# Patrologia Latina, vol. 124

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

Complete, uniform, integrated, convenient, economical, and universal library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition produced during the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared with the greatest care according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and thoroughly corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, together with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority and influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of each biblical book, and in what places of their works they have done so.

An extremely accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection, unified, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but gathered together for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. — The 1,200 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,000 French francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 800. — The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

# [Usuard’s Martyrology]

[Col. 0009]

## Usuard’s Martyrology Follows

## May Has Thirty-One Days

### Kalends — Day 1

[Note: [Col. 0009]

The Pratensis codex, Greven, and Molan are pure in almost every respect.]

[Note: [Col. 0009A]

The errors can generally be reduced to scribal mistakes, such as *Egypto*, *Schytiam*, *Hierosolimorum*, *Policarpus*, *Autisiodoro*, and so forth. Since these bear the mark of their age, most have been left untouched in the text. I read *Taphnas*, with Pratensis, [Col. 0010A] not *Taphnes*, as in Greven and Molan. The codices cited for the text, and others everywhere, write *Orientis*, perhaps incorrectly, for all today read not *Orientis* but *Orientii*.]

[Note: [Col. 0009A]

Jeremiah, or the prophet Jeremias, is called solely by his name, as though with one voice, by Bede, Rabanus, the Romanum parvum, and Ado. Notker differs from them only slightly, writing: “The repose of Jeremiah the prophet.” Therefore, the things said in our entry about his stoning were added by Usuard, just as we have shown that he did the same with the other prophets of the Old Testament. All these writers likewise mention Philip and James in their Martyrologies, as do the Hieronymian codices, some of which wrongly assign both to Hierapolis, while more of them commemorate James, or at least commemorate him on several days. In particular, [Col. 0009B] James the brother of the Lord is placed on 15 March, and James the apostle, son of Alphaeus, on 22 June.

What may surprise you more is that on this very day, after the commemoration of Philip and James has been given at the beginning, the text reads in the middle: “The birth-day of Matthew and James the apostles.” In the first place, the beginning of the Lord’s preaching is announced; on this see Florentinius’s *Exercitation*, p. 478. As for the apostles, Fronto’s Calendar records: “The birth-day of the apostles Philip and James.” Bede: “At Hierapolis, of Philip the apostle, and James the apostle, brother of the Lord.” The simple Romanum parvum: “And of the apostles Philip and James, brother of the Lord.” Ado explains that relationship briefly in the Martyrology, but in the Feasts of the Apostles he composed a more elegant commendation for each, from which Our Author was content, so to speak, to pluck the marrow, while Notker joined together more material.

Florus composed another commendation, and Rabanus a shorter one. It is not the place here to discuss all these, nor the many other matters debated among scholars concerning the Jameses, which, when we had to deal briefly with Simeon on 18 February, [Col. 0009C] we indicated here and there, as we are likewise compelled to do here, referring the reader to Henschenius’s modern dissertations, to Florentinius’s *Exercitation*, p. 95, [Col. 0010A] to Tillemont, vol. I, in various places, and to others cited elsewhere.

Thus far Ado followed the course of the Romanum parvum. The third in order is Andeolus, whom the older Martyrologists pass over. Ado composed his commendation from the commonly circulated Acts then accepted. In examining these he was by no means scrupulous, and he transferred into the sacred calendars things that cannot at all be admitted. Henschenius sufficiently recognized that the Acts themselves are neither very ancient nor entirely genuine; later scholars, with Tillemont, vol. III, p. 636, have subjected them to a harsher judgment. Our Author, always trusting Ado, copied nearly everything from his commendation almost word for word, omitting only a few matters. [Col. 0010B]

He did not even touch the encomium of King Sigismund, which is quite surprising, content merely to set down the name and place. I think this was because the entry had already grown beyond its usual limits. A commemoration of Sigismund is found appended to all the Hieronymian codices, from which Rabanus received it; Notker added something from Gregory of Tours to Ado’s commendation. See the *Deeds of Sigismund*, and the controversies concerning the translation of his body, carefully explained by Henschenius.

Here we combine from Wandelbert the final three verses concerning the apostles, Jeremiah, and Sigismund:

> Here shines James, the Lord’s brother, and Philip (or: James, the Lord’s brother, shines with Philip);  
> And Jeremiah, renowned among the prophets, likewise flourishes;  
> And King Sigismund reigns for the blood he has shed.

The final two announcements, concerning Orientius and Amator, belong to Usuard, although traces of them seem to appear in additions to the Hieronymian copies. For in Mosander they are marked with asterisks and are judged by the editor to have been added by him, [Col. 0010C] or, as Florentinius calls them, spurious. From these facts the genuine simplicity of the entry is evident. For the rest, see the Acts of Amator himself and what Tillemont thinks of them, vol. XV, p. 833 onward.]

[Note: [Col. 0011A]

HERINIENSIS: Otherwise extremely pure; in third place it inserts: “In the district of Laon, Saint Marculf the confessor.” At the end, Walburgis has recently been added in the margin.

TORNACENSIS: Pure in Jeremiah and the apostles; it also contains the others, but cuts out the commendations of Andeolus and Orientius.

PULSANENSIS: Begins with the apostles. Then, concerning Jeremiah, quite purely. It follows with Andeolus, without a commendation. The rest are absent. Amator has been added in the margin by a later hand.

MUNERATENSIS: Lacks Orientius and Amator.

ROSWEYD: Nothing concerning Jeremiah. Otherwise the text is pure in the remaining items. At the end is added: “The translation of Saint Walburgis, virgin.”

ANTVERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., and the ULTRAJECT.-BELGIAN EDITION: Almost entirely pure throughout; after “king” they add “of the Burgundians.” Then: “On the same day, Saint Walburgis, virgin.” The entry on Amator follows. In ANTVERP.-MAX. I note the word “elevation of Walburgis” inserted in yellow ink [Col. 0011B]; in the others it is “translation.” See the omitted entries.

ANTVERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.: Differ only in lacking the commendation of Jeremiah.

ALBERGEN. and DANIC.: Similar to ANTVERP.-MAX., etc., but place the apostles before Jeremiah.

ANTVERP.-MAJOR: Would be entirely pure if it had not omitted the final announcement concerning Amator. The copyist of this codex was not sufficiently diligent.

CENTULENSIS reads as follows: “The birth-day of the blessed apostles Philip and James. In Egypt, of Jeremiah the prophet, who, having been overwhelmed with stones by the people, died at Taphnas. At Jerusalem, of Saint Judas the bishop, through whom the sacred cross of the Lord was discovered.” See 4 May: “At Auxerre, Saint Amator, bishop and confessor. At the city of Sion, Saint Sigismund, king and martyr. In Gaul, in the territory of Viviers, Saint Andeolus, martyr. On the same day, Saint Marculf, abbot. Likewise on the same day, in Flanders, the translation of Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor of the church of Soissons.” [Col. 0011C] The entry is referred to his birth-day, 15 August. He is venerated at Aldenburg in Flanders.

BRUSSELS: Somewhat interpolated in the apostles; in second place it gives: “And in Germany, in the district of Sualavelda, Saint Walburgis, virgin, who followed Saint Boniface from England into Germany with her two brothers, Willebold and Winebald, where she herself became abbess; and after a most chaste life is believed to have departed to the Lord on this day.” In Jeremiah the place of martyrdom is lacking. In Andeolus it is again interpolated. Concerning Sigismund, as above. In Orientius and Amator it is almost pure. At the end is appended: “At Reims, Saint Theodulf, abbot.”

HAGENOYENSIS: Weaves long histories concerning Jeremiah, Philip, and James, which have no place here. In Andeolus it is pure. It omits the rest, closing the day in this manner: “On the same day, Saint Walpurgis, virgin, who was of noble birth in England. She came to Alemannia with her two brothers, bishops, namely Mallebald (Wilibald) [Col. 0011D] and Winebald, visiting the city of Eichstätt and building the monastery of Heidenheim, which she also laudably governed throughout her life; and in it, full of good works, she departed to the Lord.”

AQUICINCTENSIS adds at the end: “On the same day at Wapingo, the birth-day of Saint Arigius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, of Saint Walburgis.”

AMBIANENSIS adds the whole of Ado’s commendation concerning Sigismund.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of the apostles Philip and James. Of Jeremiah the prophet, who was stoned by the Jews. Of Evermarus the martyr. Of Amator the bishop. Of Walburgis the virgin.” His birth-day is considered to be 25 February, as we said there.

CLUNIACENSIS: “On the same day at Wapingo, the birth-day of Saint Arigius, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0012A]

SWEDISH REGISTER, marked no. 428: “On the same day, Saint Walburgis, virgin.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked C, and ALTEMPS: “On the same day at Wapingo, the birth-day of Saint Arigius, bishop and confessor.”

In VATICANUS no. 5949, the entries for Jeremiah, Orientius, and Amator are absent. The following is added: “At Jerusalem, Saint Quiriacus, bishop, who was first called Judas. In the city of Avellino, Saint Hippolytus, martyr.” See the Acts.

FLORENTINUS: “At Rome, Saint Calepodius the priest, who suffered under Alexander, who ordered his body to be thrown into the Tiber, as is related in the deeds of Saint Callistus the pope. Likewise, of the holy martyrs Simplicius and his entire household, sixty-eight persons of both sexes. Near the city of Catania in the province of Sicily, the passion of Saint Comitius (Cominius), martyr, under the emperor Claudius.” See the Acts and the list of omitted entries. Walburgis follows.

BURDIGALENSIS: “At the city of Bordeaux, the birth-day of Saint Macarius, bishop of Lyon.” Referred to 4 May.

LUXOVIENSIS: “The translation of the body of Saint Clement, bishop of the city of Metz, in the year 1090.” Here it is referred to 23 November.

REIMS, SS. TIMOTHY AND APOLLINARIS: “In the territory of Reims, at a place called Avenay, the passion of Saint Berta, wife of Saint Gumbert, king. At the city of Sion, in the place called Aganicum, the passion of the holy martyrs King Sigismund, his wife, and their two sons; at Reims, the deposition of Saint Theodulf, abbot; at Amiens, of the holy martyrs Actius and Aciolus.” The Acts read *Acius and Acheolus*.

LUBECK-COLONIA EDITION: Places the apostles before Jeremiah; otherwise pure up to King Sigismund, where it adds: “of the Burgundians, who built the Agaunian community in honor of the holy Theban martyrs. Captured by the Franks in the city of Sion, he died after being thrown into a well with his wife and sons. But, at the admonition of an angel, they were lifted from the well [Col. 0012C] and honorably buried in the aforesaid monastery. In Germany, in the monastery of Eichstätt, the deposition of the religious nun Saint Walburga, virgin, sister of Saint Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt, whose tomb is adorned with glorious miracles.” Amator follows. Then: “In Lesser Britain, Saint Corentin, bishop and confessor. In the district of Meaux, Saint Blandinus, confessor.” Corentin’s birth-day is 12 December.

BELIN: Almost pure up to “in Gaul,” except that it calls Andeolus “Anderolus.” It immediately follows with: “Likewise at Auxerre,” etc. Then: “Likewise at Bergamo in Cisalpine Gaul, Saint Grata, virgin. At the city of Auch, Saint Orientius, bishop. On the same day, Saint Walburga, virgin.” Note that Grata was a widow and is venerated on 25 August.

GREVEN: “Benignus and Andochius, priests, and Thyrsus, deacon, companions of Saint Andeolus.” Benignus is venerated on 1 November, the others on 24 September. “Note: Sigismund, mentioned above, was king of the Burgundians, devoted day and night to fasts and prayers. By divine revelation he built a monastery in the place where Saint Maurice and his companions rest, and finally, captured by the Franks, was thrown into a well with his wife and sons. But when he was revealed to the abbot of Agaunum and extracted by him, he became renowned for miracles. On the same day—or, as others prefer, on the day before 4 May—the birth-day of Saint Judas (also called Quiriacus), bishop of Jerusalem, who suffered under the emperor Julian.” See the Acts, 4 May. “Likewise, according to Ado—but not the genuine Ado—on this day the passion of Saints Calepodius the priest, Palmachius, and the others who are listed below on 10 May, namely the day of their burial. Also of Saints Ammon the martyr and Proculus.” This occurs here in the Hieronymian Martyrology; I do not know who the other is. “In Lesser Britain, of Corentin, bishop and confessor.” Concerning Blandinus and Marculf, as above. “Of Anne the martyr, mother of Saint Quiriacus.” She is not known anywhere else. “In Germany, in the monastery of Eichstätt, the deposition [Col. 0013A] of Saint Walburga, virgin and nun, sister of Saint Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt, renowned for her life and miracles. At Mantua, the translation of Saint John Bonus, confessor, of the Order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine.” Referred to 23 or 24 October.

MOLAN: “In the monastery of Blandinium, the translation of the body of Saint Amelberga, virgin. At Blandinium, the consecration of the first basilica by the blessed bishop Amandus.” See the omitted entries. Concerning Grata, Walburga, Marculf, and Theodulf, as above. “In Britain, Saint Corentin, bishop of the city of Aquila. At Amiens, the blessed martyrs Acius and Aciolus, who shine through holy miracles. On the same day, Saint Ultan, brother of Saints Fursey and Foillan; after the death of his brother Fursey, he attained, together with Foillan, the companionship of Saint Gertrude, whose many monuments of holiness shine in the church. The holy virgin, recognizing their sanctity, offered to God through their hands part of her inheritance, namely the estate commonly called Fosses, which she entrusted to them for the sustenance of God’s servants, so that they might build a monastery there [Col. 0014A] as a permanent lodging for pilgrims. On the same day, in the territory of Tongeren, at a villa called Rott, Saint Evermarus, martyr, who was innocently killed by wicked men. His precious death is illumined by frequent miracles.”

Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, of the holy hermits Zoerard and Benedict the martyr, whose life was written by Maurus, bishop of the Five Churches. At Furnes, the translation of the bodies of Saints Walburgis, Willibald, and Winebald, in the year 1109.” Thus far the first edition. In the others, concerning Marculf, Theodulf, Corentin, etc., as in the first. “Likewise at Blandinium, etc.

“May first consecrates the Kalends to Christ’s teaching.” Then, in smaller letters: “In Hungary, of the holy hermits Zoerard, etc. At Furnes, etc. In Scotland, of Asaph, bishop, from whose name the bishopric is now called Saint Asaph. In Lesser Britain, of the most holy Brioc, bishop and confessor.” What is inserted in italics in Molan’s text can easily be distinguished from what is genuine.]

[Col. 0009]

In Egypt, of Jeremiah the prophet, who, having been overwhelmed with stones by the people, died at Taphnas. Likewise, the birth-day of the blessed apostles Philip and James. Philip, after he had almost converted Scythia to the faith of Christ, rested with a glorious end at Hierapolis, a city of Asia. James, who is read to have been the brother of the Lord, was buried beside the temple of Jerusalem, where he had also been thrown down. In Gaul, in the territory of Viviers, the blessed Andeolus, subdeacon, whom Saint Polycarp sent from the East, together with others, to preach the word of God in Gaul. When the emperor Severus learned of his preaching, he ordered him to be most cruelly scourged with thorny clubs and thrown into prison, and finally his head to be split by a wooden sword in the form of a cross. At the city of Sion, the birth-day of King Sigismund. At the city of Auch, Saint Orientius, bishop, who is said, adorned with virtues, to have rested in a holy death. Likewise at Auxerre, Saint Amator, bishop and confessor.

### VI Nones — Day 2

[Note: [Col. 0013B]

The codices almost all agree in the text. The purer are Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antverp.-major, Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Antverpien., Max.-Lubec., Greven., and [Col. 0014B] Molan. To these may be added Antverp.-max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Ultrajectine-Belgian Edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0013B]

After Bede and Ado, our best codices consistently read *our Father*: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antverp., both minor and major, Max.-Lubec., and Greven. In Rosweyd. and Molan. *our* is absent. In others *Father* is also omitted. Greven., Molan., and several other inferior codices give *Alexandriae* instead of *Alexandrinae*. Herinien., Greven, Molan, and the codices already cited wrongly write *persecutione*, while Rosweyd. gives the still worse *praedicatione*. Antverp. and Max.-Lubec. have *contra* instead of *adversus*. Greven does not convey the complete sense when he writes: “The rulers of the earth, kingdoms, and armies gathered together.” Concerning the Arians, see elsewhere [Col. 0013C]. For *multasque … insidiis*, Antverp., Max.-Lubec., Antverp.-major, Max., etc., have *multasque … insidias*. In Herinien. *ei* is absent between *nec* and *ullus*. Again Antverp. and Max.-Lubec. give *ille superest, haec subest* instead of *supererat*. The sense seems to require that, with Greven, Molan, and a few others, we read *moverentur*. Nevertheless, we have followed Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., and most others, with *moventur*, as in the text. *Quadragesimo et sexto* should be read; Herinien. wrongly omitted the conjunction *et*, and the copyist who more recently filled the blank space in Antverp.-major with *sexagesimo sexto* made a disgraceful error, which he also entered in the margin. Antverp., Max.-Lubec., and the later codices have *Neopoli* instead of *Neopolis*. This may perhaps be correct, but the more authoritative codices are preferable to us. All these, together with Herinien., Rosweyd., [Col. 0014C] Greven, and Molan, read *quieverunt*; we prefer Praten. and Tornacen., which, after the Romanum parvum and Ado, write *requieverunt*.]

[Note: [Col. 0013C]

The illustrious and ever-venerable memory throughout the world of the great Athanasius was first entered into the sacred calendars by Bede in these words: “Of our holy Father Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria,” as also in Rabanus. The Romanum parvum writes: “Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria.” Ado combines the wording of both, explicitly asserting, in accordance with the opinion received in every age, that Athanasius died in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood. But how this can fall in the year of Christ 373, let those consider who, in order to connect Athanasius’s death with that year, continue to strive with intense study. Ado develops this and other matters more fully from Rufinus in his notable panegyric. Notker, surprisingly, interpolated and abridged its more attractive flowers with great appropriateness. We arranged Athanasius’s life, as far as possible, briefly and chronologically from Hermantius and Papebrochius in the treatise on the Alexandrian patriarchs previously cited, prefixed to volume V of June. The most learned Montfaucon carefully prepared another life along with the newest edition of the great Father’s works. Add to these the more recent French life by Tillemont, which occupies most of his eighth volume. I shall not dwell longer on this; the distich of Wandelbert requires attention:

> From this point, on the sixth day before the Nones, great Athanasius, you shine,  
> When, victorious through you, the Arian serpent first perished.

Saturninus and Neopolis are clearly expressed in some Hieronymian copies, with the place or site of martyrdom added: Alexandria. The Romanum parvum records the same persons with somewhat altered wording; Ado copied its words almost to the letter, adding only “on the same day,” and from him Our Author, as we said above, seems to have taken the entry in precisely these terms. Thus the original simplicity of the entire entry is plain and straightforward. Henschenius, however, rightly noted Galesinius’s error: he placed these martyrs, increased by two companions, at Rome; Baronius followed him in the modern Roman Martyrology without sufficiently examining the matter.]

[Note: [Col. 0015A]

PULSANENSIS: Gives an altered and mutilated commendation of Athanasius, and writes *Neapolis* for *Neopolis*.

MUNERATENSIS: Pure in the text; adds at the end: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Sicharius, martyr.”

CENTULENSIS: “At Alexandria, of Saint Athanasius, holy Father and outstanding shepherd, bishop and most steadfast confessor. On the same day, of Saints Saturninus and Neopolis, who rested in prison. In the territory of Reims, Saint Macra, virgin, with other sacred virgins.” Our predecessors rightly judged, I think, that no other person than the famous Macra is indicated here; but whether she had any virgin companions, see the index of the omitted entries and above, 6 January.

BRUSSELS writes as follows: “Of Saint Athanasius, holy Father, bishop of the city of Alexandria. Against his persecution Constantius, emperor and son of Constantine the Great, corrupted by the Arian heresy, conspired with all his supporters. While Athanasius himself was driven into exile throughout the world, and no safe place remained for him in which to hide, Blessed Maximinus received him at Trier, where, in a certain cistern that saw no sunlight, he composed the Creed ‘Whoever wishes to be saved,’ which we Catholics confess daily at Prime. After he had hidden there for six years, at last, in the time of the emperor Valentinus or Valentinian, he was restored to his see and, in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, after many struggles and many crowns of endurance, rested in peace. Likewise, the birth-day of Saints Saturninus,” etc.

HAGENOYENSIS: Is greatly interpolated from Ado in the account of the child’s baptism, etc., but this is not the place for those matters. In Saturninus and Neopolis it is pure. Today he places Amator, concerning whom he writes as follows: “At Auxerre, Saint Amator, bishop and confessor. From his childhood he was instructed in letters, and when his parents compelled him to marry, he urged his bride to preserve her virginity, which she did. He himself excelled with such a proclamation of virtues that, after Cladus—for he meant Eladius—he became bishop of Auxerre. He gave sight to the blind, healed paralytics, raised the dead, converted many unbelievers, consecrated Saint Germanus as a cleric, though unwilling, and shone with the spirit of prophecy. Finally, foreseeing his end, he summoned the clergy and people and, after strengthening them in the faith, surrendered his spirit into the hands of those attending him. His soul was seen to be carried to heaven by angels in the form of a dove.” He was treated on the preceding day.

AQUICINCTENSIS adds at the end: “Likewise, Saint Walbert, count and abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil.” More correctly, Waldebert. In the Acts he is distinguished from the others.

DAVERONENSIS: “At the fortress of Saumur, the reception of the body of Blessed Florentius, priest and confessor.” We shall discuss him with Usuard on his birth-day, 22 September.

AMBIANENSIS: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Germanus, glorious martyr.” This is a local feast. See the Acts.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT: “Athanasius, bishop. Germanus, bishop and martyr. Saturninus and Neopolis, martyrs.”

AUGENSIS OF SAINT LAURENT: “Likewise, Saint Germanus, bishop and martyr.” See the Ambianensis codex.

CAMBERIENSIS OF SAINT MARY: “Likewise, Sicharius, martyr.” See what is said about him below.

SWEDISH REGISTER, marked no. 428: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Sicharius, martyr.”

[Col. 0016A]

FLORENTINUS: “The birth-day of Saint Antoninus, confessor, of the Order of Preachers, archbishop of Florence, distinguished by the holiness of his life and every kind of learning, as is evident from his many volumes. He died in his Florentine homeland in the year of the Lord 1459, and there, with a seven-year indulgence granted by Pope Pius II, who was then at Florence, to those who kissed his hand, he was buried with the greatest concourse of people in the church of Saint Mark among the Friars Preachers.”

CODEX D. LE MARE, marked A: “Likewise, Saint Sicharius, martyr.” We have now seen him named for the third time. He was a boy, perhaps killed by Jews; but whether he may be counted among the Innocents slain at Herod’s command, Papebrochius examines in the Acts.

LUBECK-COLONIA EDITION begins: “At Bonn, on the bank of the Rhine, in the territory of Cologne, the translation of the holy martyrs Cassius, Florentius, Malusius, and their companions. After their bodies had rested buried beneath the earth for 773 years, the Lord [Col. 0016B] Reynold, archbishop of Cologne, found them, translated them, and honorably gathered them into reliquaries.” They are referred to their birth-day, 10 October. An Athanasius commendation follows, more extensively interpolated. In Saturninus, etc., it is pure. Then: “At Trier, the birth-day of Saint Theodulf, monk and confessor, nephew of the emperor Charlemagne.” He was treated on 1 May. “At Marburg in Hesse, the translation of Saint Elizabeth, widow.” Her birth-day is 19 November. “On the same day, Saint Florentius, confessor.”

FIRST EDITION OF BELIN: At the end: “At the city of Sion, the passion of Saint Sigismund, martyr, king of the Burgundians.” The second edition adds: “In the territory of Angers, Saint Florentius, priest and confessor.” Concerning Sigismund, see the preceding day.

GREVEN: “Germanus, Hippolytus, Helpidius, and Hermogenes.” Their names are better distinguished in the Acts. “At Auxerre, the birth-day of Saints Optatus, bishop, Memorius, and Sanctianus, priests.” See the omitted entries. “Evermarus, martyr, commander from the Theban legion.” See the same place. “Likewise, Waldebert, abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus. At Trier, Saint Theodulf, etc.,” as above. “Florentius, confessor. In the monastery of Saint Gall, Saint Wilberada, virgin. In the diocese of Cologne, in the town of Bonn, the translation,” etc., almost as above. “At Metz, the translation of Saint Clement, bishop and confessor.” He is especially venerated on 23 November. “At Marburg in Hesse,” etc., as above.

MOLAN: “At the city of Sion, the passion of Saint Sigismund, etc. In the territory of Angers, Saint Florentius, priest and confessor. Near Florence, the birth-day of Blessed Antoninus, confessor, of the Order of the Friars Preachers, archbishop of that city.” Concerning Sicharius, as above. “At the monastery of Luxeuil, Walpert, abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus the abbot. In Alemannia, at the monastery of Saint Gall, the birth-day of Saint Wilberada, virgin.” In later editions, concerning Florentius, Antoninus, Wilberada, Sicharius, and Walbert, as above. It follows: “At Trier, Saint [Col. 0016D] Theodulf, priest and monk.” Concerning him we said: “At Eischstätt, Cunegundis, virgin. On the second day, the return of the relics of the holy Father Athanasius to the monastery of Sithiu; the glorious elevation of the most precious body of the confessor of Christ, Bertinus the abbot, which took place in the year 1052 of the Lord’s incarnation. At Merbes, the elevation of Saint Berlendis, virgin, and of Celsa and Nona, virgins.” See the index of the omitted entries for all these.]

[Col. 0013]

The birth-day of our holy Father Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria and confessor. Almost the whole world conspired to persecute him, and the rulers of the earth were stirred up; nations, kingdoms, and armies gathered against him. After suffering many plots of the Arians, he was driven into exile throughout the world, and no safe place for hiding remained for him, while all were moved to search him out. He died in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, after many struggles and many crowns of endurance, in the time of Valentinian and Valens. On the same day, Saints Saturninus and Neopolis, who rested in prison.

### V Nones — Day 3

[Note: [Col. 0017A]

There is almost complete agreement among the codices. Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antverp.-major, Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Antverpien., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., [Col. 0018A] Greven, and Molan agree. To these may be added Antverp.-max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Ultrajectine-Belgian Edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0017A]

The first word of the entry is absent in Rosweyd: *Hierosolimis*. We have retained this form, as elsewhere, in accordance with the practice of our manuscripts. Rosweyd alone reads *Nomentana*. All the manuscripts write *Theodoli*, except Max.-Lubec., where *Theodori* is printed incorrectly. I would suppose that the Small Roman Martyrology and Ado were emended by Rosweyd’s editor, where they have *Theoduli*. In Tornac., *Arriano* is incorrectly written instead of *Adriano*, but neither reading can be accepted, since *Trajano* must be read, as we shall show below from Ado and the Acts. Pulsan. and Belin. come closer to the truth, for they give *Aureliano*, provided that we understand this person to have been a prefect, not an emperor. Molan’s meaning is confused because he writes *carceris* instead of *carceres*, without punctuation. Pulsan. is excessively discerning in seeming to wish to complete the sense after *per tota membra*, inserting *confossus* (“pierced through”). Tornac., after *peremptus*, omitted *est*. *Sequentes quoque* must likewise be read; nevertheless, quite a few manuscripts, together with Antverp., Max.-Lubec. and Molan., read *sequentes vero*. The two primary manuscripts, Praten. and Herinien., expressly give *ignibus exanimati* (“put to death by fire”). All the others disagree—and, unless I am mistaken, rightly—for Bede reads *ignibus examinati* (“tested by fire”), and thus Ado’s allusion to Scripture seems to require it. In Herinien. we find *sunt decollati* instead of *decollati sunt*. Tornac., pressed, I suppose, by the narrow limits of its columns, suppressed the final words of the entry, namely *episcopis et confessoris*.

[Col. 0017B]

As for what is read in one or another Hieronymian copy: “In Jerusalem, the finding of the holy Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ by Helena, after the Lord’s Passion, in the year 233, while the emperor Constantine was reigning”—Florentinius appears fruitlessly to argue that this belongs in any way to the genuine Martyrology of Jerome. Papebrochius more rightly rejects it, on the authority of the very ancient manuscript of Echternach and other arguments that overturn the antiquity of this feast asserted by Florentinius. For me, the form of the announcement alone would suffice: it is wholly unusual in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. It is most probable that the quoted words were taken from Florus and, with the anachronism preserved, prefixed to the Hieronymian text by some later writer. As far as our purpose is concerned, it is certain that this finding is recorded by the genuine Bede, but only in second place, after Alexander and his companions, who are adorned with a notable eulogy. It is also certain that the same feast is commemorated on this very day by the Small Roman Martyrology and, from it, by Ado, who composed a long history of the finding; concerning its truth, our Acts for this day and for 10 March, where Saint Macarius is discussed, should be consulted. Usuard, meanwhile, following his customary brevity, passed over the story and stated the event itself, removing its doubtful circumstances.

There is no doubt that Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus are recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, although in a somewhat altered order and in such a way that it nowhere certainly appears that Pope Alexander is intended there, as Florentinius observed before me. It is more surprising that the same point is not expressed more distinctly in the Calendar of Fronto, which reads: “The feast of Saints Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus.” This is almost the reading of the Gregorian Sacramentary, in which they are placed before the Finding of the holy Cross, as we said Bede did; Bede, however, more clearly and correctly names Alexander as pope and adorns him and his companions with a notable eulogy, followed here by Rabanus. They also appear in the Small Roman Martyrology and likewise in Ado, where a longer encomium is drawn from the Acts of Alexander, contracted and interpolated here and there by Notker.

Our author preferred to imitate Bede and copy his words, although he changed the tyrant’s name, contrary to Ado’s explicit statement, which expressly affirms that the emperor Hadrian was not yet emperor when the aforesaid martyrs suffered, as is also completely clear from their own Acts. Therefore everything said in the entry must be assigned to the time of Trajan—at least if anyone decides to contend more vigorously with Henschenius for the historical truth of the Acts. Baronius had long ago delivered a moderate judgment concerning them in his *Annals*, under the year 132, no. 1, in these words: “There exist Acts of Pope Alexander and his companions, but—as happens with many others—they are corrupted by excessive antiquity” (he might have added, “or by some other defect”). Henschenius did not tolerate this criticism: whenever he discussed the aforesaid Acts in various places, he invariably called them “most genuine and, because of their antiquity, worthy of veneration,” although otherwise he was sparing enough in bestowing such praise.

The commendation of so exceptional a scholar moved me to examine the praised Acts more carefully than my purpose required, in case I might be able to defend them against Tillemont, vol. II, pp. 238 and 590, and against other more recent writers who vie with one another in opposing Henschenius. The result, however, was very different. The more attentively I examined them, the more they seemed to depart from the gravity and sincerity of primitive Acts. This can more appropriately be demonstrated on 28 August, when Hermes is commemorated from the aforesaid Acts. Here I merely indicate briefly that Henschenius’s two arguments, if they prove anything, prove altogether too much. To infer the authenticity of the Acts from the brilliance and elegance of the more ancient passionaries, or from the eulogies of Bede, Rabanus, Ado, and Notker, which were taken from them, seems to me equivalent to accepting all the passions contained in those works and at the same time assuming all the eulogies of the aforesaid Martyrologists to be certain and indisputable. How foreign this is to Henschenius’s own mind is readily shown by many examples in our work. I pass over this quickly; it will be explained more fully elsewhere.

Here are the verses with which Wandalbert honors our martyrs, adding in the third line the Finding of the Cross:

> Bishop Alexander and Eventius adorn the fifth [day],  
>   
> And Theodulus, likewise slain for God’s name.  
>   
> With these also shine the lofty standards of the Cross that was found.

The Martyrologists earlier than Ado are silent about Juvenal. Ado himself recorded him simply, without assigning any position or adding any eulogy, just as Usuard copied him from Ado; his pure and genuine text is therefore presented here. In Notker the title “confessor” is suppressed, perhaps because he doubted whether Juvenal should be called a martyr. See Papebrochius’s commentary on these matters.

[Col. 0017D]

CENTULEN.: “In Jerusalem, the Finding of the holy Cross, whose solemn celebration the holy Roman Church established by decree. At Rome, blessed Alexander, pope and martyr, and Saints Eventius and Theodulus, priests. On the same day, Saint Juvenal, bishop and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN.: “In Jerusalem, the Finding of the holy Cross by Queen Helena, under Pope Eusebius and the great emperor Constantine, whose mother she herself was. At Rome, the feast of Saint Alexander, pope and martyr. He established that the water used for sprinkling should be consecrated with blessed salt, that oil should be blessed each year by the bishop, and that, just as blood and water flowed from Christ’s side, water should be mixed with wine in the consecration of the altar sacrament to signify the union of Christ and the Church. In memory of Christ’s Passion he added to the Canon of the Mass: ‘Who, on the day before he suffered,’ etc. This Pope Alexander, under the emperor Hadrian, after bonds, prisons, the rack, iron claws, and fires, was finally killed by very numerous punctures throughout his body, and was buried on the Nomentan Way; afterward he was transferred to the cemetery of Saint Sabina. On the same day, Saints Eventius and Theodulus, priests. When they had been arrested with the aforesaid Pope Alexander, after enduring a long imprisonment they were tested by fire and finally beheaded. And Saint Juvenal, bishop. Near Ponthisera in the province of Rouen, blessed Walter, abbot.” Walter’s Life is given on 8 April.

HAGENOYEN begins: “At Rome, on the Nomentan Way,” etc., with the text somewhat interpolated. It then follows with Juvenal, purely. It relates various matters about the Cross shown to Constantine and its discovery, which are given more accurately in the Acts. At the end it has more about Sigismund than we reported above.

AQUICINCT, after “they were beheaded,” inserts: “This Pope Alexander established that sprinkling water should be blessed with salt in people’s dwellings, and he joined the Lord’s Passion to the priests’ prayer when Mass is celebrated.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The Finding of the holy Cross. Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus, martyrs. Juvenal, bishop and confessor. Silvanus, bishop and martyr, with many of his clergy. Andeolus, subdeacon and martyr.” In the margin, in the copyist’s own hand, it is rightly noted that Silvanus is to be treated on the following day and Andeolus on 1 May.

[Col. 0019C]

CODEX CASTRI-KAROLI: “Saint Serenus, confessor.” He is not even named among the omitted saints. I suspect that he is the person about whom we shall speak in the Supplements on 11 October.

DIVIONEN.: “At Auxerre, the deposition and translation of the body of Saint Concordinus, bishop and confessor.” The writer intended Corcodemus, or Curcodemus, or Curcodomus—not a bishop, as he is incorrectly called here, but a deacon, who is discussed on the following day.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL.: “After Constantine the ruler”—it adds “the younger,” whose mother she herself was. “And because the Finding of this holy Cross took place in the time of Pope and confessor Eusebius, he therefore established that the feast of this Finding should be solemnly celebrated by all Catholic churches throughout the world. At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, at the seventh milestone, the Passion of Saint Alexander,” etc., purely up to “they were beheaded.” It then adds: “This most holy pope held the episcopate of the Roman Church for ten years, two months, and ten days, being fifth after blessed Peter. He established that water should be mixed with wine at Mass, to signify the union of the Church and Christ, and that the offering should be made from unleavened bread and in a small quantity. Also, in memory of Christ’s Passion, he added to the Canon: ‘Who, on the day before he suffered,’ up to ‘For this is my body.’ He also established that sprinkling water should be blessed with salt and sprinkled in people’s dwellings. On the same day, Saint Juvenal,” etc.

GREVEN.: “On the same day, Juvenal, martyr.” He is celebrated on 7 May. “Aufridius, bishop of Utrecht and confessor. Florentius and Vindemialis, bishops and confessors.” See the Acts for 11 May. “In Gaul, at a place called Cella, Philip, priest and confessor.” See the Acts. “Severina, matron, wife of Aurelian Caesar. At Bruges, a festive commemoration of the blood of Christ.” See the entry among the omitted saints. “Note: Blessed Alexander, pope, mentioned above, the fifth after Saint Peter, sat for ten years, two months, and ten days. He established that water should be mixed with wine in the chalice, to signify the union of the Church and Christ, and that the offering should be made,” etc., as EDIT. LUBECO-COL. has above.

MOLAN.: “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saints Optatus, bishop, Memorius, and Santianus, priests. On the Sunday after the Finding of the holy Cross, at Rome, Saint Catherine, virgin. She was born in the city of Siena; in her youth she assumed the penitential habit of Saint Dominic, and, renowned for frequent miracles, she rested in Rome in her thirty-third year and was buried in the church of Saint Mary above Minerva. Pope Pius II enrolled her in the catalogue of the saints.” See the entry among the omitted saints. In other editions only the following appears: “At Ponthisera, Saint Walter, abbot,” concerning whom it was said: “On the third day, Saints Timothy and Maura, martyrs.” Then, in smaller type: “In Italy, in the city of Salsena, Saint Ursus, confessor, son of the king of Dalmatia, who came as a pilgrim to this city and, full of virtues, rested there in Christ. Likewise, under the governor Festus, the martyrdom of Antonina, virgin, and Alexander, soldier.” See Papebrochius’s commentary.

[Col. 0015]

In Jerusalem, the Finding of the holy Cross by Queen Helena, under the ruler Constantine. At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, the Passion of blessed Alexander, pope, Eventius and Theodulus, priests, under the ruler Hadrian. The first of these, after bonds, prisons, the rack, iron claws, and fires, was killed by very numerous punctures throughout his body. [Col. 0017] His companions likewise, after enduring a long imprisonment, were tested by fire and finally beheaded. On the same day, Saint Juvenal, bishop and confessor.

Fourth day before the Nones. Day 4.

[Col. 0019]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Rosweyd., Antverp.-major, Greven., and Molan.

[Col. 0019D]

Concerning the various ways of writing *Palestina*, *Hierosolimis*, *Jherosolimis*, *Jerosolimis*, *Autisiodoro*, and similar forms, enough has been said elsewhere: we follow the manuscripts, which write according to the usage of their age. Rosweyd reads *Sylvani*, contrary to the Utrecht autograph. Herinien. seems to have *Suvani*; both are corrected in the text. The older manuscripts and, generally, the others consistently read *in metalla Fanensi*—not *Fatensi*, as Antverp.-major has it. Greven. and Molan., following Ado, perhaps more correctly have *metallo*. But we must adhere to the manuscripts; the place-name is given in the Acts. Greven alone writes *Antoninae* instead of *Antoniae*. Again, Greven. and Molan. have *sunt caesi* instead of *caesi sunt*, just as Antverp.-major has *adusta est* instead of *exusta est*. Likewise, *praecipitatur* appears instead of *praecipitatus est*. Herinien. has *Curcodimi*, Rosweyd *Corcodimi*, Antverp.-major *Cocordani*, Greven. and Molan. *Curcodomi*, and others have other forms. We think the reading should be as it stands in the text.

[Col. 0021A]

The author of the Small Roman Martyrology mentions Silvanus, bishop, crowned in the city of Gaza with many of his clergy, in these words. As usual, he followed Rufinus’s Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 14, and added nothing. Ado added only the well-known persecution of Diocletian. Usuard and Notker copied Ado. See what was said incidentally in the observation for 20 February, where we showed that Silvanus was wrongly joined with Tyrranion and others. In accordance with Ado, those forty companions—or rather thirty-nine—ought to have been placed here second. They were condemned to the mines together and received the same crown of martyrdom as Silvanus, but Usuard wrongly separated them from the leader, so to speak, in our entry. See Eusebius, cited in the Acts, and Ruinart, pp. 328 and 351. Tillemont gives the whole story in French in volume V, beginning at p. 432.

The Small Roman Martyrology speaks only of Silvanus; the Hieronymian Martyrologies, however, have been so corrupted that Florentinius labored greatly to restore them. In the entry for Silvanus and the forty martyrs there are many errors. Instead of *Antonia*, *Antonii* is found almost everywhere. Because of a corrupt arrangement, Florianus has been separated from Curcodemus, who is called *Codomi* there, with his first syllable diminished. Florentinius thought that it had been added by a French copyist, but Henschenius rightly judged from the Echternach, Corbie, and other manuscripts that it belongs to the text. I believe Ado drew his material from a more corrected copy. Our author followed him and transferred everything except the final announcement, which he added himself.

The feast of Judas Quiriacus is celebrated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 1 May, as also in Rabanus; Florus gives it a longer eulogy, to which today’s Notker should not be preferred. Ado and Usuard are briefer; nevertheless, they bear the scent of ancient Acts. The authority of so many Martyrologists added no more credibility to those Acts than their first compiler deserved, as was said yesterday concerning the Acts of Saint Alexander. See Papebrochius’s commentary, notes, and censures, and again his *Responses*, in various places, especially article 10, no. 129. You should remember, however, that none of this at all diminishes the saint’s most ancient cult in the Church.

Ado’s eulogy of Antonia is indeed Ado’s, although Florus’s account does not greatly differ from ours and was doubtless drawn from the same source. The purity of that source is not entirely certain, since a similar eulogy is applied by Greek and Latin writers to several women named Antonia or Antonina, if not in the same words, at least in the same sense. This can be gathered from the Acts for 1 March, from this passage, and from the omitted saints for 12 June.

Rabanus also discusses Florianus. His brief eulogy, like ours and the more extensive one of Notker, was drawn from the same Acts. Certainly, as they were first edited and illustrated by Henschenius, those Acts seem to contain nothing that so strongly supports the supposition advanced by Tillemont, volume V, p. 67. Finally, Curcodemus was added by Usuard to the others but omitted by the genuine Ado. Let the reader consult Henschenius’s brief commentary, in which he gives nearly ten different forms of the name. Thus far the genuine reading of Usuard. To it we may append Wandalbert’s couplet on Silvanus, Antonia, and Florianus:

> Silvanus with the fourth, Antonia with Florianus,  
>   
> Are adorned, encircled by perpetual virtue of mind.

[Col. 0021B]

TORNACEN. is defective in part of Antonia’s eulogy, omitting the words between “after being tortured exceedingly” and “finally” in the entry. The final announcement is also absent.

PULSAN. omits Quiriacus, the Forty Martyrs, Florianus, and Curcodemus.

[Col. 0021C]

ANTVERP. MAX.-LUBEC. and UGHELLIAN. are also defective in the final announcement.

MUNERAT., after the complete text, adds: “In Jerusalem, blessed Quiriacus, bishop and martyr, formerly called Judas, discoverer of the Lord’s Cross.” Consult the Acts.

ANTVERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG. reproduce a text that is not entirely pure and omit Curcodemus’s announcement at the end.

LOVAN. agrees with the preceding witnesses but adds at the end: “On the same day, Monica, widow, mother of our most blessed Father Augustine.”

CENTULEN.: “In Palestine, in the city of Gaza, Saint Silvanus, bishop and martyr, who suffered gloriously with a multitude of clergy and faithful people. At the Phanensian mines, the forty saints who were beheaded together. At Auxerre, Saint Corcodemus, deacon and confessor. At Nicomedia, Saint Antonia, cruelly and for a very long time [Col. 0021D] tormented. At the place called Lauriacum, Saint Florian, martyr. In the suburb of Verdun, Saints Pulchronius, Possessor, and Firminus, bishops and confessors.” In the table of omitted saints, those holy bishops are referred to their proper days, for today properly concerns their translation.

BRUXELLEN. is pure in the notice of Silvanus but has removed Quiriacus. The account of the Forty Martyrs follows correctly. Of Antonia it adds: “By the governor Priscillianus,” as Ado has it. In the account of Florianus, after “he was thrown down,” it also adds from Ado what Usuard omitted: “And immediately, while all were watching, the eyes of the one who threw him down burst. On the same day, blessed Justus, bishop of Vienne.” He is deferred to 6 May. The notice of Curcodemus is pure.

HAGENOYEN is nearly pure in the account of Silvanus. It mentions Florianus second, with an eulogy of its own. The forty martyrs follow [Col. 0022B] purely. Then comes Quiriacus, with an apocryphal narrative. Nothing is said about Antonia. The notice of Curcodemus is pure.

AQUICINCT does not call Quiriacus a bishop. It has *Nisi* instead of *Anisii*.

DAVERONEN.: “And at Tours, the feast of blessed Antonius, confessor.” The same person is mentioned by several witnesses below.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Quiriacus, bishop and martyr, formerly called Judas, discoverer of the holy Cross. Florianus, martyr. The forty holy martyrs. Tryphanes, martyr,” perhaps the boy who is celebrated on 10 November. “Antonia, martyr.”

CAMBERIEN. S. Mariae: “At the castle of Cambrai, the deposition of the holy shroud, or holy winding-sheet, of our Savior Jesus Christ.” See the entry among the omitted saints concerning the Lance, Crown, Nails, and so forth.

In VATICAN. no. 5949, “Quiriacus and Curcodemus” is absent. This manuscript frequently has omissions.

FLORENTIN.: “In the Florentine territory, the Passion of Saints Cerbonius and his companions at Vallis Cava, or Cavis, near the tomb of Saint Crescius, martyr, and his companions, under the tyrant Decius.” The first notice of this Cerbonius was supplied by the Acts of Saint Crescius, edited by Laderchius in 1707.

REMENS. SS. Timothei et Apollonaris: “At Auxerre, the deposition and translation of the body of Saint Corcodemus, deacon and confessor.”

EDITIO LUBECO.-COL. begins: “At Cologne Agrippina, in the church of Saint Cecilia, virgin, the feast of blessed Paulinus, deacon and martyr, whose head is known to have been crushed with an iron hammer for Christ, and who patiently poured out his brain together with his holy blood. In Jerusalem, the Passion of Saint Quiriacus, bishop, together with his mother, under the emperor Julian. On the same day, a commemoration of the Crown of Thorns of our Lord. At Ostia on the Tiber, the deposition of Saint Monica,” etc., with a long eulogy. The text that follows is nearly pure up to “he was thrown down.” Then: “In the city of Speyer, the feast of Saint Wido, abbot.” He is called Guido below; Henschenius does not mention him among the omitted saints. I think he is the person concerning whom we treated with Molan on 31 March, where he is recorded in the Acts under the title “abbot of Pomposa,” etc. “At Tours, blessed Antonius, confessor. At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Corcodemus, deacon and confessor. In the city of Hildesheim, the translation of Saint Godhard, bishop and confessor. At Vienne, a commemoration of Saint Justus, bishop and martyr.”

BELIN. begins: “At Ostia on the Tiber, the feast of Saint Monica, whose admirable life is gathered from the ninth book of the *Confessions* of Saint Augustine, bishop.” The text follows, almost pure. In another edition is added: “In the territory of Périgueux, a holy priest, bishop of Limoges.” He is celebrated on his own feast day, 5 May.

GREVEN.: “On the same day, a commemoration of the holy Crown of Thorns of our Lord Jesus Christ. At Cologne, etc.,” concerning Saint Paulinus, almost as above. “Also Saints Celestine, Majolus, and Quincianus.” They are more appropriately placed in the Acts. “Also the Passion of Saint Gordianus, whose feast is celebrated on the day of his burial.” It is deferred to [Col. 0023B] 10 May. “On the same day, a commemoration of Saint Justus, bishop of Vienne and martyr. At Tours, blessed Antonius, confessor. At Speyer, a commemoration of blessed Guido, abbot. In the city of Hildesheim, the translation of Saint Godebard, bishop and confessor. At Ostia on the Tiber, the deposition of Saint Monica, widow, mother of [Col. 0024A] Saint Augustine, bishop. How great her faith and devotion toward God were is clearly apparent from book IX of the *Confessions* and from other books of that holy doctor. By her abundant prayers and tears she won both her husband for Christ and her son back from the error of the Manichaeans to the unity of the faith. Helena, virgin. At Thoren, near Roermond, blessed Herswinda, abbess.” She is discussed among the omitted saints.

MOLAN.: “At Ostia on the Tiber, the feast of Saint Monica,” etc., as in BELIN. “In the territory of Périgueux, a holy priest, bishop of Limoges. And Saint Gothehard, bishop and confessor.” In smaller type there follows the notice of Saint Paulinus, as above. Then: “Also John Hauthon, of blessed memory,” etc., as given among the omitted saints. Other editions begin in italics: “At Ostia,” etc. Of the priest, as above. “At Hildesheim, Saint Gothehard, bishop and confessor.” Of Antonius, as above. “At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of Saint Paulinus, martyr, whose head is known to have been crushed with an iron hammer for Christ. [Col. 0024B] On the fourth day, Saint Pelagia, holy martyr. At Verdun, the translation of the bishops and confessors of that place, Pulchronius, etc.” It continues: “At London, John Hauthon, of blessed memory,” etc. I have already said that a summary of his life is given among the omitted saints.

[Col. 0019]

In Palestine, in the city of Gaza, the feast of blessed Silvanus, bishop of that same city, who, during the persecution of Diocletian, was crowned with martyrdom together with many of his clergy. In Jerusalem, the Passion of Saint Quiriacus, bishop, under the emperor Julian. Likewise at the Phanensian mines, the forty holy martyrs, who were beheaded together. At Nicomedia, the feast of Antonia, martyr, who, after being excessively tortured and afflicted with various torments, was hung by one arm for three days, thrown into prison for two years, and finally burned by fire in her confession of the Lord. In Riparian Noricum, Saint Florianus, who, at the governor’s command, was thrown into the river Anisus with a stone tied around his neck. At Auxerre, Saint Curcodemus, deacon.

Third day before the Nones. Day 5.

[Col. 0023]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Rosweyd., Antverp.-Maj., Greven., and Molan.

[Col. 0023C]

Tornacen. and Antverp.-major write *Euthymi* incorrectly. Rosweyd likewise has *requiescentis* instead of *quiescentis*. In Antverp.-major, *Thesalonicae* is a scribal error. The names of those burned, as they are placed in the entry, are pronounced in nearly all the manuscripts. Rosweyd has *Irenei* and *Irenis*. Molan has the somewhat more polished forms *Irenaei* and *Hyrenis*. Greven. and a few others write *Hylarii*. [Col. 0024C] Herinien., Rosweyd, and Antverp.-major read *nobilissimi viri*. The manuscripts generally have *Niceti*, except Tornacen., where *Nicecii* occurs. Greven. and Molan., closer to Ado, read *Nicetii*. In Herinien. the *a* has dropped out; likewise, instead of *Zoviniani* we should read *Jovinini*, and in Rosweyd, even worse, *Joviani*.

[Col. 0023C]

A single note may take the place of a full observation, if I say that the entire text is taken almost word for word from Ado. A few points may nevertheless be indicated for clarification. The Hieronymian copies record Euthymius under various spellings. The Small Roman Martyrology uses a phrase—I do not know from where it was taken—which Usuard and Notker transferred from Ado. The cited copies also expressly mention the Thessalonian fighters. [Col. 0023D] That the Small Roman Martyrology did not have them before its eyes may be inferred from its omission of the third person, recording only: “At Thessalonica, Irenaeus and Peregrinus.” Ado meanwhile restored the person, perhaps having learned from the lost Acts the manner of death; Usuard thought it should be preserved exactly, without removing a single syllable, and Notker also has almost the same wording.

Florentinius doubts whether the final announcements derive from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, again preferring his Echternach and Corbie manuscripts to his own. Ado, moreover, assigns Hilarius a sufficiently notable eulogy; it is surprising that Florentinius attributes it to Notker, who seems often to have done no more than combine the words of Ado and Rabanus. Our author was content with the opening elements of that encomium and omitted the rest. The remaining material can be seen in the source which Notker blended with Rabanus’s eulogy.

Notker clearly shows what the learned opinion of his own age was concerning Hilarius in these words: “At Arles, the deposition of Saint Hilarius, bishop, who detected the Pelagian heresy among the collators and strove to correct it.” This brief indication is enough; the rest is carefully and learnedly set out in the Acts by Henschenius and Papebrochius, on this day and in the appendix to volume VII for May, beginning at p. 594. Compare Tillemont, volume XV, pp. 36–97, where he judges somewhat more moderately than those who did not fear to brand so illustrious a saint, calumniously, with the charge of Semipelagianism, whatever close association he otherwise had with Augustine’s new disciples.

In the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Nicetus or Nicetius is joined with Nectarius, as also in Notker. Ado named only the first, and therefore our author, following him closely, did the same, except that he wrote *Niceti* instead of *Nicetii*. Juvenianus in Jerome, Juvianus in Rabanus, and Jovianus in Notker is announced by Ado in the form read by Usuard in our entry; here it is rendered simply and fully, as elsewhere.

The details recorded by Notker at considerable length concerning the Ascension of the Lord—the church on the Mount of Olives furnished with royal magnificence, and the final footprints of God and man impressed in the sand—are unknown to the earlier writers. It could perhaps be said that he followed Wandalbert, who sang as follows:

> Christ traversed the starry Olympus in threefold ascent;  
>   
> Arles shines with Hilarius, and Vienne with Nicetus.

[Col. 0023D]

PULSANEN. omits the Thessalonian martyrs and also Jovinianus, replacing him with: “On the same day, the Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ into heaven from the Mount of Olives.”

[Col. 0025A]

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. abridge the brief eulogies of Hilarius and Nicetius and incorrectly give Jovinianus the title of bishop.

MUNERAT., at the end, adds: “At Cella, Saint Fortunatus, bishop and confessor.” He is celebrated on 18 June. See Munerat’s eulogy and the Acts there.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., DANIC., and EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG. have the following concerning Hilarius: “In Gaul, in the city of Arles, blessed Hilarius, bishop and confessor, a most distinguished and noble man. A lover of poverty and a devout compassionate helper of the poor, he even undertook farming, contrary to his strength, to refresh the poor, although a man of distinguished birth and raised in a very different manner; yet he did not neglect himself in spiritual matters.” This material, taken from Ado and somewhat expanded in nearly Ado’s own words, is developed by ALBERGEN. at greater length; it can be drawn more purely from the same source. The remaining text of those manuscripts is pure, except that some write *Vincenti* instead of *Niceti*, and others—as these later manuscripts commonly do—contain minor errors.

[Col. 0025B]

CENTULEN.: “In the city of Arles, Saint Hilarius, bishop and confessor, a great, learned, and most distinguished man. At Auxerre, Saint Jovinianus, lector and martyr. At the castle of Douai, Saint Maurontus, abbot, a man remarkable in birth and holiness, who is said to have been the son of the most holy Richarius at baptism. At Vienne, Saint Nicetius, bishop and confessor.” Euthymius and the Thessalonians follow; the text is pure in those passages.

BRUXELLEN. begins: “Near Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives, the Ascension of the Lord.” It is correct in the notices of Euthymius and the Thessalonians. Concerning Hilarius, after “confessor,” it adds: “A noble and most distinguished man. A lover of poverty, he did not neglect himself in spiritual matters. And at Vienne, the glorious bishop Nycaesius.” The notice of Jovinianus is pure. It then continues: “And the feast of Saint Juvenal, martyr.” Is this the person celebrated on 7 May? It is surprising that he is not noted in the table of omitted saints. “On the same day, the translation of the body of Saint Audoenus, archbishop and confessor of Rouen.” He is celebrated on 24 [Col. 0025C] August.

HAGENOYEN begins with Antonia in the words reported on the preceding day. Euthymius and the Thessalonians follow, purely. Its account of Hilarius is almost like that of the middle-class manuscripts. Then: “On the same day, Saint Godhard, bishop and confessor of Hildesheim.” He was also treated on the preceding day. The remaining two announcements are pure.

AQUICINCT, at the end: “At Douai, the feast of Saint Maurontus, abbot and levite.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Audoenus, bishop of Rouen. Waldrada, virgin. Nicetius, bishop and confessor. Hilarius, bishop of Arles.”

CAMBERIEN. of the Convent of Saint Mary: “On the same day, blessed Fortunatus, bishop and confessor.” Concerning him, see above. “At Auxerre, Saint Romanus, martyr.” No other witness gives any notice of him on this day, not even our list of omitted saints. There “Romanus, abbot” is celebrated on 22 May. “Romanus, bishop,” whom someone also calls “martyr,” is celebrated on 6 October. Let someone inform us which of the two is intended here.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “At Cella, Saint Fortunatus, bishop and confessor.”

UGHELLIAN. writes *Viviani* instead of *Joviniani*.

ALTEMPS: “In Lesser Britain, Saint Buddocus, bishop and confessor.” Until now he has been unknown to me, unless this is the person whom Castellanus calls “Budocus of Vannes,” whom he records on 9 December.

FLORENTIN.: “Near Milan, the conversion”—MEDIC. incorrectly has “and translation”—“of Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor, under Saint Ambrose, bishop of that same city, and baptized by him, having put on the black monastic habit, as Ambrose himself says in his sermon on the baptism of blessed Augustine.” This should be referred to 28 August.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins with Hilarius, reproducing Ado’s entire eulogy. It then continues: “On the same day, Saint Godhard, bishop and confessor. He had first been abbot of many monks, but afterward was summoned by Saint Henry the Emperor to the episcopate of Hildesheim. After he had devoutly governed this office for many years, on the feast of the Ascension of the Lord, while ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father’ was being sung at Matins, his soul, accompanied by angels, ascended to heaven; his death was made miraculous by wonders and signs. At Trier, the feast of Saint Brito, bishop and confessor.” The rest of the text follows. Then: “On the same day, Saint Angelus, Carmelite and martyr. On the same day, the conversion of blessed Augustine, bishop and confessor,” together with various circumstances of his conversion, which are better related in their proper place.

BELIN. begins: “At Milan, the conversion of Saint Augustine,” etc., as above from FLORENTIN. Another edition prefixes: “On the Mount of Olives, the Ascension of Our Lord Jesus Christ.” Some things in the text, which is often badly printed, require correction.

GREVEN.: “The Ascension of the Lord. At the town of Leocata in Sicily, blessed Angelus of Jerusalem, a Carmelite. [Col. 0026B] As he traveled about preaching and converted innumerable souls to Christ, he was martyred for the truth of the faith and the protection of chastity. On the same day, in many churches the office is kept of the Good Thief, who was crucified with Christ and entered Paradise with him.” See the Omitted Saints. “Also, of Saints Gregory and Petivius.” Better in the Acts. “Of Tryphon, a boy and martyr, according to Vincent in Book XII, chapter 47.” See the Omitted Saints. “Of Brito, bishop of Trier and confessor. Of Nectarius, bishop of Vienne and confessor. Of Maurontus, bishop. The conversion of blessed Augustine, bishop, when, after many struggles, he was corrected from the error of the Manichaeans through the preaching of blessed Ambrose, and in the year of the Lord” 377 “(add at least ten years), when he was over thirty years of age, he burned wholly with love for Christ. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Godehard, bishop and confessor. When he was abbot of many monks, he was summoned by the holy Emperor Henry to the bishopric of Hildesheim. [Col. 0026C] Divinely admonished, he consented; and vigorously administering the office of pontifical dignity imposed upon him, when on the night of the Ascension the words ‘I ascend to my Father’ were sung, his holy soul, accompanied by angels, ascended into heaven. Of Hirenia, a virgin, daughter of the Emperor Licinius.” It would be better to say that she was the daughter of some petty king who perhaps was called “Licinius.” In any event, she is placed first in the Acts. “Also, of Saint Waldrada, virgin. At Rouen, the translation of Saint Audoenus, bishop and confessor of that city. Also, of Saint Avertinus, deacon and confessor. Of blessed memory, Bruno, a boy, to whom Saint Godehard, who had taken him in and raised him, often foretold that he would go with him to the heavenly homeland. And when the bells were rung at the death of the saint, the boy cried out: ‘Truly my lord is ascending into heaven!’ Forgetting his promise, and at the same time praying that he might not leave him longer in the flesh, he deserved to be heard.” He is venerated—or at least his Acts have been edited together with the Acts of Saint Godehard—on 4 May.

[Col. 0026D] MOLAN, concerning Jovinianus, adds as follows: “When he came with blessed Peregrinus, bishop and martyr, to Auxerre at the command of Pope Sixtus, being a man eloquent in every respect and exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures, and when he stoutly resisted the superstitions of the pagans, he was seized; and persevering in the passion of Christ, he was killed by them. This is written in the Passion of Saint Peregrinus. On the same day, of Saint Avertinus, confessor and deacon. On the Mount of Olives, the Ascension of Our Lord Jesus Christ into heaven. At Milan,” etc., as in FLORENTIN., up to “baptized.” Concerning Fortunatus, likewise as above. “In Sicily, the feast of Saint Angelus, priest and martyr, who came from Mount Carmel at divine command for the sake of preaching; and after he had converted many to repentance, he was slaughtered by certain impious heretics. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Maurontus, abbot; through whose intercession, if sick people afflicted with various illnesses are brought to his tomb, they truly receive the rewards of restored health. The holy bishop Amatus entrusted him to custody, because of his holy way of life, after the death of blessed Abbot Ultanus, at the time when King Theodoric was exercising wicked tyranny. This is written in his Life.” Then, in smaller letters: “At Bruges, the office of the Good Thief crucified with Christ is observed.”

Other editions agree with the first regarding Jovinianus. Then: “In Sicily, at the town of Leocata, or Achata, the feast of Saint Angelus,” etc. The same is true of Fortunatus. The notice concerning Maurontus is somewhat shorter in both, and obscure in each; from the Acts you will understand the matter more clearly. Concerning Avertinus, as above. “At Trier, of Brito, bishop [Col. 0028A] and confessor. On the Mount of Olives . . . . . At Milan, the conversion of Saint Augustine,” etc., as in the first edition. It is easy to observe that the aforesaid conversion of Saint Augustine was not celebrated in the Church, or entered in the Calendars, before the end of the fifteenth century. For the manuscripts first cited from FLORENTIN. are not older, and indeed the greater part is absent from the Florentine edition of Usuardus of 1386, so that this rather inadequate commemoration must almost certainly be attributed to BELIN.]

[Col. 0023]

At Alexandria, Saint Euthymius, deacon, resting in prison. At Thessalonica, the feast of Saints Hyrenaeus, Peregrinus, and Hyrenis, burned in the fire. In Gaul, at the city of Arles, blessed Hilary, bishop and confessor, a most distinguished and noble man. Also at Vienne, Saint Nicetius, bishop, a man of venerable holiness. At Auxerre, the passion of Saint Jovinianus, lector and martyr.

The day before the Nones. Day 6.

[Note: [Col. 0027B]]

The texts of Praten., Herinien., Antverp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. are entirely pure. Antverp. and Max.-Lubec., Antverp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., [Col. 0028B] Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the Ultraject-Belg. edition come close.

[Note: [Col. 0027B]]

In the purer manuscripts these matters are reduced to a few points. Herinien. and Munerat., as usual, write *Joannis*. Herinien. again reads *Cirinensis* and *Cirenen*. Munerat. has the festive *festive* instead of *festum*; Greven. and Molan. have *Venustii*. The reference to Africa was made elsewhere. The remaining manuscripts, except the major Antverp. manuscript, omit the first word, *Natalis*. The exceptional codex has *natale*. In the same place, instead of *Hic glorioso martyrio*, it has the shorter *hic gloriose*. The others seem to follow Ado rather than Usuardus when they read *melius* and *clarius*, where there was a festive gathering on the same day, etc.; but Antverp. and Max.-Lubec. have other blemishes, such as *est missus* and *cursim* instead of *concursum*, and *in Actibus Helyodori*, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0027B]]

The entire section, apart from the final announcement, derives from the Small Roman Martyrology; for in the principal Hieronymian copies you will find not a word concerning John before the Latin Gate, Evodius, or Lucius. There is nevertheless this difference between our text and the Small Roman Martyrology: John is placed first here, but last there. Anyone reading the text of the Small Roman Martyrology will see that its compiler nowhere expressed himself more distinctly. Ado also fitted a longer eulogy to John, placing him first; Our author condensed it with his customary polish. It is surprising that he read *festum concursum* less clearly, where Ado had put the clearer *festivum*. Notker here showed more judgment than his source, expanding and interpolating its eulogy.

What should be elucidated from Tertullian and Jerome concerning that celebrated passion of Saint John the Apostle, whose commemoration we have seen preserved at Rome, Henschenius rightly postpones to his feast on 27 December. Let Wandelbertus be heard here, celebrating John’s triumph:

> On the day before the Nones, the Roman temples of God  
> Celebrate lofty John, who drank in the Word from a full heart.

Ado said no more about Evodius in his Martyrology than he had found in the Small Roman Martyrology; but in the Feasts of the Apostles he quotes the words of Saint Ignatius, which Our author did not transcribe, composing his brief eulogy from the whole of Ado’s account: “He completed his life in glorious martyrdom,” etc. What is read in Mosander is Ado’s very own encomium among the Feasts. Notker did not consult it; in addition to the words of the Martyrology, he rather inappropriately brought here Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians: “Concerning whom Paul himself, writing to the Philippians, says: ‘I urge Euodius and Syntyche,’” etc. For the Apostle does not mention Evodius there, but Euodia, as is well known.

Henschenius briefly gathers what he found concerning Evodius in ecclesiastical records, and others have transmitted nothing more. The Small Roman Martyrology reports Lucius in these words: “And Saint Lucius of Cyrene, who was ordained bishop at Cyrene by the Apostles.” The rest, added by Ado, Our author transcribed word for word. Henschenius rightly observes that the Martyrologists attribute more to Lucius here than the sacred text expresses; they would have acted more correctly if they had assigned him the same eulogy that Manahen has on 24 May, namely, “a prophet and teacher under the New Testament.”

I cannot conjecture from which copy, or what kind of copy, of Jerome Usuardus received Heliodorus and Venustus with seventy-five companions; in their place, Rabanus and Notker again announce Marianus and Jacobus with companions. If Henschenius correctly divided the numerous band of martyrs in Jerome, Heliodorus, Marianus, and Jacobus belong to the same African company; but Venustus should be assigned to the—if one may so speak—Milanese delegation. As for what Henschenius notes among the Omitted Saints, namely, that Rabanus identifies Marianus as a lector and Jacobus [Col. 0028D] as a deacon, concerning whom he speaks on 30 April, the circumstances added by Rabanus make this quite plausible. We indicated there that this is the true day of their martyrdom. However the matter may stand, the reading of Usuardus found in our manuscripts appears certain and beyond doubt.]

[Note: [Col. 0027D]]

TORNACEN. has shortened the eulogies somewhat several times, and has done so again here by omitting the words, “he completed his life in glorious martyrdom in that same city.” Apart from this, it is entirely pure.

PULSANEN. is more mutilated; it omits “where the feast,” etc. It has not a word about Evodius.

ROSWEYD. begins: “At Rome, John before the Latin Gate,” and then adapts the remaining sentence of our text to this beginning: “When the same,” etc.

BELIN. is sprinkled, as usual, with many blemishes. The principal one here is that, contrary to the text concerning “Lucius of Cyrene,” it has him in the final place.

CENTULEN.: “The feast of Saint John the Apostle before the Latin Gate at Rome. At Antioch, Saint Evodius [Col. 0029A] martyr, who was the first after blessed Peter to govern the church of Antioch. On the same day, Saints Heliodorus, Venustus, Postunius, Maximus, and Nicetius, with seventy-two others.” We have already said in the Observation that Heliodorus is wrongly joined to Venustus and the other Milanese. See also what Henschenius noted here. It continues: “At Auxerre, Saint Valerian, bishop, third after Saint Peregrinus.”

BRUXELLEN.: “Saint John, apostle and evangelist. By order of Domitian, the brother of Titus, in the second persecution which he himself carried out after Nero, he was brought from Ephesus to the city of Rome; in the presence of the Senate, he was put before the Latin Gate into a vessel of boiling oil, but was not harmed at all. Thus he emerged from that punishment as unharmed as he had remained free from corruption of the flesh.” These additions to the text are taken from Ado. In the rest it is fairly pure.

HAGENOYEN. In John it is moderately interpolated; in second place it has: “Also at Salerno, the translation of Saint [Col. 0029B] Matthew the Apostle.” Some Hieronymian copies place the feast of Matthew today. Everything will be treated on the day on which he is celebrated, 21 September. “At Lauffen in the diocese of Würzburg, the translation of Saint Reguisida, virgin and martyr.” The Acts refer this to 15 July. What pertains to the text follows, with some interpolation as well.

AQUICINCT. It omits what is recited in the text concerning Saint Luke, and ends the sentence differently.

MATRIC-CARTUS ULTRAJECT.: “John before the Latin Gate. Lucius of Cyrene. Heliodorus, Venustus, with seventy-five other martyrs. Evodius, bishop and martyr.”

VATICAN. no. 5949. The notice of Heliodorus and his companions is absent. Added first is: “The feast of Saint Secundinus, bishop and confessor, in Saint Sophia. On the same day, Saint Secundinus martyr.” Who these “Secundini” are is not yet clear to me, nor do I find anything about them among the Omitted Saints. I do not think that the “Secundinians” are meant, such as are numbered among the martyrs today. In any event, these additions stand first; [Col. 0029C] at the end follows: “At Salerno, the translation of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist.” The manuscripts that follow agree.

FLORENTIN.: “At Salerno, the translation of the body of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist.
