At Rome, the translation of the body of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, in the time of Pope Pelagius I and the Emperor Theodosius; and he was buried in the church of Saint Lawrence outside the walls and in his tomb.” These matters are referred to in the table of the Omitted Saints; but that translation is postponed to 3 August or 26 December.

LUXOVIEN.: “At Autun, blessed Placidus, priest and abbot of Saint Symphorianus.” The index of Omitted Saints refers this to 7 May.

SALINEN. B. Anatoli.: “At Autun, the deposition of blessed Philibert, bishop.” Perhaps he is the same person who just above is called “Placidus.” See the Omitted Saints for this day and the Acts for 7 May.

REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.: “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Valerian, bishop and confessor.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. is fairly pure in the text; at the end it adds: “On the same day, Saint Melotis, a boy, beheaded for Christ.” See the Omitted Saints, where the name is written in various ways. “At Auxerre, Saint Valerian, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0030B] GREVEN.: “Also, Saints Matthew and Primus, Victor, and Felix.” The first two are from Tarentum; the last belong to the number of the Milanese. “On the same day, Saint Melotis, a boy, beheaded for Christ.” We have already spoken of him. “At Auxerre, Saint Valerius, bishop and confessor.” In the Acts he is joined to “Secundianus, bishop.” He is no better known by this title than “Secundinus, Benedictus, and Placidus, bishops.” See the Omitted Saints concerning each separately. “In England, Saint Eadbercht, whom they call Edbert, bishop of Lindisfarne and confessor; a man, as Bede testifies in Book IV, distinguished both by knowledge of the divine Scriptures and by observance of the heavenly commandments, and especially by the practice of almsgiving. At Constantinople, the deposition of blessed John of Damascus, an outstanding teacher, no less distinguished in life and miracles.”

MOLAN. in smaller type: “In England, Saint Eadbercht,” etc., as GREVENUS. Then: “At Constantinople, the deposition,” etc., adding at the end: “John, patriarch of Jerusalem, wrote his Life.” [Col. 0030C] Other editions, also in smaller type, have only this: “In England, Saint Eadhreсht, or Edbert, bishop and confessor of Lindisfarne, a man distinguished alike by knowledge of the divine Scriptures, observance of the heavenly commandments, and especially the practice of almsgiving.” See GREVEN. above.]

[Col. 0027]

The feast of blessed John the Apostle, when he was brought from Ephesus to Rome by order of Domitian and, in the presence of the Senate, was placed before the Latin Gate in a vessel of boiling oil, but was not harmed at all. On that day the faithful people still gather there for the feast. At Antioch, Saint Evodius, who, as blessed Ignatius writes, was ordained there by the Apostles as the first bishop. He completed his life in glorious martyrdom in that same city. Also Saint Lucius of Cyrene, who was established by the holy Apostles as the first bishop at Cyrene, and whom blessed Luke mentions in the Acts of the Apostles. In Africa, Saints Heliodorus and Venustus, martyrs, with seventy-five others.

The Nones. Day 7.

[Note: [Col. 0029]]

The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Rosweyd., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0029D]]

I attribute *Tarracinam* and *Teracenam* to the ignorance of the copyists. All the manuscripts except Greven. and Molan. read “blessed Domitilla.” Whether *beatae* has intruded in place of *Flaviae*, I do not know; certainly no one except the two just cited adds the name Flavia. Munerat., Belin., and the two aforementioned manuscripts wrongly write *Domicillae*. *Domiciani* in Praten. and Munerat. need not be noted. Rosweyd. has made a slight transposition in “niece through his sister and deported into exile.” After *Domitiani*, Belin. inserts “for the testimony of Christ.” Instead of *Pontiani* it writes *Pontianum*; instead of *inibi*, *ibi*; instead of “the faith of the Lord,” “the faith of Christ.” Thus Tornacen., instead of *martyrium*, which he had adopted, preferred to write *produxit*. Herinien. scarcely deserves to be counted among the pure manuscripts today, since it distorts the sense as follows: “Under a certain judge, in whose [house] Theodora was also confined, she completed the course of her glorious martyrdom, together with Euphrosina, her fellow virgin.” The more reliable manuscripts have *convirginibus*; only Rosweyd., Munerat., and Belin. simply have *virginibus*. All the manuscripts write *Eufrosina*. Some, however, incorrectly write *Nichomedia*. Thus Munerat., instead of “of Saints Flavius,” etc., has *Clavius*.]

[Note: [Col. 0029D]]

Although two women named Flavia are listed among many other martyrs in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on this day, it is more than certain that Flavia Domitilla is recorded in neither these manuscripts nor on any other day. The author of the Small Roman Martyrology was the first of all to give this most illustrious saint a place in the sacred Calendars, briefly announcing her here in second place: “And of Flavia Domitilla.” I would not hesitate to assert that she was most probably taken from Rufinus’s Eusebius, Book III, chapter 17, where exile, if not martyrdom, is expressly mentioned.

A fuller history was woven by Ado from the well-known Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus; Notker made it somewhat longer, while Our author gathered it into an elegant synopsis. You may vainly speculate whether, and why, Usuardus removed the name Flavia. It is evident that all commemorate one and the same woman; nor is there greater doubt concerning the most ancient, universally received, and celebrated veneration in the Church of the famous virgin and her male and female companions, even though they are commemorated on different days, almost at the discretion of the Martyrologists who record them.

In honor of Flavia Domitilla, one or two testimonies of Saint Jerome, produced by Henschenius in the Acts on 12 May, might suffice; on that day she is joined in the Roman Martyrology to Nereus and Achilleus. Thus far everything proceeds satisfactorily. The difficulty returns with respect to the Acts themselves, praised by Henschenius as being of excellent reliability, although Baronius had long before acknowledged, in volume I under the year 18, no. 13, that those Acts are not wholly trustworthy in certain respects. More rigorously, recent scholars treat them as entirely suspect; even Tillemontius, otherwise so moderate, could not here refrain from delivering a severe judgment, calling them in volume II, page 127, “a very bad work, worthy to be counted among the fabrications of the Manichaeans, who assailed the sacred bonds of marriage.” He is neither wholly right nor wholly wrong. I prefer the judgment of the eminent annalist, from whom here, as elsewhere, we are separated only reluctantly.

The Small Roman Martyrology mentions Juvenalis the martyr first; neither Ado, Our author, nor Notker supplies anything from which one could establish with certainty the place and time in which he flourished, Henschenius says, while continuing with what may be said of that saint by some plausible conjecture. Ancient veneration is also supported by Wandelbertus:

> On the Nones, holy Juvenalis honors [the day] with a pious death.

Usuardus likewise drew the final announcement from Ado, and Ado from the Small Roman Martyrology. Into the latter’s text he inserted the name Flavius among Nicomedia, Augustus, and Augustinus, and was the first to call the three brothers, reading: “On the same day at Nicomedia, the passion of Saints Flavius, Augustus, and Augustinus, brothers.” Here it is clear what Ado added to his source from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; the derivation of our text is also clear. But I should like to know by what authority the Viennese Martyrology so confidently calls Flavius, Augustus, and Augustinus brothers. “From the Hieronymian Martyrologies,” you will say. Certainly not. For although I admit that the name Augustinus is mentioned there more than once, and that some persons are likewise called brothers, neither Henschenius nor Florentinius has yet had the insight to determine whether these three may rightly be called brothers.

Whether Notker handled the matter more successfully, when removing the title of brothers from these men and assigning it instead to three others—Marcellinus, Macrobius, and Eutychius, elsewhere called Eutheius—I leave to the judgment of the curious reader. Rabanus’s wording differs from all these. Usuardus, less scrupulous in such matters, simply copied Ado, as we have said. Let this suffice concerning the truth of the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0031B]]

PULSANEN. omits the announcement of Juvenalis; otherwise it is entirely pure.

ANTVERP., MAX.-LUBEC., UGHELLIAN., ANTVERP. MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and the ULTRA BELG. EDITION. All fail in the final announcement.

[Col. 0031C] ANTVERP.-MAJ. begins as follows: “In Kent, at the monastery of Peter and Paul, the deposition of Saint Leothard, bishop and confessor, who was sent to these regions with Bertha, daughter of the king of the Franks, so that, by the example of holiness, she would not abandon the worship of the Christian religion while joined in marriage to a still-pagan king.” The remarks concerning Leothard, or Letard, in the Omitted Saints should be observed. It continues: “And the feast of Saint John, archbishop of York.” The text is pure.

CENTULEN.: “At Terracina, a city of Campania, the feast of blessed Domitilla, virgin and martyr. On the same day, at Nicomedia, Saints Flavius, Augustus, and Augustinus, martyrs and brothers.”

BRUXELLEN. is moderately interpolated in the notice of Flavia Domitilla and is pure in that of Juvenalis. Then: “At the foot of the seventh mountain, the passion of Saint Gaudentius martyr.” I confess that I do not know who this Gaudentius is. “At Nicomedia, Saints Flavius, Augustus, and Augustinus, brothers and martyrs. And Benedictus, bishop.” [Col. 0031D] This seems, I think, to indicate Pope Benedict II, whose Acts are celebrated today. “Also Donacianus, bishop.” His feast is 14 October. “Also, the translation of Saint Peter of Milan (why not ‘of Verona?’), martyr of the Order of Preachers.” See what was said about his feast on 29 April.

HAGENOYEN. In Flavia Domitilla it is also somewhat interpolated; in the rest of the text it is pure. Then it adds: “On the same day at Rome, the deposition of Saint Benedict II, pope, who from the beginning of his life served in the Church and always proved a lover of poverty. He issued constitutions and died in peace under Constantine IV.” You will find the age of this pontiff discussed in the Acts for this day.

MATRIC.-CARTUS-ULTRAJECT.: “Domitilla, virgin and martyr, with Euphrosina and Theodora. Domitianus, bishop and confessor. Juvenalis, martyr. Also Saints Flavius, Augustus, and Augustinus, brothers and martyrs.” It always mutilates the text.

[Col. 0032B] In the VATICAN manuscript numbered 5949, Juvenalis is absent. It adds: “The passing of Saint Stephen the protomartyr to Rome.” Concerning this also, see yesterday. See the day of his feast, or 3 August. Castellani’s note is misleading.

ALTEMPSIAN.: “In Kent, at the monastery of Peter and Paul, the deposition of Saint Leothard, bishop, etc.,” as above in ANTVERP.-MAJ.

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, Saint Benedict, pope and confessor. At Beverley, Saint John, bishop and confessor.” After resigning the episcopate, he wished to die in that place, from which he was called “of Beverley.”

REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.: “At Laon-la-Ferté, the deposition of Saint Bason, confessor.” He has been omitted, although Castellani nevertheless numbers him among the saints.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins: “At Rome, Saint Benedict, pope, who sat there for ten months, during the reign of Constantine Augustus.” See what was said above concerning HAGENOYEN. “At Terracina, a city of Campania, the feast of blessed Domicilla, virgin and martyr. Since she was the niece through his sister of the Emperor Domitian and married to Aurelian, son of the consul Flavius Clemens, she rejected marriage for Christ’s sake and was consecrated by Saint Clement, bishop, with the sacred veil,” etc., almost entirely pure. It places the Nicomedian martyrs before Juvenalis. Then: “In the territory of Milan, the translation of blessed Peter [Col. 0032D] priest and martyr, of the Order of Preachers. On the same day, blessed Domitianus, bishop and confessor . . . At Beverley, the feast of Saint John, bishop and confessor of York.”

GREVEN.: “The feast of the five joys of blessed Mary, Mother of God.” Concerning this, see the Omitted Saints. “Also Saints Frodisius, Macrobius, Achaicus, and Marcellinus.” From Jerome: “Celerinus, bishop and confessor.” There are two Celerini among the martyrs, but which one is this “bishop and confessor,” I do not know. “In England, Saint John, bishop and confessor of York, distinguished in life and miracles, as Bede testifies in Book V. At Autun, the deposition of Saint Placitus—Placidus—bishop. Domitianus, bishop of Tongeren and confessor. Hilary, confessor.” See the Omitted Saints. “Ceverus, confessor.” Is this “Cerenicus” or “Serenicus,” the deacon of Séez? “In England, Ezeleidis, virgin.” See the Omitted Saints and the Appendix to volume VII, May. “The translation of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, when his body was brought from Constantinople to Rome and joined to the body of Saint Lawrence, in the time of the younger Theodosius. At Milan, the translation of blessed Peter, martyr of the Order of Preachers. Mastidia, virgin,” of Troyes.

MOLAN.: “Domitianus, bishop and confessor of Tongeren, Utrecht, and Liège, resting at Huy in the church of blessed Mary. At Autun, the deposition of Saint Placitus, bishop. At Rome, Benedict, pontiff, who held the episcopate for one month, during the reign of Constantine.” Then, in smaller letters: “In England, Saint John,” etc., as GREVEN.: “The feast of the five joys of Mary.” Other editions have: “At Beverley, the deposition of Saint John, bishop [Col. 0034A] of York and confessor, distinguished in life and miracles. In the church of blessed Mary at Huy, the feast of Saint Domitianus, bishop and confessor. He is recorded to have taken part in the synod of Orléans in the time of the most glorious King Hildebert.” Concerning Placidus, as above. “At Troyes, the translation of the body of Saint Mastidia, virgin. On the seventh day, the commemoration of the sign of the cross appearing in the sky at Jerusalem, around the third hour of the day, under King Constantius. It was formed by the stars from the holy place of Calvary as far as the Mount of Olives. And the commemoration of Saint Acacius the martyr.” See the Omitted Saints concerning both of the announcements already noted.]

[Col. 0029]

At Terracina, a city of Campania, the feast of blessed Domitilla, virgin and martyr, who, being the niece through his sister of the consul Flavius Clemens and consecrated by Saint Clement with the sacred veil, was deported into exile during the persecution of Domitian, together with many others, to the island of Pontia, where she endured a long martyrdom. Finally, after converting many to the faith of the Lord through teaching and miracles, she completed the course of her glorious martyrdom when a certain judge burned the chamber in which she was confined together with her fellow virgins, namely Euphrosina and Theodora. On the same day, Saint Juvenalis martyr. At Nicomedia, the passion of Saints Flavius, Augustus, and Augustinus, brothers.

The eighth day before the Ides. Day 8.

[Note: [Col. 0033]]

Thus Praten., Tornacen., Antverp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0033B]]

The differences are almost entirely in details. Antverp.-Maj. writes *Mediolane*. Tornacen. reads “persevering in the confession of the Lord,” omitting the adverb *fortissime*, for which Munerat. has *constantissime*. Elsewhere in the text all the manuscripts have *abscisione*, although I may perhaps have corrected it in another place. Otherwise, *primeva*, *etate*, *cesus*, *nichil*, *lesus*, *poenitus*, *aput*, etc., are blemishes retaining the flavor of their period; the penultimate belongs to Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0033B]]

The memory of Victor, the martyr of Milan, famous for his fatherland and origin and surnamed Maurus, must once have been highly celebrated among the Latins, since all the ancient Martyrologists proclaim him, with the sole exceptions of Bede and Florus. The principal Hieronymian copies begin the day with this saint: “At Milan, Victor.” The Small Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Rabanus announce only him today. In the former alone we read: “At Milan, Saint Victor martyr.” Ado’s and Rabanus’s eulogies differ, although both are drawn from the same Acts. Notker first followed Ado, as did Our author, who uses Ado’s words but, in his customary manner, leaves certain things untouched; Notker transcribed them in full.

Whether the truth of the eulogy should be doubted, I do not entirely perceive. Henschenius admits that the source from which it was taken is not wholly pure; others think it should be rejected almost entirely. See what is considered in the Preliminary Commentary from no. 8 onward and in Tillemontius, volume V, [Col. 0034B] page 267 onward. There is also in the Acts a narrative by Gregory of Tours in praise of Victor. Nor should Wandelbertus’s polished poetic embellishment be passed over:

> On the eighth day before the Ides, in the city of Milan, there shines  
> The martyr Victor, to be revered for his exceptional love [or honor].

Thus far the judgment of the ancients is unanimous. The following names, Stephen and Victor, were entered by Usuardus from the aforesaid Hieronymian Martyrologies. One might wonder whether, instead of *Stephani et Victoris*, one should write *Victoris et Stephanae*, as Notker did after the Hieronymian Martyrologies, while others add Januarius. I do not know whether he has strayed far from the truth who thinks one should read “Victor and Corona.” But since Victor and Stephen recur on 1 April, and Victor and Corona on 14 May, I prefer to adhere on this day to Usuardus’s text, which I have no doubt exactly expresses his intention. Henschenius discusses these matters very briefly in our Acts for this day.]

[Note: [Col. 0033C]]

HERINIEN. In the rest of the text it is entirely pure; here it inserts the saint of its own region again, writing in second place: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Gibrianus, confessor, resting in the church of Saint Remigius.”

PULSANEN. It begins as follows: “On Mount Gargano, the apparition of the most blessed archangel Michael. There a church dedicated to his name has been erected, humble in appearance but endowed with heavenly power.” See the table of the Omitted Saints. It is pure in the notice of Victor of Milan. The final announcement is absent.

ANTVERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. add to the pure text: “Also Elladius, bishop.” They further add: “In the territory of Besançon, at the monastery of Bellevaux, the translation—or, in others, the feast—of Saint Peter, bishop and confessor.”

ROSWEYD. At the end: “At Utrecht, Wiron, confessor.” See Bollandus’s excellent commentary on him for this day.

ANTVERP.-MAX., LOVANIEN., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. EDITION. [Col. 0033D] are pure in the notice of Victor. They say nothing about Stephen, etc., but immediately add: “At Auxerre, the feast of Saint Elladius, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Besançon, at the monastery of Bellevaux, the feast of Saint Peter, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Wiron, [Col. 0034C] bishop and confessor.” In LEYDEN-BELG., the announcement of Peter is absent.

ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. begin: “In the borders of Apulia, on Mount Gargano, the discovery of the blessed archangel Michael.” It continues: “At Milan,” etc., purely. “Stephen,” etc., is absent. Concerning Elladius and Peter, as we have just said.

CENTULEN.: “At Milan, Saint Victor martyr. In Egypt, Saints Stephen and Victor. At Auxerre, Saint Helladius, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Saint Martin in Saintonge, at Vertou, Saint Martin, abbot.” This is referred to 24 October. “On the same day, the translation of Saint Gentianus martyr.” He is celebrated on 11 December.

BRUXELLEN. is usually purer in the text and adds: “On the same day, Saint Martin confessor. In the territory of Besançon, at the monastery of Bellevaux, Saint Peter, bishop and confessor. And Saint Dionysius, sixth bishop of Vienne.” This is postponed to the following day. [Col. 0034D] “At Auxerre, Saint Elladius, bishop and confessor. Also the apparition of Saint Michael the archangel. He admonished Saint Aubert, bishop of the church of Avranches, once, twice, and a third time, to found a church dedicated to his name in the sea, at the place called Tumba because of its height; as a sign, he showed him the place where he would find a tethered bull, and told him to mark out the circuit of the church according to the way he saw the animal’s feet break through the earth. From that time the memory of Saint Michael the archangel began to be celebrated there, as on Mount Gargano.” These matters, together with others, will be discussed on 29 September.

HAGENOYEN. In the first announcement it is pure; in second place it has: “In the borders of Apulia, on Mount Gargano, the discovery of the oratory of the blessed archangel Michael, which was discovered through the lost bull of Garganus” (read: “which was found through the bull of Garganus”). “Also at Vienne, Dionysius, a man most distinguished in learning.” Concerning him, see above. “Also Gybrianus, a most distinguished confessor. In Gargonia, Scanysolay, bishop and martyr.” Henschenius understands this as Stanislaus. “In Egypt, Saints Stephen and Victor, martyrs. In the territory of Besançon, Saint Peter, bishop and confessor. At Auxerre, Saint Elladius, bishop and confessor, [Col. 0035B] predecessor of Saint Amator.”

AQUICINCT. It begins: “At Rome, Saint Benedict, pope. From the beginning of his life he served in the Church and was always a lover of poverty.” He is celebrated on 7 May. See what we said there in the Appendices.

VICTORIN. and REG. OF SWEDEN no. 130. At the end they have: “The discovery of Michael the archangel; at Rome, Saint Benedict, pope.”

AMBIANEN.: “At Vertou in Saintonge, in the monastery, the deposition of Martin, priest and confessor, a man of great virtues, whose life shines gloriously with holiness and miracles. On the same day, the translation of the body of Saint Gentianus martyr.” See above.

MATRIC.-CARTUS-ULTRAJECT.: “Wiron, bishop and confessor, whose body is in the church of Saint Martin at Utrecht. Victor, martyr and soldier.”

REG. SUEC. no. 428: “In the district of Bourges, the deposition of Saint Desideratus, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN. no. 5949. First: “The apparition of Saint Michael. At Rome, Benedict, pope, who governed the Church for ten months during the reign of Constantine.” Stephen and Victor are absent.

UGHELLIAN. adds: “Also Elladius, bishop. Also Saint Peter, bishop and confessor.”

ALTEMPS. “At the monastery of Glasgow, Saint Indract, martyr, and his companions.” See the Acts for 5 February, where his sister “Dominica” is added to the companions.

FLORENTIN.: “In Africa, of the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix, who were beheaded together with John and Marinus.” See 10 July. “Also, of the holy bishop Elladius. In the territory of Tarentaise, at the monastery of Bona Vallis, of the holy bishop and confessor Peter. At Rome, of the holy pope Benedict II and confessor.”

REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.: “In the territory of Châlons, the burial of the holy priest and confessor Gibrianus.”

[Col. 0036A] EDITIO LUBECO.-COL. begins: “In the borders of Apulia, on Mount Gargano, the discovery of Saint Michael the archangel. This feast began in the following way. For at the time when Saint Pope Gregory, because of the bubonic plague, [ordered] the Litanies,” etc. How these passages are to be connected with one another, let the learned reader judge. In Victor, the text is sufficiently pure. It continues: “In the territory of Besançon, at the monastery of Bella Vallis, the feast of the holy Peter, bishop of the Church of Tarentaise and confessor of the Cistercian Order, who, renowned for many miracles and virtues, rested in peace. In Poland, in the city of Kraków, the passion of Blessed Stanislaus, bishop and martyr.” Concerning Elladius, Stephen and Victor, Martin, Dionysius, and Wiro, see above.

BELIN. places at the beginning: “In the borders of Apulia, on Mount Gargano, near the city of Sipontum, the apparition of Blessed Michael the archangel.” Then, after the text, at the end: “Also, of Bishop Eladius.” Others write “Elladius” throughout. Our Acts prefer “Helladius,” in which [Col. 0036B] see the few things that survive concerning him, taken from volume I of the Bibl. Labbeana and elucidated by Henschenius.

GREVEN. concerning Michael, as BELIN.: “According to some, on this day, the passion of Blessed Stanislaus, bishop and martyr.” It was yesterday. “On the same day, or according to others on the preceding day, of Saint Benedict II, pope, in the time of Constantine IV Augustus.” Concerning Dionysius and Peter of Tarentaise, as above. “In Lower Utrecht, of Blessed Wiro, bishop of Deivovum and confessor. In Ireland, of Blessed Cataldus, bishop and confessor, most renowned for his life and miracles.” He is commemorated on 10 May. “In the Cenonican monastery of Vercanum (how variously these names are expressed is evident from what has been said), of Blessed Martin, priest and confessor. Of Metronus, a confessor resting at Verona. Of Maximus the priest.” He is unknown, unless he is one of the martyrs. “Of Sibrianus the confessor.” He intended to say “Gibrianus.” “Of Macharius the hermit and confessor, at the end of the world near paradise.” See among the Omitted.

MOLAN. “In the borders of Apulia, on Mount Gargano near [Col. 0036C] the city of Sipontum, the apparition of Blessed Michael the archangel. Also, of Eladius, bishop and confessor, at Auxerre. On the same day, of Wiro, bishop and confessor, whose relics are kept in the church at Utrecht. On the same day, the burial of the holy Gibrianus the confessor, resting in the church of Saint Remigius. In the territory of Besançon, at the monastery of Bella Vallis, of the holy bishop and confessor Peter.” In other editions, concerning Michael and Eladius, as above. “At Kraków, of Saint Stanislaus, bishop and martyr. At Rheims, the burial of the holy Gibrianus,” etc. Concerning Peter, as in the first edition. Also concerning Wiro. “At Vienne, of Saint Dionysius, the sixth bishop of the city.” Finally, in smaller letters: “At Nivelles, on the same day, a commemoration of Yduberga.” She is also called “Itta,” and by others “Ittaberga”; after becoming a religious woman, she wished to place herself under her daughter Saint Gertrude.]

[Col. 0033]

At Milan, the feast of Saint Victor the martyr, who, a Christian from his earliest age, while serving as a soldier in the imperial forces, was compelled by Maximian to sacrifice. Persevering most steadfastly in his confession of the Lord, he was first severely beaten with clubs, but, protected by God, felt no pain; then he was covered with molten lead, but was not harmed at all; finally, he completed the course of his glorious martyrdom by the cutting off of his head. In Egypt, of Saints Stephen and Victor.

VII Idus. Day 9. [Note: [Col. 0035]

I consider the Pratensis, Antverp.-Maj., Greven, and Molan texts pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0035D]

Antverp.-Maj., before Timothy, did not add the conjunction “and.” It reads Constantine, together with Greven and Molan; I, with Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., and others, think Constant[i]us should be retained, at least according to Usuard’s intention, although Baronius, much more prudently, omitted both names in the modern Roman Martyrology. Nearly all the manuscripts write “Hermen,” and, if I am not mistaken, so does the Pratensis manuscript, corrected in our copy by Sirmond. I admit that in Ado one plainly reads “Hermae,” as is proper; but here we are dealing with Usuard, and we do not depart from him, even when he is mistaken. Add that Ado’s editors applied their correcting hand rather freely. I do not know what elegance Greven and Molan are pursuing when they vary the text thus: “Of whom the Apostle Paul makes mention when writing to the Romans.” Antverp.-maj. again neglects the particle after “acceptable.” [Col. 0038A] Again, the aforementioned Greven and Molan, instead of “firmly founded in virtues,” wrongly put “making virtues illustrious.” In the Antverp. maj. one reads “Nazanci” instead of “Nazanzi”; Ado’s “Nazianzi” is better. Likewise “Theodoli” instead of “Theologi,” and “peribet” instead of “perhibet.” I wrote “Vindicino,” as do most manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0037A]

The first announcement in our text seems so distinctly to belong to Usuard that, until now, I have been unable to discover from where he obtained it. “At Constantinople, the feast of Saint Timothy,” say the Hieronymian copies; the Viennese copy sheds light by adding: “When his sacred bones were brought from Ephesus.” Hence Notker, who always follows Ado more closely, briefly substitutes the translation of Timothy. As far as I know, no one before Usuard mentions on this day a common feast of Andrew and Luke. Would that he had done so more successfully! For it is clear that the translations of those three apostles are not properly connected, are connected even worse with the same period, and worst of all are assigned to the same day, especially this 9 May. But in what year, and on what day, the bodies of Andrew and Luke were brought to Constantinople and from there elsewhere must be discussed in their proper places. Meanwhile, let the reader see what was said on 24 January in the Preliminary Commentary, § 3, and Castellanus there, p. 394, as well as Baronius and Florentinius [Col. 0037B] here. To these may be added what Tillemont carefully observes in volume I, p. 320.

No martyrologist preceding Ado says anything about Herma today—not even Ado himself in his Martyrology—and consequently nothing appears in Notker either. This is strange and unusual in Ado: after adorning the saint among the feasts of the Apostles with a eulogy, Mosander, as I believe on his own authority, inserted it into the text of the Martyrology. This much is certain: everything Usuard reports here was taken from that source. The bishop of Philippi is called Hermas by some, but Ado does not give him this title, nor is anything else transmitted with sufficient certainty by which such a dignity can be asserted of him. Ado cites the Apostle’s passage at Romans 16, where he commands both Herman and Hermen to be greeted. He also mentions some things about the book of the Shepherd composed by Herma, which Jerome and Origen praise in Henschenius; but Tillemont explains much more about him and in greater detail in volume II, beginning at p. 3; the curious reader may consult there the other Fathers he cites [Col. 0038A]. Enough about Herma.

Gregory of Nazianzus was commemorated by the Greeks and others on various days; the first to assign him to this day was the author of the Little Roman Martyrology, taken, unless I am mistaken, from Rufinus, book II, chapter 9. Ado took the name from that source and composed from it his excellent eulogy, which Notker somewhat abbreviated; a few passages were taken from Notker by Our Author and placed in the margin. Concerning the life and deeds of this most illustrious Father, Papebrochius treated at length after Baronius and Hermantius; Tillemont likewise arranged an extensive account in French in volume IX, beginning at p. 305. Nor do I wish Castellanus’s note, appended to the Universal Martyrology, to go unmentioned. The 310 martyrs, reported first by Ado, derive from the Hieronymian Martyrologies and the Little Roman Martyrology. Usuard and Notker transcribed Ado’s words. Henschenius observed the following about them: “No one reports at what time or by what kind of death they completed their contest; and since very many persecutions were stirred up against Christians among the Persians, it is difficult to distinguish them.” Florentinius directs his attention to Sapor, king of the Persians, conjecturing that many were crowned with martyrdom under him. A certain Beatus, with the appended title “confessor,” appears in the common Hieronymian Martyrologies, but without a location. He was omitted by Bede, Florus, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado. Rabanus, I do not know on what basis, assigns him to Rome; Notker rather omitted him, but Our Author, more correctly, restored him to his proper place, the castle of Vendôme; add that he was in the diocese of Chartres, and seek the other matters concerning him, accurately explained, in Henschenius. For the rest, although only a few manuscripts agree, I plainly believe that here I have restored Usuard’s genuine text. The two final announcements in our text correspond to two verses of Wandalbert:

“Three hundred shine together on the seventh Ides,

“at last alike adorned by blessed martyrdom.”

] [Note: [Col. 0037C]

In the PRATENSIS manuscript, but, if I am not mistaken, added in the margin, appears: “At the city of Bari, the translation of the most holy Nicholas, bishop and confessor.” These words, or similar ones, passed into the text in other manuscripts.

ANTVERP.-MAJ. likewise has added in a later hand, in the margin: “On that same day, the translation of Saint Nicholas the confessor.” It could have added “bishop.”

HERINIEN., entirely the purest throughout the text, inserts in second place, in a fuller phrase: “On the same day, the translation of the body of the most blessed Nicholas, archbishop of Myra in Lycia. He was transferred, by divine dispensation, from the metropolitan see of Myra across the sea and was gloriously and suitably placed in the basilica of his honor at Bari, a city of the Apulian region, where to this day, as though living in the body, he shines magnificently through various miracles.” The same passage is found in MOLAN’S Appendix, but in more correct form.

TORNACEN. reports the text, but abridged by the eulogies of Herma and Gregory of Nazianzus. There, instead of the 310 martyrs, it gives only 305.

[Col. 0037D] PULSANEN. is pure in the first announcement and also reports Gregory purely in second place. But all the rest is absent.

MUNERAT. at the end of the text: “On the same day, the translation of Blessed Nicholas, bishop and confessor.”

ROSWEYD. substitutes “of the martyr Gengulphus” for “of Beatus.” The same occurs in the Utrecht church. But he is commemorated on 11 May.

ANTVERP.-MAX.-LUBEC., and ALBERGEN. begin with the 310 martyrs, where they are pure. Concerning Herma, after “makes mention when writing,” they omit the rest. Concerning Gregory, after [Col. 0038C] “town,” they write: “Of Blessed Gregory, who was called the Theologian, a noble and learned colleague of Blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea.” Everything else is absent—namely, the first and last announcements.

DANIC. differs from the preceding texts in reporting Herma’s entire eulogy.

MAX.-ANTVERP., LOVANIEN., and LEYDEN. add at the end, after Danic.: “On the same day, the translation of the body of the most blessed Nicholas, archbishop of Myra in Lycia.” EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG agrees. But it treats Gregory last.

ULTRAJ. adds to these: “Also, the translation of the glorious Jerome, outstanding doctor.” See among the Omitted.

CENTULENSIS: “At Rome, of Saint Hermen, whom the Apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans. In Persia, the martyrdom of the 310 saints. On the same day, the feast of Saint Andrew the apostle, when his most holy body, together with the bones of Luke the evangelist and Timothy, the disciple of the Apostle Paul, was translated to Constantinople. In Apulia, at the city of Bari, [Col. 0038D] the arrival and reception of the body of Blessed Nicholas, bishop and confessor of Myra. At the monastery of Saint Bavo, the translation of Saint Macharius, bishop and confessor of Antioch. At the castle of Vendôme, of Saint Beatus the confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. begins with Herma, quite purely. In second place it also gives the 310 martyrs purely. Then: “The feast of Saints Quirillus, Beatus, and Primulus, confessors.” This is a faulty conjunction derived from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. It continues with Gregory, where the text is interpolated: “Also, the translation of the body [Col. 0039A] of Blessed Andrew the apostle, together with the bones of Saints Luke the evangelist and Timothy, the blessed disciple of Paul, carried out to Constantinople under the emperor Constantine the Great. And the translation of Saint Nicholas, bishop. And at Ghent, the elevation of Saint Macharius, archbishop. When the unbelievers demanded a miracle, a rainbow in the form of a crown encircled the entire church courtyard, and in the middle a golden cross shone forth, followed by such clear evidence of miracles that scarcely anyone would be able to recount it.” See in the Acts on his feast day, 10 April.

HAGENOYEN. also begins with Herma, purely, as it does with the 310 martyrs. In Gregory it is slightly interpolated and wrongly calls him a “martyr.” It continues: “The feast,” etc., with the sense somewhat abridged. Then: “On that same day, the translation of Saint Nicholas, bishop, from Myra to Bari in Apulia. At the castle of Vendôme, the burial,” etc., purely.

AQUICINCT. after the word “ten,” adds: “On the same day, the translation of Blessed Nicholas, bishop and confessor, from the city of Myra to Bari. At Ghent, the elevation of Saint [Col. 0039B] Macharius, archbishop. At the castle of Vendôme,” etc.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130, at the end: “The feast of Blessed Hippolytus the martyr, when his most sacred body was translated to the monastery of Saint Saviour.” They commemorate him on 13 August. Nothing is added in the Omitted.

MATRIC.-CARTUS-ULTRAJECT. “Of Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop. The translation of Saint Andrew the apostle. The translation of Blessed Jerome. The translation of Blessed Nicholas, bishop.”

REG. SUEC., marked no. 130. Instead of “Beatus,” it writes: “At the castle, of Blessed Heraclius the confessor.”

Another REG. SUEC., no. 428: “On that same day, the translation of Blessed Nicholas, bishop, from Myra to the city of Bari.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949, “Andrew, Herma, and Beatus” are absent. It adds: “The translation of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor, to Bari.”

[Col. 0040A] In UGHELLIAN, Andrew and Beatus are also absent. I think it agrees with ANTV. and MAX-LUBEC.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins with Herma. Then the 310 martyrs. It follows with Gregory, as in ANTVERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. Then concerning Andrew, etc., where it says: “Under the younger Emperor Constantine, in his twentieth year, he was translated from Achaia to Constantinople. The translation of Blessed Jerome, priest and doctor of the Church, from Bethlehem in Judaea to the city of Rome.” Concerning Nicholas it adds: “The translation took place in the seventy-fifth year after his death (or rather in the seven hundred and forty-fifth?).” The sense makes our correction evident. Concerning Macarius and Beatus, as above.

BELIN. completely rearranged the text, beginning with the 310 martyrs. Then, concerning Gregory, it writes as ANTVERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. Afterward: “At Rome, of Saint Hermes, whom the Apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans. Also, the feast,” etc., purely, as also in the case of Beatus.

GREVEN.: “Also, of Saints Quirillus, Guideus, Zeno, Aphrodisius, and Primulus.” Again, an inept conjunction derived from the Hieronymian Martyrologies [Col. 0040B]. “On the same day, the translation of Blessed Jerome the priest from Bethlehem to the city of Rome. Also, the translation of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor, from Myra to Bari. At Ghent, the elevation of the body of Saint Macharius, bishop and confessor. Of Corinthia the virgin. At Rome, of Marina the matron.” Both of the latter are hitherto unknown, unless “Marina” is understood as “the wife of Gordian,” whom Bede and others mention on the following day. But nothing yet is known about her cult, as may be seen among the Omitted.

MOLAN. after Beatus adds: “Whose deeds are preserved.” Concerning Nicholas, as I said above, he reports the words of HERINIENSIS, somewhat polished. Then: “At Ghent, the elevation of Saint Macharius, archbishop of the See of Antioch.” In later editions he has the same concerning Macarius, but in Nicholas’s eulogy he somewhat abridges the words of HERINIENSIS.]

[Col. 0035]

The feast of Blessed Andrew the apostle, when his most sacred body, together with the bones of Saints Luke the evangelist and Timothy, the disciple of Saint Paul, was translated to Constantinople under the emperor Constantius. At Rome, the feast of Saint Hermen, whom the Apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans. He, sacrificing himself worthily to God and becoming an acceptable offering to God, firmly established in virtues, went to the kingdoms of heaven. At the town of Nazianzus, of Blessed Gregory, bishop, surnamed the Theologian, who, after many teachings, in his own place, as Jerome reports, having ordained as bishop the man instructed by him in the divine books, practiced the monastic life in the countryside. In Persia, of the 310 holy martyrs. At the castle of Vendôme, the burial of the blessed confessor.

VI Idus. Day 10. [Note: [Col. 0039C]

The Pratensis, Herinien., Rosweyd., Antverp.-Maj., Antverpien., Max-Lubec., Greven, and Molan texts are pure. To these are added [Col. 0040C] Antverp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., and Edit. Ultraject.-Belg.]

[Note: [Col. 0039C]

This is not of great importance, for Gordianus, Epimachus, Tybris, Palmacius, and matters of such minor detail may nearly be disregarded. In Rosweyd it is absent; the text is truncated before the heading. Ultraject. wrongly writes “prelate” instead of “consul.” Lovanien. [Col. 0040C] adds after “as an example,” “and terror.” Molan. reads “of Saint Quartus and Quintus” instead of “of the saints Quartus and Quintus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0039C]

The Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Our Author begin today with the celebrated miracle of patience, using the very words of the prophet Job. The Hieronymian expression is different, if indeed it belongs there; Notker’s is different again. All agree with Wandalbert in placing Job, the most ancient model of endurance among Christian athletes, and this is also the position in our Acts, adorned with a Commentary. The aforementioned Hieronymian copies also mention Gordianus and Epimachus, in distinct announcements and with a separate place of burial; on this matter Florentinius’s note should be consulted. Bede mentions them, as does the Little Roman Martyrology, which gives almost only their names. The published Ado ordinarily offers an abridgment of the Acts. Rabanus explains the matter from the same source but in different phrasing, and has Notker as his almost constant follower, though here Notker deserts his usual guide [Col. 0040C]. Our Author, without departing from the well-worn path, confined Ado’s eulogy to a few words, omitting either by accident or deliberately what the Viennese author had said more fully about Epimachus, and what Henschenius, on the authority of a single manuscript of ours, almost removes from Ado while discussing Epimachus at length; these matters may be read in his Commentary. It is evident from the Acts he himself produced that only Gordianus’s martyrdom is described. The aforementioned Henschenius does not dare to assert there whether the account is sufficiently trustworthy, recognizing with Baronius a mark of falsehood that does not necessarily corrupt the substance of the others as well—unless all the Acts that call Julian a tyrant collapse together through the same error [Col. 0040D]. I know that some, with Tillemont, volume VII, p. 722, reject them entirely; but I would rather suppose that they were interpolated by a later hand, long after Julian’s time. Certainly, the enduring memory of the distinguished martyr has been abundantly consecrated by perpetual veneration, both singly and together with his companion Epimachus, in the calendars of Allatius and Fronto and in Gregory’s Sacramentary. Thus Wandalbert honors both with Job, fully agreeing with our Martyrologies:

“Gordianus and Epimachus, old men, are cut down together

“for the one glory and faith of Christ.

“Holy Job also honors them by the example of his endurance.”

There is no mention in the Hieronymian manuscripts of Calepodius the elderly priest, as the Little Roman Martyrology writes. Bede composed for him a shorter but elegant encomium, which Rabanus transcribed almost word for word, and Notker took from Rabanus, though they differ in the number of his companions. The Viennese martyrologist exercised his style more fully, with both him and the author of these Acts having before their eyes the Acts of Saint Pope Callistus. For the rest, Usuard appears to adhere more to Bede’s words than to Ado’s, neatly condensing what could contribute to the praise of Calepodius and the others [Col. 0041B]. And this would indeed be excellent, if it had been drawn from a sufficiently clear source. I do not know what could have induced Henschenius to believe that the aforementioned Acts were written by Roman notaries, when they so openly fabricate a persecution that certainly never existed in the Church. To summarize, Baronius’s judgment is sufficient for me; writing under the year 226, no. 2, he says: “There exist Acts of his [Pope Callistus’s] passion, though they are not entirely genuine; for the edicts against Christians said to have been promulgated by Alexander, and the persecution said to have been initiated by him against them, are not accepted as historical. For these things are contradicted not only by what we cited above from Lampridius, but also by what was written by the ancient historians of Christian affairs, who all equally affirm that no persecution was raised in the Church under Alexander.” See also Tillemont, volume III, beginning at p. 250. It is entirely certain that Quartus and Quintus are mentioned in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, whatever may be the condition of some mutilated manuscripts, as Florentinius admits. The older Epternacensis expresses them most distinctly in these words: “Via Latina at the Hundred Halls, Quartus and Quintus.” This is the very phrase that passed into Ado and from him into Our Author; for the Little Roman Martyrology, Bede, Florus, and Rabanus make no mention of them. Henschenius inquires about their cemetery; but the Capuans raise another dispute, in settling which he labors there [Col. 0042B]. Ughelli’s opinion is agreeable: after Baronius and Bellarmine, he holds that we should accept the Roman Martyrology, which attributes this to the Capuans, so that the bodies of Quartus and Quintus are considered to have been transferred to Capua. See more in the aforementioned Henschenius.]

[Note: [Col. 0041B]

In the PRATEN. manuscript, added, I think, by a later hand, appears: “At the monastery of Saint Germanus, the dedication in honor of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Lawrence the archdeacon, and Saint Sulpicius the bishop.”

TORNACEN. completely cuts out the eulogy of Gordianus and Epimachus. It also removes Calepodius’s account up to “he was beheaded.” Everything else, beginning with those words, follows the text correctly and is pure.

MUNERAT., at the end: “On that same day, the feast of Saint Maturinus.” It refers the reader to 1 November.

In ALBERG. and DANIC., Job the prophet is absent.

[Col. 0041C] CENTULEN.: “The death of Job the prophet. At Rome, on the Via Latina, of the holy martyrs Gordianus and Epimachus. At Rome, at the Hundred Halls, of Saints Quartus and Quintus. Also at Rome, of Saint Calepodius, priest and martyr.” This codex arranges the text in its own manner.

BRUXELLEN. joins Januarius to Gordianus and Epimachus, with an interpolated eulogy afterward. “In the land of Uz, the burial of Blessed Job the prophet.” It then continues with Calepodius almost purely. Then: “On that same day, by order of the emperor Alexander, Palmatius the consul was beheaded with his wife and children and forty-two others of both sexes indiscriminately. Likewise Simplicius the senator with his wife and children and sixty-eight members of his household of both sexes indiscriminately. Likewise Felix with his wife Brianda [read Blanda]. Their heads were ordered to be hung at various gates of the city of Rome, as an example and terror to Christians.” It is pure in the account of Quartus and Quintus. “At Ghent, of Saint Bavo.” See 1 October.

HAGENOYEN. reverses the order of the text. First: “At Rome, [Col. 0041D] the passion of Saint Calepodius, priest and martyr. He made a cemetery at Rome, where he buried many martyrs,” etc., almost purely. Then it treats Palmatius and Simplicius separately, with an interpolated text. Next come Gordianus and Epimachus, and Quartus and Quintus, quite purely. “On that same day, of Job the prophet. Also in the bishopric of Strasbourg, of Sophia the widow.” See what is said about her among the Omitted.

MATRIC., CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT. “Of the martyrs Gordianus and Epimachus. Of Job the prophet. Of Calepodius the priest and many others of both sexes and every age, among whom Palmatius the consul suffered with his wife and the rest of his household, and likewise Simplicius the senator with his own. A perpetual abridgment here.”

AUGENS. S. Laurentii: “On the same day, at Augia, the translation of Blessed Laurence, bishop of Dublin, otherwise a martyr.” See among the Omitted, where it is referred to 14 November.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “On that same day, of Saint Maturinus the confessor.” See MUNERAT.

In VATICAN. no. 5949, Job and Quartus and Quintus are absent. It adds: “Of Saint Cataldus, bishop and confessor.” STROZZ speaks more clearly.

ALTEMPS.: “On that same day, of Saint Cataldus the confessor.”

STROZZ. “Also, of Saint Cataldus, archbishop of the city of Tarentum and confessor, in the province of Apulia. Also, the translation of the bodies of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian to the city of Venice, and their placement in the monastery of Saint Gregory Major, in the year of the Lord 1154, in the second indiction.” BELIN is almost the same.

LUXOVIEN.: “In the middle of the monastery, the translation of the holy confessors John the priest and Benignus the deacon, disciples of Blessed Hidulf, archbishop.” Their feast day is 31 July.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL.: “In the land of Uz, the burial of Saint Job the prophet.” In the account of Gordianus and Epimachus, and likewise in that of Calepodius and his companions, it is interpolated from Ado, though it reads 48 instead of 68. It is pure in the account of Quartus and Quintus. It adds: “In the territory of Bourges, of Saint Palladius, bishop and confessor.” Whether this is the first or the second, see in the Acts. “In the territory of Vexin, of Blessed Martin the confessor.” I am mistaken if this does not refer to “Maturianus, in the territory of Vexin,” concerning whom see 1 and 9 November. “Also at Rome, of Saint Januarius, sent into exile for Christ.” See among the Omitted.

BELIN. adds at the end: “Also, of Saint Christina, virgin and martyr. Also, the translation of the holy [Col. 0042D] martyrs Cosmas and Damian to Venice, to the monastery of Saint George Major, in the year of the Lord 1154, in the second indiction.” See among the Omitted.

GREVEN.: “Of Noah the prophet. At Rome, of Saint Januarius,” etc. Concerning both, see among the Omitted. “In the territory of Bourges, of Saint Palladius, bishop and confessor.” Concerning him, see above. “In the territory of Vexin, of Blessed Martirinus [for Maturinus], confessor.” See also above. “At Pontizara, of Saint William, priest and confessor, a man of great charity. In Ireland, of Congallus the abbot. Of Probate and Midaris, confessors.” I do not know what these names are. “The translation of Saint Bavo the confessor.”

MOLAN. concerning Christina and the translation of Cosmas and Damian, as above. The year 1153 is noted here. “On the same day, the burial of the Venerable Bede the priest.” See among the Omitted. Then, in smaller type: “Also, at the monastery of Gembloux, of Beatrice of Este, of blessed memory, who died at the age of twenty in the year of the Lord 1229. Albert, prior of Mont des Vignes, wrote her life at that time.” In other editions these words are inserted into the text in Italics, concerning Job: “In the land of Uz, the burial.” Some material from Ado’s eulogies has been mixed into the accounts of Gordianus and Simplicius. At the end: “Also, of Saint Christina, virgin and martyr, whose body is visited in the chief church at Palermo in Sicily, where it is buried with great veneration and attendance. In Sicily, near Leontini, of Saints Alphius, Philadelphus, and Cyrinus, brothers and martyrs, under the emperor Licinius and the governor Tertullus.” Concerning Palladius, as above. “At Milan, the translation of the body of Blessed Nazarius to the Basilica of the Apostles.” Here the account of Cosmas and Damian is correct. Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, the burial of the Venerable Bede the priest. At Gembloux, Beatrice of Este died.”]

[Col. 0039]

Of Job the prophet. At Rome, on the Via Latina, the feast of the holy martyrs Gordianus and Epimachus, the former of whom, for confessing the name of Christ in the time of Julian, was beaten for a long time with leaden clubs and finally beheaded. Also at Rome, of Blessed Calepodius the priest, under the emperor Alexander, who had him killed by the sword and his body dragged through the city and thrown into the Tiber. Palmatius the consul was also beheaded, together with his wife and children and forty-two others of both sexes; Simplicius the senator likewise with them. Their heads were ordered to be hung at various gates of the city of Rome, as an example to Christians. Also at Rome, on the Via Latina at the Hundred Halls, the feast of Saints Quartus and Quintus.

V Idus. Day 11. [Note: [Col. 0043]

The text is taken from Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Antuerp.-Maj., Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0043A]

Pulsanen. on his own authority inserts “on the old Via Salaria.” In Rosweyd, through the copyists’ negligence, I think, the noun “disaster” was omitted after “impending.” The rest are almost entirely scribal blunders: “Rhome,” “Antimi,” [Col. 0044A] “Tiberim,” “celos,” “ac” instead of “ad,” “Vihennae,” “assentionem,” “Sollempnes,” and so on. I wrote “Letania,” since the best manuscripts read it thus, as above on 25 April.]

[Note: [Col. 0043B]

You will find Anthimus in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in the Little Roman Martyrology, in Ado, and in Notker. In the earlier copies he is not announced everywhere in the same way: in the Epternacensis, leading the procession, he has the companions who are noted in the Acts joined to him. In others he is placed alone at the end, “on the Via Salaria, at the twenty-second milestone”; these words were preserved by Ado and Notker. The Little Roman Martyrology omitted the distance, and Usuard did not express it, although he examined the Acts on his own initiative and composed an eulogy of the kind we presented in the margin. Henschenius judged the aforementioned Acts correctly in his Commentary, and Tillemont does not depart far from his opinion when discussing Lucina’s affairs in volume IV, beginning at p. 554. The difficulties that arise here and there do not seem impossible to resolve. Whether Mamertus belongs among the Hieronymian manuscripts, Florentinius’s doubt is shown by the Italic type in which he is presented together with a certain Martin, concerning whom there will be discussion in the Appendices. Henschenius plainly asserts that his memory is inscribed in those most ancient Calendars and, after reporting Florus’s eulogy, thinks that Usuard, Ado, and others followed the Florus mentioned above, as he often supposes elsewhere. I do not agree: until now I have not noticed Ado having Florus’s words before his eyes anywhere, although sometimes, in composing eulogies, he uses expressions not unlike those found in the Acts of the saints [Col. 0044B]. It is most probable that the genuine wording is Ado’s own, which we have represented in the text and which Our Author copied from him exactly. Henschenius examines many other matters reported by Ado in his Chronicle concerning Mamertus, while accurately discussing in his Commentary the remaining matters concerning his age, deeds, and writings. Tillemont briefly touches on some points concerning Mamertus in volume XV. Those who continue the edition of Tillemont’s works will be able to provide the complete life. Wandalbert seems to have rendered Florus’s meaning in his verses:

“Mamertus, a bishop of eminent splendor, marks the fifth day,

“who established that a solemn offering of fasting be made to God

“for three days beneath the light of day.”

In the Pratensis manuscript, the following is wrongly appended at the end: “On the same day, the burial of Lord Maiolus the abbot.” This announcement is not Usuard’s, but was appended by some later hand, as is abundantly clear from all the manuscripts cited as witnesses for the text; it is otherwise equally certain and obvious that Maiolus lived an entire century after Usuard. Accordingly, the simple and pure wording of Usuard is what we have displayed in the margin.]

[Note: [Col. 0043C]

CONCERNING PRATEN. enough has already been said.

ANTUERP., MAX-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. append to the pure text: “On the same day, of Saint Maiolus the abbot.”

MUNERAT., at the end: “Also at Silvancium [Silviniacum], the burial of Blessed Maiolus the abbot, a man of magnificent holiness, whose life shone gloriously before the world through devotion to religion and miracles. From the cradle he was devoted to literary learning; he was also raised to the dignity of archdeacon of the Church; then, suddenly changed by divine guidance and desiring the monastic life, he became the father of monks and founder of many monasteries. Finally, exhausted by old age, he returned to God his spirit, claimed for divine works, and rested in peace.” Others treat him more briefly.

MAX.-ANTUERP., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG.: “At Langres, of Saint Gengulphus, a martyr glorious for his miracles far and wide. On the same day, of Saint Maiolus the abbot.” The rest are sufficiently pure.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, on the Via Salaria, of Saint Anthimus, priest and martyr. At Vienne, of Saint Mamertus, bishop [Col. 0044C] and confessor. At the monastery of Silviacum, of Saint Maiolus, abbot of Cluny.”

BRUXELLEN. begins as follows: “By anticipation, at Rome, on the Via Aurelia, at the second milestone, of Pancratius the martyr, who, being fourteen years old, completed his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head under Diocletian. Also at Rome, on the Via Salaria, at the twenty-second milestone, the feast of Blessed Anthimus,” etc., quite purely. It continues: “And at Nartencias, or among the Lingones, of Saint Gengulphus, an outstanding martyr, glorious far and wide.” It is almost pure in the account of Mamertus. Then: “And of Saint Mamertinus.” I think Martin is meant, whom some join with Mamertus. See among the Omitted. Finally: “At Silviniacum, the burial of Saint Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, whom Blessed Adomarus had appointed abbot in his place.”

HAGENOYEN, in addition to the fairly pure text, adds the following: “At Ravenna, Saint Gangulfus the martyr.” Unless I am mistaken, it makes two men out of one by changing two letters, having erred in the word *Varennas*, which it had found somewhere. It continues as follows: “Likewise at Lingones, the passion of Saint Gengulfus the martyr, glorified far and wide by miracles. [Col. 0045A] Because of adultery, he dismissed his wife, whom he discovered to be adulterous by God’s judgment, and served God more earnestly. Therefore the adulterous cleric, fearing that he might at some time be killed by Gengulfus, so that he might enjoy that man’s wife more freely, killed Gengulfus and made him a martyr. But the wife disparaged his miracles and called down a curse upon herself, in such a way that Gengulfus would perform miracles in accordance with what her anus [*anus*] might say. Thus, when on a Friday she was saying something with her mouth, her anus emitted foul sounds, to the hearing of everyone. On the same day, at the monastery of Silviacum, Saint Mayolus the abbot. Likewise at Reims, Saints Motanus, previously blind, restored through the milk of Eylinia, the mother of Saint Benignus.” See the *Praetermissi*.

AQUICINCT., at the end: “Likewise Saint Montanus. On the same day, the passing of Blessed Mayolus the abbot.”

VICTORIN. and the REG. SUEC. codices numbered 130 and 428: “In the territory of the Arverni, at the monastery of Silviniacum, the burial of Saint Mayolus, abbot of Cluny.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Saint Anthymus the priest and Saint Sisinnius the deacon, with their fellow martyrs. Saint Gengulfus the martyr in Burgundy. Saint Mayolus, abbot of Cluny. Saint Mamertinus [Mamertus], bishop and confessor, who instituted the Litanies before the Lord’s Ascension.” See the other material in MUNERAT’s notice.

CISTERCIEN., which belonged to Saint Benignus of Dijon: “At Varennas, Saint Gengulfus the martyr.”

VATICAN. no. 5949 adds: “On the same day, Saint Pamphilus the bishop.” See the *Praetermissi*.

ALTEMPS.: “On the same day, Saint Palladius the confessor.” Concerning him, see the preceding day. “Likewise Saint Langulfus the confessor.” Could this be Saint Gengulfus the martyr? “Likewise Saint Montanus. In Great Britain, Saint Fresmundus, king and martyr.” In the *Acts* he is called Fremundus.

FLORENTIN.: “Likewise, the passing of Saint Mayolus the abbot, whose distinguished life was made illustrious by holy merits. Likewise at Varennas, Saint Janigulfus the martyr.”

LUGDUNEN.: “The feast of Saint Villebadus,” or “Willebudus [Col. 0045C] the martyr.” The rest concerning him is unknown.

BURDIGALEN.: “On the same day, Saint Genulfus the martyr.” *Gengulfus* is better, or, as others have it, *Gengulphus*.

[Col. 0046A] BIZUNTICEN.: “At Lingones, Saint Gengulfus, the distinguished martyr.” Correctly so, as above.

The LUBECK-COLOGNE EDITION reads incorrectly: “Blessed Ancimus, bishop and priest.” After the slaughter, it adds “of wolves.” At the end: “On the same day, Saint Mayolus the abbot. On that day, Blessed Montanus the confessor.”

BELIN. has exactly the same material that we reported from the FLORENTINI, and writes it in the same manner.

GREVEN.: “In Asia, Saints Demetriaticus and Septimus.” See in the *Acts*: “Demetrius, Atticus, etc. Fremundus, king of England and martyr. In the city of Tergeste, Saints Primus the priest, Marcus the deacon, Jason and Celianus the martyrs, in the time of the emperor Hadrian. Of these, the prefect Artasius ordered Primus and Marcus to be beaten with clubs, fire to be kindled beneath their bellies, and dissolved sulphur to be poured into their mouths. When they had remained entirely unharmed by these things, and on that account many had believed, he ordered them to be led outside the city and beheaded. But he ordered Jason and Celianus to be beaten with clubs until they died.” The *Acts* assign these saints to 10 May. “At Metz, [Col. 0046B] the feast of Saints Rufus and Agathymbrus, bishops and confessors.” The latter is treated today, the former on 7 November. “On the same day, Saint Mayolus, abbot of Cluny, distinguished in life and miracles. Saint Montanus the confessor.”

MOLAN. copied almost everything concerning Mayolus from MUNERAT; concerning Gengulfus, from CISTERCIEN. It continues from Rabanus: “And the passion of Saint Evellius, who, seeing the passion of Saint Torpetes the martyr and the miracles he performed, believed in Christ. Previously he had been a counsellor of the emperor Nero, concerning how Christians were to be martyred.” These words have been twisted by Rabanus and are rendered better by Notkerus. “At Blandinium, the dedication of Paradise in honor of Blessed Andrew the apostle.” See 30 November. In later editions, MUNERAT’s notice has been abridged. Concerning Gengulfus and Evellius, as above. “Likewise at Blandinium, etc. At Martianis, the vigil of Saint Rictrudis.” Then in smaller type: “On the same day, Saint Fremundus, who was elevated on the fifth day before the Kalends of April by Birinus, [Col. 0046C] returning from the pope with apostolic letters. On the eleventh day, the feast of Genethlia of Constantinople.” See the *Praetermissi*.

[Col. 0043]

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the feast of Blessed Anthymus the priest, who, after distinguished deeds of virtue and preaching, was thrown into the Tiber and thereafter rescued by an angel, restored to his own oratory, and then punished by beheading; victorious, he departed to heaven. At Vienne, Saint Mamertus, bishop and confessor, who, because of the impending calamity, instituted solemn Litanies before the Lord’s Ascension.

## Four days before the Ides: 12 May

[Note: [Col. 0045]]

The only pure witnesses are Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven. and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] [Col. 0045D]]

Heriniensis betrays its own age when it writes *Ardiatina*, *Ponciam*, *Idolis*, *Martiris*, *Dioclitiani*, and *Karus*. Munerat. writes *the island of Pontus*. It also has *by very severe blows*. Then likewise *Idolis*, *Paucratii*, *fourteen*, and *Epyphani*. In the later edition of Greven., which we follow, *idolis* is absent. Greven. and Molanus likewise omit the word *blessed* after *of the same man*, although it is expressly found in the other codices; and instead of *capitis detruncatione* they read *obtruncatione*. Antuerp.-Maj. reads worse: “who, when he was thirteen years old, [Col. 0046D] under Diocletian completed the beheading.” Praten. has *Dionisii*, Grevenus *Dyonisii*; in the text we follow the latter, together with the others. His encomium is somewhat obscure unless it is punctuated correctly. Muneratus made it more obscure, perhaps wishing to correct it, by reading: “Who, since he was dear and worthy to God through heavenly rewards,” etc. The Adonian phrase must be preserved exactly, as we have reported it in the text from the better codices.

[Note: [Col. 0045D]]

Today the very celebrated feast of Saints Nereus and Achilleus among the Latins is found both in ancient Calendars and Sacramentaries and among all the ancient Martyrologists, generally separate from Domitilla. Jerome’s copies, Bede, and Rabanus expressly remember it, both of them being silent about the place of burial. The *Romanum parvum* determines the place more precisely: “In the cemetery of Praetextatus,” whereas our text and others call it the Ardeatine Way. Florentius says that this discrepancy concerning the places was reconciled through Notkerus as intermediary—though here and elsewhere he would better have named Ado himself, from whom Notkerus copied his material, including on this day, and from whom he habitually copied it throughout. As for this minor dispute concerning the tomb, one may also consult the preliminary Commentary on the *Acts*. In brief, the feast of those saints was celebrated in both places, for different reasons. Meanwhile, nothing is clearer than that the notice placed in the text was taken from Ado. Concerning the *Acts* themselves, from which both the Adonian and Usuardine notices were taken, I have nothing to add to what was said above under 7 May. Wandalbertus mixes Pancratius in with the others as though he belonged to the same period, although he was in fact two full centuries later. Thus he sings:

> We honor your virgin, Domitilla, fourfold,  
> Nereus, Pancratius, and holy Achilleus also.  
> The first taught and washed them in the apostolic baptism,  
> Those whom Peter joined to the illustrious virgin of Rome.

The name of Pancratius, inscribed in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and the *Romanum parvum*, is adorned by Bede and Rabanus with the same encomium that appears here in our little entry; the very same words are likewise read in Ado and Notkerus, though mixed in with other material. [Col. 0047B] Dionysius, unknown to Jerome and Bede, is placed by the *Romanum parvum*, and from there by Ado, whom our author customarily follows, preserving the phrase in which one might wish for somewhat greater clarity. Baronius judged the *Acts* of Pancratius and Dionysius genuine, as did Henschenius, although he did not conceal the difficulties involved, and labored diligently to resolve them. Tillemont raises the same difficulties again in volume V, pp. 259 and 689; but I do not see that a few blemishes are so serious that the otherwise simple and weighty *Acts* can rightly be rejected. Ado continues from the aforementioned *Acts*: “But at that time also the most sacred virgin Soteris suffered, noble in name and lineage.” Notkerus included her; Usuardus passed her over. Whether this was because he confused her with another woman of the same name, or for another reason, is uncertain. For it is not sufficiently established whether she is the Sotheris who is placed in the Hieronymian Martyrologies accompanied by companions whose names are listed in the *Acts*, or the woman of whom we spoke under 10 February, as Ruinart, p. 406, and Tillemont, vol. V, pp. 359 onward, believe. Bede, and Rabanus, who frequently copies him, read: “Saint Epiphanius, our father, bishop of Cyprus.” Ado is more precise, using exactly the words which our author transferred, to the letter, into his own little entry. Thus neither in this nor in other announcements can there be any doubt about the complete simplicity of the Usuardine text. [Col. 0048B] Papebrochius rejected the Life of Epiphanius, falsely presented under the name of his disciples, and substituted another compiled from ecclesiastical historians; it may be compared with the French account by Tillemont in volume X, pp. 484 onward.

[Note: [Col. 0047B]]

TORNACEN. abbreviates the longer notice of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, omitting what follows after “were assaulted”; otherwise it is entirely pure.

PULSANEN., pure and complete at the beginning, omits everything after “Saint Pancratius the martyr.”

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC. and BELIN. delete the notice of Dionysius. The same is done by ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC. and the ULTRAJECT.-BELGIAN EDITION. In these, the words “our holy father” are also absent from the notice of Epiphanius. From this one may infer that these belonged to religious communities where that appellation, as something foreign, was not admitted. The later LOVANIENSIS agrees with them, but suffers from another defect, mutilating the notice of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.

ROSWEYD. seems to have wished to be too clever when he corrected the Adonian and Usuardine phrase concerning Dionysius as follows: “Who, being worthy of heavenly rewards and dear to the Lord.” At the end he has nothing concerning Saint Epiphanius.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, Saints Nereus and Achilleus, brothers and martyrs, who were eunuchs of Blessed Flavia Domitilla. At Martianis, the burial of the most blessed Rictrudis, countess. Likewise at Rome, on the Aurelian Way, Blessed Pancratius the martyr. Likewise Blessed Dionysius, the uncle of that Blessed Pancratius. In Cyprus, Saint Epiphanius, our father, bishop of Salamis, distinguished in faith and teaching.”

BRUXELLEN. gives a long history of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, Domitilla, and their companions Eutychus, Victorinus, and Macrone. The reader will find it in a purer form in the source itself. [Col. 0047D] It dealt with Pancratius, by anticipation, on the preceding day. In Dionysius and Epiphanius it is nearly pure. A more recent hand adds in the margin: “The burial of Saint Modoaldus, archbishop of Trier, who was the uncle of Blessed Gertrude.” See his genealogy in the *Acts*, p. 52.

HAGENOYEN., moderately interpolated in the first announcement, invents more material concerning Pancratius; it is better read in the *Acts* themselves. In Dionysius it is nearly pure. “At the city of Salamis in Cyprus, the burial of Saint Epiphanius, our father, bishop of Alexandria, etc.” Here too there is other equally exact material, including the mutual prophecy of Epiphanius and Chrysostom.

AQUICINCT., after “he closed,” adds: “At Martianis, the burial of Saint Rictrudis.”

DAVERONEN.: “At Tours, the reception of the relics of Saint Maurice the martyr. Likewise, the burial of Saint Martin in his own tomb, together with the other bishops Brictius, Eustachius, and Gregory, at Martinopolis.” Each of these will be treated on his proper day. Concerning Maurice, see the *Praetermissi*, and likewise concerning Martin.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Saints Nereus, Achilleus, and Pancratius, martyrs. Likewise Dionysius, his uncle. Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, whom Blessed Jerome mentions.” In the margin, added by the same hand: “The bones of Saint Pancratius the martyr rest in the church of Saint Salvator at Utrecht.”

REG.-SUEC. no. 428: “On that day, the commemoration of Blessed Hippolytus the martyr, when, after his most holy body had been transferred, the storm of widespread mortality ceased.” See the *Praetermissi* and 13 August.

[Col. 0048C] In the VATICAN codex no. 5949, Dionysius is absent. It suffers more often from deficiency than excess.

STROZZ.: “Likewise Saint Soteris the virgin, who suffered under the emperor Diocletian.” From Ado.

ABDINGHOFFEN.: “Likewise at Rome, on the Aurelian Way, Saint Pancratius the martyr, brought to completion by beheading in the fourteenth year of his age under Diocletian. On the same day, Saint Dionysius, the uncle of that Saint Pancratius, who, worthy of God and dear to him, peacefully rested in peace.” It is clear that someone smoothed out the phrase of Usuardus or Ado; but this codex has fewer recurring correspondences.

The LUBECK-COLOGNE EDITION recounts much concerning the ordination of Saint Severinus, archbishop of Cologne, which will be treated in the *Acts* under 23 October. See GREVEN below. It then gives another long history of Saints Nereus, Achilleus, etc. The notice of Pancratius is also interpolated. That of Dionysius is omitted. At the end: “At Trier, Saint Modowaldus, bishop and confessor. In Cyprus, Saint Epiphanius, bishop and confessor of Salamis.” [Col. 0048D]

GREVEN.: “On the same day, Saints John, Achilleus, Aphroditus, and 405 other martyrs. Likewise Saints Quiriacus and Maximus.” The usual confusion or distinction. See the whole group in the *Acts*. “At Trier, the burial of Saint Modowaldus, bishop and confessor. At Cologne Agrippina, the ordination of Blessed Severinus, bishop and confessor of that city. When he was bishop of Sens and was present at the synod of the holy Fathers assembled at Cologne because of the blasphemous bishop Euphratas, after that man had been deposed he was unanimously appointed to govern the aforementioned church, in the presence of the holy Fathers Maximinus of Trier and Servatius of Tongeren, bishops. At Anderlecht in Brabant, Saint Guy the confessor.” He is celebrated on 12 September. “At the monastery of Marchiennes, Saint Rictrudis the virgin.” More properly, “widow.” The reference is to the monastery of Marchiennes.

MOLAN. adds to the text, in Italian type, from Ado what Usuardus had omitted concerning Pancratius: “Whose venerable body Octavilla, etc.” At the end: “On that day at Trier, Saint Modowaldus, bishop and confessor. On that day, Saint Rictrudis at Martianis.” Then in smaller type: “On the same day at Agyra, Saint Philip, who was sent by Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, to preach Christ’s Gospel to the Sicilians; after a large part of Sicily had been initiated into the sacred rites of Christ, he finally died among the people of Agyra. There he has a temple most renowned for the frequency of its miracles, and so famous for the crowds of people who flock to it that the name of Saint Philip has popularly become attached even to the city itself.” [Col. 0050A] In other editions it reads: “In Spain, Saint Dominic of Calzada, confessor, of wondrous holiness. On the same day, at Agyra in Sicily, Saint Philip the priest, whose power in driving out demons appears through frequent signs. On that day at Trier, Saint Modowaldus, bishop and confessor. At Martianis, the burial of Saint Rictrudis.” Finally, in smaller type: “At Soissons, the translation of Blessed Hippolytus the martyr, when, after his most holy body had been carried away, the terrible storm of mortality ceased.” We have already said above that this concerns the Hippolytus who is celebrated on 13 August.

[Col. 0045]

At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the feast of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, brothers and martyrs, who first endured a long exile on the island of Pontia, and afterward were assaulted with very severe blows by a certain judge. Then, when they were driven by the rack and flames to sacrifice, and said that they had been baptized by Blessed Peter the apostle and could in no way sacrifice to idols, they were beheaded. Likewise, on the Aurelian Way, Saint Pancratius the martyr, who, being fourteen years old, completed his martyrdom by beheading under Diocletian. On the same day, Saint Dionysius, the uncle of that Blessed Pancratius, who, dear and worthy to God through heavenly rewards, ended the day of this life in peace. In Cyprus, Saint Epiphanius, our father, bishop of Salamis.

## Three days before the Ides: 13 May

[Note: [Col. 0049B]]

The pure codices are Praten., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp., Max-Lubec., Munerat., Greven. and [Col. 0050B] Molan. Add also Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic. and the Ultraj.-Belgian Edition.

[Note: [Col. 0049B]]

Antuerpien. and all the middle-quality codices read *in honor of the holy ever-Virgin*. Molan. corrected this to *in honor*. The others have *Amfibulus* in the text, as Praten. writes it; Herinien. and Greven. give *Amphibulus*, which amounts to the same thing and has the flavor of the Middle Ages. Others have the better form *Amphibolus*. Munerat. has the worst form, *Manifibulus*, omitting *in* and writing *Munitii* for *Mucii*. Likewise, instead of *Tungrensis*, it has *Trugiensis*; if one attributes this to the printer’s error, I have no objection. Some write *Thungrensis*, *Servacii*, *Servasii*, *hyemis*, etc. The question is whether Usuardus read “so that all might demonstrate” or “so that men might demonstrate.” Heriniensis alone, together with Tornacensis—which is not pure—has the latter; and I think this should be retained, on the authority of Ado, Notkerus, and, unless I am mistaken, the nature of the matter itself. In Max.-Lubec., *as magnificently built* is redundant after *for demonstration*; the same occurs in Munerat.

[Note: [Col. 0049B]]

Florentius had almost thought that he had found traces in Jerome of the Pantheon of Agrippa transformed into a Christian basilica, but he himself entirely rejects his conjecture. Thus Bede is the first in whom the Dedication of Saint Mary “at the Martyrs” is found recorded in these words; the *Romanum parvum* is somewhat clearer: “The day of the dedication of Saint Mary at the Martyrs is celebrated, established by Pope Boniface.” Ado enumerates other circumstances, and Notkerus follows him, adding a little from his own material.
