Our author, following his usual practice, acted here as elsewhere, contracting the substance of the matter quite elegantly. The cited Bede and the author of the *Romanum parvum*, as well as Rabanus, commemorate Bishop Servatius. Among the Hieronymian copies, the Corbie manuscript clearly marks him as a saint, “from Tongeren, a port in Gaul.” Wandalbertus has only this verse:

> They honor Servatius, the gracious one, on the Ides threefold.

Ado developed the history at greater length, and Notkerus copied him again. Our text is taken word for word from Ado, except for the reason that moved Servatius to migrate from Tongeren to Maastricht. I would not readily approve what is asserted in the notice of Florus, nor what Rabanus records but Notkerus omits. No one who has read the Life is unaware that the ancestry and deeds of this saint are wrapped in many legends; but we do not attend to them here. Henschenius rendered outstanding service concerning Servatius; the interested reader should consult his commentary and his treatise on the bishops of Tongeren and Maastricht. Tillemont has less material in volume VIII, pp. 382 onward.

[Col. 0050B] In these two earlier announcements all the ancient witnesses agree. Before Usuardus, however, none in our series mentions Mucius, and it is not sufficiently obvious where he obtained him for this day, since the Greeks assign him to five days before the Ides, that is, 11 May, not five days before the Ides as Baronius wrongly placed him. In this uncertainty, [Col. 0050C] nothing seems more plausible than what Henschenius judged in his Commentary on 11 May, no. 5, letter F: namely, that Usuardus probably found the *Acts* in an old codex of the Queen of Sweden, numbered 569, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint-Denis, and from them entered Mucius—otherwise Mocias—for this day. This is more satisfactory than saying that Usuardus took his material from Florus, whose sole copy, of uncertain reliability, mentions *Mulius*, but in a phrase very different from ours; as is proved by comparing the two texts alone, there is absolutely no affinity between Florus and Usuardus, as I have said elsewhere. Wherever he obtained him, it is certain that Mulius is Usuardine, as are all the other items expressed in the little entry. Here Henschenius, contrary to his usual practice, adapted himself to the Greeks, elucidating the *Acts* of Mucius, as I have said, under 11 May, although the Roman Martyrology keeps him on this 13th day. Tillemont found several points in the *Acts* of Mucius to criticize, although they are written in a serious and simple style; see volume V, p. 640. Yet such minor blemishes, however much they may obscure the sun of truth shining in those *Acts*, certainly cannot obscure it altogether.

[Note: [Col. 0049D]]

TORNACEN. remains stuck in the same mire; today it has deleted the entire notice of Mucius.

PULSANEN. is mutilated in the first announcement, but is fairly pure in the notice of Mucius; it omitted Servatius entirely.

ROSWEYD. begins as follows: “The feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs, when Blessed Pope Boniface dedicated, in honor of the holy Virgin Mary and all the martyrs of Christ, the shrine previously called the Pantheon.” [Col. 0050D]

BELIN. differs slightly: “The dedication of the church of Blessed Mary and all the holy martyrs of Christ, which Blessed Pope Boniface dedicated in honor of that glorious Virgin and Mother, or of the aforementioned martyrs.” More will be said under 1 November.

[Col. 0051A] CENTULEN.: “The feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs. In the city of Maastricht, Saint Servatius, bishop and confessor of Tongeren. At Auxerre, Saint Marcellianus, a bishop most distinguished in faith.” See Henschenius’s commentary.

BRUXELLEN., beginning with Servatius, relates the following: “Saint Servatius, glorious bishop and confessor of the Church of Tongeren. He was an alumnus of Armenia, related to Christ according to the flesh by blood; miraculously he became a bishop when a pastoral staff was extended to him from the altar by an angel. Seven years earlier, Valentinus, the bishop of that same place, had forbidden it to be given to anyone until the angel who would give it came from heaven. While Bishop Servatius preached Christ in one and the same natural language with complete uniformity, the understanding of a native language flowed forth for all who heard, although in secular affairs he shamefully used an interpreter. Long beforehand he foresaw in spirit that the destruction of Gaul by the Huns was impending. Therefore, having set out for Rome and received from Blessed Peter a silver key, and having prophetically learned that the destruction of Gaul, especially of Tongeren, was inevitable, he was freed from the enemy on his return by the miracle of an eagle overshadowing him. He abandoned Tongeren and transferred his episcopal see to Maastricht, where he died; covered with silk brought by an angel, he was buried in the middle of the public road. On account of his merit,” etc. In the dedication of Saint Mary, it is nearly pure apart from interpolations from Ado. In Mucius it is fairly pure.

HAGENOYEN. begins: “At Rome (I suppose the new Rome), Blessed Mucius,” etc. Servatius follows, concerning whom we have already said enough. In the dedication it is nearly pure. Then it adds: “Likewise at Verona, Saint Metronus the enclosed monk.” This is Meiro, concerning whom see the *Acts* under 8 May.

VICTOR. gives Mucius as a bishop instead of a priest.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Saint Servatius, bishop and confessor. His body is said to be with our brothers at Confluentia; nevertheless, the people of Liège and Maastricht say the opposite concerning the same place.”

CLUNIACEN. and CODEX D. DU CHEVAL., marked C: [Col. 0051C] “On the same day, the translation of Saint Gratus, bishop and confessor, from the city of Chalon.” His Life will be given on the day of his celebration, 8 October.

REG. SUEC. no. 428: “On the same day, Saint Onesimus the confessor.” Perhaps this was taken from Rabanus.

In the VATICAN codex no. 5949, Mucius is absent.

STROZZIAN.: “The dedication of Saint Mary at the Martyrs … which is now called Saint Mary Rotunda. It was consecrated in the year 595 (better that he had omitted the year). At Volterra, Saint Victor the soldier and martyr.” See what is said in the *Praetermissi*. The following also occurs in other FLORENTINI: “In Tuscany, in the city of Romania, Saint Hilary the monk and confessor, a father and hermit.” This is undoubtedly Hilary of Galeata, concerning whom see the *Praetermissi*.

CAUDIACEN.: “The translation of Blessed Gratus the confessor, at Aqua, from the city of Chalon.”

The LUBECK-COLOGNE EDITION is fairly pure in the first announcement. It continues: “In upper Maastricht, in the diocese of Liège, Saint Servatius, bishop and confessor of Tongeren. He is said to have been related to the Savior according to the flesh through his father, Emin. He had such great abstinence even as an infant that in a day he scarcely suckled at his mother’s breasts twice. When grown, he was ordained a priest at Jerusalem and sent, at the warning of an angel, to govern the church of Tongeren, where he was honorably received by the entire clergy and people. He was accustomed to celebrate Mass daily and, content with the sacred nourishment, scarcely required the taste of any other food,” etc. In Mucius it is pure. “At Trier, the translation of Blessed Paulinus, bishop and martyr of that city.” He is celebrated on 31 August. “At Auxerre, Saint Marcellianus, bishop and confessor. At Lingones, Saint Gengulfus the martyr, glorified far and wide by miracles.” Concerning him enough has often and fully been said above under the 11th of this month.

GREVEN.: “In Burgundy, Saint Gangulfus the martyr. Born of illustrious parents and wholly devoted to acts of piety, by great faith he caused a spring that he had purchased in a foreign land to gush forth on his own estate. Finally, struck mortally by a cleric who habitually committed adultery with his wife, he died, shining with miracles, in the year of the Lord 667. Likewise Saints Gagus, Luke, Agrippa, and Sabina.” From the Hieronymian Martyrologies. “In Ireland, Carthach the bishop.” This is postponed to 14 May. Concerning Marcellianus and Paulinus, as above. “At the monastery of Syhergen, the translation of Saint Innocent and of the head of Saint Vitalis the martyr, from the Theban Legion.” [Col. 0052B] See the *Praetermissi*. “Hilary the abbot and confessor. When he was thirteen years old and was reading the letters of Blessed Paul, he was inflamed by the divine heat of faith; with an angel as his guide, he left the city of Rome and reached a solitary place. Living there in great holiness, gathering many disciples, and illustrious for miracles, he rested in peace in the time of Theodoric, king of the Lombards. Saint Rolenda the virgin, who is customarily invoked against iliac disease and stone.” Concerning Hilary, or Hilarius, we have spoken in the FLORENTINI.

MOLAN. restores in the text, in Italian type, from Ado what Usuardus had omitted. After “was built,” he adds: “By his successor, Saint Munulfus the bishop. The burial of Saint Onesimus, bishop and confessor, who endured a long martyrdom in his limbs without iron, so that what the shedding of blood had not conferred, the prolonged torment of his limbs might confer even through the wearing down of the scourge. He indeed endured the torment of sufficient martyrdom: dragging a pale face through excessive fasting, he was able to subdue the flow of lust in his body, [Col. 0052C] nor did his mind, devoted to its creator, call itself away from constant prayer. Thus, after the course of his life had run its length, seized by the pain of death, he gave his spirit back to Christ, summoned by works of divinity. When the sick come to his tomb, they obtain the remedies of health they desire. He therefore enjoys the presence of the divine majesty in the heavenly court, where both Cherubim and Seraphim incessantly proclaim, ‘Holy, Holy, Holy,’ and what follows. This is written in his deeds.”

Then in smaller type: “Saint Rolenda the virgin, who is customarily invoked against iliac disease and stone. Her body rests at Gerpinnes, in the diocese of Namur.” Here see Henschenius, who skillfully explains the matters that the people of Gerpinnes embellish with excessive wonder. Thus far the first edition. In later editions it has the same material concerning Servatius. It continues: “At Gerpinnes, Saint Rolenda the virgin, who is customarily invoked against, etc. At Douai, from Soissons, the burial of Saint Onesimus, bishop and confessor, who endured a long martyrdom in his limbs without iron. When the sick come to his tomb, they obtain the remedies of health they desire. He therefore enjoys that, etc. On the thirteenth day, Saint Glyceria the martyr.” Then in smaller type: “At Laodicea, near Trajanopolis. Likewise Saint Alexander the martyr under the emperor Maximian. And John the bishop, afterward a silentary in the Laura. For some, today is the feast of Gengulfus the martyr, who was placed on the eleventh day of this month.”

[Col. 0049]

The feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs, when Blessed Pope Boniface dedicated a church in honor of Mary, ever Virgin, and of all the martyrs. Likewise, Blessed Mucius, priest and martyr, who, first at the city of Amphibolus, was subjected to many punishments and tortures for confessing Christ, then was brought as far as Byzantium and died under a capital sentence. On the same day, Saint Servatius, bishop and confessor of the Church of Tongeren; to demonstrate his merit to men, although in wintertime snow filled everything round about, it never covered his tomb, until, through the industry of the citizens, a basilica was built over it.

## The day before the Ides: 14 May

[Note: [Col. 0053A]]

From Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerpien.-Max., Lubec., Greven., and Molan. Add Antuerp.-Max., [Col. 0054A] Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., and the Ultraj.-Belgian Edition.

[Note: [Col. 0053A]]

I read *Cimela*, or, if you prefer, *Cymela*, as Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., and Greven. have it. Perhaps *Cimella* is better, as others have it. Again, with the same codices, after *cujusdam* I have omitted the word *militis* [soldier], although it seems to be restorable from Bede and Ado. I have already said that we prefer to err with the older codices rather than correct anything. Antuerp.-Maj. wrongly has *protestatur* for *protestaretur*; Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. likewise err in putting *quoque* for *vero*. Again, [Col. 0054A] Max.-Lubec. alters the sense by writing: “Who, being distinguished by apostolic grace,” which is certainly clearer than the reading of Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., etc.: “Who, having been made distinguished by apostolic grace,” etc. The same witnesses read “Saint Pachomius the abbot.” But Antuerp.-Maj. has at the end: “He wrote a rule for monks, which he had learned at an angel’s dictation.” Greven. and Molan. have “from an angel.” The rest are trifles.

[Note: [Col. 0053A]]

Pontius, who stands first in the text—a Roman by birth and a martyr of Cimela, or Cimella (Castellanus would read *Cemenelensis*, from the French Cimiez)—is unknown, I say, to all martyrologists older than, or contemporary with, our author. It is therefore most likely to be concluded once more that Usuard found him in certain Acts, such as were occasionally published. The curious reader may consult Henschenius’s commentary on this saint and the Life itself, there illustrated in its proper place. It is certainly entangled in great difficulties, as Baronius acknowledged under the year 246, no. 9, Petavius in *De doctrina temporum*, book XI, chapter 25, and Tillemont, who assembles several more in volume V, p. 588 onward; so much so that one must almost admit that those Acts were so enormously stuffed and interpolated that they can scarcely stand unless corrected in large part, whatever the writer Valerius may testify that he saw with his eyes and received with his ears all that he relates. We know that this very thing has repeatedly been done by impostors. Henschenius judges more mildly: conceding that some things here are said by exaggeration, he considers that the rest can not incongruously be defended.

Victor and Corona are briefly celebrated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and the *Romanum parvum*, but Bede adorns them with a notable encomium. Here, with Ado, the text agrees so completely—in these two martyrs and in Pachomius—that there seems no doubt that the former took all his material from the latter. Nor should one say that Ado’s text was perhaps falsely ascribed to Bede: Rabanus, Bede’s continual copyist, who has nothing in common with Ado, has reproduced the very same words; Notkerus unquestionably copied from the Viennese author, and it is astonishing that Florentinius should err so often on this point. Moreover, the notice of those most illustrious champions which we have included in the little entry, even if not expressed in Bede’s or Ado’s very words, is at least elegantly condensed from their sense. The Acts of Victor and Corona contain matters to occupy critics; nor is it altogether certain how many pairs there were of saints bearing the same names, of whom we have already spoken more than once. Henschenius explains some points, including the place of their martyrdom. We have no more, or clearer, information. See Tillemont’s observations, volume II, p. 624. Wandalbert undoubtedly follows Bede:

> On the day before, Pachomius, and Victor together with Corona, shine forth:
> the one a mighty hermit, the other, by their joint strength,
> following God through crowns and martyrdom.

Everything said in the text concerning Pachomius is borrowed from the cited Bede or Ado, except only the final words after “which he had learned at an angel’s dictation,” together with the material about the Paschal season. Whether Usuard did not understand those final words, or regarded them as suspect, is uncertain. Otherwise, the agreement of so many codices makes the genuine reading of Usuard beyond doubt. Papebrochius published Pachomius’s Life in Greek and Latin and edited it with the greatest care; modern scholars rightly praise it. How much Tillemont made use of his study and labor is evident from volume VII, p. 167 onward.

[Note: [Col. 0053C]]

TORNACEN. is pure only in Pachomius. Pontius lacks his notice. In Victor and Corona it is also greatly mutilated, for everything after “emperor” is missing.

PULSANEN. begins with Boniface, as below. Then it gives Pachomius purely. The rest is absent.

ROSWEYD. After Saint Victor is interpolated as follows: “Seeing his constancy when he was flayed alive and then beheaded.” Then after “she protested”: “She too, having been seized and her feet bound to bent trees,” etc.

MUNERAT. At the end: “On that same day, the ordination of Saint Eligius, bishop.” See the *Praetermissi*. He is commemorated on 1 December; everything will be referred to that day.

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. prefix the pure text with: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Boniface the martyr, who suffered under Diocletian and Maximian at the city of Tarsus, but was buried at Rome on the road called the Latina. When he had long been involved in sexual immorality, he was finally struck with remorse by divine prompting; he not only abandoned the vice to which he had been enslaved, but also eagerly ran through diverse torments toward the palm of martyrdom.” Ado and Usuard treat Boniface on the Nones of June.

CENTULEN.: “In the city of Cimela, Saint Pontius the martyr, through whose preaching and diligence two Roman emperors received the faith of the Lord and Savior: namely, Philip the father and Philip the son. In Syria, the passion of Saints Victor and Corona under the emperor Antoninus. On the same day, the birthday of Saint Pachomius, our father and abbot, who, when …,” purely, except that it adds: “Likewise concerning the time of Easter. At Tarsus, the passion of Saint Boniface the martyr, whose more celebrated day is observed on the Nones of June, when his body … was buried.” The blank at Rome has been filled in by a later hand and ink.

BRUXELLEN. begins with Victor and Corona. It follows with Pontius, in which it comes very close to the pure text. Then: “At Rome, Saint Boniface the martyr, who suffered under Diocletian and Maximian at the city of Tarsus, but was buried at Rome on the Latina road. And the 404 holy martyrs.” See the *Praetermissi* concerning these. “On the same day, Saint Pachomius, our father and abbot,” etc. Near the end it restores Bede’s or Ado’s words cited above, and adds: “And after this, when he had completed 110 years of his life, he rested in peace.”

HAGENOYEN. is quite pure in Pontius; in Victor and Corona it has been somewhat interpolated. In Pachomius it is correct.

AQUICINCT. adds this at the end: “He also wrote down the Paschal limits, as is related, being taught by an angel.” Then, in a more recent hand: “At Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, the passion of Saint Boniface the martyr.”

VICTORIN. at the end: “At Benevento, Saint Constantius, bishop.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT. “Of the renowned martyr Pontius. Of the martyrs Victor and Corona. Of Pachomius the abbot.” The text is, as usual, entirely abridged.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “On that same day, the ordination of Saint Eligius, bishop and confessor.” And in the codex marked 130: “At the city of Tarsus, the passion of Saint Boniface the martyr,” etc. “At Benevento, Saint Constantius, bishop.”

VATICAN., marked no. 5949, has nothing concerning Pontius. It adds first: “At Benevento, the birthday of Saint Boniface the martyr at Saint Sophia. He suffered at Tarsus, indeed, but was buried at Rome on the Latina road.” At the end: “At Milan, the 304 holy martyrs.” Concerning these, see above under another number. “At Benevento, Saint Constantius, bishop.”

ALTEMPS.: “At the monastery of Fontanella, Saint Frembert (Erembert), bishop and confessor of the city of Toulouse.” His brief life has been elucidated.

FLORENTIN.: “The ordination of Bishops Audoenus and Eligius. The deposition of Saint Theodore, pope.” See the index of the *Praetermissi*. STROZZIAN. alone: “At Aquileia, the martyrdom of Saints Felix and Fortunatus, brothers.” In the *Praetermissi* they are referred to 11 June.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins with Boniface, concerning whom it gives much material, in Ado on the Nones of June, and today in the *Acts* in a more reliable form. It is quite pure concerning Pontius and Pachomius. In Victor and Corona it has been moderately interpolated. At the end: “On the same day, Blessed Halnard the martyr.” See Harwald.

BELIN. has concerning Pachomius only: “On the same day, Saint Pachomius the abbot.” Concerning Boniface it has the same text as ALBERGEN. and DANIC. “At Aquileia …” concerning Felix and Fortunatus, as in STROZ. above.

GREVEN.: “At Tarsus in Cilicia, the passion of Saint Boniface the martyr. When he was the steward of a most noble Roman matron named Aglaes—who, while governing the city prefecture, had 73 stewards under her, of whom Boniface was the chief—and had long wallowed with her in the filth of lust, at last, when both were struck with remorse by divine prompting, Boniface was sent, by common agreement, to seek the bodies of the martyrs, and he himself also attained the glory of martyrdom. When Aglaes learned this through an angel, she renounced the world and received such grace from God that she shone with signs of miracles in his name. Nevertheless, their feast is more celebrated on the Nones of June, when Saint Boniface was buried at Rome.”

These things are almost the same as those found in EDITIO LUBEC.-COL.; but they will be read more accurately in the source. “Likewise, Saints Victor, Secundinus, Quartus, Cyriacus, and Isidore.” The names are confused from the Hieronymian Martyrology; see the *Praetermissi*. “Halphard the martyr. At the city of Muthon, Saint Barbarus the martyr. Julian the emperor ordered him to be hung and his belly scraped with a sword until his entrails spilled out. Then, after he had been healed by an angel, he ordered him to be tied to a wheel and dragged around, with fire placed underneath and oil poured over him. But when he was not harmed even by this, he was beaten with stretched bull sinews. Then, after overcoming the fiery furnace and the bronze bull, he completed his martyrdom by decapitation. Likewise, according to the catalogue of the saints, here is the passion of Felix and Fortunatus, who are placed below on the third day before the Ides of June. Boniface, bishop of the city of Ferentinum. As Gregory relates in *Dialogues* 1, he shone remarkably from childhood in life and miracles. For when he left a lodging, he would sometimes return naked, because as soon as he found someone naked, he would strip himself and clothe that person. When his poor mother had distributed all the wheat she possessed to the needy, and he saw his mother distressed on account of this, he obtained through earnest prayer that she should have more than she had had before. At last, having become bishop and being full of good works, he rested in peace. The bishop of the East, not a confessor. Another Pachomius, a monk and confessor. Likewise, Theodore the abbot, who succeeded Saint Pachomius in governance, renowned for life and miracles. In Ireland, Maldod the confessor. Orosius the monk, companion of the blessed abbots Pachomius and Theodore, a man conspicuous for perfection of conduct. Stephana, virgin and martyr.” Concerning these last entries, except Theodore, see the list of the *Praetermissi*.

MOLAN. has concerning Boniface the same text as ALBERG. and DANIC. Concerning Felix and Fortunatus, as STROZZIAN. and BELINUS. In Boniface of Ferentinum he copied GREVEN, though in smaller type. Thus stands the first edition. Later editions changed the text by prefacing: “The passion of Saint Boniface,” etc., from Usuard on the Nones of June. At the end there is only: “At Milan, the translation of Saint Victor.” It may be doubted whether this belongs to the Grevenian class. “Victor, Secundinus,” and the others, concerning whom we dealt a little above.

[Col. 0051]

In Gaul, in the city of Cimela, the birthday of Pontius the martyr. Through his preaching and diligence, after the two emperors Philip, father and son, had been converted to the faith of Christ, he himself also obtained the palm of martyrdom under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. In Syria, Saints Victor and Corona, martyrs, under the emperor Antoninus. When Corona was the wife of a certain man and had begun to encourage Saint Victor because of his steadfastness in martyrdom, she saw two crowns falling from heaven, one sent for Victor and the other for herself. When she also proclaimed this before all who were listening, she was split apart between trees, while Victor was beheaded. On the same day, Saint Pachomius, our father, who, being distinguished by the deeds of apostolic grace and founder of the Egyptian monasteries, wrote the rules of the monks, which he had learned at an angel’s dictation.

Ides. Day 15. [Note: [Col. 0055C]

The Praten., Herinien., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Munerat. copies are pure. The Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Albergen., Danic., and Edit. Ultraject.-Belg. copies also agree.]

[Note: [Col. 0055D]

It is sufficiently clear that most of the names of the apostles of Spain are corrupt. Nevertheless, we thought that nothing should be corrected in them, lest we depart too far from the orthography of the codices, in some of which they are depicted even more disgracefully. Understand the same concerning the cities, whose names are transmitted more accurately in Ado and in the *Acts*. Ado explicitly reads “to the Spaniards, still entangled in pagan error,” and Muneratus, the Parisian editor of Usuard, followed him. Notker wrote “to the Spains … entangled.” All our Usuardine codices of the best quality read, as in the text, “to the Spains, still entangled in pagan error.” Pratens. has *Chyum*; the others, more correctly, *Chium*. Ado had written: “from whose water the possessed, those suffering from fever, and the other sick, after drinking it frequently, are healed.” But Usuard must be said to have abbreviated this, with the agreement of nearly all the codices; consequently we excluded Greven and Molan from the number of the pure copies, because they followed Ado rather than Usuard. He also reads *salvantur* (“are saved”), not *sanantur* (“are healed”), as Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Munerat. have it. All the codices read *Lamosacum*, *Lamosaco*, or *Lamosaci*; none reads *Lampsaci*. The text conforms to Ado and Usuard. The others have *Dionysiae*, since this is what the codices commonly contain.]

[Note: [Col. 0057A]

Neither the Hieronymian Martyrologies, nor Bede, Florus, or Rabanus mention the seven famous apostles of Spain. The author of the *Romanum parvum* should be considered the first to have entered them in the sacred calendars, in the sole announcement that it now contains: “Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Secundus, Indalecius, Caecilius, Esicius, and Euphrasius, who were baptized at Rome by the apostles.” From there Ado took them, adding an encomium, a substantial part of which Usuard made his own; Notker reproduced it almost word for word. The names of the individuals and the places of burial, which are considerably deformed in our text, Rosweyd seems to have polished in his edition of the *Romanum parvum* and Ado; Henschenius expressed and explained them quite accurately in the *Acts*. But who could explain where the names of these saints first became known to the author of the *Romanum parvum*, and from where Ado in turn received his entire narrative—unless perhaps they had seen some *Acts* similar to those published by Henschenius? See in the same author the hymn of the Mozarabic Breviary, the proper feast days of each, and other matters concerning these saints, whether confessors, as they are called here, or, as others wish, martyrs. Tillemont also discusses them in volume 1, page 191. Wandelbert settled the matter in a single verse:

“Seven pontiffs together adorn Hesperia on the Ides.”

Isidore of Chios, so far as I know, was recorded by no one before Ado; from him, with the phrasing and the same words preserved, he passed to Notker. Our author moderately abridged the encomium. Greven and Molan, however, while adhering to Ado’s words rather than Usuard’s, departed from the simplicity of the Usuardine text. Everyone readily concedes that the memory of this Isidore of ours has always been most celebrated, especially among the Greeks. Yet the *Acts*, published by various people with insufficient uniformity, suggested certain doubts to Tillemont, volume 3, page 714, which it is not the place to discuss here. The last four martyrs were undoubtedly taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, not from Florus; had Ado read Florus, he would have transmitted them more distinctly. Otherwise Usuard and Notker followed Ado plainly, content with the names alone and with a corrupted place of contest. Meanwhile, although the codices vary somewhat in other matters, we find them all entirely in agreement in this final announcement. It is nevertheless remarkable that only Florus explains the type of martyrdom; he must undoubtedly have received this from the *Acts* themselves, unknown to Ado, Usuard, and Notker. These *Acts*, published by Henschenius in their original wording, are excellent, genuine, and approved by all critics; see Ruinart, page 146 onward, and Tillemont, volume 3, page 392 onward. Henschenius has illustrated the diversity of the cult among the Greeks and the remaining matters.]

[Note: [Col. 0057B]

PRATEN. Castellanus testifies that the margin of the aforesaid codex contains the inscription: “The coming of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples.”

TORNACEN. continues to abbreviate the encomia, perhaps because they were longer than its usual practice. In the first announcement everything after “were sent” is missing. It is pure in Isidore. Instead of *Lamosacum*, it writes *Mosacum*. Several others vary in this name.

PULSANEN. agrees with TORNACEN. in the first class. Concerning Isidore it goes as far as “martyr”; the rest is missing.

ROSWEYD., pure in the text, formulates the final announcement as follows: “In Gaul, at Lamosacum, Peter,” etc.; and at the end, “whose deeds are recorded.”

ANTUERPIEN.-MAJ., otherwise also pure, omitted the final two names, “Paul and Dionysia.”

We discussed GREVEN and MOLAN in the variant readings. The *Auctaria* are treated separately below.

LOVANIEN. agrees with TORNACEN. and PULSANEN. in the first announcement. In the rest of the text it is pure. At the end it adds: “On the same day, Saint Dymphna, virgin, who, refusing her father’s incest, was struck by him with a sword and completed her martyrdom.”

CENTULEN. is mutilated in the Apostles of Spain, as above. “At Ramosacum, the passion of Saints Peter,” etc. “Whose wondrous passions are read.”

BRUXELLEN.: “The coming of the Holy Spirit visibly upon the apostles and disciples of Christ. In Spain, the birthday of the holy confessors,” etc., pure up to “had subjected them.” Then it adds: “After all these things, they rested in peace. And while each one [rests] in his own [place], Saint Torquatus is glorified at the city of Acci. For on his solemnity every year an olive tree at his tomb, flowering by divine power, is laden with ripe fruit.” The latter material is taken from Ado. “At the island of Chios,” etc., also from Ado, as in GREVEN. and MOLAN. “And at Lamosacum, the passion,” etc. “Elsewhere, Saints Prestabilis and Felix.” They have been torn away from their companions; see their company in the *Acts*. “On the same day, Saint Sophia. For her the emperor Justinian built at Constantinople a church of wondrous and incomparable workmanship.” This is the Holy of Holies, to be venerated from eternity and forever. “At the village of Gheele in Brabant, the birthday of the blessed martyrs Gerebern, priest, and Dymphna, virgin, daughter of the king of Ireland. Persecuted by the king, the virgin’s father, they fell together for Christ, their heads having been cut off. Gerebern was transferred to Nova Rhenensis, which is called Xanctis; but the body of Saint Dymphna, virgin, rests near the aforesaid village of Gheele, shining with many miracles.”

HACENOYEN. is deficient in Isidore of Chios; in the remainder it comes close to purity.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130: “On the same day, Saint Hilary, monk and hermit.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT. “The passion of Saints Peter, Andrew, Dionysius, and others; Robert the confessor.” This is, I think, the one who is later called count or Palatine duke at Bingen, etc. It follows: “Torquatus, Ticefontus, and the other confessors, bishops of their company.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, immediately after “Dionysia” adds “and Liberator the martyr.” See the *Acts*. “And Saints Primianus and Firmianus, martyrs.” These two are found in another, though also Lombard, manuscript. See the *Praetermissi*.

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apollin. “At Baugia, a village of Auxerre, the birthday of Saint Peregrine the martyr.” He is not placed among the *Praetermissi*. He should be referred to the following day, 16 May.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. is quite pure in the first announcement; in second place it follows Ado. “At Lamosacum, etc.” At the end it adds: “In the territory of Senones, Saint Sidromus (Sidronius) the martyr.” He is commemorated on 11 July. “In Brabant, Saint Dymphna, virgin and martyr. On the same day, Blessed Gerebern, priest and martyr, concerning whom one reads in the deeds of the aforesaid Saint Dymphna, virgin and martyr.”

BELIN. The first edition begins with Isidore. Then it treats of Peter and his companions. It follows with the apostles of Spain, with the ending mutilated. The second edition prefixes to the first: “At Jerusalem, the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete.”

GREVEN. “The coming of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples. In the territory of Senones, Sidronius the martyr. Likewise, Saints Timothy and Felix.” The usual confusion drawn from the Hieronymian Martyrology. “Likewise, Saint Auctor.” Perhaps “Victor”; see the *Praetermissi*. “Halphard the martyr, according to others on the preceding day. Simplicius, priest; Robert, Palatine duke of the Rhine and confessor. Dymphna, virgin and martyr, daughter of the king of Ireland. When her idolatrous father wished to have her in the place of a wife, she, having been instructed in the faith of Christ, recoiled from the crime and secretly left her homeland, coming to Brabant, where she was beheaded by her pursuing father together with Saint Gerebern the priest, who had baptized her.” The first edition differs from this in order. “Rosula, with four other virgins. Likewise, Saint Sophia.” See the *Acts* and the *Praetermissi*.

MOLAN. “At Jerusalem, the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. On the same day, Saint Bernard, a regular canon.” In the *Praetermissi* he is referred to 15 June. “In Brabant, in the village called Ghele, Saint Dymphna, virgin and martyr. She was beheaded by her own father, the pagan king of Ireland, on account of her faith and her love of chastity.” It continues in smaller type: “Around the year of the Lord 700, the one who was pursuing her came through the castle called Antwerp, in the diocese of Cambrai, to the aforesaid village of Rure. There those possessed by demons are freed by her from day to day. At Auvergne, Saints Cassius the priest and Victorianus with their companions, martyrs: Cassius was a disciple of Blessed Austremonius, the first bishop of Auvergne, and persevered until the times of Valerian and Gallienus. Saint Praejectus the bishop wrote their deeds. On the same day, Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia, whose life Simeon Metaphrastes excerpted from the testimony of John, one of his disciples.” His life is celebrated on 12 May. Other editions have concerning Saint Dymphna the same material recited above, up to “the pagan king of Ireland.” It follows: “At Bingen, Saint Robert, Palatine duke of the Rhine and confessor.” This is the man concerning whom we spoke above under MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJ. “At Auvergne, Saints Cassius, Victorianus, Maximus, and their companions, martyrs. Saint Praejectus the bishop wrote their *Acts*. At Jerusalem, the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete.”

[Col. 0055]

The birthday of the holy confessors Torquatus, Tesifontus, Secundus, Indalecius, Caecilius, Esicius, and Euphrasius, who were ordained at Rome by the holy apostles and sent to preach the word of God to the Spains, still entangled in pagan error. When they had evangelized various cities and subjected countless multitudes to the faith of Christ, Torquatus rested at Acci, Tesifontus at Vergium, Secundus at Abula, Indalecius at Urci, Caecilius at Heliberri, Esicius at Carcesi, and Euphrasius at Eliturgi. At the island of Chios, Blessed Isidore the martyr, in whose basilica there is a well into which he is also said to have been thrown; from its water the sick are frequently healed after drinking. At Lamosacum, the passion of Saints Peter and Andrew, Paul and Dionysia.

XVII Kal. Day 16. [Note: [Col. 0059]

The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0059B]

Herinien. and Autuerp. write *Hisauria* incorrectly; the others correctly, as in the text. Pulsanen. reads: “At Auxerre, Blessed Peregrine, the first martyr and bishop,” etc. The other purer codices contradict this, and we follow them. I do not know why the Herinien. copy omitted the title “bishop.” Molan also reads: “martyr and first bishop.” In Rosweyd., *beati* is missing. Antuerp. Maj., instead of “rested in peace,” preferred to write “rested in peace” in the opposite order.]

[Note: [Col. 0059B]

The text is Adonian, altered only very slightly by our author and expanded a little in the case of Peregrine. The first announcement flowed from copies of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which the somewhat corrupt wording can easily be restored. The *Romanum parvum* reads “in Isauria,” leaving uncertain, no less than the Hieronymian codices, whether the city itself, Isauria or Isaura, or the province of Isauria is meant. Ado suffers from the same defect—or blemish—when he writes indefinitely, “near Isauria”; Notker has “in Isauria”; our author speaks more explicitly: “in the province of Isauria.” The remaining words are copied entirely from Ado. But when he so expressly adds to the words of the *Romanum parvum* “whose deeds are recorded,” he clearly shows that he had never seen them; otherwise he would have given at least some brief encomium from them. Hence those final phrases were wisely removed by Notker. Among the Hieronymian codices, the Epternacensis and Corbeiensis explicitly record Peregrine. Rabanus does likewise. Wandelbert celebrates him—and him alone—in this verse:

“And the sixth, with ten, blossoms with Peregrine the martyr.”

He plainly transfers him incorrectly to the following day, while remembering Timothy on this day: “Whom blessed Paul taught with truthful voice”; no other ancient martyrologist mentions him on this day. Ado reads: “At Auxerre, the passion of Saint Peregrine, the first bishop of that city.” Notker is almost the same. The rest was added by Usuard, from which we learn only that Peregrine was struck with a capital sentence, the other torments with which the *Acts* first testify that he was afflicted having been omitted. These *Acts* were published and illustrated from various codices by Henschenius; they had previously been made public by others, among them Labbeus, who inserted them in volume 1 of the *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum librorum*, beginning at page 526. They are written in a serious and simple style, though not in such a way as to remove all the doubts that the reader will find among more recent scholars. See Tillemont, volume 4, page 480 onward. I consider that Henschenius has sufficiently explained the matters debated concerning the time of his mission, the translations of his relics, and other questions. To avoid disagreements, the Autissiodorense manuscript of the distinguished Castellanus, communicated to us in 1709, presents and distinguishes several Peregrines bearing the same name; perhaps there will be an opportunity to discuss them elsewhere.

The virgin Maxima of Fréjus was unknown to earlier writers and is first mentioned by Ado, whose words Notker transferred exactly. Usuard also took all his material from Ado, but omitted what Ado had undoubtedly expressed deliberately: “in a village called Calidianus,” as our codices clearly demonstrate. From these it is evident that we have reproduced Usuard’s genuine and true wording. Concerning Maxima’s cult and homeland, see the dissertations of Papebrochius and the distinguished Anselmius prefixed to our *Acts* on this day. Here I note only that some have gone astray by looking for Maxima at Fréjus in Italy, whereas it is certain that she belongs to Fréjus in Provence.]

[Note: [Col. 0059C]

ANTUERPIEN. and MAX.-LUBEC., after the pure text, add: “At Troyes, Saint Fidolus the abbot.” MAX.-LUBEC., however, altered the final word and wrote “bishop.” Others have wrongly imitated this.

MUNERAT. At the end: “At Amiens, Honoratus, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN. “In the territory of Chartres, the passion of Saints Emanus, Maurillus, and Almarius.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., and EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG. are pure in the first announcement and continue as follows: “At Auxerre, Blessed Peregrine the martyr, the first bishop of that city: ordained bishop at Rome by Blessed Sixtus, he was sent into Gaul to preach to the nations. When he came to Auxerre, after converting many to the faith of Christ and beginning to preach God publicly, he was seized by the ministers of the temples and afflicted with various punishments, then confined in a very dark prison. Finally condemned to death, he merited an everlasting crown.” They are pure in Maxima; at the end is added: “At Troyes, Saint Fidolus, bishop and confessor.”

ALBERGEN. and DANIC., similar to the preceding copies, further add: “At Amiens, Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor.”

CENTULEN.: “At Auxerre, in the village of Biaugy, the passion of Saint Peregrine, bishop and first martyr, sent from Rome by the authority of Pope Sixtus. At Amiens, the birthday of Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Troyes, Saint Fidolus, priest and confessor. In Isauria, Saints Aquilinus and Victorianus, whose deeds are recorded. In the territory of Fréjus, Saint Maxima, virgin.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “Timothy the apostle, whose birthday is celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of February.” This may easily have been taken from Wandelbert: “At the province of Isauria, etc.,” purely. “At Auxerre, the birthday of Saint Peregrine, the first,” etc., as above in ANTUERP.-MAX. “And in the territory of Fréjus, in a village called Calidianus, Saint Maxima,” etc., correctly. “At Troyes, Saint Fidolus, bishop and confessor. And at Amiens, Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor. On the island of Ireland, Saint Brendan, abbot and confessor. While searching for the Fortunate Isles in a seven-year voyage, he saw many things worthy of miracles and scarcely credible to those inexperienced in such matters, and left them commended in writing.” The compiler of this codex could have reported something more certain and more worthy of remembrance from his genuine *Acts*.

HAGENOYEN. begins with Peregrine, somewhat more fully than the other codices cited above. Then: “In the territory of Fréjus, Saint Maxima,” etc. “At Troyes, Saint Fidolus, bishop and confessor. In the city of Amiens in Gaul, Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor. In the city of Isauria, Aquilinus,” etc.

AQUICINCT. “At Troyes, Saint Fidolus the abbot.”

AMBIANEN. “At Amiens, Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor. Among the other marks of his goodness, while he was consecrating the Lord’s body on earth, he was worthy to see His hand in heaven.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT. “Peregrine, bishop of Auxerre and martyr. Honoratus, bishop and confessor. Aquilinus and Victorianus, martyrs. Maxima, virgin.”

CODEX BICOTIAN., marked E 40: “In the territory of Chartres, the birthday of Saint Emanus the martyr.”

CAMBERIEN. “At Auvergne, Saints Cassius and Victorianus.” They were treated on the preceding day.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, adds first: “At Benevento, the birthday of Saint Rosius, bishop, at Saint Sophia.” See the *Acts*.

UGHELLIAN. At the end: “At Troyes, Saint Fidolus, bishop.” See above, the first *Auctarium*.

ALTEMPS. “In Cornwall, Saint Carnoc, bishop and confessor.” Is it perhaps “Carentocus” or “Cernathus”? Concerning him, see the *Acts*. “On the same day, the presentation of the body of Blessed Edmund, king and martyr.” He is commemorated on 20 November, when this presentation will be discussed.

FLORENTIN.: “At the city of Volterra, the birthday of Saints Justus, bishop and confessor, and Clement, confessor; both brothers completed their holy life with a perfect end.” They are referred to 5 June. “At the city of Gubbio, Saint Ubaldus, bishop and confessor of that city, whose life shone with virtues and miracles. At Troyes, Saint Sydolus, bishop and confessor.” The error in writing *Sydolus* is clear; the true name is Fidolus, etc.

CODEX S. RICALDI: “In the territory of Chartres, the passion of Saints Emanus, Maurillus, and Almarius.”

BURDEGALEN.: “At Bordeaux, Fortis, bishop and martyr.” See Papebrochius’s commentary.

MONTIS SANCTI. “At the city of Metz, the translation of the body of the most blessed man Terentius, bishop, through whom the Lord displayed many miracles.” In the *Praetermissi* he is referred to his birthday, 28 September.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins with Peregrine, whose encomium it somewhat amplifies. In Aquilinus, Victorianus, and Maxima it is almost pure. It follows with Fidolus and Honoratus, as above. Then: “At Auxerre, Blessed Tricius, bishop and confessor.” See the *Praetermissi*. “In the territory of Bourges, at the monastery of Mediaco, Blessed Victorinus the martyr. In England, Blessed Brendan, abbot and confessor. On the same day, Saint Simeon, confessor of the Carmelite Order.”

BELIN., quite pure in the text, has at the end: “At Troyes, Saint Sydolus, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN. In the *Auctarium*: “Likewise, Saints Diocletian, Florentius, Heraclius, Paulinus, and Vincent.” A mixture of unrelated persons. “In the territory of Bourges, at the monastery of Madiacum, Saint Victorinus the martyr. At Amiens, Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor. At Troyes, Fidolus, bishop. At the city of Sées, Saint Alnobert, bishop and confessor. On that same day, Blessed Renobert, bishop and confessor, a man of great holiness. Tricius, bishop of Auxerre and confessor. Theobald, bishop and confessor.” See the *Praetermissi* concerning both. “Ubaldus, bishop and confessor of Gubbio, a man of great patience, distinguished in life and miracles. Aquilinus, bishop of Cologne, of blessed memory, who buried Blessed Ursula.” He is referred to the Ursuline commemoration on 21 October. “At Metz, the translation of Saint Terentius, bishop and confessor.” Concerning him, see above. “In Ireland, Saint Brendan the abbot, who, great in the virtue of abstinence, became the father of nearly 3,000 monks. At the city of Bordeaux, Blessed Simeon the confessor of the Carmelite Order, singularly devoted to the holy Mother of God and exceedingly renowned for the radiance of his miracles. At Mount Jovis, the deposition of Saint Bernard, hermit, a man of exceptional holiness. Among other kinds of illness, he received the power to cure paralysis.” In the *Praetermissi* he is said to have died on 15 June.

MOLAN. “And Saints Diocletian and Florentius.” See the *Praetermissi*. “At Troyes, Saint Fidolus, bishop and confessor. At the city of Bordeaux, Blessed Simeon Stock, Carmelite, singularly devoted to the God-bearing Virgin Mary and pre-eminent in the radiance of miracles. At the city of Sées, Blessed Alnobert, bishop and confessor of that city. On that same day, Blessed Renobert, bishop and confessor, a man of great holiness. Likewise, Saint Ubaldus, bishop and confessor.” Then, in smaller type: “Of Gubbio, a man of great patience, distinguished in life and miracles. In Ireland, Saint Brendan,” etc., as in GREVEN. “On the same day, Saint Dommolus (Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans, concerning whom Gregory of Tours speaks in book 6 of the *History of the Franks*).” Other editions have: “In Scotland, Saint Brendan the abbot, whose wondrous deeds are read. At Le Mans, Saint Domnolus, bishop.” Concerning Simeon Stock and Alnobert, as above. “On that same day, Blessed Renobert, bishop of Bayeux and confessor, a man of great holiness.” Concerning Bernard, Ubaldus, and Honoratus, as above. “In the territory of Chartres, the passion of Saint Emanus the martyr. And Saints Diocletian and Florentius.” Concerning Fidolus, as above. “On the sixteenth day, Saint Theodore the sanctified father, disciple of Saint Pachomius.” He was treated with his master on 14 May.

[Col. 0059]

In the province of Isauria, the birthday of Saints Aquilinus and Victorianus, whose deeds are recorded. At Auxerre, Blessed Peregrine, first bishop of that city, who, condemned to death, merited an everlasting crown. In the territory of Fréjus, Saint Maxima, virgin, who, renowned for many virtues, rested in peace.

XVI Kal. Day 17. [Note: [Col. 0063A]

The Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerp., and Max.-Lubec. copies are pure, as are Antuerp. Maj., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. The Antuerp. Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and Editio Ultraj.-Belg. may also be added. They depart from purity only in inserting *jubente Silvio* (“at the command of Silvius”) after “his martyrdom.”]

[Note: [Col. 0063A]

Rosweyd. moderately alters the phrasing as follows: “He was first great in the office of Nero the Caesar.” Herinien. has “he was first”; Antuerp.-Maj. “he was first”; Greven. and Molan. “he was first.” Again, those same Greven. and Molan., instead of “he was afflicted for a very long time with scourging,” read “most harshly.” Munerat. omitted the particle *ac* (“and”) before “beasts.” Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. pursue excessive precision when they write “by decapitation of the head.” Almost everyone reads “the third day before the Kalends of May”; I do not know why Greven. and Molan. wrote “of May.” Rosweyd. transposed the words, “he completed [it] on the third day before the Kalends.” In Max.-Lubec. *crebrius* (“more frequently”) occurs instead of *celebrius* (“more celebrated”), a mistake of the kind with which that edition frequently abounds. Rosweyd., instead of *recolitur* (“is commemorated”), has the simple verb *colitur* (“is celebrated”), while Pulsanen. wrote *hinc* (“from here”) instead of *hic* (“here”). Herinien. and Pulsanen. have *Nividuno*, worse in Max.-Lubec. *Innedinio*. All the others, as in the text, have *Niveduno*. So too *Heraclii* in all copies. Molan. alone has *Paulini* instead of *Pauli*.]

[Note: [Col. 0063B]

How illustrious is the memory of the martyr Torpetes, and how celebrated his cult is in Italy and elsewhere; so uncertain are the Acts that circulate concerning him, which Papebrochius discussed on this day. In the Appendices we treated him from several manuscripts on 29 April. Rabanus composed a long eulogy for him on 29 March, in which—if I am not mistaken, guided by his own inspiration—I do not know what Acts he may have had before his eyes. In the Hieronymian copies he is known neither on 29 March nor on 29 April, neither on this day nor, so far as I know, on any other. Nor does the genuine Bede ever mention Torpetes, nor Florus, nor Wandalbert; thus the first person to place him in the sacred calendars seems to have been the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*, whom Ado always carefully follows. Ado, moreover, composed an eulogy on his own initiative, entirely different from Rabanus’s, and therefore excerpted from other Acts, perhaps no less suspect. Notker copied Ado’s wording, adding a few things of his own. Our author, preserving the ancient text, elegantly adapted Ado’s more expansive narrative to his customary brevity, saying so much that it was [Col. 0063C] unnecessary afterward to insert what is recited today in the modern Roman Martyrology. For the rest, let the reader be referred to the Acts. Whoever seeks a shorter summary of the whole matter in a table should consult Tillemont, volume II, p. 497. The Acts must likewise be consulted in order to determine the place, if that can be done with sufficient confidence, to which Eraclius, Paul, and Aquilinus, together with two other named or unnamed companions, should be assigned. How extremely uncertain are the traditions concerning this entire matter, both ancient and modern, is clearly shown by the wholly hesitant conjecture of Florentinius and Henschenius, men exceptionally perceptive in such matters; I shall certainly not presume to resolve it. That group was most probably taken by Usuard from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; Notker expressed it differently, and neither of them distinguished the matter completely. I would suppose that both simply copied what they had found in their respective, whatever their quality, copies, without troubling themselves over what later writers might determine about the place—whether Nivedunum or Sivedunum—or about the number of those martyrs. It should be enough for us, on the unanimous agreement of our manuscripts, to have faithfully recorded Usuard’s intention, whether clear or confused, true or false.]

[Note: [Col. 0063C]]

**CENTULEN.:** “At Hierapolis, blessed Papias, bishop, who was a hearer of the apostle John, but a fellow disciple and companion of Polycarp.” We treated him with Usuard on 22 February. “In Tuscany, the deposition of the body of Saint Torpetes, martyr. In the city of Nivedunum, Saints Emilius, Paul, and Aquilinus, with two others.”

**BRUXELLEN.:** It has the following concerning Torpetes: “In Tuscany, Saint Torpetes, martyr. He was first a great man in the office of Caesar Nero, and was baptized by the blessed priest Anthony. When the emperor Nero learned that he was a Christian, he ordered him to be beaten, handed over to the beasts to be devoured; and when the beasts did not harm him, he ordered him to be beheaded. With him also a certain counsellor of Nero, named Evellius, was beheaded because through him he had believed in Christ.” The interpolations were taken from Ado.

**HAGENOYEN.:** It is almost pure in the entry for Torpetes, but adds in second place: “On the island of Chios, Saint Isidore, martyr, in whose basilica there is a well into which, as is said, he was thrown; from it the sick, after drinking, are often healed.” This has been wrongly transferred here from the preceding day. It continues: “In the city of Nivedunum, the passion of the saints,” and so forth.

**MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:** “Torpetes, martyr, in Tuscany. Heradius, Paul, and Aquilinus.”

**ALTEMPS.:** “On the same day, Saint Frainichildis, mother of Saint Austreberta, virgin.” See the *Life of Austreberta*, her daughter, 10 February, chapter I.

**FLORENTIN.:** “On the same day, the translation of Saint Syrus, bishop of Ticinum.” This will be treated on his feast day, 9 December. Then the **CODEX STROZZIAN.** alone has: “The translation of Saint Bernard—he meant ‘Bernardine’—of the Order of Friars Minor.” In the *Omissions* it is referred to his feast day, 20 May.

[Col. 0064C] **LUXOVIEN.:** “In the city of Nivedunum, Saints Heradius, Paul, and Aquilinus, with two others. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Liberius, bishop.” See below.

**MONTIS SANCTI:** “On the same day, the bodies of Saints Amatus, Romaricus, and Adelphius are brought from this mountain to the court.” See the list of the *Omissions*.

**EDITIO LUBECO-COL.:** “After ‘he was first,’” it inserts with the **BRUXELLENSIS**: “And he was baptized by the blessed priest Anthony, but afterward for the faith of Christ,” and so forth. “Finally, by the beheading of his head, he completed his martyrdom, at the command of Silvius, on the third day before the Kalends of May, outside the city of Pisa. Nevertheless, his feast is celebrated more solemnly here. In the city of Nivedunum, Saints Eraclius, Paul, and Aquilinus, martyrs, with two others.” The change is present, but not a substantial one.

**BELIN:** At the end: “On the same day, Saint Syrus, bishop and confessor.” In my opinion, the translation of his body reported above is better placed here. We said that his feast day is commemorated on 9 [Col. 0064D] December. It continues: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Bernardine of the Order of Friars Minor.” See above.

**GREVEN.:** “In Alexandria, Victor and Basil, Primus, Pliberus”—a joining of Roman names with Alexandrian ones. Then: “At Rome, the feast of Saints Partinus, Gallicerius, and Eponomus.” See the genuine names in the Acts. “Likewise Saints Paul, Peregrine, Martin, Adrion, and Basilla.” A second confusion. “At Rome, Liberius, bishop and confessor.” He is the same person who is called “Pliberus” in the first place, and he must be joined with “Primus,” as “martyr,” not “confessor.” It continues: “Benedict, confessor, shepherd in Avignon.” In my opinion, he is the one who erected the famous bridge, whose Acts were examined on 14 April. “The translation of Saint Cirius, bishop and confessor of Pavia. In the city of Aquila, the translation of Saint Bernardine, confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor.”

[Col. 0065A] **MOLAN.:** “On the same day, Saint Syrus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saint Bernardine of the Order of Friars Minor. At Laon-la-Chaussée, the translation of the body of Saint Montanus, monk.” This entire announcement is also included in the later editions, where [Col. 0066A] the following is additionally inserted: “On the same day, at Elnone, the bringing-in of the three Cologne virgins.” In the index of the *Omissions* it is referred to the common feast of all the virgins of Ursula, 21 October.]

[Col. 0061]

In Tuscany, Saint Torpetes, martyr. He was first a great man in the office of Caesar Nero; but afterward, for the faith of Christ, at Nero’s command, he was struck on the face, afflicted for a very long time with scourging, and handed over to the beasts to be devoured, but was not harmed at all. Finally, by beheading, he completed his martyrdom on the third day before the Kalends of May. Nevertheless, his feast is celebrated more solemnly here. In the city of Nivedunum, Saints Eraclius, Paul, and Aquilinus, with two others.

**XV Kal. Day 18.**

[Note: [Col. 0065A]]

Taken from the Patren., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerpien., and Max.-Lubec. manuscripts, Munerat., Belin., Greven. [Col. 0066A] and Molan. Also from Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Danic., and the Ultraj.-Belg. edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0065B]]

It is notable scarcely in anything except scribal errors: *egipto*; *set*; *Dioschori*, *Diostori*; *Faelicis*; *martirii*; and other such forms. Munerat. wrote “lector and martyr” concerning Dioscorus. Pulsanen. read “of Spoleto”; Belin., “of Spoletum”; Max.-Lubec., worse, “of Spelladum.” Other variations will be evident in the Appendices.]

[Note: [Col. 0065B]]

The Hieronymian copies explicitly announce Dioscorus, an Egyptian martyr; in them, except for the Epternacensis, it is unusually added that he suffered many things. The *Little Roman Martyrology*, in keeping with its brevity, gives only his name and the place of his martyrdom. The Viennese Martyrologist, however, elegantly enumerated in a few words the many and most atrocious tortures by which he was cruelly tormented, taking his account from some older source; but neither Henschenius nor anyone else has so far discovered what that older source was, or whether Acts once existed. Peter of Equilium regularly copied Ado’s eulogies; Usuard and Notker transferred the whole of Ado’s text here, unchanged, into their own entries. Wandalbert celebrates him alone on this day in these words: “On the fifteenth, Dioscorus the martyr fulfills the day.” But what are we to say about Felix, bishop of Spellatum? I observe this certainty: he is entirely unknown to all the Martyrologists older than Usuard, and to those contemporary with him [Col. 0065C]. For the fact that Felix’s memory has been inserted into the manuscript of Ado at Liège, Saint Laurence, it is plainly evident [Col. 0066B] that this is an addition made from Usuard by some later copyist. Therefore, everything transmitted about this holy bishop and martyr by Peter of Natalibus and others seems to rest solely on Usuard’s authority. But from where Our author obtained it, I confess that I cannot conjecture at all; for the writers do not agree about the authenticity or antiquity of the Acts, or even about the episcopal see. Baronius, perhaps relying too much on Belin, thought that “Spoleto” should be substituted for “Spellatum.” Others try to transfer him to Dalmatia, others to Spain. It is remarkable that there should be so much dispute about one Felix, when our Acts for the first five months alone list almost a hundred persons of that name. To avoid prolonging matters, I refer the curious reader to Henschenius’s commentary, which approaches the truth—or at least probability—as closely as possible, unless Tillemont’s objection in volume V, p. 433, proves decisive. As far as we are concerned, Usuard’s text is made certain not only by the fourteen manuscripts cited by Henschenius, but by all those that we have cited intact in the course of this work, both printed and written by hand.]

[Note: [Col. 0065C]]

**ROSWEYD.:** Adds to the pure text: “On the same day, the translation of Elgiva.” Her memory is commemorated in the Acts on this day.

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.:** Also at the end: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Mildred, virgin beloved of God.” In the *Omissions* it is referred to her feast day, 13 July. The translation is said to have taken place in the year 1030.

**CENTULEN.:** Omitted Dioscorus’s eulogy. In the entry for Felix it is entirely Usuardine.

**BRUXELLEN.:** Fairly pure in the entry for Dioscorus, it continues: “In Alexandria, Saints Parthonius and Serapion, priests.” It would have been better to write “Potamon,” with various companions, concerning whom there are Acts derived from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. It continues: “At the city of Spoleto, Saint Felix, bishop, who under the emperor Maximian obtained the palm of martyrdom. Likewise Medardus, bishop. Likewise Eugenia, virgin.” Henschenius cites this manuscript and omits this Eugenia. He does not discuss Medardus today, but does so on the following day; see the *Omissions*. Medardus’s feast is known to be on 8 June.

**HAGENOYEN.:** Begins: “Job the prophet, who reigned in the city of Bosra and at first was very wealthy, and adorned with sons and daughters, brothers and friends. While he was prosperous he greatly feared the Lord, and for the sins of his sons and daughters he always entreated the Lord to keep them from sin. Satan asked the Lord to test him, supposing that he could make God’s servant Job, blessed through poverty and bodily affliction, fall away. But the Lord intended to do something else with him, and therefore subjected him to Satan’s temptation. For the Lord wished to set him as an example to others [Col. 0066C]. While he was wealthy he always feared God, and now the Lord wished to test him in poverty, to see whether he would remain faithful. And because he persevered faithfully in affliction and poverty, the Lord therefore repented of the evil he had done to him and restored everything to him twofold. Afterward he took Dinah, the daughter of Jacob the patriarch, and begot sons and daughters by her, and saw his sons and his sons’ sons to the third and fourth generation. His feast is commemorated on the sixth day before the Ides of May.” Let the reader judge what credibility the foregoing deserves. It continues: “On the same day, Saint Felix, bishop and martyr, who at the city of Spellatum under the emperor Maximian obtained the palm of martyrdom. In Lesser Britain, in the diocese of Tréguier, Saint Ivo, confessor, and also a great jurist. Likewise Carentius, bishop and confessor.” Henschenius names him in the *Omissions*, but again says nothing about the former. “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Adolphus, bishop and confessor of Cambrai.” Nor [Col. 0066D] is he mentioned in the *Omissions*. He is commemorated on the following day.

**AQUICINCT.:** Has “Spolitanensis” instead of “Spellatensis.” At the end it adds: “At Arras, the deposition of Hadulphus, bishop.”

**MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:** “Dioscorus, martyr and lector. Felix, bishop and martyr. Bernardine, confessor.” In the margin, with an asterisk: “Elsewhere, Bernard the hermit.”

In the **VATICAN**, designated number 5949, Felix is missing, which is surprising. It adds: “In Alexandria, Saint Pontamion, priest.”

**STROZZIAN.:** In first place: “At Camerino, Saint Venantius [Col. 0067A] martyr, with 1,565 fellow martyrs.”

**CAUDIACENSIS PRIORATUS:** “At the monastery of Magni Locus in Auvergne, Saints Cassius and Victorinus, martyrs.” They are listed among those omitted on the following day. See also 15 May.

**EDITIO-LUBECO-COL.:** “At Rome, Saint John, bishop and martyr.” It is referred to 27 May. “On the same day, Saint Eric, king of the Swedes—why not ‘of the Swedes’ in the other form?—and martyr.”

**GREVEN.:** “The prophet Zephaniah.” It is referred to 3 December. “At Rome, Saint John, bishop and martyr.” Concerning him we have already spoken. “At Constantinople, Dativus, Luciosus, and Martinianus. In Alexandria, Parthonius and Serapion, priests.” See the Acts. “Eric, king of Sweden and martyr. Venantius, martyr, who, having been beaten with clubs for the faith of Christ under Decius and shut up in prison, was strengthened by an angel; then he was exposed to lions, but suffered no harm, and was hung upside down, with fire placed beneath his head. Finally [Col. 0068A] he triumphed by the cutting off of his head. Mark, bishop and martyr.” Is this the Evangelist, or another? See in the *Omissions*. “Likewise Saints Honestasius, Maximius, and Hermon.” The names are almost corrupted and altered; see the Acts. “In Ireland, Saran, confessor.” See the list of the *Omissions*.

**MOLAN.:** In small type: “Eric, king of Sweden and martyr. Near the monastery called Maricolus, Saint Quinbert, confessor, who in our days became famous through innumerable miracles.” Thus the first edition; but the later editions are somewhat clearer: “In Sweden, in the city of Uppsala, Saint Eric, king and martyr. In the city of Camerino, Saint Venantius, martyr, under Decius. After overcoming scourges, prison, and torches, and taming lions, he was beheaded and gave up his spirit to God. At Quercetum, on the same day, Saint Quinibert, confessor. On the eighteenth day, Saint Theodotus of Ancyra, holy martyr, and with him seven virgins.” See in the Acts the names of each of the virgins, and the life of all of them, published there in Greek and Latin.]

[Col. 0065]

In Egypt, Saint Dioscorus, lector, against whom the governor inflicted many and various tortures, so that he tore out his fingernails and set his sides aflame with lamps; but the attendants, terrified by the radiance of heavenly light, fell down. Finally, after being burned with heated metal plates, he completed his martyrdom. On the same day, Saint Felix, bishop, who at the city of Spellatum, under the emperor Maximian, obtained the palm of martyrdom.

**XIV Kal. Day 19.**

[Note: [Col. 0067]]

Thus have the Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp., and Max.-Lubec. manuscripts, Greven. and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0067B]]

I wrote *Calocerus* with the Praten., Tornacen., and Greven. manuscripts. Herinien. has *Calocerii*. Antuerp.-Max.-Lubec. and Molan. have *Calocerii and Parthimii*. Greven. and Molan. depart from purity in several places. First, instead of “were killed,” they read “were slain.” Then, to bring everything together, where the others have “clothed with Christ in baptism,” they put “invested with Christ by baptism” [Col. 0068B]. Finally, both omit at the end “and preserved it”; this is also absent from Antuerp.-Max.-Lubec. and other manuscripts. The Praten. manuscript alone reads “from earth to the heavens”; the others have “from the earth,” as Ado had already led the way, and we judged that it should be changed. I disregard scribal errors.]

[Note: [Col. 0067B]]

Whoever has Ado before his eyes will again easily understand where Usuard obtained the whole text for this day; for anyone comparing one with the other will see clearly that Our author represents Ado’s wording, only somewhat more condensed. The first announcement originally flows from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; and, what is extremely rare and therefore highly suspect, the whole of Ado’s eulogy is found in the Lucensis manuscript, with only the final words—“and they rest in the cemetery beside the Appian Way”—transposed by Ado from the beginning and made shorter. The Epternacensis reading is shorter and better. The *Little Roman Martyrology*, in its customary manner, mentions the same martyrs: “Calocerus and Parthenius, eunuchs.” Rabanus’s wording does not differ greatly from Ado’s; whether Notker followed him is not entirely clear, while Florus is somewhat more concise. We observed on 11 February that Calocerus and Parthenius are recorded for that day by Bede, Rabanus, and Wandalbert; Notker may be added, since he repeats them on 18 April, where they were doubtless taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Papebrochius believes that these are the very same men commemorated on those various days, as we have shown often elsewhere in this Martyrology, attempting to preserve the truth of the Acts by removing the beginning and end; others do not even admit the remaining body of the narrative, as may be seen in Tillemont, volume V, p. 617. There is one point on which I miss my teacher’s diligence: he neglected the passage in the most ancient Bucherian Calendar, where it is explicitly read: “On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, Parthenius and Calocerus, in the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the sixth of Maximian, consuls”—that is, in the year 304, more than fifty years after Decius’s death. Papebrochius subsequently saw that decisive authority, and therefore wrote in his own hand on an attached slip [Col. 0068B] that these words should be understood as referring to a translation, carried out in that year 304 to a safer place. Florentinius takes another path, supposing that two other men of the same names must be posited, who suffered martyrdom under Diocletian and Maximian, distinct from those whom the present Acts and our Martyrologies clearly attest to have been eunuchs of Decius’s wife and to have suffered under Decius. Here I suspend judgment for the time being; let the reader choose what seems more probable.

Bede mentions the virgin Potentiana, as does the *Little Roman Martyrology*, and both announce her in this form. Rabanus and Notker prefer *Pudentiana*; Ado expressed both names disjunctively, as did our elders in the Acts. Yet the manuscripts of Usuard consistently call her Potentiana. Rabanus’s eulogy differs from Ado’s, although it is clear that both were taken from the same Acts. Our author borrowed selected words from Ado; Notker transcribed everything, though I do not know why his text lacks the second announcement concerning Pudens, the virgin’s father. It is reported in the *Little Roman Martyrology* and consequently in Ado, in second place; but Usuard chose to place Calocerus and Parthenius at the head of the entry. For the rest, as suggested above, the encomium of Pudens too is woven from Ado’s words. There you have Usuard. The reader may ask whether he also has the truth. There can be no doubt about the celebrated cult of Potentiana or Pudentiana, since it is plainly established by the most ancient ecclesiastical monuments, including the Calendar of Fronto. There are some who do not so readily accept Pudens, among them Castellanus in the *Universal Martyrology*. Papebrochius labored admirably in excavating and explaining the Acts, persuading himself that, once certain things were removed, others altered, and the chaff separated from the grain, the history could be attributed to Pastor as an eyewitness. Yet Tillemont criticized so much in them in volume II, beginning at p. 615, that he raises a prudent doubt whether they truly belong to that author to whom they are commonly attributed. [Col. 0070A] Wandalbert sang only of Pudentiana:

“By twice seven, the virgin Pudentiana shines.”

] [Note: [Col. 0069A]]

**PULSANEN.:** Pure only in the second announcement; in the first it omits everything after “eunuchs,” and in the third everything after “virgin.”

**ROSWEYD.:** Adds at the end: “Likewise in Britain, in the city of Canterbury, Saint Dunstan, archbishop.”

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.:** Also at the end: “On the same day, the passing of blessed Dunstan, archbishop and confessor.”

**MUNERAT.:** “On the same day, the feast of Saint Peter Celestine, pope and confessor. In Lesser Britain, in the diocese of Tréguier, Saint Ivo, priest and confessor.”

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC.,** and the **EDITIO-ULTRAJ.-BELG.:** Begin with Potentiana, where they are pure. Then follows the entry for Pudens, where “disciple of Paul” is inserted from Ado. In the other announcement, “eunuchs of the wife of Decius” is added from the same source. At the end they append: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Adolphus, confessor, bishop of Cambrai.”

[Col. 0069B] **CENTULEN.:** “At Rome, the feast of Saint Potentiana, virgin. On the same day, of the most blessed Pudens, father of the aforementioned virgin. Likewise at Rome, Saints Calocerus and Parthenius, eunuchs of the wife of the emperor Decius. At the monastery of Blandinium, the feast of Saint Bertulf, confessor and monk.” See 5 February.

**BRUXELLEN.:** Interpolated in Potentiana and Pudens, but purer in Calocerus and Parthenius, it adds: “And the deposition of Saint Dunstan, archbishop of the English. On the same day, the deposition of blessed Hildebert, or Emebert, bishop of Cambrai, the full brother of blessed Gudila, our patroness. He succeeded Vindicianus in the bishopric of Cambrai through the agency of Saint Autbert.” He is listed among those omitted on the following day. He was treated on 15 January. “Likewise Saint Ivo, confessor, who was first advocate of the poor in the parliament of the kingdom of France and afterward bishop of Chartres.” He is commemorated on the following day. “At Rome, Saint Peter, confessor, who, when he was Pope Celestine V, freely renounced the honor and burden of the supreme pontificate. And Celestine, descending from Peter’s lofty seat so that he might ascend the heavenly seat, humbly prostrated himself at the feet of the Cardinals over whom he had presided. O glorious man, who, by the example of no one, voluntarily abandoned the papacy—than which nothing on earth is more wondrous—so that he might serve Christ more peacefully.”

**HAGENOYEN.:** Interpolated in the text, it adds near the end: “At Trier, Cyril, bishop and confessor.”

**AQUICINCT.:** Has nearly the same account of Dunstan. See below, the later editions of Molan.

**MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:** “Calocerus and Parthenius, brother martyrs. Potentiana, virgin. Ivo, confessor. Dunstan, archbishop.”

**BIGOTIAN.,** designated P. 5, formerly belonging to the Celestine Fathers: “Likewise the feast of blessed Peter, Our Father, of Murrone, confessor, formerly Pope Celestine.”

In the **VATICAN**, number 5949, it is absent: “Pudens.”

**ALTEMPS.:** “At Torres in Sardinia, Crescentianus, martyr.”

[Col. 0069D] **STROZZIAN.:** In first place, or in other copies last: “In the province of Tuscany—he should have said ‘Latium,’ or at least ‘Campania’ in the broader sense—at the city of Ferentinum, the deposition of Saint Peter, pope and confessor, formerly Celestine, who is called ‘of Murone’”—more properly read “Celestine, pope … formerly Peter”—founder of the Order of the Celestines, who founded many monasteries, became father of innumerable monks, and shone forth through many miracles and virtues. He was born in the year of the Lord 1216, lived in the world for 17 years, spent 34 years in penance, was raised to the papacy in the year of the Lord 1296—actually 1294—rested in the year of the Lord 1216, and lived 81 years. He was canonized by Pope Clement [Col. 0070A] in the year of the Lord 1306—actually 1312. On the same day at Florence, the passing of Blessed Emiliana of Circuli, who was buried at the place of the Friars Minor in Florence in the year of the Lord 1246 and shone forth through virtues and miracles. At Lucca, the deposition of Saint Theodore, bishop, who was buried in the basilica of Saint Donatus, in which he had formerly ruled admirably as bishop.”

**EDITIO LUBECO-COL.:** Interpolated in Potentiana and Pudens, it adds: “At Trier, Saint Cyril, bishop and confessor.” Then concerning Calocerus and the others, as in the manuscripts above. It continues: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Dunstan, archbishop and confessor of the English. Likewise the commemoration of the deposition of Saint Ivo, priest and confessor, and his canonization, which was carried out in the year of the Lord 1347 by Lord Pope Clement VI. And Saint Peter Celestine, confessor, from whom the Order of the Celestines is named.”

**BELIN.:** Mutilated in the entry for Pudens, it adds at the end: “On the same [Col. 0070B] day, Saint Peter Celestine of Morone, who, because he renounced the supreme pontificate, was canonized by the Church only as a simple confessor.” The Paris edition adds: “At Torres in Sardinia, the feast of Saint Crestianus, martyr.”

**GREVEN.:** “At Alexandria, Saint John, martyr, who, while serving as a military commander under Maximian and persecuting Christians, was converted from heaven, warned like Paul. Later, for the faith of Christ, he was torn on the rack, his face was crushed, he was beaten with leaden weights, shut inside a fiery furnace, and finally beheaded; he departed victorious.” See the Acts. “Urban, pope and confessor.” See the *Omissions*. Concerning Cyril, as above. “Peter, confessor, who was Pope Celestine V. On account of the holiness of his life, the Cardinals elected him when the Apostolic See had already been vacant for two years. But he wished to devote himself to God alone; after five months he laid down the burden, and, always becoming better than himself, rested in peace. Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury and confessor, who, taking the monastic habit in his youth, was esteemed admirable in life and miracles, became primate of all England, and rested with a blessed end in the year of the Lord 988. Adolphus, bishop and confessor of Cambrai. In Lesser Britain, in the diocese of Tréguier, the deposition of Saint Ivo, priest and confessor, doctor of both laws and advocate of the poor; and his canonization, carried out in the year of the Lord 1347. Likewise blessed Alchin”—I think “Alcuin.” Perhaps from Rabanus.

**MOLAN.:** “On the same day, Saint Peter Celestine of Morone, who, because he renounced the supreme pontificate, was canonized by the Church only as a simple confessor.
