On the same day, Saint Cyril, bishop of Trier. In Lesser Britain, in the diocese of Tréguier, Saint Ivo, priest and confessor, who for the love of Christ never ceased defending the causes of orphans, widows, and the poor. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Dunstan, archbishop of the English. At the monastery of Nobiliacum, the deposition of Saint Hadulphus, bishop [Col. 0070D] and confessor, resting at Arras in the church of Saint Vedastus.” In smaller type: “The deposition of Lord Alcuin.” Other editions have the same material concerning Peter Celestine, Hadulphus, and Ivo as the earlier edition. It continues: “In the city of Dorobernia, Saint Dunstan, archbishop, who built the famous monastery of Glastonbury and became the founder of many other monasteries. At his sarcophagus it is often revealed what sort of merit he now possesses in heaven.” Concerning Cyril, as above. “On the nineteenth day, Saint Patricius of Prusa, holy martyr, and his companions.” See in the *Omissions*, where it is said that they were treated on 28 April. Concerning Alcuin, as above.]

[Col. 0067]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of Saints Calocerus and Parthenius, eunuchs. The former was chief chamberlain of the emperor Decius, the latter chief secretary; because they refused to sacrifice to idols, they were killed by Decius himself. Likewise at Rome, Saint Potentiana, virgin, who, after countless struggles, after reverently providing burial for many martyrs, and after distributing all her possessions to the poor for Christ’s sake, finally passed from earth to heaven. On that same day, blessed Pudens, father of the aforementioned virgin, who, having been clothed with Christ by the apostles in baptism, guarded and preserved his innocent garment undefiled until the crown of life.

**XIII Kal. Day 20.**

[Note: [Col. 0071]]

Taken from the Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Rosweyd., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0071A]]

Apart from scribal errors, they offer nothing especially noteworthy, such as *Femanso*, *Baudelii*, *Austregisilli*, *martirii*, and so forth. All the manuscripts here write *Galieni*, except the Pratensis; with the latter I would prefer to read *Gallieni*, but I follow the general stream. Greven. corrupts the syntax by writing *accusata est*. Antuerp.-Maj., instead of *sponsum reciperet* (“she might accept a bridegroom”), has *perciperet* (“she might receive”). Greven. and Molan., instead of *morte percepit* (“she attained through death”), substitute *suscepit* (“she received”). Rosweyd., instead of *Bituricas*, has *Bituricis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0071A]]

The *Little Roman Martyrology* clearly records Basilla, virgin and martyr, on this day; and there is no doubt that this same woman appears in the Hieronymian copies, whatever the corruption of her name and its confusion with her companions. Ado composed an illustrious eulogy for her alone; Notker copied it, and Our author elegantly condensed it. If only it were sufficiently consistent with the truth. What is narrated here was taken from famous Acts—or rather from a pious drama, embellished long ago by I know not whom in honor of Saint Eugenia—from which eulogies were also fashioned for other saints. Let the reader consult Papebrochius’s dissertation for this day, and what he had to argue again in his responses to article 16, beginning at number 91. Whatever may be thought of those attractive fictions, the cult of Saint Basilla, or Basilissa, remains beyond doubt, abundantly confirmed by the Hieronymian copies and our Martyrologists. Add to this her very ancient memory in the Bucherian Calendar, where the cemetery of Basilla is mentioned more than once, and probably this Basilla, distinguished from another who is listed in that Calendar on the tenth day before the Kalends of October: “Basilla, on the Old Salarian Way, in the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian,” and whom Florentinius and Papebrochius think to be the woman mentioned in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 11 June, as may be seen in both authors on that day.

Baudelius is unknown to the *Little Roman Martyrology* and was taken by Ado from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which he is reported incompletely as *Saudeli*, *Haudeli*, and under other corruptions. Again, the whole eulogy is Ado’s, transferred into Notker’s Martyrology and expanded by a few additions, while Usuard rendered it more briefly [Col. 0072A]. It was taken from older Acts edited and illustrated by Henschenius, who acknowledges that they themselves are not of the highest merit, although he greatly prefers them to the apocryphal Acts of Orléans. The account transmitted from Gregory of Tours in the appendix to the Acts provides more reliable knowledge of the holy martyr, and together with our Martyrologies clearly establishes the antiquity of Baudelius’s cult. You will find how highly Tillemont values the aforementioned Acts in volume IV, beginning at p. 724, where, following Henschenius, he carefully explains several matters concerning whether there was one Baudelius or two, the time of his martyrdom, the translations of his relics, and other questions not relevant to the purpose of this work. Wandalbert elegantly expressed the two announcements just mentioned:

“When ten holds and supports three, Basilla,  
And Baudelius likewise, clad in blood, blooms anew.”

Ado does not mention Austregisilus, nor do authors older than him. [Col. 0072B] Notker inserted him into his calendar. There can be no doubt about Usuard, given the virtually unanimous agreement of almost all the manuscripts. Florentinius rightly judged that Austregisilus does not belong in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, although he appears in his Lucensis copy. Since that manuscript was brought from Gaul to Lucca, and, as the distinguished Castellanus observes, from the monastery of Saint Wandregisilus, it is not surprising if the name of Austregisilus was subsequently added by some monk, since it is absent from the other copies. See what Henschenius carefully collected and arranged concerning him. Also the *Acta Benedictina*, century 2, beginning at p. 95.]

[Note: [Col. 0071B]]

**PULSANEN.:** Begins as follows: “At Rome, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, the passion of the blessed martyrs Eustasius, surnamed Placidi, and his wife Theopista, with their sons Agapitus and Theopistus, whose wondrous deeds are read.” It is referred to the solemn feast on 20 September. It then continues with Basilla [Col. 0071C] and Baudelius, but with their eulogies completely truncated. Nothing concerning Austregisilus is read in that manuscript.

**ANTUERP. MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC.,** and the **EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG.:** They are almost pure, differing only in being fuller because they insert from Ado into the text: “Having been summoned, she replied that she had the King of kings as her bridegroom, and with the sword,” and so forth. Max.-Lubec., more defective than the others, omits Austregisilus at the end.

**CENTULEN.:** “At Rome, Saint Basilla, virgin, who, converted from royal stock through blessed Eugenia, rejected a very wealthy and powerful bridegroom and submitted her neck to the sword for the love of Christ. At the city of Nîmes, Saint Baudelius, martyr. At Bourges, and so forth.” Correctly so.

**BRUXELLEN.:** Begins as follows: “In Africa, the feast of the holy virgins Victoria and Marcellosa.” It then proceeds [Col. 0072B] fairly purely with Basilla and Baudelius. Then: “Also Mucius, who suffered at the hands of the Jews. Because of his confession of the Son of God, they stretched him out in bonds of rope and inflicted such wounds on his body that his limbs were fed upon by worms; yet in all these things he remained unconquered and gave up his spirit to God.” He is placed in the Acts on the following day. [Col. 0072C] “Likewise Ethelbert, martyr”—he meant Ethelbert, king of the East Angles. “On the same day, at Bourges, Saint Austregisilus, bishop and confessor. And Saint Bernardine, confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor, whom Pope Nicholas V canonized.”

**HAGENOYEN.:** Interpolating the text slightly, inserts near the end: “Likewise Celestine, confessor.” This can be no one other than Pope Celestine V, concerning whom we spoke yesterday.

**VICTORIN.** and **REG. SUEC.,** designated number 130: “On the same day, Saint Eustasius with his wife and sons.” We have already said that he is commemorated on 20 September.

**REGINAE SUECIAE,** which belonged to Prince Ursinus Rosenberg: “In the city of Aquila, Saint Bernardine, of the Order of Friars Minor.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Basilla, virgin and martyr. Of Saturnina, virgin.” In the Acts she has companions. “Of Conon the martyr and his son.” Rabanus says much about him on this day, but the entry is referred to 29 May. “Of Baudelius the martyr. Of Austregisilus, bishop.”

REG. SUEC., numbered 428: “At the monastery of Flaviacum, translation of Saint Geremar the confessor.” Referred to his feast day, 24 September.

In VATICAN. no. 5949, Austregisilus is absent. Added at the beginning, however, is: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Eustasius, who in the time of the emperor Trajan was crowned with martyrdom together with his wife and sons.”

FLORENTIN., at the beginning or end: “The feast of Saint Bernardino of Siena, confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor, distinguished in life, teaching, and preaching of the word of God. He died at Aquila, where he also rests in the church dedicated to him under his own name. By his word and example he illumined all Italy. Likewise, in Sconium [Iconium], a province of Isauria, of Saint Conon with his son, who suffered for Christ under the governor Maximian [Medic. Domitianus]. Of Saint Eustasius the martyr with his companions.” See above.

BURDEGALEN.: “At Angers, translation of the body of Saint Lucinius, bishop and confessor.” He is commemorated on 13 February.

ABDINGHOFFEN.: “And of Saint Saturnina, virgin and martyr.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL., interpolating Basilla and Baudelius, but pure in Austregisilus, adds as follows: “At the city of Aquila, the feast of blessed Bernardino, confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor. In England, of Saint Athelbert, king and martyr. On the same day, of Saint Saturnina, virgin and martyr.”

BELIN. agrees with ANTUERP. and the others cited above in the entry for Basilla. Then: “At Pavia, of Saint Theodore, bishop and confessor. On the same day, of Saint Eustasius the martyr with his companions. In Gaul, at the city of Nîmes, of Saint Baudelius the martyr. At Bourges, of blessed Aistrigilis, bishop and martyr. On the same day, of Saint Bernardino of Siena, confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor, resting in the city of Aquila, who illumined all Italy by his word and example.”

GREVEN.: “Of Athelbert, king of England and martyr. Likewise of Saints Marcellus and Victoria [read: Marceliocae]. According to some, on this day of Conon the martyr and his son, who are placed below on 29 May. Likewise, according to the Catalogue of the Saints, on this day the passion of Saint Eustasius and his companions, who are placed below on 2 November. The deposition of Saints Vellesius and Faustinus, bishops. At Pavia, of Saint Theodore, bishop and confessor. In the city of Aquila in Abruzzo, the deposition of Saint Bernardino of Siena, priest and confessor of the Order of Friars Minor. From childhood his most sincere way of life brought considerable admiration to those who observed it. For, having entered the aforesaid order, by his most fervent preaching and writings he won countless souls for Christ, and rested in peace around the year of the Lord 1343, or rather 1344. Of Saturnina, virgin and martyr.”

[Col. 0074B]

MOLAN.: “At Blandinium, translation of the bodies of Saints Guduald and Berthulf, together with the relics of Saint Amelberga, virgin.” See in the list of omitted entries the individual days to which they are referred. “At Pavia, of Saint Theodore, bishop and confessor. On the same day, of Saint Eustasius the martyr with his companions.” Concerning Bernardino he reports the words of BELINUS: “At Trier, in the monastery commonly called Horreum, of Basilissa, virgin.” See the catalogue of omitted entries. In the other editions the entries concerning Theodore and Bernardino are as in the first. It continues: “At Trier, of Saint Maximinus the martyr, the first bishop of Trier of that name.” Consult the omitted entries. Then: “And in the monastery commonly called Horreum, of Basilissa, virgin. At Hereford, of Saint Athelbert, king of the East Angles and martyr. On the twentieth day, of Saint Thalaleus the martyr.” See his companions in the Acts. “At Blandinium, translation,” etc., as above.

[Col. 0073]

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the feast of Saint Basilla, virgin and martyr, who, being of royal lineage and having a most illustrious fiancé, was accused by him of being a Christian. The emperor Gallienus decreed that she should either accept her fiancé or perish by the sword. Summoned on this matter and refusing to give her consent, she was pierced through with a sword. In Gaul, at the city of Nîmes, of Saint Baudelius the martyr, who, after being arrested and refusing to sacrifice, persevered immovable in the faith of Christ amid blows and tortures and received the palm of martyrdom through a precious death. At Bourges, of blessed Austregisilus, bishop and confessor.

XII Kal. Day 21. [Note: [Col. 0073C]

The text is found in Praten., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerpien. and Max.-Lubec., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven. and Molan. It is also found in Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., [Col. 0074C] Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic. and Edit. Ultraj.-Belg.]

[Note: [Col. 0073C]

Here again much must be attributed to the carelessness of copyists. I give only a small selection. Mauricania, Thimothei, Thymothei, Eutici, Euticii, Capadociae, Capadotia, Poliveti, Polieveti, Polionati, Polmeti, Polioti, Poliocti, and so forth. More notable is the reading offered by the Pulsan. codex, following Ado, which reads diaconorum instead of diaconi. [Col. 0074C] It also has, contrary to the text, coronati sunt. Finally, it goes most astray in this inept construction or combination: “Likewise, in the aforesaid region of Caesarea of Cappadocia,” etc. Antuerp.-Maj. preferred to write Domini verbum instead of verbum Domini.]

[Note: [Col. 0073D]

Of the whole text for today, this alone can be said: no records are found concerning any of the saints enumerated in it except those contained in the Martyrologies, so that they are known almost solely by name. Thus most of the Hieronymian codices form the first announcement: “In Mauretania, of Timothy, Polyus, and Eutychius the deacon,” leaving uncertain to which of the two Mauretanias—the aforesaid martyrs should be assigned, whether Tingitana or Caesariensis. The small Roman Martyrology removes the doubt by expressly indicating: “In Mauretania Caesariensis, of Timothy and Polyus,” although there the third companion is missing. Ado restored him and composed a fairly commonplace eulogy, such as is displayed in the entry, with this sole difference from Ado that he reads in the plural, diaconorum, whereas our author, together with the Hieronymian copies, appears to restrict whatever dignity is meant to Eutychius alone. Whether Usuard did this deliberately or by accident I do not investigate. Certainly in Notker Ado’s sentence remained intact, with only the word civitate inserted—incorrectly, as Henschenius rightly observed long ago. Wandalbertus celebrates our three martyrs in one verse; the other two lines do not belong to this text:

“On the twelfth, Polyus, Eutychius, and Timothy [are commemorated].”

The name of the leader of the Cappadocian martyrs is pronounced variously by nearly all the codices, both printed and manuscript, ancient and recent, as we have indicated above and as is also fully explained in the Acts. The Hieronymian copies generally give Policutes; the Usuardine witnesses are inconsistent with themselves. Ado, and Notker who follows him, more correctly have Polyeuctus; amid such disagreement among the codices, I thought that form preferable. For the rest, our text is Ado’s. The final martyr, Secundinus, is, I think, one of those whom Usuard brought from Spain into Gaul, relying on confused information received there. Nor do the Spanish sources provide anything from which the time of his martyrdom can be determined more precisely. Henschenius, lacking the Acts or other more reliable records, very plausibly conjectures that he belonged not to that famous persecution of the Moors, [Col. 0076A] but to the much earlier persecution under Diocletian. The commemoration of Secundinus therefore seems to rest solely on Usuard’s authority. Yet whoever unearthed him and from wherever, Usuard was the first to enter him in the sacred calendars; and in this respect the certainty of his reading is as great as the certainty that everything else was taken from Ado.]

[Note: [Col. 0075A]

HERINIEN., after the pure text, adds: “Likewise, of Saint Romanus the monk.” I think this is the Romanus who is placed in the Acts on the following day and who, in the Pratense codex, is assigned on that same day to Sens. Hence the conjecture that Romanus was specially venerated in that church or monastery which once possessed the Herinien. codex.

ROSWEYD., at the end: “At Augia, of Valens, bishop and martyr, and Januarius the martyr.” See the list of omitted entries and the following day. See also what Castellanus noted about Valens on this day in his Universal Martyrology.

CENTULEN.: “In Mauretania Caesariensis, of Saints Timothy, Polyus [Col. 0075B] and Eutychius the deacon. At Caesarea of Cappadocia, of Saints Polyeuctus, Victor, and Donatus. At Auxerre, of Saint Valis, priest and confessor. At Córdoba, of Saint Secundinus the martyr.” We have just spoken of Vale, or Valens.

BRUXELLEN., fairly pure in the first announcement, continues as follows: “And of Saint Valens, bishop and martyr. At Caesarea of Cappadocia, the feast of Saints Polyeuctus, Victor, and Donatus. On the same day, the deposition of Constantine the Great, emperor, who left to rulers the way of faith and devotion, and whom Gregory in the Register, Ambrose in his exposition of the fourteenth psalm, and Isidore in his Chronicles record as having been of great merit before God and as having ended his life happily. At the city of Córdoba, of Saint Secundinus the martyr. At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Vitalis the priest.” He is the one called Valis above.

HAGENOYEN., pure at the beginning, has in second place an entry concerning Dioscorus, the Egyptian martyr, whom we included with Usuard on 18 May. It continues with the Cappadocians and Secundinus, fairly correctly.

VICTORIN., at the end: “Who, as blessed Cyprian writes in his book On the Lapsed, completed their martyrdom through the fire of suffering. In Corsica, of Saint Julia, who was crowned by the punishment of the cross. At Auxerre, of Helena, virgin.” All these, however, belong to the text of the following day.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Timothy, Polyus, and Eutychius, martyrs; of Polyeuctus, Victorius, and Donatus.” Everything is corrupted in the customary manner.

REGINAE SUEC., numbered 428: “On the same day, of Saint Romanus the monk, who gave the monastic habit to blessed Benedict.” It is clear that the Romanus of Subiaco is meant. In the supplements he is confused, under 28 February, with Romanus of Jura; the error is amply demonstrated in the Acts for that day. Ferrarius further holds that the aforesaid Romanus of Subiaco is the same as the present Romanus of Auxerre or Sens, or rather of Fontenelle. With what probability this is asserted may be seen in Henschenius’s annotations on the foolish argument in chapter 1 of the Acts of this Romanus, 22 May; we mentioned it briefly under 28 February.

In VATICAN. no. 5949, Secundinus is absent.

ALTEMPS.: “On the same day, at Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Vitalis, Vialis, or Valens,” as above.

STROZZIAN.: “Translation of blessed Paul the martyr from Constantinople to the city of Venice, to the monastery of Saint George Major, in the year of the Lord 1222, indiction 2.” Referred to 8 July. “On the same day, of Saints Genesius and Theopontus and Saint Helena.” The first two are listed under their true names on 3 January; Helena is celebrated on her proper day, 18 August. See the observations there.

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Valis, priest and confessor.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL., in a fairly pure text, adds: “On the same day, of blessed Valens, bishop, and the three boys martyred with him: first they were bound by the feet for Christ, then raised upon the rack, repeatedly [tortured,] and finally struck with the sword, thus attaining the crown of martyrdom. At Troyes, of Saint Maurilius the confessor. At Auxerre, of blessed Vallis, priest and confessor.” There is frequent variation in the name.

BELIN., in the text, reads Hippolytus instead of Polyus. Then he adds: “Likewise, translation of blessed Paul the martyr from Constantinople to Venice, to the monastery of Saint George Major, in the year of the Lord 1222, indiction ten. On the same day, of Saints Genesius and Theopontius and Saint Helena.” See above.

GREVEN.: “Of Valens, bishop, and the three boys with him; first bound for Christ, then raised upon the rack and repeatedly tortured, and finally struck with the sword, they attained the palm of martyrdom. In Africa, the feast of Saints Victor, Maurella, Quintus, Primulus, Salustius, and Fortunatus.” See the other two companions in the Acts. “According to some, on this day the deposition of Constantine the emperor. At Auxerre, of blessed Vallis, priest and confessor. At Troyes, of Saint Maurilius the confessor. Of Valerianus the priest.” See what is said about him in the omitted entries. “Of Hospitius, confessor and man of God, who, shut up near Nuceria [Nicaea], with iron fastened against his flesh, distinguished by the virtue of abstinence, also shone through the spirit of prophecy.”

MOLAN.: “The feast of Saint Idaberga, virgin.” In the Acts she is called “Itisberga. Likewise, translation of blessed Paul the martyr from Constantinople to the city of Venice,” etc., as in BELINUS. “On the same day, of Saints Synesius and Theopontius,” also as there: “And of Saint Valens, martyr and bishop.” In smaller type it follows: “Of Hospitius the confessor,” etc., from GREVENUS. Other editions have: “At Aria, the feast of Saint Idaberga, virgin. In the city of Auxerre, of blessed Vualis, priest and confessor. In Lusitania, at the village of Miliana, the passion of Saint Maucius, killed by Jews.” The translation of Paul follows, as above. “On the same day, of Saints Synesius and Theopontius. And of Saint Valens, martyr and bishop:

‘Augia leads him through joyful delights with happy prayers.’”

“On the twenty-first day, of the great holy kings equal to the apostles, Constantine and Helena.” Then in smaller letters: “Constantine honored the Church of God with the greatest privileges, spread the faith, built churches, and, full of good works, rested in peace. When bishops had assembled, he burned the documents of accusation brought against them, saying: ‘You are gods, appointed by the true God; go and settle your cases among yourselves.’ At Nicaea in Gaul, of Saint Hospitius the confessor and man of God, who, distinguished by the virtue of abstinence, also shone through the spirit of prophecy. In England, the deposition of blessed Godric, hermit and confessor, whose illustrious Acts survive.” See Henschenius’s commentary on him and the life written by his contemporary, Geoffrey.]

[Col. 0073]

In Mauretania Caesariensis, the feast of Saints Timothy, Polyus, and Eutychius the deacon, who, spreading the word of the Lord in the aforesaid region, deserved to be crowned together. Likewise, at Caesarea of Cappadocia, the feast of Saints Polyeuctus, Victorius, and Donatus. At Córdoba, of Secundinus [Note: [Col. 0073] The name “Saint Secundinus” occupies an erasure in the codex. Who or what formerly stood in its place? There is nevertheless no difference affecting the text. BOUILLART.] the martyr.

XI Kal. Day 22. [Note: [Col. 0077]

Thus in Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven. and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0077A]

Molan., more correct than the other codices, writes Aemilius, but we have taken Usuard’s spelling from other manuscripts and printed editions. It is uncertain whether Usuard read scribit, “he writes,” or scripsit, “he wrote.” Praten., Tornacen., Rosweyd. and Munerat. have the past tense. Herinien., Pulsan., Antuerp.-Maj., Greven. and Molan. have the present. Either reading may be preferred indifferently; I favor [Col. 0078A] Ado’s reading. Munerat. is wrong to put consummavit for consummaverunt; nor is the alteration made by Greven. and Molan. more satisfactory, since they substitute compleverunt. Again, Munerato has Cortica incorrectly; Greven. has Julianae instead of Juliae; finally, Rosweyd., Greven. and Molan. prefix the title “Saint” to Helena.]

[Note: [Col. 0077A]

Florentinius devotes himself entirely to counting, distinguishing, and distributing the martyrs of this day on the basis of the ambiguous wording of the Hieronymian codices. I do not wish to claim greater knowledge than that most diligent man. But, in accordance with our purpose, I note that he wrongly attributes Faustinus, Timothy, and Venustus to Bede, whom he had not previously seen in a pure form; and even more wrongly to Usuard, who differs very greatly from the supplements of Molan. What is true is that Bede remembers Castus and Aemilius, in a phrase not far removed from Ado’s, which Rabanus borrowed. The small Roman Martyrology indicates them more briefly. As I said, Ado generally follows Bede, and Notker follows Ado. [Col. 0077B] Usuard, however, inserted in a parenthesis what others had placed at the end, concerning the testimony of blessed Cyprian. The fall of both martyrs, but also their glorious repentance afterward, is described briefly but elegantly by that celebrated Father, and the Acts reproduce it. Permit us to quote these few words:

“Thus the Lord at one time forgave Castus and Aemilius; thus, defeated in the first encounter, he made them victors in the second battle, so that those who had previously yielded to the flames became stronger than the flames, and by the very means by which they had been overcome, they overcame.”

See the notable passage concerning the same men in Augustine, cited by Tillemont, volume III, p. 126. The most ancient memory of these martyrs is also found in the Carthaginian Calendar edited by Mabillon. Wandalbertus briefly adorns them as follows:

“Castus and Aemilius the holy consecrated the eleventh.”

Mosander developed the history of Julia of Corsica at length, attributing it to Ado. Yet that this is not Ado’s eulogy is made probable by Rosweyd’s more accurate edition, and Florentinius himself freely admits it, adding that a similar narrative is given by Peter de Natalibus, book V, chapter 29. Comparison shows that the two accounts also differ, although it is certain that both flowed from the same Acts. Ado’s genuine words very briefly embrace the sequence of her martyrdom, and Notker and our author copied them without elaboration. As for what should be thought of Mosander’s and Peter’s histories, the various Acts, and the translation, let the reader gather it from Papebrochius’s commentary. There the Master sufficiently indicates his inclination toward the view that the Virgin suffered in the sixth or seventh century, contrary to Baronio’s opinion in his current annotation and to Theodoric Ruinart’s in his Commentary on the Vandal Persecution, p. 451, where he reproduces her Acts collated with another manuscript from Reims. We leave it to others to judge which opinion should be preferred.]

Concerning Helena, one may be surprised to find Florentinius writing as follows: “Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Notker remember Helena,” when this can truly be asserted only of the last two and the one before last. I say nothing about Bede, whom he possessed only in a spurious form. But the learned author could plainly see in Rosweyd’s edition of Ado that Helena is absent, having been rejected into the appendix, and that Mosander himself marked her with an asterisk, just as he had rightly observed earlier concerning Faustinus and Timothy. As for the fact that both her deposition and her translation are mentioned in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Henschenius rightly judged that these were additions made by later writers; Florentinius should have thought the same when he distinguished Helena’s commemoration from the genuine text by printing it in Italian type. However the matter may stand—whether Helena became known to Usuard through Hieronymian copies or through the Acts of Saint Amator—it is certain that Usuard himself entered her into the sacred records. The origin of the earlier entries and their insertion is now clear. See the Acts of Saint Amator, illustrated on 1 May, no. 31, and what Tillemont also says briefly about her in the Life of Saint Germanus, volume XV, p. 11.]

[Note: [Col. 0077C]

In our copy of PRATEN., near the end, we read: “At Sens, of Saint Romanus the confessor.” I have little doubt that this was added later in the margin and therefore does not affect the purity of the codex, as we have noted elsewhere. What should be thought of this Romanus, let the reader see in the Acts for this day and for 28 February. See also the supplements for the preceding day, from HERINIEN. and REG. SUEC., no. 428.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., AQUICINCT., VICTORIN. and UGHELIAN. add only at the end: “At Rome, of Saints Faustinus and Timothy.”

ANTUERPIEN.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC. and EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG. append the following concerning Helena to the pure text: “Who, as is read in the deeds of Saint Amator, was distinguished by manifold virtue of merits and shone through miracles.” Then: “At Rome, of Saints Faustinus and Timothy.” GREVEN adds another companion.

CENTULEN.: “In Africa, of Saints Castus and Aemilius, who completed their martyrdom through fire. At Auxerre, [Col. 0077D] of Saint Helena, virgin, who shone with manifold virtue. In Corsica, of Saint Julia, who was crowned by the punishment of the cross.” See below.

BRUXELLEN. differs in no matter of meaning from ANTUERP.-MAX., [Col. 0078C] etc. But it places the announcement of Faustinus and Timothy in the penultimate position.

HAGENOYEN. omitted Helena. Pure in the first announcement, it continues: “On the same day, of Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, who had been captured in Carthage and presented to Eusebius as a slave; she served him faithfully, yet did not neglect divine worship. Therefore Eusebius loved her greatly and refused to accept four other slave women from Felix, governor of the province of Corsica, in exchange for her. He also praised her excessively. Eusebius became drunk, and Julia was violently taken from the ship; because she refused to consent to sacrifice to idols, she was struck on the face, her hair was twisted, and she was suspended and scourged while hanging. Finally, she completed her martyrdom by being fastened to a cross. On the cross she prayed and died, and in the form of a dove her soul ascended to heaven before the eyes of all.” These things are almost entirely taken from the historical narrative developed above. It continues: “At Constantinople, the deposition of Saint Constantine the emperor, who was called the Great. He also fought nobly for the empire, so as to preserve peace among all nations. He is found in the Chronicles. He too, as the first emperor, granted privileges to the Roman pontiffs and to the churches. He assigned royal tithes to the churches and to the ministers of Christ. At first this Constantine was a persecutor of the Church, not personally but through his agents; therefore he became a leper, and was cleansed of leprosy by blessed Silvester in baptism, where Christ appeared to him, and thereafter he became a propagator of the Church. At Rome he also built the church of the Savior, that is, the Holy of Holies; the church of blessed Peter the apostle, which he made the head and mother of all churches; and those of Saint Paul and Saint John the Baptist at the Lateran. Thus, after arranging the state well and exalting the Church of God in a wondrous manner, he died with great devotion at Constantinople and was buried in the church of the Apostles, which he himself had built. The Greeks celebrate his feast.” The learned reader will easily distinguish for himself what is mixed here with truth and falsehood. Constantine is commemorated on the preceding day, as reported there in the Acts.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Julia, virgin and martyr. Of Helena, virgin. Of Castus and Aemilius, concerning whom blessed Cyprian writes.”

ALTEMPS.: “At Rome, of Saints Faustinus and Timothy [Col. 0079B] the martyrs. In Gaul, at the monastery called Bonaevallis [Vallilias], of Saint Romanus the confessor, disciple of Saint Benedict.” Enough has been said about him.

FLORENTIN.: “At the city of Ravenna, of Saint Martianus, archbishop and confessor.” Then STROZZIAN.: “The feast of Saint Soter, pope, is celebrated on 22 April. Likewise at Rome, the deposition of Saint Urban, pope and martyr, whose feast is celebrated on 25 May.” I do not know why these are noted there on this day.

BURDEGALEN.: “Of Quiteria, virgin and martyr.” Our Acts write Quiteria.

LUXOVIEN.: “In the district of Sens, at the monastery of Vallisdiacum, translation of the body of the most blessed Romanus the confessor.” See what we said above concerning PRATEN., etc.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL., pure in the first announcement and somewhat interpolated in the second, is otherwise like the codices cited above, ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. But it adds: “On the same day, of Saints Sanctinus and Antonius, confessors, disciples of Saint Dionysius, who successively governed the church of Meaux in episcopal office and rested in the Lord.” See the omitted entries. “At Limoges, of Saint Lupinus [Lupus], bishop and confessor. At Auxerre, of blessed Romanus, abbot.” Unless I am mistaken, he is the same Romanus assigned above in other places.

BELIN., in the first edition, at the end: “At Rome, of Saints Faustinus and Timothy.” In the other edition is added: “In Gaul, at the monastery called Vallilias, of Saint Romanus, abbot, disciple of Father Benedict.”

GREVEN.: “At Rome, the feast of Saints Faustinus, Timothy, and Venustus. Likewise of Maxentius and Felix, companions of Goswinus the martyr. On the same day, of Saints Sanctinus and Antonius, confessors, disciples,” etc., as above. “At Limoges, of Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, as is said in book III of the Ecclesiastical History, the deposition of blessed Constantine the Great, emperor and confessor. He honored the Church of God with the greatest privileges, spread the faith, built churches, and, full of good works, rested in peace. At Auxerre, of blessed [Col. 0080B] Romanus, abbot. On the same day, of Saint Bonus.” Is this Bonus or Bononus? “In Gascony, of Quiteria, virgin and martyr, and of others.”

MOLAN continues the sense: “Who, as in the deeds of Saint Amator, etc. In the city of Auxerre, of blessed Vualis, priest and confessor.” Concerning him, see the preceding day. “At Rome, of Saints Faustinus and Timothy. In Gaul, at the monastery called Vallilas,” etc. “On the same day, of Saint Bonus.” Then in smaller type: “Of Goswinus the martyr.” Enough has been said about Constantine. In the other editions the entries concerning Helena, Romanus, and Bonus are as on the preceding day. It continues: “In Gascony, of Saint Quiteria, virgin, who with many others endured a glorious martyrdom. At Rome, of Saints Faustinus and Timothy. On the twenty-second day, of Saint Basilicus the martyr.” He is commemorated on 3 March. Finally, in small letters: “At Rome, of Saint Goswinus, boy and martyr.” See the Acts concerning him.]

[Col. 0077]

In Africa, the feast of Saints Castus and Aemilius, who, as blessed Cyprian writes in his book On the Lapsed, completed their martyrdom through the fire of suffering. In Corsica, of Saint Julia, who was crowned by the punishment of the cross. At Auxerre, of Helena, virgin.

X Kal. Day 23. [Note: [Col. 0079]

The codices Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0079C]

The first variation occurs in the name of the Vandals, which we both write and pronounce as such. Nevertheless, I have followed the codices Praten., Herinien., Rosweyd., and others in which that letter is not used. Greven. wrote it correctly; Munerat. incorrectly writes Unandalorum. Tornacen. and Pulsanen. form Guandalorum, by the quite usual change of V into G, and perhaps from this root, Ganda from Wanda, as happens in various names, such as Guillelmus and Willelmus, Guido and Wido, Gualterus and Walterus, Gasconia and Vasconia, and others noted by Honoratus Bouche in the Chorography of Provence, vol. I, book IV, chap. 2, § 5, on the occasion of the city of Vapingum, commonly Gap. It will be useful to have indicated this once, since it will serve elsewhere too. Thus on this very day the supplements have Guibertus and Wibertus of Gembloux; so on 1 April, Gualericus and Walericus; elsewhere Guandelbertus for Wandelbertus, etc. Should anyone take pleasure in more such examples, I have material that would furnish a not-uninteresting dissertation.

The second variation is in quique for ovibus, as Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven., and others have it, with an incorrect sense. Pulsanen. and Molan. corrected it by introducing the conjunction, reading qui pro ovibus, or, as Munerat. has it, Qui mox pro. Either reading is purer, but we preferred the older codices. Pulsanen. omits libenter. Munerat., through a printer’s error, has alio plures for alii plures, just as it has Lingonem for Lingones at the beginning.]

[Note: [Col. 0079C]

Bede is empty on this day; the small Roman Martyrology is empty; and, if one may so speak, the Hieronymian copies are also empty, at least as regards the limits of our entry. Understand that Desiderius is not found in those codices except insofar as he was added by later hands, as Florentinius admits; and he was added in such a way that, when the manner of announcement is weighed, it remains uncertain whether the passion of Desiderius, bishop and martyr, is to be assigned to Langres or to Vienne, both of whom are commemorated on this very day. The words of the Hieronymian witnesses, copied, I think, by Rabanus from the same codices, do not remove the doubt at all. Florus, however, expressly declares that he is speaking of the bishop of Vienne. What then of Ado? In his Chronicle, under the year of Christ 583, he relates that man’s martyrdom. He wrote more about him elsewhere, as Notker recounts at length, and as other matters are reported in our Acts; we have treated these attentively under 11 February. But in his Martyrology Ado makes no mention of Desiderius of Vienne, whatever eulogy Mosander may construct under his name, compounded from the words of the Chronicle. Florentinius proves this against Baronius’s annotations, as Rosweyd had held before him: what is read concerning Desiderius of Vienne in Mosander’s Ado, Rosweyd found written not in Ado’s text but in the margin of a Cologne codex, and therefore rejected as an added and spurious matter. Thus the only material that ought to be considered genuinely Ado’s is what the praised edition of Rosweyd presents, and that same material was copied by Notker, with the insertion of a sentence rebuking those who said that a city is a city of living citizens, not of dead bodies. For matters omitted by Usuard, especially those concerning the holy martyr’s burial, and also his translations, the time of his martyrdom, and the Vandals or Alemanni of the third century, as they are called here, the reader should consult Henschenius’s learned dissertation. Yet this has its opponents, foremost among them Tillemont, vol. II, from p. 648, where, discussing the Acts of this Desiderius, he expressly attacks Henschenius’s view and maintains that Desiderius’s martyrdom should be placed not in the third century but at the beginning of the fifth. I submit the force of each opinion to the examination of others. The praised Tillemont gives the French account of the Acts themselves in the same volume, from p. 539; Ado’s text is a brief compendium of them, while ours is contracted from Ado almost word for word. This is the simple and genuine reading of Usuard. Wandelbertus praised Desiderius in this distich:

“On the tenth, Desiderius consecrates the city of Langres,

A bishop and martyr of God, armed with honour.”

] [Note: [Col. 0081A]

In our PRATEN. copy, near the end, one reads: “At the place called Sigestre, the dedication of the church of Saint Mary and Saint Sequanus.” I scarcely doubt that these words were added later in the margin and thus do not impair the purity of the codex, as we have noted elsewhere.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG. add to the pure text: “In Spain, the feast of Saints Epiticus and Basileus, bishop.” Others write “Epictetus or Epitacius, Epictasius,” or “Epitasus.” See the Acts.

CENTULEN.: “At Langres, the passion of Saint Desiderius the martyr. When he saw his people being laid waste by the army of the Vandals, he went out to entreat their king, from whom he immediately received a sentence of beheading. There suffered with him [what follows is in another hand] very many of the number of his flock.”

BRUXELLEN. begins thus: “In Spain, the feast of Saints Epictetus and Basileus. At Langres, the passion of Saint Desiderius, bishop. When he saw his people being laid waste by the army of the Vandals, he went out to entreat their king for his own people. He was immediately ordered by him to be killed; and he, gladly extending his neck for the sheep entrusted to him, was struck with the sword and passed to Christ. But his executioner soon perished, seized by madness. There suffered with him also many others of the number of his flock, who were buried with him in the same city. And at Vienne, the feast of Saint Desiderius, bishop, who in the territory of Lyon, at the estate of Priscilliacum, was overwhelmed with stones by King Theodoric at Brunhild’s counsel and gained the glory of martyrdom. Now buried as a martyr in the church at Vienne, he is honourably preserved. At Gembloux, of Saint Witbert, who, the first among the noble soldiers of Lotharingia to lay aside military service and gird himself with the belt of religion, founded the monastery of Gembloux.”

HAGENOYEN. begins with Desiderius of Vienne, much as in Mosander’s Ado. It is fairly pure in the account of Desiderius of Langres. It then wrongly adds “Helena, Faustinus, and Timothy,” who belong to the preceding day. Then: “In Spain, of Saint Epictetus, martyr, and Basileus, bishop and confessor.”

AQUINCINT. and UGHELLIAN. have at the end the same material as the eight codices above: “In Spain, of Saints Epictetus or Epiticus and Basileus, bishop.”

[Col. 0081D] MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Desiderius, bishop and martyr, with many of his flock. Of Lucius, Montanus, Flavianus, with their companions.” See both these and their companions more fully set out in the Acts. “Of Groybertus the confessor.” It indicates, I think, Guibert of Gembloux, or Wibert of Fritzlar.

REGINAE SUEC., numbered 130: “At Rome, of Saints Faustinus and Timothy. In Africa, of Saints Castus and Aemilius.” See what was said of both announcements on the preceding day.

VATICAN. no. 5949: “At Rome, of Saints Faustinus and Timothy.”

CAUDIACEN. PRIORATUS: “At Grand-Lieu, the arrival of the relics of Saint Austremonius, bishop and martyr.” He is commemorated on 1 November.

REMENS. SS. Timothei et Apoll.: “At Auxerre, the deposition and translation of the body of Saint Helena.” She is placed in Usuard’s text on the preceding day.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL., fairly pure in the text, adds: “In Spain, the feast of Saints Epicticus and Basileus, bishop, martyrs. At Vienne, of Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr, who suffered in the territory of Lyon, at the estate of Priscilliacum. This martyr is now buried in the church at Vienne, where he is honourably preserved.” See the observations above.

BELIN.: “In Spain, Epitacius the bishop and Basileus. On the same day, Saint Mercurialis, bishop and confessor.” See the entries omitted and 30 April.

GREVEN.: “In Africa, Saints Lucius and Quintus, Montanus and others. In Spain, the feast of Saints Epicticius and Basileus, bishops and martyrs. At Vienne, Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr, who indeed suffered in the territory of Lyon, at the villa of Priscilliacum [Prisciniacum], but now rests at Vienne; Saint Theopompus, bishop and martyr, who, sent into a burning furnace for the faith of Christ, remained unharmed for an entire day and night. Then shut up in prison and denied food, he was strengthened by the Lord; finally, together with Senesius, converted by him, he attained the glory of martyrdom.” We have already discussed these several times. See the index of the omitted entries. “William, martyr of Rochester, whose body, although it lay hidden, was divinely revealed through miracles. Mercurialis, bishop and confessor.” Concerning him, see BELIN. “In Frislaria of Hesse, Saint Wibertus, monk and confessor.” He is transferred to 13 August. “Calista, a noble Roman woman.” See the omitted entries.

MOLAN, concerning Epitacius and Basileus, and likewise concerning Mercurialis, copied the text of BELIN. Then: “At the monastery of Gembloux, the feast of Saint Guibert, our father and founder, a distinguished confessor renowned for miracles. Likewise at Vienne, the feast of Saint Desiderius, bishop, who suffered in the territory of Lyon.” Concerning William of Rochester, as above, but in smaller type. Other editions treat first of Guibert and then of Desiderius, as above. Then: “On the twenty-third day, Saint Michael, father and confessor, bishop of Sinada.” Concerning Epitacius, etc., and Mercurialis, as already stated. At the end, in smaller type: “In England, in the city of Rochester, the passion of Saint William.”]

[Col. 0079]

At Langres, the passion of Saint Desiderius, bishop. When he saw his people being harassed by the army of the Vandals, he went out to pray on their behalf; immediately he was ordered to have his throat cut. He willingly extended his neck for the sheep entrusted to him, and, struck by the sword, departed to Christ. Many others from the number of his flock also suffered with him and were buried in the same city.

IX Kal. Day 24. [Note: [Col. 0083A]

From Praten., Herinien., Antuerpien. and Max.-Lubec., Rosweyd., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven. and Molan. Add Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Albergen., Danic., and the Utraj.-Belg. edition.] [Col. 0084A]

[Note: [Col. 0083A]

Only the Pratensis has *conlactanei*; the others, together with the text, are better. Greven. reads “who rests at Antioch,” omitting “in Christ.” Herinien., Antuerp., Max.-Lubecana and Greven. have *Cuzae*. Rosweyd. has *Chusae*; we, with most witnesses, have *Chuzae*. Antuerp.-Major, apparently through a copyist’s error, writes *cujusdam*—“of a certain person”—instead of *Chuzae*. In the Pratensis, *Nannetis* is correctly read; in Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. it is incorrectly *Nampnetis civitate*; in Munerat. most incorrectly *Nanunetis*. We follow the stream of the manuscripts, which uniformly have *Namnetis*. In the major Antuerp. manuscript, instead of *Histriam*, on which the manuscripts agree, there is *Historiam*. The rest—such forms as *Mananen*, *Zoeli*, *Servili*, *Faelicis*, *Dyoclis*, and so forth—should be regarded as scribal errors of the scriptoria. Whether one prefers *Johannae* or *Joannae* makes no difference; let the proverb prevail: “Speak with many, think with few.”]

[Note: [Col. 0083A]

Manahen and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, are known neither to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, nor to Bede and his followers, nor to the *Romanum parvum*; they were first recorded by Ado, whose words Usuard and Notker simply copied. There is no reason at all to doubt the commendation of either saint. What is said about Manahen is taken from the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 13. Luke mentions Joanna in chapter 8, verse 3, and chapter 24, verse 10. How she is venerated among the Greeks with the other women who carried spices is explained in Papebrochius’s historical collection.

The commemoration of Vincent flows from the Hieronymian manuscripts, in nearly the same terms in which it is expressed in our text. The *Romanum parvum* had omitted the entry, but it was restored by Ado and passed from him to us. This is all that survives as having been handed down about her. In Jerome there also appear Donatianus and Rogatianus, blood brothers and martyrs, likewise called so by Rabanus; they too were drawn from the same source by Ado, but rather plainly, since they were adorned with no further commendatory account. The items recited in our brief entry are Usuardine and were taken from the Acts.

These Acts, however, are written with such gravity and simplicity, although long after the martyrdom, that they are counted among the genuine by everyone; Ruinart regarded them as such from page 294 onward. Tillemont reports them in French in volume IV, beginning at page 491, and his note on page 732 contributes nothing that seriously diminishes the authority of the Acts themselves. Notker pursued the sequence of the martyrdom at greater length from those same Acts, but that lies outside our present purpose.

Wandalbert celebrates only these two today:

> Donatianus of Namnetis, with Rogatianus  
> his brother, piously adorns the Ninth with the contest of faith.

Up to this point everything proceeds correctly. The final entry creates some difficulty, namely because those who ought rather to be called Syrians are incorrectly assigned to Istria. The author of the confusion seems to have been the author of the *Romanum parvum*, from which Ado—and, as usual, without prior examination, Usuard and Notker after him—took the material. The *Romanum parvum* had written: “In Istria, Zoellus and Silvanus,” incorrectly substituting Istria for Syria. Preserving the location, the Viennese Martyrologist added companions from the same group; thus the error passed into our Martyrology, into others, and even into the present Roman Martyrology. Florentinius and Henschenius corrected it; in their works the matter is discussed more carefully. I do not investigate whether Usuard should be excused. Even when his guide’s footprints lead him astray, he has become accustomed—as has already been shown so often—to follow them; and, in accordance with the purpose of our undertaking, we profess to reproduce his judgment, whatever it may be.]

[Note: [Col. 0083C]

TORNACEN., having removed the commendatory account of Donatianus and Rogatianus, presents Ado’s text unaltered. At the end, however, it adds: “On the same day, Saint Posinna, virgin.” She will recur below. But in the Acts she is reported under the name Pusinna on 23 April, and on that day we mention her in the appendices.

PULSANEN. remains pure as far as Vincent the martyr; it omitted everything else.

LOVANIEN. likewise reproduces Ado unaltered, with the commendatory account of the martyrs of Namnetis deleted.

CENTULEN.: “At Antioch, the feast of Saint Manahen, foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch, a teacher and prophet under the grace of the New Testament.” In the entry for Joanna it is unaltered. “In Gaul, in the city of Namnetis, Blessed Rogatianus and Donatianus, martyrs. In Istria, Saints Zoellus, Servilius, Felix, Silvanus and Diocles.”

BRUXELLEN., in its usual text somewhat purer, adds at the end: “Likewise, the translation of Saint Dominic, father and founder of the Order of Preachers.” This should be deferred to the day on which he is celebrated, 4 August.

[Col. 0083D] HAGENOYEN. begins as follows: “At Antioch, the feast of Blessed Manahen,” etc. In this it departs from the genuine text; otherwise it is sufficiently pure in the remaining matters.

MATRIC.-CARTUSIAE-ULTRAJECT. first has: “Donatianus and Rogatianus, brothers.” Concerning them it says in the margin: “A certain house of our order has been established in honor of these martyrs near Nantes, where they rest or suffered.” The text continues: “Zoellus the martyr with his companions; Manahen, Herod’s foster-brother, teacher and prophet under the grace of the New Testament; Joanna, the wife of Chuza, whom the Evangelists commemorate.”

[Col. 0084C] AUGENS., of the Canons Regular: “On the same day, Saint Posinna, virgin.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949, Manahen is absent. It has: “And in Istria, Silvanus and Felix.”

STROZZIAN.: “At Bologna, the translation of Blessed Dominic the confessor, during which such a great fragrance poured forth from his virginal body that it surpassed the scent of all spices. It was carried out in the thirteenth year after his death, by order of our lord Pope Gregory IX, by the archbishop of Ravenna and many other bishops.” The day on which he is celebrated, 4 August, is well known.

REMENS., of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “In the village of Bausion, on the river Marne, the burial of Saint Posinna, virgin.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins with Rogatianus and Donatianus, as in the text. Then: “In Istria, etc.” Next: “In the Roman port, etc.” It continues: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Manahen, etc.” Finally: “Likewise, of the most blessed Joanna, wife of Chuza, the procurator of the aforementioned Herod, whom the Evangelists commemorate. After her husband’s death, she followed the Lord Jesus Christ everywhere as he preached, and generously ministered from her resources to him and his disciples. She had as her companion one like herself both in affection and in action, namely Saint Susanna, about whom Luke speaks; and many other women followed the Lord Jesus Christ.

“In Lombardy, in the city of Bologna, the translation of Saint Dominic the confessor, first of the Order of Preachers. At Cologne, in the church at the Steps of Saint Mary, the arrival of certain relics of Saint Anno, archbishop and confessor of that city.” See 4 December, the day of his feast.

[Col. 0085A] The first edition of BELIN reverses the order and shamefully corrupts most of the names. In the second, near the end, it adds: “Likewise at Bologna, the translation of Blessed Dominic the confessor, during which such a great fragrance flowed from his virginal body that it surpassed the sweetness of every perfume. It was carried out in the thirteenth year after his blessed death, by order of our lord Gregory IX, by the archbishop of Ravenna and many other bishops.”

GREVEN.: “In the city of Tergeste, Saint Servulus the martyr, in the time of the emperor Numerian. When he refused to sacrifice, he was beaten with sinews, suspended on the rack and tortured, while his sides were torn with claws. Then, after being taken down and drenched with boiling oil, when he became still more steadfast, he was ordered to be put to death by the sword.” He is a companion of Zebellus and Secundinus, who truly belong to Istria. “Anolinus the martyr, who, while serving as a prison guard, was converted by Saint Urban together with the tribunes and, killed with them for Christ, triumphed.” He is deferred to the following day. “At Bologna, the translation of Saint Dominic the confessor, from whose body, when it was raised, a wondrous sweetness of fragrance issued. At Cologne, in the church at Mary’s Steps, the translation of certain relics of Saint Anno, bishop and confessor.”

MOLAN.: “Likewise at Bologna, the translation of Blessed Dominic, etc.,” from Belin. Then: “The translation of Saint Lambert.” His feast is 17 September. It continues in smaller type: “On the same day, at the monastery of Lérins, Vincent the priest, who wrote a truly golden book on behalf of the antiquity and truth of the Catholic faith against the profane innovations of every heresy.” In later editions I do not know why this entry is omitted, with only the translations of Saint Lambert and Saint Dominic being treated.]

[Col. 0081]

The feast of Manahen, foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch, teacher and prophet under the grace of the New Testament, resting in Christ at Antioch. Likewise, of the most blessed Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod’s procurator, whom the Evangelists commemorate. At the Roman Port, the feast of Saint Vincent the martyr. In Gaul, in the city of Namnetis, Blessed Donatianus and Rogatianus, brothers and martyrs, who, for their steadfastness in the faith, were sent into prison, suspended and torn on the rack, then pierced with a soldier’s lance, and finally beheaded. In Istria, Saints Zoellus, Servilius, Felix, Silvanus and Diocles, martyrs.

VIII Kal. Day 25. [Note: [Col. 0085]

The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Munerat., Greven. and Molan., who alone deserve to be counted among the pure manuscripts for this day.] [Col. 0090C]

[Note: [Col. 0085B]

All write *Numentana*, and so did we, although we are not unaware that *Nomentana* should be read. Again all agree on *in cujus doctrina*; only Greven. inserted on his own authority the words *cujus praedicatione et doctrina*—“by whose preaching and teaching.” Likewise, with the manuscripts, I retain *Dionisii*, although elsewhere, if I am not mistaken, I corrected it. Nearly all wrote correctly and properly *condigno honore*; Herinien. and Greven., however, have *cum digno honore*. The Pratensis manuscript correctly has *Moesiam*; let the reader forgive me if I follow all the other manuscripts, in which *Mesiam* is incorrectly but very explicitly written. We think *Pasicratis*, as required by the Greek meaning, should be preferred, but, guided by the same authority, we read *Passecratis*. The Pratensis has *duum* instead of *duorum*; here the orthography of the other manuscripts is certainly preferable. It is scarcely worth pointing out *Capadociam*, *Valencionis*, and other forms of this kind.] [Col. 0086B]

[Note: [Col. 0085B]

All the Hieronymian Martyrologies commemorate Urban in approximately the following manner: “On the Nomentan Way, at the eighth milestone, the feast of Urban, bishop”; and in the same manuscripts there immediately follows: “In the cemetery of Praetextatus, Dorostorus.” Since, arranged in this way, these items mean nothing, it seems that this cemetery ought to be joined with Urban’s entry. That would be a combination of entirely different places: the Appian Way, to which the cemetery of Praetextatus certainly belongs, and the Nomentan Way, which lies far away. Florentinius exercises his critical skill in explaining these matters.

Bede, and Rabanus after him, read more simply: “At Rome, the feast of Urban, pope and confessor, by whose teaching many were crowned with martyrdom.” Here there is certainly an allusion to Cecilia and the martyrs associated with her, who were instructed by Pope Urban. The *Romanum parvum* speaks differently: “In the cemetery of Praetextatus, Saint Urban, bishop and martyr.” This differs greatly from Bede, not only in wording but in the matter itself.

Now hear Ado’s more expansive phrasing: “At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the feast of Saint Urban, bishop and martyr, by whose teaching, under the persecution of Alexander, many were crowned with martyrdom.” Here, I think, you can see that matters have been badly combined, with the persecution of Alexander added—material that Ado had found, more or less, in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede and the *Romanum parvum*—while preserving the title “martyr.” Our author, however, rightly deleted the cemetery and borrowed the rest of his text from the aforementioned Ado.

These are the positions of our Martyrologists. They should be compared and reconciled with the wording of the Allatian and Frontonian Calendars: “On the 25th day [of May] (Allatius: the eighth day before the Kalends of June), the feast of Saint Urban, confessor and pontiff, on the Appian Way.” I know that, with Henschenius, the titles “confessor” and “martyr” can very reasonably be reconciled in a sound sense; indeed, in the Gregorian Sacramentary Pope Urban is addressed as a martyr in a prayer. I also know that Wandalbert sings as follows:

> On the eighth day Urban shines in the splendor of his merits,  
> whom mitre, teaching, and blood together blessed.

Finally, I know that the Acts themselves—which Henschenius judged to have been written by Roman notaries—describe the martyrdom of Pope Urban at length. But I do not see with equal clarity how those ancient Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, Bede and Rabanus, who everywhere and expressly habitually distinguish martyrs from confessors, can truly and solidly be reconciled with the other Martyrologists and with the cited Acts.

Tillemont opened a path in volume III, page 686, where he considers it possible that Urban the bishop and martyr was distinct from Urban the pontiff and confessor; this would also settle the disputes concerning the body preserved at Rome and elsewhere. To this should aptly be referred what Henschenius correctly argued on page 10, no. 18. What would be especially useful in this system for explaining the Martyrologies is the possibility that Urban the bishop and martyr was buried on the Nomentan Way, at the eighth milestone from Rome, and was later transferred to Gaul; while the other, the pope, was buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way, where his body remained, until it was first transferred to Rome by Paschal I and subsequently discovered in 1599.

This is a conjecture; otherwise it does nothing to undermine the title “martyr,” which is commonly asserted of Pope Urban, since he may have earned it through various confessions of faith, as did many others, as is well known. A more important question concerns the authenticity of the Acts themselves: Henschenius defended them, while the aforementioned Tillemont attacked them sharply, among other arguments maintaining that an open persecution and public martyrdoms under the emperor Alexander cannot at all be admitted.

The same considerations arise against the passion of Cecilia and her companions, as we briefly indicated on 14 April. So that we do not decide rashly here or wander beyond our purpose, we defer everything for fuller examination and explanation to 22 November.]

Milan: the burial of Dionysius, bishop, is expressly noted in the Hieronymian copies. Bede and his followers, as well as the *Romanum parvum*, are silent. The commendatory account of our author, recited here in the text, belongs to Ado; Notker did not fail to copy it, adding other material which I do not consider it our task either to report or examine. Papebrochius collected and carefully arranged from various Fathers the outstanding labors of Dionysius on behalf of the Catholic faith.

The martyrs of Dorostorus, transposed in the Hieronymian Martyrologies but nevertheless extracted from them, must have been copied by our author and Notker directly from Ado, since they are found in no other ancient Martyrologies. I have no means of determining whether there were two or three companions, or perhaps four. Nor did Henschenius determine this; he set aside the fabrications of the compiler of the pseudo-chronicle of Dexter and substituted more plausible encomia of our saints from Greek records.

Their most certain praise is found in the Acts of Saint Julius, which we shall discuss on 27 May. There the names Pasicrates and Valention are expressed, together with Esichius, unquestionably also a martyr, as reported on 15 June; but no mention is made of the others, unless Julius himself and Esichius are to be regarded as those two other companions.

Apart from Usuard, no ancient author speaks of Leo of Trecassinum; and even in several Usuardine manuscripts, not of the best quality, he is omitted. The authority of the better witnesses should suffice for us. Little survives concerning him, and Henschenius included it in his historical collection.

There remains Pope Eleutherius, placed by Ado on this day with a commendatory account and enlarged by Notker. It is certain that Usuard mentions him neither here nor elsewhere. I shall not settle the matter by conjecture or guesswork; that would be what I did if I called Ado’s text into doubt at this point or otherwise made suspicious the entry so clearly expressed in Ado. Whoever wants more should consult the Acts for 26 May. We have no doubt that we have represented the genuine Usuard on this day as well.] [Col. 0088B]

[Note: [Col. 0087B]

TORNACEN., otherwise entirely pure throughout the text, mutilates the commendatory account of Dionysius from “he first rested” through the end of the entry. The rest is exceptionally pure.

PULSANEN. is pure in the entry for Urban, but truncates the whole commendatory account of Dionysius. The third entry is absent. At the end it is pure.

ROSWEYD. adds at the end: “Likewise, on the same island of Britain, Blessed Bede the priest.” It anticipates the day, for he is celebrated on the following day.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN.-BELG., LOVANIEN. and the UTRAJ.-BELG. edition omit the final entry concerning Leo. LEYDEN.-BELG. incorrectly records the stigmata of Saint Francis; it intended to indicate the translation.

ROSWEYD. is pure in the entry for Urban; in second place it inserts: “Likewise, Pope Eleutherius, who ruled for fifteen years and was buried beside the Apostle Peter.” The remainder of the text follows. At the end: “Likewise, on the island of Britain, in the city of Magidulf, the burial of Saint Aldhelm, bishop and confessor. Likewise, of Sulpitius and Servilianus.” The Acts of the latter are given on 20 April.

ANTUERPIEN.-MAJ. makes Leo a bishop and adds at the end: “Likewise, on the island of Britain, in the city of Enagidulf [or Magidulf], the burial of Saint Aldhelm, bishop and confessor.”

MUNERAT. has at the end: “On the same day, Saints Mary of James and Salome, companions of the Mother of the Lord.” Others celebrate their translation. See what is said about them among the omitted entries.

ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG. and DANIC. begin: “At Assisi, the translation of Saint Francis (our most blessed father, say ALBERGEN. and DANIC.), which took place in the year 1230 of the Lord’s Incarnation, under Pope Gregory IX.” These same manuscripts—except LEYDEN.—after the account of Urban, add the words “were crowned with martyrdom”: “He was the sixteenth after Blessed Peter, and established that all the vessels of the altar should be of gold, silver, or at least tin.” Moreover, all omit “Saint Leo.”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, Saint Urban, pope and martyr, by whose teaching, under the persecution of Alexander, many were crowned with martyrdom. At Milan, Blessed Dionysius, bishop and confessor. In Moesia,” etc., as in the text. “In the territory of Trecassinum, Saint Leo, confessor and monk.”

BRUXELLEN. gives a longer commendatory account of Urban; but it is preferable to learn these matters from the Acts. In the rest of the text it is sufficiently pure. At the end it adds: “At Assisi, the translation of Saint Francis, founder of the Order of Friars Minor.” His feast day, 4 October, is well known; everything should be deferred to that day.

HAGENOYEN. invents other material about Urban, which must be passed over here. It is pure in the rest.

AQUICINCT. after “Pope and martyr,” inserts: “He made all the sacred vessels of silver and provided fifteen silver patens.” At the end: “In Britain, at the monastery of Maldubia, Saint Adelmus, bishop and confessor. At Rome, Saint Eleutherius, pope and martyr.”

VICTORIN.: “Likewise, Eleutherius, pope. He established that no food should be rejected by Christians that was rational and human. And in the territory of Reate, Saint Maron the martyr.” See the list of omitted entries.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Pope Urban and martyr. Mary of James and Salome; Canio the martyr with his son (Conon, I believe, who is celebrated on 29 May). Pasicrates the martyr with his companions. Dionysius, bishop of Milan, whose relics Blessed Ambrose elevated.”

REG. SUEC., marked no. 130: “And in the territory of Reate, Saint Maron the martyr.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949, Leo is absent; the following is added: “At Benevento, Saint Secundus, bishop and confessor, in Saint Sophia.” I confess that I do not know this Secundus. “At Rome, Saint Eleutherius, pope, who presided over the Church for fifteen years. And Saint Canio the martyr.” Perhaps it refers to the same man who appears in the Acts as the bishop of Aser, etc. See there.

FLORENTIN.: “At Florence, in the parts of Tuscany, the feast of the most holy Zenobius, bishop of that city. While he lived, he shone so greatly in life and miracles that, through the power of the Holy Trinity, he was deemed worthy to become the raiser of three dead persons. He lived ninety years and rested in the Lord in the year 424 from the Incarnation.

“To honor his holiness, when his body was being transferred on 26 January from the church of Saint Lawrence to the principal church of the aforementioned city, the bier accidentally touched a dried elm tree, which immediately blossomed before everyone’s eyes.

“At Assisi, the translation of Saint Francis the confessor, in the year of the Lord 1230. On the same day, Saint Boniface, pope. Likewise, the translation of the most holy Stephen the martyr from Constantinople to Venice, to the monastery of Saint George Major, in the year 1110.” See what is said about this translation—whether it concerns the protomartyr or perhaps another Stephen the Younger, etc.—among the omitted entries.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION, concerning Urban, adds to “the vessels of the altar, etc.”: “In his time the Church first began to possess estates.” It is sufficiently pure in the entries for Dionysius and the martyrs of Dorostorus; it omits Leo. Then: “At Assisi,” etc., as in ULTRAJECT. and the others above. “On the same day, Saint Adelini [Aldelmus], bishop and confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saints Mary of James and Mary Salome, sisters of Saint Mary the Mother of God. Likewise, the translation of Saint Goar, priest and confessor.” His feast day is 6 June.

[Col. 0089A] BELIN. Before Leo, inserts: “At Florence, a city of Tuscany, the feast of the most holy Cenobius (Zenobius), bishop of that city.” After Leo, it adds: “On the same day, Saint Boniface, pope. At Assisi, the translation of Saint Francis, the holy father.” Elsewhere it has: “Likewise, the translation of the most holy Stephen,” etc., as in FLORENTIN.

In the later edition everything is similar, but concerning Francis it reads: “At Assisi, the translation of Saint Francis, the holy father, founder of the Friars Minor, whose venerable body, adorned with the stigmata of the Crucified One as with the most precious pearls, was transferred in the year of the Lord 1230, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, when the brothers had gathered at Assisi for the general chapter, from the church of Saint George, where it had first received a place of rest, to the basilica built in his honor; there it remains situated with fitting honor.” We have already said that this should be deferred to 4 October.

GREVEN.: “On the same day, or, according to others, on the following day, at Rome, Saint Eleutherius, pope. He received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that through his command he might become a Christian. After ruling the Church for twenty-one years and six months, he attained the palm of martyrdom and was buried at the Vatican.

“Likewise, Saints Maximus and Venerandus, martyrs. Barctwardus and Dictwardus, martyrs.” See the omitted entries, under Worado. “Canio, bishop and martyr. Nicetius the martyr, who was a Goth by race; because he refused to deny the faith of Christ, he was thrown into the fire by the Goths and attained the crown of martyrdom.” See the omitted entries. “At Florence, Blessed Zenobius, bishop and confessor, who, as Antoninus testifies in part 2 of his Chronicle, greatly benefited the Church of God through the holiness of his life, the glory of his miracles and his health-giving teaching, especially in the regions of Tuscany, in the time of Pope Damasus.

“Adelinus [Aldelmus], bishop of Sherborne in England, confessor. Mutius the abbot, who was first the leader of robbers; afterward converted, he lived a most holy solitary life. On the Lord’s Day he tasted bread sent from heaven and required no other food. Likewise another Mutius, who entered a monastery with his eight-year-old son and, at the abbot’s command, threw that same son into a river. It was revealed to the abbot that by this act Mutius had acquired for himself the merit of the patriarch Abraham.” See the omitted entries concerning both Mutius. “At Assisi, the translation of Saint Francis the confessor. The translation of Saint Goar, priest and confessor. The translation of Saints Mary of James and Salome, sisters of Saint Mary the Mother of God.”

MOLAN.: “At Florence in Tuscany, the feast of the most holy Zenobius, bishop of that city. On the same day, Saint Boniface, pope. At Assisi, the translation of Saint Francis, the holy father, founder,” etc., from the second edition of BELIN. “Likewise, the translation of the most holy Stephen,” etc., as in FLORENTIN. In smaller type: [Col. 0090B] “Adelmus, bishop of Sherborne in England, confessor.” Other editions have: “In Britain, at the monastery of Maldubia, Saint Adelmus, bishop and confessor.” What follows concerning Zenobius, Boniface, Stephen and Francis is as above. Then: “On the twenty-fifth day, the third discovery of the precious head of the Forerunner.” See the list of omitted entries. Finally, in a different type: “On the same day, Saint Aurelius, bishop of the city of Reggio, who was buried with Dionysius, bishop of Milan, and was eventually transferred to the monastery of Hirsau by Bishop Notting, its founder.” We have found him mentioned in no other manuscript. This is deferred among the omitted entries to 9 November.]

[Col. 0085]

At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, the feast of Blessed Urban, pope and martyr, by whose teaching, under the persecution of Alexander, many were crowned with martyrdom. At Milan, Saint Dionysius, bishop and confessor, who, condemned to exile in Cappadocia for the Catholic faith, first rested there; afterward, his bodily relics, received by Saint Basil, bishop of that city, were honorably laid to rest by Blessed Ambrose. In Moesia, in the city of Dorostorus, the holy martyrs Pasicrates, Valention and two others crowned together with them. In the territory of Trecassinum, Saint Leo the confessor.

VII Kal. Day 26. [Note: [Col. 0089C]

The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Munerat., Greven. and Molan. Only these deserve to be counted among the pure manuscripts for this day.] [Col. 0090C]

[Note: [Col. 0089C]

There is little to report, and it concerns chiefly spelling. With Pratensis and Munerat., I read *Simmitrii*, not *Sinmitrii* as in Herinien., nor *Simitrii* as in Greven. and Molan.; various fuller Usuardine manuscripts and others render the name in various ways. The Acts have the better form, *Symmetrii*. Likewise, Praten., Herinien. and Munerat. write *plenum fidei*, not *plenum fide* as in Greven. and Molan. I pass over the remaining matters in silence.]

[Note: [Col. 0089C]

We have often observed above that Usuard and Notker derived most of their material from Ado. This is so clear throughout the entire text today that I can scarcely understand how it could have escaped the extraordinarily precise and penetrating eye of Henschenius, since the fact itself immediately meets the eye in the case of every single saint in this brief entry.

First, concerning “Quadratus of Athens,” Henschenius notes that Notker took the commendatory account from Jerome, whereas it is clear that Notker copied Ado’s words concerning the feasts of the Apostles exactly. The same will be evident of the others to anyone who compares them individually.

Thus the aforementioned Quadratus, omitted by the Hieronymian Martyrologies and by Bede, was first recorded by the *Romanum parvum* in these words: “At Athens, Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles,” words which are found almost exactly in Ado’s Martyrology. The commendatory account is composed by Ado in the cited place, and our author presents its compressed elegance neatly.

Here there is no disagreement among our Martyrologists: he is considered an “Athenian bishop,” a “disciple of the Apostles,” an “apologist” and a “prophet.” This is the ancient and most widely accepted view. Some more recent scholars, however, depart from it; whether with sufficient foundation, the reader may judge after comparing Henschenius’s historical collection with Tillemont’s note in volume II, page 589. In such controversies I do not wish to decide anything here.

Symmetrius and his companions likewise belong to Ado; Usuard expresses them somewhat more briefly, omitting the indication of the time, the place of burial and its guardian Praxedes. From these details it should be inferred that all our knowledge of this saint and his companions was taken from the Life of Saints Pudentiana and Praxedes, which we discussed on 19 May. The particular Acts concerning them are rejected. See what Henschenius and Papebrochius have unearthed concerning the translation and other matters.

The second Quadratus, placed second by Ado and Notker, is reported in the Hieronymian copies mixed among the companions. After those companions are omitted, Ado celebrates Quadratus alone in precisely the words copied by our author and Notker. Henschenius hopes that the sermons of Saint Augustine delivered on his solemnity may someday be published, just as the sermon concerning Saints Perpetua and Felicity was published in the Acts for 7 March.

A certain Quadratus is noted in August, after Massa Candida, in the Carthaginian Calendar; he is unquestionably this same person, although others may have transferred him to this day at their discretion.

The troop of Tudertine martyrs is likewise illustrious in the ancient Hieronymian Martyrologies, although their names have been variously distorted. From this group those mentioned here were undoubtedly again detached: the first and principal three, Felicissimus, Heraclius and Paulinus, recorded by the Viennese Martyrologist and copied by both other authors in nearly the same terms. The same applies to Priscus of Cociacum and the great multitude.

Henschenius holds that those portions of the Hieronymian Martyrologies which determine the place of martyrdom should be attributed to them, whatever Florentinius may appear to think otherwise. This is certain: Ado, Usuard and Notker list them in the same phrasing. In the Acts, Cottus is added as a companion. See there the history of both, which Tillemont considers more recent in volume IV, page 349.

The final place is occupied by Augustine, the apostle of the English, whom Bede first mentions. The commendatory account was composed not by Usuard, as Papebrochius believed, following the ancient and very common opinion of our predecessors and others, but by Ado, from whom our author and Notker transferred their material.
