Notker did so fully and word for word; Usuard excised the portions that Papebrochius thought had been added to Usuard by Ado and Notker. See the rest in Papebrochius.

This, then, is the plain and certain reading of our Usuard, which, as we said at the outset, agrees completely with the Adoan and Notkerian texts and is moreover demonstrably taken from Ado himself. Wandalbert honored Augustine alone in the following lines:

> Augustine, your name the seventh commends,  
> where the thousands of the English shine white;  
> through the prince of the word, by whom the conquered Britons  
> came to know Christ.] [Col. 0092B]

[Note: [Col. 0091B]

TORNACEN., otherwise exceptionally pure throughout the text, omits the commendatory account of the second Quadratus, beginning “on whose solemnity,” etc.

PULSANEN., more mutilated in the earlier part, has nothing except the entry for Quadratus of Athens and Augustine; all the rest is absent.

ROSWEYD. adds at the end: “Likewise, on the same island of Britain, Blessed Bede the priest.” It anticipates the day, since he is celebrated on the following day.

ANTUERP. MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN. and the UTRAJ.-BELG. edition are deficient in the commendatory account of Quadratus of Athens, in which they resemble Ado’s Martyrology. See the observations above.

ANTVERP.-MAJ. begins as follows: “In Britain, in the city of Canterbury, the feast of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, who formerly, sent by the Apostolic See together with many other ministers of the word of life, by order of Blessed Gregory, first preached the Gospel of Christ to the English people. Likewise, on the same island of Britain, the burial of Blessed Bede the priest, the most discerning teacher of the English, whose great merits and streams of teaching are attested by the honeyed examples of his good works.” The remainder of the text follows in pure form.]

ALBERGEN and DANIC begin: “At Rome, Saint Eleutherius, pope and martyr. He was the twelfth after blessed Peter, and received letters from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that through his command he might become a Christian.” In the remainder they resemble ANTUERP.-MAX.-LUBEC. and the other manuscripts cited above.

CENTULEN.: “At Athens, the birthday of blessed Quadratus, bishop and martyr, disciple of the apostles. Also of another Quadratus, martyr, on whose feast sermons of Saint Augustine are found to have been delivered. At Auxerre, in the place called Cociacum, the passion of Saint Priscus with his companions, an innumerable multitude of martyrs, in the time of the emperor Aurelian. At Rome, the blessed martyrs Symmetrius, priest, and twenty-two others, in the time of Antoninus. At Todi in Tuscany, Saints Felicissimus, Heraclius, and Paulinus. In Britain, Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor, who, sent by blessed Pope Gregory, first preached the Gospel of Christ to the English people. In the city of York, Saint Bede, priest and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. adds concerning Quadratus the bishop: “He was especially renowned in prophetic grace together with the seven daughters of Philip.” It continues: “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Eleutherius, pope and martyr. He occupied the see for fifteen years. Through him Lucius, king of Britain, asked by letter to become a Christian, and was baptized.” Concerning Symmetrius and his companions it adds: “Whom the emperor Antoninus ordered to be struck down with the sword for the faith of Christ.” The remainder is sufficiently pure, but at the end it reads:

“And the burial of the venerable Bede, priest and doctor of the English people, who, when he was seven years old, was received into the monastery by Abbot Benedict; afterward, in the thirtieth year of his age, he was ordained priest. When he was ninety and suffering in his final illness, after he had poured forth to the Lord this prayer, ‘O King of glory, Lord of hosts!’ etc., he gave up his spirit to the Lord on the day he had requested, namely on the Lord’s Ascension. He was buried in the monastery where, from childhood, he had devoted himself to knowledge and virtue.”

I have already said that the venerable Bede is commemorated on the following day.

HAGENOYEN., in the notice of Quadratus of Athens, is fairly pure and adds concerning Eleutherius almost as above. It then gives Priscus, followed by Symmetrius, fairly accurately. Next it inserts: “Also Saint Hilderticus, bishop and confessor.” It means Hildevertus, concerning whom see today in the Omissions and on the following day in the Acts. It continues with the other Quadratus of our text, the people of Todi, and Augustine, fairly accurately.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end concerning Augustine: “And he still shines forth through frequent miracles. The burial of the venerable Bede, priest, at Rome.” I have no time to examine what “at Rome” means here, or what is signified by the other material added later in the manuscript.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Eleutherius, pope and martyr. Priscus and Felix and their companions. Augustine, first bishop of the English. Quadratus, bishop, disciple of the apostles. Also Quadratus, martyr, on whose feast Augustine delivered a sermon. Bede, venerable priest and confessor. Julius, soldier and martyr.” The last belongs to the following day.

In VATICAN no. 5949 the second Quadratus is absent. It adds, however: “Saint Theodore, martyr.” See under the Omissions the two Theodores. It is unclear which of them is meant here.

ALTEMPS.: “At Périgueux, Saint Memorius, confessor. On the same day, Saint Odo, archbishop of Canterbury and confessor.” Odo is referred in the index of the Omitted Saints to 4 July.

REMENS. Saints Timothy and Apollinaris. “At Auxerre, in the place called Cotiacum, the passion of Saint Priscus martyr and his companions, with an innumerable multitude of martyrs.” Almost as in the Hieronymian Martyrology.

LUBECO-COL. EDITION. It begins: “At Rome, Saint Eleutherius, pope and martyr. He was the twelfth after blessed Peter and occupied the see for twenty-one years, six months, and five days. He received letters from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that through his command he might become a Christian. He also affirmed that Christians, especially the faithful, should reject no customary food that God had created, provided that it was rational and human.” It then treats Quadratus of Athens, the people of Todi, and Augustine. There it inserts: “Also in Britain, Saint Zacharias, bishop and confessor of that people,” concerning whom see the Omitted Saints. “In the territory of Auxerre, the passion of Saints Priscus martyr and Felix priest, with a great multitude of the faithful under the emperor Aurelian.” It then continues with the second Quadratus, Symmetrius, and the others, as sufficiently described above.

BELIN. lacks the notice of Quadratus at the beginning. Then: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Ministrius, priest, and twenty-two others.” The remaining text follows. At the end, however: “On the same day, Saint Eleutherius, pope and martyr.” Then: “Also the holy martyrs Simetrius, priest, and twenty-two others.” He did not notice that “Ministrius” is a fictitious name, where Symmetrius must be restored. In another edition there is also added: “Also the burial of Bede, priest.”

GREVEN.: “Also Saints Victor and Rufinus.” These have been wrongly joined together from the Hieronymian Martyrology. “Hildemicus, bishop of Meaux and confessor.” See above under HAGENOYEN. “Zacharias, bishop of Canterbury and confessor.” See the Omitted Saints. “On the same day—or, according to others, on the following day—in England, the burial of the venerable Bede, priest and confessor, outstanding teacher. As he himself relates of himself, when he was seven years old and had been entrusted to a monastery, amid the observance of regular discipline and the daily duty of singing in the church, he always took delight in either learning, teaching, or writing. At last, full of days and holiness, he died at the age of ninety on the day he had requested, that is, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension. For on that day, with his understanding unimpaired and his face cheerful, after singing the antiphon ‘O King of glory, Lord of hosts!’ etc., he gave up his spirit.”

MOLAN.: “On the same day, Saint Eleutherius, pope and martyr. Also the burial of Bede, priest. At Vienna, the passion of Saint Zacharias the Younger, bishop of that city.” Concerning him see the Omitted Saints. In later editions the notices of Eleutherius and Zacharias are as above. In smaller type they append the common notice of the venerable Bede in this form: “Also the burial of Bede, priest, teacher of the English people.”

[Col. 0089]

At Athens, the birthday of blessed Quadratus, bishop and disciple of the Apostles, who, during the persecution of Hadrian, gathered together by his faith and diligence the Church, which had been scattered in great terror, and also produced a book in defense of the Christian religion, full of faith and worthy of apostolic doctrine. At Rome, the holy martyrs Symmetrius, priest, and twenty-two others. On the same day, Saint Quadratus martyr, on whose feast sermons of Saint Augustine are found to have been delivered. At Todi in Tuscany, the birthday of Saints Felicissimus, Heraclius, and Paulinus. In the territory of Auxerre, the passion of Saint Priscus martyr, with a great multitude. In Britain, Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor, who, sent by blessed Pope Gregory, first preached the Gospel of Christ to the English people.

VI Kal. Day 27.

[Note: [Col. 0093B]

Our principal manuscripts generally agree: those customarily cited for the text are Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0093B]

Pratensis correctly reads Moesia, as does Muneratus; but, on the agreement of all the other manuscripts, we write Mesia, as on the 25th of this month and elsewhere. Greven. has *execraret* instead of *execraretur*, and, together with Molanus, *confiteretur constantissime*, contrary to the other manuscripts and to the text. *Eutropi* instead of *Eutropii* occurs in Pratensis, Herinien., and Tornacen.; we have followed these as older and most reliable, although the later spelling is unquestionably preferable. The typesetters’ carelessness is responsible for *Ausarica* in Muneratus and *Aurasica* in Grevenus instead of *Aurausica*, which is correctly printed in the text. Likewise, in the cited Muneratus, *Clarus* is wrongly printed instead of *Verus*, and *Agatensi* instead of *Adartensi*; also *Rudulfi* instead of *Ragnulfi*. Tornacen. has *Rasuulfi*, Greven. *Ramulfi*, and Molan. *Ranulfi*.]

[Note: [Col. 0093B]

The Roman Martyrology celebrates Julius the martyr. It was taken from Ado and adorned with a notable eulogy, the greater part of which—namely, what particularly and separately concerns Julius—Usuard transferred into our calendar. He omitted what Ado records there concerning Hesychius, whose feast is 15 June, and his conversation with the martyr; and concerning Pasicrates and Valentio of Durostorum, commemorated on 25 May. Notker preserves the ancient form, describing everything. Florus also mentions Julius, but very briefly. Yet what he and the others possess was taken from splendid and genuine Acts. Henschenius had only an epitome of them; Ruinart published them complete from page 614 onward, correctly observing that they contain no indications from which anything certain about the time of the passion can be established. Hence one may conclude that Galesinius wrongly inserted the time of the emperor Alexander.

Henschenius and Ruinart, on the basis of various characteristics, rightly judge that a certain Julius of Faesulae, or one venerated at Faesulae, was distinct from our Julius of Durostorum. Wandalbert commemorates only this Julius:

“From here Julius, soldier and martyr, adorns the sixth [day].”

Eutropius of Orange owes his first commemoration in the sacred calendars to Ado. From him Usuard and Notker took their accounts, both following their guide very closely. We suppose, by the usual conjecture, that Ado did not see the lucid sermon on the life of Eutropius by Verus, bishop, because he did not adorn the saint with any eulogy. The first part of that sermon, from the Fucquetian manuscript, was first published by Papebrochius; the curious reader should consult his Commentary for the rest.

Ragnulfus of Thérouanne, martyr near Arras, is recorded by no martyrologist older than or contemporary with our author. The few surviving monuments concerning him must be sought in Henschenius’s historical collection.

We have said that Usuard commonly calls the territory of Adartum “Atrebatian,” or, if one wishes, “Artesian,” as on 6 February, where he calls Vedastus not bishop of the Atrebates but of the Adartenses. More inquisitive etymologists may consult what Henschenius noted on this matter on that day.

There can certainly be no doubt about Usuard’s text, to which in no way belongs the addition made by a later hand in the Pratensis manuscript: “On the same day, the translation of the body of Saint Martin [Maximinus], abbot and confessor, not bishop of Trier but abbot of Micy, whose feast is 15 December.” These remarks have been made in passing.]

[Note: [Col. 0093D]

PULSANEN. abridges the eulogy of Julius. It is pure in the account of Eutropius, omits Ragnulfus, and adds at the end: “In the territory of Orléans, the translation of the body of Saint Maximinus, abbot and confessor.” This is the saint of whom we have just spoken from PRATEN.; he is to be referred to 15 December.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., and the ULTRAJECT.-BELG. EDITION add at the end: “Also the burial of Lord Bede, priest and teacher of the English people.” You will note that all the later manuscripts of middle quality write “Atrebatian territory” instead of “Adartian territory”; others do the same. They also give Ragnulfus the title “bishop,” although Henschenius thinks that “this dignity was wrongly transferred to him by Saint Hadulfus.”

ALBERGEN and DANIC have the same addition and defect as the preceding witnesses, but go beyond them at the beginning, where they read: “At Rome, the birthday of blessed John, pope, whom Saint Gregory reports to have been first held in custody for the orthodox faith and then led to death together with other equally Catholic men.” These words also occur in BELIN, taken from the Roman Martyrology, and in the later editions of MOLAN under this day; from Bede, the Small Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, Rabanus, and Notker, they appear to belong to the following day.

CENTULEN.: “The birthday of Saint Julius, martyr, who was killed by the impious king Theodoric and honorably buried in the church of blessed Peter the Apostle. At Paris, Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor.” The entries for Sardinia and Caraunus are pure.

BRUXELLEN. is not entirely pure in the notice of Julius; in second place it adds: “And Saint Hesychius martyr,” taken, I think, from Ado, although, as we said in the note, he is commemorated on 25 June. The account of Eutropius is correct. Then: “And Saints Martialis, Lucianus, and Castulus.” Should this not be Servulus, so that all are people of Tomi? “In the territory of Arras, Saint Ragnulfus, bishop and martyr.” As we said in the second supplement, the later title is sufficient.

HAGENOYEN., fairly pure in the text, continues as follows:

“On the same day, the burial of Lord Bede, teacher of the English and venerable cardinal priest. He was English by nationality, and when he was seven years old he was given to Abbot Benedict to be brought up. From him he received the monastic habit, and afterward always learned or taught, composing incomparable books together with homilies and sermons used by the Church in the divine office. At Rome he earned the name ‘Venerable,’ for he expounded Scripture, which no one before him had been able to expound. He is said to have cursed the writers of cathedral books; at last he died in a good old age, having been blinded before his death.”

AQUICINCT. omits at the end the commemoration of Saint Ragnulfus, which nevertheless more properly belongs here.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130. At the end: “In the city of Sora, the passion of Saint Restituta, virgin and martyr.”

BIGOTIAN., marked p. 5, formerly belonging to the Celestines, and UGHELLIAN.: “Also the burial of Lord Bede, priest and teacher of the English people.” As in ANTUERPIEN. and MAX.-LUBEC.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “In the territory of Orléans, the translation of the body of blessed Maximinus, abbot, and the dedication of a church in his honor and that of blessed Stephen the protomartyr.”

VATICAN no. 5949 says nothing of Ragnulfus. It begins: “At Benevento, Saint Felix martyr, in Saint Sophia.” See the Omitted Saints. At the end it adds: “At Sora, a city of Campania, Saint Restituta, virgin and martyr.”

FLORENTIN.: “At Florence, the burial of Saint Podius, bishop of that city, who died glorious in life and miracles. He was buried in the cathedral church of the aforesaid city, beside the body of Saint Zenobius in a marble sarcophagus.” See Henschenius’s Commentary.

LUBECO-COL. EDITION. It begins with Pope John, whose eulogy it supplements as follows: “In his time France was converted to Christ. He died at Ravenna in prison under King Theodoric, a supporter of the heretics; his body was transferred to Rome and buried in the church of Saint Peter in the Vatican.” The text that follows is pure, except that it makes Ragnulfus a bishop. Then: “Also the burial of the holy and venerable Bede, priest and teacher of the English people. At Alexandria, the passion of Saints Aquilinus, priest, and fourteen others.” Add “of the Gospel,” as it appears below in the Supplements of GREVEN.

BELIN. adds to a text that is not sufficiently corrected: “On the same day, Saint John, pope and martyr, whom King Theodoric of the Arians sent into exile at Ravenna, where, after long suffering in prison, he ended his life. Also the octave of Saint Bernardine of Siena, of the Order of Friars Minor.” The later edition adds: “At the monastery of Micy, the translation of Saint Maximinus, abbot.” See above in REG. SUEC. 428.

GREVEN.: “At Alexandria, Saints Aquilinus, priest, Evangelus, and fourteen others. Also Saints Salustianus, Elias, Saccius, and Restitutus.” See the Acts. “At Ravenna, blessed Symmachus, patrician and martyr, killed by the Arian King Theodoric together with his son-in-law Boethius.” Boethius is commemorated on this day, but Symmachus on 23 October. “On the same day—or, according to others, on the sixth day before the Ides of June—Maximinus, bishop of Aix, concerning whom it is read in the Acts of blessed Mary Magdalene.” See the Octave of June. “Maxentius, abbot of Poitiers, a man of great holiness. Although content with bread and water, he was nevertheless frequently nourished by divine banquets through angels; among his other miracles, he raised a dead man and brought forth a spring for his thirsty brothers.” This is referred to 26 June.

MOLAN. copied BELIN’s account of Pope John. Then, in smaller type: “The arrival of the body of Saint Adrian martyr at Mount Girard.” Other editions have the notice of John first; and near the end, in italics, they insert: “On the twenty-seventh, Saint Therapontus, hieromartyr.” See what survives concerning his miracles and translation in Greek and Latin in our Acts. “On the same day, the arrival of Saint Adrian martyr at Mount Girard, in the year 1510.” His feast is 8 September.]

[Col. 0093]

At Mesia, in the city of Durostorum, the birthday of blessed Julius. During the persecution, when he was a veteran and had completed his military service, he was arrested by officials and brought before the judge. In his presence, because he cursed the idols and steadfastly confessed the name of Christ, he was punished with a capital sentence. In Gaul, at the city of Orange, Saint Eutropius, bishop, whose life, illustrious for virtues and miracles, Bishop Verus describes in a lucid sermon. In the territory of Adartum, Saint Ragnulfus martyr.

V Kal. Day 28.

[Note: [Col. 0095D]

This is taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerpien. and Max.-Lubec., Antuerp.-Maj., Greven., and Molan. Add also Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Danic., the Ultraject.-Belg. Edition, and almost Bruxellen.]

[Note: [Col. 0095D]

All the manuscripts write *orthodoxam*, except Antuerp.-Maj., Greven., and Molan.; therefore we thought no correction necessary. *Parisius* should be retained in the ancient spelling; Molan. corrected it to *Parisiis*, while Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and all the manuscripts of middle quality have *Parisiorum*. Praten. reads “Germanus, bishop and confessor,” together with Antuerp. and the cited manuscripts of middle quality. We prefer the reading of Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Greven., and Molan., which, avoiding the repetition of *bishop*, append Usuard’s eulogy to Bede’s notice, with a more polished construction of the kind Usuard ordinarily follows. Only Herinien. has *sanctus Fortunatus*; only Antuerp.-Maj. has *Fortunatus presbyter*. Molan. wrote *quantique fuerit meriti et claruit*. In all manuscripts except Molan. the reading is *Stilo*; in all, *Emilii*; in Pratensis alone, *Felici*. That the ancient form was *Charaunus* is demonstrated by the older manuscripts, Pratensis, Heriniensis, and Antuerp.-Major, which we followed, although *Caraunus*, French *Cheron*, is now more widely accepted.]

[Note: [Col. 0097A]

We noted on the preceding day, in the third Supplement, that Pope John and martyr is placed not on 27 May, as the modern Roman Martyrology did after Belin, but on this day by all the ancient martyrologists who mention him, Rabanus alone excepted—regardless of the statement in our Acts that his translation took place and that he is commemorated at Rome on 27 May.

Bede compiled his eulogy, or the account of his captivity and death, briefly but elegantly. Rabanus and Ado copied it from him; Notker copied it from Ado, adding some details about Symmachus and Boethius. Our author, following his custom, captured the substance of the matter in an elegant abridgment. Many have written about this glorious pope; Henschenius and Papebrochius collected and arranged the more significant episodes of his life. The former began a Commentary in which he explained the sense in which the pope is sometimes attributed to him; the latter revised and completed it.

Bede also mentions Germanus, whom he honored only with the title “confessor.” I do not know why Rabanus recorded him on the preceding day with a longer eulogy. Ado, surprisingly, honors Germanus with no encomium, perhaps because he considered the memory of this celebrated saint, renowned throughout Gaul, and his deeds sufficiently famous. In Bede’s Supplements there are two eulogies attributed by our predecessors to Florus. One of them is formulated in such a way that someone might immediately object that I have wrongly denied universally, in my preface and throughout this work, that Florus was ever seen by Usuard. Yet it is easy to show that nothing in these passages shakes my assertion.

I readily admit that in our edition of Bede two supplements by Florus have been added. But anyone even moderately accustomed to using martyrologies will easily recognize that the first eulogy of Germanus is genuinely characteristic of Florus, whereas the second is not; it is supplied conditionally, indeed almost doubtfully. Nor could it have been supplied otherwise, since the Atrebatian manuscript cited there—the one I have before my eyes—makes it sufficiently clear that this and many other notices are not genuine compositions of Bede or Florus, but were transferred from Usuard into the aforesaid Atrebatian manuscript. I shall demonstrate this with many examples if necessary. Add that the eulogy in question is expressed wholly in Usuardian phraseology; in this matter I would appeal in vain to the judgment of anyone other than experts.

Rabanus on the preceding day and Notker on this day have fuller narratives. Their meaning is similar, though their wording differs; yet I would be mistaken if Notker had not had Rabanus before him as a model. Florentius excludes Germanus from the Hieronymian Martyrology, although the oldest copies represent him there. We admit that these were expanded and interpolated by the monks to whom they belonged.

Wandalbert’s metrical poem places Germanus before John:

“On the fifth day, the crowd at Paris frequents Germanus;

then Rome also celebrates its pontiff John.”

Of the Sardinian martyrs, the Small Roman Martyrology recorded only the first two, but Ado restored two companions from the Hieronymian Martyrology; Usuard and Notker followed him. Others are added in the Acts; see Papebrochius’s critical Commentary.

Caraunus, as the older manuscripts write, or Charaunus, as is now preferred, martyr of Chartres and unknown to the other ancient martyrologists, is plainly Usuardian. I think no one can call the remainder of the text into question, whatever its source. Henschenius published the Acts of Caraunus and gave his judgment that they belong to Usuard’s—or rather Hilduin’s—century. In his preliminary Commentary he most plausibly determines the saint’s date and other matters concerning him; from these you may judge whether Baronius was right to assign him to the time of Domitian.]

[Note: [Col. 0097C]

PULSANEN. abridges the eulogy of Germanus and omits the final notice.

ROSWEYD. expands the meaning in the first notice, inserting after “held”: “and afterward, by order of Theodoric, king of the Arians, he was led to death together with Symmachus the patrician and other Catholic men.”

MUNERAT. after “by miracles,” alone inserts into an otherwise pure text concerning Saint Germanus: “whose body rests in the monastery of blessed Vincent, in the suburbs of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.”

ALBERGEN and DANIC are deficient in the first notice concerning Pope John, who was wrongly recorded by them on the preceding day. BELIN agrees with them in this, as I recall having explained fully there.

CENTULEN.: “The birthday of Saint John, pope, who was killed by the impious King Theodoric and honorably buried in the church of blessed Peter the Apostle. At Paris, Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor.” The entries for Sardinia and Caraunus are pure.

BRUXELLEN. begins as follows: “The birthday of Saint John, pope. He was sent by King Theodoric the Arian to Constantinople; before the city gate he restored sight to a blind man. He was gloriously received by the Catholic emperor Justin, fulfilled his mission, returned to Theodoric, and was imprisoned by him at Ravenna with other equally Catholic men, where he died of hunger. Blessed Gregory mentions him in the Book of Dialogues.” The account of Sardinia and Caraunus is nearly pure. At the end it adds:

“At Paris, the burial of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor. When he was ill, he ordered the words ‘V Kal. JUNII’ to be carved on the wall opposite him. Since he died on the following day, it is clear that this had been divinely revealed to him. How great his holiness was,” etc.

HAGENOYEN., moderately interpolated in the text, adds the following, which I wish to place before the curious reader:

“On the same day, the burial of Saint William, duke of the province of Aquitaine, commonly called William of the Spider. He served most valiantly under Charlemagne. He recovered the great city of Orange, which Theobald, king of the Saracens, had occupied, and took its queen, named Kyburga, as his wife. He endured many dangers in war against the pagans; he crushed the Agarenes in many ways, restored peace to the Church, and exercised himself in every good work. He attended willingly to the common good, confirmed holy laws, settled disputes in the Church, governed lords, and made himself a protector and generous benefactor of churches and servants of God. He always rose before priests and commended himself devoutly to their prayers.

“Although he did these things as a layman, once he became a monk he became a cook and requested that the duties of the bakery and mill be assigned to him. He always endured everyone’s ways with equanimity. In the monastery he became renowned for miracles and the spirit of prophecy: he foretold the death of Charles, that of several others, and also his own. Finally, after laboring greatly in the active life, through the insistence of his brothers he transferred himself to the contemplative life. A hundred times by day and a hundred times by night he used to bend his knees in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion; he exchanged bodily battles for spiritual battles when, in winter, he threw himself into cold water. Strengthened by the body and blood of Christ, he happily rested in the Lord, and throughout the neighboring provinces the sound of bells is produced by divine power.”

With a few omissions, this is an abridgment of the Acts reported by Henschenius.

AQUICINCT. adds concerning John: “led away by King Theodoric Adrian.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Germanus, bishop of Paris. John, pope and martyr, whom blessed Gregory mentions in the Book of Dialogues. William the confessor, first a count and duke in the time of Charles, afterward a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict.” You have a sufficiently lengthy history above.

VATICAN no. 5949 does not have “Caraunus.” It adds: “At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, Saints Epagathus, Eustasius, and Castulus.” See the entire group of these martyrs enumerated more distinctly in the Acts.

FLORENTIN.: “At Florence, the burial of Saint Podius, bishop of that city, who died glorious in life and miracles. He was buried in the cathedral church of the aforesaid city, beside the body of blessed Zenobius in a marble sarcophagus.” See Henschenius’s Commentary.

LUBECO-COL. EDITION. Concerning John, it has him on the preceding day. The remaining text follows. Then: “At Meaux, blessed Rogomorus, bishop and confessor. At Paderborn, the arrival of Saint Liborius, bishop and confessor of the city of Le Mans.” His feast is 23 July. “On the same day, the translation of Saint Bridget, widow, from Rome to Sweden.” Her birthday is 8 October.

GREVEN.: “Fortinus, bishop and martyr.” In the Omitted Saints he is thought to be the one commemorated on 2 June. “At Meaux, blessed Rogomorus, bishop and confessor. Also William, duke of Aquitaine and confessor. In the time of Charlemagne, after many victories over the infidels, he became a monk. Once, when there was no broom available to clean the oven in which bread was being baked and he feared delaying the brothers, he entered the heated oven, cleaned it with his scapular, and emerged unharmed. Crispola, virgin,” previously unknown to me, unless perhaps a martyr named “Crispolus” is meant, such as is commemorated on the following day. “At Paderborn, the translation of Saint Liborius, bishop and confessor of Le Mans. The translation of Saint Bridget, widow, from Rome to Sweden.” We have spoken of both immediately above.

MOLAN.: “The translation of the holy relics of blessed Bridget from Rome to the monastery of Vadstena in the kingdom of Sweden.” Other editions have: “On the twenty-eighth, Saint Nicetas, holy father, and Saint Helladius, hieromartyr.” The first is commemorated on this day, the other on the preceding day. “At Paderborn, the translation of Saint Liborius, bishop and confessor of Le Mans. Also the translation of the holy relics of blessed Bridget,” etc. These are the same translations of which we have already spoken above.]

[Col. 0095]

At Rome, the birthday of blessed John, pope, whom Saint Gregory reports to have been first held in custody for the orthodox faith and then led to death together with other equally Catholic men. At Paris, the passing of Saint Germanus, confessor. This blessed bishop of the same city—how great his holiness and merit were, and by what miracles he also became renowned—Bishop Fortunatus set forth in truthful writing. In Sardinia, Saints Aemilius, Felix, Priamus, and Lucianus. On the same day, Saint Caraunus, who at the city of Chartres received martyrdom by beheading.

IV Kal. Day 29.

[Note: [Col. 0099B]

Taken from Praten., Rosweyd., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. Also from Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Danic., the Ultraject.-Belg. Edition, and almost Bruxellen.]

[Note: [Col. 0099C]

*Icnoniam* in Antuerp.-Maj. can easily be corrected to *Iconium* in Munerat. and *Ichonium* in Greven. Likewise *Aurelio* in Rosweyd., *Conoris* in Antuerp.-Maj., and *Canonis* in Munerat., which also reads *filiorum* instead of *filii*. Another error occurs in Antuerp.-Maj.: *craticula* instead of *craticulam*, and *injuriam* instead of *penuriam*. Neither is satisfactory, although the former is better than the latter. Molan. is best, writing *poenam*, and Greven. *penuriam*, elsewhere *paenam*. The manuscripts of middle quality also have *poenam*. Pratensis, Heriniensis, Rosweyd., and Munerat., however, consistently read *penuriam*, which we thought should be retained in the text. After *passi*, Molanus inserted *sunt*, thereby damaging the construction. In Greven. the name *Martyrii* is absent; Munerat. substitutes *Martirini*. Rosweyd. has *Avaniae*, Antuerp.-Maj. *Inaniae*, and the latest manuscripts *Ananiae*, correctly in the text. In Rosweyd., *viris* is omitted after *gentilibus*. Antuerp.-Max. wrongly writes *Treveris translatio*. Antuerp.-Maj. has *Maximiani* instead of *Maximini*. The last four manuscripts add *Alexandrinus* after *Antistes*. In Munerat. *Constantii* is absent. The same manuscript and Antuerp.-Maj. abound in various scribal errors, which, as minor trivialities, we deliberately disregard here and elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0099C]

The Small Roman Martyrology treats, in order, Restitutus, the seven German brothers, and Maximinus of Trier; Ado preserved it, adding the material that we shall shortly mention. Our text, even if not in precisely the same order or in exactly the same words, was transferred here wholly from Ado.

Conon with his son, who is placed first here, is mentioned by some manuscripts on the twentieth of this month, after Rabanus composed a longer eulogy, as we said there in the Supplements. This Conon, unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrology, Bede, and the Small Roman Martyrology, was first recorded by Ado and adorned with a eulogy almost transcribed by Notker. Usuard made the greater part of it his own, a fact that somehow escaped Papebrochius’s notice. In his Commentary he observed other matters that shed light on the ancient Greek-Latin Acts published by him.

The learned modern scholars admit that those Acts are venerable for their simplicity and gravity. Among them Tillemont, in volume IV, page 455, willingly accepts with Papebrochius the account of the passion as derived from the proconsular Acts. Nor do the objections he notes on page 683 prevent this, although they are such as show that the Acts are not wholly original and authentic; for that reason Ruinart did not include them among the genuine and selected Acts.

The Anaunian, or Anagnian, martyrs of the territory of Trent are mentioned in the Hieronymian copies, with their names somewhat corrupted. We therefore believe that they passed into Ado, who elaborated their praise at greater length. Our author contracted the whole matter into a shorter form from Ado. The reader will perceive, by comparing them, what agrees in Rabanus and Notker.

These holy martyrs found such an encomiast in Vigilius of Trent that nothing can be set against their Acts. Ruinart included Vigilius’s account in his collection, beginning on page 682. Tillemont abridges the Life in French in volume X, beginning on page 543, investigates everything more fully, and explains what is obscure. Papebrochius does so in our Acts.

We have already said that the Small Roman Martyrology mentions Maximinus; the Hieronymian copies mention him, and Bede does also. From Bede, Rabanus and Florus composed a brief eulogy. Ado, following the Small Roman Martyrology, added only what our author transferred word for word. Whether Notker appropriately appended other material, together with a long fragment from Augustine’s letter, is not for me to judge.

The importance of the Lives of Maximinus composed in the eighth and ninth centuries is demonstrated by Henschenius in his preliminary dissertation. More reliable information must be sought from ecclesiastical history in Baronius and others; see Tillemont, volume VIII, in various places. Hear Wandalbert, who composed this single verse today about Maximinus alone:

“Maximinus, for you, on the fourth day, lofty Trier shines.”

The memory of Restitutus, and afterward of the seven German brothers, is expressed in nearly the same words in the Hieronymian Martyrology, the Small Roman Martyrology, Ado, our text, and also Notker. But the last-mentioned, together with their mother Symphorosa, are commemorated on 18 July, as is shown there from Usuard himself—unless they are the sons of Saint Felicitas, commemorated on 10 July, or other full brothers. See volume V, 1 May, page 237, letters E and F.

Henschenius considered the Acts of Restitutus to have been written with gravity and to be highly trustworthy, a favorable judgment indeed; but those who have weighed Tillemont’s discussion in volume V, page 634, will scarcely accept it. We leave the arguments on both sides for the curious reader to examine.

Meanwhile, what I said at the beginning remains true: our text is derived from Ado, and it is no less certainly Usuard’s.]

HERINIEN. To the otherwise very pure text it prefixes this announcement peculiar to itself: “Translation of the body of blessed Remigius, apostle of the Franks, from the place where it had previously lain in the same church.” Nothing about this is found in the others.

[Col. 0101B] TORNACEN. It cuts out the eulogy of Conon, as well as that of the martyrs of Anaunia. Otherwise pure.

PULSANEN. It also removes Conon’s eulogy. It is sufficiently pure in the entry for Sisinnius and his companions. Then: “At Trier, blessed Maximinus, bishop and confessor.” There it stops, omitting the rest.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC., LOVANIEN. and ALBERGEN. are deficient only in Conon’s eulogy. BELIN is affected by the same defect.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the feast of blessed Restitutus. On the Via Tiburtina, the seven brothers. At Trier, blessed Maximinus, bishop and confessor, by whom Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, fleeing the Arians, was honorably received. Also the passion of Conon the martyr and his son. On the same day, the holy martyrs Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander.”

BRUXELLEN. differs from the purity of the text in this manuscript—which we admit is rare there—almost solely in the transposition of the announcements.

[Col. 0101C] HAGENOYEN. It amplifies Conon’s eulogy from Rabanus, unless I am mistaken, as follows:

“Near the city of Iconium in Isauria, the passion of Saint Cuno and his son. He, having left his wife, became a hermit together with his son. This Cuno commanded a river, which people could not cross, to flow elsewhere, and so it happened. Later, when they had been arrested, they first endured boiling oil, burning coals, a grating, a frying pan, hanging with fire placed beneath them, and the crushing of their hands with a wooden mallet. Yet in all these things the martyrs of God remained unharmed; and, looking toward heaven and praying, they departed to the Lord.”

It omits the martyrs of Anaunia; otherwise it is nearly pure.

AQUICINCT. Instead of *Anauniae*, it has *Auniae*.

[Col. 0102A] MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Maximinus, bishop of Trier. Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander, martyrs. At Rome, the seven brother martyrs.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. After a slight interpolation concerning Conon, it continues [Col. 0102B] as follows:

“Near the city of Trent, Saints Sisinnius the deacon and Martyrius, who, as blessed Paulinus writes, came from Cappadocia to Milan, where they stayed for some time with Saint Ambrose. From there they came to Trent, where they were gladly received by Saint Vigilius, bishop. After a few days he sent them to a village called Medo, so that there too they might proclaim the faith of the Trinity to the Gentiles. When they had already converted many there, they were seized by unbelieving men, beaten, hung up, wounded, and tortured with various punishments; finally, handed over to the fire, they obtained the crown of martyrdom. It was the day of the Lord’s Passion, and therefore the Lord’s miracles were not lacking. The relics of the saints were carried to the city of Trent by Saint Vigilius the bishop. At Trier, the translation of the body of blessed Maximinus, bishop and confessor, from Aquitania to Trier.”

“Restitutus” follows, but the final announcement is absent.

GREVEN. “Note: on this day blessed Maximinus was translated from Aquitania to Trier” [Col. 0102C]; “the day before the Ides of September is the day of his burial.” See the Preliminary Commentary to the Acts, no. 5.

“Also Saints Pollio, Crispolus, and Cyrillus.” Thus Numidia, Caesarea of Cappadocia, and Antioch are joined together.

“In Africa, the feast of Saints Primus, Accidia, Passimonius, and 143 others.” In the Acts these are distinguished more clearly.

“In Bechlem, Suicbert, bishop and martyr.” See the Omissions.

MOLAN. In the latest editions, concerning the martyrs of Anaunia, he inserts in italics, in the text itself after “On the same day,” the word “at Milan,” and so forth. At the end, in smaller type: “Their martyrdom is described on 27 June.” Why not 18 July?

[Col. 0099]

Near the city of Iconium in Isauria, under the emperor Aurelian, the passion of Saint Conon the martyr and his son. First placed upon heated iron, then upon a grating with burning coals beneath it and oil poured over it, they endured steadfastly. Afterwards, having suffered both the frying-pan and suspension on the torture-horse, as well as deprivation of fire, and finally having had their hands crushed with a wooden mallet [Note: [Col. 0099B] In the manuscript the whole passage reads: “Afterwards, having suffered both the frying-pan and suspension on the torture-horse, as well as deprivation of fire, they had their hands finally crushed with a wooden mallet”—the words are written over an erasure. Nevertheless all the codices give the same reading. The erasure, therefore, is older than any copy of the Usuardine Martyrology. BOUILLART.] they gave up their spirit in praise of almighty God.

On the same day, Saints Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander, who, in the regions of Anaunia, as Saint Paulinus writes, obtained the crown of martyrdom while pagan men were persecuting them.

At Trier, blessed Maximinus, bishop and confessor, by whom Athanasius the bishop, fleeing the persecution of Constantius, was honorably received.

At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the feast of Saint Restitutus. On the Via Tiburtina, the seven brothers.

III Kal. Day 30. [Note: [Col. 0101]

So read Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Rosweya., Antuerp.-Maj. Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0101D]

For “the emperor Claudius,” Rosweyd substitutes “Diocletian”; Antuerp.-Maj. is mistaken elsewhere in omitting “emperor.” I read *Gabini* with Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Greven., and Molan. If one prefers *Gabinii*, I do not object. Likewise, on the authority of all the codices, I read *Crispoli*, although the Romanum parvum and Ado write otherwise. Only Pulsanen. has wrongly placed *Scripuli*. It is not worthwhile to append here the variations of the other codices. Pratensis and Herinien. have *Hucberti*, and this is probably the correct reading. Others have *Huberti*: Tornacen. wrongly has *Bucberti*, and Pulsanen. is no more correct with *Bucherti*.]

[Note: [Col. 0101D]

The author of the Romanum parvum is the first to discuss Felix, pope and martyr; he may perhaps have found his name in Rufinus, Book VII, chapter 27. Ado then reproduced it in precisely those words, which Usuard transferred into his own text. Notker thought it appropriate to append a few remarks about Masses celebrated in commemoration of the martyrs; some Additions drew material from these remarks. Henschenius [Col. 0103A] and Papebrochius examine and attempt to determine the dates of this holy pontiff, finding scarcely anything that can confidently be asserted in praise of Felix apart from a fragment of a letter quoted by Cyril of Alexandria and by the Council of Ephesus. See what Tillemont added to this, vol. IV, p. 362 onward. After Papebrochius, he discusses the day of his martyrdom or death at length in the same volume, p. 687, where, from various passages of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, from the Calendar of Fronto on 29 July, and from Sacramentaries and other monuments, he considers it more probable that 30 May became more celebrated on account of some translation. Since we presently lack anything more certain, we do not wish to accumulate conjectures. The question of the confusion and distinction of the various Felixes remains to be examined in the Acts under 29 July. It will be evident below that this day was also selected by Wandalbertus.

From the same source and stream come the martyrs Gabinus and Crispolus of Sardinia. Their memory, however, is also celebrated in the Hieronymian copies, which may perhaps be called their original source. We have placed Gabinus first, although the Romanum parvum and Ado express the name differently. Likewise, instead of *Crispuli*, we read *Crispoli*, on the agreement of our oldest codices. But this is not a difficulty of great importance. Henschenius raises the more serious question whether this Gabinus is distinct from another Gabinus or Gavinus, who, with other companions, is commemorated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 25 October. Much here is again obscure; perhaps some light will be shed on it when these matters are discussed in the Acts under 25 October. Meanwhile see what Tillemont has in vol. II, pp. 230 and 587, and then in vol. V, p. 143 onward.

Hubert—or rather Hucbert—peculiar to Usuard alone and furnished with the title of bishop, makes the matter complicated. For the more recent Usuardine codices, as will appear in the Additions, make him bishop of Liège; others make him bishop of Tongeren, although he may more correctly be called bishop of Maastricht, if indeed the reference today is to that bishop, and not, much more probably, to Hubert the monk of Brétigny, as Papebrochius thinks in the Acts. The curious reader should consult his Preliminary Commentary, nos. 1 and 2.

Worth noting is Castellani’s present announcement, appended to the text of the modern Roman Martyrology, which I translate from French into Latin: “At Fura (commonly Tervuren), between Brussels and Leuven, the passing of Saint Hubert, bishop, who transferred the episcopal see from Maastricht to Liège. His body was immediately transferred to Liège and buried there in the oratory of Saint Peter. Sixteen years later it was raised from the tomb, on 3 November; and, under Louis the Pious, it was transferred to the abbey of Andain in the Ardennes, which subsequently changed its name to that of Saint [Col. 0104B] Hubert. A certain monk of the same name is honored on this day at Brétigny in the diocese of Soissons, because his true day of death was unknown.”

These details are for the most part taken from Papebrochius’s commentary just cited. See below, under 30 September, Molan’s Addition from his later editions. The remaining matters concerning Hubert the bishop will be more carefully discussed and clarified in the Acts under 3 November, when he also recently began to be honored at Antwerp with a solemn office. Here we have represented the genuine text of Usuard. Thus Wandalbertus writes of Hucbert and Felix:

“Let the third be dedicated to Hucbert, the Pope, and Felix.”

[Note: [Col. 0103B]

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. and UGHELLIAN. omit the third announcement concerning Saint Hubert, substituting in its place: “At Antioch, the feast of Saints Sicius and Palatinus, who suffered many torments.” That entire announcement has been transferred here from the Hieronymian Martyrologies or from Rabanus.

[Col. 0103C] ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., and EDITIO ULTRAJ.-BELG. insert into the cited announcement the words “suffered for Christ.” At the end, however, they retain Hubert’s commemoration in this form: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Hubert, bishop and confessor of Liège.” I have already said in the observations that these Belgian codices connect Hubert’s name more explicitly with the bishop of Liège than Usuard himself does in the genuine text.

ULTRAJECT. and DANIC. agree with the three last-mentioned witnesses, but go beyond them by appending to the text concerning Pope Felix: “He was the twenty-seventh after blessed Peter, and instituted the celebration of Masses in commemoration of the martyrs.” In the observations we noted that this was added by Notker.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, Saint Felix, pope and martyr, under Caesar Claudius.” It is pure in the entry for Sardinia. It continues: “At Antioch, Saints Isicius and Palatinus, who suffered many torments. On the same day, Saint Hubert, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Centula, [Col. 0103D] Saints Chaidocus, Fricorius, and Madelgisilus, confessors, the first two of whom were companions of blessed Richarius at the beginning of his holy way of life.” Henschenius treats the first two together in his historical commentary; one of them is also called Adrianus. He found more about Madelgisilus—so he is generally called—and illuminated it with a careful commentary.

BRUXELLEN. agrees with the preceding witnesses except in the final announcement, which it gives as follows: “On the same day, the burial of Saint Hubert, bishop and confessor of Liège. Miraculously appointed to the episcopate in succession to blessed Lambert, he transferred the episcopal see from Maastricht to Liège; and finally, on this day, at Fura in Brabant, rescued from this wicked age, he ascended to heaven, while his body was transferred to Liège, where it was honorably buried in the church of Saint Peter.” See the Observations above.

[Col. 0104B] HAGENOYEN. In addition to what has been said about Felix, it adds: “And under him the heresy of the Manichaeans arose.” In second place it has Hubert of Liège, and so forth. Then: “Also Thudebert the confessor.” He is entirely unknown in the Omissions and cannot be confused with Trudpert, the martyr in Breisgau, discussed under 26 April. For why would the same compiler repeat the same saint twice, once as a martyr and once as a confessor? What if we suppose that Hucbert the monk of Brétigny was here transformed into Thudebert through the scribe’s error? The martyrs of Anaunia follow in the codex, improperly inserted on this day. The entry for Sardinia is pure. Finally, concerning the Antiochene saints Sico, or Isicius, and Palatinus, see above.

AQUICINCT. Concerning Felix: “He instituted the celebration of Masses over the memorials of the martyrs.”

DAVERONEN.: “At Tours, the first reception of the relics of the most blessed Julian the martyr.” See the Omissions, where Henschenius notes: “He seems to be Saint Julian the martyr of Auvergne, on whose feast the Acts of his martyrdom, divided into nine lessons, are read in the church and diocese of Tours on 27 August.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Dymphna, virgin and martyr, who was beheaded by her father for her faith and chastity.” She is nowhere read of by others on this day; see 15 May. “Felix, pope and martyr. Gabinus and [Col. 0104D] Crispolus, martyrs.”

In the VATICAN codex numbered 5949, the final announcement concerning Saint Hubert is absent.

FLORENTIN.: “At Ravenna, Saint Exuperantius, archbishop and confessor.” See Papebrochius’s Historical Commentary, where he makes several careful observations about other Exuperantiuses.

DIVIONEN., of the church of Saint Stephen: “The dedication of Saint Medard in the city of Dijon.” Nothing about this appears in the Omissions. See what is said in the Acts under 9 June, Preliminary Commentary § IV, p. 77, letter A.

EDITIO LUBECO COL. gives the following concerning Felix: “After he had governed the Church for five years and ten months, he was crowned with martyrdom under the emperors Claudius and Aurelian. He was the twenty-seventh after blessed Peter,” and so forth. It continues with the Sardinian and Antiochene saints. Then: “In Apulia, Saint Nicholas the Pilgrim and confessor, famous for miracles.” Reference is made to the day on which he is honored at Trani, 2 [Col. 0105A] June. “On the same day, the feast of Saint Hubert of Liège, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN. In the next-to-last place it also inserts the Antiochene martyrs. Instead of *Huberti* it writes *Hugberti*; and in another edition it adds: “At Centula, the burial of Saint Madelgisilus the confessor.”

GREVEN.: “Note: this is the burial of Saint Hubert; his translation is on the third day before the Nones of November.” See the observations made above on this matter in more than one place.

“At Antioch, the feast of Saints Sicius and Palatinus, who suffered many torments for Christ. In Apulia, blessed Nicholas, surnamed the Pilgrim, confessor. Led by dove-like simplicity, he wished to fulfill the Lord’s command concerning taking up the cross. Carrying a wooden cross in his hand, crying ‘Kyrie eleison’ (‘Lord, have mercy’), and leading behind him innocent children who shouted the same words, he went around the places of the town. At last he rested in peace, famous for miracles.”

We have already said that reference is made to the day on which he is honored at Trani, 11 June. There the saint’s image, Life, miracles, translation, and other matters concerning him are carefully arranged by Papebrochius. [Col. 0105B] It continues:

“On the same day, according to the Catalogue of the Saints, at Venice, the translation of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor, together with the bones of his predecessors, [Col. 0106A] Theodore, bishop of Myra and martyr, and another Nicholas, bishop and confessor of the same place, the uncle of Saint Nicholas, from Myra to Venice, in the time of Pope Urban II.” See what is said about these in the Omissions.

MOLAN.: “Of the church of Tongeren. He was first buried near Saint Lambert the martyr; after some years he was transferred to a certain monastery and buried there with honor. At Ravenna, Saint Ursinus the martyr, who suffered under the judge Paulinus and was buried in the same city by blessed Vitalis, father of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.” Reference is made to 19 June.

“At Antioch, Saints Syrius (so it reads here, although below it more correctly writes Sicius) and Palatinus, who suffered many torments. At Centula, the burial of Saint Madelgisilus the confessor.” Thus far the first edition.

In the others, after “under the emperor Claudius and Aurelian,” it inserts words in italics. Likewise, after *Crispoli*, in the same type: “At Centula, the burial of Saint Madelgisilus the confessor. At Antioch, [Col. 0106B] Saints Syrius, etc. On the thirtieth day, Saint Isaac, father of the Dalmatian monastery.” Finally Saint Hubert follows, where, as in the earlier edition, “of the church of Tongeren” is inserted.]

[Col. 0101]

At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the feast of blessed Felix, pope, who, after governing the Church for five years, was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Claudius. At the Towers of Sardinia, the holy martyrs Gabinus and Crispolus. On the same day, Saint Hucbert, bishop and confessor.

The day before the Kalends. Day 31. [Note: [Col. 0105]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0105C]

Muneratus suffers from the usual defects of a corrupted edition: *sociari* for *sociare*, and *tridui induas* for *tridui inducias*. Moreover, *tridui* should be read, not *triduum*, as Pratensis has, nor *triduo*, as Antuerp.-Major has; the other codices demonstrate this. Herinien. wrongly deleted the particle *mox*. For *Cantii*, Antuerp.-Maj. wrote *Cautini*; Greven. has *Cancii*, *Canciani*, and so forth. Muneratus has *cum ducerent prosapiam Aniciorum*. Herinien. altered the wording even more severely as follows: “who were descended from the family of the Anicii.” All the others have *pedagogo* in the text, since none uses the diphthong, except Molan alone. Antuerp.-Maj. has *petagogo*. Greven. and Molan. write *Protho*, while all the others agree with the text. *Creciani* for *Crescentiani* is an error in the major Antwerp codex.]

[Note: [Col. 0105C]

Florentinius correctly observed that Petronilla, a Roman virgin, was assigned to Aquileia in some Hieronymian copies through the carelessness of scribes, although that section concerns the three brothers who follow in the text. Bede and the Romanum parvum likewise mention this Petronilla, and only within those limits. Rabanus followed the former, adding the entire portion of Marcellus’s letter that you will find quoted in the Acts. Whether what Marcellus relates there is genuine may be judged from the fact that Petronilla is called the daughter of the apostle Peter and that other details are included which do not readily win credence. Recent scholars regard them as highly suspect; see Tillemont, vol. I, p. 189. Ado compressed the matter. Notker seems to have read both him and Rabanus, while our author extracted the more certain elements from Ado’s eulogy, deliberately passing over what he recognized as open to doubt.

Furthermore, the genuine Usuardine codices clearly establish that he is cited incorrectly, as though he had named Petronilla, Saint Peter’s daughter, together with the others. He entirely avoided that designation and moderated the rest so prudently that he seems to have deliberately composed his eulogy in this manner.

Wandalbertus did not do so. The following verses of his concerning Petronilla survive:

“Then, on the day before, Petronella, holy offspring of Peter’s stock,

The radiant virgin shines, clothed in Christ’s splendor.”

The three Aquileian martyrs, recorded in Jerome and the Romanum parvum, receive no eulogy from Ado, nor do Rabanus and Notker add anything of importance. Whatever praise concerning the family of the Anicii, and so forth, appears in the entry we have presented belongs to Usuard. I believe that Usuard was given access to those Acts which, taken from Mombritius and manuscript codices, are reported on this day, and which probably had not come to Ado’s attention.

Henschenius carefully elucidated the Acts of these illustrious martyrs from the oldest manuscripts, collating them with one another and with Mombritius’s edition, and appended Analecta that accurately clarify much collected here and there about their relics, miracles, and translations. The same Acts had earlier been published by Mabillon in his volume on Gallican Liturgy, p. 467, in 1685; Henschenius was unable to see that edition, since he had died four years earlier. Tillemont considered all this in vol. V, p. 636, distinguishing what is precious from what is worthless. He approves the material that is customarily circulated under the name of Maximus of Turin, while criticizing certain points in the others, at least as insufficiently exact. We leave the whole matter to the judgment of prudent readers.

Here too Wandalbertus’s verses concerning the Cantian martyrs have their place:

“Cantius and Cantianus with Cantianilla

Shine forth. These solemnities close the month of May.”

Some Hieronymian witnesses mark Protus the pedagogue, together with Chrysogonus, whom we discuss elsewhere. Crescentianus, placed last, passed from the cited Hieronymian Martyrologies through Ado to this place and to Notker, everywhere in the same words except for the title “martyr,” which our author added. Thus we have restored the genuine Usuardine wording. Crescentianus is usually joined with Gabinus and Crispolus, discussed in the text for the preceding day, as a fellow-countryman and perhaps also as a companion in martyrdom; see the brief commentary of Henschenius.]

[Note: [Col. 0107A]

TORNACEN. Here again it cuts something from the text, namely the eulogy of the Cantian martyrs; otherwise it is extremely pure.

PULSANEN. It is additionally mutilated in the final announcement.

ROSWEYD. At the beginning it reads: “At Rome, Saint Petronilla, daughter of Saint Peter, who, after many…” and so forth. But again at the end it inserts: “On the third day, immediately after she had received from Nicomedes the priest the sacrament of Christ…” and so forth. The remainder is pure.

ANTUERP., MAX-LUBEC., and BELINUS, after “Petronilla the virgin,” insert: “Daughter of blessed Peter the apostle, who, rejecting the marriage of Count Flaccus, obtained a three-day period for deliberation and, devoting herself to fasts…” and so forth. In the rest they are pure.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN-BELG., and EDIT. ULTRAJ.-BELG. have the same addition, but after “received the Sacrament,” they further insert: “reclining on her bed, she gave up her spirit.” The LOVANIEN. codex agrees with this, but lacks the eulogy of the Aquileian brothers.

[Col. 0107B] ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. resemble ANTUERP.-MAXIMUM, but after “she gave up her spirit” they further add: “When Pope Paul opened her tomb in order to transfer the virgin’s body, it was found in her marble sarcophagus, engraved by the hand of the apostle Peter: ‘To golden Petronilla, his sweetest daughter.’” See in the Acts how well this inscription accords with the style of the apostle Peter.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, Saint Petronilla the virgin, who is said to have been the daughter of blessed Peter the apostle. Near Aquileia, Saints Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla, brothers, who, being of the family of the Anicii and unwilling to worship idols, were beheaded for Christ together with their pedagogue. At the Towers of Sardinia, Saint Crescentianus.”

BRUXELLEN.: “At Rome, Saint Petronilla the virgin, daughter of blessed Peter the apostle. After many miracles of healing, when Count Flaccus wished to marry her, which she rejected, she asked for a three-day period of deliberation and, fasting and devoting herself to prayer with Saint Felicula, her foster-sister, on the third day, immediately after receiving Christ’s Sacrament, she reclined on her little bed and gave up her spirit.”

This is almost the whole of Ado’s text, taken from his Martyrology. The well-known addition follows: “When Pope Paul opened the tomb of this virgin in order to transfer her body, he found it in her marble sarcophagus, engraved by the hand of blessed Peter the apostle: ‘To golden Petronilla, his sweetest daughter’—Peter’s act of devotion.” See what Henschenius thinks of this inscription in his Historical Commentary, no. 4. The rest of the codex is pure.

HAGENOYEN. What it has concerning Petronilla will be read more accurately in the Acts than in the material already given. I add, however, what follows concerning the Cantian martyrs:

“Near the city of Rudelphus, Aquileia, the feast of the holy martyr brothers Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantionilla, who were of the family of the Anicii and of the emperor Carinus, and were taught the faith of Christ by their pedagogue Protus. Fearing the persecution of Diocletian, they sold their inheritances at Rome and went to Aquileia, thinking that they would find Chrysogonus and Anastasia in prison; but they had already been taken away through the palm of martyrdom. They were therefore accused before Augustus by Dladius [Dulcidius] and Sysinnius, on the charge that they were Christians, and at Aquae Gradatae, beside the river Ysocium [Hysontion], they were beheaded and buried by Saint Scelius [Zoilus or Zeno].” [Col. 0108A] See the Acts themselves, from which this material was taken. The entry for Crescentianus is pure.

MATRIC-CARTUS-ULTRAJECT.: “Petronilla, daughter of Saint Paul the apostle. Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla, brother martyrs, together with their pedagogue Protus. Crescentianus the martyr.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, adds: “Saint Primianus and Firmianus.” They do not belong here at all, and I cannot clearly see whom the compiler intends to indicate.

EDITIO LUBECO COL. begins as follows: “Near Cologne, translation of the holy Maccabean martyrs, carried out in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164 by Reynold, archbishop of Cologne.” They are celebrated on 1 August, when the entire history of the translation of the holy Maccabees to Cologne will be most carefully elucidated. Concerning Petronilla it has the same material as ULTRAJECT. and the other codices cited above. The remainder is pure.

[Col. 0108B] GREVEN.: “At the city of Girona, the feast of Saints Germanus, Victor, and Sylvanus.” As usual, this writer selects some names from the Hieronymian copies. On this day he was fortunate in correctly forming the three names marked there, but I do not know why he omitted the leader of the others, “Gaulienus.” See the companions listed in the Acts.

“Also Chrysogonus.” He is celebrated on 24 November.

“Commemoration of Saints Marcellus and Exuperantius, martyrs, who are placed under the third day before the Kalends of January,” and correctly so; together with “Sabinus.”

“Near Cologne, translation of the holy Maccabean martyrs carried out in the year…” and so forth.

MOLAN. In small type: “At Rome, Saint Paschasius the archdeacon and confessor, concerning whom Gregory writes in the Dialogues.” Nothing about this Paschasius is read in the earlier Martyrologists, so it must be judged that he passed from these additions into the modern Roman Martyrology. In his Historical Commentary, Henschenius presents the entire story of Paschasius, who was in purgatory and yet famous for miracles, from Gregory’s Dialogues, and confirms it by a similar example. He rightly distinguishes this Roman deacon Paschasius, unless I am mistaken, from another Paschasius, deacon of Saint Martin, bishop of Dumium, whose Acts are treated under 20 March.

It continues: “At Clermont, Saints Alexander and Galla, confessors, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes in his book on the Confessors.” These saints were first entered in the sacred tables by MOLAN, but were omitted by Baronius. In Gregory of Tours, chapter 36, the tomb and merits of each are discussed; but who they themselves were, or where they came from, has not yet been discovered. Henschenius thinks that the “Galla” of whom we speak here is different from “Galla, wife of Saint Eucherius,” as he attempts to demonstrate in the Acts against Baronius.

The other editions have only this: “On the thirty-first day, Saint Hermias the apostle and the most holy martyr Hermaeus.” The third edition of 1583 reads the same word for word, which makes me wonder why the Acts report it differently. Meanwhile, see there whether this is one Hermias or Hermaeus, or whether two persons should be distinguished. Papebrochius thinks that the martyr of this day should be called “Hermias” and buried at “Comana”; but that “Hermaeus” of Sirmium is a different person. He nevertheless struggles to distinguish from this Hermaeus Saint Hermas, the apostle of Dalmatia, whose Acts are reported under 8 April. See more in the commentary of the Papebrochius just mentioned.]

[Col. 0105]

At Rome, Saint Petronilla the virgin, who, after many miracles of healing, when a certain count wished to marry her, asked for a three-day delay, devoted herself to fasts and prayers, and on the third day, immediately after receiving Christ’s Sacrament, gave up her spirit.

Near the city of Aquileia, the feast of the holy martyr brothers Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla, who, being descended from the family of the Anicii, were beheaded, because of their steadfastness in the Christian faith, together with their pedagogue Protus.

At the Towers of Sardinia, Crescentianus the martyr.

THE MONTH OF JUNE HAS THIRTY DAYS.

[Col. 0109]

On the Kalends. Day 1. [Note: [Col. 0109]

Thus read Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan., which alone are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0109B]

There is a difficulty at the very beginning. Pratensis writes: “At Rome, the dedication and feast of Saint Nicodemus.” Antuerp.-Maj. and Tornacen. have “the feast” or “feast-day of Saint Nicodemus”; Greven. and Molan., “the dedication of the basilica of Saint Nicodemus.” Others have “the dedication and feast.” We believe that Usuard preserved Ado’s reading, as it appears in Muneratus, Herinien., and others, and therefore in our text. Molan also seems to have recognized this, since in his later editions he printed *basilicae* in italics, distinguishing it from the text.

Likewise, with Praten., Antuerp.-Maj., and Muneratus, we correctly read *Maximini*, not *Maximiani*, as Greven. and Molan. have. In the codices it is, and should be, *Pamphili presbyteri*. [Col. 0110B] Pratensis erred in writing *episcopi*. Again, all have *se reperisse*, or, as Greven. writes, *repperisse*; I do not know what Muneratus, usually more carefully corrected, intends by *recepisse*. There are numerous scribal errors, such as *Niconedis*, *presbiteri*, *Palestinae*, *Caesariensis*, *Jeronimus*, *Hieronimus*, *inquid*, *Cresi*, and *Lirinensis*. We have thought it best to preserve those readings in which the principal codices and the others agree today.

Pratensis erred again by removing the title “bishop” from Reverianus, which he had wrongly assigned above to Pamphilus. Antuerp.-Major falls no less shamefully into error: instead of “Reverianus the bishop … crowned with martyrdom together with the others,” it has “Severianus the bishop and confessor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0109C]

We have already sufficiently noted that it is uncertain what Usuard wrote in his original wording concerning Nicodemus the priest and martyr on this day. After others, he himself connected his feast-day, or day of combat, with 17 Kalends of October, that is, 15 September. It is clear that the dedication of some church in honor of the martyr is meant. The author of the Romanum parvum seems to have been the first to mark this with the words: “The dedication of Saint Nicodemus the martyr.” Ado added “priest at Rome,” while at the same time indicating the feast-day mentioned above. Bede, perhaps older than both, expressly wrote: “The feast of Nicodemus the martyr,” [Col. 0110C] and Rabanus then added “the dedication of the church.”

Whether Usuard forged a more obscure expression from these insufficiently clear ones—*dedicatio natalis*—I leave to the judgment of the reader skilled in such matters. I preferred the syntax of the Romanum parvum and Ado, along with Usuard’s customary rule. I shall not dwell on this at greater length, since the whole matter requires a more laborious investigation, to be provided in the Acts on Nicodemus’s actual feast-day, 15 September, as the Martyrologies establish.

Papebrochius rightly judged in his Commentary that the contest of the famous martyr Pamphilus is improperly reported on this day, and that his two companions Valens and Paul are no more correctly added in the modern Roman Martyrology. They would be better joined with all the companions under 16 February. There he also makes the quite successful conjecture that some Martyrologist older than Ado and Usuard, perhaps merely at his own discretion, entered Pamphilus on this day.

This is indeed what happened; and it is not difficult to identify that Martyrologist, namely the author of the Romanum parvum, who, following his usual guide Rufinus, reads today in second place: “And Saint Pamphilus the martyr,” without adding any indication of time or place.

Ado did not doubt that the reference was to the illustrious man celebrated by Eusebius. From this source and from Jerome’s *De viris illustribus*, chapter 75, he composed the eulogy, the principal portion of which our author transferred word for word, while Notker copied it all. We therefore believe that this is the sole true reason why Pamphilus is entered separately from the others in our Martyrologies on this day.

We discussed his companions in our Observation under 16 February, cited in the final section. There we said that Tillemont set out in French, in vol. V, p. 418 onward, the continuous series of twelve martyrdoms from Eusebius and others. Almost the same material is published in Greek and Latin in our Acts on this day by Papebrochius, in two sections comprising what survives from the three books on the Life of Pamphilus written by Eusebius. These had previously been published under the name of the Metaphrast, and so seemed to have lost some of their authority.

Wandalbertus honors Pamphilus and Nicodemus:

“Your beginning, June, raises your brilliance to the stars,

Pamphilus, venerable teacher in blessed martyrdom;

And this day adorns the feast of the martyr Nicodemus.”

Reverianus of Autun and Paul with his companions were first entered into the sacred calendars by Usuard; no earlier or contemporary writer mentions them. Nor should Peter de Natalibus be followed, since he wrongly attributes them to Ado. See Henschenius’s commentary and the Acts communicated by P. F. Chifletius; to these may be added Motherius’s note appended to the French Martyrology on this day.

Caprasius, however, is plainly taken from the cited Ado and from his very words. I do not sufficiently understand why Claudius of Vienne, the eleventh bishop, noted there, was omitted. In any event, we have no doubt that what we have given belongs to Usuard. What remains concerning Caprasius may be found collected and reviewed by Henschenius.]

PRATEN. has especially much today concerning the “Dedication of the Crypts,” etc., recited in full in the Index of Matters Omitted. We were uncertain whether this longer passage should be attributed to Usuard himself; when consulted on the matter, Castellanus replied that, in the Pratensis manuscript, everything was written by the first and same hand. Is it Usuardine? I do not think so, given the manifest opposition of nearly all the other codices, and especially of another Pratensis codex, B, in which this passage is attested by the illustrious Sirmondus to have been erased; he compared our copy with the alleged autograph.

HERINIEN. is the purest throughout its entire text, and at the end adds the following material peculiar to itself:

> “At Trier, the deposition of the blessed Simeon, monk. He came forth from the monastery established on Mount Sinai, obeying the commands of his superior, and, arriving in the aforesaid metropolis, assiduously practiced a life of withdrawal for many years. There, when the Lord called him, he departed to the heavenly realms; that he lives happily there is repeatedly attested by the miracles he displays.”

TORNACEN. cuts away the second part of the eulogy of the blessed Pamphilus; otherwise it is pure.

PULSANEN.: “At Rome, the dedication and birthday,” etc. It continues:

> “In Campania, the birthday of Saint Erasmus, bishop and confessor. Under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, after being tortured by various punishments, he finally rested in a holy death when the Lord called him.”

See the third day. Moreover, in the manuscript the entire eulogy of Pamphilus is truncated. Nothing else is given.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., quite pure in the text, add at the end, the former Juvencius, the latter Vincentius. In others one finds Viventii, Viriani,” etc. See the Matters Omitted and the Acts, p. 43.

ROSWEYD. is also quite pure in the text here, but at the end adds: “Likewise, Faustinus, bishop and martyr, and his companions.” There is a certain Faustinus among the martyrs of Perugia; whether this refers to him, I do not know.

[Col. 0111D] ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN. and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. EDITION also reproduce the text, but add: “At Rome, Saint Vincentius.” We have already spoken of him. Then: “At Trier, the blessed Simeon, monk.” LOVANIEN. has the same, but is defective in the second part of the eulogy of Saint Pamphilus. ALBERG. and DANIC., however, like the first group, are acephalous at the beginning, lacking “dedication,” etc.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, Saint Nicomedes, martyr. At Caesarea in Cappadocia [Palestine], Saint Pamphilus, priest and martyr, from whom Eusebius of Caesarea took the surname Pamphilus. At Autun, Saints Reverianus, bishop, and Paul, priest, with ten others, who suffered under Aurelian.” It is pure in the passage concerning Caprasius.

[Col. 0112B] BRUXELLEN., usually purer in its text, adds:

> “At Vienne, Saint Elaudissimus [he meant Claudius], bishop. And at Trier, the deposition of Saint Symeon, monk and hermit. He was born at Syracuse in Sicily; at Trier he was confined for a long time in a tower for Christ, and departed to Christ.”

HAGENOYEN., moderately interpolated in the first three announcements, inserts before Caprasius:

> “The deposition of Saint Simeon, monk and confessor. He was born in Sicily of very noble parents, and led the eremitical life on Mount Sinai. But Puppo, archbishop of Trier, crossed the sea, brought Simeon to Trier, had him shut up above the Black Gate, provided him with necessities, and he gave his soul to God. He was buried there and shines forth through many miracles.”

Caprasius follows; and at the end: “At Rome, Saint Vincentius.” Concerning him, see above.

[Col. 0112C] AQUICINCT. begins: “At Rome, the dedication of the birthday,” etc. At the end: “Likewise, Jovinus, abbot.” He is noted in the Acts as belonging to the diocese of Poitiers in Gaul.

VICTORIN. substitutes another location for Autun: “In the territory of Nevers.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Nicomedes, martyr. Pamphilus, priest and martyr. Reverianus, martyr, with his companions.”

In the VATICAN manuscript no. 5949, “Nicomedes, and Reverianus and Caprasius” is lacking; it adds: “At Thessalonica, Saint Lucia, virgin.” See the Index of the Saints of this day and the Acts, in which she has various companions.

UGHELLIAN. at the end: “At Rome, Saint Viventius.” See above, ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.

ALTEMPS.: “At Poitiers, Saint Jovinus, abbot.”

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, Saint Vincentius. Near Bologna, the passion of Saint Proculus, martyr and bishop of Terni, in the duchy of Spoleto; by his life and miracles he converted many to the Lord.” See the Matters Omitted and the Acts. “On this same day, Saint Vivianus, confessor.” [Col. 0112D] Is this not Viventius, Virianus, Juventius, or Vincentius? “Likewise, Saint Simeon, who formerly lived in Bethlehem in the Holy Land and afterward came to Trier and ended his life there; his basilica, of massive construction, is still visible there today. Likewise, Saints Virianus the soldier and Secundarius with their companions, who suffered for Christ under the emperor Decius.” Does this concern the martyrs of Tifernum? Let our Acts be consulted.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins with Pamphilus, quite purely, and proceeds similarly with Reverianus and Caprasius. Then:

> “At Rome, Saint Viventius, martyr. At Trier, in the gate called Marcia or the Black Gate, the deposition of the blessed Simeon, monk and confessor. At Rome, the commemoration of the blessed Nicomedes, priest and martyr. [Col. 0113A] At Vienne, Saint Claudissimus, bishop and confessor.”

It should be read, as I said above, Claudius.

BELIN, concerning Nicomedes, adds from Ado: “whose martyrdom is celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.” He shortens the eulogy of Pamphilus from the middle onward. In Reverentianus, instead of Reverianus, and in Caprasius, he is pure. At the end: “Likewise, Saint Virianus, martyr.” In another edition the eulogy of Pamphilus is supplied.
