After “Virianus” is added: “At Rome, Saint Juventius, martyr.” See above concerning the confusion of the names. “At Poitiers, Saint Jovinus, abbot.”

GREVEN: “Likewise, Saints Octavius, Zosimus, Lucia, Castus, Pullus, Lupus, and Crispus.” The explanation must be sought in the Acts. “Justus and Virianus, martyrs. At Rome, Viventius, martyr.” Concerning these, see what has been said and the Matters Omitted. “Cuno, also called Conrad, provost of the principal church of Cologne and martyr. In the year of the Lord 1066, he was thrown three times from a very high mountain by wicked men; when he remained unharmed, they killed him with swords, and he became renowned for miracles. At Vienne, Saint Claudius, bishop and confessor. At Trier, in the gate called Marcia or the Black Gate, the deposition of Saint Symeon, monk and confessor. Thecla, virgin and martyr”—I think the Antiochene Thecla, together with Zosimus, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

MOLAN. inserts in italics, after “martyr,” concerning Nicomedes, Ado’s words, “whose martyrdom is celebrated,” etc. At the end:

> “Likewise, Saint Virianus, martyr. At Poitiers, Saint Lovinus, abbot. At Trier, in the city, in the gate called Marcia or the Black Gate, the deposition of the blessed Simeon,”

etc., almost as in HERINIENSIS.

“On this same day, the translation of the body of our holy father Gislenus, and of Saint Sulpitius, bishop and confessor, and of blessed Leochadia, virgin.” See the Matters Omitted. Then, in smaller type, concerning Cuno or Conrad, from GREVEN. It continues:

> “At Rothbornacum, the translation of the body of the divine Cyprian.”

He is commemorated on 14 September. Later editions also print “basilica” in italics. At the end, however:

> “At Poitiers, Saint Jovinus, abbot. At Trier, in the city,”

etc., exactly as we cited above from HERINIENSIS.

“On this same day, Saints Felinus and Gratianus, martyrs under Caesar Decius.” See in the Acts: “Felinus and Gratianus. At Clermont, Saint Medulphus, confessor, a man of great holiness. At Vienne, Saint Claudius XI, bishop. Likewise, Saint Virianus, martyr. At Rome, Saint Viventius, martyr.”

Enough has been said about these two. “On the first day, Saint Justin the Martyr, Philosopher, and the other Justin with his companions.” See the Acts. Concerning Gislenus, etc., as in the first edition:

> “At Rothornacum, the translation of the relics of the divine Cyprian. At Soissons, the elevation of Saints Principius and Lupus, bishops and confessors, Gandinus, martyr, and Agricola, priest and confessor. At the monastery of Fontenelle, the translation of Saints Maximus and Venerandus, martyrs, Wolfrannus and Erembertus, bishops, and Condedus, priest and confessor.”

In the Matters Omitted, each is referred to his proper day.

> “Likewise, at Dole, Cuno or Conrad, provost of the church of Cologne, who in the year 1066, after being thrown three times from a very high mountain, remained unharmed, and shortly afterward was killed with swords; he became renowned for miracles.”

[Col. 0109]

At Rome, the dedication of Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr. Near Caesarea in Palestine, under the persecution of Maximinus, the blessed Pamphilus, priest and martyr, whose Life the bishop Eusebius of Caesarea comprised in three books. Saint Jerome also writes that he found certain volumes written by Pamphilus’s own hand; “I embrace and preserve them,” he says, “with such joy that I think I possess the wealth of Croesus.” At Autun, Saints Reverianus, bishop, and Paul, priest, with ten others, who were crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian. On this same day, Saint Caprasius, abbot of the monastery of Lérins.

[Addit Bouill.: [Note: [Col. 0109A] This dedication of the crypts of the church of Saint-Germain is so particular to it that it is not surprising that those who copied Usuard’s Martyrology omitted it. Yet Sollerius considers it sufficient evidence that the long passage should not be attributed to Usuard, because nearly all the other codices contradict it, and especially Pratensis B, in which Sirmondus testified that it had been erased. I confess that this latter argument ought to have caused Sollerius some difficulty. Nevertheless, he is at fault when, for that reason, he denies that it was written by Usuard, since the perfect resemblance of the writing persuades us that it was written by him. Was the knot difficult to untie? He should have waited a little and restrained himself; he should have inquired by letter what crypts there were at Usuard’s monastery; why that dedication is announced once and again; and why Pratensis B silently passes it over. These were the duties of an accurate editor. I shall untie the knot briefly. Where the elegant chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary is now seen built in the monastery of Saint-Germain, there were formerly crypts, or subterranean altars, whose dedication was celebrated in Usuard’s time on the Kalends of June. Later the same dedication was celebrated on the fourth day before the Ides, as is clear from the Pratensis codices; it finally ceased to be celebrated after the chapel of the Blessed Mary was erected in place of the crypts by Hugh of Yssiaco, abbot of the Pratensis monastery. If Sollerius should then ask why the commemoration of that dedication was erased in Pratensis B, the reason is obvious. Once the altars had been demolished—which happened while this codex was in use—their dedication ceased to be announced; hence later codices, that is, those written during the last four hundred years, entirely omitted it. BOUILLART.] At Paris, at the monastery of the blessed Germanus, the dedication of the crypts in honor and veneration of Mary, Mother of God, and of the blessed apostle Peter, and of the holy martyrs George, Aurelius, and Natalia. There the principal altar was consecrated in the name of the same virgin and of blessed Peter and all the apostles; at the head of the holy martyrs there is an altar in honor of Saint Michael and of all the blessed heavenly powers; and at their feet, one of Saints Vincentius, Sebastian, Christopher, Andochius, Thyrsus, and Felix. There is also an altar in honor of Macharius, Dionysius, Rusticus, Eleutherius, and all the holy martyrs. And another of Saint Marcellus, the virgin Genovefa, Sabinus, Audoenus, Ansbertus, and all confessors and virgins.

IV Non. Day 2. [Note: [Col. 0113B]

Thus the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerpiensis, Max.-Lubeck, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts, and, remarkably, Hagenoyen as well. The Antwerp-Maximus, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, and Ultrajectine-Belgian editions also agree; in them two words are added, which will shortly be noted.]

[Note: [Col. 0113C]

Greven and Molan, as well as the manuscripts of middling authority, have “saints” instead of “blessed martyrs.” For Serenus, Max.-Lubeck wrongly has Semio. Rosweyd has Lugduno. In Greven, instead of “Saints Photinus,” there is “Saint Photinus.” I read Fotini with all the codices except Munerat and Molan, who more correctly write Photini, although most, following Jerome, prefer Pothini, from Greek πόθος (“longing”) rather than from φῶς (“light”), so that the name means “desirable” rather than “bright.” Fontinus in Max.-Lubeck is an error, as is Matudi for Maturus; [Col. 0114C] and in Molan Pagati for Epagati, which is wrongly divided in Heriniensis as Et-pagati. Antwerp-Maximus, Utrecht, Leiden, and Leuven, after “ecclesiastical history,” perhaps insert “book five,” from Ado. The Rosweyd codex likewise omitted it; “also suffered” must be read. In Rosweyd, “is” is lacking; in Greven and Molan, “also”; in Antwerp, “and.” Max.-Lubeck, instead of “from their company,” has “among.” The Pratensis alone reads “was slain”; the rest agree with the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0113D]

The excessive length of Ado, and consequently the necessity of a more concise Martyrology for ecclesiastical use, is abundantly demonstrated by this one day alone, on which his work is much more like a Legendary than a Martyrology, describing at length from the Acts themselves the history of Marcellinus and Peter, and again that of the martyrs of Lyon. All the most ancient martyrologists, however—Jerome, Bede, and the Little Roman Martyrology—speak of Marcellinus and Peter. Rabanus copied Bede, and Notker followed one or the other, adding briefly some material from Ado. Our author likewise transfers everything from Bede word for word, omitting only the angelic vision and the conversion that followed it, of Dorotheus; it is remarkable that the other martyrologists pass him over so completely that no trace of his sacred cult appears. The companions of Marcellinus and Peter who are missing here are clearly recorded in the Acts. The memory of these martyrs of ours is certain and most celebrated, being consecrated even in the Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, in the Sacramentary of Gregory, the Missal of Thomasius, and other unquestionable monuments. Would that the same could be asserted of the Acts themselves, which Baronius rightly judged to have been written in antiquity, under the year 302, no. 10. Henschenius attempted to defend them; but more recent scholars have stamped them with a very different judgment, and Tillemont did not consider them worthy material from which to compose his French Life in volume V, p. 199, referring their examination to a note on p. 663. Henschenius and Papebrochius collected much curious material concerning the cult of Marcellinus and Peter, especially concerning their relics, which were translated to various parts of the Catholic world; add to them what Janningus more recently excavated in the Supplement to June, [Col. 0115A] where, after Laderchius, he discusses at much greater length, diligence, and accuracy the question of whether there was at Rome not one church of theirs, as Tillemont thought, but two.

The martyrs of Lyon are not in the same position as the Roman martyrs. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies they are recorded in a more confused manner; in Bede they are said to number forty-seven or forty-eight (Rabanus incorrectly put sixty-eight), of whom only the illustrious virgin Blandina is named as the leading figure, with the additional mention of one Ponticus. In Ado, a very full account of the persecution at Lyon and Vienne is woven, from which the names of the individuals can easily be extracted, except for Saint the deacon; Henschenius did this distinctly. Notker transferred a large part of the foregoing narrative; but Usuard, constrained by his customary limits, selected from Ado the names arranged by him, as they are displayed in the margin, and from Bede, in more compressed wording, composed Blandina’s contest. These constitute everything announced by Usuard on this day. [Col. 0115B] It remains only to state briefly how highly learned men value the incomparable Acts of these martyrs of Lyon, or Vienne, from which perhaps no more certain, no more brilliant, no more august monument of the earliest Christian strength and evangelical beauty has come down intact to posterity—indeed, a monument that even the hypercritical receive and esteem with the greatest veneration. Eusebius transmitted to us a most precious treasure in book V of his Ecclesiastical History, from the letter of the Christians of Lyon, probably written by the hand of Irenaeus, to the churches of Asia and Phrygia. Henschenius explains the matters disputed in these Acts, whether because of variant translations or readings, carefully seeking out each of the forty-eight names of the martyrs, as Florentinius also does. Tillemont set everything out in French in volume III, beginning at p. 1. See also Ruinart’s admonition and his notes on the aforesaid Acts, beginning at p. 45. It will not be displeasing to the reader to hear Joseph Scaliger’s judgment on those very Acts, which certainly cannot be suspected by anyone. To the words of the Eusebian Chronicle—“Many were gloriously killed in Gaul for the name of Christ, whose struggles, committed to books, endure to the present day”—he makes this devout observation in his Notes, p. 202, no. 2183:

> “And today Polycarp’s martyrdom exists in Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History; these are the Church’s most ancient martyrdoms, and by reading them the mind of the devout is so moved that it never leaves them satiated. Everyone can recognize that this is so according to his own capacity and the condition of his conscience. Certainly I have never seen anything in Ecclesiastical History from whose reading I would depart more deeply moved, so that I seem no longer to belong to myself.”

We feel the same about the Acts of the martyrs of Lyon and Vienne in that same Eusebius: what more august or more venerable can be read among the monuments of Christian antiquity? Thus he speaks. It is open to everyone to experience the same movements of the soul. Wandalbertus adorned all the martyrs in our text not inelegantly in his verses:

> O sacred Marcellinus, O Peter the exorcist, on the fourth day before the Nones, offer sacrifice at the common and worthy altar;  
> and at Lyons Blandina is invoked with pious honor,  
> she who, together with forty-eight, wove a shining necklace  
> amid flames and waves.

[Note: [Col. 0115B]

TORNACEN., excessively prone to mutilating the text, cuts back the eulogy of Marcellinus and Peter here; otherwise it comes quite close to the purity of the Usuardine text.

PULSANEN., pure in the first announcement, is more abbreviated in the second, writing:

> “At Lyon, Saints Zacharias, priest, and Donatus, martyrs, with forty-six others. [Col. 0115C] All these servants of Christ, as it is written in the history,”

etc. But it says nothing about Blandina.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. is truncated in the first announcement, omitting these words: “who instructed many in the faith while in prison.”

ALBER. and DANIC. insert second today material belonging to the following day, namely:

> “In Campania, Saint Erasmus, bishop and martyr. Under the emperor Diocletian, he was first severely beaten with leaden balls, then with clubs; afterward, after being covered with resin, sulfur, pitch, lead, wax, and oil, he appeared unharmed. Then, under Maximian, after being tortured with various and most savage punishments, he finally rested in a holy death when the Lord called him.”

The rest, which belongs to the text, is pure.

CENTULEN.:

> “At Rome, the passion of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus, priest, and Peter, exorcist, under the judge Serenus. On this same day at Lyon, Saint Blandina, martyr, with forty-eight other martyrs, in the times of Marcus Aurelius [Col. 0115D] Verus and Antoninus and Lucius, his sons. On the same day, the translation of Walericus, abbot, from Flanders to his proper place.”

See the Acts of 1 April, p. 23, where this translation is discussed.

BRUXELLEN. appends the following at the end of its account of Marcellinus and Peter:

> “We commemorate them in the Canon of the Mass.”

It is almost pure in the account of the martyrs of Lyon. Then it adds: “And Saint Algisius, confessor.” There is an Adalgisus, a priest, in the little region of Theorascia in Picardy.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130, add at the end:

> “On this same day at Rome, Saints Marcellinus and Saturninus.”

I think they were taken from the great multitude of Roman martyrs, among whom there are “six Saturninae, two Saturnini, and one Marcellina,” but no Marcellinus apart from the one placed above in Usuard’s text.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs. Photinus, bishop and martyr, with forty [Col. 0116B] companions from the clergy and people, among whom Saint Blandina also suffered.”

In the VATICAN manuscript marked no. 5949, the entire announcement concerning the martyrs of Lyon is missing.

FLORENTIN.:

> “At Rome, the deposition or passing of Saint Eugenius, pope and confessor . . .”

[Col. 0116C] EDITIO LUBECO-COL., concerning Marcellinus and Peter, adds after the torments:

> “They were led into the Black Forest and beheaded there together, under the emperor Diocletian and the judge Serenus.”

It also inserts the following concerning the martyrs of Lyon:

> “As it is written in book five of Ecclesiastical History, they were crowned together in the time of Marcus Aurelius Verus and Antoninus and Lucius, his sons. Saint Blandina also suffered,”

etc. It continues:

> “Likewise, Saint Dorotheus, who saw the souls of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, splendidly adorned, carried by angels to heaven after he had beheaded them; afterward, doing penance, he was baptized under Pope Julius and rested in peace.”

See what we said above in our Observations.

BELIN, concerning the martyrs of Lyon, has:

> “On this same day at Lyon, Saint Blandina with forty-seven martyrs, in the time of Marcus Aurelius and Antoninus Verus and Lucius, his sons.”

He is pure in the first announcement. It continues:

> “In Campania, the birthday of Saint Erasmus,”

etc., as above in ALBERG. and DANIC. We, with Usuard and [Col. 0116D] the other martyrologists, shall treat of him on the following day.

GREVEN:

> “The names of the Saints who are read to have suffered at Lyon together with those mentioned above are these: Macharius, Alcibiades, Silvius, Primus, Ulpius, Vitalis, Cominus, Octuber, Philominus, Geminus, Julia, Rogata, Emilia, Potamia, Pompeia, Rodona, Biblis, Quartia, Maternia, Helpes, also called Amnes, Alexander, and Ponticus. All these rested in prison. Aristeus, Cornelius, Zosimus, Titus, Julius, Toticus, Apollonius, Geminianus, Julia, Ausonia, Emilia, Jamnica, Pompeia, Domna, Justa, Trofima, and Antonia. Algisius, confessor. Dorotheus, confessor, who, after beheading the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, saw their souls splendidly adorned and carried to heaven; he did penance, received baptism, and rested in peace. Archemias [Arthemius] with his companions.”

See 6 June.

> “Zacharias, monk, disciple of Abbot Silvanus, who, as Heraclides relates, led a very strict life in the desert, and, trampling his cloak beneath his feet, used to say that no one could become a monk unless he had likewise trampled everything underfoot in his mind.”

See what is said about this Zacharias among the Matters Omitted.

MOLAN, in his first and purer edition, has the addition concerning Erasmus given above; and, in smaller type:

> “Martyrius, monk, concerning whom Saint Gregory speaks in the Dialogues.”

He is unknown to me. In the other editions, after “he is slain,” the text in italic letters interweaves Bede’s words and those of Rabanus derived from him:

> “Then also Ponticus, a boy of fifteen years, was subjected with her to every kind of torment and, strengthened by her motherly exhortation, completed his martyrdom before her.”

There is then added, as though it were part of the text:

> “In Campania, the birthday of Saint Erasmus,”

etc. At the end:

> “On the second day, Saint Nicephorus, confessor and patriarch of Constantinople.”

See 13 March. Then, in smaller type:

> “In the territory of Lyon, the deposition of the blessed Algisius, priest and confessor. At Sandomierz, the annual celebration of the slaughter of the martyrs of Christ by the incursion of the Tartars, which is commemorated with a great gathering of the people, greatly enriched and endowed with indulgence by Pope Alexander IV. At the monastery of Lagny, the translation of Saints Deodatus, bishop, Maldegarius, Fulbertus, Amsilio, Lambertus, and one Innocent.”

See each of them in the Matters Omitted.]

[Col. 0113]

At Rome, the birthday of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus, priest, and Peter, exorcist, who, after instructing many in the faith while in prison, were beheaded under the judge Serenus after harsh bonds and many torments. At Lyon, Saints Photinus, bishop of that city, Zacharias, priest, Saint the deacon, Epagathus, Maturus, Attalus, Albina, and Grata, with forty others. All these servants of Christ, as it is written in the Ecclesiastical History, were crowned together. Saint Blandina also suffered, from their company; after being tortured on the first, second, and third day without being overcome, she was driven on the fourth day by blows, burned on grates, and subjected to many other torments; finally, she was slaughtered with the sword.

III Non. Day 3. [Note: [Col. 0117]

The Pratensis, Antwerp, Max.-Lubeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0117B]

The Pratensis and Molan correctly write Erasmi; Max.-Lubeck has Erasimi. The others, together with Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Rosweyd, and many others, generally have Herasmi, which we retained in the text. For “first with leaden balls,” etc., Max.-Lubeck and Munerat put “first.” Thus Antwerp and Molan have excruciatus instead of cruciatus. Greven, which in the first edition correctly wrote Aretinum, wrongly changed it in the edition we are following to Aretum. Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck read Arecium, and Valentini for Laurentini. Isaac is a common error among many. The final name is expressed in various ways: Munerat, Greven, and Molan thought they had corrected it properly to Liphardi, where they had found Lifardi in the older manuscripts, which is a common kind of meddling. I consider Lifardi preferable, since, as Henschenius said before me, it is more suited to the character of a Frankish name taken from the Teutonic language and signifying one endowed with a lovable disposition. Why should the same reasoning not also apply to Italian, Spanish, English, and similar names unrelated to Greek, as we have shown elsewhere? The title of bishop is wrongly assigned to Lifardus by Max.-Lubeck.]

[Note: [Col. 0117B]

The illustrious contest of Erasmus, celebrated in today’s Roman Martyrology and in the Acts, is famously related on the preceding day; it is no less certain that he is commemorated on that very day in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and by Rabanus, who gives an eulogy. Yet on this day he is mentioned by the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, and Notker. I do not dispute which day ought to be preferred. Notker almost entirely transferred Ado’s eulogy, adding the title of martyr, not merely bishop but specifically bishop of Antioch, and, unless I am greatly mistaken, incorporating some material from Rabanus’s encomium. Our author, following his usual practice, elegantly wove his garland from Ado’s flowers. Those Acts, which commonly circulate in the Legends, clearly preceded Rabanus and Ado. They are not without just suspicion of gratuitous invention, says Henschenius in his Preliminary Commentary, p. 211; Papebrochius explains this somewhat more clearly in the appendix attached to the Acts. Others reject them more categorically as entirely spurious; Tillemont, indeed, in volume V, p. 636, pronounces them, in his French phrasing, exceptionally bad. But whoever invented them cannot harm the very ancient cult of Erasmus, supported by so many monuments mentioned by Henschenius, whether only one Erasmus of Formiae is admitted, or a second, and perhaps several namesakes as well.

The Aretine martyrs are noted rather obscurely in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, with the name Laurentius given for Laurentinus and four hundred anonymous companions added. The Little Roman Martyrology more clearly distinguished the brothers, “at Aretium, etc.” Ado followed it, preferring to write Aretia, in a brief and polished eulogy, which Our author contracted, while Notker drew from it somewhat more generously. Everything was taken from ancient Acts, such as Henschenius published, which bear at least those blemishes that readily show them not to be original. Tillemont regards their excessive number of prodigies with suspicion, volume III, p. 332.

Isaac, the monk and martyr of Córdoba, celebrated by Saint Eulogius, should be counted among those whom Usuard brought from Spain; he was the first to insert him into the Martyrology, while all the other ancients were unaware of him. The martyrdom of this Isaac has been illustrated from Eulogius in our Acts.

Florentinius rejected the memory of Lifardus, Licfardus, Leifardus, or Liphardus among the additions to the Hieronymian Martyrologies—where in one manuscript he is wrongly called a bishop—for the reason mentioned elsewhere. Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado are entirely silent about him. Rabanus calls him Leofardus; Notker, Liefardus, not Licfardus. We have said enough about which form ought to be preferred. I think his first commemoration in the sacred calendars was received by Rabanus and Usuard from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. You have Florus’s particular eulogy in the genuine Bede and in the Acts; the appendices will provide a portion of it. We have recited what belongs to Usuard. See what Henschenius carefully collected from various writers concerning this saint. Wandalbert’s metrical eulogy mentions only the Aretines and Lifardus in these three lines:

> Pergentinus likewise, and Laurentinus, adorn the threefold [term uncertain] with the double splendor of blood and lineage;  
> and the people of Orléans commemorate their Lifardus.

[Note: [Col. 0117D]

HERINIEN., again exceptionally pure, adds at the end material peculiar to itself:

> “On this same day, the translation of the blessed Sindulfus, confessor.”

He is the saint honored in the territory of Rheims on 20 October; he is wrongly noted as a bishop in the Matters Omitted.

TORNACEN. is defective in the eulogy of the Aretine martyrs; otherwise it is entirely pure.

[Col. 0119A] PULSAN. treated Erasmus on the first day of this month, as we noted there. It is quite pure in the accounts of the Aretines and Isaac, but omits Lifardus.

ROSWEYD. adds at the end:

> “At Rome, Marcellus, martyr, with four hundred others.”

Many of his companions are enumerated in the Acts.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. confuses the sense, omitting the end of one passage and the beginning of the other, connecting the Aretine and Cordoban material in this way:

> “And great miracles were manifested: when they were twenty-seven,”

etc.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., AND THE ULTRAJ.-BELG. EDITION, pure throughout the text, record the following at the end:

> “In the territory of Orléans, the deposition of Saint Lifardus, priest and confessor. Renowned for many virtues and venerable in monastic habit, he rested in a holy death.”

ALBERG. and DANIC. have the same addition, or eulogy, concerning Saint Lifardus, but here lack the first announcement, which was given on the preceding day.

[Col. 0119B] CENTULEN.:

> “At the city of Aretium, Saints Pergentinus and Laurentinus, brothers. In Campania, the blessed Erasmus, bishop and martyr. At Córdoba, the blessed Isaac, monk and martyr. At Orléans, in the village of Meung, Saint Lifardus, abbot, who was the brother of the blessed confessor Leonardus. At the monastery of Centula, the glorious translation of our holy father Richarius, an excellent priest and precious confessor.”

The translation recurs elsewhere; see everything on the day of his commemoration, 26 April.

BRUXELLEN., quite pure in the text, has the following concerning Lifardus:

> “At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Lifardus, priest and confessor, who, renowned for many virtues, rested in a holy death. Likewise, Saint Ositha, virgin.”

This is Ositha, who is commemorated on 7 October.

HAGENOYEN., somewhat interpolated in its account of Erasmus, omits the Aretines. It is almost pure in the account of Isaac. Then, concerning Lifardus:

> “In the territory of Orléans, the deposition of Saint Lifardus, priest and confessor, who, renowned for many virtues and venerable in monastic habit, rested in peace in a holy death. Some say that he prophesied many things concerning the kings of France and Flanders. In the territory of Basel, Saint Morandus, a religious man venerable for many miracles.”

DAVERONEN.:

> “In the territory of Orléans, Saint Liphardus, priest and confessor.”

AMBIANEN.:

> “In the territory of Orléans, in the village of Meung, the deposition of Saint Liphardus, priest and confessor, who, renowned for many virtues and venerable in monastic habit and religious observance, rested in a holy death.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Pergentinus and Laurentinus, brothers and boy-martyrs. Erasmus, bishop and martyr. Isaac, monk and martyr. Lifardus, priest and confessor.”

In the VATICAN manuscript marked no. 5949, “Erasmus, Isaac, and Lifardus” is missing. It adds: “In Africa, Saint [Col. 0120A] Quirinus.” See his companions in the Acts, unless this is the one whom Usuard mentions on the following day.

ALTEMPS.:

> “On this same day, Saint Esitha, virgin.”

I think this is the same woman as the Ositha mentioned above.

> “Likewise, the ordination of Saint Thomas, martyr and archpres…”

Could this not be “archbishop”? If it refers to the archbishop of Canterbury, he is commemorated on 29 December.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. is quite pure concerning Erasmus and moderately interpolated in the account of the Aretines. It is pure concerning Isaac. Concerning Lifardus, it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. Then at the end:

> “On this same day, Saints Servilius and Erasmus, martyrs.”

I confess that I do not know to which class these two should be assigned here.

BELIN recorded Erasmus on the preceding day. In the remainder of the text he is not entirely pure, and announces at the end:

> “In the territory of Orléans, Saint Liufardus, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN:

> “On this same day, Saint Silvanus with eighty-two others; Abdianus and Neporius. The same four hundred martyrs.”

See the Acts.

> “On this same day, Saints Servilius and Erasmus. Morandus, confessor. In Ireland, Kelvinus, abbot.”

See the Matters Omitted.

> “Coemginus, confessor. Juliana, virgin,”

unless I am mistaken, the one counted among the African martyrs.

MOLAN: “At Treves, the burial of Saint Numerian, archbishop.” He is commemorated on 5 July. In smaller type follows: “On the same day, Saint Crotildis, queen. She departed to the Lord at the city of Tours, full of days, and was buried at Paris in the sanctuary of the basilica of Saint Peter, beside Clovis, king and her husband. Afterwards, however, she was enrolled among the saints because of the various miracles she performed there; placed in a precious coffin, she was raised up near the shrine of Saint Genevieve. Gregory of Tours mentions her honorably in Books II, III, and IV of his *History of the Franks*. On the same day, in the year 1070, at Hasnon in Ostrevent, the dedication of the old church, which Count Baldwin converted into a Benedictine monastery, by the bishops Lietbert of Cambrai, Rathod of Noyon, and Rainer of Orléans. At that dedication I find that the bodies of Saints Marcellus, Piaton, Salvius, Amatus, Donatian, Vedastus, Amandus, Audomar, Gislenus, Vincent, Bertin, Winnoc, Wandregisilus, Bavo, Everard, Eubert, Landelinus, Hugh, Aicadrus, Eusebia, Rictrudis, Aldegund, Queen Ragenfred, and Waldetrudis were present.” This has no relevance to the *Acts*, and MOLAN himself omitted it in later editions, where only this is read: “On the same day, Saint Morandus the confessor, disciple of blessed Hugh. And Saint Crotildis, queen. On the third day, Saint Lucillian, martyr.” See the four companion boys and the virgin Paula or Paulina, p. 274 in the *Acts*, and there Janning’s preliminary commentary with the Greek-Latin encomium. See also what is said about Morandus in the supplement to June.]

[Col. 0117]

In Campania, the commemoration of Saint Herasmus, bishop and martyr, who under the Emperor Diocletian was first severely tortured with leaden instruments, then with clubs, and afterwards, having resin, sulfur, lead, pitch, wax, and oil poured over him, appeared unharmed. Then, under Maximian, tortured with various and most savage punishments, he finally rested in a holy death when the Lord called him. At the city of Arezzo in Tuscany, Saints Pergentinus and Laurentinus, brothers and martyrs, who, when they were boys during the persecution of Decius, after enduring harsh tortures and displaying great miracles, were struck down with the sword. At the city of Córdoba, blessed Isaac the monk, who, when he was twenty-seven years old, was killed by the sword for the faith of Christ. In the territory of Orléans, Saint Lifard, priest.

The day before the Nones. Day 4. [Note: [Col. 0119]

The text is taken from Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0121A]

Molanus correctly reads *Illyricum*; but we, together with all the other manuscripts, have *Illiricum* in the text. *Siscia* must unquestionably be read, as in Herinien., Molan., Pratens., and others—not *Sitia*, as in Tornacen.; *Sisia*, as in Pulsanen.; *Stiscia*, as in Muneratus; or *Sicia*, as in Greven. [Col. 0122A] The title “martyr,” added by Muneratus, is found in none of the Usuardine manuscripts, nor even in Ado himself. Only the Pulsan manuscript has *fluvium* instead of *flumen*. *Optinuit* in the Herinien and Tournai manuscripts clearly retains the character of its own period.]

[Note: [Col. 0121A]

In the city of Sabaria, the Hieronymian copies mention Quirinus; for these, Florentinius’s annotations deserve consultation. From them, but especially from the *Acts*, it will be understood how the same Quirinus came to be associated with Sabaria and with other cities. The *Little Roman Martyrology* reads as follows: “At the city of Siscia in Illyricum, Saint Quirinus, bishop and martyr.” It would have been more correct to write “in Pannonia” or “near Pannonia.” The additions in the text are Ado’s, originally taken from the Hieronymian chronicle of Eusebius under the year 310. Our author, I say, took all his material from Ado, except that he omitted the name of the tyrant under whom Quirinus suffered and the translation of his relics to the Catacombs. But Notker copied these details, along with the others, wrongly reading *Fiscia* for *Sicia*. The hymn of Prudentius cited here appears in the *Acts*, where one will note in the preliminary commentary that what is attributed to Usuard as its source was in fact plainly taken by him from Ado, as is clear to anyone who compares them. Thus the millstone tied to his hand was also first incorrectly taken by Ado himself from the cited Chronicle or from the *Acts*. There it reads, “with a hand-millstone tied to his neck”; in these texts it is clearly stated, “with the millstone tied to his neck.” Moreover, those *Acts* are both very ancient and approved by everyone, and were also edited by Ruinart from p. 551 onward and translated into French by Tillemont in volume V, from p. 428 onward. Papebrochius in our *Acts*, as well as those authors, explains several difficulties concerning the place and date of the martyrdom, the governor and the tyrant, and finally the translations of the body or of parts of it. Thus Wandalbert praised him metrically:

> Quirinus, martyr and bishop, on the day before the sacred vows,  
> Adding to them, appeases Christ with his own blood.

It is entirely clear that this is, up to this point, a Usuardine entry. The Pratensian manuscript adds the following: “At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychus.” The other manuscripts disagree, except for a few that elsewhere more than once follow the erring Pratensian—namely Rosweyd., Antwerp Major, and Aquicinct.—as will be clearer in the *Appendices*. Those Nivedunian martyrs, not Ninivetan, as one manuscript has it and Rabanus especially imitated, were selected from the Hieronymian copies and detached from their companions. Henschenius, and after him Janningus in the supplement to June, p. 17, learnedly examines what region the aforementioned martyrs belonged to, or rather to which region Nivedunum should be assigned, Gaul or Pannonia. For the rest, Henschenius seems to have no doubt that the saints themselves should be attributed to Usuard. We are now asking whether Usuard really recorded them in his *Fasti*. Castellanus was consulted as to whether that announcement was inserted into the text of the Pratensian manuscript or written in the margin. After carefully inspecting the manuscript, he admitted that it formed part of the entry, since it was immediately attached to the preceding text; but he judged it to have been added by a more recent hand and therefore not to be Usuardine. In any event, we have now excluded the alleged autograph Pratensian manuscript from the number of pure manuscripts, removing that article which all the other manuscripts, at least the more reliable ones, plainly show to have nothing to do with Usuard.]

[Note: [Col. 0121C]

PRATENS.: Adds: “At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychus.”

ANTWERP MAJOR–LÜBECK and UGHELLIAN.: At the end: “Also at Rome, Saints Aretius and Dacianus.” Preface *Pictus*, as it appears in the *Acts*.

ROSWEYD.: Begins: “At Aquileia, Quirinus, bishop and martyr, and two hundred other martyrs.” It is unknown where he unearthed those martyrs; see what is said in the *Omissions*. The text follows, with *Scythia* instead of *Siscia;* at the end it adds, with the Pratensian: “At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychius.” See the *Observations*.

ANTWERP MAJOR: Also has: “At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychus.”

ANTWERP MAX., UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERG, DANISH, and the UTRECHT-BELGIAN EDITION: Add to the pure text: “His relics were translated to Rome, to the Catacombs. On the same day, Saints Aretius and Dacianus.” Most write this; but ALBERG and DANISH more correctly have *Dacianus*.

[Col. 0121D] CENTULEN.: “At the city of Siscia in Illyricum, Saint Quirinus, bishop and martyr, who suffered under Maximian, was translated to Rome and buried beside the Catacombs.”

BRUSSELS: Also has: “His relics to Rome,” etc. Then: “On the same day at Rome, Saints Aretius and Dacianus. At the city of Numidia [Nivedunum], Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Euthycus. Also the translation of Saint Poctocus the confessor.” Perhaps this refers to Abbot Petrocus in Cornwall, concerning whom see the *Acts* for this day.

HAGENOYEN: Adds concerning Quirinus: “His relics,” etc., as above. It then follows with the Aretine martyrs Pergentinus and Laurentinus, whom it had omitted on the preceding day. Finally: “On the same day at Rome, Saints Aretius and Dacianus, martyrs.”

[Col. 0122C] AQUICINCT.: “At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychus.”

MATRIC., CHARTERHOUSE, UTRECHT: “Quirinus, bishop and martyr, in Illyricum, of whom Prudentius writes that he was drowned with a stone tied to his hand.”

CAMBRAI, Saint Mary: “At Rome, Saints Pictus, Aretus, and Dacianus.”

VATICAN, manuscript no. 5949: “At Rome, Saints Pictus, Aregius, and Dacianus.”

FLORENTINE: “At Rome, Saints Aretius and Datianus, martyrs. Also Saint Ulrich, bishop and confessor.” He is the celebrated bishop of Augsburg, commemorated on 4 July.

LUXEUIL: “At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychus.” Concerning them, see what has already been said so many times.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: “Commemoration of the five wounds of our Lord Jesus Christ.” This is the first announcement, which GREVEN also has, but nothing is said of it elsewhere. The entry concerning Quirinus follows, with the addition concerning the translation of the relics taken from Ado, as above. At the end: “At Rome, Saints Aretius and Decianus, martyrs. In Sicily, Saints Expergentius, Philip, Eutychius, Saturnina, and Julia, martyrs. In the city of Sabaria, blessed Rufulus [Rutilus or Rustulus], martyr, with many others. At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychius.” All these martyrs and their companions are enumerated more distinctly in the *Acts*.

BELIN: After the text: “Also at Rome, Aretius and Datianus. Also Saint Ulrich, bishop and confessor.” See above under FLORENTINE. Note here that some wrongly duplicate Ulrich, because he is commemorated at Milan. But learned men recognize no other Ulrich there than the one of Augsburg.

GREVEN: “The solemnity of the five wounds of Christ.” I think this arose from the devotion of the people of Cologne. “In Cilicia [Sicily], [Col. 0123A] Saints Expergentius, Philip, Eustichus, Julia, and Saturninus. In the city of Sabaria, Saint Rustulus, with two others. At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychius. Also at Camasium, Italius and Cirina.” See the names more accurately expressed in the *Acts* and assigned to their proper class. “At Rome, Aretius and Dacianus. Ulrich [Uldaric], bishop and confessor. Petrocus, abbot and confessor. Helenus, monk and confessor. Tryphonia and Antonia, virgins and martyrs.” Concerning these three, see the *Omissions*. “Ausomia, Esmilia, Jamnica, and Rufina.” I think most of these names are corrupt. “Ositha, virgin and martyr, daughter of the king of the East Saxons.” We have also discussed her elsewhere and stated that in the *Omissions* she is referred to 7 October, although she is also noted on other days.

MOLAN: “Also at Rome, Aretius and Dacianus. Also Saint Ulrich, bishop and confessor, in the province of Rhaetia, at the city of Augsburg. In the city of Sabaria, Saint Rutilus with two others.” In other editions, concerning Aretius and Dacianus, as above. Then: “On the fourth day, Saint Metrophanes, patriarch of Constantinople.” See Janning’s learned commentary on him, in which everything concerning him and his predecessors, if he had any, and concerning his successor Alexander, is examined with the greatest care. No less carefully worked out are the matters concerning the same subject that you will find chronologically arranged and established in the supplement to June.]

[Col. 0119]

At the city of Siscia in Illyricum, the commemoration of blessed Quirinus, bishop, who, as Prudentius writes, was thrown into the river with a millstone tied to his hand for the faith of Christ; and after speaking for a long time with those standing around, so that they would not be terrified by his example, he scarcely obtained by his prayers that he be drowned. [Bouillart adds: [Note: [Col. 0119D] I make no complaint here against Castellanus. Indeed, at this point he seems to have been more favorable toward the Pratensian manuscript than was proper. For, as far as I can conjecture from Sollerii’s observations on this and the following day and from the preface, that learned writer was not informed that a leaf had been detached from the Pratensian manuscript and another sewn into its place. Perhaps the parchment deceived Castellanus’s eyes: it was equally worn, the ink equally faded, and the form of the letters not very dissimilar, so that it seemed almost to have been written at the same time and by the same hand, without any distinction. But our case rests on firmer supports than that we should conceal anything, especially since this kind of blemish actually favors what it might otherwise oppose. For the antiquity, elegance, and dignity of the remaining manuscript shine forth more brightly because of it, just as shadows add beauty to paintings. Therefore, for these days—3, 4, 5, and 6—I leave the manuscript to Soller’s discretion. Let him correct, alter, add, or subtract; it makes no difference to me. BOUILLART.] At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Zoticus, Attalus, and Eutychus.]

The Nones. Day 5. [Note: [Col. 0123]

Thus Herinien., Antwerp., Max.–Lübeck, Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0123B]

Muneratus has *Marciani et Appolloni*; Molan has *Martiani*; we follow the orthography of the others. In Egypt, however, we follow the practice begun above. Thus some write *Bonefacii*, while more, with the text, have *Bonifacii*. I have also spoken elsewhere about Tarsus. All write “under Diocletian” (Herinien. has *Dioclitianus*) and Maximian; Muneratus omits the latter and also the city. *Frixia* in Muneratus is an error for *Frisia*. It is certain that Ado reads *Eoban*, which Greven and Antwerp Major preserve. Hence the Pratensian, Rosweyd, and Molan form *Eobano* most correctly, as do several others; I believe Usuard himself also wrote it in this form—not *Eubanco*, as in Herinien. and Tornacen.; nor *Eubaneo*, as in Munerat.; nor *Eobanco*, as in Antwerp.; and still less *Eobantho*, as in Max.–Lübeck. In the two manuscripts cited immediately above, *episcopo* is absent. But should one perhaps read *coepiscopo*, as in Ado? The manuscripts vary. I followed Pratens., Herinien., Tornacen., and Munerat. If another reading seems preferable, it may be preferred with my consent.]

[Note: [Col. 0123B]

It could not lightly be disputed whether the three Egyptian martyrs recorded on this day are plainly the same as the three nearly synonymous names, Marciana, Nicanor, and Apollonius, whom we listed on 5 April, indicating there in the *Observations* that they had been omitted from the *Acts* on that day and referred to 5 June. Henschenius therefore holds that the very same persons are commemorated on both days, although in the Hieronymian Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, and Notker they are most explicitly distinguished both by sex and by names—except for Apollonius, who can easily be called Apollo or Apollinus here, as Florentinius allows. He does not think it unreasonable to suppose that there are three pairs of different persons on the two occasions, despite their popular names; [Col. 0123C] another, following the intention of the Martyrologists, might think this necessary. Certainly Henschenius has not yet fully persuaded us that his three martyrs of today, accompanied by seven companions, are the same as those three others of the Nones of April. Moreover, it may also be questioned whether those three who are marked on this day by the Hieronymian and other Martyrologies so explicitly and without any companions should really be confused with Henschenius’s group. If this surprises you, observe how many namesakes are celebrated in those manuscripts. The difficulty is increased by Nicander and Marcian, who are commemorated at Venafrum in the modern Roman Martyrology on 17 June, the day on which we know from the authentic *Acts*, first published by Mabillon and then by Ruinart among the *Selecta* from p. 617 onward, that they suffered martyrdom. Nicander and Marcian were soldiers, probably in the regions of Moesia, under the same judge Maximus under whom Julius, also a soldier, completed his contest on 27 May. Tillemont discusses them in volume V, p. 14 onward, and carefully examines the *Acts* in a note beginning on p. 590. But these matters belong to a longer discussion, which we leave to Janning in the supplement to June, to be fully reconstructed under the cited day, 17 June. As regards the text, it is more certain and evident to us that Usuard, according to his customary practice, followed Ado as his guide and transcribed his words exactly. This is made clearest by the agreement of all the manuscripts except, once again, the Pratensian, the Antwerp Major, and Rosweyd, which, as we recently noted, generally follow similar traces in their deviations. Castellanus, in the frequently cited letter, warned that the entry for this day had perhaps once been detached, rewritten on a second occasion (French *réécrit*), and attached or sewn onto the manuscript (French *ajouté*) by some ignoramus who had noticed that the same or similar names were recorded on the Nones of April. Certainly, so clear a deviation from the others [Col. 0124C] sufficiently proves that this manuscript, on this day as on the preceding one, is not pure.

Concerning Boniface of Tarsus, the *Little Roman Martyrology* reads as follows: “Boniface, martyr, who suffered at Tarsus on the fourteenth day of the month of May, was buried at Rome on the Nones of June.” Ado correctly noted this, and Notker, describing Ado’s longer narrative, took it from him and abbreviated it with his customary elegance. He is commemorated by others, and by the modern Roman Martyrology, on the very day of his passion, 14 May; his *Acts* were edited and illustrated by Henschenius after earlier scholars. Even if they are not the original *Acts*, they are at least such that even stricter critics do not dare reject them altogether. Among the stricter critics is Tillemont, volume V, pp. 650–651. In some Hieronymian copies, Boniface of Mainz is added as having suffered as though in Austria—that is, in ancient Austrasia. What should be thought of Bede’s Martyrology, both here in the *Acts* and before volume II of March, Henschenius explains. This is entirely certain: the elogium placed in our entry was plainly taken from Ado, as was also done by Notker, who added the names of Boniface’s companions from Rabanus. These matters abundantly demonstrate the genuine Usuardine character of the text. [Col. 0125A] In adorning the apostle of Germany, Henschenius and Papebrochius omitted nothing. To this belongs Wandalbert’s elegant metrical praise:

[Col. 0126A]

> On the Nones, the bishop Boniface shines forth, born among the English,  
> Who brought the children of the Ocean to Christ,  
> Bending the necks of the Frisians beneath the pure bath.]

[Note: [Col. 0125A]

PRATENS.: I have already said that he omitted the first announcement. He begins the second as follows: “The commemoration of blessed Boniface, etc.”

TORNACEN.: Concerning Boniface of Tarsus it has only this: “On the same day, Saint Boniface, martyr.” In the rest it is exceedingly pure.

PULSAN.: It dealt with Boniface of Tarsus above. In the remainder of the text it is sufficiently pure.

ANTWERP MAJOR: Agrees with the Pratensian in the omission. In the rest it is sufficiently pure.

ROSWEYD: It likewise agrees in the aforesaid omission, but arranges the text in this way: “At Utrecht, blessed Boniface, archbishop and martyr, who, coming from Britain to Utrecht in the time of Saint Willibrord, archbishop and first teacher of the people of Utrecht, stayed with him. After the passing of the most holy bishop Willibrord, the aforementioned Boniface, by the grace of God, was raised to the dignity of that same archbishopric. When he was steadfastly preaching the faith of Christ in Frisia and had brought a very great multitude under the Christian religion, he was finally killed by the sword by the Frisians and completed his martyrdom, together with his fellow workers, Eoban and Adalar, priests, and fifty-three others.” This is the Utrecht manuscript’s account, according to its own understanding; concerning them, see the *Acts*. Then: “Also at Tarsus, blessed Boniface, martyr, etc.,” sufficiently pure.

ANTWERP, MAX.–UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION: These approach purity most closely, differing in that they first mention: “The feast of Saint Boniface of Mainz, bishop, etc.” The Egyptians follow. Then concerning Boniface of Tarsus, purely, as we have already said.

LOUVAIN: Similar to the preceding manuscripts, but at the end cuts out Boniface of Tarsus’s elogium [Col. 0125C] after “buried at Rome.” ALBERG and DANISH, otherwise also conforming to the others, omit Boniface of Tarsus here, since they placed him above on 14 May.

CENTULEN.: “The commemoration of Saint Boniface, who was one of the first seven deacons. At Tarsus in Cilicia, twenty martyrs. At Rome, Saints Artemius, with his wife Candida and his daughter Paulina, who suffered under the judge Serenus. At Fulda monastery, the commemoration of Saint Boniface, who, ordained bishop at Rome by Pope Zachary and sent to preach in Frisia, converted many peoples to the faith and was killed by the sword by the remaining pagans, together with Bishop Eoban and other servants of God.”

BRUSSELS: Begins as follows: “Commemoration of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, instituted on account of the glorious victory which John, the first of that name, duke of Lorraine, Brabant, and Limburg, won at Woeringen on this day.” This has no relevance to our *Acts*. It continues: “At Fulda, Saint Boniface, archbishop and martyr. Pope Gregory consecrated him archbishop of Mainz when he came from England and sent him to Germany to preach the word of God. He founded the monastery of Fulda in the territory of Mainz, and afterwards, coming with his companions to preach in Frisia, after he had brought a very great multitude there under the Christian religion, was beaten with women’s fire-blackened forks and killed by the sword. His fellow bishop Eoban and other servants of God fell with him, and Boniface himself was taken back to Fulda and buried.” It is sufficiently pure concerning Boniface of Tarsus and the Egyptians. At the end it adds: “And Saint Aglaha, a glorious woman, renowned for many virtues. See 14 May, where Boniface is discussed.”

HAGENOYEN: In the first announcement, mutilated in its final words, it mixes together a great deal concerning Boniface of Tarsus, which is to be read more purely in the *Acts*. “In Frisia, the burial of Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr of Mainz, who came from Britain and preached the faith of Christ to the peoples. At that time Boniface was the legate of Pope Gregory; because of him he deprived the church of Worms of the use of the pallium and gave it to the church of Mainz, for previously Mainz had been under Worms. When he had brought a very great multitude of people in Frisia under the faith, he himself was finally killed by the sword, together with his fellow bishop Colianus, his archdeacon Adalar, and fifty-two other servants of God. Boniface’s body was translated to Fulda, but all the others were buried at Utrecht in the church of the Savior.”

VICTORIN and SWEDISH REG., manuscript no. 130: “On the same day, Saint Severa with her brothers Kalendinus and Marcus.” See 29 January.

AMBIANEN.: “At the monastery of Corbie, the reception of the body of Saint Praecordius the confessor.” See the *Acts* for 1 February, on which day Praecordius is commemorated.

MATRIC., CHARTERHOUSE, UTRECHT: “Boniface, bishop, and his companions, martyrs.” In the margin: “From them we have many relics, given to us by the college of Saint Savior at Utrecht, where many of them rest.”

VATICAN, no. 5949: Begins: “The commemoration of Saint Eleutherius, bishop, and Saint Anthia, his mother, at Saint Sophia.” Nothing concerning them belongs to this day; see 18 April. The Egyptian martyrs and the entire announcement of Boniface of Tarsus are absent.

ALTEMPS: “At Poitiers, Saint Jovinus, abbot. In the district of Boulogne, Saint Proculus, martyr.” Both are treated on 1 June. See the *Appendices* and the *Acts*.

FLORENTINE: “At the city of Ceblia, or Cellia, in a place called Pigrius, the passion of the holy martyr Severa [Col. 0126C], with her brothers Kalendinus and Marcus and their mother, who was the wife of Saint Maximus the martyr; after she had prayed, she gave up her spirit. They suffered in the time of the Emperor Claudius.” I said above that the *Acts* of 24 January should be consulted, where approximately one thousand soldier-companions are added.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: Interpolated in the section on Boniface of Mainz, it places the Egyptian martyrs second. Then: “On the same day, the canonization of Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, priest and confessor, of the Order of Hermits. Also Saint Aglaha, most glorious, renowned for many virtues. At Rome, the burial of Saint Boniface, martyr.”

BELIN: Pure in the first announcement, it omits Boniface, concerning whom it speaks on 14 May; otherwise it is pure. In the second edition it adds: “On the same day, blessed Claudius, bishop and confessor.” He is referred to the following day.

GREVEN: “Adalar, bishop of Erfurt, and fifty-three other martyrs, companions of Saint Boniface. Also Saints Marcian, Felicitas, Gregory, and Fecula.” See the Roman martyrs in the *Acts*. “In Africa, [Col. 0126D] Evasius and Probatus [read: Privatus], Pergentina, sister of Saints Laurentinus and Pergentinus.” See the *Omissions*. “The canonization of blessed Nicholas of Tolentino, priest and confessor, of the Order of Hermits of Saint Augustine.” He is commemorated on 10 September. “Aglaha, a holy Roman matron, concerning whom see above, on the day before the Ides of May.”

MOLAN: Adds only, in smaller type: “At Brussels, a commemoration of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, instituted on account of, etc.,” as we said above from the Brussels source itself. In other editions: “On the fifth day, Saint Dorotheus, hieromartyr and bishop of Tyre.” Then the commemoration given above. See Henschenius’s historical commentary on Dorotheus.]

[Col. 0123]

In Egypt, the commemoration of Saints Marcian, Nicander, and Apollonius, martyrs, whose deeds are recorded. On the same day, the passion of Saint Boniface, martyr, who suffered under Diocletian and Maximian at the city of Tarsus, but was buried at Rome on the road called the Latin Way. While he had long been engaged in sexual vice, he was finally moved by divine prompting; he not only abandoned the vice to which he had been subject, but also eagerly ran through various tortures toward the palm of martyrdom. Also Saint Boniface, bishop, who came from Britain and preached the faith of Christ to the peoples; after he had brought a very great multitude in Frisia under the Christian religion, he was finally killed by the sword and completed his martyrdom together with Bishop Eoban and other servants of God.

The Eighth day before the Ides. Day 6. [Note: [Col. 0127]

The Pratensian, Herinien., Antwerp Major, Greven., and Molan are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0127A]

Antwerp Major’s *fuit unus* instead of *unus fuit* causes no difficulty. The older manuscripts have *inclitus*; Greven and Molan have *inclytus*. We have spoken of Tarsus more than once; we do not wish to vary the form. “They glorified the Lord” is read by the Pratensian and Herinien manuscripts, as Ado has it; and, I think, as Usuard wrote it, whatever Notker may read, namely “God,” as do also the Antwerp Major, Greven, and Molan manuscripts. The Pratensian placed *Arthemii* first and *Arthemius* second. Antwerp Major also has *Arthemii*. In accordance with Usuard’s intention, *Artemii* is better, with the others, as in the text. Only the Pratensian reads *Amanti*; the others have *Amantii*.]

[Note: [Col. 0127A]

As far as the clear portions are concerned, the source of today’s text must be sought nowhere but in the *Little Roman Martyrology*, where all the same saints are named, though in a different order, who are expressly named here—apart from the Nivedunian martyrs alone, concerning whom we shall speak below. From that source the Viennese Martyrologist drew; from him, Usuard and Notker, each in his customary manner, the former more briefly, the latter more fully. Our author sampled in summary the elogium of the deacon Philip and his prophetic daughters, repeated from the celebrations of the apostles, in precisely the form in which it is presented in the entry. I have often wondered, and wonder here also, why manuscripts of middling quality cited in the *Appendices* so often cut out from the Usuardine text what is not found in Ado’s Martyrology itself. I suspect that this was done through the fault of some ignorant person who did not know the earlier part of Ado’s Martyrology, from which Usuard nevertheless borrowed many elogia. The same thing is plainly done on this day, when, following Ado’s intention, he mentions only three daughters buried with their father: namely, because Ado, following the tradition of certain persons, believed that one of the four daughters, filled with the Holy Spirit, had been buried at Ephesus. Papebrochius composed a historical commentary on Philip’s deeds, the eunuch baptized by him, his episcopate, and his cult; to this should be joined what Tillemont has in volume II, p. 65 onward, and in the notes beginning on p. 490. Let the reader consult a large part of chapter VIII and chapter XXI, verse 9, of the *Acts of the Apostles*.

[Col. 0128A] In the case of the Tarsian martyrs, all of Ado’s words have been transcribed, except only the name of the judge Simplicius. Notker correctly added that these martyrs are mentioned in the passion of Saint Boniface; in our *Acts* they are represented more briefly on this day, insofar as these martyrs are concerned. Ado discusses Artemius, his wife, and his daughter at greater length on 2 June, where he treats Marcellinus and Peter. Here he repeats the details that separately contribute to the praise of these three, which our author neatly reduced to his customary numerical form. Up to this point the material comes from the aforementioned source; neither the Hieronymian Martyrology nor Bede supplies anything. The Nivedunian or Nividunian martyrs remain, concerning whom Florentinius offers much information and Henschenius examines much, both to distinguish the genuine names and to determine the number of companions and the arena of their contest, since the ancient Martyrologies vary remarkably here. It is not our task to unravel all these threads; whoever has leisure to weigh the individual matters should consult the authors cited, but above all the recent dissertation of Janning in the supplement to June, p. 17. It seems probable to us that Usuard, as often happened elsewhere, selected these two from the Hieronymian Martyrology, since he had not found them in Ado; whether he did so more successfully than Rabanus and Notker, we leave undecided. The unanimous agreement of our manuscripts is sufficient to establish the uncorrupted Usuardine integrity of the proposed text, whose investigation is chiefly our concern.]

[Note: [Col. 0127C]

TORNACEN.: We have said that it very rarely suffers from erasure, but more often from omission, as though it fitted the text to the brackets rather than the brackets to the text. Thus once again today let the elogium of the Tarsian martyrs run on; in the rest it is exceedingly pure.

PULSANEN.: It omits not only the elogium but the Tarsian martyrs themselves; it also cuts out Philip’s elogium. Otherwise it is sufficiently pure.

ROSWEYD: Immediately before the Nivedunian martyrs it inserts: “At Blandinium, Guthuual, bishop and confessor.”

MUNERAT.: Adds at the end: “On the same day, Claudius, confessor and archbishop of Besançon.”

ANTWERP MAX., LÜBECK, ANTWERP MAJOR, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERG, DANISH, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION: These are the manuscripts of middling quality that I mentioned, mostly Belgian; they lack Saint Philip’s elogium.

CENTULEN.: “The feast of Saint Philip, who was one of the first seven deacons. At Tarsus in Cilicia, twenty martyrs. At Rome, Saints Artemius, with his wife Candida and daughter Paulina, who suffered under the judge Serenus. At Antioch, Saint Asclepiades, bishop, who was one of the distinguished company of confessors.” He is referred to 18 October. “At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Amantius and Alexander. At the Blandinian monastery, Saint Guthwal, bishop, adorned with virtues and miracles.”

BRUSSELS: Begins with Artemius. Then it treats Philip and the Tarsian martyrs sufficiently purely. It follows with: “And Benignus, martyr”—probably a companion of Saint Vincent, bishop of Mevania in Umbria. “Also Mellonius, bishop.” I think this is Mellonius of Rouen, whose feast is 22 October. “At the monastery of Brandinium, the burial of Saint Gudunalis” [Gudwal], “bishop and confessor. When his shrine was being carried back to Ghent after the procession, an image of the cross, which had venerated him with bowed face, remained immovable and did not turn back. And Claudius, confessor.” It is clear that the Nivedunian martyrs have been omitted.

HAGENOYEN: Departing little from purity, it differs almost solely at the beginning, where it writes: “At Caesarea, the commemoration of blessed Philip, who was one of the first seven deacons, elected together with Saint Stephen. He, through signs,” etc.—all correctly.

VICTORIN and SWEDISH REG., manuscript no. 130: At the end they add: “On the same day, Saint Bonitus, bishop and confessor. And Saint Gratian, bishop and martyr.” See what is said about each in the index of the *Omissions*.

MATRIC., CHARTERHOUSE, UTRECHT: “Philip the deacon, [Col. 0129A] who was one of the first. At Tarsus, twenty martyrs. Gundual, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN, manuscript no. 5949: Omits Amantius and Alexander. It adds: “In Tuscany, Saints Vincent, bishop, and Benignus, deacon, martyrs.” The place is identified above under BRUSSELS.

FLORENTINE: “At the city of Fiesole, the commemoration of Saint Alexander, bishop and martyr of that same city. At the city of Mantua, the discovery of Saint Celestine, martyr.” Concerning him, see the *Omissions*.

CODEX JURENSIS OF ST RAGNOBERT: For Nivedunum it writes: “At Lyons, Amantius, Lucius.” See what we said above in the *Observations*.

REIMS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At the city of Nivedunum, the passion of Saints Amantius and Alexander.” In the preceding entry, Lucius is substituted.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: It is moderately interpolated throughout the text, notably in the case of Artemius, concerning whom, after Candida, it continues: “and his little daughter, a virgin in fact and in name, Paulina, martyrs; Saint Peter the Exorcist converted them to the Lord while he was being held in prison among them. Artemius, then,” etc. At the end they add: “At Bourges, Saint Scariola, virgin. In Poland, the feast of blessed Vincent, bishop and martyr.” The latter is the levite of Agen; the former is Studiola, or Eustadiola, a widow and religious woman. The latter is treated on 9 June, the former on 8 June.

BELIN: In the first edition it reads *Lugdunum* instead of *Nivedunum*, which is corrected in the Paris edition. In both it adds: “At Mantua, the discovery of blessed Celestine, martyr.” He has already been mentioned.

GREVEN: “Also Lucius, Andrew, Donatus, Peregrinus, Italius, and Claudius.” See in the *Acts* concerning the Nivedunian martyrs. “In Poland, the commemoration of blessed Vincent, bishop and martyr, and his brother Benignus, deacon. The former, after overcoming the rack, burning, and wild beasts, gave up his spirit while celebrating Mass before the people; the latter was killed by the sword, together with many others.” I do not see what this refers to; unless I am mistaken, Vincent and Benignus have been confused. “Gundual, archbishop of Blandinium and confessor.” Nor is this any clearer. “Claudius, bishop of Besançon and confessor. Kilian, confessor.” See the *Omissions*. “Commemoration of Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg and confessor, of holy memory, founder of the Premonstratensian Order. At Bourges, Scariola, virgin.” See above.

MOLAN. Concerning Gudwal, Celestine, and Claudius, as above. Then:

> “The Passion of Saint Ceratus, bishop, under the emperor Gratian. At Trier, Saint Auspicius, bishop.”

This is referred to July 8.

> “At Prémontré, the commemoration of Norbert, of holy memory,”

[Col. 0130B] and so forth, in smaller type. In other editions, concerning the first three, as in the first edition. Then:

> “On the sixth day, Saint Father Bessarion, renowned for miracles. At Malbodium, the showing of the body of Blessed Aldegundis, virgin.”

See January 30. Verses by Wandalbert follow:

> Ceratus, bishop, adorns the eighth day before the Ides,  
> Who shone in the city named after the prince Gratian.

Concerning Norbert he repeats what we gave from GREVEN. See Henschenius’s historical commentary on Ceratus or Ceratius, p. 708. This same Ceratus also appears to have been inserted into the Hieronymian Martyrologies under June 7.

[Col. 0127]

The feast of Blessed Philip, who was one of the seven deacons. Renowned for signs and wonders, he rested at Caesarea; beside him lie buried his three daughters, virgins and prophetesses. At Tarsus in Cilicia, twenty martyrs, in the times of Diocletian and Maximian, who glorified the Lord in their bodies through various torments. At Rome, Saints Artemius, with his wife Candida and his daughter Paulina. Artemius was struck with the sword; his wife and daughter, however, were crushed with stones. At the city of Nivedunum, Saints Amantius and Alexander.

VII before the Ides. Day 7.

[Note: [Col. 0129C]]

Many manuscripts agree: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Antuerp., and Max.-Lubec.; Rosweyd., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Belinus’s first edition, [Col. 0130C] Munerat., Greven, and Molan. To these is added the Albergen manuscript.

[Note: [Col. 0129C]]

Pulsanen., Max.-Lubec., Rosweyd., Antuerp.-Major, and Belinus write *Constantinopolim*, accusative “Constantinople,” where the entry means “at Constantinople.” Our reading from the other sources is preferable. *Paulini*, “of Paulinus,” for *Pauli*, “of Paul,” in Rosweyd. is an error. Antuerp.-Major, Belin., and Molan. give *Constantini*, “of Constantine”; below it is shown that *Constantii*, “of Constantius,” must be read. Munerat.’s *a Constantinopolim imperatore*, “from/by Constantinople the emperor,” is ridiculous. The text rightly has *Cappadociae*, “of Cappadocia,” not *in Cappadocia*, “in Cappadocia,” as Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Belinus. All have *Cucusam* for *Cucusum*, differently inflected forms of Cucusa, except Herinien. and Molan., who have *Cucussam*, and Greven, who, worse, has *Concussam*. Muneratus errs again in *civitaculam*; [Col. 0130C] Belinus more disgracefully in *civitatiunculam*: both are defective forms of “small city.” Pulsanensis reads *expulsus*, “expelled,” for *pulsus*, “driven out”; Belinus has *compulsus*, “compelled/driven.” All regularly agree in *Arrianorum*, “of the Arians,” with the doubled r. *Exilio*, “by/in exile,” in place of *insidiis*, “by plots,” is a scribal blunder in Antuerpiensis. The best manuscripts read *Corduba*, “at Cordoba.” Max.-Lubec. has *Cordubam*; Munerat., Greven, and Molan., *Cordubae*, differing case-forms of the city’s name. Belinus’s *Everici* is an error, as are *Evencii* in Max.-Lubec. and *Eventii* in Antuerp. and another Antuerp.-Major manuscript. With the others we write *Aventii*, though *Habentii* would be more correct. Above, something has been said concerning the inflections *Jeremiae* or *Jheremie* and the like.

[Note: [Col. 0129D]]

The author of the Short Roman Martyrology is the first to speak of this illustrious victim of Arian fury, in these words: “At Constantinople, Paul, bishop.” Following him, Ado composed the brief eulogy which may also be read entire in Notker. Ours presents it somewhat abridged, preserving the author’s phrasing. Both, however, departed from their guide in preferring to write *Constantius* rather than *Constantine*—rightly everywhere and in accordance with the facts. For although the same Paul, as Athanasius expressly testifies, was first ordered by Constantine himself to go into exile in Pontus, this must necessarily have occurred before he became bishop, according to the chronology most plausibly established by our Baertius, about the year 336; having then been recalled from exile, he was not ordained bishop before the year 311 [printed 311, apparently 341 in the stated chronology], as Janning’s dissertation on the subject, in the supplement for June on this day, shows at length. From that time he endured several exiles, as Baertius’s *Commentary*, chapter 2, abundantly demonstrates. [Col. 0130D] Since this passage appears to designate the last of them, it is certain that it must refer not to Constantine but to Constantius, since it belongs to about the year 350, a full thirteen years after Constantine’s departure from this life. You will understand this more readily if you remember that 6 November is the day of his martyrdom, while this is the day of his translation, subsequently made more celebrated, as we have said in their places concerning Chrysostom and others. We touch on these matters briefly in keeping with our plan; Baertius and Janning have discussed them more laboriously. Tillemont composed Paul’s Life in French, vol. VII, from p. 251, examining related matters in notes from p. 697; there the curious reader may see that he disagrees with our colleagues on several points and, if he has leisure, weigh the arguments of both sides. See also Motherius’s short note. Wandalbert celebrates Paul alone on this day:

> Paul, your bishop, O lofty Byzantium, adorns the seventh day before the Ides.

[Col. 0131A] The same author of the Short Roman Martyrology commemorates on this day: “In Cappadocia, Lucian, martyr.” The Viennese Martyrology adds the more precise location, namely Caesarea, as do Rabanus and Notker. Nothing concerning him is found in our more authoritative manuscripts. He was added in Antuerp.-max. and other texts to be enumerated among the Supplements; and this, unless I am mistaken, came from Ado, as we have often observed elsewhere. Moreover, those who occupy Lucian’s place in Usuard [Col. 0132A] are the martyrs of Corduba, summoned from Spain with several others but, in the Usuardian manner, detached from their companions. You will find their names stated in the Acts, and the matters concerning their contests carefully collected by Papebroch from Saint Eulogius’s *Memorial*, book II, chapter 4. The simplicity of our entry is perfectly clear amid such unanimous agreement.

[Note: [Col. 0131A]]

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition append to the pure text, from Ado as we have said: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Lucian, martyr.”

CENTULEN.: “At Constantinople, Blessed Paul, bishop of the same city, who, while the Arians persecuted him for (*ad*, read *ob*, “on account of”) the Catholic faith, was driven into exile and afterward cruelly strangled, and passed to the heavenly kingdoms. At Corduba, the holy martyrs Peter, priest, Aventius, Jeremiah, and three others, whose acts are extant. In the district of Ponthieu, Saint Wulfagius, priest and confessor.” This name is not written in one way only. See [Col. 0131B] how it is pronounced in the Acts.

BRUXELLEN., almost pure in Paul, adds: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Julian (for Lucian), martyr. At Corduba,” etc., correctly. “At Nivedunum, Saints Amantius and Alexander,” taken from the preceding day. “On the same day, the translation of Saint Servatius, bishop and confessor.” This must be sought under the saint’s feast day itself, 13 May.

HAGENOVEN. is more confused in sense concerning Paul. At the end it adds: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Lucian, martyr,” like the others cited above.

The manuscript of Prince Ursini at Rosenberg: “In the city of Mantua, the discovery of the body of Saint Celestine, pope and confessor.” A double major is assigned to it. The Acts were given on 6 April.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Maximinus, bishop and confessor of the Church of Aix, who was Mary Magdalene’s teacher.” He is deferred to the following day. “Paul, bishop of Constantinople and martyr. [Col. 0131C] Peter, Aventius, Jeremiah, and three others.”

The manuscript of D. DU CHEVAL, marked B, formerly belonging to the Augustinian Fathers: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Julian, martyr.” See above.

In VATICAN., no. 5949, Peter and his companions are absent. There is added: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia,” etc., as immediately above and often already.

ALTEMPS.: “The translation of Saint Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester.” It was dealt with in the Life given on 19 January. “Likewise Saint Venantius, bishop and confessor.” See the catalogue of the Omitted.

[Col. 0132A] FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Felicula, companion of Saint Petronilla, and of Saint Nicomedes, martyr, as is read in the history of Petronilla.” Felicula is separately commemorated on 13 June.

The LUBECO-COL. edition appends to the pure text: “Near Caesarea in Cappadocia, Blessed Julian, martyr. At Maastricht, the translation of Blessed Servatius, bishop and confessor.” See above.

BELIN.’s second edition: “On the same day, Saint Godoald, bishop and confessor.” He is in the Acts.

GREVEN.: “The second [word repeated in the source] translation of Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr: namely, from Nicomedia to Rome.” [Col. 0132B] It is treated on 4 December. “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Lucian, martyr. Likewise the holy martyrs Fortunatus, Masus, Macharius, Magrus, Primosus, Victor, Lunicia, Privata, and Priscus.” I do not know from where he fashioned these names of African martyrs. See the proper names in the Acts. “In Ireland, Colman, bishop and confessor.” His Acts were illustrated on 18 February. “Dietger, abbot.” Nothing concerning him has yet been found. “Godoald, confessor. At Maastricht, the translation of Saint Servatius, bishop and confessor.”

MOLAN., immediately after “the three others,” adds: “Whose acts are extant. On the same day, Saint Godoald, bishop and confessor. Likewise at Maastricht, the translation of Saint Servatius.” In smaller type follows: “In Ireland, Colman, bishop and confessor, concerning whom Bede writes in the History of his People.” In other editions: “On the same day, Saint Godoald, bishop and confessor. At Clermont, Saint Illidius, bishop and confessor of the same city.” The Acts are given on 5 June. “On the [Col. 0132C] seventh day, Saint Theodosius, hieromartyr and bishop of Ancyra.” He is called Theodore among the Omitted, elsewhere Theodotus: everywhere the same man, whom we treated on 18 May. “Likewise at Maastricht, the translation of Saint Servatius. At the monastery of Sithiu, the translation of Blessed Folquin, bishop of the Morini.” His feast day is marked among the Omitted on 14 December. Finally, in smaller type: “Likewise the deposition of Robert, abbot of the Cistercian Order in England.” See Henschenius’s Commentary concerning him, and the short Life edited and illustrated by the same author from Capgrave in the Acts.

[Col. 0129]

At Constantinople, the feast of Blessed Paul, bishop of the same city, who, for the Catholic faith, was driven into exile by the emperor Constantius to a small city of Cappadocia called Cucusa, and was cruelly strangled through the plots of the Arians, and passed to the heavenly kingdoms. Likewise at Corduba, the holy Peter, priest, Aventius, Jeremiah, and three others.

VI before the Ides. Day 8.

[Note: [Col. 0131C]]

Thus Praten., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0131D]]

Rosweyd. has singular *Gallia* for plural *Galliis*, both used here for “in Gaul.” Antuerp.-maj. has *meriti fuerit*, “he was of [such] merit,” and *episcopi Rothomagensis*, “of the bishop of Rouen.” Moreover, all read *Rothomagensis*, “of Rouen,” except Pratensis. Some write *Senones*, a form of Sens, such as Antuerp.-Maj. and Greven.; the others as in the text. Again, Antuerp.-Maj. and Molan. rightly have *Heraclii*, “of Heraclius”; we follow all the rest. Praten. and [Col. 0132D] Munerat. give *Abundi*; Greven. and Molan., *Habundii*; Rosweyd., *Habundini*. Antuerp.-Maj., which has *Abundii*, “of Abundius,” is to be preferred; Herinien., Tornacen., and most others agree with it. The preceding *Abundi*, *Habundii*, and *Habundini* are alternative forms of this name. Elsewhere *Corduba* is regularly read; here all wrote *Cordubae*.

[Note: [Col. 0131D]]

Nowhere is Usuard richer from his own resources; nowhere is Ado poorer. The Short Roman Martyrology is entirely blank. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies, whatever is mentioned concerning Medard’s deposition is an addition. [Col. 0132D] Thus Medard derives from Bede, where he is adorned only with the title confessor. The Viennese adds bishop, but stops there. Licinius, whom Ado has in second place, belongs to 13 February; Carilefus, or, in Notker, Carlenius, [Col. 0133A] to 1 July. Therefore everything which follows in the text is purely Usuardian. No one adopted Florus’s Medardian eulogy about a dove flying from the dying man’s mouth. Rabanus sang something different, rendered somewhat more fully by Notker.
