Ours elaborated his own independently, as the manuscripts cited for the text and many others report; though Heriniensis, Tornacensis, and Belinus oppose it, being content with this more common—and therefore more certain—form: “Whose life and death are commended by glorious miracles.” Wandalbert seems to allude to the famous synchronism, to be given shortly in the Supplements, in these two little verses:

> Gildard and Medard, whom birth, holy merit, and the altar unite,  
> together honour the sixth day before the Ides.

From this you may infer that the remarkable brotherhood of Gildard and Medard either took its origin perhaps first from this Martyrology, or at least passed into the sacred calendar in the ninth century, in which he lived; neither earlier writers nor contemporaries remember it even faintly. [Col. 0133B] Ours joined them on this day, I admit, but wisely abstained from the rest. See more in the Acts concerning Saint Gildard, where Henschenius, in a notable Commentary, separates [Col. 0134A] in vol. II of June, from p. 67, what is worthy of belief from ingeniously imagined inventions. Papebroch worked out the greater part concerning Medard, producing, after Acherius, Lives by Fortunatus composed both in verse and in prose. The preliminary Commentary and the documents appended to the Lives, on the translation of Saint Medard’s body into Burgundy, collected by Pierre-François Chifflet, are most worthy of reading; I would be mistaken if anything necessary to the complete elucidation of all points could be desired. Heraclius of Sens is rightly placed on this day, although unknown to the other ancient Martyrologies. I think Henschenius has collected everything which can be adduced concerning Heraclius on the authority of the better writers. Salustianus was received from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, not as a confessor but as a martyr, as Florentinius rightly observed. What is known of this saint beyond his name will be taught by Henschenius’s collection against the inventions of recent writers. Abundius of Corduba is deferred by Spanish writers and the modern Roman Martyrology to 11 July. Nevertheless, we are wholly of the opinion that Usuard placed him thus, and that his genuine text is reported in all the other respects—[Col. 0134B] unless anyone should suspect the Medardian eulogy. Eulogius briefly describes Abundius’s martyrdom in *Memorial*, book III, chapter 12, and marks the day of martyrdom as 11 July.

[Note: [Col. 0133B]]

HERINIEN. and TORNACEN., led by I know not what scruple, substituted another notice for the eulogy just cited; certainly in every other announcement they are most pure. Indeed, they almost create doubt concerning Usuard’s true and genuine reading itself.

PULSANEN., fairly pure in Medard, continues: “On the same day, Saint Gildard, bishop of Rouen, brother of Saint Medard, who were born on one day, ordained bishops on one and the same day, and likewise removed from this light on one day.” This is the synchronism of which I spoke. Everything else is absent.

[Col. 0133C] ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., pure in Medard, after Gildard, omit Heraclius, join Salustianus, and omit Abundius of Corduba as well.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition, pure in Medard, add after “bishop” concerning Gildard: “brothers of Saint Medard [printed *fratres*], whom they report to have been born on one day, ordained bishops on one and the same day, and likewise removed from this light on one day.” The rest is as in ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.

CENTULEN.: “In Francia, in the city of Soissons, the feast and deposition of Saint Medard, bishop of Vermandois and Tournai, whose life and death shone gloriously in miracles. In the city of Rouen, the deposition of Saint Gildard, archbishop, brother of Saint Medard, whom they were [read: report] to have been born on one day, ordained bishops on one day, and likewise removed from this light on one day. In Sardinia, Saint Salustianus. At Corduba, Saint Abundius, priest and martyr. [Col. 0133D] At Sens, Saint Heraclius, bishop and confessor.”

BRUXELLENSIS, enlarging the little narrative, declares: “In Gaul, in the city of Soissons, the holy bishops and confessors Medard and Gildard, twin brothers. They were born on one day and consecrated bishops on one day: Medard to the see of Noyon and Gildard to that of Rouen; and likewise they were afterward removed from this light on one day. How great their merit was before God was shown when, at their death, the heavens were opened and divine lights gleamed before them. In Sardinia, Saint Salustianus. At Corduba, Saint Abundius, priest and martyr. At Sens, Saint Heraclitus, bishop and confessor. Likewise Saint Carilefus.” We have elsewhere said that Carilefus is commemorated on 1 July.

HAGENOYEN. supplies other matter: “In Gaul, in the city of Soissons, the deposition of Saint Medard, bishop and confessor. While still a little boy he was wholly devoted to works of mercy; consequently he gave to a blind poor man a superfluous garment [received] from his mother, [Col. 0134B] and sometimes distributed to the poor the food necessary for himself. This holy bishop of Noyon gave to the poor everything that he had and could have. How great his merit was,” etc. In Gildard it has the synchronism, of which enough has already been said. The remainder of the text follows, and at the end: “In the city of Medis [Metis; Metz], Saint Clodulf, bishop.”

AQUICINCT. inserts after “bishop of Rouen”: “Who, as is reported, on one day,” etc. There, after “Salustianus,” is inserted: “In Egypt, Saint Marcian. The translation of Saint Audomarus, bishop.” He is commemorated on 9 September, when the translation will also be considered.

[Col. 0134C] MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Medard, bishop and confessor of Noyon. Gildard, bishop and confessor of Rouen. Heraclius, bishop and confessor.” The last two alone are absent.

CLUNIACEN.: “On the same day in Egypt, Marcian.” In the Acts he has Jocundus as companion.

The manuscript of D. DU CHEVAL, formerly belonging to the Franciscan Fathers: “In Egypt, Marcian. On the same day, Syria, virgin.” In a later hand. Others read *Syra*. See the Acts.

In VATICAN., no. 5949, the commemoration of Gildard, Heraclius, Salustianus, and Abundius is absent. There is added: “At Angers, Saint Lucinius, bishop and confessor; and Saint Carilefus, confessor.” They were taken from Ado, as we said in the Observations, where feast days are assigned to each.

In UGHELLIANO, Heraclius and Abundius are absent, as in ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.

ALTEMPS. at the end: “In Egypt, Marcian.”

[Col. 0134D] BIZUNTICEN.: “At Sens, Saint Eradius, bishop and confessor.” It intended to say Heraclius.

The LUBECO-COL. edition inserts after “of Noyon”: “In youth he feared God and gave his bread at school to poor schoolboys. He foretold to his father-in-law that he would be bishop in the third year. And how great his merit was,” etc. It has the matter on Gildard already repeated. “In Sardinia, Saint Salustianus, confessor. At Angers, Saint Lucian, bishop and confessor.” Others write better *Lucinius*, or, as Ado, *Licinius*. “On the same day, Saint Carilefus, confessor.” See above concerning both. “In the territory of Troyes, Syria, an excellent matron. At Corduba, Saint Abundius, priest and martyr.” Heraclius is absent.

BELIN. reads concerning Medard as HERINIEN. and TORNACEN. It follows with Eradius for Heraclius, then Salustianus, then Abundius; after Gildard, at the end: “In the city of Metz, Saint Codulf, bishop and confessor.” See above: Clodulf is more correct.

GREVEN.: “At Nicomedia, Saint Nestor.” See [Col. 0135A] his companions in the Acts. “Likewise Marcian. At Rome, Nabor and Nazarius.” They are referred to 12 June. “At Angers, Licinius, bishop and confessor. Theodulph, also a confessor.” He appears to be the one commemorated on 24 June. “In England, William, archbishop of York and confessor. Maximinus, bishop of Marseille and confessor, according to others, 27 May. Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse and confessor, mentioned by Gregory in *Dialogue* III.” I am surprised that he is not found among the Omitted. He is commemorated on the following day. “At Metz, Saint Clodulf, bishop and confessor. Carilefus, confessor. Marcella, virgin.” This indicates Saint Martha’s maidservant. See 29 June. “Publia, widow and abbess.” See the Omitted. “Syria, matron,” concerning whom other manuscripts above.

MOLAN. inserts in the text itself, but in different type, after “lights”: “His life, full of virtues, has been written.” At the end: “In the city of Metz, Saint Clodulf, [Col. 0136A] bishop and confessor. In the territory of Troyes, Blessed Syria, matron.” Then in smaller type: “In England, William, archbishop of York and confessor; Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse and confessor, mentioned by Pope Gregory in *Dialogue* III. Publia, widow and abbess, concerning whom, in book VI of the Tripartite Ecclesiastical History, chapter 36.” Enough has already been said of these. In other editions, concerning Syria and Clodulf, as above. Then: “At the monastery of Sithiu, the carrying-back or translation of Saint Audomarus, bishop, when Folquin, after expelling Abbot Hugh, brought back his body from Lisbourg in the year 843 and buried it underground at Sithiu beside the body of Blessed Bertin. There it remained hidden from men for many years, but was revealed when the Lord willed.” In different type there follows matter on William of York. Finally: “In Gaul, in the city of Aix, the deposition of Blessed Maximinus, first bishop and confessor of that city.” He too was mentioned above.

[Col. 0131]

In Gaul, in the city of Soissons, the feast of Blessed Medard, bishop of Noyon; how great his merit was was shown when, at his death, the heavens were opened and divine lights gleamed before him. On the same day, Saint Gildard, bishop of Rouen. Likewise at Sens, Saint Heraclius, bishop and confessor. In Sardinia, Saint Salustianus. At Corduba, Saint Abundius, priest and martyr.

V before the Ides. Day 9.

[Note: [Col. 0135]]

No manuscripts are pure except Herinien., Rosweyd., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0135B]]

With Molan I retain the diphthong in *Coelio*, “on the Caelian [hill],” and in *longaevam*, “long-lived.” Herinien. has the diphthong in *Coelio*, not in *longaevam*; Rosweyd. rightly has it in *Romae*, “at Rome,” but omitted it in the others. These alone, with Pratensis, are manuscripts in which account is taken of diphthongs. *Feliciani*, “of Felicianus,” is given by Molanus alone. Rosweyd., [Col. 0135C] Molan., and others commonly write *sigillatim*; Herinien., *singulatim*, both “individually/separately.” Rosweyd. alone has *perferentes*, “enduring,” for *ferentes*, “bearing.” I read *Agenno*, “at Agen,” because that is the reading of the three cited manuscripts and almost all the others. Rosweyd., Molanus, etc., rightly have *Scotia*, the name Scotia. Herinien. wrongly has *Schotia* and *Scotheia*, elsewhere *Scothia*. Molan and Rosweyd. have *admirandae virtutis viri*, “a man of admirable virtue,” followed by Greven; Herinien., with Pratensis, Tornacensis, and the others, simply *mirandae*, “wonderful/admirable.” Molanus not improperly writes *Niceae*, “at Nicaea”; nor Rosweyd., *In Nicaea*, “in Nicaea.” Nevertheless, I follow Herinien. and the others, which have *Nicaea*, another case-form of the city name. Rosweyd. also added *martyris*, “of the martyr.”

A more noteworthy variation remains, from which arises the small number of manuscripts cited for the text; it proceeds chiefly from three causes. First, some, like Pratensis, have at the end: “At [Col. 0135D] the monastery of Saint Germanus, the dedication, in honour of Blessed Peter the Apostle.” Sirmond reports that this addition was erased in another Pratensian manuscript; Castellan confesses that it seems to him to have been added in the alleged autograph itself [Col. 0136B] by a later hand. Manuscripts conforming to Pratensis are Antuerp.-Major, Muneratus, and Greven. The second cause is that Tornacensis, Pulsanensis, and Belinus, though not guilty of this addition, suffer from other omissions. The third cause in Usuards of middling rank is the one we have indicated elsewhere: namely, that [Col. 0136C] those manuscripts and others of which we possess only extracts sometimes follow Ado’s meaning more scrupulously and set down no saints other than those expressed in that Ado. For that reason, I think, Columba and Diomedes are omitted by them on this day. Nonetheless, we consider the genuineness of our entry secure, since, apart from those four alone, all the rest agree in excluding the final notice peculiar to the Pratensian monastery. But who can determine with sufficient certainty whence Antuerp.-Maj., Muneratus, and Greven received it? Was it from the alleged autograph, where so many other dedications have been appended? It is not likely that this one alone was selected before the others. Certainly Castellan does not believe that any other manuscripts ever copied Pratensian peculiarities; he states this plainly [Col. 0136D] in letters often cited elsewhere, and it was recently clear on 1 June and frequently elsewhere. But enough and more than enough of this.

[Note: [Col. 0135D]]

As regards the sources of the text, the Calendars of Allatius and Frontinus mention Primus and Felicianus; so do the Sacramentary of Gregory, Bede, and the Short Roman Martyrology. Ado drew from the Acts a wholly remarkable commendation, nearly all of which Notker reproduces; Rabanus gives a briefer encomium. They are altogether silent about the place of their contest, which others locate on Mount Coelius, to which [Col. 0136D] the bodies were translated. Ours most elegantly compressed Ado’s eulogy into a few lines. All these notices were taken from the published Acts, polished by Surius and restored by Henschenius, through comparison of various manuscripts, to their primitive phrasing. He thus explains his opinion of them: “Nor do we believe that they are of first rank and taken from [Col. 0137A] proconsular acts; but [that they were] embellished long afterward in rhetorical style and with circumstances of speeches delivered back and forth, perhaps also of various punishments; yet we think them written long before the translation of the bodies.” That was before the year 648. Modern writers readily assent to Henschenius’s judgment; see Tillemont, vol. IV, p. 571, who thinks that the time of martyrdom can be placed in 287. The praised Henschenius continues in his Commentary with the other matters concerning the sacred relics. Thus Wandalbert:

> Primus holds the fifth day before the Ides, with Felicianus joined to him.

Florus composed the notice of Vincentius, martyr of Agen, from Gregory of Tours, concerning the whiteness of the stole, etc.; it did not pass to others. Ado, and from him Notker, again name as the place of martyrdom the place to which the body was later translated, namely Pompeiacum. But ours, perhaps more cautious, silently passing over those words, transferred the rest from Ado word for word. Florentinius rightly thought that the lacuna in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, where the martyr’s name itself is omitted, [Col. 0138A] should be supplied. See what Henschenius carefully examines concerning the ancient Acts and cult, and the several controversies about the person and relics. Tillemont joins Vincentius with Faith and Caprasius in vol. IV, from p. 543. But they will be dealt with on 6 and 20 October. See Motherius’s brief notes concerning Vincentius. The very celebrated Columba is first marked by Usuard and Notker: by the former, indeed, as we have reported in the text; by the latter, however, in a long summary of his life. In this, certain things require correction, such as “the first of all the bishops of the Irish,” and others, as Baertius teaches after Colgan; in him you will find very many matters most curiously collected, arranged, and explained. Diomedes was taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies and detached from his companions; none of the other ancients records him. Nothing concerning him or his companions is transmitted except names alone, variously connected in the Martyrologies, as will also be clear from our Supplements. Thus the simplicity of the entry is sufficiently secured.

[Note: [Col. 0137B]]

PRATEN., ANTUERP.-MAJOR, MUNERAT., and GREVEN. have the addition noted in the Observations.

TORNACEN., as often elsewhere, is mutilated in the eulogy of Primus and Felicianus; it stops at *imperatoribus*, “emperors.” Otherwise it is wholly pure.

PULSANEN. has the same defect concerning Primus and Felicianus. In second place: “At Alexandria, Saint Maximus, priest.” See the Acts. It continues: “In Gaul, at Pompeiae, the passion of Saint Vincentius. In Scotland, Saint Columbanus (it intended to write Columba), confessor.” Nothing concerning Diomedes.

BELINUS, purer than usual, omits only Columba’s eulogy.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. edition lack the last two announcements, which Ado also lacks, as we said in the Observations. VATICAN. [Col. 0137C] no. 5949 and UGHELLIAN have the same defect.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, on Mount Coelius, the holy martyrs Primus and Felicianus, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. In Gaul, in the city of Agen, the passion of Saint Vincentius, deacon and martyr. In Scotland, Saint Columba, priest, a man of admirable holiness.”

BRUXELLEN., pure in the first and second commemoration, puts the fourth before the third: “In the city of Nicaea, Saints Diomedes, Amamantius [corrected to Amantius], Mocianus, and Januarius.” The account of Saint Columba follows, fairly correctly.

HAGENOYEN.: “At Rome on Mount Coelian, the feast of the holy martyrs, the brothers Primus and Felicianus, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. First they were bound with iron and shut in prison, where an angel came to them, consoling them and freeing them from their bonds. Then they were severely beaten with rods. Next they were separated from one another; Felicianus was beaten with leaded scourges, then bound to a stake, and goads were driven into his hands and [Col. 0137D] feet; thus bound, he remained on the wood three days and nights without food or drink. But his companion Primus was beaten with very stout clubs, then suspended on the rack, and his sides were burned with lamps; afterward boiling lead was poured into his mouth, which he drank as though cold water. Then lions were sent to devour them both, but they rolled at their feet. Seeing this, fifteen hundred unbelievers were converted; they were slain by diverse deaths, and the saints were immediately beheaded.” In the rest it is fairly pure.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., no. 130, [Col. 0138B] at the end: “At Savina, Saint Getulius, martyr.” In the Omitted he is joined with others. He is undoubtedly the man whom Usuard mentions on the following day.

DAVERON.: “On the same day, the dedication of the church of Saint Mary of Josaphat.” It may be peculiar to that place.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Primus and Felicianus, martyrs. Vincentius, martyr, in the city of Agen. Columba, priest and confessor, in Scotland.”

REG. SUEC., no. 428: “On the same day in Gaul, in the territory of Paris, the body of Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite was discovered and publicly displayed to the gaze of many by a manifest revelation. This was certainly done so that the craftiness of certain envious persons, falsely claiming that they possessed the limbs of that most glorious martyr, might not instil into human minds the error of a false belief and persuade simple people of the fabrications of their deceit.” Nothing of this sort occurs in the others. I do not discuss its truth here.

FLORENTIN.: “In the city of Nicaea, Saints Diomedes, [Col. 0138C] Amantius, Motianus, and Januarius. At Alexandria, Saint Maximus, priest. At Rome, the passion of Saint Faustinus, martyr, who suffered under the emperor Julian.”

LUGDUNEN.: “In the city of Agen, at Pompeiacum, the passion of Saint Vincentius,” etc.

The LUBECO-COL. edition inserts after *ducentes*, “leading [a life],” in the notice of Primus and Felicianus: “They were accused before the emperors by the priests of the temples because they were Christians. But because they were found steadfast in the faith of Christ, therefore now separately” … and so on to the end [the editor abbreviates the citation]. Then: “They were buried at the Numentan arches, within the sandpit, fourteen miles from the city of Rome.” It has the notice of Vincentius as Ado does. It is pure in Columba. “At Nicaea, Saint Diomedes, confessor. On the same day, the holy martyrs Gentilis and Basilides.” They are referred to the following day. “On the same day, the translation of Saint Edmund, bishop and confessor.” That translation and other matters relating to it will be dealt with on the feast day, [Col. 0138D] 16 November.

GREVEN.: “At Rome, the blessed martyrs, fifteen in number, Gentilis and Basilides, martyrs.” See what has been said. “Maximus, priest; Alexander [printed *Alexandri*]. The translation of Saint Eskil, bishop and martyr.” His feast is 12 June. “The translation of Saint Edmund, bishop and confessor.”

MOLAN., in small type: “On the same day, Saint Pelagia, virgin and martyr of Antioch, who threw herself from a roof lest she fall into the hands of mockers.” In later editions: “Likewise Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, who flourished in the time of Pope Gregory.” Concerning Pelagia, the same and in the same manner as above.

[Col. 0135]

At Rome on Mount Caelius, the feast of Saints Primus and Felicianus under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. These most glorious martyrs, having lived a long life in the Lord, and now together enduring equal torments, now separately diverse and carefully devised ones, at last completed the course of their blessed contest when they were put to the sword. In Gaul, in the city of Agen, the passion of Blessed Vincentius, deacon and martyr. Likewise in Scotland, Saint Columba, priest and confessor, a man of great and admirable virtue. At Nicaea, Saint Diomedes. Bouillart’s addition: [At the monastery of Saint Germanus, the dedication

[Note: [Col. 0135B]]

This mention of the dedication seemed by no means Usuardian to Sollerius, since very many manuscripts are silent concerning it; Sirmond testifies that it was erased from Pratensis B, and Castellan finally admits that it seems to him to have been appended by a later hand. But in a matter which belongs to the monastery of Saint Germanus alone, what does the silence of other manuscripts prove? Nor does Sirmond’s observation carry any weight. After the oratory of Blessed Peter, along with the basilicas of Saints Vincentius and Germanus, [Col. 0136B] had been destroyed and burned by the Northmen, the solemnity of the dedication was also discontinued, and consequently its mention was omitted from the manuscript read in the chapter. And what, finally, am I to say of Castellan’s remark? I am weary of continually repeating “the same parchment, the same ink, the same hand”; I leave that invention to be refuted by the eyes. BOUILLART.]

of the oratory in honour of Blessed Peter the Apostle.]

IV before the Ides. Day 10.

[Note: [Col. 0139]]

Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Rosweyd., Belin., Greven, and Molan. are pure.

[Note: [Col. 0139A]]

I wrote “Madalis,” following Herinien., Tornacen., Rosweyd., Belin., and Greven., indeed also Praten., which I believe is how Usuard read it, although the Roman parvum and Ado have “Mandalis,” followed by Antuerp.-Major, Molan., and others. “Magdalis” occurs in Belin., which comes closest to “Magdalotis,” or “Macidalitis” [Col. 0139B], from which some think it was fabricated. Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. omit *via Aurelia* at the very beginning. Belin., instead of *praeside* (“under the governor”), has *praesidente* (“while presiding”). Tornacen. reads *Gentulii*, Molan. *Gethulii*, and, worse, Antuerp.-Major [Col. 0140A] *Gelucii*. Rosweyd. alone substitutes *Cerearis* for *Cerealis*. Antuerp.-Major and Rosweyd. read *in carcere* (“in prison”); the others have the reading in the text. Thus Belinus wrote *retrusi* (“thrust back”) instead of *reclusi* (“confined”). The error in Herinien. is *Zacariae*; but much worse is Rosweyd.’s addition of *Zachariae prophetae* (“the prophet Zacharias”). *Autisiodoro* is common and frequently recurring; others have *Antisiodoro*, *Antisiodori*, and *Anthisiodori*. I pass over *Nichomediam*, *Amancii*, *Censuri*, and the rest.]

### [Note: [Col. 0139B]]

The Roman parvum states the matter on this day most explicitly: “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia: Basilides, Tripolis, and Mandalis, and twenty others.” Ado follows, adding in place of a eulogy only the distance from the city, the emperor, and the governor; of these our author omitted the first and reproduced the rest. Notker copied all of Ado’s words, adding material of his own; in some manuscripts, instead of *Tripode* and *Mandale*, *Tripoli* and *Magdaletes* are found written. Henschenius used this argument to remove the last two from the Martyrologies. I do not know which manuscripts Notker implies for this day; certainly this transformation of the names ought rather to belong not to this day but to 12 June, on the basis of the Hieronymian manuscripts. Nor does the authority of the Roman parvum, Ado, and all the Usuardian manuscripts seem so easily to be dismissed.

Nevertheless, the cited Henschenius was greatly perplexed by the various other Martyrologies, because Basilides appears here, and a second Basilides on 12 June, now joined with these companions, now with others. He does not, however, admit either Tripodes or Mandalis; for today he adds seven named companions to Basilides, while excluding entirely our twenty-two anonymous ones, and he grants them no place on 12 June either. Thus, in his judgment, the names must be fabricated or corrupt, as we recently observed from Notker.

Papebrochius perhaps resolves the matter better in his annotation on 12 June, p. 510. I freely acknowledge that it is not so easy to untangle a most intricate problem; yet I do not see that the way is closed by which the authority of the Martyrologies cited can be preserved intact, provided that I presume nothing beyond my masters. The reader will find further discussions of this matter in those authors and in Florentinius. I, whose concern here is the present investigation, am more than confident that our notice—whether ultimately genuine or fabricated through the fault of certain copyists—is genuinely Usuardian in all its details, as it is expressed in the marginal column, having been transferred here from the Roman parvum through Ado.

Wandalbertus seems to have made a different path, as though it were his own, when he sang:

> On the fourth, Basilides flourishes, and twice ten martyrs.

The distinguished martyr Getulius and his companions proceed from the same sources, the Roman parvum and Ado, and are recorded neither in the Hieronymian Martyrologies nor in Bede. The Roman parvum assigns him one companion only, namely Cerealis; Ado added two others, Amantius and Primitivus, from the Acts. Notker did not reproduce Ado’s longer history from the Acts in full. Our author selected from it, in very few words, those details that sufficiently indicate and illuminate the manner of their death.

Regarding the antiquity of the Acts, Papebrochius judged that he did not dare assert that they were taken from the proconsular Acts, although otherwise he considered them sufficiently well attested. They are also admitted by more recent writers, at least insofar as they do not conflict with the famous Acts of his wife Symphorosa and their sons. Ruinartius accepted these Acts as genuine among his selected texts, beginning at p. 17. Tillemontius composed in French the history of the man, his wife, sons, and companions in vol. II, beginning at p. 241.

We shall discuss separately, according to Usuard’s understanding, certain matters concerning Symphorosa and her sons on 27 June; but the recension of the Acts themselves was deferred by our predecessors to 18 July, following the order we were instructed to observe from the Roman Martyrology. The Hieronymian copies explicitly record Zacharias of Nicomedia and Censurius of Auxerre; from them, I believe, Rabanus, Usuard, and Notker immediately took these names, while Bede, the Roman parvum, and Ado passed them over. Of Zacharias there remains only a certain memory of his cult; concerning Censurius, Henschenius gathered into a brief historical summary everything that had come to his notice from elsewhere.

In the Pratense manuscript there follows, from Castellani’s letter: “At Paris, Saint Landericus the confessor,” or, as in our copy, “bishop and confessor.” Among the Usuardian witnesses, only Munerat’s edition mentions him in the text; it was therefore excluded from the pure manuscripts together with the aforesaid codex. But the material added in the same manuscript in a more recent hand, concerning the dedication of crypts and so forth, we omit here as we do in the appendices. The remaining material placed in the text cannot fail to be Usuardian.]

### [Note: [Col. 0141A]]

**PRATEN.** Enough has already been said about its Appendix. We shall not discuss the dedication of the crypts.

**MUNERAT.** reads as follows: “At Paris, the deposition of Saint Landericus, bishop and confessor. Although he, the bishop of that same city, shines on earth less fully with signs of miracles, nevertheless he is believed to reign with the Lord in heaven.”

**PULSANEN.** supplies another text: “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, at the fifteenth milestone, Saints Basilides, Aurisius, Rogatus, and Januarius, with twelve companions.” See the Acts for this day and for 12 June. “On the same day, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Lucian the martyr [Col. 0141B] in the city of Soissons.” I find nothing else about it. “In the city of Nicomedia, Saints Restitutus, Rogatus, and Zacharias.” FLORENTINI discuss these and Basilides, etc., in the same way below; nothing was said about them in the material omitted. I think the names at the end have been joined incorrectly.

**ANTUERP. MAX.-ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVAN., ALBERG., DANIC.** and **EDIT. ULTRAJ.-BELG.** add at the end, after the text: “At Cologne Agrippina, Saint Maurinus the martyr.”

**CENTULEN.**: “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, Saint Basilides the martyr, Tripodes and Mandalis, and twenty others, under the governor Plato. On the same day, the blessed martyr Getulius, who suffered under the emperor Hadrian, together with certain companions.” In the case of Zacharias and Censurius it is pure. It continues: “At Paris, Saint Landericus, bishop and confessor. At Lysois, the translation of the blessed Ursinus, bishop and confessor, and Bertunius the martyr.” See what is said about them in the catalogue of those omitted.

[Col. 0141C] **BRUXELLEN.** begins: “Saint Judocus, abbot and confessor, son of the king of the Britons, who, as a pilgrim and hermit, rested in the district of Pontinus [Pontivo].” He is commemorated on 13 December. It then reads: “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the feast of Saints Basilides, Tripodes, Modalis, Aurisius, Rogatus, Januarius, Cassianus, Victor, Martin, and thirty others crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian.” The account of Getulius is sufficiently pure; to Zacharias it adds “the man of God.” Then: “At Cologne Agrippina, Saint Maurinus the abbot, martyred for Christ in the atrium of the church. At Mainz, Saint Bardus [Bardon], archbishop and confessor.” At the end, the account of Censurius is pure.

**HAGENOYEN.** gives a sufficiently pure account of Getulius, in first place. Concerning Basilides and his companions, after “martyrs” it adds: “who were killed by various deaths.” The account of Zacharias and Censurius is pure; at the end it adds concerning Maurinus: “At Cologne,” etc., as above.

[Col. 0141D] **VICTORIN.** and **REGINAE SUEC.**, under no. 130, add at the end: “In Persia, Saint Plato.” There is Plato the hegumen on 4 April; there is also the martyr on 22 July. I do not know who this one is. Nor is he known among the omitted entries. Or perhaps it cannot be said that this is Ivo? See **ALTEMPS**.

**MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.**: “Getulius and his companion martyrs. Basilides, Tripodes, and Mandalis, with twenty companions. Also Saint Zacharias. Censurius, bishop and confessor.”

**REGINAE SUEC.**, under note no. 428: “In the city of Paris, the blessed Landri, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Evremund, abbot.” In the Acts it is “Landericus and Ebremundus.”

**VATICAN.**, no. 5949, lacks Zacharias and Censurius. The extract notes this.

[Col. 0142A] **ALTEMPS**: “In England, at Ramsey, the translation of Saint Ivo, archpriest [he means bishop of Persia], whose sacred relics a very white dove flew over for seven miles, until they were carried to the holy land. In the city of Rochester in Britain, the deposition of Saint Ythamar, bishop and confessor.”

**FLORENTIN.**: “Also Saints Cassianus, Victor, Martin, Aurisius, Rogatus, and Januarius, with twelve others. At Nicomedia, Saints Restitutus, Rogatus, and Zacharias.” See what was said above [Col. 0143B] concerning the **PULSANEN** manuscript.

**EDITIO LUBECO-COL.** begins thus: “At Cologne Agrippina, the passion of Saint Maurinus the abbot, who suffered martyrdom in the atrium of the church of Saint Pantaleon, and whose body is decently and honorably laid to rest there.” A moderately interpolated text follows. Then: “At Trier, Saint Fortunatus, bishop and confessor.” See the omitted entries. “Also at Trier, Saint Basilissa the virgin, in the monastery commonly called Horrentum.” There is nothing about her among the omitted entries; nor can the Roman martyr Basilla or Basilissa of the following day be intended here. Rather, this concerns the abbess of the monastery of Horreum, whom I find recorded by Castellanus on 5 September.

**GREVEN.**: “Rogatus, Marcianus, and twenty other martyrs. Mammarius the priest, a holy old man of ninety-two years, and his companions Felix and Victorianus, deacons; Libosus, prefect of the city; Donatus, Albinus, Laurentius, Fauntianus, Ziddinus, Crispinus, [Col. 0142C] Leucius, Faustina, and her husband Faustinus. At the time of Valerian and Gallienus, after the rack, lamps applied to their sides, and claws, with the skin of their heads flayed, burning helmets were placed upon all their heads. Then, having been comforted by an angel in prison, they were brought out again and thrown into the fire, but were not harmed; they were roasted on a gridiron and beaten with raw sinews until their entrails were exposed. Finally, by the stroke of the sword, they obtained the palm of martyrdom. At Cologne Agrippina, Saint Maurinus, abbot and martyr, who suffered in the atrium of the church of Saint Pantaleon and lies decently buried there. Landericus, bishop of Paris and confessor. Bardus, bishop and confessor. Fortunatus, bishop of Trier and confessor.” Concerning him, see above. “At Trier, in the monastery called Horrentum, Saint Basilissa the virgin.” We have also spoken of her. “In Scotland, the translation of Saint Patrick, bishop and confessor.” He is commemorated on 17 March. “On Mount Sinai, the translation of Saint Catherine [Col. 0142D], virgin and martyr.” Her feast is 25 November.

**MOLAN.**: “At Paris, the deposition of Saint Landericus,” etc., as in **MUNERAT** above. “At Cologne Agrippina, the passion of the most holy Maurinus, abbot and martyr. Christ made known to the world, through frequent works of virtue, the merits dear to Himself of this most steadfast bearer of His cross, when He graciously revealed his sacred body.” Later editions report the same concerning Landericus and Maurinus. Then: “On the tenth day, the most sacred martyr Timothy, bishop of Prusa. On the same day, the translation of Saint Ivo, bishop from Persia.” Finally, in smaller type: “In Scotland, Saint Margaret, queen.” See her Life in the Acts.]

### [Col. 0139]

At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the feast of Saints Basilides, Tripodes, and Madalis under the emperor Aurelian, with Plato as governor, and twenty other martyrs. On the same day, on the Via Salaria, the passion of the blessed Getulius, a most distinguished and learned man, and his companions Cerealis, Amantius, and Primitivus. By order of the emperor Hadrian, they were first beaten, then confined in prison, and finally handed over to the fire. At Nicomedia, Saint Zacharias. At Auxerre, Saint Censurius, bishop and confessor.

**[Addit Bouill.]** [Note: [Col. 0139] Sollerius here provides a notable example of fairness. I have already observed that he does not once take the silence of his manuscripts as a rule by which to judge the Pratense; accordingly, he declares those saints to have been added to it by a later hand whom he did not find in his own copies. Yet, to remain consistent with himself, he draws to his side even those additions which no one has ever denied to be at least three centuries later than Usuard. What could be more unjust? [Col. 0140] He had doubtless been warned by Castellanus that Landericus had been added by a later hand. Could that be a reason why he could or should fail to count the Pratense among the pure manuscripts? I firmly believe that, given his severity, he would have acted no more leniently toward the Pratense if one of our own men had printed Francis of Assisi, Ignatius of Loyola, Teresa, or other saints of our own age in its blank spaces. **BOUILL.**] At Paris, Saint Landericus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, at the monastery of Saint Germanus, the dedication of the crypts in honor of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of the blessed Michael the archangel, and of all the heavenly powers, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the apostles and evangelists, as well as of all the holy virgins. There is also an altar of Macharius, Dionysius and his companions, and Saint Urbanus, pope and martyr, and of all the martyrs. And another of Saints George, Aurelius, and Prajectus, martyrs, and of the holy confessors Martin, Nicholas, Marcellus, and Ansbert, and of Saints Cecilia, Genovefa, and Nathalia, and of all Christ’s confessors.]

## Third day before the Ides. Day 11. [Note: [Col. 0143]]

The pure witnesses are Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. Belin., Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., Danic., and the edition of Ultraj.-Belg. may also be added.

### [Note: [Col. 0143A]]

The second class of the manuscripts cited differs from the others in reading, instead of *qui cum esset Cyprius* (“who, being a Cypriot”), *qui a discipulis* (“who by the disciples”); Belinus, moreover, after *gentium* (“of the nations”), adds *doctore* (“teacher”). Although many, with Herinien., Tornacen., and Greven., have *Ciprius*, I followed Praten., Rosweyd., Munerat., and Molanus. There is an error in Antuerp.-Major, where *episcopus* is read instead of *Apostolus*. Rosweyd. wrote *Aquilegiam*, with which all the manuscripts cited in the second place agree. We have often spoken elsewhere of *aeculeus*; the better manuscripts always write *equulei*, as in the text. In Antuerp.-Major the conjunction *atque* is missing before *ardentes*. [Col. 0144A] Our Pratense copy, contrary to all the other manuscripts, has *lampadae* instead of *lampades*, which I think occurred through the copyist’s fault. Likewise, the unanimous reading of all is: “they were drenched through the belly with boiling oil.” Grevenus and Molanus, however, omit the substantive verb *sunt* (“were”) there, placing it at the end and reading: “drenched with boiling oil . . . beheaded,” in which the sense does not change, but the simplicity of Usuard’s style is abandoned. Among the manuscripts of the second order, Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. have this peculiarity: instead of *in confessione Christi* (“in confession of Christ”), they alone substitute *in confessione Domini* (“in confession of the Lord”).]

### [Note: [Col. 0143A]]

Barnabas the apostle is not known in the Hieronymian copies, since Papebrochius observes that his memory was entered into the sacred Martyrologies very late, both in the East and in the West. At the very beginning of his Commentary he almost doubts whether the words *Barnabae apostoli* (“of Barnabas the apostle”), which are transmitted before volume II of March in the genuine edition of Bede’s Martyrology as Bede’s own words, truly belong to that Martyrologist, rather than to Florus.

I believe they genuinely belong to Bede, chiefly for the following reason among others: Rabanus, Bede’s constant copyist, places those very words on this day, without adding even a syllable either from Florus or from anyone else, so that it is perfectly clear that he had no knowledge of Florus. Thus Barnabas first obtained a place in the Christian Martyrologies through Bede, unless the Roman parvum is older, since it too explicitly mentions him.

Ado recites a eulogy among the apostles’ festivals, composed almost entirely from Jerome’s words in *De viris illustribus*, chapter 6; Florus likewise drew his material from there. Notker wished to mix in somewhat more of his own. Our author selected from Ado the individual points that we have displayed in the marginal column. I have nothing to add except to repeat what Papebrochius collected and carefully distinguished with the greatest labor and diligence. At the end of the *Analecta*, while discussing Barnabas’s Epistle, he shows that he read Tillemont’s Commentaries in the Brussels edition. Consult Papebrochius’s studies, and the ordered sequence of the whole life in Tillemont, vol. I, p. 408 onward, together with his notes beginning at p. 655. Wandalbertus mentions Barnabas alone:

[Col. 0144A]

> Barnabas, the apostle, adorns the Ides with threefold honor.

The aforesaid Roman parvum and Ado also contain, in second place, Sosthenes, a disciple of Paul the apostle, who is likewise marked by Notker. But Usuard transferred him to 28 November, followed generally by all the more recent writers, together with the present Roman Martyrology.

The pair of Aquileian brothers is not sufficiently clear in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, indeed perhaps is not recorded there, although another group of Aquileians is listed. Their commemoration is very distinct in the Roman parvum. From it Ado drew them and pursued the matter in an excellent discourse, which Notker copied in its entirety, while Usuard contracted it so that he allowed nothing connected with the illustrious struggle of the champions to be lacking. Nor do we believe that anything is missing here for the complete simplicity of Usuard’s text.

Ado’s eulogy contains the entire substance of the Acts. It recounts the pious dispute between the people of Vicenza and Aquileia as having been settled by divine assent: the people of Vicenza were to have Felix, and the Aquileians Fortunatus, but in such a way that Aquileia would receive the head of blessed Felix, while Vicenza would receive the head of Fortunatus. On this matter and on other translations or elevations of sacred relics, see Henschenius’s Commentary.

If the date indicated in the aforesaid Acts is correct, these saints ought to be referred to 14 May, as some of our manuscripts do. We displayed them on that day among the appendices. From this it will again become clear—something that occurs very frequently throughout this entire work—that perhaps the author of the Roman parvum selected this day merely according to his own inclination.]

### [Note: [Col. 0143C]]

**PULSANEN.** has again an almost entirely new text: “The feast of the blessed Barnabas the apostle. On the same day, Saints Crispulus and Restitutus. And the translation of the body of Saint Fortunatus, bishop and martyr. In the region of Aquileia, Saints Emeritus, Victorianus, Victor, Felix, and Creti.” These are almost entirely taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; see the Acts.

**CENTULEN.**: “The feast of Saint Barnabas the Apostle, who, being a Cypriot by race, was appointed apostle of the nations together with blessed Paul, and suffered martyrdom by fire at the hands of his fellow countrymen. At Corinth, Saint Sosthenes, disciple of the apostles. At Aquileia, Saints Felix and Fortunatus the martyrs, under the governor Euphemius.”

**BRUXELLEN.** begins as follows: “The feast of Saint Barnabas the apostle. He was appointed apostle of the nations by the disciples of Christ together with Paul. At Salamis in Cyprus, he was burned by Barjesus the magician and the Jews. His body, which had long remained hidden in a crypt by John Mark, his cousin and disciple, was found when the emperor Zeno was ruling, Barnabas himself revealing its location, together with the Gospel of blessed Matthew, written in Hebrew by Matthew’s own hands. Barnabas himself, while alive, always carried it with him; placing it upon the sick, he healed them.” And Saint Sosthenes, disciple of blessed Paul the apostle. “At Aquileia,” [Col. 0144D] etc., sufficiently pure.

**HAGENOYEN.** I omit what it relates about Barnabas. In the account of the Aquileians it is sufficiently pure, and then adds: “On that very day, blessed Judocus returned from Rome, carrying with him relics of the saints. He was joyfully welcomed by a large crowd, both for his own sake and because of the relics. He placed them in the church of Saint Mark the bishop. During the very solemn celebration of the Mass which he himself conducted, since he was a priest, a divine hand appeared over him, consecrating and marking him. The whole people heard a promise being made to him that whoever visited that church for Judocus’s sake would obtain whatever he devoutly requested, whether spiritual or temporal, or concerning bodily health, according to his proper need.” What these matters signify and where they lead will be explained on 13 December.

**VICTORIN.** and **REGINAE SUEC.**, under note no. 130, add at the end: “On the same day, Saint Onuphrius,” the other “Onuphrius the hermit.” See the omitted entries.

**MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJ.**: “Barnabas the apostle; Felix and Fortunatus, brother martyrs, who, afflicted by various torments, were beheaded. The translation of Saint Anthony.” See his feast on 17 January.

**VATICAN.**, under note no. 5949: “At Corinth, [Col. 0145B] Saint Sosthenes, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle. In Egypt, Saint Onuphrius the hermit.” Both have been discussed above.

**FLORENTIN.**: “At Rome, on the Via Salaria, in its cemetery, Saint Basilla the virgin. Also at Rome, Saints Crispulus and Restitutus. Also the translation of the body of Saint Fortunatus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saints Emeritus, Victorianus, Felix, Creti, and Nabor, with their companions.” These too are almost Hieronymian, as we said above concerning **PULSANEN**. See them in the Acts, in their proper places.

**LUXOVIEN.**: “The translation of Saint Spinulus the confessor, a man distinguished for his merits, disciple of the blessed Hidulphus, archbishop.” In the omitted entries he is called Spinalus and referred to 11 July.

**EDITIO LUBECO-COL.**, much interpolated in the account of Barnabas, is almost pure in the account of the Aquileians. At the end it adds: “On the same day, the discovery of the body of the blessed Anthony, abbot and confessor.” See 17 January.

**GREVEN.**: “At Corinth, Saint Sosthenes, disciple of Saint Paul. Also Emeritus, Victorianus, and Victor.” See their true names and the complete account in the Acts. “Rumbertus, bishop and confessor.” His Life is given on 4 February. “Onuphrius the anchorite and confessor, a man of God. For sixty years he lived in the vast desert of Egypt, unknown to men, living for God and himself. Spinulus the confessor, a man of the greatest humility and obedience, disciple of the blessed Hidulphus, archbishop of Trier. Before his sacred body, when he was returning to the monastery at an angel’s command, burning candles were carried, although the force of the winds was so great that it uprooted even aged oaks and firs.” These two have been discussed above. “Also the holy anchorites Timothy, John, Andrew, Thaddeus, and Philip, who are mentioned in the Acts of blessed Onuphrius.” I do not find whether, or on what day, they are commemorated in the omitted entries. “On the same day, the discovery of the body of the blessed Anthony the abbot. The commemoration of Saint Judocus, priest and confessor, over whom on this day, during the solemn celebration of Mass, the hand of the Lord appeared.” More is given above in **HAGENOYEN**, with a reference to the feast of Judocus on 13 December.

**MOLAN**, in smaller type: “Spinulus the confessor, a man of the greatest humility and obedience, disciple of the blessed Hildulphus, archbishop of Trier. Onuphrius the anchorite and confessor, a man of God.” See what was said above. In other editions: “At Bremen, Saint Rembertus, archbishop and confessor.” Concerning him, see above. “On the same day, the translation of the body of Saint Ragenfredis the virgin.” See the omitted entries. She is commemorated on 8 October.]

### [Col. 0143]

The feast of Saint Barnabas the apostle, who, being a Cypriot, was appointed apostle of the nations together with Paul. His body was found when the emperor Zeno was ruling, Barnabas himself revealing its location. At Aquileia, the passion of Saints Felix and Fortunatus, under the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian. Since they were two brothers, they were suspended on the rack; burning lamps were placed around their sides. When these were soon extinguished by God’s power, they were drenched through the belly with boiling oil, and finally, in their confession of Christ, they were beheaded.

## The day before the Ides. Day 12. [Note: [Col. 0145]]

The pure witnesses are Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

### [Note: [Col. 0145C]]

In Antuerp.-Major, *Mediolano* (“at Milan”) is a copyist’s error. All read *cum quo sanctissimum* (“with whom the most holy [one]”), except Greven. and Molan., who have *et cum eo sanctissimum* (“and with him the most holy [one]”). The text continues: *quem idem ipse nutrierat* (“whom that same man himself had raised”). In Herinien. *ipse* has been erased. In Munerat. *idem* is missing; Antuerp.-Maj. has *nutriverat* (“had nourished”); Greven. and Molan. *nutriebat* (“was nourishing”). Herinien. and Munerat. write *ferire* (“to strike”) instead of *feriri* (“to be struck”). The latter is redundant, reading: *ferire Anolinus jussit* (“Anolinus ordered [him] to strike”). Again, Greven. and Molan. prefer *beatus* (“blessed”) to *sanctus Paulinus* (“Saint Paulinus”); Munerat. omits both. In the case of Archadius and Cyrinus all agree: *repperit* (“he found”) occurs only in Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., and Greven.]

### [Note: [Col. 0145C]]

On 10 June a controversy arose concerning whether there was one Basilides or several, and concerning his companions, who were combined in different ways. Here another, no less serious, difficulty follows from a faulty reading of Usuard, which transfers Roman martyrs to Milan. The Hieronymian Martyrologies provide no great illumination, as Florentinius admits there, citing chiefly what Fronto collected in his notes at p. 92, on the occasion of Basilides alone, who is recorded in his Calendar on this day.

Nor do the ancient Sacramentaries cited by Henschenius completely resolve the matter. To explain it briefly, I first give the complete text of the Roman parvum, where today it reads: “At Milan, Nazarius and Celsus, whose discovery is on the second day before the Ides of June, and whose martyrdom is on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.” Here the difficulty begins, and Henschenius explains it more successfully than the matter we discussed on the tenth of this month.

Thus Ado, following his guide, reported here the eulogy—or rather the history—of the two Milanese martyrs, abridged from the Acts and described by Notker. Others place it on their proper day of struggle, 28 July; Notker repeats there both their feast and their commemoration. Therefore, in recording the encomium of Nazarius and Celsus on this day, Usuard did not depart at all from Ado, whose elegant abridgment he presents. Nor does the chief point of the controversy turn on this.

After these two Milanese saints, Ado simply continues: “Also the blessed Basilides, Cyrinus, and Nabor.” But also Nazarius and Celsus, whom antiquity celebrates in its records as having suffered at the city of Embrun. What should be thought about the Embrun martyrs will be seen in its proper place, and is meanwhile indicated in the omitted entries.

The difficulty concerns three others, whom Ado lists without assigning a place or arena. If Usuard had done so, everything would have been clearer. Whether he did this inadvertently or deliberately, who can say? He added from his own hand, plainly: “At the aforesaid city.” This is what the aforementioned Henschenius laboriously refutes by collecting other Martyrologies, and rightly so; for it has neither the appearance of truth nor any basis in the older sources used by Usuard.

Bede, moreover, gives the following concerning the same martyrs: “The feast of Saints Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius.” I am firmly persuaded that Ado took his material from Bede, cautiously omitting Nazarius, whom he may have thought should not be confused with the Milanese martyr.

Rabanus certainly follows Bede, determining the matter more clearly: “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, at the fifth milestone, the passion of the martyr Basilides,” etc. He adds much concerning the translation of their bodies, to be displayed in the appendices; Notker took much of this from Rabanus, although he himself, I think according to his own judgment, separates the martyrs.

Henschenius therefore argues correctly for the truth of the notice in the modern Roman Martyrology, and we too have correctly reproduced the genuine, though erroneous, text of Usuard for this day.

What should be thought about Basilides alone, and further about the Acts of Basilides and the three companions named here, Papebrochius has explained sufficiently. But the indisputable monuments attest their most certain and ancient cult. The passion, discovery, and other matters concerning Nazarius and Celsus will be examined in the Acts on 28 July.

Here is Wandalbert’s distich specifically belonging to this day:

> On the day before, Cyrinus shines, and Nazarius and Nabor;  
> With these we join Basilides in the same festival.

### [Note: [Col. 0147A]]

**TORNAC.** cuts off the final part of the Milanese eulogy, beginning with the words: “Their bodies,” etc.

**PLUSANEN.** again departs from Usuard. Here are its words: “The feast of Saints Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius, martyrs. At Rome, the feast of Saints Felix and Magilaleus, martyrs.” Felix has been intruded here from elsewhere; the other, perhaps Macidaletes, seems to belong to Tripoli. “Also Saint Helidius, bishop.” Nor do we know from where he found a place here on this day.

**ROSWEYD.** appends to the pure text at the end: “The feast of Saint Odulphus, priest and confessor.”

**ANTUERP.** and **MAX-LUBEC.** commemorate the following today: “At Milan, the festival of Saints Nazarius and Celsus the martyrs, when these blessed martyrs were discovered and translated by blessed Ambrose. They were endowed with such grace that their blood seemed to have been poured out most recently, and their heads seemed to have been cut off that very day. Everyone perceived such a fragrance that it surpassed the sweetness of every perfume. Their actual festival is celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. On the same day, Saints Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius, martyrs.”

**ALBERG.** and **DANIC.** begin as follows: “At the city of Aurelia, the feast of the blessed Basilides, who, when the Lord appeared and commanded him to sell all his possessions and distribute them to the poor, came to Aurelia to visit his parents, and there, under Aurelian, together with Saints Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius, earned the palm of martyrdom.” That these things have been embellished as fables is more than evident. It continues: “At Milan, the feast of Saints Nazarius and Celsus the boy martyrs, when these blessed martyrs were discovered by blessed Ambrose,” etc. Everything reported above from **ANTUERP.** and **MAX.-LUBEC.** is repeated.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN.** and **EDIT. ULTRAJ.-BELG.** suffer from precisely the same defects and additionally add at the end: “On that very day, Saint Odulphus, priest and confessor.” **LOVAN.**, similar to the others, is defective in the eulogy of Nazarius and Celsus; after *suavitatem* (“sweetness”) it omits *festivitas vero*, etc.

**CENTULEN.**: “At Milan, the discovery and translation of Saints Nazarius and Celsus the martyrs. Also the blessed Basilides, Cyrinus, and Nabor; and Nazarius and Celsus, whom antiquity commemorates as having suffered.” Namely, at Embrun, as we said in the Observations from Ado.

**BRUXELLEN.**: “At the city of Aurelia,” etc., as above in **ALBERGEN.**, **DANIC.**, and the others. Then: “And the feast of Saints Nazarius and Celsus the boy martyrs, whom antiquity celebrates in its records as having suffered at the city of Embrun. For the governor Anolinus, in the fury of the persecution,” etc. It mixes truth with falsehood, connecting and interpolating the two different eulogies given above. At the end: “And on that very day, Saint Odulphus the confessor.”

**HAGENOYEN.**: “At Milan, the translation of Saints Nazarius and Celsus the martyrs. Their bodies, as he writes,” etc. See what was said above. It continues: “At the city of Aurelia,” etc., as above. Finally: “On the same day, at Utrecht below, the deposition of Saint Odulphus, canon of the monastery of Saint Salvator. He converted Frisia a second time together with Saint Frederick, his bishop. Because they did not kindly heed him, he foretold that the Danes would come upon them and that many martyrs would arise in Frisia; and so it happened. Finally, near the end of his life, he built a monastery in Frisia and foretold that the sea would come there. Then he returned to Utrecht and died in peace.” These things are taken from his Life, which see in the Acts.

[Col. 0148B] **MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.**: “Basilides, Cyrinus, and Nabor, martyrs. Odulphus the confessor, canon of Saint Salvator of Utrecht. Cunera the virgin and martyr, who was one of the companions of blessed Ursula.” See Papebrochius’s Commentary.

**ALTEMPS.**: “At Orléans, the translation of Ewicus, bishop and confessor.” Perhaps Evurtius or Evortius, concerning whom we shall have to speak below on 7 September.

**FLORENTIN.** Here again there is confusion among many entries, in some respects not unlike the Pulsanensian account. **STROZZIAN.**, unless I am mistaken, reports as follows: “On that very day, at Rome, on the Via Aurelia, at the eighth milestone, in the monastery of Nirinus, the passion of Saints Basilides, Tribulus, Malchus, Daletis, Cibinus, Tropulus, Aurilius, Donatellus, and Secunda.” See the Acts for their more accurate names. “Also the feast of Saints Basilides and Cyrinus, martyrs. Also at Rome, the feast of Saints Felix and Magdalena. Also Saint Elidius, bishop.”

**EDITIO LUBECO-COL.** is marked by a peculiar reading: [Col. 0148C] “In the town of Reims, the passion of Saint Cunera, virgin and martyr, one of the company of the eleven thousand virgins. At the city of Aurelia, the feast of the blessed Basilides,” etc. Again: “At Milan, the discovery of Saints Nazarius and Celsus the boy martyrs, who likewise,” etc., as set out at length above. “At Utrecht below, the feast of the blessed Odulphus, priest and confessor.” See the eulogy of **HAGENOYEN** above and the entire history of his life in our Acts.

**BELIN.** after *repperit* (“he found”) adds: “But their festival,” etc. Another edition further adds at the end: “At Orléans, the blessed Evurtius, bishop and confessor.” We said above that his feast is celebrated on 7 September.

GREVEN: “In Scotland, of Ternan, archbishop and confessor.” In the *Acts* he is called Ternan. “In Lower Utrecht, of Saint Odulf, priest and confessor, a canon of that same Utrecht church. To make his merit evident to all, when the whole of his building had been consumed by devouring flames, the staff, nevertheless, by which he was accustomed to support his aged limbs, and on which he also kept a wax tablet for recording the names of the faithful, was found so entirely unharmed that not even a single point of writing had perished in the wax. In the town of Renen, of Saint Cunera, virgin and martyr. Since she belonged to the company of the eleven thousand holy virgins, yet survived them for some time, being greatly devoted to works of piety, she deserved to attain the palm of martyrdom.” I have already mentioned that her *Life* is illustrated in the *Acts*.

MOLANUS, continuing the final sense of the text, adds: “and of Nazarius, whose relics—Nabor and Nazarius, together with the martyr Gorgonius—the bishop of Metz, Crodegandus, transferred from Rome to Gaul, with the permission of Pope Paul of Rome, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 765; and the aforesaid bishop placed Saint Gorgonius in the monastery called Gorzia, Saint Nabor in the monastery called Novacella, and Saint Nazarius in the monastery called Loreshain, where signs and miracles frequently occur in the healing of the sick and infirm.” These things are taken from Rabanus or Notkerus. “On that same day, of Saint Odulf, priest and confessor, whose relics are kept at Saint Saviour’s in Utrecht.” Then, in smaller type: “In the town of Renen, the elevation by Saint Willebrord of Saint Cunera, virgin and martyr. Since she was,” etc., as in GREVEN. “In Mesopotamia, of Saint Maruthas, bishop and confessor,” concerning whom see the *Tripartite History*, book XI, chapter 8. He is referred to 4 December. Other editions, with the text corrupted, have the same account of the translation of Nazarius, etc., and likewise of Odulf. Then they continue: “In the town of Renen, the elevation of Saint Cunera, virgin and martyr,” stopping there. “On the twelfth day, of the holy father Onuphrius. And of the holy father Peter the Athonite.” On Mount Athos, see Janning in the *Acts*.

[Col. 0145]

At Milan, the birthday of Blessed Nazarius, whom Anolinus, during the persecution stirred up by Nero, had long tormented and afflicted in prison; with him he ordered the most holy boy Celsus, whom Anolinus himself had brought up, to be struck with the sword. Their bodies, as Saint Paulinus writes, had remained hidden until the time of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius, when Blessed Ambrose, by divine revelation, discovered them. Likewise near the aforesaid city, of the holy martyrs Basilides, Quirinus, and Nabor.

On the Ides. Day 13. [Note: [Col. 0149A]

The text is taken from Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp-Major, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0149B]

Tornacensis omitted the title “saint” before Felicula. Molanus, however, wrote *Faelicula*. The same Tornacensis substituted *sacrificare* (“to sacrifice”) for *immolare* (“to offer sacrifice”). We have spoken elsewhere of idols, as also of the torture-horse. In Molanus, instead of *nec idolis* (“nor to idols”), there is *neque* (“and not”). In Heriniensis, through an improper transposition of letters, *coaclam* is read instead of *cloacam* (“sewer”). I do not know what Greven had in mind when, instead of *Cordubam* (“Córdoba”), he read “in the city of Columba.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149B]

The ancient Calendar of Fronto, cited the previous day and often elsewhere, reads under 14 June: “The birthday of Saint Felicula,” where the rightly cited Fronto observes that it should perhaps be written under the thirteenth day, as our Martyrologists have it. In particular, the Hieronymian copies preserved by Florentinius mark *Feliculi* last on this day; but the editor does not doubt that the reference is to Felicula, having been sufficiently instructed by the most ancient Echternach manuscript. Bede explicitly mentions Saint Felicula at Rome, and after him Rabanus, with an elogium. The *Little Roman Martyrology* states more clearly: “At Rome, of Saint Felicula, virgin and martyr.” Still more clearly and explicitly does the Viennese Martyrologist, composing his entire panegyric from the account of Marcellus at Nereus and Achilleus, cited more than once under May, mention her; its epitome, most elegantly abridged by Usuard, represents our little calendar. Wandalbertus briefly and not inelegantly embraces much in a few words:

“The Ides illumines Felicula the virgin with blood,

[Col. 0149C] Milk, Petronilla, for you, whom word and age joined to her.”

Here there is an allusion to the term *collactanea* (“foster-sister”), of which we have also spoken elsewhere. Whether some manuscripts of the *Acts* improperly call her *collectanea*, see Henschenius’s Commentary. [Col. 0150B] The case of Felicula’s deeds is the same as that of the entire series of the *Acts* of Nereus and Achilleus. We know that her ancient cult is thoroughly well attested. Concerning several bodies of several persons venerated under the same name, see the historical Commentary of Henschenius and Papebrochius. On this day Bede also records the African martyrs Lucianus, Fortunatus, and Crescentianus. Rabanus omitted the last of these, contrary to the middle-quality Usuardine manuscripts, which frequently fail in the second name. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies Tecla is added; you will find her noted in the *Auctaria*. Nothing can be said about Notkerus, since there is a lacuna in him up to the thirteenth day before the Kalends. Our text entirely passed over those Africans, being more concerned with its Cordoban martyrs, of whom it commemorates several this month: on the third, Isaac; on the seventh, Peter, Habentius, and Jeremiah, etc.; on the eighth, Abundius; and to these our *Acts* add others on other days from Eulogius. We therefore consider it quite certain that Usuard celebrated the priest Fandila on this day, and that all the preceding material is genuinely his. See the *Acts of Fandila*, drawn from Eulogius’s *Memorial*, book III, chapter 1, and presented in the larger work, with a preceding synopsis concerning his cult and date.]

[Note: [Col. 0149C]

PULSANENSIS reads as follows: “In Africa, the birthday of the holy martyrs Lucianus, Fortunatus, Crescentianus, and Tecla. At Rome, at the seventh milestone, the birthday of Saint Feliculus with his companions.” I think he intended to write “Felicissimus with his companions,” concerning whom BRUSSELS also has an entry on this day. He is actually commemorated on 6 August.

ROSWEYD inserts into the text concerning Felicula, which is otherwise pure: “who was the foster-sister of the virgin Petronilla.”

ANTWERP and MAXIMUM-LÜBECK omit the place in the first announcement, namely, the Ardeatine Way. At the end they add: “In Africa, of Lucianus and Crescentianus.” Here you see that Fortunatus, who stood between them, is missing, as I noted above; this will become clearer in what follows.

ANTWERP-MAJOR, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, and the BELGIAN UTRECHT EDITION begin as follows: “In the city of Padua, the birthday of Blessed Anthony, confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor, who was most renowned for his life, miracles, and learning.” The pure text follows. At the end is added: [Col. 0149D] “In Africa, of Lucianus and Crescentianus.”

ALBERG and DANIC, equal to these up to this point, additionally add concerning Saint Anthony of Padua, after “learning”: “He used memory in place of books, so that Pope Gregory IX called him, by a special designation, the Ark of the Testament. Among the other miracles of his virtues by which he shone during life, it is also read that he raised two dead persons.”

[Col. 0150C] CENTULENSIS: “At Rome, of Saint Felicula, virgin, who was the fellow-virgin of Blessed Petronilla and suffered under the governor Flaccus. On the same day, of Saint Fandila, priest, who received martyrdom at the city of Córdoba by decapitation.”

BRUSSELS, after “martyr” concerning Felicula, inserts: “When the governor Flaccus, after the death of Blessed Petronilla, wished to take her as his wife, and she refused to marry,” etc., up to the end, where it adds: “And thus she went to Christ with the crown of martyrdom. At Rome, the birthday of Saint Felicissimus, with his companions.” This appears to refer to the one commemorated on 6 August. In the account of Fandila it continues in pure form: “In Africa, of the holy martyrs Lucianus, Fortunatus, and Crescentianus. Likewise, the translation of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.” This will be treated on 24 August. “In the city of Padua, of Blessed Anthony, confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor. He was most renowned for his life, miracles, and learning. Likewise, of Saint Priscus, bishop [Col. 0150D] and confessor. And at Ghent, the translation of Saint Landoaldus, confessor.” Concerning this and Priscus, see the *Praetermissi*.

HAGENOYEN: “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the birthday of Blessed Felicula, virgin and martyr, who was the close companion and foster-sister of Blessed Petronilla, virgin, daughter of Blessed Peter the Apostle. After the death of the virgin Petronilla, the governor Flaccus wished to have her as his wife, [Col. 0151A] but she refused to consent. But because she then refused to sacrifice to idols, she was handed over to a certain magistrate, who made her fast for seven days; then she was led to the girls consecrated to the goddess Vesta, so that she might eat with them of the sacrificial food. She refused this as well, and fasted for another seven days. Then she was imprisoned and finally raised upon the torture-horse; afterward she was taken down from the torture-horse and thrown headlong into a sewer. On the same day, the translation of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle to Benevento.” The account of Fandila is sufficiently pure. It continues: “In Africa, of the holy martyrs Crescentianus and Lucianus. At Padua, the birthday of Blessed Anthony, confessor, who is said to have raised two dead persons.”

AQUINCINCT adds at the end: “In Africa, of Lucianus and Crescentianus.”

In VICTORINUS, *Fandilae* is replaced by *Ficandi*.

MATRIC-CARTUS-UTRECHT: “Of Anthony, confessor, of the Order of Minors. Of Felicula, virgin and martyr. Of Pharaildis, virgin.” The *Life* of Pharaildis was given on 4 January. [Col. 0151B] I do not know why she is repeated on this day.

UCHELLIAN: “In Africa, of Lucianus and Crescentianus.” See ANTWERP and MAXIMUM-LÜBECK.

FLORENTINIUS: “In Italy, in the city of Padua, of Saint Antoninus of Lisbon, illustrious confessor of the Order of Friars Minor, who was most renowned for his life, miracles, and learning. In Africa, of the holy martyrs Lucianus, Fortunatus, Crescentianus, and Tecla the virgin.”

CODEX S. RICALDI: “In the territory of Forlì, of Blessed Regnabertus, martyr.” See the *Praetermissi*, where he is referred to 15 July.

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION, with Felicula moderately interpolated, is nearly pure in the account of Fandila. “In Africa, of the holy martyrs Lucianus and Crescentianus. In the city of Padua, the birthday of Blessed Anthony, confessor,” etc., as in ANTWERP-MAJOR, ALBERG, and others above.

BELINUS begins: “In the city of Padua, the birthday of Blessed Anthony, illustrious confessor of the Order of Friars Minor, who was most renowned for his life, miracles, and [Col. 0152A] learning.” The account of Felicula is pure. But near the end: “In Africa, the birthday of the holy martyrs Fortunatus, Lucianus, and Crescentianus. On the same day, of Saint Fandila, priest, martyred at Córdoba.”

GREVEN: “In Africa, of Lucianus, Fortunatus, and Crescentianus. Likewise, of Saint Landwoldus.” I think this is Landoaldus, mentioned above. “In the city of Aternum, of Blessed Cetheus, bishop, surnamed Peregrinus. He governed that [Amiternian] church in the time of Blessed Pope Gregory and, condemned to death by the Lombard tyrant Umblus, when he could not be decapitated, was thrown into the river with a huge stone tied around his neck and happily died; immediately the sacred body floated back up with the stone. At Padua, the deposition of Blessed Anthony, confessor of the Order of Minors, most renowned for his life and miracles. He used memory in place of books, and therefore Gregory IX called him the Ark of the Testament. The translation of Saint Andrew [or was it Bartholomew?] [Col. 0152B] the Apostle to Benevento.” See the *Praetermissi*.

MOLANUS: “In the city of Padua, of Blessed Anthony, the illustrious Portuguese confessor from Lisbon, a Minorite, who was most renowned for his life, miracles, and learning. In Africa, of the holy martyrs Fortunatus, Lucianus, and Crescentianus. At Ghent, the elevation of Saint Landoaldus and his companions”; in smaller type he adds: “Amantius, Adrianus, Vinciana, and Landrada.” Concerning them, see the *Praetermissi*. “At Clairvaux, Gerard the monk died, concerning whom Bernard speaks in his sermon on the *Song of Songs*, 26.” He is Saint Bernard’s brother, concerning whom there is an account in the *Acts*. In other editions: concerning Anthony and the Africans, as above. Then: “On the thirteenth day, of Saint Aquilina, martyr, and Saint Tryphillius, bishop of Leucosia in Cyprus. At Ghent, the elevation,” etc. In smaller type: “At Clairvaux, the death of Gerard the monk, etc. Likewise, of Saint Peregrinus, or Cetheus, bishop and martyr of Aternum, drowned in the river Pescara in the city of Atria, in the time of Pope Gregory.” See the *Acts*.

[Col. 0149]

At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the birthday of Saint Felicula, virgin and martyr, who, because she refused to marry and refused to sacrifice to idols, was handed over to a certain magistrate, who, after dark confinement and deprivation of food, had her, as she persevered in the confession of Christ, raised upon the torture-horse, then finally taken down and thrown into a sewer. On the same day, of Saint Fandila, priest, who received martyrdom at the city of Córdoba by decapitation.

XVIII Kalends. Day 14. [Note: [Col. 0151B]

Thus have Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, the first edition of Belin, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0151C]

The remaining manuscripts have *Helisei*, as Pratensis and the others do, although Heriniensis, Tornacensis, and Antwerp-Major lack the aspiration; no manuscript reads *Elizaei*. They all have *Palestinae*, and we have often said enough elsewhere about that place and Jerome. The most approved manuscripts uniformly write *situs est* (“is situated”); Molanus has *positus est* (“is placed”); the middle-quality manuscripts have *conditus est* (“is buried”). In Antwerp-Major, after Abdias, *propheta* (“prophet”) is missing; and in Molanus, instead of *quiescit* (“rests”), there is *requiescit* (“rests”). I say nothing further about Caesarea and Cappadocia. The first edition of Belin places the final announcement before the penultimate one; the second, fuller edition will be evident in the *Auctaria*. Antwerp-Major has *Rufi* instead of *Rufini*. Tornacensis, after *Valerii*, omitted *qui*, leaving the sense incomplete. All manuscripts read *Quintiani*; only Rosweyd has *Quintiniani*. Here, however, both Antwerp-Major and this text add the title “martyr”; all the others have only “confessor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0151C]

Bede was the first to introduce Elisha into the Latin calendars; he was content with the name alone, and Rabanus followed him. The author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* likewise read it so—perhaps that work is older than Bede—from which Ado certainly took it, expanding it with several details from Saint Jerome, while our author has compressed the material very briefly, reporting almost only the burials of Elisha [Col. 0151D] and Obadiah. In our text the second place belongs to the great Basil, whose birthday is explicitly recorded by the first person to adorn him with an elogium, Ado of Vienne, who evidently took it from the *Little Roman Martyrology*. The one who most diligently and accurately illustrated Basil’s *Acts*, our colleague Baertius, did not notice that his memory had first been entered into a martyrology there. [Col. 0152C] These are the words of the *Little Roman Martyrology*: “In Cappadocia, of Saint Basil, brother of Gregory and Peter.” Our author elegantly abridged Ado’s elogium in his customary fashion, preserving the formula of the birthday, which I find reported concordantly in most of the better manuscripts; concerning the ordination, there is not a word anywhere. I readily admit that learned men assign his death to the Kalends of January, on which day we too commemorated his memory with Usuard. But why the present festival could not equally well refer to the elevation or translation of his body, as some manuscripts suggest, or to some other cause, as well as to an ordination, I would willingly be taught, since a commemoration of his ordination is unknown in the older martyrologies [Col. 0152D] and so rare even in the more recent ones; moreover, it is established elsewhere that the word “ordination” first entered the modern Roman Martyrology toward the end of the sixteenth century. Perhaps an opportunity will arise elsewhere to discuss the matter more carefully; for now, it is enough to have shown the first origin and subsequent development of today’s festival. In Ado, Rufinus and Valerius are placed second, without an elogium, just as Rabanus announces them. But Florus explains their martyrdom more fully; our author shows that he had seen the *Acts*, since he drew only a very small amount from them. I would believe, however, that Ado and Rabanus first extracted the account of these martyrs from Hieronymian copies, in some of which they are added. Sirmondus once judged their history to be reliable and by no means doubtful. That it was also highly esteemed by Henschenius is clear from his commentary for this day. Certainly, all must acknowledge that it is venerable for its antiquity. Tillemont gave a summary of the deeds in volume IV, p. 459; but on p. 718 he expressly explains that those *Acts* ought not to be trusted. [Col. 0153B] Let the learned reader decide which of them judged better. Wandalbertus sings of Elisha with Rufinus and Valerius:

“On the eighth of July and the tenth before the beginning of the month,

[Col. 0154A] the prophet Elisha, together with Obadiah, shines forth;

here too he rejoices in the martyr Valerius and Rufinus.”

Quintianus, who occupies the last place, does not derive from Jerome, where he is marked as a martyr with companions, but was first brought forward by Usuard, I do not know from where, and substituted for Etherius, bishop of Vienne, whom Ado had noted; Usuard, as he often did, passed over the Viennese saint. Moreover, that Quintianus is commemorated as a priest and confessor, not as a bishop, seems to have been overlooked by the person who produced the more expansive 1608 edition of the modern Roman Martyrology, defended by Baronius in his notes. Henschenius rejects as his namesake a bishop of Rodez, assigning him to 13 November, on which day he is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology as a bishop of Clermont, the same man who had earlier been bishop of Rodez; Gregory of Tours mentions him in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 4, as we shall say in its proper place.
