Our genuine Bede deals with the translation of Saint Anianus, etc.; this is included in many *Auctaria*, indeed in Hieronymian copies, which makes one doubt whether it truly belongs to Bede, since Rabanus is silent about it. But the complete Usuardine reading is established with the greatest consistency by manuscripts of very different kinds.]

[Note: [Col. 0153B]

PULSANENSIS: “Of Elisha the prophet. And of Saint Felicula.” See the preceding day. “In the city of Orléans, the translation of the body of Blessed Anianus, bishop and confessor, and the liberation of that city [from] the Huns.” His birthday is 17 November. “Likewise, in the city of Soissons, the passion of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Valerius.”

ANTWERP and MAXIMUM-LÜBECK, omitting Quintianus, substitute: “At Orléans, the translation of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor.” Codex UGELLIAN agrees with them, as often elsewhere.

MUNERATUS, in second place: “At Orléans, of Saint Anianus, confessor and bishop.” The rest is pure.

[Col. 0153C] GREVEN, in third place: “At Orléans, of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor.” The remainder is extremely pure.

ANTWERP-MAJOR, concerning Basil, adds at the end of the elogium: “This same saint is also celebrated on the day of the Circumcision itself,” as has been sufficiently explained in the Observation. The final announcement is missing.

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, and the BELGIAN UTRECHT EDITION have a sufficiently pure text up to “Quintianus,” which they lack, like the preceding witnesses.

ALBERG and DANIC deal with Elisha and the people of Soissons. The rest is absent. They dealt with Basil on 1 January.

CENTULENSIS: “Of Elisha the prophet, who is buried at Samaria in Palestine, where the prophet Obadiah also rests. At Caesarea of Cappadocia, of Saint Basil, archbishop and confessor. In the territory of Soissons, the passion of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Valerius under Rictiovarus. At Orléans, the translation of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor.”

BRUSSELS: “At Caesarea of Cappadocia, the elevation [Col. 0153D] of Blessed and Great Basil, bishop and confessor, brother of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus (of Nyssa) and Peter. When Christ appeared to him with his apostles, he taught him the ministry of the Mass; and through Basil’s prayers Ephrem the Syrian spoke Greek. He also learned by revelation of the death of Julian the Apostate, who, when he went to war against Persia, had threatened that on his return he would destroy Caesarea. This great Basil, distinguished in wisdom and learning and established in every virtue, after shining wondrously in the Church of God, fell asleep in Christ on the Kalends of January. His feast is celebrated on this day of his elevation. On the same day, of the prophet Elisha, who was buried at Samaria in Palestine, which later began to be called Sebaste; there the prophet Obadiah also rests, as does Saint John the Baptist.” The account of Rufinus and Valerius is pure. It continues: “At the city of Mesana-Dorostorum, of Saint Julius, martyr, who received the palm of martyrdom under the governor Maximus.” He is commemorated on 27 May, where these matters are expressed more elegantly. “In Africa, of the holy priests and martyrs Gallianus and Bitunus.” The first is Ephesian; concerning the other, see the *Praetermissi*. “In Aquileia, the birthday of Saint Prothus, martyr.” This indicates Prothus, the tutor of the Cantiani, concerning whom see 31 May. “On that same day, the birthday of the holy martyrs Afrus and Quintianus, priests.” He perhaps intended to say Afra. “At Vienne, of Saint Eucherius, bishop and confessor.” He changes the names; he intended to say Etherius. “Likewise, of Saint Ignatius, bishop.” Is this the Ignatius of Constantinople, commemorated on 23 October? Concerning Anianus, see above. At the end: “Likewise, of Tecla, virgin.” [Col. 0154C] He perhaps indicates the martyr, namely, Quintianus’s companion.

HAGENOYEN: “The burial of Elisha the prophet, at whose birth a golden heifer gave a lowing that could be heard in Jerusalem. He was anointed prophet by the prophet Elijah, and thereafter always adhered to him. He also saw Elijah carried into heaven and divided the Jordan with Elijah’s cloak; he performed many miracles and raised two dead persons. He anointed the kings of Israel and Syria and prophesied their good and evil deeds. Then at Samaria,” etc. He cuts short Basil’s elogium; the account of Rufinus and Valerius is pure. “On the same day, the birthday of the most wonderful Blessed Brendan, abbot and pilgrim upon the sea. He was Irish by nationality.” He is commemorated on 16 May. “On that same day, the translation of Saint Quincianus, priest and confessor. On the same day, the burial of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor of Orléans.” Here there should be “translation” in the case of Quincianus, and “burial” in the case of Anianus. It continues: “On that same day, the ordination of Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra.” In the LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION and GREVEN, this ordination is assigned to 16 June. Which manuscripts are more correct need not be examined here, but on 6 December.

AQUICINCT has “priest and martyr” concerning Quintianus; but several Quintiani are listed in the *Acts* on this day. It then adds: “At Orléans, the translation of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor.” Codex BIGOTIAN also has this under its note, p. 5.

VICTORINUS and the SWEDISH REGISTER, under number 130, at the end: “In the city of Orléans, the translation of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor, and the liberation of the city itself.” See PULSANENSIS above. “Near Aquileia, of the holy martyrs Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla.” Concerning them, see 31 May.

DAVERON: “At Orléans, the translation of Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor, and the dedication of Saint Saviour of Carrosses.” If the dedication pertains to Anianus, it will be discussed on his birthday, 17 December, to which we always refer similar matters.

MATRIC-CARTUS-UTRECHT: “Of Rufinus and Valerius, martyrs. Of Basil, bishop of Caesarea. Of Elisha the prophet at Samaria. Of Quintianus, priest.”

In the VATICAN manuscript, no. 5949, “Elisha, Basil, Quintianus” is missing. Added is: “At Benevento, of Saint Marcianus, bishop and confessor.”

ALTEMPS: “On that same day, of Quintianus, priest and martyr.” The text is better with “confessor.”

FLORENTINIUS: “On that same day, of the holy martyrs Afrius, Prothus, and Quintianus.” See the African martyrs. Concerning Anianus, see PULSANENSIS. “Likewise, of Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr of Constantinople,” concerning whom see above. “In the city of Pagia, of Saint Autheonis and Saint Ludidia.” See the *Acts* for Antheon. “At Ephesus, of Magginus, Gastinus, and Vivianus. In Africa, of Afra, Quintianus, Theodulus, Theda, Festina, and Quintianilla.” See the more accurate forms of these martyrs’ names in the *Acts*.

[Col. 0155B] MONTIS SION: “In the city of Orléans, the translation of the body of Blessed Anianus, confessor and bishop.”

REIMS, SAINTS TIMOTHY AND APOLLINARIS: “At Reims, the translation of the body of Saint Rigobert, bishop and confessor.” He is commemorated on 4 January.

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION interpolates the account of Elisha. It then proceeds purely concerning Valerius, etc. Then: “At Caesarea of Cappadocia, the translation of Saint Basil, bishop and confessor. In the city of Soissons, of Saint Aristio, confessor.” See the *Praetermissi*. “At Vienne, of Saint Eucherius (Etherius), bishop and confessor. On the same [Col. 0156A] day, of Saint Quincianus, priest, and Siccius, confessors. At Orléans, the translation of Saint Anianus,” etc. The second edition of BELIN also has this.

GREVEN. Note: “On this day Saint Basil was translated; on the Kalends of January he died. Likewise, of Antheon, Galanus, and Jovinus, Theodulus, Afrus, and Prothus.” See the *Acts*. “At Vienne, of Etherius, bishop and confessor. Of Gregory, bishop and confessor.” Who this is is unknown. “Of Berthold, confessor.” Perhaps this is the one commemorated on 16 June. “At Soissons, of Saint Aristio, confessor.” Concerning him, see the index of the *Praetermissi*. “At Toul, the translation of Saint Mansuetus, bishop and confessor.” He is commemorated on 3 September. “Of blessed memory, Basil, prior of the Great Charterhouse, who, eighth in succession after Saint Bruno, governed that house for twenty-three years and, shining with miracles, fell asleep in the Lord.” See the *Praetermissi*.

MOLANUS, in later editions: “At Vienne, of Saint Etherius, bishop. At Syracuse, of Saint Martianus, [Col. 0156B] bishop, who, sent by the Apostle, converted there Seleucus, Gordius, and a great multitude. On the fourteenth day, of the holy father Methodius, patriarch of Constantinople.” Then, in smaller type: “At Orléans, the translation of Saints Anianus, Monitor, and Flosculus, bishops of that city; of Euspius, first abbot of Micy; of Baudelus and Scubilius, martyrs; and of Agia, mother of Saint Lupus, bishop; and the liberation of the city from the Huns through Saint Anianus, bishop.” In the *Praetermissi* each of them is assigned to his own proper birthday.]

[Col. 0151]

Of Elisha the prophet, who, as Blessed Jerome writes, is buried at Samaria in Palestine, where the prophet Obadiah also rests. At Caesarea of Cappadocia, the birthday of Saint Basil, bishop, who in the time of Valens, distinguished in learning and wisdom and established in every virtue, shone forth wondrously. In the territory of the city of Soissons, of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Valerius, who, after the governor Rictiovarus had inflicted torments upon them, were ordered to be decapitated. On that same day, of Saint Quintianus, priest and confessor.

XVII Kalends. Day 15. [Note: [Col. 0155]

The texts of Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp, Maximum-Lübeck, Muneratus, Belinus, Greven, and Molanus are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0155C]

The sense requires “of Saints Vitus, etc.”: Greven and Molanus alone have the singular “of Saint Vitus, etc.” Thus the conjunction *et* between Vitus and Modestus is superfluous, though Tornacensis, Antwerp, Maximum-Lübeck, Muneratus, and Belinus add it; the last reads “of Vitus and Modestus and Crescentia.” We have often and sufficiently discussed Moesia. It was not through divine inspiration that the Heriniensis manuscript wrote “At the city of Mesia, Dorostorum.” *Messia*, *Messina*, and *Dorostrum* are corruptions of Belinus. Likewise, it has *Exitii* instead of *Esichii*. Muneratus seems to have wished to display excessive learning when he changed *militaris*, as the *Little Roman Martyrology*, Ado, and Usuard consistently read it, into “soldier and martyr.” The same Muneratus, together with Belinus, wrote *Maximiano* instead of *Maximo*. I do not know whether they intended to correct Usuard from Ado; certainly both editions of Ado read it that way, while all our other manuscripts agree with the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0155D]

All the Latin Martyrologists commonly celebrate the noble triad of Sicilian martyrs. Jerome especially does so; in his copies the only variation is that the final name is improperly given in the masculine gender in one or another manuscript, *Crescentius* or *Crescentianus*. Bede, surprisingly, mentions only Vitus; but Florus, restoring his companions, adorns all of them with a respectable elogium. Rabanus also seems to deal only with Vitus, although in the course of his longer account he does not omit the companions. Let us now approach our sources more closely. The *Little Roman Martyrology* says: “In Sicily, of Modestus, Vitus, and Crescentia, martyrs.” Ado, restoring the original order of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, gives an excellent epitome of whatever kind of *Acts* they may be; Florentinius praised it, Papebrochius quoted it, and our author most elegantly constructed his own encomium from it in a more concise form. Florentinius reviews several modern opinions concerning the arena in which the martyrs fought, attempting to reconcile the Lucanian accounts with the Sicilian ones; some matters concerning these are also clarified in Papebrochius’s Commentary, to which we gladly refer more inquisitive investigators of such questions. For the present matter, we know that the older and more approved Martyrologists, without any mention of Lucania, unanimously assign these champions to Sicily. As for the *Acts* of Vitus and his companions, they are scarcely tolerated by modern writers, as may be seen in Tillemont, volume V, p. 129. We approve Papebrochius’s judgment concerning them: namely, that the widespread cult of these martyrs is in no way doubtful, however doubtful the circumstances of their martyrdom may be. Indeed, their cult is also established with the greatest consistency by the Sacramentaries cited by Tillemont. Papebrochius collected and carefully examined the records concerning their burial and their various translations. There remains Wandalbertus’s metrical song, in which I confess that I do not know what Margarita is doing, unless she has been improperly transferred here from 20 July. Hear the poet:

“On the seventeenth, Vitus with the illustrious virgin,

Margarita, shines with the splendor of martyrdom;

and Modestus and the gracious virgin Crescentia shine likewise.”

Now the man whom we, with Usuard, call Esichius is called *Isicus*, *Isicius*, *Ysicius*, etc., in the Hieronymian copies; in the *Little Roman Martyrology* he is called *Esychius*, as also in Rosweyd’s Ado, which, as we said, substituted *Maximianus* for *Maximus. Apart from that word, our author transferred each of Ado’s words most clearly into his own calendar. [Col. 0158A] This is Esichius, or Esychius, of whom we have already spoken above, on 25 and 27 May, from the *Acts of Saint Julius*, where the whole account that can be reported about him is found in Ado’s elogium. In the Pratensis manuscript, after the Sicilians, a Beneventan martyr has been inserted in these words: “In the city of Benevento, of Saint Mercury, martyr.” Two other manuscripts frequently agree with it, namely Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, together with the Aquicinct collation. But Castellanus detected that this was an obvious addition, written above an erasure of other words, and all our remaining manuscripts sufficiently prove it. Castellanus notes that the erasure on the parchment begins at the word “emperor,” from which one may suspect that the interpolator used smaller writing so that he would have enough space to insert Mercury. Moreover, our copy adds at the end—by my judgment, in the margin of the supposed autograph—“At Rome, of Saint Alexius, man of God.” Since this announcement is unknown to the manuscripts of better quality, we consider it just as certain that it does not belong to Usuard as it is certain that the text we have reported is genuinely and completely Usuardine.]

[Note: [Col. 0157B]

PRATENSIS. We have just discussed the two *Auctaria* of this manuscript. Mercury is commemorated on 25 October.

ANTWERP-MAJOR has the same account of Mercury in the same place; but at the end it adds: “On that same day, of Saint Eadburga, virgin.” See the *Acts*. In other sources she is called Eadburga.

ROSWEYD agrees completely with this, differing only in writing, as we have already said: “On that same day, of Saint Eadburga, virgin.”

PULSANENSIS: “In the province of Lucania, the passion of the holy martyrs Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia. Likewise at Dorostorum, the birthday of Saint Ysichius, martyr. Near Aquileia, of the holy martyrs Cantius, Proticius, Clemens, and Cantianus.” See the entire group more accurately distinguished in the *Acts*.

ANTWERP-MAJOR, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERG, DANIC, and the BELGIAN UTRECHT EDITION append to the pure text: “On the same day, in the territory of Valenciennes, at the monastery of Crispinus, the burial of Saint Landelinus, abbot and confessor, who was lifted from the sacred font by Saint Autbertus, bishop of Cambrai.” [Col. 0157C]

CENTULENSIS: “Near Sicily, of Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia, under Diocletian. On the same day, at the city of Dorostorum in Moesia, of Saint Esichius the soldier, who, having been arrested with Blessed Julius, was crowned with martyrdom.” It is scarcely removed from purity.

BRUSSELS, after a fairly pure text, adds: “In the city of Benevento, of Saint Mercury, martyr. Likewise, of Saint Eadburga, virgin. In the territory of Valenciennes, at the monastery of Crispinus, the burial of Saint Landelinus, abbot and confessor, who, having been converted from a robber to Christ by Blessed Autbertus, bishop of Cambrai, founded three monasteries.”

HAGENOYEN has the following: “In Sicily, the birthday of the holy martyrs Vitus the boy, Modestus his tutor, and Crescentia. Under the emperor Diocletian, after he had healed the emperor’s daughter, after the boiling lead cauldron, after the beasts and the torture-racks had been overcome by divine power, and after they had been rescued by an angel, they asked the Lord that their souls might be taken away in peace, and immediately their souls, like white [perhaps, doves], were seen to ascend to heaven.” The account of Esichius is nearly pure. Concerning Landelinus it repeats what we described above from ANTWERP-MAJOR and others. But concerning these matters, the two *Lives* of that saint, illustrated by Henschenius in the *Acts*, should be consulted; in the preliminary Commentary he carefully explains many matters concerning the translations of the body or its parts to various places, controversies about which remain and will also be touched upon elsewhere.

AQUICINCT, in second place, inserts, as we said: “In the city of Benevento, of Saint Mercury, martyr.”

VICTORINUS, after a pure text concerning Vitus, Modestus, [Col. 0158B] etc., adds at the end: “On the same day, the birthday of Saint Vitus, martyr.” He apparently believed that this was a different person.

MATRIC-CARTUS-ULTRAJECT. “Of the martyrs Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia. Of Landelinus the abbot. Of Hesychius the soldier and Julius the martyr.” Julius was treated on 27 May.

The BIGOTIAN CODEX, marked D. 9: “At Fécamp, the dedication of the church of the Holy Trinity.”

CAMBERIEN. “At Orléans, Saint Anianus the confessor.” See the preceding day.

REG. SUEC., under entry no. 130: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Vitus the martyr.” As in VICTORIN above.

FLORENTIN. Many things are again gathered here: “At Benevento, Saint Mercurius the martyr. At Aquileia, the holy martyrs Cantianus, Crotus, Clement, and the other Cantianus. At Constantinople, the holy martyrs Mitius, Migettus, and Minginus. [Col. 0158C] In Barbaria, the holy martyrs Gaianus, Jovianus, and Philip. In Lucania, the holy martyrs Nivitius, Candidus, Cantianus and Cantianilla, Prothierus, Singon, Artheon, Quintianus, and Theodolus. In Scythia, the holy martyrs Marcus, Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia.” These have the character of the Hieronymian Martyrologies; but they are corrupt and confused in a remarkable way, almost as though deliberately. You will find them expressed more distinctly in the Acts.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. changes the beginning as follows: “In Sicily, the feast of the holy Vitus the boy, Modestus, and Crescentia, his foster-parents. Who, under Diocletian,” etc. The remainder of the text is fairly pure. At the end: “On the same day, blessed Eadburga the virgin.”

GREVEN. “In Lucania, the holy Candidus, Crotus, and Chrysogonus. See the Acts. At Benevento, Mercurius the martyr.” I said above that he is venerated on 25 October. “Landelinus the abbot and confessor. In England, Eadburga the virgin.”

MOLAN. “On the same day, in the territory of Valenciennes, at the monastery of Crispin, the deposition of Saint Landelinus, confessor of Christ and abbot, who was lifted from the sacred font by Saint Autbert, bishop of Cambrai. On the same day, Saint Eadburga at the city of Winton.” I think this means Winchester. Then, in smaller type: “At Clermont, Abraham the confessor, whose life Gregory of Tours wrote.” Other editions have it thus: “At Clermont, Saint Abraham the confessor.” Concerning Eadburga, see above. “In the territory of Valenciennes, in the village called Crispin, on the river Hon, the passing of the most holy and blessed father Landelinus. He was instructed by blessed Autbert, but later, deceived by the persuasion of wicked men, abandoned the way of truth. Afterwards, terrified by his prayers and by an angelic visitation, he was recalled; and, receiving from Saint Martin the pope the office of preaching and effectively compelling others, he became the founder of many monasteries and rested in peace. Likewise on the same day, the translation of the body of that same Saint Landelinus by Godefridus, bishop of Cambrai. At Huy, the translation of Saint Domitianus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the translation of blessed Mengoldus, [Col. 0160A] duke and martyr.” See concerning both in the Index of the Saints Omitted. At the end, in smaller type: “In Cilicia, Saint Dulas the martyr.” This is “Tatianus Dulas,” whose Greek-Latin Acts we have published. Henschenius judged them thoroughly genuine, and did not consider the difficulties raised by Tillemont, volume V, p. 622, worth pursuing.]

[Col. 0155]

In Sicily, the feast of the holy Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia, who, under the emperor Diocletian, after the cauldron of boiling lead and after overcoming the beasts and the torture-racks by divine power, completed the course of their glorious contest [Bouillart inserts: [Note: [Col. 0155C] Concerning the mention of Saint Mercurius, which Sollerius asserts was introduced by Pratensis from the silence and erasure of his manuscripts, I appeal from his judgment to sound eyes. If they suspect even the slightest difference in the writing, I will not say that they do not immediately judge that it was written over the original. It is true that it was added, but by Usuardus; whence it was taken is unclear. We once possessed the Acts of that martyr, if indeed they are recorded in the index of our manuscript codices under no. 461. But I could not find them. Perhaps the person to whom they had been lent did not return them; perhaps they were even stolen. As for Alexius, added in the margin, there is no reason for it to provoke a dispute with the Pratensis codex, since there is no Martyrology, at least among those formerly in use, that is not stuffed with additions of this sort. And why should that be surprising? Would it have been necessary to copy an entire volume whenever some saint was added to the Fasti? BOUILLART.] At Benevento, Saint Mercurius the martyr.] At Dorostorum, a city in Moesia, Saint Esychius the soldier, who was arrested together with blessed Julius and was later crowned with martyrdom under the governor Maximus.

XVI Kal. The 16th day. [Note: [Col. 0159]

The following manuscripts support the text: Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Belin., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0159B]

Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Major, and Molan. correctly write *Vesuntionem*. In the Pratensis this is *Vezuntionem*; in Greven., *Vesuncionem*; and, worse, in Belin., *Vescentionensem*. Only Tornacen. has *Fereoli*; several go wrong in the second name: Antuerp.-Maj. has *Ferruntionis*; Belin., *Ferutionis*; Greven., *Ferrucionis*. Molanus, generally correcting the orthography, rightly put *Irenaeo*; the others have the form found in the text, including those who use diphthongs, especially Pratensis and Herinien. With these I wrote *poenis*. Belin. reads *postea vero et cruciati* instead of *excruciati*. *Cyrici* occurs everywhere except in Antuerp.-Maj., which, together with the others, also writes *Tulitae*; the form in the text, supported by the ancient martyrologies, is better. I collect the remaining errors of Antuerp.-Major: *graviora* for *gravia*, *Lugdunis*, *Nammetis*, *Smiriani*. Ado reads *Nannetis*, but our best manuscripts have *Namnetis*, Tornacen. *Nampnetis*, not *Nanetis*, as Belinus does.]

[Note: [Col. 0159A]

We believe that whatever is placed in our text on this day was taken from Ado, although the order has not been preserved everywhere; for in him the people of Rutochium are placed before the Bisuntines, and Similianus before Aurelianus. I think the reason for this alteration is wholly arbitrary. Bede is the first to commemorate the martyrs of Besançon on this day; from him Ado took the principal part of his eulogy, prefacing it only with those details concerning the mission of Irenaeus and the place of the contest that were lacking in Bede. Rabanus seems to have wished to add the arena. Our author, keeping Ado before his eyes, selected what would not exceed the customary brevity. These details were received from the Acts of the martyrs themselves, which are older than Gregory of Tours. Concerning their faithfulness and truthfulness, the same questions are disputed as those which we briefly mentioned on 23 April regarding the Acts of the other three disciples of Irenaeus. Later writers do not entirely deny that they are serious and simple, but nevertheless do not regard them as sufficiently sincere for Ruinart to include them among his selected texts. The venerable memory of Ferreolus and Ferrutio survives in the Gothic Missal, or ancient Gallican Missal, published by Thomasius, p. 359. Florentinius thinks that their names were added to the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 5 September, on which day their discovery, rather than their translation, is celebrated. Those who assign companions to them generally consider them to be none other than the three Valentinians—Felix, Fortunatus, and Achilleus. Wandalbertus also records the present saints on the date just mentioned, 5 September:

“On the Nones, Ferreolus shines together with Ferrutio.”

Nevertheless, the authority of the ancient martyrologists and of our author remains intact up to this point. The case is different with Cyricus, or Quiricus, and Julitta, whom the Hieronymian copies and the Small Roman Martyrology most explicitly assign to Antioch, together with four hundred and four companions. Ado agrees with them completely as to the location, and Usuardus follows him. Florus speaks in the same sense; his eulogy agrees here and there with Ado’s, although I in no way believe that Florus knew Ado. Both certainly had before them the Acts, which had long ago been rejected as apocryphal. Our author rendered Ado’s eulogy in a more contracted form, omitting the companions whom Florus multiplied to 404. These things could appear clear and certain from the venerable testimony of the aforesaid martyrologists, were it not that very weighty considerations advise changing the place of the contest and writing “at Tarsus” instead of “at Antioch,” as in the modern Roman Martyrology. Papebrochius considers the reformers to have acted correctly, explaining the difficulty at greater length on this day. He plausibly doubles the martyrs who may bear the same names, supposing that one Cyricus with Julitta may be assigned to Antioch, and another Cyricus with another Julitta to Tarsus, unless one prefers the alternatives suggested there with considerable probability. If these arguments are insufficient for anyone, let him consult Florentinius, who weighs similar considerations with adequate care. Setting aside such intricacies, let the reader see in our Acts the notable Greek-Latin account by Theodore of Iconium concerning the contest of these most illustrious martyrs. From the hands of the faithful that account should have displaced the famous condemned apocryphal narrative, which nevertheless persisted for so many centuries in certain legendary collections and can also be read in the cited Acts. Ruinart prints that very letter of Theodore, beginning at p. 527. Tillemont gives a brief account of all this in French, volume V, beginning at p. 349. Add to these Wandalbertus’s couplet:

“On the sixteenth, Cyricus with his mother Julitta  
Shines through the piety and faith of Christ.”

Meanwhile, what belongs to our field and duty we have now completed, and we continue with the two final announcements, which our author copied almost word for word from Ado, leaving them entirely untouched by the older martyrologies, except that Similianus may have been added under the name Similinus to certain Hieronymian copies, perhaps from Gregory of Tours. In the meantime, what we said at the beginning is entirely true: Usuardus borrowed all his material from Ado. Concerning these two final saints of ours, see what Henschenius and Papebrochius report in their historical collections. You will scarcely find more elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0159D]

PULSANEN.: “At the city of Besançon, the blessed martyrs Ferreolus the priest and Ferrutio the deacon. They were stretched on the rack and scourged under the judge Claudius; then they were shut up in prison, and, after their tongues had been cut out, they preached the word of the Lord. Afterwards awls were driven into both of them in their hands, feet, and chest; finally, after being struck with the sword, they died.” This is from Bede or Ado. Everything else is absent.

ROSWEYD. adds after the pure text: “At Mainz, the holy martyrs Aureus and Justina.” Their Acts have been illustrated at considerable length.

ANTUERP. MAX-LUBEC. and MUNERAT. lack the final announcement concerning Saint Similianus.

ANTUERP. MAX. ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., LOVAN., EDIT., and ULTRAJ.-BELG. have the Bisuntines almost as PULSANEN.; namely, after “under the judge Claudius,” they insert: “They were stretched on the wheel and scourged, then thrust into prison; after their tongues had been cut out, they preached the word of God. Afterwards thirty awls were driven into their hands, feet, and chest, and finally they were struck with the sword.” In the Antiochene and Aurelian entries they are pure. But, omitting Similianus, they substitute: “At Mainz, the holy martyrs Aureus, bishop of that place, and Justina, his sister.”

ALBERG and DANIC. have the same material concerning the Bisuntines, but defer the Antiochene martyrs to 15 July. In the rest they agree with the immediately preceding witnesses. DANIC., however, has its own distinctive addition concerning a popular saint: [Col. 0161B] “On the same day in Dacia, in the province of Zeeland, Saint William the abbot, famous for his life and miracles.” He is celebrated on 6 April.

CENTULEN.: At Antioch, the holy martyrs Cyricus and Julitta, his mother, and 404 others who suffered with them. At the city of Vesontio, the holy martyrs Ferreolus the priest and Ferrutio the deacon. At the city of Nantes, Saint Similianus, bishop and confessor.

BRUXELLEN. begins with Cyricus and Julitta, in words drawn almost entirely from Ado: “At Antioch, the holy martyrs Cyricus and Julitta, his mother. The former received lime mixed with vinegar and mustard into his mouth; then they were fastened together with nails, and, after their eyes had been torn out, they were scalped and flayed, roasted upon burning coals on a bronze bed; then mangled with iron instruments, and, after their tongues had been cut out and suffered grievous tortures, they completed the course of their martyrdom by decapitation, together with 404 others.” The account of the Bisuntines is almost as above. [Col. 0161C] It continues: “On the same day, the feast of Saints Diogenes and Saturninus.” I think the African Diogenes has been joined with the Sicilian one. “At Mainz, the holy martyrs Aureus, bishop of that same place, and Justina, his sister.” As the middle-class manuscripts above have it. Then follows Similianus. Afterwards the Aurelian entry is pure. At the end: “At Vienne, Saint Domnolus, bishop and confessor.” He appears in the Acts.

HAGENOYEN. has the same account of the Bisuntines as ANTUERP.-MAX., etc., above. In second place: “At Mainz,” etc., as above. In the Antiochene martyrs the text is slightly interpolated; in the Aurelian and Similian entries it is fairly pure. Then: “Likewise in England [read: in Denmark], Saint William the abbot.” Concerning him, see above under DANIC. “In France, Roland the duke and martyr.” This indicates Roland; see concerning him in the Saints Omitted.

MATRIC-CARTUS-ULTRAJEC.: “Cyricus and Julitta, martyrs. Ferreolus the priest and Ferrutio the deacon, martyrs. Aurelianus, bishop and confessor. And Saint Similianus.”

CAMBERIEN.: “On the same day, Saint Verolus the confessor.” Concerning him, see the following day. “And Saint Justina the virgin.” Is this the Mainz Justina, or another?

CODEX D. LE MARE, under entry A: “On the same day, Saint Quintianus the priest and martyr.” Perhaps this is the one mentioned on the 14th of this month. “The deposition of Saint Flavianus.” If this concerns the man of Autun, he is celebrated on 23 August.

In VATICAN., no. 5949, “Aurelianus” is absent. In UGELLIAN., Similianus is absent.

[Col. 0162A] FLORENTIN.: “At Antioch, the holy martyrs Domestus, Crescentius, and Julius with four hundred soldiers.” See the Saints Omitted. “On the same day, Saints Diogenes and Saturninus.” Concerning them, see above.

BIZUNTICEN. S. Pauli and SALINENSIS of the Franciscans: “In the territory of Langres, Saint Verolus the priest and confessor.” Here *Veroli* is correctly written, but we have already said that he is celebrated on the following day.

In the CODEX OF THE ABBEY OF GOLL: “At Lyons, the deposition of blessed Aurelius, bishop of Arles.” Read *Aurelianus*, as it is found above in the text.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. adds nothing new concerning the Bisuntines. In second place, it gives the Aurelian entry in a pure form. The Antiochene entry is heavily interpolated. It then follows with Aureus and Justina, Similianus, William, Domnolus of Vienne, as above. “On the same day, the translation of Saint Richard, bishop and confessor.” Concerning the same man, see 3 April. “On the same day, the ordination of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor.” See 6 December, when his entire life will be illustrated.

GREVEN. “Roland, count of Maine, and his companions, including Oliver, who were killed by the unbelievers in the time of Charlemagne.” See above. “The 404 martyrs who suffered, according to Ado, with Saints Cyricus and Julitta. At Mainz, the holy martyrs Aureus,” etc. Concerning Domnolus, see above. “Papponius, archbishop of Trier and confessor.” He is omitted. “At Metz, Leguntius and Strominius, bishops and confessors.” See the Saints Omitted. “The translation of Saint Richarius, bishop. In Dacia, the translation of Saint William the abbot.” Concerning him, see above. “Meander the confessor. Is this Nicander?” But the latter is a martyr on the following day. “Lutgardis the virgin. The ordination of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor.”

MOLAN.: “And at the city of Mainz, the passion of Saints Aureus and Justina, his sister, who were killed in a church by the Huns while they were devastating Germany.” This is taken from Rabanus. Then, in smaller type, concerning Roland and Oliver, as in GREVEN. Likewise concerning William. Finally: “At Aquiria, a monastery of Brabant, Saint Lutgardis died, a virgin of great devotion, whose life Thomas of Cantimpré wrote.” Later editions insert the following in italics within the text concerning the Antiochene martyrs: “Four hundred and four others suffered with them.” At the end, concerning Aureus and Justina, as above. “On the sixteenth day, Saint Tycho of Amathus, illustrious for his miracles. At Eischel, in the diocese of Constance, the elevation of the holy virgins Cunegundis, Mechtundis, and Vuibrandis. At Bergues, the translation of Saint Lewinna the virgin and martyr.” Her feast is 22 July. “At the monastery of Sithiu, the discovery of the precious body of Saint Bertinus, which was found beneath the head of the altar of Saint Martin, where it had formerly been translated and concealed by blessed Folquinus in the year 846. It had lain there for about 206 years, after having first rested in its tomb for 149 years.” It continues, in smaller type: “In Gaul, Roland, count of Maine, Oliver, and their companions, who, fighting for Christ near Pamplona beneath the Pyrenean mountains, fell while Charlemagne was emperor. At the monastery of Aquiria in Brabant, Lutgardis, an abbess and virgin of great devotion, died.” Matters concerning her cult, life, age, and so forth have been carefully elucidated in the Acts.]

[Col. 0159]

In Gaul, at the city of Vesontio, the holy martyrs Ferreolus the priest and Ferrutio the deacon, who were sent by blessed Irenaeus the bishop to preach the word of God and were later tortured with punishments under the judge Claudius and struck down with the sword. At Antioch, the feast of the holy martyrs Cyricus and Julitta, his mother, who, after dreadful blows and grievous tortures, completed the course of their martyrdom by decapitation. At Lyons, the deposition of blessed Aurelianus, bishop of Arles. At the city of Nantes, Saint Similianus, bishop and confessor.

XV Kal. The 17th day. [Note: [Col. 0163A]

The following manuscripts plainly report this form: Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerpien., Max-Lubec., Munerat., the first edition of Belin, and the later editions of Greven and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0163A]

This is almost entirely reduced to scribal or typographical errors. Thus Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. have *vetere* instead of *veteri*. Munerat. has *politi* instead of *positi*; [Col. 0164A] *divum* instead of *clivum*, where Belin has *clivium*. Again, Belin has *Vulmarii*, while Munerat. reads *ammirandae* and *et* instead of *presbyteri et confessoris*, and reads “abbot and confessor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0163A]

This is the sole and only announcement of the Small Roman Martyrology for this day: “At Rome, 262 martyrs.” The remaining words of our text are from Ado. I find nowhere what else can be said about them, unless they are judged to be the same men who, condemned while digging the arena, 260 in number, were killed by arrows in the amphitheater of the city and buried by Saints Marius and Martha—concerning whom, see 20 January—in a crypt on the Salarian Way, near the Cucumber Hill. Henschenius and Papebrochius believed this, joining in their historical collection other martyrs mentioned in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on this day; but one may rightly doubt whether those martyrs have any connection of place or time with these 262. Yet amid such great obscurity of matters, I do not see that we should depart from the opinions of our predecessors until more light comes from elsewhere. Whether Wandalbertus provides such light, you may judge from his verses:

“On the fifteenth, seven and fifty and two hundred  
Send a joyful crown of martyrs to the stars.”

To establish further the genuine, Usuardine, and primitive simplicity of our text, not only the manuscripts already cited, which are pure throughout, but nearly all the others, however much expanded, agree—except those that habitually agree with Pratensis outside the order of the rest. These are the customary companions of Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., and Aquicinctinus, concerning whom we have spoken so often. They read there in second place: “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Gundulfus, bishop and confessor.” Henschenius thinks this reading should be preferred to ours, on the basis of the favorable coincidence with the day and the support of two Pratensis manuscripts. But even if we readily concede that the feast of Vulmarus falls on 20 July, while Gundulfus is to be commemorated on this day—a matter over which we have no dispute here—this can never make our reading cease to be truly Usuardine, whatever title is assigned to it, given the agreement of the wholly unimpaired manuscripts in its favor. That agreement clearly proves that Gundulfus was subsequently intruded into the Pratensis codex, as we have often shown happened elsewhere, perhaps after the earlier announcement had been erased. This becomes even clearer if we return to Usuardus’s perpetual source, namely Ado, to whom that Gundulfus of Bourges was entirely unknown. Accordingly, returning to Vulmarus, the aforementioned Ado is the first to mention him, and he praised him in exactly the words that Usuardus most clearly transferred into his own little entry. I therefore cannot doubt that this was how it originally stood in the true autograph, from which our more reliable manuscripts received it. This is sufficient here for our present purpose; if we allow anything to be lacking, we shall abundantly make it good under 20 July in the Acts. Concerning Avitus of Orléans, there is no difficulty, since he was taken from Bede and is recorded in all the Usuardine manuscripts, with only the small difference that Pratensis and similar witnesses stop at “priest,” cutting off the ending “and confessor.” Whether this properly concerns the Hieronymian copies, Florentinius will show. Rabanus, as usual, transcribed him from Bede and adorned him with a more expansive eulogy; Florus made it much shorter. But this has nothing to do with Usuardus, and we think nothing further need be argued here in defense of his simplicity. Henschenius explains in the Commentary, p. 350, the questions and controversies concerning Avitus or the Aviti, where he also rightly observes that this Avitus is most probably the same one recorded by Ado on 19 December. Moreover, the sequence of his life as transmitted in our Acts seems sufficiently to refute the opinion of a recent scholar who thinks that Avitus of Dun should be distinguished from Avitus of Orléans, or Micy.]

[Note: [Col. 0163C]

PRATEN.: We have already indicated its additions and omissions in sufficient detail.

ANTUERP.-MAJ., conforming to Pratensis, adds at the end: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Botulphus the confessor and abbot.” Here again you notice the English supplement.

ROSWEYD., agreeing with both of the preceding witnesses in the text, forms its supplement as follows: “On the same day, Saint Buthelmus the confessor.” It then follows with a fairly lengthy summary of the entire history of Alexius, concerning which several manuscripts have supplements under 17 July.

PULSANEN.: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Quiracus.” It could have added quite a few companions. “At the city of Orléans, the deposition of Saint Avitus the priest and confessor. At the city of Nantes, the most blessed Linus the confessor.” Unless I am mistaken, this hints at a truncation of Similianus, whom we call Similianus and who is also reported by others on this day, but whom we place with Usuardus on the preceding day. “On the same day, at the city of Rouen, the translation of the body of blessed Romanus, archbishop and confessor.” This is deferred to 23 October.

The second edition of BELIN adds to the text: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Gundulfus. On the same day, Saint Possemius (Possennius), a priest, a man of remarkable simplicity.”

[Col. 0164D] MOLAN. in the first edition omitted only these words: “Who were laid on the old Salarian Way at Cucumber Hill.” The other editions, as we said, are pure and complete.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERG., DANIC., and the ULTRAJ.-BELG. EDITION seem to wish to settle the dispute, since they append to the pure text: “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Gundulfus, bishop and confessor.”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, the holy martyrs, 262 in number, who were laid on the old Salarian Way at Cucumber Hill. At Orléans, Saint Avitus the priest and confessor.” Vulmarus is absent; concerning him, see the Observations above.

BRUXELLEN., pure in the first place, inserts second: “And at Rome, the passion of Saints Diogenes and Quiracus.” Their companions are listed in the Acts. In the entry for Vulmarus and Avitus it is pure, and it adds: “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Bothulphus, bishop and confessor.” It intended to say “Gundulphus.” “On the same day at Rouen, the translation of the body of Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor.” His feast is 23 October. “And Saint Aycadrius (in others, Aichardus), abbot of Jumièges. When he had nine hundred monks, half of them, whose departure had been foretold to him by an angel during the night, migrated to the Lord on a single day. He himself followed them not long afterwards and rested in Christ.” This is deferred to 15 September.

HAGENOYEN. adds concerning the 262 that “they were beheaded under the emperor Claudius.” It continues: [Col. 0165B] “In Egypt, the deposition of Saint Onuphrius the hermit. He had previously been a monk among the most perfect monks and was himself perfect. Finally, wishing to lead the hermit life of Elijah in the Old Testament and John the Baptist in the New Testament, and reproving the brothers because they did not become what they praised,” etc. This will be taken in a purer form from the Acts, under 12 June. It continues: “In England, Saint Rotulphus the abbot.” Others write *Loculphus*, but the same man is meant, who above is called Botulphus. The entry for Vulmarus and Avitus is pure. At the end: “Likewise at Bisinicia [Vesontio], Saint Anthidius, bishop and martyr.” Concerning him, see our Supplements and the Acts for 25 June.

AQUICINCT. We already said above in the Observation that this manuscript agrees with PRATEN.

VICTORIN.: “The assumption of Elijah the prophet.” See the Saints Omitted. “And Saints Nicander and Marcianus.”

CODEX PRINCIPIS URSINI, by Rosemberg: “Volinarus, elsewhere Vulmarus.” Thus the extract reads.

AMBIANEN.: “At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Avitus [Col. 0165C] the priest and confessor. While he flourished in the fervor of holy religion in the monastery under his father Maximianus, he was finally touched by God and sought the desert. After dwelling there for some time, he became renowned also for miracles, and later rested in peace with a glorious end.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Avitus the priest and confessor. At Rome, the holy martyrs, 262 in number. Vulmarus the confessor.”

CAMBERIEN.: “On the same day, Lord Luculphus the abbot.” Unless I am mistaken, this will be Botulphus.

REG. SUEC., under entry no. 428: “On the same day, in the territory of the castle of Biddick, the arrival of the renowned confessor of Christ, Bolulphus; over whose bier, in the sight of all, a column of light sent down from heaven shone forth.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, omits “Vulmarus and Avitus.” It adds: “At Benevento, Saints Nicander and Marcianus. On the same day, the translation of Saint Bartholomew the apostle from India to Lipara.” The apostle will be treated on 24 August.

[Col. 0165D] ALTEMPS.: “On the same day, Saint Posennius the priest, a man of remarkable simplicity. On the same day, at Saint Edmund’s, Saint Bolulphus, bishop and confessor. [Could this be Adulphus, the brother or companion of Botulphus?] In the territory of Oxford, at the monastery of Hertilanda, Saint Nechtavius the martyr.” There is nothing about him on this day in our Acts, nor among the Saints Omitted.

FLORENTIN.: “At Benevento, the translation of Saint Bartholomew the apostle. At Ravenna, Saints Fronus, Candrus, Blastrus, Nicander, and Ahena. At Dorostorum, Iphicus, Cantinus, Cantiana, and Cantianilla. At Rome, the feast of Saint Quiracus. Likewise at Rome, on the Salarian Way at the seven columns, the feast of Saint Diogenes, a man most renowned for virtue and holiness. At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Diogenes and Marinus. At Aquileia, Musca, Cirina, Valeriana, and Marina.” See the Acts concerning all of these. “At the city of Rouen, the translation of Saint Romanus, archbishop and confessor. Likewise Saint Badulphus [Col. 0166A] the abbot.” We have already said that this name is pronounced in various forms.

CODEX S. RICALDI.: “At Lyons, the deposition of blessed Aurelianus, bishop of Arles.” From the preceding day.

REMENS.: SS. Timothy and Apollinaris. “In the monastery called Haraea,” or “Harcea,” “Saint Wulmarus the confessor.” See below, under Julianus.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. is pure in the first edition. It continues: “On Mount Jovis, the deposition of blessed Bernard the hermit, a man of exceptional holiness. Among other kinds of illnesses, he was accustomed to cure the disease that physicians call paralysis.” He is celebrated on 15 June. Concerning Vulmarus it adds, “a disciple of Saint Judocus the confessor.” The entry for Gundulfus is pure. “In the monastery called Arena, Saint Julianus the confessor.” The entry for Avitus is also pure. “At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Diostorus and Marinus.” See the Acts. Concerning Botulphus, as above. “On Mount Syberg, the translation of Saint Innocentius the martyr, of the company of the holy Theban martyrs.”

GREVEN. “Likewise Saints Diogenes, Blasius, and Cantianus. [Col. 0166B] At Rome, Diogenes and 264 others. Dioscorus and Marinus the martyrs.” See the Acts. “Helprardus the martyr.” He is omitted. “Nicander and Marcianus the martyrs.” Concerning Gundulfus, correctly. “In the Tuscan city of Amelia, Himerius, bishop and confessor. Veredemius, bishop of Avignon and confessor. In the district of Rouen, Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor of that same city.” Concerning him, see above. “Vultramnus the bishop.” See the Saints Omitted. “In England, Botulphus the abbot and confessor. He always held conversation concerning the progress of souls; the eulogy of the joy of eternal happiness always resounded from his mouth. Eadrius the abbot. In Ireland, Enolich the confessor.” Concerning both, see the Saints Omitted. “Julianus the confessor; Alteramnus the confessor.” Who is this? “According to some, this is Bernard the hermit and confessor, concerning whom see above, 17 Kalends of June. On this day Elijah was carried away in a fiery chariot, in the year 903 before the birth of Christ.” Above he is called the Assumption of Elijah. [Col. 0166C] See 20 July.

MOLAN. concerning Avitus: “His life shone with miracles. Among other deeds, when the other brothers were weighed down by sleep, he raised a dead monk in the church from death by pouring out a prayer to the Lord. At Vienne, Saint Domnolus the bishop.” From the preceding day. Concerning Gundulfus and Possemius (for Posennius), as above. “Likewise at Rome, Alexius the confessor, who chose voluntary poverty and, after many anxieties and insults inflicted by the servants of his father’s household, rested in the Lord in fasting and prayer, without his father or mother knowing it.” He is celebrated on 17 July. “In Arabia, the taking up into heaven of Saint Elijah, the prophet of the Lord and patriarch of the Carmelite order, who found such great favor before the Lord that he could close and open heaven.” Concerning Botulphus and Julianus, as above. In smaller type: “The translation of Innocentius the martyr from the Theban Legion on Mount Siberg.” The entire legion is celebrated on 22 September. “Fulco, archbishop of Reims and martyr.” He is omitted. Other editions repeat, concerning Avitus, Domnolus, Gundulfus, Possemius, Julianus, and Botulphus, what has already been sufficiently stated. It continues: “At Cremona, Saint Himerius, bishop of Emilia and confessor. On the seventeenth day, the holy martyrs Manuel, Sabel, and Ishmael. In the diocese of Constance, the elevation of Christiana the virgin.” See the Saints Omitted. Then, in smaller type: “Likewise at Pisa, Saint Ranerius, a nobleman and later a pilgrim, who, after visiting Jerusalem, renowned for abstinence and piety, died in the year of salvation 1161.” Concerning Elijah, as above, in the first edition. “Likewise Fulco, the martyr and bishop of Reims, who was killed in defense of ecclesiastical liberty.” We said that he is omitted. After the annotations, contrary to the usual practice, the following is appended in italics: “On the Sunday before the feast of the Baptist, at Forest, Saint Helena (or Halena), virgin and martyr. She was the only daughter of Levoldus, a pagan king, and suffered martyrdom at her father’s command. After her death she shone with so many miracles that her father Levoldus, moved by them, received the faith of Christ, the grace of baptism, and forgiveness of sins at the same time. The body of this holy virgin rests in the Forest monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, near Brussels.” See these matters fully treated in the Acts.]

[Col. 0161]

At Rome, the holy martyrs, 262 in number, who were laid on the old Salarian Way at Cucumber Hill. On the same day, Saint Vulmarus the confessor, a man of admirable holiness and religious devotion. [In Bouillart, [Col. 0163] instead of “On the same day, … a man”: [Note: [Col. 0163A] For Saint Gundulfus, the Carolingian autograph has: “On the same day, Saint Vulmarus the confessor, a man of admirable holiness and religious devotion.” Usuardus later deleted this commemoration, taken from Ado, and substituted Saint Gundulfus. He did both wisely. For Saint Vulmarus did not depart this life on this day, but on 20 July, as I shall say in its proper place; and no occasion was more suitable for mentioning Saint Gundulfus than this day. This is the place assigned by Henschenius himself, who cites the Breviary of Bourges, the tables of that same church, and the purest Usuardine codices, both handwritten and printed. At what time, and of which see, that Saint Gundulfus was bishop has until now been unknown. The author who wrote the history of his translation and miracles says that Gundulfus was archbishop of Milan. Venantius Fortunatus, in the life of Saint Radegundis, calls him bishop of Metz. Yet neither the Milanese nor the people of Metz number him among their bishops. Nor was this known to Usuardus, who would not have failed to name the see if it had been known to him. BOUILLART.] In the territory of Bourges, Saint Gundulfus, bishop and confessor.] At Orléans, Saint Avitus the priest and confessor.

XIV Kal. The 18th day. [Note: [Col. 0167]

This is reported exactly by Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., and Rosweyd.]

[Note: [Col. 0167B]

]

Ardentina is a scribal error in Rosweyd. It is absent from Antwerp-Major; [the word] “martyrs” is absent. Furthermore, both codices write *tenti ad stipitem*, omitting the conjunction *et*. What follows is a faulty construction, *in pedibus acutos acceperunt* (“they received sharp [objects] in their feet”), which occurs both in the cited codices and in nearly all the others, except Greven and Molanus. Rosweyd, altering the wording, instead wrote *in pedibus aculeos susceperunt* (“they received spikes in their feet”), perhaps from Florus, where one finds *aculeos acceperunt* (“they received spikes”). Our text follows Ado, suppressing the noun *clavos* (“nails”), which we have enclosed in parentheses. Antwerp-Major has *cessassent laudare Dominum* (“they had ceased praising the Lord”); Rosweyd has *cessassent laudare Deum* (“they had ceased praising God”). The reading in the text is better. Pratensis reads *Syderea*; Antwerp reads *Malacha*. After *Paulae virginis*, Tornacensis inserted *quae* (“who”). All agree on the name *Marina*, whereas Pratensis alone has *Maria*.

[Note: [Col. 0167B]]

All the ancient Latin Martyrologies have made the festival of the two brother martyrs Mark and Marcellianus celebrated. The Hieronymian copies, above all, are not entirely consistent with one another. Then comes Bede, after whom Rabanus composed an eulogy wholly different from Bede’s, which Henschenius judged to be Florus’s. Add the Little Roman Martyrology, from which the Viennese martyrologist derived; he composed a fuller and more elegant encomium, no less elegantly contracted by our author, as represented in the entry. Everything is drawn from the Acts of Saint Sebastian, as may be seen in our edition, especially chapter XXII, p. 277; these matters are elucidated more fully on this day. The memory of our saints is most celebrated in the Sacramentaries edited by Menardus and Thomasius, and likewise in the ancient calendars of Allatius and Fronto, whatever may be read in the former concerning Marcellinus. Wandalbertus likewise did not fail to praise them in verse, adding Balbina, whom we think should be replaced by Marina, discussed below. He writes:

> On the fourteenth, the brothers Marcellianus and Mark alike  
> Consecrated [the day] with precious blood;  
> This day too illumines Balbina’s (Marina’s) merit and glory.

We read *Siriaci*, rather than *Cyriaci*, as all the ancient codices write it; and no one before or contemporary with Usuard mentions Paula. Usuard himself, as is clear in the text, presents the martyrdom in a polished little speech. But where he obtained it is entirely unknown to us. If conjecture is permissible, one might suppose that Usuard, while he was in Spain, either saw some Acts or, from oral tradition, transferred to Francia both the saints themselves and what he had heard recounted about them; hence their memory first became known in his martyrology. Certainly no Acts worthy of credence have yet been published, nor does Henschenius’s collection offer much beyond the veneration solemnly accorded to them at Málaga as patrons of the city. The Hieronymian Epternacense and Corbeiense mention Marina, by name only, as having suffered at Alexandria. In her place the Lucense, followed by Florentius, substitutes *Marius*; the Blumianum has *Maria*; nearly all the others would probably say *Margarita*. We believe, however, that Rabanus took Marina from the earlier sources and adorned her with an eulogy, probably borrowed from elsewhere, which is largely transcribed by Notkerus, although his entry for this day is still incomplete. Why these two assign her to Antioch will be found in the index of the omitted notices, where more than one Marina is distinguished, contrary to Molanus’s confusion in his first edition. Our author adhered simply to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, except that he added from himself the little crown of a virgin. This suffices for our present purpose; the entire matter will be discussed in the Acts on 20 July from the beginning, when Tillemontius, volume XVI, p. 167, may be consulted. We judge this to be the genuine text of Usuard, not the form reported by Greven and Molanus, who, in the first announcement after *transfixi* (“pierced through”), insert these words: “Since they also confessed Christ amid their torments, they were tortured until, through the crown, etc.” Thus the wording is clumsily doubled, since the preceding phrase, “and finally, as they did not cease praising Christ,” is sufficiently clear and complete. This plainly seems contrary to Usuard’s brief and concise method; consequently, the genuine simplicity of his text is much better represented and expressed here by us from all the other codices.

[Note: [Col. 0167D]]

Belinus, approaching the text in purity, reverses the order, treating Marina second; and in the entry concerning the people of Málaga he omits the words “buried beneath stones.”

Greven and Molanus: We have already said that they expand the first announcement.

Pulsanense: “At Rome, the birthday of the holy martyrs Mark and Marcellianus. In Africa, at Marchia, the birthday of Saint Milia and Felix.” See the Acts. “At Tomis, Saints Paul and Cyriacus. At Ravenna, the birthday of the holy martyrs Martarius, Felix, Enulus, and Crispinus.” See the Acts also. “Saint Autbertus, bishop of Abricata” (Abrincata or Abrincensis).

Muneratus, at the end: “In the territory of Sens, at Cellas, the deposition of blessed Fortunatus, bishop and confessor. He was born in the city of Vercelli and, from the flower of his earliest youth, was given over to the study of letters; with shining zeal he was the philosopher of the Lombards. Later, having been recognized by blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, he fearlessly revealed to the whole circuit of the world the life of Saint Marcellus, bishop of the aforementioned city. Shortly afterward, while Saint Germanus was ill and famine was raging, he was admonished by an angelic visitation; and, wishing in the fervor of contemplation to set out for Paris, he was touched by divine power about twenty miles from the city and rested in peace.”

Antwerp-Major, Lübeck, Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition, in the first announcement after *acceperunt* (“they received”), add Ado’s words: “And persevering in hymns and praises.” But the first two omit Marina.

Albergen and Danic are similar to the preceding codices, but at the beginning they have another addition from Ado, namely: “the sons of the most illustrious Tranquillinus and Marcia.”

Centulense: “The birthday of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, when he was transferred from the island of Lipara to Benevento.” His birthday is 24 August. “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the holy twin martyrs Mark and Marcellianus, who, pierced through the sides with lances, migrated to the starry kingdoms. In Spain, in the city of Málaga, Saints Cyriacus and Paula the virgin. At Alexandria, Saint Marina the virgin. In the territory of Sens, Saint Fortunatus, bishop and confessor.”

Bruxellense, in the first announcement, has everything that Albergen and Danic have. It is pure in *Siriaco et Paula*. Then: “In Africa, the birthday of the holy Hermelius and Felix. At Ravenna, the birthday of the holy martyrs Mercury, Felix, Emilius, and Crispinus.” See the names more correctly expressed in the Acts. The entry concerning Marina follows, in pure form. At the end: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Autbertus, bishop of Abricaca.” He intended to say Abrincatensis.

Hagenoyen, after “brothers,” inserts: “Before they suffered, they began to grow faint-hearted at the words of their parents and wives; but Saint Sebastian, by his exhortations, made them strong for suffering. They were handed over by the judge Fabianus,” etc. In second place: “In the territory of Bourges, the deposition of Saint Gundulfus, bishop and confessor.” Concerning him, see the preceding day. In the rest of the text it is sufficiently pure.

Aquicinctense, in another hand: “At Alexandria, the deposition of Saint Marina the virgin.” Traces of a more accurate inscription are still visible.

Ambianense: “On the same day, the dedication of the church of Saint Firminus the martyr, situated within the walls.” He is celebrated on 25 September, where I shall note more about both saints named Firminus.

The Matric-Carthusian of Utrecht has: “Mark and Marcellianus, martyrs. Marina, virgin and martyr. Cyriacus and Paula the virgin, buried beneath stones.”

The Augustinian Canon Regular: “Likewise at Rome, in the cemetery of Damasus, Saints Marcellus and Mark, brothers. At Tomis, Saints Paul and Cyriacus.” It is not very different from our Málaga entries. But concerning these, see Usuard on 20 June: “At Alexandria, Saint Marina the virgin. At Ravenna, the birthday of the holy martyrs Martarius, Felix, Emilius, and Crispinus.” See the Acts. “On the same day, Saint Autbertus, bishop of Cambrai.” Read “of Abrincensis.”

The Swedish Register, no. 428: “In the territory of Sens, at Cellas, the deposition of blessed Fortunatus, bishop and confessor.” See Muneratus above.

In the Vatican codex, no. 5949, and in Ughellianus, Marina is absent, as in Antwerp and the Antwerp-Lübeck codex.

Altemps: “On the same day, Saint Adolphus, brother of Bodulfus the abbot.” See the preceding day in our Acts.

Florentinus: “At Rome, Saints Felix and Emilius. At Ravenna, the holy martyrs Martali, Felix, Emilius, and Crispinus. Likewise at Alexandria, Saint Marina the virgin, who, while still a child, secretly had her hair cut and sought the monastic life, assuming for herself the name Marinus; after being confined for many years, she rested in the Lord in all holiness.” See the omitted notices. “On the same day, Saint Autertus, bishop of Bricata.” It is “Autbertus of Abrincensis.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins: “In the city of Bordeaux, the birthday of blessed Amandus, bishop and confessor of that city. He received blessed Severinus, archbishop of the city of Cologne, with the highest honor at an angelic admonition; although he had never seen him before, he greeted him by his own name and yielded the episcopal throne to him.” Concerning Mark and Marcellianus, as in Albergen and Danic. The entry concerning the people of Málaga is pure. A longer history of Marina’s monastic life follows; concerning it, see the omitted notices.

Greven: “At Ravenna, Saints Felix, Emilius, and Crispinus. The birthday of the holy martyrs Potentinus the deacon, Felicius the priest, and Simplicius the soldier, resting at Steynvelt.” Concerning Amandus, somewhat more briefly than above. “In the territory of Sens, Saint Fortunatus, bishop, distinguished in life and learning. At Cremona, Saint Himerus, bishop and confessor.” See the preceding day. “In Ireland, Colmanus the abbot.” See the omitted notices. “Elizabeth, a nun of blessed memory at Schönau, to whom many secrets were revealed by the Lord, around the year 1156.” In the earlier edition, dated 1515, Cunera was added; we mentioned her on 12 June.

Molanus assigns to Marina the eulogy which Rabanus attributes to the woman of Antioch, in these words: “She suffered many torments through the prefect Olibrius for the name of Christ: bonds, prisons, and the rack. The devil also tempted her in the form of a dragon and likewise in that of an Ethiopian, but he was overcome by the sign of the holy cross. Finally, having been beheaded by the aforementioned prefect, she ended her life in sacred martyrdom.” See the omitted notices. Fortunatus follows, as above in Muneratus. Then: “At Cremona, Saint Himerus,” etc., as in Greven. Then, from the same source but in smaller type, concerning Amandus of Bordeaux and Elizabeth of Schönau. This follows: “At the port of Tripoli, Saint Leontius the martyr, whose account of his martyrdom a certain scribe named Cyrus wrote on lead tablets and deposited at the martyr’s monument, so that he might leave an excellent example for those who would come afterward, in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Thus far the first edition is fuller. In the others there is Fortunatus’s eulogy, from Muneratus, as far as “revealed”; the remainder is absent. Then: “At Lipara, Calogerus, the most holy monk, whom Gregory seems to mention in the fourth book of the Dialogues. On the eighteenth day, Saint Leontius the martyr.” This is followed, in smaller type, by: “In the city of Bordeaux, Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor. At Schönau, Elizabeth died, a nun to whom many secrets were revealed by the Lord.” Marina is omitted in these editions and relegated to the Additions for 20 July under the name Margarita.

[Col. 0167]

At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the birthday of the holy martyrs Mark and Marcellianus, brothers, whom the commander Fabianus kept bound and tied to a stake; they received sharp objects in their feet [nails]. [Note: [Col. 0167] In the German manuscript there is a blank space the length of one word. Bouillart.] And when at last they did not cease praising Christ, they were pierced through the sides with a lance and migrated with the glory of martyrdom to the starry kingdoms. In Spain, in the city of Málaga, the holy martyrs Siriacus and Paula the virgin, who, after many tortures had been inflicted upon them, were buried beneath stones and, among the rocks, gave their souls back to heaven. At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Marina the virgin.

XIII Kal. Day 19. [Note: [Col. 0169]]

Taken from Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp, Antwerp-Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus; likewise from Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, Danic, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.

[Note: [Col. 0171A]]

*Mediolano* occurs in Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, and Antwerp-Lübeck; in Rosweyd it is worse, *Mediolanis*. I read *Protasii*, with Pratensis, Herinien, and Rosweyd, although most of the others have *Prothasii*. The first two write *Astaius*; the latter, *Astacius*; Muneratus, *Artatius*; Antwerp-Major, *Anastasius*. I follow Greven, Molanus, and the other codices, together with Ado, where the correct form is *Astasius*, not *Astachius*, as in Rabanus. Molanus correctly wrote *exhalaret*. But the other codices compel me to write *exalaret*. Many have *repperit*; concerning this, see elsewhere. The text agrees with the purer witnesses. *Interempta* is an error in Antwerp and Antwerp-Lübeck. Molanus likewise wrongly has *incorupta*. We have often spoken of the spelling of *abscisio*; in that orthographic practice we are swept along by the stream of the codices. In any case, “he completed his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head” is Usuard’s own phrase, although Ado reads *consummavit* (“completed”), which amounts to the same thing. Rosweyd’s codex substitutes “he was beheaded,” for which reason it should almost have been excluded from the number of the pure witnesses.

[Note: [Col. 0171A]]

The solemnity of the most celebrated martyrs throughout the Christian world, begun and instituted by Saint Ambrose, passed into all our Martyrologies on this very day, which ought rather to be called the day of their discovery, translation, or—more properly—elevation than their birthday. Whatever the case, the Hieronymian copies place them between Nazarius and Celsus, brought back here from another day. Was this because they were elevated or translated together? Florentius decides that it was so, on the basis of Puricellus’s dissertation on Nazarius. The Little Roman Martyrology also contains a commemoration of Nazarius and Celsus, entirely omitted by Ado and therefore outside our present purpose. Bede speaks of Gervasius and Protasius with no little praise; his words form the final part of our eulogy, transferred from him by Ado and accepted from Ado by our author together with other, less certain material. When transcribing Bede, Rabanus added something from the Hieronymian Martyrologies concerning Vitalis and Valeria, the parents of our martyrs. They belong to this day only by virtue of their blood relationship, for we commemorated Vitalis on 28 April, where his wife is joined to him in the Acts. As usual, Notkerus made Ado his own rather freely, although he also altered some details. If you seek anything certain about the deeds or passion of these martyrs, you will seek in vain; nevertheless, they did not thereby attain lesser glory, since their illustrious merits are clearly demonstrated by nearly innumerable miracles, preserved in memory by irrefragable witnesses—Ambrose, Augustine, and Paulinus. Their veneration was undoubtedly transferred to Africa by Augustine and obtained a place in the Carthaginian Calendar. The often-mentioned Sacramentaries and Fronto’s Calendar likewise honor them with no less devotion. Papebrochius diligently composed a long commentary on them, to be reviewed by Janningus in the supplement to June for this day. Tillemontius arranged most matters more briefly in volume II, beginning at p. 78; add his notes beginning at p. 498. Wandalbertus sings only this verse today:

> Gervasius and Protasius crown the thirtieth.

[Col. 0172B] The other Martyrologists agree almost unanimously in the second announcement concerning Ursicinus, if Bede alone is excepted. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies he does not seem to be sufficiently separated from Hippolytus, Vitalis, and Valeria; this perhaps gave Rabanus occasion to assign him to Rome. On this matter, Florentius may be consulted. The Little Roman Martyrology more correctly assigns him to Ravenna; taking from it the arena, Ado adapted a brief eulogy for Ursicinus, which Notkerus transcribed in full, while our author mutilated only its final portion, omitting these words: “and he was buried in the same city by blessed Vitalis, the father of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.” These words could have been added to show a certain affinity between the two announcements, although they do not belong to the same day. It is not unusual for saints to be entered on a day other than their birthday, as we hinted above concerning the earlier entries. Papebrochius gives a not implausible reason for Ursicinus in his historical collection, which the inquisitive reader should consult. Whatever the truth may be, our text proceeds from Ado and is genuinely and purely Usuardine. The praised Papebrochius discusses its authenticity, and we spoke briefly of it on 28 April. Wandalbertus, however, indulged his own judgment when, contrary to the other Martyrologists, he assigned Vitalis to 20 June in this verse:

> And Vitalis, the father, follows his children on the twelfth.

[Note: [Col. 0171C]]

In Tornacensis the words “Saint Ambrose discovered their tombs,” etc. are absent. Everything else is most pure.

Pulsanense: “At Milan, the birthday of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. Ambrose, by divine revelation, discovered their bodies, so incorrupt that they seemed to have been killed on that very day. While they were being carried through the city, a blind man received his sight by touching the bier. Likewise at Rome, the holy martyrs Hippolytus and Honorius, with six others.” Concerning these, see the Acts and the omitted notices.

Centulense: “At Milan, the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, whose father, the martyr Vitalis, and mother, Valeria, a good root, produced pious shoots. At Ravenna, Saint Ursicinus the martyr.”

Bruxellense, after “brothers,” inserts: “Whom Valeria bore to her holy husband Vitalis in a single birth. Of these, the elder, namely Gervasius, was [ordered by] Count Astasius,” etc. The text is sufficiently pure. It continues: “And Celsus the boy, martyred for Christ.” His birthday, together with that of Nazarius, is 27 July. The entry for Ursicinus is pure. Then: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Hippolytus, Honorius, Evotus, Peter, Valeria, Marcellus, and Vitalis.” See the Acts concerning them. “Likewise, Saint Alena the virgin and martyr, who, the only daughter of Levoldus, a pagan king, suffered martyrdom at her father’s command. After her death she shone with so many miracles that Levoldus her father, moved by them, received the faith of Christ, the grace of baptism, and forgiveness of sins [may have received]. The body of this holy virgin rests in the county of Brussels, at the Forest monastery, in the chapel of the parish church dedicated to her.” She appears again above, on 17 June.

Hagenoyen, after “brothers,” has: “They were the sons of Saint Vitalis the martyr and Saint Valeria, his wife. Of these, the elder, namely Gervasius, Astasius ordered for so long,” etc., in pure form. It continues: “In Liguria, the birthday of Saint Ursicinus, who, under the judge Paulinus,” etc., up to “he completed.” There follows: “Although this man is placed here, he is nevertheless recorded as having suffered before Vitalis, whose feast is on the fourth day before the Kalends of May.” See the fuller account of them in the Acts.

[Col. 0172D] Victorinus and the Swedish Register, marked no. 130: “On the same day, at the Castrense monastery, Saint Romualdus the abbot.” His Acts were elucidated on 7 February.

Daveronense: “At Le Mans, Saint Innocentius, bishop and confessor.” See him in the Acts.

The Matric-Carthusian of Utrecht: “Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs. Count Roland and martyr, with many others, from the history of Emperor Charles.” See what we said in the Additions on 16 June. “Ursicinus, physician and martyr.”

Camberiense of Saint Mary: “At Rome, Saint Silverius, pope and martyr.” In Notkerus, “Silvester.” See the twentieth day.

In Vaticanus, no. 5949, “Ursicinus” is absent. Added is: “Saint Romualdus the abbot and hermit.”

Florentinus: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Hippolytus, Honorius, Evotus, Peter, Valeria, Marcellus, Vitalis, and Ursicinus.” Concerning these, who are very confused here, see elsewhere for a clearer account. “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Romualdus.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins: “At Herford, the feast of the vision of the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God.” Then it gives a sufficiently pure account of Gervasius and Protasius, except that at the end, after “killed,” it adds: “and buried, although they had lain for nearly three hundred years.” Concerning Ursicinus, it adds his burial by Vitalis, as above. It continues: “At Le Mans, Saint Innocentius, bishop and confessor. In Scotland, Saint Margaret the queen.” Her life was given on 10 June.

Belinus, at the end of the pure text, adds: “Likewise Saint Romualdus the confessor.” Concerning him, see above.

Greven: “At Herford, the feast of the vision of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God. Boniface the martyr, disciple of Saint Romualdus. Having obtained permission, he went to Russia, or Slavonia, with wondrous fervor and a desire for martyrdom, to preach the Gospel of Christ. After converting many, he was beheaded and attained the glory of martyrdom. Likewise Saints John and Benedict, who also, while evangelizing among the Slavs, merited to be crowned with martyrdom.” They are referred to 12 November. “On the same day, Saint Innocentius, bishop of Le Mans and confessor; Deodatus, bishop of Nevers and confessor; Hildegerus, the first bishop of Halberstadt and confessor, brother of Saint Liudgerus, bishop of Münster; and Romualdus, abbot and confessor, the first founder of the Camaldolese Order. Peter Damian, bishop and cardinal, describes his life, renowned for virtues and miracles, in an elegant style. He died in the 120th year of his life, during the reign of the first Emperor Henry.” We have already said that he is celebrated on 7 February. “The translation of Saint Margaret, queen of Scotland, sister of Saint Edward, king of England.” We also said that she is celebrated on 10 June, where her true genealogy will be found.

Molanus: “Likewise Saint Romualdus the confessor. Likewise Saint Alena,” etc., as above in the Bruxellense. Here, however, in smaller type, it adds: “Her elevation took place in 1193, on the Sunday before the Nativity of John the Baptist, by Godscalcus, abbot of Affligem.” Concerning Boniface and Hildegerus, as in Greven. Then: “On the same day, at the city of Besançon, a commemoration of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. When the arm of Saint Stephen, prepared with gold and gems, had been stolen by thieves, the people raised an enormous tumult, lamenting and saying that nothing remained for them except death, since they had lost their lives in the arm of their patron Stephen. Fishermen, hearing the tumult, showed the people a place in the river where the holy arm, naked and luminous, had been placed on dry ground amid the waters. All saw it together and left to posterity an unquestionable testimony of that miracle.” These and other matters concerning Saint Stephen will be treated on 26 December. This is in the first edition. The others have the account of Romualdus as in the first. Then: “At Besançon, a commemoration of Saint Stephen.” The rest, in smaller type, is as already described. At the end: “In the city of Conon, Saint Sozimus the martyr.” He was taken from the usual Greek source. See his Acts, accurately elucidated by Henschenius.

[Col. 0169]

At Milan, the birthday of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, brothers. Count Astasius ordered the former to be beaten with leaded scourges until he breathed out his spirit; the latter, after being beaten with clubs, to be beheaded. Saint Ambrose, by the Lord’s revelation, discovered their tombs and their bodies so incorrupt that they seemed to have been killed on that very day. At Ravenna, Saint Ursicinus the martyr, who, under the judge Paulinus, after excessive tortures, remaining steadfast in confession of the Lord, completed his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head.

XII Kal. Day 20. [Note: [Col. 0173]]

The text is found in Pratensis, Herinien, Tornacensis, Antwerp-Major, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0173C]]

Our codices differ in very few respects. *Potentia* in Antwerp-Major is an error, as is *Prudenciana* in Muneratus.
