We have retained the name *Potentiana*, as it also appears on 19 May, when we commemorated her birthday with Usuard. Herinien wrongly reads *Dionis* for *Tomis*, as the others write; they also all agree on *Cyriaci*, except Pratensis and Muneratus, in which the better reading is printed as *Cyriaci* as well—the intended orthographic distinction is uncertain in the supplied text. We follow the stream of the codices.

[Note: [Col. 0173C]]

The Martyrologies of Jerome and Bede, together with their related witnesses, are silent about Novatus. The author of the Little Roman Martyrology was the first to vindicate his memory, writing as follows: “At Rome, Novatus, brother of Timothy the priest, who were instructed by the apostles.” Ado begins his eulogy with those very words, and it embraces nearly everything recounted in the Acts from Pastor’s letter to Timothy. Yet nowhere in these Martyrologies is it suggested that Potentiana—or, as others write, Pudentiana—and Praxedes were the sisters of those two brothers, Novatus and Timothy. Our author was the first to assert this, and it can be sustained only in the sense in which Pastor says of Novatus, “who is our brother in the Lord,” just as elsewhere we have said that Petronilla is called the daughter of the apostle Peter—namely, as one of the first Christians, related not by flesh or blood but by the nobler affinity of faith. Thus the statements Usuard placed above his sources in the margin on this day are to be understood. Whether Novatus and Timothy can properly be called disciples of the apostles, and in what sense, Papebrochius will explain in the Acts; he can readily be inclined toward the more charitable interpretation if the terms “apostles” and “disciples” are not taken too rigidly. These matters can easily be reconciled, assuming the complete authenticity of the letter cited so often elsewhere, whose authenticity, as we said on 19 May, is challenged by Tillemontius. So that nothing rash may be asserted here, we refer the whole matter for renewed examination to 21 July, on which day Praxedes will be discussed in the Acts.

The two Tomitan martyrs, Paul and Cyriacus, are mentioned in some codices of Usuard on the preceding days; according to his intention, they should be placed on this day. He took them from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, omitting their companions, whom Notkerus lists, being somewhat more expansive than his source. For matters belonging to today’s group, see the exposition in the Acts and compare it with another group not very different, reviewed on 18 June and largely reported in our Additions, especially in the Pulsanense and Florentine codices, which in this month approach Jerome more closely than Usuard. Let these remarks suffice in passing for those who may wish to examine the matter more deeply, while the Usuardine text remains wholly intact in every respect, if not in truth, at least in its complete simplicity—which alone we have proposed to seek.

[Note: [Col. 0173D]]

Rosweyd departs from the pure form only in this: after *Cyriaci*, at the end, he adds “martyrs, and others.”

Pulsanense, celebrating its proper feast, distinguished by a special mark, has on this day: “The birthday of the most blessed hermit John, abbot of the holy Pulsanense church. While alive in the world, he mortified himself with all his strength for Christ. His venerable death occurred on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 1139 of the incarnate Word, in the second Indiction. In the city of Tomis, the birthday of the holy Paul, Cyriacus, Aprilia, Feliciana, Thomas, Felix, Emilius, Martyria, Vitalis, and Crispinus the martyr.” The Acts concerning them should be consulted.

Antwerp-Major, Lübeck, Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, the Utrecht-Belgian edition, Bigotianus marked P. 5, and Codex D. Le Mare, marked B: all add after “Paul and Cyriacus”: “Felix and Feliciana.” Ughellianus, changing the gender, reads *Feliciani* instead of *Felicianae*.

Albergen and Danic. First: “The octave of Saint Anthony.” Then: “At the Pontian Islands, the birthday of Saint Silverius, pope and martyr, who, when he refused to restore the patriarch Arthemius, deposed for heresy, was sent into exile at the request of the empress Antonina, through her agency, and, sustained there by the bread of tribulation and the water of distress, died as a confessor.” After this follows a sufficiently pure text, which at the end also adds: “Felix and Feliciana.”

Centulense: “At Rome, Saint Novatus, brother of Timothy the priest, who was instructed by the holy apostles and, persevering in holiness, departed to Christ.” “Paul and Cyriacus” are absent.

Bruxellense, pure in the first announcement, continues: “At Ravenna, Saint Vitalis the martyr, father of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. Because he secretly buried the body of Saint Ursicinus the martyr, he was stoned by Paulinus the consul, under whom his wife Valeria also, having been killed by excessive slaughter, departed to the Lord.” See 28 April. “And the birthday of Saint Silverius, pope and martyr. He sat in Rome for one year; and when he refused, at the request of the empress Theodora, to restore Arthemius, patriarch and bishop of Constantinople, infected with the Eutychian heresy, deposed and excommunicated, he was deposed by Belisarius, patrician of the emperor Justinian, made a monk, and exiled to the island of Ponza. There, living for a short time on the bread of tribulation and the water of distress, he died in exile as martyr and confessor. At the city of Tomis, the birthday of the holy martyrs Paul, Cyriacus, Felix, Feliciana, Emilius, and Vitalis. On the same day, Saint Crispinus the martyr.” Is this the one who is celebrated with Crispinianus on 25 October? “At the monastery of Fontanella, the deposition of Saint Bavius [Bainus], bishop and confessor of Cava [Thérouanne]. Likewise Regina the virgin.” See the omitted notices.

Hagenoyen, likewise pure at the beginning, has in second place: “At the Pontian Islands, the birthday of Saint Silverius, pope and martyr, who was the sixtieth after blessed Peter the Apostle, and who, having governed the Roman Church for one year and ten months, refused, at the request of Antonia Augusta, to restore Arthemius, patriarch of Constantinople, deposed for heresy. At her insistence he was sent into exile and, sustained by the bread of tribulation and the water of distress, died there as a confessor because he refused to consent to the heretics.” On the same day, Saint Florentia the virgin. See the omitted notices. Concerning the Tomitans it also adds: “Felix and Feliciana.”

Aquicinctense writes *Navati* instead of *Novati*. At the end it adds: “On the same day, the bringing of the relics of Saint George of Aquicinct.” The Aquicinctine Chronicle appended to the Martyrology records that these relics were brought in the year 1100. The Martyrology then continues, in a much later hand: “Likewise Saint Silverius, pope and martyr.”

Victorinus and the Swedish Register, marked no. 130: “On the same day, Saint Florentia the virgin.” Concerning her, see above.

The Matric-Carthusian of Utrecht: “Silverius, pope and martyr. Novatus the confessor and brother of Timothy, and Potentiana and Praxedes, virgins.”

The Cistercian Codex of Saint Benignus: “On the same day, Saint Florentia the virgin.”

Codex D. du Cheval, Dijon, marked C: “The birthday of Saint Vitalis the martyr.” Here, as do other codices, it follows Wandalbertus.

Vaticanus, no. 5949, omitted “Paul and Cyriacus.” It adds: “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Silverius, pope, who sat in the pontificate for one year. He was sent into exile by Belisarius the patrician and died there.” See the eulogy above in Hagenoyen.

Altemps: “On the same day, Saint Florentia the virgin. And Saint Genulphus, bishop and confessor.” See the index of the omitted notices. “And the birthday of Saint Vitalis the martyr.” Concerning him, see above. “On the same day, Saint Jovinus the priest and confessor.” See 1 June. “At Septonia, the translation of Saint Edward, king and confessor.” See 18 March.

Florentinus: “In the city of Tomis, Paulinus [Paul] and Cyprian [Cyriacus], Felix and Feliciana, with several others. The deposition of Saint John, abbot and hermit of the Pulsanense Church, in the diocese of Siponto in the region of Apulia; the first abbot and founder of the Pulsanense Order, [who, while alive in the world, mortified himself with all his strength for Christ. His venerable death occurred in the year 1229 of the incarnate Word,] a man of great holiness.” The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the printed edition. “On the same day, Saint Florentia the virgin.” Others write *Florentiana*; see Greven.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition: “At the Pontian Islands, the birthday of Saint Silverius, pope, who sat in Rome for nine years and eleven days. When he refused to restore Arthemius,” etc. The account of Novatus is pure. At the end: “Felix and Feliciana, martyrs.” Then: “On the same day, blessed Abagarus, ruler of the city of Edessa, who wrote a letter to our Lord Jesus Christ, asking him to deign to come to him and heal him of his illness. The Lord wrote to him, saying: ‘After my death I will send you one of my disciples, who will cure you and grant you life.’ After the Lord’s Ascension, the apostle Thaddeus was sent to him, as the Lord had promised, and baptized him with all his people, and there was great joy in that city.” See the omitted notices. “Likewise Saint Florentiana the virgin. At Trier, Saint Maximinus, bishop and martyr.” See in the Acts concerning the bishop of Tongeren. It continues: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Edward, king and martyr.” See above.

Belinus, in second place, has Florentia. Then: “On the same day, Saint Silverius, pope and martyr. On the same day, the octave of Saint Anthony of Padua, of the Order of Friars Minor. And elsewhere, in the city of Tomis,” etc., in pure form. Another edition adds: “On the same day, Saint Genulus, bishop and confessor.” I think this is Genulphus, concerning whom see the Altempsianus.

GREVEN: “Likewise at the city of Thomis, [the feast] of Felix and Feliciana.” Concerning Maximus, as above. “Of Pope Silverius and confessor, who occupied the see for one year and five months. When, however, he refused to restore Anthem­ius, deposed by his predecessor Agapitus, he was sent into exile at the empress’s instigation and ended his life in confession of the Lord. Of Baianus, bishop of Ravenna and confessor.” See the omitted notices. “At the city of Séez, of Saint Latuinus, bishop and confessor. Of Abagar, king of the city of Edessa and confessor. He [as is stated in Book I of the Ecclesiastical History] sent a letter to our Savior and received a letter from him. After the Lord’s Ascension, he was baptized with his people by Thaddeus, one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples, and rested in peace.” We have already spoken of him, as also of the translation of Edward, of Florentiana [who perhaps would more correctly be called Florentina], and of Regina.

MOLAN. After “Virgin of Christ,” he inserts in italic type: “In whose deeds Pastor writes about him to the aforementioned Timothy, his brother.” At the end, concerning Silverius, Florentiana, and Anthony, as in BELINUS. Concerning Latuinus, as in GREVENUS. Then: “The deposition of Saint Aldegundis, virgin, daughter of the blessed Basinus, king and martyr.” Then, in smaller type: “She rests with her father at Truncinium outside Ghent. On the same day, of Ida, whose body is preserved in the church of Saint John at Ghent.” In other editions, concerning Latuinus, as above. “At the monastery of Fontenelle, the feast of Saint Baimus, bishop [Col. 0177A] and confessor. At Truncinium, the deposition of Saint Aldegundis, virgin, daughter of the blessed Basinus, king and martyr.” Concerning Silverius and Florentia, as above. “On the twentieth day, of the most holy martyr Methodius, bishop of Patara,” more correctly, “of Patara.” Then: “At Berg, the glorious translation of Saint Oswald, king, and Saint Idaberga, virgin.” See the Acts concerning Iduberga on this day; Usuard mentions Oswald on 5 August.

[Col. 0173]

At Rome, the deposition of Saint Novatus, brother of the priest Timothy, who were instructed in the faith by the apostles. Their sisters were the blessed Potentiana and Praxedes, holy virgins of Christ. At the city of Thomis, of Saints Paul and Cyriacus.

### 11 days before the Kalends. Day 21

[Note: [Col. 0177A]]

Only Molan’s edition is everywhere pure.

[Note: [Col. 0177B]]

There is today great disagreement among our manuscripts, arising chiefly from the omission in some, and the different—one might call it scrupulous—wording in others, of Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine, bishop and author of the Ecclesiastical History. Before discussing this, we shall settle the more certain matters.

The Sicilian martyrs Rufinus and Martia, recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and the Little Roman Martyrology, were taken from the latter by Ado and reported in his words by Usuard and Notker. Nothing about them is found elsewhere, but Wandalbert mentions only them in this verse: “The martyr Rufinus and Martia possess power on the eleventh day.”

There is another notice of the virgin Demetria in the Little Roman Martyrology; Ado transferred it from there [Col. 0177C] and adorned it with an encomium, which Notker copied in full, while Our author shortened it somewhat. Henschenius referred what concerns this distinguished saint to the illustration of Bibiana’s commemoration on 2 December.

The abbot Leutfred, whom we report in fourth place, was first recorded by Usuard in the sacred calendar; he is entirely unknown to the other ancient authorities. On Leutfred, see Henschenius’s Commentary and the life published and illustrated by him after the works of others.

Finally, Quiriacus and Apollinaris, joined by several companions in Jerome, were selected by Our author from that group, as often happened elsewhere, as we have shown in their proper places. Their companions are arranged in their own order in the Acts. In reporting these saints on this day, the better Usuardine manuscripts generally agree.

The exceptions are the Herinien manuscript, which omits Leutfred here, and the larger Antwerp manuscript, in which the final notice is omitted. The Tournai manuscript moves Leutfred to the last place and cuts off his eulogy. We now proceed to the central point of the matter and its difficulty.

[Col. 0177D] I said that among the principal manuscripts only Molan’s is everywhere pure, both in the four commemorations mentioned above and, as I believe, also in the second notice that we have printed in full: “At Caesarea of Palestine, etc.” The Herinien, Tournai, and Belin manuscripts give this with precisely the same wording, and their authority is confirmed by the Antwerp-major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, Danish, and other manuscripts, which have the very same words but report them in third place or elsewhere.

Pratensis, together with the two related manuscripts Antwerp-major and Rosweyd, agrees in substance, though not in wording, for the manuscripts read as follows: “At Caesarea of Palestine, of Saint Eusebius the historian.” Antwerp and the larger Lübeck manuscript put this last: “Likewise of Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor.”

Only in Muneratus and Grevenus is Eusebius entirely removed. This was, I think, the scruple of the editors, who rightly suspected the doubtful reliability of Eusebius the historian on other grounds, and therefore arrogated to themselves the authority to corrupt Usuard’s text. Baronius approved this so completely that he left no memory whatsoever of the man in the modern Roman Martyrology.

Everyone readily admits, moreover, that the most ancient Hieronymian manuscript of Echternach contained the heading “Eusebius the historian.” But because in other manuscripts the entry was found only as “At Caesarea, the deposition of Saint Eusebius, bishop,” and because in some variant reading of the Corbie manuscript edited by Acherius “Caesarea of Cappadocia” may have been added by a more recent hand, Florentinius eagerly seized upon this and thought it sufficient to [Col. 0178C] substitute another Eusebius, a bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. He prepared a dissertation for this purpose, which Papebrochius arranged to have reprinted in the Acts, adding only the title “Venerable,” since he knew well that this man had never had a place in any catalogue of saints.

The very proper intention of both men is certainly worthy of praise. Yet I think it more than likely that not only in the very ancient Echternach manuscript but also in the other copies of Jerome, “Eusebius” means the historian himself. I am all the more led to believe this because Florus states it so plainly: “At Caesarea of Palestine, the deposition of Saint Eusebius the confessor, who was most devoted to the divine Scriptures and, with the martyr Pamphilus, a most diligent investigator of the divine library.” These are almost Jerome’s words in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 81.

Nor do I doubt that Usuard had Jerome before his eyes and shortened his own eulogy from him. No sensible person will deny that from these martyrologists who most closely followed the Hieronymian Martyrology, the correct understanding of the matter should be determined more securely than from Florentinius’s conjectures.

I do not, however, intend thereby to claim the title of saint for Eusebius the historian. On this matter one should consult the dissertations of Valesius and Florentinius, as well as what Papebrochius incidentally discussed concerning Eusebius of Cappadocia in volume IV of June, page 75, citing more recent writers who contend for Eusebius’s orthodoxy; others could also be added.

Nevertheless, although I greatly esteem Eusebius, I have always thought that all these men labor in vain—a view Tillemontius also urged after others, especially in the last three articles of volume VII, beginning on page 39, where he treats the controversy carefully.

This much is certainly beyond dispute: for seven centuries and more, at least from the time when Usuard’s Martyrology was everywhere received in the Western Church, the memory of this Eusebius was celebrated in the sacred calendars together with the other saints. This proves that he was honored with heavenly rites, so that it is perfectly clear that we have restored Usuard’s text in its genuine form. From its truth—or, if you prefer, its orthodoxy—we set aside the question.]

[Note: [Col. 0179A]]

Nothing further need be said concerning PRATEN., HERINIEN., TORNACEN., ANTUERP.-MAJOR, ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBECK, MUNERATUS, and GREVENUS.

ROSWEYD, in addition to the text, adds at the end: “At the city of Mainz, of Saint Alban the martyr.”

BELIN adds concerning Quiriacus and Apollinaris: “Men of wonderful holiness.” Concerning Leutfred: “In the district of Évreux,” with the eulogy removed.

PULSAN: “In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Saturninus, Albinus, Quiriacus, and Apollinaris with five others. And in the East, the feast of Saint Januaria and Primus.” See their Acts. “At Caesarea, the deposition of Saint Eusebius, bishop.”

LOVANIEN inserts in the penultimate place: “Near Mainz, of Saint Alban, priest and martyr, who, while preaching the truth of the faith to the Goths and Arians in that place, was seized by them, led outside the city, and beheaded with a sword-stroke.” It continues: “Of Quiriacus,” etc., purely.

[Col. 0179B] ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG., DANIC., and EDIT. ULTRAJECT.-BELG. run through the entire text consecutively, except that concerning Demetria they add, “sister of Saint Viviana and daughter of Faustus the martyr”; and, as we have already said, move Eusebius from second place to third. Finally, concerning Alban, they add at the end, in addition to what LOVAN. has: “The martyr of Christ, taking it up, carried it with his own hands to the place where his body now rests together with his head.” You should also note that the name “Rufinus” has been changed to “Rufina.”

CENTULEN, pure in the first notice, continues: “At Rome, of Saint Demetria, virgin, who was the daughter of the blessed Faustus. In the district of Madriacum, of Saint Leutfred, abbot. In Africa, of Saints Quiriacus and Apollinaris. At Caesarea of Palestine, of Saint Eusebius, bishop, a most learned and eloquent historian.” See the Observations.

BRUXELLEN begins: “Near Mainz, of Alban …,” as ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. It continues with the Syracusans [Col. 0179C] purely. Then: “In Africa, of the holy martyrs Quiriacus, Apollinaris, Saturninus, Albinus, Bellicus, Spes, Crisimus, and Primus.” See the Acts. “At Rome, of Saint Demetria, virgin, sister of Saint Juliana [Bibiana], who were daughters of the blessed Faustus the martyr. When she was brought before the impious apostate Julian to be killed for the faith of Christ, she gave up her spirit in confession of the Lord.” It is sufficiently pure concerning Eusebius and Leutfred; at the end it adds: “Likewise of Martin, bishop,” of Tongeren.

HAGENOYEN, pure in the first notice, adds concerning Eusebius: “He loved learning so greatly that he wished to ask nothing from Constantine the Great except that the deeds of the saints be sent to him, in which he could exercise his intellect for the benefit of many.” It continues quite purely concerning Demetria, Quiriacus, Apollinaris, and Leutfred. At the end, concerning Alban of Mainz, it is somewhat longer than the passage we quoted above.

AQUICINCT, concerning Eusebius in third place, as PRATENSIS, [Col. 0179D] except that it adds, “a most learned man.” At the end: “And of Eusebius.” But I should like to know which one.

AMBIANEN has the following concerning Eusebius: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, a man distinguished in faith and doctrine.” See the Observations.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJ.: “Of Theognestus, bishop and martyr, with his companions.” This is probably the same man who is commemorated with Alban and Ursus, as will be discussed more fully below. “Of Martin of Tongeren. Of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea. Of Laufred, abbot, of outstanding holiness. Of Alban the martyr. Of Demetria, virgin and martyr.”

BIGOTIAN, under note D 9: “In the district of Évreux, of Saint Leutfred, abbot.”

The SWEDISH REGISTRY, numbered 428: “At Caesarea of Palestine, the deposition of Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor.” The wording varies, but the matter is the same.

In VATICAN MS 5949, “of Leutfred, Quiriacus, and Apollinaris” is absent. This manuscript is often defective.

ALTEMPS: “At Bourges, of Saint Radulph [Rodulph], bishop and confessor. In Brittany Minor, of Saint Meven, confessor. In the city of Chester, of Saint Walburga, virgin.” She is commemorated on 25 February and in May. See the omitted notices.

FLORENTIN: “In Africa, of the holy martyrs Quiriacus, Apollinaris, Saturninus, Albinus, Bellicius, Crismus, Perseus, and Primus. In the East, of Saints Primus and Januaria.” Add this to the African notices. “Likewise, of the holy martyrs Hierperis, Saturnina, Sergia, Hieria, Saturninus, and Quiriacus.” See these more distinctly arranged in the Acts. The entries concerning Eusebius and Lautfred are pure.

LUXOVIEN: “In the district of Madriacum, of Saint Leufred, confessor.” The form above is better: “Leutfred.”

EDITIO LUBECO.-COL. begins: “Near Cologne [Col. 0180B] Agrippina, in the church of Saint John the Baptist and Cordula: the discovery of Saint Constance, queen, virgin, and martyr, of the company of the eleven thousand holy women, which took place in the year of the Lord 1327.” The text that follows is nearly pure. Then, concerning Alban of Mainz, it differs little from ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. Then: “Likewise at Cologne Agrippina, in the monastery of Saint Martin, the commemoration of the blessed Eliphius, martyr.” He is commemorated on 16 October. “At Trier, of Saint Martin the Second, bishop and confessor, who also presided over the Church of Tongeren.” See the Acts.

GREVEN: “Near Mainz, of Saint Alban, priest and martyr. When he steadfastly preached the truth of the faith to the Goths and Arians, after various tortures they expelled him from the city and beheaded him. Immediately the headless body, taking up its head in its hands, carried it under angelic guidance to the place where it now rests peacefully.” Concerning Eusebius he inserts: “and ecclesiastical historian.” Concerning Martin of Tongeren, as stated immediately above. “Of Monicha, virgin.” Is she one of the Ursuline group? Concerning Eliphius, as above. Likewise concerning Constance of the eleven thousand, who are commemorated on 21 October. “The consecration of Saint James the Less, apostle.” I cannot determine what this means.

MOLAN: “On the same day, of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor of the Church of Tongeren, who converted the Hasbanians and became famous for many miracles.” Rabanus’s words follow:

“At Mainz, the feast of Saint Alban the martyr, who, under the emperor Diocletian, setting out from the island of Nansia, came to Milan with Saint Theonestus and Ursus, and from there, departing with the Lord’s help, reached Gaul. Remaining there in God’s service, he was ready for martyrdom in the Savior’s name. After the blessed Ursus received martyrdom in the city of Augusta, Theonestus reached Mainz with Alban; and while he preached the word of God there, his disciple Alban completed his martyrdom and was buried there near the aforementioned city.”

In later editions [Col. 0180D] it reads: “On the same day, of Saint Martin of the Church of Tongeren, etc. At Mainz, the feast of Saint Alban the martyr. On the twenty-second day, of the most holy martyr Julian of Tarsus.” It is strange that “the twenty-first” is not given. In fact, he is commemorated on neither of these days, but on 16 March, as appears in the omitted notices.

You should also note that in these editions Eusebius has been removed from his proper place, as though relegated to an appendix after the actual Additions. Indeed, in our copy from the year 1583, which belonged to the college of Douai and in which Father John Gravius added manuscript marginal notes here and there, both the notice itself and the annotation concerning Eusebius the historian have been completely erased.]

[Col. 0177]

Near Sicily, in the city of Syracuse, the feast of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Martia. At the city of Caesarea of Palestine, of Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor, a man of outstanding intellect and historian.

[Bouillart: [Note: [Col. 0177B]] Some manuscripts announce Eusebius of Caesarea in different places and with different words. Since Sollerius therefore finds no fault here with Pratensis, why did he place it after several much more recent manuscripts that give the commemoration of Eusebius as follows: “At the city of Caesarea of Palestine, of Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor, a man of outstanding intellect and historian”? Yet if one listens to Sollerius, the shorter and simpler the eulogies, the more Usuardine they are. But this learned and scholarly brevity of Eusebius’s eulogy, preserved in the Pratensis manuscript, had falsely been enlarged in others by the title “confessor”; and it was certain that Pratensis should be disregarded whenever it differed from the others. If only his manuscripts had announced Eusebius like Pratensis, and Pratensis like his manuscripts—ah, how Sollerius would have triumphed! With what praises he would have commended Usuardine simplicity!]

“At Caesarea of Palestine, of Saint Eusebius the historian.” At Rome, of Saint Demetria, virgin. When she was brought before the impious Julian for the sake of the faith of Christ, she gave up her spirit in confession. In the district of Madriacum, of Saint Leutfred, confessor, who, as a monument to his outstanding holiness, is said by his prayers to have brought forth a spring from the earth. In Africa, of Saints Quiriacus and Apollinaris.

### 10 days before the Kalends. Day 22

[Note: [Col. 0181]]

Taken from Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Muneratus, Grevenus, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0181A]]

“Britania” is a scribal error in Pratensis. Much more serious in Tournai is the omission of the words “in the city of Verulamium.” The manuscripts express the name of that city in various ways: Herinien has *Verola*; Antwerp-Major, *Verolamino*; Muneratus, *Verolanno*; Grevenus, *Verolanio*. It was later destroyed, and the famous monastery of Saint Alban was built there; see the Acts.

Grevenus and Molan transpose some words: “bitter blows and tortures” instead of “bitter blows and tortures” in the other order. The latter reads *noluit* (“he did not wish”) instead of *noluerit* (“he would not have wished”). Thus Tournai, for the reading in the text, has “of whom Saint Gregory makes mention.” It then omits *autem* (“however”) after *claruit* (“he became famous”).

I wrote *adversus daemones* (“against demons”) with Herinien and Molan, in which the diphthong is present, and likewise with Antwerp-Major and Grevenus, which lack the diphthong. Pratensis has *adversum demonem* (“against the demon”); Muneratus, *adversum demones* (“against demons”). *Romacianae* and *Romatione* should be regarded as scribal errors.

[Note: [Col. 0181A]]

All the ancient martyrologists without exception eagerly commemorate the Alban whom the English call their Stephen, or Protomartyr. Why he is called Albinus in the Lucense Hieronymian Martyrology and in Ado may perhaps be explained by supposing that the change was made, at least in some of Ado’s manuscripts, through the agency of the Cottonian copies, so that, as Surius relates, Alban of Cologne would not be confused with Alban of Mainz. But you will find this matter examined somewhat more carefully by Henschenius, in his discussion of Saint Albinus of Cologne, beginning on page 172.

Whether this is true or false matters little to us, so long as in all the other sources the British martyr is consistently called Alban. The Hieronymian Martyrologies, and the manuscripts cited by Henschenius that interpolated Bede, do not give the number of his companions with complete uniformity.

The Little Roman Martyrology simply mentions Alban the martyr. Bede adapted for the glory of his own people a distinguished encomium, copied by Rabanus and Ado, and enlarged by Ado with two lines, which Notker transcribed along with the rest. Usuard, always more concise, excerpted only those words, and exactly those words, which our text presents.

These matters belong to our present purpose. Henschenius carefully illustrated and arranged Bede’s and the others’ accounts of Alban, together with the related materials in the *Analecta*. Tillemontius treated them more briefly in French, volume IV, beginning on page 508.

Concerning Paulinus, the Hieronymian Martyrologies plainly state: “In the city of Nola, of Paulinus, bishop and confessor.” The author of the Little Roman Martyrology is somewhat shorter. Bede is silent; Florus, however, composed an eulogy exalting almost exclusively his charity toward the poor.

Ado touches upon the story of Paulinus’s captivity in Africa, nobly endured in place of a widow’s son. Rabanus added only: “of whom Gregory relates in the Book of Dialogues.” Thus Our author, in nearly the same way, took the first part of his eulogy from Ado word for word; the rest of the story is passed over in silence, perhaps because he suspected its truth.

Certainly, it can be abundantly inferred from Florus’s entire composition that this story was unknown to him. You should examine what Papebrochius carefully discussed concerning the whole matter and the life of Paulinus, referring to another Paulinus of Nola, third in order, what Gregory seems to have attributed to the first and most celebrated.

The captivity of Paulinus among the Vandals greatly perplexed all the learned authors who illustrated his life, so much so that some, with Pagi, under the year 431, no. 54, regard it as almost legendary. For us, the authority of Gregory the Great carries greater weight, and Papebrochius supplied a not implausible means of preserving it [Col. 0182B]. The editor of Paulinus’s works, D. Le Brun, was not far from this view, nor does he seem to have rejected it so strongly, in dissertation 7, page 141, no. 4.

Tillemontius, after weighing many arguments on both sides, leaves the matter undecided in volume XIV, beginning on page 733, after setting out Paulinus’s life at length in the same volume, pages 1–146.

Meanwhile, all the points of Usuard’s text remain safe for us, expressed with sufficient caution. Wandalbert elegantly sang of the two saints who constitute our first and second notices:

> Alban on the tenth day, by his praise, defends the Britons,  
> And Paulinus illumines Nola by merit and by name.

The final notice is subject to several difficulties, explained in the Acts, especially concerning the identity of the one Nicetas, whom Baronius seems to have divided into two. Otherwise, it too proceeds from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, with the name *Niceus* changed to *Nicea*, not *Nicetius*, as Notker gives it.

Our author left entirely unchanged what he had found in Ado. Hence it is clear that almost the whole of our text here too flowed from Ado, though otherwise it is purely and simply Usuardine.]

[Note: [Col. 0181C]]

ROSWEYD inserts in the penultimate place: “Likewise at Antioch, of Julian and 815 others.” See the Acts.

PULSAN begins: “The feast of the blessed Paulinus of Nola, bishop and confessor. In Britain, of Saint Alban the martyr. Who in the time of Diocletian,” etc., up to “he was beheaded. But when he fell to the ground, the eyes of the man who struck him fell out as well. Likewise of Saint James son of Alphaeus, apostle.” See 1 May. “On the same day, of Saint Nicea, bishop.”

ANTWERP and MAX.-LUBECK omit the second part of Paulinus’s eulogy. At the end they add: “Near Alexandria, on the mountain called Ararat, the passion of ten thousand martyrs.” I confess that I do not know what the words added in MAX.-LUBECK, “numbering 660,” mean.

[Col. 0182C] ANTUERP.-MAX., LEYDEN., LOVAN., and EDIT. ULTRAJ.-BELG. place Saint Paulinus first, omitting even the words beginning “he became famous,” etc. Then comes Alban, whom they call Albinus, purely. In third place: “Near Alexandria, on the mountain called Ararat, of ten thousand holy martyrs.” At the end, concerning Nicea, purely.

ULTRAJECTIN, similar to those already mentioned, adds concerning the ten thousand: “All of whom, together with their leader Acacius, were crucified under the emperor Antoninus; after prayer had been poured out to the Lord by those devoutly celebrating their passion, and that prayer had been heard through a divine response sent from above [a sign of legendary invention], they passed to the heavenly kingdoms.”

ALBERG and DANIC differ scarcely at all from ULTRAJ., but at the end omit “of Nicea,” in the Romacian manuscript, etc.

[Col. 0183A] CENTULEN: “In Britain, of Saint Alban the martyr. At Nola in Campania, of Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor, who, following in the footsteps of Christ the Lord, handed himself over into slavery in place of a widow’s son and, with the Lord working with him, restored many to freedom. On the same day, of the blessed Nicea, bishop of the city of Romatiana.”

BRUXELLEN begins with the ten thousand, omitting only “after prayer had been poured out,” etc., which I said was a mark of legendary invention. It continues: “At Jerusalem, the feast of 480 holy martyrs.” Read 1,480, and see what is said about them in the Acts. “On the same day, the feast of 989 martyrs.” See the Acts also. “In Britain, the feast of Saint Albinus,” etc., with an eulogy taken almost entirely from Bede, which you will find in the Acts.

Concerning Paulinus, it adds to the words of the text: “But especially because, when he subjected himself to a barbarian’s slavery in place of a widow’s captive son, he freely received all the captives of his city. And the deposition of the blessed Nicea, etc. Likewise of James son of Alphaeus, apostle [Col. 0183B] and bishop of Jerusalem.” See 1 May to determine how these statements can be reconciled.

HAGENOYEN, calling him Albinus, is pure concerning Alban; it enlarges Paulinus’s captivity story and then constructs another lengthy account of the ten thousand on Mount Ararat, from fabulous Acts, which does not deserve to be reproduced here. The final notice is absent.

VICTORIN and the SWEDISH REGISTRY, under note no. 130, add at the end: “Likewise, of Saint Consortia, virgin; likewise of Saint James the apostle, brother of John, who was beheaded at Herod’s command.” He is commemorated on 25 July. “Likewise, of 1,807 holy martyrs, who were deposited in the baptistery, whose names God has in the book of the living.” Are these the companions of Saint Alban?

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-UTRAJECT: “Of Walfrid, martyr in Frisia.” He is commemorated on 3 December. “Of Paulinus, bishop and confessor of Nola. Of the ten thousand martyrs who suffered under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus.”

The SWEDISH REGISTRY, no. 428: “On the same day, the feast of ten thousand martyrs crowned on a single day.”

UGHELLIAN adds at the end: “Near Alexandria, on the mountain called Ararat, the passion of ten thousand martyrs.” See what we said concerning HAGENOYEN.

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, of Acacius with his companions—namely, 9,999.” The same martyrs on Mount Ararat are meant.

FLORENTIN: “Near Antioch, of the holy martyrs Ganthalica, Julian, and Graptus the martyr. Likewise, of the holy martyrs Rufus and Albinus with 999 others.” See all these matters more distinctly in the Acts.

LUGDUNEN, Saint Stephen’s: “In the territory of Aix, of Saint Consortia, virgin.” See the following manuscript.

CAUDIACENIS PRIORY: “In the territory of Aix, the feast of Saint Consortia, virgin, daughter of Eucherius, bishop of the city of Lyon.” She occurs several times.

REMENS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “In the district of Odominus, above the river Marne, in a village called Duromannus, the deposition of Saint Novica, virgin.” I have found nothing about her in the omitted notices or elsewhere; whether something has been incorrectly written, I do not know.

[Col. 0184A] EDITIO LUBECO.-COL. is moderately altered in the text. At the end: “At the monastery of Cluny, of Saint Consortia, virgin. Near Alexandria, on the mountain called Ararat,” etc., with a certain abridgment of the Acts. It is better to consult the Acts themselves or GREVEN.

BELIN, in third place: “Near Alexandria,” etc., “of ten thousand crucified martyrs. On the same day, of Saint Consortia, virgin.” Then, concerning “Nicea,” whom in another edition it calls “Phocas,” purely. There also: “Likewise of Saint James son of Alphaeus, apostle.”

GREVENUS gives a longer account of the Crucified:

“Near Alexandria, on Mount Ararat, of the ten thousand holy martyrs. All of them, together with their leader Agathius, were tortured under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus in imitation of Christ and hung upon separate crosses. After they had poured out a prayer for those devoutly celebrating their passion, they gave their souls back to heaven. There appeared there the signs that had been seen at the time of Christ’s Passion: for there was a great earthquake, the rocks were split, and the sun was darkened. Among them the more distinguished were Hermolaus the bishop, Alexander, Mark, Eliadis, Diaconarius, and Theodolus.

“Likewise at Alexandria, of Saint Rufinus the martyr; of Julian and many others. In Frisia, near Groningen, the translation of Walfrid the martyr, his wife Therasia, and their son.” We have said that they are commemorated on 3 December. “Of Galganus, confessor.” He too is referred to that day. “At the monastery of Cluny, of Saint Consortia, virgin,” concerning whom see above.

MOLAN: “Near Alexandria,” etc., as in BELINUS. Likewise concerning Consortia. Then: “Of Saint Ortrudis, virgin.” Then in smaller type: “Her body rests in the monastery of Sithiu, in the town of Saint-Omer.”

Concerning Walfrid, etc., he has GREVENUS’s words. “Likewise of blessed memory, John Fisher, bishop of Rochester and martyr, who, after having for many years conducted himself as a true bishop through the holiness of his life and his diligence in teaching, both by voice and in writing, and through remarkable generosity toward the needy and kindness toward students, was committed to a very long imprisonment because of his detestation of adultery; and at last, for the unity of the faith and of the Church, which he defended, receiving an axe at his neck, he departed to the heavenly kingdoms on 22 June 1535. Thomas More had preceded him by several days, shining with the same crown of martyrdom.”

Other editions insert into the text in italic type what Ado added to Bede: “At that time,” etc.

At the end: “In the district of Hainaut, above the river Haine, the deposition of Saint Domitian, confessor. He was the inseparable companion of the blessed Landelin on his pilgrimage and was established by him as a hermit in the same place. Glorious for many virtues, he passed to Christ and now rests happily with his master at Crespin.” He was treated on 15 June.

Concerning the Crucified, as above. “On the same day, of Saint Consortia, virgin, at the monastery of Cluny. At the monastery of Sithiu, of Saint Ortrudis, virgin. On the twenty-second day, of Saint Eusebius, hieromartyr, bishop of the Samo­satians,” read “of the Samosatans.” Then [Col. 0184D], in smaller type, concerning Walfrid, as above. Concerning John Fisher, as he himself writes, somewhat more briefly but with the same meaning.]

[Col. 0181]

In Britain, of Saint Alban the martyr, who in the city of Verulamium, in the time of Diocletian, after bitter blows and tortures, was beheaded. One of the soldiers also suffered with him because, though ordered to strike him, he refused. At Nola in Campania, the feast of Blessed Paulinus, bishop and confessor, whom Saint Gregory mentions in the book of the *Dialogues*. He was distinguished not only by learning and abundant holiness of life, but also by power against demons. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Nicea, bishop of the city of Romatiana.

### 9 days before the Kalends. Day 23

[Note: [Col. 0183D]]

This is the reading of Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck, Rosweyd, Muneratus, Belin, Greven, and Molan. The manuscripts of middling rank agree: Antwerp-Max., Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, Danish, and the Utrecht-Belgian edition.

[Note: [Col. 0185A]]

In Greven and Molan, the epithet *impious* is absent before Julian. Rosweyd wrongly gives the opposite of *unheard-of*, namely *heard-of*. Most and the better manuscripts write *simulacrum*; it has therefore been retained in the text. *Decolari* in Antwerp-Major is an obvious copyist’s error. Nearly all manuscripts read *Utrina*, and some *Utina*; both are incorrect. Rosweyd came closest to the true name, reading *Sutria*. *Sutrina* would be better written, but the manuscripts must be followed.

Belin’s first edition read “of Saint Felix the First,” but this was rightly corrected in the second edition. The prefect’s name is variously given: *Turtius* in Pratensis; *Trucius* in Antwerp-Major; *Turgius* in Greven and Molan. With the rest, and correctly, we have written *Turcius*. For *emitteret*, Utrecht reads *emisit*. We have spoken elsewhere of *Britania* and *Britanniis*.

There is greater difficulty in establishing the name of the holy queen and virgin herself. Antwerp-Major calls her *Edeldride*; Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and the later manuscripts, *Edeltrudis*; Rosweyd, *Ediltruda*; Belin, *Getrudis*. In the Acts she is *Ethelreda*, *Etheldreda*, or *Aetheldritha*. With Pratensis, Muneratus, Greven, and Molan, we give *Ediltrudis*; and with those same manuscripts we add only the title *Virgin*, although most of the others, following Bede and Ado, add also *Queen*. Antwerp-Major, Belin, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, etc., read ten instead of eleven; and Belin omits “when … she was.” Rosweyd reads “it was discovered.”

[Note: [Col. 0185B]]

The vigil of the Lord’s Forerunner, in the ancient Martyrologies, is expressed rather rarely. Bede is the first to announce it, but only after reporting the elogium of Ediltrudis. Rabanus follows him in wording and arrangement. Ado, however, begins his text from this point. The Little Roman Martyrology records only one commemoration today: “Saint John the priest, buried on the old Salarian Way.” The Viennese martyrologist adds a few details, composing a brief elogium, translated—as is customary—from Notker; but our author has mutilated it in the part where it says that his body was collected by the blessed priest Concordius and buried near the Martyr Assemblies, as will again be indicated from Molanus in the Additions. Here we shall note briefly that the Acts have perished, though Ado must have seen them in order to extract his elogium from them. What Papebrochius assumes incorrectly at the beginning of his Commentary must also be corrected: he supposes that Usuard had not copied Ado’s Martyrology, contrary to what we have shown extensively in our preface and throughout this work. More accurate are the discussions there concerning John’s relics, especially his head.

As for the material contained in our text [Col. 0185C], it is all taken from the aforementioned Ado: for example, the notice of Saint Ediltrude, who is reported here after Felix; of the ancient Martyrologists no one except Usuard mentions him, and even Usuard marked the place incorrectly, writing Utrina instead of the city of Sutrina, as was sufficiently indicated above. Papebrochius considers the Acts of that martyr Felix genuine, and nearly capable of being regarded as judicial records; he believes that, joined and connected with the Acts of Saint Mustiola, they had guided Usuard.

At first sight I had almost doubted whether that announcement should truly be attributed to Usuard, since I know that he very rarely commemorates foreign saints—that is, saints sought outside Spain or Gaul—whom he had not found recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies or in Ado. The silence of the two distinguished codices, Heriniensis and Tornacensis, also contributed to the doubt: in them there is absolutely no mention of this martyr of Sutrina. Yet one must yield to the uniform agreement of the other codices, and the more readily because, unless I am mistaken, I have found Papebrochius’s conjecture to be true. Usuard must have obtained the Acts of Felix and Mustiola from some source; from them he reports Felix on this day and Mustiola on 3 July, although they are unknown to the other martyrologists and omitted by the cited Heriniensis and Tornacensis codices.

You may consult the Acts themselves, which are certainly substantial and worthy of belief, although they may perhaps require some modest correction. Tillemont praises them in volume IV, beginning at page 351, and the other critics have little to criticize in them. We shall provide more from the Acts on 3 July, when Mustiola must be discussed.

For the present, let Usuard’s announcement concerning Felix stand, as well as the following one concerning Ediltrude, which passed from Bede into Ado and from Ado into our text [Col. 0186C], with almost the sole difference that our author omitted the title “Queen,” which Notker preserves. Notker, however, incorrectly reads “ten years” instead of “eleven”; in this he has as followers all the codices of later character, in which we observed above that this error occurs. Thus we present Usuard genuine and complete.

Papebrochius has illustrated the sufficiently extensive Life of Ediltrudis, or Etheldreda, and the other matters relating to her have been explained in the Commentary. There remains Wandalbert’s verse concerning her:

> On the ninth [day], Ediltrude shines forth from English stock.

] [Note: [Col. 0185C]

We have already said above that the HERINIENSIS and TORNACENSIS codices are defective at this point.

PULSANEN. speaks as follows: “The vigil of the most blessed John the Baptist. In Britain, Saint Gediltrude, virgin and queen, whose body, when it had been buried for eleven” etc., correctly. “In the city of Nicomedia, Saints Aviticus, Agapitus, Aristion, Emeritus, Aletus, with seventy-nine others.” This is again taken from the Hieronymian Martyrology. But the names are expressed differently by the others; concerning them, see the Acts.

CENTULEN.: “The vigil of Saint John the Baptist. At Rome, Saint John the priest and martyr, in the time of the apostate Julian. In Britain, Saint Eadtrudis, virgin and queen, whose body, after it had been buried for eleven years, was found incorrupt.” 

BRUXELLEN. writes “Utina,” even worse, instead of “Utrina.” See what we said above. Then: “At Nicomedia, Saints Aviticus, Capitaton, Abricio, with eighty-two others.” Concerning them, see the Acts. “In Britain, the deposition of Saint Ediltrudis, virgin and queen of the English. Having been married to three men, and having sent them before her to God, she remained a virgin; and her body, after eleven years of burial, was found incorrupt. Also, the deposition of Blessed Mary of Oegnies in Brabant, whose legend Master James of Vitry, later cardinal, composed.”

HAGENOYEN. inserts here, in third place, the notice which he had omitted on the preceding day: “On this day, the deposition of Saint Nicaea, bishop of the city of Romatiana.” It is followed by the notice of “Felix,” correctly. Then: “On the same day at Lyons, Saint Consortia, virgin.” This too belongs to the preceding day. Concerning Ediltrude, he has the same text as the ANTUERP.-MAX. codices, and so forth.

[Col. 0186D] MATRIC-CARTUS-ULTRAJECT.: “The vigil of John the priest and martyr.” In the codex itself, “vigil” is joined with the following announcement, so that one might almost doubt whether it should not refer to John the priest. Yet it is clear from other sources that John the Baptist is intended. “Ediltrudis, virgin and queen, in Britain. After eleven years of burial, she was found incorrupt. Avitus the abbot, of wondrous holiness.” The saint commemorated today is “Avitus,” the martyr of Nicomedia. I do not know whether this is the one celebrated on 17 June.

CAMBERIEN. of Saint Mary of the Conventuals: “On the same day, Saint Bonitus, bishop and confessor.” I find no further information about him in the Omissions.

FLORENTIN.: “At Nicomedia, Saints Aviticus and seventy-three others.” See above and in the Acts.

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION, which is sufficiently pure in the text, adds at the end: “At Alexandria, the passion of very many martyrs, many of whom, with their ears and noses cut off, and the tips of their hands and the other members of their bodies amputated, happily died.” [Col. 0187A] There is no mention of these in the Omissions. Perhaps they survive from a larger number?

GREVEN.: “At Alexandria, the passion of very many martyrs,” etc., as above, except for the final word, which here is “died.” “At Nicomedia, the passion of the holy virgins Pistis and Elpis, and of their mother Agape, of Avitus, Capito, and seventy-eight others.” Here GREVENUS joins separate notices together, as he does elsewhere more than once. Concerning the virgins, taken from Notker, see the Omissions; concerning the Nicomedians, enough has been said. “Hidulf, bishop and confessor.” If the bishop of Trier is meant, he is celebrated on 11 July. “In the diocese of Liège, the holy memory of Mary of Oegnies, whose most holy Life was written by James of Vitry, bishop of Tusculum and cardinal, a man worthy of God. Hezekiah and Josiah, kings of Judah, according to the Catalogue of the Saints. The translation of Saint Anthimus, bishop and martyr.” See the Omissions concerning these.

MOLAN. adds John in Italic type to the text, from Ado: “And his body was collected and buried by the blessed priest Concordius near the Martyr Assemblies.” If I am not mistaken, this means a place where many martyrs were buried. See Papebrochius’s Commentary, where the distinction between “Martyr Assemblies” and “cemeteries” is established, page 482. At the end: “At Binche, Hidulf, duke of Lorraine.” Then, in smaller type: “Fibronia, virgin and martyr, during the persecution of the emperor Diocletian.” See 25 June. “In the diocese of Liège, the holy memory of Mary of Oegnies, whose most holy Life was written by James of Vitry, a man worthy of God,” etc., as in GREVEN. Later editions have the same material in the text. At the end, however: “At Lobbes, Hidulf, duke and confessor. On the twenty-third day, Saint Agrippina, martyr.” Then in different type: “At Oignies, the passing of Blessed Mary, who was enclosed there. At Cambrai, in the year 1076, in the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre, Lord Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, died.”]

[Col. 0183]

The vigil of Saint John the Baptist. On the same day, Saint John the priest, whom the impious Julian ordered beheaded without a hearing on the old Salarian Way, before an image of the sun. In the Tuscan city of Utrina, Saint Felix the priest, whose mouth the prefect Turtius ordered to be beaten with a stone for so long that he gave up the Spirit. In Britain, the birth-day of Saint Ediltrudis, virgin, whose body, after it had been buried for eleven years, was found incorrupt.

8 Kalends. Day 24. [Note: [Col. 0187]

Thus the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp-Major, Muneratus, Belinus, Greven, and Molanus codices.]

[Note: [Col. 0187B]

In Antwerp-Major and Belinus, the particle “and” is missing between “Baptist” and “Forerunner.” It could indeed be omitted, but it must be retained because of the constant reading of the other codices. They write “in the Parisian territory,” namely the Pratensis, Muneratus, and Belinus; the others, as in the text, are better. Muneratus omitted “village.” There is now great variety in the name of the place and in the names of the two martyrs. The place is pronounced “Christolico” especially in Antwerp-Major, “Ristoilo” in Greven, “Christoilo” by the others, and “Cristolio” by Muneratus and Belinus. This is correct and, in my opinion, should be written in precisely this way. Yet the highly approved Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, and Molanus codices, with the letters transposed, read “Cristoilo,” and we have retained that form in the text [Col. 0188B]. Again, the names of the martyrs are most probably Agoardus and Aglibertus, or Agilbertus, as Molanus and Muneratus have them. In Antwerp-Major and Greven we read “Agoadi and Gilberti”; in Belinus, “Agovardi”; in others, “Agaodi”; in the Tornacensis, “Agoaldi.” I prefer the form of the Pratensis and Heriniensis, where the names are “Agoadi and Gliberti.” You may choose whichever form you prefer. There is nearly the same variation in Augustodunum. We used “Augustoduno” with Antwerp-Major, Muneratus, and Belinus; in Pratensis it is “Augustiduno”; in Tornacensis, “Augustiduni”; in Heriniensis, Greven, and Molanus, “Augustuduni.” The form in the text is best, unless I am mistaken.]

[Note: [Col. 0187B]

The present text of Ado in the Martyrology is confined to these few words: “The Nativity of the Lord’s Forerunner,” as Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Rabanus likewise read. Ado’s discourse among the feasts of the Apostles is longer. Yet it seems entirely certain that everywhere the Nativity according to the flesh is indicated, namely the special prerogative of the Forerunner, celebrated in the Church from the earliest age. According to Florentius, drawing from Ambrose through Peter de Natalibus, it is asserted that this occurred to no human being except the Savior and his Forerunner. This was, of course, at a time when the Nativity of the Mother of God had not yet been consecrated with a particular cult; but this is not the place to discuss the institution of that feast.

Wandalbert’s little verse also plainly denotes John’s Nativity:

> On the eighth day John the Baptist is honored as born.

The Hieronymian copies seem to indicate another Nativity, or birthday—or, if you prefer, the deposition of the body together with the head—when they read: “In the province of Palestine, in the city of Sebaste, the birth-day of Saint John the Baptist.” The very same words are repeated on 29 August, when his Beheading is commemorated by the others and by the whole Church today, as will more suitably be explained there from Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and our author. [Col. 0187D]

If anyone wishes to inquire further into the celebrated feast of the Forerunner of the newly born Christ—or rather into the feasts collected together in some fashion—he will find enough in the Acts today to satisfy him completely. For the present, as regards our text, it is clear that Usuard inserted only the name of John the Baptist above his predecessors. Notker’s encomium is more extensive and includes many other matters concerning the place of his birth, his death, and so forth. But these and similar matters may more conveniently be examined on the aforementioned day, 29 August, unless they have already been sufficiently discussed by Papebrochius on this day, throughout chapter II, from page 698 to page 711. These points had to be indicated in passing. It is neither the place nor the purpose of our work to raise further questions that are disputed among scholars. We began to say something on 24 February. Florentius’s Exercise 13, beginning at page 785, and another beginning at page 857, as well as Tillemont, volume I, beginning at page 82 and in the notes beginning at page 482, together with Papebrochius’s studies, may be consulted by inquisitive readers; perhaps they will meanwhile suggest new material to us, which we can examine more accurately on 29 August or even on 24 September.

The following commemoration of the martyrs of Cristolium belongs exclusively to Usuard; it is recorded by no other Martyrologist, whether ancient or contemporary. We have given their names in various forms above, and still more forms appear in the Acts. No one doubts their ancient cult; everything concerning their date is uncertain, for the commonly circulated Acts are not such that anything definite can be extracted from them. See Papebrochius’s annotation, to which the learned Frenchmen readily subscribe.

The Hieronymian copies speak of Simplicius: “In the city of Augustodunum, Saint Simplicius,” and Rabanus wrote nearly the same. Usuard and Notker added the title “bishop,” both using almost the same words. See Henschenius’s Commentary and the Life published there from Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors.

There remained in the praised Hieronymian Martyrologies the birth-day of John the apostle and evangelist. Rabanus calls it his “sleep,” Notker his “falling asleep,” and gives a fuller account there; our author more prudently postponed these details to the day on which his memory is celebrated more festively, 27 December. Otherwise, the matters represented in our little column are straightforward, and are presented by Usuard with the greatest simplicity and truth.]

[Note: [Col. 0189A]

ROSWEYD. adds to a fairly pure text at the end: “At Rome, Festus and Luceia, with twenty-two others.” See the Acts.

PULSANEN.: “The Nativity of the Lord’s Forerunner John in the Jordan. In the Palestinian territory of Ephesus, the falling asleep of Saint John the apostle and evangelist. At Rome, Saints Festus and Lucia with twenty-two others. In the city of Augustodunum, the deposition of Saint Simplicius, bishop and confessor.”

ANTWERP, MAX-LUBECK, and UGHELLIAN omit the Cristolienses and add at the end: “At Rome, Fistus, Luceia, with twenty-two others.”

ANTWERP, MAXIMUS, and LOUVAIN, after “Lord,” add: “Whose nativity, austerity of life, preaching, and passion the sacred evangelical history reveals.” Then: “At Augustodunum,” etc., correctly. Next: “At Rome, Saint Systus [read: Festus] and Luceia with twenty-two others. In the Parisian territory,” etc., fairly correctly.

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION agree with the two immediately cited, but before the final notice insert: “Also, Saint Prosper, bishop and distinguished teacher.” Whoever this Prosper is, see in the Acts. “On the same day, the translation of Saint Lebuinus, priest and confessor.” He is indeed celebrated at Antwerp and elsewhere on this day, but his feast-day is 12 November.

ALBERG and DANIC are similar at the end, except that they omit the Cristolienses.

CENTULEN.: “The Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist, whose immeasurable dignity of holiness our Savior Christ the Lord commends in his own words, saying: ‘Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist.’ At Augustodunum, Saint Simplicius, bishop and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. has John the Baptist as in ANTUERP.-MAX., and so forth. In second place: “In the Palestinian territory of Ephesus, the falling asleep of Blessed John the apostle and evangelist. In the Parisian territory, the passion of Saints Agaodus and Glibertus with,” etc. The notice of Simplicius is correct. At the end: “At Anderlacum, the elevation of Saint Guido, confessor.” His feast-day is 12 September.

HAGENOYEN. after “Lord” continues: “At whose nativity the blessed Virgin Mary, the Mother of the Lord, was present, having the Son of God in her womb. His nativity, austerity of life, preaching, service concerning the person of the Lord, and passion the sacred evangelical history reveals. This man, while still in his mother’s womb,” etc., as is set out more fully in the Acts. He is correct in the second and third announcements. He then continues: “At Rome: Saints Systus and Luceia with twenty-two others. At Mechelen in Brabant, Rumoldus, bishop and martyr.” He is celebrated on 1 July, as we said above.

VICTORIN and REG. SUEC., no. 130, add at the end: “On the same day, Saint Febronia.” See the following day.

MATRIC-CARTUS-ULTRAJECT.: “The Nativity of John the Baptist. Rumoldus, martyr, at Mechelen. Simplicius, renowned bishop and confessor.”

BIGOTIAN., marked page 5: “At Rome, Festus, Lucia, with twenty-two others.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949, Agoardus, Aglibertus, and Simplicius are absent. The following is added: “In Syria, Saint Febronia, virgin and martyr, who, in the times of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, after many kinds of tortures, was finally killed by beheading, by the solemn order of the judge.” [Col. 0190A]

ALTEMPS: “At Auxerre, Saint Hiericus, monk.” In the Acts he is called “Ericus,” and his life is illustrated there.

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, Saints Festus and Lucia, martyrs, with twenty-two others.” They recur frequently.

BURDEGALEN.: “In the Parisian territory, in the village of Christolium, the passion of Saints Agaodus and Gumbertus, with countless others of both sexes.” As in the text.

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “At Amiens, the discovery of the body of Saint Quentin the martyr.” He is celebrated on 31 October, where this translation too will be discussed.

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION, after “Lord,” continues: “The blessed Virgin Mary was present at this nativity, and with her virginal hands lifted John himself from the ground. His nativity,” etc. Then the notice of Simplicius, correctly. “At Rome, Saints Systus and Lucia, virgin, martyrs, with twenty-two others.” The notice of the Cristolienses is correct. Then: “At Poitiers, Saints Pectina, Matrina, and Columba, virgins and martyrs.” See the better-formed names in the Omissions. “The discovery of Saint Quentin the martyr.” Concerning this, see above.

GREVEN.: “The deposition of Saint John the evangelist. At Rome, Saints Systus and Lucia with many others. At Poitiers, Saints Pectina, Martina, and Columba, virgins and martyrs. At Auxerre, Heyri [Ericus], confessor. The discovery of Saint Quentin the martyr.” Reference is made to his feast-day, 31 October.

MOLAN. inserts much concerning John the Baptist in different type, which is arranged better in the Acts. At the end: “At Mechelen, the passion of Saint Rumoldus, bishop and martyr. At Lobbes, Saint Theodulf, bishop and confessor.” Then in smaller type:

“While his body, returning to Lobbes, had escaped the borders of France and had also reached Valenciennes through the district of Cambrai, it began to shine with the light of miracles. Therefore the inhabitants of that fisc-town vowed to dedicate a church in honor of their divinely appointed physician and resolved to retain Saint Theodulf among themselves forever. At length, when our people were secretly transporting the holy body to Lobbes without any display, it was almost forcibly held back at the Scheldt by those who had been cured.”

“The birth-day of Saints Urbasius, Theodorus, and Menedemus, martyrs, with seventy-seven others, concerning whom see the Tripartite History, book VII, chapter 30.” These are rightly omitted in later editions, since they are celebrated on 5 September. “On the same day, Saint Romula, virgin, concerning whom blessed Gregory speaks in a homily and in the Dialogues, book IV, chapter 15.” Reference is made to 23 July. “Also, Saint Lupicinus, hermit and confessor, concerning whom blessed Gregory of Tours writes.” Thus far the first edition. In the others, the text alone adds what we reported above from ANTUERP.-MAX. and others: “Whose nativity, austerity of life,” etc. At the end: “At Auxerre, Saint Heir, a most holy man. In the Poitevin district, Saint Pecinna, virgin.” She is celebrated separately from Macrina [Col. 0190D] and Columba, on the following day. “At Hugardia, the birth-day of Saint Odwinus, priest and martyr.” Reference is made to 25 June, on which day he is celebrated there with ecclesiastical office.]

[Col. 0187]

The Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist and the Lord’s Forerunner. In the Parisian territory, in the village of Christolium, the passion of Saints Agaodus and Glibertus, with countless others of both sexes. At Augustodunum, the deposition of Simplicius, bishop.

7 Kalends. Day 25. [Note: [Col. 0191]

The four codices—Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Greven, and Molanus—are correct.]

[Note: [Col. 0191A]

Molanus correctly writes Pyrrhi Beroea as two separate words, as Henschenius explained. In Greven it is Periberoea. We follow the two others and nearly all the rest, as in the text. Among the many errors of Antwerp-Major, the first is “Blessed Peter the apostle” instead of “Paul.” The second is “Gallicanus the priest” instead of “martyr.” Something similar is found in Heriniensis, which reads “Constantius” instead of “Constantine,” and “famous” instead of “dear.” Again, Antwerp-Major has “and a virgin of Christ,” where one should read “and the martyrs of Christ.” Likewise, it has “is converted” instead of “was converted,” and “they saw” instead of “they might see.” It also reads “coming” in place of “and Consul,” and “pouring” instead of “pouring out,” and so forth. We spoke above of *contempneret* (“might despise”). All the codices write “he made him a martyr of Christ”; in some, such as Heriniensis, the word “himself” was added above by a later hand. Molanus wished to show greater wisdom than the others and altered the text as follows: “he becomes a martyr of Christ.” The syntax is thereby improved, but at the cost of the simplicity characteristic of Usuard. The codices have “Lucia”; it would be better written “Luceia.”]

[Note: [Col. 0191B]

The whole genesis of the present text proceeds from the Little Roman Martyrology through Ado, with the order of the announcements preserved entirely. Thus the compiler of that Martyrology begins: “At Pyrrhiberoea, Sopater, a disciple of Paul.” Ado added very little to these words, and our author added nothing to Ado, being content to transcribe his words. This is once again someone from among the disciples of Christ or the apostles, entered on this day by the author of the Little Roman Martyrology, perhaps arbitrarily, and with a confused name: for that man of Beroea should be called Sopater, not Sosipater, as Henschenius judges in his historical-critical Sylloge—unless perhaps the same person is known under both names, as Tillemont seems to think in volume I, page 565. If Henschenius was mistaken in anything, the matter may be restored in the Acts on 12 July, when we shall discuss Naso, who was marked by our Martyrologists on that day in place of Jason or Mnason.

From the earlier part of the Acts of Saints John and Paul, Ado weaves a lengthy history of Gallicanus [Col. 0191C]. Our author condenses it—though more extensively than usual—while everywhere preserving the limits of his predecessor. It is polished, elegant, and unusually long, so that one may wonder how that entire history of John and Paul, circulated under the impressive name of a certain Terentianus and known also to Bede, could have pleased Ado and Usuard so remarkably; this will be clear on the following day. Its antiquity, and the fact that it is earlier than the eighth century, are therefore completely certain. No one who has examined it will dare pronounce it wholly genuine. See Papebrochius’s Commentary and Tillemont’s note in volume VII, beginning at page 719.

But enough of this; let us return to our little column [Col. 0192B]. It has the same source, the same channel, and the same words throughout by which the final announcement is expressed; hence Usuard’s simplicity is entirely clear, with the translation of Saint Eligius excluded, since it is wrongly attributed to the text in the Pratensis and Muneratus codices.

As for what should truly be thought about Lucia or Luceia and her companions, it may certainly be doubted, on account of the very divergent readings of the Hieronymian and other codices. The Hieronymian codices themselves are not entirely consistent: on the preceding day they mention Festus and Lucia with twenty-two companions; on this day, Luceia virgin and Aceia virgin, without companions; on the following day, Luceia virgin and Diogenes; and finally, on 1 July, Luceia virgin and Auceia king with eight or nine companions. Thus one finds at least four Luceias, or Lucias, multiplied beyond what is reasonable, unless I am mistaken—and multiplied still further if the texts of the individual Hieronymian codices are compared more scrupulously with one another. The others, diverging in different directions, do not shed light on these obscurities. Nor is this the place for a fuller investigation of the matter. See what Papebrochius established in the Acts with whatever probability was possible; or consult Florentius, if you wish. Meanwhile, Usuard’s text is secure. In the part concerning Luceia, Wandalbertus does not depart far from Usuard’s view, in these verses:

> By sevenfold love Luceia adorns Rome,
>
> Glad through Scampio, with twice ten and two martyrs;
>
> Among them Aceia shines with the honor of a companion.

Perhaps “Campio” should be read, so that the word means “champion” or “victress.”]

[Note: [Col. 0191D]

PRATENS. adds at the end: “Also, the translation of Saint Eligius, bishop and confessor.” He is celebrated on 1 December.

TORNACEN. omits more than half of Gallicanus’s elogium, for it has only as far as “he was converted.” The rest of the text is correct.

ROSWEYD. lacks the final announcement; in its place it substitutes: “At Deventer, the translation of Radbodus, bishop and confessor.” His feast-day is 29 November. “There also, Lebuinus, priest.” This is deferred to 12 November.

MUNERAT. also lacks Luceia. It adds: “On the same day, the translation of the body of Blessed Eligius, priest [bishop] and confessor.”

PULSANEN.: “The birth-day of Saints Gaudentius, Felix, and Agapitus.” They are deferred to 26 June. “On the same day, Saint Amandus, confessor.” He is celebrated with “Domnolenus” at Périgueux. “At Rome, Saint Lucia, virgin, with twenty-two others.”]

[Col. 0192D] In ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBECK, and UCHELLIAN, Luceia is omitted, because they thought they had dealt with her on the preceding day.

ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and the UTRECHT–BELGIAN EDITION reproduce the entire text; but after Gallicanus they insert the following: “Also, Saint Prosper, bishop and distinguished teacher.” Which Prosper this is, see in the Acts. “On the same day, the translation of Saint Lebuinus, priest and confessor.” He is indeed celebrated at Antwerp and elsewhere on this day, but his feast-day is 12 November.

ALBERG and DANIC agree through Prosper, inclusively, omitting Lebuinus and Luceia.

LOUVAIN truncates Gallicanus’s elogium, immediately connecting after “he was converted”: “But he himself,” etc. In the rest it resembles ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others.

CENTULEN. is correct in the first announcement, then continues: “On the same day, Saint Eligius of Noyon, bishop and confessor. At Alexandria, Saint Gallicanus, illustrious and most noble duke of the Romans, who, being of such dignity that he sought the daughter of the great Constantine in marriage, by divine grace going before him, became a Christian while fighting in the war against the Scythians, and rejecting all the pleasures of the world, chose the monastic life. Finally, struck with a sword by the count Arantianus, he ended his life in martyrdom.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “At Noyon, the translation of Saint Eligius, bishop and confessor.” The entire text follows. Then: “And the birth-day of Saints Gaudentius, Felix, and Agapitus, martyrs.” Concerning them, see above. “On the same day, Saints Radbodus and Adalbertus.” This is correct for today; concerning the other, I spoke above. “Also, Saint Prosper, bishop and distinguished teacher.”

HAGENOYEN. after a fairly pure text adds: “On the same day, at the city of Turin, Maximus, bishop and confessor.” In a later hand, in the margin: “Also, Saint Prosper, bishop and distinguished teacher.” See what was said above.

AQUICINCT. has “twenty-two women” instead of “twenty-two.” It then adds: “Also, the deposition of Saint Nicetius, priest and confessor.” He is unknown. Could this perhaps have intruded in place of Lebuinus?

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The translation of Saint Radbodus, bishop of Utrecht. And of Saint Lebuinus at Deventer. Also, Adalbertus the confessor. Luceia, virgin, and Ancea [Aceia], martyr, with their companions. Gallicanus the martyr, who was consul and patrician at Rome, converted through John and Paul.” See these matters more distinctly in the text itself.

ALTEMPS.: “At the monastery of Saint Alban, the blessed martyrs Amphibalus and his companions.” Concerning them, see the Acts with Saint Alban himself, on 22 June. Why they are listed here on this day, I do not know.

FLORENTIN.: “The birth-day of Saints Gaudentius, Felix, and Agapitus, martyrs.” See above. “At Thessalonica, Saints Bigarius and Luteranus, martyrs, and Agrega the king.” See the Acts. “In Gaul, Saint Lous, bishop and confessor. And the translation of Saint Eligius, bishop.” Is this not the same person recurring twice, once under a vernacular and once under a Latin name? “Also, Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.” See the Acts. “At Rome, the birth-day of Saint Lucia, virgin, with twenty-two others.”

CODEX MONTIS SANCTI. “At Geneliacum [Gemeliacum], the birth-day of Saint Amandus, confessor.”

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “At Ephesus, the falling asleep of Blessed John the apostle and evangelist.” Concerning this, see yesterday. “At Cologne, the translation of Blessed Gregory, duke, and his Moorish companions, carried out by Blessed Anno, archbishop of Cologne, five hundred years after their passion.” They are celebrated on 24 November. The notice of Sosipater and Gallicanus follows, correctly. Prosper is treated as above. Then: “At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the passion of Saints Lucia, virgin, and twelve others. Also, Saint Adalbertus, levite and first deacon of the lower church of Utrecht, who was the son of Edilbalda, king of the Deiri, himself son of Saint Oswald, king and martyr. He came from England with Saint Willibrord and his companions, and, building an oratory at Egmond in Holland, after converting many pagans and completing his praiseworthy life, rested happily in Christ, renowned for many miracles and buried at Egmond; to this day he shines through countless miracles. On the same day, the translation of Saint Eligius of Noyon, bishop and confessor. In Denmark, the translation of Saint Canute, duke and martyr.” His Acts are illustrated on 7 January. “At Deventer, the translation of Blessed Lebuinus, priest and confessor, carried out by Blessed Ludger, first bishop of Münster. Also at Deventer, the translation of Saint Radbodus, bishop of Utrecht. On the same day, Saint Molocus, bishop and confessor.” He is also called Molonachus.

BELIN. is almost correct in the notices of Sosipater and Gallicanus. He adds the notice of Maximus of Turin, whom he later repeats. Then: “On the same day, in the church of Saint Mark the Evangelist at Venice, the appearance of the same saint.” He is celebrated on 25 April. The notice of Lucia follows, then that of the translation of Eligius, and again that of Maximus of Turin. Finally: “Also, Saint Prosper, bishop.”

GREVEN.: “In Africa, Gaudentius and Felix.” See above. “Antidius, bishop of Chrysopolis, or Besançon, and martyr, killed by the king of the Vandals for the faith of Christ. Mercurius, martyr.” See the Omissions. “Molocus, bishop and confessor. Prosper, bishop of Reggio [Col. 0194B] and confessor, distinguished teacher, in the year 465.” Maximus is treated as above. Adalbertus is treated almost as in the LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. “In Sweden, Hotwidus, confessor.” He is unknown to me. “Bodardus, confessor. Severa, virgin and martyr. Constantia, virgin, daughter of the great emperor Constantine. Arthica and Arethemia, virgins, daughters of Saint Gallicanus the martyr.” Concerning Severa and Bodardus, see the Omissions. “At Venice, the discovery of the body of Saint Mark the Evangelist. Near Cologne, the translation of the holy Moorish martyrs.” Concerning these, see above. The notices of Canute, Eligius, Radbodus, and Lebuinus are as in the LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. At the end: “The translation of Saint Serena, virgin.” Perhaps this is the Serena who is celebrated at Metz as a martyr on 30 January.

MOLAN.: “At Binche, Theodulf, archbishop of Reims, who governed the church of Lobbes second after Ursmarus.” See the Omissions. “At Turin, Maximus,” etc., as above. “On the same day, in the Basilica of Saint Mark the Evangelist at Venice, the appearance of the same saint.” Eligius and Prosper are treated as in BELINUS. “Also, at Deventer, Saints Lebuinus and Radbodus, confessors. At Egmond in the regions of Holland, Saint Adalbertus, confessor and levite, of royal English stock, disciple of Saint Willibrord, the prelate. On the same day, the birth-day of Saint Vindicianus, bishop of Cambrai.” He is celebrated on 11 March. “The translation of the body of Saint Gerulphus the martyr.” His feast-day is 21 September. Antidius is treated as in GREVEN, but in different type. Thus far the first edition.

Later editions add to the text: “And Aceia the king. At Lobbes, Blessed Theodulf, bishop and confessor.” Maximus, Prosper, and Adalbertus are treated as in the earlier edition, but the royal lineage and the other details are omitted. “At Besançon, Saint Antidius, bishop and martyr, who was killed by the king of the Vandals for the faith of Christ. At Gemeliacum, the birth-day of Saints Amandus and Domnolenus, confessors. On the twenty-fifth day, Saint Febronia, holy martyr.” The appearance of Mark, the translation of Eligius, and the notices of Lebuinus and Radbodus are as above. Then: “At Tronchiennes, the translation of the body of Saint Gerulphus [Col. 0194D] the martyr.
