At the monastery of Stavelot, the translation of Saint Remaclus.” His feast-day is 3 September. “On the same day, Saint Vindicianus, bishop of Cambrai.” It was said that he is celebrated on 11 March. Here his translation is properly meant; elsewhere it is joined with the translation of Saint Eligius.]

[Col. 0189]

At Pirriberoea, Saint Sosipater, disciple of the blessed apostle Paul. In Alexandria, Saint Gallicanus the martyr. When he had been elevated with the insignia of a triumph and was esteemed and dear to Augustus Constantine, he was converted to the faith through Constantine’s daughter, named Constantia, and through the martyrs of Christ John and Paul. The reputation of this sacred profession of faith afterward grew throughout the whole world to such an extent that people coming from East and West saw a man who had been a patrician and consul washing the feet of the poor, setting the table, pouring water over their hands, diligently ministering to the sick, and performing the other duties of holy service. But afterward, when he was compelled to sacrifice under Julian and refused, he was struck with a sword in the [Col. 0191] body and made a martyr of Christ. At Rome, Saint Lucia the virgin, with twenty-two others. [Bouillart adds: [Note: [Col. 0191A] It is true. Pratensis appends to this article the translation of Saint Eligius. But what error did he commit in this matter? This translation took place in the middle of the seventh century and was especially celebrated in the Gallican churches: [Col. 0192A] the codex would therefore not have been at fault had it omitted it; and Sollerius blames it for not omitting it, although seven of the codices he examined, and eleven of those examined by me, agree with Pratensis. BOUILLART.] Likewise, the translation of Saint Eligius, bishop and confessor.]

## VI Kal. The 26th. [Note: [Col. 0195]

The sound codices are the Heriniensis and the Tornacensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0195C]

There is scarcely anything that deserves notice. “Pictavensi” is written throughout in the codices, and we have thought that it should be preserved. The principal variation was indicated above, on 31 January: on that day we placed Vigilius of Trent, who in the Pratensis and most other codices is recorded on this day. In my opinion, this is wrong and contrary to the first reading of the Romanum parvum, of Ado, and indeed of Usuard himself—the original reading—which was erased from the Pratensis codex on 31 [Col. 0196C] January and replaced on this day by a much fuller entry, subsequently transferred from this or similar codices into others. Let our very widely accepted rule prevail here: namely, that the primitive purity of a text shines forth all the more clearly the shorter and simpler the text is. The Pratensis codex also suffers, together with certain others, from another defect, of which we shall speak in the Observations.]

[Note: [Col. 0195D]

After the Gallican entry, from the Acts of Saints John and Paul, chapter XXV, which preceded it, follow the saints themselves, celebrated by all the ancient Martyrologists. The Hieronymian apographs and the Romanum parvum expressly name them. Bede praises them in an encomium, which, as usual, is read in full in Rabanus. The Viennensis, drawing more fully from the aforementioned Acts, is more expansive; nevertheless, its beginning agrees admirably with Bede’s, having been taken by Our Author from one or the other, and it merely appended the manner of their death in different words. Notker gathered a more generous harvest from Ado. These authorities rest upon the testimony of the older Usuard and his contemporaries. That authority—the one we began to examine on the preceding day—is doubtful and wavering in many respects, although nothing deserving criticism occurs in matters touching our present text. For the very constant and renowned memory of these distinguished martyrs is firmly established in ecclesiastical monuments, not only in all the Martyrologies cited, but also in the Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, in the Sacramentaries published by Menard and Thomasius, and even in the most sacred Canon of the Mass. On these matters see more in Papebrochius’s Commentary. Whatever, therefore, may rightly be censured in the Acts themselves, which are undoubtedly embellished and interpolated, the certain and indisputable veneration of these most glorious martyrs, consecrated by the whole Catholic Church, nevertheless remains. Wandalbertus adorned it in his verses with his customary elegance:

> Sixth among the martyrs is Paul, together with John,  
> Brothers by birth, love, faith, virtue, and blood,  
> With whom Constantia shines in an august crown.

Maxentius, whose Life was carefully elucidated by Henschenius in our Acts, was first recorded by Usuard; in defending this entry all the codices agree unanimously. They do not agree so well concerning Salvius of Engolisma, who is found only in the Pratensis, the Antuerpiense-majus, and the Aquicinctinus. The Rosweyd codex dissents; its author or copyist, perhaps uncertain whether to write Salvius or Perseveranda, erased both. Now the most clear-sighted Castellanus discovered that this Pratensis codex suffers here again from the defect of erased, superscribed, and perhaps substituted names. He consulted the source and expressly testified in the frequently cited letter dated 31 May 1709 that “Perseveranda is plainly erased” (*visiblement effacée*), and that “SANCTI SALVII was placed over the erasure” (*mis par-dessus l’effacure*), that is, Salvius was written over the erasure. I suspect that one of the monks of Saint-Germain thought that the Salvius found in the *Forum* should be added to the Pratensis codex, together with an encomium abridged from it; those codices that generally agree with it were undoubtedly copied from that source afterward. But the constant and decisive uniformity of the other codices must prevail entirely, in favor of the sincere and primitive simplicity of Usuard, whatever the Acts may determine in the meantime. Perseveranda, whom others commonly call Pecinna, must be venerated on 25 June, when Papebrochius carefully and laboriously examined everything that he thought pertained to her cult, her proper title, and the other circumstances of her life. It is most probable [Col. 0198B] that Wandalbertus also imitated Florus when, after John and Paul, he sang this fourth verse:

> Salvius the holy, who then visited the banks of the Scheldt.

] [Note: [Col. 0197B]

The PRATENSIS, ANTUERP.-MAJUS, and AQUICINCTINUS have the following concerning Vigilius:

> “At the city of Trent, Saint Vigilius the bishop, who under the consul Stilicho, for the name of Christ, was struck by a great shower of stones and completed his martyrdom.”

In place of Perseveranda they read:

> “At the port of Valenciennes, Saint Salvius, bishop of the city of Engolisma.”

ROSWEYD lacks both Salvius and Perseveranda, as we have said; but concerning Vigilius it agrees with the text above.

GREVEN, MOLANUS, and MUNERATUS would be entirely pure if, together with the PRATENSIS and the other codices cited above in confusion, they had not mentioned Vigilius. Their associates are the codices of middling quality.

PULSANEN has nothing concerning Vigilius anywhere in the text, nor concerning Perseveranda. In the rest, it is Usuardine [Col. 0197C] on this day.

ANTUERP, MAX-LUBEC, ANTUERP-MAX, ULTRAJECT, LEYDEN, LOVAN, ALBERGEN, DANIC, and the ULTRAJECTINO-BELGIC EDITION also include Vigilius. They further fall short of purity because they omit Maxentius’s brief encomium, “glorious in miracles.”

The first edition of BELIN substitutes another encomium for the aforesaid Maxentius:

> “Who became renowned through miracles.”

It agrees with the others concerning Vigilius. As usual, it teems with typographical errors. In the second edition is added:

> “Likewise, the passion of Saint Salvius the bishop.”

CENTULEN:

> “At Rome, the blessed martyrs John and Paul, at whose urging that most noble man abandoned the worldly pomp of the Gallic age. They too were put to death by the apostate Julian. In the district of Poitiers, Saint Maxentius the abbot, a man of admirable virtue and holiness. On the same day, Saint Perseveranda the virgin. In the territory of Cambrai, in the town of Valenciennes, the passion of Saint Salvius, bishop [Col. 0197D] and martyr of Engolisma.”

BRUXELLENSIS also speaks of him, but these and similar codices carry no authority.

BRUXELLENSIS adds concerning John and Paul:

> “They converted the Gallican patrician and consul to the faith while he was on campaign. Later the apostate Julian, because they refused to sacrifice to idols, had them killed at night in their house. And the holy martyrs Baudelicus and Nonnosa, brothers.”

They have been omitted. The entry concerning Vigilius follows. In two other announcements it is pure. At the end is added:

> “At the port of Valenciennes, Saint Salvius, bishop of the city of Engolisma. When he came from Aquitaine to the fiscal estate of Valenciennes, he was secretly killed by Winegardus, son of Genardus, the procurator of the fiscal estate. But King Charles the Great, having been warned three times by an angel to seek him, discovered by lot the man who had killed him. He severely avenged upon that man and his father the great crime itself.”

[Col. 0198B] HAGENOYEN rendered the encomium of John and Paul somewhat more fully from the Acts. It is pure concerning Maxentius and Perseveranda. In fourth place:

> “At the city of Trent, Saint Julius,”

by which he meant Vigilius, and so forth, correctly. It is followed by a corrupted and distorted history of Saint Prosper, whom we recorded on the preceding day. From this brief specimen, you may form your judgment concerning the rest. It begins:

> “On the same day, Saint Prosper, an outstanding teacher, who was of noble Spanish and Aquitanian stock [or: of noble parents?]. At first he was a soldier, filled with wisdom and eloquence. Therefore, after selling all that was his, he came to Rome and was kindly received by Saint Leo the pope. In the time of the emperor Marcian, at the Council of Chalcedon, he refuted the heresy of Nepticius and Nestorius and wrote many books for the strengthening of the Christian faith. Concerning this holy man it was revealed to [Leo] that Prosper should be ordained bishop and sent to Emilia, etc.”

These remarks are sufficient.

VICTORINUS has at the end, in place of Perseveranda:

> “On the same day, Saint Perseverantia the virgin.”

MATRIC-CARTUS-ULTRAJECT:

> “John and Paul, brothers and martyrs. Vigilius the bishop and martyr. Maxentius, abbot of Poitiers.”

In the VATICANUS, Maxentius and Perseveranda are absent. It adds:

> “In Africa, Saints Gaudentius and Felix.”

FLORENTINUS:

> “At Tudertum [Trent], Saint Julius [Vigilius] the bishop, who under the proconsul Stilicho, for the name of Christ, was struck by a great stone and completed his martyrdom. At Rome, Saint Deodatus the pope and confessor. A Roman by nation, he sat for four years, two months, and five days, after Saint Peter the seventy-eighth; he was buried in the church of Saint Peter in the Vatican. He was of such greatness and kindness that he willingly received every person, from the greatest to the least, and showed compassion to pilgrims. Everyone obtained without doubt whatever he rightly requested. After his passing, there were such great rains and thunder that even people and cattle perished from lightning.”

See the *Praetermissi*, where he is called Adeodatus and has no cult.

CAUDIACENSIS:

> “At Saintes, the feast of Saint Decentius the bishop and confessor, whose venerable body, carried to Auvergne because of pagan persecution, rests in a cell called Argedis, where, by God’s favor, he shines through many miracles of signs.”

This belongs to 28 October.

The LUBECO-COLOGNIAN EDITION is pure concerning John and Paul but interpolated concerning Vigilius. Concerning Maxentius it inserts:

> “Brother of the blessed Maximinus, bishop of Trier.”

Concerning Salvius, it is almost like CENTULENSIS. It follows:

> “At the city of Longina, Saint Pelagius the martyr.”

If it is speaking of the one from Córdoba, it would have been better to write “at the city of Córdoba.” Concerning Perseveranda, it is correct.

GREVEN:

> “In Alexandria, Saints Agatho and Diogenes. Salvius, bishop and martyr of the city of Engolisma [or Amiens]. While disseminating the word of God through the Gauls, in the ardor of divine charity, he was killed at the port of Valenciennes together with his disciple by a certain impious man, and, having been hidden, was discovered after divine warning had been given to Charles the Great. Vigilius, bishop and martyr of Auxerre, who, having become hateful to the enemies of justice because of his holiness, was killed by Warrachon, seneschal of the king of France.”

He was treated on 11 March. Concerning Pelagius, as above.

> “On the same day, or according to others, on the preceding day, Saint Radulphus, bishop and confessor of Bourges.”

He is commemorated on 21 July.

> “Likewise, the holy bishop and confessor Anthelmus, of the Carthusian order. From prior of the Grande Chartreuse he became bishop of Belley and shone through innumerable miracles, among them restoring life to a boy who had been drowned in the water. As a further sign of his holiness, as Vincent also testifies in book XXX, when his funeral rites were being celebrated, the lights standing nearby were seen to be kindled from heaven. The translation of Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor of Paris.”

His feast day is 1 November.

MOLANUS, in a different typeface, inserts concerning John and Paul:

> “They were beheaded within their own house after the military commander Terentianus had been sent; he too afterward became a Christian. The passion of these martyrs was recorded by Terentianus himself.”

At the end:

> “Likewise, the passion [Col. 0200A] of Saint Salvius, bishop of the city of Engolisma, at the port of Valenciennes.”

Then, in smaller type, concerning Anthelmus, as in GREVEN, up to the words “restored life.” Then:

> “On the same day, at the city of Córdoba, the feast of Saint Pelagius the martyr, who, at about ten years of age, was thrown into prison and, when he refused to deny Christ, gloriously completed his martyrdom under King Abd al-Rahman, around the year of Christ 846.”

This is in the first edition. Other editions, in addition to the foregoing, insert in italics:

> “At the city of León, Saint Pelagius the martyr.”

Indeed, in Roman type, as though part of the text:

> “At the port of Valenciennes, Saint Salvius the martyr.”

Then again in italics:

> “And the bishop: coming from his own city of Abbia into the Gauls with one companion to preach, he was secretly seized in a village called Beviticum by Winegardus, son of Genardus, and struck on the head with an axe; together with the aforesaid companion he received martyrdom. Both were placed in a stable, where they were honorably guarded by angels, as is found in the book of their passion. After three years, discovered by divine revelation to the emperor Charles the Great, they were buried in the place where they now lie, and to this day they shine with signs and miracles. On the sixth day before the Kalends of July, Saint Babolenus the abbot and confessor. On the twenty-sixth day, Saint David of Thessalonica.”

Finally, in smaller type:

> “Likewise, the death of Anthelmus, bishop of Belley and confessor of the Carthusian order.”

Henschenius’s commentary and his annotations on the Life of Anthelmus, written by a contemporary and associate, may be consulted.]

## [Col. 0193]

At Rome, the feast of Saints John and Paul, brothers. The first was steward, the second chief chamberlain of Constantia the virgin, daughter of Constantine; afterward, under Julian, they received the palm of martyrdom when the sword struck them. In the district of Poitiers, Saint Maxentius the priest and confessor, glorious in miracles. On the same day, Saint Perseveranda the virgin. [In Bouillart: At Rome, the feast of Saints John and Paul, brothers, the first of whom was steward and the second chief chamberlain of Constantia the virgin, daughter of Constantine; afterward, under Julian, they received the palm of martyrdom when the sword struck them. [Note: [Col. 0195A] In Sollerius’s edition, Vigilius was moved from this place and transferred back to 31 January, where Sollerius argues that it had been erased, and we acknowledge that it was. But here it will not be out of place to warn the reader by what other consideration Sollerius regards the mention of Vigilius as suspect. Namely, he is less pleased by that lengthy discourse, which is wholly alien to Usuard’s native simplicity, and which is much more extensive than the entry he had used on 31 January:

> “At the city of Trent, Saint Vigilius the bishop and martyr.”

Indeed, that brevity and simplicity so delight and captivate Sollerius that he wishes it to serve as a rule:

> “Let our very widely accepted rule prevail here,” he says, “namely, that the primitive purity of a text shines forth all the more clearly the shorter and simpler the text is.”

But, Sollerius, why did you reject on the 21st of this month the very short and simple encomium of Eusebius and prefer one composed and inflated with false titles? Why, on the 25th, did you judge the Pratensis encomium of Saint Gallicanus to be Usuardine, although it fills almost the entire article? Your Tornacensis codex represented it much more briefly and simply. Why, on 18 May, did you copy the whole encomium of Mark and Marcellianus? How short and simple was the entry offered by the Pulsanensis codex:

> “At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Mark and Marcellianus.”

On the 15th it simply names Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia; why did you prefer all three verses? The Tornacensis codex cuts off almost half of the encomium of the blessed martyr Nazarius on the 13th. Why did you think the Pratensis and other codices should be preferred to it? Why delay with many examples? I have scarcely seen a single day in your whole Martyrology on which one encomium is not shorter and simpler than another, and on which you have not at the same time departed from your own rule.

Now you do not ask me to prove by arguments that Vigilius was erased by Usuard from 31 January and rightly reserved for this day. Your own arguments admit this. “The day of his martyrdom,” they say, “is expressed by no Acts; but the Church of Trent celebrates the feast of Saint Vigilius on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, probably as his feast day.” Florus of Lyons certainly seems to have judged it so when, in his additions to Bede’s genuine Martyrology, he added the encomium of Saint Vigilius.

Nor did the critic of the Pratensis codex remove Vigilius alone from this article; he also removed Salvius of Engolisma, in whose place he thought Perseveranda should be substituted. On what arguments, finally? On the silence of his codices concerning Saint Salvius and their agreement concerning Perseveranda.

I have already said more than once that neither argument has any force: it is not surprising that Sollerius’s codices agree in mentioning a saint who is absent from the Pratensis, or that they lack saints whom the Pratensis contains. This happened because nearly all the codices were copied from the first example of Usuard’s Martyrology, and Usuard erased commemorations that he did not approve, or added those that he considered preferable.

Thus he erased Perseveranda because, after reading the Acts, he noticed that she died not on the sixth but on the seventh day before the Kalends of this month. The Acts say:

> “Her deposition is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of July,” etc.

But he substituted Salvius because the Acts testify that this was the day of his death:

> “Saint Salvius and his disciple with him were martyred under Winegardus on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.”

If Sollerius denies that Usuard read the Acts of Saint Salvius, why would he not have imitated Florus and Wandalbertus, both of whom mentioned that bishop on this day?

Here I warn that Sollerius’s inspector on this occasion was poorly sighted and thought he saw an erasure in the Pratensis codex. This entire page is sound, wholly untouched by the edge of a knife. But it is one of the few leaves substituted in place of those that Usuard himself tore out, either because they could not be read on account of the number of erasures, or because the knife had torn the parchment itself.

Why, then, Castellanus wrote that Salvius had been erased, I suspect was for the following reason. On the other leaf after Salvius, though somewhat higher up, the middle of a line had been split or cut, so that the upper part of the letters was separated from the lower. To prevent those letters from falling out, a later hand, though close to that period, wrote above the crack or cut what remained of the encomium of Saint Marcellus:

> “...tari viro martyrio coronatus est” (“... was crowned with martyrdom”; the surviving opening is fragmentary and uncertain).

Before this, in the preceding line, are the words, together with “Anastasius mili...” Thus the most clear-sighted Castellanus wrote about one leaf what he had seen on another. Nevertheless, relying on his testimony, our censor declaims against the Pratensis codex:

> “Now the most clear-sighted Castellanus discovered that this Pratensis codex suffers here again from the defect of erased, superscribed, and substituted names; he consulted the source, etc.”

He then carefully investigates where the Salvius introduced into our codex was taken from and suspects that it was one of the monks of Saint-Germain who, by this addition, interpolated the sincere and primitive simplicity of Usuard.

I shall not spend time refuting these absurdities—to use no harsher word. Sollerius will regret having said them and will wish them to be considered unsaid. (BOUILLART.)] At the city of Trent, Saint Vigilius the bishop, who under the consul Stilicho, for the name of Christ, was struck by a great shower of stones and completed his martyrdom. In the district of Poitiers, Saint Maxentius the priest and confessor, glorious in miracles. At the port of Valenciennes, Saint Salvius, bishop of the city of Engolisma.]

## V Kal. The 27th. [Note: [Col. 0199]

I consider the PRATENSIS, HERINIENSIS, ANTUERP.-MAJOR, and MUNERATUS pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0199C]

It contains rather a collection of errors. “Galaciam” is found in the Heriniensis and Muneratus. “Crescentii” in the Antuerp.-Majus. “Galathas” in the Pratensis and Muneratus. The Antuerp.-Majus reads “ordained” instead of “given,” and omits “of the Lord” after “work.” The Pratensis has “Tiburtinum.” The Heriniensis has “Simphorosae”; the Muneratus, “Simphoriense,” and it also has “Nemesiae” instead of “Nemesio.” [Col. 0200C] The Antuerp.-Majus writes “matrem” (“mother,” accusative) rather than “mater” (“mother,” nominative). All these matters are correct in the text, as is another reading which the Muneratus gets wrong: “the mother, most steadfast in faith, under Arianus.” I printed “bound,” with Ado, not “bound [feminine],” as the Antuerp.-Majus and Muneratus have. The former reads the fragment “cujus cum longo,” omitting “corpus” (“body”).]

[Note: [Col. 0199C]

The author of the Romanum parvum is the first, as is customary here, to mention Crescent, the disciple of the apostle Paul, probably from Rufinus’s History, book III, chapter 3. The Viennensis took him from the Romanum parvum and embellished him with an encomium of its own; Notker, like Our Author, moderately abridged it, omitting the matters concerning the preaching at Vienne but transcribing the rest verbatim. Papebrochius here first acknowledges having observed this concerning Usuard. Consult his discussion of Crescent’s cult among the Greeks and Latins and of the apostolate attributed to him among the Viennese and Mainz communities. See also Tillemont, volume I, pages 312 and 584.

Thus far everything in the text is straightforward. But, says Florentinius, a knot of extremely difficult resolution arises: whether, in the commemoration of seven brothers recalled here—namely, in the Hieronymian apographs, where they are unnamed—the seven sons of Saint Symphorosa or those of Saint Felicitas are intended. A careful investigation follows, whose final conclusion is:

> “For this reason I readily came to the opinion that the seven sons of Symphorosa are recalled here with the [spurious] Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Notker, since this really was their feast day, as Ado asserts; but that their memory is celebrated again on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August,” etc.

Thus Florentinius, perhaps without paying sufficient attention here, reports other names for those brothers from Ado on this day, entirely different from those reported by the Hieronymians on 18 July, where Florentinius once again rolls the same stone without completely resolving the difficulty. The problem grows and becomes more intricate because Ado’s names, perhaps with one exception, are precisely those assigned today by the Hieronymians at Córdoba. [Col. 0200D] There is no time to note the other considerations. After weighing them, Henschenius thought it better to exclude Symphorosa’s sons from this place and transfer them to their proper day, 18 July. We subscribe to this opinion, with the protestation inserted, intending, with God’s favor, to discuss the whole matter afresh in the Acts. The Acts published by Ruinart among the Select Acts, with the preliminary notice beginning on page 17, will provide guidance, as will Tillemont’s most recent treatment in French, volume II, beginning on page 241.

Meanwhile, if Wandalbert’s authority has any force or value, Zoilus with his companions will occupy this day:

> On the fifth day, the bishop and martyr Zoilus  
> Increases the number of martyrs, joined to nineteen.

But the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August the mother will dedicate to her sevenfold offspring—not as Notker did, arranging the matter so that he commemorates seven brothers from Ado on this day and seven from the Hieronymians on 18 July. That is more a cutting of the knot than a solution, if indeed it is sufficiently capable of being untied.

Yet the whole dispute properly concerns the investigation of historical truth. Here we are expressly asking about the text of our Usuard, which we may provisionally suppose to be false, as we have often had to acknowledge above. Nevertheless, it will remain certain that he copied Ado in such a way as to represent the little entry sincerely and simply. I think the same must be said of the announcement of Zoilus, whom he alone praises, after deleting Ado’s nineteen unnamed companions. We therefore judged Greven and Molanus to be interpolated because they followed Ado’s rather than Usuard’s sense.

That Zoilus, whom Wandalbert above improperly calls a bishop, was incorporated into the Acts together with twenty other companions, among whom the seven sons of our Symphorosa are named. There Henschenius begins, in his historical commentary, the controversy concerning the mother and the seven sons. In two further paragraphs you will find in him the martyrdom, discovery, and translation of Zoilus’s body, together with other matters concerning him.

Here Usuard adds from himself a miracle concerning the revelation of the sacred body. Whether it is described sufficiently accurately, I prefer that you determine from the Acts themselves rather than from our judgment.

Ado briefly mentioned something about the Seven Sleepers; Rabanus composed a fairly long history, which Notker related in almost the same words and which may be seen in the *Auctaria*. Our Author, I do not know under whose guidance, relegated them to 27 July. Once these matters are set aside, the simple and genuine reading of Usuard remains for this day.] [Note: [Col. 0201B]

We said that GREVEN and MOLANUS must be excluded from the number of pure witnesses because they insert concerning Zoilus:

> “with nineteen others.”

TORNACENSIS, pure concerning Crescent, shortens the encomium of the seven Tiburtine brothers and cuts away the encomium of Zoilus.

PULSANENSIS, pure concerning Crescent, omits the Tiburtines and has at the end only:

> “At Córdoba, Saint Zoilus the martyr.”

ROSWEYD, after the pure text, adds:

> “At Rome, Crispinianus and the seven brothers. At Ephesus, the Seven Sleepers: Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine.”

ANTUERP. MAX.-LUBECANA, ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT, LEYDEN, and the ULTRAJECTINO-BELGIC EDITION add at the end, after the pure text:

> “On the island of Hoya, the translation of Saint Florentius the confessor.”

Is this the Florentius who is commemorated on 22 September? See the *Praetermissi*. They also insert the companions of Zoilus.

[Col. 0201C] LOVANIENSIS, pure in both its first and second editions, follows Ado at the end:

> “At Córdoba, Saint Zoilus the martyr, with nineteen others,”

the rest having been deleted.

ALBERGENSIS and DANICUS are pure in their first edition but omit the second entirely. Concerning Zoilus they also insert, with GREVEN and MOLANUS:

> “with nineteen others.”

At the end:

> “On the island of Hoya,”

etc., as above.

CENTULENSIS:

> “At Galatia, Saint Crescent the bishop, whom the blessed Paul ordained and appointed shepherd of the land and people of Galatia.”

Here Usuard’s text seems not only to be abridged but also correctly emended:

> “In the city of Tibur in Italy, Saint Symphorosa, wife of the martyr Getulius, who suffered under Caesar Hadrian together with her [seven] sons, whose names were Crescens, Julian, Nemesius, Primitivus, Justinus, Stateus, and Eugenius. At the monastery of [Hoya], Saint Florentius the confessor. At the city of Amiens, the discovery of the blessed martyrs Fuscianus, Victoricus, and Gentianus.”

Rabanus also discusses them, and Notker took his account from him. They are commemorated on 11 December.

> “On the same day, the birth of Saint Nicholas the archbishop.”

See 6 December.

> “At Córdoba, Saint Zoilus and eighteen others. At Carthage, Saint Gudilene the martyr.”

Others have Guddenes or Gundenes. She is commemorated on 18 July.

BRUXELLENSIS is almost similar to LOVANIENSIS in the text. Then follows a curious history, which it is useful to append here:

> “At Ephesus, the seven holy brothers called the Sleepers. Under the emperor Decius, tortured for Christ, they withdrew from the cruelty of their torturers and hid themselves in a certain cave; there, after prayer, they fell asleep, and Decius sealed up the cave. In the time of Theodosius, when a dispute arose concerning the faith in the resurrection, they were divinely awakened from the sleep in which they had slept for nearly two hundred years. They arose and, before the emperor Theodosius, having affirmed the truth of the resurrection, again fell asleep in Christ. Later, in the time of King Edward of England, turning from one side to the other, they were proclaimed by that king in a prophetic spirit as destined to rest on that side for seventy-four years. Thus they are said to have remained motionless in rest only from the time of the emperor Lothair, grandson through his son of Charles the Great.”

How credible this is will be discussed in the Acts on 27 July.

> “At Carthage, Saint Guddenes, struck down with the sword for Christ. And the birth of Saint Nicholas the bishop. On the island of Hoya, the translation of Saint Florentius the confessor.”

We have already dealt with these three above in the CENTULENSIS.

HAGENOYEN is sufficiently pure concerning Crescent. Concerning the Tiburtines, after a moderately interpolated text, it reports the manner of each one’s death without naming them; this you will understand more clearly from Ado, where the names are repeated in order. It is again pure concerning Zoilus and adds at the end:

> “On the island of Nola [Hoya], the translation of Florentius the confessor.”

DAVERONENSIS:

> “On the island of Oya, the translation of Florentius [Col. 0202C] the confessor.”

AMBIANUS:

> “At the monastery of Roia, Saint Florentius the confessor.”

Without doubt this concerns the same translation of Florentius.

> “At Amiens, the discovery of the bodies of the holy martyrs Fuscianus, Victoricus, and Gentianus.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT:

> “The Seven Sleepers. Crescent, disciple of the blessed apostle Paul. The martyr Zoilus. Symphorosa with her seven sons, martyrs.”

CAMBERIENSIS:

> “At Vienne, Saint Crescent, the first bishop of that city.”

See Papebrochius’s Commentary.

ELORENTINUS:

> “On the island of Hera [Hoya or Oya], the translation of Saint Florentius the bishop and confessor.”

REMENSIS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris:

> “At the monastery of Oya, the translation of the body of Saint Florentius the confessor. At the city of Amiens, the discovery of the bodies of the holy martyrs Fuscianus, Victoricus, and Gentianus.”

The LUBECO-COLOGNIAN EDITION is closer to Ado than to Usuard concerning Crescent, and is pure concerning the Tiburtines. Concerning the Seven Sleepers it invents another account; what has been said above is sufficient for us. It is pure concerning Zoilus. Then:

> “On the same day, Saint Ladislaus, king and confessor of Hungary. At Hoya,”

etc., as above.

> “On the same day, the revelation of Saint Anthony the abbot and confessor.”

See his feast day, 17 January.

BELIN, pure concerning Crescent, has in second place:

> “In Hungary, in the city of Várad, Saint Ladislaus the king and confessor, who shines to the present day through his most illustrious miracles.”

It is severely mutilated in the entry concerning Symphorosa and her sons. At the end:

> “At Córdoba, Saint Zoilus the martyr.”

The second edition adds:

> “On the island of Oha, the translation of Florentinus the confessor.”

Others have it better.

GREVEN:

> “Note: the aforesaid Symphorosa was the wife of the martyr Getulius, concerning whom see above, on the fourth day before the Ides of June. Likewise, Saints Crispus and Crispinella.”

See in the Acts concerning Felix and Spinella.

> “According to some, on this day the discovery of the seven martyr Sleepers. At Ephesus, during the time of Decius, they entered a cave to escape the fury of the persecution, in which they slept peacefully for 363 years, until the time of the elder Theodosius [an enormous anachronism]. Usuard first records them on the sixth day before the Kalends of August. Ladislaus, king of Hungary and confessor, renowned for his life and miracles.”

Concerning the revelation of Saint Anthony and the translation of Saint Florentius, as above.

MOLANUS adds the manner of death of the Tiburtines from Ado in italic type:

> “For the emperor ordered Crescent to be pierced through the throat; Lucian through the chest; Nemesius through the heart; Primitivus through the navel; Justinus, stretched out limb by limb, to be torn apart at every joint and articulation of the body; Stacteus to be fixed to the ground with innumerable lances until he died; Eugenius to be split from the chest down to the lower parts. On the following day Hadrian ordered their bodies to be thrown into a deep pit. The priests of the temples gave that place the name ‘At the Seven Violent Deaths.’”

At the end, concerning Ladislaus, as in BELIN. Concerning Florentius, as so often before. Then:

> “At Ghent, the elevation of Saint Livinus the martyr and the second translation of his body.”

He is commemorated on 12 November.

> “At Crispin, the feast of Saint Adelmus the confessor, disciple of Saint Landelin.”

See his Life on 15 June, where he is more correctly called Adelinus, as below.

Then, in smaller type:

> “Here in Paris the feast of the Visitation of the blessed Mary is celebrated. In the district of Tours, Saint John the priest and confessor, of exceptional holiness. Concerning him, see Gregory of Tours.”

See the *Praetermissi*.

Later editions removed the Tiburtines. At the end, concerning Ladislaus, as above from BELIN:

> “At Châlons, Saint Poma the virgin, sister of the most holy Memmius.”

This is deferred to her brother’s feast day, 5 August:

> “At Crispin, the burial of the most blessed Adelinus, confessor of Christ. He was established by the blessed Landelin above the river Hon. As an athlete of Christ, he diligently led a life adorned with virtues and departed to Christ. He is believed to have been buried in that place, as frequent miracles have shown. But afterward he was transferred to Crispin and is shown to be present there with his master.”

See what was said above.

> “On the twenty-seventh day, Saint Father Samson, receiver of guests. In the city of Ephesus, the feast of the seven Sleepers is celebrated, namely Maximian, Malchus, Marcian, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine.”

Concerning the translation of Florentius and the elevation of Livinus, as above.]

## [Col. 0199]

In Galatia: blessed Crescent, disciple of the holy apostle Paul. As he was making his way into Gaul, he converted many to the faith of Christ by the word of his preaching. Returning, however, to the people to whom he had been specially appointed bishop—the Galatians—he strengthened them in the work of the Lord until the blessed end of his life. At the city of Tibur in Italy: the birthday of Saint Symphorosa and her seven sons, Crescent, Julian, Nemesius, Primitivus, Justin, Stacteus, and Eugenius. Under the emperor Hadrian, because of her unconquerable steadfastness, their mother was first beaten with palms, then hung by her hair, and finally, with a stone tied to her, thrown into a river. Her sons, meanwhile, were stretched upon stakes and pulleys and completed their martyrdom by various forms of death. At Córdoba: Saint Zoilus, martyr, whose body, after the place where it had been buried had long remained unknown, was revealed by divine revelation to the venerable bishop of that place, Agapius.

### IV Kalends. Day 28.

[Note: [Col. 0203B]]

Thus Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Munerat, Greven, and Molan; Antwerp and Max-Lübeck may be added to them.]

[Note: [Col. 0203C]]

For *pontificis*, Greven and Molan read *papae*; but all add *doctoris*, except Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, which read as follows: “At Rome, the birthday of blessed Leo, pope.” Concerning Hirenaeus, Polycarp, and Jerome, enough has been said elsewhere about the usage of the Middle Ages. Some have *Hyrenei* and *Jeronymus*; Molan corrected everything. Antwerp and Max-Lübeck read “Saint Jerome.” Some prefer, instead of *apostolorum*, to write *apostolicorum* with Ado; our manuscripts have the reading found in the text. Likewise, they read *temporum*, not *temporibus*, as Greven and Molan do, and still less *tempori*, as Antwerp and Max-Lübeck do. There is some variation in the names of the Alexandrian martyrs. Thus Herinien has *Potamianae*, and again, when the same name occurs later, *Potamiana*. Antwerp-Major has *Eraclidis* and *Herroris*. Munerat has *Herodidis* and *Patamene*. I pass over other matters of this kind that are of less importance. Only Greven and Molan have *igne consumpta est*, “she was consumed by fire”; the others, with the text, have *igni*.

[Note: [Col. 0203C]]

The Vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul, marked in the ancient Sacramentaries and in the Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, appears to have first been recorded among the Martyrologists by Bede, whom Ado followed; our author followed one or the other, or both. It is well established that the feast of Leo the Great, long customarily celebrated by the Church on 11 April, was also celebrated on this day; this can be shown no less clearly, although neither date is his proper deposition-day, as we explained at length under 11 April. In the Calendars cited, this is read for the present day: “Translation of the body of Blessed Leo,” plainly Leo I, as the editor rightly argues. Gregory’s Sacramentary explicitly has: “The birthday of Saint Leo, pope”; and it is clear that Leo II cannot possibly be intended. Bede, who had written on 11 April, “At Rome, Leo, pope and confessor,” adds on this day, after the Vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul: “On that same day, Saint Leo, pope.” In both places, however, Leo the Great is inferred, since it is altogether unlikely that Leo II, who lived in Bede’s time, was recorded by Bede himself in ecclesiastical calendars. The Little Roman Martyrology, when it writes “At Rome, Leo, pope,” and Ado, “On that same day, the birthday of Saint Leo, pope,” clearly indicate not Leo II, as Rosweyd incorrectly noted, but Leo the Great, since they do not mention him on 11 April. Our author, by adding the title “doctor,” identifies Leo I quite openly. Rabanus and Notker made this still clearer, although they had placed nearly the same eulogies on 11 April. Wandalbert likewise speaks most explicitly in the same sense, whatever praise he may have given Leo I on another day. Here is the verse for the present day:

[Col. 0204D]  
“The fourth rejoices in Leo, bishop and teacher of the Word.”

Such was the opinion of all the ancients, from which Papebrochius also thought one should not depart. In paragraph 4 of his *Chronological Synopsis*, he plausibly assigned the approximate time when Leo II succeeded Leo the Great in the commemoration of this day. Molan expressed this in its natural colors in his later editions, although in others he had more correctly asserted the contrary. Meanwhile, our Appendices will show how differently those men thought who, according to their individual tendencies, repeatedly interpolated our Usuard. I add nothing further concerning the duration of the cult of Leo I on this very day, since what has been said is sufficient for our purpose.

The illustrious martyr Irenaeus is clearly recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but is connected there with the Alexandrian martyrs in such a way that one might almost think him to belong to the same arena. He is not mentioned in Bede or in the Little Roman Martyrology. Ado, however, composed an eulogy containing scarcely anything other than what he could easily have obtained from Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 35, and from the tradition of Lyons. It is therefore unnecessary, with Papebrochius, to have recourse to the fictions of Florus, that venerable man, in the second book; for, as we have sufficiently proved elsewhere, these are nothing other than Ado’s own Martyrology, regarded by Usuard as Florus’s volume because he had received it headless from Lyons and therefore did not know its author. The aforesaid Ado carefully distinguished Irenaeus from the Alexandrian martyrs, adorning both the former and the latter with notable eulogies; Usuard drew out the substance of these so completely that they could not have been condensed more elegantly. The whole of Papebrochius’s historical Commentary may be consulted, in which everything else concerning Irenaeus is diligently elucidated. Ruinart inserted a brief dissertation on him in his *Selecta*, p. 59, and near the end of the work, p. 708, among the Addenda, writing as follows:

“Acts, a fragment of which Baronius says he found, we discovered complete in a manuscript of the Cistercian chief monastery. But since they do not appear to approach the age of Irenaeus, we did not think it worthwhile to publish them.”

Nor did Papebrochius consider any of the Acts of Irenaeus, of which we possessed several, worthy of publication. One may also consult what Tillemont and others cited by Papebrochius and by Tillemont have transmitted in scattered passages. In all other respects, Usuard took his entire text from Ado. It remains to be noted that Usuard gave the same names of the Alexandrian martyrs that the Little Roman Martyrology recorded. We have also touched on some of them from Eusebius in our treatise *On the Alexandrian Patriarchs*, p. 23. Consult the Acts, where more is drawn from the said Eusebius; or Ruinart, pp. 96–102. For us, it is enough here that the original simplicity of our entire table is manifestly evident.]

[Note: [Col. 0205B]]

**Tournai.** Deletes the words of Irenaeus’s eulogy after *temporum vicinum*.

**Pulsano.** Continues through *vicinum*, inclusively; everything else is missing.

**Rosweyd.** Pure throughout the text; inserts the following from the Utrecht manuscript in second place: “And the birthday of Saint Benignus, bishop and martyr, who received martyrdom for Christ at Chartres.”

**Antwerp-Maximum, Leiden, Louvain, and the Utrecht-Belgian Edition.** Have the following concerning Leo: “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Leo II, pope and confessor.” At the end: “On the same day, Saint Benignus, bishop and martyr.” The rest are pure.

**Utrecht, Alberg, and Danish.** Further add concerning Leo: “He received the holy Sixth Synod and established that whoever had been ordained archbishop should not, by any custom, be required to pay anything for the use of the pallium or for the Church’s various offices.” They agree up to this point, but the former has an addition concerning Saint Benignus.

[Col. 0205C] **Centula.** Pure in the Vigil, it continues: “At Rome, the translation of the body of Saint Leo, pope, who on account of his outstanding intellect is deservedly called Leo the Great among the Romans. At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Plutarch [read: Plutarchus], Serenus, Heraclides, Leonides, Potamiana, and Marcella, with three others. At Lyons, Saint Irenaeus, bishop and martyr, who under the emperor Severus was gloriously crowned together with almost the entire population of his city.”

**Brussels.** First treats of Leo the Great, whom it says cut off his own hand because a woman had kissed it; the most blessed Virgin later restored it. It then treats of the celebrated letter written against Eutyches, and so forth. It is sufficiently pure concerning Irenaeus. It is moderately interpolated in the names of the Alexandrian martyrs. At the end it follows with what our text has at the beginning: “The Vigil of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.”

**Hagenoy.** Writes thus concerning Saint Leo: “Likewise, at Rome, Saint Leo II, pontiff and doctor. He composed sermons, and the Church uses these sermons in the divine office. He received the Sixth Synod and established that whoever had been ordained archbishop,” and so forth, as we reported above from the Utrecht manuscript. In the remaining portions it approaches purity, but departs widely from correct orthography, as it commonly does throughout.

**Aquirinct.** Adds concerning Saint Leo that he condemned the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies and that he compelled the Council of Chalcedon. It then adds: “He established that within the action one should say, ‘the holy sacrifices,’ and that a nun should not receive the veil of the head from a bishop unless her virginity had first been proved.”

**Matrice-Carthusian-Utrecht.** “Leo, pope. Irenaeus, bishop, with his fellow martyrs. The Vigil. Benignus, bishop and martyr, whose bones are in the Utrecht church. Plutarch, martyr, with his companions. Potamiana, virgin and martyr.” In the margin it calls her Potamiaena. There it also notes that “Irenaeus of Lyons suffered martyrdom with almost his entire people.”

In the **Vatican**, after Herois, the following is added: “Likewise Serenus, Potamia, Marcella, Catechumena, and Heronima, who obtained baptism through martyrdom. Among them…” Henschenius examined the names of the Alexandrian martyrs in the Acts down to the smallest details.

**Florence.** “Likewise, the passion of Saint Cassianus, bishop of Todi and martyr, whose body rests there in the church of Saint Fortunatus.” His birthday is 13 August, on which day he is also recorded in the Roman Martyrology. Whether a translation is intended here is uncertain.

**Lübeck-Cologne Edition.** Immediately after the Vigil of the apostles it places the notice of Irenaeus, then that of the Alexandrians; both are sufficiently pure. Then: “On the same day, blessed Benignus, bishop of Chartres and martyr.” At the end: “At Rome, blessed Leo I, pope and confessor. He sat for twenty-one years, one month, and twenty-eight days. During his time the Fourth Synod, namely that of Chalcedon, took place; five hundred and thirty bishops assembled there, setting forth the Catholic faith and confessing, against the Nestorian and Eutychian heresy, a twofold nature in Christ, namely divine and human. He added to the Canon: ‘The holy sacrifice, the immaculate host.’ He cut off his own hand because of a certain temptation, but the blessed Virgin, to whom he had always been especially devoted, restored it.”

**Belin.** Concerning Leo: “At Rome, blessed Leo, pope and confessor.” At the end it is mutilated and stops at “Potancia the virgin shone forth”; it intends to say Potamiena.

**Greven.** “Note. The Leo placed here was the first of that name. By his exertions he caused the Council of Chalcedon to be assembled, and he established that within the action one should say: ‘The holy sacrifice, the immaculate host.’ Likewise Basilides, the executioner of Saint Potamiena; Serenus, Ethera, and Cathecumena, who obtained the baptism of fire; and many other martyrs from Origen’s school. Saint Potamiena appeared to them in a vision and brought crowns of martyrdom obtained from the Lord.” Consult the Acts themselves. “Benignus, bishop of Chartres and martyr, resting at Lower Utrecht. Likewise, the blessed presbyter and confessor Heymbrad, of venerable memory, resting in Hesse, in the monastery of Hasungen, which he founded.”

**Molan’s first edition** adds only: “Likewise at Utrecht, Benignus, martyr and pontiff.” In the later editions Leo’s announcement is corrected as follows: “And the birthday of blessed Leo, pope,” and so forth; then, in italics: “confessor, who sat at Rome for ten months. He was highly eloquent and learned in both Greek and Latin. He held the holy Sixth Synod, which was celebrated in the imperial city, where Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, Macarius, Stephen, and Polychronius were condemned—the new Simon, who preached one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ.” The text follows; after Herois, the following is again inserted in italics: “Likewise Serenus.” At the end: “On the twenty-eighth day, the return of the relics of Saints Cyrus and John, who became renowned for miracles.” Both are celebrated on 31 January. “Likewise at Utrecht, Benignus, martyr and pontiff.”]

### [Col. 0203]

The Vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul, and the birthday of blessed Leo, pontiff and doctor. At Lyons in Gaul, Saint Irenaeus, bishop and martyr, who is known to have been a disciple of the blessed Polycarp, priest and martyr, as Jerome writes, “a contemporary of the times of the apostles.” Later, during the persecution of Severus, he was crowned with glorious martyrdom together with almost the entire population of his city. At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Plutarch, Serenus, Heraclides, Herois, Potamiana, and Marcella, with three others; among them Potamiana the virgin shone out especially. First she endured immense and countless struggles for her virginity; then, subjected to extraordinary and unheard-of tortures for martyrdom, she was finally consumed by fire.

### III Kalends. Day 29.

[Note: [Col. 0207]]

I count Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, and Munerat among the pure copies, although they differ in some respects.]

[Note: [Col. 0207A]]

All agree in the first announcement. In Munerat, *Ostinsi* is a printer’s error. All the manuscripts read *Argentomacum*, except Munerat, who has *Argento magnum*, and Molan, who substitutes *Argentomachum*. The manuscripts cited and nearly all the others read, with the text, *capite plexus est*, “was beheaded”; Pratensis instead has the more general *martyrio coronatus est*, “was crowned by martyrdom,” and Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd usually agree with him. The authority of the others is more valuable to us, although I am not unaware that Anastasius, according to the Acts, completed his martyrdom by a different kind of death from beheading. I think Usuard simply wrote “Blessed, virgin,” as Pratensis, Tournai, and Munerat have it, and Herinien also, except that it adds “hung upon a cross.” Others express it differently, as will appear in the Appendices.]

[Note: [Col. 0207B]]

All antiquity, the Middle Ages, and all the Churches even today have revered and continue to revere this 29 June as the rightful day of the deposition or martyrdom of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Who would dare even to object against so great an authority and against the uninterrupted practice of the universal Church? These are the words of Janningus, § 5, no. 46, in the preliminary Commentary on the Acts of the apostles; he should certainly be consulted by the curious reader, since he explains various other intricate questions concerning the place, manner, and time of the martyrdom both clearly and learnedly.

More directly relevant to our purpose: apart from Calendars and Sacramentaries, all the ancient Martyrologists as a body contend for this same day, unanimously and with complete constancy—especially all the Hieronymian copies published by Florentinius, and then Bede, Florus, and Rabanus. Likewise the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, Notker, and our Usuard. Wandalbert too sang elegantly as follows:

“The third raises golden Rome to the heavens,  
with the blessed martyrdom alike of Peter and Paul.”

[Col. 0207C] These testimonies considerably strengthen the assertion recently reported from Janningus. Moreover, the Viennese Martyrologist, among the apostles’ festivals, gives the first and foremost place to many observations in praise of Peter and Paul, which could be subjected to a more exact critical examination, just as could other additions supplied by Notker. What our text presents as genuinely Usuardine was taken entirely from Ado, with the names of the consuls Bassus and Tuscus retained and incorrectly connected with Nero Caesar, from whom they were separated by almost two whole centuries. Thus it is clear that another translation, or deposition—if it may be called that—was confused with the very day of the martyrdom through Ado’s error. On this controversy, see the cited passage of Janningus, and again § 20 of the *Analecta*, as well as Henschenius and Papebrochius in the preceding paragraphs. I am persuaded that the curious reader will there find material fully satisfying the mind. If anyone prefers a sequential arrangement of events, he may consult Tillemont, vol. I, pp. 108–317, where the deeds of both apostles are followed.

Meanwhile, it is plainly evident how simply and in good faith Usuard followed Ado, his customary guide. He had no mention of Marcellus of Argentomagus and his fellow soldier, and therefore we believe that the Acts lay before him, in which it is clearly said that Marcellus was beheaded, whereas Anastasius completed his contest by another kind of death. Hence, if the martyrdom of both is joined in the entry, it remains uncertain whether Pratensis, with the usual companions, wrote more correctly, or whether the others did. For this reason we have multiplied the pure manuscripts, although they differ notably. The final announcement also moved us; in our judgment it is plainly Usuardine, but it is expressed differently in the manuscripts. The reading of our entry seems to us much the more probable, being confirmed by many arguments in the collection of Acts. Yet the authority of the other manuscripts is not to be despised: they make *Beatae* or *sanctae* an adjective or epithet meaning “blessed,” so that the proper name remains uncertain. The distinguished Castellanus devised another name not implausibly; since it has been discussed in the aforesaid collection, there is no need to repeat the matter here. From what has been said, one may gather what we think Usuard wrote in the original wording.]

[Note: [Col. 0207C]]

**Antwerp-Major.** In the rest it is like Pratensis, as usual; it lacks the final announcement concerning Beata or Benedicta.

**Pulsano.** Pure through the martyrdom of Marcellus, inclusively; everything else is missing.

**Rosweyd.** Also lacks at the end the announcement of Beata, in whose place it has: “Likewise at Rome, Novatian and 979 others.” These martyrs are recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but it is surprising that no mention of them is made either in the Acts or in the *Praetermissi*. It continues: “Fortunatus, bishop and confessor.” See the *Praetermissi*.

**Antwerp and Max-Lübeck.** Begin: “At Rome, of the most holy apostles,” and so forth. At the end, instead of “Beata, virgin,” they read “Saint Benedicta, virgin.” See the Observations.

[Col. 0208C] **Belin’s first edition**, besides many errors, also reads “Saint Benedicta.” The second inserts concerning Peter and Paul: “in the thirty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion.”

**Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Alberg, Danish, and the Utrecht-Belgian Edition** begin in this way:

“At Rome, the passion of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul. The former was fastened to a cross with his head turned toward the earth and his feet raised on high, for he declared himself unworthy to be crucified in the manner of his Lord. The latter found a precious death through the beheading of his precious head. These most illustrious athletes suffered in the year 72 of the Lord’s incarnation, the thirty-ninth year of the Passion” (Leiden alone reads “the sixty-second year of the Passion, the thirtieth”).

At the end: “In the territory of Sens, Saint Benedicta, virgin, hung upon a cross.”

[Col. 0209A] **Centula.** “At Rome, the birthday of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, who suffered under Nero” [a later hand, over erased words: “when Bassus and Tarsus were consuls”]. “The ancient and most holy Fathers relate that these two great princes of the Churches did not triumph after the lapse of a year, but in the same year and on the same day, in one city—one by the cross, the other by the sword. In the city of Strasbourg, Saint Marcellus, who was beheaded together with Anastasius.”

**Brussels.** Concerning Peter and Paul, omitting the years, nearly repeats what has already been said, adding this notable statement: “Regarding this martyrdom, blessed Ambrose says: ‘We do not think it happened without reason that Peter and Paul suffered on one day, in one place, and under the same persecutor. On one day, so that they might reach Christ together; in one place, so that Rome might not lack either of them; and under one persecutor, so that equal cruelty might bind them both.’” It is pure concerning Marcellus; concerning Benedicta, it agrees with the middle-ranking manuscripts mentioned above. [Col. 0209B] At the end it adds: “And Saint Cassius [of Narni], bishop, whose passing blessed Gregory mentions in his Homilies.” See Papebrochius’s Commentary.

**Hagenoy.** Concerning Peter and Paul, expresses the sense of the six manuscripts mentioned above in other words, assigning the seventy-first year of the Incarnation and the thirty-seventh of the Passion. Concerning Marcellus and Benedicta, it agrees with those same manuscripts.

**Aquirinct.** Reads *Argentoracum* instead of *Argentomachum*. At the end: “Saint Beata.”

**Victorin and the Swedish Royal manuscript**, under no. 130: “In the territory of Sens, Beata and Mustiola, virgins.” Concerning Mustiola, see the *Praetermissi*. “On the same day, at Nevers, Saint Agricola, bishop and confessor.” See the Acts under 26 February.

**Matrice-Carthusian-Utrecht.** “Peter and Paul, apostles. Cassius of Narni, bishop, concerning whom blessed Gregory speaks in a homily.” See Brussels.

In the **Vatican**, no. 5949, the commemoration of Marcellus and likewise that of Beata are absent.

[Col. 0209C] **Florence.** “At the city of Veroli, the passion of Saint Alban, martyr, under the emperor Diocletian. He suffered in the year of the Lord 287, yet his feast is celebrated on 22 June.” See the entry there.

**Bordeaux and Besançon.** “In the territory of Sens, Beata, virgin.”

**Caudiacum.** “In the territory of Sens, Saint Beata, virgin.” The same person is named in various ways.

**Lübeck-Cologne Edition.** Concerning Peter and Paul it agrees with the manuscripts above. It is pure concerning Marcellus. Benedicta likewise agrees with the foregoing. Then: “On the same day, Saint Novatian, martyr, with 997 other martyrs.” See the passage above in Rosweyd. “Likewise Saint Cassius, bishop of Narni and confessor, concerning whom blessed Pope Gregory writes in his Homilies: On the first Sunday, at the imperial town of Werden, the translation of Saint Swicbert, bishop of Werden and confessor.” The Acts are given under 30 April.

**Greven.** “On the same day, Novatian, martyr, with 978 others.” Concerning them, see above. “Cassius, bishop of Narni,” [Col. 0210B] “and confessor. As Gregory reports in Homily 37, it was his custom to offer daily sacrifices to God, so that scarcely a day of his life passed on which he did not sacrifice offerings of reconciliation to the almighty Lord. His life also agreed most fully with his sacrifice; for he gave everything he possessed in alms, and when the hour of offering the sacrifice came, he melted entirely into tears and sacrificed himself with great contrition of heart. Likewise, Gero, archbishop of Cologne and confessor, of blessed memory.” He is not mentioned in the *Praetermissi*. Finally: “On the Sunday nearest this feast, at Werden, the translation of Saint Swicbert, bishop of Werden and confessor.” See the Lübeck-Cologne Edition.

**Molan.** In smaller type describes the passages concerning Cassius of Narni that we have just given from Greven, and adds nothing else in either his first or later editions. See the other passages from Saint Gregory transcribed in our Acts.]

### [Col. 0207]

At Rome, the birthday of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, who suffered under Nero Caesar when Bassus and Tuscus were consuls. The former is honored in the same city beside the Triumphal Way with the veneration of the whole world; the latter, buried on the Ostian Way, is likewise held in equal honor. On the same day, Saint Marcellus, martyr, who at the fortress of Argentomagus was beheaded for the faith of Christ together with Anastasius, a soldier [Bouillart: “who was crowned with martyrdom together with Anastasius, a military man”]. In the territory of Sens, Beata, virgin.

### Pridie Kalends. Day 30.

[Note: [Col. 0209]]

Taken from Herinien, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0209D]]

The commemoration in the manuscript of Herinien is undoubtedly a scribal error. Munerat renders Usuard’s meaning rather than his exact words: “Who, killed by the sword on the same day as blessed Peter, received heaven.” I read *Marcialis*, with nearly all the manuscripts except Molan. Munerat writes *Alpiano*; the others follow the text, where perhaps *Albiniano* should be read instead, and likewise *Austricliniano*, as Greven and Molan correctly have it. With Herinien and the other older copies, I retained *Stratocliniano*. Either reading may be preferred to *Stratocliani*, found in Pratensis and Munerat. Again, three of our manuscripts, like Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, and Rosweyd, read “in Italy,” incorrectly; the other manuscripts agree with the text. In Munerat there is an error: *Variensi* instead of *Vivariensi*. Finally, he is mistaken in omitting the last word, “confessor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0211A]]

In his later editions of Usuard, under 29 June, John Molan noted that he had removed from the text “when Bassus and Tuscus were consuls,” because he had wrongly convinced himself that these words had been added to Usuard at a later date through an obvious error. “For,” he says, “I infer that this dream cannot belong to Usuard from the fact that he thought Peter and Paul suffered in different years.” This ought to have been demonstrated. Now hear him under this day, 30 June. As for the reading, an old manuscript of Usuard—not certainly the one he had followed in his first, purer edition—has: “ONE, BUT NOT ON THE SAME DAY; RATHER, AFTER THE LAPSE OF A YEAR, AS THE ELOQUENT ARATOR WRITES.” But our predecessors seem to have deleted the whole of this sentence, apart from the word “one,” as improbable. This was Molan’s view, doubtless because he did not know that what he calls a dream was not Usuard’s error but Ado’s, truly copied by Usuard, and therefore wrongly removed from the text. The same applies to Arator’s passage, which was wrongly erased, if indeed Usuard ever inserted it; so far, this does not seem probable to me. [Col. 0211B] I would rather believe that, in his commemoration of Paul no less than on the preceding day, Usuard adhered to Ado’s opinion and thus adopted another of Ado’s dreams, according to which both apostles suffered martyrdom not after the lapse of a year, but on one and the same day, in Nero’s fourteenth year, as Ado, our author’s guide, expressly asserts. Hence we think that Arator’s statement was inserted into that old manuscript by some more recent ignoramus. For that manuscript—perhaps the Pratensis—we present the usual companions, namely Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, in which the same is transmitted; for this reason we excluded them from the number of the pure copies. We have retained the reading of the other manuscripts, which we judge to be Usuard’s own simple and genuine reading, unless someone demonstrates something more certain.]

Usuard had the same guide before him in Lucina, the disciple of the apostles, copying Ado’s words exactly. Ado, in turn, took Lucina from the Little Roman Martyrology as from a source and adorned her, among the apostles’ festivals, with an eulogy transcribed from Notker, as though she too had shed her blood in confessing Christ. On this matter see Papebrochius in the Acts; there he also differs concerning another Lucina. The Hieronymian manuscripts record the deposition of Martialis of Limoges as that of a confessor; the Viennese likewise records it in the same way, adding nothing in his praise. He is similarly placed by Rabanus and Notker. Our author joined two companions to him, but they do not belong to this day, since each is commemorated on his own festival. None of the cited Martyrologists says anything about Martialis’s apostleship or discipleship among the apostles, although Florus seems to have remembered it, assuming that the words reported in our Bede are his. Let the curious reader examine what has been explained at length and accurately in the Acts concerning that celebrated controversy. Here I add only Wandalbert’s single verse about Martialis:

“On the preceding day Limoges honors Martialis,  
and June marks out the lofty world for these festivals.”

[Col. 0212B] In our manuscripts, Corsicus and Leo follow; Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, and Rosweyd assign them to Italy, whereas the others more correctly remove them from that arena, as we read them in the text. For if the place of the contest was added by Usuard, it could not fail to indicate Africa, which he must have read clearly in the very source from which he detached those two from their other companions. I do not know how Ostianus, a priest rather than a bishop, as some have it, became known to Usuard, since his Acts are entirely lacking. Certainly, the silence of the earlier and contemporary writers proves that he was first recorded by Usuard; and that he was genuinely recorded by him, as were the others above, in the manner we have reported, is abundantly demonstrated, we think, by the agreement of the more reliable manuscripts. Among the manuscripts to be cited in the Appendices, Ostianus is announced in various ways; in many, he himself and the two preceding saints are entirely omitted, as will soon appear.]

[Note: [Col. 0211C]]

Concerning Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, and Rosweyd, we have already said enough in the Observations.

**Tournai.** Lacks the end of the text, making no mention of Corsicus, Leo, or Ostianus.

**Pulsano.** In the commemoration of Paul, also mentions the lapse of a year. It entirely omits Martialis and his companions, as well as Corsicus and Leo.

**Antwerp and Max-Lübeck.** Likewise Antwerp-Maximum and Louvain simply write: “The commemoration of Saint Paul the apostle.” Belin has the same, but concerning Ostianus they read “bishop,” whereas he has only “priest.” The Utrecht-Belgian Edition agrees with the former in the commemoration of Paul but lacks both of the final announcements.

**Utrecht, Leiden, Alberg, and Danish** begin as follows:

“The commemoration of Saint Paul the apostle, who, according to the tradition of the blessed pontiffs Anacletus and Gelasius, was completed by the sword on the same day on which Peter was hung upon the cross. Concerning him, blessed Ambrose says: ‘We do not think it happened without reason that Peter and Paul suffered on one day, in one place, and under the same persecutor. On one day, so that they might reach Christ together; in one place, so that Rome might not lack either of them; and under one persecutor, so that equal cruelty might bind them both.’”

We reported these words of Ambrose yesterday as well, in the Brussels manuscript. The rest are pure, except that they make Ostianus a bishop.

**Centula.** “The birthday and renewed celebration of Saint Paul the apostle. On the same day, the most blessed Lucina, who was baptized and instructed by the apostles. At Limoges, Saint Martialis, bishop, who was ordained at Rome by blessed Peter and sent as the first bishop to the aforesaid city. On the same day, Saints Corsicus, priest, [Col. 0212C] and Leo, subdeacon. In the territory of Viviers, Saint Hostianus, priest and confessor.”

**Brussels.** “The commemoration of blessed Paul the apostle, doctor of the nations. At Rome, the birthday of blessed Lucina, and so forth. In Africa, Saints Timothy, Zoticus, and Paul.” See the Acts for the names of their other companions. “In Italy, Saints Corsicus, and so forth.” It then follows with a pure account of Martialis and Ostianus. At the end: “And in Brabant, the passing of Brother Arnulf of Brussels, a lay brother of the monastery of Villers, where the marvelous deeds of his holiness are recorded.” From this comes Molan.

**Hagenoy.** “At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Paul the apostle, which blessed Pope Gregory the Great established to be celebrated in the Church, because it seemed unjust and inappropriate to him that such great heralds of the Church should be celebrated on one day. Therefore, on the day of both apostles, he orders the entire office to be performed for blessed Peter; and on this day he established that the office should be kept for blessed Peter [rather, Paul]. At Rome, the birthday of blessed Lucina, disciple of the apostles. This Lucina gave the apostle Paul the veil of her head so that he might cover his eyes as he went to his passion. She miraculously received it back stained with his blood. In Gaul, at the city of Limoges, Saint Martialis, who was one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples, with two priests, Alpinianus and Austridianus. This Martialis was a relative of the apostle Saint Peter and of Saint Stephen the protomartyr. He was baptized at the age of fifteen with his parents, always remained close to the Lord, and became his disciple. He was sent into Gaul by blessed Peter. In Gaul, one of his holy companions died, and he raised him by the touch of his staff. This Martialis was honored by the Lord in many ways, including being admitted to certain of his secrets, namely to the washing of the feet at the Lord’s Supper, where he himself supplied the water and linen cloths.”

[Col. 0213A] And many other things were invented in the same spirit, which we pass over in silence, since these suffice as a specimen. More may be found in the commonly available legendary collections; consult Papebrochius’s Commentary concerning them. He says nothing about Corsicus, Leo, or Ostianus.

**Matrice-Carthusian-Utrecht.** “The commemoration of Saint Paul the apostle. Theobald, hermit and confessor. Martialis, bishop, with two priests. Saint Lucina, disciple of the apostles.”

**Bigot.** Under note p. 5: “Ostianus, bishop and confessor.” Thus reads the brief comparison.

In the **Vatican**, no. 5949, Corsicus, Leo, and Ostianus are absent. Whether it is pure in the remaining passages is unclear.

**Lyons, Saint Stephen.** “In the territory of Viviers, the birthday of Saint Ostianus, most glorious confessor.”

**Bordeaux.** “At the city of Angers, the translation of the body of the most blessed Albanus and the dedication of the basilica.”

**Salins, Saint Anatolius.** “At the city of Angers, the translation of the body of Saint Albinus, bishop and confessor.” Usuard treated him above, under 1 March, on which day his birthday is celebrated.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. reports concerning Paul the same things that we gave above from the ULTRAJECTIN., etc. In Lucina it is sound: “At the city of Limoges, Saint Martial, bishop, with two presbyters, Alpinian and Austriclian. Their life shone exceedingly with signs of miracles. When Martial was still a boy of fifteen years, a relative of Saint Peter the Apostle, the Lord Jesus called him while preaching through Judaea. And he said to him: ‘Remain with me, my son, and serve me, and do not take a wife, but follow me in poverty, and I [will …] you, etc.’” This too is equally apocryphal. “In Italy, Saints Corsicus, etc.” In Ostianus it is sound. It continues: “On the same day, Saint Otto, bishop of Babenberg and confessor.” This is deferred to 2 July. “At the monastery of Meyfelt, the translation of Saint Severus, presbyter and confessor.” This is assigned to 15 October.

GREVEN.: “Otto, bishop of Babenberg and confessor.” Concerning him, see immediately above. “In the territory of Constance, Saint Theobald, presbyter, hermit, and confessor. Susanna the matron and her daughter Valeria, killed for Christ, concerning whom [there is an account] in the deeds of Saint Martial”—without doubt those rejected accounts, which is why they are not discussed in the Index of the Omitted Saints either. “Erendrudis, virgin and abbess, kinswoman of Saint Rupert, bishop of Worms. At the monastery of Meyfelt, the translation of blessed Severus, presbyter and confessor.” See above. “The translation of Saint Albinus, bishop and confessor.” Concerning him also, see above. “At Metz, the translation of Saint Sigebert, confessor.” He was treated on 1 February. “At the monastery of Villers, of the Cistercian Order, Arnold, convert-brother and confessor, of blessed memory.” He is more commonly called Arnulfus, or by others Arnulphus.

[Col. 0214B] MOLAN adds concerning Ostianus: “Whose deeds are extant.” Yet they have nowhere been found; for this reason he removed those words in other editions. He continues in smaller type: “And in Brabant, the passing of Brother Arnulf of Brussels, convert-brother of the monastery of Villers, where the wondrous deeds of his holiness are extant.” Other editions insert into the text, in different type: “On the same day, according to the tradition of the blessed pontiffs Anacletus and Gelasius.” At the end: “On the same day, Saint Odo, bishop of Urgell.” This is referred to 7 July. “At Orp-le-Grand, Saint Adilia, virgin. On the thirtieth day, the assembly of the twelve holy and blessed apostles.” See the Omitted Saints. “On the same day, Saint Clothsendis, virgin.” And in smaller type: “Who has not been canonized.” Concerning Arnold of Villers, the same material appears as in the earlier edition. See his wondrous deeds in the Acts.]

[Col. 0209]

Commemoration of Saint Paul the Apostle, whom heaven received, slain by the sword, together with blessed Peter hanging upon the cross [Bouillart adds:

[Note: [Col. 0209D] These words, beginning “not however …,” were omitted by Soller in his edition of Usuard, although they are genuinely Usuardine and were written in the autograph clearly, simply, and by the first hand, without any trace of erasure, without any difference in the ink, and in the same letter-form. The Dervensis codex likewise reports the testimony of Arator, so that there can be no doubt that Usuard wrote it. Whatever Soller babbles in this passage—that Usuard adhered to the opinion of Ado; that both he and Ado dreamed that the two apostles suffered martyrdom not after the completion of a year but in one and the same year, the sixteenth of Nero; and that Arator’s opinion was inserted by some more recent ignoramus—all this is mere assertion and nothing more. Here I am not asking whether Usuard ought to have followed Ado or Arator as his guide. Dionysius of Corinth, Bucher’s Calendar, Epiphanius, Jerome, Asterius, and the Lateran Council under Gelasius favor Ado; before Arator, Prudentius, Augustine, and Nilus, as cited by Photius, had held the same opinion. But if what the Lateran Council affirms is true—that this latter opinion originated with heretics—I do not know with what reasoning Soller could say that this was Ado’s dream, unless perhaps that dream came to Ado through the gate of horn, by which true shadows are given exit.]

Not, however, on the same day, but after the completion of a year, as the eloquent man Arator writes]. At Rome, the natal day [Bouillart omits “natal day”] of blessed Lucina, disciple of the apostles. At the city of Limoges, Saint Martial, bishop, with the two presbyters Alpinian and Stratoclinian [Bouillart: Stratoclianus], whose life shone exceedingly with signs of miracles. On the same day, Saint Corsicus, presbyter, and Leo, subdeacon. In the territory of Vivarais, Saint Ostianus, presbyter and confessor.

THE MONTH OF JULY. IT HAS THIRTY-ONE DAYS.

[Col. 0213]

On the Kalends. Day 1.

[Note: [Col. 0213B]

The edition of Greven is almost the only one that is sound.]

[Note: [Col. 0215A]

Greven reads Hor, and thus Usuard ought to have copied it from the Roman Parvum and Ado. Nevertheless, all the other codices, except Molan’s, have it as it stands in the text. Again, in Greven there is Eparchius; I have written Eparchus with the others. Likewise, Aninsulae and Carilefi are written, whereas the printed text has Anynsula and Karileffi; Theoderici and Theodorici are written indiscriminately, and some have Teoderici. We have used the first form. Finally, the cited codex and Molan put “of Salvius the martyr”; we, with the others, have “confessor,” although we know that the other reading is preferable.]

[Note: [Col. 0215A]

Aaron’s memory must once have been celebrated in the Latin Church, since Wandalbert himself, who was accustomed to include very few saints, praises him today in three verses, which we shall give a little farther below. He appears in most of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, likewise in the Roman Parvum, from which he passed into Ado and from this into our text in exactly the same words. Ado was the first to insert Domitianus into the sacred calendars, accompanying him with an eulogy which Notker more generously, and our author more sparingly but elegantly, sampled. Up to this point no doubt can arise.

Monegundis, whom Ado reports second, was transferred by our author to the following day; Martinus, however, the third bishop of Vienne, was completely omitted, as we have often observed elsewhere that Usuard did. Eparchus, who follows in Usuard, is called Separcus in the Lucensian codex and Eparcus in the Corbeiensis; in both places he is a bishop, whereas our codices more correctly call him a monk and presbyter, taken by Usuard from one or the other Hieronymian Martyrology. See Surius and the Benedictine Acts, volume I, page 267.
