We believe that Carilephus, or Karilephus, also a presbyter, came from the cited Corbeiensis, where he is recorded in this manner: “At Cinomannum, in the monastery of Anisola, the burial of Saint Karilephus, presbyter and confessor.” But it may be asked in what wording Usuard expressed his announcement: whether “in the district of Cenomanum,” as Pratensis and his parallels, Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, read; or rather “at the monastery of Aninsula,” as the others have. Relying on the authority of the latter, we have written it as it stands in the text. Molan, who in his first edition had counted Carilephus among the additions, after reconsidering the matter more carefully restored him to his proper place in the later editions.

Rabanus and Notker say more about this saint; the former calls him Arilephus, the latter Arileffus. It is enough to have indicated this here; the matter must be examined at length elsewhere, when we publish the Life written by blessed Siviardus, edited among the Benedictine Acts, volume I, page 642, and compare it with the Surian and other manuscripts. Here let Wandalbert’s verses about Aaron and Carilephus have their place:

> The first who became priest of the law  
> Of the ancient people, and first offered incense upon the altar,  
> Aaron begins July and consecrates the Kalends.  
>
> Carilephus, likewise a despiser of the world, honors them.

All the codices unanimously designate Theodericus of Reims, though with this difference: Pratensis and its companions assign him only the title “confessor,” while all the others assign only “presbyter.” There is therefore no doubt that he was first recorded here by Usuard. The Life of Theodericus is found in the Benedictine Appendix, volume I, from page 614 onward.

At the end there is a more intricate difficulty. Above, under 26 June, we noted that Perseveranda had been erased in the Pratensis codex and that a commemoration of Salvius, bishop of Angoulême, had been written in its place. Here I observe that the same codex and Munerat also record: “In Britain, Saint Leonorius, confessor and bishop.” In this case Salvius’s announcement has not been omitted; rather, it is absent altogether from Pratensis, having been transferred elsewhere, and Leonarius has subsequently filled its place. He is unknown to all the others, including Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd. This explains why we excluded those two codices from the number of pure witnesses.

It should also be observed that Greven and Molan read “Salvius the martyr,” and entirely correctly; yet they sufficiently indicate that they corrected older codices, in which he is commonly honored only with the title “confessor.” Thus, if it is not completely certain, it is at least exceedingly probable that the simple and genuine text of Usuard is the one we have entered in the register. I scarcely doubt that Salvius was recorded here by Usuard himself. For the rest, see under 26 June, on which day Henschenius distinguished several Salvii who had wrongly been conflated into one. If more precise information should come from elsewhere, it may be recorded in its proper place in the Acts.]

[Note: [Col. 0215C]

PRATEN. and MUNERAT. at the end: “In Britain, Saint Leonorius, confessor and bishop.” But with the difference about which we have already spoken in the Observations.

HERINIEN. has something distinctive: it mentions Theodericus in third place, with this eulogy: “An abbot, disciple of Saint Remigius, who, through the merits of that same master assisting him, is said to have restored the daughter of the king of the Franks from the dead.” In all other respects it is the purest.

TORNACEN. omitted Domitianus’s eulogy. Otherwise it agrees completely with the text.

ROSWEYD. adds “pontiff” to Theodericus. At the end, however: “Likewise, the holy virgins Faith, Hope, and Charity, and Sophia, their mother.”

PULSANEN. begins: “The Passion of the eight hundred martyrs who suffered at the city of Verolano in the time of Diocletian.” See 22 June. In Aaron it is sound. Domitianus’s eulogy is absent. Nothing is said of Eparchus, Carilephus, or Theodericus. It calls Salvius Silvanus.

ANTUERP.-MAJ., perhaps uncertain which of the two it should designate last, Salvius or Leonorius, omitted both.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are defective at Carilephus. At the end they have additional material: “On the same day, the octave of Saint John the Baptist.”

[Col. 0216D] ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG., and DANIC. all announce, though not in the same place: “The octave of Saint John the Baptist.” In all of them “Carilephus” is absent. The first three read: “Salvius, bishop and confessor.”

LOVANIEN., at the beginning: “Near Mechelen, the Passion of Saint Rumoldus, martyr, bishop of Dunellum, son of the king of Scotland.” See the MOLAN Auctarium. The eulogy of Saint Domitianus has been removed. In the rest it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX., etc.

CENTULEN. begins: “The octave of Saint John the Baptist.” In Aaron it is sound. It continues: “At Reims, Saint Theodericus, abbot, disciple of Saint Remigius. At Le Mans, Saint Carilephus, bishop and confessor. In the city of Angoulême, Saint Eparchius, confessor and monk. In the territory of Lyon, the burial of the man of God, blessed Domitianus, abbot.” In the margin, in a more recent hand, has been added: “The burial of Saint Theobald, confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. begins as follows: “The octave of Saint John the Baptist. At Tours, the burial of Saint Monegundis, religious virgin.” Of Aaron it adds: “Brother of Moses.” Then: “At Vienne, Saint Martin, third bishop of that city, sent by the Apostles to the aforementioned city.” These words are taken from Ado. “In the territory of Lyon, at a place called the Valley of Nebronia, the burial of the man of God, blessed Domitianus, etc.” It adds “Theodericus, abbot.” In Eparchus it is sound. At the end: “Likewise Carilephus, presbyter and confessor.” It treated Salvius at length on 26 June.

HAGENOYEN. adds much about Aaron, which is more certainly known from the sacred pages. The remainder of the text is sufficiently sound. Finally, it transfers here the two announcements of the preceding day, concerning the martyrs Corsicus and Leo. Likewise, it has Ostianus, as it writes, bishop and confessor.

[Col. 0217B] AQUICINCT. has: “In the district of Cenomanum.” To Carilephus it adds “confessor,” without “presbyter.” It then adds only: “Likewise, Theodericus, abbot.” At the end: “The octave of Saint John the Baptist. And Saint Theobald, confessor.”

VICTORIN. reads with the text: “Salvius, confessor.” Then: “On the same day, Saint Quintianus, martyr. The octave of Saint John the Baptist.”

DAVERONEN.: “At the monastery of Avinsda, Saint Carilephus, presbyter.” Concerning Salvius, it is correct. “At Autun, the burial of Leo, bishop.”

AMBIANEN. “On the same day, the natal day of Saint Carilephus, bishop and confessor. He lived an eremitical life at a place called Ansula [or ‘called Ansulato’], and later became there the father of many monks; renowned for miracles, he rested in peace. In Gaul, in the city of Ambiensis (or rather Ambianensis?), the dedication of the basilica of Saint Mary the Virgin.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Aaron, priest. Salvius, bishop and martyr, with his disciples. Theodericus, abbot. Carilephus, bishop and confessor. Conradus, bishop and martyr.” I think Cunonus of Trier is meant, concerning whom see 1 June. “Domitianus, abbot.”

AUGEN. and BURDEGALEN. have the text purely: “At the port of Valenciennes, Saint Salvius, confessor.” Whether they are referring to other men, I do not know.

REG. SUEC., no. 130: “On the same day, Saint Quintianus, martyr. In Alemannia, near the city of Augsburg, the burial of blessed Udalricus, bishop and confessor, great and glorious from infancy until his death.” He is celebrated on 4 July. Another copy is numbered 428. “On the same day, Saint Leonorius, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN. mentions only Domitianus, omitting the eulogy. It adds: “The natal day of Saint Luceia, virgin, and Vuceia the king, with eight others.”

FLORENTIN.: “Near Ravenna, Saint Martial, confessor, archbishop of that same city.”

JURENSIS S. Ragnoberti: “In the district of Cenomanum, at the monastery of Anisola, blessed Carilephus, confessor and abbot.” See above.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL.: “The octave of Saint John the Baptist.” Of Aaron it adds: “As the book of Leviticus attests.” “In the territory of Privinum, blessed Theobald, bishop and confessor. He withdrew himself from the world, choosing an eremitical life for nine years; he lived in extreme poverty for Christ. Because of the holiness of his life, the angels from heaven adorned him with the episcopal mitre.” Of Domitianus it is sufficiently sound. Then: “In the city of Mechelen in Brabant, Saint Rumoldus, bishop of Ireland and martyr, son of the king of Scotland. Although he suffered on the very day of the natal feast of the Lord’s Forerunner, his solemnity is nevertheless celebrated here festively. In the territory of Reims, Saint Theodericus, abbot and confessor, who was educated by blessed Remigius, bishop, and became father of many servants of God in the monastery built by that same man; renowned for many miracles, among which he raised the king’s daughter from the dead, he himself at last rested in peace. At Tours, the burial of Saint Monegundis, virgin consecrated to God.” Of Eparchus, it is sound. “In the territory of the city of Cambrai, at the port of Valenciennes, Saint Silvius, martyr, who endured the death sentence. At Autun, the burial of Saint Leo, bishop and confessor.” Concerning Martinus, as in BRUXELLEN above. At the end: “At the port of Valenciennes, Saint Salvius, confessor.” Here the same man is mentioned twice; he was also recorded on 26 June. Carilephus, however, is omitted.

BELIN.: “The octave of Saint John the Baptist.” The order has been disturbed, and in the first edition Carilephus was wrongly omitted; he is included in the second.

GREVEN. “Note. Elsewhere it reads ‘Salvius, confessor.’ In Brabant, Saint Rumoldus, bishop of Ireland and martyr, who indeed suffered on 24 June, but whose celebration is observed here more festively. Vivianus, martyr, and his companions. Aaron and Julius, martyrs, with many others. Gaius, pope. At Vienne, Saint Martin, third bishop of that city, sent there by the Apostles. At Autun, Saint Leontius, bishop and confessor. Servanus, bishop and confessor. Pambo, abbot and confessor. Though he was uneducated and wished to learn a psalm, when the verse ‘I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue’ was read to him, he refused to hear the second verse, saying that it would be enough for him if he could fulfill the first. At Rome, the holy virgins and martyrs Faith, Hope, and Charity, sisters. Liberia, empress, and Agrippina. Mary, sister of Moses and Aaron. Eleazar, son of Aaron, and Phinehas, his nephew. Queen Esther.”

MOLAN inserts into the entry for Theodericus, in different type, the words of HERINIEN above. In smaller type: “Theodericus, son of Clovis. After Theodericus, leader of God’s flock, had performed many virtues—born of a robber father, like a rose from thorns—and had departed in glory, with angels receiving him, King Theodericus came to the monastery and carried the holy body to the tomb on his own shoulders.” At the end of the text: “He who, condemned to death, merited an everlasting crown. The octave of Saint John the Baptist. At Mechelen, the Passion of Saint Rumoldus, most glorious martyr and pontiff, son of the king of the Scots, wondrous in signs and teaching. Rejecting both the throne of royal majesty and the honor of pontifical dignity, he went to Mechelen, which had been divinely revealed to him, and consecrated it by martyrdom on 24 June. But because the birth of the most holy Baptist and Lord’s Forerunner is celebrated on that same day, Pope Alexander IV established that the Passion of our martyr should be solemnized during the octave of that birth.” It continues with Carilephus. Then: “On the same day, the burial of Saint Theobald, confessor.” Of Leonorius, as above. Again in smaller type: “Queen Esther. Aaron and Julius, martyrs, with many others, whom Bede mentions in Book I of his History. On the same day, Simeon, abbot, who because of Christ was called Salus, that is, ‘fool.’” Simeon is also noted on this day in the modern Roman Martyrology; there Baronius writes: “The Greeks celebrate the same man on this day in the Menologion.” To this Rosweyd, in the manuscript cited more than once, replies: “Indeed,” he says, “the Menologion, as also the Menaea, place Simeon Salus on 21 July. I think Baronius placed Simeon on 1 July in the Martyrology because Aloysius and Surius present his Life among the saints on that day. They seem to have formed that opinion from the end of the Life, where it is said that he died on 1 July. But the Greek text must be consulted, to see whether it has ά, from which the translator rendered 1 July, or rather κά, which is 21 July, as the Menaea and Menologion represent.” I do not know where Molan obtained this material for this day; certainly the same Simeon is again found on 21 July in his later editions, where he adds the Greek sources. Molan continues: “At Clermont, the burial of blessed Gallus, bishop and confessor of that same city. Blessed Gregory of Tours wrote his Life. Likewise, at the monastery of Donon, Saint Regina, mother of Saint Rainfridis.” In other editions it begins in italics: “The octave of Saint John the Baptist.” Then: “At Mechelen, etc.,” as above. Carilephus is placed in the text; Salvius is omitted. Concerning Theodericus, after the words of HERINIEN, he adds only: “Theodericus; and that same king carried the holy body of the deceased to the tomb on his own shoulders. On the same day, the solemnity of Saint Regina, who rests at Valenciennes in the monastery of Donon. In the territory of Pruvinum, Saint Theobald, confessor.” Of Leonorius, as above. Finally: “At Clermont, the burial of blessed Gallus, bishop and confessor.” See above for more about Gallus.]

[Col. 0213]

At Mount Hor, the burial of Aaron, the first priest. In the territory of Lyon, the burial of blessed Domitianus, abbot, who first practiced the eremitical life there, gathered many to himself in the service of God, and, exceedingly renowned for great virtues and glorious miracles, was gathered to his fathers in a good old age. In the city of Angoulême, Saint Eparchus, monk and confessor. At the monastery of Aninsula, Saint Carilephus, presbyter. In the territory of Reims, Saint Theodericus, presbyter. At the port of Valenciennes, Saint Salvius, confessor.

[At Bouillart: In the city of Angoulême, Saint Eparchus, confessor.

[Note: [Col. 0213C] Concerning the last three commemorations, the Carolinian autograph has the following: “At Aninsula, in the monastery, Saint Carilephus, presbyter. Likewise, in the territory of Reims, Saint Theodericus, presbyter. At the port of Valenciennes, Saint Salvius, confessor.” In his Usuard codex, instead of “at Aninsula, in the monastery,” he wrote “in the district of Cenomanum.” This correction occurs not only here but also in several other places. It is likely that the reason is that certain particular places are much less familiar to most people than the regions in which they lie. Thus, so that those for whom the martyrology was destined for use might more easily recognize the places where there was a veneration of some saint common to them, he designated the regions where the saints’ cult was celebrated rather than the places themselves. Perhaps another reason was also added: to vary the wording. He had already written “in the territory of Lyon” instead of the particular place where Saint Domitianus had died and was venerated; later he wrote “in the district of Cenomanum,” so that he might designate the place where Saint Carilephus was known in a different way. This also spared him from using the word “territory” in the third commemoration. I add that corrections of this kind would not occur to an interpolator. Such people are accustomed to add, remove, and transfer material; but what advantage would there be in deleting the name of a particular place in order to indicate a more general region? Concerning Saint Theodericus, there is nothing for which one need labor in defending the correction. Whether the Carolinian autograph called him a presbyter and his own codex bestowed on him the title “confessor” is immaterial; there is no time to speculate about such trifles. But how learnedly Salvius was erased here is clear from what we observed under 26 June. Finally, that Saint Leonorius was appropriately mentioned here is beyond dispute. This Leonorius is the man who, brought up from childhood and instructed by Saint Hildutus in the first elements of the Christian religion, was later made a bishop without a see, so that he might carry the name of Christ more freely wherever he wished. He was celebrated in the sixth century of the Church, during the reign of Childebert in Gaul, who held him in the highest favor. Usserius, in the Antiquities of the British Churches, and Cointius, in the Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks, relate more about him; it is not part of the present purpose to report that material here.]

In the district of Cenomanum, Saint Carilephus, presbyter. Likewise, in the territory of Reims, Saint Theodericus, confessor. In Britain, Saint Leonorius, confessor and bishop.]

VI Non. Day 2.

[Note: [Col. 0219]

Thus write Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Molan. Danic is also added.]

[Note: [Col. 0219B]

It is enough to point out Eculeus, Marcia, Symphorosa, Felicissimus, and similar names. Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., together with other codices of the second rank, read “and scorpions.” Molan alone put “concussion” in place of “bruising of the mouth.” He also correctly amended Eutychiani, but we follow the other codices, in which Euticiani is consistently found.

There is uncertainty concerning the title to be assigned to Monegundis. Praten. and its companions, namely Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, read “consecrated to God.” Very good; but we, with Herinien., Tornacen., and Greven, have “religious,” where, with Baronius, “woman” should be added. Choose whichever you prefer, provided that, with Molan and the other codices, you do not attach the laurel of virginity to her, since it is wholly unsuitable for a widow and mother of two daughters.]

[Note: [Col. 0219B]

The memory of Processus and Martinianus is illustrious in Gregory’s Sacramentary, as also in the calendars edited by Allatius and Fronto, and likewise among all the ancient martyrologists. Bede praises it simply and correctly on this day; Rabanus expands it, but likewise says nothing of the place of their martyrdom and burial.

Difficulty is introduced by the Hieronymian copies, which place them on 31 May on the Via Aurelia, but write today: “At Rome, at the cemetery of Damasus,” etc. This leaves Florentinius uncertain whether the cemetery of Damasus or some Saint Damasus is intended. The perplexity increases in Ado, who, in his Martyrology, places those saints in the cemetery of Damasus, although in the feasts of the Apostles he very clearly gives the Via Aurelia, far removed from the aforementioned cemetery.

I would suppose that the error arose from the Roman Parvum, which the Viennese followed in his Martyrology. Usuard, more prudently, composed his entire announcement neatly from the booklet concerning the Feasts. Whether those various locations indicate translations or something similar will more appropriately be discussed in the Acts; what has been said is enough for the present purpose.

I add a brief word concerning the Acts of the aforesaid martyrs, which Baronius considered more reliable in the year 68, no. 24, where they are known in a shorter form. Henschenius regarded them as very ancient under 14 March. More recent scholars think quite differently, as may be seen in Tillemont, volume I, pages 179 and 532. We shall state our opinion shortly. Thus Wandalbert played in verse:

> Processus keeps the sixth, together with Martinianus,  
> The Nones, illumined by the joyful splendor of martyrdom.

The three soldiers, companions of the Apostle Paul, were first recorded by the Roman Parvum, from which Ado took them, and from Ado our author copied everything word for word. From the same source come the following ten martyrs, crowned in Campania, though the Roman Parvum did not express all of them by name. There is no doubt that Ado had before him the deeds of Saint Sebastian, in which the names of each of these and of others are listed; see our Acts, chapter XI. Our author, following Ado in good faith, transferred his unchanged text here.

Florentinius notes that Monegundis—or rather Monegundem—is recorded in the Corbeiensis and Lucensis, but not in the very ancient Epternacensis; hence he considers it an addition by a Gallic antiquarian. Correctly, in my opinion; yet additions of this kind are not otherwise absent from the Epternacensis, which is as Gallic as the remaining copies.

From whatever source Usuard obtained Monegundis, it is certain that he mentions her on this day, whereas we observed that Ado marked her on the preceding day. In Ado the title “virgin” is expressly attached to her, as also by Rabanus on this very day; Usuard wisely refrained from it, and Molan therefore needs no defense for having failed to notice the error in the text of his first edition. Florentinius, indeed, thinks that she was a virgin. Yet he could have been better instructed by Gregory of Tours, whom he himself cites but did not consult. Here are the words of Florus, probably taken from the praised Gregory:

> At Tours, Saint Monegundis, who, deprived of her two daughters, rejected the companionship of her husband and hastened to Christ. For love of him, she shut herself away in a small cell, where she shone through great abstinence, both before and after her passing, by an abundance of miracles.

I therefore think that Usuard wrote “religious,” or, if you prefer, “consecrated to God,” as we noted above. Nor should Molan be heeded when, in his later editions, having noticed the error of the first, he thinks that she may be called a virgin because she was a nun. Surius published Monegundis’s Life from Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 19, on this day; one may add chapter 24 of *The Glory of the Confessors*. All this will be illustrated more carefully in the Acts.]

[Note: [Col. 0219D]

ANTUERP.-MAJ. adds at the end of the text: “Among the West Saxons, in the city of Wenta, the burial of Saint Swithun, a man of wondrous holiness.”

KOSWEYD omitted the announcement of the three soldiers. At the end it also has: “Among the West Saxons, in the city of Wenta, the burial of Svitbuni, bishop and confessor.”

PULSANEN. is sound through “who were crowned with blessed Paul the Apostle,” inclusive. Everything else is absent, as it often is deficient elsewhere.

[Col. 0221A] MUNERAT. adds at the end: “Likewise, the Visitation of blessed Mary the Virgin.”

GREVEN., remarkably, begins the text: “The Visitation of blessed Mary the Virgin.” See below.

BELIN. announces it thus: “The Visitation of the glorious Virgin Mary to Elizabeth.”

ALBERGEN. begins simply as GREVEN.: “The Visitation of Saint Mary the Virgin.” Others, namely ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., and LOVANIEN., speak as follows: “The Visitation of blessed and glorious Mary, ever Virgin.”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Damasus, the natal day of Saints Processus and Martinianus, who were baptized by the holy Apostles and suffered under Nero.” Refer here to Rosweyd’s note, page 222. “Likewise, the holy martyrs Ariston, Crescentianus, etc. [as in the text], all of whom were converted to the faith through blessed Sebastian and strengthened for martyrdom.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “The Visitation of blessed Mary, ever Virgin. At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, in the cemetery of Damasus, the natal day of the holy martyrs Processus,” etc. It is sound throughout the following material almost to the end, except that Monegundis is absent; as it often does, it reported her in advance on the preceding day.

HAGENOYEN. inserts concerning Processus and Martinianus: “They had been baptized while they were still being held in chains.” The remainder is sufficiently sound. Of Monegundis it says: “The religious virgin.”

AQUICINCT. after Monegundis has “consecrated to God.” It then adds: “At Rome, Pope Leo, a most eloquent man, adequately instructed in divine letters and learned in the Greek and Latin languages. He decreed that whoever had been ordained archbishop should not have to pay any customary fee for the use of the pallium in the various offices.” See the Auctaria under 28 June for a clearer rendering of this disjointed sense. Then: “In Britain, Saint Swithun, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The Visitation of blessed Mary. Processus and Martinianus, martyrs. The three holy soldiers who suffered with blessed Paul. Ariston, Crescentianus, Urbanus, Eutychianus with their companions. Monegundis, religious.”

In VATICAN., no. 5949, “the three soldiers and Monegundis” are absent.

STROZZIAN.: “Saint Vitumius, bishop and confessor.” Rather, “Swithun,” if I am not mistaken.

[Col. 0222A] CODEX CASTRI KAROLI: “On that day, Saint Adegrinus, confessor.” We possess a manuscript Life.

DIVION. of the church of Saint Stephen: “Near the castle of Dijon, the translation of the body of Saint Medardus, bishop and confessor.” See 8 June.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL.: “The Visitation of the glorious Virgin Mary. Immediately after conceiving the Son of God, she went into the hill country to the city of Judah to greet her kinswoman Elizabeth; through that greeting John, while still enclosed in his mother’s womb, was sanctified.” The text is somewhat interpolated from this point to the end. Monegundis was treated on the preceding day. At the end it adds: “On that day, blessed Swithun, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN. Note: “The feast of the Visitation of blessed Mary was instituted by Urban VI in the year of the Lord 1389 and was added here to Usuard.” He would have done better to leave Usuard’s text untouched, as he was accustomed to do elsewhere. It continues: “Mamertinus, martyr.” I am greatly mistaken if some ignorant person did not here fabricate the name of a saint, and indeed a martyr, from “the prison of Mamertinus.” “Otto, bishop and confessor, according to others on the day before the Kalends of July. In England, Swithun, bishop of Winchester and confessor. Likewise there, Sibertinus, confessor. Mary of James, that is, the daughter of Cleopas.”

MOLAN prefixes to the text in italics: “The Visitation of the glorious Virgin Mary to Elizabeth, instituted by the Lord Urban with many indulgences.” After the text he adds: “On the second Sunday after the feast of John, at Binche, the translation of Saints Ursmarus, Erminus, Theodulfus, Ulgisius, Amolvinus, Abel, Hydulphus, and Amelberga, made from the church of Lobbes to the town of Binche in the year 1409, on 20 June.” Then in smaller type: “In England, Saint Swithun, bishop of Winchester and confessor. The burial at Bamberg of Otto, bishop and confessor.” In other editions it reads: “In the city of Winchester in Britain, the burial of Saint Swithun, bishop and confessor, whose merits shine with miracles to this day. At Bamberg, Saint Otto, bishop and confessor. On the second day, the burial of the most holy robe of our Lady the Mother of God at Blachernae. On the second Sunday after the feast of John, at Binche, the translation of the saints, etc.”]

[Col. 0219]

At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the natal day of Saints Processus and Martinianus, who were baptized by blessed Peter the Apostle; under Nero they endured bruising of the mouth, the rack, sinews [or cords], clubs, flames, and scorpions, and finally, struck by the sword, were crowned with martyrdom. On the same day, the three holy soldiers who suffered with blessed Paul the Apostle. Likewise, the holy martyrs Ariston, Crescentianus, Eutychianus, Urbanus, Vitalis, Justus, Felicissimus, Felix, Marcia, and Symphorosa, all of whom were crowned at Campania with glorious martyrdom. At Tours, the burial of Saint Monegundis, religious [Bouillart:

[Note: [Col. 0219A] Soller admits that this reading of the Pratensis codex, “Saint Monegundis, consecrated to God,” is excellent. But because the Heriniensis and Tornacensis codices read “religious,” he feared that he might seem to prefer Pratensis even in matters of no importance.]

consecrated to God].

V Non. Day 3.

[Note: [Col. 0221]

Thus write Praten., Herinien., Antwerp-Maj., Rosweyd., Munerat., Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0221D]

Concerning Cneocaesarea, this has been stated elsewhere; I follow the spelling of most manuscripts. Nearly all of them, after the *Romanum parvum* and Ado, read “bishop and martyr,” but Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd correct this to “bishop and confessor.” Rosweyd alone has *faciundae*. It should be written *Clusina*, as most have it; Munerat has *Elusina*, Greven *Selusina*, and Molan *Seleusina*. [The form] *Hirenei*, as often above, rather than *Hireni*, as Antwerp-Major has it, which also incorrectly reads *Mustiolae*. Again that manuscript and Rosweyd have *Laodiciae Siria*; we, with most others, have *Laodicia Siriae*. Pratensis is better with *Laodicea*, and Molan with *Syriae*. Munerat is mistaken in giving *Antonii* for *Anatholii*. Rosweyd alone has *phylosophis*. In Greven and Molan *scripta* is lacking. Pratensis writes *reliquit*; all the others have *dereliquit*. Greven and Molan, together with several middle-quality manuscripts, join twelve companions to Tryphon. Finally, Antwerp-Major substitutes *Constantinopolim* for *Constantinopoli*, a sufficiently common medieval way of announcing a feast.

[Note: [Col. 0221D]]

The Translation of the Apostle Thomas to Edessa is celebrated in several Hieronymian manuscripts, in Bede and Rabanus, in the *Romanum parvum*, and consequently in Ado, and from Ado in our text, almost everywhere in the same terms—except that the Hieronymian Martyrology and Bede add “from India,” although those who investigated Indian matters in the sixteenth century attest that the body was still preserved there. Baronius preserves both opinions in his notes for this day; the matter will have a more appropriate place for examination when the Acts of the Apostle are discussed under 21 December.

The *Romanum parvum* mentions Gregory the martyr. Ado, taking him from there, drew out at length those descriptions from Eusebius-Rufinus, book 7, chapter 26, and Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 65; from these it is entirely clear that Gregory the Wonderworker is meant, although the Acts themselves clearly demonstrate that that holy Wonderworker did not undergo martyrdom in the strict sense, as will be explained more fully on 17 November.

Usuard, for the rest, following and abridging the judgment of his source, thought that nothing should be changed in the martyr’s crown; some later writers did so, as we have shown in the Various Readings. Irenaeus and Mustiola follow, martyrs of Clusium in Etruria, recorded by Usuard alone—if what is placed here is truly Usuard’s, as we have provisionally assumed in good faith under 23 June, where we discussed Felix of Sutrium. In our judgment, however, the manuscripts of Heriniensis and Tornacensis should have been preferred, since both these saints and Felix are entirely absent from them. We are overcome by the number and authority of the manuscripts, and from their unanimous agreement our text must be derived. See what we said about the history of their passion under the cited date, 23 June.

Anatholius is taken from the *Romanum parvum*. Ado adds scarcely anything to its wording, so that his brief eulogy must be attributed entirely to Usuard, from Eusebius-Rufinus, book 7, chapter 28, from which the name was extracted and, in all likelihood, borrowed.

The Hieronymian copies mention Tryphon of Alexandria with several companions. Even our own manuscripts differ as to their number. Bollandus correctly establishes ten in his General Preface, explaining the sense of the Epternacensis manuscript; and we believe that Usuard truly read the text in this way.

That there were several Constantinopolitans is established by the same Hieronymian manuscripts. Yet the author of the *Romanum parvum* names only Eulogius; Ado likewise names only Eulogius, and our text likewise names only him. We judge that the genuine sense of our text has been reproduced throughout, subject to the caution applied concerning the martyrs of Clusium.

In what sense Wandalbert’s verse concerning Anatholius and Eulogius should be understood will be said in the Acts. Thus today he sang his two men, whom he calls “pontiffs”:

> Anatholius and Eulogius, fifth among pontiffs,

[Note: [Col. 0223B]]

Heriniensis and Tornacensis, as we said, lack Irenaeus and Mustiola; otherwise they are completely pure.

Pulsanensis also lacks Gregory and Tryphon; in other respects it is consistently accurate.

Antwerp and Max-Lübeck expand the text concerning Gregory from Ado as follows:

> Who, when two brothers were quarrelling over a certain pond, drew the water away from the lake by prayer, and by divine will caused the abysses to disappear, leaving a green field to the brothers reconciled. And at a certain time, so that the church …

Irenaeus, Mustiola, and Anatholius are absent. They give Tryphon twelve companions. At the end they have:

> Likewise at Constantinople, Saint Eulogius, Euphemia, Acacius, and Demetrius.

Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, and Louvain place before the foregoing words about Gregory:

> Who, as ecclesiastical history relates in book 7, when two brothers were quarrelling …

The text continues:

> At Alexandria, Tryphon and twelve others. Likewise at Constantinople, Saints Eulogius, Euphemia, Acacius, and Demetrius.

Then they give the text concerning Anatholius, omitting the announcements of Irenaeus and Mustiola.

Albergen and Danish are similar to those just cited, but lack the announcement of Anatholius.

Centulensis:

> In India, the passion of Saint Thomas the Apostle, whose sacred body was brought to Edessa of Mesopotamia on 21 December, when his more celebrated feast is observed. At Cneocaesarea in Pontus, Saint Gregory, bishop and martyr, brother of the blessed Athenodorus. This Gregory was endowed with the greatest grace of miracles.

Bruxellensis places Irenaeus and Mustiola second; Tryphon and the twelve third; then Eulogius, Euphemia, Acacius, and Demetrius. Concerning Gregory it is almost identical with Antwerp above. Then:

> And at Rome, Saint Leo II, pope, who governed for ten months. This man, most eloquent and learned in the divine Scriptures in both Greek and Latin, established that peace should be given to Christ’s faithful in the Mass after the *Agnus Dei*.

Then it gives Anatholius in pure form. Finally:

> Blessed Athenodorus, bishop, brother of blessed Gregory the Wonderworker.

Hagenoyensis, after Thomas the Apostle, adds:

> This translation took place under the emperor Alexander.

I would like to know which Alexander this was. Concerning Gregory, it follows the preceding form; Anatholius is given in pure form; Tryphon and the twelve, and likewise the four Constantinopolitans, are as above. It lacks Irenaeus and Mustiola.

Matricularius-Carthusian-Utrecht:

> Translation of Saint Thomas. Mustiola, virgin and martyr, with her companions. Gregory, bishop and martyr. Anatholius, bishop and Doctor. Tryphon, martyr, and twelve others.

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949, Thomas, Gregory, and Tryphon are absent. It adds:

> At Rome, the feast of Saint Leo, pope, who governed the Church for ten months.

Leo II is more often indicated here by a longer formulation in Molan below; but see our Observations and Acts concerning him under 28 June.

Ughellianus omits Anatholius and joins three companions to Eulogius, as above.

Florentinus:

> In the city of Constantinople, Saints Eulogius, Acacius, Euphemia, and Demetrius, martyrs. At Ravenna, Saint Datus, or Dathus, archbishop and confessor.

Baronius notes from the Ravennate writers that Datus flourished during the reign of the emperor Commodus.

Luxoviensis:

> In the Senonese district, Saint Sidronius, martyr, brother of the holy blessed virgin Menrora, who rests in the village.

He is venerated on 11 July.

The Lübeck-Cologne Edition begins:

> At Cneocaesarea in Pontus, the feast of blessed Gregory, bishop and martyr, most renowned for doctrine and miracles. Who, as ecclesiastical history …

The translation of Thomas follows. Tryphon is accompanied by twelve:

> At Constantinople, Saints Evolius, Euphemia, Acacius, and Demetrius, martyrs. At Laodicea in Syria, blessed Anatholius, bishop and confessor. At the city of Clusium …

Finally:

> At Rome, blessed Leo, pope and confessor, who governed for three years, ten months, and seventeen days. He was most eloquent and learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently instructed in Greek and Latin. He established that the kiss of peace should be given after the *Agnus Dei*. He received the Sixth Holy Synod and decreed that an archbishop should owe nothing for the use of the pallium.

See 28 June.

Belin writes *Georgii* instead of *Gregorii* and adds what we reported above, substituting *ab ipsis* for *abyssis*, among other corruptions; the order of the text is also reversed. In the first edition “At the city of Clusium …” is absent. In the second, this announcement is added at the end.

Greven:

> Acacius, Demetrius, and Euphemia, crowned together with Eulogius. Leo II, pope, who governed for three years and ten months. He established that the kiss of peace should be given after the *Agnus Dei*. Lantfranc, archbishop of Canterbury and confessor, a most learned man. Attracted by his reputation, Anselm came to him and later succeeded him in the episcopate, as Lantfranc had foretold to him in the prophetic spirit. Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum and confessor, to whom several letters of blessed Jerome are extant. Bertha, widow, mother of Charlemagne.

Molan inserts in different type into the text what we reported above concerning the brothers who were quarrelling. At the end:

> Leo, pope, who governed at Rome for ten months. He was most eloquent and sufficiently instructed in the divine Scriptures, learned in Greek and Latin. He held the Sixth Holy Synod, which was celebrated in the imperial city, where Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Peter, Paul, Macarius, Stephen, Polychronius, and the new Simon were condemned, since they preached one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Then, in smaller type:

> On the same day, the feast of Saint Sidronius, martyr, under the emperor Aurelian, whose body Adela, wife of Baldwin the Pious, count of Flanders, transferred from Rome to Messines. Near Bruges, at Oostkerke, Guthagon the confessor.

In other editions Gregory is relegated to the end, deprived of his eulogy. The additions are:

> In the village of Oostkerke in Flanders, Saint Guthagon the confessor, king of Scotland, who, as a pilgrim for Christ, rests there in peace. On the third day, Saint Hyacinth the martyr, and Saint Anatholius, holy father and bishop of Constantinople. On the same day, Wibrandis and Mechtundis, virgins, who rest at Eischel.

Gregory is now placed here; after “bishop,” smaller type adds:

> Whom the Roman and Greek Churches place in November. Likewise blessed Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum.

Baronius’s note agrees with the sense of Greven. Castellanus, however, doubts whether this “Heliodorus” may not be different from the one of whom he so often speaks and to whom Jerome wrote.

[Col. 0221]

At Edessa in Mesopotamia, the translation of the body of Saint Thomas the Apostle. On the same day, at Cneocaesarea in Pontus, the feast of blessed Gregory, bishop and martyr, endowed with great glory of signs and miracles; among other things, at one time, so that sufficient space might be available for building a church, he moved a mountain by his prayers. At the city of Clusium, Saints Irenaeus, deacon and martyr, and Mustiola, a noble matron, who suffered under the emperor Aurelian. At Laodicea in Syria, Saint Anatholius, bishop, who left writings worthy of admiration not only for religious men but also for philosophers. At Alexandria, Saint Tryphon and ten others. Likewise at Constantinople, Saint Eulogius.

## 4 July — IV Non.

[Note: [Col. 0225]]

This is taken from Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Munerat, and Molan. Antwerp-Maximum and Louvain are very close to the pure text.

[Note: [Col. 0225B]]

I do not know why Molan simply writes *Osee*. This may indeed be allowed in manuscripts of the Middle Ages, in which diphthongs are generally not marked; but since he usually restores them elsewhere, I do not see why he omits them here, unless he regards the name as indeclinable. Pratensis and Heriniensis read correctly, and we follow them here. The form is *Jocundiani* in the Hieronymian manuscripts and the *Romanum parvum*, *Jucundiani* in Ado; our text restores the older reading. *Smyrmium* in Antwerp-Major and *Syrmum* in Munerat are scribal errors. All our manuscripts have *Sebastiae*. It is strange that Usuard departed from the older witnesses, in which *Sabbatiae* is written very clearly. Molan diverges still further, giving *Sebastae*, and Antwerp-Major *Sebaste*, in which no account is taken of diphthongs. The same Antwerp manuscript incorrectly has *ab Hispalim*; Munerat has *Hyspalim* and *Hyspaniam*.

[Note: [Col. 0225B]]

Usuard contributed nothing of his own on this day, but copied the entire text as it stands from Ado, with several passages truncated here and there. Thus, at the very beginning, he removed the prophet Haggai as a companion of Hosea; the Viennese manuscript had taken Haggai from the *Romanum parvum*, the announcer of the prophets, and joined him to Hosea. Again, in what is reported concerning Martin, he mutilated something. For where Ado, besides the translation and ordination, added “and the dedication of his basilica,” our text cut out this part, although it had read it also in Bede’s Martyrology. Some middle-quality manuscripts of ours, as will be said in the Additions, thought that this torn-off fragment should be restored on their own authority.

Whether the foregoing announcement may belong to the Hieronymian Martyrology as expanded in Gaul, Florentius will explain. We shall defer everything concerning Martin to his proper feast on 11 November.

The *Romanum parvum* mentions the martyrdom of *Jocundiniani*—probably, I think, through a typographer’s error for *Jocundiani*—without specifying the place or kind of martyrdom. The Lucense copy of the Hieronymian Martyrology also lacks these details and merely says “Saint Jocundianus.” The Epternacensis adds: “In Africa, Jocundianus.” The Corbeiensis, expressing everything more distinctly, reads: “In Africa, Jocundianus, thrown into the sea and martyred.”

As I have already said, our text follows Ado exactly, except that we believe it changed *Jucundiani*, as Ado wrote it, to *Jocundiani*, in accordance with the unanimous agreement of our manuscripts.

Similarly, Ado explicitly wrote *Sabbatiae* among the martyrs of Sirmium, from the *Romanum parvum*, in which the number of thirty companions is also added; the Hieronymian copies vary again in Florentius. I do not know what moved Usuard to substitute *Sebastiae* for *Sabbatiae*, since all our manuscripts consistently have *Sebastiae*—namely, those in which that announcement has not been omitted.

Whether anything survives concerning these martyrs of Sirmium and Jucundianus beyond their bare remembrance in the Martyrologies is so far unknown to me. The manuscripts of the Acts of Laurianus, which follows, were long ago communicated to Bollandus by the distinguished Andreas du Chesne; Labbe published similar material in volume 2 of his *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, beginning on page 411. I was pleased to examine them myself, but the more carefully I considered them, the less I confess that I liked them; nor do I know whether Cointius sufficiently resolves all the difficulties, under the year 517, beginning at number 14, as we shall explain more fully in its proper place.

For the present, what matters more is this: Florentius wrongly excludes Laurianus from the Hieronymian copies, since he is mentioned in the printed witnesses, whatever differences may occur in the martyr’s crown. The Epternacensis correctly writes “Laurianus the martyr”; the Corbeiensis incorrectly has “bishop and confessor.” Ado omits the title “bishop,” though the Labbean *Hagiologium* assigns it to him—surely appropriately if, as the Acts maintain, he was bishop of Seville. This also explains why the cited *Hagiologium* says that his head was carried to Seville, in Spain.

Our text, without hesitation and without departing from the footsteps of its source, took all its wording from Ado here as well. On this day Wandalbert speaks only of this martyr and the translation of the great Martin, in these two verses:

> Laurianus, in the name of merits you hold the fourth place;  
> And Martin’s bones, transferred to a tomb, lend it beauty.

[Note: [Col. 0225D]]

Tornacensis, rarely more expansive, adds today:

> In the monastery of Altovillare, eight miles from the city of Reims, the arrival and reception of the body of Saint Polycarp, priest and martyr, and of the relics of the holy martyrs Sebastian, Urban, and Quirinus.

From this it is conjectured that this manuscript was received or copied from that monastery.

Rosweyd, omitting “Hosea,” begins:

> At Tours, the translation or ordination of Saint Martin, archbishop. Likewise at Constance—or perhaps Augusta?—Saint Odalricus, bishop.

The remainder is pure.

Pulsanensis lacks the final announcement concerning Saint Laurianus.

Antwerp-Maximum and Lübeck:

> The prophets Hosea and Haggai.

From Ado it supplies what is missing in Usuard:

> And the dedication of his basilica.

“Near Sirmium,” and the rest, are absent.

Greven inserts into the text, after Jocundianus, a fourth announcement which could in no way belong to Usuard, since the saint in question lived an entire century after Usuard:

> On the same day, the feast of blessed Odolricus, bishop and confessor, who shone in the world through many unheard-of miracles.

He writes *Odolricus*; others have *Oldericus* and *Odalricus*. The more common form is *Udalricus*.

Antwerp-Maximum and Louvain are closest to the pure text, adding only Haggai.

Utrecht and Leiden also write:

> The prophets Hosea and Haggai.

At the end:

> In the province of Raetia, in the city of Augusta, the feast of Odalricus, bishop and confessor of that city.

Albergen and Danish have Haggai as in the preceding witnesses. In the section on Martin, the ordination and the entire announcement concerning the martyrs of Sirmium are absent. At the end they add:

> In the province of Raetia, the feast of Saint Udalricus …

Centulensis:

> Haggai, as above. At Tours, the ordination to the episcopate of the blessed and great confessor Martin, the translation of his body, and the dedication of his basilica. In the territory of the city of Bourges, Saint Laurianus the martyr. At Sirmium, Saints Innocentius and Sabacia, with thirty others.

Bruxellensis begins:

> At Mechelen, the translation of Saint Rumoldus, bishop and martyr. On the same day, the prophets Hosea and Haggai.

In the sections on Martin, the Sirmian martyrs, and Jocundianus it is sufficiently pure. From Ado it inserts concerning Laurianus:

> In the village of Justinus. In the province of Raetia, Saint Udalricus, of the city of Augusta, or Augsburg, bishop and confessor.

Hagenoyensis:

> Hosea the prophet, who was the son of Beeri, from the tribe of Issachar … He prophesied in the times of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and of Jeroboam, king of Israel, son of Joash. He who foretold the rejection of the children of Israel …

and much else, better understood from the sacred pages.

Concerning Martin it adds “and the dedication …,” and then:

> At the city of Augusta, the burial of Saint Odalricus, bishop and confessor. At first he refused to accept the episcopate from Martin, the supreme pontiff, because of his great humility; afterward he accepted it under compulsion and governed there amid great labor, ruling himself and his people excellently. Through his merits and prayers, the people of Noricum and Alemannia were delivered from the monstrous devastation of the Hungarians.

The text then continues with Jocundianus in pure form; the remainder is absent.

Aquicinctinus adds at the end:

> In the province of Raetia, at the city of Augusta, the feast of blessed Udalricus, bishop of that city. In the Tervanian district, the burial of Saint Bertha, a noble matron.

Victorin:

> In Alemannia, at the city of Augusta, blessed Udalricus, bishop and confessor, great and glorious from infancy until his death.

We cited similar words on 1 July from manuscript REG. SUEC. no. 130, and said that they should be referred to this day.

Matricularius-Carthusian-Utrecht:

> The translation of Saint Martin. Donatus, bishop and martyr.

A marginal note says that he “is not found elsewhere on this day.” The observation is correct: although more than twenty saints named Donatus are found, we have so far found none assigned anywhere to this day. The manuscript continues:

> Udalricus, bishop and confessor. Innocentius and Sebastia, with thirty other martyrs.

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949, Hosea and Martin are absent. In Ughellianus the Sirmian martyrs are absent.

Altemps:

> Likewise, the burial of Saint Malricus, bishop and martyr.

Could this not be “Udalricus of Augsburg”?

Bizuntinus:

> In Bavaria, the burial of Saint Oldericus, bishop, most renowned for the power of his miracles.

Rheims, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris:

> In the territory of the city of Bourges, in the village of Vescennus, the feast of Saint Laurianus, bishop and martyr.

The Lübeck-Cologne Edition:

> In the monastery of Tuicium, on the bank of the Rhine, the translation of some relics of Saint Ursula, virgin and queen, from the city of Cologne. Likewise Saint Florentia, virgin and martyr, one of the company of the eleven thousand virgins.

It continues:

> Hosea and Haggai. In the province of Raetia, at the city of Augusta, the feast of Saint Udalricus, bishop and confessor of that city. One Easter day, while he was celebrating Mass, the right hand of the Lord appeared over him; together with his own right hand it sanctified this sacrament, just as had previously happened at the Lord’s Supper.

The text continues, somewhat interpolated and transposed, in which thirty-three companions are assigned to the Sirmian martyrs.

> In Bohemia, Saint Procopius, abbot and confessor.

Castellanus incorrectly places this on 11 April. Crugerius notes in *Sacred Bohemian Dust* that he died on 25 March, but that he is celebrated more festively on this day because of his canonization.

Belin adds “Haggai.” Concerning Martin, he adds “the dedication of his basilica.” The Sirmian martyrs are placed last, in reverse order.

Greven:

> Haggai the prophet. In Bohemia, Saint Procopius, abbot and confessor. Nonna, virgin of Tongeren. The translation of Saint William, count of Poitiers and confessor.

In the monastery of Tuicium, across from Cologne, the translation of certain relics … as above. “Likewise the translation of Saint Florentia …”; above she is written as *Florentina*.

Molan inserts in different type into the text:

> And the dedication of his basilica.

At the end:

> And Haggai the prophet. On the same day, the feast of blessed Udalricus, bishop and confessor, who shone in the world through many unheard-of miracles. Likewise Saint Domitianus, disciple of Saint Landelinus.

In other editions, “Haggai the prophet” is added to the text in italic type, as is “the dedication.” At the end:

> In the province of Raetia, at the city of Augusta, the feast of blessed Udalricus, bishop and confessor, who shone through many unheard-of miracles. At Blanciacum, the burial of Saint Bertha, most devout, who ended her life there in peace and who, through many signs of virtue in that place, continues to shine to this day. On the fourth day, Saint Andrew of Crete, holy father of Jerusalem.

Castellanus distinguishes this Andrew from the one celebrated on 17 October.

[Col. 0225]

Hosea the prophet. At Tours, the translation of blessed Martin, bishop and confessor, and his ordination to the episcopate. In Africa, the feast of Saint Jocundianus the martyr, drowned in the sea. At Sirmium, the holy martyrs Innocentius and Sebastia, with thirty others. In the territory of the city of Bourges, Saint Laurianus the martyr, whose head was carried to Seville, in Spain.

## 5 July — III Non.

[Note: [Col. 0227D]]

So have Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Pulsanensis, Munerat, Greven, and Molan. Many other manuscripts are not far removed, as will appear below.

[Note: [Col. 0227D]]

Munerat makes a shameful error at the very beginning, perhaps through a copyist’s mistake, when he reads “At Sicily.” The manuscripts write *Syriam* or *Siriam* indiscriminately, so that they are not consistent with themselves. In the text I have followed Pratensis, Rosweyd, Pulsanensis, and Molan; anyone who prefers the others is free to do so. *Domitii* must be read; Antwerp-Major wrongly has *Domiciani*, and Rosweyd *Domitiani*. Tornacensis omitted the title “saint,” which should precede it. Pratensis, Heriniensis, and Molan have *Zoae*, retaining the diphthong; all the others read *Zoe*, except Munerat, who gives *Zoee* … A few have “to the Confession of Saint Peter”; most, as in the text. The cited Pratensis, Heriniensis, and Molan correctly read *arctata*, whereas nearly all the others have *artata*. Antwerp-Major has *a collo et capillis*; Rosweyd and Munerat have *collo et capillis*; the others perhaps more correctly agree with the text. Likewise, with *subter horribili* correctly supplied, whereas Pulsanensis incorrectly wrote *ibi subter*.

[Note: [Col. 0229A]]

Concerning the martyrs Domitius and Zoa, or Zoe, who alone are recorded in the text, there is nothing on this day in the Hieronymian copies, nothing in the genuine Bede, nor in Florus, Rabanus, or Notker. The *Romanum parvum*, Ado’s customary source, opened the way by saying:

> In Syria, Saint Domitius the martyr.

The Viennese manuscript gathered much into a very brief eulogy:

> Who by his virtues bestows many benefits on the inhabitants.

These same words, as is clear, were transferred by our text into its calendar. This eulogy, whatever its value, was taken from Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 100.

The martyrdom of our Domitius is mentioned briefly in the Alexandrian, or Paschal, Chronicle under the year 363, in Cangius’s edition, page 297, where *Dometius* is written instead of *Domitius*. Ruinart did not describe the story, however brief; he does mention Domitius in his discussion of the martyrs who suffered under Julian, page 645. Tillemont approves the history of Domitius, volume 7, page 422, and asks on page 744 whether he is the same person as the one listed in the Roman Martyrology on 7 August.

From the aforesaid source of the *Romanum parvum* also comes the second announcement:

> At Rome, the feast of Zoa, wife of Nicostratus.

Florus placed her on the preceding day with a longer eulogy composed from the Acts of Saint Sebastian; Ado also commemorates part of these Acts, though in his customary shorter form. The entire sequence of events may be found in the Acts of that saint under 20 January, chapter 20 of our work.

Usuard selected his eulogy from Ado, so that the whole text here also proceeds from him. Wandalbert neatly fitted its summary into verse:

> Let Domitius speak of threefold glory; and the illustrious Zoe,  
> Through martyrdom, increased the company rightly called blessed.

[Note: [Col. 0229B]]

Nearly all the middle-quality manuscripts deviate only slightly from the pure text, including Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Albergen, and Danish. In the section concerning Zoe or Zoa they insert only:

> Wife of blessed [others: holy] Nicostratus.

Belin states the same addition somewhat differently:

> Zoe the martyr, wife of blessed Nicostratus the martyr.

He alone also writes:

> To the confession of blessed Peter and Paul.

Centulensis does not depart from the purity of the first announcement concerning Domitius. Then:

> At Rome, Saint Zoe, wife of Nicostratus the martyr. She was hung by her hair from a tree; after a dreadful smoke had been applied beneath her, she gave up her spirit in confession of Christ.

Bruxellensis, first:

> By anticipation, the octave of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

It then proceeds to Domitius, in which it is pure. Concerning Zoe, after *oraret* it reads:

> Seized by pagan persecutors.

The remainder agrees with the text.

Hagenoyensis. Concerning Hosea, on the preceding day he composed a eulogy from Sacred History, for which we referred the reader to the source. He transferred Haggai to this day, whose eulogy I present here as a sample. It reads:

> Haggai the prophet, who was from the tribe of Judah and spoke to Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, leader of the people, and to Jesus the high priest, son of Jehozadak, so that they might return from Chaldea to Jerusalem in the first year of Cyrus, king of the Assyrians, who gave them permission to go. This prophet began to preach to the people more than to prophesy, and for this reason they acted slowly. Nevertheless, he prophesied the people’s return under Cyrus, the building of the temple, the recall [restoration] of the city of Jerusalem, the renewal of priestly observance, and the destruction of foreign kingdoms. This prophet did not fear King Cambyses’ decree, but strengthened the hands of those building the temple of the Lord. He also foretold barrenness of the land to the children of Judah, because they were negligent in building the temple. Haggai, the prophet of the Lord, died in Jerusalem, and all the people mourned him, and he was buried there.

Then:

> In Syria, the feast of Saint Dyomitius the martyr, who by his virtues …

in pure form. And:

> At Rome, Saint Zoe, wife of Nicostratus the martyr. While she …

almost as in the text. Finally he restores what he had omitted on the preceding day:

> At Sirmium, the holy martyrs Innocentius and Sebastia, with thirty others. In the territory of the city of Bourges, Saint Laurianus the martyr, whose head was carried to Spain.

Aquicinctinus has *Domicianus* instead of *Domitius*.

Matricularius-Carthusian-Utrecht:

> In Syria, Domitius the martyr; Zoe the martyr, concerning whom it is read in the Acts of Saint Sebastian.

We cited the passage itself from our Acts above in the Observation.

Camberiensis of the Conventuals of Saint Mary:

> Likewise Saints Demetrius and Numerianus.

The Lübeck-Cologne Edition begins:

> At Rome, Saint Zoe, wife of blessed Nicostratus the martyr, for whom blessed Sebastian obtained from the Lord, while he was still mute, the power of speech. While she was praying at the tomb of blessed Peter the Apostle, she was seized by persecutors and [placed] by the patron of the district of Naumachia for six days in a very dark prison …

and so forth, as in the text. It is pure in the section on Domitius. At the end it adds:

> At Trier, blessed Numerianus, bishop and confessor.

Greven:

> In Sicily, Saints Agatho and Trifina; Martin, Theodore, and Godepha; Tryphon.

See the Hieronymian Martyrology.

> At Trier, Numerianus, bishop and confessor. The translation of Saint Wendelinus the confessor.

Molan inserts into the text, in different type, after *arctata*:

> She was led to the patron of the naval games.

At the end:

> At Trier, the burial of Saint Numerianus, archbishop.

Then, in smaller type:

> The burial of Saint Valerius the confessor, first bishop of Couserans, concerning whom blessed Gregory of Tours speaks in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 84.

Other editions agree in the text with the first. At the end, however:

> At Trier, the burial of Saint Numerianus, archbishop. On the fifth day, Saint Martha, mother of Saint Simeon, on the Wonderful Mountain. And Saint Athanasius, holy father and God-bearing, who was on Athos. And Saint Lampadius.

[Col. 0227]

In Syria, the feast of Saint Domitius the martyr, who by his virtues bestows many benefits on the inhabitants. At Rome, Saint Zoe the martyr, who, while praying at the Confession of the Apostle Peter, was seized by persecutors, thrown into a very dark prison, then hung from her neck and hair on a tree; after a dreadful smoke had been applied beneath her, she gave up her spirit in confession of the Lord.

## 6 July — Pridie Non.

[Note: [Col. 0229]]

So have Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Munerat, the second edition of Belin, and Greven.

[Note: [Col. 0231]]

All the manuscripts write *Judeam* simply, except our Pratensis copy, in which they also have *Esaiae*, as Belin and Molan do. Tornacensis, Munerat, and others have *Isaiae*; we follow Heriniensis and Greven, as in the text. Tornacensis lacks *juxta* before the transfer of Octava; it is found in Heriniensis and Belin. The others more commonly have *Octavae*. Munerat transposes *Neronis imperii* into *imperii Neronis*, as does Tornacensis; Greven reverses the sense by reading *per Neronis impii* (“through impious Nero”). Again it has *ad … Confessionem memoraret* instead of *oraret*. Munerat has *lapidibus* for *lapidatus*. Among the pure witnesses, Pratensis alone reads *Maginensi*, as I shall discuss more fully below. The others better have *in pago Treverensi*, for which Heriniensis incorrectly writes *Trecarensi*. Others read it differently, but, unless I am mistaken, they are equally in error.

[Note: [Col. 0231A]]

Today’s text too Usuard took entirely from Ado, and Ado from the *Romanum parvum*. None of the saints mentioned is recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrology; only the octave of the Apostles is treated, with the prophet Isaiah prefixed, as was also done by Bede’s constant follower, Rabanus.

Florus does mention Tranquillinus, but in such a way that he could not in any manner have served as a source for either Ado or Usuard. Thus the *Romanum parvum* announces Joel together with Isaiah, and Ado does the same. Our text, however, omitting Joel, adds the manner of death and the place of burial to Isaiah. I think this was taken from Epiphanius, an extract from whom Surius presents on this day, together with another passage concerning Isaiah drawn from Isidore of Seville.

All the witnesses record the octave of the Apostles in the same words. They also differ very little in their wording concerning the first arrival of the blessed Apostle Paul in the city of Rome. Ado added “in the second year of Nero’s reign,” which our text transcribed, while neglecting the long account of Paul’s journeys that can be seen in Ado. The *Romanum parvum* continues:

> And Tranquillinus the martyr.

Ado composed his brief eulogy from the Acts of Saint Sebastian, already cited several times; Usuard contracted it still further, though the middle-quality manuscripts restore it almost in full, as will be shown in the Additions.

Finally, the last commemoration is expressed in the *Romanum parvum* as:

> And the feast of Saint Goar the confessor.

In Ado:

> On the same day, the burial of the most blessed Goar the confessor.

It is stated simply, without any location, which Mabilio wrongly assigns to him in the district of Trecharius, in the passage cited below, as we demonstrated in the Preface.

Rabanus composed a longer history of his life, the first part of which we shall quote from Molan in the Additions. The saint’s Life itself, composed anonymously in a similarly rough style, and another set out by Wandalbert were published and annotated by Mabillon in the second Benedictine century, beginning on page 275. A later version is also found in Surius, but Cointius prefers an earlier one, discussing Goar sporadically in his Annals under the years 617, 618, 640, and 647. We reserve all these matters for further examination.

The question here is how Usuard expressed the place of the burial. Pratensis, together with three manuscripts generally similar to it—Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and Aquicinctinus—reads:

> In the district of Maginensis, Magniensis, or Machinensis.

We frankly confess that this place is entirely unknown to us. We know well the district of Trier, recorded by the other witnesses, and we do not doubt that Usuard wrote this in his original wording. Thus some unskilled person must have inserted into the Pratensis manuscript a word unknown to him, which then passed from it into other manuscripts copied from that one.

I cannot at all conjecture what deterred Molan from claiming this final announcement for Usuard, given the manifest agreement of the streams with their source—that is, the *Romanum parvum*, Ado, and Usuard—which Wandalbertus also demonstrates. Today’s saints he elegantly comprised in five little verses:

> The eminent Prophet, cut down yesterday in the world …

Isaiah shines forth in martyrdom, in courage and speech.

Tranquillinus, at once you shine with a double splendor,

Father of saints, accompany those slain among the saints;

And then Goar, Christ’s servant and holy man, is honored.

] [Note: [Col. 0231C]

ANTUERP.-MAJ., after Isaiah, inserts in second place: “Likewise, the deposition of Saint Teufredus, deacon.” And at the end it adds: “On the same day, in Britain, the deposition of Saint Sexburga.” We have already said that, instead of Treverensis, it reads Magniensis.

ROSWEYD. begins: “The octave of the apostles Peter and Paul.” It agrees in its additions with ANTUERP.-MAJ., but reads Theofredus instead of Teufredus; and as for Sexburga, it incorrectly assigns her the title “Virgin.” Instead of Treverensis it has Machinensis.

PULSANEN. is pure up to and including Tranquillinus the martyr. The rest is lacking.

The first edition of BELINUS and MOLANUS omit the final announcement, about which we have said more above in the Observation.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.: “Of Isaiah the Prophet,” stopping there. Paul’s entrance is omitted. Regarding Tranquillinus they add what Usuard suppressed, namely: “Of the father of Marcus and Marcellianus, martyrs, who, believing in Christ through the preaching of blessed Sebastian, while to, etc.” At the end: “On the same day, of Goar the confessor.” Nothing further.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN. and LOVANIEN. are pure except for what they insert concerning Tranquillinus, as just mentioned.

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. begin, the former: “On the eighth of the apostles,” the latter: “The octave of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.” In both, Paul’s entrance is omitted, and concerning Tranquillinus they likewise have what ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. have.

BRUXELLEN.: “The translation of Saint Gudula the virgin, our patroness. In Judea, of Isaiah and Joel, the prophets, who, since Isaiah had been cut apart, etc. On the same day, the first entrance of Saint Paul the Apostle into the city of Rome. While he was being sent there in chains by Festus, the governor of Judea, after appealing to the emperor, in the second year of Nero’s reign.” Concerning Tranquillinus it has what was given above. Then—he could have inserted this again here by anticipation—“At Alexandria, of Saint Pantaenus [Panthemius], a confessor, an apostolic man adorned with every kind of wisdom. He possessed such zeal and love for the word of God that, inflamed by the warmth of faith and devotion, he even set out to preach the Gospel of Christ to all the nations hidden away in the remotest regions of the East.” See the following day. In the notice of Goar it is pure. Finally: “At Vienne, of Saint Foldo [Eoaldus], bishop, through whose efforts the relics of the holy martyrs of the Theban Legion were brought to the city of Vienne.” These are Adon’s words, transferred to the following day.

HAGENOYEN. is entirely occupied with encomia of the prophets, a specimen of which we gave on the preceding day. Here he relates a long story about Isaiah, which there is no time to transcribe. Concerning Tranquillinus, as above. In other respects it is sufficiently pure. Then: “On the same day, in the territory of Trier, of Saint Goar, priest and hermit, whose holiness was wonderfully revealed by an infant questioned by him (the text reads oudit, perhaps intending prodidit). For Archbishop Rusticus charged Goar with the sexual offense which he himself had committed, and the seven-day-old infant excused him and declared the bishop to be its father. Because of this deed the bishop ought to have been deposed by the king of the Franks and Goar installed in his place. And scarcely having obtained a few days, he asked the Lord for perpetual illness and received it: fevers which afflicted him for seven years, and in which he died.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Of Isaiah the prophet, who was cut apart in Judea. Of Goar the priest on the Rhine. Of Tranquillinus the martyr, concerning whom it is read in the Acts of Saint Sebastian.” See the Acts, chapters 12 and 20.

In VATICAN., no. 5949, Isaiah and Goar are absent. It adds: “At Autun, the feast of Saint Leontius, bishop and confessor.”

ALTEMPS.: “In Britain, of Saint Sexburga, sister of the holy and perpetual virgin queen Etheldreda, who had been married to King Ovotibricht, the younger brother of Ermenred, namely the father of Saints Aelthredus and Ethelbertus. By this Sexburga the aforesaid king begot two daughters and Ethbrichtus, his heir in the kingdom, under whom the aforementioned martyrs [I think this refers to those saints, Aelthredus and Ethelbertus] were killed.”

[Col. 0233B] FLORENTIN.: “In Tuscany, at Fiesole, the passion of Saint Romulus, bishop and martyr of that city, and of his companions, namely Carissimus, Marchitianus, Crescentius and Dulcissimus, who were disciples of blessed Peter the Apostle and were sent by him to that same city to preach the word of God.” STROZZ. continues: “The aforesaid Saint Romulus, consecrated bishop of that city by Saint Peter, endured grievous and terrible tortures together with his companions under the tyrant Repertianus, and at last willingly suffered death for Christ’s name. Thus they obtained the crown of martyrdom and were buried there at the foot of the mountain on which the aforesaid city of Fiesole is situated.” Again all have: “Saint Goar … buried in the valley of Trioricha.” Finally STROZZ. and MEDIC.: “On the same day, of Saint Syrus, bishop of Genoa and confessor.”

LUXOVIEN.: “At Lyons, of blessed Leontius, bishop. On the same day, of Saints Bertharius and Athalenus, martyrs, who were killed by the Allobroges.”

SALINEN.: “At Autun, the deposition of Saint Legontius [Col. 0233C], bishop.” The same person as the “Leontus” mentioned above, etc.

CODEX MONTIS SANCTI: “The feast of the holy martyrs [Col. 0234A] Bertharius the priest and Athalenus the Levite.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. In the text, with some transposition, it resembles ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. Concerning Goar it adds only: “A man of extraordinary hospitality and charity, whose deeds are recorded.” Then: “At Vienne, of Saint Eooldus, bishop and confessor, through whose efforts,” etc., as in BRUXELLEN. “On the same day, of blessed Sexburga the virgin, sister of Saint Etheldreda the queen. Likewise of Saint Gadalena [Godeleva], virgin and martyr. On the same day, the translation of Saint Gudula the virgin.”

GREVEN.: “In Syria, of Zotichus, Amandus and Artetes. In Tuscany, of Romulus, bishop and martyr, a disciple of blessed Peter, and of Marcianus and others. Of Palladius, bishop and confessor. Of Leutfredus, deacon and confessor. Of Gadalena, virgin and martyr. Of Sexburga, queen. In Ireland, of Nonnina, virgin. On the same day, the translation of Saint Gudula the virgin.”

MOLAN.: “In the territory of Trier, of Saint Goar, priest and confessor. Born in the province of Aquitaine [Col. 0234B], in the time of Hildebert, king of the Franks, he was from infancy a true worshiper of God. Later consecrated priest there, he abandoned his homeland and parents and chose to serve God freely in the province adjoining the banks of the Rhine, called Trigoria, which belongs to the diocese of Trier, until the end of his life.” See the remainder in Rabanus and also in Notker, who devoted several days to him. “In the Cistellensian territory, the passion of blessed Godeliva the martyr.” Then, in smaller type: “At Rotornacum, the translation of Saint Hermes the martyr, under the emperor Hadrian, from the monastery of Inda.” Other editions insert more, in different type, into the text concerning Tranquillinus. Concerning Goar, as in the cited edition. Likewise concerning Godeliva. Then: “In Britain, the deposition of Saint Sexburga, widow. In Campania, under Diocletian, of Saint Dominica, virgin and martyr, who, after breaking the idols and overcoming fire and beasts, was beheaded and departed to the Lord. Her body rests at Tropea in Calabria. On the sixth day, of the holy father Sisoes the Great.” Again, in smaller type [Col. 0234C]: “At Rotornacum,” etc.]

[Col. 0229]

In Judea, of Isaiah the prophet, who, cut into two parts, died and was buried beneath the oak of Rogel, beside the crossing of the waters. Likewise, the octave of the Apostles and the first entrance of blessed Paul the Apostle into the city of Rome, in the second year of Nero’s reign. At Rome, the feast of Saint Tranquillinus the martyr, who, while praying at the Confession of blessed Paul, was seized by pagans and stoned, and completed his martyrdom. In the territory of Trier, of Saint Goar, priest and confessor.

On the Nones. Day 7. [Note: [Col. 0233]

Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Greven. and Molan. agree. Likewise Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen. and Danicus.]]

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

The name of Pantaenus is given in various forms: some write Pantheni, others Pantemii, others Panthemii, and so forth. We approach the correct form most closely on the basis of Herinien., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. Praten., Greven. and Molan. read: “He possessed such zeal, etc.”; the others follow Ado, as it appears in the text. Antuerp., Max.-Lubec. and all the middle-class manuscripts write quite neatly: “inflamed by the warmth of faith and devotion”; but neither in Ado nor in the purer manuscripts is the word “inflamed” found. The manuscripts vary [Col. 0234D] in the final name of the five martyrs: some call him Simphorianus, others, more correctly with the Roman parvum and Ado, Simphronianus. In Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject. and Leyden, Victorinus is absent; in Lovanien the fifth is called Simplicius, which is the name of the fifth martyr in the class marked VI Idus November, where he stands first. Tornacen. has movere, “to move,” instead of commovere, “to stir”; Praten. has torquere, “to torture,” instead of torqueri, “to be tortured”; Greven. has penitus, “entirely,” instead of postea, “afterward”; Molan. has, in his own fashion, poenitus, like Faelix, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

Today Florentinius asks whether the person who in the Hieronymian Martyrologies is called Parthenus, Permenus, Parthemus, or by some other inflection—whether, I say, this person has anything in common with our celebrated Pantaenus, whom we briefly mentioned in the Chronology of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, p. 21. It is most likely, however, that there the reference is to a martyr entirely different from the apostle of the Indians. Pantaenus is likewise unknown to Bede, Florus and Rabanus. He first found a place in the calendars through the Roman parvum, together with other saints of Rufinian origin, and was adorned by Ado—if I am not mistaken, from Eusebius and Jerome—with the encomium whose more elegant portion Our Author excerpted in his customary manner, while Notker transcribed the whole. It may serve the reader’s information if I indicate briefly [Col. 0235A] the life of Pantaenus, collected and arranged from all the ancient documents by our Halloix, in the second volume of the Lives of the Fathers of the East, beginning at p. 839. Tillemont arranged his account in French in volume III, beginning at p. 170. In Wandalbert there is a single verse concerning our saint:

“On the Nones, Pantaenus’ merit and faith shine forth.”

The next class of Roman martyrs, again passed over on this day by the older authorities, is expressly recorded by the praised Roman parvum in these words: “At Rome, of Nicostratus, chief secretary, the martyr, Claudius, Castorius, Victorinus and Symphronianus.” The Viennese author transferred these names into his text and expanded them considerably from the Acts of Saint Sebastian, in which at least the first three are named individually in our edition, chapter 11. Notker, however, after reciting these saints’ names, observed concerning the last, whom he calls Symphorianus: “Or, as it is contained in the Book of Sacraments, Simproniani.” Then he continues: “We believed that we had celebrated their feast on the sixth day of the Ides of November until venerable Father Ado indicated that other and different persons were to be honored in their place; concerning these, in their proper place, with the help of their life, we shall discuss more conveniently.” What he discussed, however, we do not know, since the remainder of his Martyrology after 26 October is missing. It is worth noting the observation added by Notker, for in the Hieronymian Martyrologies the same names, except that Simplicius appears instead of [Col. 0236A] Victorinus and Simphronius or Simphonianus instead of Simphronianus, are recorded on the sixth day of the Ides of November, as also in Bede. Florus’ addition explicitly indicates that they were converted to the faith of Christ by Saint Sebastian and baptized by Polycarp, in precisely the same sense that Ado applied to our present class. By contrast, the author of the Roman parvum, on that sixth day of the Ides—that is, 8 November—introduces others, although nearly homonymous, speaking as follows: “At Rome, of the martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphronianus, Castorius and Simplicius, most distinguished artisans.” To these same persons Ado attached on that very day an encomium, so that they must be regarded as entirely distinct both from the catechumens of Saint Sebastian commemorated today and from the four or five Crowned Martyrs. It is enough for the present purpose to have indicated these matters; they will be examined fully in the Acts for July to be published next. Meanwhile it is clear that Usuard, although somewhat more concise, has departed no more from Ado’s wording here than in the preceding announcement. Evoldus, noted last in Ado, appears with the encomium concerning the relics of the Thebans brought to Vienne, which we discussed in the Additions for the preceding day. Our author omitted him, however, together with most of the bishops of Vienne. The name is written in various ways, as the various Additions sufficiently show. Perhaps the best reading is Castellan’s Eoaldus.]

[Note: [Col. 0235B]

ANTUERP.-MAJ., often augmented with English saints, adds at the end: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Thomas the martyr.”

PULSANEN. is pure in the first announcement; in the second, after somewhat changing the names, it abridges the encomium.
