ROSWEYD. adds to the fairly pure text: “At Eichstätt, of Willibald, bishop and confessor. At Alexandria, of Publius the martyr with twenty-four others.”

MUNERAT. at the end after the text: “At Canterbury, the translation of Saint Thomas, bishop and martyr.”

There is also an addition in the PRATENSI codex: “On the same day, the octave of Saint Martial”; but since it bears such a note, I think it was added in the margin, or at least belongs rather to the other codex which we call the Blessed one than to the older manuscript.

CENTULEN.: “At Alexandria, of Saint Pantaenus, an apostolic man adorned with every kind of knowledge. At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Nicostratus, chief secretary, Claudius, record-keeper, Castorius, Victorinus and Symphorianus. Saint Sebastian taught them to believe in Christ and encouraged them to the glory of martyrdom.” A later hand adds in the margin: “On the same day, of Saint Marculf, abbot.”

BRUXELLEN., omitting Pantaenus, concerning whom it had spoken the day before, anticipates again here: “In Asia Minor, of Saints Aquila and Priscilla, his wife. Concerning them it is read in the Acts of the Apostles. When they themselves had come from the city of Rome to Achaea, blessed Paul the Apostle stayed with them because of his trade; for they practiced the same craft, namely tentmaking, in which the Apostle also worked.” In the following notice it seems to make two saints out of the term Primiscrinius: Primus and Serincus. In the rest [Col. 0235D] of the text it is pure. It adds: “In Palestine, the feast of blessed Procopius the martyr. He was led from Scythopolis to Caesarea and beheaded by the judge Fabianus.” This too is anticipated from the following day. Finally: “In England, the translation of Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury and martyr.”

HAGENOYEN., fairly pure in the first notice, has the following in second place: “In the city of Eichstätt, the feast of Saint Willibald the boy [or, perhaps, ‘man’?], bishop and confessor of that same city. Likewise at Vienne, of Coldus [intended to mean Eoaldus or Evoldus], bishop and confessor.” The notice concerning Nicostratus and his companions follows in pure form. Then it transfers here from the preceding day: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Tranquillinus the martyr. While he was praying at the confession of blessed Paul, he was seized by pagans and stoned, and completed the martyrdom of the martyrs.”

MATRIC.-CARTUL.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Nicostratus the martyr [Col. 0236B] with his companions. Of Pantaenus, an apostolic man adorned with knowledge.”

CODEX DIVIONEN. S. Benigni, in three different excerpts: “At the monastery of Dijon, the translation of the bodies of Saints Urbanus, Eustasius and Hilary the confessor, and of Saints Radegundis the queen and Paschasia the virgin; and also of blessed Quieta, the wife of the aforesaid blessed Hilary.”

REG. SUEC. under no. 428: “At Canterbury, the translation of Saint Thomas, archbishop and martyr.”

VATICAN., marked no. 5949: “The feast of Saints Januarius, Laurentius and Peter in Saint Sophia. At Camerino, of Saint Answinus, priest.”

ALTEMPS.: “Likewise, the deposition of Saint Boisilus, priest and confessor, and of Saint Mary the virgin, who offered himself as a pleasing sacrifice to God for the liberty of the Church of God.” Thus it is read, though not very clearly.

STROZZIAN.: “On the same day, of Saint Willibald, bishop and confessor.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. adds after the text: “On the same day, of Saint Willibald, bishop of the city of Eichstätt and confessor. At Trier, of blessed Navitus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, of blessed Processus the confessor. In England, in the city of Canterbury, the translation of Saint Thomas, bishop and martyr. In Scotland, the translation of Saint Kentigern, bishop and confessor.”

BELINUS. in both editions: “On the same day, of Saint Willibald, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN.: “At Vienne, of Saint Eoaldus, bishop and confessor, through whose efforts the relics of the holy [Col. 0236D] Thebans were brought to the aforesaid city.” See what we said above at the end of our Observation. “Likewise, of Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt and confessor. Of Navitus, bishop of Trier and confessor. Likewise, of Walfridus, bishop. In England, of Hedda, bishop. The translation of Saint Thomas, bishop and martyr of Canterbury. Of Maternianus the confessor. Of Apollonius the confessor. Of Processus the confessor. Of Edilberga, virgin and abbess, daughter of the king of the East Angles, whom Bede mentions in Book III. At Trier, of Saint Julia the virgin. Of Mustiola, widow.”

MOLAN. adds in different type to Nicostratus “chief secretary,” to Claudius “record-keeper,” and after Simphorianus, instead of Simphronianus, inserts: “Saint Sebastian taught these men to believe in Christ, and the priest Saint Polycarp baptized them. While they were searching for the bodies of the saints along the banks of the Tiber, they were seized.” At the end: “At Canterbury, the translation of Saint [Col. 0237A] Thomas, bishop and martyr. On the same day, of Saint Bilibald, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saint Begga, widow.” And in smaller type: “In England, of Hedda, bishop. Of Edilburga, virgin,” etc., as in GREVEN. “At Clermont, of Saint Illidius, bishop and confessor of that same city.” Later editions have the same in the text. At the end, however: [Col. 0238A] “On the same day, of Saint Willibald, bishop and confessor. At Trier, the feast of Saint Navitus, bishop and martyr. On the seventh day, of the holy father Thomas in Maleo and of Saint Cyriaca, the great martyr. At Canterbury, the translation of Saint Thomas, bishop and martyr. At Antoing, the translation of Saint Begga, widow.”]

[Col. 0233]

At Alexandria, the feast of Saint Pantaenus, an apostolic man adorned with every kind of wisdom, who possessed such zeal and love for the word of God that, inflamed by the warmth of faith and devotion, he even set out to preach the Gospel of Christ to all the nations hidden away in the remotest regions of the East. At Rome, of the holy martyrs Nicostratus, Claudius, Castorius, Victorinus and Simphronianus. Judge Fabianus, having for ten days tried threats and blandishments against them, and being utterly unable to move them in any way, ordered them to be tortured for a third time and afterward thrown headlong into the sea. [Badillart. adds from the margin of the Pratensis codex: “On the same day, the octave of Saint Martial, bishop and confessor.”]

The Eighth Day before the Ides. Day 8. [Note: [Col. 0237]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen and Grevenus.]]

[Note: [Col. 0237B]

Praten. correctly wrote Scytopolis, or at least the person who copied our exemplar. Since, however, the others generally have Scitopolis, I was compelled to follow even those who are mistaken. Pulsan. alone wrote Scithopolis, while Greven. most incorrectly has Sticopolis and Molan. Nicopolis. “At Caesarea,” instead of “to Caesarea,” is an error in Pulsanen. In the same manuscript there is another error in the phrase “at the first confident response,” [Col. 0238B] where, together with the text, one should read “at the first confidence of his responses.” Again, instead of Kilianus it has Julianus. Since I find the form “Ciliani” in all the manuscripts except Greven’s, it had to be retained in the text. In Rabanus and Notker one reads Chiliani, but common usage supports the first inflection.]

[Note: [Col. 0237B]

Usuard continues in the same manner to draw from Ado, who here draws from the Roman parvum: for the first announcement is found only in them. Here are the words of the Roman parvum: “In Asia Minor, of Aquila and Priscilla, his wife.” Ado reads: “In Asia Minor,” etc., exactly as Our Author transferred it into his text. But Ado adds other material, which Notker took from him, in approximately the sense in which we reported it from the Brussels manuscript in the Additions for the preceding day. The matters commonly known from the Acts of the Apostles and Paul’s Epistles are familiar; if you wish to have them arranged in chronological order, consult Tillemont, volume I, p. 246, and other places which we shall discuss elsewhere. Castellan’s note, appended on this day in the Universal Martyrology, is not satisfactory; better are the observations made by Motherius. These matters concerning Aquila and Priscilla are proper to the four Martyrologists cited. Procopius is better known, being also mentioned by the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Rabanus and Wandalbert. Florentinius alone doubts whether there is one Procopius or two, and whether this one is different from the Procopius whom Eusebius celebrates among the martyrs of Palestine, as having been brought before the tribunal and beheaded on the eighth day of the month Desius, which among the Romans is the seventh day before the Ides of June. We shall treat that controversy in its proper place. Meanwhile, it is certain that Procopius is recorded by the Hieronymian Martyrologies on this day; whether together with Quartus, his companion in martyrdom, will be seen elsewhere. It is also certain that the Roman parvum reads: “In Palestine, of Procopius the martyr.” Finally, it is certain that the same encomium is found in Bede, Rabanus, Ado, Usuard and Notker, with only this change of a small word: Usuard writes “by the judge” instead of “by the enraged judge,” a clearer meaning. It is easy to infer who preceded whom. Rabanus and Ado borrowed their material from Bede; Our Author from Ado; Notker from one or the other. Everything points to the celebrated Procopius, with whom Eusebius begins his book on the martyrs of Palestine. The account, from Valesius’ edition, is reproduced by Ruinart beginning at p. 330, and there is appended on p. 373 a somewhat fuller history from the notes of the aforesaid Valesius, p. 172. These accounts may be accepted as true and genuine and as fitting the same person very well. As for what should be thought of the Acts of another Procopius, commander of an army, published by Surius under the name of Metaphrastes, see the Acts for 19 May, p. 304, and Papebrochius’ Response to article 5, beginning at no. 29; Tillemont adds further material in volume V, beginning at p. 605. These brief remarks will suffice here.

Nothing concerning Kilianus is found in the Roman parvum or in Ado, whom Baronius incorrectly cites; nor in Bede or Florus. As for the passage found only in the Lucensian Hieronymian copy, “In Austria, the passion of Saint Kilianus,” Florentinius considers it a fragment inserted from a marginal note by a French antiquarian. I could readily grant him this, in confirmation of what I have observed elsewhere: that the Epternacensis, no more than the other Hieronymian manuscripts, was in Gaul without having been enlarged and interpolated there. That Kilianus was known to Rabanus in that vicinity should not seem at all surprising. From him Notker received the material and adorned it with an encomium twice as long, in which you will also find that Austria distinguished from the modern one, as I have more than once mentioned elsewhere. See the two passions published by Canisius in Antiquae Lectiones, volume IV, beginning at p. 628, and Mabilio’s observations on them, second Benedictine century, p. 991 and following. There is no doubt that Kilianus was also recorded by Our Author, although it is entirely unclear from where he obtained him. Molan, here again excessively scrupulous, removed him from the text. I note that the Roman parvum also commemorates on this day Brictius, whom Ado and Our Author postponed to the following day. Concerning Kilianus and Procopius Wandalbert sang:

“On the eighth day before the Ides, Kilianus and Procopius

Shine forth, following Christ in courage and in death.”]

[Note: [Col. 0237D]

ANTUERP.-MAJ., again drawing from England, adds: “In the monastery of Ventano (see below), the deposition of Saint Grimbald, monk.”

ROSWEYD. begins as follows: “At Würzburg, of Kilianus, bishop and martyr, and his companions Colmannus and Totmannus.” Concerning these, see the BRUXELLEN. codex and others. The following text is pure.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC., MOLAN. and VATICAN., no. 5949, lack the final announcement concerning Kilianus.

MUNERAT. greatly expands the text as follows: “On the same day, of Saint Ciliarius [Kilianus] the martyr. In the territory of Pincerais, of Saint Nonius the confessor. On the same day, of Saint Theobald the confessor.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERG. and DANIC. append to the pure text: “On the same day, of Saint Kilianus, bishop and martyr, and his companions. He came from the islands of the Ocean Sea into the kingdom of Germany, reached the city of Würzburg, and there completed his martyrdom by decapitation under the judge Gozbertus.” They all agree on this, but ANTUERP.-MAX. additionally adds: “In the city of the Almuridians, of the holy martyrs Epicticus [Epictetus], priest, and Astion, monk, whose deeds are recorded.” These are, I think, the deeds published by Rosweyd in the Lives of the Fathers and disseminated from the same source by Surius; they will be illustrated in their proper place.

CENTULEN., except for Kilianus, is unusually pure in the text and adds: “At Heraclea, of Saints John and Aprus. On the same day, of Saint Quillianus and his companions.” It is quite clear that Kilianus is intended.

BRUXELLEN. begins: “In Austrasia, the passion of Saint Kilianus, bishop and martyr, and his companions. He came from the islands of the Ocean Sea into the kingdom of Germany and reached the city of Würzburg. There he rebuked Gosbertus, duke of that place, because he had taken Gayla [Geilana], formerly the wife of his brother, as his own wife. Therefore, at Gayla’s command, Bishop Kilianus and his companions were secretly killed for the sake of truth and justice.” A new anticipation follows: “At Rome, at the ever-flowing Gutta, the feast of Saint Zeno the martyr and of ten thousand two hundred and three others. Likewise, of Julianus the martyr. And of Grimbald the confessor. At the monastery of Belisia, of Saint Landrada, virgin and abbess. She was an illustrious descendant of those whom the Franks call Mayors of the Palace and a kinswoman of our patroness, blessed Gudula. When she died, she immediately appeared to blessed Lambert, bishop, and showed him the place of her burial. When the people did not agree to carry this out, she was buried at Belisia; but after three days she was found, together with the sarcophagus, miraculously transported to the place she had foretold.” Her Life is found in Surius, where these matters may be seen.

HAGENOYEN., after reporting the earlier announcements fairly purely, adds much about Kilianus. But consult Rabanus or Notker; it is abundantly clear from the material given above here and there that they deserve greater confidence than this compiler.

AQUICINCT., at the end after the complete text: “At the city of Winchester, the deposition of blessed Grimbaldus, priest and monk of Sithiu.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Epictetus and Astion, martyrs. The translation of Saint Barbara. Of Procopius the martyr. Of Kilianus, bishop and martyr, with his companions. Of Landrada, virgin. Of Norbertus, archbishop and founder of the Premonstratensian Order.” This undoubtedly concerns some translation. Another is solemnly commemorated at Antwerp on 11 July.

REG. SUECIAE, no. 428: “In the territory of Pintiavum, of Saint Nunnus the confessor.” Castellan writes “Nummius.”

ALTEMPS.: “The passing of Saint Grimbaldus, priest and confessor, a man of great holiness.”

STROZZIAN.: “Likewise, of Saint Paul, martyr of Constantinople.” [Col. 0239D] Is this the bishop mentioned on 7 June?

ABDINGHOFFEN.: “On the same day, of Saint Kilianus with his companions Calamus and Totmannus.” The others are more correct.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins: “At Würzburg, the passion [Col. 0240A] of Saint Kilianus, bishop and martyr, and of his two companions Colonatus and Thotuanus. Kilianus came from the islands of the Ocean Sea to Rome for the salvation of souls. There he was consecrated bishop and, having obtained permission to preach, proceeded to the regions of Germany and came to the city of Würzburg. There he converted Gosbertus, duke of Franconia, to Christ. But because he had illicitly retained his brother’s wife, named Erilana, and the holy bishop urged him to leave her, he caused the holy man and his companions to be punished for this.” In the first two announcements it is fairly pure. At the end: “At Trier, of Saint Auspicius, bishop and confessor. At Heraclea, of Saints John and Primus, confessors. On the same day, of Saint Grumbaldus, priest and confessor. On the same day, of blessed Disibodus, bishop and confessor.” See his Life in Surius on this day.

BELIN. is not entirely pure in the text; at the end it has: “Likewise, of Saint Paul, martyr of Constantinople.”

GREVEN.: “The first translation of Saint Barbara, virgin [Col. 0240B] and martyr, from Nicomedia to the place of her burial. Of Colonanus, priest, and Tornanus, deacon. After setting out from Scotland with blessed Kilianus, bishop and martyr, and preaching Christ in Würzburg, the city of Franconia, they were deemed worthy to attain with him the palm of martyrdom. Of Epictetus, priest, and Astion, monk, martyrs. Coming from the East into the territories of Scythia in the time of Diocletian, they were seized on account of the faith of Christ and, amid all the tortures inflicted upon them, frequently uttered these words: ‘We are Christians, O tyrant; may the will of our God be done in us.’ At last, after various tortures, they were beheaded and completed their martyrdom. At Trier, of Auspicius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, of Disibodus, bishop and confessor. Likewise, of Wazo, bishop of Liège and confessor. In the city of Rouen, the translation of Saint Evodius, bishop and confessor. At Heraclea, of John and Primus. Of Sumniva, virgin, and her companions, martyrs. Having departed from Ireland, they attained the crowns of martyrdom in Norway.”

[Col. 0240C] MOLAN.: “In the territory of Austria, and in the fortress called Würzburg, situated beside the river Main, the feast of Saint Kilianus the martyr and his two companions, who came from Ireland, the island of the Scots, preached the name of Christ in the aforesaid regions, and there were slaughtered under a certain judge Gozbertus for confessing the truth. Later, through many signs, they became manifest as true martyrs of Christ.” These are Rabanus’ words. “Likewise, of Saint Paul, martyr of Constantinople. In the territory of Pincerais, of Saint Nonius the martyr. At Gembloux, the arrival of the body of Saint Exuperius, standard-bearer of the Theban Legion and glorious martyr. At Trier, of Saint Auspicius, bishop. At Vermand, the discovery of the body of Saint Quintinus the martyr. At the monastery of Belisia, of Saint Landrada, virgin.” Concerning Disibodus and Suinniva, or Summiva, as in GREVEN. In other editions there is this difference: the following is added: “At the city of Winchester, the deposition of blessed Grimbaldus, abbot and monk of Sithiu.” And concerning Disibodus: “In the territory of Trier, of Saint [Col. 0240D] Disibodus,” etc. Finally, in smaller type: “In England, of Saint Withburga, virgin.” She is celebrated on 17 March. See Henschenius there.]

[Col. 0237]

In Asia Minor, of Saints Aquila and Priscilla, his wife, concerning whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles. In Palestine, the feast of blessed Procopius the martyr, who was led from Scythopolis to Caesarea and, at the first assurance of his replies, was beheaded by the judge Fabianus. On the same day, [Note: [Col. 0237A] the Carolinian autograph adds companions to Saint Kilianus. There is, however, no erasure here in the Pratensis manuscript, because it is another leaf—a fact I have always noted—where no erasure is visible, although the codex nevertheless differs from the Carolinian autograph. BOUILLART.] of Saint Kilianus the martyr.

The Seventh Day before the Ides. Day 9. [Note: [Col. 0241]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., and also from Albergen. and Danic. Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven. and Molan. [also agree].]

[Note: [Col. 0241A]

I wrote Milius and Cyrillus uninjured, in accordance with the nearly unanimous agreement of the manuscripts. Instead of “for his eager preaching,” Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. incorrectly have “for his eager persecution”; Munerat. has it still worse, reading “for the altar” instead of “for his eagerness.” In Tyre the manuscript reading had to be retained; Antuerp.-Maj. and Greven. have Tiro, but neither form is correct, as I shall show below. I think the Pratensis manuscript correctly reads “in prayer she was pierced through,” but on the authority of the others the construction had to be transposed. Instead, Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. [Col. 0242A] have “pierced through in confession she is,” and Munerat. has “pierced through, she completed her martyrdom.” I read Brictius with Tornacen., Munerat., Greven. and Molan. In Praten. it appears to be written Brixius; others have Bricius or Briecius. Munerat. has the erroneous es instead of est. Molan. omitted item, “likewise,” before “great multitudes of peoples,” etc. Finally, Antuerp.-Maj. has secundo instead of sancto and at the end lucrificans, “winning gain,” rather than “rested in Christ.”]

[Note: [Col. 0241A]

The same method of Usuard once again appears in his description of Ado, and the same method of Ado in following the Little Roman Martyrology, in which, however, as we said on the preceding day, Brictius is placed on 8 July. Thus Zeno, together with that immense multitude of companions, unknown to the other older authorities, is recorded only by our four writers, who are all pulling the same rope. [Col. 0241B] If fuller information should subsequently become available, it will be given in our Acts.

In the Little Roman Martyrology it reads: “Cyril, bishop and martyr,” who does not occupy the same place everywhere, but is praised in nearly the same words by Ado, Usuard, and Notker; in the earlier writers without a location, or place of combat, although he is placed in that manner in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Bede is silent about him; but Florus specified both Egypt and the emperor Decius and the governor Lucius, as well as the fire by which he is said to have been consumed. Rabanus speaks in the same sense, composing a fairly long eulogy. Notker likewise, although following Ado in his wording, added several such characteristics of his own. Meanwhile some name Gortyna in Crete, for which Baronius stands, while others name Rome. All these matters will furnish material for discussion in the Acts when they are elucidated.

The Acts themselves are included in Surius’s collection for this day, composed in a brief, simple, and weighty style; yet the difficulties already mentioned by us led Tillemont to suspect that perhaps two Cyrils had been combined into one. See him, vol. III, p. 715. Nor do I think Castellani’s brief notes on this and the following announcement should be disregarded. When I said that Cyril is praised by Usuard also in nearly the same words, understand that Usuard has abridged Ado’s eulogy in his customary manner.

The following announcement is reported in the Little Roman Martyrology cited above in these words: “In the city of Tyre, Anatolia and Audax.” Instead of *Tyriae*, Bede writes *Tirae*, from which Ado and Rabanus copy their entire eulogy, and consequently Notker as well. Perhaps fearing ambiguity in the word *Tyro*, which Rabanus uses, Notker deliberately added “not far from the city of Rome.” This was certainly necessary, as the circumstances of the eulogy sufficiently indicate: it is not the Phoenician city of Tyre that is intended here, but some Italian town.

This would have fitted Usuard better, for he gathers only the flowers, so to speak, of the eulogy, and, contrary to Ado’s intention, also reads *Tyro*. He therefore forms his announcement in such a way [Col. 0242A] that anyone reading it could scarcely doubt that it refers wholly to the aforementioned city of Tyre, otherwise very well known.

Whether our *Anatholia* should also be considered to be mentioned in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, see Florentinius’s Note for this day and the next, on which, in the Savini manuscripts, she is joined to Victoria. For the rest, Baronius will teach that one should read neither *Tyriae* nor *Tirae*, much less *Tyri* or *Tyro*, but *Thorae*, which is situated beside Lake Velinus in the diocese of Rieti—unless, with our Father John Gravius, who added marginal manuscript notes to Molan’s 1573 edition, called by our predecessors the Douai edition of Molan, and who attributed those notes to Schottus, one should substitute *Turii* in Calabria for *Thorae*. But this will properly be a matter for the Commentary on the Acts of these saints.

Surius published the Acts themselves, somewhat polished in his usual manner, but not so thoroughly purged that they are free from suspicion of interpolation. I like the history as Tillemont arranged it, vol. III, p. 329. Yet there Audax seems to be excluded, although Wandalbert joined him with Anatolia:

> On the seventh day Audax, and likewise Anatolia, shine.

Brictius, recorded by the Little Roman Martyrology on the preceding day in the city of Martula, is reported on this day by Ado with a eulogy, which you will find transcribed in Notker. Our author selected from it [Col. 0242C] piecemeal whatever suited his brevity; and thus, as I said at the beginning, the whole text has been taken from Ado and faithfully transmitted by us.

What should be thought about this history of Brictius may be gathered from the Acts of Chrysopolitus and his companions, discussed by Henschenius under 12 May, and more briefly by Tillemont, vol. V, p. 132.

In Bede and Wandalbert, the deposition of our holy father Ephrem is also commemorated on this day. In Ado: “Likewise in Egypt, Serapion, bishop and confessor.” Our author treats the first on 1 February; he may perhaps have hesitated about Serapion. Certainly he does not mention him on this day, but records three others on different days: the Anchorite and martyr on 21 March; the Antiochene on 30 October; and the Alexandrian on 14 November. More will have to be discussed in the Acts concerning the distinction among the Serapions, in addition to what was discussed on 21 March. But enough of this, lest we wander farther than is proper.

[Note: [Col. 0241D]

TORNACENSIS, which usually shortens longer texts, here omits the eulogies of Cyril and Brictius; in all other respects it agrees completely with the text.

PULSANENSIS proceeds correctly as far as “under the emperor Decius”; everything else is lacking.

ROSWEYD, after the pure text, adds at the end: “In Egypt, Ephrem the monk.” This must certainly be a different person from the deacon of Edessa.

ANTWERP-MAXIMUS, UTRECHT, and LEYDEN prefix to the pure text: “The octave of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.”

LOVANIENSIS, in the cited augmentation, similar to the preceding copies, is additionally defective in the eulogy of Brictius, which it omits entirely.

CENTULENSIS, in the entry for Zeno, is pure: “On the same day, Cyril, blessed bishop, who completed his martyrdom by being beheaded. In the city of Syria [for *Turiae*, unless I am mistaken], Anatolia and Audax, under the emperor Decius. In the city of Martula, Brictius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, our holy father Ephrem, deacon, a man of great virtues and outstanding intelligence.”

BRUXELLENSIS dealt with Zeno on the preceding day. In Anatolia, Audax, and Cyril it is fairly pure. It continues from the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “At Rome, the birthday of the holy virgins Floriana, Faustina, and Felicitas, with seven priests.” It is also correct concerning Brictius, but enlarges his eulogy with these words: “Those standing by saw his soul received into heaven in the form of a snow-white dove.” At the end it adds: “On the same day, our holy father Ephrem.”

HAGENOVENSIS is pure in the entry for Zeno, but in second place has: “Likewise at Cologne Agrippina, Agilolfus, bishop and martyr.” See 31 March. “On the same day, Cyril, blessed bishop and martyr, who preached the word of God in Egypt and therefore was seized by King Lucius and thrown into the flames. But when he was not harmed, the judge was astonished and allowed him to depart. Afterwards he converted many to the faith; therefore the judge, grieving over his release, ordered him to be beheaded. Those standing by saw his soul ascend to heaven in the form of a snow-white dove.” The rest is pure.

MATRICULARY–CARTUSIAN–UTRECHT: “The octave of the Visitation. Cyril, bishop and martyr. Anatolia, virgin and martyr, and Audax. At Rome, Zeno the martyr and ten thousand two hundred who suffered with him.”

VATICAN MS 5949: “In Egypt, Serapion, bishop and confessor. And the deposition of Ephrem.” See the Observations.

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, Everildis, virgin.”

STROZZIAN: “In Egypt, Serapion, bishop and confessor.”

THE LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: “The octave of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. At Cologne Agrippina, the deposition of Agilolfus, archbishop of that city and martyr. When he had been summoned by Charles Martel, whose tutor and counsellor he was, he was killed on the road by certain enemies of his near the town of Malmandar; but he was transferred afterwards to Cologne and honorably placed in the church of Saint Mary at the Steps. Likewise at Cologne Agrippina, the commemoration and ordination of Heribert, blessed archbishop and confessor, which took place under Otto III, emperor of the Romans, in the year 999 from the Incarnation of the Lord.”

It continues: “At Rome, beside the ever-flowing Gutta,” and so forth, where it enumerates at length the various kinds of torture inflicted upon Zeno and his companions. Of Cyril it adds, as above, “his soul in the form of a dove,” and so forth. In the entries for Anatolia, Audax, and Brictius it is fairly pure. At the end: “In Egypt, Serapion, bishop and confessor. At Sens, Theraclius, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0244A] BELIN begins: “The octave of the glorious Virgin Mary’s Visitation.” At the end the eulogy of Brictius is lacking; in the second edition he is called Luricius.

GREVEN: “The octave of the Blessed Mary’s Visitation. At Cologne Agrippina, Agilolfus, blessed bishop and martyr. Because of his love of justice, he became hateful to the wicked and was killed by them; brought back to Cologne, he was honorably placed in the church of Saint Mary at the Steps. At Heliopolis, which is near Lebanon, Cyril, deacon and martyr. As is said in Book VI of the Ecclesiastical History, when he had destroyed many idols under Constantius, he was killed by pagans under Julian. In Egypt, Serapion, blessed bishop and confessor. Maternus, Galendus [the first edition has *Galendinus*], Gaius, and Basil, bishops of Milan and confessors. At Sens, Theraclius, bishop and confessor. At Cologne Agrippina, the ordination of Heribert’s episcopate, bishop and confessor, performed in the year of the Lord 999. In Egypt, Ephrem, our holy father, hermit and confessor. In Ireland, Germanus, confessor. Salvia, virgin. Likewise Wichburga, virgin. The translation of Oda, holy widow.”

MOLAN: “The octave of the glorious Virgin Mary’s Visitation. On this very day, our holy father Ephrem. At Cologne, Agilolfus, archbishop and martyr of that same city.” Then, in smaller type: “Who, because of his love,” and so forth, as in GREVEN. Likewise: “At Heliopolis, which is beside Lebanon,” and so forth, also as in GREVEN.

In other editions, after “beside the ever-flowing Gutta,” the following is inserted, improperly printed in different letters: “which is otherwise called the church of Saint Mary of the Oil Fountain across the Tiber,” although these places are very far apart, as Baronius correctly shows in his Notes. At the end only this is added: “At Cologne, Agilolfus, archbishop and martyr of that same city.” His eulogy has already been reproduced above more than once.]

[Col. 0239]

At Rome, beside the ever-flowing Gutta, the birthday of Zeno the martyr and of ten thousand two hundred and three others. On the same day, Cyril, blessed bishop, who, after being thrown into the flames and emerging unharmed, and after being released by the judge in amazement at so great a miracle, was again beheaded by the same judge because of his urgent and zealous preaching concerning Christ.

In the city of Tyre, the passion of the holy Anatolia and Audax under the emperor Decius. Anatolia, Christ’s virgin, was afflicted with various kinds of blows and finally was pierced through with a sword while at prayer. Audax too was handed over to custody; and without delay he was crowned by sentence of death.

In the city of Martula, Brictius, bishop and confessor, who, after suffering many things for confessing the Lord and being strengthened by a holy angel and blessed Peter the Apostle, also winning great multitudes of believing peoples for almighty God, fell asleep in peace.

## 6th day before the Ides. Day 10

[Note: [Col. 0243]

The only completely pure copies are Pulsanensis, Muneratensis, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0243C]

I have written *Martialis* with Herinien., Antwerp-Maj., and others, although Praten. and certain others differ. Molan alone has *Sylvani*. With Greven, he writes *carceres* for *carcerem*; Belin has “the mortification of prison”; and again, *plumbatis* for *ad plumbatas*, where Antwerp-Maj. has *ad plumbatas*. Some, with Greven and Molan, read *interemptus est* (“was killed”), but Praten., Herinien., Antwerp-Maj., and others omit *est*. The last, however, incorrectly wrote *puniti sunt* (“were punished”), which Belin also has; he likewise lists four African martyrs in last place. *Decolatorum* is incorrectly written in Antwerp-Maj., as is *Cristinae* for *Rufinae*. All the manuscripts have *Galieni*, and therefore that is retained in the text. For “the other, with neck cut,” Greven and Molan read “the other, to the neck,” namely, with the sword having struck it; but Usuard’s construction is different. Belin, for clarity, I suppose, inserted “to heaven” before “they departed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0243C]

The related Martyrologies follow their accustomed paths: the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, and, for the greater part, Notker. Of the illustrious company of the mother and her sons, only the first records: “At Rome, seven brothers.” The Hieronymian copies are so confused that Florentinius needed outside assistance [Col. 0243D] to distinguish the true names of the sons of Saint Felicitas from *coemeterus* and other interpolated material. Nor does Fronto’s Calendar speak with sufficient clarity: “the seven brothers of Apius and Salaria.” On these see the editor’s observation, p. 103, concerning the three Masses and so forth.

The accounts given by Bede and, after him, Ado are clearer. Both express the same opinion, though not in exactly the same words, since one is somewhat shorter than the other; and unless our author were consistently dependent on Ado, one might wonder whether he had Ado rather than Bede before his eyes. Rabanus certainly copied Bede, and Notker Ado, adding a brief clause.

Whether all those brothers were killed on this day, or together with their mother, or in the same place were executed and buried, will be discussed in its proper place, with Bucherius’s most ancient Calendar leading the way; Ruinart reproduces its words, p. 20. I will append the actual Acts of the passion as genuine, collated with Surius’s and Ughelli’s editions and with other manuscripts. It is remarkable how meagerly Tillemont treats these matters, vol. II, p. 312.

We dealt with seven other brothers, likewise seven in number, the Tiburtines, on 28 June, and must deal with them again on the 18th of this month.

Our four Africans are announced by the Little Roman Martyrology in this manner [Col. 0245A]: “In Africa, Januarius, Narinus, Nabor, and Felix.” The wording of the Hieronymian Martyrologies is the same, except that companions seem to be added, whereas our copies have removed them. The Vienne copy, and Notker from it, added to the words just cited “the beheaded,” and also: “Their bodies were transferred to Milan.” Usuard seems to have regarded this translation with suspicion; certainly he completely concealed it in silence, while otherwise taking the entire announcement from Ado.

There is a strong resemblance, at least between the last two and Victor Maurus, whom we discussed on 8 May, so much so that the Acts are said to agree in many respects. See Tillemont, vol. V, beginning at p. 267.

The famous virgins Rufina and Secunda are named by the Little Roman Martyrology only by their names: “At Rome, Rufina and Secunda.” Florentinius observes that, in the Hieronymian manuscripts, they are mixed with the brothers mentioned above, and he gathers several details in their praise. Ado, however, pursued the matter more fully and adorned them with an extended eulogy—an elegant abridgment, evidently, of their Acts. It is surprising that Notker did not transcribe it in full. [Col. 0246A] Our author sampled only a few passages, quite sparingly, if I may speak frankly, considering the abundance of material so extensively arranged by Ado.

It is clear that Ado took his material from the Acts themselves, later published by Mombritius and Surius; these have Aldhelm, the encomiast of the Virgins, and other ancient writers as witnesses to their antiquity. Baronius defends their integrity; more recent writers think otherwise, and Tillemont largely agrees with them, vol. IV, p. 5, especially p. 584.

Their illustrious memory at Rome is confirmed by the very ancient bishopric of Silva Candida, later united with Portus after the destruction of the place. But whatever may eventually be decided about them, it is meanwhile clear, as I said above, that our Martyrologies agree and that the Usuard manuscripts preserve Usuard’s own native simplicity.

Wandalbert mentions only the first group:

> On the sixth day, Felicitas, blessed mother,  
> For Christ’s sake, gives a crown to seven sons,  
> Whom she bore and sent beforehand, pleasing to God, to the altar.

[Note: [Col. 0245B]

TORNACENSIS enumerates the names of the seven brothers, but omits the eulogy. Everything else is pure.

PULSANENSIS is pure in the first entry and adds: “Likewise at Rome, the holy virgins Rufina and Secunda.” The remainder is lacking.

ROSWEYD, after the pure text, adds: “Likewise, Amelberga, holy virgin.”

ANTWERP-MAX., UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOVANIENSIS, ALBERGEN, and DANIC all, with Belin, place the Africans last and add: “At the port of Ghent, in the Blandinian monastery, Amelberga, holy virgin.” LOVANIENSIS lacks the eulogy of the seven brothers, and DANIC adds its own local entry: “In Dacia, in the city of Odense, the birthday of Canute, holy king and martyr.”

CENTULENSIS: “At Rome, the birthday of the seven brothers, sons of Saint Felicitas, namely Januarius, Felix, Philip, Alexander, Vitalis, Silvanus, and Martialis, who suffered under Antoninus and were brought before the prefect—whether publicly or privately? [Col. 0245C] Then they were sent before various judges to be torn apart by various punishments. In Africa, Januarius, Marinus, Nabor, and Felix, holy beheaded martyrs. Their bodies were transferred to Milan. Likewise at Rome, the birthday of the holy sisters Rufina and Secunda, noble by birth and wealth, whom the prefect Archesilaus ordered to be beheaded for the name of Christ. In the Blandinian monastery, the birthday of Amelberga, holy virgin.”

BRUXELLENSIS, concerning the seven brothers, adds after “were punished”: “And after the martyrdom of her sons, Felicitas their mother was beheaded for Christ. Gregory calls this blessed woman more than a martyr, because she bravely suffered martyrdom seven times in her sons and an eighth time in her own body.” It then proceeds with Rufina and Secunda, correctly, and likewise with the Africans. At the end it adds: “At Tenseca, beside the Scheldt, the deposition of Amelberga, holy virgin of Christ, niece of blessed Gudila, our patroness. Charles Martel, the prince, broke the bone of her arm when he himself was still young, in order to take her for his bride. He would indeed have made her his wife if [Col. 0245D] virginal chastity had not completely prevented it. The relics of this holy virgin were later transferred to Ghent, to Blandinian Mount.” See Castellani’s brief note.

HAGENOVENSIS is somewhat interpolated in the account of the seven brothers and has in second place: “Likewise Theodora, the chosen one, whose repentance is recorded. Likewise Patinianus, confessor.” In the rest of the text it is pure. At the end it changes the name: “At the port of Ghent, in the Blandinian monastery, Quielberga, holy virgin.” It is clear that Amelberga is intended.

AQUICINCTENSIS adds after the text: “And Amelberga, holy virgin.”

MATRICULARY–CARTUSIAN–UTRECHT: “The seven brother martyrs, sons of Saint Felicitas, namely Januarius, Felix, Philip, Silvanus, Alexander, Vitalis [Col. 0246B] and Martialis, who suffered gloriously at Rome. Rufina and Secunda, virgins and martyrs. Amelberga, virgin, at Ghent.”

THE LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION, somewhat interpolated in the first announcement, has in second place: “Likewise at Rome, at the tenth milestone, the holy sisters and virgins Rufina and Secunda. They were born of a most distinguished father named Asterius and a most illustrious mother named Aurelia, and under the persecution of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, with Junius Donatus the prefect and Archesilaus the count as judges, they were martyred by various kinds of torture. Finally, one of them departed to the Lord with the sword striking her head, the other with her neck cut.” The account of the Africans is pure. Then: “In Flanders, at the port of Ghent, in the Blandinian monastery, Amelberga, holy virgin; in Dacia, Canute, blessed king and martyr.”

GREVEN: “In Dacia, Canute, king and martyr. Because of his love of justice and holy religion, after many persecutions he was killed by the wicked in the church of Saint Alban, the proto-martyr of the English, while praying with outstretched hands. Patinianus, bishop and confessor. In Flanders, at the port of Ghent, in the Blandinian monastery, Amelberga, holy virgin.” See BRUXELLENSIS above.

MOLAN. In different type he inserted into the text: “Their bodies were transferred to Milan,” as in the copies above. At the end: “At the port of Ghent, on the mountain called Blandinian, Amelberga, most holy virgin of Christ. At Binche, Amelberga, the chosen widow, who, after resting in peace, was buried at Lobbes in the basilica of blessed Ursmar and, famous for miracles, is venerated with extraordinary devotion by the faithful. At Fiscia, the birthday of Etto, holy bishop and confessor.”

Then, in smaller type: “In Dacia, Canute, king and martyr. Who because of his love,” and so forth, as in GREVEN. Finally: “At Lens, a town in Artois, Pacificus died, the first minister of the Friars Minor in France.” Other editions preserve the same text. At the end, concerning Amelberga, as in the first edition. Then: “On the same day, at the monastery of Lobbes, the deposition of Amelberga, the chosen one. Famous for miracles, she is venerated with extraordinary devotion by the faithful. In the city of Odense, Canute, holy king and proto-martyr of the Danes, who in the year 1086, in the basilica of Saint Alban the martyr, while praying with his hands extended to the ground in the form of a cross, suffered death for Christ at the hands of one of his household. Benedict his brother and seventeen others suffered with him. At Laëtis, from Fécamp, the birthday of Etto, holy bishop and confessor. On the tenth day, the forty-five holy martyrs at Nicopolis in Armenia.” Finally, in smaller type: “At Lens, a town in Artois, Pacificus died, the first minister of the Friars Minor in France, whom Bonaventure mentions.” These differ little from the earlier edition.]

[Col. 0243]

At Rome, the seven brothers, sons of Saint Felicitas, namely Januarius, Felix, Philip, Silvanus, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis. Of these, Januarius, under Antoninus, after being scourged with rods and imprisoned, was killed with leaded clubs. Felix and Philip were killed with cudgels. Silvanus was killed by being thrown over a precipice. Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis were punished by sentence of death.

In Africa, the birthday of the holy Januarius, Marinus, Nabor, and Felix, who were beheaded. Likewise at Rome, the holy virgins Rufina and Secunda, who, subjected to tortures under the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, finally departed, one with a sword striking her head, the other with her neck cut.

## 5th day before the Ides. Day 11

[Note: [Col. 0247]

Only Pulsanensis, Muneratensis, Greven, and Molan are entirely pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0247A]

Pulsanensis has *Nycopoli* and *eculeo*. Muneratensis has *Pellagii* and *Sidroni*. Some write “in the district of Poitiers,” as Pratenensis and others do. But our copies, with Herinien., Tornacen., and most others, read as in the text. Muneratensis reads *Albini* for *Sabini*. This confusion will frequently recur in the Appendices.]

[Note: [Col. 0247A]

The translation of the body of Saint Benedict from Italy to Gaul is inserted or added as a commemoration in most ancient Martyrologies, indeed even in the Hieronymian copies themselves, especially those of Lucca and Corbie, despite the Cassinese continuing to resist this even to the present day, as I have occasionally been able to hear from their own complaints in person.

[Col. 0247B] Instead of “translation,” Bede wrote “deposition”; Florus, who describes the translation, corrected him at this point, although Rabanus thought the reading should be retained. The Little Roman Martyrology mentions neither. Ado, however, composed a brief history of the translation, somewhat enlarged by Notker, whose abridgment we will provide in the Appendices.

Our author, omitting the rest, was content to record the translation itself, as the earliest manuscript notes prove. In one of these, namely the Herinien manuscript, the passage was very probably erased with a knife, leaving an empty space. It is not marked in the Tornacensis, and for that reason both manuscripts, although otherwise completely pure, have been excluded from the class of genuine copies.

Let the curious reader consult the entire history of this translation to the monastery of Floriacum, set out at length in our Acts under 21 March, together with the account of the miracles performed there, from p. 299 to p. 357. We will give Wandalbert’s verses below.

The Armenian martyrs Januarius and Pelagia have been somewhat disfigured in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. The Little Roman Martyrology commemorates Januarius alone. Ado, I think, joined both from the Hieronymian Martyrologies or from the Acts, adding a brief eulogy, which our author transcribed word for word. Notker differs only in the final word; but Florus and Rabanus, although they agree in the substance of the matter, differ completely in wording from Ado. It therefore always seems more probable to me that those two, although older than Ado, had never seen him.

I have nothing to add here except Wandalbert’s metrical encomium, which also embraces Benedict’s translation:

> Januarius adorns the day with fivefold martyrdom,  
> And holy Pelagia with a like splendour. [Col. 0248B]  
> Then the lofty Loire now honours the sacred remains  
> Of Father Benedict, translated from the Beneventan mountains.

What follows is found in the Pratensis and similar copies. Antwerp-Maj., Rosweyd, and Aquicinct: “In Caesarean Mauretania, Marciana, holy virgin and martyr,” inserted into the cited Pratensis manuscript over several erased words, as the most clear-sighted witness, the distinguished Castellani, informed me; we indicated the same matter again above under 10 January.

I do not discuss the true day of the passion, since on this day also a certain Martianus in Mauretania is commemorated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, perhaps for Martiana. The sole purpose of our inquiry is whether, from the nearly unanimous agreement of the other manuscripts, the genuine opinion of Usuard is not entirely clear. That is indeed how it seems to us, although we will willingly and readily yield to stronger arguments.

The final two announcements are purely Usuardine, unless perhaps one finds an affinity with these saints in the corrupted names of the Hieronymian Martyrologies and supposes, for example, that *Basinus*, attached to the Lucensis manuscript, should be understood as our Sabinus. Whether this Sabinus should be brought from Brescia, Castellani’s note for this day will teach; there he adds another note concerning Sabinus and Cyprian, recorded in the modern Roman Martyrology. We will examine both in our Acts.

From what has been said it is clear what Usuard’s genuine and pure reading is. It is remarkable that it passed over Pope Pius, whom Ado presents so distinctly on this day and whom Notker postponed to the following day.]

[Note: [Col. 0247C]

Concerning PRATENSIS and the copies connected with it, as well as HERINIENSIS and TORNACENSIS, we have already said enough.

ANTWERP and MAXIMUS–LUBECK, as well as the U GHELLIAN edition, omit the translation of Saint Benedict at the beginning. Sidronius and Sabinus are also absent; in their place appears: “At Rome, the passion of Stephen and Leontius.”

ANTWERP-MAX., UTRECHT, and LEYDEN: “The translation of blessed Benedict the abbot and of his sister Saint Scholastica. At Rome, in the Vatican, the birthday of Pius, holy pope [Col. 0247D] and martyr. An angel announced to him that Easter was to be celebrated on Sunday.” The Armenian entries are fairly pure. Then: “Likewise at Rome, Stephen and Leontius.” Finally: “In the district of Poitiers, Sabinus, holy confessor.” Sidronius is absent.

In LOVANIENSIS, Sidronius and Sabinus are absent; the rest is as in the preceding copies. ALBERGEN omits Benedict’s translation. DANIC likewise omits it, but adds its own local saint at the end in these words: “In Dacia, in the city of Wiburg, the birthday of Ketellus, holy confessor.” He appears to have been a martyr.

CENTULENSIS: “In Gaul, at the monastery of Floriacum, the arrival and translation of the body of Benedict, most holy father and abbot, together with blessed Scholastica, his sister. In Armenia, in the city of Nicopolis, Januarius and Pelagia, holy martyrs. In the district of Poitiers, Sabinus, holy confessor. He was one of the disciples of the great father Saint Germanus.”

BRUXELLENSIS: “At Floriacum, the arrival or translation of Benedict, holy abbot. His body was transferred from Italy, from Monte Cassino, to Gaul, to the monastery of Floriacum.” The Armenian entries are fairly pure. It continues: “At Rome, in the Vatican, the birthday of Pius, holy pope and martyr. He established, at the announcement of an angel, that the Lord’s Easter should always be celebrated on Sunday. [Col. 0249A] Likewise at Rome, the passion of Stephen and Leontius, holy martyrs. In Caesarean Mauretania, Marciana, holy virgin and martyr.” He forgot that he had recorded her on 9 January. The entry for Sidronius is pure. Then: “In the district of Poitiers, Albinus, holy confessor.” He meant Sabinus, unless he is referring to Albinus, or Albanus, the companion of Lisianus, as below.

HAGENOVENSIS: “At Rome, in the Vatican, at Saint Peter’s, the deposition of Pius, holy pope and martyr. He was the ninth after blessed Peter and governed the Church for eleven years, four months, and twenty-one days. He suffered under the emperor Antoninus. He established that Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, so that we would not seem to Judaize with the Jews. He established that a heretic coming from the heresy of the Jews should be received and baptized. He also established that a sentence of excommunication should be issued against violators and despoilers of ecclesiastical property and churches. Likewise, that a cleric who laid an ambush for his bishop should be deposed and handed over to the secular court.” In the Armenian entries it is pure. Then: “At Rome, the passion of Stephen and Leontius, holy martyrs.” It is correct concerning Sidronius. Then: “On the same day, the translation of Benedict, holy abbot, and of Scholastica, his sister. After the destruction of his monastery by the pagans, his body [the syntax is defective] was carried to Gaul, together with the body of Saint Scholastica.” The entry for Sabinus is pure.

AQUICINCTENSIS: Concerning Martiana, what was said above is sufficient. After Sabinus it adds: “And Albanus, holy confessor, and Lisianus. Likewise, Savinus and Cyprian, holy martyrs. At Rome, Pius, holy pope. In his time Hermes wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, because an angel appeared to him in the dress of a shepherd.” These final remarks about *The Shepherd* were taken from Ado.

REG. SUEC., which belonged to Ursinus of Rosemberg: “In the city of Mantua, Speciosa, holy virgin. Double, second class.”

DAVERONENSIS: “In the territory of Sens, Sedronius, blessed martyr. Likewise, in the territory of Poitiers, Albinus, holy confessor, and Lisianus.”

[Col. 0249C] MATRICULARY–CARTUSIAN–UTRECHT: “The translation of Benedict, holy abbot. Sidronius, martyr, in the territory of Sens. Sabinus, confessor. Januarius and Pelagia, martyrs. Joel and Ezra, prophets.” They are treated in the Usuardine text under the 13th of this month.

BIGOTIAN, signed P. 5: “At Rome, the passion of Stephen and Leuticius, holy martyrs.” Above, Leontius.

REG. SUEC., under note no. 428: “At Paris, Albinus, confessor.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL., signed C: “In the territory of Poitiers, Albinus, holy confessor, and Lisianus. And Savinus and Cyprian, holy martyrs.”

In VATICAN, Benedict’s translation is absent. Nothing is said about Sidronius or Sabinus. It adds: “At Rome, Pius, holy pope, who sat in the episcopate for eleven years. Likewise at Rome, Leontius, Stephen, and Maurice, holy martyrs.”

ALTEMPS: “In Caesarean Mauretania, Marciana, holy virgin and martyr. Likewise Lisianus, Savinus, and Cyprian, martyrs.”

FLORENTINIUS: “At Rome, the passion of Stephen and Leontius, holy martyrs. In the territory of Poitiers, Albinus, holy confessor.”

BURDEGALENSIS: “In the territory of Sens [something is missing] of Poitiers, Albinus, holy confessor. And in the territory of Bordeaux, Sabinus.”

LUXOVIENSIS: “The deposition of Hidulfus, archbishop, resting in the monastery of Moyenmoutier, a man of glorious holiness.”

THE LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: “At Rome, in the Vatican, the birthday of Pius, holy pope and martyr. He sat in the episcopate for eleven years, three months, and twenty-one days. An angel announced to him that Easter was to be celebrated on Sunday. He also established that a heretic coming from Jewish heresy should be received and baptized. Likewise at Rome, Stephen and Leontius, holy martyrs.”

[Col. 0250B] The Armenian entries are fairly pure. Then: “At Trier, Hildulfus, blessed bishop and confessor. On the same day, Savinus and Cyprian, blessed brother martyrs. In the territory of Poitiers, Albinus, Lucianus, and Sevianus, holy confessors. At the monastery of Floriacum in the territory of Orléans, the translation of the holy bodies of Benedict the abbot and his sister Scholastica the virgin, from Italy to Gaul.”

BELIN begins: “At Rome, Pius, blessed pope and martyr.” At the end it places Sabinus before Sidronius. In the second edition it adds: “Likewise, the translation of Scholastica, holy virgin.”

GREVEN: “At Rome, in the Vatican—according to Ado—Pius, holy pope and martyr, who sat in the episcopate for nineteen years [Ado has eighteen]. During his time Hermes wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, because an angel appeared to him in the dress of a shepherd. On the same day, Savinus and Cyprian, blessed brothers and martyrs. At Rome, Stephen, Leoncius, Maurice, and Militio. Bertinus, martyr. In Syria, Marcial, holy. At Caesarea of Mauretania, the passion of Mary, holy virgin, who suffered under Budarius. Hildulfus, archbishop of Trier and confessor, brother of Saint Erhard, bishop of Regensburg. When he laid down the burden of pastoral care, which he bore with great difficulty, he led the life of a hermit in the Vosges forest, distinguished equally by his manner of life and by miracles; he deserved to have many men of great holiness as imitators of the same way of life. In the territory [Col. 0250C] of Poitiers, Lucianus and Savinus, confessors. In Britain, the translation of Maclovius, holy bishop and confessor. In Dacia, the translation of Ketellus, holy priest and confessor. Scholastica, his sister, was translated together with Saint Benedict and buried in the region of Le Mans through the devotion of religious persons. Likewise, holy Eulogius.”

MOLAN, after Benedict the abbot, inserts into the text in different type: “For after, as he himself foretold while alive, his monastery had been ravaged by foreign peoples, his body was discovered through the Lord’s revelation, transferred to Gaul, and suitably buried in the monastery called Floriacum. The body of blessed Scholastica, his sister, was likewise transferred and buried in the region of Le Mans through the devotion of religious persons.”

At the end he adds only: “And Lisianus. At Rome, Pius, blessed pope.” In the other editions the history of the translation is shorter. At the end, however, one finds: “At Rome, Pius, blessed pope [and martyr]. At Trier, [Col. 0250D] Hidulfus, holy bishop and distinguished confessor. At Wiburg in Dacia, Ketellus, holy confessor.” The readings concerning him in our manuscripts will be elucidated in their proper place.]

[Col. 0247]

Translation of Saint Benedict the Abbot. In Lesser Armenia, in the city of Nicopolis, the feast of the holy martyrs Januarius and Pelagia, who, tortured for four days on the rack, with claws, and with fragments of pottery, completed their martyrdom [Bouillart inserts: **[Note: Col. 0247A]** Since the love of truth alone impelled me to undertake this small work, I am far from wishing to conceal or even disguise the truth, including when it is inconvenient to me. Therefore I freely acknowledge that this article is disfigured by an erasure from the word *cruciati* to the end; and that the writing now occupying the space of the erasure is by another hand, although contemporary with Usuard. **[Col. 0248A]** Nevertheless, I would not dare to affirm, as Sollerius does, that Martiana was inserted. I leave the matter undecided; the reader may determine it, if he wishes, on the authority of the three manuscripts Antwerp-major, Rosweyd, and Aquicinct, which Sollerius testifies followed the Pratense, and of the three Pratense manuscripts B, D, and E, together with Conches and Montisburg, which report the same reading. **BOUILLART.**] In Caesarean Mauritania, the holy virgin and martyr Martiana. In the territory of Sens, blessed Sidronius the martyr. Likewise in the territory of Poitiers, Saint Sabinus the confessor.

## Fourth day before the Ides. Day 12. **[Col. 0249]**

The Pratense, Heriniense, Antwerp-Major, and Munerat manuscripts are pure.

**[Col. 0251A]**

Antwerp-Major reads *Ermagoree*. Munerat reads *Ermagore*, both disregarding the diphthong; but the form in the text is better. The same Munerat incorrectly writes *conversationem* instead of *conversionem*. **[Col. 0252A]** In the Pratense manuscript the reading is *Dyi*, in Antwerp-Major *Disi*; I take it as certain from the manuscripts and numerous excerpts that it should entirely be read *Dii*, as the text has it.

**[Col. 0251A]**

Today the *small Roman Martyrology* has, if I am not mistaken, inserted two announcements at will, the second of which is presented in this form: “In Cyprus, of Nason, an ancient disciple of Christ.” Insert “the feast of blessed,” and you will have the sense of Ado, and it will become clear what our author took and from where. There is no doubt that, as Rosweyd correctly observed, Jason—or Mnason—is meant here, the man mentioned in chapter 21 of the Acts of the Apostles. Indeed, the modern Roman Martyrology calls him Jason, but all our manuscripts, as well as the *small Roman Martyrology* and Ado, consistently retain this reading. Nothing about him is found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, at least on this day, nor in Bede, Florus, Rabanus, or Wandalbert. Notker differs very slightly from our text. Whatever the case may be, I consider it certain that this concerns that Cypriot Mnason who was one of Christ’s disciples, as Henschenius long ago demonstrated on 25 June, beginning at page IV; and, if necessary, we shall discuss him more fully in the *Acts*. The memory of Hermagoras being commemorated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies seems to be indicated by the accompanying characteristics, **[Col. 0251B]** although his name is corrupted in all the manuscripts: some read *Armiger*, others *Armigirus* or *Armagerus*, with the name Fortunatus everywhere prefixed, whom Florentinius wrongly reports as absent from our text. In any case, Hermagoras is clearly expressed first in the *small Roman Martyrology*: “At Aquileia, Hermagoras, bishop, disciple of Saint Mark.” Ado added little to this apart from indicating that he was the first bishop of that same city. Thus the entire eulogy represented in our little entry, together with the association of the archdeacon Fortunatus, is purely Usuardine, extracted from certain Acts. Such may perhaps be those published by Mombritius in volume II, page 2, or those we possess in manuscripts, in a different style and order, to be examined in their proper place. Wandalbert honored Hermagoras with this couplet:

**[Col. 0252A]**

> On the fourth day Aquileia frequents Hermagoras suppliantly,  
>   
> the bishop who by his prayers illumined the people and the city.

We have shown with no implausible probability in the treatise on the Alexandrian Patriarchs, in the foundational dissertation, § 2, no. 20, how it could be said that Mark the Evangelist was at Aquileia and established Hermagoras there as bishop. The remaining matters will be discussed in the *Acts*. Florentinius admits that *Dium* or *Divum* is read in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, with the same saint explicitly mentioned by Ado: “At Caesarea, Saint Dius.” These are almost also Usuard’s words and, in my judgment from the agreement of the most reliable manuscripts, certainly his, although neither Belin, nor Greven, nor Molan, nor certain other manuscripts included this announcement. This omission was undoubtedly the reason why it was also neglected by Baronius, since it was not found in his usual sources. This, then, is the complete and integral Usuardine text.

Ado follows with: “At Milan, the translation of the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix,” sufficiently in conformity with what was said on the tenth of this month. Among others, however, that translation underwent a change of appearance. Thus the present Roman Martyrology clearly indicates the day of their death, or the day on which they suffered at Milan, as do the manuscripts cited in the Appendices. Castellanus notes that another place is suggested in their Acts, while others cast still other darkness over the matter, so that this harvest is entangled in a mass of complicated questions to be clarified elsewhere. Add also the commemoration of Saint Pope Cletus recorded in the same Ado, but likewise omitted by our author, perhaps because he believed him to be the same person as Anacletus, whom he noted on 26 April. The famous controversy over Cletus and Anacletus—whether they were one or two, the same or different—is well known, as are the confusion and opposition of the Martyrologies. We indicated this fully on the aforementioned day, and it will be discussed more extensively, perhaps from the beginning, in the *Acts* for July, on this or the following day.

**[Col. 0251C]**

The Tournai manuscript, entirely pure in its text, adds at the end: “On the same day, Felix and Nabor, martyrs.”

The Pulsano manuscript omits “Dius,” substituting for it: “At Milan, the feast of the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix.”

Rosweyd, Antwerp, and Maximum-Lübeck, as well as Greven and Molan, all fail to include the final announcement.

Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Albergen, and the Danish manuscript have first: “At the city of Milan, the feast of the blessed Nabor and Felix. Accused before the emperor Maximian because they worshiped Christ, they were detained in prison for twelve days without food. Then handed over to the governor Anolinus, [and] beaten with clubs, they were ordered to be consumed by fire. Remaining unharmed, they finally received the sentence of death.” After this follows the material on Nason, Hermagoras, and so forth, in pure form, but the final announcement is also absent.

The Centulense manuscript: “At Aquileia, Saint Hermagoras, bishop and martyr, who, together with his archdeacon Fortunatus, **[Col. 0251D]** by capital punishment merited an everlasting triumph. In Cyprus, Saint Nason, an ancient disciple of Christ. At Milan, the translation of the holy Nabor and Felix.”

The Brussels manuscript: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Anacletus, pope and martyr. After blessed Clement, he governed the Church for nine years and was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Domitian. He ordered priests to be honored above all others and prohibited them from presuming to celebrate without witnesses.” Then it gives the material on Nason and Hermagoras in pure form, omitting Dius. Then: “At Milan, the feast of the blessed Natalis, Felix, Nabor, and Primitius. Accused before the emperor Maximian because they worshiped Christ, **[Col. 0252C]** they were detained in prison for twelve days without food, then beaten with clubs and handed over to the flames; remaining unharmed, they finally received the sentence of death.” A much later hand has added: “And blessed Wilgefortis, virgin and martyr, daughter of the king of Portugal.” She is placed by others on 20 July.

The Hagenoyen manuscript, pure at the beginning, relates much about Hermagoras mixed together from the Acts, material deserving to be sifted. It also has no little concerning Nabor and Felix, which must be verified more carefully from other sources. It agrees with the text: “At Caesarea, Saint Dius.”

The Aquicinct manuscript writes *Disi* instead of *Dii*, as Antwerp-Major does above. At the end it adds: “At Rome, Saint Cletus, pope and martyr. By command of blessed Peter, he ordained twenty-five priests in the city of Rome; he was also buried beside the body of blessed Peter.” This material is taken from Ado.

Victorinus and the Swedish Register, sign no. 130: “At Rome, **[Col. 0252D]** Saint Pius, pope. During his pontificate Hermes wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, because an angel appeared to him in the form of a shepherd.”

The Matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht manuscripts: “Felix and Nabor, brothers and martyrs. Their bodies were transferred to Cologne with the Three Kings. Hermagoras, bishop, disciple of Saint Mark the Evangelist.”

In the Vatican manuscript no. 5949, Hermagoras is absent. It adds: “At Milan, the feast of the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix. At Rome, Saint Anacletus, pope, who presided over the Church for twelve years. At Lyons, Saint Viventiolus, bishop.” This is correct; the others are incorrect.

The Florentine manuscript, differing in a few words, has nearly everywhere: “In Tuscany, in the territory of Florence, **[Col. 0253A]** at the monastery of Saint Michael of Passignano, in the diocese of Fiesole, the passing of Saint John the abbot, founder of the order of Vallombrosa. While still living in the world, he mortified himself with all his strength for Christ. His venerable death occurred in the year 1073 of the Incarnation of the Word (elsewhere 1074). Nevertheless, his feast is celebrated in Tuscany on the sixth day before the Ides of October. In the region of Tuscany, in the city of Lucca, the feast of Saint Paulinus, first bishop and confessor of that same city, and of Severus and Theobald. Their bodies are buried in the cathedral church of that city. At Antioch, the passion of forty-six holy martyrs (as is read in the Acts of the holy martyrs Quiricus and Julitta), who were martyred under the emperor Julian and put to death by the governor Alexander by sentence of execution.”

The Abdinghof manuscript: “On the same day, blessed Henry, emperor and confessor.” This belongs to 14 July.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition has the material on Nabor and Felix as Antwerp-Major and the others do. The material on Nason and Hermagoras is somewhat interpolated. Concerning the latter, it notably adds: **[Col. 0253B]** “He rests at Osnabrück.” Then: “At Lyons, Saint Juventiolus, bishop and confessor. At Caesarea, Saint Disus, confessor.” I do not know where it found this title, “confessor.”

Belin writes: “Hermacora and Hermagorius.” Dius is absent. At the end is added: “At Milan, the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix. In Tuscany, in the city of Lucca, blessed Paulinus, first bishop of that city, who under Nero, at the foot of Mount Pisa, after many struggles, completed his martyrdom. Likewise, Saint John Gualbert.”

Greven: “On the same day, at Milan, the feast [or, as Ado prefers, the translation] of Felix and Nabor, martyrs. Since they were citizens of Milan, they were accused of worshiping Christ and were sent into prison, food being denied them. Then, after being beaten with clubs and overcoming the fire, they completed their martyrdom by beheading under Maximian. Their bodies were transferred to Cologne with the holy Magi and rest there. The passion of Pope Anacletus **[Col. 0254A]** here, but his burial on the following day. Vincent the martyr. In Tuscany, in the city of Lucca, blessed Paul, first bishop of that city. Under Nero, at the foot of Mount Pisa, after …,” and so forth, as in Belin. “At Milan, Saint Magdun, a disciple of Christ. At Lyons, Saint Juventiolus, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Bourges, Saint Menulphus, bishop and confessor. Likewise Saint Cletus, pope, who, as Ado says, sat at Rome for twelve years. By command of Saint Peter, he ordained twenty-five …,” and so forth, as in the Aquicinct manuscript from Ado. “Note that Ado has Cletus here, but on the sixth day before the Kalends of May Anacletus.” Greven says this correctly. “Usuard, however, has Anacletus here on the following day.” This is false. “At Caesarea, blessed Dius, confessor. Theodora, a devout woman, who in the time of the emperor Zeno, deceived by a sorcerer, committed adultery, but soon repenting entered a monastery of men; falsely accused of the crime, she endured it most patiently, and, shining with miracles, finally rested in **[Col. 0254B]** peace. Likewise, the sainted John Gerson, most Christian doctor, outstanding in life and learning, who died in the year of the Lord 1429.” Here sanctity, cult, and the like are lacking.

Molan: “In the territory of Bourges, blessed Meinulphus, prelate. At Milan, the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix. In Tuscany, in the city of Lucca, blessed Paulinus, of that city,” and so forth, as in Belin. “At Pompeii, the passion of Saint Vincent the martyr, whose passion is recorded. At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of Saint Juventiolus, bishop. Likewise Saint John Gualbert.” In smaller type: “Blasius Milanesius, Minister General of the Order of Vallombrosa, published his life.” In other editions the material on Nabor and Felix, Paulinus of Lucca, Gualbert, Juventiolus, Vincent, and Meinulph is as in the earlier edition. I note that these editions read *Viventiolus*; they would more correctly have written *Viventiolus*. Here is also added: “On the twelfth day, the holy martyrs Proclus and Hilary, and Saint Father Michael Maleinos.”

## [Col. 0249]

In Cyprus, blessed Nason, an ancient disciple of Christ. At Aquileia, the feast of Saint Hermagoras, bishop, disciple of blessed Mark the Evangelist, who, amid miracles of healing, persistent preaching, and the conversion of peoples, experienced many kinds of punishment and at last, together with his archdeacon Fortunatus, merited an everlasting triumph by capital punishment. At Caesarea, Saint Dius.

**[Note: Col. 0249D]** Saint Dius was added here by Usuard after the first copy of his Martyrology had been presented to King Charles. **[Col. 0250D]** Nothing concerning this saint is found in the Dervensis manuscript. The Hieronymian indexes and Ado mention him. **BOUILLART.**

## Third day before the Ides. Day 13. **[Col. 0253]**

This is taken from the Pratense, Heriniense, Antwerp-Major, and Munerat manuscripts, as in my preceding note.

**[Col. 0253C]**

The Pratense reads *Joel* and *Esrae*; Heriniense, *Johel* and *Ezrae*; Antwerp-Major, *Johei* and *Hesdrae*; Munerat, *Joelis* and *Ozeae*. Let me write *Esdrae* with Ado, on the authority of the others. I consequently placed *Sileae*, with the Pratense and Heriniense, although the other manuscripts have the better form *Silae*. Antwerp-Major errs by writing “and to the Apostles,” having deleted the preposition *ab*. The Pratense alone has *Carthaginensis*, quite correctly, but I followed the current of the others. For *universi cleri*, Antwerp-Major reads *universalis*, very badly. Thus in the Pratense and Munerat, *nobilissimus* occurs instead of *nobilissimi*. Likewise in Antwerp-Major: “driven into exile.” Other scribal errors occur in Munerat: *Murita*, *glorioso*, and *mirae simplicitatis*. In Antwerp-Major *Tauriavi* is correctly read; in all the others, including our Pratense copy, the form is *Turiani*, as it is now commonly printed from the life published by Surius from Baralli, whatever Castellanus may write when he says that he read *Turiavi* in the Pratense. He likewise advises in the margin of his universal Martyrology that it should be read in French as *Turiaf*, adding that his body rests in Paris.

**[Col. 0253C]**

Above, on 6 July, we observed that our author had omitted the prophet Joel, whom he had found joined to Isaiah in the *small Roman Martyrology* and in Ado. It is now sufficiently clear that he was right to do so, since the same prophet occurs again here, joined to another; whether through design or error I do not examine. Our entire announcement **[Col. 0254C]** is taken from the Martyrologies already cited, which repeat the same name in both places, while Notker omits Joel, whom he had mentioned above. Ado, as far as I know the first among the ancients, briefly records Sila—or, better, Silas, or, if one prefers, Silvanus—here, but among the festivals of the apostles, with an eulogy almost entirely transferred by our author into his little entry, as we have reproduced it. His remaining deeds can be historically derived in the *Acts* from the Acts of the Apostles and the letters of Peter and Paul; Tillemont seems to have prepared the way for this in various places in volume I, where the matter will be examined more carefully. Notker, remarkably, does not mention him even once, substituting in his place Margaret of Antioch, with a summary of her life composed almost word for word from Rabanus. The *small Roman Martyrology* speaks of the Africans as follows: “And the holy confessors Eugenius, bishop, and the entire clergy of the Church.” To this is added Ado’s brief panegyric, copied almost word for word by our author; Notker is more expansive, and in him one should note that the reading *lectores infantulique* is not inept, contrary to Ado and Usuard, who, I believe, expressed it less clearly. Material for the eulogies of these most renowned confessors was not lacking in Victor of Vita, who relates at length that barbarous persecution of Huneric from the beginning of book II; see the editions of Chifflet and Ruinart, or Surius himself. **[Col. 0255B]** The ways in which Gregory of Tours differs from Victor **[Col. 0256A]** near the beginning of book II of the *History of the Franks* will be discussed in the *Acts*. In the meantime, Tillemont may be consulted in volume XVI, where he describes the Vandal persecution in French beginning on page 492; he treats Eugenius and the others from article 21, page 541, and discusses the difficulty in question on page 800. In the meantime it is perfectly clear that the entire text so far has been borrowed directly from the aforementioned Ado, while the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and Florus are silent. Turianus is recorded only by Usuard, who may have taken part in the translation of the sacred relics mentioned in the Life of Saint Leufredus on 21 June, page 112. Thus there can be no doubt that we have given the genuine and simple text, excluding Anacletus, whom Greven and Molan, I do not know from what source, inserted here in second place, although he is entirely unknown to the purer manuscripts. Wandalbert departs very far from Usuard’s text; his verses are these:

> On the third day Serapion presents Egypt,  
>   
> and Attalus, the martyr, shines with heavenly blossom.

**[Note: Col. 0255B]**

The Tournai manuscript has the material on Sila as far as “he completed,” and that on the Africans as far as “they were driven out”; the remainder of the eulogies is absent.

The Pulsano manuscript is quite pure in the first and second sections, but omits the rest, substituting: “On the same day, Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr.”

Antwerp-Major and Lübeck are pure as far as “they were driven into cruel exile”; they omit everything else that follows in the text.

Rosweyd has nothing about Turianus, but adds at the end the following: “Likewise Margaret. And Mildrada, virgin, sister of Saint Lebuin, beloved of God, buried in Kent. Attalus the martyr. In Egypt, Serapion the monk.”

Greven and Molan insert in second place: “At Rome, the burial of Anacletus, pope.” See the remaining manuscripts below.

Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, and Leiden, pure in the first section, add: “At Antioch, the feast of Saint Margaret, virgin, who, when she was fifteen years old, under the governor of the region, Olybrius, after various kinds of torture and astonishing miracles, finally completed the contest of martyrdom by beheading. At Rome, the feast of Saint Anacletus, pope and martyr, who, third after blessed Peter, governed the Church for nine years and was crowned with martyrdom in the persecution of Domitian.” They are pure in the section on Sila. In the African material, they lack what follows after “they were driven into cruel exile.” Nothing is said about Turianus.

Albergen and the Danish manuscript agree with the three just cited, but place Joel and Ezra in third place, after Anacletus. Louvain is more faithful in the order of the announcements, but cuts out the entire eulogy of the Africans.

The Centulense manuscript: “The feast of Saint Sila the apostle, who, glorifying Christ in his sufferings in Macedonia, afterward rested. At Alexandria, Saint John the patriarch, who is called Ele… [Eleemosynarius, ‘the Almsgiver’]. In Africa, the holy confessors Eugenius, **[Col. 0255D]** bishop of Carthage, Salutaris the archdeacon, and Muritta, second in the office of the ministers, together with the entire clergy of that church. In Lesser Britain, Saint Cerianus, bishop and confessor.” This is undoubtedly Turianus, or, as in the text, Turianus.

The Brussels manuscript, first, has the material on Margaret, almost as above. It is quite pure in the prophets and Sila.
