In the African material it stops at “they were driven into exile.” It continues: “At Alexandria, blessed John the patriarch, a man of God, most devout in compassion and generosity of alms. Likewise at Alexandria, Saints Menas, Serapion, Zeno, and Naseus, priests.” Finally, its text on Turianus is entirely pure, although it too writes *Turiani*.

The Hagenoyen manuscript omits Ezra and adapts Joel’s eulogy to the form we gave for Hosea on the fifth of this month. It is quite pure in the section on Sila. A longer history of Saint Margaret follows, in which even the red dragon is not lacking, and so forth. The Africans and Turianus are absent; in their place are: “In Bavaria, the translation of Saint Castulus the martyr. At Bamberg, Saint Henry, emperor and confessor.”

The Aquicinct manuscript adds after the text: “At Alexandria, blessed John, bishop, the Almsgiver.”

Victorinus and the Swedish Register, sign no. 130, at the end: “On the same day, Saint Minulphus, confessor. On the same day, Saint Cletus, pope. By command of blessed Peter, he ordained twenty-five priests in the city of Rome; he was buried beside the body of blessed Peter.”

The Matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht manuscripts: “Henry, emperor. Cletus, pope and martyr. Marcellinus, pope and martyr.” See 26 April. “Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, exiled together with the entire clergy.”

In the Vatican manuscript, Joel and Ezra are absent.

The Florentine manuscript: “Likewise Saint Artsius, one of Christ’s ancient disciples.” Then the Strozzi manuscript alone: “At Lyons, the burial of Saint Bonaventure, cardinal bishop **[Col. 0256C]** of Albano, of the Order of Friars Minor.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins with Margaret, as above. It is correct in the prophets. Then: “In the city of Bamberg, the burial of Saint Henry, most Christian emperor. He reigned for twenty-two years, about the year of the Lord one thousand; his wife was Saint Cunegund, daughter of the Count Palatine of the Rhine, a most devout virgin. Both of them, likewise vowing their virginity to God, remained secretly virgins until the end of their lives.” Concerning Anacletus it adds that “he was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican,” and that “he established that the clergy should grow neither beard nor hair.” Concerning John, it agrees with the Brussels manuscript above. It is quite pure in the section on Sila; in the African material it becomes confused near the end. Then: “At Poitiers, Saint Cyprian the martyr.” The section on Turianus is pure. Then: “At Carthage in Africa, blessed Salutaris,” and so forth, supplying what was missing above. “On the same day, Saint Milarida, virgin.” It indicates “Mildrida” or “Mildritha.”

Belin inserts before Turianus: “At Rome, Saint Anacletus, pope and martyr.” Concerning Bonaventure, it agrees with the Florentine manuscripts above.

Greven: “At Poitiers, Saint Cyprian the martyr. Likewise, the burial of Saint John, patriarch of Alexandria, surnamed the Almsgiver, according to others on the tenth day before the Kalends of February. At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of Saint Bonaventure, bishop of Albano, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, of the Order of Friars Minor. By his life, talent, and writings—for in these he so devoted himself to the illumination of the intellect that he referred everything to religious feeling and piety—he greatly illumined the Christian religion, and deservedly acquired the name ‘Seraphic.’ His feast is observed on the second Sunday of July. In the city of Bamberg, the burial of Saint Henry, most Christian emperor, the first of that name among the emperors who received the imperial blessing, or crown. His wife Cunegund, a most holy virgin and exceedingly beautiful young woman, induced her husband to preserve perpetual virginity with her by their common vow. In this state Saint Henry, serving Christ, died a blessed death in the year of the Lord 1021, renowned for miracles.” This belongs to the following day; in the Roman Martyrology it is deferred to the fifteenth. “Serapion, confessor. Likewise the sainted Peter of Luxembourg, cardinal, resting at Avignon. At Antioch, Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr. When she was fifteen years old, after the squalor of prison, scourging, the tearing of her flesh with claws, and burning with lamps, she completed her martyrdom by the cutting off of her head. According to others, she suffered on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August. Mildrida, virgin. Nehemiah; Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel; and Jesus, son of Jehozadak, who are numbered among the holy Fathers of the Old Testament in Ecclesiasticus 40.”

Molan, after “they were illumined,” inserts in smaller type: “under Elpidophorus, whom the venerable deacon Muritta had received as a child from the basin of the font. While Elpidophorus sat and raged, before he was stripped, Muritta took up the cloths with which he had earlier covered him at the font, the *sindon*—and is said to have moved the whole city to weeping and tears with these words: ‘These are the linen cloths, Elpidophorus, minister of error, which will accuse you when the majesty of the Judge comes, while my careful guardianship serves as testimony to your destruction, to plunge you into the abyss of the sulphurous pit. These covered you, spotless, as you rose from the font. These will pursue you more fiercely when you begin to possess the flame of Gehenna.’” At the end: Concerning Bonaventure, as in the Florentine manuscript: “At Antioch, Saint Margaret, virgin, who through many kinds of torments merited from the Lord the triumph of the heavenly homeland. At Bamberg, Saint Henry, emperor and confessor. Likewise Saint Mildrada, a virgin in Kent, now translated to Deventer.” Again in smaller type: “On the Sunday after this feast of blessed Margaret, at Brussels, the feast of Corpus Christi, most renowned for miracles, which the Jews pierced through in the year 1369, as may still be seen today.” Other editions are somewhat shorter in their first supplement. At the end, concerning Mildrada [whom others often call Mildrida, while Castellanus thinks she should be called Miltritha], as above. “On the thirteenth day, the commemoration of Saint Father Joseph, confessor, at Thessalonica.” In smaller type: “On the same day, among many, the feast of blessed Margaret. On the following Sunday, at Brussels, the feast of Corpus Christi, most renowned for miracles.” See the first edition.

## [Col. 0253]

Joel and Ezra, prophets. In Macedonia, the feast of blessed Sila the apostle, who, being one of the first brothers and sent by the apostles to the churches of the Gentiles, diligently completed the ministry of preaching, full of the grace of the Lord; and, glorifying Christ in his sufferings, afterward rested. In Africa, the holy confessors Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, glorious in faith and virtues, and the entire clergy of that Church, who, weakened by slaughter and hunger—nearly five hundred or more, among whom were many very young readers—rejoicing in the Lord, were driven far away into cruel exile. Among them were the most distinguished: an archdeacon named Salutaris, and Muritta, second in the office of the ministers. Having become confessors for the third time, they were honored with the title of glorious perseverance in Christ. In Lesser Britain, Saint Turianus, bishop and confessor, a man of remarkable simplicity and innocence.

## Day before the Ides. Day 14. **[Col. 0257]**

Thus read the Pratense, Heriniense, Antwerp-Major, Pulsano, Munerat, the first edition of Belin, Greven, and Molan—and, what is especially rare, also the Centulense.

**[Col. 0257C]**

The Pratense and Molan correctly have *Phocae*, but, by the unanimous agreement of all the others, it was necessary to write *Focae* in the text, as we likewise did above on 5 March, where Molan, like the Pratense, agreed with the others. The Centulense alone has *Foceae*. Here it reads *Synopis* with Greven and Molan, while all the others have the form found in the text. I do not know what the Pulsano manuscript means by “of the city itself.” In Munerat, the *et* before *ferrum* is redundant; in Belin, *etiam* is absent after *ignem*. Molan and the Centulense read, as they should, *Heraclae*, but again the remaining manuscripts compel us to write the form found in the text—or, worse, *Eracleae*, or, worst of all, with Belin alone, *Eradii*. Antwerp-Major has *properavisse* instead of *properasse*, which has the same meaning; Belin’s *properasse historiam* is worse. The Centulense, if not pure, at least rendered the phrase elegantly in this form: “Because of his most celebrated reputation, Africanus, the noble historian, says that he hurried to him.” I collect the scribal errors, such as *Aput*, *Ponthum*, *civitate Sinapis*, *ignes*, *Ystoriographus*, *Aphricanus*, *Affricanus*, and so forth.

**[Col. 0257C]**

We mentioned Phocas of Antioch on 5 March, from our Usuard and other earlier sources. Another Phocas, likewise very well known among the Martyrologists, occurs here. The Hieronymian Martyrologies especially remember him on this day under the name *Phocus* or *Phocas*, as we have written it in the text, with the title of bishop. Florentinius notes that Combefis reproached Baronius for not having distinguished Phocas sufficiently; certainly, even Combefis himself was not entirely able to do so. Meanwhile, the *small Roman Martyrology* announces our bishop and martyr as follows: “At Pontus, Phocas, bishop of the city of Sinope.” Ado also speaks in this way, proceeding to describe the emperor, the governor, **[Col. 0257D]** the kinds of torture, and the translation or burial of the relics at Vienne in Gaul, in nearly the same words used by Bede and, after him, Rabanus. Since Notker describes Rabanus or Ado, it is clear that these four eulogies are entirely similar. Our author says nothing about the governor or the relics, which are supplied in the Appendices; but he took everything else verbatim from the account of Vienne. Thus far, almost all the Martyrologists have held a consistent opinion. On their authority, as we indicated on 5 March with Henschenius and Florentinius, at least two martyrs named Phocas must be affirmed, differing at minimum in status, whatever the possibility that they may be called fellow citizens by origin. Whether the encomium on Phocas by Asterius, bishop of Amasea, confused the two, as Baronius thought, is not entirely clear. Combefis, already cited, published his conjectures together with Asterius’s oration, first printed by Surius on 22 September; Ruinart presented his own in the preliminary notice to the *Selecta*, page 627. Tillemont reconsidered most of the arguments of these highly learned men in volume V, beginning on page 581. I see before me a thorny and tangled forest, whose clearing or cutting down, with Baronius, Florentinius, and others, will have its proper place in our *Acts*. Wandalbert agrees with the other Martyrologists, adorning the other Phocas, namely the bishop, in this way:

> On the day before, Phocas, bishop and martyr, seeks the heavens.

**[Col. 0258D]**

All the Martyrologists, whether older than Usuard or contemporary with him, are silent about Heraclas, patriarch of Alexandria. It is therefore evident that he first received a place among the saints from Usuard—something certainly remarkable in one who very rarely adds foreign saints, especially those summoned from so far away, to the material of his guides. Nor do I sufficiently see why he placed Heraclas especially on this day, since in our chronological series we have shown in our treatise, on page 24, that he more probably died on 4 December. These matters, however, are reserved for examination in their proper place. It is enough here to have reproduced the true text of Usuard, in which what is brought forward in praise of that patriarch can be found in Rufinus’s translation of Eusebius, book VI, chapter 23.

**[Col. 0259A]**

The Tournai manuscript begins the text: “Phocatus, bishop and martyr.” After this comes a pure and complete text, in which that Phocatus is considered distinct from Phocas, as you will soon see in several manuscripts. In the margin, in a similar but later hand, it adds: “Vincent the confessor, of Haonia.”

Rosweyd, after the pure text, adds: “Likewise Marcellinus, confessor, companion of Saint Lebuin. Likewise Phocatus, bishop.” See the Luxovien manuscript.

The Antwerp and Maximum-Lübeck manuscripts, in the first section, insert “and the African governor,” from Ado. Heraclas is entirely omitted. They continue: “At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of the holy bishops Justus and Amatus. Likewise Phocatus, bishop.”

Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, and Louvain likewise have in the first section “and the African governor.” They continue: “At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of Justus and Amatus.” Their text on Heraclas is pure. Finally: “On the same day, Phocatus, bishop.”

In Albergen, Heraclas is absent; the rest is similar to the others. The Danish manuscript agrees completely, but in the margin, in a much later hand, it has concerning Bonaventure: “At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of the Seraphic doctor Saint Bonaventure, bishop, cardinal and confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor.”

The Brussels manuscript begins: “At Senoges [more probably Soneges], Saint Vincent the confessor and husband of blessed Waldetrudis of Mons, niece of blessed Gudila. By the exhortation of Saints Autbert and Gislenus the abbot, he became a monk from being a count and strove to serve Christ in all his actions.” Concerning Phocas it agrees with Antwerp-Major, inserting “and the African governor”; at the end it also adds from Ado: “His relics are preserved at Vienne in the basilica of the Apostles.” Its text on Heraclas is pure, except that it writes *Eraclei*. At the end: “And at Lyons in Gaul, the burial of the holy bishops Justus and Amantius. On the same day, Saint Phocatus, bishop. Likewise Germanus, bishop.” In the margin, in a very recent hand, is written **[Col. 0259C]** “Saint Henry, Roman emperor and confessor.”

The Hagenoyen manuscript agrees with Antwerp-Major and the others in the section on Phocas. Then: “In Africa, the martyrdom of holy Eugenius, bishop, glorious in faith and virtues, and of the entire clergy,” and so forth. Likewise: “In Lesser Britain, Saint Turianus,” and so forth; these passages have been transferred here from yesterday’s text. “At Alexandria, Saint Heraclitus,” and so forth, instead of *Heraclas*.

The Daveron manuscript: “At Poitiers, Saint Cyprian the martyr.” See the other manuscripts on the preceding day.

The Amiens manuscript: “On the same day, the dedication of the oratory of blessed Paul the Apostle. In this church, on this day, the principal commemoration is venerated of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of our Saint Firminus the Elder, on account of the battle nobly fought in the suburb of this city in the year 957 from the Lord’s Incarnation.”

The Bigot manuscript, marked P 5: “At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of the holy bishops Justus and Amatus. **[Col. 0259D]** And elsewhere, Saint Phocatus, bishop.”

Codex D of Du Cheval, marked B: “On the same day, Saint Phocatus, bishop.” In another manuscript of the same collection, marked C: “In Africa, Donatus.”

The Florentine manuscript: “At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of the holy martyrs Justus, Amatus, and Phocatus.” But I do not understand why this Phocatus, so often repeated, is here connected with the people of Lyons. See the following manuscript.

LUXOVIEN: “At Pontus, Saint Phocas … whose relics are kept in the basilica of the Apostles in the Gallic city of Vienne.” These are additions from Ado.

SALINEN: “At Lyon in Gaul, the deposition of Saints Justus and Amatus, bishops.”

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: “In Dacia, the translation of two heads of holy virgins from the company of the eleven thousand. At Pontus, the feast of Saint Phocas,” etc., with additions from Ado, as above. [Col. 0260A] “On the same day, Saint Constantine the Great, emperor, who built the Lateran church at Rome in honor of Saint John the Baptist. At that place he deserved to be cleansed of leprosy by Saint Pope Sylvester. He endowed the holy church with the greatest gifts and honored the clergy. At Lyon in Gaul, the deposition of Saints Justus and Amicus, bishops and confessors. On the same day, Saint Phocas, bishop and confessor. In Lower Britain, Blessed Turiavus, bishop and confessor.” Undoubtedly, “Turrini” stands for Turiavi [perhaps Turiavus]. “At Alexandria, Saint Heraclius, bishop and confessor, on account of whose …” etc. “At Deventer, the feast of Blessed Marcellinus, confessor, disciple of Saint Lebuinus the priest. In Africa, Saints Peter and Donatus. In the territory of Cleves, in the city of Rees, the deposition of Saint Dentlinus, a boy. Also, on the Tuesday immediately following the feast of Saint Margaret the virgin, the commemoration of Saint Brigid the virgin.”

The second edition of BELIN adds at the end: “In Africa, Saint Donatus. On the same day, Saint Vedastus, confessor and bishop of Arras.” Perhaps this concerns the translation of his body [Col. 0260B], which is commemorated on the following day in the Auctaria.

GREVEN: “In Africa, Saints Peter and Donatus … Lubbertus, abbot and martyr. At Lyon, Saints Justus and Amicius, bishops and confessors. Phocas, bishop and confessor. At Deventer, Marcellinus, priest and confessor, companion of Saint Lebuinus, but disciple of Saint Willebrord, bishop. On the same day, according to some, Constantine the Great. But, more truly, according to others, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. Vincent, count of Hainaut and confessor. In the territory of Cleves, in the city of Rees, Saint Dentlinus, a seven-year-old boy and confessor. Phoca the virgin. In Dacia, the translation of two heads of holy virgins,” etc., as above in the Lubeck–Cologne edition.

MOLANUS also inserts into the text, though in different type: “Whose relics are kept in the basilica of the Apostles, in the city of Vienne in Gaul.” At the end: “On the same day, the discovery of Saint Libertus the martyr, glorious in life and merits [Col. 0260C]. Whom the illustrious and most blessed martyr Rumoldus, when he had been dead from drowning for three days, raised by divine power and imbued with faith and instruction. At the time when the Northmen, Danes, and Huns were laying Brabant and the neighboring provinces waste with fire and sword, he completed his life in glorious martyrdom before the altar of Saint Trudo. At Soignies, the deposition of Blessed Vincent, confessor of Christ and abbot, who built High Mount (Altus Mons). At Aicura, Saint Ragenufla the virgin. On the same day, Saint Henry II, emperor of the Romans and confessor, who died in the year of the Lord 1021. The passion of Saint Basinus, king and martyr.”

Then, in different type: “He rests in the monastery at Tronchiennes outside Ghent. At Deventer, Saint Marcellinus,” etc., as in GREVEN. “In the territory of Cleves, in the city of Rees, Saint Dentlinus, a seven-year-old boy and confessor; though he was not canonized.” Other editions begin in italics: “At Lyon, the deposition of Saint Bonaventure, cardinal and bishop of Albano, of the Order of Friars Minor.” In the text, the same as above. At the end: “At Bamberg, Saint Henry II, emperor of the Romans and confessor, who died in the year of the Lord 1024. At Soignies, the deposition of Blessed Vincent, confessor of Christ. He lived in the monastery called Mons, with his head tonsured, for many years under the holy Rule, preserving charity while separated from his holy wife Waldetrudis. In Hasbaye, on the same day, the discovery of Saint Liberius,” etc., as above. “At Deventer, Saint Marcellinus, priest and confessor, disciple of Saint Willibrord, bishop. He governed the regions beyond the IJssel, the places Oudenzeel, Drenthe and Twente, Coevorden and Deventer, and by God’s providence won almost the entire population for Christ by preaching. At Tronchiennes monastery, the passion of Saint Basinus, king and martyr. At Aicura, Saint Ragenufla the virgin. At Trier, Saint Justus the confessor.”]

[Col. 0257]

At Pontus, the feast of Blessed Phocas, bishop of the city of Sinope, who under the emperor Trajan endured prison, chains, iron, and even fire for Christ. At Alexandria, Saint Heracleas, bishop, on account of whose most celebrated reputation the historian Africanus says that he hastened to him.

On the Ides. Day 15. [Note: [Col. 0261]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0261A]

All the codices, both the pure and the others, simply have “at Nisibis,” except Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck, which have “in the city of Nisibis.” They likewise all read: “He was one of the number,” etc.; but in Greven and Molanus “of the number” is missing. Again, “under the persecution of Maximinus,” although Ado explicitly reads “of Maximian.” The cited codices and almost all the others write “at the Nicene council,” [Col. 0262A] but in Herinien. it is incorrectly “at the council.” The same applies to “of Arius and Homoousius,” although Ado has “of Arius and Homousius.” I have spoken elsewhere about Carthage, as also about “they condemned” and similar spelling—or rather pseudo-spelling. In Molanus one reads “they condemned.” Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck have Catilini instead of Catulini.]

[Note: [Col. 0261A]

The Small Roman Martyrology restricts the first announcement to a few words: “At Nisibis, James, bishop.” The Hieronymian Martyrologies have Nisivis, Nizibae, or Nisibini; in them, contrary to custom, a story—or perhaps a fable—is appended in the following form: “He performed many signs in the body, and alone saw Noah’s Ark on the mountain; no one else among those who went with him was permitted to see it.” This passage, inserted there and not very correctly, is shown by the silence of the very ancient Echternach codex to be extraneous. What, moreover, survived in the early centuries of the Church on Mount Ararat or Mount Taurus concerning Noah’s Ark, Florentinius investigates at considerable length, though I do not know at what cost in labor. He also indicates other feast days, perhaps of different Jameses.

As for the vision mentioned above, whether natural or miraculous, Ado said nothing. Instead, [Col. 0261B] drawing from Gennadius another eulogy—which, if I am not mistaken, conforms more closely to historical truth—he hastened to provide it; Usuard composed a most polished epitome of it, which we have reproduced in the text. Notker, however, unsatisfied with the material from Ado, wished to append the vision taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies to the words of the earlier account.

Surius extracted the life of James from Theodoret’s *Philotheus*, in Hervetus’s translation; further material could have been added to it from the history of the same author. Tillemont composed a historical account in French from Theodoret himself, Gennadius, and others, in volume VII, beginning on page 260; it will be of considerable use in illuminating the acts of this distinguished saint.

The first line of Wandalbert’s couplet [Col. 0262A] does not belong here; the second is attributed to James:

“On the Ides Cassianus and Cyricus shine forth,

And James the bishop is celebrated for his abundant merits.”

The second announcement is found in full in the Small Roman Martyrology and in Ado, and almost in full in the Hieronymian copies, where the names are more corrupt and confused here and there. Certainly our predecessor faithfully followed his models. See Baronius’s note.

The Small Roman Martyrology is silent about the Carthaginians and Alexandrians. Ado undoubtedly took both commemorations from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but expressed certain names somewhat more clearly: in the first class he omitted Pollutana, and where the copies mentioned above read Nasei among the Alexandrians, he put Marsei [Col. 0262B]. The name of the martyr Catulinus is illustrious on this day in the frequently praised Carthaginian Calendar. A treatise by Augustine in his honor is also cited, but we have not yet seen it published. Of the Alexandrians, only the names seem to survive. In any case, Usuard copied both classes word for word from Ado, placing one before the other and, so to speak, taking a middle course: instead of Nasei and Marsei he substituted Narsei, as all our codices unanimously pronounce it; more recent copies have Narseus. Thus the entire compilation of the text is both Adonian and Usuardian.]

[Note: [Col. 0261B]

IN THE HERINIAN CODEX, a later hand adds in the margin: “On the same day, the division of the apostles.” Others also have this.]

TORNACEN. cuts the eulogy of James of Nisibis; otherwise it is pure.

ANTWERP–MAJOR appends to the pure text at the end: “And the translation of Saint Swithun.” [Col. 0261C]

PULSANEN. is both abbreviated and expanded. It begins: “At Antioch, the passion of the holy martyrs Quiricus and Julitta, his mother.” But in the text it omits James and the martyrs of Porto.

MUNERAT. adds at the end after the text: “On the same day, the division of the apostles for preaching.”

ROSWEYD begins: “The division of the apostles.” Then: “Plechelm, confessor and bishop.” The first announcement of the text concerning James follows, etc. Then: “Also, Philip, Agrippinus, and Reginswindis the virgin. Cassianus the martyr.” After this the remainder of the text follows, with the addition at the end: “On the same day in Britain, the deposition of Blessed Deusdedit, archbishop and confessor. And the translation of Swithun.” In the English copies it often agrees with ANTWERP–MAJOR.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM and LOUVAIN differ little from the pure text, prefacing it only with: “The division of the apostles, which, as Bede writes, took place in the twelfth year after the Passion of the Lord.”

[Col. 0262B] UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC agree with the two preceding copies, but all place before them: “At Antioch, the feast of the holy Tyritus, Tyricus, Quiricus, and Julitta, his mother. After their eyes had been torn out, they were first sent to prison; afterward they were flayed and roasted on an iron bed, then crushed with irons, and, after their tongues had been cut out, they completed the course of their martyrdom by beheading. Four hundred and four others also suffered with them.” We discussed these with Usuard on 16 June. See what is said there, and more fully in the Acts.

CENTULEN.: “The feast of Saint James, bishop of the city of Nisibis, a man of great virtues. At Carthage, Saints Catulinus the deacon, Januarius, Florentius, Julia, and Justa, who are buried in the basilica of Faustus. At Alexandria, Saints Philip, Zeno, Narsenus, and ten infants. At Arras, the return of Blessed Vedastus to his proper place.”

BRUSSELS begins: “The division of the apostles, which, as Bede writes, took place in the twelfth year after the Passion of the Lord, under the emperor Claudius. In the city of Nisibis, Saint James, bishop and confessor. He was one of the number of the saints under the persecution of Maximian, and of those who condemned the perversity of Arius at the Council of Nicaea; and he was otherwise a man of great virtue, so that often through his prayers the city was delivered from danger. After he had been buried within the city walls, and afterward, through the zeal of Julian the Apostate, had been buried outside them, the city soon fell under Persian rule.” [Col. 0263A] The account of the Alexandrians follows, then that of the Carthaginians, and finally that of the Romans in its pure form.

HAGENOYEN, in third place, after the class of the Porto martyrs, inserts: “On the same day, the division of the apostles, which, according to Bede, took place in the thirteenth year after the Passion of the Lord, when they were divided throughout the whole world and preached the word of the Lord. For under Pope Cornelius there took place the division of the bones of the apostles Peter and Paul, when half of Peter’s bones were placed at Saint Paul’s and, conversely, half of Paul’s bones were placed at Saint Peter’s.” I do not understand at all what this “for” means, or what the division of the bones has to do with the apostles’ dispersion. The account of Cyricus and Julitta follows, almost as above. Then: “At Lyon in Gaul, the deposition of Saints Justus and Amicius, bishops. On the same day, Saint Phocas, bishop.” See the preceding day.

AQUICINCT omits the name of Florentius. At the end it adds: “On the same day, the return of the body of Saint Vedastus [Col. 0263B] from the city of Beauvais to its proper place.”

VICTORIN and the Swedish Royal Codex, marked 128, have at the end: “At Antioch, the feast of Saints Cyricus and Julitta, his mother. On the same day, the holy city of Jerusalem was liberated.” See the year in MOLANUS.

MATRICHT–CARTUSIAN–UTRECHT: “The division of the apostles. Plechelm, bishop and confessor. Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa, sisters and martyrs. Philip, Narseus, Zeno, and ten infant martyrs. James, bishop of Nisibis.”

SWEDISH ROYAL CODEX, no. 428: “On the same day, the division of the apostles for preaching.”

VATICAN CODEX, no. 5949: “At Tarsus, the metropolis, the feast of the holy martyrs Cyricus and Julitta, his mother.”

FLORENTINUS: “At Antioch, Quiricus and Julitta … The translation of Saints Senator, Viator, Cassiodorus, and Dominata, their mother.” These passages require some clarification. STROZZIAN: “At Pavia, Saint Felix [Col. 0263C] bishop and martyr.”

BURDIGALEN: “Saint Benedict, bishop of Angers.” Castellanus also places him on this day.

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “The division of the apostles for preaching the word of God throughout the whole world. This, as Bede writes, took place in the twelfth year after the Passion of the Lord. Peter came to Antioch, then settled at Rome, where he was crucified. Paul enlightened the world by his preaching and was beheaded at Rome. Andrew was crucified in Achaea. James the son of Zebedee was beheaded at Jerusalem. John died peacefully at Ephesus. Philip was stoned and crucified in Phrygia. James the son of Alphaeus was killed with a fuller’s club. Bartholomew was flayed and beheaded in India. Thomas was pierced in another India, which is at the end of the world. Simon and Thaddeus were killed in Persia. Matthew was pierced with a lance in Ethiopia before the altar. Matthias completed his martyrdom in Judea. [Col. 0264A] This division was made at Christ’s command, so that the Psalmist’s saying might be fulfilled: ‘Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.’”

The complete text follows, with this appended: “Also at Alexandria, Saints Catholinus, bishop, and Zosima, confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saint Swithun, bishop, and his companions, bishops and confessors. On the same day, Saint Plechelm, bishop and confessor. Also, the return of Saint Vedastus, bishop and confessor of the people of Arras.”

BEDIN places last: “In the city of Nisibis,” etc. Then adds: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Quiricus and Julitta. At Pavia, Saint Felix, bishop and martyr.”

GREVEN: “The division of the apostles for preaching, made, according to Bede, in the twelfth year after the Passion of the Lord. Also, according to some, Cyricus and Julitta, whom Usuard records on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July. Plechelm, bishop and confessor of Twente, resting at Oldenzaal. Deusdedit, archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 0264B] and confessor. At Alexandria, Saints Catholinus, bishop, and Zosima, confessors. On the same day, in England, the translation of Saint Swithun, bishop of Winchester, and his companions, bishops and confessors. Also, the return of Saint Vedastus, bishop and confessor of Arras. Reginswindis, virgin and martyr. Fausta and Julia, sisters, virgins and martyrs. The dedication of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre in Jerusalem.”

MOLANUS: “On the same day, the feast of all the apostles, that is, when they were separated from one another. On the same day, the holy martyrs Cyricus and Julitta. At Pavia, Saint Felix, bishop and martyr. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 893, the return of the body of Saint Vedastus from Beauvais to its proper place, after twelve years, nine months, and twenty-four days.”

Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, Jerusalem was captured by the Christian army, in the year one thousand two hundred less one”; he means 1199. Concerning Plechelm, Deusdedit, [Col. 0264C] and the translation of Swithun, as in GREVEN above. Finally: “Ansuerus the monk, with his companions, stoned at Ratzeburg.”

Other editions, after “a man of great virtue,” insert in different type: “So that often through his prayers the city was freed from danger.” At the end, concerning the division of the apostles, as above. “At Canterbury, the deposition of Saint Deusdedit, sixth archbishop and confessor. In the city of Oudenaarde, the feast of Saint Plechelm, bishop.” Concerning Felix, as above. “On the same day, Saint Reginswindis the virgin. At Arras, in the year of the Lord,” etc., as in the earlier version. Concerning Swithun, as above. Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, Jerusalem was captured by the Christian army in the year one thousand one hundred less one,” correcting the earlier error, where it had written “one thousand two hundred,” etc. “At Ratzeburg, Ansuerus the monk, with his companions, was stoned; Helmold discusses them in his history of the Slavs.”]

[Col. 0261]

At Nisibis, the feast of Saint James, bishop, a man of great virtue. He was one of the number of confessors under the persecution of Maximinus, and of those who condemned the perversity of Arius at the Nicene Council by opposing Homoousius. At the harbor of Rome, the feast of the holy sisters Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa. At Carthage, Saints Catulinus the deacon, Januarius, Florentius, Julia, and Justa, who are buried in the Basilica of Faustus. At Alexandria, Saints Philip, Zeno, Narseus, and ten infants.

The seventeenth day before the Kalends. Day 16. [Note: [Col. 0263D]

The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Antwerp–Munerat., Belin., [Col. 0264D] Greven and Greater Molan., Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck.]

[Note: [Col. 0263D]

Syria had to be discussed elsewhere as well; I write in accordance with Praten., Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck, Munerat., Belin., and Molanus. If the codices are not consistent with one another, neither will our spelling be uniform. All our codices, following the Small Roman Martyrology and Ado, read Eustachius; nevertheless, Eustathius must certainly be read, as we shall say in the Observations. The best-quality codices—Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antwerp–Major, [Col. 0264D] Pulsanen., Rosweyd., Munerat., and Belin.—correctly write in the text “under the emperor Constantine,” whatever the others, followed by the modern Roman Martyrology, may wish to have our bishop “banished by order of Constantius.” This is what Antwerp, Max.-Lubeck, and the middling-quality copies have, together with Greven and Molanus, who read “under the emperor Constantius”; others have “under Constantius the prince.” Baronius claims in his Notes that this is established from Athanasius’s not sufficiently strong testimony, while others prove the contrary from the sequence of history. Some, along with Notker, incorrectly write “within Janopolis.” Others agree better with the text. “Of Thrace” in some copies, and “Thrace” in Antwerp–Major, are easily corrected. Belin changes the meaning by writing “there he found rest in exile” [Col. 0266A]. “Ostia” is read in many copies, but Praten. and Herinien. correctly agree with the text. Belin has “Hilarianus”; Munerat., “Hilarius,” with the addition “and martyr,” properly enough, but not according to the author’s intention.]

[Note: [Col. 0265A]

The Small Roman Martyrology provided the source for the text. Ado drew from it, and from Ado it passed, naturally, into ours. It differs only in this: Hilarinus, who is placed first in the earlier accounts, occupies second place in Usuard. Otherwise, as I indicated above, both the Small Roman Martyrology and Ado, as well as almost all our Usuardian codices throughout, consistently read Eustachius; Baronius writes Eustathius instead, correctly, since the reference is to that most celebrated defender of the faith against Arius, well known in the history of that period. But in the text we have transmitted the Usuardian reading; there we also show that “under Constantine the prince” is better than “under Constantius the prince,” even against Ado’s most explicit opinion. See Baronius’s Note and what will be discussed in its proper place in the Acts.

The greater difficulty is whether our Eustathius or Eustachius is listed in the Hieronymian Martyrologies together with other martyrs. I would not dare resolve that question on the basis of a single footstep, whatever Florentinius may conjecture. It is safest to defer that question also for clarification in its proper place. For now we give the words of the Small Roman Martyrology: “At Antioch in Syria, Eustathius, bishop.” The rest is Adonian, copied by our author and by Notker.

Scholars know the entire sequence of the deeds of the great Eustathius, which must be assembled from various ancient ecclesiastical documents. Several have long labored on it; among them Tillemont, in volume VII beginning on page 21, supplies most of the evidence, which will serve us in due course.

[Col. 0266A] Concerning Hilarinus, the Small Roman Martyrology also has only a brief notice: “At Ostia, Hilarinus the martyr.” The eulogy placed in the text must originally have been composed by Bede, if the material attributed to him in our edition before volume II of the March Acts is genuine. From there it passed into Rabanus and Ado, and from Ado into ours.

Notker, perhaps alluding to the name of the saint, thought it appropriate to insert these few words: “The most cheerful receiver and sustainer of the saints.” Whether these were taken from the Acts of Saints John and Paul, there is no time—or need—to investigate here. What if an example from Gallicanus had flowed in from elsewhere?

This much seems certain: the same Hilarinus, placed in the same location, is mentioned by the Hieronymian copies, namely, “in the city of Hostia,” for us Ostia, as the recently cited martyrologists also indicate, contrary to Florentinius’s reading—unless he too, along with the modern Roman Martyrology, thinks that Hilarinus completed his contest at Arezzo and was afterward transferred to Ostia. This is Baronius’s sufficiently well-founded opinion, which must likewise be examined in its proper place.

See Ado on 7 August concerning Donatus, and on the same day Florentinius concerning the same saint. Of the companion Cyricus or Cyriacus only the Hieronymian Martyrologies make mention. Whatever historical truth may require in the meantime, the simple and genuine text of our Usuard is entirely beyond dispute. Wandalbert celebrates Hilarinus as follows:

“When the tenth marks August—or August marks the seventh month—

Your feast, excellent martyr Hilarinus, shines forth.”

] [Note: [Col. 0265B]

TORNACEN begins: “Bertinus, abbot.” The text that follows is entirely pure.

PULSANEN, pure in the first announcement, completely omits the second.

ROSWEYD adds to the pure text at the end: “Munulfus and Gundulfus, bishops and confessors. The translation of Saint Bertinus, abbot.”

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, LOUVAIN, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC also append to the pure text: “On the same day at Utrecht on the Meuse, Saints Mondulfus and Gondulfus, bishops.” The final two form the names as Monolfus or Monolphus, and Gundulfus or [Col. 0265C] Gundolphus.

CENTULEN: “At Antioch, Saint Eustathius, bishop, who, driven into exile for the Catholic faith, found rest there. At Ostia, Saint Hilarinus, monk and martyr, under Julian the Apostate.”

BRUSSELS is fairly pure in the text, but adds: “At Utrecht on the Meuse, the deposition of the holy confessors Monulfus and Gundulfus, bishops. At Xantas in Brabant, the feast of Saint Regnildis, virgin and martyr, sister of our blessed patroness Gudila. Content with the company of one servant and one maidservant, she made a pilgrimage to the holy city of Jerusalem and to each place where the Lord Jesus had physically walked. After seven years, she returned to her homeland with many relics of the saints and remained at Xantas until she herself, together with Grimoaldus the subdeacon and Gundulfus her household servant, received the palm of martyrdom from the Huns for the faith of Christ. On the same day, the elevation of Saint Bertinus, abbot.”

[Col. 0265D] HAGENOYEN, pure in the first place, reports in the second: “At Carthage, the feast of the holy martyrs Catulinus the deacon, Januarius,” etc. Concerning them, see the preceding day. Again: “At Alexandria, the feast of the holy martyrs Philip,” etc., also as yesterday. It continues: “In the city of Ostia, the passion of Saint Hilarinus, monk,” etc., purely. “At Utrecht on the Meuse, the deposition of the holy confessors Munulfus and Gundulfus, who are said to have been those two deceased bishops, raised again by Saint Pope Leo and his companions [who] dedicated the church of Aachen together with other bishops.”

MATRICHT–CARTUSIAN–UTRECHT: “Eustathius, bishop of the city of Antioch. Hilarinus, monk.”

VATICAN, marked no. 5949, has at the end: “At Benevento, the feast of Saint Vitalianus, bishop and confessor.” In the modern Roman Martyrology it is recorded as Capua.

FLORENTINUS: “At Rome, Saint Leo, pope IV …” This is how I read it here, although elsewhere I find no evidence of liturgical cult. I think Leo IV is meant, concerning whom see below. The same codices continue: “The canonization of Blessed Francis, celebrated by Pope Gregory in the year of the Lord 1228, in the second year of his pontificate.”

In the CODEX OF THE MONASTERY OF MONTE SANTO: “The dedication of the basilica of Blessed Stephen the protomartyr, on this holy mountain of Saint Romaric.”

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “At Rome, the feast of Blessed Leo IV, pope and confessor. He sat for eight years, three months, and six days. Constantly devoted to prayers and vigils, he was buried in the church of Saint Peter.”

The account of Eustathius follows, purely. Then: “At Ostia, the passion of Saint Hilarinus, monk. When, by order of Julian the sacrilegious emperor, he was seized at Arezzo, a city of Tuscany, by the judge Quadracius and compelled to sacrifice together with Blessed Donatus, bishop, and when they refused, Donatus was imprisoned, while Hilarinus was beaten with clubs until he gave up his spirit; his bones are preserved buried at Ostia.

At Lower Utrecht, situated above the Meuse, Saints Monulfus and Gundulfus, bishops and confessors. These men, by God’s will, as is reported, rose alive from their tombs and, with Blessed Pope Leo III, consecrated at Aachen a church in honor of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God. After this was done, they returned to Utrecht to their tombs and restored one another to their former sleep. At Caesarea, Saints Paulinus and Mammes, martyrs.”

Notker gives much information about Mammes on this day; but Usuard places him on 17 August. [Col. 0267A] “On the same day, Saint Marinus, bishop and martyr. At Trier, Blessed Valentinus, bishop and martyr. On the same day, the translation of Saint Osmundus, bishop and confessor. Also, on the second Sunday of July, the feast of Saint Bonaventure, or of Saint Eustathius, bishop of Albano and confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor.”

GREVEN: “Valentinus, bishop of Trier and martyr. Marinus, bishop and martyr. At Caesarea, Saints Paulinus and Mammes, martyrs. At Antioch, Saint Theodotus. Leo IV, pope and confessor, who sat for eight years: a very holy man, greatly devoted to vigils and prayers, having been brought up from childhood among holy monks. Anatholius, bishop and confessor. At Upper Utrecht on the river Meuse, Saints Monulfus and Gundulfus, bishops and confessors, who are said to have risen from their tombs and, with Pope Leo III, consecrated the church at Aachen in honor of the holy Mother of God, and, after completing that service, returned to their former rest. At Trier, Helia the virgin. Also Regnildis, virgin and [Col. 0267B] martyr. The translation of Saint Osmundus, bishop and confessor. The canonization of Blessed Francis the confessor.”

MOLANUS: “At Utrecht, Saints Monulfus and Gundulfus, confessors, bishops of the Church of Tongeren. At Sanctis, Saint Raineldis, virgin and martyr.”

[Col. 0268A] Then, in smaller type: “Blessed Gudila’s sister. Content with the company of one servant and one maidservant, she made a pilgrimage to the holy city of Jerusalem and to each place where the Lord Jesus had physically walked; after seven years, she returned to her homeland with many relics of the saints and remained at Xancthas in Brabant until she herself, together with Grimoaldus the subdeacon and Gundulfus her household servant, received the palm of martyrdom from the Huns for the faith of Christ.”

This appears to have been copied from BRUSSELS, as we have shown was also done elsewhere. In other editions it reads: “At Utrecht, Saints Monulfus,” etc., as in the earlier account. “At Trier, Saint Valentinus, bishop and martyr. At Sanctis, Saint Raineldis, virgin and martyr, sister of Blessed Gudila, who, together with Grimoaldus the subdeacon and Gundulfus her servant, received the palm of martyrdom from the Huns for the faith of Christ. On the sixteenth day, Saint Athenogenes, hieromartyr, and his ten disciples. Also, the canonization of Blessed Father Francis. At the monastery of Sithiu, the body of Saint Father Bertinus is transferred and reinterred by Blessed Folquinus in the year 846.” Bertinus is celebrated on 5 September. “In Spain, the triumph of the holy cross, on account of the splendid victory achieved against the Moors through the sign of the cross.”]

[Col. 0263]

At Antioch in Syria, the feast of Blessed Eustathius, bishop and confessor, under Constantine the prince, who, driven into exile at Trajanopolis, a city of Thrace, on account of the Catholic faith, found rest there. At Ostia, the passion of Saint Hilarius, monk, who, when he refused to sacrifice during the persecution of Julian, was beaten with clubs and suffered martyrdom.

The sixteenth day before the Kalends. Day 17. [Note: [Col. 0267]

Praten., Herinien., Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck, Munerat., Greven, and Molanus are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0267C]

Concerning Carthage, nearly enough has already been said to cause nausea. Those who write “of the Scillitans,” such as Munerat. and Greven, were quite evidently correct. The difficulty lies in the form of the names, which in the case of some are different almost everywhere. I pass over the Hieronymian Martyrologies here.

Bede has: “At Carthage, of the Scillitans: Marcialis, Cithius, Vesturius, Felix, Aquilinus, Lactantius, Januarius, Generosus, Vesta, Donata, and Secunda.” Here you see that Speratus is missing, although he is the first in the other accounts; this is undoubtedly due to a copyist’s carelessness, since he is explicitly placed first in Rabanus.

In the Acts reported by Baronius they are listed in this form and order: Speratus, Narzalis, Cittimus, Veturius, Felix, Acyllinus, Letantius, Januaria, Generosa, Vestina, Donata, and Secunda. The differences in other Acts are very slight. It is sufficiently clear how all these forms are to be reduced to a single standard.

Among our codices, Munerat. reads Narchalis; Praten. and Molanus, Cythinus; Herinien., Beaturius, and also Letatus; Praten. and most of the others, Letacius. I scarcely doubt that the original form was Laetantius.

Nearly all vary between Januarius and Januaria; we have written Januarius with Ado, which is most probably correct. Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck not incorrectly read “after the first confession of Christ,” but all the other codices, without exception, forbid that reading. In Greven and Molanus the construction is corrupt, since they write: “after the first confession in prison, and on the wood,” etc. The syntax in the text is clear and straightforward.

Herinien. simply has “Then they were beheaded,” omitting the word “with the sword.” I should likewise have mentioned above that the name Bessia is missing in Munerat. Nothing else deserves notice.]

[Note: [Col. 0267C]

The triumph of these twelve Scillitan martyrs has been illustrious throughout every age, celebrated competitively by the Carthaginian Calendar and by our ancient Martyrologies. We have already said that Speratus is missing in Bede through a copyist’s error. Otherwise, between Bede and Ado—Rabanus following the former, and Notker as well as our author following the latter—there is no discrepancy except in the inflection of some names; and you readily understand that these can easily be restored by comparing one with the other.

The Small Roman Martyrology does not give the individual names, writing only: “At Carthage, of the Scillitan martyrs: Speratus, Narthalis, Cythinus, Beaturius, Felix, and seven others.”

Ado then added the seven by name, I suppose from the Acts, or perhaps from Bede. I am inclined to believe this all the more because he adopts Bede’s entire eulogy, adding at the end the following translation in his own words: “Their relics, together with the bones of Blessed Cyprian and the head of Saint Pantaleon the martyr, were translated from Africa into Gaul and are venerated at Lyon in the basilica of the most blessed John the Baptist.”

But our author, perhaps deliberately, omitted this passage, copying all the rest of Ado word for word; therefore there should be no doubt concerning the true and genuine Usuardian text.

Florentinius labors greatly to reconcile the twelve names of these Scillitan martyrs with the Proconsular Acts, which the most eminent Baronius brought forth as a truly precious treasure of venerable antiquity in volume II of the *Annals*, under the year 202, no. 2. I do not deny that the confusion in the Hieronymian codices between African and Asiatic martyrs casts shadows over Baronius’s Acts that are not easily dispelled; nor do the other Acts published by Theodoric Ruinart among the genuine and selected works, beginning on page 73, sufficiently clarify matters that trouble Florentinius.

Nevertheless, the constant authority of the other martyrologists, more consistent with those Acts, sufficiently proves that our Scillitans were twelve in number and suffered together at Carthage, whatever difficulty may be caused by the slight differences in the names and the assigned days, corrupted by copyists.

But here we determine nothing. It is enough to have pointed out the difficulties, which must be examined in their proper place. I mean our Acts, in which another controversy will recur for discussion, also touched upon by Ruinart: whether the relics of all the martyrs, or only some, were translated to Rome or Lyon, and from there to Compiègne, to the royal chapel. Tillemont also discusses this, describing the passion of these martyrs in French in volume III, beginning on page 131.

Meanwhile, Wandalbert’s verses also contribute to proving the number twelve, elegantly expressing the feast of the Scillitan martyrs:

“On the sixteenth Carthage looks toward the rich votive offerings,

Joyfully honoring the twelvefold people of martyrdom;

Whom their Scillitan homeland sent together to the capital.”]

[Note: [Col. 0269A]

TORNACEN, although rarely more expansive, already had one or two additions at the beginning. Thus it begins today’s text: “Alexius the confessor.” In the rest of the text it is entirely pure.

ANTWERP–MAJOR adds to the pure text: “On the same day, Saint Kenelm, king and martyr.”]

PULSANEN. It brought here the part of the text that had been lacking on the preceding day, namely: “At Hostia, the passion of Saint Hilarinus the monk. When he was unwilling, etc.” The entire present text follows, pure.

ROSWEYD. After the pure text it adds: “On the same day, in Britain, Saint Kenelm the martyr. Also the feast of Saint Marcellina the virgin, sister of Saint Ambrose the bishop. Also the burial of Saint Theodosius the bishop and confessor.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN, LOVANIEN., [Col. 0269B] ALBERG., DANIC. have the following first:

“At Rome, on the Via Latina, the feast of Saint Alexius the confessor. Having abandoned his father, home, and possessions, and having lived for some time as a poor and wandering man, he finally returned to his father’s house and remained there, disguised as a pilgrim, for the whole period of his life. His acts and deeds were made known to everyone by a document found in his hand after his death.”

The pure text follows.

CENTULEN.: “At Carthage, of the holy martyrs of Scillium, namely Speratus, Marchalus, Cithinus, Beturius, Felix, Aquilinus, Lactatius, Januaria, Generosa, Bassia, Donata, and Secunda, beheaded under Saturninus the prefect. At Auxerre, Saint Theodosius the confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. has Alexius first, as above. Then comes the text. At the end, however: “On the same day, Saint Fredegundus the confessor. Also King Kenelin [Kenelm].” See below for a fuller account.

HAGENOYEN. is sufficiently pure in the text, but adds the following concerning Alexius [Col. 0269C]:

“At Rome, on the Via Latina, the burial of Saint Alexius the confessor. This Alexius was the son of Euphemianus, first among the chiefs of the imperial palace under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. Euphemianus gave Alexius Marina as a bride, a woman sprung from imperial blood. But he urged his bride to live chastely, and thus abandoned her and all that he possessed for God’s sake, taking only a few things with him, which he soon gave to the poor. Alexius therefore went to Laodicea, where for seventeen years he lived most humbly as a poor man among the poor, beside the church of the blessed Virgin. After this he was warned by the Lord to return to Rome, and he did so. His father received him into his house as just another poor man, for the salvation of his son, and supplied him with food, unaware that he was his son. Alexius remained there for seventeen years, patiently and willingly enduring many insults from his father’s servants. At last, sensing that death was approaching, he wrote his life with his own hand on a document, and, holding it in his hand, died; afterward he shone forth through many miracles. [Col. 0269D] In England, Saint Konelin [Kenelm], a royal boy, innocently killed. Also Marcellina the virgin, sister of Blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan.” There is no doubt that “of Milan” must be read.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end: “On the same day, the passing of Saint Alexius the confessor.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., sign. no. 130: “On the same day, the passing of Saint Alexius the confessor and Marina the virgin.” One might say that this conjunction indicates that Marina should be understood as Alexius’s bride. But see GREVEN below.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Alexius, the outstanding confessor, at Rome; Speratus and his eleven fellow martyrs, who are called the Scillitan martyrs; Marcellina the virgin, sister of Saint Ambrose.”

[Col. 0270A] VATICAN., no. 3949: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Alexius.” Or, as BELIN has it: “On the same day, Saint Alexius the confessor.” See above, the manuscripts of the intermediate class, etc.

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, Saint Alexius … in the year of the Lord 398, in the fifty-first year of his life. Also Saint Marina the virgin.” GREVEN composed a longer history of her, which is also attributed to others.

THE LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “Commemoration of the relics of the holy father Severinus, archbishop of Cologne, at Agrippina, a confessor, a man of many virtues and distinguished miracles. At Rome, on the Via Latina, the feast of Blessed Alexius, etc.” as in the six manuscripts above. The sufficiently pure text follows. At the end: “In England, the burial of Saint Kenelm, king of the Mercians and martyr. At Milan, Saint Marcellina the virgin. In Dacia, Saint Florentia the virgin.”

[Col. 0270B] GREVEN:

“In England, Kenelm, king of the Mercians and martyr, a boy of seven years. When his dying father, Kenulf, had entrusted him to his sister to be brought up, she, out of desire to reign, had the boy killed. It is said that at that very moment the boy began the angelic hymn, ‘We praise you, God,’ and was struck down as he was saying, ‘You, the white-robed company of martyrs, …’ Immediately at Rome, above the altar of blessed Peter, a parchment fell from heaven, carried by a white dove, and disclosed the death of the holy martyr and the place of his burial.

“In Hungary, in the church at Nitra, the holy martyrs Andrew and Benedict. Theodosius the bishop and confessor. Evodius the bishop and confessor. Fredegandus the bishop and confessor. At Rome, on the Via Latina, Saint Alexius the confessor. Born to a very wealthy father and married to a most noble bride, he was nevertheless inflamed by the fire of faith. After abandoning everything, he lived for some time abroad in the poorest condition; at length he returned and remained unknown in his father’s house until the end of his life. [Col. 0270C] At Milan, Saint Marcella the virgin, a favorite of Blessed Ambrose the bishop. In Dacia, the translation of Saint Florentia the virgin, disciple of Saint Hilary the bishop. Also, according to the Catalogue of the Saints, Saint Marina the virgin. Having changed her clothing, she entered a monastery of men and was falsely accused of fornication. She bore this most patiently and did penance as though she had actually been guilty. Her holy body was translated to Venice in the year of the Lord 1113 and is preserved there with due honor.

“Also a commemoration of the relics of Saint Severinus, archbishop of Cologne at Agrippina, a man of great holiness. At Aachen, the dedication of a basilica in honor of the most glorious Mother of God Mary, by Pope Leo III, in the presence of 365 bishops and very many other Fathers. Although this took place on the feast of the Epiphany, it is nevertheless commemorated here with greater festivity.”

MOLAN. adds from Ado the translation of the relics, mentioned above:

“On the same day, Saint Alexius the confessor, [Col. 0270D] who, after a glorious and praiseworthy life, was buried at Rome in the monastery of Saint Boniface the pope. The canonization of our most blessed father Francis. At Milan, Saint Marcellina the virgin. On the same day, Saint Enodius the bishop and confessor. On the same day, the dedication of Saint Mary at Aachen. On the same day, Fredegundus the confessor.”

Then, in smaller type:

“He came from Ireland with Saint Fursey and rests in the monastery of the Ladies on the River Sambre, not far from Namur. In England, Kenelm, etc.,” as far as GREVEN’s words “had the boy killed.”

Other editions, concerning the translation of the Scillitan martyrs and Alexius, have the material given above. Then:

“At Pavia, Saint Enodius the bishop and confessor. At Milan, the burial of Saint Marcellina the virgin. In England, Saint Kenelm, the boy, king of the Mercians, and [Col. 0271A] martyr. At the monastery of Argenton, on the same day, Saint Fredegundus the confessor.”

Castellanus places him in his Universal Martyrology at Dorne, or rather Deurne, near Antwerp.]

[Col. 0267]

At Carthage, the feast of the holy martyrs of Scillium, namely Speratus, Natalis, Cithinus, Berturius, Felix, Aquilinus, Letatius, Januaria, Generosa, Bessia, Donata, and Secundina, under Saturninus the prefect. After their first confession they were sent to prison and affixed to wood; afterward they were beheaded with the sword.

XV Kal. Day 18.

[Note: [Col. 0271]

Only Pulsanen. and Molanus are pure throughout.]

[Note: [Col. 0271A]

I read Gundenes with the Short Roman Martyrology, Ado, and our manuscripts of better quality. In Antuerp.-Major, Guildene is incorrectly written. Rosweyd. gives Gundenes; Munerat. gives Gaudenes. The Short Roman Martyrology adorned her with two garlands, calling her both virgin and martyr. Ado wrote “virgin,” and Molanus also printed it. Pulsanen., however, together with the other [Col. 0272A] manuscripts, gives her only the title “martyr,” perhaps because Usuard had doubted the crown of virginity. Molanus alone correctly wrote Aemilius, in my opinion by his own correction, since all the other manuscripts simply read as the text has it.]

[Note: [Col. 0271B]

On this day the Short Roman Martyrology supplied Ado and his followers with the following material: “At Carthage, Saint Guddena the virgin and martyr,” who is known neither to Jerome today nor to Bede. Ado gives both the time of her martyrdom and the manner of her death, from which Our Author adopted only the final part.

Everything concerning this announcement is quite straightforward, unless one should think, with Tillemont, volume III, page 125, that Gaudentus or Gaudentius of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, marked in Africa on 26 June, can be understood as this Guddena, or Gudenne, or Gudente. In support of this one might cite Augustine’s sermon 294 in the new edition, delivered on 27 June at the feast of the martyr Gaudentius, of whom Ruinart also makes mention among his selections, page 197.

It is entirely plausible, however, that what the same Tillemont conjectures at the cited place is correct: that some genuine Acts once existed, from which Ado derived his encomium, distinguished so explicitly by the consular dates. Would that they might someday be brought to light!

Emilianus, or rather Aemilianus, can appear to have been taken only from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, detached from several companions; elsewhere we have shown sufficiently and more than sufficiently that Usuard was accustomed to do this. Let the annotations of Baronius be consulted, together with what Tillemont collected from ancient sources concerning the distinguished martyr, volume VII, pages 354–355.

Thus far, at least, nearly all our manuscripts agree; hence Usuard’s reading, as transmitted by us, is rendered certain.

It must now be observed that on this day Ado, Rabanus, and Notker mark Arnulf of Metz as bishop. Rabanus gives him a long encomium, Ado a short one; Usuard deferred him to 16 August, reproducing there Ado’s very words. It is therefore certain that all manuscripts that treat Arnulf of Metz today are in this respect in no way Usuardian. We shall give the words of each in the appendices.

It is less easy to determine whether Usuard did not enter in his martyrology Arnulf the bishop and martyr, whom the manuscripts of Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Major, Munerat., and Greven., otherwise of excellent quality, expressly mention. These manuscripts would indeed prevail, unless there were reasons compelling us to reject them: namely, that we judge this Arnulf to have been neither properly a martyr nor in any way a bishop, and that he was not entered by Usuard himself but added by others.

To begin with the Pratensis, the illustrious Castellanus warned me in the frequently cited letter that the announcement “in the district of Castrensis, Saint Arnulf the martyr and bishop” does not belong to the original text at all, since it is plainly sewn into that manuscript in a later hand. What the Herinien. has concerning the episcopate of Tours—as I shall report among the appendices—is commonly regarded as fictitious; moreover, it alone speaks from its own understanding, adding to the Usuardian text, unless I am mistaken, something proper to the province of Reims. The others either use a different phrasing, from which it is completely clear that the matter is an addition, or they took their material from the Pratensis or some manuscript of that kind, and therefore do not offer anything purer than their source.

Furthermore, our other manuscripts agree excellently with Pulsanen. and Molanus, and would be pure, except where they exceed them concerning Arnulf of Metz or something else. Baronius long ago noted on this day—when he inserted Arnulf of Metz into the Roman Martyrology—that Usuard placed him, as we have said, on 16 August. He noted, I say, that some confusion occurs among the Arnulfs; and it is surprising that this could have happened between Arnulf of Metz and Arnulf of Soissons, separated by so many centuries.

It is more likely that modern writers have confused, and continue to confuse, Arnulf of Aquila or Avellino, whom we are discussing here, with another Arnulf of Mousson, or one translated to Mousson. Their Acts, which circulate in varied and sufficiently remarkable forms, may perhaps easily have been mixed together, one being attributed to the other. There is no time here to distinguish the matter: we are touching knots to be untied in a larger work.

For the present, the question may be asked which Arnulf Bede intended when he wrote on this day: “The feast of Saint Arnulf the confessor.” Florus adds there: “Whose life was of the greatest holiness.” It does not seem probable that Arnulf of Metz is meant, since Bede could hardly have been unaware of that man’s dignity. I do not deny, however, that Bede sometimes honors bishops with the title “confessor” alone, as can be seen on 28 May in the case of Saint Germanus, on 8 June in the case of Saint Medardus, and elsewhere.

You may argue that being called simply “confessor” fits our Arnulf of Aquila no better. Yet whatever Bede and Florus assert here may certainly be predicated of him once the titles “martyr” and “bishop” have been removed; whether these titles rightly belong to him is at least uncertain.

Unless one prefers to distinguish the Arnulfs in this way: that our Arnulf of Castrensis or Aquila, killed by robbers, should be regarded as a martyr, while another or others enjoy only the title “confessor.” From this may have arisen the great multiplication of sacred relics under the same name, a multiplication that could also have been increased by different locations or place-names. But these matters must again be reserved for the Acts.]

The famous seven brothers of Tibur could also seem relevant here. On this day they are marked by the Hieronymian Martyrologies and by Notker under entirely different names, whereas we have recorded them on 22 June. Since, however, they have nothing to do with Usuard at this point, it would be pointless to linger here over reconciling them; especially since we consider that enough and more than enough has been said about that controversy on the date mentioned, and we shall say more in the Acts. See the verses of Wandalbertus cited above in Molanus. The remaining matters concerning these martyrs will be found in the Appendices.]

[Note: [Col. 0273A]

PRATEN. We have already given the words. Note that it has Castrinse instead of Castrensis, and, contrary to custom, “martyr and bishop.”

HERINIEN. uses an entirely different phrasing: “On the same day, in the forest called Equilina, the feast of Blessed Arnulf, bishop and martyr of Tours, who is known to have been a contemporary and disciple of Blessed Remigius.” That forest, called Aquilina, is named Yveline in French. See Castellanus.

TORNACEN. begins: “Bruno [elsewhere Bruni], bishop and confessor. In the district of Castrensis, Saint Arnulf the bishop and martyr.” The first announcement follows; the second, concerning Aemilianus, is lacking.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. adds to the pure text: “On the same day, Saint Ernulf the martyr.” Note the different manner of expression from that of the others.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. and UGHELLIAN., at the end after the pure text: “At the city of Metz, Saint Arnulf the bishop, who, illustrious for holiness and the grace of miracles, loving the eremitical life, rested in a blessed death.” These words, taken from Ado, are found on 16 August.

MUNERAT. also has the following at the end, but with a different phrasing: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Arnulf the bishop and martyr.” See the observations above.

GREVEN. comes closest to the PRATENSIS: “In the district of Castrensis, Saint Arnulf the bishop and martyr.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN. report the pure text, to which they append: “At the city of Metz, Saint Arnulf the bishop, who in holiness,” etc., as above from Ado. At the end: “On the same day, Saint Frederick, bishop and martyr of Utrecht.”

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. place first: “At Tibur in Italy, the feast of Saint Symphorosa with her seven sons,” etc., as may be seen on 27 June. The text follows, and at the end the material concerning Arnulf, bishop of Metz, as above.

CENTULEN.: “In France, at the castle of Crespy, the feast [Col. 0273C] of Blessed Arnulf, bishop of the see of Tours, whom they report to have been a disciple of Blessed Remigius, bishop of Reims; returning from him, he was killed by the impious.” See the Castellanus cited above. “On the same day, the octave of Saint Benedict the father and abbot.”

BRUXELLEN. anticipates at the beginning the feast of Justa and Rufina; see the following day concerning them. The material about Guddena and Aemilianus follows, quite purely. Then:

“Near the Aquiline forest, Saint Arnulf the bishop and martyr. At Lower Utrecht, the feast of Saint Frederick the bishop and martyr, who was killed for the justice of divine law by order of the empress—or rather by the incestuous inhabitants of Walcheren—and was renowned for many miracles. At Reims, the translation of Saint Nicasius the bishop and martyr.”

HAGENOYEN. brings here the prophet Ezra, whom we treated above on 13 July, and assigns him an encomium composed, as is customary, from the sacred Scriptures. The entire text follows. Then:

“In the city of Metz, the burial of Saint [Col. 0273D] Arnulf, bishop of that city,” with a longer encomium, which I would prefer to read in the Acts themselves. Then:

“In the district of Castrensis, Saint Arnulf the bishop and martyr. At Utrecht, Saint Frederick the bishop and confessor.” I do not know why he is not likewise called a martyr here.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end: “At the castle of Crespy, Saint Arnulf the archbishop and martyr.” I think this is the same Arnulf as the one mentioned by CENTUL. The entry continues: “The octave of Saint Benedict the abbot.”

VICTORIN.: “In the city of Metz, Saint Arnulf the bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Severinus the confessor. The octave of Saint Benedict the abbot.”

DAVERONEN.: “In the district of Castrensis, called the Aquiline Forest, the feast of Blessed Arnulf the bishop and martyr, together with his wife Scariberga.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Frederick, bishop of Utrecht and martyr. He rests at Saint Saviour’s. [Col. 0274A] Arnulf, bishop of Tours and martyr. Guddena, who endured many things.”

CODEX BIGOTIAN. III, under note D, 9: “Also Saint Clarus the martyr.” These words were added by another hand. He is honored today at Paris, but elsewhere on his proper feast, 4 November.

REG. SUEC., sign. no. 130: “On this very day, Saint Veterinus the confessor.”

In VATICAN., no. 5949, Aemilianus is lacking. Symphorosa with her seven sons is added. “Also Saint Arnulf of Metz,” as above.

FLORENTIN.: “In Tuscany, Saint Raphilus, archbishop of Ravenna. Blessed Robert the confessor of Salle, of the order of the Celestines.”

CODEX MONTIS SANCTI: “The translation of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, who was distinguished for holiness of life and the grace of miracles,” etc.

THE LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “At Hoya, in the territory of Liège, the translation of Saint Odilia the virgin and martyr [Col. 0274B] from the city of Cologne, from that noble company of eleven thousand virgins. At the city of Tibur in Italy, Saint Symphorosa,” etc. The account of Guddena follows, purely. Then:

“Near the Aquiline Forest, Saint Arnulf, bishop of Tours and martyr. At Metz, Saint Arnulf the bishop and confessor, who, in holiness,” etc. “At Dorostorum, Saint Emilianus the confessor. At Lower Utrecht, the passion of Blessed Frederick the bishop and martyr. In the territory of Jülich, in the village of Arnswilre, the feast of Blessed Arnold, harpist of Charlemagne and confessor. On the same day, Saint Eadburga the virgin.”

BELIN. begins with Symphorosa, etc. Then Arnulf of Metz. After that Aemilianus. Then:

“On the same day, Saint Aquilinus the bishop. On the same day, Saint Maternus the bishop and confessor. At Carthage, Saint Gaudenis the martyr.”

GREVEN.:

“Eugenius II, pope and martyr, who was blinded and killed by the Roman laymen and buried at Saint Peter’s. At Lower Utrecht, Saint Frederick [Col. 0274C] the bishop and martyr, who, when he reproved the unlawful marriage of the emperor Louis with zeal for justice, encountered another Herodias and was crowned with martyrdom.” See what we said concerning BRUXELLEN.

“Answerrus the martyr and his companions. Clarus the martyr. Aquilinus the bishop. Maternus the bishop and confessor. At Metz, the translation of Saint Arnulf the bishop and confessor. In the territory of Jülich, in the district of Arnswilre, the feast of Blessed Arnold, Charlemagne’s harpist and confessor, a man of great compassion toward the poor. According to some, this is Symphorosa with her sons, concerning whom see above, 5 Kal. July. At Hoya, in the territory of Liège, the translation of Saint Odilia the virgin and martyr, from the company of the eleven thousand virgins. On the same day, Saint Eadburga the virgin.”

MOLAN.:

“At the city of Tibur in Italy, etc. At the city of Metz, etc. On the same day, Saint Aquilinus the bishop. At Milan, Saint Maternus the bishop and confessor.”

Then, from Ado or from the appendix to Ado in Rosweyd:

“At Brescia, the burial of Saint Philastrius, bishop of that city. Having been ordained a presbyter, he was moved by love of God, abandoned everything, and traveled through almost the entire world, following in the footsteps of the apostle Paul, so that in every place he might free by his preaching from eternal destruction souls deceived by the devil’s fraud. Therefore he fought with the strength of faith not only against pagans and Jews but also against nearly all heresies, and especially against the Arian perfidy, which at that time was exceedingly powerful. For this reason he was chastised with blows and bore the marks of our Lord Jesus Christ on his body.

“In the city of Milan also he was an able guardian of the Lord’s flock, and, supported by divine grace, he resisted Auxentius, the bishop of Arian perfidy, before Blessed Ambrose was chosen. At Rome too he stayed for a considerable time and won many to the faith by public and private disputation. Since he attacked heretics with great force, he wished to compose a book concerning each of their sects and their most wicked doctrines, so that, once the error of each heresy had been exposed, no one, however simple, established in the Church, could be ensnared by them. Concerning him Blessed Augustine said: ‘Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, in the very extensive book that he composed concerning heresies, judged that 128 heresies should be counted.’

“Also at Utrecht, Frederick, bishop of that place and martyr, who, though innocent, was killed by the guilty for the sake of truth before the holy altar of God, after the celebration of Mass; he was buried in the same place. In the district of Castrensis, Saint Arnulf, bishop and martyr of Tours.”

Then, in smaller type, the account of Arnold the harpist, as in GREVEN.

“On the same day, the feast of Blessed Theodoric, bishop of Metz, cousin of Otto [Col. 0276A] I. In Normandy, Saint Clarus the monk and martyr, concerning whose passion there is a sermon by Nicholas of Nise.”

This is what the first edition has. Other editions prefix to the text: “At Tibur,” etc. At the end, concerning Aemilianus, they add “martyr,” and “Saint Hyacinthus the martyr at Anastride.” Concerning Arnulf of Metz, as above. “On the same day, Saint Maternus the bishop and confessor at Milan.” Concerning Arnulf of Castrensis, it has almost the same account as HERINIEN. Concerning Frederick of Utrecht, as in the earlier edition. “At Brescia, the burial of Saint Philastrius, bishop of that city, who fought with the strength of faith against nearly all heresies, and especially against the Arian perfidy, which at that time was exceedingly powerful; for this reason he was chastised with blows and bore the marks of our Lord Jesus Christ on his body.” Concerning Odilia of Huy, Arnold the harpist, Theodoric the bishop of Metz, and Clarus, as above.]

[Col. 0271]

At Carthage, Saint Guddena the martyr, who, by order of Rufinus the proconsul, because of her confession of Christ, was tortured four times at different periods by stretching on the rack and tormented by the dreadful tearing of hooks; she was also afflicted for a very long time by the squalor of prison, and finally killed with the sword. At the city of Dorostorum, Saint Emilianus.

[Bouillart adds, in italics: In the district of Castrensis, the burial of Saint Arnulf, martyr and bishop.]

XIV Kal. Day 19.

[Note: [Col. 0275B]

The following agree: Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Major, Antuerp.-Max., Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and [Col. 0276B] Molan. They are joined by Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Albergen, and Danicus.]

[Note: [Col. 0275B]

Pulsanen., Greven., and Molan. correctly give Epaphrae. In the text I follow all the others. Some have Colosis; Herinien. has Colosensis, better than the others, as we wrote it. Munerat. added the title “martyr.” The forms Beati Paulo (“by Blessed Paul”), Thebaidam (“the Thebaid”), servorum (“of servants”) for seniorum (“of the elders”), lacrimarum and lachrimarum (both “of tears”), exalavit (“breathed out”), etc., can easily be corrected.

Belin. and Molan., together with the manuscripts of the intermediate class, omit patris nostri (“our father”) after sancti (“Saint”). For redundationem (“abundance” or “overflow”) they have, with Greven., redundantiam, or, as Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., redundanciam; the more authoritative manuscripts follow Ado, and so do we in the text.

Belin. and five recent manuscripts depart from Bede’s and Ado’s phrasing by reading habuit (“he kept”) instead of habuerit (“he may have kept”). Greven. and Molan. are occasionally distinctive, as has often been clear above: here alone they substitute Hispaniis (“in the Spains”) for Hispania (“in Spain”).

They also add, after “in prison”: “afflicted by hunger and tortures.” Finally: “Rufina’s neck was broken in the confession of the Lord.” These readings are peculiar to Greven. and Molan., the latter having copied them here from the former.

Otherwise, all the manuscripts unanimously read In Hispania; in the second matter they vary somewhat. Herinien. reads: “after prison, afflicted by hunger and pains”; Antuerp.-Major: “after imprisonment, etc.” The greater number, together with Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., have: “after imprisonment, afflicted by hunger and various pains.”

The phrasing closer to Ado, however, is that taken into the text from Pratensis and Munerat. Finally, Herinien. has: “the neck was broken in the confession of the Lord”; Antuerp.-Major: “the neck was broken in confession.” All are good Latin syntactically, but when Usuard’s manner of expression is at issue, the form closest to Ado seems preferable: that found in Praten., Munerat., Belin., Antuerp., and Max.-Lubec., together with the others whom we preferred to place before the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0275C]

The agreement of our manuscripts on this day is as great as the clarity with which the whole text has been transferred from Ado.
