According to Florentinius, the Hieronymian Martyrologies contain nothing relevant here, although there is no serious obstacle to taking the Hispanian Justus recorded there as Justa, especially since the Corbeian manuscript expressly writes Justa.

As for Florentinius’s belief that Notker settles the matter, I cannot regard it as sufficiently proven unless, with that same author, he supposes that two Justuses are to be listed in Spain on this very day—a supposition whose probability you will understand in its proper place.

Meanwhile the Short Roman Martyrology gives today simply: “At Seville, Saints Justa and Rufina.” Bede names Arsenius, and after him Rabanus, in exactly the same terms used by Ado. Here, then, is the genesis of the little entries.

The encomium of Epaphra was copied word for word by Our Author from the Feasts of the Apostles. It is clear that the greater part was taken from Paul’s letters. But where Ado learned that Epaphra received the palm of martyrdom at Colossae in manly combat, I confess that I have not yet discovered; nor did Tillemont find it, volume I, in the Life of Paul, article 44, beginning on page 292. But these matters belong elsewhere.

I have already said that the account of Arsenius is common to Bede and Ado, and was also transcribed by Usuard. Arsenius could have been adorned with a fuller encomium from the very source touched upon by the Viennese manuscript. But these matters are left to us to develop more fully in the Acts, from the Lives of the Fathers and other writers more reliable than Metaphrastes, whose various narratives Tillemont arranged in order in volume XIV, beginning on page 676.

Wandalbertus composed a metrical encomium only for Arsenius:

“Arsenius adorns the fourteenth day with the beauty of the hermit.”

Finally, the praise of Justa and Rufina, although somewhat abridged here and there, is entirely composed from Ado’s words. It was undoubtedly drawn from older Acts, from which Maldonatus seems to have extracted the choicest marrow, as you may see in Surius on this day.

It is surprising that Notker, so faithful an imitator of Ado, omitted Epaphra and substituted others in his place, persons not sufficiently known everywhere—not even in the Hieronymian manuscripts, however greatly expanded. But we need not labor greatly over this, since from what has been said above the text’s origin is revealed simply and clearly as entirely certain.]

[Note: [Col. 0277A]

TORNACEN. begins: “At the Thebaid,” etc.; then the account of Epaphra, with the encomium removed in both places. The rest is pure.

ROSWEYD. is enlarged at the end with these words: “At Lyon, Rusticus the presbyter.”

PULSANEN. is pure in the accounts of Epaphra and Arsenius, but is silent concerning the last two, Justa and Rufina.

LOVANIEN. is pure in the first two, but cuts out the encomium of Justa and Rufina.

CENTULEN. is fairly pure at first and continues as follows:

“On the same day, our holy father Arsenius, in life and conduct wholly worthy of Christ the Lord. In Spain, at the city of Seville, Saints Justa and Rufina, who were seized by Diogenianus the governor and torn apart under severe torture.”

BRUXELLEN. again anticipates material:

“In Judea, the feast of Blessed Joseph, who was called Justus and was chosen together with Blessed Matthias by apostolic lot; while serving the office of preaching and enduring much persecution for the faith [Col. 0277B] of Christ, he is said to have drunk poison, from which he suffered no harm, but rested in peace with a victorious end.

“At Colossae, the feast of Saint Epaphras, who was ordained bishop of the Colossians by Blessed Paul. Distinguished for his virtues, he received the martyr’s palm there, in manly combat, for the sheep entrusted to him.

“At Tibur in Italy, the feast of Saint Symphorosa with her seven sons. She was hung by her hair and afterward, tied to a stone, thrown into a river. Then all her sons were martyred through various tortures.”

These accounts also are not appropriately assigned to this day. It continues:

“At the Thebaid, our holy father Archenius, who from a distinguished senator became a monk in the desert. Concerning him it is reported in the Sayings of the Elders that, because of …,” etc.

At the end: “At Lower Utrecht, the burial of Saint Barnulfus, bishop and confessor.” In GREVEN. he is called “Bernoldus.”

HAGENOYEN. is fairly pure at first. Then:

“At the Thebaid, the burial of our holy father Arsenius, brother of Saint Euphemianus, father of Saint Alexius. [Col. 0277C] When he was in the world, he was at least clothed in imperial garments, was exceedingly refined, and was very dear to the emperor Theodosius, so much so that he lifted his two sons from the sacred font. After his conversion he was extremely abstemious and wore the most wretched clothing. Therefore, like the prophet Daniel, he shone with the spirit of prophecy. Concerning him it is reported in the Sayings of the Elders that, because of …,” etc.

The account of Justa and Rufina is fairly pure.]

[Col. 0278A] AQUICINCT. adds at the end a local entry of its own:

“At Aquicinctum, the translation of Saint Sambaria the virgin and martyr.”

But these words are from a later hand, as is noted in the copy.

VICTORIN. and REG. OF SWEDEN, under note no. 130: “At Milan, the discovery of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.” See Usuard on 19 June concerning them, and the Acts for that day, where they are treated more fully.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Justa and Rufina. Arsenius the confessor and solitary, formerly a senator at Rome. Epaphra, bishop of Colossae, disciple of Blessed Paul the apostle.”

In VATICAN., no. 5949, Arsenius is lacking. The following is added: “The Assumption of Saint Elijah the prophet.”

FLORENTIN.: “At Spoleto, the passion of the holy martyrs Eutychus, Britius, John, Theudilius, Isaac, Laurence, Herculanus, and Parietalis. The tyrant Martianus ordered their heads to be cut off and their unburied bodies to be abandoned. But a certain noble widow buried them on her estate in the Pontian cemetery, [Col. 0278B] not far from the aforementioned city, as is recorded in the Acts of Saint Proculus [the printed edition has Paul], bishop and martyr. Their names are as follows: Eutychius … Theudila … At Trier, Saint Severa the virgin.”

THE LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “At Colossae, Saint Epaphra, bishop and martyr, who was ordained by Blessed Paul,” etc. The remainder of the entire text is fairly pure. At the end it adds: “At Trier, Blessed Martin, bishop and martyr. At Constantinople, Saint Daria the virgin. At Lyon in Gaul, the burial of Blessed Rusticus the bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN.: “At Trier, Blessed Martin, the first bishop of that city and martyr. Symmachus the pope. At Lyon in Gaul, Saint Rusticus the bishop and confessor. Also Saint Justus. At Constantinople, Saint Daria the virgin. Also Blessed Bernoldus, bishop and confessor of Lower Utrecht, remembered with honor.”

MOLAN. in the first edition has no appendices. In later editions he adds these few items:

“At Trier, Blessed Martin, the tenth bishop of that city and martyr. [Col. 0278C] On the same day, Symmachus the pope. On the nineteenth day, Saint Father Dei and Saint Macrina, sister of Basil the Great.”

It should be noted that in the text of these editions, after “Justa and Rufina, who,” the following words are inserted in italics: “selling earthen vessels,” with a marginal citation to the office of the saints of Spain, Maldonatus, and Surius; from these sources the words were evidently taken. In the earlier edition, reading 2 of the Burgundian church is marked.]

[Col. 0275]

The feast of Saint Epaphra, who was ordained bishop at Colossae by Blessed Paul. Distinguished for his virtues, he there received the palm of martyrdom in manly combat for the sheep entrusted to him.

At the Thebaid, our holy father Arsenius, concerning whom it is reported in the Sayings of the Elders that, because of the abundance of tears that had to be wiped away, he always kept a handkerchief in his bosom or in his hand.

In Spain, at the city of Seville, the passion of Saints Justa and Rufina, who were seized by the governor Diogenianus and first tortured by stretching on the rack and tearing with hooks; afterward they were afflicted in prison by hunger and pains. Finally Justa breathed out her spirit in prison, while Rufina’s neck was broken in confession.

XIII Kal. Day 20.

[Note: [Col. 0277]

We consider Herinien., Max.-Lubec., Antuerp.-Max., and Lovanien. pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0279A]

Some read “serving in the office of preaching and holiness”; the construction of our text is better, where *inserviens* agrees with Ado, not *serviens*, as others have it. In all the Damascene manuscripts the order here is Sabinus, Maximus, Julianus, etc. Only Greven and Molanus transpose them as follows: [Col. 0280A] Julianus, Sabinus, Maximus—undoubtedly because of the diversity among the Hieronymian manuscripts; concerning this, see Florentinius. Herinianus wrote *Macrabii* instead of *Macrobii*, wrongly, as did others write *Pauli* for *Paulae*, and so forth. The remaining matters are dealt with in the immediately following observation.]

[Note: [Col. 0279A]]

There is absolutely no difficulty concerning the first and second announcements of our text. Joseph, first inserted by the author of the Little Roman Martyrology into the sacred Calendars, is there celebrated thus: “Joseph, who was called Justus, who suffered many things from the Jews for Christ and, victorious, rested in Judaea.” Ado expanded the eulogy, which was copied by Notker. Our author, as he usually does whenever the texts of Ado are somewhat more expansive, elegantly compressed the principal points. I believe that what is said about his having drunk poison without harm was taken from Rufinus’s translation of Eusebius, Book III, chapter 28. The rest must be gathered from the Acts or from the tradition of the Fathers, as Tillemont did in various places in Volume I, especially on page 119; these matters will be discussed more carefully in our Acts. The Damascene martyrs, as they are listed here, were taken by Ado from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, and from him passed into our Martyrology and that of Notker. Florentinius discusses a certain discrepancy between the very ancient Echternach manuscript and the other Hieronymian [Col. 0279B] manuscripts; the curious reader should consult him.

Thus far, at least, Usuard’s text is consistent with itself, on the agreement of all the manuscripts: the poison or difficulty lies at the end. To proceed clearly and in order, I shall first quote the words of the Pratensis manuscript. After the two commemorations mentioned above, it adds: “In the district of Bologna, Saint Ulmarus the confessor.” It then appends our copy: “On the same day, Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr”—yet, from the subordinate marking, I can easily understand that these words were transferred from the margin into the text. This was later confirmed by the distinguished Castellanus, who inspected the manuscript himself and asserted that a more recent hand had written there, not “Margaret,” but the following: “On the same day, Saint Marina, virgin and martyr.” We began to discuss when and by what means that Marina could have been confused with Margaret under June 18; but, to speak frankly, this is a matter for a more elaborate inquiry than can be undertaken here.

For the present, it is enough to have shown that this announcement, unknown to the ancient Martyrologists, is plainly an addition in the Usuardine manuscripts, and [Col. 0279C] that all the manuscripts adopting it are so far from the purity of the text—namely, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, Munerat, Greven, and others. The knot concerning Vulmarus remains, although we have now almost entirely cut him out under June 17. Here we need only add Castellanus’s observation, which he wrote to me in French: “The 20th [of July] ends with an erasure, over which is rewritten in a very ancient hand: ‘In the district of Bologna,’ etc.” This means that the announcement previously placed there had been erased and that the one now appearing had been written over it in a very ancient hand. It must be remembered that under June 17 Vulmarus was crossed out in the same manuscript and Gundulfus of Bourges substituted for him—as we have shown elsewhere to have been done more than once in similar cases. Thus we shall plainly discover that the corrector, whoever he was, removed Paul of Córdoba on this day in order to transfer Vulmarus there; because of the lack of space, he could not express him in Ado’s wording, just as the other manuscripts agreeing in that announcement do not conform to it either.

From this you may infer that Paul’s announcement ought to be restored to its proper place; for this reason we have placed it in the text as it is explicitly marked by the four manuscripts cited above, and in addition by Tournai, Antwerp, Munerat, Greven, Utrecht, and other manuscripts and excerpts. Molanus, who had correctly treated Vulmarus under June 17 in his first edition, rightly omitted him on this day; but why he neglected Paul I do not sufficiently understand, much less why in other editions he placed both: one would think he had forgotten himself, unless in a note he indicated some unknown reason for this duplication. Having weighed everything, we therefore have no doubt that Paul, magnificently celebrated by Saint Eulogius in Book II of the *Memorial*, chapter 6, together with several other martyrs of Córdoba whom Usuard had gathered in Spain, was brought from there into France and entered on this day, the actual day of his martyrdom—not Vulmarus. We may therefore regard the original and genuine simplicity of Usuard as vindicated.]

[Note: [Col. 0279C]]

We have already spoken of the Pratensis manuscript. In its additions it is, as usual, similar to ANTWERP-MAJOR.

TOURNAY begins: “Margaret, virgin.” In Joseph’s eulogy it is mutilated at “about whom it is related,” etc. The rest is pure.

ROSWEYD has at the end only: “In the district of Bologna, Saint Wulmarus, abbot and confessor.” I prefer to write *Vulmarus* with the others.

ANTWERP and UGHELLI have the following concerning Margaret: “At Antioch, the passion of blessed Margaret, virgin and martyr.”

MUNERAT appends to the pure text: “On the same day, Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr.”

BELIN also has the pure text, but adds: “At Antioch, the passion of blessed Margaret, virgin and martyr. Also on the same day, the Octave of Saint Bonaventure, bishop and confessor, of the Order of Friars Minor.” Similar feasts are often noted here.

GREVEN alone, after the pure text, adds within the text itself [Col. 0279D]: “On that day, Saint Arnulfus the confessor,” without any identifying designation by which he could be recognized. Then: “On the same day, Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr.” See the Observation above.

MOLANUS is defective, as stated above, in the announcement of Paul, martyr of Córdoba.

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC add to the pure text: “At Trier, Saint Severa, virgin, sister of Saint Monwaldus, bishop of the same place.” [Col. 0280C] See below under BRUSSELS, etc.

CENTULE: “The birthday of blessed Joseph, who was called Justus, who was worthy to bury the Lord’s body in his own tomb.” The confusion is sufficiently clear. In the Damascene section the text is pure, except that it writes *Maximinus* for *Maximus*: “In Thebaid, Saint Victor. At Córdoba, Saint Paul, deacon and martyr. In the district of Bologna, Saint Vulmarus, abbot.” In the margin, however, a wholly new hand has added: “At Antioch, the passion of Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr.”

BRUSSELS speaks of blessed Joseph on the preceding day. Moreover, after the Damascene martyrs and Paul it has, in a pure form: “In the district of Bologna, the deposition of Saint Vulmarus, priest and confessor. At Trier, Saint Severa, virgin, sister of Saint Modoaldus, bishop of the same place. At Antioch, blessed Margaret, virgin and martyr.”

[Col. 0280D] HAGENOYEN begins as follows: “In Judaea, the deposition of blessed Joseph, who was called Justus. He was the son of Alphaeus and Mary of Clopas, who was the sister of blessed Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the brother of James the Less, Simon, and Judas the apostles. He was one of the seventy-two disciples of the Lord; and after the Lord’s ascension, he cast lots with Matthias for the apostolate, by election of the apostles. He was present at the Lord’s great mysteries and received the Holy Spirit with the apostles. Later, serving in the office of preaching and holiness,” etc., purely. In the Damascene section and under Paul it agrees with the text, and at the end adds: “At Trier, the deposition of Severa, virgin, sister of Modoaldus, bishop of that city.”

AQUICINCT has *Bassi, Pauli* instead of *Cassi, Paule*. “At the city of Córdoba” is absent, etc. But at the end: “On the same day, Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr. In the district of Bologna, the deposition of Saint Vulmarus, abbot.” The same feature recurs here several times.

VICTORINUS: “At Antioch, Saint Margaret, virgin.” See below the eulogy in MOLANUS.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-UTRECHT: “Margaret, virgin and martyr. Joseph who was called Justus. The holy martyrs Sabinus, Maximus, Julianus, with the others. Bernoldus, bishop of Utrecht, who rests at Saint Peter’s.”

CLUNIAC, CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked C, and CAUDIAC add: “On that day, at the monastery of Cluny, the glorious reception of the relics of blessed Pope Gregory.”

In the VATICAN manuscript Paul is absent. Added: “At Cassino, the birthday of Saint Severus, bishop.”

ALTEMPS: “At Cluny, the reception of the relics of blessed Pope Gregory.”

LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION begins: “Elijah was taken up into heaven in a chariot of fire, while Elisha stood by and watched.” What follows concerning Joseph and the Damascene martyrs is sufficiently pure. Then: “In Thebaid, Saint Victor the confessor. At the city of Córdoba,” etc. “In the district of Bologna, the deposition of Saint Wulmarus, abbot, priest, and confessor. At Trier, Saint Severa, virgin, sister of Saint Monwaldus, bishop and confessor of the same place. She rests in the church of Saint Eucharius.” Elsewhere *Modoaldus* is read more correctly.

[Col. 0282A] GREVEN: “In Thebaid, Saint Victor the confessor. Magnus the priest and Amorinus. In the district of Bologna, Saint Vulmarus, abbot, priest, and confessor. Also Placeria. In Tuscany, Saint Ambrose, priest and confessor, of the Order of Preachers, of holy memory. Also Saint Wilgefortis, virgin and martyr, daughter of the king of Portugal. Severa, virgin, sister of Saint Modoaldus, bishop of Trier.” See Baronius’s note.

MOLANUS: “At Antioch, the passion of blessed Margaret, virgin and martyr. At Trier, Saint Severa, virgin, sister of Saint Modoaldus, bishop of the same place. On the same day, in the district of Bologna in Gaul, at the monastery of Silmacum, the deposition of Saint Vulmarus, abbot.” Later, in smaller type: “Also Saint Wilgefortis, virgin and martyr, daughter of the king of Portugal, whom some call in Latin *Liberata*, but in German *Ontcommera*.” Other editions, after the complete pure text, append: “At Antioch, the passion of blessed Margaret, virgin and martyr. She [Col. 0282B] suffered many torments for the name of Christ under the prefect Olybrius: bonds, prisons, scourges, and the rack. The devil also tempted her in the form of a dragon and likewise in that of an Ethiopian, but he was overcome by the sign of the holy Cross. Finally, having been beheaded by the aforesaid prefect, she ended her life in holy martyrdom.” Concerning her, see elsewhere, for example under July 13, etc.

In these editions the following is then included as though it were part of Usuard’s text: “On the same day, in the district of Bologna in Gaul, Saint Vulmarus the confessor, a man of admirable holiness. At Trier, Saint Severa, virgin, sister of Saint Modoaldus, bishop of the same place. In Portugal, the birthday of Saint Wilgefortis, virgin and martyr, who, for love of chastity and the Christian faith, passed happily to the Lord while dying on the cross.” The name is not Portuguese.]

[Col. 0277]

The birthday of blessed Joseph, who was called Justus. Serving in the office of preaching and holiness, and enduring much persecution from the Jews for the faith of Christ, he rested in Judaea after a most victorious end. It is related of him that he drank poison and suffered nothing grievous from it, because of faith in the Lord. At Damascus, Saints Sabinus, Maximus, Julianus, Macrobius, Cassius, and Paula, with ten others. At the city of Córdoba, Saint Paul, deacon and martyr. [Bouillart: . . . . . with ten others. [Note: [Col. 0277D] After the Damascene martyrs, the Carolingian autograph has: “At the city of Córdoba, Saint Paul, deacon and martyr. On the same day, Saint Margaret, virgin.” Neither of these two commemorations is ever found written by Usuard. Only a single line was scraped away with a knife; that space could never have contained both Paul and Margaret. Why, then, do all the manuscripts except the Pratensis mention both? Perhaps Usuard dictated Margaret from memory; perhaps she was added shortly after Usuard. The knot cannot be untangled until the actual manuscript presented to King Charles emerges from some library. As for Saint Paul, it is difficult to say why Usuard erased him, for the saints of Spain seem to have been dear to him, and Paul would have occupied his proper place here—if, as Lord Eulogius the martyr testifies, he died on July 20, Monday, in the year 851. As far as conjecture can reach, when two saints fell on the same day, one from a distant region and the other nearby, Usuard preferred the latter to the former. You will find the Life of Saint Vulmarus in Part I of the third century of the Benedictine Acts, p. 234.] In the district of Bologna, Saint Vulmarus the confessor. And in the margin: “On the same day, Saint [Mar]garita, virgin and martyr.”]

XII Kalends. Day 21. [Note: [Col. 0281]]

The text is taken from the Pratensis, Herinianus, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp and Lübeck-Major, Munerat, the first edition of Belin, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0281C]]

All correctly read *assiduously devoted to prayers and fasts*; I do not know why the word *erudita* was inserted in the Antwerp manuscript, producing the absurd construction “learned in prayers and fasts assiduously,” whereas the same word had already been properly placed in “learned in divine law,” etc. *In Christo quievit* is a transposition in Antwerp-Major, as Belin, Greven, and Molanus do elsewhere; they change *juxta suam sororem* (“beside her sister”) to *juxta sororem suam* (“beside her sister”). We have said elsewhere that *Prudentiana* is written for *Potentiana*, but here all the manuscripts agree with the text. Munerat and Belin have *Marsilia*. Again, where the text reads *et nec militare, nec idolis*, Belin writes *et non militare nec*. Antwerp-Major, moreover, omits *et* and badly forms what follows in this way: “First [Col. 0282C] when he was thrown into prison, there by,” etc. Belin again has *angelo* (“by an angel”) instead of *angelis* (“by angels”). The others have *poenis* (“punishments”) in the text, although nearly all the manuscripts lack diphthongs; here and in similar cases orthographic uniformity can scarcely be maintained. Belin, using different words, wrote “punished with various tortures.” The sense requires “finally crushed in a baker’s millstone,” but Antwerp and Lübeck-Major have *constrictus* (“bound”), and that edition and Belin omit *in*. Greven and Molanus again depart from the common reading: where all the others read “three soldiers suffered with him,” they omit *three*. *Longius*, for *Longinus*, is an error in Antwerp-Major. I pass over the lesser errors, both those arising from this and those found in other manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0281D]]

Bede treats the prophet Daniel today in second place, after Praxedes. The Little Roman Martyrology is followed by Ado, by our author and by the others, all in nearly the same terms. In due course it will be seen how highly one should value the account of Daniel and the three Babylonian boys that appears in Surius under this day—the entire commentary of Symeon Metaphrastes. Praxedes is also mentioned by the Little Roman Martyrology and by Bede, as I have already said. Rabanus, taking her from Bede, composed a eulogy quite different from Ado’s. Our author neatly compressed Ado’s somewhat longer text in his customary manner. It is unnecessary to repeat here from where the Viennese obtained the material for his narrative; see what was said on May 19 and June 20.

Victor of Marseille, the illustrious martyr, is noted in the Little Roman Martyrology only in these words: “At Marseille, Victor the martyr.” In the Hieronymian Martyrologies, however, he is accompanied by the same soldier-companions whom Ado also lists by name, adding the boy Deutherius, who breathed his last while praying at the martyrs’ tomb. Notker followed the same traces, making all of Ado his own both in these martyrs and in Praxedes. Usuard, however, reducing the panegyric according to his customary method, commemorated only the soldiers and omitted the boy.

Nor are the things the Viennese relates about that boy as well established as the Acts of the most glorious Victor and the other three, which all learned men have praised highly and which were first published by C. V. Francis Bosquet; concerning him, see Ruinart’s preliminary notice in the *Selecta*, p. 299. Tillemont reviewed the same material in French in Volume IV, beginning on p. 549. The *Annals of Marseille* by P. Guesnay, p. 131, should also be consulted. We shall elucidate all these matters fully in the Acts.

Moreover, Usuard alone adds Julia of Troyes, unknown to or omitted by the ancient authorities, although she must plainly be regarded as Usuardine no less than the others, on the unanimous agreement of our manuscripts. The history of her passion was transferred from Camuzat, p. 381, into Surius, but the author of the Tricassine *Promptuarium* admits that it was inelegantly written. Others criticize it more severely; see the Tillemont cited above, in the same volume, p. 348. You will note that on this day Bede mentions Symphorosa with almost the same eulogy that Ado placed under June 27, an epitome of which we presented there in Usuard’s style. Rabanus, following the learned leader, added many other things. Since these do not belong to Usuard at all, it will be enough here to point out Bede’s divergence from the others, which some of our Usuardine manuscripts imitate.

An Oedipus is needed to understand what Wandalbert intended to suggest in his third verse. Unless he is alluding to the dedication of Saint Peter’s church, in which the body of Saint Wandregisil was deposited, as the Hieronymian Martyrologies mention. But then that verse would belong to the following day. Thus on this day he sang:

“The twelfth shines bright with the virgin Praxedes and the prophet Daniel, in name, end, and faith.

On this very day is the solemn dedication of holy Peter.”]

[Note: [Col. 0283B]]

ROSWEYD, between the Massilian martyrs and Julia of Troyes, places: “On the same day, Saint Arbogast, bishop and confessor of Strasbourg.” He meant Strasburg, instead of Argentinas or Argentoracum.

PULSAN is pure through Saint Victor inclusively, but everything else is absent.

ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN change the order of the announcements, placing Julia of Troyes before the Massilian martyrs. At the end they add: “On the same day, Saint Arbogast, bishop and confessor of Argentinas.” See what Baronius noted about him.

ALBERGEN and DANIC begin with Praxedes, followed by Daniel. The remainder is similar to the immediately preceding manuscripts. In DANIC, the following is added in the margin: “The Octave of Saint Bonaventure.”

CENTULE: “The death of Daniel the prophet. At Rome, Saint Praxedes, virgin, who was the sister of blessed Potentiana, virgin. At the city of Marseille, the passion of the most blessed martyr Victor, and with him Alexander, Felicianus, and Longinus, soldiers. At Troyes, Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, whose body rests in the church of blessed Mary at the monastery of Jordar.”

BRUSSELS begins: “At Rome, Saint Praxedes, virgin. Learned in all chastity and in divine law, she remained a virgin with her sister, blessed Potentiana, after the death of her father Pudens, and, assiduously devoted to fasts, vigils, and prayers, full of good works and almsgiving, she departed to Christ. Her body was buried on the Salarian Way beside her aforementioned sister. Also Daniel the prophet.” In the account of Victor it is pure up to “tormented with punishments,” after which it continues: “Finally he was thrown into a baker’s mill, in which an animal scattered around by the turning wheel is customarily crushed, and thus, having been ground to pieces, he completed his martyrdom under the prefect Asterius. And with him three soldiers suffered,” etc. The account of Julia is pure. At the end it adds: “At the city of Argentinas, Saint Arbogast, bishop and confessor of that place.” [Col. 0283D]

HAGENOYEN, according to his custom, has conflated the prophetic eulogy; there is no room to transcribe it here. In Praxedes he is somewhat interpolated, omits the Massilian martyrs and Julia of Troyes, and adds the following concerning Arbogast at the end: “At the city of Argentinas, the deposition of Saint Arbogast, bishop and confessor of the same city. Among his other miracles of virtue, he restored to life by his prayers the only son of Dagobert, king of France, after he had been torn apart and killed by wild beasts; for this reason the king granted the castle and town of Rubiacum to the church of Saint Mary at Argentinas. Arbogast himself lived many years, shone with numerous miracles, ended his life in peace, and had himself buried in the church of Saint Michael.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-UTRECHT: “Praxedes, virgin, sister of Saint Potentiana, who rest together at Rome. Daniel the prophet. In Gaul, at the city of Marseille, Victor the soldier and martyr, crushed in a baker’s mill. Also the three soldiers who suffered with him.” See their names above.

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked C: “Also Saint Symphorosa.” This recurs frequently.

VATICAN no. 5949 lacks Daniel and Julia. I am uncertain whether the rest is pure.

ALTEMPS, at the end: “Also Saint Symphorosa, virgin.” He meant “widow.”

BORDEAUX: “At Troyes, Saint Juliana, virgin and martyr. Also Saint Symphorosa. At Salvia, Saint Serenetus—or Serenedus?—the confessor.”

CAUDIAC: “In Gaul, the arrival and reception of the body of Saint Domninus, or Douminus, martyr, from the sacred province of Aquitaine, translated to Selula, in the district of Toloricum, at a place anciently called Magno Loco, later by the name stated, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 889.” I confess that I do not sufficiently understand what all this means.

[Col. 0284C] RHEIMS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At the city of Chartres, the deposition of Saint Leobinus, bishop and confessor.” Is this not “at Chartres, of Leobinus”? Concerning him, see September 15.

LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION begins with Praxedes, where it is somewhat interpolated. Daniel and Julia follow, purely. Then Victor, in whose account only the names of the tyrants Diocletian and Maximian are inserted. At the end: “Also at Troyes, the passion of the holy martyrs [the name of Claudius could be inserted here], emperor of the barbarians, Justus and Secundinus, and five others under the emperor Aurelian. On the same day, Saint Arbogast, bishop and confessor of Argentinas. On that day, the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Pontus, Cussion, Papirius, Saturius, with seven others.” GREVEN has *Custion*.

The second edition of BELIN adds at the end: “Also Saint Symphorosa.”

GREVEN: “In Africa, Helias and Stertio. Vastradis the martyr. Dionysius and Pontus, Cussion, Papirius, [Col. 0284D] Saturius, and seven others. Eleutherius [Deutherius] the boy and confessor, who, while praying at the tomb of Saint Victor, breathed his last. Arbogast, bishop and confessor of Argentinas, who came from Scotland, led a life full of virtues, and gloriously presided over the aforesaid church in the time of King Dagobert; by his earnest prayer he also restored to life the king’s only son, who had been thrown from a horse during a hunt and trampled. Albinus the confessor. In Egypt, Daniel, abbot, priest, and confessor. At Troyes, the passion of the holy martyrs [Claudius], emperor of the barbarians, Justus and Secundinus, with five others under the emperor Aurelian.”

MOLANUS adds the following concerning Julia: “Her sacred body was translated into the territory of Meaux, to the church of blessed Mary of the monastery of Jordar, where it is honorably venerated after burial. On the same day, at the monastery of Celle, Saint Sulpitius, bishop, and Saint Leochadia, virgin. At Troyes, the passion of Saint Claudius, emperor of the barbarians, Justus, Jocundinus, with five others under the emperor Aurelian. On the same day, Saint Arbogast, bishop and confessor of Argentinas.” Then, in smaller type: “Who came from Scotland,” etc., as in GREVEN above.

In later editions the same additions are made concerning Julia of Troyes. Then: “There, the passion of Saint Claudius, emperor, Justus, Jucundinus,” [Col. 0286A] etc. Concerning Arbogast, simply, without a eulogy. Then: “On the twenty-first day, Saints Simeon the Father, who on account of Christ was called Salus, and John, his fellow ascetic.” See what has been said about Simeon Salus in our Appendices under July 1, from Rosweyd’s longer observation reported there. “On the same day, at the monastery of Celle, the translation of Saint Sulpitius,” etc., as in the earlier edition.]

[Col. 0281]

Daniel the prophet. At Rome, Saint Praxedes, virgin. Learned in all chastity and in divine law, and assiduously devoted to vigils, prayers, and fasts, she rested in Christ and was buried beside her sister Potentiana on the Salarian Way. In Gaul, at the city of Marseille, the birthday of Saint Victor, who, although a soldier, was unwilling either to serve as a soldier or to sacrifice to idols. First he was thrown into prison, where he was visited by angels; then he was tormented with various punishments; finally he was crushed in a baker’s mill and completed his martyrdom. Three soldiers suffered with him: Alexander, Felicianus, and Longinus. At Troyes, Saint Julia, virgin and martyr.

XI Kalends. Day 22. [Note: [Col. 0285]]

This is how the Pratensis, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Munerat, and Greven manuscripts have it.]

[Note: [Col. 0285B]]

I follow the common reading of the manuscripts, “Ancyra of Galatia”; some have the slightly better “Ancyra of Galatia,” and Molanus alone, with Ado, has the best form, “Ancyra of Galatia.” The Pratensis and Herinianus appear to write *Magdalenis*, but all the others, as in the text, have *Magdalenae*, except that many neglect the diphthong, which I think must be written here and elsewhere in order to avoid confusion. The same does not apply to *Syntyche*, which the others therefore retain as it appears in the manuscripts. Tournai and Munerat have *Sintyche*, which is equally erroneous. The Pratensis with *Synticen*, Greven with *Sintiches*, and finally Molanus with *Syntiches* do not come sufficiently close either; correctly, in the Little Roman Martyrology, undoubtedly corrected by Rosweyd, the form is *Syntyches*.

The Pratensis, with its usual companions, reads “In the district of Rouen,” but we, with the others, prefer the more Usuardine “At the monastery of Fontenelle.” This will be discussed below in the Observations. Some have *Wandregisili*, but nearly all agree with the text, except that Munerat wrongly forms *Wandregisilli* and adds the title “abbot,” which Antwerp-Major also assigns to him, together with some later and less authoritative manuscripts. *Arvernensis* in Munerat and *Arnivernensis* in Rosweyd are perhaps scribal errors, as is *Menelai* for *Menelei* in the last manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0285C]]

The Little Roman Martyrology speaks today as follows of the first three saints of this day. First: “Saint Mary Magdalene.” Second: “And Syntyche, who sleeps at Philippi.” Third: “At Ancyra, Plato the martyr.” Ado preserves the same order and adds nothing especially to their praise. Our author, reversing the order slightly, mentions Plato first, in Ado’s exact words, which he seems to have taken here from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, corrected according to the position in the Little Roman Martyrology, where the reading was corrupt: “At Ancyra, or Auritia, of Galatia or Gallatia,” in almost the same manner as it is read in Rabanus.

Plato’s deeds are said to be found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but I believe they were different from those embellished by Metaphrastes and found in Surius, which Tillemont, Volume V, p. 563, and other modern critics by no means approve. We shall treat of these matters in their proper place.

Bede gives the second announcement as follows: “The birthday of Mary Magdalene.” Thus Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Rabanus, and Ado scarcely differ from one another in substance. The Viennese, however, among the feasts of the apostles, notes as a sort of eulogy her expulsion of seven demons and the first appearance of Christ the Lord to her after the resurrection; all this was recited from Molanus in the Appendices. The occasion naturally gives rise to the observation that our Martyrologies everywhere specify Mary Magdalene most distinctly, but nowhere Mary of Bethany, still less the anonymous sinful woman in the Gospels. For I have not yet found it sufficiently proved that the seven demons expelled from her ought to be understood as sins.

It is commonly known that Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, are listed in the ancient Martyrologies on January 19, as we noted there in our Appendices. It will be useful to append here the opinion of our Father Grothusius concerning the old manuscript Calendar of Paderborn on that very day, January 19. “Truly,” he says, “Mary, Martha’s sister, is entirely different from that Mary Magdalene who is celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, since from the Gospel history it is altogether necessary, with many holy Fathers, to assert that there were three different persons, all nevertheless holy and serving Christ, who are commonly indicated by the name Mary Magdalene. The first was from the village of Magdala near Capernaum, from whom the Lord expelled seven demons; the second was the sinful woman of Nain, who obtained mercy; the third was from Bethany, the sister of Lazarus.”

I find this opinion of a most learned man confirmed today by the judgment of many scholars who have debated this highly contentious question. Nevertheless, I shall not prematurely define anything here; I refer the resolution of the whole controversy to the Acts. Meanwhile, see Tillemont’s brief discussion of it in Volume II, beginning on p. 28. Hear Wandalbert:

“On the eleventh, blessed Mary, by Christ’s mercy,

adorns the day—she who was freed from seven demons,

whom her origin marks as born at Magdala.”

Ado also touched on Syntyche quite briefly, so that our author transferred almost all his words into his table. Paul commends her in Philippians 4:2. Her death and burial will be considered elsewhere.

But what the joining together of such disparate persons means here I do not wish to guess. It is certain and evident that Usuard wrote it thus. Meneleus is not found in the Martyrologies mentioned above. The Hieronymian copies create doubt concerning Wandregisil; nevertheless, we have absolutely no doubt that both are genuinely Usuardine, although Castellanus reports that he observed some erasure in the Pratensis manuscript where these two final announcements appear to have been written.

But, what is remarkable, he says, only these words—“In the district of Rouen”—are by another hand, while all the others are evidently formed in the same script in which the entire Pratensis autograph was written. Whether so long an erasure was made in the aforesaid manuscript cannot be established with certainty; for me, the agreement of nearly all the manuscripts sufficiently proves that both saints were truly entered by Usuard.

Yet an erasure and corruption plainly appear in those words, “In the district of Rouen,” since they are found in no manuscripts except the Pratensis and those resembling it—Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and Aquicinct—all the others consistently reading with the text: “At the monastery of Fontenelle.” This was undoubtedly how the Pratensis manuscript originally read as well; nevertheless, we have not on that account excluded it from the pure manuscripts.

I would not dare assert that Wandregisil was borrowed from the fuller Hieronymian Martyrologies; but the holiness of both he and Meneleus, likewise an abbot, was sufficiently well known to enrich the sacred Calendars, and we firmly believe that Usuard did this, whatever Molanus—once again excessively scrupulous here—may have thought when he omitted one of them.

The Lives of both abbots were published by Mabillon among the Benedictine Lives: that of Wandregisil in Volume II, beginning on p. 524; that of Meneleus in Volume III, Part 1, beginning on p. 404. Wandalbert composed a verse on Wandregisil; perhaps the saint mentioned in third place on the preceding day should be joined with him. Here is today’s verse:

“Wandregisil, on this day the monks’ vows return to you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0287A]]

HERINIANUS, otherwise extremely pure, adds at the end: “On that day, the translation of Saint Theodosia, virgin.” I believe this refers to some local feast.

PULSAN begins: “The birthday of the most blessed Mary Magdalene.” It is pure in the account of Plato and slightly interpolated in that of Syntyche. It omits Wandregisil; in Meneleus it is again pure.

ANTWERP and LÜBECK-MAX, as well as UGHELLI, are defective in the final announcement; otherwise they are pure.

MOLANUS lacks Wandregisil.

ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN begin: “The birthday of blessed Mary Magdalene, of whom, as the Gospel relates, the Lord expelled seven demons.” What follows concerning Plato, Syntyche, and Wandregisil is sufficiently pure. The final announcement of Meneleus is absent.

ALBERGEN and DANIC begin as follows: “The birthday of blessed Mary Magdalene. This is that most blessed sinful woman who, cleansed by flowing tears, washed the feet of the reclining Lord. This is that Gospel woman who, pouring out the sweetness of devotion, anointed the Lord’s head with the most precious ointment at the time of his passion. This is that apostle of the apostles who deserved to be the first among the others to see and announce the glory of the risen Lord.” In the remainder, concerning Plato, etc., they agree with the preceding manuscripts. [Col. 0287C]

CENTULE: “The birthday of the most blessed Mary Magdalene, of whom, as the Gospel relates, the Lord expelled seven demons. And blessed Syntyche, who lies buried at Philippi, whom the blessed Apostle commends in his speech. At Ancyra of Galatia, Saint Plato the martyr. At the monastery of Fontanella, the deposition of Saint Wandregisil, illustrious confessor and abbot. In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Meneleus, abbot.”

BRUSSELS begins with the same words as ALBERGEN and DANIC above. Then it treats Syntyche and Plato quite purely. Finally: “At the monastery of Fontenelle, the deposition of Saint Wandregisil, abbot and confessor. He was the son of Walachisius, brother of Ansegisus the duke, and grandson through his son of blessed Arnulfus. He was the first founder of the monastery of Fontenelle, where, after laying down the burden of the flesh, he himself departed to Christ. Later, however, his body was translated to Blandinium.” There also he is announced in the Little Roman Martyrology.

HAGENOYEN begins:

“**At the city of Aix in Provence, the deposition of Saint Mary Magdalene**, who was noble by birth but wholly given over to wantonness. She loved Christ, washed his feet with tears of repentance, and anointed them with perfume; she gave all her wealth to Christ and his followers; she used to sit at his feet and listen to his words. Because of her love, Christ raised her brother Lazarus. At the banquet she anointed the Lord’s head, for which Judas grumbled, while Christ rejoiced. She stood beside the cross; she also helped bury the Lord and wished to anoint his dead body. She was the first to see him after the resurrection, and was then made by the Lord the apostle of the apostles, when she announced the Lord’s glory to the disciples. Angels consoled her at the tomb, but she could not be consoled. Christ spoke to her in the likeness of a gardener, and she did not recognize him.

“After the Lord’s ascension, she was sent into exile by the Jews with other Christians. They were placed on a ship without oars and, by God’s favor, came near Marseille. There, through the miracles of Mary Magdalene and her companions, the whole population was converted to the Lord: a miracle was performed at sea concerning the rescue of the prince’s child and the death of his wife.

“Then, out of desire for Christ and weariness of human beings, as Josephus says, she lived for thirty years in the wilderness, unknown to human beings, taking neither human food nor drink. At every canonical hour the angels carried her into the air, where she heard heavenly songs with the ears of her heart, and then brought her back to her cave, satisfied. At the end of her life she received Communion from the blessed Bishop Maximinus. She then prostrated herself before the altar and died while everyone was praying. The odor of her body was perceived there for many days afterward, and her body stood without its soul until the blessed Bishop Maximinus prepared a tomb for her. Many miracles are performed there through her merits. Magdalene was buried in the city of Aix, but was later translated to Vézelay.”

These and similar inventions, devised more piously than plausibly, will provide material for us to excavate in the Acts. What follows concerning Syntyche, Plato, Meneleus, and Wandregisilus is fairly pure.

[Col. 0288C] **AQUICINCT.** Instead of “on the same day,” it has “at Vézelay.” After “writes,” it adds, “to the Philippians.” “In the district of Rouen, the deposition of Saint Wandregisilus, abbot and confessor.”

**MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:** “Mary Magdalene. Wandregisilus, first a soldier, afterward a monk and abbot. The martyr Plato, whose acts are available.” In the margin is added: “The dedication of the church at Utrecht, which took place in the presence of the Roman emperor and twelve bishops.”

**CAMBERIEN.:** “At the city of Philippi, the blessed Syntyche, a disciple of Paul.”

In **VATICAN. 5949**, Wandregisilus and Meneleus are absent. It adds: “The feast of Saint Jerome, bishop of Pavia, at Saint Sophia.”

**LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION.** Its account of Mary Magdalene nearly agrees with ALBERGEN. and DANIC. Its account of Plato is fairly pure. Then: “At Philippi, the falling-asleep of Syntyche, who lies buried at Philippi, concerning whom the apostle Paul writes to the Philippians: ‘I exhort Euodia [Evodia] and I beseech Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord.’” The remainder is fairly pure.

**BELIN.** It begins thus: “The feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, from whom the Lord cast out seven demons, and who was worthy to be the first to see the Savior himself risen from the dead.” Wandregisilus is absent; the rest is fairly sound.

**GREVEN.:** “Likewise, Saints Cyril, Andrew, Thebellus, Aurilius, and Apollonius. At Pavia, Saint Jerome, bishop. Lewina, virgin and martyr.”

**MOLAN.** In italics he inserts into the text Ado’s words concerning Magdalene: “Of whom, as the Gospel relates, the Lord cast out seven demons; she also, among her other notable gifts, was worthy to be the first to see Christ risen from the dead.” Then at the end: “At Blandinium, our most holy father Wandregisilus, first founder of the monastery of Fontanella, whose acts are available. [Col. 0289A] At Pavia, Saint Jerome, bishop. The passion of Saint Lewina.” In smaller type follows: “Her venerable bones, together with the bones of Saint Oswald, king of the English, and Saint Iduberga, were raised up in the city of Bergues; but during the last invasion of Flanders by the Franks, they were lost in the devastation of Bergues. Saints Eulogius and Protogenes, bishops, with others, concerning whom see Trip., book VII; Apollo, concerning whom Acts 18 and 1 Corinthians 1 and 16 speak.” Thus far the first edition. The later editions contain the same material concerning Mary Magdalene and, at the end, concerning Wandregisilus, followed by Jerome of Pavia. Finally, as something peculiar to these editions, they add: “On the twenty-second day, the translation of the remains of the holy hieromartyr Phocas.”

[Col. 0285]

At Ancyra in Galatia, the feast of Saint Plato, martyr, whose acts are available. On the same day, Saint Mary Magdalene and the blessed Syntyche, who lies buried at Philippi, concerning whom the apostle Paul writes.

[Note: [Col. 0285B] Sollerius does not doubt that Wandregisilus and Meneleus belong to the Usuardine tradition, although, he says, Castellanus warns that he observed some erasure in the Pratensis manuscript, in which the two final announcements seem to have been written. I believe that Castellanus was warning us that Saints Wandregisilus [Col. 0286B] and Meneleus were written over an erasure, since the parchment is so bright and clean—contrary to the statement of Sollerius’s not very perceptive informant. Only this appears in the erasure: “In the district of Rouen”; but it is by the same hand. BOUILLART.]

In the monastery of Fontinella [Bouillart: In the district of Rouen], the deposition of Saint Wandregisilus, confessor. In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Meneleus, abbot.

**The tenth day before the Kalends. Day 23.**

[Note: [Col. 0289] The text is taken from Praten., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Majore, Pulsanen., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0289B] Greven. and Molan. again have something distinctive. Where all the other manuscripts simply begin, “The feast of the blessed…,” they themselves prefix, “At Ravenna.” The manuscripts Antuerp.-Major and Munerat., generally not very carefully corrected, write *Apollinaris* for *Apollinaris*. I read *caedes*, although a few manuscripts use diphthongs, as in *Romae*, *caesare*, and so forth; as I have often remarked above, this should be done to avoid confusion.]

[Note: [Col. 0289B] The most renowned martyr, Apollinaris, the first of the bishops of Ravenna, is celebrated on this day in the calendars of Allatius and Fronto. All the Martyrologists except ours celebrate him: Jerome, Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Rabanus, Ado, Notker, and Wandalbert. In the Lucense Hieronymian he is called Apollenaris; in the oldest Epternacensis, Apollinaris, but in that manuscript he is assigned to the preceding day. Bede composed a distinguished eulogy for him, transcribed by Rabanus and somewhat abridged by Notker. In the Little Roman Martyrology he is announced in these words: “At Ravenna, Apollinaris, bishop and martyr.” The Viennese Martyrologist pursued him with a double encomium, in a manner until then unusual. He placed him among the festivals of the apostles; this must be said to have been taken from Bede, unless one maintains that material from Ado was transferred to Bede, or invents a miracle to explain the remarkable agreement between the two. In his Martyrology, however, Ado prefaced and expanded a lengthy sequence of the Acts, embracing nearly the whole life of the apostolic man. Usuard took a few details from these, with which he abundantly proclaims the martyr’s praises in his customary form. All these accounts have nearly the same meaning, and all flow from the same source—namely, those very Acts, published by Surius, which plainly display their antiquity through these Martyrologies. No one doubts their antiquity; but more recent writers are unwilling to acknowledge that they are genuine or derived from reliable records. For that reason Tillemont, in volume II, p. 102 onward, preferred to gather from Chrysologus, Gregory, and others what he judged more reliable. It will be our task to examine, arrange, and illustrate in its proper place everything concerning the Acts, the relics, and the miracles. Wandalbert’s single verse praises Apollinaris in this way:

“Here glorious Apollinaris honors the tenth day.”

] [Note: [Col. 0289C] **HERINIEN.** Again appends to its very pure text something peculiar from the province of Rheims, as follows: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Nicasius with his companions.” In **STROZZIAN.**, Eutropia is mentioned.]

**ROSWEYD.** is also very pure in the remainder and adds at the end: “On the same day, Saint Liborius, bishop and confessor of Le Mans.” He intended to write “of Cenomanum.” Surius contains a history of his life and translation; see Bollandus’s short work concerning them.

Many manuscripts today also add, after the pure text: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Primitiva,” or simply: “At Rome, Saint Primitiva.” Such are ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., UGHELLIAN., BIGOTIAN. marked P 5, and CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked B, as well as several to be cited below.

**ALBERGEN. and DANIC.** add as follows: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Primitiva, virgin. At the city of Cenomanum, Saint Liborius, bishop and confessor. In the fiftieth year of his ordination he passed from this world to the Father and to his homeland.”

**CENTULEN.:** “At Ravenna, Saint Apollinaris, martyr and bishop, who, having been instructed for a long time and at great length in the discipleship of the blessed apostle Peter and ordained bishop by him, was entrusted as shepherd to that city and province. He suffered under the Caesar Vespasian, under the patrician Demosthenes.”

**BRUXELLEN.** is fairly pure in the text and also adds: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Primitiva. At the city of Cenomanum, Saint Liberius [Liborius], bishop and confessor. In the fiftieth year of his ordination, he happily passed from this world to the eternal homeland.” See what was said under ROSWEYD.

**HAGENOYEN.:** “At Ravenna, the passion of Saint Apollinaris, bishop [Col. 0290C] and martyr. He was a disciple of the blessed apostle Peter, by whom he was ordained bishop and sent to Ravenna to preach. The pagans made him stand barefoot on burning coals; afterward he was stripped and beaten, and boiling water was poured over his wounds. Finally, under the emperor Vespasian, amid successive tortures, he was beaten with clubs until he seemed dead. He survived for seven days and completed the course of his martyrdom. In Gaul, at the city of Marseille, the feast of Saint Victor, who, being a soldier and unwilling either to serve in the army or sacrifice to idols, was first thrust into prison, where angels visited him. Then he was tortured with various punishments; finally, he was bound in a milling-mill [and], under the governor Asterius, completed his martyrdom. Three soldiers also suffered with him: Alexander, Felicianus, and Longinus. At Troyes, Saint Juliana, virgin.”

This material has been transferred here from the twenty-first day. It continues: “At the city of Cenomanum, the deposition of Saint Liborius, bishop [Col. 0290D] and confessor. In the fiftieth year of his priesthood in the episcopate, he happily passed from this world to the Father and the homeland. He was translated by the emperor Louis to Paderborn, and there he is patron throughout the whole diocese. He cures stone and gravel-related illnesses. At Rome, Saint Primitiva.”

**MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:** “Apollinaris, bishop and martyr. Sent by the blessed Peter to Ravenna, he completed a glorious martyrdom. The translation of the three kings from Milan to Cologne. Brigitte, widow and religious, from whom the observant members of that Order derive their origin; they began to arise in modern times in the diocese of Utrecht.” See her Life in Surius. The margin notes: “On this day every year a solemn procession is held around the city of Utrecht with the Blessed Sacrament and the relics of the saints.”

**VATICAN., marked no. 5949:** “At Rome, Saints Vincent and Primitiva.”

**STROZZIAN.:** “On the same day, Saint Rasiphus, martyr.”

**REMENS.** has something peculiar concerning Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At Rheims, the translation of the bodies of Saints Nicasius, bishop and martyr, and Saint Eutropia, his sister.”

**LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION:** “At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of the bodies of the three Magi, who, as we read in the Gospel, offered gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—to the Savior born at Bethlehem. Their venerable relics were requested from the emperor Frederick by Reynold, bishop of Cologne, and transferred from Milan to Cologne in the year of the Lord 1164 amid the joy and exultation of all; he honorably placed them in his cathedral church, where, through the operation of divine grace, frequent miracles shine forth through their merits. Likewise at Cologne Agrippina, the translation of Saints Felix and Nabor, soldiers and martyrs, which was also carried out from the city of Milan at the same time by the aforementioned Reynold, archbishop of Cologne. Likewise, the feast of the blessed Apollinaris, bishop and martyr. He followed the apostle Peter from Antioch to the city of Rome, was ordained bishop there by him, and was sent to Ravenna. There he ruled the Church for twenty-eight years, one month, and four days. He also preached in the regions of Corinth and Nicaea, on the banks of the Danube, and in the regions of Thrace. In those places he was sent into exile, and wherever he arrived he performed countless miracles. Later he endured various and countless slaughters for the faith of Christ. Finally, under the Caesar Vespasian and the patrician Demosthenes, amid successive tortures, etc. At Rome, the feast of Saint Primitiva, virgin. At the city of Cenomanum, Saint Liborius, etc.,” as in ALBERGEN. and DANIC.: “On the same day, Saint Brigitte, widow, who during her life, through the Lord working in her, raised fourteen dead persons.”

**BELIN.** has the pure text but adds: “On the same day, Saint Rasiphus, martyr.”

**GREVEN.:** “At Cologne Agrippina, the translation [Col. 0292A] of the three Magi, with two others. Note: the bodies of the holy Magi, as Vincent says in book XXX, were formerly transferred by the emperor to Constantinople and from there miraculously carried to Milan. When the emperor Frederick I destroyed Milan, they were transferred to Cologne by Reynold, archbishop of Cologne, who had come to the emperor’s aid, in the year of the Lord 1164, together with Saints Felix and Nabor, and were deposited in the cathedral with great exultation by all; there too they shine forth through many miracles. On the same day, the holy martyrs Ravennius, a priest, and Rasiphus, brothers of Cenomanum, and Saint Liborius, bishop and confessor, a man of great holiness. When he died in the fiftieth year of his episcopate, the blessed Martin of Tours buried him. At Rome, Saint Primitiva, virgin. At Ravenna, Saint Thecla, virgin. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Brigitte, widow, noblewoman of the kingdom of Sweden. Having passed through the state of virginity and marriage with great integrity, she went as a pilgrim to Jerusalem after receiving a divine summons. Returning from there to Rome, she spent the remainder of her life there in great holiness, visited by the Lord through continual revelations. She also established a new monastic order and became renowned through many miracles.”

**MOLAN.:** “On the same day, Rasiphus, martyr. At Rome, the feast of Saint Brigitte, widow, who during her life visited the Holy Land and various distant places of the saints, and under Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord 1373, at the age of seventy, after receiving the sacraments, rested in a blessed death. At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of the three Magi, who, as we read in the Gospel, offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the Savior born at Bethlehem. Their relics, together with the bodies of the holy martyrs Felix and Nabor, were requested from the emperor Frederick by Reynold, archbishop of Cologne, and honorably transferred from Milan to Cologne.”

In other editions he writes: “On the same day, Saint Rasiphus, martyr.” Concerning Brigitte, as in the earlier edition. Then: “At Cenomanum, the deposition of Saints Pavicius and Liborius, bishops and confessors.” The translation of the three kings, and likewise of Felix and Nabor by Reynold, is expressed in the same words as in the first edition.

[Col. 0289]

The feast of the blessed Apollinaris, bishop, who was ordained by the apostle Peter at Rome and sent to Ravenna; afterward, for the faith of Christ, he endured various and manifold slaughters. Finally, under the Caesar Vespasian, amid the tortures succeeding one another, he completed a glorious martyrdom.

**The ninth day before the Kalends. Day 24.**

[Note: [Col. 0291] Thus Praten., Herinien., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0291D] “Concerning the Via Tiburtina, it has been said elsewhere. Greven. writes *Vincentii*, and Munerat. *militis* instead of *militaris*. Again, Greven. has *Antinogeno* instead of *Antiogeno*. Praten. reads *diversis exterminatus suppliciis*, which suits the matter well, as we have elsewhere judged it preferable. Greven. and Molan. speak more forcefully: *per diversis exterminatus suppliciis*. But the others here, with Ado, read *diversis examinatus*, and so forth. Herinien. has it wrongly as *Tiro*; likewise *Cristinae*, with Munerat. and Greven., while the others, more correctly, agree with the text in *Christinae*. All consistently have *tormenta constanter perferens*; I do not know where *tormenta multipliciter exacta* crept into Herinien. Likewise *confessione* instead of *confixione*, while in Greven. it is *infixione*. Herinien. and Munerat. write *Nicae* instead of *Nicetae*, as Florus has it on the following day. Perhaps Pratensis, following Ado, correctly placed *Aquilae*, and one or two manuscripts agree with him; but it was necessary to yield to the majority. I read *Christofori*, with the greatest number of manuscripts, although Herinien. and Molan. more correctly have *Christophori*. *Amiterina* instead of *Amiternina* is an error in Munerat.]

[Note: [Col. 0291D] You will reach the true and single source of this entire text, which is very doubtful and confused, if you compare Ado with ours, although the order is not the same in both. What appears first in the Little Roman Martyrology—“At Rome, on the Via Tiburtina, Vincent”—also appears in Usuard, but in Ado it is placed second, where he inserts “at the nineteenth milestone,” which you see our text has omitted. Perhaps this is because he understood those milestones to extend beyond the city of Tibur. Thus, however, it is generally read in the Hieronymian manuscripts on the preceding day, unless one prefers the Epternacensis manuscript, which simply has: “At Rome, Vincent.” You see that the only surviving monument of this martyr of ours is the church of Saint Vincent that, according to Baronius, exists at Tibur and was probably so named after him. Again, the Little Roman Martyrology continues: “At Emerita in Spain, Victor, a soldier,” who occupies third place in Ado. Whatever Usuard added to the Little Roman Martyrology, he copied word for word from the Viennese Martyrology. Whether the Viennese received this material from sufficiently reliable documents may rightly be doubted because of Castellanus’s note, by which he thinks that perhaps, on the basis of the Hieronymian manuscripts, ten disciples of Athenogenes are indicated here, who were killed with him on 17 July, the day on which Surius reports the Acts of their master. We shall discuss these matters more fully elsewhere, either on that day or on this one.

Concerning Christina, Bede wrote most prudently: “The feast of Saint Christina, virgin.” Rabanus prefixed “At the city of Tyre” and added an encomium composed by himself. But the author of the already twice-mentioned Little Roman Martyrology followed Bede’s caution, reading: “Near Lake Bolsena in Italy, Christina, virgin.” From this distinguished virgin Ado begins today: “On the same day, in Italy, at Tyre, near the lake,” and so forth. He then relates in greater detail the various tortures she endured with incredible fortitude. Usuard considered it sufficient to extract a few of these, represented fairly elegantly in our text.

Baronius and Florentius, against Cluverius, inquire what that Tyre of Tuscany was—the place we nearly encountered above on 9 July—and where it was ever situated. Many other matters are mixed into that discussion, but they are not to be settled here; they will more suitably be examined elsewhere together with Christina’s Acts. Wandalbert includes her and the following two virgins in a single verse:

“Soon Christina, Aquila, and Niceta hallowed the ninth.”

Thus the two aforementioned virgins, Niceta and Aquilina, are placed fourth both in Ado and in our text, in exactly the same words in both. We call them both by that name here on the authority of the principal Usuardine manuscripts, although perhaps the latter should more correctly be called Aquila according to Ado’s meaning. The learned Castellanus asserts in his Universal Martyrology that both were unknown before Wandalbert; rightly so, unless Florus, published by our editors, is considered earlier, since on 25 July he connects their eulogy with that of Christopher. Whether this is sufficiently accurate will have to be investigated elsewhere.

The final announcement is genuinely and wholly derived from Ado, so that no one can doubt, even in the slightest, the origin and simplicity of our entire entry. In accordance with the purpose presently before us, these matters have therefore been fully and plainly brought into conformity with their standard, although I readily admit that considerable roughness remains in the Hieronymian manuscripts, especially concerning the people of Amiternum and Emerita. Another tool will still be needed to smooth it away besides the one Florentius employed in reconciling them, as we have just said concerning Christina.

Victorinus of Notker may be added, as well as Victorinus and Severinus, brothers, whom Rabanus commemorates. Meanwhile, see the cited notes of Castellanus on the Universal Martyrology, where eighty-three soldiers are changed into eighty-three miles, while only Victorinus’s name is retained—he is said to have obtained the crown of martyrdom at that distance on the Salarian Way. The Hieronymian copies, correctly compared with one another, appear to support this reading. But concerning doubtful matters, this is more than enough.]

[Note: [Col. 0293C] **TORNACEN.** begins: “The feast of Saint Christina, virgin.” Whether he means Christina of Hasbania, commonly called “the Miraculous,” who died in the century when this Martyrology was written, I do not know. Certainly, in the continuation of the text he writes again: “In Italy, at the city of Tyre, Saint Christina, virgin,” omitting the encomium. The rest is pure.]

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.** omits Vincent and confuses the text in this manner: “At Rome, on the Via Tiburtina, the feast of Saint Victorinus, a soldier, who with his two brothers, etc.” The remainder that follows is fairly pure, except that at the end it reads: “At Amiternum, eighty soldiers.”

**ROSWEYD.**, pure throughout the text, adds at the end: “The vigil of the apostle Saint James.”

**PULSANEN.** lacks two announcements, namely the second and the last.

**ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN.** are missing only the first announcement.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., and LOVANIEN.** give the complete text, changing only the position of Christina, whom they place first with Ado. At the beginning, however, they prefix: “The vigil of the apostle Saint James.”

**ALBERGEN. and DANIC.**, conforming to the first four, also omit Vincent.

**BRUXELLEN.** Although rarely deficient, is deficient on this day in the same entry concerning Vincent.

**HAGENOYEN.** begins: “The vigil of Saint James.” It is pure in the account of Vincent and the people of Emerita. It continues: “In Italy, at the city of Tyre, the passion of Saint Christina, virgin and martyr. Since she was noble and fifteen years old, her father shut her up with twelve girls and placed golden gods beside her so that she might worship them [the gods]. But, inspired by God, she despised them. Because of this her father, enraged, beat her naked with rods, and twelve men were stripped naked over her. Then he had her bound to a wheel and presented her to the judge, who shut her in a bronze vessel and applied fire together with pitch, resin, and oil, but it harmed her not at all. After this her breasts were cut off, and milk came forth instead of blood. Then she stained the judge’s face with one of her breasts and knocked out his eye. Under a third judge her tongue was then cut out, and finally she was killed by three blows of arrows.” The rest is fairly pure.

**CENTULEN.** “At Emerita in Spain, Saint Victor, martyr. In Italy, at the city of Tyre, the passion of Saint Christina, virgin. On the same day, Saints Niceta and Aquilina, who are commemorated in the passion of Saint Christopher.” See the Observations.

**AQUICINCT.** Instead of “Stercatius and Antinogenus,” reads “Sunteatius and Antiogenus.”

**VICTORIN.** adds at the end: “And Saint Victorinus, martyr.” Other manuscripts announce it in the same way.

**MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:** “Christina, virgin and martyr. The vigil. At Rome, Vincent, martyr. Niceta and Aquilina, martyrs. Judocus, confessor. Likewise, eighty-three soldier martyrs.”

**REG. SUEC.**, marked no. 130: “Ninety-three soldiers. And Saint Victorinus, martyr.”

[Col. 0294D] **VATICAN.**, under no. 5949, also has at the end: “And Saint Victorinus, martyr.”

**ALTEMPS.:** “In the territory of Conventium, at the monastery of Stanes, Saint Wulfad, martyr, who for the faith of Christ was killed by the sword by his father, King Wulferus, and deserved to receive an eternal crown, making the sign of the cross upon himself and manifesting by clear signs that he lived.”

**CODEX MONTIS SANCTI:** “The feast of Saint Segolena, consecrated to God.” Castellanus writes *Siggolena*.

**LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION:** “The vigil of the apostle Saint James. In Italy, at the city of Cyro, which is near Lake Bolsena, Saint Christina, virgin. She who believed in Christ,” and so forth. After “completed,” it adds: “in the eleventh year of her age.” The account of Victor is pure. Concerning Vincent it adds “at the nineteenth milestone.” The account of the Amiternines is pure; concerning the two virgins Niceta and Aquilina it inserts: “Who in Lycia, at the city of Samos, [were converted by] the blessed Christopher,” and so forth. At the end: “At Cenomanum, the deposition of Saints Pavacius, Turibius, and Gundanifolius, bishops and confessors.”

[Col. 0295A] **BELIN.** begins: “The vigil of the apostle Saint James.” The remainder of the text is fairly pure, but it moves the people of Emerita to the final place.

**GRIVEN.** “The vigil of the apostle Saint James. At Cenomanum, the deposition of Saints Pavacius, Turibius, and Gundanisolius, bishops and confessors of the aforesaid city. Segolena, widow.”

**MOLAN.:** “The passion of Saint Lewinna, who, adorned with many virtues, flourished under a king of the English named Euberus. Later, under the same king, she completed her life through martyrdom, while the archbishop named Theodore was still alive. The vigil of the apostle Saint James.”

Then, in smaller type: “She is celebrated in many places in observance of the fast. In the territory of Hasbania, Christina, virgin of holy memory, whose Life was written by Thomas of Cantimpré.”

The later editions begin in italics: “The vigil of the apostle Saint James.” At the end: “At Bergues, from England, the passion of Saint Lewinna, who, adorned with many virtues, flourished under the king of the English, etc. On the twenty-fourth day, Saint Parasceve, holy martyr of Christ.” This is not noted in the Latin manuscripts.]

[Col. 0291]

At Rome, on the Via Tiburtina, the feast of Saint Vincent. At Emerita in Spain, Saint Victor, a soldier, who with his two brothers, Stercatius and Antinogenus, after being subjected to various tortures, completed his martyrdom. In Italy, at the city of Tyre, Saint Christina, who, believing in Christ, first endured tortures steadfastly under two judges and finally, under their successor, completed the course of her martyrdom by the cutting out of her tongue and being pierced with arrows. On the same day, the feast of Saints Niceta and Aquilina, who, converted to Christ through the preaching of the blessed martyr Christopher, received the palm of martyrdom by decapitation. At the city of Amiternum, eighty-three soldiers. [Bouillart adds in the margin: At Sens, Saints Ursicinus and Pavacius, bishops.]

**The eighth day before the Kalends. Day 25.**

[Note: [Col. 0295] Thus Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Greven.]

[Note: [Col. 0295B] Enough has been said concerning *Hierosolimus*, *Jherosolimus*, *Hierusolimis*, *Jerosolimis*, and so forth. Likewise concerning Lycia and Christopher. Here it must especially be noted that in the Herinien manuscript the second announcement is placed first. Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. substitute *sacra ossa* for *sacratissima ossa*. It should be read *Samo*, as Greven. correctly has it. But all the others write *Samon*, not *Samson*, as Antuerp.-Major does. Pratensis reads “and from the seething flames,” etc.; Herinien. and Antuerp.-Maj. have the worse reading “and flames.” We have followed Ado and the other manuscripts in reading “and from the flames.” Antuerp. alone, and incorrectly, wrote *Barcilonona*. Likewise, both it and Max.-Lubec. have “the sons of Cucufatus,” while Antuerp.-Major has *Cucufati*; we follow the larger and stronger majority in reading *Cucufatis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0295B] The memory of James son of Zebedee, the first martyr among the apostles, is recalled in the Gregorian Sacramentary; the Little Roman Martyrology recalls it in nearly the same words: “The feast of the apostle Saint James, son of Zebedee.” Florentius does not doubt that the same things reported on this day concerning James in the Hieronymian Martyrology are to be attributed to Zebedee. Ado’s eulogy among the festivals of the apostles is brief and polished, and Usuard scarcely removed anything from it, transcribing almost everything word for word. What Notker adds to these matters is not very important.

Florus reports other things concerning the apostle, apparently received from Clement of Alexandria, but they must be examined in their proper place, together with many other matters concerning James’s life, journeys, martyrdom, translation, discovery, and innumerable miracles. These certainly require extensive investigation, begun by Tillemont in volume I, p. 324 onward, and in the notes from p. 594 onward. There, with his customary diligence, he cites the authors from whom several controversies may be more fully explained and resolved in their proper place.

The Little Roman Martyrology continues: “At the city of Samos, Christopher, martyr.” His memory is also treated in Florus’s additions to Bede—Florus assigned him to 28 April—which contain a fairly long eulogy. But Ado concerns us more directly here; he expressed the whole matter so elegantly and briefly that Usuard found nothing he could remove from it. There is no doubt that the Hieronymian copies also commemorate this same Christopher, whatever distortions may appear in his name and placement. Concerning his gigantic statues and other related matters, see Florentius and Papebrochius’s note on the Greek-Moscow Ephemerides [Col. 0295D] before volume I of May, p. XXVI, column 1; from it you will first understand what judgment should be formed concerning the commonly circulated Acts of Christopher.

“**At the city of Barcelona, Saint Cucufas, martyr**,” writes Florus; I am completely convinced that Ado had never seen him. Thus it appears certain that not some older Martyrologist but the Acts themselves, whatever their quality, preceded the Viennese Martyrology. That Martyrology produces a notable epitome of them, copied almost entirely by Notker but contracted by Usuard in the manner visible in the text. The Hieronymian manuscripts should be consulted not on 15 February, as Castellanus notes, but on 16 February, [Col. 0296C] together with what Florentius observed there. Tillemont gives what is certain concerning this saint in volume V, p. 58, and what is doubtful on p. 609.

Thus far everything in our text is derived from Ado. In Ado himself follows the deposition of Saint Germanus, placed, I believe, through a typographical error instead of “translation,” as the Usuardine manuscripts correctly read; for we have shown that Ado himself treats the deposition of Germanus on 28 May. In the aforementioned Ado, the text concludes: “At Metz, the feast of Saint Clodesindis, virgin.” Why Usuard omitted her, I can assign no other reason than that she was probably absent from his copy. Whatever the truth of the matter, the most reliable manuscripts demonstrate that she was omitted, just as they clearly show the original and genuine wording of the remainder.

Wandalbert bound our first three martyrs together in his verses as follows:

“James, son of Zebedee, adorns the eighth;

He first gave apostolic blood for the King;

After him come Cucufas and Christopher.”

] [Note: [Col. 0295] **TORNACEN.**, otherwise entirely pure, omits Cucufas’s eulogy.]

**PULSANEN.** is complete concerning James but lacks the eulogies of Christopher and Cucufas. It says nothing about Saint James’s translation.

**ROSWEYD.** appends to the complete text, together with Ado: “At Metz, the feast of Saint Glodesindis, virgin.”

[Col. 0296D] **MUNERAT.**, also pure in the text, adds: “At Cenomanum, the translation of Saint Julian, bishop and confessor.” His feast is 27 January.

**MOLAN.** omitted the final announcement concerning the translation of Saint Germanus.

**ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC.** also add to the otherwise pure text: “At Metz, the feast of Saint Glodesindis, virgin. At Trier, Saint Magnericus, bishop and confessor.”

**ANTUERP.-MAX.** adds to these: “Likewise on the same day, Saint Judocus, hermit, son of the king of Britain.”

**CENTULEN.:** “The feast of the blessed apostle James, brother of John the Evangelist, who was beheaded by Herod at Jerusalem, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles relates. In Lycia, at the city of Samos, Saint Christopher, martyr, who, bound with iron rods and exposed to the flames of a blazing fire, was saved by the power of Christ and finally, pierced by arrows, completed his martyrdom by decapitation. At the city of Barcelona, the glorious martyr Saint Cucufas. At Rome, Saint Nemesius, martyr. At Paris, the translation of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor. In the district of Ponthieu, the discovery of the body of Saint Judocus, confessor.”

**BRUXELLEN.** is fairly pure in the first three entries; in fourth place it has: “At Metz, the feast of the glorious virgin Saint Glodesindis, who, fleeing her bridegroom, was worthy to receive a veil from the hand of an angel.
