At Trier, Saint [Col. 0297B] Magnericus, bishop and confessor, who enrolled the blessed Gaugericus in the clerical service.” It then follows with “the translation of Saint Germanus.”

**HAGENOYEN.** recites lengthy accounts of James and Christopher, which must be discussed elsewhere. Its account of Cucufas is fairly pure. It has nothing concerning the translation of Saint Germanus, but substitutes in its place: “Likewise, the translation of Saint Judocus, confessor,” which above in CENTULEN. is called the “discovery,” and so forth. See his feast day, 13 December.

**AQUICINCT.** After the translation of Saint Germanus, a later hand adds: “And Saint Judocus.”

AMBIANEN.: “On the same day, of Saint Judocus, confessor.” We have already said that he is commemorated on 13 December.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJET.: “Of the apostle James. Of Christopher the martyr. Of Cucuphas the martyr. Of Glodesindis the virgin. Translation of blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, and of Felix the martyr.”

BICOTIAN., sign. P 5: “In the city of Paris, translation of Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor.” See further concerning Marcellus on the following day.

DIVIONEN. of Saint Benignus, which is at Cîteaux: “On that day, of blessed Julian, bishop. He was one of the seventy disciples of Christ, whom blessed Peter the apostle sent to the city of Le Mans to preach the word of God.” See under MUNERAT.

REG. SUEC., under note no. 428: “At Le Mans, translation of Saint Julian, bishop and confessor. At Beauvais, of Saint Ebrulfus, confessor.” In French he is called Evrols. Concerning him, Castellanus notes in the Universal Martyrology that he was an abbot at “Saint Fuscianus,” buried near Amiens in an oratory in the Beauvais district, and that his body was subsequently transferred to the city of Beauvais, to Saint Peter.

IN VATICAN., no. 5949. The entire final announcement in our text, concerning the “translation of Saint Germanus,” is absent.

ALTEMPS.: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Eutychian, pope, who buried 362 martyrs; crowned with martyrdom, he was buried on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Callistus.” See Florus on this day concerning him, or the account published under his name in our Bede, and Rabanus. He is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 8 December.

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, of Saint Eutychian, pope and martyr.” We have already spoken of him.

LUXOVIEN.: “At Metz, of Saint Glotsindis, virgin.”

EDITIO LUBECO.-COL., moderately interpolated in its first three sections, adds: “At Jerusalem, of Saint Josias the scribe, who gained Christ by the law of the cup, as is related in the Acts of blessed James the apostle.” Concerning Magnericus, as above. Then: “At Metz, the feast of Saint Glodesindis, whose tomb is made illustrious by frequent miracles. In the district of Meaux, the burial of Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor of Troyes. On the same day, of Saint Ursicius, bishop and confessor.” Concerning the translation of Germanus, as above. Finally: “On that day, discovery of the body of Saint Judocus, priest and confessor.”

BELIN., in third place: “In the city of Paris, translation,” etc. After this announcement follows: “In the city of Barcelona, the feast of blessed Cucuphas the martyr,” where it stops, the eulogy having been deleted.

[Col. 0298B] GREVEN.: “At Trier, of Saint Magnericus, bishop and confessor. He was educated by Saint Nicetius, bishop of that same city; when Nicetius was driven into exile by Chlothar because of his zeal for justice, Magnericus did not abandon him and afterward worthily succeeded him. In the district of Meaux, the burial of blessed Ursus, bishop and confessor of Troyes. Also, of Saints Rusticus and Florentius. At Metz, the feast of Saint Glodesindis, virgin, whose tomb is adorned with frequent miracles. At Le Mans, translation of Saint Julian, bishop and confessor. On that day, discovery of the body of Saint Judocus, priest and confessor.” See what we said above under HAGENOYEN.

MOLAN.: “On that day, at Metz, the feast of Saint Glodezindis, virgin. At Trier, of Saint Magnericus, bishop. In the city of Paris, translation of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor. In the district of Meaux, the burial of blessed Ursus, bishop and confessor of Troyes.” Then, in smaller type: “In the city of Autun, of Saint Reticius, confessor, bishop of that same city.” Other editions read: “On that day, at Metz, etc. At Trier, etc. In the district of Meaux, etc. On the twenty-fifth day, commemoration of the holy women Olympias and Eupraxia.” Concerning the translation of Saint Germanus, as above. Finally, in smaller type: “In Palestine, in the city of Gaza, of the holy women Valentina and her companion. Firmilianus the governor, to whom they freely and most boldly opposed themselves, with a courage plainly manly, condemned them at last to be consumed in the fire. In the same place, of Saint Paul the martyr, who, after pouring out a prayer for the judge, the executioner, and all who were in error, willingly submitted his neck to be struck by the sword.” See concerning these most celebrated martyrs the Roman Martyrology for this day and Castellanus’s two exceptionally careful notes on it. They are taken from Eusebius, *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, book VIII, chapter 8, in the Valesian edition, which Ruinart reproduces among his *Selecta*, p. 341. There he observes that the exceptionally courageous virgins are commemorated by the Greeks on 18 July, and that the other, anonymous in Eusebius, is called “Thea” by them.]

[Col. 0295]

The feast of blessed James the apostle, brother of John the evangelist, who was beheaded by King Herod. His most sacred bones were transferred from Jerusalem to Spain and buried at its farthest extremity; they are honored with the most celebrated devotion of those peoples. In the Lycian city of Samon, of Saint Christopher, who, after being crushed with iron rods and saved by the power of Christ from the flames of a blazing fire, was finally pierced by arrows and completed his martyrdom by decapitation. In the city of Barcelona, the feast of blessed Cucuphas the martyr, who, for the name of the Lord, endured the most atrocious kinds of torture under three judges and finally departed victorious by the sword. In the city of Paris, translation of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor.

VII Kal. Day 26. [Note: [Col. 0297]

The following manuscripts are pure: Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp., and Max.-Lubec., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0297D]

In “Herasti” there is no disagreement among the manuscripts, all forming the name in precisely this way. I admit that the following name should more properly be called “Hyacinthi,” as it is in the Short Roman Martyrology and in Ado. Praten. comes nearest with “Hiacinti”; but the others consistently and uniformly read “Jacincti,” as in the text. Antuerp.-Maj. alone writes “from there in a very strong torrent” instead of “from there into a very strong torrent.” The text is correct after this in reading “by the consular,” etc.; but Antuerp.-Maj. and Herinien. omit the preposition “by,” etc. “Leuncio” in Antuerp. and “Lenucio” in Max.-Lubec. are both written incorrectly, as is “Leoncio” in Greven. After “the Latin Way,” Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. lack the word “saints.” The names of the martyrs are variously corrupted, even in our text, where we retained “Simpronii,” following Praten., Herinien., etc., as closer to the true name “Sempronii,” which appears in the Acts, although others more commonly read “Simphronii.” Antuerp.-Maj. has “Simphrosii,” followed by “Olimphii, Theodoli, Exuperii,” forms which we have written differently on the basis of the agreement of the other witnesses. Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. omit “Olimpii.” Greven. reads “and as” instead of “as in the Acts,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0299A]

Concerning Erastus, who is placed here first, there is nothing on this day in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, nothing in Bede, Florus, or Rabanus, nothing in the Short Roman Martyrology, and nothing in Ado’s Martyrology itself as edited by Rosweyd. In it you will also notice this defect: although the name “Herastus” is marked in the index, we are referred to the appendix, in which the saint is nevertheless absent; in the booklet *On the Feasts* he is correctly given without the aspirate. I do not sufficiently understand what scruple led Rosweyd to remove him from Ado’s Martyrology mentioned above. To me, at any rate, he seems just as Adonian as Hyacinth, who is commemorated there; and I think this is altogether demonstrated by the fact that both Notker and Usuard report him in the very words of Ado himself as found in Mosander, except that he is also celebrated most explicitly in Rosweyd’s Ado itself, among the cited Feasts of the Apostles, and everywhere with the same wording. The praise of Erastus is truly to be drawn from the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles of the apostle Paul. One may consult what Tillemont briefly collects concerning him, especially in volume I, p. 113. Concerning Hyacinth, likewise unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies and to Bede, the Short Roman Martyrology says: “At Rome, in the Portus, of Saint Hyacinth the martyr.” From there he passed into Ado, where both his martyrdom and burial are described at greater length, as you will also find in Notker. Usuard, however, content with the first part alone, explained the entire matter more briefly and with his usual elegance—if only with equal truth! For, to speak candidly, the Acts of his martyrdom as published by Surius contain not a few things that a reader experienced in such matters will not readily accept. Tillemont rightly criticizes some of them in volume II, p. 573.

The following group of martyrs is also absent from the Hieronymian Martyrologies and from Bede. It was first recorded by the Short Roman Martyrology, not on this day but on 4 December, where it is said to have become more celebrated because of the translation performed by Saint Sixtus, although they are said to have suffered on 26 July, that is, VII Kalends of August. All these matters are explained more fully by Ado on the aforesaid day, 4 December, after a long eulogy composed from the Acts of Saint Stephen the pope. It is surprising that Ado did not observe that the aforesaid martyrs are reported to have been buried by Pope Saint Stephen on the day before the Kalends of November, and therefore most probably completed their martyrdom not in July but at the end of October. Florus chose another day, namely 27 July, speaking as follows: “On the same day, at Rome, the passion of Saint Symphronius; with him, Olympius, together with his wife Exuperia and his son Theodolus, were burned in the fire at the command of Valerian and Gallienus.” As far as our Usuard is concerned, I scarcely doubt that he took all his material from Ado. Following Ado’s judgment concerning the day of their passion, he moved the martyrs themselves from 4 December to 26 July. Baronius did the same, not sufficiently remembering that in the Acts of Pope Saint Stephen, which he published in his *Annals* under the years 259 and 260, an entirely different day is indicated. But these matters will have to be examined later in the Acts themselves, which we shall illustrate. Here I wished only to show that everything which we have recounted above, purely and simply according to the author’s mind, in the Usuardine entry derives from one and the same Adonian source. See what we shall say concerning the Acts of Saint Stephen on 2 August. Wandalbert connects Adrian with Aemilius and Marcian on this day; the latter two are found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but I have absolutely no idea where that conjunction originated.]

[Note: [Col. 0299C]

TORNACEN. lacks the eulogy of Hyacinth and has at the end: “In the city of Paris, translation of Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor. MUNERAT has more.”

ROSWEYD. adds after the pure text: “Also, of Rusticus and Florentius, martyrs.”

PULSANEN. has the second announcement truncated, its eulogy having been deleted.

MUNERAT. adds after the text: “At Paris, translation of Marcellus, a man of great praise and outstanding excellence, pastor of that same place, whose body rests (thus also in another place) in the nourishing church of the blessed virgin Mary of Paris. Also, the feast of blessed Anna, mother of Mary, the Mother of God.”

PRATEN. likewise reports an addition, which I gather from the sub-virgulation to have been written in the margin, in these words: “Translation of Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT. and LEYDEN. begin: “The feast of blessed Anna, mother of the virgin Mary. Also [Col. 0299D] the feast of Saint Pastor, confessor.” You should note that Olympius is absent from these two and the three following manuscripts.

LOVANIEN. has the same concerning Anna, mother of the most blessed Virgin, but nothing concerning Pastor.

ALBERG. and DANIC. begin as follows: “The feast of Saint Pastor, confessor.” The former adds at the end of the text: “Also, of Saint Anna, mother of the most glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God.” This announcement is added in different words and by a different hand in the later Danish manuscript.

CENTULEN.: “The feast of blessed Erastus, who, ordained bishop at Philippi by blessed Paul, there rested, crowned with martyrdom. At Rome, in the Portus, of Saint Hyacinth the martyr. Also at Rome, of Saints Symphronius, Olympius, Theodolus, and Maxima (Exuperia), who, burned in the fire, obtained the palm of martyrdom.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “Of Saint Anna, mother of blessed Mary the Virgin, glorious mother of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Transfiguration of the Lord, which took place on Mount Tabor and was made known by the three disciples who were present, after the Lord’s Ascension, to their fellow apostles.” The text follows, almost pure. Then: “And commemoration of the holy martyrs Victorianus, Frumentius, another Frumentius, and two brothers. All of them were crowned in Africa during the Vandal persecution. At Laodicea, the feast of Saints Vivianus and Felix. On the same day, the burial of Warmudi, who was patriarch of Jerusalem.” At least under this form of the name, he is not known to us thus far. “Also, of Saint Pastor, confessor.”

[Col. 0300D] HAGENOYEN. is quite pure in Erastus; in second place it has: “Also, the feast of blessed Pastor, confessor.” Two other announcements follow, also fairly pure. Then: “On the same day, of Saint Anna, mother of the Mother of God, who is said in Sacred Scripture to have had three husbands . . .” and other material of this kind, which I pass over. He places here the translation of Saint Germanus. He also has: “At Metz, the feast of Saint Glodeswindis, virgin. Also, of Desideratus, bishop and confessor.” An imperfect construction concerning the translation of Saint Helena follows. Finally: “At Trier, of Saint Magnericus, bishop and confessor.” See the preceding day.

[Col. 0301A] AQUICINCT., for Exuperia, has Exuperantia.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Anna, mother of blessed Mary. At Rome, of Hyacinth the martyr. Of Symphronius, Olympius, Theodolus, and Exuperia, martyrs. Of Erastus, disciple of blessed Paul.”

REG. SUEC., sig. no. 128: “In the city of Paris, translation of Saint Marcellus, bishop of Paris.”

CODEX D. LE MARE, sig. A: “At Autun, of blessed Reticius, bishop and most learned man.”

VATICAN: “In Syria, of Simeon the monk, who stood upon a pillar.” The extracts for this day are confused.

UGHELLIAN. generally agrees, as we have often said, with ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., which here, together with it, omit the announcement of Olympius.

FLORENTIN.: “Also, of Saint Pastor, cardinal priest.” IN STROZZIAN. additionally has: “At the monastery of Saint Benedict, in the Mantuan territory, of Saint Simeon the monk and hermit, who, famous for many miracles, rested in a good old age.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins: “The feast of Saint Anna [Col. 0301B] the widow, mother of the most glorious and illustrious virgin Mary, Mother of God, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ. She was from the city of Bethlehem, descended from the tribe of Judah, and betrothed to blessed Joachim. At Rome, in the Title, of Saint Pastor, priest and confessor, brother of Saint Pius the pope. After countless struggles, after the burials of many saints, and after innumerable works of piety, he rested in the Lord during the reign of the emperor Antoninus. On the same day, of Saint Valerius, son of Albana, whom blessed Eucharius, the first bishop of Trier, raised from the dead.” It is fairly pure in Erastus. Concerning Hyacinth, it adds his burial. In another class it is moderately interpolated. At the end: “In the territory of Trier, near Confluence, on the mountain, the feast of Saint Beatus, priest and confessor.”

BELIN. begins: “The feast of Saint Anna, mother of the virgin Mary.” The text follows, and at the end: “On the same day, of Saint Pastor, priest and confessor. [Col. 0302A] At the monastery of Saint Benedict, in the Mantuan territory,” etc., as above in STROZZIAN.

GREVEN.: “The Dormition of Saint Anna, worthy mother of God, mother of the ever-virgin Mary. Of Eobanus, bishop and martyr. Also, of Saints Vivianus, Felix, and Julianus. At Rome, of Saint Pastor, priest and confessor, brother of Saint Pius the pope. Saint Pudens, disciple of Saint Paul, entrusted his daughters Potentiana and Praxedes to him and established the title in his name. He himself, after countless struggles and after reverently providing burial for many saints, rested in peace. Of Valerius the confessor, son of Albana,” etc., as above. “At Trier, of Saint Beatus, priest and confessor. In Bohemia, of John Ovicula, confessor, of the Order of Preachers, a man of good and holy memory.”

MOLAN., in Italic type before the text: “The feast of Saint Anna, mother of the virgin Mary.” At the end: “On the same day, of Saint Pastor, priest and confessor.” Concerning Simeon of Mantua, as above. Also concerning the translation of Saint Marcellus, as in MUNERAT. Then: “In the city of Teneramunda, of blessed Christina, virgin. She was the only daughter of Migranim, king of the English, and according to the tradition of her fathers was most devoted to her gods and idols. Almighty God, looking upon her, sent her from heaven an angel in the guise of a poor man, who was to catechize her and commanded her to be baptized in the name of Christ; under his guidance she also reached Diclivenne.” Then, in smaller type: “At Trier, of Saint Beatus, priest and confessor. Of Eobanus, bishop and martyr.” Other editions begin the Usuardine text itself in Italic type as follows: “In the city of Acon, the feast of Saint Anna,” etc. At the end, concerning Pastor, Simeon of Mantua, and Christina of Teneramunda, as in the first edition. Then: “At the Carthusian monastery near Confluence, of Saint Beatus, priest of Trier and confessor.” Finally, concerning the translation of Marcellus of Paris, also as above.]

[Col. 0297]

The feast of Saint Erastus, who, left by blessed Paul as bishop at Philippi, there rested, crowned with martyrdom. At Rome, in the Portus, of Saint Hyacinth the martyr, who was first thrown into the fire and then hurled into a very strong torrent, from which he emerged unharmed; afterward he was struck with the sword by the consular official Leontius and ended his life. On the Latin Way, of Saints Symphronius, Olympius, Theodolus, and Exuperia, who, burned in the fire, obtained the palm of martyrdom, as is recorded in the Acts of Pope Saint Stephen. [Bouillart adds in Italic type: Translation of Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor.]

VI Kal. Day 27. [Note: [Col. 0301]

Only four manuscripts are pure: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., and Antuerp.-Major.]

[Note: [Col. 0301C]

The first difficulty is whether Usuard enumerated individually the names of the brothers commonly called the Sleepers, since they are distinctly expressed in many manuscripts. Together with the four cited and most reliable witnesses and Munerat, we judge that it should be written as it stands in the text. A second difficulty arises in forming the names of the two companions of Hermolaus, which perhaps only Molan writes correctly: Hermippus and Hermocrates. Nevertheless, because of the unanimous orthography of the other manuscripts, the inferior reading must be followed; all have Hernempi or Ernempi, and all likewise give Hermogratis, except Praten. I am not speaking of those who, having omitted this announcement, substitute another from Ado and mingle other material into our text that conflicts with it. Antuerp.-Major suffers from two faults: at the beginning it inserted “the feast of the seven holy Sleepers,” and at the end, before Etherius, it added “saint.” We excluded Molan because he gives the names of the seven brothers and, in the second announcement, after “capital sentence,” deleted “for confessing Christ.” Greven did the same, in addition to other expansions. Concerning scribal errors in Nicomedia, priest, veins, Auxerre, etc., enough has been said elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0301C]

On 27 June we briefly brought in Ado as celebrating the memory of the seven Sleepers on that day. Here we add that he gives none of their names, which, unless I am mistaken, were first produced by Rabanus. Thus Ado simply says there: “On that day, the deeds of the seven Sleepers,” almost as they are reported in the Corbie Hieronymian manuscript on 10 August. The eulogies of Rabanus and Notker for the aforementioned day, 27 June, compiled from the widely circulated Acts, may be consulted; concerning them, Baronius must certainly be consulted in his notes for this day. Usuard prudently omitted what he perhaps did not judge credible. But as to under whose guidance or authority he placed these seven brothers on this day, despite the silence of all the martyrologists, both earlier and contemporary, no trace appears anywhere by which we can plausibly explain it, unless perhaps he found something in their aforesaid Acts, of whatever kind, that led him to think it belonged here rather than elsewhere; or finally unless he arranged the matter arbitrarily. In any case, we have shown above from the better manuscripts that Usuard did not enumerate all the names of those Sleepers individually. Nor do the names given in Latin agree with the Greek nomenclature, although in the remarkable story they do not differ greatly. Whether the account of Gregory of Tours or of others can add authority to those Acts is sufficiently explained by Baronius; add Tillemont, volume III, beginning at p. 348, and in the notes p. 712.

The Short Roman Martyrology and Ado mention only Hermolaus; the middle-quality manuscripts in the Additions will present his eulogy unchanged. Our author added two companions, taken from the passion of Saint Pantaleon, while removing what is said there concerning Pantaleon himself in the Viennese manuscript. What remains concerning their passion is to be taken from the Acts of Pantaleon. Wandalbert sings only of Hermolaus:

“On the sixth day, the priest and martyr Hermolaus shines forth.”

[Col. 0304A] “In Sicily, of Simeon the monk,” writes the Short Roman Martyrology, followed by Ado; Usuard and Notker follow him, unless one prefers to say that they drew from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which he is recorded in almost the same words. I still do not sufficiently understand why the reformers of the modern Roman Martyrology excluded him from the text. Concerning Etherius of Auxerre, whom Bede, the Short Roman Martyrology, and Ado pass over, it seems certain that Usuard took him from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; Rabanus and Notker likewise mention him. But however each item entered our text, I am certain that what is presented in the entry is truly Usuardine. In our manuscript concerning the bishops of Auxerre, Etherius is known almost by name alone.]

[Note: [Col. 0303A]

ROSWEYD. begins: “On the Latin Way, of Saints Boni the priest, Faustus, Maurus, and seven others, who are described in the Acts of Pope Saint Stephen.” He is deficient in the seven Sleepers; the rest of the text is pure. At the end he adds: “Of Saint Artemia, mother of Saint Nicetius the bishop.”

[Col. 0303B] PULSANEN. is also deficient in the Sleepers; otherwise it is fairly pure.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. read: “At Ephesus, the feast of the seven holy Sleepers, Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine, whose deeds are recorded.” The Adonian text follows: “At Nicomedia, of Saint Hermolaus the priest, through whose teaching blessed Pantaleon was converted to the faith of Christ and completed his life in glorious martyrdom. When he was seized by Maximian, he was punished by capital sentence for confessing Christ.” At the end, Etherius is placed before Simeon.

MUNERAT. is mistaken at the beginning with the words: “The Transfiguration of Christ on Mount Tabor.”

GREVEN. continues the same at greater length: “On Mount Tabor, the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ, when he took Peter, James, and John with him.” He has all the names of the Sleepers and is additionally deficient in the second announcement, in which the words “for confessing Christ” are absent.

MOLAN. likewise has the names of the Sleepers, as stated in the Variants, and also suffers from the same omission as Greven.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., and ALBERGEN. agree with ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. See there.

DANIC., similar to the foregoing, prefixes at the beginning: “At Nicomedia, the passion of blessed Pantaleon, who, seized by Maximian for the faith of Christ, was tortured by the punishment of the rack and the burning of torches, but in the midst of these torments was refreshed when the Lord appeared to him; finally he completed his martyrdom by a stroke of the sword.” See the following day.

CENTULEN.: “At Nicomedia, of Saints Hermolaus the priest, Hernempus, and Hermocrates, brothers, who suffered under Maximian. At Ephesus, of the seven holy Sleepers, namely Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine the martyrs. In Sicily, of blessed Simeon the monk. At Auxerre, of Saint Etherius the bishop.”

[Col. 0303D] BRUXELLEN., after enumerating the names of the Sleepers, adds: “Their deeds are mentioned above on V Kalends of July, on which day almighty God raised them from death to life as a testimony to the resurrection. At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Hermolaus, priest and martyr, through whose teaching blessed Pantaleon was converted to the faith of Christ. And of the blessed brothers Hermippus and Hermocrates. All of them, after being seized and subjected to many punishments, were crowned with illustrious martyrdom by the emperor Maximian and punished by capital sentence for confessing Christ.” Here you see Ado’s text mingled with ours. Simeon follows; concerning him it adds: “He was born at Syracuse in Sicily and, after being confined for a long time in a tower at Trier for Christ, departed to the Lord.” The combination of disparate persons: concerning Simeon of Trier, see 1 June. For it is not likely that these Simeons should be confused, although both were Sicilians. The one is older and perhaps less well known; the other is younger and very well known at Trier. In any case, there is no Simeon on this day in Baronius. The following is: “At Metz, of Saint Frominius, bishop and confessor.” At the end, concerning Etherius, the text is pure.

HAGENOYEN.: “At Ephesus, the feast of the seven [Col. 0304B] Sleepers, Malchus, Maximian, Martinian, Dionysius, John, Constantine, and Serapion. These seven holy men were officials of the court of the emperor Decius; and when he compelled everyone to sacrifice to idols, they fled to a mountain, taking some money with them, and fell asleep in tribulation until the time of the most Christian emperor Theodosius the Great. Before him they asserted that they had been raised up as a demonstration of the future resurrection, because at that time the resurrection of the dead was being attacked by heretics. After they had proved the general resurrection before the emperor and the whole people by the radiance of their faces and their words, they again fell asleep in Christ.” Concerning Hermolaus, he has almost the same material as above from Ado. Then he adds: “On the same day, of the holy martyrs Hernempus and Hermocrates, brothers of Saint Hermolaus the priest, who endured many punishments inflicted on them by Maximian and were finally punished by capital sentence for confessing the name of Christ.” In Simeon and Etherius he is fairly pure.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Lutgardis, virgin (concerning whom, 16 June). Of Beatrice, virgin (see the 29th of this month). Of Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, and four other martyrs. Of Hermolaus with his companions, martyrs in the passion of Pantaleon, the illustrious and glorious young man, whom God miraculously comforted during his passion, and from whose body milk flowed in place of blood.” Referred to the margin with an asterisk, these words leave it uncertain whether they should be assigned to this day or rather to the following day, to which they properly belong.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. differs little from Ado’s text in the entry for Hermolaus; it adds: “Also, at Nicomedia, of the holy martyrs Hernempus and Hermocrates, brothers, beheaded under the emperor Maximian.” It is fairly pure in Simeon and Etherius. Then follows: “At Ephesus, the feast of the seven holy Sleepers on Mount Celyon, in a cave, who were sealed in with square stones by order of Caesar Decius. On the same day, translation of blessed Charlemagne, emperor and confessor, at Aachen.”

BELIN. is pure in the first, second, and third places; in fourth place it has: “At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Pantaleon the martyr, who, when seized,” etc., as Usuard announces in the text on the following day. Instead of Etherius, it writes Ethercius; otherwise it is pure.

GREVEN.: “In Campania, of Saints Felix, Julia, and Jucunda. Also, according to some, on this day the passion of Boni the priest, Faustus, and ten others from the clergy of Pope Saint Stephen, whom Usuard has below, on the Kalends of August. At Metz, of Saint Frominius, bishop and confessor. At Aachen, translation of Saint Charlemagne, emperor and confessor. On the same day, of Guigo, confessor, of holy memory, distinguished in life and learning. After Saint Bruno, he held the priorship of the Great Charterhouse in fifth place; he organized the Constitutions of the Carthusian priors in writing and demonstrated them by his example.”

MOLAN.: “At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Pantaleon the martyr, who, when seized,” etc., as on the following day. “In the city of Noyon, of Felix, Julia, and Jucunda. At Metz, the burial of Saint Frominius, bishop and confessor. Translation of Saint Charlemagne.” Thus the earlier edition. In the others, this is prefixed to the text: “At Nicomedia, the passion of blessed Pantaleon,” and in Italic type, “the glorious martyr. This sacred young man and athlete of Christ, while studying the art of medicine under Hermolaus the priest, was converted to the faith of Christ and performed many miracles.” Then again in ordinary type: “Who, seized for the faith,” etc. And then follows: “At Ephesus, the feast of the saints” (in Italic type, “the seven Sleepers”), “Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, Dionysius, John,” etc. In the rest of the text everything is fairly pure, and at the end concerning Frominius and the translation of Charlemagne, as above.]

[Col. 0301]

At Ephesus, the feast of Saints Maximian, Malchus, Martian, and four others, whose deeds are recorded. At Nicomedia, of the blessed martyrs Hermolaus the priest, Hernempus, and Hermocrates, brothers, who, after suffering many punishments inflicted on them by the emperor Maximian, were punished by capital sentence for confessing Christ. On the same day, in Sicily, of blessed Simeon the monk. At Auxerre, the burial of Etherius the bishop.

V Kal. Day 28. [Note: [Col. 0305]

From Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Major, and Munerat.]

[Note: [Col. 0305C]

They consist almost entirely of scribal errors; to note them is to correct them: “Nichomediam,” “Pantaleonis,” “eculei,” “pena,” “apparente,” “Sansoni,” “beatitudine.” It is uncertain whether Usuard wrote *Lampadum* or rather, with Ado, *Lampadarum*. The latter form is found in Herinien.; the others have the former and therefore have the stronger numerical support. Choose whichever you prefer, but do not read, with Munerat, “the burning of stones.” In Tornacen. the title of bishop is mistakenly attributed to Peregrinus.]

[Note: [Col. 0305C]

It is very well known that the most illustrious martyr Pantaleon, otherwise Pantaleemon, is celebrated in the modern Roman Martyrology on the preceding day, apparently because Baronius made this change in the final revision on the authority of the Greeks. Certainly, among the principal Latin martyrologists, namely the Hieronymian Martyrologies, the Short Roman Martyrology, Florus (in which he is assigned to Lyon), Wandalbert, Ado, and those who follow him, he is explicitly recorded on this 28th day. See Rosweyd’s note on his old Roman Martyrology, p. 219, where, instead of 18 January, you should substitute 18 February, when the memory of his translation is celebrated, as it is recorded there on that day in Greven’s Additions. I do not know what moved Rabanus to place not only Pantaleon but also Hermolaus, Hermippus, and Hermocrates together on 18 February, on which day, unless I am mistaken, only the translation of Pantaleon is celebrated among the people of Cologne. Molan, following Usuard in the first edition, accommodated himself to the Roman Martyrology in later editions; hence Usuardine purity is often lacking in these matters, as we have noted more than once elsewhere. Florentinius collected much concerning the name and relics of Pantaleon, and more will remain for us to explain in the Acts. Meanwhile, what Usuard records in his brief eulogy has been copied entirely from the Viennese manuscript, with an Adonian beginning and ending joined to it, while the intermediate material, which is reported as altered and interpolated by Notker, has been omitted. Even our martyrologists, otherwise sufficiently credulous, seem almost to have doubted the truth of the Acts. Baronius was content to attribute them to Metaphrastes, from whose style they certainly do not depart. But, I confess, they are not a single work; would that even one of them presented a genuine sequence of events! See Tillemont’s judgment, volume V, p. 642. Wandalbert places Pantaleon after Nazarius and Celsus, adding four other verses that have no connection with this day. He sings as follows:

“On the fifth day Nazarius with Celsus possesses this place, and Pantaleon the martyr consecrates it to himself with his own honor.”

Concerning Samson—thus we write the name with all the manuscripts—the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in Florentinius, speak of him as monk, abbot, and bishop; without doubt our author took him from them, unless he recorded him on his own initiative. In any event, all the copies clearly show that he is listed on this day. There exists a lengthy account of his life, which Mabillon preferred to others and illustrated with notes in volume I of the Benedictine *Annals*, beginning at p. 165. Finally, Peregrinus was transferred here from Ado, once again in Ado’s very words. We await from the people of Lyon, if they possess any records concerning this saint, monuments to be illustrated in our Acts. It remains to note that some manuscripts repeat Nazarius and the boy Celsus on this day; we discussed them with Ado and Usuard above, on 12 June. Among these, Praten., as Castellanus writes, displays them in the margin in a very ancient hand, referred by an asterisk * to the second place in the text; Rosweyd, Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Greven, Molan, and others add them at the end. But this repetition of the same saints is far removed from Usuardine simplicity, which throughout this work we have chiefly undertaken to investigate, uncover, and establish; consequently, nothing is lacking here for our purpose.]

[Note: [Col. 0307A]

PRATEN. As I have already said, writes in the margin: “On the same day, the passion of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus.”

ROSWEYD. after the text: “At Milan, of Nazarius the martyr with the boy Celsus.”

PULSANEN. begins: “The feast of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus the boy.” It is fairly pure in Pantaleon and complete in Peregrinus, but says nothing concerning Samson, who is reported second from last.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. at the end: “On the same day, the passion of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus the boy.” The following manuscripts are almost the same.

GREVEN. and MOLAN. add after the text: “At Milan, [Col. 0307B] of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus.”]

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN, and LOVANIEN begin with Pantaleon, with the text. In second place they insert from 12 June:

> “At Milan, the anniversary of blessed Nazarius the martyr, whom Anolinus, during the fury of the persecution aroused by Maximian, tortured for a long time and struck with the sword. Together with him he ordered the most holy boy Celsus, whom Nazarius himself had raised, to be struck with the sword. Their bodies, as blessed Paulinus writes, after having remained hidden until the time of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius, were discovered by blessed Ambrose, the Lord revealing them. At Rome, Saint Victor, pope and martyr. He was the thirteenth after blessed Peter; after ruling the Roman Church for ten years, he was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Severus. Likewise at Rome, at the Ursus Pileatus, Saint Innocent, pope and martyr.”

These two announcements seem to have been translated from Rabanus or Notker. Victor is commemorated on 20 April; Innocent—not a martyr but a confessor—on 12 March. The remainder of the text [Col. 0307C] is sound.

ALBERGEN., similar to the preceding, adds concerning Victor:

> “He established that from the fourteenth day of the first month through the twenty-first, holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday.”

Concerning Innocent it likewise has:

> “He banished many Cataphrygians whom he found in exile to a monastery. And he established that everyone, even one born of a Christian woman, ought to be born again through baptism, which the heretic Pelagius denied and condemned.”

These statements are not sufficiently clear; see Rabanus and Notker.

DANIC. differs in that it dealt with Pantaleon on the preceding day and here begins with Nazarius.

CENTULEN.:

> “At Nicomedia, the passion of Saint Pantaleon the martyr. When, at the command of the emperor Maximian, he was learning the medical art from the presbyter Hermolaus, he was converted to the faith of Christ, performed many miracles, and subjected his father Eustorgius, a senator, to the faith of Christ.”

Place this before the text, and you will have Ado’s [Col. 0307D] eulogy.

> “In Lesser Britain, at the monastery of Dol, Saint Samson, bishop and confessor, a man of admirable virtue and holiness. At Milan, Saints Nazarius and Celsus, martyrs.”

BRUXELLEN adds to the text concerning Pantaleon:

> “His head, together with the bones of blessed Cyprian of Carthage, was sent into France by Aaron Amiras to Charlemagne.”

Concerning Nazarius and Celsus it gives Usuard’s eulogy from 12 June, as above in ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. Then:

> “At Rome, Saint Victor, pope and martyr. After ruling the Roman Church for ten years, he was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Severus. He established that the fourteenth day, etc.”

—as in ALBERG., etc. To these are added:

> “For at that time many bishops of Asia and the East were celebrating Easter with the Jews. At Rome, at the Ursus Pileatus, the anniversary of Saint Innocent, pope and martyr. [Col. 0308A] He sat for fifteen years. He established that the kiss of peace should be given at Mass, and that not only presbyters but also other Christians should use oil consecrated by the bishop for the benefit of the sick. In Lesser Britain, at the monastery of Dol, Saint Samson, bishop and confessor, with six brothers who were likewise holy priests, whom their mother bore in England in a single birth. She was otherwise a matron of great charity and justice. If by chance a woman had borne twins in her womb, she suspected her of fornication, not believing that one woman could conceive several infants at the same time from one man, until she herself experienced God’s power in her own case and gave birth to seven whom she had conceived together. Out of shame she sent them into a reed-bed to be drowned, but they were snatched from danger and brought up by a passing bishop.”

In Peregrino the text is sound.

HAGENOYEN compiles a long eulogy of Pantaleon, which I would rather have read in Metaphrastes. He says that Victor was the twelfth after Saint Peter. Concerning Easter, he has nearly the same as above. He adds:

> “He also established that, when necessity required it, whether in a river, at sea, or in martyrdom, each person should be baptized through the belief of the Christian profession.”

The passage concerning Samson is sound. At the end:

> “At Milan, Saints Nazarius and Celsus, martyrs, under Nero Caesar and the governor Anolinus.”

Peregrinus is absent; he transferred him to the following day.

AQUICINCT at the end has:

> “At Lucas Castle, Saint Ursus the confessor. On the same day, at Milan, Saints Nazarius and Celsus the boy,”

as in the preceding entry.

DAVERONEN after “Peregrinus” has:

> “At Lucas Castle, Saint Ursus the confessor.”

[Col. 0308C] MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Nazarius, Celsus, and Pantaleon, martyrs.”

In the margin concerning the first two is added:

> “Blessed Ambrose discovered their bodies and raised them from the earth.”

REG. SUEC., no. 428:

> “On the same day, Saint Anne the matron, mother of the most glorious mother of God, Mary. In the basilica of Saint Dionysius, the consecration of an altar in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul by blessed Pope Stephen.”

See Wandalbert.

CODEX MONTIS SANCTI:

> “The anniversary of Saint Augustina, virgin.”

This is stated without further specification and supplies little information about this saint.

EDITIO LUBECO.-COL., much interpolated in the entry for Pantaleon, also inserts some material concerning Nazarius and Celsus; see it in Ado, 12 June. Concerning Saint Victor it is similar to ALBERGEN., and likewise concerning Innocent. Then:

> “In Lesser Britain, at the monastery of Dol, Saint Samson, bishop and confessor, whose body was transferred to Orléans.”

In Peregrino it is sound and continues:

> “At Troyes, the deposition of Saint Camelianus, bishop and confessor. At Lucas Castle, blessed Ursus the confessor. On the same day, Saint Botuidus the martyr.”

BELIN dealt with Pantaleon on the preceding day. Here it places Nazarius and Celsus first, as above in ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. It follows with Peregrinus, soundly.

> “On the same day, the passion of Saint Victor, pope and martyr. And of Saint Innocent, pope and martyr. In Greater Britain, Saint Saxon, etc.”

In the second edition it has:

> “In Lesser Britain, Saint Sason.”

See the text. At the end it adds:

> “At Loches Castle, Saint Ursinus the confessor.”

Others have the better reading, “Ursus.”

GREVEN., after those additions to the text mentioned above:

> “At Milan, Saints Nazarius and Celsus, martyrs.”

Thus the Auctarium begins:

> “Note: Nazarius and Celsus suffered here, but on the day before the Ides of June they were discovered. [Col. 0309A] According to some, this is Victor, the first pope and martyr, whom Usuard has on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May. At Rome, at the Ursus Pileatus, Saint Innocent, the first pope and martyr. Usuard and Ado have him on the fourth day before the Ides of March. Botuidus the martyr. At Lucas Castle, Saint Ursus the confessor. On the same day, Saint Augusta, virgin. At Troyes, the deposition of Saint Camalianus, bishop and confessor.”

MOLAN inserts concerning Pantaleon, in different type:

> “The glorious martyr. This consecrated youth and athlete of Christ, while learning the medical art from the presbyter Hermolaus, was converted to the faith of Christ and performed many miracles. When he was seized for the faith of Christ, etc.”

At the end, after “Celsus,” he adds:

> “The boy whom Anolinus,”

and so forth, up to:

> “ordered to be struck.”

Then:

> “On the same day, the passion of [Col. 0310A] Saint Victor, pope. And of Saint Innocent, pope. At Lucas Castle, Saint Ursus the confessor.”

Thus far the first edition; the later editions contain scarcely anything Usuardine. They begin with Samson. Then comes Peregrinus. The entire announcement of Nazarius and Celsus follows, as above. Next:

> “At Rome, the anniversary of Saint Victor, pope. After blessed Peter, the fifteenth, he ruled the Church for ten years and was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Severus. Likewise at Rome, blessed Innocent, bishop.”

Thus far is the text, to which “and martyr” is appended in parentheses and in italic type. Finally, as Auctarium, there is:

> “At Lucas Castle, Saint Ursus the confessor.”

Castellanus interprets the place in French in the Universal Martyrology as “from Loches in Touraine,” in Latin, *Lucis*.

[Col. 0305]

At Nicomedia, the passion of blessed Pantaleon, who, seized for the faith of Christ by Maximian, was tortured by the punishment of the rack and the burning of lamps; but amid these torments the Lord appeared to him and refreshed him. At last he completed his martyrdom by a sword-stroke.

[Bouillart adds in the margin: “On the same day, the passion of Saints Nazarius and Celsus the boy.”]

In Lesser Britain, at the monastery of Dol, Saint Samson, bishop and confessor. On the same day at Lyons, Saint Peregrinus the presbyter, whose blessedness is attested by the glory of miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0305B]

I do not know by what accident Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix entered this article in the Dervensis codex; the Pratensis codex mentions them in the following article. For in this one there is no erasure here and no other leaf. Nor would they have been properly placed here. Thus the Acts read in Monbritius:

> “Then blessed Beatrix, together with the blessed presbyters Crispus and John and other Christians, raised the bodies of the holy martyrs Simplicius and Faustinus from the river Tiber, into which they had been thrown under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, and buried them there in the sixth [milestone] of Philippus, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.”

See also Aringhus, *Roma subterranea*, book II, chapter 20, pages 365–366. If the Acts of those saints published by Monbritius can be trusted, it would be easy to determine in what year they obtained the glory of martyrdom. For those Acts relate that, after Beatrix had performed the last service for her brothers on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, she went to a certain venerable matron named Lucina and stayed with her for seven months; that she was thrown into prison by a certain Lucretius; that at night she was strangled in prison by the servants of that wicked man; and that she was buried by Lucina in the sixth [milestone] of Philippus, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

[Col. 0305C] Thus Beatrix died one year after her brothers. In the same year, it seems, Lucina, terrified by the severity of the punishments and preparing to flee, was warned by Beatrix not to depart, because peace would be granted to the churches of Christ in that month; and that month was August. The death of Maximin, which occurred in August of the year 312 or 313, restored peace to the churches. Simplicius and Faustinus therefore suffered in 311 or 312, while Beatrix suffered in 312 or 313. Tillemont, volume V, page 560, suspects that Beatrix’s prophecy should be understood of the year 305, when Diocletian withdrew from imperial rule. But can the peace that followed that withdrawal be called peace? Moreover, Diocletian withdrew in May, and I have seen nothing in the Acts indicating that Lucina was warned in May. Nor do I think this conjecture is contradicted by the opening words of the Acts: “In the time of Diocletian and Maximian, etc.” For this vague way of assigning the time can just as easily refer to the life of both or either of them as to their imperial rule. And even if the Acts were faulty in this respect alone, I have no doubt that they would be approved by everyone. BOUILLART.]

IV Kal. Day 29. [Note: [Col. 0309A]

The Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, Max.-Lubeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan codices agree. Also Antwerp-Max. and Utrecht.]

[Note: [Col. 0309B]

Munerat and Max.-Lubeck erroneously put *Constantino* for *Constantio*. Greven, Molan, Antwerp-Max., Utrecht, and nearly all the codices of the second class read simply *gloriose occubuit* (“he died gloriously”) instead of *gloriosissime* (“most gloriously”). Munerat alone has: “Likewise on the Via Portuensis.” Greven and Molan somewhat transpose the sentence. Where the others immediately add “in the time of Diocletian” to the names of the martyrs, they transfer it elsewhere, reading:

> “They were ordered to undergo the death sentence in the time of Diocletian.”

In Antwerp-Major the reading is *praefocata in carcerem* (“strangled in prison”). Again, Greven and Molan [Col. 0310B] write *civitate Trecis* (“in the city of Troyes”). The title “bishop,” which is added in Antwerp, Max.-Lubeck, and other middle-grade codices, is absent from all the best codices. In these codices there is also a change: after “confessor” they add, “He, together with blessed Germanus ... and fifty,” etc. Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck indeed write *venit Britanniam* (“he came to Britain”) and omit *venerabiliter* (“reverently”). Antwerp-Major explains it thus: “For fifty [L, i.e. 50] years he reverently fulfilled the office of a priest.” It was accidentally omitted that Antwerp-Max. has *Fausti* for *Faustini*.]

[Note: [Col. 0309C]

The Little Roman Martyrology commemorates today our first martyr Felix in these words:

> “At Rome, Felix, pope and martyr, under Constantius.”

The Hieronymian Martyrology, in my judgment, does not name him. Bede, however, joins a certain Felix to the three who follow, as though he had been their companion and leader. He is likewise associated with them by Wandalbert and in Fronto’s Calendar, making it more than doubtful whether this Felix can truly be understood as a pope. A more precise account is supplied by Ado, from whom Our Author condensed his brief eulogy. The Viennese notes there that Felix was crowned with martyrdom on the fourth day before the Ides of November and buried in the basilica that he had previously built, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. Yet, he says, his anniversary is celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, without assigning any reason for that celebration. See what Florentinius has assembled on this matter, although he does not sufficiently prove that this pope Felix belongs to the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

Moreover, Baronius has discussed at length the many and serious controversies surrounding his Acts; these will have to be examined more fully by us in their proper place. We indicated the disputed question briefly at 30 May, where Felix the pope and martyr was treated. It is perfectly clear that Ado designates Felix II, substituted for Liberius; but scholars have not yet agreed whether this Felix truly belongs among the saints, much less among the martyrs, or indeed whether he can be counted among the Roman pontiffs. Henschenius and Papebrochius formerly touched upon the controversy: the former in the *Tables of the Ancient Pontiffs*, before volume I of April, page XXXI, and in volume III of that month from page 999; the latter most recently in his *Response to Article XI*, beginning at number 116. Felix has very determined adversaries. Among them Tillemont attacks him, with a sharper style than usual, in volume VI at various places, especially from page 778. I do not list more of his compatriots, since they all eagerly incline to the side opposed to Felix. Fronto is milder in his notes on the Calendar, from page 108 onward. We are dwelling on this too long here; in the Acts there will be an opportunity to examine the entire controversy more carefully.

The Hieronymian copies certainly commemorate the three of Porto, although some seem to associate them with companions, as the aforementioned Florentinius explains at greater length. As I said, Bede also mentions the same three; Rabanus follows him, adding more material from the Acts. Ado, receiving the text either from these earlier sources or from the Little Roman Martyrology, honored the brothers with a longer eulogy, of which Our Author compiled an elegant epitome. He also associates them all together, although the summary of the Acts makes it entirely clear that the brothers and their sister suffered on different days.

Baronius’s note on these three saints must certainly be consulted, where he reports their contests in the Acts of Saint Anthimus, in Surius under 11 May. Let the reader consult the appendix in our Acts and the annotation placed there; we refer all these matters to their proper place, where more circumstances concerning the martyrdom and burial of our saints will be examined, as well as the translation carried out by Leo II and the marble tomb—or stone tablet with epitaph—in the sacristy of the Basilica of Saint Mary Major. Tillemont briefly touches upon this from Baronius and Aringhus in volume IV, page 550.

I should also note here that these saints are marked as joined to Pope Felix in the Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, with this difference: in the latter the words “on the Via Portuensis” are added, while they are absent from the former. Tillemont cites the Roman Missal, or the Sacramentary of Thomasius, correctly, for there only the three are commemorated in this form:

> “Simplicius, Faustinus, and Viatrix.”

The codices of the Gregorian Sacramentary are not uniform, as the notes and observations of Menardus, page [Col. 0312A] 171, demonstrate. Certainly, in the printed edition there is no Mass except that of Saint Felix, martyr and pontiff. But enough of this here.

The Hieronymian Martyrologies mention the celebrated Lupus of Troyes; Florentinius considered the mention an addition, at times with excessive scrupulosity. Bede praised him briefly, and the Viennese copied all his words; in Our Author these are abbreviated so that the proper title of bishop is missing. From the authors cited by the aforementioned Baronius one must draw whatever may be useful for illuminating the deeds of this illustrious prelate; these have already been collected with care by Tillemont in volume XVI, from page 126 onward.

For the rest, the entire text is Adonian and thoroughly Usuardine. Notker copied Ado nearly word for word in everything. Wandalbert neatly summed up the matter in two little verses:

> “Felix, Simplicius, Faustinus, and gracious Beatrix,  
> and Lupus of Troyes, jointly adorn the fourth.”  
> [The final reading may be *ornant* (“adorn”).]

[Note: [Col. 0311B]

ROSWEYD adds the title “bishop” to Lupus, which others omit. At the end he adds:

> “Likewise, the anniversary of Olaph, king of the Danes.”

PULSANEN does report all the saints in Our Text, but, in a manner quite familiar to him, truncates all their eulogies.

LEYDEN has a lacuna through the copyist’s fault; otherwise it would belong among the sound copies.

LOVANIEN inserts in second place:

> “The passing of venerable Martha, the hostess of Christ, concerning whom more is found in the Gospel.”

At the end the eulogy of Lupus of Troyes is missing:

> “who came into Britain with blessed Germanus,”

etc.

ALBERGEN is sufficiently sound in the text, but unusually adds a long history of Martha. See GREVEN and the other codices concerning her.

DANIC adds only this to an otherwise sufficiently sound text:

> “In Norway, Saint Olav, king and martyr.”

CENTULEN.:

> “At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, Saint Felix, [Col. 0311C] pope and martyr. On the same day at Rome, Saints Simplicius and Faustinus and their virgin sister Beatrix. At Troyes, Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor, who came into Britain with Saint Germanus and flourished with many virtues.”

The final words of the eulogy could have been added:

> “He spent fifty-two years in the priesthood,”

etc.

BRUXELLEN begins:

> “Saint Martha, virgin, hostess of Christ, and the blessed Lazarus and Mary Magdalene, her sister. And the octave of blessed Mary Magdalene. At Rome, the passion of blessed Serapia, virgin, under the emperor Hadrian. At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the anniversary of Saint Felix II, pope and martyr. He sat for one year. He declared the emperor Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, rebaptized and a heretic. Therefore, in defense of the Catholic faith, he was expelled by that same Constantius Augustus from the papacy and his seat, and finally killed by the sword; he died gloriously.”

It then gives the passage concerning the three of Porto in sound form. Next:

> “At Troyes, the deposition of Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor. He came with blessed Germanus into Britain for the purpose of preaching against the heretics and served reverently in the priesthood for fifty-two years. When Attila, leader of the Huns, was coming to Troyes, Lupus asked him who he was. When Attila replied that he was the scourge of God, Lupus said: ‘And I am Lupus, the disperser of sheep, in need of the scourge.’ Having said this, he opened the gates. Attila and his men entered, passed from gate to gate through the city, saw no one, harmed no one, and then departed. At Orléans, the deposition of blessed Prosper, bishop and confessor.”

See Notker.

> “On the same day, Saint William the confessor.”

HAGENOYEN begins with the three of Porto, in whose account it is somewhat interpolated. He invents some material concerning Felix, not very coherently. It continues:

> “On the same day at Lyons, Saint Peregrinus the presbyter, whose blessedness is attested by the glory of miracles.”

In the account of Lupus [Col. 0312B] it is nearly sound. Concerning Peregrinus, see the preceding day.

AQUICINCT at the end has:

> “On the same day, Saint Olav, glorious king and martyr.”

In a much more recent hand:

> “Likewise, blessed Martha, sister of Saint Mary Magdalene and Lazarus.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., no. 130:

> “On that same day, Saint Serapia, virgin.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Felix [pope], Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix, their sister, martyrs. Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor, a holy man who went into Britain with Saint Germanus. Flora and Lucilla, virgins and martyrs, together with Eugenius the king, who had first taken them captive and afterward suffered martyrdom with them.”

In VATICAN the entry for Lupus is missing. It adds:

> “At Rome, Saint Seraphia, who converted blessed Savina to the faith and afterward suffered under the emperor Hadrian and the judge Berillus.”

ALTEMPS.:

> “Likewise in Norway, Saint Olav, king and [Col. 0312C] martyr.”

Others likewise commemorate him.

FLORENTIN.:

> “Martha . . . . Likewise, blessed Marcella, servant of blessed Martha, who after Martha’s death went to Slavonia and preached the Gospel of Christ there; one year after Martha’s falling asleep, she rested in peace.”

STROZZIAN alone additionally has:

> “In the city of Mamis, Saint Seraphina.”

BIZUNTICEN assigns Saint Lupus of Troyes only forty-two years in the priesthood. Read fifty-two with the others.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. gives a longer eulogy of Martha than can be copied here. The text that follows is almost entirely sound. Then:

> “On the same day, Saint Olan” [Olav], “king and martyr of Norway.”

It also has:

> “At Rome, the passion of Saint Serapia, virgin and martyr.”

BELIN, after a text that is not entirely sound, adds:

> “Likewise on the same day, the feast of Saint Martha, virgin, sister of Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Lazarus, hostess of our Savior Jesus Christ. In the [Col. 0312D] city of Mamis, Saint Seraphina.”

In the second edition it adds:

> “In Norway, the passion of Saint Olav, king and martyr.”

GREVEN:

> “Olav, king and martyr of Norway and Denmark. As soon as he had accepted the faith of Christ, inflamed with zeal for that faith, he proclaimed the Gospel in various parts of his kingdom and won an innumerable people for the Lord. At last, his face veiled, crowned with thorns, and bound to a cross by his own brother on account of the faith of Christ, he yielded up his spirit on a Friday in the year 1026.”

(The first edition records 1028.)

> “At Orléans, the deposition of Prosper, bishop. At Rome, Serapia, virgin and martyr, who suffered here, but was placed in a new tomb on the third day before the Nones of September. In the city of Mametum, Saint Seraphina. Eugenius, king of the Barbarians, Flora and Lucilla, virgins, and many others crowned with martyrdom. In the noble castle of Tarascon, the falling asleep of Saint Martha, hostess of Christ and his apostles. At her funeral, as is read, our Lord Jesus Christ, together with Saint Fronto, bishop of Périgueux, performed the solemn obsequies.”

These matters are to be examined elsewhere.

MOLAN adds concerning Lupus from Ado:

> “In the time of King Attila, who was devastating Gaul, as is sung in his hymn: ‘while they were destroying all things in war, he fortified Troyes by praying.’ And the deposition of blessed Prosper, bishop. Likewise on the same day, the feast of Saint Martha,”

etc., as in BELIN. Likewise concerning Seraphina.

> “In Norway, the passion of Saint Olav, king and martyr. As soon as he accepted the faith, etc.”

This is printed in smaller type, from GREVEN. Then it continues:

> “In the city of Évreux [read Briocensis], Saint William, bishop and confessor of the same city. Innocent IV canonized him at Lyons in the fourth year of his pontificate. At Rome, the holy virgin martyrs Flora and Lucilla, with many others; their passion is extant, and there is a sermon concerning them by Peter Damian. The revelation of the head of blessed John the Baptist, made to King Pepin in Aquitaine.”

Later editions have the same material concerning Lupus, but read, “he fortified Troyes by praying.”

> “At Orléans, the deposition of blessed Prosper, bishop. In Norway, Saint Olav, king and martyr, in the year 1028”

(in the earlier edition it read 1026).

> “In the city of Briocensis, Saint William, bishop and confessor.”

Concerning Seraphina, as above.

> “On the twenty-ninth day, Saint Callinicus, martyr.”

Then in smaller type:

> “At Rome, the holy virgin martyrs Flora and Lucilla, with others, etc. Likewise the revelation, etc.,”

adding at the end concerning the revelation of the head of Saint John the Baptist:

> “Concerning this there is a treatise in the works of the martyr Cyprian.”

GREVEN.:

> “Likewise Saint Tiburtius. At Auxerre, Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor. In Sweden, Brunolph, bishop of Skara and confessor. Lupinus, bishop. In Sweden, Helena, a military woman.”

[Col. 0309]

At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, the anniversary of blessed Felix, pope, who, expelled from his seat by Constantius Augustus for the defense of the Catholic faith and killed by the sword, died most gloriously. Likewise on the Via Portuensis, Saints Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix, martyrs, in the time of Diocletian. After many and various punishments, two of them were ordered to undergo the death sentence. Beatrix, their sister, was strangled in prison in the confession of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0309B]

Apart from the words “in the city of Troyes,” the entire commemoration of Saint Lupus has been covered by erasure. Yet there is no indication or trace of this erasure in either the Dervensis or the Sollerian codices. This circumstance frees the Pratensis codex from every suspicion of interpolation. For even Sollerius could not deny that the erasure is older than any other example and therefore was made by the author himself. If the remaining corrections were written by the same hand as this one, it will be certain that all the corrections were written by the author himself. Whether all belong to the same hand must be left to the judgment of the eyes. BOUILLART.]

At Troyes, Saint Lupus the confessor, who came into Britain after being sent with blessed Germanus. He served reverently in the priesthood for fifty-two years.

III Kal. Day 30. [Note: [Col. 0313]

The Pratensis, Heriniensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan codices are sound.]

[Note: [Col. 0313B]

Herinien and Antwerp-Major read *Sennis*, as it appears in the Pratensis; it cannot be determined from our copy whether this is so. I would prefer *Sennen*, but the other codices agree with the text. We write *Cordula*, as we did above; see the Observations below. In Rosweyd, “by Decius” is missing. Pratensis, Tornacensis, and Munerat read *Romae* (“at Rome”); the others have the better *Romam* (“to Rome”), although Antwerp-Major somewhat alters the sense in these words:

> “At last he brought us to Rome in chains.”

*Aput* is peculiar to Antwerp-Major. We have spoken of Galienus elsewhere. All the codices, like the text, have “and also thrown to the beasts,” except Rosweyd, which inserts the particle *etiam* (“also”):

> “and also thrown to the beasts.”]

[Note: [Col. 0313B]

The most celebrated holy martyrs Abdon and Sennen, says Florentinius concerning this day, received veneration at Rome from the most ancient times and are indicated in all the martyrologies of the Western Church. He adduces other distinguished evidence in their praise from Calendars and Sacramentaries. Accordingly, they are celebrated in succession by the Hieronymian copies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, Notker, and Wandalbert.

Bede’s eulogy was copied by Rabanus and altered by Florus. Our Author also used an abridgment: since he found in Bede the substance of Ado’s encomium, which had been drawn from the Acts of Saint Lawrence repeatedly cited elsewhere, he made the whole of it his own word for word. Notker preferred to follow Ado.

Concerning the city Cordula—whether one inflects it as Corduba, Cerduba, Credula, Corduena, Cerduna, or in any other way—see what was said on 15 and 22 April. As for the Acts, since they were taken from the Laurentian Acts, what should be thought of them must be determined from the authenticity of those sources. See 10 August. Baronius admits that there are ancient manuscripts containing the deeds of our saints that require correction. Tillemont gives very little concerning them, in volume III, pages 328–329.

Yet, as I was saying, their veneration is abundantly established by the most ancient monuments. Nothing is older than the Bucherian Calendar; in it they are expressly announced on this very day in these words:

> “The third day before the Kalends of August: Abdon and Sennen, at the church of Pontianus, which is at the Ursus Pileatus.”

The Calendars of Allatius and Fronto are simpler; they contain only these words:

> “The anniversary of Saints Abdon and Sennen.”

The Sacramentaries of Menard and Thomasius likewise differ only in the way the names are expressed, the latter writing:

> “Abdo and Senis.”

What Tillemont reports concerning the translation of their bodies by Gregory IV, or concerning translations to Florence or Soissons, will be examined more carefully elsewhere.

Wandalbert’s fairly elegant eulogy should not be omitted:

> “Abdon and Zennen, the third day designates the saints,  
> whom Rome, sprung from Persia, assigns to its kingdom.”

The African virgins are announced in this way today by the Hieronymian codices:

> “In Africa, in the city of Tuburtulum of Caesarea, the anniversary of Saints Maxima, Secunda, Donatella, Rufus, etc.”

In some codices fourteen companions are named individually; in the most ancient Epternacensis only nine, who were nearly all gathered by Notker into a single group. Consult Florentinius’s learned Notes concerning them.

The Little Roman Martyrology mentions none of the companions and announces only the virgins in a different form:

> “At Tuburbo of Lucernaria, Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, virgins.”

Florentinius admits that he did not discover this place of contest—or arena—any more than the preceding one. Nor did Usuard remove any obscurity when, omitting Tuburbo, he simply read:

> “In the city of Lucernaria.”

But concerning these matters see the preliminary Commentary on the Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas, 7 March, and what may be reconsidered and debated in its proper place from Ortelius and other geographers concerning one, two, or three Tuburbos or Tuburbis, as well as in the authors cited by us above under that same day, 7 March. There we said that these virgins and martyrs should properly be called *TUBURBITANAE*, “the Tuburbitaean women,” just as they are designated on this day in the Carthaginian Calendar:

> “The holy Tuburbitaean women and Septimia.”

This is sufficient concerning the arena for our present purpose. For more, see the preliminary notice of Ruinart cited elsewhere on the Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas, in the *Selecta*, from page 81 onward. Concerning the text itself, Ado, following the Little Roman Martyrology, compiled from the Acts of the most noble virgins the history of their most courageous struggle. Notker reports it mutilated; Our Author, omitting the circumstances concerning Secunda, who voluntarily joined the earlier captives, and many other details, sampled only what we have elegantly set out in the brief entry.

I do not know whether the Acts that preceded Ado were sufficiently authentic. It is to be hoped that, just as Mabillon discovered the Acts of Crispina, which mention three of our saints, someone may also find the passion of the Tuburbitaean women. See the notes of the aforementioned Mabillon on the Carthaginian Calendar, volume III of the *Analecta*, page 409; Ruinart, in the *Selecta*, from page 493.]

[Note: [Col. 0315A]

PULSANEN is sound in the first announcement and has nothing concerning the second.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., UGHELLIAN., and BELIN at the end have:

> “At Auxerre, Saint Ursus, bishop.”

See the Roman Martyrology.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN, LOVANIEN, ALBERG., and DANIC. differ from the others by a single word, for they read:

> “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Ursus, bishop.”

CENTULEN.:

> “At Rome, Saints Abdon and Sennen, martyrs and petty kings, whom Caesar Decius ordered to be brought before him from Corduba, a city of Persia. In Africa, in the city of Lucernaria, Saints Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, virgins. They suffered [printed *passi*, for *passae*] under Gallienus and the judge Anolius. At Auxerre, Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor. [Col. 0315B] On the same day, the vigil of Saint Germanus, most illustrious in birth, faith, doctrine, and the glory of miracles.”

BRUXELLEN, slightly interpolated in the text, has at the end:

> “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor. And at Trier, blessed Pantho, presbyter.”

Unless I am mistaken, he meant Banto, concerning whom others speak on the following day.

HAGENOYEN, also somewhat expanded in the text, adds at the end:

> “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor.”

AQUICINCT has the smaller reading “or Decius” written above the name Gallienus. At the end:

> “And Saint Ursus, bishop of Auxerre.”

Nearly all note this.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., no. 130:

> “On the same day, Saint Ursus, bishop of Auxerre.”

AMBIANEN:

> “On the same day, the vigil of Saint Germanus, bishop, most illustrious in birth, faith, doctrine, and the glory of miracles. He has the feast of his burial on the Kalends of October, when the more solemn day is also celebrated.”

See, therefore, what we shall say with Usuard on the following day. [Col. 0316A] And again what is reported in various places on 1 October concerning his translation.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Abdon and Sennen, martyrs. Martha, hostess of Christ.”

Concerning her, see the preceding day.

> “Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, virgins and martyrs.”

VATICAN, no. 5949:

> “At Auxerre, Saint Ursus, bishop.”

I have already said that this recurs in various places.

ALTEMPS.:

> “In Kent, the deposition of Saint Tadwin, bishop and confessor.”

See Castellanus.

FLORENTIN. It is doubtful whether they refer to this day or the following day what they place in this form:

> “At Rome, on the Via Latina, Saint Tertullinus the martyr, in an underground crypt, as is read in the deeds of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr.”

Florus notes him on this very day with a eulogy; others on 4 August, and we there, with Usuard.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL., after “they were killed by the sword,” adds:

> “And they were thrown before an image of the Sun, where they lay unburied for three days; the subdeacon Quirinus secretly buried them.”

In the second announcement the text is sufficiently sound. At the end, together with the other codices, it adds:

> “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN.:

> “Likewise Saint Tiburtius. At Auxerre, Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor. In Sweden, Brunolph, bishop of Skara and confessor. Lupinus, bishop. In Sweden, Helena, a military woman.”

MOLAN: “At Auxerre, [the commemoration] of Saint Ursus, bishop.” Then, in smaller letters, he described Brunolphus and Helena, as GREVEN has them. Finally he adds: “On the same day at Assisi, the feast of Saint Rufinus the martyr.” Later editions have the material on Ursus and Brunolphus as above. “Likewise, in Sweden, of Blessed Helena.” And in smaller type only this: “At Assisi, the feast of Saint Rufinus the martyr.” Regarding the Roman Martyrology, Baronius notes that a sermon by Peter Damian exists about him. See Surius.]

[Col. 0313]

At Rome, the feast of the holy petty kings Abdon and Sennen, who, while suffering imprisonment in the city of Cordula in Persia under Decius, were finally brought to Rome in chains, weakened by various punishments; there they were first beaten with leaded clubs and then killed with the sword. In the African city of Lucernaria, of the holy virgins Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, who during the persecution of Gallienus were first given vinegar and gall to drink, then beaten with savage blows, tortured by stretching on the rack, afterward burned on grates, and also thrown to the beasts; but when the beasts left them unharmed, they were finally slaughtered with the sword.

The day before the Kalends. Day 31. [Note: [Col. 0315C]

The Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., and Antuerp. codices agree, as do Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., [Col. 0316C] Greven., and Molan. To these may be added Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., and Danicus.]

[Note: [Col. 0315C]

You should note that the Tornacen. codex is entirely sound, but at the beginning treats Saint Germanus, doubtless according to the usage of that church. Antuerp. reads Fabiani. In Belin, ferre is absent. Herinien. has “thrust into prison.” Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and the remaining middling-quality codices alter the sense somewhat as follows: “Then, having been questioned once and again, since he persevered in the confession of Christ”; Antuerp.-Max. has “persisted.” Some have “then he was condemned.” The reading in the text is better, [Col. 0316C] deriving from Ado’s phrase. In Pratensi there is Sinada; in Munerat., Sinnenda; in Belino, Synoda and Cinoda. Others have Sumada, Synnada, and so forth. In the text we follow the better witnesses. There is no less variation in the name Democritus. For this, Tornacen. has Dimocritus; Max.-Lubec., Democertus; Antuerp.-Max., with some others, Demotricus; [Col. 0316D] Danicus, Democritus. The text’s reading seems certain. I pass over the matters of Caesarea, “is condemned,” Auxerre, Dionysius, and so on.]

[Note: [Col. 0315D]

The Hieronymian Martyrologies have nothing here about Fabius, nor does Bede, or Bede’s followers Florus and Rabanus. Accordingly, the first notice is owed, as to its source, to the Little Roman Martyrology, which writes: “At Caesarea, of Fabius the martyr.” From this source Ado borrowed it and adorned it with a historical panegyric, the earlier and more important part of which Usuard transferred into his own text, while Notker, as usual, thrusts his sickle more freely into another’s harvest. [Col. 0316D] Peter records nothing about Fabius in his Catalogue, nor does Surius, apart from Ado’s sole eulogy, which Henschenius illustrated with a brief commentary, assigning him as a martyr to Caesarea in Mauretania. The Acts that we possess from the Mossiacensis codex in D. Joly, transcribed by Papebrochius, seem to display not the character of a serious narrative but rather the ornamentation of an exuberant pen exercising its style, by which Ado’s eulogy is rhetorically expanded. [Col. 0317A] Wandalbertus speaks metrically only of Fabius:

“On the eve, pious glory covered Fabius with martyrdom;

July, passing away, leaves these solemn rites to the world.”

Ado commemorates the most glorious bishop Germanus on this day in the briefest terms: “At Auxerre, of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor.” The rest concerning that most celebrated defender of the faith he treats at length on the Kalends of October; Usuard therefore seems to have taken his brief eulogy from there. The Hieronymian Martyrologies correctly record Germanus on this day as well. Bede joins him on the following day with Eusebius of Vercelli, whose words Rabanus transferred from there to this day; from Rabanus, unless I am greatly mistaken, Notker took what he reports about Germanus on this day too, observing that his feast is celebrated more solemnly by the Gallican churches on the Kalends of October—almost as we noted on the preceding day among the additions from the Ambianensis codex. Surius published the Life of Germanus written by Constantius; we possess it in manuscript [Col. 0317B], also with the verse version attached by Ericus, [Col. 0318A] together with several other documents concerning the saint’s deeds, which Tillemont excerpted in volume XV, beginning at page 1. See Baronius’s note.

The final class of martyrs seems to have flowed directly from the Hieronymian Martyrologies into Usuard, since nothing is read about them either in the Little Roman Martyrology or in Ado. Rabanus also mentions them, as does Notker; both read “in the African city of Sinnada,” adding their companion Thyrsus, so that there can be no doubt that Notker took this material from Rabanus. “It is remarkable,” says Florentinius, “how greatly the codices differ among themselves in assigning the place of the saints’ contest,” and so forth. I would believe that Usuard had also noticed this long ago and, perhaps doubting whether they should be assigned to Phrygia or Africa, cut through the knot of the difficulty by withdrawing them from either region and writing simply “Sinnada.” Whether Baronius was right to add “of Phrygia” or “in Phrygia,” or whether rather, following Florentinius’s view, these martyrs should be assigned to Africa, will be examined in its proper place. Meanwhile the evidence of our codices is clear, and the reading of the whole Usuardine text remains secure.]

[Note: [Col. 0317B]

ANTUERP.-MAJ., just as it was expanded in England, here too—as has often been observed above concerning other saints—adds an English saint to the text, in these words: “On the same day, of Saint Neot, priest and confessor.”
