ROSWEYD. alters Germanus’s eulogy, for after “bishop” he adds: “Who often defended the Catholic faith against the Pelagian heresy.” The entire final notice is absent.

PULSANEN. lacks the first notice concerning Fabius; everything else is sound.

CENTULEN.: “At Ravenna, a city of Italy, the passing of Saint Germanus, an apostolic man, a wondrous teacher of the Church and adorned with every wisdom. At Caesarea, of Saint Fabius the martyr. In the city of Sinnanda, of the holy Democritus, Secundus, and Dionysius.”

BRUXELLEN. begins with Germanus and, after “most illustrious,” adds: “Who died at Ravenna, but whose body, with the splendor of miracles, was brought back to Auxerre.” [Col. 0317C] The remainder of the text is almost sound.

HAGENOYEN., in its first and last parts fairly sound, has the following about Germanus: “At Ravenna, the passing of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor of Auxerre. He was noble by birth, born at Auxerre, educated in liberal studies in Gaul and in the science of law at Rome; there he obtained the dukedom of Burgundy, and in his youth devoted himself more to vanity than to the Christian religion. Later Bishop Amator ordained him cleric against his will. After becoming a cleric, he never consumed wheat bread, wine, vinegar, oil, pulses, or salt for seasoning; he always fasted until evening, and sometimes fasted from Thursday until Sunday; he mixed ashes into his bread. In summer and winter he had no clothing except a hair shirt, tunic, and hood; he used neither bed nor pillow, never removed his clothing, and rarely removed his shoes or belt, and in the community of the brothers he led a hermit’s life. Twice he went to England against the heretics, and in various places raised three dead persons. Finally, in the house of Queen Placida (Placidia), he raised her dead donkey and, departing from her, died at Ravenna in the thirtieth year of his episcopate.”]

VICTORIN. and REG. SUECIAE, sign. no. 130, at the end: “Likewise, of Saint Serapia with her three daughters, Pistis, Elpis, and Agape.” On the following day the mother is called Sophia, otherwise Sapientia.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Germanus, bishop and confessor. Of Fabius the martyr. Likewise, of Democritus, Secundus, and Dionysius.”

VATICAN., no. 5949, lacks the final notice; in its place it substitutes: “In the castle of Saint Agnellus, the feast of Saint Dodo, abbot.”

[Col. 0318B] ALTEMPS.: “In the city of Canterbury, of Saint Catwin, archbishop and confessor. Likewise, of Critullinus the martyr.” Is this not Tertullinus, concerning whom the preceding day was discussed?

LUXOVIEN.: “At the Medianum monastery, the burial of the blessed confessors John, priest, and Benignus, deacon, who, brothers in flesh and spirit, were educated by Blessed Hidulf, archbishop of Trier; departing together, they were buried in a single mausoleum.”

ABDINGHOFFEN.: “At Trier, of Saint Banto, confessor of Christ.” Others write “of Banti and Panthon.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins: “At Ravenna, the passing of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor of Auxerre, most illustrious in the time of the emperor Valerian [Valentinian] by birth, faith, doctrine, and the glory of miracles. From the time of his episcopal consecration for thirty years he tormented his body so cruelly that he never ate wheat bread, wine, vinegar, oil, [Col. 0318C] pulses, or salt for seasoning. He drank no wine except once at the feasts of Easter and the Nativity of Christ, and then only a great deal diluted with water. He always fasted and ate only in the evening, and at his meal he always set ashes before himself. He had no clothing apart from a hair shirt, tunic, and hood, which clung to his body until they were loosened by excessive wear; and just as he was noble by birth, so he was distinguished in faith, doctrine, and the glory of miracles. His mother, named Placida, buried his most holy body with her own hands.” The rest of the text is fairly sound. At the end it adds: “At Trier, of Saint Banto the confessor. On the same day, of Saint Neot, abbot and confessor”; Castellanus reads Neothus.

GREVEN.: “Of Tertullinus, priest and martyr (concerning whom in the Acts of Blessed Stephen the pope); here, his burial. Yet, according to Ado, on the day before the Nones of August there is a more solemn gathering at his tomb. Likewise, of Saint Thyrsus. On the same day, of Saint Fantinus the confessor. From childhood he lived a holy life; when he was twelve years old, he converted his father Fantius and his mother Deodata to the faith. With them he was seized for the faith of Christ, beaten with leaded clubs, and thrown into prison. Finally, when his parents completed their martyrdom by decapitation, Fantinus was freed by an angel; renowned for miracles, he rested in peace. At Trier, of Panthon [otherwise Banto], priest and confessor. In England, of Neot, abbot and confessor. Of Morandus the confessor. Of Flora, virgin and martyr.”

The first edition of MOLAN adds at the end only: “At Trier, of Saint Banto, confessor of Christ.” In the others, however: “At Milan, the birth of Saint Calimerus, bishop and martyr. In England, of Blessed Neot, a priest distinguished for merits and miracles.” Concerning Banto, as above. “In Calabria, in the town of Tabritanum, of Saint Fantinus, confessor of Syracuse, whose parents Fantius [Col. 0319A] and Deodata, because they refused to sacrifice to the gods, were beaten with leaded clubs and beheaded at Syracuse. On the thirty-first day, of Saint Eudocimus, holy and just.” Then, in smaller type: “At Rome, the most blessed Ignatius of Loyola died, founder of the Society of Jesus, which he saw multiplied throughout almost the whole world. He also learned that many thousands of barbarians had through it been recalled from the depths of barbarism to submit to the gentle yoke of Christ. For all his counsels and efforts were directed toward preserving, restoring, and multiplying through himself and his followers the purity of the Catholic faith.” To the greater glory of God.]

[Col. 0315]

At Caesarea, the passion of Fabius the martyr. When he refused to carry the standards of the governor, he was first thrust into prison for several days; then, questioned once and again, he persevered in the confession of Christ. Soon he was condemned to death by the judge. At Ravenna, the passing of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, most illustrious by birth, faith, doctrine, and the glory of miracles. In the city of Sinnada, of the holy Democritus, Secundus, and Dionysius.

THE MONTH OF AUGUST. IT HAS THIRTY-ONE DAYS.

[Col. 0319]

On the Kalends. Day 1. [Note: [Col. 0319]

The Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Major., Greven., and Molan. codices are sound.]

[Note: [Col. 0319B]

The remaining codices read Vercelli, following Praten. and Herinien. Others generally read Vercellis more correctly. Greven. has “under the ruler Constantius”; Molan., “under the ruler Constantine”; Antuerp.-Maj. omits principe but retains Constantino. The others simply have the form found in the text. I write Scitopolis with Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., and most of the others. Pratensis has Scithopolis, Greven. Scytopolis, and Molan. Schytopolis. All have Spei, Fidei, and so forth, except Antuerp.-Maj., which, with some others, places Fidei first. In Antuerp.-Maj. the construction is broken: “whom the judge Dacianus,” with the verb iussit omitted. Molan. has Decianus, if I am not mistaken through a typesetter’s error. Then, with Greven, it reads “to be torn away by chains,” instead of “by claws.” Both likewise have “the wounds being renewed for so long”; Herinien., “the wounds restored by blows.” Pratensis and Antuerp.-Maj. correctly agree with Ado, as in the text. But Antuerp.-Maj. incorrectly has reddit for reddidit. Antuerp.-Maj. consistently writes Filadelfia; Herinien., Filadelphia; I prefer the other three. Pratensis alone reads “in the Parisian territory,” almost against everyone else. In Antuerp.-Maj. the name Justinus is not distinguished. It likewise has Bisuino and Menesii; Greven., Lisuyno. The authority of the codices supports the text; I have considered the other minor details unworthy of notice.]

[Note: [Col. 0319B]

The text is scarcely more extensive anywhere in the year, yet it is derived for the most part from the customary sources, especially Ado. That the Maccabean brothers were always held in great veneration from the earliest centuries of the Church is demonstrated by the encomia of the Fathers collected by Florentinius and by the agreement of our martyrologists. The Hieronymian Martyrologies [Col. 0319C] in particular commemorate them in fuller language, which entered the middling-quality codices. Our author follows Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado only very briefly, differing from them in announcing them first. You may read more in their praise in Florentinius, who enumerates individually the names of the mother and sons. Notker also attempted something beyond Ado.

Again, the Hieronymian Martyrologies relate more about the dedication of the first church by Blessed Peter and about release from the Chains; these matters were also somewhat expanded by Notker, while Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado dispose of them very briefly, exactly as they are read in the text. The learned Florentinius discusses the first church dedicated by Peter at Rome. Eusebius of Vercelli is marked in the Hieronymian Martyrologies as a confessor. Bede, by whom we recently said Eusebius was joined to Germanus of Auxerre, expressly says that he suffered martyrdom when the Arians stirred up persecution. Consult Tillemont, volume VII, page 529 onward. The Little Roman Martyrology alone says: “At Vercelli, of Eusebius, bishop.” The Viennese title connects both descriptions, and all our material was taken from it once the doubts had been removed. [Col. 0319D] Notker explains both how he suffered martyrdom and how, in the peace of the Church, he completed the course of his confession. For what has been said thus far, Surius supplies documents, and Wandalbertus agrees with our sources, beginning August in this way:

“August, now filled with ripe grain,

Let us show in song which saints new rites commemorate:

Those whom savage Antiochus forced to death with their mother,

Who willingly dedicated their blood to Christ who was to come,

The Maccabees rightly hold the August Kalends.”

“Rome celebrates Peter in prison, restored from his chains;

And Vercelli duly frequents its own Eusebius.”

There follow the virgin sisters with their widowed mother. I confess that I do not know where Usuard obtained them, since they are unknown to all the older Martyrologies. I am aware that on 23 June three sisters are listed among the additions, bearing the same Greek names—Pistis, Elpis, and Agapis—and that there Notker, and he alone, says that they suffered at Nicomedia. Baronius sufficiently indicates in his Notes that he found them in Usuard, as is clear from our codices. But why he separated the mother from the daughters and relegated her to 30 September, I have not yet sufficiently determined. It is scarcely worth mentioning, much less refuting, the absurdities invented by Geddes on the occasion of these holy women. I would readily believe that Usuard found some Acts, such as those preserved by Surius, and from them placed their commemoration together on this day. I refrain from discussing more here; they will be examined expressly elsewhere. Meanwhile, let the curious reader see what we said about Sophia and her daughters in the Chronology of the Alexandrian Patriarchs, p. 18, no. 92.

The following class, concerning Bonus and his fellow martyrs, likewise does not come from the usual sources. Among the older writers it is recorded only by Florus, published together with Bede, and in language so different from ours that it is entirely impossible to think that Usuard received it from that writer. We must therefore suppose that it was transferred from the Acts of Saint Stephen himself. Concerning Felix, there is no doubt that the notice derives from Ado; from his longer eulogy, copied by Notker, Our author composed his abridgment. Felix is also known from the Hieronymian Martyrologies and from the Florus just cited. As for whether Ado assigned the day accurately, see Florentinius and the Acts, which are to be elucidated in their proper place; [Col. 0322A] their authority will be discussed there. Certainly what Prudentius and Gregory of Tours relate cannot be called into question.

Among the Philadelphians there is likewise some difficulty concerning the Synod mentioned by the Hieronymian Martyrologies and distinguished by Notker from our own martyrs; Florentinius carefully investigates this matter, as well as the Councils of the Martyrs. As far as our subject is concerned, the Little Roman Martyrology mentions them without giving the individual names; Ado restored those names, having found them elsewhere, and Usuard took all the words of his notice from Ado. Justinus and Nemesius, who close the procession, seem first to have been brought into the sacred calendar by Usuard. Whatever may have grown beyond the customary bounds in the text, we nevertheless judge the whole of it to be genuinely and simply Usuardine.]

[Note: [Col. 0321B]

TORNACEN. begins: “At Rome, at Saint Peter at the Chains.” Then it treats the Maccabees soundly. It abridges Eusebius’s eulogy. It is sound in the virgins and likewise in Justinus. All the remaining material is absent, replaced by: “At the castle of Corbeil, of Saint Exuperius, bishop and confessor, whose body, driven from the city of Rennes by the persecution of the Danes and honorably received by the inhabitants of Gaul, is venerated at the aforesaid place with great devotion.”

ROSWEYD. begins: “At Rome, at the Chains of Saint Peter.” It is good in the Maccabees. The notices of Hope and the others, and of Bonus and his companions, are absent; so is that of Nemesius.

PULSANEN.: “At Rome, the release of Blessed Peter the apostle from his chains.” It is fairly sound in the Maccabees and Eusebius. The eulogy of Bonus and his companions is absent, as is everything that follows.

MUNERAT., in second place: “At Rome, of Saint Peter at the Chains.” The rest is fairly sound; at the end it has almost the same material as TORNACEN above concerning Exuperius, whom the REG. SUEC. codex, under note no. [Col. 0321C] 128, also announces in the same way.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJ., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. begin: “At Rome, of Saint Peter at the Chains.” Then, with the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “At Antioch, the passion of the seven holy Maccabean brothers with their mother, who suffered under King Antiochus.” The remaining material follows fairly soundly, except that the two final notices are missing.

LOVANIEN., similar to the preceding, has the additional defect of lacking Felix’s eulogy.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, at the Chains of Saint Peter, a festive and solemn gathering. At Antioch, of the holy Maccabees. In the Italian city of Vercelli, of Saint Eusebius, bishop and martyr. In the Arabian city of Philadelphia, of the holy martyrs Cyril, Aquila, Peter, Domitila, Rufus, and Menander, crowned on one day. In the territory of Paris, of Saint Justin the martyr. In the district of Silvinus, of Saint Nemesius the confessor. At Rome, on the Latin Way, of the holy martyrs Bonus, priest, Faustus, and Maurus, with seven others. Likewise at Rome, of the holy virgins Faith, Hope, and Charity, and their mother Sophia, who suffered under the emperor Hadrian. In Spain, in the city of Gerona, of Saint Felix the martyr.” In a much later hand in the margin is added: “At the castle of Corbeil, of Saint Exuperius the confessor.” He was bishop of Bayeux; see above.

BRUXELLEN.: “At Rome, Saint Peter at the Chains: for the pope placed in the church a triple chain made from the two chains with which Herod had bound Blessed Peter and from the one with which he himself had been bound under Nero; he dedicated that church on the Kalends of August in honor and under the title of Blessed Peter at the Chains.” Concerning the Maccabees it has the same material as ANTUERP. and the others above. The Philadelphians follow, fairly soundly. Eusebius is moderately interpolated; the sections on Felix, the three virgins and their mother, and Bonus and his companions are fairly correct. It then adds: “In Aquitania, in the city of [Col. 0322B] Vienne, of Saint Severus, bishop, who was one of the disciples of the apostles. And of Saint Nectarius, bishop. At Ghent, the translation of the body of Saint Bavo the confessor.” He is celebrated on 1 October.

HAGENOYEN.: “At Antioch, the feast of the holy martyrs, the seven Maccabean brothers with their mother, who suffered under the Old Testament. But the Church venerates their martyrdom in memory of all the Fathers of the Old Testament. The passion of these holy Maccabees is contained in the Second Book of Maccabees. At Rome, of Saint Peter at the Chains. This feast was once celebrated in honor of Octavian Augustus, prince of the Romans; Eudoxia, together with Pope Pelagius, abolished it and established its celebration in memory of the prince of the apostles. Thus the queen, coming from Jerusalem, brought the chains with which Peter had been bound by Herod, and the pope immediately brought forth the chain with which Peter had been bound by Caesar Nero in Rome. These two chains were miraculously joined into one [the text has: ‘was miraculously joined’].” [Col. 0322C] The section concerning the virgins follows, and has been interpolated. Then the material on Bonus and his companions, the Philadelphians, and likewise Justinus and Nemesius, is fairly sound. Everything else is absent.

AQUICINCT., before the commemoration of Blessed Eusebius of Vercelli, inserts: “At Marciana, the burial of Saint Jonatus, abbot.” For Nemesius it has Nenesii. At the end: “Likewise, of Saints Freardus and Secundellus.” From Gregory of Tours, On the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 10.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., sign. no. 130, at the end: “In Italy, the feast of Saint Justa.”

DAVERONEN.: “In the Parisian territory, of Justinus the martyr.” What it has concerning the rest is uncertain.

MATRIC.-CARTUS., ULTRAJECT.: “Of Peter at the Chains. Of the holy Maccabean brothers. Of the virgins Faith, Hope, and Charity, and their mother Sophia, martyrs. Of Eusebius of Vercelli, bishop and martyr.” It is clear that the text is badly mutilated.

In VATICAN., no. 5049, the virgins, Justinus, and Nemesius are absent. It adds: “In Italy, of Saint [Col. 0322D] Justa the virgin.”

UGHELLIAN. also lacks the commemorations of Justinus and Nemesius. See ANTUERP. and the others.

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, of Bonus the priest, Faustus, Maurus, Primitivus, Calumniosus, John, Exuperantius, Quirillus, and Honoratus . . . . In Italy, of Saint Justa the virgin. Likewise, of Saint Ruphinianus (MEDICAEUS reads Ruffinianus), bishop and confessor, disciple of Saint Peter the apostle.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. has sufficiently treated the Chains and the Maccabees. The text then continues through the Philadelphians, inclusively. Then: “In England, of Saint Ethelwold, bishop and confessor.” Next, the notice of Justinus, soundly. Afterward: “At Vienne, of Saint Severus, bishop and confessor, who was one of the disciples of the apostles. At Bourges, of Blessed Arcadius, bishop and confessor. At Soissons, of Blessed Bandaridus, bishop and confessor. In the district of Lisy, of Blessed Nemesius the confessor. On the same day, of Saint Nectarius, bishop and confessor. On that day, of Saints Friardus [Col. 0323A] and Secundellus, confessors. Likewise, of Blessed Facinola, virgin. And of Saint Justa, matron.”

BELIN. begins and reads concerning the Chains and the Maccabees as ANTUERP. and the others. It is sound in Eusebius, the virgins, Bonus and his companions, and the Philadelphians; it adds: “In Italy, of Saint Justa the virgin.” It is sound in Justinus. “In the district of Tisuinus, of Saint Menesius the confessor.” Felix appears last, without a eulogy. The second edition places the Maccabees “At Jerusalem,” and so forth. In other respects it resembles the first, but at the end adds: “In the territory of Blois [clearly, of the city], of Saint Bethasius the confessor.” Castellanus reads Betarius.

GREVEN.: “Likewise, of Saints Primitivus, Calumniosus, John, Exuperantius, Quirillus, Theodosius, Castus, Basilius, and Honoratus, concerning whom in the Acts of Blessed Stephen. At Vienne, of Saint Severus, bishop and confessor, disciple of the apostles. At Bourges, of Saint Arcadius, bishop and confessor. At Soissons, of Saint Bandaridus, bishop and confessor. Of Exuperius, bishop of Bayeux and confessor. In Britain, of Ethelwald, bishop and [Col. 0323B] confessor. Of Nectarius, bishop. Of Friardus and Secundellus, confessors. Of Justa the martyr, mother of Saint Sylvester, thrown into a well. Of Facinola the virgin. At Verona in Italy, of Saint Mary the virgin, surnamed the Consoler.”

MOLAN.: “At the castle of Corbeil,” and so forth, as in TORNACEN. [Col. 0324A] above. “At Ghent, the elevation of Saint Bavo, the pious confessor. At Rome, the dedication of the first church constructed and consecrated by Blessed Peter. At Blandinium, the translation of Saint Winwaloc, abbot.” Then, in smaller type: “In Britain, of Ethelwald, bishop and confessor, in the city of Winchester; his deeds were written by Wulstan, cantor of Winchester. Of Saint Secundellus, abbot, and Friardus, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes. On the same day, the feast of Saint Jonathus the confessor, disciple of Saint Amandus.” In other editions he inserts in italics the material about the Maccabees found in ANTUERP. and the others, and adds “and their teacher Eleazar.” Of Eusebius, “and confessor”; and concerning the virgins, their Greek names, together with the statement that “they were Milanese by nation.” Finally, concerning Justinus: “whose body rests in the great church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Paris.” Then at the end: “At the castle of Corbeil,” and so forth. Likewise: “Of Friardus and Secundellus. In Britain, the feast of Saint Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester and confessor. At Marciana, the burial of Saint Jonatus, abbot.” Concerning Bavo, Winwaloc, [Col. 0324B] and the dedication of the first church by Blessed Peter, as above. Finally: “On the first day, the procession of the venerable pieces of the venerable and life-giving Cross.” This is taken from the Greek Horologion, which we have discussed several times elsewhere.]

At Antioch, the feast of the holy Maccabees. At Rome, at Saint Peter at the Chains. In the Italian city of Vercelli, of Blessed Eusebius, bishop, who, because of his confession of the faith, was exiled by Constantius to Scitopolis and thence to Cappadocia; afterward he returned to his church and, finally, when the Arians were persecuting him, suffered martyrdom. Likewise at Rome, the passion of the holy virgins Hope, Faith, and Charity and their mother Sophia, who under the emperor Hadrian obtained the crown of martyrdom. On the Latin Way, of the holy martyrs Bonus, priest, Faustus, and Maurus, with seven others, who are described in the Acts of Pope Stephen. In the Spanish city of Gerona, the feast of Saint Felix, whom the judge Dacianus, after inflicting various kinds of torture, ordered to be torn with claws and then mangled to the bones, and the wounds to be renewed with further wounds until he surrendered his unconquered spirit to Christ. In Arabia, in the city of Philadelphia, of the holy martyrs Cyril, Aquila, Peter, Domicianus, Rufus, and Menander, crowned on one day. In the Parisian territory, of Justinus the martyr. In the district of Lisuinum, of Saint Nemesius the confessor.

The fourth day before the Nones. Day 2. [Note: [Col. 0323]

The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0323C]

We have mentioned the Cemetery of Callistus elsewhere and shall do so again; in the text I follow the reading found in the greater number of codices. Pratensis reads Cemeterio, Herinien. cymiterio, though they are not always consistent with themselves. Calixti is found in all except Pratensis. All write Cum insequeretur in the passive voice. But what are we to make of this phrase: “In the same place, just as in his seat he is beheaded”? Ado does not have it so, but more elegantly: “In the same place, they beheaded him in his seat.” Yet our construction is found in almost all the codices, with only this difference: Munerat., Greven., and Molan. read “he was beheaded in his seat,” and Tornacen. “Thus in his seat”; for the fact that Herinien. also has sic is clearly due to the error of an over-clever corrector, since two letters, ut, have been erased. [Col. 0324C] We therefore suppose that Usuard, although incorrectly, nevertheless wrote it as we have placed it in the text. Molan. alone correctly has Bithynia; Munerat. incorrectly has Bitinia; the others agree with the text, except that Pratensis seems to put Bithyniae in the oblique case. It likewise reads Euodus or Evodus, together with Munerat. Greven. distorts the sense by reading “the consular [official] first acted in Bithynia,” and with Molan. at the end has “he ordered him to be consumed”; Antuerp.-Maj., with all his sons, a reading also found in Pratensis marked B. Concerning solempnia, solemnia, sollemnia, Nicea, cedi, and other matters of this kind, I do not think it worthwhile to make further notes.]

[Note: [Col. 0323C]

The Acts of Blessed Stephen the pope have been cited above more than once and will be cited again. From them not a few martyrs, whether jointly or separately, are drawn out for their respective days; you will find most of them collected by Molan on this day in his annotation, while we have distributed them among their proper feasts according to Usuard’s arrangement. The Hieronymian copies also commemorate Stephen himself here, though they do not express his dignity very distinctly. Bede more clearly and explicitly calls him pope and martyr, adding a brief eulogy transferred by Rabanus. This subsequently, I do not know how, passed into almost all the middling-quality Usuardine codices, which deviate from the pure text in this respect alone. But it is evident that Usuard did not take his material from Bede but from Ado, since he imitates Ado’s phrase and words with the greatest precision. There is scarcely any doubt that the passage flowed from the Little Roman Martyrology into Ado, where it reads: “At Rome, of Stephen, pope and martyr.” Ado’s longer account may be regarded as an abridgment of the Acts, especially in the parts that properly concern Stephen.

The question is whether the Acts, taken in summary form, should be judged, with Baronius in the Annals under the year 259, no. 20, to be utterly faithful, genuine, known, and authentic—indeed, the more candid, the truer—or whether, with more recent scholars, they should be regarded as corrupt and interpolated. The reader will permit this most difficult controversy to be deferred to its proper place. Meanwhile, let him see what Tillemont sets against these Acts in volume IV, p. 592. [Col. 0324D] A brief observation by Motherius may also be noted. Wandalbertus elegantly celebrates Stephen:

“On the fourth day before the Nones, blessed Stephen, martyr and pope,

grants Rome the pious joys of his feast.”

The Little Roman Martyrology just as briefly includes the second notice: “In Bithynia, of Theodota with her three sons.” Ado speaks in exactly the same sense, adorning both mother and sons with a notable encomium; this appears in Bede, and in Rabanus from the same source of the Acts, but in a more compressed form—unless one prefers to say that Bede in some measure preceded Ado. Certainly it can be inferred with some clarity that Usuard adheres more to Bede’s words than to Ado’s, removing what both relate about the tyrant Diocletian and the count Leucadius.

But how all this can be reconciled with the Hieronymian codices, I simply do not see. For there the text from the Lucensis and Corbeiensis reads as follows: “And in Caesarea of Mauretania, of Theodota and her seven sons, whose deeds are recorded.” Florentinius did not perceive this sufficiently either; he admits that he searched in vain for the Acts of that Caesarean woman and her sons. Hence he rightly thought that in the very ancient Epternacensis the name of the province should be supplied and corrected, writing Bithyniae instead of Bitia, so that it might agree better with the other Martyrologies. These brief observations are more than sufficient for our purpose, [Col. 0326A] for whatever may be the truth concerning one or two Theodotas—or Theodoras—one from Caesarea and the other from Nicaea, a matter which we defer to a full discussion of the Acts, the origin and genuine purity of our text have been amply demonstrated, though it is not entirely free from blemish. The Acts published by Surius under 25 December, I think, belong among those refuted by Ruinartius on p. 420. What should be decided concerning the Combefisian Acts, published in Greek and Latin among the “Select Triumphs,” p. 247, belongs elsewhere. Here it is enough to have identified the sources.]

[Note: [Col. 0325A]

ROSWEYD., concerning Stephen the pope, inserts into the text: “When he had already sent many ahead to the crown of martyrdom.” The rest is sound—indeed, more than sound, since it simply reads: “In the same place, in his seat he is beheaded,” and so forth.

PULSANEN. is fairly sound in the first notice but deficient in the second, where it abridges the eulogy.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., and DANICUS. These are the codices into which, as I said, Bede’s eulogy passed, with the Usuardine material expunged. Thus they read concerning Stephen [Col. 0325B] the pope: “Who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of the emperor Valerian.” See above in the Observations.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus, the feast of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr. On the same day, of Saint Theodota with her sons, who suffered her ordeal in the time of Diocletian under the consul Nicecius and the count Leucadius.” Here there is generally alteration and abridgment.

BRUSSELS. Under Stephen, after “pope and martyr,” it continues as follows:

> “Who, after converting many pagans and burying the bodies of many martyrs, was persecuted during the persecution of Valerian. Fearlessly celebrating Mass before the altar, he was beheaded. And [the feast] of the holy martyrs Nemesius, Leucilla, Olympius, Exuperius, and Theodolus.”

These persons are discussed in the Acts of Saint Stephen, but they belong to other days. The first two are commemorated on 21 October. See what we said about the others on 26 July. After “Theodota and her sons,” after *consumi* (“to be consumed”), it adds:

> “As is written in the Passion of Saint Anastasia the virgin” [Col. 0325C].

Anastasia is commemorated on 25 December.

HAGENAU. He appears to have taken his material concerning Pope Stephen piecemeal from Ado, in the following form:

> “At Rome, in the cemetery of Callixtus: the birthday of blessed Stephen, pope and martyr. When the emperor Valerian was persecuting the Christians, he was arrested with many of his clergy. Then he alone fearlessly went to Valerian, reproving him for the slaughter of the faithful, and immediately he was led to the temple of Mars, either to sacrifice or to be beheaded. Then Pope Stephen prayed, and part of the temple collapsed, and everyone fled in fear. He himself, with his companions, went to the cemetery of Lucina and encouraged the Christians who came to him. He began the solemn Mass and continually completed what he had begun. When Valerian’s soldiers saw him, they immediately beheaded him at the altar, together with some others.”

The remainder is pure.

MATRICHT–CHARTREUX–UTRECHT:

> “Of Stephen, pope and martyr, whose illustrious deeds are recorded and frequently cited [Col. 0325D]. Of Boni, Faustus, and Maurus with seven others, concerning whom it is read in the Acts of Blessed Stephen, but who are found on the first day in other Martyrologies. Of Theodota with her three sons.”

ALTEMPS:

> “On the same day, the discovery of the body of Saint Alban, protomartyr of the English.”

Why not “Albani”?

STROZZI and perhaps other FLORENTINES:

> “At Rome, the burial of blessed Severinus, pope, who was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle. He was kind beyond all men, a lover of the poor, generous, and exceedingly gentle. He was the seventy-first after the apostle Peter. In his time the most Christian emperor Heraclius, after destroying Chosroes, brought the Lord’s cross back to Jerusalem” [Col. 0326A].

I admit that Severinus lived at that time, but I do not understand that he was a pope.

> “At Padua, Saint Maximus, bishop of that city, who, famous for miracles, rested in a blessed death. The dedication of the church of Saint Mary of the Portiuncula, in which Blessed Father Francis obtained from Pope Deodatus the greatest indulgence” [Col. 0326B].

Deodatus lived in the seventh century, whereas Saint Francis lived in the thirteenth. Therefore read, as BELINUS does, “from God and from the pope.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. Concerning Stephen it says:

> “He governed the Church for four years, two months, and fifteen days, and suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. On account of his confession of Christ, while fearlessly offering sacrifice in the cemetery of Saint Lucina, they beheaded him in that same place, as he sat in his episcopal seat before the altar. The faithful of Christ who were present buried him in the same crypt, together with his chair, already drenched with his sacred blood. His blood is shown on a marble stone before the high altar at the catacombs. He established that priests and deacons should not use priestly vestments in daily life, except in church.”

In the account of Theodota there is a moderate interpolation. It continues:

> “In Italy, in the city of Verona, of the blessed martyrs Felix and Nicetius. On the same day, of the holy martyrs Nemesius, Lucilla, Olympius, Exuperia, and Theodota [Col. 0326C]. On that day also, of blessed Adrenuldus, bishop and confessor.”

BELINUS. In the account of Stephen he likewise uses Bede’s eulogy, as above. At the end he adds:

> “At Padua, Saint Maximus, bishop of that city, who, famous for miracles, rested in a blessed death. On the same day, the consecration of the church of Saint Mary of the Portiuncula near Assisi, in which Blessed Father Francis obtained from God and the pope the greatest indulgence.”

GREVEN:

> “In Italy, in the city of Verona, of Felix and Nicetius, martyrs. Likewise of the holy Nemesius, Lucilla, Olympius, Exuperia, and Theodola. Of Stephen II, pope and confessor, who was a lover of churches and especially a supporter and nourisher of Christ’s poor. In the last year of his pontificate he transferred the empire from the Greeks to the Germans, in the person of Charlemagne. Likewise of Stephen III, pope, a most holy man. Of Adrenuldus, bishop and confessor. Of Medanus, bishop.”

MOLANUS. At the end he adds Bede’s words:

> “It is written in the Passion of Saint Anastasia. At Padua, Saint Maximus, etc. On the same day, the consecration of the basilica of Saint Mary of the Portiuncula,” etc.

These passages were copied from BELINUS. Later editions change the name Theodota to Theodora. At the end are the same additions, mixed with a new one:

> “At Chartres, Saint Betharius, bishop of that city, famous for holiness and miracles.”

At Rome, in the cemetery of Callixtus, the birthday of blessed Stephen, pope, who, during the persecution of Valerian, when he was being pursued because of the martyrdom of Christ, stood fearlessly before the solemn rites of the altar and continually completed what he had begun; in that same place, as he sat in his episcopal seat, he was beheaded. In the province of Bithynia, in the city of Nicaea, Saint Theodota with her three sons. Of these, she caused the firstborn, named Evodius, who was boldly confessing Christ, first to be beaten with clubs by the Bithynian consul; then she herself and all her sons were consumed by fire.

## 3 August

[Note: [Col. 0327]]

The following are pure: Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Pulsano, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0327A]]

All the manuscripts read *beatissimi*, except the Pratensis alone, which simply has *beati*. Rosweyd writes *Abibae* instead of *Abibon*, and not without justification, since he is also called Abibas, the son of Gamaliel. “These seven, etc.” should be read with reference to all the bodies. Munerat wrote *Hoc*. The same witness has *principiis* instead of *principis*, doubtless a printer’s error. “Of the emperor Honorius” appears in the Tournai manuscript; the others agree with the text. Likewise, some witnesses, such as Herinien and Molan, read “and by the blessed presbyter Lucian,” and we have followed the larger number of manuscripts. But Greven, as on several other occasions, once again twists the construction here, reading: “and written by the blessed presbyter Lucian”; Pulsano has “described.” Antwerp-Major did not approve the phrase “person of the whole Church,” which Our Author copied from Ado, but preferred to read “persons of the whole Church.” Together with Pulsano, it wrote *Constantinopolim* instead of *Constantinopoli*. Again, Antwerp-Major has *Emelli*, Greven and Molan *Ermelli*; the others have the better form with aspiration. There remain the spellings *Iherosolimis*, *Jerusolimis*, *Jerosolimis*, *protomartiris*, *Gamalihelis*, *Nichomedi*, and *Nychodemi*, which it is sufficient to indicate.

[Note: [Col. 0327A]]

Ado embellished the revelation or discovery of the body of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen, an event celebrated throughout the world, with a notable narrative taken chiefly from Lucian. The substance of his text, unless I am mistaken, he derived from the Little Roman Martyrology, where it is written:

> “At Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of Blessed Stephen, of Gamaliel, Nicomedes, and Abibon” [Col. 0327B].

Our Author, moreover, extracted everything from Ado’s lengthy historical panegyric, departing not by a hair’s breadth from the steps of his customary guide—and even reproducing the same error that Baronius notes in the years of Honorius, where the twenty-first year should be read instead of the seventh.

Rabanus follows an entirely different route, joining the translation at Antioch found in yesterday’s Hieronymian Martyrologies to today’s discovery. From him Notker took everything that he mentioned on the preceding day concerning one of the stones preserved at Antioch and famous for miracles.

These are the words of the Hieronymian Martyrologies for 4 August:

> “At Antioch, the birthday of the relics of the protomartyr Stephen and deacon, who was stoned at Jerusalem. Following the revelation of the presbyter Lucian, his little body was transferred from Jerusalem.”

Following these words, Notker adds from Rabanus:

> “Where one of the stones with which he suffered in his passion is said to be kept,” etc.

Florentinius, reflecting on this passage, as elsewhere attributing too much to Notker and being unaware of his sources, takes occasion here to indulge in further commentary [Col. 0327C]. Among other things, together with Baronius he wonders whether *Ancona* should be written instead of *Antioch*, since one of these stones is held there in great veneration. He cites sermons of Saint Augustine for this purpose. All these matters will be examined on 26 December, together with what more recent scholars have collected from Augustine and others.

Thus far for Notker on the preceding day. But the Hieronymian Martyrologies cited on this day agree more closely with the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and therefore also with Our Author, when they read:

> “At Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of the most blessed Stephen, the first martyr, and of the holy Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibon.”

But here Notker again suggests something different. He wishes Stephen to have been stoned on this day, or at least buried by Gamaliel, so that today his passion might be commemorated according to Notker’s view, while on 26 December—the seventh day before the Kalends of January—his sacred body was revealed and transferred to Jerusalem. “With the Life as our companion,” he says, “we shall take care to set this forth,” etc. But proof of this is still lacking, since his Martyrology fails after 26 October.

Nevertheless, we do not think that Notker is wrong in every respect, since Lucian’s account makes it clear that the bodies were discovered in December. Why, then, the feast of this same discovery is celebrated on 3 August, I would not dare rashly to assert. For the time being, see Baronius’s conjecture and his other notes, as well as those of Florentinius; also Surius for this day and Tillemont, volume II, page 1 onward, and in the notes page 462 onward.

In any case, what has been said in no way harms the primitive simplicity of Usuard’s text. As we have already said, he did not depart from his Ado, taking even the final announcement concerning Saint Hermellus verbatim from him, almost exactly as it appears in the Little Roman Martyrology. For the reading of the Hieronymian Martyrologies [Col. 0328C] is somewhat obscure: it changes the name or inflects it differently, as the frequently cited Florentinius will explain more fully. I find no mention of Hermellus anywhere else.

Wandalbertus adorns the first announcement metrically as follows:

> Soon the solemn feast is kept of Stephen, discovered:
>
> The first to follow Christ’s death by dying.
>
> Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibon likewise,
>
> Having been discovered, shine in devotion and everlasting praise.

[Note: [Col. 0327C]]

ANTWERP, MAX–LÜBECK, ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEIDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANICUS likewise construct their text for this day from Ado:

> “At Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen and of the holy Nicodemus [Antwerp: Nicodemus], Gamaliel, and Abibon; as was revealed by the Lord to the blessed presbyter Lucian in the seventh year of the emperor Honorius [Col. 0327D]. At Constantinople, the birthday of Saint Hermellus the martyr. At Autun [Max–Lübeck: Augustodimum], the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop.”

CENTULA:

> “At Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, and with him of Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Abibon, as was revealed by the Lord to the blessed presbyter Lucian in the seventh year of the emperor Honorius. At Rome, on the Appian Way, Saint Tarsitius, acolyte and martyr.”

BRUSSELS:

> “At Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of blessed Stephen the protomartyr and of the holy Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Abibon. This discovery is said to have been revealed by the Lord in the seventh year of the emperor Honorius and on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, and to have been written down by the blessed presbyter Lucian. But the feast is celebrated on this day, on which that same blessed Stephen was stoned for Christ” [Col. 0328C].

These statements agree with Notker’s opinion. What follows concerning Hermellus is pure. Then:

> “At Autun, the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop.”

HAGENAU begins:

> “At the city of Novara, the birthday of blessed Gaudentius, bishop and confessor. He was Saint Martin’s secretary. Saint Simplicianus ordained him the first bishop of the city of Novara. Together with Bishop Eusebius of Vercelli he endured exile, and before that he was detained in chains for several days at Milan. Then Saint Ambrose wished to pass by without seeing him and the others, but could not. At last he dismounted from his horse and comforted the saints placed in prison in the Lord. Gaudentius died in exile, and his body was brought back to Novara. Agapius, who had been appointed his successor, had a costly tomb prepared for him; and therefore he remained unburied from January until August, while his nails and hair grew as though he were alive. At Jerusalem, the discovery of Saints Stephen, Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abilion. This discovery took place in the seventh year of the emperor Honorius, with the blessed priest Lucian arranging it; a revelation concerning them had also been made to him by God.”

In the account of Hermellus he is pure. At the end:

> “At Autun, the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0329A] AQUINCUM adds at the end:

> “At Autun, Saint Euphronius.”

This is better than in the preceding witness.

MATRICHT–CHARTREUX–UTRECHT:

> “The revelation of blessed Stephen the protomartyr. The discovery or revelation of Saints Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibon, which the blessed presbyter Lucian wrote down. Hermellus the martyr.”

The account could have added the place of his struggle.

VATICAN, under number 5949, adds:

> “At Rome, Saint Diogenes.”

He is unknown to the others.

UGHELLI:

> “At Autun, the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop.”

Write, as above, “Euphronius.”

FLORENTINE:

> “At Novara, Saint Gaudentius, bishop and confessor. At Rome, in the cemetery of Callixtus, Saint Tarsitius the acolyte, as is read in the Acts of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr.”

BESANÇON:

> “The discovery of the body of the most blessed Stephen . . . Likewise at Chrysopolis, now called Besançon, the arrival of the relics of the aforementioned protomartyr.”

This is a local addition, concerning which nothing is found among the others.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. Almost pure in the text, it adds [Col. 0329B]:

> “At Autun, the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop and confessor. In Italy, in the city of Novara, Saint Gaudentius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, blessed Fiacrius, hermit and confessor. At Vienne, Saint Justus, bishop and martyr, a man of exceptional holiness, under the emperor Antoninus, surnamed Pius” [Col. 0330A].

This is another Justus. Ado places him on the following day.

BELINUS. In the discovery of Saint Stephen he follows the wording of the Antwerp and other witnesses mentioned above. Then:

> “At Constantinople, the birthday of Saint Hermolus the martyr. At Autun, the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop. At Novara, Saint Gaudemius, bishop,”

instead of Gaudentius, just as above he wrote Hermolius instead of Hermellus.

GREVEN:

> “At Vienne, in the time of Antoninus surnamed Pius, Saint Justus, bishop and martyr, a man of exceptional holiness. At Autun, the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop and confessor. In Italy, in the city of Novara, Saint Gaudentius, bishop and confessor. At Constantinople, Saint Metropolus, bishop.”

Should this not be Metrophanes? See Florentinius.

> “Fiacrius, hermit and confessor. Likewise Waltenus, abbot and confessor. Martin, confessor. In Hesse, of blessed memory, Conrad of Herlesheim, monk, priest, of the Cistercian order, and confessor.”

[Col. 0330B] MOLANUS:

> “At Autun, the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop. At Novara, Saint Gaudentius, bishop.”

In later editions he repeats exactly the same, adding only:

> “On the third day, of the holy Fathers Isaac, Dalmatius, and Faustus.”

[Col. 0329]

At Jerusalem, the discovery of the body of the most blessed Stephen, protomartyr, and of the holy Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibon. This was revealed in the seventh year of the emperor Honorius and written down by the blessed presbyter Lucian; it is proclaimed in the person of the whole Church, among almost all nations. At Constantinople, Hermellus the martyr.

## 4 August

[Note: [Col. 0329]]

Only the following manuscripts are pure: Pratensis, Herinien, Pulsanen, Antwerp, Max–Lübeck, and Munerat.

[Note: [Col. 0329C]]

Only Pulsano reads “the birthday of Saint Aristarchus”; all the others have the form found in the text. In the same place, before Tertullinus, the title “saint” is lacking. There is no manuscript, whether handwritten or printed, that does not read “under the emperor Aurelian.” Ado, however, from whom all this was taken from the Acts of Saint Stephen, called the tyrant “the emperor Valerian.”

Again, all agree on the impious beating with clubs; Antwerp and Max–Lübeck, however, together with Molan, write *macerationem* (“tormenting”) instead of *mactationem* (“slaughtering”). Pulsano, instead of “and the crushing of his mouth,” has “and of his mouth”; likewise, instead of “and the stretching of his sinews,” he reads “and of the sinews.” Where Antwerp and Max–Lübeck have *conquassationem*, they simply put *quassationem* (“shaking”).

These matters are minor. Three manuscripts otherwise of excellent reputation—Antwerp-Major, Greven, and Molan—are defective in part of the eulogy, reading:

> “and the burning of the fires around his sides and the stretching of his sinews”

or, in Antwerp-Major:

> “and the cutting of his sinews,”

omitting the intervening words. This is why we exclude them from the number of the pure witnesses, besides the fact that Greven has another addition, to be quoted later. Pulsano writes *consumavit*; Munerat has *Tertulini*, etc. These points scarcely require notice.

[Note: [Col. 0329C]]

There is no mention today of either Aristarchus or Tertullinus in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, or Wandalbert. The Little Roman Martyrology mentions both in these words:

> “Aristarchus, a disciple of the apostles. In the sand-pit crypt at Rome, Tertullinus the martyr.”

The Viennese Martyrology transferred both from there into its own text; and the words concerning Aristarchus in our text proceed from it verbatim. One may wonder that Usuard, who was accustomed to consult the feasts of the apostles, did not consult them on this day in order to extract material for some eulogy. Molan inserted such material in full, in italic letters, in his little panel, as will be evident in the Additions.

The further additions made by Notker do not belong to this place. Apart from Ado’s eulogy, little can be offered from elsewhere concerning Aristarchus. Tillemont gathers almost everything said about him here and there from the Acts of the Apostles and Paul’s Epistles, in volume I; in the note on page 571 he also examines and refutes various Greek eulogies, about which we shall say more elsewhere.

We have elsewhere mentioned that Tertullinus is noted by Florus on 30 July, which may perhaps be considered the true day of his passion, since Ado expressly states that his body was buried by Pope Saint Stephen on the second day before the Kalends of August. Why, then, the feast of the blessed martyr is celebrated only on this day, Ado gives the reason there: namely, that a solemn gathering takes place at his tomb on 5 August.

Moreover, Ado’s eulogy was taken from the Acts of Pope Saint Stephen, most recently cited the day before yesterday, and was elegantly abridged by Our Author. Nevertheless, he wrongly changed the emperor’s name, writing Aurelian instead of Valerian, as we showed in the Variant Readings; in the modern Roman Martyrology one will find the name correctly amended [Col. 0330D]. Whether this happened deliberately or through inattention is not easy to determine. For since Usuard follows Ado extremely closely in everything else, what reason can one give for his departing from him in this passage?

The Viennese Martyrology continues:

> “The arrival of Justus, bishop, from the desert,” etc.

The Hieronymian copies also remember him, but Our Author omitted this brief commemoration, content to copy the remainder from Ado.

Wandalbertus adorns another martyr today, concerning whom more will immediately be said in the Additions. He sings:

> Justin is celebrated on the preceding day with his own honor,
>
> A presbyter numbered among the saints, slain by cruel death,
>
> Who, seeking out the tombs, adorned them.

[Note: [Col. 0331A]]

TOURNai begins as follows:

> “The birthday of Saint Oswald, king and martyr,”

concerning whom see Usuard’s text for the following day. The remainder is most pure.

ANTWERP-MAJOR suffers from the defect noted above. In the rest it is also pure.

ROSWEYD begins with Justin in this form:

> “At Rome, of Justin the presbyter, most devoted to burying the bodies of the martyrs.”

Whether this and the eulogies that follow were taken from Rabanus or Notker, I leave to others to judge. In the rest it is pure and complete.

GREVEN is pure in the first announcement; in the second place he inserts:

> “At Rome, at Saint Lawrence, the birthday of blessed Justin, presbyter and martyr, whom blessed Sixtus ordained and who buried many bodies of saints.”

He is defective in the eulogy of Tertullinus, as stated above.

MOLANUS agrees with ANTWERP-MAJOR and GREVEN in the defect mentioned.

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEIDEN, and LOUVAIN [Col. 0331B] add concerning Aristarchus:

> “Who, appointed bishop of the Thessalonians, after long and most blessed struggles, was crowned by Christ and came to rest.”

Then:

> “At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, the birthday of Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr, who during the persecution of Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus was most distinguished by the glory of his confession.”

They are sufficiently pure in the account of Tertullinus. The three later witnesses are exceeded by ANTWERP-MAXIMUM in that it has, in a somewhat more recent type, the following addition:

> “At Eydan, the birthday of Saint Walburgis the virgin, who, burning with love of God, abandoned her homeland and inheritance and strove to please God alone.”

ALBERGEN and DANICUS are almost like UTRECHT and the two preceding witnesses, but place Justin before Aristarchus.

CENTULA:

> “At Rome, at Saint Lawrence, Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr, who was most distinguished by the glory of his confession. At Rome, in the sand-pit crypt, blessed Tertullinus the martyr. On the same day, Saint Aristarchus [Col. 0331C], a disciple of the apostles, ordained bishop by the Thessalonians and, after long and most blessed struggles, crowned by Christ.”

BRUSSELS begins:

> “At Lyons, the arrival from the desert of the body of Saint Justus the martyr. At Thessalonica, the birthday of blessed Aristarchus, disciple of blessed Paul the apostle. Appointed bishop of the Thessalonians, after long struggles he was crowned by Christ and came to rest. At Rome, on the Latin Way, in the sand-pit crypt, the passion of Saint Tarculinus the martyr. Under the emperor Aurelian, after clubs, burning of his sides, crushing of his mouth, the rack, and cutting of his sinews, he completed his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head. Likewise at Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, the birthday of Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr. Under the persecution of Decius Gallus and Volusianus, he was distinguished by the glory of his confession. And in Germany, the elevation of Saint Walburgis the virgin, who departed to the Lord on the Kalends of May.”

See our Acts for 25 February.

[Col. 0331D] HAGENAU adds concerning Aristarchus almost the same thing as above. Instead of *Tertullii* he writes *Tertullini*. After the text he adds:

> “Likewise at Rome, Saint Gregory the pope, who is called the Penitentiary. Likewise at Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, the birthday of Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr, who under the persecution of the emperors Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus was most distinguished by the glory of his confession. He buried many martyrs, and hid many Christians in his own house, supplying them with food. At last he was thrown into the Tiber from a bridge and completed his martyrdom.”

AQUINCUM adds at the end:

> “On the same day, Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr.”

MATRICHT–CHARTREUX–UTRECHT:

> “Of Julian [rather, Justin], presbyter and martyr. Of Aristarchus, disciple of blessed Paul. Of Tertullinus, martyr at Rome, who after various torments was beheaded.”

[Col. 0332A] REGINA OF SWEDEN, marked number 428:

> “On the same day, Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr.”

VATICAN, number 5949:

> “At Rome, Saints Crescentianus and Justus, and Saint Apollonius with his companions.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins:

> “The octave of Saint Pantaleon the martyr. At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, at Saint Lawrence, the birthday of Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr. He committed to burial the bodies of Saints Lawrence, Hippolytus, Concordia, Irenaeus, Abundius, Cyrilla, and many other saints. During the persecution of Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus, he was most distinguished by the glory of his confession.”

Concerning Aristarchus it adds, as above:

> “At Rome, on the Latin Way, in the sand-pit crypt, the passion of Saint Terculinius the martyr. Who under the emperor Aurelian,” etc.

Then:

> “On the same day, blessed Justin, bishop and confessor. On that day also, blessed Valentinus, bishop and confessor.”

This concerns the “Patavian” in Noricum; see Surius for this day.

> “Likewise the arrival of Saint Walburga the virgin. At Lyons, the arrival from the desert of the body of Saint Justus [Col. 0332B], bishop and confessor.”

BELINUS, sufficiently pure in the text, adds:

> “On the same day, at Rome, Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr.”

GREVEN:

> “Of Justin, bishop and confessor.”

Then he extracts from Ado:

> “At Lyons in Gaul, the arrival from the desert of the body of Saint Justus, bishop. After living in the desert for several years a life close to that of the angels and happily falling asleep there, his little body was sought out through the care of the venerable citizens of Lyons, brought back joyfully and reverently from distant regions, and buried.”

It continues:

> “Likewise the arrival of Saint Walburga the virgin. The translation of Saint Valentinus, bishop of Patavium and confessor. In Spain, Saint Joanna, widow. Likewise in England, of good memory, Simon, earl of Leicester, martyr.”

MOLANUS inserts concerning Aristarchus what I said in the Observation, namely:

> “Concerning him the blessed Apostle writes to the Colossians: ‘Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you.’ He remained the Apostle’s constant companion until his confession; appointed bishop of the Thessalonians, after long and most blessed struggles he was crowned by Christ and came to rest” [Col. 0332C].

At the end, after “he completed his martyrdom,” there is added:

> “Blessed Stephen baptized him in the white garment, ordained him a presbyter, and not long afterward he was buried by that same blessed pontiff, after earning martyrdom by the cutting off of his head. At Lyons, the arrival from the desert of the body of Saint Justus, bishop. On the same day at Rome, Saint Justin,” etc., as in BELINUS above. “Likewise Saint Walburgis the virgin.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “She rests at Furnes. On the same day, the burial of Saint Euphronius, the eighteenth bishop of Tours and confessor, concerning whom his near successor Gregory of Tours writes several things in his History of the Franks and in On the Glory of the Confessors.”

Other editions begin in italic letters:

> “In the city of Bologna, Saint Dominic, confessor, founder of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man most illustrious in holiness and learning. It is evident that, on account of the exceptional grace of his merits, he raised three dead persons while he lived and preserved his virginity inviolate throughout his life.”

Concerning Aristarchus, as in the first edition. Concerning Tertullinus, “in the sand-pit crypt” is added, and at the end the material given above. This fuller text has:

> “At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, the birthday of Saint Justin, presbyter and martyr, who during the persecution of Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus was most distinguished by the glory of his confession.”

Then again, in italic letters:

> “Whom blessed Sixtus ordained. He buried in tombs the blessed martyrs Hippolytus, Concordia, Irenaeus, Abundius, and Cyrilla, daughter of Caesar Decius, together with many others. At Rome, blessed and holy Perpetua, mother of Saint Nazarius. Likewise Saint Walburgis the virgin, whose sacred relics are kept at Furnes. At Tours, Saint Euphronius, bishop and confessor.”

See what Baronius noted about him on this day.

[Col. 0329]

The birthday of blessed Aristarchus, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle. At Rome, on the Latin Way, the passion of Saint Tertullinus the martyr, who under the emperor Aurelian, after the impious slaughter with clubs, the burning of fires around his sides, the crushing of his mouth, the stretching on the rack, and the cutting of his sinews, completed his martyrdom by the sentence pronounced and the cutting off of his head.

## 5 August

[Note: [Col. 0333]]

Taken from Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0333A]]

I write *Retiae*, as all the manuscripts have it, except Antwerp, which has *Reciae*. Molan followed Ado rather than Usuard and added *martyr* after Afra; on the authority of the other manuscripts we have excluded that word. Antwerp-Major presents an imperfect sense when it reads “she was handed over on account of the confession of the Lord,” omitting “to the fire.”

Tournai correctly wrote *Oswaldi* yesterday; today Herinien, Molan, and others correctly have *Oswaldi*. Here observe the custom of the Gauls, who either do not wish or are unable to become accustomed to doubling the W; hence Pratensis and Antwerp write *Oswaldi* [Col. 0334A].

Again, in Antwerp-Major the construction is defective. Bede venerably records his deeds. I read: “At Autun,” since that is how the manuscripts have it today; Antwerp has *Augustoduno*. *Cautalaunis* is an error in Antwerp-Major, as is *Memini*. Antwerp has *Cathalaunis* and *Cataulanis*; the others correctly read, as in the text, “of Memmius, bishop.” Most of the manuscripts simply read “Memmius, bishop”; Molan adds “and confessor.” I pass over other matters, such as *aput*, *Affrae*, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0333A]]

The text of the Little Roman Martyrology reads as follows on this day:

> “In the city of Augusta, in Rhetia, Saint Afra the martyr.”

The Hieronymian Martyrologies do not speak of her on this day, nor do Bede or Florus. The earlier witnesses explicitly record:

> “In the city of Augusta, the passion of Saint Afer.”

Some say that he was the uncle of Saint Afra, and that for this reason he is commemorated under that title on 5 August at Augusta Vindelicum, as can be read in the notes of Marcus Welser, page 54 verso. There one will also learn that Saint Afra is celebrated by the people of Augsburg not on this day but on 7 August, as Raderus likewise testifies in *Bavaria Sancta*.

She is also placed on the aforementioned day, 7 August, by Florus and Wandalbert, and, if we believe Florentinius, by the Hieronymian Martyrologies, although on the following day, 6 August, they expressly read:

> “The passion of Saint Afra.”

This should not seem strange, since the Acts do not specify the date distinctly.

Notker wished to resolve all these matters, defining the whole question today as follows:

> “At Augusta on the Euphrates, the birthday of Saint Afer the martyr.”

Because of the similarity of the names—that is, both Augusta and Afer—our countrymen were led to suppose that on this day, at Augusta in Rhaetia, or Vindelicia, the passion of Saint Afra was completed. We shall speak of her in what follows, God willing.

Nor is the evidence far to seek. On 7 August Ado almost recites the same words, adding her companions, whom he repeats on the 12th. Yet the aforementioned Ado, who was by no means a follower of Notker, followed the author of the Little Roman Martyrology, undoubtedly an Italian, and on this day, 5 August, included Afra with a short eulogy. Our Author copied the whole of it, except for the single word *martyr*.

Here we have touched on several difficulties that must be discussed in their proper place in the Acts, when the errors of English critics scattered through the Roman Martyrology and sufficiently refuted in the preface will be more fully demolished insofar as they concern Afra.

Meanwhile, see the illustrated Acts of Saint Narcissus for 18 March; Tillemont, volume V, page 270 onward; and Ruinart, among the *Sincere and Selected Acts of the Martyrs*, page 500 onward.

King and martyr Oswald is mentioned on this day by no ancient martyrologist except Wandalbert. I have no doubt that Usuard introduced him into the sacred calendars from Bede’s History. See Surius for this day.

Ado announces Cassian as follows:

> “At Autun, the birthday of Saint Cassian, bishop.”

What Usuard added and omitted is clear from our index. The eulogies proceeding from Florus will be listed in the Additions; for the time being, see the Bede edited by us before volume II of March.

I do not sufficiently understand why Florentinius, using another typeface, namely italics, treats him as an addition. The same judgment should be made concerning Memmius of Châlons, who is explicitly mentioned no less in the Lucerne manuscript than in the Corbie and Echternach manuscripts. The editor cited above added only this:

> “I am readily persuaded that these holy bishops, Cassian and Memmius, were added by a Gallic writer to an older Martyrology.”

He could have been persuaded more readily if he had wished to remove all saints added by Gallic antiquarians.

Meanwhile, Rabanus celebrates Memmius in a somewhat fuller phrase, from whom Notker took his account, though with some variation. It is strange that Florentinius never observes this, although he is accustomed repeatedly to swear by Notker’s words.

As for Memmius, Mosander assigned him entirely to Ado, while Rosweyd relegates him to an appendix without giving a reason. It seems sufficiently plausible to me that he, like Cassian, was taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, noted by Ado in the same way, and transferred from there into Our Author.

Nor do I wish to argue the point. If another view is preferred, I shall say that the latter, Memmius, was extracted by Usuard himself from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Certainly, that he and all the others are genuinely and purely Usuardine cannot be demonstrated more clearly than by the agreement of all the manuscripts.

I will not conceal that Mabillon claims everything rejected by Rosweyd for Ado. But these matters were discussed in the preface.

There are Acts of the two last saints, although they require careful examination. Gregory of Tours mentions both in *On the Glory of the Confessors*: Memmius in chapter 66 and Cassian in chapter 74.

Wandalbert sang of both together with Oswald, since, as we said, he postponed Afra to 6 August. The metrical Martyrologist has it thus:

> On the Nones, Cassian, Memmius, and Oswald,
>
> The pious king of the English, are remembered for merit and virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0333D]]

TOURNAI, which dealt with Oswald on the preceding day, inserts in his place:

> “On the same day, in the city of Bologna, blessed Dominic, confessor, of the Order of Friars Preachers.”

The remainder of the text is most pure.

ROSWEYD omitted the first announcement here, placing it last on 7 August, or the seventh day before the Ides, with some additions.

PULSANO is sufficiently pure in the first two announcements but defective in the last two.

MAX–LÜBECK, in addition to several errors, has at the end [Col. 0334D]:

> “In the city of Bologna, the burial of Saint Dominic, confessor.”

UGHELLI likewise has this.

MUNERAT is not especially polished even in the text; at the end he adds:

> “At Corbeil Castle, Saint Yonius the martyr. On the same day, Dominic, confessor, father and founder of the Order of Preachers.”

GREVEN. He has a pure and complete text, but, with the sign LL appended, inserts Dominic, who belonged to the Appendices. Thus, in second place, he reads: “In Italy, in the city of Bologna, the feast of blessed Dominic, an apostolic man, mighty in work and word, founder of the Order of Preachers. How great was his merit before the Lord, his resplendent miracles testify.” I am not unaware that, by the sign LL, Greven wishes to indicate that the saint prefixed by it has been added to Usuard. But since he did this on his own initiative, it is nonetheless excluded from the pure witnesses for that reason, as is the case on 1 April and again on 20 August, 13 September, and elsewhere.

ANTWERP-MAX. begins: “In Italy, in the city of Bologna, the feast of Saint Dominic the Confessor. He possessed such zeal for the salvation of souls that he not only devoted himself, in word and example, to evangelical preaching, but also instituted the Order of Preachers for this very purpose.” After the entries for Afra and Oswald, which are pure, it continues: “At Autun, blessed Cassianus, bishop and confessor. When Saint Germanus the bishop had once come to his tomb, marvelous to relate, he called him from the grave after praying and said: ‘What are you doing, brother Cassianus?’ And he replied from the tomb: ‘I enjoy sweet repose in peace, and await the coming of the Redeemer.’ At Châlons, Saint Memmius, bishop and confessor.”

LOUVAIN agrees with the preceding witness, but is defective in Afra’s eulogy and writes Memnius instead of Memmius.

UTRECHT and LEYDEN are almost like ANTWERP-MAX. Throughout the text they prefix: “At Rome, the feast of the glorious Virgin Mary of the Snows.”

ALBERGEN: “The feast of the Snows of the blessed Virgin Mary.” DANICUS, however, in second place: “On the same day, the feast of the Snows.” The same is expressed in various ways.

CENTULA: “In France, in the city of Châlons, Saint Memmius the confessor, the first bishop of that city. At Autun, Saint Cassianus, bishop and confessor.” It is pure in the entry for Afra. Then: “In Britain, Saint Oswald, king and martyr of the English, whose venerable priest Bede commemorates his deeds in the history of his people.”

BRUSSELS, by anticipation: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, blessed Sixtus, etc.” This belongs to the following day. It then proceeds with Afra, quite purely; then with Memmius, as above. Likewise with Cassianus, as in ANTWERP-MAX. Then: “On the same day, Saint Gregory of Nyssa.” See 9 March. “And Saint Oswald, king of the English. When he had assumed the kingdom, he shone forth in the faith of Christ above all the kings of Britain. The Venerable Bede commemorates his deeds in the history of the English. At Rome, the feast of the blessed Virgin Mary, which is called ‘at the Snows.’ In Italy, in the city of Bologna, the burial of Saint Dominic the Confessor, founder of the Order of Preachers.”

HAGENAU begins with Oswald, concerning whom it narrates many admirable deeds, to be examined elsewhere. It follows with Cassianus, in wording not very different from ANTWERP-MAX; likewise with Memmius. Then comes a eulogy of Dominic too long to insert here. It postpones Afra to 7 August. The URSINI-ROSEMBERG codex has Dominic as ANTWERP-MAX and additionally says: “On the same day, Saint Mary of the Snows at Rome.” Both feasts are of the second class with double rite.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-UTRECHT: “Dominic the confessor, who, as is said, received the habit in the house of the Great Charterhouse, for previously he had been a canon regular, and was founder of the Order of Preachers. His feast is already celebrated on the preceding day. The feast of the blessed Mary of the Snows. Oswald, king of the English. Cassianus, bishop and confessor. Afra the harlot, who was converted with her entire household and handed over to the fire.”

SWEDISH REGISTER, marked no. 428: “At Corbeil, Saint Paul the martyr” (MUNERATUS has Yonius).

FLORENTINIUS: “At Bologna, Saint Dominic the confessor of the Friars Preachers, illustrious in life, teaching, and miracles, who departed to the Lord in the year of the Lord 1221. At Ascoli, Saint Migdias, bishop and martyr. At Rome, at Saint Peter’s, Saint Hormisdas, pope and confessor . . .” See the Appendices for the following day.

BESANÇON: “At Châlons, Saint Memmius, bishop, who, among the other distinctions of his virtues, raised a dead man.”

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION: “At Rome, the building of the church of Saint Mary Major, a feast called the Snows of the blessed Virgin Mary. In Italy, in the city of Bologna, the feast of Saint Dominic the confessor, a man of great piety and holiness. He possessed such zeal, etc.” At the end it adds: “How great was his merit before God, his resplendent miracles testify.” It follows with Oswald, purely; with Cassianus, as above. For Memmius it writes Meminius and adds: “sent first from the city of Rome to that city, who, among other miracles, raised a dead man. On the same day, blessed Yonius, priest and martyr, companion of Saint Dionysius.”

BELIN begins: “At Rome, Saint Mary, Mother of God, of the Snows. In the city of Bologna, Saint Dominic the confessor, founder of the Order of Friars Preachers.” His text is not entirely pure. The second edition gives Dominic as MOLANUS reported him more fully on the preceding day.

GREVEN: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Mary of the Snows, when, from the resources of John Patricius, during the time of Pope Liberius, a church was built in honor of the Mother of God. She herself indicated the site by the descent of abundant snow, contrary to the nature of the autumn season (or should it be summer?). It is called Saint Mary Major. Emigius, bishop of Ascoli and martyr. After departing from Germany, he was ordained bishop of Ascoli at Rome by Pope Marcellus. When he had converted many to the faith and shone with countless miracles, he completed his martyrdom by being beheaded for that same faith. At Corbeil, Saint Yonius, priest and martyr, companion of Saint Dionysius. Hormisdas, pope and confessor; according to some, his feast is celebrated here, while his burial is on the following day. According to Ado, he organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms; he sat for seventeen years and was buried in the church of blessed Peter, on 8 August.” See Ado’s appendix.

MOLANUS, after Oswald, but in different type, adds: “Among other things, relating that one day, as he was sitting at dinner, he ordered a silver dish placed before him to be broken into pieces and the food distributed to the poor.” At the end: “At Rome, Saint Mary, Mother of God, of the Snows. In the city of Bologna, etc.,” as on the preceding day. “At Corbeil, Saint Jonius the confessor. At Binche, Abel, archbishop of Reims.” Later editions begin in italics: “At Rome, Saint Mary, etc.” With Oswald, as above. To Memmius they add: “the first sent to that city from Rome, who, among countless other miracles, raised a dead man.” Of Jonius, as above. “At Lobbes, the feast of Saint Abel, archbishop and confessor. On the fifth day, Saint Eusignius the martyr. And the eve of the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ. At Bergen, the arrival of Saint Lewina, virgin and martyr.” Finally, in smaller type: “At Ascoli, Saint Emigius, bishop and martyr, in the time of Pope Marcellus.” Others have often wrongly written Esculum above instead of Asculum.

[Col. 0333A]

In the province of Raetia, in the city of Augsburg, the feast of Saint Afra, who, although she was a pagan and a prostitute, was converted to Christ through the teaching of Saint Narcissus the bishop, baptized with her entire household, and handed over to the fire for her confession of the Lord. On the same day, Saint Oswald, king of the English, whose Acts the Venerable Bede the priest commemorates in the history of that people. At Autun, blessed Cassianus, bishop and confessor. At Châlons, Saint Memmius, bishop.

VIII Ides. Day 6.

[Note: [Col. 0337A]]

The following are pure: PRATEN., HERINIEN., ANTWERP-MAJOR, ROSWEYD, ANTWERP, MAX.-LÜBECK, MUNERATUS, BELIN, GREVEN, and MOLANUS. To these are added ANTWERP-MAX and LOUVAIN.

[Note: [Col. 0337A]]

The greatest difficulty occurs at the beginning, because of which several codices would almost have to be excluded from the pure witnesses. I am not concerned about Xystus or Sixtus: prefer whichever you wish; the older spelling has been preserved in the text. All the purer witnesses, with Ado, read “bishop,” although the Small Roman Calendar has “pope.” Here the difficulty begins. ROSWEYD especially shapes the beginning so that after “martyr” he adds “who presided for two years,” and “and Saints Felicissimus and Agapitus,” etc., omitting the cemetery of Praetextatus. ANTWERP and MAX.-LÜBECK, however, write: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr.” Two other witnesses, ANTWERP-MAX and LOUVAIN, have “blessed Sixtus II, pope,” etc. Our text is purer, being composed in Ado’s own words. In MUNERATUS the conjunction “and” is missing before “in the cemetery.” After “who were beheaded,” it continues: “And with him also four,” etc., without repeating “were beheaded.” HERINIEN, ROSWEYD, MUNERATUS, and GREVEN read: “Blessed … also suffered with them.” But there the conjunction “and” seems redundant. In ROSWEYD, “in the city of Complutum” is missing. MUNERATUS wrongly wrote Compultum and, after “of the brothers,” added “title and martyrs,” which appears neither in Usuard’s text nor in Ado’s. The name Justus is not correctly expressed in ANTWERP-MAJOR. The latter, together with ROSWEYD, has “while they were still being instructed in childish letters.” Several read “school,” some “exhortations,” and others “were led,” but all these are better expressed, in accordance with Ado’s meaning, in our column, which, as we have already said, consists chiefly of Ado’s words.

[Note: [Col. 0337B]]

The memory of Pope Sixtus the martyr is so illustrious that scarcely that of any other Roman pontiff has been consecrated by more ancient monuments. The Bucherian Calendar explicitly records on this day: “Sixtus at Callistus and Praetextatus, Agapitus and Felicissimus.” In the Frontonian Calendar it is placed on 5 August: “The feast of Saint Sixtus, Felicissimus, and Agapitus.” The Allatian Calendar changes the name Felicissimus to Felix on this day. Add to these the Sacramentaries edited by Menardus and Thomasius, although they do not agree about the companions. Nor is there a uniform opinion in the Martyrologies, especially the Hieronymian ones, concerning the companions, whether anonymous or expressly named; Florentinius discusses this controversy at length. The Small Roman Calendar briefly concludes its entry: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, Xystus, pope and martyr; Felicissimus and Agapitus, deacons, in the cemetery of Praetextatus.” Ado wove a longer historical account from the Acts, partly described by Notker, whose beginning and end Our author has suitably joined in the words of the Viennese witness. What Bede records here with his companions does not differ much, though he omits Quartus, whom Florentinius also acknowledges as praised by Saint Cyprian, although, he says, it is unknown from another source when he suffered. It may be doubted whether the four named subdeacons completed their glorious contest on the same day as Sixtus; indeed, the same appears to apply to the deacons, as we shall examine more fully in due course. Meanwhile Castellanus judges, in a note appended to his universal French Martyrology, that only Quartus suffered martyrdom with Sixtus, on the basis of a letter of Saint Cyprian. We shall say on 10 August that Sixtus and the others belong not to the time of Decius but to that of Valerian, when we discuss the Acts of Laurence. Although learned men reject those Acts, the account can easily be supplemented from otherwise certain monuments cited by Baronius and others. We shall give Wandalbert’s eulogy below.

Concerning Justus and Pastor, our Florus mentions them on this day, but I find nothing about them among the earlier witnesses.
