Nor is it in any way likely that the Viennese author took his account from this Florus. Although he agrees with him sufficiently in substance, he uses such different wording here and elsewhere that they cannot be connected by any relationship at all. I would believe that both drew from the same Acts, which survive in Surius, and that each composed the eulogy independently. Moreover, Usuard here follows Ado’s wording so closely that he took everything from him to the letter, omitting only the place of the passion, “in the praiseworthy field,” and the brief final sentence: “Where they also rest in a basilica bearing their name.” Baronius noted several things about these saints, mostly repeated from Tillemont, volume V, page 59. It is therefore clear that the entire text is both Ado’s and Usuard’s. The Transfiguration of the Lord, added in some codices, does not belong to this text, and was never included by Usuard; Greven wrongly tried to persuade himself of the contrary on 27 July, as will be repeated below from him in the Appendices. The authority of our codices is sufficient. Among the ancients, only Wandalbert mentions the Transfiguration, which he places before Sixtus and his companions as follows:

On the eighth Ides, the holy flesh of Christ  
Will suffer death and the cross, having first displayed  
Its heavenly form. Sixtus, bishop and martyr,  
Is honored at Rome, and Felicissimus and Agapitus  
Triumph beside him.

[Note: [Col. 0337C]]

TORNACEN begins: “The Transfiguration of the Lord on Mount Tabor.” The final entry is missing.

PULSANEN: “On Mount Tabor, the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ before three disciples.” It is deficient in the final five companions of Sixtus and also in the eulogy of the martyrs of Complutum.

[Col. 0337D] UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANICUS, though otherwise pure in the text, insert in second place: “Likewise at Rome, Saint Hormisdas, pope. During his time the heretical emperor Anastasius was struck by lightning and perished.”

CENTULA: “The Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ on Mount Tabor, when his face shone and his garments became white like snow. At Rome, the passion of Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr, and with him Felicissimus and Agapitus, deacons; Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, and Stephanus, subdeacons. Blessed Quartus also suffered with them, as blessed Cyprian writes.” Nothing concerning the martyrs of Complutum.

BRUSSELS: “The Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ on Mount Tabor. It is believed to have taken place near the beginning of spring, at which time his Gospel is read. The three disciples who had been present at it proclaimed it to their fellow apostles after the Lord’s Ascension, on 26 July. Later, on this day, 8 August, by decree of the whole apostolic council, the Transfiguration itself began to be publicly preached. At Rome, Saint Hormisdas, pope and confessor.” It is quite pure in the account of the martyrs of Complutum. It treated Sixtus on the preceding day.

HAGENAU: “On Mount Tabor, the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ, when he took Peter, James, and John and showed them the glory which the saints will possess after the general resurrection. There they also heard the Father in a voice, saw the Son in glorified flesh, and the Holy Spirit in a shining cloud. There they also saw Moses and Elijah speaking with him, and the Law and the Prophets agreeing in the person of Christ. At Rome, on the Appian Way, the passion of Saint Sixtus II, pope. He was Greek by nationality, at first a philosopher, and afterward elected vicar of Christ. After governing the Church for two years and eleven months, he suffered under the persecution of the younger Decius and the emperor Valerian, and completed his martyrdom by decapitation. He established that Mass should be celebrated upon an altar, which had not previously been done, and that the altar should face east and no other direction. In the cemetery of Praetextatus, blessed Felicissimus,” etc., quite purely. “Likewise at Rome, the burial of Saint Hormisdas [Ormisdas], pope. During his time the heretical emperor Anastasius was struck by lightning and perished. He established that if anyone celebrated Mass without first having been properly ordained, he should by that very act be permanently deposed from holy orders.” Some material is taken from Ado’s appendix.

VICTORINUS, after Cyprian, inserts: “Likewise in the same place, Hormisdas the pope. He organized the clergy during the time of the emperor Anastasius. On the same day, the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-UTRECHT: “Sixtus, pope; Felicissimus and Agapitus, martyrs; Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, Stephanus, and Quartus, martyrs. These suffered with blessed Sixtus; Justus and Pastor, boyish brothers and martyrs.” As usual, the text is abbreviated.

CAMBRAI, Saint Mary’s: “On the same day, Lord Leonard, abbot.” I think this refers to the Aquitanian Leonard, disciple of Saint Remigius, who is commemorated on 6 November.

VATICAN, marked no. 5949, adds at the end: “At Rome, Saint Hormisdas, pope, who presided over the Church for seven years, in the time of the emperors Theodoric and Anastasius.” I have already said that Hormisdas is treated in Ado’s appendix.

[Col. 0339C] THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION: “On Mount Tabor, the Transfiguration of the Lord, which took place in the presence of the disciples, namely Peter, John, and his brother James, when his face shone like the sun, while his garments became white as snow, prefiguring the true renewal of his natural and mystical body. At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, the feast of blessed Sixtus II, pope and martyr, whom Caesar Decius caused to be beheaded. He governed the Church for two years, eleven months, and six days, established that Mass should be celebrated upon an altar, which had not previously been done, and was the spiritual father of Saint Laurence the deacon. Likewise at Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the passion,” etc., almost purely. Concerning Hormisdas, as in UTRECHT, etc.; concerning Justus and Pastor, as in the text.

BELIN is close to the purity of the text, although disfigured by many errors. At the beginning it prefixes: “On Mount Tabor, the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ.” See the fuller account above in BRUSSELS.

GREVEN: “The Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ on Mount Tabor, which Usuard has above on 27 July.” I said in the Observations that Usuard did not treat this feast; whatever Greven may have thought otherwise. “Here the burial of Pope Hormisdas. Among the Persians, Hormisdas the confessor. Concerning him, Book X of the Tripartite History relates that, although he was very noble, he was stripped of his wealth, rank, and clothing for Christ, and ordered, naked beneath the fiercest sun, to lead an army of camels. When the king again tried to soften him by restoring him and mentioning the benefit of clothing, he immediately tore the garment apart, left naked, and departed, expelled by the royal command. Likewise, blessed Gezelinus the confessor, resting at Slebusrode in the duchy of Mont.”

MOLANUS, after “were likewise beheaded,” inserts in different type: “At night, the clergy and the greater part of the Christians came and buried the bodies of the saints with fitting honor.” At the end: “On Mount Tabor, the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ. And the feast of blessed Hormisdas, pope, who sat at Rome for seventeen years. He organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms. During his time the heretical emperor Anastasius was struck by lightning and perished. The same pontiff was buried in the church of blessed Peter.” In smaller type it follows: “Among the Persians, Hormisdas the confessor.” Concerning him, etc., as in GREVEN, up to “to drag a camel’s army.” Other editions prefix the text in italics: “On Mount Tabor, etc.” In the text they have the same as the first edition. At the end: “At Rome, in the church of blessed Peter, the feast of blessed Hormisdas, pope, who organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms. During his time Anastasius,” etc. Finally, in smaller type: “Likewise, blessed Gezelinus the confessor, who rests in the duchy of Mont.” At Slebusrode, as GREVEN reported above.

[Col. 0335]

[In the margin: “The Transfiguration of the Lord Jesus on Mount Tabor,” Bouillart.]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of blessed Xystus, bishop and martyr. And in the cemetery of Praetextatus, Saints Felicissimus and Agapitus, his deacons, who were beheaded with him under Decius. Four others were beheaded with him also, namely Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, and Stephanus, subdeacons, as is read in the pontifical Acts. Blessed Quartus suffered with them, as Saint Cyprian writes. In Spain, in the city of Complutum, Justus and Pastor, brothers, who, while still boys and being instructed in letters, threw down their school tablets and voluntarily hastened to martyrdom. Immediately ordered by Dacianus to be arrested, while strengthening one another with mutual exhortations most steadfastly, they were led outside the city and slaughtered by the executioners.

VII Ides. Day 7.

[Note: [Col. 0339C]]

Many codices are pure on this day: PRATEN., HERINIEN., TORNACEN., ANTWERP-MAJOR, ANTWERP, MAX.-LÜBECK, MUNERATUS, BELIN, GREVEN, and MOLANUS. Likewise ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANICUS.

[Note: [Col. 0339D]]

The reading should follow the text from Bede, as Pope Gregory mentions it in the books of the Dialogues. MUNERATUS has “in the book of the Dialogues”; BELIN writes “in the books of the Dialogues.” ANTWERP more awkwardly combines both, writing “in the book of the Dialogues he mentions.” ANTWERP-MAJOR contracts the two martyrs into one boy, reading: “The holy martyr-boy Julian,” unless “boy” is taken as a proper name, or, more probably, this is a scribal error. MUNERATUS inserts the conjunction, “and Peter and Julian.” GREVEN and MOLANUS write: “At Milan, the feast of Saint Faustinus,” etc. Among other scribal errors, MUNERATUS also has “Aurelianus Commodus” instead of “Aurelius Commodus.”

[Note: [Col. 0339D]]

Florentinius rightly notes that Donatus, the bishop of Arezzo, well known in all the Martyrologies, was a martyr. He therefore wonders why in some Hieronymian copies he is called only a confessor; and here, to repeat the point, we always understand these names in their strict and mutually distinct senses. It is also necessary to observe in his index the entry which reads: “The feast of Saints Donatus, bishop and confessor, Auxentius, and Garpenforus,” as though the latter two had been companions of Donatus and crowned on the same day. Yet Florentinius does not dare assign them to the city of Arezzo. Whether they were from Cumae, Novum Comum, or another place will be said elsewhere. The matter is clearer in the Small Roman Calendar: “At Arezzo, Donatus, bishop and martyr.” To this the Viennese witness appends a long series of Acts, in which several saints are treated, Donatus’s teachers, companions, or contemporaries, especially Hilarinus the monk, as we indicated in our Observations on 16 July. It does not appear that Usuard took anything from Ado’s more elaborate discourse, copied by Notker, except the name of the emperor Julian, by which the time of the martyrdom would be indicated. The rest of the words placed in our text are Bede’s, expressing only the circumstance of the broken cup being restored, taken from Gregory’s Dialogues. It is more than probable that Bede received this from the holy pontiff’s own Acts, since Ado also narrates it at greater length from the same source. Baronius, in his present notes, gave a criticism worthy of his learning concerning the source itself, as it was published by Mombritius, volume I, page 234; we shall say more about it in the Acts. Meanwhile, Donatus’s commemoration in Thomasius’s Sacramentary should be noted.

The Small Roman Calendar mentions at Rome Peter and Juliana with eighteen others. Ado likewise expressly writes Juliana rather than Julianus, and I do not know why Usuard altered it, since in all other respects he took everything from Ado verbatim. Baronius followed Usuard in preference to the others; I confess that so far I do not see why one name should be preferred to the other, whatever all our codices may say. Another question remains: whether the two martyrs named here should be counted among the twenty-five or twenty-six anonymous persons recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on this day; and likewise whether they should not themselves be assigned to Augusta, as Florentinius briefly discusses. But these matters require a more intricate investigation than is compatible with the purpose of the present work. The final entry is no less Ado’s; in the Small Roman Calendar it originally read: “At Milan, Faustus the martyr.” The Hieronymian witnesses, however, consistently write Faustinus, and I think Ado borrowed the name from them, as it is also found in Rabanus and Notker. The present Roman Martyrology preferred Faustus, for which Baronius cites the Milanese records, which we shall examine elsewhere. For our present purpose, the genuine and pure simplicity of Usuard has been sufficiently demonstrated. We have spoken fully on 5 August about Afra of Augsburg, recorded on this day by Florus and others. I do not know what the passion of Mamas of Caesarea in Cappadocia is doing in the aforementioned Florus today: it belongs to 17 August. Wandalbert connects Afra with Donatus on this day as follows:

Together, Donatus and Afra likewise blessed the seventh day.

[Note: [Col. 0341B]]

ROSWEYD, whom we noted above as having omitted Afra on 5 August, appends her here to the pure text: “In the city of Augsburg, the feast of Saint Afra. Although she was a pagan and a prostitute, she was converted to Christ through the teaching of Saint Narcissus the bishop and, baptized with her entire household, was handed over to the fire for her confession of the Lord, together with three girls.”

PULSANEN is quite pure in the first two entries but completely omitted the third.

CENTULA: “At Rome, Saints Peter and Julian, martyrs, with eighteen others. In Tuscany, in the city of Arezzo, the feast of Saint Donatus, bishop and martyr, in the time of Julian.”

BRUSSELS is pure concerning Donatus, but here repeats Hilarinus, whom it had also treated above on 16 July, joining him to Donatus in these words: “And Saint Hilarinus the monk, killed by the sword.” It is pure in the second entry; in the third, it writes Aurelius instead of Aurelianus.

HAGENAU begins: “In the province of Raetia, in the city of Augusta, the feast of Saint Afra the martyr. Although she was a pagan and a prostitute, she was converted to Christ through the teaching and preaching of Saint Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem [more correctly, of Gerona], because of the fear of the devil whom she saw and the miracles which she witnessed from Saint Narcissus. Thus blessed Afra was baptized with her entire household and handed over to the fire for her confession of the Lord.” The final two entries follow quite purely. Then, concerning Donatus, also almost purely, it adds: “For this reason more than eighty pagans were converted and baptized by him.” Thus far not unreasonably; but what follows confuses two Donatuses, whom GREVEN distinguishes below by different type. Our codex reads here: “He also killed a dragon by praying and cleansed a spring poisoned by the dragon. At last he completed his martyrdom by being beheaded.”

AQUICINCT at the end adds what the other Appendices have on the preceding day, namely: “Likewise at Rome, Saint Hormisdas, pope. He organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms. During his time the heretical emperor Anastasius was struck by lightning and perished. After the pontiff died, he was buried in the church of blessed Peter.”

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-UTRECHT: “The Transfiguration of the Lord. This belongs instead to the preceding day (which are also the words of that codex). Donatus, bishop and martyr. Faustinus the martyr. Peter and Julian, martyrs, with eighteen others.”

STROZZIAN: “In Italy, at Cumae” (two other FLORENTINE codices omit the location), “the passion of Saints Carpophorus, Exanthus, Cassius, Severinus, and Secundinus, who suffered under the sacrilegious tyrant Maximian.” These are generally assigned to Novum Comum in the present Roman Martyrology.

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION begins: “Commemoration of blessed Mary of Egypt. In the twelfth year of her age, she left her parents and went to the city of Alexandria. Because she was beautiful and wanton, she exposed her body for eighteen years to every lustful act for temporal profit, excluding no one who approached her. Later converted by God’s will, she entered the desert and there, unknown to all human beings for sixty years, performed the harshest penance. Blessed Jerome describes her life in the Lives of the Fathers. She died happily in the year of the Lord 273, on the Lord’s Supper, which is celebrated on 2 April.” See there. It might have added why such a commemoration is made on this day. It continues: “In Tuscany, in the city of Arezzo, the feast of blessed Donatus, bishop and martyr, beheaded under the emperor Julian and the judge Quadracianus. Among other miracles, as Pope Gregory mentions in the books of the Dialogues, while he was administering the sacred mysteries to the people, a pagan jostled the deacon, and a glass chalice slipped from his hands and broke, causing the pagans to laugh. The holy bishop gathered the fragments and restored it by his prayers.” The next two entries are pure. It continues with Afra, nearly as on the fifth of this month. Finally: “On the same day, blessed Albert the confessor, of the Carmelite Order.” See the Roman Martyrology and Castellanus’s note.

GREVEN: “Donatus, bishop, and Hilarinus, the monk, martyrs, under Julian.” The repetition is superfluous. “At Antioch, Saints Suffronius, Veneria, and six others. Likewise Juliana, Dyomada, Memmia, Agape, and other martyrs. In Gaul, in the city of Rouen, the burial of Saint Victricius, bishop and confessor. Donatus, bishop of Eurea in Epirus and confessor. Concerning him the Tripartite History, Book IX, relates that he killed a dragon, terrible to all, by making the sign of the cross and spitting into its mouth; without delay he destroyed it and obtained a spring for his companions, fatigued by the journey. In the city of Messina, blessed Albert of Trapani, provincial prior throughout Sicily of the Carmelite Order, distinguished by the holiness of his life and the glory of his miracles. Commemoration of blessed Mary of Egypt.”

MOLANUS, after “he restored it,” inserts in different type: “He was arrested by Quadracianus the Augustal together with Hilarinus the monk and ordered to sacrifice to idols. When he refused, Quadracianus ordered Hilarinus to be beaten with clubs in Donatus’s presence until he gave up his spirit; then he ordered blessed Donatus to be struck with the sword. Christians buried their bodies reverently near the city.” This is abridged from Ado. At the end: “In the year of the Lord 1312, the burial of most blessed Albert of Mount Trapani, priest and confessor, provincial prior of the sacred Carmelite Order, resplendent with many miracles in life and after death. In Gaul, in the city of Rouen, blessed Victricius, bishop and confessor of that city.” Then, in smaller type: “Donatus, bishop of Eurea in Epirus,” etc., as in GREVEN above. Then: “In the city of Novara, Saint Godescalcus the martyr, bishop of that city, whose passion is recorded.” Other editions conclude: “In the city of Messina, in the Sicilian strait, the burial of most blessed Albert of Mount Trapani, priest and confessor and provincial prior of the Carmelite Order throughout Sicily. Illustrious by birth, character, learning, holiness, and miracles, he died in the year of the Lord 1292.” Of Victricius, as above. “In the city of Châlons, the burial of Saint Donatianus, bishop and confessor. On the seventh day, the most sacred martyr Dometius.” Finally, in smaller type: “In the city of Novara, Saint Godescalcus,” etc., as in the first edition.

[Col. 0339]

In Tuscany, in the city of Arezzo, the feast of blessed Donatus, bishop and martyr, under the emperor Julian. As Pope Gregory mentions in the books of the Dialogues, while celebrating Mass he restored the holy chalice broken by pagans. At Rome, Saints Peter and Julian, martyrs, with eighteen others. At Milan, Saint Faustinus, martyred in the time of Aurelius Commodus.

VI Ides. Day 8.

[Note: [Col. 0343A]]

Thus read PRATEN., HERINIEN., TORNACEN., ANTWERP-MAJOR, ROSWEYD, the earlier edition of BELIN, GREVEN, and MOLANUS.

[Note: [Col. 0343B]]

The reading should be Cyriacus, with PRATEN., ROSWEYD, and BELIN; but the others prevail, even when they are in error. “Ostian” or “Ostianus” has been noted elsewhere. ROSWEYD, after “deacon,” adds “and martyr.” All read “in the time of the emperor Diocletian,” although Ado most distinctly wrote “of Augustus Maximianus,” about which we spoke elsewhere. MOLANUS omitted “emperor.” TORNACEN substituted Severinus for Severus. Upon reaching the aforementioned city, all write with the text, except GREVEN and MOLANUS, who have “when he came to the aforementioned city.” I pass over “martyrs,” “Vienna,” “of the Gospel,” and similar matters.

We dealt with the holy martyrs placed here first, Cyriacus, Largus, and Smaragdus, together with Usuard and the other martyrologists on the very day on which they are considered to have suffered martyrdom, namely 17 Kalends of April, or 16 March; and there, in the Observations, we noted that their companions, both those named and those anonymous, passed from Bede into Ado, together with nearly the whole of their eulogy [Col. 0343C]. On this day many things are confused, both in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and in others, which it is not easy to explain briefly. Florentinius distinguishes some matters quite accurately, but leaves still more unresolved. Bede, who on the aforementioned day, 16 March, had reported five names, here simply reads, “The feast of Saint Cyriacus,” leaving it somewhat doubtful whether this Cyriacus is the same one of whom he had spoken above. Nor do the additions made, I think, under the name of Florus provide much illumination, any more than does Rabanus, who follows Bede as though Cyriacus had suffered on this day with twenty-one others. The small Roman Martyrology is somewhat clearer: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, Cyriacus the martyr with twenty-one others, when they were laid to rest on the eighth day of the month of August.” But even so the difficulty is not removed, for it remains to be asked who these twenty-one are, since the same small Roman Martyrology, on the aforementioned 16 March, distinctly mentions Cyriacus, Largus, Smaragdus, and Crescentianus with twenty others.

Nevertheless, the things Ado records here are obscure. At the beginning he names only Cyriacus with twenty-one persons of both sexes indiscriminately; at the end, however, he writes as follows: “The passions of the blessed martyrs, namely Cyriacus, Largus, and Smaragdus, have been recorded in their proper places in the present Calendar on 17 Kalends of April.” I ask again whether it can safely be inferred from this that all those reported on 16 March were laid to rest on this day, or only some of them; likewise, whether only Cyriacus, Largus, and Smaragdus were buried by Pope Marcellus; or whether, as Bucherius’s Calendar notes, the following were buried together: Ballestaria, Cyriacus, Largus, Crescentianus, Memmia, Julianus, and Smaragdus; or rather all those who are enumerated today in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. If one says that all of them were transferred or moved, one will scarcely find a number that can be established with certainty. If Notker is added, [Col. 0344B] he seems to complicate still further the day of their martyrdom and translation, as well as the number of martyrs. Thus Our Author, making no mention whatever of the translation or elevation of the bodies, writes plainly: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the feast of the blessed man, etc.,” as though he had never mentioned them before. He names three principal martyrs with twenty others, and thus counts the same twenty-three whom he had also placed on 17 Kalends of April—there under Maximian, here under Diocletian.

But concerning the persecutor and the persecution we have spoken sufficiently above; we leave the remaining knots to be untied in the Acts, where the whole history of this passion will have to be discussed in full. Bollandus admitted, in his correction under 16 January, that it requires amendment. In the Annals, under the year 298, no. 13, and under the year 309, no. 6, he indeed shows clearly that not a few things displease him; but later critics add so much to these observations that they expose almost the entire narrative to contempt. Meanwhile, all the cited manuscripts support the genuine reading of the entry. The more recent witnesses, which will be brought forward in the Appendices, differ somewhat from them: wishing to correct the author, they substitute a translation performed by Pope Marcellus, as will soon become clear.

The more involved the foregoing statements are, the clearer is the final announcement taken from Ado, with a few small excisions. Ado, as the first writer and as one to whom the matter was better known, placed it there [Col. 0344D], and Notker transcribed the whole from him. Perhaps the Viennese cited those Acts which survive among our manuscripts, composed in one case in a shorter and in another in a more expansive style. We reserve judgment on how much weight they deserve until the proper place. Wandalbert mentions Cyriacus here as though he alone were commemorated today and were different from the earlier Cyriacus. In this he may have followed ancient Calendars, such as those published by Fronto and Allatius, which are completely in agreement with Gregory’s Sacramentary. What is more, Cyriacus is also noted alone on 15 July in the Fronto Calendar. You see here abundant material for discussion elsewhere. Here now is Wandalbert’s own verse:

> Cyriacus enters the honor of the aged one.

[Note: [Col. 0345A]]

Pulsanen, pure in the first place, puts in the second: “At Jerusalem, the passion of Saint Quiriacus the bishop, under the emperor Julian.” Then: “At the Gallic city of Vienne, Saint Severus the priest and martyr,” stopping there.

Antwerp and Max-Lübeck append to the text: “Likewise Saint Agape the virgin.”

Munerat, after the text: “On the same day, Saint Justin the martyr, whose body rests in the great church of the Blessed Virgin at Paris.” This is the same saint whom we placed under 1 August among the Appendices of Molanus, with the same eulogy, though somewhat corrected, because he is venerated at Paris on this day.

Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, and the Danish witness express the first announcement as follows: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the blessed Cyriacus the deacon, and the holy martyrs Largus and Smaragdus, when their bodies were raised by the blessed Marcellus and honorably buried. They suffered, however, on 17 Kalends of April.” [Col. 0345B] In the second announcement they are fairly pure. At the end: “Likewise Saint Agape the virgin.”

Centulen: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Cyriacus the deacon [and] his companions, who suffered on 17 Kalends of April, but now, since their bodies have been raised by the blessed Pope Marcellus and reburied with greater honor, a greater celebration and more frequent gathering take place. At Milan, Saint Faustinus the martyr.” From the preceding day. “At Vienne, Saint Severus the priest and confessor, who, serving diligently in the Lord’s vineyard from early morning until the end of his life, deserved to be crowned. At the Tuscan Colonia, Saints Secundianus, Marcellianus, and Verianus.” See the following day.

Brussels: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, at the seventh milestone, the elevation of the blessed Cyriacus the deacon and of the holy martyrs Largus and Smaragdus. They suffered with twenty-one others on 17 Kalends of April, but on this day their bodies were raised by the blessed Pope Marcellus and honorably buried. And at Nicaea in Bithynia, Saint Arsacius the confessor, under Licinius the persecutor. After abandoning military service, he led a solitary life in a certain tower of the aforesaid city, and shone with such great virtues that he expelled demons and killed a monstrous dragon.” In the entry for Severus it is pure; it ends: “Likewise Saint Agape the virgin.”

Hagenoyen: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the translation of the holy martyrs Cyriacus, Largus, and Smaragdus, when their bodies were raised by the blessed Pope Marcellus and honorably buried. These saints suffered under the emperor Maximian on 17 Kalends of April, but their feast is celebrated on this day.” In the entry for Severus it is fairly pure. It continues: “Likewise Saint Agape the virgin.” Then: “In Spain, in the city of Gerunda, the feast of Saint Felix the martyr, whom the judge Decianus, during the persecution of Diocletian, after inflicting various kinds of tortures, ordered to be stripped with hooks, then torn to pieces down to the bones, and his wounds continually renewed with further wounds, until he returned to God his unconquered spirit.” See our text above under 1 August.

Aquicinct, at the end: “Likewise Agape the virgin.”

Matrice-Carthusian-Utrecht: “Cyriacus, Largus, and Smaragdus the martyrs, with twenty others. Severus the priest and confessor, who converted a great multitude at Vienne to the faith.”

Ughellian adds at the end: “Likewise Saint Agape the virgin.” This entry recurs frequently.

Florentin: “At Ancona, the translation of Saint Quiriacus the bishop and martyr. Likewise Saint Agape the virgin.”

Lübeck-Cologne Edition: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, at the seventh milestone, the translation of the blessed Cyriacus the deacon and the holy martyrs Largus and Smaragdus with twenty-two others, when their bodies were raised by the blessed Pope Marcellus and honorably buried. They suffered on 17 Kalends of April. Nevertheless, this day is considered the more celebrated.” In the entry for Severus it is pure. At the end it adds: “On the same day, Saint Agape the virgin. In the territory of Troyes, Saint Leonides the martyr.” I think there is an error in the name.

The second edition of Belin adds at the end: “Likewise Agape the virgin. At Bordeaux, the deposition of Mommuralis, abbot of the monastery of Fleury.”

Greven: “In Hungary, the arrival of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise the feast of the Fifteen Helpers, whose names are these: the glorious ever-virgin Mother of God Mary, Blaise, Dionysius, Erasmus, Pantaleon, Vitus, George, Cyriacus, Christopher, Agathius, Eustace, Giles, Barbara, Catherine, Margaret. Cyriacus, bishop of Ostia and martyr. Paymon the martyr. At Philadelphia, the feast of Saint Leonides. Likewise Justin the martyr. In the territory of Troyes, Leovaldus the martyr. Likewise Secundus. At Ancona, the translation of Saint Quiricus the bishop and martyr, from Jerusalem to the aforesaid city. Agape the virgin. Likewise the blessed-memory confessor Hilger, [Col. 0346C] of the Order of Preachers, son of a count.”

Molanus appends to the first announcement, in italic letters: “Whose passions have been recorded in their proper places in the present Calendar.” At the end: “Likewise Agape the virgin. At Bordeaux, the deposition of Mommuralis, abbot of the monastery of Fleury. On the same day, Saint Justin the martyr, whose body rests in the great church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Paris.” See these same entries under 1 August in the later editions of Molanus. These editions, moreover, have in the text today the same material as above. At the end: “At Bordeaux, the deposition of Mommolus, abbot of the monastery of Fleury. Likewise Saint Agape the virgin. On the eighth day, Saint Aemilianus the confessor at Cyzicus.” In the Horologium the title “bishop” is added.]

[Col. 0343]

At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the feast of the blessed Cyriacus the deacon and the holy martyrs Largus and Smaragdus with twenty others, in the time of the emperor Diocletian.

[Note: [Col. 0343B]]

The place where the commemoration of Saint Severus is now read was once erased. Likewise, the following entry has been completely mutilated with a knife from beginning to end, while Sollerius says nothing and admits the correction. Who were the saints formerly commemorated in these places? Where, Reverend Father, are those ancient codices of yours, from which you think the original and native simplicity of Usuard is to be recovered? Bring them forward, as you usually do; display them. Is there no fraud and imposture concealed here? Was there not some associate of Usuard who judged that he ought to adapt his own style to that of Usuard? But, setting aside the jest, admit at last that erasures and corrections do no harm whatsoever to the purity of the Usuardine text, since the same hand that copied the entire codex also corrected it.]

At the Gallic city of Vienne, Saint Severus the priest and confessor, who, as his Acts testify, undertook a laborious journey for the sake of preaching the Gospel and, arriving at the aforesaid city, converted a great multitude of pagans to the faith of Christ by word and miracles.

### 5 Ides. Day 9.

[Note: [Col. 0345D]]

Thus read Praten, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molanus. [Col. 0346D] Likewise Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, and the Danish witness.

[Note: [Col. 0345D]]

You will note that Rosweyd is counted among the pure witnesses, although he differs greatly from the others—not in the wording of the text, but in the transposition of the announcements. For he relegates the Vigil to the final place and substitutes the Roman entry in first place. Similarly, the last six manuscripts of the middle class report the Roman entry in second place.

Now to the particulars. Rosweyd reads “Secundianus, and Marcellianus, and Valerianus.” In place of Promotus he has Promortus. Greven has Promotio, Molanus Promotio. Munerat reads “they were first beaten.” Antwerp, through a scribal error, repeats *assati* in this fashion: “and roasted at the sides by fire, roasted being added.” All these matters are set more accurately in the text. Greven and Molanus insert *in* before *confessione*: “who in confession”; the others, together with the older witnesses and Our Author, are simpler. Thus the same two read: “he was brought forth with clubs and beheaded,” omitting the conjunction *and*. Antwerp-Major and the six final witnesses remove *with*: “Decius ordering, with clubs,” which Munerat also does [Col. 0348A] in another place, going beyond the others, for after *exhibited* he adds: “and finally he was beheaded.”]

[Note: [Col. 0347A]]

The Vigil of Saint Laurence. Thus it is given by Bede, the small Roman Martyrology, and Ado. Why it was omitted by Rabanus I cannot conjecture; I would rather suspect that it is not a genuine announcement of Bede. Even so, it would remain a very ancient celebration, or custom observed from the earliest times of the Church, as the Calendars of Fronto and Allatius prove, together with the Sacramentaries published by Menardus and Thomasius, whatever the Hieronymian manuscripts may say by not mentioning it. You will find the origin of such vigils, prolonged for one or more days, explained most plausibly by Baronius [Col. 0347B]. Notker follows the cited martyrologists, but Our Author adds the title “martyr.” Wandalbert, singing only the Roman entry today, shows that, while he was writing at his monastery of Prüm, that rite had not yet been adopted there.

Concerning the following class of martyrs I find nothing among Usuard’s usual predecessors. Florus says briefly: “At Cologne, the feast of Saints Faustinus, Marcellinus, Secundianus, and Sixtus.” But Our Author certainly did not derive his entry from this. I think it more probable that the martyrs expressed in the text flowed from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in one of which Usuard may have read: “In Tuscany, Verianus, Marcellianus, Secundianus …”; and that he selected these as the principal martyrs, as he often does, omitting the others noted by the Echternach manuscript. When another manuscript read “In Colonia,” he himself may have combined the two locations into one: “At the Tuscan Colonia”; and then, having found the Acts somewhere, composed his eulogy from them.

As for the truth of those Acts, and also the disputed place where the martyrdom began and ended [Col. 0348A], more remains to be examined elsewhere. For the present, Notker’s judgment may suffice. On this day he writes: “At Colonia, Faustinus, Marcellinus, Secundianus, and Verianus, according to the Martyrology of blessed Jerome. Since, by our countrymen, who pursue the ravings of apocryphal writings, they are said to have been baptized by Saint Sixtus because of the succession of the times, and to have been killed by Decius.” I do not yet understand clearly whom or what Notker is specifically attacking here. I nevertheless think that he is demolishing the Acts that connect the time of Pope Sixtus with Decius; hence Baronius, under the year 253, no. 29, calls them corrupt. See what Papebrochius discussed concerning these same Acts in volume I of June, p. 34 onward; Tillemont, volume III, p. 704, may also be consulted. See further in Florentinius’s Notes.

For the rest, it is perfectly clear from all the Usuardine manuscripts that Our Author wrote as the table presents it. Concerning the famous Roman martyr there is no difficulty at all. He is simply recorded by the Hieronymian Martyrologies and the small Roman Martyrology. Bede embraced his passion in a concise eulogy, from which Rabanus and Ado took their accounts, and from Ado Usuard and Notker, preserving everywhere nearly the same details. It is evident that the Acts of Romanus have been mixed into those of Laurence, and therefore the same judgment must be applied to both.

Florus, Rabanus, and Notker speak of Firmus and Rusticus, the Veronese martyrs, but I do not know from where Belin transferred them; certainly they have nothing whatever to do with the Usuardine text. Wandalbert’s verse concerning Romanus is elegant:

> Romanus, soldier and martyr, shines with fivefold glory.

[Note: [Col. 0347B]]

Tournai, having scarcely set down half of today’s text, continues to be defective until 26 September.

Pulsanen begins as follows: “The Vigil of Saint Laurence the Levite and martyr.” In the second announcement the eulogy has been deleted. In the third he is pure concerning Romanus.

[Col. 0347C] Centulen: “The Vigil of Saint Laurence. At Rome, Saint Romanus the soldier, who, moved by the confession of the blessed Laurence, asked to be baptized and was immediately, at the command of Decius, brought forth with clubs and beheaded.” He dealt with the others on the preceding day.

Brussels: “The Vigil of Saint Laurence the martyr, who alone among all the martyrs has a Vigil. At Rome, Saint Romanus the soldier, who was baptized by the blessed Laurence and immediately, at the command of Caesar Decius, beaten with clubs and beheaded.” In the other martyrs it is fairly pure, but instead of Verianus, which is in the text, it writes Nerianus.

Hagenoyen, fairly pure in the first two, announces the third as follows: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Romanus the soldier and martyr. During the passion of Saint Laurence he was moved because he saw a very beautiful young man wiping his wounds, and therefore asked and obtained baptism from him; for this reason he was beaten with clubs by the younger Caesar Decius, and because he was strong in faith, Decius ordered him to be beheaded.”

[Col. 0347D] Matrice-Carthusian-Utrecht: “The Vigil. Romanus the soldier and martyr. Secundianus, Verianus, and Marcellianus, martyrs.”

Strozzi: “At Verona, Saints Rusticus and Firmus the martyrs.” See the preceding Observations.

Bordeaux: “At Briva, Saint Martin the martyr.” Castellanus calls it “Briva Curretia.”

Codex of the Castle of Charles: “In the suburb of Lyon, the feast of the holy martyrs Amor and Viator.” This is doubtless a local feast.

Besançon, concerning the Tuscan martyrs, reports the words of the text and adds: “Of these Secundianus was later transferred to Gaul, in the territory of Langres, and gloriously buried in the monastery of Saint Leodegarius [Col. 0348B], where, by God’s gift, he does not cease to reveal himself through distinguished miracles.” The same words are read in the Martyrology of the Franciscan brothers of Salins. This, however, concerns Secundianus alone.

Saussayus, in his Gallican Martyrology, gives a completely different account, writing on this day: “In the monastery of Jouarre, the veneration of the most sacred relics of the illustrious martyrs of Christ, Secundianus, Verianus, and Marcellianus, who today at Rome, under Decius, under the consul Promotus, having been tortured with clubs, fire, and iron, finally earned the eternal crown of glory by the cutting off of their heads. Their bodies, brought from Rome into Gaul and deposited there for veneration, are still preserved with exceptional honor, together with the relics of many other blessed martyrs.”

The compiler of the great Martyrology ought to have shown in his Apodictic writings what documents concerning this translation remain; but since these are lacking, they will have to be sought elsewhere later in our Acts, when the claims of the Italian cities disputing over the precious deposit are carefully weighed.

The Lübeck-Cologne Edition is nearly like Antwerp-Maximum and the others, namely, in announcing Romanus in second place. At the end it adds: “At Metz, the feast of Saint Auctor, bishop of that place and confessor.” See the following day.

Belin also places Romanus before the Tuscan martyrs. Then, at the end [Col. 0348D]: “On the same day, at Verona, Saints Rusticus and Firmus the martyrs.”

Greven: “At Verona, Saints Firminus and Rusticus the martyrs. Because of their confession of Christ, they were rolled for a long time over burning tiles, and when they had remained unharmed even in the fire, they were mangled with clubs and attained the glory of martyrdom by beheading. At Alexandria, Saints Antoninus, Tiburtius, and Valerianus. Likewise Ericus, king of Dacia and martyr, of blessed memory.” Is this perhaps the same one who is commemorated on 18 May? Certainly he does not seem to be the one mentioned in the Acts under 13 March, who is venerated at Perugia. The phrase “of blessed memory” seems to indicate something else, as it sounds in Greven.

Molanus, at the end: “On the same day, at Verona, Saints Rusticus and Firmus, citizens of Bergamo.” Then, in smaller type: “The feast of Saints Numidicus the priest and martyr with many others. Concerning them Cyprian writes in his letter to the deacons, priests, and people of Carthage.” See Ruinart, p. 198. In other editions it reads: “On the same day, at Verona, Saints Rusticus and Firmus the martyrs. At the city of Châlons, Saint Domitianus the bishop and confessor.” He is included in the Roman Martyrology.]

[Col. 0345]

The Vigil of Saint Laurence the martyr. At the Tuscan Colonia, the feast of Saints Secundianus, Marcellianus, and Verianus, who in the time of Decius were first beaten under the consul Promotus, then suspended on the rack, scraped with hooks, and roasted by fire applied to their sides; finally, beheaded, they earned the triumphant palm of martyrdom. At Rome, Saint Romanus the soldier, who, moved by the confession of the blessed Laurence, asked to be baptized by him and was immediately, at Decius’s command, brought forth with clubs and beheaded.

### 4 Ides. Day 10.

[Note: [Col. 0349]]

The pure manuscripts are Praten, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Munerat, the first edition of Belin, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0349A]]

For *Tiburtina*, Belin and Molanus write *Tyburtina*; Antwerp and Max-Lübeck have *Laurencii*. Antwerp-Major alone transposes the phrase, placing “after the many torments of prison” later. Herinien has *Lamminarum*. Rosweyd removes “one hundred and sixty-five martyrs” from the second announcement, reading “sixty-five soldiers.” In Antwerp-Major *soldiers* is absent. Belin, however, has: “At Rome, one hundred and sixty-five saints.”]

[Note: [Col. 0349B]]

“Everything concerning Saint Laurence,” says Florentinius, “is better known than to require anything to be added.” So it is; for all our Martyrologies, indeed even the most ancient Calendars—such as that of Polemius Silvius and another published by Bucherius, as well as the Carthaginian, Allatian, and Fronto Calendars, and the Sacramentaries—unanimously commemorate throughout the Church his most glorious passion. You will observe this particular distinction in this most illustrious saint: he alone, apart from the feasts of our Redemption and of the apostles, alone among mortals possesses a solemn and universal celebration, prescribed not only for the clergy but also for the people; or perhaps because for him alone, who was not Jewish by origin, nearly the first feast in the Church was decreed.

Apart from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, the small Roman Martyrology says this today concerning Laurence: “At Rome, Laurence, archdeacon and martyr.” Ado devotes himself entirely to setting out the Acts at length, the greater part of which Notker transferred into his Martyrology. Our Author, however, pursuing greater brevity, preferred to transcribe Bede’s eulogy [Col. 0349C]. There you will notice that the only element prefixed from Ado is the place of combat—or, if you prefer, of burial—“at Rome, on the Tiburtine Way”; likewise, from Ado and the small Roman Martyrology, and even from some Hieronymian manuscripts, the title “archdeacon,” which the holy Fathers long ago bestowed in a rare example.

Our Author, however, wrote “in the presence of the emperor Decius,” beyond what he had read in his sources. Rabanus adheres more closely to Bede’s words, in which it is not the presence of Decius but the persecution of Decius that is expressly indicated; Ado likewise took this from the Acts, using the same words in both places: “Under Decius.” But concerning this matter, Baronius’s most careful Notes for this day must be read. There he proves easily from the chronology that neither the martyrdom of Sixtus nor that of Laurence can be reconciled with the years of Decius, and consequently that “Valerian” should be written instead of “Decius,” as we shall explain more fully elsewhere.

How much weight should be given to the commonly circulated Acts of Laurence, from which other accounts are also drawn and which we have cited elsewhere, Cardinal Norisius will show at the end of his third dissertation on the epochs of the Syro-Macedonians, p. 394 of the Leipzig edition. Recent scholars agree with him, and their arguments will be examined in due course. If we cannot defend even the Acts that concern Laurence separately, the loss can easily be compensated elsewhere by the many eulogies of the holy Fathers, which have begun to be collected among Ruinart’s selections, p. 180 onward.

The small Roman Martyrology continues: “And one hundred and sixty-five soldiers.” Nothing is said of these in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, nor in Bede or Bede’s followers. Ado, following his custom at first, reads: “On the same day, at Rome, one hundred and sixty-five soldiers,” and adds: “Then Claudius, Severus, Crescentio, and Romanus suffered, on the same day on which the blessed Laurence suffered, three days after the passion of Saint Sixtus.” These matters will have to be considered in their proper place.

Meanwhile, Notker appended the final material to Laurence’s eulogy, forming the second announcement as follows: “On the same day, at Rome, one hundred and forty-five soldiers.” The reason for this alteration is nowhere apparent. But if one considers only the number, I do not see why Notker should have departed from Ado; hence it may be suspected that it was badly copied through the carelessness of a scribe. As for his separating Claudius and his companions from the one hundred and sixty-five soldiers, this perhaps happened because he believed that, although they suffered on the same day, they did not suffer at the same time. Baronius certainly assigns their contest to the persecution of Aurelian in the modern Roman Martyrology. Whether rightly or wrongly I leave aside here. It is enough to observe that Usuard, the perpetual follower of Ado, did not depart from Ado’s judgment concerning those soldier-martyrs.

It deserves to be added that Wandalbert composed a metrical encomium of Laurence, in which he alone is sung, with no mention of companions or of the one hundred and sixty-five soldiers:

> On the fourth day, Laurence, you shine with richly deserved splendor,  
> who, having suffered fire, overcome the unjust torturer.

[Note: [Col. 0349D]]

Pulsanen reads: “of the most blessed Laurence.” He omits the one hundred and sixty-five soldiers, replacing them with: “At Ephesus, the feast of the seven holy Sleepers, namely Maximian, Malchus, Martyrianius, John, Dionysius, Constantine, Serapion, and four others, whose Acts are extant.” I do not know why those four are added. See Usuard under 27 July.

Antwerp-Maximum, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, and the Danish witness add to the text: “At Metz, the deposition of Saint Auctor the bishop.” Correctly below: “in the monastery of Maurus.”

Centulen: “At Rome, the feast of the blessed Laurence the archdeacon, who, after many torments of imprisonment, various scourges, and burning plates, was finally roasted on an iron grid and completed a glorious martyrdom worthy of every praise. On the same day, at Rome, one hundred and sixty-five soldiers.”

Brussels, with an otherwise fairly pure text, adds only: “At Metz, in the monastery of Maurus, the deposition of Saint Victor, bishop of Metz and confessor.” Read *Auctor*, as the manuscripts correctly have.

Hagenoyen: “At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, the passion of Saint Laurence the martyr, who was ordained archdeacon of the Roman Church by the blessed Pope Sixtus II. He devoutly fulfilled his office; therefore, when Sixtus went to his passion, he entrusted his treasures to him so that he might distribute them to the poor. He did so, and by the sign of the cross he himself gave sight to the blind and converted many to the faith by word [Col. 0351A] and example. After imprisonment and various kinds of scourging, he endured burning plates; he was strengthened by a divine voice speaking to him; then he was again beaten with scorpions, and while praying for those standing by he was imprisoned. Then, at night, he was brought before Decius, and every kind of torture was inflicted. Laurence was then stretched upon an iron grate, compressed with iron forks, and coals were placed beneath the grate; he was roasted, and thus that martyr of Christ was consecrated. Likewise, on the same day at Rome, one hundred and sixty-five soldiers. At Metz, the deposition of Saint Auctor, bishop and confessor.”

Victorinus and the Queen of Sweden manuscript, marked no. 130, at the end: “In the Ephesian city, the seven Sleepers.”

Matrice-Carthusian-Utrecht: “Laurence the martyr. At Rome, one hundred and sixty-five soldiers.” Something is always lacking here.

The Swedish Royal manuscript, marked no. 428: “At Paris, the reception of the holy crown of the Lord.” Nothing is said of this by the others; it belongs to the following day.

[Col. 0351B] Vatican manuscript, marked no. 5949: “At Ephesus, the seven holy Sleepers.” See under Pulsanen.

The Lübeck-Cologne Edition: “At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, the feast of the blessed Laurence the archdeacon, of the blessed Pope Sixtus. [Col. 0352A] He was Spanish by birth, and outstanding in purity, innocence of life, freedom [or perhaps generosity?] of works of mercy, and, in the presence of the emperor Decius, after many torments,” etc. The entry concerning the one hundred and sixty-five soldiers is pure. At the end it adds: “In Scotland, Saint Blane, bishop and confessor.” See Castellanus.

The second edition of Belin forms the final announcement as follows: “On the same day at Rome, one hundred and sixty-five, and the seven Sleepers.” The construction must be divided.

Greven: “Likewise Saints Claudius, Severus, Crescentianus [or perhaps Crescentio?], and Romanus the martyrs; at Metz, Saint Auctor the bishop and confessor. At Tongeren, Saint John the bishop and confessor, who was also called Agnus. When he was a farmer, he was appointed to govern the aforesaid church through the miracle of a flowering staff. In Scotland, Saint Blane, bishop and confessor. At Maastricht, the translation of Saints Monulphus and Gundulphus, bishops and confessors.” [Col. 0352B] They are placed on 16 July, and by Castellanus on 26 July.

Molanus, in all editions, has this single addition: “At Metz, the deposition of Saint Auctor the bishop.” His body rests in “the monastery of Maurus.”]

[Col. 0349]

At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, the feast of the blessed Laurence the archdeacon, who, in the presence of the emperor Decius, after many torments of imprisonment, various scourges, and burning plates, was finally roasted on an iron grid and completed his martyrdom. On the same day, at Rome, one hundred and sixty-five soldiers.

### 3 Ides. Day 11.

[Note: [Col. 0351]]

The text is taken from Praten, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, Belin, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0351C]]

What occurs elsewhere concerning the Tiburtine Way recurs here concerning Tiburtius. Belin and Molanus again write *Tyburtina*; Antwerp-Major has *Tiburcius*. This same manuscript also has a broken and mutilated construction. Where the text correctly reads “when he confessed Christ with greater steadfastness,” it reads: “he confessed Christ with urgency.” The final clause of Herinien is likewise corrupt, or rather the last part of the clause, and is not even half the first: “and there he caused him to be punished by the sword,” instead of “he was ordered.” Concerning Gaius, mention has been made more than once; we follow the spelling of the manuscripts.

Praten, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, and Belin explicitly place the entry “in the city of Cambrai.” Those who prefer *Cameracum* may do so as far as I am concerned. *Gauritius*, instead of *Gaugericus*, is an error in Belin. Hieronymus of Lucca wrote *Gauricus*. Molanus was careless when he read “bishop and martyr,” but corrected his acknowledged oversight in later editions. He also added at the end “Taurinus, bishop and confessor”; the final word is absent from all the other manuscripts except Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, which mutilate the announcement at the beginning: “On the same day, Saint Taurinus the bishop and confessor.” All read *Ebroas* rather than *Ebroicae*, and Antwerp-Major does not improve matters with *Eborias*. Another has *Ebora*.]

[Note: [Col. 0351C]]

Some Hieronymian manuscripts mention Tiburtius in such a way that they seem plainly to identify him as the brother of Valerian, Cecilia’s bridegroom. Florentinius therefore rightly suspects that, through the ignorance of a careless ancient copyist—one who knew nothing of another Tiburtius—the names of those two companions were wrongly inserted there. In the same Hieronymian manuscripts the following is immediately added [Col. 0351D]: “The feast of Saint Susanna.” Bede embraces the two in a single announcement, as briefly as possible: “At Rome, Saint Tiburtius the martyr and Susanna.” The small Roman Martyrology distinguishes them somewhat more clearly: concerning the first, “At Rome, between the Two Laurels, Tiburtius the martyr”; concerning the second, “And Susanna the virgin martyr.”

The Viennese inserted extended histories of both into his Martyrology. He took the first from the Acts of Saint Sebastian, especially chapter 21 in our collection; the second from the very Acts that Molanus calls most celebrated, the deeds of the illustrious martyr, which are to be seen in Surius and praised by Baronius and by our earlier scholars. Some have completely rejected them, but we shall examine and elucidate them from time to time. Whatever judgment may eventually be made concerning those Acts, the venerable memory of Susanna is amply confirmed, apart from the cited Martyrologies, by Fronto’s Calendar and the Sacramentaries cited by him; in that same Calendar Tiburtius is commemorated on this day. Both are also recorded in the Allatian Calendar [Col. 0352C].

As for the text, Our Author selected a few of the more notable details from two eulogies of Ado and arranged them in the order in which they appear in the entry. Notker drew more extensively from the same sources, in his customary generous fashion. Florus and Rabanus also have shorter eulogies, but they contribute nothing to the present purpose.

Wandalbert sang of Tiburtius and of Gaugericus, who follows him, while Susanna, I do not know for what reason, was entirely omitted:

> Threefold, you seek the stars as a flower and pious glory, Tiburtius.

> This holy confessor Goericus also possesses (in Brabant, Goeric).

The edition of Mosander attributes Gaugericus of Cambrai to Ado; Rosweyd relegated him to the Appendix, rightly, I think, since otherwise Notker would probably not have omitted him. For the present, he is recorded in the Lucan and Corbie Hieronymian manuscripts. Whether he was added more recently by a copyist I do not discuss. I would believe that Usuard received him from some similar manuscript, perhaps the Corbie manuscript, in which Taurinus is also named. He is unknown to all the other martyrologists except Florus, who joins him to Gaugericus in such a way that he does not hesitate to assert that he was his brother.

The origin of the well-known chronological error is evident in certain Acts, I do not know which, adorned by someone named Adeodatus in such a way that their fabrication is easily demonstrated [Col. 0353A]. Our Author proceeded more securely, asserting nothing that is not abundantly established by more reliable monuments; perhaps for this reason he deliberately abstained from the title “confessor” or “martyr.”

Castellanus regards as suspect in the eulogy of the modern Roman Martyrology only the part concerning the mission sent by Saint Clement the pope. The Life of Gaugericus preserved by Surius is more genuine, but it is abridged from a more extensive history, which we shall elucidate in its proper time. These observations suffice to establish the origin of the entire text and its plainly genuine simplicity.]

[Note: [Col. 0353A]]

Rosweyd inserted into the text concerning Tiburtius: “son of Chromatius, prefect of the City, taught by Saint Sebastian.” The rest is fairly pure to the end, where the final announcement alone is lacking.

Pulsanen is pure up to “Susanna the virgin”; everything else is absent.

MUNERAT. Appends to the uncorrupted text:

> “At Paris, the reception of the sacred Crown of Thorns of the Lord, happily rescued from the unbelievers by the blessed Louis, king of the Franks. It—or a portion of it—is honored and venerated in the most holy chapel of the palace at Paris, and rests there.”

[Col. 0353B] GREVEN. At the end also adds:

> “At the city of Paris, the translation of the sacred Crown of Thorns of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

MOLAN. More cautiously excluded it from the text.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. are sufficiently pure in the first three entries, but formulate the last as follows:

> “At the fortress of Ebroas, Saint Taurinus, bishop, whom the blessed Dionysius ordained and appointed bishop of that city, where, crowned with glorious martyrdom, he shines forth through many miracles.”

This is also the reading of the other codices.

In LOVANIEN. the whole of this announcement has fallen out, as it commonly abbreviates certain passages.

CENTULEN.:

> “At Rome, between the Two Laurels, Saint Tiburtius the martyr, son of Chromatius, prefect of the City, who, instructed in the faith by the blessed Sebastian, endured a glorious martyrdom. On the same day at Rome, Saint Susanna, who rejected the marriage proposed by the Roman emperor so that she might obtain communion with Christ the Lord. At Cambrai, Saint Gaugericus, bishop and confessor.”

In a more recent marginal hand [Col. 0353C] was added:

> “At the city of Ebroicas, Saint Taurinus, bishop and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. begins:

> “At the city of Cambrai, the deposition of Saint Gaugericus and confessor.”

Later, after “the martyr,” it inserts concerning Tiburtius:

> “Son of Chromatius, prefect of the City. When he was a young man under the judge Fabianus, while barefoot,”

and so forth, almost without corruption. In the entry for Susanna it is likewise correct. Concerning Taurinus, it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others.

HAGENOYEN.:

> “In the city of Ebroa, Saint Taurinus, bishop and martyr, whom the blessed Dionysius sent to the fortress of Eboras, ordaining him and appointing him bishop of the city, where, gloriously, and so forth. At Rome, between the Two Laurels, the feast of Saint Tyburtius the martyr. Tyburtius was the son of Cromacius, a senator of very noble birth. When he had been converted by the preaching of Saint Sebastian, after the healing of his father, he received such devotion in the faith of Christ that, when all the Christians were fleeing from Rome, he alone remained in the City out of love for martyrdom. Betrayed by Torquatus, a false Christian, to Fabianus the prefect, he was made to go barefoot,”

and so forth.

> “Also at Rome, Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr. She was a noble and beautiful virgin, and Diocletian sought her as a wife for his son Maximian. She was taught to preserve her virginity by her father, Saint Gabinus, by her uncle Gaius, the supreme pontiff, and by the empress Serena. Because she refused to consent, she endured unheard-of tortures both for her virginity and for the faith. Finally, she ended her life by the sword.”

Concerning the Crown, it has the same as GREVEN.:

> “Also in Scotland, Saint Arata, virgin and religious woman, who is invoked for the liberation of captives and assists people during pestilence.”

[Col. 0354A] Castellanus calls her Athracta. The entry for Gaugericus is uncorrupted.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “The illustrious martyr Tiburtius, concerning whom many excellent deeds are read in the acts of the blessed Sebastian; likewise concerning his father Chromatius. Gaugericus, bishop and confessor. At Rome, Susanna, virgin and martyr. The feast of the Crown of the Lord. Taurinus, bishop and confessor.”

CODEX D. Marked by Le Mare with the letter A, formerly belonging to the college of Canons of Autun:

> “On the same day, the martyr Andeolus is venerated.”

See 1 May.

In VATICAN. the entries for Gaugericus and Taurinus are lacking.

[Col. 0354B] UGHELLIAN:

> “At the city of Paris, the translation of the sacred Crown of Thorns of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

LUXOVIEN.:

> “At the city of Metz, the deposition of Saint Autor, bishop and confessor.”

See what we said in the supplements for the preceding day.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL.:

> “At Rome, between the Two Laurels, the feast of Saint Tiburtius the martyr, son of Chromatius, prefect of the City, whom Sebastian, the blessed Tranquillinus, and the glorious presbyter Polycarp instructed in the faith. When, under the judge Fabianus, he entered barefoot upon burning coals and confessed Christ with even greater steadfastness,”

and so forth.

After “he is ordered,” it adds:

> “And he is buried in the same place by a certain Christian relative.”

Concerning Susanna it has almost the same material as HAGENOYEN. The entry for Gaugericus is pure. Concerning Taurinus, it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others.

> “At Paris, the translation of the Crown of Thorns of our Lord. At Trier, in the principal church, the translation of the head of Saint Matthias the Apostle.”

GREVEN.:

> “Chromatius, prefect of the City, father of Saint Tiburtius, with many others. As Ado says, avoiding the brutality of the persecution on the advice of Gaius [Col. 0354C], the pontiff, they departed for Campania and entered the kingdom of God through many tribulations. At Aquileia, Saint Chromatius, bishop and confessor, to whom several letters of the blessed Jerome survive. According to the Catalogue of the Saints, on this day occurred the watching over, or discovery of, the Seven Sleepers at Ephesus. At Trier, in the principal church,”

and so forth, as above.

MOLAN. Inserts into the text, in different type, the following material concerning Susanna taken from Ado:

> “Her body was gathered at night by Serena Augusta, who adorned it with her own hands with linen cloths and spices. The martyr’s blood, which had been shed, she wiped away with a cloth in the place of her house and placed it in a silver chest in her palace, where day and night, through secret prayers, she poured herself out before the Lord.”

Likewise concerning Gaugericus:

> “He ruled the church of Cambrai for thirty-three years, was conspicuous for the holiness of his life, shone through his miracles, and rested in peace.”

Then at the end:

> “At Paris, the reception of the sacred Crown of Thorns,”

and so forth, almost as in MUNERAT.

> “At Sarchinium, the translation of the bodies of Saints Trudo and Eucherius, confessors of Christ. On that same day, the elevation of those same saints, solemnly carried out by Lord Rudolph, bishop of Liège.”

All these same items are also reported by the later editions, in which, in addition, the following is appended concerning Taurinus in different type:

> “Whom the blessed Dionysius ordained and appointed bishop of that city.”

Here one observes that the words concerning the glorious martyrdom of Taurinus, which other codices had eagerly added, have been cut away.]

[Col. 0351]

At Rome, between the Two Laurels, the feast of Saint Tiburtius, who, under the judge Fabianus, when he had entered barefoot upon burning coals and confessed Christ with greater steadfastness, was ordered to be led three miles from the city and there put to death by the sword. Also at Rome, Saint Susanna, virgin, who, born of noble lineage and niece of the blessed pontiff Gaius, earned the palm of martyrdom in the time of Diocletian by the cutting off of her head. At the city of Cambrai, Saint Gaugericus, bishop and confessor. At the fortress of Ebroas, Saint Taurinus, bishop.

The day before the Ides. The 12th day.

[Note: [Col. 0355]

Only Herinien., Greven., and Molan. are entirely uncorrupted.]

[Note: [Col. 0355]

Herinien. wrongly writes *Sycilia*, and Greven. wrongly writes *Cachyna*; nor is *Cathina* or *Catina* correct in the text. Nevertheless, everyone reads these forms, especially the first, while elsewhere they give the somewhat better form “in the city of the Catanians.” Greven. has *Eupoli*, and this is also found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. I have placed *Hilaria* with Greven. and Molan. Herinien. has *Hilara*, while others have *Hylara* and *Hylaria*. The following construction, “They also suffered on the same day in the aforesaid city,” is Usuardine, as I shall show below. Molan. neglected the particle *also*; Herinien., however, wrote “in the aforesaid town.” The five martyrs’ names are correctly given [Col. 0356A], although some codices vary; among them Molan. reads *Nymmia*. He substitutes *Phalari* for *Falari*; perhaps neither is suitable, as Baronius judges. I do not know whether some codices noticed this, for they removed *palaestra*. “Whose mouths first,” and so forth, is common to all; Molan. transposed it to “whose first mouth.” Again Molan., with Greven. and others, differs by reading “they received the desired palm of martyrdom.” Most follow Herinien. in reading “they received the desired crown of martyrdom,” as in the text. Concerning Syria and Macarius, see what has been said elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0355B]

Euplus, Euplius, or Eupolus is discussed by the calendars of Allatius and Fronto and by practically all the Martyrologists after the Hieronymian Martyrologies. In the latter, Nericia and Veneria are added as companions, unknown to all the others and even to the Acts themselves. These Acts, cited and examined, may be found in volume I of February, page 598, where Bollandus adduces them as an example by which the freer interpolations of Metaphrastes may be recognized. Baronius was the first to unearth this exceptional treasure and make it public in the *Annales* under the year 303, no. 146 onward. From him Surius received it, and most recently Ruinart included it among the *Selecta*, beginning on page 437, after a preliminary admonition and with observations added for future use, together with the Greek edition prepared by Coleterius. From those highly praised Acts Bede composed a concise eulogy, and Ado a longer one. Our author, I believe, saw both and drew his material from them. Nor did Wandalbert pass over the illustrious martyr; he honored him in this verse:

> “On the day before, Euplus, you gain the everlasting palm of martyrdom.”

[Col. 0355C] What follows concerning Hilaria is properly Adonian, taken from the Acts of Saint Afra, which we discussed above, and copied word for word by Usuard from Ado, so that there is consequently no difficulty. It is not, however, so easy to determine what the third commemoration means in the Pratensis codex, which is plainly corrupt, according to the distinguished Castellanus. In that alleged autograph he found that all the words between *Euprepia* and *Quiriacus* had been erased, and that the following words had been substituted there, set out more closely:

> “On the same day they suffered at Rome under the prefect Pertinax.”

In this alteration the Pratensis is characteristically supported by Antuerp.-Major and Rosweyd. Yet among all the others Usuard’s reading seems the most certain. One might ask whether it is genuine, or whether it was corrected by Usuard himself—as someone might perhaps wish to maintain [Col. 0356B], by Usuard himself, I say. What I think about this I have explained fully in the preface. The Acts of Saint Afra of Augsburg, illustrated with notes by Marcus Welser, lie between the two possibilities. If Usuard had them before his eyes, he could not have written otherwise than as the text stands. If you say that he consulted the Hieronymian Martyrologies for 8 August, the day is then transposed; indeed, two classes are confused, and perhaps a third as well, since in the aforesaid Hieronymian Martyrologies an anonymous group is placed on 7 August. I see here difficulties and precipices which will not easily be explained unless our twenty-five Augustan martyrs are distinguished from an equal number of Romans, nearly alike in name, concerning whom see 7 August. Let the curious investigator read what Florentinius recorded on those cited days, 7 and 8 August. We defer the remaining matters to the Greater Work, while for the present having no doubt about Usuard’s intention, whether he wrote what is true or what is erroneous. Thus far, then, we have indeed excavated the sources; but where that Gracilianus—called Gratilianus by others—and Felicissima entered the little list, I frankly confess that I have no idea. Nevertheless, the consensus of all the codices most clearly proves that these are Usuard’s incontestable words [Col. 0356C]. What that *Falaris*, or *Falare*, may be must be investigated in Baronius’s Notes. After examining the Acts from time to time, I think I can conjecture that Usuard saw the copies preserved among our manuscripts, of more than one of which you have a specimen at 15 May, volume III, page 458, under Eutitius. Tillemont, volume V, page 126, regarded as intolerable only the note concerning the fourth year of Claudius, which is consistently marked by all. There are other matters that must be subjected to prudent examination in their proper place. Macarius and Julianus are praised by the Hieronymian Martyrologies, the *Romanum parvum*, and Ado. We believe that they were taken word for word from the last of these. Notker preferred to transcribe the words of the Hieronymian Martyrologies. So far I have found nothing concerning these last two.]

[Note: [Col. 0355]

PRATEN., ANTUERP.-MAJ., and ROSWEYD. have the alteration I mentioned above in the Observations.

ROSWEYD. additionally adds at the end:

> “In Aquitaine, Saint Radegundis, virgin.”

See Usuard on the following day.]

[Col. 0356D] PULSANEN., pure in the first and last announcements, lacks all the intervening ones.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are sufficiently pure throughout the text, but fail in that they contract the penultimate announcement [Col. 0357A] in this manner:

> “Also, the passion of Gracilianus and Felicissima, virgin.”

MUNERAT., whether through the fault of the copyist or of the printer, joins unrelated passages. For immediately after “with twenty others” it adds:

> “Whose mouths first for Christ,”

and so forth, omitting what should have been inserted between them, namely:

> “Also at the city of Falari, the passion of Gracilianus and Felicissima.”

ANTUERP.-MAX. adds after Euprepia, from Ado:

> “Who were the holy girls of Saint Afra.”

It omits the location, or place of combat, of Gracilianus and Felicissima. At the end it has:

> “At the city of Assisi, the feast of Blessed Clare, virgin.”

ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG., and DANIC. begin:

> “At the city of Assisi, the feast of Blessed Clare, virgin. When she heard the preaching of the blessed Francis and saw his penitence, she became his spiritual daughter and the chief exemplar of holy poverty. She was the foundation and glory of the order of poor women, a mirror and lamp of every perfection.”

[Col. 0357B] In the rest they resemble ANTUERP.-MAX. ALBERGEN., however, is more defective than the others and has only this in the penultimate entry:

> “Also, the passion of the holy Gracilianus and Felicissima, virgin.”

LOVANIEN., pure in the first entry, omitted Hilaria’s eulogy and the remainder relating to it. Concerning Gracilianus and the others, it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX. Also at the end it has the entry for Clare.

CENTULEN.:

> “In the city of Catina in Sicily, the passion of Saint Euplus, deacon and martyr, in the time of Diocletian under the judge Calvitianus. In Syria, Saints Macarius and Julianus. On the same day, Saint Hilaria, mother of Saint Afra, who suffered by fire with Digna, Eumenia, and Euprepia. At the city of Falaret, the passion of Saints Gracilianus and Felicissima, virgin.”

BRUXELLEN. is somewhat interpolated in the entry for Euplus, whom it calls Empli. In Hilaria it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX. It continues:

> “At Rome, Saints Chrysanthus and Daria, virgin. Since they could not be harmed by any kind of torture, by order of Numerianus they were finally buried under earth and stones for Christ.”

The Hieronymian Martyrologies commemorate them today. [Col. 0357C] They are celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 25 October; our author places them on 1 December. In the entry for Gracilianus and Felicissima, and in those for Macarius and Julianus, it is uncorrupted. Then:

> “At the city of Assisi, the deposition of Saint Clare, virgin. She was the first spiritual daughter of the blessed Francis, a mirror and lamp of poverty and of every perfection. At the mountains of Hainaut, the translation of Blessed Waldetrudis, the elect, and niece of Blessed Gudila.”

See 3 February and 28 March.

HAGENOYEN., in the first three entries, only moderately interpolated, continues:

> “Also, the passion of Saints Graciliana and Felicissima, virgins.”

Concerning Macarius and Julianus it is pure. At the end, concerning Saint Clare, it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130:

> “Also, the passion of Saint Gracilianus and Felicissima, virgin.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Clare, virgin of the Order of Friars Minor. Hilaria the martyr with three others. Quiriacus, Largio, Crescentianus with twenty-two martyrs. [Col. 0357D] Gracilianus and Felicissima, martyrs.”

In VATICAN., no. 5949, Gracilianus and Felicissima are lacking. I do not know whether the remainder is pure.

[Col. 0358A] ALTEMPS.:

> “On the same day, Saint Ethelwold.”

See 1 August.

> “At the city of Canterbury, Saint Lambert, archbishop and confessor.”

FLORENTIN.:

> “At the city of Assisi, the feast of Saint Clare, virgin. She was the first plant of the order of poor women and shone both by her life and by her miracles. She migrated to the Lord in the year of the Lord 1253.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. begins:

> “At Cologne Agrippina, the commemoration of Saint Ursula, queen, and her companions, eleven thousand virgins, in their church.”

In the entry for Euplus it is pure. It continues:

> “At the city of Assisi, the feast of Blessed Clare, virgin,”

and so forth, almost as above in ANTUERP.-MAX.

Then:

> “At the city of Augsburg, Saint Hilaria, mother of Saint Afra the martyr. When she and her brother Saint Dionysius and several others had buried Blessed Afra and were keeping vigil at her tomb, they were seized there; and because they refused to sacrifice to idols, they were handed over by the persecutors to the fire with Blessed Digna, Eumenia, and Euprepia, who had been [Col. 0358B] buried, the holy girls of Saint Afra, and all suffered honorably together in that place,”

and so forth.

> “At the city of Salari, the passion of Saints Gracilianus and Felicissima, virgin.”

In the final entry, after Julianus, it adds “confessor.” Finally it adds:

> “On the same day, Saint Vuibertus, confessor.”

GREVEN. below writes *Wibertus*.

BELIN., not entirely pure in the text, immediately adds after the Augustan martyrs:

> “In Syria, Saints Macarius and Julianus.”

Then:

> “At the city of Assisi, Saint Clare, virgin, the first plant of the order of poor women, who shone through her life and miracles. Also at the city of Falarius, the passion of Saint Gratianus and Felicissima, virgin.”

Read it as the others have it above.

GREVEN.:

> “On the same day, Porcarius, abbot of the monastery of Lérins and martyr, with five hundred fellow monks, crowned under Geiseric, king of the Vandals, for the truth of the faith. Also Wibertus, confessor. At Assisi, the passing of Blessed Clare, virgin. When she was eighteen years old, having abandoned the world and the bond of marriage, she was consecrated by Saint Francis to Christ, the immortal bridegroom; she became the foundation, glory, and rule of the order of poor women, and a mirror of every perfection. Finally, after completing forty-two years in her holy purpose, she rested, shining with many miracles. At Prague in Bohemia, Saint Agnes, virgin. At Cologne Agrippina, the second commemoration of Blessed Ursula, queen, and her companions, eleven thousand virgins, in their church.”

These items concerning Cologne are often repeated as local material.

MOLAN.:

> “At the city of Assisi, Saint Clare, virgin, the first plant of the order of poor women, who shone through her life and miracles. At the monastery of Jotro, Saint Agliberta, abbess. On the same day, Porcarius, abbot,”

and so forth, as above in GREVEN.

See the Acts in Surius.

In other editions, at the beginning, he places in different type the material concerning Clare that he had previously put at the end. Here, however, he writes:
