> “On the same day, Porcarius, abbot of the monastery of Lérins and martyr. At the monastery of Jotro, Saint Agliberta, abbess. On the twelfth day, Saints Photius and Anicetus, martyrs. At the mountains of Hainaut, the translation of Saint Waldetrudis.”]

[Col. 0353]

At the city of Catina in Sicily, the feast of Saint Euplus, deacon, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. After he had been tortured for a very long time for his confession of the Lord, he finally received the palm of martyrdom when the sword struck him. At the city of Augsburg, Saint Hilaria, mother of Saint Afra the martyr, who, while keeping vigil at her tomb, [Col. 0355] was there handed over by the persecutors to the fire for the faith of Christ, together with Digna, Eumenia, and Euprepia. They also suffered on the same day in the aforesaid city: Quiriacus [Bouillart.: [Note: [Col. 0355A] Instead of “on the same day,” “they suffered at Rome under the prefect Pertinax,” which Usuard added to his own copy; in the Carolingian autograph it read: “They also suffered on the same day in the aforesaid town.” No one with sound eyes could doubt that the correction was made by Usuard. But where he learned that those martyrs had suffered on the same day, that Pertinax was then prefect of the City, that Nymmia and Juliana and twenty other companions were to be joined to Quiriacus, Largio, and Crescentianus, and finally that all those martyrs had migrated to heaven on 12 August, I simply do not know. I do not recall seeing any of this in the Acts of Blessed Marcellus in Monbritius, nor anywhere else. Yet all these matters prove that Usuard took from Ado and other Martyrologies whatever he could use as his own when he had nothing better, and that he read many things which they had never read. Would that the Acts of those holy martyrs which he saw might now emerge from darkness! For in the published Acts, there are almost as many fables as lines. BOUILLART.] On the same day Quiriacus, Largio, Crescentianus, Nimmia, and Juliana suffered at Rome under the prefect Pertinax, with twenty others. Also at the city of Falari, the passion of Gracilianus and Felicissima, virgin, whose mouths were first battered with stones for Christ, and then, struck by the sword, they received the desired crown of martyrdom. In Syria, Saints Macarius and Julianus.

The Ides. The 13th day.

[Note: [Col. 0357A]

Nearly all the codices agree: Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Major, Rosweyd., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., and Danicus also agree.]

[Note: [Col. 0359A]

Only Molan. correctly has *Hippolyti*; Praten. has *Hippoliti*, Greven. *Hipoliti*, and Herinien. *Yppoliti*. All the others, as in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, have the form found here in the text and on 30 January. Antuerp.-Maj. omitted *pro* in “for the glory of his confession,” and so forth. Rosweyd. has “bound by the feet . . . thus through thorns,” instead of *carduos*, as Bede has it. Everyone writes *Cardetum*; Ado has *Carduetum*. Neither form is pleasing. “Of untamed horses” occurs in Antuerp.-Major. Greven. and Molan. read of Concordia: “who, having been struck with leaden scourges, suffered martyrdom beforehand”; Rosweyd. and Munerat. also alter the final words to “was martyred”; Antuerp.-Max., with the others, has “migrated to the Lord.” Again, all of these, together with Antuerp. [Col. 0359B] and Max.-Lubec., have “who were beheaded together with him.” Greven. and Molan. invert it: “were beheaded together, and nineteen others from his household.” Antuerp.-Maj. and others wrongly read “and other people.” All write *Forosillae* as one word except Molan., who correctly separates it as *Foro Syllae*. Rosweyd. disgracefully changes *die* into *sanctae*: “on the same day of Saint Forosilla.” Antuerp.-Max. and its companions read “of Cassianus, bishop and martyr.” Rosweyd. has “had become hated”; Greven. and Molan. “had been made hated.” “To kill him” is replaced in Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. by “to punish him.” Antuerp.-Maj. has “permission was given to them”; Munerat. “permission was given them,” and afterward “they prolonged the death.” All this is simpler in the text. Greven. and Molan. read: “At Poitiers, the deposition of Saint Radegundis, queen, whose life shone widely through her virtues and miracles.” The word *deposition* also occurs in Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Antuerp.-Max., and so forth. In the first two, *widely* is lacking, for which Munerat. substituted *with light*, reading “the deposition of Saint Eradgundis.”]

[Note: [Col. 0359B]

Hippolytus must plainly be numbered among the illustrious martyrs of the Church. He is highly praised in all the most ancient calendars and Martyrologies, whatever may rightly be debated concerning the authenticity of his Acts and their identification with those of the other presbyter Hippolytus, martyr of Ostia, owing to the confusion of the Martyrologists. The Hieronymian Martyrologies have this further peculiarity: they seem to join companions to him, giving their names explicitly, although no other source mentions them. Usuard was pleased by Bede’s encomium, which could not have been more elegantly condensed by him from Ado’s longer history, while preserving most of the words from the Acts reported there. [Col. 0359C] Hence arose the doubt whether that eulogy should truly be attributed to Bede. But since Rabanus also reports it, whatever difficulty appears at first sight is easily removed. Notker is closer to Ado than to Bede, though he errs in the number of those said to have suffered from Hippolytus’s household. Here at least Florentinius clearly indicates that Notker, as usual, took his material from Ado—a point he could have observed elsewhere so many times and more clearly. These matters are again sufficiently straightforward, insofar as the purpose of this work requires; yet we must note what we indicated at the beginning: our Martyrologists confuse two Hippolyti here when Concordia is called his nurse, and so forth. Thus the illustrious and repeatedly celebrated martyr is the same one about whom we spoke on 30 January, and in all likelihood the same one celebrated by Prudentius, who at some point became involved in the Novatian schism, and so forth. Concerning him, see Ruinart among the *Sincera*, beginning on page 155, and Tillemont’s note, volume III, page 675, and elsewhere. We also remember another companion of Laurence, whom we shall distinguish more carefully from the other Hippolyti in the Acts [Col. 0359D].

As we said above, these matters are sufficiently straightforward for the simplicity of the text. But what are we to do with Cassianus, whom the Hieronymian Martyrologies—if indeed they are speaking of this Cassianus—place among Hippolytus’s companions? Bede likewise, and Rabanus after him, explicitly assign him to Rome. The *Romanum parvum*, Ado, Notker—deficient in orthography—and others, however, assign him to Foro Syllae, today Imola; and this is the opinion of the poet Prudentius himself. See it in Ruinart, page 593, or expressed in prose in Surius on this day. Add what Tillemont carefully observes in volume V, pages 531 and 794. Baronius notes some matters that might resolve the issue, unless the difficulty is increased by Cassianus of Todi, bishop and martyr, inserted into the modern Roman Martyrology, whom others prefer not to separate from the former. We defer such difficult investigations to their proper place. [Col. 0360C] It is certain that Usuard followed Ado’s wording and condensed from his eulogy, which is precisely the same in Bede, Rabanus, and Notker. The Hieronymian Martyrologies mention Radegundis, as they mention many others added later in various places; Florus also mentions her. Why should we not say that Ado too included her, although Rosweyd relegated her to an appendix? Mosander held this view, and I am drawn still more strongly to it because Notker records her. Whatever the case, our author could append her, as she was sufficiently well known from elsewhere, with the brief praise common to all holy women—whether virgins, married women, or widows—as is clear from the text. The text itself shows that it is purely and plainly Usuardine. The Life of Radegundis, written by Fortunatus and Bandoninia, or Bandonivia, was published by Surius; Mabillon later issued it, with various notes, in the first Benedictine century. The remaining material must be taken from Gregory of Tours. The observation will end with Wandalbert’s metrical encomium of the first and last saint in our text:

[Col. 0360D]

> “On the Ides, Laurence received Hippolytus, his companion, among the stars,  
> who suffered an equal contest for Christ.  
> Then the Aquitanian earth, venerating Radegundis,  
> frequents the queen, worthy to be honored for her merits, virtue, and faith.”

]

[Note: [Col. 0359D]

PULSANEN.:

> “At Rome, the blessed Hippolytus the martyr and his companions. He, for the glory of his confession . . . and thus through thorns and briars gave up his spirit. In the city of Modomul, at the place called Forum Cornelium, the feast of Saint Cassianus the martyr.”

All the rest is lacking, as this codex is often mutilated here.

[Col. 0360D] CENTULEN.:

> “At Rome, the passion of Hippolytus the martyr and Concordia, his nurse, with nineteen others who were beheaded. At Poitiers, Saint Radegundis, queen, whose life shone widely through her virtues and miracles. At Foro Syllae, Saint Cassianus the martyr.”

BRUXELLEN. is moderately interpolated in the entry for Hippolytus. Concerning Cassianus, it copies Ado or a similar source in this manner:

[Col. 0361A]

> “On the same day, at Foro Syllae, Saint Cassianus the martyr. When he refused to worship idols, the persecutor asked him what profession he practiced. He replied that he taught children their letters. He was immediately stripped of his clothing and, with his hands bound behind his back, was set in the midst of them. The children were summoned, and permission was given to those whom he had made hateful by teaching to kill him. As much as they had grieved while learning, so much did they rejoice in taking revenge: some struck him with wax tablets, others wounded him with awls and styluses. The weaker their hands were, the more severe the punishment of his martyrdom they inflicted by prolonging his death. At Poitiers, the deposition of Saint Radegundis, queen, who, having been captured in Thuringia, was taken as wife by Lotharius, king of the Franks. Later, having changed her clothing, she shone widely through virtues and miracles. Also, Saint Wicbertus, abbot.”

HAGENOYEN.:

> “At Rome, the feast of the blessed Hippolytus the martyr and his eighteen companions from his household. The blessed Laurence converted him to the faith after he saw the miracles that the Lord performed through him. After Hippolytus had committed Laurence’s body to burial, he was seized by Valerianus and presented to Decius. He was stripped of his clothing and beaten with clubs. Since he refused to sacrifice to idols, all the members of his household were ordered to be beheaded. Blessed Concordia, Hippolytus’s nurse, also suffered on that day, when she was beaten to death with clubs. Hippolytus himself gave thanks to God for the steadfastness of his servants, and then Hippolytus was dragged by untamed horses through thorns and briars until he gave up his spirit.”

The entries for Cassianus and Radegundis are also somewhat interpolated.

DAVERONEN.:

> “In the district of Poitiers, Saint Vinianus [or perhaps Julianus, or rather Junianus?], abbot of the monastery of Nobiliacum.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Hippolytus the martyr, who, dragged through thorns and briars, gave up his spirit. Radegundis, queen; Concordia, the nurse of Hippolytus; and nineteen others from his household. Cassianus the martyr; Euplus the martyr.”

This has been transferred here from the preceding day.

[Col. 0361C] FLORENTIN.:

> “At Milan, Saint Simplicianus, bishop, disciple of Saint Ambrose. He composed the life and history of Saint Zenobius, bishop of Florence.”

STROZZIAN. adds:

> “His life was glorious, and thus he rested in peace.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition differs little from HAGENOYEN. in the entry for Hippolytus. It is almost pure in that for Cassianus. Then:

> “In the district of Poitiers, Saint Julianus, abbot. At Poitiers, the deposition of Saint Radegundis,”

and so forth. Enough has been said about her.

BELIN., not sufficiently corrected in the text, adds at the end:

> “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Simplicianus, bishop and confessor.”

The second edition more correctly writes *Simpliciani*. See the following supplement of GREVEN.

GREVEN.:

> “On that same day, Wichbertus, bishop and confessor. Potentianus [or perhaps Pontianus?], bishop. At Milan, the deposition of the blessed Simplicianus, bishop and confessor. Because of the celebrated reputation of his holiness, he succeeded the blessed Ambrose, an aged hermit worn out by his years; just as he had been especially devoted to the Lord in the solitary life, so, once appointed to govern the church, he proved an energetic imitator of Saint Ambrose. In the district of Poitiers, Saint Julianus, abbot. Near Milan, the translation of Saints Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander, martyrs. Also Saint Laudulphus. Ermendrudis, virgin.”

MOLAN. inserts into the text, in different type, concerning Cassianus, the words of Bede or Ado:

> “The poet Prudentius writes this.”

At the end, concerning Radegundis, he adds:

> “Written by the presbyter Fortunatus. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Simplicianus, bishop and confessor. On that same day, Saint Laudulphus. In the province of Germany, the feast of Saint Wigbertus, presbyter and confessor.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “In England, Saint Higbald, confessor, abbot at Lindsey. Concerning him Bede writes in the *Deeds of the English*, book IV, chapter 3. On the same day, Saint Hariolphus, first abbot of Elwangen.”

Other editions scarcely differ in the text. At the end:

> “On that same day, Saint Laudulphus, bishop of Évreux.”

Concerning Simplicianus and Wigbertus, see above. Then:

> “On the thirteenth day, Saint Maximus, father and confessor.”

Finally, in smaller type:

> “On the same day, Saint Hariolphus,”

and so forth, as in the earlier edition. See Castellanus, who reads *Herulfus* instead of *Hariolphus*.

[Col. 0357]

At Rome, the blessed Hippolytus the martyr, who, for the glory of his confession, by order of Valerianus the governor, had his feet bound to the necks of untamed horses and, thus dragged through thorns and briars, gave up his spirit. Concordia, his nurse, also suffered; she was struck with leaden scourges before him and was martyred. Nineteen others from his household, who were beheaded together with him, also suffered. On the same day at Foro Syllae, the feast of Saint Cassianus. Because he refused to worship, the children whom he had made hateful through teaching were summoned and given permission to kill him; the weaker each person's hand was, the more grievous a punishment of martyrdom it inflicted by prolonging his death. [Note: [Col. 0357D] Saint Radegundis was added to this article by a hand equal to, but certainly not the same as, the original hand. Sollerius nevertheless accepts her as having been written by Usuard, without mentioning any erasure of the earlier writing, which he conceals whenever nothing appears in his codices that would enable him to charge the Pratensis codex with interpolation [Col. 0360A]. Nor is there any trace of this erasure in the Dervensis codex, although two entire lines had certainly been erased. They must therefore have been erased before any other copy existed, and thus by the author. BOUILLART.] At Poitiers, Saint Radegundis, queen, whose life shone widely through her virtues and miracles.

The nineteenth day before the Kalends. The 14th day.

[Note: [Col. 0361]

The codices Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Major, Munerat., Greven., and Molan. are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0361C]

The entire matter consists of two discrepancies among the codices. The first is that Antuerp.-Major and Munerat. wrongly write *Constantino* instead of *Constantio*, something we have often observed elsewhere. Greven. departs still further from the others, and Molan. is his constant follower in such variants. Both therefore begin as follows: “The vigil of the Assumption of Mary, Mother of God.” From the others it is sufficiently clear that the reading of Ado and Usuard is correct.]

[Note: [Col. 0361D]

From what time, above all, the Vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary first began to be celebrated—at least in Gaul—must be inferred entirely from the period of Ado, who appears to have been the first among the martyrologists to enter it into the sacred Calendar; all the more ancient writers, such as the Hieronymian Martyrologies, the Small Roman Martyrology, Bede, Florus, and Rabanus, being completely silent about it. Wandalbert likewise mentions only Eusebius, as we shall say below. Meanwhile Usuard, just like Notker, transcribed the same number of syllables from Ado. Here again I would have the detractors of the Small Roman Martyrology warned how far they are led astray by their prejudices when they insist, importunately, that that Martyrology was abridged from Ado, although both on this day and on others they find in Ado so many things which plainly could never have been known to the author of the Small Roman Martyrology.

The codices of the Hieronymian Martyrology likewise mention nothing about this Eusebius of ours at Rome; among them, indeed, some Eusebius is recorded, but with characteristics distinguishing him—or, if you prefer, confusing him—including even the title of founder, which demonstrate that he was someone other than this Roman Eusebius of ours. Bede confines his notice to a few words, without even stating the place: “The nativity of Saint Eusebius the priest.” The Small Roman Martyrology explains the matter more fully: “At Rome, Eusebius the priest and confessor, under Constantius the Arian, buried in the cemetery of Callistus.” Ado gathers more details from his Acts, some of which require correction, as do the additions which Rabanus made to Bede. See Baronius under the year 357, no. 45, where the schism between the clergy who followed Liberius, recalled from Rome, and those who adhered to Felix is discussed more fully, and in which Eusebius appears to have played a considerable part.

Again, in volume XII, p. 887, certain details are added which may probably be assigned to this Eusebius, but they must be examined in their proper place along with the others. Following Ado, Notker likewise opposes Liberius, while additionally calling Eusebius a bishop. Our author, as though deliberately avoiding controversial matters, is content to extract from Ado those details which sufficiently adorn the excellent confessor who suffered and died in defense of the integrity of the faith against the Arians; yet he nowhere grants him the martyr’s crown. The Acts also refrain from doing so. They were first published by Mombritius, vol. I, p. 258, and later by Baluze, *Miscellanies*, book II, p. 141; they are not much unlike the material contained in Ado’s panegyric.

It must be admitted, as I have already said, that the aforesaid Acts require some correction. Yet Tillemont, volume VI, beginning at p. 776, and others opposed to Pope Felix II, exaggerate the matter beyond measure when they regard as suspect everything consistent with that pontiff’s deeds, as will be explained more fully in its proper place. Meanwhile, I consider it evident that the ancient Calendars of Fronto and Allatius, together with Gregory’s Sacramentary, praise no other Eusebius than this one of ours, whatever Fronto may appear to have confused two Eusebiuses on pp. 53 and 121, and whatever his wish that Eusebius the pope should have been a martyr. It is remarkable that Tillemont cites this, since in volume V, p. 100, he does not grant that small crown to the pope.

To this belongs a note by Motherius in the recent translation of the Roman Martyrology. It is the same Eusebius of ours whom Wandalbert sings of on this day:

> Which is the nineteenth before the Kalends of September,  
> He declares and celebrates blessed Eusebius at Rome.

[Note: In ROSWEYD the word “Vigil” is absent. It then reads: “The nativity of blessed Eusebius the priest and confessor, at Rome on the Appian Way. Since Constantius Augustus had confined him in a certain room of his house because of his defense of the Catholic faith, and there, etc. On the same day, in the island of Betuwe, in the village of Elst, Saint Werenfrid the priest, who had been sent as a preacher to that people by Saint Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht, and, after completing his blessed preaching, rested in peace in the place mentioned above.” His Life is found in Surius.

PULSANEN begins as follows: “The Vigil of the Assumption of the most holy Mother and Virgin of God, Mary.” In the entry for Eusebius it is sufficiently accurate.

ANTWERP–MAX-LÜBECK and UGHELLIANA, accurate in the text, add: “In Africa, Saint Demetrius.” ALBERGEN and DANICUS agree with them. It is also found in the modern Roman Martyrology.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN likewise have this addition; they further add: “On the same day, Saint Werenfrid the priest and confessor.”

CENTULEN reads: “The Vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary. At Rome, Saint Eusebius the priest, who, after being committed by the faction of the Arians to a most stringent [the intended meaning is ‘most confined’] custody, was tormented there for many days and received his repose. At Aquileia, Saints Felix and Fortunatus, brother martyrs.” See the Additions for 14 May.

BRUSSELS reads: “The Vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary, perpetual Virgin. At Rome, on the Appian Way, Saint Eusebius the priest. He boldly reproved Constantius Augustus and the heretic. Therefore he was committed to prolonged custody and confined in a room of his own house; persevering steadfastly in prayer there, he fell asleep in Christ. And Saint Gregory the priest and confessor. In Africa, the nativity of Saint Demetrius.” I think the reference is to the Gregory mentioned above, who buried Eusebius.

HAGENAU reads: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the nativity of blessed Eusebius the priest and confessor, who, when he reproved Constantius the heretical emperor [and affirmed] that he was acting unjustly against orthodox bishops and clergy, was confined by that same Constantius, for the defense of the Catholic faith, for seven months in a room of his house, which was four cubits wide; persevering in prayer there, he received his repose. At Complutum, a city in Spain, the passion of Justus and Pastor, brothers,” etc., concerning whom the account was given on 6 August. “In Africa, Saint Demetrius.” He intended Demetrius, as above.

MATRICULARY–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT reads: “Eusebius the confessor; the Vigil; Werenfrid the confessor, patron at Elst, in Betuwe, in the diocese of Utrecht.”

CAMBRAI reads: “Near Aquileia, the beheading of Saints Felix and Fortunatus, brothers.” See above.

The VATICAN codex, no. 5949, adds: “The nativity of Saint Peregrinus.” Nothing about him is found in the others.

FLORENCE reads: “In the city of Vicenza, Saints Felix and Fortunatus, martyrs. At Rome, Saints Irenaeus and Abundius, martyrs, as is read in the Acts of Saint Hippolytus the martyr. Saint Justin buried them beside the body of blessed Lawrence the martyr in the Veranian field on the Tiburtine Way, on the twentieth day after the passion of those martyrs.” See 26 August.

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition reads: “The Vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary the Virgin.” In the entry for Eusebius, after “of his house,” it adds: “which was four feet wide; confined there, and persevering steadfastly in prayer, after seven months he received a blessed repose. Also at Rome, Saint Gregory the priest and confessor. Because this man had buried the body of blessed Eusebius the priest, the emperor Constantius had him confined alive in the same crypt; the priest Orosius found him there at night, half alive, and, when he had breathed his last, buried him beside the body of blessed Eusebius. In Africa, the nativity of Saint Demetrius, bishop and confessor. At Elst, the deposition of Saint Werenfrid the priest and confessor, who came from England with Saint Willibrord and was sent as far as Betuwe; he faithfully governed the newly converted people of Christ at Elst, Westervoort, and in the surrounding region. Glorified by countless miracles, both in life and in death, he happily fell asleep in the Lord and was miraculously buried at Elst.” See the miracle in GREVEN.

BELIN reads: “The Vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary the Virgin.” In the entry for Eusebius it is nearly accurate; at the end it adds: “In Africa, Saint Demecius.” I think this is a printer’s error, and that it should read, with the others, “Demetrius. In [Col. 0364C] Vicenza, Saints Felix and Fortunatus.”

GREVEN reads: “In Africa, the natal feast of Saint Demetrius, bishop and confessor. In Ireland, at Fachua, [Fachnan], bishop. At Rome, blessed Gregory the priest and confessor. When he and the priest Orosius had buried the body of blessed Eusebius in the crypt, with the inscription EUSEBIUS, MAN OF GOD, Constantius the emperor, hearing this, ordered Gregory to be confined in the same crypt. Orosius found him there at night, half alive, and, after he had died a short time later, buried him beside blessed Eusebius. Also Saint Felix. The deposition of Saint Werenfrid the priest and confessor. He came from England with Saint Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht; he cleansed the island of Betuwe of its ancient errors and governed it diligently, renowned for many miracles both during life and after death. When people were disputing over the possession of his sacred body, it was placed on a ship without a pilot, and by angelic guidance it proceeded to the farther bank. There, after it had again been placed upon a wagon drawn by oxen, it was conveyed without human direction to the place called Elst, where it now rests peacefully. Eusebius the confessor, a disciple of blessed Jerome, a native of Cremona: after Jerome’s death, when he had commendably governed his monastery, and was already being committed to burial, a certain monk who had lost his sight kissed his body and recovered his vision.”

MOLAN adds to the account of Eusebius from Ado: “His body was gathered by the priests Gregory and Orosius, who buried it in a crypt beside the body of blessed Sixtus, bishop and martyr, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus. Writing his inscription there, they set it down as follows: EUSEBIUS, MAN OF GOD. When Constantius heard that Gregory and Orosius had buried the body of blessed Eusebius, he ordered Gregory to be confined alive in the same crypt in which they had placed it. Orosius found him there at night, half alive, and, after he had died a short time later, buried him beside the body of Saint Eusebius. A most severe persecution of the Catholic Church by the Arians then took place, while Liberius occupied the apostolic see. In Africa, Saint Demetrius. In Vicenza, Saints Felix and Fortunatus. Also Werenfrid, the priest and confessor, whose body rests in the Duchy of Guelders, in the village called Elst.” Then, in smaller type: “Also our holy mother Athanasia, whose life, rule, and miracles are found in Symeon Metaphrastes, related by a pious man who partly saw them himself and partly heard them from women who were companions of that holy mother.” Other editions repeat the same material about Eusebius and Demetrius. There “Werenfrid and Guelders” is written more correctly. Finally, in smaller type, it adds: “This outstanding preacher, sent toward Betuwe, happily governed the newly converted people of Christ at Elst and Westervoort, in that region.” See more in the GREVEN Addition. “Also our holy mother Athanasia.” See her Life in Surius.]

[Col. 0361]

The Vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary. At Rome, on the Appian Way, the natal feast of blessed Eusebius the priest and confessor, who, because of his defense of the Catholic faith, was confined by Constantius Augustus in a certain room of his house and, persevering steadfastly in prayer there, received his repose.

XVIII Kalends. Day 15. [Note: This is how it appears in Praten, Herinien, Antwerp–Major, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.

[Note: Only Molan substitutes “most holy” for “most sacred.” Likewise, with Greven he writes “is found.” He reads “as regards the condition” instead of “according to the condition,” where all the others have the latter form. Munerat reads “But what” instead of “But since,” etc. Antwerp–Major has “sobriety with piety chose more,” while the others, more correctly, have “the sobriety of the Church.” The remaining codices in the text have *apocryphum* from Praten and Greven. Most of the others have *apocrifum*; Molan alone correctly has *apocryphum*, but, with Greven, omits the following word *inde*. There is variation in the name of the succeeding martyr: some write Tharsius, others Tarsicius, and others Tharsicius; we follow the more common form, Tharsicius, with Herinien, Munerat, and others. In *acolyte* we follow the reading of Antwerp–Major and Greven. Others have *accolyte*; Molan’s *acolyti* is somewhat better. For *discutientibus*, Antwerp–Major has *decutientibus*. In Munerat the word *pagans* is absent. Greven and Molan omit the conjunction *et*, producing a smoother sense but one not corresponding to the text. The matter of *exalaret* has been discussed elsewhere.]

[Note: The one opinion of the Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, so often cited, concerning today’s feast is: “Solemnities concerning the repose of Saint Mary.” The Sacramentaries state the Assumption; yet the Dormition of Saint Mary is expressed in the same terms today by Bede, the Small Roman Martyrology, and Ado, although on the preceding day Ado had expressly read, “The Vigil of the Assumption.” Rabanus, who usually describes Bede, nevertheless here wrote “The Assumption of Saint Mary,” which is also how Florentinius reports it from his Lucensian manuscript; for the Corbeiensis of Acherius, in second place, wrote: “And the Assumption of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord,” while the most ancient Epternacensis is silent on these matters.

It is not the place here to pursue at length all the controversies formerly debated back and forth by Baronius, Gretser, and Florentinius concerning the Assumption and Dormition, death and resurrection; more recently by Joli, Launoy, Billius, and Lambecius; and by the most recent writers, Tillemont in volume I, Castellanus under 16 January, and others. I am exceedingly surprised that someone should recently have asserted with confidence that here, at least, it clearly appears that Usuard and Ado did not transcribe one another (“without one being able to say this time that one took it from the other”). Thus he writes after Tillemont, p. 477, although perhaps nowhere is the contrary demonstrated more clearly.

Let the curious reader consult Ado’s *Feasts of the Apostles*, at the last of all the notices, on 6 September, and call the witnesses to his eyes: does Usuard bring forward anything that he did not transcribe word for word from Ado, except for passages here and there which he either deliberately or for the sake of brevity left untouched? What Notker discusses more fully does not concern us; nor do I wish to reopen the question why, in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, the deposition of the most blessed Virgin is recorded on 18 January. We have dealt with Usuard’s sources on other days among other writers, and this is sufficient for our purpose. Those who desire more should consult the authors named above; yet let them beware of attributing to Usuard, with Lambecius in the sacred journey through the monastery of Celle, p. 31, material which was added later, as will be seen in the Additions from the Utrecht, Leyden, and other codices.

One point may be worth noting: the famous controversy over Usuard’s words, debated at Paris with such intensity for more than forty years, must originally be referred to Ado’s authority. There remains the elegant couplet with which Wandalbert accompanies the triumphant Mother of God:

> On the eighteenth, Mary, light and flower of the world,  
> The Virgin, accompanied by an angelic choir, seeks the heavens.

The foundation of our other notice is laid by the Small Roman Martyrology as follows: “Saint Tharsicius, acolyte and martyr.” The more ancient writers do not mention him. Ado composed a sufficiently polished panegyric, which Notker transcribed. Usuard did not take everything from it, but he has nothing which he did not receive from it word for word. Thus everything contained in this little notice of ours today is both Ado’s and plainly Usuard’s. Tharsicius’s contest is described in the Acts of Saint Stephen the pope; nothing further need be said about them here. See Tillemont, volume IV, p. 32.]

[Note: ROSWEYD begins: “The Dormition or Assumption of Saint Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin.” The remainder follows quite accurately. In place of Tharsicius it substitutes another name, reading: “The nativity of blessed Eutychianus the priest,” etc., as in the text.

PULSANEN reads: “The most glorious Assumption of the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ and perpetual Virgin Mary.” The remainder is correct, but Tharsicius is absent.

[Col. 0366D] ANTWERP and MAX-LÜBECK read: “The most holy Assumption of Mary, Mother of God,” with the remainder deleted. Then they give a fuller account of Tharsicius from Ado in these words: “On the same day, Saint Tharsicius, acolyte and martyr. When the pagans found him carrying the sacrament of the body of Christ, they began to ask what he was carrying. But he, judging it unworthy to cast pearls before swine, was beaten with clubs and stones until he breathed out his spirit. When the sacrilegious interrogators turned over his body, they found none of Christ’s sacraments in his hands or clothing. The Christians gathered the martyr’s body, and he was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.”

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM reads: “The most holy Assumption of Mary, Mother of God, or, according to the Carthusians from the Martyrology of Saint Jerome, the Dormition of the Mother of God, concerning whom, etc. At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, the nativity of Saint Tharsicius, acolyte and martyr. When the pagans found him,” etc.

LOUVAIN simply reads: “The most holy Assumption of Mary, Mother of God. Although her most sacred body, etc.” In the remaining details it resembles the preceding account.

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANICUS begin as follows: “The most holy Assumption of Mary, Mother of God. For the honorable burial and venerated funeral rites of her body, as is read in the book *On Divine Names*, the Prince of the Apostles Peter and the other apostles assembled. Timothy, Dionysius the Areopagite, and the teacher of that same Dionysius, Hierotheus, were also present, together with many other holy men, praising the divine goodness.” This is the material which, as we said above, Lambecius wrongly attributed to Usuard. In the rest they continue with the text: “Although her most sacred body is not found,” etc., through the end, exactly as in ANTWERP–MAXIMUM and the others.

CENTULEN reads: “The happy and blessed Dormition of our glorious Lady Mary, ever-Virgin and Mother of God. Although her most sacred body is not found upon the earth, the pious mother Church nevertheless celebrates her venerable memory so festively that, according to the condition of the flesh, she does not doubt that she departed. At Rome, on the Appian Way, Saint Tharsicius, acolyte and martyr. In Palestine, Saint Eusebius the martyr.”

BRUSSELS reads: “The Assumption of blessed Mary, ever-Virgin, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the burial and venerated funeral rites of her sacred body, as is read in the book *On Divine Names*, blessed Peter and the other apostles, together with many holy men, assembled, praising the divine goodness. Therefore the pious mother Church celebrates her memory so festively that she does not doubt that she departed according to the condition of the flesh; but whether her most blessed soul, reunited to her sacred body, or with that body left on earth, ascended into heaven, she preferred in sober wisdom not to know, rather than to teach something apocryphal by asserting it: At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, the nativity of Saint Thartius, acolyte and martyr. When the pagans found him,” etc., as above.

HAGENAU begins with: “The Dormition of Mary, Mother of God.” It then agrees in every respect with UTRECHT and the others, and after “by asserting it” adds: “Nevertheless, all the holy teachers say that she was assumed into heaven with flesh and soul, except Jerome alone, who asserts nothing certain about her Assumption.” The statement is excessively general.

MATRICULARY–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT reads: “The Assumption of the glorious Virgin. Tharsicius, acolyte and martyr. Arnulf of Metz, bishop and confessor.” In the margin it notes: “Some place Arnulf on the following day; and that is how he was placed.” See therefore our Usuardian text on the following day.

FLORENCE writes Tarsius instead of Tharsicius.

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition differs little in its first notice from UTRECHT and the others, and agrees with them concerning Tharsicius. At the end: “In Palestine, Saint Eusebius the martyr, beheaded for Christ. At Nicomedia, the passion of Saints Strato, Philip, and Eutychianus and their companion martyrs. In the monastery of Flechtdorf, the arrival of Saint Landolinus the confessor, who had previously been transferred by Charlemagne from Gaul to the village of Boek.” It should be written Landelinus. See the whole history of this translation—whether genuine or pretended—in the preliminary Commentary for 15 June, beginning at p. 1062.

BELIN reads: “The Assumption of Mary, the most holy Mother and Virgin of God. On the same day, Saint Tarsicius …” as in ANTWERP and MAX-LÜBECK.

GREVEN reads: “At Rome, Eutychianus the priest and martyr.” I think Tharsicius is intended. “In Palestine, Saint Eusebius the priest and martyr, beheaded for Christ. At Nicomedia, Saints Strato, Philip, and their companion martyrs. In the city of Soissons, Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor. Born in Brabant of noble parents, he abandoned everything; entering the monastery of Saint Medard near the walls of Soissons, he exercised himself in great works of virtue. Later made abbot of that place, and from abbot bishop of Soissons, he rested in peace, full of good works. In the monastery of Flechtdorf, the arrival of Saint Landolinus the confessor, from the district called Boek, where he had been transferred by Charlemagne. Also the holy memory of Altfrid, bishop of Hildesheim and confessor, who rests in the monastery of Essen.”

MOLAN inserts into the text, in different type, after “to cast them before the pagans”: “Judging it unworthy to cast pearls before swine.” At the end: “And when his body was turned over,” etc., as above. “At Nicomedia, Saints Strato, Philip, and Eutychianus, with their companions.” Then, in smaller type: “On the same day at Aldenburg, the deposition of Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor. Born in Flanders of noble parents,” etc., as in GREVEN; but at the end it adds: “In the year of the Lord 1087.” Other editions have the same in the text and at the end add only as far as “they found none of Christ’s sacraments.” Concerning Strato and his companions, as above. Concerning Arnulf, somewhat more briefly. Then, also in smaller type: “On the same day, Saint Jacicus or Jacinctus, of the Order of Preachers, who, after enduring many labors in Poland and Russia for the Christian religion, died in the year 1255; many years later, because of the holiness of his life and his miracles, he was enrolled in the number of the saints in our own time.” He is transferred to 16 August.]

[Col. 0365]

The Dormition of Mary, holy Mother of God, whose most sacred body, although it is not found upon the earth, is nevertheless so festively commemorated by the pious mother Church that, according to the condition of the flesh, she does not doubt that she departed. But as to by what will and divine counsel that venerable temple of the Holy Spirit has been hidden, the sobriety of the Church, together with piety, preferred not to know, rather than to teach something frivolous and apocryphal by asserting it. At Rome, on the Appian Way, Saint Tharsicius, acolyte and martyr, who, while carrying the sacrament of Christ’s body one day and refusing to disclose it to the pagans who were interrogating him, was so long tormented by them with clubs and stones that he breathed out his spirit.

XVII Kalends. Day 16. [Note: The pure codices are Praten, Herinien, Antwerp–Major, Rosweyd, Munerat, Belin, Greven, and Molan.

[Note: I wrote “at Nicaea in Bithynia” simply, as elsewhere, on the basis of the agreement of nearly all the codices. Greven has “Bitinia”; Molan, best of all, has “Bithynia.” Belin adds “in the city of Bithynia.” Here too, instead of Ursacius, he writes Ursicius. More disgracefully, Antwerp–Major has Velatius, and then barbarously says “under the emperor Clitimus.” Rosweyd has Licinianus; Munerat, Limo, adding “and soldier” after “confessor.” In Rosweyd there is *expulisset*; in Munerat, *drachonem*. In Belin, the printed readings are corrupt, as is *Methensium* in Herinien for *Metensium*. Finally, Munerat has Arnustus instead of Arnulfus. Belin alone corrupts the text, reading: “In the city of Metz, the translation of Saint Arnulf,” etc. Greven and Molan, unlike the others, write: “Arnulf, bishop and confessor.” They likewise have “the glory of miracles,” together with Antwerp–Major, Rosweyd, and Munerat—not incorrectly, but the others, following Ado, more correctly have “the grace of miracles.” Antwerp–Major wrongly inserts “he was illustrious.” Praten reads “choosing a hermit’s life,” which, if properly construed and compared with what precedes, seems to be demanded by the sense; but all the others, following Ado, agree with our text in the word *diligens*, “loving,” which for that reason was preferred. Belin alone again has “he rested in peace with a blessed end.” Rosweyd has “the nativity of Saint Serena.” The others conform to the text. The forms Dioclesianus and Diocletianus, and other minor details of this kind, are sufficiently evident.]

[Note: Concerning Ursacius—whom the Greeks, whom Baronius preferred to follow, commonly call Arsacius—the Hieronymian Martyrologies say nothing on this day; Bede is also silent, as are his followers Florus and Rabanus. In the Small Roman Martyrology, however, he is recorded in these words: “At Nicaea in Bithynia, Ursacius the confessor, under Licinius.” From book V of the *Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts*, as he himself indicates, Ado composed a brief panegyric, which Notker transcribed in its entirety, while Our Author contracted it only very slightly, omitting merely the passage where Ursacius is said to have led a solitary life in a certain tower of the aforesaid city, together with the final words already quoted by us and to be repeated more than once in the Additions. Everything may be read more fully in the passage cited by Ado, or in Sozomen, book IV, chapter 16, or in Surius on this day.

Above we said that Arnulf, the illustrious bishop of Metz, had been recorded by Ado on 18 July, and there we discussed at somewhat greater length the various Arnulfs and their confusion. Here it must especially be observed that the translation of Arnulf of Metz, which took place in the eleventh month after his death, was substituted by many for his nativity. Molan was so persuaded of this—on the authority, I think, of Belin—that he thought the word “translation” should be inserted into Usuard’s text on this day. Baronius and others, likewise following Ado, consistently place Arnulf’s blessed passing on 18 July. They are wrong; for we shall prove in its proper place with many arguments that he was taken from the living on this very day and not on another. Since this was not unknown to Usuard, we believe that this was the reason why, abandoning Ado’s opinion, he transferred his words here in full from 18 July.

The Life presented by the aforementioned Surius on this very day was reproduced more accurately and illustrated with observations by Mabillon, *Benedictine Ages*, volume II, beginning at p. 149; there the words of Paul the Deacon are also reported. The final commemoration again has no other source than the Small Roman Martyrology: “At Rome, Serena, wife of Diocletian Augustus.” The words “holy” and “formerly” were added by Ado and were thus transcribed by Our Author and Notker. What must finally be decided about that Serena will be examined in its proper place. It is useful here to append Wandalbert’s verse in support of the true opinion concerning the heavenly nativity of our Arnulf, as we have said:

> You hold the seventeenth, Arnulf, priest.

[Note: PULSANEN reads: “At Nicaea in Bithynia, the natal feast of blessed Ursicinus the confessor” [instead of Ursacius or Arsacius]. “Near the city of Metz, Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor.” Everything else is absent.

ANTWERP and MAX-LÜBECK, accurate in the first and last notices, have concerning Arnulf, or Arnolphus: “In the city of Metz, blessed Arnulf, bishop and confessor of that same city.”

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN add Ado’s words concerning Ursacius: “It is written in book V of the *Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts*.” “In the city of Metz, the translation of Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor of that same city.” In the final notice they are accurate.

ALBERGEN and DANICUS likewise append the same material concerning Ursacius. They are also accurate concerning Serena. They have nothing concerning Arnulf, since they deal with him on 18 July.

CENTULEN reads: “At Nicaea in Bithynia, Saint Ursatius the confessor, who shone with such great virtues that he cast out demons and killed a great dragon by prayer. In Gaul, in the city of Mediomatricum, Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor, a man of illustrious lineage and admirable holiness. Also in Flanders, the deposition of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons, who, among other praises of his miracles, both obtained by prayer and prophetically foretold the birth of Louis, king of the Franks.” It is accurate concerning Serena.

BRUSSELS begins: “In the city of Metz, Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor. He was the son of Arnold, son of Ansbert and Blichild, daughter of Lothair I, the first king of the Franks; and father of Ansegisus, husband of Saint Begga, sister of blessed Gertrude. This Saint Arnulf, from being master of the royal household, became bishop of Metz; and from bishop became a solitary. He was more illustrious through the wondrous holiness of his life and the glory of his miracles than he had previously been distinguished, and finally rested in Christ with a blessed end. In Africa, Saints Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servius and Rusticus the subdeacons, Rogatus and seven monks, and Maximus the boy, seven martyrs. During the Vandal persecution, at the command of King Huneric, they were killed with the shafts of oars for the Catholic faith, and thus each of them was put to death like a dog, with his skull crushed.” This is again an anticipation by this codex; see the Usuardian text on the following day. The notice of Serena is sufficiently accurate; at the very end it deals with Ursacius, in which it has the reading found in the codices above. At the end, in a much more recent hand: “And blessed Roch the confessor.”

HAGENAU, similar to the preceding codices concerning Ursacius, adds: “At Vercellae, a city of Italy, blessed Eusebius, bishop and martyr, who, because of the truth of the faith which the Arians were striving to corrupt, was sent by them and by the emperor Constantius into exile; there he was committed to a very narrow prison, deeper in height, shorter in length, and narrower in width, so that he could not turn from one side to the other. Later, however, he returned to his church; and when those same Arians persecuted him for the last time, he was dragged down from step to step in his own church and crowned with martyrdom.” See 11 August. “Near the city of Metz, the translation of Saint Arnulf the bishop, when his body was exhumed from the castle of Habendum and brought to the city of Metz with great solemnity. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Serena, empress and wife of the emperor Diocletian, who in her time was of great benefit to Christians and prolonged the lives of many Christians so that they would not be punished.”

DAVERON reads: “Saint Gemma.” I find three Gemmas somewhere; it is uncertain which one is meant here.

MATRICULARY–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT reads: “Saint Serena, wife of Diocletian. Ursacius the confessor. Jheron the martyr and confessor.” See the following day.

The VATICAN codex, numbered 5949, lacks Arnulf. “In Persia, the natal feast of Simplicius.” Among the thirteen Simpliciuses I find, none is Persian.

STROZZIAN reads: “At the city of Todi, the natal feast of blessed Philip the confessor, of the Order of the Servants of Saint Mary, originally from Florence and otherwise a Florentine citizen. His life was glorious for its miracles.”

BORDEAUX reads: “At Angers, the translation of Saint Maurilius.” He is celebrated on 13 September.

CAUDIAN reads: “In the monastery of Magnilocum in Auvergne, Saint Domninus, illustrious martyr, and his companions.” This entry recurs above more than once.

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition is almost entirely Ado’s in the entry for Ursacius. It then adds: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Serena, martyr, formerly the wife of Diocletian Augustus. At the Castle of Ramerude, the nativity of blessed Balsamius, glorious martyr, and his companions. In the city of Metz, the translation of blessed Arnulf, bishop and confessor of that city, a man of admirable holiness. On the same day, the translation of Saint Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim and confessor. The exposition of Saint Hunfrid, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the nativity of Saint Roch, confessor and pilgrim.”

GREVEN reads: “On the same day, Saints Orion, Thyrsus, and Agnitus. At the Castle of Ramerude, the nativity of Saint Balsamius the martyr and his companions. The translation of Saint Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim and confessor. The exposition of Saint Hunfrid, bishop and confessor. At Lyon in Gaul, blessed Roch, pilgrim and confessor. Born of distinguished Aquitanian parents and of excellent conduct from childhood, he received from the Lord a singular grace for curing people of epidemic disease. Finally, after many good works, he was detained in prison for five years as a spy, and there rested in the Lord. At Milan, the deposition of blessed George of Cremona, who shone remarkably in life and miracles. Also Carloman the confessor. Artemia, virgin and martyr, daughter of Saint Serena and the emperor Diocletian. Liberated from a demon and baptized by Saint Cyriacus, she was crowned with martyrdom by her brother Galerius Maximianus, who ruled after their father’s death.”

MOLAN inserts into the text, in different type: “It is written in the book,” etc., and concerning Arnulf: “the translation.” At the end: “At Milan, in the monastery of Coronata, of the Order of the Hermit Brothers of blessed Augustine, the deposition of blessed George of Cremona, who was distinguished by the holiness of his life and the grace of his miracles. At Lyon in Gaul, blessed Roch the confessor, helper against pestilence. At the Castle of Ramerude,” etc., as above. In other editions: “In Gaul, the deposition of blessed Roch,” etc. Concerning Balsamius likewise, as above. “On the same day, Theodulus, bishop and confessor of Sion. On the sixteenth day, Saint Mandelius and Saint Diomedes the martyr. And the removal from the city of Edessa of the image of our Lord Jesus Christ not made by human hands. Among the Morini, the exposition of Saint Hunfrid, bishop and confessor.” Finally, in smaller type, concerning blessed George of Cremona, as above.]

[Col. 0367]

At Nicaea in Bithynia, the natal feast of blessed Ursacius the confessor, who, under the persecutor Licinius, abandoned military service and led a solitary life, shining with such great virtues that he is said both to have expelled demons and, by prayer, to have killed an enormous dragon. Near the city of Metz, Saint Arnulf, bishop, who, illustrious for the holiness of his life and the grace of his miracles, loving the life of a hermit, rested with a blessed end. At Rome, Saint Serena, formerly the wife of Diocletian Augustus.

XVI Kalends. Day 17.

[Col. 0371C]

**The Pratenses, Herinien., Antuerp.-Major, Rosweyd., Antuerpien. and Max-Lubec., Munerat., Greven. and Molan. are pure.**

[Note: [Col. 0371C]]

Some codices read *Bonefacii* (“of Boniface”); we follow the others and the more common *Bonifacii*, as it stands in the text. Praten., with Munerat., has *Servi* (“of Servius”), correctly following Ado. But the second Praten. codex and all our other copies, together with the small Roman Martyrology, have *Servii* (“of Servius”). Concerning the letter *W* we have spoken elsewhere: “Wandalica” and “Uuandalica” are Gallic modes of writing; we follow Antuerp.-Maj., etc. Here it writes “of the Vandals,” and moreover construes the sense unfaithfully. For where the text reads “for the confession of the Catholic faith and the defense of the one baptism, [they] gloriously …,” it simply has “for the confession, gloriously …” For “Huneric,” Munerat. gives “Himeric”; Greven. has “Honeric.” Furthermore, Antuerp. and Max-Lubec. also vary in the earlier construction, giving “for the defense of the Catholic faith and the one baptism.” Rosweyd., instead of *perfecerunt* (“completed”), substitutes *perceperunt* (“received”). Herinien. and Munerat. write *Octabae* in the old manner; the latter, at the end, together with Antuerpien.-Major, omits *martyris* (“of the martyr”). Concerning *Affricam*, *Aphricam*, *dyaconi*, *Capadociae*, and other matters of this kind, what has been said elsewhere will suffice.

[Note: [Col. 0371C]]

The small Roman Martyrology today reads as follows: “In Africa, the martyrs Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servius and Rusticus, and others, under the persecution of the Vandals.” This is the first Martyrologist to mention these saints, and indeed on this day, although it is sufficiently established that they completed their martyrdom on 2 July. Ado, consulting the source of the announcement—namely, Victor of Vita, p. 81—expressed the names of each of them and treated the history of their martyrdom more fully. Notker, as usual, made a complete harvest of the material; our author adapted to his own style what is given in the little calendar. But whether the celebrated history of this passion should be attributed to Victor of Vita, Ruinart carefully investigates in the latest edition of his *History of the Vandal Persecution*, beginning at p. 94, where several matters concerning the time, manner, day, and place of the martyrdom are discussed; add to these his notes on p. 209.

Concerning the celebrated Mammes, Mammas, or Mamma—whether one person or several—Florentinius investigates at length from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which he is called a monk. Baronius attributes to this one, under the name Mammas, the panegyrics of Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and others. Various authors consequently offer various materials, which we again defer for discussion in their proper place. Meanwhile, consult the summary of the Acts of Mammes in Rabanus, which Notker took from him in almost exactly the same words.

As for the Metaphrastic Acts published by Surius, more recent scholars do not dare to trust them, composing the history of Mammes from more reliable records, which you will find indicated in Ruinart among the *Selecta*, beginning at p. 276. Tillemont presents the history in French in vol. IV, beginning at p. 358.

The small Roman Martyrology gives this brief notice of Mammes: “At Caesarea, Mammes the martyr.” Whether Ado had seen any Acts of that martyr is doubtful; his eulogy is unusually brief, since he says nothing beyond what Usuard copied from him. Wandalbert praises him alone in these words:

> On the sixteenth, blessed Mammes shines forth in martyrdom.

There remains the Octave of Saint Laurence the martyr, noted by all the Usuardine codices, although the learned Castellanus observed that in the Praten. codex the announcement seems almost to have been added later—written in a hand scarcely different, but filling the space left at the end of the line. If this is true, it must have happened not only in that codex but in all the most ancient ones. Mosander judged the commemoration wholly Adonian; Rosweyd relegated it to the appendix. You may judge which is preferable. But is the “Octave of Saint Laurence” explicitly marked in the genuine Bede? I admit that it is; yet I do not understand why Rabanus omitted it. In any case, the reading of our Usuard is certain and indisputable, however strange it may seem that in this work the Octave of only Laurence and the apostles Peter and Paul should be mentioned.

[Note: [Col. 0373A]]

Pulsanen begins: “The Octave of the most blessed Laurence, deacon and martyr.” It continues with the African martyrs through “Maximus the boy,” inclusive; everything else is absent.

Belin., Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovani., Albergen. and Danic. approach the text so closely that they are excluded only because of their order: they begin with “The Octave of Saint Laurence the martyr.” Concerning the Africans, they write, together with Antuerp. and Max-Lubec., “for the defense of the Catholic faith and the one baptism”; in Belin this is ineptly repeated at the end as “defense.”

Centulen.: “At Rome, the Octave of blessed Laurence. In Africa, the holy martyrs Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servius and Rusticus the subdeacons, Rogatus and seven lector-monks, and Maximus the boy. All of them, by order of the most cruel king of the Vandals, were consumed by various punishments. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Mammes, a monk and martyr, who suffered under the emperor Aurelian.”

[Col. 0373B] Bruxellen begins: “The Octave of Saint Laurence the martyr.” It treated the African martyrs on the preceding day. In the notice of Mammes it is sufficiently pure. It continues: “At Rome, blessed Julius the senator and martyr, who, by order of the emperor Commodus, was beaten with clubs for so long that he gave up his spirit.” This is anticipated from the nineteenth of this month.

Then: “Likewise, Karloman, prince of the Austrasians, son of Charles Martel. Out of love for Christ he abandoned the kingdom and glory of the world and professed himself a monk on Monte Cassino. There, excelling in every virtue, when he was once assigned to kitchen duty for the week and made a small mistake, he was cruelly beaten by the cook and said: ‘May God forgive you, brother, and Karloman.’ Later, coming with holy Pope Stephen II into France so that King Pippin, his brother, might restrain Aistulf, king of the Lombards, from oppressing the Church, he obtained this. On the return journey, seized by illness at Vienne, he died a holy death.” Truth mixed with falsehood.

Hagenoyen.: “In the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Mammes the martyr, who, fearing the emperor Aurelian, fled into the desert and lived there with his companions. All the wild beasts gathered around him; he milked them and made cheese. After he had converted many to the faith, he called a wild lion to defend him, and it happened so. He was suspended on the rack by the governor Alexander and was comforted there by a heavenly voice. After this he was imprisoned, to be thrown later into a furnace, where an angel brought him honey and milk. On the third day he was thrown to the beasts, but was not harmed; then he was buried under stones, and, called by a heavenly voice, he died.”

The account of the Africans follows, purely; likewise that of the Octave of Saint Laurence.

Aquicinct. has *Rustitius* instead of *Rustici*.

Daveronen.: “At Tours, the dedication of Saint Mary and of Saint Julian the martyr.”

Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraject.: “The Octave of Saint Laurence the martyr. Mammes the boy and martyr. Liberatus the abbot, with several others of his companions, martyred by the Vandals for the faith.”

Codex Gollian.: “At Sion, Saint Theodore the bishop.” Which Theodore this is among the many Theodores will be seen later.

The Lubeco-Cologne edition, in the Octave of Saint Laurence and the African martyrs, is pure. After “martyr” in the notice of Mammes it reads: “When he was seven years old and utterly rejected the worship of idols, he suffered various torments for the faith of Christ; finally he was stoned, under Aurelian, with Alexander as governor. At Nortwich, the feast of blessed Jerome, priest and martyr.” See what Castellanus noted with sufficient care concerning this very day.

Greven.: “In Holland, in the village of Norwich, the feast of blessed Jerome, priest and martyr. In Bethulia, blessed Judith the widow. Likewise, Euphemia.”

Molan., after “they completed,” inserts into the text in different letters: “Blessed Victor, bishop of Africa, writes in the history of that same Vandal persecution, which he himself endured with the others and composed in a faithful and distinguished style.” At the end: “On the same day, in a village of Holland, Saint Jerome, priest and martyr.” Then in smaller type: “Likewise, Karloman the confessor, prince of Austrasia, who became a monk on Monte Cassino.” Later editions agree with the first in the text. At the end, however, they have: “In a village of Holland, at the monastery of Egmond, Saint Jerome, priest and martyr. On the seventeenth day, Saint Myron the martyr.” Finally, in smaller letters they add: “At the city of Ptolemais, the holy martyrs Paul and Juliana.” See the Acts in Surius. In the modern Roman Martyrology they are said to have suffered under Valerian.

[Col. 0371]

In Africa, the holy martyrs Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servius and Rusticus the subdeacons, Rogatus and Septimus, monks, and Maximus the boy; under the Vandal persecution, by order of King Huneric, for the confession of the Catholic faith and the defense of the one baptism, they completed the splendid course of their struggle, with the Lord crowning them. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Mammes the martyr, who suffered under the emperor Aurelian with Alexander as governor. On the same day, the Octave of Saint Laurence the martyr.

**XV Kal. Day 18.**

[Note: [Col. 0373]]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Major, Rosweyd., Antuerp. and Max-Lubec., Munerat., the first edition of Belin, Greven. and Molan. The Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden. and Albergen. codices also agree.

[Note: [Col. 0373D]]

Only Molan. writes *Praenestinam* with a diphthong; the others follow the text. Antuerp., Max-Lubec., Belin and others read “from the city of Rome.” In Munerat. there is an error, “twenty-third” instead of “thirty-third,” as all have it with Ado; likewise, “he burned with love of Christ’s martyrdom,” except Greven. and Molan., who, by omitting *martyrio*, make the sense smoother. Notker’s construction is not exact: “he burned with love of Christ’s martyrdom.”

Among the older codices, only Rosweyd. wrote *Aureliani* instead of *Aurelii*, following Ado and Notker; this is retained by the middle-grade codices. Why Usuard prefers *Aurelii*, I confess I do not know, unless, as often happens, the names were used indiscriminately—a thing that could easily have occurred in that age.

From this point most read *exhin*, others *exin*, others *exhinc*. Belin., after “by the emperor’s command,” wrongly inserts “he was seized and [given] to lions,” etc.; Rosweyd. again not ineptly corrected *subjiceretur* (“was subjected”) to *objiceretur* (“was thrown to”). In Munerat., after “through whose merits,” the words “they themselves also” are omitted. Greven. and Molan. again differ from the others, reading “the joys of eternal life,” contrary to Ado and our codices. Belin, concerning Helena: “Likewise at Rome, on the Via …” I say nothing about the blemishes of the middle-grade codices, such as *tercio*, *aput*, *Anthiocho*, *Johannis*, *Dyocletiani*, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0375A]]

As illustrious and celebrated from ancient times as the glory of Agapitus of Praeneste the martyr is—proclaimed by all our ancient calendars, sacramentaries and martyrologies—so corrupted are his Acts, according to Cardinal Baronius himself, that it seems safe to say that they were produced in the same workshop as those concerning Saint Venantius, discussed under 18 May; or perhaps that the Acts of both are the same, or that one has been adapted from the other. In any case, they require much correction, as will be demonstrated more fully in its proper place; and the matter must again be discussed below, under 20 and 21 August.

I know that two sets of Acts exist; which should be preferred will be said in its proper place. The glorious struggle of the young man is also reported by the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Rabanus, the small Roman Martyrology, Ado, Notker and Wandalbert. The Hieronymian Martyrologies also state the distance from the City, with slight variation among the codices; this is ignored by the small Roman Martyrology. Rabanus’s eulogy mentions King Antiochus.

The account given by Ado is more credible: he explicitly names the emperor Aurelian, as Notker does after him. It is therefore surprising that “by order of Aurelius” entered almost all the ancient Usuardine codices, although it is perfectly clear that everything else was taken from Ado. Only Agapitus is celebrated by Wandalbert in this verse:

> Agapitus seals the fifteenth with his contest.

The following announcement was first produced on this day by the author of the small Roman Martyrology in these words: “At Rome, John and Crispus, priests.” Ado composed a brief encomium, which our author copies almost in full, omitting only the words “at the Sixth of Philip,” which are certainly not very clear, and the name of the other tyrant, Maximian. I would believe that Usuard did not wish to name a cemetery unknown to him. The curious reader may consult Aringhi, *Roma subterranea*, book II, chapter 20, p. 365, where he will find these same words of Ado cited. Castellanus notes that these saints have been brought together here from other days.

The rest elsewhere. Mosander marked Helena, found in the Adonian codices, with an asterisk as an interpolation; Rosweyd held the same opinion. It therefore remains uncertain from where Usuard took her, but it seems entirely certain that he marked her, as we have reproduced her in the text.

Among our manuscripts there is a life of Helena by Altmann of Altivillar, addressed to Hincmar, together with accounts of the translation and miracles, as well as other lives and various narratives by Notker, both manuscript and printed, all to be carefully examined specifically in due time. Surius proceeded more cautiously here, drawing several things from Eusebius and Theodoret, assigned to 7 February. Flodoard’s history of the translation to Altivillar, discussed more thoroughly by Mabillon, is found in the fourth century of the Benedictine works, part II, beginning at p. 153. But Tillemont paved a more laborious path by which a more reliable sequence of Helena’s life might be extracted from the testimonies of the ancients, as may be seen in vol. VII, beginning at p. 1, and in the relevant notes.

[Note: [Col. 0375B]]

Pulsanen is pure in the first and last notices; it entirely omits the second.

Lovani. is deficient in Agapitus’s eulogy; otherwise it is pure.

Danic. cuts off the final part of the second announcement, beginning with “whose merits they themselves later joined,” etc.

Centulen.: “In the Italian city of Praeneste, Saint Agapitus the martyr, under the governor Antiochus. On the same day at Rome, at the Sixth of Philip [Ado: ‘at the Sixth of Philip’], the blessed priests John and Crispus, who during the persecution of Diocletian very carefully buried many bodies of martyrs. On the Lavican Way, Saint Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine.”

[Col. 0375C] Bruxellen is almost pure; it also adds “in the city of Rome,” and reads “of Aurelian”; there are minor blemishes elsewhere. Then: “And at Rome, at the Sixth of Philip, the holy priests, etc. Likewise at Rome, on the Lavican Way,” etc.

Hagenoyen.: “At the city of Praeneste, thirty-three miles from the city of Rome, the feast of Saint Agapitus the martyr. When he was fifteen years old and burned with desire for martyrdom, he offered himself to the persecutors. By order of the emperor Aurelian he was seized, first beaten severely with raw sinews, and sent to the governor Antiochus, by whom he suffered grievous torments. First he was imprisoned; then burning coals were placed on his head, but he was not harmed. He was beaten with whips, his head turned downward, and a dreadful smoke was made beneath him. Then boiling water was poured over him and his jaws were crushed; when the judge saw this, he expired. Then the emperor ordered him to be thrown to lions, but they did not harm him; afterward, when his head had been cut off, he completed his martyrdom.”

It is pure in the notice of John and Crispus. Then: “At Rome, on the Lavican Way, the deposition of Saint Helena, queen, mother of the great emperor Constantine. This Helena was first a pagan and greatly devoted to works of mercy; afterward she was Jewish and perfect in that law. Finally she became Christian and greatly beneficial to the Christian religion, because she discovered the Lord’s cross. She brought many bodies of saints from overseas to the Christians and built many monasteries in Asia, Gaul and Italy. She persevered in good works and died in peace.” The matters related here require another witness if they are to be believed.

Aquicinct. appends to the text: “Likewise, Saint Pontinus.” See below for the true name and title.

[Col. 0376B] Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraject.: “Agapitus the martyr. At Rome, Helena the queen, mother of the emperor Constantine. John and Crispus, priests, who, after burying many bodies of holy martyrs, themselves also were crowned with martyrdom.” In the margin, concerning Agapitus, it adds: “This boy endured many things and greatly confounded the judge, whom God also struck in vengeance for the holy martyr.”

Codex D. du Cheval, marked C: “Likewise, Pontinus.” I think “Pontimus” should be read, following the Hieronymian Martyrology.

Altemps.: “Likewise, Pontinus the martyr.” Correctly “martyr,” not “confessor,” as the Lubeco-Cologne edition has it.

[Col. 0376C] Florentin.: “Helena … whose body now lies at Venice.” Or: “Whose body is now buried at Venice.” The dispute is still undecided.

Lugdunen.: “In the village of Sisteric, on the mountain called Lura, Saint Donatus,” etc. See the following day.

Codex Castri-Caroli: “In Gaul, in the village of Sigisteric, on the mountain called Lura, Saint Donatus the priest.” Usuard treats him on 19 August.

The Lubeco-Cologne edition begins: “At Rome, on the Lavican Way, Saint Helena, mother of Saint Constantine the emperor and discoverer of Christ’s cross, a most noble native of Trier.” It then gives the account of Agapitus, quite purely. In John and Crispus it adds from Ado what Usuard omitted. Finally: “In the city of Amasea, blessed Pontinus the confessor.” I have already said that the reading is “Pontimus,” and that he was a martyr.

The second edition of Belin adds at the end: “Likewise, Pontinus.” [Col. 0376D] See what has already been said. The Hieronymian copies name companions—or rather female companions.

Greven.: “According to some, this is the commemoration of Saint Helena; her deposition, however, is on 17 Kalends of May. Martin the pope. Demetrius the martyr. Privatus the martyr. Potentinus the confessor.”

Molan.: “At Bronium, the translation of Saint Eugenius, bishop and martyr. At the city of Metz, the deposition of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor.” Other editions write *Aureliam* in italics in the text. At the end: “At the city of Metz, the deposition of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor. On the eighteenth day, the holy martyrs Phlorus and Laurus. At Bronium, the translation of the body of Saint Eugenius, archbishop and martyr.”

[Col. 0373]

At the city of Praeneste, thirty-three miles from the City, the feast of Saint Agapitus the martyr. When he was fifteen years old and burned with love for Christ’s martyrdom, he was seized by order of the emperor Aurelius and first beaten for a very long time with raw sinews; then he suffered grievous punishments from the governor Antiochus. Afterward, when he was to be thrown to the lions by the emperor’s command, and was not harmed at all, he was struck by the sword of the attendants to be crowned. On the same day at Rome, the blessed priests John and Crispus, who during the persecution of Diocletian buried many bodies of saints with the greatest devotion; through whose merits they themselves were afterward joined to them and deserved the joys of eternal life. On the Lavican Way, Saint Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine.

**XIV Kal. Day 19.**

[Note: [Col. 0377]]

Thus Praten., Antuerp.-Major, Rosweyd., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven. and Molan.; likewise Antuerp.-Max., Lovani. and Danic.

[Note: [Col. 0377A]]

Muneratus stumbles at the beginning: “The feast of Saint Magnus and Saint Andrew the martyrs.” All read “with their companions,” except Praten., which omits the final word. I write “thousands,” since all likewise have it. Antuerp.-Maj. gives 2,598 companions; Rosweyd., 2,167; Greven., 2,527. Usuard took the number from older sources, and we reproduce it in the text.

Antuerp. differs from the associated Maxima edition and from the others in Donatus’s title: it alone calls him a bishop. It also writes *anacoreticam*; the others have *anachoriticam*. [Col. 0378A] Greven., at the beginning of the announcement, reads “In Gaul, in the village,” etc.; the customary imitator Molan. also has this, and both write “he carried out [his life] for many years,” and afterward “famous by the glory of miracles” instead of “by the grace of miracles.” In Munerat. both are absent; in Antuerp.-Major and Rosweyd., the conjunction *et* is found before “miracles.” Antuerp.-Major has “he was beaten with clubs.” Antuerp. substitutes “Martin” for “Marian”; Max.-Lubec., together with Antuerp.-Max., Lovani. and Danic., has “Marinus.”

[Note: [Col. 0377A]]

It is highly probable that our Latin martyrologists made Andrew, the most renowned *megalomartyr* among the Greeks, into a double name from the Greek designation: Magnus, or Andrew. Thus Bede, and from him Rabanus, the small Roman Martyrology, Ado and our author, all use precisely the same phrase. They might perhaps better have read “the great Andrew.” For I do not think it likely that our martyrologists intended to confuse Andrew the military tribune with Magnus, bishop of Anagni.

Wandalbert took another route: according to the number of names, he doubled and joined the designation, as I shall soon show. Whether Ado saw the Acts of Andrew as they are commonly circulated, I do not know; certainly he added nothing to his predecessors. We shall examine them in their proper place as they are known from the editions of Metaphrastes, Lipomanus and Surius.

Baronius judged the aforesaid Acts genuine under the year 301, no. 5, and believed that they had been collected and written by Peter, bishop of Tarsus. Today there are not lacking those who think otherwise. Tillemont’s note may be consulted in vol. V, beginning at p. 588; the Acts will be examined more carefully in their proper place. For now, hear Wandalbert:

> Magnus and Andrew shine forth on the fourteenth:
>
> Five hundred and ninety-seven accompany them,
>
> And two thousand holy ones likewise follow with them.

The Donatus who follows in our little calendar was first introduced into the sacred calendars by Ado, with a fuller history of his life and an identification of the mountain on which he lived in solitude. Mosander calls it Tura; Rosweyd, Jura, but with a note added in his own hand warning that I should be changed to L, and therefore that it should be read Lura, since it is as far from Mount Jura as Provence is from Burgundy.

Whatever the truth, Usuard transferred his entire eulogy from Ado. From where Ado took his account is unclear. Peter, in his *Catalogue*, book VII, chapter 78, as usual copies Ado’s words. The Life of Marius, under 27 January, mentions Donatus. We possess a manuscript Life of the saint himself, to be illustrated elsewhere.

Concerning Julius, the small Roman Martyrology says very briefly: “At Rome, Julius the senator and martyr.” Ado derives more from the Acts, but our author uses a summary. See the observations under 25 August, concerning the Acts of Eusebius, Pontianus, etc. Not long ago the body of a certain Julius martyr was discovered at Rome; whether it may be said to be this senator’s body, I have not yet learned.

In some Hieronymian copies one finds the addition: “At Biturium, in the village of Villaunus, the deposition of Saint Marianus the confessor.” Florentinius discusses him more fully and notes, from Labbe, that the feast of this holy hermit is celebrated in the diocese of Bourges on 19 September. Whether, in order to preserve a distinction of cult, one should rightly have recourse to another Marianus, we shall explain elsewhere.

It might seem sufficiently strange that Usuard did not know, not only the true day of his death—which cannot be determined at all—but also the day of his cult customary in his own time, while he recorded Marianus on this day. The agreement of our codices, both in Marianus and in the preceding notices, is entirely unanimous. Labbe published a brief Life of Marianus, though I do not know whether it is sufficiently genuine, in vol. II of the *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, p. 432, where he also reports chapter 81 of Saint Gregory of Tours. In our library there are two other manuscript summaries of his life, to be examined more accurately in a larger work.

[Note: [Col. 0377C]]

Herinien. is entirely pure in the whole text, but for some reason the following notice is inserted second: “At the monastery of Bobbio, the deposition of Saint Bertulf the abbot.”

Pulsanen.: “The feast of Saint Magnus the martyr. At Rome, Saint Julius the Senator, etc.,” correctly. It continues: “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Marcianus the confessor.” Everything else is absent. See above what we said about Magnus, as well as Castellanus’s note in the *Universal Martyrology* and Greven. below.

Ultraject. and Leyden. begin: “In Sicily, the feast of Saint Louis, bishop and confessor. The feast of Saint Magnus the martyr with his companions,” etc., purely. Each has the following announcement disordered and confused. Instead of Marianus, they write Marinus.

Albergen. uses another wording: “At Marseilles, the feast of Saint Louis, bishop and confessor, who, being the firstborn son of the king of Sicily, professed the order of the Friars Minor.” The rest is pure, except that the end of this day is confused with the beginning of the next, though this was corrected in some copies.
