It also reads Marinus.

Centulen.: “The feast of Saint Magnus, or Saint Andrew the martyr, with his 2,597 companions. In Gaul, in the village of Sigisteric, Saint Donatus the priest and confessor. On the same day at Rome, Saint Julius the Senator, who suffered under the emperor Commodus, with Vitellius as judge.”

Bruxellen writes of Andrew’s companions “more than 2,500, ninety-nine,” rather than “more than 2,500, ninety-seven.” Concerning Donatus it adds, “on the mountain called Lura.” Elsewhere it is only slightly interpolated. At the end it adds: “At Marseilles, Saint Louis, bishop and confessor, son of the king of Sicily, bishop of Toulouse, of the order of the Friars Minor.”

Hagenoyen begins with Julius, in which it is pure. Nor does it depart greatly from purity in Donatus. Then it treats Marianus; finally Andrew, also fairly correctly. Two announcements anticipated from the following day follow, namely: “On the island of Herio, the deposition of Saint Philibert the abbot, who first followed earthly military service, then was devoted to Christ’s service and became a devoted founder of many monks. In the city of Cordila (Corduba), the holy monks and martyrs Leovigild and Christopher, whose bodies were delivered to the fire after their heads had been cut off.” See concerning them on the following day.

Ambianen. copies the eulogy of Saint Donatus from Ado, more purely from that source.

Matric.-Carthus.-Ultraject.: “Magnus the martyr with his companions. Louis the confessor, who was the king’s son, afterward a monk in the order of the Friars Minor and bishop of Toulouse. Julius the Senator, martyr.”

In Vaticanus 5949, Marianus is absent.

Florentin.: “Saint Louis: …” I find no more; perhaps the remainder will conform to the present Roman Martyrology or to Belin, who often agrees with these codices. Other codices mentioned above and the Lubeco-Cologne edition may also be consulted.

[Col. 0379B] Burdegalen.: “In the territory of Bourges, Marinus the confessor.” It intends Marianus.

Codex Salinen.: “In the territory of Besançon, Saint Marianus the confessor. Read ‘of Bourges.’”

The Lubeco-Cologne edition is pure concerning Andrew; in Donatus it is somewhat interpolated from Ado, as also in Julius. It continues: “At Marseilles, the feast of Saint Louis, bishop of Toulouse and confessor, who, being the firstborn son of the king of Sicily, professed the order of the Friars Minor; glorious in life and miracles, he deserved to be enrolled among the saints.” Instead of Marianus, it writes Marinus.

“In the city of Nuremberg, Saint Sebald, pilgrim and confessor, son of the king of Denmark. In the city of Anagni, forty miles from the city of Rome, on the road called the Latina, the deposition of Saint Magnus, bishop and confessor. Born in Apulia, in the city of Trani, he guarded the sheep of his neighbors in the pastures for payment, so that he might support his poor parents from it. Later, baptized under the guidance of the angel by Saint Redemptus [Col. 0379C] the bishop, and perfectly instructed in the faith, he was also sufficiently taught in literary studies in a short time. After a few years had passed, he was ordained bishop, and, having suffered many plots against him, finally rested in a blessed death.”

Belin.: “The feast of Saints Magnus and Andrew with …” The rest is sufficiently pure, except that it writes Martinus instead of Marianus. Then it adds: “On the same day in Provence, at the castle of Brignoles, the deposition of Saint Louis, bishop and confessor. From there he was carried to Marseilles and buried honorably in the church of the Friars Minor. Likewise, the Octave of Saint Clare the virgin. At the city of Mantua, Saint Rufinus the confessor.”

Greven.: “Magnus, king of the Norwegians and martyr. At Marseilles, the feast of blessed Louis, bishop and confessor, who, being …,” etc., as above. In Magnus of Anagni it differs very little from the Lubeco-Cologne edition. It continues: “Bertulf the abbot and confessor. Sebald the confessor, son of the king of Denmark. Having obtained a most noble bride, he abandoned her, his parents and all his possessions, following the example of blessed Alexius. Living a solitary life and offering God the purest service, he shone with many miracles. Among them, by prayer he obtained a loaf baked beneath the ashes for his traveling companions; placing a hair shirt upon the waters, he crossed a river. Finally, full of good works, he died near the town of Nuremberg. Richardis the virgin. Ermelina the virgin.”

Molan. concerning Marianus: “whose deeds are recorded.” In Louis, he describes Belin. “At Mantua, Saint Rufinus the confessor. At Bobbio, Saint Bertulf the abbot.” Then in smaller type: “Sebald the confessor, son of the king of Denmark, who, full of good works, died near the town of Nuremberg.” Other editions, concerning Louis, give “at the castle of Brignoles,” with the rest as in Belin. Concerning Rufinus and Bertulf, as above. “On the same day, Saint Elaphius, bishop of Châlons and confessor. In the city of Nuremberg, the deposition of Saint Sebald the confessor, son of the king of Denmark.”

[Col. 0377]

The feast of Saint Magnus, or Saint Andrew the martyr, with his 2,597 companions. In the village of Sigisteric, blessed Donatus the priest, who, endowed from the earliest beginnings of childhood with the wondrous grace of God, led an anchoritic life for many years and, famous for the glory of miracles, departed to Christ. At Rome, Saint Julius the Senator and martyr, who, by order of the emperor Commodus, was beaten with clubs for so long that he gave up his spirit. In the territory of Bourges, Saint Marianus the confessor.

**XIII Kal. Day 20.**

[Note: [Col. 0379]]

From Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Major, Rosweyd. and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0379D]]

I first note matters of orthography: *Samuhelis, Jeronimus, Jheronymus, Hieronimus, Archadius, Judea, Traciam, Porphirii, Filiberti, Phyliberti, Philiberti, tyrocinio, tirocinio, Christophori, Christofori, Cristofori, abscisionem*, etc. In writing all these here and now, uniformity cannot always be maintained, since I do not find it in my codices. Accordingly, here and elsewhere I form the readings according to the greater authority of the agreeing codices. I know that *Hieronymus, Arcadii, Judaea, Thraciam, Porphyrii, Filiberti, tirocinio, Christophori, abscissionem* are preferable; nevertheless, let no one blame me for following another reading. Molan., instead of *hominis Dei* (“of the man of God”), wrote *viri Dei* (“of the man of God”). Praten., instead of *Christi tirocinio* (“Christ’s service”), has *Christo* (“to Christ”).

[Note: [Col. 0379D]]

The prophet Samuel is noted by Bede; Rabanus, changing the case, wrote “of the prophet Samuel.” The small Roman Martyrology has it in this same form. Ado added not an encomium of the prophet but a brief history of the translation from Jerome’s work *Against Vigilantius*, which you will find among the additions of Molan. and others. We shall give Wandalbert’s verses below. Usuard took from Ado only what we have represented in the little calendar.

Concerning Porphyrius, the small Roman Martyrology reads: “And Porphyrius, a man of God,” whom the earlier writers do not mention. Whatever Ado added from the Acts of Agapitus, our author copied word for word. To make clearer the confusion between the Acts of Agapitus of Praeneste and those of Venantius of Camerino, consult the latter’s readings in the Roman Breviary under 18 May. There Cornicularius is said to have been baptized by the blessed priest Porphyrius together with his household, etc. These accounts are so closely alike that they must have been transferred from one set of Acts to the other, unless we wish to invent a new miracle. But enough has been said about this according to the purpose of our work.

Wandalbert mentions Philibert on 20 July:

> And holy Philibert adorns the thirteenth.

On that same day he is found added to the Adonian codices, joined to another abbot, Vulmarus. On this day he was added to one or another Hieronymian copy, and is also mentioned by Florus and Rabanus. I do not think he passed into Usuard from any of them; rather, our author seems to have composed the entire announcement on his own initiative.

Surius published the Life of Philibert, written by a contemporary monk, exercising his customary liberty in altering the style. Mabillon restored it to its original phrasing in the second century of the Benedictine works, beginning at p. 816, while referring the translations and other matters to the fourth century. See there, part I, beginning at p. 537.

Leovigild and Christopher likewise owe their inclusion to him alone; they were brought from Spain together with several others, as we have said elsewhere more than once. Consult the *Memorial of Eulogius*, book II, chapter 11.

Concerning Samuel, Wandalbert praises him today as follows:

> On the thirteenth Samuel excels, whom from his very cradle  
> His devout mother consecrated to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0381A]]

Pulsanen is pure in the first two notices and omits the last two.

Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. are pure, except that they are deficient in the notice of Porphyrius; at the end, however, they exceed the text with a new announcement concerning Saint Bernard: “In the territory of Langres, the deposition of blessed Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, a man glorious in life, doctrine and miracles.”

Munerat. faithfully appends to the pure text: “In the territory of Langres, blessed Bernard.”

Greven., also pure throughout the text, uses at the end the sign LL, concerning which we spoke on the fifth of this month under Saint Dominic and elsewhere. By this sign it indicates that the saint marked with it was added to Usuard. It should therefore have been placed among the additions. Today it reads: “Likewise, at Clairvaux, Saint Bernard the abbot.”

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN, in the second place after Samuel, insert:

> “In the territory of Langres, the deposition of blessed Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, a man glorious in doctrine and miracles.”

The rest of the text follows in its pure form. At the end:

> “On the same day, Saint Auctor, bishop of Trier.”

Or was he bishop of Metz, on 10 August?

ALBERG and DANIC differ from the preceding witnesses in placing Bernard first and entirely omitting the commemoration of Porphyry, which the others place in its proper location.

CENTULEN:

> “Of the prophet Samuel, whose sacred bones Augustus Arcadius transferred from Judea to Thrace, while the bishops carried them and all the peoples of the churches came together with such joy as though they saw him present, alive, and living. On the same day, Saint Porphyry, a man of God. On the island of Herio, Saint Philibert, abbot, who, having been enlisted in Christ’s service after the service of this world, became a devoted founder of monasteries. In the city of Córdoba, the holy monks Leovigild and Christopher, whose bodies were handed over to the fire after their beheading.”

BRUSSELS begins with Bernard, as above. Then:

> “Also, Saint Samuel the prophet, whose sacred bones Augustus Arcadius transferred from Judea to Thrace. When the bishops carried them and the peoples of all the churches came to meet them, such joy arose as though they saw and welcomed him present and alive, so that from Palestine to Chalcedon the crowds of peoples joined together and resounded with one voice in Christ’s praise. Saint Jerome records this.”

For Porphyry it reads: “Agapitus or Agatho.” In the entry for the people of Córdoba it is pure. Concerning Philibert it adds:

> “And especially of the monastery of Cinégy, in the territory of Rouen. He abandoned the abbacy which he himself held—or governed—because of the tyranny of Ebroin [or, perhaps, Ebronius], the apostate.”

At Trier, Saint Auctor, bishop and confessor. See the additions for 10 August, unless the two are different men.

HAGENOYEN constructed a long commentary on Samuel from the sacred writings, which there is no time to transcribe. The entry for Porphyry is pure. It dealt with Philibert and the people of Córdoba on the preceding day. It now continues:

> “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux in the territory of Langres. He was born of noble parents from Burgundy, his father being Celmo and his mother Aleyde, both highly religious. He had five brothers and one sister. Bernard himself was third among the sons. His mother foresaw him in her womb as a completely white puppy, shaved on the head and back, and heard him barking loudly. While he was still a little boy, on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, he saw Christ, as a newborn child, being born of the Blessed Virgin. As a young man he greatly loved chastity, and, becoming a monk in the twenty-second year of his life, he devoted himself entirely to works of patience, abstinence, humility, and charity throughout all the days of his life. Having performed many miracles, written many books, and built one hundred and sixty monasteries of his Order, he died in peace in the sixty-third year of his age, leaving his brothers a testament of charity, humility, patience, and abstinence. Also in England, Saint Oswin, king and martyr. At Trier, Saint Auctor, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0382B] AQUICINCT. adds at the end:

> “At the castle of Caino, Saint Maximus the confessor.”

Then, in a notably more recent hand:

> “The deposition of Saint Bernard, abbot.”

The sufficiently long eulogy is given above.

AMIENS:

> “On the same day, Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT:

> “Bernard, abbot. Samuel the prophet. Porphyry, who instructed the child Saint Agapitus. Philibert, first a soldier and afterward an abbot.”

CLUNY and ALTEMPS:

> “At the castle of Caino, Saint Maximus the confessor.”

He was a disciple of Saint Martin of Tours; in French he is called Meme.

SWEDISH REGISTER, no. 428:

> “In the regions of Burgundy, at the place called Clairvaux, the deposition of Saint Bernard, abbot.”

In the VATICAN manuscript, no. 5949, Samuel and Philibert are absent. It adds:

> “In Lucania, Saint Leontius.”

[Col. 0382C] UGHELLI omits Porphyry. At the end:

> “In the territory of Langres, the deposition of blessed Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux.”

FLORENCE:

> “Saint Bernard. … Saint Stephen. … Saint Potitus, a child, who, I think, is intended by the abbreviation *q. a.* to mean ‘who suffered,’ in the province of Apulia during the time of the emperor Antoninus.”

BORDEAUX:

> “At the castle of Caino, Saint Maximinus the confessor.”

CODEX OF THE HOLY MOUNT:

> “On the same day, the annual celebration of the holy confessors Amatus, Romaricus, and Adelphus is renewed. On the same day, the translation of Saint Gebetrudis.”

See Castellanus, p. 785, and the index.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. The entry concerning Samuel is almost identical with that of BRUSSELS. It continues:

> “In the territory of Langres, in the monastery of Clairvaux, the deposition of blessed Bernard, first abbot and confessor of that place, a man glorious in life, doctrine, and miracles. He was an illustrious founder and father of monasteries and monks.”

[Col. 0382D] In the entries for Philibert, the people of Córdoba, and Porphyry, it is sufficiently pure. Then:

> “At Trier, blessed Auctor, bishop and confessor, who rests at Brunswick by translation. On the same day, blessed Stephen, king of Hungary and confessor. Also, the commemoration of Saint Malachy, bishop and confessor.”

In the Roman Martyrology his deposition is placed on 3 November.

BELIN. The entry for Samuel is pure; that for the people of Córdoba is corrupt. Again, the entry for Porphyry is pure, but in the entry for Philibert the entire eulogy is omitted. Then:

> “In Hungary, in the royal city of Alba Regalis, Saint Stephen, king, who first converted the Hungarians to the faith.”

The entry for Bernard resembles ANTW.-MAX.–LÜBECK:

> “At the castle of Caino, Saint Maximus the confessor.”

GREVEN:

> “Oswin, king of the province of Deira and martyr. When Saint Aidan, bishop, foretold his impending death—for so Bede writes in Book III—he said: ‘This people is not worthy to have such a ruler.’ In Lucania, Saints Valentinian and Leontius. Stephen, king of Hungary and confessor. When, at the persistent urging of his most holy wife Geisila, sister of the emperor Saint Henry, he accepted the faith of Christ, by his own efforts he led his people to the same faith, and, full of good works, rested in a blessed death. At Trier, Saint Auctor, bishop and confessor, resting at Brunswick. Juliana, virgin and martyr, and four others. The commemoration of Saint Malachy, bishop and confessor.”

See above.

MOLAN. Concerning Samuel, he inserts into the text, in different type:

> “When the bishops carried them and the peoples of all the churches came forward with such joy as though they welcomed him alive, so that from Palestine to Chalcedon crowds of peoples joined together and resounded with one voice in Christ’s praises. Saint Jerome writes this in his book *Against Vigilantius*.”

At the end:

> “In Hungary, in the royal city of Alba Regalis, Saint Stephen, king, who first converted the Hungarians to the faith.”

This is taken from BELIN, as is also the material concerning Bernard and Maximus:

> “On the same day, Saint Auctor, bishop of Trier.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “Who rests at Brunswick.”

In the entry for Oswin, it copies GREVEN. It continues:

> “At Deventer, blessed Gerard, surnamed the Great, died. And in the monastery of Villers, of the Cistercian Order, blessed Gobert, formerly count of Aspermont, a monk of outstanding holiness in that place.”

Other editions, besides the material already mentioned, also insert Bernard’s announcement into the text in the entry for Samuel. At the end, concerning Stephen, Maximus, and Auctor, as above:

> “In England, Saint Oswin, martyr of Deira, whose impending …”

and so forth. Then, in smaller type:

> “At Deventer, the death of blessed Gerard, surnamed the Great, who gave the beginning to the Brothers of the Common Life. In the monastery of Villers, the death of Gobert, formerly count of Aspermont,”

and so forth, as in the earlier edition.

> “At Worms, the death of Burchard, bishop.”

[Col. 0379]

Samuel the prophet, whose sacred bones, as Jerome writes, Augustus Arcadius transferred from Judea to Thrace. On the same day, blessed Porphyry, a man of God, who instructed the holy martyr Agapitus in the faith and teaching of Christ. On the island of Herio, Saint Philibert, abbot, who, after his service in the world, devoted to Christ’s service, became a devoted founder of monasteries. In the city of Córdoba, the holy monks Leovigild and Christopher, whose bodies were handed over to the fire after their heads had been cut off.

XII Kalends. Day 21. [Note: [Col. 0383]

The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Antwerp-Major, Munerat., Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0383B]

Only Antwerp-Major reads “who suffered under persecution”; all the others omit the particle *sub* (“under”). Munerat’s reading *Ganalitanae* should, I think, be attributed to a printer’s error. Likewise *Bodosi* for *Bonosi*. The same should be said of *Maximi* for *Maximiani* in Greven, who also, together with Molan, writes “whose Acts are preserved.” All read “And in the city of Salona”; I do not know why Molan omitted the particle *in*. Here Usuard again becomes entangled in the confusion mentioned above concerning the names Aurelian and Aurelius, whereas Ado most explicitly reads the former, as we said above under Agapitus on 18 August. Whether one or the other should be preferred must be discussed elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0383B]

“In the territory of the Gabali, in the district of Mimate, the passion of the martyr Privatus,” say the Hieronymian copies, placing him last. Florentinius’s Notes and Baron’s notes on the Roman Martyrology may also be consulted on this matter. Rabanus copied his entry directly from the Hieronymian Martyrology, without mentioning episcopal dignity. Florus expresses more fully the dignity that is desired, the time of the contest, and the barbarians by whom he is believed to have been martyred. The small Roman Martyrology does not mention Privatus. I therefore believe that Ado took his material from Gregory of Tours, whose account he merely touches upon briefly, and that Our Author copied it, except for the words “in the district of Minat,” which should read “in the district of Mimate,” as we shall demonstrate more fully in its proper place from the Gregory cited and from others cited by Baronius. Tillemont will provide useful assistance in Volume IV, p. 221 onward, and in the notes from p. 651 onward. Wandalbert adorns the present day with a single verse concerning Privatus:

> “Here the twelfth day shines with the blood of the martyr Privatus.”

Bonosus and Maximian, omitted by all the more ancient witnesses, I do not know from where they first entered Ado’s notice; from him they were entered into the sacred calendars in the very words which, taken from him by Usuard, we supplied in our index. This is all the more remarkable because Ado expressly asserts that their Acts exist; yet it is certain that he never saw them, since he says not a word from them, producing only bare names from which one can infer nothing either about the place or the time of their martyrdom. Baronius admits that they had not been found in his time, and we likewise admit that our predecessors nowhere found them. Therefore the greatest thanks are owed to Theodoric Ruinart, who unearthed them from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Mary of the Greater Forest in the diocese of Bordeaux and first published them in *Sincera et Selecta*, p. 663, where he also illuminates them here and there with learned observations. From those Acts it is gathered that 21 August was selected by Ado almost arbitrarily; although whether Castellanus was right to prefer 20 September is nearly equally uncertain. The arena was Antioch; the tyrant was Count Julian, uncle of the apostate emperor and himself an apostate, exceedingly hostile to Christians. The martyrs were soldiers by profession, cruelly tortured because, for the sake of the Christian Labarum, they steadfastly refused to change it into a pagan standard. Finally, the name of one of them should be given not as Maximian but as Maximilian. It is enough to indicate these points briefly here. Meanwhile, see Tillemont, Volume VIII, pp. 406 and 739. The small Roman Martyrology treats on this day only of Anastasius: “At Salona, Anastasius the martyr.” Ado supplies a little more from the Acts of Saint Agapitus, where he is called a *cornicularius*, a military officer. Usuard copied no more than what we presented in the entry, retaining the earlier change and the change mentioned above in the names Aurelius and Aurelian. The additions will provide more from the aforesaid Ado. What was observed on the preceding day concerning Porphyry recurs here exactly with Anastasius: in the cited readings of Venantius, the same *cornicularius* whom Ado reports here is placed among those converted by Venantius’s astonishing steadfastness, and he is placed in the modern Roman Martyrology on 11 May. We shall say more in the Acts, where Anastasius of Salona must doubtless be distinguished from this *cornicularius*, and from the Hieronymian entries to be placed on 26 August, on which day the Acts cited by Tillemont, Volume V, p. 148, assert that he was crowned. It is again perfectly clear here that everything we have recited is Adonian and Usuardine.]

[Note: [Col. 0385A]

ROSWEYD adds to the pure text:

> “In Spain, Saint Julian the martyr with four others.”

The manuscripts vary.

PULSANEN, also pure in the text, adds at the end:

> “On the same day, the consecration of the altar of blessed Andrew the apostle.”

ANTWERP and MAX.–LÜBECK add:

> “Also, Quadratus the bishop.”

See the Roman Martyrology and Baronius’s relevant note.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC, pure in the first and second sections, construct the third from Ado as follows:

> “In the city of Salona, Saint Anastasius the martyr. When he was a soldier and saw Saint Agapitus confessing Christ bravely amid torments, he cried out: ‘The God of the Christians is great, and there is no other besides him.’ When the governor reported this to the emperor Aurelian, Anastasius was killed by the emperor’s command.”

Then at the end:

> “Also, Saint Quadratus the bishop.”

CENTULEN:

> “In the territory of the city of Gabali, Saint Privatus, bishop and martyr, who suffered under Gallienus. On the same day, the holy martyrs Bonosus and Maximian.”

BRUSSELS, not unlike ANTWERP–MAXIMUM and the other codices in the first three announcements, adds:

> “And in Spain, the feast of the holy martyrs Julius and Julian. And Saint Quadratus the bishop. And blessed Florus, abbot, disciple of Saint Maurus, abbot.”

HAGENOYEN:

> “In the city of Gabali, in its territory, the passion of Saint Privatus, etc.,”

as in the text.

> “Also, Saint Quadratus the bishop.”

It is pure in Bonosus and Maximian. Concerning Anastasius, it is nearly as above from ANTWERP–MAXIMUM and so forth. Finally:

> “At Rome, Saint Antonius the martyr, who, when he openly confessed himself a Christian, was condemned to death by the judge Vitellius and buried on the Via Aurelia.”

See the following day.

AQUICINCT. at the end:

> “Also, Saint Quadratus the bishop.”

See what was said above.

MATRIC.–CARTHUS.–UTRECHT:

> “Privatus, bishop and martyr. Bonosus and Maximian, martyrs. Anastasius, martyr.”

VATICAN, no. 5949, adds:

> “The feast of Saints Valentius and Leontius in the Church of Holy Wisdom. In Spain, Saints Julius, Julian, Vincentius, Augurius, and Fructuosus. In Sardinia, Saint Quadratus the bishop.”

In the others the deposition is absent.]

[Col. 0386A] UGHELLI:

> “Also, Quadratus the bishop.”

The same entry recurs frequently; see above.

FLORENCE:

> “In Sardinia, in the city of Cagliari, the passion of the holy martyrs Ruso­rius [MEDICI: Ruxorius], Casellus, and Camerinus, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, while Dalasius was presiding over the tribunal.”

STROZZI adds:

> “They suffered for Christ. The head of Saint Rusorius was afterward transferred from there to Florence and placed in the Church of All Saints.”

See also the martyrdom and the names of the places as more accurately expressed in the Roman Martyrology. Cardinal Aguirre, in Papebroch’s *Responsiones*, article 18, no. 42, will indicate how highly the material scraped together by Tamayo on this day concerning Luxorius and Camerinus should be valued.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION:

> “In the territory of the city of Gabali, in the district of Minacum, the passion, etc.”

It then gives the entry for Anastasius as in ANTWERP–MAXIMUM and the others above. The entry for Bonosus and Maximian is pure. Finally:

> “On the same day, Saint Quadratus, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0386B] BELIN begins:

> “The feast of the holy martyrs Luxorius, Cesellus, and Camerinus.”

If this was taken from FLORENCE, the names appear to have been polished. The entry for Privatus is sufficiently pure. It continues:

> “On the same day, the holy martyrs Bonosus, Maximus, and Maximian, whose deeds, etc.”

The entry for Anastasius is pure; at the end it adds:

> “Also, Quadratus the bishop.”

GREVEN:

> “Julian and four other martyrs. Also, the holy martyrs Luxorius, Cisellus, and Camerinus. Quadratus, bishop and confessor. In Alexandria, Contes, a nobleman. Cyriaca, a Roman matron and martyr, resting in Upper Wesel.”

MOLAN copied the entry for Luxorius and his companions from BELIN or GREVEN. Then:

> “Also, Quadratus the bishop.”

In smaller type:

> “Cyriaca, a Roman matron and martyr, resting in Upper Wesel among the Carmelites, concerning whom see the passion of blessed Lawrence.”

Later editions, following BELIN more closely, place before the text in different type:

> “The feast of the holy martyrs Luxorius, Cisellus, and Camerinus.”

At the end, concerning Quadratus, as in the first edition. Then:

> “And Saint Bassa the martyr. At Rome, in the Veranian district, Saint Cyriaca the martyr, who, having been translated to Wesel, rests there.”

Concerning Cyriaca and Bassa, see the Roman Martyrology, where the eulogies of both are found.]

[Col. 0383]

In the territory of the city of Gabali, the passion of Saint Privatus, bishop and martyr, who suffered in the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus. On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Bonosus and Maximian, whose deeds are preserved. And in the city of Salona, Saint Anastasius the martyr, who was killed for confessing the name of Christ by order of the emperor Aurelius.

XI Kalends. Day 22. [Note: [Col. 0385]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0385D]

In Greven it is “of Ostia”; in Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, “Ostian.” In Herinien and Antwerp-Major, “of Timothy.” Likewise in those two and in Rosweyd, “third.” After *caesus* (“struck”), Antwerp-Major omitted the particle *et*. Most noteworthy is that Greven and Molan added to *praefecto* (“governor”) the name Tarquinius, as do the more recent codices; but that Usuard omitted it appears certain. Herinien has *adtractatus* for *attrectatus*, and Antwerp-Major, worse, *attractus*. All write *Augustuduni* or *Augustuduno*. Munerat and Molan have *Symphoriani*; the others simply follow the text. [Col. 0386D] Again the old codices agree on *Aurelii*, although Ado gives *Aureliani*. Note that Munerat, after *Symphoriani*, adds *martyris* (“of the martyr”). Here he also writes *Marcialis*, together with Antwerp-Major and Greven; likewise *Epictei*, with the same Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd; Greven reads *Epiceti*. I have spoken elsewhere concerning *Dampnatus*. Rosweyd places *est* later; Antwerp-Major moves it to the end. Greven and Molan vary the wording somewhat at the beginning: “when he openly confessed himself a Christian.” Moreover, Molan writes *Anthonini* instead of *Antonii*.]

[Note: [Col. 0387A]

The present entry is composed entirely from Ado’s words, preserving the order of the announcements; nevertheless, its first source may be traced farther back. To begin with the first: the commemoration of the very illustrious martyr Timothy was inserted with remarkable agreement into the ancient calendars—the Bucherian, Carthaginian, Allatian, and Frontonian—as well as into the Sacramentary of Gregory and all the Martyrologies. The Hieronymian Martyrologies therefore celebrate him, but with the title “disciple of the apostle Paul”; Florentinius examines and explains this confusion in his Notes, although the matter is full of uncertainty. Bede, Rabanus, the small Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Wandalbert speak more clearly. The first to compose an eulogy for him was the aforementioned Bede; Rabanus copied it, Ado shortened it moderately, and from Ado Our Author elegantly condensed it, as the text above shows. I do not here debate the authority on which the history of this Timothy rests. Since both Bede and Ado admit that it was taken from the Acts of Saint Sylvester, the learned reader will easily judge its truth, while preserving the integrity of the most ancient and renowned cult—provided, of course, that both the calendars and the Martyrologies record the same Timothy who is mentioned in the Acts of Saint Sylvester. I confess that I have not yet been able to see this clearly enough. On this day Baronius noted many things concerning Timothy, but they do not touch our present difficulty. Tillemont briefly samples some of the material in Volume II, p. 618; many more matters will have to be examined in the Acts. As our task here requires, we append Wandalbert’s verses, which embrace this and the following announcement:

> “The eleventh day honors Timothy, who suffered at Rome,
>
> and the people celebrate their Aeduan Symphorian,
>
> whom his mother dedicated to Christ, destined likewise to die.”

The memory of the aforementioned Symphorian of Autun is no less illustrious and supported by more certain Acts. Although it is not marked in the ancient calendars, it is nevertheless both very well known and widely celebrated throughout Gaul. The Hieronymian codices mention him, as do Bede and, in exactly the same words, Rabanus. Florus adds a brief eulogy, specifying the time under the emperor Aurelian and the consul Heraclius. Ado preserves the same details, doubtless taken from the Acts published by Mombritius and Surius and approved by Baronius. The Acts themselves exist among our manuscripts; Ruinart, editor of the *Selecta* and restorer of their original purity, rejects the stated chronological details from p. 69 onward and thinks that *Aurelii* should be written instead of *Aureliani*, as Our Author has done more than once, abandoning Ado’s reading, although he copied all the rest from Ado exactly. Which chronological reckoning should be preferred is not for this place to determine. Tillemont may be consulted in Volume III, p. 43 onward, but especially p. 609, where he discusses those chronological details at length. See also the Mass sent in the Gothic or Gallican Missal, in Thomasius, p. 371.

The “foreign martyrs”—whether they truly are the persons named here—is made doubtful by the Hieronymian copies, which Florentinius attempts to reconcile. The small Roman Martyrology says:

> “And of the foreign martyrs, Martial, Epictetus, Saturninus, with their companions.”

Ado added Apris and Felix, prefacing the location from the Hieronymian Martyrology, in which other names are also listed more confusedly. Their index will more appropriately be arranged in the Acts. Usuard copied his announcement word for word from Ado. Antonius the martyr, or Antoninus, is first mentioned by the author of the small Roman Martyrology; from there he passed into Ado, whose eulogy was composed from the Acts of Saint Eusebius. Our Author joined together its beginning and end and, as I said above, is entirely Adonian in all respects.]

[Note: [Col. 0387C]

PULSANEN begins:

> “The octave of the Most Blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary.”

The entry for Timothy is pure. In that for Symphorian it remains pure up to “of the emperor Aurelian.” Everything else is missing.

ANTWERP and MAX.–LÜBECK, sufficiently pure in the text, add:

> “And the octave of Saint Mary, Mother of God.”

The wording varies among the different codices.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, and LEYDEN place before the text:

> “The octave of the Assumption of Saint Mary.”

They read “the governor Tarquinius” and substitute *Anthonini* for *Antonii*.

ALBERGEN and DANIC resemble the preceding witnesses, but, before “in the Roman harbor,” they also insert:

> “Also, the feast of blessed Hippolytus the martyr.”

Usuard treats him on the following day.

LOUVAIN also begins with the octave of the Assumption, and so forth. The entry for Timothy is pure; it cuts short Symphorian’s eulogy. Again, the entry for the Portuenses is pure, but it omits Antonius’s eulogy.]

[Col. 0387D] CENTULEN:

> “The octave of the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, who, glorified by a heavenly message and made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, exalted above all by him who assumed flesh from her, is venerated forever as blessed. At Rome, Saint Timothy the martyr. At Autun, Saint Symphorian the martyr, in the time of the emperor Aurelian. Also at Rome, blessed Antonius the martyr. In the Roman harbor, the foreign martyrs Martial, Epictetus, Apris, and Felix with their companions.”

BRUSSELS:

> “The octave of the Assumption of blessed Mary, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

In blessed Timothy it reproduces Bede’s eulogy. In the other three entries it is sufficiently pure. At the end it adds:

> “In the city of Reims, the feast of fifty martyrs. And the translation of the bodies of Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor, Innocent the martyr, and Saint Peregrine, bishop and martyr, in the basilica of Saint Dionysius.”

HAGENOYEN begins with the octave of the Assumption and appends a history which I would prefer to see supported by greater authority. Then:

> “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the feast of blessed Timothy the martyr, who, during the persecution of Nero, was arrested by Tarquinius, prefect of the city, and weakened by prolonged imprisonment. When he refused to sacrifice to idols, he was beaten three times, subjected to the most severe punishments, and his wounds were sprinkled with hot lime. The martyr of God gave thanks to God. Then two angels said to him: ‘Look upward.’ He looked and saw a crown prepared for him in the Lord’s hand, and so he was beheaded. On the same day, Saint Apollinaris the martyr, who witnessed the glory of Saint Timothy and therefore had himself baptized; he was beheaded together with Timothy.”

The confusion is sufficiently obvious and needs no explanation from me. See the following day.

After “of the emperor,” concerning Symphorian, it reads:

> “Who in his youth was so grave in his conduct that he seemed to anticipate the life of the aged. When he refused to adore the statue of Venus, he was first beaten under the governor Heraclius, then handed over to prison, and finally punished by beheading. In the Roman harbor, the holy foreign martyrs Martial, Epictetus,”

and so forth, purely.

MATRIC.–CARTHUS.–UTRECHT:

> “The octave of the Assumption of blessed Mary. Timothy and Symphorian, martyrs.”

In the margin:

> “This Timothy is mentioned in the life of blessed Sylvester.”

Then:

> “Martial, confessor.”

Again, in the margin:

> “You will find Martial the confessor nowhere else.”

The text continues:

> “In the Roman harbor, the holy foreign martyrs Martial, Epictetus, and ten of their companions.”

These matters are expressed more clearly in the text.

SWEDISH REGISTER, no. 428:

> “On the same day, the translation of the bodies of the saints in the monastery of Saint Dionysius; namely, Peregrine, Patroclus, Innocent, and Hilary, bishop and confessor.”

FLORENCE:

> “Saint Andrew the deacon and minister of Saint Donatus of Scotland, bishop of Fiesole, whose body was honorably buried in the monastery of Saint Martin of Mensola [MEDICI: Lamensola] in the Florentine territory.”

SALERNO:

> “In Gaul, in the city of Autun, the feast of Saints Medard and Aemilian with their eight sons.”

REIMS, manuscript of Saint Timothy and Apollinaris:

> “At Reims, the passion of Saint Maurus the priest and fifty martyrs with him.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION:

> “The octave of the glorious Virgin Mary’s Assumption. At Rome, on the Ostian Way, in its cemetery, the feast of blessed Timothy the martyr, who came from Antioch to Rome in the time of Pope Melchiades and, after preaching there for a year and three months and converting many to the faith of Christ, was arrested … and was devoutly buried beside the apostle Paul by Pope Saint Melchiades and Saint Sylvester.”

Concerning Symphorian, after “he completed,” it adds:

> “When he was being led to the place of beheading, his mother, crying out from the wall, said: ‘Son, son, remember eternal life; look upward and behold him reigning in heaven. Your life is not being taken from you, but changed for the better.’ Strengthened by such exhortation, he was led to execution like a lamb, like a child in its innocence. After he was beheaded, he was honorably buried.”

The entry for the Portuenses is pure.

> “Also at Rome, Saint Antoninus the martyr and executioner. Who, when … At Xonis, a city of Gaul, fifty holy martyrs.”

I believe these are the same persons who are assigned above to Reims. See GREVEN.

BELIN exceeds the beginning and the end. It begins:

> “The octave of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary.”

At the end it adds:

> “Also at Rome, Saint Hippolytus the martyr.”

[Col. 0390A] GREVEN:

> “The octave of the Assumption of the glorious Mother of God and Virgin Mary. Maurus the priest and martyr and forty others [the earlier edition has sixty, but XLIX should be written]. At Xonis, a city of Gaul, fifty holy martyrs.”

MOLAN inserts into the text, in different type, from Ado concerning Timothy:

> “This is found written in the history of Saint Sylvester.”

Concerning Antonius, he copies almost the whole of Ado’s text. At the end:

> “The octave of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. At Rome, Saint Hippolytus the martyr. At Reims, a city of Gaul, blessed Maurus and fifty martyrs with him.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “At Montefalco, in the city of Bevagna, the deposition of blessed James of the Blanchoni, who, renowned for his life, conduct, and miracles, already worn out by old age, departed to heaven in 1301, his face, clothing, and hands sprinkled with blood flowing from an image of the Crucified. God has not yet permitted his body to see corruption, but it still preserves the Lord’s blood in its hand.”

The other editions are corrupted. In different type they preface the text with “The octave,” and so forth. Worse, the text gives, in second place:

> “In the harbor of the city of Rome, the holy Hippolytus,”

in Italian:

> “who is called Nonnus, and his companions. At Ostia, the feast of the holy Quiriacus and Archelaus,”

in Roman type. The rest is as in the earlier edition. At the end:

> “In Reims, a city of Gaul, the feast of Saint Maurus the martyr with his companions. He came from Rome to Reims with blessed Timothy, and after spreading the word of God there and baptizing Apollinaris with many others, he was beheaded by the governor Lampadius together with the holy companions whom he had baptized. On the twenty-second day, Saint Agathon the martyr.”

This comes from the customary Greek source.]

[Col. 0385]

At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the feast of blessed Timothy the martyr, who was arrested by the prefect of the city and weakened by prolonged imprisonment. When he refused to sacrifice to idols, he was beaten three times and subjected to the most severe punishments; finally, he was beheaded. On the same day, at Autun, Saint Symphorian, in the time of the emperor Aurelius, who, when he refused to sacrifice to idols, was first beaten, then handed over to custody, and finally completed his martyrdom by beheading. In the Roman harbor, the holy foreign martyrs Martial, Epictetus, Saturninus, Apris, and Felix with their companions. Also at Rome, Saint Antonius the martyr, who, when he openly confessed himself a Christian, was condemned to death by order of the judge Vitellius and buried on the Via Aurelia.

X Kalends. Day 23. [Note: [Col. 0389B]

Only Herinien, Munerat, Greven, and Molan are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0389C]

All write simply “Zachaeus,” except Molan. Munerat reads incorrectly: “the Church of Jerusalem shone most clearly.” Lycia, Aegea, Hippolytus, and so forth, as elsewhere. Most of the other errors in Munerat are scribal, such as *Neronis* for *Neonis*, *afflixii*, *Achillei*, *vero Deo digni*, *Apollinaris*, *Minervi*, and so forth, where the conjunction *et* (“and”) is absent. Contrary to the common reading of all the codices, Greven and Molan write not “with his sons” but “with eight others,” failing to notice that Eleazar is a feminine name, like Glyceria from *Glycerium*, Eustochia from *Eustochium*, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0391A]

On this day I find no remembrance of the Antiochene champions older than Ado’s Martyrology, nor did Usuard have any other source, since he drew his material from Ado without changing a syllable. We seek Ado’s source, but so far nothing has been discovered. The small Roman Martyrology mentions Zachaeus the bishop, perhaps from Rufinus, Book IV, chapter 5, but omits all the identifying features which Ado added and Usuard in turn transferred individually from him. Neither the small Roman Martyrology nor Ado says anything about the following group. In the more accurate Hieronymian copies only Claudius, Asterius, and Neon are named; we reported them above and do not doubt that they were taken from those sources. The form of their martyrdom must have come from the proconsular Acts, which were published long ago by Surius on this day, by Baronius under the year 285, no. 3 onward, and more recently by Ruinart. It is not sufficiently clear whether Rabanus saw those Acts in their complete and authentic form when he composed his eulogy, since he says not a word about the punishment of the cross, which Florus expressly asserts from the aforesaid Acts.

Nevertheless, I believe that the women Domnina—or, as others have it, Donuina—and Theonilla were taken by Rabanus from those Acts. Someone, with the text corrupted, thought they should be inserted into the Praten codex. This was pointed out to me by the exceptionally keen observer, the distinguished Castellanus, who noticed an erasure in that codex between “they were crowned” and “at Alexandria.” The erasure is exclusive at both ends; everything found in our text was inserted there with a knife and the material reported first in the Additions was written above it. I suspect that the corrector wished to follow the aforementioned Rabanus. In any case, the usual companions of the Praten codex, Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, agree with it; they too are excluded from the group of pure witnesses, and Aquincum may perhaps be similar, as I shall say below.

Concerning Lycia—or rather Cilicia—and the other controversies surrounding these martyrs, see Florentinius’s Notes and Ruinart’s *Sincera et Selecta*, p. 278 onward.]

[Col. 0392A]

The greater difficulty concerns the martyrs of Porto and Ostia, who are distinguished in the Hieronymian Martyrologies but joined and confused in the little Roman Martyrology in this fashion: “At Rome, Hippolytus, Quiriacus, and Archilaus.” Ado reads: “In Roman Porto.” Our author copied all of this. The identity and diversity of the several Hippolyti have been discussed more than once, especially under 30 January and 13 August, and much will remain to be examined elsewhere: namely, whether our Hippolytus is to be celebrated on the preceding day, or called Nonnus for purposes of distinction, and whether he alone suffered martyrdom in Roman Porto; whether two others suffered at Ostia; whether they were companions of yesterday’s foreign martyrs; and finally, whether this Hippolytus was a bishop—indeed that famous Hippolytus distinguished by his writings—and other questions of this kind, which must be treated more fully in their proper place. You will find the first beginnings of these inquiries in Baronius and Florentinius under this and other days. Tillemont carefully collected the deeds and writings of the great Hippolytus in volume III, beginning at page 238.

The remainder has already been stated sufficiently above, in accordance with the purpose of this work. The little Roman Martyrology wrote: “The bishop Theonas”; Ado supplied a brief eulogy, the first part of which our author excerpted. See our Patriarchal Chronology, no. 173 onward. Florus also discusses Timothy and Apollinaris, but Usuard considered that nothing in Ado’s wording needed alteration. Whether they belong to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Florentinius will say. See what Surius reports about them from Gregory of Tours. Longer Acts are not lacking, but they appear spurious; they also discuss Maurus and his companions, who were noted yesterday among the Additions. Consult Florentinius also concerning Minervius and Eleazarus.

The text of Usuard is to be sought nowhere other than in the Ado mentioned so often above; and from that source it may be concluded that everything was copied from it except one announcement, about which we have already said enough. Wandalbert’s verse does not belong here.]

[Note: [Col. 0391C]]

In the PRATENSIS, Castellanus transcribed for me, from the supposed autograph, the words found between “they were crowned” and “Alexandria,” with the abbreviations:

“At Aegea, a city in Lycia, the holy martyrs Claudius, Asterius, Neon, Domnina, and Theonilla, who were tortured with various punishments and put to death under the governor Lysias. In the harbor of the city of Rome, the holy Hippolytus, Quintus [Quiriacus], and Archilaus. On the same day, the blessed Zachaeus, who, fourth after James, most illustriously ruled the church of Jerusalem.”

[The reading “ruled” is supplied for *rex*, because of the restricted space; and in ANTUERP.-MAJOR it was copied exactly in this form.]

I have already said that ROSWEYD. agrees both in order and in sense. Concerning AQUICINCT., see somewhat below.

PULSANEN. is pure in the Antiochene entries and in the notice of Zachaeus; extracting something from the notice of Theonas, it reads:

“At Alexandria, the holy bishop Theonas, truly worthy of God.”

Everything else is lacking.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are pure in the text and add at the end:

“Also, Flavianus and Synodius, bishops.”

[Col. 0391D] See Castellanus’s notes.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECTIN., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERG., and DANIC. place at the beginning:

“The vigil of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.”

At the end they add:

“Also, Flavianus and Sydonius, bishops.”

All the rest are pure.

CENTULEN.:

“The feast of the holy martyrs Donatus, Restitutus, Valerianus, Fructuosa, and twelve others, who were crowned at Antioch. At Alexandria, the blessed bishop Theonas, venerable and truly worthy of God. On the same day, the holy bishop Zachaeus, who, fourth after James, ruled the church of Jerusalem. At Lyon in Gaul, the holy martyrs Minervius and Eleazarus with their eight sons. In the harbor of the city of Rome, the holy Hippolytus, Quiriacus, and Achilleus. At Rheims, the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris. At Aegea, a city in Lycia, [Col. 0392C] the holy Claudius, Asterius, and Neon, who were fastened to a cross after severe tortures.”

BRUXELLEN. reverses the order and begins:

“At the city of Rheims, the holy Timothy,”

and so forth. It is pure in the notices of Zachaeus and the Antiochene martyrs. Instead of *Theonae*, it writes *Theonis*, and at the end adds Ado’s words:

“Who nourished the blessed bishop and martyr Peter in all purity. At the city of Aegea in Lycia,”

and so forth. It is also pure in the notices of the martyrs of Porto, but again attaches Ado’s words to the final announcement:

“Whose bodies are buried in the place called Inscripta, which overlooks the city from the west.”

At the end:

“Also, Flavianus and Sydonius, bishops.”

HAGENOYEN. begins:

“The vigil of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.”

The text follows, with some alteration in the order of the announcements, but is otherwise sufficiently pure. At the end:

“On the same day, Saint Flavianus, bishop and confessor. Also Saint Sydonius, bishop.”

AQUICINCT. inserts after “Neon,” together with PRATEN.:

“Domnina and Theonilla, who were tortured with various punishments and put to death under the governor Lysias.”

[Col. 0392D] I have not found it recorded whether it also changed the order. At the end it adds:

“Also, Saints Flavianus and Sydonius, bishops.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

“The vigil of Claudius, Asterius, and Neon, brothers, martyrs and children, whom the judge had crucified through various tortures; and with them two women suffered, together with a little child. Eleazarus with his sons.”

UGHELLIAN. has at the end:

“Flavianus and Sidonius, bishops,”

as above in ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.

ALTEMPS.:

“In Scotland, Saint Ebba, abbess.”

She is commemorated on 25 August.

STROZZIAN.:

“On the same day, Saint Flavianus, bishop.”

It does not mention Sidonius.

[Col. 0393A]

CAUDIACEN.:

“At Caudiacum, the feast of Saint Ainandus and Saint Domninus the martyr.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition begins:

“The vigil of the blessed Bartholomew the Apostle.”

The text follows, somewhat altered in order and interpolated. At the end:

“At Autun, the blessed Flavianus and Sidonius, bishops and confessors. At Le Mans, the blessed Victor, bishop and confessor.”

Is this Victor the one commemorated on 1 September?

BELIN. is more or less pure in the first three entries; fourth, it has the notice of Timothy, and so forth. It then follows:

“Also, the vigil of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.”

Then it gives the notice of the people of Lyon in pure form.

“At Alexandria, Theonas, bishop.”

The first edition adds at the end only:

“On the same day, Saint Flavianus, bishop.”

But the second reads:

“On the same day, Saints Flavianus and Sydonius, bishops.”

Although on the preceding day it had discussed Saint Hippolytus, it adds here:

“In the harbor of the city of Rome, Saint Hippolytus, Quiriacus, and Achilaeus.”

GREVEN.:

“The vigil of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle. [Col. 0393B] Also, according to some, on this day, Adam, the first man. Justus and Abundius, martyrs. At Autun, Saints Flavianus and Sidonius, bishops and confessors. [Col. 0394A] At Le Mans, Victor, bishop and confessor, and Brumbertus, confessor. In the desert of Scetis, Theonas, abbot. At the city of Aegea, Saint Theonilla. Osanna, virgin. Ebba, virgin.”

MOLAN.:

“On the same day, Saint Flavianus, bishop, and Sidonius, bishop. On the same day, the blessed Fraubaldus, abbot and confessor. Also, the vigil of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.”

Then, in smaller type:

“This feast is celebrated in many places by observing a fast. Also, according to some, on this day Adam, the first man, who, although lifted up in pride and eating from the forbidden fruit, miserably destroyed himself and his offspring by afflicting and infecting them wholly with the stain of original sin, was nevertheless, through the second Adam, delivered from his offense and brought to possess the joys of eternal life, as the Catholic Church holds.”

This is as far as the first edition goes. In the others only the following are added:

“On the same day, Saint Flavianus, bishop of Autun. At Clermont, the feast of Saint Sidonius, bishop. At Le Mans, the blessed Fraubaldus, abbot and confessor. On the twenty-third day, Saint [Col. 0394B] Lupus, martyr. Also, the vigil of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle.”

Most of the other codices cited above also discussed this matter.]

[Col. 0389]

The feast of the holy martyrs Donatus, Restitutus, Valerianus, Fructuosa, and twelve others, who were crowned at Antioch with the glorious honor of confession. On the same day, the blessed bishop Zachaeus, who, fourth after James, most illustriously ruled the church of Jerusalem. At Aegea, a city in Lycia, the holy Claudius, Asterius, and Neon, who were fastened to a cross after bitter tortures. In the harbor of the city of Rome, the holy Hippolytus, Quiriacus, and Archilaus. At Alexandria, the holy bishop Theonas, venerable and truly worthy of God.

[Bouillart, with a different order and a few additions: “[lacuna] they were crowned; at Aegea, a city in Lycia, the holy martyrs Claudius, Asterius, Neon, [Note: [Col. 0389C] The Carolingian autograph differs greatly. Zachaeus, who appears here in fourth place, is placed second in the Dervensis codex. Claudius and his companions, who occupy second place in the Pratensis and third in the Dervensis. Finally, that Saint Claudius, who has four companions in the Pratensis, has only two in the Dervensis, namely Asterius and Neon. To correct all this, Usuard obliterated five whole lines in his own codex. I will not say that the same hand was responsible; it is enough to have repeated this a hundred times. Let us see what reasons moved Usuard to make the correction. As for the order in which he arranged those saints, I suppose Sollerius will not bring the author to trial. It is a trivial matter over which it would be foolish to linger in defense. Nor will the censor of the Pratensis codex deny that Domnina and Theonilla were rightly added to Claudius, Asterius, and Neon. We possess their complete and genuine proconsular Acts, in which those five martyrs are named individually as summoned to confess the faith and tortured; and at the end it is stated: ‘This passion took place in the city of Aegea, under the governor Lysias, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Augustus and Aristobulus.’ These words—‘who were fastened to a cross after bitter tortures’—were not in the Carolingian autograph, although Sollerius inserted them in his article on Usuard. The three martyrs Claudius, Asterius, and Neon are named without addition in the Dervensis codex. BOUILLART.] Domnina and Theonilla, who were tortured with various punishments and put to death under the governor Lysias. In the harbor of the city of Rome, Saint Hippolytus, Quiriacus, and Archilaus. On the same day, the blessed bishop Zachaeus, who, fourth after James, most illustriously ruled the church of Jerusalem. At Alexandria, the holy bishop Theonas, venerable and truly worthy of God.”]

Also, the feast of the holy Timothy and Apollinaris, who, having completed their martyrdom at the city of Rheims, merited the heavenly kingdoms. At Lyon in Gaul, the holy martyrs Minervius and Eleazarus with their eight sons.

IX Kal. Day 24. [Note: [Col. 0393B]

From the Pratensis, Herinien., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0393C]

All the codices write *Bartholomei*, except Molan. and perhaps the Pratensis. Numerous other scribal errors recur in the same way; I gather them here, such as *Lipparis*, *Cartaginem*, *Galieni*, *Rotomago*, and so forth. Munerat., instead of *denique post*—“finally, after”—wrote *deinde*, “then,” producing a construction no more correct; see the Observations and Additions concerning it. He likewise wrongly writes *Musa candida* instead of *Massa candida*. Herinien. transposed the words *salubriter saeculum despiciens*, “wisely despising the world.” It is uncertain what should be preferred: *episcopi honorem* or *episcopii honorem*, “the honor of a bishop” or “the honor of the episcopate.” The first form is written by Praten., Herinien., and Rosweyd.; the second by Munerat., Greven., Molan., and Antuerp.-Maj. The latter is more polished; the former seems to reflect the usage of its own age. We have therefore retained the former in the text. Greven. and Molan. place *sancti*, “saint,” before Patricius; the others omit the title.]

[Note: [Col. 0393C]

It is sufficiently established that the feast of Bartholomew the Apostle was formerly celebrated on various days, especially among the Greeks, and that even at the present time it is observed in the Church not everywhere on the same day. In Gregory’s Sacramentary it is placed on the twenty-fourth; in Allatius’s Calendar, on the twenty-fifth. The accounts circulated concerning his deeds are no less confused and uncertain, but they do not concern us here, nor do the matters recently debated concerning his translation.

The Hieronymian copies, moreover, assign Bartholomew’s feast in Persia to 13 June, and some of our codices discussed him there among the Additions. Today the same Hieronymian Martyrologies express the matter differently: “In India, Saint Bartholomew the Apostle,” words which are read on the following day in the most ancient Epternacensis. Whether one of these announcements should be understood as referring to a feast of translation may be seen in Florentinius under the cited days and under the Index of the Apostles. See also Baronius in his Notes.

In Bede one reads explicitly today: “In India, the feast of Bartholomew the Apostle.” Rabanus nearly follows him, interpreting the name and asserting that he was flayed alive by barbarians. The little Roman Martyrology places it thus: “Bartholomew the Apostle and Martyr.” Ado in his Martyrology is closer to Bede, but the brief eulogy that he arranged among the feasts of the Apostles our author copied almost in full from him.

How much value should be assigned to the encomia composed about Bartholomew—one of which Surius published—you will readily understand from Tillemont, volume I, beginning at page 387, and from the notes to which he refers, as well as from the other matters concerning the translations. What Castellanus observes in a brief note about the apostle’s true name had already been investigated more laboriously by others.

Wandalbert’s metrical eulogy is longer than usual; he joins Genesius, the apostle of the following day, to Bartholomew, together with Audoenus, about whom more below:

> Blessed Bartholomew adorns and holds the ninth day;  
>   
> Under whose teaching India learned the honor of God,  
>   
> Scarcely rescued from the mad rites of Hercules and Bacchus.  
>   
> Tradition says that, according to the varying fate of his tomb,  
>   
> He possesses temples in Aeolia, Lipara, and Benevento.  
>   
> Then Rome also shines with Genesius the martyr,  
>   
> And Rouen honors the pious Audoenus.

The Hieronymian codices perhaps mention Massa Candida, of Carthage—or rather of Utica—somewhat obscurely under 18 August, where Florentinius’s commentary may be read. It is likely that it was commemorated on the same day in the Carthaginian Calendar. On this day it was first recorded by the little Roman Martyrology in these words: “At Carthage, Massa Candida.” Ado, probably following Prudentius, increased the number of martyrs to three hundred; Baronius rightly argues for this number from Pontius the deacon, against others who infer from the sermons of Saint Augustine that it was smaller.

From what source Ado, the writer just mentioned, derived the kind of martyrdom and its other circumstances is not sufficiently clear to me. Usuard shortened his eulogy in such a way that he made the construction more difficult, using the adverb *denique*, “finally,” although nothing precedes to which it can properly refer. This was doubtless why some scribes returned to the source in order to speak more clearly, as the Additions show. Relevant here are Ruinart’s careful remarks about these martyrs in the *Selecta*, pages 199 and 518. See also Tillemont, volume IV, pages 175 and 640.

The burial of Audoenus at Rouen is prefixed to the Lucensis Hieronymian Martyrology. Florus preserves the same placement but more correctly writes *Audoeni*, with a brief eulogy. Mosander attributed it to Ado; Rosweyd removed it. Which is better is a problem; I certainly consider the eulogy, whatever its quality, to be Usuard’s own. We preserve several manuscript Lives of Audoenus, including one in verse. But it is not for this place to determine how far all of these differ from the Surian version. In due time they will be compared with what the editor of the history of the royal abbey of Saint Audoenus reports in book I, and with Cointius under various years from 634 to 683 and 687.

The Patricius added at the end gave some codices an opportunity to confuse him with the apostle of Ireland. In the Hieronymian additions he is called *Pectricius*, which Florentinius corrects. The Gauls pronounce the name *Parrize*, from which *Parrizius* would seem to follow by no inappropriate formation. Let these remarks be understood as made in passing and to be discussed in their proper place; for now it is enough that we have reproduced the true, simple, and genuine text of Usuard.]

[Note: [Col. 0395A]

The CODEX PRATENSIS, designated among us by the letter B, adds in the margin:

“At Cervidunum, Saint Eptadius, confessor.”

ANTUERP.-MAJ. is pure in the text up to the final announcement, which it expands as follows:

“In Ireland, Saint Patricius, abbot, and Gildardus, confessor. [Col. 0395B] This Patricius is said to have been the first Master of the Irish. But because he was unable to correct even them, he went into exile; he reached the monastery of Glastonbury, and there ended his life, distinguished by virtues, as his bones, dead though they are, seem even to this day to attest.”

The AQUICINCT codex has the same account, with only slightly better correction.

ROSWEYD.:

“In India, the blessed Bartholomew the Apostle, who, preaching the Gospel of Christ in that same province, first had his skin flayed from him alive by order of Astyages, and afterward was beheaded, thus completing his martyrdom. Whose,”

and so forth. In the Carthaginian notice it is pure; after “honor,” concerning Audoenus, it adds:

“After many notable miracles and after faithfully dispensing the talents entrusted to him, he entered into the joys of his Lord. In Britain, at the monastery of Glastonbury, the burial of Saint Patricius, abbot.”

PULSANEN. is deficient in the first entry and fairly pure in the second. Then:

“At the city of Rouen, Saint Audoenus, archbishop and confessor.”

The remainder is lacking, [Col. 0395C] as this codex is usually abbreviated.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC., while also fairly pure in the first entry, announce the second as follows:

“On the same day, at Carthage, the three hundred martyrs who suffered in the time of Valerian and Gallienus. For it is said that, among the other punishments then inflicted, the governor had a lime-kiln heated and burning coals with incense brought to its mouth, and said to the Christians: ‘Choose one of the two: either offer incense to Jupiter upon these coals, or be plunged into the lime.’ Then three hundred men, armed with faith, confessing with the utmost speed that Christ is the Son of God, threw themselves into the fire and were submerged amid the vapor of the powdered lime. Hence that white-clad host of the blessed deserved to be called Massa Candida—*massa* because of their number, *candida* because of their merit. At the city of Rouen, Saint Audoenus, bishop and confessor.”

MAX.-LUBEC. writes *Audo*. In all of them Patricius is absent.

CENTULEN., fairly pure in the first entry, continues:

“At Carthage, the three hundred holy martyrs, who, because they suffered unanimously and at one moment, are called Massa Candida. At the city of Rouen, the burial of Saint Audoenus, archbishop and confessor. In the territory of Nevers, Saints Patricius, abbot, and Gildardus, priest and confessor.”

See above, ANTUERP.-MAJ.

BRUXELLEN. inserts concerning Bartholomew:

“Who was flayed for the faith of Christ and afterward beheaded. Whose,”

and so forth. Concerning the Carthaginians:

“For after various punishments [lacuna] they were consumed; hence that army of the blessed is customarily called Massa Candida—*massa* because of the number, *candida* because of the merit.”

In the notice of Audoenus, which is fairly pure, it adds:

“And after he had ruled the church of Rouen for forty years, he happily departed to Christ at the age of ninety.”

It is silent about Patricius.

[Col. 0396A]

HAGENOYEN.:

“Bartholomew the Apostle, who is described as having been the only nobleman among all the other Apostles.”

I omit the rest of this kind. Its account of the three hundred Carthaginians is almost like that of ANTUERP. and the others. It says nothing about Audoenus or Patricius.

VICTORIN. and REGINAE SUEC., no. 130, add after “to be called”:

“In Gaul, in the city of Nevers, Saint Gildardus, priest and confessor. Also, in the same territory, Saint Patricius, abbot. In the territory of the city of Autun, at the monastery of Cervidunum, the burial of Saint Eptadius, priest and confessor.”

See the Additions under 16 April.

DAVERON.:

“At the city of Le Mans, Saint Rigomerus, priest and confessor.”

See the Acts under 17 January and Castellanus’s first two-month section.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

“Bartholomew the Apostle; the three hundred martyrs who, after various tortures, were thrown into a lime-kiln, whereby they deserved to be called Massa Candida. Audoenus, bishop and confessor of Rouen. The abbot Theodoricus, a man of admirable holiness.”

CISTERCIEN. S. Benigni:

“On the same day, the blessed Ursinus, martyr.”

I do not know which Ursinus is meant.

REG. SUEC., no. 428:

“At Nevers, Saints Gildardus and Patricius, confessors.”

[Col. 0396C]

CODEX D. LE MARE, designated A:

“On the same day, at Cervidunum, the feast of Saint Eptadius, confessor.”

In the VATICAN. codex, no. 5949, Audoenus and Patricius are absent. It adds:

“At Capua, the feast of Saint Rufinus, bishop and confessor.”

In the Roman Martyrology he is commemorated on 26 August.

REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.:

“In the territory of Nevers, Saints Patricius, abbot, and Gildardus, priest, confessors.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition resembles ROSWEYD. in the first entry and ANTUERP. and the others in the second. It omits Audoenus’s eulogy. It then continues:

“At Le Mans, the blessed Rigomerus, priest and confessor. In the territory of Nevers, the blessed Patricius, abbot, and Geldeldus, confessors. On the same day, the blessed Elizabeth, mother of the Lord’s precursor.”

More correctly, this belongs under the twenty-sixth.

BELIN., in everything like ANTUERP. and the others, adds at the end:

“At Livernis [for Nevers], Saint Patricius, abbot.”

The second edition adds:

“In the district of Le Mans, Saint Rigomarus, confessor, and the most blessed Tenestina, virgin.”

[Col. 0396D]

GREVEN.:

“Gildardus, otherwise Gildeldus, priest and confessor. Sandradus, abbot and first abbot of the monastery at Gladbach, confessor. The abbot Theodoricus. At Le Mans, the blessed Rigomerus, priest and confessor. On the island of Samum, Saints Gregory, Theodore, and Leo, confessors. When they were soldiers in the time of Constantius, they avoided the persecution of the Arians, served Christ with the utmost devotion on the island mentioned above, and rested there together. Domnina, martyr.”

This should have been placed yesterday.

“Engra, virgin and martyr, with others. At the monastery of Moalbodium, Ansoaldis, virgin. On the same day, Saint Elizabeth, widow, mother of the Lord’s precursor.”

MOLAN. After “preaching,” in the notice of Bartholomew, inserts in different type:

“While still alive he was flayed by barbarians, and by order of King Astyages he was beheaded,”

and so forth. After “to be called,” it adds:

“In whose praises there are homilies of Saint Augustine, bishop.”

At the end:

“In the district of Le Mans, Saint Rigomarus, confessor.”

Others would say *Richmirus*. See DAVERON. The other editions have the same material in the text and likewise add the notice of Rigomerus at the end. Then:

“In the diocese of Gladbach in the province of Cologne, Saint Sanderadus, first abbot of that monastery. On the twenty-fourth day, Saint Eutyches, hieromartyr, disciple of Saint John the Theologian.”

Then, in smaller type:

“At the monastery of Andain, the abbot Theodoricus died in the year 1085. Living and dead, he was renowned for many signs and virtues. His body, taken from the earth, was reduced to ashes and embers by the savagery of the Huguenots.”

See Castellanus.]

[Col. 0393]

The feast of the blessed Bartholomew the Apostle, who, preaching the Gospel of Christ in India, completed his martyrdom by decapitation. The most sacred body of this Apostle, first translated to the island of Lipara and afterward to Benevento, is honored by the pious veneration of the faithful. On the same day, at Carthage, the three hundred martyrs who suffered in the time of Valerian and Gallienus; finally, after the punishments inflicted upon them, they confessed Christ, the Son of God, as God, and were plunged into a burning lime-kiln. Hence that white-clad host of the blessed also deserved to be called Massa Candida. At the city of Rouen, Saint Audoenus, confessor, who wisely despised the world and, by the merit of his holiness, attained the dignity of the episcopate. At Nevers, Patricius, abbot.

VIII Kal. Day 25. [Note: [Col. 0397A]

Only four are pure throughout: Praten., Antuerp.-Major, Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0397B]

Apart from the orthographic errors with which Antuerp.-Maj. generally abounds—such as *Potentiani*, *eculeo*, *distensi*; the omission of *sunt* after *caesi*; the omission of *etiam* after *lampadibus*; *michi*, *Aretensis*, *impii* instead of *impia*, and *Christiana* instead of *Christiani*, and so forth—and apart from the word *milies*, which all have except Greven., two matters should be noted.

First, Greven. and Molan. immediately append after *occidar*—“I am killed”—the words *ipsum mihi de corde auferre*, “to take him from my heart,” and so forth, omitting the preceding words, *ipsum mihi de ore*, “from my mouth.”

Second, Praten. and Rosweyd. read *Civitate Italica*, “at the city of Italica”; Antuerp.-Major has the equivalent *In civitate Italica*, “in the city of Italica.” Greven. and Molan., however, have *In Hispaniis civitate Italica*, “in Spain, at the city of Italica.” Finally, Herinien. and Munerat., whose text is pure, have *In Hispania civitate Italica*, “in Spain, at the city of Italica.” We have preferred this form, though we do not consider the others wholly incompatible with the surrounding phrasing.]

[Note: [Col. 0397C]

The little Roman Martyrology places today’s section third:

“At Rome, the four martyrs Eusebius, Pontianus, Peregrinus, and Vincentius.”

They are likewise placed in this order by Ado, who adds an abridgment of their Acts, published more than once by Surius and others. Our author reduced it not inelegantly to his usual brevity, giving them first place in the column and transposing the last two names.

It seems certain that earlier martyrologists do not discuss them; Florentinius himself admits that Pontianus was added separately from the others to the Lucensis codex by local people. I do not yet dare to determine what judgment should be made concerning these Acts. Tillemont found some matters in them, volume III, page 59, that are displeasing, including the section concerning Julius the Senator, mentioned above under 19 August. But these matters must be discussed elsewhere.

Genesius, the most illustrious martyr who had been a mime, is placed by Allatius’s Calendar and by the Hieronymian Martyrologies under 24 August. Florus does likewise, calling him a soldier in his eulogy drawn from the Acts. Finally, Wandalbert also places him there, as we showed yesterday. The little Roman Martyrology expresses the matter more explicitly today:

“At Rome, Genesius, martyr and mime.”

He was a teacher of the theatrical art, that is, of the stage. He also appears in the Calendar of Fronto and probably in the Carthaginian Calendar. Acts that are truly remarkable exist in various copies, most recently published by Ruinart beginning at page 282. From them it is clear that Ado had sincere and genuine Acts before him when he inserted them almost intact into his Martyrology. Usuard was content to select the principal points from Ado, though he expanded them somewhat more than usual; Rabanus extracted a few details from the aforementioned Acts rather dully. The Acts cited above may also be seen in the French edition by Tillemont, volume IV, beginning at page 418.

A second Genesius follows, the one of Arles, whom some have wrongly confused with the former, as Florentinius explains in his notes on the Hieronymian Martyrologies, where he is recorded on this day, as also by Florus, who merely hints that he was baptized in his own blood. The little Roman Martyrology simply reads:

“And Saint Genesius of Arles.”

Ado drew several details from the beautiful Acts, also reproduced by Ruinart in the *Selecta*, beginning at page 601; our author summarized the substance of the entire matter in fewer words. One may consult Prudentius’s hymn in the Ruinart volume cited above, page 517, and Gregory of Tours, *Miracles*, chapter 68. If desired, see also Tillemont, volume V, beginning at page 569. The single verse of Wandalbert concerning this Genesius is also worth noting:

> From this point Arles, on the eighth day, celebrates you, holy Genesius.

Gerontius, or Geruntius, is unknown to all the earlier martyrologists, and I do not sufficiently discern where Usuard could have obtained him, unless he learned something about him during his journey in Spain and subsequently judged it worthy of a place in the sacred Calendars. He nowhere suggests that Gerontius lived or preached in the time of the Apostles. It must therefore have been added by the reformers of the Roman Martyrology on the basis of other documents; for the matter, one may provisionally consult Baronius’s note. We have shown that all the preceding material was copied from Ado, but our codices altogether establish that this final announcement is also entirely Usuard’s.]

[Note: [Col. 0399A]

HERINIEN., extremely pure throughout the text, adds at the end:

“In the district of Vermandois, the feast of Saint Hunegundis, virgin.”

ROSWEYD., somewhat corrupted in the text, inserts after “received,” in the notice of Genesius of Arles:

“And where his blood fell, a great sycamore tree grew.”

At the end it adds:

“Also, the feast of the blessed Gregory, abbot, bishop and confessor of the people of Utrecht.”

Castellanus’s note is mistaken here.

PULSANEN. has the notice of Bartholomew fairly purely on this day. It then gives the notice of Eusebius and so forth up to “under the emperor Commodus.” Everything else is lacking.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN., instead of Gerontius, have:

“In the province of Syria, Saint Julianus, martyr.”

The preceding material is pure.

MUNERAT., fairly pure throughout the text, adds at the end:

“Also, the burial of the blessed Louis, most illustrious and glorious king of the Franks, whose body rests in the monastery of Saint Denis in France, while his head is honored and venerated in the most holy chapel of the palace.”

This phrasing is peculiar to it.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN. would be pure throughout if they did not omit the final announcement, in place of which they substitute:

“In the province of Syria, the feast of Saint Julianus, martyr. Also, the feast of Saint Louis, confessor and king of France. On the same day, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor of Utrecht. In the district of Vermandois, the feast of Saint Hunegundis, precious virgin of Christ.”

LOVANIEN. has the same omission and the same Additions, but abridges some of the eulogies.

ALBERGEN. begins:

“The feast of Saint Louis, king and confessor.”

It also lacks the final announcement about Gerontius, in whose place it gives only:

“In the province of Syria, Saint Julianus, and so forth.”

DANIC. differs from the preceding only in inserting second:

“At Paris, at Saint Denis, the blessed Louis, king and confessor.”

CENTULEN.:

“At Rome, the holy Eusebius, Pontianus, [Col. 0399C] Peregrinus, and Vincentius, in the time of the emperor Commodus, under the judge Vitellius. Also at Rome, Saint Genesius, martyr, who suffered under Diocletian. On the same day, Saint Genesius of Arles, who was struck with a sword and died on the bank of the Rhône. In the territory of Vermandois, Saint Hunegundis, virgin of Christ. In Spain, at the city of Complutum, the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor”—another hand adds, “brothers.” See above, under 6 August. “At the city of Italica, Saint Gerontius, bishop, resting in prison. In France, Saint Louis, king of the Franks and most glorious confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. begins with Genesius of Arles, whose notice is somewhat interpolated. It continues:

“At Rome, the feast of Saint Genesius, soldier and martyr. When the emperor Diocletian wished to turn him back from the faith, he stood firm, saying: ‘There is no king except Christ; for whom, if I am killed a thousand times, you will not be able to take him from my [lacuna].’ And when the emperor achieved nothing, he ordered him to be beheaded after the rods, the rack, the hooks, and the torches.”

It is pure in Eusebius and his companions.

“In Spain, at the city of Italica, Saint Gereon, bishop, resting in prison.”

The notices of Julianus and Hunegundis are as above.

“On the same day, the burial of Saint Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, whom Pope Boniface VIII enrolled in the catalogue of the saints.”

HAGENOYEN., pure in the first class, continues:
