“Also at Rome, Saint Genesius, soldier and martyr, in the time of Diocletian Augustus. In his youth he so mocked the Christians that he eagerly examined all the sacraments of the Church, writing the divine mysteries in a book and proposing the same as a joke to his companions. Finally, having been wonderfully converted to the Lord, first with clubs,”

and so forth, fairly purely. It then gives Julianus as above. Finally:

“In Spain, at the city of Italica, Saint Gerontius,”

and so forth. The announcement of Genesius of Arles is absent.

[Col. 0400A]

AQUICINCT. begins:

“At Humularia, the feast of Saint Hunegundis, virgin.”

At the end:

“In the district of Limoges, Saint Aredius, abbot.”

Then, in a much later hand:

“On the same day, at Paris, the translation of the blessed Louis, confessor.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., manuscript no. 130, have at the end:

“On the same day, the blessed Aredius, abbot.”

See the Observations under the following day.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

“Louis, king of the Franks; Gregory, the third bishop of Utrecht, noble by birth, who succeeded Saint Boniface and was instructed by his teaching; his body is in the church of the Holy Savior.”

BIGOTIAN., under the note numbered P. 5:

“In the province of Syria, Saint Julianus, martyr.”

REG. SUEC., designated no. 428:

“At Carthage, the burial of the blessed Louis, king of France, glorious in holiness and merits.”

Here the placement is marked more correctly.

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, designated C.:

“In the district of Limoges, Saint Arethius, abbot.”

[Col. 0400B]

In the VATICAN. codex, no. 5949, Gerontius is absent. I do not know whether the rest is pure.

ALTEMPS.:

“On the same day, Saint Hilda, virgin.”

Others place her under 17 November.

STROZZIAN.:

“Saint Louis, king. [lacuna] Saint Nemesius. [lacuna] His sacred relics lie translated in the monastery of Saint Mary of the Angels.”

Perhaps *Genesius* should be read, as in BELIN. Yet some Nemesius is also commemorated on this day. Others, including FLORENTINI, have:

“At Rome, Saint Lucius, pope and martyr.”

BIZUNTICEN. adds after the first announcement:

“Of these, Vincentius and Peregrinus were transferred to Gaul in the time of Pope Nicholas by Count Gerard and decently buried in the territory of Langres, in the monastery of Saint Peter called Pulterae. Note: in the Chronicle of Auxerre, under the year 865, it is said: ‘The body of Saint Eusebius was deposited at Pulteriacum, but the body of Saint Pontianus at Vercelliacum.’”

More about these matters will be given in its proper place.

[Col. 0400C]

The LUBECO-COL. edition:

“At Cologne in Lower Germany, the translation of the arm of the blessed Anno, archbishop and confessor of that city, from Mount Siberg to the church of Saint George the Martyr.”

It has a long eulogy of Louis, which we shall give more briefly under GREVEN. In Eusebius and his companions, and likewise in Genesius of Rome, it is moderately interpolated; in Genesius of Arles, it is pure. It writes:

“Gerontius, bishop and confessor.”

Concerning Gregory it adds:

“He sent the blessed Lebuinus, priest of the Lord, to Deventer.”

On the same day, Saints Aredius, abbot, and Justinus, priest and confessor. In Denmark, in the church of Roskilde, the translation of Saint Lucius, pope and martyr. At Rome, the passion of the blessed martyrs Nemesius, deacon, and Lucilla, his daughter, who were beheaded under Valerian and Gallienus. Also, the translation of Saint Adalbertus, bishop and martyr.”

BELIN begins: “At Rome, Saint Lucius, pope and martyr.” In the entry for Eusebius and his companions he is exact. Then: “Likewise at Rome, Saint Nemesius,” in place of “Genesius,” etc. [Col. 0400D] In the Arelatensian edition he is sufficiently accurate. “In the province of Styria,” instead of Syria, etc. In Gerontius he is accurate. At the end: “Likewise at Paris, Saint Louis, confessor and king of France.” A second edition adds: “In the district of Limoges, Saint Aredius, confessor.”

GREVEN: “In Syria, Saint Julian, martyr. At Rome, the passion of Saints Nemesius the deacon and Lucilla his daughter, whom Usuardus has on the day before the Kalends of November, namely the day on which their bodies were raised by Saint Sixtus. The five martyr brothers, namely Benedict, John, Matthew, Isaac, and Christina.” Of Gregory, almost as in the LUBECK–COLOGNE edition. “Of Turibius and Gundanisola, bishops and confessors of Le Mans. According to others, however, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August. Likewise, according to the Catalogue of the Saints, here [is commemorated] Titus, bishop of Crete, whom Usuardus has on the day before the Nones of January. At the city of Agde, Saint Severus, abbot, who, born of the royal race of the Syrians, despising great riches, devoted himself to the strictest way of life near the aforesaid city. Afterwards made father of many monks, full of holiness, he rested in the Lord in a blessed end. Aredius, abbot, and Justin, priest and confessor. Louis, king of France and confessor, a man of great holiness. When his mother Blanche repeatedly told him that she would rather see him incur temporal death than offend the Creator through any mortal sin, her words adhered so firmly to the heart of her pious son that he is said never to have committed a mortal sin. Finally, after many works of piety, when he was already preparing a second expedition in aid of the Holy Land, he was called by the Lord during the journey itself and entered the land of heavenly promise. The translation of the head of blessed Lucius, pope and martyr, from the city of Rome to Dacia, to the church at Roskilde.” Concerning the translation of Saint Adalbert, and likewise of the arm of Saint Anno, [he has] as in the LUBECK–COLOGNE edition. Of Hunegundis, as in HERINIENSIS above.

MOLAN inserted Adon’s encomium of Genesius into the text in different type. At the end: “At Rome, Lucius, pope and [Col. 0402A] martyr.” Of Julian, as above. Of Saint Louis, as in MUNERATUS, to which he adds: “God bearing witness to his precious death through frequent miracles, Lord Boniface VIII, with the solemnity of his brethren and clergy, enrolled this saint in the catalogue of the saints.” Of Hunegundis, as in ANTUERP–MAX., etc. Of Aredius, as above. Of Gregory he adds: “Who was the teacher of Saint Ludger, bishop of Münster,” and, in smaller type, “the first [author] who wrote the Life of that same Gregory. Of Hilda, abbess of the monastery of Scruwelhalt, whose feast in the city of Lübeck is held in the highest renown by the makers of rosaries.” Other editions have the same material in the text concerning Julian, Louis, Hunegundis, Aredius, and Gregory as the first edition, except for what has been added in different type. Then: “On the twenty-fifth day, the return of the relic, Saint Bartholomew the apostle.” Finally, in smaller type: “On the same day there was a fire in the town of Deutz, in which the Lord’s body remained untouched amid the surrounding flames.”

[Col. 0397]

At Rome, the feast of Saints Eusebius, Pontianus, Vincentius, and Peregrinus, martyrs, under the emperor Commodus. They were first raised upon the rack, stretched with cords as well, and then beaten with clubs, while flames were applied around their sides; but because they remained most faithful in praising Christ, they were put to death with lead-weighted scourges until they gave up the spirit. Likewise at Rome, Saint Genesius, martyr, in the time of the emperor Diocletian. First beaten most cruelly with clubs, then hung upon the rack and tormented by the prolonged tearing of hooks, and also burned with lamps, he persisted in the faith, saying: “There is no king besides Christ. Even if I am killed a thousand times for him, you will not be able to take him from my mouth, nor from my heart.” He earned the crown of martyrdom by decapitation. On the same day, blessed Genesius of Arles, who served as a court clerk; when he refused to record the impious edicts by which Christians were ordered to be punished, he was arrested and beheaded, and received the glory of martyrdom, baptized in his own blood. In Spain [Note: [Col. 0397B] The Dervensis codex has: “in the Spanish city of Italica.” Usuardus deleted “in Spain” in his own codex. Who could say why? Perhaps because, when speaking of a sufficiently well-known city, he judged it unnecessary to name the region in which it was situated? There is nothing concerning Saint Geruntius in the martyrologies earlier than Usuardus. Without doubt he learned of his cult in Spain. The oldest account preserved concerning this Geruntius is an epigram of Isidore of Seville [Col. 0398B], which John Tamayus Salazar read in a handwritten copy and incorporated into his Spanish martyrology. In that epigram Geruntius is said to have suffered the punishments of prison and hunger under Nero. From this Salazar concludes that he suffered around the year 68, when Nero’s cruelty was raging more fiercely in Spain. BOUILLART.] in the city of Italica, Saint Gerontius, bishop, who rests in prison.

**Seventh day before the Kalends. Day 26.** [Note: [Col. 0401]

The Antwerp and Maximum–Lübeck editions, Muneratus, Greven, and Molan are exact.]

[Note: [Col. 0401B]

I read Zephyrinus plainly, in agreement with nearly all the codices. Likewise I read Irenaeus, although HERINIENSIS has Hereneus; MUNERATUS, Hyreneus; more correctly MOLAN, Irenaeus. ANTWERP and MAXIMUM–LÜBECK write Abundius incorrectly, and GREVEN’s Habundius is no better. I do not know why MUNERATUS altered the text, reading “in the passion of blessed Hippolytus” instead of “in the passion of blessed Lawrence.” In the first edition of MUNERATUS, moreover, after “commander from the legion,” *saints* is lacking. Pergamis may be questioned; for it some, together with ANTWERP and MAXIMUM–LÜBECK, substitute Bergamis. We, however, prefer the common spelling of the codices, perhaps more agreeable to popular usage. ANTWERP and MAXIMUM–LÜBECK have “who was also one of them,” where *he himself* is lacking. On the other hand, in this same announcement they redundantly have *saints* before *of Thebes*. I have written this word plainly, in agreement with the codices. Enough has been said elsewhere about *abscisione*; MUNERATUS substitutes *obtruncatione*. Most have Autissiodoro; GREVEN and MOLAN have Autissiodori, and Antissiodori. The same editions also write Eleutheri and Eleutherii; the rest use the simpler form, although it is worse in relation to the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0401C]

The entire text, except for the final announcement alone, was derived from the little Roman Martyrology into Ado, and thence into Usuardus, with only this difference: that one of the Theban martyrs is preferred to the other. The Hieronymian Martyrologies say nothing of either of them on this day; they postponed Zephyrinus to 20 December, which Papebrochius considers, with greater probability, to be the true day of his death. Rabanus and Wandalbert follow the traces of the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Hence some rightly think that 26 August became more celebrated because of the translation or elevation of his body, and this opinion is also preferred by the aforementioned Papebrochius. He is commemorated on this day in the modern Roman Martyrology; see Baronio’s note there, together with what Tillemont has in volume III, beginning on page 236. What the bishop of Vienne adds to the little Roman Martyrology—namely, that Zephyrinus ruled the Church for eight years, seven months, and ten days—was prudently omitted by Usuardus, as he often does, perhaps because he regarded the calculation as suspect, since the chronological tables of the Roman pontiffs show that he occupied nearly twice that length of time. But these matters, and the deeds of Zephyrinus, will be treated more fully elsewhere. Bede is the first to speak of Irenaeus and Abundius; Rabanus copied his words, as elsewhere, correctly, I think, reading “to be killed in a sewer” instead of “to be thrown into a sewer.” The latter reading, however, was retained in the genuine edition of Bede by Henschenius and Papebrochius, and Ado also adopted it, taking his encomium word for word from Bede. Our author compressed the wording of both into fewer words. See the Acts of Saint Lawrence, repeatedly mentioned above. Wandalbert celebrates only these two in the following verse:

> Irenaeus and Abundius adorn the sevenfold [crown] by martyrdom.

In the little Roman Martyrology, Alexander is placed before Secundus among the Theban martyrs [Col. 0403A]; Usuardus followed Ado’s order. Of Secundus he copied the entire first part of Ado’s encomium, leaving the second untouched. The Viennese bishop composed a longer history of Alexander of Bergamo, from which Usuardus extracted a few items, presented in the short entry; these are sufficient to show that the whole text up to this point flows from Ado. The Acts of Saint Secundus are found in Mombritius, volume II, page 261 verso, where he is described as one of the Thebans. Ado could therefore at one time have taken his encomium from them. But why he counted Alexander among the Thebans I still do not know; for the Acts reported by that same Mombritius, volume I, page 24, do not contain a word from which Alexander might be judged to have been a Theban rather than a Roman. I do not examine how genuine these accounts are. For Tillemont, when discussing the Thebans in volume IV, page 431, it was enough to mention the names of both in the martyrologies. From elsewhere Usuardus added Eleutherius of Auxerre, mentioned by all our codices except three, which often disagree—namely the Pratensis, Antwerp Major, and Rosweyd codices—to which Aquicinctensis may be added, generally following the same line. At the end they write: “In the territory of Limoges, Saint Aredius, priest,” whom we have often mentioned among the supplementary entries on the preceding day. Castellanus observed, however, that the announcement of Eleutherius had been erased in the Pratensis codex, so that another was improperly inserted on this day, although it seems certainly to belong to 25 August. It is likely that Usuardus took Eleutherius from some fuller Hieronymian codex. Whatever the case may be, we have again excluded those discordant codices from the pure witnesses and followed the genuine and sincere reading of the others.]

[Note: [Col. 0403B]

Concerning the PRATENSIS and ANTWERP MAJOR editions we have already said enough in the notes.

ROSWEYD, in addition to the alteration mentioned above, inserts into the text concerning Irenaeus and Abundius: “Whom Valerian ordered to be thrown alive into a sewer.” This is taken from Bede’s encomium, with some correction.

PULSANENSIS is sufficiently accurate up to “who himself was one of the Theban legion.” There it stops.

ANTWERP MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC begin as follows: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of blessed Zephyrinus, pope and martyr. He was the fourteenth after blessed Peter to rule the Church, and, crowned with martyrdom, was buried in his own cemetery beside the cemetery of Callistus.” In the rest they are accurate.

CLUNIACENSIS: “At Rome, Saints Irenaeus and Abundius, martyrs, whom Valerian—or his prefect—caused to be killed alive in a sewer because they had raised the body of Concordia the martyr from the sewer. [Col. 0403C] At the fortress of Victimilium in Italy, Saint Secundus, martyr. In the city called Pergamis, Saint Alexander, martyr. In the city of Salona, Saint Anastasius, martyr.” See 21 August. “At Auxerre, Saint Eleutherius, bishop. In the year 1131 from the Lord’s incarnation, the church of Saint Richarius was burned, together with the entire village and nearly three hundred men and women of both sexes, on Wednesday, the seventh day before the Kalends of September.” It is clearly a local addition.

BRUSSELS begins: “At Rome, the feast of Saints Irenaeus and Abundius, martyrs. Valerian ordered them to be thrown into a sewer because they had raised the body of blessed Concordia from the sewer. And when their bodies had been raised, the priest Justin buried them in a crypt beside blessed Lawrence. Likewise at Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of blessed Zephyrinus, pope and martyr. He sat [as bishop] for nine years and decreed that the sacrifice should be celebrated in glass or tin vessels, whereas previously it had been celebrated in wooden ones. He also decreed that all Christians twelve years old should receive the Eucharist on Easter Day [Col. 0403D]. Likewise, the burial of Saint Anastasius, priest and martyr.” After “of the Thebans” in the entry for Secundus, it adds: “Who, before Saint Maurice and the others, after bonds and imprisonment, completed his martyrdom by decapitation. In the Italian city called Pergamus, Saint Alexander, martyr. He was one of the Theban legion; and when he most steadfastly confessed the name of the Lord, he was beheaded by order of Maximian.” All this has been expanded from Ado. At the end: “At Auxerre, Saint Eleutherius, bishop.”

HAGENOYEN tells other stories concerning Zephyrinus and likewise concerning Irenaeus and Abundius, which I do not wish to transcribe. In the rest it is sufficiently accurate.

AQUICINCTENSIS, after *pope*, adds: “He decreed that, with all the faithful clergy and laity present—that is, a deacon or priest, together with the priests standing by—Masses should be celebrated.” It lacks Eleutherius and substitutes Aredius [Col. 0404B], although on the preceding day it had dealt with Aredius of Limoges, the abbot.

VICTORINUS has at the end: “At Auxerre, Saint Eleutherius, bishop and confessor. In the city of Nevers, Saint Eulalius, bishop and confessor.”

MATRICENSIS–CARTHUSIANA–UTRECHT: “Alexander, martyr, of the Theban legion. Isaac and Maximian, martyrs. Anastasius, martyr.”

SWEDISH REGISTER, marked number 130: “In the city of Nevers, the feast of Saint Eulalius, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN, under number 5949: “At Benevento, the translation of Saint Mercury, martyr, from the fifteenth [place or day] to Saint Sophia.” I do not understand what this means. Something seems to be missing.

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Guthlaor, hermit.” Is this not Guthlac the hermit, who is commemorated on 11 April?

BURDEGALENSIS: “Saint Sulpicius, bishop and confessor.” I think this refers to the one commemorated on 17 January.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition: “At Cologne, the translation of certain relics of blessed Andrew, apostle and martyr, to his church [Col. 0404C]. At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of blessed Zephyrinus, pope and martyr. He was the fourteenth after blessed Peter to rule the Church for nine years, seven months, and ten days; and, crowned with martyrdom, he was buried in his own cemetery beside the cemetery of Callistus. He decreed,” etc., with the same material as in BRUSSELS. In Irenaeus and Abundius it is nearly exact. In Secundus it has what BRUSSELS has. In Alexander it additionally adds: “A certain matron named Greta [Grata] buried him in her own estate. At Auxerre, Saint Eleutherius, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN, after “pope” in the entry for Zephyrinus, adds “and martyr.” It renders the place-name of Secundus as follows: “At Viginti Milium.” Then: “Likewise in Cisalpine Gaul, in the city of Bergamo,” etc. It continues: “On the same day, the octave of Saint Louis, bishop and confessor. At Auxerre, blessed Eleutherius, bishop, worthy of God.”

[Col. 0404D] GREVEN: “At Carthage, Saints Isaac and Maximian, martyrs. Anastasius, martyr, and Asclepia, widow. Theodolus, bishop and confessor. Aurelius, priest. Maximian, confessor. Grata, holy matron, who buried blessed Alexander. At Cologne, the translation of certain relics of Saint Andrew, apostle.”

MOLAN: “Likewise, the translation of Saint Lambert, from the crypt to the altar of the Holy Cross.” Then, in smaller type: “Maximian, confessor. In the town of Ceresano in Spain, blessed Victor, martyr. He was granted the crown of martyrdom by the Moors and was numbered by Christ among the heavenly host; his feast is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of September in the diocese of Burgos.” Other editions, in italic type, insert “and martyr” into the text after “pope.” At the end, however: “In the town of Ceresano in Spain, blessed Victor, martyr, who was granted the crown of martyrdom by the Moors.” He is included in the Roman Martyrology.]

[Col. 0401]

At Rome, the feast of blessed Zephyrinus, pope, and of Saints Irenaeus and Abundius, martyrs, who are mentioned in the passion of blessed Lawrence. At the fortress of Victimilium in Italy, the feast of blessed Secundus, martyr, a distinguished man and commander from the legion of the holy Thebans. Likewise, in the city of Pergamis, Saint Alexander, who himself was also one of the Theban legion; and when he most steadfastly confessed the name of the Lord Jesus, he completed his martyrdom by decapitation. [Bouillart: ... completed it. [Note: [Col. 0401B] Saint Aredius is absent from the Carolingian autograph; in his place: “At Auxerre, Eleutherius, bishop.” Afterwards Usuardus erased Eleutherius from this place, having apparently read the Acts of that holy bishop, which record his death not on 26 but on 16 August. He is counted as the sixteenth bishop of the Church of Auxerre, and is said to have died in the year 551. If this is true, all the chronological notes used by the Anonymous author in the new Labbe Library, volume I, page 419, are false. As for Saint Aredius, Usuardus must have been misled by certain Acts of that saint [Col. 0402B] different from those made public by the chief glory of our Society, Mabillon, volume I of the Acts, page 349. For these say that on the ninth day before the Kalends of September Aredius summoned his disciples and warned them of his imminent death, and at the second hour of the night gave up his soul. If “the second hour of the night” means the second hour after midnight, Aredius died on the eighth day before the Kalends of September; but if it means merely the second hour after sunset, he died on the ninth day before the Kalends. Bernard Gui testifies in the Labbe Library, page 631, that the feast of Saint Aredius is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. BOUILLART.] In the territory of Limoges, Saint Aredius, priest and confessor. At Auxerre, Eleutherius, bishop.

**Sixth day before the Kalends. Day 27.** [Note: [Col. 0405]

Thus have the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Maximum–Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molan editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0405A]

HERINIENSIS incorrectly wrote Cappua, as did MUNERATUS Appollinaris. The same edition has Tomis, but here we had to yield to the current of the remaining witnesses. Again, MUNERATUS, GREVEN, and MOLAN have Manea; the others, more correctly in agreement with the text, have Mannea. There is considerable variation in some witnesses here. GREVEN and MOLAN at the end, after “Peter,” add “their sons.” I think this is gratuitous, for if anything could be added, it should have been taken from Ado, whom ANTWERP and MAXIMUM–LÜBECK closely followed; after Mannea they read: “Of John, his son, and Serapion the cleric, and Peter the soldier.” Both groups, however, clearly depart from Usuardian purity in this matter [Col. 0406A]. MUNERATUS inserts *and* after George the deacon. He also writes Natalia, with ROSWEYD; the others have Nathalia. A second difficulty follows in the encomium of Caesarius, which GREVEN and MOLAN formulate from Ado as follows: “a man of extraordinary holiness, piety, and zeal.” ROSWEYD has “a man of extraordinary holiness and piety.” ANTWERP and MAXIMUM–LÜBECK have “a man of extraordinary holiness.” Our construction seems less precise, but it is the Usuardian one. Ado and Notker write Syagrius, as does MOLAN; PRATENSIS has Siagrius. The rest read as we have preserved them in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0405A]

Today Florentinius discusses the name, dignity, and aureole of Rufus or Rufinus of Capua, prompted by a certain Rufinus recorded by the Hieronymian Martyrologies at Capua, of the sort we have often found among the supplementary entries. But Ughellus does not prove with arguments sufficient to convince his opponents that episcopal dignity, in addition to the aureole of martyrdom, can be assigned to this Rufus of ours. Baronius makes two Rufuses and, in defending the title of bishop for this one, cites Bede—namely the edition then current—Usuardus, and Ado, although none of them assigns that dignity to Rufus. More deserving of praise is the learned material he collected concerning patrician dignity. But these matters are not to be pursued at present. Everything concerning one Rufus or several, together with the Acts themselves, which we mentioned under Apollinaris on 23 July, will be discussed more fully in its proper place in the larger work. For the moment, the source of our commemoration seems to be sought in the little Roman Martyrology, which reads: “At Capua, Rufus, martyr, disciple of Apollinaris.” What has been added in our text Usuardus received from Ado, except that he removed one word after “he taught,” namely “and was baptized.” Notker, emerging here for the first time from his lacuna, rendered Ado’s wording somewhat more concisely. Wandalbert elegantly writes:

> Remembering your triumphs, Rufus, the sixth [day] displays them:

[Col. 0405C] The manuscript copies of the Hieronymian Martyrologies commemorate the martyrs of Tomis. Florentinius, with completely useless effort, explains his Notker as though he had been unable to observe that every one of its phrases was copied from Ado. The little Roman Martyrology had briefly preceded it in this form: “At Tomis, Marcellinus and Mannea.” Ado is more similar to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, from which he seems to have taken the characteristics of each person, which we said were then received by Notker. Our author distinguished the wife and, omitting the cleric and the soldier, was content to enumerate only the proper names. The Cordoban martyrs who follow, with George as their leader, properly belong to Usuardus; they were unknown to the older martyrologists but were gathered by Usuardus, along with many others, from the Spanish harvest. Baronius marked them in the modern Roman Martyrology on 27 July and established from Eulogius that this was their feast day; he makes other observations to be explained elsewhere. Eulogius himself treated their Acts admirably in Book II of the *Memorial*, chapter 10, where the day of their passion is expressly noted as the sixth day before the Kalends of August. Nevertheless, the monks of Prüm follow Usuardus in error. For the translation of George and Aurelius, see 20 October. Florentinius considers Caesarius of Arles and Siagrius of Autun to have been additions to the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Rabanus treats both. I do not know what moved Florus to call Caesarius a martyr. Usuardus and Notker, following their constant guide, both copied their announcements from Ado. Those saints are too celebrated for anything further to need adding here; for the moment, read Baronio’s careful notes on each of them.]

[Note: [Col. 0405C]

ANTWERP MAJOR is truncated today, for immediately after “in the city of Tomis, of the holy martyrs,” it adds “George,” etc., omitting the intervening material. At the end it adds: “On the same day, Saint Bernard, abbot.” I think it intended to say: “The octave,” etc.

PULSANENSIS is exact in the first entry but omits the second. In the third it cuts out the encomium. In the fourth it is exact. The fifth is absent.

ANTWERP MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC follow Ado in the account of the Tomitan martyrs, as above. They then add: “Who, under the governor Culcianus, after overcoming the ferocity of beasts and surviving the flames, are struck down by the sword, and finally their bodies are burned by fire.” I think the encomia of Maurolycus and Galesinius were composed from this.

LOUVAIN is purer than the preceding witnesses, but the encomium of the Cordoban martyrs is absent.

CENTULENSIS: “At Capua, Saint Rufus, martyr, whom blessed Apollinaris taught and baptized, since Rufus was of patrician rank. On the same day, Saints George the deacon, Aurelius, Felix, Natalia, and Liliosa, all of whom suffered for Christ. At Autun, Saint Siagrius, bishop and confessor.” The second and fourth announcements are absent.

BRUSSELS is purely Adonian in the entry for Rufus. Then: “At Nola, Saint Felix, bishop, martyred together with thirty others under the governor Marcianus.” Of the Tomitan martyrs, as in ANTWERP MAXIMUM, etc. “At Cordoba, the feast of Saints George,” etc. It is also sufficiently exact concerning Caesarius and Siagrius.

HAGENOYEN: “At Capua, the feast of blessed Rufus, martyr, who was converted to the faith because blessed Apollinaris, the disciple of the apostle Peter, raised his only daughter from the dead. Rufus was a patrician at Ravenna, and therefore during the persecution he was brought to Capua and beheaded there.” In the account of the Tomitan martyrs it is similar to ANTWERP MAXIMUM, etc. In the account of the Cordobans it is exact. Then: “On the same day, in the city of Arles, Saint Caesarius, bishop and confessor, a man of extraordinary holiness, piety, and zeal, and an excellent teacher, who also composed homilies and sermons. At Autun, the burial of Saint Siagrius, bishop and confessor.”

AQUICINCTENSIS adds at the end: “At Bourges, Saint Sulpicius [bishop] and confessor.”

MATRICENSIS–CARTHUSIANA–UTRECHT: “Rufus, martyr, formerly of patrician rank; the sixteen holy martyrs in Egypt. Isaac and Maximian, martyrs.” It is correctly noted in the margin: “I plainly do not find them on this day in the Roman Martyrology or elsewhere”; nor have we found them. It continues: “Caesarius, bishop of Arles.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, under a note: “In the territory of Bigorre, in the city of Horea, the feast of Saint Licerius, bishop and confessor, most renowned as a performer of miracles.”

VATICAN, number 5949, omitted George and his companions. It added first: “The feast of Saints Arontius, [Col. 0407B] Honoratus, Fortunatianus, and Sabinianus. At Capua, the feast of Saints Rufus and Carponius [also Carpophorus], martyrs.”

FLORENTINIUS: “At the city of Potentia, the four holy martyr brothers Aruntius, Honoratus, Fortunatus, and Sabinianus. Their feast is celebrated on the Kalends of September.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition begins: “At Milan, Saint Simplicianus, bishop and confessor. Because of the celebrated reputation of his holiness, he was taken from the life of a hermit and, after the death of Saint Ambrose, raised to the episcopate of the Church of Milan. Just as he had previously been devoted to God in monastic life, so in pastoral care he proved an energetic imitator of blessed Ambrose. While this venerable bishop was still a hermit, by his teaching and exemplary life he also led Augustine, a rhetorician and teacher of that city, to detest the errors of the Manichaean sect and converted him to faith in the most holy Trinity. And because Augustine himself had been converted to the Catholic faith by the admonitions and examples of that holy elder, he therefore received from the same holy old man the habit of holy conduct and a pattern of life, which he later caused to flourish and spread in Africa. At Capua, the feast of blessed Rufus, martyr, a Roman patrician. He held command at Ravenna; there blessed Apollinaris, the disciple of the apostle Peter, raised his dead daughter from the dead. Consequently, he himself, together with his wife and daughter and his entire household, numbering 324, were baptized in Christ. Blessed Rufus, however, completed his martyrdom at Capua.” Of the Tomitan martyrs it has what ANTWERP MAXIMUM has. “At Cordoba, the feast,” etc., accurately. The rest of the text is likewise accurate. At the end: “At the city of Metz, Saint Rufus, bishop and confessor.” His feast is recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 7 November.

[Col. 0408A] BELIN moves the Cordoban martyrs to the penultimate position and removes their encomium. In the account of the Tomitan martyrs it is also not exact. It writes Ruffus, etc. The Paris edition adds: “In the city of Bourges, Saint Sulpicius, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN: “Note that elsewhere the companions of Marcellinus the tribune are listed in this manner: John and Babylas, his sons; Serapion and Hiron, clerics; Ammon, and Peter, the soldier. All of them, together with Marcellinus and his wife, under the governor Culcianus, after overcoming the ferocity of beasts and surviving the flames, were struck down by the sword and completed their martyrdom. Miletius, bishop. Theogenes, Aristion, Festus, Victor, Susanna, Zoilus, Domnus, and Memmo, martyrs. At Metz, Saint Rufus, bishop and confessor. Likewise, according to some, on this day Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, whom others commemorate on the Ides of August; Ebbo, bishop and confessor. At Bourges, the translation of Saint Sulpicius, bishop and confessor. In Scotland, Malkubius, abbot.”

MOLAN, in the first edition, lacks the additions. In later editions: “On the twenty-seventh day, Saint Pastor, holy father. In the city of Constance, the feast of Saint Gebehard, bishop and confessor. Likewise, the translation of Saint Lambert, from the crypt to the altar of the Holy Cross.”

I append here Rosweyd’s observation on Baronius’s *Martyrology*, concerning the words: “In the Thebaid, Saint Poemen, hermit.” Baronius had noted: “The Greeks also speak of him on this day in the Menologion. More is found in the Lives of the Fathers.” Likewise in the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 343: “It is also recorded in the *Lives of the Fathers* that the same holy Athanasius once summoned to Alexandria Abbot Poemen, a man of outstanding holiness.”

Now hear Rosweyd in the manuscript letter cited above: “As for what Baronius says about Poemen, either his memory deceived him, or he thought Poemen the same as Pammone. Concerning Pammone, you have this account here in Rufinus, Book III, number 164; from Pelagius, Book III, no. 14, and Book XVII, no. 11, you will infer that he is the same as Pambo, not Poemen, since the same sayings are related under the name Pambon which Rufinus has under the name Pammon. Another is Piammon or Pyaminon, concerning whom see Rufinus, Book I, chapter 31; in Palladius, chapter 72, he is Ammonas. I had already noted this long ago in the Life of Saint Antony. I now add that Poemen was distinct from Pammone or Pambo. This is clear from Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 9, where Pampus is placed in the Cells and Poemen on Mount Pispiri. He says: ‘Macarius of the upper desert, and another Macarius of the lower; Isidore in Scetis; Pambus in the Cells; Moses and Benjamin in Nitria; Scyrion, Elias, and Paul in the East; another Paul in Phocis; Poemen and Joseph in Pispiri.’” Thus far Rosweyd’s careful observation.]

[Col. 0405]

At Capua, the feast of Saint Rufus, martyr, whom blessed Apollinaris, the disciple of the apostle Peter, taught, since Rufus was of patrician rank. In the city of Tomis, Saints Marcellinus, tribune, and his wife Mannea, and John, Serapion, and Peter, martyrs. On the same day, the feast of Saints George the deacon, Aurelius, Felix, Natalia, and Liliosa. The first of these, a monk of extraordinary abstinence, came from Jerusalem to Cordoba; together with the others, who were descended from a distinguished family of the same city, he was granted the long-desired martyrdom that the Lord had shown him beforehand. In the city of Arles, Saint Caesarius, bishop, a man of extraordinary holiness, piety, and zeal. At Autun, Saint Siagrius, bishop and confessor.

**Fifth day before the Kalends. Day 28.** [Note: [Col. 0407]

Thus have the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp Major, Muneratus, Greven, and Molan editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0407D]

At the very beginning Antwerp Major omitted *feast*. It then somewhat confused the text, placing the final announcement concerning Julian of Brioude second, and writing Viensis instead of Viennensis. Again, instead of Constantinopoli it has Constantinopolim. MUNERATUS expands our third article as follows: “The burial of Saint Augustine, bishop and doctor”; MOLAN has “Augustine, the excellent doctor and bishop.” HERINIENSIS wrote Ticini relatus, while GREVEN and MOLAN, with better syntax, have Ticinum. Yet it is certain that Bede, Rabanus, Ado, and Notker have Ticinis, as preserved by PRATENSIS, ANTWERP MAJOR, MUNERATUS, and others [Col. 0409A]. “Of the city of Ariminum” instead of “of Arvernia” is an error in MUNERATUS, and MOLAN’s Avernae is also incorrect; the text is more accurately preserved by the others. The typesetter of MUNERATUS again errs in omitting the *g* from *desecto*, writing *defecto*. The same edition has Juliani instead of Vibiani, an error also found in ANTWERP MAJOR. There is otherwise great diversity in this name. FLORUS and ADO read Bibianus, followed by GREVEN and MOLAN. BELIN has Julianus in the first edition and Vivianus in the second, as do our more recent codices and Baronius. I followed the Pratensis and Heriniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0409A]

The ancient calendars preserved by Florentinius and all our martyrologies show Hermetes, a most illustrious martyr, celebrated by the oldest and continuous cult; in these sources he occupies the first place, except in Rabanus, where the order is reversed. His acts have been mixed into the Acts of Saint Alexander, pope, illustrated under 3 May. The curious reader may consult them in the meantime, until, in its proper place, his translation to Renaix, a town of Flanders, and other matters relating to the same saint can be more carefully elucidated. Ado’s lengthy encomium nearly encompasses his Acts. Notker, contrary to his usual practice, took a few things from it [Col. 0409B], and our author fewer still, adapted to his own style. Florentinius shows that the companions of Hermetes were improperly added in the Lucensis codex. Ariomastus Alexander is also illustrious in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and the little Roman Martyrology; Baronius praises him in many places, both in his notes and in the *Annals*, and we shall adorn him more fully elsewhere. Our fellow Janning has already treated no small part of the subject on 4 June, in his commentary on Saint Metrophanes. The scholarly dispute concerning Alexander’s date has been debated more sharply; it seems to have been satisfactorily settled by the same author in the June Supplement, in the appendix to the Life of Saint Paul, Alexander’s successor. The brief Usuardian entry concerning him is abridged from Ado, with the passages omitted for which certain codices had to be rejected. The martyrologists who have just been cited, and also Bede, described by Rabanus and our author, remember the great father Augustine. Ado set out a fairly long sequence from his Life, whose beginning and end Usuardus clearly expresses, although I think that here he had Bede before his eyes more than Ado [Col. 0409C]. In due time a vast field will be opened by the splendid deeds of this incomparable teacher, which he himself, in a very rare example, pursued brilliantly up to his priesthood in his golden work on his Confessions. His disciple Possidius, almost his constant companion and an eyewitness, carefully set out the remainder of his course of labors. No one will deny that the whole sequence of his life must be drawn chiefly from these sources, and illuminated from Augustine’s own writings and those of others, as well as from his countless struggles in defense of the Catholic faith [Col. 0410A]. Many writers who have long treated the same subject will provide assistance, but it would be pointless to enumerate them here. Tillemont has allowed nothing to be lacking in this section, having treated the deeds of Augustine at great length throughout volume XIII. Wandalbert places a metrical encomium of Augustine between Hermetes and Vivianus, scarcely ever more lavish in praise. It reads:

> On the fifth day, blessed Hermes manifests himself by a happy death.
>
> O light of the Church, sacred and faithful rule of the people,
>
> Africa shines under your pastoral care, and the world under your teaching;
>
> Father Augustine, you are celebrated on the same feast,
>
> Whom golden churches in Italy now preserve buried.
>
> At Saintes, Vibianus shines on this day in the high honor of his [feast].]

Julian of Brioude is held in such great veneration by the people of Auvergne that his renown is known throughout all Gaul. The Hieronymian Martyrologies, Florus, Ado, Usuard, and Notker commemorate him with solemn observance. Here, somewhat more briefly, Our Author, drawing from Ado’s encomium, omitted only this detail after Ferreolus: that Julian had been his companion in military service. He translated everything else word for word. See Baronius and Florentinius. Some acts were published by Labbe in volume II of the *Bibliotheca manuscripta*. Surius transcribed Gregory of Tours. See what Tillemont examined more carefully in volume V, beginning at page 279, but especially from page 696, where further material is drawn from the cited Gregory of Tours. The Vivianus who in the Hieronymian Martyrologies is joined with Alexander is either no one at all, or, unless I am mistaken, the very same man who is there also called Julian in the additions; Florus more correctly calls him Bibianus, though wrongly assigns him to Sconis, Scottiis, or Comis. Ado likewise calls him Bibianus, but Notker calls him Vibianus. We have preferred this spelling from the Pratensis and Heriniensis manuscripts, taking, with Baronius, a kind of middle course between the older and more recent codices. Consult his annotations on this matter. It is certain that Usuard took his entire announcement from Ado; and thus, from what has been said, the origin of our text is shown to be entirely pure and simple.

[Note: [Col. 0409C]

The ROSWEYD manuscript is not entirely pure; moreover, it is defective in the final announcement.

The PULSANEN manuscript gives Saint Augustine first and then Hermetes, quite purely. But everything else is missing.

The ANTUERP and MAX.-LUBEC manuscripts have been excluded from the pure witnesses because, in the entry for Alexander, they use Ado’s wording: “Arrius, condemned by divine judgment, burst open in the middle, and his entrails spilled out.” At the end, they have Viviani.

The ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN manuscripts begin with Augustine, of whom they add “the outstanding teacher”; and the LEYDEN manuscript [Col. 0409D] further adds “our Father.” The other readings are pure, including those concerning Hermetes and all the rest, except Alexander; concerning him they also have Ado’s wording, “burst open in the middle,” etc. At the end, too, they write, with several others, Viviani.

The ALBERGEN manuscript differs from the preceding ones only in this respect: concerning Augustine, it omits the elogium and simply reads “bishop and confessor.”

The DANIC manuscript agrees in all respects, but after “at Ticinum,” intending to identify the place more clearly for purposes of explanation, it adds “that is, at Pavia.”

The LOVANIEN manuscript reads: “In Africa, the burial of our holy Father Augustine, bishop and outstanding teacher,” etc., purely. It likewise treats Hermetes. Concerning Alexander, it agrees with the above. In Julian’s entry it truncates the elogium. In Vibianus, it is correct.]

[Col. 0410C] The CENTULLEN manuscript reads: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Hermetes the martyr, whom the blessed Pope Alexander, while he was prefect, baptized together with his wife, his sons, and his sister Theodosia. At Constantinople, Saint Alexander the bishop, a glorious old man. In Africa, in the city of Hippo, Saint Augustine the bishop and confessor, who multiplied the talents entrusted to him by God, [so] that no one could admit to having read all his writings. At Privatus, the passion of Saint Julian the martyr, whose passion Gregory of Tours describes in a faithful style. At Saintes, Saint Lubinianus the bishop and confessor.” The variation in the name is remarkable, although everywhere the same man—Vibianus, Vivianus, or Bibianus—is meant. The codex that follows calls him Lubianus.

The BRUXELLEN manuscript begins with Augustine, and in this is almost identical with ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. In Hermetes, it is almost pure. In Julian it inserts Ado’s words, omitted by Usuard, as I said in the Observations. Concerning Alexander, it has the reading given above. Instead of Vibiani, it writes Lubiani.

The HAGENOYEN manuscript is moderately interpolated in Hermetes and Alexander, and gathers several details concerning Saint Augustine that may be read more purely in Ado. It then proceeds to Vivianus. At the end it reads: “Also, on this same day, Saints Julian and Ferreolus the martyrs,” etc. He is commemorated on 18 September.

[Col. 0411A] The AQUICINCT manuscript reads: “At Saintes, Vibianus the bishop and confessor.” This is in a much later hand.

The MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT manuscripts read: “Augustine, bishop and confessor. Hermetes the martyr. Alexander, bishop and confessor, at Constantinople, who condemned Arius. Julian the martyr. Tubianus [Vibianus], bishop and confessor.”

In VATICAN manuscript no. 5949, Vibiani is absent. The following is added: “At Salerno, Saints Fortunatus, Gagus, and Anthes the martyrs. And Saints Septiminus, Januarius, and Felix the martyrs. And the dedication of three altars of this church.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition contains much concerning Saint Augustine, expressed more elegantly by MOLANUS. It continues: “At Rome, the blessed Hermetes the martyr, a most illustrious man. As is read in his Acts, the blessed Pope Alexander baptized him, while he was prefect of the city of Rome, together with his wife, his sons, and his sister Theodora; with them he likewise first granted freedom to 1,052 of his slaves, together with their wives and children. When this deed came to the ears of Count Aurelian, he ordered Hermetes to be committed to prison, then struck with the sword; and by such a martyrdom he departed to Christ.” Julian’s entry is somewhat interpolated. Concerning Alexander, etc., it agrees with the other codices cited above.

BELIN reads: “In the African city of Hippo, the feast of our holy Father Augustine, bishop and confessor, and outstanding Doctor of the Church. He first,” etc., not very purely. It also varies in Hermetes. In Alexander, it agrees with the above. Julian’s elogium has been removed. We have spoken above concerning Julian and Vivianus.

GREVEN reads: “Abundius and Abundantius the martyrs. Pelagius the martyr, who in the province of Acarnania, during the reign of the emperor Numerian, was beaten with rods and clubs; after overcoming the rack, hooks, and boiling oil, he was finally consecrated to Christ as a martyr by a sword-stroke. Saint Uranius the presbyter, who had instructed him in the sacred writings, buried his body.” Wandalbertus sings of him; see below under MOLANUS. “Pelagius the pope and confessor. John the abbot and confessor. Also, blessed Agnes the virgin, sister of Saint Clare, who, when dying, had told her to follow her quickly to the Lord. Taysis, once a sinner, whom Saint Paphnutius the abbot converted and shut up in a narrow cell, where, after spending three years in the greatest penitence, she afterward rested in peace.”

MOLANUS, after “the excellent Doctor,” inserts in Italic type, abridged from Ado—or rather from Possidius—the following:

“He received from God, through the most acceptable priest Ambrose, illustrious among the best of men and a most frequent preacher of the word of God, by the gracious assistance of divine providence, both saving instruction and the divine sacraments. Immediately afterward, from the inmost marrow of his heart, he abandoned every hope that he had placed in the world. It then happened that, after some time had passed, through the action of the holy bishop Valerius, and with everyone rejoicing, he was compelled to accept the episcopate while his bishop was still living. This occurred so that, as bishop, he might preach the word of eternal salvation to the Church of the Lord, which was flourishing and growing, with much greater urgency and fervor and with greater authority. Until the very extremity of his illness, he preached the word of God in the Church without interruption, with sound mind and sound judgment.”

It continues in smaller type:

“He always showed hospitality, and at table he preferred reading or discussion to eating and drinking. As a safeguard against the pestilence of human custom, he had written this at the table:

> Whoever loves to gnaw at the lives of absent people  
> should know that this table is forbidden to him.

And therefore he warned every guest that he ought to abstain from superfluous and harmful stories and from slander. He both reproved and tolerated the undisciplined transgressions of his people against the right rule and propriety, insofar as it was fitting and necessary; especially in such matters he taught that no one’s heart should be turned toward words of wickedness, in order to make excuses for sins. He always ordered the Church’s library and all its books to be carefully preserved for posterity. He did not treat his blood relatives, whether they were within or outside his religious commitment, according to common custom either in life or in death.”

Again in Italic type, from Ado:

“He made no will, because, being God’s poor man, he had nothing from which to make one. In the third month of the siege—for his city was enclosed and besieged for fourteen months by the Vandals, Alans, and other mixed peoples—he took to his bed with fevers, and was exercised by that final illness. This blessed bishop, touched by the divine Spirit, wrote in the holy Catholic Church, for the instruction of souls, books, treatises, and letters numbering 1,030, apart from those that cannot be counted, because he did not specify their number. He first concerning his own,” etc., purely.

At the end: “At Constantia, a city of Gaul, the feast of Saint Pelagius the martyr, who under the emperor Numerian, by order of the judge Evilasius, suffered martyrdom.”

Finally, in smaller type: “At Buchau, Saint Adelindis the abbess.”

Other editions announce Augustine first, but abridge the foregoing elogium to approximately one quarter of its length. Concerning Hermetes, they have almost the same material that we gave above from the LUBECK–COLOGNE edition. In Italic type, they insert the name Brivate in Julian’s entry. At the end: “At Buchau in Swabia, Saint Adelindis the abbess. On the twenty-eighth day, Saint Moses the Ethiopian the Father.” This has been taken from the *Horologium*. See Baronius’s note on him, our Observations for 7 February, and the Acts for the same day.

Finally, two concluding verses by Wandalbertus are added for this day:

> The city of the Alemanni, Constantia, commemorates the holy man;  
> here too Pelagius, renowned for blood poured out.

Above, Pelagius was assigned to Constantia in Gaul, which lies far from the Rhine—unless “Gaul,” or rather the Frankish empire, is understood in the broadest sense, which it is known once to have possessed.]

[Col. 0407]

At Rome, the feast of the blessed Hermetes, an illustrious man, who, as is read in the Acts of Pope Alexander, first was committed to prison and then attained martyrdom when the sword struck him. At Constantinople, Saint Alexander the bishop and confessor, a glorious old man, by whose power of prayer Arius was condemned by divine judgment. In Africa, the burial of Saint Augustine the bishop, who was first transferred from his city to Sardinia because of the barbarians, and recently brought back by the king of the Lombards to Ticinum and honorably buried. On the same day, the feast of Saint Julian the martyr, who during the persecution, at the urging of the blessed Ferreolus, secretly departed from the city of Vienne and moved to the territory of the city of Auvergne, where at last he was killed by having his throat cut, suffering a horrible death. At Saintes, Saint Vibianus the bishop and confessor.

**IV Kalends. Day 29.** [Note: [Col. 0411]

Thus the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0413A]

The Pratensis reads “the finding of the head of John,” etc. Antwerp-Major has “the finding of the most blessed John.” Rosweyd agrees with the Pratensis, but the Heriniensis and the others explicitly give the reading found in the text. We have spoken elsewhere about *solemnitatem*, which the codices commonly write elsewhere. Munerat, in support of the evangelical reading, substitutes “is proved by evangelical authority” for “is confirmed by the evangelical reading.” Greven and Molan differ from the others in saying “when his head was found for the second time at Edessa.” It ought to be written “Emesa,” but we do not depart from the codices. Instead of *conditum*, Munerat has *reconditum*. Also, Sabina the virgin and martyr. [Col. 0413B] See the Observations. In Heriniensis it is *Trecasino*. In [Col. 0414A] Antwerp-Major, *Leginae* appears instead of *Sabinae*, or *Savinae*, as Munerat writes. Castellanus noted an erasure in the Pratensis codex, beginning at *Parisius dep.* and continuing to the end; above it he observed the inscription *ositio Mederici presbyteri et monachi*, etc. The constant companions of the Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd codices follow this same way of writing. Previously it had read *Mederici episcopi*, as Molan reads it. But the reading of Heriniensis and Greven is preferable: “the burial of Medericus the presbyter,” not “of Saint Medericus the abbot,” as found in Munerat. Nevertheless, those codices have been counted among the pure witnesses.]

[Note: [Col. 0413B]

Concerning the finding of the head of John the Forerunner, we summarized briefly at 24 February what needed to be said; it would be superfluous to repeat it here. Moreover, for 24 June it was stated that in most Hieronymian copies, both on that day and on this one, his feast is commemorated at Sebaste, although Florentinius disputes the true and genuine text of this day in Admonition 6, pages 26 and 28. Bede distinctly reads today: “On the same day, the beheading of Saint John the Baptist.” Yet what is added there sufficiently suggests that the translation of the head is understood. The Small Roman Martyrology and Ado indicate that the beheading is venerated today. The remaining material found in the latter is Bede’s own wording, also copied by Rabanus and Notker. Nor are the statements that Ado reports on this day in the festivals of the Apostles any clearer. Our author seems to have drawn from Ado’s text of 24 February the beheading, which could not be celebrated around the feast of Easter—for example, on 1 April—and therefore entered it on this day because the second finding of the sacred head had taken place on this very day. But if everything is carefully weighed, you will easily see that this is almost entirely conjectural. Perhaps Castellanus’s conjecture is better: he believes that the feast of the beheading was established because of the dedication of the temple founded by Theodosius, which took place today. Others devise other explanations, which can be examined more fully in their proper place, and to which may be added what Papebrochius set out at length and learnedly in volume IV of the June Acts, beginning at page 711, and what the cited Tillemont discussed under 24 February. To these must be added the arguments that the same author made against Father l’Amy in volume II, beginning at page 714. What Wandalbertus thought about this festival you will understand from his verses. The Roman Sabina also has a place here; she follows, celebrated here as a virgin:

> John, herald of God, voice of the Word, and Baptist,  
> whom the heavens granted to the commands of the dancing girl,  
> marks the fourth with the enduring praise of his merits.  
> The virgin Sabina likewise revisits her own temples at Rome.

[Col. 0413D] Bede places first today: “At Rome, Saint Sabina the virgin and martyr”; Rabanus has only “Sabina the martyr.” It is probable that this was how Bede originally wrote it, since the Acts establish that she was the wife of the once-famous Valentinus, whom the Acts of the virgin Serapia mention; these will be treated on 3 September. In the ancient Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, as also in the Gregorian Sacramentary, she is marked by name alone. The Small Roman Martyrology added nothing except the title of martyr, although it does add the location, at the Arch of Faustinus. Ado composed a fuller account from the aforementioned Acts of Serapia, and Usuard took this principal material from him, by which he praises the most illustrious martyr. Notker runs briefly through a few points in summary. Baronius’s and Florentinius’s Notes will provide more. From the Annals of the former, under the year 432, no. 37, you will learn that a church was dedicated to her at that time, still highly celebrated today; the first and more solemn station is held there on Wednesday of the Ember Days, as may be seen in Fronto, page 33.

Castellanus rightly observed that Sabina or Savina of Troyes was improperly inserted here by Usuard, since he could have known that she was celebrated by her fellow citizens everywhere with public solemnity not on this day but on 29 January, as you will find more fully proved in the Acts for that day; essentially the same elogium of Usuard is also reported from several manuscript Martyrologies. The cited Castellanus sufficiently suggests in the first *Bimestre*, page 452, that Usuard consecrated this day to Sabina of Troyes because the aforementioned homonymous Sabina of Rome was commemorated on it, although he could have been better informed about the true festival of the other woman.

Medericus is also noted only by Our Author—not as a monk, abbot, or bishop, as we demonstrated above, although we do not deny that he was a monk and, if you wish, an abbot, but as a presbyter, as our text presents him. See what Mabillon reports and observes about him in the third part of the third volume of the Benedictine age, beginning at page 8. There he carefully investigates and explains, in his customary manner, many matters concerning the saint’s age, the author of his Life, his monastic profession, the various places—whether monasteries or others—in which Medericus was honored, and finally the cell in the suburbs of Paris, dedicated under the name of the prince of the apostles, in which he lived out the remainder of his life and finally died. More will be set out elsewhere. The oldest Hieronymian manuscript, that of Echternach, brings forward a certain Roman virgin Candida mixed in with other companions; I would readily believe that Usuard drew her from a copy of this sort. Certainly our codices sufficiently prove that she belongs to Usuard, and they equally clearly show the genuine simplicity of the whole text.]

[Note: [Col. 0413D]

The PULSANEN manuscript is quite pure in the first announcement, then continues: “In the district of Troyes, Saint Sabina the virgin.” The remainder is missing.

The ANTUERP and MAX.-LUBEC manuscripts are plainly mutilated and read: “The beheading of Saint John the Baptist. At Rome, Saint Sabina [Col. 0414D] the virgin and martyr. On the same day, Saint Candida the virgin. In Antioch of Syria, Saints Nicea and Paul. In Sirmium, the feast of Saint Basilla.” The last two have been added from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

The ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN manuscripts are quite pure through the penultimate announcement. Thus they do not speak of Medericus; instead, they immediately append to Sabina of Troyes: “On the same day, Saint Candida,” etc., as we have just said.

The LOVANIEN manuscript is also similar to these, except that it removes the elogium of Sabina of Troyes.

The ALBERG and DANIC manuscripts begin: “The beheading of Saint John the Baptist.” In the remainder they agree with ANTUERP.-MAX., etc.

The CENTULLEN manuscript reads: “At Rome, at the Arch of Faustinus, the most blessed Sabina the martyr. On the same day, the beheading of Saint John the Baptist is venerated; Herod the Tetrarch, as the Evangelists report, ordered him to be beheaded in prison. On the same day, Saint Candida the virgin. At Paris, the burial of Clericus the presbyter”—I think, instead of Medericus, who is not called a monk here either.

The BRUXELLEN manuscript reads: “The beheading of Saint John the Baptist, which the evangelical reading records as having taken place around Easter; but his feast is commemorated here, when his head was found for the second time and buried in the church of the city of Edessa. At Rome, in the Adventine district, in the town of Vindinum, at the Arch of Faustinus—for this is clearer in Ado—the feast of Saint Sabina, the most illustrious martyr, who was once the wife of the most famous Valentinus and the daughter of Herod Metellarius. Under the emperor Hadrian, she suffered under the prefect Helpidius and, struck by the sword, received the palm of martyrdom.” In Sabina of Troyes, the reading is pure. It then proceeds concerning the Antiochians and Basilla as above. In Candida it is pure. Then: “And Saint Aurea the virgin. At Metz, the burial of Saint Adelphus the bishop and confessor.” In Medericus, an *o* has been inserted into the first syllable, producing *Modericus*.

The HAGENOYEN manuscript reads: “The beheading of Saint John the Baptist—or rather, the finding of his head, the burning of his bones, the translation of his finger, and the dedication of his basilica. Hence some record this festival in different ways. For it is called the beheading, the collection, the finding, and the dedication. John was beheaded around the feast of Easter, as the authority of the Gospel proves, by Herod the Tetrarch of Galilee, the son of Herod the king under whom the Lord was born. His bones were burned by the emperor Julian. The collection of his bones was carried out by Jerusalemite monks, who mingled with those burning them and stole many of his bones. The finding of John’s head was accomplished through two monks, by his own revelation. The translation of his finger and the dedication of the church were carried out near Milan by Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards. Therefore, on account of all these events, it was established by the Lord Pope that this day should be celebrated throughout the world in honor of the Baptist.” What it records concerning Sabina of Rome is better reported by Ado. It is silent about the woman of Troyes and about Medericus. It continues: “In Sirmium, Saint Basilica the virgin.” She is better called Basilla. It treats Candida purely, and the Antiochians as above.

The AQUICINCT manuscript calls Medericus a monk, along with the PRATENSIS and the other companions cited above.

The MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT manuscripts read: “The beheading of Saint [Col. 0415D] John the Baptist. Sabina the virgin and martyr.” Concerning her, a marginal note correctly remarks: “We are now commemorating her, as though she were not a virgin. Medericus the abbot and confessor. Sabina the virgin. Candida the virgin.”

The CODEX BIGOTIANUS, marked P 5, formerly belonging to the Celestines, has written in the margin, in a more recent hand: “In the city of L’Aquila, the coronation of our holy Father Peter Celestine, in which there is an indulgence from baptism.” The codex can be identified from this as well.

[Col. 0416A] In the VATICAN manuscript, Medericus and Candida are absent. The following is added: “The feast of Saints Vitalis, Sator, and Repositus.” They are not known among the others.

The UGHELLIAN manuscript contains nothing concerning Sabina of Troyes or Medericus. Concerning the Antiochians and Basilla, it agrees with the ANTUERP and MAX.-LUBEC manuscripts above.

The CODEX CASTRI-KAROLI reads: “On the same day, Saint John the confessor.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION reads: “The beheading of Saint John the Baptist. He was first buried in Samaria, now in Alexandria. Moreover, his head was carried from Jerusalem to the Phoenician city of Edessa.” Bede, Rabanus, Ado, and Notker have almost the same wording. “At Rome, in the Adventine district, in the town of Vindinum, at the Arch of Faustinus,” etc.; I would rather read this in Ado. Concerning Sabina of Troyes, it inserts “sister of Saint Savinianus the martyr.” Concerning the Antiochians it says, “Nicea the virgin and Paul the martyr. At Metz, Saint Adolphus the bishop and confessor.” Concerning Medericus, it adds “and confessor.” Concerning Basilla of Sirmium, it agrees with the above. In Candida, it is pure.

BELIN begins: “The beheading of Saint John the Baptist.” Concerning Sabina, it omits the title “most illustrious.” It continues: “Also Saint Elisha the prophet.” In Candida, it is pure. In the Antiochians, it agrees with the above. Instead of *Basillae*, it writes *Basiliae*. In Medericus, it is pure. What was absent from the earlier Venetian edition is included in the later one: “In the district of Troyes, Saint Sabina the virgin.”

GREVEN reads: “Also the nine hundred martyrs who suffered on the same day. In Antioch of Syria, Saints Nicea the virgin and Paul the martyr. At Metz, Saint Adolphus the bishop and confessor. At the city of Ostia, Saint Aurea the virgin and martyr. Born of noble parents, she was tortured by hunger in prison for the faith of Christ under Claudius; then, after overcoming the rack and being beaten with clubs, she was sent into exile. There she endured various tortures again, was thrown into the sea, and completed her martyrdom. At Sirmium, Saint Basilla the virgin. At Verona, a virgin.” [Col. 0416C] See what MOLANUS says about her.

MOLANUS reads: “At the city of Metz, the burial of Saint Adelphus the bishop and confessor. Also Saint Elisha the prophet. His sacred body, even after death, glorified by the raising of the dead—a distinctive miracle—was translated to Ravenna and is honored there with fitting reverence. In Antioch of Syria, the feast of Saints Nicea and Paul. In Syria, the feast of Saint Basilea. At Venusium, a city of Apulia, the feast of Felix the bishop. At the city of Tubzoz, Januarius the presbyter, and Fortunatianus and Septimius the readers, who under the emperor Diocletian were put to death by the sword by the procurator Magdellianus.” See concerning them 24 October. “At Verona, a blessed virgin, in the church of the Holy Cross.” Then, in smaller type: “A mile from the city of Louvain, on the mountain that took from it the name of Saint Verona. She was the daughter of Louis, a royal Alemannic woman and nun in the monastery she founded on the Rhine, which is called Vorenhaute, and she fell asleep in the Lord at Mainz.”

The later editions correct the earlier one to Medericus, but in Italic type add “abbot.” Concerning Elisha, they agree with the above. Then: “Near the city of Louvain, the feast of Verona, a blessed virgin, in the church of the Holy Cross.” Here everything that was explained more fully above from the earlier edition concerning Saint Verona is omitted. It continues: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Adelphus, bishop and confessor of Metz, to the monastery of Villers-la-Ville, at the request of Lantfrid, bishop under Drogo of Metz, in the time of Louis the Pious.”]

[Col. 0411]

The beheading—or rather, the finding of the head—of the most blessed John the Baptist. For the Gospel reading proves that his beheading occurred about the Paschal solemnity; nevertheless it is commemorated here as a feast, because on this day his head was found for the second time in the city of Emesa and placed in a church. At Rome, the feast of Saint Sabina, most illustrious martyr, who, under the emperor Hadrian, was struck with the sword and attained the palm of martyrdom. In the district of Troyes, Saint Sabina the virgin, who, having undertaken a most arduous pilgrimage for Christ’s love, glorious also in virtues and miracles, rested in peace. [Note: [Col. 0411D] I would gladly leave Sollerius uncorrected here. For, although he noticed some fault in the Pratensis codex, he nevertheless thought fit to count it among the pure witnesses. For this I am grateful to him. But it will not be inappropriate to weaken Castellanus’s testimony even in the smallest matters. That most keen-eyed inspector wrote that there was an erasure in the Pratensis manuscript from *Parisius dep.* to the end. This is true. He then says that there is now written in the erasure *ositio Mederici presbyteri et monachi*, etc. But I wholly deny this: immediately after *dep.* follows *sancti Mederici et monachi*. Finally, Sollerius’s allegation that *Mederici episcopi* had formerly been written is utterly false, since the Dervensis codex calls Medericus not a bishop but only a presbyter. Nor was he ever a bishop; he was first a monk, then abbot of one of the two monasteries which existed at Autun at that time, and finally, at Paris, whither he had come for prayer, exchanged life for death on the fourth day before the Kalends of September. These facts are from his Acts, which our Mabillon published, part I, third century, p. 10. Before leaving this point, I have some difficulty in seeing how Sollerius would extricate himself. In the same erasure in which Saint Medericus occurs, Saint Candida also occurs. The handwriting of the correction is the same for both. Yet Sollerius says of Saint Candida: “Certainly our codices sufficiently prove that she belongs to Usuard.” Therefore, what was added concerning Medericus is equally Usuardian. I now ask Sollerius himself to come and teach us what difference there is between the handwriting of this correction and that of the other corrections. For neither I nor any of this city’s learned men see any. BOUILLART.] At Paris, the burial [Bouillart adds: *of Saint*] of Medericus the presbyter. On the same day, Saint Candida the virgin.

**III Kalends. Day 30.** [Note: [Col. 0417]

The following are pure: Heriniensis, Pulsanensis, Antwerp, and Max.-Lubec.; Belin’s first edition, Greven, and Molan. Likewise Antwerp-Major, Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., and the Danish manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0417]

They consist almost entirely in minor blemishes. Thus: *Rhome*, *Hostiensi*, *eculei*. In Heriniensis, *deduceretur* stands for *duceretur*. Belin reads *obvius fuit ei*; Max.-Lubec., *obvius ei quidam fuit*. In Antwerp, after *Adauctum*, *eum* is omitted. Finally Belin writes *Felice* for *sancto Felici*.]

[Note: [Col. 0417A]

We had to discuss the confusion of the various martyrs bearing the name Felix under 14 January, where we identified the sources from which the inquisitive reader will find further material useful also for this day; I neither wish nor have leisure now to repeat it or to reconsider it more laboriously. The difficulty may seem more involved on this day because the martyrologists disagree among themselves. For Bede, and Rabanus, who follows him with a shift of one day, commemorate the martyrs whom we listed among the Auctaria on the preceding days: namely Felix the bishop, Adauctus or Adactus, and the presbyters Januarius (some vary slightly in all these names), Fortunatianus, and Septimius or Septiminus, readers—whom we recently referred from Molan to 24 October. On that day they are celebrated in the very words of Bede by Ado, and by Usuard from Ado. This gave later writers an occasion to doubt whether our Felix and Adauctus should truly be claimed for Rome. Let them see on what basis they establish this. Certainly the ancient Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, often cited, the Sacramentary of Gregory, the Hieronymian copies, the Small Roman Martyrology, Rabanus, Ado, Notker, Wandalbert, and Our Author alike most explicitly mark today Felix alone and Adauctus—or Audactus by metathesis—on the Ostian Way; and they distinguish them by so many further marks and circumstances that I do not yet see what they could have in common with the foregoing African martyrs. I grant that Ado suggests two brothers named Felix on this very day; but since he narrates the deeds of only one, he sufficiently shows that it was this one who won the crown of martyrdom on the Ostian Way with Adauctus as an added companion. Some reject Ado’s Acts. I do not yet venture to vouch for them as genuine; nevertheless, I judge the authorities adduced to be such that our two Ostian martyrs must be wholly distinct from the others. If anyone wishes to attach to this day also the glorious contest of the Africans—at least of Felix the bishop, who suffered at Venusia—I shall not at all oppose it; indeed, I shall endorse Ruinart, who argues this not implausibly from p. 374. It is enough for us to have defended the authority of our Martyrologies. Moreover, as regards the entry, it is plain that Usuard abridged everything from Ado’s longer narration. Florentinius relies heavily on a manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, but did not know that the material reported there belongs properly to Bede and therefore can change nothing in this matter. Wandalbert followed the common judgment of the martyrologists when he wrote:

> With holy Felix, Adauctus excels in a threefold company.

[Col. 0418B] In the Hieronymian Martyrologies, the virgin Gaudentia is marked first, together with the other three. These occur in Rabanus in exactly the same words; I should like some light to be supplied from some source. Gaudentia was omitted by Ado and Notker; hence I have no doubt that Usuard received her from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Whether she should be adorned with the title of martyr, see Florentinius. Rabanus next has: “The burial of Agilus the abbot,” unknown to all the other more ancient Martyrologies. Someone—I know not who—wanted to attach him to the Pratensis codex with the phrase: “In the district of Meaux, Saint Agilus the confessor”; from this he passed into its regular companions, which were for that reason excluded from the pure witnesses. We say that Saint Agilus was sewn on or added in the Pratensis codex because, as Castellanus testifies, he was not entered by the first hand. But whatever hand it was, it must have been ancient, since Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, which we call companions of the Pratensis codex, also report him in the same words. Munerat presents the same man in a different phrase; but both he and the aforementioned codices are so refuted by all the others cited above for the text that the unquestionable, most genuine purity and simplicity of our Usuardian reading remains. Whoever wishes to read more about Agilus should consult Mabillon, *Benedictine Century* II, from p. 315.]

[Note: [Col. 0417C]

PRATENSIS and ROSWEYD add at the end: “In the district of Meaux, Saint Agilus the confessor.”

ANTWERP-MAJOR has the same addition and is moreover mutilated in Felix’s entry.

MUNERAT adds to the pure text: “At the monastery of Resbacus, called Jerusalem, Saint Agilus, abbot of that same monastery, who shone in many virtues. In the territory of Meaux, Saint Fiacrius the confessor.”

CENTULLEN reads: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the blessed martyrs Felix and Audactus, in the time of Diocletian, under Draco, prefect of the city. Also at Rome, Saint Gaudentia the virgin. At the monastery of Restacum, the burial of Saint Agilus the abbot.”

BRUXELLEN reads: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the passion of the blessed martyrs Felix the presbyter and Adauctus, beheaded under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. When the first, after the torture of the rack and the passing of sentence, was being led to death, the other met him; and when he freely confessed himself a Christian, he was immediately beheaded together with the first. Since Christians did not discover the name of this second martyr, they called him Adauctus, because he had been added to the holy martyr Felix, and because for his confession of the faith the crown of martyrdom had been added to him. Also at Rome, Saint Gaudentia the virgin. On the same day, at the monastery Jerusalem, the burial of Saint Agilus, confessor and abbot.”

HAGENOYEN reads: “At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the feast of the blessed Felix the presbyter and of a certain other Christian, Adauctus, under Diocletian and Maximian. When Felix had been led before many statues, namely those of Serapis, Mercury, and Diana, all of which fell down, and when he had been raised on the rack and tortured, and afterward led to a sacrilegious tree, which he likewise cast down, the image, temple, and altar collapsed; then the governor ordered him to be beheaded and his body left to wolves and dogs. Then a certain Christian sprang into the midst, confessing Christ, and they kissed one another and were beheaded together. Since Christians did not know his name, they called him Adauctus, because he had been added to Saint Felix for the crown.” See this stated more purely in Ado. “In the city of Troyes, Saint Savinianus the martyr and Saint Savina his sister,” etc. A long history of these saints follows [Col. 0419A]; see the Acts for 29 January.

AQUICINCT adds after “Gaudentia the virgin”: “At the monastery called Respacis, the passing of Saint Agilus, abbot and confessor of the same place.” In a much later hand it adds: “In the territory of Meaux, Saint Fiacrius the confessor.” See what Surius has for this day, and more recently Mabillon, *Benedictine Century* II, from p. 599.

DAVERONEN reads: “At the monastery Jerusalem, called Resbacis, the passing of Saint Agilus, first abbot and confessor of that place.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT reads: “Felix and Adauctus, martyrs. Lazarus, brother of Martha, bishop of Marseilles.” See 17 December. “Fiacrius, hermit and confessor. Agilus, abbot and confessor.”]

[Col. 0417]

At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the feast of the blessed martyrs Felix and Adauctus, under Diocletian and Maximian, emperors. When the first, after the torture of the rack and the passing of sentence, was being led to death, another met him; when he freely confessed himself a Christian, he was immediately beheaded with the first. Since Christians did not discover the name of this second martyr, they called him Adauctus, because he had been added to Saint Felix, the martyr. Also at Rome, Saint Gaudentia the virgin.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “At the monastery of Resbacus, surnamed Jerusalem, Saint Agilus, who, as abbot of that same monastery, shone with many virtues. In the Meldese district, blessed Fiacrius the confessor, a man glorious in life and miracles.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949, “Gaudentia” is absent.

ALTEMPS.: “At the monastery of Ceneyo, Saint Ealdwold the confessor, brother of blessed Edmund the martyr. On the same day, Saint Junion, bishop and confessor. Also Saint Decimavus the martyr.”

FLORENTIN.: “At the monastery of Jerusalem, Saint Agilus, abbot and confessor.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition introduces scarcely anything new concerning Felix and Adauctus. It continues: “At the monastery of Tuici, on the bank of the Rhine, the translation of the body of blessed Heribert, archbishop of Cologne at Agrippina and confessor. This was carried out by Lord Arnold, the first archbishop of Cologne, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147. At the monastery of Resbacus, Saint Agilus, abbot and confessor, who, having reached his hundredth year and remaining a virgin, happily departed from this world at his calling.” In the entry for Gaudentia, it is pure. Finally: “On the same day, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Januarius the presbyter, Fortunatus and Septimus the readers.” See the Observations.
