BELIN. in its second edition has at the end: “In the Meldese district, Saint Fiacrius the confessor.”

GREVEN.: “On the same day, according to the Catalogue of the Saints, Saint Terentianus, bishop and martyr. At the time of Hadrian, when he refused to sacrifice at Todi in Tuscany, he was hoisted upon the rack and beaten with scorpions, and fire was applied to his sides. Then, after his tongue had been cut out, when nevertheless he continued to confess Christ clearly, he was beheaded together with Flaccus, a priest of the idols who had been converted and baptized by him. Also the holy martyrs Hippolytus and Savinianus, concerning whom see the Acts of Saint Aurea the virgin. In the Meldese district, blessed Fiacrius, abbot and confessor, a man of great virtue. At the monastery of Resbacus, Saint Agilus, abbot and confessor, who died a virgin in the hundredth year of his life. At the monastery of Tuici, on the bank of the Rhine, the translation of Saint Heribert, archbishop of Agrippina-Cologne and confessor, carried out in the year of the Lord 1147 by Lord Arnold, archbishop of that city. On the same day, according to some, the commemoration of the holy Januarius the presbyter, Fortunatus and Septimus, who are commemorated below on the ninth day before the Kalends of November.”

MOLAN.: “At the monastery of Resbacus,” etc. Then: “In the Meldese district,” etc., word for word from MUNERATUS. It continues: “In the year 1056, the translation of Saint Donatianus, bishop of Rheims.” In the later editions, concerning Agilus and Fiacrius, the same material appears as in the first edition. Then: “At Bruges, the translation of Saint Donatianus, bishop of Rheims.”

[Col. 0415]

At Rome, on the Ostian Way, the passion of blessed Felix the presbyter, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. After being tortured on the rack, when sentence had been pronounced and he was being led away for beheading, a certain Christian met him; and when this man voluntarily confessed himself a Christian, he was immediately beheaded together with him. Since the Christians did not know his name, they called him Adauctus, because he had been added to Saint Felix for the crown. Also at Rome, Saint Gaudentia the virgin. [Bouillart adds: [Note: [Col. 0417] Castellanus was mistaken and misled Sollerius when he wrote that Saint Agilus had not been entered by the first hand. BOUILLART.] In the Meldese district, Saint Agilus the confessor.]

The day before the Kalends. Day 31. [Note: [Col. 0419]

The Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Muneratus, Greven, and Molan codices are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0419C]

There is a difference between the codices cited here for the text and Belin, with which our manuscripts of the middle recension agree. Although all drew from the same source, the latter nevertheless transferred the first announcement concerning Paulinus of Trier into a somewhat different form, speaking as follows: “At Trier, Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor, who, during the time of the Arian persecution, was harassed by the emperor Constantius through various exiles even unto death for the Catholic faith, and at last received from the Lord, in Phrygia, the crown of blessed suffering.” Otherwise there is scarcely any difference among our pure witnesses. Antwerp-Major and Muneratus erroneously write “Constantine” instead of “Constantius.” Molan has “relegated into exile,” but Greven distorts the sense still further by entangling the construction thus: “Relegated into exile for the Catholic faith.” Pratensis has “Phrigia”; Molan more correctly “Phrygia,” but we, with all the others—including those whom elsewhere we have followed even when they were mistaken—simply write “Frigia.” In Heriniensis there is “Aristhidis.” Concerning Auxerre or Antisiodorum, etc., it has often been said. The remaining points are not worth noting.]

[Note: [Col. 0419C]

Athanasius, Hilary, Jerome, and other ecclesiastical writers rightly celebrate the illustrious struggles of Paulinus of Trier against the Arians for the Catholic faith; and the martyrologists everywhere adorn him as an outstanding confessor—and why not also as a martyr?—especially the Hieronymian martyrologies. After the entry has been placed on this day, “At Trier, the deposition of Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor,” it is repeated again on 4 September: “At Trier, the deposition of Saint Paulinus.” Florentius found no explanation for this doubled feast, nor is it easy to provide one unless we have recourse to the translation, elevation, or discovery of the body, or to its return from Phrygia; concerning these matters Sigebert may be consulted in Florentius. For all these possibilities seem to be ruled out by the fact that in both places “deposition” is expressly written. There is nothing about Paulinus in Bede, Florus, or the Little Roman Martyrology, but Rabanus mentions him, briefly noting that he was exiled under Constantius and died there. Ado expressed the matter somewhat more fully and elegantly; I do not know why Notker did not follow him with sufficient fidelity. Our author, adhering closely to Ado’s words and somewhat abridging them, must plainly be judged to have formed his eulogy according to our older codices, as we have placed it in the little calendar—not as Belin and the more recent manuscripts report it, which will have to be cited more distinctly in the Appendices. Florentius’s annotations say rather more; there you will wonder that we are referred to Mersaeus in the Annals of the Archbishops of Trier, so that we may learn that Saint Paulinus—who certainly died under Constantius and therefore, as Florentius admits, at least before 363—was consecrated by Saint Martin of Tours and loved and cultivated by Saint Ambrose. Baronius will teach us sounder things, and in its proper place we shall produce material from Book II of Sulpicius Severus’s Sacred History and from other more reliable ecclesiastical records. From these it will be clear that our Paulinus of Trier completed the glorious course of his confession before either Martin or Ambrose had scarcely become catechumens; for he was probably sent into exile in 353, after the Council of Arles, and five years later, in 358, reached the end of his labors and hardships. Here may be inserted Wandalbert’s poem about Paulinus, with which he concludes the month of August:

“Paulinus, on the day before, surveys the walls of Trier,

A bishop illustrious in exile for the true doctrine.

With these feasts the lights of August are finally closed.”

[Col. 0421B]

Nothing is said of Aristides in the Hieronymian martyrologies, Bede, or Rabanus; hence it seems certain that he was first entered into the sacred calendars by the Little Roman Martyrology, undoubtedly from Rufinus’s Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 3, in these words: “At Athens, Aristides, who presented books concerning the Christian religion to the emperor Hadrian.” These facts are indeed confirmed by ecclesiastical history and by Jerome’s work On Illustrious Men, chapter 20; but not the things added by Ado concerning his most eloquent speech before Hadrian. Thus it is again clearly evident how foolishly some wish to claim that the Little Roman Martyrology was abridged from Ado. More on these matters elsewhere. For the present, note that the Viennese wording was plainly and almost entirely copied by our author, with Notker altering or transposing some words. Optatus of Auxerre was undoubtedly added by Usuard from the Hieronymian codices, which expressly mention him, whatever Florentius may wish to add. From this the whole structure and method of our text becomes clear.]

[Note: [Col. 0421B]

ROSWEYD. adds English supplements to the text: “In Britain, at the monastery of the Glastonbury people, Saint Aidan [more probably Aidan], bishop and confessor.” See Surius. “In Kent, the deposition of Saint Eanswitha the virgin. On the same day, Saint Cuthburga the virgin.”

PULSANEN. abridges Paulinus’s eulogy. In the entry for Aristides he is pure: “Nothing concerning Optatus.”

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. These eight codices, together with BELIN, form the first announcement, as I said above in the readings. Otherwise the codices are pure; we shall speak of the other matter below.

CENTULEN.: “At Athens, blessed Aristides, most renowned for faith and wisdom. At Trier, blessed Paulinus, bishop, who fought bravely and faithfully against the Arians. At Arras, Saint Hadulf, bishop and confessor.” See in our Acts, on his feast day, 19 May. In MOLAN. the translation is noted below.

[Col. 0421C] BRUXELLEN. copies Ado’s text concerning Paulinus and adds the following from its own source: “By whom he is now wondrously glorified. His body was brought back to Trier, where it rests in the church bearing his name, in an underground crypt with the bodies of many martyrs who suffered under Rictiovarus.” In Aristides it is sufficiently pure. “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Optatus, bishop and confessor. Also Bishop Andanus.”

HAGENOYEN. writes “Aristion” instead of Aristides, but is otherwise pure in that entry; in Paulinus it is entirely Adonian. Then: “Also at Paris, the deposition of Saint Medericus, bishop and confessor.” See above, 29 August. “On the same day, blessed Genesius, martyr of Arles, who served as a court clerk. When he refused to record the impious edicts by which Christians were ordered to be punished, he was arrested and beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom after being baptized in his own blood.” In this codex the days are often changed and transposed, almost at the writer’s discretion; see Usuard, 25 [Col. 0421D] of this month. In Optatus it is sufficiently pure.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end: “On the same day, Saint Aidan, bishop, whose soul Saint Cuthbert saw being carried into heaven by angels. Also Saint Elladius, bishop.” He is recorded in the Hieronymian martyrologies on this day; see 8 May.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Aidan, bishop and confessor. Paulinus, bishop and confessor, sent into exile. Aristides the confessor, a most learned man.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL. sign. C: “Also Bishop Elladius.” I have already said that this belongs to 8 May.

In VATICAN. no. 5949, Optatus is absent.

ALTEMPS.: “In Kent, the deposition of Saint Eanswitha the virgin.” See above, ROSWEYD.

FLORENTIN.: “Also Saint Julian the confessor, who killed his father and mother; his life and death are recorded. Julian has been discussed elsewhere.”

BURDEGALEN.: “At Auxerre, Saint Optatus, bishop and confessor. Also Bishop Heraclius.” If this concerns the bishop of Sens, he is honored on 9 July.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition: “At Trier, the commemoration of Saint Paulinus, bishop and martyr. During the time of the Arian persecution, he was harassed by the emperor Constantius through various exiles for the Catholic faith even unto death, and at last, in Phrygia, in the year of the Lord 361, received from the Lord the crown of blessed suffering.” In Aristides it is pure up to “he concluded his speech”; it adds, “and proved it by many testimonies of the prophets.” In Optatus it is pure. At the end: “On the same day, blessed Belladius and Aulanus, bishops and confessors.” I would be mistaken if this did not indicate Elladius and Aidan, mentioned above. “In England, Saint Cuthburga the virgin.”

BELIN., besides the alteration in the first announcement, [Col. 0422C] adds at the end: “Also the holy martyrs Robustianus and Marcus.” See the Roman Martyrology, in which the former is also commemorated on 24 May.

GREVEN. adds Coloman the martyr. If this concerns Kilian’s companion, see 13 July. “In England, Saint Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne and confessor. As Bede testifies in Book III, he was renowned in life and miracles and took care to omit nothing of all that he had learned from the Gospel, Apostolic, or Prophetic writings ought to be done, but strove to fulfill everything according to his strength. Also at Marseilles, Saint Lazarus, bishop and martyr, whom the Lord raised from the dead. Usuard has him on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January. Justus and Clement, bishops and confessors. In England, Cuthburga, virgin and abbess. Potamia the virgin. In Egypt, very many virgins.”

MOLAN.: “At the place called Blandinium, the dedication and consecration of the basilica of the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. Also the holy martyrs Robustianus and Marcus. [Col. 0422D] The translation of Saint Hadulf, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Jotra, Saint Ebrarsilus, bishop and confessor.” Others call him Ebrigisilus. From that point, in smaller type: “In England, Saint Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne and confessor. As Bede testifies in Book III, renowned in life and miracles, he took care to omit nothing of all that he had learned from the Gospel, Apostolic, or Prophetic writings ought to be done, but strove to fulfill everything according to his strength.” These words are copied from GREVEN., as is what follows: “In England, Cuthburga, virgin and abbess.” Other editions have: “Also the holy martyrs Robustianus and Marcus. At the monastery of Jotra,” etc., as above. “On the same day, Saint Aidan, bishop, whose soul Saint Cuthbert saw being carried into heaven by angels. In England, Saint Cuthburga, virgin and queen. In the same place, the deposition of Saint Eanswitha, virgin and abbess.” See what was said above. [Col. 0423A] “At Arras, the translation of Saint Hadulf, bishop and confessor. At the place called Blandinium, the dedication,” etc., as in the earlier version. “On the thirty-first day, the deposition [Col. 0424A] of the most venerable girdle of the most holy Mother of God,” to which, in smaller type, is added: “On the anniversary of the dedication of the church at Chalcoprateia.” See Surius for this day.]

[Col. 0419]

At Trier, the feast of Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor, who, exiled by the emperor Constantius for the Catholic faith, was harassed even unto death, even beyond the Christian name, by changing places of exile, and at last died in Phrygia, receiving from the Lord the crown of blessed suffering. On the same day, at Athens, blessed Aristides, most renowned for faith and wisdom, who presented books concerning the Christian religion to the emperor Hadrian and, in the emperor’s presence, argued most eloquently that Christ Jesus alone was God. At Auxerre, Saint Optatus, bishop and confessor.

THE MONTH OF SEPTEMBER HAS 30 DAYS.

[Col. 0423]

On the Kalends. Day 1. [Note: [Col. 0423A]

Only Greven and Molan are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0423B]

For Sens, Greven reads “Senones.” Both he and Molan differ from the other codices in having “in his holy chalice”; nevertheless I have followed the others, although in one respect they depart from purity. The common addition of all is “Egidus the abbot,” placed in different locations and expressed by each in different wording. Castellanus reports concerning the Pratensis that beneath the final line of the calendar column, which is also the last line of the page, he found this addition in an ancient hand: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Egidius the abbot.” [Col. 0424B] In the Heriniensis, in the third-to-last place, it reads: “Also Saint Egidius the abbot.” In Antwerp-Major, after “chalice”: “On the same day, Saint Egidius, abbot and confessor.” In Rosweyd, in the final place: “In Provence, the feast of blessed Egidius, whose life was venerable for many signs of miracles.” Muneratus inserted, in the third place: “In Provence, Saint Egidius the abbot.” Such variation in the codices is, unless I am mistaken, clear evidence that Egidius did not belong to Usuard’s original reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0423C]

The prophets, placed here first, were transferred from the Little Roman Martyrology into Ado and thence into our text; Notker removed the title “prophets.” I do not yet understand why Castellanus claims that the final item should be referred to 12 December. The blessed prophetess who follows was first entered by Ado among the Feasts of the Apostles; later she was placed in the Martyrology after Priscus, whom Usuard put before her, taking from the aforesaid Feasts whatever eulogy he added. For the remainder, see Luke’s Gospel, chapter 2. Concerning Priscus, the Hieronymian codices read approximately as follows: “At Capua, on the Aquaria or Aquiri[a] Way, the feast of Saint Priscus.” The Little Roman Martyrology, omitting the way, has: “At Capua, Priscus the martyr, one of those ancient disciples of Christ.” Ado gives the more precise “on the Aquaria Way,” which Notker strangely suppressed. Our author transferred everything from Ado word for word. Whether the few things Peter has about him in Book VIII, chapter 17, of his Catalogue are sufficiently supported will be seen elsewhere. Sixtus, or Xystus, of Rheims, omitted by the older writers, was entered into the sacred calendars by Usuard, but in the simplest form, as is evident here; the additional material found in the modern Roman Martyrology will be shown in its proper place to be not equally certain, based on the tradition of Rheims preserved by Flodoard, Marlot, and others. Lupus of Sens is adorned by Ado with this sole eulogy: “Most illustrious in holiness and signs of miracles.” From this it may easily be inferred that the Viennese did not know the Acts of Lupus, which I judge Usuard clearly to have seen from the miracle reported. In some Hieronymian codices he is entered with Victor, Victorius, or Victurius of Le Mans; Florentius considers both additions foreign. Surius published the aforesaid Acts of Lupus, but in wording very different from the autograph; in due time we shall provide the text in its genuine and complete form. Wandalbert is more generous in his treatment of Joshua, and also rightly praises Priscus and Lupus, adding Verena, concerning whom see Molan in the Appendices. Thus he honors the others:

“The Lawgiver, who leaves his heir the honors properly due,

Joshua, who marked out for the people the promised land,

Distinguishing it perhaps through the stars, the places, the lofty mountains,

And the cities, holds and begins the Kalends of September;

Priscus, the martyr clad in blood, purifies these days.

And Bishop Lupus of Sens shines in a lofty church.”

Furthermore, Florus and Rabanus discuss Victor; their eulogies are entirely different, and other accounts published by more recent writers will provide abundant material for discussion in the Acts. Meanwhile see the notes of Baronius and Florentius. Also see the note of Father Mothier in the latest French translation of the Roman Martyrology, published in 1705, for this day. It is uncertain where Usuard obtained Victor—perhaps he saw some Acts, or perhaps he copied the name from Gregory of Tours. Henschenius excavated some material concerning the deeds of the bishops of Le Mans in his treatment of Thuribius, 16 April, p. 415 onward; Papebrochius collected more concerning their chronological succession on 19 June, in the Life of Innocent or Innocentius, p. 854 onward, after the Acts published by Mabillon in volume III of the Analecta, p. 46 onward. Whether the difficulties have been exhausted, judge from Tillemont, volume IV, p. 739 onward. But these matters must be decided elsewhere. Whatever conclusion one reaches, it is meanwhile clear from our codices that the text transmitted thus far is genuinely Usuardine; above we showed that Egidius must be excluded from it. Concerning Longinus in Ado, see the Appendices.]

[Note: [Col. 0425A]

Concerning DE PRATENS., we have spoken sufficiently above in the variant readings. See the cited Father Mothier concerning Egidius.

HERINIENS. inserts a proper Rheims entry in second place, namely: “At Rheims, the deposition of Saint Sixtus, the first bishop of that city, and of blessed Sinicius, his successor.” Concerning Egidius, see above. At the end another proper entry is added: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Nivardus, bishop.”

ANTUERP.-MAJ. is truncated in Priscus’s eulogy. More disgracefully, it confuses Sixtus with Lupus, assigning to the former Lupus’s eulogy concerning the gemstone, etc. Egidius has already been discussed.

ROSWEYD. improperly inserts, in fourth place: “At Alexandria, Peter, bishop and martyr, who first condemned the presbyter Arius with the bond of anathema.” See 26 November. In the penultimate place it inserts: “Saint Verena the virgin.” At the end it treats Egidius as above.

PULSANEN. is pure in the first, second, and third entries, but omits Sixtus. It continues: “At Sens, blessed Lupus, bishop and martyr. On the same day, Saint Egidius the abbot.”

[Col. 0425B] ANTUERP., MAX-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. are sufficiently pure, but add at the end: “Also Egidius the abbot.” The first omits Anna’s name. Instead of Victor, they write Victurius and Victurius, perhaps not incorrectly. He is also called Victorius.

MUNERAT. has “Agnes” instead of Anna. In the third place, concerning Egidius, as above. Instead of “holy chalice,” it reads “sacred chalice.” At the end it adds: “At Amiens, the passing of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor.” The recent dissertations of D. l’Estocq and others concerning this Firminus should be consulted.

ANTUERP.-MAX. and LOVANIEN. are sufficiently pure, but in the penultimate place have: “Also, the feast of Saint Egidius the abbot.” They also have Victurius or Victurius.

ULTRAJECT. and LEYDEN. begin: “At Benevento, the feast of the twelve holy martyr brothers: Donatus and Felix, Aruntius and Honoratus, Fortunatianus and Savinianus, Septiminus and Januarius, Felix and Vitalis, Saturninus and Repositus. After converting very many by their preaching, they suffered capital punishment under the emperor Maximian and the judge Valerian.” See their Acts, written in hexameter verse, in Surius for this day. The Prophets and Anna follow as in the text. Then: “In the territory of Constance, at the place called Aquae Durae, Saint Verena the virgin.” A long eulogy by Notker may be consulted concerning her. The remaining items of the text follow; in the penultimate place: “Also, the feast of Saint Egidius the abbot.”

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. are almost identical with the Beneventan entries above; in second place they put: “In Provence, Saint Egidius the abbot, a man of great virtues.” Then come the Prophets and Anna. “In the territory of Constance,” etc., as above. Then the text.

CENTULEN. is pure in the prophets. “On the same day, the most blessed prophetess Agnes, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, whose holiness the Gospel records. At Rheims, the metropolis of the Franks, the holy confessors and pontiffs Sixtus, Sinicius, and Nivardus. At Sens, Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor. At Amiens, Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor. At Capua, on the Aquaria Way, Saint Priscus the martyr, who was one of those ancient disciples of Christ. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Egidius the abbot, whom every class of people seeks and venerates because of the merit of his holiness.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “Saint Egidius, abbot and confessor, a man of great virtues. Coming from Greece to Provence, he became renowned for marvelous holiness. During the solemn celebration of Mass, an angel brought him upon the altar a letter containing a certain hidden sin of King Charlemagne, which the king himself had never dared confess to anyone. After confessing it, Saint Egidius the abbot departed to the Lord.” In the entries for the prophets, Anna, and Priscus, it is sufficiently pure. Then: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Longinus the soldier and martyr, who is said to be the man who opened the side of the Lord hanging on the cross with a lance. Later baptized by the Apostles, he was beheaded for the faith of Christ; and Aphrodisius the record-keeper was beheaded and crowned together with him.” This is substantially from Ado; see Usuard, 15 March. Concerning the Beneventans, it has almost the same material as above. In Lupus, Sixtus, and Victurius it is sufficiently pure. Instead of Verena, it writes Serena, concerning whom it says the same things as above in ULT., etc.

HAGENOYEN. deals only with Joshua, attaching to him a eulogy from sacred history. Then: “In the territory of Constance, at the place called Aquae Durae, that is, Zurziatum, the deposition of Saint Verena the virgin, illustrious in the glory of miracles and holiness.” In Lupus it is not entirely pure. Then: “Also Vivardus [perhaps Nivardus?] and Firminus, bishops and confessors.” Concerning Anna, it adds some material from the Gospel. “Also Saint Longinus, the soldier and martyr who pierced the Lord’s side. Also the seven brother martyrs.” In Priscus it is pure. It tells much about Egidius, which there is no time to transcribe. At the end, concerning Sixtus and Victurius, it is sufficiently pure.

AQUICINCT. places third: “On the same day, Saint Egidius the abbot.” At the end, in a more recent hand, it adds: “On the same day, at Amiens, blessed Firminus, bishop and confessor, who, while celebrating Mass, saw the hand of the Lord in the heights above the consecrating chalice [or perhaps above the consecrated or consecrating chalice].”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130, have at the end: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Egidius the abbot, resting beside the sea’s pond. In Tuscany, Saint Terentianus, bishop. At Benevento, the twelve brothers.”

AMBIANEN.: “At Amiens, the passing of blessed Firminus, bishop and confessor. Among the other signs of his goodness, while he consecrated the Lord’s body on earth, he deserved to see his hand in heaven.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Sixtus and Sinicius, bishops. Lupus, bishop and confessor. Egidius, abbot. Sanina, virgin.” A marginal note says: “I cannot find Sanina, but Verena is correct. The twelve brother martyrs,” undoubtedly those of Benevento. “Also Joshua and Gideon.”

REGINAE SUEC. no. 428: “In Provence, Saint Egidius the abbot. At Amiens, the translation of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949, Joshua, Gideon, Sixtus, and Victor are absent. It adds: “At Benevento, the feast of the twelve brother martyrs. At Todi, Saint Terentianus, bishop and martyr.”

STROZZIAN., etc.: “In the territory of Todi, Saint Terentianus, bishop and martyr. At Capua, Saint Priscus . . . Also Saint Fidelis the confessor, who was the companion of Saint Cerbonius, bishop of Populonia, and rests near that city, a man of great holiness. In Africa, Saint Regulus, bishop and martyr, whose body rests in the basilica of Saint Martin in the city of Lucca. Also Saint Mamertinus the abbot, at the monastery of Saint Germanus, where he became abbot after Saint Alodius and, living laudably there before God and men, rested in peace.”

LUGDUNEN.: “In the territory of Menosus, the feast of Saint Egidius.” Others give more about him.

BIZUNTICEN. after Victor adds: “Also at Autun, the reception of the body of Saint Lazarus, whom the Lord Jesus raised from the dead.”

REMENS. SS. Timothei et Apoll.: “At Rheims, the deposition of the blessed confessors and likewise of the pontiffs of that same city, Sixtus, Sinicius, and Nivardus.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition is pure in its first form; in the second it inserted “daughter of Phanuel.” Then: “In Provence, Saint Egidius the abbot, a man of great virtues. Born at Athens from a royal and most Christian lineage and adequately instructed in sacred letters, after the death of both his parents he distributed his patrimony to the poor. Fleeing the danger of human praise, he withdrew into a more remote wilderness near the river Rhône, to a place called Septimania, and, remaining there for three years, lived only on the roots of herbs and the milk of a certain doe. At last the Lord revealed to him through the Spirit the day of his death; he announced it to the brothers and happily departed to the Lord. At Trier, the translation of Saint Matthias the Apostle from Rome to Trier,” etc., as we shall describe more fully below from GREVEN. It continues: “At Benevento,” concerning the twelve brothers, as above. “In the city of Amiens, the deposition of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor. He flourished with such knowledge and holiness that he became the teacher and ruler of all the churches of Europe. Then he was ordained bishop of the church of Amiens, and after completing forty-seven years of life, passing to Christ, he rested in a holy death. He was buried in the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary beside the body of his predecessor, Saint Firminus, martyr and bishop, whose name he himself had received.” [Col. 0427B] In Priscus and Sixtus it is pure. Concerning Lupus of Sens, it joins Ado’s eulogy to Usuard’s. “At Le Mans, Saint Victurius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Vivardus, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN., although not sufficiently polished in the text, adds: “Also Saint Egidius the abbot. On the same day, at Benevento, the twelve holy brother martyrs.” In the second edition: “On the same day, Saint Lazarus the martyr.”

GREVEN.: “On this day, according to Ado, Longinus the soldier and martyr, who opened the Lord’s side with a lance. Baptized by the Apostles, while he was living as a leading man in Cappadocia, he was arrested for confessing Christ; his tongue was cut out, his teeth were knocked out, and he was beheaded, triumphing. Usuard has him on the Ides of March. With him was crowned Aphrodisius the record-keeper, who, after his tongue had been cut out, spoke of Christ fluently. At Bethsaida Prima, the feast of Saint Marcialis [first edition: Marcianus], bishop, Sisinnius, and Amantius. Peter, bishop [Col. 0427C] of Alexandria and martyr.” In the Beneventan entries, almost as above. “Terentianus, bishop and martyr. According to others, however, on the third day before the Kalends of September. In the Tuscan city of Lucca, Saint Regulus, bishop and martyr. Also Saints Constantius and Felicianus. At Rheims, Vivardus, bishop and confessor. At Amiens, Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor, who was named Firminus by his father Faustianus, a nobleman, in honor of Saint Firminus of Amiens, the glorious bishop and martyr whom he himself had buried. Since he was outstanding in life and learning, and had energetically governed that church for many years, he fell happily asleep in the Lord. On the same day, according to the Catalogue, Saint Bercharius, abbot and martyr. First instructed in character and wisdom under Saint Vivardus, bishop of Rheims, and then under Eustasius the abbot in the monastery of Luxeuil, he was once drawing drink from a vessel when, summoned by the abbot’s command, he immediately left everything behind and hastened to answer the summons without even stopping the vessel from which he had been drawing. While liquid continued to flow constantly from that vessel, when it became full the liquid began to rise upward—so that the merit of his obedience might be made known—and none of it flowed down onto the ground. Later he was killed by a son whom he had rebuked for a fault and deserved to be numbered among the martyrs. At Rheims, Saint Sinicius, bishop and confessor. Near the town of Arles in Provence, Saint Egidius, abbot and confessor. In the year of the Lord [Col. 0428A] 715, coming from Athens, where he had a distinguished ancestry, he remained for two years with Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles. But desiring the wilderness and fearing the danger of human praise, he secretly departed to a place called Septimania, where the Rhône flows into the sea, and lived for three years on roots of herbs and the milk of a certain doe. At last, after building a monastery and instructing many in contempt for the world and the monastic life, he rested in peace, full of faith and good works. Rothildis, queen of France. In the diocese of Constance, Saint Verena the virgin, from the company of the holy Thebans. At Trier, the translation of Saint Matthias the Apostle from the city of Rome. When, at the request of Saint Helena, a native of Trier, Pope Sylvester was sending the blessed Agricus, patriarch of Antioch, as bishop to the people of Trier, the aforesaid empress handed over to him through Saint Sylvester the seamless tunic of the Lord, together with one of the nails and the knife [the first edition: Christ] which he had used at the supper. In addition, she gave him the body of Saint Matthias the Apostle, which she herself had transferred from Judea to Rome, so that she might bring these relics to her own city with fitting honor. When he came to Trier, he distributed the sacred relics in various places; but he honorably placed Saint Matthias beside the bodies of the holy fathers Eucharius and Valerius, bishops. Also at Trier, the discovery of the same Apostle at Saint Eucharius.” The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition likewise has this.

MOLAN., after Victor the bishop, adds: “Whose deeds are recorded as outstanding in holiness and miracles. Also Saint Egidius the abbot in Provence. At Amiens, the passing of Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor. The translation of Saint Matthias the Apostle from Rome to Trier. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Nivardus. At Rheims, the deposition of blessed Sinicius, successor of Saint Sixtus, the first bishop of that city. On the same day, at Benevento, the twelve holy brother martyrs. At Aquae Durae, the feast of Saint Verena the virgin.” Concerning this same Saint Verena, Wandalbert sang in his final verse:

“Here too shine the solemn rites of holy Verena.”

Then, in smaller type: “On the Sunday before the Nativity of blessed Mary, Mother of God, at Louvain in the basilica of Saint Peter, the solemn commemoration of the feasts of that same most blessed Virgin, which is celebrated festively with the joy of the entire city.” Other editions have the same eulogy concerning Victor that we gave above. “Also in Provence, Saint Egidius the abbot.” Concerning the Beneventans, as in the first edition. “At Altvillare, the deposition of Saint Nivardus, bishop of Rheims.” Concerning Firminus, briefly, as above. “In the territory of Coutances, at Aquae Durae, etc. On the first day, Saint Aithalas the martyr, and the forty holy women martyrs, and Ammon the deacon and teacher of those women; and the holy martyrs Callistes, Evodius, and Hermogenes, brothers. Also the beginning of the indiction and of the new year, and the commemoration of the most blessed Mother of God, at Masinis. At Trier, the translation of Saint Matthias the Apostle from Rome.” Again, in smaller type: “On the first Sunday of September, at Louvain in the basilica, etc.,” as above. With no less ceremony, the same solemnity of the feast of Recollection, etc., is celebrated each year at Antwerp on the Sunday after the octave of the Assumption of the same most blessed Virgin.]

[Col. 0423]

Joshua son of Nun and Gideon, prophets. Also the birth-feast of the most blessed prophetess Anna, whose holiness the Gospel narrative reveals. At Capua, on the Aquarian Road, Saint Priscus the martyr, who was one of Christ’s ancient disciples. At Reims, the burial of Saint Sixtus, the city’s first bishop. At Sens, blessed Lupus, bishop and confessor, of whom it is related that one day, while he was standing before the sacred altars in the presence of the clergy, a jewel fell from heaven into his holy chalice. At Le Mans, Saint Victor, bishop. [Bouillart adds, in italic type: “[Note: [Col. 0423B] The ancient hand inserted Aegidius into this entry, and so ancient is it that the distinction is obscure. Nevertheless, Sollerius knew that it was different from the first, and we readily acknowledge this ourselves. Why, then, does he erase the Pratense codex from the list of pure witnesses for so slight a reason? BOUILLART.]”] On the same day, the birth-feast of Saint Giles, abbot.

## IV Non. Day 2. [Note: [Col. 0427]

Thus read the Pratense, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0429A]

There is a notable variation between the older and more recent manuscripts. The former, following Usuard’s intention, present the eulogy of Justus contracted from two entries of Ado, namely from this day and from 14 October; others, such as the Antwerp and Max-Lübeck manuscripts, seem to have drawn it from this day alone, as will become clear to anyone comparing the Appendices with Ado.

Among the pure manuscripts the principal difference is this: the Pratense, Antwerp-Major, and Munerat form an imperfect construction: “he earned the kingdom of heaven by blessed gain, ascending”; others have the smoother reading, “to ascend the kingdom of heaven by blessed gain,” and so forth. See Ado on 14 October, where you will find: “and, as a worthy end should crown such great labours, promising the kingdom of heaven,” and so forth. The reading expressed by us in the text seems certain.

We have spoken elsewhere about *heremum* or *eremum*. Muneratus writes *Elipidii* instead of *Helpidii*, and *In Appia* instead of *In Appamia*. Greven, Molan, and others have *Apamia*: whichever way you write it, I am indifferent.]

[Note: [Col. 0429A]

Justus of Lyons, the most renowned bishop after Irenaeus, “has the appearance,” says Florentinius, “of an addition by an antiquarian to the Hieronymian Martyrologies,” although he notes several things from Theophilus Raynaudus and others that may shed light on the Acts. You will find him marked on this very day by Florus and Rabanus, so that there is no apparent reason why some should attack Ado for placing Justus on this day.

Perhaps no one deserves less criticism, since today he explains most clearly that Justus departed to the Lord on the day before the Ides of October, while his body, together with the bones of blessed Viator, his attendant, was brought back to Lyons by devout citizens and buried with fitting honour in the basilica of the blessed seven brothers, the Maccabees, and the most glorious martyrs, on 4 September.

If you compare Ado’s words, both here and on 14 October, with the eulogies of Florus and Rabanus, you will rightly doubt whether each of them drew his account from the same Acts. Notker, almost reproducing Ado here, contrary to Ado’s express statement, refers the translation of the body to 14 October.

It is certain concerning Usuard that he celebrates the saint’s birth-feast today, although he had read and compared both of Ado’s announcements and had extracted from each of them what he needed to compose his own eulogy. Some unlearned copyists of later manuscripts, failing to notice this and altering Usuard’s wording, thought that everything had to be taken from the little entry of Ado for this day alone; we shall give their words in the Appendices.

Baronius, Severtius, Hermantius in his treatment of Ambrose, and others will provide further material, to be considered in their proper places. Among these Tillemont will not be the least important, in volume VIII, pages 546 and 798.

The Latin Acts are extant in Surius on this day, but, as usual, with their style polished away; we shall restore them to their integrity from several of our manuscripts. Wandalbert sings briefly of Justus alone:

> Hence, on the fourth before the Nones, Justus honours Lyons.

There is no memory of Helpidius in the sacred Calendars earlier than Ado, from whom Usuard and Notker received a somewhat contracted form of the wording. The praised Severtius says little about him on page 39.

Antoninus—whoever he may be, whether one person or several—provides material for many controversies. Thus the Hieronymian copies have him today: “In the regions of Apamia, the birth-feast of Saints Anthony and Antoninus.” Florentinius carefully collects much concerning these entries: concerning the place of martyrdom, whether it should be sought in Syria or in Aquitania; and concerning the distinction or identity of Anthony and Antoninus, who are joined together in the aforesaid copies.

Others debate whether this is the same Anthony who is read on this and the following day in those same copies; and again, whether Ado, Usuard, and others rightly assign some Antoninus to Capua on the following day. On all these matters Baronius, Chiffletius, and finally Tillemont have different opinions, the latter in volume IV, in his treatment of Dionysius of Paris, article 10 and note 15, pages 464 and 720.

The curious reader may consult these works for the present, until the Acts—rejected by the last-mentioned scholar and his followers—are examined by us more carefully in their proper time and place. See also the Appendices in the Utrecht, Centula, Victorine, and other manuscripts.

The author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*, who omits the first two, explicitly records Antoninus, in the simple form through which the entry passed into Ado and Usuard; Notker writes *Antonii* instead of *Antonini*. The Capuan Antoninus, a boy of twenty years, will be treated on the following day. Let these remarks suffice concerning the genuineness and simplicity of our Usuardian reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0429C]

The Rosweyd manuscript, not entirely pure in the text, adds at the end:

> “At the city of Toul, Saint Mansuetus, bishop. At Nicomedia, Saint Anicetus. Also Photinus with his companions, who, having been thrown into the public baths, gave up their spirit amid the flames.”

See the Acts of these saints published by Surius.

The Pulsen manuscript is quite pure at the beginning and end but is defective in the middle, where Helpidius is concerned.

The Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, Antwerp-Major, and Louvain manuscripts belong to those that alter Usuard’s wording in this way:

> “The birth-feast of Saint Justus, bishop of Lyons, a man of remarkable holiness and prophetic spirit, who indeed died in Egypt, but whose body, together with the bones of blessed Viator, his attendant, was brought back to Lyons by devout citizens and buried with fitting honour in the basilica.”

The rest is pure, except that the Antwerp-Major manuscript writes *Anthony* instead of *Antoninus*.

The Utrecht, Albergen, and Danic manuscripts begin as follows: [Col. 0429D]

> “At Apamia, Saint Antoninus the martyr. When he was seized and struck down by pagans, his body was torn by them into many pieces, but in a moment it was divinely reunited, so that the individual limbs, previously scattered, were restored to one and the same structure.”

They have Justus as the Antwerp manuscript and the others do. They are pure in the entry for Helpidius.

The Leiden manuscript agrees with the preceding ones in substance but differs in order, announcing Justus first, as he appears in the Usuardian text.

[Col. 0430C] The Centula manuscript:

> “In Gaul, in the territory of Cahors, Saint Antoninus, priest and martyr. On the same day, another Saint Antoninus, a boy and martyr. At Lyons, Saint Justus, bishop. And in the same place, Saint Elpidius, bishop and confessor.”

The Brussels manuscript begins:

> “At Apamia, the birth-feast of Saint Antoninus the martyr. He was seized and struck down by pagans; and when his body had been torn into many pieces, in a moment …,”

as above.

> “At Lyons in Gaul, Saint Justus, bishop and confessor, a man of remarkable holiness and prophetic spirit. Secretly abandoning his episcopate, he went to Egypt; there, withdrawing into the desert, he lived for several years among monks a life close to that of angels, and fell asleep in peace. His body, together with the bones of blessed Victor, his attendant, was brought back to Lyons and buried in a basilica.”

The entry for Helpidius is pure.

The Hagenoyen manuscript:

> “At Lyons in Gaul, the birth-feast of Saint Justus, bishop and confessor, a man of remarkable holiness and prophetic spirit. He withdrew into the desert, etc.”

The text is fairly pure. The entry for Helpidius is also pure. It continues:

> “At Beneventum, the birth-feast of the holy martyrs and brothers Donatus, Felix, Arontius, Honoratus, Fortunatus, Savianus, Septiminus, Januarius, Felix, Vitalis, and Repositus. After they had converted many to the faith by their preaching, under the emperor Maximian and the judge Valerian they received the sentence of death. Their feast is celebrated on the Kalends of September.”

Why, then, are they recorded on this day? For Antoninus it agrees with the Utrecht manuscript and the others.

The Aquicinct manuscript has at the end:

> “At the city of Toul, Saint Mansuetus, bishop and confessor.”

See the manuscripts among the Appendices for the following day.

The Victorine manuscript also has at the end:

> “In the city of Bruges, the passion of Saint Antoninus the Levite, with John the priest and Almachius the boy. Also Saint Zeno with two boys.”

The Matrician, Carthusian-Utrecht manuscripts:

> “The translation of Agnes to Utrecht. Aigulphus, abbot and martyr, with his companions. Helpidius, bishop and confessor. Justus, bishop. Antoninus, martyr.”

The Swedish Royal manuscript, shelfmark 130:

> “Also Saint Zeno with two boys.”

The Florentine manuscript:

> “At the city of Volterra, Saint Octavian, hermit and confessor, an African by birth, a man of remarkable holiness and renowned for miracles. He came with Saint Regulus, bishop, to the aforesaid city; at last he ended his life in a single elm tree, and his body rests there in the cathedral church. Also Saint Terentius the martyr, who suffered under the emperor Alexander and rests at the city of Todi, in a place called Petroso, at the eighth milestone.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins:

> “In the territory of Constance, at the place called Aquae Durae, the birth-feast of Saint Verena, virgin. She accompanied the company of the holy Theban martyrs.”

See the Appendices for the preceding day. In the entry for Antoninus it is nearly like the Utrecht manuscript. After “was torn apart,” it inserts:

> “together with his severed head, it was immediately plunged into the river, so divinely …”

Then, after “were restored,” it adds:

> “and were honourably buried by the faithful.”

In the entry for Justus it agrees with the Antwerp manuscript. In that for Helpidius it is pure. At the end:

> “On the same day, Saint Nonnosus the monk.”

See Molan and the Roman Martyrology.

The Belin manuscript, whose text is fairly pure, adds:

> “Also Saint Cosmas, confessor and hermit.”

Greven:

> “At Nineveh, Saint Tobias the prophet. At Nicomedia, the holy brothers Anicetus and Photinus, martyrs, who, after overcoming countless torments, were finally thrown with others of both sexes into a fiery furnace and surrendered undefiled spirits to their Creator, in the time of Diocletian.”

See Surius.

> “Elpidius, abbot, a man of remarkable abstinence. Antonius, confessor. Joseph. Nonnosus, monk and confessor. Justinus, confessor. Cosmas, confessor, who, leading the eremitical life on the island of Crete, fell asleep in peace. At Lower Utrecht, the translation of Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr. Agricola, bishop of Avignon and confessor.”

Molan:

> “Also Saint Cosmas, confessor and hermit. At Lower Utrecht, the translation of Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr. At Reims, the burial of Saint Alpinus, bishop.”

Then in smaller type:

> “Nonnosus, monk and confessor, of whom Gregory writes in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 7, that among other miracles he moved a huge stone by his prayers, repaired a broken lamp, and increased oil.”

Other editions read as follows:

> “Also Saint Cosmas, confessor and hermit, whose body was translated from Crete to Venice. On the same day, blessed Brocard, priest and prior general of Carmel, a man of great holiness. On the second day, Saint John the Faster, holy father. On the same day at Utrecht, the translation of Agnes, virgin. At Donzy, the elevation of the body of Saint Ragenfredis, virgin.”

She is commemorated on 8 October.]

[Col. 0427]

At Lyons in Gaul, the birth-feast of Saint Justus, bishop and confessor, who withdrew into the desert and, after living for several years a life close to that of angels, when a worthy end had come to such great labours, earned the kingdom of heaven by blessed gain. His holy little body, together with the bones of blessed Viator, his attendant, was later brought back to Lyons. On the same day, in the aforesaid city, Saint Helpidius, bishop and confessor. At Apamia, Saint Antoninus the martyr.

## III Non. Day 3. [Note: [Col. 0431]

The Antwerp-Major, Greven, and Molan manuscripts are pure and complete.]

[Note: [Col. 0431C]

Molan correctly writes *Phoebe*; Greven has *Febes*; I follow the others, who generally have *Feben*. In *Seraphia*, Antwerp-Major follows the spelling of the *Little Roman Martyrology* and Ado, rather than the more common form found in our manuscripts.

Some read “the Kalends of August,” such as the Pratense and Herinien manuscripts, but the others agree with the text. In Greven and Molan, *tradita* is placed after *viris*. All write *Aristei*, not *Aristaei*.

The Pratense is excluded because at the end it added: “At Rome, the ordination of Saint Gregory the pope,” as is explicitly reported in our copy. Nevertheless, I am surprised that this addition escaped the sharp eye of Castellanus.

The Herinien manuscript, whose text is otherwise pure, also adds:

> “On the same day, the birth-feast of Saint Remaclus, bishop and confessor.”

Rosweyd has:

> “At Stavelot, Saint Remaclus, bishop.”

Others have other additions, which we shall list in the Appendices.]

[Note: [Col. 0431C]

Ado is the first to mention Phoebe among the feasts of the apostles; Usuard took the entry from him. Concerning her, the blessed Apostle writes to the Romans—“I commend to you …”; Usuard omitted the Apostle’s words from Romans 16, though the aforesaid Ado sets them out there.

Concerning the following virgin, the *Little Roman Martyrology* reads:

> “At Rome, Saint Seraphia, virgin, who suffered on the fourth before the Kalends of August and was buried on the second before the Kalends; on the third before the Nones of September the memory of her passion is celebrated with greater solemnity.”

Ado derives from the Acts, at greater length, both this account and the entire outstanding martyrdom of the virgin, preserving the name Seraphia and likewise noting the day of her passion, the fourth before the Kalends of August.

Here you will observe that Ado did not err, as though the day of the blessed Sabina’s struggle had to be reckoned, which falls on the fourth before the Kalends of September, or 29 August. We treated that most illustrious martyr, together with our present subject, from the same Ado. For the Acts indicate there that, after several days had intervened, Seraphia first suffered and was buried before Sabina became a participant in the same glory. How easily those several days could extend into a month!

Apart from this, Notker greatly contracted Ado’s eulogy here; our author extracted everything that we have transmitted in the text together with it. The Acts have been examined with sufficient scrupulousness by some recent scholars and will be illustrated by new studies at the proper time. Surius published them on this day; they must then be compared with the manuscripts. See also Tillemont’s French translation, volume II, beginning at page 246, and the notes relating to it beginning at page 597.

The difficulty mentioned on the preceding day recurs here concerning Antoninus, whom Ado placed at Capua with the bishop Aristaeus, contrary to the very explicit testimony of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, which clearly place that Antoninus—or Anthony, whoever he may have been—in Syria, together with other circumstances. Rabanus follows them, reproducing part of their words.

But we have already said that these matters provide material for many controversies. Castellanus meanwhile roundly asserts that today’s Antoninus is the same as the one commemorated on the preceding day. Others, even more categorically, combine four Antoninuses into one: the Syrian Antoninus of Apamia, the Gallic Antoninus of Apamia, the Capuan Antoninus, and the Piacenzan Antoninus, who is placed on 30 September.

Here again you see many doubts and complexities. Florentinius labours diligently to clarify them, and we shall discuss the same matters more carefully elsewhere. I do not know whether Notker suspected the Capuan Antoninus; certainly he says nothing about him.

Usuard copied his entire announcement from Ado, even noting that Acts existed which, in all likelihood, neither he nor Ado had ever seen. Wandalbert’s verses, unless I am mistaken, support the more common opinion:

> On the third day, Antoninus, boy and martyr, you triumph,
>
> and then Bishop Aristaeus, blessed in death.

In the same Ado, both in Mosander’s and in Rosweyd’s editions, I read Remaclus of Utrecht and Mansuetus of Toul. One might almost doubt whether they are genuinely Ado’s, given the silence of our Usuardian manuscripts, at least the purer ones, and of Notker.

Even if we grant that Ado recorded them, I nevertheless consider it certain that Usuard omitted them. His pure and complete text, as produced by me, seems beyond any doubt once everything rejected above in the Variants has been excluded.]

[Note: [Col. 0433A]

As I have already said, the Pratense adds at the end:

> “At Rome, the ordination [Col. 0433B] of Saint Gregory the pope.”

The Herinien also has at the end:

> “On the same day, the birth-feast of Saint Remaclus, bishop and confessor.”

In the margin, written in nearly the same hand, it adds:

> “Also at Provins, Saint Aigulphus, glorious martyr.”

See Surius concerning both.

Rosweyd reads *eleven years* instead of *a boy of twenty years*; others have *ten years*. He also has at the end:

> “At Stavelot, Saint Remaclus, bishop.”

The Pulsen manuscript is pure up to “she was beheaded.” Everything else is missing.

The Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, and Ughellian manuscripts lack the first entry. At the end they add:

> “At the city of Toul, Mansuetus, bishop.”

The Munerat manuscript adds after the text:

> “At the city of Sées, Saint Godegrand, bishop and martyr.”

The Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Albergen, and Danic manuscripts all lack the first announcement. They are pure in the second. It continues:

> “At the city of Toul, Saint Mansuetus, bishop. In the territory of Liège, at the monastery of Stavelot, the birth-feast of Saint Remaclus, bishop and confessor.”

They are pure in the last entry. All except Antwerp-Major add to Remaclus the title “glorious bishop.”

The Centula manuscript:

> “The birth-feast of Saint Phoebe, disciple of the Apostles. At Rome, Saint Seraphia, virgin, who came from Antioch, converted blessed Sabina, and completed her martyrdom at Rome. At Capua, Saint Aristaeus the martyr. At Rome, the ordination of blessed Gregory the pope, teacher of the whole Church and apostle of the English.”

The Brussels manuscript:

> “In the territory of Liège, at the monastery of Stavelot, the burial of Saint Remaclus, glorious bishop and confessor. He came from Aquitania to the monastery of Solignac, where under blessed Eligius he trained himself in Christ’s service; later he was ordained bishop of Utrecht above the Meuse. But finally, wishing to flee the tumult of the crowd, he had blessed Theodard appointed in his place in the episcopate and undertook the governance of the monastery of Stavelot, where he fell asleep in peace.”

The entire text that follows is fairly pure. It adds:

> “At the city of Toul, Saint Mansuetus, bishop and confessor. At Prüm, Saint Aigulphus, abbot of the monastery of Lérins [his name is pronounced in various ways, but, to state it once, read ‘of Lérins’], and martyr. At Ghent, on Mount Blandinium, the translation of the holy bodies of Ausbert and Wulfrannus, archbishops, and Wandregisilus, abbot. Also at Rome, the ordination of blessed Gregory the pope.”

See the Greven Appendix.

The Hagenoyen manuscript writes *Paphen* instead of *Phoebe*. In second place:

> “At the city of Toul, the burial of Saint Mansuetus, bishop and confessor, the first bishop of that city. He was born of noble Scottish stock and derived his name from the gentleness of his mind. This saint, who surpasses human praise. This holy man was a disciple of the blessed apostle Peter, etc.”

This material is taken from Acts that are not sufficiently trustworthy. The entry for Seraphia is somewhat interpolated. For Remaclus it agrees with Antwerp-Major above.

> “At Rome, the ordination of blessed Gregory the pope, an ordination which the emperor Maurice ordered to be carried out and compelled him to become supreme pontiff. At Capua, the holy martyrs Aristaeus, bishop, and Antoninus, a boy.”

The Aquicinct manuscript inserts in the penultimate place:

> “On the same day, Saint Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren.”

At the end:

> “At the monastery of Lérins, the passion of Saint Aigulphus the martyr.”

Then, in a more recent hand:

> “And the ordination to the episcopate of blessed Gregory the pope.”

The Victorine and Swedish Royal manuscripts, shelfmark 130, have at the end:

> “At the city of Toul, Mansuetus, bishop. At the monastery of Lérins, Saint Aigulphus the martyr.”

The Matrician, Carthusian-Utrecht manuscripts:

> “Seraphia, virgin and martyr. Remaclus, bishop of Tongeren. Mansuetus, bishop, disciple of blessed Peter.”

The Swedish Royal manuscript, number 130, additionally has:

> “At Rome, the election and ordination of the distinguished and most learned Gregory the pope.”

[Col. 0434C] In Vatican manuscript 5949, Phoebe and Seraphia are absent. It adds:

> “At Aquileia, Saint Syricus and Saint Euphemia.”

The Florentine manuscript:

> “At the city of Toul, Saint Mansuetus, bishop. At Rome, the ordination of Saint Gregory the pope. In the district of Liège, at Scapachel [by which it means Stavelot], Saint Remaclus, bishop and confessor.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins:

> “The ordination to the supreme pontificate of Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, a supreme and incomparable man and confessor.”

The entry for Seraphia is interpolated from Ado.

> “At the city of Toul, Saint Mansuetus, bishop and confessor, whom blessed Peter sent into Gaul, etc.”

For Remaclus, it is much as above, etc. The entry for Antoninus is fairly pure.

> “At the monastery of Lucca, Saint Aigulphus, abbot and martyr. On the same day, blessed Emeric, duke of Hungary and confessor.”

The Belin manuscript omits Phoebe. Its entry for Seraphia is mutilated. At the end it adds:

> “At the city of Toul, Saint Mansuetus, bishop [Col. 0434D] and confessor. On the same day at Pavia, Saint Marinus. The ordination to the supreme pontificate of the incomparable Gregory the pope. And the birth-feast of Saint Sebenda, whom the Apostle mentions in his Epistle to the Romans.”

Whether there is any relationship between Sebenda and Phoebe, judge for yourself; nevertheless, they are combined in this way in another edition. Then:

> “On the same day, Saint Arnulfus, abbot of the monastery of Lérins,”

instead of Aigulphus.

Greven:

> “At the city of Sées, Saints Godegrand, bishop and martyr, and Godegrand, bishop and confessor of that same city. At the monastery of Lucca, Saint Aigulphus, abbot and martyr. At Rome, the ordination to the supreme pontificate of the most blessed and incomparable Gregory the pope and doctor of the Church, performed in the year of the Lord 592.

> At the city of the Leuci, or Toul, the burial of Saint Mansuetus, bishop and confessor. Born of illustrious Scottish blood, he was ordained bishop at Rome by blessed Peter, announced the Gospel of Christ as the first bishop to the aforesaid city, and, renowned for his life and miracles, fell asleep in peace.

> In the territory of Liège, at the monastery of Stavelot, the burial of Saint Remaclus, bishop of Upper Utrecht and confessor. Born of noble parents from the diocese of Bourges, he was entrusted to Saint Eligius and placed by him in the monastery of Solignac; there he grew in great holiness. He was then taken to govern the aforementioned church, but, out of love for the solitary life, eventually obtained permission for another to succeed him. By word and example he encouraged many to give themselves to the service of the Almighty, and he fell asleep after a blessed end.

> Ambrose, bishop of Sens and confessor. The translation of Saint Renobertus, bishop and confessor. In Hungary, Saint Emeric, duke and confessor, son of Saint Stephen, king of Hungary. Warned from heaven, he preserved bodily integrity with the virgin betrothed to him to the end, and became renowned for miracles.

> At Pavia, Saint Maricius. At Aquileia, the passion of Saints Euphemia, Dorothea, Thecla [the first edition has ‘Tecla’], and Erasma, virgins and martyrs. For the faith of Christ, they were first beaten with rods, then their heads were crushed with iron hammers, and finally, after being burned with torches and having their breasts cut off, they attained the glory of martyrdom through beheading.”

Molan:

> “On Mount Blandinium in the territory of Ghent, the arrival of the holy bodies of Wandregisilus, abbot, and Ausbertus and Wulfrannus, archbishops. At the city of Toul, Saint Mansuetus, bishop and confessor. On the same day at Pavia, Saint Marinus. The ordination to the supreme pontificate of the incomparable Gregory the pope. On the same day, Saint Arnulfus, abbot of the monastery of Lérins.”

He took this from Belin, but, unless I am mistaken, it is Aigulphus himself who follows:

> “Also at Prüm, Saint Aigulphus, glorious martyr. On the same day, in the territory of Liège, in the Ardennes, at the monastery of Stavelot, the burial of Saint Remaclus, bishop and confessor. At the city of Sées, Saint Godegrand, bishop and martyr.”

Then in smaller type:

> “His passion is contained in the Life of Saint Oportuna, his sister, the virgin. Also Godegrand, bishop and confessor of that same city.”

Other editions:

> “At the city of Sées, Saint Godegrand, bishop and martyr. On the same day, Saint Aigulphus, abbot of the monastery of Lérins, glorious martyr.”

For Remaclus, Mansuetus, and Marinus, as above. Then:

> “At Aquileia, Saints Euphemia, Dorothea, Thecla, and Erasma, who in the time of Nero, after very severe and manifold torments, were beheaded and buried by Hermagoras. On the third day, Saint Theoctistus, holy father and great companion of Euthymius.”

For Gregory’s ordination and the arrival of the bodies on Mount Blandinium, as above. Finally:

> “At Fosses, the translation of the body of blessed Foillanus the martyr.”

See what is recorded about him in the Appendices for 31 October.]

[Col. 0431]

The birth-feast of Saint Phoebe, of whom the blessed Apostle writes to the Romans. At Rome, the passion of blessed Seraphia, virgin, under the emperor Hadrian. When she had been handed over to two lustful men and could not be mocked or afterwards set on fire with burning lamps, by order of the governor she was beaten with clubs and then beheaded with a sword. The day of her passion is the fourth before the Kalends of August, but the day of her burial is commemorated here, when the memory of her martyrdom is celebrated with greater solemnity. At Capua, the holy martyrs Antoninus, a boy of twenty years, and Aristaeus, bishop, whose Acts are extant. [Bouillart adds: “[Note: [Col. 0431C] With his customary fairness, our censor did not consider the Pratense manuscript pure because Saint Gregory’s ordination was added to this entry, although the difference in the writing is not now conspicuous. BOUILLART.]”] At Rome, the ordination of Saint Gregory the pope.

## Pridie Non. Day 4. [Note: [Col. 0435]

The Pratense, Herinien, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0435C]

All the Usuardian manuscripts write *Moysi*, although the *Little Roman Martyrology* and Ado have *Moysis*. In the Pratense and Molan manuscripts the reading is *Ancyram*; the others simply have the form found in the text. Greven has *Galaciae* and *Victalici*. Herinien incorrectly has *Calonis* instead of *Cabilonis*. The Pratense, Greven, and Molan manuscripts have *prophanum*; I prefer *profanum* with the others. I have spoken elsewhere about *ydolis*, *Sylvani*, *tercio*, and similar forms.

Here it is especially important to observe that the Pratense codex, following Ado, has *defodiri*, although I find this reading in no other manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0435C]

From the *Little Roman Martyrology* into Ado, and from him into Usuard and Notker, there flowed the entry for Moses the prophet, whom neither the Hieronymian Martyrologies nor Bede nor Bede’s followers mention. As we have said more than once in the preface and elsewhere, he is one of the distinctive saints of the *Little Roman Martyrology*. Among such figures we count not a few prophets of the Old Testament, several disciples of the apostles from the New Testament, illustrious men known through Eusebius and Rufinus, and certain feasts proper to Rome. It is useful to remind the reader of these repeatedly.

He is also found in Wandalbert, though I do not know from what source, since it is very likely that Wandalbert never saw the *Little Roman Martyrology*. Thus the martyrologist poet adorns the Hebrew lawgiver:

> Bearer, receiver, and author of the divine law,  
> deemed worthy of frequent converse and vision of God,  
> Moses, you are buried on the lofty mountain on the day before;  
> no one afterwards was permitted to know your tomb.

The martyrs of Ancyra derive from the same source, being recorded by the *Little Roman Martyrology* as follows:

> “At Ancyra, three boy martyrs, Rufinus, Silvanus, and Vitalica.”

Ado also wrote *Vitalica*, using somewhat more words but without an eulogy, and recording the same things that were later copied by our author and Notker, with this sole difference: they changed the last name, *Vitalica*, into *Vitalici*.

Several knots of difficulty recur here. First, why are only three listed from the larger group, extended by the Hieronymian Martyrologies to seventeen, with absolutely no mention of their companions? Also, why are they called boys, when no indication of greater or lesser age appears in the Hieronymian Martyrologies? Finally, why was the name *Vitalica* transformed by later writers into *Vitalici*? Other matters may perhaps arise for discussion, but it is not the task of this place to resolve all of them.

The cited Hieronymian copies read concerning Marcellus:

> “In Gaul, in the city of the people of Chalon, the birth-feast of Saint Marcellus the martyr.”

The Echternach manuscript, somewhat more abbreviated than the others, nevertheless adds the title “bishop,” which the rest omit. With it agree the other martyrologists—Florus, Rabanus, Ado, Usuard, Notker, and Wandalbert—who record him on this very day, content with the crown of martyrdom alone.

The eulogies of Florus, Rabanus, and Ado differ greatly, agreeing only in reporting an unusual form of martyrdom. Apart from this, what Florus has is fairly commonplace. Rabanus devotes himself entirely to describing various forms of torture. Ado takes another path: he first gathers what concerns Marcellus’s flight from Lyons toward Chalon, where he fell into another slaughter.

From this you may readily infer that they did not all consult the same Acts. What period those Acts reflect is not yet clear to me. The versions that have been published, after examination by more recent scholars, are not approved, and I find nothing in Gregory of Tours that can help illuminate them.

Our author took everything from Ado, cutting away the first part, in which Marcellus’s flight from Lyons to Chalon is indicated. Thus Wandalbert celebrates him after Moses:

> Then Chalon too grows green with Marcellus’s blood.

Magnus and Castus were added by Usuard. Whether they were taken from the Roman entries or from those of Ancyra in the Hieronymian copies, who can determine? For in those copies they are announced twice. It is equally uncertain who first added Maximus to Usuard, concerning whom we shall speak in the Appendices. Saturninus would seem rather to be their companion, with Maximus far separated from them.

Whatever the case may be, our text is genuinely and simply Usuardian.]

[Note: [Col. 0437A]

The Antwerp-Major manuscript adds after the pure text:

> “And the translation of the relics of Saint Cuthbert, bishop.”

It is plainly English. See also the following codex.

Rosweyd adds at the end:

> “And the translation of the relics of Saint Guthbert, bishop. Also in the regions of Britain, the translation of Saint Berinus, bishop and confessor. Strengthened first by the wondrous constancy of Catholic preaching, he fearlessly entered the long-pagan province of the West Saxons, converted King Cynegils to the knowledge and worship of Christ, regenerated him and his people for Christ the King in the sacred font, and, after many years, was buried in the aforesaid city. Revealed there by the heavenly signs of God’s providence, he is venerated in that place with fitting honours. At Rome, Boniface, bishop, who made the Pantheon a church of Christ.”

[Col. 0437B] The Pulsen manuscript cuts away the entire eulogy of Marcellus; the rest is fairly pure.

The Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, Ughellian, Swedish Royal no. 130, Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Albergen, and Danic manuscripts are all close to purity, suffering only from the defect that at the end, after Magnus and Castus, they add Maximus. See the Observations.

The Centula manuscript:

> “Moses the prophet, the man of God. At Ancyra in Galatia, Saints Rufinus, Silvanus, and Vitalica, martyrs. At Chalon, Saint Marcellus the martyr.”

The Brussels manuscript begins:

> “Moses the prophet and lawgiver.”

It then follows with the entry for Marcellus and afterwards that for the martyrs of Ancyra, fairly purely. To Castus it also adds Maximus. Then:

> “At Verdun, Saints Maurus and Silvinus, bishops and confessors. Also the translation of Saint Cuthbert.”

The Hagenoyen manuscript usefully appends a eulogy of Moses from the sacred writings, as it contains many such passages. It reads:

> “Moses the prophet, who was the son of Amram and Jochebed, of the tribe of Levi. He was cast into the river and submerged; Pharaoh’s daughter found him and adopted him as her son. When he had grown up, moved by zeal for the law, he struck down an Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Then he fled to Jethro, his kinsman, and took his daughter Zipporah as wife; by her he fathered two sons, namely Gershom and Eliezer.
>
> Afterwards he saw God in the bush. At God’s command he returned to Egypt with two signs: a rod changed into a serpent and a leprous hand. Then he brought ten plagues upon Egypt; in the tenth he went out of Egypt with all the people and livestock through the Red Sea, where Pharaoh the king was drowned with all his people.
>
> Coming into the desert, he received the law from the hand of the Lord, and his face appeared horned from his converse with the Lord. At the Lord’s command he established the priestly vestments, the altar vessels, the ark, and the candlestick. He established the everlasting priesthood for his brother Aaron and Aaron’s sons through the flowering of his rod.
>
> When Dathan, Abiram, and Korah quarrelled over the priesthood and leadership of the people, he caused the earth to swallow them alive. In the desert the Lord displayed miracles through him. He fought in prayer against the kings Amalek, Sihon, and Og, and conquered them.
>
> The Lord always loved Moses and therefore always protected him, and he always rebuked those who cursed him. He blessed the children of Israel and died in the plains of Moab. His grave was never found, nor were his bones ever discovered, and he was buried by the hand of the Lord.”

See Moses’ very lengthy Life published by Surius on this day, in which you will find all these matters set out somewhat more elegantly and distinctly.

It continues:

> “Also at Sion, the translation of Theodulus, Mauritius, and their companions.”

The entries for the Ancyrean martyrs and Marcellus are fairly pure. It adds Maximus. Then:

> “At Viterbo, Saint Rose, virgin and abbess, whose body, preserved through many ages, is still displayed intact.”

I myself saw it in 1697, when it was still exposed for visitors arriving there. Castellanus notes, however, that the translation is commemorated here, while her birth-feast is on 7 March.

Also:

> “The translation of Saint Barbara, virgin, from Arezzo to Rome. On the same day, Saint Peter Chrysogonus the confessor.”

Or perhaps *Chrysologus*? But this saint is commemorated on 11 December.

AQUICINCT adds at the end: “And the translation of the relics of Saint Cuthbert, bishop.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of the illustrious martyr Marcellus. Of the three child-martyrs Rufinus, Silvanus, and Vitalicus. Of the prophet Moses.”

In VATICAN MS 5949, Moses, Magnus, and Castus are absent. It adds: “At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the burial of Saint Boniface, bishop.” [Col. 0438D]

The FLORENTINE manuscripts add Maximus. Instead of Castus, they read Festus. “Also, Saint Maurus the confessor. The translation of Saint Gudbert the confessor.”

LUXOVIEN.: “At Verdun, of the holy confessors and bishops Maurus, Silvanus, and Arator.” BRUXELLEN. mentions only two.

CAUDIACEN.: “In Auvergne, at the monastery called Magni Locus, the arrival of the relics of Saint Sebastian, and the arrival of the body of the blessed martyr Ferreolus.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition is fairly pure in Moses, Marcellus, and the martyrs of Ancyra; it adds:

“At Verdun, of the holy confessors and bishops Maurus, Salvinus, and Arator. On the same day, of the holy martyrs Magnus, Castus, and Maximus. At Trier, of the blessed confessor Paul. Also at Trier, of the blessed Marcellus, bishop and martyr. On the same day in Britain, the translation of Saint Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne and confessor.”

BELIN. has Maximus. “And Saint Maurus the confessor. On the same day, the octave of Saint Augustine, bishop.”

[Col. 0438C]

GREVEN.: “Of the prophet Haggai. At Trier, of the blessed Marcellus, bishop and martyr, who governed both the church of Trier and that of Tongeren. At Rome, the burial of Saint Boniface, bishop. At Verdun, the translation of the holy confessors and bishops, etc. At Trier, of the blessed confessor Paul. In England, the commemoration of Saint Birinus, bishop of Dorchester and confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saint Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne and confessor. Also, the canonization of Saint Switbert, bishop of Werden and confessor. On Mount Titano, of Saint Marinus the Levite and confessor, who, being skilled in hewing stones and employed by Diocletian, generously assisted the poor from the proceeds of his labor; he also helped Christians who, because of their faith in Christ, were burdened with work. Later, by order of the Roman Pontiff, he was ordained deacon and rested in peace. In Ireland, of Vultanus the abbot. Of Museus, priest of Marseille and confessor. In Africa, of Simpliciola the virgin and Galla her mother. Of Rosa the virgin. Of Herentrudis the virgin. [Col. 0438D] Of Irmgard the virgin, in the major church of Cologne. Also, of Saint Ida, a noble widow, who in the time of Charlemagne, in Westphalia near the Lippe, after completing her married life, established a place of enclosure for herself in the church porch that her husband had built at his own expense; living in great holiness and truly showing herself a widow, she rested in peace.”

MOLAN. gives, from BELIN: “And Maximus, and Saint Maurus the confessor.” Then, in smaller type: “Irmgard the virgin, in the major church of Cologne.” Concerning Cuthbert and Ida, he follows GREVEN above. Other editions have, concerning Maximus and Maurus, as above: “At Trier, Saint Marcellus, bishop and martyr. In the territory of Münster, above the river Lippe, the burial of the blessed Ida, a widow of great holiness.” [Col. 0439A] Then, in smaller type: “At Cologne, in the major church, Irmgard the virgin, on whose vigil bells are rung there, as on the vigils of the saints, although she has not been canonized.” That is, on account of the immemorial cult which she has continued to enjoy there for so many centuries. [Col. 0440A]

[Col. 0435]

Of Moses the prophet. At Ancyra in Galatia, the feast of the holy martyrs, the three children Rufinus, Silvanus, and Vitalicus. At Chalon-sur-Saône, Saint Marcellus the martyr, who, when he had been invited by the governor Priscus to a profane banquet and, condemning such food, openly rebuked all who were present for serving idols, was buried upright up to the waist by order of the governor in an unheard-of act of cruelty. Thus the holy martyr of God, persevering for three days in the fear and praises of God, surrendered his undefiled spirit. On the same day, of the holy martyrs Magnus and Castus.

## On the Nones. Day 5

[Note: [Col. 0439]]

The texts of Herinien., Antuerp.-Max., Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. are pure. Also Antuerp.-Max., [Col. 0440A] Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., and Danicus.

[Note: [Col. 0439B]]

Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Alberg., Danic., and Belin. read *has attained* for *attains*; omitting *inde* (“therefrom”), they immediately append *postmodum* (“afterwards”), etc. Belin. has the scribal error *qui cum per triduum* (“who, when for three days”) for *quod cum per triduum* (“which, when for three days”). Again, instead of *migravit ad Dominum* (“he departed to the Lord”), it reads *migravit ad Christum* (“he departed to Christ”), in which Munerat. agrees. Scribal errors include *Amiterniae putrentes* and *Heriniani* for *Herculani*; in the first edition of Bellin.: “Quincii, Arconcii, Aconcii,” [Col. 0440B] etc. Praten., with his two usual companions, reads at the end: “In the district of Tarvannes, Saint Bertinus the abbot.” But Castellanus observed that the words “on the same day” had been deleted in that manuscript and that the new words “in the district of Tarvannes” had subsequently been written in; he believes this was done by the first hand. Ant.-Maj. and Rosweyd. have the same reading. We shall report it in the Additions.

[Note: [Col. 0439B]]

Concerning the martyr Victorinus, the short Roman Martyrology speaks in this way today: “At Rome, Victorinus the martyr, brother of Severinus, who, after astonishing repentance, became bishop and martyr of the city of Amiternum.” You have the whole story described at greater length in Ado, where his unfortunate fall, his utterly remarkable repentance, and other matters relating to it are narrated; [Col. 0439C] but Baronius judges that all these things must be attributed to another Victorinus of Septempeda, the brother of Severinus. Consequently, the short Roman Martyrology and Ado must be entirely mistaken here. Surius nevertheless copied this story from Ado, and Notker likewise reports it. Our author, following his customary practice of not abandoning his guide, selected from Ado what he judged most suitable for weaving an encomium; and in his uniform manner of reporting it, one sees the remarkable agreement of our Usuardine manuscripts. Yet although that descent is so manifest and certain, the source from which it originally flowed is itself so suspect. Since the facts have not yet been sufficiently examined, I have no firm conclusion to offer. Castellanus notes that the Victorinus commemorated today rested in peace, and therefore differs from the one to whom the glory of martyrdom is attributed among the people of Amiternum. The curious reader may consult Baronius’s note, which exposes Ado’s error. See also the Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, 12 May, in our chapter 5, where one will find a Victorinus whose martyrdom agrees exactly with today’s account; therefore this Victorinus must be the same as the one celebrated with Maro and Eutyches on 15 April.
