Henschenius should be consulted there, p. 374, no. 5. I consider this sufficient to indicate the difficulties, which must be discussed fully elsewhere.

The short Roman Martyrology places, second, “At Rome, of Herculanus.” Our announcement is plainly Ado’s. The Hieronymian Martyrologies vary in the number of the martyrs of Portus: some count four, others three, and others only two. Rabanus followed the last; yet it is generally characteristic of our manuscripts to select one, or at least a few, from the larger number in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. [Col. 0440C] The Capuans, taken from the same copies of Ado, are more faithfully reproduced, their wording being almost entirely preserved. Usuard closely follows Ado’s words; I do not know on what authority Notker added two companions. Rabanus wrote only: “In Campania, of Quintus.” What Henschenius discussed concerning Quartus and Quintus under 10 May may be relevant here, as may what we briefly indicated there in the Observations. Wandalbert, apart from Ferreolus and Ferrutio, concerning whom we treated with Usuard on 16 June, celebrates only the two Capuans in this way:

> Donatus and likewise Arcontius adorn Capua.

For more concerning the martyrs of Portus and Capua, see Florentinius’s notes. Up to this point the purity and simplicity of our text are evident. Among the ancients, only Florus speaks of Bertinus, in these words: “On the same day, the burial of Saint Bertinus the confessor and monk, who, prudent in divine matters and simple in evil things, shone with divine virtues.” This is a commonplace encomium, which could be attributed to almost any saint. It is hardly plausible that Usuard saw this. To what extent Bertinus truly belongs to him, however, we explained above in the Variants. Surius published the Life of Bertinus, but more material may be found collected in Mabillon, *Benedictine Century III*, part I, pp. 104–169.

[Note: [Col. 0439D]]

PRATEN. and ANTUERP.-MAJOR: “In the district of Tarvannes, Saint Bertinus the abbot.”

ROSWEYD. has exactly the same addition, but is not entirely pure in the text. It writes “Tarvernensi” instead of “Tarvenensi.” At the end it also adds: “Also Saint Aper the confessor.” If this is Aper of Toul, he is commemorated on 15 September.

PULSANEN.: “At Rome, the blessed Victorinus the martyr.” The entire encomium is absent. It is fairly pure in Herculanus and the Capuans. For Bertinus, following the text, it writes “Libertinus.”

CENTULEN.: “In the suburb of Rome, the blessed Victorinus the martyr. At Capua, of the holy martyrs Quintus, Arcontius, and Donatus. On the same day, of the holy Magnus and Castus. At Rome, Saint Herculanus the martyr. In the territory of the Morini, Saint Bertinus the abbot, a man of great holiness and innocence.”

[Col. 0441A]

BRUXELLEN.: “At Rome, in the suburb, the feast of the blessed Victorinus, bishop and martyr. He, distinguished by holiness and miracles, attained the highest priesthood of the city of Amiternum by the election of the whole people. Under the emperor Nerva, at the place called Cotilia, where foul and sulphurous waters flow, he was ordered to be hung head downward. When this had been done for three days, he was gloriously crowned and, victorious, departed to the Lord.” It is pure in Herculanus and the Capuans. “On the same day, the burial of the blessed Bertinus, abbot and confessor.”

HAGENOYEN begins: “Of Gideon, prophet and judge of Israel. This Gideon was Joash’s son, of the family of Ezri, of the tribe of Manasseh. He was greeted by an angel and called a very brave man. To him Gideon offered flesh upon a rock for food. After he destroyed the altar of Baal, he was called Jerobaal. Having received a sign in his fleece, with three hundred men,” etc.—things sufficiently well known from the sacred history itself. It continues: “At Lausanne, [Col. 0441B] of Genebaudus, bishop and confessor.” It is fairly pure in Victorinus, Herculanus, and the Capuans. At the end: “In Italy, Saint Bertinus the abbot.” I leave it to others to guess how Italy was introduced here.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Victorinus, bishop and martyr. Of Bertinus the abbot, whose solemn monastery stands near Saint Omer.”

CLUNIACEN. and CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked C: “At the Cluniac monastery, the glorious reception from Auvergne of the blessed Marcellus, pope and martyr, distinguished not a little by the renown of his miracles and the crowds of peoples.”

REGINAE SUEC., marked 428: “At Sées, Saint Godegrannus, bishop and martyr.” See what was said above under 3 September.

In VATICAN MS 5949, Victorinus and Bertinus are absent.

FLORENTIN.: “At the monastery of Pulsano, in the diocese of Siponto, near Manfredonia, the burial of Saint Jordan, abbot of that monastery.” It is strange that in the proper Martyrology of that monastery, so often cited by us, no mention is made of this Jordan.

BURDEGAL.: “At Bordeaux, Innocentia the virgin.”

CAUDIACEN.: “In Burgundy, in the district of Mâcon, at the Cluniac monastery, the glorious reception from Auvergne of the blessed Marcellus, pope and martyr,” etc., as above in CLUNIACEN.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition: “At Cologne, in the church of Saint Clement, the translation of Saint Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne and confessor. At Rome, in the suburb, the blessed Victorinus, priest and martyr. He, distinguished by holiness and miracles, attained the priesthood of the city of Amiternum by the election of the whole people. Then, by the judge Aurelian, he was exiled with the servants of God Eutyches and Maro, from the Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, sixty miles from the City on the Salarian Way. [The printed reading is *Amicerrimae*; read *Amiterninae*.] Thereafter, under the emperor Nerva, he was ordered to be hanged,” etc., purely. In [Col. 0441D] Herculanus and the Capuans it is pure. Then: “In Flanders, at the monastery of Sithiu, the burial of Saint Bertinus [Col. 0442A] abbot and confessor. On the same day, the feast of the blessed Genebald, bishop of Laon and confessor, concerning whom one reads in the deeds of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims.”

GREVEN.: “Saint Bertinus, born in the territory of Coutances, left his homeland and came with two others to Saint Omer, his countryman and bishop of Thérouanne; sent by him to the work of God, he rested in glory of life and miracles. In Alexandria, Nympius and Saturninus. In Gaul, in the city of Besançon, the discovery of the blessed martyrs Ferreolus and Ferrutio by Saint Anianus, in the time of the emperor Julian. There, through the Lord’s working, many miracles occur.” To this refers Wandalbert’s verse for today, which is placed first:

> On the Nones, Ferreolus shines with Ferrutio.

“In Promia, Agigulphus, abbot and martyr, with others.” See the preceding day. “In Campania, Quintinus, bishop and confessor. At Cologne, in the church of Saint Clement, the translation of Saint Cunibert, bishop and confessor of that city. On the same day, the burial of the blessed Genebald, bishop of Laon and confessor, concerning whom it is read in the deeds of Saint Remigius. On the same day, the discovery of Saint Taurinus. Victorinus the confessor, who, since at Rome on account of his wisdom he had earned a statue in Trajan’s Forum, in old age gave himself to the faith of Christ and rested in peace. At Troyes, the commemoration of Saints Sabina the virgin and Sabinian the martyr, her brother.” What is this conjunction doing here? Usuard commemorated the former on 29 January and the latter on 29 August.

MOLAN.: “The burial of our blessed Father and confessor, in the district of Thérouanne, at the monastery called Sithiu; distinguished by his life and miracles, he departed to the Lord in the year 698 from the Incarnation of the Lord. There, when the dog-days come to an end, as the venerable Gregory, bishop of Tours, writes, at the close of the final day the invincible labors of the holy man were changed, for when he ended the day, in living regeneration he received an everlasting day, Jesus Christ our Lord. At Laon-Clavato, Saint Genebald, bishop and confessor, and Saint Proba the virgin.” Then, in smaller type: “In Gaul, in the city of Besançon, the discovery of the blessed martyrs Ferreolus and Ferrutio,” etc., as above in GREVEN. “In Campania, Quintinus, bishop and confessor. Victorinus the confessor, who, since at Rome on account of his wisdom he had earned a statue,” etc., also as GREVEN has it. In later editions, between “on the same day” and “of Saint Bertinus,” another entry is inserted: “In the district of Thérouanne, at the monastery called Sithiu.” Then: “Our blessed Father,” etc. “At Laon-Clavato, Saint Genebald, bishop and confessor, and Saint Proba the virgin. In Gaul, in the city of Besançon, the discovery of the blessed martyrs Ferreolus,” etc., as above. Finally, in smaller type: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Eudoxius, also called Marianus, Romulus, Zeno, and Macarius, who were crowned martyrs under Trajan.” See the announcement in the modern Roman Martyrology [Col. 0442D] and Castellanus’s appended note.

[Col. 0439]

At Rome, the blessed martyr Victorinus, who, distinguished by holiness and miracles, attained the priesthood of the city of Amiternum by the election of the whole people. Thereafter, under the emperor Nerva, he was ordered to be hung head downward at the place where foul and sulphurous waters flow; after suffering this for three days for the name of Christ, he was gloriously crowned and, victorious, departed to the Lord. Also at Rome, at Portus, the feast of Saint Herculanus. At Capua, of the holy martyrs Quintus, Arcontius, and Donatus. On the same day [Apud Bouillart., [Note: [Col. 0439B] In the Carolingian autograph: “On the same day, Saint Bertinus the abbot.” Since this was contrary to the custom of our work, he deleted the entire line and restored it in smaller letters, so that there would be space to designate the place where Bertinus was chiefly venerated. That place was appropriately designated by the words “in the district of Tarvannes.” At that time the monastery which he first governed, or whose construction he completed, stood several leagues from Thérouanne. It is now enclosed within the walls of Saint Omer. BOUILLART.] in the district of Tarvannes, instead of “On the same day”], Saint Bertinus the abbot.

## The Eighth Day before the Ides. Day 6

[Note: [Col. 0441]]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Major, Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0443A]]

In our Pratense copy *Zachariae* is written. Herinien., Antuerpien.-Maj., and Greven. have *Caldea*, better supported by the others, as it stands in the text. Antuerp.-Maj. omitted the particle *de*, which immediately precedes it. The same manuscript reads *Aggeam*; Munerat., *Ageum*; Molan., most accurately, *Aggaeum*; but we follow the remaining codices. Again, Antuerp.-Maj. writes *confessorum episcoporum* (“confessor-bishops”), omitting the conjunction *et* (“and”). Munerat. has *Donaciani*, [Col. 0444A] Antuerp.-Maj. *Donatii*. In the same manuscript, *ascertione* occurs for *assertione*. Finally, in it, after *concrematus*, *est* is missing. We have spoken elsewhere about Cappadocia. Greven. and Molan. read as follows: “Also, at the Cappadocian city of Reate, Saint Cottidus the deacon.” Others agree with the text, except that Munerat. writes *Cotidi*. *Strennuus* in Molan. is a typographical error; it correctly reads *Praesidii* and *Laetus*, but we follow the others in using the simpler form.

[Note: [Col. 0443A]]

Bede, Rabanus, the short Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Notker all commemorate the prophet Zachariah in precisely these words. Our author, as we have said more than once, often adds something distinctive to the Fathers of the Old Testament whom he finds adorned in older sources with only their names, as is evident here from our register. Today Wandalbert sings of him alone:

> The prophet Zachariah holds the eighth day before the Ides.

The short Roman Martyrology continues: “And Onesiphorus, Paul’s disciple.” Ado reads “a disciple of the apostles,” supplying, in place of an encomium, among the Feasts of the Apostles everything that Paul mentions (2 Tim. 1): “May the Lord grant mercy,” etc. Notker did not take this from Ado, but copied only the words of his Martyrology. It is certain, meanwhile, that Onesiphorus was omitted by Usuard; whoever can may guess the reason. The class of illustrious African prelates who suffered under the Vandal persecution during Huneric’s reign is briefly described by the cited short Roman Martyrology: “and the confessors Donatianus and his companions.” Ado’s account is somewhat fuller, naming each confessor individually, taken, unless I am mistaken, from Victor of Vita’s *History of the African Persecution*, book II, near the end. Notker transcribed almost all Ado’s words; Usuard, more concise, omitted some, which are supplied in the Additions. The final announcement remains, unknown to the short Roman Martyrology and to Ado, which Usuard translated from the Hieronymian Martyrologies alone. In them it is read approximately as follows: “In the territory of Cappadocia, in the city of Reate, the feast of Saint Quottidus with his companions.” The copies vary in the name of the city. Rabanus reads: “In the territory of Cappadocia, in the city of Ructa, the feast of Saint Cuttidus,” adding also Eugenius the bishop and his companions. Our author, following his customary practice, as I have often said, neglecting the companions, mentions only Quottidus or Quottidius, whom, following the common spelling of our codices, we have called Cottidus. Florentinius discusses that city at length. Whether Reate, Reaten, Readden, Seriate, Teriate, or some similar or related place in Cappadocia can be found to which our Cottidus truly belongs will be examined elsewhere in detail. We have shown from where Usuard received the first saints and from where he received this final one; consequently, by the agreement of the codices, his text retains its original and unalloyed simplicity.

[Note: [Col. 0443B]]

PRATEN. is counted among the pure, although in the text, near the end, our exemplar contains the following: “At Sens, Saints Sanctianus and Beata, brother and sister, and Saint Augustine the bishop.” Since these words have been marked with underlining by Sirmond or Cortasius, this indicates that they entered the text from the margin.

[Col. 0443C] ROSWEYD. is fairly pure, but omits the final announcement.

PULSANEN. has everything correctly through *Fusculus*, but, as that codex is already deficient in many places, here too it omits the remainder.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. add to the text: “At Rome, Eleutherius the bishop.” The Roman Martyrology concerns Eleutherius the abbot, a servant of God; see Castellanus’s note.

LOVANIEN. is fairly pure in the text and adds at the end: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Magnus the confessor.” See Surius and the encomia below.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. have the same addition; moreover, after *Fusculus*, they insert into the text: “Who, in the Vandal persecution, by order of Huneric, the Arian king, for the assertion of the Catholic faith,” etc.

CENTULEN.: “The death of the prophet Zachariah. On the same day, Saint Onesiphorus, whom Saint Paul mentions with full praise. In Africa, the holy confessors and bishops Donatianus, Praesidius, Mansuetus, Germanus, and Fusculus, who under the Vandal persecution reached the end of this life.”

BRUXELLEN. places second: “And the feast of the blessed Onesiphorus, a disciple of the apostles.” In the African martyrs it resembles ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. “In Cappadocia, near the city of Reate, Saint Cottidus the deacon. On the same day, Saint Magnus the confessor. Also, Saints Donatus and Eleutherius, bishops.”

HAGENOYEN. again contains a long prophetic history, as we have noted more than once is customary in this codex. In the African martyrs it has the same material as ANTUERP.-MAX., etc., above. Then: “Also at Rome, Saint Eleutherius the bishop.” In the final entry it is nearly pure. At the end it adds the following, which we have thought worth transcribing:

“Also in the diocese of Augsburg, at the monastery in Fautibus, the burial of Saint Magnus, or Magnoaldus, abbot. He was once deacon of the blessed abbot Gallus. For twenty-five years he laudably exercised the priesthood, during which time he also became renowned for miracles, converting many to the faith. To him, by means of a wild bear, veins of iron were shown. The bears living there also served him, as did domestic oxen. After this the blessed Magnus died in peace.”

AQUICINCT. adds at the end: “Also Saint Humbert the confessor. At Rome, Eleutherius the bishop.” Concerning Humbert, see Surius.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Humbert the priest and confessor [added in the margin: elsewhere, Humbert]. Zachariah the prophet. Donatianus, Praesidius, with the others.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked C: “At Rome, Eleutherius the bishop.” See what we noted above.

In VATICAN MS 5949, Zachariah and Cottidus are absent. It adds: “At Iconium, Saint Onesiphorus, disciple of the blessed apostle Paul.”

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, Saint Eleutherius the bishop. The passion of Saint Potitus the martyr.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition is pure in Zachariah and continues:

“In Africa, the holy confessors and bishops [Col. 0444D] Domicianus, Praesidius, Mansuetus, Germanus, and Fustolus. In the Vandal persecution, by order of Huneric, the Arian king, they were beaten most cruelly with clubs for the assertion of Catholic truth and driven into exile. Among them also was a certain bishop, etc. At Fauces, the feast of Saint Magnus the confessor, renowned for miracles, a disciple of the blessed Columbanus. In Cappadocia, near the city of Reate, Saint Cottidus the deacon and confessor. In Asia, Saint Onesiphorus, a disciple of the apostles.”

BELIN., near the end, inserts: “At Rome, Saint Eleutherius the bishop.” See above.

GREVEN.: “Zachariah, son of Jehoiada, or of Berechiah. When he rebuked the transgression of the king and the people, they stoned and killed him in the court of the house of the Lord, 2 Chronicles 24. On the same day, according to Ado, the feast of the blessed Onesiphorus, a disciple of the apostles. At Rome, Saint Eleutherius the bishop. In Ireland, Mastulinus the bishop. At Metz, Saint Gundulphus, bishop and confessor. Mamertinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre and confessor. At Fauces, Saint Magnus, also called Magnoaldus, a disciple of Saint Columbanus the abbot. Humbert the confessor. Eleutherius the abbot and confessor, a man of remarkable simplicity and compunction. Concerning him, blessed Gregory reports in the Third Dialogue, among other things, that when he was ill he obtained the power of abstinence, and that by prayer and tears he obtained life for a certain dead man.”

MOLAN. After *concrematus est*, in different type, he inserts from Ado into the text:

“Then Huneric the Arian king, as though the bishops had been summoned to a council at Carthage, closed the churches of all Africa in a single day and bestowed all the bishops’ property upon his own bishops.”

At the end he adds:

“And the feast of Saint Humbert, confessor of Christ. On the same day, at Fauces, Saint Magnus the confessor. At Rome, [Col. 0445B] Saint Eleutherius the pope. And the feast of the blessed Onesiphorus, [Col. 0446A] disciple of the apostles, concerning whom the Apostle says: ‘May God grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus.’”

It continues in smaller type:

“For he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain, but when he came to Rome, he diligently sought and found me. And how many services he rendered at Ephesus, you know better.” See Ado among the Feasts of the Apostles. Then:

“Mamertinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre and confessor. Eleutherius, abbot and confessor, a man of remarkable simplicity and compunction, concerning whom blessed Gregory reports in the Third Dialogue, among other things, that when he was ill he obtained the power of abstinence, and that by prayer and tears he obtained life for a certain dead man.”

In other editions Ado’s concluding clause is also inserted into the text. Concerning Magnus they have as above. “And the feast of the blessed Onesiphorus, disciple of the apostles,” through “the household of Onesiphorus.” “On the same day, the translation of the body of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Humbert, distinguished by virtues and miracles. On the sixth day, the commemoration of the miracle performed by the archangel Michael at Colossae, or Chonae.”

[Col. 0441]

Of the prophet Zachariah, who, an old man returning from Chaldea to his homeland, lies buried near the prophet Haggai. In Africa, the blessed confessors and bishops Donatianus, Praesidius, Mansuetus, Germanus, and Fusculus, who were beaten most cruelly and driven into exile for the assertion of Catholic truth. Among them also was a bishop named Laetus, a vigorous and highly learned man, who, after the prolonged squalor of prison, was burned to death. Also in the Cappadocian city of Reate, Saint Cottidus the deacon. [Bouillart adds in the margin: [Note: [Col. 0441D] This commemoration—“At Sens, Saints Sanctianus and Beata, German siblings, etc.”—did not enter the text from the margin, as Sollerius conjectured from ambiguous indications; it is also read [Col. 0442D] in the margin, and indeed in the upper margin. BOUILLART.] At Sens, Saints Sanctianus and Beata, brother and sister, and Saint Augustine the bishop.]

## The Seventh Day before the Ides. Day 7

[Note: [Col. 0445B]]

Taken from Praten., Antuerp.-Major, Rosweyd., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Greven., and Molan. Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Albergen., and Danicus also agree.

[Note: [Col. 0445C]]

I write *discerpsit* with Praten., Herinien., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Greven. The sense requires this, although Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Molan., and most others have *descerpsit*. Antuerp.-Maj. and Rosweyd. read: “with such great cheerfulness of face and hope,” so that the abbreviation appears to represent *specie* rather than *spiritus*. Nearly all have *Evurtii* according to the usage of Orléans. Rosweyd. alone has *Evorcii*, Greven. *Evurcii*, and Molan. *Evortii*. The last two, together with Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. and the more recent copies, add the title “bishop,” which is absent from the older witnesses. In Greven., *dehinc* appears instead of *dein*. I read *Augustodunensi* according to the older usage; others have *Augustudinensi*, Molan. *Augustodunensi*, and Greven., most incorrectly, *Andegavensi*. Rosweyd. has “under the consul Olibrius”; the others read as in the text. But Antuerp.-Maj. and Molan. have *lampadum*; Antuerp., “was ordered to bring to an end”; Max.-Lubec., “was ordered to be punished”; Rosweyd., “to end his life.” The others have *Chlodoaldi*, as the older witnesses do, not Rosweyd.’s *Cloaldi* or the *Clodoaldi* of others. Rosweyd. likewise substitutes *perspicui* for *conspicui*.

[Note: [Col. 0445D]]

The first mention of the illustrious martyr who is anonymous in Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* and in Eusebius—his first mention, I say, under the name John—is owed to the short Roman Martyrology. On this day, chosen at its discretion, it reads: “Of John the martyr, who at Nicomedia under Diocletian tore the book of the wicked law into pieces.” Ado recounts the event at greater length from Rufinus, book VIII, chapter 5; our author took his encomium from Ado, and Notker also abridged it. Castellanus proposes another name and declares that the martyrdom was most probably completed around 24 February 303. Papebrochius plausibly conjectures that what is attributed here to our John may be attributed to George; see the preliminary commentary on the Acts of Saint George, 23 April, § 4. Others think differently, such as Baluzius in Ruinart, *Selecta*, p. 319, in the notes. Ado appears to be dealing with this one John alone, whatever Mosander’s supposition of three others may imply; and in this I agree even more strongly with Rosweyd, since Notker, Ado’s constant copyist, omits the others as well.

Evurtius of Orléans, *Evotus* in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and called by others *Evortius*, *Euritius*, and *Emirtius*, but, according to his own subscription, properly *Eortius*, is celebrated by Florus in a long encomium, plainly taken from Acts that had long ago been published by various authors and are judged by more recent scholars to have been at least interpolated. Rabanus and Usuard must likewise have had those Acts before their eyes, each extracting from them what was proper to him. Regina of Autun is also mentioned by Rabanus, but adorned almost solely with her name, although her deeds are cited. Those deeds, published by Peter and by Mombritius and apparently rejected by Surius, are treated by others as pure fiction, cobbled together from similar Acts; on these matters we have so far formed no judgment. In any case, Usuard’s encomium was drawn from such Acts, and all the codices prove that it truly belongs to him. Bede writes “Saint Clodoaldus the confessor”; Rabanus, *Chlodoaldus*; the additions to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, *Chlonevaudus* and *Clodoaldus*; Aimonus, according to Castellanus, *Fludualdus*. However one writes it, the same person is meant: the grandson of King Chlodoveus and son of Chlodomir, happily rescued from the impious murder of his brothers by their uncles. See the authors cited by Baronius who write about him; in due time we shall compare them with the Acts published by Mabillon and others. Usuard’s encomium says much in few words, and I believe it was transferred from him into the *Hagiologium of Franco-Gaul*. Certainly it seems beyond doubt that it is Usuardine, like the other material transmitted today. Wandalbert joined our second and fourth announcements to his verses as follows:

> Bishop Evurtius keeps the seventh day, and  
>   
> Clodoaldus, a priest illustrious in royal descent.

[Note: [Col. 0447A]]

HERINIEN., entirely pure throughout the text, adds at the end its own entry: “On the same day, blessed Vincent, archbishop of Reims” [intending Vivent[i]us].

PULSANEN. is pure through *expendi in eum*. It immediately continues: “In the territory of Autun, Saint Regina the virgin.” There it stops.

MUNERAT. adds to the pure text, in its own wording, concerning Clodoaldus: “Whose body rests in the church of Saint Clodoaldus near Paris.”

LOVANIEN. is deficient in the encomia of Eortius of Orléans and Regina of Autun.

CENTULEN.: “At Nicomedia, the blessed martyr John, under Diocletian. At Alesia, once a very strong city but destroyed by Julius Caesar, Saint Regina the virgin, who, suffering much for the faith under the governor Olybrius, met her end. At Orléans, Saint Evurtius, bishop and confessor. At Paris, Saint Clodoaldus, priest and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “In Gaul, in the city of Orléans, the burial of Saint Evorcius, bishop and confessor. Who,” etc. It continues: “On the same day, Saints Felix, Lucas, Polianus, Victor, Laderus, and Dativus, martyrs. After being grievously beaten with clubs under Decius, then bound in fetters and assigned to dig in the mines, they completed their martyrdom.” See Usuard speaking of them more fully on 10 September. In John, Regina, and Clodoaldus it is fairly pure. At the end: “Also, the burial of Saint Magdalberta the virgin, who rests at Liège, daughter of Saint Aldetrudis and niece of the blessed Gudula.” A more recent hand appended: “And Saint Clodoaldus,” etc., as though he were different from the preceding one.

HAGENOYEN is fairly pure in John and adds a reasonably good account of Regina. Then: “In the district of Lausanne, Saint Wlpecla the virgin. Also, the translation of Saint Anastasia. Also, Saint Madelberta the virgin.” The remainder of the text is pure.

DAVERON writes: “Saint Clodoaldus the priest, both in lineage and in mind,” etc.

MATRIC.-CARTUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Regina the virgin and martyr. Madelberga the virgin. Nemorius [others write Memorius] with his companions. The illustrious martyr John. Evurtius, bishop and confessor.”

CAMBERIEN. S. Mariae: “At Augusta, a city of Savoy, the burial of the body of Saint Gratianus, bishop of that city.”

In VATICAN MS 5949, Evurtius and Regina are absent.

FLORENTIN.: “The feast of the holy martyrs Desiderius and Januarius.” See GREVEN.

[Col. 0447D] BIZUNTICEN.: “At Châlons [for *Catalaunis*], Saint Alpinus, bishop and confessor, whose praiseworthy virtue is attested by the most illustrious miracles.”

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “At Châlons, Saint Alpinus, bishop and confessor.”

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION, in John it is quite pure, but inserts concerning Evortius: “bishop and confessor, a most holy man.” Again, in the entry for Regina it is pure; concerning Clodoaldus it writes:

> “In the territory of Paris, in the village of Novigentum, of Saint Clodowaldus, priest and confessor, son of King Clodomer of France, “both in birth,” etc.

Then:

> “In the territory of Troyes, of blessed Nemorius, martyr, and of the glorious deacon of Bishop Lupus, whom King Attila of the Huns killed together with his companions. At Châlons, the deposition of Saint Alpinus, confessor, disciple of the aforesaid Saint Lupus the bishop, so that from the merits of the disciples it may be evident how great was the holiness of the master. On the same day, of blessed Magdelberta, virgin.”

BELIN. In John and Evortius it is quite pure. In place of Clodoaldus he has Dodaldus, whose eulogy he deletes. He then follows with Regina, even more briefly.

GREVEN:

> “In the territory of Troyes, of blessed Memorius, martyr, deacon of Saint Lupus the bishop, whom King Attila of the Huns killed together with his companions. At Châlons, of Saint Alpinus, confessor, disciple of the same blessed Lupus, from whose disciples’ merits one may estimate the holiness of the master. In Campania, near Benevento, of Saints Innocentius, Januarius, and Festus. In Aquileia, of Anastasius, martyr, who was a fuller’s comb-maker. Of Vincentius—he means Viventius—archbishop of Reims and confessor. On that same day, of Stephen, bishop of Die, of the Carthusian Order, a man of great holiness and most renowned for miracles, worthy of holy memory. Having been taken from the priory of Portes and appointed to govern the aforesaid church, besides his other astonishing works he zealously sought the salvation of souls. Therefore, when he saw that the people were stiff-necked, in order to frighten them beneficially and make them know what enemies they had served, he caused demons of gigantic stature to appear before everyone [the first edition has: ‘before all the people assembled in the church’], and then to depart again [the first edition: ‘who at his command departed again’]. Also, of blessed memory, of Gorlinus, bishop of Toul and confessor, of whom it is said in the Acts of blessed Mansuetus that he was approved by pious and most holy works. At Arles, the deposition of blessed Augustalis, and of Magdelberta, virgin.”

Some read Madelberta.

MOLAN, concerning Clodoaldus, has an addition from MUNERATUS:

> “Also at Liège, of blessed Madelberta, virgin. On the same day, of blessed Vincentius, archbishop of Reims.”

He copied the following from GREVEN:

> “At Arles, of Saint Augustalis, bishop. In the city of Dendermonde, of blessed Hildelwardus, bishop and confessor, who, under Duke Magriptius, was first afflicted by various tortures and torments; but, steadfast in faith amid adversity and cheerful as in prosperity, he urged the faithful people to acknowledge the truth and preached the Catholic faith with the greatest constancy. Finally, by holding up the mirror of truth to Magriptius, he overcame him so completely that, rejecting the error of unbelief, Magriptius declared Jesus Christ to be the Son of God and loudly proclaimed that he wished to be baptized, together with his people. After this, the man of God built an oratory at Dikkelvenne, in which, after departing from this fleeting life, he rested in a glorious end. From that place the men of Dendermonde transferred his venerable bones, renowned for every virtue, to Dendermonde with the greatest rejoicing. Also on the same day at Dendermonde, the arrival of the body of blessed Christiana, virgin. In Aquileia, the feast of Saint Anastasius, martyr. He was a fuller, but through the merit of his faith he was numbered among the martyrs. In the territory of Troyes, of blessed Nemorius, glorious archdeacon of Bishop Lupus, whom King Attila of the Huns killed together with his companions.”

Other editions, concerning Clodoaldus and Hildewardus, are as above. Concerning Madelberta they add:

> “Who, after her aunt Aldegundis and her sister Aldetrudis, governed the monastery of Maubeuge as its third abbess.”

In place of Vincentius, Viventius is correctly read here. Concerning Anastasius, Augustalis, and Nemorius, as above.

> “On that same day, the deposition of Saint Gratus, confessor, bishop of Aosta, a man of marvelous holiness and miracles. On the seventh day, of Saint Sozantas, martyr. And the eve of the Nativity of the most holy Mother of God, Mary. At the port of Valenciennes, the translation of Saint Salvius, martyr and bishop of the city of Angoulême, and of Superius, his disciple. Also on the same day at Dendermonde, the arrival of the body of blessed Christiana, virgin.”

[Col. 0445]

At Nicomedia, the feast of the most blessed John, martyr. Inflamed by an excessive ardor of faith, he seized with his hand and tore apart a book containing cruel edicts against Christians. When this had been reported to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, who were then established in the same city, they raged with extreme cruelty and ordered every kind of torture to be inflicted upon him. That most noble man endured them with such cheerfulness of face and spirit that he could not even have appeared sad on account of them. At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Evurtius, confessor, who, as the Acts relate, was first a subdeacon of the holy Roman Church and then, by divine favor, was designated bishop of the aforesaid city through a dove. In the territory of Autun, of Saint Regina, virgin, who, under the proconsul Olybrius, endured the tortures of the rack, prison, and lamps, and was finally ordered to be put to death by capital sentence. Also in the territory of Paris, of Saint Clodoaldus, priest, distinguished both by nobility of descent and of character.

[Note: In the Carolingian autograph: “of Saint Clodoaldus, priest and confessor.” Sollerius ought not in this matter to have preferred the Pratensis manuscript to his own, since he wished to admit nothing except what was original: for this addition to the eulogy was made by Usuardus. BOUILLART.]

VI Idus. Day 8.

[Note: From Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Muneratus, Belin, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: Among the pure witnesses are counted Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, and Belin, who could easily have been excluded because of the defect from which they suffer. For where the older manuscripts read “The Nativity of the most blessed Mother of God Mary, ever-virgin,” Antwerp and Belin omit “ever-virgin,” while Max-Lübeck has “of the virgin Mother of God Mary.” Pratensis and Muneratus write *et aliorum viginti duum* (“and of twenty-two others”); Greven, confidently, *aliorum XXII*; we, with the remaining witnesses, *viginti duorum*. Antwerp-Major erroneously has: “Also at Antioch, of Timothy and Faustinus”; the text is purer. The remaining errors are generally scribal, or old forms of writing: Nicomedia, Diocletian, Dioclician, Ammon, Theophilus, Neoterius, and so forth.]

[Note: The Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of the Lord, or the feast of holy Mary, Mother of God, or, as it stands in the text, under equivalent expressions, is celebrated by all the martyrologists. For the earliest origin of the institution of this feast, Baronius and Florentinius’s Notes should be consulted. No less curious are the observations made by Fronto on pages 129 and 130 concerning the Calendar, in which, as also in the Allatian Calendar and Gregory’s Sacramentary, the memory of Hadrian is appended to the Nativity of the blessed Virgin Mary, whereas it is excluded in the Thomassian Calendar. But why, in the most ancient Echternach Hieronymian Martyrology, the Nativity of the Mother of God is placed on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, that is, 16 August, I cannot reach by conjecture. Ado today connects several feasts of the same most blessed Mother of God among the feasts of the apostles. Our author used the wording which, from the reading of our older manuscripts, we judged preferable in the text. Wandalbert agrees with the other martyrologists in these verses:

> “Whereby God assumed human form from the Virgin,  
> Mary’s birth illumines the sixth rising with light.”

[Col. 0449C]

> “Then the martyr Hadrian accompanies Rome with blood.”

But the Hadrian celebrated in the final verse seems to be assigned by Wandalbert to Rome: “Rome accompanies him with blood.” Nevertheless, the other martyrologists generally and consistently assert that he suffered at Nicomedia; and on this day most of them do so. Their list may be found in our Acts under 4 March, among the omitted materials. Nothing can be decisively determined from the Hieronymian Martyrologies in favor of either side, since his passion or feast is expressly placed both on 4 March and on 8 September. Bede also has: “The feast of Saint Hadrian, martyr, with thirty-three others.” Baronius, moreover, criticizes Ado for asserting that Hadrian’s passion is celebrated today; I do not see what such grave fault is involved in this. Whatever the truth may be concerning the actual day of his martyrdom—which cannot be sufficiently established even from the Acts themselves—it is certain that Hadrian’s feast is observed more solemnly on this day, whether this custom arose from the first translation, the second translation, the dedication of the basilica, or some other cause. The curious reader should consult Baronius and Florentinius, who discuss these matters at somewhat greater length. His Acts have been published several times; from them Ado compiled an extensive narrative, Notkerus a shorter one, and our author the briefest of all, but one free from every difficulty and therefore the most credible. The Acts themselves, although Baronius considers them sincere and Florentinius regards them as affecting, are regarded by some scholars as doubtful; indeed, Tillemont, volume V, page 818, bluntly asserts that they can neither be proved nor defended (*insoutenables*). See his notes in the cited volume, beginning at page 641. We shall give our judgment concerning them, their place, and their date in due course. Thus far the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Wandalbert, Rabanus, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, Notkerus, and Usuardus agree. The feast of Natalia is also attached to this day by the author of the Little Roman Martyrology. Ado determines no date; our author postponed it to 1 December, I suppose because Ado mentions that she was buried on that day. The Alexandrian martyrs who follow in the short entry above seem to have been taken by our author from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, with three selected at will from the seven whom he might have named individually. The Antiochene Timothy and Faustus come from the same sources, though they are not everywhere arranged or named in the same way. On all these matters see Florentinius. Our reading is genuinely Usuardine and, on the agreement of the manuscripts, sufficiently clear and well established.]

[Note: ROSWEYD, in capital and illuminated letters, has:

> “The Nativity of holy Mary, ever-virgin.”

At the end, after the text, he adds:

> “At Freising, of Corbinianus, bishop and confessor.”

See his Life in Surius.]

PULSANEN. It would be quite pure if it did not lack the final announcement.

[Col. 0449D] ANTWERP-MAX, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN omit “ever-virgin.” Then, after “the Emperor Diocletian,” they insert:

> “After several years had passed, the body of blessed Hadrian was transferred to Rome on 8 September and honorably placed in a church.”

UTRECHT, ALBERGEN, and DANIC, similar to the preceding witnesses, further insert in third place:

> “At Rome, the feast of Saint Sergius, pope. He found in the shrine of blessed Peter a portion of the Lord’s Cross of marvelous size, which every year, on the day of its Exaltation, is kissed and worshiped by all the people in the basilica of Saint Salvator, which is called Constantinian. He established that, at the breaking of the Lord’s Body, the Agnus Dei should be sung by clergy and people.”

See the Additions for the following day.

CENTULE. “The Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, whom the Holy Spirit guarded and sanctified as the chosen one, so that from her womb the exalted God-man might be born. At Alexandria, of Saints Ammon, Theophilus, Neoterius, and twenty-two others. At Rome, the feast of Saint Hadrian, martyr, who suffered at Nicomedia with twenty-three others on 4 March. On the same day at Freising, of Saint Corbinianus, bishop and confessor.”

BRUSSELS. In the first announcement it continues, quite purely:

> “At Rome, the translation of Saint Hadrian, martyr. He and twenty-three others, after many tortures, completed their martyrdom at Nicomedia on 4 March under the Emperor Diocletian, their legs being broken. And after several years the body of blessed Hadrian was transferred to Rome on this day.”

The rest is quite pure.

HAGENOYEN:

> “The Nativity of blessed Mary, virgin, which was discovered through a certain hermit who heard every year on this night, and on no other night, a heavenly and sweet harmony from the angels. At last he asked the Lord what this signified. He received a divine answer that blessed Mary, virgin, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, had been born on earth from blessed Anna, her mother, and that for this reason the entire choir of angels and saints in heaven rejoiced. He was commanded from heaven to go to Rome and report this to the pope, so that the Church militant on earth might rejoice on that day with the Church triumphant in heaven. And so it happened. On the same day, the translation of Saint Hadrian, martyr, when his body was transferred to Rome. He had suffered under Diocletian at Nicomedia with thirty-three others. At Rome, the feast of blessed Sergius, pope,” etc., as in UTRECHT above. In the rest it is quite pure.

MATRICHT–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT: “The Nativity of blessed Mary, virgin. Of Hadrian, martyr, with twenty-three martyrs.” It is noted in the margin:

> “The head of this martyr is kept in the church of Saint Martin, together with the head of Saint Esisius, martyr, in a sufficiently solemn place.”

In the VATICAN manuscript, under note no. 5949, the entries for Ammon and his companions, and for Timothy and Faustus, are missing.

REIMS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At Reims, the feast of Saint Viventius, bishop and confessor.” He was discussed extensively among the Additions for the preceding day.

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION:

> “The Nativity of the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, who brought joy to the whole world. Therefore let our earth rejoice with the greatest exultation, illumined by the Virgin’s birthday.”

Concerning Sergius it has, as above, more distinctly expressing that the Agnus Dei is to be sung three times by clergy and people. It follows:

> “In the city of Freising, the feast of Saint Corbinianus, bishop and confessor.”

It is quite pure in the Alexandrian and Antiochene entries. At the end:

> “At Nicomedia, the translation of Saint Hadrian, martyr, from Constantinople to the city of Rome. Although the day of his passion is celebrated on 4 March, this day is nevertheless held in greater honor in the Church, when his body was transferred to Rome and honorably placed in a church.”

GREVEN: “Of Corbinianus, bishop of Freising. On that same day, of Saint Clodulphus, bishop of Metz, and Doda, his mother.” See 8 June.

MOLAN. In the text, in letters other than those used for “the Emperor Diocletian,” he inserts:

> “After their legs had been broken and their feet cut, and after the hand of blessed Hadrian had also been cut off, they sent forth their spirit while praying and giving thanks to God. The tyrant ordered their bodies to be burned, but suddenly flashes of lightning, thunder, and rain arose, and the fire was extinguished. Then Christians, snatching up the martyrs’ relics, boarded ships, fled to Byzantium, and buried them with reverent honor. Not long afterward the body of blessed Hadrian was transferred to Rome.”

These words are excerpted from Ado. At the end he adds:

> “In the suburbs of the church of Mainz, of Saint Disibodus, confessor [more properly, Disibodus]. And at Freising, the deposition of Saint Corbinianus, bishop, whose life, renowned for its virtues, shone forth in Bavaria.”

Later editions have only:

> “At Freising, the deposition of Saint Corbinianus, bishop, whose life was renowned for its virtues,”

and so forth, as in the first edition.

[Col. 0449]

The Nativity of the most blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God. At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Hadrian, martyr, with twenty-three others, all of whom, after many tortures, completed their martyrdom by the breaking of their legs under the Emperor Diocletian. At Alexandria, of Saints Ammon, Theophilus, Neoterius, and twenty-two others. Also at Antioch, of Timothy and Faustus.

V Idus. Day 9.

[Note: Thus have Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Muneratus, Belin, Greven, and Molan. Also Antwerp-Max, Utrecht, Leyden, Louvain, Albergen, and Danic.]

[Note: After *laniari* I read *exin*, with the principal manuscripts, whatever Muneratus, Greven, and Molan may have as *exinde*. Belin is wrong, as are those who incorrectly write *nudoti* for *nudatis*. The name Hyacinthus recurs several times above; from several forms we have established *Hiacinti*, as Pratensis now has it. Here we write *Jacincti* with Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Greven, and Molan. Muneratus has *Jacinti*, Belin *Jacinthi*; I do not take account of the blemishes of the last six manuscripts. In the first edition Molan put *Alexandriae* in place of *Alexandri*, which, if I am not mistaken, caused Florentinius to attribute this reading to Usuardus. I write *Taruanensi* with Herinien, Greven, and Molan. The others vary: Pratensis has *Taruennensi*, Antwerp-Major *Taruenensi*, Rosweyd *Taruernensi*, Muneratus *Ternanuensi*, the first edition of Belin *Daraunensi*, the second *Tervanensi*, and Utrecht, very badly, *Tornacensi*. I think we should adhere to Pratensis, but I preferred the number of the other witnesses. Nearly all read *Audomari*; but from Pratensis, Herinien, and Greven we retained *Autmari*, which Muneratus also seems to have intended to write. In the second edition of Belin and in Molan the title *saint* is omitted. Concerning Scotland, see elsewhere more often. Herinien has *Queranni*, Rosweyd *Cherani*, better, with the others, in the text.]

[Note: Among the countless Nicomedian martyrs, Dorotheus and Gorgonius, the chamberlains of the raging Diocletian, hold no minor place. They are celebrated by Eusebius, Rufinus, Lactantius, and others, and are placed on this day by the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuardus, and Notkerus—not very appropriately, as many rightly think—since it plainly appears that they are the very men who are reported by the Hieronymian Martyrologies with Migdomius, Peter, and several others on 12 March, when they are discussed in the Acts. The account of the Nicomedian slaughter in Eusebius, Book VIII, should certainly be read, or at least the excerpt from it presented and annotated in the selected Acts of the Martyrs by Theodoricus Ruinart, beginning on page 317. See also Tillemont, volume V, beginning on page 180, where he treats the deeds of Dorotheus, Peter, and Gorgonius with clarity and learning. What singular information the various surviving records among us provide concerning these saints, apart from their translations, will be explained elsewhere. Our Bede, having struck the contest, reads on this day “the feast of Saint Gregory,” through, I suppose, a copyist’s error, since there can scarcely be doubt that “Gorgonius” should be read, as Rabanus has it. Rabanus adds a great crowd of companions—not Nicomedian, but Roman martyrs under Licinius, distinguished in both place and time. The Hieronymian Martyrologies also have Gorgonius alone today. Wandalbert likewise has:

> “Gorgonius, celebrated for fivefold fame and merits,  
> Rome retains; now Gaul seeks him, worshiping”

(another reading: “now Gaul seeks him, venerating”).

Was he a Nicomedian? Baronius seems to assert this; Florentinius and Castellanus doubt it; others deny it. Consult the authors cited, until their opinions are examined more carefully by us in their proper place. As for our preceding short entry, Usuardus customarily followed Ado, simply copying both his sense and his words, omitting only what exceeded his desired brevity. The following announcement of the Sabinian martyrs is taken word for word from the aforesaid Ado, though expressed somewhat more briefly by the Little Roman Martyrology. Rabanus gives more information about Hyacinthus, but does not name his companions. In most Hieronymian Martyrologies there are three, and they are reported in the same manner as here by us. How Rabanus makes Hyacinthus a deacon, and Peter of Natalibus a bishop, I simply cannot conjecture. No ancient authors mention Autmarus or Audomarus, except Florus, who embellishes him with this eulogy: “Dead to the world, living to God, and dispelling it by signs of many virtues, he converted the people of the city of Thérouanne to divine worship.” But it is quite clear from our text that this was not known to Usuardus. From this one may easily conclude that both Audomarus and Queranus obtained a place in the sacred tables through Usuardus’s particular diligence; and you should have no doubt that his reading is simple and genuine. Certainly, concerning Pope Sergius, there can be no question whether the entry is Usuardine; whether it is Adonian is disputed by Mosander and Rosweyd: the former attributes it to Ado, the latter rejects it. Which is better is uncertain. Notkerus has everything attributed by Mosander to Ado; Usuardus does not, though both are either copyists or abbreviators of Ado. Let the reader decide as he wishes. The Life of Audomarus, which Surius had supplied in abridged and interpolated form, was restored to its integrity and furnished with notes by Mabillon in the second Benedictine century, beginning on page 559. Whether it agrees fully with our manuscripts will be seen in its proper place. We possess a manuscript Life of Queranus, Kiranus, or Kirianus, together with various notes on it, which will be arranged in due course.]

[Note: HERINIEN, in the margin, added by another but still ancient hand, has:

> “In the territory of Troyes, of Saint Memorius, martyr, with his companions.”

He also recurs on the immediately preceding days, now under the name Nemorius, now under Memorius; but whatever the manuscripts vary, he is placed in the Roman Martyrology on 7 September.]

PULSANEN. It leaves a large blank space; it then treats the Nicomedians, whose eulogy it entirely cuts short, along with everything else except the final announcement.

ANTWERP, MAX-LÜBECK, and UGUELLIAN are quite pure in the text, but lack the final announcement.

CENTULE:

> “At Nicomedia, of Saints Dorotheus and Gorgonius, martyrs, under Diocletian. On the same day, of Saint Audomarus, bishop of the people of Boulogne and of the Morini, whose glorious conduct is praised by the proclamation of miracles. On that same day, of Saints Hyacinthus, Alexander, and Tiburtius. In Scotland, of Saint Queranus, abbot.”

The name of this saint has been expressed above in various ways; Castellanus calls him *Kiaranus*.

BRUSSELS. At the end of the first announcement, after “Rome,” it adds:

> “And afterward he was transferred to Gorze, seven miles from the city of Metz. At Rome, of Saint Sergius, pope, who instituted that the Agnus Dei should be sung three times during the distribution of Communion at Mass. In the territory of Thérouanne, or of the Morini, the deposition of Saint Audomarus, bishop and confessor. Although he was blind, he was given sight at the elevation of the body of blessed Vedastus; then he asked for and obtained the return of his blindness.”

HAGENOYEN:

> “At Nicomedia, the passion of the holy martyrs Gorgonius and Dorotheus. Dorotheus was a master in the offices performed within the palace; the other was prefect of the royal chamber. Through their excellent instruction, almost all the servants of the chamber persevered vigilantly and freely in the faith of God. These two boldly reproved Diocletian for the death of the Christians and freely confessed themselves Christians. Then he ordered them to be seized, their entire bodies torn by scourges, and, once their entrails had almost been laid bare, to be sprinkled with salt and vinegar. After they had cheerfully endured these torments, a gridiron with coals laid beneath it was ordered to be placed in the middle [the text has *prunis subtracta*; perhaps *substrata*], and whatever remained of their bodies after the scourging was placed upon it and burned—not suddenly, but gradually. Finally, he ordered them to be killed by hanging them with a noose. After some time, blessed Gorgonius was transferred to Rome and buried there on the Latin Way [others: the Labican Way] between the Two Laurels. In Ireland, of Saint Osmanna, most Christian queen.”

The following announcement is punctuated as follows:

> “In the Sabine territory, at the thirtieth mile from the city of Rome, of the holy martyrs Hyacinthus, Alexander, and Tiburtius. In the territory of Terni, the deposition of Saint Audomarus, bishop and confessor. In Scotland, the feast of Saint Queranus, abbot and confessor.”

VICTORINUS. In the penultimate place:

> “At Rome, of Saint Sergius, pope. He established that, at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s Body, the Agnus Dei should be sung by clergy and people, and he ordained that on the days of the Annunciation and Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Simeon, which in Greek is called *Hypopanti* [the Meeting], processions should go out from Saint Adrian’s and meet at Saint Mary’s.”

See below the addition of MOLAN, who writes more clearly from Notkerus, “and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s”; there the preceding matters are also explained somewhat better.

MATRICHT–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT: “Of Gorgonius, martyr. Of Audomarus, bishop and confessor. Of Sergius, pope and confessor.”

REGINA OF SWEDEN, no. 428: “On that same day, of most blessed Osmanna, virgin.” Castellanus notes that this saint is honored with particular devotion in the town bearing her name, in the province of Maine, and at Saint-Denis in France, where her relics are preserved.

SWEDISH REGISTER, shelfmark 130: “In the territory of Thérouanne, of Saint Autmarus, bishop and confessor.”

In the VATICAN manuscript, no. 5949, Audomarus and Queranus are missing. It adds:

> “At Rome, the feast of Saint Sergius, pope, who governed the Church for thirteen years.”

ALTEMPS: “On that same day, of Saint Modwida, virgin.” Perhaps Modovena, whom Castellanus places on 9 July. “At the monastery of Barking, of Saint Wilfida, abbess.”

DIJON: “The revelation of blessed Medardus, bishop, whom the Lord James, cardinal, revealed among us.”

REIMS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “The translation of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris, and of the saints Jovinianus and Tonans.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. After “on the Latin Way,” it inserts:

> “between the Two Laurels, while Dorotheus remained in Greece as patron.”

After Tiburtius it adds:

> “martyrs, of whom blessed Hyacinthus foretold to his torturer: ‘Today a serpent will devour you; but the fire and water with which you caused me to be punished will harm me not at all’; finally he was beheaded.”

In the two final entries it is pure. Then:

> “In the city of Bamberg, the translation of blessed Cunegundis, virgin.”

GREVEN:

> “Blessed Audomarus [also Autmarus], as Vincentius relates from his Acts, was born of noble parents near Constance. With his father he became a monk in the monastery of Luxeuil under Saint Eustasius, the abbot, and not long afterward became bishop of Thérouanne. After gloriously presiding for thirty years alike by word and example, he surrendered his spirit to the Creator, while an ineffable fragrance remained. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saints Donatus, Fortunatus, and Ammonius. At Rome, the deposition of blessed Sergius, pope and confessor. A Syrian by nation, he laudably governed the Church for thirteen years. At Mass he instituted that, after the breaking of the Lord’s Body, the Agnus Dei should be said three times by clergy and people, and he rested, full of good works. Of Berlendis, virgin, and her companions [translation], in the city of Bamberg, the translation of blessed Cunegundis, virgin and empress.”

MOLAN. Concerning Audomarus he inserts:

> “Who died in the year 191 of the Incarnation of the Word”;

other editions have 695. At the end, from Notkerus:

> “Of Sergius, pope, who sat at Rome for thirteen years. He found in the shrine of blessed Peter a portion of the life-giving wood of the Lord’s Cross, of marvelous size. He established that, at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s Body, the Agnus Dei should be sung by clergy and people; and he ordained that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Dormition and Nativity of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Simeon, which in Greek is called *Hypopanti*, litanies should go out from Saint Adrian’s and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s.”

Later editions have:

> “On the ninth day, of Saint Severianus, martyr. At Bethnei, which more recent writers call Stadfort, of Saint Bertellinus, hermit and confessor. At Alto Monte, the finding of Saint Marcellus, pope and martyr. At Merbeke, the translation of Berendis, Celsa, and Nona, virgins.”

Concerning Pope Sergius they repeat almost the same things that we reported from the earlier edition.

[Col. 0451]

At Nicomedia, the passion of the blessed martyrs Dorotheus and Gorgonius. In the presence of Diocletian, they detested the persecution which he was inflicting upon Christians; therefore they were first ordered to be suspended and their entire bodies torn by scourges. Then, after the skin had been stripped from their entrails, they were sprinkled with vinegar and salt, roasted on a gridiron, and finally killed by a noose. After some time, blessed Gorgonius was transferred to Rome and buried on the Latin Way. In the Sabine territory, thirty miles from the City, of Saints Hyacinthus, Alexander, and Tiburtius. In the territory of Thérouanne, of Saint Autmarus, bishop and confessor. In Scotland, of Queranus, abbot.

[Note: All the witnesses, including Dervensis, have these words: “In the territory of Tarvenna.” Nevertheless, erasures are inscribed in Pratensis. The erasure must therefore have been made by the author and is older than all the witnesses. BOUILLART.]

IV Idus. Day 10.

[Note: Thus Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: Hylarius has been discussed elsewhere. There is no single consistent method for forming the names of the African bishops. Antwerp-Major incorrectly has Menesianus for Nemesianus. Some read Lacius in place of Lucius. There is great variation in Litteus, which we prefer. Molan, with Ado, has Liteus; Greven, Liceus; Muneratus, Licteus; Antwerp-Major, Luteus. Here, too, he has Jaredus, while Greven no better has Vaderus. Greven and Molan read “bound in chains for digging,” omitting the conjunction “and.” In Muneratus it is written incorrectly: “There is a letter of blessed Cyprian to them and to them,” and so forth. What is surprising is that Molan, who uses diphthongs, placed *gloriose* before *confessionis* adverbially, whereas Pratensis, Herinien, and Rosweyd, with Ado, more correctly have “of glorious confession.” No judgment can be made concerning the remaining readings. Greven and Molan have “of Saint Cyprian” instead of “of blessed Cyprian.” Antwerp and Max-Lübeck write *Calcidonia*, Muneratus *Calcidona*, omitting the preposition *in*. Molan alone correctly wrote *Sosthenis*; in the text we had to follow all the others. Max-Lübeck deleted the final words, “they sent forth their spirit.”]

[Note: What we observed on the preceding day concerning the announcement of blessed Sergius, pope, is again uncertain here: namely, whether the Viennese martyrologist meant Hilary or Pope Hilary, since, as there, the editors Mosander and Rosweyd disagree. Mosander, in second place, gave: “At Rome, the deposition of blessed Hilary, pope,” almost exactly as our author speaks here; Notkerus, on the contrary, says nothing at all about Hilary. Rosweyd judged that the words cited from Mosander’s edition should be rejected into the appendix. Meanwhile, it is certain that Hilary is marked in most Hieronymian Martyrologies, from which we think he passed into Rabanus. His announcement is:

> “At Rome, the deposition of Hilary, pope, through whom Victor wrote the Paschal cycle.”

Castellanus, following Papebrochius’s reckoning, moves Hilarus back to 21 February, on which day, in his first bimonthly section, he observes several matters worth reading, no less than the notes of Baronius and Florentinius. In any event, wherever Usuardus obtained Hilary, as we write him, we consider it evident from our manuscripts that he is Usuardine. Many things accomplished and written by him are collected in Labbe’s Councils, volume IV, column 1029 onward. See also Tillemont, volume XV, in various places.

Concerning the nine famous African bishops, the Little Roman Martyrology has:

> “In Africa, of the bishops Nemesianus, Felix, and seven others.”

Ado names them individually, taking most of their eulogy from the letter of Saint Cyprian cited there, among the published letters numbered 77. What our author recounts more briefly in the short entry was elegantly abridged from the aforesaid Ado. It is well known that those champions of confession completed their course on different days and in different places, but here I believe they were gathered into one company because Cyprian counts them together. Their replies are preserved in Letters 77, 79, and 80. On them see Tillemont, volume IV, beginning on page 171, and the note on page 640. Castellanus records the proper episcopal sees of each in his Universal Martyrology for this day; we shall treat the rest more fully in its proper place. Sosthenes and Victor are unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Florus, and Rabanus, just as the preceding figures are. The Little Roman Martyrology briefly says of them:

> “At Chalcedon, of Sosthenes and Victor.”

From whatever kind of Acts of the famous virgin and martyr Euphemia Ado composed his eulogy, Notkerus reproduced it almost in full, while our author treated the matter more briefly, as we displayed in the short entry. Wandalbert likewise commemorates them:

> “Sosthenes and Victor are remembered on the fourth, having together  
> Received the same crown of praise for Christ’s kingdom.”

[Note: HERINIEN is exceptionally defective: it remains pure up to “they completed,” omitting the final construction and everything Usuardus says about Sosthenes and Victor.]

ROSWeyd. After the text he adds:

> “Also of Saint Odgerus, deacon and confessor.”

Others write Othgerus.

[Col. 0456D] PULSANEN, in the first and last portions, is quite pure but says nothing at all about the Africans.

ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, and LEYDEN, quite pure in the text, add:

> “On the same day, the passion of Saint Theodardus, bishop of Thérouanne. He was the successor of blessed Remaclus and the teacher of Saint Lambert.”

See Castellanus’s note.

LOUVAIN has the same addition, but is defective in the eulogy of the Chalcedonian martyrs.

ALBERGEN and DANIC add concerning Hilary:

> “He established that no cleric should receive investiture from a layman.”

The rest is similar to ANTWERP-MAX and the others.

CENTULE:

> “At Rome, the deposition of Hilary, pope, through whom Victorinus wrote the Paschal cycle. In Africa, of the holy bishops Nemesianus, Felix, Polianus, Victor, Jaderus, and Dativus [two added in the margin are missing], who suffered under Decius and Valerian. At Chalcedon, of the holy Sosthenus and Victor, who were converted through blessed Euphemia.”

BRUSSELS begins:

> “The passion of Saint Theodardus, bishop and martyr of Thérouanne above the Meuse. He was the successor of blessed Remaclus and the teacher of Saint Lambert.”

Hilary follows, purely. Then:

> “At Rome, on the Lavican Way, between the Two Laurels, the feast of the holy martyrs Hyacinthus, Alexander, and Tiburtius.”

See the preceding day. In the African entry the final sentence concerning Cyprian’s letter is missing. In the Chalcedonian entry it is pure.

Hagenoyen agrees with Alberg in the entry for Hilary. In the African and Chalcedonian entries it is quite pure. It continues: “Also Salvius, bishop and martyr.” In the Roman Martyrology he is called a confessor, but there are several different Salvii. “On the same day, the Passion of Saint Theodard, bishop of Trajectum, successor of Saint Remaclus, and instructor of Saint Lambert, bishop after him, according to his prophecy.”

Aquicinctus adds at the end: “Also Saints Nemesius and Ammonius.” In the Hieronymian Martyrologies they have several companions. See Florentinius there.

Matricularius–Carthusianus–Ultraiectinus: “Theodard, bishop and martyr. Hilary, pope and confessor. Otger, confessor.”

Reginensis–Suecicus, no. 428: “At Liège, Saint Theodard, martyr and bishop of Tongeren.” See above.

Codex D. du Cheval, sign. C: “Also Demesius [Col. 0457C] [others: Demetrius] and Ammonius.” See Aquicinctus.

In Vaticanus no. 5949, Hilary the pope is absent.

Altemps: “On the same day, at Evesham, the translation of Saint Egwin, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Besançon, at the monastery of Bella Vallis, Saint Peter, bishop and confessor.” See the Auctaria for 8 May.

Strozzianus: “In the city of Carontasia [Carontasiensis], Saint Peter, archbishop and confessor, who shone with many virtues and miracles.” Perhaps this is the same Peter mentioned immediately above; and it should therefore be read: “At Tarentaise. Also, Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, confessor, of the Order of the Hermit Friars.”

The Lübeck–Cologne edition, in the entry for Hilary, has the same text as Albergensis and the others above. In the African and Chalcedonian entries it is quite pure. Concerning Theodald [*Theodaldo*], it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others. It continues:

“At the city of Tolentino, the burial of Saint Nicholas, priest and confessor. He was a man of marvelous abstinence, a follower of the eremitical life; living under the rule of blessed Augustine, he led among the brethren, beyond the ordinary observance of the rule, [Col. 0457D] a stricter way of life. How great his merit was became clear when, for six continuous months before his death, he was deemed worthy to be [Col. 0458A] honored by the ministry of angels with heavenly melodies. Afterwards he rested in a holy death; his tomb is to the present day made illustrious by frequent signs and miracles. On the same day, Saints Demetrius and Dmmonius [printed *Dmmonii*, apparently Ammonius], martyrs. Also blessed Otger, deacon and confessor.”

Belin begins: “At Tolentino, the burial of Saint Nicholas, confessor, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine.” It continues with Hilary and the Africans, quite purely. Then:

“On the same day, Saint Peter, archbishop, who shone with many virtues and miracles. On the same day, in Chalcedon, Saints Sosthenes and Victor, who, after many torments, gave up their spirit in prayer.”

Greven:

“On the same day, the Passion of Saint Theodard, bishop of Upper Trajectum and martyr. He worthily succeeded Saint Remaclus when the latter went into the wilderness; he was the educator of Saint Lambert. Demetrius and Ammonius, martyrs. In Alexandria, Saints Ammon, Orion, Orosius, and 806 others. Also, the burial of blessed Silvius, bishop of Albi and confessor. Having despised the world, [Col. 0458B] he entered a monastery; forgetting what lay behind and constantly stretching himself toward what lay ahead, he was elected abbot. But judging it more useful to remain hidden among the monks than to bear the name of abbot before the people, he entered a place of seclusion. From there he was later brought out and compelled to preside over the aforesaid church; finally, when called by the Lord, he received with many others the reward of his labor. Otger, deacon and confessor. In England, the translation of Saint Adelwold, bishop of Winchester and confessor. At Novara, Saint Gabius [*Gabii*], bishop and confessor. Also, the burial of Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, of the Order of the Hermits of blessed Augustine, who shone greatly through the virtue of continual prayer and marvelous abstinence. As a judgment of his outstanding holiness, for six months before his death he was deemed worthy to hear angelic choirs; delighted by them, he desired and obtained release and to be with Christ. Felicitas, widow, and her daughters.”

Molanus:

“At Tolentino, the burial of the most holy Nicholas,” [Col. 0458C] etc., as in Belin. Concerning Peter also, as there. “Also, in the city of Liège, the feast of Saint Theodard, bishop and martyr. He was the successor of blessed Remaclus and the instructor of Saint Lambert; he rests at Liège, in the basilica of Saint Lambert. Also, Saint Otger, confessor. And the burial of Salvius, bishop, concerning whose holiness Gregory, bishop of Tours, wrote, reporting that by revelation he had seen a sword drawn by the divine voice hanging over the roof which King Chilperic had ordered to be built. The truth immediately followed this vision, for twenty days later the king’s two sons died.” See Rabanus.

It continues, in smaller type: “On the same day, Saint Eunucius, bishop of Noyon and confessor.”

Other editions have other entries, as above. It continues:

“At the city of Albi, the burial of Saint Salvius,” etc., as above. “Also, Saint Otger, confessor, who was a companion in pilgrimage from Britain of the holy bishops Wiro and Plechelmus and, after many acts of piety, received burial in [Col. 0458D] the church of Mount Peter, near Roermond. On the same day, Saint Eunucius, bishop of Noyon and confessor. On the tenth day, Saints Menodora, Metrodora, and Nymphodora, martyrs.”

[Col. 0455]

At Rome, blessed Hilary, pope. In Africa, the feast of the holy bishops Nemesianus, Felix, Lucius, and also Felix, Litteus, Polianus, Victor, Jader, and Dativus. Under Decius and Valerian, when the fury of persecution arose, they were first beaten severely with clubs for their steadfast first confession of Christ; then, bound in fetters and assigned to dig in the mines, they completed the struggle of their glorious confession. A letter of blessed Cyprian, written to them and concerning them, is extant. On the same day, in Chalcedon, Saints Sosthenes and Victor, who, for confessing the faith, endured prison, chains, and wild beasts under the consul Priscus and, finally called from heaven while at prayer, gave up their spirit.

**The third day before the Ides. Day 11.**

[Note: [Col. 0457]

The text is taken from Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp–Major, Pulsanen, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0457D]

Antwerp–Major, Greven, and Molan write *Prothi*, “of Protus”; with the others, we use the simpler form found in the text. Hyacinthus was discussed on the ninth day of this month. Here again most witnesses, such as [Col. 0458D] Herinien, Antwerp–Major, Rosweyd, and Greven, compel the form *Jacincti*, “of Hyacinthus.” Pulsanen has *Jacinthi*, Munerat *Jacinti*, Molan *Hyacincthi*, and Pratensis *Hiacincti*—[Col. 0459A] unless this should perhaps be attributed to the copyist rather than to the manuscript itself. The common reading is *tuncque pariter decollantur*, “and then they are beheaded together.” Antwerp–Major varies: *atque pariter decollati sunt*, “[Col. 0460A] and they were beheaded together.” Greven and Molan have *Tunc pariter decollati sunt*, “Then they were beheaded together.”]

[Note: [Col. 0459A]

For the very ancient and continuous cult of the two brothers, commonly called twins, there stand the oldest ecclesiastical monuments—namely, the calendars edited by Bucherius and Fronto (the Allatian calendar is corrupt for this day) and Gregory’s Sacramentary. It is commonly held that a more solemn office for them continued to be celebrated up to the thirteenth century, when the octave of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary is thought first to have been instituted.

To these witnesses must be added all the ancient Martyrologists, without exception. Their only difference is that in the manuscripts of Florentinius Eugenia and Basilla are added; the latter we included with the Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Usuard on 20 May, and the former we shall give with those same authorities on 25 December. These are the words of the Lucan codex:

“At Rome, on the old Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Basilla, the feast of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, Eugenia and Basilla.”

Eugenia and Basilla are absent from the Echternach and Corbie manuscripts; in the latter the brothers are more probably called *Didymi* [*Dydimi*], that is, twins. Bede writes:

[Col. 0459B] “At Rome, Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, who were eunuchs of Saint Eugenia.”

Florus adds: “But through the fervor of faith they became teachers of Christian law, and therefore received the sentence of death.”

Rabanus’s eulogy derives from the same source from which Ado drew his own, namely, the Acts of Saint Eugenia; but it is entirely different from Ado’s. The Roman Parvum reads briefly:

[Col. 0460A] “At Rome, Hyacinthus and Protus, eunuchs.”

Ado appended to these words his longer narrative from the aforesaid Acts. Nearly the whole of it appears in Notker, compressed by our author into shorter limits, so that it contains scarcely anything that does not seem sufficiently consistent with historical truth, although the Acts themselves from which Ado drew require some criticism, as Baronius admits; others reject them as wholly fictitious. This matter will be treated expressly elsewhere, unless what Papebrochius has touched upon in his replies to Father Sebastian, article 16, no. 91 onward, should suffice.

Here are Wandalbert’s verses:

> Next, Protus and his brother Hyacinthus honour the third day before the Ides;  
> Together they taught Eugenia the sacred law.  
> Felix too consecrated this day by his blessed death at Zurich,  
> Together with the holy martyrdom of blessed Regula.

Of the latter martyrs I find nothing among the older Martyrologists. Only Notker adorns the local saints—namely, [Col. 0460B] those of Zurich—with a great encomium. I refer the reader to him, since these matters have nothing to do with our Usuard. What was subsequently added in certain Usuardine manuscripts I shall place among the Auctaria, where some manuscripts record more about these two saints as companions of the Theban Legion.]

[Note: [Col. 0459B]

Rosweyd, whose text is pure throughout, adds at the end: “Saint Eugenia, virgin. Felix the martyr and his sister Regula, virgin and martyr.” Eugenia is commemorated on 25 December. Concerning the last two, see Wandalbert.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. at the end: “At Lyons, the burial of Saint Patiens.”

ANTUERP.-MAX. and LOVANIEN.: “At Lyons, the burial of Saint Patiens, bishop.” See the Roman Martyrology.

Utrecht, Leiden, Alberg, and Danish: they have the same Auctarium concerning Patiens of Lyons; they add:

“At Zurich, the feast of Saints Felix and Regula, martyrs, his sister, companions of the Thebans. [Col. 0459C] Decius the governor, by order of the emperor Maximian, first subjected them to various torments and finally ordered them to be put to death by the sword.”

Centulensis:

“At Rome, in the cemetery of Basilla, Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, martyrs, who were eunuchs of blessed Eugenia the virgin. At Lyons, Saint Patiens, bishop and confessor, at whose urging the life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre was written.”

Bruxellensis, whose text is quite pure, adds the same account of Felix and Regula that we gave above from Utrecht and the others. Then:

“On the same day, Saint Dagobert, king and martyr. At Lyons, Saint Patiens, bishop. And Saint Muciana, virgin.”

I think Vinciana is intended; see Castellanus.

Hagenoyen:

“At Rome, on the old Salarian Way, the feast of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, brothers and martyrs. Together with Eugenia, daughter of Philip, later prefect of Alexandria, they were given over to study. Although they ought to have learned philosophy, [Col. 0459D] they learned the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ; and thus they converted Eugenia to the faith. They were then sent to Alexandria with Philip, but left him and entered a monastery with Eugenia. Afterwards they appeared miraculously to Philip and converted him to the faith. After his death, Claudia, Philip’s wife, returned to Rome with all her children and with Protus and Hyacinthus. While many were being converted through them, they were led to sacrifice; but when they prayed, the idol immediately collapsed and was reduced to ashes. The pagans were ashamed, and soon beheaded them. Also, in the castle of Habut, Saint Adolphus, confessor.” See below for a better identification of this saint.

“At Zurich, the Passion of Saints Felix and Regula, his sister, martyrs, and Exsuperantius. [Col. 0460B] After the glowing iron wheels [printed *rotassiti*, read *rotas*, “wheels”], enduring long imprisonment and other afflictions, and after being tested with pitch and boiling lead, they heard the Lord calling them in these words: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,’ etc. Not long afterwards, by order of the governor Decius, they were beheaded. Then, an hour later, the bodies of the saints rose, took up their own heads, carried them forty cubits, and rested there. At that place Charlemagne established a canonry [the printed *fideles … canoiniam contraxit* is defective; the editor asks whether it means “gathered the faithful”], and later his son Louis built a monastery of nuns [the source has plural *aedificaverunt*, “they built”]. At Lyons, [Col. 0460C] Saint Patiens, bishop and confessor.”

Aquicinctus at the end: “On the same day, Saint Patiens, bishop of Lyons.”

Matricularius–Carthusianus–Ultraiectinus: “Protus and Hyacinthus, martyrs.” It adds:

“These were the eunuchs of blessed Eugenia, virgin and martyr; they were converted to the faith with her, as is found in her Life.” It continues: “Felix and Regula, martyrs.”

Florentinus:

“Protus and Hyacinthus . . . Their most sacred bones, together with the relics of Saint Nemesius the martyr, were transferred in the year of the Lord 1420, during the pontificate of Martin V, to the monastery of Saint Mary of the Angels at Florence. On the same day, Saint Elias, abbot.”

There are several Eliases; this one will be discussed later.

Codex Montis Sancti:

“The natal day of Adelfius, a noble man nobly descended from the illustrious race of the Sicambri, shines forth; his mother was the daughter of the most noble Romaricus, our holy ruler and sweetest patron.”
