[Col. 0460D]

The Lübeck–Cologne edition, after “eunuchs,” inserts: “of blessed Eugenia, virgin, with whom they were baptized by Helenus, bishop. Not long afterwards, under the emperor Gallienus, because they were,” etc.

It continues:

“At Zurich in Germany, Saints Felix,” etc., almost as above in Utrecht and the others:

“At Lyons, the burial of Saint Patiens, bishop and confessor. In Sicily, blessed Euplus and Serapion, confessor.”

This is better in Greven below.

Belin, whose text is quite pure, adds at the end, as above: “At Lyons, the burial of Saint Patiens.” But I do not know why the second edition has *Saint Patiens* in the feminine, unless this is a typographical error.

Greven:

[Col. 0461A] “At Zurich in Germany, Saints Felix and Regula, his sister, martyrs of the holy Theban Legion. Decius the prefect, by order of the emperor Maximian, after subjecting them to various punishments, ordered them to be executed by the sword. At Lyons, Saint Patiens, bishop and confessor. Bodo, bishop of Toul and confessor, who, having been translated to Lugdunum Clavatum (Laon), is venerated with marvelous devotion by the faithful. Also, a commemoration of Saints Leo, Basilla, and Eugenia. In Sicily, Euplus and Serapion, confessors. Also blessed Maura. On the island of Palmaria, the burial of Saint Venerius, abbot. In the time of the emperor Phocas, while leading an eremitical life on that same island, he rested in peace, famous for many miracles, and was buried there by angelic hands. Oil was also seen to flow at that place, effective for the health of many. Also Venerius, another monk and confessor. Out of love for the solitary life, he left the cenobium, climbed a certain rock inaccessible to human beings, and remained there for four years without human food, except for the four loaves he had taken with him. At last he died and was buried in the same place, [Col. 0462A] where he became famous for miracles in the time of Otto III. In Egypt, Saint Elias, abbot and confessor. Also, of blessed memory, Wilbert, bishop of Cologne Agrippina, and confessor.”

Molanus:

“At Lyons, the burial of Saint Patiens, bishop. At his urging, the presbyter Constantius wrote the life of blessed Germanus, bishop, full of miracles. At Vercelli, Saint Aemilianus, bishop and confessor. And Saints Felix and Regula.”

Then, in smaller type:

“Bodo, bishop of Toul and confessor, who, having been translated to Lugdunum Clavatum (Laon), is venerated with marvelous devotion by the faithful. Vinciana, virgin.”

Later editions have the same entries concerning Patiens and Aemilianus as the earlier edition. It continues:

“On the same day, at Zurich, the feast of Saints Felix and Regula. At the port of Ghent, Saint Vinciana, virgin. On the eleventh day, Saint Theodora, holy mother of Alexandria.”

In smaller type:

“Also Bodo, confessor and bishop of Toul, who, having been translated to Lugdunum Clavatum (Laon), is venerated with marvelous devotion,” etc.

Understand “the fortified Lugdunum,” commonly called Laon, where his body is honored.]

[Col. 0457]

At Rome, on the old Salarian Way, the feast of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, eunuchs and martyrs. Under the emperor Gallienus, when they were discovered to be Christians, they were compelled to sacrifice; but because they refused, they were first beaten with extreme severity and then beheaded together.

**The Day before the Ides. Day 12.**

[Note: [Col. 0461]

Again taken from the same sources: Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp–Major, Pulsanen, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0461B]

Greven and others write *Tycinum*, a spelling of Ticinum, but incorrectly. The manuscripts differ greatly concerning Iventius, and confusion could therefore arise with another saint or with one or more nearly synonymous names. The saint under discussion is called *Juventius* in our Acts, on 8 February. Today Pratensis, together with Pulsanen, writes *Yventius*; Greven, *Yvencius*; Munerat, *Juventius*; and de Gasparis, author of the Ticinian Breviary, consistently calls him *Inventius*. We follow Herinien and Molan in the text. Antwerp–Major reads *Syri Eventii*, “of Syrus [and] Eventius,” omitting *et*, “and.” [Col. 0462B] Greven and Molan likewise omit the same particle before “with great virtues,” although all the other manuscripts unanimously retain it. *Choruscantes*, “shining,” in Antwerp–Major and Munerat is an error for *coruscantes*. Herinien, Antwerp–Major, and Munerat have *illustraverunt*, “they illumined,” in place of contracted *illustrarunt*; it makes no difference, but I prefer the readings of the others. Pulsanen lacks *glorioso fine*, “with a glorious end”; Munerat, perhaps through a printer’s error, has *gloriose*, “gloriously.”]

[Note: [Col. 0461B]

I observe that a certain Syrus and also a certain Eventius, Evantius, or Iventius are recorded by the Hieronymian Martyrologies on this day, but neither of these can in any way be brought back to Ticinum. Nor are those whom Rabanus mentions, taking almost everything from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, any nearer to Ticinum. Wandalbert also has:

> Next, on the day before the Ides, the exalted martyr Syrus seeks the heavens.

But even this martyr, crowned with martyrdom, should be attributed still less to the people of Ticinum. We have said that Juventius is found in the Acts on 8 February, where several matters concerning him and Syrus are clarified, [Col. 0461C] although Syrus’s deeds are referred to 9 December. Many things in the Acts of both saints raise doubts, especially concerning the periods in which they are said to have flourished and concerning the mission undertaken from Hermagoras, the disciple of Saint Mark; these matters, however, must be examined by a more laborious investigation.

In the meantime, the Ticinian writers may be consulted—vigorous defenders of their antiquities—Gualla and de Gasparis: the former in the *Sanctuary of Pavia*, the latter in the *Breviary of the Holy Bishops of the Ticinian Church*. [Col. 0462B] The former, in flagrant contradiction and apparently unaware of it, but perhaps truly, asserted that Juventius fought vigorously against the Arians at Milan. Yet on this basis the entire history of Syrus, Pompeius, and Juventius would be overturned. See the cited day, 8 February, Bolland’s Commentary and Tillemont, volume II, page 561.

In any case, neither in the Hieronymian copies nor in the genuine Bede, Florus, or the others are those two Ticinian bishops and confessors joined together. The sole source of their joint commemoration on this day is [Col. 0462C] the author of the Roman Parvum, from whom it passed into Ado, from Ado into our author and Notker. The first speaks as follows:

“At Ticinum, Syrus and Eventius, confessors [printed singular *confessoris*], disciples of Hermagoras, the first bishop of Aquileia.”

Ado added much in his customary manner; from this Usuardus made his abridgement, which we have presented here in the text, so that there can be no doubt at all about Usuardine simplicity. I do not know whether Usuardus deliberately avoided certain things; certainly, what is said in our text seems more easily capable of being tested against historical truth than some of the material Ado inserted from the Acts. More elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0461C]

Rosweyd, whose text is pure, adds at the end: “At Trier, the feast of Saint Maximinus, bishop.” See below.

Antwerp, Max–Lübeck, and Ughelli, whose text is also pure, add: “At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of blessed Sacerdos, bishop.” In French, Serdot or Sardot; Castellanus notes in the margin of the Martyrology that he died at Paris.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERG., and DANIC. append to the text:

“In Aquitaine, the feast of Saint Maximinus, archbishop of Trier, [Col. 0461D] who was transferred to Trier on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.” [Col. 0462C] (Utrecht and Alberg note the fourth day before the Kalends of July.) “At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of blessed Sacerdos, bishop.”

Centulensis:

“At the city of Ticinum, also called Pavia, the feast of the holy confessors and pontiffs Syrus and Hiventius [*Hiventii*], whom blessed Hermacoras [*Hermacoras*] of Aquileia ordained and sent to the aforesaid city. By the word of faith they illuminated not only that region but also the neighboring cities of Verona, Brixia, and Lodi, and completed their course with an excellent [end, supplied by the editor with “unless I am mistaken”].”

[Col. 0462D]

Bruxellensis:

“At the city of Ticinum, [Col. 0463A] also called Pavia, Saints Syrus and Evencius, confessors. Sent to the aforesaid city by blessed Armagoras, disciple of Saint Mark the Evangelist, they first preached the Gospel of Christ there and, shining with great virtues and miracles, also illumined the neighboring cities by divine works. Thus, in pontifical dignity, etc. In Sicily, the Passion of Saint Serapion, bishop, and thirteen others. In Aquitaine, the burial of Saint Maximinus, archbishop of Trier. His body was transferred to Trier on the fourth day before the Kalends of June and buried in the cemetery of Saint Eucharius. At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of blessed Sacerdos, bishop. At Anderlach, a village of Brabant near us, the burial of Saint Guy, confessor. His bodily relics are venerated there; many accounts of his life and miracles are also read. And Saint Regina, virgin. Also Saint Edippa, virgin.”

Hagenoyen is almost identical in the text to Bruxellensis. It continues:

“On the same day, Verona [called Verena below], virgin, at Zurzach in the diocese of Constance. She was of Theban descent [Col. 0463B] and came to Italy with blessed Maurice and his companions as a pilgrim. Entering Milan, she visited the prisons of the saints during the persecution of Diocletian and ministered to them from her resources as far as she could. What she could not do with money, she did by her will and bodily service.

When Maurice and his companions had suffered martyrdom, Verena crossed the Alps and stayed with one who had escaped from the Thebans—not because he had fled through fear of death, but following the example of the Lord. Thus Verena became the mother of many virgins; she illuminated the blind, drove demons from the possessed, and the Lord worked many other miracles through her. Therefore a certain Roman, after subjecting her to various insults, imprisoned her; there she was visited and comforted by Saint Maurice.”

I omit the rest; whether it deserves greater credence will be discussed in its proper place. See the Auctaria for 1 September.

“Also, Saint Maximus [*Maximi*], bishop and confessor of Trier. At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of blessed Sacerdos, bishop and confessor.”]

[Col. 0463C] See above under Antwerp and the others.

Aquicinctus at the end: “At Lyons, Saint Sacerdos, bishop.” See what was said above.

Victorin and Reginensis–Suecicus, under note no. 130: “On the same day, Saint Patiens, bishop of Lyons.” We transferred him from various manuscripts to the preceding day.

Matricularius–Carthusianus–Ultraiectinus: “Cyrus and Urentius, bishops, who, sent to Ticinum by blessed Hermagoras, converted a great multitude.” The margin correctly urges: “Elsewhere, Syrus and Yvencius; in the Roman Martyrology, Juventius.”

Florentinus: “At Lyons in Gaul, the feast of Saint Patiens. Also Saint Serapion.”

The Lübeck–Cologne edition begins:

“In Aquitaine, the feast of blessed Maximinus, archbishop and confessor of Trier. Anastasius, bishop of Alexandria, fleeing the persecution of the emperor Constantius, was [Col. 0464A] honorably received by him at Trier. He also deposed Euphratas, bishop of the Church of Cologne, as a heretic, and replaced him with blessed Severinus, a most discerning man. At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of blessed Sacerdos, bishop and confessor. At the city of Ticinum, also called Pavia, Saints Syrus and Quentius, confessors and pontiffs, who were sent to the aforesaid city by blessed Hermagoras, bishop of Aquileia and disciple [printed *discipuli*, “of the disciple/disciples,” corrected to *discipulo*, “by the disciple”] of Saint Mark the Evangelist. There they first preached the Gospel of Christ and, shining with great virtues and miracles, also illumined the neighboring cities—namely Verona, Brescia, and Lodi—by divine works. Thus, with the faith of the believing peoples founded and strengthened in pontifical dignity, they rested with a glorious end. At Autun, Saint Evantius, bishop and confessor.”

Belin, after the text: “At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of Saint Sacerdos, bishop.”

Greven:

“Also at Antioch, Saint Timothy. At Nicomedia, Saint Nicetas, martyr, who was also called [Col. 0464B] Victor. For the faith of Christ he overcame sharp swords, fire, smoke, and the cutting off of his hands and feet; when his limbs had been restored to him by divine power, he was again beaten with clubs and afterwards departed happily. In Aquitaine, the burial of Saint Maximinus, bishop and confessor of Trier. Born in Aquitaine, he was attracted by the reputation for holiness of Agricius, bishop of Trier, and came to him. Agricius raised him in every holiness, and by divine revelation Maximinus succeeded him. Finally, while visiting his native land, he rested there. At Lyons, blessed Sacerdos, bishop and confessor. Also Serapion, bishop. Marcellinus, bishop. At Autun, Saint Evantius, bishop and confessor. The translation of Saint Hermagoras, bishop of Aquileia. In the Norman city of Bayeux, blessed Reverentius, priest and confessor. In Egypt, Saint Bona, virgin, also called Mundicorda, “pure-hearted” [the first edition has *est, quae*, “is, who,” instead of *dicta*, “called”], who served Christ her bridegroom in great holiness.”

[Col. 0464C]

Molanus:

“At Lyons in Gaul, Saint Sacerdos, bishop. Among us”—he means at Anderlach near Brussels—“the burial of Saint Guy, confessor. After a seven-year and arduous pilgrimage, he chose this place for his rest, where the relics of his sacred body are honored amid frequent miracles. In Aquitaine, the feast of Saint Maximinus, archbishop of Trier, who was transferred to Trier on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. On the same day, blessed Reverentius, priest and confessor.”

Then, in smaller type: “In the Norman city of Bayeux.”

Later editions have the same entries concerning Sacerdos, Guy, and Maximinus as above. Then:

“On the same day, at Bayeux, blessed Reverentius, priest and confessor. In the Gallic city of Autun, the burial of blessed Evantius, bishop. On the twelfth day, the most holy martyr Autonomus.”

See the Roman Martyrology and the Acts of the Saint in Surius.]

[Col. 0461]

At the city of Ticinum, Saints Syrus and Iventius, confessors. They were sent to the aforesaid city by blessed Hermagoras; there they first preached the Gospel of Christ and, shining with great virtues and miracles, also illumined the neighboring cities by divine works, and thus, in pontifical dignity, rested in peace with a glorious end.

**On the Ides. Day 13.**

[Note: [Col. 0463]

Thus Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp–Major, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0463D]

Egypt has been discussed more than sufficiently. In this matter Munerat surpasses the others, reading *apud Aegiptum Alexandriae*, “in Egypt, at Alexandria,” and adding the title “bishop and martyr” to Philip. The difference concerning the dignity of *episcopi*, “the bishop,” *episcopatus*, “the episcopate,” or *episcopii*, “the episcopal office” was also noted above. [Col. 0464D] I followed the last form, chiefly on the authority of Pratensis and Herinien; Antwerp–Major writes the second form, Munerat and Molan the first. *in orationem constitutus*, “placed in prayer,” with accusative *orationem* instead of ablative *oratione*, is found only in Antwerp–Major; the others have the form found in the text. Ado incorrectly writes *Perennius* [Col. 0465A] for *Terentius*; Antwerp–Major altered it still worse to *Perhennius*, and Molan to *Perhemmius*. All, with Ado, have “of Volusianus and Gallienus”; [Col. 0466A] concerning this conjunction, see below. *Romanici* for *Romarici*, “of Romaric,” and *anachoritae*, “of an anchorite,” for *anachoriticae*, “of an anchoritic [life],” are errors in Antwerp–Major.]

[Note: [Col. 0465A]

Baronius, under 25 December, speaks as follows concerning the Acts of Saint Eugenia mentioned above:

“They nevertheless contain some things requiring criticism, such as what is read there about Philip, Eugenia’s father, who, as the author says, became bishop of Alexandria. The lists of the Alexandrian bishops … [the citation is abbreviated] plainly show that this is entirely fictitious.”

If one adds what the same Baronius notes on this day, one will easily perceive that the aforesaid Acts suffer not merely from that one fiction. As we have already said above, they were examined and rejected by Papebrochius in his replies to Father Sebastian, article 16, no. 91 onward. Philip is not mentioned by the Hieronymian copies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, or Wandalbert. Here again the author of the Roman Parvum leads his followers, saying:

“In Alexandria, Philip, bishop and martyr, who was previously prefect.”

From the cited Acts Ado drew the material recorded there concerning Philip’s episcopate and other matters relating to him. [Col. 0465B] Usuardus and Notker each rendered a summary in his own manner, everywhere preserving the association of the emperors Volusianus and Gallienus and the name of the prefect Perennius, who is called Terentius in the Acts published by Surius and whom Baronius calls by that name in the modern Roman Martyrology. This may suffice for our purpose.

The following announcement concerning Amatus, priest and abbot, is wholly Ado’s and is not older; nearly the whole of it was copied word for word by our author. Our announcement is Ado’s, I say, but not of that Ado whom Mabillon usually cites in the Benedictine Acts [Col. 0466A] and who differs from all our witnesses, both manuscripts and printed editions, as we have also observed elsewhere. See the preliminary notes to the Life of this Saint Amatus of ours, in Benedictine century II, page 129, where it is given in full; in Surius it is abridged and altered.

Notker differs in having written *Anianus* for *Amatus*, but we believe this entered through a copyist’s error. Thus Wandalbert writes of our Amatus alone:

> On the Ides the abbot Amatus shines, beloved (*Amatus*) in merit as well as name.

Besides Philip and Amatus [printed *Lmatum*], Mosander assigns to Ado [printed *Ldoni*] the bishops Maurilio of Angers [printed *Ludegavensem*, apparently *Andegavensem*] and Littorius of Tours, whom Rosweyd rejected into an appendix. That Usuardus did not treat the latter—whom Rabanus records in the words of the Hieronymian Martyrologies—is shown by our best manuscripts. I would believe that he took Maurilio [*Maurilionem*] from the same Hieronymian Martyrologies; today he is more commonly called Maurilius [*Maurilium*], [Col. 0466B] and Mosander and Labbe’s Hagiologium commemorate him in precisely the same terms.

We judge all these entries to be genuinely and purely Usuardine, which is entirely sufficient for the purpose of this work. We leave for another place the examination of the mass of material concerning several Lives preserved among our manuscripts. Besides those published earlier, there is a manuscript and printed Life by Magnobodus of Angers, another in prose, and also the metrical Life by Marbode of Rennes on very old parchment; their reliability has already become a matter of dispute among scholars, following Launoy.]

[Note: [Col. 0465B]

Rosweyd adds at the end from the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “Also in Apulia, Felicissimus and Secundinus, martyrs.”

Pulsanen, quite pure at the beginning and end, removed the second entry concerning Amatus.

Antwerp, Max–Lübeck, and Ughelli append to the text: “At Tours, Saint Litorius, bishop.”

[Col. 0465C] Greven attaches to the text under the sign LL: “At Trier, Saint Maternus, bishop. We discussed that sign on 5 and 20 August; for the same reason we exclude Greven from the number of the pure witnesses.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., and DANIC. add concerning Maurilio: “He was conspicuous for the holiness of his life and flourished in many virtues. At Tours, Saint Litorius, bishop and confessor.”

Albergensis adds to these: “At Trier, the feast of Saint Maternus, bishop, disciple of the Apostle Saint Peter.” See below, the Lübeck–Cologne edition.

Louvain removes everything concerning Amatus after *Romarici*, “of Romaric.” Its text concerning Maurilius is pure. At the end, concerning Litorius, it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others above.

Centulensis:

“At Alexandria in Egypt, Saint Philip, martyr, father of Saint Eugenia the virgin. At Angers, Saint Maurelius [*Maurelii*], bishop and confessor, a man of great virtues. In the territory of Boulogne, Saint Maximus of Riez, bishop and confessor. [Col. 0465D] On the same day, Saint Amatus, abbot of Mount Romaricus.”

Concerning Maximus, or rather his discovery, see Greven below.

Bruxellensis, moderately interpolated in the text, adds at the end only this single auctarium:

“At Tours, Saint Litorius, bishop and confessor.”

Hagenoyen treats Philip at greater length from the Acts of Eugenia, as follows:

“At Alexandria in Egypt, the Passion of blessed Philip, bishop, father of Saint Eugenia the virgin. He was wonderfully converted through his daughter Eugenia when he saw her in the state of the monks and she had been accused of rape. She opened her garment and showed that she was his daughter; he was pierced in heart, was baptized, and, abandoning the prefecture, obtained the honor of the episcopate, since everyone chose him. Not long afterwards, while he was engaged in prayer, [Col. 0466B] the prefect Perhennius had him slaughtered with the sword, in the time of the emperors Volusianus and Gallienus.

On the same day, Saint Amatus, priest and abbot of the monastery of Romaricus in the diocese of Metz, who possessed marvelous abstinence,” etc., adding at the end, “and died in peace, the father of many monks. In Aquitaine, the feast of Saint Maximinus, [Col. 0466C] archbishop of Trier, who was transferred to Trier on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. At Angers, the burial of Saint Maurilianus, or Maurilius, bishop and confessor. He,” etc., as in ANTUERP.-MAX. “At Tours, the burial of Lydorius [*Lydorii*],” etc.]

AQUICINCT. After “emperors,” inserts: “At Douai, the translation of Saint Amatus, archbishop of Sens, who was expelled from the episcopate by Theodoric, king of the Franks, at the instigation of Ebroin, mayor of the palace, and was exiled to this province by order of the aforesaid king. Having been made abbot of the monastery of Romaricus, he was a follower of extraordinary abstinence,” etc. After “king,” the words “Likewise, of another Saint Amatus,” or something similar, have been omitted, lest two different men be confused as one.

DAVERON.: “Saint Lidorus, bishop of Tours. The reception of the relics of blessed Julian the martyr.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Philip, bishop and martyr, father of Saint Eugenia the virgin, who was converted in a sufficiently miraculous manner through his daughter, resigning the prefecture of Alexandria. Maurilion, bishop. Amatus [Col. 0466D], abbot.”

In VATICAN., no. 5949, Amatus and Maurilion are absent. Added first: “At Benevento, the feast of Saint Felicissimus, bishop, in Saint Sophia. On the same day, Saint Mamilianus the confessor.”

ALTEMPS.: “On that same day, the translation of blessed Augustine, apostle of the English, and of the holy archbishops and confessors Laurence, Mellitus, Justus, Honorius, Deusdedit, Theodore, and Saint Adrian the abbot, together with the virgin Milareda, beloved of God.”

FLORENTIN.: “Amatus . . . . . [abbot or otherwise Donaticus]. His body was granted to blessed Ambrose by the supreme pontiff Saint Damasus and transferred from the Roman city to the city of Florence, and buried in the church of Saint Laurence; there also rest the bodies of Saint Marc, pope, and Concordia, martyr. [Col. 0467A] At Angers, Saint Auxilius, bishop and confessor. In place of Maurilius: at Tours, Saint Littorius [MED., Litoris], bishop and confessor. At the city of Lamus, the passing of Saint Venerius, whose body was transferred to Reggio. In Sicily, the seventy-nine holy martyrs who suffered under the tyrant Profasius in the city of Admimundula, as is recorded in the passion of Saints Lucia and Geminianus.” The Acts are available in Surius, but neither the tyrant’s name, nor the place of martyrdom, nor the number of martyrs agrees with the present account.

CODEX MONTIS SANCTI: “Already the orbit of this solemn day flashes forth, on which the illustrious confessor of Christ, Amatus, leading a heavenly life, joyfully obtains the supreme hall of the heavenly court; whoever wishes to read his miracles, that is, his deeds and life [should consult them]. He was a follower of extraordinary abstinence,” etc.

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “At Tours, Saint Littorius, bishop and confessor.” There is constant variation in the name; it should consistently be written Lidorus.

LUBECO-COL. edition: “At Cologne Agrippina, the deposition [Col. 0467B] of Saint Maternus, bishop and confessor, disciple of the holy apostle Peter. He presided as archbishop over the churches of Cologne, Trier, and Tongeren. Yet, at a good old age, he gave back his spirit to God at Cologne in the one-hundred-and-twenty-eighth year from the Incarnation.” See the following day. The entry on Philip is sufficiently pure. It continues: “On the same day, Saint Venerius the priest, of remarkable origin. He led a solitary life on the island of Tyre, and there restored a drowned boy to life by prayer; he also cured many people of various illnesses, and afterward happily fell asleep in the Lord.” On Maurilion it has the same as ANTUERP.-MAX. The entry on Amatus is pure. On Lidorus, as above: “At Augustodunum, Saint Neocarius, bishop and confessor.” This name too is formed in various ways; GREVEN below writes Necarius, but with MOLAN it should be read Nectarius. “The discovery of Saint Maximus, bishop and confessor of Riez.”

BELIN., in his first announcement sufficiently pure, writes Romancius instead of [Col. 0468A] Romaricus, and cuts short Amatus’s eulogy. In the case of Maurilion, whom he calls Maurilius in the second edition, he is accurate. He adds: “On the same day, Saint Venerius the confessor, a man of admirable holiness.” In the second edition there is also: “At Tours, Saint Lidorus,” etc.

GREVEN.: “On the same day, Saint Ligorius the martyr. He was killed in the regions of Greece for the name of Christ and afterward translated to Venice. Since the day of his passion was unknown, he himself designated this day in a vision.” See Castellani’s note. “In Apulia, Saints Felicissimus and Secundinus. At Tours, Saint Lidorus, bishop and confessor. At Alexandria, Saint Theodulus, bishop. At Augustodunum, Saint Necarius, bishop and confessor. The discovery of Saint Maximus, bishop and confessor of Riez. Adolphus, abbot and confessor. At Angers, Saint Nectarius.” I do not know who this Nectarius is; perhaps he has been inserted on account of another person. “On the same day, Barsanuphius, the glorious abbot and confessor. Having been instructed in all worldly wisdom in Egypt during the reign of the emperor Justinian [Col. 0468B], he sought a solitary life after receiving a divine admonition. There, together with companions of the same resolve, amid hunger, thirst, nakedness, vigils, and labors, he devoted himself to the mortification of the flesh and the restoration in himself of the divine image; at last, full of days and holiness, he came to rest. According to some, on this day: Venerius the confessor, who is mentioned above on the third day before the Ides.”

MOLAN.: “At Broylo, the deposition of Saint Amatus, bishop and confessor. At Tours, Saint Lidorus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Venerius the confessor, a man of admirable holiness.” Other editions read: “At Douai, from Broylo, the deposition of Saint Amatus, bishop and confessor. The merciful Savior of all glorified his virtue during his temporal life, through the grace of his merits.” On Venerius and Lidorus, as above. “At Augustodunum, the deposition of Saint Nectarius. On the thirteenth day, the dedication of the church of the holy resurrection of Christ and our God, and the eve of the life-giving cross.”

[Col. 0463]

At Alexandria, in the Egyptian city, the blessed Philip, bishop, father of Saint Eugenia the virgin. Having abandoned the dignity of the prefecture and received the grace of baptism, he afterward attained the honor of the episcopate. While he was engaged in prayer, the prefect Perennius ordered him to be beheaded with a sword, in the time of the emperors Volusianus and Gallienus. On the same day, Saint Amatus, priest and abbot of the monastery of Romaricus, who, as a follower of extraordinary abstinence and an anchoritic life, led an illustrious way of life through the grace of his virtues and miracles. At Angers, Saint Maurilion, bishop and confessor.

XVIII Kal. Day 14. [Note: [Col. 0467]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0467C]

I write Heraclius with Praten., Greven., and Molan., although others commonly have Eraclius. Enough has been said about Jerusalem; Herinien. has “brought back to Jerusalem.” All read repperit, “found.” Munerat., instead of osculatur atque adoratur, transposes the words as adoratur et osculatur, “is worshiped and kissed.” Again, instead of “he was beheaded on the same day,” it has “under the same head,” etc. In Greven. and Molan. sub, “under,” is absent, and after Cypriani, episcopi, “of the bishop,” is absent. Antuerp.-Maj. incorrectly writes sex miliario ex Cartagine, “six miles from Carthage.”]

[Note: [Col. 0467C]

The Exaltation of the saving cross is celebrated with the greatest solemnity by all the Martyrologists, although it is omitted in the oldest Hieronymian manuscript, the Echternach codex. From this, using Florentinius’s customary manner of argument, one might infer that it was an addition by a Gallic copyist in the other manuscripts. On the antiquity and prominence of this feast, and other matters relating to it, see, among others, Baronius and Florentinius, who rightly judge that the Exaltation of the cross has an origin older than Heraclius; and, if Castellano is to be believed, it was instituted at least in Jerusalem more than two hundred and forty years before that emperor’s time. Hence perhaps in the Hieronymian manuscripts, Bede, and Rabanus, where Heraclius is not mentioned, it simply reads: “The Exaltation of the holy cross.” The Romanum parvum, unusually but as though treating the proper feast at greater length, reads: “The Exaltation of the holy cross, brought back from the Persians to Jerusalem by the emperor Heraclius, when also at Rome the saving wood of the cross was discovered by Pope Sergius and is venerated by all the people.” A longer history was set out by Ado, from whom Usuard composed his shorter version, while Notker did not abbreviate it quite so much.

In the calendars frequently cited and in all the Martyrologies, except the Sacramentary of Gregory and the Hieronymian manuscripts, the memories of Cornelius and Cyprian are placed first; they are celebrated throughout the whole world. On this day, all the ancient Martyrologists agree in recording Cornelius; among them Cornelius and Cyprian are eagerly joined together on the same fourteenth day of September—that is, on the same day, as they assume—although they were crowned in different years, since one survived the other by six years. Among scholars, however, considerable effort has been expended to establish that the death or martyrdom of blessed Cornelius can be assigned to September. Papebrochius tried to explain this quite suitably by reference to the transfer of his body from Centumcellae to Rome and its burial there, and some have followed him. There is greater difficulty concerning the time, explicitly assigned by Bede, Ado, and their followers to the reign of Decius, since it appears certain that Decius, or the Decii, had already perished altogether before Cornelius’s end. To loosen this knot, the usual wedge may help to some extent, if one says that what is meant is the persecution of Decius while it was continuing, rather than Decius while he was alive. Apart from this, some conjecture that Ado’s history was taken from Acts composed by Hilduin; their authority and reliability will be discussed elsewhere. Tillemont has arranged an impressive series of Cornelius’s Life in volume III, which will be useful in its proper time. [Col. 0469B] Meanwhile, our Usuard’s eulogy seems to have flowed principally from Bede, with its wording somewhat transposed, altered, and polished.

“Everything is known,” says Florentinius, “about Cyprian, the most celebrated martyr and bishop of Carthage—indeed, his Acts, preserved for posterity by Pontius, his deacon, who was present and an eyewitness, are exceedingly well known and entirely trustworthy, apart from the consular records published together with the earlier materials.” Equally well known is the fame of his holiness in all the Martyrologies and in the more ancient monuments.” On these matters see Baronius and Florentinius again in their notes for this day. Ruinart published the highly praised Acts in full and furnished them with learned notes among the Selecta, beginning on page 193. Tillemont, likewise, among many others, arranged Cyprian’s acts with equal accuracy and diligence in volume IV, beginning on page 45. What bears more directly on the present matter is that our text was again taken from Bede; insofar as it follows his words, it is true and certain. For what is added from Ado concerning Cyprian’s companions is not equally established, as Florentinius carefully observes. Thus the descent and genuine simplicity of the entire text are clear up to this point. It is not the place here to investigate the translations of Cyprian’s relics—or indeed those of Saint Cornelius—to Gaul and other regions. See what Henschenius learnedly discussed concerning the booklet on Cyprian’s Life composed by Pontius, under 8 March. Wandalbert agrees with our text, but in the final verse adds a certain Eparchus, whom I think is the same person about whom we spoke on 1 July. I append the remaining verses:

[Col. 0470B]

On the eighteenth, when October is called the coming month,

the shining banners of the cross, brought back, are raised;

Heraclius carried it victoriously from unworthy Persia;

and Cornelius, the bishop, supports his Rome

by virtue and blood, while joyful Carthage

glitters with Cyprian, the distinguished teacher and martyr,

and throughout the world they write the sacred words

of the Church.

] [Note: [Col. 0469B]

ROSWEYD. adds at the end to the pure text: “At Trier, Saint Maternus, bishop and confessor.” Others wrongly place this on the preceding day.

PULSANEN., sufficiently pure in the first announcement, has only this concerning the other two saints: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, blessed Cornelius, pope. In Africa, Saint Cyprian, bishop.”

“ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and BELIN. truncate the first announcement as follows: “The Exaltation of the Holy Cross, under the most devout emperor Heraclius.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN.: “The Exaltation of the holy cross, under the most devout emperor Eraclius, who [Col. 0469C] brought it back from Persia to Jerusalem. But also, with the years advancing . . . . .” up to the end of the text, sufficiently purely. Then is added: “At Trier, Saint Maternus, bishop, disciple of the holy apostle Peter. At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of Saint Evergisilus, bishop and martyr.”

LOVANIEN. begins like the preceding manuscripts up to “brought back,” omitting the rest. In the entry on Cornelius it is pure. In that on Cyprian it cuts out the companions. Otherwise it resembles the preceding manuscripts.

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. have only the beginning, up to “most devout,” as in ANTUERP.-MAX.-LUBEC. They are sufficiently pure in the entries on Cornelius and Cyprian. ALBERG. has nothing concerning Maternus. In both, after “martyrdom,” the following is added concerning Evergisilus: “killed by arrows at Tongeren.”

CENTULEN.: “The Exaltation of the holy cross. At Rome, blessed Cornelius, pope and martyr under Caesar Decius. At Carthage, the passion of the magnificent and admirable teacher Cyprian, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Gallienus, with Galerius Maximus as proconsul.”

[Col. 0469D] BRUXELLEN. is interpolated from Ado in its account of the Exaltation. It is also somewhat interpolated in the entries on Cornelius and Cyprian. It then adds the following: “And the feast of the holy martyrs Senator, Viator, and Cassiodorus, brothers, and of their mother Dominata. At Trier, Saint Maternus, disciple of blessed Peter the apostle, through whose staff he himself was raised from the dead after forty days, and afterward sat in the episcopal chair for as many years as he had lain buried in the earth for days. At Cologne Agrippina, blessed Evergisilus, bishop and martyr. While he was serving as archdeacon, he heard with his master, Saint Severinus, the angelic hymn at the passing of the most blessed martyr, and afterward was killed by arrows at Tongeren, which is also called Octavia. On the same day, the dedication of this church and the translation to it of the body of blessed Gudila the virgin.”

[Col. 0470B] HAGENOYEN constructs another history of the Exaltation of the holy cross. He also inserts various details concerning Cornelius. Then: “At Cologne, the feast of Saint Evergisilus, bishop of Cologne, killed by arrows at Tongeren.” His account of Cyprian is also somewhat interpolated. At the end he adds: “Likewise in Swabia, Saint Aurelius, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The Exaltation of the holy cross. Cornelius and Cyprian, martyrs. Crescentianus, Victor, Rosula, and Generalis, who are reported to have suffered with blessed Cyprian.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, sign. B.: “At Cologne [Col. 0470C] Agrippina, the feast of Saint Evergisilus, bishop and martyr.”

FLORENTIN.: “In Calabria, the holy martyrs Senator, Victor, Cassiodorus, and their mother Dominatia.” See above under BRUXELLEN.

REMENS. SS. Timot. et Apoll.: “At Rome, blessed Cornelius, pope and martyr. His sacred body, transferred from Rome by Charles the Younger, Augustus, was placed in the monastery that he built within the palace buildings at Compiègne. At Carthage, the passion of the most blessed Cyprian, an outstanding teacher, whose most holy body was transferred to France in the time of the emperor Charlemagne and reverently deposited at Lyon.”

LUBECO-COL. edition: “The Exaltation of the holy cross, under the most devout emperor Heraclius, who brought it back from Persia to Jerusalem, five hundred years and more having elapsed since the Lord’s passion.” Concerning Cornelius it adds: “He established that priests might swear for a definite cause, if they wished.” The account of Cyprian is moderately interpolated. It continues: “At Trier, the celebration of the feast of Saint Maternus, archbishop and confessor. At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of Saint Evergisilus, bishop and martyr, killed by arrows at Tongeren.”

GREVEN.: “At Tongeren, the passion of blessed Evergisilus, bishop of Agrippina Cologne and martyr. While he was fulfilling the office of archdeacon and traveling through the holy places with blessed Severinus, bishop of Cologne, he was privileged to hear the choir of angels carrying the soul of Saint Martin of Tours into heaven. Ferreolus, martyr. Likewise, Saints Dionysius and Felix. According to some, on this day, the deposition of blessed John Chrysostom, and on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, his translation. Maternus, bishop and confessor. He was sent by the blessed apostle Peter, together with Saints Eucharius and Valerius, to preach the Gospel of Christ to the Gauls and Germans. After his companions had fallen asleep, he himself governed the churches of Trier, Agrippina, and Tongeren alike [in the first manuscript, ‘with the greatest vigilance’]; and he came to rest at Agrippina [the first manuscript: ‘Cologne’], where his feast is celebrated in advance [the first manuscript: ‘especially’] on the Ides of September. Aurelius, bishop.”

MOLAN.: “At Trier, Saint Maternus, bishop, disciple of the holy apostle Peter, who presided as archbishop over the churches of Tongeren, Cologne, and Trier alike, and finally gave up his spirit at Cologne; he rests together with them in the church of Saint Father Eucharius, now called Saint Matthias. On the same day, the dedication of this church and the translation to it of the body of blessed Gudila the virgin.” See BRUXELLEN. “At Blandinium, the translation of Saint Ansbert [Col. 0472A], archbishop of the church of Rouen.” Then, in smaller type: “The feast of Saint Anastasius the martyr, concerning whom there is a sermon by Peter Damian. At Mareuil, in the territory of Arras, the elevation of blessed Bertilia. On the Wednesday after the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, the three-day autumnal fast, or fast of the seventh month, concerning which there are nine homilies of Saint Leo I, pope.” Later editions truncate the commemorations of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian and transfer them to the sixteenth day, indicating this in the following words: “Their feasts are transferred to the day after tomorrow.” Then, concerning Maternus, as in the earlier edition: “At Brussels, the dedication of the church and the translation to it, etc. At Blandinium, the translation of Saint Ansbert of Rouen, etc. At Mareuil, the elevation of blessed Bertilia.” Finally, in smaller type: “On the Wednesday after the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, the three-day autumnal fast,” etc., as above.]

[Col. 0467]

The Exaltation of the holy cross, when the emperor Heraclius brought it back from Persia to Jerusalem. But as the years passed, Pope Sergius, by divine revelation, found a portion of that wood of extraordinary size in the shrine of blessed Peter; every year, on the very day of its Exaltation, it is kissed and worshiped by all the people. At Rome, on the Appian Way, blessed Cornelius, pope, whose mouth, after his banishment into exile, Decius ordered to be beaten with leaden scourges; thus, together with twenty-one others of both sexes, he was beheaded. The soldier Cerealis and his wife Salustia, whom Cornelius himself had instructed in the faith, were also beheaded on the same day. In Africa, Saint Cyprian, bishop, who under the emperor Valerian, after a long exile, completed his martyrdom by decapitation, six miles from Carthage, near the sea. Crescentianus, Victor, Rosula, and Generalis are reported to have suffered with him.

XVII Kal. Day 15. [Note: [Col. 0471]

The texts of Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Major, Munerat., and Molan are pure. The same applies to Antuerp.-Max., Lovanien., and Danicus.]

[Note: [Col. 0471B]

Very many codices write Nichomedis; nevertheless, I have followed the earlier orthography, which we used on 1 June when discussing the same Nicomedes. I retain Domiciani in accordance with the more common judgment of the manuscripts, although Herinien. and Molan more correctly write Domitiani. Molan differs from all the others, having, I think, followed Greven. For where they read, “When, as he was being compelled to sacrifice, he said: ‘I do not sacrifice except to almighty God, who reigns,’” etc., he construes it differently: “When he said to those compelling him that he could not sacrifice except to God,” etc. In Antuerp.-Major, Cabilenensi is written incorrectly as Cabilonensi. Molan has Tulli and Carnoti. More disgracefully, Antuerp.-Major has Cartono for Carnoto, and “of Saint Leobidus”; Munerat. has “of blessed Leobinus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0471B]

We discussed briefly on 1 June the dedication of a certain basilica, as we suppose, of our Nicomedes, the renowned martyr, correcting either the error or at least the confusion of various Usuard manuscripts. Today the Hieronymian manuscripts, which Florentinius regards as his own, celebrate his feast. Bede uses the same wording today as on the cited day, 1 June; but since the manuscripts from which we gave the genuine text before volume II of March appear to be disordered here, perhaps the reading of Rabanus, taken from Bede, should be preferred. On the earlier day he expresses the dedication of the basilica; here he reads, “The passion of Nicomedes the martyr.” An ancient memory of him also appears in the calendars of Fronto and in Gregory’s Sacramentary, through Menardus, where the notes of both editors may be consulted; nor is he absent from Allatius’s calendar. The Romanum parvum also reads very briefly: “At Rome, Nicodemus the martyr.” As is his custom, Ado draws more extensively from the Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, or rather from the letter of Marcellus, which we have cited more than once elsewhere. He draws, I say, on more details proper to this saint; Notker reports them briefly, and Our Author contracts them still further, though almost in Ado’s own words. Whether Nicomedes suffered under Domitian or rather under Trajan will be explained in its proper place. See what was said above in various places, especially on 12 and 31 May; it need not be repeated here. I shall append below Wandalbert’s metrical eulogy. In assigning Valerian to this day, the Hieronymian manuscripts agree as closely as they differ in expressing and distinguishing the place of his martyrdom: some say Castro Tremorcio, others Canlomo castro, and others Castro Ternocio, the last coming closest to Tournus. It is not sufficiently certain whether Bede truly remembered Valerian, since it is doubtful whether the words assigned to him there can be attributed to him: “In the territory of Chalon, at the castle of Trimorchium,” unless Rabanus contributes something. His words are: “In the territory of Chalon, at the castle of Nortium, the feast of Saint Valerian the martyr,” which are almost copied by Notker, the longer panegyric of Ado having been left aside, though Rabanus’s place of martyrdom was removed, perhaps because it was considered suspect. However these matters may stand, Our Author had no other guide than his customary one; he seems to have taken these details from the Acts of Saint Marcellus, likewise of Chalon, whom we discussed on 4 September, and from whom they passed into several others. Usuard selects little, but even in this brevity he clings scrupulously to Ado’s words. Whatever the confusion of Bede’s manuscripts may be, it is nevertheless clear that they record: “On the same day, Saint Aper, bishop.” Then: “Leobinus the confessor,” who are reported by Rabanus in exactly the same manner. There is nothing about the last one in Ado; of the first he says: “On the same day, the deposition of the most blessed Aper, bishop and confessor of Toul.” Determine, by comparison, which of the two Usuard copied, or whether he took something from both. Whether this Aper is the same person who had a relationship or correspondence with Saint Paulinus is a matter for another place and inquiry. For the present, consult the latest Paris edition of blessed Paulinus’s Works, from 1685, Dissertation V on the Life of the saint, toward the end of the volume. Since I find nothing about Leobinus in Usuard’s usual sources, it may reasonably be supposed that the name itself was taken from Bede, to whom Our Author added the episcopal see from another source. Certainly, according to the evidence of our manuscripts, this entry and all the others are properly and genuinely Usuard’s. Wandalbert sang of the two final bishops after Nicomedes; these are his verses:

[Col. 0472D]

On the seventeenth, Nicomedes the priest adorns the day;

your virgin Petronilla, blessed companion and martyr;

the bishops, to be revered for their merits and life,

Leobinus, Aper, and the Leuci (or, according to another reading, “Leo, all alike”) protect the altar.

] [Note: [Col. 0473A]

ROSWEYD., sufficiently pure in Nicomedes and Valerian, is lacking in the last two announcements.

PULSANEN., sufficiently pure in the first, cuts short the eulogy in the second and also lacks the final two.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. are both lacking only in the final announcement. MAX.-LUBEC., however, differs from the earlier text in having at the end: “And the octave of the holy mother of God, Mary.”

GREVEN., after the pure text, adds: “Likewise, the octave of the blessed Virgin Mary.” It is surprising that he could include this among the Usuardine entries.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG., and DANIC. begin: “The octave of the nativity of the glorious Virgin.” The entries on Nicomedes and Valerian follow, not entirely purely. Then: “At the city of Toul, the feast of Saint Aper,” etc. Leobinus is absent.

LOVANIEN. also begins: “The octave of the nativity of the glorious Virgin.” In Nicomedes it is almost pure. It cuts short the eulogy of Valerian: “At the city of Toul,” etc., as above. Leobinus is also absent.

[Col. 0473B] CENTULEN.: “The octave of the nativity of blessed Mary. At Rome, the passion of Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr. In the territory of Chalon, at the castle of Tenortium, Saint Valerian the martyr. Likewise at Chartres, Saint Leobinus, bishop and confessor. At Toul, Saint Aper, bishop and confessor, whose precious death in the sight of the Lord is attested by frequent miracles.”

BRUXELLEN.: “The octave of the nativity of the glorious ever-virgin Mary.” In Nicomedes and Valerian it is somewhat interpolated from Ado. Then: “Likewise at Chartres, Saint Leobinus, bishop and confessor. At the city of Toul, blessed Aper, bishop and confessor of that church. In the territory of Rouen, at the monastery of Ginegium, the deposition of Saint Aycadrus, abbot and confessor. When he had nine hundred monks there, half of them, as an angel had foretold to him during the night, departed to the Lord on a single day. He himself followed them not long afterward and rested in peace.” Surius published his Life. On it, see Mabilion’s preliminary observations to the second Benedictine century, beginning on page 952, where he produces another Life of the same saint, to be compared with our manuscripts in its proper place.

HAGENOYEN. collects various material on the octave of the Nativity that is irrelevant to the matter. He continues no more appropriately: “At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, the feast and translation of blessed Nicomedes, priest and martyr, whose day of passion is on the Kalends of June.” See what we said above in the Observations. He is sufficiently pure in Valerian. A long history of Aper, bishop of Toul, follows, of which I give a specimen: “At the city of Toul, the deposition of Saint Aper, bishop and confessor. While still a boy, this man possessed such generosity and compassion toward the poor that many times he gave his clothes to the poor and returned home naked. Blessed Aper was venerable in appearance, gentle in speech, serene in countenance, lacking truth [rather, “free from falsehood,” or “having experienced truth”], and pleasing to all through his tranquil gentleness. It was also his custom to visit all the saints in order to imitate them, and therefore he possessed bodily continence, cheerfulness of spirit, diligence of heart, watchfulness [vigilance], fasting, prayers, sackcloth, ashes, patience, and charity.” I omit the rest, which I do not know how it could apply to our Aper if compared with his Acts, as we shall show more fully elsewhere. At the end is added: “Likewise, at Chartres, the deposition of Saint Leobinus, bishop and confessor.” Almost as it stands in the text.

AQUICINCT. At the end: “And Saint Aicadrus, abbot.” See above under BRUXELLEN.

DAVERON.: “At the city of Chartres, the translation of Saint Leobinus, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The octave of the nativity of blessed Mary the Virgin. Nicomedes, martyr. Valerian, martyr. Leobinus, bishop and confessor. Aper, bishop and confessor.”

In VATICAN., no. 5949, Aper and Leobinus are absent. Added: [Col. 0474B] “At Benevento, Saint Constantius in Saint Sophia.” He is not known among the others.

UGHELLIAN. is also lacking the final announcement, concerning Leobinus of Chartres, like ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. above, with which it usually agrees.

FLORENTIN.: “The feast of Saint Arcadius, bishop and confessor.” Unless I am mistaken, he means Aicadrus.

LUBECO-COL. edition: “The octave of the nativity of the glorious Virgin Mary. At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, the feast of Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr, who had honorably buried the body of blessed Felicula, virgin and martyr; for this reason he was arrested by Count Flaccus under the emperor Domitian [and] when he said, to those compelling him,” etc. The account of Valerian is sufficiently pure. “At the city of Toul, the feast of Saint Aper, bishop and confessor. At Chartres, blessed Leobinus, bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN.: “At Alexandria, the three holy brothers Cyrinus, Leontius, and Serapion. Likewise Seleucus and Constantius. Decoratus the martyr, and others with him. Clement [Col. 0474C], bishop. In Scotland, Merenus, bishop. Aichadrus, abbot. Luthardus, count of Cleves and confessor. Ludmilla, widow and martyr, grandmother of Saint Wenceslaus, duke of Bohemia and martyr.”

MOLAN.: “On the same day, the octave of the nativity of the Virgin Mary. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Aichadrus, abbot. At Lyon, the deposition of Albinus, bishop.” Then in smaller type: “In Gaul, Saint Eutropia, widow, concerning whom Sidonius writes in his letter to Pragmatius. Luthardus, count of Cleves and confessor, who founded the monasteries of Wissel and Nüssen.” Other editions: “On the same day, the octave of the nativity,” etc. Likewise concerning Albinus of Lyon and Aichadrus the abbot, as above. “On the fifteenth day, Saint Nicetas the martyr. In Cleves, Luthardus, count and confessor, who founded the monastery,” etc., as may be seen in the previously cited edition.]

[Col. 0471]

At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, the feast of blessed Nicomedes, priest and martyr, under the emperor Domitian. When those compelling him to sacrifice were saying this, he replied: “I do not sacrifice except to the almighty God who reigns in heaven.” After being beaten for a very long time with leaden scourges, he departed to the Lord. On the same day, in the territory of Chalon, Saint Valerian the martyr. When the governor Priscus saw that he remained steadfast in confessing Christ and continued with joyful spirit in his praises, although suspended and tortured by severe tearing with hooks, he ordered him to be put to death by the sword. At Toul, Saint Aper, bishop and confessor. Likewise at Chartres, Saint Leobinus, bishop.

XVI Kal. Day 16. [Note: [Col. 0473]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Rosweyd., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. Likewise Antuerp.-Max., Lovanien., and Danicus.]

[Note: [Col. 0473D]

I note first that the last three codices are indeed pure, but differ from the others in placing Euphemia second. Rosweyd. also differs from the others, beginning as follows: “At Chalcedon, Euphemia the virgin,” etc. Herinien. and Greven. retain Chalcedon, but Munerat. has Chalcedone. I say nothing about the form Eufemiae, since all write it that way except Molan, who correctly has Euphemiae. In Antuerp. the epithet sanctae, “holy,” is absent; in Max.-Lubec. it is beatae, “blessed.” Belin. reads tormenta, carceres, “torments, prisons,” with the conjunction et, “and,” removed. Again, the same Belin., perhaps better following Bede, writes sartagines ignitas, “heated frying pans,” instead of sartagines igneas, “fiery frying pans.” It is doubtful whether rursum morsum bestiae, “again the bite of the beast,” or rursus morsum bestiae, “once more the bite of the beast,” should be preferred. Bede reads the former, from whom it was more probably taken. Herinien., Antuerp.-Max., Lubec., and Munerat. have rursus morsum, etc. Greven. [Col. 0476A] and Molan. are once again singular in reading nobilissimae matronae, “of the most noble matron,” instead of nobilis matronae, “of a noble matron.” Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. expressed neither form.]

[Note: [Col. 0475A]

The holy and most blessed Chalcedonian martyr Euphemia—or, as others call her, the most precious and most blessed martyr—is celebrated everywhere, both in the East and in the West, with innumerable praises and the most certain memorials. This is so even if we grant that the Acts of her published by Metaphrastes, Surius, and others are of little reliability and authority, as perhaps are also those that we possess in several ancient Passionaries and other manuscript documents, where perhaps illustrious accounts, better than those published until now, may be found; Papebrochius mentions them in the Greek-Muscovite Ephemerides. However, even if all those accounts are assumed to be insufficiently proven, indeed doubtful, the notable narrative about Euphemia by Asterius, published by Surius and most recently by Ruinart, and illustrated with observations, is certainly not doubtful. Nor are the many other arguments doubtful that Tillemont carefully assembled after Baronius and Florentinius in volume V, beginning on page 405. How highly the metrical Life of Saint Euphemia, composed by Paschalis [Col. 0475B] Verrone and published at Naples in 1592, should be valued, and likewise the encomium of Theodore Bestus, which exists among us in a Greek and Latin manuscript, will be considered later. In any case, all our Martyrologies stand as witnesses to her most ancient cult. Among the Hieronymian manuscripts, the only difference is that in the oldest Echternach manuscript Euphemia appears to be assigned to Rome, as the calendars of Allatius and Fronto also suggest, since they join her to Lucia. Yet in the aforementioned Hieronymian manuscripts, Euphemia of Chalcedon is found on the following day; on this matter see Florentinius for both days. The Romanum parvum reads: “At Chalcedon, Euphemia the virgin.” Ado’s eulogy extends more fully from the Acts cited above; Bede, Rabanus, and Notker treat it more briefly, though it is nevertheless evident that the last took it from the first. But from whom did Usuard take it? Certainly he described the kinds of tortures in Ado’s words, where Ado has not clubs but blows from rods; where the words “sharp saws” are absent; and finally where he has “fiery frying pans,” not “heated frying pans.” Yet the final words, “again she overcame the bite of the beast for Christ,” plainly flow not from Ado but from Bede. Here you have the formation of the text in this section.]

The celebration of the Roman matron Lucia and Geminianus is also famous and ancient, although neither is recorded by the Hieronymian Martyrologies on this day. Is this the Lucia whom we most recently cited from the Calendars of Allatius and Fronto? Some doubt it. Bede, and after him Rabanus, explicitly announce both, but omit the place or arena. The Small Roman Martyrology is clearer: “At Rome, of the martyrs Lucia and Geminianus.” Ado gives a lengthy account extracted from the Acts, which Surius included in his collection—no doubt because he lacked the Acts themselves, published by Mombritius in volume II and preserved also among us in manuscript in an ancient parchment codex. These, I believe, are the same Acts that Baronius saw, correctly observing that they require correction. I am surprised that Tillemont claims not to have possessed them, as though he could not have found them in Mombritius or elsewhere. There is no occasion here either to debate or to decide anything about their authenticity. Whatever their character, it is sufficiently clear that the whole of Ado’s account was extracted from them, and that Our Martyrologist abbreviated it from Ado so briefly that our little notice contains nothing that can reasonably be called into serious doubt, provided only that “the persecution of Diocletian” is replaced by the name of the persecutor himself, as we have often said must be done elsewhere. Wandalbert begins his metrical encomia for this day with Pope Martin, whom I do not find marked in any of our codices; Castellanus indicates that this is the day of his death. The poet-martyrologist sings as follows:

> Hence, on the sixteenth, Pope Martin is blessed;  
> And with devout love we venerate holy Euphemia;  
> Lucia likewise excels here with Geminianus;  
> The laurel of Christ together adorns those who suffered.

[Note: [Col. 0475C]]

**ANTWERP–MAJORITY.** In addition to the pure text, as we have shown above frequently happens, adds a proper English entry in these words: “On the same day, Saint Eadipa, virgin.” I think Edith is intended.

**PULSANO.** In the first announcement it is unaltered. In the second it likewise continues unaltered as far as Geminianus; all the rest is missing.

**ALBERGEN.** It resembles **ANTWERP–MAJORITY**, etc., in the transposition. At the end, however, it adds: “Likewise, the feast of the blessed Stigmata of Saint Francis.”

**UTRECHT and LEYDEN.** They begin: “The feast of the sacred Stigmata. For that blessed confessor of Christ, Francis, two years before he returned his spirit to heaven, after the course of his preaching, the excess of charity, and the title of poverty, at the sight of the crucified Seraph, as though he were driven by seraphic desires, was bodily marked in his hands and feet and right side—not by human agency, but inscribed by the fingers of the living God.” In the remainder, the text is as in **ANTWERP–MAJORITY**, etc.

[Col. 0475D]

**CENTULENSE.** “The birth of Saint Euphemia, virgin, who suffered under the emperor Diocletian and the proconsul Priscus in the city of Chalcedon. At Rome, of the holy martyrs Lucia and Geminianus, under the consul Megasius. On the same day, Saint Aicadrius, abbot.” See the preceding day.

**BRUSSELS.** In the entry for Euphemia it is slightly interpolated; in the second entry, after Geminianus, it inserts: “This most blessed Lucia, accused by her son Euprepius of being a Christian, was ordered by Diocletian to be brought to him together with the aforementioned Geminianus. He subjected them to punishments,” etc. At the end it adds: “On the same day, the reception of the sacred Stigmata of blessed Francis.”

[Col. 0476C]

**HAGUENAU.** “In the city of Chalcedon, Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr. She was the daughter of a certain priest of idols, and every day she heard Christians singing as they passed her house: ‘All the gods of the nations are demons,’ etc. She was converted to the faith of the Lord, and under the persecution of Maximian, by the governor Priscus, endured tortures and imprisonment, etc. At Rome, the passion of Saint Lucia, widow, and Geminianus, martyrs. This widow Lucia taught her son Euprepius to observe the Christian faith steadfastly. She was accused and handed over to the emperor Diocletian by that same son Euprepius and cast into prison, where the Lord appeared to her and brought forth from the prison a river which overthrew half the city together with the royal palace,” etc. From these examples, which are extended more than is proper in their remaining portions, you will easily form a judgment. At the end is added: “Likewise in England, Saint Edith, queen and virgin.”

**DAVERON.** “At Le Mans, the deposition of Saint Principius, bishop and confessor.”

**CARTHUSIAN MATRICULARIES–UTRECHT.** “Lucia and Geminianus, martyrs. Euphemia, virgin and martyr. Justin, presbyter and confessor.” A marginal note states that in the Roman Martyrology he is placed on the following day, and that he is called a martyr.

**FLORENCE.** “Likewise, of the holy martyrs Sosthenes and Victor.” These do not belong to this day, but perhaps some ignorant person placed them here so that they might be associated with Euphemia, since we said that they were taken from her Acts on 10 September. It continues: “as also of the forty-nine holy martyrs.”

**LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION.** “At Rome, of the holy martyrs Lucia, a noble matron, and Geminianus, a very powerful man. This most blessed Lucia, after remaining a widow for thirty-six years and having completed seventy-five years over the course of her whole life, was accused by her son Euprepius of being a Christian. The emperor Diocletian ordered her to be brought before him together with the aforementioned Geminianus. After subjecting them to very severe punishments and torturing them for a long time, he finally handed them over to a certain most wicked judge, who tormented them for a long while and at last, after their glorious victory of martyrdom, had them put to death by the sword. Saint Maxima, a devoted servant of Christ, properly buried them.” The entry for Euphemia is almost pure; afterward it adds “and completed her martyrdom for Christ.” It continues: “On Mount Alvernia, the reception of the holy Stigmata of Saint Francis, confessor and founder of the First Order of Friars Minor. At Le Mans, Saint Principius, bishop and confessor. In England, Saint Edith, virgin.”

**GREVEN.** “The feast of Saint Joachim, father of the glorious Mother of God, Mary, ever virgin. And the commemoration of Saint Anne, her mother. At Rome, Felix, pope. Likewise Saint Victor. In Scotland, Ninian, bishop and confessor. At Le Mans, the deposition of Saint Principius, bishop and confessor. Likewise, Saint Louis, of blessed memory, archbishop of Arles, cardinal of Saint Cecilia. In England, Edith, virgin and abbess, daughter of Edgar, king of the English. Having been consecrated to Christ at the age of two by religious parents and having lived most holily, she was ignorant of the world rather than left it.” Castellanus reads Eadgitha.

**MOLANUS.** In smaller type: “In England, Edith, virgin and abbess, daughter of Edgar,” etc., as in **GREVEN** above. “In Scotland, Ninian, etc. In the territory of Strasbourg, Saint Einbeth, virgin, of outstanding holiness. Agnes, virgin of Montepulciano, whose life Master Raymond of the Order of Preachers wrote.” In later editions, the texts of approximately two days have been confused. For on this day Cornelius and Cyprian, from 14 September, are recorded, and the entire present text is appended to them. At the end is added: “In England, Saint Edith, virgin, daughter of King Edgar. In the territory of Strasbourg, Saint Einbeth, virgin, of outstanding holiness.” Then, in smaller type: “In Scotland, Ninian, bishop of Candida Casa and confessor. Likewise, the death of Agnes of Montepulciano, whose Life was written by Master Raymond of the Order of Preachers.” See the Roman Martyrology and the Acts for 20 April.]

[Col. 0473]

At the city of Chalcedon, the feast of Saint Euphemia, virgin and martyr, who under the proconsul Priscus overcame tortures and prisons, blows and the contrivances of wheels, fires and the weights of corner-stones, beasts and blows of rods, axes and fiery frying-pans, and once again the bite of a beast, for Christ. At Rome, of the holy martyrs Lucia, a noble matron, and Geminianus, whom Diocletian, after subjecting them to very severe punishments and torturing them for a long time, finally ordered to be put to death by the sword after their glorious victory of martyrdom.

**XV Kal. Day 17.** [Note: [Col. 0477]]

Thus read Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp–Majority, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Maximum–Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus. Antwerp–Maximum and Louvain may also be added to them.

[Note: [Col. 0477C]]

I said that Antwerp–Maximum and Louvain could be added; for although they report the entire text, they nevertheless differ from the others in treating Lambert first and in invariably reading *perpetuo victurus intravit* (“he entered, destined to live forever”) at the end of the sentence, contrary to all the older witnesses. Together with Pratensis and Molanus, they write *Tyburcina*, but the others have the stronger claim. Again, together with Molanus they omit the name Gallus; Muneratus has Gaulus. Antwerp–Majority omits *confessionis* after Volusianus, and, together with Antwerp, Maximum–Lübeck, Antwerp–Maximum, and Louvain, writes *insignis* rather than *insignissimus*. Muneratus, however, changed *confessionis* into *confessoris*. Pratensis has *Narcyssi*, Molanus *Narcisci*, Antwerp and Maximum–Lübeck *Narcissae*; but what does *Marcillae* mean in Greven? Antwerp–Maximum and Muneratus turn the name Crescention into Crescentianus, and the Small Roman Martyrology has the same form; Louvain is worse, with Crescentis. Pratensis seems to have written *Leodicum*, which I find in no other codex. Likewise *Lantberti*, as Rosweyd alone has it. We have preferred, from Ado and the other codices, the more common orthography, certainly customary in the ninth century, including in Wandalbert—and why not also in Bede?—although Rabanus and others use *Landebertus*. Antwerp–Majority is wrong in *innocentum* for *innocenter*, and in *Britannia* for *Brittanniis*, as we frequently find elsewhere. I pass over the remaining scribal errors, such as *Niveduni* for *Niveduno*, *Matrini* or *Martini* for *Macrini*, *Cordubae*, and *Eliani* for *Emiliani*, as the codices preserve them: *Dyaconi*, *Hiremiae*, *Jeremiae*, *Jheremiae*.

[Note: [Col. 0477D]]

The author of the Small Roman Martyrology begins his text for today as follows: “At Rome, Justin, presbyter, to whom blessed Lawrence came by night in the Vicus Patricius.” No older martyrologist mentions him, at least not on this day. Ado records him in third place, recalling several details from the Acts of Saint Lawrence, the beginning and end of which Our Martyrologist joined together in the wording of his source. We have marked this same Justin among the additions for 4 August, on which day Wandalbert sings of him as follows:

> Justin is celebrated on the preceding day with his own honor,  
> A presbyter numbered among the saints, slain by cruel slaughter,  
> Seeking out tombs, which he adorned.

Baronius also attributes to him the crown of martyrdom in the strict sense, led, as he says, by the authority of Wandalbert and other ancient monuments. Among these he doubtless counts his deeds, set down separately and written at greater length, from which it appears that he survived into the time of Claudius—understand Claudius II—and was then crowned with martyrdom. All these matters will be examined more carefully in their proper place. In the aforementioned Small Roman Martyrology there follows: “Likewise Narcissus and Crescentianus,” whom Ado assigns more distinctly in the penultimate place to Rome, in an underground sand-quarry, calling the second Crescention, as Usuardus copied from him. What the Acts of Saint Lawrence contain in their praise will become clear on 10 August. The fifth and final place in Ado is occupied by the illustrious bishop and martyr Lambert, whom Bede and Rabanus also mention; they call him Landebertus, if one is willing to follow certain copies of Bede. Florus gives him a plainly ordinary eulogy. Rabanus draws several details from his deeds, Ado fewer, and Notker abbreviates Ado. Usuardus wished to speak here in his own fashion and language, following Ado’s meaning but expressing the matter in entirely different formulas. To what extent Lambert or Landebert belongs to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, you will learn from Florentinius. We know of several Acts written about him; see the authors in Baronius’s notes for this day, Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedictini*, century III, part I, p. 66 onward, and other more recent writers. Nor should Wandalbert be passed over; on this day he celebrates only Lambert:

> Lambert, fifteenth in virtue, wins his crown;  
> The ever-trembling faction, having slain him, continually fears him.

[Col. 0479A]

Bede, Rabanus, Ado, and Notker speak of Socrates and Stephen in nearly the same terms. Our Martyrologist plainly borrowed his account from Ado, where they are placed first. Among the Hieronymian Martyrologies they are also mentioned by the oldest copy, that of Echternach, while almost all the others are silent. Ado’s next, or second, announcement is: “At Nivedunum, the feast of the holy martyrs Valerian, Macrinus, and Gordianus.” Here you see that Our Martyrologist changed nothing except the final name. The Hieronymian Martyrologies speak in the same way, except that most write *Magrinus* and *Gurdianus*. What remains of this twofold group in authentic ecclesiastical monuments will be investigated in its proper place. Up to this point Usuardus had his sources and followed them in the manner we have explained. But the last two martyrs of Córdoba were first recorded by him—or rather, recorded by him alone—from the harvest of the Arabic persecution gathered in Spain, which he brought back to Gaul, as has often already been said above. I scarcely doubt that he changed the name of the first and formed *Emilianus* from *Emilla*, who is reported together with Jeremiah by Eulogius in Book II of the *Memorial*, chapter 12. Why they have no place in the modern Roman Martyrology, and why Columba from Book III, chapter 10 of the *Memorial* was substituted in their place, I see no other reason than that its reformers followed Galesinius, neglecting Bellinus, Maurolycus, Felicius, and others, whom they nevertheless certainly used. But that our two martyrs are genuinely Usuardine, just like the others, our codices clearly demonstrate.

[Note: [Col. 0479A]]

**PULSANO.** The first announcement is truncated; the second is unaltered; the third is missing; the fourth is unaltered; the fifth is missing again. In the sixth, the final word of the entire text, *decollatorum* (“of those beheaded”), is missing.

**UTRECHT and LEYDEN.** They expand Ado’s eulogy of Lambert in this way: “At Liège, blessed Lambert, bishop. When, inflamed by zeal for religion, he had rebuked the royal household, and, returning, was engaged in prayer in his church, he was innocently killed by the guilty and entered the hall of the heavenly kingdom, destined to live forever.” The remainder follows the text in question.

**ALBERGEN and DANIC.** They have the same beginning, but say nothing about Justin, Narcissus, or Crescention.

**CENTULENSE.** “At Rome, the holy martyrs Narcissus and Crescention. At Córdoba, the holy deacon Emilianus and Jeremiah, whose bodies were handed over to the fire after their heads had been cut off. At Nivedunum, the holy martyrs Valerian, Macrinus, and Gordianus. In Britain, the holy Socrates and Stephen. On the same day, the passion of Saint Lambert, bishop of the church of Tongeren.”

**BRUSSELS.** It begins: “At Liège, the passion of blessed Lambert, bishop and martyr. He was the son of Count Aper, whom Saint Landoaldus led into the way of God; thus he himself succeeded blessed Theodard in the episcopate of Tongeren. But after being driven from the episcopate by the faction of Ebroin, he became a monk for seven years in the monastery of Stavelot. At last Pippin restored him to his see. And because, inflamed by zeal for religion, he dared to rebuke the aforementioned Prince Pippin for having taken Alpaida as a concubine in addition to his lawful wife Plectrude, he was martyred by Dodon, Alpaida’s brother.” In Justin, and then in Narcissus and Crescention, it is slightly interpolated. The Cordoban martyrs follow, then the martyrs of Nivedunum and Britain, unaltered. At the end: “At Waslagium, Saint Ervagindus, confessor. Likewise Saint Maurice, bishop and confessor.”

**HAGUENAU.** Nothing about Justin. In Narcissus and Crescention it is unaltered. Then the Cordobans and those of Nivedunum are given fairly well. The Britons are missing. Then: “Likewise at Merantii, the holy Desiderius, bishop, and Reginfridus, martyr. In the monastery of Saint Rupert at Bingen, in the diocese of Mainz, Saint Hildegard, nun and prophetess. At Liège, blessed Lambert, bishop and martyr,” etc. We have already said enough about him. “On the same day, Saint Floscellus, martyr.”

**CARTHUSIAN MATRICULARIES–UTRECHT.** “Lambert, bishop and martyr. Floscellus, child and martyr. Hildegard, virgin. Narcissus and the other martyrs.”

**CODEX BIGOTIANUS**, marked D. 9: “On the same day, Saint Floscellus, martyr.” He is recorded in most codices, but see his eulogy below among the additions of **GREVEN**.

**CAMBRAI, SAINT MARY.** “Likewise at Rome, blessed Justin, presbyter.” I do not know whether the rest is unaltered.

In **VATICANUS 5949**, the final announcement of Emilianus and Jeremiah is missing.

**FLORENCE.** “The feast of the sacred Stigmata of Jesus Christ in the body of Saint Francis.” Then the **STROZZIANUS**: “On the same day, Saint Stesellus—almost certainly to be read as Floscellus—an outstanding martyr.”

**CODEX OF THE HOLY MOUNTAIN.** “The discovery of Saint Gebetrudis and Saint Desiderius, martyr and bishop of Rodez.”

**BELNEN.** “The feast of Saint Floscellus, martyr.”

The **LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION**, in the entry for Lambert, is almost like **UTRECHT**, etc. In second place it treats the Britons, then those of Nivedunum; fourth, Narcissus and Crescention; fifth, the Cordobans; and finally Justin, everywhere quite faithfully.

**BELLINUS**, not entirely unaltered in the first four entries, adds in fifth place: “On the same day, the octave of Saint Nicholas, confessor of Tolentino. On the same day, the feast—that is, the impression of the sacred Stigmata of Our Lord Jesus Christ in the flesh, that is, in the body of Saint Francis, on the sacred mountain of Alvernia, in the diocese of Arezzo.” It then continues with the martyrs of Nivedunum and Córdoba, unaltered. At the end: “On the same day, Saint Flesellus, outstanding martyr.”

**GREVEN.** He has longer eulogies of many saints. “On the same day, Desiderius and Reginfridus. The passion of Saint Floccellus, a child, who in the time of the emperor Antoninus, when he was comforting Christians placed under torture, was sent into prison with a lion to be devoured by it; but while he prayed, the lion died. He was brought out of prison and thrown into the fire; when the fire had been extinguished, he later completed his martyrdom. Tarrasis, confessor, whose body was found near Constantinople in a cave, with this inscription: ‘Here rests the body of Saint Tarrasis, confessor’; it was first transferred to the imperial city and then to Venice, where it rests in the monastery of blessed Zacharias. Leandra, virgin. At Bingen in the diocese of Mainz, the deposition of Saint Hildegard, of blessed memory, virgin. In the time of Saint Bernard, abbot, she spread the fragrance of her holiness far and wide, so much so that many Roman pontiffs and writers commended themselves and the Roman Church to her prayers. Although she was ignorant of the Latin language, taught by the Holy Spirit she dictated in Latin everything she wrote to those who took it down. On the mountain called Alvernia, near Assisi, the impression of the sacred Stigmata on the body of Saint Francis. For when that man of God was at a certain time carried upward to God by the ardor of seraphic desires, and, in the gracious sight of Christ crucified, who appeared to him with such wondrous familiarity, conceived an extraordinary joy, while the dreadful fastening of the Cross pierced his soul with the sword of compassion, after a secret conversation with Christ his flesh appeared marked in conformity with the Crucified One—namely, with signs of nails protruding from the flesh in his hands and feet, and with a red scar on his right side.”
