**MOLANUS.** After *insignissimus fuit*, in different type, he inserts from Ado: “Whom blessed Sixtus ordained. He buried blessed Hippolytus and Concordia, Irenaeus and Abundius, and Cyrilla, daughter of Caesar Decius, martyrs, and many others.” He also inserts much about Lambert from the same Ado, in the same type. At the end: “On the same day, Saint Frecillus, outstanding martyr. On the mountain called Alvernia, near Assisi, the impression of the sacred Stigmata on the body of our most blessed father Francis. On the same day, the elevation of Saint Hiltrudis, virgin.” Then, in smaller type, the entries for Hildegard and Tarrasis, as in **GREVEN**. Finally: “The deposition of the holy confessors and presbyters Justin and Similinus, concerning whom Gregory of Tours [writes].” In other editions Justin is placed on 4 August and omitted on this day; Lambert is placed first with additions, as in the first edition. At the end, Floscellus is treated as above. “At Bingen, Saint Hildegard, virgin, who in the time of Saint Bernard, abbot, spread the fragrance of her holiness far and wide.” The entry for the Stigmata of Saint Francis is as above, except for the word “our.” Finally: “At Laetiis, on the same day, the elevation of Saint Hiltrudis, virgin.”]

[Col. 0477]

At Rome, on the Via Tiburtina, the feast of Saint Justin, presbyter, who in the persecution of Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus was outstanding in the glory of his confession. Likewise at Rome, the holy martyrs Narcissus and Crescention. At Liège, blessed Lambert, bishop of Tongeren, who, innocently killed by the guilty, entered the hall of the heavenly kingdom, destined to live forever. In Britain, the holy Socrates and Stephen. At Nivedunum, the holy martyrs Valerian, Macrinus, and Gordianus. Likewise at Córdoba, Saint Emilianus the deacon and Jeremiah, the beheaded.

**XIV Kal. Day 18.** [Note: [Col. 0481]]

The text agrees in Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp–Majority, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0481B]]

Molanus, departing from the writing of the older witnesses, correctly set down *Olympi Lyciae* (“of Olympus in Lycia”); Pratensis, Antwerp–Majority, Muneratus, Greven, and others generally have simply *Olimpi Liciae*. In Heriniensis and Rosweyd, the copyists’ excessive cleverness tried to improve the text: in the first, *pi* has been erased, so that it reads *olim Liciae*; in the other, *pi* has been joined to *Liciae*, producing *olim Piliciae*. We have followed a somewhat better—or at least more common—orthography. Heriniensis and Molanus correctly write *Tyri*; we, with the others, have followed the form in the text. Muneratus adds *et martyris* after *episcopi*. Pratensis alone reads *Colcide* incorrectly; all the others have *Calcide*, except Heriniensis, who has *Chalcide*, and Molanus, who has *Chalcide*. I read it as Saint Jerome writes it, with everyone except Pratensis and Antwerp–Majority, who omit the article τό (“the”) before *sanctus*. I have spoken elsewhere about *Hieronimus*. *Fereoli* for *Ferreoli* is an error in Antwerp–Majority. Muneratus has *deinde catenarum onustus* (“then burdened with chains”); Greven and Molanus better have *deinde gravi catenarum* (“then with the weight of chains”), etc.; but we, with the others, have *dein*. Thus the aforementioned Greven and Molanus, after *trusus est* (“he was thrust”), complete the sense and begin a new sentence: “Afterward, however,” etc. All the others have the form that we have written in the text.

[Note: [Col. 0481B]]

Bishop Methodius, teacher and martyr, illustrious in writings no less than in holiness and the crown of martyrdom, is celebrated in many encomia by both ancient and modern writers. Among these, Tillemont collected in volume V, beginning at page 466, almost everything that later generations have left scattered elsewhere. Among the ancients, Jerome praises Methodius especially in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 83. From Jerome it seems that he was received by the author of the Small Roman Martyrology—for he is not mentioned in the Hieronymian codices, Bede, Florus, or Rabanus—in these words: “Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterward of Tyre, who was crowned with martyrdom under Diocletian.” Ado added only the arena, or place of martyrdom, namely Chalcedon in Greece; Notker took this from him, with the variation that he wrote *Ebacide* instead of *Chalcide*, probably through a copyist’s error. Our Martyrologist additionally indicates the source from which everything was copied and from which more could have been copied. Wandalbert also rightly praises Methodius in these verses:

> Methodius, a bishop renowned for speech, faith, signs, and martyr’s blood,  
> Honors the fourteenth day by his celebration.

[Col. 0482B]

Although Ferreolus was a very celebrated martyr of Vienne, no martyrologist before Ado spoke of him on this day. Nevertheless, he seems to have a place in the oldest copy of Echternach, whose entry Florentinius considers to have been badly treated by a careless scribe, since he is recorded there on the following day. Consult him there. In the meantime, Notker extracted only a few things from Ado, but did so in such a way that he also transferred the martyrdom to Brioude. This does not sufficiently agree with the more authentic Acts—which Ado probably did not know—as you will be able to recognize for yourself if you consult what Surius formerly published and what Ruinart published not long ago among the *Selecta*, beginning at page 509. The well-known association of Ferreolus with Julian of Brioude, whom we discussed on 28 August, led Tillemont to join the deeds of both in volume V, beginning at page 279. There you will find briefly set out whatever will elsewhere require fuller illumination in praise of both. Our Usuardus prudently adapted his encomium from Ado so that he asserts nothing that does not agree most aptly with the cited Acts. An ancient Mass for Ferreolus is preserved by the Gothic—or rather Gallican—Missal edited by Thomasius, p. 359.

[Note: [Col. 0481D]]

**PULSANO.** The first announcement is mutilated; it also writes *olim Ciliciae* instead of *Olympi Liciae*. In the second, concerning Ferreolus, it is unaltered.

**ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, LÜBECK, AQUICINCT, VICTORINUS, BIGOTIANUS** under letter P 5, **SWEDISH REG.** under number 130, and **UGHELLIANUS**, all sufficiently faithful in the text, add at the end: “Likewise, the holy Trophimus, Oceanus, and Eustorgius.” For their true distinction and placement, see the Hieronymian copies in Florentinius.

**ANTWERP–MAXIMUM, UTRECHT and LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC.** They also report a sufficiently faithful text, at the end of which they add: “At Milan, the deposition of Saint Satyrus, confessor, brother of Saint Ambrose.” He is placed on the preceding day in the modern Roman Martyrology. It continues: “Likewise, the holy Trophimus—in some copies, Trophinus—Oceanus, and Eustorgius.” It is strange that **DANIC** writes *Neapoli* at the beginning instead of *natale*.

**CENTULENSE.** “The feast of Saint Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterward of Tyre, who under Diocletian was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcedon in Greece. At Vienne, Saint Ferreolus, martyr.”

**BRUSSELS.** Alone among all the witnesses, it begins the day in this way: “At Rome, Saint Martin, pope and martyr. While he was celebrating Mass, a swordsman sent by Olympius to kill him raised his sword for that purpose and was struck blind. Afterward the pope himself was sent into exile. His memory is chiefly celebrated on 13 November, the day on which he happily departed to the Lord.” I do not yet know why Brussels recalls him on this day, nor do I consider it worth investigating. See what we said on 16 September concerning Wandalbert’s verse. The text that follows is fairly pure. Then at the end: “At Milan, the deposition of Saint Eustorgius, bishop, and blessed Satyrus, confessor, brother of Saint Ambrose. Likewise, the holy Trophimus, Oceanus, and Sixtus.”

**HAGUENAU.** In the entry for Methodius, after *episcopi*, it inserts: “the outstanding teacher and distinguished martyr.” In the remainder the text is only slightly interpolated. At the end it adds: “At Milan, the deposition of Saint Satyrus, confessor, brother of Saint Ambrose, bishop of that same city. On the same day, the passion of the holy martyrs Trophimus, Oceanus, and Eustorgius, and others. At Fandela, Saint Richardis, virgin and empress. In the district of Castina, Saint Severius, confessor, a man remarkable and distinguished for holiness.” See Castellanus, who speaks more clearly about these two in his *Universal Martyrology*, p. 472. See also Molanus below.

**CARTHUSIAN MATRICULARIES–UTRECHT.** “Ferreolus, tribune and martyr. Methodius, bishop and martyr. Satyrus, confessor, brother of blessed Ambrose.”

**CODEX D. DU CHEVAL**, marked B, could have been added to the preceding witnesses; after the text it reads: “Likewise, the holy Trophimus, Oceanus, and Eustorgius.”

In **VATICANUS 5949** the following is added: “At Nicomedia, the holy Oceanus, Xistus, and Eustorgius, bishop.” I said above that the Hieronymian copies should be consulted concerning these. Eustorgius the bishop belongs elsewhere.

**FLORENCE.** “Likewise, the holy martyrs Tryphon—Tryphinus in some copies—Oceanus, and Eustorgius.” Then the **STROZZIANUS**: “At Milan, the deposition of Saint Satyrus, confessor.”

The **LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION**, somewhat interpolated in the text, adds: “At Milan, the deposition of Saint Satyrus, confessor, brother of Saint Ambrose, bishop. Likewise at Milan, the feast of Saint Eustorgius, bishop and confessor. He transferred the bodies of the three holy Magi from Constantinople to Milan and, renowned for many miracles, rested in peace. On the same day, the holy martyrs Trophimus, Oceanus, and Eustorgius. Likewise, the twenty-four elders.”

**BELLINUS** adds to the text: “On the same day, Saint Eustorgius, bishop and confessor. At Milan, the deposition of Saint Satyrus, confessor.”

**GREVEN.** “The twenty-four elders whom the Apocalypse of John commemorates. On the same day, according to the catalogue of the saints, Victor and Stephana, which in Latin is called Corona. Victor, who was a soldier from Cilicia, remained unharmed for three days in a fiery furnace after his fingers had been torn out for the faith of Christ. Then, by order of Sebastian, duke of Alexandria, after he had swallowed poison, after boiling oil and lamps had been applied to his sides, after vinegar mixed with lime had been poured into his mouth, and after he had been blinded and flayed, he earned the triumph of everlasting victory by the cutting off of his head. Concerning Stephana, see 14 May, where Usuardus records these martyrs. Florentius, martyr. Trophimia, Oceanus, and Eustorgius, martyrs. At Milan, Saint Eustorgius, bishop and confessor. He brought the bodies of the blessed Magi,” etc., as above. “Marianus, bishop. Synerius, bishop and confessor. At Milan, the deposition of blessed Satyrus, confessor, brother of Saint Ambrose, bishop, who, elegantly illuminating his virtues in the book he entitled *On the Death of His Brother*, says that he preserved undefiled the gifts of holy baptism with a chaste body and pure heart. Likewise, Egbert, bishop of Trier and confessor, of blessed memory. Also Arnulf, his brother, third count of Holland, of blessed memory, innocently killed by the wicked. And Herlindis, virgin, their sister, equally of holy memory.”

**MOLANUS.** “At Avranches, the deposition of Saint Sinerius, bishop and confessor of that same city. At Milan, Saint Eustorgius, bishop and confessor. At Milan, the deposition of Saint Satyrus, confessor and brother of the illustrious teacher and bishop Ambrose. In the book that he composed on the death of his brother, he said the following in his praise, among other things:

> ‘I had nothing, dearest brothers, among human things more precious than such a brother, nothing dearer. The ox bears witness to its affection with frequent lowing if the one with whom it was accustomed to draw the plow by the neck should be absent. And should I not seek you, brother? Or could I ever forget you, with whom I always bore the plow of this life? For I was inferior in labor, but closer in love. You enclosed my side with your side: with affection, as a brother; with care, as a father; with solicitude, as an elder; with reverence, as a younger man.’”

Other editions have the same material about Eustorgius and Satyrus as the first. Then follows: “At Avranches, the deposition of Saint Sinerius,” etc., also as above. Castellanus calls him Senator; consult him there for further information. Then: “In Germany, at the monastery of Andelaha, the deposition of Saint Richardis, empress, wife of Charles the Fat and a virgin. On the eighteenth day, Saint Father Eumenius, bishop of Gortyna, wonder-worker of Bergis; the glorious translation of the body of our most holy Father Winoc, abbot.”]

[Col. 0481]

The feast of blessed Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterward of Tyre, who under Diocletian, at Chalcedon in Greece, as Saint Jerome writes, was crowned with martyrdom. At Vienne, Saint Ferreolus, who, although he held tribunician authority, was seized by order of a most impious governor, first flogged with extreme cruelty, then loaded with the heavy weight of chains, and thrust into a most dreadful prison; afterward he received the palm of martyrdom by the cutting off of his head.

**XIII Kal. Day 19.** [Note: [Col. 0483]]

Thus read Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp–Majority, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.

[Note: [Col. 0483D]]

In Heriniensis, *In Neapolim* instead of *In Neapoli* is an ancient but erroneous manner of writing. Greven has *Festi* and *Procli* instead of *Proculi*. The codices commonly have *Eutici*, as in the text; Antwerp–Majority has *Euticii*. The same witness reads *Pelei et Lini*. Muneratus has *Pelei et Julii*. Again, where all the codices have *pro Christo* (“for Christ”), Muneratus substitutes *pro Christi nomine* (“for the name of Christ”). In the same place, *apud Miceriam* appears instead of *apud Nuceriam*. Again, for *Nerone imperatore*, Greven, following Ado’s manner, wrote *Linguonicae*. Heriniensis, together with the older martyrologists, likewise has *Sigonis* instead of *Sequani*. We have retained *Sequani*, because it is more widely received in our codices. Antwerp–Majority and Muneratus call him *Signi*. In other witnesses one also reads *Sigoni* or *Sigonei*. Greven, for clarity, inserted into the text the parenthesis *Sequani (al., Sigonis)*. But it is sufficiently certain that these different names—or rather the various inflections—everywhere indicate one and the same person.

Of the first group of martyrs, much is discussed on this day by Baronius in his notes, and more by Florentinius on September 12 and 19; these matters will furnish ample material for discussion elsewhere. Tillemont [Col. 0484D] collected and carefully arranged the principal events and chief points of their martyrdom in volume V, beginning at page 365. The Hieronymian copies are sufficiently confused and mutilated on both of the days just mentioned. Bede, followed by Rabanus and likewise by Ado, gives exactly the same eulogy for the entire group. I would believe that Bede composed his encomium from older Acts—for the deacon John, who wrote another account [Col. 0485A], lived much later than Bede. Whatever authority those Acts may possess, the immortal glory of Januarius throughout the Catholic world can in no way be obscured, as will be shown in its proper place from numerous manuscript monuments collected for that purpose. Here I follow the Martyrologies.

The Little Roman Martyrology wrote as follows: “At Naples, Januarius, Sosius, Festus, Desiderius, Proculus, Eutyches, and Acutius.” In our present connection it must especially be noted that all of these, as well as Notker and Ado’s abridger, count seven martyrs. Usuard took all his material from Bede or Ado, but since both of them commemorate Sosius separately again on September 23, our author judged that he should be omitted here, in order to avoid repetition. How Baronius followed this course can readily be seen by anyone who consults the present Roman Martyrology.

I find Peleus, Nilus, and several others commemorated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, not in Palestine but at Alexandria [Col. 0485B]. Florentinius discusses them at length from Eusebius, On the Martyrs of Palestine, chapter 13, and Ecclesiastical History, book VIII, chapter 13; but he joins Patermuthius as a companion to the first two. In place of Patermuthius, Marcus has slipped into Notker, and elsewhere Elias; perhaps the reading should rather be *alius*, namely, an anonymous presbyter not named by Eusebius. Bede and Rabanus do not mention them. The Little Roman Martyrology has only this brief entry: “Also Peleus and Nilus,” as that author commonly extracts only the names of martyrs from Eusebius through Rufinus. Ado added little of importance, but shaped the announcement as our author copied it from him, though omitting the tyrant’s name. Where Ado clearly says “those who suffered in the persecution of Diocletian,” our author says indefinitely “those who suffered in the time of the persecution,” perhaps because he thought the most violent persecution was sufficiently understood *antonomastically*—that is, by a name used in place of the thing itself. Ado joined these two bishops to Tyrannion, Silvanus, Zenobius, and [Col. 0486A] the anonymous Tyrian martyrs on February 18. See what we said there.

There is considerable corruption in the Hieronymian Martyrologies concerning Felix and Constantia. Since they are entered twice, on this day and the following day, they have been so intermingled and confused in gender that Florentinius can scarcely find their true names or a definite setting to which he may safely assign them while they remain entangled with others. There is no need to look far for the source of our author’s material, since he copies each word from Ado, as Notker also nearly did. Florus, differing from all the others, announces them on the preceding day, but without a location: “Also the passion of the holy Felix and Constantius, who suffered under the emperor Nero.” The person who occupies the last place here, Sigo, Sequanus, or Signus, according to the various nomenclature of the ancients, seems to have been taken by Ado from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, and from there passed word for word into our author and Notker. Florentinius doubts whether Sigo, or Sigonus, and Sequanus are one and the same person. But if plurality can be inferred from such [Col. 0486B] variation, that saint might already be fourfold, or even fivefold. In the Florus just mentioned the same person is commemorated in these words: “In the territory of the city of Langres, in the monastery of Segestro, the burial of Saint Sigo, priest and confessor.” Other Usuardine manuscripts also use a similar phrase. Nevertheless, both in this passage and in the rest of the text, it is perfectly clear that we have transmitted Usuard’s genuine reading. Surius found nothing concerning Sequanus except chapter 88—which he incorrectly calls chapter 8—of Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*. We possess a manuscript Life of the kind published by Mabillon in the first Benedictine century, beginning at page 263, together with another somewhat shorter version; both may be compared and illustrated in their proper time. Wandalbert today sings of Eustathius, or Eustachius; whom he means will be stated elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0485C]]

Rosweyd has a sufficiently pure text, but at the end adds: “Also Turgius, bishop; Pius, deacon, with 154 others. At Bourges, Marianus, bishop and confessor.” See what we said with Usuard on August 19.

Pulsanen is nearly pure at the beginning. He immediately adds: “At Nocera, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Felix and Constantia.” Everything else is absent, as so often above.

Antwerp-Major-Lübeck, Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, and the Danish manuscript add after Sequanus: “abbot, a priest of extraordinary righteousness. At Tours, Saint Eustachius, bishop, a man of great virtues.” The manuscripts must here generally be corrected, for the true name is Eustochius, as Molanus correctly has it below.

Centulen: “At Naples in Campania, the commemoration of the holy Januarius, bishop of the city of Benevento, with Sosius, deacon of the city of Misenum, and his deacon Festus and his lector Desiderius, under the judge Dracontius. In Palestine, the holy bishops Peleus and Nilus, who were consumed by fire with many clerics for their confession of Christ. At Nocera, the holy Felix and Constantia, who suffered under Nero. In the territory of the city of Langres, Saint Sigo, priest and monk, who was a follower of remarkable abstinence.”

Brussels begins: “At Rome, the holy martyrs Eustachius, surnamed Placidus, and his wife Theospis, with their sons Agapitus and Theospistus. Their deeds, pilgrimage, and conversion under the emperor Trajan are read as extraordinary. Since they refused to sacrifice to the gods, at the beginning of the reign of the emperor Hadrian they were burned in a bronze bull heated with fire.” We have already said that Wandalbert also commemorates these saints on this day. In the present Roman Martyrology they are placed on the following day, to which Ado likewise moved them; we shall treat of them with Usuard on November 2. What follows is transposed. First comes “At Micena,” instead of “At Nocera,” and so forth. Then come Januarius and his companions, followed by the Palestinians. The following is then inserted: “Also Theodore the martyr. At Tours, Saint Eustachius, bishop, a man of great virtues. In the territory of the city of Langres, the burial of Saint Sequanus, abbot, and Saint Sigo, a priest of extraordinary righteousness.” Here, clearly but wrongly, if I am not mistaken, Sequanus and Sigo are treated as distinct persons; we have said enough about them above in the Observation. “In the territory of Bourges, the burial of Saint Marianus the confessor.”

Hagenoyen, sufficiently pure in the first and second sections, adds: “At Metz, the burial of Saint Goericus, bishop and confessor.” See Surius. “Also Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor.” Is this the bishop of Gap? It continues: “At Nocera, the commemoration of the holy …,” and so forth, purely. Finally it gives Sequanus and Eustachius of Tours, as Antwerp and the others above.

Aquicinct, at the end: “Also Saint Zeno the martyr.” Below he is called Genon.

Victorin and the Swedish Register, marked no. 130: “Also in the territory of Bourges, Saint Marianus.”

Matrician–Carthusian–Utrecht: “Maternus, bishop and confessor. Januarius, bishop and martyr, with his companions. Peleus and Nilus, bishops, who were consumed by fire with many clerics.”

Codex D of Du Cheval, marked B: “At Trier, blessed Maternus, bishop and confessor.” See September 14. Codex C of the same collection: “Also Genon the martyr.” He may be the person whom others call Zeno. He is not commemorated here under either form of the name.

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949, Sequanus is absent.

Ughellian: “At Tours, Saint Eustachius, bishop, a man of great virtues.”

Florentinian: “Saint Sequatius, abbot … Also, in the same place, Saint Marianus the confessor.”

Bordeaux: “In the territory of the city of Langres, Saint Signus, priest. Also Beo, the martyr.”

Codex Castri-Caroli: “In the territory of the city of Langres, Saint Signus, priest.” Here it is clear that Sequanus is intended, as in the preceding manuscript.

Besançon: “At Metz, Saint Gohericus, bishop and confessor.” He is the same person called Goericus above.

[Col. 0487A] Reims, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “In the territory of the city of Langres, in the monastery of Segestro, the burial of Saint Sigonius, priest and monk.”

The Lübeck–Cologne edition is nearly pure in its first three sections, then adds: “At Trier, Saint Miletus, bishop and confessor. At Metz, Saint Goericus, bishop and confessor. In the territory of the city of Langres, the burial of Saint Sequanus, abbot, a priest of extraordinary righteousness.” Concerning Eustachius of Tours, as above. “On the same day, Saint Zeno the martyr. On this day, the commemoration of Saint Maternus, archbishop and confessor, at Tongeren.”

The first edition of Belinus inserts near the end: “At Tours, Eustachius, bishop, a man of great virtues.” The second edition adds at the end: “Also Genon the martyr.”

Greven: “At Alexandria, the holy Aemeterius, Nicetius, and Castor. Also Zeno the martyr. At Metz, Saint Goericus, bishop and confessor. At Trier, Saint Miletus, bishop and confessor. At Tours, Saint Eustachius, bishop and confessor, a man of great virtues. In England, blessed Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury and confessor. He”—as Bede testifies in book IV—“was born at Tarsus in Cilicia, trained in divine and human literature in both Latin and Greek, of upright character and venerable age. When he was sixty-six years old, he was consecrated by Pope Vitalian as bishop of Doruvernus, or Canterbury. Filling the churches of all England by his example and teaching, full of days, he rested in peace.” His Life is found in Surius. “Turgius, bishop and confessor. Eligius, bishop and confessor. At Tongeren, the commemoration of Saint Maternus, bishop and confessor.”

Molanus: “At Tours, Saint Eustachius, bishop, a man of great virtues. At Trier, Saint Melitus [Miletus], bishop. In England, blessed Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury and confessor. He was born at Tarsus,” and so forth, as in Greven, except that at the end it adds: “Bede writes this in book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapters 1 and 2, and in book V, chapter 8. At Metz, Saint Goericus, bishop and confessor, surnamed Appo, admirable for the holiness of his life and lovable to all entrusted to him.” Other editions have Miletus as above. It continues: “At Messina in the Sicilian strait, the holy Nicander, abbot, and his companions Gregory, Peter, Demetrius, and Elizabeth. They lived as solitaries under a certain cave, enduring hunger, thirst, heat, and cold for Christ, where together they rested in peace.” Concerning Eustachius, as above. Then: “On the nineteenth day, the holy martyrs Trophimus, Sabbatius, and Dorymedon. At the city of Metz, Saint Goericus, bishop and confessor, who was admirable for the holiness of his life and lovable to all entrusted to him.” At Castellum he is the patron of the women’s canonesses of Spilans.

[Col. 0483]

At Naples in Campania, the commemoration of the holy Januarius, bishop of the city of Benevento, Festus and Proculus, deacons, Desiderius, Eutyches, and Acutius, who, after imprisonment and confinement, were beheaded in the city of Pozzuoli under the emperor Diocletian. Also in Palestine, the holy bishops and martyrs Peleus and Nilus, who, during the persecution, were consumed by fire with many clerics for Christ. At Nocera, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Felix and Constantia, who suffered under Nero. In the territory of the city of Langres, Saint Sequanus, priest.

The twelfth day before the Kalends of October. Day 20.

[Note: [Col. 0487]]

Only Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, Munerat, and Molanus are pure.

[Note: [Col. 0487C]]

Everyone writes “Cizico,” except Molanus, who has “Cyzico”; but Antwerp-Major has it very badly as “Crito” or “Erito.” Molanus seems to have wished to correct Usuard by reading “and he himself, believing in Christ” instead of “and he himself, believing, Christ”; unless he received this reading from Greven. Munerat omitted *Christi* before “martyrs.” Antwerp-Major polished—or at least altered—the whole phrase in this form: “Eulogius the priest, crowned with martyrdom for the love of Christ.” Then, instead of Phrygia, as nearly all the manuscripts write, he put “in Africa.” Molanus correctly has Phrygia; Munerat and others have Frigia. We have said enough about this elsewhere, while following a different orthography from that of the manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0487D]]

The first commemoration of the first martyrs in this small section, unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, is found in Bede, where one finds certain excerpts from longer Acts that Tillemont, quite reasonably, pronounces difficult to believe, in volume V, pages 160–161. Apart from this, some details seem to be narrated differently by Surius, after Metaphrastes on February 6; others by Bede here; and still others by Baronius, who makes Evilasius a priest of idols. We shall examine these matters in their proper place. Here it must especially be noted that Rabanus and Ado followed Bede so closely that they transcribed his entire history. The Little Roman Martyrology reads briefly: “At Cyzicus, Fausta the virgin and Evilasius.” Whether our author had Ado or Bede before his eyes, he shaped the eulogy as we have reported it in the text, not as it appears in the manuscripts of the intermediate recension. Although they contain the same account, the wording has been changed. See what Baronius noted concerning Cyzicus, the tonsure of virgins, and related matters; and what Molanus noted in the first edition of Usuard concerning the *maforte*, *maphorte*, or *mavorte*, a woman’s head-covering. Wandalbert today commemorates only Fausta and Evilasius in these words:

“Fausta the virgin twice six [that is, twelve years old], and Evilasius adorn the day.”

Concerning Eulogius, the most celebrated priest and martyr of Córdoba, who follows next in our text, Usuard alone among the ancients speaks. Among later authors he was followed, among others, by Maurolycus, Felicius, and Galesinius. But since Galesinius noted that Eulogius was struck down with a sword on the fifth day before the Ides of March, Baronius judged that he should be transferred there, although Galesinius himself asserts: “On this day he is celebrated with the divine offices of the appointed hours, according to the usage of the church of Córdoba …” But in our Acts, in the preliminary Commentary for March 11, section 1, this is refuted from the Scholia of Ambrosius Morales. Whether rightly or wrongly, let the reader decide. For my part, I have no doubt that Usuard, who witnessed the struggles at Córdoba almost at close range, had a serious reason, appropriate to that time, for placing Eulogius on this day rather than on March 11. For the remaining matters concerning Eulogius, see in our Acts for the aforementioned March 11 the accurate and diligent treatment by Henschenius. Unless I am very much mistaken, the Phrygian martyrs were taken from one of the Hieronymian manuscripts. We recently indicated that certain matters in those manuscripts are disturbed, mutilated, and confused on this day and the preceding one. Furthermore, from the tables of various manuscripts compared by Florentinius, Dionysius and Privatus can readily be extracted from the number of the martyrs of Synnada, whatever corrupt and displaced names we may recognize there. It would be most welcome if someone should supply some historical monuments concerning these last martyrs. Finally, it may be briefly observed that Molanus, pure in his first edition, inserted Eustachius with his wife and sons into the text in later editions, although Wandalbert had sung of him alone on the preceding day. Florus mentions him on November 1; Usuard on November 2. The latter’s words were attached by the Herinien manuscript to this day, as we shall say shortly in the Supplements.

[Note: [Col. 0489A]]

Herinien, although generally complete and reliable, is remarkably corrupted today. It begins: “The vigil of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist.” The first announcement of the text follows in a very pure form. Then, however, the passage I mentioned earlier is inserted: “Also, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, the passion of the blessed Eustachius, surnamed Placidas [or Placidus], and his wife Theospis, with their sons Agapius and Theospistus, whose marvelous Acts are read.” It also lacks the passage on Eulogius of Córdoba.

Rosweyd, not entirely pure in the text, adds at the end: “The vigil of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist.” This recurs several times below.

[Col. 0489B] Pulsanen begins: “The vigil of Saint Matthew the apostle.” The text is plainly truncated, for it contains only: “At Cyzicus, the commemoration of the holy martyrs,” and so forth, up to “emperor.” Everything else is absent.

Antwerp and Major-Lübeck belong chiefly to the group of manuscripts that, as I said, altered Usuard’s wording from Bede or Ado, in this form: “At Cyzicus, the holy martyrs Fausta the virgin and Evilasius. Fausta was first shorn by that same Evilasius, stripped to her shame, hung up, and tortured. Then, when he wished to cut her in two but the executioners were unable to injure her, Evilasius, astonished, believed. While he too was being cruelly tortured by Maximian, Fausta, her head pierced, her whole body nailed through, and placed on a heated frying pan, passed away with Evilasius when a voice from heaven called them.” The remainder of the text is pure, but at the end it adds: “Also, the vigil of Saint Matthew the apostle.”

Greven, pure in the text, also adds at the end, but as an announcement belonging to the text: “Also, the vigil of Saint Matthew the apostle.”

[Col. 0489C] Antwerp-Major, Leiden, and Leuven begin in this way: “The vigil of Saint Matthew the apostle and evangelist.” In all other respects these three manuscripts resemble Antwerp and Major-Lübeck.

Utrecht differs from the three immediately preceding manuscripts in omitting Eulogius.

Albergen and the Danish manuscript: “The vigil of Saint Matthew the apostle. At Rome, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, the passion of the blessed Eustachius, surnamed Placidus, and his wife Theospis, with their sons Agapius and Theospistus, whose marvelous Acts are read.” The text continues as in Antwerp-Major and the others.

Centulen: “The vigil of Saint Matthew. In Phrygia, the holy Dionysius and Privatus. At Cyzicus, the holy Fausta the virgin and Evilasius, under the emperor Maximian. Fausta was a girl of thirteen years, and Evilasius was eighty years old. At Córdoba, Eulogius the priest, beheaded for faith in Christ.”

[Col. 0489D] Brussels: “The vigil of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist.” It mixes many details about Fausta and Evilasius from Ado, which one will read in a purer form in Molanus’s Supplement. It then continues with Eulogius and the Phrygians, purely. Then: “At the monastery of Elnone, the elevation of the body of Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.”

Hagenoyen, concerning the vigil, is as above. In Fausta and Evilasius it also nearly follows Ado or Bede. It is pure in the final two sections. It adds: “At Trier, Saint Quiriacus, priest and confessor.” See March 6; below the translation is mentioned.

Aquicinct inserts near the end: “The elevation of the body of Saint Amandus, bishop.”

Victorin and the Swedish Register, marked no. 130, at the end: “Also at Rome, Euthius or Eutychius [Eustachius], with his wife and two sons.”

Matrician–Carthusian–Utrecht: “Fausta the virgin and martyr. And Evilasius. Dionysius and Privatus.”

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949, the announcements of Eulogius, Dionysius, and Privatus are absent.

Florentinian: “Saint Lauri, bishop and confessor—Laudi, I suppose,” concerning whom see the following day.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition: “The vigil of Saint Matthew the apostle. At Rome, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, the passion of the blessed Eustachius, etc.,” nearly as above. The account of Fausta and Evilasius is somewhat more interpolated than in Antwerp and the others. The final two sections are pure. It continues: “On the same day, Saint Quiriacus, apostle and martyr. On this day, the translation of Saint Quiriacus, priest and confessor.” We spoke above concerning Hagenoyen. The nativity of this Quiriacus is commemorated on March 6. See there, in the Acts, the historical commentary; here the translation is more appropriately commemorated.

Belinus. In Fausta and Evilasius he resembles Antwerp and the others. He immediately adds: “On the same day, Saints Eustachius and his companions. Also on the same day, the vigil of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist. In Phrygia, the holy …,” and so forth. Eulogius of Córdoba is absent from the first edition, but is added at the end in the second: “In the city of Córdoba, blessed Eulogius the priest.”

Greven: “Florentius, bishop and martyr.” Among the many Florentiuses, it is not easy to guess whom he intends here. “Quiriacus, philosopher and martyr. Also Saint Cuthbert. On this day, the translation of Saint Quiriacus, priest and confessor. According to some, here belong Eustachius and his companions, who are commemorated on the fourth day before the Nones of November. Also the holy memory of Gerhard, hermit and confessor. As is related in the Acts of Blessed Lidwina the virgin, he was born in the diocese of Cologne, in the territory of Agrippina. Desiring a solitary life, he went to Egypt, where, living on the manna of heaven, excessively stout in body but angelic in countenance, he was found in a cave. At last he rested in the Lord in a blessed death, in the year of the Lord 1426 [in the first edition, 1425]. The aforementioned virgin saw his soul carried by angels into heaven. Eustochia the virgin.”

Molanus, after “he suffered,” inserts into the text in different type, from Bede or Ado: “Since the executioners were unable to injure her with their instruments, Evilasius, astonished, began to believe in Christ. When this had been reported to the emperor, he sent a prefect to have him hung up and cruelly tortured. He also ordered Fausta to be stripped naked and beaten without her *maforte*, imprisoned, her head pierced, and her eyes impaled. Later not only her head and face but also her breast and entire body down to the thighs were filled with nails. After this he ordered a frying pan to be heated, but while she sang psalms it grew cold. Meanwhile a voice came from heaven and called them, and so they gave up their spirit. Fausta was thirteen years old, and Evilasius eighty.”

At the end he adds: “Also on the same day, Saints Eustachius and his companions. Also on the same day, the vigil, etc. On this day, in the monastery of Sonegia, the translation of blessed Vincent, confessor and monk.” This concerns the husband of Saint Waldetrudis, who is also called Madelgarius. See the Supplements for his feast day, July 14. Other editions begin with Eustachius. At the end, concerning the vigil, as above. Also the translation of blessed Vincent. Finally:

[Col. 0491A] At Elnone, the elevation of the body of Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor. After 150 years from his death his body was found intact, and drops of blood are said to have flowed from his mouth after the discoverer removed two teeth. See concerning this elevation the sermon of Milo the monk in the Acts for February 6, page 891.

[Col. 0487]

At Cyzicus, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Fausta the virgin and Evilasius, under the emperor Maximian. Evilasius, who was first in the palace, ordered her first to be dishonored, hung up, tortured, and cut in two as though she were a piece of wood; but afterward he himself believed in Christ and suffered together with Fausta. [Note: [Col. 0487C] The Carolingian autograph inserts the following between the first and second announcement: “Also, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, the passion of the blessed Eustachius, surnamed Placidus, and his wife Theospis, whose marvelous deeds are read.” It contains not a word about Eulogius of Córdoba. Nevertheless Sollerius rejected the Herinien Codex, which was extremely pure, for this day. I ask for what reason. Four lines had been erased in the Pratensis Codex; Herinien, his Achilles, contradicted Pratensis. Was there some other reason elsewhere why he rejected the Pratensis? In any event, I am not surprised that Usuard removed Eustachius from his manuscript; but I am very surprised that he could ever have admitted him. Concerning Eulogius of Córdoba, and whether he attained the palm of martyrdom on this day or on March 11, there is much controversy. It is not credible that Usuard, Eulogius’s contemporary and almost an eyewitness of his martyrdom, was mistaken. I embrace Sollerius’s opinion and explain it in his own words. For my part, I have no doubt that Usuard, who witnessed the struggles at Córdoba almost at close range, had a serious reason, appropriate to that time, for placing Eulogius on this day rather than on March 11. BOUILLART.] In the city of Córdoba, blessed Eulogius the priest, beheaded for the martyrdom of Christ. In Phrygia, the holy Dionysius and Privatus.

The eleventh day before the Kalends of October. Day 21.

[Note: [Col. 0491A]]

Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Major-Lübeck, Munerat, Belinus, Greven, and Molanus agree. Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, and the Danish manuscript also join them.

[Note: [Col. 0491A]]

The differences are nearly reduced to orthography: everyone writes *Mathei*, except Molanus, who correctly has *Matthaei*. Rosweyd has *Ethyopiam*; Belinus and most others have *Ethiopiam*; we follow Pratensis and Herinien. The same applies to *Hebraeo*, and so forth. Belinus has *laceratione* instead of *laniationem*, and Rosweyd *exuperans* instead of *superans*.

[Note: [Col. 0491B]]

Besides other ancient monuments, all the Martyrologies prove the very ancient commemoration of the apostle and evangelist Matthew in the sacred calendars. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies he is indeed listed on four different days: May 1 and 6, and again October 7. Today they read: “And in Persia, in the city of Tarseum [or Tarrium], the commemoration of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist.” The Epternacensis more prudently does not specify the place. Bede more simply wrote: “The commemoration of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist.” Florus added “in Persia,” and even “in the city of Tharim.” Rabanus has “in Ethiopia,” adding a few details from the commonly circulated Acts. The Little Roman Martyrology has only, very briefly, “Matthew the apostle.” Ado supplied little in his Feasts of the Apostles, drawing chiefly, indeed almost exclusively, from Jerome; the material he took from there was neatly abridged by our author. Notker, more sparing than usual, adds rather coldly: “whose passion is commonly recounted everywhere.” We shall discuss that history and several similar histories rejected in various places elsewhere, as well as the much-disputed place of his martyrdom, the translations of his relics, and other matters relevant here. Preliminary material can be found in Baronius’s notes, in Florentinius’s preliminary index to the Martyrology, pages 158–159, and in the notes for this day; more recently, see Tillemont, volume I, in the series of the Apostles. Castellan’s brief annotations on the Universal Martyrology for this day may also be consulted. Wandalbert sang as follows:

“He who abandoned the world’s gains when Christ called him,

Matthew consecrated the eleventh day with his evangelical voice.”

[Col. 0492B] No Martyrologist today mentions Alexander the bishop except Ado, who honors him on November 26 with a long eulogy. There the Little Roman Martyrology records him in this way: “And blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, who suffered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October and was transferred by Pope Damasus on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, when he dedicated a feast to him.” From Ado’s history Usuard brought here what he has elegantly, though briefly, compressed in our eulogy. Baronius noted that this Alexander is certainly entirely different from Pope Alexander. “Of what city he was bishop,” he says, “we have not yet discovered. Nor has any light thus far appeared to us by which we could determine anything concerning his episcopal see; this will be examined more carefully in its proper place together with his Acts.” The final place here is occupied by Pamphilus the martyr at Rome, without any other distinguishing note or designation. Baronius asserts that ancient manuscripts support Usuard in this. Yet he nowhere indicates what or of what kind they are, perhaps because he found the name only in the manuscripts cited by Galesinius, who is quite liberal in calling things by such names. I confess that I am very greatly surprised that Usuard attached this Pamphilus to the day, since none of the ancients or his contemporaries mentions him. I have elsewhere observed that one rarely finds a saint in Usuard—apart from the people of Córdoba and the popular saints of Gaul—whose traces do not occur at least somewhere in other authors. Nevertheless, from all our manuscripts it is indubitable that he really is commemorated by Usuard on this day.

[Note: [Col. 0491C]]

Pulsanen is pure up to and including Alexander the bishop; everything else is absent.

Centulen: “The commemoration of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, who first wrote the Gospel of Christ in Hebrew in Judea, and afterward, preaching in Ethiopia, suffered martyrdom. On the same day, Saint Alexander the martyr, whom Pope Damasus honorably buried. At Rome, Saint Pamphilus the martyr.” Thus it commonly abridges the text.

Brussels: “The commemoration of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, who, chosen by Christ from the ranks of the publicans, first preached the Gospel in Judea, afterward preaching in Macedonia and Ethiopia, and suffered martyrdom in Persia. His Gospel, etc.,” purely. “On this day, at Rome, on the Claudian Way, twenty miles from the city, the passion of Saint Alexander the pope.” This is erroneous, for Pope Alexander is commemorated on May 3, as we said there. The remainder of the text follows, fairly purely, and is supplemented in the same false supposition: “He established that the water of sprinkling should be blessed with salt, that the altar offering should be made with unleavened bread, and that water should be mixed with wine, to signify the union of Christ and the Church. He also added to the Canon of the Mass: ‘who, on the day before he suffered.’” The section on Pamphilus is pure. Then: “And at Tronchiennes, Saint Gerulphus the martyr. And the translation of the body of Saint Landelin the confessor, whom Saint Autbert converted to Christ; and after his own conversion he founded the monasteries of Aulne on the Sambre and Lobbes.”

Hagenoyen: “The commemoration of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, whom the Lord called from the customs house and made his apostle. He prepared a great banquet for the Lord in his house. After he came to the Lord, he did not leave him, nor did he return to public business. He was among the Lord’s intimate companions with the other apostles. He saw the Lord rise from the dead and ascend into heaven, and received the Holy Spirit with the others. First preaching in Judea, he was the first to write the Gospel in the Hebrew language. [Col. 0493A] He added the article to the Creed. Later, preaching in Myrmidonia, he was blinded and restored to sight through the Apostle Andrew. Then he went down to Ethiopia to preach the word of God, where Taroes and Arphaxat, magicians, were very hostile to him. After raising the king’s son, he converted a large part of the city and country, built many churches, ordained priests, bishops, and other clergy, and consecrated the king’s daughter Iphigenia with the sacred veil. Because Hircatus, after King Eglyppus, had intended to take her as his bride, he caused the Apostle Matthew to be struck from behind with a sword after the solemn celebration of Mass and thus consecrated him a martyr of Christ. His Gospel, etc. Also Saint Landelin the martyr.” But this manuscript makes Landelin a martyr along with the others, although everywhere the subject is the same disciple of Saint Autbert, bishop of Cambrai, whom our Supplements and the Roman Martyrology commemorate on June 15; his Life is illustrated on that day. “Also blessed Laudo, bishop and confessor.” In Alexander and Pamphilus it is nearly pure.

[Col. 0493B] Aquicinct, at the end: “At the city of Apt, the commemoration of blessed Castor, bishop and confessor.”

Matrician–Carthusian–Utrecht: “Matthew, apostle and evangelist. Alexander, bishop and martyr, who endured many torments.”

Cistercian of Saint Benignus: “The dedication of the altar of Saint Eustadius and Saint Paschasia.”

Swedish Register, marked no. 428: “At Rouen, Saint Laudo, bishop.” More properly he should be called *Lauto*, shortened in French to *Lo*.

Codex D of Le Mare, marked A, unless I am mistaken: “In the city of Apt, the commemoration of blessed Castor, bishop and confessor.”

In the Vatican manuscript under note no. 5949, the last two announcements are absent. It adds: “On the same day, Saint Vincent the martyr.” I do not know which Vincent is meant, unless it refers to what is found in the Besançon manuscript on September 23.

[Col. 0493C] Altemps: “Also Saint Laudo, bishop. In Britain, Saint Werburga the virgin.” See February 3.

Caudiac: “At the city of Apt, the commemoration of blessed Castor, bishop and confessor.” Above someone had read “at the city of Atta.” Greven below has “Castor, bishop of Athens,” but the reading should be “at the city of Apt.” [Col. 0494A] See some other material about the same saint in Castellan’s Martyrology.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition: “In Ethiopia, in the city of Nadaber, the commemoration of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, who was also called Levi. He first wrote the Gospel of Christ in Hebrew in Judea; afterward, while preaching in Ethiopia, he suffered martyrdom from King Hircanus. Although this Gospel had been hidden for some time, it was nevertheless found by divine providence, when the apostle himself revealed it, in the time of the emperor Zeno.” The account of Alexander is slightly interpolated; that of Pamphilus is pure. It continues: “On the same day, in the territory of the city of Constancia, Saint Laudus, bishop and confessor. In the district of Troyes, Saint Maura.” The word “of the city” is added at the end, although it contributes nothing to the matter; perhaps the intended reading was “of the virgin.”

Greven: “Landelinus the martyr.” See what was said under Hagenoyen. “Gero the martyr. In Flanders, Gerulphus, a boy and martyr. In Lower Normandy, in the city of Coutances, blessed Laudo, bishop and confessor. He was appointed bishop at the age of twelve by divine providence, and after illuminating the aforesaid church by word, life, and miracles, he rested in a blessed death. Castor, bishop and confessor of Athens.” See Caudiac. “Also Victor. Geremar, abbot. In the district of Troyes, Saint Maura the virgin.”

MOLAN. Regarding Alexander, after “gloriously,” inserts into the text, in different type:

> “To whom Pope Damasus, having made a fitting crypt, transferred him there on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, when he also instituted a feast for him; there his passion was recorded.”

See Ado in the *Observations* cited above. At the end he adds:

> “At Coutances in Lower Normandy, of blessed Laudus, the first bishop of the aforesaid city, whose life flourished with miracles and whose death was likewise precious in the sight of the Lord. The passion of Saint Gerulphus the martyr.”

The later editions have the same material concerning Alexander in the text, as we have already said. At the end they likewise have the passage concerning Laudus. Then:

> “At Tronchiennes near Ghent, the passion of Saint Gerulphus. On the twenty-first day, of the holy Apostle Quadratus at Magnesia. At Crespin, the elevation and removal of the body of the most blessed father Landelin by Odo, bishop of Cambrai.”

Here the reference is rightly to Landelin, father—or abbot—and confessor, and not to his burial, but to his elevation, and so forth.

[Col. 0491]

The nativity of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, who, while preaching in Ethiopia, suffered martyrdom. His Gospel, written in the Hebrew language, was discovered, through his own revelation, in the time of the emperor Zeno. On the same day, on the Claudian Way, at the twentieth milestone from the City, the passion of Saint Alexander the bishop, who for the faith of Christ, under the emperor Antoninus, overcame chains, clubs, the rack, burning lamps, the tearing of flesh with hooks, wild beasts, and the flames of the furnace, and at last attained a glorious life by the sword. Also at Rome, of Saint Pamphilus the martyr.

**The tenth day before the Kalends. Day 22.**

[Note: [Col. 0493]]

Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan have this form.

[Note: [Col. 0493D]]

I retained “at Agaunum,” together with our older manuscripts, Pratensis and Heriniensis, and because the Eucherian *Acts* and other ancient authorities read this way. The number of his companions cannot so readily be determined from those manuscripts or from others, since the *Acts* themselves do not state it, although they indicate the customary strength of a legion according to the more common opinion; Viennensis likewise hesitated within those limits. Florus seems to have been the first to determine the number as 6,666, and this reading is found in most of our manuscripts, namely in Heriniensis, Rosweyd, Greven, Molan, and nearly all the manuscripts of middling age. Since I think that Florus was never seen by Usuard, I readily believe that he adopted another reckoning, which has remained in Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, and Munerat; we have followed that form in the text, as perhaps closer to the true calculation, although we would prefer to leave the number undetermined.

I think Usuard wrote *Beuuaria*, for which some have *Bejovaria*, others *Bannaria*, and others *Bavaria*; Rosweyd has the more precise *Ratispona*. There is remarkable diversity in the saint’s name. Pratensis has *Himmerani*; Heriniensis, *Amtrani*; Antwerp-Major and Munerat, *Avitramni*; Molan, *Emerami*; others have other forms. I have allowed myself to choose for the text the form that comes closest to the truth, from Rosweyd and Greven: *Emmerammi*, instead of *Emmeramni*.

Pratensis read incorrectly *crimen stupri a quodam commisso* (“the crime of sexual misconduct committed by someone”); Heriniensis somewhat better has *commissi*; others, best of all, *commissum*. Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan, contrary to the older witnesses, read at the end: “In the territory of Bourges, of Saint Silvanus,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0495A]]

The martyrdom of the most renowned Theban Legion is confirmed and established by so many ancient and indisputable records that I cannot sufficiently marvel at the audacity of a certain Anglo-Savoyard minion who dared, with reckless speech, to gnaw away at that most sacred host. The time will come when, with God’s favor, we shall tear apart his hypercritical dissertation, published in English and French—unless Tillemont, although I have never seen the work, has already sufficiently crushed it in advance in volume IV, beginning on page 421, together with several others who, in other respects, are sufficiently critical and highly skilled in uncovering historical truth.

The records I mentioned rest chiefly upon our Martyrologies and upon those excellent, indeed venerable, *Acts of Saint Eucherius of Lyon*, first published by our Chifflet and then edited and illuminated by Ruinart in the *Selecta*, beginning on page 285. I do not see what the sophistries of Dubourda have so greatly diminished in them to this point.

As for the exact number of those martyrs, just as the *Acts* cited above state nothing certain, so here also I do not wish to determine anything. In the Hieronymian copies they are commemorated as follows:

> “In Gaul, in the city of Sion, the nativity of Saints Maurice, Exuperius, Candidus, Victor, Innocentius, and Vitalis, with their companions: V CIC D and eighty-five.””

The manuscript copies of Bede do not agree in their number. If we seek Bede in Rabanus, he should probably be understood to have written:

> “Of the holy martyrs of the Theban Legion, Maurice, Candidus, and Exuperius,”

which are the names expressed in the *Acts*. In one manuscript Victor is added, and rightly so; in another, the anonymous companions are listed as 6,085. Florus, more neatly and according to the reported strength of the ancient Roman legions, has:

> “With their companions, whose total number was 6,666.”

The *Small Roman Martyrology* wisely and truthfully says:

> “Of Maurice with his companions, who are reported to have been Thebans and to have suffered under Maximian.”

Ado also did not express the number of the martyrs more precisely, since he found no such number in Eucherius, from whose most genuine *Acts* he transferred the greater part into his Martyrology. I repeat: he could not find it at all in Eucherius. Our author carries out his brief eulogy from Ado, with the aforesaid number of the martyrs varying in the manuscripts, as we have amply shown above.

Thus there is complete agreement concerning the martyrdom of our Thebans among all the ancient Martyrologists, including Wandalbert and Notker. Nor should the authority of the Gothic, or ancient Gallican, Missal be passed over. It is nine hundred years old, as the illustrious editor Thomasius, later cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, testifies on page 373; it contains a Mass in which the most illustrious memory of the army of 6,600, indeed of the Thebans, is preserved.

These are Wandalbert’s verses concerning the Thebans and Emmeram:

> At last Maurice crowns [the day] with his companion legion,  
> which by pouring out its blood likewise conquered death.  
> Emmeram accompanies him with equal honor,  
> whom illustrious Britain claims by voice.

Only Rabanus and Wandalbert remembered Emmeram or Emmeramn. Usuard may have found the name in Wandalbert, but it seems more likely to me that he obtained it elsewhere, taking the name from a Life in which it is rather crudely stated that he caused the sexual offense committed by another to be attributed to himself. In the Roman Martyrology Baronius judged that this should be expressed in somewhat more restrained language. The truth of the whole matter will be elucidated in due course from the *Acts* of Emmeram, published by various authors, when Wandalbert’s verse will also be examined:

> whom illustrious Britain claims by voice.

Florentius of Poitiers and Silvanus of Bourges were entered in the sacred registers by no one before Usuard, something quite familiar to him in the case of local saints. The *Acts* of the former, connected with those of Saint Florian, were partly published by Cointius under the year 1194, no. 13 onward. Whether the manuscripts we possess, divided into four parts, are as unreliable as a more recent writer contends will be seen later. I know nothing reported about Silvanus except what Labbe suggests in volume II of the *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, beginning on page 444.

[Note: [Col. 0495C]]

PULSANEN., in its first announcement, is fairly pure and adds:

> “Also of Saint Silvanus the confessor with his companions.”

Everything else is lacking.

ANTWERP, MAX.-LUBECK.:

> “In Gaul, in the city of Sion, or Octodurum in Valais, at the place called Agaunum,”

and so forth. They give the number as 6,666, like all the manuscripts of middling age, and conclude the announcement:

> “Having suffered for Christ, they illuminated the world by their glorious passion,”

as the Roman Martyrology reads today. Then follows:

> “In the territory of Poitiers, of Saint Florentius the priest and confessor. In the territory of the city of Coutances, of Saint Laudus the bishop.”

The other items relevant to the text are lacking. Laudus—or rather, as we noted above, Lauto—is celebrated on the preceding day, where he is also called Laudus by others.

ANTWERP-MAJOR reads 6,660. It has the same conclusion: “Having suffered,” and so forth. It calls Florentius a bishop. Then it gives Laudus, as we have just said. Finally:

> “At Bavaria, of Saint Emmeram, bishop and martyr.”

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, and DANIC agree for the most part with the preceding witnesses. They write 6,666. Concerning Florentius, they read “priest,” in agreement with the text. In writing the name of Emmeram they vary greatly, as has also been said concerning the others.

ALBERGEN is defective, like Antwerp and Max.-Lubeck, in the announcement of Emmeram; in all of them, Silvanus of Bourges is absent.

CENTULEN.:

> “In Gaul, in the territory of Sion, at the place called Agaunum, the nativity of the holy martyrs of the Theban Legion, Maurice, Exuperius, Candidus, Vitalis, Innocentius, and Victor, together with their companions, whose total number was 6,666 men. Having suffered for Christ under the emperor Maximian, they were crowned most gloriously. At Auxerre, the arrival and reception from Italy of the body of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor. In Bavaria, of Saint Hameramus the martyr. On the same day, the translation of Saint John of Réomay.”

BRUSSELS, fairly pure in its first announcement, has in second place, concerning Silvanus:

> “But with his companions.”

Then:

> “At Regensburg, a city of Bavaria, the passion of blessed Hemmeram, or Autean, bishop and martyr. He allowed the crime of sexual misconduct committed by someone else to be attributed to him, an innocent man, for Christ’s sake, and so forth. In the territory of the city of Coutances, of Saint Laudus the bishop. In the territory of Poitiers, of Saint Florentius the bishop and confessor.”

Read “priest,” as in the text.

HAGENOYEN gathered much material concerning the Theban martyrs, which we consider apocryphal. Then it treats Silvanus. Next comes Florentius, fairly purely. It follows with Laudus, as above. Here is some material concerning Emmeram:

> “At Petivaria, the city of Regensburg in Germany, of Saint Emeram, bishop and martyr. He was born in Aquitania, in the city of Toulouse. From his youth he despised the world and adhered to Christ; he acquired a knowledge of letters and attained the highest priesthood. For he was a true worshiper of God. After this he left his homeland and all that he possessed in order to preach the word of God to the Huns [and other peoples]. Having entered Germany, which Deodo, a man of lively intelligence and vigorous in arms, governed, he preached for three years in that province at Deodo’s command. At that time the duke’s daughter committed sexual misconduct, which she confessed to him together with her fornicator. Imposing penance upon them, he caused it to be imposed upon himself, and so forth.”

AQUICINCT does not call Saint Emmeram a bishop and, after “martyr,” continues:

> “He allowed the crime of sexual misconduct committed by someone else to be attributed to him for Christ’s sake, and therefore patiently endured the danger of death.”

Besides what has been noted above, Cointius should not be overlooked; while investigating many matters carefully, he treats the subject under the year 649, from page 243 to page 256.

MATRIC-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT.:

> “Of Maurice and his companions. Of Salaberga the abbess. Of Lintrudis the virgin. Of Emmeram, bishop and martyr. Of Florentius, bishop and confessor.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, signature B:

> “In the territory of the city of Coutances, of Saint Laudus the bishop.”

In the Vatican manuscript marked no. 5949 there is nothing concerning Emmeram, Florentius, or Silvanus.

UGHELLIAN also lacks Emmeram and Silvanus. It adds:

> “In the territory of the city of Coutances, of Saint Laudus the bishop.”

ALTEMPS writes *Hautramnus* instead of Emmeram:

> “At Coutances, of Saint Laudus the bishop.”

FLORENTIN.:

> “In the territory of the city of Coutances, of Saint Laudus the bishop and confessor.”

LUXOVIEN.:

> “At Laon-Clavato, of Saint Salaberga, servant of Christ, who became the mother of three hundred religious women; at whose tomb, after her death, illustrious miracles appeared.”

CAUDIACEN.:

> “Of Saint Lauto, bishop and confessor.”

He is the same person whom others call Laudo, Lando, Laudus, and so forth, in French Lo, as we have said.

REMENS., Saints Timothy and Apollinaris:

> “At Auxerre, the arrival from Italy and reception of the body of Saint Germanus, bishop of that same city.”

The Lubeck-Cologne edition, fairly pure in its first announcement, adds:

> “Also there, at the place called Agaunum, of blessed Victor the veteran, who, after the slaughter of the blessed Thebans, was killed there by the persecutors and joined to the holy martyrs. At Regensburg, of Saint Emmeram, bishop and martyr.”

It treats Florentius correctly.

> “In the province of Bavaria, the nativity of Saint Haytramus, bishop and confessor.”

Is this not a repetition?

> “In the territory of Tornodorum, of blessed John the abbot.”

Concerning Silvanus, as above.

> “On the same day, of Saint Luttrudis the virgin.”

BELIN, in the first edition, also reads 6,666 and has the conclusion given above. It follows with Florentius, as in Antwerp-Major. Then Laudus, and so forth. The passage concerning Silvanus is somewhat mutilated:

> “At Bavaria, of Saint Antranus, and so forth. The crime of sexual misconduct was attributed to him, and therefore the danger of death,”

and so forth.

GREVEN.:

> “Of Landelin, Romaric, and their 585 companions. Of Plato the martyr. Of Victor the martyr, who, when he was blessing the martyrs of Agaunum, saying that he would count himself happy if he had been killed with them, was immediately slaughtered by the same executioners. According to some, Jonius the priest and martyr, companion of blessed Dionysius, is commemorated here; according to others, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August. When he had come to Gaul for the sake of preaching, he was seized and beheaded; then, taking his severed head in his hands, he carried it for nearly a mile to the place where he had chosen to rest. According to the *Catalogue of the Saints*, Saint Santinus, bishop of Meaux and confessor, is commemorated here, a disciple of blessed Dionysius, bishop and martyr of Paris. Also of Silvanus, bishop of Nazareth and confessor, a man of great holiness and especially close to Saint Jerome, as is clear from his deeds. In the Scetis desert, of Saint Silvanus the abbot and confessor. In the territory of Tornodorum, of blessed John the abbot. Of Lutrudis the virgin. On the same day, of Saint Salaberga, widow and abbess. She was born of noble parents in the suburb of Leuca. After recovering her sight through the intervention of Saint Eustasius the abbot, and after the death of the husband whom she had married at the command of King Dagobert, she first lived in her paternal inheritance in the suburb of Langres; then, at Lyon, having built a monastery and presiding over nearly three hundred servants of Christ, she died renowned for her life and miracles.”

MOLAN, in the text, after “they were crowned,” inserts in different type material from Ado:

> “But Victor the martyr was neither of that same legion nor a soldier, but a veteran who had already completed his military service. While traveling, he came upon these men, who were feasting everywhere in delight over the spoils of the martyrs. Invited by them to join their meal, and having learned from the rejoicing men the reason for their celebration, he rejected the feasters in disgust. They immediately seized and slaughtered him, and he was joined in honor to the other martyrs. But the bodies of the most blessed martyrs were revealed many years after their passion to Saint Theodore the bishop, and a basilica was honorably built in their honor.”

At the end it has the passage concerning Laudus, as often above.

Then:

> “At Laon-Clavato, the burial of Saint Salaberga the abbess, who, instructed in divine law and constantly devoted to vigils and prayers, led an illustrious life through the grace of virtues and miracles. In the territory of Tornodorum, of blessed John the abbot.”

Finally, in smaller type:

> “At Corbie, of Lutrudis, a religious virgin.”

The other editions abridge some things concerning Victor, but add concerning Emmeram what the first edition also inserts in italic type:

> “Why were all his limbs severed one by one?”

Moreover, these editions truncate and alter the announcement, again reading in italic type:

> “The crime of sexual misconduct was attributed to him.”

Then, in Roman type, that is, in the proper text:

> “and therefore the danger of death,”

and so forth. At the end:

> “At Laon-Clavato, the burial of Saint Salaberga,”

and so forth, as above. These editions treat Laudo or Laudus on the preceding day, as do several other manuscripts.

> “In the territory of Tornodorum,”

and so forth.

[Col. 0493]

In Gaul, in the city of Sion, at the place called Agaunum, the nativity of the holy martyrs of the Theban Legion, Maurice, Exuperius, Candidus, Victor, Innocentius, and Vitalis, with their 6,500 companions, who suffered for Christ under Maximian and were crowned most gloriously. At Bavaria, [Note: [Col. 0493D] In this article the words “of Saint Emmeram” have been erased and written over; likewise, whatever wording occurs between “sexual misconduct” and “in the territory.” Yet no trace of either erasure appears in the other manuscripts. But what correction is older than all the copies, and to whom should it be attributed except its author?—Bouillart.] of Saint Emmeram, bishop and martyr. He caused the crime of sexual misconduct committed by someone else to be attributed to him for Christ’s sake, and therefore patiently endured the danger of death. In the territory of Poitiers, of Saint Florentius the priest and confessor. Also, of Saint Silvanus the confessor, in the territory of Bourges.

**The ninth day before the Kalends. Day 23.**

[Note: [Col. 0497C]]

Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Greven, and Molan agree. Antwerp-Max., Leyden, Louvain, and Albergen also join them.

[Note: [Col. 0497D]]

Heriniensis wrote “of blessed Sosius” instead of “of Saint Sosius.” Antwerp-Major has *Sossii*. The place-name is written in various ways. Rosweyd and Molan have the best form, *Misenatae*; Heriniensis incorrectly has *Messeratae*; Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, and Greven have the form retained in the text. Rosweyd reads *ascendere* (“to ascend”) instead of *flammam exsurgere* (“for a flame to rise”). Pratensis and Antwerp-Major have *Theclae*. All the others have the simpler *Teclae*. I say nothing about such blemishes as *dyaconus*, *yconium*, and the like. Pratensis writes *Seleucia*, but the others generally, and better, have the form used in the text.

At the end there is a more significant variation: Pratensis and the two usual companions, Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, dissenting from all the others, read:

> “In the territory of the city of Avranches,”

whereas all the others, without exception, have:

> “In the territory of the city of Coutances,”

which we considered must be retained. See below in the *Observations*. Note, however, that Castellanus, otherwise the most accurate examiner of the Pratensis manuscript, did not indicate this difference from Molan’s edition among the others.

[Note: [Col. 0499A]]

We have already spoken sufficiently elsewhere about Sosius, the famous deacon of Misenum, on September 19, when Januarius was discussed; what was said there need not be repeated here. Bede, Rabanus, and Ado have the same eulogy, from which our author elegantly abridged his own summary. The *Small Roman Martyrology*, together with others, also announces Sosius on this day, in second place:

> “At Mesenata, of Sosius the deacon, a martyr of thirty years.”

Notker alone wrote:

> “Of Sosius the deacon,”

concerning whom one may read under the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October. Wandalbert praises him in his third verse:

> The Levite Sosius rightly shines with honor.

All the Martyrologies celebrate the most illustrious virgin Thecla—and, if one wishes, the protomartyr among virgins—and indeed the Hieronymian Martyrologies do so on various days, as Florentinius carefully notes in his annotations on this and the other days cited there. Whether the same disciple of the Apostle is everywhere being commemorated, or perhaps another woman—since there were several rivals in virtue—may be uncertain.

No Hieronymian copy speaks more simply than the most ancient one from Echternach, in which only this is read:

> “In the East, of Thecla.”

Florentinius’ text is somewhat fuller:

> “At Seleucia, the nativity of Thecla the virgin, who escaped being burned at Rome.”

Bede, and Rabanus from him, provide a brief but sufficiently polished eulogy, most of which our author transferred into his own little register. The *Small Roman Martyrology* uses its customary brevity:

> “And of Thecla the virgin, resting at Seleucia.”

Ado’s account is longer, extracted from the commonly circulated *Acts*; their reliability will be discussed elsewhere from Baronius and others. The well-known story of the ancient fabulist concerning the *Acts of Paul and Thecla* was long ago rejected, although I would not dare deny that other, sufficiently extensive narratives grew from it in Surius.

Yet even if we acknowledge that such sources are corrupt, the venerable authority of the holy Fathers has supplied so much material from elsewhere that a sequence of her life can be arranged from it, as Tillemont attempted, not unsuccessfully, in volume II, beginning on page 60.

Wandalbert alone among the Martyrologists seems to assert that she was crowned by a genuine martyrdom, when he sings:

> The ninth, Thecla, is drenched in rosy blood.

More probably this should be understood in a broader sense, and some infer this from the fact that the Church did not assign her a place in the Canon of the Mass. This is sufficient for our purpose.

Paternus, added by Usuard to the two preceding entries, is placed by Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, and Rosweyd not in the territory of Coutances but in that of Avranches, contrary to the uniform reading of the other Usuardine manuscripts:

> “In the territory of the city of Coutances,”

as it is also read in the present Roman Martyrology, where Baronius observes in his note that he was first bishop of Coutances.

Henschenius proves in his preliminary commentary on the *Acts of Saints Paternus and Scubilio*, April 16, that this distinguished man had here suffered a lapse of memory. There he also shows that our Paternus was precisely that bishop of Avranches who, because he died at the monastery of Sesciacum in the diocese of Coutances, was therefore designated “in the territory of the city of Coutances.” Thus we think Usuard read it, whatever may be objected by Pratensis with his two usual companions.

It is furthermore certain that Paternus died in peace on April 16, and so far I have found no reason why Usuard placed him on this day. Some also mention Linus, following, unless I am mistaken, Florus or Rabanus; from there the name passed into some of our manuscripts and into the Roman Martyrology, although Usuard treats him on November 26. But why was Pope Liberius omitted, when the Hieronymian Martyrology and Wandalbert commemorate him on this day, and Rabanus on the following day? Perhaps the reason will be assigned elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0499C]]

PULSANEN. In the first announcement the eulogy has been completely deleted. In the second it is pure. The third is absent.

ANTWERP, MAX.-LUBECK, UGHELLIAN, FLORENTIN, and several other manuscripts mention Pope Liberius today in these same words:

> “At Rome, of Saint Liberius the bishop.”

See the *Observations* above and Castellanus’ note.

MUNERAT, after the pure text, adds:

> “On the same day, of Paxentius the martyr, whose body is honored and venerated in the monastery of Saint Martin de Campis.”

You will note that this phrasing is peculiar to this manuscript.

UTRECHT, ALBERGEN, and DANIC begin:

> “At Rome, the nativity of blessed Linus the pope. After he had governed the Roman Church for twelve years as the first after the Apostle Peter, he was crowned by martyrdom and buried in the Vatican.”

See the *Observations*.

CENTULEN.:

> “In Campania, of Saint Sosius the deacon and martyr. On the same day, of Saint Thecla the virgin, resting at Seleucia. At Beauvais, of Saint Geremar the abbot.”

See the Roman Martyrology on the following day.

BRUSSELS begins as follows:

> “The nativity of Thecla the virgin, resting at Seleucia; she had been instructed by the blessed Apostle Paul after coming from the city of Iconium. When her mother saw that she was a Christian and rejecting marriage, she accused her. In her confession of Christ she overcame fire and wild beasts, and after many struggles, coming to Seleucia for the instruction of many, she rested in peace with the double crown of virginity and martyrdom. At Rome, of blessed Linus the pope.”

It follows with the first and last entries, namely Sosius and Paternus, in pure form.

HAGENOYEN gathers much material concerning Thecla, of which I give part here:

> “At Seleucia, the burial of Saint Thecla the virgin, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle. She was born in the city of Iconium. Because she abandoned her bridegroom and adhered to Paul, her own mother accused her of being a Christian; therefore she was thrown into the fire and was not harmed. She wished to cut her hair so that she might live with Paul, but he forbade her. Again, because she refused to marry, she was thrown to wild beasts at Antioch, but was not consumed. Then she was cast into a pit full of serpents, but when she prayed, they died. Again she was thrown into the fire, but was not burned. Then she was tied to a lioness, and so forth.”

It follows with:

> “Also at Rome, of Liberius the bishop.”

The passage concerning Sosius is fairly pure. There is nothing concerning Paternus.

AQUICINCT adds at the end:

> “At Rome, of Saint Liberius the bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT.:

> “Of Thecla the virgin. Of Zozius the deacon and martyr, with his bishop Januarius. Of Paternus the bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0500D] In the Vatican manuscript no. 5949, Paternus is absent.

LUGDUNEN places here:

> “Of Victor, Innocentius, … with their companions, 6,066.”

See the Thebans, September 22.

BIZUNTIC.:

> “Also the feast of Saint Vincent the martyr, when his most sacred body was transferred from Spain to Gaul and decently buried in the monastery called Castrum.”

LUXOVIEN.:

> “On the same day, the reinterment at the Middle Monastery of the body of blessed Boniface the martyr from the Theban Legion.”

CABILONEN.:

> “The discovery of the body of blessed Vincent the Levite and martyr.”

See Bizuntic.

The Lubeck-Cologne edition begins:

> “At Rome, the nativity of blessed Linus, pope and martyr. After blessed Peter the apostle, he was the first to govern the Roman Church, for twelve years, three months, and twelve days, and was crowned by martyrdom. At the command of blessed Peter, he established that a woman should enter the church with her head veiled; he was also buried beside the body of blessed Peter the apostle in the Vatican.”

At the end of the entry for Sosius it adds these three words:

> “in the time of the emperor Diocletian.”

The eulogy of Thecla is somewhat interpolated here and there; in the last announcement it is fairly pure.

BELIN has altered the order of the announcements. First:

> “In the city of Iconium, of Saint Thecla the virgin,”

and so forth. Second, concerning Paternus, purely. Then Sosius. At the end:
