> “On the same day, at Rome, of Saint Linus the pope and martyr, who after Peter was the first to govern the Roman Church for twelve years and was crowned by martyrdom and buried in the Vatican, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.”

See the following *Auctaria*.

GREVEN.:

> “At Rome, of Linus the pope and martyr; his passion is given here, although his feast is more solemnly celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, on which day he is said to have been translated. At Rome, of Liberius the bishop and confessor. Of Adamnan the bishop. Of Constantius, bishop of the city of Aquino, concerning whom blessed Gregory relates in the third book of the *Dialogues* that he was renowned for the spirit of prophecy. Of Stabilio the confessor, a disciple of blessed Paternus the bishop.”

Note that Greven assigns Paternus to April 16, but under the erroneous title “bishop of Poitiers.” For the rest, see what is said in the *Observations* and, more fully, in the *Acts* for April 16, where you will find the true name of the disciple.

GREVEN continues:

> “On the same day at Ancona, of Saint Constantius the confessor, concerning whom blessed Gregory I relates in the *Dialogues* that this same man of God, utterly despising earthly things, burned with all the effort of his mind for heavenly things. When the oil with which he lit the lamps had run out in the church where he served as a caretaker, he filled the lamps themselves with water and, bringing fire, set them alight; thus the water burned as though there had been oil in the lamps.”

See Castellanus’ note.

> “Of Adumianus the abbot.”

Read “Adamnan.”

> “Of Digna and Emerita, virgins and martyrs.”

These belong to the preceding day. See the Roman Martyrology.

MOLAN.:

> “On the same day, at Rome, of Saint Linus the pope and martyr, who after…”

and so forth, as in Belin above.

> “Also at Rome, of Saint Liberius the confessor.”

How carefully this is stated, when Wandalbert openly declares:

> Liberius, pope, shall speak throughout the Roman city.

Then:

> “On the same day, of Paxentius the martyr, whose body is honored and venerated,”

and so forth, as in Munerat.

> “At Gembloux, the elevation of the body of our holy patron Guibert, confessor of Christ, renowned for miracles.”

He adds in smaller type:

> “The second assumption of Saint Mary the Virgin.”

He reports exactly the same material concerning Constantius of Aquino and Constantius of Ancona from Gregory’s *Dialogues*. Finally:

> “In Scotland, in the monastery of Iona, of Saint Adamnan, abbot of that place, famous for holiness and learning, concerning whom Bede speaks in book V, chapters 10 and 22.”

The other editions place Linus before the Usuardine text. After “virgin,” they insert in different type concerning Thecla “the first martyr,” and after “Seleucia”:

> “with the double crown of virginity and martyrdom.”

At the end:

> “Also at Rome, of Saint Liberius, pope and confessor.”

Concerning Paxentius the martyr, they reproduce the material from Munerat and concerning the elevation of the body of Saint Guibert of Gembloux, as above in the earlier edition. They also add, in smaller type, the second assumption of Saint Mary the Virgin.

[Col. 0497]

In Campania, the nativity of blessed Sosius, deacon of the city of Mesenata. Once, while reading the Gospel in the church of the aforesaid city, in the presence of Bishop Januarius, the same bishop suddenly saw a flame rising from his head and declared that he would become a martyr. After not many days, when he was thirty years old, he suffered martyrdom by beheading together with that same bishop. On the same day, of Saint Thecla the virgin from the city of Iconium, who in her confession of Christ conquered fire and wild beasts and, after many struggles, coming to Seleucia for the instruction of many, rested in peace. In the territory of the city of Coutances, of Saint Paternus the bishop and confessor.

**The eighth day before the Kalends. Day 24.**

[Note: [Col. 0501]]

Only Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, and Rosweyd are pure.

[Note: [Col. 0501C]]

Enough has been said elsewhere about *Joannes* and *Johannes*. In our Pratensis copy one reads simply *Augustodunum*, but Castellanus explicitly notes that it has:

> “And at Augustodunum,”

as Heriniensis and the others also read it; we have therefore thought that form should be retained, although *et* is absent in Antwerp-Major and both particles are absent in Rosweyd.

Antwerp-Major has *Andocii* instead of *Anaochii*. Of the four manuscripts cited, only Rosweyd writes *Tirsi*; the others have the form in the text, and none has *Thirsi*. Concerning Polycarp, see elsewhere.

All have “under Aurelian” after Bede and Ado; but Usuard corrected this chronological indication elsewhere, and in the *Acts* we shall show that it should more probably be rejected. Heriniensis alone substitutes “under the emperor” for “under the prince.” In Antwerp-Major *conbusti* is incorrectly written for *combusti*.

[Note: [Col. 0501C]]

I shall complete all the necessary observations in a few words by saying that our little register was copied word for word from Ado, and that Ado, like Rabanus, took his material from Bede. There is this difference between Bede and Ado: Ado, after “they were struck,” repeats unnecessarily:

> “and thus they completed their martyrdom most gloriously on the eighth day before the Kalends of October,”

whereas Bede adds more appropriately:

> “At that time Symphorian, who was twenty years old and who later suffered martyrdom, was always engaged in vigils and prayers.”

We have said enough about this Symphorian, for our purposes, on his feast day, August 22.

The kinship of the martyrs of Autun extends more broadly. You will find it explained at length in the *Acts of the Three Brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus*, January 17. There it is said that Benignus the priest—whom we must treat on November 1—was sent into Gaul with these holy men, and also with Andochius the priest, Thyrsus the deacon, and Felix, by Polycarp. There, with far greater probability, Felix is considered to have been the last of them, a native layman and merchant who received the crown of martyrdom together with the apostles whom he had welcomed.

I have nothing to add concerning the *Acts of the Three Brothers*. As for the authenticity of the manuscripts that exist among us concerning Andochius and his two companions celebrated today, it will be enough to quote them, when there is more leisure and opportunity to examine them carefully.

Meanwhile Florentinius shows that they were also inserted, or rather added, to the Hieronymian Martyrologies. There one reads:

> “In Gaul, in the city of Autun, at the village of Sedelocus, the nativity of Saints Andochius, Thyrsus, and Felix the martyr.”

Several Usuardine manuscripts of what we call middling age used almost the same wording, not badly. On this matter see the *Observations* for January 17. The *Small Roman Martyrology* says nothing about them; its author had certainly never seen the *Acts of Warnacharius* or anything similar. Notker contracted Ado or Rabanus more than usual. I shall append Wandalbert’s verse at the end.

Concerning the Conception of Saint John the Baptist, which occupies the first place in our text, this one brief observation must be made: it is recorded in absolutely all the ancient Martyrologies and has always been held in veneration from the earliest times, in both the Eastern and the Western Church.

Florentinius admits that he does not know why such a celebration was omitted from the revised Roman Martyrology. Whether he achieves this through his conjectures I leave to the reader’s judgment; I urge the reader to consult the *Exercise* of Florentinius appended to this day, concerning the office of John the Baptist, who had not yet been established as the Forerunner, and concerning the place of his conception and birth, where he discusses Machaerus, at which place some Hieronymian manuscripts mark the conception of the Baptist.

If this is not sufficient, let Papebrochius be consulted, since he has most carefully illuminated all these matters in volume IV of June, chapter 2, §§ 2 and 3, beginning on page 701. Rosweyd’s note in *The Feasts of the Apostles*, page 223, may also be consulted.

Here now are the promised verses of Wandalbert:

> The eighth, John sanctifies, conceived in a barren womb,  
> and Andochius, a holy martyr and priest;  
> Thyrsus and Felix accompany him with equal devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0503A]]

PULSANEN is pure up to “they were crowned,” but everything else is lacking.

ANTWERP and MAX.-LUBECK are good in the first announcement. They continue:

> “In the territory of the city of Autun, at the fortress of Sedelocus, of Saint Andochius.”

At the end:

> “At Clermont, the burial of Saint Rusticus the bishop.”

MAX.-LUBECK has “Rusacus.”

MUNERAT adds to the text:

> “At the fortress of Blois, of Saint Solennis the bishop and confessor.”

This occurs in the Roman Martyrology on the following day. See there our variant readings.

GREVEN also adds, and indeed as part of the text: [Col. 0503B] “Likewise, Saint Solemnis, bishop.”

MOLANUS in the first edition omits the Conception of Saint John the Baptist, as BARONIUS also did. But in later editions he restored that announcement.

ANTWERP-MAXIMILIAN, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN are similar to ANTWERP-MAXIMILIAN and LÜBECK, differing from them chiefly in this: in the Auctaria they omit the word *depositio* (“burial”) concerning Rusticus and add the title “confessor.”

ALBERGEN and DANICUS lack the first announcement; in the remainder they agree with the last-mentioned witnesses.

CENTULEN in the first is pure. Then: “At Augustodunum, Saint Judochius, priest and martyr; Thyrsus, deacon; and Felix, who under the emperor Aurelian were gloriously crowned.”

BRUSSELS, pure in the first, in the second has the same beginning as ANTWERP and MAXIMILIAN-LÜBECK, etc., though at the end it is somewhat transposed. Then: “At Arvernis, Saint Rusticus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, [Col. 0503C] in the territory of Beauvais, Saint Gummarus [it intends Geremarus], abbot.”

HAGENOY: “The Conception of Saint John the Baptist, which took place after the completion of the priesthood of Zachariah, his father.” In the Augustodunensian material it is somewhat interpolated. Then: “In the territory of the city of Constance, Saint Patrinus [for Paternus], bishop and confessor.” See the preceding day. “In the district of Poitiers, Saint Florentius, priest and confessor.” Concerning him he dealt again above, on 22 September. “At Arvernis, the burial of Saint Rusticus, bishop and confessor. Likewise, Saint Silvatus, confessor.” Or was it Silvanus, concerning whom he also wrote above on the 22nd? “In Hungary, Saint Gerard, bishop and martyr.”

AQUICINCT omits the Conception of Saint John the Baptist; otherwise it is pure.

DAVERON: “The burial of blessed Solemnis, bishop of Chartres, a man of magnificent holiness and renowned for miracles.”

AMIENS, after John’s Conception, adds: [Col. 0503D] “On the same day, the vigil of the most glorious bishop and martyr of Christ, Firminus.”

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT: “The Conception of Saint John the Baptist. Solemnis, bishop and confessor.”

THE SWEDISH REGINA manuscript, designated no. 428: “At Beauvais, the burial of Saint Geremarus, confessor.”

[Col. 0504A] UGHELLI: “At Arvernis, the burial of Rusticus, bishop.”

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, the dedication of the church of the Holy Trinity at Norwich. In the territory of Beauvais, Saint Germanus, abbot.” For Geremarus.

FLORENTINE: “In the borders of Germany, the passion of the holy martyrs who suffered for Christ in the time of Maximian, as is related in the Acts of Saint Domninus.”

MONT-SAINT: “In Gaul, in the city of Augustodunum, at the village of Sedulum, the feast of Saints Andochius,” etc.

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION. After “Baptist” it adds: “the Lord’s Forerunner.” In the Augustodunensian material it is almost similar to [Col. 0504B] ANTWERP, etc., above. At the end: “At Arvernis, Saint Rusticus, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN begins: “At Augustodunum,” etc., purely. Then: “At Arvernis, the burial of Saint Rusticus, bishop. Likewise, in Hungary, Saint Gerard, bishop and martyr. Likewise, the Conception of Saint John the Baptist.” This transposition of the Conception misled PAPEBROCHIUS in the cited passage, in the observations where he says that Belin was the first to omit this feast—namely, because he did not find it at the beginning of the calendar entry. A second edition of Belin adds: “In the territory of Beauvais, Saint Germanus, abbot.” See above.

GREVEN: “In Pannonia, or Hungary, Saint Gerard, bishop and martyr, who, according to the Catalogue, suffered on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. Rupert, bishop and martyr. In Chalcedon, forty-nine holy martyrs, who, together with blessed Euphemia, were handed over to Priscus the proconsul for the faith of Christ and won the palm of martyrdom. Fymbertus, bishop. At Arvernis, the burial [Col. 0504C] of Saint Rusticus, bishop and confessor. Genianus, abbot. Epigenia, virgin and abbess, and Euphemia her mother, concerning whom it is related in the Acts of Saint Matthew the Apostle. Rosa, virgin.”

MOLANUS: “At Arvernis, the burial of Saint Rusticus, bishop. Likewise, in Hungary, Saint Gerard, bishop and martyr. Likewise, the Conception of Saint John the Baptist. In the territory of Beauvais, Saint Germanus, abbot. At Cambrai, the translation of Saint Gaugericus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the burial of Solemnis, bishop. One day, when he encountered a man blind and deaf from birth, he embraced him and kissed him on the neck, and immediately restored him to health. He was also bishop of the people of Chartres and regenerated King Louis, together with three hundred and seventy nobles, in the sacred font; and thus, after this saint of God had spent three Olympiads in the episcopate, he departed to the Lord. And Saint Rupert, confessor”; then, in a different type: “the translation of the bishop of Worms and Salzburg.” Concerning the later editions, I have already said that in them the Conception of Saint John the Baptist was restored, where it is inserted into the text in a different type as: “the glorious Prophet and Forerunner.” At the end, concerning Rusticus and Gerard, as above. “In the territory of Beauvais, Saint Germarus, abbot. At Cambrai, the elevation of Saint Gaugericus, bishop and confessor.” See above, 11 August.]

[Col. 0501]

The Conception of Saint John the Baptist. And at Augustodunum, the feast of Saint Andochius, priest, Thyrsus, deacon, and Felix, who, sent from the East by Bishop Polycarp to teach Gaul, were gloriously crowned under the emperor Aurelian. For after being beaten with scourges, suspended all day at the end with their hands inverted, and cast into the fire without being burned, at last their necks were struck with rods.

VII Kal. Day 25. [Note: [Col. 0505]

Among the pure witnesses, only Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus are numbered.]

[Note: [Col. 0505A]

I wrote *Emaus*, as the manuscripts commonly have it, although some prefer *Emmaus*. Some read “Lupus, bishop and anchorite,” or “anachorite,” but Molanus and others after Ado more correctly have *ex anachoreta*, “from an anchorite.” Likewise, following the same Ado, Molanus writes *Herculanus*, not *Herculianus*. The principal and more difficult variation remains concerning the announcement of Saint Solemnis, or, as the manuscripts write it, *Sollempnis*. It is certain that this belongs not to this day but to the preceding day, as Bollandus correctly observes on 4 February, in connection with the Life of Saint Aventinus, and as others also observe. On the preceding day we excluded Muneratus and Greven from the pure witnesses because in that announcement they differed from all the rest, although, if it is to be included, it seems that it should be assigned to that day.

The question is whether Usuard placed Solemnis on this day, and whether he was not rather added by someone else. Molanus, I think, perceived this, for he reported him on neither day. But Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and Belin take the opposite position; in their manuscripts he is most explicitly placed last: “Likewise, Saint Solemnis or Solennius, bishop.” [Col. 0506A]

Nevertheless, I am compelled to think that this is not Usuardine, especially because Castellanus, the most careful examiner of the Pratensis manuscript, observed that in the first hand only the announcement of Saint Aunarius had been placed last; it was subsequently erased, and then rewritten in smaller characters so that the other announcement of Saint Solemnis could be added. The fact that Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and also Aquicinct have the same reading is not surprising, since they frequently derive from the same source.

Only the authority of the Herinien manuscript would restrain me, if it too were not fuller at this point. As for Belin, nearly every day his Auctaria are so abundant that he rarely appears uncorrupted. Thus I judge the following more probable: if anyone wishes to claim Solemnis for Usuard, I shall readily yield to the arguments; meanwhile, let me prefer Muneratus, [Col. 0506B] Greven, and especially Molanus to the other manuscripts here. Concerning Solemnis, see Rabanus on 24 September. Bollandus indicates, in the passage cited above on 4 February concerning Aventinus, etc., that his Acts are not sufficiently reliable.]

[Note: [Col. 0505B]

There is nothing concerning Cleophas in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, or Wandalbert. The first to record him was the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*, in these words: “Cleophas, to whom the Lord appeared on the road after the Resurrection.” Ado prefixes in his Martyrology: “The feast of the blessed,” and Notker described him in almost the same way. Usuard’s elogium, however, is contracted word for word from the *Feasts of the Apostles*. So far I have not discovered on what authority Ado’s assertion of his martyrdom rests.

Others, with Tillemont, volume I, pages 366, 459, and 622, examine his kinship or relationship with Christ the Savior; we too have dealt with this elsewhere and shall discuss it more fully in its proper place. What the cited Tillemont relates from Luke, chapter 24, is indubitable, page 368.

Concerning Firminus, Rabanus reads: “The feast of Saint Firminus the martyr.” Wandalbert writes:

> The people of Amiens shine through Firminus the martyr.

Florus records more. Mosander attributes him to Ado. Yet, unless I am greatly mistaken, Usuard had no other guide than the Acts themselves. Although they may not be wholly genuine, it will nevertheless be shown in due time that they were weighty and ancient for their period.

Much has been debated, formerly and most recently, even amid the shadows, concerning one or several translations of this Firminus and of another confessor bearing the same name; these matters too will then be examined more carefully.

The burial of Lupus is recorded on the preceding day by the Hieronymian Martyrologies, being assigned by the Corbie manuscript to Lyon and by the Echternach manuscript to Augustodunum. Ado seems to have followed the former when he correctly writes: “At Lyon, Saint Lupus, bishop, formerly an anchorite.” Thus you can already see from what source Our Author obtained his material. Wandalbert sings this elogium of him:

> Lupus, the bishop, returns for the seventh time to the walls of Lyon,  
> A memorable shepherd to the devoted city.

His deeds can be gathered from what Severtius set out at considerable length in his *Historical Chronology*, beginning on page 84, and from the other sources he cites.

Herculanus, mentioned in the Acts of Saint Alexander, bishop—concerning whom we dealt above on 21 September—and mentioned by Ado on 26 November, appears to have been placed on this day merely at Usuard’s discretion, since all the other ancient Martyrologists pass him over. Here you will also notice that Our Author improperly, or at least without evidence, gives him the title “soldier,” whereas Ado merely calls him “a young man in the service of Antoninus.”

Aunarius follows, or, as Castellanus writes, Aunacharius. He was first recorded by Usuard. More concerning his Acts is scattered through the first volume of Labbe’s *Library*, especially on pages 419 and 528; our own Auxerre compilation, likewise a manuscript and drawn for the most part from Labbe for this section, may also be consulted, page 53.

Up to this point all the manuscripts of better authority agree, so that there can be no doubt about the genuine text. What is to be thought of Solemnis or Selenne has already been discussed sufficiently above.]

[Note: [Col. 0505D]

PRATENSIS, ANTWERP-MAJOR, and ROSWEYD have Solemnis as we stated above. In Rosweyd there is additionally: “In the monastery of Gleste, Saint Ceolfrith.”

HERINIEN inserts at the second place its own entry: “On the same day, Saint Principius, bishop of Soissons, brother of blessed Remigius.” At the end, concerning Solemnis, as above.

PULSANEN is fairly pure in the first part; in the second it truncates the elogium and then immediately adds, together with the preceding witnesses: [Col. 0506D] “Likewise, Saint Solemnis, bishop.” Everything else is absent.

ANTWERP and MAXIMILIAN-LÜBECK omit the announcement of Aunarius and, correctly, that of Solemnis as well. Instead of “Alexander, bishop,” they have “Alexander, pope.”

BELIN also reads “Alexander, pope,” and at the end: “Likewise, Saint Solemnius, bishop.” A second edition reads more distinctly: “Likewise, at Blois,” etc.

ANTWERP-MAXIMILIAN, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN write “Alexander, pope”; they omit Aunarius and have at the end: [Col. 0507A] “At Chartres, the feast of Saint Solemnis, bishop and confessor.”

UTRECHT, ALBERGEN, and DANICUS differ from the immediately preceding witnesses in adding the following concerning Solemnis: “He restored sight, hearing, and the use of speech to a man blind, deaf, and mute from birth. He also initiated King Clovis of the Franks and three hundred and sixty-four persons with him in the water of sacred baptism.”

CENTULEN: “The feast of blessed Cleophas, who was one of the seventy-two disciples. At Amiens, the passion of Saint Firminus the martyr, the first bishop of that city. At Lyon, Saint Lupus, bishop, formerly an anchorite. On the same day, Saint Herculanus the soldier. At Auxerre, Saint Aunarius, bishop and confessor. Likewise, Saint Solemnis, bishop. In the monastery of Caesarea, Saint Robert, bishop and confessor.”

BRUSSELS begins with Firminus, fairly purely. Then it has Cleophas. Next it has Herculanus, whom it calls Arculanus. It continues: “At Chartres, the feast of Saint [Col. 0507B] Solemnis, bishop and confessor. He restored sight, hearing, and the use of speech to a man blind, deaf, and mute from birth. At Lyon, the burial of Saint Lupus, bishop, formerly an anchorite. At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Januarius [for Aunarius], bishop and confessor. And on the same day, Saints Sergius and Bacchius.” Read *Bacchus* and see 7 October.

HAGENOY, concerning Cleophas, develops the evangelical history at greater length. In the entry for Firminus it is fairly pure. Likewise in that for Lupus. Then: “At Chartres, Saint Solemnis, bishop. He restored sight, hearing, and the sense of smell to a man blind, deaf, and mute from birth.” It continues: “But King Clovis of the Franks, and six hundred and sixty-four persons with him, with the water,” etc. The entry for Herculanus and Aunarius follows with a fairly pure text.

AQUICINCT has Sebastianus instead of Rictiovarus; at the end, concerning Solemnis, as above.

AMIENS: “In the city of Amiens, the feast of Saint [Col. 0507C] Firminus, martyr and first bishop of that city.”

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT is more abbreviated on this day and reads: “Cleophas, disciple of Christ. Firminus, bishop and martyr. Principius, bishop of Soissons, brother of blessed Remigius, bishop.”

The Swedish Regina manuscript, designated no. 130, also has: “Likewise, Saint Solemnis, bishop.”

In the VATICAN manuscript designated no. 5949, the last two announcements are absent.

In the UGHELLI manuscript Aunarius is absent here, as above in ANTWERP-MAXIMILIAN-LÜBECK.

ALTEMPS: “In Glasconia, Saint Ceolfrith, abbot and confessor. Likewise, Saint Fausta, virgin. Likewise, Saint Solennius.” The same person as Solemnis.

[Col. 0508A] FLORENTINE: “On the same day, Saint Solemnis, bishop.”

CAUDIAC: “At Magno Loco, Saint Georgia, virgin.” See this same manuscript cited on 15 February, where it records the translation of this Georgia.

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION: “In the territory of Jerusalem, at the castle called Emmaus, the feast of Saint Cleophas, who was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ and who, on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, was going with another disciple to that same castle, where the Lord appeared to them on the road. They also say that he was killed there and in the same house in which he had prepared a table for the Lord, for confessing him, etc. At Cologne, the ordination of Saint Cunibert, archbishop of that city and confessor. In the city of the people of Amiens, blessed Firminus, bishop and martyr. Under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian and the governor Rictiovarus, after various threats of torture, he was secretly beheaded at night in prison, and thus completed his martyrdom. Faustinianus, who had been baptized by him, seized and buried his body; out of love and reverence [Col. 0508B] for the holy martyr, he named his only son Firminus. The son eventually advanced in learning and holiness, became a teacher of all the churches of Europe, and was ordained bishop of the aforementioned church of Amiens.”

In the entries for Lupus and Herculanus it is almost pure. Concerning Solemnis it has the same as UTRECHT and ALBERGEN above. “At Auxerre, Saint Amantius.” It undoubtedly intended to write Aunarius.

GREVEN: “In Asia, Saints Eucarpus, Bardumanus, and twenty-six others. At Soissons, Saint Principius, bishop and confessor, brother of blessed Remigius. Zacharias, bishop. In Ireland, Barrea, bishop and confessor. Germanus, abbot and confessor. At Cologne, the ordination to the episcopate of Saint Cunibert, bishop and confessor of that city. Likewise, Gerard of blessed memory, confessor of the Order of Friars Minor, a most devout man.”

MOLANUS: “Likewise, Saint Solemnis, bishop and confessor, at the castle of Blois. On the same day, Saint Principius, [Col. 0508C] bishop of Soissons, brother of blessed Remigius.” This appears to have been taken from HERINIEN. Other editions read: “Likewise, at Blois, Saint Solemnis, bishop. He kissed a man blind and deaf from birth, and immediately restored him to health. He was also bishop of the people of Chartres and regenerated King Louis, together with three hundred and seventy nobles, in the sacred font. Thus this saint of God, after spending three Olympiads in the episcopate, departed to the Lord. On the same day, Saint Principius,” etc., as in the earlier edition. “At Cusance, in the territory of Besançon, the burial of blessed Hermenfredus, abbot and confessor. In Glasconia, the burial of Saint Ceolfrith, abbot and confessor.” See Castellanus concerning both.]

[Col. 0503]

The feast of blessed Cleophas, whom they say was killed by the Jews at the castle of Emmaus, in the same house in which he had prepared a table for the Lord, for confessing him, and was buried there in glorious memory. In the city of Amiens, blessed Firminus, bishop, who under the governor Rictiovarus, after various tortures, underwent martyrdom by decapitation. At Lyon, the burial of Saint Lupus, bishop, formerly an anchorite. On the same day, Saint Herculanus [Col. 0505] the soldier, who is mentioned in the passion of Bishop Alexander. At Auxerre, [Note: [Col. 0505A] Castellanus correctly observed that the announcement of Aunarius had been erased and rewritten in smaller characters so that Saint Solemnis could be added. But this correction is by the same period and author as the other three that we have already seen this month. For the manuscript of Dervensis agrees with the Herinien manuscript and records Saint Solemnis. The correction, therefore, belongs to both autographs and is consequently either older than, or contemporary with, the first exemplar. BOUILLART.] Saint Aunarius, bishop and confessor. [Bouillart adds: “Likewise, Saint Solemnis, bishop.”]

VI Kal. Day 26. [Note: [Col. 0507]

The pure witnesses are Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0507D]

Here Tournai again appears among the pure manuscripts; it had been empty from 8 August up to this day because several leaves had either been torn out or at least lost. Moreover, that manuscript, as well as Antwerp-Major and Greven, writes *Cipriani*; the others more correctly have the form found in the text. Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and Molanus appropriately add *verum* after “with his magical arts”; but from the other manuscripts I judge that Usuard did not write it that way. Perhaps, following Bede, he would more correctly have written *with his magics*, since Bede genuinely reads *magiis suis*, while Rabanus simply has *magis suis*. For *dementare*, Antwerp-Major has *temptare*. The same manuscript omits *a* before *Christianis*. Rosweyd forms the final announcement as follows: “At the city of Alba, the feast of Saint Senator.” But whichever way it is written, the true location cannot easily be determined. Muneratus adds the title “bishop” to him at the end.]

[Note: [Col. 0509A]

There are many things that make the history of our most celebrated martyrs Cyprian and Justina confused and perplexing. It has been published from Metaphrastes by Lipomanus, Surius, and others in such a way that it very plainly confuses that illustrious Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, with our Cyprian, more probably an Antiochene—an identification commonly attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus.

The praise of the empress Eudocia departs somewhat from that confusion; still more so does the confession attributed to Cyprian himself, whether genuine or, as others think, spurious. The writers of their deeds do not agree sufficiently either about the time of their martyrdom or about many other circumstances, as Baronius admits.

Tillemont’s work deserves praise here: he carefully arranged what is credible and probable in volume V, beginning on page 329, and some of it will be useful in due course.

Turning now to our text, I first note that Cyprian and Justina are entirely omitted from the Hieronymian copies. The *Little Roman Martyrology* mentions them as follows: “At Rome, Cyprian the bishop, who suffered at Antioch and was transferred to Rome with the martyr Justina.” The Viennese Martyrologist composed a lengthy narrative, but one in which Metaphrastes’ confusion is avoided so successfully that the truth of the whole of his Acts, even as edited by Surius, seems capable of being preserved without serious difficulty.

Our Author, however, abbreviated from it those features concerning the bishop and the man who became a noble teacher, so that, unless I am mistaken, we must understand him to be clearly designating the Carthaginian Cyprian. Hence it should not seem surprising if the revisers of the Roman Martyrology wished to remove those details.

Nevertheless, Usuard wisely took care not to assert that Justina and Cyprian alike suffered many things for Christ under Diocletian and were finally martyred under the emperor Claudius, as is read in Bede and Rabanus. The fact that both are assigned to Antioch and Nicomedia must be explained by saying that their passion began in the first place and was completed in the last.

Let us leave the remaining matters to their proper place, adding here only Wandalbert’s metrical encomium:

> On the sixth day, the martyr Cyprian rejoices, and the blessed virgin Justina,  
> Through whom he came to know the kingdom of God,  
> After at last abandoning his mad arts and his rages.

Senator of Alba—whether martyr, confessor, or, if you prefer, bishop—provided Baronius and Florentinius with much material for conjecture. He seems to be known to no ancient Martyrologists except the Hieronymian ones, in which I read: “And at Alba, the feast of Saint Senator.” What was subsequently added by someone connected with Ado is amply demonstrated by Mosander’s asterisk and Rosweyd’s appendix.

I have scarcely any doubt that Our Author received him from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, while leaving the boundaries equally uncertain, so that even among scholars there is not yet complete agreement about where that city of Alba, or *Albanum*, should be sought.

Whether Castellanus found him successfully in Scotland against the opinions of others, as his note to the universal Martyrology indicates, will be considered later. Meanwhile, it is entirely certain that Usuard placed him as he appears in our index.]

[Note: [Col. 0509B]

PULSANEN is pure in the first part but lacks the second announcement, as it is often mutilated.

ANTWERP, MAXIMILIAN-LÜBECK, BELIN, UGHELLI, ANTWERP-MAXIMILIAN, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANICUS append to the pure text at the end: “At Rome, Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor.” His burial is recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies “on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus,” in the manner in which confessors are usually designated. Florentinius may be consulted, as he cites several who assert for him the martyr’s crown.

In any case, Eusebius passes from the Hieronymian Martyrologies into Bede and Ado, and even into the Auctaria of Usuard, as is clear from our most trustworthy manuscripts cited for the text. Concerning Eusebius the pope, see the Usuardine Auctaria for 2 October.

CENTULEN: “At Antioch, the feast of the holy martyrs Cyprian, bishop, and Justina, virgin, who suffered under the emperor Diocletian. At the city of Alba, Saint Enathor.” Thus the manuscript reads, but traces remain of an erased initial *S*, so that it should be read “Senator.”

BRUSSELS: “The feast of the holy martyrs Cyprian, once a magician, bishop, and Justina, virgin, and Theognitus. Justina, after suffering many things for Christ, converted Cyprian himself, when he was a magician and was attempting through his magical arts to drive her mad and turn her away from the worship of Christ. Later, when he had become a bishop and a noble teacher, he was crowned with martyrdom together with her under the emperor Diocletian. Their bodies were afterward, etc. At Rome, Saint Eusebius, bishop. At the city of Alba, Saint Senator.”

HAGENOY: “At Antioch, Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr, and Justina, virgin and martyr. This Cyprian was formerly an enchanter and magician; by his arts he drove many mad. For when he was a boy of seven years, his parents consecrated him to the devil, and he long abstained from meat, fish, wine, and sexual intercourse so that he might serve the devil more fully. In short, he did every evil that he could devise in order to please the demons more, and in some evils he surpassed the demons themselves in wickedness; he was himself a cause of sin to many Christians.

When he could not incline the virgin Justina to consent to him, although he sent many demons against her, he asked one of them why he accomplished nothing. The demon replied that Christ would not permit it. Cyprian then said to him: ‘Is Christ, therefore, greater than we are?’ The demon answered: ‘He is greater than all creatures.’ Cyprian therefore despised the devil and was baptized. Later he himself performed miracles, and after a year he was ordained a priest. After sixteen years, when Anthimus, bishop of Antioch, had died, he himself was ordained bishop. He converted many to the faith and greatly strengthened the faithful in it; he also placed Justina in charge of several virgins in a monastery.

Then he was arrested together with Justina and imprisoned. Afterward he was hung on the rack and torn with iron claws. Next they were struck on the face and scourged with raw sinews. Then they were placed in a frying pan filled with burning pitch, wax, and fat, in which they praised God without injury. The governor Eucolinus then sent them to the emperor Claudius at Nicomedia. He ordered them to be beheaded, and their bodies were transferred to Rome and afterward to Piacenza.

At the city of Alba, Saint Senator, martyr. In Greater Armenia, Saint Ripsima, queen and virgin. When she rejected the marriage proposal of King Tiridates of Armenia out of love for Christ, she was killed, together with several other virgins, by unheard-of tortures.”

It indicates Ripsima, concerning whom see Castellanus’s note and the Roman Martyrology on 29 September. Concerning Eusebius, see above.

AQUICINCT at the end: “At Rome, Saint Eusebius.”

MATRICULA-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT: “Justina and Cyprian, martyrs; he was first a magician but was converted through Saint Justina, the virgin.” The same hand adds in the margin: “Their relics are kept in the church of Saint John at Utrecht.”

In the VATICAN manuscript, designated no. 5949, Senator is absent. It adds: “At Rome, Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor. The feast of Saint Januarius, priest of Antioch.” I know many Januarii, but who this Januarius, priest of Antioch, may be, I should like to be told.

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION prefixes a rather remarkable announcement, in these words: “At Cologne, in the church of Saint Maximianus, the discovery and translation of Saint Gorgonius, bishop and martyr, and his companions. This Gorgonius was the confessor of the king and queen of Spain and belonged to the company of the eleven thousand holy virgins.” Concerning Cyprian and Justina, after he had become a teacher, it writes: “He underwent martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian, before the judge Eutellius. When these two martyrs were being led to the city of Nicomedia by order of the emperor, after enduring many punishments, in order to be beheaded there, a certain Christian joined them, returning from pilgrimage, named Theognitus. As he kissed the necks of the saints, he too was beheaded together with them. Their bodies were taken at night by sailors onto their ship and carried to Rome. At the city of Alba, Saint Senator, confessor.” Concerning Eusebius, see above.

GREVEN: “Likewise, at Cologne, in the church of Saint Maximinus, the discovery and elevation of Saint Gorgonius, bishop and martyr. He was the confessor of the king of Spain and belonged to the company of the eleven thousand virgins. [Col. 0512A] At Rome, Eusebius, bishop and confessor. At Arvernis, the burial of Saint Apollinaris, bishop and confessor. The translation of Saint Meynulfus, deacon.”

MOLANUS: “At Rome, Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor.” Then, in smaller type: “On the same day, Amantius, priest and confessor, concerning whom blessed Gregory speaks in the *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 35.” See Castellanus’s note. Later editions have the entry for Eusebius as in the earlier edition. Then they add: “On the twenty-sixth day, the passing of Saint John the Theologian, apostle and evangelist.” This announcement was customarily taken from the Greek *Horologion*, or from an abbreviated *Menologion*, concerning which we have spoken elsewhere. But this and the other generous claims circulated by the Greeks concerning John the Evangelist should be assigned to his feast in the Latin Church on 27 December.]

[Col. 0507]

The feast of the holy martyrs Cyprian, bishop, and Justina, virgin. Justina, after suffering many things for Christ, converted Cyprian himself, when he was a magician and was attempting through his magical arts to drive her mad, to Christ. Later, when he had become a bishop and a noble teacher, he suffered martyrdom together with her. Their bodies were afterward brought by Christians to Rome. At the city of Alba, Saint Senator.

V Kal. Day 27. [Note: [Col. 0511A]

Thus Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0511B]

I find *Aegea* in our Pratensis copy and in Molanus, but all the other manuscripts simply write as in the text. I do not know whether Castellanus touches the matter precisely when he prefers another form of the name, *Aegae*, *Aegarum*. For *lapidationem*, Molanus has *lapidationes*. Pratensis and Antwerp-Major seem to read *Eoprepius*; in this singular reading we follow the others. Ado first writes *Euprepius*, then *Eutropius*. In Greven and Molanus, with excessive scrupulosity, one reads *Adulphi*; concerning this inflection we have said enough elsewhere, but in Antwerp-Major it is incorrectly *Aldulfi*. What remains is *Pseudunum*, which must unquestionably be written that way, as the excellent manuscripts Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Rosweyd, and Greven have it—not *Seudunum*, as in Antwerp-Major, nor *Sedunum*, as in Molanus and others. See below in the observations.]

[Note: [Col. 0511B]

Florentinius, in his lengthy note on Saints Cosmas and Damian for this day, writes among other things as follows:

“Baronius saw various Acts of these holy martyrs, filled with errors and confusions, such as are found in the Legendary collections. If anyone wishes to defend them, he must make them different Cosmas and Damianus, and indeed admit some as martyrs at Rome and others as confessors elsewhere, duplicating them more than once. Wangnerechius and Dehnius, both members of our Society, did precisely this, drawing from what they call ancient monuments of Greece in their historical *Syntagma concerning the three pairs of holy Anargyri named Cosmas and Damian*, published at Vienna in 1660. In it the threefold Greek distinction is vigorously defended against Latin confusion, on the supposition that the Greeks commemorate one Cosmas and Damian on 1 July, others on 17 October, and others on 1 November or on other days.

Baronius had long known these things but rejected them; nor do I know whether they can safely be arranged in this way, although Papebrochius in the Greek-Muscovite *Ephemerides* seems inclined toward that opinion. Yet, so that I do not rashly decide anything here, where a lengthy and mature examination is required, I shall restrict the matter to the authority of our Martyrologies.

The Hieronymian Martyrologies say: ‘At the city of Adacia, the feast of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian.’ Decide for yourself whether Florentinius correctly explains the place as *Ad Acia*, *Adacia*, whether separately or joined together. I consider it an error for *Aegea* or *Aegaea*, as Bede writes and Rabanus derives from him, as do the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*, Ado, Notker, and others.

Among these, the *Little Roman Martyrology* reads: ‘At the city of Aegea, Cosmas and Damian, Anthimus, Leontius, and Euprepius.’ The Viennese Martyrologist added much from the Acts, and these additions themselves require thorough examination.

Our Author copied the first part of his elogium from Bede and borrowed the second from Ado. Up to this point all the ancient Martyrologists agree, including Wandalbert, who—if the Hieronymian witnesses are excepted—mentions only the Anargyri on this day; for the saints added by Mosander are not Ado’s.

Let us hear Wandalbert:

> On the fifth day, Cosmas excels with his brother Damian;  
> Anthimus follows them, and Leontius and Euprepius,  
> Who dedicated one garland to you, Christ, by their death.

Florus recorded Timothy on this very day, unquestionably receiving him from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; concerning him, see above on 22 January, etc.

The Cordoban martyrs are purely Usuardine, and I see nothing to note about them except what has often been said elsewhere: namely, that they were brought from Spain and recorded by Our Author, and that they were the first to find a place in the sacred calendars.

A brief but distinguished elogium of both appears in the *Memorial*, book II, chapter 8, beyond the middle. There Eulogius says that their deeds, shining like the stars of heaven, were composed in a broader style for the benefit of the holy Church and the example of the weak by his old man, teacher, and most illustrious master, Sperandeus, of blessed recollection and memory.

He says this in connection with their mother Artemia. Eulogius again names them in book III, chapter 17, when he describes the illustrious confession of their sister Aurea.

We believe that the Acts themselves have perished, and our Martinus de Roa rightly laments this perhaps irreparable loss in his volume on the Cordoban Martyrs, page 153. If those writers who thrust so many pseudo-chronicles upon us had devoted their efforts to searching for monuments of this kind, what solid glory would they have won for the whole nation, and what genuine praise for themselves!”

Florentinus is recorded last in the Hieronymian Martyrologies as follows:

> [Col. 0512D] In the territory of the Aeduan city, the feast of Saint Florentinus.

Mosander reports his name with an asterisk; Rosweydus relegates it to the appendix—and rightly so, as we demonstrated in the preface, chapter 3, against Mabillon. Usuard must have obtained more extensive information from elsewhere, [Col. 0513A] since he identifies the place more precisely and names Hilary as his companion in martyrdom, writing correctly *Pseudunum*, a place of which, it is said, nothing remains today except a village which Castellanus calls Semont in French-speaking Lugdunensis Gaul, not far from the Arar. Hence one may see that those are mistaken who understand this as Castrum Sedunum on the Rhône, commonly called Sion or Sitten. One may also conclude that the variation of the readings is not sufficient reason [Col. 0514A] for these martyrs to be duplicated in Florentinius. The more common opinion of Baronius, Florentinus, and others is that they suffered under the Vandal persecution—or, preferably, the Vandal devastation and depopulation. I do not know why Castellanus departs from this in his universal Martyrology, assigning the year of Christ 264. However matters may stand, it is enough here to have represented Usuard’s simple and genuine wording.]

[Note: [Col. 0513A]

The Herinian manuscript has an appendix of its own: “On this same day, the translation of Saint Gibrianus the confessor.” See the Additions for 8 May, where from the same codex we reported Gibrianus’s deposition at Saint Remigius, who is at rest.

The Tournai manuscript, in the first commemoration, is pure; it cuts away the two final elogies.

Rosweydus appends to the complete text at the end: “Also, of the martyrs Fidentius and Terentius.” See the Roman Martyrology.

The Pulsano manuscript is likewise pure in the first item, but lacks all the remaining ones.

The Antwerp, Maximilian-Lübeck, Antwerp-Maximilian, and Louvain manuscripts give the first announcement as follows: “At the city of Aegea, [Col. 0513B] the feast of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, who, under the persecution of Diocletian, after many tortures, bonds, and imprisonments, were plunged into the sea, brought out by divine power, and placed upon a great fire; but when the fire cooled, they remained unharmed. Since they proved superior to the tortures, the impious proconsul ordered them to be suspended on prepared crosses and crushed with stones. Then he ordered them to be attacked with arrows and finally killed with the sword. They are reported,” and so forth, without interpolation.

The Munerat manuscript adds at the end: “On this same day, Saint Ceraunus, confessor and bishop of the city of Paris.” See Castellanus in his Universal Martyrology.

The Utrecht, Leiden, and Danish manuscripts agree with the Antwerp manuscript and the others, but at the end add: “At Metz, the deposition of Saint Peter, bishop and confessor.” In the Danish manuscript there is also a marginal addition: “The solemn feast of Saint Elzearius the confessor”—that is, because the codex was intended for the use of the Franciscan Friars.

The Bergen manuscript further adds: “On this same day, Saint Elyasius the confessor,” in place of Elzearius.

[Col. 0513C] The Centulensis manuscript reads: “At Aegea, the passion of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, with whom their three brothers, Anthimus, Leontius, and Euprepius, also suffered. On the same day, the holy brothers Adulfus and John, who were crowned for Christ at the city of Córdoba. In the territory of Augustodunum, the holy martyrs Florentinus and Hilary.”

The Brussels manuscript is almost similar to the Antwerp manuscript and the others in the first item. In the second and third it is sufficiently pure. It also adds at the end: “At Metz, the deposition of Saint Peter, bishop and confessor.”

The Hagenau manuscript, interpolated in the entry for Cosmas and Damian, adds: “In Armenia, Saint Gaiana, a widow, and another virgin.” See Castellanus, who adds two virgins. In the final two announcements it is sufficiently pure. Then: “Also, the translation of Virgilius, bishop and confessor of Salzburg.” He is celebrated on 27 November. “On the day of Cosmas and Damian, Saint Elzearius, the Arian count and confessor, recently canonized by Pope Urban [Col. 0513D] the Fifth.” Concerning Peter of Metz, as above.

The matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht manuscripts read: “Cosmas and Damian, martyrs. Florentinus and Hilary, martyrs. Fidentius and Terentius, martyrs. Lioba, virgin. Anthimus, Leontius, and Euprepius.” It is noted in the margin that Lioba occurs in the Roman Martyrology on the following day, which is true.

The Augiensis manuscript reads: “At Flaviacum, Saint Geremar, confessor and abbot.” This is placed first. He has been discussed above more than once. See 24 September.

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949 the final two announcements are lacking. It adds: “At Ephesus, Saint Timothy.” See the Observations.

The Florentine manuscript reads: “At Ravenna, Saint Adentis [Aderitus], archbishop and confessor.” Then the Strozzi manuscript: [Col. 0514A] “Saint Eleazarius the confessor, of the Third Order of Saint Francis.”

The Jurensis manuscript reads: “In the city of Amiens, Blessed Firminus, bishop,” and so forth. See above, 25 September.

The Dijon manuscript reads: “In the territory of Augustodunum, the passion of the holy martyrs Florentinus and Hilary.”

The Reims manuscript inserts, in the words cited immediately above concerning Saints Timothy and Apollinaris, the actual location—or place—namely, the castle of Pseudunum, as it stands in the text.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition reads: “At Ephesus, the sending into exile of Blessed John the Evangelist, together with Saint Prochorus the deacon, under the emperor Domitian. At [Col. 0514B] the city of Aegea in the province of Arabia, the feast of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, brothers and physicians. They, under the persecution of the emperor Diocletian, by the governor Lysias, after many tortures,” and so forth, as above in the Antwerp manuscript and the others. Concerning the martyrs of Córdoba, it is sufficiently pure. Then: “In the territory of Augustodunum, at the castle of Seudunum, the feast of the holy Florentinus and Hilary, who, by order of Crocus, king of the Vandals, after having their teeth knocked out and their tongues torn out, were killed by the sword.” Concerning Peter of Metz, as above. “On the same day, Saint Elsiarius, count and confessor, of the Third Rule of Saint Francis the Confessor.”

Belin has the same account of Cosmas and Damian as the Antwerp manuscript and the others above. The remainder is pure in the final announcements, except that in the first edition it reads *Florentii* instead of *Florentini*. At the end it adds: “On the same day, Saint Elzearius the confessor, of the Third Order of the holy Father Francis.”

[Col. 0514C] Greven reads: “The sending into exile of Blessed John the Evangelist, together with Saint Prochorus the deacon, under the emperor Domitian. Also, the holy martyrs Eleutherius, Andronicus, Timothy, Fidentius, and Terentius. Felicianus and Benedictus, martyrs. The translation of Blessed Stanislaus, bishop and martyr. At Metz, the deposition of Saint Peter, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Elsiarius, count and confessor, of the Third Rule of Blessed Francis. In Dacia, the falling-asleep of Saint Ketillus the confessor, regular provost of the church of Viborg. Theodota, matron, mother of Saints Cosmas and Damian. At Cologne Agrippina, the dedication of the greater church of Saint Peter the Apostle.”

Molan, after Euprepius, inserts into the text from Ado, in different type, the following concerning Cosmas and Damian: “Their bodies were buried by religious men in a venerable place, not far from the city of Aegea. The memory of the two brothers Cosmas and Damian is also solemnly celebrated at Rome, in a temple built for their name with splendid workmanship.” At the end: “At Paris, on the same day, Saint [Col. 0514D] Eleazarius the confessor, of the Third Order of the holy Father Francis. On the same day, Saint Ceraunus, confessor and bishop of the city of Paris. At the city of Sées, the dedication of the aforementioned city’s basilica, to be celebrated throughout the diocese wherever appropriate. The feast of Saint Hiltrudis, virgin, who, fleeing on earth from a spouse for the love of Christ, manfully clung to the one she had chosen and brought her good purpose to a praiseworthy conclusion.” Then, in smaller type: “Her body rests in Hainaut, in the monastery of Liessies.” Concerning Ketillus he has the same as Greven. Later editions concerning Cosmas and Damian insert only: “Renowned for abstinence from money and for miracles.” At the end, concerning Elzearius and Ceraunus, as in the earlier edition. Then: “At Liessies, the feast of Saint Hiltrudis, virgin, who, for the love of Christ, and so forth. On the twenty-seventh day, Saint Callistratus the martyr and his companions. At the city of Sées, the dedication of the basilica,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0511]

At the city of Aegea, the feast of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, who, under the persecution of Diocletian, after many tortures, bonds, and imprisonments, after divinely overcoming the sea and fires, the cross, stoning, and arrows, were punished by decapitation. It is also reported that three of their own brothers suffered in their company, namely Anthimus, Leontius, and Euprepius. On the same day, the holy brothers Adulfus and John, who were crowned for Christ at the city of Córdoba. At the castle of Pseudunum, Saint Florentinus, who, together with Blessed Hilary, was ordered to be struck with the sword after his tongue had been cut out.

**IV Kal. Die 28.**

[Note: [Col. 0515]

Taken from the Praten, Herinian, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, Maximilian-Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0515A]

They linger over details. The Herinian manuscript has *extiterit sibi* (“he will have been for himself”). The Tournai manuscript omits *natalis* (“feast”) after *Romae*. The Antwerp-Major reads *Stractei*; Maximilian-Lübeck, *Stracteti*; Munerat and Greven, *Tactei*. Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck write *Salomonis* instead of *Salonis*; Molan, *Saloni*. There is no point in noting anything concerning *Tholosam*, *Hieronymus*, *Jeronymus*, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0515A]

Today our author abandoned his usual guides, the Romanum parvum and Ado. For, following Notker, they mention only the martyrs of Córdoba—Faustus, Januarius, and Martial—about whom Wandalbertus also writes; Usuard postponed these saints to 13 October. Whether this was because he had then obtained more reliable information in Spain about the proper day of their cult will be considered elsewhere. Bede is entirely silent on this day.

Only the Hieronymian codices therefore remain, from which our author could have gathered his harvest. Yet from them he did not take Exuperius of Toulouse, who is omitted by all the Martyrologists. Nothing is more probable than that Usuard found in Jerome’s own works what he proclaims in this brief notice concerning the most holy bishop. Baronius makes further observations about this saint in his Notes on the Roman Martyrology; but Catellus arranged the sequence of his life more carefully in his Commentaries on the History of Occitania, book V, beginning on page 827, [Col. 0515B] where one will find the sources from which the passages recited here from Jerome in praise of the saint were extracted, together with many other relevant materials. See also the testimonies collected by Surius.

Rabanus mentions Stacteus together with our author. Both write the name in the same way, and both took it from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which the name is variously formed as *Stactae* and, in the most ancient Epternacensis, repeatedly as *Stertei* and *Stactei*. This gave Florentinus reason to suspect that they were different martyrs and that Sterteus was absent from several codices. He also disputes the office and title. But, unless I am mistaken, Sterteus and Stacteus are one and the same person—not a confessor or bishop, but a Roman martyr known almost solely by name, whose relics were for the most part transferred to Fulda, as Henschenius indicates in the Life of Blessed Rabanus, illustrated under 4 February, page 57.

[Col. 0516A] Salo, Salon, Salonus, or Salonius, as Florentinus acknowledges, is recorded in several Hieronymian copies, whatever the fact that he marks it as an addition and prints it in another type in these words: “At the city of Geneva in Gaul, the deposition of Saint Salon, bishop.” Rabanus transcribed the same words, but the editor Canisius wrote *Salomonis* in the margin of the book, undoubtedly from the modern Roman Martyrology. Our author, perhaps having long ago sensed the difficulty, removed the word *Gaul* and wrote *Januis*. Baronius, finding no Salon at Geneva, substituted Salomon from Belin and other more recent sources.

You see the tangled problem, to which Castellanus attached this note in his universal Martyrology, referring by a dismissed asterisk to Salomon: “This is,” he says, “according to the ancient Martyrologies: at Geneva, Saint Salon, probably the first of that name [among the bishops], omitted in the catalogues; he subscribed with his father, Saint Eucherius, to the First Council of Orange. He should rather be understood here [Col. 0516B] than the second, who subscribed to the Fourth Council of Paris, together with another Salon, bishop of Embrun.”

The learned conjecture is supported by the cited reading of the Hieronymian Martyrologies and Rabanus: “At the city of Geneva, in Gaul.” In my judgment these words seem clearly enough to exclude the famous Genoa of Liguria, which medieval writers called *Janua* or *Januis* rather than *Genua*, and which, at least in our ancient Martyrologies, is never named, so far as I know. Geneva itself also occurs rarely; nevertheless, for the moment we shall suppose that it is meant here, until the Acts clarify the matter. We may seem to have strayed rather far from our subject, while in the meantime nothing particularly doubtful arises concerning the purity of Usuard’s text.]

[Note: [Col. 0515C]

Rosweydus is not entirely pure in the text; at the end he adds: “In Bohemia, Saint Wenceslaus the martyr. Also Martial and thirty-three other martyrs.” In the Hieronymian Martyrologies fifteen companions are named, together with twenty anonymous ones.

The Pulsano manuscript, almost pure in the first and second items, omits the third, a frequent defect.

The Antwerp-Major, Louvain, Bergen, and Danish manuscripts add after the text: “At the city of Prague in Bohemia, Saint Wenzelai, or Wenceszlai (Wenceslaus), duke and martyr. He was exceedingly devoted to the Christian religion, so much so that, forgetting the dignity of his rank, during the season of harvest and vintage he himself reaped and gathered grapes, so that the produce might be offered by the hands of priests as sacrificial offerings.” It should be noted that only the Louvain manuscript writes *Salonis*; the others have *Salomonis*.

The Utrecht and Leiden manuscripts correctly have *Salonis*. In the passage concerning Wenceslaus they agree with the preceding manuscripts; but at the end they add: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Elearius [for Elzearius] the confessor, of the Order of the Third Rule of Blessed Francis.” See what has often been said on the preceding day [Col. 0515D].

The Centulensis manuscript reads: “In the Spanish city of Córdoba, the holy [Col. 0516C] Faustus, Januarius, and Martial.” I have already said in the Observations that Usuard postponed them to 13 October, where one will also find Wandalbertus’s duplicated metrical elogies. “At Rome, the feast of Saint Stacteus. At Auxerre, Saint Alodius [the Hieronymian Martyrologies and Rabanus write *Alodi*], bishop and confessor, who was one of the disciples of Saint Germanus. At the city of Januis, Saint Salomon the martyr.”

The Brussels manuscript begins from Ado: “At Córdoba, the feast of the holy Faustus, Januarius, and Martial. After the rack, their eyebrows were scraped off, their ears and noses cut off, and their upper teeth pulled out; thus disfigured, they were finally consumed in the fire.” It then proceeds, purely, concerning Stacteus. Then: “At the city of Prague in Bohemia, the feast of Saint Wenceslaus, duke and martyr. He was so devoted to the Christian religion that he himself personally reaped and gathered grapes, so that what was offered to God as sacrificial offerings might be presented by the hands of priests. At Lyon, Auremundi the martyr.” The better reading is Enemundus or Annemundus, called Chaumond in French; see Castellanus. At the end, concerning Exuperius and Salon, as in [Col. 0516D] the text.

In the Hagenau manuscript some things in Exuperius’s elogium have been altered and [Col. 0517A] transposed to a considerable distance. Concerning Wenceslaus it has the text above up to “might be offered,” but adds: “He also cut wood in the forests belonging to him with his own hands and carried it on his back to the door of a poor man who otherwise could not obtain wood. Sometimes he was severely beaten by his servants who guarded the wood, yet he did not desist. Finally he was killed by his own brother, so that the latter might possess his dominion.” In the passage concerning Stacteus it is pure. Instead of *Salonis*, it writes *Salomonis*. Then: “Also, Lioba the virgin.” Concerning her, see Rabanus and what Molanus will give from him below; also the Life in Surius. “Also, Saint Eustochia the virgin, instructed or formed, I think, by Saint Jerome.” See Castellanus’s note. “At the city of Córdoba, the holy Faustus, Januarius, and Marcellianus. Also Martial, bishop and confessor.” See above, the first Addition.

The Aquicinctine manuscript inserts, before the commemoration of Saint Stacteus: “On the same day, Saint Martial, bishop and confessor.” I think this is the martyr mentioned above.

[Col. 0517B] The matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht manuscripts read: “Wenceslaus the martyr, duke of Bohemia. Exuperius, bishop and confessor, of whom Jerome writes.”

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949 the text is absent; in its place are substituted: “In the Spanish city of Córdoba, the feast of the holy martyrs Faustus, Januarius, and Martial. In the city of Prague, Saint Wenceslaus, king and martyr.” Various elogies of him occur here in the codices; see the shorter and more elegant version in the Roman Martyrology.

The Florentine manuscript reads: “In the Spanish city of Córdoba, the holy martyrs Faustus, Januarius, and Martial. Also Saint Foroseus, bishop and confessor, whose history the venerable Bede wrote.” The name appears corrupt; perhaps Furseus is intended, whom Bede celebrates? But he is commemorated on 16 January, under the title of confessor alone. See Greven.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins with Wenceslaus, concerning whom it also agrees with the preceding manuscripts up to “might be offered,” [Col. 0517C] after which it adds: “His brother Boleslaus, having summoned his servants and companions, stabbed him together with them using swords and spears, and by such a passion made him a martyr of Christ. The blood of Christ’s martyr, as though crying from the earth to the Lord against the fratricide, could neither be scraped away nor wiped up from the place of his passion for many years.” Concerning the martyrs of Córdoba it reads as the Brussels manuscript above. It then proceeds, purely, concerning Exuperius. “At Rome, the feast of Saint Stacteus the confessor.” Instead of *Salonis*, it writes *Salomonis*. At the end: “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Alodius, bishop and confessor.”

Belin is almost pure in the passage concerning Exuperius; in second place he has: “On the same day, Saint Wenceslaus the martyr, king of the Bohemians, glorious in holiness and miracles [*gloriosi*].” [Col. 0518A] In the passage concerning Stacteus he is almost pure; instead of *Salonis* he writes *Salomonis*. Finally: “At the city of Córdoba, the holy martyrs Faustinus, Januarius, and Marcialis.”

Greven reads: “Some here observe a feast of their own angel. Terentianus, bishop and martyr. At Prague in Bohemia, Saint Wenceslaus, duke and martyr, who, after succeeding his father in the principality during the time of Otto I, conducted himself with such devotion to the Christian religion that, forgetting his dignity, he privately reaped and gathered grapes during the season of harvest and vintage, so that they might be offered in the sacrifice of Christ by the hands of priests. Though he abounded in great virtues, he was innocently killed by his pagan brother Boleslaus and obtained the palm of martyrdom. In Asia, Saint Maximus the martyr, who by order of the emperor Decius was beaten with clubs, raised upon the rack, and then raked with claws so that his flesh, together with his blood, flowed onto the ground. Finally, covered with stones, he gloriously died. Also, according to Ado, Faustus, Januarius, and Marcialis, whom Usuard has on the third day before the Ides of October. [Col. 0518B] At Auxerre, Saint Alodius, bishop. Marnulphus, bishop. Aaron, bishop. Furseus, bishop. Justinus, priest. On the same day, Saints Convallus and Maucharius, priests and confessors. On the same day, Eustochia, virgin, daughter of Saint Paula the widow. The frequent letters addressed to her and her mother testify to the great veneration in which the holy Jerome held her; as does also the fact that he calls her the precious jewel of virginity and of the Church. In Britain, Saint Thecla the abbess. In the monastery of Fulda, Saint Lioba the virgin.” See Castellanus’s note, where instead of Lioba he writes *Leobgytha* and says that her proper name was Truthgebe.

Molan also largely describes the account of the martyrs of Córdoba from Ado. He then follows Rabanus: “In Germany, Saint Lioba the virgin, who was summoned from the island of Britain by Saint Boniface, archbishop of the church of Mainz, to instruct the servants of God in the monasteries of Germany in the divine Scriptures. There she performed many miracles while alive; indeed, after her death, buried in the Buchonian forest, in the monastery of Fulda, according to the decree of Saint Boniface, she continues to shine through not a few miracles. On the same day, Saint Wenceslaus the martyr, king of the Bohemians, glorious in holiness and miracles. He was exceedingly devoted to the Christian religion, and so forth,” as in the Antwerp-Major manuscript above. Concerning Eustochia he prints in smaller type Greven’s words through “calls her,” adding: “In her mother’s epitaph, where he also recounts her services to her sick mother.” Other editions have the account of Wenceslaus as above. Then: “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Alodius, bishop.” This is followed by the account of Lioba, nearly as above. At the end: “On the twenty-eighth day, Saint Chariton, holy father and confessor.” See the Martyrology of Castellanus.]

[Col. 0515]

At Toulouse, Saint Exuperius, bishop and confessor, concerning whom the holy Jerome gave a memorable account of how sparing he was toward himself and how generous toward others. At Rome, the feast of Saint Stacteus. At the city of Januis, Saint Salon, bishop and confessor.

**III Kal. Die 29.**

[Note: [Col. 0517D]

Thus nearly all the codices: Praten, Herinian, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Rosweydus, Pulsano, Antwerp, Maximilian-Lübeck, Munerat, Belin, Greven, and Molan. [Col. 0518D] Also Antwerp-Maximilian, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, and Bergen.]

[Note: [Col. 0517D]

Pulsano, Munerat, and Belin read *Michaelis archangeli* (“of Michael the archangel”). Rosweydus has “The feast of Saint Michael,” and so forth. All have *scemate*, except Molan, who more correctly has *schemate*. Yet there is some variation in that construction. Here are the words of Antwerp-Major: “Where a church consecrated in his name is held to exist, made indeed with humble workmanship, but endowed with heavenly power.” Rosweydus: “but the basilica is held to be endowed with heavenly power.” Belin: “made indeed with humble workmanship.” Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck: “endowed with heavenly power.” Our reading is uncorrupted and derived from Ado.

We have said enough elsewhere concerning [Col. 0518D] Thrace. Pulsano alone assigns its martyrs to “In Africa.” All write *Eutici*, except Antwerp-Major, which has *Euticii*. The more recent codices have *Plati*, as do Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck; Munerat has *Plati*, Belin *Paulati*. In a few manuscripts one finds *Heracleae*. Greven and Molan incorrectly have *Eracletae*; but Molan corrected this in later editions to *Heracleae*. Concerning *Autisiodoro*, *Antisyodoro*, and so forth, see above. Antwerp-Major wrongly substituted *Firmini* for *Fraterni*.]

[Note: [Col. 0519A]

I find three principal and more celebrated apparitions of the archangel Michael enumerated by writers. The first occurred in the Asian region of Chonae; Pantaleon records much about it in the account of Metaphrastes, published by Surius. The second in chronological order, but involving several manifestations, occurred at Mount Garganus. There is also an account of the Norman apparition on Mount Tumba, otherwise called the Mount of the Peril of the Sea; concerning it, see Mabillon, Benedictine Century III, part I, beginning on page 84. The Usuardine additions speak of it more explicitly on 16 October.

The event commemorated on this day in the Martyrologies seems chiefly to concern the dedication of his temple, which is most famous on the aforementioned Mount Garganus. The Hieronymian Martyrologies speak in much the same way: “The dedication of the basilica of Saint Michael,” as in the most ancient Epternacensis; or, as in the Corbeiensis: “The dedication of the basilica of the archangel Michael, on the mountain called Garganus.” Bede is similar to the former: “The dedication of the church of Saint Michael the angel”; Rabanus adds, [Col. 0519B] “on Mount Garganus.” Wandalbertus agrees:

> Mighty in heavenly power, and prince of the heavenly  
> Host, Michael consecrated temples for himself threefold.

I think it is clear that all these references to dedication must be understood of the dedication on Mount Garganus, and that the same applies to what is found in the calendars edited by Allatius and Fronto, and in the Gregorian Sacramentary edited by Menard, as well as in the other ancient monuments cited by Florentinus.

The author of the Romanum parvum seems to follow a different path, explaining the matter in two entries. First: “On Mount Garganus, the venerable memory of the archangel Michael.” But what kind of memory this is—whether of an apparition or of a dedication—is left uncertain. He then continues: “And at Rome, the dedication of a church of the same archangel, built by Pope Saint Boniface in the Circus, a place called *Inter Nubes*.” Ado describes that memory on Mount Garganus in precisely the words which our author transferred from him to the heading, but I do not see that these words express clearly and precisely the dedication already mentioned. I therefore suppose that Baronius was moved to restrict the wording in such a way that he might indicate somewhat more clearly a solemnity of consecration performed on this very day.

In Ado one finds a longer account of the history of Garganus, to be illustrated at its proper time. At the end, the dedication of the Roman church situated *Inter Nubes* is appended from the Romanum parvum; concerning it, see Baronius’s Notes. Florentinus tries to reconcile the history itself with sound chronology, and we shall undertake the work elsewhere. For the present, it may be useful to note that the present celebration is observed by the universal Catholic Church as belonging not to Michael alone but to all the angels.

The following class of martyrs in Thrace is rightly said by Florentinus to be involved in obscurity and confusion, because in the Hieronymian copies the names of the martyrs and of the places are so confused that one cannot easily distinguish one from another. Meanwhile Rabanus and our author drew from the same source; but the discrepancy between them shows that it was not pure, since the former writes: “In the city of Heraclea in Thrace, the feast of Eutychius and Plautus.” Florentinus considers many other matters. However that may be, our reading is genuinely Usuardine among all the codices, and Baronius followed it in the modern Roman Martyrology.

The deposition of Fraternus, bishop of Auxerre, is recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, from which Rabanus again took it in exactly the same words. Our author added “confessor,” to which the word *depositio* in the Hieronymian Martyrologies refers. Others call him a martyr, notably the catalogue of the bishops of Auxerre in Demochare and another manuscript preserved by us. Castellanus seems to remove the title of martyr and, I do not know for what reason, thinks that he should be transferred to 9 July. Whether he was recorded by Ado is doubtful, but Usuard’s simplicity, according to every part of our table, is beyond dispute. Tillemont, volume XV, page 26, offers a few remarks about Fraternus; nor do the notes on pages 838 and 839 provide anything that could contribute much to illuminating his Life [Col. 0520C].]

[Note: [Col. 0519C]

The Danish manuscript, sufficiently pure in the text, adds at the end: “At Trier, Saint Lincwinus, bishop.” The name is formed in various ways, as will be evident below. Whether Castellanus surpasses the others by writing *Ludovinus* will be examined elsewhere in detail.

The Centulensis manuscript reads: “On Mount Garganus, the venerable memory of Blessed Michael the archangel, where a church consecrated by that same archangel is held to exist, made with humble workmanship but endowed with heavenly power. Also at Rome, the dedication of the oratory of Saint Michael the archangel, which Pope Boniface dedicated at the summit of the Circus, raised to a great height with marvelous workmanship. At Auxerre, the passion of Fraternus, bishop and martyr. In Thrace, Saints Lucius, Plautus, and Heraclea.”

The Brussels manuscript reads: “The venerable memory of Blessed Michael the archangel, patron of this church; and on Mount Garganus, the dedication of the church which is held to have been consecrated there in his name, made indeed with humble workmanship,” and so forth. The names of the martyrs in Thrace are somewhat distorted. It continues: “At Trier, in the monastery of Medelocus, the deposition of Saint Lindeminus, archbishop and confessor.” In the passage concerning Fraternus it is sufficiently pure.

The Hagenau manuscript, after reporting the account of the archangel Michael quite purely, adds: “On this day it also pleased holy Mother Church that the memory of all the holy angels should be solemnly celebrated, because each human being is believed to have one angel assigned to him by God for his protection. At Chartres, the feast of Saint Solemnis, bishop and confessor. By praying, he restored sight, hearing, and speech to a man who had been blind, deaf, and mute from birth. He also initiated Clovis, king of the Franks, and three hundred and sixty-four persons with him, by the water of baptism; afterward Remigius, bishop of Reims, consecrated him king.” He has been discussed above in the Additions for 24 and 25 September; his history will be examined more fully elsewhere. “In Thrace, the feast of the holy martyrs Eutychius, Plautus, and Heraclea.” The account of Fraternus is sufficiently pure. At the end: “At Trier, Saint Lintwinus, bishop and confessor.”

The Swedish Register, which belonged to Ursinus of Rosemberg, reads: “At Trier, Saint Lintwinus, bishop and confessor.” The same name is often formed differently. See what we said above concerning the Danish manuscript.

The matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht manuscripts read: “Michael the archangel. Lutwinus, bishop of Trier. Eutychius and his companions, martyrs. Fraternus, bishop and confessor.” Concerning him, see the Observations.

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949 Fraternus is absent.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition, after the text concerning Michael up to “endowed with power,” adds: “In it, however, we celebrate the solemnity of all the angels, and adore and [Col. 0520D] honor them all. In Thrace, the feast of the holy martyrs Eutychius, Plutius, and Heraclea. In the monastery of Melacum, near Trier, the deposition of Saint Lutwinus, bishop and confessor of Trier. He was first a duke in France; after building a monastery there, he became a monk. Then he became archbishop of Trier, shining through many miracles, and afterward rested in the Lord. At Auxerre, Saint Fraternus, bishop, whom they say was killed on the very day on which he was ordained bishop. At Troyes, Blessed Ursio, monk and confessor. On the same day, Saint Blandinus the confessor.”

Greven reads: “Also Saints Placidus and Sosius. Aquilinus, bishop. At Trier, Saint Ludwinus, bishop and confessor. Also, according to the Catalogue, on this day the deposition of Saint Maximus, bishop of Riez, whom Usuard has on the fifth day before the Kalends of December. In India, Saint Josaphat, king and confessor, whose birth, conversion, and illustrious deeds Vincent relates at length in the *Speculum*, book XVI. Blandinus the confessor. At Troyes, Ursio, monk and confessor.”

Molan, after “endowed with power,” inserts into the text from Ado concerning Michael: “At the summit of the lofty mountain, a cave hollowed out in the body of the same rock, like a cavern, is seen. When the Roman pontiff and the bishop of Sipontum were inquiring about the consecration of that place, and were therefore observing a three-day fast with the citizens, on the final night of the fast Saint Michael appeared in a vision to the bishop of Sipontum and instructed him to enter the church which he himself had dedicated and celebrate Masses there according to custom. Countless benefits are also bestowed there through the merits of the holy archangels [Col. 0522A].” The remainder of the text follows. At the end: “On the same day, in the monastery of Mediolacum near Trier, the feast of Saint Lutwinus, archbishop and confessor of that same aforementioned city. On this same day, the finding of the body of Saint Gislenus, bishop and confessor. At Troyes, Blessed Ursio the monk.” In later editions the first sentence of the material inserted from Ado is omitted, for in them the text begins, “For when the Roman pontiff and the bishop of Sipontum,” and so forth. At the end, concerning Lutwinus of Trier, they have the same as in the first edition.
