Then: “At Troyes, Blessed Ursio the monk.” Then: “On the twenty-ninth day, Saint Cyriacus, holy father and anchorite.” See the account of Metaphrastes in Surius for this day. Finally, the statements made above in the earlier edition concerning the discovery of the body of Saint Gislenus, bishop and confessor, are repeated.]

[Col. 0517]

On Mount Garganus, the venerable memory of Blessed Michael the archangel, where a church consecrated in his name is held to exist, made with humble workmanship but endowed with heavenly power. In Thrace, the feast of the holy Eutychius, Plautus, and Heraclea. At Auxerre, Saint Fraternus, bishop and confessor.

**Pridie Kal. Die 30.**

[Note: [Col. 0521]

Thus only the Praten, Herinian, Tournai, Greven, and Molan manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0521B]

They are completed by two brief notes. In the Herinian manuscript, instead of *erepti sunt* (“they were snatched away”), one reads *erecti sunt* (“they were raised”). In Greven and Molan, [Col. 0522B] *mense tertio* (“in the third month”) occurs instead of *mense sexto* (“in the sixth month”). Concerning *choruscante*, Bethlehem, Jerome, and so forth, we have said enough.]

Marked first among them are the twin martyrs Victor and Ursus, who are at least named in the Acts of Eucherius as members of the celebrated Theban Legion; in the more ancient Martyrologies, such as the Hieronymian, Bede’s, and the Little Roman Martyrology, they are entirely passed over—whatever some more recent writer may vainly allege concerning both the Hieronymian codices and the Florentine editor. We dealt with another Victor, numbered among the Mauritian martyrs, and with others, on 22 September. Those who are commemorated today were first entered by Ado into the sacred calendars, with a panegyric which, I think, was abridged from longer Acts; Usuard reproduced its substance selectively in his text. Surius published certain Acts brought from Gaul, but what their date may be, or what authority they possess, is at the very least uncertain; nor do I think it probable that they preceded Ado, although at the beginning they differ little from his encomium. Whether the manuscripts of the Acts preserved among us provide anything new will be examined in its proper place. Another Victor, whose translation to Milan the Hieronymian Martyrologies celebrate on this day, is believed not to have belonged to the Theban number but to have been brought there from elsewhere, perhaps from Africa. The Martyrologies and other monuments speak everywhere of the most glorious doctor of the Church, Jerome, and everything is so clear, says Florentinius, that it does not seem to require reworking. The Hieronymian Martyrologies read as follows: “In the territory of Jerusalem, the deposition of Saint Jerome the priest.” Bede: “In Bethlehem of Judah, the deposition of Saint Jerome the priest.” It is added that he died in his ninety-first year. Florus inserted a brief panegyric, Rabanus a somewhat longer one, but they differ from Bede in the number of years. The Little Roman Martyrology notes the matter most briefly: “At Bethlehem, Jerome the priest.” Ado compensates for this brevity by treating it at greater length, with a list of his works, from which Usuard extracted very little, while preserving an age designation that agrees neither with Bede nor with Rabanus. See Baronius’s Notes. After others, Marianus Victorius compiled Jerome’s Life with greater diligence; others made their own promises; for us Tillemont pointed the way in volume XII, arranging many things learnedly which will be of the greatest service in elucidating the Acts of Jerome, as will also the observations made by Martianaeus in the recent edition of Jerome’s Works and in the subsequent edition of the Gallic Life, together with many of our own monuments, both manuscript and printed, to be examined in their proper place in the Acts and to be more splendidly adorned in accordance with the merit of so illustrious a saint. Here the metrical encomium of Wandalbert, not altogether uncouth, claims its place:

> Approved interpreter of the law, both old and new,  
> Instructor in doctrine, condemner of wicked heresy,  
> Jerome closes the rejoicing month of September on its eve.

The final place is filled at Piacenza by Antoninus, called “our confessor”; in the Corbie manuscript he is called Antoninus the martyr, while in other Hieronymian copies he is simply Anthonius or Antonius, without any title. Florentinius investigates him at length, referring readers to 2 and 3 September, on which days we too dealt fully with various Antonini and Antonii; nor does anything of importance now occur that might dispel with new brilliance the darkness already discussed there. The Acts preserved by Peter in the Catalogue, book VIII, chapter 133, proclaim him a martyr who, having departed from the territory of Piacenza, passed through the eastern provinces and performed many miracles, finally returning to his own city, and so forth. He is nevertheless supposed to have belonged to the Theban Legion. I would believe that both the title and the office entered the present Roman Martyrology incorrectly from Peter, if I am not mistaken. Ferrarius and Florentinius recognized that the Acts of this Antoninus and of the other Antoninus of Apamea had somehow been confused; to avoid becoming entangled here in such complications, we leave all these matters to be discussed in their proper place. Certainly there is no doubt that Usuard received Antoninus from some Hieronymian source, since he is unknown to all the other Martyrologists, even to Ado, to whom Usuard’s words were attributed by someone but rejected by Mosander and Rosweyd. Nothing more is needed to establish the integrity of Usuard’s text.

[Note: The Antwerp–Major edition adds beneath the unadulterated text: “Also on this day, in the city of Canterbury, Saint Honorius, archbishop and confessor.”]

[Note: Rosweyd’s text is not entirely pure, and at the end adds: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Honorius, archbishop, who, fifth after blessed Augustine, preached the word of God to the English people. Also, Saints Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus, whose Acts are extant.” Indeed, the Acts themselves, serving as the official record, were published in full by Rosweyd in 1607 and also by others. But why they are listed on this day I do not know, since they suffered martyrdom on 11 October, as we shall say there.]

[Note: The Pulsanen edition places Jerome first, without alteration. Then: “At Rome, the passion of the holy virgins Faith, Hope, Charity, and their mother Sophia, that is, Wisdom.” See 1 August. In the entry concerning the martyrs of Solothurn it removes the panegyric. It assigns the title “martyr” to Antoninus of Piacenza.]

[Note: The Antwerp and Maximilian–Lübeck editions, in their first form, insert after “priest,” concerning Jerome: “He acquired a knowledge of every branch of literature and became an imitator of the most approved monks. He died in the year …,” and so forth, as in the text. Concerning Antoninus, they are correct.]

[Note: Muneratus, after the unaltered text, adds: “At Paris, the solemnity of the sacred relics of our redemption, honorably deposited there in the royal holy chapel by the most blessed king Louis.”]

[Note: The Antwerp–Maximilian, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, and Danish editions begin as follows: “At Bethlehem of Judah, the deposition of Saint Jerome the priest, a most holy man and exceedingly learned in Sacred Scripture. He acquired a knowledge of every branch of literature and became an imitator also of the most approved monks. He died in the year 423 [Antwerp–Maximilian: 403] of the Lord, in the ninety-eighth year [Danish: plainly, ninety-ninth] of his age, in the sixth month.” Others more correctly place Jerome’s death in the year 420. In the rest, the codices are sufficiently pure.]

[Note: The Alberg edition, concerning Saint Jerome, adds after “priest,” besides what has already been mentioned: “the glorious doctor and cardinal of the Roman Church. He acquired a knowledge of every branch of literature,” and so forth, as in the preceding editions.]

[Note: The Centulian edition reads: “In Gaul, at the fortress of Solothurn, Saints Victor and Ursus, martyrs, who belonged to the glorious Theban Legion. At Bethlehem of Judah, the deposition of Saint Jerome the priest and abbot, through whom all Sacred Scripture among the Latins was restored to the standard of truth. At Piacenza, Saint Antoninus the confessor.” See the Observations above.]

[Note: The Brussels edition, after “imitator,” enlarges Jerome’s panegyric with these words: “Having completed the same number of years as the other minister of the Mother of God, John the Evangelist, he rested in Christ in the ninety-ninth year of his age. Concerning him, someone heard in a nocturnal vision a person apparently reading the following verses from a book:”]

> Wondering Greece takes joy in no pupil more;  
> If it were to count his ancestors, tracing them back to the first beginning,  
> There is more in him to praise than can be praised.

[Note: In the entry concerning Victor and Ursus, whom it lists second, the text is also interpolated, inserting, among other things, the following from Ado: “When they had withdrawn there to avoid the fury of the tyrant Maximian, at his command they were first tortured with dreadful punishments; but when a heavenly light shone over them,” and so forth. At the end it is unaltered.]

[Note: The Hagenoyen edition is somewhat interpolated at the beginning and tells more about Jerome, though these details are more properly derived from Ado. It then adds: “In Greater Augia, in the diocese of Constance, Saint Fortunata, virgin and martyr, and her brothers Terponius, Evagistus, and Priscianus, martyrs.” These saints are also celebrated and listed in the codices on 14 October; see the Appendices for that day. At the end the text is unaltered.]

[Note: The editions of Matricularius, the Carthusians, and Utrecht read: “Jerome the priest and confessor. Victor and Ursus, martyrs of the Theban Legion. Antoninus the confessor [added in the margin: in the Roman Martyrology, martyr]. At Rome, Arethas the martyr and five hundred others (again noted in the Roman Martyrology on the following day), and Leopardus the martyr.” See also the Roman Martyrology concerning him.]

[Note: The Swedish Register, no. 428, reads: “On the same day, Saint Seraunus, bishop of Paris.” See the Usuardine Appendices at 27 September.]

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, no. 5949, adds: “At Rome, the holy virgins Faith, Hope, Charity, and their mother Sophia.” I have already said that one should refer back to 1 August.]

[Note: The Castle Charles Codex reads: “In Gaul, at the fortress of Solothurn, which is situated on the River Aare,” and so forth.]

[Note: The Besançon edition reads: “At Châlons, Saint Leudomir the confessor.” Others write Leodemirus, and so forth.]

[Note: The Reims manuscript of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris reads: “At Châlons, Saint Ledomarus, bishop and confessor.”]

[Note: The Lübeck–Cologne edition reads: “At Bethlehem of Judah, the deposition of the glorious Jerome, priest and doctor, cardinal of the Roman Church. He acquired a knowledge of every branch of literature and was learned in Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and Chaldean. He came to Jerusalem, and after visiting the holy places asked and obtained from Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, the place of the Lord’s manger. There he founded a monastery; having become an imitator of the most approved monks, he began to live with the brothers joined to him in charity, according to the rule established by the holy apostles. After a perfect life pleasing to the Lord, and after many labors spent in writing books for the edification of the Church, he finally died in the year of the Lord 423, in the ninety-ninth year of his age, and was buried at the mouth of the cave of the Lord’s manger.” Concerning Victor and Ursus, it is almost as above. The entry for Antoninus is unaltered. Then: “At Châlons, Saint Leodomerus, bishop and confessor of that city. On the same day, Saint Laurus, bishop and confessor. At Bamberg, the translation of Saint Otto, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Leopold the martyr.”]

[Note: Belin places Jerome first, as do the Antwerp and Maximilian–Lübeck editions. Antoninus comes second, without alteration. Victor and Ursus follow, also without alteration, except that it reads Ursicius instead of Ursus. At the end: “On the same day, Saint Sophia the widow,” omitting her daughters.]

[Note: Greven reads: “At Rome, Saint Leopardus the martyr, now resting at Aachen. In England, Saint Honorius, archbishop of Canterbury, fifth after blessed Augustine. Leodomerus, bishop of Châlons and confessor. The translation of Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg and confessor. At Rome, the deposition of blessed Simeon the monk and confessor, son of the count of Vermandois. Laurus the priest and confessor. On the same day, blessed Sophia the widow. Rachel, wife of Jacob the patriarch, whose name is interpreted as ‘sheep.’ Also, the holy memory of James of Viniacum, of the Carthusian order. He was deeply devoted to the pursuit of the contemplative life; he held the priorate at Chartreuse first in the eighteenth place and then in the twentieth, and after his death began to live through miracles. Also, the good memory of John Cornerius, a monk of the Carthusian order, a man of the greatest holiness. On the day when he was about to celebrate his first Mass, when he was summoned by the sacristan, his cell was found shining with fiery brilliance, and the man of God himself was burning like a flame of fire. Through his merits also, certain writings which had accidentally been thrown into a great fire and withdrawn after a long interval were found entirely unharmed.”]

[Note: Molanus inserts in the text, in different type, concerning Jerome, nearly the same material as above from the Antwerp and Maximilian–Lübeck editions. At the end, concerning Sophia, as in Belin. Also concerning the solemnity of the relics at Paris, as in Muneratus. Then: “The translation of the body of Saint Vedast from the place of his burial to the place where he now rests. Blessed confessors Aubert and Audomar transferred him. On the same day, the feast of Saint Leopardus the martyr.” Then in smaller type: “At Rome; now resting at Aachen.” Concerning the translation of Saint Otto and Saint Honorius, as in Greven above. Then: “At Châlons, Saint Leudomir, bishop and confessor of that city; concerning whom the Church sings:

> Father Leudomir, come powerfully to the aid of your children,  
> So that they may live in health and seek eternal joys.”

In later editions, Jerome appears in the text as above. At the end, concerning Sophia, as above. “At Bamberg, Saint Otto, bishop and confessor, who converted the Pomeranians. In England, Saint Honorius, archbishop of Canterbury.” Concerning Leudomir, nearly as in the first edition. “At Aachen, on the same day, the feast of Saint Leopardus the martyr. On the thirtieth day, Saint Gregory, the most sacred martyr, in Greater Armenia.” Concerning the solemnity of the Parisian relics and the translation of Saint Vedast, as in the first edition. It continues: “At the monastery of Andain, the translation of the body of the most blessed Hubert, bishop and confessor of Tongeren: when Bishop Vulcand, of blessed memory, transferred his sacred bones from Liège to Andain in the year 825 of the Lord’s incarnation. There the glory of miracles declares his merits, and the benefits he bestows are celebrated through the devotion of the faithful.”]

In Gaul, at the fortress of Solothurn, the passion of Saints Victor and Ursus, martyrs of the glorious Theban Legion. They were first tortured with dreadful punishments; but when a heavenly light flashed over them, the executioners fell to the ground and the martyrs were rescued. Then they were thrown into the fire, but were not harmed at all; finally they were completed by the sword. On the same day, at Bethlehem of Judah, the deposition of blessed Jerome the priest, who died in the ninety-eighth year of his age, in the sixth month. At the city of Piacenza, Saint Antoninus the confessor.

## The month of October has thirty-one days.

### On the Kalends — Day 1

[Note: The Prato, Greven, and Molanus editions are unaltered, or closest to unaltered.]

[Note: At the outset, one must note the transposition of the announcements in many codices, including those which we consider more accurate. The Prato manuscript treats of Piaton before the translation of Germanus and Remigius; Greven and Molanus, however, place the translation first. All write Arethas. Likewise they write Thomis, although the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Notker read Tomis, and the modern Roman Martyrology adds “in Pontus.” Florentinius argues at length whether the Hieronymian reading should be Thumuis or Thomis in Egypt, or rather Tomis in Pontus; but that belongs to another investigation, whereas we are seeking the Usuardine reading from the codices. Molanus corrects the text by writing Lusitanian. The name is rendered Olisepona, Olesipona, Olesipoma, and in other ways; the more accurate witnesses write it as in the text. The Prato manuscript, with a few others, has Pyatonis. Greven and Molanus omit episcopo after Dionysius and put gubernavit for rexit. Greven changes migravit ad Christum to migravit ad Dominum; and for “In the port of Ganda” substitutes “in the port of Ghent.” What remains to be noted is the greatest variation among the codices concerning the translation just mentioned, which in the Lucca Hieronymian is instead treated as the natal feast of several persons joined together: “In Gaul, in the city of Auxerre, Saint Germanus the bishop, and Saints Vedast, Remedius, and Piaton.” I do not know whether the confusion in some Usuardine codices may have arisen from this, so that the Antwerp–Major edition writes: “On the same day, the translation of the holy confessors and bishops Germanus, Remigius, and Vedast; of whom the first governed the Church of Auxerre, the second that of Reims, and the third that of Arras”—almost the same form found in Antwerp, Maximilian–Lübeck, and the middle-grade codices, together with Belin and the modern Roman Martyrology. Herinien preserves the announcement correctly, but gives it first place; after three others, also in an unaltered form, it inserts: “At the fortress of Arras, Saint Vedast the bishop.” In place of this, the Prato codex has, I think, added in the margin: “And the translation of Saint Vedast the bishop.” Molanus asserts that this translation was moved back to the preceding day because the feast of Remigius occupied this day. Incidentally, note Florentinius’s error: he inadvertently attributed to Notker the words of Rabanus concerning Vedast, which will be quoted below. See the rest in the Observations and Appendices.]

[Note: It has been observed more than once above that few saints occur in Usuard’s Martyrology—excepting always the popular saints of Gaul and Córdoba—who are not mentioned by at least one of the ancients. We have supplied examples to the contrary here and there, most recently on 21 September in the case of Pamphilus the Roman martyr, entirely unknown to the other Martyrologists. Here is another example in the first announcement of this day, concerning Arethas and his five hundred and four companions. I labored intensely to find even a trace of these saints elsewhere, but in vain; for it is perfectly clear that Ado is repeatedly cited here and elsewhere incorrectly by Baronius and his followers. Galesinius, Ferrarius, and other recent writers invent and reinvent that number, to such an extent that Bartholomew Piazza in his Calendar reduced the companions to only seven, claiming that the memory of their glorious confession survived and that their relics were scattered through various churches of Rome. The cited Galesinius and Ferrarius seem to guess at the time of their martyrdom; I frankly confess that I have learned nothing certain about the whole announcement. We briefly touched on another Arethas, a martyr among the Homerites, who suffered with many companions under the tyrant Dhu Nuwas; Metaphrastes discusses him in Surius under 24 October, and we treated him cursorily in the Treatise on the Alexandrian Patriarchs, p. 64. Whatever may meanwhile be the truth concerning our Roman Arethas, it cannot be denied that Usuard truly recorded him, however he may ultimately have received the information. The source of the second announcement is completely evident, since the Hieronymian Martyrologies mention those three martyrs, although the notice is dislocated in various places. The Little Roman Martyrology clearly records them, from which Ado took it, and from Ado Notker and our author, everywhere in the same terms, except that Usuard wrote Crescentis instead of Crescentii, or, as the Hieronymian has it, Crescenti. Among the ancient writers, Florus alone mentions the martyrs of Olisipo, in an appendix to Bede, and he also composed their panegyric. But if you compare the texts of Florus and Usuard, you will easily see—as I have pointed out elsewhere—that neither was known to the other. Florus writes: “In the city of Olisipo, the passion of Saints Verissimus, Maximus, and Julia, who suffered under the governor Datianus,” and so forth. Baronius reads in the Roman Martyrology: “who suffered in the persecution of Diocletian.” Our author supplied no chronological indication, perhaps because, as I infer, he had found no such information in Spain, from which he may have brought those martyrs together with the Cordoban martyrs. The memory of Piaton or Platon, otherwise Piatus, is considered by Florentinius to have been added to the Hieronymian Martyrologies; Usuard should not have received it from there, and undoubtedly saw the Acts from which the panegyric was composed. Some have struggled over the names of Dionysius and Quintinus, one of whom is said to have set out from Rome for Gaul with the other as companion. But the difficulty is easily removed if we maintain that both traveled together. The Acts of Platon are suspect because they seem to have arisen from other similar accounts; that controversy will be dealt with in its proper place. The confusion concerning the translations has been discussed above. Here it should be observed that Bede wrote: “The feast of Saint Remigius, in the city of Reims.” The Little Roman Martyrology: “And in the city of Reims, Saint Remigius the bishop.” Ado added something in the place of a panegyric, and from him Notker did likewise; the material concerns a natal feast or deposition more than a translation. Rabanus accordingly speaks as follows of Germanus and Vedast; his words deserve to be quoted here: “In Gaul, in the city of Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Germanus the bishop. In the city of Reims, Remedius the bishop. In the city of Arras [for Atrebatis], blessed Vedast the bishop. At the monastery of Ganda, Saint Bavo the bishop. The lives and deeds of all these, full of miracles, are preserved in writing.” Concerning the solemn feast of Remigius, or, as the people call it, the feast for the diocese of Reims, we spoke on 13 January; we treated Germanus on 31 July and Vedast on 6 February. The illustrious deeds of Remigius, developed both historically and rhetorically, will occupy a considerable portion of October in our Acts, although the most ancient collection of them, from which Fortunatus of Poitiers made an abridgment, is said to have perished. Concerning Germanus of Auxerre, the Viennese author tells here everything that ought rather to have been placed on his proper day, and Notker abridges it. In the midst of such great variation among the readings, I think that we have reproduced Usuard’s text faithfully. Baronius’s Notes may be consulted. The codices agree concerning Bavo, who should be attributed first not to Ado but to Usuard. Mabillon published his original Acts in volume II of the Benedictine century, beginning on p. 394; compared with the Theodorician materials, they will be elucidated in their proper time. The following verses of Wandalbert belong to the final announcements:

> Remigius, who first taught and subdued the fierce Franks,  
> Marks October with his own distinction;  
> And Germanus, likewise renowned in doctrine and deed,  
> Strengthens Auxerre, his own city, by his merits;  
> He drove into the ocean the deserters from the faith and their wicked doctrine,  
> And covered you, painted Britain, with signs.  
> Bavo accompanies them in virtue and holy honor.]

[Note: The Herinien edition, besides what has been stated, has this distinctive feature: concerning Piaton it begins: “In the district of Medenentia, the natal feast of Saint Piaton,” and so forth. See the Variants.]

[Note: The Tournai edition lacks the first two announcements. In the rest it is unaltered, but at the end adds: “On the same day, Vedast, Wasnulph, and Trudo.”]

[Note: The Antwerp–Major edition was recopied here for several leaves by a later hand and is full of scribal errors. We have already spoken of its Appendix.]

[Note: Rosweyd begins: “At Reims, Remigius the bishop and confessor. At Auxerre, Germanus the bishop and confessor. At Arras, Vedast the bishop and confessor.” Then the entries concerning Bavo, Piaton, Arethas, the people of Tomis, and the Lusitanians are fairly pure.]

[Note: The Pulsanen edition has Hermes instead of Arethas. The announcements concerning the Lusitanians, Piaton, and Bavo are lacking, as is almost daily the case.]

[Note: The Antwerp and Maximilian–Lübeck, Ughellian, and Daveron editions are fairly pure in the first three entries. Then: “On the same day, the translation of the holy confessors Germanus, Remigius, and Vedast. The first of them governed the Church of Auxerre, the second that of Reims, and the third that of Arras and Cambrai.” The remainder is pure.]

[Note: Muneratus is close to the unaltered text, adding only at the end: “At Chartres, Piaton the martyr.” This was perhaps added through ignorance. See the Bordeaux edition.]

[Note: The Antwerp–Maximilian, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, and Alberg editions begin: “In the city of Reims, the translation of Saint Remigius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the translation of the holy confessors Germanus and Vedast, the first of whom governed the Church of Auxerre, while the other governed those of Arras and Cambrai.” The entry concerning Arethas, the people of Tomis, and the Lusitanians follows, unaltered. All except Alberg give Piaton the title of bishop. At the end they write concerning Bavo: “In the port of Ghent, the deposition,” and so forth.]

[Note: The Danish edition is similar to the preceding ones but inserts, in the penultimate place: “At Trier, Saint Nicetius the bishop.” He is celebrated on 5 December.]

[Note: The Centulian edition reads: “At Rome, blessed Arethas the martyr, with his 504 companions. At Auxerre, the deposition of the most sacred body of blessed Germanus, bishop and confessor, who died at Ravenna in Italy on 31 July. At Reims, the metropolis of the Franks, the translation of Saint Remigius, archbishop and confessor. At Arras, the translation of Saint Vedast, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Tournai, Saint Piaton, priest and martyr, who came from Rome to Gaul in the company of Saint Quintinus. At the monastery of Ganda, the deposition of Saint Bavo, confessor and monk, whom the blessed pontiff Amandus, after converting him from the vanity of the world, thoroughly instructed to hasten toward the glory of heaven. In the district of Ponthieu, the natal feast of Saint Wulflagius, priest and confessor.” He is celebrated on 7 June. See his Acts, elucidated on that day.]

[Note: The Brussels edition reads: “At Reims, the translation of Saint Remigius, archbishop and confessor. Before he was born, he was announced by name through Montanus, a blind monk. After he was born, the same Montanus anointed his own eyes with the milk of Cilinia, Remigius’s mother, and recovered his sight. He departed to Christ on the Ides of January, but on this day the feast of his translation is celebrated. At Auxerre, the translation of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor, whose day of deposition falls on the eve of the Kalends of August. At Arras, the translation of Saint Vedast, bishop and confessor. Ordained bishop by Saint Remigius, he governed both the churches of Cambrai and Arras, and departed to Christ on 6 February.” The entries concerning Piaton, Arethas, the people of Tomis, and the Lusitanians follow, fairly pure. Then: “Also Saint Wasnulph the martyr. In the district of Medenetia, Piatus suffers for Christ. In the port of Ghent, the deposition of blessed Bavo the confessor. Converted from being a most ferocious count of Hasbania, he established for himself a monastery at Ghent under blessed Amandus and appointed Florbert abbot. At the hour of his death he appeared to Saint Gertrude, his kinswoman, while she was praying at Nivelles, asking her to prepare suitable burial garments for him at once. At Trier, Saint Nicetius, bishop and confessor.” See the Danish edition, where we said that he is celebrated on 5 December.]

[Note: The Hagenoyen edition is unaltered in its first and second entries; in the third it reads: “In the district of Medenentia, in the city of Tournai, the natal feast of Saint Piaton the martyr. He …,” and so forth. In the translation it joins the three together, as do the Antwerp and Maximilian–Lübeck editions, and others. In the entry concerning the Lusitanians it is fairly pure. Then: “In the district of Ghent in Flanders, the deposition of Saint Bavo the monk and confessor. In the bishopric of Tridemi, Saint Remedius the confessor.” I do not understand “Tridemi,” nor “Tridentini,” as others render it. See Castellanus in the first Bimester, p. 231, where he discusses Remigius. It continues: “At Bamberg, Saint Otto, bishop and confessor.” He was treated on the preceding day. “At Salsa, the translation of Saint Adelaide the empress.”]

[Note: The Aquicinct edition also joins the three translations and adds concerning Vedast: “The body of the third was transferred by the holy bishops Aubert and Audomar, through an angelic revelation, from the episcopal see to the place where he is now venerated.” At the end: “And the deposition of Saint Wasnulph the confessor.”]

[Note: The Amiens edition reads: “At the monastery of Centula, the dedication of the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Richarius the confessor.” It is quite astonishing that such a church dedication is not recorded in the Martyrology of that very monastery.]

[Note: The editions of Matricularius, the Carthusians, and Utrecht read: “Remigius, bishop and confessor, whose feast is celebrated here in the Order, namely when his translation occurred, because on the day of his death there is no free observance on account of the octave of Epiphany and the commemoration of Saint Hilary. Piaton, the first bishop and martyr of Tournai.” It is noted in the margin: “I have seen a great controversy concerning Piaton’s episcopate. Bavo the confessor at Ghent, where his body rests.”]

[Note: The Swedish Register, no. 130, reads: “Also Saint Vedast.”]

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript, no. 5949, the Lusitanians, Piatus, and Bavo are lacking.]

[Note: Florentinius reads: “At Trier, blessed Nicetius, bishop and confessor.” We have already said that he is celebrated on 5 December.]

[Note: The Bordeaux edition reads: “In the city of Chartres, the passion of Saint Picton, priest, who, together with blessed Dionysius,” and so forth. If one reads “At Tournai” and “Piaton,” one will have the text. See Muneratus and the passage below.]

[Note: The Besançon edition reads: “In the district of Chartres, the natal feast of Saint Platon, who, together with blessed Dionysius,” and so forth.]

[Note: The Lübeck–Cologne edition divides the three translations into three separate articles. Concerning Piaton, after “he sought,” it adds: “and afterward, under Diocletian, having completed his martyrdom, he departed to the Lord. In the city of Trier, at the monastery of Saint Maximinus, the natal feast of Saint Nicetius, bishop of that city, a man of complete holiness, who while still in the body freed the people of Trier from the groin plague through his prayers.” The entry concerning the people of Tomis and the Lusitanians is fairly pure. Concerning Bavo it reads as in the Antwerp–Maximilian edition and others. Then concerning Arethas, without alteration. “On the same day, Saint Melor the martyr.” See Castellanus. “Also Saint Wasnulph,” elsewhere Basanulph.]

[Note: I have already said that Belin also joins together the translations of Germanus, Remigius, and Vedast. In the remainder, the first edition is fairly pure, except that it writes Gada instead of Ganda and Pavonis instead of Bavonis. The second edition corrects these, but at the end gratuitously repeats: “At Arras, Saint Vedast, bishop and confessor.”]

[Note: Greven reads: “Melor the martyr. At Trier, the deposition of Saint Nicetius, bishop and confessor. Also the holy confessors Remedius, Abra, also called Deodatus, David, disciples of Saint Germanus the bishop. Imerius the confessor. Also Wasnulph the confessor. At Arras, the translation of Saint Vedast, attended by Saint Lambert of Tongeren, Aubert of Rouen, and Audomar of Thérouanne, who had lost the sight of his eyes. When, through the prayers of the holy bishops present and the merits of blessed Vedast, he recovered his sight, he was distressed and obtained that he might be blinded again. The translation of Saint Aubert, bishop and confessor of Cambrai. Also, the Catalogue places here the memory of certain ancient righteous men, namely Mattathias, father of Judas Maccabaeus, and Jonathan and Simon, his sons. The Books of the Maccabees fully teach how much they did and suffered for their fatherland and the holy laws of God. John, the son of the aforesaid Simon, is added to them. Also the memory of Onias, the high priest, a man of extraordinary modesty and sobriety, innocently killed by the wicked Andronicus. Also Eleazar, a man among the foremost of the scribes, of excellent conduct from childhood, who, when he was pressed against the law to eat pork, refused with marvelous freedom and courage, endured tortures, and, leaving a courageous example to the young, met an honorable death.” Nothing concerning these men appears in the other codices.]

[Note: Molanus reads: “Also Saint Fronto, bishop, whose deeds, full of miracles, are preserved in writing.” See Rabanus. He is celebrated on 25 October under the name Fronto. “Also in the cemetery of the city of Hainaut called Condé, Saint Wasnulph the confessor, who, coming from the island of Scotland, lived laudably for many days in the Cerisian forest, at the place now called Cell. Later he reached the monastery of the Mother of God Mary, called Condé, and there served the Lord until his death. At Trier, Saint Nicetius, bishop and confessor, who was holy from his mother’s womb; for from the time of his birth he was miraculously marked out as a cleric. When he had been delivered at birth, he emerged with his entire head bare of hair, as is customary among newborns, while a small circular arrangement of hairs appeared around it.” Other editions put Quintinus instead of Dionysius. In the entry concerning Bavo, they add in another type: “whose deeds are extant.” Then the following is attached to the text: “In the city of Trier, Saint Nicetius, bishop, a man of complete holiness,” and in another type, “who from the time of his birth was miraculously marked out as a cleric. At Condé, Saint Wasnulph the confessor.” Concerning Fronto, as in the first edition. Finally: “On the first day, Saint Romanus the Melodist,” from the usual Horologion.]

At Rome, the natal feast of blessed Arethas the martyr and five hundred and four others. In the city of Tomis, Saints Priscus, Crescens, and Evagrius. In the province of Lusitania, in the city of Olisipo, Saints Verissimus, Maxima, and Julia, sisters, martyrs. In the city of Tournai, the passion of Saint Piaton the priest, who, together with blessed Dionysius the bishop and his companions, set out from the city of Rome for Gaul for the sake of preaching; afterward, having completed his martyrdom, he departed to Christ. On the same day, the translation of the holy confessors Germanus and Remigius, the former of whom governed the Church of Auxerre and the latter that of Reims. At the port of Ganda, Saint Bavo the confessor.

[Note: Bouillart adds in italic type: “All seven verses of this little column were shamefully mutilated with a knife. A rich opportunity for Sollerio to guess, had Castellanus warned him. But if he had warned him? Could that inspector, who so skillfully noted even the slightest variations, have failed to act at so crucial a point? He did not notice so ugly an erasure, although he suggested to Sollerio that the translation of Saint Vedast, a matter of no importance, had been attached to the article by a more recent hand. Yet that same severe critic of the Prato codex copies all those saints. I think that someone from Saint-Germain, noticing that his codex differed from Greven and Molanus, adapted his own pen to Usuard. Bouillart.”] And the translation of the body of Saint Vedast the bishop.

### The sixth day before the Nones — Day 2

[Note: In the text the Prato, Herinien, Antwerp–Major, and Greven editions agree.]

[Note: The principal difficulty lies at the beginning, where the Prato and Antwerp–Major editions have syntax that is not sufficiently correct: “of whom, at the command of Diocletian, collected in heaps, some by swords,” and so forth. Muneratus’s construction is not exact either: “of whom the multitude, collected in heaps at the command of Diocletian, some by the sword,” and so forth. Herinien is better, together with Antwerp, Maximilian–Lübeck, and others: “of whom, at the command of Diocletian, the most savage emperor, some by swords,” and so forth. But the epithet “most savage” appears to have been added, so that, in my opinion, Greven and Molanus read more briefly and elegantly: “of whom, at the command of the emperor Diocletian, some by swords,” and so forth. In Greven there is concremabantur, “they were burned up.” Then it has “long torture”; the others have it as in the text. The Antwerp–Major edition, as I recently said, teems with errors; a few will suffice: Adaracensi for Adartensi, Eborinus, Serini, and so forth. Nevertheless, like all the others, it reads afflictum, “afflicted,” contrary to the solitary reading affectum in the Prato manuscript. See Ado.]

[Col. 0531]

Here, very probably under a single announcement, all those most valiant athletes are celebrated again who were crowned at Nicomedia, perhaps toward the end of March, on the occasion of the famous burning of Diocletian’s palace. On this, see Eusebius and Lactantius, cited by us elsewhere when we were discussing the individual saints of this group, especially on 12 March, 27 April, and 9 September. Today the Hieronymian Martyrologies name only Eleutherius, in these words: “At Nicomedia, Eleutherius, whose Acts are preserved.” Rabanus cut away the final part, perhaps because he could find no Acts of this saint. The Short Roman Martyrology briefly and elegantly gathers the whole matter together:

> “At Nicomedia, Eleutherius the martyr under Diocletian, and innumerable others whom the enraged Diocletian, because of the burning of his palace, killed by various tortures out of hatred for the Christian name.”

Ado’s account is somewhat fuller; Peter transferred it from there into the *Catalogus*, and Our author likewise condensed his entire eulogy from it. Tillemont carefully examines the Nicomedian slaughter in volume V, beginning at page 23.

It is doubtful whether Leodegarius refers to the Hieronymian codices. Florus, as edited by us, certainly included him, although with a eulogy so different from the wording of Ado and Usuard that they have nothing in common except the substance of the event. Rabanus is mistaken when he reads: “In Gaul, the feast of Saint Leudegarius, bishop and confessor”; and he seems confused in naming Leudegarius on this day as distinct from Leutgarius, bishop of Autun, whose passion he celebrates somewhat more fully on the following day. Ado places the martyrdom in the territory of Arras, at the village of Siricinium (Notker described it as “in Atratis”). Our author, taking everything else from Ado, [Col. 0531C] expands the location in such a way as to substitute the district or province of Artois for the village of Siricinium. The *Hagiologium Franco-Galliae*, edited by Labbe, wrote it in the same way; as we have said elsewhere, that work was often copied from Usuard.

There are two sets of Acts of Leodegarius, edited by Mabillon and others; later they are to be compared and reviewed more carefully by us against our manuscripts. In the old Gothic or Gallican Missal he is honored by a Mass, as may be seen in Thomasius’s edition, page 375. Today Wandalbertus alone celebrates him:

> “Soon Leodegarius adorns the sixth day before the Nones,  
> Whom the duke and people, mighty in sedition, put to death.”

Up to this point our text has flowed from Ado. Serenus occupies the final place; he is first recorded by Usuard from private information, and is omitted in the modern Roman Martyrology, perhaps because he was not found in Belinus, or because he was insufficiently known to its revisers, since Usuard indicated him only by name. Maurolycus correctly assigned him to Castrum Cantumerulae, and I find the same noted in our manuscript Acts, which are in some respects very remarkable, with the French name *Chante-merle* added; this is an abbey of Canons Regular of the Order of Saint Augustine. Castellanus, otherwise a most diligent investigator of the names of persons, saints, and places, and their Latinizer—pardon the barbarous term—neglected this on this day in his universal Martyrology, where he states that Serenus is especially honored at Montier-la-Celle, not far from the city of Troyes. He evidently assumed that the monastery of Celle, or a monastery named from a *cella*, would readily present itself. To speak more clearly, understand the priory of Celle, of the Order of Saint Benedict, [Col. 0532C] situated one quarter of a league from the aforesaid abbey of Cantumerula. This is sufficient, according to our purpose, for knowledge of the saint.]

[Note: [Col. 0531C]]

**Tournai.** Lacks the first announcement concerning the Nicomedian martyrs; in all other respects it is entirely sound.

**Rosweyd.** Fairly sound in the first and second announcements; omits the third.

**Pursanne.** In the first it is mutilated, with everything after *innumeris* (“innumerable”) deleted. Sound in the other two.

**Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, Ughellian, and Antwerp-Major.** Fairly sound in the first and second; they nevertheless have Leodegarius’s location from Ado. In place of the third they read:

> “On the same day, Saint Gerinus the martyr, brother of the blessed Leodegarius. At Antioch, the feast of Saints Primus, Quirillus, and Secundianus.”

The Roman Martyrology treats these men.

**Muneratus.** For the text derived from Ado and our text, he reads:

> “After having had his eyes torn out and his tongue and lips cut off, since he did not cease preaching the word of God, Ebroinus, mayor of the royal household, had him beheaded.”

For Serenus he has *Severus*.

**Molanus.** Improperly inserts into the text: “In the territory of Arras,” and, in italics, “the village of Siricinium,” from Ado. But his principal defect is that he has deleted the final announcement.

**Louvain.** Similar to Antwerp-Major, Lübeck, etc., except that it is truncated in the first section.

**Alberg.** Has the entire text, as Antwerp, etc. But it prefixes:

> “At Rome, the feast of Saint Eusebius, pope and martyr. He was the thirty-second after the blessed Peter. In his time the Lord’s cross was found at Jerusalem on the fifth day before the Nones of May, and Judas was baptized, to whom the name Quiriacus was later given.”

In the Roman Martyrology he is placed on 26 September. See Castellanus’s note there.

**Utrecht, Leiden, and Danish.** Prefix to these:

> “In the city of Assisi, the translation of Saint Clare the virgin.”

In the Danish manuscript these words are out of order and, so far as appears, were added by another hand.

**Centule.**

> “At Nicomedia, Saint Eleutherius the martyr. In the territory of Arras, the passion of Saint Leodegarius, bishop and martyr of Autun. On the same day, Saint Serenus the confessor. Also on that day, Saint …”

The name is missing and has been added in a smaller, more recent hand as *Huini*—perhaps *Gerinus* was intended—concerning whom see above.

**Brussels** begins:

> “In the territory of Arras, at the village of Siricinium, the passion of Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun. For the justice of truth he was first confined in the monastery of Luxon; recalled from there, he was captured, and Ebroinus, mayor of the royal household, ordered him beheaded after his eyes had been torn out and his tongue and lips cut off. His merit was made manifest after death by many miracles. On the same day, Saint Gerinus the martyr, brother of the blessed Leodegarius. Ebroinus killed him by burying him beneath stones. At Rome, the feast of Saint Eusebius, pope and confessor. In his time, as he himself writes in his letter, the Holy Cross was found; and therefore he instituted that the Finding of the Holy Cross should solemnly be celebrated on the fifth day before the Nones of May.”

What follows concerning Eleutherius and his Nicomedian companions is sound. At the end:

> “At Antioch, the feast of Saints Primus, Quirillus, and Secundianus.”

Then follows Serenus, also sound.

**Hagenoy.**

> “At Rome, the feast of Saint Eusebius, pope and martyr. He was the thirty-second after the blessed Peter, and suffered under the persecution of Diocletian. In his time the Holy Cross of the Lord is believed to have been found at Jerusalem on the fifth day before the Nones of May; he himself also established that day as a celebration for Christians, and Judas, who was also called Quiriacus, was baptized.”

In the section on Eleutherius it is fairly sound. It has a long history of Leodegarius, which may be read more faithfully in Surius. Then:

> “On the same day, Gerinus, brother of Saint Leodegarius the martyr, whom that same Ebroinus ordered, after he had been bound to a stake, to be buried under stones. Also Saint Apollinaris, bishop and martyr.”

The location is lacking.

**Daveron, Codex Castri-Caroli, Gollian, and Caudiac.** At the end they write somewhat more briefly: “Saint Serenus the confessor.”

**Chartreuse-Utrecht Matriculary.**

> “Leodegarius, bishop and martyr. Eleutherius the martyr, at Nicomedia with many others.”

In Vatican manuscript 5949 Serenus is absent. It adds:

> “At Benevento, the feast of Saint Modestus, levite and martyr. At Rome, the feast of Saint Eusebius, pope, who sat in the episcopate for two years.”

**Florence.**

> “At Antioch, Saints Primus, Cyrillus, and Secundianus the martyrs. Saint Eusebius the pope.”

[Col. 0533B]

**Lübeck-Cologne edition.**

> “At Rome, the feast of Saint Eusebius, pope and confessor, who sat in the episcopate for seven years. He was the thirty-second after the blessed Peter. In his time there was found,” etc.

In the sections on Eleutherius and Leodegarius it is fairly sound:

> “Also Saint Gerinus the martyr, brother of the aforesaid blessed bishop Leodegarius. At Antioch, the feast of Saints Primus, Quirillus, and Secundianus the martyrs. At Assisi, the translation of Saint Clare the virgin, of the Order of Friars Minor. In England, Saint Thomas, bishop and confessor. At Castrum Cantumerulae, the blessed Serenus, monk and confessor. The showing-forth of Saint Maximus, bishop of Riez and confessor.”

**Belinus.** In the section on Eleutherius he gives Julian instead of Diocletian and, besides many other errors, omits the announcement of Serenus. After *interfecit* (“killed”) he adds:

> “On the same day, Saint Gerinus the martyr, brother of the blessed Leodegarius. At Antioch, Primus, Quirillus, and Secundianus. On the same day, the translation of Saint Clare the virgin.”

More clearly above, and in Greven.

**Greven.**

> “At Antioch, Primus, Quirillus, and Secundianus. In Tuscany, Colmerus, bishop and martyr. [Col. 0534A] At Rome, the blessed Eusebius, pope and confessor. Theylaidius, abbot and martyr. In England, Saint Thomas, bishop and confessor of Hereford, renowned for his life and miracles.”

See Castellanus’s marginal note in the universal Martyrology.

> “Also Saint Garinus the martyr, brother of the blessed Leodegarius, bishop, whom the vile apostate Ebroinus, brought back from exile, ordered to be buried beneath stones. Beregisius the confessor. Also Gericus, of blessed memory, duke of Savoy and confessor. The showing-forth of Saint Maximus, bishop of Riez and confessor. At Assisi, the translation of Saint Clare the virgin.”

**Molanus.** At the end, after *interfecit*, he adds:

> “His body rests at Bronn. At Binche, the translation of Ursmar and others from old chests into new ones. On the same day, Saint Gerinus the martyr, brother of the blessed Leodegarius. At Antioch, Primus, Quirillus, and Secundianus. On the same day, the translation of Saint Clare the virgin. On that same day, Saint Serenus the confessor. At the monastery of Dain, the feast of Saint Beregisius, abbot.”

Then, in smaller type: [Col. 0534B]

> “He took up the habit of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Saint Trudo.”

Concerning Thomas of Hereford, from Greven. Other editions agree with the earlier one in the text, in the section on Gerinus, and in that on the Antiochene saints. Then:

> “At the monastery of Andain, the feast of the blessed Beregisius, abbot. He was born in the village of Condé among the Austrasians and was educated in letters within the monastery of Saint Trudo in Hasbaye. When he had been elevated to a position in the household of Pepin the Younger, he desired the solitary life more earnestly. It happened that Plectrude, the wife of that ruler, was passing through the forest of the Ardennes; and behold, she saw a little tablet fall among the rocks, on which was written that the place had been chosen by God and that many souls of the faithful were to be directed from there into heaven. Beregisius willingly offered himself, took possession of the place, cleared it, built a monastery, and gathered many there, by his example, for a good life.”

Concerning Serenus, as above.

> “In England, Saint Thomas, bishop of Hereford and confessor. At Assisi, the translation of Saint Clare the virgin. Among the Morini, the showing-forth of Saint Maximus, bishop of Riez and confessor.”]

[Col. 0529]

At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Eleutherius the martyr, with innumerable others, of whom, at the command of the emperor Diocletian, some were beheaded with swords, others burned in fires, and others thrown into the sea. But Eleutherius, the first of these, after enduring prolonged tortures and becoming stronger through each successive torment, completed the martyrdom of his victory, tested by fire like gold. In the territory of Adartum, the passion of the blessed Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, whom Ebroinus, mayor of the royal household, killed after he had been afflicted with various injuries and different punishments for the sake of truth. On the same day, Saint Serenus the confessor.

## V Nones. Day 3

[Note: [Col. 0533C]]

So read Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, and Max-Lübeck. Muneratus, Belinus, Greven, and Molanus. [Col. 0534C] Antwerp-Max, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, and Danish are added.

[Note: [Col. 0533D]]

I pass over Dionysius, Aristides, Aristodes, and similar matters. There is variation in Aristides’ eulogy: Greven and Molanus express it as “a man of faith and wisdom”; Antwerp has “a man of wisdom and faith.” Belinus and Max-Lübeck omit “faith”; the reading in the text is sound. Muneratus has *complevit* (“completed”) instead of *composuit* (“composed”). According to our usual practice, the reading should be *Ewaldorum*, as found in Antwerp-Major, Max-Lübeck, Greven, and Molanus. Pratensis and Heriniensis write *Euualdorum*, which amounts to the same thing but is less correctly written. Antwerp has *Egualdorum*; Belinus, *Eugualdorum*. [Col. 0534D] The sense seems to require “to their bodies,” as found in Antwerp and Belinus from Bede, Ado, and others, or “over whose bodies,” as in Muneratus. Nevertheless, we follow the better manuscripts Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Greven, and Molanus, from which the text is derived. Muneratus abridged the final part of the sentence, including “and whose they were,” etc. The others have “to Ursus Pilleatus,” which nearly all write in this way; Belinus perhaps more correctly deleted those words.

It is surprising that Usuard, in today’s entry, omitted the designation “Areopagite,” since it is evident from the text itself that the subject is none other than that famous Athenian bishop. The entry derives from Ado, both here and in the feasts of the apostles, and ultimately and most clearly from the Short Roman Martyrology. The Hieronymian Martyrologies say nothing of the Areopagite, nor do Bede, Florus, or Rabanus. [Col. 0534D] We have indicated the source of the text, and so certain is it that no learned person today would dare defend Hilduin’s opinions, so openly rejected by Ado and Usuard, his contemporaries—whatever Wandalbertus, also a contemporary, may appear to do in following Hilduin when he celebrates that Dionysius on 9 October:

> “The teacher of learned Gaul, blessed, instructed by Paul,  
> Whom Gaul deserved as a blessed teacher, instructed by Paul, adorned and joined to a twofold minister.”

[Col. 0535A]

We are dealing with a matter well known even to the general body of scholars, in which Baronius is repeatedly contradicted. He seems to have followed Hilduin both in his Notes and in the *Annals* at the year 109, number 38 onward. I think it will be welcome if I present here to the curious reader Rosweyd’s observation in a manuscript letter often cited elsewhere. It shows that this most learned man had long before observed what so many others in the same century confirmed by their judgments.

He first reports all the words of Usuard from Belinus, expressed here in the text, and adds:

> “I am surprised that these things were omitted from Baronius’s Roman Martyrology, since they were displayed in Belinus’s Martyrology a hundred years ago. What is more, did not the Roman Church believe this a thousand years ago? For the old Roman Martyrology, which I once prefixed to Ado’s Martyrology in the Moretian edition—where Rosweyd’s own note may also be seen on page 219—clearly presents it thus: ‘At Athens, Dionysius the Areopagite, who suffered under Hadrian through various tortures, as Aristides testifies in the work he composed concerning the Christian religion.’ [Col. 0535B] This work is held among the Athenians as one of the most renowned memorials of antiquity. The same account is found in the spurious Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Notker; consequently, it ought reasonably to be considered whether this Dionysius the Areopagite should be left in his proper place with so many accompanying witnesses, especially since the Greek *Menologion* and the *Menaea* likewise present Dionysius the Areopagite on this day. Now, since these same authors place Dionysius of Paris on another day, namely 9 October, who can doubt that they distinguished Dionysius the Areopagite from the Parisian? Therefore, in Baronius’s text for 9 October, where Dionysius of Paris is discussed, it seems that, in order to establish conformity among the ancient Martyrologies—the Roman Martyrology of Gregory the Great’s time, Belinus’s Roman Martyrology of a hundred years ago, Usuard, Ado, and Notker—the word ‘Areopagite’ should be deleted, as should ‘by Blessed Clement,’ since these expressions were inserted and forced in by later writers. All the most ancient Roman Martyrologies at Rome may be consulted. I do not think that any can be found from before the time of Hilduin the abbot that presents Dionysius the Areopagite on 9 October. Perhaps, if Baronius had seen the old Roman Martyrology prefixed to Ado’s, which he desired so greatly, he would have adopted another opinion.”

Thus far Rosweyd. Castellanus’s very brief but highly plausible observation in the universal Martyrology should also be consulted. From all these sources it is clear that the Dionysian monks constructed—though incorrectly, whether one should call it a confusion or a distinction of several Dionysiuses—a theory already abundantly refuted by the Short Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, and Notker. Anyone wishing to pursue the matter further should consult Papebrochius’s *Responsiones*, article XI, entire paragraph 4.

Concerning the Ewalds, Euualds, or Egualds—we have explained elsewhere in sufficient detail the etymology of such names and the change of the letter *w* into *g*—Bede speaks clearly in his Martyrology; Rabanus, Ado, Usuard, and Notker follow and transcribe him, although the last two express the story somewhat more briefly. [Col. 0536B] They are not known in the Hieronymian Martyrologies or the Short Roman Martyrology. Wandalbertus sings:

> “The Ewalds, equal in merits, race, surname, altar, and teaching,  
> Dedicated the fifth day to themselves by death.”

The sequence of their Acts will be clarified from Bede. Meanwhile, Castellanus’s brief note deserves attention; some manuscripts touch on it in the appendices. Here again the source of Usuard’s text is evident. But where did that Candidus of Ursus Pilleatus come from? I find him nowhere. There is indeed, in some Hieronymian manuscripts, a commemoration of Candida or Candidus on this day; but from where Usuard took the location “at Ursus Pilleatus,” since we know no Acts of this saint, is uncertain. Rosweyd thought that the material added to Ado by Mosander from the Hieronymian manuscripts should more plausibly be distinguished from Ado’s text.]

[Note: [Col. 0535C]]

**Tournai.** Reports the first entry only up to “he was crowned”; the second part is missing. It omits the second entry entirely and is sound in the third. At the end it adds:

> “In the district of Dulcomium, Saint Juvinus the confessor.”

**Rosweyd.** Fairly sound in the first. In the second he is closer to Bede than to Usuard, inserting:

> “Coming into Germany with Saint Willibrord, they began to preach to the Saxons; they were seized by the pagans and killed,” etc.

**Centule.** Fairly sound in the first; in the second it cuts away the entire eulogy. For *Ewaldorum* it writes *Guandolorum*. The third is also missing.

**Alberg.** Before a fairly sound text it prefixes:

> “In the monastery of Werden, the translation of Saint Ludger, the first bishop and confessor of Münster. He himself founded this monastery with divine assistance. There, by a revelation from the Lord, he also foresaw that he would await the final day.”

**Centule.**

> “The feast of Saint Dionysius, bishop and martyr. Among the ancient Saxons, two holy presbyter martyrs, both named Ewald, who were killed by the pagans for preaching the word of God.”

In the last section it is sound.

**Brussels** begins:

> “Among the ancient Saxons, the two holy Ewalds, presbyters, one of whom was called Ewald the White and the other Ewald the Black. Coming from England into Germany with the blessed bishop Willibrord, they crossed over to the Saxons; and when they had begun there to preach Christ, they were killed by the pagans. A pillar of light appearing at night over their bodies revealed where they were and what their merit was; and by order of Pepin they were buried at Cologne. On the same day, the feast of the blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop and martyr. Instructed by the apostle Paul, he believed in Christ and was the first bishop ordained by that apostle at [probably ‘Athens,’ but the word was erased and another hand wrote] Corinth; after the most grievous kinds of torture, under the glorious emperor Hadrian, he received a glorious martyrdom,” etc.

Then:

> “At Rome, at Ursus Pilleatus, the feast of Saint Candidus the martyr. On the same day, the elevation of Saint Ludger, bishop, renowned for his virtues. And the burial of Lord Madulitus, bishop of Verdun.”

Castellanus has Madelveus on the following day.

**Hagenoy.** Fairly sound in the first; in the second, after “the Saxons,” it inserts “who are now called Frisians.” Then:

> “At Antioch, the feast of the holy martyrs Primus, Quirillus, and Secundianus.”

See the preceding day. A long history of Nicetius of Trier follows; enough has already been said about him at 1 October. Finally:

> “In England, Saint Thomas, bishop and confessor.”

See also the preceding day.

**Chartreuse-Utrecht Matriculary.**

> “The two Ewald martyrs. Gerard, first a soldier and later an abbot. Dionysius, bishop and martyr.”

**Augsburg.**

> “In the district of Dulcomium, Saint Vivinus the confessor.”

Tournai has Juvinus, elsewhere Jovinus.

**Swedish Register**, numbered 428:

> “Also on the same day, Saint Francis the confessor.”

See the following day.

**Florence.**

> “Also Saints Victor and Spargius the martyrs.”

See the Hieronymian manuscripts and the note of the Florentine manuscript.

**Luxeuil.**

> “The burial of Saint Madalnus, bishop and confessor of Verdun.”

As I have already said from Castellanus, he is better called Madelveus and is honored on the following day. These matters will be discussed more fully in their proper place.

**Caudiac.**

> “At Saint Andrew of the Elms, the arrival of Saint Ragnobert, soldier and martyr.”

Castellanus places him on 13 June; he is also found among our appendices on that day, but in the Acts he is referred to 15 July. The reason will be given later.

**Dijon.**

> “The feast of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, who, instructed by the apostle Paul, believed in Christ.”

**Reims, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris.**

> “In the suburb of Reims, the feast of Saint Jovinus the confessor.”

**Abdinghof.**

> “On the same day, the arrival of the body of the blessed Felix the martyr.”

I do not know which Felix is meant among the many saints of that name.

**Lübeck-Cologne edition.**

> “Among the ancient Saxons, the feast of the two holy martyr brothers Ewald. Since they were presbyters and had begun there to preach Christ, they were seized by the pagans, killed, and thrown into the Rhine. Over their bodies a great light appeared at night for a long time, revealing where they were and what their merit was. The current did not swallow their bodies, but, flowing back for almost forty thousand paces, carried them, accompanied by divine light, to Cologne, where the bodies of the saints were buried with fitting veneration by Pepin, duke of the Franks, who at that time governed the Roman realm, together with all the clergy, in the church of Saint Clement beside the Rhine. Also, among the ancient Saxons, Saint Willibrord, bishop and martyr.”

What follows concerning Dionysius and Candidus is sound. Then:

> “Among the Warins, the blessed Gandulphus the confessor. On the same day, Saints Felix and Castus the martyrs. On that same day, the burial of Saint Madalnus, bishop and confessor of Verdun.”

Concerning the translation of Saint Ludger, it has the same account as Alberg above.

**Greven.**

> “Among the ancient Saxons, Saint Willibrord, bishop and martyr.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition likewise placed this above, but I know no other Willibrord than that famous bishop and confessor of Utrecht, who is honored on 7 November.

> “In Africa, Victor, Urbanus, and Spargius. And elsewhere, Felix, Ammonius, and Castus. At Antioch, Cheugenus.”

In the Hieronymian manuscripts he is called Thugenus, Theugenes, Theogenes, and so forth.

> “Gerard, abbot of Bronn and confessor. Among the Warins, the blessed Gandulphus the confessor. Scopilio, archpriest and confessor. At the monastery of Werden, the translation of Saint Ludger, the first bishop of Münster and confessor, founder of the aforesaid monastery, where, by revelation of the Lord, he foresaw that he would await the day of the general resurrection.”

See his feast in the Acts on 26 March.

**Molanus.**

> “And in the monastery of Bronn, the feast and translation of Saint Gerard, abbot, who, after temporal military service, was devotedly enlisted in the service of Christ and became the founder of this monastery by the command of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Later, with Christ as author, he became father and abbot of six monasteries. His body rests at Bronn. In the district of Dulcrimium, Saint Juvinus the confessor.”

Later editions report the same things as the first, adding only:

> “At Moson, the feast of the blessed Arnulf the martyr.”

They differ from the earlier edition in that they place the announcement of Dionysius after the appendix, inserting the surname “Areopagite” in italics. I leave it to others to judge whether a sufficient explanation of such frequent variations is given in the preface to these editions. Here, at least, the correction has been added quite appropriately.]

[Col. 0533]

The feast of the blessed Dionysius, bishop and martyr, who, after the most illustrious confession of faith and after the gravest kinds of torture, was crowned with a glorious martyrdom, as Aristides of Athens testifies—a man remarkable for faith and wisdom—in the work he composed concerning the Christian religion. Among the ancient Saxons, the two holy martyr Ewalds, who, being presbyters and having begun there to preach Christ, were seized by the pagans and killed; over their bodies a great light appeared by night for a long time, revealing where they were and what their merit was. At Rome, at Ursus Pilleatus, Saint Candidus the martyr.

## IV Nones. Day 4

[Note: [Col. 0537]]

Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Greven, and Molanus are sound.

[Note: [Col. 0537C]]

Heriniensis has *Corintum*, but correctly corrects himself to *Corinthiis*. He likewise writes *Martiani*, whereas the others agree with the text. Pratensis alone reads *cruciatus horribiles* (“horrible tortures”). In Antwerp-Major the words “and some were also beheaded” had been displaced; in their place stood *non sine etiam capite caesi* (“not without also being beheaded”). Nor did the person who deleted *non sine* and substituted *alii etiam* (“others also”), etc., produce a sound sense. Heriniensis wrote not badly *capite deorsum verso* (“with the head turned downward”), but better, with Ado, *capite deorsum presso* (“with the head pressed downward”). There, probably through a typographical error, Molanus has *quidem* (“indeed”) instead of *quidam* (“some”), and shortly before has *inedta* instead of *inedia* (“starvation”). He is overly scrupulous in *Parisiis* instead of *Parisius*. Concerning *Caii*, *Gaii*, *Gaji*, *Gagi*, and so forth, we have often spoken elsewhere: the manuscripts are not consistent.

Crispus, formerly ruler of the synagogue, is prominently mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 18. Gaius is described as the apostle’s host in the final chapter of the Epistle to the Romans. I believe the reason for associating the two is that they alone are said by the apostle to have been baptized by him, in 1 Corinthians 1. From that passage, for the most part, what can certainly be said in their praise must be extracted.

Their first mention in the Martyrologies is owed to the Short Roman Martyrology, where they are simply recorded: “At Corinth, Crispus and Gaius.” What is added here in the text was appended by Ado, fully described by Our author, and almost fully by Notker, while the things which Ado seems to have mixed in elsewhere in the feasts of the apostles are omitted. It is plausible that three Gaiuses, disciples of the apostles, must be distinguished: this one, Paul’s host, in Romans chapter 16; another from Derbe, also Paul’s disciple, clearly distinguished in Acts chapter 20; and a third, to whom John addresses his Third Epistle. Some think that Ado went astray here by confusing the last with the first, and that the spurious Bede and hence Molanus inserted this confusion into their texts. But what if someone should doubt whether a fourth ought also to be added, the one mentioned with Aristarchus in Acts chapter 19? These matters belong to another place and investigation.

Marcus and Marcianus are expressly placed in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and are distinguished from Marcus and Marcellianus by so many identifying features that it is astonishing that they could have been confused. Rabanus writes *Marti et Mauriciani*, which we attribute to the carelessness of copyists. The Short Roman Martyrology says briefly:

> “In Egypt, Marcus and Marcianus, brothers, with an innumerable multitude.”

Ado’s encomium is evidently drawn from Eusebius, book 8, chapter 8. In Eusebius all those glorious athletes are anonymous, as are those enumerated by the same Eusebius in the following chapter. Nevertheless, the application made by Ado to these two martyrs is so widely accepted that, so far as I have discovered, no one has yet called it into question. Usuard and Notker followed it; Usuard more elegantly contracted the wording in the text, while Notker substituted Marcellianus for Marcianus. Wandalbertus adorns only the brothers with these verses:

> “Marcus and Marcianus fulfill the fourth through their office,  
> Brothers in birth, martyrdom, nature, and burial.”

[Col. 0539A]

Aurea of Paris is purely Usuardine; she is unknown to all the other ancient Martyrologies, or at least passed over by them. Mosander himself recorded her among Ado’s additions together with Marsus of Auxerre. Saint Audoenus mentions her in the *Life of Saint Eligius*. From that work and from any other surviving monuments, those matters concerning her and her abbey, founded by Eligius at Paris in honor of Martial of Limoges, his countryman among the saints, later destroyed, and other related matters, can be elucidated in their proper place. Meanwhile, see the index of saints omitted in the second Benedictine century, page LVIII.]

[Note: [Col. 0539A]]

**Tournai.** Sound in the first and last sections; in the second, almost half is mutilated. In the margin: “On the same day, Francis the confessor.”

**Rosweyd.** Fairly sound in the text; he adds: “Also Saint Marsus the presbyter.”

**Pursanne.** Fairly sound in the first and third; in the second it has only up to “of either sex and every age,” with the rest missing.

**Antwerp and Max-Lübeck.** Both have the addition concerning Saint Francis, but the former reads: “On the same day, the burial of blessed Francis.” Max-Lübeck differs by omitting τὸ *depositio* (“the ‘burial’”) and adding *confessor*.

**Muneratus.** Begins:

> “At Assisi, the feast of the blessed Francis the confessor, founder or institutor of the Order of Friars Minor.”

The text follows. At the end, after the virgin Aurea, it adds:

> “Her body rests in the church of Saint Eligius, *prope palatii, Parisii* (‘near the palace, at Paris’).”

[Col. 0539B] Molanus corrects this to: “*prope palatium, Parisiis* (‘near the palace, at Paris’).”

**Antwerp-Max.** Comes fairly close to the sound text, prefixing only:

> “At Assisi, the feast of the blessed Francis the confessor, founder and first minister of the Order of Friars Minor.”

**Louvain.** Has the same, but is mutilated in the eulogy of the Egyptian martyrs.

**Utrecht, Leiden, Alberg, and Danish.** They place Saint Francis first:

> “At Assisi, the feast of the blessed Francis the confessor, founder and first minister of the Order of Friars Minor. To him irrational creatures showed wondrous obedience, as though recognizing that original innocence had been restored in a human being. He was carried by such desire toward God that those who were present saw him, while absorbed in the spirit of prayer, lifted above the earth with his whole body; and in prayer he therefore obtained the spirit of prophecy and revelation of hidden things. Two years before his blessed passing, after the course of his preaching, his desire for martyrdom, his zeal for souls, his excess of charity, and his title of poverty, when he gazed upon the crucified seraph, as he was moved by seraphic desires, he was bodily marked on his feet, hands, and right side with the stigmata of Jesus Christ.”

The rest is fairly sound.

**Centule.**

> “The feast of Saints Crispus and Gaius, whom the blessed Apostle recalls having baptized at Corinth. In Egypt, Saints Marcus and Marcianus, brothers, with whom innumerable men and women, as well as boys and old men, suffered for the faith of Christ. At Auxerre, Saint Marsus the presbyter and confessor. At Paris, Saint Aurea, virgin and abbess.”

**Brussels.**

> “At Assisi, the burial of the blessed Francis, confessor and founder of the Order of Friars Minor. Two years before his blessed passing, he was bodily marked on his feet, hands, and side with the stigmata of Jesus Christ.”

The first and second announcements follow and are fairly sound. Then:

> “In the city of Paris, the burial of the blessed Aurea, virgin, whom the blessed Eligius placed over the monastery of girls that he himself built there.”

**Hagenoy.** Fairly sound in the first and second; it omits the third, replacing it with:

> “At Assisi, the burial of the blessed Francis the confessor, founder of the Friars Minor, etc.”

The wording above from Utrecht and the others is more polished.

**Aquicinct.** At the end, in a recent hand:

> “On the same day, Saint Francis the confessor.”

See above, Utrecht and the others.

**Daveron.**

> “In the district of Tours, Saint Quintinus the martyr.”

See Castellanus’s universal Martyrology concerning this martyr of chastity.

**Chartreuse-Utrecht Matriculary.**

> “Francis the confessor. Aurea the virgin, abbess at Paris. In Egypt, Marcus and Marcianus, brothers, with innumerable others who suffered in various ways.”

**Ughellian.**

> “Also Saint Francis the confessor.”

**Florence.**

> “Saint Francis … Also Saint Petronius, bishop and confessor.”

**Reims, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris.**

> “At Auxerre, Saint Marsus [it intended Marsus] the presbyter and confessor.”

The Lubeck–Cologne edition begins:

“Near Trier, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Tyrsius, commander of the most sacred legion of the three hundred Thebans, and of Saint Boniface. The Emperor Maximian Herculius, because of the frequent disturbances of the Gauls, summoned Theban soldiers from the East as auxiliaries. These Thebans were baptized by the bishop of Jerusalem and instructed by the blessed Pope Marcellinus [Col. 0540B] how, under Roman arms, they ought to preserve Christian innocence. The prefect of the city, Rictiovarus, asked them whether they wished to worship the gods of the Romans and defeat their detractors by force of arms. When Tyrsus, commander of the legion, replied that he and all his companions and soldiers preferred to die for the love of Christ rather than be defiled by such sacrilege, Rictiovarus then spread the soldiers throughout the entire field and ordered them all to be killed, leaving their bodies to be devoured by wild beasts and birds. This multitude of soldiers was therefore martyred on the bank of the Moselle near the capitol, which was later dedicated in honor of Mary, the Mother of God and ever-Virgin; and that place, in memory of the martyrs, received the name ‘Bank of the Martyrs.’”

What follows concerning Francis is as in the Utrecht edition and elsewhere above. The entire text then is sufficiently pure. Concerning Quintinus, as in the Daveron edition. At the end: “At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Marsus, priest and confessor.” See what was said above concerning the Reims manuscript.

[Col. 0540C] Belin:

“In the city of Assisi, the commemoration of blessed Francis the confessor, founder of the Order of Friars Minor. After the order he founded had been wonderfully multiplied and spread more widely throughout the world, he spent twenty years leading a celibate life in it; then he was led from the prison-house of the flesh amid this world's misery to the heavenly homeland.”

Join this with the Utrecht edition and the others.

Greven has little concerning the people of Trier, but we have said enough about them. Concerning Quintinus, as above:

“On this day, according to the Catalogue, Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor, concerning whom it is related in the Acts of Saint Mark the Evangelist that, when he was a shoemaker and was repairing the blessed Mark’s shoe, he pierced his own hand. But he was healed by Saint Mark and ordained a priest. He displayed such great faith that he is said to have moved a mountain. Afterwards ordained bishop, he rested in peace; later transferred to Venice, he is preserved buried in the monastery of Saint Clement.” See the Treatise on the Alexandrian Patriarchs before volume V of the June collection.

“Saint Madalveus, bishop of Verdun and confessor. Also Saint Petronius, bishop of Bologna and confessor, who is said to have written the Lives of the Fathers. In the Spoletan valley, near the city of Assisi, etc.” This is somewhat shorter than the Utrecht edition and others, where it is said that he died in the year 1224.

“At Auxerre, Saint Marsus, priest and confessor, a Roman by nationality. Saint Dasius the confessor.”

Molanus, after writing about Crispus and Caius, inserts the following in different type:

“Caius is mentioned by the same Apostle in the Letter to the Romans: ‘Gaius, my host and that of the whole Church, greets you,’ he says. Blessed John also mentions him when writing his Epistle: ‘The elder to the most beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth.’”

At the end, concerning Aurea, he adds the words of Muneratus; concerning Francis, he reports Belin’s words, adding only after “was led away”: “in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1226”; and:

“His illustrious life, full of miracles, is described by Bonaventure. Also at Trier, Saints Tyrsus and his companions, under the governor Rictiovarus.”

Then, in smaller type, concerning Quintinus, as above. The following then succeeds:

“Baptista Mantuanus, in the Ecclesiastical Fasti, book X:”

This same light, most renowned Petronius,  
Chief of the Flaminian race, is consecrated to your Felsina,  
Which once was accustomed to be the Tuscan capital  
Of the Empire and preserves monuments of praise; you were  
Both father and shepherd, most worthy of so great a city, etc.

Thus far the first and purer edition. In later editions, the commemoration of Saint Francis is printed in Italic type and placed first. Concerning Caius, the material given above is added. At the end, concerning Aurea and Tyrsus, likewise as above. Then:

“At Bologna, Saint Petronius, bishop and confessor.”

What follows concerning Quintinus is as in the first edition. Then:

“At Verdun, Saint Madalveus, eminent bishop and confessor.”

We have already said more than once that this should be read as Madelveus. “On the fourth day, Saint Hierotheus, bishop of Athens.” See Castellani’s note; if it is accurate, this entry must be removed both here and from the Roman Martyrology.]

[Col. 0537]

At Corinth, the commemoration of the blessed Crispus and Caius, whom Saint Paul the Apostle mentions in writing to the Corinthians. In Egypt, Saints Mark and Marcian, brothers, and countless others with them, of no lesser glory, of both sexes and every age.
