Some of them, after scourging and horrible tortures of various kinds, were handed over to the flames; others were thrown into the sea; some were beheaded; very many were consumed by hunger; others were fastened to gallows; and some, with their heads pressed downward and their feet raised aloft, merited the most blessed crown of martyrdom. At Paris, Saint Aurea, virgin.

III Non. Day 5.

[Note: [Col. 0541]

The pure manuscripts are Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0541B]

Only Pratensis writes “Syciliam”; only Antwerp-Major has “Ceciliam.” In the Antwerp manuscript there is “Placiti,” as some Hieronymian manuscripts have it; Max-Lübeck is full of scribal errors. Eutychius is rendered in various ways, while the others have Euticius, supported by the majority of witnesses—namely Rosweyd, Greven, Tournai, and so on. Pratensis has Eutichii; Herinien, Euthici; the Antwerp manuscripts, Eutici; Muneratus, Ethici; only Molanus correctly has Eutici. The same issue recurs with Thrasea, whose name I formed from Pratensis, Herinien, Greven, and Molanus. In the others it appears as Traciae, Tarseae, Tharseae, Transeae, and so on. [Col. 0542B] Again, I wrote “Smyrna” simply on the basis of almost all the manuscripts, except Pratensis and likewise Molanus. I read “whose life and virtues,” contrary to Pratensis and Herinien, who omit the conjunction “and,” which Usuardus certainly seems to have taken from Ado, from whom he derived everything else. I do not know why Greven and Molanus deleted “saints” before “brothers,” just as Rosweyd deleted “blessed” before “Thrasea.” Nothing need be said about “Nichilominus, deacon,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0541B]

The Lucan and Corbie Hieronymian manuscripts, both in manuscript form and in the edition published by Acherius, explicitly read: “In Sicily, Placidus—or Placitus—Eutychius, and thirty others.” The Epternacensis appears mutilated, since it records only: “Eutychius and eight others.” Rabanus agrees with the latter in the name, but in the number of anonymous companions agrees with the others. Here Florentinius twists himself about in various ways, as though smoothing out spirals, convolutions, winding passages—in fact, a labyrinth of errors—which arose from the pseudo-Gordian Acts. How difficult this was, Baronius clearly recognized in the year 529, number 10, and elsewhere. Even the Benedictines themselves now admit that the source from which Maurolycus and others drew was wholly turbid and muddy; so much so that Theodoric Ruinart, in the recently published Appendix to the Apology of the Mission of Saint Maurus, took an entirely different path to preserve the cult of Placidus, the disciple of Benedict.

No method is more expedient than distinguishing one Placidus from the other. It certainly seems indisputable that none of the ancient Martyrologists, when they mention Placidus, Eutychius, and their anonymous companions, even remotely imagined that they were monks, much less Benedictines. Those writers, who were themselves monks, would surely not have failed to indicate this, as they do everywhere else, despite Ruinart’s futile and timid protest here. Castellanus observed that an interpolation had been made in the modern Roman Martyrology, probably from Maurolycus’s abridgment of the Acts; this interpolation was subsequently altered more than once, as will become clear to anyone who compares even the Plantinian editions alone. Belin was the first to make Placidus himself a disciple of Benedict, while leaving the rest of the text untouched. But this too is disproved by its novelty, since, among the very large number of our manuscripts—most of them written by Benedictine monks—not a single one can be found in which even a syllable has been added to Usuardus’s wording.

Meanwhile, nothing is read about Placidus or his companions in Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Florus, or Wandalbert. Our author copies Ado’s words; Notker slightly abbreviates them. Moreover, Acherius and Mabillon have tried to free the aforementioned Acts from their atrocious errors. On these matters, see Papebrochius’s brief Responses to article XI, numbers 238 and 239. We reserve the rest for its proper place.

Concerning Thrasea, the author of the Little Roman Martyrology is the first today to mention him, following his usual source, Rufinus, book V, chapter 24: “At Eumenia, Thrasea, bishop, crowned at Smyrna, who was one of the ancients.” Ado expanded this somewhat from Eusebius; Usuardus and Notker then took it from him. It is not entirely certain whether the words of our text accurately convey Rufinus’s meaning. For Polycrates speaks differently in Eusebius: he does not assert that Thrasea was brought to completion through martyrdom at Smyrna, but that he is—or was—at rest, κεκοίμηται, where Rufinus simply translates “brought to completion.” But more on this elsewhere.

In the Viennese manuscript, Apollinaris precedes the entry with a eulogy that has been transferred verbatim into our text; Notker, as immediately above, shortens it moderately. Surius published some material about this saint, but in due time we shall produce more certain evidence from other records. I think Ado took Apollinaris from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; from these he also passed more accurately into Rabanus, together with the final commemoration of the brothers of Auxerre. [Col. 0542D] Whether Florentinius is right, on his own authority, to identify these saints from additions made by a Gallic antiquarian is not sufficiently clear to me. Nor do I understand why Rosweyd deprived Ado of this final commemoration, which he could have taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies just as he took the immediately preceding one. Castellanus conjectures that this Flaviana, changed into Flavia—as she is otherwise called—was added to the Sicilian martyrs, among whom was also her brother Firmatus; similarly Victorinus and Faustus are expressly placed with the conjunction “and elsewhere” in the Hieronymian copies. I do not know why, in the final Plantinian edition of the Roman Martyrology, dated 1701, [Col. 0543A] Firmatus of Auxerre is called Firmanus. This will suffice for the present. But what does Wandalbertus mean when he composes these verses about Apollinaris, which would more properly refer to 23 July, although he also mentions Apollinaris there?

On the third Nones Apollinaris is honored,  
The bishop whose frequent temples Ravenna crowns.

] [Note: [Col. 0543A]

The Tournai manuscript would be counted among the pure ones if the words “completed in martyrdom at Smyrna” were not missing.

The Pulsan manuscript is pure in its first two commemorations, but is entirely deficient in the final two.

Antwerp-Major and Leuven are pure in the first, third, and fourth entries. They render the second as follows: “At Smyrna, Saint Thrasea, bishop of Eumenia and martyr, whom the fifth book of Ecclesiastical History mentions.” See Ado’s text below.

Utrecht, Leiden, Alberg, and Danish have the same addition, but further append: “He was one of the ancients and claimed to have received, as if from the tradition of his predecessors, that the Savior had commanded the Apostles not to depart from Jerusalem before the twelfth year.” These are Ado’s words, taken from Eusebius, book V, chapter 18.

Centule: “In Gaul, in the city of Valence, Saint [Col. 0543B] Apollinaris, bishop and confessor. Near Sicily, Saints Placidus, Eutychius, and thirty other martyrs. At Auxerre, Saints Firmatus, deacon, and Flavia, virgin consecrated to God.” Observe that “Flavia,” not “Flaviana,” is read here.

Brussels is pure in the first entry. It formulates the second as follows: “At Eumenia or Smyrna, blessed Thrasea, bishop and martyr, whom … mentions,” as above in Utrecht and the others. In the third, it slightly rearranges the construction. In the last, it is pure.

Hagenoyen is pure in the first and in the second is almost like Utrecht and the others, except that he makes Thrasea both a confessor and a martyr. In the third and fourth he is sufficiently pure. At the end he reports material belonging to the preceding day: “At Paris, the deposition of Saint Aurea, virgin.” See there.

The matricularies of the Carthusian Utrecht: “Placidus and Eutychius with thirty others. Firmatus the deacon and his sister.”

In the Vatican manuscript numbered 5949, the final commemoration of the people of Auxerre is absent.

[Col. 0543C] Florentinus:

“At Ravenna, Saint Marcellus [elsewhere Marcellinus], bishop of that city and confessor. At Iconium, blessed Thrasea, bishop.” Concerning Marcellinus of Ravenna, see Surius.

Abdinghof:

“On the same day, Saint Meinulfus the confessor”; others read Magenulfus. See Surius.

The Lubeck–Cologne edition:

“At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of the most holy father Severinus, archbishop and confessor of that city. This translation was carried out, at the prompting of an angel, by devout citizens of Cologne from the city of Bordeaux in Aquitania to Cologne, to the church of the holy martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian. The most blessed confessor of God, Severinus, had raised this church from its foundations, dedicated it in their honor during his lifetime, and established there a community of brothers in the love of Christ. God, who is always glorious in his saints, also adorned his translation with new miracles, as the account of the transfer of his body testifies.

At Trier, the passion of the holy martyrs Palmatius, consul and patrician of the city, with eleven princes whom the prefect of the city, Rictiovarus, ordered to be punished by the sword because they confessed the name of Jesus Christ. These are the names of the princes: Maxentius, Constantius, Crescentius, Justinus, Leander, Alexander, [Col. 0544A] Sother, Hermisda, Papirius, Constans, and Jovanius. Their bodies rest there in a crypt beside the body of Saint Paulinus, bishop and martyr.

In the territory of Paderborn, in the monastery of Bodeken, the deposition of Saint Maynulfus, deacon and confessor.”

The text that follows is as in Utrecht and the others. At the end: “On the same day, blessed Faustinus the confessor.”

Belin:

“Near Sicily, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Placidus the monk, the most blessed disciple of Benedict the abbot, Eutychius, and thirty others.”

He is sufficiently pure in the entries concerning Apollinaris and the people of Auxerre. At the end he places:

“At Iconium, blessed Thrasea, bishop, crowned with martyrdom at Smyrna.”

Greven:

“Note: Antoninus, part II, title 15, chapter 14, says that this Placidus was a disciple of Saint Benedict, whom Maurus had drawn from the waters, and that he was sent to Sicily to administer the possessions his father had bestowed on the monastery.

At Trier, the passion of the holy martyrs Palmatius, consul and patrician of that city, with eleven princes: Maxentius, Constantius, Crescentius, Justinus, Leander, Alexander, Sother, Hormisda, Papirius, Constans, and Jovinianus. Rictiovarus, prefect of the city, ordered all of them to be killed by the sword because they confessed the name of Christ.”

Concerning Severinus’s translation, he has almost the same account as above. Then:

“In the diocese of Paderborn, in the monastery of Budiken, Saint Meinulfus, deacon and confessor. In the time of Charlemagne, while distinguished by his life and miracles at the foundation of the church of Paderborn, he rested in a blessed death. Faustinus the confessor. Osytha, virgin and martyr.”

See Surius and Castellanus on 8 October.

“Galla, a most noble widowed religious woman, concerning whom Gregory, book IV of the Dialogues, reports that, after she had been widowed, physicians told her that unless she returned to the embraces of a man she would grow a beard; and this indeed happened. Fearing no outward deformity, she devoted herself to the service of almighty God, giving herself to simplicity of heart, prayer, and generous almsgiving. When the blessed Apostle Peter, whose face is of the most kindly appearance, appeared to her, she departed from this world.”

Molanus, after Placidus, inserts in the text, in different type:

“Monk of the most blessed Benedict the abbot.”

At the end:

“Also at Trier, the holy martyrs Palmatius and his companions, under the governor Rictiovarus. At Cologne, the translation of Saint Severinus, bishop.”

Then, in smaller type, concerning Meinulfus, as in Greven. Next:

“Galla, a most noble widowed religious woman, concerning whom Gregory speaks in book IV of the Dialogues. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Attilanus, bishop of Zamora, whom Pope Urban II enrolled among the saints after his death.”

See Surius. In other editions, the famous story of the pirate Manucha is additionally inserted concerning Placidus, sent by Abdallah, king of Spain—a person whom one will search for in vain among the Spanish historians. Concerning Thrasea, “whom he mentions,” etc. At the end, after “virgin,” “consecrated to God” is added. Concerning Palmatius, as in the earlier edition. Then:

“In the monastery of Budiken, in the diocese of Paderborn, Saint Meinulfus, deacon and confessor. At Zamora, the commemoration of Saint Attilanus, bishop, whom Urban II enrolled among the saints. On the fifth day, Saint Charitina, martyr.”

See the Menologion of Symeon Metaphrastes in Surius for this day.]

[Col. 0541]

Near Sicily, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Placidus, Eutychius, and thirty others. At Eumenia, blessed Thrasea, bishop, completed in martyrdom at Smyrna. In Gaul, in the city of Valence, Saint Apollinaris, bishop, whose life was distinguished by virtues and whose death likewise was adorned with signs and wonders. At Auxerre, the deposition of the holy siblings Firmatus, deacon, and Flaviana, virgin.

The day before the Nones. Day 6.

[Note: [Col. 0545]

Taken from Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus; also from Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Alberg, and Danish.]

[Note: [Col. 0545A]

All write simply “Emilius,” except Molanus, who has “Aemilius.” Tournai reads “saint” instead of “blessed Sagaris.” In the Pratensis copy one finds “Laudicensis,” perhaps through a copyist’s error; certainly neither “Laudicensis” nor “Laudunensis,” as Muneratus has it, is correct, since it appears certain that he was bishop where he died, namely at Laodicea. Muneratus says of him: “He was one of the disciples of the blessed Apostle Paul.” Among the intermediate manuscripts are some in which “Aginno” and likewise “Agynno” are read. I do not dispute whether our reading, which is older, is also purer and more accurate.]

[Note: [Col. 0545A]

The entire table for today is wholly and literally derived from Ado; Notker also copied it, with this difference: Our author moved Fides the virgin, placed second by Ado and Notker, into third place. Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Florus, and Wandalbert are silent about the Capuan martyrs. Rabanus reads only: “In Apulia, Castus and Emilius.” Our commemoration seems originally to have been taken by Ado from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, where almost the same words are read: “At Capua, the commemoration of Saints Marcellus, Castus, Emilius, and Saturninus”; and in certain copies the following is repeated lower down on this very day: “In Apulia, Castus, Emilius, Saturninus,” etc. [Col. 0545B] Other witnesses render the names differently. Florentinius tries to reconcile the discrepancies, but we have no time to linger over them here. Baronius’s conjecture is sufficiently plausible: it is based on the similarity of the names Castus and Aemilius among the Africans, whom we discussed on 22 May, whatever Ferrarius may object. These matters will be examined more fully in their proper place.

The second commemoration, if I am not mistaken, was taken from Rufinus and appears in the Little Roman Martyrology as follows: “Sagaris, bishop of Laodicea, one of the ancient disciples of the Apostle Paul.” The bishop of Vienne added little, apart from the title of martyr, which Polycrates suggested to him in the letter to Pope Victor cited on the preceding day, concerning the controversy over the observance of Easter in Eusebius, book V, chapter 24. There Polycrates cites Sagaris as evidence for the antiquity of the Asian custom and asserts that he died at Laodicea, placing him after Thrasea, whom we discussed yesterday. Yet I do not see either one proclaimed in that passage as an ancient disciple of the Apostle Paul.

The Hieronymian Martyrologies, Ado, Usuardus, and Notker most explicitly remember the virgin Fidis—not “Fidei”—using the same inflection. Rabanus alone reads “Fidei”; but the scribe Laurentius of the Epternacensis manuscript seems to have changed Fidem into Felicem and Agennum into Genua. [Col. 0546B] Her Acts have otherwise been published by several authors, most recently by Labbe in volume II of the Manuscript Library, beginning on page 528; Tillemont examined them with sufficient care in volume IV, beginning on page 543, and again in his notes beginning on page 752. There we observed that the matters concerning Caprasius and Vincent of Agen, who were likewise martyrs, should be joined together in our observations on 9 June. This is not the place either to examine or refute Tillemont’s criticism, since we shall illustrate all these matters more carefully in their proper time. Thus Wandalbertus sang of our Fides in a single hexameter:

The virgin Fides triumphs here yesterday by a blessed death.

] [Note: [Col. 0545C]

Antwerp-Major, in an otherwise sufficiently pure text, adds at the end:

“At Auxerre, Saint Romanus, bishop and martyr. On the same day at Lincoln, the translation of Saint Hugh, bishop and confessor.”

Rosweyd, pure in the text, adds:

“At Auxerre, Romanus, bishop and martyr.”

Pulsan is pure in the first two entries but deficient in the third, a characteristic of this manuscript that we have noted more than once elsewhere.

Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, and Ughellian begin as follows:

“At Rome, Saint Balbina, virgin.”

The rest is pure. I believe Balbina was inserted here from some Hieronymian manuscript in which she is recorded on this day. See Florentinius’s note. We discussed her on 31 March. The Ughellian manuscript seems to read “Sabina,” as do others below.

Herinien, otherwise extremely pure in the text, has the following added in a smaller and more recent hand in the margin:

“In Calabria, the deposition of blessed Bruno the confessor, first founder of the Carthusian Order.”

[Col. 0545D] Centule:

“At Capua, Saints Marcellinus, Castus, Emilius, and Saturninus. In the city of Agen, the passion of holy and glorious Fides, virgin, by whose example blessed Caprasius was encouraged to undergo the contest of martyrdom. At Auxerre, Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor.”

Brussels begins:

“The octave of blessed Michael the archangel, patron of this church.”

The pure text follows. At the end:

“At Rome, Saint Balbina.”

Hagenoyen gathers much material concerning the patriarch Abraham, which there is no room to transcribe here. See below, 9 October. The Capuan martyrs follow, purely. Then:

“At Rome, Saint Balbina, virgin. On the same day, Saint Sagaris, bishop of Laodicea and martyr.”

Nothing concerning Fides.

Aquicinct, at the end:

“Also Saint Rogatus.”

Who this Rogatus was—martyr, confessor, or bishop—I still do not know.

Daveron:

“At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Romanus, bishop.”

The Carthusian-Utrecht matriculary:

“Fides, virgin and martyr. Caprasius the martyr, who endured martyrdom following the example of the virgin Fides.” See 20 October.

“Marcellus, Castus, Aemilius, and Saturninus, martyrs.”

In the margin is written:

“This is the day of our holy father Bruno, yet he has been omitted; from this one may observe the antiquity and authenticity of this calendar.”

These are the words of the scribe who copied the manuscript.

Cluny and Codex D of the Cheval, marked C:

“Also Rogatus.” See above.

The Vatican manuscript numbered 5949 adds:

“Near Sorrento, Saint Renatus the confessor.”

Add “bishop.”

Altemps:

“Also Rogacius the martyr.”

Perhaps “Rogatus”?

Florentinus:

“In Judea, in the metropolitan city of Hebron, the deposition of the holy patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, [Col. 0546D] and Jacob. Their bodies were discovered in the same church, in the double cave, by divine revelation by the Latin canons of that church in the year of the Lord 1120. At Rome, Saint Sabina, virgin.”

The Medicean manuscript perhaps reads more accurately “Balbina.”

The Reims manuscript of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris:

“At Auxerre, Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor.”

The Lubeck–Cologne edition:

“The octave of Saint Michael and all the angels. At Trier, the passion of innumerable martyrs killed by the prefect of the city, Rictiovarus, [who] carried out a slaughter among the people of both sexes and every age for the name of Christ. A few Christians who escaped this storm by flight, after the persecution had abated somewhat, buried some of the bodies of these martyrs and filled with their bones a well of enormous capacity, neglected through age and drained of its water. In this well Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, hid unknown for six years. A monastery of Saint Maximin was dedicated at that place; in its crypt, in the same well, the bodies of those martyrs, etc., rest.”

The Capuan entry is pure. It says that Fides suffered under Dacianus, governor of the Spanish provinces. Then:

“Also at Agen, a city of Gaul, the passion of Saint Caprasius the martyr, who, following the example of the aforementioned blessed virgin Fides, was encouraged to undertake the contest of martyrdom.”

We have already said that he is commemorated on 20 October. The entry concerning Sagaris is sufficiently pure. What follows is:

“On the same day, Saint Rogatus the martyr. At Auxerre, Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor. In England, in the town of Lincoln, the translation of Saint Hugh, bishop and confessor of the Carthusian Order. Also on this day, the commemoration of the holy patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In the monastery of Schönau, the translation of Saints Caesarius and Verena, virgin, and their other companion martyrs from the company of the eleven thousand virgins.”

[Col. 0547B] Belin, in the first edition, begins:

“At Rome, Saint Balbina, virgin.”

In the second he adds at the end:

“Also Saint Rogatus, bishop.”

The rest of the text is pure, though corrupt in its spelling.

Greven:

“The octave of Saint Michael and all the blessed spirits.”

Concerning the patriarchs, as in the Lubeck–Cologne edition:

“Some preserve here the memory of Raphael the archangel. In Sweden, Eskillus, bishop and martyr.”

He gives the Trier material somewhat more briefly than above.

“Also Saints Primus and Felicianus, who are reported to have suffered with blessed Fides.”

See 9 June.

“According to the Catalogue, the passion of Saint Gangulphus the martyr, who is mentioned above on 3 May. At Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor. Dulcidius, bishop of Agen. In Calabria, the deposition of Saint Bruno the confessor. Born of illustrious parents at Cologne Agrippina, he was exceptionally learned in both secular and divine literature and a famous teacher, a canon of the church of Reims, a kind of embodiment of honesty, gravity, and complete maturity. [Col. 0547C] After leaving the world with six other men of the same purpose—salutarily terrified and already burning with divine love by that dreadful incident at Paris in which a certain deceased man cried out that he had been accused, judged, and then condemned—he entered the desert of Chartreuse, where at that time Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, had seen God building a dwelling for his majesty and seven stars showing him the direction of his journey, since there were seven of them as well. There he established the sufficiently arduous discipline of monastic life, namely the religious order of the Carthusians, in the year of the Lord 1084.

“But he was summoned by Pope Urban II, whose teacher he had once been, and was compelled to go to Rome and assist the Supreme Pontiff in ecclesiastical affairs. Unable to endure the noise of the Curia, and rejecting the archbishopric of Reggio, to which he had been elected, he withdrew to the desert of Calabria, burning with love for the solitude and quiet he had abandoned. There, after gathering many brothers around him and living in great holiness and austerity, while also caring for the first monastery—that is, the desert of Chartreuse—he rested in peace, renowned for his life and miracles, in the year of Christ 1101, on a Sunday.”

Concerning the people of Schönau and the translation of Saint Hugh of Lincoln, as above in the Lubeck–Cologne edition. At the end: “Babilla, virgin.”

Molanus:

“At Rome, Saint Balbina, virgin. The deposition of Romanus, bishop of Auxerre. Also Saint Rogatus, bishop. In Calabria, the deposition of Saint Bruno the confessor, first founder of the Carthusian Order.”

Then, in smaller type:

“Whom Leo X enrolled in the Catalogue of the Saints.”

Greven’s material concerning Eskillus and the Trier martyrs is copied. In other editions, Bruno is placed first in different type. At the end, concerning Romanus and Balbina, as above. Then:

“In Gaul, Saint Enimia, virgin, daughter of King Clovis, of outstanding holiness.”

Perhaps she is more properly called Enimia; see Castellani’s Martyrology. Enough has been said here about the Trier martyrs; their eulogy is abbreviated here.]

[Col. 0543]

At Capua, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Marcellus, Castus, Emilius, and Saturninus. On the same day, blessed Sagaris, martyr and bishop of Laodicea, who was one of the ancient disciples of the Apostle Paul. In the city of Agen, the commemoration of Saint Fides, virgin and martyr, by whose example blessed Caprasius was encouraged to undertake the contest of martyrdom.

On the Nones. Day 7.

[Note: [Col. 0547]

From Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Muneratus, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0547D]

Pratensis, together with his usual two companions, Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, differs from all the others in placing the commemoration of Marcellus and Apuleius second. Molanus has “saint” instead of “blessed Mark.” Rosweyd gives him the title “martyr.” Only Pratensis omits “Augusta” before “Euphratesia.” Otherwise I write “Euphratesia,” “Bacchus,” “coturnis,” “Apuleius,” and so forth, according to the common practice of the manuscripts in expressing these names. In Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, “martyrs” is missing before “Sergius.” Molanus transposed the words “for so long he was beaten with raw sinews.” Again, he put “Mark” in place of “Marcellus,” which was corrected in later editions. Pratensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and Muneratus write “Simon.” Rosweyd, moreover, together with Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, adds “the Magian.” Antwerp-Major, besides numerous scribal errors such as “Bacchii,” “Bacus,” “discissus,” and “confescione,” has the particular feature that almost caused it to be excluded from the pure witnesses: following Ado, it reads “with Aurelianus, a consular man, pronouncing sentence.”]

[Note: [Col. 0549A]

Today’s section has the same origin as yesterday’s: namely, the transfer of the entire text from Ado, whom Usuardus and Notker habitually followed here. Ado, in turn, took all the saints from the Little Roman Martyrology. Saint Mark the pope is read in Bede, joined likewise to Pope Linus; from this the following verse of Wandalbertus probably arose, in which both are praised together, though not with sufficient metrical accuracy:

The pontiffs Linus and Mark keep the Nones.

Among the Hieronymian Martyrologies, the oldest Epternacensis speaks more distinctly, in these words: “At Rome, the deposition of Mark, bishop.” In other copies there is varied combination and confusion, with many entangled matters that Florentinius takes considerable trouble to explain. The Little Roman Martyrology, not unlike Bede, has: “At Rome, Mark, pope.” Ado composed a brief eulogy, in which Notker wished to alter something. Our author merely specified his position. What the Pontificals transmit about Mark may be seen in the ancient Catalogues prefixed to volume I of the April collection. From them Fronto extracted a few items for his present note on the Calendar, where it is marked in this way: “In the month of October, on the seventh day, the commemoration of Saint Mark”; more distinctly in the Allatian Calendar and the Sacramentary of Gregory: “On the Nones of October, the commemoration of Saint Mark the pope.” These sufficiently establish the very ancient cult of this holy pontiff in the Church. Tillemont found nothing further concerning his life or deeds in volume VII, page 268.

Julia, Sergius, and Bacchus are joined under one commemoration in the Hieronymian manuscripts, the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Notker. Much could be observed about this, but, to avoid repetition, I refer readers to Florentinius’s note. Ado composed a sufficiently elegant abridgment of the Acts; I would not dare assert that he used a pure and trustworthy source. Baronius acknowledged in the final note on the year 309 that certain matters required correction. Some reject the entire account as deriving from Metaphrastes, as it appears in Surius, or as interpolated or corrupted. Among them, Tillemont, in volume V, beginning on page 491, was content carefully to collect what concerns their ancient and celebrated cult throughout the Church. We leave all those matters untouched here, to be examined in their proper place.

Usuardus separated Julia from the other two, distinguishing two entries from one and composing each in Ado’s words. He did the same in the final commemoration, which he made somewhat obscure by abbreviating it too much. Whether Marcellus and Apuleius belong to the Hieronymian Martyrologies may be gathered from Florentinius, who incorrectly asserts that Usuardus writes Mark instead of Marcellus. He doubtless read this in Molanus’s first edition, about which we spoke above. The Little Roman Martyrology clearly announces both:

“Marcellus and Apuleius, who first adhered to Simon Magus and afterwards to the Apostle Peter; under Aurelianus, a consular man, they were crowned with martyrdom.”

Ado gives more, and our account, as I said, was taken from him; but elsewhere we shall determine with what reliability all these matters are narrated. The whole story is rejected by those who do not accept the Acts of Saints Nereus and Achilleus or of Processus and Martinianus. See Tillemont, volume I, pages 189 and 538. Meanwhile, in support of their ancient cult, the Sacramentary of Thomasianus stands with the Martyrologies; on page 174 it explicitly contains prayers “for the commemoration of Saints Marcellus and Apuleius on the Nones of October.”]

[Note: [Col. 0549B]

The Tournai manuscript would be extremely pure if, after “under the Emperor Maximian,” it did not cut off the remainder of the eulogy.

Pulsan suffers from the same defect as Tournai; in addition, it deletes everything after “Julia the virgin” and after “Marcellus and Apuleius.”

Greven departs from purity today through a peculiar addition, namely the proper entry of the place where it once belonged:

“In the city of Chartres, the discovery of the body of Saint Caletricus, bishop of that city.”]

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT. and LEYDEN. are not entirely pure, differing only in the first announcement, which they express as follows: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Balbina, the burial of Saint Mark, pope and confessor.” Julia is not placed immediately after Sergius and Bacchus, but in the last place, with her position repeated.

LOVANIEN. agrees with these, but omits the entire entry for Sergius and Bacchus.

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. differ from the others in placing Sergius and Bacchus first and Mark second-to-last.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, Saint Mark, pope and confessor. He sat in the pontificate for three years, eight months, and twenty days. Also at Rome, the holy martyrs Marcellus and Apuleius. They first adhered to Simon Magus, but, seeing the miracles that were performed against him by the Apostle Peter, abandoned Simon’s impurity and received the sincerity of faith. In the province called Augusta Euphratesia, the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus. Also in the same province, Saint Julia, virgin and martyr.” In the first two entries it expands the text; here it abridges it.

BRUXELLEN.: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the burial of Saint Mark, pope and confessor. He established that the Creed of the faith should be sung aloud at Mass, and was buried at Saint Peter’s in the cemetery of Balbina.” What follows concerns Marcellus and Apuleius, then Sergius and Bacchus, and then Julia, quite purely. At the end: “At the city of Bourges, the burial of blessed Augustus, presbyter and confessor.”

HAGENOYEN. begins with Marcellus and Apuleius, and is not far from purity in that entry. In the entry for Sergius and Bacchus it mixes together many details that can be found more purely in Ado. It should be noted [Col. 0550B] that it asserts that these martyrs were translated to the town of Wittemburg. In the entry for Julia it is moderately interpolated. Finally: “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, in the cemetery of Balbina” (it is equally erroneous here and in BRUXELLENS.), “the burial of Saint Mark, pope. He was the thirty-fifth after blessed Peter the Apostle, succeeded Saint Sylvester, held the see under the great Emperor Constantine for eleven years and eight months, and established that the bishop of Ostia should consecrate the pope, and that he should use the pallium; and he died in peace.” He held the apostolic see for scarcely nine full months.

AQUICINCT. adds after “Saint Mark, pope”: “He established that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the city’s bishops, should use the pallium.” These statements agree sufficiently with what was said just above, and were almost certainly taken from Notker or from the papal lists.

VICTORIN. and REGINAE SUEC., marked with number 130, read: “Also Saint Linus, pope.” I do not know how this announcement slipped into these two codices. See Usuard, 26 November, and what we said at the end of the Observations for 23 September.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Mark, pope and confessor. Sergius, Julia the virgin, and Bacchus the martyr. Marcellus and Apuleius, martyrs.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949 Julia is absent. The following is added: [Col. 0550D] “At Rome, Saint Linus, pope and martyr.”

ALTEMPS.: “Among the East Saxons, the passion of Saint Ositha, virgin and martyr. Her head was cut off by the Danes; she herself, a martyr, took it up and carried it from place to place.”

FLORENT.: “Saint Mark, pope … And he now lies at Florence in the church of Saint Lawrence. At the city of Padua, Saint Justina, virgin and martyr.” See below.

BURDEGALEN.: “At the city of Xaintes, Saint Palladius, bishop and confessor.” He is mentioned by Saussay and others, but it is surprising that Castellanus omitted him from his Universal Martyrology.

BIZUNTICEN. and SALINEN. of the Franciscans: “At the monastery of Besançon, the reception of the body of Saint Prudentius, martyr.”

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “In the district of Rheims, in a village called Buxiosus, the burial of Saint Elami, presbyter and confessor.” The modern Roman Martyrology and others more correctly write Helanus.

The LUBECO-COL. edition is somewhat interpolated in the entry for Sergius and Bacchus; it is purer in that for Marcellus and Apuleius. Then: “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, in the cemetery of Balbina, the burial of Saint Mark, pope and confessor. He sat in the episcopate for two years, eight months, and ten days.” The entry for Julia is quite pure. “On the same day, blessed Osgida, virgin. At Padua, Saint Justina, a noble virgin and martyr, who, when she refused to sacrifice to idols there by order of the Emperor Maximian, was struck with a sword through the side and, praying, departed to Christ her bridegroom. Also, the translation of Saint Wolfgang, bishop and confessor, and his canonization. On the same day, the canonization of Saint Bridget, widow.”

BELIN. begins: “At the city of Padua, Saint Justina, virgin and martyr.” A text follows that has not been entirely corrected. A second edition adds at the end: “On the same day, the most blessed Linus, pope.”

GREVEN.: “Sysai, bishop and confessor. At the city of Bourges, the burial of Saint Augustalis, bishop. The translation and canonization of Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg and confessor. The octave of Saint Jerome, presbyter and doctor, Cardinal of the Roman Church. Learned in the Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and Chaldean languages, he withdrew from the city of Rome because of his rivals and obtained from Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, the site of the Lord’s manger. After traveling through many deserted places, he built a monastery and began to live with his companions according to the rule established by the holy Apostles; finally, after many labors for the benefit of the Church, he fell asleep in the Lord in the year of the Lord 423. At Padua, Saint Justina, virgin and martyr. Born of royal stock, when she refused to sacrifice to idols at Maximian’s command, she had her side pierced with a sword and attained the glory of martyrdom. Jotha, abbess. On the same day, Osgida, virgin. Also, the canonization of Saint Bridget, widow.” I prefer to read Birgitta.

MOLAN.: “At the city of Padua, Saint Justina, virgin and martyr. At Chartres, the discovery of the body of Saint Caletricus, bishop of that city. In the district of Rheims, in a village called Buxiolus, the burial of Saint Helanus, presbyter and confessor. At Rome, in the church of Saint Peter, the canonization of blessed Bridget, widow, by Boniface IX, in the second year of his pontificate. He issued a solemn document in which, by apostolic authority, he commanded that the said bride of Christ should be venerated perpetually in the Church of Christ as a holy widow.” In other editions, material concerning Sergius and Bacchus is inserted into the text from Ado, in italic type: “the first chief and second chief of the school of the gentiles.” At the end, the entries for Justina and Helanus are as above. Then: “At Bourges, Augustus, presbyter and confessor.” Concerning the discovery of Caletricus of Chartres and the canonization of blessed Bridget, everything is presented as in the first edition. Finally, in smaller type, it adds: “At Toulouse, the discovery of the holy confessors Silvius, Hilary, and Honoratus, bishops, and of Pappulus, bishop and martyr.” I do not know where these notices were taken from; in any case, Papulus is said to have been found in October of the year 1255.

[Col. 0547]

[Note: [Col. 0547C] This entire article is completely pure. It is wholly Usuardine; Sollerius rejects neither a syllable nor adds a stroke. He merely relegates the holy Marcellus and Apuleius to the last place, although Usuard had placed them second. Nevertheless, everything from “blessed Mark, pope” to the end has been obliterated. Let the reader forgive us if we repeat the same things so often, and let him lay the blame on Sollerius, who, although he used erasures so frequently in discrediting the Pratense codex, nevertheless leaves so many erasures unnoticed [Col. 0548C]. It is especially important for us to point out repeatedly that affected silence of Sollerius, since his entire criticism is chiefly undermined by it. For if the erasures report Usuard just as the intact passages do, it is obvious that erasures cannot serve as a rule for rejecting a codex. There is no rule common to truth and falsehood. What is proper, as the logicians teach, cannot be marked by a common sign. BOUILLART.]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the burial of blessed Mark, pope. In the province called Augusta Euphratesia, the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus, under the Emperor Maximian. Bacchus was beaten with raw sinews until, his whole body torn apart, he breathed out his spirit in confession of Christ; but Sergius, having been shod in boots lined with nails and remaining firm in the faith, was sentenced and ordered to be beheaded. Also in the same province, Saint Julia, virgin, who completed her martyrdom under the governor Marcian. On the same day, the holy martyrs Marcellus and Apuleius, who, through the Apostle Peter, abandoned Simon and devoted themselves to apostolic teaching, and afterward, under Aurelian the consular official, won the crown of martyrdom, and were buried not far from the city of Rome.

VIII Idus. Day 8.

[Note: [Col. 0551]

The Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. copies are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0551C]

Greven. and Molan. read “of blessed old Simeon” instead of “of the most blessed old Simeon.” Praten. here again writes Symeon with the others, but the codices are inconsistent, often writing according to their preference; here we follow the majority. In Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. the first word of the announcement, namely “the feast,” is absent. Tornacen. omitted “his” after “the Lord.” I have placed Thessalonica as elsewhere, although some copies have Thessalonicam. Concerning Hispalis, see what was said above. Praten. reads: “In the territory of Lyon-Clavat,” in which only Antuerp.-Maj. agrees with it. Munerat. and Max.-Lubec. have “in the territory of Lyon.” We follow all the others. In Herinien. it is incorrectly written pecatris instead of peccatrix. Munerat. substitutes “is called” for “is named.”]

[Note: [Col. 0551C]

On 11 April we briefly indicated that Philip, bishop of Gortyna in Crete, is also commemorated on this day by the Short Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Notker. I have not yet found the reason for this repetition, nor do I wish to investigate it more laboriously, since it has no bearing on our Usuard. Ado is the first to mention blessed old Simeon, also among the Feasts of the Apostles, where, from Luke chapter 2, those things are reported that can truly be commemorated about him. Our author includes everything briefly. It is surprising that Notker omitted him and substituted in his place the celebrated virgin and martyr Reparata, with an elogium abridged from Rabanus. [Col. 0551D] What Leo Allatius wrote about Simeon in his dissertation On the Simeons, on page 100, under the name of Methodius or Timothy, presbyter of Jerusalem, will be discussed in its proper place. In the meantime, see Tillemont, volume I, page 424. Concerning Demetrius, the author of the Short Roman Martyrology has this: “At Thessalonica, Demetrius, martyr.” From there he was received by Ado, and from Ado by our author and Notker. Wandalbert presents his encomium metrically:

“On the eighth before the Ides, holy Demetrius, you are blessed,

Having suffered in Christ’s name against unjust persecutors.”

Baronius’s Notes enumerate much that various writers have composed about this most celebrated martyr; Tillemont collects the more select material in volume V, beginning on page 149, where he also asserts that the Greeks called him the Great Martyr and Wonder-worker. [Col. 0552C] We shall present all these materials and, as far as we can, elucidate them carefully, comparing the Metaphrastic Acts published by Surius with the passion composed by Anastasius the Librarian, which appears among Mabillon’s Analecta, volume I, beginning on page 65. I nowhere find Peter of Hispalis, martyr, outside Usuard; therefore, it may be suspected that he belongs to the number of those whom our author transferred from Spain to France, as must often be supposed elsewhere—namely, when no other source is available from which we might conjecture that he drew it. Benedicta of Auriniacum, or, as others have it, of Origniacum, was also first entered by Usuard into the sacred registers, as often happens with Gallic saints, and should be assigned to the territory of Laon, not Lyon. Our predecessors long ago noted, under 26 May in the Index of the Omitted, volume VI, page 353, that the Acts of this martyr are exactly the same as those of Saturnina, virgin and martyr, with only the names changed; these Acts were published by us on 20 May. If, nevertheless, any particulars should occasionally be found, whether concerning her life or her translation, they will find a place in the Acts for October. One may consult what Tillemont briefly noted about her and other virgins, perhaps her companions, in his discussion of Lucian of Beauvais, volume IV, page 540. It is certain that some Pelagia is commemorated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies; Florentinius doubts whether she is the penitent woman whom Baronius assigns to Jerusalem. [Col. 0553A] In this obscure matter we are not yet permitted to decide anything. It is sufficiently probable that Usuard took the name Pelagia from the Hieronymian Martyrologies and added the surname “the sinner” at his discretion, since she was the best-known among those bearing the same name. In any case, according to Usuard’s intention, all later writers understand today’s Pelagia as the sinner. Her life, written by James the deacon, was published in Surius’s collection, taken from Rosweyde’s Lives of the Fathers; it is followed by another composed by Metaphrastes.]

[Note: [Col. 0553A]

ANTUERP.-MAJ. lacks Pelagia, in whose place it has: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Oswald, archbishop and confessor.” The English addition is evident.

ROSWEYD. in the first edition resembles GREVEN. and MOLAN. In the second and third it is pure. Then: “In the territory of Lyon-Clavat, that is, at Auriniacum, Saint Benedicta, virgin. At Antioch, Dionysius, bishop, and his companions. Also Saint Regenfledis, virgin. And Saint Reparata, virgin. On the same day, Saint Pelagia, who is called the sinner.”

PULSANEN., in the entries for Simeon, Peter of Hispalis, and Benedicta, is sufficiently pure; it lacks the others.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG. and DANIC. are pure in the first entry. After “Demetrius the martyr,” they add: “Whom the Emperor Maximinus [some copies: Maximianus], while he was teaching the people in the aforesaid city, ordered to be pierced with spears; and by such an end he completed his glorious martyrdom.” In the rest of the text they remain pure and add: [Col. 0553B] “At the city of Caesarea, the feast of Saint Reparata, virgin. Under the governor Decius, she was drenched with boiling lead, then had her breasts cut off with burning lamps, and, after her entrails had been torn out [some copies: dismembered], overcame a furnace kindled with fire; finally, by beheading, she completed her martyrdom. At Belisia, the burial of Saint Amator [some copies: Amor], confessor.” He is venerated at Munsterbilsen near Tongeren.

LOVANIEN. differs from the preceding copies in having omitted the elogium of Demetrius.

CENTULEN.: “The feast of the most blessed old Simeon, who is read in the Gospel to have received the Lord into his arms. At Thessalonica, the holy and glorious martyr Demetrius. In Gaul, in the territory of Lyon-Clavat, the passion of Saint Benedicta, virgin, under the judge Matroclus. On the same day, in the territory of Arras, Saint Ragemfledis, virgin and abbess. On the Mount of Olives, Saint Pelagia, transformed from a sinner into a religious and most holy woman.”

[Col. 0553C] BRUXELLEN. begins: “The feast of Saint Benedicta, virgin and martyr.” After “into his arms” in the entry for Simeon, it adds: “and to have uttered the canticle Nunc dimittis. At the Cretan city of Cortina [read: the city of Cortina in Crete], blessed Philip, glorious bishop.” See above at the beginning of the Observations. It has the entries for Demetrius and Reparata as ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others. Then, concerning Peter of Hispalis, it is pure. It follows with: “At Belisia, the burial of Saint Amor, confessor. Also Richarius, confessor.” See 26 April. The entry for Pelagia is pure. Finally: “And Saint Ragenfredis, virgin.” This name is inflected variously in the codices.

HAGENOYEN., beyond what has already been said about Simeon, adds, in its usual but not very plausible manner: “This Simeon is said to have been one of the seventy-two interpreters who were sent by the high priest Onias to King Ptolemy to translate the law of God from Hebrew into Chaldean.” It then inserts Saint Faith with a fairly long elogium; we dealt with her fully on 6 October. [Col. 0553D] The entry for Demetrius follows as above in ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others. Finally, that for Benedicta is pure. Peter of Hispalis and Pelagia are omitted here.

AQUICINCT. inserts, in second place after Simeon: “On the same day, Saint Ragenfledis, virgin.” Instead of “in the territory of Laon,” it has “at Lyon-Clavat.”

VICTORIN. ends with: “At the city of Caesarea, Saint Reparata, virgin and martyr.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Saint Simeon, the old man. Reparata, virgin and martyr. Benedicta, virgin and martyr. Pelagia, the Antiochene prostitute, who was called Margarita because of her beauty; she was wondrously converted by Saint Nonnus, bishop.”

REG. SUEC., under no. 428: “The vigil of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius. At Caesarea, Saint Reparata, virgin and martyr.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949 the commemoration of Simeon, Demetrius, Peter, and Pelagia is absent. It adds: “In Crete, the feast of Saint Philip, bishop. And Saint Reparata, virgin.”

STROZZIAN.: “The passion of the holy martyrs Terentianus, presbyter, Probus, and Andrian [MED. has Adrianus], who suffered for Christ at the city of Nicaea under the tyrant Maximian.” I think the names are corrupt. Could Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus be intended, the saints whom Usuard commemorates on 11 October? “The dedication of the church of Saint Mark the Evangelist in the august city of Venice.”

CABILONEN.: “At Chalon, the passing of Saint Gratus, bishop and confessor.” See Castellanus.

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apol.: “In the district of Laon, Saint Benedicta, virgin and martyr.”

ABDINGHOFFEN.: “In the territory of Lyon, Saint Benedicta, virgin and martyr.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition is pure in the entry for Simeon and has the entry for Demetrius as above. It is pure in that for Peter. Concerning Benedicta it adds: “Who, in the time of the Emperor Maximian, was cruelly afflicted by various tortures in the city of Auriniacum under the judge Matroclus; finally her temples were shattered with an axe. In the district of Blion, Saint Susanna, virgin.” It has the commonly known elogium of Pelagia. Concerning Reparata of Caesarea, it agrees with the text above. Then: “At Belisia, the burial of Saint Amor, confessor. He was born in Aquitania of very noble parents; outwardly he tormented his flesh with a hair shirt, inwardly strengthened it with fasts; he devoted himself continually to vigils and prayers, abstained from idle speech and laughter, and, renowned for many miracles, rested in peace. At Trier, Saint Metropolus, bishop and martyr. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Flavian, martyr. Also, the translation of Saint Erhard, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN. has not been purified in the text, as usual. At the end it adds the dedication of the church of Saint Mark, as above. Then: “Also Saint Reparata, virgin.” A second edition adds: “In the territory of Sens, Saint Porcaria, virgin and martyr.”

GREVEN.: “At Trier, Saint Metropolus, bishop and martyr. At Antioch, the holy Dionysius, Januarius, Faustinus, and Marcialis. The commemoration of Flavian the martyr. Philip, bishop of Gortyna and confessor.” Concerning Saint Amor it has almost the same material as the LUBECO-COL. edition above. “In England, Ewigus, confessor. The translation of Saint Erhard, bishop and confessor.” Concerning Reparata it is also almost the same as ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others. “In the district of Bleon, Saint Susanna, virgin. At Humeltoet, Valeria, virgin. Rainfredis, virgin. On the same day, Saint Triduana, virgin.”

MOLAN.: “The arrival of Saint Gerulphus, martyr.” [Col. 0554D] Then, in smaller type: “From Merendra to Tronchinium. He was anointed with sacred chrism by Bishop Eligius in the monastery of Blandinium; after entering the church of the Mother of God on his journey, he prayed longer than his godfather, who was escorting him, wished, and therefore was beaten by him so severely that death followed shortly afterward. Mejerus writes this in his Commentary on the Affairs of Flanders under the year 915.” Then, again in the customary italic type: “At Walchiodorum, Saint Eloquius, presbyter and confessor. On the same day, the dedication at Venice of the church of Saint Mark the Evangelist. And at Humelioet, Saint Valeria, virgin. Also Dionysius, bishop, Januarius with his companions. Also at Belisia, the burial of Saint Amor, presbyter and confessor. In [Col. 0555A] the territory of Sens, Saint Porcaria, virgin and martyr. At Rouen, blessed Evodius, bishop and confessor of that city. In the district of Blion, Saint Susanna, virgin. On the same day at Dondey, Saint Rainfredis, virgin. Also Saint Reparata, virgin.” Concerning her, three verses from Baptista Mantuanus’s *On Sacred Days*, book X:

“I was Caesarean while living; after death, my corpse

Came to the fields subject to Fiesole and lies

Where the Tuscan Arno runs with rushing waters.”

[Col. 0556A] Other editions read: “And at Hemuleurt, Saint Valeria, virgin. Also the burial of Saint Amor, who rests in the monastery of Belisia.” Concerning Porcaria of Sens, Evodius of Rouen, Susanna, Metropolus, and Reparata, as above. Then: “At Dononium, the solemnity of Saint Ragenfredis, virgin.” Concerning the dedication of the church of Saint Mark and the translation of Saint Eloquius, as above. Finally: “From Merendra to Tronchinium, the arrival of Saint Gerulphus, martyr.”]

[Col. 0551]

The feast of the most blessed old Simeon, who is read in the Gospel to have received the Lord into his arms. At Thessalonica, the passion of Saint Demetrius, martyr. Also at the city of Hispalis, Saint Peter, martyr. In the territory of Laon, Saint Benedicta, virgin and martyr. On the same day, Saint Pelagia, who is called the sinner.

VII. Idus. Day 9.

[Note: [Col. 0555]

This is how the Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., and Molan. copies read.]

[Note: [Col. 0555B]

I read “at Paris” from Praten., Molan., and also Greven., although others commonly write “at Parisius.” The reason is that I think Usuard found this form in Ado. Likewise, “he came to the aforesaid city” should stand without a preposition, as most of the purer copies read, except Antuerp.-Maj. and Molan. Again, Antuerp.-Maj. placed “the work entrusted to him”; Molan., wishing to add force, inserted *solerter* before *ardenter*, reading “skillfully and zealously.” Only Antuerp.-Maj. appears to have taken from Ado the form “Fescenninus Sisinnius.” The penultimate particle, *gloriose*, is absent from Pratense. Antuerp.-Maj. writes *Dompnini*, but this, as well as *nichilominus*, *Dionisii*, and so forth, may be disregarded.]

[Note: [Col. 0555B]

The author of the Short Roman Martyrology supplies a richer harvest of the patriarchs of the Old Testament. From him Abraham is received on this day, Lot by many on the following day, and others on other days. Ado copied his words, and from him Usuard and Notker have the same material. See below the four verses of Wandalbert drawn in praise of Abraham. The controversy now returns, which we touched upon on the third of this month and which Baronius treated most fully in his Notes. There one will find neither Lucas Holstenius nor the learned Frenchmen nor most of the others who support him in defending the Areopagitic writings of Abbot Hilduin. We, bound by the limits of the martyrologists, shall bring forward only what seems capable of being established by their authority. Here are the words of the Corbie Hieronymian Martyrology: “At Paris, the feast of the holy Dionysius, bishop, Rusticus, presbyter, and Eleutherius, deacon.” Bede agrees: “At Paris, the feast of the holy martyrs Dionysius, bishop, Rusticus, and Eleutherius,” with a somewhat fuller form in Rabanus. The Short Roman Martyrology adds: “At Paris, Dionysius, bishop, struck down with his companions by the sword of Fescenninus.” The same is Ado’s unmistakable opinion, and our text was plainly taken from him, as was also Notker’s customary practice. There is, however, this difference, correctly noted by Castellanus in the preface to the first two-month section, page 25: Ado, and Notker after him, call Eleutherius a presbyter and Rusticus a deacon, whereas Usuard’s text correctly reverses these designations. I would be greatly mistaken if any trace of the Areopagite doctrine could be extracted from all these sources. Compare this, then, with the words of the Short Roman Martyrology, Ado, Usuard, and Notker cited for 3 October, and you will see most clearly that, in their view, today’s Dionysius is very far removed from the Areopagite. The Dionysius of whom we are speaking today is therefore regarded as the first bishop of Paris. Much has been debated, especially during the past century, concerning his date, birthplace, mission, companions, and deeds; these matters will be carefully examined and arranged in their proper place. In the meantime, one may consult—selecting only two authors from so many—Dubois, *History of the Church of Paris*, book I, chapter 3, and book VI, chapter 6, and the more recent Tillemont, volume IV, beginning on page 439, where other authors are indicated. In the Lucensian Hieronymian tables, Saint Domnin, martyr, is placed first; Florentinius made several observations about him. Nothing about him is read in the Epternacensis or Corbie Hieronymian Martyrology, nor in Bede, the Short Roman Martyrology, Ado, or Notker. Rabanus marks him with a brief elogium, but one different from Usuard’s. I believe that Usuard received this martyr from some Hieronymian codex and read the same Acts that Mosander published in Surius, since the material briefly presented in our text appears to have been taken from them. Some recent writers suspect those Acts, but that controversy does not belong here. Under 3 October we said toward which opinion concerning the Dionysuses Wandalbert seems to incline in his fuller elogium, which is preserved intact in Molan. Here we append his final verse on Domninus to four others about Abraham:

“An example of faith, obedience, and salutary rule,

First called by the surname of the exalted father,

Then named father of nations by heavenly destiny,

And blessed Abraham keeps the holy sevens.”

[Col. 0556D] “And they shine with Domninus, the famous Italian martyr.”]

[Note: [Col. 0555D]

TORNACEN., which frequently tends to shorten elogia, has the entry for Dionysius only as far as “he came to the aforesaid city.” The remainder of his elogium is absent. Otherwise it is pure.

ROSWEYD. is interpolated, for after “by the Roman pontiff” it inserts “Clement, successor of the Apostle Peter.” Likewise, after “with his companions” come the words “he was beheaded with blunted axes.” The rest pertaining to the Usuardine text [Col. 0556D] is sufficiently pure.

PULSANEN., in the first and second editions, is almost pure; it fails in the third, as so often above.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. are pure throughout the text and add at the end: “Also the feast of Saint Gislenus, confessor.”

MUNERAT. is also interpolated, for it reads: “by Fescenninus, prefect of Rome.” After “completed,” it adds in its own wording: “Their bodies rest in the monastery of Saint Dionysius in France.”

GREVEN. adds to the pure text: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Richarius, confessor.” See 26 April.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN. insert concerning Dionysius: “the blessed bishop who was sent by blessed Clement, Roman pontiff …” Concerning Domninus: “Nevertheless, his head was cut off with a sword; by divine command he raised his severed head from the ground and carried it the distance of a stone’s throw from the place of the blow, and so gloriously died.” At the end: “Also Saint Gislenus, confessor.”

LOVANIEN. resembles the two preceding copies in the first two entries; in the third it cuts out the entire elogium. It agrees again in the entry for Gislenus.

ALBERG. differs from ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others only in order, placing Dionysius first and Abraham second.

[Col. 0557B] DANIC. has the entire text as ALBERGEN. But in the lower margin of two pages I find, written in another hand: “At the city of Ceuta in Spain [the writer means at Septa in Africa], the passion of the holy martyrs Daniel, Samuel, Angelus, Dempnus, Leo, Nicholas, and Hugolinus, of the sacred order of Friars Minor. While they fervently preached the Catholic faith to the Saracen king and his people in that city, after enduring for Christ with the greatest patience iron chains, prisons, blows, and the most savage scourging, they were all cruelly slain by the same Saracens by the sword and cut limb from limb in the year of the Lord 1221. A major double feast.” They are mentioned elsewhere on 13 October.

CENTULEN.: “The death of Abraham the patriarch. At Paris, the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, archpresbyter, and Eleutherius, archdeacon, who completed their martyrdom after being beheaded with axes. In Italy, on the Claudian Way, Saint Donninus, martyr. At the monastery of Centula, the welcome translation of the precious body of our most holy father Richarius, from the wilderness to the site of the monastery formerly founded by him, so that he might strengthen Christ’s soldiers by his presence—those whom he had previously trained by word and example. In the territory of Haumacum, Saint Gislenus, confessor.” We spoke above about Richarius of Centula, who is commemorated on 26 April.

BRUXELLEN. begins with Dionysius, almost as above. Then: “On the same day, Saint Abraham the patriarch, who is named in the Canon of the Mass.” The entry for Domninus is also expanded, as above. Finally: “In the county of Hainaut, the burial of Saint Gislenus, archbishop and confessor. Coming from Athens into Hainaut, he built the monastery of Cellensis, whose church was dedicated by blessed Authertus, bishop of Cambrai.”

HAGENOYEN. piles up much material about Dionysius, which I prefer to omit. See below, the LUBECO-COL. edition. In the entry for Domninus it is almost like the preceding copies. Then: “At the city of Hispalis, Saint Peter, martyr,” concerning whom see the preceding day. Finally: “Also Saint Gislenus, confessor.”

[Col. 0557D] AQUICINCT. has “with an axe” instead of “with a sword” in the elogium of Dionysius. It is silent about Domninus. “On the same day, Saint Gislenus, confessor. And the translation of the body of Saint Richarius.” The additions concerning Saint Gossuinus are from a recent hand.

AMBIANEN.: “In the district of Pontinus [I think Pontivus], the translation of Saint Richarius, magnificent confessor. In the same place where he now rests, he established a monastery from his father’s palace and there became the father of many monks and a great performer of miracles.”

[Col. 0558A] MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, martyrs. Abraham the patriarch. Nicasius, bishop and martyr, with his companions Quirinus and Stanilus.” I do not know what name this is; see 11 October. “At Rome, Domninus, martyr. Gislenus, presbyter and confessor.”

CODEX BIGOTIAN., marked E 40: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Richarius, confessor.”

In VATICAN. no. 5949 Abraham and Domninus are absent. It adds: “At Cologne, Saint Gereon with 358 others,” and so forth. The Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and Notker deal with the same persons; we shall do so with Usuard on the following day.

ALTEMPS.: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Oswald, archbishop. And of Reparata, virgin.” See the Auctaria for the preceding day. “The feast of Saint Richarius, abbot and confessor.” The subject is the translation; see what was said above.

FLORENT.: “Also Saint Gilibertus, confessor.” [Col. 0558B] Others call him Gislerius; above, Gislenus is preferable.

The LUBECO-COL. edition: “At Paris, the feast of the holy martyr Dionysius, bishop … Who, blessed Bishop Dionysius, while he was staying at Athens in the district of the Areopagus, was instructed by the Apostle Paul and believed in Christ; he was ordained by that same apostle as the first bishop at Athens. When he learned that the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul were being held captive at Rome by Nero, burning with love for them and a desire for martyrdom, he hastened there so that he might suffer with them. After the apostles had completed their martyrdom, Saint Clement, pope and successor of Saint Peter, sent him into Gaul to preach; thus he came to the aforesaid city of Paris, where he remained for years, and so forth,” almost as above. “Also Abraham the patriarch.” Concerning Domninus it adds “the chamberlain of Maximian.” In the rest it differs little from ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others.

BELIN., sufficiently pure in the text, adds at the end: “Also the feast of Saint Gislerius, confessor.” For Gislenus, unless I am greatly mistaken.

[Col. 0558C] GREVEN.: “On the same day, Saint Dionysius, archdeacon of Rheims, and his companions. At Rome, the feast of the holy Marcellinus, Geminius, and Nivus. Also Saint Theodore. Gislenus, abbot and confessor. At Rome, between the Two Laurels, Saint Primina, virgin.” He often gathers much material here, which must be distinguished expressly elsewhere.

MOLAN. inserts, in different type within the text, the words of MUNERAT: “Their bodies rest in the monastery of Saint Dionysius in France.” At the end: “In the district of Hainaut, in a place then called by the surrounding country people Ursidongus, now called Cellensis, the feast of Saint Gislenus, bishop and confessor, a man of extraordinary holiness. He was bishop of Athens and, for Christ’s sake, abandoned that highest earthly honor, choosing to become poor. Coming to Rome to visit the thresholds of the chief Apostles Peter and Paul, he was there commanded by a divine voice to hasten into Gaul, build an oratory there in honor of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and await the end of this sorrowful exile. [Col. 0558D] Also on the same day, the elevation of his body. Also Saint Domninus, who was beheaded under the Emperor Maximian because of the faith of Christ.” Is this to be distinguished from the preceding person? In smaller type it reads: “At Aquicinctum, the death of blessed Gossuinus, abbot; he neither listened to rumors nor willingly repeated them.” Other editions agree in the text. At the end: “Also the feast of Saint Gislerius, confessor. On the same day at Cambrai, on the road to Arras, the feast of Saint Olla, virgin.” The entry for Gislenus follows, as above. But what is meant by Gislerius, which, unless I am mistaken, was taken from BELIN? “On the ninth day, Saint Audronicus, father.” In smaller type, concerning Gossuinus, as above.]

[Col. 0555]
of the patriarch Abraham. At Paris, the feast of the holy martyrs Denis, bishop, Rusticus, priest, and Eleutherius, who, the blessed bishop having been sent by the Roman pontiff into Gaul for the purpose of preaching, reached the aforesaid city, where, ardently pursuing the task entrusted to him for several years, he was finally put to death by the prefect Fescenninus, together with his companions, by the sword, and completed his martyrdom. At Julia, on the Claudian Way, Saint Domninus the martyr, under Maximian. When he wished to evade the fury of the persecution, he was immediately pursued and nevertheless struck down by the sword; thus he fell gloriously.

## Sixth day before the Ides. Day 10.

[Note: [Col. 0559]]

Thus Pratensis, Heriniensis, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0559A]]

I write simply *Piniti*. Pratensis and Greven have *Pyniti*; no one correctly has *Pinyti*. Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck, together with Greven, read “left behind for himself a living image,” which is better, as in the other editions, in the text. In Greven and Molan the correct form is *Agrippinensi*, but all the others prevail by their agreement. Antwerp-Major, among numerous scribal errors, has *subdiderant* instead of *subdiderunt*. It must certainly be read *Cassius and Florentius*, not, as in our Pratensian copy, *Florentini*. Pratensis [Col. 0560A] and Heriniensis write *Brittannia*; all the others have *Britannia*, which we follow here. Antwerp-Major added concerning Paulinus, “archbishop of York.” Antwerp, Maximilian-Lübeck, Aquicinct, and Ughelli’s edition add “and Eubrachii,” which I do not doubt has entered in place of *Eboraci*, since I have no knowledge whatever of such a saint, although I find the reading in the Cambrai manuscript, “and Eubrachii the confessor,” as you may see in the Appendices.

[Note: [Col. 0559A]]

The prophet Lot, as I mentioned yesterday, is placed today in the *Romanum parvum*, from which he passed into Ado and Notker; he was omitted by Our Author, but Wandalbert adorned him with this couplet:

> Holy Lot is adorned with the titles of an old man’s righteousness.

The other announcement in the *Romanum parvum*, probably from Rufinus, Book IV, chapter 23, reads as follows: “In Crete, Pinitus, most distinguished among bishops.” He is first recorded here; he is unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, and Wandalbert. Our eulogy is wholly Ado’s. His deeds must be drawn from the authors cited by Baronius in the Note and from his [Col. 0560B] *Annals* at the year 172, no. 8, and 175, no. 15. A summary appears in the already cited passage of Rufinus or Eusebius, from which Jerome derived his account in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 28.

Much concerning Gereon and the other martyrs along the Rhine remains to be examined later with mature scrutiny. Above all, the Hieronymian entries for this day and the preceding one are confused—in their names, the number of martyrs, and even their nationality: whether they were Mauri or Thebans, or whether separate companies from both peoples should be admitted. Florentius attempts to explain all this. Our predecessors doubted whether Gereon with 315 companions was genuinely recorded by Bede on the preceding day. This becomes still more uncertain to me because Rabanus does not mention them.

The published Florus reads today: “At Cologne, which is called Agrippina, the feast of Gereon the martyr, with 318 others.” Notker on the preceding day counted 319 companions, and on this day, following Ado, mentions Mallosus and Victor. Bede, without specifying the place or scene of the contest, has: “The Passion of Saint Victor the martyr.” [Col. 0559C] In Ado, Gereon appears first, with 318, whom, he says, “are reported to have been Thebans, and to have belonged to the legion of Saint Maurice,” and so forth.

Then, after Lot and Pinitus, there follows a longer commemoration of Mallosus and Victor; [Col. 0560A] to them he assigns no companions, nor does the purer edition of Rosweyde mention Cassius or Florentius. What are we to decide here? Usuard saw Ado, for he took Gereon’s eulogy from him. Nevertheless, what Ado established as a proper name Usuard turns into a surname—namely, Mallosus.

If conjecture is permissible, I would suppose that Usuard knew some Acts older than those of Elinand, in which he found no Mallosus (as neither is there one in the Elinand Acts), but found distinctly expressed only the four principal champions, Gereon, Victor, Cassius, and Florentius, whose commemorations follow in our text. If you deny that Usuard saw Acts older than Elinand’s, I shall not strongly resist; but I shall say [Col. 0560B] that the names of the latter three were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, confused though they are.

But how did Victor acquire only seventeen companions, when in both the Hieronymian Martyrologies and the Acts, indeed even in Mosander, 330 are counted? And who are those “many others” with Cassius and Florentius? I repeat: all these matters are so tangled and confused that they require laborious discussion, which must be deferred here to its proper place, while the faith of the Church of Cologne remains inviolate. Tillemont has begun the treatment of the subject with no little care in volume IV, beginning at page 429. What Molan thought is shown by the notes added to the later editions. Wandalbert’s verses also include only the four named athletes:

> Cassius and Gereon, Victor, Florentius, and  
> the companions of their martyrdom—then the united people triumph.

Bede described Paulinus of York’s life in his *History* and recorded him in his *Martyrology* in these words: “And in Britain, Paulinus, bishop of York,” which he borrowed from Rabanus. Ado’s eulogy, abridged by Notker, was omitted by Our Author. The life published by Surius may be consulted.

[Note: [Col. 0559C]]

Tournai lacks the first announcement; the remaining text is pure. It adds: “At the monastery of Jotro, Saint Teclechildis, virgin and abbess.” Castellanus writes *Theodolechildes*, in French *Thelchide*.

Rosweyde, not entirely pure in the text, after “Cassius and Florentius with many others,” adds: “Victor of Tournai and Florentius of Verona [that is, Bonn] are buried and rest.” But why is that Victor joined to this Florentius?

Pulsano lists all the saints except Victor, but cuts short all the eulogies and expresses some names incorrectly.

Antwerp-Major and Louvain begin: “Of the prophet Lot, son of Aran, brother of Abraham.” Then: “At Populonia, the feast of Saint Cerbonius, bishop and confessor.” They are pure in *Pinitus*. After *Agrippinensi* they insert “which is called Cologne.” Later: “Also in the territory of the same city, at a place called Xanctis, Saint Victor the martyr and 330 others. Also at Verona, the holy martyrs Cassius and Florentius with seven others.” After “bishop,” concerning Paulinus, they add “of York.”

[Col. 0560C] Utrecht and Leiden differ from the immediately preceding manuscripts only in adding this eulogy to Cerbonius: “When he was accused before Pope Vigilius and summoned by him, he did not wish to appear empty-handed; therefore, presenting wild geese that followed him like domesticated birds to the supreme pontiff, he compelled him to rise before such a sign.”

Albergen and the Danish manuscript differ from the preceding codices only in order, placing Cerbonius first and Lot second.

Centule: “At Crete, the blessed Pinitus, most distinguished among bishops. At Cologne Agrippina, Saint Gereon the martyr with his companions, 219, who are reported to have been Thebans. Also there, the holy Mallosus and Victor. Also the holy Cassius and Florentius with many others.” Concerning Paulinus, between “bishop” and “confessor,” it inserts “of York.”

Brussels joins Gereon, Victor, Cassius, and Florentius in one announcement at the beginning, “with their companions,” and so forth, as above; then adds from Ado: “All of whom are reported to have been Thebans and to have crossed into Gaul with that legion of Saint Maurice, by order of the emperor Maximian; and, rejecting the tyrant’s deadly rule on the banks of the Rhine, patiently submitted their necks to the swords for Christ.” Concerning Lot, as above. It is almost pure in *Pinitus*. Concerning Cerbonius, as Utrecht and Leiden. Then: “In Britain, the burial of Saint Paulinus, confessor and bishop of York. Also, the discovery of Saint Austreberta.” She is commemorated on 10 February.

Hagenoyen is fairly pure in the first two entries and has nearly the same account of Victor as above. Then: “In the territory of the same city, which is called Bonn, the feast of Saint Cassius and Florentius with seven others, who fell under the same persecutor for the faith of Christ.” In the account of Cerbonius it is somewhat fuller, adding at the end: “And thus he returned in glory to his own see and died in peace.”

Aquicinct inserts Domninus here in second place, concerning whom see yesterday. To Victor it adds “and 330 others.” At the end it appends “and Eubrachii,” as in Antwerp and Maximilian-Lübeck, etc.; concerning this, see the Variants.

Victorin and the Swedish Register, no. 130, add at the end: “At Nevers, Saint Troesius the abbot, who, full of days, departed to the Lord.” Castellanus places him on 17 October in his *Universal Martyrology* and calls him *Trojecius*.

Amiens: “On this same day, the entry of the blessed martyr Firminus into the city of Amiens.”

Matricularies of the Carthusians at Utrecht: “Of Victor the martyr. And of Gereon, Cassius, Florentius, etc.” In the margin is added: “A feast in the city of Utrecht. Paulinus, bishop and confessor. Pontius [Pinitus], bishop and confessor.”

Bigotian, marked P. 5: “Also, the dedication of the churches of the Celestine Order, established today and solemnly celebrated everywhere.”

Cambrai: “In Britain, at York, the blessed Paulinus [Pauline], prelate, and Eubrachii the confessor.” See the Variants.

In the Vatican manuscript marked no. 5949, Gereon, Cassius, and Florentius are absent. A later hand adds: “On the Claudian Way, the feast of Saint Domninus the martyr, whose body, through divine revelation, was transferred by venerable monks to the sacred monastery of Sculeularum, where it clearly rests.”

Florence: “At the city of Populonia, in the region of Tuscany, Saint Cerbonius, bishop and confessor of that city, a man of great holiness. At the city of Narni, Saint Cassius, bishop of that same city, and Saint Florentius with seven others.” One might say that these saints were transferred from here to Bonn, or from Bonn to here. “In the Florentine territory, at a place called Pasignano, the translation of Saint John Gualbert, abbot of Vallombrosa.” Strozzi adds: “He died in the flesh and reigns with Christ, in the year 1073 from his Incarnation.”

Bordeaux: “Saint Clarus, bishop and confessor.” See Castellanus.

[Col. 0561D] Chalon: “In the territory of Mâcon, at the monastery of Cluny, the reception of Saints Valentine, priest and martyr, and Felix, bishop and confessor, who held the episcopal see at Clermont.”

Reims, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At the monastery of Jotro, the burial of Saint Theodebildis, abbess.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition contributes scarcely anything new concerning Gereon and the others. See Greven below. It follows with Lot, as in Antwerp-Major, etc. Concerning Cerbonius, as Utrecht. But after “sign,” it adds: “He received Christian soldiers as guests; for this reason he was exposed by the king of the Goths [Col. 0562A] to a fierce bear, which licked the feet of the holy man; and, having thus been freed, he afterward rested happily in the Lord.” It is fairly pure in *Pinitus* and inserts “of York” after Paulinus. At the end: “At Troyes, Saint [Saint] Ancha, virgin and martyr.” It should be read *Tanca* or *Tancha*, who is commemorated on this day.

Belin, at the end of the text, which is not entirely pure, adds: “On this same day, Saint Zerbonius, bishop and confessor.” Another edition reads *Cerbonius* and adds: “At Limoges, the translation of the distinguished confessor of Christ, Martial.” His feast day is 30 June.

Greven: “The prophet Lot. Note: Saint Gereon and his companions belonged to the Theban legion. Likewise Saint Victor, who suffered with 330 companions at Troyes, which is now called Xanctis. Cassius and Florentius, with seven others, belonged to the same legion and suffered at Verona, which is also called Bonn. All these glorious martyrs, although killed in different places, were killed for one faith in Christ, and their bodies were cast into deep places.
