In Africa, Saints Eusebius, Heraclius, and Venustus, martyrs. Cerbonius, bishop and confessor of the city of Populonia. Concerning him, Blessed Gregory III reports in the *Dialogues*, among other things, that, being very devoted to hospitality, he received passing soldiers as guests and hid them from the Goths. When for this reason he had been exposed to a bear, and the beast, laying aside its ferocity, licked the bishop’s feet, he was released. When his body was being carried by ship for burial, a violent storm poured down around both sides of the ship, but not a single drop fell upon it. Virgil, bishop of Arles and confessor.” See the Acts for 5 March. “Atticus, bishop and confessor of Constantinople, whose virtues are touched upon in Book XII of the *Tripartite History*. At Troyes, Saint Ancha, virgin and martyr.” Concerning her, see above. Whether Atticus deserves to be counted among the saints we shall inquire elsewhere.

Molan, in other type, inserts concerning Victor: “At a place called Xanctis.” Then: “At Verona, commonly called Bonn.” At the end, concerning Paulinus: “He converted to the Lord by preaching the word of faith the nation of the Northumbrians—that is, the people of the English who dwelt north of the River Humber—together with their king Edwin.” On the same day, “Saint Cerbonius, bishop and confessor.” Concerning the translation of Martial, from Belin: “The prophet Lot. At the monastery of Jotro, Saint Telechildis, virgin and abbess. At Troyes, the passion of Saint Ancha, virgin. On this same day, the dedication of the Celestine Order, to be solemnly celebrated everywhere by the said order on one day.” Then, in smaller type: “John, prior of Bridlington in England, of the Order of Canons Regular, who was canonized by Boniface IX. In Gaul, near Area, Saint Venantius, a truly noble martyr.”

Later editions preface the text in different type with “The prophet Lot.” In the text, besides what has been mentioned, instead of “seventeen,” they read “his companions.” Concerning them, see Molan’s Note there. “At York” is also inserted. The expansion begins with the words “who converted that nation,” etc. Concerning Cerbonius, after “confessor,” is added: “of Populonia, whose relics Brother Robert of Pisa brought into Gaul.” Concerning Tanca of Troyes, as above. “At the monastery of Jotro, Saint Telechildis,” etc. “In England, at the monastery of Bridlington, the burial of Saint John the confessor and prior of that monastery, of the Order of Canons Regular.” Concerning Saint Venantius, as above. “In Hasteria, Saint Nuntius the confessor. On the tenth day, Saints Eulampius and Eulampia, martyrs. On this same day, the dedication of the Celestine Order, everywhere by the said order,” etc., as in the earlier edition.

[Col. 0557]

At Crete, the blessed Pinitus, most distinguished among bishops, who in his writings left behind, as in a mirror, a living image of himself. At the city of Agrippina, Saint Gereon the martyr, surnamed Mallosus, with 318 others, who, during the persecution of the tyrant Maximian, patiently submitted their necks to the swords for true piety. [Col. 0559] Also in the territory of the same city, Saint Victor the martyr and seventeen others. Also the holy martyrs Cassius and Florentius with many others. In Britain, Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor.

## Fifth day before the Ides. Day 11.

[Note: [Col. 0563]]

Only Pratensis, Greven, and Molan are entirely pure.

[Note: [Col. 0563A]]

I write *Tarsum*, *presbyteri*, *Scotia*, etc., as I have often said above, although the codices vary on this point. *Tharaci* is the more common spelling, and this is found in the older codices, Pratensis, Heriniensis, etc.; not *Taraci*, as in some, or *Tarati*, as in Greven. No one has written *Tarachi*, although that is how it should be read from the Greek. In Pratensis, Heriniensis, and others the form is *Vilcasini*, which we have preserved, although Greven and Molan prefer *Vilcassini*; choose whichever you wish. Greven writes *Nycasii*; Molan’s *Nicasii* is better, and many follow him—indeed, best of all, if I am not mistaken. Pratensis has *Nigasii*, to distinguish him from Nicasius of Reims. I do not understand why [Col. 0564A] Heriniensis omitted this announcement, unless perhaps the copyist, since he belonged to the diocese or province of Reims, thought that in this way his own Nicasius was being transferred elsewhere. Greven and Molan write *Canici*; I prefer *Cainichi*, as coming closest to the true formation of the name, as Pratensis, Heriniensis, and Aquicinct have it. Nevertheless, I think it should truly be read *Kainnichi*, as it appears in the Life. The codices pronounce the name *Uzecia*, *Uzechia*, and in other ways; I prefer *Uzetia*, together with the principal witnesses.

[Note: [Col. 0563B]]

The genuine and authoritative Acts of these three most illustrious martyrs are exceedingly precious and can never be praised enough. They were first published by Baronius, more accurately by Rosweyde, and subsequently by others, as the man who prepared the latest Greek-Latin edition explains at greater length in his preface: Theodoric Ruinart, among the *Select and Sincere Acts*, beginning at page 454.

The Hieronymian Martyrologies commemorate them not only on this day but also on the ninth and tenth of the month, with differing forms in different codices. Among them, the very ancient Antwerp or Epternacian manuscript explicitly places them today “at Anazarbus of Cilicia.” This place-name, which is much better rendered *Anazarbi*, shows from the Acts themselves that they suffered there, not at Tarsus.

The author of the *Romanum parvum*, however, appears to have been the first to place them at Tarsus, in these words: “At Tarsus, the martyrs Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus.” From there this placement passed into Ado, Usuard, Notker, and all later writers. The title “priest” added to Andronicus in the Epternacian manuscript certainly entered through the copyist’s carelessness. Ado’s eulogy is elegantly drawn from the Acts themselves and was adapted by Our Author from it to his customary brevity. Wandalbert probably derived his own verses from the same source:

> Soon Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus crown the fifth [day],  
> equal in virtue and death, whom glory makes renowned.

Thus far Usuard’s guides are clear. From where he obtained the other saints I do not see so clearly. He may indeed have found in some Hieronymian manuscript, perhaps one like the Corbie manuscript, “Nicasius and other martyrs”; but there he certainly did not find the names of his companions. Moreover, the uncertain edition of Mosander’s Ado mentions Bishop Nicasius and the deacon Subiculus. Our Author, meanwhile, says nothing of the latter and assigns only the title of priest to the former.

Nor does any light come from the other martyrologists. It remains to conjecture that Usuard possessed particular information from which he inserted that company into his Martyrology. On the proper inflection of the names, one may consult Father Motherius’s notes on the latest French version of the Roman Martyrology. For the rest, see Tillemont on Denis of Paris, volume IV, article 18, page 485.

Venantius, abbot of Tours, was added to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in Florentius’s view; he is known to Florus, Rabanus, Ado, Mosander, and Notker, and Our Author postponed him to 13 October. But from Scotland he introduces Cainichus, mentioned by no other writer—perhaps because he regarded him as an abbot of his own order, or because he was honored with a special cult in Gaul. We possess a manuscript Life in which he is called *Kainnechus*, and Rosweyde left many notes on its chapters, to be published in the Acts. Firminus of Uzès is plainly also Usuardine. Various writers have described his deeds; we shall collect everything in its proper time.

[Note: [Col. 0563C]]

Heriniensis would be extremely pure and complete if it did not omit the second announcement, which I discussed above.

Tournai suffers from the same defect as Heriniensis. The rest is fairly pure.

Antwerp-Major, under Nicasius, after “Quirinus the priest,” continues as follows: “And Subiculus the deacon and Pientia the virgin. They were sent with blessed Denis from the city of Rome into Gaul to preach, and, having been seized in the same district by the prefect Sisinnius, they were crowned with glorious martyrdom.” At the end it also has: “In Britain, Saint Ethelburga the virgin, whose Life the Venerable Bede mentions in his history of the English.”

Rosweyde reads the entry concerning Nicasius as follows: “Also, the passion of Saints Nicasius,” etc. At the end: “Also Saint Onesta the virgin.”

Pulsano entirely removed the eulogy of the Tarsian martyrs. Then: “In the district of Vexin, the passion of Saint Nicasius the priest and his companions Subiculus, Quirinus, and Pientia, virgin and martyr.”

Antwerp, Maximilian-Lübeck, and Ughelli begin: “At the city of Rennes, Saint Melanius the confessor.” Read *Aemilianus*. They write “Nicasius the bishop and his companions” but name none. The final announcement concerning Firminus is absent.

Munerat also writes “Nicasius the bishop,” but then, changing the location, has: “At Corbeil, the most blessed Quirinus and Poenitentia.”

Antwerp, Utrecht, and Leiden begin: “The translation of Saint Augustine, our father, bishop and confessor, from Sardinia to Pavia.” They are fairly pure in the Tarsian martyrs. Concerning Nicasius and his companions, after Pientia they add: “They were sent by Pope Clement, together with blessed Denis, to preach in Gaul; and, when the prefect Fescenninus pursued them, they attained the glory of martyrdom.” They have “Cainichus the abbot,” but say nothing about Firminus.

Louvain also has “our father,” from which it is clear that the text was for the use of the Augustinian Fathers. Otherwise it resembles the preceding witnesses, except that it entirely removes the eulogy of the Tarsian martyrs.

Albergen and the Danish manuscript begin: “The octave of blessed Francis the confessor.” In the rest they have the text of Antwerp-Major, but nothing about the translation of Saint Augustine.

[Col. 0565A] Centule is pure in the first entry, apart from the eulogy: “In the district of Vexin, Saints Nicasius, first bishop of Rouen, and his companions Quiriacus and Pientia, martyrs. In Syria, Saint Eustachius the martyr. At Tours, the burial of Saint Venantius, abbot and confessor.”

Brussels begins: “At Lier, a town of Brabant, the burial of Saint Gummarus the confessor.” It follows with Nicasius and his companions as Antwerp-Major. It is fairly pure in the Tarsian martyrs. Then: “At Acervo in Sicily, the feast of Saints Anastasius the priest, Placidus, and Martial. At Antioch, the feast of Saint Heraclius. At Cologne Agrippina, the burial of Lord Bruno, archbishop. At Verdun, the burial of the blessed Sanctinus, bishop and confessor. In Scotland, the burial of Saint Canute, abbot and confessor. On the same day, the translation of the blessed Augustine, glorious bishop and confessor.”

Hagenoyen begins with Nicasius and his companions, expanded as above. It is fairly pure in the Tarsian martyrs. Then it inserts: “At the city of Caesarea, the feast of Saint Reparata the virgin,” etc., as may be seen in the Appendices for 8 October. “At Pelusia [for *Belisia*], the burial of Saint Amour,” etc., in the same place. “In Scotland, the burial of Saint Canichus the abbot. In the city of Uzès, the burial of Saint Firminus,” etc.

Aquicinct adds at the end: “Also Saints Placidus and Athanasius.” The same is found in codex D, marked C by Cheval.

Victorin, Swedish Register, marked no. 130, adds at the end: “The translation of Saint Augustine, our father and bishop, from Africa into Sardinia.” The second translation is discussed above. Then: “At Tours, Saint Venantius the abbot.”

The Carthusian matricularies at Utrecht: “Sanctinus the bishop and martyr; Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus, martyrs; Melanius [as I said above, *Aemilianus* should be read], bishop and confessor; Gummarus the confessor; the translation of Augustine.” It is uncertain which translation is meant.

Bigotian, marked P 5, has first: “At the city of Rennes, Saint Melanius the confessor.”

Bigotian, marked D 9: “On this same day, Saint Nicasius the bishop, Quirinus the priest, and Subiculus the deacon.”

Augsburg has added in another hand: “At Rouen, Saint Nicasius the martyr and his companions.”

In the Vatican manuscript no. 5949, the commemoration of Cainichus and Firminus is absent; nothing has been added.

Altemps: “In Scotland, Saint Canuchus the abbot. At the city of Uzès, Saint Firminus,” etc.

Florence: “The first translation of the body of Saint Augustine, bishop and doctor, from Hippo to Sardinia.”

Bordeaux: “At Tours, Saint Melanius, bishop and confessor.” Is this not Aemilianus of Rennes, or of Roton?

Besançon: “In Scotland, Saint Canute,” etc. In my opinion, *Cainichus* should be read. “In the city of Uzès,” etc.

Luxovium: “Saint Sanctinus, first bishop of Verdun.” See also above.

Reims, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At Tours, Saint Venantius the abbot.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins with Nicasius, as Antwerp-Major. It is fairly pure in the Tarsian martyrs. Instead of *Cainichus*, it writes *Carachus*. Then: “Also, the translation of the body of the eminent doctor Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor, from Sardinia to the city of Ticinum, now called Pavia, where, by the devout king of the Lombards, named Liutprand, it was honorably brought back and deposited, as was fitting, in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, called the Golden Heaven, in the year of the Lord 723, in the time of Pope Gregory II and the emperor Leo III, [Col. 0566A] 283 years after his death (the chronological calculations do not agree). This is called his second translation. On the same day, Saints Anastasius the priest, Placidus, and Genesius, with their companions, martyrs. At Verdun, Saint Sanctinus, bishop and confessor of that place. At the city of Eurecia, Saint Firminus,” etc. “On this same day, Saint Athelburga the virgin. Also Saints Justus and Artemius and the virgin Honesta, martyrs. And at Tours, Saint Venantius the abbot.”

Belin begins: “At Pavia, the translation and reburial of the body of the most blessed father Augustine, bishop and confessor. At the city of Rennes, Saint Emilianus the confessor.” It is correct in the Tarsian martyrs. Then: “On the same day, the octave of Saint Francis the father.” The entry for Nicasius and his companions is absent. It is fairly pure in Cainichus and Firminus. Another edition adds at the end: “Also Placidus and Athanasius.”

Greven: “On this same day, Saints Anastasius the priest, Placidus, Martial, Genesius, and their companions, martyrs. At Antioch, the feast of Saint Heraclius. Saint Venantius the martyr. Saints Justus, Artemius, and Honesta the virgin, martyrs. At Verdun, the blessed Sanctinus, bishop and confessor of that place. Gummarus the confessor. Melanius the confessor. The translation of Saint Augustine the bishop. When Liutprand, the devout king of the Lombards, heard that the island of Sardinia had been devastated by the Saracens—the island to which the bones of the eminent doctor had once been transferred from Hippo because of the barbarians’ invasion—he sent his messengers there with all speed and, having provided a large sum of money, had the sacred relics brought to Pavia in the year of the Lord 723, 283 years after the saint’s death. This is said to be his second translation; the first is celebrated at the end of February. Some, however, celebrate the first here and the second there. Athelburga, virgin and abbess. Also Blessed Bruno, archbishop of Cologne Agrippina and confessor, the brother of the emperor Otto I.” See Surius.

Molan inserts the entire eulogy of Ado concerning the Tarsian martyrs in different type; it can be read in the source. At the end he describes, from Belin, the translation of Saint Augustine and Aemilianus. Then: “At Lier, the burial of Saint Gummarus, an illustrious confessor, who, among the other marks of his virtues, brought forth a spring from the earth with a blow of his staff; he also raised up a tree that had been cut down and thrown to the ground by divine assistance, and strengthened it so completely that no sign of injury appeared on it. As a testimony to so great a virtue, it remained unharmed for many years.” Then, in smaller type: “On this day died Blessed James the German, of the Order of Preachers. Athelburga, virgin and abbess.” Concerning Sanctinus, as in Belin. “From the calendar of the dead at Cologne, at Saint Pantaleon: Lord Bruno died, the pious shepherd of the holy Church of Cologne, who, among the other marks of his praiseworthy life, which his book of deeds recounts more fully, also raised this place from its foundations and richly endowed it with whatever was sufficient for those serving God there.”

In other editions [Col. 0566D] the text is simple. At the end, concerning Gummarus, Aemilianus, and Sanctinus, as above. “At Besançon, Saint Germanus, bishop and martyr. In England, Saint Ethelburga, virgin and abbess. On the eleventh day, Saint Theophanes, father, writer and poet, bishop of Nicaea. At Pavia, the translation and reburial,” etc., as in Belin. “On the same day, the burial of the blessed Bruno, archbishop of the Church of Cologne Agrippina. Who, among his other works,” etc. Then, in smaller type, concerning James the German, as above. Finally he repeats: “At Cologne, at Saint Pantaleon, Lord Bruno died, the pious shepherd of the holy Church of Cologne and founder of that monastery.” See what the cited author has here at the end of his Note.

[Col. 0561]

At Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia, the feast of the most blessed martyrs Tharacus, Probus, and Andronicus, who, during the persecution of Diocletian, were afflicted for a long time by the squalor of imprisonment, were examined three times by different tortures and punishments, and attained the triumph of glory in their confession of Christ. In the district of Vexin, the passion of Saints Nicasius [Col. 0563] the priest and his companions Quirinus and Pientia.

[Note: [Col. 0563A] Not certain words here, nor a few lines, but the entire section from beginning to end has been miserably defaced and torn apart by the knife, and no trace of the former section remains. Turn over your codices, Reverend Father: where has the original simplicity of Usuard gone, if not the author himself but a treacherous corrupter introduced the corrections into the Pratensian codex? BOUILLART.]

In Scotland, Saint Cainichus the abbot. At the city of Uzès, Saint Firminus, bishop and confessor.

## Fourth day before the Ides. Day 12.

[Note: [Col. 0567]]

Taken from Pratensis, Heriniensis, Munerat, Belin in the first edition, Greven, and Molan. The Danish codex is also added, although otherwise it is not sufficiently correct.

[Note: [Col. 0567A]]

Munerat reads *via Laurentia* instead of *via Laurentina*. The martyr’s name is variously expressed, but especially *Edistius* or *Hedistius*. The first form is supported by Greven, Molan, and others together with Ado; the second by Pratensis, Heriniensis, and the more reliable codices together with the *Romanum parvum*, and we agree with these. All the codices read *milium*, as I have also said elsewhere. Heriniensis has “four thousand,” etc. Greven and Molan have *Honericus*; Munerat has *Himericus*, and above he omitted the final number, six. Greven and Molan’s first edition reverse the order, reading “priests, deacons, bishops.” All have *Heremi*, except Molan alone. Here again, together with Greven, he has the names reversed: Felix and Cyprian. Munerat and Belin write *celebraverunt*. Heriniensis, clearly through a copyist’s error, reads *Africa* instead of *Syria*. Belin has *Scythia*. Munerat writes *Eustacius* instead of *Eustachius*.

[Note: [Col. 0567A]]

There is today a notable disagreement among the Hieronymian codices and also among the other martyrologists. The very ancient Epternacian manuscript announces first: “At Rome, the feast of Hedistus,” in which form Rabanus copied it from a similar manuscript. Other Hieronymian manuscripts explicitly read: “At Ravenna, on the Laurentine Way, the feast of Saint Edistus.”

I do not know where Florentius found the following in Notker: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Bodistus the martyr,” instead of Hedistus. I do indeed find, in third place, “Bedistus the martyr,” but at the beginning he clearly wrote: “At Ravenna, Saint Edistus,” in which he does not depart at all from his sources. For the *Romanum parvum* has simply: “At Ravenna, [Col. 0567B] Hedistus.” Ado, somewhat more distinctly and in accordance with the Hieronymian tradition, has: “At Ravenna, on the Laurentine Way, the feast of Saint Edistus.” From where Our Author took his entry is evident, and there is no doubt concerning Notker either, although he omitted the words “on the Laurentine Way.”

Whether *via Lauretina* should be substituted for *via Laurentina* may be learned from Florentius, from the grove planted with laurels. In any case, it seems beyond dispute that Hedistus was a martyr of Ravenna, Wandalbert also attesting this in the following verses:

> Then Edistus, by his merits, augments the fourth Ides,  
> by which Ravenna rejoices in its celebrated martyr.

Of the very strong and most glorious legion of African martyrs, the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* is the first to make mention: “In Africa, of four thousand nine hundred and seventy-six holy confessors who suffered under the Vandal persecution.” Victor of Vita draws forth tears—not now witnesses of compassion, but rather of a rejoicing spirit—when he describes the savage brutality of the barbarian Hunneric, book II, in the Chifflet edition, p. 24. From this, without doubt, the Viennese martyrologist drew the material for his encomium, following the *Little Roman Martyrology* in the number of martyrs; the author of that Martyrology, however, consulted a copy different from Chifflet’s *History of the Vandal Persecution*, since in the aforementioned Chifflet edition the entire company of martyrs is reduced to four thousand nine hundred and sixty-one. Ruinart, who revised the Vita text with renewed care, gives the number in full, p. 30. Baronius differs from both, reading “four thousand nine hundred and sixty-six.” The reckoning of our martyrologists seems altogether preferable, as it agrees with the most recent edition. Whatever the truth may be, Usuard, elegantly abridging Ado’s eulogy, rightly embraced his view even in determining the number of the champions.

As for our final announcement, disagreement exists among the Hieronymian codices, just as with the first: see Florentinius as arbiter. It is certain to us that, from a copy similar to the Epternacense, “In Syria, Eustachius—or Eustatius—the presbyter” was accepted, with his companions, if he had any, left out, as Our Author commonly does. Certainly, it could not be shown more clearly from the codices that this announcement is Usuardine. Rabanus also seems to have drawn from this very source when he writes: “And in Syria, Eustatius the presbyter”; there is added: “And Eucharistus, Burrus, Bonatus” (the Epternacense has *Donata*), concerning whom, since they do not belong to Usuard, we have no question here. Rosweyd included Eustachius with several others in an appendix, as though added to Ado; this is also indicated by the asterisk placed by Mosander. See the note appended by Castellanus to his universal Martyrology, in which he attempts to distinguish the confused martyrs. Whether he has done so successfully, I still would not dare assert, amid such disorder in the Hieronymian tables—a disorder which we shall attempt to resolve elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0567C]]

**TORNACENSE** lacks the entire first announcement; in the others it is exceptionally pure.

**ANTWERP-MAXIMUM** does not read “for the defense of the Catholic [truth],” etc., but rather “for the Catholic confession of God,” etc. At the end it adds: “In Britain, Saint Wilfrid, bishop and confessor, who, among his other virtues, is also said to have restored life to a dead man.” Wilfrid’s life was treated on 24 April. See also Surius for this day.

**ROSWEYD** adds beneath the text: “In Britain, the deposition of Saint Wilfrid, bishop and confessor.”

**PULSANENSE** is mutilated in the eulogy of the Africans after “King Hunneric”; otherwise it is fairly pure.

**ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK,** and **UGHELLIAN** add at the end: “At Bourges, Saint Epion, presbyter.”

**ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT-LEIDEN, LOUVAIN,** and **ALBERGEN**, whose text is fairly pure, have the same addition as those above: “At Bourges, Saint Epion, presbyter.”

**CENTULENSE**: “At Ravenna, on the Laurentian Way, Saint Hedistus the martyr. In Africa, of nine hundred and seventy-six holy confessors [Col. 0568C] and martyrs” (the four thousand are omitted). “At Meaux, Saint Santinus, bishop and confessor.” See the preceding day.

**BRUSSELS** begins: “In Burgundy, the feast of Saint Gangulphus the martyr, who was secretly killed by a certain cleric, the violator of his wife. In revenge for his death, while that same cleric was emptying his bowels, he poured out his entrails like Arius.” His life is published in the Acts on 11 May. “At Ravenna, on the Laurentian Way, the feast of Saint Hedistus the martyr and of Saints Caelestius and Saturus. In the province of Syria, of Saints Quirinus the presbyter and Evagrius. In Egypt, Saint Eustachius the presbyter. In Campania, Saint Eucharistus. [Col. 0568D] At Bourges, the deposition of Saint Epion the presbyter. Also Saint Wilfrinus, bishop and confessor.” I think Wilfrid is meant. It transfers the Africans to the following day.

**HAGENAU** brings here the prophet Lot, together with a summary of his life customarily gathered from Sacred Scripture. It then treats the African martyrs, in whose entry it is almost entirely pure. The remainder is missing.

**AQUICINCT** reduces the number of African martyrs to “three thousand nine hundred and seventy-seven.” At the end it adds: “At Bourges, Saint Opion. And Saints Saturus and Calixtus.”

**MATRICULENSE, CARTHUSIAN, UTRECHT**: “Amicus and Amelius, soldiers and martyrs, whose acts are read. Four thousand and more holy confessors and martyrs.”

In the **VATICAN**, no. 5949, Eustachius is absent. It adds: “At Rome, Saints Caelestinus and Saturus.”

**FLORENTINUS**: “At Bourges, Saint Epion the presbyter. Also Saint Vilstidius [or perhaps Wilfrid?], bishop and confessor. Also Saint Eulalgius.”

The **LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION** gives the pure text, except that at the end, concerning Eustachius, it adds “and confessor.” Then: “At Bourges, Saint Epion the presbyter and confessor. In the city of Meaux, Blessed Schynnius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Wilfrid, bishop and confessor of the city of York.” “On that day, Saint Maximilian, bishop and confessor.”

The second **BELIN EDITION**, at the end: “At Bourges, Opion the confessor.” See above.

**GREVEN**: “At Apamea, Blessed Marcellus, bishop and martyr, who, after destroying many temples of idols in the time of Theodosius the Elder, was seized by the pagans and crowned with martyrdom for confessing the name of Christ. In Campania, the feast of Saints Eucharistus, Fortunatus, and Priscianus. In Syria, the feast of Saints Syrus and Evagrius. At Rome, the feast of Saints Caelestis and Saturus. Also Saints Amelius and Amicus, whose remarkable acts are read in Vincent’s *Speculum*, book XXIV, chapter 162. Since they were wonderfully alike, they were eventually killed, together with many others, in the war which Charlemagne waged in Italy against Desiderius, king of the Lombards; rich in many works of piety, they obtained the palm of martyrdom. Of Maximilian, bishop and martyr of Lauriacum, who, having obtained the crown of martyrdom in the time of the emperors Carus and Numerian, was afterward translated by the duke of the Bavarians to Patavium, on the bank of the Enns, and is held in great veneration. Of Lucinius and his sister, martyrs. In England, Saint [Col. 0570A] Wilfrid, bishop of York and confessor, whom Bede had mentioned in book IV and, returning as it were to the earlier account in book V, describes more carefully from childhood his most virtuous life; he also adds an epitaph written in verse, in which, among other things, it is read that, after being tossed about by many dangers at home and abroad for a very long time, he finally rested in peace. He caused the four books of the holy Gospels to be written in letters of gold and a suitable golden case to be made for them. Of Anianus, bishop. Of Namaatus, bishop. In the city of Meaux, Saint Schynnius, bishop and confessor. Of Symperthus, bishop. At Bourges, Saint Opion, presbyter and confessor. In Aquitaine, Saint Gerald, abbot and confessor, of whom it is related in the acts of Saint Arnulphus, bishop of Soissons, that he succeeded that Arnulphus in governing the monastery; but, expelled by ambitious men, he went to Aquitaine and built a monastery, and his life and death shone with signs of virtue and the glory of miracles. Of Ardanus, abbot. In [Col. 0570B] Scotland, Moveus, abbot. Of Euphrasia, virgin and martyr. Of Harlindis, virgin and martyr.”

**MOLANUS**: “At Bourges, Opion the confessor.” Then, in smaller type, he describes from Greven everything concerning Wilfrid of York. He likewise treats Amelius and Amicus, noting them in Vincent’s *Speculum*, book XXIV, chapters 62 and following. At the end: “Of Maximilian, bishop and martyr of Lauriacum.” In other editions, concerning Opion, as above. “At Milan, the translation of Saint Mona, archbishop. In England, the feast of Saint Wilfrid, bishop of York and confessor. At Celena in Pannonia, of Maximilian, bishop and confessor of Lauriacum, whose body Saint Rupert, apostle of the Bavarians, translated to Lauriacum, dedicating many churches in his honor. Finally, Emperor Henry II translated his relics to Patavium.” Then, in smaller type: “At Pavia, of the holy martyrs Amelius and Amicus, whom King Desiderius killed in the war against Charlemagne.” From Castellanus you will learn that the relics are at Mortara.

[Col. 0565]

At Ravenna, on the Laurentian Way, the feast of Saint Hedistus the martyr. In Africa, of four thousand nine hundred and seventy-six holy confessors and martyrs under King Hunneric. Since they were bishops, priests, and deacons of the churches of God, accompanied by crowds of faithful peoples, they were driven into exile in a dreadful wilderness for the defense of Catholic truth, [Col. 0567] and at last, after being tortured in various ways, they completed their martyrdom. Among them were Cyprian and Felix, eminent priests of the Lord. In Syria, Saint Eustachius the presbyter.

The Third of the Ides. Day 13. [Note: [Col. 0569]]

Taken from the Praten, Herinien, Tornacense, Antwerp-M maximum, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0569D]]

The older manuscripts, together with Ado, write *Trodam*; printed editions, such as Munerat, have *Troadam*. Belin reads “disciple of the holy apostle Paul.” He likewise gives *Faustini* for *Fausti*, as well as *superciliciis*, and other errors. Again, Belin, Greven, and Molan write: “who held the pontificate of the Church from the apostle Peter.” Rosweyd, however, has: “who was sixth from the blessed apostle Peter in the Church of Antioch,” etc. I think Usuard read it as it stands in the text. Belin again wrongly substitutes *Amantii* for *Venantii*. We excluded the Praten codex from the pure witnesses because at the end it has the addition: “On that day, of the holy confessors Gerald and Leobonus.” I infer that this is by a more recent hand also from the fact that the customary witnesses, Antwerp-Maximum and Rosweyd, do not include that announcement.

[Note: [Col. 0569D]]

No martyrologist before the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* mentions Carpus, the apostle’s host and disciple; that author celebrates him as follows: “At Troas, Carpus, disciple of the apostle Paul.” From there the notice passed into Ado, and from Ado into his followers Usuard and Notker. Its first and certain source is 2 Timothy 4:13. Baronius hints at another matter in his Notes, which will be useful in its proper place. See what Tillemont thinks of these matters, volume I, pp. [Col. 0570D] 310 and 581.

Some Hieronymian manuscripts present the Cordoban martyrs distorted both in place and in names; Florentinius occupies himself with reconciling them. Rabanus drew his material from these; Our Author, however, followed his customary guide Ado, copying almost everything from him word for word—not from this day, but from 28 September, on which they were noted by the *Little Roman Martyrology* and adorned by Ado with the aforementioned eulogy. Why Usuard postponed them to this day, no other reason can be conjectured than the one we briefly touched upon on 28 September: namely, that he may have discovered that they were honored in Spain on this very day. Theodoric Ruinart collected more material on this subject, including their Acts among the genuine and selected texts, beginning at p. 597. The difficulties proposed by Tillemont, volume V, p. 796, are not so serious that they cannot easily be resolved. Our Cordoban martyrs are also praised in a hymn by Prudentius, in the same Ruinart, p. 517.

Wandalbert sang of those martyrs both on 28 September and on this day; perhaps he thought them different because of the distinction between Martial and Marcellus in his text. First he writes:

> Faustus, Martial, and Januarius adorn the fourth [day],  
> Famous alike in the robe and contest of martyrdom.

Today, however, he sums them up in a single verse:

> Marcellus, Faustus, and Januarius complete the threefold [company].

[Col. 0572A]

Theophilus, praised with distinction by Jerome in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 25, also first appears in the *Little Roman Martyrology*, in these words: “At Antioch, Theophilus, bishop, who was sixth after the apostles.” I scarcely doubt that this was taken from Rufinus, book IV, chapter 24. Ado expanded the phrasing very slightly, but I do not know from where Notker enlarged it. Our Author drew his entry from Ado, omitting the final two words, “a most learned man”—words which he could certainly have preserved, since his distinguished learning is amply established by the Eusebius and Jerome cited there, as you will find at greater length from the other writers cited by Baronius in his Notes. The work of our Halloix will be especially useful to us, to be compared with Tillemont’s French Commentary, volume III, beginning at p. 49.

Venantius has been discussed more than once in the Appendices. It is clear that this is the first day marked for him by Usuard, but Castellanus observed in his universal Martyrology that this is rather the day of his burial than of his death. His life is known chiefly from Gregory of Tours.

[Note: [Col. 0571B]]

**PRATEN**: We noted his addition above among the variants: “On that day, of the holy confessors Gerald and Leobonus.”

**TORNACENSE**, more defective than usual here, lacks the first and last announcement; in the two middle ones it is entirely pure.

**ANTWERP-MAXIMUM** again has an English addition: “On the same day, at Westminster, the translation of Saint Edward, king and confessor.”

**PULSANENSE** is defective in the eulogy of the Cordobans; otherwise it is fairly pure.

**ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK, THE BIGOTIAN CODEX no. P. 5,** and **UGHELLIAN** all add at the end after the text: “Also Marcellus, Adrian, and Marcus.” They seem to have been taken from the Hieronymian codices, but, as very often happens, they have been wrongly joined.

**ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEIDEN, ALBERGEN,** and **DANIC** all write *Faustini* instead of *Fausti*. All restore from Ado the words omitted by Usuard, namely “a most learned man.” All insert near the end: “Also at Chalcedon, Saints Marcellus [Antwerp-Maximum alone, among the others, reads *Marcellia*], Adrian, and Marcus.”

**LOUVAIN** agrees with the preceding witnesses but is defective in the Cordoban eulogy.

**CENTULENSE**: “At Troas, Saint Carpus, bishop, disciple of the apostle Paul. At Córdoba, Saints Faustus, Januarius, and Martial, who completed their martyrdom through the suffering of fire.”

**BRUSSELS** transfers here the African martyrs of whom we treated on the preceding day, enlarging the account from Ado. It is pure in the entry for Carpus. The entry for Theophilus follows as above. It is fairly pure in the Cordobans. “At Chalcedon, the feast of Saints Marcellus, Adrian, and Marcus. At Alexandria, Saint Athanasius, the orthodox.” The great Athanasius seems to be intended, but he is celebrated on 2 May. It continues: “At Clermont, Saint Gerald the confessor.” He is called Geraldus. See Castellanus and the codices below. Venantius will be treated on the following day.

**HAGENAU**, after “of the apostle,” adds concerning Carpus: “Of whom the same apostle makes mention in his Epistles.” It places here the Ravenna Hedistus, of whom we treated yesterday. To Theophilus it also adds the eulogy “a most learned man.” Then it adds: “Who composed the book of the four Gospels in a single volume. At Tours, the deposition of Saint Venantius, abbot, in the monastery of Saint Martin. On that day at Chalcedon, the passion of Saints Marcellus, Adrian, and Marcus.”

**AQUICINCT**, before Tours, inserts: “Also Saints Marcellus, Adrian, and Marcus. On the same day, Saint Gerald the confessor, who, although in lay dress, clung manfully to the Christian religion; how dear he was to God was demonstrated by the miracles which he performed while alive and which he worked in many ways after his death.”

[Col. 0572B]

**VICTORIN** and the **SWEDISH REGISTRY**, marked no. 130: “On that day, Saint Gerald the confessor.”

**MATRICULENSE, CARTHUSIAN, UTRECHT**: “Of Venantius, abbot and confessor. Of Carpus, disciple of blessed Paul. Of Faustus, Januarius, and Martial, who suffered grievously. Of Theophilus, bishop of Antioch.”

In the **VATICAN**, no. 5949, Faustus and his companions are absent, as is Venantius. It adds: “In Gaul, the deposition of Saint Gerald the confessor. The translation of Saint Gilbert the confessor. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Honorius, pope.” Greater authority will be needed before anything can be established concerning his cult.

**LYONS**: “The deposition of Blessed Gerald, confessor of Christ.” Concerning him, see the numerous earlier references.

**BORDEAUX**: “The translation of Saint Gerald the confessor.” Read with the others: “the deposition.”

**CHARLES-TOWN**: “At the city called Orlacus, Saint Gerald the confessor.”

**REIMS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris**: “In Aquitaine, [Col. 0572C] in the monastery of Aurillac, the deposition of Saint Gerald the confessor.”

The **LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION**: “At Cologne Agrippina, in the monastery of Saints Pantaleon, Cosmas, and Damian, physicians of God, the discovery of the body of Blessed Maurinus, abbot and martyr, under Emperor Otto I and his brother, Lord Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, in the year 956 from the Incarnation of the Word.” The text then follows as above in Antwerp-Maximum, etc. Then: “At Chalcedon, Saints Marcellus, Adrian, and Marcus, confessors. In the territory of Trier, the translation of Saint Lubentius, presbyter and confessor. On the same day, Saint Gerald the confessor. In Austria beside the Danube, the passion of Saint Coloman, martyr and pilgrim of Christ. On that day, the triumph of Saint Lambert, bishop of Liège and martyr. In England, the translation of Saint Edward, king and confessor.”

The second **BELIN EDITION** has the text as the first, but at the end joins together: “Also Marcellus, Adrian, Marcus, and Gerald.” The last confessor is wrongly connected with the first martyrs.

**GREVEN**: “At Chalcedon, Saints Marellus [Marcellus], Adrian, and Marcus. In Austria beside the Danube, the passion of Saint Coloman, martyr and pilgrim of Christ. At Cologne Agrippina, the discovery of Saint Maurinus, abbot and martyr. When Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, of blessed memory, was building the monastery of Saint Pantaleon in that city in the year of the Lord 966, and the ground was being dug to lay the foundations, a sacred body was found with this inscription: ‘Here rest the bones of Maurinus, abbot of good memory, who suffered martyrdom in the church courtyard on the fourth day before the Ides of June.’ On that day, the triumph of Saint Lambert, bishop of Liège and martyr. At Alexandria, Athanasius, an excellent teacher, who expounded the faith. In Usuard he is found on 2 May. In England, the translation of Saint Edward, king and confessor. In the territory [Col. 0573A] of Trier, Blessed Lubentius, presbyter and confessor. Conganus, abbot. Also Belixenda, of blessed memory, daughter of Charlemagne and wife of Saint Amelius, count and martyr.” Whether she has a cult will be considered later.

**MOLAN**: “On that day, the triumph of Saint Lambert at Steps. At Ceuta, a city of the Saracens, Saints Daniel, Samuel, Anglus, Domnus, Leo, Nicholas, and Hugolinus, martyrs of the Order of Friars Minor, who, burning with the desire for martyrdom, preached the Catholic faith there with undaunted mind and the greatest steadfastness. At last, after suffering insults, affronts, mockery, scourging, and imprisonment, they were crowned with martyrdom by beheading in the year of the Lord 1221, six years before the death of our blessed Father Francis. At Alexandria, the feast of Saint Anastasius, bishop, and Saint Lupentius, presbyter, and Saint Gerald, confessor. At Cologne, in the monastery of Saints Pantaleon, Cosmas, and Damian, physicians of God, the discovery of the body of Saint Maurinus, abbot and martyr, [Col. 0573B] which was found in the year 964 from the Lord’s Incarnation, while the foundations of that church were being dug, with an inscription of this kind: ‘Here rest,’ etc.” Then, in smaller type, concerning Coloman, as above. “Also Saint Gerbrand, abbot and confessor. Of Simpert, the twelfth bishop of the church of Augsburg, around the year 756, whose body rests in the monastery of Saints Ulrich and Afra. Through his merits, amid various miracles, a certain poor woman recovered the use of one arm and hand, which she had lacked for several years. After receiving her health, she gave praise and left there a wax arm as a sign of her recovery.” Other editions: “At Ceuta of the Saracens,” etc., as above in the first edition. “In Gaul, Saint Gerald the confessor. At Trier, Saint Lupentius the presbyter. At Augsburg, Saint Simpert, bishop and confessor. On that day, the triumph of Saint Lambert at Steps. At Cologne, in the monastery of Saint Pantaleon,” etc., as above. Finally, in smaller type: “Also Saint Gerbrand, confessor and first abbot at Floricampus, of the Cistercian order.” See Castellanus in his universal Martyrology.

At Troas, the feast of Blessed Carpus, disciple of the apostle Paul. In Spain, in the city of Córdoba, the passion of Saints Faustus, Januarius, and Martial. First tormented by the punishment of the rack, then with their eyebrows shaved, their ears and noses cut off, and even their upper teeth pulled out, they finally completed their martyrdom through the suffering of fire. At Antioch, Saint Theophilus, who, sixth after the apostle Peter, held the pontificate of the Church. At Tours, Saint Venantius, abbot. [Bouillart adds, in Italian type: [Note: [Col. 0569C] “The Praten codex,” says Sollerins, “we excluded from the pure witnesses because at the end it has the addition: ‘On that day, of the holy confessors Gerald and Leobonus.’” [Col. 0570C] Forgive me if he was not warned that those holy confessors had been added by a more recent hand. Bouillart.] On that day, of the holy confessors Gerald and Leobonus.

The Second of the Ides. Day 14. [Note: [Col. 0573]]

Taken from the Praten, Herinien, Tornacense, Antwerp-Maximum, Rosweyd, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0573B]]

I discussed elsewhere the forms *Calixtus*, *Callistus*, *Calistus*, and *Calestus*, as you may see under 16 April. Here again I follow our older codices, Praten and Herinien, together with the Hieronymian witnesses. Enough has also been said about *cotidie*. Among other typographical errors, Munerat has *tantem vero*. Praten, Herinien, and Munerat read *Tutertina*; I am compelled, with all the others, to write the better form *Tudertina*. Munerat has another error in *affugandis*, for *effugandis*. [Col. 0574B] The greatest variation concerns the final verb, *enituit*, which is written in this way by Praten, Tornacense, and Munerat. Herinien wrongly changes the verb *pollebat*, which Gregory uses, into the past form *polluit*. Antwerp-Maximum, Greven, and Molan have *emicuit*. The copyist of Rosweyd’s codex, uncertain which reading to prefer, wrote *emicuit* and added *enituit* above it. We think we should read as Usuard does.

[Note: [Col. 0573C]]

The feast of Calixtus, Callistus, or Calistus the pope—whether this is the day of his death or rather, according to Ado’s view, the day of his burial—is solemnly commemorated in the oldest monuments of the Church on the day before the Ides of October. On this very day, the calendars of Bucherius, Allatius, Fronto, and other very ancient writers, as well as Gregory’s Sacramentary and all the Martyrologies, speak of him. The Hieronymian codices do indeed remember Calixtus, Callistus, or Calestus, though not in the same wording. Florentinius attempts both to reconcile the disagreement among these copies and to identify his companion.

Bede, and Rabanus after him, adorn Callistus with a notable eulogy, which is more fully given in Ado, though taken from the same source—a source which Baronius recognized as insufficiently clear and purified, both in his Notes and in his Annals, under the year 226, no. 2, as we noted more fully above under 10 May. The material published by Surius may be consulted. In any case, what Our Author produced in today’s entry seems to have been taken from Bede rather than Ado.

The *Little Roman Martyrology* had briefly preceded Ado: “At Rome, Callistus, pope and martyr, and Privatus the soldier.” Florentinius prefers to join Saturninus as Callistus’s companion; Wandalbert leaves the companion unnamed:

> Callistus, on the preceding day, bishop and martyr,  
> Outstanding in triumph and shining, accompanied by a martyr.

[Col. 0574C]

Tillemont gave a brief collection concerning the pontificate of Saint Callistus in volume III, beginning at p. 250. Part of the Acts was published under 10 May, where Calepodius, Palmatius, and their companions were treated; the remainder will be explained in its proper place.

All the ancient Martyrologies are silent about Fortunatus, bishop of Todi; consequently, he is plainly Usuardine, having undoubtedly been found in the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory, whose words, for the most part, form the basis of our announcement from book I, chapter 10. Yet in Gregory, who is concerned only with reporting miracles, Our Author did not find the day of his death, whatever Ferrarius may confidently mark as the day before the Ides of October. Hence, it may not rashly be conjectured that this day was selected above all others at Usuard’s own discretion and subsequently became established among later writers, as often happened with other saints transferred from Gregory’s *Dialogues* into the sacred calendars.

Why the memory of Fortunatus is celebrated more festively at Todi on 30 June, see Baronius’s Notes. Castellanus observes that his feast is solemnly commemorated in that city on 30 August; whether this is because the inhabitants consider it the day of his death will be investigated in its proper place. Meanwhile, see what is extant concerning Fortunatus in Surius for this day. Today Ado again includes Justus of Lyons, concerning whose deposition and translation we treated fully on 2 September.

[Note: [Col. 0573D]]

**PULSANENSE** continues to be defective: almost every day it is mutilated in the saints’ eulogies. Today concerning Callistus it has only as far as “pope and martyr,” with everything else removed. It is fairly pure in the entry for Fortunatus.

**ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK,** and **UGHELLIAN** again agree here, as usual: they are pure in the Usuardine text, but at the end add: “Also Saturninus and Lupus.” These are Cappadocian martyrs; see their companions in the Hieronymian codices.

**UTRECHT, LEIDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN,** and **DANIC** have: “Also Saints Saturninus and Lupus.”

**ANTWERP-MAXIMUM** has the same addition and further adds: “On the same day, at Bruges, Blessed Donatian, seventh archbishop of Reims.”

**CENTULENSE**: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Calixtus, pope and martyr, who sat in the episcopate for seven years, two months, and ten days, and under the rule of Alexander obtained the glory of martyrdom. In the city of Todi, Saint Fortunatus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the feast of Saint Donatian, seventh bishop of Reims, whose body is held in great reverence at the castle of Bruges. On that day, Saint Viator, lector and companion of Saint Justus, bishop.” See the Observations.

**BRUSSELS**: “At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, the feast of Saint Callistus, pope and martyr, who instituted the fasts of the four seasons. Under the persecution of Emperor Alexander, he was imprisoned and cured a certain soldier both of the foulness of his ulcers and of unbelief. When Emperor Alexander heard this, he ordered the soldier to be beaten with leaden clubs, but Blessed Pope Calixtus to be thrown from the window of the house and plunged into a well with a stone tied around his neck. After seventeen days, the presbyter Asterius, with the clergy, lifted his body by night and buried it in the cemetery of Calepodius, who had completed his martyrdom before him.” See Ado. “At the monastery of Maurus, Saint Celestis, bishop, disciple of blessed Peter the apostle. He came with blessed Clement and Felix to the city of Metz; afterward, having been made bishop in that same city, he led a heavenly life and finally departed to Christ. And at Córdoba, the feast of the holy martyrs Saturninus, Lupus, and Aurelia.” See the second Appendix. It is pure in the entry for Fortunatus. “On the same day, Saint Donatian, archbishop of Reims. At Tours, the deposition of Saint Venantius, abbot and confessor. In the city of Beauvais, Saint Angadrisma, virgin, bride of Saint Ausbert, archbishop of Rouen.” Castellanus calls her Angadrisma. [Col. 0575C] “Also the passing of Saint Justus.” See the Observations.

**HAGENAU**, besides the fast of the Four Seasons, introduces other statutes of Callistus, which I would rather find elsewhere. It is fairly pure in the entry for Fortunatus. Then: “In Britain, Saint Paulinus, bishop and confessor in the city of York.” See above under 10 October. “Also Saints Saturninus and Lupus, martyrs.”

**AQUICINCT** adds at the end: “Also Saints Saturninus and Lupus. In the district of Beauvais, Saint Angadrisma, virgin. At Bruges, Saint Donatian, archbishop and confessor.”

**VICTORIN** at the end: “Also Saint Fortuna, virgin,” for Fortunata. See below.

**MATRICULENSE, CARTHUSIAN, UTRECHT**: “Of Calixtus, pope and martyr. Of Donatian, bishop and confessor. Of Fortunatus, bishop. Of Eutropius, bishop” (a note in the margin says: “I find him nowhere else on this day”), “of Fortunata, virgin and martyr, with her three brothers.”

The **SWEDISH REGISTRY**, marked no. 428: “At Beauvais, Saint Angadrisma, virgin.” See Brussels.

The **SWEDISH REGISTRY**, marked no. 130: “Also Saint Fortunata, virgin.” See the following column.

In the **VATICAN**, no. 5949, Fortunatus is absent. It adds: “On the same day, the passing of Saint Justus the hermit. In Campania, Saint Fortunata, virgin, who suffered with her three brothers, Carponius, Evaristus, and Priscianus, at Caesarea, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian and the governor Urbanus.”

**FLORENTINUS**: “Also Saints Saturninus and Lupus. Also Saint Gaudentius.” The **STROZZIAN** adds “bishop.” See Greven.

[Col. 0576A]

**LUXOVIENSE**: “The passing of Saint Justus the confessor in the desert. On that day, Caelestis, bishop of that city.”

The **LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION**, interpolated in the entry for Calixtus, besides the fast of the Four Seasons adds: “which he instituted so that the promotions of the ecclesiastical orders would take place gradually, and introduced the practice of perpetual chastity among the ministers of the Church.” The rest is given above. In the entry for Fortunatus it is pure. Then: “On the same day, Saints Saturninus and Lupus, martyrs. At Trier, Saint Rusticus, second bishop and confessor. At Würzburg, Saint Burchard, first bishop and confessor of that city. In the desert, the passing of Saint Justus the hermit. In the city of Metz, Saint Caelestis, second bishop and confessor of that city. In the city of Reims in Gaul, Saint Donatian, bishop and confessor.”

**BELIN**, after “he obtained,” inserts: “He established that the fast should be held on Saturday four times a year, of grain, wine, and oil according to the prophecy.” At the end: [Col. 0576B] “Also Saints Saturninus and Lupus.”

**GREVEN**: “On the same day, Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Rimini and martyr. Born at Ephesus, he was ordained priest at Rome in the time of Pope Damasus and became famous for miracles. Then consecrated bishop of the Church of Rimini, after converting many to the faith, he was killed in defense of the Catholic faith with clubs and stones until his spirit was released. In the city of Córdoba, Lupus and Aurelia. Of the martyrs Saturninus and Lupus. At Vienne, Saints Agratus and Casturius, bishops of that same city. At Trier, Saint Rusticus, second bishop and confessor of that city. At Würzburg, Saint Burchard, first bishop and confessor of that Church. He was a relative of Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr of Mainz, and was ordained bishop of the aforementioned Church by him in the year of the Lord 751. After governing it vigorously for a long time, he appointed another in his place out of desire for the solitary life; devoting himself to God and to himself, [Col. 0576C] he died in the fortieth year of his priesthood. Here is the deposition of Justus, bishop and confessor of Lyons. Loving the solitary life himself, he lived most holily for several years in the desert and, as he was dying, foretold to his minister Viator that he would soon follow him. In the city of Reims in Gaul, Blessed Donatian, archbishop and confessor. At Metz, Blessed Caelestis, second bishop and confessor of that city, disciple of blessed Peter the apostle. Of Vitalis, confessor. At Beauvais, Saint Angadrisma, virgin, bride of Saint Ausbert of Rouen.” See above, 5 February. “Of Fortunata, virgin and martyr, and her three brothers.”

**MOLAN**: “Also Saints Saturninus and Lupus. At Trier, Saint Rusticus, bishop and confessor. At Bruges, Saint Donatian, archbishop of Reims. At Lyons in Gaul, the passing of Saint Justus in the desert. In the territory of Châlons, Saint Manegildis, virgin.” Then, in smaller type, concerning Burchard from Greven, through “in the year of the Lord 751.” Then: “Also Placilla, of blessed memory, wife of Emperor Theodosius. On the same day died Dominic Loricatus, whose life Peter Damian wrote, in volume VIII of Aloysius.” In other editions, concerning Saturninus and Lupus as above. “At Würzburg, Saint Burchard, bishop and confessor.” Concerning Donatian, Rusticus, and Manegildis, as above. Then concerning Angadrisma, as in Greven. Then: “And Saint Cosmas of Hagia Polis, father and poet, bishop of Maiuma.” In smaller type: “On the same day died the venerable Dominic Loricatus.”

[Col. 0573]

At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, the feast of Blessed Callistus, pope and martyr. Emperor Alexander ordered him to be tormented by hunger during prolonged imprisonment and beaten daily with clubs; at last, thrown from the window of the house in which he was confined, he obtained the triumph of victory. In the city of Todi, Saint Fortunatus, bishop, who shone with the grace of immense power in driving away unclean spirits.

The Ides. Day 15. [Note: [Col. 0577]]

I consider the Praten and Munerat witnesses pure. Rosweyd and the first edition of Belin come very close to them.

[Note: [Col. 0577A]]

I said that the last two approach textual purity most closely, for at the beginning both are corrupt: Rosweyd has “At Cologne, 340 holy Moors,” and Belini “300 martyrs.” It is entirely certain that *fifty* must be read, as the older manuscripts have it: Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Pulsanen., Aquicinct., and Munerat. from Ado. Munerat. subsequently omits the word *sacred* after *from the legion*. Likewise, instead of *they completed*, he reads *they fulfilled*, and instead of *Basoli* he has *Bajoli*.

Here I note that I have excluded the Herinien. manuscript because, in second place, it inserts: “On the same day, Saint Oswald, bishop and confessor.” At the end it also has: “In the territory of Rheims, the translation of Saint Basolus the confessor, which was carried out by Hincmar, archbishop, a venerable man.” This is indeed what he writes, although it is not purely Usuardine. It seems likely to me that the Oswald mentioned here is Oswald of Worcester and York, whose feast is kept on 29 February; yet he could also be identified with Ethelwald of Lindisfarne, who was likewise called Oswald, as Henschenius thought in volume III for February, page 750. See what we said about the Herinien. manuscript in the preface. Antuerp.-Maj. discussed the translation of some Oswald on 8 October; but here that same manuscript adds at the end: “In Britain, Saint Wulfun, bishop and confessor,” for which Henschenius, at the cited place, reads *Wlfranni*.

[Col. 0577A]

That the feast of the holy Moors is recorded today in the Hieronymian Martyrologies is clear. The fact that Rabanus, following those manuscripts, places these martyrs in the territory of Pinus is easily corrected, for he intended to read: “In Gaul, at Cologne Agrippina, the feast of the Moors.” Until now I have found no record of the number of these champions.

[Col. 0577B]

Whether the groups of Thebans and Moors, which Florentius distinguishes from Elinandus, or Helinandus, a writer of the thirteenth century, are sufficiently well founded is another question; so too whether these men belonged to the Theban Legion, as Ado most explicitly asserts, followed in this by Usuard and Notker, or rather constituted another group brought to Cologne from the shores of Africa, as Grevenus and other popular writers maintain.

For my part, I find no older—and therefore no more reliable—information concerning their number and nationality than that found in Gregory of Tours, in the *Book of the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 62, from which Ado plainly took his account. Gregory says there:

“THEY ARE SAID TO HAVE BEEN FIFTY MEN FROM THAT SACRED LEGION OF THE THEBEANS.”

And because the basilica shines with marvelous workmanship, gilded, as it were, with mosaic, the inhabitants wished to call the basilica “the Golden Saints.” These are Gregory’s words, transferred by Ado into his Martyrology. From them one may judge how admirably the later writers presumed to correct—or, rather, to corrupt—Usuard, as Molanus candidly admits having done. Above I showed that others attempted the same thing improperly, and this will become still clearer from the subsequent additions, which do not differ at all from the Utrecht Breviary published at Leiden in 1508, a work later, of course, than the Utrecht Carthusian Register, which will also be cited below.

The exceptional devotion of the people of Cologne toward their martyrs is certainly worthy of praise. From the time of Gregory of Tours, throughout so many centuries, they have continuously preserved and honored, with ever greater adornment, both the basilica gilded in this manner and the Golden Saints. I myself have been privileged more than once to behold them there with the greatest pleasure. Let this be said only in passing.

Wandalbert adorns the Moors without deciding anything concerning the disputed matters:

> On the Ides, therefore, the throng of Moors is commemorated for you,
>
> At Agrippina, joyful alike in blessed spirits,
>
> Who devoted their service to Christ through courage and death.

The text then continues with Fortunatus the martyr. I have no doubt that Usuard took him from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; and I readily agree with Rosweyd that he was altogether wrongly attributed to Ado, since in Notker he is recorded quite differently. For Notker, following Rabanus, joined Libulus of Capua with Fortunata. Indeed, if we consult the first source in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, it seems that *Fortunata*, not *Fortunatus*, should be read; there one reads: “On the Via Aurelia, in her cemetery, Saint Fortunata.”

Ado is the first of all to mention Antiochus of Lyon. Notker took from him only the name and location, while our author contracted part of the eulogy quite elegantly. Severtius collected some records concerning Antiochus’s life, beginning on page 37. He is also known from the *Life of Saint Justus*; see what we said about him on 2 September.

At the end, according to the reading of our manuscripts, Basolus is placed here. This is incorrect if the reference is to the day of his death, since that certainly belongs to 26 November. For this reason the Herinien. manuscript more properly reported above the translation of his body by Hincmar on this day; that manuscript was accustomed to add here and there local notices from Rheims to Usuard. Mabillon reports and discusses various matters concerning Basolus in the second volume of the Benedictine work, beginning on page 64. But what is there quoted under Ado’s name concerning Basolus is a mere addition, which I was able to find only in the Lobbes manuscript. It is therefore clear that Basolus is properly Usuardine: because he had become famous through a celebrated translation in Usuard’s time, Usuard thought that he should be commemorated on this day.

[Col. 0577C]

Concerning the HERINIENSI and ANTUERP.-MAJ. manuscripts, see what was said above in the section on variants.

TORNACEN. says nothing about the Moors, but adds at the end: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Bercharius, abbot and martyr.” This feast is found on this day in the Roman Martyrology. See there Castellanus’s note, which is discussed elsewhere.

PULSANEN. is pure in the first notice. It omits the second. Of the third it has only: “At Lyon, Saint Antiochus, bishop.” In the fourth it writes *Bassoli*.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. have “300 martyrs.” At the end: “At Capua, Saints Lufilus and Fortunatus.”

[Col. 0577D]

GREVEN. has 360, and after the text adds: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Gregory the pope from the city of Rome.”

MOLAN. follows GREVEN. in the number, 360, and omits the final notice.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., and ALBERG. DANIC. all give the number of the martyrs as 360. They insert into the text: “under the persecution of Maximian, and with their leader Gregory.” At the end: “At Capua, Saints Lufilus [Lusyli, Lusili, Infili] and Fortunatus.”

CENTULEN.: “At Cologne Agrippina, fifty holy martyrs. At Lyon, Saint Antiochus, bishop. At the monastery of Fontenelle, the translation of Saint Wulfrannus, formerly archbishop of Sens and confessor. In the territory of Rheims, the feast of Saint Basolus, confessor and monk, whose holy way of life also shone forth through miracles.”

BRUXELLEN. has the Moors as ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. It is pure in the notice of Fortunatus. Then: “At Capua, Saints Lusilus and Fortunatus.” It is again pure in the notices of Antiochus and Basolus. At the end: “At the monastery of Fontenelle, the elevation and translation of Saint Wulfrannus, archbishop and confessor.”

HAGENOYEN.: “At Cologne Agrippina, outside the walls, the feast of the holy Moors, with forty.” I think *CUM* was formed from *CCC*, so that *CCCXL* should be read. The remainder is generally like ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. In the rest of the text it is fairly pure. Instead of *Basoli* it has *Basili*.

[Col. 0579A]

At the end it adds: “At Capua, Saints Lusius and Fortunatus, martyrs. In Syria, Saint Eustachius, priest and confessor. At Bourges, Saint Epionus, priest and confessor.” Both were discussed above, on 12 October.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end: “At Capua, Saints Lupilus and Fortunatus. On the same day, Saint Wulfrannus, archbishop of Sens.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked number 130: “In the territory of Limoges, Saint Leonard, confessor.” Others assign his location more accurately below.

DAVERON: “In the district of Le Mans, Saint Leonard, confessor.” See Castellanus.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Basolus, abbot and confessor. The translation of the fifty holy martyrs from the Theban Legion. On this day Saint Hedwig, duchess of Moravia, Silesia, and Slavonia, died in the year of the Lord 1243. She was the maternal aunt of Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia, who was canonized by Clement IV. When he delayed her canonization, he prayed at Mass that, if she were so meritorious before God and if it were God’s will that she be enrolled in the catalogue of the saints, his blind daughter—whom he had had by his own wife while still in the lay state—might receive her sight through Hedwig’s merits. This occurred; therefore he canonized her immediately, in the year of the Lord 1267, although Urban IV had intended to canonize her but was prevented by death.” The copyist says that this was written below the margin.

BIGOTIAN. sign. P 5: “At Capua, Saints Lufilus and Fortunatus.”

BIGOTIAN. sign. E. 40: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Gregory the pope from the city of Rome.”

AUGEN.: “On that day, the feast of Saint Beracharius, abbot and martyr.”

CODEX D. LE MARE sign. A: “In the region of Augustodunum, Saint Leonard, abbot.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL sign. B: “At Capua, Saints Lusilus and Fortunatus.”

In the VATICAN manuscript numbered 5949, the commemoration of Fortunatus and Basolus is absent. The following is added: “At Benevento, the feast of the holy martyrs Lupulus and Modestus, at Saint Sophia. And Saint Tammarus, bishop and confessor.”

ALTEMPS.: “On that day the bodies of Saints Sebastian and Gregory were translated from Rome. In Lesser Britain, Saint Erkletus, martyr.”

FLORENTIN.: “At Capua, Saints Rufilius, or Rufilus, martyrs, and Fortunatus.”

LUXOVIEN.: “At Luxeuil, the dedication of the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition is somewhat fuller concerning the Moors, adding: “With their leader Gregory and blessed Constantius, they completed the course of their contest; and together with blessed Gereon and his companions, they chose perpetual rest for their blessed bodies in the basilica, which shone, as it were, gilded with mosaic through marvelous workmanship. At Trier, the feast of Saint Severus, bishop and confessor.”

The rest of the text follows and is fairly pure. Then: “At Capua, Saints Lufilus and Fortunatus, martyrs. At Vienne, Saints Agratus and Castulus, bishops and confessors of that same city. At Limoges, blessed Austridinus, confessor. On the same day, Saint Hedwig, queen. Likewise Saint Wulfrannus, bishop and confessor. At Strasbourg, the feast of Saint Aurelia, virgin, who was one of the eleven thousand virgins and, having fallen ill there on her return from Rome, died there.”

BELINI’s second edition has in the first notice “three hundred martyrs.” At the end: “At Capua, Lupinus and Fortunatus, martyrs.”

GREVEN.: “At Capua, Saints Lufilus and Fortunatus, martyrs. At Vienne, Saint Deodatus, bishop and confessor. At Trier, the feast of blessed Severus, bishop and confessor. Wulfrannus, bishop and confessor. At Limoges, Saint Austridinus, confessor. Speciosa, virgin. At Antioch, Saint Margaret, virgin. To escape the sea of this world, she abandoned her bridegroom, entered a monastery of men in male clothing, and took the name Pelagius. Living there in great holiness and placed over a monastery of virgins, she was falsely accused of fornication, did penance, and, full of holiness, entered into rest. Note. The aforementioned 360 martyrs were from Mauritania, which is part of Africa, not from the Theban Legion, although Ado and Usuard have it so: ‘and they came to Cologne by ship with their leader Gregory.’ Likewise Saint Leonard of Corbignac, confessor. As Vincent reports in book XXII, in the time of King Lothair, he built a monastery for himself and his followers in the district of Le Mans. He displayed such humility among all that, avoiding the title of prior, he showed himself inferior to everyone. At length, renowned for his life and miracles, he entered into rest around the year 559.”

Rather, somewhat later.

“At Strasbourg, Saint Aurelia, virgin, who belonged to that noble company of eleven thousand virgins and, having fallen ill in the aforesaid city on her return from Rome, died in peace. On the same day, Saint Placidia, virgin, daughter of the emperor Valentinian. Rejecting the world and attaching herself to her grandmother Galla, she devoted herself to fasting, almsgiving, and continual prayer; at length she entered into rest at Verona, resplendent with signs. On that day, Saint Hedwig, duchess of Poland, maternal aunt of Saint Elizabeth, landgravine. This most holy matron showed herself toward the poor pious beyond what can be expressed: she supplied them with food on bended knees and kissed their washed feet. She was also intensely devoted to continual prayer, chastising her body severely with cold, nakedness, fasting, and scourging. Shining with the prophetic spirit, she entered into peace.”

MOLAN. adds the following concerning the Moors in the text, in different type and drawn from Ado: “Buried in the basilica, which shines, as it were, gilded with mosaic through marvelous workmanship; hence the inhabitants have become accustomed to calling them the Golden Saints.”

At the end, from HERINIENSI: “On the same day, Oswald, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Rheims, the translation of Saint Basolus, confessor, which was carried out by Hincmar, archbishop, a venerable man.” Then: “On that day, Saint Severus, bishop of Trier.”

Next, in smaller type: “In Silesia, on that day, Saint Hedwig, duchess of Poland, maternal aunt of Saint Elizabeth, landgravine. In Scotland, Saint Malcolm, king, who took blessed Margaret as his wife from Hungary and, renowned for holiness, entered into rest in the Lord in the year 1097.”

Other editions have the text as in the first edition. At the end: “On the same day, Oswald, bishop of Worcester and confessor.” See above in the section on variants. Concerning Severus, see above.

“At Krakow, Saint Hedwig, duchess of Poland. At Strasbourg, Saint Aurelia, virgin. On that day, Saint Theodoric, confessor, of the Carmelite order. At Verona, Saint Placidia, most holy virgin, daughter of the emperor Valentinian.” Concerning the translation of Basolus, see above. Finally: “At the port of Valenciennes, the elevation of the most precious body of blessed Salvius, martyr and bishop of the city of Angoulême.” This clearly seems to designate that Salvius about whom our Observation of 1 July should be consulted.

[Col. 0575]

At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of the fifty holy martyrs, who, being from the sacred Theban Legion, completed the course of their contest in that same city. At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, Saint Fortunatus. At Lyon, Saint Antiochus, bishop, who, having energetically administered the episcopal office to which he had been appointed, attained the heavenly kingdom. In the territory of Rheims, Saint Basolus, confessor.

**XVII Kalends. Day 16.**

[Col. 0581]

Among all the manuscripts, Molanus alone is either pure or very close to purity.

[Col. 0581A]

Molanus has *Satyriani*; we, with nearly all the others, have *Satiriani*. *Saturiani* ought to be read, as I shall say below. Again, he agrees with Grevenus in reading *in exile through banishment*; the others have the reading found in the text. Finally, instead of *she also suffered*, he writes *but she suffered*.

Let us now examine the corruptions of the other manuscripts. Concerning the notice of Ambrosius, in which Praten., Antuerp.-Maj., and Rosweyd. disagree with the others, we shall speak in the Observations.

Praten. also has the addition: “At the monastery of Clervo”—perhaps it reads *Derno* or *Dervo*—“Saint Bercharius, martyr and abbot.” He died on 26 March; therefore Herinien. more appropriately, though not more in accordance with Usuard, writes: “On that day, the translation of Saint Bercharius, abbot and martyr.”

Tornacen. is mutilated in the first notice and adds at the end: “At the monastery of Jotro, the feast of Saint Priscus, martyr.”

Antuerp.-Maj. begins: “The dedication of the basilica of blessed Michael the archangel on Mount Tumba, where God displayed many miracles,” adding near the end, “and the reception of his relics.” These words are absurd unless *his* refers to the basilica, so that the meaning is the reception of the relics of that basilica whose dedication is under discussion.

Rosweyd. has at the end: “In Alemannia, Saint Gallus, abbot and confessor. At Cologne, Saint Eliphius, martyr.”

Pulsanen., mutilated in the first notice and pure in the second, adds: “Likewise the dedication of the basilica of Saint Michael the archangel in the sea, on the mountain called Tumba.” These examples are sufficient; we shall give the rest in the additions.

[Col. 0581B]

Among the Hieronymian tables, the difference occurring today is that some write: “And in Africa, the passion—or the sufferers—of Cacra, or Cecra, and 270 others”; while others have: “In Asia, Cereas and 270 others.” Rabanus follows this latter reading; others prefer the former. Yet there is nowhere even a word about the Vandal persecution. Florentius is therefore right to judge that our anonymous group of 270, even if we admit them to have been Africans, must at least be separated chronologically from those named individually in the list, whose illustrious struggles Victor of Vita describes in book I, in the Chifletian edition beginning on page 10. There you will not find even a letter that can be reduced to these 270, unless from the indefinite number of martyrs who suffered here and there one arbitrarily gathers a definite number.

The *Small Roman Martyrology*, however, speaks differently, expressly joining these anonymous martyrs with the others—Martinianus, Saturianus, and so forth—in these words: “The holy martyrs Martinianus and Saturianus, with their two brothers and 270 others, likewise crowned, under the Vandal persecution.”

Certainly the author of this Martyrology could not have extracted this from Victor, nor can one easily identify another source. Again, this day seems to have been chosen by him purely at will. In all other respects Ado follows him, placing the 270 anonymous martyrs at the beginning but connecting them so closely with those who follow that he refers all of them to the same persecution. In the meantime, however, in his longer narrative he develops from Victor only those matters that properly concern Martinianus and Saturianus with their two brothers, and the illustrious handmaid of Christ, Maxima the virgin, treating them separately and individually.

Usuard and Notker, each in his customary manner, embraced Ado’s view. Both contracted the eulogy, each according to his own judgment, and from them it passed into all the later Martyrologies.

Florentius thinks that Belini intended to divide the groups completely, since after the anonymous martyrs he begins another notice separately with: “Likewise the saints Martinianus, etc.” As though Baronius had not also divided them by writing “There,” and so forth, while nevertheless affirming that the former too suffered in the Vandal persecution and, indeed, that they were taken from Victor.

[Col. 0581D]

Wandalbert expresses the number of the anonymous martyrs in such a way that he leaves entirely undecided their nationality, location, and date:

> Two hundred and seventeen are said to have been slain,
>
> Whom an unjust fury slaughtered with equal honor for Christ.

Nor would I dare determine anything concerning these matters until it has been possible to examine each point more carefully. For the present, it is enough to have set out the differing opinions. I mention in passing only one point: the names of two martyrs have been dislocated in our Martyrologies. Instead of *Martiani* and *Satiriani* or *Satyriani*, one should read with Victor and Baronius *Martinianus* and *Saturianus*.

The manuscripts agree in recording the commemoration of Ambrosius, but they differ completely in its wording. Praten., together with Antuerp.-Maj. and Rosweyd., reads: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Ambrosius, bishop of Cahors.” Munerat. nearly agrees, writing: “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Ambrosius, confessor, bishop of Cahors.”

Herinien., Tornacen., Pulsanen., Belin., Greven., and Molan., on the contrary, simply give him the title of confessor, reading: “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Ambrosius, confessor.”

I admit that the former reading is also genuine, but I judge the latter, which is ours, to be truly Usuardine. Guilielmus de la Croix investigated with considerable care the matters relating to this Ambrosius’s life and deeds in his *Bishops of Cahors*, beginning on page 32. Everything will be illustrated more fully in its proper place.

We discussed Gallus the abbot with Usuard on 20 February, where we noted that Notker and others more appropriately place him on this day, as does the Rosweyd manuscript, together with several other fuller Usuardine manuscripts to be cited in the additions. Wandalbert also agrees with them:

> Gallus the confessor is honored,
>
> Who marks the coming of November on the seventh and ninth.

But since these lines are foreign to today’s text, we refer them to the Acts. His Life is found in Surius on this day.

[Col. 0581D]

Concerning PRAT., HERIN., TORN., ANT.-MAJ., ROSV., and PULSAN., enough has been said above in the section on variant readings.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC., and UCHELLIAN. say nothing about Maxima. At the end: “Likewise Saturninus and Nereus with 365 others.” See Castellanus’s note in the universal Martyrology.

MUNERAT. inserts after *to perish*: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Lucianus, Maximianus, and Julianus.” Then: “She also suffered,” and so forth. Concerning those martyrs of Beauvais—Lucianus, Maxianus, and Julianus—see 8 January. Their discovery is recorded in DAVERON. Tillemont reports other matters in volume IV, pages 538–539, largely taken from Bollandus.

BELIN, in second place after the Africans: “Likewise Saturninus and Nereus with 365 others. On the same day, Saint Gallus, abbot.” See the Observations.

GREVEN. lacks the name of the virgin Maxima. In addition, at the end he adds: “At Chartres, the feast of Saint Priscus, martyr, beside the river Eure.”

ANTUERP.-MAX. and LOVANIEN. have *beheaded* instead of *crowned*. They insert: “Who, during the Vandal persecution, under Geiseric, the Arian king.” Then follows: “In Alemannia, the deposition of Saint Gallus, abbot. He was born a Scot and lays his limbs to rest among the Suebi.”

They add no title to Ambrosius, nor do ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. above. At the end: “Likewise Saturninus and Nereus with 365 others.”
