ULTRAJECT. and LEYDEN. correctly have *crowned*. They likewise insert the notice concerning the persecution and otherwise have the same text as the two preceding manuscripts. In addition, at the end they add: “At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of Saint Eliphius, martyr. Since he frequently preached to the pagans the truths of the Christian faith, he was finally beheaded under Julian the Apostate, at the city of Grandis, and crowned with the glory and honor of exalted martyrdom.” See Surius.

DANIC. is similar to the manuscripts just cited, but omits the words: “Maxima also suffered,” and so forth.

ALBERG. has the same omission and also writes 260 instead of 270. It surpasses all the others in this addition after *to perish*: “And while the innocent bodies were dragged, taken and brought back, through thickets of wood, by the sharp points of branches, and beside them untamed horses were running, they said farewell to one another in these words: ‘Brother, pray for me. God has fulfilled our desire; by this path one reaches the kingdoms of heaven.’ Thus, praying and singing psalms, while their angels rejoiced, they gave up their souls.” See Ado.

CENTULEN.: “The octave of our blessed Father Richarius, glorious confessor of the Lord. In Africa, the 270 holy martyrs, and Maxima, the distinguished handmaid of Christ, virgin and abbess. At Beauvais, Saints Lucianus, Maxianus, and Julianus, martyrs. At Bourges, Saint Ambrosius, priest and confessor.” See the Observations.

BRUXELLEN. begins: “In the regions of Alemannia, at the castle of Arbon, the deposition of blessed Gallus, abbot. He came from Ireland, or Scotland, to Alemannia with blessed Columbanus and remained there. Without receiving any messenger’s report, he learned of the death of that same blessed Columbanus, who died in Italy. In Africa, the holy martyrs Cacra and 270 others, likewise crowned.”

[Col. 0583D]

“Likewise Saturninus and Nereus with 365 others. At the camp of Solercius, the feast of Saint Eliphius, martyr. Since he fervently preached to the pagans the truths of the Christian faith, he was finally beheaded under Julian the Apostate at the city of Grandis, and crowned with the glory and honor of martyrdom. His body was translated and now rests at Cologne Agrippina.”

It is nearly pure in the notice of Ambrosius. “At the city of Noviomagus, the deposition of Saint Nummolinus, bishop and confessor. In the city of Nazareth, the commemoration of blessed Gabriel the archangel, the heavenly attendant. Likewise, on the mountain in the sea called Tumba, the dedication of the church of Saint Michael the archangel.”

It says nothing here about Martinianus and the others, whom it transferred to 24 October.

HAGENOYEN. is similar in its first notice to ANTUERP.-MAX. Concerning Saturninus and his companions, see above. Then: “In the diocese of Constance in Alemannia, the deposition of blessed Gallus, abbot, disciple of Saint Columbanus, abbot. An ardent lover of the monastic life, he entered a certain wilderness, where through the power of God he became very strong, so that he drove beasts and demons from it. And just as he then drove demons from the place of solitude, so afterward he drove them from possessed people. Finally, after performing many miracles, receiving many disciples, converting many to the faith, and building monasteries, he died in peace.”

It transferred Ambrosius of Bourges to the following day.

AQUICINCT. has at the end: “Concerning Saturninus, and so forth, as above. On that day, Saint Giles, confessor.” See 1 September. “At Cologne, Saint Eliphius, martyr. In Alemannia, Saint Gallus, priest and confessor. In the territory of Limoges, Saint Junianus, confessor. At the city of Noviomagus, the deposition of blessed Nummolinus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the feast of Saints Lucianus, Maxianus, and Julianus.” See below the DAVERONENSE manuscript.

VICTORIN. and REG.-SUEC. no. 130: “In Alemannia, the feast of Saint Gallus, abbot.” VATICAN. manuscript no. 5949 has “the deposition,” and so forth.

DAVERONEN.: “At Beauvais, the discovery of Saints Lucianus, Maxianus, and Julianus, martyrs. On that day, Saint Magnibodus, bishop and confessor. At the city of Le Mans, the deposition of Saint Berarius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, in the district of Chartres, beside the river Eure, Saint Priscus, martyr.”

AMBIANEN.: “On the same day, the reinterment of Saint Firminus, bishop and martyr.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Eliphius, martyr, whose head is in the church of Saint Martin at Utrecht. Gallus, abbot and confessor. The 270 holy martyrs. Bercharius, abbot and martyr.” See what Surius has about him on this day.

Codex D. LE MARE, marked A: “In the territory of Ratina, Saint Vitalis, confessor.” I freely admit that this person is entirely unknown to me.

FLORENT.: “The second apparition of Saint Michael the archangel, which is said to have occurred around the year of the Lord 710. Likewise Saints Saturninus and Nereus with 365 others.” We have already discussed these more than once.

BURDEGALEN. introduces a new saint, writing: “Saint Bertrand, bishop of Comminges.”

LUXOVIEN.: “On Mount Falcon, the most blessed Balderic, confessor, whose merits are demonstrated by frequent miracles. In the territory of Toul, Saint Eliphius, martyr.” See the longer history below.

SALINEN.: “In the territory of Besançon”—for *Bourges*—“Saint Ambrosius, confessor.”

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “In the territory of Bourges, Saint Ambrosius, priest and confessor.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition: “In a pleasant meadow, above the river called the Vera, between the cities of Grandis and Toul, the feast of Saint Eliphius, martyr. Since he fervently preached the truths of the Christian faith to Jews and pagans, he was finally seized under Julian the Apostate and commanded to deny Christ. He replied: ‘Enemy of truth and adversary of your own salvation, follow my counsel in this matter and repent that you have erred, so that you may escape eternal death.’ When Julian heard this, he raged and ordered him to be beheaded, saying: ‘Now I shall see in what way your God prevails.’ Beheaded, he completed his martyrdom with glory and honor.”

[Col. 0584D]

“After this, the lifeless body moved itself from the ground, embraced the severed head with both hands, and carried it for nearly a mile to a high mountain that it had previously chosen for its burial. But it now rests at Cologne Agrippina, in the monastery of Saint Martin the bishop, through translation.

“In Alemannia, the deposition of Saint Gallus, abbot and confessor, in the monastery of Avernus, disciple of Saint Columbanus, abbot. He was born a Scot and lays his limbs to rest among the Suebi. While absent, he learned of the death of his master Columbanus and announced it to his brothers. Full of virtues, he migrated to the Lord at the castle of Arbon. Then a small chest was found in his cell, and in it an iron chain with which the holy man mortified his body.”

See Notker, who discusses more fully, on this day of his birth, the founder and organizer of his monastery.

Concerning the Africans, see ULTRAJECT., etc. Then: “At the place called Tumba, beside the sea, six miles from the city of Avranches, the apparition of Saint Michael the archangel.”

The notice of Ambrosius is pure. “In the district of Limoges, Saint Silvanus, martyr. At Le Mans, the deposition of Saint Betharius, bishop and confessor. On that day, Saints Magnibodus and Mammolenus, bishops and confessors. The former governed the Church of Angers, and his life became glorious through miracles. At Mainz, Saint Lullus, bishop and confessor.”

Concerning Betharius of Le Mans—also called Berarius—Gallus, and Balderic, see the preceding edition. “At the monastery of Dervo, the translation of Saint Bercharius, and so forth. Ninianus, monk and confessor. Berta, abbess and martyr. Heriburgis, virgin. On the same day, blessed Maxima,” and so forth, as above.

GREVEN.: “In the territory of Avranches, the apparition of Saint Michael the archangel, who around the year of the Lord 707 appeared to Aubert, bishop of Avranches, warning him to found a church in the place by the sea called Tumba because of its elevation, and also because of the dangers of the sea, wishing in fact that he should receive there in the open sea a veneration equal to that which is offered on Mount Gargano.”

Concerning Saturninus, see above. Concerning Eliphius, see what has already been said; here the address is absent.

“In the district of Limoges, Saint Silvanus, martyr. On the same day, Saint Lullus, archbishop of Mainz and confessor, who deserved worthily to succeed Saint Boniface, whose kinsman he was. Arnulfus, bishop. Magnibodus, bishop and confessor of Angers, who shone brightly in life and miracles in the time of King Dagobert. Benedictus, bishop. Mammolenus, bishop and confessor.”

Concerning Betharius of Le Mans—also Berarius—Gallus, and Balderic, see the preceding edition. “At the monastery of Dervo, the translation of Saint Bercharius, and so forth. Ninianus, monk and confessor. Berta, abbess and martyr. Heriburgis, virgin. On the same day, blessed Maxima,” and so forth, as above.

MOLAN. has at the end “bishop of Cahors.” Concerning Saturninus, enough has been said. “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Gallus, abbot, whose life, full of virtues, is preserved in writing. At the monastery of Jothro in Chartres, the feast of Saint Priscus, martyr, beside the river Eure.”

Concerning Bercharius, he has the translation. Concerning Balderic, see above. “At the city of Noviomagus, Saint Nummolinus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the passing of Saint Gurdiellus, confessor [at Douai]. At Lyon, blessed Antiochus, bishop. And Eliphius, martyr. Since he fervently,” and so forth, as in BRUXELLEN.

Then, in smaller type: “He rests here at Cologne Agrippina, in the monastery of Saint Martin.”

Then concerning Lullus, as in GREVEN.; likewise concerning Magnibodus and Berta.

In other editions Gallus the abbot is assigned to the text, and instead of “in the addition” one finds: “a man of extraordinary holiness. Born a Scot, and so forth. And whose life, and so forth.”

Concerning Saturninus and Priscus, as in the first edition. “On that day, at the monastery of Dervo, Saint Bercharius, abbot and martyr.” Concerning Balderic, see above. “At Cologne, Eliphius, martyr. Since he,” and so forth, as above, except for the addition printed in smaller type in the first edition. “At Mainz, the feast of Saint Lullus,” and so forth, as in GREVEN. “At Angers, Saint Magnibodus,” and so forth, likewise as in GREVEN. Concerning Nummolinus, as in the first edition. “At Douai, on that day, the passing of Saint Gurdiellus, confessor. In the territory of Avranches, the apparition of blessed Michael the archangel, in the Storm of the Sea—that is, on Mount Tumba.” See above.

[Col. 0579]

In Africa, 270 holy martyrs, likewise crowned, and the holy martyrs Martianus and Satirianus with their two brothers. For their steadfastness in the Catholic faith, they were first beaten with knotted clubs and lacerated to the bone. Although they endured such treatment for a long time, on the following day they were always restored unharmed. Finally, during their banishment into exile, their feet were bound behind the chariots as they ran, and they were ordered to perish together among the thorny places of the forests. The virgin Maxima also suffered with them.

In the territory of Bourges, Saint Ambrosius, confessor.

[Bouillart.: **[Col. 0581A]** For *in the district of Bourges*, Sollerius writes *in the territory of Bourges*. On whose authority? Is it because there is an erasure in the Praten. manuscript? Yet he accepts Saint Ambrosius of Cahors as having likewise been written in an erasure. Then he says rather weakly: “Praten. also has the addition: at the monastery of Dervo, Saint Bercharius, abbot and martyr.” And for that reason Molanus alone is either pure or very close to purity. This reason nevertheless does not seem sufficient, unless he conceals the fact—of which he was well aware—that the addition was written by a later hand. The Dervensis manuscript calls Ambrosius of Cahors not a bishop but a confessor, and adds: “Likewise in the territory of Toul, Saint Eliphius, martyr.” BOUILLART.]

Saint Ambrosius, bishop of Cahors; and he adds, in cursive writing: “At the monastery of Dervo, Saint Bercharius, martyr and abbot.”

**XVI Kalends. Day 17.**

[Col. 0585]

Three manuscripts are pure: Herinien., Tornacen., and Molan.

[Col. 0585C]

Tornacen. writes *Jeronis* for *Heronis*, and *Aurasica* for *Arausica*. Praten. seems to have had *Aurausica*, which in our copy was corrected by the revisers Sirmond or Cortas. Thus in the same codex I believe *Florentii* was originally written, and was changed to *Florentini*, as it is also read in Herinien. and Tornacen. [Col. 0585D]; but the other, more authoritative witnesses, together with Ado, Notker, and Wandalbert, more correctly have *Florentii*. Greven. and Molan., closely following the aforesaid Ado, read as follows: “In Gaul, in the city of Aurasica [for Arausica], of Saint Florentius,” etc. Here again I excluded many codices from the number of the pure ones, because they abound in additions. Praten., especially, adds at the end: “In the territory of Nivernum, of Saint Vincent, priest and confessor,” where Castellanus noted that these words were written by the same hand but with different ink. Moreover, the two ordinary followers, Antuerp.-Maj. and Rosweyd., again agree with Praten., although they have omitted the title “priest,” and the former incorrectly writes *Vincii* instead of *Vincentii*. We shall speak of the others below; here, on the authority of the remaining most reliable codices, I judge that this notice is wholly an addition.]

[Note: [Col. 0585D]

The older Martyrologies—such as the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, the Little Roman Martyrology, Florus, and Rabanus—make absolutely no mention of today’s saints, Heron and Florentius. What is presented here in the text has been taken from Ado. Yet Our Author did not follow the illuminating Ado in every respect. For the first notice in Ado and in the earlier Little Roman Martyrology is that of Martha, Lazarus’s sister; Usuardus does not speak of her today, but transfers her to 13 December. In both of the works just cited Aristion follows; we discussed him on 22 February, where, from the Observations, you will understand that Ado repeated him here without justification, having found him on this day only in the Little Roman Martyrology. Notker blindly copied Ado; Our Author made a selection. Thus the saint who occupies third place in Ado takes first place here: Heron—or rather Heros—the successor of the great Ignatius in the see of Antioch, as Eusebius has it in book III, chapter 16 of Valesius’s edition. The final words of that chapter are: “After Ignatius had died, Heros assumed the episcopate of the church of Antioch.” Rufinus has a different order of chapters, but exactly the same statement. In Rufinus, after the final words of book III, chapter 25—“Thus far concerning Ignatius”—chapter 26 begins: “After him Heros governed the Church of the city of Antioch.” Nothing further has been handed down by the ancients in his praise, since the letters of Ignatius allegedly addressed to him are today judged spurious by the common agreement of scholars. Whatever, therefore, is mentioned in the text about his imitation of his teacher and his pouring out his blood for the flock entrusted to him rests, so far as I know, solely on Ado’s authority.

Florentius of Arausica, the only one after Eutropius among that city’s bishops to have been entered in the catalogue of the saints, was first recorded by Ado, and Notker copied all his words; Our Author cut away only the opening words, “In Gaul,” which we have shown were restored by Greven. and Molan. Sammarthani derive a summary of his life from him, and our manuscript Catalogue supplies certain further details, from which material for other investigations may in due course be drawn. I append Wandalbert’s verse:

“The bishop Florentius adorns the sixteenth [day] above.”]

[Note: [Col. 0587B]

PRATEN. Above, in the Variants, we already noted its addition concerning Vincent of Nivernum.

ANTUERP.-MAJ., similar to the preceding witness, adds at the end: “In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent [for Vincentius], confessor.”

ROSWEYD. likewise has at the end: “In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, confessor.” Then: “In Britain, Saint Edeldrutha, virgin and queen. This is the feast of her translation. See our Acts, 23 June. In Mauretania, Marianus and Maximus, martyrs, with twenty-three others.” See the Hieronymian copies concerning them.

PULSANEN. mutilates Heron’s eulogy in the first notice. It is pure in the second. Then it adds: “In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, bishop and confessor.”

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC. and UGHELLIAN. append to an otherwise sufficiently pure text: “Also Victor, Alexander, and Marcianus.”

GREVEN. again exceeds his proper Carnotian material. First: “At Chartres, Saint Solina, virgin.” Then: [Col. 0587C] “Near the same city, the dedication of a basilica in memory of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

MUNERAT., sufficiently pure in the text, adds a proper Parisian entry: “On the same day, Saint Cerbonius, bishop of Populonia, whose relics Brother Robert of Pisa brought here.” See the Additions under the day on which Saint Cerbonius is commemorated, namely 10 October. At Paris he has a feast today because of part of the aforesaid relics; concerning these, see below in the codex of the King of Sweden, under no. 428.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERG. and DANIC. also append to the text, almost as in ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC.: “In Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Victor, Alexander, and Marianus.” Florentinius attempts to extract these men from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

CENTULEN. also repeats what it had placed on 22 February, namely: “The feast of the blessed Aristion, who was one of Christ’s ancient disciples. At Antioch, Saint Heron, bishop, successor of the blessed Ignatius, who steadfastly died for his sheep. In the city of Arausica, Saint Florentius, bishop and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN., pure in the first notice, has in second place: “At Auxiopolis, the feast of Saints Hermetes and Taxius. In Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Victor, Alexander, and Marianus. In Gaul, in the city of Arausica, etc. In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, priest and confessor. On the same day, Saint Austrudis, virgin.”

HAGENOYEN., after Ignatius the martyr, inserts: “Who was made bishop after him by Polycarp, disciple of Saint John the Evangelist; to him Ignatius entrusted the Church when he was going to Rome as a captive to be killed. He who followed the way of his teacher,” etc. “At Cologne Agrippina, the feast of Saint Eliphius, martyr. After he had zealously preached to the pagans the things belonging to the Christian faith, he was finally arrested under the emperor Julian [Col. 0588B] and brought in chains to the city of Grand. There he was beheaded by that same man and crowned with the honor of supreme martyrdom.” See the preceding day. “In the city of Aurasica, the deposition of Saint Florentius,” etc., purely. “In Nicomedia, the feast of the holy martyrs Victor, Alexander, and Marianus. Also, in the territory of Biturix, the deposition of Saint Ambrosius, confessor.” He is commemorated on the preceding day.

AQUICINCT. at the end: “Also Saints Victor, Alexander, and Martianus.” Then, as it often does, it agrees with PRATENSI: “In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Aurelius, martyr, with his wife and their other companions. Saint Heron, martyr; Florentinus, bishop and confessor.” I think Florentius of Arausica is intended.

REG. and SUEC., under no. 428: “On the same day, Saint Cerbonius, bishop of Populonia, whose relics our brother Robert of Pisa brought to us.” Anyone who knows that Robert of Pisa will know what church or monastery the codex in question once belonged to. Then: “In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, priest and confessor.”

Codex D. LE MARE., marked A: “On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Anna, Lucius, and Victor.”

In VATICAN., under no. 5949, the following is added at the end: “The feast of the blessed Aristion, who was one of the Seventy disciples. In Sannia, Saint Pardus, bishop.” Concerning Aristion, see the remarks on 22 February.

ALTEMPS.: “At Ramesey in England, the translation of the brothers and precious martyrs of Christ, Etheldred and Ethebrith, born of royal stock. Their bodies, wickedly killed and secretly buried beneath the royal seat, were revealed when, at midnight, a light brighter than the sun was sent down from heaven through the roof of the royal palace. Not long afterward, their killer, to expose his madness and proclaim the glory of the martyrs, was swallowed alive by the earth and sent to hell. On the same day, Saint Etheldreda, perpetual virgin, whose most sacred [Col. 0588D] body, after many years, was revealed—by divine mercy, at the very translation—as preserved incorrupt, to demonstrate the merit of her outstanding virginity.” See above under ROSWEYD.

FLORENTIN.: “In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, bishop and confessor. Also Saints Victor, Alexander, and Marianus, martyrs. Also Saint Aristion, who was one of the Seventy disciples of Jesus Christ. Also, the feast of Saint Rufinianus.”

BURDEGALEN.: “At Angers, Saint Lupus, bishop. See Castellanus.”

LUXOVIEN.: “At Luxeuil, the dedication of the church of Saint Martin.”

DIVIONEN. of Saint Benignus: “In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, priest and confessor.”

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “The feast of blessed [Col. 0589A] Martha, Lazarus’s sister.” See the Observations. At Arausica, Florentius.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. inserts after “disciple” in the entry for Heron, “and deacon.” For the rest, the text is sufficiently pure. Then: “In Nicomedia, the feast of Victor, Alexander, and Marianus, martyrs. At Trier, Saint Florentinus, bishop and martyr. At Chartres, Saint Solina, virgin. On the same day, the translation of Saint Martha, the hostess of Christ, sister of blessed Lazarus and Mary Magdalene. In England, the translation of Saint Etheldreda, virgin. At Angers, Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Nivernum [read, with the others, Nivernensi], blessed Vincent, priest and confessor.”

BELIN. has *Aurisica* instead of *Arausica*. The first edition adds at the end: “Also Victor, Alexander, and Marianus.” The second adds to these “and Marcus.”

GREVEN.: “At Trier, Saint Florentius, bishop and martyr. At Nicomedia, Saints Alexander and Victor. In Mauretania, Saints Marianus, Maximus, [Col. 0589B] Ninus, Lucius, Sacratus, Veneria, Prima, Donata, Victoria, Basilla, and others.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies. “Also, according to Ado here, the blessed Aristion, who was one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples. Usuardus has him on 22 February. On the same day, or according to others on the preceding day, the passion of Saints Silvanus, Alexander, and Marcus, martyrs. Saint Privatus, martyr, who, while he was a soldier and covered with ulcers, was healed and baptized by blessed Pope Calixtus and was killed for Christ with leaden clubs until he died.” See above, 14 October. “At Angers, Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor. In Kent, Nodelinus, bishop and confessor. In Ireland, Monachus, confessor. In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, priest and confessor. Meinardus, confessor. Gordinellus, confessor. On the same day, the translation of Saint Martha, hostess of Christ. In England, the translation of Saint Etheldreda, virgin; Liliosa, virgin, relative of Saint Natalia; Austrudis, virgin.” You will find more about her in the following addition.

MOLAN.: “Also Victor, Alexander, and Marianus. At Chartres, Saint Solina, virgin. On the same day, Saint Cerbonius, bishop of Populonia, whose relics Brother Robert of Pisa brought here. At Laudunum Clavatum, the feast of the holy and most illustrious Austrudis, virgin and abbess, who, endowed wondrously with God’s grace from the first beginnings of childhood, glorious also in virtues and miracles, departed to Christ. Also the blessed Aristion, who was one of Christ’s Seventy disciples.” Then, in smaller type: “Meinardus, confessor.” In later editions he has the same material as in the first concerning Victor and his companions, concerning Solina the virgin, and concerning Florentinus of Trier. “Also the blessed Eutychius, confessor, a man of great holiness, of the Carmelite order. At Laudunum Clavatum, the feast of the holy and most illustrious Austrudis,” etc., as in the earlier edition. Then: “On the seventeenth day, Saint Andrew, martyr, at Crisi.” Then, in smaller type: “Who was gloriously crowned because of his veneration of the sacred images under the wicked Constantine,” namely that iconoclast surnamed Copronymus. Surius published Andrew’s disputation and struggles from Metaphrastes.]

[Col. 0585]

At Antioch, the feast of Saint Heron, disciple of the blessed martyr Ignatius. Having been made bishop after him, he followed the way of his teacher as a devout imitator and, as a lover of Christ, died for the flock entrusted to him. In the city of Arausica, Saint Florentius, bishop, who, renowned for many virtues, rested in peace. [Bouillart adds: [Note: [Col. 0585C] Sollerius considers the commemoration of Saint Vincent to be a mere addition on the authority of the most reliable codices, Herinien. and Tornacen., although he himself lists ten codices that imitate Praten. and have the same reading, as do all our own witnesses. For a long time I have restrained myself from attacking those two codices. But I have been patient too long. The reader may perhaps wonder how I can disparage the authority of codices that I have neither seen nor could see. Yet this is the advantage of Sollerius’s judgment: the very supports on which he chiefly relies are betrayed by him, whether in good faith or through negligence. How highly those two codices should be valued [Col. 0586C] will be indicated, if by nothing else, by the use they have so far served Sollerius. On the following days of this month—1, 11, 15, 16; of September—1, 3, 7, 10, 20, 25, 27; of August—19, 25; of July—1, 11, 18; of June—1, 3, 8, 21, 23; of May—1, 9, 29; of April—30; of March—16, 25; of February—3, 10, 15; of January—23—both are excluded from the pure witnesses. And the number of days on which one or the other is excluded is so great throughout the year that I could not endure the tedium of counting them. In one place there is an addition, in another an omission; now an abridgment of a eulogy, elsewhere faulty and corrupt readings. It is from these codices, then, that Sollerius corrects Praten., naturally. BOUILLART.] In the territory of Nivernum, Saint Vincent, priest and confessor.]

XV Kal. The 18th day. [Note: [Col. 0589]

The pure witnesses are Praten., Herinien., Greven., and Molan. The first edition of Belin comes closest.]

[Note: [Col. 0589C]

All our codices, together with Ado, write “seventy-three”; I do not know where Greven. and Molan. got “eighty-three.” Molan. correctly wrote *Bithynia*, but all the others have the form found in the text. I said that Belin came closest to the pure witnesses; for it is deficient in reversing the order of the notices, relegating Asclepiades to the last place. Moreover, it corrupted the text by substituting “translated to Padua” for “translated to Constantinople.” Concerning this translation to Padua Florentinius notes today: “Although Ferrarius affirms it in his Catalogue of the Saints of Italy on this very day, Peter de Natalibus had nevertheless already rejected it as a fable in book IX, chapter 7.”]

[Note: [Col. 0589C]

I find Luke the Evangelist recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies in more than one place. Yet Florentinius wrongly sends us here to 25 September, when he should have indicated the 21st of the same month, on which day the following is expressly placed: “In the city of Paralice, the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist”; and also 27 November: “At Milan, Luke.” Today, however, in those same copies we read: “In the East, the translation of the body of Luke the Evangelist”; unless you prefer, with the very ancient Epternacensis, to assume a feast, as all the other ancient Martyrologies do—Bede, from whom Rabanus derives his entry; the Little Roman Martyrology, from which Ado and his followers derive theirs. Florentinius adduces other translations, made to other places, and partly, as we said above, refutes them. The curious reader may consult the learned author concerning these and other related matters. Ado enlarged Bede’s eulogy, shortening the age by one year: where Bede has seventy-four, Ado writes seventy-three years. The Menologion of Sirlet extends it to eighty; Greven. and Molan. to eighty-three; Jerome to eighty-four. Meanwhile Our Author follows the Viennese Martyrologist and plainly abridges from him the entire eulogy set down in the calendar entry. The question of Luke’s martyrdom is disputed on both sides. Baronius cites various sermons composed in his praise, some of which Surius reproduced. Tillemont set out the course of his life rather accurately from more reliable records, volume II, p. 130 onward. Nor should Wandalbert’s metrical encomium be omitted:

“Luke, thrice five, dedicated to festive service,

Shows Christ speaking through your discourse, O Paul.”

Concerning Asclepiades, the author of the Little Roman Martyrology is the first to mention him from Rufinus’s Eusebius, book VI, chapter 9: “And Asclepiades, bishop of Antioch.” Ado has somewhat more, and Our Author follows him; I do not know where all this material came from, especially if “to suffer gloriously” is understood of the penalty of death. For Eusebius clearly indicates that he truly suffered when, speaking of him as Serapion’s successor, he says in book VI, chapter 11: “Who, having confessed the faith of Christ during the persecution, carried away the greatest glory”; or, as Rufinus translates it, whose words are inserted into Usuardus’s text: “Who himself also was one of the distinguished number of confessors.” Yet violent death is certainly not established, nor can it be said that he suffered under Decius; this observation led Baronius to substitute Macrinus for Decius. In its proper place we shall examine the whole matter more carefully from the beginning. For the present it may plausibly be observed that Ado confused two Asclepiades: this Antiochene bishop, who suffered under Severus, and another, a companion of Pionius, whose struggle belongs to the time of Decius. See the preliminary commentary on the Acts of Pionius, 1 February, § 3. The few details that survive in praise of our Asclepiades are briefly set out by the aforementioned Eusebius in the cited passage. For the rest, this entire text of ours also derives from Ado.

Again, concerning Triphonia, whom Bede, Rabanus, and Ado report in almost exactly the same words, the Little Roman Martyrology announces her more briefly; Notkerus somewhat mutilates the wording of his source, and Our Author, as usual, reduces it rather elegantly to fewer words. Everywhere the assertion is the same: that she was the wife of Caesar Decius—the son, or the younger Decius, as Baronius holds. The historical truth depends on the authenticity of the Acts of Saint Laurence, which we treated briefly on his proper day, 10 August, and elsewhere. Wandalbert’s verse agrees with the others:

“Triphonia too shines forth, treading upon the kingdom.”

Inserted in the Corbie Hieronymian codex is the deposition of Justus the boy. This is probably the Justus whom Usuardus commemorates today, either from that codex or from his own source, explicitly assigning him to Beauvais. Whether this Justus is the same as Justinus of Paris, whom Muneratus commemorates on 8 August, is not for this place to examine; nor is it for us to determine whether the Acts circulated under Bede’s name are sufficiently trustworthy. Certainly Bede’s genuine Martyrology, which alone we follow here, says nothing at all about Justus. Meanwhile, see Tillemont on Lucian of Beauvais, volume IV, p. 540. The Acts are found in Surius for this day.]

[Note: [Col. 0591A]

TORNACEN. lacks the second notice concerning Asclepiades; in all the rest it is pure.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. reads “Saint Asclepiades”; it lacks his eulogy and likewise the notice concerning Triphonia.

ROSWEYD. begins as follows: “In Bithynia, the feast of blessed Luke the Evangelist, who, a disciple of the apostles, afterward followed Paul and, being seventy-three years old, died in Bithynia, full of the Holy Spirit, whose bones,” etc. It is pure in the two middle notices; in the last it is again longer, adding concerning Justus: “Who was brought to completion by martyrdom for Christ’s name.”

PULSANEN. In the first notice the words “in the twentieth year of Constantius” are absent. The second is missing. In the third it is pure; it lacks the final notice but adds: “On the same day, Saint Hermelandus, abbot and confessor.” I think this is the saint commemorated on 25 March.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC, UGHELLIAN., BIGOTIAN. marked P 5, and ALTEMPS. append to the text: “Also Alexander and Victor.”

MUNERAT., sufficiently pure in the text, adds: “At Angers, Saint Herblandus, abbot.” In French he is called Hermeland.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN. and DANIC. insert after “Caesar” in the notice of Triphonia, from Ado: “Having been baptized by the blessed Justinus, she died the following day and departed to the Lord.” At the end they have the earlier addition: “Also Alexander and Victor.”

CENTULEN.: “The feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist, who was by nationality a Syrian of Antioch, a physician by profession, and a disciple of the apostles. At Antioch, the blessed Asclepiades, bishop, who was one of the distinguished number of confessors. In the territory of Beauvais, Saint Justus, boy and martyr, in the time of Rictiovarus. At Rheims, metropolis of the Franks, the dedication of the church of Saint Mary.”

BRUXELLEN.: “Saint Luke the Evangelist, disciple of the apostles. He was a Syrian by nationality and a physician by profession; following the apostle Paul, at Achaia he wrote the Gospel, which he had learned from the same blessed Paul, and the Acts of the Apostles. After many struggles, he died at the age of seventy-three in Bithynia. His bones were translated to Constantinople in the twentieth year of the emperor Constantius, together with the relics of the blessed apostle Andrew.” What follows concerning Asclepiades and Justus is pure. Then: “Also Alexander and Victor.” Next: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Triphonia, or Cephinia, wife of Caesar Decius. After her husband had been divinely punished following the killing of the blessed Sixtus and Laurence, she asked to be baptized, together with Decius’s daughter Cyrilla, by the priest Justinus. She died the following day, departed to the Lord, and was buried in a crypt near Saint Hippolytus. On the same day, Saint Hermelandus, abbot and confessor.”

AGENOYEN.: “In Bithynia, the deposition of Saint Luke the Evangelist, who was born in the city of Antioch in Syria, was a physician by profession, and yet some say that he was an outstanding painter; in speech he was Greek, not knowing the Hebrew letters. Some say that he was one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ. But Jerome says that he was converted only after the Lord’s Passion and became a disciple of the apostles. [Col. 0592A] This man was a virgin and therefore was the secretary of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of the Lord; it is believed that he heard from her what he wrote in his Gospel after Matthew and Mark. As is read, he was dear to God, whose Gospel he had written; dearer to the blessed Virgin, whose attendant he had been; and dearest to the apostle [Col. 0592B] Paul, whose inseparable companion and excellent fellow-worker in all his deeds he was. After the Gospel he also composed the Acts of the Apostles. Finally, after performing many miracles, building many churches, converting many to the faith, and ordaining many bishops and clerics, he died in Bithynia, full of the Holy Spirit. His bones, etc. On the same day, Saint Asclepiades, bishop and martyr of Antioch. This Asclepiades is highly commended in the letters of Alexander of Jerusalem, who calls him a most holy man. He was one of the distinguished [number], etc. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Triphonia, wife of the younger emperor Decius. She was sufficiently cruel, and yet reproved him for the killing of the saints. After her husband’s death, she became a Christian with her daughter Cyrilla through the blessed Justinus, and the following day, while praying at the memorials of the saints, departed to the Lord.” The Justus of Beauvais is transferred to the following day.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Luke the Evangelist. [Col. 0592C] Justus, boy and martyr. Mononus, martyr. Asclepiades, bishop and martyr of Antioch.”

REGINAE SUEC. under no. 428: “At Angers, Saint Erblandus, abbot.” See above.

In VATICAN., marked no. 5949, “Justus” is absent.

FLORENTIN.: “Also Saints Alexander and Victor. Also Saint Hermelandus, abbot. And Saint Monnonus or Mononus, martyr.”

BURDEGALEN.: “In the territory of Beauvais, Saint Justus, martyr. Alexander, Victor.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL. agrees substantially with the witnesses cited above concerning Luke. In the notice of Asclepiades it is pure. In that of Triphonia it agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others. “In the territory of Beauvais, Saint Justus, boy and martyr, who was beheaded in the time of the emperor Diocletian under the judge Rictiovarus. On the same day, Saint Alexander and Saint Victor. On the same day, Saint Aquilinus, bishop and confessor.” See the following day.

The second edition of BELIN adds at the end: “On the same day, [Col. 0592D] blessed Marcus, most illustrious teacher.” It is otherwise similar to the first. I know many Marci, but I do not know which one is intended here. If it is Marcus of Jerusalem, he is commemorated on 22 October.

GREVEN.: “Mononus, martyr. At Auxiopolis, Saints Hermetes and Rexius.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies, from which these entries have been badly copied. “In Campania, in the city of Puteoli, Januarius.” See 19 September. Here there is a typographical error. “Also Victrix and Marcialis. In Nicomedia, Victorinus and Hermetes. In Africa, Victor and Faustus. Aquilinus, bishop of Evreux [Ebroicensis], and confessor, according to others on the following day. At Angers, Saint Herblandus, abbot.”

MOLAN., concerning Luke, adds after “were translated,” in different type and from Ado: “He was a Syrian by nationality, an Antiochene, a physician by profession, a disciple of the apostles; he followed Paul to his confession, serving the Lord without blame and never having a wife.” Again, after “Caesar Decius”: “After her husband had been divinely punished following the killing of Sixtus, Laurence, and Hippolytus, she asked to be baptized, together with Decius’s daughter Cyrilla, by the priest Justinus, and died the following day and was buried in a crypt near Saint Hippolytus.” At the end: “On the same day, at Nassonia, at Saint Hubert’s in the Ardennes, the blessed Mononus, martyr. At Angers, Saint Herblandus, martyr.” I think this is the same person as the abbot Hermelandus mentioned above, as the other editions correct it. “At Mechelen, the translation of the blessed Rumoldus, martyr and bishop.” Later editions add concerning Luke alone, in different type: “He was a physician by profession and followed Paul to his confession.” Concerning Triphonia they have the same as the first edition. At the end: “At Angers, Saint Herblandus, abbot. At Nassonia, the feast of the blessed Mononus, martyr, who came from Scotland to the Ardennes at an angel’s command; there he served God alone for a long time and was stabbed by assassin-bandits and happily died. He was buried in the church that he himself had built.” Concerning the translation of the blessed Rumoldus, as above.]

[Col. 0589]

The feast of blessed Luke the Evangelist, who, being seventy-three years old, died in Bithynia full of the Holy Spirit; his bones were translated to Constantinople in the twentieth year of Constantius. On the same day, Saint Asclepiades, bishop of Antioch, who was one of the distinguished number of confessors who suffered gloriously under Decius. Also at Rome, Saint Triphonia, wife of Caesar Decius. In the territory of Beauvais, Saint Justus, martyr.

XIV Kal. The 19th day. [Note: [Col. 0593]

Thus Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., the first edition of Belin, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0593B]

Concerning Egypt, we have spoken frequently. The name is written *Phtolemei*, *Tholomaei*, *Ptolomaei*, and in other ways; we have followed the simple inflection of most codices, although we think *Ptolomaei* should be read. Antuerp.-Maj. reads: “When he affirmed the teaching of Christ,” etc. Belinus, however, changes what immediately follows, “he confirmed it by public confession [Col. 0593C] and testimony.” He likewise writes *Antiochia*; Antuerp.-Maj. has *Antyochia*, etc. Herinien. and Antuerp.-Maj. [Col. 0594B] have forty-nine; the others have the form found in the text. In our copy of Praten. I find added: “On the same day, the translation of Saints Savinianus and Potentianus and their companions.” But since these words have been crossed out, I infer that they were added more recently in the margin, as Castellanus also noted; [Col. 0594C] therefore they do not affect the integrity of the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0593C]

As we have more than once stated above, with the agreement of experts in these matters, that the author of the Little Roman Martyrology compiled his Martyrology chiefly from Rufinus’s Eusebius, so this is plainly evident today in his notice of Ptolemaeus and his companions: “And Ptolemy, who is handed over by a certain centurion to Urbicius the judge; and Lucius and Tertius, beheaded together, who were buried at Alexandria.” Except for the final phrases, this is clearly taken from Eusebius, book IV, chapter 17; Ado expanded it from the same passage, while preserving two features that are wholly objectionable in the cited wording. First, Tertius appears to be taken as a proper name, whereas in Eusebius he is third in order and remains anonymous. Second, they are said to have been buried at Alexandria, although it is clear from the source of this history, Justin’s Apology, in Halloix, p. 48, that they suffered at Rome. The Viennese Martyrologist further adds that they suffered under Antoninus surnamed Pius; but, as Halloix clearly states in his notes, p. 361, these events took place under Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, son of Pius. Our Author avoided the first error concerning Tertius, but falls into a worse one by beginning the notice: “At Alexandria, the metropolis of Egypt,” which he found neither in Ado nor elsewhere—unless he honestly assumed that the martyrs suffered where he found them buried. I will not deny, however, that the place of martyrdom is left sufficiently uncertain in Eusebius; indeed, the whole context provides grounds for understanding Ptolemy and his companions to have suffered elsewhere, especially at Alexandria. Nevertheless, Baronius corrected all these matters most properly in the modern Roman Martyrology from Justin’s own Apology. Ruinart examines questions of this kind in the preface to his *Acta sincera et selecta*, beginning on p. 35. See also Tillemont, volume II, p. 312 and from p. 395 onward.

For the rest, the whole text reported by us is abridged from Ado. Nevertheless, its order differs from that of both of the leading witnesses: they place the Antiochenes first, whereas Our Author places them after Ptolemaeus, though in such a way that Usuardus copied the entire notice concerning the Antiochenes from the aforesaid Ado, who had transferred it from the Little Roman Martyrology. The Hieronymian codices also preserve on this day a memory of this Antiochene group, with Pelagius’s name prefixed as that of their leader or chief officer. Concerning him and related matters, see Florentinius. As for the Pelagia commemorated today, the matter will have to be investigated more laboriously in its proper place. I am certain that she is not the penitent whom Rabanus and Notkerus inappropriately insert here. Whether she is that celebrated Antiochene virgin and martyr praised by Ambrose, concerning whom our Acts on 9 June contain an excellent discussion by our colleague Janningus in the preliminary commentary, volume II, pp. 154 and following, will have to be determined there. Meanwhile, on p. 157C you will find almost a preliminary refutation of Castellanus’s note concerning Domnina, whom he considers Pelagia’s mother, and her sisters Bernice and Prosdoce. I confess that I still do not sufficiently understand how the learned Castellanus extracts the names of the first and last from the present Hieronymian tables and joins them to these Antiochene women. But, lest I exceed the limits set here, I refer these and any other disputed matters to a larger work. It was enough to show fully the source from which Usuardus took both his text and the opportunity for error. Wandalbert does not mention Ptolemaeus and his companions; concerning the Antiochenes he sings the same as Our Author:

“On the twice-seventh [day], Beronicus and Pelagia shine,

And forty-nine accompany them together.”]

[Note: [Col. 0595A]

TORNACEN. lacks the first notice; it is pure in the second, and then adds: “On the same day, the feast or translation of the blessed martyrs Savinianus and Potentianus and their companions. Although their feast had been celebrated from ancient times on the day before the Kalends of January, it was transferred by the Fathers to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, because on that day their bodies were translated and angelic voices were heard in heaven, as is read in the sacred account of their translation. Their solemnity is therefore held here as more venerable, since on this day their holy bodies were also buried with greater honor.”

[Col. 0595B] ROSWEYD., pure in the text, adds: “At Beneventum, Januarius, bishop, and his companions, martyrs.” See 19 September. “Proculus, martyr, with forty-four others. The translation of Saint Willibrord, bishop.”

PULSANEN. is mutilated in the first notice, its eulogy having been cut off. Instead of Beronicus it has Berontius and fifty-nine others, as Notkerus has.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., LOVANIEN., ALBERGEN. and DANIC., sufficiently pure in the text, add: “In the city of Puteoli, the feast of Saints Proculus and Nicea, his mother.”

MUNERAT. at the end: “At Sens, Saints Savinianus and Potentianus and their companions.” See above under TORNACEN.

GREVEN. distinguishes the matter more carefully: “At Sens, the passion of the holy martyrs Potentianus, Savinianus, Altivus, and Totaldus.” He reads the last names incorrectly; other witnesses have Altinus and Eodaldus.

CENTULEN.: “At Alexandria, the blessed martyrs Ptolemaeus [Col. 0595C] and Lucius. At Antioch, Saints Belonicus and Pelagia and forty-nine others. At the monastery of Centula, the dedication of the eastern crypt in honor of Saint Mary and Saint Richarius, the glorious priest.”

BRUXELLEN. begins with the Antiochenes, in which notice it is pure. Then: “And in the city of Puteoli, the feast of the holy martyrs Proculus and Nicea, his mother.” The notice concerning Ptolemaeus and Lucius follows, purely. It adds: “Also Amatus, bishop of Sens, who for the sake of justice and truth was long afflicted in harsh exile by King Theodoric.” See the Additions on 28 April and 13 September. “At Tours, the deposition of Saint Columbanus, abbot.” Below he is called a bishop of Tours, but he is not known as such.

HAGENOYEN, contrary to its usual practice, adds in pure form: “In the territory of Beauvais, the birthday of Saint Justus the martyr.” See what was said on the preceding day. “Likewise, Saints Alexander and Victor, martyrs.” See there also. “In the city of Puteoli, the passion of the holy martyrs Proculus and Nicaea, his mother.”

[Col. 0595D] AQUICINCT begins with the proper commemoration of the neighboring town: “At Douai, the translation of Saint Amatus, archbishop and confessor.” At the end, however, it adds: “At the fortress of Évreux, the birthday of Saint Aquilinus, bishop and confessor.”

VICTORIN and REG. SUEC., marked with number 130, at the end without indication of its position: “On the same day, Saint Aquilinus, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Ptolemy and Lucius, martyrs. Ethbin, confessor. Beronicus, Pelagia, and forty-nine other martyrs.”

BIGOTIAN, marked P 5: “In the city of Puteoli, the birthday of Saints Proculus and Nicaea, his mother.”

BIGOTIAN, marked E 40: “At Sens, the passion of the holy martyrs Sabinianus, Potentianus, Altinus, [Col. 0596A] and Eodaldus.” It is established from TORNACEN above that today the translation is commemorated, which took place in the year 1026, or, according to others, 1030.

Codex D. DU CHEVAL, marked B: “In the city of Puteoli, the birthday of Saints Proculus and Nicaea, his mother.” UGHELLIAN is doubtless similar here also to ANTUERP.-MAX., LUBEC., and the others. In our extract, however, the first name is written as follows: “In the city of Puteoli, the birthday of Saints Paul and Nicaea, his mother.”

ALTEMPS: “In Britain, in the city of Oxford, Saint Frideswide, virgin. And Saint Aquilinus, bishop [Col. 0596B] and martyr.”

FLORENTIN: “In the city of Puteoli, Saints Proculus and Nicaea, his mother, martyrs. Likewise, Saint Amatus the confessor.” The STROZZIAN codex alone adds: “At Rome, Saint Asterius, priest and martyr.” See 21 October.

BIZUNTICEN: “At Sens, Saints Sabinianus and Potentianus, martyrs, and their companions.”

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “At Tours, the deposition of Saint Columbanus, abbot and confessor.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION inserts into the first commemoration, after “and Lucius”: “and Tertius under Antoninus, surnamed Pius, and his son.” The remainder is sufficiently pure up to the end, where it adds: “In the city of Puteoli, the birthday of Saints Proculus and Nicaea, martyrs. In England, in the city of Oxford, Saint Frideswide, virgin.”

The second edition of BELIN, similar to the first in its text, appends at the end: “On the same day, Saint Eadnoth, martyr, [Col. 0596C] bishop of the men of York. In the territory of Orléans, the deposition of Blessed Veranus, bishop and confessor.” See Usuard on 11 November.

GREVEN: “In the city of Puteoli, Saints Proculus and Nicaea, his mother, martyrs. In Istria, Saints Austerius, Neopolis, Desiderius, and Festinus. On the same day, the commemoration of Saints Januarius and his fellow martyrs. Columbanus, bishop of Tours and confessor. Bevagius, bishop of Senlis and confessor. Folquinus, bishop. Desiderius, bishop. Geremar, abbot of Flayac and confessor.” See the Supplements for 21, 23, and 24 September. “Amatus, abbot of Luxeuil and confessor. In Ireland, Saint Ethbin, Levite and confessor, disciple of Blessed Samson, archbishop of Dol. While traveling with Saint Winwaloe, priest and most worthy confessor (concerning whom there is discussion above on the sixth and fifth days before the Nones of March), he deserved to receive Christ in the form of a leper and to tend to him with wondrous ardor of faith, and also to hear the voice of the ascending Lord promising salvation to those who should remember both of them in their prayers. At last, renowned for his life and miracles—including, as is read, the raising of a dead man—he rested in the Lord in a blessed end.” You should note that the parenthesis inserted here reads as follows in the first edition: “who ought not to have been passed over without distinguished commendation on 6 and 5 March.” It continues: “The translation of Saint Willibrord, bishop and confessor. In England, in the city of Oxford, Saint Frideswide, virgin.”

MOLAN: “On the same day, Saint Eadnoth, martyr, bishop of the men of York. In the territory of Orléans, the deposition of Blessed Veranus, bishop and confessor. At Sens, Saints Sabinianus and Potentianus, martyrs, and their companions. Since their feast had been celebrated by the ancients from early times on the day before the Kalends of January, it was transferred to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, because on that very day their bodies were translated and angelic voices were heard, as is read in the account of their translation. At Douai, the translation of Saint Amatus, bishop and confessor. After he had abandoned the episcopate by the detestable command of King Theuderic, grieving for his flock but commending it to the Holy Trinity, he endured many sufferings for Christ by mortifying his flesh. And Saint Aquilinus, bishop and confessor; [Col. 0598A] then, in smaller type, Ébroïcensis [Ebroicensis]. In England, in the city of Oxford, Saint Frideswide, virgin.” Other editions have: “At Évreux, Saint Aquilinus, bishop and confessor. At Oxford, Saint Frideswide, virgin. On the nineteenth day, Saint Varius, martyr.” Concerning Sabinianus and his companions, and likewise concerning Amatus, it is exactly as in the earlier version. At the end, in different lettering, others add: “In Britain, Saint Ethbin, abbot of Nectis.”

[Col. 0593]

At Alexandria, the metropolis of Egypt, the birthday of the holy martyrs Ptolemy and Lucius, under Antoninus surnamed Pius. The former, after being worn down for a long time by the filth of prison, and finally publicly bearing witness to the teaching of Christ, was ordered to be led away to death. The latter also, when he freely confessed himself a Christian, received a similar sentence. At Antioch in Syria, the holy martyrs Beronicus, Pelagia, and forty-nine others.

[Bouillart adds in the margin: [Note: [Col. 0593B] Although a later hand wrote in the margin “Saints Sabinianus and Potentianus,” nevertheless Soller included the Pratense among the pure codices. I beg the reader to observe what moved him to do this: “because,” he says, “things added in the margin at a later date do not compromise the integrity of the text.” He showed the same fairness on 18 January, 21 February, 13 and 25 April, 15 May, 8 and 28 July, and 6 September. I ask you, Sollerius, tell me what difference there is between things added later in the margin and things added later in the remaining space of the article. In your preface you say that you have disputed and examined nothing against the Pratense codex except for the sake of seeking the truth. By that love of truth with which you burn, I beg and implore you to indicate this difference to me. But if you cannot, with what fidelity and what devotion to truth did you disdain to count the Pratense codex among the pure codices on 10 June because of Saint Landericus; on 18 July because of Saint Arnulf; on 1 September because of Saint Giles; on the 3rd of that same month because of Saint Gregory; and on 19 November because of Saint Odo? Again, if things added later in the margin do not compromise the integrity of the text, why on the 24th of this month do you reject the Pratense codex, although Maglorius is written outside the text and in the margin? You vainly conceal the fact that Castellanus had warned you. No one will believe that this escaped the notice of one whom you everywhere praise as an exceptionally sharp observer. BOUILLART.] The translation of the holy martyrs Sabinianus, Potentianus, and their companions.]

XIII Kal. Day 20. [Note: [Col. 0597]

The only codices that are altogether pure are Praten., Antuerp. Maj., Munerat., and Greven.]

[Note: [Col. 0597B]

Munerat. and some more recent codices write “Anianus,” but all the older ones support “Avianus,” although the place is not known today in the Vestini, where it once existed; consequently, it may be counted among those villages or towns of which one may rightly say: “These names existed then; now they are without a name.” Moreover, that same Munerat. [Col. 0598B] omitted the title “blessed.” It should read patiendi desiderio, “from the desire to suffer.” Greven. has incorrectly patiendo, “by suffering.” In Munerat. and Greven. there is responsionis constantiam, “steadfastness in his answer”; the others have it as in the text. The error of Caprasius is in Antuerp.-Majore. Greven. has passionis, “of the passion,” instead of passionum, “of the sufferings.” Finally, in Antuerp.-Majore the particle et, “and,” has been omitted after properavit, “he hastened.”]

[Note: [Col. 0597C]

None of the ancient Martyrologists mentions this Maximus of ours of Avia, except Usuard alone; where he obtained him, I simply cannot guess, unless we suppose that the passion of that martyr, or some brief Acts, came into his hands, such as Peter de Natalibus more or less published in book IX, chapter 85. Other manuscripts exist with us, and indeed various ones; in some of them a manifest confusion among the Maximi appears. On this subject see Tillemont, volume III, pages 710–711. Baronius asserts that he received in manuscript the history of his martyrdom and translation from the church of Aquila—namely, I think, those very Acts from which an ecclesiastical office proper to the diocese of Aquila was subsequently composed, printed at Rome in 1604. We possess a copy of it, and from it Ferrarius transcribed whatever he notes about Maximus in the Saints of Italy, page 657. He is honored by the people of Aquila, possessors of the sacred deposit, as their special patron on 19 October; on one or the other day [Col. 0597D] we shall illuminate his life and deeds with as much probability as we can. The Hieronymian Martyrologies certainly mention Caprasius, and there is no reason for Florentinius to regard him as an addition, unless perhaps he was absent from the Lucense codex; in any case, his note deserves consultation. Earlier, on 6 October, when we had to discuss Faith, we briefly indicated what concerned the Acts of that most celebrated virgin; Caprasius’s deeds must be drawn from them, so there is no need to repeat them here. From the aforesaid Acts Ado took Caprasius and adorned him with a brief eulogy, whose substance Our Author reproduces; but more recent codices, contrary to Usuard’s intention, restore the complete account, as will become clear in the Supplements. Notker, condensing Ado’s words, [Col. 0598C] placed him on the preceding day. Wandalbert sang of him alone today:

“Caprasius the martyr, you are honored with thrice ten.”

Next comes the group of Cologne virgins. I had sought them for a long time, though unsuccessfully, among Martyrologists and other ancient writers, and even among the people of Cologne themselves, until by chance I came upon Crombach’s discussion of Ursula, book II, chapter 12. There he maintains that Usuard, by the words of our text, remembered the first virgins slain on the day before the general Ursulan catastrophe, adding that the people of Cologne either do not honor these women or honor them only on the following day together with the whole Ursulan company. This brief information taught me why I had searched in vain; but it remains equally uncertain where Usuard obtained or fashioned his virgins. Whether Crombach’s judgment concerning our Usuardine commemoration is sufficiently well established, and likewise whether it is sufficiently consistent with the commonly circulated Acts of Ursula concerning the other place and event, remains to be considered. Yet from Usuard, who bears witness as to an opinion accepted in his own age, namely the ninth century, it follows that several virgins at Cologne—as Wandalbert too will testify on the following day—were martyred there for the faith. Perhaps Martha and Saula may someday provide material for more inquisitive investigation. Meanwhile, if they are thought to have belonged to the company of the eleven thousand, one may wonder that, among so many Ursulan women named individually by some writers, these two names are almost everywhere absent. We discussed George, Aurelius, and their fellow Cordoban martyrs with Usuard on 27 August, on which day he incorrectly entered them, since it is certain from Eulogius that they were killed on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, that is, 27 July. Here the solemn reception of the sacred bodies brought from Córdoba by Usuard himself and Odilard is commemorated; because of its notable solemnity, Our Author wished to insert it into the Martyrology. There exists [Col. 0600A] a history of its translation, carried out in the year 858, compiled from Usuard’s account by Aimoinus, his fellow monk, and reprinted by Mabillon in the fourth Benedictine century, part II, from page 45.]

[Note: [Col. 0599A]

HERINIEN, entirely pure in the text, adds a Rhemish addition of its own: “On the same day, the deposition of Sindulfus the confessor, whose life was pleasing to God is testified by the miracles performed through his merits.”

TORNACEN omits Maximus’s eulogy; it is pure in the passages concerning Caprasius and the Cologne women, but says nothing about the reception of the relics, and so forth.

ROSWEYD, not entirely pure in the text, has the principal defect that it lacks the penultimate commemoration concerning Martha and Saula.

PULSANEN cuts out the eulogies of Maximus and Caprasius; everything else is pure.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., and, I think, UGHELLIAN, are pure at first. Afterward, concerning Caprasius, they copy Ado, beginning “then, in the cave,” and add: “Finally, hearing how blessed Faith would contend for Christ, he was encouraged to endure sufferings and prayed to the Lord that, if He judged him worthy of the glory of martyrdom, the clearest water might flow from the stone of the cave. By the Lord’s granting this, he hastened confidently to the contest and won the palm, and so forth.” The last two commemorations are absent.

MOLAN, in the first edition, is sufficiently pure; in the second it is mutilated; in the third it is pure, but lacks the fourth.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN have Caprasius as do ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. They say nothing about Martha and Saula; in the first and last they are pure. At the end: “In the district of Rheims, the deposition of Saint Sindulfus, priest and confessor.” I note that ANTUERP.-MAX. reads Maximinius instead of Maximus.

ALBERG. and DANIC. resemble the preceding witnesses in the first and second sections, but lack the remainder, as above in ANTUERP., and so forth.

LOVANIEN agrees with ANTUERP.-MAX., and the others, but has removed the whole eulogy of Caprasius.

CENTULEN: “In Gaul, in the city of Agen, Saint Caprasius, martyr. In the province of Avia, Blessed Maximus, Levite [Col. 0599C] and martyr. In the city of Cologne, the holy virgins Martha and Saula with many others.”

BRUXELLEN begins with Caprasius, for whom it has the same account as ANTUERP. and the others. It follows with Maximus, purely. Then: “At Rome, the birthday of Saint Austerius, priest.” See the following day. “In the city of Puteoli, the birthday of the holy martyrs Zosimus, Januarius, and Dorothea.” This is from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, as is also Austerius. It then follows with the reception of George and the others, and of the holy women Martha and Saula, purely. Then: “In the district of Rheims, the deposition of Saint Syndulfus [for Sindulfus], priest and confessor. And Saint Austreberta, virgin.” See 10 February; the translation is indicated below.

HAGENOYEN, sufficiently pure at first, has nothing of the rest of the text, but substitutes: “At Alexandria, Saint Pelagia, who is called the Sinner; Saint Nonnus [printed Nummus] the bishop converted her wondrously to the faith and baptized her in the assembly of the clergy and the whole city of Alexandria. Yet before this, while she was still a prostitute, he had prophesied concerning her that she herself would precede the priesthood of eight bishops. Later he saw a wondrous vision concerning her, which she fulfilled in herself: for she put on male clothing and, known only to Bishop Nonnus, from whom she received a hair shirt, fled. Entering a solitary cell, she called herself Pelagius. There she lived for many years in great abstinence and penance. Before her death she was greeted by Bishop Nonnus through the deacon James, greatly comforted, and died in peace.” See what is said about Pelagia and the Pelagias in the Observations for 8 and 19 October.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Caprasius, martyr. Maximus, Levite and martyr. The holy virgins Martha and Saula with many others, martyrs.”

CLUNIACEN: “Likewise, Neon, martyr.” I know of seven Neons; which one is designated here, I do not know.

In VATICAN no. 5949, the text is prefaced with: “At Benevento, Saint Zosimus, bishop.” The last two commemorations are absent.

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, Saint Neotus, priest and confessor. Likewise, Neon, martyr. Likewise, the translation of Saint Austreberta, virgin.”

FLORENTIN: “Likewise, the holy martyrs George the deacon and Aurelius. On that day at Rome, Saint Asterius, priest and martyr, under the Emperor Alexander, who ordered him to be thrown from a bridge.” See the following day.

BIZUNTICEN: “At Paris, the reception of the holy martyrs George the deacon and Aurelius.”

CABILLON: “Saint Veranus, bishop of Chalon.” [Col. 0600B] See Usuard on 11 November and the others on the preceding day.

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “In the territory of Rheims, in a village called Alsontia, the deposition of Saint Sindulfus, priest and confessor.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “At Cologne Agrippina, in the church of the eleven thousand holy virgins, the commemoration of Saint Hippolytus the martyr and his companions, whose body rests there by translation. Likewise, at Cologne, the passion of the holy virgins and martyrs Martha,” and so forth. It is sufficiently pure concerning Maximus. “In Gaul, in the city of Agen, the feast of the translation of Saint Caprasius the martyr. While he, through fear, was avoiding the fury of persecution,” and so forth, as in ANTUERP. up to “by the Lord’s granting,” where it adds: “And so it happened. Therefore, confident, he hastened to the contest of suffering; there, beheaded together with Blessed Faith, he thus won the palm,” and so forth. Then: “Seeing the endurance of these saints in suffering and patience, the brothers Primus and Felicianus [Col. 0600C] were converted to Christ and beheaded together with them.” See how this agrees with what was said on 9 June. “At Troyes, Saint Arandus, confessor.” Could this be Adroldus or Alderaldus? “On the same day, Saint Quirinus, priest and martyr.” I do not know this Quirinus. “At Minden, Saint Felicianus, martyr.”

BELIN, not entirely pure in the first edition, has in the second the same account as ANTUERP. and the others. In the third it is pure, but the last item is absent. Another edition of his adds at the end: “Likewise, Saint Neon, martyr.”

GREVEN: “Avelsius and Valerianus, disciples of Christ. Quirinus, priest and martyr. At Minden, Saint Felicianus, martyr. Felicia, martyr, and Justus the boy. At Nicomedia, Saints Eutychus, Promasius, Lucius, and Marcellinus. In the city of Puteoli, Saints Zosimus, Januarius, and Dorothea. At Foligno, Felicianus, bishop and confessor. Sindulfus, confessor. Priscus, confessor. At Troyes, Saint Arandus, confessor.” See above in the LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. “At Cologne [Col. 0600D] Agrippina, in the church of the eleven thousand holy virgins, the commemoration of Saint Hippolytus the martyr, resting there by translation, and his companions.”

MOLAN, drawing from Ado, has the same material as the text, but inserts in different lettering what we reported above in ANTUERP. and the others. We said above that it is mutilated in this very commemoration because it gives even the final words, “and by fighting bravely he earned the palm of martyrdom,” in italic type. At the end, however, it regards the following as an addition: “On that day, the reception of the holy martyrs George the deacon and Aurelius.” Then: “Likewise, Neon, martyr. On the same day, the deposition of Sindulfus the confessor, whose life, how pleasing it was to God, is testified by his miracles.” This is from HERINIEN, but somewhat altered. “In the city of Troyes, the birthday of Saint Arandus, confessor and archdeacon.” Other editions agree with the text. At the end: “In the district of Rheims, the deposition of Sindulfus the confessor, whose life, how pleasing it was to God, is testified by his miracles. In the city of Troyes, the birthday of Saint Araldus, confessor and archdeacon. Likewise, Saint Neon, martyr. [Col. 0602A] And the passing of Saint Wendelin, confessor. At Minden, the birthday of Saint Felicianus, bishop and martyr.” Castellanus thinks that the same Felicianus of Foligno is designated everywhere. “On the twentieth day, Saint Artemius, the great martyr. On that day at Paris, the reception of the holy martyrs George the deacon and Aurelius.” See in Surius the lengthy history of that great martyr Artemius from Metaphrastes.]

[Col. 0597]

In the province of Avia, the birthday of Blessed Maximus, Levite and martyr, who, from a desire to suffer, openly presented himself to the persecutors who were seeking him. After steadfastness in his answers, he was suspended on the rack and tortured, then beaten with clubs, and finally overwhelmed, and so died. In Gaul, in the city of Agen, Saint Caprasius, martyr, who, while hiding in a cave to avoid the fury of persecution, was at last encouraged to endure sufferings, hastened to the arena of combat, and by fighting bravely won the palm of martyrdom. In the city of Cologne, the passion of the holy virgins Martha and Saula with many others. On that same day, the reception of the holy martyrs George the deacon and Aurelius.

[Note: [Col. 0597B] The Dervensis codex adds: “On this same day, the deposition of Saint Sindulfus the confessor, who, struggling in the school of contempt for the world, turned the wandering sun to his use and, utterly despising the present age, followed Christ with his whole heart. His conversion, shining with virtues and miracles, shows that he led a celibate life. Effectively fleeing the twofold earth and leaping away from it, he sowed in tears with the patriarchs and left behind the fruit of holy conduct; sacrificing himself for Christ with the apostles; with the martyrs, stretching both hands from the salt of this pilgrimage toward the shore; with the confessors, filling his fingers with the finest myrrh; with the virgins, he answered the bridegroom of his soul with a new song, until he met him upon the mountains of spices, like a doe and a fawn of the deer.”

This was drawn from the Life of Saint Sindulfus, which Almannus, a monk of Hautvillers, wrote in the ninth century and our Mabillon published in volume I of the Acts, page 368. No one is unaware that the monasteries of Hautvillers and Der were first founded by Saint Nivard; from this relationship it came about that the feast days of both were shared. BOUILLART.]

XII Kal. Day 21. [Note: [Col. 0601]

Among the codices, the only ones pure in every respect are Praten. and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0601B]

Gaius, Jerome, Ostia, and Callistus have been discussed more than once. Molan, I think from Greven, somewhat transposed the phrase, reading: “Jerome writes his life, full of virtues.” Our reading is closer to Bede and Ado. Here I note that there is also a principal variation of reading among the older codices: Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd, Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Munerat., and Greven, with the sign L, add to the text those celebrated Cologne virgins, eleven thousand in number, of whom we began to speak on the preceding day on the occasion of Martha, Saula, and their many companions; Castellanus believes that they were transferred from that day to this one. This much is certain: these present entries are certainly not Usuard’s, nor are they known under that number in any ancient Martyrology. I gladly append the verses of Wandalbert, recently cited, from which all that follows is finally established—and this we readily grant—that a numerous multitude of virgins was crowned with martyrdom at Cologne. Thus he writes:

“Then, in great numbers, along the banks of the Rhine they shine,

Trophies raised for Christ by virgin battalions,

For the city of Agrippina, whose impious fury once

Sacrificed thousands led by illustrious holy women.”

Here the number plainly seems to be determined at the poet’s discretion. In any event, we consider it so indisputable that there were illustrious virgins by the thousands and by tens of thousands that one must be iron-hearted—“I speak according to the Master’s judgment”—to dare deny credence to the Cologne tradition, founded upon these and ancient testimonies. I certainly approve none of the Acts as they are commonly circulated, nor is this the place to discuss them, since they have rightly been corrected in various ways by various authors. Let Baronius’s note be consulted, but compared with what our Browerus examined most diligently in the third book of Venantius Fortunatus, beginning at page 61; likewise with Papebroch’s Responses to article XIX, number 15, and the matters he indicates there. In due time we shall examine the remaining points from Crombach and others.]

[Note: [Col. 0601C]

I begin with the confusion that must undoubtedly be found in the manuscript codices of Ado, both because of the added Ursulan virgins and because of the names transposed in the Little Roman Martyrology, which Rosweyd successfully restored to their proper places but which Mosander, and still more Notker, confused. As for our text, it was plainly either copied or abridged from Ado; let us follow the individual points in order. Among the Hieronymian codices, the Epternacensis is both the oldest and today the most correct. Where the others generally read: “At Nicomedia, Dasius, Zoticus, Gaius with twelve thousand,” an enormous number unknown even to the Greeks, this codex more correctly restricts it in the following manner: “with twelve soldiers.” Notker followed the first reading on the preceding day, but the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Our Author, following him, adhere to the better reading.

Now the words “with twelve thousand” led Florentinius to wonder whether the contest of Saint Ursula and her companions might not be celebrated under this number. Nor does this unfounded suspicion seem so very remote, especially if what Castellanus asserts in his note is true: namely, that in some ancient codices not twelve thousand but only eleven thousand are counted, and that the number is not referred to the Nicomedians but applied to the Cologne martyrs themselves. To these matters we return again, though enough has been said about them; scarcely anyone even moderately learned is unaware of the conjectures of other scholars concerning the origin of this famous number. Some may be seen in Motherius’s Note, in the recent French translation of the Roman Martyrology for this day.

I have nothing to add concerning Hilarion to Baronius’s note. Bede and, after him, Rabanus celebrate him in the same words: the Little Roman Martyrology has only a few: “And Saint Hilarion the monk.” Ado, however, inserted a fairly long account into his Martyrology from the distinguished Life written by Jerome; Notker reported little from it, and did so incorrectly on the preceding day; Our Author selected and transcribed only the first period, which closely resembles the wording of Bede and Rabanus. See what we briefly indicated on 21 March, and the Life in Surius.

Bede also mentions Asterius, as do Rabanus and Ado, all in precisely the same terms. Whether Usuard followed Bede or Ado is equally uncertain; certainly he took from one or the other, more probably from his usual forerunner, the few points that we have reported in the text. Concerning the Acts, see what we observed about Callistus on 14 October. Wandalbert praises Asterius and Hilarion as follows:

“Priest Asterius shines with twelvefold praise,

An outstanding man who taught many saints to conquer

The cruel wars threatening pious people everywhere with death;

And good Hilarion, a dweller in the desert, accompanies him.”

“Concerning the holy traveler,” says Florentinius, “everything is clear among Gallic writers.” I agree; but whether his conjecture is so well founded in restoring what he calls the addition of the Gallic antiquary, let others judge. We discussed Justus, this traveler’s teacher, at length on 11 September; other matters will be examined fully elsewhere. Some Supplements report both together, or separately on different days; but this has no bearing on the text. For the present, it is enough to observe that Usuard, in the case of Viator as in that of the other saints, transferred everything from Ado, as we warned at the beginning.]

[Note: [Col. 0603A]

HERINIEN, entirely pure throughout the text, again inserts an addition proper to Rheims in second place: “Likewise, in the fortress of Laon, Saint Cilinia, mother of Blessed Remigius, archbishop of Rheims.” In the lower margin of the codex, a later hand adds: “At Cologne Agrippina, the passion of the eleven thousand holy virgins.”

TORNACEN is also entirely pure in the text, but inserts near the end: “In the city of Laon, Saint Cilinia.” Then, after Viator, at the end: “In the city of Meaux, Saint Cilinia, virgin.” Castellanus thinks that the mother of Remigius was entered because of this nearly homonymous virgin.

ANTUERP.-MAJ., not sufficiently correct in the text and no more elegantly at the end, adds: “In the city of Cologne, the passion of the eleven thousand holy virgins.”

ROSWEYD, concerning Asterius: “Who is read of in the passion of Callistus, pope of the city of Rome.” At the end: “In the city of Cologne, eleven thousand virgins.”

[Col. 0603B] PULSANEN has everything sufficiently pure except the final commemoration, which is lacking.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN add to the text: “At Bordeaux, Severinus, bishop. In the city of Cologne, the birthday of eleven thousand virgins.”

MUNERAT: “Dasius, Zoticus with twelve thousand.” At the end: “On the same day, at Cologne, the eleven thousand holy virgins and martyrs.”

GREVEN, with the sign L, as we said, adds at the end: “At Cologne Agrippina, the passion of the eleven thousand holy virgins.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN are pure in the first section; they render the second as follows: “In Palestine, the birthday of Saint Hilarion, abbot, whose Life,” and so forth. Then: “At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of eleven thousand virgins.” Concerning Asterius they add: “Who, as is read in the passion of Pope Callistus, was thrown from a bridge at the command of the Emperor Alexander because he had buried the body of Saint Callistus, and thus attained the glory of martyrdom.” They are pure in Viator, and add: “In the fortress of [Col. 0603C] Laon, Saint Cilinia, mother of Saint Remigius, apostle of the Franks. At Bordeaux, Saint Severus, bishop of Trier.” Severus of Trier is honored on 15 October. Here Severinus is intended, on the 15th, as we shall explain more fully elsewhere.

LOVANIEN differs from the preceding witnesses in having removed Asterius’s eulogy.
