ALBERG. and DANIC. differ from ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others only in order: they announce Hilarion first, the Ursulan women second, and the Nicomedians third; the rest is as above.

CENTULEN: “At Nicomedia, Saints Dasius and Sotitigius with ten other soldiers. In Palestine, the passing of Blessed Hilarion, great father of the monks, whose life Blessed Jerome describes as full of the glory of holiness and miracles. In the city of Ostia, Saint Asterius, priest and martyr. At Laon-Clavatus, Saint Cilinia, mother of Saint Remigius, archbishop.”

[Col. 0603D] BRUXELLEN begins: “At Cologne Agrippina, outside the city walls on the northern side, the passion of Blessed Ursula and, with her, of eleven thousand holy virgins. They came from Britain to Rome and from there to Cologne, and were martyred there beside the Rhine.” It names four of the Nicomedian martyrs individually, namely Elasius, Dasius, Zoticus, and Gaius, or Gagius, and so forth. Concerning Hilarion it has the same account as ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others. Then: “At Bordeaux, the deposition of Saint Severus, archbishop of Trier.” See ANTUERP.-MAX. “At the monastery of Fontenelle, the deposition of Saint Condedi [also Condedus], confessor. At Laon, the deposition of Saint Cilinia, mother of Blessed Remigius.” Read “Laon,” as above.

HAGENOYEN gives a lengthy account of the Ursulan virgins, but appears to have selected what is especially improbable. See below in the LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION and GREVEN. Concerning the Nicomedians it adds only “with eleven [Col. 0604A] soldiers.” Concerning Asterius it is nearly the same as ANTUERP.-MAX. Then: “Likewise, in the fortress of Lyon, the deposition of Saint Cilinia, mother of Saint Remigius, apostle of the Franks.” Hilarion and Viator are absent.

AQUICINCT adds to the text: “At Bordeaux, Saint Severinus, bishop. On the same day, the discovery of the body of Blessed Audomar, bishop. And Saint Cilinia, mother of Saint Remigius. At Cologne, the eleven thousand holy virgins.” The copyist who collated the codex with Molan’s second edition and recorded the variants notes—he notes, I say—that one or two pages were inserted here by a later hand, containing various additions, and especially that one from which we attempted to infer the age of the codex in the preface.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The eleven thousand virgins. Hilarion, confessor. Dasius, Zoticus, Gaius, with twelve soldier-martyrs. Asterius, priest and martyr.”

REG. SUEC., under number 428: “At Cologne, the eleven thousand [Col. 0604B] virgins.”

CODEX D LE MARE, marked A: “In the city of Bordeaux, Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN, no. 5949, has Claudius instead of Dasius.

FLORENTIN does not agree completely, but reads approximately as follows: “Ursula with eleven thousand, and the passion of the holy martyrs Cyriacus the pope, who was eighteenth after Peter, and also James, archbishop of Antioch; Vincent, cardinal priest; Maurice, bishop of Lavicani; Follanus, bishop of Lucca; Sulpitius, bishop of Ravenna; Clement, bishop; Marculus, bishop; and Hereus, the husband of Saint Ursula. At Bordeaux, Saint Severinus, bishop.” This final commemoration of Saint Severinus is read in the same words in the BURDEGAL codex.

CODEX MONTIS SANCTI: “At Toul, the translation of Saint Gerard, bishop and confessor.” See in our Acts on 23 April.

EDITIO LUBECO-COL.: “At Cologne Agrippina, the passion of Saint Ursula and her companions, eleven thousand holy virgins and martyrs. Their holy Ursula, a virgin and daughter of the king of the Britons, was their lady and queen. When she had been betrothed to Etherius, son of the king of England, she chose these holy virgins for the dedication and preservation of her virginity; with them she travelled to Rome and from Rome reached Cologne. Associated with these holy virgins were Pope Saint Cyriacus, Cardinal-Priest Innocent, Pantulus, bishop of Basel, and Saint Marculus, bishop; many bishops and priests, princes and nobles joined this holy company. Together with these virgins, on one day, under the one most holy faith of the Trinity, on the bank of the Rhine at the aforesaid city, together with the blessed Gerasina, queen of Sicily, and her daughters Babilla, Juliana, Victoria, and Aurea, her little son Adrian, and the blessed virgins Cleomatha, Theomata, Cristantia, Pynnosa, Theusta, Thamaria the queen, and Officia, they were slaughtered by the Huns and barbarians after a cruel ordeal in the time of the emperor Marcian, [Col. 0604D] around the year of the Lord 450. At the city of Bordeaux in Aquitaine, the memorial of the most holy father Severinus, archbishop and confessor of Cologne; this glorious feast is celebrated today with joyful solemnity among the inhabitants of that city.”

It also has more concerning Hilarion, but I prefer to read that in Ado. In the Nicomedian entry he has “with twelve thousand.” Concerning Asterius, as in ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. In Viator it is almost pure. Concerning Cilinia likewise as in ANTUERP.-MAX., but instead of *matris* it has *martyris*. Then: “On the same day, the passing of Saint Wendelin the confessor, whose merits are revealed by frequent miracles. At Meaux, Saint Celinia, virgin. On the same day, Saints Victor and Sindulf, confessors.”

BELIN., in the text, is quite accurate, except that he reads “with twelve thousand.” At the end he adds: “At Bordeaux, [Col. 0605A] Saint Severinus, bishop. On the same day, in the city of Cologne, the feast of the holy thousand virgins, who completed their lives in martyrdom for the steadfastness of their virginity.”

GREVEN.: “Note. The blessed Ursula was queen and leader of the eleven thousand virgins. She was the daughter of Denotus, king of the Britons, and betrothed to Conan, king of Armorica, or Brittany Minor. All these virgins, together with countless others who flocked to them, were crowned with martyrdom at Cologne—as is read in the Acts of the Britons—in the time of the emperor Gratian, who began to reign in the year of the Lord 381. Others think differently.” Compare with this EDITIO LUBECO-COL.: “To commend their sanctity, not only custom but also a quasi-sacramental observance has arisen, so that within the bounds of the virginal burial-place no one dares to bring in the body of any deceased person. There were, moreover, four virgins over the army with blessed Ursula; their names were Pynnosa, Cordula, Eleutheria, and Florentia. After these, eleven others presided, each over a thousand; their names are: Jota, Benigna, Clementia, Sapientia, Corpophora, Columba, Benedicta, Odilia, Celyndris, Sibilia, and Luca. Also at Nicaea in Bithynia, Saints Macarius, Proculus, and Modestus with 272 others. Mauruntus, bishop of Marseilles and confessor. Severus, bishop of Trier and confessor. At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Condelus, priest and confessor. Also the burial [Col. 0606A] of Saint Wandelin, confessor of Trier, whose merits are revealed by frequent miracles. Malchus the monk. In Ireland, Nummius the confessor. At Bordeaux, a city of Aquitaine, the solemn memorial of the blessed Severinus, archbishop and confessor of Cologne. At Meaux, Saint Celina, virgin. At the fortress of Laon, Saint Cilinia, mother of Saint Remigius, apostle of the Franks. ‘This has already recurred several times above.’”

MOLAN.: “At Bordeaux, Saint Severinus, bishop.

On the same day, at Cologne Agrippina, the holy” etc., as in BELINUS: “Likewise, at the fortress of Laon, Saint Cilinia, mother of the blessed Remigius, archbishop of Reims. In the city of Meaux, Saint Edinia, virgin. On the same day, the passing of Saint Wandelin, confessor.” In smaller type is added: “Of Trier, whose merits,” etc., as in GREVEN. “Malchus, monk. On the same day, the blessed Wimon, bishop of Bremen, who rests at Birka. Other editions have the entries concerning Ursula as above. Concerning Cilinia, [Col. 0606B] Remigius is given the title ‘apostle of the Franks.’ ‘In the city of Meaux, Saint Celinia, virgin. At Sithiu, the discovery of Saint Audomar, bishop of Thérouanne.’ Finally, in smaller type: ‘At Birka, the blessed Wimon, bishop of Bremen, who preached the word of God to the Goths.’ Castellanus calls him Vimo, in French Guimon, and says that he was the third bishop of Bremen.”

[Col. 0601]

At Nicomedia, the birthday of the holy martyrs Dasius, Zoticus, Gaius, with twelve soldiers. On the same day, our holy father Hilarion, whose Life Jerome wrote as full of virtues. In the city of Ostia, Saint Asterius the priest, who is mentioned in the passion of the blessed Pope Callistus. On the same day, Saint Viator, minister of the blessed Justus, bishop of Lyon.

[Note: [Col. 0601B] In the Dervensis manuscript, before the final commemoration: “In the city of Lyon, Saint Cilinia, mother [Col. 0602B] of the most blessed Remigius, archbishop of Reims.” BOUILLART.]

XI Kal. Day 22. [Note: [Col. 0605B]

Many manuscripts agree, such as Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Belin., Greven. [Col. 0606B] and Molan. Likewise those of Antuerp.-Max., Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, and the Danish manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0605C]

Some write *Hadrinopolim*, as Praten. and Molan.; the others have *Adrianopolim*, except Belin, who reads *Andrianopolim*. I shall say no more about “of Thrace,” or likewise “of Jerusalem,” etc. For *doctissimi* Antuerp.-Max. has *devotissimi*; Antuerp.-Maj. calls him “of Mark.” Antuerp., Max.-Lubec, and all the more recent manuscripts write *fuisse sollicita*. Nowhere is there such variation as in the name *Nunilonis*, for which I find written *Mumilonis, Munilonis, Mulinonis, Numelonis, Numilionis, Minulionis, Mymilionis, Mivilionis, Milionis*, and what not? The remaining manuscripts have *Elodia* in the text, as all codices do except Molan alone, who correctly writes [Col. 0606C] *Alodia*, as the Memorial of Eulogius altogether demonstrates should be written. In Antuerp.-Maj. *custodia maceratae* is not well expressed; Belin is even more defective, mutilating the phrase in this way: “Mulinus and Zoledia, who, punished by capital sentence, completed their martyrdom”; the words “who, worn down by prolonged imprisonment for the confession of Christ,” etc., are entirely missing. Greven. and Molan. have *celebraverunt* instead of *celebrarunt*. The last six manuscripts, which we call of middling quality, differ from the purer ones in beginning the second announcement thus: “At Jerusalem, blessed Mark,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0605C]

At Atriopolis, or Adrianople, in Thrace, Philip the bishop, Eusebius, Hermes, and Severus are commonly read in the Hieronymian copies preserved by Florentinius. From these Ado very probably took the first three, which seemed more closely associated; from Ado Our author copied his material word for word, listing first the group that stands last in Ado. In the case of Severus, or Severi, who may perhaps be different persons, the cited manuscripts seem to have confused the names; but from where they introduced Eusebius here, I confess that I cannot discover even by conjecture.

We possess excellent Acts of this Philip—not bishop of Adrianople but of Heraclea—of Severus the priest, and of Hermes the deacon, in manuscript; Mabillon published them in volume IV of the *Analecta*, p. 134 onward, and Ruinart later published them more accurately among the *Selecta et sincera*, p. 442 onward. From these it is clear that Philip had only two companions in martyrdom: Severus the priest and Hermes the decurion and deacon. Castellanus’s note expressly excludes the first of these, namely Severus, asserting that only the decurion-deacon suffered with the bishop; but anyone who consults the Acts will plainly discover that the aforesaid Severus was crowned with the glory of martyrdom together with two others. [Col. 0606C] Rabanus alone among the martyrologists appears to have read the Acts themselves, correctly distinguishing and identifying the companions and composing a brief eulogy from those same Acts. Notker follows Rabanus in part, but wrongly mixes his words with those of Ado, and again goes astray here in the order of the Kalends.

In my opinion those are mistaken who think that Philip completed his contest under Julian; nor does Baronius rightly number him among the bishops of Adrianople. It is clear that Wandalbert held the same view as Ado from his verses:

“Philip the bishop increases the eleventh feast;

On this same day Hermes shines, and blessed Eusebius.”

The author of the *Romanum parvum* is the first among the martyrologists to speak of Mark of Jerusalem, from his usual source Rufinus, book IV, chapter 7, in these words: “At Jerusalem, Mark, who was the first from the Gentiles to be made bishop there.” The Viennese follows him first, composing a brief eulogy of Mark, partly taken from the cited passage. Our author took everything from Ado, as did Notker, though on the preceding day. In the praised Rufinus, however, Ado did not find [Col. 0607A] the statement that Mark, not long after his election, completed his life by martyrdom; the first claim is false, while the second, concerning martyrdom, is at least doubtful. See the *Chronological History of the Bishops of Jerusalem*, prefixed by Papebrochius to volume III of the May volume, p. XI. Baronius and others provide more material, which should be reviewed in its proper place.

Salome, omitted by the other ancient martyrologists, is also owed to the author of the *Romanum parvum*: “And Salome, who is read of in the Gospel.” The name Mary is assigned to her somewhere, but nowhere, so far as I know, is she called this among the ancients. The Viennese transferred her from the *Romanum parvum*; Our author removed only what did not properly belong to her, namely “with the other holy women”; everything else is plainly Ado’s. Let the Evangelists be consulted, especially Matthew, chapters XV and XVI, and what has already been set out in the Acts concerning Mary of Clopas on 9 April.

The final Spanish entry is peculiar to Usuard. We have already said more than enough above about the variation of the names. You will find their Life and Acts excellently described in Eulogius, book II of the *Memorial*, chapter 7. See also what Ambrosio de Morales discussed and noted more fully concerning their passion in the scholia on Eulogius, found in volume IV of *Hispania illustrata*, p. 285.]

[Note: [Col. 0607A]

TORNACEN. is accurate in the first three announcements but entirely deficient in the fourth.

ROSWEYD. is accurate throughout the text, but at the end adds: “At Naples, Saints Festus and Modestus, martyrs, and 271 others.” See the Hieronymian tradition for the preceding day. “At Ravenna, Saint Severus, bishop and confessor.” See below EDITIO LUBECO-COL., GREVEN., and MOLAN. Also the supplements for 1 February. [Col. 0607B]

PULSANEN. is accurate in the first entry; in the second everything after “the most learned man” is missing. He is also accurate in the third; the fourth is absent.

MUNERAT. is not entirely accurate in the text, and at the end adds: “In Gaul, in the city of Rouen, the birthday of Saint Mellonius, who governed the church of that city as its first archbishop and, buried there, rested most gloriously.” What fabrications concerning this saint were made by certain Spanish writers, you will learn from Cardinal Aguirre, as reported in Papebrochius’s *Response*, article XVIII, no. 37.

CENTULEN.: “At Jerusalem, blessed Mark, who was the first from the Gentiles at Jerusalem, after the bishops from the circumcision, to hold the priesthood of that church. At Adrianople in Thrace, Saints Philip the bishop, Eusebius, and Hermes. In the city of Huesca, the holy virgins Nunilo and Elodia, who suffered for the faith of Christ in the persecution of Dacian [Col. 0607C] (let the Acts themselves be consulted). Likewise, Saint Salome, who in the Gospel is read to have been concerned about the Lord’s burial.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “Mary of James and Mary Salome, maternal aunts of our Lord Jesus Christ. As is read in the Gospel, they anxiously cared for the burial of that same Lord Jesus. At Cologne Agrippina, the passion of the blessed Cordula, virgin and martyr. At Adrianople in Thrace, etc. At Jerusalem, the birthday of the most illustrious and learned man, Saint Mark the bishop, etc. In the city of Ostia, the birthday of the blessed Asterius the priest. Concerning him it is read in the passion of Pope Callistus that, because he had buried the body of that same Pope Callistus, the emperor Alexander ordered him to be thrown from a bridge, and thus he gained the palm of martyrdom. In that same city of Ostia”—clearly an error—“the birthday of the holy virgins Munilodia and Elodia. Who, for their confession,” etc. Also Valerius, bishop and martyr. At Lyon, the burial of Saint Viator the confessor, lector, companion, and minister of the blessed Justus, [Col. 0607D] bishop of Lyon.” Concerning him and Asterius, see the preceding day. “And Mellonius the confessor, archbishop of the church of Rouen.”

HAGENOYEN. errs at the very beginning, writing “Mary Magdalene” instead of Salome and mixing together much material that must be sorted out elsewhere. In the Adrianopolitan entries he is accurate. “At Jerusalem, the birthday of Saint Mark, bishop and martyr, who was the first from the Gentiles,” etc. “In Britain, Saint Mellonius, bishop and confessor. In the city of Huesca, the birthday of the holy virgins Mynidenis, Mymilion, and Elodia. Who, for the confession of Christ,” etc., accurately. “On the same day, Saint Cordula, virgin, with several others who belonged to the company of the eleven thousand virgins. Terrified by the prospect of death, they hid during the night in ships; but when they saw the other glorious virgins ascending to heaven, they voluntarily handed themselves over to the executioners on the following day. [Col. 0608A] Since they could not be buried with the other virgins, they therefore do not rest in the church of the Hospitallers, where many miracles have been performed through their merits. At the city of Ravenna, the burial of Saint Severus, bishop, who is said to have been a craftsman and to have been chosen bishop through his flowering staff. He received from the Lord the knowledge of governing his subjects, governed well, performed miracles, and, while still alive, entered the tomb and died like John the Evangelist.” See ROSWEYD above.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Severus, bishop. Cordula, virgin. Philip, bishop and martyr, with his companions. Mary Salome. Mark, bishop of Jerusalem.”

BIGOTIAN., marked D 9: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Mellonius, archbishop of Rouen.”

REGINAE SUEC., under no. 428: “In the city of Rouen, the burial of Saint Mellonius, bishop and confessor. He governed the church of that city as its first archbishop and, buried there, rested in a glorious end.”

IN VATICAN., marked no. 5949, the last two announcements are absent. At the end is added: “At Benevento, the birthday of Saint Cassius, bishop, in Saint Sophia.” Who this Cassus is will be investigated later.

ALTEMPS.: “Also the passion of Valerius, archdeacon of the city of Langres, who, when the Vandals invaded Gaul, was crowned with glorious martyrdom for the name of Christ.”

FLORENTIN., first: “In the regions of Tuscany, at Fiesole in the Florentine territory, Saint Donatus the Scot, bishop and confessor of that city, who, renowned for virtues and miracles, rested in the Lord and was buried in the basilica of the aforesaid city. Also Saint Mallonius, archbishop and confessor of the church of Rouen.”

DIVIONEN. S. Benigni: “In the territory of the city of Langres, Saint Valerius, archdeacon and martyr.”

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “In the district of Châlons, Saint Lupentius, martyr.”

EDITIO LUBECO-COL.: “In Cologne Agrippina, the passion of Saint Cordula, queen, virgin, and martyr, one of the eleven thousand virgins. When she saw the most terrible slaughter of her companions, she hid herself in a ship that night, terrified by fear; but on the following day, offering herself voluntarily to death, she received the crown of martyrdom. Also the vigil of the blessed Severinus, archbishop and confessor.” [Col. 0608D] In the Adrianopolitan entries and in that concerning Mark it is quite accurate. “At Ravenna, Saint Severus, bishop and confessor. He was chosen bishop by all the clergy and people from the wool-working trade, through the manifestation of a dove. Seeing this, his wife Vincentia and his daughter Innocentia entered a monastery and dedicated themselves to God. The holy man himself, foreknowing his death, after celebrating the sacred mysteries and dismissing the people from the church, went to the tomb of his wife and daughter. With the stone rolled away by itself, he said to them: ‘At the Lord’s command I am called; give me a place to sleep with you.’ When they gave him a place, he entered alive, destined to die. Also Saint Mary Salome, who in the Gospel is read to have been concerned, with the other women, about the Lord’s burial. Coming from the Roman city into Campania, she moved to Christ at the city of Merulana [Verulana], and there received a tomb beneath a certain cave. Her body was later discovered by her son James and honorably transferred to the aforesaid city. In the city of Ostia, the holy virgins and martyrs Mivelon and Helodia. Who, for their confession,” etc., with the Usuardine text quite accurately.

GREVEN.: “In the district of Amiens, blessed Gratian, martyr. Leogatus, martyr. Ebidius, bishop and martyr. In Gaul, in the city of Rouen, Saint Mellonius, bishop, who was first ordained bishop of that city by Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, and rested there in a glorious end. On this day, but according to others on the Kalends of February, at Ravenna, blessed Severus, bishop and confessor. He was taken from the wool-workers’ trade and made bishop through the miracle of a dove sent from heaven. After diligently carrying out the office entrusted to him and foreknowing the day of his death, he ordered the tomb of his wife and daughter to be opened so that they might grant him a place to rest with them; when they gave him a place, he entered the tomb, destined to die. [Col. 0609B] At Cologne Agrippina, Saint Cordula, queen, virgin, and martyr. Since she belonged to the company of the eleven thousand virgins, she hid herself in a ship, terrified by the slaughter of her companions; but when morning came, she offered herself voluntarily and received the crown of martyrdom.”

MOLAN., after Hermes, in different type, inserts into the text: “When persecution was raging, they resisted the closing and plundering of Christian churches, ordered by Emperor Julian and carried out through wicked governors; for this reason they were subjected by the governor Bassus, and also by Justinus, to many tortures, namely prisons, chains, scourges, and finally burning in flames. But strengthened by the power of the Lord, they persevered until the end in confessing his name.” This was taken from Rabanus, with the name Julian wrongly inserted, since it is absent there.

At the end: “In Gaul, in the city of Rouen, the birthday of Saint Mellonius, who was the first of that city, etc.,” from MUNERAT. “Severus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Cordula, virgin.” Then in smaller type: “Who, since she belonged to the company of the eleven thousand,” etc., from GREVEN. “Lupentius, abbot of Gabalum and martyr, concerning whom see the *Chronicle* of Gregory of Tours.” Other editions have these entries in the text itself. At the end, concerning Mellonius, as above. Then: “In the city of Gabalum, Saint Lupentius, abbot of the basilica of Saint Privatus and martyr. At Cologne, Cordula, virgin and martyr. On the twenty-second day, Saint Abercius, bishop of Hierapolis, who was renowned for miracles in the time of the apostles.” [Col. 0610B] See Metaphrastes in Surius. “At Oosterhout, the birthday of Saint Oelbert, martyr.” You will find the few things surviving by tradition about this saint in the *Lives of the Saints of Belgium* for this day. “On the same day, the translation of Saint Severus the confessor, bishop of Ravenna, with his wife and daughter, to the diocese of Mainz.”]

[Col. 0605]

At Adrianople in Thrace, the birthday of the holy martyrs Philip the bishop, Eusebius, and Hermes. Also the blessed Mark, bishop, a most illustrious and learned man, who was the first from the Gentiles to undertake the governance of the church of Jerusalem and not long afterward merited the palm of martyrdom. Also Saint Salome, who in the Gospel is read to have been concerned about the Lord’s burial. In the city of Huesca, the holy virgins Nunilo and Elodia, who, worn down by prolonged imprisonment for the confession of Christ and punished by capital sentence, completed their martyrdom.

X Kal. Day 23. [Note: [Col. 0609]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0609C]

Only the manuscripts Praten. and Antuerp.-Maj. have *Theodoriti*; we preferred this reading from his Acts, although the other ancient manuscripts have *Theodorici*, others *Theodori* with Sozomenus, while the *Romanum parvum* and Ado have *Theodoreti*. Antuerp.-Maj. and Munerat. write “priest and martyr.” Concerning “priest,” “of Syria,” and similar matters, enough has been said. Praten. writes *durissimos cruciatus*; we, with the rest, have *durissimos*. [Col. 0610C] Again, Praten. separates *etiam*, reading *et jam*; in Antuerp.-Maj. it is *et lampadibus*. Greven. and Molan. place *impii Juliani* instead of *Juliani impii*. In Munerat., after Germanus, *martyris* is added; and instead of *martyrii sui* it reads *martyrii socii*. In listing the tortures, Molan. continues with substantives, “filth, prisons”; the others have it as in the text. Likewise, instead of *Pictavensi*, as everyone reads, he corrects it to *Pictaviensi*.]

[Note: [Col. 0609C]

In the whole entry for today, neither the Hieronymian manuscripts nor Bede and those who follow him have any part. The first memorial, therefore, of Theodiritus or Theodoretus, Theodorus or Theodoricus, is taken from the *Romanum parvum* in these words: “At Antioch, Theodoretus the priest.” Ado thus gives the name, although Sozomenus, book I, chapter 8 of Valesius’s edition, calls our martyr Theodorus, as we said. I think Ado saw the Acts, which were carefully written by an eyewitness, since his eulogy appears to have been abridged from them. Here Molan. cites manuscript Acts from the Amsterdam Charterhouse, in which the day of the passion is expressly marked as the tenth day before the Kalends of November, as some manuscripts among us also read; others have it differently. All these will in due time be compared more carefully with Mabillon’s edition in volume IV of the *Analecta* and Ruinart’s edition among the *Selecta et sincera*, p. 658 onward.

For the rest, Usuard took everything from Ado, as did Notker on the preceding day. The author of the *Romanum parvum* is also the first to mention Servandus and Germanus: “In Spain, Servandus and Germanus.” Ado gave a brief eulogy, perhaps having seen some Acts resembling those of Surius, extracted from Lucius Marineus Siculus. We possess fuller material compared with other sources, concerning which there is neither time nor place to make many observations; meanwhile, what Baronius noted may be consulted. Our author here too transferred his entire text from Ado.

Mosander today begins the Adoian entry thus: “At Cologne, the burial of Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor.” Rosweyd considered this an addition and therefore relegated it to the appendix; rightly, I think, since it was omitted by Notker, Ado’s faithful copyist. Nothing at all remains doubtful concerning Usuard in view of the common agreement of the principal manuscripts. That his feast was solemnly celebrated at Bordeaux on 21 October is clear from the supplements for that day. What Fortunatus is said to have written about this most illustrious saint has not yet seen the light. Other Acts by a more recent author were published by Surius, together with an extract from Gregory of Tours and also an account of the translation; other manuscripts exist among us, to be illustrated elsewhere together with the earlier material. Baronius’s note should again be consulted.

Today Severinus alone is celebrated by Wandalbert in these verses:

“Severinus, sacred one, on the tenth day thereafter you behold your Colonian people,

shining from the summit of the first temple.”

[Col. 0611A] The final entry follows, likewise wholly Usuardine, namely Benedict of Poitiers, the confessor, who is also assigned to Usuard in the supplements. Castellanus, in his French translation, reads *Bonizet*, “in the manner of the people of Poitiers,” but Motherius prefers to restore the customary form of that language, *Benoist*. If any Acts or deeds of his have been committed to memory, they will be brought forth in due course. So far I have found nothing worthy of note. When Saussay praises him as richly adorned with the privileges of grace, you understand that this applies so well to our Benedict that it deserves to be said of all saints, whatever their sex or rank.]

[Note: [Col. 0611A]

TORNACEN. is quite accurate in the first and the two final entries; it entirely lacks the second, concerning Servandus and Germanus.

ROSWEYD. is not entirely accurate in the text; after Severinus he adds “archbishop and confessor.” “At the hour of Saint Martin’s passing, when after Matins he was going around the holy places with his clergy, he heard a choir singing above.” At the end he adds: “In Caesarea of Cappadocia, Severus, bishop and confessor.” In the Hieronymian manuscripts a certain Suresus is found, but he must, I think, be called a martyr, not a bishop.

PULSANEN. removes the eulogies from the first two entries. He is accurate in the third. Then: “At Rouen, the burial [Col. 0611B] of Saint Romanus, archbishop and confessor.”

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. are nearly accurate in the text, but omit the final entry.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERGEN., and DANIC. all write *Theodori*. They are accurate in the first two; they form the third thus: “In the city of Cologne, which is called Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor. At the passing of the blessed Martin, he merited to hear the voices of angels singing.” Here too the final announcement is absent, as in PULSANEN., etc.

LOVANIEN. would entirely agree with those just cited if it did not lack the eulogy of the two Spanish martyrs Servandus and Germanus.

CENTULEN.: “At Antioch in Syria, Saint Theodoricus the priest, who, during the persecution of Julian, completed his martyrdom by the sword. In Spain, Saints Servandus and Germanus, martyrs. In the district of Poitiers, Saint Benedict, confessor. In the city of Cologne, Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor. In the city of Amiens, Saint Domitius, confessor. In the territory of that same city, Saint Gratian, martyr; to prove his sanctity, the Lord each year causes a hazel tree within the space of a single night to put forth leaves, blossom, and produce nuts.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “At Cologne Agrippina, the burial of Saint Severinus, archbishop of that same city. He immediately learned of the passing of the blessed Martin of Tours and together with his archdeacon then merited to hear voices of angels singing in heaven. At Antioch in Syria, the birthday of Saint Theodore the priest. During the persecution of the impious apostate Julian, after the torture of the rack and many very severe tortures, he was also burned by lamps placed around his sides. But when the ministers, terrified by the sight of angels, fell on their faces, and professed belief in Christ, the impious Julian ordered them to be plunged into the sea. The blessed Theodore said to them: ‘Go ahead, brothers; I, overcoming the enemy, will follow to the Lord.’ Thus, himself remaining steadfast in the confession of Christ, he was beheaded.” See Ado. In the entry for Servandus and Germanus he is accurate. Then: “And elsewhere, Saint Longinus. Also Oda, widow, daughter of the duke of Lorraine and surviving wife of Count Lambert, our founder. At the translation of the body of the blessed Gudula and the establishment of the college of this church, she was her husband’s faithful helper both in counsel and in assistance. On the same day, Saint Romanus, archbishop and confessor. And the translation of Saint Theodore the abbot.” Nothing concerning Benedict of Poitiers.

HAGENOYEN., somewhat interpolated in the first and second entries, has the third as follows: “In the city of Cologne, which is called Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor of that city. He governed that same church most excellently during the time of the Arian persecution and is himself said to have been appointed by God. He is read to have led a pilgrim’s life in his episcopate; and when at a certain time he was going around the churches in the customary manner with his clergy, at the passing of Saint Martin he merited to hear the voices of angels singing.” Here the final announcement, transferred to the following day on the authority of this manuscript, is absent.

AQUICINCT. At the end, in a later hand: “On the same day, Saint Leotadius, bishop and confessor.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEG., marked no. 130, and CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked with the letter C: “On the same day, Saint Leothadius, bishop and confessor.”

DAVERON.: “The feast of the blessed Gratian, martyr.” It is accurate concerning Severinus and Benedict.

AMBIANEN.: “In the city of Amiens, the birthday of Saint Domitius [Col. 0612B] the confessor, a man of great virtues. In the territory of that same city, Saint Gratian, martyr.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Severinus, bishop of Cologne. Oda, widow. Theodoricus, priest and martyr. Servandus and Germanus, martyrs.”

CLUNIACEN.: “On the same day, Leotadius, bishop and confessor.” This recurs several times on this day.

CAMBERIEN. and REG. SUEC. under no. 428: “In the district of Amiens, the blessed Gratian, martyr.”

In VATICAN., marked no. 5949, the announcements of Severinus and Benedict are absent.

ALTEMPS.: “On the same day, Saint Ethelfleda, queen. And Saint Leotadius, bishop and confessor of Canterbury.” See Castellanus’s Martyrology.

FLORENTIN.: “Also Saint Romanus, archbishop.” Then STROZZIAN.: “In the territory of Amiens, Saint Domitius, bishop and confessor.”

CASTRI-KAROLI writes, with the preceding sources: “Saint Leothadius, bishop and confessor.”

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll.: “In the district of Poitiers, [Col. 0612C] Saint Benedict, bishop and confessor.”

EDITIO-LUBECO-COL.: “In the city of Cologne, which is called Agrippina, the passing of our most holy father and protector Severinus, archbishop and confessor of that same city, a man of great authority and holiness. He was born in Aquitaine, in the city of Bordeaux, of respectable parents, noble according to worldly fortune; sufficiently educated in the liberal arts, he was first ordained bishop at Sens and afterward, as had been foretold to him by the Lord through an angel, was ordained archbishop at Cologne Agrippina on the fourth day before the Ides of May. Through his Catholic faith, his immense labor, and his sound doctrine, the churches of Cologne, Bordeaux, Tongeren, and their neighboring churches were defended from the attacks of the Arian heresy in the time of Pope Saint Damasus and the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian; for this reason he suffered many plots from Arians and wicked men.

The miracles that shine forth testify how great his merit was before God. [Col. 0612D] Like the blessed patriarch Jacob, standing in prayer at night, he saw a golden ladder extending to heaven, with angels ascending and descending. At the passing of the blessed Martin, bishop of Tours, he merited to hear the voices of angels singing. He is read to have restored one dead youth to life. He also possessed the grace of prophecy: whoever he saw, he knew that person’s mind. After many distinguished works of virtue and miracles, he summoned the brethren and foretold that he would pay the debt of death and announced the day and hour of his departure. Thus, at Bordeaux, in the presence of the blessed Amandus, bishop of that place, and many faithful of both sexes, after giving an exhortation and the kiss of peace, laden with every virtue, he departed from the world on the day he himself had foretold, the day on which our Lord rose victoriously from the dead. He saw the Lord Jesus Christ and the holy glory of God the Father; angels came and received his soul. [Col. 0613A] But he was carried back to Cologne on the third day before the Nones of October and, as is believed, was honorably placed there during those days. His tomb is very frequently illumined by divine miracles, as the deeds of his life testify.”

Here you have an abridgment of the published Acts, which must be examined in their proper time. “Also the translation of the blessed Maternus, first archbishop of Cologne, third of Trier, and likewise first of Tongeren, and confessor. To avoid a revolt among the peoples of these three churches, his body had been placed at Cologne on a ship after mature deliberation. And behold, that ship, set in the middle of the Rhine without a human pilot, driven by a heavenly oar, ascended against the current toward Trier.” These matters too will have to be carefully examined on 14 September.

Concerning Theodoricus of Antioch, see what was said above in BRUXELLEN.; this edition agrees with it almost entirely. It is accurate concerning Servandus and Germanus, and likewise concerning Benedict. Then: “On the same day, Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor. In the district of Amiens, the blessed Gratian, martyr. At Vienne, Saint Eodicius, bishop.”

[Col. 0613B] BELIN. is quite accurate throughout the text, but in the penultimate place inserts: “On the same day, Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor.” At the end: “In the territory of Amiens, Saint Domitius, bishop and confessor.” Another edition adds still further: “In the city of Rouen, the burial of Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor.” See the supplement of MOLAN below.

## GREVEN

“Note. The aforementioned blessed Severinus was born of a noble family in Aquitania and sufficiently instructed in the liberal arts. First bishop of Sens, and afterward—as had been foretold to him by an angel—made bishop of the church of Cologne, by his own exertions, Catholic faith, and sound teaching, though at great labor, he defended the churches of Cologne, Tongeren, Bordeaux, and those neighboring them from the infestation of the Arian heresy in the time of Pope Damasus. He was granted to hear the choir of angels and, in spirit, to recognize those who were carrying the soul of blessed Martin of Tours into heaven. [Col. 0614A] Finally, renowned for his life and miracles—among them he is said to have raised a dead man—he rested in peace; he is the singular patron and protector of the church of Cologne, shining forth even to this day through many miracles. Of the martyr Longinus. At Adrianople, Saints Severus and Dorotheus. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Severus, bishop. At Rouen, Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor. While presiding over the aforesaid church in the time of Clovis, among his other remarkable works he restored by prayer a small vessel of chrism that had been accidentally broken; immediately afterward the sacred chrism withdrew itself drop by drop into the same vessel. At Vienne, Saint Eodicius, bishop and confessor.” Concerning the translation of Maternus, see what has already been said. At the end: “Queen Ethelfreda.”

MOLAN, in another type, adds to the text concerning Severinus: “Of our most holy protector, by whose Catholic faith, greatest labor, and sound doctrine the churches of Cologne, Bordeaux, Tongeren, and the neighboring churches were defended from the infestation of the Arian heresy; he also deserved, at the passing of blessed Martin, to hear the voices of the singing [Col. 0614B] angels.”

At the end: “In the territory of the Amiens people, Saint Domitius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Romanus, bishop and confessor, in the city of Rouen, whose life shone with miracles and whose precious death in the house of the Lord is daily proclaimed. At Mantua, the burial of Saint John Bonus, confessor, of the order of the Hermit Brothers of Saint Augustine, whose life was illustrious for holiness and the glory of miracles. In the territory of the Amiens people, the glorious martyr Saint Gratian. On the same day, Oda, widow, aunt of Saint Hubert, at the village of Anania on the river Meuse.”

Other editions agree in sense with the first concerning Severinus, Domitius, Gratian, Romanus, and Oda. Then: “At Helnone, the restoration of the body of Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.” Concerning Amandus’s translation, elevation, and so forth, see 6 February, p. 841, and from p. 889 onward. Finally, the same edition has the smaller type concerning John Bonus as above.]

[Col. 0609]

At Antioch in Syria, the birthday of Saint Theodoricus, priest, who, during the persecution of the impious Julian, after the punishment of the rack and many exceedingly harsh tortures, was also set aflame by lamps placed around his sides; since he persisted in confessing Christ, he completed his martyrdom by execution with the sword. In Spain, Saints Servandus and Germanus, who, after scourging, the squalor of prison, the injury of thirst and hunger, and the hardship of a very long journey, finally completed the course of their martyrdom when their necks were struck off with the sword. Of these, Germanus was buried at Mérida, but Servandus at Seville. In the city of Cologne, Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor. In the district of Poitiers, Saint Benedict, confessor.

### Ninth day before the Kalends. The 24th.

[Note: [Col. 0613]

From Herinien., Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0613C]

Molan, as is his custom, writes *Felicis*; Rosweyd, *Apuliae*; I omit other details of this kind. Antwerp-Major reads “of the holy martyrs Felix, etc.,” and before *occisione* the preposition *in* is lacking. There is very great variation in the final member of the entry. Rosweyd, Greven, and Molan read: “Felix died a virgin in his fifty-sixth year,” and this appears the more polished way of writing it. Nevertheless, we preferred the other reading, although less proper, “in the fifty-sixth year of his age,” with Herinien, Antwerp-Major, and the Pratense manuscript, because it comes closer to Ado, in whom the better and more correct reading is: “fifty-six years old.” Antwerp-Major alone correctly reads *Vertavo*; Herinien and Rosweyd have *Vertao*; Greven and Molan, *Vercano*; others, *Vertano*, etc. In our third Pratense copy, the following is added in third place: “In Britain, Saint Maglorius, bishop and confessor.” The Tornacense has: “On the same day, Maglorius, bishop and confessor.” Muneratus places the same saint in another wording, as I shall say below. From nearly all the remaining manuscripts, however, it is sufficiently clear that Maglorius was not recorded by Usuard.]

[Note: [Col. 0613C]

We have already discussed the various saints named Felix more than once and have repeatedly attempted to resolve the doubts that arise concerning them. The Felix of whom we are now speaking recurs on 30 August in our Observations, where he is expressly recorded by Bede—more accurately than by Rabanus on 29 August—and was transferred to this day more accurately still than in the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and their followers.

These are today the words of the Little Roman Martyrology: “At Venosa, Felix, bishop of Tubzoca, and Audactus and Januarius, priests, and Fortunatianus and Septimus, lectors.” Ado preserves precisely the same names of the companions and the same designation of the episcopal see, although he plainly describes the entry from Bede, who nevertheless reads *Audacti* for *Audactis*, and *Septimini* for *Septimi*. What must especially be noted is that, where Bede merely adds in the entry the distance between Tubzoca and Carthage, the Viennese copy, omitting this, inserts on its own authority: “They were honorably buried between Carthage and Utica,” which is wholly inconsistent with the Acts of Saint Felix.

As for Usuard, he contracted his shorter encomium, apart from that omitted circumstance, entirely from the aforementioned Ado, [Col. 0615A] as did Notker, who here again places the Kalends one day too early. Moreover, concerning the day of the martyrdom of these champions, the true names of their companions, their arena, the date, Felix’s episcopate, and matters of that kind, there are many confused and controversial questions, to be examined fully in their proper place. Meanwhile, one may consult Baronius, both in the present Annotation, which requires some correction, and in volume II of the Annals, year 302, from no. 118 onward. From there our Janning, while staying in Rome in 1698 at the request of Cardinal Coloredo, obtained readings to be formed and arranged for the use of the church of Venosa; they were approved and published there in the following year.

Also consult Ruinart in the *Sincere and Selected Acts*, p. 374 onward, and Tillemont, volume V, p. 202 onward. The Acts themselves pleased learned men so greatly that, after Surius and Baronius, they published them again and attempted to make them more accurate: Lucas d’Achery in volume XII of his *Spicilegium*, p. 634, and Étienne Baluze in volume II of his *Miscellanea*, p. 77. They are also said to have been reprinted at Oxford in 1680. Add Castellan’s brief note. All these materials will have to be compared with many other manuscripts collected by us from various libraries, as we shall provide fully in its proper place. For now, it is enough, in accordance with our purpose, to have briefly touched upon the main points.

Martin of Vertou has no author older than Usuard, but it is entirely clear from our manuscripts that he was genuinely recorded by Usuard. Baronius’s Annotation confuses this Martin with the other Martin of Saintes, reported by Ado not on the fifth but on the seventh day before the Ides of December; on that day one should consult Castellan’s observation, as well as the present one, both of which carefully distinguish several Martins.

I find an edited Life of this Martin of Vertou in volume I of the *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 371 onward; it is followed by a Book of Miracles, probably by the same author, and an additional Life and account of miracles is appended. In both places it is assigned to approximately the year 600; hence it is surprising that his Acts should be counted among those considered spurious, as though he were one of the saints who died before Saint Benedict.

The aforementioned Castellan, in the inner margin of his universal Martyrology, writes in Roman numerals that the year of his death was approximately 789. In this he departs very far from Mabillon’s opinion, and on the outer margin calls him in French “saint Martin le seul,” as though by this distinguishing characteristic to separate him from the other Martins. The Acts are preserved among our manuscripts [Col. 0616B] in various forms, which can in due time be catalogued and illustrated together with those cited above.

We have already shown abundantly in the Variants that Maglorius does not at all belong to Usuard’s text. Wandalbert today commemorates “forty and six,” renowned in Rome for military service and holy combat; they belong to the following day.]

[Note: [Col. 0615B]

PRATENSE and TORNACENSE. We have already recounted the passing of both above.

PULSANENSE, reasonably pure in the first announcement, completely lacks the second; this is not unusual in this manuscript.

ANTWERP, MAX.-LÜBECK, UGHELLIAN, ANTWERP-MAX., UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERG, and DANIC: all fail to contain the final part of the entry of Saint Felix and his companions, where the age of the former is indicated; all add at the end: “Also Saint Vitalis,” or, as UTRECHT has it, “Also the birthday of Saint Vitalis.” I think this was taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; for it is not likely that Felix’s companion Vitalis, who is mentioned in the Acts, is meant here.

MUNERATUS is entirely pure in the text and adds at the end: “On the same day in Britain, the passing of blessed Maglorius, bishop and confessor.” Thus the first edition; in the second edition there is added: “Whose body is honored and venerated in the monastery of Saint Maglorius, in the city of Paris.”

CENTULENSE: “In Apulia, in the city of Venosa, Saint Felix, bishop of Tubzoca, and Audax and Januarius, deacons, and Fortunatus and Septimus, lectors, who were brought to completion by execution with the sword. At Paris, Saint Maglorius, bishop and confessor.”

BRUSSELS. It refers here to the African martyrs whom we discussed on 16 October. It reads: “In Africa, the birthday of the holy martyrs Marcianus and Saturianus with their two brothers. During the persecution of the Vandals under the Arian king Geiseric, for the constancy of the Catholic faith they were first beaten with knotted clubs and torn almost to the bones; and although they suffered such things for a long time, each following day they were restored unharmed. Finally, in banishment, with their feet bound behind them to the backs of running chariots, they were ordered to perish together among the thorny places of the forests; and when the untamed horses ran, they gave up their devout souls while praying and singing psalms. The distinguished handmaid of Christ Maxima, a virgin, also suffered with them. Eventually released to her freedom, she afterward became the mother of many virgins of God and grew old gloriously in confessing the truth. At Adrianople, the birthday of the holy martyrs Severus and Dorotheus.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies on the preceding day.

Likewise, in *Nemesia* instead of *Venusia*, a city of Apulia, etc., it is reasonably pure up to: “Of whom Felix, fifty-six years old, a virgin and martyr, obtained a double crown. At Nicomedia, the passion of Saints Felix, Paperius, and Flavianus.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies again here. [Col. 0616B] “At the monastery of Vertou, the burial of Saint Martin, abbot. On the same day, the burial of Saint Maglorius, bishop and confessor. Also Saint Vitalis.” See what was said above.

HAGENOYEN. In the first announcement it is not entirely pure; in second place it records: “In Palestine, the birthday of Saint Hilarion, monk and hermit, disciple of the great Saint Antony, who shone with the spirit of prophecy, suffered many persecutions from unbelievers, and at last, full of good works, departed to the Lord in peace. Blessed Jerome describes his life in the *Life of the Fathers*.” See above, 21 October. The author of this manuscript moves the saints here and there quite arbitrarily. Here is another example from 23 October: “In the district of Poitiers, Saint Benedict, confessor.” Again: “In the territory of the Amiens people, Saint Domitius, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Vertou, Saint Martin, abbot. Also Saint Vitalis, martyr.”

AQUICINCT adds at the end: “Also Saint Vitalis. In the district of Tours, at Lucas castle, Saint Senoch, confessor and abbot.”

DAVERONENSE, after Martin, adds: “Also Saint Vitalis. At Lucas castle, Saint Senoch, confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT: “Evergisclus, bishop and martyr. Maglorius, bishop and confessor. Martin, abbot and confessor. Felix, bishop and martyr, with his companions.”

BIGOTIAN, fol. D, 9: “Saint Frotmund, martyr.” Castellan calls him Fromundus.

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, marked C: “On the same day, Saint Amandus, confessor. Lucianus, Marcianus, and Florus.” Concerning these, see 26 October.

[Col. 0616D] In the VATICAN manuscript, no. 5949, Martin is lacking.

ALTEMPS: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Dulcardus, confessor. Also Saint Fremundus, martyr.”

FLORENTINE, in first place: “In the territory of Florence, in Tuscany, the passion of Saint Crescius, martyr, and his companions. They suffered in the year of the Lord 258 [more probably the following year] under the persecution of the tyrant Decius, at a place called the Hollow Valley, where they rest in a church dedicated under the title of Saint Crescius. Also Saint Vitalis. Saint Macrenius (the name is not correctly expressed), bishop and confessor. Also at Saint Mark’s, the translation of the holy martyrs Senator and Viator, Cassiodorus and Luke, abbots.”

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION begins: “At Cologne Agrippina, the birthday of Saint Evergisclus, archbishop and martyr of the same city, killed with arrows at the city of Tongeren. Through the prayers of blessed Severinus the archbishop, of whom he was first archdeacon, he deserved to hear on high the voices of singing angels. Also at Cologne, the passion of blessed James, bishop of Antioch and martyr, from the company of the eleven thousand virgins.” In Felix and his companions it nearly reproduces Ado. Then: “At Trier, Saint Severinus, first bishop and martyr. Also at Trier, Saint Felix, first bishop.” It is quite pure in Martin. Then: “At Nicomedia, the passion of the holy martyrs Vitalis, Papirius, and Flavianus. At Paris, blessed Maglorius, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Tours, at a castle called Lucas, blessed Enoch, abbot.” Other copies have Senoch. “On the same day, blessed Oda, widow.”

BELIN. In the first edition it resembles ANTWERP and the other manuscripts cited above. In the second it has a pure text, also adds Vitalis, and further: “In the territory of Tours, Saint Senec, confessor. On the same day, Saint Maglorius, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0617B] GREVEN: “At Cologne Agrippina, Saint Evergisclus, bishop and martyr, who, although he suffered on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, is nevertheless more festively commemorated here. In the same city, the passion of blessed James, bishop of Antioch and martyr, from the company of the eleven thousand virgins. At Trier, blessed Severinus, first bishop and martyr. At Nicomedia, Severus, martyr. At Nicaea, the birthday of Saints Vitalis, Felix, Rogatus, Flavianus, Papirius, and Victoria. At Hierapolis in Phrygia, Saints Claudianus, Eucherius, Justus, Victor, and [Col. 0618A] Flavianus. On the same day, or according to others, on the following day, Pope Boniface I, who sat in Rome for three years and was buried on the Salarian Way beside the body of blessed Felicity. He decreed that a slave should not become a cleric, nor be subject to the curia or to any obligation.”

These words are attributed to Ado in Mosander’s edition. It continues: “Bishop Heraclianus. At Trier, Saint Felix, first bishop and confessor. In Britain, the passing of Saint Maglorius, bishop and confessor of Dol, who, succeeding blessed Samson, was renowned for his life and miracles. He was warned by an angel to seek the solitary life; and when, obeying the heavenly command, he had spent many years in this purpose, celebrated for miracles, he learned from the angel, on the vigil of Easter, that his death was approaching, and visibly received viaticum from him. From that day until the day of his calling, unless unavoidable necessity interrupted him, he constantly repeated this verse: ‘One thing have I asked of the Lord; this I will seek,’ etc.

In Ireland, Daluath, bishop and confessor. [Col. 0618B] In the territory of Tours, at Lucas castle, Saint Enoch, abbot. Columbanus, monk. On the same day, the feast of blessed Oda, widow.”

MOLAN describes Maglorius as MUNERATUS does. Then: “Also Saint Vitalis. In the territory of Tours, Saint Senoch, confessor, in the castle called Luchas. Also Saint Evergisclus, bishop of Cologne and martyr, archdeacon and successor of Saint Severinus, bishop. He was born at Tongeren, was a martyr, and was buried there.”

Other editions add: “On the twenty-fourth day, Saints Arethas and his companions, martyrs.”]

[Col. 0613]

In the city of Venosa in Apulia, the birthday of Saints Felix, bishop, Audactus and Januarius, priests, and Fortunatus and Septimus, lectors, who in the time of Diocletian were long tormented by many chains and prisons in Africa and Sicily and finally were brought to completion by execution with the sword; Felix died a virgin in his fifty-sixth year. At the monastery of Vertou, Saint Martin, abbot. [Bouillart, in the margin: In Britain, Saint Maglorius, bishop and confessor.]

### Eighth day before the Kalends. The 25th.

[Note: [Col. 0617]

The Pratense, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and Antwerp-Major manuscripts are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0617C]

In Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck, the phrase τὸ *natalis* (“the birthday”) is lacking at the beginning. Likewise, instead of “one hundred twenty-one,” they read only “one hundred twenty,” and Antwerp-Major agrees with them. The latter writes *Petragoritas* for *Petragoricas*. Again, it changes *Georgius* into *Gregorius*; and, together with two others, writes not *Suessionem* but *Suessionis*. [Col. 0618C] Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck read “they obtained the crown,” omitting “of martyrdom”; Antwerp-Major more simply has “they were slaughtered with the sword and crowned.” Finally, in Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck, *Item* is lacking at the beginning of the final announcement. Minor details have been disregarded, such as *Dionysio*, *presbytero*, *Mineatis*, *Hilari*, *Hylarii*, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0617D]

The first announcement is double or composite. It was initially taken by Bede, as he testifies, from the Acts of Saint Xystus. Some cite the Acts of Saint Lawrence, others those of Saint Hippolytus, but all are speaking of the same persons.

As for the first part, it alone is also mentioned by the Little Roman Martyrology, with all the other material omitted: “At Rome, on the Salarian Way, forty-six soldiers who, having been baptized by Pope Dionysius, were beheaded at the command of Claudius.” Ado took more from the aforementioned Bede and from the Acts themselves, both in this part and in the other; our author reduced both to his customary brevity.

The Hieronymian Martyrologies say nothing of the forty-six, but name Maximus and another 120 soldiers without names, “whose names God knows.” Rabanus, Ado, Usuard, and Notker preserve the number determined by Bede, 121, presumably because Maximus is included among them; but four others from the same company are named individually, with this difference [Col. 0618D]: the one called Theodotius by Bede is called Theodosius by all the others.

Florentius discusses and attempts to resolve with considerable care whatever doubts remain; we shall examine them more laboriously elsewhere. Fronto’s commemoration was first brought into the sacred tables by Ado, and the entire wording of the entry, unless I am mistaken, was taken from those Acts which Bollandus, in the Appendix to volume I of the January Acts, p. 1085, following Bosquet, declares to have been composed by some recent and ridiculous writer not more than forty or so years ago.

Concerning Peter’s Catalogue, it seems hardly doubtful that in book IX, chapter 109, some other abbot Fronto is confused there with our Fronto. Much else in Peter and in other writers is obscure and uncertain, as may be seen in Tillemont’s Commentaries, volume IV, p. 501 onward. For the rest, our Usuard’s entry is merely an abridgment of Ado’s.

[Col. 0619A] Those illustrious twin martyrs of Soissons are recorded by Bede as follows: “At Soissons, the birthday of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian.” Florus added an encomium; Rabanus a longer history from the same source, I think, from which Ado also received his own, though in a different and shorter wording. Our author contracted it further from Ado; Notker more probably from Rabanus.

The memory of these most celebrated champions is older in the Hieronymian manuscripts: “In Gaul, at Sessona or Sesso, Crispin and Crispinian,” with companions added who seem to have been transferred from elsewhere. What age the Acts reflect we shall discuss elsewhere. They were published by Mombritius, somewhat abridged by Surius, and are to be restored by us to their original wording, illustrated, and, if possible, defended against more recent critics.

I find nothing anywhere concerning Miniatus among the older writers, nor can I adequately conjecture from where Usuard received him; for he cannot be thought to have seen the Acts published by Surius, since he speaks of him so briefly. Hilary is no better known among the ancients. I suspect, however, that Usuard possessed some fuller Hieronymian manuscript, such as the Corbeiensis now is, in which alone one reads: “At Gabalum, the burial of blessed Hilary, bishop and confessor.” [Col. 0620A] This is better understood as referring to a district or territory than to a city. In any case, our author undoubtedly borrowed it from there.

See what Baronius and Castellan noted concerning Miniatus; concerning Hilary, no further record, so far as I know, has been handed down. See Motherius’s note.

Wandalbert, who on the preceding day had treated of the forty-six soldiers, today celebrates Hilary last, after Crispin and Crispinian, Chrysantus and Daria. Rabanus also records the latter two today in first place, and Notker after him; they are likewise placed in the ancient calendars of Allatius and Fronto. But our author, following Ado, postponed them to 1 December, as we shall say there.

Here I append Wandalbert’s verses:

> On the eighth, Crispin is joined with Crispinian,  
>   
> Who, having suffered flames, overcame the savage tyrant.  
>   
> We venerate on the same feast (the word *festo* could be deleted) the twin gems of martyrdom—  
>   
> Chrysantus and Daria, newly brought by Christ’s gift,  
>   
> Whom Rome now adorns with a new shrine and tombs,  
>   
> Which (read *qua*) the waters of the Rhine follow through the lofty forests.  
>   
> Here too Hilary shines in the great honor of a bishop.

] [Note: [Col. 0619B]

HERINIEN. Entirely pure throughout the text, it adds its own entry for Rheims: “On the same day, the burial of Saint Celsinus, priest and confessor.” See Castellan.

TORNACENSE. Pure in the first, third, and fifth entries; it omits the second and fourth.

ANTWERP-MAJOR is deficient only in the fourth announcement and is reasonably pure in the rest of the text.

ROSWEYD, in fourth place, inserts: “Also at Rome, Maximus and another 120 soldiers.” It follows simply: “Miniatus, martyr.” Then: “At Rome, the birthday of the holy martyrs Chrysantus and Daria, virgin. After many sufferings which they had endured for Christ, they were ordered by the emperor Numerianus to be placed in a sandpit on the Salarian Way and buried alive under earth and stones.” We have already said that Ado transferred these saints to 1 December.

[Col. 0619C] PULSANENSE has only this: “The birthday of the holy martyrs Chrysantus and Daria, virgin. They suffered at Rome in the time of Numerianus under the judge Celerinus. At Rome, the birthday of fifty-six soldiers. Also, in the city of Gabalum, Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor.” It writes and abbreviates in its own manner.

MUNERATUS writes “the birthday of six thousand soldiers” instead of “forty-six soldiers.” Other matters in the text are not sufficiently exact. At the end: “At Corbeil, Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor.” See Castellan.

GREVEN adds to the text: “At Chartres, the dedication of the church of Saint John the Baptist, and Saint Vincent, deacon and martyr.”

UTRECHT, LEYDEN, ALBERG, and DANIC begin: “At Rome, Saints Chrysantus and Daria, virgin. After many sufferings, they were ordered by the emperor Numerianus to be placed in a sandpit on the Salarian Way and there buried alive under earth and stones. At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the birthday of blessed Boniface I, pope. He decreed that a slave should not become a cleric, nor be subject to the curia or to any obligation.” It might almost be doubted whether this final material is Ado’s. Certainly Notker treats of Boniface, and Mosander also included him; Rosweyd, however, relegated him to an appendix under 24 October. The text that follows in the cited manuscripts is reasonably pure.

LOUVAIN is close to purity, failing only in Fronto’s entry.

CENTULENSE: “In Gaul, in the city of Soissons, the passion of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian, who contended under the cruel examination of Maximian. At Périgueux, Saint Fronto, bishop, sent there from Rome. On the same day at Rome, forty-six soldiers whom Pope Dionysius baptized and who were immediately beheaded at the command of Claudius. In the city of Gabalum, Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor.”

BRUSSELS: “At the city of Soissons, the birthday [Col. 0620B] of Saints Crispin and Crispinian. Under the persecution of Diocletian, after monstrous tortures inflicted upon them by the governor Rictiovarus, they were crowned by being struck down with the sword, having followed blessed Quintinus.”

In Fronto it is also somewhat interpolated from Ado. “At the city of Florence, the passion of blessed Miniatus [Nimetus] under Caesar Decius. At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the birthday of the holy martyr Chrysantus and Daria, virgin. Since they could not be conquered by any kind of torture, at last, by order of the emperor Numerianus, they were buried under earth and stones for Christ. At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the birthday of Saint Boniface, pope, who decreed that no slave or person subject to the curia should become a cleric.” It is reasonably pure in Hilary. At the end: “At Bourges, in the monastery of Ambiliacum, blessed Dulcardus, confessor.” Castellan writes *Amiliaci*, in French *Amblis*.

[Col. 0620C] HAGENOYEN has forty-seven soldiers instead of forty-six and is reasonably pure in the rest of the announcement. It continues: “At the city of Soissons in Gaul, the passion of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian. They were noble by birth and, fleeing from the persecution which Maximian inflicted upon Christians in the East, came to the same city. Since they then had neither food nor clothing, they devoted themselves to the shoemaker’s trade and worked freely for the poor, for those without pay, and for everyone; and they surpassed all shoemakers. Accused out of envy of being Christians, they did not deny it; therefore, under Diocletian, they suffered monstrous tortures at the hands of the governor Rictiovarus, and at last were ordered to have their throats cut with the sword.” Concerning Boniface it has nearly the same as above. It writes *Mymates* for Miniatus. Concerning Fronto and Hilary, see the following day.

AQUICINCT adds at the end: “In the district of Tours, Saint Spanius, martyr.” Others likewise write this, or *Sperani*, etc. Castellan has *Hispadii*, in French *Epain*. “On the same day, Saints Benignus and Beatus with their companions.” See also their vernacular names in Castellan. Then, by a more recent hand: “At Rome, Saint Boniface, pope. He decreed that a cleric should not become … subject to any obligation.” The sense is broken; above you have it complete.

VICTORIN inserts in second place: “Also at Rome, Saint Boniface, pope. He decreed that a slave should in no way become a cleric.” At the end: “Also Chrysantus and Daria, martyrs.”

DAVERONENSE: “At Bayeux, Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor. In the district of Tours, Saint Speranius, martyr.” See under AQUICINCT.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT: “Crispin and Crispinian, martyrs; Boniface, pope and confessor. [Col. 0621A] At Rome, forty-six soldier martyrs. Fronto, bishop of Périgueux.”

CLUNIACENSE and ALTEMPS write, as the AQUICINCT manuscript cited above: “In the district of Tours, Saint Spanius, martyr.”

SWEDISH ROYAL MANUSCRIPT, no. 428: “At Corbeil, Saint Lupus, bishop and confessor.” See DAVERONENSE, etc.

SWEDISH ROYAL MANUSCRIPT, no. 130: “Also at Rome, Boniface, pope. Also Chrysantus and Daria, martyrs.”

VATICAN, no. 5949, lacks Miniatus and Hilary. It adds: “The translation of Saint Bartholomew from the island of Lipari to Benevento.”

FLORENTINE, in first place: “At Florence, the passion of Saint Miniatus, martyr, with his companions, who suffered under the tyrant Decius in the year of the Lord 248.” It was undoubtedly somewhat later. “In Sardinia, in the city of Turris, Saint Gravinius, soldier and martyr, who suffered under the governor Barbarus during the persecution of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian.” In the Roman Martyrology Protus and Januarius are included. See our observation on 30 May. “At Rome, Saint Boniface V, pope, who …” See the material above attributed to Boniface I.

BORDEAUX: “At Angers, the translation of Saint Albinus.” His birthday is 1 March.

LUXEUIL: “The translation of Saint Simeon, bishop and confessor, the most devout pastor of the church of Metz.”

REIMS, SS. TIMOTHY AND APOLLINARIS: “At Reims, Saint Celsinus, disciple of Saint Remigius.”

THE LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION adds to what was already said concerning Boniface: “He ruled the Church for three years.” It further adds: “He also decreed that no woman or nun should touch or wash the consecrated cloth of the altar. He was buried beside the body of Saint Felicity.”

The first and second announcements follow and are reasonably pure. Then: “In Gaul, in the city of Soissons, the passion of the holy brothers Crispin and Crispinian. Since they were most noble Romans, they left Rome to spread the faith of Christ and preach the same faith elsewhere. Wherever they went, no one was willing to receive them as guests; therefore they learned the shoemaker’s trade, so that they might assist the poor. Whatever they earned from their occupation, apart from their food, they distributed entirely to the poor. When it was discovered that they were Christians, they were beaten with clubs and stretched upon racks; their fingers were pierced with awls, pieces of flesh were cut from their backs, and thus they were harassed by various tortures. Under the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, while the governor Rictiovarus was in charge, they were slaughtered with the sword and crowned with glorious martyrdom.” In Miniatus and Hilary it is reasonably pure. Concerning Beatus and Benignus, as in the AQUICINCT manuscript above. Finally: “At Bourges, Saint Dulcardus, confessor.”

BELIN begins with Chrysantus and Daria, approximately as ROSWEYD above. Then: “Also at Rome, the birthday of Saints Marius and forty-six soldiers,” etc. It places Fronto last. In the second edition it adds: “On the same day, Beatus and Benignus with their companions.” Then: “In the territory of Tours, Spanius.” Finally, at Reims, Celsinus, as above.

GREVEN adds at the end: “On the same day, according to Vincent, book 26, the translation of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle from the island of Lipara to Benevento, accomplished in the year of the Lord 808. At Rome, the holy martyrs Maximinus and another 120. On the same day, or according to others on the following day, at Nicomedia, Saints Lucianus, Marcianus, Florus, Heraclius, Tutus, Florinus, Beatus, and Benignus, martyrs, and others with them. In England, the translation of Saint John, bishop of York and confessor. In Normandy, Saint Lupus, bishop of Bayeux and confessor. Marnocus, bishop and confessor. At Bourges, Saint Dulcardus, confessor. Also the translation of the holy martyrs Chrysantus and Daria from Rome to the monastery of Eystia.”

MOLAN, after Peter, adds in another type, from Ado: “When they saw armed men coming toward them, they asked that they might be beheaded first. This is written in the Passion of Saints Sixtus, Lawrence, and Hippolytus.”

At the end, concerning Chrysantus and Daria, nearly as in ROSWEYD. “On the same day, Beatus and Benignus with their companions. In the territory of Tours, Saint Spatius, martyr.” See AQUICINCT. “At Reims, Saint Celsinus, confessor and priest, disciple of blessed Remigius.” Concerning Lupus, as in MUNERATUS. “Boniface, pope, who sat in Rome for three years. He was buried on the Salarian Way beside the body of Saint Felicity. He decreed that a slave,” etc.

Other editions prefix within the text: “Chrysantus, Daria, and Diodorus, priest,” etc. [Col. 0622C] After Peter, the same as above. At the end: “Beatus and Benignus, Spatius and Celsinus,” as above. To Lupus they add “bishop of Bayeux,” etc. “At Bourges, in the monastery of Ambiliacum, blessed Dulcardus, confessor. On the twenty-fifth day, the holy martyrs and notaries Marcianus and Martyrius. At Rome, on the Salarian Way, Boniface, pope.” See above.]

[Col. 0617]

At Rome, the birthday of forty-six soldiers who were baptized together by Pope Dionysius and immediately beheaded at the command of the emperor Claudius and buried on the Salarian Way, where 121 other martyrs were also placed. Among them were four soldiers of Christ: Theodosius, Lucius, Marcus, and Peter.

On the same day, in the city of Périgueux, Saint Fronto, who was ordained bishop at Rome by blessed Peter and, arriving at the aforesaid city with the priest Georgius—whom on the journey he restored from death as his companion through the apostle’s staff—converted a great multitude of that people to Christ and, renowned for many miracles, rested in peace.

At the city of Soissons, Saints Crispin and Crispinian, who, during the persecution of Diocletian, after monstrous tortures inflicted upon them, were slaughtered with the sword and obtained the crown of martyrdom.

At the city of Florence, the passion of blessed Miniatus under the ruler Decius. Also in the city of Gabalum, Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor.

[Note: [Col. 0617] In the Dervense manuscript the entry concludes: “At Reims, the metropolitan city, Saint Celsinus, confessor.” BOUILLART.]

### Seventh day before the Kalends. The 26th.

[Note: [Col. 0621]

Thus the Pratense, Herinien, Tornacense, Antwerp-Major, Muneratus, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0621C]

They stumble over orthography, such as *Aphricam*, *Affricam*, *Rogaciani*, and *Ciprianus*. Antwerp-Major could have been excluded from the number of pure manuscripts, because the entire first announcement of the present day [Col. 0622C] was omitted by the first hand; but since it was subsequently entered in full and is pure, we have assigned it a place here.]

[Note: [Col. 0621C]

Rogatian and Felicissimus are passed over by the Hieronymian copies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, and Wandalbert; they are first recorded by the author of the Little Roman Martyrology in these words: “In Africa, Rogatian the presbyter and Felicissimus the martyr.” What our text further sets out somewhat more fully and elegantly is taken word for word from Ado, with the sole omission of the commendation of the great Cyprian, quoted from his Letter 81 in the Viennese manuscript: “namely,” he says, “that in all things you should follow the presbyter Rogatianus . . . who, together with our brother Felicissimus, always calm and sober, receiving the attack of the raging people,” and so forth. Baronius cites several other letters of the same Cyprian in his Notes, and treats these saints more fully in volume II of the *Annals*, under the year 253, no. 42, and likewise under 254, no. 35; but more explicitly under 209, nos. 59 and 60, where he appears to depart from the received chronology, postponing the death of the saints too far, contrary to the authority of our text. Perhaps for this reason we observe that the names of the emperors have been altered in the modern Roman Martyrology.

Meanwhile, our Martyrologists seem to have drawn chiefly from the aforesaid Letter 81 of Cyprian what they proclaim about the illustrious crown of martyrdom. Whether they do so with sufficient certainty, I would not dare to assert. For, if what Tillemont carefully observes in volume III, p. 389, is correct, it is indeed established that Rogatian and Felicissimus suffered the first assault of the raging people, but not that they ended their lives under torture. Notker uses a different phrase from Ado, but does not hesitate to call them martyrs also. Castellanus, on the other hand, plainly declares that he has found no foundation for that claim. The further controversies concerning several saints named Rogatian—and why not also several named Felicissimus?—whether this Rogatian is the same man of whom Cyprian speaks, and likewise concerning the time of death, the rank and office of each, and other matters of this kind, I reserve for their proper place.

Rusticus of Narbonne is purely Usuardine, being recorded today by no earlier or contemporary authority. Baronius’s note briefly indicates whatever should be observed concerning his life or deeds from the letters of Jerome and Leo; Catellus records nothing more, except an inscription which exercised the minds of many scholars and which we shall examine in full elsewhere.

In Ado, in second place, we read: “Commemoration of the holy bishops Vedastus and Amandus, whose life and death were glorified by very many miracles.” Wandalbert also sings of them on this day:

> The seventh displays the pontiffs, resplendent in fame, signs, and tombs:  
> Amandus by his true name, and Vedastus likewise,  
> United in merits and in time.

Elsewhere we have shown how rightly those two prelates are joined on one day. Notker adds more about Vedastus, formerly a presbyter of Toul, and so forth. Here the Canisian edition of Notker ends, since from this day to the end of the year the remainder is missing. Usuardus, moreover, reproduced the cited words of Ado on 6 February, as we said there, silently passing over both saints here. Most of the more recent manuscripts are also silent about Vedastus; but many remember Amandus, or his ordination, translation, or elevation, and the dedication of his church. I shall now set these out. See what we said on 6 February.

[Note: [Col. 0623B]]

Rosweyd adds at the end: “The natal day of Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.”

The Pülsanen manuscript announces the first entry as follows: “In Africa, the natal day of the holy martyrs Rogatian the presbyter and Felicissimus. Likewise at Thessalonica, Saint Demetrius the martyr.” I think this is the Demetrius celebrated on 8 October. What follows concerning Rusticus is pure.

Antwerp-Major, Lübeck, and Ughellian have nothing about Rusticus; instead, in his place they read: “On the same day, Amandus the confessor.” They append, in the same text, Lucian and Florus, as you will also find on the preceding day.

Antwerp-Major and Louvain, fairly pure in the first place, have in second place: “At Nicomedia, the holy Lucian and Florus.” See their companions in the Hieronymian manuscripts. Ruinart included their Acts among the *Selecta*, beginning on p. 151; his preliminary warning should be consulted there. Then: “On the same day, the elevation of Saint Amandus the confessor.” They are pure in the entry on Rusticus. Finally: “Likewise Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr.”

Utrecht has all the same material, except that it speaks of Evaristus first in this manner: “At Rome, the natal day of Saint Evaristus, pope, who governed the Roman Church fourth after blessed Peter. Crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Trajan, he was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican.”

Leiden and Utrecht agree, but repeat at the end: “Likewise Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr.”

Alberg and the Danish manuscript differ from those immediately above in omitting Rusticus and writing simply, instead of “the elevation of Saint Amandus”: “On the same day, Saint Amandus the confessor.” As though they meant someone other than the bishop of Utrecht.
