Centulen has: “In Africa, the holy Rogatian the presbyter and Felicissimus, under Decius and Valerian. At Florence, blessed Minias, under Decius.” See the text on the preceding day. It continues: “At Ephesus, Saint Polycrates, an outstanding and most noble bishop.” Whoever can determine which Saint Polycrates this is may do so; I know no other bishop of Ephesus named Polycrates except the one who resisted Pope Victor in the controversy over the celebration of Easter and was excommunicated. “At Narbonne, Saint Rusticus, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Elnone, the translation of blessed Amandus, bishop and confessor.”

Brussels begins as follows: “The translation of the body of blessed Amandus, bishop and confessor. He governed the church of Utrecht above the Meuse for three years; then, choosing a hermit’s life, he remained in a certain cell for fifteen years, always clothed in a hair shirt and water,” and so forth. The remainder is missing. The manuscript is defective from this point to 31 October.

Hagenoyen has: “At the city of Périgueux, the burial of Saint Fronto, bishop. He was ordained bishop at Rome by blessed Peter the apostle, together with Gregory the presbyter, whom he restored alive from death on the journey by means of the apostle Peter’s staff as his companion; and, coming to the aforesaid city, he converted a great multitude of that people to Christ. With the Lord [Col. 0624B] Jesus Christ he buried blessed Martha in a cave; her glove and ring remained there, although later they sent back one glove with the episcopal ring, keeping the other there. Finally, after many miracles and salutary teachings, he died in peace. At Rome, the natal day of Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr, who governed the Roman Church fourth after blessed Peter for ten years and seven months. He was a Greek by nationality, born of a Jewish father named Judas, from the city of Bethlehem. He divided the titular churches in the city among the cardinal presbyters and deacons. He established that a marriage should be publicly pledged in the presence of witnesses and afterward blessed by a priest. He was crowned with martyrdom under the persecution of the emperor Trajan and buried beside Saint Peter. In the city of Javols, the natal day of blessed Hilary, bishop and confessor.”

The entry concerning him and Fronto is treated on the preceding day. At the end it has: “At Narbonne, the burial of Saint Rusticus, bishop and confessor.”

Aquicinct, after the confessors, inserts: “The translation of the body of Saint Amandus, bishop, his episcopal ordination, and the dedication of his church.”

Victorin and the Swedish Register, marked no. 130, have: “Likewise Saint Amandus, bishop,” and so forth.

Matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht have: “Rogatian and Felicissimus. Evaristus, pope and martyr. Rusticus, bishop and confessor.”

Cluny and Altemps have: “Lucian, Marcian, and Florus.” Florus treats these with a brief eulogy.

The Swedish Register, under no. 428, has: “On the same day, Florentius the confessor.” Is this the man discussed on the following day?

Codex D. Lemare, marked A, has: “At the city of Nevers, the burial of Saint Trogenus the confessor.” It means Trojecius, called *Troe* in French, who is celebrated on 17 October.

The Vatican manuscript adds: “At Thessalonica, Saint Demetrius the martyr.” See Pülsanen. Perhaps he is celebrated on this day among the Beneventans and in other parts of Italy.

The Florentine manuscript has: “Saint Demetrius the martyr. At Rome, Saint Evaristus, pope. The ordination of Saint Amandus’s episcopate, the translation of his body, and the dedication of his church.”

The Bordeaux manuscript has: “Saint Amandus the confessor, Lucian, Marcian, and Florus.” See above.

The Lübeck-Cologne edition has: “At Cologne Agrippina, in the church of Saint Mary at the Steps, the feast of the arrival of the holy Cross of Christ. At Rome, the natal day of Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr, who, fourth after the apostle blessed Peter, governed the Roman Church for nine years, was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Trajan, and was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican. He established that a marriage should be publicly pledged by the parents and then solemnly blessed by a priest.” See the fuller account in Hagenoyen.

It continues with the Africans, fairly purely. Then: “On the same day, Saint Pelagia the virgin. When a certain noble young man sought her in marriage, she cut her hair, put on men’s clothing, secretly fled, and entered a monastery of highly esteemed monks; there, unknown to everyone until her death, she served God devotedly [Col. 0625A] and finally died happily.” See Greven. The entry on Rusticus is good. Then: “At Nicomedia, the natal day of the holy martyrs Lucian and Florus. Likewise at Nicomedia, Saint Ursa the virgin. On the same day, the translation of Saint Amandus, bishop of upper Utrecht and confessor.”

Belin, in second place, has: “On the same day, Amandus the confessor. Lucian and Florus.” At the end: “At Rome, Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr.”

Greven has: “Jacob the patriarch. Likewise, according to some, Evaristus the pope is commemorated here, but according to Ado and others on the following day. He occupied the see for nine years and was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan; he was buried in the Vatican. He divided the titular churches in the city among the presbyters and ordained seven deacons to guard the bishop while he preached. Demetrius the martyr. At Rome, the natal day of the holy Mariander, Lucius, and Vietus. On the same day, but according to others on 27 October, in Phrygia, the holy Tharsus, Polycarp, Gaius, Metrobius, Eumenia, Januarius, Terreius, Corminius. At Ephesus, Polycarp, bishop [Col. 0625B] and confessor.” If there was a bishop of Ephesus of this name, he is no more honored in the Church than Polycrates, discussed above.

It continues: “Beanus, bishop. The translation of Saint Amandus, bishop of upper Utrecht, confessor. At Cologne Agrippina, at Mary of the Steps, the arrival of a large portion of the holy Cross. At Augsburg, a town in Raetia, the conversion of blessed Aphra, who, when she was a prostitute and had received blessed Narcissus as a guest, was converted by him.” She is celebrated on 5 August. “At Nicomedia, Saint Ursa the virgin. Likewise, according to some, Margaret the virgin, who is also Pelagia. Others have her on the Ides of October.” The matter is confused. In my opinion, she is the same woman who is called Pelagia in the Lübeck-Cologne edition.

Molan has: “On the same day, Lucian and Florus. At Rome, Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr. A commemoration of Saint Vedastus and Amandus, whose life and death were glorious through very many virtues.” In smaller type: “In Gascony, the burial of Ceolfrid, abbot and confessor.” Other editions have material concerning Lucian, and so forth, and also Evaristus as in the first edition. Then: “At Utrecht, the ordination of Saint Amandus’s episcopate; and at the monastery of Elnone, the translation of his body from the church of Saints Peter and Paul to the basilica of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, under the direction of blessed Bishop Eligius; and the dedication of that basilica. At Douai, the elevation of Saint Erminus, bishop. On the twenty-sixth day, a commemoration of the great earthquake.”]

[Col. 0621]

In Africa, the natal day of the holy martyrs Rogatian the presbyter and Felicissimus, who were crowned with illustrious martyrdom during the persecution of Decius and Valerian; blessed Cyprian also writes about them in his letter to the confessors. At Narbonne, Saint Rusticus, bishop and confessor.

## 27 October — 6 Kalends

[Note: [Col. 0625B]]

Taken from Pratensis, Munerat, Greven, and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0625C]]

The principal variation is that many manuscripts, including highly reliable ones such as Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and the rest, either place before or append to the text: “The vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude,” or “of Simon and Jude.” One might doubt whether that announcement is Usuardine, especially since it is set out so expressly in Ado. I would certainly be convinced that it should be attributed to Usuardus if uniformity were maintained in the manuscripts cited; since it is lacking, I have judged the others preferable, as I shall say again on 31 October.

In Munerat, *Abulla* is erroneous; the others generally have *Abula*, although the Little Roman Martyrology and Ado write *Abela*. Perhaps *Christetae* would be better written, but we have followed our manuscripts. Molan transposed the words “of their limbs.” Pratensis reads *Datiano*, which is better, as in the common Munerat, *Daciano*; Greven and Molan have the incorrect *Deciano*. In our Pratensis copy, at the end there is added: “On the same day, the discovery or translation of Saint Vincent the Levite and martyr.” But because these words are underlined, Sirmond’s preface makes it clear that they were added later in the margin.]

[Note: [Col. 0625C]]

Many martyrs distinguished by the name Vincent are frequently commemorated, but perhaps scarcely any one of them has left fewer and less genuine ancient records than this Vincent of Ávila and his two sisters, Sabina or Savina and Christeta. Thus Ruinart calls them in the *Sincere and Select Acts*, p. 389. He may perhaps have seen the Acts in the form in which they are preserved by us, transcribed by Papebrochius from a very ancient manuscript belonging to Canon Joly at Paris. In them they are said to have suffered on 28 October, that is, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November. If he had considered them genuine, he would certainly not have failed to publish them.

The Viennese Martyrologist, however, possessed these or similar materials, since the eulogy appears to have been taken from them; Peter reproduced it in his *Catalogue*, book 9, chapter 114, where he writes *Christina* for *Christeta*, and our author copied the whole account, changing only *Abela* to *Abula*, *Christetes* to *Christetae*, and *supposita* to *superposita*.

If you ask what I think of the Acts themselves, I prefer for the moment to suspend judgment rather than decide anything rashly, although there are sufficient indications to show that they were fabricated, or at least embellished in imitation of other Acts, several centuries after the martyrs’ passion. Tamayus de Salazar, otherwise very accommodating in gathering everything together, therefore thought that a considerable portion of them should be excised. Yet this has not diminished in the least the very ancient and celebrated cult throughout Spain of these illustrious martyrs, whose earliest memory, unless I am mistaken, flows from the Little Roman Martyrology: “At the city of Abela, Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, martyrs.”

Florus also records them explicitly on the following day in these words: “On the same day, the passion of the holy Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, who suffered in the city of Ávila.” The remainder of the eulogy comes from the customary Adonian source, though expressed in different wording. Add Wandalbert, whose metrical eulogy deserves to be read:

> Hence Vincent, fighting as a martyr, adorns the sixth;  
> Christeta likewise triumphs, and the virgin Sabina.

Ado continues: “On the same day, at the fortress of Tyle, the natal day of Saint Florentius the martyr.” These words have been transferred into our calendar exactly, with *Tyle* changed to *Tile*. In Mosandrus’s Ado there is another Florentius, a confessor, concerning whom more will recur in the additions. Since the Hieronymian manuscripts also mention someone named Florenctis or Florentius, they do not sufficiently explain whom they mean.

I ask who might shed some light in these matters of darkness, but so far I find no one, unless we choose to follow Saussay, who recites from memory the place, time, kind of martyrdom, and so forth. Nor do the materials noted among us by conjecture by Rosweyd, if I am not mistaken, provide any solid explanation: he assigns this Florentius to Thebes and places the arena of his martyrdom at Tiel, a town of Gelderland situated on the river Waal. The Belgians readily incline to this opinion.

In my judgment it may be enough to identify a single Theban Florentius in the region of the Rhine, whom we discussed on 10 October. I do not think Tile or Tyle should be sought by the Euphrates, in Pontus, Africa, or Spain, but probably in Burgundy, where it is called *Trichâteau* in French, between Langres and Dijon, as our Motherius examines more carefully in an observation on this day, which the inquisitive reader should certainly consult.

He will deserve great credit concerning our Acts and the saints themselves if he supplies more certain evidence about Vincent and his sisters, as well as about Florentius—more certain, I say, than the Higuerian, Dextrian, and similar fabrications amassed by Tamayus. I would not mention them here at all if the poverty of the purer sources had not compelled me to return to them.

In third place Ado places Pope Evaristus, crowned with martyrdom under Trajan; we treated him at length on the preceding day. Florus also remembers him, but Usuardus entirely omitted him.]

[Note: [Col. 0627A]]

Herinien begins: “The vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.” The rest is very pure.

Tournai, in a pure text, adds: “On the same day, the vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.”

Antwerp-Major also appends to an otherwise pure text: “At Auxerre, Saint Desiderius, bishop and confessor. And the vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.”

Rosweyd inserts in second place: “At Nicomedia, Lucian the martyr.” See the preceding day. The entry on Florentius is pure. Then: “Rumoldus the martyr. See below. Rictrudis the virgin.” He means the nun and abbess who, however, was a widow and the mother of blessed Eusebia; she is celebrated on 12 May. “The vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.”

Pülsanen has: “The vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.” In the second copy the eulogy is missing. The last copy is pure.

Antwerp-Major and Lübeck, pure in the text, also add: “On the same day, the vigil of Simon and Jude.”

Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, and the Danish manuscript all begin: “The vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.” The text is pure.

Alberg adds at the end: “Likewise Saint Yvo the confessor.” Below the translation is given more explicitly.

Centulen has: “The vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude. In Spain, at the city of Elvira, the holy martyrs Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta. In the district of Poitiers, Saint Florentius the presbyter and monk.” This is the man placed in our Martyrologies on 22 September, and whom we said above is repeated on this day in Mosandrus’s Ado; the same also occurs in other Usuardine manuscripts. The various translations of this saint and the various disputes concerning his sacred body could easily have occasioned these different feasts, since he is also commemorated in other months. What if this was perhaps the first translation of his body to Rodium in Picardy?

The cited manuscript continues: “At Auxerre, Saint Desiderius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, at the fortress of Tile, Saint Florentius the martyr. At the monastery of Blandinium, the arrival of Saint Amelberga the virgin.”

Brussels: I have already said that this manuscript is defective through 31 October.

Hagenoyen: Through the copyist’s negligence, 27 October was omitted, and 28 October is prefixed with “the sixth day before the Kalends,” where “the fifth day before the Kalends” should have been written.

Aquicinct begins: “At Rome, Evaristus, pope and martyr. He divided the titular churches in the city among the presbyters and ordained seven deacons to guard the bishop while he preached.” In the same place, instead of *Florentii*, it has *Florentiani*.

Victorin has: “At Rome, Saint Evaristus, pope. He divided the titular churches in the City among the presbyters and appointed seven deacons to guard the bishop. The vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.”

Ambianen has: “In the district of Poitiers, the natal day of Saint Florentinus, presbyter and monk, a man of great holiness and innocence.” In my opinion, the same Florentius is meant as the one discussed under Centulen.

Matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht have: “The vigil. Pharo, bishop and confessor.” See the following day concerning him. “Vincent, Sabula [Sabina], and Christeta, martyrs. Florentius the martyr.”

The Swedish Register, marked no. 130, adds: “At Rome, Saint Evaristus, pope,” and so forth.

The Vatican manuscript adds: “At Rome, the natal day of Saint Evaristus, pope, who presided over the Church for thirteen years and was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan.”

The Florentine manuscript has: “Likewise Saint Gertrude [the Medicean manuscript has *Gertrudis*; or is *Rictrudis* better?], virgin. In Britain, the translation [the Medicean manuscript has ‘ordination’] of Saint Yvo the confessor, a man of great holiness. In Sardinia, at the city of Torres, the holy martyrs and brothers Protus the presbyter and Januarius the deacon, under the governor Barbarus, during the time of Diocletian and Maximian.”

The Reims manuscript of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris has: “In the district of Poitiers, Saint Florentius the presbyter and monk.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins: “The vigil of the holy apostles Simon [Col. 0628B] and Jude.” It then continues with Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, purely. Then: “At the fortress of Tile, the holy Florentius, Heraclius, Florus, and Tutus, martyrs.” This is a confusion of distinct persons. “On the same day, a commemoration of blessed Yvo, presbyter and confessor. At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Desiderius, bishop and confessor.”

Belin, whose text is disfigured by various errors, adds at the end: “Likewise on the same day, the vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude. On the same day, Saint Yvo the confessor of the Third Order of Friars Minor.”

Greven has: “The vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude. At Carthage, the natal day of Saint Suffrasianus” (the first edition is better arranged). “On the same day, Saint Eucharius, bishop and martyr. In Sardinia, the holy Marianus, Protus, and Januarius. In Phrygia, Eumenus and Canon. The translation of Rumoldus, bishop and martyr. In the district of Poitiers, Saint Florentius, bishop.” He means, I think, presbyter; otherwise there would be two Florentiuses of Poitiers. “Desiderius, bishop of Auxerre and confessor. In India, Saint Frumentius, bishop, who, sent there as bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, brought almost all upper India under the faith of Christ and, renowned for his life and miracles, rested in peace. In Ireland, Oranus, bishop and confessor. In lesser Britain, the translation of Saint Yvo the confessor, a lawyer and advocate of the poor. Rictrudis the virgin. On the same day, the discovery of the body of Vincent the Levite and also martyr.”

Molan has: “At Mechelen, the translation of blessed Rumoldus, bishop and martyr. On the same day in Britain, the translation of Saint Yvo the confessor, doctor of both laws, of the Order of Penitents of blessed Francis. At Rome, Evaristus, pope, who occupied the see for nine years. He was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan and buried in the Vatican. He established two presbyters in the City and ordained seven deacons to guard the bishop while he preached. At the place called Marcinas, Saint Rictrudis with her daughter Eusebia. At Blandinium, the arrival of the most holy virgin of Christ, Amelberga’s body. Likewise on the same day, the vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude.” Then, in smaller type: “Which is celebrated with the observance of a fast.” Then: “In India, Saint Frumentius, bishop, who was sent by Athanasius,” and so forth, as in Greven.

Other editions have: “Likewise on the same day, the vigil,” and so forth. Concerning Yvo’s translation, as above. It continues: “At Elnone, a commemoration of the ordination of blessed Amandus. Although it is believed to have taken place on the preceding day, as did the translation of his body and the dedication of the church, it is nevertheless commemorated more particularly on this day.” Concerning Rumoldus, as above. Then: “On the same day, the elevation of the bodies of the holy Eusebia and Gertrude.” Concerning Amelberga’s arrival, as above. Finally, in smaller type: “On the same day, the discovery of the body of Saint Vincent the Levite and martyr.”]

[Col. 0625]

In Spain, at the city of Ávila, the passion of the holy Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta, who were first stretched upon the rack so violently that all the joints of their limbs were dislocated; then their heads, placed upon stones, were beaten with heavy bars until their brains were crushed, and thus they completed their martyrdom under the governor Dacianus. On the same day, at the fortress of Tile, Saint Florentius the martyr. [Bouillart adds in the margin: “On the same day, the discovery or translation of Saint Vincent the Levite and martyr.”]

## 28 October — 5 Kalends

[Note: [Col. 0629]]

Taken from Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, Antwerp-Major–Lübeck, and Greven. Antwerp-Major agrees with Antwerp and Antwerp-Major–Lübeck; Utrecht, Leiden, and Louvain also agree with them.

[Note: [Col. 0629A]]

Some write *Symonis*, but in this name, as also in *Chananaeus* and *Thaddaeus*, I have followed the greater part of the manuscripts. Antwerp, Antwerp-Major–Lübeck, and others have *Thaddaeus*, who is also read as “Judas of James,” as is generally found in Ado. There is greater variation in explaining the apostles’ preaching. Antwerp-Major, after *Simon*, omits the preposition *apud*. Antwerp, Antwerp-Major–Lübeck, and others read: “Of whom Simon preached in Egypt and Thaddaeus in Mesopotamia.” Almost all write *Cirillae*, as in the text. Greven wrote “she was slaughtered and killed.” Herinien omitted “and killed.” Antwerp-Major has “At Paris, Saint Genevieve the virgin” instead of “the translation.” There is no need to add more concerning *Persidam* or *Persidem*, *Faronis* or *Pharonis*, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0629A]]

The celebration of the apostles Simon and Jude is commonly joined on this day in our Latin Martyrologies—for as to what the Greeks maintain, we have not concerned ourselves with it throughout this work. In the Hieronymian copies especially we read: “And the natal day of the holy apostles Simon the Cananaean and Jude the Zealot.”

Florentius considers that more should be read in the *Index of the Apostles*, p. 160, where he gathers the other days on which, perhaps for different reasons, both apostles are commemorated together in those same copies. He further appends two fairly lengthy investigations explaining the doubtful, confused, and complicated matters surrounding the names, surnames, kinship with others, preaching, martyrdom, and other questions concerning these apostles. There are many such questions, and they cannot be settled briefly here. Consult Florentius himself and Baronius’s Notes, as well as Tillemont, volume I, beginning at p. 399.

As required by the purpose of our work, we shall indicate the remaining Martyrologists and, together with them, the source of our text. In Bede we read briefly: “The natal day of the holy apostles Simon and Thaddaeus.” This was almost certainly copied from Rabanus. The Little Roman Martyrology is shorter: “Simon and Thaddaeus, apostles.” Ado in his Martyrology has: “The natal day of the holy Simon and Jude.” But in his *Feasts of the Apostles* he treats the matter more fully, and from there Usuardus evidently condensed his entire eulogy.

Among other things, the Viennese Ado rebukes those who think that the apostle Simon, one of the Twelve, is the same person who suffered crucifixion under Trajan. There are nevertheless some who still defend this and other claims. But, as I have already said, those controversies require another and more laborious investigation and cannot be sketched here superficially.

Finally, hear Wandalbert’s encomium:

> Simon and Jude, outstanding in the fifth place of honor,  
> Whom Persia, receiving them when God sent them,  
> Deserved to bury as faithful patrons in martyrdom and signs,  
> If afterward she had remained a cultivator of the faith.

[Col. 0630A]

The Little Roman Martyrology has in second place: “At Rome, Cyrilla, daughter of the emperor Decius.” Venerable Bede added a few details from the frequently cited Acts of Saint Laurence; these were copied by Rabanus and Ado, without any distinction ever being made between the two Decii. Our author probably took the first part from Ado, the part explaining the martyrdom, while leaving untouched the second part concerning the burial arranged by the presbyter Justinus. Hear Wandalbert on this matter also:

> Born of Caesar Decius, Cyrilla here shines,  
> A virgin with blessed courage, whose father was not Decius.

From these things it is clear that the story discussed in connection with Tryphonia on 18 October had long since gained currency; we shall examine it more carefully elsewhere.

No one except Usuardus remembers Pharo, elsewhere called Burdunus, bishop of Meaux. That distinguished prelate had more than one saint among his relatives. The Acts, published under the name of Hildegarius, were edited by Mabillon in the second Benedictine century, beginning on p. 606, and more briefly by Surius. We possess several versions, both fuller and shorter, which nevertheless do not entirely agree with the published texts. A comparison of all of them with one another will provide material for the investigations to come in our Acts. I have not yet seen the life said to have been written in verse by Fulcuinus. We have this single line from Wandalbert:

> Here too Pharo is honored along the banks of the Matrona.

On 3 January we recorded the illustrious virgin Genevieve, together with Usuardus, on her own natal day. There Bollandus enumerates several other feasts celebrated in her honor, among them this translation, probably carried out by Saint Eligius in the year 630. Usuardus certainly included it, whatever scruple led Molan to reject it among the additions. This is enough for our present purpose; for the rest, see Bollandus and the writers cited by him. There are also more recent authors from whom some details may perhaps be noted in the January Supplement.]

[Note: [Col. 0629C]]

Tournai has the whole text, pure except for the third announcement concerning Saint Pharo.

Rosweyd begins in large red letters: “The natal day of the blessed apostles Simon and Jude.” He then continues: “Of whom Thaddaeus preached in Mesopotamia, but Simon,” and so forth. After this, where they had inserted something, he adds: “Killed by the priests of the temples, they suffered martyrdom,” and so forth.

Pülsanen is more or less pure in the first copy and lacks all the rest.

Munerat is fairly pure throughout; at the end he adds concerning Genevieve: “Whose body is honored and venerated in the monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul, on the mountain of Paris.”

[Col. 0630C]

Molan is otherwise pure but omits, as I said, the final announcement.

Alberg and the Danish manuscript, also fairly pure in the text, add: “On the same day [Alberg: ‘the natal day’], Saint Ferrucius the martyr.” See Molan below. “At the city of Metz, Saint Terentius, bishop and confessor.”

Centulen has: “The natal day of the blessed apostles Simon the Zealot and Jude, who is called Thaddaeus and is written as Judas of James. At Rome, blessed Cyrilla the virgin, who was the daughter of the emperor Decius and whom the emperor Claudius ordered to be beheaded. At Meaux, Saint Pharo, bishop [Col. 0630D] and confessor. At Paris, the translation of the glorious virgin Genevieve, who shone with wondrous virtue and holiness.”

[Col. 0631A]

Hagenoyen, changing the Kalends, writes today as follows:

“7 Kalends of November. In Persia, the natal day of the blessed apostles Simon and Jude. These two apostles are called by other names. Simon is called Cananaean or Zealot”—in which he makes a quite correct observation—“but Jude is called Thaddaeus, and in ecclesiastical history he is called Lebbeus. These two apostles were brothers of James the Less”—at least one of them—“and sons of Alphaeus and Mary of Cleopas. The first of them, namely Simon, preached in Egypt, converted many to the faith, performed many miracles, founded churches, and appointed priests and bishops there. Jude had been associated with the blessed apostle Thomas, and with him converted the three kings who had offered gifts to the Lord in the manger. He cured and converted King Abgarus of leprosy, performed many miracles there, and built churches there. Then, preaching in Mesopotamia and Pontus, he instructed those untamed and beastlike peoples in his doctrine. Finally Jude came into Egypt to his brother Simon, with whom he went to Persia, where they confounded two magicians, Aroes and Arfaxat. They baptized Xertes, king of Babylon, with sixty thousand men, not counting women and children. They remained there for a year and three months, built churches, appointed bishops and priests, converted a large population from error, and afterward were arrested in the city of Swanyr. There they commanded the demons to come out of the idols and to break them, which they did. Then the priests attacked the apostles and suddenly killed them.”

Here he has a compendium of the commonly circulated Acts.

“At Rome, blessed Cyrilla the virgin, daughter of the younger Decius Caesar, who, after the death of her father, became a Christian with her mother Tryphonia; she was beheaded for the faith of Christ under the emperor Claudius. Likewise Saint Fidelis the martyr. Likewise Saint Joseph, son of Jacob, translated to Britain. At the city of Metz, the burial of Saint Terentius, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0631C]

Aquicinct has: “At Paris, the translation of Saint Genevieve.” It is unclear whether the rest is pure.

Codex Ursini, from Rosemberg, has: “At the city of Metz, Saint Terentius, bishop and confessor.”

Ambianen has: “In the district of Poitiers, the burial of Saint Salvius, bishop and confessor, who, while King Theuderic ruled Gaul, full of holiness and grace, obtained the episcopate of that place. His body was transferred to the village of Mosteriol and decently adorned with due honor.” See Castellanus.

Matricular, Carthusian, and Utrecht have: “Simon and Jude, apostles. Cyrilla, daughter of Decius Caesar, virgin and martyr.” Concerning Pharo, see the preceding day.

In the Vatican manuscript, under no. 5949, Pharo and Genevieve are absent, as they are found in the excerpt.

Altemps has: “At the monastery of Monstroil, Saint Silvius, bishop and confessor.” See Ambianen.

The Reims manuscript of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris has: “At Soissons, the burial of Saint Divitianus, bishop and confessor.”

[Column 0631D] LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: The first entry is fairly pure; in the second it adds from Ado: “and was buried by the presbyter Justinus with his mother near Saint Hippolytus.” In Pharo, the text is pure. “In Phrygia, the holy martyrs Tharsus, Polycarp, Gaius, Eminus, Januarius, Terreus, Corminius, and Florentius.” The names are confused with those in the preceding day’s Hieronymian Martyrology. “On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Ferrucius the martyr. The octave of blessed Ursula and her eleven thousand companions, the Virgins.” The translation of Genovefa is pure.

BELINUS, though not entirely pure in the text, adds at the end: “In the city of Cumae, Saint Fidelis the martyr.” See the Roman Martyrology.

GREVEN: “The octave of the eleven thousand holy virgins. Blessed Pharo was brought by his sister, Saint Fara, to despise the world; after his wife Blidechild had been consecrated under the sacred veil, he himself, formerly a count palatine, succeeded his brother, blessed Walbert, in the bishopric of Meaux. Once, as he was passing before a prison and heard the cries of the prisoners, he said, ‘Come out, free men, since you repent,’ and immediately their chains were loosed. Finally, after governing the aforesaid church for sixty-six years in great holiness, he rested in peace. In Lucania, Saints Quintus, Felicianus, and Sancinctus.” See these more fully on the following day. “Saint Ferrucius the martyr. Saint Felix the martyr. At Metz, the deposition of Saint Terentius, bishop and confessor. Bodo the confessor. Likewise blessed Chillenus, who was sent from Scotland by Saint Pharo into the province of Arras; by his sound teaching and the signs of his miracles he won that province for Christ. Among other things, while he was refreshing his body with the aforesaid Pharo, he restored by prayer a glass vessel that had accidentally been broken. The translation of Saint Cunera, virgin and martyr, from the company of the eleven thousand virgins.” See what was said on 12 June.

MOLANUS, after “Chananaeus,” inserts in different type “who is also called Zelotes.” At the end: “At Paris, the translation of Saint Genovefa,” etc., as Munerat has above. “In the city of Cumae, Saint Fidelis the martyr. On the same day, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Lambert the martyr. This dedication was made in the sixth year of the episcopate of our bishop Baldric, by the most holy man of God, Herebert, archbishop of Cologne. Likewise Saint Cunera, virgin, who completed her martyrdom in the town of Rhenen.” Concerning Terentius, as above. “On the same day, the deposition of blessed Dodo the monk, disciple of Saint Ursmarus, bishop.” Other editions, concerning Fidelis and Cunera, agree with the first. “On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Ferrucius the martyr, whom Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, moved by his very celebrated miracles, transferred with great honor to the monastery of Laetantius, which is called Bleidenstadt. At Fama, the deposition of blessed Dodo,” etc. Concerning Terentius, as above. “On the twenty-eighth day, the holy martyrs Terentius and Neonilla, and Saint Stephen of Saba, the holy father and poet.” Here it has Genovefa as in the pure text. Finally: “At Liège, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Lambert,” etc., as in the earlier edition, except that the word “our,” which [Column 0632D] occurs there, is omitted here.

[Column 0629]

The commemoration of the blessed apostles Simon the Cananaean and Thaddeus, who is also called Judas; Thaddeus is said to have preached in Mesopotamia, and Simon in Egypt. Thereafter, entering Persia together, when they had subjected an innumerable multitude of that nation to Christ, they completed their martyrdom. At Rome, Saint Cyrilla, daughter of the emperor Decius, who was slain and killed with the sword for Christ under the emperor Claudius. At the city of Meaux, Saint Pharo, bishop and confessor. At Paris, the translation of Saint Genovefa, virgin.

## IV Kalends. Day 29

[Note: [Column 0631]

From Pratensis, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Munerat, Belin, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Column 0631D]

What has been said about Jerusalem is sufficient. Variants of much the same sort are Narcissi (“of Narcissus”), paciencia (“patience”), hystoria (“history”), Sydonem (“Sidon”), Synodem (“synod”), Senobii (“of Zenobius”), Feliciani (“of Felicianus”), and so forth. Rosweyd transposed the words somewhat; in the Ecclesiastical History it is narrated. [Column 0632D] The difficulty is how Usuard wrote about Zenobius, since, certainly having Ado before his eyes, he read in him: “who was crowned with martyrdom in the persecution of Diocletian”; the Antwerp-Major, Lübeck, Belin, and most of the later copies followed this wording from our manuscripts. Others, on the contrary, have: “who under the final persecution,” etc. It must altogether be said that the alteration was made by Usuard, as we have preserved it in the text. Munerat omitted “blessed” before Zenobius and the preposition “under” before “final.” In the second edition of Belin one finds Lucana instead of Lucania; in both, provincia is absent. He alone writes Hiacinthi, but all the others have Jacincti, except Herinien and Munerat, who have Jacinti, and Antwerp-Major, which has Jacingti. Max-Lübeck omitted the name. In the Hieronymian Martyrology one finds Sanecinti and Sacinti. Whether Hiacynthus or Hyacinthus can satisfactorily be formed from these, I do not determine; here and elsewhere we have adhered to the reading of the best-attested manuscripts.]

[Note: [Column 0633A]

Narcissus of Jerusalem, called “the Great” by some, is entirely distinct from the Narcissus of Gerunda, who converted Saint Afra of Augsburg; he is celebrated by Eusebius in various places, as may be read in Baronius’s notes. But, so that one need not search for scattered material, one will find almost everything collected by Ado in his praise. He received him from the Little Roman Martyrology, as we noted that he did with Alexander on 18 March, when the memory of each was first recorded there in the sacred calendars. Thus, in the very source, one has: “Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, a man commendable for holiness, patience, and faith.” These are almost the words of our text, transcribed from the aforesaid Ado. Papebrochius briefly explains his withdrawal from the episcopate into solitude because of the monstrous slander of wicked men, his subsequent return, and the probable resignation of his office to his successor Alexander, divinely designated on account of his advanced age of one hundred and sixteen years, in the Chronology of the Bishops of Jerusalem before volume III of the Bollandists’ May. Tillemont derives the whole sequence of his life somewhat more carefully from Eusebius and others in volume III, beginning at page 177. Motherius’s note for this day may also be consulted.

According to Eusebius, History, book VIII, chapter 13, Zenobius was a presbyter at Sidon and the most distinguished of all physicians. He was taken to Antioch with Tyrannion, bishop of Tyre, and is said to have died bravely amid tortures after Tyrannion had been cast into the deep sea. The author of the Little Roman Martyrology therefore transferred him from Rufinus in these words: “At Sidon, Zenobius the presbyter and martyr.” From there he passed into Ado, and from Ado into our Martyrology, with the difference of wording noted in the Variants. But the addition made in the modern Roman Martyrology—that he exhorted others to martyrdom—certainly could not have been drawn from the Eusebius cited by us. That exhortation was perhaps taken from the aforesaid text of Ado discussed on 20 February, where we showed that Tyrannion and Zenobius had been incorrectly confused with the martyrs of Tyre.

Among the older Martyrologies, no one mentions either Narcissus or Zenobius, except Wandalbert, who finally sang:

> Here, retaining the fourth, Zenobius adorns.

The final Adonian class is not Adonian, but has been plainly transcribed from the Hieronymian Martyrologies by Rabanus and Usuard, though the names have not been preserved in complete conformity. No one should wonder at this, since the manuscripts themselves contain the variation discussed in the Variants.

Moreover, the martyrs should rightly be assigned to the province of Lucania, not to Lucana or to the city of Lucense, as Florentinius candidly admits, whatever others may dream. The matters relating to this can be read in his work; among other things, he indicates that when Pope Gregory mentions a certain Hyacinthus, he means not this man but another, who was famous in the Sabine territory and was venerated on 9 September, on which day Usuard also speaks of him and his companions. The aforementioned Florentinius is mistaken, however, when he asserts that Usuard wrote Julii instead of Lucii.

Finally, Ado reports: “The deposition of Saint and most blessed Theodarius, abbot,” etc.; but you will not find him in the genuine Usuard, since Usuard omitted this and several other Viennese saints, both here and elsewhere. In Molan’s supplement we shall give the remainder of the Adonian announcement, from which one will gather that Ado commemorates a translation on this day rather than a deposition, although in some of our manuscripts a commemoration of the feast may seem to be recorded here and there.]

[Note: [Column 0633C]

PULSANO, in the first and third announcement, is fairly pure; it lacks the second, concerning Zenobius.

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC add to the text concerning Narcissus, from Ado: “When he saw that on the vigil of Easter there was no oil for the lamps, he ordered the ministers to bring water, and, while everyone watched, the blessed water was changed into oil.” Concerning Zenobius, they write, with the others, “under the persecution of Diocletian,” etc.

CENTULA: “The commemoration of Saint Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, a man commendable for holiness, patience, and faith. At the city of Sidon, Saint Zenobius, presbyter and martyr.”

AGEN: Concerning Narcissus it almost agrees with Antwerp-Maximum, adding: “And in that deed he changed the nature of the elements.” In Zenobius it is fairly pure. Then, from the preceding day: “In the city of Meaux, Saint Pharo, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Ferrucius the martyr. At Paris, the translation of Saint Genovefa, virgin. This translation took place on the preceding day, but is commemorated here. In the province and city of Lucania, the holy martyrs,” etc. “Likewise in Gundabyzavia [perhaps he means in Rugusta of Swabia], Saint Narcissus, bishop and martyr, who converted Saint Afra.” See the Acts for 18 March.

AQUICINCT adds at the end: “In the territory of Vienne, the commemoration of Saint Theuderius the confessor.” Ado reads Theodarius; other manuscripts differ.

VICTORIN and the Swedish Royal Manuscript, numbered 130: “In the district of Vienne, Saint Theudericus the confessor.” In the Swedish Royal Manuscript it is Teuderii.

MATRICULAE–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT: “Narcissus, bishop [Column 0634C] and confessor. Ermelindis, virgin, who left her homeland for the sake of chastity.” See Castellanus.

The VATICAN manuscript, numbered 5949, adds: “At Capua, the commemoration of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor, whose soul blessed Father Benedict saw being carried by angels to heaven in a fiery sphere.” See the following day.

ALTEMPS: “In the district of Vienne, Saint Cauderius the confessor.” Through the copyist’s carelessness, both the place and the saint seem to have been duplicated, although without doubt it is the same Theuderius or Theodarius.

LYONS: “In the territory of Vienne, Saint Theuderius the confessor.”

BORDEAUX: “Saint Terentius, bishop and confessor.” See the preceding day.

LUXEUIL: “In Gaul, in the city of Vienne, the deposition of Saint and most blessed Theodorius, abbot.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION: In the text it resembles Antwerp-Maximum, etc. Then: “At Augsburg in Swabia, the commemoration [Column 0634D] of Saint Narcissus, bishop and martyr. He was sent by God to that city and there converted blessed Afra with her maidens.” This is perhaps inserted because of Narcissus of Jerusalem, with whom he was wrongly confused by Peter in the Catalogue and by others. We have already said that he is treated on 18 March. “In Gaul, at the city of Metz, Saint Terentius, bishop and confessor, a man of admirable goodness, the seventeenth bishop of that city.” See the preceding day. “At the city of Vienne in Gaul, the deposition of Saint Theodore [for Theodarius], abbot. On the same day, the arrival of the heads of the two holy Ewalds, presbyters and martyrs.”

GREVEN: “At Augsburg in Rhaetia, the commemoration of blessed Narcissus, bishop and martyr. In the time of Diocletian, he was sent by God to the aforesaid city; after converting blessed Afra with her maidens, he filled the whole province with the Gospel of Christ, and afterwards endured a glorious martyrdom.” See what we have most recently noted. “Quintus the martyr. Likewise Socioctus. At Xanten, the translation of Saint Victor, commander of the Theban Legion. Apianus, bishop and confessor. Honoratus, bishop and confessor. Abdias, bishop and confessor, who was converted to the faith by the holy apostles Simon and Judas, wrote their passion in Hebrew, and rested in peace. At Vienne, the deposition of the most blessed Theodarius, abbot. In the monastery, the arrival of the heads of the two holy Ewalds, presbyters and martyrs. Aquilina, virgin and martyr. Ermelindis, virgin. Eldetrudis, virgin. Kenneria, virgin.

MOLAN: “At the village of Meldert, Saint Ermelindis, virgin. On the same day, Saint Apianus, bishop and confessor. Likewise Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor. And at the castle called Lens, Saint Vulganus [Column 0636A], bishop and confessor. On that same day, Saint Rictrudis. On the same day, the second translation of blessed Vincent, confessor. In Gaul, at the city of Vienne, Saint Theodarius, bishop and confessor; and his translation to the place called Vallis Rubiana. Dodo the confessor, whose body rests at the monastery of Fama.” Concerning him, again on the preceding day. Then, in smaller type: “In the city of Passau, the triumph of Saint Maximilian, bishop and martyr, and Valentinus, confessor.” Other editions have the same concerning Ermelindis and Vulganus. For Theodarius they give only the deposition, omitting the translation, and more correctly write “abbot,” not “bishop.” “On the twenty-ninth day, Saint Abraham, the holy father. In the monastery of Sonegiacas, on the same day, the second translation of blessed Vincent, confessor.” See what we said about him on 14 July. Again, in smaller type but somewhat differently: “In the city of Passau, the triumph of the holy bishops, Maximilian the martyr and Valentinus the confessor.”]

[Column 0631]

At Jerusalem, the commemoration of blessed Narcissus, bishop, whom ecclesiastical history relates to have been commendable for holiness, patience, and faith. On the same day, at the city of Sidon, blessed Zenobius the presbyter, who was crowned with martyrdom under the severity of the final persecution. In the province of Lucania, the holy martyrs Jacinctus, Quintus, Felicianus, and Lucius.

## III Kalends. Day 30

[Note: [Column 0635]

Only Herinien, Greven, and Molan are found to be entirely pure.]

[Note: [Column 0635B]

I do not discuss the excision and variations of this kind; there are two more noteworthy cases in which the stream differs from the source, Usuard from Ado, namely, when the principal and best manuscripts write Tingitina and Agricolano instead of Tingitana and Agricolao, as the other manuscript expressly read. Many have been excluded from the number of manuscripts pure in every respect, especially the Pratensis, which at the end adds: “On that same day, [Column 0636B] Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua”; and in the margin, what has been struck through in our copy: “Likewise Saint Lucanus the martyr.” These are part of the text in manuscript B. The customary manuscripts Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, and Aquicinct follow this reading, but with a different and fuller wording, so that there can be no doubt that the addition belongs to them.]

[Note: [Column 0635B]

“Almost all the Latin Martyrologies venerate on this day the phalanx of two hundred and twenty anonymous holy soldiers,” says Florentinius. But all those Martyrologies derive from certain copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology, and likewise from the Little Roman Martyrology, which reads: “In Africa, two hundred and twenty martyrs.” From there it passed to Ado, and then to our Martyrology, which transcribed its customary guide. Among the other ancient writers these martyrs are unknown; only Wandalbert, I do not know on what plausible basis, added to the troop of combatants the centurion Marcellus as their standard-bearer, in these verses:

[Column 0635C]

> On the thirtieth, Marcellus, helmeted with the love of Christ,  
> consecrated a century and a double century worthy of heaven,  
> accompanied by two hundred and twice ten martyrs.

These verses, plainly connected by Wandalbert without basis, clearly demonstrate the genuine and authentic Acts of Saint Marcellus of Tangier, published today by Surius, at the beginning of Baronius’s account for the year 298, and more recently edited and annotated among the Selecta by Theodoric Ruinart, beginning at page 311, and translated into French by Tillemont in volume IV, beginning at page 575. Spanish writers relate much about this illustrious martyr; but on what right they claim him as their national saint, or attribute twelve sons, likewise martyrs, to him, will be discussed in its proper place, as will the other matters briefly noted here by Baronius.

The first among the martyrologists to mention Marcellus in this way is the author of the Little Roman Martyrology: “In Tingitana, Marcellus the centurion and martyr.” It is surprising that Ado should compose so meager an encomium, although he seems not to have been ignorant of the Acts themselves. Usuard certainly considered it most suitable and transferred it whole into his text, changing only what has been noted in the Variants.

Moreover, the man called Agricolaus by Ado, Agricolanus by our author, is called Auriculanus by others. Cassianus, who was converted to the faith of Christ on the occasion of this glorious martyr and afterwards crowned with an equal victory, will be treated on 3 December; the aforementioned Ruinart first brought his Acts to light and appended them to the Acts of Marcellus.

No one before Ado entered Serapion of Antioch into the Christian calendars. Usuard slightly abridged Ado’s words. His life, deeds, and writings must be gathered from various passages of the ancients, especially Eusebius, as Tillemont has already done with considerable care in volume III, beginning at page 168. Jerome, On Illustrious Men, chapter 41, should also be consulted, together with the scholia of Aubertus Miraeus there; Baronius drew upon them both in his note here and in the Annals, especially under the year 191.

Felicianus, whoever he was, with his companions, and Germanus of Capua are, in the judgment of Mosander and Rosweyd, denied to Ado. Whether the last is Usuardine, we have sufficiently explained above. In Rabanus there is only Pope Pontianus, whom Florus mentions on the preceding day. See 20 November.]

[Note: [Column 0635D]

PRATENSIS. Concerning it and the other Pratensis manuscript marked B, I have divided the material in the Variants.

TOURNAY, at the end of the pure text: “On the same day, Saint Lucanus the martyr.”

ANTWERP-MAJOR, in the text with the others, adds: “On that same day, Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, whose soul Father Benedict saw,” and then, after some erasures, below the line: “being carried into heaven.” [Column 0637A] Several manuscripts treat the same matter, with this or somewhat different wording.

ROSWEYD, with slightly fuller wording, adds: “On that same day, Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, whose soul Father Benedict saw being carried by angels into heaven.”

PULSANO begins: “The commemoration of blessed Germanus, bishop of Capua.” Then, pure in the first and last announcements, it omits the second.

ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK, and UGHELLIAN, pure in the text, add: “At Toulouse, Saint Saturninus.” In others it is a translation, and correctly so, since in Usuard his commemoration is placed on 29 November.

MUNERAT, at the end: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Lucanus the martyr.”

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOUVAIN, ALBERGEN, and DANIC, also pure in the text, add: “On the same day, Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, whose soul Father Benedict saw being carried into heaven.” [Column 0637B] Almost as above.

CENTULA: “At Capua, Saint Germinus, whose soul Saint Father Benedict saw being carried by angels to heaven in a fiery sphere. In the province of Lucania, the holy martyrs Jacinctus, Quintus, Felicianus, and Lucius.” From the preceding day. “On the same day, Saint Lucanus the martyr. In the city of Tingitana, Saint Marcellus the centurion, who was beheaded for Christ.”

AGEN: “In Africa, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Rogatianus the presbyter and Felicissimus [for Felicissima], who under the persecution of the emperors Decius and Valerian were crowned with an illustrious martyrdom. Blessed Cyprian also writes about them in his letter to the confessors.” This manuscript often confuses the order of the calendar, assigning saints on various days according to its own inclination, although it nowhere finds them recorded elsewhere in that manner. Concerning these martyrs, see above, 26 October. It continues: “Likewise Theodegarius the confessor.” One might think this is Theodarius, who was mentioned on the preceding day; but later it writes: “At Vienne, Theodore the abbot.” It gives three fairly pure texts of the announcement. Then: “At the city of Regensburg in Bavaria, the deposition of Saint Wolfgang, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, a man commendable in every respect; his soul Saint Benedict the abbot, father of the black monks, saw being carried into heaven by angels, as blessed Gregory says in the second book of the Dialogues.” Add chapter 35.

AQUICINCT, after the text, adds: “On that same day, Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, whose soul Father Benedict saw being carried into heaven. On the same day, Saint Gervasius the martyr.” Others mark this as a translation, and rightly, since the true day of his commemoration is 19 June.

VICTORIN and the Swedish Royal Manuscript, numbered 130, at the end: “At Toulouse, Saint Saturninus. At Capua, Saint Germanus the bishop. And Maximus the martyr.”

DAVERON: “At Toulouse, Saint Saturninus the martyr.” See above, Antwerp, etc.

MATRICULAE–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT: “Germanus, bishop of Capua [Column 0637D]. Serapion, bishop and confessor. Jero, martyr at Egmond.” See 17 August in the supplements. Then: “The two hundred and twenty holy martyrs.”

BIGOTIAN, marked P. 5: “At Toulouse, Saint Saturninus the martyr.” Concerning him, see above repeatedly.

CLUNIAC: “On the same day, Saint Gervasius the martyr.” See the Aquicinct manuscript.

The Swedish Royal Manuscript, numbered 428: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Lucanus the martyr. In the city of Capua, Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor,” etc., as we have often reported from other manuscripts.

[Column 0638A] Manuscript D of Du Cheval, marked C: “At Toulouse, Saint Saturninus the martyr. On the same day, Saint Genesius the martyr.”

ALTEMPS: “On that same day, the ordination of our most holy bishop and patron Swithinus.” See 2 July. From this it is rightly inferred, I think, that this Usuardine manuscript was augmented in England and belonged to the church of Winchester.

FLORENTIN: “At Toulouse, the commemoration of Saint Saturninus, a man most distinguished in virtue.”

CAUDIAC: “The translation of Saint Gervasius the martyr.” Better than the others above.

REIMS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris: “At the city of Toulouse, the translation of the body of Saint Saturninus, bishop and martyr.”

LÜBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins: “The octave of the deposition of the most holy father Severinus, archbishop and confessor.” A fairly pure text follows. Then: “On the same day, Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor of Capua; his soul Saint Father Benedict [Column 0638B] saw being carried into heaven. He, namely, freed Paschasius, archdeacon of the Roman Church, from purgatory by the saving sacrifice. Likewise on that day, Saint Theonestus, bishop and martyr. At the city of Troia, which is called Xanten, the translation of Saint Victor the martyr.”” This is certainly Victor, whose commemoration with seventeen companions was discussed above on 10 October.

BELIN, at the end: “At Toulouse, Saint Saturninus. On the same day, Germanus, bishop of Capua, a man of great holiness.”

GREVEN: “At Nicomedia, Saints Kalendion, Marcialis, Theophilus, Januarius, Peter, and Mark.” See the Hieronymian Martyrology. “Likewise Felicianus and his companions, martyrs. Eusebius the martyr. On that same day, the commemoration of Saint Theonestus, bishop and martyr, and his companions. Jero the martyr. Lucianus the martyr. The translation of blessed Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse and martyr. Germanus, bishop and confessor of Capua, whose soul Saint Father Benedict saw being carried into heaven. He freed Paschasius, archdeacon of the Roman Church [Column 0638C], from purgatory by the saving sacrifice. Talaricanus, bishop. In Dacia, Theotgarus the confessor. At Terracina, a city of Campania, Saint Leontius, a consular official and confessor. Concerning him it is read in the Acts of blessed Caesarius that, believing in his confession, he covered the holy martyr who was naked with his own cloak. After being baptized, when he had received Holy Communion, he gave up his spirit. Likewise Dorothea of Prussia, of blessed memory, an enclosed woman.”

MOLAN, after “most distinguished,” adds in smaller type: “Of whom Eusebius speaks in the Ecclesiastical History, book V, chapters 19 and 22, and book VI, chapter 1.” Then, in italics: “At Cagliari, a town in the province of Sardinia, the commemoration of blessed Saturninus the martyr, who was beheaded with the sword under the persecution of Diocletian. On the same day, Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, a man of great holiness. On the same day, the feast of Saint Lucanus the martyr. The translation of Saint Victor, our patron,” again in smaller type, “in the city called Xanten. At Terracina in Campania,” etc., as in Greven. Other editions have: “At Paris, the feast of Saint Lucanus the martyr.” Concerning Saturninus of Cagliari and Germanus of Capua they resemble the earlier edition. Then: “At Altinum, the commemoration of Theonestus, martyr and bishop, who began preaching the true faith at Mainz and saw Albanus slaughtered by the Arians. In Denmark, Saint Theodgarus the confessor, who, by preaching the word of life and devoutly celebrating the hours, Masses, and other offices, served the heavenly King in place of the earthly King Olaf. On the thirtieth day, Saints Zenobius and Zenobia, martyrs. At Xanten, the translation of Saint Victor.”]

[Column 0635]

In Africa, the commemoration of the holy martyrs, numbering two hundred and twenty. In the city of Tingitana, the passion of Saint Marcellus the centurion, who completed his martyrdom by beheading under Agricola, acting in place of the prefects of the praetorium. At Antioch, Saint Serapion, bishop, most distinguished for learning. [Bouillart adds in the text: [Note: [Column 0635] “We acknowledge that Lucanus was added at the edge of the manuscript. In the case of Germanus, it is in the first hand. BOUILLART.”] And in the margin, in cursive script: “And Saint Lucanus the martyr.”]

## The day before the Kalends. Day 31

[Note: [Column 0639]

From Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, Munerat, Belin, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Column 0639A]

Concerning Sollemnitas, Sixtus, and similar matters, enough has been said elsewhere. Munerat uses nativitas instead of natalis, and likewise has “deacon and martyr.” Belin substitutes Lucina for Lucilla. The reading should be as the text has it: since they could in no way be turned away from the faith of Christ. In Munerat it is corruptly printed “who turns with the faith of Christ,” etc.; in Antwerp-Major the verb has been changed to “who could not be separated from the faith of Christ.” The same manuscript writes this under the Augustan Kalends, on the eighth day. Greven and Molan [Column 0640A] have hic tamen instead of hic autem; Belin has the worse reading: “Nevertheless, the solemnity of these same people is considered more venerable.” Almost all read Virmandensi with Ado; Antwerp and Max-Lübeck have Viromandensi; Belin, Viromadensi. Herinien, Tournay, Antwerp, Max-Lübeck, and Belin, not improperly in my judgment, write “His body,” etc.; I have nevertheless preferred the reading of the others. Belin has revelante Domino instead of revelante angelo.]

[Note: [Column 0639A]

The Vigil of All Saints is genuinely and purely Usuardine, for neither Mosander nor Rosweyd thinks it should be attributed to Ado. Here one may rightly doubt, as I also noted above, whether Usuard omitted the vigil of the holy apostles Simon and Judas, expressly placed by Ado, while placing before his text this vigil, found nowhere among the older authorities. Nevertheless, our manuscripts clearly show that this is how the matter stands, both on 27 October and on this day.

We have observed more than once elsewhere, especially on 2 August, that the Acts of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, are a rich mine from which various saints commemorated on various days may be extracted. Among them are those commemorated today, Nemesius the deacon and his daughter Lucilla. The author of the Little Roman Martyrology first began to include them in the sacred records; his sole announcement for today is: “Nemesius the deacon and Lucilla his daughter suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of September”—so it is written—“but were buried on the day before the Kalends of November by Pope Sixtus.” These details are taken from the aforementioned Acts of Saint Stephen. Ado composed a fuller summary of them, and our author drew from it everything that he adapted to his customary brevity.

See the cited Acts in Baronius’s Annals under the year 259, beginning with number 8, and, in the section concerning these martyrs, number 22; also in Surius, 2 August. Modern scholars generally do not consider those Acts authentic or wholly uncorrupted. I certainly do not see why Tillemont, when discussing Pope Stephen in volume IV, beginning at page 28, should have thought—indeed, I do not see why he should have thought—that this Nemesius and his daughter Lucilla, baptized by the holy pontiff, ought to be passed over in silence above all others. The matter deserves longer reflection, and we shall therefore discuss it more fully in the larger work under 2 August.

The famous martyr Quintinus is recorded in the Epternacensis and Corbeiensis Hieronymian Martyrologies at Augusta Viromandorum. But how the copyist of the Florentinian manuscript could aptly derive Quirinus in Italy from this, I cannot imagine. Bede, and Rabanus after him, do not distinctly state the place; Ado records it, making the remaining words of Bede his own, while Usuard rejoices in the spoils of both.

I do not know why Rabanus gave fifty-two years instead of the fifty-five years after which the body is said to have been found. Anyone wishing for a longer encomium should consult Florus, who has abridged much from the Acts. But he should rather consult the source in Surius for this day; although later critics do not consider it entirely clear or free of dregs, they at least do not deny that it breathes great antiquity and approaches the original purity. Among them Tillemont has expressed the substance of the Acts quite clearly in volume IV, beginning at page 433; other writers are listed there, whom we shall examine more carefully in their proper place.

Wandalbert celebrates Quintinus in this metrical eulogy:

> On the preceding day they celebrate the feast of blessed Quintinus,  
> Who, victorious in a remarkable and varied struggle for Christ,  
> Brings October to its close as it falls in the enclosed sphere.

] [Note: [Column 0639C]

TOURNAY lacks the eulogy of Nemesius and Lucilla; otherwise it is entirely pure.

ROSWΕYD adds at the end: “On the same day, Saint Foillanus the martyr.” Others generally write Foillanus. Castellanus prefers Fullanus, French Foignan, whose relics he says are honored at Péronne. “Likewise Saint Wolfgang, confessor.”

PULSANO omits the entire eulogy in the second announcement. In the entry for Quintinus it is mutilated, for what occurs in the text after “he suffered” is missing.

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, and LEYDEN add at the end to the fairly pure text: “At Fosses, the commemoration of Saint Foillanus the martyr. Coming from Ireland to visit his brother Ulcanus, who governed the church of Fosses [others: Fossense], he was martyred in the forest now called the Carbonaria.”

LOUVAIN has the same concerning Foillanus, but expunges the entire eulogy of Nemesius and Lucilla.

ALBERGEN and DANIC resemble Antwerp-Maximum, [Column 0639D] etc., except that between Quintinus and Foillanus they insert: “At Regensburg, Saint Wolfgang [DANIC: Wolfgandus], bishop and confessor.”

CENTULA, written in a later hand in the margin: “The Vigil of All Saints.” In the text: “At Rome, blessed Nemesius the deacon and his daughter Lucilla, virgin. Saint Stephen the pontiff baptized them. In Gaul, in the town of Vermand, the passion of Saint Quintinus, a man glorious in birth, faith, and martyrdom. In the territory of Liège, Saint Foillanus, monk and martyr.”

BRUSSELS, after the lacuna mentioned above, is still incomplete today; nevertheless, I think the text was fairly complete. What is added to it follows: “In Macedonia, the commemoration of Saints Vitalis, Peter, Crescentius, and Alternus. And the commemoration of Saint Eusebius the martyr, whose passion is recorded. At Regensburg, Saint Wolfgang, bishop and confessor. Likewise Saint Rictrudis, virgin.” Concerning her, see the Supplements under 29 October.

AGEN has nothing concerning the vigil. In Nemesius and Lucilla it is fairly pure. Concerning Foillanus it reports almost the same as Antwerp-Maximum, etc., above. Concerning Quintinus it is somewhat fuller, as follows: “In Gaul, in the city of the Viromandenses, the passion of Saint Quintinus the martyr, who was crowned under the emperor Maximian [the words are supplied]. This Quintinus was a Roman citizen and noble by birth. He preached in the city of Amiens [for Ambianensis] and performed many miracles. Therefore, by order of Maximian, he was cruelly beaten and committed to prison; but he was released by an angel, preached again, was captured again, tortured on the rack until his sinews were torn, and beaten with raw nerves. He endured boiling oil, pitch, and fat, and mocked the governor. Because of this, the governor threw lime, vinegar, and mustard into his mouth. The captive martyr of God was taken to the city of the Viromandenses, where two nails were driven from his head to his thighs, and ten more were struck through his flesh between his fingernails; finally, he was beheaded.”

AQUICINCT, after “it was found,” adds from Ado: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of July.”

CODEX URSINI of Rosemberg: “At Regensburg, Saint Wolfgang, bishop and confessor.” The name should properly be formed as Wolfgangi, as above.

MATRICULAE–CARTHUSIAN–UTRECHT: “The Vigil of Quintinus and Foillanus, martyrs.” The conjunction is foolish; but concerning the first alone it continues: “After many tortures, Quintinus was finally beheaded; after fifty-five years he was found with his body incorrupt and fragrant.”

ALTEMPS: “At the monastery of Glasgow, Saint Benignus the confessor. He faithfully departed to the Lord after an excellent manner of life.”

## Lubeck–Cologne Edition

In the vigil and in the notice of Nemesius it is sufficiently pure; concerning Quintinus it reads as follows:

> “In Gaul, in the town of Viromandis, [Col. 0641B] the feast of Saint Quintinus the martyr. He was beheaded under the emperor Maximian, while Rictiovarus was governor, after various tortures, and his body was submerged in the river Somme. Nevertheless, after fifty-five years, when an angel revealed the place, it was found and buried on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. At Fosses, the feast of Saint Foillanus the martyr. He came from Ireland,” etc., as above in ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others; it continues:

> “At Cologne Agrippina, the burial of blessed Neitburg, virgin. She now rests, having been translated, on Mount Saint Beatus, near Confluentes. At the city of Regensburg, Saint Wolfgang, bishop of that city and confessor, renowned for many miracles.”

### Greven

> “Foillanus, bishop and martyr. In Macedonia: Vitalis, Peter, Crescentius, Alternus.” See the Hieronymian Martyrology. “Eusebius the martyr, whose acts are preserved. And the passion of Saint Philip. Romanus, priest. Vincentius, deacon. At Regensburg, Saint Wolfgang, bishop and confessor. He was born of the noble blood of the Suebi. Ordained a cleric at Trier, he abandoned the pomp of the world and assumed the monastic habit. Afterwards, having been made a priest by Saint Udalric of Augsburg, and with the approval of Otto II, he was appointed the eleventh bishop of the Church of Regensburg. Illustrious in life, teaching, and miracles, he rested in the year of the Lord 994. At Cologne Agrippina, the burial of blessed Neitburga, virgin. Born of the noble blood of the Franks, she shone in holiness in the time of Pepin. To commend her merits, two lights sent from heaven were seen standing beside her funeral bier. She now rests on Mount Saint Beatus, in a monastery of the Carthusian order near Confluentes. Begha, virgin.” See Castellanus.

### Molanus

> “At Fosses, the feast of Saint Foillanus, bishop. Coming from Ireland to visit his brother, who governed the Church of Fosses, he was martyred in the forest now called the Carbonaria. His life is illumined by glorious virtues and very numerous miracles. On the same day, Saint Wolfgang, bishop and [Col. 0642B] confessor, at Regensburg. Also Saint Eusebius the martyr.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “whose acts are preserved. At Cologne Agrippina, the burial of blessed Neitburga, virgin, who was born of the noble blood of the Franks,” etc., from Greven.

Other editions, not entirely identical with the earlier one, read:

> “At Fosses, the feast of Saint Foillanus, bishop, who came from Ireland to his brother Ultanus, who governed the Church of Fosses; and in the forest which in the rustic language is called the Carbonaria, he was martyred. His life is illumined by virtues,” etc., as above.

> “At Regensburg, Saint Wolfgang, bishop and confessor. At Cologne, Saint Neitburga, virgin, who, having been translated, rests near Confluentes, on Mount Saint Beatus. Also Saint Eusebius the martyr. On the thirty-first day, the holy Apostles Stachys, Amplias, and their companions. And Saint Epimachus the martyr.”

I think that this is the companion of Alexander, whom we shall discuss on 12 December. His acts, embellished by Metaphrastes, are found in Surius.

## [Col. 0637]

### Vigil of All Saints

At Rome, the feast of blessed Nemesius, deacon, and Lucilla, his daughter. Since they could in no way be bent away from the faith of Christ, they were beheaded by order of Valerian and Gallienus on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. Their solemnity, however, is held in greater honor when their bodies were more honorably buried by blessed Sixtus on the Appian Way. In Gaul, in the town of Virmandis, Saint Quintinus, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Maximian; his body was found after fifty-five years, when an angel revealed the place.

## The month of November has thirty-one days

---

## [Col. 0641]

### On the Kalends. Day 1

#### Note: [Col. 0641]

This is how the first edition of Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus read it. Many other codices come very close, as will become clear below.

#### Note: [Col. 0641C]

Muneratus is generally full of errors. Here, at the beginning, he adds “of the Virgin Mary.” Greven has *very severely* instead of *the most severe tortures*. In the three editions cited, the reading is *perforari* (“to be pierced through”); nevertheless, following Bede and Ado, I retained *forari* (“to be pierced”), as found in the others. Molanus always corrects *Parisius* to *Parisiis*. [Col. 0642C] The remaining errors of Muneratus are these: instead of *a Terentio* (“by Terentius”), he reads *ea* (“these things”); instead of *custodia* (“custody”), he has *custodi* (“to the guard”). He adds the title “bishop” to Marcellus. Then: “the monk from Bithynia.” Also: “Mary, virgin and martyr.” Finally, he has *Vuastensi* instead of *Vuastinensi*.

[Col. 0643A] We were compelled to exclude our best codices from the number of the pure ones, especially the Pratense, because the text has erased the entry for Mary of Neocorus (Neocorensis), which here stands sixth, leaving an empty space, as the distinguished Castellanus testifies. He also observed that she had been rejected to 21 November, where another entry had been inserted for her. The usual companions of the Pratense follow: ANTUERP.-MAJ. and Rosweyd; both likewise lack the aforementioned notice. Indeed, in ANTUERP.-MAJ. the monk Severinus is also absent. The aforementioned codices have this further peculiarity: they begin the second member of the first notice with “The third Gregory,” whereas all the others read indefinitely, “But also Gregory”; the middle-grade codices, however, more accurately identify Gregory IV. In the Herinian codex, otherwise exceedingly pure, the encomium of Marcellus has been altered, as will be seen below.

#### Note: [Col. 0643A]

The first notice here concerning the feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of All Saints is not to be sought in the ancient calendars or in the Hieronymian Martyrology. We began to discuss its first institution, or the transformation of the Pantheon into a Christian church, together with the *Romanum parvum*, on 13 May. From that same Martyrology one should derive the somewhat more distinct outline of today’s solemnity:

> “The feast of the Saints, which is celebrated as a solemn and general feast at Rome.”

It does not say that it was celebrated generally throughout the Church, but only at Rome. Thus the author of that Martyrology shows that he was writing at a time when the aforesaid feast, instituted in the city itself by Gregory III—who sat from the year 731 beyond 740—was being celebrated with greater festivity. From this we derived the chronology of the *Romanum parvum* in chapter 2 of the preface. Concerning the same feast, see the notes of Baronius on 13 May and 1 November, but especially the observations of Fronto on the Calendar, beginning on page 142.

Our Bede reads today: “The feast of all the Saints” in the first place; but since these words are set down by Rabanus in a very different manner and order, it is doubtful whether they were really marked by Bede or Florus. Ado’s account is clearer; our author abridged it, without explicitly specifying Gregory III, which specification is wrongly inserted in the Pratense and its companion codices. For the extension of the feast to the universal Church is thought to have been secured not by Gregory III but by Gregory IV, a full century later. Accordingly, we correctly said in the Variants that the name of Gregory IV had been better inserted by the middle-grade codices, although it is not Usuardine.

Concerning Benignus of Dijon, or, as others call him, the first apostle of Burgundy, the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in Florentinius, speak together with Bede; from Bede, Rabanus and Ado do so as well. They all have the same encomium, which the latter somewhat shortened, while Usuard reduced it to much less. The *Romanum parvum* says nothing about Benignus; and where Ado has five commemorations, only three are found in the other work. From this alone one might infer that the author of the *Romanum parvum* was an excellent abbreviator of Ado.

Gregory of Tours discusses Benignus in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 51. What Henschenius thought of the published acts, and of those which we shall later publish, can be seen under 1 May, in the entry on Andeolus, page 35. See also our observations above on that day.

In the Hieronymian Martyrologies there is a group of several Terracinenian martyrs and virgins, concerning whom Florentinius argues. All the other Martyrologies mention only Caesarius and Julian, as does Rabanus from Bede, and in our series the *Romanum parvum*, Ado, and Usuard. Their encomia agree, having been drawn from those same acts, which Ferrarius, in Florentinius, noted should be corrected from Baronius. There are some who think that rather more could be demanded. The calendars of Allatius and Fronto, as well as Menard’s Sacramentary, mention Caesarius alone separately. Whether this Caesarius should be counted as a second person, or at least distinguished from the one whom Baronius placed here, must be investigated by the one who will examine our manuscript acts.

Marcellus follows in the text; on this day he was first recorded by Usuard—by Usuard, I say, in accordance with the wishes of our codices, for he is not known to the earlier or contemporary martyrologists. Why he is reported in another edition of Muneratus and by others on 3 November I do not discuss here; nor do I address the question concerning Fortunatus, the author of the Life or Miracles of Saint Marcellus. On that matter I prefer, for the present, to remain with Gerard du Bois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, part I, page 46, rather than publish uncertain conjectures. The Life itself, of whatever kind, will in due time be carefully illuminated from this author and others, but especially from our manuscripts.

The monk Severinus, received by Ado from the *Romanum parvum* or from Bede, was transferred by Usuard in nearly the same words. What the “monuments of his Church” cited by Baronius may be, I do not yet know; if anything concerning him survives, it will be given in its proper place.

Mary of Neocorus (Neocorensis), excluded here by the Pratense and its companion codices and transferred elsewhere, is certainly Usuardine according to the others. She was drawn from the customary Viennese source, with an encomium composed in Ado’s words and taken from ancient acts which, in Vincent, Mombritius, and others, are incomplete and mutilated, but were more recently published in full by Baluzius in volume II of the *Miscellany*, beginning on page 115, with several observations added from page 491. We shall discuss more about these elsewhere. The same Mary seems to be indicated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, as Florentinius concludes, although, unless I am mistaken, he was confused about the place of her martyrdom.

Vigor of Bayeux and Maturinus are likewise purely Usuardine, unless Rosweyd was mistaken when he relegated Vigor to Ado’s appendix. The Life of the former should be compared in Surius with our manuscripts and with what Cointius reports under the year 530, page 365. More than one Life of Maturinus is found among our materials, and these too must then be illuminated.

From the following verses of Wandalbert you will understand which of so many saints commemorated on this single day he omitted, and how much he sang metrically:

> November is marked first on its brow by Caesarius,  
>   
> Whose splendid triumph fills Rome with joy.  
>   
> This month too, surpassing the others with starry crown,  
>   
> Joins all the saints together in a single honor,  
>   
> Whom the heavenly kingdom alike receives and cherishes.

#### Note: [Col. 0643D]

PRATEN. lacks, as we have already said, the entire notice concerning Mary. Its usual companions, ANTUERP.-MAJ. and ROSWEYD., are similar; the former also lacks Severinus, while the latter is not free from several minor blemishes.

HERINIEN. would be entirely flawless throughout the text, except that it has attached to Marcellus another encomium:

> “Whose illustrious life the bishop Fortunatus admirably describes through virtues and miracles.”

TORNACEN. is pure in the first notice; in the second the encomium is lacking; it lacks the third, fifth, sixth, and seventh entries. In the case of Marcellus it agrees with HERINIEN.

PULSANEN., reasonably pure in the first notice, continues:
