> “In Campania, in the city of Terracina, the holy martyrs [Col. 0644D] Caesarius, deacon, and Julian, priest.”

Everything else is absent.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. are pure throughout the text, but at the end they add:

> “At the city of Poitiers, Saint Hilary the confessor.”

ANTUERP.-MAX. ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG., and DANIC. deserve to be counted among the pure ones; but some things have been altered in the text, such as “Gregory IV,” and the end of the notice has been transposed. Likewise, the third notice has been placed before the second, and several other things are not sufficiently exact.

LOVANIEN. agrees entirely with the preceding codices, but lacks the encomium of Saint Benignus.

CENTULEN.:

> “The feast of All Saints. In Burgundy, at the castle of Dijon, the passion of Saint Benignus, priest [Col. 0645A] and martyr. At Terracina, Saint Caesarius, deacon and martyr. At the city of Bayeux, the burial of Saint Vigor, bishop and confessor, whose body, translated by divine direction to Ponthieu, has been celebrated with great love and honor in the church of Saint Richarius. On the same day, the passion of Saint Mary, virgin, who, though she was a slave, and could not be induced to eat food sacrificed to idols, completed her martyrdom through many afflictions. At Paris, the burial of Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor. Also Saint Severinus, monk, from the city of Tibur. In the district of the Vexin, Saint Maturinus the confessor.”

BRUXELLEN., somewhat interpolated in the first notice, treats second of Caesarius and Julian. After *maceratus* (“tormented”), it inserts from Ado:

> “For when he had reached the temple of Apollo, at his prayer the temple itself fell and killed the priest named Firminus; and afterwards, together with the same Julian,” etc.

It also adds something concerning Benignus, namely:

> “He was sent with Andochius, a fellow priest, and Thyrsus, a deacon,” [Col. 0645B] etc.

It postpones everything else to the following day.

HAGENOYEN.:

> “The feast of the holy Mother of God and of All Saints, which blessed Pope Boniface IV instituted, the Pantheon—that is, the temple of all demons—having been granted to him by blessed Gregory the Great, with the emperor Phocas consenting. He decreed that this solemnity should be celebrated only in the city of Rome and nowhere else. At that time the feasts of confessors were not yet celebrated; but afterwards Gregory IV decreed that it should be celebrated throughout the whole world, in honor of all the Saints, at the beginning of the Kalends of November, transferring the day which had been festive on the fourth day before the Ides of May. This feast was established for four reasons: first, to complete what had been omitted; second, to expiate negligences; third, to obtain our prayers more easily; fourth, for the consecration of a certain temple.”

This is sufficient; for the material that it subsequently mixes together concerning Benignus, Caesarius, and Julian does not deserve to be described in detail. At the end it reads: [Col. 0645C]

> “In the city of Paris, the burial of Saint Severinus the monk, who was born in the city of Tibur.”

Everything else has been omitted.

AMBIANEN.:

> “At the monastery of Centula, Saint Vigor, bishop and confessor.”

See above in the CENTULEN. codex.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end:

> “On the same day, Saint Lautenus the abbot. At Clermont, Saint Austremonius, bishop.”

VICTORIN., marked in the Swedish Royal register, no. 130, add:

> “At the city of Clermont, Saint Austremonius, bishop and martyr.”

See Castellanus’s note.

> “Also in the same district, Saint Florus, bishop and confessor, who was one of Christ’s seventy disciples.”

DAVERON.:

> “At the city of Bayeux, Saint Vigor, bishop and confessor. At Poitiers, Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “All Saints. Caesarius the martyr. Julian, priest and martyr. Mary, Virgin and martyr. Marcellus, bishop of Paris. Vigor, bishop, who raised a little child.”

DIVIONEN. of Saint Benignus, after the encomium given in the text, adds:

> “Although the solemnity of this blessed martyr is celebrated on the same day with the others, nevertheless, out of devotion to his martyrdom and veneration of his body, which is presently contained in this monastery, it is repeated on the following day with the greatest and most splendid festivity.”

CLUNIACEN.:

> “At Poitiers, Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Lautenus the confessor.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL also marks him, C.

CODEX D. L. MARE., marked A:

> “At Autun, Saint Pigmenius, bishop and confessor.”

Castellanus places him on the preceding day.

VATICAN., no. 5949, is lacking in the entries for Marcellus, Severinus, Vigor, and Maturinus.

ALTEMPS.:

> “At the city of Poitiers, Saint Hilary the confessor. At Clermont, the feast of blessed Austremonius the martyr, the first pastor of that city. On the same day, Saint Lauthenus the abbot.”

FLORENTIN. mentions Hilary as above. Then:

> “At the city of Reggio, the translation of the body of blessed Venerius the confessor, from the territory of Lucca to the aforesaid Reggio.”

See 13 September.

LUXOVIEN.:

> “At the monastery of Median., Saint Spinulus the confessor, the chief of Saint Hidulphus’s disciples. After commendably completing an anchoritic life, he departed to the Lord, renowned in the world for miracles.”

See Castellanus, 1 August.

The Lubeck–Cologne edition is somewhat interpolated from Ado in the first notice and greatly so in the other two. In the case of Marcellus it is correct. Concerning Severinus it adds only “confessor.” At the end of Maturinus it adds:

> “After the display of miracles, among which he delivered Maximian’s daughter from a demon, he joyfully gave his spirit back to the Lord.”

In the case of Mary it prefixes the place of combat, but incorrectly:

> “At the city of Neothorium.”

It also gives her condition:

> “A certain rich woman’s slave.”

Finally, it gives the period:

> “Under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus.”

It then proceeds to Vigor. At the end it adds:

> “In the territory of Nevers, Saint Patrick the martyr.”

BELIN. agrees almost entirely with the text in the first notice; the second and third differ little. It lacks the encomium of Marcellus. It is fairly good concerning Severinus, Mary, Vigor, and Maturinus. But what is the meaning of this repetition at the end?

> “On the same day, Saint Caesarius the martyr?”

And again:

> “Also Severinus the monk, from the city of Tibur?”

These had already been recorded above. In the other edition the repetition concerning Severinus is omitted, but the following is added:

> “At Poitiers, Saint Hilary the confessor. At Clermont, Saint Austremonius, [Col. 0646C] first bishop and martyr of the people of Clermont.”

GREVEN.:

> “In the territory of Nevers, Saint Patrick the martyr. In Africa, the holy Poplianus, Victor, Hermes, Justus, Vitalis, and Papias. Also the passion of Saint Agricola, and of Amancius, bishop. At Tarsus in Cilicia, Saint Eustochia, virgin and martyr. When she refused to sacrifice, by order of the emperor Julian she was beaten with ox-hide thongs, and she was clawed with the horns of young goats. Her hair was pulled out and nails were driven into her head. Then sentence was passed that she should be cut limb from limb and roasted in a frying pan; while praying to the Lord, she gave up her spirit.”

MOLANUS, doubtless from BELIN, adds to the text:

> “On the same day, Saint Caesarius the martyr. At Poitiers, Saint Hilary the confessor. At Clermont, Saint Austremonius, first bishop and martyr of the people of Clermont.”

Then:

> “At Blandinium, the burial of our most holy Father Florbert, first abbot of the monastery of Blandinium.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “In Spain, Saint Ermengaud, bishop of Urgell.”

Other editions insert into the text, in italics, concerning Marcellus:

> “Whose body rests in the venerable church of the Blessed Virgin Mary. His illustrious life,” etc.

Concerning Mary they supply material from Ado. At the end:

> “Whose body is honored and venerated in the territory of the diocese of Sens.”

The rest contributes nothing new, but merely transposes the notices concerning Florbert, Austremonius, Hilary, Caesarius, and Ermengaud.

---

## [Col. 0641]

The feast of the Blessed Mother of God and of all the martyrs, which Pope Boniface instituted to be celebrated solemnly and generally every year in the city of Rome. But Pope Gregory later decreed that the same feast should be solemnly observed perpetually by the whole Church in honor of all the Saints.

At the castle of Dijon, Saint Benignus, priest, who was sent by blessed Polycarp to preach in Gaul. After he had been afflicted in many ways by Terentius the count with the most severe tortures, at last an iron bar was ordered to be struck against his neck and his body to be pierced with a lance.

In Campania, in the city of Terracina, the holy Caesarius, deacon, and Julian, priest. Caesarius, in the time of Claudius, was tormented for many days in custody; afterwards he was put into a sack with the same Julian and thus thrown into the sea.

At the city of Paris, the burial of blessed Marcellus the confessor, who, to show that he was destined to become a worthy bishop, by his merits caused water sometimes to be changed into wine and at other times into balsam.

Also Saint Severinus the monk, from the city of Tibur.

And the feast of Saint Mary, virgin, who, afflicted with dreadful scourging, tortured by stretching on the rack and by the tearing of flesh with hooks, completed her martyrdom.

Also at the city of Bayeux, Saint Vigor, bishop.

In the district of the Vexin, Saint Maturinus the confessor.

---

## IV Non. Day 2

#### Note: [Col. 0647]

The purer witnesses are ANTUERP.-MAJ., ROSWEYD., ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., GREVEN., and MOLAN.

#### Note: [Col. 0647A]

I read *Pitabionensis* with most of the older codices. Some of them have *Pythabionensis* or *Pictavionensis*; none has *Pictaviensis*. This latter form crept into the more recent witnesses, as Molanus and others carefully noted, doubtless from Saint Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 74. Some prefer *Petavionensis*. However one writes it, it is not plausible that Poitiers in Gaul is intended here, but rather Poetabium or Poetavium of ancient Pannonia, or Noricum, today in Styria, commonly Pettaw, formerly a cathedral city and now in the diocese of Salzburg.

All read *Eustachii*, not *Eustathii*, although perhaps the latter is how he should be called. The older codices give *Placidae*, from *Placidas*; we, with the greater number, retain the form found in the text, as well as *Theospite*, with the manuscripts, Greven, Molanus, and others who write *Theospito*. Rosweyd differs from all the others by inserting into the encomium of Eustachius the phrase “first master of the soldiers.” In Greven there is *Theodoci* by mistake. Likewise, in ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. we find *coronatus* instead of *ornatus*. A few witnesses have *Acaunensis*; the more common form is *Agaunensis*. It is certain that Ado writes *requievit*, as do some codices, but we thought it necessary to yield to the greater number.

#### Note: [Col. 0647A]

Among the ancient ecclesiastical writers, Victorinus holds no lowly place; Saint Jerome praises him abundantly in the passage cited above. Those who seek judgments about writings such as are supplied by bibliographers now commonly known may consult Miraeus’s observations. Nothing further need be said here about his episcopal see; more can be discussed elsewhere with Launoy, to whom recent writers generally subscribe. See also the notes of Baronius, and Tillemont, volume V, beginning on page 311, where much is said about his writings, although scarcely anything is found concerning the events of Victorinus’s life or the acts of his martyrdom.

Nothing on this day was received from the Hieronymian Martyrologies or from Bede. The entire notice is from Ado, augmented by Usuard with little more than a citation of Jerome. Wandalbert also mentions him, together with Benignus and Julian, whom he seems to have transferred here because of the excessive number of saints on the preceding day. Thus he sings of Victorinus first:

> “On the fourth, Victorinus, sacred martyr, you are blessed.”

The second place in the Usuardine codices is consistently occupied on this day by the celebrated Eustachius—elsewhere Eustathius—with his wife and two sons, although he is now, perhaps on the basis of Greek sources, customarily recorded on 20 September, as in the Calendar of Allatius; Fronto incorrectly notes him on 11 September. And indeed our sources say that they suffered on 1 November, at least according to the greater number of codices.

Eustachius is rightly denied to Ado, unless I am very much mistaken. Certainly the material rejected by Rosweyd into the appendix does not sufficiently agree with the Usuardine witnesses, nor any more with what is attributed to Florus in our edition of Bede. It is therefore a notice proper to Usuard, deliberately placed in such a way that it contains nothing deserving criticism.

That the Acts of Eustachius and his companions are extraordinary is rightly attested; whether they are equally true—whether those published by Metaphrastes, Combefisius, or others, since they all agree in substance—you will understand from Baronius under the year 120, no. 4. Recent scholars reject them entirely, and Tillemont did not consider them worthy of serving as the basis for his history. See him in volume II, page 226, and from page 585 onward.

I am not unaware of how much Kircher labored to defend those Acts. Letters of his on that subject, addressed to our predecessors, still exist here. Nevertheless, although Nicephorus and Damascenus cite them, no one, in my opinion, will easily prevail against Baronius in denying that much was added to those Acts, at the very least. We shall endeavor in its proper place to purge them, if possible.

Meanwhile, see what the aforementioned Baronius observes in his note concerning the ancient cult of Eustachius. It would be strange if he had substituted the virgin Eustochia of Tarsus, of whose acts we possess some, for Eustachius on this day from Peter’s Catalogue, as Castellanus’s note maintains. I do not think that the following verses sung by Wandalbert on 19 September can refer to anyone other than our Eustachius:

> “A model of virtue, and the beauty and glory of endurance,  
>   
> Eustathius triumphs on the thirteenth day through martyrdom.”

The Theodotus who follows, bishop of Laodicea, is the only person whom the author of the *Romanum parvum* marked on this day:

> “At Laodicea, Theodotus, bishop, who was a physician by profession.”

There is no doubt that this author again consulted his Rufinus, book VII, chapter 29, from which Ado’s longer encomium was also taken. Here is the stumbling-block first cast by Theodotus’s friend, Eusebius of Caesarea, book VII, chapter 32, in Valesius’s edition. Our writers took it from there, but Valesius attacked it more sharply, as we showed in chapter 2 of our preface. Here you have the source from which that Theodotus—unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Florus, Wandalbert, and Rabanus—obtained a place in the Martyrologies of our series.

I possess a letter from our most learned fellow member, Peter Possinus, written at Rome on 30 December 1677. Among other things, speaking about the Reverend Father Leander of the Oratory, later Cardinal Coloredo of the Holy Roman Church, he writes:

> “He incidentally asked me to consult you in his name concerning the dispute recently raised here about Theodotus, bishop of Laodicea. The illustrious Michael Angelo Ricci and other learned men think, or strongly suspect, that he was unjustly introduced into the Roman Martyrology, where an especially honorable mention of him occurs on 2 November, although in every account of the Arian controversy he appears stained with that pitch, and nowhere is there a suitable indication of his repentance. For this reason Henry Valesius, in his booklet on the Roman Martyrology, published at the end of his Notes on Eusebius, does not hesitate to declare that the name was wrongly forced into that place, and that Baronius’s diligence requires correction.”

What was set aside I infer from the surviving note, which confirms the opinion of the Roman scholars. Eusebius, the eulogist of Theodotus, had intruded into Usuard on 21 June, but was omitted from the Roman Martyrology; perhaps the same thing will eventually happen to Theodotus here.

I confess that I have labored no less than others to unearth from somewhere even slight traces of his repentance, but thus far the result has not answered the labor. I see that Baronius, under the year 325, no. 40, and all the learned writers generally number Theodotus among the Arian deceivers. On this matter see Tillemont, volume VI, page 740, and elsewhere. Enough has been said concerning the origin and spread of his cult, unknown among all Eastern peoples.

Ambrosius, first father of the monastery of the Island of Barbara near Lyons and later abbot of the Agaunian monastery, was first marked by Ado, with a brief but more distinctive encomium; our author records him more concisely. Baronius cites Peter in the Catalogue and Trithemius, but they speak rather sparingly about Ambrosius, which may be why Mabillon lists him among the “omitted.” Nor do the manuscripts of our Lives of the abbots of Agaunum supply much. Perhaps more will be furnished from another source. This is, unless I am mistaken, the true and complete text of Usuard.

#### Note: [Col. 0649A]

PRATEN. is again not to be counted among the pure witnesses, because here it lacks the final member of the second notice, namely:

> “Although their feast is held on the Kalends, it is nevertheless commemorated here more fully.”

HERINIEN. suffers from exactly the same defect, which, in agreement with the other witnesses, must truly be called a defect. It also displays an evident erasure, contrary to its usual practice, over which two first notices have been written in a reversed order and in longer lines, although it dealt with Eustachius on 20 September. This shows the incompetence of the corrector, or of the original scribe himself, since the script scarcely differs. In addition, at the end it adds:

> “On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Benignus the martyr.”

This was doubtless proper to the place, having been transferred here because the preceding day was obstructed, as it appears yesterday in DIVION.

TORNACEN. is pure in the first notice; in second place it records Ambrosius, and in third Eustachius, but with the defect mentioned in the earlier codices. It entirely expunged Theodotus. At the end it adds:

> “On the same day, the commemoration of all the faithful departed.”

PULSANEN. is sufficiently pure only in the first notice. It then deals with Ambrosius, whose encomium it entirely expunged. The rest is absent.

MUNERAT. writes Victor instead of Victorinus. It lacks the section:

> “Although their feast,” etc.

At the end:

> “On the same day, the commemoration of all the faithful departed.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN. begin:

> “The commemoration of all the faithful departed.”

The entire text follows, although somewhat transposed; at the end it adds:

> “At Vienne, Saint George, the distinguished bishop of that city.”

This is found in the Roman Martyrology.

LOVANIEN. agrees in all respects with the codices just cited, but differs from them by omitting the encomium of Theodotus.

ALBERGEN. and DANIC. lack Eustachius, whom they treated on 25 September. Otherwise they resemble ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others.

CENTULEN.:

> “At Rome, the passion of Saint Eustachius, formerly called Placidas, who suffered by fire under Hadrian together with his wife Theospis [Col. 0649C] and his two sons Agapius and Theopistus. At Laodicea, Saint Theodotus, bishop, a man adorned not only in words but also in deeds and virtues. On the same day, Saint Ambrosius, abbot of Agaunum, remarkable for holiness.”

The first notice is absent.

BRUXELLEN. begins:

> “The commemoration of all the souls of the faithful departed.”

It is mutilated in the account of Eustachius. Omitting Victorinus, whom it treats on the following day, it records here those whom it omitted yesterday. In particular:

> “And the feast of blessed Mary, virgin and martyr, who, although she was a slave and fasted on the birthday of the Son of her Lord, could in no way be persuaded to eat with idolaters; through dreadful wounds,” etc.

It continues:

> “At Cologne Agrippina, Saint Evergislus, third archbishop of that city.”

Then it gives Severinus of Tibur, from the preceding day. Next it treats Theodotus, fairly accurately. It gives George of Vienne together with the codices mentioned above. Again it gives Marcellus, Vigor, and Maturinus, as we did on the preceding day. Finally:

> “At Mons in Hainaut, the canonization”—MOLANUS has “translation”—“of Saint Waudru, the chosen one and niece of blessed Gudula, virgin.”

HAGENOYEN. begins with Eustachius and gives a summary of his sufficiently well-known Acts, but I do not wish to follow it in describing them here. It then treats Victorinus, fairly well. Next:

> “Also Saint Namatius, bishop and confessor.”

It says nothing about Theodotus. It postpones Ambrosius to the following day. At the end it reads:

> “On the same day, the commemoration of all the faithful departed, which was established for those deceased persons whose memory no one observes; and because such people do not have particular intercessions, they should have general ones on this day.”

This reason is tolerable, but the other reason for the institution, which it adds concerning the abduction of Saint Peter’s guardian, does not deserve to be described.

AQUICINCT. begins:

> “The general and festive commemoration [Col. 0650A] of all the faithful departed.”

VICTORIN. and the Swedish Royal register, marked no. 130, add at the end:

> “On the same day, Saint Lautenus the abbot.”

In Castellanus he is listed on 1 November.

DAVERONEN., pure in the first and second notices, adds:

> “At the monastery of Dol, Saint Justus, monk and martyr.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Eustachius with his companion martyrs. The commemoration of the souls. Victorinus, bishop and martyr. Theodorus, bishop and confessor. Ambrosius, abbot of the monastery of Agaunum.”

VATICAN., marked no. 5949, lacks Eustachius and Ambrosius. It adds:

> “In the Sabine territory, the holy martyrs Valentinus and Hilary. At Benevento, Saint Marcianus, bishop and martyr, disciple of blessed Peter. And the passing of the lord Amicus, priest.”

See Castellanus’s Martyrology.

FLORENTIN.:

> “At Trieste, Saint Justus the martyr, under the governor Monatius.”

The Lubeck–Cologne edition:

> “The commemoration of all the [Col. 0650B] faithful departed, which holy Pope Boniface IV instituted to be celebrated every year as a general observance in the churches of God. At Rome, the venerable memory of Saints Eustachius, surnamed Placidas, with his wife and sons, martyrs.”

It then treats Victorinus, fairly accurately, and likewise Theodotus. Next:

> “At Vienne, Saint George, the distinguished bishop and confessor of that city. At the monastery of Dol, Saint Justus, monk and martyr. On the same day, at the monastery, the translation of the holy martyrs Victorinus and Florianus.”

The account of Ambrosius is fairly pure.

BELIN. begins:

> “The commemoration of all the faithful departed.”

In second place it writes Theodorus instead of Theodotus. The account of Victorinus is fairly pure; that of Eustachius is mutilated. Then:

> “On the same day, the passion of blessed Justus the martyr, who was crowned at the city of Trigesina”—another edition, less incorrectly, has “at the city of Trigestina.”

Finally it includes Ambrosius, but with his entire encomium cut away.

**GREVEN:** “Commemoration of all the faithful departed, [Col. 0650C] which Saint Boniface IV instituted to be observed generally in the churches. At the city of Tergeste in Istria, the birthday of Saint Justus, precious martyr, who under Diocletian and Maximian, having been sent to prison for the faith of Christ and then brought out, was scourged with raw sinews and finally, after many weights of lead had been fastened to him, thrown into the sea. In Persia, Saints Alenidinus, Pigasius, Anepodistus; who, under King Shapur, were most cruelly beaten with rods, endured fire and iron beds, and at last, together with twenty-eight others who believed through their confession, were cast into the fire. As they gave their souls back to Christ, they were taken up by angels into the clouds. A certain soldier named Antoninus also believed through their confession; he was arrested and beheaded. At the monastery of Dol, Saint Justus, monk and martyr. At Vienne, Saint George, bishop and confessor of that city. Saint Malachy, bishop, primate of all Ireland and confessor, whose life, illustrious from childhood for virtues and miracles, Saint Bernard the abbot carefully described in his honeyed style of speech. He was Irish by nation and first a monk, then became a bishop; when he was traveling to Rome a second time on ecclesiastical business, he died at Clairvaux, as he had wished, and was buried by that same holy abbot. Saint Volganus, bishop and confessor, brother of Saint Foillan the martyr. In Ireland, Saint Doranus, bishop. Saint Odilo, confessor. Vitalis. At Monastery, the translation of Saints Victorinus and Florianus, martyrs. Florbert, abbot of Blandinium and confessor.”

**MOLANUS**, at the beginning in italic letters: “Commemoration, etc.” At the end: “On this same day, the passion of Blessed Justus,” etc., as in **BELINUS**. The other editions agree, but lack Eustachius. They have the entry concerning George as **GREVENUS** does. Then: “On the second day, Saints Acindymus, Pegasius, Aphtonius, Elpidephorus, and Anempodistus, martyrs.” **GREVENUS** yesterday recorded other names: “At Monts in Hainaut, the translation of Saint Waldetrudis.”]

[Col. 0645]

The birthday of Blessed Victorinus, bishop of Pitabronum, who, after many teachings, as Saint Jerome testifies, was crowned with martyrdom in the persecution of Diocletian. At Rome, in the time of the Emperor Hadrian, the passion of Blessed Eustachius, surnamed Placidus, and of his wife Theospis, with their sons Agapius and Theospes, whose wondrous deeds are read. Although their feast is observed on the Kalends, it is nevertheless commemorated here more fully. At Laodicea, Saint Theodotus, bishop, who was adorned not only with words but also with deeds and virtues. On the same day, Saint Ambrose, abbot of the monastery of Agaunum, who, illustrious for the great virtues of his life and holiness, rested in the Lord with a blessed end.

**III Non. Day 3.** [Note: [Col. 0651]

From Praten., Antuerp., and Max.-Lubec., Greven. and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0651A]

This is almost the only disagreement among the manuscripts cited for the text: Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. mark only three Cappadocian martyrs, omitting the name of Caesarius. Among the typographical errors in Max.-Lubec. let *Caesaraugusto* be counted. Otherwise, *Cappadocia*, *Datianus*, etc., recur elsewhere as well. In Ado of Mosander, two further announcements are added for this day, concerning Domninus and Hubertus. Rosweyd, excluding the first, retained the second, expressed as follows: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Hubertus, bishop.” [Col. 0652A] I do not see the reason for this inclusion; since both are absent from Usuard, I would readily believe that neither is Ado’s. As for Hubertus alone, whether he is Usuardine may be called into doubt by the Heriniensis, Rosweyd, and middle-recension manuscripts; but since he is excluded by several, and the others use different wording in commemorating him, I conclude plainly that he does not belong to our text. I judge that everything else is unmistakably Usuardine.]

[Note: [Col. 0651A]

We have more than once said elsewhere that one of the distinctive characteristics of the *Little Roman Martyrology*—and not the least important—is that it gathered from the New Testament the names both of the first deacons and of many others whose memory is celebrated either in the Acts of the Apostles or in the Epistles of the Apostle Paul. Such on this day is Quartus, in Romans 16:23, among the household members, honored by the Apostle with a somewhat distinguished title when he writes: “There greets you … Quartus, the brother.” No other earlier martyrologist mentions him anywhere. Thus he was first recorded by the compiler of the *Little Roman Martyrology*: “Quartus, disciple of the apostles.” Add “the birthday of Saint,” and you will have Ado’s announcement, from which ours has been copied word for word. Nor do we think that our saint should be adorned with any other title. For the *Synopsis* of Dorotheus, cited by Baronius and so often torn apart elsewhere by our predecessors, is not an adequate authority for us to assert, in agreement with the Greeks—among whom he is celebrated on 10 November—that he was either one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ or bishop of Berytus. This will have to be demonstrated more fully elsewhere.

The Cappadocian martyrs are marked by the same author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* as follows: “In Cappadocia, the martyrs Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Vitalis, under the persecution of Decius.” A somewhat longer wording of Ado, although with some transposition, was transferred into our text by Usuard. It may be doubted whether the praised author of the *Little Roman Martyrology* did not receive these saints from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; certainly there too the names of the martyrs that we have presented are read, with Egrinius or Egritius added, so that their very ancient cult is altogether certain. Caesarius is absent from Rabanus, just as from two of the manuscripts cited above for the text; but three others are substituted, namely Domninus, Justus, and Eremitis, whom we believe to have been wrongly confused with the Cappadocians. Baronius further notes here [Col. 0652A] that Peter, in his *Catalogue*, book X, chapter 18, briefly describes their Acts from ancient records. He might have added that these were cited as derived from the Martyrology of Saint Jerome. Yet if all the words of the bishop of Equilinum are carefully weighed, he reports nothing peculiar to these saints that he did not receive from Usuard; for this is plainly the Martyrology that in Peter’s age used to be called Hieronymian, as we have observed elsewhere with Molanus. Thus Wandalbert sings of our four Cappadocian martyrs in one distich:

[Col. 0652B]

“Germanus, Vitalis, and Caesarius, three together,  
and Theophilus, shine with equal light of festal glory.”

Above, under 22 January and under 15 and 16 April, we had to discuss the martyrs of Caesaraugusta, especially Vincentius and the fixed number of eighteen others. Here Usuard alone—for they are found in no other ancient martyrologists—gathers an innumerable host, which Papebrochius rightly considers to have been taken from the Acts, accurately elucidated by him on 16 April; unless we should think that Prudentius’s hymn 4 came first, when he does not hesitate to compare the multitude of the Caesaraugustan martyrs with the Carthaginians and Romans, in these words:

“Scarcely does populous Carthage, parent of the world,  
scarcely Rome itself, enthroned in its majesty,  
deem it worthy in this gift  
to surpass you, our glory.

At every gate sacred blood was sacrificed,” etc. [Col. 0652C] See the hymn itself on the cited day, 16 April, or the passages excerpted here by Baronius in his Annotation. Tillemont briefly mentions our martyrs, plucking passages here and there from the Acts, in volume V, page 230. If anything can or ought to be added by us to Papebrochius’s Commentary or to the elucidation of the Acts themselves, we shall provide it in its proper place.]

[Note: [Col. 0651C]

**HERINIENSIS**, otherwise thoroughly pure in its text, adds at the end, if I am not mistaken: “At the monastery of Andaginum, the deposition of Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor.”

**TORNACENSIS**, also extremely pure, adds: “On the same day, Saint Juvenalis, confessor.” If this concerns the Juvenalis of Narnia, it belongs to 3 May. I would rather think that Guinailus is meant, concerning whom see below.

[Col. 0651D] **ANTUERPIENSIS-MAJOR**, also pure, but at the end has: “On the same day, Saint Paul, bishop and martyr, disciple of the Apostle Peter.” I do not know who this is.

**ROSWEYD:** also pure, reads: “Likewise, the birthday of Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor. Likewise, Pirminius, bishop. Valentinus, priest.”

**PULSANENSIS**, fairly pure in the first two, lacks the third announcement.

[Col. 0652C] **MUNERATUS**, after the text, continues: “At Corboil Castle, the deposition of Blessed Guinailus, abbot and monk, whose life and miracles are preserved. On the same day, in the city of Paris, Blessed Marcellus,” etc., as on 1 November, but at the end: “Whose body rests in the venerable church of the Blessed Virgin Mary.”

**ANTUERPIENSIS MAXIMUS, ULTRAJECTENSIS, LEYDENENSIS,** and **LOVANIENSIS** likewise append to an otherwise pure text: “At the monastery of Audaginum [Antuerp.-Max. has *Augadinum*], the deposition of Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor.”

**ALBERGENSIS** gives an equally pure text, to which it adds more simply and in Ado’s wording: “On the same day, Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor.”

**DANICUS**, also following a pure text, adds: “At Viterbo Castle, Saints Valentinus, priest, and Hilarius [Col. 0653A] deacon, who, after being torn apart for a long time under Maximian, were drowned in the Tiber; but, rescued by an angel, they completed their martyrdom by the cutting off of their heads.” See the Roman Martyrology.

**CENTULENSIS**, pure in the first announcement, is mutilated in the second, reporting only the names; the third is absent and is replaced by: “In the district of Vilcassinum, Saint Clarus, priest and martyr.” See Usuard himself on the following day.

**BRUXELLENSIS** begins: “At Liège, the elevation of Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor, performed sixteen years after his death. His body was found intact, with his hair having grown, the crown undamaged, and his face clearly covered with sweat. Charles Martel, prince of the Austrasians, brother of Pippin, later king of the Franks, was present at this elevation.” It then gives Quartus, purely. Next comes Victorinus of Pitabionum, from the preceding day. Among the Cappadocians it inserts the name of Victor. Then it anticipates the following day’s text as follows: “At the city of Bologna, the birthday of Saints Agricola and Vitalis, martyrs; the latter had formerly been the former’s servant, but is now his companion and fellow in martyrdom. The ministers of every kind of torture exercised their torments upon them, and finally killed Blessed Agricola by fastening him to a cross. At Viterbo Castle, the birthday of Saints Valentinus, priest, and Hilarius, deacon, who were long torn apart under Maximian.” The Caesaraugustan martyrs follow, fairly purely. Finally it gives Ambrose of Agaunum from the preceding day.

**HAGENOYENSIS** begins: “In the city of Paris, the deposition of Saint Marcellus, bishop and confessor, who, as one worthy,” etc., from 1 November, adding another eulogy: “Whose illustrious life, full of virtues and miracles, Fortunatus,” etc. It then gives Mary from the same day. Quartus is absent. The Cappadocians are given fairly purely. The Caesaraugustans are deferred to the following day. Then comes Ambrose of Agaunum from the preceding day. Next: “On the same day, Saint Pirminius, bishop and confessor, a man of complete holiness. Likewise [Col. 0653C] in England, Wenefrida, virgin, of most holy religion. Likewise, Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor.”

**AQUICINCTENSIS** lacks the name of Caesarius. At the end: “The deposition of Parmenus, bishop.” Rabanus writes *Permenius*, but it should be read, with the others, as *Parminius*. It continues: “In the Ardennes, Saint Hubertus, bishop of Liège. On the same day, at Viterbo Castle, the passion of Saints Valentinus, priest, and Hilarius, deacon, who under Maximian and the consul Demetrius were long torn apart, made the renowned temple of Hercules into ashes by their prayer, and [were cast] into the Tiber,” etc., as above in the **DANICUS** manuscript.

**VICTORINUS** has at the end: “At Interbentium Castle, the passion of Saints Valentinus,” etc., as in the preceding entry, except that here *Demetrius* is read instead of *Demetius*. The manuscript marked no. 130 in the **REGIA SUECIAE** agrees with this custom, but seems to read: “At Viterlencium or Viterbencium Castle.” Why not *Viterbiensium*?

**DAVERONENSIS:** “The deposition of Saint Pirminius, bishop. In the district of Tours, the birthday of Saint Adventius, confessor.” [Col. 0653D]

**MATRICENSIS-CARTHUSIENSIS-ULTRAJECTENSIS:** “Quartus, disciple of the apostles. Hubertus, first bishop of Liège. At Caesaraugusta, an innumerable number of holy martyrs, under the governor Dacianus.”

**CAMBERIENSIS:** “At Corboil Castle, Blessed Guinardus, abbot and monk.” I think he is the same person whom **MUNERATUS** calls Guinailus and Castellanus Vinailus, in French Guenau. See also the following entry.

**REGIA SUECIAE**, marked no. 428: “At Corboil, the deposition of Guinailus, abbot and monk, whose life and miracles are preserved. On the same day, at the city of Magubium in Mauritania, the passion of Saints Martianus, Pelagia, and Maurus.” I do not know these saints as joined together in this way.

**Codex D. LE MARE**, marked A: “The translation of Saint Andochius, priest.”

In the **VATICAN** manuscript, no. 5949, the Caesaraugustan martyrs are absent; I do not know whether the remainder is pure.

**ALTEMPS:** “In Britain, Saint Rumwold, confessor, resting at Bockingham. At Corboil, the deposition of Saint Guinaldus, abbot and confessor. Likewise, Pirminius, bishop.” [Col. 0654A]

**FLORENTINUS**, in first place: “In the territory of Florence, at the castle of Pauzen, Saint Euphrosynus, bishop and confessor of Pamphylia, who, illustrious for great virtues and miracles, rested in the Lord in the time of Pope Sylvester and was buried there in a basilica dedicated in honor of his name. Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor.”

**LUBECO-COLONIENSIS EDITION** begins: “The birthday of Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor of Liège, most illustrious for his virtues. While he was a soldier devoted to paganism, occupied with hunting on Good Friday, Christ appeared to him in the form of a crucifix between the antlers of a stag and brought him back to the faith of the Christian religion. By divine warning through an angel, he was ordained bishop of Rome by Pope Sergius and sent to govern the church of Tongeren. In the thirteenth year [Col. 0654B] of his episcopate, by the Lord’s revelation, he transferred from Maastricht to Liège the relic of Saint Lambert, his predecessor. After he had laudably governed the churches of Tongeren and Liège for almost thirty years, he rested in peace with a holy end; but the body was transferred by Louis, king of the Franks, son of Charlemagne and most Christian emperor, from Liège to the monastery of Andaginum.” The text that follows is fairly pure. Then: “On the same day, Saint Pirminius, hermit. Wishing to inhabit a deserted place full of beasts and serpents, and finding it occupied by flies of various kinds, revered animals, and stinging scarabs, he made a wooden cross and, invoking the name of the Lord Jesus, drove out all those poisonous creatures that occupied the place. At last he was elected bishop, and after many distinguished virtues he rested in peace. At Vienne, Saint Domnianus, glorious bishop and confessor. In the district of Vilcassinum, the passion of Blessed Clarus, priest and martyr. In the district of Tours, Saint Adventius, confessor. On the same day, Blessed Baya, virgin. [Col. 0654C] At Bardewic, Saint Marianus, deacon and martyr. And on the same day, Saint Wenefreda, virgin and martyr.”

**BELINUS**, fairly pure in the text, adds at the end: “On the same day, Saint Malachy, bishop, who in his time shone with many virtues.”

**GREVEN:** “Valentinus, priest, and Hilarius, deacon, martyrs. In Brabant, in the district of Bardewic, Saint Marianus, deacon and martyr. Hubertus, bishop and confessor of Liège. While he was a soldier devoted to the worship of idols, in the time of Theoderic, king of the Franks, he was converted during a hunt when Christ appeared to him in the form of a crucifix between the antlers of a stag. Then, instructed more carefully in faith and morals by Saint Lambert, bishop of Liège, he sought the wilderness and for some time led an austere life. Later, warned by an angel, he went to Rome and, by divine revelation, was appointed by Pope Sergius as successor to the aforementioned Lambert, who had already been crowned with martyrdom. After he had energetically administered the episcopal office for nearly thirty years, he rested in peace in the year of the Lord 731, on the third day before the Kalends of June. Nevertheless, his feast is solemnly celebrated here when his sacred body was raised from the earth. At Vienne, Saint Domninus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Priminius, hermit.” Concerning him, see the **LUBECO-COLONIENSIS EDITION**. “In Britain, Romuldus, confessor. William, confessor. In the district of Tours, Saint Adventius, confessor. Likewise, Wenefreda, virgin and martyr. In Scotland, Haya, virgin. Likewise, Saint Alpaidis, who, as Vincent relates in book 30, afflicted by illnesses for many years, lived without bodily food; although lowly by birth and a herdswoman by occupation, she was nevertheless endowed with the gift of wondrous wisdom, very prudent in counsel, careful in speech, and effective in exhortation. She was moreover visited by God with many revelations and finally rested.”

**MOLANUS**, concerning Malachy, Guinalus, Marcellus, and Adventius, as above: “In the monastery of the Ardennes called Saint Hubertus, [Col. 0655A] the deposition of Saint Hubertus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Pirminius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Odrada, virgin.” In smaller type: “At Alem in Brabant. In the cathedral city of Barduyc, Saint Marianus, etc. Likewise, Wenefreda, virgin and martyr.”

The other editions read as follows: “At the monastery of Andain, the birthday of the most blessed Hubertus, pontiff and confessor of the church of Tongeren. Having succeeded Blessed Lambert the martyr in the episcopate, in the twelfth year of his ordination, warned by a divine oracle, he transferred the sacred bones of that martyr, and the episcopal seat, from Maastricht to Liège, where he had suffered. Then, increasing in many virtues, he converted many from idolatry to the faith of Christ and, while alive, freed many possessed persons, and after his death very many more. That precious pontiff of the Lord and outstanding athlete died on the third day before the Nones of November and was buried in the church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. In the ninetieth year, however, he was transferred to Andain by Vulcandus, bishop of Liège of blessed memory, with the approval of Louis, most pious emperor. There, what his spirit accomplished while alive is wonderfully attested to this day, for the praise and glory of the Lord, by countless virtues, glorious prodigies, and continual miracles.” Concerning Pirminius, Adventius, and Guinalus, as above. Then: “In the district of Maasland, in the village of Alem, Saint Odrada, virgin.” Concerning Valentinus and Hilarius, as above. “In England, Saint Wuenefreda, virgin and martyr, whom Cadoc, son of King Alan, killed for her chastity.” Castellanus notes this in a note to the Roman Martyrology. “In Gascony, Saint Benignus, bishop and confessor. On the third day, Saints Acepsimas, Aithalas, and Joseph, martyrs. And the dedication of the divine temple of Saint George, the great martyr, in Lydia, and the deposition of his holy body. In the village of Florin, the reception of the body of Saint Maurus, distinguished martyr. At Liège, on the public hill, the dedication of the monastery of Saint Lawrence.”]

[Col. 0651]

The birthday of Saint Quartus, disciple of the apostles. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saints Germanus, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Vitalis, martyrs, who under the persecution of Decius endured martyrdom with great distinction. At Caesaraugusta, an innumerable number of holy martyrs, who under Dacianus, governor of the Spains, wonderfully fell for Christ.

**Pridie Non. Day 4.** [Note: [Col. 0655]

The following are pure: Praten., Herinien., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0655B]

The first and almost greatest variation concerns the name of the first saint. Only Molanus gives it in the more received form, *Pierius*, as it appears in Eusebius of Valesius and is commonly called. But since it was taken from Rufinus, who writes *Hierius*, it has been preserved in that form in the *Little Roman Martyrology*, Ado, and Usuard; some manuscripts have distorted it into *Herii, Jerii, Hierei, Hyerii, Hyrei, Hyerei*, and so forth. Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., and others have the form found in the text. Another variation concerns the designation of the city of Rotenus. Together with Ado, and on the basis of Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., and others, we formed its name according to the usage of that age as *Rotenus*, not *Rotemis*, as in Praten., [Col. 0656B] nor *Rotenis* or *Rotenius*, as in others, and much less *Redonis*, as Molanus most wrongly corrected it. The Ruteni belong to Aquitania; the Redones to Armorica, or Lesser Britain. I wrote *Vilcasino*, as most manuscripts have it; the printed editions commonly have *Vilcassino*, while some prefer *Vulcasino*. Among the pure witnesses, Greven. and Molan. give Proculus the title of martyr, and Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Belin. read it likewise; hence it also passed into the Roman Martyrology. But the principal manuscripts stand for our reading, which is both preferable and more genuine. Concerning Augustodunum and similar matters, enough has been said elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0655B]

Hierius or Pierius proceeds from the same source—or rather from the same book and chapter—from which Theodotus of Laodicea was taken two days ago, namely Rufinus, book VII, chapter 29. From this the entire eulogy of Ado was again compiled, whose more elegant substance is represented in our text. Thus the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*, who first included this saint in his calendar, had first written: “At Alexandria, Hierius, priest, of most pure life, nobly learned in the Scriptures.” He too belongs to the number of those saints whom we call peculiar to the *Little Roman Martyrology*, since one seeks them in vain among other martyrologists or outside our series. What can be said about the deeds or writings of Pierius should be drawn from the cited Eusebius or from Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 76. Tillemont collected most of the material from those sources and from Photius and arranged it in French in volume IV, pages 582–583. We have offered a few remarks in our treatise on the Patriarchs of Alexandria, page 36a, no. 191.

The following commemoration is entirely Ado’s, at least under these terms, and was first marked here. Florentinius considers it to have been added to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but those manuscripts contain very many additions of this sort. Certainly I scarcely doubt that Rabanus derived his announcement from them, phrased almost in Hieronymian words; whether Ado also consulted the same source matters little to investigate further. See also the notes of Baronius and Florentinius. A certain sequence not so much of deeds as of several miracles has been left to us either by Fortunatus or by some other compiler of that synopsis, which is found in Surius, neither sufficiently complete nor sufficiently trustworthy; it should therefore be corrected from other sources, especially our manuscript and volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, page 474, and restored in the Acts. Wandalbert correctly wrote that the Rutenian city is adorned by Saint Amantius, not the Redonian, as Molanus wrongly and so insistently maintains, deceived by the similarity of the names and leading others, perhaps even Ferrari, into error. See what was observed above in the Variants concerning the difference between these places. This is the metric martyrologist’s sole verse:

“On the eve, the confessor Amantius adorns the Ruteni.”

Clarus of Vilcassinum is known to no ancient martyrologist except ours. He is furnished with no eulogy, doubtless because Usuard saw no Acts from which he could draw more distinct details of his mission, preaching, life, martyrdom, or time. Much has been investigated with care and learning by Henschenius and Papebrochius concerning another Clarus, bishop and martyr, greatly renowned among the Aquitanians; other matters have been conjectured with Baluzius concerning the quite plausible confusion of various synonyms. All this may perhaps provide guidance for examining what Denyaldus and others seem to have amassed concerning this Clarus of Vulcassinum, if not rashly, at least with great liberality. [Col. 0656D] Which other ancient manuscripts, agreeing with Usuard, Baronius cites, we entirely do not know. But it is unnecessary here to cross the established limits.

The Hieronymian manuscripts certainly remember Proculus, whether the entry belongs to the first or the later hand. Hence we believe that he was taken over by Rabanus and by Our Author, unless, contrary to the view of Mosander and Rosweyd, he should also be attributed to Ado. Certainly everywhere I find him a bishop, nowhere a martyr; therefore above in the text we rightly established that he should be read with the purer Usuardine manuscripts. But what Peter’s *Catalogue* has in book II, no. 309, to which Baronius refers us—“Proculus the martyr suffered at Augustodunum on this very day”—is sufficiently undermined by the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Rabanus, and Usuard. Would that monuments of his life were as certain as we consider the asserted title owed to Proculus to be. In the remaining matters as well, we judge the Usuardine reading to be true and straightforward.]

[Note: [Col. 0657A]

**TORNACENSIS** would have to be counted among the very pure manuscripts, unless it had cut out the entire eulogy of Hierius.

**ANTUERPIENSIS-MAJOR**, pure in the first two announcements, wrongly joins the final two into one as follows: “In the district of Vilcasino, Saint Proculus, martyr.”

**ROSWEYD** is fuller, for after the text it adds: “In the city of Wenta, the deposition of Saint Birnstanus, bishop of that diocese, who, shining with the virtues of sacred merits, rested with a blessed end. In Italy, Saint Domninus, martyr. In Africa, Saints Primus and Caesarius with ten others.” The last two are taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, where Domninus is assigned not to Italy but to Nicaea.

[Col. 0657B] **PULSANENSIS:** the eulogy is absent in the first manuscript. The second and third are pure. It is lacking in the fourth.

**ANTUERPIENSIS, MAX.-LUBEC,** and **UGHELLIANUS** somewhat enlarge the eulogy of Hierius and construct it in Ado’s manner, putting everything in the genitive. They lack the third announcement. In the fourth they read “Proculus the martyr.”

**ANTUERPIENSIS-MAXIMUS, ULTRAJECTENSIS, LEYDENENSIS,** and **LOVANIENSIS** also imitate Ado in the first announcement. In the second they read: “On the same day, the birthday of Saint Perpetua, wife of Blessed Peter the Apostle.” I do not know who first inserted this. There is a Roman Perpetua, but she is Peter’s disciple on 4 August. The manuscripts are fairly pure in the entry for Amantius. Nothing is said of Clarus. They add the title martyr to Proculus. Finally: “In Gaul, in the town of Dinant” [*Dinacensi, Clinatensi*, more correctly in **LOVANIENSIS**, *Dinantensi*], “Saint Perpetuus, bishop of Tongeren.” The manuscripts differ concerning the place in the same way.

**ALBERGENSIS** and **DANICUS** agree with the matters already mentioned, but prefix to the entire text: “At the city of Bologna, the birthday of Saints Agricola and Vitalis, martyrs. The latter had previously been the former’s servant, but is now his companion and fellow in martyrdom. Finally, when the persecutors compelled him to deny Christ, and he confessed the Lord Jesus Christ all the more, they inflicted every kind of torture upon him. At last they killed Blessed Agricola by fastening him to a cross.” **BELINUS** also placed this on the same day, and from him it entered the modern Roman Martyrology; but in our series it belongs to 27 November.

**CENTULENSIS**, Adonian in the first announcement but mutilated, lacks the eulogy in the second; the third is absent; the fourth is pure. At the end: “At the monastery of Centula, the translation of Saint Angilbertus, abbot, who, twenty-eight years after his death, was found incorrupt.” Angilbertus is celebrated on 18 February.

**BRUXELLENSIS** begins: “The birthday of Saint Perpetua, wife of Blessed Peter the Apostle.” In the entry for Hierius it is fairly pure. Then concerning Proculus, as above. In the entry for Amantius, fairly correctly. Clarus is absent. Various additions follow, especially: “At Reims, the deposition of Saint Gamatus, bishop. In Gaul, at the town of Dinant, the birthday of Saint Perpetuus, bishop of Tongeren, who performed many miracles. In Africa, the birthday of Saints Primus, Caesarius, Gregorius, and Porphyrius.” See their companions in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. “Likewise, Brustanus, bishop and confessor.” Castellanus writes *Biristanus*.

**HAGENOYENSIS** begins: “In the monastery of Epta, Saint Clarus, priest and martyr.” In second place it reports the Caesaraugustan martyrs, concerning whom Usuard writes on the preceding day. Then it gives Theodotus from the text of 2 November. In the entry for Hierius it is fairly pure. To Amantius it adds the title “bishop of Rouen.” Just as this manuscript commonly confuses many things, so it deferred Clarus of Vilcassinum and Proculus of Augustodunum to 6 November. [Col. 0658A] Here at the end it adds: “In Gaul, in the town of Dinant in Brabant, the deposition of Saint Perpetuus, bishop and confessor of Tongeren or Liège.” See Castellanus.

**AQUICINCTENSIS** calls Proculus a bishop and martyr. At the end: “In the city of Bourges, Saint Lusor, bishop.” Our Florus celebrates Lusor today at Bourges, not as a bishop but as a boy, called *Lude* in French, who was placed in Castellanus’s Martyrology on 1 November.

**DAVERONENSIS**, incomplete in the text, adds: “Saint Luxor, bishop, in the district of Bourges.”

[Col. 0658B] **MATRICENSIS-CARTHUSIENSIS-ULTRAJECTENSIS:** “Amantius, bishop in Gaul. Perpetuus, bishop of Liège. Hierius, priest of Alexandria, concerning whom Blessed Jerome writes.” See the Observations.

**CAMBERIENSIS:** “In the city of Aachen, Saint Nutricius, martyr.” Nothing about him appears in the other manuscripts.

In the **VATICAN** manuscript, marked no. 5949, the entire final announcement is absent.

**ALTEMPS:** “Likewise, in the city of Wenta, Saint Brinstanus, bishop and confessor.”

**LUGDUNENSIS**, instead of Amantius, writes *Amonius*.

**BURDEGALENSIS:** “In the city of Bourges, Saint Lusor, bishop.” See what we said under **AQUICINCTENSIS**.

The **LUBECO-COLONIENSIS EDITION** smells of Ado in the first announcement. The second is fairly pure, retaining *Redonis*, as others do. Then: “In Gaul, in the town of Dinant, the birthday of Saint Perpetuus, bishop and confessor of Tongeren.” It omits Clarus. Concerning Proculus, as in the others above. Then it adds this history: “On the same day, Saint Perpetua [Col. 0658C] the martyr, wife of Saint Peter the Apostle. When the torturers were pressing her toward martyrdom, Saint Peter boldly exhorted her in the Lord with these words: ‘My wife, remember that the Lord Jesus Christ suffered for you, and do not fear those who kill the body but cannot destroy your soul.’ Strengthened by these words in the Lord, she gladly, patiently, and courageously endured death for Christ. At Trier, Saint Modesta, virgin. In the territory of Nevers, Saint Honoratus, confessor. On the same day, Saint Quilianus, confessor.”

**BELINUS** is not altogether pure in the first announcement. Concerning Amantius and Proculus, as above. Then: “In Hungary, at Alba Regalis, the deposition of Blessed Emericus, confessor, son of Saint King Stephen. Likewise, on the same day, at the city of Bologna, Saints Vitalis and Agricola, martyrs, the latter of whom was the former’s servant,” etc., as in **ALBERGENSIS**, but with the names transposed so that Vitalis is the servant, and with the ending added: “and thus they completed [Col. 0658D] their martyrdom.” Then: “In the district of Vilcassinum, Saint Clarus, martyr.” A second edition adds: “Likewise at Bourges, Saint Lusor, bishop.”

**GREVEN:** “According to the Catalogue and others here, the birthday of Saints Agricola and Vitalis, whom Usuard has below, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December. In Africa, Saints Primus, Caesarius, Gregorius, Porphyrius, and others.” From the Hieronymian Martyrologies. “In Gaul, in the town of Dinant, the deposition of Saint Perpetuus, bishop and confessor of Liège. Briscanus, bishop and confessor. Annianus, bishop. In the territory of Nevers, Honoratus, confessor. Quilianus, confessor. Lusorius, confessor. Likewise, Saint Gregory, abbot, son of the king of Greece, first founder and ruler of the monastery of Porcetum near Aachen. At Trier, Saint Modesta, virgin. Odrada, virgin. On the same day, Saint Perpetua, martyr, wife of Blessed Peter the Apostle. When she was being led to punishment for the faith of Christ, Saint Peter called out to her: ‘O wife,’” and the rest as above.

**MOLANUS:** “Likewise at Bourges, the deposition of Saint Lusor, boy and confessor, who is said to have died in white garments as the son of a certain senator. This is written in the book of miracles by Gregory, bishop of Tours.” Concerning Modesta and Emericus, as **GREVEN**. Concerning Agricola and Vitalis, as **BELINUS**, but correctly. Concerning Perpetuus and Perpetua, almost as in the manuscripts above. Then, in smaller type, concerning Gregory, as **GREVEN**. Next: “The deposition of Blessed Florus, bishop and confessor, whose episcopal see is now called by his name. Likewise at Tours, the seven Sleepers, Clement, Primus, Cletus, Theodorus, Gaudentius, Quiriacus, and Innocentius, nephews of Blessed Martin through two brothers, whose celebrated life and conduct Gregory, archbishop of Tours, described.” [Col. 0660A]

Other editions insert Agricola and Vitalis into the text at the beginning. At the end, concerning Emericus, as we said from **GREVEN**. It continues: “At Dinant, Saint Perpetuus, bishop and confessor of the church of Liège.” Concerning Perpetua, as in the manuscripts. “Near Aachen, at Porcetum, the passing of Saint Gregory, abbot. Likewise at Bourges, the deposition of Saint Lusor, boy,” etc., as in the earlier edition. Then concerning Modesta. Hence: “At Velay, the deposition of Saint Florus, bishop and confessor, whose episcopal see is now called by his name. On the fourth day, Saint Nicander, martyr and bishop of Myra. And Saint Joannicius, the great father.” The distinguished Acts of this most celebrated saint, in Greek and Latin, will be issued in due time, as we promised long ago.]

[Col. 0655]

At Alexandria, Blessed Hierius, priest, who, nobly learned in the divine Scriptures, of most pure life, and naked and wholly free of worldly attachments for Christian philosophy, was an incomparable teacher of the Church. He rested in the time of the Emperor Philip. In Gaul, in the city of Rotenus, Saint Amantius, bishop, whose life was glorious in holiness and miracles. In the district of Vilcassinum, Saint Clarus, priest and martyr. At Augustodunum, Saint Proculus, bishop.

**Nonis. Day 5.** [Note: [Col. 0659]

Many are pure on this day: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0659B]

Some codices insert between “father” and “John” the appropriate title “saint” or “blessed.” I preferred those which come closest to the *Romanum parvum* and to Ado. *Tracina* and *Caesareum* are errors in *Antuerp.-Maj.*, as is *Cesarem* in Muneratus. Belin has *converterent* [Col. 0660B] instead of *converteret*; Rosweyd has *baptizavit* instead of *baptizabat*. Belin again changed *inde* to *deinde*, and the name *Laeti* to *Leviti*. Muneratus alone adds *confessoris* after *presbyteri*.

### Note [Col. 0659B]

This is the first announcement for this day in the *Romanum parvum*, and the first marked by it itself: “Zacharias the prophet, father of John the Baptist.” The words are the same in Ado and Usuard, as is clear from our text; nor is any memory of this Zacharias found in the older Calendars or Martyrologies of Jerome, Bede, Florus, or Rabanus. Hence one may again readily infer that the day was selected arbitrarily. Was it selected by the author of the *Romanum parvum*? I certainly think so, since we have already observed so many times that he was accustomed to do this throughout.

But how did this day become known to Wandalbertus before the others, since I have elsewhere said that it is unlikely that Wandalbertus saw the *Romanum parvum*? Ado certainly speaks as though he were the first to bring to Gaul a treasure unearthed in Italy. Yet one must admit that at least some knowledge—perhaps from the city of Rome itself—had reached Wandalbertus earlier, for such open agreement concerning several prophets could not have been accidental. In any case, wherever the metrical Martyrologist found that Zacharias was especially to be celebrated on this day, he sings of him as follows:

> On the Nones, Zacharias, prophet and priest of the temple,  
> Stands forth: he who, through the gift of his son,  
> Received again his prophet’s voice and office,  
> Long forgotten according to the ancient custom.

More certain records concerning this holy Prophet must be drawn from the Gospel. Baronius discusses several disputed matters in the *Annals* and in his note for the present day; Tillemont likewise treats them in volume I, beginning at page 482. We shall discuss these matters more fully elsewhere, as well as the conjunction with Elizabeth made in the Roman Martyrology.

Felix and Eusebius, taken by Bede from the Acts of Saint Caesarius—whom we treated on 1 November—and entered into the sacred lists, were therefore clearly copied in their entire eulogy by Ado. Our author has not inelegantly abridged the text from one or the other of them. Rabanus followed Bede in the usual manner. In the *Romanum parvum* one simply reads: “At Terracina, Felix the presbyter and Eusebius the monk.”

The Acts of Caesarius were discussed on the first day of November already cited. I have nothing to add here until they can be reviewed more carefully and perhaps defended against Tillemont’s note in volume II, beginning at page 574. Here the Viennese Martyrograph ends, unless someone wishes to attribute to it the announcement rejected by Rosweyd to the appendix: “At Capua, the city, the holy martyrs Eura, Quartus, and Pardus.” On this, see Florentinius’s final note for this day.

Meanwhile I append Wandalbertus’s final verse:

> And these the sacred Felix and the monk Eusebius increase.

Laetus is genuinely and properly Usuardine: he is called a presbyter, although the life published from the Floriacensian Library by Surius and Gononus calls him only a deacon. Some find much to criticize in the aforementioned life. It exists separately in print and manuscript in our Museum, together with a learned man’s observation on it, published at Charleville in 1675. He says that it displays pure verbosity, except for what it reports concerning the relics with sufficient authenticity. It is not our task rashly or prematurely to decide anything in these matters. We give Usuard here; that is sufficient.

### Note [Col. 0659D]

**Pulsanen.** In the first part it is sufficiently pure; the second continues only as far as “of the emperor”; the rest is missing.

**Antwerp and Max.-Lübeck.** At the end they add to the pure text:

> In the territory of Langres, in the monastery of Clairvaux, the feast of Saint Malachy, bishop and confessor.

**Antwerp-Max., Utrecht, Leiden, and Leuven.** They have the same as the two preceding witnesses, except that Antwerp-Max. incorrectly writes “in the territory of Linge,” but all add:

> Whose life shone forth full of virtues.

**Alberg and Danish.** Besides Malachy they add: “At Trier, Saint Abrunculus, bishop and confessor.” Alberg indeed writes this, but the other has the better reading *Fibitius*.

**Centulensian.** The first part is pure. The following words occur:

> As above in the monastery;

Nothing is added by which one might know whether the reference is to the monastery of Centula or to another, perhaps Clairvaux and Malachy. Then:

> In Campania, in the city of Terracina, the holy Felix the presbyter and Eusebius the monk, martyr.

The final announcement is missing.

**Brussels.** Also sufficiently pure in the first part, after “of the emperor Claudius” it inserts:

> They were arrested by Leontius, the son of Leontius the consul, chiefly because they had buried Caesarius, who had made his father a Christian, as well as Julian and other holy martyrs of God, and because Eusebius converted many,

and so forth. Then:

> And the holy Domninus, Epiphanius, Antoninus, Marcia, Secunda, and Quartus. At Trier, the burial of Saint Fibitius, bishop and confessor.

Then it gives Malachy as the Antwerp-Max. witness above does, and at the end Laetus purely.

**Hagenoyen.**

> At Jerusalem, the birth-feast of Zacharias the prophet, father of Saint John the Baptist. He was a prophet of the New Testament. An angel closed his mouth in the temple when he did not believe concerning the birth of the son whom the angel foretold would be born. Thus, after the birth of John the Baptist, he received speech and prophecy again by divine power, and prophesied concerning Christ, while he was still enclosed in his mother’s womb, and concerning his own son after his birth. Some say that this Zacharias was stoned by Herod of Ascalon.

On the same day at Rome, the passion of Saint Perpetua, wife of Saint Peter the Apostle, who suffered under the persecution of Nero Caesar. As she went to her passion, blessed Peter cried out behind her: “O wife, remember the Lord.”

See the preceding day. In the entry for Felix and Eusebius it is not pure, and it notes the time of the emperor Commodus. It continues:

> At Bayeux, the burial of Saint Vigor, bishop.

This belongs to 1 November.

> In Hungary, Saint Henry [I think, for Emeric], duke and confessor.

From 4 November. Finally:

> In the district of the Vexin, Saint Maturinus.

You see the great confusion, for Maturinus belongs to 1 November.

**The principal codex of Ursinus by Rosemberg:**

> At Trier, Saint Feberius, bishop.

For *Fibitius*.

**Matric.-Carthus.-Utrecht:**

> Of Malachy, bishop, who rests at Cîteaux; concerning whose passing blessed Bernard preached a sermon.

**Cambrai:**

> On the same day, Saint Modesta, virgin.

**Vatican**, marked no. 5949, lacks the announcements of Zacharias and Laetus. It adds:

> At Benevento, the feast of Saint Pardus, martyr in Saint Sophia. And Saint Trophima, virgin and martyr.

**Ughellian.** At the end:

> At Clairvaux, the burial of Saint Malachy, archbishop and confessor.

**Dijon**, church of Saint Stephen:

> At Langres, the translation of Saint Gregory, bishop.

**Lübeck-Cologne edition.** The first part is sufficiently pure; the second is moderately interpolated; the third adds “and confessor.” Then:

> At Trier, Saint Fibitius, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Langres, in the monastery of Clairvaux, Saint Malachy, bishop and confessor, who was patriarch of all Ireland and is said to have founded fifty-four collegiate churches. His life also shone forth full of virtues.

He is placed on 2 November in Castellan II, and on 3 November in the Roman Martyrology.

### Note [Col. 0662B]

**Greven.**

> At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the holy Domninus, Epiphanius, Antoninus, Mark the bishop, and ten others. At Capua in Campania, the feast of the holy Marcia, Secunda, Sechiruda, and Quartus. At Trier, Saint Fibitius, bishop and confessor. Also Saint Caesarius. Among the Cistercians, the memory of Saint Malachy, patriarch of Ireland, is celebrated as a feast on this day. The elevation of Saint Emeric, duke of Slavonia and confessor. At Ideburga, a matron, mother of Saint Gertrude the virgin.

She is called *Ydubega* or *Itta* by others. See what we said in the appendices to Molanus, 8 May.

**Molanus.**

> In the territory of Langres, in the monastery of Clairvaux, Saint Malachy, bishop and confessor, whose life blessed Bernard described as glorious in miracles. On the same day, Saint Febitius, bishop of Trier.

Later editions insert concerning Malachy:

> who shone forth in his time through great virtues.

Concerning Fibitius, as in the earlier edition. At the end they add:

> On the fifth day, the holy martyrs Galaction and Episteme.

See their deeds in Surius.

[Col. 0659]

Zacharias the prophet, father of John the Baptist. In the city of Terracina in Campania, the feast of the holy Felix the presbyter and Eusebius the monk, in the time of the emperor Claudius. When Eusebius had buried the holy martyrs Julian and Caesarius, and was converting many to the faith, whom Felix the presbyter was baptizing, both were arrested and brought before the judge’s tribunal, but were not overcome. They were then confined in prison, and on that same night, when they refused to sacrifice, they were beheaded. In the territory of Orléans, Saint Laetus the presbyter.

## Eighth day before the Ides. Day 6

### Note [Col. 0661]

From Pratensis, Tornacensis, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.

### Note [Col. 0661C]

The reading is *Toniza* in all the codices except Greven, who incorrectly has *Tonza* in his customary African manner. Others write *Thimissa*. Yet Baronius also supports *Toniza*, from the Itinerary of Antoninus, where his corresponding note constructs another, nearly synonymous, African city, *Tynissa* or *Tunissa*, commonly Tunis. Hence it becomes doubtful whether interpreters correctly render our *Toniza* as Tunis. If I am not mistaken, the manner of writing found in all the ancient codices ought to be retained, although I entirely recoil from the change of *m* to *n*, which suggests something of a Hispanic dialect.

*Theophili* for *Theopoli* is an error in Muneratus and Greven. Here again appears *Phrygia*, and it is found in nearly all the codices; only Pratensis and Greven have *Phrigia*; Molanus correctly has *Phrygia*. Tornacensis and Muneratus read *Atici*. We regard the remaining matters concerning *Africae*, *solemnitate*, and similar details as minor points. It will be evident in the appendices that some codices, such as Belin, Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and others, incorrectly substituted “In Africa” for “In Phrygia.” In our Pratensis copy, the following was written beneath a line and therefore appears as an addition:

> In the district of Lenovium, in the noble village, the feast of Saint Bernard the confessor.

The reading *Bernardi* is incorrect, but no one fails to understand what is intended. See the appendices.

### Note [Col. 0661D]

The Hieronymian copies at Florentinius unanimously read today:

> And at Toniza, or Tonize, in Africa, Felix;

or:

> the feast of Felix;

or:

> the feast of Saint Felix.

The commentator observes concerning these that a memory of Saint Felix exists in Augustine, *Tractate on Psalm 127*. That is, the present Roman Martyrology, following Ado as I think, asserts as certain what he had put forward conjecturally. The author of the *Romanum parvum* had simply written:

> At Toniza in Africa, Saint Felix the martyr.

Add the words of our text. They constitute Ado’s wording in full, where that Martyrologist, explicitly expressing doubt, appears to explain it. He appends all the words of the holy Doctor from the tract just cited. Whether these truly apply to this Felix rather than to another—for there are several of that name—has not yet been established with certainty, as Castellan rightly observed; although otherwise I readily agree with Baronius, until we can examine the whole matter more carefully.

The appendices to Bede attribute forty companions to Felix, but their authority completely vanishes when compared with the Martyrologies cited. I would not hesitate to conjecture that some ignorant enlarger of Bede’s Martyrology combined two announcements of the *Romanum parvum* into one. In any case, if what is reported from Augustine was truly said about the Felix of this day, it may be illustrated more fully in its proper place.

Wandalbertus sang only of Felix:

> On the eighth Ides, the martyr Felix is celebrated.

I do not rightly understand what the author of the *Romanum parvum* intends by his second and final announcement:

> In the city of Theopolis, eleven martyrs.

I understand Theopolis as Antioch, which we have discussed elsewhere; Baronius’s note for the present day may also be consulted. But who are those forty martyrs? Ado, who ought to have shed light on the matter, made it more complicated through the text which our author again copied here in full. Only ten are introduced there, said to have suffered under the Saracens in the Acts of the Forty Saints, as though he were beginning to speak of something universally known.

But this is precisely what I investigate: who are those forty whose Acts say that ten suffered under the Saracens? Why are the other thirty, joined together by the *Romanum parvum*, excluded here? What are those Acts cited by Ado but probably never seen by him? At what time are we to believe that they suffered—whether the ten alone or all forty?

Baronius refers to the time when Antioch was plundered by the Saracens under Chosroes, king of the Persians. Yet the matter might perhaps with equal probability be assigned to the year 637, or rather 638, when that city was captured by the same Arabs. I confess that here I do not see where I can safely stand unless someone supplies more certain evidence. Would that my doubts might at least bring about the discovery of the evidence somewhere!

The six Phrygian martyrs are named individually in all the codices cited; of them the Roman Martyrology, following Usuard, records only Atticus. This is Florentinius’s correct observation on the Hieronymian Martyrologies, also used by Castellan, to which I add our own observation, repeated elsewhere more than once: it is customary among our Martyrologists, especially Usuard, to select one or two individuals from the larger groups of martyrs in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, without any mention of their companions. This has been evident above in many places, and here too it is clear that the entire entry is genuinely and simply Usuardine.

### Note [Col. 0663B]

**Pratensis.** Concerning the appendix added to this codex, perhaps in the margin, I spoke in the *Variants*. Sirmond notes that the same reading is found in the first hand of codex B.

**Herinien.** Entirely pure throughout, but at the end, perhaps as a local addition, it has:

> At Bergues, the burial of Saint Winoc.

**Antwerp-Maj.** At the end:

> In the district of Limoges, the feast of Saint Leonard the confessor. On the same day, the burial of Saint Winnoc the confessor.

**Rosweyd.** Everything else:

> In Africa, Paul with seven other martyrs; Willebald, bishop and confessor; Herculian, confessor.

**Pulsanen.** Begins:

> In the territory of Dunois, the burial of the most blessed Leonard, eminent confessor.

Felix is missing. It reads “fifty saints.” Nothing concerning Atticus.

**Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, and Ughellian.** In the first and second parts sufficiently pure, they continue:

> In Africa, Saint Atticus.

At the end:

> At Rennes, Saint Melanius the confessor.

See Greven below.

**Antwerp-Maj., Leuven, and Belgian Leiden.** Their text largely agrees with the two preceding witnesses, but at the end:

> Also the feast of Saint Leonard the confessor.

What these place at the end, the Danish witness puts at the beginning:

> The feast of Saint Leonard the confessor.

**Leiden.** Its text is like the others, but at the end it adds in a somewhat fuller form:

> Also the feast of Saint Leonard the confessor. Because of his merits, which were to be demonstrated to all, when the brothers were transferring his body for burial, snow fell contrary to the season and covered the place where the saint wished to be buried. Once buried there, he performs wonderful works, especially for captives.

Utrecht and Alberg have this same eulogy of Saint Leonard at the beginning.

**Centulensian:**

> At Toniza in Africa, Saint Felix the martyr. In the territory of Orléans, Saint Laetus the presbyter.

The entry concerning Atticus follows purely.

> In the district of Limoges, Saint Leonard, eminent confessor. On the same day, the burial of Saint Winnoc the abbot, who was a monk of Saint Bertin. In the eastern city of Theopolis, the ten holy martyrs who suffered under the Saracens.

See the Observations.

**Brussels.** Begins:

> At Nobiliacum, near Limoges, the burial of Saint Leonard the abbot and confessor, disciple of blessed Remigius. He shone forth with his brother Lifard through miracles and holiness.

The announcement concerning Felix is confused and is interpolated from Ado; it is purer in the second part. It also places Atticus in Africa. Then:

> At Rennes, the burial of Saint Melanius, bishop and confessor. And Saint Winnoc, abbot and confessor, who came from Britain and shone forth in Gaul through the holiness of his life.

**Hagenoyen.** The first part is sufficiently pure. The second concerns Clarius of the Vexin, and the third Proculus of Autun. Then comes the entry concerning the ten from Theopolis, reasonably correctly. The entry concerning Malachy follows. Then:

> On the same day, the burial of Saint Leonard the abbot. He was raised from the sacred font by Saint Remigius the archbishop and was instructed by him in discipline. His parents had initially held positions at the palace of the king of France. He obtained such favor from the king that all prisoners whom he visited were immediately released, etc.

I would rather have this read in the *Life* published by Surius. Instead of *Attici*, it reads *Amri*.

**Aquicinct.** At the end it adds to the text:

> At Rennes, Saint Melanius the confessor. In the district of Limoges, Saint Leonard the confessor, who was a disciple of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims. The burial of Saint Winnoc the abbot.

**Victorin and Swedish Register no. 130.** They place Atticus in Africa. At the end:

> At Rennes, Saint Melanius the confessor.

**Daveronensian:**

> In the territory of Tours, Saint Lupantius the confessor. In the district of Limoges, Saint Leonard the confessor, who in the time of King Clovis, born of a noble Frankish lineage and baptized and instructed by blessed Remigius, archbishop of Reims, abandoned his homeland and chose the eremitical life.
