He died at Nobiliacum, renowned for miracles, especially the liberation of those in chains, and lives in Christ.

**Ambianensian:**

> On the same day, Saint Leonard the confessor.

**Matric.-Carthus.-Utrecht:**

> Leonard the abbot. Willehad, bishop and confessor.

Concerning the latter, see the Roman Martyrology on 8 November.

> The ten holy martyrs. Felix the confessor.

Is this the one placed at Fundi in Latium in the Roman Martyrology?

**Swedish Register no. 428:**

> In the district of Limoges, the burial of Saint Leonard the confessor.

**Codex and Le Mare, marked A:**

> On the same day, the arrival of the relics of Saints Nazarius and Celsus from the Italian regions.

In Vatican no. 5949 the final announcement is missing. It adds:

> At Benevento, Saint Castus, bishop and martyr.

**Altemps:**

> In Britain, Saints Winnebald and Winnoc, abbot and confessor. In Lesser Britain, Saint Thenteonicus the abbot.

The name is not correctly expressed; it may also be read *Thenteonici*. Perhaps it will be better understood once it has been trimmed from some fuller account.

**Florentinian:**

> Saint Leonard … Saint Appianus the confessor, who, a Ligurian by birth, was a monk at the Golden Heaven. At Rennes, Saint Melanius the confessor.

**Besançon:**

> The translation of Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres.

This was placed on the preceding day from the Dijon codex.

**Lübeck-Cologne edition.** It begins:

> In the district of Limoges, at the place called Nobiliacum, the burial of Saint Leonard the abbot and confessor. He was raised from the sacred font by blessed Remigius, bishop of the church of Reims, and instructed by him in salutary disciplines. He entered a certain forest and, having built a monastery there, lived in it with some monks under the strictest discipline; finally he ended his life there in peace. To demonstrate his merit to all, when the brothers transferred his body for burial and looked out over the entire province, they found the whole region covered with snow, contrary to the season, while the place in which the holy man had wished to rest was completely free of snow, where, once buried, he performs wonderful works, especially for captives.

The remainder is sufficiently pure. At the end:

> In the territory of Tours, Saint Lupantius the confessor.

**Belin.** In the first and second parts it is moderately pure; in the third it has:

> In Africa, Saint Atricius.

At the end:

> At Rennes, Saint Melanius. On the same day, Saint Leonard the confessor.

Another edition reads *Melanius*. In second place, however, it inserts:

> At Nicomedia, Saint Adrian the martyr.

**Greven:**

> At Nicaea, the feast of Saints Adrian, Julia, and Eusebius. In Africa, Saints Donatus, Paul, and Balsam. Also Eustasius and Julius.

See the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

> According to some, on this day, Melanius, bishop of Rennes, whom Usuard has above on the eighth day before the Ides of January, and Ado on the second day before the Ides of November.

Rosweyd therefore rightly rejected to the appendix some uncertain announcement for this day. It continues:

> At Bergues, the burial of the four holy brothers Winnotus, Quadenotus, Ingenotus, and Madenotus. In the territory of Tours, Saint Lupantius the confessor. In the district of Limoges, the burial of Saint Leonard the abbot and confessor. He was raised from the sacred font by Saint Remigius and instructed in salutary disciplines. Entering a certain forest, he led an austere life with his companions, shining forth even during his life through many miracles, especially the liberation of captives, and finally rested in peace. When his disciples wished to transfer his sacred body to another place, they saw the entire province covered with snow except for the place where it had pleased the man of God to rest. Also Saint Christina of Stommeln, resting at Nybeck [also Nydeck] in the Duchy of Jülich.

She has now been transferred to Jülich, where her relics are exposed for veneration. See the Acts for 22 June.

**Molanus:**

> On the same day, the restoration of our holy Father Gislenus. In the territory of Tours, blessed Lupantius the confessor. At Rennes, Saint Melanius the confessor. On the same day, Saint Leonard the confessor, disciple of Saint Remigius the bishop, in the city of Limoges, in the province of Aquitaine. At Bergues, in the territory called the cell of Aoromholt, the burial of Saint Winnoc the abbot, an eminent confessor of Christ, whose life shone forth full of virtues and miracles. He persevered for a long time in the work of God in the aforementioned place, gathered many into the service of God, and, very renowned for great virtues and glorious miracles, was gathered to his fathers in a good old age.

Then, in smaller type:

> Concerning him it is read in his life that he considered it an eminent duty to serve the brothers subject to him, because he knew that Christ had not come to be served but to serve; and that whatever tasks other hands avoided as arduous and burdensome, he did not fear to undertake eagerly and without hesitation, although he possessed the title of royal nobility. For a long time he turned with his own hands a mill built for the use of the poor brothers. On the same day, Severus, bishop of Barcelona, who was one of the seventy bishops who established the Gothic laws in Spain. He was crowned with martyrdom by the Gothic barbarians who inhabited Catalonia: they pierced his head with a nail. This occurred in the year 638 of the redemption of Jesus Christ.

The question is from which Martyrology Molanus took this final material. Other editions contain the same, but most of it is contracted much more briefly.

[Col. 0661]

At Toniza in Africa, the feast of Saint Felix. On his solemnity, blessed Augustine appears to explain a certain psalm to the people. In the eastern city of Theopolis, the ten holy martyrs who are said to have suffered under the Saracens in the Acts of the Forty Saints. In Phrygia, Saint Atticus. [Bouillart adds in the margin of the text: “In the district of Limoges, at Nobiliacum, the feast of Saint Leonard the confessor.”]

## Seventh day before the Ides. Day 7

### Note [Col. 0665]

The following are pure: Pratensis, Herinien, Antwerp-Maj., Antwerp, Max.-Lübeck, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus.

### Note [Col. 0665D]

Only Antwerp-Maj. reads *Achillei*; this is also found in the *Romanum parvum*, but was more correctly restored by Ado and Usuard as it stands in the text. Greven, and Molanus, who copies him here, read *qui in eruditione*; in all the others the preposition *in* is redundant. Muneratus alone adds *et martyris* after “Herculani episcopi.” There are many other scribal errors, such as *Achilli*, *Prusinam*, *Albiensem*, and so on. In Antwerp-Maj. and Molanus, *et confessoris* has been added at the end after *episcopi*. The greatest variation concerns the formation of the name Willibrord, which we have taken from Greven; all the others differ, writing *Willeboldi*, *Wullebrodi*, *Willebrordi*, *Villebrordi*, *Wllebrordi*, *Vuellebrodi*, and so forth.

I have placed here the difficulties concerning the eulogy of Herculanus. First, the best authorities leave no room to doubt that it is Usuard’s own, indeed all the codices except the Tornacensian and Pulsanensian, which we have so often found mutilated in their eulogies elsewhere. Second, it is plainly taken from Gregory’s *Dialogues*, book 3, chapter 13. But how are we to say that it was formed in such a way that it does not convey Gregory’s meaning?

Pratensis reads:

> Whose body, after the cutting off of his head, remained so intact;

all the others have:

> remained so joined,

and so forth. Muneratus has:

> Whose body was so joined to the severing of his head,

where, in accordance with Gregory’s meaning, he should more correctly have said:

> was so joined to the severed head.

Gregory’s reading is:

> His head had been so joined to his body as though it had not been severed at all, so that no traces of the cut appeared. When they turned him onto his back and examined whether any sign of another incision could be shown, the whole body was found so healthy and unviolated, as though no cut of iron had touched it.

What if Usuard did not possess a genuine Gregorian exemplar? In every other respect it is as certain that the eulogy is Usuardine as the unanimous agreement of all the codices, both manuscript and printed, is certain.

In our Pratensis *astigraph*, however, the entire passage is marked beneath the line as though it were an addition. Castellan testifies that in the margin of the supposed autograph it was written by a later hand—“in the margin and in letters less ancient than the text.” I ask which hand is the autograph. If one examines this and similar passages recurring throughout the codex without distinction, I am mistaken if one does not conclude that neither the earlier nor the later hand is Usuardine. More on this in the Preface.

### Note [Col. 0667B]

At the beginning of this month there recurs a third citation of book VII, chapter 29, of the Eusebius-Rufinus history. From it Achillas here, as well as Theodotus on 2 November and Plerius or Hierius on 4 November, was taken by the author of the *Romanum parvum*, who extracted all of them from that source and noted them in this form:

> At Alexandria, Achillas the bishop.

Ado more correctly has *Achillae*. He also took from the cited passage the material for the eulogy, changing the wording slightly; our author copied it word for word. Here again this is a saint who should not be sought among other Martyrologists outside our series. Nor should one labor in vain to discover why he is commemorated on this day rather than any other, since I plainly believe that this was done here and in many other places solely at the discretion of the author of the *Romanum parvum*.

See what I determined more plausibly as the true day of his death in my treatise *On the Patriarchs of Alexandria*, chapter 3, page 36, beginning at number 188. There I have also briefly collected the matters relating to his life, which should be compared with Tillemont’s article in volume VI, pages 213–214.

### Note [Col. 0667C]

In the *Romanum parvum* cited above, the second and final place is occupied by:

> At Perusia, Herculanus the bishop and martyr.

For the sake of clarity Ado inserted “a city of Italy,” marking Herculanus as the third entry but without any further eulogy. The whole eulogy, expressed in Usuard’s words and taken from Gregory’s *Dialogues*, although not quite correctly, must therefore be regarded as having been derived from there, as we abundantly demonstrated above from the best codices.

These matters are sufficiently certain on the authority of Gregory, whom Usuard cites as his witness. As for the two Herculanuses, bishops of Perusia, Baronius attempts to explain the matter in his note. Yet he applied Gregory’s eulogy to that Herculanus whose feast or translation is commemorated on 1 March. It is therefore easy to understand that uncertainty and doubt have remained here, just as they remain with all who do not allow themselves to be led astray by local prejudices.

Our Janningus will in due time provide a most careful investigation of these twin Herculanuses—or perhaps of several—together with the other multiplied saints of Umbria. Through it, most of those dense darknesses in which Umbria was long enveloped, as Bollandus once testified, may be dispelled.

Amarantus was first placed in second position by the Viennese Martyrologist, from whose brief eulogy Usuard took all his words. The source is Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 57, who calls him *Amarandus*. I do not know that anything else about this saint’s deeds has been handed down to memory.

Wandalbertus honored him together with Willibrord as follows:

> Amarantus, you hallowed the seventh [day] by a holy death.  
> Willibrord too has this [honour], under whose leadership  
> Many of the Frisian people perceived Christ calling them.

Rosweyd rightly separated Willibrord from Ado, whatever Mosander may insert him into the text of Ado’s Martyrology without an asterisk. Rabanus places him on the preceding day, following the author of Alcuin’s *Life*. But here I infer from this alone that the passage is genuinely and specifically Usuard’s: our wording is plainly quite different from that attributed to Ado.

In any case, the memory of this most illustrious saint is held in the highest veneration not only among the Frisians and Batavians but also among the Brabantians and especially the people of Antwerp, as the many outstanding monuments show in the *Annals of Antwerp*, recently prepared by our teacher Daniel Papebrochius but still in manuscript. His memory is also dear in our Museum because of that celebrated and very ancient codex of the Hieronymian Martyrology, commonly called the Antwerp and Echternach codex. The Preface to the Bollandist work, page XLVI, shows that this holy man used it and that it was written by Laurentius.

A life of him, composed by Alcuin in both prose and metrical form, exists in Surius and was reproduced by Mabillon and illustrated with notes in *The Benedictine Century III*, part I, beginning at page 601. The eulogies of Bede and others may be added to it.

[Col. 0665]

In Alexandria, the blessed Achillas, bishop, who was distinguished in learning, faith, conduct, and morals. At Perugia, a city of Italy [Note: [Col. 0665C] Sollerius raises many questions concerning Herculanus. He rightly maintains that the eulogy of Herculanus should be attributed to Usuard, since all the best manuscripts, both handwritten and printed, agree. Yet because this eulogy is found not in the text of the Pratensis codex but in the margin, written by a more recent hand, this led the acute critic to doubt which hand was the author’s—or, as he himself puts it, which hand was the autograph. He removes this doubt by holding that neither the earlier nor the later hand was Usuard’s, and that anyone who, laying aside partisan zeal, examines this and the other defects of the Pratensis codex will reach the same judgment.

I appeal to all scholars: can a few words added in the margin or in the blank space between verses by a more recent hand—which is the one defect of the Pratensis codex, if indeed it is a defect—incline anyone to doubt that the Martyrology is an autograph, when its chronological indications and the form of its letters show that it was written in the ninth century, in Usuard’s own age; when it was composed at the abbey of Saint-Germain and arranged for the use of that same abbey by a monk of the same abbey; when it was publicly read in the chapter for three hundred years or more; and when it was preserved with the greatest care in a library that was never plundered or burned, at least from the ninth century onward? What can be certain in this branch of literature, if this is not?

I have already explained in a letter concerning the eulogy of Herculanus, added to the margin of the codex, how it happened that it was absent from the autograph codex and yet found in all the copies. BOUILLART.], the birthday of Saint Herculanus, bishop. After his head had been cut off, his body was found on the fortieth day so united and sound, as Blessed Pope Gregory writes, as though no cut of iron had touched it. On the same day, Blessed Amarantus, martyr, who, after completing the course of his faithful contest near the city of Albi, was buried and lives in glory. In Frisia, the deposition of Saint Willibrord, bishop.

VI Idus. Day 8. [Note: [Col. 0671A]

The Pratensis, Heriniensis, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts agree. Likewise the Antwerp-Maximilian, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Albergen, and Danish manuscripts.] 

[Note: [Col. 0671A]

The reading should be *Symphroniani* in the Roman parvum and Ado, not *Simphoriani*, as Rosweyd, Max-Lübeck, Greven, and Molan incorrectly have. Nevertheless, *Simproniani* had to be retained on the authority of the better manuscripts. In our Pratensis copy *Castorii* is missing. Some manuscripts read “sent into prison,” but the purer ones read it as in the text. The copyists seem to have hesitated chiefly over the final formula of the text—namely, whether it should say “under the names of the five martyrs mentioned above,” or rather “of four martyrs.” The Pratensis and Munerat manuscripts incorrectly read “four”; Greven and Molan suppress the number; the others, following the Roman parvum and Ado, and consequently also Usuard, correctly read, as the sense requires, “of the five martyrs mentioned above.” The others have *Carpofori* in the text and *repperiri*. There is little worth noting about *Nichostrati*, *Severini* for *Severi*, or *coleretur* for *recoleretur*. In the Pratensis, however, the particle before *Domino* seems to be missing; the construction should therefore be formed as in Munerat, *statutum est autem*.]

[Note: [Col. 0671B]

The author of the Roman parvum first joined these two classes of martyrs in the Martyrology, though he was not himself the first author of the combination, since he could have found it in the Roman Sacramentaries, especially the Gregorian, where the first five are named individually and the four Coronati anonymously are joined in the same Mass. Thus, in the first prayer Claudius, Nicostratus, and the others are expressly named, while the Preface speaks of the four anonymous Coronati. The following explanation is prefixed to that Mass:

> “The names of the Four Crowned Ones are these: Severus, Severianus, Victorinus, and Carpophorus. Their birthday, through negligence, had been disregarded and could not be found at all. Therefore it was decreed that in their church the birthday of these five saints, who are recited in the Mass, should be celebrated, so that their memory also might be commemorated together with these.”

On this subject see the variant manuscript readings in Menard’s notes, p. 185, where he also discusses the church of the Four Crowned Ones, its title, and so forth.

Now compare with this the following words of the Roman parvum:

> “At Rome, the martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, most distinguished craftsmen. And on the same day, the Four Crowned Ones, Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus; Pope Melchiades decreed that their feast should be celebrated under the names of five martyrs, because their names could not be found, but after some years they were revealed to a certain holy man.”

Here you see almost the same opinion of the Sacramentary being reported. Menard, and with him some more recent writers, asks how the names of the holy Coronati could have been unknown in Melchiades’ time, especially since they are said to have suffered under the persecution of Diocletian. But I see nothing here that should cause such astonishment—as though not several, indeed very many, had been crowned during that savage slaughter, perhaps in the presence of Melchiades, whose distinct names nevertheless did not come to his attention.

Here belongs the criticism of Saussay, who, scrutinizing every corner of the Roman parvum, a little work hateful to him, loudly declares that he has encountered something ridiculous: the Four Crowned Ones are celebrated under the names of five martyrs. But this has been solidly refuted by Florentinius in Preliminary Admonition IV, p. 19, as we also indicated in chapter 2 of our Preface. Saussay might rather have attacked Bede—if he had known the real Bede. For Bede provided the occasion for these quibbles when he wrote, without distinction:

> “At Rome, the Four Crowned Ones, Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius,”

where the names of some seem to have been substituted for those of others, though they must in the end be brought back to the same explanation. If this explanation is not satisfactory, let Saussay first contend with the Roman Order before attempting to tear apart the Martyrologies.

In the calendars of Allatius and Fronto this is simply entered for the day:

> “The birthday of the holy Four Crowned Ones.”

But the Sacramentary of Thomas shows itself to confuse the whole matter anew:

> “Of the holy Four Crowned Ones, Cassianus, Claudius, Castorius, and Sympronianus.”

However one turns or twists these statements, they must be understood according to the earlier explanation.

Another question concerning the Coronati may arise from the calendar of Bucherius, which reads:

> “On the seventh day before the Ides of August, Secundus, Carpophorus, Victorinus, and Severianus, at Albano and Ostia.”

There are four names, except for the first; but what do “at Albano and Ostia” mean? Is this really a reference to our Coronati? I confess that I have not yet sufficiently investigated the matter.

There is an equally difficult problem, which we touched upon on 7 July. At that time, together with the Roman parvum, Ado, Usuard, and Notker, we thought that the five craftsmen celebrated today should be distinguished from the nearly five homonymous catechumens of Saint Sebastian, about whom the discussion there concerned, since the Acts adapted by Ado for the two groups are clearly different. I know that the present supplement under the name of Florus adorns our five with material from the Acts of Saint Sebastian, and I know that others think likewise. Yet so far I do not see that they should be confused, if they can be properly distinguished.

Florentinius discusses more at length on this day, in his notes, but does not settle the matter so completely that much does not remain to be resolved more carefully in the Acts for the following month of July. Wandalbert does not mention the Coronati, unless we wish to suppose that he followed Bede and introduced the name of the crown in his second verse. Meanwhile he sings of the first five in such a way that the entire praise could be applied to any homonymous martyrs:

[Col. 0672D]

> “Claudius, Castorius, Simplicius, Symphorianus,
>
> Nicostratus, you shine with the equal light of a crown,
>
> Rightly adorning the sixth Ides by merit and blood.” ]

[Note: [Col. 0671D]

ANTWERP-MAJOR. Also uncorrupted in the first; the second continues through “they were killed,” but is mutilated thereafter.

PULSANEN. The first extends through Simplicius; the second through “they were killed,” both inclusive; there is nothing else.

Then it treats the Four Crowned Ones, but the text is badly composed and even worse corrected. Then, after Simplicius, it inserts the following concerning the other five:

AQUICINCT, at the beginning, has *Latina* in place of *Lavicana*, and, together with the manuscripts cited for the text, reads *Simproniani*.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT. A feast of relics; as the margin explains, this is in the Carthusian order. But whose relics, or the relics of which saints, it concerns I do not yet understand. It continues:

and so forth, as in GREVEN.

Finally, in smaller type:

As above.] 

[Col. 0669]

At Rome, on the Lavican Way, the passion of the holy martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, [Note: [Col. 0671] These five martyrs are written over an erasure; nevertheless, no copies differ from the Pratensis. I ask to whom the correction should be attributed. BOUILLART.] who were first thrust into prison and then severely beaten with scorpions. But since they could not be turned from the faith of Christ, Diocletian ordered them to be thrown headlong into the middle of the sea. Likewise on the Lavican Way, the birthday of the Four Crowned Ones, Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus, who, at Diocletian’s command, were beaten to death with blows from leaded scourges. Since their names could not be found at all, but were later revealed after some years through a revelation from the Lord, it was decreed that their anniversary should be commemorated under the names of the five martyrs mentioned above.

V Idus. Day 9. [Note: [Col. 0673C]

The Pratensis, Rosweyd, Greven, and Molan manuscripts are uncorrupted.]

[Note: [Col. 0673D]

All write *Amasiam* with the designation *Marmaritanorum*, as though it referred to some particular region or people, whereas the subject is a legion of soldiers wintering at Amaseia in Pontus. Rosweyd alone writes “Theodore, soldier and martyr.” He likewise, together with Molan, has “Maximianus and Maximinus.” Again, Rosweyd seems to have wished to polish the ending of the eulogy, reading “handed over to the fires, he gave up his spirit.” “At the city of Bourges” is the customary expression of the martyrologists; Greven perhaps wished to correct it to “at the city of Bourges.” Ado certainly wrote *Ursicinus*, and Usuard follows him in nearly all manuscripts; Greven and Molan substitute the true name *Ursinus*, although this is not properly Usuard’s reading, as is also found in Pratensis B.]

[Note: [Col. 0673D]

This Theodore, our soldier, who bears the surname of Amaseian or Euchaitan, may rightly be called a great martyr and, if there are several, should be venerated above the other Theodores with special devotion. He is celebrated on this day in the calendars of Allatius and Fronto, in the Sacramentary of Gregory, and in nearly all the Martyrologies among the Latins. He does not appear to belong to the Hieronymian manuscripts, as Florentinius readily admits; but Bede, Florus, Wandalbert, and those in our series consistently proclaim him. Bede, together with the calendars and Sacramentary mentioned, simply has: “The birthday of Saint Theodore, martyr.” The Roman parvum is somewhat more explicit: “At Euchaita, Saint Theodore, martyr,” designating not the place of his birth or martyrdom, but of his most glorious burial.

Nor does Ado mention the arena of his struggle, nor does Usuard seem to have abridged his eulogy—at least not in this commemoration. I am quite convinced that Usuard consulted the Acts themselves, from which he rather inappropriately formed that city of his as “Marmaritanorum” from the legion of soldiers so designated there. This word is much more suitably removed in the eulogy published under the name of Florus.

From the aforesaid Acts, together with the excellent panegyric on Theodore by Gregory of Nyssa published by Surius, Tillemont compiled his historical series in French, volume V, p. 369, making many observations in the relevant notes, both concerning the Acts themselves and concerning this Theodore and the Heracleian Theodore, about whom our Acts treat on 7 February. All these matters will be examined more carefully in a larger work. For the present, see Baronius’s Note and Ruinart’s Genuine Acts, beginning at p. 531.

We possess various Greek documents concerning the passion of Theodore the Recruit and his miracles, which should in due time be illustrated together with those long since published. He alone is honored by Wandalbert in this metrical verse:

[Col. 0676A]

> “Soon the Ides bloom with Theodore the martyr.”

The entire announcement concerning Ursicinus—or, more correctly, Ursinus—of Bourges is also attributed to the Florus cited above. But it was certainly first recorded by Ado and taken from him by Usuard; hence, unless I am gravely mistaken, it was taken from that Florus of ours. This may be inferred even from the fact that the very name—namely Ursicinus—has been preserved, although it was incorrectly formed by Ado.

But we have discussed this Florus, of whatever quality, published by our predecessors, elsewhere. Here it is enough to say that the entries presented in both commemorations are genuinely Usuardine.

Concerning the life and deeds of Ursinus, those things are approved and accepted which Gregory of Tours transmitted in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 8, rendered into French by Tillemont in volume IV, beginning at p. 477, and explained on p. 726. Labbe published a longer life in volume II of the *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, beginning at p. 5. In his *Catalogue of Writers* he says that its author is uncertain but later, and that he collected many scarcely credible details from popular rumors—a fault common to the lives of many others. The same may perhaps be true of those from whom our manuscripts concerning the life, revelation, and translation of Ursinus derive; I would not wish to decide anything prematurely concerning their reliability and authority.

I note only that some regard this day as the day of his elevation, while his birthday is placed on 29 December. I have not yet been able to investigate this matter with sufficient certainty.]

[Note: [Col. 0675B]

HERINIEN is entirely uncorrupted, but at the end, from the local or provincial cult, adds:

> “At Verdun, the deposition of Blessed Vito, bishop and confessor of that same city.”

TORNACEN is largely mutilated in the first part of Theodore’s eulogy; in the second it is uncorrupted.

ANTWERP-MAJOR is pure and complete in the first part, but forms the second as follows:

> “On the same day, at the city of Bourges, Saint Ursinus, confessor.”

PULSANEN in the first part extends through “martyr”; in the second through “confessor,” with the eulogies removed. At the end it adds:

> “On the same day at Verdun, the deposition of Saint Vito, bishop of that same city.”

The name is sufficiently well known.

ANTWERP, MAX-LÜBECK, and UGHELLIAN, after the text:

> “At Verdun, Saint Vido, bishop and confessor.”

MAX-LÜBECK writes *Virdini* and *Widoni*; UGHELLIAN more correctly has *Vitoni*.

MUNERAT, although the text is more or less pure, adds:

> “On the same day, Maturinus, confessor, whose body is honored and venerated in the territory of the diocese of Sens.”

I know that Usuard celebrates him on 1 November and others on this day, but I do not know why MUNERAT entered him on both days.

ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, LEIDEN, and LEUVEN append to the pure text:

> “At Verdun, the deposition of Saint Vito, bishop and confessor of that same city.”

This or a similar phrase is often repeated by the manuscripts today.

ALBERGEN and DANIC add further:

> “The dedication of the basilica of the Savior.”

See BELIN below.

CENTULEN:

> “At the city of Amaseia of the Marmaritans, the passion of Saint Theodore, martyr, under Diocletian. [Col. 0675D] On the same day, Saint Ursinus, first bishop of Bourges and confessor. At Verdun, Saint Vito, bishop and confessor.”

BRUSSELS introduces another Theodore:

> “At Rome, Saint Theodore, martyr.”

Our first announcement follows, nearly uncorrupted. Then:

> “At Arras, Saint Ragnulfus, martyr.”

The entry on Ursicinus is sufficiently Usuardine. At the end, with the other manuscripts:

> “In the suburb of Verdun, Saint Vito, bishop and confessor of that same city.”

HAGENOY begins, transposing the days:

> “At Trier, Saint Hildulfus, bishop. In the city [perhaps Beirut], the passion of the image of the Crucified One.”

After “he was revealed,” it inserts:

> “And a crowd of men in white began to sing psalms with him. When the prison guards saw and heard these things [for ‘saw and heard’], they fled. Then Saint Theodore was hung on wood and torn with iron claws, and his sides were scraped. The governor said: ‘Do you wish to be with us, Theodore, or with Christ?’ And he replied: ‘I have been, am, and shall be with my Christ.’ Immediately he was ordered to be consumed by fire. When placed in the fire, he gave up his spirit at the voice of the Lord, and his body was not burned; and many saw the heavens opened above him.”

Then follows a new piece of learning:

> “On the same day, at the city of Bourges, Saint Ursicinus, confessor and bishop. He was formerly called Nathanael, the one mentioned in the Gospel of John. Ordained bishop at Rome by the successors of the apostles, he was appointed the first pontiff of that city. After converting many to the faith, performing many miracles, and building churches, he died in peace. At Verdun, the deposition of Blessed Wido, bishop and confessor. In Africa, Saint Atticus, martyr. At Rennes, the deposition of Saint Melanius, confessor.”

These entries belong to 6 November.

AQUICINCT adds at the end:

> “In the territory of Adart, Saint Ragnulfus, martyr; at Verdun, Saint Vitonius, bishop.”

Read *Vitoni*, as above.

VICTORIN and REG. SUEC. no. 130:

> “On the same day, in the territory of Nevers, Saint Maturinus, Levite and confessor.”

The second manuscript, namely REG. SUEC., more correctly reads *Maurinus*.

AMBIANEN.:

> “In the suburb of Verdun, the deposition of Saint Vito, our father, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT.:

> “Theodore, martyr. Nathanael, bishop, brother of Saint Philip, apostle of the Lord. Vito, bishop of Verdun. Ursinus [Col. 0676D], bishop and confessor.”

If the scribe of this codex had seen HAGENOY, he would have conflated Ursinus and Nathanael.

REG. SUEC., numbered 428:

> “At the fortress of Verdun, Saint Vito, bishop.”

The LUXOVIEN codex reads almost the same.

FLORENTIN.:

> “At Verdun, Saint Victorinus, bishop and confessor of that same city.”

Read *Vitoni* for *Victorini*.

RHEMENS. SS. Tim. and Apoll.:

> “In the suburb of Verdun, the birthday of the most holy Vito, bishop and confessor.”

BELNEN.:

> “The translation of the body of Blessed Floscellus, martyr, resting in this church of Beaune. This body was translated from one place to another, to a more venerable place, on the aforesaid day by the venerable fathers Lord Simon, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia and legate of the Apostolic See in France, and Gerard, by the grace of God bishop of Autun, in the year of the Lord 1265.”

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition begins:

> “At the city of Edessa, the commemoration of the holy blood of Christ from an image of the Crucified Lord.”

The first announcement is moderately interpolated. In the second it adds:

> “This Ursicinus was formerly called Nathanael, the apostle of Christ, to whom the Lord said: ‘Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.’ He rested in peace, buried at the aforesaid city and afterward rediscovered through divine revelation. In Spain, Saints Faustus and Martialis, martyrs. At Verdun, Saint Wido, bishop and confessor of that city. Likewise at Verdun, Saint Nicanus, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Nevers, Saint Maurus [more correctly, above, Maurinus], Levite and confessor. At Nicomedia, Saint Damianus, confessor.”

See the Hieronymian Martyrology.

BELIN begins:

> “The dedication of the basilica of the Savior.”

Then follows a fairly pure text.

[Col. 0677B] GREVEN:

> “The commemoration of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which miraculously flowed at the city of Edessa from an image of the Crucified One struck by a Jew. In Spain, Saints Faustus and Martialis. At Rome, the birthday of Saints Clement and Symphronianus. Likewise at Nicomedia, Saint Gamasus, otherwise Damianus.”

See the Hieronymian Martyrology.

> “At Rome, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Savior, that is, of the holy Lateran church, by Blessed Sylvester. Ragnulfus, martyr. At the city of Heraclea in Macedonia, Saint Theodore, martyr. Under King Licinius, for the faith of Christ, he was beaten for a very long time with rods and leaded scourges, torn with claws, burned with torches applied to his wounds, and rubbed with extremely sharp saws. Then he was ordered to be crucified and shot with arrows, and finally, by beheading, he attained the glory of martyrdom.”

We have already said that this belongs to 7 February, unless he is the same as the Amaseian Theodore.

Here is another namesake:

> “Theodore, bishop of London and confessor. Vito, bishop of Verdun and confessor. Dethmarus, confessor. Likewise Saint Donatus. In the territory of Nevers, Saint Maurus, Levite and martyr. Paurilia, a sacred virgin, whom the apostle Paul is said to have baptized. In the Hellespont, Saint Eusebia, virgin. Among the Carthusian monks, the commemoration of the deceased brothers and sisters of that order.”

MOLAN:

> “The dedication of the basilica of the Savior, the first basilica in Constantine’s palace at the Lateran, performed by Blessed Pope Sylvester. In the district of Arras, the passion of Saint Ragnulfus, martyr, who was placed in the basilica of Saint Vedastus. On the same day, Maturinus, confessor, whose body is honored and venerated in the territory of the diocese of Sens.”

FROM MUNERAT:

> “On the same day, the crucifixion of an image of our Lord Jesus Christ in Syria, in the city of Beirut. At Verdun, the deposition of Blessed Vito, bishop and confessor of that city.”

Later editions begin:

> “At Rome, the dedication of the basilica of the Savior by Constantine,”

and so forth. Concerning the crucifixion of the image, Ragnulfus, and Vito, they follow the earlier edition. They add:

> “On the ninth day, the holy martyrs Onesiphorus and Porphyrius. And Saint Matrona, holy mother.”

See Castellani’s Martyrology.]

[Col. 0673]

At the city of Amaseia of the Marmaritans, the birthday of Saint Theodore, martyr. Under the emperors Maximianus and Maximinus, he was bravely beaten and sent into prison for confessing the Christian faith. Then, after the Lord and Savior appeared to him and exhorted him to act steadfastly and courageously, he was strengthened. Finally, after being hung on the rack and torn with claws, so that his entrails were exposed, he was handed over to the burning fires. On the same day, at the city of Bourges, Saint Ursicinus, confessor, who, ordained at Rome by the successors of the apostles, was appointed the first bishop assigned to that city.

IV Idus. Day 10. [Note: [Col. 0677]

Thus the Pratensis, Heriniensis, Munerat, Greven, and Molan manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0677B]

Munerat writes “for the Catholic faith of Christ” and, through faulty punctuation, tortures the construction in the rest. Most manuscripts read *Constantino*, a few *Constantio*; neither reading is correct. Usuard certainly followed the form found first in Ado; but in the modern Roman Martyrology the name is more correctly given as Constans, who ruled from 641 to 666, under whom Pope Martin suffered that most unworthy persecution and martyrdom through blows and hardships.

Again, all the manuscripts mark the place of exile as *Cersona*, except Molan, who has *Chersona*, as in the Roman parvum and Ado. But what is this Chersona of Lycia? I would believe that the same place is indicated which Pope Clement formerly made famous by his exile and martyrdom; Rosweyd discusses it learnedly in his notes on the booklet *On Feasts*, pp. 221–222. It is enough to indicate this briefly here.

The others in the text retain both *Cersona* and *Lycia*, following the manuscript forms. The Agathensis manuscript does the same, although Greven and Molan more correctly read *Agathensis*. It seems that *Tiberii* should be written, from which the French form is *Tubery*, as Greven and Molan again have; but I prefer the manuscripts. Likewise *Aniani*, for which some have *Aviani*; I do not know which is preferable.]

The feast of Pope Martin, the most resolute defender of Catholic orthodoxy against the Monothelites and a martyr, is perhaps observed at this time, on 12 November, according to the preference of more recent Usuardine codices; by Wandalbert, however, it is assigned to the more probable day of his death, namely 16 September. Among the other ancient martyrologists, it is celebrated only in our series, having first been entered in the sacred registers by the Small Roman Martyrology, with this single announcement: “At Chersona in Lycia, of Pope Martin, who, having been exiled there on account of the Catholic faith, ended his life.” From there it passed into Ado, from whom our entire announcement was excerpted by Usuard himself, following his guides, and marked on no other day than this, as the testimony of all the ancient codices proves. The Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, when they mention some Martin without any distinguishing indication on 12 November, refer not to this martyred pope—for he was not celebrated on that day even in the ninth century—but, as I think, to that famous Martin of Tours, because the feast of Menas had been transferred there to the following day. If anyone should perhaps find Fronto’s notice in the Calendar for that day more convincing, I shall not strongly resist him. The Acts of Pope Martin, published by Surius, are excellent; we shall illuminate them in their proper place together with the writings of Anastasius and others. To that discussion must also be referred the many complicated controversies concerning the beginning and end of his pontificate, the time of his exile, and the chronological order of all his deeds. It is better to pass over them here altogether than to touch on them too briefly and contrary to our purpose; most of them, after Baronius, have already been excavated, if not completely explained, by Cointius, Papebrochius, Pagius, and others. Here I may repeat in its proper place Wandalbert’s verse, which we gave under 16 September:

> Hence on the sixteenth, Pope Martin is honored.

[Col. 0679A] The martyrs of Agde are unknown to the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, and even the Small Roman Martyrology, but are sung by Wandalbert; they are more distinctly marked by Ado: “In the territory of Agde, at Cessarion”; the rest Usuard copied verbatim from him into our text. Peter published some Acts in his Catalogue; Catellus, in his *Occitania*, p. 279, cites but does not reproduce others, more extensive ones, from which he thinks the former were abbreviated. I am greatly mistaken if Possinus did not send Catellus’s own text to Bollandus in 1656, divided into twenty-seven readings. To speak frankly, I do not like them at all; but judgment concerning them belongs elsewhere. Hear Wandalbert’s metrical eulogy:

> On the fourth, Modestus, Florentia, and Tiberius  
> Shine through threefold martyrdom, for the threefold Name.

In the Hieronymian Martyrologies, this day begins with: “At Antioch, the birthday of the holy Demetrius the bishop, Aniesus the deacon, Eustosius, and his companions.” Florentinius rightly struggles with this, seeking to assign that Demetrius either under the name Demetrianus or under another name to a definite see. The names of the companions are not uniform in the copies, nor is their number anywhere determined. Rabanus seems closely to follow the Hieronymian Martyrologies when he writes: “At Antioch, the birthday of Demetrius the bishop, Amnesus, Eustachius, and his companions.” Rosweydus correctly judged that it does not belong to Ado’s text; in the appendix it reads: “Anianus the deacon, Eustosius, and their companions.” Usuard’s different wording shows that he drew immediately from that source. But how shall we explain the addition of that closing clause and of the other twenty? It is not easy to untie that knot unless we openly admit that Our Author was mistaken and wrongly gathered into one group other saints belonging to other regions. Nor does Castellani’s note, insofar as it concerns Eustosius, clarify the matter; indeed, it seems rather to entangle it, though he may have guessed more accurately when he separated the other twenty Africans from the first three. In any event, it must be admitted on the evidence of the codices that Usuard wrote in this way and that our text concerning Martin and the Agde martyrs is genuinely Usuardine.

[Note: [Col. 0679B]]

**Tournai.** Not entirely pure; the eulogy of the Agde martyrs is lacking.

**Antwerp–Major.** In this codex the first announcement is confused, the second is incomplete, and the third is omitted.

**Rosweydus.** In the text sufficiently pure; at the end he adds: “On the same day, in Britain of Kent, the deposition of Saint Justus, archbishop and confessor, who was fourth after Saint Augustine. At Orléans, of Monitor the bishop. The vigil of blessed Martin the bishop.” Remember that this is the Utrecht codex, in which the cathedral, later the metropolitan church, was dedicated to Martin.

**Pulsanus.** In the first announcement almost complete; in the second he cuts away the eulogy; the third is absent.

**Antwerp, Maximus–Lübeck, and Ughellian.** Sufficiently pure in the text; they add: “At Orléans, of Monitor, bishop.” This occurs in many codices.

**Antwerp–Maximus, Utrecht, and Leiden.** Pure in the text, but in second place they introduce this new announcement: “The birthday of the holy martyrs Tryphon and Respicius.” At the end they append: “At Orléans, of Saint Monitor the bishop.”

**Louvain.** In the text purer than those mentioned above, since it lacks the interpolated announcement concerning Tryphon and Respicius.

**Alberg and Danish.** They assume a more recent form. After Martin the pope has been transferred to the 12th, they begin the present text as follows: “The birthday of the holy martyrs Tryphon and Respicius. Also of Saint Nympha the virgin, daughter of Aurelian, whom Bishop Maximilian baptized.” In the announcements concerning the Agde and Antiochene martyrs they are pure. At the end, concerning Monitor, as already more than once above.

**Centula.** “The birthday of Saint Martin, pope and martyr, who, because of the Catholic faith, was exiled by the heretical emperor Constantius to the island of Chersona and there rested in the Lord. His body, brought back to Rome, shines with many miracles.” In the second announcement, instead of Tiberius, it reads Vitius; otherwise it is pure in this and the third announcement. At the end it adds: “At Orléans, of Saint Monitor the bishop.”

**Brussels.** “The birthday of blessed Pope Martin. He celebrated a council at Rome, at which he condemned Paul of Constantinople, an advocate of an evil doctrine and a patriarch of false name. Because of this, the heretical emperor Constantius dragged him from the church, sent him into exile at Chersona in Lycia, and there he departed to Christ, with many signs in that same place,” and so forth. It increases the number of the Agde martyrs, writing: “In the territory of Agde, at Cesarion, of the holy martyrs Liberius, Tiberius, Modestus, and Florentia. Who, in the time, etc.” It is pure in the Antiochene material. Then: “On the same day, the birthday of the holy martyrs Tryphon and Respicius. And of Saint Nympha the virgin, daughter of Aurelian, whom Saint Mamilianus the bishop baptized. On the same day, the deposition of Bernard, who was the first of the Latins to be patriarch of the Church of Antioch. At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Monitor the bishop. At Rome, of Saint Leo the pope.” See Castellani’s note. “At Verdun, the deposition of Saint Maurus, bishop of that city.”

**Hagenoyen.** It begins with the Agde martyrs, but not very purely. Then concerning Nympha, as in the preceding source. The Antiochene material is fairly good, followed by Tryphon and Respicius as above. It continues: “On the same day, of Saint Martin, pope and martyr, who was wholly devoted to God and Catholic in faith, because he assembled a council against the heretics and bishops Cyrus, Sergius, and Paul. Because he expelled them from their dignities, he was ordered by Olympius the *spatarius* to be killed; but Olympius was not permitted by God to see Saint Martin, because he was struck blind. Their heresy was that they did not confess that there was either one or two wills or operations in Christ. At length the blessed man was seized by force and brought to Constantinople; nor did he then yield so as to tolerate the wicked. Therefore, for this reason, he was sent into exile at Chersona, where Blessed Pope Clement once lived; and there Martin happily departed to the Lord, both martyr and confessor. At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Monitor, bishop and confessor. In Bohemia, of Saint Ludmilla, grandmother of Saint Wenceslaus.” See below under Greven.

**Aquicinct.** At the end: “At Orléans, of Saint Monitor the bishop. On the same day, of Saint Probus the confessor.” Is this the bishop of Ravenna?

**Matrice–Carthusian–Utrecht.** “Of Tiberius the martyr with his companions. Of Martin the pope and confessor. Of George, disciple of Christ.”

**Swedish Register**, marked no. 428: “In the territory of Orléans, of Saint Veranus, bishop and confessor.” He is the bishop of Cavaillon, known from his burial; concerning him, see Castellani on the following day.

In the Vatican codex no. 5949 the final announcement is absent. It adds: “At Benevento, of Saint Menas the confessor.” Nothing concerning him is found in the others.

**Strozzi.** “At the city of Cologne, the deposition of Saint Cunibert the bishop. At the castle of Millidunum, of Saint Leo the confessor.” See concerning both under 12 November.

**Bordeaux.** “At Orléans, of Minor the bishop.” Read Monitor. “On the same day, of Saint Maurus, bishop and confessor.” In the Roman Martyrology it is on 8 November.

**Luxeuil** writes, with the others above: “At Verdun, of Saint Maurus, bishop and confessor.”

The Lübeck–Cologne edition begins: “At Rome, the birthday of the holy martyrs Tryphon and Respicius.” It follows with Nympha, as above. In the Agde and Antiochene announcements it is fairly pure. Again concerning Monitor, as above. Then: “At Chersona in Lycia, the deposition of blessed Martin, pope and martyr, who, because of the Catholic faith, etc. On the same day, of blessed Justus, bishop of Canterbury and confessor, who, together with Mellitus and many others, was sent by blessed Pope Gregory into Britain to assist blessed Augustine in preaching. He was first made bishop of the church of Rochester, and afterward, fourth in succession in the episcopate of the Church of Canterbury, succeeded Augustine.”

**Belin.** It begins: “The birthday of the holy martyrs Tryphon and Respicius and of Nympha the virgin.” Martin has been transferred. In the second and third announcements it differs little from the pure text. Then: “At Orléans, of Saint Notarius the bishop.” At this point it has Monitor: “At the city of Cologne, the deposition of Saint Cumbert [Cunibert] the bishop. At the castle of Milludun, of Saint Leo the confessor.” Concerning this I said that Castellani should be consulted.

**Greven.** “According to some, on this day is the passion of Saint Felix, pope and martyr, whose feast is chiefly celebrated on 27 July; but he is said to have been buried on 17 November. At Rome, of the holy martyrs Tryphon and Respicius. Of Monitor, bishop of Orléans and confessor. At Rome, the deposition of blessed Leo the bishop. In Britain, of Saint Justus, bishop and confessor. He was sent into Britain with Mellitus and others by blessed Pope Gregory for the work of the Gospel; first indeed bishop of Rochester, then of the Church of Canterbury, and after Saint Augustine the fourth archbishop. Shining with holy works, he rested in peace. Of Theodore, bishop of Sicca and confessor. At Ravenna, of Saint Probus, bishop and confessor. Of Maurus the bishop. At Antioch, of Saint Theodore the young confessor, concerning whom Book X of the *Ecclesiastical History* relates that, for the faith of Christ under Julian, from first light until the tenth hour he was tortured with such cruelty and by so many successive executioners that no age remembers a similar deed. At Rome, of Saint Nympha the virgin, daughter of the emperor Aurelian. The translation of Ludmilla, duchess of Bohemia and martyr. At Paris, of Catulla, a most noble matron. Of Ermegardis, countess of Zutphen.”

**Molanus.** “The birthday of the holy martyrs Tryphon and Respicius and of Nympha the virgin. At Aurelia, of Saint Notarius the bishop.” From Belin. “In the city of Cologne, the deposition of Saint Cunibert the bishop. At the castle of Milledun, of Saint Leo the confessor.” From the same source. “At Orléans, the deposition of Monitor the bishop.” Then in smaller type: “In Britain, of Saint Justus,” etc., as in Greven, except that it writes Brocensis. In the Roman Martyrology the episcopal see is not added. It likewise takes from the same source the account of Theodore the young man of Antioch. Later editions transfer Martin to the 12th. In the first place, in italic type, they treat of Tryphon, Respicius, and Nympha. At the end: “In Britain, of Saint Justus, bishop and confessor, whom Pope Gregory sent there with others for the work of the Gospel. On the same day, of Saint Probus, pontiff of Ravenna, buried in the church dedicated to him. At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Monitor the bishop. On the tenth, of the holy apostles Erastus, Olympius, and their companions.” From the Greek Horologion. Finally, in smaller type, there is added: “Also, of Saint Theoctista of Lesbos.”

[Col. 0677]

The birthday of blessed Martin, pope, who, on account of the Catholic faith, was snatched from the Church by the heretical emperor Constantine, brought to Constantinople, and exiled at Chersona in the province of Lycia; there he ended his life, still shining to this day in that same place through many signs of miraculous power. In the territory of Agde, of the holy martyrs Tiberius, Modestus, and Florentia, who, tortured with various torments in the time of Diocletian, completed their martyrdom. At Antioch, of the holy Demetrius the bishop, Anianus the deacon, Eustosius, and twenty others.

**The third day before the Ides. Day 11.**

[Note: From Prato, Herinien, Rosweydus, Antwerp and Maximus–Lübeck, Munerat, the first edition of Belin, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0681C]]

Molanus varies somewhat at the very beginning: “In Gaul, in the city of Tours.” Rosweydus, adorning the patron of the city of Utrecht with large illuminated letters, reads “most blessed Martin.” Munerat alone inserted “who was the resuscitator of three,” etc. Likewise he has *meruerit*, for which Antwerp has *mereretur*; Maximus–Lübeck, worse, has *meretur*; Belin, however, has *mereretur esse suscitator magnificus*, “would deserve to be a magnificent resuscitator.” We have said more than once in what ways *Scythia* and *Phrygia* are written; here again I follow the larger number of codices. It is certain that *Scythia* was wrongly introduced here by Ado, in place of which Baronius substituted *Cotyaei*. Greven and Molanus wrongly read *meruit* for *studuit*. In all copies the word is *heremo*; in Prato, *exanimatus*; in Herinien, *examinatus*. In several copies the final syllable is so abbreviated that it can equally be read *examinatur* or *examinatus*; choose either reading—we retain the latter. Prato reads *Veriani*; Rosweydus, *Valeriani*; the majority support *Verani*. But Molanus seems to have been uncertain which Veranus was meant, and therefore wrote simply: “Also, of Saint Veranus,” etc. The rest are minor matters, such as *Thuronis*, *Salutaris*, *coelesti*, *Nerani*, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0681C]]

Florentinius truly pronounced judgment in the note for this day: “Everything concerning the holy and wonder-working Martin is so well known that it is unnecessary to repeat anything here.” Nevertheless, we must extract a few points relevant to our purpose. Thus, in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, the Small Roman Martyrology, and Ado, he is commemorated in a phrase not very different and in a concise form, with this sole distinction: the author of the Small Roman Martyrology praises him as a worker of miracles. Usuard did not wish to pass over in silence a saint so universally venerated throughout every age and so famous, at least throughout the whole of the West. Something is also attributed to Florus, but Rabanus adorned Martin with a longer eulogy. Wandalbert will return below. Baronius made many observations about Martin in his notes and more in his *Annals*, perhaps requiring correction here and there, especially in fixing the year of his death. Hardly any saint has left behind so many illustrious monuments, or found so many celebrated encomiasts. The principal and best known are Sulpicius Severus, Benedict, Paulinus of Périgueux, Fortunatus, and Gregory of Tours, whose works have been explained and illuminated by the notes of many learned men. Gervasius collected, examined, and arranged most of the material in a *Life* published at Tours in French in 1699; Tillemont treated it more briefly in volume X, beginning at p. 309. We shall gladly use their labors at the proper time to elucidate the earlier material. The poet-martyrologist places Menas before Martin and appends to Martin some Domitilla whom I do not recognize. Although she may perhaps be entered in the Hieronymian Martyrology, since she is not mentioned in ours today, we shall describe only the encomia of the former saints. Thus he sang—not from Molanus, but from Acheri’s *Spicilegium*:

> Holy Menas rejoices in threefold virtue and faith,  
> A confessor by merit, a priest by office and speech,  
> And Martin, a martyr through faith, famous throughout the wide world,  
> Is invoked by vows and celebrated on the same feast.

The matters concerning Martin are almost all clear and straightforward; those concerning Menas, otherwise an illustrious martyr, appear very obscure. In the first place, it is not established that in the Hieronymian Martyrologies he is marked by the formula “At Alexandria, the metropolis, the birthday of Saint Minatas,” although Florentinius seems to wish to derive this. Bede reads: “On the same day, the birthday of Saint Menas the martyr.” The same name occurs in the Calendars of Allatius—though on the fourth day before the Ides—and of Fronto, as well as in Gregory’s Sacramentary. His once-famous memory at Rome is also shown, among other things, by Homily 35 preached by Saint Gregory; see Fronto’s note concerning it. Yet in these later sources he is distinguished by no particular indication of place or time. The Small Roman Martyrology reads: “In Scythia, of Menas the martyr, translated to Constantinople.” Rabanus has a fuller eulogy, but nothing can be firmly established from it unless it is determined from the Ado tradition; and even there the position indicated by Our Author, from whom it is taken word for word, does not sufficiently clarify the matter: “On the same day, in Scythia, the metropolis of Salutary Phrygia, etc.” *Palaestra* is more correctly placed in the Roman Martyrology, and Castellani observes that this is a different person from another Mena or Menas surnamed Calliceladus, whose account, together with Hermogenes and Eugraphus, occurs in the Roman Martyrology on 10 December. Indeed, different Acts for the two days were published by Surius from Metaphrastes; we shall pass judgment on them elsewhere. When those Acts and the Martyrologies are examined more carefully, it is not so easy to decide whether there was one Menas or several, or whether the Acts of one were transferred to another saint. Many obscure and ambiguous statements recur; meanwhile, see Tillemont, volume V, pp. 441 and 758. Our text, in the meantime, is plainly abbreviated from Ado, with *palaestra* retained, as stated in the Variants.

Veranus, undoubtedly the bishop of Lyon, is mentioned not in the appendix, as Florentinius says, but in the text itself by the Viennese Martyrologist, from whom all the elements of our announcement were taken. He is also read in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but Florentinius would not doubt that he comes from additions to the older Martyrology. Whatever the case, the cited author notes several Verani: one the bishop of Gabalum, or of Cavaillon; another of Vence; and distinguishes them from the bishop of Lyon and from the Veranus of our present text, on the basis of the *Hagiologium* of Labbe, Saussay, and Raynaud. Castellani seems to think otherwise, for he declares the Veranus accompanied by the note “of Vence” to be the saint transferred here from 9 September, who is called *Veran* in French; but he identifies the second, called *Vrain* in French, as the bishop of Cavaillon. On that reasoning, Veranus of Lyon would be entirely excluded. These controversies must be discussed more fully elsewhere; our text unmistakably designates the man of Lyon, and it too is Usuardine. See Tillemont, volume XV, p. 849.

[Note: [Col. 0683B]]

**Tournai.** Pure in the first announcement; in the second it ends at “Menas the martyr,” with the eulogy deleted. In the third it is again pure.

**Antwerp–Major.** This codex lacks the entire section for this day.

**Pulsanus.** Pure in the first; it truncates the second and third after “martyr” and after “bishop.”

**Antwerp–Maximus, Utrecht, Leiden, Louvain, Alberg, and Danish.** They would be pure throughout if, after the words concerning Martin, “so that he deserved to be a magnificent resuscitator of three dead men,” they did not add: “In the year of the Lord four hundred, he happily returned his spirit to heaven.”

**Centula.** “In Gaul, in the city of Tours, the passing of Saint Martin, archbishop and confessor, whose sacred tomb is made illustrious by frequent miracles through the power of Christ. On the same day, in Scythia, of Saint Menas the martyr, who ended his life by the sword. At Lyon, of Saint Neron—[the name Veranus has been written incorrectly]—the bishop, renowned for his life and miracles.”

**Brussels.** In the first announcement sufficiently pure, it continues: “And in Scythia, the metropolis of Salutary Phrygia, the passion of Saint Menas the martyr, who, during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, although he was a soldier born in the province of Egypt, renouncing earthly military service, secretly and under a hidden manner of life strove to serve the heavenly King in the desert. Then, when he came out into public during the birthdays of the prefects of the emperors, he openly professed with a free voice that he was a Christian. He was first beaten so that the streets overflowed with blood; afterward, overcoming the rack and fire, he was dragged by his bound hands and feet over thorns and iron stakes. Finally, kneeling in prayer and giving thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, he was struck with the sword, and his body was handed over to the fire. At Cyprus, in the city called Amathus, the deposition of John Eleymon, of holy memory, archbishop of the city of Alexandria.” See 23 January.

**Hagenoyen.** “In Gaul, in the city of Tours, the deposition of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, whose entire life is described as having been miraculous, so that he deserved to be the resuscitator of three dead men. He is said to have existed in three conditions, namely military, monastic, and episcopal, and in all these states he pleased God. In military service he served the emperor blamelessly, so that he did not offend God in it. In the monastic life he served God and adhered faithfully to him, so that he was himself a model of religious life for others. In the episcopate he served Christ, for the honor of God, the benefit of his neighbor, and his own advancement in good works. Finally, blessed Martin, after performing many miracles, building many churches, converting many to the faith, enduring many snares both from pagans and from heretics, and destroying various idols, full of good works departed in peace to the Lord.” The account of Menas is only moderately interpolated. In the account of Veranus it is pure, and adds: “Also, of Saint John the Almsgiver, bishop and confessor.”

**Aquicinct.** At the end: “In the village called Malonia, the birthday of Saint Bertuin, bishop and confessor.”

**Matrice–Carthusian–Utrecht.** “Of Martin, bishop and confessor. Of Menas the martyr. Of Bertuin, bishop and confessor. Of Verianus, bishop and confessor.”

**Altemps.** “On the same day, of Saint Livinus, archbishop of Dorobernia.” It is uncertain what he intends.

**Florentine.** “At Ravenna, of Saint Probus, archbishop and confessor.” See the preceding day.

The Lübeck–Cologne edition, after the material given above from Antwerp–Maximus and others, adds: “His passing was divinely revealed to Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, and to blessed Severinus, archbishop of Cologne.” Concerning Menas: “Who, during the persecution of the emperor Diocletian, although he was a most noble soldier of Egyptian origin, renouncing the world, strove in a hidden manner of life to serve the heavenly King in the desert. Then, coming out into public during the birthdays of the prefects of the emperors and declaring himself a Christian before them in a free voice, he was handed over to the judge Pyrrhus for punishment, who first tortured him with dreadful torments,” and so forth. In the final announcement it is pure. At the end: “On the same day, of Saint Theophila the virgin and martyr.”

The second edition of Belin has: “On the same day, the passing of Saint John the Almsgiver, bishop of the city of Alexandria.” See, as we said, 23 January.

**Greven.** “At Rome, the birthday of the holy martyrs Valentinus, Felicianus, Victorinus; at Ravenna, of Felix, Valentina, Hovella, Octavius, Januarius, and Erundinus. See them in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Of Bertuin, bishop and confessor. Of Ganfred, bishop of Sora and confessor, of the Cistercian order. According to some, on this day is John the Almsgiver, who is listed above under 22 January. Also, of Saint Menas the solitary, a man of great holiness. Blessed Gregory relates concerning him in the Third Book of the *Dialogues* that it was his practice to possess nothing in this world, seek nothing, and kindle in all who came to him out of charity a desire for eternal life. Among the offerings sent to him, he recognized by the spirit and rejected the offering of a certain adulterer. Of Theophila the virgin and martyr. In Gaul, of Roga, a matron.”

**Molanus** adds after his account of Martin, in different type: “His life and teaching shine before almost all the faithful through the miracles that the Lord performed through him. Nor is it necessary for us to recall anything here, because Sulpicius clearly described his life, virtues, and signs in a splendid discourse, and Gregory, bishop of the same city, discussed them most fully in his books on miracles.” At the end: “At Malonia, of Saint Bertuin, bishop and confessor.” Then, in smaller type, concerning Menas the solitary, from Greven above. Finally: “The deposition of Theophanius the confessor, count of Centumcellae, concerning whom blessed Gregory speaks in Book IV, chapter 27 of the *Dialogues*.” Other editions treat Martin somewhat more briefly: “His life Sulpicius clearly described in a splendid discourse,” and so forth. At the end: “At Namur, in Malonia, of Saint Bertuin the bishop, who, coming from the island of Ireland into the forest commonly called Marlagne, founded an oratory in the aforesaid village of Malonia above the Sambre, in honor of Mary, ever Virgin. There, serving God for a long time, he happily completed his course. On the eleventh, of Saint Stephanida the martyr, and of Saint Theodore the Studite, father and confessor.” From the Greek Horologion.

[Col. 0681]

In Gaul, in the city of Tours, the birthday of blessed Martin, bishop and confessor, whose life was so glorious in miracles that he deserved to be the resuscitator of three dead men. In Scythia, the metropolis of Salutary Phrygia, the passion of Saint Menas the martyr, who, after striving in a hidden manner of life to serve the heavenly King in the desert during the persecution of Diocletian, came out into public and openly declared himself a Christian; first he was subjected to dreadful tortures, and finally, kneeling in prayer and giving thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, he was struck with the sword. Also at Lyon, of Saint Veranus the bishop, whose life was illustrious for the merits of faith and virtues.

**The day before the Ides. Day 12.**

[Note: Thus Prato, Herinien, Tournai, Antwerp and Maximus–Lübeck, Munerat, Greven, and Molanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0685B]]

Munerat writes *Terraconensi*; the others agree with the text. There is considerable variation in the name of the city: Prato, Antwerp, and Maximus–Lübeck read *Tyrassona*; Tournai, *Terrassona*; Munerat, worse, *Trasona*. The authority of the others prevails. Only Molanus has *Aemiliani*; the other codices, including those that use diphthongs, have the simple form. Greven has *ammirabilem*; Maximus–Lübeck has the more corrupt *annumerabilem*. Only Herinien and Munerat have *Chuniberti*. In Greven and Molanus *Mileduno* is correctly read, but with all the others it ought to be written *Mileduno*. Antwerp, Maximus–Lübeck, and the codices of the middle class call the final saint Leo; Munerat has *Leoni*; it should be read as *Leonii*, French *Liene*.

[Note: [Col. 0685B]]

The present Usuardine text has this distinctive feature, shared with another text that we cited under 28 September: it does not flow from the usual sources, the Small Roman Martyrology and Ado. It can therefore appear, and in a definite sense ought to be regarded, as plainly Usuardine and genuinely and completely Usuardine, although we admit that Cunibert and Leonius—called by others Leonus or Leo—could have been derived from Wandalbert if Usuard had known him. Of the four saints recorded here, none is mentioned by the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, Florus, Rabanus, or in our series, nor by the author of the Small Roman Martyrology or by Ado. The first, Aemilianus, surnamed “the hooded,” a name rendered in French as *Milhan* or *Milhar*, was probably obtained by Usuard from Spain, or at least received from Braulio through Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men*. Baronius cites Ildefonsus’s words here: “He commends and illuminates in due order the life of a certain monk Aemilianus, and the memory and virtues of that man.” See Ildefonsus himself in Mireus’s edition, chapter 12, p. 97, and the other records cited in the notes by the aforementioned Baronius; Castellani’s brief observation is also useful. Mabilio published the aforementioned *Life* in the first volume of the Benedictine century, beginning at p. 205. In his preliminary observations he again brought forward his own Ado, differing everywhere and in every respect from all our printed and manuscript copies. With his kind permission, Aemilianus will be, for us, purely Usuardine; for we do not portray that martyrologist as so impoverished that we leave him not even a little of his own.

The other three saints did not have to be sought far away. Cunibert, once famous under the first dynasty of the Frankish kings and already more than once listed among the additions in the preceding material, was suggested either by Fredegar or by Cologne itself; concerning him, Baronius’s note should also be consulted. The Acts published by Surius seem to me quite meager, and do not adequately cover his forty-year episcopate or the very extensive series of distinguished deeds performed chiefly in Austrasia. I omit the fact that Bollandus long ago noted that they require considerable correction; in due time, therefore, they will have to be gathered, restored, and illustrated more laboriously from the Lives of Saint Sigebert the king and of Blessed Pippin, mayor of the palace.

Paternus, a monk and martyr of Sens, perhaps became known to Usuard through Acts composed by an unknown author, not through Ado, whom Mabilio also wrongly forces into this place under 13 November. For on neither day is he genuinely entered by that martyrologist; nor is he recorded in Mosander, Rosweydus, or Rosweydus’s appendix, or in our manuscripts, except the Lobbes manuscript. The Acts are reported by the aforementioned Mabilio in the third Benedictine century, part I, p. 463, as having first been written with “rough Minerva,” then somewhat polished; both authors are anonymous, and their reliability and sincerity will be considered later.

The Roman Martyrology reads under 10 November: “At the town of Milledun, of Saint Leo the confessor.” For this, old manuscripts and the old Roman Martyrology are cited in Baronius’s notes—namely, as I think, the edition published by Belin, whom we cited in the additions for that day together with Florentinius and others, where also some Leo from the Hieronymian Martyrologies is celebrated at Rome by someone. Castellani’s note appended to the Roman text understands Leo to be Pope Leo I: “He died,” he says, “on 30 October, but was deposited on 10 November,” concerning which we have treated in the proper places, namely 11 April and 28 June. There, against Pagius’s new opinion and against Papebrochius and Castellani, on the basis of the clear determination of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, we judged it more probable that 10 November is the true birthday of Leo the Great. Here, however, we are certain that Leonius of Milledun, French *Liene*, properly belongs to this day; concerning his life and deeds we would like to be informed. Here is Wandalbert’s paired verse concerning Cunibert and Leonius:

> Agrippina, your Cunibert will shine forth the day before;  
> The banks of the Seine likewise honor holy Leonius.

[Note: [Col. 0685D]]

**Antwerp–Major.** In the first announcement the eulogy is absent, though almost the same text has been added in the margin by the same hand. The other material is also confused here and there.

[Col. 0686D] **Rosweydus.** Paternus is absent from the text, nor is the remainder entirely pure. At the end is added: “At Deventer, of Saint Lebuinus the confessor.”

[Col. 0687A] **Pulsanus.** In the first announcement it lacks the eulogy; in the second it writes “Cunibert the abbot.” In the fourth it writes Leo instead of Leonius.

**Louvain.** Fairly pure in the text; it adds: “Also at Rome, of Saint Boniface IV, pope and confessor. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Lebuinus.” Leiden–Belgium agrees almost completely.

**Antwerp–Maximus.** It has the same additions, but inserts into the text: “At Alexandria, of blessed John the bishop and confessor, who is called the Almsgiver.”

**Leiden.** Pure in the first announcement; concerning Cunibert it adds: “On one occasion, while he was celebrating the solemn Mass in the aforementioned city, in the basilica of the eleven thousand holy virgins, a dove of snowy whiteness, flying peacefully around in the sight of all the people and clergy who were present, settled upon the holy head of the venerable bishop.” It then gives the material concerning Paternus and Leonius—whom all the codices of the middle class call Leo—purely. Then: “Also at Rome, of Saint Boniface IV, pope and confessor. He obtained from the emperor Phocas the temple called the Pantheon at Rome and converted it into a church of Saint Mary and all the Martyrs of Christ, so that where once worship had been offered not to gods but to demons, there afterward the memory of all the saints might be celebrated.” Finally, concerning Lebuinus, as above. Utrecht has all the same material, but places the commemoration of Boniface first.

**Alberg and Danish.** They transfer here the announcement concerning Pope Martin that we gave with Usuard under 10 November. Then follows Boniface, Aemilianus, Cunibert, and so forth, as in the two preceding sources; but they have nothing concerning Lebuinus.

**Centula.** “In Africa, the commemoration of the holy Archadius, Paschasius the priest, and Euthychius the martyr. In the district of Brabant, of Saint Livinus, bishop and martyr. At Rennes, of Saint Melanius, bishop and confessor, who, after innumerable signs of virtue, constantly intent upon heaven, departed from the world; his deeds are preserved. In Spain, in the city of Tarazona, of Saint Aemilianus the priest and confessor.”

BRUSSELS begins: “At Ghent, Saint Livinus, archbishop and martyr: He came from Scotland, crossed the sea on foot, and was kindly received by Florebertus, the first abbot of the monastery of Saint Bavo at Ghent. He preached to the fiercest people of Brabant and at last suffered martyrdom for Christ at Esch, a village in the diocese of Cambrai. His body was brought back to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Bavo. At Cologne Agrippina, the burial of Saint Cunibert, seventh archbishop of that city. Being the son of Duke Crallo, he governed the church of Cologne most excellently for forty years and was a support to Duke Pippin, administrator of the royal household. When on one occasion he” etc., almost as above. “In Africa, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Arcadius, Paschasius, Probus, and Eutychianus. Since they absolutely refused to fall into the Arian perfidy, they were first proscribed, then driven into exile, tortured with the most savage punishments, and finally killed by various deaths; they met their end in a glorious and wondrous martyrdom.” They belong to the following day. In smaller type it continues: “Likewise at Tours, the seven holy Sleepers, Clement, Primus, Cletus, Theodore, Gaudentius, Quiriacus, and Innocent, the nephews of Saint Martin, descended from two brothers. Gregory, archbishop of Tours, described their life and distinguished conduct.” Then the entry for Paternus, correctly. For Boniface, as in LEYDEN, etc. Next, for Veranus of Lyons, whom it calls Serianus, from the preceding day. The entries for Aemilianus and Leonius are pure. Finally: “On the same day, the burial of Saint Walericus the confessor.” See Usuard on 12 December.

HAGENAU is pure in its first part. Concerning Cunibert, in the words of LEYDEN it adds: “And he fully demonstrated where Ursula, queen of virgins, was.” It correctly gives Paternus and Leonius. Then: “At Rome, Saint Boniface IV, pope. He obtained from the emperor Phocas that [I think: the chair of] the blessed apostle Peter should be the head of all the churches, because Constantinople was writing itself to be the first of all the churches. He himself also instituted the feast of All Saints and All Souls’ Day. On the same day, in the territory of the diocese of Utrecht, the burial of Saint Lebuinus the confessor. He was archdeacon of Saint Willibrord the bishop, a man in every respect praiseworthy, and converted many pagans to the faith.”

AQUICINCT adds: “At Rome, Saint Boniface, pope. He obtained from the emperor Phocas that the Apostolic See of the blessed apostle Peter should be the head of all the churches, because etc.,” as in HAGENAU. At the end, in a more recent hand: “At Ghent, Saint Livinus, Irish archbishop and martyr.”

VICTORINUS has at the end: “In the territory of Nevers, Saint Honoratus the confessor.” Castellanus does not note him. Then: “At Rome, Pope Martin,” without the title “martyr”; he is likewise marked in that manner, but alone, in the REG. SUEC. manuscript numbered 130.

[Col. 0688B]

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Lebuinus the confessor. Cunibert, bishop of Cologne. Paternus the martyr. Leonius the confessor. The Seven Sleepers. Brictius, bishop and confessor.” See the Usuardine text for the following day.

VATICAN, no. 5949, has nothing Usuardine, but takes its text from elsewhere: “The feast of Saint Melanius, bishop of the city of Redon.” Others also record him on this day and on other days, but he belongs to 6 January. “In Africa, the holy martyrs Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Luticianus, who, being originally from Spain and held in high honor and affection by Genseric, king of the Vandals, and refusing to yield to the Arian perfidy, were first proscribed, then driven into exile,” etc., from the text of the following day.

In UGHELLIANUS the entry for Paternus is lacking.

FLORENTINE: “Likewise Saint Melanius, bishop and confessor of the city of Redon, who, after innumerable signs of virtue, ever intent upon heaven, departed from the earth.” These are almost the very words of the text we cited for 6 January.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “At the city of Agrippina, Cologne, the feast of Saint Cunibert, archbishop and confessor. At one time he” etc., as in LEYDEN. Then it gives Boniface as in the same manuscript, except that after “where once,” it inserts “in the time of Domitian.” The rest of the text follows, quite purely.
