Then: “At Vienne, [Saint Esichius, bishop,] who presided over the church after Blessed Pantagathus. At the city of Deventer, the feast of Blessed Lebuinus, bishop and confessor. At Conflans, the translation of Saint Castor, priest and confessor. On the same day, the passion of Saint Livinus, bishop and martyr.”

BELIN is fairly pure in the first part; the second concerns Paternus. Two other entries are missing, and in their place almost the whole text from 10 November is appended. The second edition adds Cunibert, whom it calls Cumbert. At the end: “In the territory of Ghent, Saint Livinus, bishop [Col. 0688D] and confessor.” Why not “martyr”? Lebuinus is not mentioned here.

GREVEN: “Ahiah the Shilonite, prophet, concerning whom see 3 Kings 2. Note. Blessed Cunibert’s future merit, from the very beginning of his adolescence, was prefigured when King Dagobert, in whose court the boy was staying, once saw the place where he slept illuminated by an immense heavenly light.” This cannot, apparently, be understood of Dagobert. “When he had become bishop and was offering the mystery of our redemption in the basilica of the holy virgins, the clergy and people standing by saw a most splendid dove settle upon his head, truly approving him as a priest worthy of Christ. On the same day, Blessed Livinus, bishop and martyr. He was Scottish by nationality, illustrious from his earliest age in life and miracles, and possessed such great faith that he is even said to have walked upon the waters. At last, leaving his homeland for God’s work, after converting very many to the faith, he was killed by unbelievers in Brabant and earned the crown of martyrdom. Likewise, according to Ado [in the form] published by Mosander, this was Boniface IV, pope, who sat for eight months and twenty-two days and consecrated the Pantheon, obtained from the emperor Phocas, in honor of all the saints. In Africa, Marius and Publius. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the holy Germans, Theophilus, Caesarius, and Eusebius.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies. “Graphildis, matron and martyr. When she proclaimed that the holy martyr Livinus was innocent and was suffering unjustly, the impious killed her as well, together with her little son Brictius; thus she obtained the glory of martyrdom. In Ireland, Saint Laurence, archbishop. Renatus, bishop and confessor. At Vienne, Saint Eusebius [in the first edition, Esichius], bishop and confessor. Macarius, bishop. On the same day at Deventer, the burial of Saint Lebuinus the confessor. He came from England and, when our Savior appeared to him in a vision and commanded him to go forth, announced the Gospel of God to the Saxon people around the river IJssel. After enduring many tribulations for the word, he rested in peace. Imarius the confessor, from whom Saint Malachy first received the model of holy life and conduct. On Mount Nitria, Saint Hor, abbot and confessor.”

MOLANUS, concerning Martin and Tiberius, etc., from 10 November: “At the port of Ghent, the burial of Saint Livinus, bishop and martyr. On the same day, beside the river IJssel, in the town of Deventer, Saint Lebuinus, priest and confessor.” Then, in smaller type, Renatus and Imarius from GREVEN. Other editions have Livinus and Lebuinus as the earlier edition. “Likewise Saint Renatus, bishop and confessor of Angers. At Vienne, Saint Isicius, bishop.” Then, in smaller type: “Likewise Blessed Graphildis and the boy Brictius, martyrs with Saint Livinus, whose bodies are kept at Ghent in portable tombs. At Prague, the feast of five hermits who suffered martyrdom in the wilderness of Greater Poland, where the town of Kazimierz now stands.” You will note that these editions do not preserve the Usuardine text, since Martin is placed first.]

[Col. 0685A]

In the province of Tarragona, at the city of Tarazona, Blessed Emilianus, priest and confessor, whose admirable life Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, described in simple language. At the city of Agrippina, the burial of Saint Cunibert, bishop. In the territory of Sens, Saint Paternus the martyr. At the castle of Melun, Saint Leonius the confessor.

On the Ides. The 13th day. [Note: [Col. 0689]

Among all the manuscripts, I consider only HERINIAN and the first edition of MUNERATUS pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0689C]

In HERINIAN nothing noteworthy occurs apart from “Pascasius.” MUNERATUS is everywhere full of typographical errors, at least in the second edition. It contains an addition concerning Gendulfus, which Rosweydus, collator of both editions, says is absent from the earlier one. Instead of “Mitrius,” it has “the most renowned Nutrius,” omitting, perhaps deliberately, the title “martyr.” MOLANUS alone reads “Eutichianus”; the small Roman Martyrology and Ado have “Eutychianus”; the others have “Eutychii.” We, with the manuscripts, read “Euticiani”; MUNERATUS incorrectly has “Uticiani.” In the text the others have “Briccius,” while the manuscripts, GREVEN, MOLANUS, and others read “Brictius,” with Ado; Bede has “Briccius.” I pass over the remaining minor points in order to examine variations of somewhat greater importance.

The distinguished Castellanus, who more than once compared the first edition of MOLANUS with the Pratensis manuscript, gave the following warning concerning the manuscript’s present additions: At the end: “At Toledo, Saint Eugenius, bishop and confessor. At Malbode, Saint Aldegundis, virgin.” And in the margin: “At Paris, Saint Gendulfus, bishop.” There is no controversy about the last, since it certainly does not belong to Usuard. Enough has been said about Aldegundis under 30 January; it is clear that she was erased from that day and transferred to this one by someone unknown. Here one should write “at the monastery of Malbode,” as our copy reads and as the manuscripts ANTUERP.-MAJ., ROSWEYDUS, and AQUICINCT also read—the customary companions of the Pratensis manuscript. It is therefore sufficiently clear that the aforesaid manuscripts cannot be counted among the pure ones for this day. The question is whether Eugenius of Toledo belongs to Usuard, since in the Pratensis copy and the three companions just mentioned he is marked as follows: “At the city of Toledo, Saint Eugenius the prelate,” not, as Castellanus read above, “bishop and confessor.” The doubt is increased especially by GREVEN and MOLANUS, in whom Eugenius is entirely absent. But, unless I am mistaken, these two have confused the Eugenius of this day with another who is celebrated on 15 November. GREVEN sufficiently suggests this by calling him a martyr in the additions; MOLANUS, although he also places the present Eugenius in the additions, expressed it so clearly in italic letters in the text for 15 November that our conjecture seems certain. It can also be extended without hesitation to other manuscripts, especially those of middling quality. We therefore follow HERINIAN and the first edition of MUNERATUS as the purest, under the entry that we have presented in the text and that can be abundantly defended from many other manuscripts and, in substance, from the Pratensis itself and its cited companions. We believe that this Spanish saint was also probably included by Usuard with many others, and that his commemoration was first and authentically entered by him in the sacred Martyrology. Another conjecture will be proposed below.]

[Note: [Col. 0689D]

The first three martyrs are recorded on this day in almost all the Hieronymian manuscripts as follows: “In the city of Ravenna, Saints Valentinus, Solutor, and Victor.” Florentius notes from Galesinius that there were three Ravennate martyrs bearing the name Valentinus, and says that the one commemorated today is the one mentioned in the Acts of Dalmatius. Baronius supplies some additional information, but no one so far has brought to light either Acts of their martyrdom or any certain knowledge of their life. In due time we shall see what substantial evidence the people of Ravenna produce. The small Roman Martyrology, in its customary brevity, has: “At Ravenna, Valentinus, Salutor, and Victor, martyrs.” Ado’s entire entry has been reproduced fully in our text.

Likewise, the entry placed second, concerning Mitrius, Mitria, or Metria, first recorded by Ado in precisely those words, is unknown to all the other Martyrologists. The crown of the most renowned martyr is read most explicitly both in Ado and Usuard; but from all that Gregory of Tours reports in On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 71, nothing can be gathered beyond the fact that he was a confessor, as is also expressed in the title itself. If you wish to call him a martyr because of certain struggles on behalf of the faith, or perhaps because he endured tortures, you may do so as far as I am concerned. Before me, Surius and Castellanus observed that he did not suffer a violent death. Gregory calls him Metrias; Mitrias is found in the manuscript Life, or rather in some encomium, which is preserved among us and which, if only it could in some measure compensate for the loss of the earlier Acts.

The glorious firstfruits of the Vandal persecution are celebrated by the small Roman Martyrology on the preceding day, 12 November: “In Africa, Arcadius, Paschasius, Probus, and Eutychianus, martyrs in the persecution of the Vandals.” Ado narrates the history at greater length from Prosper’s Chronicle under the year 437, marked by the consuls Aetius II and Sigisvultus, or Sigevultus. This, then, is the entire origin of their cult and feast; it is not to be sought among the earlier Martyrologists who are incorrectly cited. See what Baronius noted about these martyrs and their companion Paulillus, and what Ruinart discussed somewhat more carefully in his History of the Vandal Persecution, pages 431–441. Tillemont treats the matter more briefly in volume XVI, page 500 onward.]

[Col. 0692A]

Bede writes “At Tours, the feast of Saint Brictius, bishop,” and adds an encomium under the name of Florus. Rabanus, following Bede in the rest, merely indicates that he was Martin’s successor. Ado also follows Bede, and Our Author follows him, in nearly the same terms. Florentius considers Brictius an interpolation in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. The notes of Molanus and Baronius should be consulted. His fairly concise Life is found in Surius, drawn from Gregory of Tours; we shall discuss it more fully elsewhere with our manuscript collections. Wandalbert thus depicts Brictius in his native language:

> On the Ides, your heir, O Martin,  
> Brictius resumes [his charge], proven by exile, tears, and signs.

Above we showed that Eugenius of Toledo, the second of that name, was first and authentically recorded by Usuard, either from particular Spanish information or, if one prefers, from Ildefonsus’s book On Writers, just as we recently mentioned Braulio. In Miraeus’s edition it is on page 98, where in chapter 14 [Col. 0692B] one finds an excellent encomium, together with a distinguished note by the editor. More will be collected elsewhere for future use from Nicolaus Antonius and other Spanish writers.]

[Note: [Col. 0691B]

PRATENSIS: The additions to this manuscript have been discussed sufficiently above under the Variants.

TORNACENSIS lacks Eugenius; in the rest of the text it is by no means entirely pure. At the end it adds: “On the same day, Saint Gendulfus, bishop.”

ANTWERP-MAJOR continues to contain some disorder in the text; but it has Eugenius and Aldegundis as the Pratensis does, in the same words.

ROSWEYD begins with Brictius; the rest agrees with the Pratensis, especially concerning Eugenius and Aldegundis, discussed above.

PULSANEN has a distinctive beginning: “The feast of the most blessed John of Constantinople, surnamed Chrysostom, bishop, who greatly benefited the Christian religion by word and example.” Then it gives Brictius and the Ravennate martyrs. The rest is absent.

ANTWERP, MAX.-LÜBECK, and UGHELLIAN have the text through Brictius, inclusive. Then they add: “On the same day, Saint Kilianus the confessor.” Castellanus calls him Kallenus.

The second edition of MUNERATUS, pure in the text, adds: “At Paris, the passing of Saint Gendulfus, bishop, ordained by Blessed Sixtus, at whose command he raised from the dead the son of a pagan; the head of this man rests in the great church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Paris.”

We have already said that GREVEN and MOLANUS both lack the entry for Eugenius of Toledo.

ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, and LEYDEN, LOVANIUM, ALBERGEN, and DANIC begin: “At Tours, Saint Brictius, bishop and confessor, who succeeded Blessed Martin, of whom he had been deacon, in the episcopate.” The first three entries of the Usuardine text follow, fairly pure. Nothing is said of Eugenius. At the end, however, they add: “On the same day, Saint Kilianus or Kylianus the confessor.”

CENTULA: “At Ravenna, the holy martyrs Valentinus, Solutor, and Victor. At the city of Toledo, Saint Eugenius the prelate, a most learned man. At Tours, Saint Brictius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the translation of Aldegundis, virgin. On the same day, Saint Quillia [undoubtedly Kilianus], confessor. At the monastery of Saint Bertinus, Saint Folquinus the confessor.”

BRUSSELS begins as follows: “At Tours, the burial of Saint Brictius, bishop and confessor. Although he had greatly and unjustly assailed Blessed Martin with insults, he heard that he would become bishop after him but would suffer much in the episcopate; and the outcome proved this true.” To the three Ravennate martyrs it adds Maurilius and Publius. It is pure in the entry for Mitrius. It continues: “In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, Saint Columbanus, abbot, of Scottish origin.” See 21 November. In a somewhat later hand the following is inserted: “At Alexandria, the feast of the fifty pagan teachers whom Blessed Catherine, defeating them in debate, converted to the faith of Christ; the emperor Maximinus had them baked in fire and made them martyrs worthy of God.” This is from the commonly circulated Acts. Mitrius is wrongly repeated. Then: “At the monastery of Malbode, Blessed Aldegundis, virgin. On the same day, Saint Kilianus the confessor.” Enough has been said about Aldegundis.

HAGENAU is pure in the first part. It continues: “Likewise Saint Kylianus the confessor, companion of Saint Leobinus, bishop [Col. 0692C] and martyr. Likewise Saint Dalmatius, bishop and confessor.” It is correct in the entry for Mitrius. Then: “Likewise Saint Maxellendis, virgin and martyr.” It reports the commemoration of the African martyrs fairly purely, but gives Brictius as follows:

“At the city of Tours, Saint Brictius, bishop and confessor. This Brictius, because he scandalized eight bishops and several clerics by his life, was given by them to Blessed Martin as a son. Brictius, who was three days old, denied that Martin was his father and proclaimed a certain John to be his father. Blessed Martin made this Brictius his archdeacon and endured many scandals and accusations from him. As his reward, Martin obtained the episcopate for him and foretold that he would have to endure many adversities. For in the thirtieth year of his episcopate he was expelled, accused of sexual misconduct, and proscribed for seven years, until he came to recognize the wrong he had done to Martin. Then he was restored, sat honorably for seven years, and died in peace.”

[Col. 0692D]

AQUICINCT writes “Demetrius” instead of “Mitrius.” In Eugenius and Aldegundis it agrees with the Pratensis and its other companions mentioned above. It also has: “In the territory of Cambrai, the feast of Saint Maxellendis, virgin and martyr.” See Castellanus’s Universal Martyrology.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Brictius, bishop and confessor. Livinus, bishop and martyr, at Ghent.” See the additions for the preceding day. “Arcadius the martyr, with his companions. Valentinus the martyr, with his companions.” It usually abbreviates everything.

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “At Paris, the translation of Saint Gendulfus, bishop, ordained by Blessed Sixtus, at whose command he raised the dead son of a pagan.” See the second edition of MUNERATUS above.

Codex D. DU CHEVAL, siglum C: “And Amandus, bishop.” It concerns the bishop of Redon.

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, Saint Albo, abbot and confessor” [the manuscript has Abbo]. Castellanus explains the place and manner of his death in the Universal Martyrology. “Saint Adorator, martyr.”

FLORENTINE: “In Italy, at Cremona, Saint Homobonus the confessor. Likewise Saint Kilianus.” Then one of three manuscripts, probably the STROZZIAN, has: “On the same day, Saint Veranus, bishop.” Concerning him, see 11 November.

MONTIS SANCTI: “The elevation of Saints Romaricus, Amatus, and Adelphius, by whose merits and intercession we hope to be helped.”

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition begins: “At the city of Tours in Gaul, the feast of Saint Brictius, bishop and confessor, to whom the holy man Martin, when he was his deacon, foretold that he would become his successor in the episcopate and would suffer many adversities in it; all these things happened just as the holy man had foretold. At Alexandria, the fifty orators whom the virgin of Christ, Catherine, converted to God. But the tyrant Maxentius had them all burned in fire in the time of the emperor Constantine.” It is pure in the Ravennate martyrs and in Mitrius. In the African martyrs, after “Probus,” it inserts: “and Eutychianus and Paulillus.” Then, at the end, the tyrant is wrongly noted; under the king of the Vandals, Syrus, it makes Kilianus a bishop.

BELIN has the entire text, but before Eugenius it adds: “In Italy, at the city of Cremona, Saint Homobonus, whose holiness shines through frequent miracles.” See Surius. The second edition adds at the end: “Likewise Amandus, bishop.”

GREVEN: “Likewise, with Saints Arcadius, etc., the holy boy Paulillus [Paulissus] was condemned to servitude by Syrus, king of the Vandals. At the city of Toledo, Eugenius, bishop and martyr. Antoninus, martyr. Likewise the fifty martyred orators who believed through the confession of Blessed Catherine. In Thrace, Saints Edictus, Eutychus, and Hermogenes. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saints Antonius, Gehenna, and Adrian, with others. Likewise Saints Amantius and Antonia. At Paris, Saint Gundulfus, bishop and confessor. Paternianus, bishop and confessor. Divinicus, bishop. Kilianus, bishop and confessor. At Cremona, Saint Homobonus the confessor. He was first a merchant; then, touched by heavenly inspiration and longing with all his heart for heavenly profits, he gave up his spirit while engaged in prayer. Likewise Saint Folquinus. Maxellendis, virgin. Aldegundis, virgin.”

MOLANUS: “In Italy, at the city of Cremona, Saint Homobonus, whose holiness shines through frequent miracles.” The entry for Eugenius follows. Then Gendulfus, word for word from the second edition of MUNERATUS. “At Cambrai, the feast of Saint Maxellendis, virgin and martyr.” Then, in smaller type: “Kilianus, bishop and confessor, at Albinia in the territory of Arras. At Clermont, the burial of Saint Quintianus, bishop and confessor of that place.” Other editions mix into the text: “But the boy Paulillus, beaten with clubs and condemned to miserable servitude, was therefore, as appears, not killed, so that even that age might glory in the enemy’s cruelty having been overcome.” At the end, Gendulfus, Quintianus, Kilianus, Maxellendis, Homobonus, and Eugenius are given as in the earlier edition. Then: “At Piacenza, the revelation of Saint Antoninus the martyr. At the monastery of Malbode, the translation of Saint Aldegundis, virgin. At the monastery called Sithiu, the first elevation and translation of the body of Saint Folquinus, bishop of Thérouanne, in the year 928.” Finally, in smaller type: “In Palestine, the holy martyrs Antonius, priest, Zebinas, and Germanus, whom the governor Firmilianus, when they offered themselves voluntarily, ordered to be beheaded without any other form of punishment. On the same day, Saint Ennatha, virgin, who, brought before the same judge, was burned in fire after severe tortures.” See Eusebius describing their triumph among the Palestinian Martyrs in Ruinart’s Selecta, page 343, and Surius on this day.]

[Col. 0689]

At Ravenna, the feast of the holy martyrs Valentinus, Solutor, and Victor. In Provence, at the city of Aix, Blessed Mitrius, the most renowned martyr. In Africa, the holy martyrs Arcadius, Paschasius, Probus, and Eutychianus, who, since they would not in any way yield to the Arian perfidy, were first proscribed, then driven into exile, afterward tortured with the most savage punishments, and finally killed by various deaths [Bouillart, in the page margin: “At Paris, Saint Gendulfus, bishop”]. At Tours, the burial of Saint Brictius, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0689B] This is how the Pratensis manuscript has it here. These three words, “At the city of Toledo, Saint,” do not differ from the rest of the page. The first two syllables of the name Eugenius are by the same hand, but in darker ink. The remaining letters of that name and of “prelate” are written over an erasure, together with the first four letters of the word “Malbode.” The rest is sound. Nevertheless, I suspect that the original letters were covered with new ink so that they would not fade. The conjecture is strengthened by the last two syllables of “Aldegundis” and the intact word “virgin,” which, because they were not renewed in the same manner, begin to strike the eye less and less. BOUILLART.]

At the city of Toledo, Saint Eugenius, bishop and confessor. [Bouillart: “Saint Eugenius the prelate. At the monastery of Malbode, Saint Aldegundis, virgin.”]

The eighteenth day before the Kalends. The 14th day. [Note: [Col. 0693C]

Almost all the manuscripts agree: PRATENSIS, HERINIAN, TORNACENSIS, ANTWERP-MAJOR, ROSWEYD, PULSANEN, ANTWERP, MAX.-LÜBECK, BELIN, GREVEN, and MOLANUS. Likewise ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, LOVANIUM, ALBERGEN, and DANIC.]

[Note: [Col. 0693C]

With the purer manuscripts we write *Thraciam* (“Thrace”), rather than the variant spellings *Trhaciam*, *Trachiam*, and *Traciam* found in some others. Most have “Eraclea”; in PULSANEN, ANTWERP, and MOLANUS it is correctly “Heraclea”; in HERINIAN it is most incorrectly “Araclea.” ANTWERP-MAJOR omitted Clementinus; LEYDEN omitted Theodotus. MUNERATUS writes “Clementius” and likewise “Theodotius”; BELIN has “Theodocius.” ROSWEYD has “Phylominus,” PULSANEN “Philemonis.” ROSWEYD differs most from the others by adding to those three “and many other martyrs,” but this does not exclude it from the number of pure manuscripts. In the second entry there is greater agreement. MUNERATUS alone, instead of “they might cast him down,” incorrectly reads “they cast him down,” with a faulty construction, and then completes the sense: “and thus the holy martyr of Christ is made.” ROSWEYD, GREVEN, and MOLANUS have “and thus he is made a martyr of Christ”; ANTWERP-MAJOR has “and thus he would be made a martyr of Christ,” as in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0693D]

The Hieronymian copies cited by Florentius do not entirely agree in reporting our first commemoration. The manuscripts from which the editor usually constructs his text read there: “At Eraclea, a city of Thrace, the feast of Saints Clementinus, Theodota, Philominus, and many others whose names God knows.” The Corbie manuscript, even as edited by Acherius, has a somewhat fuller form: “Saints Clemens, Clementinus, Theodota, Philominus, and many others.” In Rabanus, who certainly had a Hieronymian manuscript before him, the wording grows: “The feast of Saint Clentinus” [it is quite clear that one should read Clementinus] “and Theodota, Philominus, at Heraclea, Martialis, Donatus, and many other holy ones.” But who can determine anything distinctly about all these many saints, when, apart from the evidence of the Martyrologies, no other documents are known to survive from which their number can be established? The very ancient manuscript of Echternach seems preferable to all these manuscripts, since it records the matter briefly and simply: “At Eraclea, Clementinus and Theodotus, Philominus.” The small Roman Martyrology, Bede, and Florus do not mention them. Nor does the very old parchment Calendar of the distinguished church of Brioude, written easily five hundred years ago and shown to us here at Antwerp in 1711 by the eminent Cardinal Bullionius, read the names accurately enough; it gives them as follows: “The feast of Clementinus, Theudota, Erdeli.” Nevertheless, it agrees with the Echternach manuscript in naming only three martyrs and recording no anonymous companions. I am fully convinced that Ado had before him a model similar to the aforesaid Echternach manuscript, from which he expressed his entry in the form in which Usuard copied it from him in the text; the only difference is that, instead of Ado’s “Philumenus,” Our Author restored the better form from older sources, “Philominus.” For the rest, see the cited Florentius. Whoever brings the Acts of these saints to light from some other source will uncover a treasure. Wandalbert praises these three in the following verses:

> Clementinus, Theodotus, and Philominus hold  
> The eighteenth day before the Kalends of December;  
> Together they suffered the commands of the bloody torturer.

The entry for Serapion is owed to the author of the small Roman Martyrology. Consulting his principal source, he took it from the same letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Fabius of Antioch, preserved in Rufinus, book VI, chapter 31; from that letter we previously gave Metra on 31 January, Cointa on 8 February, and Apollonia on 9 February. He summarizes the matter briefly: “At Alexandria, Serapion, who, cast down under Decius, was made a martyr.” Ado took somewhat more from the cited history, which in the Mantuan edition of 1479 reads as follows: “They also inflicted the most cruel punishments on Serapion, found in his own house, so that after first loosening all the joints of his limbs, they cast him down from above.” Our entire text is plainly derived from the Ado cited above, while retaining the name of the tyrant Decius, which was wrongly introduced by the small Roman Martyrology. For it is most clearly evident from the aforesaid letter of Dionysius, as we have also observed elsewhere, that Metra, Cointa, Apollonia, and Serapion were killed in a furious popular riot before the horrible and terrifying edicts of Decius. The curious reader may consult again our historical-chronological Treatise on the Alexandrian Patriarchs, page 31, no. 164, or rather the original source itself in Eusebius, in the Valesian edition, book VI, chapter 41, from which Ruinart took it for his Selecta, page 104.]

[Note: [Col. 0695B]

CENTULA, fairly pure in the first edition, continues as follows: “At Alexandria, Blessed Serapion the martyr. At Laodicea, Saint Anatolius, bishop.”

BRUSSELS: “At Alexandria, Saint Serapion, glorious martyr. Whom the persecutors under Caesar Decius, etc.,” ending, “and thus he became Christ’s martyr.” Among the Heracleans it calls the third man Philomonus. It continues: “Still in Thrace, the feast of the holy martyrs Edictus, Eutyches, Hermogenes, and Felicianus. Likewise Rufus the confessor.”

HAGENAU: “In England, Saint Laurence, bishop and confessor. Likewise Saint Rufus, first bishop and confessor of the church of Avignon.” He is in the Roman Martyrology on 12 November. “At Vienne, Saint Eustichius, bishop.” See the additions under the cited day, where he is called Esichius or, elsewhere, Hesychius. A longer history of the patriarch Isaac follows, part of which I insert here:

“Isaac the patriarch. He was born from aged parents through the Lord’s promise, and an angel gave him his name. His merit and dignity were prophetically foretold. He softened the grief of his mother’s death through his union with his wife Rebecca, by whom he himself fathered two sons, namely Esau and Jacob,” etc.; these matters are set out better in the sacred pages. Then it treats Serapion, and afterward the Heracleans, quite purely. Finally: “At Alexandria, the fifty rhetoricians who were martyred, whom Blessed Catherine converted; among them the principal ones were Eustorgius and Agro.” It ventures somewhat more than the other manuscripts on the preceding day.

AQUICINCT has at the end: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Vntigius the confessor.” Codex D. DU CHEVAL, marked C, has the same. See Castellanus, who calls him Antidius.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Clementinus the martyr with his companions. The renowned martyr Serapion.”

AUGENSIS: In another hand is added: “On the same day, Saint Laurence, bishop of Dublin, legate of all Ireland, who, passing through the final day of temporal life, attained unending glory and illuminates the Church by miracles.” His Life is found in Surius. See also the note of P. Mothier. More will be supplied by the various manuscripts in our possession.

In VATICAN, no. 5949, in red letters in the margin of the manuscript, but written by the same hand, is: “Saint John, hermit and confessor.”

ALTEMPS: “On the same day, the translation of Erkenwald, bishop of London.” He is celebrated on 30 April. “At Laodicea, Saint Anatolius, bishop.”

FLORENTINE: “In the territory of Rouen, at the village of Eu, Saint Laurence, archbishop and confessor, who was so glorious before God in life and miracles that, among many other miracles, he is said on reliable testimony to have raised seven dead people.”

CLAUDIAC: “The feast of Saint Antigius the confessor.”

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition begins: “At Alexandria, Saint Serapion, whom the persecutors, having found him in his house under the emperor Decius, etc. Likewise at Alexandria, the passion of the holy martyrs Meleus, Trophonius, Martialis, Alexander, and Silvanus, with their companions. In Thrace, the feast of the holy martyrs Clementinus the bishop, Theodorus, and Philominus, who suffered at the city of Heraclea. At Cologne Agrippina, in the church of Saint Andrew the apostle, the commemoration of Saint Cunibert, archbishop and confessor.” I do not know what is intended here; Cunibert’s feast is above, on 12 November.

GREVEN: “Plato the martyr. At Alexandria, Saints Meleus, Trophinus, Marcialis, Alexander, and Silvanus, martyrs, with many others. Albricus, bishop and confessor of Utrecht. Heraclius, bishop. Fridolinus, bishop. Modanus, bishop. Piamunus, abbot and confessor. Rufus, confessor. Attingus, confessor. In Gaul, Veneranda, virgin and martyr. In the time of Antoninus, she was stretched out on wood for the faith of Christ and beaten with raw sinews. Then, overcoming by Christ’s power a cauldron boiling with water, oil, pitch, and sulfur, as well as other tortures, she attained the glory of martyrdom by beheading, together with several others who believed through her confession. Likewise Placilla, of blessed memory, wife of the emperor Theodosius.”

MOLANUS: “On the same day, Blessed Laurence, bishop and confessor.” In smaller type is added: “Of Dublin [Col. 0696D] and primate of Ireland, whose most holy life is preserved.” Later editions concerning Laurence of Dublin read: “At Rouen, Blessed Laurence, bishop and confessor of Dublin.”]

At Heraclea, a city of Thrace, the feast day of the holy martyrs Clementinus, Theodotus, and Philominus. At Alexandria, Saint Serapion, whom the persecutors under the emperor Decius subjected to the cruellest punishments: first dislocating all his limbs, they threw him down from an upper story, and thus he became a martyr of Christ.

**Seventeenth day before the Kalends. Day 15.** [Note: [Col. 0697]

Pratensis, Tornacensis, Antwerp-Major, and Molanus simply and accurately reproduce the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0967A]

Antwerp-Major reads incorrectly: *ex uno aetatis suae anno* instead of *a quinto decimo anno*, and moreover produces an incoherent sense by writing *miraculorum insignis* while omitting the word *gloria*. I have written *Martiano*, with most witnesses; Molanus has *Marciano*, Tornacensis, worse, *Martiniano*. Antwerp-Major again has *martyrium sumpsit*. Molanus almost always tends to correct *Parisiensem* to *Parisiacensem*; Tornacensis makes the matter more disgraceful with *per, aput pagum Parisiacensem urbem*. Antwerp-Major has *consumpmata*.

It is asked whether Macutus, Machutus, Magutus, Machutes, Maclovius, or Machlonius—for this is how the name is rendered in the manuscripts—belongs to Usuard; that is, whether Usuard placed him here. In the Pratensis manuscript the following is added in the margin: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Macutus, bishop and confessor.” Rosweyd reads: “On the same day, Saint Machlonius,” and so forth. Antwerp, Maximilian of Lübeck, and Ughelli: “On that very day, the feast of Saint Macutus.” Greven: “In Lesser Britain, the deposition of Saint Machutus,” and so forth. The manuscripts of middling authority have: “On the same day, blessed Magutus,” and so forth. Muneratus gives a longer and different wording from all of them; Belinus abbreviates the name. I judge that this is not Usuardine, on the basis of the manuscripts from Herinis, Pulsano, and those cited for the text, since I consider the addition in Pratensis to be supplementary. Add the variant wordings, which sufficiently show that all these forms do not derive from one and the same source. The rest is found in the appendices. Consult Motherius’s note on the Roman Martyrology for this day.]

[Note: [Col. 0697A]

Bollandus, the parent of our work, rightly observed and demonstrated long ago that the notices and commemorations of saints named Felix are confused and shamefully disordered in the Martyrologies, when he was discussing that celebrated Felix of Nola, or Paulinus, on 14 January, beginning at page 937. We have had to acknowledge the same point more than once above, but especially on the cited days, 14 January, 24 October, and elsewhere.

Here the Felix recurs whom writers commonly identify as the first bishop and martyr of Nola, while reviewing certain Acts reported by Ughelli in volume VI, column 286. The views of the aforementioned Bollandus agree with these Acts, and I do not see how the distinction of this Felix from the others can be denied or refuted, without rashness, against the express authority of the ancient Martyrologies.

Castellanus nevertheless seems to have wished to forestall or somehow weaken this conclusion when, in a note to the Universal Martyrology, he remarks that before the author of the Little Roman Martyrology no mention anywhere had been made of any Felix of Nola except the celebrated confessor of 14 January. I do not deny that this is so; but unless we imagine that author to have been dreaming or—something impious—that he deliberately imposed a falsehood, we must accept the earlier records from which he could so explicitly state: “Of Felix, bishop, who from his fifteenth year was renowned for the glory of miracles and, under Martianus, completed his martyrdom with twenty-five others, buried in the church of Nola.”

What Ado added about Elpidius, the guardian of the burial, does not belong to the Little Roman Martyrology, nor did Usuard intend to reproduce it in such detail. In any event, here we have Felix, bishop, crowned with martyrdom together with thirty companions and buried at Nola; the doubts of modern writers, especially those of Tillemont in volume IV, pages 655–656, will not easily deprive us of him.

His Acts, in Ughelli and elsewhere, need neither be examined nor defended by me here. But I shall not allow the credibility of the Little Roman Martyrology and of those who followed it to be diminished on the basis of mere conjectures, whatever the age of that Felix may finally have been, and whatever place may be assigned to him among the bishops of Nola or of another locality. These matters will have to be discussed elsewhere more fully and accurately.]

[Col. 0698A] The other notice, concerning Eugene the martyr of the Parisian region, is entangled in no fewer difficulties—at least as it is now commonly understood after Maurolycus, Molanus, and the more recent Martyrologists. We said above that Molanus, on 13 November, excluded Eugene, bishop of Toledo, from Usuard’s text, suspecting that he did so because he had thought the present martyr to have been a bishop of Toledo.

And indeed this is now a widespread opinion, although I cannot understand on what grounds it can be made plausible—any more than the further claim that he was a disciple of Dionysius the Areopagite, or was ordained by that same Dionysius. I well know that several men have laboured diligently on this question, and that their writings are preserved among us; nevertheless, I dare not defend what seems to me unfounded. Nor, accordingly, can I assert that our Eugene, the martyr in the Parisian region, was a bishop of Toledo sent across the Alps by Peter or Clement together with the Areopagite.

If there were leisure to set out the evidence, there is no doubt that even the Spaniards themselves would readily agree, and would rather adopt the opinion of Miraeus in the Belgian Fasti for this day. I do not, however, wish to act as judge here. I merely point out that Floharius, writing in the twelfth century in Surius, or similar writers, are not sufficiently reliable witnesses for safely deciding so ancient and uncertain a matter.

In my judgment Usuard rightly and truthfully marked the matter when—whether he transferred it to the sacred Fasti from Wandalbertus’s metrical work or from elsewhere—he simply said that Eugene, having completed the course of martyrdom, received from the Lord the crown of blessed suffering, mentioning nothing at all about episcopal dignity, which in Usuard’s age was not yet known at Saint-Denis.

See more in Du Bois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, volume I, beginning at page 33, and in Tillemont, volume IV, pages 453 and 717. We shall discuss these matters more suitably in their proper place, meanwhile leaving untouched the authority of Baronius and others who may have chosen to adhere to the more recent opinion.

Wandalbertus may have preceded Usuard, or rather both may have drawn from a common source. Certainly the following verse plainly shows that he agrees with our Usuard:

> Eugene the martyr shines with seven and ten.

]

[Note: [Col. 0697D]

**Pratensis.** The marginal addition has been sufficiently discussed. “The dedication of a church in honour of Saint John the Baptist,” and so forth, does not properly belong here.

**Herinensis.** To the pure text he adds: “On the same day, blessed Junianus the confessor, whom blessed Remigius washed in baptism.” It is plainly a local addition.

**Rosweyd.** In the first section he is pure; the second he gives as follows: “In the Parisian district, Saint Eugene the martyr. On the same day, Saint Machlonius, bishop and confessor of Antioch, Valerian the martyr, with fifteen others.”

**Pulsanensis.** He begins: “At Cologne, a city of Campania,” and so forth, correctly; the second entry reads: “On that very day, Saint Eugene.” The remainder is absent.

**Antwerp, Maximilian of Lübeck, Ughelli, and Greven.** We have reported the appendix to these manuscripts among the Variants. See also Castellanus’s note on the Universal Martyrology.

**Muneratus.** After the text: “In Britain, at the city of Aleth, the feast of blessed Macutus, bishop and confessor, who from the first training of his youth shone splendidly through countless miracles: in one and the same instance, restoring a very bright glass cup from a stone, wine from water, and a man from death, wondrously bringing him back to life.”

**Antwerp-Major, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Alberg, and the Danish manuscript:** “On the same day, blessed Magutus, bishop and confessor.” Some have *Machutus*.

**Centulensis:** “The feast of Saint Felix, bishop and martyr. [Col. 0699A] In the territory of Paris, Saint Eugene the martyr. In Britain, which is now called Cornwall, Saint Macutus, bishop and confessor.”

**Brussels.** He begins: “At Antioch, the feast of the holy martyrs Donatus, Restitutus, Valerian, and Fructuosa, with twelve others.” See Greven below. In the notice of Felix he is sufficiently pure. Then: “At the city of Toledo, the passion of Saint Eugene, bishop of that same city, who at Paris, having completed the course of martyrdom,” and so forth. These are the first traces in our manuscripts of Toledo as a city. “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Macutus, bishop and confessor.”

**Hagenoyen.** In the first entry he is fairly pure, except that he inserts “and under Martianus, governor of Spain, while Maximian was reigning.” The second is more complete. It continues: “On the same day, in Lesser Britain, the feast of Saint Mathurus [for Machutus], bishop and confessor. Also Saint Kilian the confessor. In the city of Toledo, the feast of Saint Eugene, bishop and confessor. In the city of [Col. 0699B] Marseille, the passion of Saint Victor the martyr, who was in every respect praiseworthy in morals and in life. He suffered,” and so forth. See the text and appendices for 21 July; I do not know why this manuscript transfers the entry here. Finally: “In the bishopric of Coutances, at the monastery of Kniauge, Saint Findanus the confessor, who greatly benefits the Eugenes.” Unless I am mistaken, this is the same man who is placed by Castellanus on the preceding day.

**Aquicinctus.** At the end: “On the same day, Saint Macutus the confessor.” This entry has already recurred often enough.

**Matricularius–Carthusian–Utrecht:** “Maclovius, who is also Machutes, bishop and confessor, whose wondrous deeds are read. At Nola in Campania, Felix, bishop and martyr, with the others.”

**Cambrai, Saint Mary of the Canons Regular:** “On that very day, Saint Maximus the confessor.”

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949 there is nothing about Eugene. Added: “In Africa, the holy Secundinus, Martialis, Kalendio, Valerius, and Fructuosus, with twelve others.” See these more distinctly in the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

[Col. 0699C] **Altemps:** “Also Saint Cessator, bishop and confessor. At Cahors, Saint Desiderius, bishop and confessor.” See Castellanus.

**Reims, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris:** “In the Parisian territory, Saint Eugene the martyr.”

**Lübeck–Cologne edition.** To Felix it adds Ado’s conclusion: “His body was buried in the church of Nola by Elpidius the priest. On the same day, Saint Eugene, bishop, companion of Saint Dionysius, who at the Parisian district called Diolium, having completed the course of martyrdom, received from the Lord the crown of blessed suffering; and he was buried on his own estate at Toledo. In Africa, the holy martyrs Secundinus, Martialis, Saturninus, Valerian, and Fructuosus, [Col. 0700A] with twelve others. In Lesser Britain, Saint Machutus, bishop and confessor. He is said to have deserved wondrously to become the raiser of three dead persons. On the same day, Saint Maurinus the confessor. Also on that day, Saint Madonius the confessor.” Further clarification must come from elsewhere.

**Belinus.** To the text, which is not sufficiently pure, he adds: “Also on the same day, the feast of Saint Aracutus, bishop and confessor.” I would be very much mistaken if this were someone other than Macutus, a point which it will be evident below that Molanus failed to notice.

**Greven:** “In Africa, the holy Secundus, Fidentianus, Varricus, Saturninus, and Martialis. Also, according to some—but rather according to the Hieronymian Martyrologies—Donatus, Restitutus, and the others mentioned above under the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September [he intended the tenth day before the Kalends]. Madonius the confessor. Maurinus the confessor. At Cologne, the deposition of Albert, of worthy and holy memory, surnamed the Great, bishop of Regensburg, of the Order of Preachers, a man distinguished both for the purity of his life and for his learning. When worn out by old age and residing at Cologne, he announced to the brethren, with tears, the death of blessed Thomas Aquinas, which he had perceived through the spirit. He died in the eighty-seventh year of his age, after having been in the Order for nearly seventy years. The Lord manifested his merits and glory through many miracles.”

**Molanus.** After Eugene, in different type, he inserts into the text: “Archbishop and martyr of the see of Toledo, who was ordained by blessed Dionysius and sent to preach the Holy Trinity to the nations.” At the end, after “whose body now rests at Bronias in the district of Lomma,” see the notes in the later editions. Then, from Belinus: “Also on the same day, the feast of Saint Aracutus,” and so forth. Then, concerning Machutus, from Muneratus as far as “shone splendidly.” Concerning Junianus, from Herinensis. “In Austria, Saint Leopold, margrave of that province and outstanding confessor, whom Innocent VIII enrolled among the saints.” Finally, in smaller type, concerning Albert the Great, he somewhat abridges Greven’s eulogy.

The later editions retain the same material [Col. 0700C] about Eugene. Then: “On that very day, at the city of Saintes, the deposition of Saint Maclovius, bishop and confessor, in Britain, at the city of Aleth; he shone splendidly from the first training of his youth through countless miracles. At Strasbourg, Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.” Concerning Junianus and Leopold, as in the earlier edition. “On the fifteenth day, the holy martyrs and confessors Gurias, Samonas, and Abibus.” Finally, in smaller type: “Albert the Great, bishop of Regensburg, died at Cologne; he was most distinguished in the Order of Preachers for his life and learning. The Lord declared his merits and glory through many miracles.” See above Greven’s longer eulogy.]

[Col. 0695]

At Nola, a city of Campania, the feast of blessed Felix, bishop, who from the fifteenth year of his age was renowned for the glory of miracles and, under the governor Martianus, completed his martyrdom with thirty others. On that same day, Saint Eugene, who, at a village in the Parisian district, having completed the course of martyrdom, received from the Lord the crown of blessed suffering.

[At Bouillart, in the margin: “On the same day, Saint Macutus, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Saint Germanus, the dedication of a church in honour of Saint John the Baptist, and of Saint John the apostle and evangelist and Saint Martial; of the holy martyrs Laurence, Sebastian, and Christopher, and also of the holy confessors Martin, Gregory, and Benedict, and of Saint Mary Magdalene.”]

**Sixteenth day before the Kalends. Day 16.** [Note: [Col. 0699C]

The Pratensis, Herinensis, Tornacensis, Pulsanensis, Muneratus, Greven, and Molanus manuscripts are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0699D]

Pulsanensis and Muneratus are mistaken in the name itself: the former writes *Heucherius*, the latter *Eleutherius*. Greven and Molanus read “bishop and confessor”; we, with the others, use the simpler form. Muneratus again changes the wording when, instead of the [Col. 0700D] words of the text, he substitutes “who was of the rank of the noblest senators.” The remaining defects are such forms as *aput*, *sollemniter*, *sollempniter*, and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0699D]

After Irenaeus, the other most brilliant star of the city of Lyons—or rather of the whole Church—Eucherius is extolled with the highest praises by the most celebrated Fathers of the fifth century: Hilary of Arles, Cassian, Salvian, Claudian Mamertus, and many others. He has also been treated by numerous writers of the immediately preceding age, especially Raynaud and Chifflet.

The controversies are well known concerning one or two bishops of Lyons named Eucherius; Eucherius’s wife Galla; their daughters Consortia and Tullia; and the matters relating to their sons Salonius and Veranius, or Veranus. We probably dealt with the sons on 28 September and 11 November. Tillemont examined these difficulties with his customary diligence in volume XV, beginning at page 120, and in the notes associated with that discussion.

As far as our immediate subject is concerned, Eucherius seems to be recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, whatever distortion the name has suffered there; Florentinius’s note should be consulted. Rabanus expressed his notice from some Hieronymian manuscript, since he had not found Eucherius in Bede or Florus. The Little Roman Martyrology is silent on this day, so that among the Martyrologists no one has treated the affairs of Eucherius more fully than Ado, at least his call to the episcopate.

Was everything stated with sufficient accuracy? Recent critics disagree: some gnaw away at his narrative, while others reject it entirely. Yet it would certainly be astonishing if the bishop of Vienne, a man neither ignorant nor incompetent, had stumbled so disgracefully for nearly nine centuries, [Col. 0702A] as though he had been wholly unaware of the history of Eucherius, which was not so very remote from his own age.

As usual, we refer these matters to another place, where they may be examined and illustrated from Baronius and the earlier writers. It is certain that Usuard’s shorter eulogy was condensed from Ado’s words. Wandalbertus, perhaps deliberately and in order to increase the praise of Eucherius, joined him with Gregory the Wonderworker in a single distich on this day:

> Eucherius and Gregory fill the sixth with ten;
>
> the one is a priest of Lyons, the other of Neocaesarea.

]

[Note: [Col. 0701A]

**Antwerp-Major.** A more recent strip has been sewn onto an old, torn membrane to supply the text; in it one can read, though rather obscurely: “On the same day, Saint Edmund, archbishop and confessor.” For more about him, see Motherius’s annotation in his version of the Roman Martyrology, which we have mentioned several times elsewhere.]

**Rosweyd.** To the fairly pure text he adds: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Othmar, abbot and confessor.” See Castellanus’s note.

**Antwerp, Maximilian of Lübeck, and Ughelli.** After the text they extract from the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Rufianus [for Rufinianus], Marcus, Valerius, and Honoratus.” See the source for more companions. Then: “In the territory of Auxerre, at the monastery of Pontigny, the deposition of blessed Edmund, archbishop and confessor.”

**Antwerp-Max, Utrecht, Leiden, Leuven, Alberg, and the Danish manuscript.** In the first addition they agree with the preceding witnesses: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Rufianus, Marcus, Valerius, and Honoratus.” It continues: “In Germany, the feast of Saint Othmar, abbot. In the territory of Antere, at the monastery of Pontigny, the deposition of blessed Edmund of Canterbury, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0701C] **Centulensis.** He renders our text in different wording: “At Lyons, Saint Eucherius, bishop and confessor, who, from secular nobility, devoted himself to the service of the Lord; and when divinely chosen beforehand as bishop, would not consent unless he were dragged out after the doors had been broken, and finally hauled away bound. At last he duly governed the church and rested after an excellent end.”

**Brussels.** He begins: “At Capua, the feast of the holy martyrs Vitalis and Justus. In Africa, the feast of the holy martyrs Rufianus, Marcus, Valerius, and Honoratus.” The text follows with this interpolation: “Then, brought out of the cave by an angelic revelation, by the election of the clergy and the consent of the whole people, at the aforesaid city, in the episcopal office,” and so forth. Then he adds: “His wife Galla, entering his cave, spent all the time of her life there in the holy habit. Their two daughters, Consortia and Tullia, shone through the grace of virginity and the glory of miracles.” Then: “In the territory of Anthere, at the monastery of Pontigny, the deposition of Edmund of Canterbury, archbishop [Col. 0701D] and confessor. In Germany, the deposition of blessed Othmar, bishop or abbot and confessor. Also Felicitas the virgin.”

**Hagenoyen.** His text is moderately interpolated; concerning Rufinianus and his African companions he has what appears above. Then: “In Germany, in the monastery of Saint Gall, in the diocese of Constance, the feast of Saint Othmar, abbot and confessor. This man was entirely devoted to good works and suspended in profound contemplation. He took great care of the poor, washing their feet and heads and supplying them, as he was able, with bodily necessities; he also bathed lepers and cleansed their filthy wounds. Because he refused to consent to the avarice of certain tyrants and their squandering of the temporal goods of his monastery, he accused them before Prince Pepin; but they accused him of fornication, alleging that he consumed the monastery’s goods with prostitutes, and he was exiled to an island in the Rhine. There, worn down by many hardships, [Col. 0702A] he rested in the Lord. In the territory of Antere, at the monastery of Pontigny, the deposition of blessed Edmund, bishop and confessor of Canterbury. He was very devoted to the Blessed Virgin. Also at Arethon in Auvergne, Saint Vitalina the virgin.” See Castellanus on 21 February and our Acts for that day.

**Aquicinctus.** At the end: “On the same day, blessed Othmar, abbot. At Capua, the feast of the holy Vitalis and Justus.”

**Daveronensis:** “At Orléans, Marcellus.”

**Matricularius–Carthusian–Utrecht:** “Edmund, archbishop of Canterbury and confessor. Eucherius, bishop and confessor. Othmar, abbot and confessor.”

In Vatican manuscript no. 5949 there is added: “The feast of Saint Augustine, bishop, and Saint Felicitas, his mother, at Saint Sophia.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies on the following day, at the first position. “In Africa, the holy Rufinianus, Marcus, Valerius, and Fronto, with their companions.”

**Altemps:** “At Pontigny, the deposition of Saint Edmund, archbishop of Canterbury, resting at Pontigny, whose death and life are commended by glorious miracles.”

**Florentinius:** “In Africa, the holy martyrs [Col. 0702C] Rufinus, Marcus, Valerius, and Honoratus. In the territory of Auxerre, at the monastery of Pontigny, the deposition of Saint Edmund, archbishop and confessor of Canterbury.” Then, in the Strozzi manuscript alone: “Saint Fidentius, third bishop of Padua and confessor.”

**Bordeaux manuscript:** “Aemilianus the confessor, who, being a man of great holiness and shining with many miracles, was honourably buried in the basilica which he built near Dordogne with marvellous workmanship.”

**Lübeck–Cologne edition.** It begins: “At Cologne, in the church of Blessed Clement, the translation of the bodies of the two blessed Ewalds, priests and martyrs, from their tomb to shrines, by blessed Anno, archbishop of Cologne. Also at Cologne, the translation of the arm of blessed George the martyr in his own church. At Rome, Saint Martin, a boy and martyr, the son of a senator, who, when he refused to sacrifice to idols and despised the threats of the emperor Martianus, was ordered to be stretched out, and his back and belly cut open; then to be bound, hung, cut, and afflicted with various punishments [Col. 0702D], and finally beheaded.”

Concerning Eucherius and the Africans, it has what appears above in the Brussels manuscript. Then: “In Germany, the feast of Saint Othmar, abbot and confessor of the monastery of Saint Gall, who, having been exiled to an island in the Rhine by two wicked Alemannic princes, Warinus and Ruthardus, died there. After his death, when ten years had passed, his body was found untouched by the brothers in the monastery of Saint Gall and translated.” Concerning Edmund, as so often above. “At Orléans, Saint Marcellus the confessor. On the same day, Saint Secundanus the confessor.”

**Belinus.** In a text that has not been sufficiently corrected, he adds at the end: “In Africa, the holy martyrs Rufinus, Marcus, and Valerius. On the same day, the feast of Saint Fidentius, bishop and confessor, the third bishop of Padua.”

**Greven:** “In Africa, the feast of Saint Ruphianus,” and so forth. “Also Saints Secundianus, Aurelianus, and Marcellus. Note: Galla, the wife of Saint Eucherius, as Ado says, entered his cave and spent all her life there in religious devotion. Their two daughters also, one called Consortia and the other Tullia, shone through the grace of virginity and the glory of miracles.

At Rome, Saint Martin the boy. Since he was the son of a chief senator of the city of Rome, he refused to sacrifice to idols and disregarded the threats of the governor Martianus; he was raised onto the rack and ordered to be torn with hooks. Then, since he could not be harmed by various kinds of torture, he completed his martyrdom by beheading. Usuard has him on the seventh day before the Kalends of January under the name Marinus.

At the monastery of Pontigny, the deposition of Saint Edmund, archbishop and confessor of Canterbury. He was most devoutly raised by his mother Mabilia from the very beginnings of childhood, and, devoted to the mortification of the flesh and constant prayers, grew in the greatest holiness. Finally made bishop, he rested full of good works.

Othmar, abbot and confessor. By birth an Alemannian, distinguished for holy deeds, he was placed over the monastery of Saint Gall and unjustly condemned by the impious to exile on an island in the Rhine. There, after enduring many hardships, he rested in the Lord.

At Herford, in the diocese of Paderborn, Saint Waltger the confessor, the first founder of that church.” In Castellanus I find the form *Valdoger*.

“At Orléans, Marcellus the confessor. On the same day, Saint Secundanus the confessor. At Suestris, the abbesses Benedicta and Cecilia. In Scotland, Saint Margaret [Col. 0704A], queen.” Concerning the translation of the Ewalds and of Saint George’s arm, almost as above.]

**Molanus.** Concerning Eucherius, in different type, after “the aforesaid city,” he inserts into the text: “When the entire church, after the death of the bishop of Lyons, according to the custom it had observed from ancient times, was asking the Lord through three days of fasting and supplication to reveal who should assume the governance of that same church.”

At the end: “In Africa, the holy martyrs Rufinus, Marcus, and Valerius. On the same day, Saint Fidentius, bishop and confessor, the third bishop of Padua. In the territory of Auxerre, at the monastery of Pontigny, the deposition of Saint Edmund, bishop and confessor of Canterbury, and the deposition of blessed Othmar, abbot.”

Then, in smaller type, from Greven: “At Herford, in the diocese of Paderborn, Saint Walgerus the confessor, the first founder of that church. In Scotland, Saint Margaret, queen, whose life was written by Turgot, bishop.”

In the other editions the same material is given concerning Eucherius in the text, and the same concerning the Africans, Fidentius, and Edmund. Then: “At Vienne, the deposition of Saint Leonianus, abbot, who was the brother of Anianus, bishop. In Westphalia, the deposition of blessed Walgerus the confessor, founder of the church of Our Lady at Herford. In Germany, the deposition of Saint Othmar, abbot. At Capua, the feast of Saint Augustine.” Elsewhere the name is *Augustianus*, unquestionably the same man mentioned above in the Vatican manuscript. In smaller type: “In Scotland, Saint Margaret, queen.”]

[Col. 0699]

At Lyons, the feast of Saint Eucherius the confessor, who, having turned from the noblest rank of senators to a religious life and habit, served Christ for a long time voluntarily enclosed within the walls of a cave; then, at the aforesaid city, when an angel had revealed the matter, he was solemnly placed in the episcopal chair.

**Fifteenth day before the Kalends. Day 17.** [Note: [Col. 0703B]

The text is taken from Pratensis, Herinensis, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Maximilian of Lübeck, Muneratus, Beami’s first edition, and Molanus; likewise from Antwerp-Max, Utrecht, Leiden, Alberg, and the Danish manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0703C]

The text writes *Dionysius*, as usual. Muneratus alone has “Dionysius, bishop and martyr.” It should read: “Here, often distinguished in many confessions,” as the more authoritative manuscripts have it together with Ado. Pratensis omitted *in*; Muneratus and Belinus frequently do likewise. Molanus, perhaps following Greven, moved *saepe* after *confessionibus*, producing *saepe satis*; in Rosweyd it is *clarus satis*. Antwerp and Maximilian of Lübeck, with Belinus and the manuscripts of middling authority, have *passionibus*; Belinus again has *diversitatibus*. Molanus, I think again following Greven, substituted *meritorumque* for *tormentorumque*.

In the text I preferred *Acisclus*, from Pratensis and Rosweyd, indeed from Ado. The others vary: some have *Ascisclus*, others *Ausclus*, *Atisdi*, *Ascisdi*, and so forth. Pratensis lacks the epithet *pretiosae* before *mortis*, but we restored it from the others and from Ado himself. I counted Antwerp-Major among the pure witnesses, although not everything in the sewn strip discussed above is sufficiently legible.]

[Note: [Col. 0703C]

Castellanus rightly hints at some confusion in the Roman Martyrology in the note attached to 3 October. From the companions listed there he concludes that the great Dionysius of Alexandria himself has been brought into that day, since he is commemorated thus by the Greeks. It may be that the most learned reformers suffered a lapse of memory when they refer to the same man here more explicitly.

Neither day is his proper day of death, whether according to our chronological calculation or that of others; see the *Treatise on the Patriarchs of Alexandria*, beginning at page 29 and from number 157. According to our calculation there, Dionysius must be said to have died on 9 March 265; others contend for 10 March, others for 14 September 264, and others for another day.

But this controversy need not be reprinted here, since it is entirely irrelevant to our subject. I am convinced that the author of the Little Roman Martyrology, entirely and solely according to his own choice—as we have so often observed in other cases—consecrated this day rather than another to the cult of Dionysius, in these words: “At Alexandria, Dionysius, bishop, often distinguished in many confessions, in the times of Valerian and Gallienus.”

This was taken from the usual source, Rufinus’s Eusebius, from which Ado also subsequently compiled his longer eulogy; our author contracted it as the text presents it. In the cited treatise on the patriarchs we touched briefly upon that illustrious exile and most courageous confessor of the faith, as the plan of the work then permitted; but the matter was explained more fully by Ruinart among the *Selecta*, beginning at page 164, and historically developed by Tillemont in volume IV, beginning at page 242, in eighteen articles.

In due time we may use the works of Baronius and these writers in the Acts, just as his doctrine and writings may be investigated more fully from Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 69, and other bibliographers.]

Aurelius Prudentius, *On the Crown*, hymn 4, sings as follows:

> Corduba shall give Acisclus and Zoilus,
>
> and three crowns.

Here we have the first martyr of our second notice, joined, I think, with Zoilus, concerning whom we dealt with Usuard on 27 June, and more extensively on that day in the Acts, to which we referred readers there.

Our predecessors believed that by the words “and three crowns” the third martyr of this day, Victoria, was meant. But Ruinart’s conjecture seems more fortunate to me: on page 517 he substitutes the three Cordoban brothers and martyrs, Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis, so that Victoria is excluded.

Nevertheless, whatever omission Prudentius may have made, there can be no doubt that Ado saw the Acts of both as connected, and from them narrates a perpetual miracle, expressed in our text in the same words. Whether Baronius regarded this as suspicious, or perhaps thought the Acts themselves, since they give the years of Christ, to be more recent, I do not know. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies, on the following day, only Acisclus is recorded; roses are mentioned there only in the Lucensian manuscripts. See Florentinius’s differing account of these.

Florus’s eulogy, reported on the following day, connects the martyrdom of both saints, mentioning only the tortures and the governor Sidonius; but it is not easy to pronounce an opinion on the matter here. Baronius’s note cites many writers, from whom the Acts of Acisclus and Victoria may in due course be illustrated. Tillemont is later, in volume V, page 59.

Apollinaris Sidonius adorned Anianus of Orléans, even in a brief passage, with a truly excellent eulogy in book IX, letter 15, proclaiming him “the greatest and most complete pontiff,” equal to Lupus in one respect and not inferior to Germanus. If only he had pursued the rest of his deeds in the same style! Gregory of Tours transmitted part of them to posterity in book II of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 7. Charles Saussey, in Surius, collected more material from the records of the Church of Orléans; these matters must be discussed elsewhere.

As far as concerns us now, the Hieronymian manuscripts, whatever hand may finally have written them, record him: “In Gaul, in the city of Orléans, the deposition of Anianus, bishop and confessor.” As elsewhere occasionally, Bede omits the title of bishop; here he has: “At Orléans, the feast of Saint Anianus the confessor,” which Rabanus renders more distinctly.

Florus’s encomium adds a miracle concerning a little boy designating the bishop. But it is most probable that no Acts were known to Ado, since he reads most simply: “At Orléans, Saint Anianus, bishop.” It follows that the fairly ordinary eulogy in our text must be attributed to Usuard alone.

In Bede, Gregory the Wonderworker follows Anianus; Rabanus places him first. Gregory is consistently celebrated on this very day in the Roman Martyrology, although the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Usuard place him on 3 July.

Let us now hear the notable metrical eulogy of Anianus composed by Wandalbertus:

> On the fifteenth, Anianus shines along the banks of the Loire,
>
> and among the festal peoples, in eternal praise,
>
> by merit, miracles, prayer, and counsel:
>
> he redeemed his own city from hostile destruction.

]

[Note: [Col. 0705B]

**Tornacensis** lacks the second notice concerning the Cordoban martyrs; everything else is pure.

**Pulsanensis** begins: “At Neocaesarea of Pontus, blessed Gregory, bishop, endowed with the glory of signs and miracles, who, among other things, once moved a mountain by his prayers so that there might be sufficient space for building a church.” Then: “At Alexandria, blessed Dionysius, bishop.” The remainder is absent.

**Greven**, marked with the sign L, about which we have spoken elsewhere, assigns to the text: “In Britain, in the city of Lincoln, blessed Hugh, bishop and confessor.” For this reason, as elsewhere, we exclude him here from the pure witnesses.

[Col. 0705C] **Leuven** adds to the pure text: “In Britain, in the city of Lincoln, Saint Hugh, bishop and confessor.”

**Centulensis.** In the text he is not indeed pure, but is less abbreviated than usual. In third place he inserts: “At Pontus, Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea, bishop and martyr, who was endowed with great glory of miracles. On the same day, Saint Odo, abbot.” See the appendices for 18 November.

**Brussels.** In the first notice he is fairly pure; he continues: “At Pontus, the feast of Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea, bishop and martyr, who was endowed with great glory of signs,” and so forth. The second notice follows, fairly pure, as is the third; but between the two, taken from some Hieronymian manuscript, one reads: “At Rome, across the Tiber, the feast of Saint Cecilia.”

HAGENOYEN. He often heaps together much at his own discretion, generally not with sufficient exactness. Thus he begins: “At Chur, Saint Florinus the Confessor.” Castellanus assigns Confluencia and Schönau. See the later editions of Molanus. “Also Hugh, bishop of Lincoln [Lincolniensis], of the Carthusian order. In Britain, Augustine, bishop and confessor.” See 26 May. What follows is tolerably sound. Then comes a certain eulogy of Lupus of Sens, whom he placed with others on 1 September, while here too he acknowledges that this is his feast; I transcribe a little:

“At Sens, the commemoration of Saint Lupus, bishop, who was born of royal blood at Orléans. Since he excelled in every virtue, he was elected archbishop of Sens. This man was so pious that he kept nothing for himself and gave all that was his to the poor,” etc.

VICTORIN. At the end he adds: “At Tours, the deposition of Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor, worker of miracles.” This should rather be attached to the Gregory immediately following, unless the meaning is the one Molanus gives in his later editions: “Also Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus, bishop of Neocaesarea. And Saint Thecla, virgin.” Undoubtedly these are taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. The codex REG. SUEC., shelfmark no. 130, contains the latter two announcements [Col. 0706B]; another codex has the former under a single entry, no. 428.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Hugh, bishop and confessor; Anianus, bishop and confessor. Ausclius and Victoria, martyrs, on whose feast roses miraculously arise by divine power. Gregory, bishop of Tours; Florinus, confessor.”

CAMBERIEN. S. Mariae: “On this day, the blessed bishops Abraham and Florinus.”

VATICAN, no. 5949, adds: “At Neocaesarea in Pontus, the commemoration of Saint Gregory, bishop and renowned worker of miracles. On the same day, divinely produced roses are gathered.” Where, and for what reason? Perhaps these words [Col. 0706C] were disseminated from Acisclus and Victoria through the carelessness of a copyist. That is my opinion.

FLORENTIN.: “At the city of Florence, in the region of Tuscany, the commemoration of Saint Eugenius, deacon, disciple of Saint Zenobius, bishop of Florence, who, renowned for great virtues, rested in the Lord in the thirtieth year of his life, in the year of the Lord 423.” These may be the Florentine tables cited by Baronius. In the same codices follows: “At Rome, the passion of eight holy martyrs, who suffered under the emperor Alexander, as is read in the passion of Saint Martina, virgin.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition, after the existing entry for Dionysius, adds:

“He too, bound in chains with the blessed Gaius and Peter in the most desolate desert of Libya and afflicted with various torments during the reigns of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, later returned to his church and rested in peace.”

In the Corduban manuscripts the text is sufficiently pure. Then:

“At Orléans, Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor, who, endowed with wondrous holiness, was one day offering the solemn sacrifice to almighty God at Mass when the right hand of God the Father was seen to bless the host placed upon the altar. His death also, in the sight of God, etc. On the same day, Saint Hugh, bishop of Lincoln and confessor, of the Carthusian order. In England, the translation of Saint Erkenwald, bishop of London and confessor. Also on the same day, Saint Abraham, confessor. At Tours, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor. At Vienne, Saint Mammas, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN. In his second edition he adds this further item: “Also Gregory of Tours.”

GREVEN., continuing the addition mentioned above, has as follows:

“This blessed Hugh, a most holy man, was made prior of the house of his Order at Witham in England after serving as procurator of the Grande Chartreuse. There, distinguished by exceptional virtues, he was elected to govern the church of Lincoln. As he had previously shown himself a most exemplary monk, so now he displayed himself as an exceptionally vigilant shepherd and defender of ecclesiastical liberty, the most energetic of all his contemporaries [Col. 0707A], shining with many miracles both in life and after death. He rested in peace in the year of the Lord 1200 and was solemnly enrolled in the catalogue of the saints. At Rome, across the Tiber, the commemoration of Saint Cecilia. At Nicomedia, Saint Ammon. At Carthage, Saints Dubitatus, Tuscus, and Valentinus. At Rome, eight martyrs whom Saint Martina converted. Here is the burial of Pope Felix, martyr. At Vienne, Saint Mammas, bishop and confessor. At Tours, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor, who, 172 years after the death of blessed Martin, succeeded to his see and shone greatly in life, learning, and miracles. In England, the translation of Saint Erconwald, bishop of Cologne [in the earlier edition, better, London] and confessor. In the province of Raetia, Saint Florinus, priest and confessor. On the same day, Saint Abraham, confessor. Saint Martina, martyr. In England, Saint Hilda, virgin and abbess, whom all who knew her, as Bede testifies in Book IV, were accustomed to call ‘mother’ on account of her outstanding piety and grace. She was not an example of life only to those present in her own monastery [Col. 0707B], but also to those living farther away, to whom the fortunate report of her diligence and virtue brought an occasion of salvation and correction. After accomplishing many things on earth, she passed to heavenly works and to receive the rewards of heavenly life in the year of the Lord 630.”

In Castellanus’s Martyrology the year 675 is noted [Col. 0708A]. See what he likewise observes concerning her lineage, relics, and so forth.

MOLANUS:

“At Nicomedia, Saint Ammon. Also Saint Valentinus and Saint Thecla, virgin. On the same day, Saint Stuerus or Severus, confessor—the name is not clearly expressed. Also Gregory of Tours. In Britain, in the city of Lincoln, blessed Hugh, bishop and confessor.”

Then, in smaller type:

“Whose deeds have been written by various authors and rendered in verse by Henry of Morens. In England, Saint Hilda, virgin and abbess, whom all who knew her, as Bede testifies in Book IV, were accustomed to call mother on account of her outstanding piety and grace.”

The later editions place Gregory Thaumaturgus first, as mentioned above, with interpolations and so forth. At the end:

“In Britain, in the city of Lincoln, blessed Hugh, bishop and confessor.”

Then, concerning Ammon, as in the earlier edition. Next:

“Also at Tours, Saint Gregory, archbishop and confessor, author of a book of miracles. On the same day, at Chur, Saint Florinus.”

Finally, in different type:

“In Palestine, [Col. 0708B] the commemoration of Saints Alphaeus and Zacchaeus, who, after scourging and razor-blades, after various interrogations under torture, after their feet had been stretched and pulled apart day and night in wooden shackles with four-hole intervals, and after being beheaded, departed from this light.”

See Eusebius, *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 1, or Ruinart, p. 331 onward.]

[Col. 0703]

At Alexandria, blessed Dionysius, bishop. After often becoming sufficiently renowned through many confessions and proving magnificent amid the diversity of his sufferings and torments, he rested during the reigns of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. At Córdoba, the passion of the holy martyrs Acisclus and Victoria; because of the distinction of their precious death, roses that have arisen by divine power are gathered on the same day. At Orléans, Saint Anianus, bishop and confessor, whose death is attested by frequent miracles to have been precious in the sight of the Lord.

XIV Kalends. Day 18. [Note: [Col. 0707]

From Praten., Antwerp–Major, Antwerp and Max.–Lübeck, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0707C]

Herinien, today entirely intact, must certainly be counted among the purest codices, but it is excluded because of its own addition, concerning which see the Supplements. Greven and Molan, on the other hand, are counted here among the pure manuscripts, although in the second announcement they vary the construction as follows: “So that whoever did not sacrifice to idols would incur the sentence of death, he removed the military belt.” Indeed, Molan continues the sense, explaining the reason. The other [Col. 0708C] variations chiefly concern names. With Ado and the principal codices we call the boy Baralas; Greven has Barulus; Molan, Barulas; others have other forms. There is no less diversity in another name. The remaining manuscripts have Esichius in the text, close to the purity represented by Ado’s Hesychius. Some write Esicius, the Hieronymian manuscripts Isicius, and so forth. Concerning the idols, etc., enough has been said elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0707C]

The first and more polished and simpler account of Roman, deacon of Caesarea, a most distinguished martyr comparable with Laurence and Vincent, is transmitted in the oldest Epternacensian Hieronymian Martyrology. There both the little Baralas and Hesychius are clearly included under one and the same commemoration in these words [Col. 0707D]:

“At Antioch, the commemoration of Romanus, Barilus, and Isicius, martyrs.”

Confusion is introduced by the added designation “monk” found in other Hieronymian codices. It is certain that Rabanus did not find it, for he drew a fairly lengthy eulogy from the Acts. From where Florus, published by our editors, obtained his material, I do not sufficiently understand. A certain Roman is placed among the Caesarean martyrs in the cited Hieronymian manuscripts on the preceding day. From these arose Florentinius’s longer and more elaborate Note, which, against Valesius and in agreement with Baronius, inclines to the view that there must be two Roman martyrs who suffered at Antioch: one a monk, the other a deacon, although both were crowned in nearly the same kind of martyrdom, in the same place, at the same time, and perhaps even on the very same day. Support for this is also supplied by the differing accounts of Roman’s martyrdom, so that the two narratives of Eusebius—the one on the Martyrs of Palestine, in Ruinart, p. 331, the other from Book II *On the Resurrection*, in the same author, p. 379—seem scarcely capable of being suitably reconciled [Col. 0708C]. The difficulty is increased by the passion with the boy and the passion without the boy; hence Prudentius’s hymn, in the cited Ruinart beginning at p. 282, which confuses several matters; and finally other encomia of the holy Fathers cited by the aforementioned writers. Tillemont’s historical treatment, beginning at p. 699, is carefully worked out. He considers Baronius’s and Florentinius’s opinion concerning two Romans improbable, together with Valesius and Ruinart. I frankly confess that I still do not clearly discern to which side one should chiefly adhere, especially since the *Little Roman Martyrology* expressly marks: “At Antioch, Romanus the monk and martyr,” as he is called in the Mombritian Acts, whereas Ado frames his eulogy so that, like Rabanus, he does not mention the designation “monk” any more than “deacon”; nor does Our author, who drew everything from his Viennese manuscript. Whether one or two Romans who suffered at Antioch are to be admitted will be declared when it has been possible to weigh and examine more carefully the individual arguments of both opinions, together with the Acts themselves and the various panegyrics.

In the much-praised Acts of Roman, edited by Mombritius in volume II, beginning at p. 244, the contest of another of our martyrs, Hesychius or Isicius, the companion of the former in the Hieronymian manuscripts cited above, is added near the end.
