I do not see how he can be understood under the name Zocius, joined with other Antiochene martyrs and with a certain Roman and Baralas in the often-mentioned codices on 15 February, since that Zocius is there explicitly called a presbyter. However that may be, it is certainly clear that Hesychius is entered there on this day, as also in Florus, and much more distinctly in our series, where the *Little Roman Martyrology* reads: “And Saint Hesychius Palatinus and martyr”; while Ado narrates somewhat more, from which all our material represented in the text is taken verbatim [Col. 0710A]. “Palatinus” in the *Little Roman Martyrology* alludes to some office exercised in the imperial palace, and this agrees with the Mombritian Acts, which assert that he served in the household, indeed that he was prefect of the palace. Wandalbertus speaks only of Romanus and Hesychius when he honors both:

“Hesychius the martyr and Romanus crown the fourteenth day; joyful Antioch keeps their recurring feast.”

] [Note: [Col. 0709A]

HERINIEN. As I have already said, it is very pure; but it adds something proper to the province of Rheims:

“On the same day, blessed Oriculus the martyr and his companions, who suffered under the Vandal persecution.”

TORNACEN. Pure in the first announcement; in the second, as often happens, it is mutilated.

ROSWEYD. Pure in the text; in large letters it adds an item proper to Utrecht: “The octave of Saint Martin.”

MUNERAT. Also transmits the text, but adds at the end: “On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Auda.” Of Auda.

PULSANEN. In the first announcement it reads:

“At Antioch, the commemoration of blessed Romanus.”

The second is pure.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM and LEYDEN–BELGIAN. After the text:

“At Confluencia, the commemoration of Saint Florinus, confessor.”

See the preceding day.

“Also at Rome, the commemoration of Saint Gelasius, pope. Also, the octave of Saint Martin.”

LOVANIEN. The codex has precisely the same Supplements, but entirely removes our eulogy of Hesychius.

ULTRAJECT. It begins:

“At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Gelasius, pope. He, as blessed Gregory relates, composed the Canon; also five books against the heretics Nestorius and Eutyches, and two against Arius. Moreover, he composed hymns after the manner of Saint Ambrose.”

The text follows. At the end, concerning Florinus and the octave of Martin. So also LEYDEN–LATIN, but it places Gelasius second-last.

ALBERG and DANIC. In place of Martin’s octave, they substitute at the end:

“The dedication of the basilicas of the apostles Peter [Col. 0709C] and Paul.”

The rest is as in ULTRAJECT.

CENTULEN:

“At Antioch, Saint Romanus the monk, who, suffering torments in defense of the Church, endured martyrdom. On the same day and in the same place, Saint Hesychius the soldier, who abandoned military service for the faith of Christ and received the crown of martyrdom. On the same day, the octave of blessed Martin, bishop. At Tours, Saint Gregory, bishop, who wrote many passions and lives of various saints and committed the early deeds of the Franks to memory.”

See the preceding day.

BRUXELLEN. It begins:

“The octave of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours.”

In the account of Romanus, after “they contradicted,” it is interpolated as follows:

“whereupon his tongue was cut out; after it had been cut off, he himself spoke, and afterward together with a certain little boy,” etc.

In the second announcement it changes the order, writing:

“At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Esichius,” etc.

At the end it adds: “and thus he completed his martyrdom.”

Then:

“At Rome, Saint Gelasius, pope, who sat for four years. He composed the daily preface of the Mass and other prayers and hymns after the manner of Saint Ambrose, as well as five books against the heretics Nestorius and Eutyches and two against Arius, as blessed Gregory testifies. At Confluencia, Saint Florentius [Florinus], confessor. And Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny. Also Saint Hugh, of the Carthusian Order and bishop of Lincoln.”

See the preceding day.

“On the same day, Saint Eusebia, virgin.”

HAGENOYEN. In the text, as usual, somewhat purer; it adds only one announcement:

“At Rome, the commemoration of blessed Gelasius, pope. He, as is said, composed the Canon before becoming pope; after he became pope, he ordered that it be recited at Mass, according to what Pope Gregory says. Others, however, say that a certain scholar named Cuno composed the Canon, but that Pope Gelasius instituted its recitation. This Pope Gelasius composed five books, etc. Moreover, he composed hymns after the manner of Saint Ambrose. He also composed the prayers of the Mass and of the hours, together with the chants of Septuagesima. He likewise decreed that no priest should neglect to recite after Mass the hymn of the three youths, namely, ‘Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord’ [Col. 0710A].”

AQUICINCT. Adds at the end:

“On the same day, the passing of Saint Odo, abbot.”

VICTORIN. At the end:

“On the same day, in the district of Valagia, the deposition of Saint Theofredus, martyr. Also at Tours, Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny. Also at Antioch, Saint Eutychius, martyr.”

I think the name “Hesychius” is repeated [Col. 0710B].

“On the same day, the octave of Saint Martin.”

As usual, this agrees with codex REG. SUEC., no. 230, except that the octave is absent from that codex.

DAVERON. He frames his announcement as follows:

“Blessed Odo, abbot of the monasteries of Gaul.”

MATRIC.–CARTHUS.–ULTRAJECTIN.:

“Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria.”

From the preceding day.

“Romanus the martyr and Barulas. Hesychius the soldier and martyr. Severus, priest and confessor. The illustrious and great martyr.”

The author of the marginal note found this nowhere else, nor do I understand what it means.

DIVION. S. Benigni:

“On the same day, the passion of Saint Theofredus, martyr. On the same day, the deposition of blessed Odo, abbot, whose life was exceedingly distinguished by holy merits.”

CLUNIACEN.:

“On the same day, the passing of blessed Odilo, abbot.”

He intended to say Odo.

CAMBERIEN. S. Mariae:

“On the same day, the blessed confessors Mombolus and Odo.”

[Col. 0710C] REG. SUEC., no. 428:

“On the same day, Saint Auda, virgin. On the same day, the deposition of Lord Odo, abbot, most devoted father of monks.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, shelfmark B:

“Also at Rome, the commemoration of Saint Gelasius, pope.”

VATICAN adds:

“The commemoration of Saint Flavius, martyr.”

ALTEMPS:

“On the same day, blessed Odo, abbot. In Ireland, the deposition of Saint Romanus, bishop. Anigus, son of Amardarch, king, stole his left arm; it is kept intact with the flesh in the metropolitan church. And Saint Hilda, abbess.”

See the preceding day.

FLORENTIN.:

“In Tuscany, at the city of Lucca, Saint Fridianus, bishop and confessor of that same city, whose life was as glorious before God and human beings as it was extraordinary in the depth of its miracles. Not only after his death, but also while he was alive in the body, God deigned to perform many miracles through him, of which blessed Gregory, in the book of the *Dialogues*, records one as especially distinguished and the greatest of the miracles.”

This is Fridianus, whose commemoration is on 18 March, but whose Life was transferred here in the Acts. GREVEN will give below the miracle mentioned here.

Then STROZZIANUS alone:

“Also the passing of Saint Odo, abbot.”

Add: of Cluny.

LUGDUNEN and CAUDIACEN agree on the commemoration of Saint Theofredus, martyr.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION begins with the octave of Saint Martin. Concerning Romanus, after “they contradicted,” it has:

“For this reason he was ordered, together with a recently weaned little boy named Barolus, to be stretched on the rack, severely beaten with clubs, torn with claws, have his tongue cut out, and finally be strangled with a noose; and thus he was crowned with celebrated martyrdom. But the boy Baralas was at last beheaded.”

The second announcement is sufficiently pure. Then concerning Florinus, as in ANTWERP–MAXIMUM; concerning the dedication, as in ALBERG. Concerning Mombolus and Odo, as in CAMBERIEN.

BELIN. It begins:

“At Rome, the dedication of the basilicas of the Apostles Peter and Paul.”

The text that follows is sufficiently pure [Col. 0711A]. Then it adds:

“On the same day, Saint Fridianus, bishop and confessor. Also the passing of blessed Odo, abbot.”

GREVEN:

“The octave of Saint Martin. Oriculus the martyr and his companions under the Vandal persecution. On the same day, or, according to others, on the following day, at Rome, Saint Gelasius, pope and confessor, who held the episcopate for four years. He was a lover of the poor, enlarged the clergy, composed treatises and hymns, and issued the prefaces and prayers of the Sacraments that are in use in careful and polished language; he was buried in the church of Saint Peter on 12 Kalends of December. At Rome, the dedication of the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. In Tuscany, in the city of Lucca, Saint Fridianus, bishop and confessor, a man of wondrous virtue. As Gregory says in the Third Book of the *Dialogues*, he caused the river Auser, which flowed beside the city walls and often inflicted damage by its flooding, after prayer had been made, to abandon its own channel and flow elsewhere. At Coutances, a city of Lower Normandy, Saint Rumphart [Col. 0711B], bishop and confessor. Also Saint Mombolus, abbot. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Auda. In Spain, in the city of Córdoba, the passion of Saint Thecla, virgin. At Rome, Saint Eusebia, virgin. The chosen virgin.”

MOLANUS. Concerning the dedication of the basilicas, from BELIN. Also concerning Odo. Then:

“At Coutances in Lower Normandy, blessed Rumpharius, bishop and confessor of the aforementioned city.”

Concerning Oriculus, from HERINIEN:

“At Auxerre, the dedication of the basilica of Saint Germanus, bishop, together with the crypts above it. On the same day, Saint Fridianus, bishop and confessor. Also Saint Florinus, confessor of the monastery of Confluencia. And the deposition of Saint Eusebia, virgin. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Auda.”

And in smaller type:

“At Paris, in the monastery of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Also Saint Mombolus, abbot.”

Other editions improperly introduce the word *vellet* into the text. The Supplements concerning the dedication of the basilicas, Odo, and Fridianus are the same.

“At Confluencia, Saint Florinus, confessor.”

Again concerning Rumpharius and Oriculus, as above.

“At Paris, the commemoration of Saint Auda. Also in Gaul, Saint Mombolus, abbot.”

Then the dedication of the basilica of Saint Germanus. Finally, in smaller type [Col. 0712B], there is added:

“On the island of Lérins, Saint Anselm, abbot.”

[Col. 0707]

At Antioch, the commemoration of blessed Romanus, who, in the time of Diocletian, when a certain prefect attempted to break into a church and tried to destroy it utterly, urged the other Christians to oppose him; consequently, together with a certain little boy named Baralas, he was crowned with celebrated martyrdom. Also in the same city, Saint Hesychius, who was a soldier and, when he heard the command that whoever did not sacrifice to idols should lay aside his military belt, immediately removed his belt. For this reason, after a great stone had been tied to his right hand, he was ordered to be thrown into the river.

XIII Kalends. Day 19. [Note: [Col. 0711]

The pure manuscripts are Herinien, Antwerp–Major, the first edition of Munerat, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0711C]

Antwerp–Major incorrectly reads “Maximus, bishop” for “Maximus, priest.” All the codices except Pratensis explicitly read “during the persecution of Maximian”; in Ado and in the cited Pratensis, however, the reading is Maximinus. The second edition of Munerat is defective in that it combines the first two announcements, reading “he was placed at the city of Astiaga, head,” etc., while omitting the intervening material [Col. 0712C]. The others have Sixtus, together with nearly all the codices. Only Molan has “who was in the city,” etc. Also “of Severianus” instead of “of Severinus”: Antwerp–Major; and “of Superius” instead of “of Exuperius.” Greven and Molan change “to the clergy and people” into “among the clergy and people.” In *grandaevus* the diphthong must be preserved.]

[Note: [Col. 0711C]

We have already discussed Maximus in the Variants. The Pratensis codex, together with Ado, identifies the tyrant as Maximinus, undoubtedly the first of that name; but our codices placed Maximianus, perhaps because they assumed that the other Maximinus had been read incorrectly, since he did not rule at Rome. Which reading they chose more correctly remains uncertain, since it is unknown who this Maximus was, as Baronius candidly admits. He ultimately inclines to the belief that Maximus was a *commentariensis* baptized by Saint Stephen and thrown from the bridge into the Tiber during the persecution of Decius, since his burial at Saint Sixtus, in the cemetery of Callistus, suits this identification. The deeds of his passion, cited there by Baronius, must be discussed elsewhere. Here I merely observe that Baronius’s aforementioned note does not agree with the text of the Roman Martyrology, since the latter expressly specifies the persecution of Valerian. This is enough for a matter so plainly uncertain. No other source places the announcement of the *Little Roman Martyrology* earlier:

“At Rome, Maximus, priest and martyr.”

What Usuard added beyond this in our little column he copied word for word from Ado.

I find Crispinus of Astiaga only in Usuard. Baronius cites the hymn of the Toledan Breviary, in which his deeds are contained. Peter, in Book X, chapter 84 of the *Catalogue*, dispatches the matter in a few words, naming Ado in the Martyrology as his author; but I entirely fail to understand what Martyrology this was, unless it resembles the Ado of Mabillon, compiled from various collections [Col. 0712C]. If one asks for Usuard’s true source, I admit that I do not know it, but I would rather return to a harvest gathered in Spain than to some Mabillonian Ado so enormously interpolated.

Peter could truly have asserted that he copied Ado, although he suppresses the fact, in chapter 82 of the same book, when discussing the martyrs of Lyon, whose memory, so far as I know, survives nowhere except in Ado, or in the very little catalogue of the Lyon martyrs neglected by Raynaud. The aforementioned Viennese chronicle has the following under the year 163:

“Severinus, Exuperius, and Felicianus were crowned with martyrdom shortly beforehand at Vienne.”

What is narrated in the Martyrology properly concerns the discovery and translation of the aforementioned martyrs, whose memory was more recent while Ado himself is said to have cared for the basilica of Saint Romanus, before he was transferred to the Viennese islands. All our material was transferred from that source. Whether the things mentioned by others beyond Ado’s account can be sufficiently proved belongs to another place for a more precise investigation. Meanwhile, see Tillemont, volume II, p. 321. Wandalbertus rendered only this announcement of ours metrically:

“On the thirteenth, Felicianus with Severianus,

and with Exuperius he seals the faith by contest.”

[Col. 0713A] The fourth announcement in the *Little Roman Martyrology* reads:

“And Faustus the deacon and Eusebius, his companion, martyrs who visited.”

It flows from Rufinus, Book VII, chapter 10, from which it is clear that Ado’s entire eulogy was taken, and that our text was abridged from it. In our text only Faustus is mentioned; he may perhaps later have become a priest and thus be the same man who, advanced in years, suffered martyrdom with Peter of Alexandria, under which name he will recur on 26 November. Yet because he is there joined with such companions, it seems more probable that he is a different person. No other Latin Martyrologies celebrate Eusebius, who is omitted even from the modern Roman Martyrology [Col. 0714A]. Tillemont conjectures that he is the same man who later governed the Church of Laodicea in Syria as bishop, as he indicates in volume IV, beginning at p. 304. Moreover, the *Little Roman Martyrology* calls both men “companions who visited,” because, despite everyone’s opposition, they continually carried the necessities to the confessors detained in prison . . . as Ado describes more fully from the aforementioned Rufinus. But I will not dwell on these matters longer. We have Usuard, whose genuine text we are chiefly seeking.]

[Note: [Col. 0713A]

PRATEN. He is rightly excluded, since at the end he adds:

“At Tours, Saint Odo, abbot.”

Castellanus did not observe the difference in handwriting, but our most learned Chamillart, who recently, for my sake, graciously inspected the codex again, testified that some difference does appear. It has the added dedication, etc.

TORNACEN. Pure in the first and second announcements; in the third it removes the eulogy; it entirely lacks the fourth. In the margin, however, in a somewhat more recent hand, is added:

“In Germany, at the castle of Marburg, blessed Elisabeth.”

The eulogies will be given below.

ROSWEYD. Pure in the text; it adds:

“In Heraclea, the eleven holy widows.”

This is nearly the same announcement as that of the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

PULSANEN. Pure in the first announcement; the other three have completely removed all the eulogies.

ANTWERP, MAX.–LÜBECK, and UGHELLIAN. Pure in the text; they add:

“Also Simplicius, bishop. On the same day, the deposition of blessed Elisabeth.”

MUNERAT. The truncation of his second edition has been discussed in the Variants.

ANTWERP–MAXIMUM and LEYDEN–BELGIAN begin:

“At the territory of Mainz, the commemoration of blessed Elisabeth, daughter of the king of Hungary.”

The entire text follows, and at the end:

“At Autun, the deposition of Saint Simplicius [Col. 0713C], bishop.”

The same appears in the LOVANIEN codex, but it is more mutilated in the passage concerning Faustus.

ULTRAJECT and LEYDEN–LATIN expand the earlier wording at the beginning as follows:

“Since she was married to the Landgrave of Thuringia, she devoted herself to works of piety and humility as far as was permitted under her husband. But once released from the law of marriage, having entirely rejected royal and secular ornaments, girding her loins with a rope and walking barefoot, she served the Lord under the title of perfect poverty. She built a hospice, where, going beyond the apostolic command, she washed the feet of the poor with her own hands, filtering and wiping away the pus of loathsome invalids. Restoring sight to a man blind from birth and shining with countless miracles, she brought her blessed life to a close with an even more blessed end and now reigns most blessedly in heaven.”

The entire Usuardine text follows, with Simplicius of Autun added at the end, as above.

ALBERG and DANIC have the same material concerning Elisabeth, but [Col. 0713D] immediately append to that commemoration the entire announcement for the following day concerning Pope Pontianus. These two codices differ in that the latter lacks Simplicius.

CENTULEN:

“At Rome, on the Appian Way, Saint Maximus, priest and martyr. At Vienne, the holy martyrs Severinus, Exuperius, and Felicianus. On the same day, Saint Faustus, martyr; Saint Crispinus, martyr, who suffered martyrdom in the city of Astiaga after being beheaded.”

Some material concerning Elisabeth is added in a more recent hand in the margin, but it cannot be sufficiently distinguished.

BRUXELLEN begins:

“At Magdeburg [for Marburg], the deposition of Saint Elisabeth, daughter of the king of Hungary and wife of the Landgrave of Thuringia. Shining with countless miracles, she brought her blessed life to a more blessed end and now reigns most blessedly in heaven.”

The text follows, transposed and interpolated here and there. At the end:

“At Autun, the deposition of Saint Simplicius, bishop.”

[Col. 0714A] HAGENOYEN. In the first and second announcements it is sufficiently pure; it adds:

“Also at Autun,” etc.

Here it has nothing concerning the martyrs of Lyon. In the passage concerning Faustus it is sufficiently pure. Then:

“In the territory of Trier, in the town of Confluencia, the commemoration of blessed Florinus, confessor. In Hesse, in the town called Marburg, the deposition of Saint Elisabeth, widow, [Col. 0714B] daughter of the king of Hungary and wife of Ludwig, Landgrave of Thuringia, whose whole life was full of miracles and works of mercy from her childhood to her death. Her bones were found floating in oil at the time of their translation. Many sick people were anointed with it and cured.”

AQUICINCT. At the end:

“Also Saint Simplicius, bishop. At Rome, Saint Gelasius, pope. He recalled Bishop Misenus, whom his predecessor Felix had condemned, and restored him to communion with his church. He composed books against Eutyches and Nestorius.”

This has been treated under the preceding day in the Supplements; in the Roman Martyrology he is placed on 31 November, where see the observation of our Father Motherius.

VICTORIN. Has “Faustinianus” for “Faustus.” At the end:

“At Rome, Gelasius, pope.”

MATRIC.–CARTHUS.–ULTRAJECT:

“Elisabeth, widow, daughter of the King of Hungary. Simplicius, bishop and confessor. Odo, abbot of Cluny, a man of great holiness.”

[Col. 0714C] REG. SUEC., no. 140:

“At Rome, Gelasius, pope.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL, shelfmark B:

“At Autun, the deposition of Saint Simplicius, bishop.”

VATICAN, no. 5949, is lacking in the second and fourth announcements concerning Crispinus and Faustus.

ALTEMPS:

“At Périgueux, Saint Leontius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, blessed James, hermit.”

FLORENTIN.:

“In a German town called Barbuth [Marburg; the other two words cannot be read], Saint Elisabeth, daughter of Andrew, king of the Hungarians . . . At Rome, Saint Gelasius, pope . . . Also Saint Simplicius, bishop.”

The matter is given more distinctly above.

BURDEGALEN:

“Saint Simplicius, bishop.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION first treats Elisabeth, almost as in ULTRAJECT above. Then:

“At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Gelasius, pope and confessor. He, as blessed Gregory relates, composed the Canon of the Mass, also five books against the heretics Nestorius and Eutyches and two against Arius. Moreover, he composed hymns after the manner of Saint Ambrose, bishop. He also composed the preface of the Mass, ‘It is truly worthy and just,’ to be sung in daily use, and held the episcopate for four years.”

Concerning Pontianus it has the text of the following day. In the text it is unusually pure. Finally, concerning Simplicius, as above.

BELIN begins with Pontianus, as we have already said. In the first three announcements it is sufficiently pure. Then it continues:

“On the same day, in a German town called Marchburg, the deposition of Saint Elisabeth, daughter of Andrew, king of the Hungarians. Also Saint Simplicius, bishop and confessor.”

It abbreviates the fourth announcement as follows:

“On the same day, Saint Faustus the Deacon.”

GREVEN:

“In Caesarea of Cappadocia, the commemoration of Saints Maximus, Mutianus, Nicophorus, Januarius, Zephyrus, and forty others.”

He mixes various material from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

“Also, according to some, on this day, the passion of Saint Pontianus, pope, whom Usuard has on the following day. At Autun, blessed Simplicius, bishop and confessor. [Col. 0715A] Also Saint Odo, first abbot of Cluny, a man of wondrous holiness and incomparable zeal in monastic discipline, so much so that through his zeal and diligence the lukewarmness of the monks of that time was turned into ardor. He finally rested in the year of the Lord 938, renowned for miracles both in life and in death. At Heraclea, forty widows and martyrs. In the city of Marburg in Hesse, the commemoration of Saint Elisabeth, a most holy widow, daughter of the king of Hungary. From childhood she bore a most religious disposition toward God; when married to the Landgrave of Thuringia, she devoted herself, as far as was permitted under her husband, to deeds of piety and humility. When she reached the state of widowhood, she entirely rejected secular ornaments and pomp, girded her loins with a rope, walked barefoot and in humble clothing, presented herself as an apostolic widow, raised children, received strangers into hospitality, washed the feet of the saints, assisted those suffering tribulation, and pursued every kind of good work. She rested, glorified by the greatest number of miracles, in the year of the Lord 1230.”

[Col. 0715B] Molan, concerning Pontianus, like the others, from the text of the following day. [Col. 0716A] Then:

“On the same day, in a town of Alemannia called Marburg, the deposition of Saint Elisabeth, daughter of Andrew, king of the Hungarians. She built a hospice where, as a widow, she washed the feet of the poor, wiping away with her own hands the loathsome matter from the sick.”

Concerning Simplicius, as above. Concerning Gelasius, as in Aquicinct., except that it adds, “he also composed hymns,” etc. Finally, in smaller letters:

“In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Patroclus, an outstanding confessor, of whom Gregory of Tours says in *History of the Franks*, Book V, chapter 10: ‘There was in the territory of Bourges a recluse named Patroclus, endowed with the dignity of the priesthood, of extraordinary holiness and religion; concerning his life we have written a little book.’”

Later editions place Pontianus first in the text, followed by Elisabeth, but in italic letters. At the end:

“In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Patroclus, an outstanding confessor. Also Saint Gelasius, pope, who held the pontificate for four years. On the nineteenth day, Saint Barlaam the martyr.”

See the Roman Martyrology and Castellanus’s note for this day.]

[Col. 0711]

At Rome, on the Appian Way, the feast of Saint Maximus, priest and martyr, who suffered during the persecution of Maximian and was placed at Saint Sixtus. On the same day, Saint Crispinus, bishop, who attained the glory of martyrdom at Asti, after being beheaded. Near Vienne, the holy martyrs Severus, Exuperius, and Felicianus, whose bodies, after the passage of many years, were discovered when they revealed themselves, and were honorably raised by the city’s bishop, clergy, and people and buried with fitting honor. Also Saint Faustus the deacon: this man, having continued as a confessor to advanced old age and fullness of days, was consummated by perfect martyrdom through beheading.

[In Bouillart., in the text in italic type: “At Tours, Saint Odo the abbot”; and in the margin: “At Paris, the dedication of a church in honor of the holy cross, and of the holy Mother of God Mary, and of the holy martyrs Stephen and Vincent, and of Saint Germanus the confessor.”]

**The twelfth day before the Kalends. Day 20.**

[Note: [Col. 0715]

Thus read Pratensis, Herinien., Antwerp., Max.-Lübeck, Muneratus, and Greven.]

[Note: [Col. 0715C]

In Muneratus, *Potentianus* is an error for *Pontianus*. Through the ignorance of scribes, *Maximianus* entered Antwerp., Max.-Lübeck, and Greven in place of *Maximinus*, as we have observed elsewhere, although the two emperors are separated by almost an entire century. From most manuscripts we retain *Ypolitus*, as elsewhere. Herinien. wrongly transposed the words, “killed in martyrdom with clubs.” Greven errs less seriously in writing Pope Fabianus, but Muneratus speaks differently: “His body, revealed by blessed Fabianus, was buried in the cemetery of Pope Callistus.” What I said about Ypolitus, consider also to apply to the cemetery of Callistus. The manuscripts preserve different forms of spelling in *Mesana*, *Gagius*, *Gaius*, and *Octavius*. As usual, we have left *Gaius* in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0715C]

The reformers of the Roman Martyrology followed Belinus rather than Usuardus in assigning the feast of Pope Pontianus to the preceding day, that is, 19 November. Molanus—strange to say—in the very first edition excluded the saint from the Usuardine text on both days. In our series he is certainly recorded on this day, with the *Little Roman Martyrology* leading the way: “At Rome, Pontianus, pope and martyr.” As Rosweydus observes, Ado’s eulogy was taken from the *Pontifical Book*; yet I still do not see how it can be reconciled satisfactorily with our Catalogues, published before the first volume of April. Moreover, I encounter many matters discussed by Baronius, Henschenius, Pagius, Papebrochius, and others concerning Pontianus’s age, exile, and so forth, [Col. 0715D] which require a more laborious examination and which Tillemont, volume III, pages 276 and 692, has not yet clearly explained—if, indeed, they can be fitted together by any chronological method. Some matters concerning his martyrdom are also uncertain; but who would rashly call the martyrdom itself into question, confirmed as it is by so many ancient records? In any event, what is presented in our text Usuardus copied from Ado. In the Hieronymian manuscripts, on 13 August, there is “Pontianus, bishop”; the same appears on that day in Bucherius’s Calendar: “And Pontianus at Callistus.” Florentinius thinks that these entries should be understood as referring to a translation; on what basis will be seen later. Rabanus moves Pontianus’s feast to 30 October. I may safely say that much arbitrariness enters into the selection of days of this kind, as we have very often demonstrated in the case of the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*; perhaps more ancient records guided both him and Wandalbertus, when the metrical Martyrologist praised Pontianus on this very day in these words:

> Pontianus, Rome consecrates her twelfth day to you  
> in devoted observance, O blessed bishop and martyr.

Silvester of Chalon is purely Adonian. Usuardus altered the beginning; for where Ado reads, “At Chalon, of the most blessed Silvester,” our author has, “At Chalon, Saint …,” and so forth. The brief eulogy is taken from Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 85; nor, as far as I know, does anything further survive concerning his life or deeds. The records of Chalon, both manuscript and printed, relate the revelation and translation of Silvester and others; we shall discuss them elsewhere.

The following announcement appears thus in the *Little Roman Martyrology*: “At Messina, Ampelius and Caius.” The Hieronymian Martyrologies write the names in different ways, but all have the same meaning, as does Ado, from whom our commemoration derives. Florentinius found little concerning their origin or the time of their passion, nor do we possess anything capable of greatly illuminating their deeds.

The martyrs of Turin are listed in various sequences by various authorities, but in the Hieronymian Martyrologies they occur in exactly the order found in our text: “At the city of Turin, Octavius, Solutor, Adventor.” In this wording other companions are numbered as though they belonged to the same group, although Florentinius rightly considers them to be separated from it. These three are the celebrated patrons of Turin, transferred to the church of the Society of Jesus there from some older church. They were especially attacked in a mordant dissertation by that little English Savoyard minister concerning whom we spoke on 22 September, when discussing the Theban Legion. Our three are considered to have belonged to that sacred legion; they were long ago praised by Ennodius and Maximus of Turin, and Baronius states that he received their manuscript Acts from the Church of Turin. Much more was formerly sent to us from Turin concerning both their Acts and their translation; it will be set out carefully in its proper place.]

[Note: [Col. 0717A]

Tornacen. truncates Pontianus’s eulogy at “he completed.” It omits Silvester; the rest is correct.

Antwerp.-Maj. has the complete text, but in the next-to-last place, before the Taurinian martyrs, it inserts: “On the same day, Saint Edmund, king and martyr.”

Rosweyd. appends to the text: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Edmund, king of the English and precious martyr.” See Surius.

Pulsanen. In the first copy the entire eulogy is lacking; in the second and third it is pure; the fourth is lacking.

Molan. I have said that it lacks the first announcement.

Antwerp.-Max., Utrecht, Leiden, and Codex D of Du Chesne, marked B, add after the text: “In England, the feast of Saint Edmund, king and martyr, whose head, long hidden, revealed itself by its own voice at the divine command.” Codex Lovan. has the same, but cuts short Pontianus’s eulogy.

Alberg. and Danic. transferred the announcement concerning Pontianus to the preceding day. Here they treat Edmund as the manuscripts just cited do, but place him first. In three [Col. 0717B] others they are sufficiently pure.

Centulen.: “At Rome, Saint Potentianus, pope and martyr. In the city of Messina in Sicily, the holy martyrs Ampelius and Caius. In England, the passion of Saint Edmund, king and martyr. In the territory of Senlis, Saint Maxentia, virgin and martyr. At Chalon, Saint Silvester, bishop and confessor. At Amiens, the discovery and translation of the holy confessors Warlesius and Luxorius.”

Bruxellen. is not entirely pure in the first copy. It continues from the Hieronymian Martyrologies: “And the feast of the holy martyrs Maximus, Mucianus, and Neophorus. In the city of Heraclea in Thrace, the feast of the holy martyrs Bassus, Dionysius, Orion, and Basilius.” Then, together with the text: “At the city of Messina in Sicily, the feast of the holy martyrs Ampelius and Caius.” Concerning Edmund, as in Antwerp.-Max., etc. It is sufficiently pure in the case of Silvester. Finally: “On the same day, the deposition of Fulcherius, who was patriarch of the Jerusalem Church.”]

[Col. 0717C] Hagenoyen: “At Rome, the feast of blessed Pontianus, pope and martyr, who was sixteenth from blessed Peter the apostle. Because he refused to sacrifice to idols and to deny the faith, under the persecution of Maximinus, who was raging against the Church of God, he was deported into exile in Sardinia with Hippolytus the priest,” etc. It is sufficiently pure concerning Silvester. Then:

“In England, the feast of Saint Edmund, king and martyr, who in the first years of his life joined himself to the Lord, and to whom, while he was still a boy, the Lord appeared in company, saying to him: ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth.’ He was punished by beheading, and this was afterward hidden for a long time,” etc.

In the third section it is sufficiently pure; I do not know what it adds:

“At Alexandria, Helie, empress, wife of Olaxentius.”

Then:

“Also the translation of Saint Corbinianus, bishop of Freising.”

In the final section it is sufficiently pure.]

Aquicinct. adds to the text:

“In Britain, among the East Angles, the most blessed and most Christian king and martyr Edmund, who, for the unconquerable truth of the Catholic faith, was cruelly killed by pagans and obtained the heavenly kingdoms.”]

[Col. 0717D] Ambianen.: “In the district of Amiens, the discovery and translation of the bodies of the holy confessors Warlesius and Luxorius.” Thus it was written by the first hand, as Centulen. has it above. Someone, however, changed the second name to Luxoenus.

Matric.-Carthus.-Utrecht: “Potentianus (the error is evident), pope and martyr. Edmund, king and martyr, in England. Octavius the martyr with his companions. Silvester of Chalon, bishop. Bernard, bishop of Nordhausen.” The copyist notes in the margin: “Perhaps Berwaldus, bishop of Hildesheim. See below concerning him.”

Reg. Suec., no. 428: “In the territory of Beauvais, the feast of Saint Maxentia, virgin and martyr. In Britain, the passion of blessed Edmund, king of the East Angles, who, suffering beneath the pirates’ dreadful blows of arrows, finally obtained the prize of martyrdom and received the crown of immortality.”

In Vaticanus, no. 5949, the announcement of Silvester is lacking. The following is added: “On the same day, Saint Theogenes the martyr. And Saint Dorius, bishop of Benevento.”

Florentin. insert in the next-to-last place: “In England, Saint Edmund, king and martyr.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins: “In England, the feast of Saint Edmund, king and martyr, whose head,” etc., as above. It placed Pontianus yesterday. It then follows with Silvester, the Sicilian martyrs, and the Taurinian martyrs, sufficiently purely. At the end: “At Hildesheim, the feast of Saint Berwardus, bishop and confessor.” See the lengthy Life published in Surius, 1618 edition. “On the same day, Saint Regenfledis, virgin.”

Belin. contains many corruptly printed readings, such as *Babylonia* for *Chalon*. He placed Pontianus on the preceding day. The second edition adds at the end: “In England, Saint Edmund, king and martyr.”

[Col. 0718B] Greven, from the Hieronymian Martyrologies:

“In Heraclea, the feast of the holy martyrs Bassus, Dionysius, and Orion. In Antioch, Basilius and Dionysius. In England, Saint Edmund, king and martyr, who, after various torments inflicted by pagans, attained the glory of martyrdom by beheading. His head was thrown into a forest and carefully guarded by a wolf; when it was found and buried together with the body, after the passage of years it was discovered completely reunited with the body. At Constantinople, Saint Antipas, priest and martyr. At the city of Edessa, the passion of the holy martyrs Samonas and Gurias, who, while going about everywhere proclaiming Christ and strengthening Christians, were arrested, first hanged, then weakened by starvation, and finally, having overcome various tortures through the power of Christ, completed their martyrdom by beheading. Orion, bishop. Berwaldus, bishop of Hildesheim and confessor, who, in the time of Otto III, feeding the aforesaid church by word and example, rested, renowned for miracles. At Constantinople, blessed Stephen, priest and confessor, who, leading a most continent life in the time of the emperor Leo and devoting himself to continual prayers, rested in the Lord with a blessed end, renowned for many miracles. At Orléans, the holy Waclesius and Luxorius. Regenfledis, virgin. Maxentia, virgin. Agapita, virgin.”

Molan.:

“On the same day, Saint Edmund, king and martyr. The feast of blessed Raphael the archangel. At Amiens, the discovery and translation of the glorious bodies of the holy confessors Warlesius and Luxorius.”

In smaller type:

“On the same day, by order of the impious and wicked emperor Constantine the Iconoclast, Stephen the recluse was crowned with martyrdom at Saint Auxentius. They tied his foot with a rope and dragged him as far as the Pelagian praetorium, where, after tearing him apart, they threw his honorable relics into the place of those who had died violent deaths, because he had admonished many and led them to the monastic life and persuaded them to despise royal dignities and wealth. The venerable man was respected by everyone because he had spent nearly sixty years in monasteries and had shone with many virtues.”]

Concerning Samonas and Gurias, as in Greven. Other editions have the same account of Edmund and Raphael as the first edition. Then:

“At Milan, Benignus, bishop and confessor. In the city of Hildesheim, Saint Bertwaldus, bishop, who in the time of Otto III fed the aforesaid,” etc., as in Greven.

“On the twentieth day, Saint Proclus, father and archbishop of Constantinople; and Saint Gregory of Decapolis; and the vigil of the entrance into the temple of the most holy Mother of God.”

Concerning Warlesius and Luxorius, as above. Finally, in smaller type:

“At Caesarea in Palestine, the feast of Saint Agapius, who, on the birthday of the tyrant Maximinus, when he was dragged into the arena with a murderer and saw the murderer who had killed his master released in the manner of Barabbas, was himself given to a bear to be devoured and then, still alive, was thrown into the sea.”

See the Roman Martyrology.]

[Col. 0715]

At Rome, the feast of blessed Pontianus, pope, who, when Maximinus was stirring up persecution against the priests of the churches, was deported to Sardinia with the priest Hippolytus, and, everywhere beaten with clubs, completed his martyrdom. His body was brought back by blessed Pope Fabianus and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. At Chalon, Saint Silvester, bishop and confessor. In the forty-second year of his priesthood, full of days and virtues, he departed to the Lord. In the city of Messina in Sicily, the holy Ampelius and Caius. On the same day, in the city of Turin, Octavius, Solutor, and Adventor.

**The eleventh day before the Kalends. Day 21.**

[Note: [Col. 0719A] Herinien., Tornacen., Antwerp., Max.-Lübeck, and Molan. are pure today. Likewise Antwerp.-Max., Utrecht, Leiden, and Alberg.]

[Note: [Col. 0719B]

I read “most blessed” with most of the manuscripts, and I have no doubt that Usuardus copied it from Ado. Here I retain “monasteries,” since all have it except Molanus alone. Antwerp. and Max.-Lübeck omit the conjunction *and* after “founder,” together with almost all those whom we call the manuscripts of middle quality. The same manuscripts read *Ystria* or *Hystria*; some have *Ytalia*, while all the rest have *Histria*. Herinien. and Tornacen. are indeed very pure, but place Columbanus last.

It should be noted that on this day and the two following days Pratensis departs from the pure manuscripts, indeed from almost all manuscripts, together with his usual companions Antwerp.-Maj. and Rosweyd. Castellanus, who inspected the alleged autograph, observed that in today’s text everything after the announcement of Rufus had been erased, and that Mary of Neocorensis, properly belonging to 1 November, had been wrongly inserted here. The remainder, which I transcribe from his often-cited letter of 31 May 1709, reads:

“At the city of Neocorensis, Saint Mary the virgin, who suffered under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus. In the province of Histria, Saint Maurus the martyr. At the city of Hostia, the holy martyrs Demetrius and Honorius. At Autun, Saint Pragmatius [Col. 0719D] the bishop.”

Everything there must be in extreme confusion, since the same Castellanus testifies that on the 22nd only Cecilia is treated. On the 23rd, moreover, the entire text after “thrown into martyrdom” was again erased and “is crowned” inserted:

“On the same day, Saint Felicitas,” [Col. 0720B] etc.

Then concerning Columbanus, and so forth, but with the announcement badly mutilated, if our copy is correct, as we shall say later. For the 24th, a different hand is observed; hence it could almost be inferred that it is precisely the same hand that, on the 19th, 21st, 22nd, and 23rd of this month, runs through all the texts. How much all these matters commend the authenticity and genuineness of the Pratensis manuscript, experts in such matters will readily perceive.

I believe that the scribe of the manuscript had at some point found Columbanus on 23 November in a Hieronymian Martyrology or in Rabanus, and from those or other sources confused several matters improperly. In my judgment, Usuardus did not depart at all from Ado. That Ado, on this day, marked Columbanus in the very words of our text is indisputable, whatever may perhaps be brought forward against it by some Pratensis Ado, whom we have repeatedly shown to be interpolated and expanded. For among our examples, both manuscript and printed, I find none—except Lobien., unquestionably descended from Pratensis—that records Columbanus on a day other than this. Thus certain more recent critics are easily refuted. Our Usuardine reading, confirmed plainly and completely by so many manuscripts, remains intact once those three manuscripts, so often wandering outside the sequence, have been rejected. It remains, I say, on the true day of his death, correctly noted by Jonas, contrary to Florentinius’s opinion, who must be corrected here together with the others.]

[Note: [Col. 0719D]

Our first two commemorations are copied from Ado word for word. There is only one in the *Little Roman Martyrology*, expressed in these terms: “Rufus, whom the Apostle greets when writing to the Romans.” The author of that Martyrology first marked him out, along with so many other apostolic men whose names he found either in the Acts or in the Epistles of the apostles. Usuardus could without hesitation have transferred the Apostle’s very words in Romans 16:13 from Ado: “Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.” This is Rufus’s chief and true praise. For what is often fabricated concerning his episcopate at Thebes, once Dorotheus’s rejected *Synopsis* has been set aside, must not be accepted unless it is proved from another source. Rufus is distinct from the one praised by Polycarp, who is commemorated on 18 December. Whether either of them should be identified with the brother of Alexander, son of Simon of Cyrene, the bearer of the cross, will be investigated elsewhere. What the pseudo-chronicles of Spain invent, see Tillemont, volume I, page 447. Rosweyd once carefully recorded all these matters; had he lived, he would have refuted them brilliantly, just as he had exposed many other impostures of theirs.

We have already said that the announcement of Columbanus is purely and completely Adonian. That it truly belongs also to Usuardus on this very day is abundantly clear from the Variant Readings. His Life, written by Jonas, appears in Surius; it was reviewed and illustrated by Mabillon in the second Benedictine century, beginning on page 5. There we shall also find the metrical work of Frodoardus, the little book of Miracles, and other materials concerning the most celebrated abbot, which in due course must be compared and elucidated with several of our manuscripts through renewed study. Wandalbertus likewise discovered this as the true day of Columbanus’s death, undoubtedly from the author of the Life, when he celebrated him today in these three verses:

> On the eleventh day Abbot Columbanus keeps his feast, coming from the very  
> Ocean; he spread among many the teachings of holy life  
> through pious devotion, by word and by hand.

[Col. 0722A] I have nothing to say concerning Maurus of Istria: what happened to him, when he suffered, or from where Usuardus took the entry, I honestly confess that I do not know, unless we judge him to be one and the same with Maurus the Roman martyr, concerning whom Rabanus gives at length on this day the history of his martyrdom. Baronius undoubtedly held this opinion when he removed the name of Maurus of Istria from the Roman Martyrology. I cannot go further. It is as certain that he was entered by Usuardus, whether correctly or incorrectly, as it is certain that he appears in all the better manuscripts and is repeated again on the following day.]

[Note: [Col. 0721A]

We have reported the alterations and additions of Pratensis in the Variant Readings. Here I note only that our copy of the manuscript has Pragmatius of Autun not on this day but on the following day—a strange thing to have escaped the attention of the copyist, Sirmondus, and the sharp eyes of others. I did not think that on this day and the two following days I should rely on Castellanus’s latest testimony. The aforementioned Chamillart investigated the matter more carefully.

Antwerp.-Maj. and Rosweyd. present the Pratensis text, copied rather poorly in places. They treat Pragmatius on the following day in its proper place. It therefore seems to follow that this is how it also appears in Pratensis, although Castellanus testifies to the opposite—perhaps because Pragmatius was referred to that place by an asterisk which Castellanus did not notice.

Pulsanen. would be sufficiently pure if it did not cut out the entire eulogy of Columbanus.

Muneratus adds at the end of the text: “On the same day, the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.”

Greven begins: “The Presentation of the most blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, when she was presented in the temple.” The remainder is in its proper place.

Lovanien. begins: “The Presentation of the most blessed Virgin, Mary the Mother of God.” The rest is pure, as it is in Danic., which places the aforementioned announcement below but refers it by an asterisk to the first place, in the same hand in which the rest was written.

Centulen.: “The feast of blessed Rufus, concerning whom Paul writes to the Romans: ‘Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord.’ In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, Saint Columbanus, abbot, a man of admirable life and teaching.”

Bruxellen. begins: “The Presentation of Saint Mary, ever-virgin and Mother of God, in the temple.” In the text concerning Columbanus it inserts: “Who, coming from Scotland and leaving Gallus in Alemannia, built the monastery of Bobbio in Italy, and was founder of many other monasteries and of innumerable,” etc. In the case of Rufus it describes Ado, adding, however, the title of bishop. It is sufficiently pure concerning Maurus. Then, from the Hieronymian Martyrologies:

“In Antioch, the feast of the holy martyrs Basileus, Auxilius, Matrona, Demetrius, Quincianus, Sisinnius, and Eutychius.”

Here it moves the previous day’s announcement concerning the Theban Taurinians. Then:

“At the city of Hostia, the passion of the holy martyrs Demetrius and Honorius. At the city of Neocaesarea, the feast of Saint Mary the virgin, who suffered under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus.”

Here the name of the city is changed; we have discussed it elsewhere. It should read: “At Neocorensis,” etc.]

[Col. 0721D] Hagenoyen. is sufficiently pure in the first copy and continues:

“Also the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin in the temple, in the third year of her birth. Also the translation of Saint Burkardus, bishop of Würzburg.”

See the Additions for 14 October.

“At Vienne, the feast of the holy martyrs Severinus,” etc., taken from 19 November.

“In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, the deposition of Columbanus the abbot, who was born in Scotland and left his homeland for the sake of preaching, with several highly respectable disciples, namely Saints Gallus and Kilianus, Bonifacius, and many others; after many monasteries had been built and many virtues performed in Alemannia and Italy, and many brothers had been joined to him in the Lord, he finally rested in peace in Italy.”

There follows a story concerning the miraculous presentation of the right arm of Saint John the Baptist and of a thorn from the Lord’s crown; these matters do not properly belong here. [Col. 0722B] In the final copy it is pure.

Aquicinct. inserts:

“At the city of Ostia, the holy martyrs Demetrius and Honorius.”

A little earlier it also inserts:

“At the city of Neocerensis, Saint Mary the virgin, who suffered,” etc.

It is sufficiently clear that it should be written as I said above: “At Neocorensis,” etc. It is no less evident that this manuscript, as so often elsewhere, does not depart from the traces of the alleged autograph and its associated manuscripts. Whether Columbanus is included or omitted, however, is not expressed in the transcript.

Matric.-Carthus.-Utrecht:

“Columbanus the abbot, who became the father of innumerable monks. Rufus, disciple of blessed Paul. The Presentation of the glorious Virgin in the temple.”

In Vaticanus, no. 5949, Columbanus is referred to 23 November. The following is added:

“At the city of Asti, Honorius, Stephen, and Eutychius. And the holy Samonas, Abilius, and Gurias.”

See these more properly in the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

[Col. 0722C] Altemps.:

“In the province of Histria, Saint Maurus the martyr. At the city of Ostia, the holy martyrs Demetrius and Honorius.”

Florentin.:

“At Ravenna, Saint John, archbishop and confessor.”

Is this the same person who is commemorated on 12 January?

The Lübeck-Cologne edition begins:

“The Presentation of the glorious Virgin Mary at Jerusalem, when, after she had been weaned and was three years old, she was presented by her parents in the temple; and she herself climbed the fifteen steps by which one ascended into the temple, as though she had already been of mature age.”

Concerning Rufus, it follows Ado, with the title of priest. The entry concerning Columbanus is pure. In place of Maurus it writes, with Greven., *Maurinus*. Finally:

“On the same day, the presentation of the right arm of Saint John the Baptist.”

Belin. has first:

“At Jerusalem, the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, in the temple.”

Greven.:

“Note. The feast of the Presentation of Blessed Mary, when, at the age of three, she was presented by her parents in the temple, and climbed the fifteen steps by which one ascended, ascending them herself as though she had already been of mature age. It began to be celebrated around the year of the Lord 1460.”

On the same day, at Antioch, Basileus, Auxilius, and Matrona. Also Demetrius, Quincianus, Sisinnius, Saturninus, Eutychius, Basilla, and Zepherius. See the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

“The Presentation of the right arm of Saint John the Baptist. The translation of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan and doctor of the holy Church. Also Columbanus, monk and confessor, disciple of another Columbanus, who was of such innocence that birds and beasts obeyed him at his command. At the city of Neocaesarea [read: Neocorensis], Saint Mary the virgin and martyr. Mabilia, a holy matron.”

Molan., concerning the Presentation, follows Belin., adding:

“which the Roman popes Pius and Paul established with indulgences. At Laon-la-Clavato, the passing of Saint Autbodus.”

Then, in smaller type:

“On the same day, at the city of Reims, Albert, a man of extraordinary holiness, bishop of Liège and brother of Henry the Great, duke of Lorraine and Brabant, was killed and died on the orders of the emperor Henry, for the protection of ecclesiastical liberty.”

Later editions differ from the first only in this respect: they placed the feast of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin, Mother of God, etc., in italic letters at the first place in the text.]

[Col. 0719]

The feast of the most blessed Rufus, concerning whom the Apostle Paul writes to the Romans. In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, the deposition of Saint Columbanus, abbot, who was the founder of many monasteries and the father of innumerable monks, renowned for many virtues, and rested in a good old age. Also in Histria, the passion of Saint Maurus the martyr.

[Bouillart.: “The feast of the most blessed Rufus, concerning whom the Apostle Paul writes.” [Note: [Col. 0719A] Here Sollerius first notes on his own that the Pratensis manuscript departs on this day and the two following days from the pure manuscripts, indeed from almost all manuscripts. I, who on the following day saw no erasure in the manuscript, no different hand, no different ink, immediately began to wonder, turned the page, ran through Sollerius’s text, eager to know what fault the censor found in Pratensis. There was nothing different from Pratensis. But what was his state of mind when, immediately after the text, I read: “Everywhere Pratensis, Herinien., etc., are pure”? I confess that I could scarcely keep from laughing.

I continue reading the variant readings for this day, 21 November:

“Everything there must be in extreme confusion, since Castellanus testifies that on the 22nd only Cecilia is treated; moreover, on the 23rd the entire text was again erased,” etc. Then concerning Columbanus, and so forth. For the 24th a different hand is observed; hence it could almost be inferred that it is precisely the same hand that runs through all the texts on the 19th, 21st, 22nd, and 23rd of this month. The reader believes that these things are being said seriously and begins to fear for the Pratensis manuscript on the basis of Castellanus’s testimony. I ask him to look at the opposite page; he will be freed from all fear.

“I,” says Sollerius, “did not think that on this day and the two following days I should rely on Castellanus’s latest testimony in the Additions.”

What a splendid criticism! Let us examine the rest. First, Sollerius is annoyed that Mary of Neocorensis was added here, although there is no argument that the death of the holy virgin should be assigned to the first day of this month rather than to this day. Then he asserts that Columbanus was commemorated here by Usuardus. I admit that it would have been better to leave Columbanus in the place where he first announced him. For, according to Jonas, the author of his Life, that holy abbot died on this day. But Usuardus placed greater trust than Ado did in a Calendar compiled in the time of Louis the Pious for certain churches of Gaul that wished to adopt the Roman rite prescribed by Charlemagne. Perhaps he also encountered the Gellone Martyrology, which likewise commemorates Saint Columbanus not on this day but on the 23rd of this month.

Demetrius and Honorius are taken from the Hieronymian indices, which add eleven others, at least in our very ancient manuscript.

Bouillart.]

At the city of Neocorensis, Saint Mary the virgin, who suffered under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus. In the province of Histria, the passion of Saint Maurus the martyr. At the city of Hostia, the holy martyrs Demetrius and Honorius.

**The tenth day before the Kalends. Day 22.**

[Note: [Col. 0723]

Pratensis, Herinien., Tornacen., Antwerp.-Maj., Muneratus, Greven, and Molan. are pure throughout. Several others approach purity closely.]

[Note: [Col. 0723A]

No manuscript writes *Caeciliae* in this form; in the text I followed those that use the diphthong *ae*, namely Pratensis, Herinien., Rosweyd., and Molan. Tornacen. alone reads “his own brother” in place of “his brother.” The same manuscript has “to believe in Christ”; Greven. and Molan. have “to believe Christ.” Greven. alone added “and confessor” at the end of the text. [Col. 0724B] The rest are trifles, such as *Tyburtius*, *martirium*, *Marcius*, *Aurelius*, *Scelerianus* for *Celerinus*, *Augustidunum*, *Pragmatius*, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0723B]

The venerable name of Cecilia is celebrated throughout the universal Church, both Greek and Latin, in all ecclesiastical and sacred records and monuments. Her memory is consecrated by a special cult in the Gelasian, Gregorian, and Gothic Sacramentaries, in the Calendars of Allatius and Fronto, in the Litanies, and in the very Canon of the Mass.

Let us hear our Martyrologies. The Hieronymian Martyrologies first read as follows:

“At Rome, Saint Cecilia the virgin,”

where they also add the companions whom we listed from the same manuscripts on 14 April. The *Little Roman Martyrology* has almost the same words:

“At Rome, Cecilia, virgin and martyr.”

In Bede a brief eulogy is attached, copied by Rabanus, expanded by Ado, and reduced by our author almost to its original form, with Ado’s chronological note added concerning the reigns of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus. That very note must plainly be rejected if the illustrious Acts of the saint are sound, such as those published from Metaphrastes by Lipomanus and Surius and most diligently illustrated by Antonius Bosio, which we know to have been widely accepted and highly praised by the judgments of our predecessors on 14 April, 25 May, and on this day in the Greek-Moscow Calendars.

The Adonian chronological note must, I say, be rejected, since in the Acts just mentioned the martyrdom of Cecilia and her companions is expressly connected with Pope Urbanus and therefore with the emperor Alexander. In defense of this position Baronius, Florentinius, and other celebrated writers contend; and the widespread opinion of the entire Catholic world contends with them. The Greeks, taking another path, prefer to move Cecilia to the time of Diocletian, but we shall not delay over them.

The chief objection raised by more recent writers—and the fundamental difficulty—consists principally in this: as I have also suggested elsewhere, the fierce and savage persecution described in these Acts does not seem at all to fit the times of Alexander; nor do the atrocious tortures repeatedly inflicted on Christians seem to belong to that period. “The Martyrologies must be followed,” you will say. By no means, for in that case the Acts of Pope Urbanus would be entirely overturned.

Nor is the Viennese Martyrologist consistent with himself, connecting Cecilia’s age here with that of Urbanus under Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, while on 25 May he says that, through Urbanus’s teaching, many were crowned with martyrdom under the persecution of Alexander. These considerations and others of the same kind impelled Tillemont, cited above on the aforementioned days, to summon Cecilia from Sicily, following Fortunatus of Poitiers; for that ancient poet sings:

> Sicily brings forth Cecilia, and Selencia Thecla.

Such an opinion will seem paradoxical to many, as it does to me. But what can one do? The more common alternative is burdened by many difficulties that it is not easy to reconcile with the rules of exact criticism, and even less appropriate to this place. I have already solemnly declared, on the aforementioned days, 14 April and 25 May, that I do not wish to decide anything through premature judgment, and here I declare the same again.

For the rest, I have wished to report briefly the various opinions that will cause no small trouble to our colleagues or successors who will illuminate the Acts for the month of November. [Col. 0724C] The discoveries of the body, concerning which see Baronius under the year 821, will not be the only source of difficulty. Wandalbertus alludes to the commonly circulated Acts in a not inelegant metrical eulogy:

> Holy Cecilia immediately illumines the tenth day with her splendor,  
> Forever to be proclaimed through bright triumphs,  
> A virgin supported on one side by her kinsman, on the other by her holy husband.]

Yesterday our Martyrologist commemorates Maurus in Istria, today in Rome, thereby doubling him. Concerning the Istrian Maurus—if he can perhaps be different from the one commemorated today—we said on the preceding day that nothing at all is found. If he is the same as the Roman Maurus, Rabānus’s lengthy encomium, cited the day before, may be consulted. Peter’s account at the place cited there is shorter, but it lays out the matter so clearly that it is evident that Maurus, African by origin, suffered at Rome and was then conducted, under the guidance of an angel, to the shore of the city of Parentium in the province of Istria, by a ship saved from Celerinus’s deliberately set fire. All these matters can in due course be elucidated more fully from our various manuscripts, composed in both prose and verse concerning this saint. [Col. 0724D] If Usuard had seen such Acts, he would not have divided one Maurus into two. We must believe that he followed another guide, by whom he was led into error.

Pragmatius of Autun is likewise Usuardine, but was undoubtedly taken from the Hieronymians, although Florentinius considers him a Gallican antiquarian addition, sometimes excessively scrupulous in such matters. I find no account of his deeds, nor anything besides what Baronius noted; see him under the year 490, beginning at no. 24, where you will find only two of his subscriptions and a letter of Sidonius Apollinaris addressed to him. I do not know why Castellanus claims that, although he died on 20 November, he was buried on this day.]

[Note: [Col. 0723D]

ROSWEYD., in the pure text, adds at the end: “Of Longinus the martyr, who opened the Lord’s side.” See what we said about him after Usuard, on 15 March. Here too see the Hieronymian notation and Florentinius’s note.

In PULSANEN. the first [manuscript] proceeds correctly as far as “was martyred.” In the second, the third [item] is missing.

[Col. 0724D] ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., BELIN., ANTUERP.-MAX. ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN, and LOVAN. seem to speak in Adonian style, thus altering the first announcement: “She thoroughly instructed them to believe in Christ and then encouraged them to martyrdom. Almachius had her detained after their martyrdom and brought her to completion through a glorious passion. She suffered [Col. 0725A],” etc. The last four codices, at the end of the entry concerning Pragmatius, add with GREVEN., “and confessor.”

ALBERG., DANIC., and Ursinus’s codex from Rosemberg are throughout similar to the codices just mentioned, but add at the end: “At the city of Altinum, the natal feast of Saint Theonestus, bishop of Philippi, who, coming to the aforesaid city during the persecution of the Arians, there completed with the utmost glory, together with his two disciples Trabaham and Trabatham, the contest of martyrdom by decapitation.” In the Roman Martyrology he is placed on 30 October. See the Usuardine Appendices there.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Cecilia the virgin, who instructed her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius in the faith and encouraged them to the glory of martyrdom. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Longinus the martyr.” See ROSWEYD.

BRUXELLEN. begins: “At Rome, the natal feast of Saint Cecilia the virgin, who, having converted her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius, was slaughtered with the sword when she could not be harmed by fire.” Then: “And the natal feast of Saint Crescentianus the martyr, who, suspended on the rack, beaten with clubs, and lacerated with hooks, was then roasted for a long time by flames applied around his sides and gave up his spirit.” See below, 24 [November]. Concerning Theonestus it has, as ALBERG. and the others do, etc.; at the end, “and confessor.” Nothing concerning Maurus.

HAGENOYEN. adds concerning Cecilia: “She had an angel as guardian of her virginity, whom she allowed her husband Valerian to see if he wished to be purified—and he did so. With him she received from the angel in heaven a crown of roses and lilies. She displayed Bishop Urban in an angelic appearance. She distributed to the poor everything she was able to possess and taught others to do the same. Finally, when she refused to sacrifice, during the reign and persecution of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, she was placed in a hot bath for a night and a day, but was not harmed; thereafter Almachius the prefect ordered her to be beheaded.” In the entry for Maurus, the text is pure. Concerning Theonestus, besides what was stated above, it inserts: “He was expelled from his see by the Arians [Col. 0725C] and preached with his disciples, wandering through Germany, Burgundy, and Italy, and brought many back to the faith. At last [Col. 0726A], coming to the aforesaid city with only two disciples, the others having suffered for the faith,” etc. At the end, the text is pure.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Cecilia the virgin and martyr. Of Pragmatius the bishop. Of Gobertus the confessor.” In others, Gothbertus. He is commemorated on the following day.

REGINAE SUEC., sign. no. 428: “On the same day, Saint Medrisma the virgin.” In Rabānus she is Mederasma. See where she is commemorated, in Castellanus.

VATICAN., no. 5949, deals only with Cecilia.

FLORENTIN.: “Likewise, of the holy martyrs Theonestus, bishop of Philippi, Thrabaea, and Trabata, as well as Albanus and Ursus, disciples of the said bishop.”

DIVIONEN. S. Benigni: “The translation of the body of Blessed Benignus the martyr.” He is commemorated on 1 November.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition differs little concerning Cecilia from the middle-class codices cited above. “Likewise at Rome, Saint Maurus the monk and martyr, who, after various tortures had been inflicted, suffered capital punishment under the prefect Celerinus during the reign of the emperor Numerian.” [Col. 0726B] Concerning Pragmatius it adds, “and confessor.” Concerning Theonestus, as ALBERG. and the others above.

GREVEN.: “In Cappadocia, Saints Longinus, Leontius, and Faustus. At Alexandria, Felix, Demetrius, and Honoratus.” See the Hieronymians. “At Philippi, Saint Theonestus, bishop and martyr, who, during the persecution of the Arians, came to the city of Altinum with his disciples Tabraham and Tabrata and there completed the course of his martyrdom by decapitation. Of Romaricus the abbot and confessor. Likewise, the ordination of Saint Willibrord to the episcopate.”

MOLAN. in the first edition lacks the additions. The later editions corrupt the Usuardine text. First, in Italic type, between “then” and “was martyred,” these words are inserted: “After their martyrdom, by Almachius.” The end of the announcement is likewise altered so that, in place of “and Commodus,” the name Alexander is substituted, making the sense that Cecilia suffered during the reigns of Marcus Aurelius Alexander. We have already stated more than once that in these later editions the editor, attributing excessive weight to the judgments of his friends, did not preserve Usuardine purity with sufficient scrupulousness.]

[Col. 0723]

At Rome, the natal feast of Saint Cecilia the virgin, who thoroughly instructed her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius to believe in Christ and to embrace martyrdom; she herself was then martyred, overcoming fire but killed by the sword. She suffered during the reigns of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus. Likewise at Rome, Saint Maurus the martyr, who contended under the prefect Celerinus. At Autun, Saint Pragmatius the bishop.

IX Kal. Day 23.

[Note: [Col. 0725]

Complete purity is found only in Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0725D]

The three Praten., Antuerp.-Maj., and Rosweyd. have again been excluded; between Felicitas and Trudo they treat of Columbanus, as we shall say in the Appendices, to which Herinien. must also be relegated because of its proper entry for Rheims, etc. Among those cited for the text, the difference is that the first two, along with the ancient manuscripts, read “is crowned,” while the three printed editions read “has been crowned.” I followed the former, as being more in conformity with Ado. Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. alone substitute “third” for “fourth from blessed Peter.” In Greven. “the martyr Felicitas” is wrongly printed in place of “Felicitas the mother.” Basbanio and Parisii are errors in Munerat.; Antonio is an error in the aforementioned Greven. All the codices cited for the text have: “Likewise, at the city of Emerita,” except Molan., whose older witnesses agree with us; “In the city of Emerita”—the matter is not worth disputing.]

[Note: [Col. 0727A]

Everything we said here concerning yesterday’s celebration of Cecilia could be repeated concerning the apostolic pope Clement: namely, that his feast is as ancient in the ecclesiastical offices as are the monuments themselves in which the memory of any other saint is recorded. I except Bucherius’s Calendar, in which Pope Clement does not seem to be recorded on the fifth Ides, that is, 9 November, in these words: “Clement, Sempronianus, Claudius, Nicostratus in the Comitatum”; nor is yesterday’s Cecilia found in that same calendar. It is more probable that in the Carthaginian Calendar, immediately before Chrysogonus, one should read Chrysogonus, for which reading I venture; in both places the date-mark for Saint Clement has been worn away. But in all the other calendars, sacramentaries, martyrologies, and other sacred books cited for the preceding day, the solemnity of Pope Clement is celebrated in common. There is no doubt concerning the Hieronymian copies, whatever Clement—also recorded there on the 21st of this month—may be intended; concerning that controversy Florentinius should be consulted on both days. Bede and his copyist Rabanus report the same encomium, abridged from the commonly circulated Acts. In our series, the Romanum parvum says very briefly: “Saint Clement the bishop.” Ado has little in his Martyrology, more in the Feasts of the Apostles; our author gathered only the principal points here and there, shaping the encomium so that even the critics themselves can object to little, except insofar as some attack his martyrdom. Clement’s Acts are very well known; concerning them see Baronius and Rosweyd’s note, p. 221. Various accounts have been published by various writers, but to defend their complete authenticity one encounters brief passages that are reefs and shoals in a great sea, which I leave to our successors to navigate. For many matters concerning his deeds, age, exile, and writings, whether genuine or spurious, remain to be disentangled. Even after the way has been cleared by many highly learned men, they require the most laborious investigation; nor do I know whether our various manuscripts will sufficiently smooth the path. See especially what Tillemont attempted with great diligence: he carefully examined everything contributing to Clement’s indisputable praise, in volume II, p. 149 and from p. 549 onward. Thus Wandalbert sang:

“On the ninth, Pope Clement holds the contest, and with lofty

titles of virtue, he who suffered death in the waters

found a temple built by divine favor.”

[Col. 0728A] There follows the most courageous mother, more than a martyr, who, after sending seven children ahead to the kingdom, died before herself as many times, etc., as Magnus Gregory praises her magnificently. In nearly all the ecclesiastical calendars cited above, she is joined to Pope Clement on the same day. The Hieronymians mention her: “And Saint Felicitas.” Bede: “On the same day, Saint Felicitas, mother of seven martyr sons, who, by order of Antoninus, was beheaded for Christ.” Rabanus is much the same. Wandalbertus, the Romanum parvum, Ado, and Usuard also join them. The Viennese account is longer; our author was content to copy Bede’s shorter phrase. We have treated fully of the genuine Acts of the mother and sons among those edited by Ruinart as sincere, on 10 July. This place must also be given to Wandalbert’s couplet, to which we join the third verse, concerning the following saint:

“Then too the sevenfold mother with her offspring, Felicitas,

shines forth, blessed, pre-eminent in triumph.

Here also Trudo, despiser of the world, adorns his own.”

He is the man from whom the town of Trudonopolis in Hasbania, belonging to the diocese and territory of Liège, is named; formerly called Sarchinium, it is famous for many saints. I find Trudo in the Florus published by our writers, where the title “priest” is omitted, and likewise in Rabanus. Otherwise the wording of the two is different, and so is that of our author, making it easy to see that neither had seen the other. Nor does the addition agree any better—the addition made to the Corbie Hieronymian codices and attributed by Mosander to Ado, wrongly in my opinion, since it is not recorded even in the very extensive Pratense copy. Rosweyd therefore rightly rejected it into the appendix. A Life by Theodoric the abbot, polished in more elegant prose from Donatus’s autograph, appears in Surius. Mabillon examined and discussed everything more carefully in the second Benedictine century, beginning at p. 1069. These matters may in due course be compared with and illustrated from our various manuscripts.

Severinus, who is treated here, must be attributed solely to Usuard, as must Lucretia of Emerita, reported from Spain, unless I am mistaken. Consult Baronius’s note concerning her. Severinus is placed in the Roman Martyrology on 27 November, doubtless from Belinus; Castellanus records his deposition on that date, but his death on this day. What deeds concerning him may survive is not yet known to me.]

[Note: [Col. 0727C]

PRATEN., ANTUERP.-MAJ., and ROSWEYD. We have already said in the Variants that these three refer to Columbanus in third place. In the Pratense, everything after Clement had been erased; in order to insert Columbanus into that space, the announcement placed by us on the 21st had to be shortened. The codices at least read as follows: “In Italy, blessed Columbanus the abbot, founder of many monasteries.” Castellanus and Chamillart read otherwise in the Pratense; I certainly cannot understand it unless a new interpolation was added after Sirmond’s time.

HERINIEN. has the entire text completely pure, but inserts in second place its proper entry for Rheims: “In the territory of Rheims, the deposition of Saint Gotbertus the confessor.” Elsewhere, Godebertus.

TORNACEN. is deficient only in Trudo.

PULSANEN., pure in the first [entry], omits the second and third; in the fourth it is pure. The last [entry] is missing.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LOVAN., LEYDEN, and BELG. insert in the penultimate place: “At the city of Metz, Saint Clement, uncle of Pope Clement and the first bishop of the people of Metz.” They are sufficiently pure throughout.

ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN. LAT., ALBERG., and DANIC. have the same addition concerning Clement of Metz, but further add to the first announcement: “He was the second after blessed Peter and, at Peter’s command, undertook the governance of the Church as pontiff. Although Linus and Cletus are written before him, according to Haymo and others who investigated the apostolic see, they did not hold the Roman see as pontiffs, but as assistants to the supreme pontiff.”

CENTULEN.: “The natal feast of Saint Clement, pope and martyr, concerning whom the Apostle says: ‘With Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.’ At Rome, Saint Felicitas, mother of seven sons, who suffered with those same sons under Antoninus. In the district of Hasbania, the deposition of Saint Trudo the abbot and confessor, a man distinguished in birth and holiness.”

BRUXELLEN. forms the first entry as follows: “At Rome, the natal feast of Saint Clement, pope and martyr, who, under the persecution of the emperor Trajan, had an anchor tied around his neck and was thrown into the sea, and so was crowned by martyrdom. When the sea had receded four miles, his body was found in a stone coffin in a marble temple and brought to the city of Rome, where a church built in his memory preserves it to this day.” The account of Clement of Metz follows, almost as above. Then the remainder of the text, but with this inserted in the penultimate place: “Near the city of Bourges, Saint Facerius the priest.” I think this should be Faretrius or Pharetrius, in French Phalier.

HAGENOYEN. gathers much concerning Clement, beyond what is contained in the Acts, but there is no time to transcribe everything from this codex. It continues: “On the same day, the natal feast of Saint Felicitas the martyr, mother of seven brothers, who, seeing her sons die and grieving for them deeply in body, nevertheless rejoiced wholly in spirit because she had sent them to heaven. By order of the emperor Antoninus she was finally beheaded. Gregory calls her ‘more than a mother’ in his homilies. In the district of Hasbania, that is, Haspegonne, the deposition of Saint Trudo, priest and confessor, a man of admirable holiness.” It gives the pure text concerning Severinus and refers Lucretia to the following day.

AQUICINCT. adds concerning Clement: “He divided the Church into seven regions among faithful notaries, who were to investigate carefully and diligently the deeds of the martyrs. At the command of Blessed Peter he undertook the pontificate of the Church. Linus and Cletus are written before him because they were ordained bishops by the prince of the apostles himself for the priestly ministry.” See Ado’s appendix in Rosweyd’s edition.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Of Clement, pope and martyr. Of Felicitas the martyr and widow. Of Severinus the monk. Of Lucretia the virgin.”
