Codex D. LE MARE, sign. A: “The deposition of Saint Porcianus the confessor.” He is commemorated on the following day.

In VATICAN., no. 5949, the last three saints of the Usuardine text are missing. Added is: “In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, Saint Columbanus the abbot.”

Codex CASTRI KAROLI: Saint Laurence the martyr.

BIZUNTICEN. reads incorrectly: “In the district of Austuvium, or Austunium, Saint Trudo.”

RHEMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.: “In the district of Laon, Saint Godebertus the priest and confessor.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition has concerning Clement nearly all the material already reported and also adds: “He decreed that one who had been baptized should be confirmed as soon as possible, since otherwise he would not be a perfect Christian. During the persecution of the emperor Trajan, he was thrown into the sea by the judge Aufridianus; while the Christians prayed and wept, the sea receded into its basin for nearly three miles, and the people, entering over dry ground, found a marble temple prepared by angelic hands, and in it the body of Blessed Clement buried, with the anchor placed beside him. It lay there for seventy-six years. In the time of Pope Nicholas I, the body of Saint Clement was translated to Rome and placed in the church now called Saint Clement’s.” In the rest it is generally similar to the middle-class codices, also inserting Clement of Metz in the penultimate place.

BELIN. transferred Severinus to the 27th. Much else is badly confused.

GREVEN.: “At Metz, the deposition of Saint Clement, the first bishop of that city and uncle of Saint Clement the pope, sent there by blessed Peter together with two others, namely Caelestis and Felix. At Cambrai, of Sarius the priest and confessor. In the territory of Rheims, Saint Gobertus the confessor. At Bourges, Saint Faterius the priest. Of Queen Faustina, who, believing through the confession of blessed Catherine, later suffered for the faith of Christ and, after the extraction of her breasts, was beheaded. Of Theodora, wife of blessed Sisinnius the martyr.”

MOLAN. inserts Clement’s encomium into the text in Italic type: “He divided the Church into seven regions among faithful notaries, who were to investigate the deeds of the martyrs carefully. At the command of blessed Peter he undertook the pontificate of the Church. Linus and Cletus are therefore written before him because they were ordained bishops by the prince of the apostles himself for the priestly ministry. At Trajan’s command he was sent into exile beyond the Pontic Sea, into the wilderness; after calling many to the faith by his miracles and teaching, he was thrown into the sea with an anchor tied around his neck. But, while his disciples prayed, the sea receded three miles, and they found his body in a stone coffin in a marble temple, with the anchor beside it; thus, as Peter’s disciple, he was crowned by such a martyrdom.” Concerning Trudo, after “Hasbania,” it adds, “in Sarchinium, the deposition,” and after “confessor,” “a man of admirable holiness.” At the end: “At Cambrai, in the church of the Mother of God, Blessed Mary, of blessed Sarius the priest and confessor. At the city of Metz, Saint Clement, his uncle, etc. In the territory of Laon, Saint Gobertus the confessor.” Later editions have in the text concerning Clement only “with an anchor tied around his neck,” before “by such a martyrdom.” Afterwards, concerning the notaries alone, etc. Concerning Trudo, as in the first edition. Likewise concerning Sarius and Clement of Metz. It places Gobertus “in the territory of Rheims.” Then, from the Horologium, it adds: “On the twenty-third, Saint Gregory of Agrigentum, and Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium.” The Acts of both exist in Surius through Metaphrastes. For a judgment concerning them, see Papebroch in the Greek-Moscow Menologion, before volume I of the May Acta Sanctorum, p. LI.]

[Col. 0725]

The natal feast of Saint Clement the bishop, who, fourth after the blessed apostle Peter, held the pontificate of the Roman Church and, thrown into the sea during the persecution of Trajan, was crowned by martyrdom. On the same day, Saint Felicitas, mother of seven martyr sons, who, by order of Antoninus, was beheaded for Christ.

[Bouillart inserts:

[Note: [Col. 0725D]

Sollerius disputes that Columbanus was commemorated by Usuard on this day. There are two arguments. The first he derives from Ado’s authority, whom he is certain to have mentioned Columbanus on the twenty-third. The second is the date of Columbanus’s death, which Jonas, the author of his Life, attests to have been the twenty-first of this month. I have said more than once that, whether or not Usuard was in error, it makes no difference to us: the work cannot be denied to its author because of certain errors. Yet I judge the final argument so poor that I wish it could serve Sollerius’s cause well.

I do not know what Chamillartus said to Sollerius about this article, but in the Appendices I see that he read it differently from Castellanus. “I certainly cannot understand it,” says Sollerius, “unless a new interpolation was added after Sirmond’s time.” I would avenge so grave an accusation if I were not angry. BOUILLART.]

In Italy, blessed Columbanus the abbot, founder of many monasteries. In the district of Hasbania, Saint Trudo the priest and confessor. At Paris, the deposition of blessed Severinus the monk and solitary. In the city of Emerita, Saint Lucretia the virgin.

VIII Kal. Day 24.

[Note: [Col. 0729C]

There is agreement among many codices on this day—namely, Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., [Col. 0730C] Greven., and Molan. Likewise Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Lovanien., Albergen., and Danic.]

[Note: [Col. 0729D]

Molanus alone correctly wrote Chrysogonus; among the codices some have Crisogonus, others Grisogonus, Esogonus, Grisogonius, and so forth. Praten. and Herinien. come closest to the purity found in the text. Antuerp.-Maj. reads *constanti* instead of *constantissima*. Munerat. and a few others have Crescencianus. In Antuerp.-Maj. there is the error *preconii*, as well as *Florete* and *Perusitam*, for which some have *Perusium*. All the rest have “at the fortress of Blavia,” as all the older codices indicate. Max.-Lubec. has *Blama*; Greven., *Blavie*; Molan., *Blavio*. Munerat. omitted “for Christ” after “long imprisonments.” Some codices have *diutinos* instead of *diuturnos*. Only Molan. has *Thusciae*.]

[Note: [Col. 0729D]

On this day too we present a saint who, together with Anastasia, whose Acts contain his account, is found inscribed in all the ancient fasti, both Greek and Latin. Basilicas were built at Rome in honor of both, and their names were also inserted into the Canon of the Mass from the earliest centuries of the Church. Florentinius asks whether the celebrated martyrdom of the saint should be assigned to Rome or Aquileia, since both locations are found in different Hieronymian copies. The knot of the question seems to be untied if, assigning to Chrysogonus, as a noble Roman, the beginning of his confession in his homeland, one places its completion at Aquileia or near Aquileia. If this solution is not satisfactory, suggest a more suitable one that reconciles the discrepancies among the martyrologists and the Acts. See other matters carefully noted by the Florentinius cited above. Bede, Rabanus, and our entire series support the Roman location, led by the Romanum parvum, in which Zoilus is also added: “At Rome, of Chrysogonus the martyr, and Zoilus.” Ado, composing a lengthy history from the Acts, testifies that Zoilus did not go to the Lord on this day, but on the thirtieth day after Chrysogonus’s passion, and therefore either on the day itself or the day before Anastasia was crowned, 25 December. Usuard, speaking only of Chrysogonus, briefly followed his struggles and glorious contest. When discussing the Acts of Agape and her sisters on 3 April, against Henschenius’s opinion, we preferred with Baronius and others those accounts that were not mixed into the Acts of Anastasia, since the latter are encumbered by more serious difficulties, as may be seen in Ruinart’s *Selecta*, beginning at p. 419, and in Tillemont, volume V, beginning at p. 323. Since the contest of our Chrysogonus was taken from the aforementioned Acts of Saint Anastasia, care must in due course be taken that, if any impure seed is found mixed in there, it be removed after careful examination. Thus Wandalbertus praises Chrysogonus alone:

[Col. 0731B] “Chrysogonus by his merits sanctifies the eighth day and by his burial.”

On 8 August we reported from Bucherius’s very ancient Calendar the following text: “Ballistaria, Cyriacus, Largus, Crescentianus, Memmia, Juliana, and Smaragdus.” Earlier, on 16 March, we had pointed out the present Crescentianus, placed there on that day by the Romanum parvum and Ado but omitted there by Usuard. The reason for the omission is now apparent: our author transferred the saint here. He is also reported on this day by Bede with an encomium, and I am exceedingly surprised that Usuard took nothing from it. What should be thought concerning the Acts of Marcellus, from which this and several other saints were derived, we discussed fully on 16 January and on the days cited above.

Usuard found Romanus in no earlier martyrology; he himself first placed him on this day, taking him from Gregory of Tours’s book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 46. The written Lives mentioned by Gregory have probably been lost. We learn from the aforementioned bishop that Martin had arranged his burial and that his tomb was beside the fortress of Blavia, on the bank of the Garonne, where Romanus often saved those about to perish in shipwreck by appearing through the exercise of his power. We possess a manuscript Life of Romanus filled with numerous miracles of the saint, from which the office now used in the parish church of Etrahaam near Bayeux seems to have been extracted. There is no time now to pass judgment on it; here it is enough to have shown that Romanus is truly Usuardine, just as are the following Cordoban virgins with Felicissimus. Eulogius, the most worthy encomiast of the Cordoban martyrs and himself a glorious martyr in the same Arab persecution, described the victories and trophies of Flora and Maria admirably in book II, chapter 8, of the *Memorial*. Usuard learned of them from him, or rather from the most recent memory of the Spaniards, and rightly inserted them into his Martyrology. What Eulogius elsewhere recorded concerning the distinguished virgins, with his pen dipped in the pyx of the Holy Spirit, is carefully cited here by Baronius. Felicissimus of Perugia, moreover, was added from the Hieronymians, distinguished only by his name and the glory of martyrdom.]

[Note: [Col. 0731B]

In PRATENSI, whether in the margin or at the end of the text, the following has been added by a later hand and therefore marked with a subvirgula in our copy: “At Aprutium, Saint Flavianus the bishop and confessor.” I cannot determine where this Flavianus was taken from; Castellanus records Flavianus of Vercelli on the following day.

[Col. 0731C] TORNACEN., pure in the first [entry], omits the second concerning Crescentianus; it cuts out the entire encomium of Romanus and finally also omits the Cordoban virgins Flora and Maria.

ROSWEYD., pure in the text, adds: “Likewise Carpasius, who, after the rack, clubs, and hooks, was thrown into the flames and gave up his spirit.” I read Carpasius in Bede’s encomium of Crescentianus, where, acting as deputy, he carried out savage slaughter against the martyr. I would not be surprised if he had slipped in here in place of the saint; certainly all the words seem to have been taken from the aforementioned encomium of Crescentianus.

PULSANEN., mutilated in the first [entry], pure in the Cordobans, omits everything else.

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, Saint Chrysogonus the martyr, who, having been tormented in prison for two years under Diocletian, finally reached the palm by the stroke of the sword. Likewise at Rome, Saint Crescentianus the martyr, under the judge Carpasius. At the fortress of Blavia, Saint Romanus the priest [Col. 0731D] and monk, whom Bishop Martin of Tours rejoiced to bury after his death. At Córdoba, the holy virgins,” etc., purely. Felicissimus is missing.

BRUXELLEN., somewhat mutilated in the first [entry], is pure in the second. It continues: “In Gaul, at the city of Riez, Saint Maximus the bishop and confessor, who, endowed from his earliest age with every virtue, was first father of the monastery of Lérins and then bishop of the church of Riez, renowned for signs and wonders; among his other magnificent deeds, he is said, while still alive, to have raised three dead men.” We have already said more than once that saints are often transposed in this codex. See concerning Maximus on 27 November. It is sufficiently pure concerning the Cordoban virgins and Felicissimus, but deferred Romanus to the following day.

HAGENOYEN. begins: “At the city of Metz, the deposition of Saint Clement the bishop, uncle of Pope Clement, whom that same Clement sent there as the city’s first bishop.” See the Appendices for the preceding day. Then: “At Aquileia, the passion of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr. He was very noble in body, but much nobler in faith. He instructed blessed Anastasia, the virgin of God, in the faith; and when he was placed in chains, she greatly comforted him in her letters. He had long endured chains and imprisonment at Rome, and was brought bound to Aquileia by Diocletian; when he refused to sacrifice there, he was beheaded and thrown into the sea.” The text concerning Crescentianus, the Cordobans, and Romanus is sufficiently pure; at the end, in place of Felicissimus, it substitutes yesterday’s announcement concerning Lucretia of Emerita, whom it calls Lucrena, as it often habitually distorts many things.

VICTORIN. and REGINAE SUEC., sign. no. 130, at the end: “Likewise, near the city of Reate, Saint Eleutherius the martyr.” Is this perhaps the one who is commemorated with his mother Anthia on 18 April?

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECTIN.: “Of Chrysogonus the martyr. Of Crescentianus the martyr. Of Flora and Maura, virgins and martyrs. Of Porphyrius the soldier and martyr, with his companions converted by blessed Catherine.”

In VATICAN., under no. 5949, the last three announcements are again missing. Added, however, is: “Of Flavianus, bishop and confessor of Constantinople.” See the Roman Martyrology, 18 February.

[Col. 0732D] STROZZIAN.: “In the city of Reggio, Saint Prosperus the bishop and confessor.” Did BELINUS take this from here? See the Roman Martyrology and the Acts on 25 June, and GREVEN below. I do not know which Prosperus Castellanus reports on the following day with only the title “confessor,” unless perhaps he took him from the Hieronymians.

BIZUNTICEN.: “The discovery of the body of blessed Benignus the priest and martyr.” See 1 November.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition begins: “At Cologne Agrippina, the translation of blessed Gereon and his Theban companions, carried out by Lord Frederick I, archbishop of Cologne, and Rudolph, abbot of Saint Pantaleon, in the year 1121 from the Incarnation of the Lord. Likewise at Cologne, in the church of the aforementioned martyr Saint Gereon, the commemoration of blessed Gregory and his Moorish companions.” The usual text follows, somewhat purer, with this inserted in third place: “At Alexandria, blessed Porphyrius the martyr, with certain other soldiers whom the blessed virgin Catherine converted to Christ.”

[Col. 0733A] BELIN. inserts in third place: “Likewise, at the city of Reggio, Saint Prosperus the bishop and confessor.” See STROZZ.

GREVEN.: “At Alexandria, Saint Porphyrius and his companions, soldiers and martyrs, who are said to have believed during the passion of blessed Catherine. Of Ignatius the martyr. Near Cologne Agrippina, the discovery and elevation of Saint Gereon the martyr. When in the year 1121 Norbert of Prémontré had come to Cologne for the relics of the saints and had spent the night in prayer in the basilica of the aforementioned martyr, he ordered the ground to be dug in the middle of the basilica in the morning; the intact body of the holy martyr was found and was raised with fitting honor by Frederick I, archbishop of Cologne, Rudolph, abbot of Saint Pantaleon, and the faithful people. Likewise, in the same city and basilica, the commemoration of blessed Gregory the leader and his Moorish companions, [Col. 0734A] martyrs. In the territory of Morienne, Saint Marinus the martyr. The translation of Saint Prosperus, bishop of Reggio, an outstanding teacher. On the same day, Saint Eleutherius.”

MOLAN. at the end, from BELIN.: “In the city of Reggio, Saint Prosperus the bishop and confessor.” Then, in smaller type, he describes from Greven the discovery and elevation of Gereon, adding: “In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Portianus the abbot and confessor, concerning whom Blessed Gregory of Tours wrote the fifth book of the *Lives of the Fathers*.” Other editions insert in Italic type, in third place, a new announcement: “At Milan, Protasius the bishop and confessor.” At the end: “In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Portianus the abbot and confessor. On the twenty-fourth, Saint Mercury the martyr.” See his Acts in Surius.]

[Col. 0729]

At Rome, the natal feast of blessed Chrysogonus the martyr, who, after enduring long chains and imprisonments for his steadfast confession of Christ, was beheaded and thrown into the sea at Diocletian’s command and completed his martyrdom. Likewise at Rome, Saint Crescentianus the martyr, who is mentioned in the passion of blessed Pope Marcellus. At the fortress of Blavia, Saint Romanus the priest and confessor, whose holiness is proclaimed by the glory of his miracles. In the city of Córdoba, the holy virgins Flora and Maria, who, after long imprisonments, were killed by the sword for Christ. At Perugia, a city of Tuscany, Saint Felicissimus.

VII Kal. Day 25.

[Note: [Col. 0733]

Very many codices have the entire text complete, but the only four that are pure and not augmented in any part are Praten., Herinien., Rosweyd., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0733B]

I say nothing about Egypt, Erasmus, and such trifles. In our Pratenian copy, *cleris* has been written incorrectly instead of *clericis*. There is one noteworthy variation in which Molan differs from all the others: undoubtedly following Ado, he reads “almost six hundred and sixty clerics and laymen.” This is certainly correct and not without good sense, but Usuard constructed these words differently. That number, already uncertain for other reasons, was increased by others, who extended the entire multitude of Peter’s companions, even more incorrectly, to six hundred and sixty-six. The most common variation, by which so many codices were excluded from the pure texts, arises from the addition of Saint Catherine. Since the four codices cited lack this addition, their antiquity can, with the greatest probability, be recognized as superior to the others; as we did not fail to note in the preface.]

[Note: [Col. 0733B]]

Peter, bishop of Alexandria, the most renowned martyr—or rather, by antonomasia, *the Martyr*, commonly called the “end” or “seal of the martyrs”—is highly praised by Eusebius and the other ancient writers for the integrity of his conduct and his teaching, no less than for his continual labors and his endurance of innumerable hardships during the time of the most savage persecution. He is commemorated especially on three days in the Latin and Greek ecclesiastical calendars, namely 24, 25, and 26 November. In all the Hieronymian copies I consistently find him assigned to the 26th: “At Alexandria, Peter”; Florentinius’s annotation may be consulted concerning this. The other Martyrologists—Bede, Rabanus, Wandalbert, and our entire series—have entered upon what, unless I am mistaken, is the truer path, unanimously dedicating this 25th day to Peter’s cult; and I believe this continued among the Latins until Catherine’s growing fame in the West so overshadowed Peter that he withdrew to the following day.

As for the first two codices—or rather Bede alone—their splendid eulogy is almost entirely composed in the words of Rufinus, Book IX, chapter 6, and was transcribed by Our Author from Bede, with only the final clause added. We believe that clause to have been supplied by the Little Roman Martyrology; in it, certainly, the indefinite number of Peter’s companions in Rufinus is extended, on I know not what basis, to six hundred and sixty. The words of the Little Roman Martyrology are: “Saint Peter, bishop of Alexandria, with six hundred and sixty others.” He would have spoken more truly, in accordance with Rufinus, Book VIII, chapter 14, had he said that “innumerable persons, together with bishops, endured the noblest martyrdoms.”

Ado’s fuller narrative begins from the final chapter of the praised Book VII of Rufinus; the remainder he compiled himself from those Acts whose authenticity is so disputed that scarcely any learned man today, after Hermantius, Valesius, Pagius, Papebrochius, and others, dares to accept them as genuine—whether as published and translated into Latin by Metaphrastes, or as issued in both languages by Combefis among the *Lecti Triumphos*, p. 189 onward. We have briefly arranged a few points concerning the praises of this supreme pontiff in our chronology of the Alexandrian Patriarchs, p. 34, no. 180 onward. But no one, so far as I know, has collected, arranged, and examined Peter’s deeds, and the matters connected with them, more carefully than Tillemont, volume V, p. 436 onward, and in the notes p. 755 onward; all of this will have to be reconsidered in the Acts.

This is Wandalbert’s encomium:

> Peter, bishop and martyr, beautifies the seventh day;
>
> under his leadership the people of Alexandria,
>
> strengthened by him, spurn the crooked and blind paths of error.

The other martyr named in our text, Erasmus, seems entirely unknown to all the other Martyrologists—indeed, I might almost say to all writers—unless he is precisely the same as that Erasmus, so famous in Campania of Italy, whom we reported from Usuard and others on 3 June, as can easily be understood from Henschenius’s learned commentary, volume I, p. 211 onward. I cannot even guess what moved Usuard to devise such a commemoration on this day; meanwhile, the agreement of nearly all the codices, at least the most reliable, leaves no doubt that it was placed here by him.]

[Note: [Col. 0733D]]

PRATENIAN. In this codex, according to Castellanus, a much later hand adds: “At Alexandria, Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr.” All the more recent codices cited here are full of praises of this saint. To mention them once for all, see the Greek-Moscow *Ephemerides* before Volume I of May, p. LI, and Papebrochius’s *Responsiones* to article XI, no. 77 onward, etc.

HERINIEN. In the lower margin of the codex, in a hand quite different from and later than the text, an asterisk refers back from the end of the text: “On the same day, blessed Catherine, virgin and martyr, who suffered at the city of Alexandria under the emperor Maxentius.”

ANTWERP-MAJOR inserts into the middle of the pure text: “At the same city, the passion of Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr.”

PULSANEN has this text: “The feast of blessed Mercury the martyr. On the same day, the passion of Saint Catherine the virgin, who, at the command of the emperor Maxentius, was crowned with martyrdom at Alexandria. Afterwards she was carried by angels to Mount Sinai, where splendid miracles frequently occur through her.” Peter has been relegated to the following day; nothing is said about Erasmus.

[Col. 0735B] ANTW. MAJOR, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK, and UGHELLIAN add at the end of the pure text: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr, who suffered under the emperor Maxentius.” LOVAN and LEYDEN-BELGIAN have almost the same, but at the beginning. ANTWERP-MAXIMUM likewise has this, but here Erasmus is absent.

MUNERAT gives this beginning: “At Alexandria, the feast of blessed Catherine, virgin and martyr. When she refused to sacrifice to idols, by order of the emperor Maxentius she was thrust into a dark prison cell, deprived of food and drink for twelve days, and there sustained by a dove with angelic bread. Afterward, with the Lord’s help, she overcame many other kinds of torture and, persevering most steadfastly in the faith of Christ, was finally beheaded. Immediately afterward the holy angels came; visibly carrying the blessed virgin’s body high through the air, they miraculously placed it on Mount Sinai. That mountain is twenty days’ journey and more distant from the place of her beheading.”

[Col. 0735C] BELIN speaks as follows: “On Mount Sinai, the most holy Catherine, virgin and martyr, daughter of King Costus in the city of Alexandria. Imprisoned by the emperor Maxentius because of her confession of the Christian faith, and afterward beaten for a very long time with scorpion whips, she finally completed her martyrdom by the cutting off of her head. Milk flowed from her body in place of blood. After her death angels came, took her body, carried it to Mount Sinai, and honorably buried it in that same place. From her tomb there flows oil which heals the bodies of the sick.” He then proceeds, in pure form, to Erasmus. Then: “On the same day, in Emilia, Saint Jucunda, virgin.” Peter has been moved to the following day.

GREVEN: “At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Catherine, glorious martyr and virgin of Christ, whose bones are found divinely to drip oil. After she was beheaded, she was carried away by angels and buried on the summit of Mount Sinai.” The pure text follows.

[Col. 0735D] THE UTRECHT and LEYDEN LATIN codices begin: “At Alexandria, blessed Catherine, virgin, who, after many contests and tortures endured for the love of Christ and the steadfast defense of the faith, was punished by capital sentence at the command of Maxentius. After her head had been cut off, her most sacred body was carried by the service of angels and honorably placed on Mount Sinai, where, shining forth in many miracles, it produces healing oil as a salutary and effective remedy for the sick.” The pure text follows this. ALBERG and DANIC have the same concerning Saint Catherine, but Peter is moved backward. Thus, in second place: “In Numidia, the feast of Saint Marculus the martyr, killed by being thrown over a precipice.” In the Roman Martyrology it is Marcellus, on the 26th. See Castellanus’s note here and also p. 723; likewise Tillemont, volume VI, p. 712. At the end these two codices have Erasmus in pure form.

CENTULEN: “At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Peter, bishop of that city, outstanding among the foremost, who was killed by the sword during the Decian persecution [an obvious error] and died; together with him many other bishops were slaughtered, as well as six hundred and sixty clerics and laymen. On the same day at Alexandria, Catherine, virgin, under Maxentius, son of Diocletian.” What he means is sufficiently clear.

BRUSSELS places Catherine first, almost as the UTRECHT codex does, etc. It expands Peter slightly, also has Marculus as the codices cited above do, and is pure in Erasmus. Then: “On the same day, Saint Benedict, priest and martyr.” There is no way to identify him unless what the LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition gives below is correct. It then proceeds with the Roman of Blavia, from the preceding day. At the bottom of the page an asterisk refers back here, written in almost the same hand: “On the same day, at the city of Rheims, Albert, a man of remarkable holiness, bishop of Liège, brother of Henry, the great duke of Lorraine and Brabant, was killed and died, by order of the emperor Henry, for defending the liberty of the Church.”

> Liège elected him; Rome advanced him;
>
> Rheims consecrated him, and, once consecrated, martyred him.

We have already treated him in the *Auctaria* for 21 November.

HAGENOYEN, whose text is in any event pure, adds a longer eulogy of Catherine, which, apart from what was given above, contributes nothing especially new, except the conversion of fifty philosophers, including Porphyry, etc., matters commonly known and not to be repeated here to the point of nausea. Finally: “In Numidia, the feast of Saint Marculus the martyr,” etc.

AQUICINCT. The copyist notes in two words that the text ends with Catherine.

VICTORIN: “On the same day, Saint Catherine, who was beheaded under Caesar Maxentius.”

CODEX URSINI OF ROSEMBERG: “In Numidia, the feast of blessed Martillus the martyr, killed by being thrown over a precipice.” We said above that the Roman Martyrology reads Marcellus. Other codices have Marculus. See what we said concerning the UTRECHT codex, etc.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT: “Catherine, virgin and martyr. Peter, bishop and martyr, with six hundred and sixty companions. Erasmus the martyr.”

SWEDISH REGISTRY, no. 130: “And the feast of blessed Mercury the martyr.” See the Roman Martyrology.

VATICAN, no. 5949, has this text: “At Benevento, the feast of blessed Mercury the martyr, who, in the time of Decius, after enduring many torments with courageous spirit, completed his martyrdom by beheading.”

FLORENTINE: “In Italy, at the city of Reggio, the translation of the body of Saint Prosper, bishop and confessor of that same city, from the church outside the walls, by a divinely granted revelation. Concerning him Thomas, who was then bishop of the same city, writing, says: ‘He was born in the regions of Spain, an outstanding teacher, Catholic in faith, angelic in appearance, distinguished in speech, holy in work, chaste in body, subtle in intelligence, provident in counsel, and abounding in charity; and he was ordained bishop in the said church by Pope Leo I.’” I have said elsewhere that his Life is celebrated on his feast day, 25 June. They continue: “Likewise, Saint Mercury the martyr, whose deeds are recorded.” Then the STROZZIAN alone: “On the same day, in Emilia, Saint Jucunda, virgin.”

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition begins with Catherine, as the UTRECHT codex does, etc., above. Peter is transferred to the following day, and Erasmus is omitted. It continues: “In Numidia, the feast of Saint Benedict, also called Marculus, the martyr, killed by being thrown over a precipice. On the same day, Saints Lucian, Marcian, and Claudian, martyrs.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

GREVEN: “In Africa, Lucian, Claudian, Marcian, Cyprian, and Quiriacus. In Numidia, Saint Benedict the martyr, also called Marculus, killed by being thrown over a precipice. At Metz, Saint Livarius the martyr. On the same day, the feast of Saints Julian, Cunctor, and Quiriacus.” See the LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition.

[Col. 0737A] MOLAN begins in Italic type, reporting the entire BELIN announcement concerning Catherine. A pure commemoration of Peter of Alexandria follows with the text, but a long history, likewise in Italic type, is appended to it, taken from Ado, in which Peter’s warning to Achillas and Alexander concerning Arius is chiefly described, etc. There is no room to insert it here, either because it is sufficiently well known or because it can be read in the source. At the end he adds, again from BELIN: “On the same day, in Emilia, Saint Jucunda, virgin.” Later editions have the same beginning and the same typography, and also append the same expansion, but the entire announcement of Peter of Alexandria has been postponed to the following day.]

[Col. 0733]

The feast of blessed Peter, bishop of Alexandria, who, adorned with every virtue and inferior to none of his predecessors in the divine Scriptures, both priest and victim of God, was suddenly seized and beheaded by order of Maximinus. Together with him many other bishops from Egypt were slaughtered, almost six hundred and sixty clerics and laymen. Likewise at Antioch, Saint Erasmus the martyr. [Bouillart, in the margin of the page: At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr.]

VI Kal. Day 26. [Note: [Col. 0737]]

From the Pratenian, Tornacian, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp, and Maximum-Lübeck codices, and from Munerat’s first edition, Greven, and Molan. [Col. 0737B] The Antwerp-Maximum, Louvain, and Leyden-Belgian codices are also included.

[Note: [Col. 0737B]]

Our codices suggest nothing especially worth observing except that Antwerp-Major, the second edition of Greven, which we follow, and Molan omitted the word *primus* after Peter, although it should be inserted on the authority of Ado and almost all our Usuardine codices. The remaining errors are scribal mistakes: *Augustidunum* in the Tornacian; *Viatico* for *Vaticano*, and *Maximo* for *Maximino*, in the Antwerp-Maximum. If Munerat’s first edition is entirely in agreement with the second, it is nevertheless never free from typographical defects. We shall say below in what respect the later edition surpasses it.]

[Note: [Col. 0737B]]

Under 23 September, near the end of the Observations, we indicated that Pope Linus is reported by our Florus and by Rabanus, and also in some of the fuller Usuardine codices; from these we believe the notice in the modern Roman Martyrology for that day was derived. From this you may understand what Usuard Baron could have cited in his note there—namely, Belin, in whom the Usuardine announcement taken from the present day has been moved back into September.

Whether Greven correctly divined that the passion is commemorated on 23 September in the *Auctaria*, while on this day the more solemn celebration is observed because Linus is said to have been translated, I would not dare assert amid such antiquity and such confusion of feast days, whatever inclination Henschenius may show in that direction, together with several arrangers of pontifical chronology. Linus is also reported on other days, such as 7 October, etc., but I entirely do not know the reason for this variation.

It is certain that the Little Roman Martyrology, which undoubtedly first placed him in the sacred calendars on this day, marked him in this way: “At Rome, Linus the pope.” It is also certain that Ado composed for him on this day a brief eulogy from the *Pontificals*, which Our Author transferred almost intact into his text, where Linus is most explicitly established in the succession of Roman pontiffs, after Peter, as the *first*, or second in order, vicar of Christ the Lord. I know that learned men have debated many matters on this account since Baron; but one should not depart from the opinion of that eminent Annalist. Consult him under the year 80 and in the present note.

The most learned chronologists have labored abundantly over distinguishing the years of the first pontiffs, and we shall have to labor further when Linus’s Acts are collected and elucidated. For the present, see Tillemont’s attempt, volume II, p. 546. Wandalbert also stands for assigning this day to Linus’s cult with this single verse of his:

> Sixth, Linus, pope, you sanctify with rosy blood.

On 19 November we seemed to wonder whether the Faustus reported there could not be confused with the present Dii, Ammonius, or indeed Peter of Alexandria’s companion in the passion, who, having been a deacon under Dionysius, may have been ordained priest by one of his successors and, worn out by old age, finally attained the crown of martyrdom. This, I say, we proposed there with hesitation.

It is clearer that Ado received our three martyrs from Rufinus, Book VIII, chapter 14, as equal to Peter in merit, office, and martyrdom. This entire announcement must therefore be attributed solely to Ado, who, having placed the bishop on the preceding day, thought that the ministers should be added on the following day; although perhaps those whom Rufinus calls innumerable suffered after a great interval of days—or even months, and why not years. Everything in our text was copied exactly, in every detail, from the aforementioned Viennese codex.]

The following is added at the end of all the Hieronymian copies in Florentinius: “At Autun, the burial of Saint Amator, bishop.” Rabanus took his announcement from this source. Did Ado do so as well? Mosander denies it, having added an asterisk; Rosweyd denies it, consigning the entire commemoration to an appendix. It follows from this that Usuard first received and entered it here from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. I seek the Life or deeds of this saint, but nowhere do I find anything; see the few remarks Baron made about him.

In the Little Roman Martyrology this is noted for the day: “And blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, who suffered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October; transferred by Pope Damasus on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, when he dedicated a feast to him.” We already gave these words above under 21 September, on which day Usuard received this Alexander from Ado and adorned him with a eulogy from the longer history of the present day. Whether Our Author rightly or wrongly transferred the saint according to his own judgment I do not discuss; it is enough to have indicated the change here once again in words.]

[Note: [Col. 0737D]]

HERINIEN has a very pure text, but in second place again inserts its own Rheims notice: “On the same day, the passing of blessed Basolus the confessor, who profitably led the eremitical life in the territory of Rheims and was divinely illumined with the radiance of miracles both in life and after death.”

ROSW EY D, also pure in the text, exceeds it at the end: “At Aquileia, Valerian, bishop and confessor.” Undoubtedly from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

[Col. 0738D] PULSANEN has this text: “The feast of Saint Peter, bishop of Alexandria, outstanding among the foremost. He spent twelve years in the episcopate of that city, three before the persecution and the remaining nine amid various kinds of trials. At Rome, the feast of Saint Linus the pope.”

ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK, and UGHELLIAN add to the pure text: “At the monastery of Vendopera, Saint Leonard the confessor.” This occurs in many codices, either alone or joined with Faustus. See Castellanus concerning him under 15 October.

MUNERAT, pure in the first edition, adds in the second: “On the same day, Saint Genevieve and Saint Marcellus, concerning the miracle of the Burning Ones, performed in the church of Blessed Mary at Paris.”

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN add to the text: “At the monastery of Vendopera, the feast of Saints Leonard and Faustus, confessors.” The UTRECHT codex nevertheless differs from the others in placing the Alexandrians first and Pope Linus last.

ALBERG and DANIC. We said yesterday that Peter of Alexandria had been transferred to this day in these codices. They treated Linus under 23 September. Here they are pure in the notices of the Alexandrians and Amator. In the expansion concerning Leonard and Faustus they agree with the preceding codices.

CENTULEN adds the length of Linus’s rule, namely twelve years, three months, and twelve days. It is pure in the Alexandrian notice. In place of Amator it has: “On the same day, Saint [Col. 0739B] Alexander, bishop and martyr of Alexandria, glorious in miracles.” See the Observations at the end.

BRUSSELS adds concerning Linus: “He established that a woman should enter the church with her head covered; he drove demons from the possessed, raised the dead, and performed many miracles. Finally, the consul Saturninus, after afflicting him with various punishments, beheaded him. On the same day, blessed Alexander, bishop, who received the palm of martyrdom under the emperor Antoninus. At Alexandria, the feast of the holy martyrs Agricola, Faustus the priest, Elius, and Ammonius. Together with blessed Peter, bishop of that city, they were beheaded by order of Maximianus. At Toulouse, at the monastery of Vendopera, the feast of Saints Faustus and Leonard, confessors. Likewise, Saint Genevieve, virgin.” Perhaps this indicates the miracle about which MUNERAT speaks above.

HAGENOYEN: “At Rome, the feast of blessed Linus, pope and martyr. He was, as some say, the first pope at Rome after blessed Peter, although blessed Peter did not give him as much authority as he gave Clement. At Saint Peter’s command he established that a woman should enter,” etc., almost as in BRUSSELS. In the Alexandrian notices it is almost pure, and at the end it is purer still. “At the monastery of Vendopera, the burial of the holy confessors Leonard and Faustus. At the city of Constance, the burial of Saint Conrad, bishop and confessor. From his earliest age he was devoted to God and a faithful companion of Saint Ulrich, bishop of the imperial city.” See GREVEN.

AQUICINCT and BORDEAUX: “At the monastery of Vendopera, the feast of Saint Leonard the confessor, and of Saint Flavian the confessor.”

DAVERON, BICOTIAN, sign. P. 5, and CISTERCIAN OF SAINT BENIGNUS: concerning Leonard as above.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-UTRECHT: “Linus, pope and martyr. Basolus, confessor and hermit. Faustus the priest, Dedii [Dii], and Ammonius, who suffered [the sufferers] with blessed Peter the bishop. Amator, bishop.”

[Col. 0739D] SWEDISH REGISTRY, no. 428: “On the same day, Saint Genevieve and Saint Marcellus, concerning the miracle of the Burning Ones in the church of Blessed Mary at Paris. At the monastery of Vendopera, Saint Leonard the confessor. In the territory of Rheims, the feast of Saint Basolus the confessor.”

VATICAN, no. 5949, omitting Linus and Amator, has: “The feast of Saint Nicander at Saint Sophia.” Then it gives the notice of Peter of Alexandria. Finally: “At Rome, blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, under Antoninus,” etc., with a eulogy that was undoubtedly taken from Ado’s Martyrology.

FLORENTINE: “The passing of Saint Gaudentius, monk, abbot, and confessor, from the regions of Spain, who, renowned for many virtues, rested in the Lord. He was buried in an abbey constructed in honor of his name in the territory of the diocese of Fiesole in Tuscany.” Up to this point they agree; I think what follows is found only in the STROZZIAN: “On the same day, at the city of Avion, in the regions of Novara, Saint Gaudentius, bishop of that same city. At Vendopera, etc. It has *Leonis* instead of *Leonardi*. Saint Alexander, bishop and martyr, etc. Likewise Saint Bellinus, martyr and bishop of Padua.” See the Roman Martyrology.

CAUDIAC: “Flavian, confessor.”

RHEIMS, SAINTS TIMOTHY AND APOLLINARIS: “In the territory of Rheims, the burial of Saint Basolus, priest and confessor.”

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition begins with Peter of Alexandria, inserting the vision of the torn garment. Linus has been treated elsewhere. Two other pure announcements follow. Then: “At the monastery of Vendopera, the feast of Saints Leonard and Faustus, confessors. At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Linus, pope and martyr. At Trier, Saint Sabaudus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Conrad, bishop of the church of Constance and confessor. In the territory of Rheims, the feast of Saint Basolus, bishop and confessor, renowned for many virtues. On the same day, Saint Mercury the martyr.”

BELIN gives Peter first place, but the text is not sufficiently pure. Then: “On the same day, Saint Bellinus, martyr, bishop of Padua.” Next comes the Alexandrian notice, also not sufficiently pure. The preceding notice is in the third position. Concerning Linus he almost repeats the announcement previously placed under 23 September.

GREVEN: “The feast of the bringing of the Blessed Virgin Mary into the Temple at Jerusalem, or of the purification of Saint Anne, namely on the eightieth day after her birth. At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Mercury, soldier and martyr. As the *Catalogue of the Saints* says, when he was influential under Decius, he refused to sacrifice; he was beaten with clubs, and, when a fire was placed beneath him, he was roasted, but the fire was extinguished by a copious outpouring of blood. Then, overcoming fire and blows once more, he completed his contest by the cutting off of his head. At Rome, the translation of Saints Alexander, bishop and martyr, and Herculanus, a young man. Likewise there, the feast of Saints Siricius and Saturninus. Sabaudus, bishop and confessor. Conrad, bishop of Constance and confessor, who, born of a noble family in Germany, was chosen bishop by blessed Ulrich of Augsburg and the clergy of the aforesaid church. He was so eminent in faith and religion that he is even said to have walked upon the waters. In the territory of Rheims, Saint Basolus, bishop and confessor. At Aquileia, Saint Valerian, bishop and confessor. Mercurialis, bishop of Liviensis and confessor. In the territory of Troyes, Saint Justus the confessor. Berengar, priest, concerning whom see the Life of Blessed Ida, widow.” Concerning Leonard and Faustus, as above. “Likewise, John Ruysbroeck, priest and confessor, of blessed memory, a man, as his writings attest, most enlightened and devout. Salome, virgin and widow, wife of the brother of Saint Elizabeth. The translation of blessed Ida, widow.”

MOLAN, concerning Peter of Alexandria, follows BELIN. Concerning the miracle of the Burning Ones, he follows MUNERAT; concerning Basolus, HERINIEN. “On the same day, blessed Alexander, bishop and martyr, under the emperor Antoninus, who, among other miracles, raised a dead man. At Nicomedia, blessed Marculus, priest and martyr, who in the time of the tyrant King Constans endured the greatest persecutions and finally was thrown from a high cliff.” See the second edition, p. 234, and what we said yesterday in the *Auctaria*. “At Rome, Siricius, bishop.” See Florentinius’s exercise. “Likewise Conrad, bishop of Constance. On the same day, Saint Bellinus, martyr and bishop of Padua.” Then, in smaller type: “A noble but avaricious man, Thomas Capivacius, having been justly convicted and sentenced by Bellinus to pay tithes on the fields which he possessed extensively under the diocese of Padua, brutally killed him in the year 1149. After he began to shine beyond measure through miracles after his death, he was honorably entered into the catalogue of martyrs by Eugenius IV two years after his death.” Oedipus cannot explain this unless Eugenius III is substituted for Eugenius IV. The other editions treat Peter of Alexandria first, adding much in Italic type concerning the torn tunic from Ado. Linus is not mentioned. The remaining text is pure. Then [Col. 0741A] Basolus, from the earlier edition; Conrad, Sebaudo [rather, Sebalao], and Siricius, as above. “On the twenty-sixth day, Saint Father Alipius of Cion.” Finally, concerning Leonard [Col. 0742A] as above; concerning Bellinus and the miracle of the Burning Ones, as in the first edition.]

[Col. 0737]

The feast of blessed Linus the pope, who, first after Peter, governed the Roman Church for twelve years, was crowned with martyrdom, and was buried in the Vatican. At Alexandria, the holy martyrs Faustus the priest, Dii, and Ammonius, who, together with blessed Peter, bishop of that city, were slaughtered by order of Maximinus. At Autun, Saint Amator, bishop.

V Kal. Day 27. [Note: [Col. 0741A]]

The text is taken from the Pratenian, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp, and Maximum-Lübeck codices, and from Munerat, Greven, and Molan. The Antwerp-Maximum, Louvain, and Leyden-Belgian codices are also included. [Col. 0742A]

[Note: [Col. 0741A]]

GREVEN and MOLAN begin: “At the city of Bologna.” MUNERAT has the worse reading “at the city of Vienne,” and afterward also improperly inserts *inde* at the end. That Usuardine phrase is noteworthy: “Finally, when he was compelled,” where nothing precedes to which that particle could signify a conclusion. Nevertheless, all the codices clearly prove that Usuard read it this way. Only Antwerp-Major has *antea fuit* instead of *fuit antea*. All the others read *isdem*; Greven and Molan seem to have wished to emend it to *idem*. Rosweyd shows excessive ingenuity by adding *et occiderunt* after *et exercuerunt in eum*. Only Molan reads *Regiensis*; the copyist’s ignorance in Rosweyd wrongly produced *Remensis*. Nor does he write *Cirinensis* correctly for *Lirinensis*; Antwerp-Major has the even more disgraceful *Sirutensis*. All the others simply have *Lirinensis*. Here again they twist the construction with Greven: “he was renowned in signs and miracles.” Rosweyd and Maximum-Lübeck have “he was renowned.”]

[Note: [Col. 0741B]]

The most holy bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church, Ambrose, among the many precious remains of holy martyrs which he himself diligently sought, excavated, and raised, recovered these men, our celebrated patrons of Bologna, glorious in the signs of their martyrdom, from among Jewish corpses; and, bringing them forth amid the great joy of the faithful, displayed them in a suitable place of veneration. Their relics, distributed from there throughout various parts of the Catholic world, wonderfully spread the glory of the saints.

Furthermore, Agricola and Vitalis found in Ambrose the very discoverer of their relics as their encomiast, as may be seen in Ruinart’s *Selecta*, p. 514 onward; his preliminary admonition is highly suitable for clarifying the history. Tillemont contributed a discussion in volume V, p. 314 onward; all of this will usefully serve in elucidating their Acts. Nor should we omit what Gregory of Tours recalls concerning the glory of Agricola and Vitalis, chapter 44, where he asserts that both were crucified, though not correctly according to Ambrose’s account.

Our principal task here is to examine the Martyrologies in which both are recorded—not on 4 November, as Baron, unless I am mistaken, noted them from Belin, but on this very day, with the Hieronymian Martyrologies pointing the way: “In Italy, at the city of Bologna, Agricola and Vitalis.” Florentinius correctly observes concerning this that a Gallic scribe in the Corbie copy, as it was also published by Acherius, incompetently transferred Bologna in Italy to Gaul; the praised commentator carefully notes other matters worthy of attention as well.

In Bede, Florus, and Rabanus these otherwise distinguished martyrs are not known. But in the Little Roman Martyrology, with greater regard for martyrdom than for rank, the servant is placed before the master, in accordance with the custom now received in our ecclesiastical Offices: “At Bologna, Vitalis and Agricola, martyrs.” Ado preserves the same order, intent more on describing their discovery than their passion, and, narrating with Gregory of Tours that both completed their martyrdom by crucifixion. Our Author composed his eulogy more successfully from Ambrose’s own words, changing the order of the names, which is also the order in Wandalbert’s verse, in which he praises the saints thus:

> Agricola and Vitalis honor the fifth day with martyrdom.

Maximus of Reggio is purely Adonian, praised by Ado in words which Usuard for the most part borrowed from him verbatim, leaving aside the final clause, which is restored below in some codices. Baron says that it happened through error that Reggio Emilia, which is in Cisalpine Gaul, was placed instead of Reggio in Narbonensian Gaul. The eminent man carefully notes many matters there, which will have to be examined more accurately in their proper place, especially whether this Maximus of Reggio can be identified with the one to whom a fourfold solemnity is assigned at Thérouanne; or whether, as is far more probable, he was another of that name who died at Vinay, a conclusion which Molan admits he is compelled to adopt by many arguments in the *Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium*, p. 270.

Maximus of Reggio also had an excellent panegyrist, the patrician Dynamus, mentioned more than once elsewhere; Surius seems to have been able to improve his style. Others have written about the deeds, virtues, and miracles of Maximus, among them the Gregory of Tours praised above, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 83. From all these sources Tillemont composed the sequence of his life, volume XVI, p. 392 onward.]

[Note: [Col. 0741C]]

TORNACIAN lacks the eulogy of Maximus of Reggio but is otherwise entirely pure.

PULSANEN offers this text: “The feast of the holy martyrs Martial, Vitalis, and Agricola, who at the city of Bologna in Italy, after various tortures, finally completed their martyrdom by crucifixion.”

[Col. 0741D] UTRECHT and LEYDEN-BELGIAN append to Maximus, from Ado, the clause given above: “Among his other magnificent deeds, while alive he raised three dead men, and one of them merely by touching the bier in which he was being carried to the tomb.”

ALBERG and DANIC treated Agricola and Vitalis under 4 November. Here the first is pure in Maximus; the other adds the words of Ado just cited. Both agree in the following: “At Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Marcellus, Peter, and Serena. At Milan, the feast of Saints John, Severus, and Euphemia.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

CENTULEN: “In Italy, at the city of Bologna, Saints Vitalis and Agricola, who, after other tortures, completed their martyrdom by crucifixion. Their bodies, while they lay buried among the Jews, were raised by blessed Ambrose upon their revelation and honorably reinterred. In the territory of Bologna [I think Bologna in Picardy is meant], the burial of Saint Maximus, bishop of the church of Reggio, most illustrious for holiness of life and the glory of miracles.”

[Col. 0743A] BRUSSELS differs little from the preceding in the eulogy of Agricola and Vitalis, but, like PULSANEN above, places the name Martial before theirs. It continues: “At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy martyrs Marcellus,” etc. Then the Milanese saints, also as above. “At Autun, the feast of Saint Amator, bishop and martyr.” See what we said yesterday. It follows: “Likewise, the burial of Saint Oda, daughter, as is said, of the king of the Scots. While living as a pilgrim at Rode in Texandria of Brabant, she founded the place, and now rests there bodily as its patroness.” See the Roman Martyrology. Maximus has been omitted here; he is placed on 24 November.

HAGENOYEN. He makes an egregious mistake at the beginning: “At the city of Honomus,” etc. For the rest, the text is nearly pure, including the entry for Maximus, to which only the closing clause from Ado is added. Then:

“At Persia, the passion of blessed James the soldier, surnamed Intercisus [the Dismembered]. He was born in the city of Elape of noble and Christian parents; he himself was a Christian, and had a Christian wife. He had been very intimate with the king of the Persians, and out of affection for him had converted to idolatry. His mother and wife recalled him from this with indignation, saying that henceforth they did not wish to live with him. He therefore repented and confessed himself a Christian, and for that reason was cut apart limb by limb with knives. First they cut off his fingers, secondly his toes, then his feet, afterward his arms; finally they cut the shins of both legs up to the thighs, and nothing remained of him except the trunk. At last one of the executioners, enraged, cut off his head, and thus they made him a martyr of Christ.”

CODEX Ursini a Rosemberg. Regarding the martyrs of Nicomedia and Milan, as in ALBERG., etc.

DAVERON.: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Esichius the confessor.” Castellanus reads *Eusitius*.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Agricola and Vitalis, martyrs. Maximus, bishop of Riez. Siffridus, bishop and confessor.” See Castellanus, who in the index calls him Sigifridus. “Papinius and Mansuetus, bishops and martyrs. Rufus the martyr with his companions.” These last two announcements belong to the following day.

ALTEMPS.: “In the territory of Bath, Saint Congarus the confessor.” Castellanus writes *Cungarus*, among the *Aemeri*, that is, those lacking a fixed day of cult.

FLORENTIN.: “In Spain, Saints Secundus and Primitivus, martyrs.” Then STROZZIANUS alone: “At Antioch, Saint Basil the bishop, and Saint Saturninus. At Paris, the burial of Saint Severinus, monk and solitary.” Concerning Severinus, see Castellanus on this day and Usuardus on 23 November. Concerning Basil, etc., see the Roman Martyrology.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition, in its first form, after the words “they inflicted every kind of torture upon him,” inserts: “so that there was no place on his body without a wound; but he prayed to the Lord, and in that prayer he departed to Christ.” These are almost Ambrose’s words, from which it is clear that Vitalis was not fastened to the cross. After “afflicting,” it adds a chronological note: “In the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian.”

In Maximus, the passage from Ado reads:

“In Gaul, in the city of Riez, Saint Maximus, bishop and confessor, who from his earliest age was endowed with the grace of every virtue. First he was father of the monastery of Lérins, then bishop of the church of Riez, and became renowned for signs and miracles; for among his other magnificent deeds, by touching a bier once, he raised three dead youths.”

It then proceeds with the martyrs of Nicomedia and Milan, as already several times above. Then:

“At Persia, the commemoration of Saint James the soldier and martyr, wonderfully dismembered. At Mainz, the burial of Saint Bilhildis, widow, who was abbess of many devout matrons. On the same day, Saints Acharius of Noyon and Optatus, bishops and confessors. In the district of Bourges, Saint Esichius the confessor. On that same day, Saints Secundus and Primitivus, confessors.”

See the other editions of MOLANUS, where Facundus, etc., occur.

BELIN. The announcement of Primitivus is placed on 4 November. Here he gives a good account of Maximus. Then:

“At the monastery of Vendopera, Saint Leonard the confessor.” See the supplements for the preceding day. “At Antioch, Saint Basil the bishop and Saint Saturninus. At Paris, the burial of Saint Severinus, monk and solitary. Also Saint James Intercisus, the distinguished martyr.”

GREVEN.: “In Persia, Saint James the martyr, surnamed Intercisus. Since he was well known to the king of the Persians and first among the nobles, he was mutilated limb by limb for the faith of Christ through cruel and prolonged torture, and at last struck with a sword, he completed his martyrdom. At Nicomedia, the feast of Saints Marcellus, Peter, Serenus, and Nemorius. In Galatia, Facundus and Primitivus, martyrs. Also, according to the Catalogue, Barlaam and Josaphat. At Milan, Saints John, Severus, and Euphemia, martyrs. Virgilius, bishop of Salzburg and confessor. Syfridus, bishop of Verden. Acharius and Optatus, bishops of Noyon and confessors. In the district of Bourges, Saint Esichius the confessor. In France, Menna the virgin. At Mainz, Saint Bilhildis, widow and abbess of many, etc. At the monastery of Wile, Saint Electa the virgin.”

MOLANUS: “At the monastery of Vendopera, Saint Leonard the confessor. At Antioch, Saint Basil the bishop and Saint Saturninus. At Paris, the burial,” etc. He also gives the passage about James Intercisus, word for word from BELIN. Then, in smaller type:

“In Galatia, Facundus and Primitivus. Also, according to the Catalogue, Barlaam and Josaphat, whose wonderful deeds John Damascene wrote. Syfridus, bishop of Verden.”

Concerning Esichius, as above.

“At Mainz, Saint Bilhildis, widow and abbess of many devout matrons. She founded the monastery of the Old Cell at Mainz for holy virgins; today it bears the name of the White Ladies. On the same day, among the Greeks, Saint Symeon Metaphrastes, whose Life Psellus composed in an encomiastic discourse.”

The other editions speak only of Maximus. Then they give Basil and James Intercisus as above. Next:

“In Galicia, near the river Ceta, the feast of Saints Facundus and Primitivus, martyrs, to whom, after they had endured many tortures, two crowns were brought by angels. When the prefect Atticus heard this, he said: ‘Let their heads be cut off, so that there may be no place for crowns.’”

Concerning Oda, as in BRUXELLEN.

“At Mainz, the feast of Saint Bilhildis, widow and religious woman. She was buried by the clergy and people of Mainz in the basilica which she herself had ordered to be built at her own expense. On the same day, Saint Acharius, bishop of Noyon and confessor. On the same day among the Greeks, Saint Symeon, who received the surname Metaphrastes.”

Among the Greek writers who collected the Lives of the saints, he is the most celebrated; he even earned among them the name of saint. The Greek collection of the Acts embellished by Metaphrastes himself has not yet appeared. Surius published many of them in Latin translation from Lipomanus, and these have long occupied the attention of critics. Much has been said here and there in our Acts about his style, reliability, and period; other matters have been treated by Allatius concerning the writings of the Symeons. If excessive credence is given to today’s hypercritics, his entire Metaphrase will shortly be discredited and consigned to moths and cockroaches. Our opinion is that the embellishments of Metaphrastes, inserted here and there into the Lives of the saints, even if somewhat liberally, ought no more to be regarded as fraudulent or defective in sacred history than the embellishments of profane historians in profane history.

[Col. 0741]

At the city of Bologna, the feast of Saints Agricola and Vitalis, martyrs; the latter had formerly been the former’s slave, but now is his companion and fellow in martyrdom. Finally, when the persecutors compelled him to deny Christ, and he continued more firmly to confess the Lord Jesus Christ, they inflicted every kind of torture upon him. At last they killed blessed Agricola, fastening him to a cross. In Gaul, in the city of Riez, Saint Maximus the confessor, who from his earliest age was endowed with the grace of every virtue; first he was father of the monastery of Lérins, then bishop of the church of Riez, and became renowned for signs and miracles.

## Fourth day before the Kalends — 28 November

[Note: The manuscripts Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. agree. Add Antuerp.-Max., Ultrajectin., Leyden, and Lovanien.]

[Note: It ought to be written *Sosthenes*, on the authority of the small Roman Martyrology and Ado, unless Rosweydus perhaps corrected both. Certainly no manuscript has it in this form—not even Molanus, who wrote *Sosthenes*; hence, from almost all the others, it must be judged that Usuardus wrote it as it stands in the text. Likewise, *Papinianus* is found correctly written in no manuscript; but this is not surprising, since both the small Roman Martyrology and Ado wrote *Papinii*, while some manuscripts incorrectly have *Papini*. Belinus alone reads “with plates of iron.” Antuerp.-Maj. and Max.-Lubec., Greven., and Molanus wrote “made him a martyr of Christ”; nevertheless, with Praten., Herinien., and others, we thought that *made him a martyr for Christ* should be retained, all the more because Ado had that reading earlier. Munerat. gives neither form but completely omits the word. Belinus changes the order: “Diocletian made him a martyr for Christ.” The remaining errors are *Corrinthum*, *Corrinthiis*, *aput*, *Affricam*, *Aphricam*, *Vandalicae*, *defensionem* for *pro defensione*, *Rufi*, etc.]

[Note: Neither in the Hieronymian Martyrologies nor in the sequence of Bede is any Sosthenes found. In the small Roman Martyrology and in Ado, by contrast, there are either two or the same person repeated twice: namely, on 11 June, after Barnabas, and on this day. The variety of the announcements seems clearly to indicate some difference. The small Roman Martyrology—which, as we have often said, was compiled by its author from apostolic men—has this on 11 June: “And Sosthenes at Corinth, a disciple of Paul”; here, however, with different identifying features: “Sosthenes, a disciple of the apostles.” Ado follows precisely the same wording in the first place: “On the same day at Corinth, Saint Sosthenes, disciple of Saint Paul the apostle”; in the second, that is, on this day: “The feast of Saint Sosthenes, a disciple of the apostles.”

Eusebius, in Valesius’s Book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 12, places a certain Sosthenes among the seventy-two disciples, although Rufinus, in chapter 14, gives another sense. In the modern Roman Martyrology, Sosthenes is taken to be the ruler of the synagogue who, in Acts 18, was severely beaten before Gallio the proconsul and, in a distinguished beginning, consecrated the first fruits of his faith. It is assumed, naturally, that this Sosthenes, still a Jew at that point, is the same as the one whom the Apostle himself joins to him as a companion when he begins the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes the brother.”

Castellanus, however, rightly observes that it is quite uncertain—at least from the cited Acts of the Apostles—whether and when that ruler of the synagogue was brought to the faith of Christ. Meanwhile, if I correctly understand the intention of the small Roman Martyrology and Ado, I think that they distinguish the Sosthenes of Eusebius, a disciple of the apostles, or one of the seventy-two, from Sosthenes the brother, who is named by Paul and with Paul in the Epistle to the Corinthians; thus they celebrate the latter on 11 June and the former on this day. Our Usuardus, however, clearly holds another opinion, undertaking here to commemorate one and the same disciple of the Apostle, mentioned in the aforesaid Epistle.

The truth concerning their identity or distinction will be discussed elsewhere, as will the episcopate of Colophon, which we shall not readily admit on the testimony of Dorotheus alone. Wandalbertus sang of Silas today; concerning him, we follow Usuardus on 13 July. This is the verse:

“Silas, Paul’s companion, you increase and adorn the fourth.”

The Vandalic persecution in Africa has had to be treated more than once above. The two bishops recorded on this day suffered rather during the first barbarian plundering than in an open and declared persecution. See Victor of Vita, who, near the very beginning of his history, speaks as follows:

“Who could explain how many priests, and how numerous they were, were then tortured by them? At that time Papinianus, the venerable bishop of our city, was burned over his entire body with plates of glowing iron; likewise Mansuetus of Uricitana was burned at the Fornarian Gate.”

The author of the small Roman Martyrology first formed the announcement from Victor: “In Africa, Papinius and Mansuetus, bishops”; so that I do not hesitate to assert that this African history was the particular source from which the aforesaid author took these saints. Ado, taking the kind of martyrdom almost entirely from the Victor just cited, joined several other bishops—not as true martyrs or companions of these martyrs, but as confessors of the faith, subsequently condemned to various exiles. We shall supply them in the supplements below; but in the names listed, the aforesaid Ado appears to err here and there. Some of them are recorded on their proper days, such as Valerianus on 15 December, etc. Usuardus closely followed his customary guide.

Rufus is listed in second place in the order of announcements by the small Roman Martyrology and Ado; the former has these words: “And Saint Rufus the martyr, won together with his whole household through Chrysogonus.” Ado expands the same in only slightly longer wording, adding these final words, copied by Usuardus: “Whom Diocletian, having punished him together with his whole household, made a martyr for Christ”; hence what we said in the Variants about this phrase is clear. The Acts of Rufus and Chrysogonus are of the same character; see what was said on 24 November.]

[Note: TORNACEN. would be entirely pure if it did not fail in the brief encomium of Sosthenes.

ROSWEYDUS, generally quite pure in the whole text, adds at the end: “Also Silas the apostle, who was a disciple of Saint Paul the apostle.” We have said that Usuardus placed him on 13 July.

PULSANEN., defective in Sosthenes, writes: “The feast of Saint Sosthenes, disciple of the apostles.” In second place it has: “On the same day, Saint Rufus the martyr, whom the Lord Jesus Christ, together with his entire household, through blessed Chrysogonus …” A line has been cut off. It then proceeds to the Africans, in whose encomium it is again defective, with the first part of the announcement also cut away.

ALBERG. and DANIC., also pure in the text, prefix this commemoration: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Gregory III, pope and confessor. He assembled a synod of nine hundred and three bishops in the city of Rome, in which they confirmed the veneration of the holy images and anathematized their violators by a general sentence.”

CENTULEN.: “The feast of Saint Sosthenes, disciple of the apostles. On the same day, Saint Rufus, whom the Lord Jesus, together with his entire household, won through Chrysogonus his confessor. Also on the same day, in Africa, Saints Papinius and Mansuetus, bishops and martyrs, with whom other bishops—that is, Quodvultdeus of Carthage, Valerianus, Urbanus, Crescens, Habendeus, Etheus, Tiatius, Crescentianus, Cresconius, Felix, Hortolanus, and Florentianus—completed the course of their lives with an equal confession.” Some names are corrupted and confused. See below under MOLANUS, or rather Ado himself.

BRUXELLEN., quite pure in the first part, adds: “And Saint Silas the apostle, who preached the Gospel of Christ to the Gentiles with blessed Paul.” It is also fairly good in the entry for Rufus. Then: “In Syria, the feast of Saints Tryphon, Theodulus, Eucherius, Lulius, and Eusebius, martyrs.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Concerning the Africans it inserts: “under the Arian king Geiseric.” Finally: “At Rome, the feast of blessed Gregory III, pope and confessor. He added to the secret of the Mass: ‘Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world.’ He also assembled nearly a thousand bishops in the city of Rome, in which, confirming the veneration of the sacred images, he [anathematized] their violators,” etc., as in ALBERGEN. above.

HAGENOYEN., whose text is deficient in purity only in having placed Rufus second and the Africans third, continues:

“At Rome, the feast of blessed Gregory III, pope and confessor. He assembled in the Roman city a synod of nine hundred and three bishops to refute the heresy of the emperor Leo, who burned the images of Christ and the saints and ordered others to do the same. Gregory himself anathematized Leo; and because he refused to correct himself, Gregory caused Rome, Italy, and Spain to withdraw from his authority and prohibited the payment of tribute to him. In that council the veneration of the sacred images was confirmed, and he anathematized their violators by a general sentence. He was besieged by the Lombards and liberated by Charles Martel; he died in peace.”

Several things are mixed together here and will be explained more accurately elsewhere.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., under number 130, celebrate another Gregory in this manner: “Also at Rome, Saint Gregory IV, pope, who ruled the Church for ten years.” The chronology agrees with Gregory III.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT., apart from the text, has this: “Silas the apostle. Gregory III, pope. He confirmed in a council of nearly a thousand bishops the veneration of the sacred images.”

FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, Gregory III, pope.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition has Gregory first, as in ALBERGEN. above. Then it gives Sosthenes, quite purely. In the Africans it adds the names of other bishops, but most are mutilated or altered; we shall give them more accurately below. It forms the third entry as follows:

“Also at Rome, Saint Rufus, a consular, whom the Lord Jesus Christ, through Chrysogonus the martyr, won together with his entire household, whom Diocletian the emperor, in his persecution, punished in person.” At Vienne, Saint Philip, bishop of that city and confessor. In the territory of Valence, at the monastery of Crispinus, the burial of Saint Landolinus the confessor, who was raised from the sacred font by blessed Autbert, bishop of Cambrai.”

I do not know why these saints are recorded on this day.

GREVEN.: “Silas the apostle, whom Usuardus records on the third day before the Ides of July. In Syria, the feast of Saints Trophimus, Theodulus, Eucherius, Julius, and Eusebius. Also in Africa, the holy bishops whose names are Quodvultdeus of Carthage, Valerianus, Urbanus, Crescens, Habetdeus, Eustachius, Crescentianus, Cresconius, Felix, Hortolanus, and Florentinus. All these, as Ado says, having been condemned to the harshest exile under the Vandalic persecution for confessing the truth, completed the course of their lives in the confession of piety. At Rome, blessed Gregory III, pope and confessor. At Vienne, Philip, bishop and confessor. Theodulus the confessor. Liberia, virgin and martyr. Oda, virgin, daughter of the king of Scotland.”

MOLANUS, in a passage printed in different type and also taken from Ado, inserts:

“At that time other holy bishops also—namely, Quodvultdeus of Carthage, Valerianus, Urbanus, Crescens, and he who is called Habetdeus, and Eustachius, Cresconius and Crescentianus, Felix, Hortolanus, and Florentinus—were condemned to exile and completed the course of their lives.”

See the Observations. At the end he adds:

“Gregory, the pope who ruled the Church for ten years; he was buried in the church of blessed Peter the apostle.”

Then, in smaller type:

“Oda, virgin, daughter of the king of Scotland, who rests bodily as patroness at Rhodum in Taxandria, Brabant. Also Saint Acharius, bishop of Noyon and confessor.”

The later editions have the same material about the African bishops in the text and at the end about Gregory. Then:

“On the twenty-eighth day, Saint Stephen the Younger, holy martyr;” and, in smaller type:

“Imprisoned at Saint Auxentius. They tied his foot with a rope and dragged him as far as the place called Pelagia from the praetorium. There, tearing him apart, they threw his honored relics into the place of the *biothanatoi* [those who died violently], because he had admonished many and led them to monastic life and persuaded them to despise royal dignities and wealth.”

We gave this encomium above, from the first edition of MOLANUS, on the twentieth of this month, on which day GREVEN also treats Stephen. But the later editions more correctly place him on this day. See the whole celebrated history of this Stephen, related at length by Surius.

[Col. 0743]

At Corinth, the feast of blessed Sosthenes, disciple of Saint Paul, whom the Apostle himself mentions when writing to the Corinthians. On the same day, in Africa, Saints Papinius and Mansuetus, bishops and martyrs, who, during the Vandalic persecution, were burned over their entire bodies with plates of glowing iron for the defense of the Catholic faith and completed their glorious contest. At Rome, Saint Rufus, whom Diocletian, after punishing him together with his entire household, made a martyr for Christ.

## Third day before the Kalends — 29 November

[Note: The manuscripts Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. are pure. Albergen. and Danic. are also added.]

[Note: In the other edition of Greven, which we follow, *Romae* has inadvertently been omitted before *via Salaria*. This is a small matter; but the manner of announcing the entry in both editions almost caused them to be excluded from the pure texts, since those editions follow Ado’s rather than Usuardus’s wording: “The feast of Saint Saturninus the martyr, Senes and Sisinnius the deacons.” The matter is discussed more fully below in the Observations. Molanus is not entirely correct either: he reads “Saturninus the martyr” and “Saint Sisinnius.” Belinus, apart from other disorderly, erroneous, and badly punctuated features, omits *ad latera* after “he ordered flames for them,” as do Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. Molanus alone, for *capite truncari*, writes *capite detruncari*. The remaining errors are almost entirely typographical, such as *Dyaconi*, *Sisinii*, *Maximo eculeo excusoque*, *exalavit*, etc.]

[Note: The antiquity of the small Roman Martyrology is clearly demonstrated, among other things, by the small number of vigils marked in that manuscript; Florentinius sometimes uses the same argument to establish the antiquity of his manuscripts. Thus neither in the Hieronymian Martyrologies nor in the aforesaid small Roman Martyrology is the vigil of Andrew the apostle, which is marked in the text, found. It is present in Bede, if the words of the announcement of Saturninus appended to it truly belong to Bede; they are absent from Rabanus. It is also present in the calendars of Allatius and Fronto, even in second place; but Ado assigns it first place, and from him it passed into our text.

The commemoration of Saturninus, the celebrated Roman martyr, has also become confused and expanded in the Hieronymian manuscripts, which write: “At Rome, Arason, Saturninus, Chrysanthus and Daria, Maurus and seventy-two others,” or, as the very ancient Echternach manuscript has it, “and sixty others.” But that manuscript begins more clearly: “At Rome, Saturninus,” etc. It is most probable that Florentinius is correct in carefully observing that the beginning of the commemoration must be corrected and emended from a fragment of the very ancient Bucherian Calendar, where it reads—not 30 December, as Tillemont wishes, but the third day before the Kalends of December—“Saturninus at the cemetery of Thrason”; that is, instead of “At Rome, Arason,” we should restore “At Rome, at the cemetery of Thrason.” You will find more about the cemetery of Thrason there.

In Ado, moreover, from the Acts of Saint Marcellus the pope, we learn that Thrason, together with John the presbyter, collected the bodies of our martyrs and buried them on his estate on the Salarian Way. Florentinius also notes other matters there concerning Chrysanthus and Daria, whose celebration on various days is shown by the ancient Martyrologies themselves, as will become clear on 1 December.

To return to Saturninus: the aforesaid calendars of Allatius and Fronto commemorate him alone and without companions. Bede, together with his sources, adds Senes and Sisinnius. Rabanus wrote the former *Serius*; the editor Canisius thought it should be formed as *senex*, so that it would mean “Saturninus the old man”—in my opinion most correctly and truly—although, according to the encomia of Bede and Ado, *Senes* is altogether the proper name of a martyr, whom you will nevertheless seek in vain in the Acts of Saint Marcellus. The small Roman Martyrology likewise read: “At Rome, Saturninus the martyr, and Senes and Sisinnius the deacons.”

Our Usuardus, deliberately and doubtless after consulting his source, noticed that the word *Senes* should be removed, retaining only Saturninus and Sisinnius, whose deeds are narrated in the aforesaid Acts of Saint Marcellus, together with the passions of Papias, Maurus, Cyriacus, Largus, Smaragdus, and others—matters examined elsewhere and to be considered more carefully later.

Wandalbertus joins Maurus, not Sisinnius, to Saturninus. Whether he means the one celebrated with Papias on 29 January, or another about whom Florentinius gives a fuller account, I have so far been unable to determine. He sings:

“Saturninus, we dedicate the third to you and to Maurus.”
