Castellanus, in the note appended to his universal Martyrology, thinks that our Saturninus is another person, the apostle of Toulouse, appended by the copyists of the Hieronymian manuscripts to Saturninus of Rome in the sacred tables because they had not found the true day of his martyrdom in the Acts. Let the conjecture stand insofar as the day of death is concerned; but, excepting the Corbie manuscript, the others mark Saturninus in such a way that they seem to proclaim either a bishop of Nantes or some Spanish bishop.

This is the more explicit commemoration of the Corbie manuscript, even as edited by Achery: “In Gaul, in the city of Toulouse, the feast of Saturninus, bishop and martyr.” The Viennese Martyrologist embellished the saint at greater length, in wording entirely different from that which our predecessors attribute to Florus, although it is sufficiently clear that both encomia arose from the same Acts. Ruinart included the Acts themselves, truly excellent, among the *Sincera et Selecta*, beginning at page 109. I refer readers to his learned admonition, lest I repeat here what has been carefully observed there, as well as in Tillemont, volume III, beginning at page 297. The aforesaid Acts may also be consulted in Surius on this day, together with what Gregory of Tours discussed in praise of Saturninus in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 48.]

[Note: TORNACEN. lacks the encomium of Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse; in the rest it is entirely pure.

ROSWEYDUS again mixes in some material from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. In the first place he is pure, but he announces the second as follows: “At Rome, the feast of Saints Chrysanthus the martyr and Daria the virgin, who, after enduring many sufferings which they had gained for Christ, were ordered by the emperor Numerian to be placed in a sandpit on the Salarian Way and buried alive under earth and stones.” This is Usuardus’s encomium for 1 December. It continues from the aforesaid manuscripts: “Also blessed Maurus and seventy-two others.” Then it gives Saturninus of Toulouse, fairly correctly. Next: “The feast of Saint Radbodus, bishop of Utrecht.” Finally, in large letters at the end: “The vigil of Saint Andrew.”

PULSANEN. correctly has the vigil. It continues: “On the same day at Toulouse, Saint Saturninus the bishop. Also on the same day, Saint Saturninus the martyr, Senes, and Sisinnius the deacons, under the emperor Maximian.”

ANTUERP. MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN, and LOVANIEN. all add: “On the same day, Saint Radbodus, bishop and confessor.”

CENTULEN.: “The vigil of Saint Andrew the apostle. At Rome, Saints Saturninus, Senes, and Sisinnius the deacons, under the emperor Maximian. At Toulouse, Saint Saturninus, bishop and martyr, under Caesar Decius. Also at Rome, Saints Chrysanthus and Daria the virgin, in the time of Numerian.”

BRUXELLEN., pure in the vigil, adds:

“At Rome, the feast of Saints Chrysanthus, Maurus, and Daria the virgin, martyrs. Since they could not be harmed by any kind of torture, by order of the emperor Numerian they were finally beheaded for Christ and buried under earth and stones. At Rome on the Salarian Way, the feast of Saint Saturninus, bishop and martyr, and Senes and Sisinnius the deacons. They were condemned by the emperor Maximian to dig sand for the construction of the Baths of Diocletian, and afterward, having been long tormented in prison, … Their bodies, when John the presbyter had collected them, were buried by Thrason, a most Christian man, on his estate along the Salarian Way. While these events were taking place amid the struggle, two soldiers, Papias and Maurus, believed in Christ; they were soon arrested, as the Acts of Marcellus the pope relate.”

It interpolates the account of Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse, slightly as follows:

“At Toulouse, the feast of Saint Saturninus the bishop. In the time of Decius, he was seized by the pagans in the Capitol of that city and thrown from the highest summit of the Capitol down all the steps. With his skull shattered, his brains dashed out, and his whole body torn apart, he breathed forth a soul worthy of Christ.”

At the end it adds: “On the same day, the burial of Bernard, who was the first of the Latins to be bishop of the church of Nazareth.”

HAGENOYEN., pure in the first place, treats Saturninus of Toulouse second, composing the following from the Acts in his own manner and style:

“At Toulouse, the feast of Saint Saturninus, bishop and martyr, who was ordained bishop by the disciples of the apostles and sent there. As he entered the city, the demons ceased giving responses through the idols. Then one of the priests said that unless Saturninus were killed, they would obtain nothing at all from the gods. They seized Saturninus, who refused to sacrifice, tied him by the feet to a bull, and, driving it with goads, threw him from the highest summit down the steps of the Capitol. Thus, with his head broken, his brains dashed out, and his whole body weakened, he completed his martyrdom.”

Then:

“On the same day, at Rome on the Salarian Way, the feast of Saints Saturninus the soldier and Sisinnius the deacon, whom the prefect, under the emperor Maximian, after tormenting them for a long time in prison and chains, ordered to be raised onto the torture horse, stretched with cords, and beaten with clubs and scorpions.”

Finally:

“At Milan, the feast of Saints John, Severus, and Euphemia, martyrs.”

See the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 27 November.

AQUICINCT. writes *Appian* instead of *Salarian*. At the end, however, it has:

“At Rome, Saint Gregory the pope. He established that the following be said by the priest in the Canon: ‘Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty.’ Also: ‘Among whose company admit us, we ask, not as one who weighs merit, but as the giver of forgiveness.’”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Saturninus the martyr. Radbodus, bishop of Utrecht, whose body rests at Deventer in the church of Saint Lebuinus.”

VATICAN, under number 5949: “On the same day, Saint Maurus the martyr.” See Florentinius.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition, pure enough in its first and second forms, is interpolated in its last form after “bishop” as follows:

“Who, in the time of the emperor Decius, was seized by the pagans in the Capitol of that city because, in his presence, all their gods had become mute and could give no response to those who sacrificed according to custom. A bull prepared for sacrifice was tied with ropes, and, when it was goaded more violently, from the highest part of the Capitol …”

At the end it adds: “At Deventer, the feast of Saint Radbodus, bishop of Lower Utrecht and confessor.”

GREVEN.: “Maurus the martyr. According to some, here are Chrysanthus and Daria, who are recorded below on the Kalends. At Ravenna, Saint Sisinnius the bishop. On the same day at Deventer, Saint Radbodus, bishop of Lower Utrecht and confessor. Around the year of the Lord 90 [read 900], he was appointed over that church. Administering the priesthood for seventeen years with distinguished virtue, he strove so to attain the summit of abstinence that even his closest associates could scarcely perceive it. On the same day, according to the Catalogue, Paphnutius the abbot. Also Saints Mark and Mary.”

MOLANUS adds at the end: “Also Saint Radbodus, bishop and confessor of Utrecht, at Deventer.” Then, in smaller type:

“Also the death of the venerable Ida of Nivelles, a nun of the monastery of Rameya, of the Cistercian order, in the Namur region.”

Other editions, in italics, insert into the text after “beheaded”: “It is written in the Acts of Marcellus the pope.” At the end: “Also at Deventer, Saint Radbodus, etc. On the twenty-ninth day, Saints Paramon and Philumenus, martyrs, and Saint Acacius, who was in the military rank.” The same material concerning Ida appears here as in the earlier edition, and in the same type.

[Col. 0747]

The vigil of Saint Andrew the apostle. At Rome, on the Salarian Way, the feast of Saint Saturninus the martyr and Sisinnius the deacon, under the emperor Maximian. After tormenting them for a long time in prison, the prefect of the city ordered them to be raised onto the torture horse, stretched with cords, and beaten with clubs and scorpions. Then he ordered flames to be placed at their sides, and, after they had been taken down from the torture horse, to cut off their heads. On the same day, at Toulouse, blessed Saturninus the bishop, who was seized by the pagans in the Capitol of that city and thrown from the highest summit of the Capitol down all the steps. With his skull shattered, his brains dashed out, and his whole body torn apart, he breathed forth a soul worthy of Christ.

## Day before the Kalends — 30 November

[Note: The manuscripts Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. are pure. Eleven others would also belong here if they did not add at the end the passion of Saint Justina.]

[Note: These matters concern minor details. I wrote *Scythia* with the greater number of manuscripts, although here Greven himself correctly has *Scythiam*. Likewise, all have *Aegea* except Pratensis, which has evidently been corrected, and Molanus. In Munerat. there is *ibi* instead of *inibi*; and in Antuerp.-Maj., *manifestabat* instead of *manifestat*.]

[Note: [Col. 0751C]

Andrew is customarily called by the Greeks *Protocletus*, or “first-called,” as Papebrochius reports in the *Greek-Muscovite Menologion* before volume I of May, p. LXII. Nothing prevents us from using the same sense when we call him the Proto-Apostle, that is, the first apostle chosen, and one endowed with public and more distinguished worship throughout the universal Church from among the earliest apostles—as could be demonstrated at greater length, if all the ancient ecclesiastical tables, calendars, sacramentaries, and martyrologies were not sufficient.

No one will find it strange that Andrew’s name does not occur in the Bucherian Calendar who remembers that this calendar was so specifically Roman that it contains only two foreign notices, namely those of Perpetua and Felicity, and of Cyprian. But the Calendar of Carthage displays the antiquity and breadth of his cult, in which it explicitly places, “[lacuna] before the Kalends of December, Saint Andrew the apostle and martyr,” although scarcely three other apostles are found in the whole of that calendar.

I pass over other evidence so that I may remain with the Martyrologies. Among them, the Hieronymian Martyrologies celebrate no apostle with so many repeated feasts [Col. 0751D]. Whether this is true everywhere is disputed, and I do not think it can be admitted that some copies place Andrew on 10 February, since it appears that the apostle Andrew has slipped in there in place of another Andrew and Aporius or Apponius, martyrs under Herod in Bethlehem of Judea. Henschenius observed this on that day, and after many turns Florentinius eventually subscribed more or less to his opinion. The curious reader should consult Florentinius’s notes and discussions on the *Index of the Apostles*, beginning at p. 116.

Moreover, in the aforesaid copies there is, on 5 February, “the ordination of the episcopate of Andrew the apostle.” Again, on 9 May, there is at Milan some commemoration in the basilica at the Roman Gate. On that day we treated at greater length with Usuard concerning the translation of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy to Constantinople. But another translation is indicated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies [Col. 0752C] on 3 September. Add the dedication of the basilica of Saint Andrew on 3 November; and finally, on this day:

“In Achaia, or in the province of Achaia, in the city of Patras, the feast of Saint Andrew the apostle.”

From these notices you will readily see that the recently asserted prominence of the cult of Saint Andrew is amply demonstrated.

The notice in the *Little Roman Martyrology* is extremely simple: “Andrew the apostle.” Bede likewise has only the words doubled: “The feast of Saint Andrew the apostle.” The fuller notices found in Florus and Rabanus, together with the eulogy of Ado included among the Feasts of the Apostles, cannot be compared with these. The latter took his account from the famous Acts which, under the name of the presbyters and deacons of Achaia, have been circulated by almost the entire Christian age; but our author transferred his text here from Ado.

Florentinius, in the cited place, observes that Baronius hesitated concerning those Acts through fear of apocrypha. Nor could the exceptionally acute father of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* reasonably doubt that they had been stuffed, corrupted, or interpolated by Manichaeans and other heretics—or at least that this had happened to them in the form in which they once existed—and that they were rejected by Eusebius and others [Col. 0752D]. Whether, however, in Florentinius’s view, the Acts found in the Passionals, both manuscript and printed, are the same Acts purged of errors, or whether they are different, must be examined elsewhere at greater length.

For my part, I do not think that a narrative strengthened by the testimony of so many Fathers should be rejected on account of certain falsifications and corruptions by those impious hands from which even the sacred Scriptures did not remain untouched, as our Bartholomaeus Germon most learnedly demonstrated not long ago in a work published on this subject. He should certainly be consulted from p. 221 onward, throughout chapter 2. Drawing on Philastrius of Brescia, a writer of the fourth century, he shows that some original and genuine Acts of Andrew were disfigured and polluted by the foulest additions of heretics [Col. 0753A].

Here I extract a few points from the sound conclusions of this most learned man, who was also my close friend:

“I would believe,” he says, “that the letter was given the title ‘of the presbyters and deacons of Achaia’ because most of what it contains was taken from older Acts of Saint Andrew. Those Acts were in fact originally written by the disciples of that apostle, but were later miserably disfigured and corrupted by heretics. Then, through the study and care of some Catholic writer, around the end of the seventh century or the beginning of the eighth, they were purged of the errors and fables with which the treachery of the heretics had filled them.”

He supports his conjecture with several arguments, especially with the excellent testimony of the aforementioned Philastrius, from which it can be understood that, in a book written by Andrew’s disciples about his deeds, the heretics “ADDED AND TOOK FROM IT WHATEVER THEY WISHED.” The reader may consult the remaining arguments drawn out with great skill by Germon.

Nevertheless, I cannot deny that Tillemont’s arguments in volume I, beginning at p. 589, are such as to inspire fear even in reluctant readers concerning the complete reliability of the account of the presbyters of Achaia, even after its purification [Col. 0753B]. The writer mentioned above has constructed a sufficiently clear sequence of Andrew’s life from indisputable documents; see the cited volume from p. 317 onward. Motherius’s observations on this day and at p. 442 may also be consulted.

Furthermore, from the large volume on Andrew’s glory by de Saussay, and from other records, all the doubts that arise concerning the time, place, manner of his martyrdom, and many other matters, will in due course be resolved in our Acts.

Finally, here we give place to Wandalbert’s elegant metrical encomium:

> Andrew, the apostle, shines forth on the preceding day,  
> Radiant throughout the world with the broad rays  
> And honors of his virtues, who subdued the untamed Achaeans  
> By word and signs.  
> These vows of the peoples close the wintry November.

The second person mentioned is Trojanus, bishop of Saintes, whom Ado took from Gregory of Tours’s *Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 59, and first entered into the sacred Fasti, using almost Gregory’s exact words; these also compose our text. If anything else worthy of mention concerning Trojanus is found, it will be explained by us in its proper place [Col. 0754B].

[Note: [Col. 0753B]

TORNACENSIS, under Andrew, is complete; it lacks only the eulogy of Trojanus.

ROSWEYD begins with large illuminated capital letters and is quite complete in the first notice; he carries the second only as far as “of the holiness of the man.”

PULSANENSIS has, in the first notice, text through “preached”; in the second he is entirely complete.

ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK, UGHELLIAN, BELIN, and ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, together with six other middling manuscripts, add to the complete text: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Justina the virgin”; or, “On the same day, Saint Justina,” and so forth. All write *Throphianus* for *Trojanus*; but the second edition of BELIN, more accurately, has *Trojanus*.

CENTULENSIS: “In Achaia, in the city of Patras, the passion of Saint Andrew the apostle under the proconsul Aegeas, who also preached in Scythia. At Saintes, Saint Trojanus the bishop, a man of great virtue.”

BRUSSELLENSIS, beginning with Andrew and preserving the text, inserts [Col. 0753C]: “the brother of blessed Peter. He also preached in Scythia, and afterward, having been captured in Achaia by the proconsul Aegeas, was shut up in prison, severely beaten, and finally hung upon a cross, on which he survived for two days. His sacred bones were translated to Constantinople in the twentieth year of the emperor Constantius.” See 9 May. In the second notice he is complete. Then: “At Aquileia, the burial of Saint Valerianus, bishop and confessor. On the same day, the passion of Saint Justina the virgin.” Valerianus recurs in the Appendices on 26 November, while in the Roman Martyrology he is placed on 27 November.

HAGENOYEN assembled a longer account of Andrew in his own fashion, the first part of which is taken from the Gospel. The reader may decide what should be thought of the second part, and indeed of the first. Here is the account:

“In the city of Patras, the passion of Saint Andrew the apostle. He was the son of John, from the village of Bethsaida, and the brother of Peter the apostle. He was also the first disciple of John the Baptist; at John’s voice he left John himself and adhered to Christ, and he was the first and second apostle [Col. 0753D] of Jesus Christ. He brought his brother Peter to Jesus and converted him. While the Lord was alive, he preached, baptized, and performed miracles with the other apostles; he added an article to the Creed. After the Lord’s passion he received Scythia as his allotted field of preaching. In Myrmidonia he restored sight to the apostle Matthew, who had been deprived of his eyes, and made him depart. When he was being punished there, he converted them by praying, built churches, ordained bishops, as in Scythia, raised forty-one dead persons, shattered idols, and expelled demons.

“At last he entered the city of Patras and converted many there, together with Maximilla, the wife of Aegeas. There he was seized by the proconsul Aegeas, shut in prison, beaten most severely, and bound with ropes to a cross so that he might live longer and be tortured more extensively. He lived on the cross for two days, taught the people, and breathed his last in a great light. Aegeas, however, died miserably, and the whole people was converted to God.”

This is a very long narrative. In the second notice he is complete. Then he adds: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Ida the virgin and martyr.” We know *Idae* as virgins and widows, whether saints or venerable women. Finally follows: “At Nicomedia, the feast of the holy martyrs Marcellus, Peter, and Serena.” See the Appendices under 27 November.

MATRIC.-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT: “Andrew the apostle. Trojanus the bishop and confessor.”

In the VATICAN manuscript no. 5949 is added: “At Milan, Saint Amator the bishop.” Is this Ambrose’s reception of baptism, as it is found on this day in the Hieronymian Martyrologies?

FLORENTINE: “Saint Justina the virgin.”

[Col. 0754C] LÜBECK-COLOGNE EDITION: After “apostle” follows “the brother” [*germanus* for *germani*] “of Peter the apostle. He was first a disciple of Saint John the Baptist, but after the death of Saint John he was called by Christ Jesus to be an apostle. He also preached Christ in Scythia after the Lord’s ascension. This most blessed man, captured by the proconsul Aegeas, at first in prison … His most sacred body was reverently taken down from the gallows and buried by Maximilla, the most powerful of women.” In the notice of Trojanus it is complete. Then: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Justina the virgin and martyr.”

GREVENSIS: “At Rome, the feast of the holy Castulus, Maurilus, Centulus, and Theodulus. On the same day, the feast of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan.” See the Hieronymian copies concerning these. “Tugdualus, bishop and confessor.” In Castellanus there is *Pabutugdualus*, formed as though from a double name, by which he is called in French, Pabut and Tugal. “At Ravenna, blessed Peter, bishop and confessor.” See below, under 2 December [Col. 0754D]. There is no doubt that the famous Peter surnamed Chrysologus is intended here. “Justina the virgin and martyr.”

MOLAN, together with BELIN and the others mentioned above: “On the same day, the passion of Saint Justina the virgin.” See Castellanus’s brief note on her. In other editions there is only the addition: “And the baptism of Saint Ambrose.” The source of this last notice can be understood from MOLAN’s letter to the reader, §§ 11 and 12. Otherwise, I have nowhere found anything about Ambrose’s baptism in the other Usuardine manuscripts. See above what we said in the VATICAN manuscript from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, namely: “Ambrose’s reception of baptism.”]

[Col. 0751]

In the city of Patras, in the province of Achaia, the feast of Saint Andrew the apostle, who also preached in Scythia. This most blessed man was seized by the proconsul Aegeas, first shut up in prison, then beaten with extreme severity, and finally hung upon a cross, on which he survived for two days. At Saintes, Saint Trojanus the bishop, a man of great holiness, who, buried in the earth, shows through many virtues that he lives in heaven.

## The month of December has thirty-one days.

[Col. 0755]

### On the Kalends. Day 1.

[Note: The manuscripts PRATENSIS, HERINIENSIS, MUNERATIAN, GREVENSIS, and MOLAN are complete and pure.]

[Note: I am compelled to write *Crisantus* on the reading of all the manuscripts except PRATENSIS, which has *Chrisantus*, and MOLAN, which alone, more correctly, has *Chrysanthus*. MUNERATIAN has *arenaria*. GREVEN and MOLAN read somewhat harshly *ac illic* for *atque illic*. GREVEN alone has *Diodolus* and *celebraverunt*. In “to Mainz,” the manuscripts vary; the larger number supports the text. In GREVEN, “in the city of Novio,” I think is a printer’s error. All the manuscripts cited for the text, and all the more reliable ones, consistently write *Nathaliae* and *Proculi presbyteri*.]

[Note: We said under 29 November that Chrysanthus and Daria were commemorated on more than one day in ancient Martyrologies. In the Hieronymian copies they are found neither under 25 October nor on this day; but on 12 August they have: “At Rome, the feast of the holy Chrysanthus and Daria, and of those who suffered with them, Claudius, Hilaria, Jason, Maurus, and seventy soldiers.” Our pair is entered again on 29 November, where we supplied the text in the Observations; but on neither day is Diodorus or Marianus counted among their companions.

Moreover, on 29 November the Sacramentary of Thomasius adopted them in almost the very words of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, together with Saturninus, Maurus, and others, and the commonly circulated Florus followed it. What Wandalbertus intends on 13 October I do not sufficiently understand.

The calendars of Allatius and Fronto commemorate only Chrysanthus and Daria on 25 October, a day which the modern Roman Martyrology stably consecrated to their solemn feast—not from Rabanus, whom Baronius did not know, but, unless I am mistaken, from Belin and other fuller Usuardine manuscripts. It is certain, however, that Usuard himself is wrongly cited for that day, since here he did not depart by so much as a finger’s breadth from his usual guides.

The *Little Roman Martyrology* speaks in this way on this day: “At Rome, Chrysanthus and Daria, martyrs, and Diodorus and Marianus, with an infinite multitude of martyrs.” Ado follows, also writing *Marianus*, and elegantly condensing the longer history of the entire martyrdom. From him our author formed the first two notices of his little list, which others have not correctly separated, although I admit that it is not entirely certain on what day all, or some of those mentioned in the Acts of Chrysanthus, suffered.

Indeed, the Acts themselves, as they were published by Lipomanus and Surius from Metaphrastes, do not deserve much confidence. Baronius testifies to this under the year 284, no. 7, where he declares them corrupt and says that learned investigators have brought them under suspicion of imposture. Tillemont investigated them not long ago, volume IV, [Col. 0755C] p. 762, and found much that confirms the judgment of the eminent annalist. Whether we shall find shorter and more reliable Latin copies, of which Baronius mentions there, I do not yet know.

Nevertheless, the truly certain records reported here, in addition to what Gregory of Tours has in *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 38, do not permit us to doubt altogether either the genuine martyrdom or the ancient cult of these saints throughout the Church. On the translations of the saints, see Mabillon, century IV of the Benedictines, part I, p. 611, and Surius, 17 January.

We discussed Albanus of Mainz at greater length in the Appendices under 21 June, on which day he is recorded by Rabanus and Notker. Usuardus appears to have been the first, and the only one, to assign him to this day, perhaps because he had learned that he was then solemnly commemorated at Mainz. But on this point greater trust must be placed in Rabanus, bishop of the Church of Mainz, who expressly recorded not Albanus’s feast on this day, but the dedication of his basilica. Hence I do not see what purpose is served by Castellanus’s note under 21 June, as though 1 December ought to be considered the day of his passion. Let this suffice here; you will find the remaining matters concerning Albanus laboriously explained in the Acts.

As Eligius of Noyon is rightly counted among the apostles of the Flemish and Brabant peoples, so throughout our whole homeland he has customarily been celebrated with singular and perpetual veneration. Ado certainly entered him into the sacred Fasti, perhaps from some fuller Hieronymian manuscript, which Florentinius considers an addition, since he is absent from the older Epternacensis. Our author copied him from Ado, with the wording somewhat modified. The fuller account given by Florus is not relevant here.

The famous saint’s Life, composed by Audoenus of Rouen, is well known; scholars have not yet agreed whether an authentic copy of it exists anywhere. Surius did not reproduce his copy faithfully; the text published by Acherius in volume V of the *Spicilegium* is fuller. What should be thought of our manuscript, compared with several copies, will be discussed more carefully in its proper place.

Wandalbertus sang only of Eligius at the beginning of the month, today:

> Eligius, O Noyon, under the light of December  
> Marks its beginning for you with worthy episcopal honor.

Natalia, the wife of the martyr Adrianus, is explicitly placed by the *Little Roman Martyrology* on 8 September: “And Natalia.” On that same day, at the end of the narrative, Ado asserts that she sailed to Byzantium and, a few days after her arrival, received her dormition; but that she was buried on the Kalends of December. It is quite clear that Usuard took the occasion from this to place Natalia on this day. For the rest, what we said about her husband’s Acts on 8 September may be consulted.

A greater difficulty is presented by Proculus of Narnia, known to no other ancient Martyrologist. There are many Proculi, for more than thirteen recur in the Hieronymian manuscripts, though only two days are found on which some Proculus is assigned to Interamna: 14 and 18 April. I am certain that the same man is recorded twice there. Whether he recurs again on 1 May is not equally clear; but, unless I am greatly mistaken, the same person is concerned, just as in Ado on 14 February, taken from 14 April. On the latter day we treated Proculus with Usuard, venturing to conjecture nothing beyond Henschenius, and we likewise dare not do so now.

Meanwhile we know of other sufficiently certain Proculi: the Bolognese, Veronese, Puteolanian, Augustodunian, and others. In the case of the Proculi of Umbria, the matter remains unclear. Who that bishop and martyr of Interamna was, recorded confusedly in the manuscript of Saint Cyriacus as being from Interamna or Narnia; for what reason Baronius asserts that he was beheaded by the Goths on this day; and from where Usuard obtained the present-day presbyter of Narnia—all these matters appear exceedingly uncertain.

It is no surprise if our author errs when, abandoning his guides, he wanders beyond the boundaries of Gaul or Spain. But whoever the present Proculus may be, Usuard describes him most clearly not as a martyr or bishop, but only as a presbyter. More recent manuscripts have completely entangled the matter, as the Appendices will show.

But those patriotic enthusiasts seem to weave the labyrinth still tighter, multiplying Proculi, as well as other saints, in a remarkable fashion. To restore them to the truth as far as possible, our Janningus prepared an outstanding dissertation, praised above under 7 November, to be published elsewhere. It is better to refer readers to it than to weary them longer with uncertain and tangled observations. Meanwhile, see our Acts under 1 June, pp. 50 and 79.]

[Note: TORNACENSIS lacks the second notice; the rest is pure.

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM lacks the second and third article of the text.

ROSWEYD lacks the first; the second is pure. Then: “Also at Rome, Candida the virgin.” Nothing is said of Albanus. The final three notices are fairly pure. He adds: “At Milan, the translation of Saint Ambrose, bishop and confessor. Candidus, bishop and confessor.”

PULSANENSIS lacks the first two notices. He is pure only under Albanus. Then: “On the same day, Eligius of Noyon, bishop. At Byzantium, at Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Natalia, wife of Saint Adrianus the martyr. On the same day, Saint Candidus.”

ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK, UGHELLIAN, ALTEMPS, and almost all the middling manuscripts add to Proculus the title not of presbyter but of martyr. These four add at the end: “On the same day, Maurus the martyr.” See Florentinius, 29 November.

[Col. 0757C] ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN, besides what was mentioned concerning Proculus, have at the end: “At Verdun, the passing of Saint Agericus, or Agericus the bishop.”

ALBERGEN and DANIC have the same, but placed the first notice under 25 October. Albanus is also absent. They are fairly pure in the rest.

CENTULENSIS begins with Albanus, correctly. Then: “In France, in the city of Noyon, the passing of the most blessed and holy Eligius, a precious bishop, whose life and deeds the blessed bishop Audoenus described in truthful style. In the city of Byzantium, the dormition of Saint Natalia, the wife of …” The remainder is lacking.

BRUSSELLENSIS begins with Eligius, correctly; then: “At Rome, Candida, Lucius, and Marina, Ambonius and Philatus, Chrysanthus, Maurus, and Daria, saints.” It mixes in more material from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. It then gives Diodorus and Marianus, fairly correctly. For Natalia, it agrees with PULSANENSIS. Then: “And the commemoration of the holy martyrs Papinus and Mansuetus, bishops, whose feast day was the fourth day before the Kalends of December. At Mainz, Saint Albinus the martyr.” For Proculus and Agericus, it agrees with the middling manuscripts cited above.

HAGENOYEN composed a long eulogy of Chrysanthus and Daria in his own fashion, which I do not wish to transcribe here. In second place he treats Natalia, correctly. Then Diodorus and Marianus, tolerably well. It continues:

“In the city of Noyon, the burial of Saint Eligius, bishop and confessor, who from early childhood was a goldsmith by his parents’ profession. Nevertheless, because of the divine worship that he carried in his heart, he directed his workshop by prayer [rather] than by labor. By a miracle shown by God he was made a bishop. It is not easy to recount how many virtues then shone in him, since he became all things to all people. When he was dying, he not only prayed to the Lord for the people entrusted to him, but earnestly begged the Lord to appoint a worthy bishop over them after him, and he died in peace. The remarkable life of this man, filled with signs before and after his death, is commended by a great number of witnesses.”]

DAVERON: “At Le Mans, Saint Domnolus, bishop and confessor.” See Castellanus.

AMBIANENSIS: “On the same day, Saint Constantianus, abbot and confessor, who raised three dead persons.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUSIAN-UTRECHT: “Albanus the martyr, at Mainz. Candida the virgin. Chrysanthus and Daria. Arvisanus and Maxima.” See GREVEN. “Agericus of Verdun, bishop. Natalia, wife of Saint Adrianus the martyr.”

The VATICAN manuscript no. 5949 treats only Eligius and Proculus, omitting the rest.

FLORENTINE: “The feast of Saint Evasius, bishop and confessor.” See the Roman Martyrology on the following day. “In the city of Narnia, Saint Proculus the martyr. Also, Saint Maurus the martyr. At Rome, Candida the virgin and martyr. In the territory of the city of Siena, Saint Ansanus the martyr. At Ravenna, Saint Peter, archbishop and confessor.” See the following day.

[Col. 0758C] LUXOVIENSIS: “At Verdun, which is a city of the province of Gaul, the passing of blessed Agericus, confessor of Christ, who was the tenth bishop of that city and shone with so many virtues that if a sick person received a blessing from his hand, he immediately recovered his health.” This is found in the Roman Martyrology.

The LÜBECK-COLOGNE edition adds after Chrysanthus and Daria: “and thus they departed to Christ; now, through the translation from the city of Rome, they rest in the monastery of Eyfflia.” In the second notice it is fairly pure. Then: “Also at Rome, the holy Jabinus, Latinus, Superatus, Lucius, Candida, Marina, Ambonius, and Philatus, confessors.” Why not martyrs? “At Byzantium, a city called Constantinople, the feast of Saint Natalia, widow, wife of …” and so forth. In the notice of Eligius it is pure. For Proculus, as above. For Agericus, as in LUXOVIENSIS. “At Trier, the enclosure of Saint Simeon the confessor.”

BELIN: The first notice is placed under 25 October; here comes the second, tolerably well. The third is correct. The fifth is as above. The sixth is fairly pure [Col. 0758D]. Then: “On the same day, Saint Maurus the martyr. Also in the city of Noyon, Saint Eligius, bishop and confessor. At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria. On the same day, Saint Evasius, bishop and confessor.” In another copy there is added: “At the monastery of Floriacum, the reception of the relics of Saint Martial, bishop.”

GREVEN: “At Rome, the feast of the holy Jabinus, Latinus, and others. In Africa, Victor, Rogatus, and nineteen others. On the same day, the holy martyrs Anisanus and Maxima the virgin. Anisanus, a noble Roman, was instructed in the faith of Christ by the presbyter Protasius and raised from the sacred font by Saint Maxima the virgin. Later, under the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, he was killed with her for the same faith and received the palm of martyrdom. In Italy, in the suburb of Casale, the feast of Saint Evasius, bishop and martyr. At Verdun, Saint Agericus, bishop and confessor. As the tenth ruler of that church, he shone with such virtues that anyone who received a blessing from his hand while sick immediately obtained the desired health. Candidus the bishop. Maternianus, archbishop of Reims and confessor. The translation of the head of Saint Martin, bishop. At Trier, the enclosure of Saint Simeon the confessor.”

This concerns the famous Simeon of Syracuse, whose Acts were explained by Henschenius on 1 June.

MOLAN, after “confessor,” inserts into the text in italic type: “and patron of this church.” Then, after “commended,” in smaller type:

“He constructed many tombs of the saints. He labored greatly among the Flemings: with continual persistence he fought at Antwerp and converted many erring Suebi. Protected by the shield of Christ and with apostolic authority, he destroyed certain shrines; wherever he found idols of various kinds, he utterly overthrew them. In the midst of these labors he was frequently harassed by an ungrateful and faithless people and provoked almost to insult, yet he was in no way deterred from the doctrine he had begun. Rather, gentle, patient, humble, and meek, he prayed to the Lord for them.”

At the end: “On the same day, the translation of Saint Maurus the martyr. On the same day, Saint Evasius, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Floriacum,” as in BELIN, and so forth. “At Verdun,” and so forth, as in the middling manuscripts. Then: “The translation of Landoaldus, archbishop and confessor. The arrival [Col. 0760A] of the holy relics from the city of Constantinople,” and again, in smaller type, “at the holy church of Laetia, concerning which there are documents there from the patriarch Theodore and the emperor Henry, issued in the year 1208. In the territory of Auvergne, Saint Amabilis, presbyter and confessor of Riom, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes.”

Other editions, in the text, with the section on Eligius printed in italics and placed first, have:

“This blessed man, among the other distinctions of his good works, constructed many tombs of the saints in gold, silver, and gems. Moreover, anxious with the care of a shepherd, he labored greatly among the Flemings …” through “he utterly overthrew them.”

The text also contains Natalia and Proculus, with the other notices omitted. At the end, concerning Evasius, as in the earlier edition. Then: “At Milan, Saint Castricianus, bishop and confessor. At Castro Ambasius, Saint Florentinus, presbyter and confessor, a man of wondrous virtue. At Siena, Saint Ansanus the martyr, in the time of Diocletian.” For Agericus, as before. “On the first day, the holy prophet Nahum.” The translation of Maurus and the relics of Martial are also as in the first edition. Then: “In the village of Wintershoven, the translation of Landoaldus the confessor and his companions, performed by Saint Floribertus, bishop of Liège. At Laetia, the arrival of the holy relics from the city of Constantinople.” See above, in the earlier edition, concerning these relics.]

[Col. 0755]

At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria the virgin, who, after enduring many sufferings for Christ, were ordered by the emperor Numerianus to be placed in a sand-pit on the Salarian Way and buried alive there beneath earth and stones. Also at Rome, the holy martyrs Diodorus the presbyter and Marianus the deacon, with many others, who, at the command of the aforementioned ruler, celebrated the glory of martyrdom. At the city of Mainz, the feast of blessed Albanus the martyr. Also in the city of Noyon, Saint Eligius, bishop and confessor, whose remarkable life is commended by a great number of miracles. On the same day, Saint Natalia, wife of Saint Adrianus the martyr. In the city of Narnia, Saint Proculus the presbyter.

### Fourth day before the Nones. Day 2.

[Note: PRATENSIS, HERINIENSIS, TORNACENSIS, ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, ROSWEYD, ANTWERP, MAXIMUM-LÜBECK, MUNERATIAN, GREVEN, and MOLAN reproduce Usuardus correctly.]

[Note: There is one point in which the Pratensis manuscript falls short of the purity of the others: at the end it reads, “he gave back his spirit to the Lord.” I suspect that *Domino* was written by mistake for *donec*, unless perhaps it intended to say, “until he gave his spirit to the Lord,” and so forth [Col. 0760B]. Again, instead of *reddidit*, all the others have *redderet*; ANTWERP-MAXIMUM transposed the words: “until he gave back his spirit.” Enough has been said about *Affricam*, *Aphricam*, *tandiu*, and similar forms.]

[Note: The first two martyrs, Verus and Securus, are not known from Usuardus’s usual forerunners, nor from Bede. In the Hieronymian manuscripts the Mauritanian or Moorish army consists of approximately twenty-one soldiers, of whom our pair, placed at the front, appear to have been the principal ones. Rabanus transcribed the first group of four from the aforesaid manuscripts: “In Mauritania, Verus, Securus, Januarius, Victorinus.” The Plantinian Bede, Belin, and Maurolycus changed *Verus* to *Severus*. The latter and that Bede also mention four companions, from whom Baronius took them, deleting the Vandalic persecution, which I do not know why Peter’s *Catalogue*, book I, chapter 21, attributed to Ado and which Maurolycus adopted. The selection of companions is plainly arbitrary; our author reported only the first two, precisely those found in Wandalbertus.

For Verus and Securus, Africa sacrifices on the fourth day before the Nones.

This almost led me to believe outright that the metrical Martyrologist had sometimes preceded Usuardus, but I was somewhat deterred by the assertion in the text that they were brothers. From this it is easily inferred that our author found another source of information, much like the one we cited from the Catalogue, in which Verus and Securus are also called brothers. We seek light in vain because the Acts are lacking.

Florentinius attempts to extract Bibiana—called Vibiana by others and Viviana by our manuscripts, but not found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies—from the corrupt names in Rabanus, referring to the same Hieronymian Calendar of his own in which Viviana is recorded on this day.

In the ancient Roman Calendars or Sacramentaries there is no memory of her, nor is she found in any other Martyrologist outside our series. The author who leads the procession, the writer of the *Little Roman Martyrology*, formed the two notices in this way: “At Rome, Viviana the martyr. Faustus the martyr and the daughter of Dafrosa.” In Ado these are confused so as to produce an entirely different meaning: “The feast of Viviana the martyr, and of the blessed martyrs Faustus and the daughter of Dafrosa.”

Here Faustus is said to be Dafrosa’s husband and Bibiana’s father; there Faustus is Dafrosa’s father and therefore Bibiana’s grandfather. Both statements are false. For whatever may be the character of the Acts of Pimenias and Bibiana, rejected by our predecessors, in those Acts a certain Faustus is indeed a governor converted to the faith by Dafrosa; but her husband, and the father of Bibiana and Demetria, is consistently named Flavianus.

We spoke about these Acts on 4 January and 24 March. Ado does not identify the tyrant clearly enough, calling him a sacrilegious emperor; Usuardus expressed Julianus more distinctly. In the meantime, after much debate, it has still not been established with certainty under which persecutor Bibiana and the others mentioned in the cited Acts suffered. Tillemont prefers the time of Diocletian; Baronius and others believe that they have found circumstances which fit the age of Julianus more suitably, as the Acts assert. Consult Baronius’s Notes and our Acts on the cited days. It is better to define nothing positively until there has been leisure to investigate everything more deeply and examine the truth more maturely in the Acts for this day. Henschenius referred the whole controversy to that place under 21 June, and we mentioned it there briefly while discussing Demetria.]

[Note: PULSANENSIS gives Bibiana’s notice correctly, but places it first. In second place he has only: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Verus and Securus.”

ANTWERP-MAXIMUM, UTRECHT, LEYDEN, and LOUVAIN add concerning Bibiana: “By order of the emperor her body lay in the forum for two days. Finally, it was taken away at night by the presbyter John and buried in a house where her mother and her sister Demetria had already been buried.” See Ado.

ALBERGEN begins: “At Rome, the feast of Saint Viviana the virgin and martyr, [and] of the blessed martyrs Faustus and the daughter of Dafrosa.” This is the beginning of Ado. The words of the text and of the Adonian addition reported above follow. The first notice concerning Verus and Securus is placed second.

DANIC varies in such a way that it approaches the *Little Roman Martyrology* more than Ado, thereby damaging the construction. After “virgin and martyr,” it continues: “Also, the blessed martyrs Faustus and Dafrosa’s daughter.” It wrongly connects with them: “who, at the command of …,” since at that point everything refers to Dafrosa rather than to Bibiana. Otherwise it resembles the ALBERGEN manuscript cited above.

CENTULENSIS: “At the monastery of Centula, a great, distinguished, exalted solemnity: the beheading of the saints gathered in that same monastery at different times. Since their days could not be celebrated individually, Pope Adrianus decreed that their solemnity should be observed on this day. At Rome, Saint Viviana the virgin and martyr. On the same day, Verus and Securus, who were crowned with martyrdom in Africa.”

BRUSSELLENSIS: “The octave of Saint Catherine the virgin and martyr. At Rome, the holy Pimicius, Pontianus, Vivianus, and three others. In Mauritania, the feast of the holy brothers Severus and Securus, and of Victorinus and Fortunatus, who were crowned with martyrdom in Africa.” In the notice of Bibiana it resembles ALBERGEN.]

HAGENOYEN.: “In Africa, the commemoration of the holy brothers Verus and Secundus, who were crowned with martyrdom under the Arian king Hunneric.” In the entry for Bibiana it does not differ much [Col. 0761C] from ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. Then it adds: “Also at Rome, the commemoration of the blessed martyrs Faustus and Dafrosa, his daughter.” Thus the saints gradually increase and are incompetently multiplied. Then: “At the city of Narnia [for Narnia], the burial of the priest Proculus.” From the preceding day. Again: “On the same day, the burial of the holy bishop and confessor Evasius.” But in the Roman Martyrology he is placed on this day. Finally: “On this day, the commemoration of the blessed martyr Maurus.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Eligius, bishop and confessor.” See the preceding day. It follows: “Longinus, martyr, who pierced the Lord’s side during the Passion.” See Usuard on 15 March, and the Additions elsewhere [Col. 0762A]. Among the ancients only Florus mentions him. At the end: “Bibiana, virgin and martyr.”

IN THE VATICAN CODE, no. 5949, the first entry concerning Verus and Secundus is absent. It adds, however: “Also at Rome, Saints Primentius and Pontianus.”

STROZZIAN.: “Also at Rome, Saint Pontianus, martyr.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition begins as follows: “At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Bibiana, virgin and martyr, and of the blessed Faustus and Dafrosa, his daughter. This Bibiana, when Julian ordered her,” etc., as in the medieval-form codices cited above. At the end it is somewhat mutilated, so that it does not properly begin the entry concerning Verus and Secundus.

BELIN writes Severus instead of Verus; and, where all the other codices have Viviana, he alone has Bibiana. At the end he adds: “Also at Rome, Saint Pontianus, martyr.”

GREVEN.: “In Mauretania, Saints Securinus, Victorinus, Fortunatus, Agnes, and Secunda.” The Hieronymian copies should be consulted. “Longinus, martyr; Pigmenius, Fausta, and others.” In my opinion, Faustus would be the more correct reading [Col. 0762B], as an allusion to all the saints mentioned in the Acts of Bibiana. Then: “At Rome, Saints Primitivus, Potentianus; at Ravenna, Saint Peter, archbishop and confessor, who was ordained bishop of Ravenna by Pope Sixtus III through the apparition and command of Saints Peter the Apostle and Apollinaris the Martyr. Through his outstanding learning and the elegance of his speech he earned the surname Chrysologus, that is, ‘golden in speech,’ or ‘golden preacher.’ His chalice and paten also cure, by contact, the bite of a rabid dog. Bishop Ethermanus. Valeria, virgin.”

MOLAN.: “Also at Rome, Saint Pontianus, martyr. The consecration of Saint Gertrude, virgin.” In smaller type it follows: “At Ravenna, Saint Peter, archbishop and confessor, who earned the surname Chrysologus. On the same day in India, in the Chinese city of Cantana, the death of Francis Xavier, who, as leader of those evangelizing in India, most illustrious for many virtues, the conversion of peoples, and various miracles during life [Col. 0762C] and after death, returned his incorrupt spirit to the Lord. This is recorded in the Indian letters. Also the death of Lord John Ruysbroeck, first prior of the Canons Regular of Groenendael, renowned for learning and holiness. His Life is extant.” Other editions write “Pontianus,” as does the first. Then: “At Imola, Blessed Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, renowned for character, learning, and miracles. At Nivelles, the consecration of Saint Gertrude, virgin.” Finally, in smaller type, they treat of Saint Francis Xavier and Lord John Ruysbroeck, retaining the wording from the first edition already cited.]

[Col. 0759]

The commemoration of Saints Verus and Secundus, brothers, who were crowned with martyrdom in Africa. At Rome, the Passion of Saint Bibiana, martyr, who, by order of the sacrilegious emperor Julian, was beaten with leaded scourges for so long that she gave up her spirit.

III Non. The 3rd day. [Note: [Col. 0761C]

The Praten., Herinien., Antuerp., and Max.-Lubec. codices are pure. Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. add material. Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., Leyden., Albergen., and Danic. also contain additions.] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0761D]

All the medieval-form codices read: “At Rome, on the Salarian Way.” Thus also Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., when they begin the second entry from Ado: “At Tingis, the metropolis of Mauretania Tingitana.” Munerat. wrote Turgi; the second edition of Belin, Trugi; Greven, Tyngi. Belin incorrectly placed the conjunction and after Claudius, thus reading: “Claudius and the tribune and his wife Hilaria,” etc. With Praten., Herinien., Munerat., Greven., and Molan., we read: “bloody, serving the slaughter of Christians,” although the construction is harsher. To avoid this, Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Belin, and the medieval-form codices omitted the word “bloody”; indeed, in Antuerp.-Maj. the phrase was softened to “serving bloody executions.” In Greven. and Molan., before “Christians” and “confession,” the word “under” is absent. These same two also disagree with the others in the first entry, where, instead of “bound to a huge stone,” as Usuard copied it from Ado, they preferred the somewhat more grammatical “bound with a huge stone.” Molan., omitting the conjunction between “but” and “sons,” reverses the sense: “but the soldiers, the sons,” etc. Munerat.’s construction is also incomplete at the end: omitting “to the same office,” under “Christiana,” he has only: “therefore renouncing, by confession the triumph,” etc. We disregard Hylariae, renuntians, optinere, and similar matters.] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0763A]

What we observed on 1 December, on the occasion of Chrysanthus and Daria, concerns these martyrs Claudius, Hilaria, Jason, Maurus, and the unnamed soldiers. As we showed there, all of them are placed in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 12 August, with some of them repeated in the same copies on 29 November. Our four martyrs, together with those seventy soldiers, were first recorded on this day by the Little Roman Martyrology as follows: “At Rome, Claudius the tribune, his wife Hilaria, Jason and Maurus, and seventy soldiers under Numerianus.” Ado’s eulogy is fuller, and Usuard condensed his entry from it. I shall not dwell on these matters longer, since, apart from what was said about Chrysanthus and Daria, nothing further remains to be observed.

Cassian of Tingis is explicitly placed in all the Hieronymian Martyrologies, however somewhat distorted and corrupted his name and the name of the place where he suffered may be. The Lucense copy, or that of Saint Wandrille, reads most distinctly: “And at Tingis, Cassianus.” Rabanus undoubtedly took this from there, but incorrectly added the title “priest” on his own authority. Cassian is unknown on this day to the Little Roman Martyrology, Bede, and Florus. The Viennese martyrologist seems to have had another source besides the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but I do not know what it was. I am certain that he had not seen the Acts, since he speaks of Cassian rather meagerly: “At Tingis, the metropolis of Mauretania Tingitana, the feast of the holy and glorious martyr Cassian.” More information, indeed the Acts themselves, must have reached Usuard, from which he composed a splendid encomium, discussed above among the Variants. They are brief but remarkable and genuine, and the cited Acts clearly express the day of his Passion. Ruinart published them among the Sincere and Selected Acts, with a preliminary notice and notes, beginning on page 314. With Usuard we counted our Cassian on 30 October, since, on the occasion of the unjust sentence pronounced against Marcellus, he was inspired from heaven and then first converted to the faith of Christ, although Tillemont doubts this, volume IV, page 577. Prudentius’ verse concerning Cassian is well known:

“Tingis shall send forth its own Cassian.”

Wandalbert, alluding to Verus and Secundus, yesterday’s African martyrs, adds Cassian to them today in these words:

“And Africa likewise offers tribute to Cassian, a martyr, on the third [day].”] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0763B]

TORNAC.: entirely pure in the first entry; in the second it cuts out the whole eulogy of Cassian.

ANTUERP.-MAJ.: not sufficiently corrected in the text; at the end it adds: “Also the burial of Saint Birinus, confessor.” This is plainly an English addition, amplified still further in the following codex.

ROSWEYD.: “At Pentana, the metropolis of the West Saxons, Saint Birinus, bishop, who first preached the Gospel of Christ there.” He is pure throughout the Usuardine text.

PULSANEN. transposes both entries and cuts the eulogies from each.

[Col. 0763C] LOVAN. is defective in Claudius’ eulogy.

CENTULEN.: “At Tingis, the metropolis of Mauretania Tingitana, the feast of Saint Cassian, who, scorning the office of tax collector, suffered martyrdom for his confession of Christ. At Rome, Saints Claudius the tribune, his wife Hilaria, and their sons Jason and Maurus, together with seventy soldiers, all of whom believed in Christ through the preaching of Blessed Chrysanthus and suffered under Numerianus.”

BRUXELLEN. begins with “Agnes Secunda.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies on the preceding day, where you will find Agnes and Secunda, or Secundus, mixed in with others. It then proceeds to Cassian, with reasonable purity. Then: “At Nicomedia, Saints Merobius, Claudius, and Felix.” It is fairly pure in Claudius and his companions. Then: “In Africa, Saints Magna, John, Stephen, Victor, and Martin. At Bologna, the elevation of Saint Agricola, martyr.” The whole little list is interwoven with Hieronymian saints. Then: “At Blandinium, the arrival of the bodies of Saints Bertulphus and Gudualus. When the shrine of Saint Gudualus was being carried back to Ghent after the procession, an image of the cross, with bowed face, remained motionless in homage to him and did not straighten itself. Also Birinus, bishop.”

HAGENOYEN., fairly pure in the first entry, adds: “Also at Chur, the feast of Saint Lucius, confessor, that same apostle, who abandoned his kingdoms for Christ.” See the Roman Martyrology. “Also at Strasbourg, the monastery of Saint Stephen, and Saint Achela, virgin and abbess of that same monastery.” I cannot make out clearly whether it reads Athela; Castellanus calls her Atala. It follows: “In the diocese of Eystein, Saint Solus, confessor.” See Castellanus, where he is called Solas. The codex is pure in Cassian. Finally it adds: “In England, Saint Birinus, bishop and confessor.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC. no. 130: “Also the feast of Saint Crispina, virgin and precious martyr, under the emperor Diocletian.” There is some Crispina in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on this day, but consult the texts themselves. See 5 December and Usuard on the same day.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Claudius the tribune, with seventy soldier-companions.” It should read “with seventy soldiers.” I do not know why the wife and sons are omitted. It follows: “Eloquius, abbot.” See Castellanus.

THE VATICAN CODE, no. 5949, adds: “The feast of Saints Graficus, Septimus, and Quincelus, at Saint Sophia.”

LUXOVIEN.: “The burial of Saint Firminus, bishop of Verdun.” He is seventh in order among the Sammarthani. Castellanus placed him among the Aemeri, that is, those without a fixed day, on page 783.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition begins: “The return of blessed John the Apostle from exile on Patmos, after the death of the emperor Domitian.” It is somewhat interpolated in the Roman martyrs and pure in Cassian. It adds: “On the same day, Saint Birginus, bishop and confessor.” See above, ANTUERP.-MAJ. and ROSWEYD. Finally: “On this day, Saint Osmund, bishop and confessor.” See the Roman Martyrology on the following day.

GREVEN.: “The return of blessed John the Evangelist from exile after the death of Domitian. In Frisia, Radfrid and Wandelfrid, martyrs. In Africa, the feast of Saints Crispinus, Magna, John, Stephen, Victor, and Martin. At Bologna, Saints Agricola and Cassian. In England, Birinus, bishop of Dorchester.” See below the later editions of MOLAN. “Peter, archbishop. In Britain, Saint Lucius, king and confessor, who, in the time of Pope Eleutherius, received the faith of Christ, as Bede says in Book I. Also in England, Saint Osmund, bishop and confessor, illustrious for the glory of his life and miracles. Firminus, bishop. Solus, priest and abbot. Galganus, confessor. Eloquius, abbot. At Strasbourg, Saint Atala, virgin. Also Blessed Emerita, sister of Saint Lucius the king.”

MOLAN. inserts in italics into the text, after “sentenced to punishment,” a passage from Ado: “There was an ancient underground passage at the place where they were beheaded. The Christians, clearing it out during the night, buried all the bodies together on the Salarian Way. Saint Hilaria, the martyr who remained behind, gathered the bodies of Jason and Maurus; while she devoted herself to continual prayers there, she departed to the Lord.” At the end: “At the monastery of Blandinium, in the castle of Ghent, the arrival of the bodies of Saints Gudualus and Bertulphus.” In smaller type he gives the words of GREVEN concerning Radfrid and Waldefrid, King Lucius, Osmund, and Solus. The later editions have the same material in the same manner. At the end: “At Milan, Mirocles, archbishop and confessor.” See the Roman Martyrology. “In England, Saint Birinus, bishop of Dorchester. In the territory of Eystein, Solus, priest and abbot. On the third day, Saint Zephaniah the prophet. At Vualchiodorum, the feast of Saint Eloquius, priest and confessor. At Strasbourg, Saint Atala, virgin.” Concerning the arrival of the bodies of Gudualus and Bertulphus, as above. Finally, in smaller type: “In Frisia, Radfrid and Waldefrid, martyred by the Normans near Groningen.” See Castellanus’ Universal Martyrology.] [End note.]

[Col. 0761]

At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Claudius the tribune, his wife Hilaria, and their sons Jason and Maurus, together with seventy soldiers. Numerianus the emperor ordered Claudius to be bound to a huge stone and cast into the middle of the sea, while the soldiers and Claudius’ sons were punished by capital sentence. At Tingis, the metropolis, the Passion of Saint Cassian, who, having long held the office of a clerk, was finally inspired from heaven and judged it abominable, though blood-stained, to serve in the slaughter of Christians. Therefore, renouncing that office, he deserved to obtain the triumph of martyrdom under the confession of Christ.

Pridie Non. The 4th day. [Note: [Col. 0765]

The Tornacen., Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Greven., and Molan. codices are completely pure.] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0765B]

Greven writes Melecius; worse, Molan writes Meletius. Where the Tornacensis reads eruditione praerogativa (“with the prerogative of learning”), I think eruditionis praerogativa (“the prerogative of learning”) is intended; otherwise all the codices read as in the text. Greven and Molan read synceritas (“integrity”). Tornacensis has scolis (“schools”); most of the other codices, indeed almost all, reproduce the pure and complete text. But the Pratensis, with its associates, adds at the end: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Syranus, abbot,” or, as Castellanus recorded it, “Saint Sigirannus.” The first form is also found in Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd, and Aquicinct. [Col. 0766B] Moreover, in the Pratensis, in the margin: “At the German monastery [for Fleury], the translation of the most holy confessor of Christ, Benedict, abbot”; Castellanus more briefly: “At Fleury, translation of Saint Benedict.” The Herinien. codex, otherwise exceedingly pure throughout, adds Barbara at the end; many others likewise either added or prefixed her, as we shall show more fully in the Additions. Here you should note that the Barbara mentioned above is recorded by the Little Roman Martyrology, Ado, and Usuard not on this day but on 16 December.] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0765B]

On this day Usuard celebrates saints whom he could find in no earlier martyrologist. The Little Roman Martyrology had placed only this single entry: “At Rome, Symphronius and Olympius, Exsuperius and Theodulus, who suffered on 27 July, and were translated by Blessed Sixtus on 4 December, when their feast is celebrated more solemnly.” Ado constructed a longer history from the Acts of Pope Stephen, but even in Ado it is the sole commemoration. Since Usuard had already included it on 26 July, he plainly had to turn elsewhere in order to assign particular saints to this day. He did not consult the Hieronymian copies; Bede and Florus are silent; Rabanus is almost entirely occupied with Barbara. Thus, following his usual guides, he found in Rufinus or Eusebius two saints whom he could propose for commemoration on this day according to his own judgment. Consequently, the entire text is genuinely and properly Usuardine. Eusebius suggested Meletius, bishop of Pontus, in Book VII, chapter 29, where this saint is magnificently praised for his manifold adornment with every kind of learning. From this Usuard took the entire substance of his brief eulogy, transcribing Rufinus’ very words, as will plainly appear to anyone who compares our text with the cited passage. What could be added to such sweetness of character and such gentleness that his companions called him “honey-like”? What to his learning, when he is declared perfect in every branch of knowledge? See all these matters presented in French by Tillemont, volume VII, page 41, who in the immediately preceding volume, page 641, defends this same Meletius against the stain of Arianism maliciously imposed upon him by Philostorgius. We shall gather the remaining material more laboriously when his Acts are to be studied.

As great and genuine as the praises Eusebius heaped upon Meletius are, so splendid, or perhaps even greater, are those deserved by the illustrious and celebrated writer Clement, surnamed Alexandrinus—not from his origin or birth, since learned men still dispute his homeland, and it is no more certain where he died, but rather from his teaching office. Eusebius speaks more than once in Book VI of his History of the Church about Clement’s vast learning and the books he composed on various subjects; the ancient Fathers and other ecclesiastical writers are no less lavish in praising him in many ways. From these sources Tillemont constructed a kind of account of his life in volume III, beginning on page 181. Many more recent writers have contributed to the same subject, whom we shall consult in due course, especially bibliographers and those who have expressly treated ecclesiastical writers; it is not worthwhile to list their names here. We have already said that no martyrologist earlier than or contemporary with Usuard recorded Clement’s name, so that he must be credited solely to Our Usuard, just as Meletius is. I do not sufficiently understand what scruple could have led the reformers of the Roman Martyrology to wish to remove so illustrious a man from the sacred calendars. See Henschenius, volume VI of May, page 777, letter F. Some think Baronius was deterred because Clement’s works are listed among the apocrypha by Gelasius. This is sufficient for our purpose. What Wandalbert’s verse means I entirely fail to understand:

“Then, on the preceding day, when Heracleus excels with Victorius.”

At any rate, this further confirms my opinion that Usuard did not follow Wandalbert, who on this day seems to have sought his saints elsewhere.] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0765D]

PRATEN. We discussed its additions above under the Variants.

[Col. 0766D] HERINIEN., exceedingly pure in the text, brings here part of the entry from 16 December: “In Tuscany, the Passion of Saint Barbara, virgin, under the emperor Maximianus. After terrible tortures, she was finally put to the sword and completed her martyrdom.” Other codices cited below will provide more.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. We said above that this codex again agrees here with the Pratensis. It reads: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Siranus, abbot. And the translation of Saint Benedict, abbot.”

ROSWEYD. likewise adds to the text, together with the Pratensis: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Syranus, abbot.” The entire entry for Barbara follows, copied from 16 December. I do not wish to reproduce it here yet again, since it is repeated in other codices as well.

PULSANEN. substitutes an entirely different text for the Usuardine one: “At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Symphronius and Olympius, in the time of Valerian and Gallienus.” See above under the Observations. “Also Saint Barbara, virgin. In Africa, the feast of Armogastus, Archiminus, and Satyrus.” See Usuard on 29 March concerning these three martyrs.

MUNERAT. incorrectly writes Electus for Meletius. In addition to the text he adds: “On this day, Saint Benedict, abbot. At Paris, relics were received into the church of Blessed Mary: namely, part of the hair of Blessed Mary; three teeth of Blessed John the Baptist; the arm of Saint Andrew the Apostle; the stones with which Blessed Stephen was stoned; and also the most precious head of Blessed Dionysius, martyr. These relics were found in the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. On this day, Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr.” Other codices treat her more fully.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., and LOVANIEN. All these codices, together with the two following, place first the entire entry for Saint Barbara as it appears in Usuard on 16 December, to which we have already referred readers above. They are pure in the text.

ALBERG. and DANIC., besides placing Barbara at the beginning, add at the end: “At Cologne, the feast of Saint Anno [the other, more simply: ‘At Cologne, Saint Anno’], bishop and confessor.”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, Saints Symphronius and Olympius, Exsuperia and Theodulus, martyrs, in the time of Valerian and Gallienus.” With a few changes, this codex has the same entry on 26 July. It continues: “At Nicomedia, the Passion of Saint Barbara, virgin, whom her own father Dioscorus beheaded with a sword. In Africa, Saints Armogastus, Archiminus, and Satyrus, who, although they were most brilliant members of the Church, endured many and various tortures for their confession of the truth.” See what we said concerning PULSANEN. “At the monastery of Fleury, the burial of the most holy body of our blessed Father Benedict.” The entire Usuardine entry is absent here.

BRUXELLEN. begins with Barbara, almost certainly also drawing upon the text for 16 December. It differs scarcely at all from the preceding entry in Armogastus and his companions. Then, from truncated Hieronymian material: “At Laodicea, the metropolis, Felix and Merobius.” A fairly pure text follows. Then: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Cyrianus, abbot. At Cologne, the burial of Saint Aimo [Anno], bishop and confessor. At Rome, Saints Symphronius and Olympius, martyrs, in the time of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. On the same day, the translation of Saint Benedict, abbot.”

HAGENOYEN. first treats of Meletius and at the end of Clement of Alexandria, in both places fairly purely; but between these two entries it inserts a long history of the martyrdom of Saint Barbara, which anyone can easily find in the Acts in Surius, in a much more polished form.

AQUICINCT. begins: “The Passion of Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr.” The text follows. At the end, together with the Pratensis, it adds: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Syrianus, abbot. At the monastery of Fleury, the second burial of Saint Benedict, abbot.”

The Ursini codex of Rosemberg: “In Italy, at the city of Parma, Blessed Bernard of the Uberti family, from Florence, glorious bishop of that city of Parma, whose deeds are extant. At Cologne, Saint Anno, archbishop and confessor.”

DAVERON.: “At the monastery of Fleury, Saint Benedict, holy Father of monks, an outstanding confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Barbara, virgin and martyr. Meletius, bishop and confessor. Clement, priest and confessor.”

CAMBERIEN.: “In Pontus, Blessed Electus, bishop.” Thus MUNER. above, but incorrectly for Meletius.

REG. SUEC. nos. 130 and 428: “On the same day, I think it reads, the burial of Saint Benedict, abbot.” Then only codex no. 428: “At Paris, the reception of sacred relics.”

THE VATICAN CODE, no. 5949, lacks the text. It has material concerning Barbara, I believe from 16 December. It also has Symphronius, Olympius, etc., from 26 July.

ALTEMPS.: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Syranus, abbot.” See the other codices above.

FLORENTIN.: “Saint Barbara . . . Also Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, who suffered together with the aforementioned Barbara. At Rome, Saints Symphronius, Olympius, Exsuperia, and Theodulus, martyrs, who suffered in the time of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. In Africa, the holy martyrs Armogastus, Archiminus, and Satyrus, who, although they were most brilliant members of Christ, completed the course of their glorious contest by enduring many grievous punishments and insults from the Arians for the confession of the faith. Also Saint Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Salvus near Florence, a citizen of Florence, who afterward became abbot of Saint Mary of Vallombrosa and was then ordained bishop of the city of Parma.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition: “At Cologne in Gaul, which is the metropolitan city of Germany, the passing of blessed and worthy-to-be-remembered Anno, archbishop and confessor of that same city, who was founder of many churches. Once, while he was celebrating the sacred mysteries, a certain blind man asked to be given water poured over the fingers of the venerable bishop by the altar minister. Having received it, he devoutly washed his whole face with it and joyfully proclaimed with loud applause that the light of this world had then first shone upon him. The tomb of blessed Anno is also made illustrious by frequent miracles through the divine grace.” Barbara follows, in somewhat fuller wording; then the text is fairly pure.

BELIN.: “At Nicomedia, Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr. On the same day, Saints Symphorianus and Olympius [the second edition has Olympius].” He adds further: “At the monastery of Fleury, the translation of Saint Benedict, abbot.”

GREVEN.: “Note. Today the more solemn feast of Saint Barbara is celebrated, which Usuard records below on 16 December. At Laodicea, the metropolis, Felix and Merobius. On the same day, Heraclius, Christianus, and Prudentius. The commemoration of Saints Armogastus, Archiminus, and Saturus, who are mentioned above on 29 March. At Rome, the translation of Saints Symphronius, Olympius, Exsuperia his wife, and Theodulus their son. Their bodies, as Ado says, were buried by Pope Stephen on 26 July and afterward translated by Saint Sixtus, and thus made this a celebrated day on 4 December. At Cologne, the burial of Saint Anno, bishop and confessor, who was founder of many churches. To commend his sanctity: once, while he was celebrating the sacred mysteries, a certain blind man washed his face with water poured over it from the fingers of the holy bishop and received the light of his eyes. At Verdun, Saint Possessor, bishop. At Fleury, the arrival of the body of Saint Benedict, abbot.”

MOLAN. copies from BELIN what we supplied above concerning Barbara, Symphronius and Olympius, and likewise concerning the translation of Saint Benedict. Then: “At Cologne, the burial of Saint Anno, bishop of that same city,” adding in smaller type the words “who was founder of many churches,” etc., from GREVEN. Later editions insert between Meletius and Clement, as part of the text, the entry for Barbara from 16 December, as above. At the end: “On the same day, Symphronius and Olympius, martyrs, at Rome, in the time of Valerian and Gallienus. Also Saint Bernard, bishop of Parma. In the district of Bourges, Saint Sigirannus, abbot. In England, Saint Osmund, bishop and confessor, illustrious for the glory of his life and miracles. At Cologne, the burial of Saint Anno, bishop of that city. On the fourth day, Saint John Damascene, holy Father. At the monastery of Fleury, the translation of Saint Benedict, abbot.” See the other codices above.]

[Col. 0765]

In Pontus, Blessed Meletius, bishop and confessor, who, although magnificent through the precedence of his learning, was still far more magnificent in the virtue of his character and the integrity of his life. Also at Alexandria, Saint Clement, priest, who flourished exceedingly in the schools of divine learning. [Bouillart adds in the text: “In the district of Bourges, Saint Syranus, [Note: [Col. 0765B] The commemoration of Syranus was added by a first hand without any erasure, though it was added by Usuard. This Syranus, or Sigirannus, is well known. Labbe published his deeds in the Bibliotheca, and Mabillon in the Benedictine Acts. BOUILLART.] abbot.” And in the margin: “At the monastery of Fleury, the translation of the most holy confessor of Christ, Benedict, abbot.”]

Nonae. The 5th day. [Note: [Col. 0769]

Most of the codices are pure, such as Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0769A]

They chiefly contain scribal or typographical errors. Antuerp.-Maj. begins as follows: “In Africa, at Thebestia,” omitting the noun “colony.” Munerat. reads Thesbatina; Greven. and others, Tebestina. I was compelled to write Dalmatius and Nicetius. Only Antuerp.-Maj. has: “At the city of Trier.” The more reliable codices give Thagora; others, Tagora; Munerat. incorrectly, Ragora; Belin, very badly, Ragona. Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. read “Saint Julius,” etc. I do not enumerate the remaining minor details.] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0769B]

The names Crispina and Crispinus recur more than once in the Hieronymian Martyrologies on 3 December, as was shown in the Additions, and on this day as well. Among all the codices, however, the oldest Epternacensis is by far the clearest and least confused, reading as follows: “At the city of Tegora, the feast of Julius, Potamia, Crispina, and seven others.” A difficulty arises because it places Crispina at Tegora—elsewhere Thegura or Thagara. But this is easily resolved if we acknowledge that our Crispina was a native of Thagura or Thagora, while she suffered at Thebeste, where our martyrologists most correctly record her together with the genuine Acts. Closely corresponding are the words of the Carthaginian Calendar: “On 5 December, the holy martyrs Bili [undoubtedly for Juli or Julii], Felix, Potamia, Crispina, and their companions.” Those demand too much from the Hieronymian codices who try to explain them with excessive precision; it is enough that the name of our martyr can safely and truly be extracted from them. We shall treat of Julius and Potamia last; illustrious Crispina alone occupies the first place, doubtless because she was crowned separately from the others and also has different Acts. Therefore, passing over the observations of Florentinius and others, and another confusion introduced by Rabanus into the Hieronymian text, we shall follow the thread of our martyrologists. The Little Roman Martyrology says only: “Crispina, martyr.” Ado, a lavish composer of eulogies, most probably did not see the Acts; nevertheless, he obtained sufficient information from somewhere to identify the emperors and the proconsul appropriately, using precisely the words which Our Usuard transferred from him into his little list. Augustine praises this most illustrious woman, rich and delicate yet courageous, in several passages. The Acts, which had long lain hidden in darkness, were first brought forth by Mabillon in volume III of the Analecta, page 423; his note on the Carthaginian Calendar in the same work, page 417, deserves to be read. Ruinart published the same Acts, compared with another manuscript, among the Selected Acts beginning on page 493, with a preliminary notice and notes that will be useful in due course. Tillemont’s French Life, volume V, beginning on page 317, will also not be without value. Wandalbert honors only Crispina and Dalmatius today in a single verse:

“Martyr Dalmatius and Crispina keep the Nones.”

Dalmatius, praised here by Wandalbert, is first celebrated by the Little Roman Martyrology in this way: “And Dalmatius, martyr.” Rabanus likewise has: “The feast of Dalmatius, martyr.” Ado’s wording is the same: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Dalmatius, martyr.” Usuard ventured somewhat beyond his predecessors by adding “in Italy.” Yet Baronius incorrectly cites Bede of the Plantinian edition, Ado, and the Roman entry for this notice: “At Pavia, Saint Dalmatius, bishop and martyr, who suffered in the persecution of Maximianus,” since none of them indicates Pavia, the title of bishop, or a persecution. Read Ferrarius’ note for this day, which will be discussed more fully elsewhere, together with the Acts themselves, poetically embellished by Jerome Vida, bishop of Alba; Tillemont criticizes many elements of them in volume V, beginning on page 637. Clearer and more certain are what Gregory of Tours wrote about Nicetius of Trier in the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 17, and likewise in On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 94. From the latter the Viennese Martyrologist first recorded him and took the material for his eulogy; Usuard then followed him, merely removing the place of burial, which we shall restore below from the Pulsanensis codex. See Baronius’ note for further information. Julius and Potamia were placed by Usuard alone, separated from the other Hieronymian companions mentioned above.
