These were Crispina’s companions, if not in martyrdom, at least fellow countrymen and very probably crowned with the martyr’s laurel at the same time. Baronius, following Bede of the Plantinian edition, I think, wrote: “At Thagura in Africa, Saints Julius, Potamia, Crispinus, Felix, Gratian, and seven others.” Rabanus had divided them into two groups. I admit that the confusion was already present in the Hieronymian codices, but I do not know whether Castellanus’ note arranges all the details sufficiently exactly. I agree with him in asserting that Usuard prudently selected only Julius and Potamia, leaving aside the others, who are not expressed clearly enough in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. In all other respects, the purity and authenticity of our text are sufficiently established.] [End note.]

[Note: [Col. 0769D]

ROSWEYD. adds to the text: “In Africa, Fulgentius, martyr, and twenty-six others.” Fulgentius is found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but where so many companions came from in this codex must be investigated.

PULSANEN. lacks the eulogy in the first entry. It is not pure in the second. In the third, concerning Nicetius, it adds from Ado the words discussed in the Observations: “Who rests buried in the basilica of Saint Maximinus, bishop.” It is defective in the fourth.

ANTUERP.-MAX., LOVAN., and LEYDEN. BELG., add to the pure text: “In the province of Cappadocia, in the city of Mutalassa, the feast of Blessed Sabas, abbot and confessor.”

ULTRAJECT. and LEYDEN.-LAT. extend the addition as follows: “In the province of Cappadocia, the feast of Blessed Sabas, abbot and confessor, who, abandoning the world in his youth, first led a virtuous life in a community, then in the desert, and afterward in the governance of monks.” DANIC. has the same, but places it first and lacks Nicetius’ entry in the text.

ALBERG., also pure in the text, prefixes to it: “The feast of Saint Sabas, abbot and confessor.”] [End note.]

CENTULEN.: “In Africa, at the city of Thebeste, the feast of Saint Crispina, virgin, under the proconsul Anolinus. On the same day, Saint Dalmatius, martyr. At Trier, Saint Nicetius, bishop, a man of complete holiness.” The final entry is lacking.

BRUXELLEN., fairly pure in the first part, adds: “Likewise in Africa, the feast of Saints Humilis, Felix Julius, Potamia, Crispinus, Trophinus, and eight others. In the city of Thegora, the feast of Saints Julius and Potamia.” See the Hieronymian codices. It is pure in the entry for Dalmatius. Concerning Saba, it has the same text as ULTRAJ., etc., above. For Nicetius it reads *Nicesius*, but in that entry it is otherwise pure. Finally: “And elsewhere, Saints Fulgentius and Amantius.” These too have been taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

HAGENOYEN. begins with Saba, almost as in the ULTRAJECT. cited above. It then gives Crispina and Dalmatius fairly correctly. Nicetius of Trier is absent here. In the final entry, it reads *Nyli* for Julius. It continues:

“In the city of Cologne Agrippina, the deposition of blessed Anno, bishop and confessor, of that same city. This blessed man established monks at Saal and expelled the canons from there. He also founded four other solemn monasteries: two outside Cologne, in which he placed black monks, namely Siegburg and Garsdorf; and he built two within the city, namely Saint Mary at the Steps and Saint George, in which he placed canons. This blessed man excommunicated the aldermen of the city of Cologne for a false judgment—he undoubtedly means ‘excommunicated,’ although the text says *exoclavit*—and died in peace, choosing burial at Siegburg, where he rests.” See the supplements for the preceding day and Surius.

VICTORIN. adds at the end: “In Judea, the feast of Saint Saba, abbot and confessor.”

[Col. 0772A] MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Nicetius, bishop of Trier. Anno, bishop of Cologne.”

REG. SUEC. no. 130: “And Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr.” See the preceding day.

Codex D. LE MARE, marked with the letter A, reports this special entry: “At the city of Aitna, the translation of Saint Bacho, bishop and confessor.”

In VATICAN no. 5949 the final entry is absent. It adds: “The feast of Saint Saba, abbot.”

FLORENTIN.: “Saint Saba, abbot.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition is pure in the first part and then inserts: “Likewise, the feast of Saint Saba, abbot and confessor.” Three other fairly pure entries follow. Then: “On the same day, Saint Tryphon, boy and martyr, who shone with many miracles from childhood and, after various tortures, was beheaded under the emperor Decius while Aquilinus was acting as prefect.” See GREVEN below, also concerning the following entry. “On that same day, Saint Diolinicius, martyr.”

BELIN. at the end: “Likewise, in the city of Mutalassus, which [Col. 0772B] belongs to the province of Cappadocia, Saint Saba, abbot and confessor.”

GREVEN. begins, as usual, his supplements from the Hieronymian Martyrologies:

“In Africa, Saints Humilis, Felix, Crispinus, Trophinus, Evarpion, and eight others. Likewise, Fulgentius and Amantius, martyrs, and twenty-six others. At Caesarea, Saint Domninus, martyr, and twelve others. Likewise, Saints Paul and Julius. Likewise, according to some authorities, Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse, here; Usuard and Ado place him on 29 November. Likewise, according to some authorities, Tryphon, boy and martyr, here; according to Vincentius, book twelve, on 5 May. Diolinicius, martyr. At the city of Embrun, Saint Gallicanus, bishop and confessor. Humilis, confessor. On the same day, blessed Saba, abbot, who was born in the province of Cappadocia and, in the time of Theodosius, endowed with great virtues and renowned for the glory of his miracles, rested in the year of the Lord 524.”

MOLAN. inserts into the text, in italics, a single word that expresses Dalmatius’s location more clearly: *Pedonae*, “at Pedona”; concerning this, see Ferrarius, cited by us in the Observations. At the end, from BELIN.: “Likewise, in the city of Mutalassus, in the province of Cappadocia, Saint Saba, abbot and confessor.” Nothing further is added in the later editions.

[Col. 0769]

In Africa, at the city of Thebeste, the feast of Saint Crispina, martyr, who, in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, having refused to sacrifice, was beheaded by order of Anolinus, the proconsul. On the same day, in Italy, Saint Dalmatius, martyr. At the city of Trier, Saint Nicetius, bishop, a man of complete holiness. Likewise, at the city of Thagora, Saints Julius and Potamia.

**VIII Ides. Day 6.**

[Note: [Col. 0771C]]

From Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0771C]]

Among the codices cited for the text, some could have been excluded because they changed the wording at the beginning. Thus Antuerp.-Maj. begins: “The feast of blessed Nicholas, bishop, concerning whom,” etc. Rosweyd. is somewhat more expansive, in large red capitals: “The feast of blessed Nicholas, bishop and confessor, radiant with the glory of miracles, concerning whom, among other things, this is related,” etc. The first edition of Belin had: “In Apulia, at Bari, the feast of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor,” etc.; but the second, somewhat better, has: “At Myra, the metropolis of Lycia.” Only Herinien. has “archbishop.” In the others the text reads *Mirorum*, for which some have *Mirrorum*, others *Mirreorum*; only Molan. has *Myreorum Lyciae*. In Praten. our copy incorrectly has *mirabile* for *memorabile*. Molan.’s emendation has no significance when, for *ab interitu quorumdam*, he himself reads *ab interitu quodam*. Likewise, together with Greven., he reverses the following words: “he was moved to mercy by the vision and by exhortations and threats.” The others support the reading that Usuard had the text as it stands, and therefore that Rosweyd. wrongly wrote “by exhortations and threats through the vision.” Belin also errs when he prefixes to the African martyrs the title “holy virgins”; nor is *Datianae* acceptable in place of *Dativae*. Herinien. pursues unnecessary elegance with *per et Dativae et Leontiae*. He wrote *Emiliani*, whereas *Emelii* would be better—not *Juliani*, as in Max.-Lubec. In Munerat., *Christi* is absent after *confessorum*. Max.-Lubec. and Belin. inflect the final words as *sociati sunt*, and Antuerp. no better as *associati sunt*. *Nicholai*, *Tercii*, *Bonefacii*, and similar forms may be disregarded.

[Note: [Col. 0773A]]

The spread of the extraordinarily devoted cult of Saint Nicholas throughout the whole Church, both Eastern and Western, is astonishing, with temples, altars, statues, and other monuments of singular veneration erected everywhere. The principal reason for this may reasonably be judged to be that God wished to make the enormous merits of this most holy and illustrious man publicly known throughout the Catholic world through the almost incredible multitude of various signs and miracles, and in this way, if one may so speak, to compensate to some extent for the silence of the ancient writers concerning him. What position Nicholas holds among the Greeks as a wonder-worker is shown, to say nothing of other evidence, by the Greek-Moscow Ephemerides before volume I of May, pages LV and LVIII.

His life was first composed in Greek by Methodius, patriarch of Constantinople, and from that work in Latin by John the Deacon, in the ninth century; thus it was written almost five full centuries after the saint himself. It does not seem sufficient to satisfy true devotees of Nicholas by removing their desire for more ancient Acts. It exists in Mombritius, volume II, beginning on page 162, but, since it is truncated before the author’s preface, it has offended the critics. Metaphrastes composed another, published by Surius and known to everyone. Concerning that work and many others—both histories and encomia—relating to Nicholas, which are available among us in Greek and Latin, we shall speak more fully in the Acts at the proper time.

Here we must chiefly note that in many ancient martyrologists, such as the Hieronymian Martyrologies, Bede, and Florus, and in the Roman Sacramentaries or Calendars, no memory of our saint is found. I should think that he first began to be celebrated at Rome when the author of the *Romanum parvum* compiled his brief Martyrology, being the first to speak of him in these words: “Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Lycia.” Ado adds nothing to this except the prefixed title “saint,” so that one may easily infer that no life of him was yet known to Ado. Or did none exist in his time? By no means, I think, since in Rabanus, whose martyrology is older, there is a lengthy account of the celebrated miracle of Nepotianus, Ursus, and Eupoleon, military commanders, who were rescued from prison at Constantinople through the apparition of Nicholas while he was still living. Usuard has indicated this more briefly in our text. It therefore seems possible to conclude that this account of the miracle is older than both Methodius and John the Deacon.

Indeed, in the preface of a manuscript preserved among us, John the Deacon testifies that he abridged Methodius, while otherwise referring the reader to the ornate inventions of the Greeks. These must certainly have existed earlier and were probably also circulated in the West, although the Viennese author had not seen them. Meanwhile, Tillemont’s French Life of Nicholas is extremely meager, volume VI, page 688; in its first note, page 823, he sharply attacks Metaphrastes and concludes that nothing certain remains concerning the saint’s deeds. I know that some, pressed by arguments of this kind, would make Nicholas one or two centuries younger; but in my judgment, while fleeing Scylla, they do not at all avoid the Charybdis of difficulties.

It will be our task elsewhere to examine whether the materials collected by the writers mentioned above from unquestionably older monuments are really so contemptible, or at least whether they cannot be sifted so that the genuine seed may be separated from the chaff. Wandalbert is more sparing on these matters, singing of Nicholas in only one verse:

“On the eighth of the Ides, Bishop Nicholas adorns the day.”

The African martyrs, first introduced by the *Romanum parvum*, are enumerated by it as follows: “In Africa, Dionysia, Dativa, Leontius, and Aemilianus the physician, and others.” Ado does not seem to have consulted the source, since he too wrote *Leontis* for *Leontiae* and confused other details that could and should have been explained much more distinctly and splendidly—for example, if Majoricus the youth had been joined to Dionysia, his most noble mother, and if the remaining persons had been named in their true order, with somewhat greater accuracy derived from Victor of Vita’s fifth book on the African persecution.

Let the curious reader consult Victor himself at the beginning of the fifth book cited, where he repeatedly says that it cannot be expressed in human speech with what punishments that bloody beast, Huneric, afflicted the Catholics, dispatching the most savage torturers throughout the provinces of the African land at one time, so that he declares it impossible for a human being to calculate the number of martyrs or even confessors. Our Usuard, abridging Ado’s account, correctly restored the name Leontia; he could also have written *Emelii* instead of *Aemiliani*. In another respect he seems preferable to Ado, since he left three persons anonymous. This is sufficient for our text; the remaining matters concerning the distinguished confessions of those Africans must elsewhere be more carefully elucidated from the Victor just mentioned.

[Note: [Col. 0773C]]

TORNACEN. is extremely pure throughout the text, but I do not know what relevance this addition has here: “Likewise, the feast of Saint Nicholas, archbishop.”

PULSANEN. changes the text as follows: “The feast of the most blessed Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Lycia. In Africa, Saints Dionysia, Davita, Leontius, Aemilianus, Decimus, and the religious man named Tertius, Boniface, Severus, Victor, and the youth Loris.” See Ado, or rather Victor himself, cited in the Observations, and likewise Castellan’s note for today.

ANTUERP., MAX.-ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG., and DANIC. are fairly pure throughout the text, but add concerning Nicholas: “He died in a good old age and was gathered to his fathers in the year of the Lord 358.”

LOVANIEN. agrees with the preceding witnesses in its supplement but mutilates the account of the Africans.

CENTULEN.: “The feast of blessed Nicholas, archbishop of Myra in Lycia, a man filled with the fountain of charity and with every form of piety. In Africa, Saints Dionysia, Dativa, Leontius, Aemilianus the physician, and the religious man named Tertius, Boniface, Servius, Victrix, and Majoricus the youth, all of whom were crowned under the Vandal persecution.”

BRUXELLEN. reports the first entry fairly purely, but lacks the second, which it has transferred to the following day. It adds: “At Saintes, blessed Martin, abbot, disciple of Saint Martin, bishop of the city of Tours. He rests in peace in the monastery that he himself built; at his tomb, miracles are very frequently performed by divine power.” It would have been better to postpone this entry to the following day. At the end it adds: “At Rome, Saint Eutacianus,” for *Eutychianus*.

HAGENOYEN. reports more about Nicholas than the Acts themselves mention. It has almost the entire second entry, but transposed according to its own preference.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Nicholas, bishop and confessor. Dionysia, Dativa, Leontia, and many other martyrs.”

[Col. 0774D] The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition adds concerning Nicholas: “And how distinguished this saint was among the foremost prelates, how renowned for miracles, how profitable in doctrine, how splendid in example, human speech can scarcely suffice to recount. He died in a good old age and was gathered to his fathers in the year of the Lord 358.” In the second entry, after “and Boniface” with three others, it adds, with corrupted names: “namely, Zerinus, Victor, and Meroicus, youthful martyrs. All of them, for confessing the Catholic faith under Huneric, king of the Arians, having been tortured with the gravest and innumerable punishments, were counted among the confessors of Christ.” At the end: “On the same day, Saint Ozella [for Asella], virgin.” See Surius.

[Col. 0775A] GREVEN.: “The names of the three martyrs who suffered in Africa with those named above are Servius, Victrix, and Majoricus the youth, who, following the example of the others and strengthened by the exhortations of his mother Dionysia, gave up his spirit under King Huneric in the contest of confession. Likewise in Africa, Saints Zelotus, Fortunatus, Hermogenes, Rogatus, Thegulus, and Agatha, virgin.” Concerning these, see the Hieronymian copies. He continues: “At Rome, blessed Nicholas, pope and confessor, concerning whom Martin testifies in his *Chronicle* that after Gregory the Great he was the holiest man. Asella, virgin.” I have already said that *Asella* should be written. See the Roman Martyrology and Castellan’s note.

[Col. 0776A] MOLAN. in the first edition adds only in smaller type: “Asella, virgin, blessed in her mother’s womb, as Jerome testifies.” Nothing is said of her in the later editions, in which one reads: “At Marcian, the feast of Saint Gertrude.” The notes added here and there in manuscript are by our John Gravius. She was a widow and the first abbess of Hamaticum, on the river Scarpe, not far from Douai. The same Gravius notes in the margin: “She died at Hamaticum in the year 655 and was later translated to Marcenas.” Castellan, in his universal Martyrology, forms the name somewhat differently, writing not *Gertrudis* but *Geretrudis*.

[Col. 0771]

The feast of blessed Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Lycia, concerning whom, among his many distinguished miracles, this notable event is related: while far away, he turned the emperor Constantine from the destruction of certain men to mercy by admonitions in a vision and by threats. In Africa, Saints Dionysia, Dativa, Leontia, and the religious man named Tertius, and Aemilianus and Boniface with three others, all of whom, for confessing the Catholic faith, were tortured with the gravest and innumerable punishments and deserved to be numbered among the confessors of Christ.

**VII Ides. Day 7.**

[Note: [Col. 0775A]]

So have Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0775B]]

Praten. and Munerat. read *Agatho*; the others more correctly have the form found in the text. Antuerp.-Maj. not improperly has *capitis*—“of the head”—instead of *pietate*, “for piety,” etc., but all the others have *capite*, “by beheading.” Molan. seems to have followed the second edition of Belin in transposing the final two entries, placing Fara before Martin. He too writes *Pharae*, as does Antuerp.-Maj.; but it is clear enough that this name has no connection with the Greek language. Greven. and Molan. read “miracles are very frequently performed by divine power,” etc., correctly according to Ado’s intention, but we prefer the spelling of the other Usuardian codices.

[Note: [Col. 0775B]]

Baronius, taking the opportunity presented by Julianus and Euno—concerning whom we treated with the *Romanum parvum*, Ado, and Usuard on 27 February—added on the same day the soldier who suffered on their account and who, in Christophorson’s Eusebian edition, is called Besa, as though he were their companion in martyrdom. On this day, however, while identifying Agatho in Ado’s or Usuard’s words, he observes:

“He seems here—Agatho—to have undergone a contest similar to that of the man whom Eusebius, from Dionysius of Alexandria, describes in Rufinus’s translation, book VI, chapter 30 [31 in our numbering], and who in Christophorson’s edition is also called Beza, book VI, chapter 34; concerning him we treated above on 3 March. His different name and a different date of death persuade us that he is another person.”

Thus writes the eminent man, whom I observe to have been deceived by the differences in the wording with which the translators rendered Eusebius. Let us identify the source itself, and it will become obvious that the soldier who is anonymous in Rufinus, book VI, chapter 31, whatever name may eventually be assigned to him, cannot possibly be divided into two persons.

The author of the *Romanum parvum*, consulting his usual source, named the aforementioned soldier—probably on his own authority and perhaps taking the designation from a notable work—“Agatho” because of his piety toward the dead, and read as follows: “At Alexandria, Agatho, martyr and soldier, under Decius.” Ado, transcribing and slightly expanding Rufinus’s passage, and Usuard, somewhat abridging it, identify Eusebius’s Besa so clearly—both in Christophorson’s chapter 34 and in Valesius’s chapter 41—that anyone comparing Rufinus with the present text can have no room for doubt.

Here are Rufinus’s own words:

“But when a certain military man was standing by and forbidding some people who wished also to mock the corpses of the dead, suddenly the entire crowd raised an outcry against him. The strongest of soldiers, now the Lord’s soldier, was brought before the judge; and, showing himself inferior nowhere, persevering in confession, he was condemned by the corrupt reading *capitis proprietate* [read: *pro pietate*, ‘for piety’].”

Our text could not point to its source more clearly; the same will again become evident in Macarius on the following day. Nor can anything be proved from the different dates of death, since I have so often shown that the author of the *Romanum parvum*, entirely at his own discretion, assigned most of the days to the cult of the saints whom he found in Rufinus. Add that this difference of dates was introduced solely by Baronius, who had found the name Besa on 28 February in no ancient Martyrology and was himself the first to note it there. By the same right he could have joined Macarius to the following day, as well as so many others mentioned in the same chapter of Rufinus. It therefore seems clear to us that Besa and Agatho are one and the same martyr described by Rufinus.

We discussed the confusion of the various Martins on 24 October, citing Castellan, who carefully distinguishes these saints of the same name both on that day and on this. The martyrologist of Vienna was the first to introduce into the sacred Fasti Martin of Saintes, who is commemorated here. He depicted him in such a way as clearly to show that he had before his eyes chapter 57 of Gregory of Tours’s *Glory of the Confessors*. I do not know whether any other records survive from which we might learn more fully about his deeds.

Our author abridged both of Ado’s entries in the text transmitted here. Burgundofara recurs in our Usuardian supplements on 3 April; on that day, we believe, it was transferred by mistake from the account found in her Life. Otherwise, it is certain that Usuard correctly and appropriately first recorded her on this day under the name Fara, elsewhere Burgundofara. Concerning the etymology of this name, see Mabillon, *Benedictine Century* II, page 438, where he produces from the Acts of Saints Columbanus, Eustasius, and Attala material concerning Burgundofara, or concerning the virtues and miraculous events performed in her time at the monastery of Eboriacum.

In the Roman Martyrology she is assigned to England on 3 April; on this day, to the district of Meaux. See Motherius’s note. I find much other material in my manuscript collections, from which the remaining matters may later be elucidated. Only Wandalbert followed the Hieronymian copies on this day, while omitting—or perhaps not knowing—our saints; he sang as follows:

“Polycarp with Theodore keeps the seventh day.”

[Note: [Col. 0777A]]

PRATEN. In our copy the following is placed at the end: “On the same day, the ordination of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan.” Since these words are underlined, I suppose they were added in the margin, although Castellan did not observe this; nevertheless, on the following day he carefully distinguished the supplement.

TORNACEN., pure in the first part, carries the second entry only as far as “abbot.” The rest is absent.

ROSWEYD., fairly pure in the text, adds: “The octave of Saint Andrew the Apostle.”

PULSANEN. is pure in the first part as far as “emperor.” Then: “Martin, abbot, disciple of blessed Martin, bishop of Tours.” The third entry is absent. It adds: “At Spoleto, the passion of Saint Sabinus, bishop, and Exuperantius and Marcellus, deacons.” Other codices speak only of Sabinus; his account may be seen in Rabanus.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN. begin: “In the monastery of Liberiacum, the feast of Saint Gerebald, [Col. 0777B] bishop.” The text follows. At the end all add: “The ordination of blessed Ambrose, bishop. And the octave of Saint Andrew.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., LOVAN., and LEYDEN-BELG. add to the pure text at the end: “In the monastery of Liberiacum, the feast of Saint Gerebald, bishop. On the same day, the ordination of Saint Ambrose, bishop. And the octave of Saint Andrew.”

LEYDEN-LATIN agrees with the preceding witnesses but describes Ambrose’s ordination more fully as follows:

“On the same day, the ordination of blessed Ambrose, bishop and confessor. When he came to Milan and was trying by his address to calm the disturbance that had arisen among the people concerning the election of a bishop for themselves, at the voice of a child who called him bishop, everyone suddenly agreed upon him with extraordinary unanimity. Fleeing the honor offered to him, he hid for some time, but at last, recognizing the divine will concerning him, he consented.”

[Col. 0777C] ULTRAJECT. agrees completely with this codex, but places Ambrose’s ordination first. ALBERG. and DANIC. do the same; they lack the final supplement concerning the octave of Saint Andrew.

CENTULEN.: “At Alexandria, blessed Agatho, martyr, under the emperor Decius. At Saintes, blessed Martin, abbot, who was a disciple of Saint Martin of Tours. At Spoleto, Saint Salvius [it means Sabinus or Savinus], bishop and martyr. And the octave of Saint Andrew the Apostle.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “The octave of Saint Andrew the Apostle.” The entry concerning Agatho follows, fairly purely. Then it gives Dionysia and the other African martyrs from the preceding day. Next:

“In the city of Spoleto, Saint Sabinus, bishop and martyr. And the feast of blessed Palmatius, illustrious martyr. In the district of Meaux, Saint Fara, virgin. In the city of Avennis, the feast of Saint Aricola. In the monastery of Liberiacum, the feast of Saint Gerebald, bishop. At Milan, the ordination of Saint Ambrose, bishop and [Col. 0777D] confessor.”

HAGENOYEN begins with the octave of Andrew, as does the preceding entry. It is also fairly pure in the entry for Agatho. Then:

“At Milan, the ordination of blessed Ambrose, bishop, who came there not as a bishop but as a judge; fleeing the honor offered to him, he wished to hide and flee, but could not. Then, when he understood the divine will toward him, he consented. His election was confirmed by the emperor Valentinian.”

It is fairly pure in the entries for Martin and Fara. Finally, at the end it adds as above: “In the monastery of Liberiacum, the feast of Saint Gerebald,” etc.

[Col. 0778A] VICTORIN. adds at the end: “At Spoleto, Saint Sabinus, bishop.” Others have *Savinius*, etc.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Fara, virgin, who fought wondrously for chastity. The octave of Andrew. Gerebaud, or Gereband, bishop.” Elsewhere: *Gerebald* or *Gerebold*.

BIGOTIAN. marked P. 5, places first: “In the monastery of Liberiacum, the feast of Saint Gerebald, bishop.”

REG. SUEC. marked no. 130: “At Milan, Saint Ambrose, bishop. At Spoleto, Saint Sabinus, bishop.”

In VATICAN no. 5949 Fara is omitted, but the following is added: “At Milan, the feast of Saint Ambrose, bishop and confessor. At Spoleto, Saint Savinus, bishop and martyr.”

FLORENTIN.: “At Spoleto, Saint Savinus, bishop and martyr. Likewise, Saints Venustianus, martyr, with his wife and children, as is related in the Acts of the aforesaid saint. In the monastery of Liberiacum, Saint Gerebald, [Col. 0778B] bishop. At Sens … Likewise, at the aforesaid city, Saint Eutropius, martyr.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition: “The octave of Saint Andrew the Apostle.” Concerning the ordination of Saint Ambrose, it has the account given above in LEYDEN-LATIN. The entry for Agatho is fairly pure. Then:

“At the city of Saintes, Saint Martin, abbot, disciple of Saint Martin, bishop of the city of Tours. At his tomb miracles are very frequently performed by divine power. He rested in peace in the monastery that he founded. In the city of Spoleto, the deposition of Saint Sabinus, bishop and confessor.”

Concerning Gerebald it has the text given above; concerning Fara, it is pure.

BELIN.: “At Milan, the ordination of Saint Ambrose, bishop and confessor, whose holiness adorns the entire city of Milan.” It lacks Martin; the rest is fairly pure. In the second edition, concerning Ambrose it reads: “whose holiness adorns the universal Church.” Martin is added at the end.

GREVEN.: “The second finding of the holy cross. The octave [Col. 0778C] of Saint Andrew. At Antioch, Saints Polycarp and Theodosius. Near Milan, the episcopal ordination of blessed Ambrose. When he wished to calm the disturbance that had arisen among the people concerning the election of a bishop for themselves, the voice of a child rang out, saying, ‘Ambrose, bishop.’ Immediately, by unanimous consent, he was carried away and, although he resisted strongly, consecrated bishop. At Spoleto, blessed Sabinus, bishop and confessor. Marcellus, bishop. In the monastery of Liberiacum, Saint Gerebold, bishop of Bayeux and confessor. Out of zeal for chastity, he refused an assault and, like another Joseph, was shut in prison so that he might perish from hunger, but enjoyed the company of angels. Then, tied to a millstone, he was thrown into the sea, but by divine providence he reached the shores of Normandy unharmed. At his arrival the trees there blossomed, the blind were given sight, and the lame received the ability to walk. He himself, made bishop of Bayeux by a heavenly oracle, illustrious in life and miracles, rested in peace. On the same day, Dodovald, priest. In Ireland, Boethius, confessor.”

[Col. 0778D] MOLAN.: “At Bayeux, in the monastery of Liberiacum, the deposition of blessed Gerebald, bishop and confessor of the aforesaid city. At Milan, the ordination of Ambrose, bishop and confessor, whose holiness adorns the universal Church.” He adds in smaller type: “When he was lying in his final illness, he said: ‘I do not fear dying, because we have a good Lord.’” The later editions, in italics, prefix to the text “At Milan,” etc., through “adorns,” from the second edition of BELIN. At the end they have the entry concerning Liberiacum as in the first edition. Finally, an entry not found in the others: “On the same day, Saint Giraldus, bishop of Velletri and confessor.”

[Col. 0775]

At Alexandria, the feast of blessed Agatho, martyr, under the emperor Decius. He was a soldier and forbade certain people who wished to mock the corpses of the martyrs; suddenly the entire crowd raised an outcry against him. When he was brought before the judge and persevered in confession, he was condemned to death by beheading for his piety. At the city of Saintes, Saint Martin, abbot, at whose tomb miracles are very frequently performed by divine power. In the district of Meaux, Saint Fara, virgin.

**VI Ides. Day 8.**

[Note: [Col. 0779]]

Taken solely from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0779A]]

Molan. correctly wrote *Eutychiani*; Praten. has, not altogether wrongly, *Euthiciani*; the others generally have *Euticiani*, as in the text. Praten. reads *trecentos*, “three hundred,” which is better than the form used by the others; some use numeral letters. *Macharii* is the established spelling of the codices both here and elsewhere. In the Herinien. codex, after *majori constantia*, the word *ad* has slipped in; it is incorrect and contrary to the construction.

[Note: [Col. 0779A]]

The oldest surviving memory of Eutychian, the pope, in ecclesiastical calendars is found in the Bucherian Calendar, under the heading “Depositions of Bishops,” in these words: “6 December: Eutychian at Callistus.” In most of the Hieronymian Martyrologies one reads on this day: “At Rome, Eutychian”; or, as in the most ancient Epternacensis: “At Rome, the deposition of Eutychian [Eutychianus], bishop,” whom it had also placed on the preceding day: “And at Rome, Eutychian, bishop.” From this, however, uncertainty arises concerning the true day either of his death or of his martyrdom, which others assign to 25 and 27 July; whether this resulted from some translation is unknown. His martyrdom is likewise uncertain, since his deposition is so clearly expressed; but these matters must be discussed elsewhere.

Meanwhile, the author of the *Romanum parvum* explicitly recorded: “At Rome, Eutychian, pope and martyr, who buried 342 martyrs with his own hand.” Just as Ado expanded this from the *Pontificals*, so our author copied it word for word, retaining the number 342, which in the Catalogues published before volume I of April, page XXVIII, is extended to 362—easily a mistake caused by the transposition of letters, or perhaps because the compiler of the *Romanum parvum* consulted a different catalogue.

The Viennese author adopted another error, reducing Eutychian’s eight-year pontificate to a single year; he also made a second error in the name of the emperor Aurelian, which should correctly be connected with the beginning, not the end, of Eutychian’s reign. Yet this earlier error, combined with the supposed brevity of the pontificate, which Eusebius also asserts, could have placed Eutychian’s final day near the end of Aurelian’s reign. We prefer the opinion of Baronius, Henschenius, and other learned men concerning the longer duration.

Whether Baronius correctly changed the tyrant’s name in the modern Roman Martyrology to Numerian is a more difficult question. As far as I know, no Acts of Eutychian survive; in due time a historical collection could be composed from documents gathered here and there, such as Tillemont began in volume IV, page 365. Here is Wandalbert’s metrical encomium:

“Eutychian, pope, you shine with the blessed blood of an old man.”

Just as our author copied his first entry from Ado, so he transferred the second word for word, except for three words: “who was of Libyan race.” This is Macarius, called *Macar* by some, whom the author of the *Romanum parvum* took from chapter 31 of book VI of Rufinus’s History, cited above. There he immediately follows the soldier, or military man, of the preceding day, as follows:

“Another man, named Macarius, of Libyan race, when the judge tried at length to persuade him to deny, and he professed his faith with still greater constancy, was finally ordered to be burned alive.”

Epimachus and Alexander follow there; concerning them and the other martyrs contained in the cited chapter of Rufinus, the account is given on 12 December. Thus it is entirely clear that the selection of such days or festivals depended solely upon the discretion of the author of the *Romanum parvum*.

[Note: [Col. 0779B]]

PRATEN. has added in the margin, or at least in another hand: “The conception of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God.” More about this will be given below from other codices. See Castellan’s note and Motherius, page 445.

TORNACEN., pure in the first part, cuts out the whole account of Macarius, beginning with “who, when,” etc.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. adds at the end after the text: “The conception of Saint Mary, Virgin.”

ROSWEYD. at the end: “At Trier, Eucharius, bishop [Col. 0779C] and confessor, who was one of the seventy-two disciples sent by the Apostle Peter to evangelize Gaul. On the same day, Zeno and Syrus, confessors.” Concerning Syrus, see 12 September. Wandalbert placed Zeno after Eutychian on this day:

“Zeno too possesses this day, joined to it in the honor of martyrdom.”

PULSANEN. is pure in the first part as far as Callistus. Then: “On that same day, at Alexandria, blessed Macarius, subdeacon [it would be better to read ‘under Decius’].” All the rest is absent. In the margin, in a very recent hand, is added: “The conception of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God,” as above in the first codex.

MUNERAT. begins: “The conception of the glorious Virgin.”

GREVEN. begins: “The conception of the most blessed Mary, perpetual virgin and glorious mother of the Lord.” At the end of the text he also adds: “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Leonard, bishop and confessor.” I do not know this bishop, nor do I know sufficiently who the priest named below may be, unless he has been confused with another Leonard.

MOLAN. prefixes to the text, in italics and from BELIN.: “The conception of the most sacred Virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 0780B] ANTUERP.-MAX., LOVAN., and LEYDEN-BELG. have MUNERAT.’s opening: “The conception of the glorious Virgin.” The text follows, and near the end they add: “At Trier, Saint Eucharius, the first bishop and confessor of that place, who was one of the seventy-two disciples of the Lord.”

ULTRAJECT. has another opening: “The conception of blessed Mary, Virgin.” Concerning Eutychian, after “buried,” it inserts into the text:

“He established that only grain, beans, and grapes should be blessed upon the altar, and that whoever buried a martyr should not bury him without a dalmatic or a purple colobium.”

LEYDEN.-LAT. has its beginning and end as ANTUERP.-MAX., etc. In the entry for Eutychian it agrees with ULTRAJECT. It also agrees with ALBERG. But the latter writes concerning the Conception: “The feast of the glorious Conception of the Virgin Mary,” which was added in the more recent hand in DANIC. In the remaining details the cited codices agree.

CENTULEN.: “The pious solemnity of this night and day proclaims the beginning of human redemption and the dawn of our illumination, when, by God’s favor, Mary, mother and virgin, was conceived, destined to bear the Son of God. At Rome, Saint Eutychian, pope and martyr, who buried 342 martyrs in various places. At Trier, Saint Eucharius, bishop and confessor, whom blessed Peter ordained at Rome and sent into Gaul with Maternus and Valerius. At Alexandria, blessed Macarius, martyr under Decius.”

[Col. 0780D] BRUXELLEN.: “The Conception of blessed Mary, ever-virgin and mother of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The text follows in its unaltered form. Then: “At Rome, Saints Zeno, Eusebius, and Successus, bishops, and Uranius, priest.” Zeno does not belong here; see the Hieronymian Martyrologies. [Col. 0781A] “At Trier, blessed Eucharius, the first bishop of that city and confessor, who was,” etc., as in ANTUERP.-MAX. “And Saint Romaric, confessor. On the same day, in the territory of Dun, the deposition of Saint Leonard, outstanding confessor.”

HAGENOYEN recounts certain things about the feast of the Conception which I do not think worth describing. He moved Eutychian to the following day. Thus, in second place, he has: “In the city of Trier, the deposition of Saint Eucharius, the first bishop of that city. He was one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples. There, while preaching, he raised two dead persons; and when at a certain time he made the sign of the cross over a paralytic, a dead man who had been lying hidden beneath the ground rose there, and because of this miracle he converted and baptized the whole city, turning it away from idolatry. He performed many other miracles; he built churches, sat as bishop there for twenty-three years, and died in peace.” His entry for Macarius is fairly pure. Then: “Likewise, blessed Leonard, bishop and confessor. In the city of Avignon, beside the Rhône, Saint Caesaria, virgin and martyr.” [Col. 0781B] I know this Caesaria no better than I know the bishop Leonard. This evidently refers to Casaria; see Castellanus. We have collected various materials concerning her, to be published in the Acts under 9 December. “In the monastery of Habetum, Saint Romaric, abbot.”

AQUICINCT inserts into the text concerning Eutychian almost the following: “He decreed that whoever buried a martyr was under no circumstances to bury him without a dalmatic and purple colobium, and that only grain, beans, and grapes were to be blessed upon the altar.”

The Codex of Ursinus a Rosemberg: “In the city of Verona, Saint Zeno, bishop and confessor.” See 12 April, and Castellanus’s note for this day. “At Trier, Saint Eucharius, the first bishop and confessor of that church, who was one of the seventy-two disciples.”

AMBIANEN.: “In the territory of Dun, Saint Leonard, outstanding confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT. begins as follows: “The sanctification of blessed Mary.” The following note is added: [Col. 0781C] “But in the year 1470 the following ordinance was issued by our General Chapter: For the praiseworthy uniformity to be observed in our order, and especially in the celebration of divine worship, we decree that the feast of the Virgin Mary, which the Church now solemnly celebrates on 8 December, shall henceforth be universally celebrated throughout the order under the name of the Conception, as it has otherwise been determined by the Church, notwithstanding the statute that mentions sanctification.” Finally there follows: “Of Romaric, abbot. Of Eutychian, pope. Of Macarius, martyr.”

ALTEMPS.: “Likewise, the translation of Saint Sebastian, martyr, and of Gregory, teacher of the English.” See the Additions for the following day.

FLORENTIN.: “At Verona, the feast of Saint Zeno, bishop and confessor, a man of complete holiness. Likewise, the passion of Saint Zeno, bishop and martyr, who suffered and was buried at Nicomedia, under the sacrilegious emperor Julian.” Then only STROZZIAN.: “At Rome, [Col. 0781D] in the cemetery of Priscilla, Saint Crescentian, martyr, as one reads in the Acts of Saint Marcellus, pope.” See above, 24 November.

MONTIS SANCTI.: “The celebrated feast of Saint Romaric, eminent duke and accomplished confessor, is commemorated. Though he was of the noblest lineage, he despised the showy trappings of wealth and indicated that he wished to belong to almighty God and Saint Peter. He enriched his monastery—which in ancient times was called the fortress of Habendum and is now named Mount Saint-Romaric—with all his slaves and estates, together with certain privileges. Rome, too, by the authority and decree of the kings, determined and judged that it had been subjected.” These statements are obscure.

[Col. 0782A] GAUDIACEN.: “In the territory of Lyon, at a place called Sapiniacus, the translation of Saint Baldomer, man of God and confessor.”

DIVIONEN.: “In the territory of Dijon, the deposition of Saint Leonard, outstanding confessor.”

REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.: “In the territory of Dun, the deposition of Saint Leonard, confessor.”

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition: “The Conception of the glorious Virgin Mary, mother of God, as she was conceived in the womb of blessed Anna, her mother.” Concerning Eutychian it has what ULTRAJECT. has above. Its entry for Macarius is unaltered. Then: “At Trier, Saint Eucharius, the first bishop and confessor of that place. He was one of the seventy-two disciples of the Lord and was later sent to preach by the blessed apostle Peter, together with his disciples Valerius and Maternus, who in the course of time succeeded him in the same bishopric. He recalled the people from the worship of idols and converted them to the faith of Christ. In the territory of Dun, the deposition of Saint Leonard, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0782B] BELIN. begins: “The immaculate Conception of the most holy Virgin Mary, mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The text follows fairly purely, but at the end: “On the same day, at Verona, Saint Zeno, bishop and confessor.” See above. “Likewise, Saint Martin, abbot.” From the preceding day. In another edition, *τὸ immaculata* has been struck out. Martin is omitted, but the following is added: “On the same day, Saint Leonard, priest.”

GREVEN. at the end: “On the same day, according to the Catalog and others, blessed Zeno, bishop and martyr of Verona, whom blessed Gregory mentions in the third book of the *Dialogues*, chapter 5. Usuard places him on the day before the Ides of April. At Trier, Saint Eucharius, the first bishop and confessor of that city. He was one of the seventy-two disciples of the Lord, and was sent by blessed Peter to Trier with two others, Valerius and Maternus; he recalled the people from the worship of idols, and, full of good works, rested in the Lord. Genebandus, bishop of Laon and confessor, concerning whom see the Acts of blessed Remigius. At Rome, the feast of blessed Eusebius, bishop. Here is the feast of Syrus, first bishop and confessor of Pavia. Usuard places him on the second day before the Ides of September, that is, on the day when his memory and that of Yventius, his disciple and successor, are commemorated together. On the same day, Saint Romaric, abbot and confessor. When he was prominent at the palace of King Theudebert of the Austrasians, he renounced everything and, at the monastery of Luxeuil, first became a monk under Saint Amatus and then an abbot. Once, in the Vosges, after the vessel containing wine had been emptied the previous day and left without a tap, he restored it full by prayer and the sign of the cross. To the astonishment produced by the miracle there was this further circumstance: when the vessel itself was opened, not a drop of the liquid given from heaven flowed onto the ground. Likewise, Eutychian, monk and confessor, who, as the first book of the *Tripartite History* says, lived on Mount Olympus in Bithynia. Filled with divine grace for curing diseases and performing miracles in deeds and things, he was held in very high esteem by Constantine Augustus because of the excellence of his life.”

MOLAN. at the end: “On the same day, at Verona, Saint Zeno, bishop and confessor. Likewise, Saint Martin, abbot. On the same day, Saint Leonard, priest and confessor, in the territory of Dun. At Trier, the feast of Saint Anastasia.” In smaller type: “On the same day, Saint Romaric, abbot of Luxeuil and confessor. Likewise, Eutychian, monk,” etc., taken from GREVEN. Other editions: “At Trier, the deposition of Saint Eucharius, bishop and confessor. And of Saint Anastasia. On the same day, Saint Romaric, confessor. In the territory of Dun, Saint Leonard, priest.” Concerning Zeno, as in the first edition. “On the eighth day, the holy father Patapius.” See the eulogy in the Roman Martyrology.]

[Col. 0777]

At Rome, the feast of blessed Eutychian, pope, who governed the Church for one year and was crowned with martyrdom under Aurelian. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus, and he himself buried 342 martyrs with his own hand in various places. On the same day, at Alexandria, Saint Macarius, martyr, who, when a judge tried to persuade him with many words to deny the faith, and he professed it with all the greater constancy, was finally ordered to be burned alive. [Bouillart, in the margin: “The most blessed Conception of Mary, virgin and mother of God.”]

V Idus. Day 9. [Note: [Col. 0783]

The entries of Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. are pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0784A]

Antuerp.-Maj. and Molan. correctly write *Leocadiae*, but in the text the reading of the other codices has been retained. Dacian has been discussed elsewhere; here again some read *Datiano*, while TORNACEN. has *Deciano*, and so forth. But what does Munerat. mean by *praefecto Hyspaniano*? I suspect that the two words *Hispaniarum Daciano* were erroneously fused into one by the typographer’s incompetence, just as another edition of Greven. [Col. 0784A] very badly formed *Lualiae* in place of *Eulaliae*. Munerat. has *dire* for *dira*. Molan. reads “he gave back his spirit to Christ,” which is an Adonian reading; but Usuard’s reading is supported by the other codices. Some codices have *Cipriani*, as does Greven., but Praten., Herinien., and others more correctly have the form found in the text. Antuerp.-Maj. is mistaken in giving *Petragoricae* instead of *Petragorici*.]

[Note: [Col. 0783A]

The illustrious Toledan virgin Leocadia, who is reported here first, is known neither in the Hieronymian codices, nor in Bede’s series, nor in Wandalbert. She was first and very simply recorded by the author of the *Little Roman Martyrology*: “Of Leocadia, virgin,” with no mention of place, time, or martyrdom. From this one may most plausibly infer that the compiler of this Martyrology had seen none of the saint’s Acts. Nevertheless, some materials must once have existed from which the Martyrologist of Vienne drew the circumstance of her death that was transferred from his work into our text. One might ask why Leocadia is celebrated on this day, if it is true that she gave up her spirit to Christ when she heard the grievous tortures of blessed Eulalia and the other martyrs; for Eulalia of Mérida, who is undoubtedly indicated here, suffered on 10 December. The solution accepted by us, and the only true one, is now sufficiently well known: namely, that it was entirely arbitrary for Ado, the pioneer of this practice, to assign such celebrations to fixed days. Ado himself, and after him Usuard, followed this practice in good faith. Leocadia’s widespread remembrance derives from the councils of Toledo held in her church, and likewise from three basilicas in the city of Toledo alone dedicated to her name. On these see Baronius’s note, where her bodily translation is also discussed, a matter which Molanus, in the *Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium*, calls into question. We shall discuss that controversy elsewhere and publish some manuscript Acts of Leocadia, which, so far as I know, have not yet appeared in print. I do not discuss their authenticity here; indeed, I readily admit that the longer passion preserved among us seems rather a panegyric than an exact account of events. Surius found nothing apart from the Adonian eulogy, to which he added Marineus’s words about the saint’s being thrown from the walls of the city of Toledo by others—words that indicate a genuine martyrdom—whereas Leocadia is called only “the most blessed and holy confessor” by the Fourth Council of Toledo, in Labbe, volume V, column 1702. One may consult the few things Tillemont says about our saint in volume V, page 57. Whoever wishes to investigate more closely the basis on which Leocadia was assigned to the Carmelite order should consult Papebrochius’s *Responses*, article XVI, no. 77 onward. For now, let what has been presented suffice concerning the origin of our text and its transmission into Usuard.

Cyprian, abbot of Périgueux, was introduced by Ado alone. Here he consulted another source of his, namely Gregory of Tours’s *Book on the Glory of the Confessors*, as he often does elsewhere, extracting the eulogy from chapter 100, which Our author adopted in full. We know of no further information handed down about the saint’s deeds. Neither Peter, in the *Catalog*, book I, chapter 51, nor Trithemius, in *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, cited by Baronius, could supply anything more from elsewhere. Whether this Cyprian should be counted among the Benedictine order will be examined elsewhere. On this day Wandalbert is entirely occupied with the translation of Saint Sebastian; we shall give his verses among the Additions.]

[Note: [Col. 0783C]

PRATEN. remains among the pure witnesses, although on this day it reports the text only as far as “worn down in custody”; the leaf was cut away for the remainder, as Sirmundus testifies. He supplied the rest of the text from another codex, which we call B.

TORNACEN., pure in the text, adds: “At the monastery of Jotro, Saint Balda, virgin.”

ROSWEYD. adds at the end: “The translation of Saint Sebastian, martyr.” This is the translation that, as I said, Wandalbert celebrated in verse as follows:

> We celebrate Sebastian, transferred from Rome  
> on the fifth day, for whom the fields of Gaul rejoice  
> in their own patron; for him a vast temple rises  
> on the shore, its heights shining with ancient splendor.

In the aforementioned codex there follows: “In Africa, Successus, bishop and martyr, and twenty-four others. At Antioch, Aherontius, martyr, and nine others.” These entries must be corrected from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

PULSANEN. reports the first entry as follows: “The feast of Saint [Col. 0783D] Leocadia, virgin.” In another witness it comes somewhat closer to the pure form.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., UGHELLIAN., ANTUERP.-MAX., together with six codices of middling authority, and BIGOTIAN., marked P. 5: all agree in this addition: “In Africa, Saints Peter, Successus, Bassinus, Porphyrius, and Urbanus.” Some of these write *Basini* and omit *et*.

CENTULEN.: “In Spain, Saint Leocadia, virgin, who at Toledo, lacerated by the harshest imprisonment, gave back her undefiled spirit to Christ. At Périgueux, Saint Cyprian, abbot, a man of magnificent holiness and a confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “At Rome, Melchiades, pope and martyr, who decreed that under no circumstances should a fast be held on the Lord’s Day, because on that day the pagans observed what was almost a sacred fast.” This recurs repeatedly above, under 10 January and on the following day. It continues: “At the monastery of Celles, the feast of Saint Leocadia, virgin. She, by the prefect,” etc., in pure form. Notice that this indicates the monastery commonly called Saint-Ghislain, where they say her body was brought from Spain; whether it was transferred there after Toledo is disputed. Then: “In Africa, Saints [Col. 0784D] Peter, Successus, Bassinus, Porphyrius, Urbanus, Victor, and Boniface, martyrs. At Antioch, Saints Gerontius, Polentia, Silvana, Valentinus, Felix, and Eutychianus, martyrs.” All these were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; see there. The final announcement is fairly pure.

[Col. 0785A] HAGENOYEN transferred Pope Eutychian here; enough was said about him on the preceding day. Then: “At Pavia, the feast of Saint Syrus, bishop of that city, a man of great holiness.” He recurs frequently both on the preceding day and here; I have already said that he is treated under 12 September. Leocadia follows, but is not reported entirely purely. Then: “In Africa, Saints Peter, Successus, Passinus, Porphyrius, and Urbanus, martyrs.” Something has also been altered in the entry for Cyprian. Then: “In the district of Vimacium, the feast of Saint Waleric, priest and confessor.” See 12 December. “Likewise, in Jerusalem, the nativity of Saint Joachim, father of the holy Virgin Mary, mother of God. In the territory of Limoges [read: Lemovicum], Saint Valeria, virgin.” She is in the Roman Martyrology; see Castellanus’s note.

AQUICINCT, along with many other codices, writes *Datiano* for *Daciano*. At the end: “At Ticinum, the deposition of Saint Syrus, bishop and confessor.” See what was said concerning HAGENOYEN.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130: “On the same day, Saint Syrus, bishop.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT. lacks the entire text for this day and reports only this announcement: “Eucharius, bishop of Trier.” Concerning him, see the Additions for the preceding day.

REG. SUEC., under no. 428: “On the same day, the reception of the bodies of the blessed Sebastian and Pope Gregory.”

CODEX D. DU CHEVAL., marked B: “In Africa, Saints Peter, Bassinus, Porphyrius, and Urbanus.” It would agree with the codices of middling authority, etc., except that the name of Successus is missing.

In the VATICAN codex marked no. 5949 the following is added to the text: “And Saint Zeno, confessor.” See what was said under the preceding day.

FLORENTIN. at the end: “At Ticinum, or Pavia, Saint Syrus, bishop and confessor.”

[Col. 0785C] The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition: In the entry for Leocadia it inserts the names of the tyrants Diocletian and Maximian. In second place: “In Africa, Saints Peter, Successus, Bassinus, [Col. 0786A] Porphyrius, and Urbanus, martyrs.” The entry for Cyprian follows, fairly pure. Then: “On the same day, the commemoration of blessed Joachim, patriarch, father of the glorious Virgin Mary. At Trier, Saint Anastasia, virgin. At Soest, the arrival of Saint Patroclus, martyr.” See GREVEN.

BELIN. in the first edition adds to the text: “In Africa, Saints Peter, Successus, and Bassianus. On the same day, blessed Syrus, bishop of Pavia.” The second edition adds: “At Limoges, Saint Valeria, virgin and martyr.”

GREVEN.: “The solemn commemoration of Joachim, patriarch and father of the glorious mother of God, Mary, is observed here. The translation of Saint Bartholomew the apostle from Benevento to Rome. In Africa, Saints Successus, bishop, Peter, Bassinus, Porphyrius, Urbanus, Victor, Boniface, and eighteen others. At Antioch, Saints Gerontius, Polentia, Silvana, Valentina, Felix, and Eutychianus. At Verona, Saint Proculus, the fourth bishop of that city and confessor. When, under the emperor Maximian, he burned with the desire for martyrdom and voluntarily offered himself to the pagans, they beat him with blows and clubs as though he were a senile madman and drove him outside the city; at length, renowned for signs and virtues, he rested in peace.” See what we said about the various Proculi in the Observations for 1 December. Then: “At Soest, a town in the diocese of Cologne, the arrival of Saint Patroclus, martyr, transferred there from the city of Troyes by Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, of holy memory. Caesaria, virgin and martyr.” See what was said on the preceding day. “At Trier, Saint Anastasia, virgin.”

MOLAN.: “In Africa, Saints Peter, Successus, and Bassianus. On the same day, blessed Syrus, bishop of Pavia.” He copied both entries from BELIN. He continues: “At the monastery of Jotro, Saint Balda, abbess.” See Castellanus. “At Limoges, Saint Valeria, virgin and martyr.” In smaller type: “Of whom Martial writes in his second letter to the people of Toulouse, chapter 8.” Later editions [Col. 0786C] have exactly the same material concerning the three African martyrs, Syrus, and Balda; nothing concerning Valeria, but she has been transferred here to the following day.]

[Col. 0781]

The feast of Saint Leocadia, virgin, who, after being worn down by the harsh imprisonment inflicted by Dacian, prefect of the Spains, at Toledo [Bouillart, [Col. 0783] “cruel”], gave back her undefiled spirit to Christ, having heard of the most grievous tortures of blessed Eulalia and the other martyrs, with her knees placed in prayer. [Note: [Col. 0783A] At this point the leaf was torn from the codex. But the person who restored it, because he used larger letters, left this article incomplete and cut off more than half of it. What was missing was supplied from Pratensis B by Sollerius. I commend the action and imitate it. BOUILLART.] On the same day, Saint Cyprian, abbot of Périgueux, a man of magnificent holiness and outstanding in miracles.

IV Idus. Day 10. [Note: [Col. 0785]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0785D]

The principal and more noteworthy question concerns the name of the place where Carpophorus and Abundius suffered. The *Little Roman Martyrology* clearly named Spoletum, unless Rosweydus perhaps applied a correcting hand. In Ado it is certainly written “at the city of Hispolis.” The Usuardine codices vary. Among them, Praten. and Belin. distinctly read *Spoletanam*; Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., *Spolitanam*; Roswey. and Molan., *Hispalitanam*; the rest generally have *Hispolitanam* with Ado, and there is no sufficient reason to persuade us that Usuard departed from him.

But where, finally, is that city of Hispolis to be sought? Here lies the difficulty. To solve it, the Plantinian Bede inappropriately introduces Hispalis of Baetica; those who do so, if I am not mistaken, vainly contend that these martyrs belonged there, as they habitually transport any saints whatsoever into Spain on the basis of even the slightest similarity of names. If there was a Carpophorus who was bishop of Seville, he is entirely distinct from ours. Here the more cautious Baronius refrained from naming the place. I would not hesitate to choose Spoletum, or at least its territory, which is more or less what Castellanus’s note comes down to: the place would be Sassovivo, near Foligno, between Spoleto and Spello—called *Hispellum* in Latin—from which the formation of the city-name *Hispolitanam* would be very easy. We discussed Spello, or Hispello rendered otherwise in Latin, on 18 May under Saint Felix; see the Acts, volume IV for May, page 167. If anyone finds something better, we shall gladly accept it. Janningus will provide more in the dissertation cited several times, to be published in its proper place.

Another difficulty concerns Eulalia’s age. Some codices make her only twelve years old, whereas, following the most authoritative witnesses and Ado, we think Usuard wrote thirteen years. Munerat. wrongly reads *jugulata* (“throat-cut”) for *exungulata* (“torn by clawing”). We have retained *Carpofori*, etc., according to the usual orthography of the codices. *Abundi*, *Abundacii*, *Datiano*, and so on are for the most part scribal errors.]

[Note: [Col. 0787]

Our first announcement here again derives from the *Little Roman Martyrology*. It is marked there in second place, after Eulalia, in these words: “At Spoleto, Carpophorus, priest, and Abundius, deacon.” Rabanus wrote without giving a location: “On the same day, Saints Habundius and Carpopholus, martyrs.” Ado shaped the location in such a way as to provide material for many complications; otherwise he composed an eulogy whose greater part Usuard extracted, as it is transmitted in our text. No other Martyrologist preserves any memory of these saints.

The Acts, in the form published by Mombritius, preceded Ado. In the judgment of Baronius—and indeed of anyone not wholly inexperienced—they are very corrupt, so much so that I do not see how they could easily have been purged of all their errors. Whether this was accomplished by John Baptist Bracchescus, a Dominican, in the Life cited by Baronius, I cannot determine, since I have not yet seen it. We have discussed these saints and their companions, the saints of Umbria, elsewhere with Bollandus, and have more than once referred readers to Janning’s treatise on the Twelve Saints of Umbria. An appropriate place may be given to it on 9 July, when Brictius, one of the twelve, is to be discussed. I do not think it worthwhile to linger over the matter here. Elsewhere we cited Tillemont, volume V, page 132. The question of the place has been treated in the *Variants*; our manuscript collections concerning the passion and translation of the saints will be illustrated in due course.

Among the Spanish virgins crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, Eulalia is rightly considered one of the most celebrated—not the Eulalia of Barcelona, whom we discussed on 12 February, but the one who suffered at Mérida. In my view, she is mentioned on the preceding day in the eulogy of Leocadia. One or the other—for the moment we assume there were two—is known in the Carthaginian Calendar: “On the fourth day before the Ides of December, Saint Eulalia.” In the Hieronymian codices the name of Eulalia recurs on three consecutive days, this day, 11 December, and 12 December: in the first and last entries at Almeria or Almería, and in the middle one at Rome. I would not deny that there may have been several women of that name; but unless I am greatly mistaken, *Almeria* has intruded there in place of *Emerita*, with some codices explicitly reading *Eremita*. Florentinius discusses this matter, as well as the repetition, at greater length.

Bede celebrated no Eulalia on 12 February; hence Baronius assigned the woman of Barcelona to that day: “The feast of Saint Eulalia, virgin, at Barcelona,” etc. Rabanus followed him in this, while nevertheless reporting the Eulalia of Mérida on 12 December. The *Little Roman Martyrology* also distinguishes them, expressing Barcelona on 12 February, but here giving: “Eulalia, virgin and martyr,” thus apparently assuming that they were certainly different. Ado likewise gives different eulogies to each, although he confused some things when he claimed that he had taken the Barcelonan woman from the passion of Saint Leocadia.

Whatever our text reports on either day is Adonian. Yet the confusion has still not been removed. Henschenius discussed it at greater length in the Acts under 12 February; it must again be examined and clarified in the same work on this day. The principal question is whether there was one Eulalia or two. Those who wish Eulalia to have been born at Barcelona and suffered at Mérida, or those who transfer one born and martyred at Mérida to Barcelona, avoid the difficulties of the Acts only to fall into others. Certainly the documents of the Sacramentaries or Missals cited by Ruinart suggest that there were two, whatever may have been attributed from the Acts of one to the other.

Let us acknowledge with the distinguished writer that neither side offers certain arguments capable of settling the matter completely; this is also the direction taken by Tillemont’s note in volume V, page 713. Meanwhile, Prudentius sang the praises of the Eulalia of Mérida magnificently in the third hymn of his often-cited work *On Crowns* (*περὶ στεφάνων*), which should be consulted with the notes of the distinguished Ruinart, beginning on page 497. Baronius’s note lists other encomiasts, whose enumeration I omit. From all these materials, setting aside the Acts—of which we possess many—Tillemont constructed another sequence of her Life in volume V, beginning on page 320.

The distinction between the Eulalias is most clearly supported by two distichs of Wandalbert. We assigned one to the Eulalia of Barcelona on 12 February; here we append the other:

> On the fourth day we venerate with holy love  
> Eulalia, the Spaniard, whose blood and bones  
> preserve Mérida.

But what are we to say of Julia, Eulalia’s fellow virgin? I find nothing on which I can safely rely. Prudentius’s silence sufficiently shows that she was unknown to him. Nor do the Acts preserved by Mombritius, or the other manuscripts in our possession, ever mention Julia. Those who derive her from the present text of the Echternach codex easily observe that the name Julia has been substituted there for Eulalia. It remains, therefore, that she rests solely on Ado’s authority, since he may have found her in other Acts of Eulalia. We shall investigate this more carefully elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0787C]

TORNACEN. lacks the first entry; in the second it is pure, while in the third it is mutilated, stopping at the words: “Julia, virgin.”

ROSWEYD., fairly pure in the text, has at the end: “At Rome, Melchiades, pope and martyr.”

PULSANEN. has the entry for Eulalia first, as far as “virgin.” The second, concerning Julia, is partly cut away and partly mutilated. The entire eulogy of Carpophorus and Abundius has been deleted.

ANTUERP.-MAX., together with six other codices of middling authority, places before a fairly pure text at the beginning: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, Saint Melchiades, pope, who, after governing the Roman Church for four years, was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callistus.” See AQUICINCT.

CENTULEN.: “At Mérida, a city of Spain, Saint Eulalia, virgin, who, after suffering many tortures under Dacian, was finally hung on the rack and burned with fire placed beside her. In confessing Christ she gave up her spirit. On the same day and in the same place, Saint Julia, her attendant. Likewise, in the same province, Saints Carpophorus, priest, and Habundius, deacon, who, after many tortures inflicted upon them, were executed with the sword.” This is the only Usuardine codex in which those two martyrs are assigned to Spain on this day; on 12 December BRUXELLEN. adds them.

BRUXELLEN. begins with Eulalia and adds to the text: “And in the sight of the Christians she rose toward heaven in the form of a snow-white dove. By order of the prefect her sacred body hung upon the wood for three days, but snow fell upon the girl’s body from above, and by divine grace it was whitened and covered with snowy brightness.” Its entry for Julia is not entirely pure. At the end: “And the feast of Saint Paul, whose passion is recorded.” More precise information is needed.

HAGENOYEN. is somewhat interpolated in the first and second entries. Then follows: “On the same day, at Rome, the feast of Saint Melchiades, pope and martyr, who governed the Roman Church for three years, six months, and eight days. He was the thirty-first after Peter, and [Col. 0788D] decreed that Christians should under no circumstances fast on Sunday and Thursday, because the pagans observed those days as though they were a sacred fast. He too was crowned with martyrdom under Maximian. At Vienna, Saint Sindulf, bishop and confessor.” Mosander assigns this to Ado, but Rosweydus rejected it into an appendix. “In the district of Chur, Saint Eymerica, virgin and martyr. Likewise, Saint Lucius, king, who was burned for the faith of Christ.” Julia is reported last, in a reasonably pure form.

AQUICINCT. adds at the end the entire announcement concerning Melchiades, which Mosander likewise attributes to Ado, while Rosweydus rejected it. It reads: “At Rome, the deposition of Melchiades, pope. He decreed that on Sunday [add: and Thursday] no believer should fast, because the pagans celebrated those days as though with a sacred fast. And he decreed that, from the consecration of a bishop, offerings should be sent through the churches on account of the heretics. In the district of Limoges, Saint Valeria, virgin and martyr.” See Castellanus.

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., under no. 130, at the end: “At Rome, Saint Melchiades, pope.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Eulalia, virgin and martyr. Leocadia, virgin.” The latter has been wrongly transferred from the preceding day to this one. It continues: “Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, who was the companion of Eulalia, virgin. Carpophorus, priest, and Habundantius [Abundius], deacons, martyrs.”

REG. SUEC., marked no. 428: “At Limoges, Saint Valeria, virgin and martyr.”

In the VATICAN codex no. 5949 Julia is absent.

ALTEMPS.: “On the same day, Saint Antigonus and Saint Euphrasia.” Clearer information about these saints is lacking. The codex adds: “At Limoges, Saint Valeria, virgin and martyr.”

[Col. 0789B] FLORENTIN.: “At Rome, Saint Melchiades, pope. . . Likewise, Saint Sabinus, bishop and confessor.” I think the Sabinus of Piacenza is indicated, but he is celebrated on the following day. See our Additions there and the Roman Martyrology.

The LUBECK–COLOGNE edition begins with Melchiades, concerning whom it records nearly the same material as AQUICINCT. above. Our first announcement is fairly pure. It reads as follows concerning Eulalia: “In Spain, in the city of Mérida, the passion of Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr. When she was twelve years old, in the time of the emperor Diocletian, and born of very noble parents, she voluntarily presented herself before Dacian, who was seated in judgment, and bitterly reproached him for the cruelty he had exercised against God’s saints. For this reason she suffered many tortures at his hands. Finally, she was hung upon the rack and torn by claws, with burning torches placed on both sides, until she was gradually consumed by the fire. But as she prayed, the flame turned upon the torturers; and while she continued in prayer, she gave up her spirit in the form of a dove, with the people looking on and saying: ‘Glory to you, Lord.’” The entry for Julia is fairly pure. Finally: “At Vienna, Saint Sindulf, bishop and confessor.”

BELIN. adds to the fairly pure text, as above: “At Rome, Saint Melchiades, pope and martyr.”

GREVEN.: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, blessed Melchiades, pope. After governing the Church for four years before blessed Sylvester, he was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He himself decreed that fasting should not be observed on Sunday or Thursday, because the pagans regarded those days as profane fasts. On the same day, the passion of blessed Paul, bishop, whose passion is recorded. Likewise, Saints Victor, Adrian, and Cecilia. Likewise, Silvinus and Valentinus. Paul, pope and martyr, who according to the Catalog is commemorated on the sixth day before the Kalends of February. At Vienna, blessed Sindulf, bishop and confessor. Pontiana, virgin. In the city of Armenia, the feast of Saint Agricola.”

[Col. 0790B] MOLAN. in the first edition has one addition, which he copied from BELIN.: “At Rome, Saint Melchiades, pope and martyr.” In later editions he places the two words following *pope* in parentheses, thereby calling the martyrdom into question. See the Roman Martyrology and Baronius’s note. Castellanus rightly argues from the ancient Bucherian Calendar that Melchiades’ feast should be assigned to 10 January; see the Additions for that day. Moreover, the later editions add: “At Vienna, Saint Sindulf, bishop and confessor. At Limoges, Saint Valeria, virgin and martyr. At Leontini in Sicily, twenty holy soldier-martyrs, one of whom was called Mercurius, under Tertyllus the prefect and Licinius the emperor; they had been converted by Saints Alphius, Philadelphus, and Cyrinus. On the tenth day, the holy martyrs Mena, Hermogenes, and Eugraphus.” See Surius.]

At the city of Hispalis, the holy martyrs Carpophorus, a presbyter, and Abundius, a deacon, who during the persecution of Diocletian were first most cruelly beaten with clubs; then, after food and drink had been denied them, were confined in prison; again tortured on the rack; afterward weakened for a long time in prison; and finally put to the sword. In the Spanish city of Emerita, the passion of Saint Eulalia, a virgin, who, when she was thirteen years old, endured many tortures for her confession of Christ by order of the governor Dacianus. Finally, hung upon the rack and torn with claws, with burning torches applied on both sides, she gave up her spirit after swallowing fire. On the same day, near the aforesaid city, Saint Julia, a martyr, who was the fellow-virgin of Saint Eulalia and her inseparable companion as she hastened to martyrdom.

## The Third Day before the Ides. Day 11

[Note: [Col. 0789]]

It is taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven. and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0789C]]

Greven. and Molan. omit *natalis* at the beginning. Almost all the codices write *Trasonis*. Ado reads *Maximino*, and this is supported by the most authoritative codices, against many others in which the name has been changed to *Maximiano*. Herinien. has *was crowned*. Greven. and Molan., instead of *Christianissimus*, simply have *Christianus*. In the Ambian manuscripts arranged according to Usuard there is a difficulty, on account of which Pratensis and his companions would almost deserve to be excluded from the pure witnesses: contrary to the evidence of the Acts, Pratensis reads at the beginning, “of Gentianus and Fuscianus,” but at the end, “with Saint Victoricus, his host.” You might say that Usuard could have written this and could have made such an error; I do not think so, since he had the Acts themselves before his eyes. Herinien. does better by making Gentianus the host, but is not correct at the beginning in putting the three together: Victoricus, Gentianus, and Fuscianus. Antuerp. [Col. 0790C] and Max.-Lubec. perhaps read best, “of Fuscianus and Victoricus”; nevertheless, I judge Munerat., Greven., and Molan. preferable, since, beginning with Ado, they have “of Victoricus and Fuscianus.” Finding them arranged in this way, Usuard undoubtedly preserved them in that order, adding the rest from the Acts, without troubling himself over which of the two he should place first. Praten., Herinien., and a few others have *naribus vel auribus* (“in the nostrils or ears”); but the sense requires that, with Greven., Molan., and the greater number, we read *naribus et auribus* (“in the nostrils and ears”). I do not dislike Molan’s conjecture, by which he thinks that *tarincas* or *taringas*—an old French word, as the Acts of Saint Quintinus preserved by Du Cange testify—should be understood as *ringen*, which in Flemish means “a ring.” If you prefer *sudes*, as in Florus, that is acceptable to me. I retain *Euticii* with most of the codices.

[Note: [Col. 0789C]]

The ancient veneration of Pope Damasus in the Martyrologies is proved by his repeated commemoration, as some think, in the Hieronymian codices: both on the preceding day and on this day. They read either “At Rome, of Damasus, bishop,” or “The deposition of Damasus, bishop.” These words are read on the tenth day. Yet it is not sufficiently clear whether, when the Epternac manuscript begins today’s table with “The deposition of Damasus, of Eulalia, of Trasonis, etc.,” Damasus the pope is intended; for he is not known on this day in the other codices. Bede, however, expressly reads here: “The birthday of Saint Damasus, pope,” to which Rabanus added a few details. The Little Roman Martyrology simply has: “At Rome, of Damasus, pope.” The Viennese adds nothing except the duration of his episcopate, which it extends to eighteen years, three months, and two days. This must be investigated elsewhere, as must many other matters ordinarily disputed concerning the life and deeds of Damasus. See Baronius’s note, where he refers the reader to his Annals, in which he admirably defended the faith and morals of this outstanding pontiff against the slanders of his detractors, the Luciferians. The remaining material may be supplied by Jerome and the other Fathers and writers, from whom Tillemont constructed the course of his life in volume VIII, beginning on page 386, in fifteen sections. I shall append Wandalbert’s verses below.

After Damasus, the Little Roman Martyrology adds: “And of the martyrs Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Thrasonis, who supplied the martyrs with provisions from his resources.” Ado speaks in the same sense and in the same order, and from him Our Author took the whole substance of his notice, although he changed the sequence of the names. I would say that he wished to adjust it to the sense of the Hieronymian codices, in which the name of Thrasonis is placed first, if he had not omitted Capitulinus, who is reported between Pontianus and Praetextatus. I am surprised that he made this announcement correspond with the first one as though those martyrs belonged to the same period as Damasus. Florentinius’s note may be consulted. Their Acts should be treated in the same way as the deeds of the other martyrs taken from the Life of Saint Marcellus, as has been indicated more than once above.

In the Ambian manuscripts the Hieronymian copies vary again. Among them the Corbie manuscript reads more accurately, saying: “At Ambianis, the birthday of Victoricus, Fuscianus, and Gentianus, martyrs”; Rabanus also presents them in almost the same way.
