Florus, producing some material from their Acts, writes: “The passion of the holy Gentianus, Victoricus, and Fuscianus.” There is nothing about them in the Little Roman Martyrology; nor is it likely that Ado knew the Acts of these martyrs, since he names only Victoricus and Fuscianus, with this notice: “Who adorned their most glorious confession of faith with the blood of their passion”—words which can be applied to any martyrs. But it is clear that Usuard had seen the aforesaid Acts. I would not dare to assert that he saw them in the form in which they now exist; for, if Tillemont’s conjecture is correct, they scarcely surpass the twelfth century. We must therefore admit that there were other, different, and much more ancient Acts, if those truly were written by Florus which are attributed to him in our edition of Bede. There *sudes* is substituted for *tarincas*, and at the end a miracle common to many saints is added, concerning the carrying away of one’s own head in one’s hands, etc. There is no doubt that Usuard plainly copied the manner of their passion from the Acts themselves, as they were published by Bosquet, *On the Gallican Churches*, part II, p. 157 onward. Tillemont gives their summary in French in volume IV, pages 454–455, where he also describes the translation of their bodies, which is found in Mabillon, *Benedictine Century IV*, part II, p. 487; the preliminary admonition there should be consulted. Our Motherius’s brief note may also be added. We shall treat all these matters more fully in our larger work.

Wandalbert honors only Victoricus and Fuscianus, as placed by Ado, after Damasus in his verses:

> Rome celebrates the solemn rites of Pope Damasus threefold.
>
> Victoricus and Fuscianus likewise appear,
>
> And together possess the splendor of festival and vow;
>
> Their blood now makes the fields of Ambianis green.

Eutychius was taken by Ado from the Hieronymian codices and was copied by Our Author in exactly the same words. We should like to be informed what deeds were formerly associated with him, as the Hieronymian codices testify. Their silence concerning his deeds shows that neither Ado nor Usuard received them. Incidentally, note that the prophet Daniel, marked by the Little Roman Martyrology and Ado on 21 July, is repeated by both in the same words on this day, I do not know for what reason; hence he was transferred into our Appendices.

[Note: [Col. 0791C]]

**TORNACEN.** Concerning the Ambian martyrs it has: “At the city of Ambianis, the holy martyrs Gentianus and Fulgentius.” The rest is missing. In other respects it is pure.

**ANTUERP.-MAJ.** In the Ambian notice it resembles **PRATEN.**, and is pure in the rest, but lacks the last item.

**ROSWEYD.** After Damasus it distinguishes the announcement as follows: “Likewise, the passion of Thrasonis, who, when he was . . . was crowned, and of countless others, whose names God knows.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Concerning the Ambian martyrs, it agrees with **PRATEN.** It is pure in the last item.

**PULSANEN.** It has: “Of the prophet Daniel. At Rome, of Saint Damasus, pope, who ruled the Church for ten years, three months, and three days. On the same day, of the holy martyrs Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Thrasonis.” It says nothing about the Ambian martyrs. It is nearly pure in the last item.

**ANTUERP. MAX.-ULTRAJECT. and LEYDEN.** Begin the text from Ado: “Of the prophet Daniel.” Then: “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the birthday of Saint Damasus, pope and confessor. At the request of Blessed Jerome, he established that at the end of the psalms ‘Glory be to the Father’ should be said, with the following verse.” Then follows: [Col. 0791D] “On the same day, the passion of Saint Thrasonis,” etc., pure throughout the text. **LOVANIEN.** has the same, but cuts short the notice of the Ambian martyrs.

**ALBERG.** begins more briefly: “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the birthday of Saint Damasus, pope and confessor.” Then: “On the same day, of the prophet Daniel.” The text follows as above. **DANIC.** agrees in the manner. But concerning Daniel it has what **ANTUERP.-MAX.** has.

**CENTULEN.** “Of the prophet Daniel. At Rome, the deposition of Damasus, pope and confessor. On the same day, of the holy martyrs Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Thrasonis, the deacon, martyrs. In Gaul, at the city of Ambianis, of the holy martyrs Fuscianus, Victoricus, and Gentianus, who adorned their glorious confession of faith with the blood of their passion.” Nothing about Eutychius.

**BRUXELLEN.** “The octave of Saint Barbara. Of the prophet Daniel. [Col. 0792C] At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, of Saint Damasus, pope and confessor, who, at the urging of blessed Jerome, established that at the end of the psalms ‘Glory be to the Father,’ etc., should be said. On the same day, the passion of Saint Thrasonis,” etc., quite pure, as also in the Ambian notice. “In Spain, of Saint Eutychius.” This is added in a different ink, with the statement that his deeds are recorded. Finally: “Likewise, the passing of the venerable Ida of Nivelles, a nun of the Cistercian monastery of Rameya.”

**HAGENOYEN.** Begins with the Ambian martyrs, not badly. It is less pure in Thrasonis and his companions and in Eutychius. It continues: “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the birthday of blessed Damasus, pope and confessor, who ruled the Church for eighteen years and three months. He had an elegant talent for composing verses and published many brief works in heroic meter. He established that psalms should be sung in the Church day and night, and that the choir should be divided into two parts and sing antiphonally. He discovered many bodies of saints, whose tombs he adorned with verses. He established that ‘Glory be to the Father’ should be sung. At the Council of Constantinople he condemned the heretic Macedonius with one hundred and fifty Fathers; he died in peace and was buried at Saint Peter’s. In Jerusalem, Saint Elisabeth, mother of Saint John the Baptist. Likewise, in Judaea, the holy prophet Nahum.” He is placed here today according to the intention of this codex. See the Roman Martyrology, 1 December.

**AQUICINCT.** After “Pope Damasus” it adds: “He established that psalms should be sung day and night,” etc., as will be seen below in Molan’s additions. After *the judge*, the name Rictiovarus is added.

**AMBIANEN.** Concerning its own martyrs it writes: “In Gaul, at the city of Ambianis, the birthday of the holy martyrs Fuscianus, Victoricus, and Gentianus.”

**MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.** “Of Pope Damasus and [Col. 0793A] confessor. Of Fustianus [for Fuscianus] and his fellow martyrs. Of Glodulphus, bishop”; in others, “Clodulphus.” See Castellanus’s Martyrology. “Of Thrasonis, martyr, and his companions.”

**VATICAN**, under no. 5949, extends the second announcement after Damasus from Ado as follows: “And of the holy martyrs Pontianus, Praetextatus, and Thrasonis, who, being powerful and wealthy, supplied many Christians from his resources through the deacons Sisinnius and Cyriacus. Not long afterward he himself was arrested by Maximianus and, together with two others, deserved to receive the palm of martyrdom.”

**ALTEMPS.** “On the same day, of Saint Mary, virgin and martyr.” It is undoubtedly taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. See Florentinius.

**JUREN.** “At the city of Ambianis, of the holy martyrs Gentianus, Fuscianus, and Victoricus.”

The **LUBECO-COL. edition** begins: “At Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, the birthday of Saint Damasus, pope and confessor, who [Col. 0793B] ruled the Church for ten years, two months, and ten days. He established that psalms should be sung day and night by bishops, presbyters, and religious persons in churches and monasteries, and that the choirs, divided into two parts, should sing the psalms antiphonally. To this most holy man Blessed Jerome sent many writings on ecclesiastical religion, among them two verses, namely, ‘Glory be to the Father’ and ‘As it was,’ etc. He also discovered many bodies of saints. Likewise, of the prophet Daniel.” The remaining text is fairly pure, except that at the end it reads: “Of Eutychius, confessor.”

**BELIN.** Comes close to purity, beginning: “At Rome, of Saint Damasus, pope and confessor. On the same day, the passion,” etc. It forms the names of the Ambian martyrs as “Ambiani and Victoricus,” and below, “with Saint Agentianus, his host.” It also reads: “The governor Rictiovarus ordered.” I pass over the other blemishes of this edition. In the second edition it has “of Eutychius, bishop.”

**GREVEN.** “The octave of Saint Barbara, virgin and [Col. 0794A] martyr. Note. Saint Damasus ruled the Church for eighteen years and established that psalms should be recited day and night by ecclesiastical persons, with choirs singing antiphonally. Blessed Jerome also sent him many Catholic writings, among them those two verses, ‘Glory be to the Father’ and ‘As it was,’ etc., to be sung at the end of the psalms. Finally, after his death, he was buried on the Ardeatine Way. Of the prophet Daniel. Likewise, of Joseph, the patriarch, son of Jacob. At Myra, of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor, uncle of the other, namely the great Nicholas. On the same day, of blessed Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza, a man of extraordinary holiness. Full of faith, as Gregory reports in Book III of the *Dialogues*, when the river Po, overflowing, was taking possession of the Church’s fields, he wrote a warning and ordered the document itself to be thrown into the water; immediately the water subsided and did not dare to overflow any farther. At Metz, the translation of Saint Glodulphus, bishop and confessor. Likewise, of David, of blessed memory, a monk of the Cistercian Order, resting in the monastery of Hemerode.” [Col. 0794B]

**MOLAN.** In different type, he inserts into the text after “Pope Damasus”: “who ruled the Church for eighteen years, three months, and two days. He established that psalms should be sung day and night in all the churches. He searched for and found many bodies of saints, whose memory he also commemorated in verse.” At the end, in smaller type, he copied Greven’s words concerning Sabinus: “On the same day, of blessed Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza, of extraordinary holiness,” etc., also adding the miracle concerning the restraining of the waters of the Po, etc. In other editions the same material about Damasus appears in different type within the text; in addition, after *Christianus*, he inserts from Ado the following concerning Thrasonis: “Powerful and wealthy, he supplied food from his resources to the holy martyrs condemned to prisons and mines through Sisinnius and Cyriacus. Not long afterward, by order of …” etc. At the end: “On the eleventh day, of the holy Father Daniel the Stylite.” See his Life in Surius.

[Col. 0789]

At Rome, the birthday of blessed Damasus, pope, and the passion of Saint Thrasonis, martyr, who, being most Christian, was arrested by order of Maximinus and, together with two others, Pontianus and Praetextatus, crowned with martyrdom. At the city of Ambianis, the holy martyrs Victoricus and Fuscianus. The judge ordered *tarincas*—rings—to be inserted into their nostrils and ears and their heads to be pierced with glowing nails; then their eyes were torn out, and finally missiles were hurled through their bodies. Thus, after their heads had been cut off together with Saint Gentianus, their host, they departed to the Lord. In Spain, Saint Eutychius, [Note: [Col. 0789B] Eutychius was lost in the Dervensis codex. Bouillart.] whose deeds are recorded.

## The Day before the Ides. Day 12

[Note: [Col. 0793]]

The following are counted among the pure witnesses: Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. Antuerp.-Max., Ultraject., and Leyden may be added to them.

[Note: [Col. 0793C]]

Molan scarcely deserves a place among the pure witnesses today. At the very beginning he writes “of Paul, bishop and confessor,” a title from which all the others abstain. Munerat. omitted the word *ordained* after *apostle*. Again, Molan, with the same witness, reads *cumque eodem* (“and with the same”) instead of *quique cum eodem* (“who, together with the same”); Belin. has *cumque*; Munerat. has *qui cum eodem*. Belin. corrupts the sense with “after the office had been completed, distinguished in office,” instead of the reading he ought to have had, “having diligently fulfilled the office.” Praten. errs in writing *claris miraculis* (“with clear miracles”) instead of *clarus miraculis* (“famous for miracles”). The same witness has *Epymachii*; Greven., *Epymachi*. I would prefer *Epimachi*, with Belin. and Molan.; but Herinien., Rosweyd., Munerat., and even the Little Roman Martyrology and Ado compel us to write *Epimachii* with the text. In Belin., *ante perdurassent* is redundant. There is greater confusion in the same witness, since it places the Alexandrian women last. The greatest divergence, both in this witness and in Molan., is found in those who, after Mercuria, have dared to insert from Ado “and Dionysia and again Ammonaria”; because of this variation they have almost been excluded from the pure witnesses. [Col. 0794C] Rosweyd. placed *capita* before *ferro caedente*. In Greven., *cadente* is a printer’s error. A few witnesses have *percipiunt*; the second edition of Belin. has *perceperunt*. The reading in the text must be retained. *Viginti duum* is a phrase found only in Pratensis. The district of Wimacensis, which Castellanus calls Vinemacensis, is inflected differently by almost everyone. Ado of Mosandrus had written on 1 April *Winnoiensi*; Ado of Rosweyd, *Wimnoensi*; here one finds *Vimnacensi*, *Vinmacensi*, *Vivacensi*, *Vininacensi*, *Vianensi*, *Vimmocensi*, *Numuacensi*, etc. For the moment I have preferred *Vinnacensi*, following Munerat., Greven., and Molan. There is also great diversity in writing the proper name; Rosweyd. differs from the others by reading “of Walericus, abbot,” while Belin. falls more disgracefully into error by substituting “of Valentius, bishop.” Munerat. has the error *Malerici*. Note here that in Rosweyd. the announcement of Hermogenes, etc., has two Alexandrian women inserted into it; more noteworthy still, three middling-quality codices place “At Emerita” before Hermogenes and Donatus. See the Observations.

[Note: [Col. 0795A]]

We began to discuss Paul of Narbonne rather fully in the Observations for 22 March. On that day he ought to be placed according to the judgment of the Hieronymian codices and, indeed, of nearly all the ancient Martyrologists. Up to now I cannot see why Usuard, departing from his customary guides, postponed Paul until this day. Yet although he abandons the Kalends marked by Ado, he wholly embraced Ado’s opinion, current in the ninth century, that the first preachers of the Gospel in Gaul should be traced back to the apostolic age. He did so because he took his entire notice from the Feasts of the Apostles, prudently omitting the statement by which the Viennese identifies Paul of Narbonne with Sergius Paulus the proconsul.

Prudentius’s encomium of our Paul is brief but elegant:

> And splendid Narbo shall rise for Paul.

Henschenius long ago worked out the remaining matters soundly from Bosquet and others, under 22 March, so that little remains to be observed here. Those who delight in concise accounts should consult Tillemont, volume IV, in the section on Dionysius of Paris, especially article 12, beginning on page 469.

The present entry in the Little Roman Martyrology contains only the Alexandrian martyrs, taken from the frequently cited Book VI, chapter 31, of Rufinus, or rather directly from the famous letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Fabius of Antioch. From this source we recently gave Agatho on 7 December and Macarius with the same Little Roman Martyrology on 8 December. These are its words for this day: “At Alexandria, of Epimachus and Alexander. And of the four holy women Ammonaria, Mercuria, Dionysia, and Ammonaria.” The Viennese drew more generously from the aforesaid source by describing all their struggles; from this, in turn, Our Author customarily extracted both his notices, leaving the last two women unnamed. Here again it is evident—something we repeatedly emphasized on 7 and 8 December and elsewhere—that it is entirely futile to seek the reason why these martyrs were marked by the author of the Little Roman Martyrology on this day rather than another, since he distributed most of the saints taken from Rufinus, entirely according to his own whim, among various days which he happened to regard as unoccupied by other saints. I know that the Greeks assign Epimachus to 31 October, as I noted there in the Appendices; but why he was separated from his companions, or at least from his companion, and why he is honored by them especially on that day, is entirely uncertain, unless a translation or something of that sort provided the occasion.

I said in the *Variants* that Hermogenes and Donatus are assigned by inferior codices to Emerita; I would readily suppose that this was taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, or rather from some Rabanian codex. But the Epternac codex is preferable, in which we expressly read: “And in another place, of Hermogenes, Donata, and twenty-two others.” The Blumian codex agrees exactly, nor does the Corbie codex differ. In all of them *Donatae* is found instead of *Donati*, but without the expression “at [that place].” Galesinius should not be followed in asserting Alexandria. I would rather believe that they were Spaniards, although Ado refrained from naming the place, as did Usuard in copying him. Whether the *Thesaurus of Preachers* is correct in reporting, on Baronius’s authority, that they completed their contest after being plunged into a marsh will be examined in its proper place. Wandalbert praised both these martyrs, together with their twenty-two companions, not inelegantly:

> Hermogenes and Donatus shine forth twice at last.
>
> Then, on the preceding day, the two holy men, joined in blood.

Walericus, or Walaricus, abbot of Leucona, is plainly Usuardine for this day. Ado certainly placed him on 1 April, whatever Mabilion may again thrust upon us here from his Adonian codex, for we have found no similar one among ours except a single Lobbes codex. Let the person who has weighed Henschenius’s arguments under 1 April decide with certainty the day of his death; we refer readers there. For our purposes here, it is enough to have asserted his true and genuine text from the best-quality Usuardine codices.

[Note: [Col. 0795C]]

**TORNACEN.** The first part is missing. In the Alexandrian notices it reports only the names found in Usuard, with the notices omitted. It is pure in the final two announcements.

**PULSANEN.** Begins with Hermogenes, etc., in pure form. Then continues: “At Alexandria, of the blessed martyrs Epimachus and Alexander. In Septimania, at the city of Narbonne, the deposition of Saint Paul, bishop and confessor.” The rest is missing.

**LOVANIEN.** Would be pure, like **ANTUERP.-MAX.**, if it did not fail in the notices concerning the Alexandrians.

**ALBERG. and DANIC.** Lack the final announcement. Both reported it, each with different wording and differently from ours, on 1 April. In the rest they resemble **ANTUERP.-MAX.**, etc.

**CENTULEN.** Treated Paul on 22 March; on this day it begins: “The birthday of the holy martyrs Hermogenes, Donatus, and twenty-two others. At Alexandria, of the blessed martyrs Epimachus and Alexander, who passed through the ordeal of fire. And there, of the holy women [Col. 0795D] Ammonaria the virgin, Dionysia, Mercuria; likewise Ammonaria, who preserved the Lord’s faith through various kinds of tortures.” Here it repeats: “At Narbonne, of Saint Paul, bishop and confessor. In the district of Viminacum, of Saint Walericus, abbot, who, leading the eremitical life beside the river Somme, also became famous for miracles.” It speaks not of his birthday but of his translation on 1 April.

**BRUXELLEN.** Begins: “By anticipation, of Saint Autbertus, bishop of Cambrai.” It continues with Paul, fairly purely. Then: “At Alexandria, the birthday of the holy martyrs Sammon and Emeritus.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies for the preceding day. In all the Alexandrian notices it departs little from purity. It continues: “In Spain, the birthday of the holy martyr Carpophorus, presbyter,” etc., almost as Usuard above under 10 December. See what was said there. It proceeds: “At the city of Emerita, [Col. 0796C] the birthday of the holy martyrs Hermogenes, Donatus, and twenty-two others. In the district of Viminacum, of Saint Walericus, abbot and confessor. On the same day, the translation of blessed Nicasius, [bishop] and martyr.” Perhaps the translation of some relics to Brussels took place, since the other codices are silent about it. See his birthday, 14 December.

**HAGENOYEN**, in the first, second, and third editions, is usually more pure. It gives the fourth as follows: “At the city of Emerita in Spain, the birthday of the blessed martyrs Hermogenes and Donatus, with twenty-two others, under the governor Dacianus.” It says more, unless I am mistaken, than it found elsewhere. It treated Walericus, in its own manner and wording, on 1 April.

**DAVERON.** “In the district of Vimiacum, of Saint Walaricus, confessor.” Another local variation.

**AMBIANEN.** “In the district of Vimacum, the birthday of Saint Walericus, who, leading the eremitical life beside the river Somme, also became famous for miracles.”

[Col. 0796D] **MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.** “Of Paul, bishop of Narbonne. Of Hermogenes, Donatus, and twenty others. Of Epimachus and Alexander. Likewise, of the holy women Ammonaria and three others.”

**VATICAN**, under no. 5949, has nothing about Paul of Narbonne or Walericus.

**BURDEGALEN.** “In the district of Vimacum, of Saint Walericus, bishop.” The reading in the text is better.

**REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.** “In the district of Vinmacum, the birthday of Saint Walericus, presbyter,” etc.

The **LUBECO-COL. edition**, in its first form, is fairly pure, as is the second. In the third it is somewhat altered: “Likewise at Alexandria, of the four holy women Ammonaria, Mercuria, again Ammonaria, and Dionysia, martyrs,” etc. “At the city of Emerita, of Hermogenes,” etc. “In the district of Vimacum, of Saint Wallericus, presbyter, abbot, and confessor.”

[Col. 0797A] **GREVEN.** “Note. Ado has this Walericus on the Kalends of April. See there. At Alexandria, of Sammon and Emeritus, saints.” See what we said concerning the **BRUXELLEN** codex. “On the same day, at the city of the Auraricenses, the passion of the holy Eustratius, Eugenius, Orestes, and many others. In the time of Diocletian and Maximian, they steadfastly endured and overcame the punishments exacted for the faith of Christ. Finally, Eustratius was consumed by fire, while the others were beheaded, and they obtained the glory of martyrdom.” See this more carefully in the Roman Martyrology, and Castellanus’s note for the following day; Surius reports their Acts as composed by Symeon Metaphrastes. “In Ireland, of Finnian, abbot and confessor. Of Empress Alheidis, according to others, on 17 December.”

**MOLAN.** Concerning the Alexandrian women, after “and again Ammonaria,” he inserts into the text in different type: “while they displayed excessive steadfastness before the judge, and he was ashamed to be defeated by women.” And again, after “they receive,” he adds: “Saint Dionysius writes this in his book *On the Martyrs*.” See Ado. Other editions add at the end: “In Gaul, near Tournai, in the monastery of Cisoing, the translation of Saint Everard, duke of Friuli.” The Appendix speaks more distinctly; it should be assigned to 16 December, on which day Castellanus’s universal Martyrology should also be consulted.

[Col. 0793]

At Narbonne, the birthday of Saint Paul the confessor, whom blessed Paul the Apostle ordained and appointed bishop for that city. He went with the same Apostle to Spain for the purpose of preaching and was left there. Having diligently fulfilled the office of preaching, he became famous for miracles, was crowned, and rested. In Alexandria, the holy martyrs Epimachus and Alexander, who, after spending a long time in chains and enduring various punishments while persevering in the faith, were finally ordered to be consumed by fire. Likewise at Alexandria, the holy women Ammonaria and Mercuria, with two others, who, after enduring and overcoming unheard-of forms of torture, received the final end of all their torments as the sword struck them down. Likewise, the holy martyrs Hermogenes, Donatus, and twenty-two others. In the district of Vinnacum, Saint Walericus, presbyter and confessor.

## The Ides. Day 13

[Note: [Col. 0797]]

The following are pure: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0797B]]

I wrote *Siracusam*, as the best codices—Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., etc.—have, not *Syracusas*, as Greven. and Molan. prefer. *Siraculam* in Munerat. is an error; Antuerp.-Maj. and the middling-quality codices read *Siracusanam*. The same Antuerp.-Maj. omits the title *saint*. Tornacen. alone has *paribus pluribus* (“with several pairs”) instead of *boum paribus plurimis* (“with very many pairs of oxen”). In Munerat. *lenones* is missing, and *Auberti* is written in place of *Autberti*. Praten. writes *Camberacensis*, and Antuerp.-Maj. seems to agree with it; all the others preserve the more usual spelling found in the text.

[Note: [Col. 0797B]]

Everything concerning Saint Lucia, virgin of Syracuse and most renowned martyr, is clear both in Surius and in all the Latin Hagiologies, as well as in the Greek Menologies. The Sacramentary of Gregory and the ancient Frontonian Calendar mention her. In the latter, Fronto records several churches dedicated to Saint Lucia at Rome and seems to think that one of them bears the title of another Roman widow distinct from this Lucia. This is Florentinius’s observation. He attributes to Fronto what his note on the Calendar does not express, since Fronto seems rather to name churches dedicated to Saint Lucia as though they had been consecrated to this Sicilian woman of ours. I consider this beyond dispute, just as I also think that her name was inserted into the sacred canon of the Mass, whatever more recent critics may seem to wish to call into question. Let them observe, I beg them, that Lucia, the most noble matron who is celebrated on 16 September, is joined with Geminianus, while the most illustrious virgin of Syracuse is commemorated in an entirely different manner and with a different cult in the Gregorian Sacramentary mentioned above, in the calendars of Fronto and Allatius, and indeed in the other ecclesiastical books. She stands among Agatha, Agnes, and Cecilia, whose virginity and honor by the whole Catholic Church are altogether beyond doubt. These facts abundantly demonstrate that the feast of Lucia of Syracuse was celebrated in the city of Rome from the earliest times; the testimony of the Martyrologies in support of her celebration is no less clear. In the Hieronymian Martyrologies I read: “At the city of Syracuse in Sicily, the birthday of Saint Lucia, virgin.” *Lucae* in the Epternac codex is an error; nor can Lucia, repeated on the following day in those same copies, be said to be the same as our Lucia, since she is associated, rightly or wrongly, with the Antiochene martyrs. Even those who expose some of their errors do not deny that the Acts of the illustrious virgin are ancient and weighty. Adelmus saw them, and so did Bede, who composed his shorter notice from them; Rabanus copied it word for word. The author of the Little Roman Martyrology, who guides our series, reads briefly: “At Syracuse, of Lucia, virgin and martyr.” Ado’s account is long; but Our Author, accustomed to favor shorter accounts, found more suitable material for his notice in Bede and preferred to form his own notice from it, leaving aside the final section concerning communion in the Lord’s body, which some codices restore in the Appendices. We possess a Life composed in verse, undoubtedly the work of Sigebert; see Molan’s note concerning it. There are also many other monuments relating both to the Acts themselves and to the disputed translations, as well as some more recently composed in honor of Lucia. We reserve all these for their proper place and time, and shall not omit the exceptional veneration shown by the people of Antwerp toward the memorable virgin and her relics, received in the last century through the illustrious Capello from Fabio Chigi, later Pope Alexander VII.

Here may be added Wandalbert’s verses, in which the poet of the Martyrology joined Judocus. He would have been more faithful to our text if he had added Autbertus. Thus he sings:

> The Ides of Syracuse, Lucia, have dedicated to you,
>
> You who endured Paschasius the tyrant for Christ’s name;
>
> The holy Spirit made you unmoved before wicked men.
>
> Likewise you are honored by Judocus and the priest,
>
> Distinguished, before whom the storms of Ocean often yield.

Moreover, Usuard alone and the first among those who compiled the sacred calendars introduced Autbertus of Cambrai. Molan rightly testifies in *The Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium* that he was a most approved priest of Christ, under whom and through whom Hainaut wonderfully began to flourish and grow in the Christian religion. There he says that it is regrettable that the Life of so great a pontiff is largely unknown. Surius published the Life in whatever form he possessed it; but the manuscript we have seems somewhat fuller. This is not the place to examine the matter more scrupulously. Still less do I wish to ask what is meant by the Spanish account, which assumes that our Autbertus of Cambrai had previously been archbishop of Braga in Lusitania—namely, because it is sufficiently characteristic of those peoples to claim foreign saints for themselves. Tamayus does refute this in his Spanish Martyrology, but I do not understand whether he substitutes anything much sounder.

[Note: [Col. 0797D]]

**ROSWEYD.** After the text, which is fairly pure, adds at the end: “On the same day, of Saint Odilia, virgin.”

[Col. 0798D] **PULSANEN.** After “martyr” it has concerning Lucia: “She suffered during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, under the consul Paschasius. She suffered on the Ides of December, and a basilica was afterward built at the place where she was struck.” Nothing concerning Autbertus of Cambrai.

**BELIN.** After “she was struck” supplies Bede’s notice: “Yet she did not die until priests arrived and she received communion of the Lord’s body and blood.” Then: “Likewise, of Saint Ursinus, martyr.” It has *Anthiberti* for *Autberti*; in the second edition this is corrected somewhat better to *Auberti*.

**ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC., and also, I believe, UGHELLIAN., together with ANTUERP.-MAX. and all its usual companions**, place in Lucia’s notice almost the same material that we gave from **BELIN.** They all likewise write *Siracusanam*. The last six add “and confessor” at the end.

**CENTULEN.** “At the city of Syracuse in Sicily, the passion of Saint Lucia, virgin, under the consul Paschasius. At Cambrai, of Saint Autbertus, bishop and confessor. [Col. 0799B] In the district of Pontivum, of Saint Judocus, priest and confessor, who withdrew from the height of his hereditary kingdom to the poverty of Christ and most holily completed the course of his praiseworthy life.”

BRUSSELS. Anticipated the feast of Saint Autbert. In the entry for Lucia it is sufficiently similar to the manuscripts cited above. It adds the following:

> “In Ireland, Saint Finnian, abbot and confessor. At Ravenna, Saints Ursianus and Leuchadius, confessors. And Saint Odilia, who rests at Orpe near Geldonia, a village of Brabant.”

It confuses Odilia with Adilia of Orpe; the latter is commemorated on 30 June. Finally:

> “On the same day, the deposition of Saint Athanasius, abbot and confessor.”

Which Athanasius he wishes to indicate cannot be adequately determined from the title “abbot” alone.

HAGENOYEN. On Lucia it inserts:

> “She first freed her own mother from an issue of blood and distributed all that she possessed to the poor. For this reason she was accused by her pagan betrothed before Paschasius [Col. 0799C] of being a Christian, and, after a long disputation concerning the faith, was ordered to be taken to a brothel. But when the pimps…”

and so forth, almost as in the manuscripts above.

> “On the same day, in the monastery of Hoenberg, in the diocese of Strasbourg, the deposition of Saint Odilia the virgin. This Odilia was the daughter of a great prince and was born blind; for this reason she was hated by her father, who wished to kill her, but her mother and brother saved her. Later, at baptism, she was given sight. After her father’s death she became mother of two hundred virgins, dedicating her father’s entire inheritance to God and building two monasteries. She is said to have freed her father’s soul from hell [others: from purgatory] and to have performed many other miracles, and she died. On the same day, the deposition of Saint Jodocus, son of the king of England and hermit, who, after abandoning the world in his youth, lived for many years in great abstinence and patience. Because he despised an earthly kingdom in favor of a heavenly one, he became king in heaven after, through great labor, enriching it with the relics of the saints; and he hears those who petition him, in accordance with God’s promise. On the same day, the deposition of Saint [Col. 0799D] Autbert, bishop of Cambrai, glorious in teaching and life.”

AQUICINCT. In second place, after “she was struck,” it inserts:

> “On the same day, the glorious reception of Blessed Martin from Burgundy, whom not only miracles made illustrious, but whom the generosity of great nobles and the attendance of a mixed multitude of both sexes rendered famous.”

The manuscripts DAVERON, ALTEMPS, and CAUDIACEN report the same. Our earlier manuscript adds at the end:

> “And Saint Jodocus the confessor.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked with number 130:

> “On the same day, Saint Eustachius with his companions.”

They intend Eustratius; concerning him, see Surius and the Roman Martyrology.

> “In the Spanish city of Mérida, the passion of Saint Eulalia the virgin.”

See above, under her proper feast, 10 December.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Lucia the virgin and [Col. 0800A] martyr. Jodocus the confessor. Autbert, bishop of Cambrai.”

VATICAN. Under number 5949 Autbert is absent, but the following is added:

> “At Sebaste, the passion of Saint Eustratius the martyr and his companions Auxentius, Nandarius, Eugenius, and Orestes, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, with Agricola as judge.”

FLORENTIN. add:

> “At Ravenna, Saint Ursicinus the martyr.”

He is commemorated on 19 June.

BURDEGALEN.:

> “The return of Saint Martin, the most glorious bishop of Tours.”

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. The entry for Lucia is almost like the manuscripts of intermediate character. Concerning Autbert it adds “and confessor.” It continues:

> “In the district of Pontinus, Saint Jodocus, priest and confessor, son of the king of Britain. Desiring to serve God, he handed over the kingdom to his elder brother, named Michael, and came with his disciple Volmarus to the wilderness of Pontinus. He settled beside the river [Col. 0800B] Altea, where the Lord appeared to him in the form of a pilgrim four times, asking alms from him. Although he had only one loaf for himself and his disciple, he divided it into four parts and gave it to the petitioner; and, by divine providence, he deserved miraculously to receive four little boats laden with wine and bread. Finally, with Christ as his guide and the angels in attendance, he passed to the heavenly realms. At the fortress of Landun, the birth-feast of Saint Odilia the virgin and abbess of one hundred and thirty nuns, daughter of Duke Adalric of Hohenburg. She was of such great holiness before God that, through her tearful prayers, she freed her father, whom God had assigned to her in purgatory, from the place at the side of the mountain where her monastery is situated. Afterward, returning to life for a short time, she also said that she had been in the company of Saint Lucia and had seen the joys that ‘eye has not seen, nor ear heard.’”

More is narrated here than I find in any other manuscript.

[Col. 0800C] GREVEN.:

> “At Ravenna, Saints Urcianus”—[I think Ursicinus is intended, whom others wrote as Ursinus]—“and Leuchadius, confessors. At Milan, the finding of Saints Nazarius, Protasius, Gervasius, and Celsus the boy. On the same day, the deposition of Blessed Jodocus, priest and confessor. Since he was the son of the king of the Britons, and after his father’s death was being pressed to assume the government of the kingdom, he fled and came to the district of Pontinus, where he began to lead a solitary life. There, renowned for his life and miracles, he once brought forth a spring from the earth by his prayers for Duke Haymo, who was in danger from thirst. Finally, full of holiness, he rested about the year of the Lord 653. In Alsace, at the fortress of Landun, the birthday of Saint Odilia, virgin and abbess. Although born of illustrious Frankish blood, she was born blind; when for this reason her father ordered her killed, she was saved by her mother and baptized by Saint Erhard, bishop of Regensburg, divinely warned, and received her sight. Afterward restored to her father’s favor, she was entrusted with governing the monastery her father had founded. There, gathering many virgins around her, living in great holiness [Col. 0800D] and shining also through miracles, she rested in peace.”

MOLAN. Along with BELIN, in different type, he adds after “she was struck”:

> “Yet she did not die until, when the priests arrived, she had received communion of the Lord’s body and blood,”

and so forth. Then:

> “Likewise, Saint Ursinus the martyr.”

At the end, concerning Autbert:

> “and confessor; whose illustrious life shone with glorious signs of virtue in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks. On the same day, Saint Jodocus the confessor. On the same day, in the territory of Strasbourg, Saint Othilia the virgin. At Ravenna, Saint Leuchadius.”

Finally, in smaller type:

> “The Wednesday after Lucia, the winter three-day fast, or of the tenth month, concerning which Pope Leo I has eight homilies. At Orpe, a district near Geldonia, Saint Adilia, virgin and abbess.”

I said above that Adilia is commemorated on 30 June; see the Acts on that day. The later editions have the same text concerning Lucia, and almost the same concerning Autbert, except for the chronological notice. They then read:

> “In the district of Pontinus, Saint Jodocus the confessor, [Col. 0801A] son of the king of the Britons, a pilgrim. In the territory of Strasbourg,”

and so forth, as in the earlier edition.

> “On the thirteenth day, Saints Eustratius, Auxentius, Eugenius, [Col. 0802A] Mardarius, and Orestes, martyrs.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “At Nicaea, Saint Bassus, who died pierced by two nails.”

Finally, concerning the fast of the tenth month, as above.

[Col. 0797]

At Syracuse, a city of Sicily, the birthday of Saint Lucia, virgin and martyr, under the persecution of Diocletian. When, at the command of Paschasius the governor, the pimps wished to violate her, they were utterly unable to move her, even after ropes had been attached and very many pairs of oxen had been harnessed. She received pitch, resin, and boiling oil without injury, but at last she was struck after a sword had been thrust into her entrails. On the same day, Saint Autbert, bishop of Cambrai.

19 days before the Kalends. Day 14. [Note: [Col. 0801]

From Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0801B]

Herinien. and Antuerp.-Maj. write *Ciprum* here; all the others more correctly have *Cyprum*. In Munerat. it is *Spiridonis*; more foolishly, in Belin., *Spilidionis*, which was corrected in the second edition. But the older books must be excused, since typographical carelessness corrupted them. Thus Belin. reads *pollice* (“thumb”) for *poplite* (“knee”), as does Greven. Likewise some have *Datiana* for *Deciana*, and *Artenii*, *Ysidori*, *Hysidori*, *Dursii*, *Nichasii*, and so forth. “He had condemned [them] to the mines” (*per metalla damnaverat*) is Rufinus’s phrase, preserved by Ado and copied from him by Our author; Antuerp.-Maj. preferred *damnavit* (“he condemned”). Belin. reads “when he saw them steadfast” (*cum pari constantia videret*), which is better in the text. Antuerp. reads “at Reims, of the saints”; Max.-Lubec., “at Reims, the passion of the saints”; Molan., however, inserts the heading “Saint” before Eutropia.]

[Note: [Col. 0801B]

In Book X, chapter 4, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, after recounting the glorious confession of Paphnutius the Egyptian—one of those who, after their right eyes had been gouged out and their left knees cut through, were condemned to the mines—Rufinus begins the immediately following chapter as follows:

> “It is said that among their number, and even more eminent than they, was also Spyridon, bishop of Cyprus, a man from the order of the prophets,”

and so forth. From this the author of the Little Roman Martyrology extracted the name, to which he assigned a place in our Calendars on this day:

> “In Cyprus, Spyridon the bishop.”

Ado also found it there and embellished the man of admirable blessedness somewhat more fully; from Ado, Usuard copied the whole announcement. More about Spyridon can be read in the cited chapter, and more in Socrates, Sozomen, and others, from whom Tillemont composed his French Life in volume VII, beginning at page 242. He did not dare to rely on the *Metaphrastic Life* published by Surius, although the latter may perhaps have possessed the metrical version which is believed to have been composed by Tryphyllius, Spyridon’s disciple. See what Papebrochius noted concerning the Greek Lives preserved among us on 12 December, in the *Greek-Muscovite Calendar*, page LV, and Tillemont’s notes in the cited volume VII, beginning at page 693. We shall produce below the verse of Wandalbert, who placed Spyridon after Nicasius.

The fruitful harvest of martyrs, praised so often in the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria preserved in Rufinus, Book VI, chapter 3, suggested the following four Alexandrian champions to the author of the Little Roman Martyrology, who, on his own authority, entered them second on this day:

> “At Alexandria, Heron, Arsenius, Isidore, and Dioscorus.”

Ado’s longer eulogy was again taken from Rufinus; ours is a sufficiently elegant abridgment of the Adonian one. Those saints could not have received a better encomiast than Eusebius’s history. The same was not the case with the three Antiochenes, whose names alone seem to survive, first recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrologies; but in such a way that it remains uncertain whether Drusus—or Drusina, or, as Castellanus wishes, Drosides—had two or three companions:

> “At Antioch, Drusus and his companions, three in number: Zosimus, Theodorus, and Saint Lucia the virgin.”

Others express and number them differently, and the matter is not adequately resolved except when the Roman Martyrology is read:

> “At Antioch, the birthday of Drusus and his companions Zosimus and Theodorus.”

The Little Roman Martyrology doubtless found them somewhere in this form also, when it entered them first with these words:

> “At Antioch, Drusus, Zosimus, and Theodorus.”

The Viennese Martyrologist found nothing more, from whom our entire text has so far been transferred.

Nicasius, although he is found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, is plainly Usuardine here because he is joined with his sister Eutropia; in Ado’s appendix he was wrongly assigned to Lyon. The somewhat fuller wording of our Florus counts among the companions citizens slaughtered in the same barbarian incursion:

> “Rabanus, more briefly, wrote *Sacrepi* for Eutropia, or rather copied this name from the Hieronymian Martyrologies as referring elsewhere and wrongly attached it to Nicasius.”

Surius published two Acts concerning the martyrdom of Nicasius and his companions: one earlier and shorter, the other longer, composed by Flodoard four hundred years after the martyrdom. No judgment concerning their reliability and authenticity is required here. The cult of Nicasius is famous throughout Gaul, especially in the province of Reims, and from there throughout Belgium as well. Wandalbert’s metrical eulogy honors Nicasius together with Spyridon as follows:

[Col. 0802D]

On the customary ninth-and-tenth Kalends of January, Bishop Nicasius adds honor;  
And on the same day the bishop Spyridon is celebrated.

[Note: [Col. 0801D]

TORNACEN. Lacks the first announcement, is mutilated in the second, and is complete only in the last two.]

ROSWEYD. After the Antiochenes he inserts into the text:

> “At Lyon, Saint Viator the bishop.”

Florus and Rabanus also discuss him. Then:

> “At Vienne, Lupicinus the bishop and confessor.”

See Rabanus and Ado’s appendix. Concerning both saints, Viator and Lupicinus, the Hieronymian copies may also be consulted. Concerning Nicasius the following is added:

> “Bishop and martyr with his companions.”

PULSANEN., omitting Spyridon, begins as follows:

> “At Antioch, Saints Drusimus, Zosimus, [Col. 0802D] and Theodulus, martyrs.”

It deprives the Alexandrians of their eulogy and deprives Nicasius of his sister.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., and LEYDEN. append to the pure text at the end:

> “At Vienne, the birthday of Saint Lupicinus, bishop and confessor.”

LOVAN. has the same, but cuts the eulogy of the Alexandrians.

ALBERG. and DANIC., in addition to the augmentation already mentioned concerning Lupicinus, add the following concerning Nicasius and his sister:

> “They were beheaded by the Huns and completed a glorious martyrdom.”

CENTULEN.:

> “At Antioch, Saints Drusus, Zosimus, and Theodulus, martyrs. At Alexandria, the blessed [Col. 0803A] martyrs Heron, Arsenius, Isidore, and Dioscorus. In Cyprus, Saint Spyridon the bishop, illustrious by the merit of his confession. At Reims, the metropolitan city of the Franks, Saint Nicasius the archbishop, who was beheaded by the Vandals together with his virgin sister Eutropia and many members of the clergy and people.”

BRUSSELS. Begins:

> “At Reims, the passion of Saints Nicasius and Eutropia the virgin, his sister, who were slaughtered with a multitude of the clergy and people of that city by the Huns.”

It then follows with the Antiochenes, Spyridon, and the Alexandrians, quite accurately. Then:

> “At Vienne, the deposition of Saint Lupicinus, bishop and confessor. At Lyon, the deposition of Saint Viator, bishop and confessor. At the monastery of Sithiu, the passing of Saint Folquinus, bishop and confessor of the Morini.”

See Castellanus concerning him.

HAGENOYEN. Places the Alexandrians first, then Spyridon, then the Antiochenes, all quite accurately. But concerning Nicasius it reads:

> “At Reims, the passion of Saint Nicasius, bishop and martyr, and of Eutropia, his sister. [Col. 0803B] He had come there as bishop from Greater Britain by divine providence, born of royal blood, and governed his church commendably in every respect in the word of the Lord. He foretold that his death was near, consoling his people so that they would not be frightened by his example. During that same sermon he was beheaded by the Huns. He himself then took up his head, stood before the altar, and finished his sermon; turning toward the altar, he set himself to prayer and died. His sister Eutropia, however, tore out the eyes of her brother’s executioner; for this reason she was killed by a miserable death.”

AQUICINCT. At the end of the text, after “his sister,” adds:

> “and their companions, who were killed by the Vandals. Likewise, the passing of Saint Folquinus, bishop and confessor of the Morini.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Nicasius, archbishop of Reims, and his sister Eutropia, martyrs. Spyridon, bishop and confessor.”

In VATICAN, number 5949, there is nothing concerning Nicasius. The following is added: [Col. 0803C]

> “At Naples, Saint Agnellus the confessor.”

ALTEMPS.:

> “The deposition of Avitus the priest. Aticius the monk. Lotharius the abbot.”

For this day and under these descriptions they are all equally unknown.

BURDEGALEN.:

> “Fortunatus, bishop and confessor of Poitiers.”

See Castellanus, who distinctly enumerates the whole series of his names.

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. Begins:

> “At Reims, the metropolitan city, the passion of Saints Nicasius, bishop, and Eutropia, [Col. 0804A] his virgin sister, of remarkable holiness. When this bishop had been beheaded by the Huns and Vandals inside the church for the faith of Christ, he lifted up his severed head with his own hands and placed it before the altar. Eutropia, seeing that she was being reserved for mockery, struck at the enemies with her hand and wounded some of them with a sword; thus provoking them against herself, she was martyred. Countless others from the same city suffered with them.”

It follows with Spyridon, the Alexandrians, and the Antiochenes, quite accurately. At the end:

> “At Vienne, the birthday of Saint Lupicinus, the ninth bishop and confessor of that church. On the same day, Saint Folquinus, bishop and confessor.”

See MOLAN below.

GREVEN.:

> “The octave of the Conception of holy Mary, Mother of God.”

I omitted noting above that, in the upper margin of the DANIC manuscript, in a plainly recent hand, is written:

> “The octave of the Conception of the most glorious Virgin Mary. A lesser double feast.”

GREVEN continues: [Col. 0804B]

> “In Africa, the birthday of Saints Faustinus, Candidus, Caecilianus, and twenty-eight others.”

This agrees sufficiently with the ROSWEYD manuscript mentioned above; but that number of thirty-one African martyrs does not seem capable of being derived from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

> “Folquinus the confessor.”

Could this perhaps be Folquinus of the Morini, treated yesterday, with his name duplicated?

> “Likewise, the blessed John Cornerius, monk and priest of the Carthusian order, whose merits the Lord deigned to display through many miracles. Saturnina the virgin.”

MOLAN. After “of Nicasius the bishop,” in italic type within the text, inserts:

> “After the solemn celebration of the Mass, he suffered martyrdom from the Vandals inside the church of Reims; for the faith of Christ he was beheaded within the church.”

At the end:

> “At the monastery of Sithiu, the passing of Blessed Folquinus, bishop of the Morini. The merit of his life and holiness is commended by the great depth of water which, with the south wind blowing, froze in a single night so that his body could cross over it.”

Then, in smaller type:

> “At Naples, Saint Agnellus the abbot. On the same day, Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers. After reaching Tours according to his own vow, he passed through Poitiers, settled there, and wrote the deeds of many saints there, partly in prose and partly in verse.”

The other editions report the same concerning Nicasius in the text, but err in also printing Eutropia in italics. Concerning Folquinus, they have the same as in the first edition. Then:

> “Likewise, Blessed Lupicinus, eighth bishop of the church of Vienne.”

Finally, in smaller type:

> “At Ascalon, Saints Aris, Promus, and Elias, martyrs. The first of these was thrown into the fire because of his confession of faith; the heads of the other two were cut off.”

See Eusebius’s *Book on the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 10, in Ruinart’s *Selecta*, beginning at page 344. Finally:

> “At Liège, at Saint Giles, the death of Blessed Odilia, a widowed recluse.”

[Col. 0801]

In Cyprus, the birthday of Blessed Spyridon the bishop, who was one of those confessors whom Maximian, after gouging out their right eyes and cutting through their left knees, had condemned to the mines. Since he led a prophetic life, he was also renowned for the glory of his miracles. At Alexandria, Saints Heron, Arsenius, Isidore, and Dioscorus the boy, martyrs, whom the judge, under the persecution of Decius, tore apart with various tortures; when he saw them armed with equal steadfastness of faith, he ordered them handed over to the flames. Dioscorus, however, after being scourged in many ways, was released by divine will for the consolation of the faithful. At Antioch, the birthday of Saints Drusus, Zosimus, and Theodorus, martyrs. Likewise at Reims, the passion of Saint Nicasius the bishop and Eutropia, his virgin sister.

18 days before the Kalends. Day 15. [Note: [Col. 0803]

The manuscripts agree for the most part: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. Antuerp.-Max. and the associated manuscripts of intermediate character are also added.]

[Note: [Col. 0803D]

Greven. and Molan. write *Valerianus*, who was more than eighty years old; all the others, with Ado and the actual source from which this material was taken—namely Victor of Vita—write otherwise. Belin. alone reads *et ita praeceptum est* (“and it was ordered thus”), and so that reading has been adopted. Herinien. alone somewhat attempted to correct *dimitteret habitare* (“would permit him to dwell”) by *sineret habitare* (“would allow him to dwell”). Greven. and Molan. disagree with the others, writing *sed in strata publica* (“but on the public road”); the reading in the text is better. Again, both read *nudo sub aere* (“naked beneath the open sky”). I admit that this is how it appears in Chifflet’s edition of Victor of Vita, but Our author followed the Viennese manuscript, which has *nudus sub aere* (“naked beneath the open sky”), and Ruinart restored this reading from the manuscripts in his latest edition. Munerat. erred by corruptly writing *multorum temporum* (“of many times”) for *multo tempore* (“for a long time”). Tornacen. perhaps wished to speak more correctly when it changed *defensione sanctimonii* (“defense of religious observance”) to *defensione sanctimoniae* (“defense of holiness”). Molanus will explain below what *sanctimonium* and *strata* mean. Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Belin., and all the manuscripts of intermediate character created another meaning by reading:

> “in the confession and defense of Catholic truth.”

The final announcement is expressed in Usuardine wording: not *Aurelianis*, nor *in civitate Aurelianensi*, nor *in territorio Aurelianensi*, as Belin., Greven., and Molan. have, but *in territorio Aurelianensium* (“in the territory of the people of Orléans”). The question is whether, with Pratensis and the customary followers Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., and Aquicinct., he read *Maximini abbatis* (“of Maximinus the abbot”) or *Maximini confessoris* (“of Maximinus the confessor”). The others follow the latter form, which we prefer; the second edition of Belin. combined both titles. A few write *Maximi*, with the first edition of Belin., but we need not delay over them.]

[Note: [Col. 0805A]

When discussing the African bishops Papinianus and Mansuetus on 28 November, we noted there that Ado enumerates several local bishops together on that day who suffered in the Vandal persecution, including Valerianus, whom we believe to be the same as our saint of today, whom Victor of Vita magnificently praises in Book I of *The Vandal Persecution*, in Chifflet’s edition, page 13. He is called bishop of the city of Abensis there; in Ruinart’s edition, page 16, of Abbenza. But that variation is of little concern to us. More relevant is Ruinart’s correction, by which Valerianus’s age is confirmed as eighty, whereas Chifflet’s edition indicated only that he was more than seventy years old. See further in Ruinart’s notes, page 159.

Let this suffice concerning the source from which the author of the Little Roman Martyrology first drew, in these words:

> “In Africa, Valerianus, bishop and confessor, during the Vandal persecution.”

Examine all the other ancient Martyrologies: you will find no remembrance of this saint in any of them. This adds new weight to the opinion mentioned elsewhere, namely that most African saints who suffered in the Vandal persecution were first entered into the ecclesiastical calendars by the author of the Little Roman Martyrology. We discussed this matter near the end of chapter 2 of our preface.

Ado, the compiler of longer eulogies, carefully investigated the persecution indicated and found the material for his eulogy in the history of the aforementioned Victor, adding a few words concerning the defense of religious observance, which are not found in that author—at least not in the passage transmitted by us. Usuard, for his part, borrowed everything from Ado.

[Col. 0806A] In the oldest Hieronymian manuscript, the Epternacensis or Antwerp manuscript, our second announcement is clearly marked:

> “In the city of Orléans, Maximinus the priest and confessor.”

In other copies one reads *Maximi* (“of Maximus”), for which Florentinius argues in vain from Belin., Maurolycus, or others of this sort, to which Usuardine manuscripts could also be added. Florus did no better in modifying the saint’s name to *Maximianus*, nor does he provide such a distinctive eulogy that it could not be applied to any confessor:

> “Living in the highest devotion, the Lord deigned to perform many miracles through his merits.”

Nor are these words of Ado more specific:

> “At Orléans, Blessed Maximinus the priest, a man of venerable holiness.”

Here I observe that the Hieronymian Martyrology, Florus, and Ado all intend to designate the city of Orléans, which is not the true location of Maximinus of Micy. Our author, therefore, expressing the matter more simply but also somewhat more distinctly through *the territory of Orléans*, seems deliberately to have abstained from every eulogy. How we should suppose that he formed his announcement was stated above in the discussion of variants.

Our Maximinus is unknown to the Little Roman Martyrology, Bede, and Rabanus. Mabilio, however, published much about him in the appendix to the first century of the Benedictines, beginning at page 580, reporting two Lives together with a book of miracles, preceded by observations and supplemented with notes that will be of no small assistance in illustrating the saint’s Acts in our larger work. The poet-martyrologist praised only this Maximinus in the following distich:

On the eighteenth, Maximinus, you hold your place;  
The fruitful fields of Orléans offer you the wine of Bacchus.

[Note: [Col. 0805B]

ROSWEYD. Adds to the sufficiently pure text:

> “In Africa, Faustinus the martyr, with thirty others.”

In the Hieronymian Martyrologies there is a Faustinus or Faustus with several companions, but I do not know how their number came to be increased to thirty.

PULSANEN. Of the first announcement has everything through “confessor,” with the entire eulogy deleted; the second he expands as follows: [Col. 0805C]

> “In the territory of the people of Orléans, the deposition of Blessed Maximus, priest and abbot, a man of venerable holiness.”

CENTULEN.:

> “In Africa, Saint Valerianus, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Orléans, Saint Maximinus the abbot. He was the brother of Saint Vitonus, bishop of Verdun.”

BRUSSELS. Anticipates:

> “At Babylon, in the time of Nebuchadnezzar the king, the passion of the three holy youths Ananias, Azarias, and Misael. Their bodies were placed beneath a certain cave. In Africa, Saint Aurelianus”—for Valerianus—“bishop and confessor. Because of his steadfastness in the orthodox faith, Gaiseric, king of the Arians, ordered that no one should receive him in house or field. Since he was more than eighty years old, on the public road…”

and so forth, quite accurately.

> “At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Maximus, bishop and confessor. Likewise Valerianus, bishop and confessor. And the deposition of Blessed Maximinus the abbot, a man of great holiness [Col. 0805D].”

This passage is noteworthy because it shows how easily the ignorance of scribes multiplied saints: here the two placed in our text become four.

HAGENOYEN. Begins with a long history of the patriarch Jacob, which is better known and more certain from elsewhere than to be transcribed here from this manuscript. Throughout the text it is sufficiently pure, but between Valerianus and Maximinus it inserts from the preceding day:

> “At Vienne, the birthday of Saint Lupicinus, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.:

> “Valerianus, bishop and confessor, who, when he was eighty years old, was expelled and, naked beneath the open sky, completed his life in the confession of the truth.”

Nothing concerning Maximinus.

[Col. 0806B] VATICAN, marked number 5949, adds:

> “At Ravenna, Saints Nanlavis and Concordius.”

The martyrs of Ravenna are commemorated on the following day, but under other names; among them is “Navalis,” whom I consider certainly to be designated here by “Nanlavis.” See Usuard there, his supplements, and the Roman Martyrology.

[Col. 0806C] BIZUNTIC.:

> “In the territory of the people of Orléans, Saint Maximus the confessor.”

See above.

REMENS. SS. Timoth. et Apoll. agrees with the earlier manuscript and many others in the name Maximus, but writes “priest and confessor.”

LUBECK–COLOGNE EDITION. Concerning Valerianus it mixes in a few details:

> “When he was more than eighty years old, during the Vandal persecution, by order of King Gaiseric, he was ordered to be expelled alone outside the city, and thus it was ordered…”

and so forth, as in ANTUERP. and many others. Concerning Maximinus it reads:

> “In the territory of Orléans, Saint Maximinus, priest and confessor, a man venerable for holiness.”

AMBIANEN reads almost the same.

GREVEN.:

> “The octave of the Conception of holy Mary, Mother of God.”

I omitted noting above that in the upper margin of the DANIC manuscript, in a plainly recent hand, is written:

> “The octave of the Conception of the most glorious Virgin Mary. A lesser double feast.”

GREVEN continues: [Col. 0806D]

> “In Africa, the birthday of Saints Faustinus, Candidus, Caecilianus, and twenty-eight others.”

This agrees sufficiently with the ROSWEYD manuscript mentioned above; but that number of thirty-one African martyrs does not seem capable of being derived from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

> “Folquinus the confessor.”

Could this perhaps be Folquinus of the Morini, treated yesterday, with his name duplicated?

> “Likewise, the blessed John Cornerius, monk and priest of the Carthusian order, whose merits the Lord deigned to display through many miracles. Saturnina the virgin.”

MOLAN. After “of Valerianus,” in italic type, inserts after “eighty”:

> “During the Vandal persecution, when, by order of Gaiseric, the Arian king, all the priests of the Lord were being forced to hand over the divine mysteries or books, so that those impious Arians even made shirts and breeches for themselves out of the altar cloths, he fought manfully so as not to hand over the divine sacraments, and was expelled…”

and so forth.

At the end, in smaller type, he adds:

> “The deposition of Blessed Sanctulus, priest and confessor. Gregory speaks of him in the books of the *Dialogues*.”

Castellanus places him among the *Emeri*, as he calls and writes them, in the *Universal Martyrology*, page 890. I have found no other evidence of his cult. He is omitted in the other editions, in which, besides Valerianus’s eulogy, only the following is added at the end:

> “On the fifteenth day, Saint Paul the Father, who was hidden.”

[Col. 0803]

In Africa, Blessed Valerianus, bishop and confessor, who, when he was more than eighty years old, was ordered to be expelled alone outside the city. It was ordered that no one should allow him to dwell either in a house or in a field. Thus, lying naked beneath the open sky on the public road for a long time, in confession of Catholic truth and defense of religious observance, he completed the course of his blessed life. In the territory of the people of Orléans, Saint Maximinus the confessor.

17 days before the Kalends. Day 16. [Note: [Col. 0807]

The pure manuscripts are Praten., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0807B]

Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., Belin., and Greven. write *Misahelis*; with the others I have retained the more common form. Likewise, they simply have *Babiloniam*, although some read *Babyloniam*. Praten. alone reads *duram carceris macerationem* (“the harsh mortification of imprisonment”). All the others have *diram* (“dreadful”); Munerat. transposed the phrase to *diram macerationem carceris* (“the dreadful mortification of imprisonment”) and omitted “and the cutting off of the breasts.” Instead of *gladio data* (“given to the sword”), Belin. incorrectly substituted *gladio donata* (“presented with a sword”). Munerat. has *Valenciani*, *Naulis*, and so forth. In the first case he alone is in error; in *Naulis*, nearly all the manuscripts have it, and we ought to follow them. Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Molan. more correctly have *Navalis*; not incorrectly, on the basis of certain Hieronymian manuscripts, Belin. has *Novalis*. I have discussed Tuscany elsewhere: all read it as it stands in the text, except Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0807B]

The author of the Little Roman Martyrology, who placed several Fathers of the Old Testament in the series of Christian heroes, was also the first to insert those three famous Babylonian youths into the Martyrology on this day, solely by his own arrangement:

> “The martyrdom of Saints Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, otherwise Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago.”

Nothing was added in Ado beyond the words “three holy men.” Whatever is added here as an eulogy is therefore Usuardine, as we noted elsewhere concerning the other patriarchs and prophets. Usuard received these eulogies, such as they are, from Isidore of Seville, *On the Life and Death of the Saints of Both Testaments*. Whatever else can subsequently be gathered about these saints you will find carefully indicated in Baronio’s annotation.

I would not dare assert with sufficient certainty where Wandalbert derived our Babylonians; meanwhile, he adorned them with a distinguished eulogy in this fashion:

[Col. 0807C]

Those who scorned the impious commands of the Assyrian tyrant,  
Whom neither the crackling flame of the raging furnace  
Could frighten in their faithful and steadfast spirit—  
On the seventeenth, the three youths are commemorated.

]

The second entry also belongs to the aforementioned author of the Little Roman Martyrology, and is formulated there as follows: “In Tuscany, Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr.” Ado summarized the history of her entire passion in a few words, and Usuard in still fewer, here and there following Ado’s sense rather than his words. These are the three ancient martyrologists in whom the illustrious virgin Barbara is certainly commemorated on this day; Rabanus recorded her on 4 December with a different eulogy, omitting—as though deliberately—both the place of martyrdom and the chronological indications, [Col. 0807D] which that martyrologist, being a learned man, may perhaps have found insufficiently compatible with Barbara’s Acts.

And indeed the deeds of this otherwise most renowned virgin and martyr are entangled in such grave difficulties, whoever the author or authors may have been who embellished them, that so far I do not see how they can be so purged as to be reduced to a sufficiently tolerable standard. Baronius saw those knots and acknowledged that some copies appeared corrupt, in which the place, time, and other matters had been thoroughly confused. We earnestly wish that someone would produce for us other faithful copies, whether Greek or Latin, from which a historical probability might be extracted.

Here are some of the complications. Our martyrologists expressly name Tuscany and the time of Maximian. Some versions of the Acts name Maximinus, [Col. 0808B] and identify him as the first successor of Alexander, so that Barbara would have been contemporary with Origen, whose disciple she would have been, at least by correspondence. They think this is conveniently confirmed by the Oriental Chronicle published by Ecchellensis, concerning whose authority we have spoken elsewhere. Others have recourse to the second Maximinus, placing Barbara with Catherine in Egypt. There is no less dispute about whether she suffered martyrdom at Heliopolis or Nicomedia; Bede’s Additions add Antioch. But who will find those cities in Tuscany, or Tuscany in the East?

These and similar considerations led recent critics to reject contemptuously whatever Acts they could find. They also displeased Papebrochius, as he sufficiently indicates in the Greek-Muscovite Ephemerides, pp. XXVI and LIV, and again in his Responses to Article XI, beginning at no. 106. Yet he readily allowed those points to be corrected which do not agree with our Observations, especially those concerning the beginnings of Saint Barbara’s cult. He himself places its origin at the end of the ninth century, although it is certain that the saint must have been commemorated in the West even before that century, since she is expressly marked in the Little Roman Martyrology. It is well established that its author did not ordinarily assign cults to saints without historical records.

It is no less evident that either some calendars or some Acts had reached Rabanus around the year 850, from which he entered Barbara into his martyrology. For to have recourse here to interpolation—what else would that be than to tear down certainties by doubtful conjectures? From these considerations it follows that Barbara’s cult was received in the West before Catherine’s.

Furthermore, the fact that the pure and genuine copies of Ado and Usuard, as well as the other manuscripts cited above by us, include Barbara makes this certain; Papebrochius was misled because he looked for her on 4 December. These brief remarks suffice for our present purpose; we refer the rest to the place where the Acts will be examined in full. The equally thorny questions concerning her body and its translations we leave untouched here.

Valentine with his companions at Ravenna is recorded most distinctly in the Hieronymian Martyrologies as follows: “At Ravenna, Valentine, Navalis, Agricola, Concordius.” The old Echternach manuscript reads “Novalis” and “Concordia,” and the Corbie manuscript adds Justin to them. Rabanus copied his entry from the aforesaid copies, and Usuard likewise, but omitted Concordius. Their ancient Acts, if any existed, are found nowhere; those published by more recent writers will be discussed in due course.

[Note: [Col. 0809A]]

HERINIEN. By the time this codex was written, Barbara’s commemoration on 4 December had become established; at approximately the same time Saint Blaise was moved from 15 February back to 3 February. I believe this was clearly done around the tenth century. Thus the aforementioned codex lacks Barbara; see her under 4 December.

TORNACEN. Pure in the first and last entry, it cuts away the entire eulogy of the second.

ROSWEYD. Also pure in the first and last, it omits the second, which is placed above under 4 December. At the end it adds: “On the same day, Lazarus, whom the Lord Jesus raised from the dead. Also Martha, his sister.” See the following day.

PULSANEN. Pure only in the first entry. Then: “On the same day, the blessed martyrs Rufus and Zosimus. At Spoleto, Saint Meletius, bishop and confessor.” Castellanus places him here; concerning the others, see Usuard under 18 December.

ANTUERP.-MAX. together with all its companions. These manuscripts give the pure Usuardine entry under 4 December, [Col. 0809B] but here substitute another in second place: “At Rome, the birthday of the holy martyrs Irenaeus, Antonius, Theodorus, Saturninus, Victor, and seventeen others. They completed a glorious martyrdom under the prefect Aelius together with the blessed virgin Lucia and Anceia [Auceja], king of the Persians, whom she converted to the faith of Christ.” See what we said on 25 June and the Acts for that day. They are sufficiently pure in the first and last entries.

CENTULEN. “The three boys Ananias, Azariah, and Misael,” etc., purely. The rest of the text is missing, in whose place stand: “On the same day, the holy martyrs Rufus and Zosimus, whose blessed struggle Saint Polycarp describes in his letter to the Philippians. At Pontus, Saint Meletius, bishop and confessor, who, although magnificent in learning, was far more magnificent in the virtue of his soul and the sincerity of his life.” This has been wrongly transferred here from 9 December.

BRUXELLEN. begins: “In Africa, the birthday of the holy Faustinus, Candidus, and Caecilianus.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies on the preceding day. It continues: “At Ravenna, the birthday of the holy martyrs Valentine, Navalis, Agricola, and Concordius.” See the Observations. Concerning Irenaeus and his companions it agrees with the manuscripts of the middle class. “In Tuscany, Saint Barbara, virgin and martyr.” It appears to suppose that this is a different Barbara from the one it placed above under 4 December. It continues: “At Spoleto, the burial of Saint Malecius, bishop and confessor.”

HAGENOYEN gives two long histories: one concerning the Babylonian boys, which is more familiar and more certain from the sacred writings than the account given here; the other concerning the virgin Luceia [Col. 0810A] and King Auceja, which I would prefer you to take from the Acts themselves under 25 June.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “The three Babylonian boys; Valentine, Naulis [otherwise Navalis], and Agricola, at Ravenna.”

VATICAN, no. 5949, contains nothing here about the Babylonian boys or Barbara.

FLORENTIN.: “At Spoleto, Saint Meletius, bishop and confessor. Also, the holy martyrs Florianus and his forty companions.” Do they perhaps indicate the Eleutheropolitans, concerning whom see the following day?

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition is similar in the text to ANTUERP.-MAX. and the other manuscripts of the middle class. It adds: “At Spoleto, Saint Meletius, bishop and confessor. On the same day, Saint Everhard, soldier and confessor.” See the MOLAN Appendix.

GREVEN: “At Ravenna, Concordius and five others suffered together with the aforesaid. Mammetus, boy and martyr, whom Usuard has under the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September. At Rome, the holy Herenaeus, Antonius, Theodorus, [Col. 0810B] Saturninus, Victor, and seventeen others. Also Simplicius and his companions. At Spoleto, Saint Meletius, bishop and confessor. At Vienne, Saint Odo, bishop and confessor. In Ireland, Beano, bishop and confessor. In the territory of Tournai, Saint Everhard, soldier and confessor. The Empress Adelheid, according to others on the day before the Ides of December.”

MOLAN. At the end: “At Vienne, the blessed Ado, bishop.” GREVEN has wrongly written Odo above. The reference is to the man whom we have so often cited in this work, namely the author of that martyrology from which almost the whole of Usuard was abridged. It continues: “Also the Empress Adelheid.” Then, in smaller type:

“In the territory of Tournai, Saint Everhard, soldier and confessor; who, as Mayerus writes in the Annals of Flanders, was regarded as Count of Cisoing, illustrious by his wife and the noble succession of his children, as well as by his wealth, retainers, military skill, and holiness of life; and he founded the Cisoing monastery near Lille. In Ireland, [Col. 0810C] Beano, first bishop of Aberdeen and confessor.”

Later editions have the same entry concerning Ado. Then:

“In Gaul, at Tournai, in the Cisoing monastery, the burial of Evrard, duke of Friuli. Also the burial of Saint Adelheid, empress. In Ireland, the birthday of Beano, first bishop of Aberdeen and confessor. At Amiens, the reception of the face of blessed John the Baptist. In Spain, by decree of the Tenth Council of Toledo, the feast of the Annunciation of Blessed Mary.”

It is not worth asking how long this rite continued.

[Col. 0807]

The three boys Ananias, Azariah, and Misael, whose bodies have been placed near Babylon beneath a certain cave. In Tuscany, the passion of Saint Barbara, virgin, under the emperor Maximian. After cruel imprisonment, the cutting of her sinews, burning with lamps, the cutting off of her breasts, and the torment of other sufferings, she was finally put to the sword and completed her martyrdom. At Ravenna, Saints Valentine, Navalis, and Agricola.

The sixteenth day before the Kalends. Day 17.

[Note: [Col. 0809]]

Thus the Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0809D]]

Among the manuscripts cited for the text, none correctly reads “outside the Daphnitic Gate.” I followed Praten. and Herinien. Greven. and Molan. have “Dampnitic”; Antuerp.-Maj. has “Dampnitian”; Munerat. has “Davithic”; only Rosweyd comes closer to the correct form with “Daphnitic.”

Nearly all have “in the cemetery”; Praten. and Molan. more correctly have “in the burial-ground.” In the Pratense manuscript, “Maria” has wrongly crept in for “Martha.” In Munerat., or through the printer’s error, we find “evicinio” for “e vicino.” All correctly read “whose venerable memory”; I do not know why Antuerp.-Maj. prefixed the particle “in.” Again, all agree in “Sarracens,” except the aforementioned manuscript and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0811A]]

The Hieronymian copies contributed nothing to the text for today. In describing Bede, Rabanus reports his eulogy, which celebrates rather the birthday of the saint than a translation. This should not seem surprising, since neither of them mentioned him on 1 February.

The text of the Little Roman Martyrology is clearer for today’s feast: “The translation of Ignatius, bishop and martyr, at Antioch.” The Viennese manuscript adds only this here: “He governed the Church of Antioch as the third after the Apostle Peter.” Since our author reported these words under 1 February, they are rightly omitted here and replaced by other statements from the feasts of the apostles, which properly and exclusively suit a translation.

There is no reason to dwell on this longer, since Henschenius treated the various translations of Saint Ignatius at length under 1 February, beginning on p. 33. There you will also find from what time the birthday of Saint Ignatius was assigned to 1 February in the Roman Church, as you will also find in the Greek-Muscovite Ephemerides under 29 January.

Wandalbertus celebrates the most illustrious martyr on this day in such a way that he too seems to be commemorating the birthday of Rufus and Zosimus, whom Polycarp praises together with Ignatius. He adds that these men are referred by our martyrologies to the following day. Let us hear the metrical eulogy:

> Holy Ignatius triumphs on the sixteenth day,  
> > shepherd and martyr of the city of Antioch;  
> > the teeth of wild beasts made him living bread.  
> > Rufus and Zosimus follow him,  
> > having poured out their blood for Christ.
