The foundation, so to speak, of our second entry is again given by the author of the Little Roman Martyrology: “And Lazarus, whom Christ raised, and Martha his sister, in Bethany.” Here I would have you observe that both the brother and the sister are placed IN BETHANY.

Ado derived this somewhat differently; all the words are his, and from them our eulogy is constructed. Bede, Florus, and Rabanus do not deal with these saints, at least not on this day, from which one may infer that Tillemont and others wrongly cite the latter. I also note that our martyrologists do not sufficiently specify what they are commemorating here concerning Lazarus, since the Greeks are said to have various feasts concerning him.

It nevertheless appears more probable—at least from the first author of the entry, the Little Roman Martyrology—that they intend to indicate Lazarus’s final death and his burial at Bethany with his sister Martha, so that they seem to have been entirely unaware of his burial in Cyprus, and even more so of his migration to Provence. Whether they correctly or incorrectly placed these matters I do not discuss here; it is clear that Lazarus and Martha were honored under one celebration on this day in the eighth and ninth centuries.

We spoke briefly of the two sisters under 22 July, on the occasion of Mary Magdalene, but here we have deliberately abstained from other controversies, intending to examine everything in the Acts next July. Meanwhile see Baronius’s notes, Tillemont, vol. II, p. 31 onward, and Castellanus in the First Bimester, p. 342 onward.

The Eleutheropolitan martyrs are purely Adonian; Usuard did nothing else for them except transfer here into his brief entry the words of the Viennese manuscript as well. In both, the number of martyrs is fixed at fifty; in both, all are anonymous. Baronius abandoned our martyrologists and followed, unless I am mistaken, a manuscript of the passion’s Acts, of which we possess a copy transcribed from the archives of Saint Peter in Rome, where a fuller description of the entire martyrdom is found.

He calls Florianus and Calanicus the principal figures of the whole company and adds the names of all the others, which together rise to sixty; from this the entry in the modern Roman Martyrology was formed. Peter must have seen other Acts in the Catalogue, book I, chapter 73, where only forty companions are joined to Florianus and Calanicus.

Baronius incorrectly assigns the thirty-seventh year of Heraclius; perhaps the twenty-seventh would be preferable, although neither in the Miscellany nor in Theophanes can sufficiently certain indications be found from which anything definite can be established concerning the number of these martyrs or the time or place of their passion. I leave the rest to further investigation.

[Note: [Col. 0811C]]

TORNACEN. has everything except the eulogy fitted above into the text for Martha and Lazarus.

ROSWEYD. inserts from Ado concerning Ignatius: “Who, third after the Apostle Peter, governed the Church of Antioch.” It begins another entry as follows: “Here is celebrated the birthday of blessed Lazarus and Martha.” The rest is sufficiently pure.

PULSANEN. begins: “The translation and burial of the body of Saint Ignatius the martyr.” It is more abbreviated concerning Lazarus and Martha. Nothing concerning the fourth entry.

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. concerning Ignatius: “Who, third after the Apostle Peter, governed the Church of Antioch. Here he suffered at Rome from the teeth of wild beasts; afterward he was translated and lies at Antioch.” In the other commemorations they are sufficiently pure.

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN, and LOVANIEN. All lack the first entry, in whose place they put the last concerning the fifty martyrs. They are sufficiently pure concerning Lazarus and Martha.

[Col. 0811D] ALBERG. and DANIC. agree with the preceding manuscripts, but at the end add: “At Andecenna, Saint Begga, widow, sister of Saint Gertrude.” See below under MOLAN. and the others.

CENTULEN. “At Antioch, the translation and burial of the body of blessed Ignatius, bishop and martyr, who suffered at Rome on the Kalends of February.” It is sufficiently pure concerning Lazarus, but omits Martha with the entire eulogy. It is again sufficiently pure in the last entry.

BRUXELLEN. begins with Lazarus and Martha, quite purely. Then, concerning Ignatius, after “martyr” it adds:

“Who suffered at Rome on the Kalends of February and was brought from Rome to Antioch; outside the Dampnitic Gate he was placed on this day in the cemetery of the church. At the monastery of Andemna, the burial of Saint Begga, widow, daughter of Duke Pippin, sister of Saint Gertrude, and widow of Duke Ansigisus. While devoting herself and her possessions to God in the state of widowhood, she founded the monastery of Andemna and was the first to establish the Beguines and Beghards, who derive their name from her.”

The institution both of the women and of the men is known from elsewhere well enough that there is no need to go back to Begga’s time.

HAGENOYEN begins: “In the city of Marseille, the burial of Saint Marsilius, bishop and confessor, brother of Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Martha.” From the very corruption of the name you can understand how accurate the more extensive accounts given here concerning Lazarus and Martha must be. I certainly pass over the task of describing stories of this sort.

What it has concerning Begga is generally more tolerable, as follows:

“At Andecenna, the burial of Saint Begga, sister of Saint Gertrude the virgin. From her husband Anthysus [for Ansigisus] she conceived Pippin the Elder—rather, she was his daughter—the duke [Col. 0812D] of the Franks; and after her husband’s death she remained in holy widowhood all the days of her life, and, filled with good works, departed to the Lord.”

It treats the translation of Ignatius on the following day, as well as the fifty martyrs.

Codex Ursini of Rosemberg: “At Andemna, Saint Begga, widow, sister of Saint Gertrude.” We have said more about Begga above.

AMBIANEM. “At Amiens, the reception of the face of Saint John the Baptist.” See MOLAN. on the preceding day.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Martha, the hostess of Christ, and Lazarus, her brother. The fifty holy martyrs.”

In VATICAN, shelfmark no. 5949, the first three [Col. 0813A] entries are absent. It adds: “In Africa, Saints Victor, Victor, and thirty-three others.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

LUXOVIEN. reads as follows: “In the monastery of Salsa, Saint Adelheid Augusta.”

SALINEN. has another entry concerning Lazarus: “In Bethany, Saint Lazarus the martyr, whom the Lord raised; his body rests at Autun.”

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition begins: “The birthday of blessed Lazarus, bishop and confessor, brother of the blessed Mary Magdalene and Martha, whom the Lord, as is read in the Gospel, had raised from the dead. Whose venerable memory,” etc., quite purely, though three are joined where there were two. It then gives the entry concerning the fifty martyrs, also well. Concerning Ignatius, after “Church” it adds: “Where, by the Lord’s favor, very many miracles are wrought through his merits. At Andemna, Saint Begga, widow, sister of Saint Gertrude the nun.”

BELIN. In the first entry it resembles ANTUERP., etc. It contains nothing about Martha. In the fourth it is pure.

GREVEN: “Also in Africa, Saints Victor, Victorianus, Adiutor, Honoratus, Felix, Vincentius, Quartus, Quintus, and twelve others. The commemoration of the worthy and holy memory of Bernard, bishop of Die, formerly of the Carthusian house of Portes, confessor. The dead whom he raised, the lepers whom he cleansed, and other miracles which the Lord deigned to perform through him testify to his holiness. Because of his exceptional holiness he was most closely associated with Saint Bernard of Clairvaux; and at his urging that man of God composed the divine work On the Song of Songs. Sturmius, first abbot of the monastery of Fulda and confessor. Begga, widow, sister of Saint Gertrude.”

MOLAN. At the end: “On the same day, at the Seven Churches, the passing of blessed Begga, widow.” Then, in smaller type:

“Widow of Duke Ansigisus and sister of Saint Gertrude. While devoting herself and her possessions to God in the state of widowhood, she founded the monastery of Andemna and was the first to establish the Beguines, who derive their name from her.”

These seem to have been taken from the BRUXELLEN codex. Then:

“At Bigard, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict near Brussels, Saint Wivina, virgin, who was its first superior.”

Other editions insert the following concerning Ignatius into the text in different type: “Third after blessed Peter, he governed the Church of Antioch. Here he suffered at Rome from the teeth of wild beasts.”

At the end:

“At Andemna, [Col. 0814B] at the Seven Churches, the passing of blessed Begga, widow, sister of Saint Gertrude. On the same day at Bigard, blessed Wivina, virgin, whose great merit before the Lord is faithfully proclaimed by the deaf, the crippled, and the possessed, who recovered their former health.”

You will note that in these editions Usuard’s text has again been corrupted, with Martha and her entire eulogy removed. In this respect the purity of the first edition is far preferable.

[Col. 0809]

The translation of Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr, who was brought from the city of Rome to Antioch and lies outside the Daphnitic Gate, in the cemetery of the church. On the same day, blessed Lazarus, whom the Lord Jesus is read in the Gospel to have raised from the dead. Also blessed Martha, his sister; their venerable memory is preserved by a church built not far from Bethany, where their house had stood nearby. In the East, at the city of Eleutheropolis, the fifty holy martyrs who suffered under the Saracens.

The fifteenth day before the Kalends. Day 18.

[Note: [Col. 0813B]]

The manuscripts that are pure on this day are Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan. Add Antuerp.-Max. [Col. 0814B] together with all its companions of the middle class.

[Note: [Col. 0813C]]

Praten. alone has “Zozimus”; the other manuscripts agree better with the text. It also correctly writes “at Philippi,” but afterward incorrectly has “Philippians.” Antuerp.-Maj. has made Philippi into the name of a city. This manuscript and Greven. often write “hii” for “hi.” All have “these from that number,” etc., but Munerat. omitted the particle “that.” In Praten., “Jews” is not written out in full. Praten. and Herinien. read “Moysitis,” but there is no doubt that Usuard followed Ado. The principal variation concerns the name of the bishop of Tours, which only Molan. and Antuerp. have correctly formed as “Gatianus”; Praten. and Herinien. have “Catianus,” Antuerp.-Maj. “Cancianus,” Munerat. “Gacianus,” and others “Gratianus,” etc. Greven’s caution did not help him when he wrote “Cacianus,” otherwise “Gratianus.” Here the first has “directed,” omitting “bishop.” Molan. writes “first directed” somewhat better, but also omits “bishop.”

[Note: [Col. 0813C]]

Rufus and Zosimus, linked with Ignatius by Wandalbertus on the preceding day, are recorded in the Little Roman Martyrology on the next day as follows: “Rufus and Zosimus, among the first disciples of Christ, through whom the primitive Church was founded among Jews and Greeks.” The place where they suffered or were buried is not stated.

Nevertheless, this martyrologist asserts more here than he found in his Rufinus, book III, chapter 35. There Rufus and Zosimus are indeed praised excellently with Ignatius from Polycarp’s celebrated letter to the Philippians, as was said under the preceding day; but they are not said there to have been among Christ’s first disciples, nor does this seem capable of being understood in the stricter sense, [Col. 0813D] unless Rufus here is confused with the one of whom we spoke under 21 November.

Consult Rufinus’s words, which Ado includes among the feasts of the apostles, or approach the source itself, where Polycarp says: “I beseech you all to give yourselves to obedience and to practice the patience which you saw in Ignatius, Rufus, and Zosimus, blessed men,” etc., without adding a word about their discipleship or the foundation of the primitive Church.

For the rest, Ado followed the sense of the Little Roman Martyrology, adding at the end on his own: “They rest at the city of the Macedonians, Philippi.” This seems to me highly uncertain. Perhaps Polycarp’s letter provided the occasion, since it is addressed to the Philippians.

Usuard began from the aforesaid statement and copied the remainder of Ado’s eulogy. These entries are marked in our series, while they are unknown to or omitted by the others.

Wandalbertus was not ignorant of the saints’ names; we gave his metrical encomium on the preceding day. Incidentally, note that the Plantinian Bede under 26 December shamefully interpolated Ado’s text. Where Ado mentions only Pope Zosimus, the other wrote: “On the same day, Saint Ignatius, Rufus, and Zosimus the pope, who sat,” etc., transcribing the remainder of Ado’s commemoration.

[Col. 0814D] The Little Roman Martyrology mentions only the first entry. In the Viennese manuscript, the second place is occupied by the same person who appears in our text: Moses or Moysetes, a martyr in Africa, of whom I do not recall having read anything elsewhere, except for a doubtful note by Molan in the later editions. Among the many other African martyrs in the Hieronymian Martyrologies appears the name Monsitis; I do not know whether it can suitably be reduced to Moysetes.

Whatever the case may be, Wandalbertus also knew and celebrated Moysetes in this single verse for the day:

> Finally, the fifteenth day blooms with Moysetes’ blood.

[Col. 0815A] The third commemoration is again most purely Adonian, if not copied word for word, at least transcribed by Usuard in all the essential points of its meaning. Ado assigned no definite age to Gatianus of Tours, nor did Usuard; they were content with this chief praise of him, that he had been the first bishop of that Church, sent from the city of Rome.

Baronius inserted the time of Pope Fabian into the Roman Martyrology quite appropriately, and this can easily be confirmed from Gregory of Tours, as Tillemont demonstrates in volume IV, p. 723. This is now the more widely accepted opinion among learned Frenchmen, and has been asserted more than once in our Acts: namely, that the earliest apostles of Gaul—this Gatianus of Tours, Trophimus of Arles, Paul of Narbonne, Saturninus of Toulouse, Dionysius of Paris, [Col. 0816A] Austremonius of Clermont, Martial of Limoges, and others—belonged to approximately the same period.

Bosquetus, whom we cited not long ago, Fraissius, and others may be consulted; they agree in the same view, drawing from Gregory of Tours at the places cited by Baronius. It is regrettable that no Acts of so illustrious a saint survive, at least none that I have seen. What can be gathered in due course from the aforementioned Gregory, from the beginning and end of the History of the Franks—whose principal material Surius published—from the Glory of the Confessors, chapters 4 and 30, or from elsewhere, will supply the deficiency. Castellanus assigns Gatianus’s death to the year 289; this too will be examined more carefully in its proper place. See Motherius’s note on this day.

[Note: [Col. 0815A]]

TORNACEN. carries the first entry through “was founded.” It is pure in the second. Then: “Gatianus, bishop and confessor,” and no more.

ROSWEYD. adds to the fairly pure text: “In Africa, the martyr Rogatianus and thirty-five others. Auceia, king [Col. 0815B] and martyr, with eighteen others. Honoratus the martyr, with thirty-one others.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which Auceias is mentioned more than once.

PULSANEN. lacks the first entry and is pure in the second. Then: “On the same day, the birthday of Saint Anatolia, virgin, who was seized together with blessed Victoria, her fellow virgin, and crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Decius.” Usuard records Anatolia under 9 July and Victoria under 23 December; see the Observations under both days. The last entry follows in abbreviated form: “At Tours, Saint Gratianus, bishop.”

ANTUERP. and MAX.-LUBEC. have the first and second entries pure. The third is: “At Tours, Saint Gatianus, bishop.”

CENTULEN. “At Rome, Saint Anatolia, virgin, who was seized together with blessed Victoria, her fellow virgin, and martyred under Caesar Decius. In Africa, Saint Moysetes, martyr.” It is also sufficiently pure concerning Gatianus. It has nothing concerning the first entry of Rufus and Zosimus.

BRUXELLEN. is quite pure in the first entry and adds: “At Laodicea, the birthday of the holy martyrs Theotimus and Basilianus.” It continues with the fifty Eleutheropolitan martyrs from the preceding day. Then:

“In Africa, the passion of Saints Moysetes, Victor, Victorianus, Adiutor, Honoratus, Felix, Vincentius, and twenty-three others. At Rome, the birthday of Saints Antoninus, Irenaeus, and Theodolus. Also the birthday of Saints Quintus, Simplicius, Paulus, Privatus, and Januarius.”

These have been variously collected from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Instead of Gatianus it writes Tatianus. Otherwise the entry is fairly pure. At the end: “On the same day, the birthday of Saint Anatolia, virgin, who was seized together with blessed Victoria, her fellow virgin, in the time of the emperor Decius and crowned with martyrdom.” See what we said under PULSANEN.

HAGENOYEN begins with the translation of Saint Ignatius, fairly purely. See the preceding day’s text. It continues: “In the territory of Eichstätt, Saints Wunibald and Walburga, glorious confessors. At Salsa, Saint Adelheid, empress.” Then it gives the first entry fairly purely, except that it writes: “Rufus, Rufinus, and Zosimus.” It is reasonably accurate concerning Moysetes and Gatianus. Then: “In the East, at Eleutheropolis,” etc., as on the preceding day. Finally: “On the same day, the burial of Saint Flavitus, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Rufus and Zosimus, who flourished in the primitive Church. Moysetes the martyr. Tatianus, bishop of Tours.” See the Variants.

[Col. 0816A] BIGOTIAN, shelfmark D. 9: “On the same day, Saint Flavius the confessor.” This is undoubtedly for Flavitus.

ALTEMPS.: “On the same day, Saint Wunibald the confessor.” Concerning his sister, see 1 May, etc.

FLORENTIN. has the following, as above: “Saint Anatolia, virgin, [Col. 0816B] who was seized together with blessed Victoria, her fellow virgin, and crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Decius. Also Saint Catianus, bishop and martyr.” I think Gatianus is intended, whose name, distorted in this way, has been transformed into that of a martyr.

REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll. gives a different form: “At Tours, Saint Tatianus, the first bishop of that same city.”

The LUBECK-COLOGNE edition, fairly pure in the text, adds the entry concerning Anatolia, etc., as we have already given it more than once. Then: “On the same day, Saint Paul the Simple, confessor, disciple of blessed Anthony the abbot. In the territory of Eichstätt, Saint Wunibald, abbot and confessor, brother of Saints Willibald, bishop, and Walburga, virgin. At the castle of Conflans, the translation of Saint Florinus, priest and confessor.”

BELIN. is fairly pure in the first and second entries; in the third it resembles ANTUERP., etc. One edition adds primi civitatis ipsius after “bishop.” “On the same day, Saint Flavitus, priest and confessor.”

[Col. 0816C] GREVEN. contains much from the Hieronymian Martyrologies:

“At the city of Laodicea, the birthday of Saints Thetianus and Basilianus. In Africa, Saints Quintus, Simplicius, Paulus, Victoria, Privatus, Caecilianus, and Evasus. Also Saints Dignus, Bodegisilus, and Honoratus, with thirty others. In Africa, the martyr Rogatianus and thirty-six others. Also the holy martyrs Auceias, king of the barbarians, and Lucia, virgin.

“When Auceias wished to violate Lucia, a Roman virgin whom he had captured, he was moved by divine prompting, began to venerate her greatly, and afterward traveled with her to Rome, where he obtained the palm of martyrdom together with twelve others who were then being held in prison for the faith. Usuard has these on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, but others on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

“On the same day, according to the Catalogue, Saint Ildephonsus, archbishop of Toledo. Having abandoned the world and assumed the monastic habit, he attained the dignity of archbishop through the merit of his exceptional holiness; finally, filled with holy works, he happily departed on the day when he had established that the feast of the glorious virgin Mary—in whose devotion he was most ardent—should be celebrated in his church, namely, the eighth day before the Nativity of Christ.

“Maurinus, bishop. In Ireland, Flamianus, bishop. In the territory of Eichstätt, Saint Wunibald, abbot and confessor, brother of Saints Willibald, bishop, and Walburga, virgin. On the same day, Paul the Simple, confessor, disciple of blessed Anthony the abbot, a man of extraordinary patience and obedience. At the castle of Conflans, the translation of Saint Florinus, priest and confessor. Anatolia, virgin and martyr, who was seized together with blessed Victoria, her fellow virgin,” etc., as above. Then: Maximilla, virgin.

[Col. 0813]

In Macedonia, at the city of Philippi, the birthday of the blessed martyrs Rufus and Zosimus. They belonged to the number of those disciples through whom the primitive Church was founded among Jews and Greeks; Saint Polycarp also writes of their blessed struggle in his letter to the Philippians. In Africa, the passion of Saint Moysetes, martyr. At Tours, Saint Gatianus, bishop and confessor, who was sent from the city of Rome as the first bishop to that same city and, renowned for many miracles, rested in peace.

The fourteenth day before the Kalends. Day 19.

[Note: [Col. 0817A]]

The majority of the manuscripts agree: Praten., Herinien., Tarnacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Antuerp., and [Col. 0818A] Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. Also Antuerp.-Max. together with all its companions.

[Note: [Col. 0817A]]

Tornacen. alone differs from the others. Instead of “bearing the likeness of the Savior,” it reads “bearing the Savior,” etc. Belin., together with the manuscripts of the middle class, has “who with the robbers,” omitting the particle “together.” Antuerp.-Maj. reads “Dari” for “Darius,” but Munerat. has disastrously transformed the name into “Clarus.” Belin., again together with the cited manuscripts, adds “and confessor” after “bishop” at the end of the text. Concerning the varying spellings of Egypt—Egyptum, Egiptum—Antissiodorum—Anthisiodori—Nicaea—Nycea—and so forth, enough has been said elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0817B]

We have seen Alexandrian martyrs, distributed among various days of this month—namely the 7th, 8th, 12th, and 14th—taken from Rufinus, Book VI, chapter 31, or from the often-mentioned letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Fabius of Antioch. But the one who first distributed them in this way, the author of the Little Roman Martyrology, does not stop there. Today’s Nemesius is taken from the same place; on the following day Ammon, Zenon, and others will follow, and again on the 22nd the memory of Ischyrion and very many others will be commemorated, among them the old man Chaeremon. Thus, in this month alone, seven announcements are presented drawn from the cited chapter of Rufinus, none of which is marked elsewhere among the martyrologists outside our series.

Accordingly, on this day the Little Roman Martyrology celebrates Nemesius:

> In Egypt, Nemesius the martyr, who was accused before the judge as a robber through calumny.

The Viennese Martyrology transcribed the rest of his passion from the aforesaid passage of Rufinus. Our author, following his custom of using a summary, extracted the whole substance neatly. Motherius rightly evaluated the martyrdom of our Nemesius in his French translation of the Roman Martyrology, mentioned elsewhere, p. 447, where he observes that he is sometimes called Nemesianus. Nevertheless, the Greek name Νεμεσίων appears to be rendered either *Nemesius*, with Rufinus, or *Nemesion*, with Valesius—not *Nemesis*, as Christophorsonus has it, and certainly not *Nemesianus*. These remarks should suffice in praise of the distinguished martyr and for clarifying our text.

The Little Roman Martyrology speaks only of Nemesius; in Ado, however, Avitus of Orléans follows. We placed him, together with Usuard, on 17 June, so that nothing further need be said about him here. I merely observe in passing that Ajutus, found in some fuller Usuardine codices—such as those which we call FLORENTINE in the Appendices—was formed from Avitus, and that from there he was placed under that form in the Roman Martyrology. Castellanus, if I am not mistaken, rightly noticed that the same saint is understood under different names.

The rest of our text does not recognize its usual guides. But from where shall we say that Usuard received Darius of Nicaea, the martyr? The Hieronymian Martyrologies do not express him clearly enough, and record him even more obscurely at Nicaea; indeed, they join Darius, or Daria, with Chrysanthus in such a way that these may seem to be repetitions of those celebrated by Usuard on 1 December. One might say that he could have taken them from Wandalbert. I do not think so, for why would his companion Zosimus have been left out? Indeed, it might be inferred from this very point that Wandalbert’s Martyrology was never seen by Usuard, as we indicated near the end of the first chapter of the preface.

I would believe that some Hieronymian Martyrology, similar to the Lucense, had guided both men: in it, with Gregory excluded, all the martyrs listed there may have been assigned to Nicaea. From this Usuard borrowed only the last, while Wandalbert borrowed the two, praising them in his single verse:

> Zosimus and Darius crown the fourth with ten.

Gregory of Auxerre, bishop, thirteenth in order, inserted in the Lucense codex, was added to the Corbeiensis. In our Florus he has the same eulogy that Florentinius transcribed from the Martyrology of Saint Sabinus at Levitania; his other observations may be consulted. He is also in Rabanus in the same words which Florentinius set down in different lettering in his commemoration of the Lucense Hieronymian codex. I shall refrain from asking how he entered Usuard, since Ado added so many other local saints that he could easily have added this one on his own.

I know that in Ado of Mosander he is placed on the following day with an asterisk, and in Rosweyd in the appendix; but these facts sufficiently show that the Gregory is not Ado’s. Apart from the indicated eulogy, I have nowhere been able to find a Life or Acts. Our manuscript collection has a little concerning the deeds of the bishops of Auxerre, where his deposition is noted on the 14th day before the Kalends of June, that is, 19 May. If more exists elsewhere, we earnestly desire that it be supplied to us.

[Note: [Col. 0817D]]

PULSANEN, having for some time been divergent from the others, begins here:

> “At Auxerre, the blessed Gregory, bishop, who sat for twelve years, seven months, and three days, and was buried in the church of Saint Germanus, bishop.”

It cuts out the entire eulogy beginning with Nemesius. Then:

> “At Alexandria, the blessed Clement, bishop and martyr.”

I have not hitherto known such a Saint Clement; see the following codex. Darius is omitted.

CENTULEN:

> “In Egypt, the blessed Nemesius the martyr, who was burned with the robbers. At Orléans, Saint Avitus the abbot, who was full of the spirit of prophecy and rested in a glorious end.”

See the Observations. Then:

> “At Alexandria, the blessed Clement the presbyter, who flourished exceedingly in the schools of divine learning, whose authority is also very frequently preferred in narratives of divine history.”

Usuard mentioned Clement on 4 December.

BRUXELLEN invents a new announcement about Darius from the Hieronymian Martyrologies:

> “At Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, the feast of the holy martyrs Darius, bishop, Zosimus, Paul, Cyriacus, and Secundus.”

In second place it has Nemesius, but not entirely accurately:

> “At Alexandria, the blessed Clement, presbyter and martyr, who flourished exceedingly in the schools of divine learning.”

It is almost similar to the middle-grade codices in the case of Gregory. Finally:

> “At Orléans, the blessed Avitus, abbot, who was illustrious in the spirit of prophecy.”

HAGENOYEN, sufficiently accurate in the case of Nemesius, inserts a long history, of which I shall give the beginning:

> “At Aquileia, the passion of the holy martyrs Felix and Fortunatus, who suffered at the time when Diocletian and Maximian issued an order that no one could sell or buy unless he had first sacrificed to idols, and that whoever concealed a Christian should be punished. Accordingly, a certain Apamius presented the holy brothers Felix and Fortunatus to the governor for punishment. But they were singing, ‘Behold how good and how pleasant,’ etc.; and when they refused to sacrifice, they were beaten with clubs, and they invoked Jesus Christ. The governor said to them: ‘Do you not know that the Augusti have been born?’”

and so forth; these can be read more fully in Ado on 11 June. See what was said there in our Observations, or more fully in the Acts. I do not know what moved this writer to transfer those saints here. It continues:

> “In the city of Nicaea, the feast of Saint Darius the martyr. On the same day at Auxerre, the deposition of Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor.”

AMBIANEN:

> “At Orléans, Saint Avitus the abbot, who was illustrious in the spirit of prophecy and was honorably buried in the same city.”

We have already said in the Observations that he is commemorated on 17 June.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT has only:

> “Nemesius the martyr. Darius the martyr.”

Codex D. DU CHEVAL, marked with the letter C:

> “At Auxerre, Saints Paul and Gregory.”

VATICAN, under note no. 5949, says nothing about the martyrs Nemesius and Darius. It adds:

> “At Orléans, Saint Avitus the abbot.”

ALTEMPS:

> “In the district of Cabilon, Saint Cyprian the abbot.”

FLORENTIN:

> “At Orléans, Saint Ajutus the abbot, who was illustrious in the spirit of prophecy and was buried there.”

Without doubt, it was from some such codex that this Ajutus entered the Roman Martyrology.

LUGDUNEN:

> “In the city of Auxerre, Saints Paul and Gregory.”

REMENS, Saints Timothy and Apollinaris:

> “At Orléans, the deposition of Saint Avitus the abbot.”

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition:

> “In Egypt, the blessed Nemesius the martyr, who was first accused before the judge Aemilianus as a robber through calumny; when acquitted of that charge, he was thereafter accused because he was a Christian. In this matter, however, the judge showed no restraint, but, tortured by the same judge Aemilianus with repeated punishments, he was ordered to be hung with the robbers, bearing the likeness of the Savior, who endured the cross together with the robbers.”

An excessive similarity has been sought here. In the case of Darius and Gregory it is sufficiently accurate. At the end:

> “At Orléans, Saint Avitus the abbot and confessor.”

GREVEN:

> “At Nicaea in Bithynia, Saints Zosimus, Paul, Secundus, and Cyriacus. Also Anastasius and Sidonius.”

See the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

> “Ammon, bishop of Orléans and confessor. On the same day, according to Ado, at Orléans, Saint Avitus the abbot, who, from desire for the solitary life, left the monastery with Saint Karileffus and rested, illustrious for great virtues and the spirit of prophecy. Usuard has him on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July. Dignus the confessor. Megaudius the confessor, father of Saint Alheidis the virgin. Also Peter, presbyter, a regular canon, provost of Aroldus, of blessed memory. Also William, a convert of the house of Casula, of the Carthusian Order, confessor, a man of admirable virtue. Once, while riding a donkey on the business of his house, robbers attacked him. Full of faith, he pulled the donkey’s foot away and, threatening the robbers with it, threw them into astonishment and flight. Then he put the foot back on the animal and completed his journey.”

MOLAN, in italics, after “Nemesius,” inserts into the text:

> “who was first accused before the judge Aemilianus as a robber through calumny; when acquitted of that charge, he was thereafter accused because he was a Christian; in this matter no mercy is shown, but …”

At the end:

> “On the same day the body of Saint Hubert was placed in the crypt.”

In other editions “and confessor” is added at the end of the text, also in italics. Nothing further.

[Col. 0817]

> In Egypt, the blessed Nemesius the martyr, who, tortured by the judge Aemilianus with repeated punishments, was ordered to be burned with the robbers, bearing the likeness of the Savior, who endured the cross together with the robbers. In the city of Nicaea, Saint Darius the martyr. Also at Auxerre, Saint Gregory the bishop.

## Thirteenth day before the Kalends. Day 20.

[Note: [Col. 0819]]

Taken from Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., Munerat., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0819C]]

In Antuerp.-Maj. it is incorrectly written *Amonis*, and in Munerat, incorrectly *Tholomei*. All preserve *Ingenii*; Greven has the worse reading *Nigenii*. Is Molan’s *Ingenui* preferable? This is how it should be read from Rufinus, the Little Roman Martyrology, and Ado, and this is also how Valesius translated it. The modern reformers of the Roman Martyrology seem to have followed Christophorsonus, who wrote *Ingenes*. Antuerp.-Maj. and Munerat erred even more seriously by omitting the last two names, *Ingenui* and *Theophili*, which for us are *Ingenii* and *Theophili*.

Again, Antuerp.-Maj. has *etiam* in place of *et jam*, and Munerat has *eripere* in place of *erigere*. All the codices agree on *illico Christus gloriosissime triumphavit*, and this must certainly be read from Ado. Greven wrote *victoriosissime triumphavit*, and Molan followed him; he added a further defect, *per Christus illico victoriosissime triumphavit*. I have spoken elsewhere about Thrace; for the moment I follow those whom I previously followed. Antuerp.-Maj. substituted *Amphitre* for *Amphitrea*, a form in no way Usuardine; but whether, in the matter itself, the earlier or the later location is more genuine, I confess that I do not know.

[Note: [Col. 0819C]]

Here now is that other group of Alexandrians, about which we began to speak on the preceding day, proceeding from the same passage of Rufinus, Book VI, chapter 31, and from the same letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Fabius of Antioch. The author of the Little Roman Martyrology seems to have followed the order of the martyrdoms set out in that chapter of Rufinus; he is the first among the martyrologists to enumerate the five most courageous athletes:

> “At Alexandria, Ammon, Zenon, Ptolemy, Ingenius, and Theophilus.”

Following this guide, and nearly exhausting the Rufinian source, Ado transferred the order of the history from it. Our author, although somewhat more briefly, embraced the whole matter quite elegantly. The Little Roman Martyrology and the Viennese Martyrology have nothing further; therefore Usuard consulted another source to supplement his text, but thrust upon us two announcements entangled in difficulties.

There is no doubt that both were taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, but he himself seems to have become even more entangled in the confused reading of those codices. Let us display the source. The Lucense codex reads:

> “In Thrace, in the city of Gildo, Bajuli.”

The water is muddy in the last two words, *Gildo* and *Bajuli*. Now hear the very ancient Epternacensis:

> “In Thrace, the feast of Julius.”

Thus it has it in today’s entry; on the following day, however:

> “In the city of Gildoba in Thrace, Julius.”

The Corbeiensis or Corbeienses and the Blomianus place this same announcement on this very day. From these facts it is easily apparent that some such Hieronymian codex came into Usuard’s hands, from which he fashioned his *Gelduba*. You will search the geographers in vain for the part of Thrace where Gelduba or Gildoba was situated, since I do not think it can be found there; indeed, it very plausibly arose from the mutilated names of saints, no less than *Amphitrea*, to which our last saint Liberatus is assigned.

I do not deny that an ancient Gelduba, today Geldub or Gelb, is found along the Rhine in the territory of Cologne. But to place the martyr Julius there with Saussayus is as absurd as it would be ignorant to carry the Rhine into Thrace or transplant Thrace to the Rhine. Castellanus places Gelduba on the borders of Bulgaria and modern Romania, but I am looking for an ancient geographer who will assign it to us.

Furthermore, Baronius assigns our Liberatus to Rome, reporting the second announcement in the Roman Martyrology today as follows:

> “At Rome, the holy martyrs Liberatus and Bajulus.”

This departs very far from all the Hieronymian Martyrologies, including the codex of Saint Cyriacus and Rabanus, for in these Liberatus is consistently placed with Thecla in the East.

Castellanus observes concerning the aforesaid Roman announcement that it was composed from three elements: first, the location “at Rome,” which in the Hieronymian Martyrologies is assigned only to Pope Zephyrinus; then the name Liberatus, torn away from the East; and finally, from the last syllable of the earlier location *Gelduba*, joined to the name Julius, the name *Bajulus* was assembled.

I acknowledge the confusion, but I believe it is not Baronius’s confusion; rather, it belonged to some codex from which he took those names thus joined together. Castellanus will not deny that in some Hieronymian codices, and also in Rabanus, *Bajulus* is clearly expressed, so that the entire error consists solely in the location—namely, that Liberatus and whatever Bajulus may be were placed at Rome.

But who will find that Usuardine *Amphitrea*, either in the East or anywhere in the West? Perhaps the eminent man thought a well-known place found somewhere should be preferred to an unknown or fictitious one. Florentinius attempts to substitute other locations; his method is well known, but it only further entangles matters already very confused.

I shall say what I think: I am greatly mistaken if Usuard did not use some Hieronymian codex so corrupt that from the worn, torn, and badly connected elements of words he fashioned some *Amphitrea*, whose discovery we pursue in vain. Nor do I wish, with Castellanus, to join together scattered syllables from which he produced *Bajulus* and I might attempt to produce *Amphitrea*. Whether our author ultimately put forward something true or false, it is certain that he left us such a text as we have represented here as sincere and genuine.

[Note: [Col. 0821B]]

TORNACEN, in first place, extends the eulogy as far as “they testify,” with everything else deleted. The last two announcements are accurate.

ROSWEYD, in second place, has:

> “At Rome, Pope Zephyrinus and martyr.”

We treated him with Usuard on 26 August; see the Observation there. Here is Wandalbert’s verse for today:

> Zephyrinus, bishop, shines as the thirteenth.

Our codex is accurate in the case of Julius and Liberatus, adding at the end in capital letters something that will recur in other codices:

> “The vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle.”

PULSANEN: In the first phrase the wording is somewhat changed and made more suitable to Ado. The second and third are absent.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., and UGHELLIAN immediately append after Liberatus, or rather join to it:

> “and Gregory the bishop.”

Peter of Equilinum took his material from such a codex in the Catalogue printed by Florentinius. He is as uncertain as we are about this Gregory. It may be a repetition of Gregory of Auxerre, about whom we spoke on the preceding day. The cited codices continue:

> “At Rome, the deposition of Saint Zephyrinus, bishop.”

ANTUERP.-MAX. and all the other middle-grade codices begin:

> “The vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle.”

At the end, after Liberatus, they add as above:

> “and Saint Gregory the bishop.”

CENTULEN has only the first announcement, mutilated here and there and sometimes interpolated; it is unnecessary to transcribe it here.

BRUXELLEN begins:

> “At Rome, Saint Zephyrinus, pope, who established that all Christians, when twelve years old, should receive the Eucharist on the feast of Easter, and that the ordinations of priests and Levites should solemnly take place at the appointed time.”

Announcements formed at will follow:

> “In the city of Gelduba in Thrace, the feast of the holy martyrs Julius or Julianus and Liberatus. Also at Amphitrea, Saints Gregory the bishop and Liberatus.”

In the Alexandrian martyrs it is not entirely accurate. At the end it adds:

> “In the East, Saint Thecla the virgin.”

See what we said about Thecla on 23 September.

HAGENOYEN also begins:

> “At Rome, the feast of Saint Zephyrinus, pope and martyr, on the Appian Way. He established that all Christians twelve years old should receive the Eucharist on Easter Day in the presence of the clergy and faithful laity. He also decreed that all altar vessels should be of glass or tin, and that the orders of priests and Levites should be conferred at the appointed time and in the presence of many bystanders. He suffered under the emperor Severus.”

In the case of the Alexandrians it is sufficiently accurate. Then:

> “In Thrace, in the city of Geldula, the feast of Saint Julius the martyr. Also, in the city of Amphitrea, the feast of the blessed Gregory the bishop and Liberatus.”

VICTORIN and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130, have at the end:

> “At Rome, on the Appian Way, Saint Zeverinus the bishop.”

For Zephyrinus. Then:

> “In the East, Saint Thecla the virgin and martyr.”

DAVERONEN:

> “In the district of Cabilon, Saint Cyprian the abbot.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT:

> “Ammon with his companions, the martyr. Julius the martyr.”

[Col. 0822C] In VATICAN, no. 5949, there is nothing about Liberatus.

FLORENTIN has, like ANTUERP. and the others above:

> “and Saint Gregory the bishop. At Rome, Saint Zephyrinus the bishop.”

It also adds:

> “In Spain, Saint Domitian the abbot.”

I think Dominic the abbot is meant; see Castellanus and MOLAN below.

BURDEGALEN:

> “In the territory of Cynula, Saint Hospitius the confessor. In the monastery of Lérins, Saint Columbus the abbot.”

I know neither of them under these names.

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition begins:

> “The vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle. At Alexandria, the blessed martyrs Ammon,”

and so forth, sufficiently accurately, as also in the case of Julius. It gives the final announcement an entirely new form:

> “At Amphitrea, Saints Liberatus and Gregory, bishops and confessors.”

BELIN agrees with ANTUERP. and the others in the addition of Gregory the bishop and in the deposition of Zephyrinus. At the end it additionally adds:

> “Also on the same day, the vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle.”

GREVEN:

> “The vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle. At Rome, the deposition of the blessed Zephyrinus, bishop. In the East, Saint Anastasius, bishop and confessor. At Amphitrea, Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor.”

Thus, little by little, others were added who are scarcely indicated in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. It continues:

> “In Ireland, Saint Fregius, abbot. Also Henry Calkar, presbyter and confessor, a man of outstanding holiness, of the Carthusian Order, of blessed memory. In the East, Saint Thecla the virgin.”

MOLAN copied from BELIN at the end:

> “and Saint Gregory the bishop. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Zephyrinus the bishop. Also on the same day, the vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle,”

to which he adds in smaller letters:

> “which is celebrated in many places as an observance of fasting. Also the blessed Philogonius, who, from being an advocate, became a bishop; John of Constantinople, surnamed Chrysostom, celebrated his memory in a notable homily five days before the Nativity of Christ.”

See the homily itself in Surius under this day. Later editions say nothing about Gregory or Zephyrinus. They speak of the vigil as in the earlier edition. Then:

> “In Spain, at the monastery of Silos, Saint Dominic the abbot, who, illustrious for the holiness of his life and the frequency of his miracles, departed in the year 1074.”

These editions have the same material about Philogonius as the earlier one, and in the same form.

[Col. 0819]

> At Alexandria, the most blessed martyrs Ammon, Zenon, Ptolemy, Ingenius, and Theophilus, who were standing at the tribunals when a certain Christian, placed under torture, trembled and was already almost inclining toward denial. By their expression, eyes, and gestures they attempted to strengthen him. When, for this reason, the shouting of the whole crowd broke out against them, they came forward into the midst and declared that they were Christians. Through their victory Christ immediately triumphed most gloriously and gave his own people steadfastness of spirit. In the city of Gelduba in Thrace, Saint Julius the martyr. Also at Amphitrea, Saint Liberatus.

## Twelfth day before the Kalends. Day 21.

[Note: [Col. 0823]]

The text is taken from Praten., Herinien., Tornac., Antuerp.-Maj., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Belin., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0823A]]

Some codices write *Partis*, but the principal ones have *Parthis*, as in the text. *Ewangelium* occurs only in Antuerp. In Munerat, *idem* is inserted between *inde* and *translatus*. Belin, however, constructed another phrase in this way:

> “and after that he was transferred not long afterward to the city of Edessa.”

Another edition, Greven., and Molan. read *Edissam*; Tornacen has the worse reading *Edissem*. The text has been taken from the remaining witnesses. I shall say no more here about Tuscany, nor about John. The copyist of the Antwerp codex shamefully corrupted the second announcement, writing:

> “John and Paul Festus.”

Neither Max.-Lubec. nor any other codex ever mentions Paul.

[Note: [Col. 0823B]]

We dealt with the translation of the body of Saint Thomas the Apostle, together with the whole series, on 3 July. On that day it is also placed in the Hieronymian copies, but in such a way that it is repeated again on this day. The Lucense codex reads:

> “In Mesopotamia, in the city of Edessa, the translation of the body of Saint Thomas the Apostle, who was transferred from India; his passion is celebrated there on the fifth day before the Nones of July.”

This directly conflicts with what is read in the same codex on the cited day, 3 July. Florentinius labors to reconcile these and other such contradictions, especially in his *Indiculus of the Apostles*, beginning on p. 145.

But in the translation reported here, the aforesaid Hieronymian codices do not entirely agree. In the very ancient Epternacensis it is recorded:

> “The passion of Thomas the Apostle in India.”

The Corbeiensis, however, joins both festivals:

> “In Mesopotamia, the feast and translation of Saint Thomas the Apostle,”

and so forth.

Wandalbert does not seem to acknowledge the feast, or day of the passion—about which there is certainly no agreement—anywhere; he sings only of the translation on this day, as will be clear from the verses given below. Bede, on the other hand, plainly reads here:

> “The feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle.”

Florus states in a brief eulogy that the body was transferred to the city of Edessa on the fifth day before the Nones of July. Rabanus says to the same effect that he died, pierced by a spear, in the city of Calamia in India and was buried there with honor on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

Our series is perfectly clear: since the translation was already recorded on 3 July, the Little Roman Martyrology simply has on this day:

> “Thomas the Apostle.”

The sacramentaries edited by Menardus and Thomasius agree more closely with Bede. Ado, however, records in the Martyrology only this:

> “At Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia, the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle.”

He reports the rest briefly among the Feasts of the Apostles, from which Usuard drew his eulogy.

Let the reader observe that only Rabanus designates the city of Calamia as the place where Thomas suffered; likewise, only he and our authors indicate the Parthians and Medes to whom the apostle preached the Gospel. Motherius notes other matters in his observations on his French translation of the Roman Martyrology.

As for the other regions, the place of martyrdom, the remaining deeds of Saint Thomas, and the arrival of his body in Italy, there are several controversies which there is no time to examine here. Baronius pointed out most of the sources from which many details concerning the apostle’s labors may be collected; but Tillemont’s compilation is fuller, in volume I, beginning on p. 355. It should be compared with the other Lives, both manuscript and printed, ancient and recent.

For the present, it is enough to have established the true simplicity of the Usuardine text. Here are Wandalbert’s verses concerning the translation alone:

> The twelfth day celebrates the honor of Thomas’s translation,  
> Through whom, as God’s builder, India deserved to know  
> The golden kingdom, attended by awe-inspiring signs.

Among the Hieronymian copies, only the very ancient Epternacensis reads after Thomas on this day:

> “And in Tuscany, John and Festus.”

In the same codex, doubtless the same men are repeated on 23 December in these words:

> “And elsewhere, John and Festus,”

for which others have:

> “John and Felix.”

Florentinius makes the following observation in today’s entry:

> “Ferrarius, in the Catalogue of the Saints of Italy, admits that they appear to have been venerated nowhere in Tuscany, or that he was unable to find them.”

Perhaps they are the same men mentioned below on the tenth day before the Kalends of January. Nevertheless, whether they were known in Tuscany or unknown, it is certain that Rabanus recorded them from some Hieronymian codex; certain that the forerunner of our series announces them today in this way:

> “In Tuscany, John and Festus”;

and finally, certain that in Ado, and through him in our author, they are remembered in almost the same words.

What, however, may survive anywhere concerning their life or deeds is still entirely hidden. In second place Ado reports Memmius of Châlons, about whom we dealt at greater length on 5 August; at that time, I candidly confess, we were unaware that he was celebrated by the Viennese Martyrology on this day. You have his text for today below among the Florentine codices.

Here I ask only that readers remember that what we said more cautiously about Ado’s meaning on 5 August is abundantly confirmed by this passage—especially the point that Memmius there does not belong to Ado at all. Meanwhile it remains probable that Usuard on that day adopted a Hieronymian rather than an Adonian wording.

[Note: [Col. 0823D]]

ROSWEYD extends the announcement of Thomas after the city of Edessa as follows:

> “He was laid there in a silver coffin with apostolic honor.”

In the other entry it is accurate.

PULSANEN interpolated the same text from Ado. After “India” it continues:

> “and his body was transferred to the city which the Syrians call Edessa, and there it is buried with due honor.”

It is also accurate in the second announcement.

ANTUERP.-MAX., together with all its companions, adds at the end:

> “In the city of Heraclea, the feast of Saint Passus.”

He is so called in the Lucense Hieronymian Martyrology; the Corbeiensis writes *Passinus*, the Epternacensis *Bassus*.

CENTULEN:

> “The feast of the blessed Thomas the Apostle, who, preaching to the Parthians and Medes, suffered in India on the fifth day before the Nones of July. His body was transferred to the city which the Syrians call Edessa, and there it was buried with due honor. At Châlons, Saint Memmius, bishop and confessor, the first of that city.”

See the following codex. In the final entry it is accurate.

BRUXELLEN, reasonably accurate in the first entry, continues:

> “At Rome, Saint Innocent, pope, who decreed that the kiss of peace should be given at Mass and established the use of consecrated oil for the sick.”

It then follows with John and Festus. Then:

> “In Heraclea, the feast of Saint Passus the martyr. At Châlons, the deposition of Saint Memmius, the first bishop sent to that city from Rome. Among countless other miracles, he raised a dead man, and his tomb is now distinguished by very frequent miracles. At Trier, Saint Zephyrinus, bishop and confessor.”

See below:

> “And elsewhere, Saints Phocas, Florius, and Honoratus, bishops and confessors.”

I find the names in the Hieronymian codices, but not the titles.

HAGENOYEN:

> “In India, the passion of Saint Thomas, God’s chosen apostle, who had such fervor toward the Lord, while he still existed in the flesh, that he wished to die with him and encouraged others to do likewise when the Lord wished to go to raise Lazarus,”

and so forth; see this in Surius. Then a new confusion:

> “In the city of Trier, Saint Severus, bishop and confessor of that city. Coming from the city of Trier into Aquitaine, where he had been born, he was already an old man. Through the grace of God which he possessed, he recognized everyone he saw and greeted them by their proper names; and, what was more remarkable, those whom he recognized outwardly he also knew inwardly, so that he revealed to many of them their good or evil thoughts. Full of good works, he died there in peace. On the same day in Tuscany, the feast of the holy martyrs John and Festus. In the city of Heraclea, Saint Passus the martyr.”

AQUICINCT adds at the end:

> “In the district of Cavilon, Saint Cyprian the abbot.”

He was noted yesterday and the day before yesterday, but I am still asking who he is.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT:

> “Thomas the Apostle. John and Festus the martyrs.”

[Col. 0826A] FLORENTIN:

> “At Châlons, Saint Memmius, the first bishop, sent to that city from Rome. Among other miracles, he is said to have raised a dead man; his tomb is now distinguished by very frequent miracles.”

See what was said above near the end of the Observations. It continues:

> “At Rome, Nicodemus, who, as is related in their Acts, took from the river the bodies of the holy martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Castorius, and Simplicius and buried them in his own house.”

See the summary of those Acts in Ado on 8 November, where Nicodemus is also discussed.

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition adds concerning Thomas:

> “and there it was laid with due honor. In Tuscany, the feast of the holy confessors John and Festus. In the city of Heraclea, the feast of Saint Passus the martyr. At Trier, Saint Severinus, the second bishop and confessor of that city.”

GREVEN:

> “In Heraclea, Saint Passus the martyr. Also Saints Phocas and Honoratus. At Rome, the deposition of Saint Innocent the bishop. Also, according to Ado here, at Châlons, Saint Memmius, the first bishop of that city, sent there from Rome, who among other things raised a dead man, whose tomb is still distinguished by very frequent miracles. Usuard has him on the Nones of August. At Trier, the blessed Severinus, the second bishop and confessor, who is also called Severus. Also, according to the Catalogue here, the memory of the blessed Dionysius, bishop, disciple of Saint Thomas the Apostle, and Pelagia, daughter of the king and his bride, whom the same apostle converted. Dionysius was later ordained bishop and went to the Lord full of holiness. Pelagia, however, consecrated with the sacred veil after his death, since she was unwilling either to marry or to sacrifice, completed her martyrdom by being beheaded.”

MOLAN at the end:

> “At Châlons, Saint Memmius, bishop, the first sent to that city from Rome, who among countless other miracles raised a dead man. On the same day, Saint Severinus, bishop of Trier.”

In later editions there is only this addition:

> “On the same day, Saint Severinus the second, bishop of Trier.”

See GREVEN.

[Col. 0823]

> The feast of the blessed Thomas the Apostle, who, preaching the Gospel to the Parthians and Medes, suffered in India and was transferred from there not long afterward to the city of Edessa. On the same day in Tuscany, Saints John and Festus.

## Eleventh day before the Kalends. Day 22.

[Note: [Col. 0825]]

Thus Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan.

[Note: [Col. 0825D]]

Here I have used greater freedom than anywhere else in this entire work, restoring the proper and true name of Ischyrion, which is found in no codex. Praten. came closest in *Schyrionis*, Molan. in *Schirionis*. Herinien., Tornacen., Munerat., and Greven write *Chirionis*; Belin, *Chyrionis*; others, *Chiridionis* or *Scirionis*. I thought myself permitted to make that emendation.

In place of *praeacuta sude*, Herinien. has *post acuta*. Antuerp., Max.-Lubec., and Belin err more shamefully by completely omitting those two words, *praeacuta sude*. Here I join the remaining elements. Concerning *blandiciis*, *contempneret*, *Hostia*, and so forth, see elsewhere.

[Col. 0827A] The final and more serious variation separated some codices from the accurate ones, especially Pratensis, which its usual companions Antuerp.-Maj. and Rosweyd partly imitate.

Regarding Pratensis, the distinguished Castellanus testified to me that from 8 December through the 23rd nothing had been erased in it and nothing added—“nothing erased and nothing added”—and therefore it must be clear that the third announcement for today was written by the first hand of that codex’s scribe in this form:

> “In the city of Ostia, Saint Basil.”

These words cannot possibly be attributed to Usuard unless we wish to say that he wrote while asleep and confused the distinguished little indexes of the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in which the first entry plainly reads:

> “In Antioch, Saint Basil.”

This is how the other two codices, generally followers of Pratensis, read it more correctly. In the aforesaid Hieronymian Martyrologies our first entry follows:

> “At Rome, on the Lavican Way,”

and so forth. Then:

> “And at Ostia, the feast of Saints Demetrius,”

which announcement we ascribe to Usuard from all our codices. Pratensis was therefore rightly excluded from the number of the accurate codices. Let the patrons of that codex decide whether so palpable an error greatly commends its authenticity. We also excluded two others because they certainly do not belong to Usuard in that final commemoration.

[Note: [Col. 0827A]

We assigned the crown of thirty martyrs who suffered at Rome under Diocletian to 1 January, but at a specified place, the Appian Way: here we have another crown, or band, perhaps of three hundred rather than thirty champions. The number is rendered doubtful by the Lucensis and Blumianus Hieronymian codices, whereas the others read more distinctly:

[Col. 0827B] “At Rome, on the Lavican Way, between the two laurel trees, the commemoration of three hundred holy martyrs, all crowned on one day.”

If the times of Diocletian had been added, our entire announcement would seem to have been taken from this source; and the other Hieronymian codices would support this even more strongly, since they express only thirty. “But,” says Florentinius, “a number of three hundred is more worthy of the savage cruelty of Diocletian.” What did the martyrologists write? Rabanus differs from the Lucensis only in the number of martyrs; nor does the little Roman Martyrology differ greatly: “At Rome, thirty martyrs buried under Diocletian on the Lavican Way between the two laurel trees.” Ado spoke more distinctly and accurately with the Lucensis, in precisely the words that constitute our entire text. So far I have found nothing else concerning these martyrs. Wandalbert agrees with the other Martyrologies in this verse:

> Rome celebrates on the eleventh day a martyr-band of thirty.

There follows the seventh announcement of this month, taken from a single chapter of Rufinus, as I explained at greater length on 19 December.

[Col. 0827C] The little Roman Martyrology contains the article: “At Alexandria, the martyr Ischyrion. And many others, among whom was the old man Chaeremon.” The Viennese martyrology enlarges those two commemorations from the often-mentioned passage of Rufinus, but Usuard deals only with Ischyrion, copying all the words of his eulogy from Ado and omitting the notable circumstance that Ischyrion was not condemned by a judge, but was slaughtered—so to speak—by a master, that is, by some powerful man whose affairs he managed for wages, in an unprecedented act of cruelty. Alexandria is consistently given by our sources, although Eusebius nowhere asserts this; indeed, it may seem not implausible to others that he was killed somewhere else in Egypt. Concerning the many other martyrs consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, illness, robbers, and wild beasts, the Usuardine Addenda, composed in various forms, will supply much material below.

In the Variants we showed above that the Pratensis codex was mistaken when it assigned Basil of Antioch to the city of Ostia; the customary companion codices were likewise mistaken when they substituted another announcement for Usuard’s. Here the question arises: which Hieronymian codex did he have before his eyes when he took the final section concerning the three Ostian martyrs, Demetrius, Honoratus, and Florus? For the oldest Epternacensis, Lucensis, and Blumianus read:

“Of Demetrius and Honoratus, Felix, Florus.”

To such questions, often raised elsewhere, no more suitable answer presents itself than to say that Usuard, according to his own preference, selected saints from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. Would that the Acts or passions of these three martyrs, and of the thirty martyrs mentioned above, could be found somewhere!

[Note: [Col. 0827C]]

**PRATEN.** We gave its supplement above in the Variants; there we also discussed **ANTUERP.-MAJ.**, which moreover reads *between two trees* instead of *between the two laurel trees*.

**ROSWEYD.** Agrees in the supplement with **ANTUERP.-MAJ.**, but additionally adds at the end: “Theodosia, virgin and martyr.”

**PULSANEN.** Pure in the first part, it continues from Ado as follows: “On the same day, of very many martyrs who, wandering through the deserted mountains of Egypt, were consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, robbers, and wild beasts.”

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG.** and **DANIC.** insert in third place, from Ado: “In Egypt, the commemoration of Saint Therimon [others: Cherimon, better Chaeremon], bishop of the city of Nicopolis, and of many others who, wandering through the deserts and mountains of Egypt, were consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, illness, robbers, and wild beasts, and crowned with the glory of martyrdom.” In the fourth announcement all agree with the codices cited for the text.

**LOVANIEN.** Agrees with the others in the supplement, but omitted the entire eulogy of Ischyrion.

**CENTULEN.** “At Rome, on the Lavican Way between the two laurel trees, of the thirty holy martyrs who suffered under Diocletian. At Alexandria, of the blessed martyr Scirion. In Egypt, of innumerable martyrs who, laboring in the mountains and valleys, in the forests and amid various hardships, were consumed by hunger, thirst, illnesses, cold, robbers, and wild beasts. On the same day, Theodosia, virgin and martyr, and Saint Didymus, [Col. 0828C] a most learned man.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies and the observations of Florentinius.

**BRUXELLEN.** Pure in the first part, it continues as follows: “In the city of Spoleto, the passion of Saint George the martyr. In the Roman port, the commemoration of Saint Ariston. And at Rome, on the Portuensian Way, the burial of Saint Felix the bishop.” It is fairly pure in the notice of Ischyrion. Then: “In Egypt, the commemoration of Saint Cheremon, bishop of Nicopolis, and of many other martyrs who, wandering through the deserts and mountains of Egypt, were consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, illness, robbers, and wild beasts, and crowned with the glory of martyrdom. And Bishop Ceremon, when he had withdrawn to the Arabian mountain with his very aged wife, was seen by no one thereafter.” See these matters more elegantly in Ado, or in Rufinus himself. The notice of the Ostians follows in pure form. Then: “And elsewhere, the passion of Saint Theodosia, [Col. 0828D] virgin and martyr, and of Saint Didymus the monk. At the city of Antioch, Saint Basil.”

**HAGENOYEN.** In the customary text it is purer, adding concerning the Egyptian martyrs: “In Egypt, the commemoration of Saint Cheremon, bishop and martyr, who was prelate of the city of Nicopolis, and of many others,” etc. The following history is appended:

“On the same day, at Auxerre, the passion of Saint Justus the boy, who was Justus in both name and deed. This Justus was the son of Justin, a Christian man, who was repeatedly reproached by his son for not redeeming his brother Justianus from captivity. When he set out to redeem his brother, his son Justus wished to go with him; but his father forbade him because of the grief of his mother, since he was her only child. But she said: ‘Let our son go with you’; and so they proceeded. When the pagans arrived, his father hid himself, but the boy Justus went out to meet them. They said: ‘Where are the Christian men who were going with you?’ But Justus said: ‘I know them, but I will not disclose them to you.’ Immediately they cut off his head. Justus took his own head into his hands and sat down to pray. When his father was uncertain what he should do with it, Justus said: ‘Bury my body at Beauvais, and carry my head to my mother Felicia.’ When she saw it, she gave thanks to God, and such a brightness shone over Justin’s house that Saint Amator the bishop asked what had happened there. When he heard of the boy’s passion, he buried him in his own tomb.”

This is the Justus, unless I am mistaken, who is commemorated on 18 October.

**AQUICINCT.** After “he was handed over to death,” it inserts: “In the city of Antioch, Saint Basil.”

**MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.** “Theodosia, virgin. Fronius, bishop and confessor. At Rome, thirty martyrs. Cerion, martyr [or perhaps, [Col. 0829B] Chaeremon?]. Also three other martyrs.”

In **VATICAN.**, no. 5949, Demetrius and his companions are absent. It adds: “On the same day, of many martyrs,” etc., from Ado.

**ALTEMPS.** has, like **AQUICINCT.**: “In the city of Antioch, Saint Basil.”

**FLORENT.**: “Also of many others,” etc., likewise from Ado. “Also, Saint Theodosia, virgin and martyr. In the city of Ostia, Saint Flavian the martyr, under the emperor Julian the Apostate.” He is included in the Roman Martyrology.

**REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.** “In the suburb of Reims, the commemoration of Saint Jovinus the confessor.”

**LUBECO-COL. EDITION.** “At Spoleto, a city of Tuscany, the passion of Saint Gregory, priest and martyr, in the times of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. He was first beaten with knotted clubs under Count Flaccus; then, after the gridiron and prison, struck on the knees with iron cords, and also burned along the sides with blazing lamps. When he had already been condemned to death by the governor Tyrcanus, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: ‘Behold, Gregory, you have already been crowned and enrolled among my saints. Enter, therefore, to me, blessed of the Lord, for my dwelling has been prepared for you.’ While the angel was still speaking, Aquilinus the officer cut off his head. His body now rests at Cologne in the principal church, having been transferred there by Lord Bruno, archbishop of Cologne.” See also the Addenda for the following day. In Usuard he is placed on the 24th. The first and second announcements follow and are fairly pure; then much is given concerning Chaeremon and the Egyptians, as above. Finally, the notice of the Ostians, correctly.

**GREVEN.** “In the Roman port, the commemoration of Saint Ariston. [Col. 0830B] And the burial of Saint Felix the bishop. And the burial of blessed Gregory of Spoleto, priest and martyr, resting at Cologne in the principal church. Usuard and Ado, however, place him on the ninth day before the Kalends of January. On the same day, the passion of Saints Theodosia and Dimidius, or Didymus. Also, according to Ado, of many martyrs who, wandering through the deserts and mountains of Egypt,” etc. See Ado himself. It follows: “Ethernasius the confessor. Theodosia the virgin. Also, Saint Jutta, the enclosed woman, of blessed memory.”

**MOLAN.** In the first edition and in the other editions has no other supplement apart from the often-cited article of Ado concerning the many Egyptian martyrs, etc.; see above concerning them.

[Col. 0825]

At Rome, on the Lavican Way between the two laurel trees, the commemoration of thirty martyrs, all crowned on one day during the persecution of Diocletian. At Alexandria, of the blessed martyr Ischyrion. When he was compelled by flatteries and insults to sacrifice, but refused, he was pierced through the entrails with a sharpened stake and handed over to death. In the city of Ostia, of Saints Demetrius, Honoratus, and Florus.

**[Bouillart.: [Note: [Col. 0825C]]**

I admit that Basil was not correctly announced here by Usuard. For if he followed the Hieronymian lists, he ought to have written: “In the city of Ostia, of Saints Demetrius and Honoratus” —for there is no mention of Florus in our very ancient codex. Or, if he intended to commemorate Basil, the city assigned ought to have been Antioch, not Ostia.

While seeking the cause of this error, I remembered 21 November, where I had read: “In the city of Ostia, of the holy martyrs Demetrius and Honorius.” I immediately examined our codex of the Hieronymian Martyrology that most nearly approaches Usuard’s time, and which it is plausible was copied from the very one that Usuard consulted in writing his work. There, on both days—that is, 21 November and 22 December—I see the same saints mentioned from the same verses: “At Ostia, Saints Demetrius and Honorius; at Antioch, Saint Basil,” with this one difference, that on 22 December the reading is Honoratus instead of Honorius.

I myself conjecture that the error arose from the similarity of the saints and cities. Perhaps Usuard had closed his article with the commemoration of Saints Demetrius and Honoratus. Later, recalling that the same saints had been entered on 21 November, he suspected a scribal fault and erased what he had written—for Castellanus falsely stated that there was no erasure—substituted Saint Basil, and, through a lapse of memory, wrote Ostia instead of Antioch.

Whatever the case may be, the Pratensis codex loses none of its authority on this account; it will be regarded as occupying the place of the autograph until there are people who prefer to draw from the source rather than chase the streams. BOUILLART.]

In the city of Ostia, Saint Basil.

**Ten days before the Kalends. Day 23. [Note: [Col. 0829]]**

I consider only four codices pure: Praten., Herinien., Antuerp.-Maj., and Greven.

**[Note: [Col. 0829C]]**

All read “joined to the number of the blessed saints,” as is also found in Ado. **Antuerp. Maj.** may perhaps have the more elegant reading *in the number of blessed saints*, but that is not Usuardine. **Greven.** and some others write *he made them martyrs of Christ*; our reading, which conforms to Ado, is preferable. **Antuerp.-Maj.** changed the name Victoria to Victorina; and instead of *had gathered virgins together*, wrote *virgins gathered together*. **Greven.** is incorrect, reading *from her earliest age* instead of *because from her earliest age*; Molan corrected this somewhat better to *because from her earliest age*. In the text, I retain the final two articles because I find them in the principal codices, although they do not concern saints. For this reason I suspect that some copyists of the codices omitted them, while others later restored them, as can easily be inferred from the Addenda.

**[Note: [Col. 0829C]]**

The Lucensis Hieronymian codex begins its list for this day, in Florentinius, as follows: “In the city of Nicomedia, the commemoration of 245 holy martyrs together, whose names the Lord knows.” It is commonly held that this refers to the most savage persecution begun by Diocletian at Nicomedia in barbarous fury, about which we have spoken more than once elsewhere, especially on 27 April.

[Col. 0829D] According to Eusebius, on that occasion a great multitude of martyrs was consumed by every kind of torture on the occasion of the burning of the palace. Yet I do not see how this number could have been determined here; hence it perhaps happened that the Hieronymian copies vary so widely on this point. In the Blumianus, indeed, only thirty martyrs are commemorated; but in the oldest codex one reads: “At Antioch, the commemoration of thirty-five martyrs,” and Rabanus, preserving this number, restored them to Nicomedia.

See Florentinius on these matters and, if you wish, marvel with him that in the Roman Martyrology, as well as in Usuard, Ado, and other more recent writers, the Nicomedian martyrs, under unknown names, are extended only to twenty. The reason for the wonder may perhaps be removed if you remember that all those martyrs are commemorated in a single solemnity with Anthimus, mentioned above on 27 April. You will search in vain for the reason why twenty are repeated here. I think I can conjecture with sufficient certainty that this present number was reduced at the author of the little Roman Martyrology’s own discretion. Ado composed the customary eulogy, which Our Author copied word for word; but it is of such a kind that it seems to allude no more to that savage rage of Diocletian than to any other execution carried out by the same tyrant.

Migdonius and Mardonius, who are not expressly named by Eusebius, have been added in the Roman Martyrology. Here we disclose the source from which our twenty martyrs flowed. Nor do I wish, with some others, to guess that “twenty thousand” may once have been written instead of “twenty martyrs.” This is shown to have appeared somewhere from the addition found in later editions of Molan; and certainly the Greek-Moscow Ephemerides before volume 1 of May, p. 57, refer to twenty thousand on 28 December. Whether the number in our Usuardine codices is true or erroneous, we have no liberty to depart from their simplicity.

Anatolia, together with her fellow virgin Victoria, is entered more than once in the Addenda under 18 December. We discussed her and Audax according to Usuard’s intention on 9 July; the martyrologists transferred her here, both in Bede’s series and in ours. The Hieronymian copies on 10 July read: “In the Sabine territory, of Anatolia and Victoria.” There one may again see in Florentinius what we indicated above on 9 July.

Bede’s account is brief and polished, and Rabanus’s eulogy is taken from it; ours is so similar to this that I do not hesitate to believe that for the greater part it was copied from the earlier text. Ado’s history is longer; Tillemont gnaws at it here and there in volume III, beginning on p. 703, in his notes, although in the work itself, beginning on p. 329, he does not appear to depart so greatly from it. We shall declare our opinion in the Acts under 9 July. Meanwhile, no one could deny that the passion is ancient, since Adelmus composed his poem from it, and that poem was published together with Ado’s eulogy by Surius.

The Viennese account sufficiently suggests that Victoria did not suffer in the city of Rome itself. For the place of her burial, consult Holstenius’s *Observations on the Roman Martyrology*, p. 108 onward, where he accurately refutes the fables of Dexter and the errors of others. Hear Wandalbert now, singing of Victoria in one verse:

> Victoria of Christ shines forth on the tenth day, a virgin.

Servulus is known only in our series, having first been entered in the little Roman Martyrology as follows: “At Rome, Servulus, dissolved by illness, buried in the church of blessed Clement, where the Lord deigns to work miracles through him.” Consulting the great Gregory, the Viennese writer took from him the source of this brief encomium and drew a longer account, sufficiently accurate, of which our text presents an epitome.

Here one should consult the outstanding annotation of Baronius, which vigorously rebukes the hypercritics of the present day in Melchior Cano—those, namely, who dare to call into question and diminish the credibility of the books of Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues*, which for a thousand years and more the Western as well as the Eastern Church has followed with the greatest faith, worthy veneration, and immense praise. Those men have dared to do this in other matters; but so far I have found no one who has called the history of Servulus into doubt.

Concerning the Dedication of the Basilica of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, I have nothing further to add here; the codices cited for the text prove that Usuard included it. The burial of King Childebert belonged rather to a necrology than to a Martyrology.

**[Note: [Col. 0831B]]**

**TORNACEN.** Proceeds correctly in the text as far as “at the request of her betrothed.” Everything else has been omitted.

**ROSWEYD.** Continues as far as “occur very frequently”; omitting the rest, it substitutes: “Also at Rome, Eleutherius and 835 others.” See how Florentinius attempts to compose this from the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

[Col. 0831C] **PULSANEN.** Begins: “At Spoleto, the commemoration of Saint Gregory, priest and martyr, in the times of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, under the judge Flaccus.” He is found today in Rabanus with a longer eulogy; Usuard marks him on the following day. See the Addenda for yesterday and today. In this codex, the notice of Victoria continues as far as “emperor”; concerning Servulus, it writes as far as “pope.” Everything else is missing.

**ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC., BELIN.** and **MOLAN.** stop at the final two articles, which they undoubtedly did not think should be attributed to Usuard.

**MUNERAT.** has a smaller omission, since it includes the final notice concerning Childebert.

**ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN., ALBERG.** and **DANIC.** agree sufficiently with the preceding codices and with the text in the first three announcements; they likewise omit the dedication and Childebert, but add in their place: “On the same day, Saint Dagobert, king of the Franks.” I think this refers to the man whom Castellanus records today in the universal Martyrology.

[Col. 0831D] **LOVANIEN.** In the supplement it resembles those immediately above, but omitted the entire eulogy of Victoria. This is why, as we said above, she is often excluded from the codices of middle quality.

**CENTULEN.** “At Rome, Victoria the virgin, under the emperor Decius. At Nicomedia, twenty holy martyrs. Also at Rome, the blessed Servulus, of whom blessed Gregory writes: ‘Poor in possessions, rich in merits.’ Also on the same day, Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr.” He is commemorated on 26 October. There is another Evaristus on this day in the Hieronymian Martyrologies.
