**BRUXELLEN.** Begins: “At Rome, Saint Evaristus, pope and martyr, whose more solemn feast is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of November.” It is not entirely pure in the account of Victoria, reading as follows: “And at Rome, the commemoration of Saint Victoria, virgin and martyr. When she had been betrothed to a certain pagan and was unwilling either to marry or to sacrifice, after many miracles, at the insistence of her betrothed, during the persecution of the emperor Decius, she was struck in the heart with a sword by the executioner. Taliarchus, her executioner, became a leper and, consumed by worms within three days, died.” Then: “And the commemoration of Saint John the priest, placed at Saint Hermen.”

In the notice of the Nicomedians it is somewhat mutilated, and instead of twenty it gives twenty-five. Then: “Also at Rome, the commemoration of Saints Eugenius, Eleutherius, Urbanus, Cornelius, Trajan, Victor, Castula, and 830 others [he meant 830].” In the notice of Servulus, slightly interpolated, it ends like the preceding codices: “On the same day, Saint Dagobert, king of the Franks.”

**HAGENOYEN.** In the first notice gives Victoria, not entirely purely. It is somewhat better in the Nicomedians. Concerning Servulus, after “he lay,” it inserts: “in great patience of heart and body; and likewise he was poor in possessions. At his death heavenly voices were heard. At his tomb, too, miracles occur very frequently.” I find nothing else added.

**AQUICINCT.** In the commemoration of Victoria introduces some confusion; after “she was struck with a sword,” it adds: “and thereafter she was buried by the executioner at the request of her betrothed.”

In **DAVERONEN.** and **CAUDIACEN.** two articles have been added concerning the dedication of the Basilica of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and the burial of Childebert, as found in the text.

**MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.** “Victoria the virgin. Twenty holy martyrs. Servulus the paralytic, of whom blessed Gregory writes in a homily.”

**REG. SUEC.**, no. 428, is similar. **MUNERAT.** deals only with the burial of Childebert.

**VATICAN.**, marked no. 5949, adds: “At Spoleto, the commemoration of Saint Gregory the martyr.” “With a eulogy,” says Papebrochius, but he does not transcribe it; perhaps because it is identical with the Usuardine notice for the following day.

**ALTEMPS.** “At Nicomedia, the commemoration of thirty-five martyrs.” See what we said in the Observation. “Also at Rome, 835. And the burial of Lord Childebert the king.” The abbreviation **D.** is used not for *divi* but for *Domni*.

**FLORENTIN.** “Also, Saints Rufus and Zosimus, who was one of the ancient disciples of Christ.” The two names are joined without punctuation, as though they were one person. See Usuard above under 18 December.

**LUBECO-COL. EDITION.** In the announcement of Victoria [Col. 0833A] is somewhat interpolated; at the end it adds this unusual statement: “Her head now rests at Cologne in the church of the Carthusians, having been transferred there.” In the notices of Servulus and the Nicomedians it is fairly pure. It adds at the end: “On the same day, Saint Dagobert, king of the Franks.” I have already said that Castellanus’s note in the universal Martyrology should be consulted.

**GREVEN.** “At Rome, the commemoration of Saints Eugenius, Eleutherius, Urbanus, Cornelius, Trajan, Victor, Castula, and 830 others.” I have already said above that Florentinius’s observation on these saints in the Hieronymian Martyrologies should be consulted. “Also Sixtus and Apollonius. Dagobert, king and confessor of the Franks. Also Gregory the boy. On the same day, the commemoration of Saint John the priest. Mazotha the virgin.”

**MOLAN.** Considering the final two announcements of our Usuardine text suspect, counted them in italic letters at the end among the additions. He also has: “On the same day, the translation of blessed Lambert from the church of Saint Mary into the crypt, and the dedication of that crypt in honor of all the saints.”

Later editions read at the end: “On the twenty-third day, the ten martyrs in Crete.” See their names and Acts in Surius. The notice concerning the translation of blessed Lambert follows, etc., as in the first edition. Then: “At Paris, the dedication of the basilica,” etc., and concerning Childebert, as above. Next: “On the same day, Dagobert, king of the Franks.” Finally, in smaller type: “At the city of Brixen, the burial of blessed Hermann the confessor, bishop of that same city, renowned for miracles.” See Castellanus on this day in the universal Martyrology, where he is called Hartemannus.

[Col. 0829]

At Nicomedia, twenty holy martyrs whom the persecution of Diocletian, after torturing them with the most severe torments, made martyrs of Christ and joined to the blessed saints in heaven. At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Victoria the virgin, under the persecution of the emperor Decius. She had been betrothed to a certain pagan, but was unwilling either to marry or to sacrifice. After many miracles, among them the gathering of many virgins, she was struck in the heart with a sword by the executioner at the request of her betrothed. Also at Rome, Saint Servulus, of whom blessed Gregory writes that from his earliest age until the end of his life he lay paralytic; at his tomb miracles occur very frequently. At Paris, the dedication of the Basilica in honor of the holy cross and Saint Vincent the martyr, and the burial of Lord Childebert the king.

**Nine days before the Kalends. [Day 24.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0833B]]**

All the codices are pure: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Munerat., Belin., Greven., and Molan. Antuerp.-Max. joins them with all its companions. Centulen. is also complete; if it continued throughout as it began on the ninth day before the Kalends of January, it would rightly be numbered among the purest Usuardine codices.

**[Note: [Col. 0833B]]**

Belin. deserved to be excluded from the pure codices, since it begins as follows: “The vigil of the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Several codices write *Syria*, but since they are inconsistent with themselves, here, as elsewhere, we preserve *Syria* with the older witnesses.

In Max.-Lubec. and Munerat., *Daciana* is badly printed; no better is the reading *Datiana* in Belin. Again, Munerat. reads *Poletum* instead of *Spoletum*.

Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Belin., Greven., and Molan. seem to want to correct the text by reading *priest and martyr*; but it is sufficiently certain that Usuard did not depart from Ado’s wording. Therefore we have preserved it from the better codices.

Belin. completely corrupted the construction by reading: “burned with fiery iron thorns, but also struck along the sides with blazing lamps.” What is meant by *thorns* is explained in Molan’s note.

Munerat. writes *Lucini* instead of *Luciani*. The errors of the middle-quality codices have not been examined so scrupulously; in this matter they follow Ado rather than Usuard, since instead of *commemoration* they read *nativity*.

**[Note: [Col. 0833C]]**

The older the Martyrologies, the rarer is the commemoration of any vigil in them. I am not speaking here of Calendars or Sacramentaries. None can be found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies. A few vigils occur in Bede, and, surprisingly, fewer in Rabanus, who noted none except the vigil of the Epiphany and the vigil of Saint John the Baptist.

Yet Rabanus, who everywhere copies Bede, places a vigil where Bede does not at all, for example the vigil of the Epiphany; on this day, however, he does not mark a vigil, although Bede expressly has: “The vigil of the nativity of the Lord.” The same words are found in the little Roman Martyrology, and the same in Our Author; the Viennese does not differ, except that instead of *nativity* he writes *birth*, a practice followed by some Usuardine codices.

Wandalbert explains the same thing in verse, joining the vigil with the following virgins:

> On the ninth day, gathering gifts for the coming light,  
> we prepare lamps and sleepless altars and temples.  
> The forty virgins also shine here, who for heaven  
> devoted a worthy life through vow and virtue.

Those forty virgins are known from copies of the Hieronymian Martyrologies. I have no doubt that Ado received them from these, and Usuard from Ado. The oldest Epternacensis reads: “At Antioch in Syria, of forty holy virgins.” The Lucensis codex adds *canonesses*, and Rabanus transferred this designation into his text from some similar codex.

We discussed such canonesses briefly in our Observations under 9 April. Even now, we do not believe that anything more is meant by *canonesses* than simply virgins, who are known to have adorned the Church wonderfully by the radiance of their chastity from the very beginning of Christianity. Consequently there is no need at all to resort to *asceteria* and *gynaecea*, that is, monasteries of religious women.

Florentinius attempts to establish this from Eusebius, book II, chapter 17, where he describes Philo’s Therapeutæ and Therapeutrides. But the learned man does not persuade me at all that before the time of the emperor Decius there existed in the Church Christian religious virgins bound by vows and enclosure. Without entering into a lengthy dispute, I shall say briefly: until someone clearly proves that those Therapeutæ and Therapeutrides of Philo were truly Christian, asceteria and gynaecea before the time of Decius will remain, at the very least, entirely uncertain.

The recent attempt of the most learned Montfaucon appears to have been sufficiently overturned in the Trevoltian Ephemerides for the year 1712, p. 929 onward. Let these remarks be understood as incidental. Our retired elder Papebrochius long ago discussed these matters solidly; his *Responses* are in everyone’s hands.

I return to the forty virgins. The Hieronymian Martyrologies mark them without a date; Ado says—whether with sufficient certainty I do not know—that they completed their martyrdom under the persecution of Decius. All Ado’s words have been transferred into our text, and I do not know whether any Acts of those virgins survive.

In the Addenda for the preceding day I said that Gregory of Spoleto is celebrated by Rabanus there with a eulogy, and Castellanus thinks that he belongs rather to that day. Nevertheless, the author of the little Roman Martyrology, who did not know the forty Antiochene virgins, expressly writes on this day: “At Spoleto, Gregory the priest and martyr.”

The remarkable Acts of this martyr, in which his passion is described quite beautifully, as Tillemont himself admits in volume V, p. 347, were published in the Surian collection. The Viennese undoubtedly possessed such materials and presents an abridgment of them, abbreviated by Our Author so cautiously that he leaves critics no opportunity to cavil.

In the Addenda for 22 December it is asserted that the body of this Gregory was transferred to Cologne. The people of Spoleto contradict this. Since the merits of the controversy have not yet been sufficiently examined, I leave the dispute undecided.

The customary Usuardine guides do not mention Lucian of Tripoli; the copies of the Hieronymian Martyrologies do, and these are always Our Author’s final refuge. The announcement of the oldest Epternacensis is especially explicit and stands first: “At Tripoli, the commemoration of Lucian.” The Lucensis codex agrees, but writes *Tropoli* incorrectly for *Tripoli*. Both, however, expressly assign the following martyrs in the same list—Metrobius, Paul, and the others—not to Tripoli but to Rome.

The Plantinian Bede, or some similar codex joining different martyrs under one entry, misled Baronius. As far as I know, nothing historical survives concerning Lucian. Meanwhile, I think that nothing is lacking from the complete purity of our text.

**[Note: [Col. 0835B]]**

**PULSANEN.** Would be pure in the first two notices, except that instead of “the persecution of Decius” it reads “the persecution of Diocletian.” It entirely omitted the other two notices; this is not unusual in this codex.

**BRUXELLEN.** “The vigil of the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. At Antioch in Syria, the commemoration of forty holy canonesses and of two others, Donatus and Drusus, who under Decius,” etc. Concerning Gregory it inserts: “under the judge Flaccus.” At Rome: “the commemoration of the holy martyrs Metrobius, Paul, Zenotus, Temistus, and Lucian.” The final announcement follows: “At the city of Tripoli,” etc.

**HAGENOYEN.** “The vigil of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ.” It is pure in the notice of the Antiochene virgins and of Gregory of Spoleto. It continues:

“On the same day, the burial of Saint Dagobert, king of France, a man who was entirely good and Catholic and a defender of the poor; who built churches from his possessions and enriched many others with his wealth. When God, wondrously testing and examining him, stirred up many wars under him, he nevertheless settled them courteously; he likewise gave him a daughter who was deaf, blind, and mute, whom he cured through the hermit Florentius, and a son who had died a bad death, whom he raised through Saint Arbogast, bishop of Strasbourg.”

Finally, concerning Lucian, it is fairly pure.

**MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.** “The vigil. At Antioch, of the forty holy virgins who suffered various torments. Gregory the martyr. Saint Lucian.”

**CASTRI-KAROLI.** “At Spoleto, a city of Tuscany, Saint Alnulf, martyr and priest, in the times of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian.” I think it is obvious that our Gregory of Spoleto was incompetently transformed here into Alnulf.

**LUBECO-COL. EDITION.** “The vigil of the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh.” The notice of the forty virgins follows in pure form. Concerning Gregory it dealt extensively above under 22 December. Concerning Lucian it reads: “In the city of Tripoli, Saint Lucian the confessor.”

It continues: “At Trier, in the monastery called the Barn, the burial of Saint Irmina the virgin. Her father, Dagobert, king of France, after her mother’s death, made her a religious woman in that place and had a church consecrated from his barn. He established a monastery of virgins and endowed it with many revenues, appointing his daughter superior over the other holy virgins; there she now rests in a mausoleum.”

See Castellanus’s note concerning this Irmina: “On the same day, Saint Ismenerus, king and confessor.”

**GREVEN.** “Obadiah and Nahum, the prophets. At Rome, Saints Metrobius, Paul, Zeno, Drusus, and Saturninus. Ismenerus, king and confessor. In the monastery of Gladbach, Saint Alberic, hermit and confessor. Also Saint Anno the First, bishop of Cologne, of blessed memory. At Rome, Saint Tarsilla, a religious virgin and aunt of Saint Gregory the pope. See above, on the Nones of January. At Trier, in the monastery called the Barn, the burial of Saint Irmina the virgin, daughter of King Dagobert. Her father had made her superior of the monastery of virgins that he had built from his barn and endowed with many revenues; she rested there, full of holy works. Appollonia the matron.”

MOLAN, in smaller type, adds to the text: “In England, Saint Theorithgitha, virgin, disciple of Saint Ethelburga, whom the venerable Bede praises at length in his *Chronicle of the English*. At Rome, Saint Tarsilla, virgin and nun, aunt of Saint Gregory the pope. At Trier, in the monastery called the Granary, the burial of Saint Irmina,” and so forth. Later editions give Irmina more briefly: “At Trier, in the monastery of the Granary, the burial of Saint Irmina, virgin, daughter of King Dagobert. The aforesaid king built this place from his granary and endowed it with many revenues.”]

[Col. 0833]

[Note: [Col. 0833B] All the Pratensian manuscripts, except one, begin the year here, according to the ancient custom customary in Usuard’s age; countless others follow them. Sollerius’s Martyrology, however, begins at the Circumcision of the Lord, that is, at the Kalends of January. BOUILLART.]

The vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. At Antioch in Syria, the birthday of forty holy virgins, who, under the persecution of Decius, completed their martyrdom through various torments. At Spoleto, a city of Tuscia, Saint Gregory, martyr and priest, in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. He was first beaten with knotted clubs; then, after the rack and imprisonment, struck on the knees with iron hooks; he was also burned at the sides with blazing lamps, and finally beheaded. At the city of Tripoli, Saint Lucian.

VIII Kal. Day 25. [Note: [Col. 0835]

I consider the manuscripts of Herinien, Munerat, Greven, and Molan pure. Centulen is also included at the beginning of the codex, and is exceptionally pure.]

[Note: [Col. 0837A]

There are two or three variations of no great importance. Centulen begins, “The Son of God, Jesus Christ,” and at the words “she herself by fire, but the others …,” through the copyist’s carelessness *the others* is wrongly placed between *herself* and *by fire*. In Molan there is an error: in the final announcement, after the words “after the sacred choirs of virgins,” he inserts “under Nicetius, prefect of the City.” The more serious disagreement among the manuscripts concerns the chronological notes attached to the Nativity of the Lord, and it is not sufficiently certain how Usuard actually wrote them. The Pratensian manuscript, together with Antwerp-Major and Rosweyd, and also Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, with certain manuscripts of middling quality, reads between “in the thirteenth year of Caesar Augustus” and “of the 193rd Olympiad”: “the sixty-sixth week, according to the prophecy of Daniel.” I do not consider these last words part of the text, guided by the authority of the five manuscripts mentioned above; moreover, Usuard, abbreviating Adon and excluding the note concerning the founding of the City that appears in the Viennese text, does not seem to have inserted on his own another note not found in earlier witnesses. This is my opinion, although I would readily yield if anyone produced stronger evidence.]

[Note: [Col. 0837B]

Baronius, Florentinius, and other extremely learned men discuss at length the various ways in which the most solemn feast of the Nativity of the Lord was celebrated in the Church’s earliest centuries, its confusion with the Epiphany or Theophany, and the many other matters pertaining to this festival. Several pages here would not suffice even to enumerate their principal arguments. To pursue only our own subject: it is certain that in the fourth century itself, and undoubtedly much earlier, the Lord’s Nativity was fixed on 25 December, as Bucherius’s Calendar clearly proves: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of January, Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea,” to which other calendars and the familiar Sacramentaries agree. The most ancient copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology have the same entry in somewhat fuller words: “At Bethlehem, the Nativity of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ according to the flesh.” Bede comes closer to the earlier wording: “The Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ,” which Rabanus reduced again to the Hieronymian form. The short Roman Martyrology has it most briefly: “The Nativity of the Lord according to the flesh.” The Viennese martyrologist was the first to enlarge this entry and distinguish it with chronological notes, adding the year of Augustus, the Olympiads, and the founding of the City; he also indicated the firmest and truest peace and the census of the people ordered to be taken by decree of the Senate. We think that Usuard, abbreviating Adon to suit his own brevity, accepted only the first two eras, excluding the year from the founding of the City and adding no mention of Daniel’s weeks, as stated above in the Variants. Other chronological computations, now added from the calculation of the Seventy translators, are found in no manuscript and in no Martyrology earlier than Belin’s edition, whose text we shall give in its proper place among the Additions. Wandalbert’s metrical elogium will be placed at the end.

The calendars, Sacramentaries, Missals, Martyrologies, Menologies, and other ecclesiastical books, widely and universally known, loudly proclaim the most ancient, renowned, and celebrated festival veneration of Anastasia, both in the East and in the West. They are joined by the basilicas built, the altars erected, and every other monument of religious worship that may rightly be offered to the saints. We spoke almost similarly of Chrysogonus on 24 November, where, concerning the Acts, we noted what applies to the passions of both. The controversy over the place of Chrysogonus’s martyrdom was mentioned there; here it would have to be discussed more fully if anything sufficiently certain could be found to disperse the difficulties, which are neither few nor easily resolved. No less complicated are the questions concerning one or several Anastasias—one a widow, another an unmarried virgin, and a third finally an enchantress, or rather a maker of potions—who have wrongly been confused into one person, or one person divided into three different women. I read and weigh each point; but, to speak frankly, nothing has yet been offered by which I can plausibly extricate myself, briefly, clearly, and neatly, from the arguments as stated, while preserving the authority of the Roman Martyrology. I therefore judge it preferable to reserve all these matters for examination in their proper place in the Acts. Anyone wishing meanwhile to sample the principal points of this intricate controversy should consult Tillemont, volume V, beginning at page 713. For our present purpose I observe only that on this day Anastasia is recorded at Sirmium in the Hieronymian Martyrology: “And at Sirmium, Anastasia.” Hence, contrary to Florentinius, it is not openly established that the woman of Sirmium is different from her who, slain by the sword under Diocletian, is commemorated on this same day in almost all Martyrologies. It is clear that Bede, and after him Rabanus and Ado, consulted the same Acts; indeed, the latter copied most of his elogium from the former. Our author, however, abbreviated his entire entry from the Viennese Martyrology, omitting from all of them the definite arena of martyrdom—unless we wish to understand Anastasia and all her companions as crowned on the island of Palmaria, or, with Florus, place before Bede’s text the words “At Sirmium.” The author of the short Roman Martyrology plainly disagrees with the others, reading alone: “At Rome, Anastasia.” This concerns the origin of our text.

Eugenia and her Acts should have been discussed on 11 September, where, on the occasion of Protus and Hyacinthus, their reliability and authenticity were not approved, following Baronius. Here we shall confine ourselves to the Martyrologies. The Hieronymian Martyrology demonstrates the ancient and renowned cult of this illustrious virgin of the Church, praised by Adelmus, in these words: “And in the cemetery of Apronianus, on the Latin Way at Rome, the passion of Saint Eugenia, virgin”; or more briefly in the Echternach manuscript: “At Rome, Saint Eugenia, virgin.” The location is absent from Bede, who reads: “And Saint Eugenia, virgin.” Rabanus, however, added a long historical account drawn from the Acts. In the short Roman Martyrology nothing else is read than “And Eugenia.” Ado restored the place of the passion, embellishing the rest only slightly; our author borrowed his text directly from him. Thus it is manifest that the entire entry was transmitted to Usuard. Castellanus has a note which may perhaps seem insufficiently weighty to someone. It remains for me to render our three announcements from Wandalbert in verse:

> In the eighth, the Creator deigned to assume the form of a servant  
> and, coming, to recall wandering humanity;  
> through a virgin birth he clothed mortal limbs.  
> Then we commemorate Eugenia also, and Anastasia,  
> who accompanied Christ with a like mind and faith.

] [Note: [Col. 0837D]

I discussed PRATEN, ANTWERP-MAJOR, and ROSWEYD in the Variants. The second manuscript is additionally mistaken in reading “two hundred women.” The third has a different beginning to the text, beginning thus: “The Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh.” [Col. 0838D]

TORNACEN, after “forty-second,” continues as follows: [Col. 0839A] “Who, in the power of his divinity, both foresaw the time of his birth and chose the mother through whom he would be born; she conceived from the Holy Spirit and remained both mother and virgin.” In the two other commemorations it is pure.

PULSANEN reads: “At Bethlehem of Judea, the Nativity of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ according to the flesh, in the forty-second year of Caesar Augustus, the 193rd Olympiad, and, from the founding of the City, the 740th year; for by his most holy coming he consecrated the sixth age of the world. On the same day, the birthday of Saint Anastasia.” All the rest is absent.

ANTWERP, MAX-LÜBECK, ANTWERP-MAX, UTRECHT, and LEYDEN agree with PRATEN and the others in the chronological notes. They also fall short of purity in that, omitting “after the sacred choirs of virgins,” they substitute “under Nice­tius, prefect of the City.”

DANIC would agree with the preceding witnesses if it had not moved the words “Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judea” to the end of the announcement.

[Col. 0839B] LOVANIEN suffers from a defect, omitting the entire elogium of Saint Eugenia.

ALBERG, similar to the preceding witnesses at the beginning, adds “from the founding of the City, the 752nd year,” and continues from Ado: “With the firmest and truest peace established throughout the whole world by divine ordinance through Caesar Augustus, Quirinus was sent to Judea by decree of the Senate and was taking the census of the people and their possessions; and by his most holy coming he consecrated the sixth age of the world.”

BRUSSELS begins: “At Bethlehem of Judea, the Nativity according to the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, in the forty-second year of Octavian Caesar Augustus. He who consecrated the sixth age of the world,” and so forth. Concerning Eugenia, after “the sacred choirs of virgins whom he had joined to Christ,” it adds: “Bound to a rock and thrown headlong into the Tiber, she could not be drowned; then enclosed in a blazing bath, she was found unharmed; finally, under Nicetius, prefect of the City, after long striving for Christ, she was slaughtered with the sword while in custody.” In Anastasia it copies a large part of Ado’s elogium, adding at the end: “And the memory of this holy Anastasia is made daily in the canon of the Mass.”

HAGENOYEN, as usual, scrapes together something concerning the Nativity from the Gospel. Two Eugenias follow; of the first it reads: “At Rome, the passion of Saint Eugenia, virgin, daughter of Philip, prefect of Alexandria, who, in the guise of a man, entered a monastery of men, served God faithfully, and eventually became abbot. Accused before her own father of fornication, she tore her garment and revealed herself to be a woman, converting her father, mother, brothers, and many others to the faith. Finally she returned to Rome and converted many virgins to God; she was beheaded in her own house.” Then: “Also at Rome, in the cemetery of Apronianus,” and so forth; it reports the present text. Concerning Anastasia it renders, in a more barbarous style, what Ado had composed more elegantly from the Acts.

AQUICINCT records the following concerning Christ’s birthday; that codex was compared with the second edition of MOLAN: [Col. 0839D] “After the commemoration of Christ’s Nativity, it mentions the oil that flowed at Rome, across the Tiber, throughout the entire night.”

MATRIC, CARTHUSIAN, and UTRECHT: “The Nativity of Christ. Anastasia, virgin and martyr. Eugenia, virgin and martyr, noble by birth, who for a long time, in male clothing and acting as father of monks, served God.”

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition resembles ALBERG at the beginning. It then continues: “In Illyricum, the passion of Saint Anastasia, martyr, under the emperor Diocletian. [Col. 0840A] For confessing the Lord, she was subjected to prolonged imprisonment and torment by her husband Publius; nevertheless she was consoled and strengthened by the letters and exhortations of blessed Chrysogonus. After her husband’s death and a long imprisonment under the prefect of Illyricum,” and so forth. See this more fully in Ado. In the final announcement it inserts the same material found in the MOLAN cited above in the Variants.

BELIN forms his initial entry as follows: “In the year from the creation of the world, when in the beginning God created heaven and earth, five thousand one hundred ninety-nine years—which number was completed in the following month of March, on the twentieth day of that month, for on that day the world was created. From the Flood, in the two-thousand-nine-hundred-fifty-seventh year, which number was completed on the seventeenth day of the following April. From the birth of Abraham, in the two-thousand-fifteenth year. From Moses and the exodus of the people of Israel from Egypt, in the one-thousand-five-hundred-tenth year. From the destruction of Troy, in the one-thousand-one-hundred-seventy-ninth year. From David’s anointing as king, in the one-thousand-thirty-second year. In the 193rd Olympiad. From the first Olympiad, in the eight-hundredth year. From the founding of the city of Rome, in the 752nd year. The sixty-third week, according to the prophecy of Daniel, that is, in about the 440th year. In the forty-second year of Octavian’s reign. In the sixth age of the world, with the doors closed and the whole world established in peace, Christ Jesus, eternal God and Son of the eternal Father, wishing to consecrate the world by his most holy coming, conceived from the Holy Spirit, and after nine months had elapsed from his conception, is here proclaimed in a loud voice: ‘In Bethlehem of Judea he is born of the Virgin Mary, made man’; here, however, more loudly and in the tone of the Passion: ‘The Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh.’” Anastasia follows, with a text somewhat interpolated from Ado. In Eugenia it inserts the same account as MOLAN, or rather MOLAN took it from this source, concerning the prefect of the City, whom this manuscript incorrectly calls “Nicene.” [Col. 0840C] The second edition adds: “At Gordian Castle, Saint Romulus, confessor.” MOLAN copied this as well.

GREVEN: “Note that our Savior was born in the sixty-sixth week, according to the prophecy of Daniel, and in the 752nd year from the founding of the City, when the disturbances of all the nations throughout the world had been suppressed and the firmest peace established by Caesar Augustus, when Quirinus, sent to Judea by decree of the Senate, was taking the census of the people and their possessions; by his most holy coming he consecrated the sixth age of the world. Also, among the companions of blessed Anastasia, a certain man suffered, as Ado says, named Euticianus, of entirely innocent character, who, whenever he was heard and whenever he was questioned, said nothing other than: ‘No one will take Christ from me, not even he who takes my head.’ On the same day, at Gordian Castle, Saint Romulus, confessor. At Bethlehem, blessed Charitas, abbess. Chariton, abbot, and all his brothers departing together.” [Col. 0840D]

MOLAN prefaces the text in italic type with the long series of eras described above from BELIN, but notes in the margin: “This calculation is very erroneous, up to the calculation from the founding of the City.” At the end, from the same BELIN: “At Gordian Castle, Saint Romulus, confessor.” See Castellanus’s Martyrology. Nothing is added in the later editions.]

[Col. 0835]

“Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judea in the forty-second year of Caesar Augustus” [Bouillart inserts: [Note: [Col. 0835D] Sollerius does not approve that the Pratensian Usuardine codex, together with certain others, reads between “in the thirteenth year of Caesar Augustus” and “of the 193rd Olympiad”: “the sixty-sixth week, according to the prophecy of Daniel.” He does not consider these words part of the text because they are entirely absent from the five codices that he regards as pure at this point. [Col. 0837A] But these codices are later in date than the Pratensian. Which should be preferred to the other: the source to the stream, or the stream to the source? Why the other codices do not have the words, I do not know. For there is no erasure here in the Pratensian. I suspect that Usuard originally wrote them; but when he dictated the Martyrology to be offered to the king, frightened by the variety of opinions on this matter, he may have feared transmitting something uncertain. BOUILLART.] “the sixty-sixth week, according to the prophecy of Daniel,”] of the 193rd Olympiad. On the same day, the birthday of Saint Anastasia under the emperor Diocletian, who, after being tormented by prolonged imprisonment for confessing the Lord, was then taken with two hundred men and seven hundred women to the Palmaria Islands. She herself was martyred by fire, while the others completed their martyrdom through various deaths. At Rome, in the cemetery of Apronianus, the passion of blessed Eugenia, virgin, who, in the time of the emperor Gallienus, after distinguished deeds of virtue and after the sacred choirs of virgins, strove long for Christ and was finally slaughtered with the sword.

VII Kal. Day 26. [Note: [Col. 0841]

Thus read Praten, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Greven, and Molan. Antwerp-Max, Utrecht, Leyden, Lovani­en, and Centulen also agree.]

[Note: [Col. 0841A]

I do not enumerate the various ways of writing *Jerusalem*, *protomartyr*, *the Appian Way*, *Dionysius*, and so forth. Antwerp-Major reads “the passion of the Lord” instead of “the passion of Christ.” In Greven, *of his* is absent after *ascension*. Centulen did not write so badly: “shone brilliantly”; but Antwerp and Max-Lübeck have the worse reading “shone forth,” in addition to other typographical errors found in the latter. The readings *Martianus* or *Marcianus* amount to the same thing, but not *Martinianus*, as in Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Utrecht, and Leyden, still less *Maximianus*, as in Antwerp-Max and Lovani­en. The names of other emperors placed after it do not clarify the matter, since in the Mombritian Acts Martianus is mentioned without a title of rank, and the entire passion is embellished in so incredible a manner that it is extremely difficult to extract historical probability from it.]

[Note: [Col. 0841A]

We cannot deny that learned men hold differing opinions concerning the birthday, discovery, and translation of the most holy Protomartyr, as was shown clearly enough under 3 August, when his discovery is commemorated in the Martyrologies, although from Lucian’s account it is clear that it took place on 19 December. Hence some reasonably infer that today’s festival may most suitably be assigned to the first translation, from the ancient tomb to the new. However probable this may be proclaimed, it cannot be denied that this plausibility is outweighed by the gravest authority: the universally received judgment of the whole Church, which from the age of Saint Augustine has most steadfastly celebrated this day as the true birthday, martyrdom, or burial day of the illustrious Stephen. The Carthaginian Calendar proves this, as do other published calendars and Sacramentaries, and our Martyrologies, among which the most ancient Hieronymian Martyrology reads, most explicitly in Florentinius: “In the Jerusalemite settlement, in the village of Caphargamala, the passion of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, deacon and apostle, who was stoned by the Jews.” The entry of the Echternach manuscript alone is shorter, but it agrees sufficiently with the three others represented by Rabanus, who here follows the Hieronymian manuscripts more than Bede, in whom we read only: “The birthday of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr.” Florus’s elogium is irrelevant to us. The short Roman Martyrology, guide of our series, could scarcely have stated the matter more briefly, speaking today only of Stephen: “Stephen, protomartyr.” Among the feasts of the apostles there is a somewhat longer account of Stephen’s passion; Usuard consulted Ado’s Martyrology, from which he borrowed, if not the words, at least the sense of his elogium, adding something about the discovery that had already been sufficiently explained under 3 August. No saint could have received more illustrious Acts than our protomartyr, since they were dictated by the Holy Spirit; scarcely any saint’s relics have been so widely dispersed throughout the Church, and certainly none have been celebrated by Augustine and other holy Fathers with so many wonders and so many indisputable miracles. Motherius adds another note on these matters. In short, Stephen’s glory in the Catholic world has always been so great that nothing seems capable of adding to it. Much concerning all these matters may be collected in the Acts, which Tillemont arranged in advance near the beginning of his second volume. Let Wandalbert’s metrical praise follow here:

[Col. 0842A]

> From here, on the seventh day, Stephen, Levite and first martyr,  
> shines forth: the blessed one who followed the king born and suffering  
> in life, faith, struggle, and death.

Pope Dionysius is recorded by Ado not on this day but on the following day, in wording very different from that which our author expressed in the present text, and so general that it could almost be affirmed of any Roman pontiff. Why he departed from his predecessor, and from where Usuard obtained his material, I shall not investigate. The day of Dionysius’s death or burial seems uncertain, for the most ancient Bucherian Calendar gives: “The sixth day before the Kalends of January, Dionysius at Callistus.” In contrast, the Hieronymian Martyrology records today: “At Rome, the burial of Saint Dionysius”; or, as in the Echternach manuscript: “And the burial of Dionysius, bishop.” Tillemont argues for 26 December in volume IV, page 671, where he also touches on other matters concerning Dionysius. Baronius discussed this holy pontiff at greater length in the *Annals*; here, in the Notes, he assigns the sources from which his deeds may have been derived. In the text of the Roman Martyrology, however, the same Baronius seems deliberately to have removed the period of the emperor Claudius, although Usuard had marked it not incorrectly if Claudius is understood as Claudius II, or the Gothic. Tillemont composed a sufficiently lucid account of Dionysius’s life in the cited volume IV, beginning at page 341.

Marinus, the Roman martyr who occupies the third place in the entry, belongs to Usuard alone and is nowhere known to the ancient martyrologists. I do not know from what source his notice reached our author; but I see that it must have been a foul and muddy source if it stated that Marinus won his triumph at Rome under the emperor Martianus. The designation of the tyrant was changed more than once in the Roman Martyrology, as Castellanus observes. Nor do the Acts preserved by Mombritius contain any trace by which Marinus’s story could be assigned more to the time of Carinus or Numerian than to that of any other pagan emperor. The story is otherwise woven from so many marvels that it compels even the most credulous reader to doubt, at the very least, the truth of the events. Tillemont does not hesitate to reject it as a pure fabrication in volume IV, page 568. It will be our task to determine in its proper place whether, once stripped to some extent of its incredible and poorly arranged marvels, the substance of the story can be reduced to historical probability.]

[Note: [Col. 0841C]

TORNACEN is again defective here, omitting the elogium of Dionysius.

PULSANEN has the following concerning Stephen: “Not long after the Lord’s Ascension, when he was full of faith and the Holy Spirit, he was ordained deacon by the apostles, and in the same year in which Christ suffered, he was stoned by the Jews.” The entire announcement of Dionysius is absent; in Marinus it has removed the elogium after “the most illustrious man.”

MUNERAT interpolates Stephen’s elogium, inserting “in the month of August” after “his ascension”; and between “revelation” and “discovered” it places “today.” It then adds: “These festivals, as the Doctors assert and history relates, were transferred for this reason.” See the Observations on these matters.

ALBERG and DANIC, concerning Dionysius, add after “shone forth”: “He divided churches and parishes among priests and established dioceses.” These words are taken from Ado, as is the following announcement concerning Pope Zosimus, which I do not know why Usuard omitted. They read: “Also at Rome, Saint Zosimus, pope, who, forty-third after blessed Peter, established that a candle should be blessed on Holy Saturday.” Consult Ado himself, and also determine whether Castellanus rightly appended this note concerning Zosimus in the *Universal Martyrology*: “without an established tradition of cult.”]

[Col. 0843A] BRUSSELS: “At Jerusalem, on the road to Caphargamala, the birthday of blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, who not long after the Lord’s Ascension was ordained deacon by the apostles and, in the same year in which Christ suffered, was himself stoned by the Jews. His discovery is celebrated on the third day before the Nones of August; yet the discovery took place on this day, on which his passion is commemorated. The celebration of his passion was transferred to this day both because it is more worthy and because it was fitting that the first martyr after Christ should be placed immediately after him.” See the Observations. Concerning Dionysius, besides what we have reported from ALBERG and the others, it adds: “commanding that each should be content with his own boundaries and not usurp those belonging to others.” In Zosimus it agrees with ALBERG and the others, except that it omits “forty-third after blessed Peter.” It is pure in Marinus. At the end it continues: “At Antioch, Saints Julian and Marcian, martyrs.”

HAGENOYEN composes, in its customary fashion, a history of Stephen, which it would have described far better from the Acts of the Apostles, adding certain details about the discovery and so forth that agree sufficiently with what was stated in the preceding codex. It continues: “At Rome, the birthday of blessed Dionysius, pope and martyr. He divided the cemeteries and parishes in the city of Rome and ordered them to be observed elsewhere; he assigned to each its own right, commanding that each should be content with its own boundaries and not usurp the boundaries of others; and he appointed individual priests for the individual parishes. He suffered under the emperor Valerian.” In the final entry it is sufficiently pure.

AQUICINCT, after “shone forth,” adds: “He assigned churches to priests, and gave and established parishes of the diocese.” At the end: “Also at Rome, Zosimus, pope. He established that deacons should cover the left side with cloaks.” See MOLAN’s annotation at the end.

MATRIC, CARTHUSIAN, and UTRECHT abbreviate the text as follows: “Stephen, the protomartyr. Marinus, or Marianus, the most illustrious martyr. Dionysius, pope and confessor.” It preserves the ancient form.

[Col. 0843C] CAMBERIEN draws back here saints who do not belong to this day: “At Bourges, Saint Ursinus, bishop. On the same day, blessed Perpetuus, pontiff.” See 29 and 30 December.

The VATICAN manuscript, numbered 5949, lacks the announcements of Dionysius and Marinus. It adds: “At Rome, Zosimus, pope and confessor, who sat in the episcopate for one year.”

[Col. 0844A] ALTEMPS: “In the district of Oxford, Saint Ebrulf, bishop. At Bourges, Saint Ursus, bishop and confessor.”

FLORENTIN: “At Rome, Saint Zosimus, pope …”

The LÜBECK–COLOGNE edition inserts into the text concerning Stephen: “Since he was full of the Holy Spirit, he was ordained deacon by the apostles and, in the same year, namely the year of his Ascension, was stoned; blessed Luke explains his most holy passion to us in the Acts of the Apostles. His venerable body,” and so forth. It continues: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the burial of Saint Dionysius, pope and martyr, who sat in the episcopate for six years. He established churches, parishes, and cemeteries, and assigned to each its own jurisdiction, commanding that each should be content with its own boundaries and not usurp those of others; he likewise established dioceses. Who, of the faith, …,” and so forth. After “shone forth” it adds: “he was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.” Then: “Also at Rome, the birthday of Saint Zosimus, pope and confessor, who sat for one year. He was the forty-third after blessed Peter and established [Col. 0844B] that a candle should be blessed on Holy Saturday.” In the Maurine edition it is sufficiently pure.

BELIN is close to purity in both editions; concerning Dionysius alone, after “shone forth,” they add: “He divided churches and parishes among priests and established dioceses.” This is from Ado, as above.

GREVEN: “At Constantinople, Saint Anastasius. At Antioch, Saints Julian and Marcian. At Rome, Zosimus, pope and confessor, who was forty-third after blessed Peter, sat for one year, and established that a candle should be blessed on Holy Saturday. At Spoleto, Abundantia, a holy matron who buried blessed Gregory.”

MOLAN reads: “On the same day, Zosimus, pope. He was the forty-third after blessed Peter and established that a candle should be blessed on Holy Saturday.” Then, in smaller type: “At Rome, Saint Theodore, the custodian (*mansionarius*) of Saint Peter, concerning whom blessed Gregory speaks in *Dialogues*, book III. Also Saint Spes, abbot and confessor, at Nursia, concerning whom blessed Gregory speaks in *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 10.” Note that at the beginning, after “Jerusalem,” *Caphar Gamala* is inserted in italic letters from the Hieronymian manuscripts. The later editions have the same material; in them, after Zosimus, only this is added: “On the twenty-sixth day, Saint Euthymius, martyr and bishop of Sardis.”]

[Col. 0839]

At Jerusalem, the birthday of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr, who was stoned by the Jews not long after Christ’s Passion, in that same year, namely the year of his Ascension. His venerable body was discovered by divine revelation in the time of the emperor Honorius. At Rome, on the Appian Way, the burial of Saint Dionysius, pope, who shone gloriously through his teachings of the faith under the emperor Claudius. On the same day, Saint Marinus, a most illustrious man, who won the triumph of martyrdom at Rome under the emperor Martianus.

VI Kal. Day 27. [Note: [Col. 0843C]

The text is taken from Praten, Herinien, Antwerp-Major, Rosweyd, Antwerp and Max-Lübeck, Munerat, Belin, Greven, and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0843D] [Col. 0843D]

There are many typographical errors in the printed editions, and no fewer scribal mistakes in the manuscripts. Concerning *Johannis*, *apud*, *eandem*, *evangelistae*, *Asiae*, and so forth, I have spoken elsewhere; here the peculiar forms are *Apocalypsis* and *apochalypsis*. A more notable variation occurs in Munerat, which writes “the revelation of the Gospel.” Rosweyd badly contracted the years marked after “churches,” reading: “And, worn out by old age, he died in his ninety-ninth year.” Antwerp-Major gives “he departed in his ninety-eighth year.” Herinien and Munerat insert “and ninth.” Belin uses the singular *church* instead of *churches*, and connects what follows thus: “but after the Lord’s Passion, in the year of his age.” The same manuscript also places “the revelation of the divine Apocalypse” in third position, after the description of the Gospel. All read “under the heading ‘Confession,’” except Munerat, which has “from the heading,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0843D]

That John, surnamed and antonomastically called “the Theologian,” was once venerated among the Evangelists as the Eagle, on various days—not only among the Greeks but also among the Latins—is clearly demonstrated by the Hieronymian manuscripts alone. For on 25 May they read: “At Ephesus, John the apostle”; concerning which Florentinius rightly observes that it is uncertain on what day Saint John the Evangelist was translated or fell asleep at Ephesus. Another festival is placed on 24 June: “At Ephesus, Saint John, apostle and evangelist.” In the Echternach manuscript it is “the reception of John,” in the Luccan manuscript “the birthday of John,” and so forth. But no one can attain a sufficiently probable conjecture as to which solemnity these entries, like the preceding ones, are to be understood as indicating.

The Hieronymian manuscripts speak nowhere more clearly than on this day, whose entire text I append: “The assumption of Saint John the Evangelist at Ephesus, and the ordination of Saint James, the brother of the Lord, who was the first of the Jews to be ordained bishop at Jerusalem by the apostles and was crowned with martyrdom in the middle of Easter.” There is no opportunity here to discuss at greater length the questions concerning John’s assumption or dormition, life or death, and the other sufficiently thorny controversies in this subject. See Florentinius’s *Dissertation*, beginning at page 123; he adds an explanation of the aforementioned ordination of James beginning at page 144. The curious reader will find many matters there discussed with sufficient accuracy, which cannot be adapted to our brevity.

We dealt with John’s martyrdom together with the Catholic Church on 6 May; here, with the same Church, we certainly believe that the Evangelist’s birthday is commemorated on this 27 December. We also believe that the festival is clearly designated on that very day in the Carthaginian Calendar, although it reads there: “On the sixth day before the Kalends of January, Saint John the Baptist and James the apostle whom Herod killed.” The reason is sufficiently probable: since the names of saints are not ordinarily repeated in that Calendar, and the Baptist is expressly placed in his proper position on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, it is not likely that the Forerunner was joined with James, but rather the Evangelist John, as we have already shown from the Hieronymian manuscripts. All the remaining martyrologists support the present birthday, and in them James is also asserted in his own festival.

Bede’s words are clear: “The birthday of Saint John, apostle and evangelist, beloved of the Lord.” Florus’s elogium contains nothing especially worthy of notice. Rabanus preferred to copy his entire text from the Hieronymian manuscripts rather than from Bede. The short Roman Martyrology, in its customary fashion, says briefly: “John, apostle and evangelist, at Ephesus.” The Viennese martyrologist composed a panegyric among the Feasts of the Apostles, from which, together with the brief index of the Martyrology, our author fashioned his shorter encomium. This belongs properly to the purpose of our work. Baronius carefully noted further details; Tillemont arranged the whole course of John’s life and deeds in volume I, beginning at page 330, in twelve sections, illustrated with nineteen notes beginning at page 600. These may be compared with what Surius published and with the various manuscripts and printed works concerning Saint John that exist among us. Let Wandalbert’s metrical poem have its place here:

> Beloved of the Lord and beholder of the divine Word,  
> John, who deserved to draw from Christ’s breast  
> the perennial fountain, consecrates and illumines the sixth lustrum.

The preceding day we noted that Pope Dionysius is mentioned by Ado on this day, while Pope Zosimus occupies his place in the preceding calendar entry. As for Maximus, patriarch of Alexandria, the Viennese Martyrology mentions him nowhere separately, nor have I found him recorded in any other Martyrology. Some sort of memorial of him does indeed occur in Ado’s eulogy of Dionysius of Alexandria on 16 November, where, drawing on Rufinus, book VII, chapter 10, [Col. 0846B] he recounts his outstanding labors on behalf of the faith. Hence I suspect that Usuard extracted Maximus from that passage, where he is mentioned only as a presbyter. Yet since Usuard himself could easily have consulted the source directly and read there the words of Rufinus or Eusebius—which state that Maximus, whom he had called a presbyter, succeeded Dionysius himself in the episcopate at Alexandria—he could just as easily have combined the titles, adapted the eulogy, and assigned this day at will.

Moreover, if one seeks the true day of his death, it is sufficiently clear from our Alexandrian Chronology that he ceased to live not on 26 December but on 9 April. See the few remarks that we collected there in his praise, p. 32, no. 171. I do not approve Castellan’s brief observation, in which he says that Maximus first began to be recorded on this day in the ninth century because of the vigil of his successor Theonas—as though the learned man did not know that Theonas is commemorated by Usuard and his guides on 23 August. Since, furthermore, we consider the certain day of Theonas’s death to be not 28 December (as Castellan assumes here [Col. 0846C]) but, more probably, 3 January, as we have tried to demonstrate elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0845C]

TORNACEN. is pure in the first entry but once again omits the other’s eulogy.

PULSANEN. begins: “The feast of Saint John the apostle and evangelist, the Lord’s beloved.” These are almost Bede’s words. It continues: “After this he …,” etc., but in abbreviated form. Nothing about Maximus.

ANTUERP.-MAX. adds to the text, together with its companions: “In the regions of Aquileia, Saint Zoilus [also Zoelus], priest and confessor. After he had buried blessed Chrysogonus, the latter appeared to him, and on the thirtieth day after his passion Zoilus went to the Lord.”

CENTULEN. is extremely pure in the text and adds: “At Aquileia, Saint Zoilus, priest and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN.: “The feast of Saint John the apostle and evangelist, the beloved of our Lord Jesus Christ. After his exile …,” etc., through “the churches.” It then continues: “And worn out by old age, being twelve years younger than Christ himself, in the ninety-ninth year of his life and [Col. 0845D] the seventy-eighth year after Christ’s passion, without being burdened by any pain, he rested at Ephesus on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, on the nativity of blessed John the Baptist. But he yielded to him whose equal had not arisen among those born of women, and his feast was transferred to this third day of Christ’s nativity, so that the Bridegroom, who is white and ruddy, might have all his companions.” These statements rest on no great authority.

It continues: “On the same day, the ordination to the episcopate of Saint James, the Lord’s brother. He was the first of the Jews to be ordained bishop at Jerusalem by the apostles, and was crowned with martyrdom in the middle of Easter.”

In Maximus, the codex is pure. At the end, however, it adds: “In the regions of Aquileia, the feast of Saint Zoilus,” etc., as in ANTUERP.-MAX. above.

HAGENOYEN has a lengthy eulogy of John, of which I give part here: “At Ephesus, the feast of blessed John the apostle and evangelist, who was the son of the maternal aunt of Jesus Christ and the brother of James the Greater. When he wished to marry, he was called by the Lord away from the wedding, and for that reason was admitted by the Lord to all his secrets,” etc. In Maximus it is also pure, and concerning Zoilus it has the same as the preceding codex.

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “John the evangelist. Maximus, bishop and confessor.”

VATICAN., marked no. 5949. On this day this codex is wholly Adonian, for, omitting Maximus, it restores Pope Dionysius.

REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll. transforms Zoilus, previously a priest, into a bishop: “In the regions of Aquileia, Saint Zoelus, bishop and confessor.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition, after “the churches,” inserts the following concerning John: “And worn out by old age, knowing that the day of his departure had arrived, he summoned his disciples and, after giving many proofs of Christ by signs, descended into the excavated place of his burial. After praying, he died, as free from the pain of death as he was found untouched by corruption of the flesh; sixty-eight years after the Lord’s passion,” etc. Concerning Maximus and Zoilus it has the same as above.

GREVEN.: “On the same day, the ordination to the episcopate of Saint James, the Lord’s brother. Zoilus, priest and confessor, who, after he had buried Saint Chrysogonus, went to the Lord on the thirtieth day after Chrysogonus’s passion, when Chrysogonus appeared to him. Aspaliana, virgin. Claudia, mother of Saint Eugenia. Patronilla, holy matron. Fabiola, holy matron, praised by blessed Jerome.”

MOLAN.: “In the regions of Aquileia, Saint Zoelus, priest and confessor, who is mentioned in the passion of blessed [Col. 0847A] Chrysogonus.” In smaller type he then adds from GREVEN. this entry: “Fabiola, holy matron, praised by blessed Jerome.” Nothing about her appears in the later editions. After Zoelus [Col. 0848A] they add: “On the same day, Saint Theodore, holy father and confessor, writer, and his brother Theophanes, the poet.” See the excellent Acts of the two brothers in Surius.]

[Col. 0843]

At Ephesus, the feast of blessed John the apostle and evangelist, who, after his exile and banishment, after the revelation of the divine Apocalypse, and after the composition of the Gospel, continued until the time of the emperor Trajan and founded and governed the churches of all Asia. Worn out by old age, he died in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord’s passion and in the ninety-ninth year of his own life, and was buried near that same city. At Alexandria, Saint Maximus, bishop, who became sufficiently renowned and distinguished through the title of confession.

The fifth day before the Kalends. The 28th day.

[Note: [Col. 0847]

Thus the purer codices: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp.-Maj., Rosweyd., Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec., Greven. and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0847A]

Antuerp. and Max.-Lubec. begin: “At Bethlehem,” in which they disagree with all the others; Molan. begins similarly, “Bethlehem of Judea.” The codices vary between *Innocentum* and *Innocentium*; we have preferred the latter. “Ancyra of Galatia” is the more common spelling among the codices; others have *Anchira*, *Ancyra*, *Antira*, [Col. 0848A] *Galathiae*, *Galaciae*, etc. There is greater agreement concerning *Eutici*, in which nearly all concur. It is probably to be written *Eutychii*, as the Roman Martyrology reads; only Antuerp.-Maj. has *Euticii*. The best manuscripts have *Domitiani*, while quite a few have *Domiciani*. In Rosweyd. the final word, “deacon,” is omitted.]

[Note: [Col. 0847A] [Col. 0847B]

Until now the Church has neither sought nor determined on which precise day the Innocents—infants from two years old and younger, most cruelly slaughtered at the command of the impious Herod—suffered martyrdom. Nor does the choice of the fourth day after the feast of the Nativity seem to contribute anything toward establishing in what year the massacre of the children occurred. On these matters, see Florentinius’s note for this day and his *Exercitation* beginning on p. 229 concerning the history of the Magi who came to Christ and the length of their journey. Papebrochius discussed several matters relating to the adoration of those same Magi and the slaughter of the infants in the Greek-Muscovite Ephemerides under 29 December, and most recently in his *Responsiones*. Here we are investigating specifically the institution of the feast and the origin of the Martyrology.

It will not easily be proved that the memory of our Innocents was celebrated in the Church in Origen’s time, nor does it seem possible to infer from Augustine that they were then honored with an octave, to use the ecclesiastical term. Yet there is nothing to prevent us from asserting that their solemnity was already a feast before Augustine’s time.

You have a sure monument of their most ancient cult in the frequently cited Carthaginian Calendar, which on this day reads: “The fifth day before the Kalends of January: the holy Infants whom Herod killed.” Other Calendars, Sacramentaries, and whatever ancient monuments of religious veneration survive follow. Among the copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology, the most ancient, that of Echternach, has: “Bethlehem of Judah, the feast of the Infants.” Others say somewhat more fully: “Bethlehem, the feast of the holy infants and sucklings who suffered for Christ under Herod.”

I do not see that there can be any doubt [Col. 0848B] that, instead of *lactantium*, one should plainly read *lactentium*, as it stands in the Corbie Hieronymian, although Rabanus followed the former reading. Florentinius’s observation seems more scrupulous than necessary when he suggests that the mothers might almost be joined with the infants.

Bede says clearly and elegantly: “The feast of the holy martyrs, the Innocents.” Florius’s eulogy is of no great importance. The little Roman Martyrology, in its usual style: “Bethlehem, of the holy Innocents.” Ado added a few things, which we shall give below as they are recorded in the supplements. Usuard could have selected from either the Viennese Martyrologist, his constant guide, or the Hieronymian Martyrologies themselves whatever he thought better suited to his own phrasing.

In Surius there is a prayer concerning the Infants which, together with other encomia of the holy Fathers, may be examined in a larger work. Thus Wandalbertus sang of those first little flowers of Christ’s martyrs:

> Whom harsh ambition tore from their mothers’ breasts,  
> While Herod, thirsting to reign, desired to destroy  
> The newborn Christ, we venerate the Infants on the fifth day.

Eutychius and Domitian are martyrs almost only in name and status, and are known solely from copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology; hence Usuard certainly transferred them from there. The dislocated entry in the Lucca codex must be corrected on the basis of the Echternach and Corbie manuscripts, which write distinctly, as in our text: “Ancyra of Galatia, Eutychius, priest; Domitian, deacon.” Above, in the *Variants*, I said that I read *Eutychii*, conforming myself to Baronius and to the more polished orthography.]

[Note: [Col. 0847C]

PULSANEN., which generally abbreviates Usuard’s texts, here again copied from Ado certain things that have absolutely no bearing on our Usuard. Thus, after “the Innocents,” it added: “When Herod had learned of Christ’s birth through the report of the Magi, he ordered them killed in the thirty-sixth year [Ado has thirty-fifth] [Col. 0847D] of his reign. In the thirty-sixth year he died miserably and deservedly of dropsy, worms swarming throughout his body.” See the source itself, which is somewhat purer. The final entry is omitted in this codex.

MUNERAT. adds to the text: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Victor, Castor, and Rogatianus.” They are taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, in this or another order; they are also reported by others.

BELIN. changes the order slightly, and ANTUERP.-MAX. and all the other middle-grade codices agree with it, reading: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Castor, Victor, and Rogatianus.”

CENTULEN. again departs from the purity of the text: “Bethlehem, the feast of the holy Innocents, whom Herod, when he had learned of Christ’s birth through the report of the Magi, ordered killed in the thirty-fifth year of his reign, among them slaughtering two of his own sons.” Nothing concerning Eutychius and Domitian.

BRUXELLEN. has: “In Bethlehem of Judah, the feast of the holy Innocents. When King Herod learned from the Magi of Christ’s birth, he ordered them killed; and afterward he died miserably of dropsy, worms swarming throughout his body, as was fitting. In Africa, the feast of Saints Castor, Victor, and Rogatianus.” In the final entries concerning Eutychius and Domitian it is sufficiently pure.

HAGENOYEN. The well-known question concerns the number of the martyred Innocents, which the Greeks, without any foundation, extend to fourteen thousand. Hear what the author of this codex invents: “At Bethlehem of Judea, the feast of the blessed Innocent martyrs, whose number is one hundred forty-four thousand. These were killed by the impious King Herod the Ashkelonite, a foreigner, although they had never harmed anyone. But because they lived at the time when the Lord Christ had been foretold by many, he killed them in order to kill Christ in them; and for that reason the Church celebrates them in Christ’s place.

“At Rome, the feast of Pope Zosimus. He was Greek by nationality and sat for two years and eight months. He decreed that a candle should be blessed on Holy Saturday of Easter; that a slave should in no way be made a cleric; and that no cleric should sell drink in public. He also decreed that the deacon should read the Gospel in church, that people should stand during the Gospel and listen with great reverence, and that at Mass a Christian should offer something to God. He was buried in the Vatican.”

In the second entry it is sufficiently pure. At the end it adds Castor and his companions, as above.

MATRIC.-CARTH.-ULTRAJECT. The whole text is abbreviated in the usual manner: “The holy Innocents. Eutychius, priest, and Domitian, deacon.”

VATICAN., marked no. 5949, is deficient throughout the second entry.

The LUBECO-COL. edition has: “At Bethlehem of Judea, the feast of the holy Innocents, whom Herod the Ashkelonite, when he had learned of Christ’s birth through the report of the Magi, ordered killed, all those from two years old and younger, as the Gospel history relates.” It is pure in the entries concerning Ancyra. [Col. 0849B] At the end it adds: “In Africa, the feast of Castor,” etc.

GREVEN.: “In Africa, Castorius, Victor, and Rogatianus. Also, according to the Catalogue, Alphege [Col. 0850A], bishop and martyr of Canterbury, who according to others is listed above, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May [he means the thirteenth day before the Kalends].”

It continues: “The translation of Saint John, pope and martyr, from Ravenna to Rome. On the same day, Saints Eutychius and Florentius, monks and confessors. Of these, Eutychius, as Gregory says in the Third Book of the *Dialogues*, exercised himself in spiritual zeal and in the fervor of virtues, and strove by exhortation to lead many souls to God. Florentius lived a life devoted to simplicity and prayer. Both, distinguished by the glory of miracles, rested in the Lord.” See Gregory’s account in Surius. It continues: “Theodora, Roman matron.”

MOLAN. inserts into the text concerning the Innocents, after “they were killed,” in different type, from Ado: “in the thirty-fifth year of his reign; in the thirty-sixth year he died miserably and deservedly of dropsy, worms swarming throughout his body.” At the end: “In Africa, the feast of Saints Castor,” etc. Concerning Eutychius and Florentius, it copied GREVEN’s words given above. The later editions agree entirely with this earlier one.]

[Col. 0847]

Bethlehem, the feast of the holy Innocents, who were killed by King Herod. Ancyra of Galatia, Saints Eutychius, priest, and Domitian, deacon.

The fourth day before the Kalends. The 29th day.

[Note: [Col. 0849]

The edition of Molan alone is pure in every respect.]

[Note: [Col. 0849C]

Only two things displease me in Molan: that he writes *Trophini* instead of *Trophimi*, and *Ebrulphi* instead of *Ebrulfi*. The principal Variants must now be displayed, on account of which so many codices have been excluded from the number of the pure ones.

The alleged Pratensian autograph, with its two usual companions, Antuerp.-Maj. and Rosweyd.—to which the Aquicinctine codex, here its third companion, often joins itself—disagrees with all the others in adding at the end of the text: “Also at Jerusalem, Saint Melania, consecrated to God,” of whom absolutely no other codex on this day makes mention, except one single supplement of Greven.

The Herinien codex would be extremely pure if it did not insert in second place a distinctly Rheims entry: “The transfer of the most precious body of blessed Remigius from the city of Rheims.” Nearly all the others deal with Thomas of Canterbury, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place in the supplements.

Castellan notes that at the end of the aforementioned Pratensian codex there is additionally written: “And Saint Thomas of Canterbury.” But, he says, it is in a Gothic hand, whereas Melania is written in the Carolingian script with which, as he often testified, the whole codex was written.]

[Note: [Col. 0849D]

Let me repeat here, at the close of the work, something that we have clearly demonstrated more than once above: namely, that one of the distinctive characteristics of the little Roman Martyrology is that, unlike the other Martyrologists, it presents several patriarchs and prophets from the Old Testament inserted into Christian sacred observance.

King David is found recorded neither by any Hieronymian Martyrology nor by Bede or his followers Florius and Rabanus. He is first recorded by the author of that little Martyrology, in these words: “David the king.” Ado simply transcribed this, while our author expanded it only by adding the preceding preposition and omitted the eulogy, although he did not neglect to apply such eulogies to other saints of this kind. This became entirely clear in several places; see 6 July, 6 September, and elsewhere, most recently 16 December.

Whether Wandalbertus saw the little Roman Martyrology, or whether both consulted an older source, I have tried diligently to investigate, but I confess that it remains uncertain. Meanwhile, the poet-martyrologist honored both saints, celebrated on this day by the praised author of the little Roman Martyrology, in these verses:

> The pious prophet and king, source also of the divine lineage,  
> David distinguishes the fourth day by word and faith.  
> And the city of Arles, rejoicing in Trophimus as shepherd, shines.

Our second entry, therefore, was originally also placed in the little Roman Martyrology as follows: “And Trophimus, bishop, disciple of the apostles.” Those holy apostles, or disciples of the apostles, drawn from the New Testament, recur frequently above and are altogether characteristic of this little Martyrology, no less than its patriarchs and prophets. There seems no doubt that the Trophimus meant here is the one whose name appears in Acts 20:4 and again in 21:29, and whom the Apostle testifies in 2 Timothy 4:20 that he left sick at Miletus.

Why our author ascribes episcopal dignity to this man I do not sufficiently understand, unless he too held the opinion that Ado was the first to introduce more openly into the Martyrologies, when, among the Feasts of the Apostles, he fitted this encomium to Trophimus. Usuard subsequently adopted it in full, and it was transferred into all the more recent Martyrologies, and even into the Roman Martyrology.

Here we encounter once again the question that has had to be examined elsewhere many times, particularly recently on 18 December: namely, the question of the first preachers of the Gospel, and therefore of the bishops sent from the apostolic see into Gaul. The solution of this article depends largely upon whether Trophimus of Arles is to be identified with the disciple of the Apostle Paul.

I know that in his note for this day Baronius accuses Gregory of Tours of the most manifest error because he asserts that Trophimus was sent into Gaul during the time of the emperor Decius. Yet Gregory’s account has so many highly learned defenders and is supported by so many solid arguments that I would not dare subscribe to the opinion of the eminent Annalist.

This is not the place either to report or to weigh the force of the arguments. Let the curious reader consult the authors cited under the 18th of this month [Col. 0852A], and Tillemont, who discusses Trophimus separately in volume IV, beginning on p. 703. For the present we determine nothing here in this controversy concerning Trophimus on either side, until the entire matter can be examined more carefully in the *Acts*.

If the identity of Trophimus, Paul’s disciple and the bishop of Arles, is false, we must acknowledge that this error arose chiefly from Ado. Yet on this very day another error, or at least a useless repetition, is offered, when he mentions Crescentius, likewise a disciple of Paul, whom he had portrayed in his native colors on 22 June.

Usuard did better to omit Crescentius and substitute from his own storehouse Ebrulf, abbot of Ouche, who was wrongly ascribed by Mabillon to the Pratensian Ado, so often refuted above. See Mabillon, *Benedictine Century*, beginning on p. 354, restoring the Acts of Ebrulf to their integrity after they had been abridged in Surius. The translation of the saint is discussed by the same Mabillon, *Benedictine Century V*, beginning on p. 226.

We have already proved sufficiently above that Melania was an addition to the Usuardine codices. From all these statements the genuine simplicity of our entire calendar entry is most evident.]

[Note: [Col. 0851B]

The PRATEN. and HERINIEN. codices were discussed in the *Variants*. In the latter, Thomas of Canterbury is written at the bottom margin of the codex in a later hand, as GREVEN. has below.

TORNACEN. inserts in second place: “In England, in the city of Canterbury, the passion of blessed Thomas the martyr, archbishop of that city, who was cruelly killed by the ministers of the king of England in defense of justice.” The rest is pure.

ANTUERP.-MAJ. begins: “At Jerusalem, David the great king.” For Ebrulf it writes *Brullus*. In the entry concerning Melania it agrees with PRATEN., etc. At the end: “In the city of Canterbury, Saint Thomas, archbishop and martyr, who, in defense of justice, was struck with a sword in the church of his see and departed to Christ.”

[Col. 0851C] ROSWEYD. gives David as “the great king and prophet.” It has Melania as do the earlier companions. At the end: “At Rome, Felix.” From the Hieronymian Martyrologies.

PULSANEN. writes: “The burial of David.” After “Trophimus, bishop,” it adds the Adonian sentence: “Of whom the Apostle writes to Timothy: ‘But I left Trophimus sick at Miletus.’” The rest is missing, and in the margin another hand writes: “At Canterbury, Saint Thomas, bishop and martyr.” There is more in the other codices.

ANTUERP., MAX.-LUBEC. and UGHELLIAN. have at the end: “In Britain, in the city of Canterbury, Saint Thomas, bishop and martyr, who, in defense of justice, was struck with a sword in the basilica of his see and departed to Christ.”

MUNERAT. is fairly pure in the text and adds: “At Canterbury, the passion of Saint Thomas, bishop, cruelly slaughtered by executioners within the precincts of his own church, for the cause of that Church. At Bourges, primatial city of Aquitaine [or: ‘the primate of Aquitaine’?], the burial of the most blessed Ursinus, confessor, the first archbishop of the people of Bourges, sent there by blessed Clement to preach the faith of Christ. The histories relate that the Lord called him Nathanael and that at the Lord’s supper, when he was about to suffer immediately for the redemption of the world, he performed the office of reader.”

BELIN. First: “In England, in the city of Canterbury, Saint Thomas, archbishop and martyr, who, in defense of justice, was struck with a sword in his basilica and departed to Christ.” Then: “David, king and prophet.” Much is badly printed.

GREVEN. It is astonishing that Thomas of Canterbury could have been ascribed by this codex to Usuard, and without the usual mark L. It uses the same wording as ANTUERP. and its usual companions above, except that it inserts *feliciter*—“happily”—before “departed to Christ.”

ANTUERP.-MAX., ULTRAJECT., LEYDEN. and LOVANIEN. have Thomas of Canterbury in second place, with the same words as ANT. and the others above, except that instead of “to Christ” they read “to the Lord.”

ALBERG. and DANIC. have the same, but in first place; David is in second.

CENTULEN.: “At Jerusalem, the burial of King David. At Arles, Saint Trophimus, bishop and confessor, whom blessed Paul the Apostle ordained and sent to that city. In the district of Ouche, Saint Ebrulf, abbot. On the same day, the passion of Saint Thomas of Canterbury, archbishop.” Others have more.

BRUXELLEN.: “At Jerusalem, the burial of King David and prophet.” It is sufficiently pure concerning Trophimus. Concerning Thomas of Canterbury, it has the same as ANTUERP. and the others above. It then continues: “At Rome, the ordination of Saints Felix and Boniface, bishops. In the district of the Aisne, at the monastery of Origny, [Col. 0852C] the burial of Saint Ebrulf, confessor, whose deeds are recorded. In Africa, Saints Crescentius and Libosus, bishops. At Bourges, Saint Ursinus, bishop and confessor.”

HAGENOYEN. In first place it gives a summary of David’s entire life, in its own manner and style; but these matters may be drawn more suitably from Sacred Scripture. It is sufficiently pure concerning Trophimus. A long history of Thomas follows, which there is no time to transcribe.

AQUICINT. has Melania at the end, as do PRATEN. and the others, as stated in the *Variants*. It additionally adds: “At Canterbury, the passion of Saint Thomas, archbishop and martyr of that city.”

VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked no. 130, have at the end: “On the same day at Bourges, Saint Ursinus, bishop and confessor.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Thomas, bishop and martyr. Ebrulf, confessor. Trophimus, bishop. David, king of Israel.”

[Col. 0852D] DIVIONEN. of Saint Benignus: “On the same day, Saint Albert, abbot, whose life shone with many miracles.” Castellan calls him abbot of Gembloux.

In VATICAN., under no. 5949, there is nothing concerning David and Ebrulf. It adds: “At Ravenna, Saint Barbatianus, priest and confessor.” In the Roman Martyrology he is placed on 31 December.

FLORENTIN.: “Also Saint Florentius, bishop of the city of Haroisa, or Auroisa, and confessor.” I think Florentius of Orange is meant, concerning whom we dealt with Usuard under 17 October. Castellan notes that he is honored at Florentiola. Perhaps his elevation, translation, or something similar is commemorated here.

The codices continue: “At Compostela, the translation of Saint James the Apostle, as is clear from his legend. At Rome, Saint Felix, bishop.” Then only STROZZIAN. adds: “Also the feast of Raphael the archangel.”

BURDEGALEN. has a special feast: “The translation of Saint Renatus, bishop.” See Castellan in the index under Renatus and Rene.

The LUBECO-COL. edition has: “At Jerusalem, Saint David, king and prophet.” In the entry concerning Trophimus it is sufficiently pure. Then: “In Britain, in the city of Canterbury, the feast of Saint Thomas, bishop and martyr, under Henry, king of the English. In defense of justice, in the basilica of his see they cut off the sacred crown of his head with a sword, cruelly scatter his brain together with his blood, and through such martyrdom his soul departed to the Lord.”
