Concerning Ebrulf it adds “abbot.” Finally: “At Rome, Saints Boniface, bishop, and Felix, confessor.”

GREVEN.: “In Africa, Libosus, bishop. On the same day, according to Ado, Crescentius, the Apostle Paul’s disciple and the first teacher of the Church of Vienne. Usuard has him on the fifth day before the Kalends of July.” Yet Ado also records Crescentius on that very day, as we noted in the *Observations*.

“At Rome, Boniface, bishop, and Felix [Col. 0854A], confessor. Helduard, bishop and confessor. Also David the hermit, of whom it is read in the *Lives of the Fathers* that from a robber he became a most exemplary monk. Also a commemoration of Jesse, David’s father, and Nathan the prophet. On the same day, Saint Melania, Roman matron, consecrated to God at Jerusalem.”

MOLAN. adds at the end concerning Ebrulf: “Whose deeds are recorded. In England, in the city of Canterbury, Saint Thomas, archbishop,” etc., from BELIN. The later editions, in italic type and in second place, deal with Thomas of Canterbury, also from BELIN. At the end they likewise add the entry concerning Ebrulf. Then: “Also the feast of blessed Hildeward, bishop of Toul.” He is the patron of the town of Termonde; see Castellan. Finally, in smaller type: “On the same day, Saint Marcellus, holy father and archimandrite of the monastery of the Sleepless.” The monks of that monastery are commonly known by the name *Acoemetae*.]

[Col. 0849]

At Jerusalem, David the king. At Arles, the feast of Saint Trophimus, whom Paul mentions when writing to Timothy; ordained bishop by that same Apostle, he was sent to the aforesaid city to preach Christ’s Gospel there for the first time. From his source, as Pope Zosimus writes, all Gaul received streams of faith. In the district of Ouche, Saint Ebrulf, confessor. [Bouillart adds: [Note: [Col. 0849B] Here indeed Sollerius is astonishing, rejecting all manuscript codices, even the ancient ones, and adhering only to Molan’s edition. As though the Pratensian codex, which he himself admits to be at least the most ancient, if not the original, were not of greater authority. Nor does it matter that Saint Melania has been added at the end of the entry, since she is read in several codices, both those praised by Sollerius himself and in the Pratensian codices B, D, E, and Montisburg. Moreover, this addition was written not by a foreign hand but by the principal hand. For what reason Usuard mentioned Melania on this day remains unknown. Her feast is commonly celebrated on 31 December.

As for Saint Thomas of Canterbury, whom the illustrious Castellan asserts in that famous letter so often praised by Sollerius to have been written in a Gothic hand and added at the end, that claim is altogether contrary to the truth. There is not even a word concerning Saint Thomas [Col. 0850C] in the Pratensian codex. From this the reader devoted to truth may already perceive how much credence should be given to Castellan in the remaining matters. BOUILLART.] Also at Jerusalem, Saint Melania, consecrated to God.]

The third day before the Kalends. The 30th day.

[Note: [Col. 0853]

Thus: Praten., Herinien., Tornacen., Greven. and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0853B]

There is scarcely anything noteworthy among the codices cited for the text. The little Roman Martyrology writes *Exsuperantii*, while Ado has *Exuperantii*; most of the manuscripts follow Ado, and that form has been retained in the text.

Munerat. and Greven. read *relegationem*; the others have *religationem*, which seems more appropriate to the sense, although neither produces an entirely clear construction. In Molan the wording is even less satisfactory because of *carceris revelationem*.]

[Note: [Col. 0853B]

The martyrs praised in the first commemoration of the text are known only in our series. The little Roman Martyrology, the leader of the others, preceded it in this form: “At Spoletum, Sabinus, bishop, Exsuperantius and Marcellus, and Venustianus with his wife and children, who suffered martyrdom on the seventh day before the Ides of December and have the feast of their burial on the third day before the Kalends of January.”

This account, given so briefly, does not entirely agree with the published Acts. The Viennese Martyrologist undoubtedly saw the Acts themselves and drew from them a somewhat more distinct and expansive eulogy, although still not so accurate that it clearly explains everything that may be disputed.

Usuard, reducing Ado’s longer account [Col. 0853C] to an elegant epitome, deliberately avoided several matters that cause difficulties elsewhere; Castellan explained these fairly well in the note attached to his edition.

It is established that more than one version of the Acts of the aforementioned martyrs has been published, and that the versions are not entirely consistent. There can be no doubt that Baronius had the manuscripts themselves, since in the *Annals*, under the year 301, no. 18, he praises the most authentic Acts and says that they deserve to be reproduced word for word: “Would that, just as we found them faithful, so we had found them complete in every respect, and finished with the same brightness with which they were begun.”

More complete, and perhaps more authentic, versions were published by the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius in volume II of the *Miscellanea*, beginning on p. 47. In his notes, p. 465, he unhesitatingly asserts that they are the most authentic and best versions, worthy to come into the hands of learned men.

That all these saints were incorrectly assigned by our Martyrologists to Spoletum is clear from the Acts themselves. Nor can it be sufficiently inferred from them of what city Sabinus—or Savinus—was bishop. He is presented as the leader of the others, although we readily acknowledge that he was crowned with martyrdom at Spoletum.

Concerning Venustianus, Papebrochius, on the day when he is celebrated by the people of Todi, 18 April, found certain matters in the long-published Acts which he thought should be explained along a path different from Baronius’s, without in any way attacking their truth.

The more recent Tillemont, however, is not satisfied even with the Baluzius Acts. In volume V, pp. 603–604, he accumulates several arguments by which he attempts to weaken their credibility. I will not deny that there are some features which rightly make a critical reader pause. Yet who does not know that even golden Acts are not free from blemishes here and there, especially in proper names, which are sometimes distorted or, when erased in ancient parchment, wrongly supplied?

Certainly so many rays of simple authenticity shine through the darker little clouds that I do not doubt that the praised Acts will someday be vindicated by us or by our successors against Tillemont’s judgment, whatever Ruinartius may have found objectionable in them. His undertaking was to publish only those Acts that could not be called into question either by Dodwell or by any heretic, however persistent.

The following entry was once wrongly attributed to Ado: “Also on the island of Oya, Saints Florentius, Serenus, Paul, Stephen, Papianus, and Cletus.” Mosander distinguished it with an asterisk, while Rosweyd relegated it to an appendix. Florentinius restores to Alexandria and joins to Mansuetus the companions wrongly connected with Florentius on the island of Oya. In the Echternach manuscript he found nine names, in the Corbie manuscript eleven, whereas in the Lucca manuscript ten had been added, with Florentius improperly mixed into the entire series.

You can easily infer which Hieronymian codex Usuard followed. I have no doubt that he had one resembling the Lucca manuscript before his eyes, and that from it he extracted Mansuetus by name, leaving the other ten companions anonymous.

Whether Wandalbertus believed Mansuetus and Florentius to be companions I do not know; at least he combined both in this single verse of his for the present day:

> Mansuetus and likewise Florentius adorn the third …]

[Note: [Col. 0855A]

ANTUERP.-MAJ. begins: “The translation of Saint James the Apostle.” In the rest of the Usuardine text it is pure.

ROSWEYD. The present and the following calendar entries are not sufficiently distinct. Otherwise, on this day it adds to the fairly pure text: “On the island of Oya, Saint Florentius.” He seems to have been taken from the Hieronymian Martyrologies. “At Tours, Saint Perpetuus, bishop and confessor.” He is clearly expressed in the Hieronymian Martyrologies and is marked by our authors under 8 April. Rabanus follows the earlier codices.

PULSANEN. substitutes another text: “At Tours, the feast of Saint Perpetuus, bishop and confessor.” Then, from the following day: “At Sens, blessed Sabinianus, bishop, and Pontianus, martyrs. Sent by the blessed apostles to preach, they made the aforesaid city illustrious through the confession of their martyrdom.”

ANTUERP. MAX.-LUBEC. and UGHELLIAN. add to the pure text: “At Rome, Felix, bishop. At Tours, Saint [Col. 0855B] Perpetuus, bishop.”]

ANTUERP.-MAX., together with all the codices of middling quality, is pure in the first entry but entirely omits the second. At the end, however, it adds: “At Rome, Saint Felix the bishop.” ALBERG. alone adds above the others: “At Tours, Perpetuus the bishop and confessor. He was the founder of many churches.”

CENTULEN.: “At Spoleto, Saint Sabinus the bishop, Exuperantius and Marcellus the deacons, and Venustianus with his wife and children, who suffered under the emperor Maximian. At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop and confessor.”

BRUXELLEN. begins: “On the island of Oya, the birthday of the saints Florentius, Serenus, Paulus, Stephanus, Papianus, and Cletus. At Alexandria, the birthday of the saints Mansuetus, Securus, Donatus, Honorius, Poleditus, and Appianus.” See the Hieronymian Martyrologies, and there Florentinius, who assigns those martyrs to their proper group. In the first announcement concerning the martyrs of Spoleto it is slightly interpolated. At the end: “At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop and confessor. He was the founder of many churches.”

HAGENOYEN. is sufficiently pure in the first announcement; it presents the second as follows: “At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Mansuetus, bishop and martyr, with ten others.” It then follows the preceding day: “In the district of Oximus, the birthday of Saint Ebrulf the confessor. On the same day, the birthday of Saint Leporius, bishop and martyr. At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop and confessor.”

AQUICINCT. writes *Marcellinus* instead of *Marcellus*. At the end it adds: “At Rome, Felix the bishop. At Tours, Perpetuus the bishop and confessor, who was the founder of churches.” Some add “many.” The codices VICTORIN. and REG. SUEC., marked with the number 130, have the same additions in the same form.

DAVERONEN.: “At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop, who built the basilica of Saint Martin with marvelous workmanship.”

[Col. 0855D] MATRIC.-CARTHUS.-ULTRAJECT.: “Perpetuus the bishop. Sabinus the bishop and martyr with his companions.” He dealt with these above, on 15 January. “Mansuetus, with ten other martyrs.”

Codex D. LE MARE, marked A: “The translation of Francoveus, confessor and bishop of the church of Sens, from the basilica of Saint Columba to the monastery of Saint Symphorianus. On the island of Oya, the deposition of Saint Florentius.”

Codex D. DU CHEVAL., marked C: “At Tours, Saint Perpetuus . . .,” as in AQUICINCT. and the others.

In the VATICAN codex, no. 5949, the first announcement is absent. To Mansuetus it adds the following companions, who are also found in the Roman Martyrology: “Severus, Appianus, Donatus, Honorius.”

ALTEMPS: “At Evesham, Saint Egwin the bishop and confessor.” See Castellani’s *Martyrologium*.

JURENSIS has, as several other codices cited above report: “On the island of Oya, Saint Florentius.”

REMENS. SS. Tim. et Apoll.: “At Soissons, the translation of the body of Saint Onesimus, bishop and confessor. At Reims, the translation of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris [and] their companions,” added by a more recent hand.

The LUBECO-COL. edition: The first entry is sufficiently pure. Then: [Col. 0856B] “At Rome, Saint Felix the bishop and confessor.” It then gives the entry for Mansuetus, purely. Next: “At the monastery of Dol, Saint Albert the abbot. At Tours, Perpetuus the bishop and confessor. He was the founder of many churches, etc. On the same day, the translation of Saint James the apostle, brother of Saint John the Evangelist.”

BELIN. at the end: “At Rome, Saint Felix the bishop. At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop and confessor.”

GREVEN.: “In Apulia, Saint Liberalis, bishop of Canosa and martyr. Born of a senatorial father, he was entrusted to a certain holy bishop to be instructed in letters, and by that bishop was ordained bishop of the aforesaid church.” I think Rugerius or Rogerius is meant; see Castellani concerning him. The account continues: “When he diligently carried out the office entrusted to him, he also deserved to attain the palm of martyrdom—surmounting unharmed an iron bed, a gridiron with fire placed beneath it, a frying pan filled with boiling oil and fat, and a furnace—together with the prefect Cerberus, who believed through his confession, and his mother Euanthia, by decapitation. On the island of Oya, Saints Florentius, Serenus, Paulus, Stephanus, Papianus, and Cletus. Likewise at Alexandria, Saints Securus, Donatus, Honorius, Poleclytus, and Appianus, companions of Saint Mansuetus.” I have already said that Florentinius’s observations on these should be consulted. “At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop and confessor, whom Usuardus places on the fourth day before the Ides of April. According to the Catalogue, at Rome, Felix III, pope [according to others, Felix IV], and confessor. Likewise at the monastery of Dol, Saint Albert the abbot. On the same day, the translation of Saint James the Greater, apostle.”

MOLAN.: “At Rome, Saint Felix the bishop. At Tours, Saint Perpetuus the bishop and confessor. He was the founder of many churches, etc. On the same day, Florentius the confessor.” Later editions have it as follows: “At Milan, Eugenius the archbishop. On the thirtieth day, Saint Anysia the martyr, and Zoticus the presbyter, nourisher of orphans.” [Col. 0856D] Concerning Felix, as above. Then: “At Compostela in Galicia, the arrival of the body of Saint James the apostle, who, by what he could do with a living voice and with a severed corpse, impressed Christian piety upon the minds of the Spaniards. On the same day, the arrival of the body of Saint Winnoc at Bergues, in the year 900 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the third indiction.” See 6 November.

[Col. 0853]

At Spoleto, the birthday of the blessed Sabinus the bishop, Exuperantius and Marcellus the deacons, and Venustianus with his wife and children, under the emperor Maximian. Of these, Marcellus and Exuperantius were first suspended on the *equuleus*, then severely tortured with clubs, afterward scraped with claws, and roasted by the burning of their sides; thus they completed their martyrdom. Venustianus, however, was not long afterward killed by the sword together with his wife and children. But Saint Sabinus, after his hands had been cut off and he had been kept in prison for a long time, was beaten to death. Thus, although their martyrdom occurred at different times, it is commemorated on one day. At Alexandria, Saint Mansuetus the martyr, with ten others.

The day before the Kalends. Day 31.

[Note: [Col. 0857]

The Herinien., Tornacen., Antuerp., and Max.-Lubec. codices, Munerat., and the first edition of Belin are entirely pure. Greven. and Molan.]

[Note: [Col. 0857A]

I said that the cited codices are entirely pure, by which I sufficiently indicated that others are nearly pure but do not attain complete purity. Such are Praten., Antuerp.-Maj., and Rosweyd. They go beyond the others in adding, after “she was beheaded,” “by order of the emperor Aurelian”; I believe that these words, which are neither Adonian nor consequently Usuardian, were transferred from Bede’s Martyrology into the cited codices, as also into the Aquicinctine codex. Certainly, it is sufficiently clear from all the other better codices that they should not be referred to the present text. The remaining variations of the codices in the text cited are extremely slight and are generally scribal blunders, such as *Sylvestri*, *Saviniani*, *aput*, *eandem*, and *Pontiani* in Molan. instead of *Potentiani*, *Reciariae*, *Reuariae*, and so forth. Greven. and Molan. transpose the words *in sanctae virginis Columbae*.]

[Note: [Col. 0857B]

The first and most ancient memorial of the glorious pontiff Sylvester is expressed most clearly in Bucherius’s Calendar, so often cited by us: “On the day before the Kalends of January, Sylvester at Priscilla’s.” All the remaining sacred ecclesiastical monuments that survive agree. To come closer to our own sources, he is mentioned in all the Hieronymian copies: “The deposition of Saint Sylvester the bishop.” The same words occur in Bede, and the same in Rabanus, who alone adds “and confessor.” What is attributed to Florus need not be considered here. The guide of our series, the Little Roman Martyrology, has: “At Rome, Sylvester the pope and confessor.” Such is Ado’s eulogy, taken from the *Pontifical*, that one must admit either that he did not see the famous Acts, known in the time of Gelasius, or that, contrary to his custom, he deliberately avoided matters which he had noticed could not be reconciled with historical truth. Our author appears to have taken nothing from Ado, merely indicating that his famous Acts were available; that he did not entirely approve them can easily be gathered from his more meager account. We have a most illustrious saint and the first pontiff of the Church granted peace by Constantine, worthy of veneration for his great deeds and holiness. If only his history were equally true—so much debated in writings on both sides—and had not, not long ago, after many other learned men, been shown in no small part to be false by Papebrochius and Janningus. This is now the nearly universal opinion among scholars, despite Combefis’s unsuccessful effort, while he imagines that he has brought something new to light among the *Lecti triumphos*. I am dealing with a matter widely discussed at the present time; see the preliminary Apology before volume 1 of June, beginning on page 16, and the Responses to articles 2 and 3. It is entirely worthy of notice that among all the ancient martyrologists no one touched upon the story of Constantine’s baptism except Wandalbertus alone, whose metrical eulogy of Saint Sylvester is as follows:

> On the day before the Kalends, Pope Sylvester through the Roman city  
> Subdues the rejoicing peoples to himself with friendly vows,  
> He who, first among pontiffs, deserved to behold peaceful tranquility  
> And cleanse the rulers of the world in the laver.

[Col. 0857D] Sabinianus and Potentianus are known neither in the Hieronymian Martyrologies, nor in Bede’s series, nor in the Little Roman Martyrology. Ado marked them, but each in a simple form, whereas Usuardus first assigns them the title of bishop. They differ again in that Our Author writes that, sent by the Roman pontiff to preach, they made the same metropolis illustrious through the confession of their martyrdom; Ado, however, says that they were sent by the apostles to preach and that they made the aforesaid city illustrious, and so forth. Perhaps Usuardus regarded that apostolic mission with suspicion. Certainly, from their Acts, whether published by Mombritius or by Surius, it does not seem any more probable that those two saints were immediate disciples of the apostles than that the first bishops of Gaul were, concerning whom we have spoken at length elsewhere. Tillemont discusses them in his treatment of Dionysius of Paris; see volume 4, page 727. We possess many manuscript documents submitted by various persons, which we defer for examination to their proper place. Wandalbertus celebrates them after Columba; we shall give the metrical eulogies, woven together, below.

Moreover, the most celebrated virgin Columba is mentioned with complete clarity in all the Hieronymian codices in Florentinius: “At Sens, or in the city of Sens, the passion of Saint Columba the virgin.” Bede gives a fuller account: “And the passion of Saint Columba the virgin at Sens, under the emperor Aurelian, who, after overcoming the fire, was beheaded.” Rabanus follows Bede word for word. The Little Roman Martyrology more briefly has: “And Saint Columba the virgin.” Our eulogy, however, is plainly Adonian, with the tyrant’s name omitted; above, in the Variants, we noted that this name entered some Usuardian codices from Bede. The cult of the illustrious virgin is widespread, and various Acts are not lacking; we possess them both in manuscripts and in printed editions. In them, to put it most mildly, the marks of authenticity are wanting; nor has anyone adequately explained the marriage proposed to the virgin by Aurelian, the son of Caesar, whom history does not know. Whether everything else can be sufficiently excused will be examined in its proper place. Hermes the exorcist, not marked by Our Guides, may be called purely Usuardian, but he was drawn from the Hieronymian Martyrologies; concerning him, see Florentinius and Castellani’s note. Of his Acts or deeds there is profound silence. Here I append Wandalbertus’s final eulogy of the martyrs of Sens, with which both the month of December and the entire sacred year are brought to a close:

> The virgin Columba, likewise, received the palm of everlasting virtue,  
> And, accompanying Christ, received it with her own blood;  
> Together with Potentianus, Sabinianus on the same day  
> Comes forth, equal in feast, altar, and triumph—  
> They who, as its first patrons, instructed the city of Sens.  
> These at last close the final festivals of December.

] [Note: [Col. 0859A]

PRATEN. Concerning the interpolation of its codex and those of its companions, it was said above in the Variants.

PULSANEN. after Sylvester adds the following: “He was the thirty-fifth after blessed Peter and ruled the Church for three years, ten months, and eleven days. Through his diligence the most illustrious synod of 318 Fathers was held throughout the world at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, under the consuls Constantine Augustus and Licinius, on the day before the Kalends of January. On the same day, at Sens, the passion of Saint Columba the virgin.” Nothing further.

ANTUERP.-MAX., with six companions of middling quality, [Col. 0859B] interpolates the first three announcements. In the first, after “pope,” it inserts: “Who, thirty-fifth after blessed Peter, ruled the Roman Church, and, full of virtues, died in peace and was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, whose …,” and so forth. In the second, after “Potentianus”: “Who, one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ, was sent by the pontiff …,” and so forth. In the third, after “virgin”: “Who under the emperor Aurelian …”

CENTULEN.: “At Rome, Saint Sylvester the pope and confessor, whose holiness of life and nobility of deeds are celebrated in God’s Church with perpetual praise. At Sens, Saints Sabinus and Potentianus, bishops, sent there by blessed Peter. In the same city, Saint Columba the virgin, under the emperor Aurelian. At Retiaria,” and so forth. Pure.

BRUXELLEN.: “At Rome, Saint Sylvester the pope, who, full of virtues, died in peace and was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way. His Acts, etc. Likewise at Rome, the birthday of Saints Zeno and Donatus.” This is found in the Hieronymian Martyrologies; could one have entered in place of the city of Sens? In Sabinianus and Potentianus it is similar to ANTUERP.-MAX. and the others. It then proceeds to Columba and Hermes, but the final leaf of the codex is torn.

HAGENOYEN. gives three long eulogies, the first concerning Sabinianus and Potentianus, the second concerning Columba, and the third concerning Sylvester. They are composed from the commonly circulated Acts; I would rather refer readers to those than linger here over transcribing material arranged at such length and without elegance. It improperly enlarges the final announcement by a new placement: “In the province of Raetia, in the city of Retiaria, the deposition of Saint Hermes the exorcist.” Castellani places Retiaria in Serbia.

[Col. 0860A] AQUICINCT. adds the following after the material concerning Sylvester: “He established that chrism should be made by a bishop, that a priest should baptize, that a layman should dare to bring no charge against any cleric, and that dalmatics should be used in church.” In the account of Columba it generally agrees with Praten. and the two others cited above, adding “under the emperor Aurelian.”

MATRIC.-CARTHUS. ULTRAJECT.: “Sylvester the pope and confessor. Odilo the abbot.” See 1 and 2 January. It continues: “Columba the virgin and martyr. Sabinianus and Potentianus the martyrs.”

In the VATICAN codex marked no. 5949, the final announcement is absent; another is substituted from the Hieronymian Martyrologies, namely: [Col. 0860B] “Likewise at Rome, Saints Donata, Paulina, and Serotina.” See there how the names are to be formed.

JUREN. I do not understand why the following is added here on this day: “In Gaul, the birthday of Saint Eligius the confessor.”

The LUBECO-COL. edition adds much concerning Sylvester, which I do not care to transcribe. In Sabinianus and Potentianus, and likewise in Columba, it is similar to the codices of middling quality. Concerning Hermes, it adds “and confessor.”

The second edition of BELIN has at the end: “On the same day, Saint Odilo the abbot.”

GREVEN.: “At Carthage, Saints Saturninus and Caelestinus. Likewise, Saints Hilary and Donatus. At Ravenna, Saint Barbatianus the presbyter and confessor. Coming from Antioch to Rome, when the fame of his holiness and miracles spread everywhere, the Empress Placidia, together with her son Valentinian, invited him and built a monastery for him, where, completing the course of his life in holy works, he rested in peace.”

MOLAN.: “And Saint Barbatianus the confessor.” Later editions write: “On the same day, Saint Barbatianus,” and so forth. Then: “On the thirty-first day, Saint Melana of Rome” (*Melana* for *Melania*). Nearly all the codices add here, word for word, the customary conclusion for each day: “And many other saints, martyrs, confessors, and virgins.” The response is: “Thanks be to God.” I repeat Wandalbertus’s final verse, the conclusion of the entire Martyrology.]

[Col. 0857]

At Rome, the birthday of Saint Sylvester the pope, whose illustrious deeds are recorded. At Sens, the blessed Sabinianus the bishop and Potentianus, who, sent by the Roman pontiff to preach, made that same metropolis illustrious through the confession of their martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0857A] Prat. Sollerius argues that the codex, together with Antuerp.-Maj. and Rosweyd., goes beyond the others because, after “she was beheaded,” they add “by order of the emperor Aurelian.” Who could fail to see that these words were written by the author himself, so that the time of Saint Columba’s martyrdom might be indicated more precisely? These words, “by order of the emperor Aurelian,” although the place was erased, were written by the first hand. The same reading is found in codices Pratenses B and D, Colbert. [Col. 0858A] B, Victorin. B, Conchensis, Pontisar., Sandionys., and Montisburgensis. It should be noted that in this same article the words “who was sent by the Roman pontiff to prea—” are under erasure; there is no trace of them in the Dervensis codex, and the erasure was therefore made before the Martyrology was presented to Charles. There are consequently two erasures in this article, made at different times. I ask learned men to inspect it and determine whether the handwriting is different. BOUILLART.]

And in the same city, Saint Columba the virgin, who, after overcoming the fire, was beheaded [Bouillart adds: “by order of the emperor Aurelian”]. At Retiaria, Saint Hermes the exorcist.

And at last these close the final festivals of December.

TO THE GREATER GLORY OF GOD.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 877. CHARLES THE BALD, KING OF THE FRANKS.

[Col. 0861]

LETTERS OF CHARLES THE BALD

LETTER ONE TO POPE NICHOLAS. He intercedes for Bishop Adventius and asks that he be received back into favor.

[In Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VIII, p. 445.]

[Col. 0861A]

To the most holy and reverend Father Nicholas, supreme pontiff and universal pope of the Catholic and apostolic See: Charles, king by the grace of God and your spiritual son.

Because, thanks be to God, our devotion toward the holy apostolic See and toward your honor in these regions beyond the Alps is known far and wide, and because your paternal kindness toward our filial affection is cultivated with the reverence of the greatest love and has become known not only to our well-wishers but also to our rivals, through sure indications—as befits, by God’s authority, the summit of your sanctity and religion: Adventius, the venerable bishop of Metz, sent to us this brother named Betto, faithful to us, as we believe, regularly brought up from infancy in a monastery of our kingdom and granted to him through our munificence, as had been agreed between us. He asked us to send letters on his behalf to your most loving fatherhood, believing that they would be useful to him and would provide him with no small support before your authority.

He also instructed me that he wished to send through this brother to your apostolate his profession, subscribed with his own hand, containing the correction of past deceptions and caution for the future, as the holy rules prescribe, so that he might obtain pardon for his offenses, communion with the apostolic See, and the favor of your apostolic power.

Therefore, since our venerable and most beloved uncle Drogo—although he had lived in the kingdom of our brother Lothair, formerly emperor, after the death of our lord and father, because the see had fallen within that part of his kingdom—was nevertheless joined to us by uniquely sweet affection and steadfast loyalty, and since he had brought up the same venerable Adventius and kept him in domestic familiarity, while Adventius himself remains faithful and friendly toward us, we most devoutly beseech you, as though kissing the most holy footsteps of your fatherhood, that through our petition he may, as he hopes, feel himself assisted before your authority, and that neither he nor his see may in any way—God forbid—be dishonored. That see deserved to be honored by the apostolic See at the petition of our grandfather, the emperor Charles of blessed memory, so that Engilramnus, his chief chaplain and representative of the apostolic See in these regions, might for some time hold that office; and afterward, through the entreaty of our lord and father, the pious Augustus of holy memory, it had been honored by the apostolic See in the person of our venerable uncle Drogo, the bishop of distinguished character, so that, together with the aforesaid ministry of the emperor and of the apostolic See, he might also enjoy the use of the pallium.

For even if this venerable man Adventius, driven either by the superstition of his prince or teachers, or drawn by favor from the agreement of the majority, or deceived or misled in some other way, proved in something less careful than he ought to have been—for, as Augustine says, “God loves to spare those who confess, and not to judge those who judge themselves; and divine vengeance ceases if human conversion goes before it”—the most gentle and excellent kindness of your apostolate toward all who are converted will follow the judgment of your predecessor Leo, who says: “The moderation of the apostolic See maintains this restraint: that it act more severely toward the hardened, but desire to grant pardon to the corrected, so that pardon may be granted if the error is abolished.”

We ask that you kindly and familiarly receive this religious monk Betto, not merely his but also our envoy, instructed by God’s grace and diligent study in knowledge of letters and in intellectual ability, so that he may relate to the gentleness of your apostolate, in a private conversation, the matters entrusted to him. May almighty God deign to preserve your holiness, who pray for us, for a long age in accordance with his will, most holy and reverend Father in the Lord.

LETTER II, A SYNODAL LETTER TO THE BISHOPS AND COUNTS OF GAUL, in the name of King Charles.

[In Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VIII, p. 246.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, illustrious king by the grace of God, sends greetings to the bishops, beloved men, illustrious faithful envoys, and our counts.

Let your fidelity know that on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in accordance with sacred authority, [Col. 0863A] we caused a synod of venerable bishops and an assembly of our faithful to convene at Carisiacum. With them, among other matters concerning ecclesiastical welfare and the needs of the kingdom, we considered how the acts of plunder and devastation which, partly because of the incursions of the pagans and partly because of the fickleness of certain of our faithful in our kingdom, are being perpetrated even by those who ought to provide for the defense and protection of God’s Church and for the stability and peace of the kingdom, might in some way, with the Lord’s approval, be quieted and removed.

By their counsel we decreed that, because sins which at their beginning are judged to be, as they are, of great weight, through a pernicious progression speak to the mind itself in an even more destructive manner and, as though insensible, [Note: [Col. 0864D] The passage is corrupt; it should be read: “are lifted up by depraved minds through custom,” and so forth.] bind people more often to their own misfortunes when they attempt to recover their senses, so that, if they wish to rise again, they may be unable to do so, before ecclesiastical censure and legal judgments strike such plunderers with terror and condemnation, each bishop in his parish, the envoys in their districts, and the counts in their counties shall likewise hold assemblies, so that all ministers of the state and royal vassals, and all persons, whoever they may be or whosever men they are, in those parishes and counties, may assemble without any respect of persons, excuse, or delay.

The bishops of those parishes shall briefly record and read aloud to everyone the judgments concerning such a matter—namely, those of evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic authority, as well as apostolic and canonical decrees—and shall take care, in plain speech, to make known to all what a great and serious sin it is, what great and serious penance it demands, and what enormous and most severe vengeance it requires, together with the other appropriate, necessary, and useful exhortations.

The envoys likewise shall record the legal judgments as they know them, and the chapters of our predecessors, the kings and emperors, and our own chapters concerning this matter, collected into one body, shall be made known to all. The bishops shall forbid such depredations to everyone by the authority of God and the apostles; our envoys and counts shall firmly endeavor to prohibit them to all by our royal ban; and everyone shall know that if from now on anyone in our kingdom presumes to do such things, he shall receive a sentence specifically according to the divine judgments, shall be compelled to make amends according to the laws and royal chapters, and shall suffer a fitting punishment according to the judgment of our faithful.

And if such a person is of a kind that our bishops, envoys, and counts can correct the wrongful act committed within their jurisdictions, they shall endeavor to correct it according to the instructions set forth above, or shall cause him to come into our presence through sureties. But if anyone at all proves disobedient, they shall make the matter known to us with the greatest haste, so that we may order him to come into our presence as quickly as possible and suffer a fitting punishment according to the judgment of our faithful.

And if—God forbid—someone should arise who sets aside the fear of God, despises ecclesiastical authority, and refuses royal power, let him know, whoever he may be, that according to canonical authority he will be made an outsider to the assembly of all Christians and to the fellowship of the holy Church, both in heaven and on earth; and by royal power and the unanimity of all the faithful of the kingdom he will be pursued as an enemy of God and the Church and as a devastator of the kingdom, until he is expelled from the kingdom.

And if there is a count who commits such acts in his county, or permits such things to increase there and does not correct them himself, or does not make them known to us so that our authority may correct them, let him know that he will suffer the sentence imposed in such a case, as was customary in the time of our predecessors.

And if traveling men commit depredations and acts of plunder throughout our kingdom, and the bishops, envoys, or counts cannot correct this, they shall take care to make it known to us as quickly as they can, so that we may order the plunderers to return along the same road with our envoy and to make legal restitution for everything the others have done, and to undergo such an armed punishment as we shall command, or such a judgment as we shall determine in consultation with our faithful.

But if they are the men of our beloved brother or our nephews who have committed such acts, and this becomes known to us, so that we may inform them of it, let them arrange to punish their men for such offenses as they deem best, just as we wish to punish our own men. If in their kingdoms they should presume—God forbid—to commit any unbecoming or harmful act, [Note: [Col. 0864D] In the Sirmond edition: COLLECTION CONCERNING PLUNDERERS. Gregory says in the *Pastoral Book*: “Those who are to be admonished …”] those who strive to seize what belongs to others must be admonished to hear attentively what the Lord will say when he comes in judgment: “I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and so forth; to them he says: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25). From this, therefore, it must be gathered how great a condemnation awaits those who seize what belongs to others, if those who indiscriminately kept what was theirs are struck with such severity. Let them consider by what guilt the seized property binds them, if property not handed over subjects a person to such punishment. Let them consider how deeply the injustice inflicted condemns them, if kindness not shown deserves such a blow.

Let the plunderers hear, those who multiply what is not theirs everywhere and heap up thick mud against themselves (Habakkuk 2). To heap thick mud against oneself means to accumulate earthly profits together with the weight of sin.

Let them hear what Christ says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16)—that is, what does it profit a man if he gathers to himself everything outside himself and condemns only that which he himself is?

Let those who seize things in this world hear that “they will perish, and in this world they will leave them behind”; but they will carry with them to judgment the causes of their plunder—that is, condemnation—as it is written elsewhere.

Let them hear that the prophet Isaiah says: “The plunder of the poor is in your house, and the cause of the widow does not enter to them” (Isaiah I, III), and “the widow’s tear descends to her cheek; and the Lord will not be pleased with them” (Ecclesiasticus 35).

Let them hear that in whose house there is plunder—whether in the house of the body or in the house of one’s dwelling—the Holy Spirit does not dwell in that house, but an evil spirit does. And if such a person approaches communion of the body and blood of Christ before making worthy satisfaction, through that communion he is not cleansed from sin; rather, more fully, like Judas, when at the supper, full of plunder and iniquity, he presumed to receive communion from Christ’s hand, he is possessed by the devil, and therefore, when hanged, burst open in the middle. The cause of the widow does not enter to such a person, nor will he himself, unless he has made worthy satisfaction, be able to enter the heavenly Church.

Let the plunderers hear what the prophet says again: “You who plunder, will you not yourself be plundered?” (Isaiah 33). For the one who plunders the possessions of the poor, the churches, and the servants of God is plundered by the devil and becomes his prey.

[Col. 0865D] Let them hear what the holy Apostle says, through whom Christ spoke, who was caught up to the third heaven and caught up into paradise and heard secret words such as it is not lawful for human beings to speak. He says: “Neither the rapacious, nor murderers, nor adulterers shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6). Let him consider what a great and serious sin plunder is, since the holy Apostle compared it with adultery and murder.

The same Apostle also says: “If anyone is a fornicator, or an adulterer, or a plunderer, or a murderer, a disciple of Christ—that is, a Christian—may not even take food with such a person before satisfaction, that is, correction or amendment, and worthy penance” (1 Corinthians 5).

Let them hear that the holy apostle John, the chosen and beloved disciple of Christ, who reclined upon his breast at the supper, forbids greeting such a person, saying: “Do not even say, ‘Hail,’ nor receive him into your house” (2 John 10).

(24, question 3, chapter 21.) [Council of Toledo I, chapter 11.] Let them hear what the holy bishops at the Council of Toledo—who reign in heaven with God and shine forth on earth through miracles, having been gathered from all parts of the world—decreed. “If any one of the powerful has stripped a cleric, or any poor person, or a religious person, and the bishop has sent to him that he should hear the matter, but he has refused, letters shall immediately pass in turn through all the bishops of the province whom they are able to reach, so that he may be held excommunicated until he gives a hearing and returns what belongs to another.” Behold the judgment concerning plunderers of the poor.

(12, q. 2, c. 6.) Let the plunderers and robbers of ecclesiastical property hear what holy Pope Anacletus, ordained presbyter by the Apostle Peter himself, judged together with the priests of the whole world. For he says:

“Whoever takes anything away from father or mother is an accomplice of a murderer.” Our father is undoubtedly God, who created us; our mother, however, is the Church, which regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever robs or defrauds Christ of his money, or the Church of hers, is a murderer and will be reckoned as a murderer before the sight of the righteous Judge. Whoever robs his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but whoever takes away the Church’s money or property commits sacrilege and is to be judged as a sacrilegious person. [Col. 0866C] (17, q. 4, c. 18.)

Likewise, holy Pope Urban and martyr says:

“The property and resources of the Church are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor. If anyone robs them, he is liable to the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira, and such a person ought to be handed over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.” (17, q. 4, c. 5.)

Likewise, holy Pope Lucius says:

“We expel and condemn, by apostolic authority, the robbers of ecclesiastical property and resources from the thresholds of the holy Church as anathematized, and we judge them to be sacrilegious. And not only them, but also all who consent to them, because not only those who do such things are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them (Rom. I): an equal punishment encompasses both the perpetrators and those who consent.” [Col. 0866D]

And Saint Augustine says in his sermon on the Gospel of Saint John (tract. 50):

“Judas is the sacrilegious thief of the sacred and Lord’s money-boxes; and whoever steals and robs anything from the Church is compared with the lost Judas.”

Likewise, it is written in the sacred canons dictated by the Holy Spirit and confirmed by the blood of Christ (Gangr. VII):

“If anyone wishes to receive or give the Church’s obligations outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop and of the person to whom such responsibilities have been entrusted, and does not wish to act with that person’s counsel, let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0867A] The bishop, however, must tell everyone what anathema is; and, so that they may not despair, he must show how long the anathema lasts—that is, how long a person persists in his error without correcting it and making amends through worthy satisfaction, so that he may be able to merit reconciliation and pardon. But if anyone dies while persevering in his sins before satisfaction and the pardon of reconciliation, an eternal anathema will then be his, and the sin will be a sin unto death, concerning which the Apostle does not say that one should pray (I John V). Moreover, if necessary, each bishop should take care to collect and state further provisions.

# LETTER III OF CAROLUS TO POPE NICHOLAS I

Written shortly before the Council of Soissons, requesting permission to entrust the Church of Bourges to Vulfad for the interim.

[In Labbe, ibid., p. 811.]

[Col. 0867B]

To the most holy and reverend Father Nicholas, supreme pontiff of the catholic and apostolic see and universal pope, CAROLUS, by the grace of God king and your spiritual son.

If we were granted the privilege of seeing the holiness of your fatherhood every day with bodily presence, as though with the sight of the mind, we would rejoice with manifold—indeed, unspeakable—joy; and we would embrace with a humble and devoted embrace the one whom we hold close in the innermost parts of our heart. But since the distances of the earth deny us the opportunity to do this as we desire, whenever the occasion arises we wish often to send messages to the height of your holiness, so that, conversing at least through the speech of letters, we may be worthy to learn of your holy well-being, about which many people, bringing various reports from other regions, never cease to alarm us. [Col. 0867C] For we would rejoice with no small joy if we frequently received one of your people bringing us favorable news about you. And since you report to us such great thanks for the reception of one man whom we received, not as we wished, but as circumstances at that time dictated, for your honor and love, our devotion would appear greater if we were often able to do this.

For if, as we desire and as almighty God in his mercy may grant, we were at some time worthy either to receive your holiness in these regions or to see you there, then you would truly recognize how devoted and faithful we are toward you and toward the Church entrusted to you by God. Indeed, just as divine providence placed you over his universal Church as its special father, so we specially love your holy fatherhood in the charity of Christ and desire to obey your sacred commands. [Col. 0867D] For what is commanded by you is fortified by wisdom and piety.

Therefore, considering these matters, whatever your holiness recently commanded us to do concerning our faithful minister Vulfad and his companions, who were deposed because of the ordination of Ebbo, formerly archbishop of Rheims, we have carried out as far as we were able. We have also labored by every means at our disposal to persuade the venerable Archbishop Hincmar to acknowledge the justice of your holiness’s command concerning them. He promises this in sweet words, but we still do not know what may lie hidden beneath the honey.

But since you instructed us that, if we were unable to draw him over to our side so that he would obey you, we should carefully beware lest he draw us to himself by whatever arguments he could, so that he might either have us as supporters in not obeying you or turn our mind against the deposed men mentioned above, we earnestly beg, on the contrary, that you not abandon what you have begun to do for the love of God merely because someone advises you to do so, and that what we are doing at your command may not turn out to our disgrace and humiliation. [Col. 0868A]

For, as you commanded, we shall hold a synod on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, at which all the bishops and faithful of our kingdom are prepared to attend unanimously for the restoration of the aforesaid deposed men, to carry out what you commanded and also to preserve your portion in the matter. And lest you wonder why we now impress such matters upon your holiness through such messengers, although we sent you similar messages, after you had sent to us, through Eric, the man of our most beloved nephew Louis the emperor, we shall briefly explain to you, so that you may not attribute this to any frivolity or fickleness of mind.

Rudolf, archbishop of the Church of Bourges, has recently died, and that Church needs a wise, energetic, and manly pastor, because of the frivolity of certain people’s morals and the inconstancy of that nation. [Col. 0868B] Accordingly, after taking counsel, all the bishops and faithful of our kingdom, and the diocese itself as well, unanimously agreed on the election of the aforesaid Vulfad. For if we did not have such a man in our kingdom, he would have to be brought in from elsewhere, because of the great need of that place.

This is especially so because we have entrusted that kingdom and that Church to our beloved son and namesake, whose infancy and weakness—things that have befallen him because of our deserved sins—we have taken into consideration, and we have not been able to find a comparable remedy. [Col. 0868C] But since the matter of his restoration had not yet been decided at the forthcoming synod, we did not wish to place him over that Church before consulting you, to whom we entrust all our counsels, our wife, our children, our kingdom, and everything that belongs to us; and through you, we entrust him in every way to the holy princes and apostles, whose protection we daily implore and whose help we ask in humble supplication.

For this reason we have now sent back word to your holiness so quickly, because we fear that someone might by some device delay his ordination. [Col. 0868D] For it is utterly neither fitting nor just to abandon the matter; nor will we and our bishops permit this, since we possess such great authority. Therefore we ask that, by the authority of your holiness, so that the aforesaid Church may not remain widowed for long contrary to canonical authority, he may be ordained to the priestly office in the month of September, so that the future bishop may immediately perform the duties appropriate to this ministry.

Otherwise so great a mother, the Church, may be shaken everywhere by no small disturbance. It is solely because of this necessity that we urgently request that the matter be expedited. But if this displeases you, before word is brought to you about the aforementioned synod, may I be permitted, because of the aforesaid necessity, to entrust the Church itself to him, so that it may not be shaken on every side by wicked men.

For we confess that, if you had known his life as we know it, you would draw him to the episcopal order even against his will. [Col. 0869A] And because we know what kind of man he is, we wish to place him where the greatest necessity of our kingdom presses—or rather, divine providence does, without whose will we do not now believe that it has happened in any way that such a man should be placed over such a position: a man who could and would know how to govern it according to God, while laboring with the greatest energy.

For if we sent him among barbarian nations, we could procure for him neither greater labor nor greater reward for his service. And unless we had been touched by divine zeal and animated by hope of the fruitful reward of his labor, we would in no way have wished to separate him from our presence, knowing that he is useful to our interests and that, through the support of his service, we are partly relieved of our duties. [Col. 0869B]

Whatever remains, we entrust entirely to the wisdom of your holiness. And just as you entrusted him and his companions beneath the shield of our protection, so we commend him and his colleagues to your holiness, so that you may not be disappointed in the hope they received from you, and so that amid innumerable blessings you may receive eternal reward on their behalf.

# LETTER IV TO THE SAME

Concerning what had been done at the synod.

[In Labbe, ibid.]

Praising Hincmar’s obedience, he writes that the complete restoration of the clerics has been reserved by the synod to the pontiff, and meanwhile commends the Church of Bourges to Vulfad. [Col. 0869C]

We reverently received the letters of your holy fatherhood, in which you disclosed that the cries and groans of those deposed by Hincmar, the honored bishop—namely, Vulfad and his companions—had reached the ears of your graciousness. Moreover, you resolved to commend our filial devotion most earnestly, so that we might encourage that same venerable bishop and take care, for the love of God, to admonish him. You instructed us to strive by our skill to bend him to obedience to your excellence; but if that proved impossible, to take careful precautions lest he be able, by any arguments whatsoever, to incline us toward disobedience to you.

Accordingly, with the utmost zeal and in accordance with your fatherhood’s request, we acted. Addressing the aforementioned bishop reverently concerning the same matter, we found him, as devoted in other respects, so also most ready in this matter to obey you and us. Indeed, not only did he not resist, but he even hastened, as the first, most readily to obey the commands of your apostleship. [Col. 0869D]

Why, however, he did not complete the restoration of the aforementioned men with his suffragans, in accordance with your notification to him, will be made clearer by the letter sent by your command from the synod assembled at Soissons concerning that matter. As for the protection of those men, which your holiness requested and communicated to us, your son, we would have accomplished it with the greatest care if the need had arisen.

But, by God’s favor, the bishop about whom we are speaking, kindly receiving your decision, like an affectionate father, together with the other venerable bishops assembled with him, settled their case with the gentlest deliberation, obeying most willingly in every respect the expressions of your mildness in your letters. [Col. 0870A] Having recognized the intention of your excellence’s pious wish, he treated them with a tranquil, peaceful, and kindly disposition until the presence of that same synod, as we clearly learned; and thereafter, relying on the counsel of your moderation, he did not cease to support the aforesaid brothers in every respect and to console them with pious assistance.

He would have hastened to complete all these matters in every respect with the other fellow priests, except that, in accordance with the privilege of your predecessor, lord Benedict, and of yourself, the documents concerning the restoration of the men indicated that the final decision in the matter was to be reserved to you. [Col. 0870B]

Since the aforesaid bishop, however, devoted to your eminence, obeyed in every respect both the apostolic decree of your constitution and our own exhortation, receiving them all with the greatest gratitude and attempting to refuse nothing, let him rejoice that, through our humble petition, he has received from you a fuller generosity of grace, and let him therefore feel himself entirely more acceptable to you.

After this, because we have found that the brother Vulfad, about whom the matter is concerned, is eminent among us in character and learning, we hastened to commend the Church of Bourges to him, together with the property belonging to it, just as we informed your holy fatherhood in other letters. Since we delayed giving it to him without the determination of your apostleship, we commended that same Church to him so that the persistent attacks of wicked men seeking to seize what is not theirs and to ravage another’s property cruelly might not prevail entirely in its destruction. [Col. 0870C]

Therefore, so that his diligence may be able to prosper and flourish in that place, may your fatherhood’s reverence deign to reveal more quickly what your holy mind has decided concerning him and the others, and may your eminence more speedily accomplish concerning him what our humble petition has so often requested of you on his behalf. For, with the greatest necessity pressing upon them, the men of good will who are in that kingdom ask this very thing in continual supplication.

Yet the obstacles of many disturbances are known to have been present in that kingdom not only in our time but also in the times of our predecessors, either scarcely ever or never absent. [Col. 0870D] Thus it is necessary that, to assist our son, who has been weakened by an event well known to you, and those who are attached to him by loyalty to us and to himself, the man about whom we plead may be sent more promptly, with the support of your fatherhood’s assistance, so that they may be able to resist their adversaries in every way, O most blessed and greatly desired lord, father, and pope.

# LETTER V TO THE SAME

Concerning Ebbo’s case, he writes at great length as the pontiff had commanded through Ansegisus. He then excuses Vulfad’s accelerated promotion and requests the pallium for him; he also commends the bishop Actard as his legate.

[In Labbe, ibid.]

To the lord and most reverend Father Nicholas, supreme pontiff of the catholic and apostolic see and universal pope, CAROLUS, by the grace of God king and your spiritual son. [Col. 0871A]

Although the support of all priests who minister to God must be sought and their venerable eminences honored, our generosity has found it fitting and most appropriate, most holy father and most excellent of bishops, to submit our royal neck to your reverence above all others, and to subject the ear of our heart to your most salutary counsels with the utmost humility and devotion.

For we clearly perceive that, amid the turbulent abyss of the world, you have been established as the Church’s most steadfast anchor and immovable stake, to which we may suspend the burden of our sins; and we believe that this has been granted by the most gracious clemency of God. Our human affection therefore burns more fervently with love for your benevolent piety the more clearly we see that you alone have stood forth to defend the Church of Christ against cruel beasts who seek most savagely to tear it apart. [Col. 0871B]

Accordingly, since in letters from your holiness you commanded the bishops of our kingdom to write to you whatever they could discover truthfully concerning Ebbo’s case, while you commanded us—not by letter, but through your servant Ansegisus [variant: Ansegisum], a monk, when he returned to Rome for the second time this year to your fatherhood because Archbishop Egilo had fallen ill—to write the truth of the matter to you and to authenticate it with our signature, in order that we may obey your holy fatherhood in all things, we faithfully communicate to you what we have seen and know concerning him.

For no bishop now survives, except Rothad, who was present at his case at that time. And lest we allow anything to pass untouched, we have decided first to relate his birth and origin. [Col. 0871C]

Ebbo, then, born from the household of the royal treasury, was received through the royal kindness of our pious and glorious grandfather Charles. He was trained to no small degree in palace affairs, granted his freedom, and, because of the nobility of his vigorous intellect, gradually advanced through the sacred orders. He was assigned by that same glorious ruler to serve our father, Louis the most pious Augustus, who governed the kingdom of Aquitaine.

When our father found him energetic in service and quick in intellect, he appointed him librarian not long afterward. After the death of our grandfather Charles, the most excellent emperor of blessed memory, our father Louis, the most pious Augustus, having attained the paternal empire by God’s gift, came to the city of Rheims. There your predecessor, Stephen, supreme pontiff of holy memory, came to meet him and, inspired by God, consecrated him in honor of the empire. [Col. 0871D]

At that time Vulfarius, the venerable archbishop of the aforementioned city, was suffering from a serious illness, from which he also died. After his death, and after the emperor had granted the people the right of election in accordance with the institution of the sacred canons, it happened that they elected a certain man named Gislemar to the honor of the pontificate.

While he was seated before the bishops to be examined, a Gospel book was brought to him. When all had recognized together that he was able to read it to some extent but understood nothing, he was rejected and cast down by everyone as though he were a fool. [Col. 0872A] Then the lord emperor decided that the aforesaid Ebbo should be promoted to the said episcopate on account of his learning and the respect due to his merits. When this was reported to the people and to all men of sound judgment, they unanimously declared that it pleased them; and thus, in accordance with canonical institution, he was ordained archbishop.

The first time, when, at the devil’s instigation, the people of the Franks attempted to drive from his empire the emperor appointed by God and crowned by the apostolic see, Ebbo remained immovable in his loyalty to him and, as was right, persevered until his restoration.

The second time, when, at the urging and plotting of our brother Lothair, the whole people withdrew from our father of pious memory, and, after his wife had been taken to Italy, to the city of Tortona, confined him in custody, they also assigned us—though not yet ten years old, as though we were guilty of many crimes—to be confined in the monastery of Prüm. [Col. 0872B]

After the emperor had been taken by Lothair to the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons, Ebbo, together with nearly all the other bishops—some willingly, some unwillingly—removed the aforementioned emperor, though neither confessed nor convicted by anyone, from communion with the Church and stripped him of his dignity, while his wife, son, and all his faithful were with him.

But at last the mercy of the compassionate God, looking upon the humility of the pious emperor, touched the hearts of those whom he wished and, through his mercy, inspired them to bring him out of custody and restore him to the empire. [Col. 0872C] The archbishops and bishops brought him out of custody from the monastery of the most blessed martyrs Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius. As was fitting, they humbly confessed that they had sinned against him and earnestly begged his forgiveness. They urged Lothair to withdraw from imperial power. Accordingly, he and those who were with him withdrew from him into other regions.

When Ebbo learned these things, while he was staying at Rheims, he was frightened and fled to the city of Paris, to a certain recluse, so that, hiding there with him at least, he might escape the emperor’s anger. When the emperor heard this—for he was not far away—he sent energetic and faithful messengers, ordered Ebbo to be apprehended and confined, and entrusted the Church of Rheims to Fulco, the venerable abbot.

From there Ebbo was taken to the city of Metz, where he mounted the ambo in the church of Saint Stephen before everyone and declared that it had not been right for him to bring a judgment against the glorious emperor, his lord. [Col. 0872D] There, too, the same most pious emperor was honorably crowned by all the bishops, clergy, and people, and restored to his former empire.

After this, when a general assembly had again been convened, he ordered the aforesaid Ebbo to be brought before him. Because of the insult of the injuries inflicted upon him, and in the presence of several bishops—who, desiring to satisfy the emperor and preserve episcopal reverence, obtained from that same emperor that Ebbo’s case should be settled not before laymen but in the sanctuary—he proceeded against him.

Ebbo, however, deprived of every temporal resource and abandoned by all human consolation, took thought for the present. [Col. 0873A] He summoned a certain recluse named Framegaud and sent through him to our mother, Judith, the glorious empress, a ring that he had once received from her and that he used to send whenever he was touched by any misfortune. He tearfully begged her to have mercy on him.

Our mother had sent him that same ring at the very moment of our birth, because he was archbishop, out of her religious devotion and reverence, so that he might remember us continually in his prayers. Recalling this then and recognizing his tearful sighs, she took care, through pious persuasion, to obtain from the bishops who had gathered there that they should both soften the emperor’s disposition by making satisfaction and not violate the divine laws. Otherwise, by exercising the vengeance of severity against one who had sinned against them, they might appear not to render to God a worthy requital, since he had mercifully freed them from so great a danger. [Col. 0873B]

For she had resolved that, out of reverence for so great a ministry, she would in no way consent to the deposition of any bishop. For this reason she obtained from the pious emperor that he should no longer press for Ebbo’s deposition, provided that, in accordance with the very moderate counsel of our glorious mother the empress, they satisfied the most pious emperor and imposed on Ebbo no other sentence than the one he himself had issued in writing.

Hincmar, the venerable archbishop, received this authentic document from the aforementioned Fulco, the venerable abbot to whom the Church of Rheims had then been entrusted, and, as he himself told us, transmitted it to you. [Col. 0873C] But whether it was sent to you purely and simply, we do not know. This, however, we know with complete certainty: none of the bishops signed it with his own hand.

For Ebbo, recognizing the inescapable crisis in which he stood, produced three witnesses, as it were his confessors—namely, the archbishop Aiulf and the bishops Moduin and Badaradus. Acting on his behalf, they were to say that, if it was indeed true as Ebbo confessed to them, they would advise him to abstain from the episcopal ministry. These three also associated with themselves three others who had seen him confessing to them: namely, the archbishop Nothon and the bishops Theuderic and Actard.

When these proceedings were completed, he was led back into custody. [Col. 0873D] After the bishops had thus settled the matter, the lord emperor sent through Godefrid, the venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Gregory, a letter bearing his own authority to your predecessor, the lord Pope Gregory, asking for his consent, if this could be obtained, to Ebbo’s deposition.

That pope, however, sent him back through the aforementioned abbot a letter of his own authority. But what had been inserted in it is unknown to all the bishops and to every order of our kingdom. Your holiness’s diligence, however, may investigate through the archives of your dignity what that same predecessor of yours thought about the matter.

We nevertheless believe that, if the lord emperor had had that predecessor of yours as a supporter in Ebbo’s rejection, he would immediately have appointed another bishop over the vacant Church. [Col. 0874A] By delaying this action through very moderate counsel, he acted with effective prudence, so that both the boldness of rash men in such matters might thereafter be restrained and the condition of the Church might not be shaken.

After the death of the lord emperor, the aforesaid Ebbo was taken from the man who was guarding him and brought to our brother Lothair. Our same brother received him honorably and kindly. With the bishops who were then associated with him, and following their counsel, Ebbo had earlier composed a written confession in order to satisfy the emperor; by the unanimous agreement of those bishops he was restored to his rank.

When we withdrew into the regions of Aquitaine because of pressing affairs, Ebbo was eagerly sought by the entire clergy and people of the Church of Rheims, and was finally restored to his former see by his fellow bishops and suffragans. [Col. 0874B] All who were present communicated with him, and all the suffragans who had been ordained in his absence received from him rings, staffs, and written confirmations of their office, according to the custom of the churches of Gaul.

While all those who had access to him communicated with him, he ordained Vulfad and certain other sons of that Church.

We have briefly outlined these matters concerning Ebbo’s deposition and restoration so that the prudence of your sagacity may determine from them whether these circumstances pertain to Vulfad’s deposition or not. But if anyone has informed your holiness that Ebbo was canonically summoned to the synod of Soissons and signed or presented the documents of his own condemnation, know that this is entirely untrue, because he was not present at that synod. [Col. 0874C]

After these events, we deemed it necessary to make ourselves excusable, with the utmost humility and devotion, before the presence of your majesty through our letters, because, before the return of Egilo, the reverend archbishop, or the rescript of your episcopate, we commended to the aforesaid Vulfad the see of the archbishopric of Bourges, and the bishops promoted him to the honor of the episcopate not rashly, but under the pressure of great necessity and trusting in the greatness of your mercy.

For this reason we sent him into those regions of Aquitaine to our son and namesake, and entrusted that Church to him: because, in the education of another of our sons, Carloman, your servant, whom we have specially commended to your blessedness, and in our other interests, we have found him energetic in intellect, upright in character, and entirely faithful to us. [Col. 0874D]

If anything in this acceleration displeased the mind of your holy serenity, we ask your holy fatherhood to forgive it to us. Moreover, because a great persecution by pagans was raging in that kingdom—pagans whom the merciful Lord has often overthrown through our son and the faithful—and because on that account an equally serious assault by wicked Christians was spreading and raging more widely, as the bearer of this letter can tell you orally, the bishops, stirred by the urgent need of that kingdom, hastened his ordination so that greater evils might not grow, present evils might be quieted, and, since that see holds primacy in the region, they might more easily suppress the evils that had arisen by relying on his prudence and vigor, as well as on the authority of the see. [Col. 0875A]

Because your permission was not awaited in the hastening of his ordination, on account of the danger already mentioned, we ask your most gracious holiness for pardon. Furthermore, we earnestly implore your glorious and beloved fatherhood above all others that, if we dare to trust in your holy promises, you may show that we possess great influence with you by overlooking whatever in the matters mentioned ought to be overlooked, and by adorning your most faithful servant Vulfad with the pallium of apostolic authority, honoring and confirming him through that honor.

We send to your most holy fatherhood as our faithful legate Actard, formerly venerable bishop of the see of Nantes. He has endured exile, chains, the sea, and severe dangers, but has been freed by the grace of God. His city lies very close to the Northmen and the Bretons; and the city entrusted to him, once most flourishing, is now seen, after ten years, burned, utterly destroyed, and reduced to a wilderness. [Col. 0875B] What our letters state less fully, he will explain to you orally for such time and interval as may please you.

Since no hope remains for him in his own see, we most earnestly desire—if the vigilant skill of your discernment approves and favors it—that he be appointed to the chair of a vacant see, so that he may carry out the ministries entrusted and assigned to him and may serve ecclesiastical interests and obey our commands.

He has arranged to remain in Rome for some time, so that, when the Bretons arrive, he may confront them in person and expose the damage they have inflicted upon his churches and those of the neighboring regions. For this reason the synod of Soissons and that of Troyes had resolved to undertake a legation, so that the reckless, deceitful, and barbarous people might be restrained by the apostolic sword from such daring excesses and from their present presumption. [Col. 0875C]

For this fosterling of ours and client of yours, we pray, as is customary, that the most loving heart of your piety may remain open, so that his mind, shaken by long sorrow, may be strengthened and refreshed by living and leaping streams.

# LETTER VI TO ADO, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE

Concerning the ordination of Bernarius as bishop of Grenoble.

[In Dom Bouquet, vol. VII.]

[Col. 0875D]

King Charles sends greetings to Ado, venerable archbishop and most dear to us.

Through Odo and our other faithful men we have disclosed our wishes to you; when you come to us, we shall make you more fully informed. [Col. 0876A]

We command your most faithful holiness to know that we have granted the bishopric of Grenoble to a certain cleric, formerly deacon of the venerable Archbishop Remigius [of Lyons], and afterward of our dear nephew Lothair, on the condition that, if you find him canonically qualified, he be ordained bishop there by your holiness’s judgment. For it is not fitting that that same bishopric should remain long without a bishop.

You know the canonical authority concerning this matter. Whatever is neglected will undoubtedly be charged to you by the Lord, since you ought to have appointed and ordered the bishop himself, the bishopric, and all the affairs of that Church—even if our beloved nephew, intent on other matters, passed it by—so that the people of God might not wander without a shepherd.

For Christ our God has entrusted his entire Church to you and to all his bishops; and we too ought to submit reverently to him in all things. Thus, when you diligently complete the things that belong to him, we shall have no doubt that you will intercede with him more confidently on behalf of us and our kingdom.

Farewell, and always remember us in your prayers.

Received on the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

# LETTER VII TO ADRIAN II

[In P. Delaland, Supplement to the Ancient Councils of Gaul.]

[Col. 0876B]

To the most holy and reverend Father Adrian, Charles, by the grace of God king.

Your venerable Paternity sent us a letter concerning Hincmar of Laon, formerly bishop. Its opening runs as follows:

“Our opening address to you, dearest son, is with the prophet. Behold what he says: ‘This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me’ (Isaiah 29).”

We would not have wished to speak to your Reverence in one voice and make another petition, if pressing necessity had not compelled us to request what we speak of unwillingly and under constraint. You often send us letters of reproach and lay against us charges unknown to you except insofar as you hear them from the mouths of our ill-wishers [Col. 0876C]. Such conduct is neither proper nor fitting for your sanctity’s ministry. Nor did your predecessors or those before them make or issue such accusations against our predecessors.

For, as we read in the letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see and of Christian kings and emperors, devout kings and emperors called the successors of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, “Fathers”; and the pontiffs of the apostolic Roman see, until your time, called Christian kings and emperors “Sons” and “Lords.” Now, on the contrary, although the Apostle says, “Children, obey your parents,” which we would most devotedly wish to do, if we were permitted, he also says, “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” [Col. 0876D] (Colossians 3).

We have not confessed perjury, tyranny, or treachery, nor have we been legally and regularly convicted of them according to judicial procedure. For, as blessed Augustine, instructed by divine and human laws, says: “No one dares to assume both roles for himself, so as to be at once his own accuser and judge.”

We have been provoked to anger by such grave injuries, contrary to the Apostle’s command, that—leaving aside the royal person—we have never yet heard of any commoner, or any freeborn man, being provoked by any priest, when that priest had not received him into his judgment after he had been accused according to ecclesiastical rules or public laws, or had voluntarily confessed, or had been openly convicted legally and regularly. For your predecessor, Nicholas of blessed memory, when he discovered our former nephew Lothair in public adultery, while preserving the honor due to royal authority, did not address him in his apostolic letters as you address us [Col. 0877A]. Yet you hold neither that we have confessed nor that we have been convicted, and you threaten to excommunicate us without authority or reason.

We are not ignorant, from the course of sacred Scripture and the teaching of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, where, how, in what manner, and according to what procedure any pontiff ought regularly to excommunicate anyone.

We are certain that your Paternity and the holy Roman Church know what letters your predecessors and those before them sent to the Christian Roman and Frankish emperors and to our forefathers, and how they admonished those among them whom necessity required. They did not reproach them, bring charges against them, or inflict accusations upon them [Col. 0877B]; rather, they instructed and admonished them concerning matters belonging to their ecclesiastical ministry, and they did not usurp the affairs of the kingdom or of the secular order. They knew that, as Saint Gelasius says:

“There are two things by which this world is principally ruled: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and royal power. For Christ, mindful of human frailty, tempered by magnificent dispensation what suited the salvation of his own people. He assigned to each, in accordance with their proper actions and distinct dignities, the functions of their authority, wishing that they should be saved by medicinal humility, not once more destroyed by human pride.
