Thus Christian emperors would need the pontiffs for eternal life [Col. 0877C], while pontiffs would make use of the emperors’ arrangements for the course of temporal affairs, so that spiritual action might remain separate from carnal incursions, and so that the one who serves God might not become entangled in secular business” (2 Timothy 2)—and, conversely, so that one who was entangled in secular affairs might not appear to preside over divine matters.

It has also been written to us, in your own words, that in Hincmar’s case I acted not as a devout king but as another kind of person, namely an impious tyrant. For just as there is no middle position—one who cannot be called good must consequently be called evil—so one who is not a devout king is to be understood as an impious tyrant. Yet although I confess that I am a sinner, I deny that I am impious.

When the prophet Nathan reproved King David for deadly sins, he did not say to the confessing king, “You are that impious man.” He said instead, “You are the man who did this” [Col. 0877D]. And when David confessed his deeds, Nathan did not condemn him as a judge; rather, he suitably absolved him (2 Samuel 12).

But since it is written, “The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2), and since the Lord forbids anyone to say to his brother without cause, “Raca” or “Fool” (Matthew 5), we do not believe that such words concerning me—a king of whatever kind, yet a Catholic king who remains devoutly within the Catholic religion—proceeded from your mouth, by which, through sacred supplication, the body and blood of Christ are consecrated, Christ having died, as the Apostle testifies, for the ungodly (Romans 5).

Nor do we rashly believe that you sent us this message at the prompting of lies, since you retain the scriptural commands that must be followed: “I will go down,” says the Lord, “and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me; or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Genesis 18); and, “The case I did not know, I investigated most diligently” (Job 29).

Indeed, holy and learned pontiffs, who themselves had already suffered from such prejudgments, did not call Constantius an Arian and Julian an apostate in this manner. And if you review all the letters we possess from the time when the Roman pontiffs began writing to the Frankish kings, you will find nothing of this sort in them.

It has also been written to us in your own words that you would entrust to us all the possessions committed to Hincmar by the Church, until he returned to his own, so that they might remain unharmed and suffer no loss. To this we reply that, as blessed Gregory says, we kings of the Franks, born from royal stock, have until now been regarded not as bishops’ stewards but as lords of the land [Col. 0878A].

[Col. 0878B]

And, as Leo and the synod of Bourges wrote:

“Kings and emperors, whom divine power has commanded to rule over the lands, have permitted holy bishops the right of distinguishing matters according to the imperial constitutions; they have not, however, become the stewards of bishops.”

Augustine also says: “Possessions are held by the rights of kings; but through episcopal authority kings do not become agents of villages.” And the Lord commands that what belongs to Caesar be rendered to Caesar and what belongs to God to God (Matthew 22); he also paid the tax to the king (Matthew 17).

The Apostle wished kings to be served and honored, not trampled upon: “Honor the king,” he says (1 Peter 2). And again: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities”; “Therefore render to all what is owed” (Romans 13) [Col. 0878C]. And a little earlier: “Therefore be subject of necessity, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience” (ibid.).

Regarding what has been written by you about summoning bishops from our kingdom to Rome, read the records of the pontiffs of the Roman see and the letters of blessed Gregory to the king of the Franks, and also to Brunhild—even though she was a woman, she was nevertheless a queen—and you will find that your predecessors and those before them wrote to our predecessors and those before them concerning the summoning of bishops and the assembling of synods in a different manner.

In the same letter it was written to us that we should permit the men of our kingdom, Celsanus, Walco, and Berno, to remain safe and unharmed with their possessions; and that, if we acted otherwise, we would not be able to share in your communion until true satisfaction had been made. We were also told that we should know that we would not escape your censure if decrees or admonitions issued by you were further violated [Col. 0878D].

To this we reply that the pontiffs of the apostolic see have not been accustomed to give such commands to the kings of the Franks concerning those who in their time fled for refuge to the threshold of the apostles. Nor is Catholic teaching such that, for this or a similar cause, a king who corrects the wicked ought to be separated from communion with the apostolic see, as blessed Augustine patiently demonstrates:

“Those who are spiritual, or who advance toward this very end through devout zeal, do not go outside; for when they seem to be expelled by some perversity or necessity among human beings, they prove themselves more within [Col. 0879A] than if they remained inside, since they in no way rise up against the Church, but are rooted upon the solid rock of unity by the strongest strength of charity.”

To this belongs what is said in Abraham’s sacrifice: “But he did not divide the birds” (Genesis 15).

Therefore it should not be believed that these commands proceeded from your apostolic mouth. For whoever wrote in this manner, as though anyone had withdrawn his communion from me, who remain in Catholic and apostolic communion, has not understood properly. He has separated not me but himself from Catholic and apostolic communion.

On this point blessed Gregory says even of the ruler of the Church:

“Often, in binding and loosing his subjects, the movement of his own will governs the one placed over Christ’s Church, rather than the merits of the cases. Thus it happens that the one who exercises this power of binding and loosing according to his own wishes, and not according to the conduct of his subjects, deprives himself of that power” [Col. 0879B].

Although these things are so, we nevertheless acted concerning Celsanus, who falsely accused me before your Holiness, the pontiff of the apostolic see, on behalf of the lying Hincmar, whose Church we had increased by approximately two thousand *mansi* beyond what it had possessed in the time of our predecessors, and during whose own tenure we increased it by more than six hundred [Col. 0879B].

We also complied concerning Walco and Berno, who, as was written to us from your side, were marked by perjury and infidelity toward our royal authority and were fugitives. We did so without considering their lies or the slanders spoken against us, but out of honor and reverence for the apostolic see [Col. 0879C].

Therefore, with your peace and pardon, let us say that we accept and obey the commands of the apostolic see concerning matters belonging to your ministry, supported by evangelical and apostolic truth, canonical authority, the course of sacred Scripture, and the tradition of our forebears.

We wish to preserve this privilege of honor and, by obeying you as pontiff of the apostolic see, to render what is due to the primacy of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—a primacy received at the Lord’s command, which, with the Church following it, he has always held and still holds. This is demonstrated by the holy canons and the sacred laws promulgated by Christian emperors, which defer to that first see; and likewise by what our predecessors and those before them deferred to that holy see.

In the same way, may your Paternity exhibit to us the honor that is due, just as your predecessors and those before them exhibited it to the Christian Roman emperors and Frankish kings, and likewise to the Roman and Frankish emperors who were our forefathers [Col. 0879D].

As for such letters—unsuitable to your ministry and inconsistent with our royal dignity and authority—as are sent to us in your name, I would not believe that they were dictated by you or by the holy Roman Church, which has always been supremely prudent and cautious in all things. For that holy see has always been accustomed to correct with moderation and discretion, and to correct beneficially, according to each person’s rank and order.

Therefore preserve for our royal authority what belongs to us, and allow us to preserve for your pontifical authority what belongs to you.

It has also been written to us that we sent you a letter containing wicked accusations against Hincmar, and that we ought not to have written this, because we did not write to you wicked accusations against him. Rather, we wrote to you what many bishops, other ecclesiastical men, the leading men of our kingdom, nobles, middling persons, and men of low status were then admitting, and still admit, about him, reporting it lest, when we wished to correct him before he reached the point to which he had driven himself and fell, anyone should secretly forestall you before you learned the truth of the matter [Col. 0880A].

But because we admonished him repeatedly and in many ways, without being able to correct him, he reached the point at which he now stands, as you will find in the synodal records sent to your authority.

We therefore earnestly implore your authority that, just as your predecessors and those before them preserved for us and for our predecessors, and for the archbishops and bishops of our kingdom, the privileges due to them and belonging to the Church, as well as the distinctions of rank decreed and established by the sacred canons according to ancient custom, so you may strive to preserve them for us and for them in this matter also. Thus, as Saint Gregory says, the apostolic see may retain its proper vigor and may not diminish the rights it has granted to others [Col. 0880B].

There are many matters concerning which, if he had been judged according to rule together with those by whom he was judged, a definite judgment could have been rendered, had he been permitted to remain longer in the synod.

But it was necessary for us, together with certain bishops, to hasten to a conference with our brother for the reconciliation of his sons with their father and our brother. We had to do so as quickly as possible, lest, once sedition had arisen and relatives were already fighting among themselves, Christian blood—like the blood of parricides—be shed, and lest for this reason the possessions of the churches of God be divided, the resources of priests and servants of God be seized, and the poor be despoiled [Col. 0880C].

The synod could not determine definitive judgments concerning everything of which he was accused. Nevertheless, in the records sent to your authority, you will be able to learn how long we, the bishops, and the leading men of our kingdom endured, with the greatest difficulty, his detestable and intolerable conduct and actions.

Therefore, concerning him, your pontifical authority will, as we believe, do what the sacred rules prescribe. Yet we assure you most certainly that, for as long as God preserves us in the government of the kingdom, Hincmar will not hold the bishopric of Laon in his administration.

Although he does not deserve it, out of consideration for piety we have granted him this: that any member of the clergy or household of the bishopric of Laon who wished to depart should have permission to do so.

Finally, concerning the venerable Actard—whom the clergy and people of the metropolitan church of Tours request to be incardinated in that church, where he was baptized, tonsured, and brought up, and through each rank advanced to the episcopal order; whom your Paternity commended to us for incardination and, should a place become available in our regions, in a metropolitan see; and to whom, at your request, we granted a church vacant of a pastor until a suitable place should open in your kingdom, so that he might there be regularly incardinated—we refer the matter to your authority.

If it pleases you, incardinate him as archbishop in the aforesaid metropolitan church on this condition: after his death, a metropolitan bishop shall be ordained for that metropolitan church by the suffragan and provincial bishops there, through the election of the clergy and people, as the sacred rules command and ancient custom requires [Col. 0881A].

Finally, in honor of almighty God and in veneration of the holy apostles, we beseech you not to send any further to us, to the bishops of our kingdoms, or to the leading men of our realms such letters insulting to our honor, or such commands, as have until now come to us in your name. Do not compel us by your commands to despise your letters as dishonorable or to dishonor your messengers, since in matters belonging to your ministry we wish to obey you according to the requirements of our own ministry [Col. 0881B].

We say these things for the honor of your privilege, because we desire to obey you, as is truly due, in all things as the vicar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; we wish by every means to prevent matters from turning out otherwise, and we humbly beseech your Holiness to take care likewise.

May almighty God deign to preserve you through all the years of your life, for the honor, salvation, and exaltation of his holy Church, most holy and reverend Father in the Lord.

## LETTER VIII. TO THE SAME

Exasperated by two letters from Adrian, he responds to both with a somewhat more agitated spirit.

[From the Works of Hincmar, volume II, page 701.]

[Col. 0881C]

To the most holy and reverend Father Adrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, Charles, by the grace of God king and your spiritual son.

We read in the Book of Chronicles that the children of Israel went to battle with peaceful intent, because they fought not out of revenge born of hatred but for the sake of obtaining peace.

We say this again because, through your letters—dishonoring royal authority, burdening us with commands unsuitable to episcopal modesty, and disgracing us with insults and reproaches—you compel us to write back to you with a peaceful mind, though in a manner different from what we would wish [Col. 0881D]. We do so in order that you may finally recognize that, although subject to human disturbances, we are nevertheless a man who walks in the image of God; that, by God’s grace, we possess understanding through paternal and ancestral succession and have been exalted by royal name and rank; and, greater than all this, that we are a Christian and Catholic devotee of the orthodox faith, educated from infancy in sacred letters and laws, both ecclesiastical and secular, and publicly accused of no crime before an episcopal hearing, nor legally and regularly convicted of any.

To say nothing of other things we might add, lest we seem rather to boast than to speak the truth—although we read that the Apostle was compelled by necessity to say many things about himself for the benefit of others—we have often spoken to you humbly, yet have been unable to obtain writings from you that were kind, peaceful, and honorable. We therefore wrote to you through Actard, the bishop and legate of our gentleness [Col. 0882A], setting out individually and one by one how unsuitable were the things written to us in your name concerning Hincmar, formerly bishop of Laon.

We did not believe that these things had proceeded from you. We thought that, once you had learned the facts, you would recall your pen from matters that had been written to us under the influence of others. But our vain hope was disappointed, and matters turned out otherwise than we expected.

At the head of the letter that your Paternity sent us through the aforesaid bishop Actard, we found that you had first proclaimed the greatness of our reputed charity and wisdom [Col. 0882B]. Immediately afterward, however, we found ourselves branded with the charge of an ascertained murmur and a tumultuous outcry of improper criticism against your Paternity.

Thus you praised our reputed wisdom in such a way that, as though more honorably—and in reality more heavily—you wished to burden us with your customary insults. You represented us as committing an offense against proper charity, not through folly but through deliberate purpose, by murmuring and crying out against it. And, as though these later letters had been smeared with honey around the rim of a vessel, they offered us a harmful drink from the same fountain from which the earlier letters had been sent, acknowledging that the things we had believed were written at the instigation of others and had not proceeded from you were in fact yours.

In the earlier letters you called us perjured, tyrannical, treacherous, and a dissipator of ecclesiastical possessions, although we had neither confessed nor been legally and regularly convicted according to judicial procedure [Col. 0882C]. In these letters, however, you charged us with the crime of murmuring and branded us with the stain of a tumultuous outcry.

The Lord, through the prophet, rebukes carnal Israel for this very thing, and you rebuke us because Israel “did not act justly, but cried out” (Isaiah 5). The Apostle says: “Let all outcry and indignation be taken away from you” (Ephesians 4). Murmuring is no lesser evil than those things with which you previously branded us, for the Apostle says: “Nor murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Corinthians 6).

And, as blessed Gregory says, no one who murmurs is permitted to enter the kingdom of God. From this it must be understood how great a sin murmuring is, since it bars the kingdom of God, just as do those grave sins after whose enumeration the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5).

We did not, as you wrote, criticize your Paternity improperly with a tumultuous outcry. We merely replied in our own voice to what had been written to us in your name—not with the many voices by which tumults are usually made.

And because we did not at all believe that you had sent such things, or that they had been dictated by the holy Roman Church, which has always been supremely prudent and cautious in all things, we made this known to you. For that holy see has always been accustomed to correct with moderation and discretion, and to correct beneficially, according to each person’s rank and order.

Therefore, if we have spoken wrongly, “bear witness to the wrong”; but if we have spoken rightly, why are you angry with us?

It is written that Abraham, although holy and sanctified by God as a man, nevertheless said to God: “Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? That is not like you, who judge the whole earth” (Genesis 18). The Lord did not receive this complaint with resentment.

Do you rebuke us because, in humble appeasement, we suggested to you that it was not fitting for you to write such things about one who had neither confessed nor been legally and regularly convicted, and who, by God’s grace, was endowed with royal authority, as though he were a commoner convicted of crimes?

We know how serious it is to call a brother “Fool,” a lesser insult than those imposed upon us (Matthew 5), and that no one should be slandered or cursed contrary to right—least of all a king—as is shown by apostolic teaching, by the reverence of holy David toward Saul, who had already been rejected by the Lord (1 Samuel 26), by Solomon’s wisdom, and by the history of Naboth handed down (1 Maccabees 9) [Col. 0883B].

We also find in the same letters a piece of advice given to us—if it can be called advice—that is contrary to the example of the Lord and opposed to the decrees of the saints: namely, that, to use your own words, we should receive with an eager mind everything that has been sent from the apostolic see over which, by God’s grace, you preside.

For it has been written to us in your name that we are perjured, tyrannical, treacherous, and dissipators of ecclesiastical possessions. Are we then to receive these things with an eager mind, embrace them with a grateful spirit, and accept them always with humble intention?

[Col. 0883C]

Perhaps the writer wishes us, with the common people, to call Ethiopians “silver-colored,” and thus to make someone appear handsome because he is called *bellus* (“pretty”); perhaps he wishes us to sing with Persius, “Whatever you tread upon, may it become a rose,” and to incur the prophetic condemnation: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5).

When the Jews said to the Lord, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” he acknowledged the charge of being a Samaritan, consenting to it by remaining silent, and patiently rejected the false accusation he had heard by saying: “I do not have a demon” (John 8).

Following this example, in our own small measure, we have humbly and patiently excused ourselves before your Paternity concerning things we do not recognize in ourselves. Christ did not disdain to show by reason that he was not a sinner, although by the power of his divinity he could justify sinners. We acted likewise so that, if we remained completely silent, we would seem by silence and consent to admit that we were what we had been branded as being, and so that we would be judged as having confessed and been convicted by our own confession [Col. 0883D].

We also find in the letter delivered to us from your name by Bishop Actard this exhortation: that we should always receive humbly everything that comes to us from the apostolic see. As we have already said, this is opposed not only to evangelical truth but also to the decrees of the saints.

In those decrees we read that no one can be absolved who has stated against himself a capital charge which, if stated against another, would be punished—namely, false testimony—for anyone who is the cause of his own death is a greater murderer.

For this reason they decreed (Council of Valence, canon 4):

“Whoever, while under the order of deaconate, presbyterate, or episcopate, declares that he has been polluted by a mortal crime is to be removed from the aforesaid orders” [Col. 0884A].

If we were silently to consent to such charges imposed upon us, we would separate ourselves not only from royal government but also from communion with the Catholic Church.

Therefore we ought not to receive with an eager mind, embrace with a grateful spirit, or accept with always humble intention such things written to us on behalf of the apostolic see and in your name. As is added in those same letters, quoting the judgment of the wise Solomon (Ecclesiastes 12), they appear to be “like goads, and like nails driven deep,” because they do not soothe the faults of sinners but prick them.

To this judgment we reply with the words of the Wise One: “Before you investigate, do not blame anyone; and when you have investigated—that is, when you have established the facts—correct him justly” (Ecclesiasticus 11) [Col. 0884B]. Thus Nathan first questioned King David and then, after establishing the matter through questioning, rebuked him; when the cause for rebuke was absent, he humbly bowed down, as we read in sacred history (2 Samuel 7 and 12).

Command and write what is appropriate to your ministry and ours, as your predecessors commanded and wrote to us and to our predecessors, and we will receive it with an eager mind and grateful heart.

The letters sent in your name, however, always prick us without questioning—that is, without investigation—and do not show that the sins for which they unwillingly prick us were either voluntarily confessed or legally and regularly established through judicial procedure. When manifest and proven sins are absent, they do not strengthen us with the remedies of kind exhortation and encouragement [Col. 0884C].

The Lord rebuked the harsh rulers of the people for this, saying: “But you ruled over them with harshness and with power” (Ezekiel 34).

The Apostle gave them a rule for admonition, saying to each: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and doctrine” (2 Timothy 4). They should mingle severity with gentleness, showing the sternness of a teacher and the affection of a pious father.

That is, they should rebuke the undisciplined and restless more harshly; they should entreat the obedient and patient so that they may advance toward better things; they should certainly reprimand and correct the negligent and contemptuous; and concerning criminal sins, they should judge according to the measure of the fault, legally and regularly, those who have either confessed them voluntarily or have been legally established and convicted of them through judicial procedure.

[Col. 0884D]

“The Apostle,” says blessed Augustine (*Homily 2 on Penance*, chapter 4), “did not wish a human being to be judged by another human being according to the arbitrary suspicion or even the extraordinary usurpation of a judgment, but rather according to the law of God and the order of the Church, whether the person had confessed voluntarily or had been accused and convicted.

“Otherwise, why did he say, ‘If anyone is named a brother who is a fornicator or a servant of idols’ (1 Corinthians 6), and so forth? He said this because he wished that ‘being named’ to be understood as occurring when a sentence is pronounced against someone in judicial order and with integrity.

“For if merely naming someone were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, because crimes are often falsely alleged against someone. Many good Christians remain silent and tolerate the sins of others that they know because those sins often lack evidence, so that they cannot prove before ecclesiastical judges what they know.

“For even when certain things are true, a judge ought not readily to believe them unless they are demonstrated by certain indications and established according to judicial procedure. Thus, if the wicked cannot be removed from communion with the Church through judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest, by perversely avoiding the wicked, someone leave the Church himself and bind to Gehenna those whom he appears to flee” [Col. 0885A].

What was written in those same letters in your name—namely, that you had discovered that we did not patiently listen to the admonitions and corrections of your pontificate—plainly shows that you still have, at least, something lacking of that perfect charity of which the Apostle says:

“Charity is patient, it is kind, it is not puffed up, it is not irritated, it does not act improperly, it bears all things, it endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13) [Col. 0885B].

We would very much wish to learn the measure and perfection of this charity—in kindness and patience, humility and endurance—from the example of your holy Paternity in your letters, if God were not pleased to honor us through it.

We could also learn this from you if, in the matters concerning which we replied to your Holiness about what had been written to us in your name, you would “bear with a little of our folly and support us” (2 Corinthians 11).

The great Peter, first bishop of the apostolic and first see, accepted the rebuke shown to him by his fellow apostle Paul not only patiently but even joyfully. He praised Paul’s letters, in which he read that he had been rebuked, with the greatest approval (2 Peter 3).

[Col. 0885C]

He could not have praised them so highly unless he had read them; and because he read that he was reproved in them, and praised them so greatly, he showed how gladly he accepted his just rebuke and how patiently he bore it.

When he was rebuked by his juniors because he had entered among the Gentiles, he did not answer them with a bare and arrogant speech, demanding that they patiently endure everything he had done, nor did he invoke his authority in response to their complaint. Rather, he appeased them with humble reasoning and even called witnesses in the matter of his rebuke (Galatians 2).

“For if,” as blessed Gregory says, “he had said anything about his authority in the complaint of the faithful, he certainly would not have been a teacher of gentleness.”

If, therefore, the pastor of the Church and prince of the apostles, who performed signs and miracles in a singular manner, did not disdain to give a humble account in the matter of his rebuke, how much more, says blessed Gregory, pontiff of the apostolic see, ought we sinners, when we are rebuked concerning some matter, to appease our reprovers with humble reasoning?

The letters sent to us in your name did not appease us with humble reasoning, nor did they demonstrate by reason and authority that we had sought anything contrary to reason. Rather, they sought to close our mouth with an improper reprimand, although, by God’s grace, we can still speak freely about the things imposed upon us through letters sent in your name [Col. 0885D].

The aforesaid letters sent to us in your name also say concerning Hincmar:

“By apostolic authority we wish and command that Hincmar himself, bishop of Laon, relying upon your power, come to the threshold of the saints and to our clemency. When he comes, let a suitable accuser also come, one who cannot be rejected by any legitimate authority. Then, in our presence and before the entire Roman see, after his case has been examined with prudent judgment by a synodal assembly and carefully investigated, it will be concluded without any delay according to God and the constitutions of the sacred canons, issued by the Spirit of God” (Council of Carthage, canon 105) [Col. 0886A].

When we reread this, we found that, contrary to the custom of your predecessors and those before them, it introduced into the Church the shadowy arrogance of the world, whereas that Church offers the light of simplicity and humility to those who desire to see the day of the Lord.

Nevertheless, we did not doubt your intention, since what accords with deliberation can easily be snatched away by the human mind and later be changed.

[Col. 0886B]

But we were greatly astonished to discover where the author of the letter delivered to us through Bishop Actard had found it written that apostolic authority should command that a king who corrects the wicked, disciplines the guilty, and avenges crimes according to ecclesiastical and secular laws should send to Rome, relying on his royal power, someone legally and regularly condemned for his offenses.

This is especially astonishing in the case of one who, even before his deposition, was discovered in three synods to have plotted against public custody and public peace, as is contained in the episcopal records sent to your Paternity [Col. 0886C], and who, after his deposition, did not cease his obstinacy either on his own or through anyone he could employ.

We are not surprised, however, if in the later letters sent to us in your name it was inserted that one legally and regularly condemned—whom no law decrees should be restored by anyone to any rank or to his possessions and resources before, if he has not been found to have plotted against public custody and peace, he is perhaps found innocent in a renewed judgment, with the authority of the apostolic see renewed, in the province where he was judged—should come to you relying upon our royal power.

For one condemned as the author of his own wrongdoing is owed zeal for uprightness, not the clemency of release.

If these things did not flow from the same opening, they nevertheless sprang from the same undertaking as the earlier letters, in which it is stated that you would entrust to us all the possessions of the Church committed to Hincmar until he returned to his own, so that they might remain unharmed and suffer no loss [Col. 0886D].

Therefore, as we replied to you—and now have not hesitated to write to you again, although necessity requires it—because we kings of the Franks, born of royal stock, have until now been regarded not as episcopal stewards but as lords of the land: as Leo and the Roman synod wrote, kings and emperors, whom divine power has commanded to preside over the earth, have permitted holy bishops the right to distinguish matters according to the divine constitutions; they have not become the bishops’ bailiffs. Saint Augustine also says that possessions are held by the laws of kings; but by episcopal authority kings are not made stewards and agents of bishops. And the Lord commands that what belongs to Caesar be rendered to Caesar, and what belongs to God to God (Matthew XXII); he also paid the tax to the king (Matthew XVII). The Apostle wished kings to be served, wished them to be honored and not trampled upon: “Honor the king,” he says (1 Peter II). And again: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.” “Render therefore to all what is owed” (Romans XIII); and a little earlier: “For this reason you must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience” (ibid.).

And if you review the records of your predecessors and forebears, you will in no way find that such commands as are contained in letters sent to us in your name through Bishop Actard were received by our predecessors from yours. Therefore we have thought it necessary to write you a few things out of many.

Saint Gregory, pontiff of the apostolic see, distinguished for the merit of his life and the teaching of his wisdom, and to be revered and imitated by the whole world, wrote to the Frankish kings Theuderic and Theudebert, our predecessors, concerning the injury suffered by a certain bishop—not, as you wrote to us on behalf of one who was lawfully, regularly, and justly deposed on account of his conduct—in these words (Book VII, Letter 120, indiction 2):

> “Our brother and fellow bishop Ursinus, bishop of the city of Turin, is said to be suffering extremely serious prejudice in his parishes situated within the bounds of your kingdom. Indeed, contrary to ecclesiastical observance, contrary to priestly dignity, and contrary to the definitions of the sacred canons, another bishop did not fear to be ordained there, although Ursinus had committed no offense requiring it. And, as though it were too little that unlawful acts should be joined to unlawful acts, even the property of his church is said to have been taken away. If the truth is indeed so, since it is altogether intolerable that a man whom guilt has not harmed should be oppressed, after first conveying our paternal greeting, we ask that your Excellency graciously strive to grant, through our humble intercession, what you can voluntarily bestow out of love for ecclesiastical reverence and consideration of equity; and, as we trust in your goodness concerning justice, cause it to be preserved for him in every respect, and, once the truth has been disclosed, cause what was unlawfully done there to be corrected. May this exhortation of ours therefore find a place with you for the benefit of your soul, and so forth.”

He also wrote to the exarch of Ravenna, a man of lesser dignity than we possess by God’s grace in royal power, concerning a certain bishop, in these words (Book I, Letter 32):

> “It has come to our attention that Blandus, bishop of the city of Ortona, has now for a long time been detained by Your Excellency in the city of Ravenna. As a result, the church remains without a ruler, and the people, as though without a shepherd, perish; and infants there die without baptism because of their sins. Again, since we do not believe that Your Excellency has detained him except for some credible reason of misconduct, it is necessary that, once a synod has been held, it be made clear whether any charge is being brought against him, and whether such guilt is found in him as would lead to degradation from the priesthood. If so, we must seek another ordination, lest the Church of God remain uncultivated and destitute of those without whom the Christian religion does not permit it to exist. But if Your Excellency discovers that the matter is otherwise than has been said concerning him, permit him to return to his own church, so that he may fulfill his office among the souls entrusted to him.”

Compare these commands of blessed Gregory, your predecessor, concerning men who had not yet been lawfully and regularly deposed for their crimes by synodal judgment, with the writings sent to us in your name concerning one who is held to have been lawfully and regularly deposed for his offenses by synodal judgment, commanding us to send him to Rome relying on our power; and judge which ought rather to be followed.

We, however, trust that Your Authority will judge that we should follow what your predecessors and forebears wrote in accordance with the course of Scripture and the preaching of the elders, rather than what the writer of the aforementioned letter sent to us in your name fabricated. For blessed Augustine says in his book to Januarius (Letter 119, chapter 19):

> “I consider all such things to be cut away as are contained neither in the authorities of the holy Scriptures, nor found established in councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the universal Church.”

And Saint Leo, concerning matters established by the sacred canons and promulgated by decrees of the apostolic see in such a way that they cannot be overturned by any reasoning, decreed:

> “Whatever differs from their constitution is to be entirely void of authority.”

It is as though he were saying with Paul that the apostolic see cannot contradict itself in its constitutions: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you something beyond what we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians I).

But, as is read in the controversy of Quintilian, just as bees are said to have been killed by the flowers poisoned through the cunning of deceivers, although those flowers ought to have supplied them with honey, so blessed Peter shows from the sacred Scriptures what is being done when he speaks of Paul’s letters: “The ignorant and unstable,” he says, “twist them, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (2 Peter III). And concerning ecclesiastical traditions, Saint Innocent writes to Decentius (Letter 29):

> “When each person believes that what seems right to him, rather than what has been handed down, is to be held, the result is that different things appear to be held or celebrated in different places or churches, and scandal arises among the peoples. For, not knowing that ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, they think either that these things do not suit them or their churches, or that contradiction has been introduced by the apostles or apostolic men.”

Against this disease Saint Celestine offered a salutary antidote for all, saying (Letter 2):

> “Let no priest be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy thing will be preserved by us if, through the license of some people, the standard of the decretal constitutions is broken?”

And Saint Gelasius says in his decrees:

> “Our Fathers—namely, Catholic and learned pontiffs—whenever any sect arose, at whatever time, once they had assembled, established whatever they had determined for the faith, for truth, and for Catholic and apostolic communion according to the course of Scripture and the preaching of the elders. They wished it thereafter to remain unshaken and firm, and did not permit what had once been established in the same matter to be reconsidered through any recent presumption.”

We must therefore see what this course of the holy Scriptures and the preaching of the elders define. For we read in sacred history that the Lord said through the prophet to King Jehoshaphat:

> “You give help to the ungodly and join friendship with those who hate the Lord; therefore you deserved the Lord’s wrath. Yet good works have been found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah” (2 Chronicles XIX).

And in the Gospel the Lord commands that a person who has been admonished once, twice, and three times, yet does not obey the correction due to him, be regarded as a pagan and a tax collector (Matthew XVIII). Blessed Gregory, too, in his decrees—as you can find in the acts of the synod—defines as accursed the one who seizes not only another’s property but also the church entrusted to him. Indeed, if another person has done this, the man who presides over the Church, if he himself either orders it to be done or neglects to punish what was done without his order with an appropriate penalty, is himself anathematized.

We therefore cannot sufficiently wonder from where the writer of the letter delivered to us in your name produced this law, engraved in gold before him: a law that the Lord did not write with his finger, nor inspire anyone to write, nor give, ordained through angels, into the hand of his mediator; a law that no pagan promulgated, no Christian introduced, and no ecclesiastical man decreed; a law which, beneath this heaven, resounds written not with the ink of the hand of justice, nor by the Spirit of the living God. By this law I, established king by God and marked with the double-edged sword—that is, as the avenger of the guilty and defender of the innocent—for the punishment of evildoers, as the Apostle explains (Romans XIII), and for the praise of the good, am commanded to become the supporter of a criminal, condemned man, and one under anathema; and am ordered to make Hincmar, a transgressor of the sacred laws, a reviler of the holy priesthood, a dissuader from royal dignity contrary to apostolic rule, a disturber of the kingdom, a perjurer and instigator of seditions, an afflicter of the church entrusted to him, a sacrilegious defrauder and destroyer of ecclesiastical resources, a scandal to bishops and to the entire people of our regions, an invader of others’ property, and one condemned by himself through acting contrary to his own subscriptions and professions, come to Rome relying on royal power.

Who, then, has vomited forth this entire law from hell? What Tartarus has belched it from its hidden and dark tunnels? Against it, the sacred writings have shown us the way we should follow and provided a model to which we should conform.

The prophet, it says, cried out to the king of Israel and said:

> “Your servant went out to fight hand-to-hand; and when one man fled, someone brought him to me and said: ‘Guard this man; if he slips away, your life shall stand for his life, or you shall weigh out a talent of silver.’ But while I, troubled, turned this way and that, suddenly he disappeared. And the king of Israel said to him: ‘This is your judgment, which you yourself have decreed.’ Immediately he wiped the dust from his face, and the king of Israel recognized that he was one of the prophets. Then he said to him: ‘Thus says the Lord: Because you have released from your hand a man worthy of death, your life shall stand for his life, and your people for his people.’ So the king of Israel returned to his house, refusing to listen, and came furiously to Samaria” (3 Kings XX).

What madness has seized you, when you know that Christ, the power and wisdom of God, said: “Through me kings reign, and lawmakers decree what is just” (Proverbs VIII)? And the sacred canons, as we believe and have frequently read in the apostolic letters, were created by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the entire world.

Let us therefore see what the holy canons and sacred laws decree concerning such matters. The African Council says (Canon 29):

> “It should also be requested that the rulers of the earth deign to establish that, if a cleric of any rank has been condemned by the judgment of bishops for any crime, it shall not be permitted for him to be defended either by the churches over which he presided or by any person, with the penalty of loss of money and honor imposed; and they should decree that neither age nor sex is to serve as an excuse.”

Then Valens, Gratian, and Valentinian established the following (Theodosian Code):

> “Let anyone who, with the priests sitting in judgment, has been expelled from and deprived of an episcopal position and title, if he is discovered to have plotted anything against public security or public peace and then seeks again the priesthood from which he appears to have been expelled, live one hundred miles from the city he has defiled, according to the law of the divine memory of Gratian. Let him be separated from the gatherings of those from whose fellowship he has been set apart. Let it also be unlawful for such persons, under the force of this law, to approach our sacred secrets or obtain written documents; and let whatever has been obtained by persons deprived of the priesthood through guilt remain invalid. Let those on whose defense they rely know that they will not be free from blame if they promise them such assistance, since they do not appear to have deserved divine judgment.”

For this reason Pope Leo also petitioned the imperial authority concerning Eutyches, the author of scandal and wickedness (Letter 47 to Pulcheria):

> “That he be transferred farther away from the place that was too near the city of Constantinople, so that he might not use more frequent support from those whom he had drawn into his impiety.”

And Gregory decreed (Book X, Letter 33) that Paul, formerly bishop of the city of Diadina, should be sent to a monastery until he restored everything he had squandered or taken from the substance of the church. If, after his deposition, he should at any time shamelessly and perversely attempt to speak about the episcopate or seek it again with any presumptuous effort, Gregory ordered, through the diligence of John, bishop of the First Justiniana, that he be deprived of communion in the Lord’s body and blood and confined in a monastery until the day of his death to do penance, so that he might learn to correct the stains of his committed crime with fitting tears.

This was in accordance with the law of the emperor Justinian, who decreed in the Book of Constitutions:

> “If any expelled bishop dares to enter the city from which he has been driven, or to leave the place in which he has been ordered to reside, we command that he be handed over to a monastery situated in another province, so that, living in a monastery, he may correct what he committed in the priesthood.”

It is fitting that we preserve these laws, promulgated and decreed by emperors and kings—namely, by our predecessors—without mutilation and without dispute, just as the bishops of the apostolic see wrote to lords and rulers of the earth.

For Leo says to Leo Augustus (Letter 92):

> “You ought undoubtedly to recognize that royal power has been bestowed upon you not only for the governance of the world but especially for the protection of the Church, so that by suppressing wicked attempts you may defend what has been rightly established and restore true peace to things that have been disturbed.”

And Gelasius says to Anastasius (Letter 10, at the end):

> “For, Augustus Emperor, if anyone should perhaps attempt anything contrary to the public laws—which God forbid—it could not be admitted by any reasoning.”

They also wrote that these laws, promulgated by imperial authority, ought to be observed not only by any bishops but even by the pontiffs of the apostolic see themselves, as blessed Leo demonstrates in writing to Leo Augustus. He says (Letter 80) that he ought not to oppose imperial edicts or what his predecessors had established according to the course of Scripture and the preaching of the elders:

> “If I destroy what I have built, I make myself a transgressor and subject myself to the conditions of vengeance that not only the authority of the blessed emperor Marcian but also I myself, by my consent, have confirmed.”

And Saint Gelasius says to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 10, at the beginning):

> “If, so far as concerns the order of public discipline, we recognize that the empire has been conferred upon you by heavenly disposition, and the ministers of religion themselves obey your laws, lest they appear to oppose a sentence excluded from worldly matters, with what disposition, I ask, is it fitting for you to obey those who have been appointed to dispense the venerable mysteries?”

We also wish, in accordance with the exhortation of blessed Gelasius, to carry this out without hesitation and willingly, in matters belonging to their ministry, toward all priests who rightly administer divine things, and especially toward the prelate of that see whom the supreme Divinity willed to preside over all priests and whom the continuing devotion of the Church has honored. Our orthodox predecessors and forebears, emperors and kings, acted in this way, so that both the pontiff of the apostolic see and the other priests of the Lord might provide us with what God has ordained.

We know—as that same blessed Gelasius says (in the *Tome of Anathema*, near the end)—that Christ, mindful of human frailty, magnificently tempering what suited the salvation of his own, distinguished the offices of the two powers through their proper actions and dignities. He wished his people to be saved by medicinal humility, not again destroyed by human pride. Thus Christian rulers would need pontiffs for eternal life, while pontiffs would make use of imperial arrangements for the course of temporal affairs, so that spiritual action might remain apart from carnal intrusions and the one serving God might not become entangled in worldly business (2 Timothy II). Conversely, the one occupied with worldly affairs would not appear to preside over divine matters. In this way the moderation of both orders would be maintained, so that no one might be exalted by being supported by both, and each profession might be specially fitted to the qualities of its actions.

“The whole pontiff,” says the Apostle, “chosen from among men, is appointed on behalf of men in matters pertaining to God, so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins” (Hebrews V)—namely, not only for the people but also for his own sins, because he too is surrounded by weakness. It is the king’s task to administer the affairs of the kingdom, as the divinely inspired writings insist.

Since, therefore, the course of the holy Scriptures and the preaching of the elders show—and Gelasius also bears witness (Letter 10)—that “there are two things by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power”; and since through the King of kings and the supreme pontiff of all pontiffs, who alone could become both king and priest, lawmakers decree what is just (Proverbs VIII); and since the chief authorities have called these laws eternal, while the sacred canons were created by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world; and since blessed Ambrose says to Valentinian:

> “The emperor issues laws which he himself must first observe, because what he prescribed for others he prescribed for himself, so that no one might be free to judge otherwise,”

and blessed Augustine says:

> “After laws have been subscribed and confirmed, it is not permitted for a judge to judge about them, but according to them”—

then, in accordance with your pontifical ministry, we wish obediently and willingly to heed the admonitions of your paternity through our royal ministry. Permit us to preserve what your predecessors and ours established concerning the matter at issue, and, by preserving what has been done, let us show that what we do ought to be considered valid.

For how will the laws of rulers rightly be called eternal if, when rulers pass away, the constitution of the law passes away with them? Pope Symmachus also says to Aeonius (Letter 1):

> “Since, in the likeness of the Trinity, whose power is one and indivisible, the priesthood is one though exercised through different bishops, how is it fitting for the statutes of those who came before to be violated by those who follow? To this is added that, if such a variety of judgments should arise, we believe it concerns the sacred religion itself, whose entire power is weakened unless all things once established by the priests of the Lord remain perpetual. How else could this occur except if a successor failed to give firmness to the acts of his predecessor and, by strengthening what has been done, made valid what he himself had done? For how great would the reverence for the vicars of blessed Peter the Apostle be judged to be if what they command in the priesthood were dissolved when they themselves pass away?”

Let all things established by the priests of the Lord remain perpetual. They receive what they establish from the divine oracle, like Moses—not like those of whom the prophet says: “Woe to those who make unjust laws and, when writing, write injustice” (Isaiah X). Nevertheless, let what is established by the vicars of blessed Peter remain unshaken, because, as Leo says (*Sermon 3 on the Anniversary*):

> “There is neither excessive severity nor laxity where nothing is established except what proceeds from the equity of blessed Peter.”

We know that these things are canonical, strengthened by apostolic authority, and decrees of the apostolic see. As Gelasius says (Letter 10 to Dardanus, at the beginning), the apostolic see:

> “both confirms every synod by its authority and guards it through continuous moderation, in accordance with its primacy, which blessed Peter the Apostle received at the Lord’s command and which the Church, following thereafter, has both always held and continues to hold.”

And a little earlier:

> “We are confident that no one who is truly a Christian is now ignorant that, of all sees, the first ought more than any other to carry out the constitution of each synod that has been approved by the assent of the universal Church.”

And again, the same writer says (Letter 6 to all the bishops):

> “Since we desire to be permitted to do nothing rashly against the reverence due to salutary rules, and since the apostolic see, by the Lord’s favor, diligently seeks in pious and devoted purpose to preserve what has been established by the canons of the Fathers, it is exceedingly unworthy for anyone—whether pontiff or one of the ranks that follow—to reject this observance, which he sees the see of blessed Peter both follow and teach. It is altogether fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance, which it sees flourishing where the Lord placed the primacy of the entire Church.”

And concerning the sacred laws, both ecclesiastical and secular, which the Catholic Church observes together with the holy canons, the same Gelasius says, as we have already stated, in his letter to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 10):

> “So far as concerns the order of public discipline, recognizing that the empire has been conferred upon you by heavenly disposition, the ministers of religion themselves obey your laws, lest they appear to oppose a sentence excluded from worldly matters.”

Since, then, sacred laws—both ecclesiastical and secular—decree concerning a bishop condemned by episcopal and synodal judgment, it is not the duty of our royal ministry to send anywhere, relying on our power, a guilty man condemned by the judgment of the sacred canons and anathematized by the definition of the apostolic see, as you can find in the acts of the synod. The sacred canons, the laws of Justinian, and the edicts of the other Catholic emperors most clearly define how, for what reasons, and by whom a bishop ought to be judged, and, after judgment, what is to be done concerning him, in what manner, and by whom, before the apostolic see. We do not reject these provisions; rather, we assent to them without hesitation and appropriately.

No one is permitted to deviate from these definitions, because, as Saint Hilary the pope says:

> “One sins no less against the sanctions of the holy traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

Therefore, since the Lord says through the prophet, “The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel”—that is, the messenger—“of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi II). Do not permit matters that are not contained in the sacred laws established by God’s wisdom or in his holy rules promulgated by the same Spirit.

The prophet—that is, the priest giving the command—also says: “Hearing, you shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel III): “from me,” he says, and not “from yourself.” Those who speak from their own heart are reproved, because “the one who speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John VII).

Therefore, as we have already said, we beg you not to permit, in your name or under the authority of the apostolic see, commands or threats of excommunication to be sent to us any longer, at anyone’s prompting, against the course of the sacred Scriptures, the preaching of the elders, and the constitutions of the sacred laws and holy canons. For you know, and we know, that whatever differs from their constitution is entirely invalid.

Saint Leo says (*Sermon 3 on the Anniversary*):

> “It is said by the Lord to the most blessed Peter: ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven’” (Matthew XVI). “The right of this power indeed passed also to the other apostles, and the constitution of this decree came to all the leaders of the Church; but it was not without reason that what was communicated to all was entrusted to one alone. For this reason it is uniquely entrusted to Peter: because Peter’s form is placed before all the rulers of the Church. Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is rendered from his equity.”

From this statement it is evident that Peter’s privilege does not remain where judgment is not rendered from his equity. Since, when it says “wherever,” just as no place is excluded, so no ruler of the Church who renders judgment from Peter’s equity is excluded, nor is one commended who delivers judgment contrary to that equity, shall we obey a command there where Peter’s privilege does not remain because no judgment is delivered from his equity? Shall we accept a judgment that has not been issued from Peter’s equity and is therefore deprived of his privilege?

Concerning this episcopal judgment, blessed Gregory sufficiently emphasizes what all bishops should follow and what the sons of the Church should hold and preserve. Therefore, command and judge by the privilege of the great Peter, according to his judgment of equity, what ought to be commanded and judged, lest, as his fellow Apostle says, your ministry be reviled (2 Corinthians VI).

For we too, according to our royal ministry, wish, insofar as it lies with us, to preserve what is written: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord” (Ephesians VI)—that is, whatever has been commanded or judged by the Lord. For he says individually to those who, in place of the apostolic fathers, are born as sons of the Church from apostolic men: “But you, hearing, shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel III).

The divine reading teaches us that even Balaam, although King Balak pressed him insistently and, seduced by the lure of greed, corrupted him when he sought counsel, could nevertheless not be persuaded or forced, by any person or anyone’s prompting, to speak anything else in the judgment of justice against Israel than what he had heard from the Lord (Numbers XXII).

Concerning what is contained in the letters sent to us in your name—“When Hincmar comes to Rome, let a suitable accuser come who cannot be rejected by any legitimate authority”—we reply that, although this recommendation is supported by no reason or authority, if perhaps Hincmar alone is considered an outlaw among you, under a new law contrary to the ancient public and ecclesiastical laws, indeed under a new order and custom, so that he may be judged only by you and at Rome for these offenses, even though there are certain decrees of the sacred canons and laws concerning them which, as Leo says, cannot be overturned by any reasoning, then—even in a case of faith, as Gelasius says—it is permitted to any pontiff, according to the rule concerning a previously condemned error, to separate anyone from Catholic communion.

And I am so exempt from all accusations—not only from those in which the lawful and regular right of accusation against oneself is denied, but also from those in which accusation in one’s own cases is not denied—that, as the laws and rules command, matters arising in the province where they originated cannot be settled there, and, according to the canons of Antioch, cannot be subjected to the examination of provincial synods, if you obtain for us the means to go there with the will and consent of our most beloved nephew, your emperor. We do not wish to go there against his affection and the honor due to him, provided that he strives to show us mutual affection and fitting honor. If, with the Lord’s assistance, peace has been secured in our kingdom against the pagans by force or by whatever arrangement of God, we will not delay coming to Rome at the proper time.

And since we accused him lawfully and regularly in a synod of bishops from many provinces on definite charges, we shall show ourselves to be his suitable accuser. We shall bring with us so many suitable witnesses of different orders and dignities that, with them, we shall prove most fully that we lawfully and regularly accused and convicted him.

Finally, because we gather from the letters delivered to us by Bishop Actard that you have neither read nor heard what we previously sent to your paternity through him, we write again what we wrote then. We beseech you, in honor of almighty God and in veneration of the holy apostles, not to send to us, or to the bishops and leading men of our kingdom, any longer such letters dishonoring us or such commands as we have hitherto received in your name; and do not compel us to disregard and dishonor your commands and letters, and to dishonor your envoys. We desire to obey you in matters belonging to your ministry, insofar as they are indeed within your ministry.

We say these things for the honor of your privilege, because, as you are truly the vicar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we desire to obey you duly and appropriately in all things. We wish in every way to take care that the opposite does not occur, and with humble prayer we ask your holiness to take care of the same, lest you compel us and our people, very much against our will, to resort to what is found in the Fifth Ecumenical Council and is praised and accepted by the apostolic see—as we read in the apostolic letters, especially in the synodical letter of blessed Gregory to the four patriarchs and in his other letters, together with the four preceding councils—and which we find that we must uphold.

We have not yet wished to insert this in our letters as an example, until we know whether we can turn the harshness of your commands toward us to kindness by another means. For we do not fail to know that what is written in the name of the apostolic see according to the course of the holy Scriptures, the preaching of the elders, and the decrees of the orthodox must be followed and held; and we recognize that whatever has been compiled or fabricated by anyone to the contrary must not only be rejected but also reproved.

If, finally, in writing back to your most reverend paternity I have become foolish in a way unsuitable to us and to you, you compelled me to do so. But we ask almighty God to inspire your heart to treat us kindly, so that it may no longer be necessary for us to write to you in this manner, but, as we desire, to submit our necks and hearts humbly and devotedly, in veneration of the apostles, to your apostolic pontificate.

May almighty God deign to preserve you for many years, for the honor, salvation, and exaltation of his holy Church, most holy and most reverend lord and father in the Lord.

## LETTER IX TO THE SAME, SENT AT THE SAME TIME AS THE PRECEDING LETTER

*[From the works of Hincmar, p. 716.]*

To the most holy and most reverend Father Hadrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, Charles, by the grace of God king and your spiritual son.

Because, compelled by necessity, we have been forced to respond at greater length to the letters delivered to us by the venerable archbishop Actard in the name of your holy paternity, we have thought it necessary, contrary to our custom, to write our response in a small booklet sealed with our ring, so that it may be read more clearly and so that the reasons which compelled us to respond may become more fully known to the reader. May your holy paternity receive this response not with disdain but kindly; you will find that it has been composed by us not defiantly but with a peaceful mind.

We beseech you, in honor of almighty God and in veneration of the holy apostles, not to send to us, or to the bishops and leading men of our kingdom, any longer such letters dishonoring us or such commands as we have hitherto received in your name. But may it be permitted us, in veneration of God and the holy apostles, to submit humbly and devotedly, as we desire, our necks and hearts to your apostolic pontificate.

May almighty God deign to preserve you for many years, for the honor, salvation, and exaltation of his holy Church, most holy and most reverend lord and father in the Lord.

# INDICTMENT OF LORD KING CHARLES AGAINST WENILO, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

Presented by his own hand in the holy synod of the twelve provinces at the parish of Toul, in the suburb of that same city called Saponarias, to the appointed judges: Remigius, archbishop of Lyon; Herard, archbishop of Tours; Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen; and Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 859, indiction 7, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July.

## I

As Saint Gregory says, and as you recognize from the ancient custom received long ago [Note: *Olitana*, that is, received formerly and in ancient times, not abolished or obsolete], kings in the kingdom of the Franks arise from royal stock. By divine disposition, a portion of the kingdom among my brother-kings was handed over to me by my lord and father, Louis Augustus, of pious memory.

At that time the metropolitan see of Sens was vacant of a shepherd. In accordance with the custom of my predecessors, I entrusted it for governance to Wenilo, then my cleric, serving me in my chapel, who had commended himself to me according to the custom of a free cleric and had promised me fidelity by oath. With the consent of the holy bishops of that metropolitan church, I obtained, insofar as it depended on me, that they ordain him archbishop there.

## II
After this, a very well-known dispute arose concerning the division of the kingdom between my brothers and me. Accordingly, I undertook to hold and govern my share of the division with mutual oaths—namely, our own oaths and those of our faithful—as the leading men of the whole kingdom had likewise determined. Wenilo himself swore to me and to my brothers that henceforth I should substantially retain this division between us, as did the other bishops who were present there. Wenilo also confirmed by oath peace and mutual assistance between me and the aforesaid brother, Louis.

### III

But afterward, by his own election and that of the other bishops, and by the will, consent, and acclamation of the other faithful of our kingdom, Wenilo, together with the other archbishops and bishops, consecrated me king according to ecclesiastical tradition in his diocese, at the city of Orléans, in the Basilica of the Holy Cross. He anointed me with sacred chrism for the governance of the kingdom and raised me upon the throne of the kingdom with the diadem and royal scepter.

After this consecration and elevation to the kingdom, I ought not to have been overthrown or expelled by anyone, at least without a hearing and judgment by the bishops through whose ministry I had been consecrated king—bishops who are called the thrones of God, in whom God sits and through whom he issues his judgments. I was prepared to submit to their paternal corrections and disciplinary judgments, and at present I have submitted to them.

### IV

Finally, when disturbances in our kingdom began to multiply through the actions of irreverent men, with the consent of the bishops and of our other faithful, we jointly drew up a written agreement setting out how, with the Lord’s help, I wished to act toward them, and how those same faithful of ours were afterward to bring me support by counsel and assistance. Wenilo signed this document with his own hand at the estate of Bajern, as you can see at present.

### V

Then, when I proceeded against the pagans toward the island called Oscelus, with our faithful, traveling both by land and by ship, as you know, certain men who had defected from us fled. Wenilo, however, saying that because of his infirmity he could not go there, returned to his see.

While we were staying there in the field, weakened by illness, our brother Louis, as you know, invaded our kingdom from his own kingdom with an armed force and seditious men. Wenilo went to meet him without my will or permission. No other bishop from our kingdom did what he did—namely, become my overthrower.

### VI

Afterward, when I proceeded against the aforesaid brother and against my enemies, the devastators of the Church and the ravagers of the kingdom who were with him, together with God’s faithful and ours, Wenilo provided no assistance, either personally or through the proper support that my royal predecessors and I had customarily received from the Church entrusted to him—especially although I had devoutly requested this from him.

### VII

When circumstances and necessity compelled me to withdraw from the aforesaid brother at the estate of Breona, and my brother Louis returned to my part of the kingdom in order to seize my nephew from me, withdraw my men from me, and violently press upon [or oppress: *imprimeret*; *opprimeret*] my faithful, Wenilo came against me to the aforesaid brother Louis with whatever support he could provide.

With Louis were excommunicated men of this kingdom and seditious persons, concerning whose excommunication Wenilo had received letters from his fellow bishops. In my palace at Attigny, and in the parish and province of another archbishop who was our faithful, Wenilo celebrated public Masses for my brother, with whom those seditious men were associated, without that archbishop’s permission and without the consent of his fellow bishops, for excommunicated persons or participants in the excommunicated party.

He also took part in that council and deliberation by which my nephew Lothair, through the lies of his seducers, insofar as it depended on them, was to be seized, and by which the support and assistance owed to me and promised by oath were to be withdrawn from me.

### VIII

Notwithstanding the foregoing, Wenilo participated with his special intimates in the councils of my brother’s advisers and in their public and secret negotiations, and did so familiarly among their leading men, with those whom episcopal judgment—as we have said—had excommunicated and whom the judgment of the kingdom had condemned. The purpose was that the aforesaid brother should obtain the part of the kingdom that he and Wenilo had sworn to me, and in which Wenilo had consecrated me king, while I should lose it.

### IX

Wenilo took part in the council and negotiation by which the bishops who were bound to me by their pledged faith, and who ought to have brought me counsel and assistance confirmed by their own hands, would defect and turn themselves toward the service and subjection of my brother Louis.

### X

Concerning the abbey of Saint Columba and the possessions and honors of my kingdom, Wenilo obtained an order from my brother Louis and secured letters to the envoys Echard and Theodoric, directing them to restore that same abbey.

But in those same letters to the aforesaid envoys, Wenilo obtained from my brother Louis an order granting them permission to take stones from the wall of the castle of Melun, although that right belongs to royal authority. From this it is clear that he was striving and laboring to make Louis honored and established among the people of this kingdom, which God had given to me.

### XI

Wenilo was present with the aforesaid excommunicated men at the council and negotiation where it was considered how those men who were faithful to me and had promised me fidelity by oath might be made—whether unwillingly or willingly—to swear to my brother Louis, so that they would bring him assistance and he might obtain my kingdom against me.

Wenilo not only participated in this council, but himself gave this same counsel to my brother Louis against the fidelity that he had promised me by oath.

### XII

Wenilo, both personally and through his retainers—namely, the excommunicated men mentioned above—obtained from my brother Louis that the vacant bishopric of the city of Bayeux should be given to his kinsman, my cleric named Tortoldus, who had commended himself to me and promised me fidelity by oath.

He accepted that bishopric in violation of his fidelity to me and against the fidelity he had promised me, with the consent of my brother Louis.

### XIII

Finally, after God had granted me the strength to recover myself, through the support of my faithful, against my brother, I proceeded near Wenilo’s city. He knew that I was advancing against my brother in order to recover my kingdom, yet he provided no assistance—neither personally, in accordance with the counsel he had promised and signed, nor through the military force that customarily issued from the Church entrusted to him.

---

## In the Year of the Lord 878. Adrevald, Monk of Fleury

## Historical Notice on Adrevald

*(In Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

Adrevald, a monk of the Benedictine order at Fleury, is shown by Ruinart in his *Apology for the Mission of Saint Maur*, published in French, pp. 52 ff., to have lived during the time of Louis the Pious.

His *History of the Translation of Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica* appears in John Bosco’s *Fleury Library*, Paris, 1605, octavo, p. 1; in the *Acts of the Saints* under 21 March; and in Mabillon’s second-century volume of the *Acts of the Benedictines*, p. 253.

Adrevald composed the first book of the *History of the Miracles of Saint Benedict*. Its appendix was composed by Adelerius, likewise a monk of Fleury; the second and third books by Aimoinus, in A.D. 1005; and the fourth by an anonymous author. They are found in John Bosco, p. 13, in the *Acts of the Saints*, and in Mabillon’s second-century volume, pp. 67, 80, and 369.

The book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, against John Scotus, was published by Dacherius in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, and in volume I of the new edition, p. 150.

The *Life of Saint Aigulfus*, abbot and martyr of Lérins, killed in the year 675, appears anonymously in Surius under 3 September. It was restored to its author and made more complete in the second century of the *Acts of the Benedictines*, p. 656.

---

# History of the Translation of Saint Benedict, by Adrevald the Monk

*(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, from John Bosco’s *Fleury Library*, Bollandus, and manuscripts.)*

## [History of the Translation of Saint Bernard]

### The Lombards Ravage Cassino

#### 1

Since the Lombard people had long refused to abandon the darkness of their unbelief and, rejecting the yoke of the Lord, had resolved to attack those who bore it, they came into Italy to attack the Christian name and subject the country to their rule. By a hidden judgment of God, its inhabitants were delivered to their sword to be struck down.

Extending the cruelty of their slaughter far and wide, this people attacked the province of Benevento. Leveling its cities with the ground, devastating monasteries and estates, they inflicted no small slaughter upon Christians. For, tearing the Lord’s sheep from their folds in various forms of slaughter, they overthrew the Lord’s sheepfolds, so that places once desirable appeared transformed into a wilderness.

Among their other crimes, they ravaged the monastery of the eminent Father Benedict and made it uninhabitable in every respect.

How this happened is clear to anyone who reads the second book of the *Dialogues* of Blessed Gregory. In that work, having pursued all the deeds of this most holy man in lucid style, Gregory relates, among other things, that Benedict learned through the spirit of prophecy and foretold that the same monastery would be overthrown after all its possessions had been removed.

**Note:** We assigned this destruction to approximately the year 580 in *Life of the Holy Father Benedict*, chapter 17, first century of the Benedictines.

### With Chlodoveus’s Support, Leodebodus Founds the Monastery at Fleury

#### 2

After this destruction had been carried out and many years had passed, the same place, reduced to a wilderness, began to be inhabited by wild animals, although previously it had been a dwelling-place of human beings. This continued until Chlodoveus, son of Dagobert, acquired control of the Frankish kingdom.

He was a most noble man and extraordinarily skilled in the administration of public affairs. This king, distinguished by excellent character and accustomed to grant assent to just requests suited to the service of God, was approached by Leodebodus of blessed memory, abbot of the monastery of Saint Aignan, situated near the walls of the city of Orléans.

Leodebodus asked that he might build in the territory of Fleury a monastery suitable for the monastic order, giving in exchange for that territory estates that he possessed by hereditary right and that had been left to him by his parents. For the territory of Fleury was then a royal fisc.

When the king heard this, he most willingly granted the abbot’s request and judged that his desire, which had grown through long delay, should be fulfilled. Thus mutual exchanges were made by both parties: the aforesaid abbot gave the estate that had been left to him by his parents—Attimacum on the Aisne—and the aforesaid king, in reciprocal exchange, gave a certain small estate called Fleury, with its dependencies, not far from the bank of the Loire.

The charter of this mutual exchange is preserved to this day in the public archives of our monastery.

After completing this transaction, the aforesaid man of God, Leodebodus, did not forget his intended purpose. In the aforesaid estate he began to build dwellings suitable for monks. Applying himself to the work with shrewd industry, he completed it with marvelous success. He built there a basilica in honor of Saint Peter and another in honor of Saint Mary, which he wished to be dedicated to the Lord.

Soon, so that the prepared dwelling would not be empty and without inhabitants, he gathered there many men prepared to serve the Lord and live under the rule of the Rule.
