He placed over them as father and abbot a man named Mummolus, who, for as long as he remained among human beings, diligently cared for the flock entrusted to him as a capable shepherd.

**Note:** Some prefer Rigomarus to Mummolus. See the eulogy of Saint Mummolus below under the year 678, where we shall also discuss Leodebodus and the monastery of Fleury.

### Aigulfus Is Sent by Mummolus to Cassino for the Relics of Saint Benedict

#### 3

As the years passed, the aforesaid Leodebodus, having departed from the body—as we believe—to the heavenly dwellings, the aforementioned Mummolus, carefully guarding the flock entrusted to him and devoting himself continually to reading, found among other things in the books of the blessed and most eminent man Gregory, bishop of Rome, how Saint Benedict, beloved of God, had completed the course of his struggle in the province of Benevento.

Remembering that this venerable Father, warned by a divine oracle and foreseeing future events, had foretold that the monastery would be utterly destroyed—and that what Benedict had seen with spiritual eyes, Mummolus saw accomplished with bodily eyes—he sent to the aforesaid province one of his fellow soldiers, a monk named Aigulfus.

For he said that it had been divinely revealed to him that this man should go there and transfer the body of the aforesaid Benedict.

Aigulfus was a venerable man who earnestly desired in every way to please God. The degree of his sanctity and virtue was proved by his end, in which all praise may safely be sung. Although he excelled in good works, and although he had been asked to remain for a time in the monastery of Lérins as an example because of his zeal for good works, he suffered the plots of men hostile to divine religion and attained the palm of martyrdom. His passion is also preserved among us below.

### The Men of Le Mans Join Aigulfus

#### 4

Meanwhile, a vision corresponding to this one appeared in the city of Le Mans—namely, that they too should go to the same province and transfer the body of Saint Benedict’s sister, Scholastica, so that those whom the space of a single urn had contained might be shown to be transferred together.

While efforts were being made on both sides to ensure that suitable executors of the manifest vision would not be found lacking, only a few days after leaving the aforesaid city of Le Mans, the hearers of the divine oracle began the journey leading to Italy.

Turning aside to the monastery of Fleury to find lodging, they learned that the aforementioned venerable man Aigulfus, obeying the commands of his abbot, also wished to undertake the same journey.

**Note:** This vision evidently concerned Saint Bercarius, bishop of that city, as is related in the *Life of Bercarius* and in the account, or narrative, of the *Translation of Saint Scholastica*.

### After Visiting Rome, Aigulfus Proceeds to Cassino

#### 5

By common decision they therefore determined to accomplish the work they had begun together. They remained joined and inseparably attached to one another until, arriving at Rome, they entered the Basilica of Saint Peter to pray.

But when, under the pretext of visiting the holy places, they separated from one another in that city, the truth of the matter was that they intended to complete the task they had begun. Aigulfus, abandoning for the time being what he had openly displayed a desire to do—namely, visit the holy places—devoted himself to the undertaking, striving to complete more quickly the sacred commission entrusted to him.

At last he reached the site of the fortress called Cassino. There he briefly brought his journey to a halt and awaited the outcome, praying to him who had deigned to reveal the vision mentioned above and who had appointed him to this task, that he might not wish such a long journey to be spent in vain but, as he had promised, might deign to reveal to him the shrine of his treasure.

### An Unknown Old Man Reveals the Location of the Tomb

#### 6

As he traveled through the area seeking some sign, diligently looking about and turning his eyes here and there like an attentive investigator, a certain man who had often seen him doing this, and who was advanced in years, addressed him first:

“Hey, you,” he said, “from what regions have you come to our dwelling, and for what business?”

Aigulfus did not dare reveal to him the secret entrusted to him. But when the old man questioned him again about the matter, and he still feared to disclose it, he heard these words from him:

“Why,” he said, “do you not make me a participant in your secret? For if you fear the scandal of a betrayer, be confident: you will find trustworthy faith in me. And if you place confidence in my words, they may perhaps also benefit your undertaking.”

When the aforesaid servant of God had heard these words, he reflected that wisdom and knowledge of past events reside in the aged. He also considered—as the outcome later proved—that the Lord had sent this man beforehand for this very purpose. Accordingly, he related in order the history of what had happened: why he had come and what vision had been shown him for this purpose.

The old man then fixed his gaze upon the ground for a while, held his voice down in his throat, and finally opened his mouth:

“If you repay me with the worthy reward due for such a service, then, with God’s favor, I think I can quickly bring your business to completion, so that, after accomplishing what caused you to undertake the labor of so long a journey, you may return home in triumph.”

When the man of God heard the old man’s speech, he replied:

“There will be no difficulty in giving the reward. I shall give you everything you ask of me. Only remember your promise and repay your words with deeds.”

The old man answered:

“When you see that the hours of the night that flees the light are approaching the limits of silence, do not allow yourself even a little rest. Leave the recesses of the dwelling and remain an indefatigable watcher beneath the open sky.

When you see some place in this solitude shining with an exceedingly bright light, like a snowy mountain, mark the place firmly in your mind. For there you will find that by which the end of your care will be accomplished.”

### He Carries the Sacred Relics to Gaul with the Men of Le Mans

#### 7

Trusting the old man’s words and burning with desire, the aforesaid man, after taking his first sleep, threw himself from his bed. He proved himself an eager observer of the old man’s instructions.

Looking toward the region of the aforesaid solitude, he saw in the distance a place glittering with bright light, as when some location is flooded with the illumination of many lamps and torches.

When he saw this, the reverend hero was filled with great joy. Blessing the Governor of the world and Ruler of the ages, he awaited the end of the night in those same praises.

After waiting there for a long time, and while the sun’s globe had not yet filled the wide spaces of the world with its radiance, he boldly hurried to the place that he had marked. There he found everything exactly as he had long desired and offered countless thanks to the one who had prospered his journey.

Approaching the place, he found there a little chest, outwardly worthless but inwardly containing pearls of great price. Before its entrance—namely, on the rock placed above it—inscriptions had been fixed, and within lay the bodies.

When he had found what he had long desired, he opened the side and emptied the chest, enclosed the treasure he had discovered in a single basket, and carried it in his bosom. That basket is still preserved among us, almost as new.

**Note:** Paul the Deacon, in book VI, chapter 2 of his *History of the Lombards*, says that the sacred ashes remained at Cassino. The monk Notker of Saint Gall agrees with him in his *Martyrology* under 2 July:

“Not long,” he says, “did that place, Cassino, remain empty of the relics of the saints, venerable as it was to the gathering of the faithful. For the brothers who were able to escape the hands of the enemy, gathering together again and being increased by others in place of those who had been dispersed, carefully tending themselves with greater caution, reverently cared for the sacred ashes—until recently scattered by the invasion of the Saracens in every direction; namely, the monks.” We have said that this occurred in the year 884.

After all this had been accomplished, his companions suddenly arrived—the men mentioned above who had set out from the city of Le Mans. They too were seeking the blessing they had long sought but had not obtained.

Then, for the first time, they disclosed to one another the purpose of their journey: they too had been warned by a divine revelation to go and bring back the body of Blessed Scholastica.

They immediately began the return journey and hastened back together, carrying the precious pearls they had found by divine gift.

### They Are Protected by a Cloud from the Attendants of the Roman Pontiff

#### 8

As the bearers of the holy bodies of Benedict and his sister Saint Scholastica were rapidly returning and had already reached the borders of their own territory, a loud voice, sent by God through the deep silence of night, forbade them to delay on their journey.

At that same hour, someone appeared in a vision to address the Roman pope as follows:

“Why does sluggish sleep, pressing upon you at this urgent hour, prevent you from leaving your bed and keeping watch over your province? And why, abandoning public responsibilities, are you entangled in private concerns? For, to tell you plainly what you should know, you are without the protection of great men—namely, Benedict and his sister Scholastica. Certain men arriving here from the shores of Gaul are carrying their bodies away to be buried elsewhere.”

Having heard this, the Roman pontiff immediately left his bed, sought weapons and companions, and attempted to pursue those departing, joining to himself the assistance of the Lombards.

When the servants of God received this vision, fearing the sorrowful arrival of some misfortune, they looked behind them and saw enemies pursuing them. Filled with fear and thrown to the ground, they begged the one who had deigned to reveal to them the bodies of his servants to command that they carry them to the appointed place.

The divine mercy was pleased to grant their prayer. For the power of the Almighty concealed them in such a density of darkness that it did them no harm, but deprived their pursuers of every ability to find them. Thus, with their fear of danger removed, the servants of God returned more quickly.

### The Blind Man Bonodius Is Given Sight

#### 9

At last, although they had completed so great a journey with hardship, they nevertheless turned aside safely to a small estate called Bonodium, compelled by weariness. It was situated in the territory of Orléans.

**Note:** Bonodium is Bonnée, a village one league above the monastery of Fleury. No basilica now exists there except the parish church dedicated to Saint Martin. About one stone’s throw from it, however, there is a mound called Mount Saint Benedict, where ruins and foundations of an old building are sometimes unearthed—without doubt the remains of a church once dedicated to Saint Benedict.

While they rested there for a short time, a man who had been born without eyes came forward and addressed the saint with loud cries from his mouth and with faith, asking him to grant him the light that nature had denied him.

As he continued his cries, after a short interval—scarcely an hour had passed—the darkness of blindness was dispelled. He began to see the light that had long been denied him and to exalt its giver, together with Blessed Benedict, with loud praises.

### A Cripple Is Raised Up

#### 10

It also pleased the Divinity to join another miracle to this one in the same place, in order to show how great was the sanctity of him whose body was being carried.

A certain weak man who could not walk upright came, dragging himself by crawling along the ground, since he was deprived of the use of all his limbs. He implored help from Almighty God through his servant Benedict.

Then, in a marvelous manner, his long-contracted sinews began to stretch, and his long-dried veins became moist with an inundation of blood. Thus, by God’s will, after receiving strength, he joyfully stood upon his feet and blessed his healer with loud cries.

That place still preserves a basilica dedicated to the Lord in honor of Blessed Benedict.

### Sight Is Restored to a Blind Man

#### 11

When they decided to move on from that place, they reached another small estate, situated about fifteen hundred paces from the monastery toward which they were traveling, called Novavilla—commonly, *la Mairie de Neuville*.

When they had decided to rest there for a short time, a blind man came toward them. With great force and violent determination, he seized the basket in which the ashes of the blessed man were being carried.

The man of God, Aigulfus, tried to correct him with measured reproof and restrain him from his unlawful presumption.

But the man, grieved by the loss of his sight, replied that he could in no way be separated from the basket unless he immediately received his sight. He declared that he had such faith that Saint Benedict, with the Lord granting his request, could grant whatever he himself asked.

### At Old Fleury, the Men of Le Mans Request the Relics of Scholastica

#### 12

After this, as they proceeded without any delay, bands of monks together with the people of the territory of Orléans went out to meet them a mile from the monastery, in a village called Old Fleury.

There, with joy, gladness, and great honor, they received the bodies of the saints mentioned above on the fifth day before the Ides of July. On that same day they celebrated the same solemnity there with immense joy in praises of God.

While they remained there, the people of the city of Le Mans—whose citizens, as we said above, had gone to bring the body of Blessed Scholastica—came forward to meet them with their fellow citizens. They rejoiced that they had sent these men to carry away the heavenly treasure.

When they arrived at the aforesaid place and learned the truth of what had happened, together with all the acts of the venerable Aigulfus, they asked him to grant them the gift that had been promised and shown to them by God.

But the same venerable man replied that he absolutely did not wish to separate the bodies of the holy siblings from one another. Just as, as was evident, they had been buried together in the earlier tomb, so he testified that he wished to place them together and indivisibly in the second.

Then all the noble and wise men contradicted these words. They said that it was not right that those whom the divine will had made participants in the heavenly oracle, who had together approached the place of the saints’ shrine, and who had been equal in undertaking the labor, should not also share equally in the fruit of their labor.

Above all, they said that it was not fitting for the narrowness of a single place to confine two great lights, since separate places were sufficient for each.

At last, therefore, the aforementioned venerable man Aigulfus yielded to the counsels of the venerable men and decided that he himself, retaining the body of Blessed Benedict, should send his companions away with the body of his venerable sister.

**Note:** Notker disapproves of this action. “Woe,” he says in the passage cited, “to the merits of those through whom she suffered separation, although by the disposition of the Holy Spirit she deserved to be joined with him.”

### The Sacred Relics Are Distinguished by the Raising of the Dead

#### 13

But since it was not certain how the bones could be distinguished, for the hollow of a single basket held them together in confusion, the difficulty of distinguishing them led to the decision that the bones which appeared smaller should be placed separately, while the larger ones should be gathered on the other side.

As the person dividing them hesitated and no certain judgment could be made, it pleased the Divinity to bring this doubtful decision to an end in the following manner.

For after both peoples had spent the night continually beseeching God to reveal this important matter to them, at dawn they saw in the distance the funerals of two small corpses. One was male, the other female.

Having received this salutary counsel, they ordered the lifeless bodies to be brought to them. When this had been done, they had the body of the boy placed near the bones that appeared greater in size. In a marvelous manner, as soon as the body of the dead boy touched the dead bones of the one lying there, life was restored to the dead through the dead.

Likewise, they decided that the body of the dead girl should be placed near the smaller bones.

But God, in order to show that those whose bodies were being carried were truly siblings, willed that, just as they had been equal by one generation of flesh and at one and the same time, so they should be equal in the miracle.

Thus the girl rose from the funeral rites at that same hour. She had been carried to the tomb by her grieving friends, and she returned home with those same people rejoicing.

This is clearly an ancient and unusual miracle, recalled after the deed of Elisha (4 Kings XV), because the hand of Almighty God, to show that Blessed Benedict was not inferior to either the new or the ancient Fathers, made him equal in merit to the works of the prophets. The truthful voice of Truth was fulfilled when it promised: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do” (John X, 12).

All therefore bless the Lord with joyful hearts and loud voices, because he had deigned to reveal with light brighter than day what had been hidden from them.

**Note:** Near the village of Fleury—which is called Old Fleury and lies one stone’s throw from the town and monastery of Saint Benedict—there is a chapel dedicated to Saint Scholastica at the place where these two miracles occurred. Solemn processions are often held there to obtain rain.

### The Men of Le Mans Build a Basilica and Monastery for the Relics of Saint Scholastica

#### 14

Once every doubtful question that had long occupied their minds concerning the division of the bodies had been removed, the people of Le Mans turned with sound judgment toward the body of Blessed Scholastica.

They lifted it with the greatest speed, placed it upon their shoulders, and carried it joyfully to its own place. There they built a church at great expense. After the necessary arrangements had been made for women serving God, within a short time a great number of noble women gathered in the same monastery and devoted themselves to the service of the Lord after abandoning the world.

That monastery too continues to be honored by the Lord with great manifestations of miracles.

### The Body of Saint Benedict Is Deposited in the Church of Saint Peter and Buried in the Church of Saint Mary; the Place Is Celebrated for Its Miracles

#### 15

But Abbot Mummolus and the venerable Aigulfus lifted the body of Saint Benedict, which they knew by clear signs had been granted to them by God, and deposited it for safekeeping in the Basilica of Blessed Peter.

**Note:** This church of Saint Peter no longer exists. Only the basilica dedicated to Saint Mary remains; both it and the town surrounding the monastery took the name of Saint Benedict, commonly Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire.

While guarding it with extraordinary care, they discussed among themselves where in the same monastery they should bury it, in agreement with the divine will. A considerable uncertainty concerning this matter occupied their minds.

But God, who in his merciful kindness had determined that the body of the holy man should be transferred from its former place, provided a suitable place for burial in the subsequent place.

For when Mummolus of blessed memory had long been pondering this matter and seeking useful counsel, he rose during the dead of night to undertake his customary stolen moments of prayer. As usual, he left his bed and went out of the dormitory. Beneath the open sky he began, among other prayers, to ask that divine mercy suggest a sound plan to him concerning the place where he should lay the most holy remains.

The merciful ear of the Almighty, accustomed to hear his servants when they ask what is right, attended to these prayers.

Suddenly a light sent from heaven, burning like a torch, appeared before the façade of the basilica of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, and seemed to extend toward the place where the body is now buried.

When the man of God, Mummolus, saw this, he set aside all doubt and became completely certain that this place was suitable for the remains of the holy man.

Accordingly, putting aside his gnawing anxieties and giving complete credence to the vision, he carefully adorned the place that had been shown to him. On the day before the Nones of December, with great honor and divine praises, he eagerly committed a precious treasure to the earth and enclosed it in a poor vessel.

**Note:** The burial of Saint Benedict is recorded on this day in many manuscript martyrologies. Saint Odo, in the sermon that follows, chapter 2, likewise mentions two solemnities of Saint Benedict: the Translation and the Burial. Adrevald, in the *Book of Miracles*, chapter 22, calls the Burial the solemn feast of Saint Benedict, confessor of Christ, which according to ancient custom is celebrated annually on the day before the Nones of December.

After many years, on this same recurring day, the *Account* or *Bringing* of the body of Saint Benedict from the city of Orléans to the monastery of Fleury took place during the reign of Carloman, son of Louis the Stammerer.

This latter festival, which was still celebrated under the ancient name of Burial in the eleventh century—as is clear from the thirty-third chapter of Rodulfus Tortarius’s *Book of the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, published by John Bosco in fourth place under the name of an anonymous author—later acquired the name of the Bringing and obscured the memory of the earlier celebration of the Burial.

For how beloved of God and how worthy of love this treasure itself is, innumerable healings of weak bodies testify, and especially the cures of souls that the Lord continues to grant to mortals in honor of so great a man.

The nobility of this place itself can also be understood from the deeds of the blessed man. For when the same man had been shown a structure in the form of a sphere, it must be believed that he loved above all other places that place where he foresaw that his own bones would be transferred after leaving their former seats.

So many miracles have been manifested there to this day that, if they were written down, they would require a book of their own, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

# APPENDIX. From the proper history of the Translation [of the relics of] Saint Scholastica

[Note: This Translation is solemnly celebrated every year in the city of Le Mans on 11 July; on that day the sacred relics of Blessed Scholastica are carried through the city, which is decorated with hangings and carpets. After the monastery in which Saint Berarius had deposited Blessed Scholastica’s body was burned by the Normans [Col. 0909C] toward the end of the ninth century, the sacred casket containing her remains, rescued from the fury of the Normans, was transferred on 4 November, at the beginning of the tenth century, through the efforts of Count Hugh, into the urban church of Saint Peter, which is now collegiate. “During this storm of the Normans,” says the Old Author, whose fragment is reproduced in volume III of André Chesne’s *History of the Franks*, “the city of Le Mans was devastated, and the monastery of the holy virgin Scholastica, situated outside the city wall, was burned; but the body of that holy virgin was placed and preserved within the enclosure of the same city.” We learn from the very ancient anonymous chronicle prefixed by André Chesne to his *Deeds of the Normans* that this occurred in the year 669. Nor was it by a lesser miracle that the silver casket of Saint Scholastica was divinely snatched from the hands of the savage Calvinists. In 1562, on 3 April, they had been admitted into the city through the false persuasion of a certain utterly impure scoundrel named Merlin and through the treachery of certain citizens; after plundering sacred and secular possessions, on 10 July, the eve of Saint Scholastica’s Translation, they were suddenly seized by terror and turned to flight, with no one pursuing them [Col. 0910C]. The people of Le Mans attribute this to the merits of Saint Scholastica, whom they venerate as their protectress and principal patroness. What is circulated concerning the greater part of Saint Scholastica’s relics, transferred by Richildis, wife of Charles the Bald, in 874 to the monastery of Juvigny, is uncertain. Certainly Aigulf brought the dry bones of Saints Benedict and Scholastica from Italy; nevertheless, it is said that Saint Scholastica’s arm, complete with bones and flesh, is preserved in that monastery, as is also her girdle, which Anne of Austria, of happy memory, Queen of the Franks, used in childbirth when our most invincible king Louis XIV, now reigning, was born. Moreover, the Juvigny convent of nuns of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated on the border of the diocese of Trier, two leagues from the town of Satenay on the river Carus, has since its foundation been called Saint Scholastica’s, and she is still said frequently to perform miracles there.]

## Saint Scholastica

[Col. 0909]

At last, therefore, with the providence of the Lord going before them, following them, and accompanying them, they approached the city of Le Mans. The venerable lord Berarius, bishop, met them with the greatest devotion, together with vested priests and clerics of every rank, and reverently received the most sacred pledge of Saint Scholastica’s body. Entering the city, he carried it with the utmost veneration to the monastery which, as we have said, he had nobly and suitably founded from its foundations for this very purpose between the city wall and the river Sarthe. There he placed it decorously and solemnly behind the altar in the church that he had already dedicated [Col. 0910B] in honor of Saint Peter. Having arranged what was necessary for women consecrated to God and leading the regular life, within a short time he gathered into the same monastery for the service of the Lord a great number of noble women—no fewer than one hundred and sixty—and nobly enriched the monastery from the possessions of his bishopric. He also decreed that it should remain forever subject, with everything belonging to it, to his own see and to the mother church over which he presided.

[Col. 0909]

# MIRACLES OF SAINT BENEDICT PERFORMED IN GAUL AFTER THE TRANSLATION, DOWN TO THE MIDDLE OF THE NINTH CENTURY

Written by Adrevald.

(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, from the Floriacensis Library of Jean Bossier, etc.)

[Col. 0909]

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE. Praise and Description of Italy

[Col. 0909D]

The supreme and splendid glory of the Italian kingdom has clearly been treated and published with such application by the exceptionally powerful intellects of ancient authors that nothing now seems capable of being found which the diligence of our forefathers did not anticipate. For the most distinguished writers, the excellent subject matter of that laudable land seemed to offer abundant material: the temperate climate, the healthfulness of its places, the fertility of its soil, the exceedingly abundant shade of its forests, the sunny exposure of its hills [Col. 0911A], the lavish yields of its olive trees and vines, the charm of its new cities, the beauty also of its ancient towns, the fortunate course of its noble rivers, and, together with all these, the most prosperous abundance of every kind of thing.

But although the abundance, power, and most fitting vigor of Italy were attributed by the diligence of the ancients to so great an extent, the entire extent of the fatherland, stretched out in different directions, demands that it be considered with careful attention. For its excellence does not seem to embrace merely the advantages of a single region; rather, the beauty of the whole country and the prosperity of the kingdom appear compressed into a brief account, as though into a kind of collection. Since the vastness of the Italian kingdom—which was formerly called Magna Graecia because its cities and fortresses were, for the most part, founded by Greeks—when measured equally in length and breadth, exceeds its breadth by no small amount in length, resembling indeed an oak leaf, whose height exceeds its width, it has nevertheless become the mother of very many provinces and embraces them all in its most tender bosom.

But when the distinguished power of the Roman Empire wished to possess the conquered world by the right of war, it resolved to divide the extensive realms stretching far across Asia, Europe, and Libya into provinces and colonies, and thus to establish tributary territories among the legions. Among these, Italy too, having undergone the greatest division of the kingdoms of the western region, produced from itself eighteen provinces [Note: Paulus Warnefridus counts the same number of Italian provinces in book II of his *History of the Lombards*, chapters 15 and following.]. Of all these, the most distinguished is Valeria; adjoining it is Nursia, situated between Umbria, Campania, and Picenum [Col. 0911C], looking eastward toward the boundary of the Samnites, while Etruria marks its own limits.

Thus, as we have already indicated, although Italy abounds with singular nobility and overflows exceedingly with the fruits of every good, and although it is found to have been the nurturer of outstanding men in ancient times, it was nevertheless able to surpass itself through one most exalted offspring, when it brought forth the birth of the most blessed Father Benedict, desired by all mortals.

## [MIRACLES OF SAINT BENEDICT]

### CHAPTER X [Note: Jean Bossier divided the book of Miracles, which Adrevald wrote as one continuous work—as appears from the manuscript copies—into thirty-nine chapters, to which he added two sections by Adelerius. From the first nine chapters, which are merely repetitions collected from the Acts of Saints Benedict and Maurus and from other authors accessible to everyone, we have excerpted only a few verses [Col. 0911D]. In this chapter, after the preceding material, Adrevald describes Saint Benedict’s family and origin:

“Here indeed is Benedict, beloved of the Lord. According to the testimony of the eminent bishop Gregory, he arose from Nursia, which, as I have already stated, joined to Valeria and Etruria forms a single province. He not only illuminated that province by his birth, but also made all Italy, whose happiness is traced back to an ancient origin and is briefly described for this reason, illustrious through his gift. Finally, the ruins of their palace, together with a small building situated near the walls of the city of Nursia, testify to the great rank of the parents from whom he was born. From the foundations one may infer that the structure, of such immense and intricate workmanship, surpassed the palaces of any of the most powerful kings and could not be restored at moderate expense.”

The Bollandist companions reject this testimony of Adrevald and prefer the silence of Leo of Marsica concerning Saint Benedict’s more distinguished lineage, although they generously grant him noble birth. Benedict will undoubtedly be grateful to them; yet it is not worthwhile to quarrel over his nobility, sufficiently attested by Gregory the Great [Col. 0912C]. Nevertheless, these most fair-minded men seem somewhat too exacting toward Adrevald, who, although he has slipped in some matters, surpasses in learning and authority very many authors whom they themselves approve and have edited with great care and reverence. We do not reject the judgment and criticism of learned men concerning our subjects, but their prejudices.

In chapter 7, certain details in Adrevald deserve notice, since they shed some light on the departure of Saint Maurus from Cassino into Gaul:

“Accordingly, having departed from the monastery of Cassino during the days of Epiphany, on Thursday, they reached on that day an estate belonging to the same monastery, not far away.”

In the commonly circulated Faustus, however, it reads: “Therefore, on the Thursday of Epiphany, we undertook the journey,” etc. In the year of Christ 543, when, as we have said, Saint Maurus departed from Cassino, Epiphany fell on a Tuesday; consequently, if the former account is to be preferred, Maurus left Cassino on Thursday of the week of Epiphany, the third day. After Adrevald has narrated Saint Benedict’s death as it became known to Blessed Maurus in Gaul, he treats of the destruction of Cassino in chapter 10. From that point onward we reproduce the author’s complete work, supplying the chapter headings of Bossier’s edition.]

#### The Destruction of Cassino

[Col. 0912A]

When the emperor Justin, driven mad by the enormity of his crimes and shortly afterward deprived of life, Tiberius Constantine, a man energetic in governing the state, assumed the imperial insignia with the support of the entire nation. After governing it properly for seven years, he appointed Maurice as his successor, a man descended from the Greeks and born in Cappadocia. During his reign, Blessed Gregory was appointed bishop to the holy and apostolic see at Rome.

Meanwhile, Queen Brunhild firmly governed the kingdom of the Franks with Theodebert and Theoderic, sons of King Childebert, who had now reached the age of maturity. The nation of the Lombards, having entered Italy from the region of Venetia long ago, as we mentioned above, and inflicting devastation over most of it, was attempting to bring it under its own power.

As time went on, while Phocas was administering the Roman Empire—he had treacherously killed the emperor Maurice and his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine when he was the *strator* of Priscus the Patrician—the aforesaid people, under Agilulf, whom they had made their king, burst into almost the whole of Italy [Note: Do not understand this as referring to the first Lombard invasion of Italy, which took place under Alboin during the reign of the emperor Justin. We discussed the date of the destruction of Cassino in chapter 17 of the Life of Saint Benedict.], and attacked the city of Rome.

Not long afterward, the monastery of the most blessed Father Benedict, situated at Cassino, was invaded at night by the robbers of that people, plundered, and destroyed. Although they plundered everything, they could not seize even one of the monks, so that the prophecy of the venerable Father, which he had foreseen long before, might be fulfilled. He had said: “I was scarcely able to obtain from the Lord that souls should be granted to me from this place.”

The monks, fleeing from that place, came to Rome, carrying the book of the holy Rule which the aforesaid Father had composed, together with some of his other writings, as well as a weight of bread, a measure of wine, and whatever else of the furnishings they had been able to carry away.

After eight years, during which he had utterly ruined the entire empire, Phocas was killed by a fitting kind of death, and Heraclius succeeded him, ruling the empire for twenty-six years. Heraclonas [alternative reading: Heracleonas], together with his mother Martina, succeeded him for two years. Then Constantine, the son of Constantine [Note: This passage must be emended from Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 51, as follows: “His son Heraclon, with his mother Martina, assumed the government and ruled the empire for two years. When he died, his brother Constantine, another son of Heraclius, succeeded him and ruled for six months. When he too had died, Constantine, his son, ascended to the royal dignity and held the kingdom for twenty-eight years.”], succeeded according to the order of succession for twenty-nine years. During his reign, Grimoald seemed to be successfully organizing the Italian kingdom for himself, while Chlodoveus, son of Dagobert, governed the Franks very well.

### CHAPTER XI. The Translation of Saints Benedict and Scholastica. The Testimony of Paul the Deacon

At this time, therefore, Mummolus, abbot of the monastery of Floriacum, situated in the territory of Orléans [Col. 0913B] above the river Loire, having been warned by God in a dream, sent, with the consent of those who served God alongside him, one of his own venerable monks, named Aigulf, so that he might transfer here the body of Christ’s most holy confessor Benedict. For he asserted that this had been divinely revealed to him.

Unexpectedly, envoys of the bishop of the city of Le Mans joined him. They too had been invited by divine revelation to transfer the body of the most blessed virgin Scholastica, sister of the eminent Father. Since the history of this matter is readily available—namely, because it was written by Adrevald himself—we have judged it superfluous to insert it in this brief work.

Paul the monk, whom I mentioned above, bears witness to this most sacred translation of the blessed brother and sister, Benedict and Scholastica, in book VI of the history of his people, saying:

“About this time”—there can be no doubt that he means during the reign of Constantine—“when, after some years had passed, the fortress of Cassino, where the body of the most blessed Benedict rested, had become deserted, Franks came from the region of Le Mans and Orléans. Pretending that they would spend the night beside the sacred body, they removed the bones of that Father and of his sister and carried them into their own country, where two monasteries were built separately in honor of each of them.”

### CHAPTER XII. The Condition of Frankish Affairs

[Col. 0913D]

When Justin the Younger had assumed the empire after the death of Constantine and had completed ten years in power, he was deprived of the imperial dignity by Leo and banished into exile. Tiberius took up arms against him, removed him from the imperial burden, and thrust him back into prison.

At that time, in Gaul, as the glory of the Franks declined, the royal household was administered by the prefects of the palace, while the kings, through ignorance and indolence, bore only the empty royal name. For both the wealth and power of the kingdom remained in the hands of the palace prefects, who were called mayors of the palace and to whom supreme authority belonged. Nothing else was left to the king except to be content with the royal name, sit on the throne with his hair flowing loose and his beard hanging down, and present the appearance of a ruler; to hear envoys arriving from every direction; and, when they departed, to return from his supposed authority the answers that he had been taught or even ordered to give.

Apart from the useless name of king and the precarious allowance for life which the prefect of the palace supplied to him as he thought fit, he possessed nothing of his own except a single estate, and that one of very small income. There he had a house and a few servants to provide him with what he needed and render him service.

Whenever he had to go anywhere, he traveled in a cart drawn by yoked oxen and driven in rustic fashion by an oxherd [Note: Adrevald seems excessive here in disparaging the condition of the kings of that period, although everyone agrees that it was entirely degenerate.]. In this way he used to go to the palace, to the public assembly of his people, which was held every year for the benefit of the kingdom, and in the same way he used to return home.

The prefect of the palace, however, managed the administration of the kingdom and everything that had to be done or arranged at home or abroad. At that time Arnulf [Note: Saint Arnulf was neither mayor of the palace nor did he govern the palace under those indolent kings; certainly he was not a monk before he became a bishop. Read his Life under the year 640.]—a man of exceptional nobility and commendable life—administered this office together with his son Ansegisel.

Later, renouncing the glory of the world, Arnulf was ordained bishop of Metz by the acclamation and choice of the clergy and people, and strove to live magnificently in his episcopate. At length, choosing the eremitical life and offering every service to lepers, he lived with the greatest continence until his death. Anastasius was then governing the insignia of the Roman Empire, while Liutprand, after Aripert, had brought the leadership of the Italian kingdom under his own rule.

### CHAPTER XIII. The Monastery of Cassino Is Restored by Petronax

About this time a certain citizen of Brescia named Petronax, preserving the continence of a religious life, came to Rome while Blessed Gregory was exercising the episcopate, to reveal the desire of his holy devotion. Finally, at the urging of that most holy bishop, the aforesaid Petronax approached with the greatest devotion the monastery that had once been built by the eminent Father Benedict in the fortress of Mount Cassino and, by the permission of almighty God, destroyed by the Lombards.

There, together with several men endowed with prudent simplicity who had already desired to inhabit that place, he began to live in the religious habit with the closest bond of charity. They appointed this same man as their elder.

Not long afterward, with divine mercy cooperating and the merits of the outstanding Father Benedict lending their support, he became the father of many monks, both noble and humble, who gathered there around him. Thus, after repairing dwellings suitable for the monastic order, they began to live under the yoke of the holy Rule and according to the institution of the most blessed Father Benedict.

In this manner that most holy monastery of Cassino was restored to the condition in which it is now seen, when nearly one hundred and ten years had elapsed [Note: This calculation, as well as almost the entire section, is taken from Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 40. Yet, from what we said in chapter 17 of the Life of Saint Benedict, nearly one hundred and forty years seem to have elapsed between the destruction and restoration of Cassino.] since, by the hidden will of God, that place had begun to lack human habitation.

Afterward, Pope Zacharias, beloved of the Lord, provided much assistance to this venerable man Petronax: books of Holy Scripture, as well as other things that could benefit the monastery. Moreover, with paternal generosity, he granted the Rule that the eminent Father himself had written with his holy hands.

### CHAPTER XIV. The Deeds of Charles Martel. His Sons Pippin and Carloman. Carloman Becomes a Monk

Meanwhile, in Gaul, after Ansegisel the mayor of the palace and his son Pippin had passed from human life, Charles, the son of Pippin, took control of the entire Frankish nation. Although this occurred after many wars, with God’s help he wrested power from the tyrant Reinfred (Reginfred in Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 42) [Col. 0915C] and subjected it to his authority.

Applying himself with the greatest energy to military affairs, he crushed the tyrants throughout France who claimed dominion for themselves. For this reason he removed many estates from ecclesiastical ownership and joined them to the royal treasury, then endeavored to distribute them among his own soldiers.

Furthermore, he defeated the Saracens, who were attempting to occupy Gaul, in two great battles: one in Aquitaine near the city of Poitiers, and the other near Narbonne beside the river Berre. He defeated them so thoroughly that he compelled them to return to Spain.

Because he knew how never to yield to those who opposed him and to spare no one, he long bore among later generations the nickname *Tudites*, acquired from the conduct of affairs. *Tudites* are the hammers of smiths, whose blows crush every hardness.

He made a treaty with Liutprand and sent him his son Pippin, so that, according to the custom of faithful Christians, Liutprand might first cut his hair and become his spiritual father. Liutprand fulfilled this most gladly and sent the boy, richly endowed with gifts, back to his father (Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 53).

As a result, when the most sacred bishop Gregory sent an embassy to him, entreating him to free the holy Roman Church from the tyranny of the Lombards, he, weighing earthly things more heavily than heavenly ones, treated the request with contempt.

When Charles had therefore been removed from human affairs after a long administration of the kingdom, his two sons, Pippin and Carloman, assumed the government, divided in harmonious partnership, for several years under Childeric, king in name only.

After some time had passed, Carloman left to his brother the portion of the kingdom that he had undertaken to govern and, inflamed with love for a contemplative life, withdrew to Rome for leisure. This occurred at the urging of Blessed Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, who, having been expelled from his own see by Carloman’s father without any fault on his part, had been exiled to Hasbainia, to Saint Trudo; and also at the urging of Saint Boniface, bishop of the Frisians. Both of them showed Carloman in bodily visions the damnation of his father among the dead [Note: Baronius and others consign this to the realm of fables; the matter will be treated in the Life of Saint Eucherius in the following century.].

Despising with all the effort of his mind the laborious dignity of temporal kingship, and changing his habit, he merited to receive the grace of ecclesiastical tonsure from Blessed Zacharias, Roman pope.

Finally, having adopted the discipline of monastic life, he enjoyed the desired leisure for some time on Mount Soracte, at the church of Blessed Sylvester, where he built a monastery together with the brothers who had joined him for this purpose.

But when many nobles from Francia traveled solemnly to Rome to fulfill their vows and refused to pass him by as their former lord, interrupting with frequent greetings the leisure in which he took the greatest delight, they compelled him to change his residence. When he saw that such crowds obstructed his purpose, he left the mountain and withdrew into the province of Samnium, to the monastery of Saint Benedict situated in the aforementioned fortress of Cassino. There he completed the remainder of his mortal life in religious conduct.

### CHAPTER XV. Pippin Is Made King. The Monks of Cassino Appeal to Pope Zacharias Concerning the Body of Saint Benedict. Zacharias’s Letter on This Matter

While these things were taking place, Pippin, having attained supreme authority in the Frankish kingdom, by order of Stephen, Roman pontiff, deposed Childeric, the most ineffectual of kings, cut his hair, and forced him to live privately after thrusting him into a monastery. Then, by the authority of that same pontiff, he was made king, having previously been prefect of the palace, and for approximately fifteen years or somewhat more governed the Frankish kingdom alone with great ability.

At that time the monks of the aforesaid monastery of Cassino, with the support of Carloman, whom we mentioned above, came to Rome to lay before the most holy pope Zacharias their grievance and sorrow concerning the body of the most sacred Father Benedict, which had been transferred from its own soil into Gaul.

Their grief had long since grown cold in their hearts because of the distance between the lands and the passage of time, and they no longer had hope of obtaining what they sought. But when Carloman entered their holy community, their long-dead hope revived. They approached the holy bishop and asked him to send a letter to Pippin, king of the Franks, so that, honoring the authority and petitions of so great a pontiff, he might restore the body of the eminent Father to its ancestral place.

The aforesaid pontiff, yielding with tears to their petitions, composed a letter of apostolic authority and sent it through Carloman and the brothers who had come with him to Pippin, king of Francia. The form of the sacred letter was as follows:

“Zacharias, bishop, servant of the servants of God, presiding over the holy see of the prince of the apostles, Blessed Peter, sends greetings to all the bishops and priests of the Church of the Franks.

“The eminent Apostle says: ‘For those who love God, all things work together for good’ (Romans 8). And again the same Apostle says: ‘While we have opportunity, let us do good to all’ (Galatians 6). Scripture likewise says: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things’ (Romans 10).

“The religious abbot and priest of the monastery of Blessed Benedict at Cassino, and Carloman, a monk beloved of God and brother of our son Pippin, the most excellent mayor of the palace, have made known to us through these present religious servants of God, monks, that words of concord and peace should be arranged between him and his brother Grifo. By giving this very admonition, we direct our message to the eminence of our aforesaid son Pippin, so that they may return to the concord of peace, with you as mediators of peace for God’s sake.

“Moreover, concerning the body of Blessed Benedict, which was stolen from its tomb, we urge your love and holiness to lend a willing ear so that it may be restored to him. First of all, let brother return to brother in the right of peace, and let iniquity be put to shame in their midst; and let the love of God, as you preach and administer it, increase among them.

“Then, at the request of the servants of God, let the eminence of our beloved son Pippin, with your holy cooperation, undoubtedly send back the body of the aforesaid Blessed Benedict to its proper place, so that those servants of God may rejoice in having their Father restored to them, while you may possess an everlasting reward and praise because you will have acted justly in ensuring that the most holy man’s body is returned to the tomb from which it was secretly taken.

“Your holiness need not fear that God will take offense at this good work of restoration. For it is believed that the aforesaid religious servants of God have been moved to obtain this through the prayers and will of the very man whose body they seek. Farewell.”

### CHAPTER XVI. Carloman’s Embassy to Gaul. Remigius, Bishop of Rouen, Demands the Body of Saint Benedict from the Monks of Floriacum

[Col. 0918A]

Having received the letter of the holy pope, Carloman [Note: Carloman came from Cassino into Gaul during the pontificate of Stephen III, as is clear from Einhard, Anastasius the Librarian, Herkempert, the Annals of Bertin, and other contemporary or nearly contemporary authors, all of whom are silent concerning this first embassy of Carloman. It is indeed more likely that Carloman, fleeing the company of secular men, after obtaining from Pope Zacharias a letter concerning the recovery of Saint Benedict’s body, did not carry this out personally but through envoys sent to Gaul, as a manuscript history of the bishops of Rouen, composed in the eleventh century, teaches in these words:

“Pippin, at the request of Carloman, his monkish brother, commanded the aforesaid Remigius, archbishop, to go to the place called Floriacum and to return to the envoys of Carloman the body of Saint Benedict, which rested there,” etc.

Perhaps Adrevald, having examined Zacharias’s letter, was led to write that Carloman himself had served as ambassador. Later Hugh of Floriacum, who asserts that this occurred in the tenth year of the emperor Constantine, and others received the account from Adrevald.]

and the brothers who were with him set out for Gaul. They approached Pippin and produced the sacred apostolic letter. With tearful lamentation they submitted their grievous complaint, begging that the pious ashes and bones of the Father, worthy of reverence by all mortals and secretly removed, be restored in abundance by the authority of the king and with regard for justice to his most devoted sons.

They did not fear that they would incur guilt for any offense in this matter, since the blameless path of righteousness was recognized as supporting them.

The merciful prince was moved by these mournful complaints. At the same time, by agreeing with the holy see, he offered it his support; and, consulting his brother’s wishes, he sent Remigius, bishop of Rouen and his kinsman, to the monastery of Floriacum with authority to fulfill the petition of Carloman and the brothers. By the king’s command, even if the brothers were unwilling, Remigius was to exhume the sacred relic and return it as quickly as possible to Carloman and the brothers traveling with him.

Having accepted the commission, the bishop hurried to the monastery, announced the king’s orders, and attempted to carry them out.

At that time Medo was abbot over this holy flock. When he had received the royal commands with great distress, he said that he could not return what had been entrusted to him, since he rejoiced that he had received it for preservation, not for restoration. He added:

“The most holy Father himself permitted himself to be brought here of his own will; he himself, through a sacred vision, invited his servants to convey him here for his own sake. We unworthy men received the most sacred limbs of the eminent Father; we welcomed his pious ashes and have devotedly taken care to preserve them until now.

“But if, because of sins committed by us, it should please him to leave Gaul and seek his native fields, I confess that this lies within his power, and that it is in no way lawful for us to oppose his will.

“But if—as has remained fixed in our hearts with the most certain faith—by divine command and merciful providence, for the salvation of many souls, he voluntarily sought these distant places, situated almost at the very edge of the ocean, after leaving his native ones, know with certainty that you will return to your own country unable to obtain your desire.”

After saying this, shedding many tears, he ordered the doors of the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, where the sacred members lay, to be opened, and instructed his men to keep watch before the doors.

### CHAPTER XVII. The Matter Is Prevented by Divine Power

He himself, remaining inside the church of the blessed prince of the apostles with the brothers of the entire congregation, prostrated on the ground and with his face wet with tears, implored the Lord’s help, asking that he not permit the pledge of his beloved confessor—bestowed on his servants not because of any preceding merits but solely as a gratuitous gift—to be taken away because of the enormity of any crimes.

Who among mortals could express with what tears, sighs, and cries of lamentation this prayer was uttered? Who could adequately describe the hearts of the Father and his sons, struggling in grief—men of the most mature, sometimes even extreme, age, of differing character and varying health?

Certainly, one could see the hearts of the Father, worn down by the wound of sorrow, looking upon the tearful faces of the grieving sons, while from neither side could a comforter arise. From one side, the old men, who had long been accustomed to show the younger brothers the affection of love, could offer no comfort; from the other, the younger men could give their fathers no strength of assistance.

The situation was dragging their troubled hearts now here, now there. While the two parties contended with such intense emotion and those whose entire spirit was invested in the matter fortified themselves with prayers, the all-powerful Majesty chose, in its accustomed mercy, to settle so great a dispute.

Indeed, when Bishop Remigius entered the church with his men and approached the sacred tomb, they were suddenly struck by such blindness that they could neither see one another’s faces nor even discern by touch in which direction they ought to proceed.

Overcome by great terror, they could think of nothing except the loss of their lives. Some threw themselves upon the ground to await the Lord’s mercy; others, seeking safety in flight, ran here and there, crying out and begging that help be brought to them.

While they were in great confusion and tumult, the abbot, summoned, came running with the brothers. Taking them by the hand, he led the violators of the holy church out of it; they had experienced the divine vengeance sufficiently and abundantly.

Then, after they had prostrated themselves on the ground and asked pardon, he mercifully forgave them and most kindly gave them relics from the body of that most precious confessor.

After they had recovered and all necessities for the journey had been generously supplied, he sent them back to their own country.

When they returned to the palace, they reported to the most excellent King Pippin the great power of God active in that place through the merits of holy Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, and of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as well as through the intercession of the eminent Father Benedict. By their earnest exhortations they diligently induced him to be generous toward this sacred monastery [Note: An anonymous author of a manuscript history of the bishops of Rouen describes this event more briefly, writing of Remigius:

“When he came to the place, and summoned the abbot who at that time governed the monastery and was called Medo, explaining the king’s commands, he entered the church with Carloman’s envoys. When they approached the tomb of the blessed man, they were struck by sudden blindness. Then, shaken by great terror, they prostrated themselves flat on the ground before the aforesaid abbot and the brothers of the place, begging for mercy and asking them to pray to the Lord on their behalf, so that he might forgive them. Blessed Remigius promised that he would never again remove the saint’s body from that place. What more need be said? They were immediately heard, and Blessed Remigius and his companions recovered their former health. He then asked the aforesaid abbot to give them relics of the man’s body, lest the place where he had devoutly served God should be deprived of so great a protection. The abbot willingly consented. Thus the envoys returned to their own country, and Remigius returned to his.”]

### CHAPTER XVIII. Charles and Carloman Succeed Their Father Pippin. King Carloman Dies. The Deeds of Charles. — The Rapacity of Count Raho Is Punished
Meanwhile, King Pippin, as we believe, having departed to the heavenly realms, [Col. 0920A] his sons Charles and Carloman undertook the administration of the kingdom. Having solemnly convened a general assembly, they divided the whole body of the kingdom equally between them: Charles took for governance that part of the kingdom which their father Pippin had chiefly held, while Carloman took that over which their uncle Carloman had presided.

[The words enclosed in brackets are missing from our Saint-Germain copy.]

But after administering the kingdom for two years, Carloman died of illness. Charles, therefore, after his brother’s death, with the consent of all the Franks, assumed the monarchy of the entire people. He undertook war against the Lombard people, who possessed Italy—long since withdrawn from Roman authority—under various forms of right, at the request and entreaties of Adrian, bishop of the city of Rome. Previously, this undertaking had been assumed with great difficulty by his father as well, at the supplication of Pope Stephen, [Col. 0920B] for certain of the leading Franks with whom he used to consult resisted his will so greatly that they openly proclaimed that they would abandon him as king and return home.

Nevertheless, the campaign was then undertaken against King Aistulf and very swiftly completed. For, by besieging that king for only a few days at Pavia, he compelled him both to give hostages and to restore the towns and fortresses seized from the Romans, and to pledge by oath that he would not reclaim what had been returned.

Indeed, Charles did not allow the war he had begun to be interrupted until he had forced King Desiderius, wearied by a long siege, to surrender; compelled his son Adalgis, in whom everyone’s hopes seemed to be placed, to withdraw not only from the kingdom but also from Italy; [Col. 0920C] restored everything taken from the Romans; subjected all Italy to his authority; and set his own son Pippin over the conquered land as king.

Finally, since royal power had been enlarged, it was necessary to appoint dukes over the kingdom and the subjugated people, men who would compel them to observe both the administration of the laws and the customs customary among the Franks. For this reason the palace came to be emptied of the leading men and dukes of the people, because he had assigned many men of Frankish noble birth to his son, so that they might defend and govern with him the kingdom newly acquired.

On this account, as some think—and, in the view of most, probably because he had grown suspicious of the loyalty of the Franks, which he had once tested during the conspiracy when the Saxon war began, and again during the conspiracy of his natural son Pippin—[Col. 0920D] he entrusted the care of the kingdom to certain of his servants whose fiscal obligations had been relieved, and above all appointed Ragon count over the people of Orléans, Sturmin over those of Bourges, Bertmund over the Auvergnats, and placed others over other regions as he saw fit.

But Raho, as his nature demanded, growing excessively insolent through cunning and becoming more cruel through greed, observed that everything apparently contained within the boundaries of Orléans was subject to him, except only the monastery of Saint Benedict, which was then governed by Abbot Radulf. He therefore resolved, after killing the abbot, to seize that monastery. He would have carried this out without delay, had the most merciful piety of the Creator not decided to oppose so great a crime.

Trusting in the confidence that he would accomplish his wickedness, he sent one of his henchmen to the king to report that Abbot Radulf was dead; then, immediately and almost at once, he sent another to summon Abbot Radulf to a personal interview. The envoy sent to the king hastened to the palace, carried out his instructions, and, since the business had not yet been completed, remained for some time in the palace. Meanwhile, Abbot Radulf mounted horses with a few companions and hastened to the interview with his deceitful friend.

As he was making his journey, the count entered the bath and was attending to his body. While he was still sitting in the bath, the abbot entered the little monastery of Saint Gundulf [Note: [Col. 0921D] The little monastery of Saint Gundulf, commonly called Saint-Gondon, in the diocese of Bourges on the Loire, is now a priory subject to the abbey of Saint-Florent at Saumur.]—for the count was then staying there—and encountered a certain dwarf [pomilionem; pumilionem seu nanum, “dwarf”], named Gauringisus. He served the count by entertaining him and, by gestures as well as speech, warned the abbot of the count’s ambush and urged him to seek the aid of flight.

Accordingly, the abbot turned back, drove his horse forward with his spurs, and at a swift pace regained the bed of the Loire. Boarding a boat, he crossed to the nearer bank and quickly returned to the monastery.

Meanwhile, word was brought to the count [Col. 0921C] that Abbot Radulf had been there but had quickly returned. Seeing that the abbot had outstripped him completely and that no opportunity remained for his malice and deceit, the count, violently stirred by gall, leapt from the bath, wrapped himself in a linen cloth, and threw himself upon a bed to rest for a while, with his concubine Deutheria sitting at his head.

When he had been sunk into a deeper sleep, an old man wearing a monk’s habit appeared before him in a vision; a boy dressed in the same manner followed him. The old man addressed him as follows:

“Count, what have I done to deserve this, that you wished to kill my abbot?”

When the count answered by denying that he had wished to kill his abbot, the old man looked at him with a grim expression, struck his head with the curved staff he was carrying, and said:

“By this head I assure you that you will most certainly repent this deed—but uselessly.”

Awakened by the blow, he leapt from his bed and, frantic with fear, cried out:

“Woe is me, woe is me! I am dying now!”

When those standing around him asked in terror why he was uttering such words as though he were out of his mind, he answered their questions, pale and trembling:

“While I was resting in bed, Saint Benedict stood before me, venerable and beautiful with white hair. A little boy, himself also a monk, followed him, and he began to accuse me of why I wished to kill his abbot. When I replied that I had absolutely no wish to kill his abbot, he struck my head violently with the staff he was carrying and brought me near to death. At the same time he threatened that I would very quickly undergo a useless repentance for this deed.”

As he said these things, pain quickly penetrating his inward parts, on the following night he joined the death of his body to the death of his soul and, through the service of “Manum” [daemonum, “demons”], hurled his most wretched soul down to the depths of Erebus. But Abbot Radulf, having learned of his swift, though belated, death, sent an envoy to the king to announce both his own survival and Raho’s fatal funeral rites.

## CHAPTER XIX. The ships of the people of Fleury are exempt from tolls

[Col. 0922B]

By royal munificence, the most sacred monastery had long ago received from the ancient kings of the Franks, by a document of their own decree, the privilege that four ships should sail freely along the course of the Loire, exempt from every fiscal obligation.

When, therefore, in the time of the aforementioned count, one of these ships had reached the city of Nantes to transport salt, and on its return had passed safely, in accordance with the royal decree, through all the ports and cities along its route [Note: [Col. 0922D] See this charter among the writings of Louis the Pious, volume 104 of the *Patrologia Latina*.], it arrived at the city of Orléans. There the city’s toll collectors detained the ship, and its master was brought to trial on account of the toll.

Although he protested the royal privilege, the collector, disregarding royal authority, confiscated the ship laden with salt for the treasury and entrusted it, together with the other ships, to the port administrator.

These events took place on a Sunday; but at about the third hour of the day, while everyone was occupied with the celebration of Mass, the ship that was being held with the others in the fiscal port suddenly moved away without a human pilot and made for the middle of the Loire, where the stronger current usually flows. There, swimming vigorously against the opposing stream, it reached the place called Posterula, which to this day is called Saint Benedict’s, and came to land there.

People came running from every part of the city to see the unknown miracle, and in their amazement they uttered cries of wonder and encouragement:

“See, citizens! Behold how Benedict, the beloved of the Lord, the new sailor, guides his own ship through the middle of the waves without a mortal pilot!”

Finally, the entire boldness of the treasury officials was thrown into confusion, and thereafter they restrained themselves from such folly.

## CHAPTER XX. Louis succeeds Charlemagne. The condition of the kingdom and the Church under him. The savagery of Count Odo. Saint Benedict cares for his own

[Col. 0922D]

When the august Charles the Great, emperor of the Franks, died, his son Louis assumed the reins of imperial government. During his reign, as the Frankish kingdom was worn down by various disturbances, the condition of the Church also seemed to be shaken by a great and severe storm.

For while his sons were plotting various measures against their father, internal conflict arose, insofar as the state of the entire kingdom was concerned: the father sought to strip some men of their honors on account of their merits and to heap wealth upon others, while the sons, for their part, tried to raise up those whom he had cast down and to depose those whom he had exalted. Like a maritime storm, they scattered their subjects in every direction. Consequently, the affairs of the various churches of Christ suffered the gravest losses.

Among them, the Church of Orléans, together with the neighboring holy places that appeared to stand under the rule of clerics or monks belonging to the Lord, was afflicted by no small harassment. For when Count Matfrid, formerly count of Orléans, had been deprived of his honors on account of negligence, Odo was substituted in his place.

He, lifted up by gross insolence against his own nature, attempted to bring under his personal control everything subject to the jurisdiction of the Church of Orléans, except the matricula—that is, the property of the poor—and also the abbey of Saint Aignan and that of Saint Benedict.

When the monks of the monastery of Saint Benedict saw this, they took counsel, entrusted themselves solely to the mercy of the Lord, and sent a very large number of their brothers to the aforementioned count, who was raging with excessive tyranny, carrying with them the relics of the saints. With every kind of prayer they begged him not to incur so great a sacrilege, nor to transfer to wicked uses the property entrusted to the sacred order, but rather to allow the servants of God freely to administer the possessions committed to them by the Lord. This petition had no effect upon him.

At that time he had begun to prepare an expedition, gathering forces from every direction, against Lanthert, Matfrid, and their associates, who were living in the regions of Neustria and had defected from the emperor to Lothar. He had also ordered the venerable Jonah, bishop of Orléans, and Boso, abbot of Saint Benedict, to take part in this expedition, although he had unjustly claimed their property for himself.

Meanwhile, auxiliary forces from Upper Burgundy, hastening toward that war and occupying both banks of the Loire, devastated everything with their plundering. Abbot Boso confronted their madness and ordered boats to be kept ready in the port, so that if the people arriving from the upper regions occupied the nearer bank, the sailors could transport across the river all the monastery’s property—its entire wealth in large and small animals and in other movable goods. If the army proceeded along the farther route, they were, conversely, to do the same with the aforesaid possessions, transporting everything to this side of the river.

A priest named Hercambald, a man of good life and reputation, was placed in charge of this undertaking. He had lived according to the rule in this same monastery, and he confidently declared to everyone, under oath to the truth, that he had certainly learned by personal observation the events I have undertaken to record.

While the army’s departure lasted for three days, the labor not only of the sailors but also of the animals themselves became excessive, and severe weariness likewise prevailed because of the sleepless watches. Exhausted by continuous vigils, the priest went home toward twilight on the third night. Overcome by impatience for sleep, he threw himself upon the straw of a bed; and as soon as he was able to obtain some sleep, he saw in a vision a person standing before him in monastic habit and holding a staff in his hand. A boy in the same habit followed him.

The figure therefore addressed the astonished priest kindly:

“What is it, brother? Why are you lying here in this fashion?”

Looking at the figure’s venerable countenance, he replied:

“Lord, it is known to you and to everyone how much harm Count Odo and the people who support him inflict upon us and our household. Therefore, while I anxiously and zealously attend to the duty imposed upon me by the abbot, so that our household may be able to save its possessions from the plunderers by escape across the river, I have been overcome by sleep and thrown myself upon this straw.”

The elder, approving the priest’s words, answered:

“I know that what you say is true. But before I satisfy, with a most truthful promise, the things over which you sorrowfully complain, I wish to raise a small complaint myself. It is very strange that our brothers accuse me of negligence, as though I had no concern for their distress, and as though, oppressed by lethargy, I were sleeping while they were exposed to it. This certainly cannot happen.

“For if you apply yourselves to obeying the commands of the Almighty, and if you do not sluggishly carry out the precepts of the rule handed down to you by God through me, everything adverse will become prosperous, enemies will be made friends, and the supporter of all good things will deny you his grace in nothing.

“As for the wrong now being done to you, know that the judgment of the most merciful Creator of all has already become favorable toward you, and that he who wickedly took up the weapons of tyranny against the Church will certainly not pass the seventh sunrise before he suffers repentance for this deed.

“Therefore, have confidence in the Lord and take strength in him.”

While the elder was speaking these pleasing words, the priest asked the boy by whatever gestures he could make who this person of such great veneration was. The boy answered in a low voice:

“He is our Father, Saint Benedict.”

## CHAPTER XXI. The death of Odo and the others

When the aforementioned priest had learned that the most blessed Father had conversed with him in a vision, he began, in the sight of everyone present, to drag himself from the same little bed with outstretched arms, as though he might be able to grasp the footprints of the one whom he had seen standing before him. At the same time, he anxiously uttered sounds like a murmur, which those standing around could not understand at all.

At last he awoke and, turning his gaze this way and that, ran about, repeating once and again in a supplicating and almost tearful voice:

“Where has my lord, Saint Benedict, gone?”

“I call upon the Lord, knower of all hidden things, as witness that just now I saw him here in bodily form and that he spoke with me.”

Without delay, the priest himself came to the monastery and carefully related to the fathers of that place everything he had learned through the vision, as well as the most holy Father’s warnings and exhortation.

By this report the saddened brothers were relieved, and they encouraged one another to give thanks to God, who was protecting those abandoned by human aid with his customary defense.

The days of the promised period had not yet run their course when, behold, a certain cleric named Herrardus, having escaped from the army’s camp, arrived at the monastery about the eighth hour of the day after the battle had ended [Col. 0925A], and struck the whole monastery with a terrible report.

He announced that the bloodiest slaughter had occurred among our men, that the victorious hand of the enemy had prevailed, and that all the forces, together with the auxiliaries gathered from every direction, had scattered here and there in flight. He reported that the leaders of the war—Odo; his brother William, count of the people of Blois; Theuto, abbot of Saint Martin; and Guido, count of Maine—had died, along with many other men of high reputation.

The brothers, deeply afflicted by this report, devoted themselves intensely to entreating the Lord for the great slaughter of the Christian people. Although some of those who had taken part in so great a disaster had severely oppressed the property subject to the rights of the Church—not merely oppressed it, but completely carried it away in the manner of pagans—the hearts of the servants of God were nevertheless shaken by compassion according to human nature. They recalled what the souls of those who persevere in evil suffer among the dead beneath the final light of life, by what torments they are tortured, and what a deadly recompense the end of their lives had deserved.

Therefore, mindful of the divine command:

“Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5),

they resolved by common counsel to pour out prayers to the Lord for these men, so that, even if they did not deserve to be released from everlasting torments, they might at least be punished by the strict Judge with milder penalties.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] It was the opinion of certain ancient writers that the damned might be treated more mildly through the intercessions of the living. The later school of theologians holds the contrary opinion, although the former view had not yet been condemned by the Church.]

## CHAPTER XXII. The solemn feast of Saint Benedict. Benedict provides it with fish

[Col. 0925C]

The solemn feast of Saint Benedict, Christ’s confessor, was approaching. By ancient custom it is celebrated every year on the day before the Nones of December, when crowds of many peoples ordinarily gather at the monastery in memory of so great a Father. In addition, a considerable number of religious men and servants of God are present.

A custom handed down from ancient times had occupied a long period: after the abundant gift of spiritual refreshment, the bodies also were to be most carefully refreshed with earthly food, as an act of generosity. But although supplies of every kind suitable for this purpose flowed in from every direction, there was a complete lack of an abundance of fish sufficient to lend some grace to so great a celebration.

The abbot was extremely anxious, and the brothers assigned to procure them likewise sent people in every direction, to see whether they might somehow be relieved of so great a shortage of fish through someone’s assistance.

But when human industry failed, and all had already despaired, cast down in spirit and possessing nothing in which they could hope, they were roused from so great a sleep of sorrow by the merits and intervention of the illustrious and truly blessed Benedict.

As the vigil of the aforesaid feast was approaching, a certain brother, according to custom, was lying at night in his own bed with the other brothers. In a vision he saw that he had been transported across the Loire and was standing at the place where the stream commonly called the Obla flows into the Loire, on the bank of that little river.

On the opposite bank of the aforesaid river he saw a cleric—namely, a monk—standing. The monk’s appearance was unknown to him, but his countenance was venerable. Carrying a staff curved in the ancient manner of bishops, he was driving out of the deep water an enormous herd of swine, pushing it with a great din toward the side on which the monk appeared to be standing.
