After awakening and completing the nocturnal office, the brother secretly summoned the monastery’s dean, related the dream, and urged him to go with the brothers to the river, eager to fish. He said that he knew for certain that the beloved soldier of Christ would grant his fellow soldiers an exceedingly abundant catch of fish.

This, he thought, was what the vision signified: the swine evidently represented fish, while the unknown person in venerable dress signified the great Benedict.

Strengthened in spirit by this vision, the brothers prepared their nets with eager rivalry and ran to the river. Having spread their nets here and there, they pulled an abundance of the scaly herd from the water, so great that transporting the fish required a cart.

The blessed Father knew how to raise his novices by such benefits, as they clung tirelessly to the Lord’s commandments. Although he was still burdened with a mortal body, he had been able to help disciples suffering from a shortage of bread by providing two hundred measures of flour.

If, then, he so greatly comforts bodies with earthly nourishment, how much assistance do we suppose he gives to the salvation of souls, and how does he enable them, laden with the fruits of good works, to enter joyfully into the delights of eternal happiness?

## CHAPTER XXIII. A man disabled in both feet is healed

When the report spread throughout the world that the saving grace of Christ was available to mortals suffering from bodily affliction, people from every direction began to seek the monastery and the threshold of Christ’s confessor Benedict, so that they might obtain the desired gift of health.

Among the others, a certain man who was disabled in both legs arrived. He had never been able to make a journey on his feet; rather, with the aid of little stools, he had been accustomed to drag himself along the ground on his knees.

He kept vigil for a long time in the basilica of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, beside the sacred ashes. At last, through the regard of divine mercy and the intervention of the beloved Lord Benedict, he was restored to health and did not delay in giving thanks to the Lord and to his intercessor according to the measure of understanding granted to him.

Since unfamiliar pain and considerable exertion in extending his long-contracted sinews had severely afflicted the man, who was still very weak, he could not immediately travel along an unknown road. His trembling knees first had to become firmer and steadier after the pain had been removed.

He was therefore kept in the house assigned as lodging for the poor, where he received a sufficient meal with the other residents of the *ptochium* (πτωχεῖον, a poorhouse or lodging for the poor). After several days the sick man grew stronger, and his feet, which had previously straddled this way and that, learned to walk more correctly.

Finally, while the brothers were seated, at about the third hour of the day, after the reading of the regular chapter and the commemoration of the saints, Abbot Adalgaud [al., Adalguado; Boscio, Adalcaldo] ordered the man, formerly ill, to present himself before the sacred community. To remove the doubts of certain people who thought that he had not yet recovered full health, he was also ordered to carry a bucket full of water.

This was immediately done. It was therefore a miracle to behold: the man who had formerly clung to the ground on his knees now stood with a firm and steady step and moved rapidly in a straight path wherever he wished. Only recently he had scarcely been able to advance with a staggering leg, supported by any staff he could find.

What joy and exultation must then have filled the hearts of mortals when they saw the patron of so great a flock and the bishop of so great a place demonstrate his presence by such works? Their minds, burning with heavenly desire, could not cease praising the Almighty. Rather, at that time they rejoiced more abundantly in Christ with hymns of exultation, because they recognized that they had been endowed with this gift.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The judge hostile to Saint Benedict’s possessions is punished by death

When Boso [Note: [Col. 0927D] Boso governed the monastery of Fleury after Adalgaud. He was mentioned above in chapter 20 and will be mentioned below in chapter 27.] had assumed the government of this monastery by regular election and was administering it honorably, a very great dispute arose between the advocate of the present church, named Epitagius, and the advocate of another holy place, concerning a considerable number of serfs.

Theodoinus was the name of the vicar of Mariacum; the concentration and settlement of these same people had existed in his office from the time of their ancestors. The advocate of the other place came to him, corrupted him by offering a gift, and turned him away from the law of equity.

The day was now approaching on which the dispute was to be settled in the castle called Nandonis (Château-Landon in the Gâtinais). But Abbot Boso, lest he should appear insufficiently cautious, sent two monks to the aforesaid vicar. He also sent him two silver vessels of considerable weight as a gift, begging him, as one who favored justice and right, not to obstruct our official.

But he, already corrupted by the gift of the other party, despised the monks and rejected the gifts. Swollen with pride, he mounted his horse and said to the servants of God:

“Go away, monks, with your vessels, back to the monastery from which you came here. By this sword I swear that from this day forward not one of these serfs shall serve Saint Benedict.”

Having said this, he urged his horse with his spurs and began to proceed at great speed. He had not yet gone far from his own house when, behold, the foot of the horse on which he was riding slipped and threw its rider from its back.

He fell to the ground, broke his shoulder, and suffered injuries to almost his entire body. His attendants carried him back to his own house. Then, as the pain grew worse, on the third day thereafter he met the end of his life.

The advocate of Saint Benedict, arriving at the castle of Nandonis, lodged his complaint before the judges, recovered the serfs by their lawful judgment, and returned home.

## CHAPTER XXV. Again, another man loses the use of his tongue—A judicial combat

After a considerable time had passed, another dispute arose between the aforementioned advocate of this place and the advocate of Saint-Denis. Many legal experts and judges were gathered from both sides to argue on behalf of their respective parties.

Moreover, at the same hearing there were royal envoys sent directly from the king: Jonah, bishop of Orléans, and Donatus, count of Melun. But since they could not conclude the dispute at that hearing—because the judges under Salic law could not properly decide ecclesiastical property, which was governed by Roman law [Note: [Col. 0927D] The Salic law was observed by the Franks from the Loire toward the Rhine; Roman law was observed by the Gauls or Aquitanians, who were therefore called Romans]—the royal envoys thought that the hearing should be transferred to Orléans.

When the legal experts and judges came to the appointed place, they argued fiercely on both sides. Legal scholars were present both from the province of Orléans and from the Gâtinais.

The dispute was prolonged at great length before the judges, because neither side wished to yield to the other or give assent to its opponents. At last it was adjudged that witnesses should come forward from both parties and, after giving the oath, settle the dispute by fighting with shields and staves.

Although this seemed just and right to everyone, a certain legal scholar from the region of Gâtinais, whose name had been bestowed upon him by a kind of omen and was bestial rather than human, had come on behalf of Saint-Denis after being corrupted by a gift. Fearing that, if two men fought one another, his witness might be found unacceptable, he delivered the judgment that it was not right for witnesses to fight in battle over ecclesiastical property; rather, the advocates’ serfs should be divided between them.

Genesius, the viscount, supported this opinion and said that it was more proper for the serfs to be divided than for witnesses to settle the matter by combat. The entire council adopted this view.

But Saint Benedict did not forget that judge and legislator, who had first cunningly and bestially, in keeping with his name, pronounced the sentence that the serfs should be divided. For as soon as the same serfs had been divided into two parts, he was struck by the just judgment of God so severely that he could not speak at all: the entire function of his tongue had been taken away.

When his relatives who were present there learned the truth of what had happened, they led him to the monastery of the holy confessor of Christ whom he had gravely offended. He remained there for almost a month, asking by whatever gestures he could make for the help of the illustrious Father.

At last he recovered a little health and returned to his own people. Yet for as long as he lived, he was never able to obtain the power to pronounce the name of the holy Benedict with his own tongue.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Christian, the pious church custodian, recovers bracelets stolen by thieves

The office of watchmen assigned to holy temples is known to have existed not only in modern times. In ancient times, under blessed Moses, we read that the Lord appointed custodial duties from the tribe of Levi for the sacred tabernacle. As time passed, these duties were arranged in a more extensive order by the holy prophet and wondrous king David, and thus, so to speak, they suggested a custom to us and to our religion.

In ancient times this same office was indeed received by hereditary succession; in our own age, however, officials are admitted not through the propagation of offspring, but rather through purity of life and uprightness of conduct.

Accordingly, while this sacred custom flourished everywhere with the greatest solemnity, the basilica of the present place, dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, and all the virgins of Christ devoted to God, in which the venerable body of the most holy Benedict is also preserved with fitting honor, received as custodian a monk named Christian, outstanding in every religious virtue and moral excellence.

What merit and holiness he possessed shines more clearly than daylight for those who knew his sincere life and innocence. He was accustomed to approach the sacred tomb with the greatest confidence and, in the ordinary human manner, to complain to Saint Benedict whenever anything adverse happened externally to this place. He did so with the confidence of one who knew that he would by no means be despised by the saint.

This will also become sufficiently clear in the work we are writing.

In the same basilica, for the sake of honor and utility, bracelets made of bronze by the work of a metalworker and beautifully gilded hung from cords. According to custom, the bells were rung with them at the appointed hours for the celebration of the office.

One day, thieves entered the church mixed in with the crowd. They saw the bracelets hanging from the cords and, supposing them to be of considerable weight in fine gold, conceived, from their customary greed, a most wicked crime. By common agreement they began to dig through the wall.

At night they carried out what they had planned. Entering the church, they carried away the bracelets together with the finely worked rods attached to them, and departed through the same opening, filling the entrance to the ditch with earth. The theft was committed in such silence that none of the watchmen could perceive how such a crime had been completed.

When the hour for rising arrived and the venerable custodian Christian learned of so great a crime, I confess that it is not easy to say what grief entered his heart or what tears flowed from his eyes. As usual, he came to the tomb amid such lamentations and began bitterly to complain that the saint had allowed him to be robbed by thieves.

Since he had acquired an excessive confidence that he would be heard by blessed Benedict, he even expressed his rustic complaint in a foreign language—for he was by birth a German—saying:

“Saint Benedict, why do you sleep in such laziness? Why do you care for your house so negligently that you allow thieves to steal what I have contributed by my work in your honor? Certainly I do not care if they even take your breeches, since you did not defend the bracelets. Believe me, if they do not restore your bracelets to me, I will not light even a single candle for you.”

Threatening him in this and many other ways, and at the same time striking with his staff the stone placed before the tomb, he went away sadly.

But Almighty God did not allow his servant to remain sorrowful for long. Rather, through the merits and intervention of the blessed Father, with whom he was accustomed to complain so confidently, he very quickly relieved him of his sadness and filled him with fitting joy.

For the aforementioned thieves, repeating the crime they had once attempted, returned after a few days to the opening in the dug-through wall, which they had previously filled with earth. They removed the earth and prepared to enter.

Immediately, however, they were captured by the watchmen and subjected to interrogation. They confessed to the crime and said that they had entered the church at that hour in order to remove and carry away all the gold and silver, together with the jewels, from Saint Benedict’s tomb.

When asked how they had carried out so great a crime with their bare hands—especially since they had brought with them neither large awls, nor heavy hammers, nor any implement of a smith’s workshop with which they could destroy such finely crafted work—they drew knives from their sleeves and confessed that they had accomplished everything with them.

They were kept until daylight and then presented to the venerable Christian. He asked them what they had done with the bracelets they had stolen, and received the answer that they had them hidden with them.

He severely rebuked them and bitterly denounced them for daring to undertake so great a crime, something detestable to God and to human beings. Moreover, he said that human laws would order them to be deprived of life by hanging, without any consideration of mercy.

Finally, following the example of the prophet Elisha—who, after the Syrian raiders sent to kill him had been captured and brought into the middle of Samaria, forbade the king of Israel, when he asked the prophet whether he should strike them with the sword, and instead ordered them to be refreshed with bread and water and sent back to their own people—he pitied the thieves’ labor. He ordered them to be refreshed with food and drink and to return unharmed to their homes, forbidding them ever again to rush into attempts of this kind.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Under Louis the Pious, Francia is disturbed—The arm of a soldier who wished to slaughter a monastery cow becomes rigid

[Col. 0930D]

In the time of the divine Augustus Louis, when, according to the Lord’s evangelical saying, the love of many was growing cold because iniquity had abounded (Matthew 24), the public affairs of that kingdom were afflicted in many ways through the discord of the Frankish people. For, through the counsels of wicked men, while deliberation concerning the commonwealth was transformed into arrogance and domination, and while the leading men preferred to envy and malign one another rather than promote the welfare of the kingdom, good men began to become more suspect to the kings—for, as Crispus says, “another man’s virtue is always a cause of fear”—and, above all, they began to hold views contrary to the people. The result was that, while the emperor pursued the nobility of the veterans by humiliating them, they, remembering their former valor, strove to defend their liberty by revolting against the emperor and prepared the kingdom’s great ruin.

But since it is not our purpose to encompass the deeds of kings in writing, but rather to commit to letters the wondrous works of God performed through His servant Benedict, leaving aside what was done—if I may put it so—wrongly or even recklessly, let us return to what we began.

The emperor, as has been said, regarding the leading Franks with suspicion, summoned the peoples of Germany as he was about to depart for Aquitaine: namely, the Saxons, Thuringians, Bavarians, and Alemanni. To them he entrusted, without proper order, the administration of the kingdom’s affairs that the father of the Franks had subdued by arms through his valor. It is easy to recognize how the Franks received this. Having thus gained freedom across the Rhine, supposedly for the emperor’s protection, they surrendered themselves and their entire army to vices: the plundering of the poor, the dishonoring of good men, the violation of sacred places, and the other evils that it is painful to enumerate.

But while the emperor, campaigning against his son, was approaching the Loire on his way toward Aquitaine, it happened that certain leaders of the peoples mentioned above reached the little estates of the monastery of Saint Benedict while laying them waste. When, amid the savagery of the plunderers, nothing remained for them to seize from the poor, they approached the monastery, intending to do the same there as in the other places.

Not far from the monastery a considerable herd of cattle was grazing. It had been assigned to serve the brothers’ continual needs. A powerful band of plunderers attacked it and threatened to strike down some of the animals with axes for their own feasts, while taking others suitable for themselves away with them. When the herdsman told them that they ought not to touch the herd belonging to Saint Benedict, and that if they did so they would not escape with impunity, they became indignant and ordered that the fattier young cow they had noticed, separated from the rest of the herd, be slaughtered.

After it had been tied up, one of them, who seemed the bolder, drew his sword, bared his arm, and attempted to strike the cow. But at that very attempt he remained fixed and bound by unbreakable bonds, so that he retained the arm he had raised together with the sword and could turn it in no direction. You might have seen the wretched man standing there, bound by his own effort with unyielding restraints, and experiencing in his own person the divine power that he had despised in his offense.

[Col. 0931D]

When his companions saw heavenly vengeance unleashed against their fellow, they were overcome with terror, confessed their guilt, and begged mercy from the one whom they had proudly despised—namely, Saint Benedict. Finally, laying down their weapons, unfastening their shoes from their feet, and sprinkling earth upon their heads, they hastened to the monastery to seek a remedy, bringing with them the robber divinely held fast.

When they approached the basilica, they prostrated themselves before the door and confessed their guilt with tears. They declared not only that the man was guilty of the crime, but that all of them together were accomplices in the offense. Finally, they bound themselves by a vow never to inflict any trouble upon anyone belonging to Saint Benedict’s household, if only they might obtain his favor.

Meanwhile, the guardians of the holy house, seeing the men’s devotion and that they were wholly inclined to obtain the mercy of the compassionate Judge, raised them from the ground. Consoling those cast down in mind and body, they led them into the church and brought them to the holy tomb.

After the prayer had been completed, the wretched man was released. Giving thanks to the Lord, as far as he could, together with his companions, and to his liberator Benedict, he returned to his own people, openly proclaiming everywhere that divine power was present in this place in a superior manner and that no one who had deliberately plotted anything wicked against Saint Benedict could escape its judgment.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Translation of Saint Sebastian. The Relics of Saints Dionysius and Sebastian Granted to the Monks of Fleury. The Author’s Age.

While Louis Augustus, as has been stated, was governing the monarchy of the Franks, the venerable abbot Hilduin of the monastery of the holy martyr Dionysius sent envoys to Rome and obtained from Pope Eugenius the body of Saint Sebastian the martyr. He brought it to the basilica of Saint Medard and temporarily placed it in a portable shrine beside the saint’s body. In that place Christ performed innumerable miracles through the intervention of the holy martyr.

At a later time, Boso, abbot of the monastery of the holy confessor Benedict, had been summoned to the palace and had gone there. On his return he had a suitable opportunity to pass through the monastery of Saint Dionysius. Turning aside, therefore, to the monastery just mentioned, he held a friendly conversation with the revered abbot Hilduin. During their familiar conversation he asked him for relics of the holy martyrs—namely, Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, as well as Sebastian.

The most noble abbot willingly granted his request and provided what was sought on the condition that, each year when the feast day of those martyrs arrived, their most celebrated festival should be held among us according to monastic custom.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Ebbo, bishop of Reims, was deposed by the emperor Louis the Pious and was entrusted to Abbot Boso for safekeeping in the monastery of Saint Benedict. He was living in exile under Boso’s authority when the lord emperor entered upon the way of all flesh in the year 840, as these words are read in the account of the clergy of Reims. After that emperor died, as the synodal letter of the Council of Troyes to Pope Nicholas I relates, Lothair came from Italy into France. Ebbo met him at the city of Worms, escorted by Abbot Boso, to whose custody he had been entrusted. Boso was succeeded by Rodulf, and Rodulf by Bernard; see below.]

Having received the saints’ relics with the greatest gratitude, Abbot Boso returned joyfully to his own monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] Here the manuscript of Pratensis ends.]

[Col. 0933A]

On the day of his arrival at the monastery, he sent a messenger ahead and ordered that the brothers meet him at a suitable distance from the monastery with fitting honor. Obeying his orders, the brothers received the relics of the holy martyrs with as much honor as mortals can offer, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, and placed them in the Church of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God.

A considerable multitude of men and women followed the relics with the greatest devotion, because of certain miracles performed by the Lord through the blessed martyrs. But since an ancient rule had decreed that women were in no way to pass inward beyond the monastery’s outer gates, those who had followed the relics from far away turned to prayer. They asked that, for the sake of prayer, they might be permitted to enter the church in which the relics of the saints had been deposited and fulfill their vows.

Because this was contrary to monastic discipline, they could obtain permission in no way. While they continued in prayer, many of the nobles also began to assemble for this exceedingly venerable spectacle, roused by the magnitude of the commotion. By joining their prayers, they were scarcely able, by whatever means, to obtain from the abbot and the brothers that he order a tent to be erected outside the monastery gate, on the western side, in a wooded place. There the relics were to be carried at the appointed time, namely, on the eve of the Lord’s Day, and were to remain there under the reverent guard of both monks and clerics until the same hour of the Lord’s Day, when they would again be carried back into the sacred buildings.

When this had been done, crowds of common people flowed there not only from the neighboring places but also from distant regions, hoping to obtain healing of soul and body. The Lord performed through His renowned martyrs unbelievable gifts of power, some of which we ourselves, mere children, witnessed. It became plainly evident that even now, in these beloved witnesses of His, He was fulfilling what He had once promised to those who would believe in Him with true faith, saying:

> Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these. (John 14)

Those whose eyes were afflicted by any bodily disorder—whether by the worst kind of diseased discharge or by cataracts—received again the clear use of sight. The weak, burdened by afflictions of the feet, who had never walked on their feet, recovered with the greatest joy the ability to walk. Demons were driven from the bodies of the possessed, and the lunatics obtained the healing they desired.

Moreover, certain people who had suffered a burning affliction of particular limbs—a type of disease that physicians, using a name derived from *cancer*, call *cancerauma*—rejoiced that they had received perfect health. Thus the Lord performed innumerable gifts of healing, as we have said, through the relics of the blessed martyrs while they were being carried at the appointed time to the tent, for the praise and glory of His name, who glorifies His chosen everywhere—not only by granting the rewards of eternal blessedness, but also by honoring them in the present mortal age through miracles.

## CHAPTER XXIX. A Paralytic Healed.

But so that Jesus Christ, the same Creator and Redeemer of the human race, would not show Saint Benedict inferior in merits—or rather, so that those less capable of understanding the divine dispensation would not think that the martyrs who had won for themselves the crown of everlasting happiness by the shedding of their own blood were especially more glorious before the Lord than the man who, without the palm of martyrdom, had sent his soul in peace to the dwellings of his heavenly homeland—the Lord was pleased to perform, through His most beloved servant, miracles no less remarkable at the most sacred shrine where the remains of that same Father are preserved.

A small boy was carried by his parents to the relics of the holy martyrs. He had long sought healing in vain and could not obtain it. His legs were withered and his tendons contracted, and he was so weak that his ankle bones were firmly attached to his buttocks; from birth he had never been able to experience the act of walking. He was carried by bearers to the tomb of the often-mentioned confessor of Christ, Benedict.

After he had remained there throughout the day, on the following day, while we and all the brothers present were singing—for the evening office was then being celebrated—the tendons that had long been contracted began to extend, and the dry channels of his veins were moistened by the infusion of blood. The bones that had been so tightly fastened to his buttocks gradually began to separate from them. Soon the little boy stretched out and lay with his whole body against the pavement. A little later he rose healthy and, although his steps were unsteady, began freely to run about in different directions.

## CHAPTER XXX. A Possessed Man Is Liberated.

When this miracle had been accomplished by God’s grace, a certain man suddenly arrived, driven by demonic madness and fury. His name was Maldabertus. Shortly before, he had been seized by the citizens of the city of Orléans, beaten with rods like a madman, bound in chains, and committed to custody.

But overcoming every restraint, he made swiftly for the monastery. There he began most miserably to rave throughout the place: twisting his limbs, striking himself against the apse, whirling his hair, thrusting his belly forward with his back arched, hurling himself into the air in leaps and revolutions, and suffering torment through every movement of his body under diabolical impulses.

Alas, what a miserable spectacle! At last he was bound with chains and, at that part of his body where his clothing was gathered by a belt, the wretched man was fastened with extreme harshness to a church column.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] A note on the use of exorcism.]

Priests approached him and performed exorcisms and all the other rites that ought to be carried out for possessed persons. Asked his name, he declared that he was called Legion. He was finally rolled in different circuits around the columns, and, twisting his wretched body with the most dreadful movements, he revealed what he carried within him.

Those troops of demons were struggling, if one may say so, against the intercessions of the saints. Indeed, at the urging of the devout monks, who pressed him to implore the Lord’s mercy and the intercession of all the saints, the wretched man was accustomed, as though unwillingly uttering a prayer, to say:

> God, deliver me from the ancient enemy who besieges me. Saint Benedict, prick him.

He uttered this not willingly, certainly, but while driven by unclean furies, jokingly, as he said innumerable other things.

Why say more? Through the intervention of the serene Father, and by divine mercy, he was freed from the devil’s snares and remained safe and peaceful within the church. When he spoke with others, he explained how he had been seized by demons. He confessed his guilt and proclaimed, with a contrite heart and humbled spirit, that because of the enormity of his crimes he had been handed over to unclean spirits. He gave thanks to the Lord his liberator and to the blessed intercessor Benedict, and so returned unharmed to his own home.

From then onward, for as long as he lived, he adopted the custom of returning each year, at the season when he had recovered his health, to the threshold of the holy confessor of Christ with a vow; after completing his prayer, he would return home.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Another Case.

After this man had been freed from demonic madness by such great mercy of God, another man, bound with terrible chains, was brought from the upper reaches of the Loire valley. He too was possessed by a most cruel demon.

He was finally tied to a church column. His eyes were bloodshot, his complexion pale, his face emaciated, and his expression fierce—such that he would inspire great terror in mortals. He was forbidden to eat bread, for his master did not permit him to use food in the human manner.

He was accustomed to pass three days without nourishment. At times he drank plain water; when forced, he accepted water that had been exorcised, shouting and twisting his limbs. Sometimes, if meat was given to him, he ate it greedily but filthily, like a dog. By such food the wretched man dragged out his unhappy life.

After he had long been tormented at the holy shrine by various and monstrous tortures, he was finally led, bound by the wrists, to the relics of the holy martyrs, where the ashes of the aforementioned confessor of Christ, Benedict, were also venerated by the faithful people.

He was tied to the tent’s post and was afflicted there most severely. The wicked torturer knew that, through the power and merits of the saints, he would soon be driven from the possessed man; therefore he raged against him all the more cruelly in every manner.

But around the third hour, when Masses were already being celebrated, the wretched man fell asleep after the Gospel reading. While the priest was consecrating the offered host, one of our brothers, whose name was Garno, and also certain clerics, seemed to see three large and exceedingly black flies emerge from the mouth of the afflicted man and fly outside the tent.

After this vision, the sick man began to behave more quietly and, through the Lord’s mercy and the intervention of His saints, was rescued from the persecutor of the human race and restored to health. Having thus recovered his safety, he returned to his own home.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Another Count Driven Mad.

A certain castle in the region of Burgundy, situated on the side of a mountain above the river Armançon, gave its name to the surrounding territory. For the neighboring region is called Tonnerrois from Tonnerre.

A man of noble birth named Raculfus was in charge of the castle, exercising the office of count’s deputy. Because of the wickedness of his character and the enormity of his evil deeds, he became mentally deranged and was transformed into a madman.

When he wished to attack himself and all those standing around him with a sword, clubs, and whatever other weapons happened to come to hand, his own people seized him. Bound, and with a great retinue appropriate to a man of wealth, he was brought to the monastery.

There he raged for a long time, to such an extent that, gnashing his teeth, he threatened that, if he were permitted, he would tear to pieces with his bites anyone who approached him. After approximately fifteen days had passed, through the intervention of the blessed Benedict he began to regain his senses. Not long afterward he was completely restored to health and returned joyfully to his native land—not merely to the delight of one man, but of many.

At that time the Lord deigned to perform these and many other wondrous works through His servant, who had been freed from the burden of the flesh. They were omitted because of the negligence of those whose efforts ought to have made them known to the people. As for the things we were able to learn by bodily sight, and those we discovered through trustworthy testimony, we have taken care to transmit them to the knowledge of posterity, in a modest style of speech—the style that is especially effective in recounting events—at the urging of our elders.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The Kingdom of Louis the Pious’s Sons Is Divided. The State of Affairs at That Time. The Incursions and Terrible Deeds of the Northmen.

But after the most pious Augustus Louis had been stripped of the burden of the flesh, the Frankish kingdom, which had been formed into a single body from diverse nations, was divided into three parts and received for governance by three sons of the same emperor.

The eldest, Lothair, possessed Francia together with Italy; Louis possessed all Saxony and Germany; and the younger Charles possessed Burgundy together with Aquitaine.

But, leaving aside the kingdoms—whether they declined after being worn down by wars or flourished somewhat under unbroken peace—I wish to run briefly through the misfortunes of our own region.

After Charles had obtained no small part of the kingdom, misfortune joined to fortune devastated the commonwealth with the greatest destruction. First, when the margraves of the Breton frontier were divided among themselves by grave rebellion, a mournful war arose for both sides.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] In that ninth century the name “margrave” was first heard. They were so called from *marca* or *marchia*, a word meaning “boundary,” because they guarded the borders of the region, just as dukes and counts had done previously.]

Although Lambert emerged victorious after Rainald fell, he did not carry away wholly victorious standards from the enemy. When he saw thousands of his own followers perish, and when Heriveus, Rainald’s eldest son, took up arms to avenge his father’s death, Lambert fought him unsuccessfully, was defeated, and handed him over to death after he had been pierced by weapons.

As warriors on both sides perished in this kind of discord, nearly the whole region was left without its own defenders and became prey to foreign peoples. For the neighboring force of the Britons crossed the ancient boundary and, laying waste to the region of Nantes and also Anjou as far as the river Mayenne, brought it under its own control through slaughter and fire.

Lambert had previously resisted those efforts. But when he withdrew from the place at the king’s command, he allowed the Britons to carry out their barbarous designs.

Moreover, the Northmen, a northern people well known—more than is desirable—to our race, no longer merely practiced piracy: they ruined the entire coast and, to speak more accurately, reduced it to a desolate wilderness.

Their wicked efforts had often been frustrated by the successive commanders of those regions, namely Lambert, Robert, and Rainulf. But when those men perished by differing fortunes, nearly all Neustria—which extends across the land from the city of Orléans to the town of Paris—lay open to Northmen savagery.

They roamed everywhere, devastating all things by their frequent incursions. At first they traveled on foot, because they lacked skill in riding; later, mounted on horses, they traversed everything in our manner.

Meanwhile, establishing the station of their ships—as though it were an asylum for all robbers—on an island below the monastery of Saint Florentius, they constructed a fortified settlement resembling a cluster of huts. There they kept herds of captives bound in chains and, for a time, rested their own bodies from labor, ready to serve the next expedition.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] The monastery of Saint Florentius was on Mount Glonna, in the diocese of Angers, not far from the Loire, at the extreme limits of Aquitaine. It is now called Vieux-Saint-Florent, to distinguish it from another monastery of the same name. After the former was destroyed by the Northmen, the latter was first built in the castle of Saumur, likewise situated on the Loire, and later near the town of Saumur. It retains the name of the abbey on which it depends. The older monastery and the newer one were both assigned to the congregation of Saint Maur.]

From there they made unexpected raids, traveling sometimes by ship and sometimes on horseback, and destroyed the entire surrounding province. On their first arrival they burned the city of Nantes with fire (in the year 853).

Passing through the region of Anjou, they burned the city itself; as for the fortresses and villages of Poitiers and the whole country from the sea to that same city of Poitiers, they plundered and devastated it, filling everything with slaughter.

At a later time they came by ship to Tours and, after filling it with slaughter as was their custom, finally gave it over to the flames. After devastating the entire surrounding region, not long afterward they sought the upper reaches of the Loire by ship and reached Orléans. They ransomed the captured city for gold, while Agius was then governing its episcopal see.

[Note: [Col. 0938D] Agius was ordained bishop of Orléans in the year 843, as is established by canon 10 of the Second Council of Verneuil, held the following year. He later subscribed to various councils: the Council of Beauvais in 845, the Council of Paris in 846, the Fourth Council of Tours in 869, the Second Councils of Soissons and Verberie in 853, the Council of Saponaria in 859, the Council of Tusiacum in 860, and the Third Council of Soissons in 867. He was succeeded by Walter, of whom more below.]

After withdrawing for a time, they destroyed that city by fire on their second arrival. Only the mother church, which had been consecrated in honor of the Holy Cross by the blessed Bishop Evurtius at the command of Augustus Constantine, remained through the efforts of good men.

Why, then, should we prolong our account by recalling the devastation of Neustria alone? It was not only the four cities mentioned above that suffered the calamities of destruction. What of Paris, that noble capital, once resplendent with glory, wealth, the fertility of its soil, and the profound peace of its inhabitants—a city that I might rightly call the wealth of kings and the marketplace of peoples? Can one see anything there now more readily than burned ashes rather than a noble city?

What of Beauvais, what of Noyon, and those once most distinguished cities of Gaul themselves? Did they not also fall beneath Northmen incursions and the enemy’s sword?

It is painful to recount the destruction of the most renowned monasteries, both of men and of women devoted to serving God; the slaughter of populations of no low standing; the captivity of married women; the abuse of virgins; and all the unspeakable forms of torture that victors can inflict upon the vanquished.

Why should I recount the immense affliction of the Aquitanian people, once the nurse of wars but now presenting a cold right hand to war, deprived of its own eyes and in need of foreign leaders? For Aquitaine itself, crushing within itself the best men of its native soil, now lies open as prey to foreign peoples.

From the very shore of the Ocean, so to speak, eastward as far as Auvergne, that most illustrious city of ancient Aquitaine, no region has been able to retain its freedom—no town or village, no city, finally, that has not fallen beneath the savage slaughter of the pagans.

Poitiers, once the most fertile city of Aquitaine, bears witness to this; so does Saintes, so does Angoulême, so does Périgueux, so does Limoges, and so certainly does Auvergne, now the furthest limit of the barbarian sword. Bourges itself, the capital of the Aquitanian kingdom, proclaims that it was gravely overthrown by the enemy’s attack, with no military force opposing it.

After nearly thirty years of such evils, through which the Gauls were worn down—not without the guilt of all concerned—it is readily perceptible to anyone, even one of slow understanding, how the worship of divine religion proceeded and whether or not it flourished.

For what order of Christian religion fully carries out its rule according to the intended standard, so that, if the execution of its works is properly examined, it is not judged rather to be a transgressor of Christ’s commandments?

Therefore it seems that He is not unjustly inflicting upon such people—that is, upon us, the transgressors of His commands—the vengeance of punishment once promised through the prophet. For He says, threatening through the prophet Jeremiah:

> Because you did not listen to my words, behold, I will send for and take all the families of the North, says the Lord, and I will bring them against this land, against its inhabitants, and against all the nations that surround it. I will destroy them and make them an object of astonishment and hissing, and perpetual desolations. I will take away from them the sound of joy, the sound of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstone, and the light of the lamp. And all its land shall become a desolation and an object of astonishment. (Jeremiah 25)

Likewise, through the prophet Ezekiel:

> Make a chain, for the land is full of judgments of blood, and the city is full of iniquity. I will bring the worst of the nations, and they shall possess their houses. I will put an end to the pride of the powerful, and they shall possess their storehouse. When distress comes, they will seek peace, and there will be none. Trouble will come upon trouble, and report upon report. They will seek a vision from the prophet, but the law will perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders. (Ezekiel 7)

And shortly afterward:

> I will deal with them according to their ways, and I will judge them according to their judgments; and they shall know that I am the Lord. (Ibid.)

Thus it is possible to see the prophetic threat assigned to our own age, when, because of the enormity of their crimes, the people once belonging to God and the sheep of His hands have been given over to the nations for plunder and the harshest captivity; and when the land, which until recently had flourished, rich in soil and abundant in every possession, has been reduced to utter devastation and desolation.

Let us therefore truthfully exclaim with the prophet David:

> You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right. (Psalm 118)

And let us humbly implore with another:

> Lord, have mercy on us; for we have waited for you. Be our arm in the morning and our salvation in the time of tribulation. (Isaiah 33)

I have wished to commit this brief account of the destruction of our most delightful homeland to writing, so that I might prepare a clearer path to the matters that were to follow. Leaving aside, then, the unspeakable disasters of these evils—which by their very horror and execration force the course of the pen to grow dull—let us now return to our subject.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The Monastery of Fleury Is Plundered and Burned by the Northmen.

Meanwhile, as we briefly mentioned above, the Northmen attacked Orléans on their second incursion and burned the city. Some of them, under the leadership of Bareto and with forty ships, made for the monastery of Saint Benedict, which lies eighteen miles from the city of Orléans.

Finding it empty of inhabitants but filled with all the temporary goods of mortals, they plundered and scattered everything according to their familiar custom, and finally set it on fire and burned it.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] This occurred in the year 865, as is written in the Bertinian Annals and in the chronicle of the anonymous author whom Andreas Chesnius placed before the other writers who composed accounts of the deeds of the Northmen. The same monastery was also burned by the Northmen on another occasion, as is said in the account of the translation of Saint Benedict in the fourth volume of the Benedictine history.]

At that time the most sacred body of the confessor of Christ, Benedict, was absent. For during the first devastation of the aforementioned city, while Bernard, a man of the noblest birth, was governing this holy place, the most holy body was removed from its tomb, placed with fitting honor in a chest, and then set in a portable shrine, so that, whenever the necessity of flight compelled them, the brothers could carry it as a safeguard during their flight.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] This Bernard, or Bertaldus, took part in the Second Council of Soissons, held at Saint Medard in the year 853, and succeeded Rodulf, mentioned in connection with the council held at Saponaria in 859, canon 11. At last the general synod humbly petitioned, prostrating itself on the ground before King Charles and Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges, beseeching and adjuring them by the cross and the blood of Christ to endeavor to preserve valid and unshaken the privilege of the monastery of Saint Benedict, which they had confirmed with the king’s approval and which the same Rodulf had subscribed, although he irregularly retained the aforementioned abbey.]

But, through Christ’s grace, when the pagan sword returned to the dwellings prepared for it, the most holy members were restored to their proper place.

During the second incursion of the enemy, when the aforementioned abbot was already passing through the final days of his administration, the most holy body was again removed and placed in a portable shrine. The brothers carried it here and there as the opportunity for flight arose.

Yet throughout this period divine grace did not deign to forget its servants, though they had been pitiably driven into exile and tossed among uncertain dwelling places. Rather, it consoled them through miracles performed by its beloved servant, so that the hearts of men, wavering because of so many adverse events, might be strengthened more abundantly by the presence of so great a Father and by the power displayed before their eyes.

After the monastery had been consumed by the raging fire, with no blessing of the site remaining—for neither temples suitable for divine worship, nor dwellings constructed for various uses, nor granaries, nor stores, nor anything at all of beauty or utility had survived—the bare walls of the ruins presented to the eyes of those who saw them astonishment and, more than beauty or glory, horror.

The brothers were therefore compelled to divide the house once fitted for quiet living by inserting arches. From one part they fashioned the shade of a smaller chapel, in which, after constructing an altar, they celebrated the divine office during the day.

[Col. 0940D]

In this place too they brought the body of the blessed Benedict, still lying in its portable shrine.

[Note: [Col. 0940D] From this the Bollandist scholars infer that the events reported in the history of the Translation of Saint Benedict as having occurred after the departure from the city of Orléans are suspect—namely, that ice melted and dissolved of its own accord and that trees flowered in winter. They think that these events could have occurred only on this occasion and that Adrevald would not have omitted them here if they were true. More on this elsewhere.]

While the holy remains were resting there, God brought about the following miracle.

## CHAPTER XXXV. A Perjurer Is Punished through Saint Benedict. A Penitent Recovers.

[Col. 0940D] At the appointed time—that is, on Saturday—throughout the course of the year people customarily gather from the nearby villages at a place situated beside the monastery, called Old Floriacum, to sell or purchase merchandise. One Saturday, therefore, two companions came to the place for the purpose of trading. One of them had twelve denarii in a purse, as he himself maintained; they had received them together from the goods they had sold and had agreed to divide them between themselves there.

But when the man who had received none of the money demanded from his companion the share owed to him, while the other admitted that he had paid it back, a dispute arose and the market judge, named Engilraus, hurried over. When he wished to settle the quarrel, and the man who had held the money affirmed in every way that he had repaid it to his companion, but his words were not believed, he was compelled by necessity to extend his right hand toward the basilica and, in fury, uttered an oath, saying:

“By this Saint Benedict, I returned those denarii to him.”

[Col. 0941B] Because he had sworn rashly and falsely, he by no means enjoyed impunity. Indeed, he could not draw back the hand which, together with his arm, he had imprudently extended in the act of perjury; it stiffened in his effort and remained numb. All who were present were terrified and immediately investigated what ought to be done. No more salutary counsel was found than that the guilty man, having already experienced divine power, should go to the sacred church to seek pardon.

He promptly did so. Cast down and supplicating, he went to the church, carrying in his other hand—which had not been similarly afflicted—a three-pronged iron fork as an offering. Finally, he prostrated himself before the most sacred tomb, empty indeed of the saint’s body, but filled with divine power through the former association with those bones. He begged pardon for the rashness and the crime contracted through his perjury, and at the same time implored the Lord’s mercy, so that through the intervention of the most merciful shepherd—whose venerable name he had treated in his oath as though it were a most worthless thing—he might be found worthy to regain his health.

The Creator’s clemency attended the earnest prayers of the wretched man seeking the help of the outstanding leader. Through Benedict’s intercession the sick man obtained healing and returned joyfully to the marketplace. Yet, lest he be consumed by excessive sorrow over the money he had lost, the Lord deigned to console him through the power of the one whose aid had brought him salvation.

For—marvelous to relate!—when almost the entire crowd had withdrawn from the marketplace to their homes and only a very few remained, he looked back toward the place where the greatest throng of people had been and saw lying there the purse with the money he had lost. Picking it up, he was filled with even greater joy, not only because of his bodily recovery but also because he had found the hard-earned profit of his poverty. To this admirable sign another was added, with Christ’s grace consenting, although at a greater distance from the place.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. A Lame Woman Is Cured

Within the walls of the city of Orléans there is a church built in honor of the most holy Benedict by the venerable abbot of the present place, named Medo. It was small, indeed, but situated in a more secluded part of the city—as it was thought at that time—and therefore very suitable as a dwelling for the monks and the abbot when they had necessary business to conduct.

Around the winter season, when the pagans were planning an incursion into the upper parts, the brothers were compelled by necessity to withdraw there. Certainly, as we briefly mentioned above, after the city had twice been consumed by fire and a third time devastated, it seemed to offer no further use for defense or protection. Then the venerable bishop of that city, Galterius—whose name must be spoken with the greatest reverence—, inspired by God, restored and adapted for the defense of the inhabitants the walls of the city, which had been almost entirely destroyed, employing the keen intelligence for which he is known to have been pre-eminent.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] From this it appears that Adrevald devoted himself to describing these miracles while Galterius—or Ganterius, Walterius—was still seated as bishop. According to Sausseyo, this was the Walterius who subscribed to the Council of Pontigon in 876 and was still presiding over the see of Orléans in 885. He writes that the little church of Saint Benedict mentioned here was converted into a parish church, called Saint Benedict of the Return, commonly Saint Benoist du Retour, taking its name from the return of Saint Benedict’s body to the monastery of Floriacum, which occurred under Bishop Walterius.]

Thus the servants of God came there and spent the time in a manner suitable to the religious life. Meanwhile, near the sacred little church, there was a certain woman from the city’s suburb who was entirely unable to walk on her feet. She crawled along the ground and dragged herself forward with the aid of little stools [or: footstools, *scabella*]. By keeping watch at the church doors, she was accustomed to live on the alms of the religious brothers. She waited to see whether, through God’s mercy and the merits of the most blessed confessor, she might somehow be found worthy to obtain bodily healing.

After she had done this for a long period of time, at last, through divine mercy and by the merits and intervention of the most holy Benedict, she was restored to health. She remained healthy and unharmed in that same place for a long time; afterward, having entered into marriage with a man and having children, she continued to live in the same city.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. A Fire Is Extinguished

A certain man from the household of the holy Father Paul, in the village of Pauliacum—Pouilly, a town in the Nivernais—had built a small dwelling of light materials, namely wicker and broom, upon his own inheritance. Bringing together there everything he was able to acquire, he had placed all his hopes of prolonging his extremely poor life in it.

At last, by an accidental occurrence, the dwelling caught fire and began to send out a mass of flames. Amid the din and uproar—as commonly happens in such a situation—the people of the neighboring villages began to run together. But when they saw the pyre rising higher in flames and already close to being consumed, they restrained their steps, saying that no one could save a structure made of wicker and packed with broom, which offered easy nourishment to the devouring fire.

Moreover, when human assistance withdrew, the poor man turned to divine help and said:

“O Lord, have mercy on me, lest I die of hunger! Saint Benedict, come to my aid and help your servant, for I had gathered all my poverty into this little hut.”

While he repeated these and many other words amid his tears, the Divinity, moved to mercy by the merits of the most sacred Father Benedict, extinguished the fire, and the whole hut remained safe except for a single wall, which had been woven of wicker. Everything belonging to the man remained unharmed.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. A Man Invading the Monastery’s Vineyard Is Seized by Death

Caput Cervium, Sacerge, was a village in the province of Aquitaine, donated to the monastery of Saint Benedict by royal generosity. Through the many attacks of its neighbors, and especially of the leading men of the region, it had defected from the authority of this place.

After a long period of time, however, it was restored to its proper authority through the greatest labor of the servants of God. It was then necessarily decided that a suitable dwelling should somehow be built there for the monks, and that two or three monks should remain there continually, until the easily swayed dispositions of the Aquitanians, readily softened toward every new development, ceased—through the brothers’ persistence—from hoping to regain possession of the property.

The monk Raganarius, a man of great religious virtue, was sent to undertake this effort. He had once been sent by the emperor Louis with others to Jerusalem. With him went Segevertus, a priest and monk. They built a cell at the place mentioned above and removed from the people of Aquitaine all confidence that they could recover these possessions.

At that time there was a certain man of no insignificant standing among that people, named Stephen, who sold a part of his own estate to one of the servants of Saint Benedict for an agreed price. The servant acquired the estate without any fruitful cultivation, but did not allow the land to remain empty. He cultivated it carefully, planted a vineyard there, and retained it for his own use for as long as he lived.

When he died, the owner of the land of which we have spoken attempted to reclaim what he had sold. The advocate, arriving at the place of the land transfer together with the monk Raganarius, according to legal custom, was endeavoring by his authority to restore the aforesaid vineyard to the jurisdiction of Saint Benedict.

Therefore Stephen, stirred by the impatience of a light-minded temper, approached the monk Raganarius, who was sitting on his horse, and spoke furiously:

“I say to you, monk Raganarius, who sought Jerusalem across the sea: by this sword I call to witness that, when you and I have left this place, Saint Benedict will have no authority over this vineyard.”

To him in his fury Raganarius replied:

“Certainly I do not know; but you do not know whether we shall be able to leave this place as we wish.”

Again shaking his sword, the man repeated his oath and affirmed that he would depart from that place without Saint Benedict’s favor. As soon as he had said these words, he collapsed. With all his limbs crushed and broken, he was carried by his servants in a litter to his own house. The vineyard, indeed, was left under Saint Benedict’s authority, while Stephen himself, consumed by a prolonged illness, died.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Unfortunate Reign of Charles the Bald. A Boy Rescued from a Wolf’s Jaws

While King Charles was governing the kingdom of the Franks, a very severe famine seized all Gaul. A considerable disaster, also, arising from the attacks of the pagans, afflicted the entire people along the shores of the Ocean.

But, so that the world might experience a third plague, according to the prophet [II Kings 14], savage beasts were sent, which received those fleeing famine and barbarian devastation with gaping mouths.

At that time it happened that a certain woman, leaving an estate at Matriniacum, took with her a very small child so that he might play with other children of his age, while she herself watched from a distance with many men and women. Suddenly a wolf came out of the forest, seized the woman’s son, and, lifting him up, did not return to the forest but began to carry him away across the open fields.

When the unhappy woman saw this, she mourned with the most wretched cries and immense lamentation. Then, joining the crowd, she began to pursue the wolf. But the animal was not at all frightened and dragged the little boy farther away.

[Col. 0944B] When the exhausted crowd stopped pursuing the wolf, despairing that it could in any way wrest the prey from it, the woman—whose grief at losing her son urged her on with greater force—did not cease her attempted pursuit. Rather, she hurried forward as quickly as she could, invoking Saint Benedict and asking that he bring her aid by restoring her own son and not permit his servant to be carried outside his boundaries.

Then, through the mercy of the divine Majesty and the intervention of the precious confessor, she obtained what she had requested. For the wolf, coming to the boundaries of Saint Benedict’s territory, left the child unharmed and safe, and returned to the remote hiding places of the forests.

The woman, joyfully receiving her little boy, gave thanks to God and to the liberator of her son, Saint Benedict, as best she knew how, and returned to the poor home of her poverty.

## APPENDIX OF ADELERIUS THE MONK

## CHAPTER XL. Saint Benedict Appears on the Feast of the Translation. He Secures the Salvation of Deceased Brothers. Miracles

The wondrous power and wisdom of our Lord, which glorifies the most blessed Father Benedict, while keeping him glorified with itself in the heavenly court, never ceases continually to make wondrous on earth, by a multitude of miracles, his body reverenced by all mortals.

For, as we have learned by credible report from men of an earlier time in our own age, rendered trustworthy by their zeal for truthful testimony, the bountiful majesty of God has often deigned, through the merciful gift of its favor and by means of its often-mentioned beloved one, to perform a memorable deed wrought in former ages.

It once happened that the feast of his most sacred translation occurred; when the cycle of time brought it round again, great crowds of diverse numbers had gathered from every side—not only from the surrounding districts but also from the remotest places of the provinces.

After the praises appropriate to the celebration of so great a feast had been duly offered during the night, and before the dawn had brightly poured forth its rays, each person sought his own bed for the sake of rest.

One of the brothers, who had been entrusted with the care of guarding the basilica, was sitting before the altar of the sacred body. He was continually intent on attaining the joys of eternal life and was asking the Lord, with every devotion of a devoted heart, for forgiveness of his sins. He was striving, according to his customary practice, to offer most devoutly the melody of psalms and prayers. Extending the beginning of his office at greater length, however, he fell asleep, compelled by weariness.

At once a certain elder appeared to him, distinguished by the beauty of his dignity and clothed in a venerable habit. In a pleasant manner he asked what the brothers were doing and where they had withdrawn.

The brother immediately replied that they had gone to sleep, so that, after a little refreshment for their bodily needs, they might be able to perform the daytime office more abundantly.

Wondering who this person might be who was giving him such instructions, the most blessed man said to him:

“Do not be surprised at my presence, which you see. Know with complete certainty that I am called Brother Benedict, appointed prelate and defender of this place.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] In the various appearances of Saint Benedict related both in the Cassinese Chronicle and elsewhere, Benedict is always said to have called himself “Brother.” From this one may understand that it was the custom of those times for any monk, when speaking of himself, to use the title “brother” out of humility.]

“Tell the brothers greetings from me in the general assembly, and let them be aware at the celebration of solemn Mass that I was unable to be present with my brothers while they were singing the nocturnal office. For I obtained from the Lord forgiveness of sins for Brother Aimericus as he departed for the regions of Britain, and, rescuing him from the jaws of the enemy, I raised him happily to the seats of eternal life.

“Let them therefore know, with you bearing witness, that after, by God’s arrangement, the presence of my body was transported from the eastern regions to these western lands, none of them suffered the loss of eternal rest; rather, Christ placed those who had been granted protection in the exalted places of the heavenly homeland.”

When he had said this, the vision of the man standing and conversing with him vanished.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] From this it is inferred that Benedictine monks in that age performed the morning office at midnight; otherwise, on the feast of the Translation—that is, in high summer, or on 11 July—no interval would have remained after the nocturnal prayers for sleep before daylight.]

When the light of day had poured its brightness over the earth, the brothers awoke from sleep. The same man then summoned Abbot Theotbertus [Note: [Col. 0946D] It is established from the preliminary Dissertation, no. 13, that Abbot Theodbert was in office in 878.], together with the others, by the sound of the cast metal board, which had formerly been fashioned for giving the signal to reopen speech [Note: [Col. 0946D] Observe that the end of the nightly silence prescribed by Saint Benedict in chapter 42 was formerly indicated by a signal.], and uttered words of greeting. He then reported to them in order everything that Father Benedict had commanded him to say.

They bowed their whole bodies toward the ground in worship and, with joyful hearts, offered countless praises to God and to his guardian in unanimous devotion. Each one also took care to prepare himself, lest the appearance of the one who was coming reveal anything inappropriate.

Although he had made known that he was especially to be awaited by the brothers in person, while they remained faithful to the Lord’s commands, so that no one should be absent anywhere, even for a short time, nevertheless, to display the power of his virtue and the common joy of all, he showed himself present through the efficacy of divine action.

For something great happened, which all believers either saw or came to know: after the holy Gospel had been recited, all who were suffering from any ailment, and all whom the thresholds of the sacred basilica had retained, returned each to his own home with the gift of the desired health.

In all, sixty people of both sexes and every age were healed. With complete magnificence they jointly offered praises to God, thanks to God, and thanks to the most blessed Father Benedict.

For it was plainly evident to all, through so great an accomplished work of God, that our Benedict had been present during the solemn celebration of Mass.

## CHAPTER XLI. Charles the Bald Is Praised. Returning from Rome, He Dies by Poison at Pavia (A.D. 877). Louis Succeeds Him; the Northmen Renew Their Attacks and Are Defeated by Hugh

Meanwhile, after two of his brothers had departed this human life and the third, Lothair, had become a monk at the monastery of Prüm because of the repentance he felt for having confined his father in prison, King Charles obtained the whole of his father’s empire. Showing himself agreeable and favorable to everyone, he had attracted some of the Franks to the imperial dignity through their common allegiance to him.

Thus, daily advancing toward the stature of a perfect man, he exercised the devotion of a most Christian [variant: Christian] spirit so vigorously in enriching the monasteries of the saints that he seemed inferior in no aspect of holy religion to any of the former kings who had shone with the dignity of the royal name.

Among the many gifts he generously bestowed on this place, he devoutly granted a priestly vestment which he had taken from the chapel of his brother Lothair when he was returning from the battle of Fontenay [Fontenay in Burgundy, in 841]. He also took care, for the healing of his soul, to give solemnly and personally two golden vessels valued at [lacuna] pounds, together with a Gospel book produced with elaborate workmanship of various kinds.

But, as was mentioned above, after the death of his brothers he set out for Rome with magnificent equipment and, through the favor of the entire people, was proclaimed emperor and Augustus of the Roman Empire. When, on his return, he reached the borders of Italy, he was enticed by the malicious deception of certain men and, at the city of Pavia, amid the greatest grief of his followers, ended his life by poison on the day before the Nones of October.

Afterward his son, named Louis, took up his father’s kingdom. For scarcely two years, he devoted its difficult beginnings to all the nobles of his realm.

For the Northmen, the people who had already twice emerged from the sheath of their homeland and so often practiced piracy, regained strength after the death of his father. With few people resisting them, they continually inflicted the devastation of their wickedness within the boundaries of the Frankish kingdom.

First attacking the regions of Neustria, they devoted themselves with the full perversity of their efforts to slaughter and plunder, striving to seize and convert to their own wicked uses everything that had previously seemed desirable and beneficial to human life.

They would have completed what they had begun, had not Hugh [Note: [Col. 0947C] This is Abbot Hugh, who subscribed to the Council of Pontigon in 876 and to whom two letters of Pope John VIII survive in volume III of the Councils of Gaul, concerning the protection of the monastery of Pultariacum. Regino and others say that he died in 887 in these words: “Hugh, an abbot of great piety and great prudence, dies at Orléans and is buried at Saint-Germain at Auxerre.” The duchy which he had held and governed vigorously was entrusted by the emperor to Odo, son of Robert, who at that time was count of Paris.], the most noble abbot, vigorously governing the commonwealth by both arms and counsel, repressed their barbarous efforts through his own courage and killed a very large number of them.

How he accomplished this powerfully through the virtue of Father Benedict should be briefly related.

As we have said, the Northmen passed through the harbors of many cities without opposition and came to Orléans. From there, advancing farther, they attempted to approach the monastery of Floriacum in order to inflict devastation.

The brothers had already learned of this through widespread report. It seemed appropriate to them, therefore, to withdraw from the place and fortify themselves with whatever protection circumstances required.

Accordingly, they prepared wagons of various kinds, loaded them with their valuables, and decided to make their way with the rest of their possessions to the estate at Matriniacum, so that there their entire property might somehow be safe.

But when that treacherous nation reached the monastery and found its hopes frustrated, discovering nothing there worth plundering except the walls, it finally noticed the fresh tracks of the wagons and decided to proceed to the place where it suspected, in its anxiety, that the brothers had gone, so that, after plundering their better possessions, it might return with its victory accomplished.

The omnipotence of merciful God anticipated their wicked plan. By his power he would crush them and, by kindly defending it, save the innocent people from their evil attack.

For at that time the venerable man Hugh had come from the region of Burgundy to these territories, perhaps summoned by God’s counsel for the fulfillment of his necessary duty. When he had drawn near the monastery, he learned from his men that the brothers were being pursued by the enemy and would very soon be plundered [variant: pillaged] unless they were delivered by God’s wondrous power.

When he learned this, he was pulled in different directions in mind. Since he had very few soldiers with him at that moment, he began to be troubled and distressed in many ways, turning over within himself how he might confront so great a multitude.

At last, encouraged by Girboldus, the most noble count of Auxerre, he took courage to engage in battle, asserting that no one who had joined the opposing army for the sake of serving Blessed Father Benedict would ever suffer disaster.

Thus, strengthened by this exhortation, trusting in the merits and help of the outstanding Father, they pursued the enemy from behind not far from the monastery. Joining battle with great courage and engaging in a fierce struggle, they raged against them with such slaughter and devastation that, from so numerous a people, scarcely anyone remained to report the outcome of the battle to posterity.

After the desired victory had been achieved, the commander of the battle questioned his men and asked whether any of them had actually seen, amid the dense ranks of the enemy, a monk of venerable appearance opening a path for him.

When they answered that they had seen no monk in that battle, he immediately said:

“Saint Benedict protected me throughout the entire course of this battle. With his left hand he directed and guarded the reins of my horse; in his right hand he held a staff, striking down many of the enemy and handing them over to death.”

Thus, through the intervention of Father Benedict, punishment was returned to the guilty and security to the innocent, by the gift of the blessed Son of God, whose blessed name remains forever and ever.

[Col. 0947]

# ADREVALD, MONK OF FLORIACUM: ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST, AGAINST THE FOLLIES OF JOHN SCOTUS

*(In Acherius, Spicilegium, vol. I, p. 150, from manuscripts of the abbey of Floriacum.)*

[Col. 0947D] When blessed Jerome was explaining the mysteries of the Lord’s body in his Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, he added the following:

“Now while they were dining” [Matthew 26:26], and so forth. “After the typical Passover had been fulfilled and he had eaten the flesh of the lamb with the apostles, he takes bread, which strengthens the human heart, and passes over to the sacrament of the true Passover, so that, just as Melchizedek, priest of the most high God, had prefigured it by offering bread and wine, he too might represent it in the truth of his body and blood.”

[Note: Blessed Jerome. Acherius notes that he found this little work in the parchment manuscripts of Floriacum. It consists entirely of passages stitched together by Adrevald from the Fathers.]

Likewise, in his letter to Hedibia, concerning what is written in Matthew, “I tell you: from now on I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine” [Matthew 26:29], he says:

“Let us hear that the bread which the Lord broke and gave to the disciples is the body of the Lord the Savior, since he himself says to them: ‘Take and eat; this is my body’ [ibid., 26]; and that the cup is the one of which he again said: ‘Drink from it, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’ [ibid., 27–28].

“This is the cup of which we read in the prophet: ‘I shall take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord’ [Psalm 115:4]. And elsewhere: ‘Your cup, making drunk—how splendid it is!’ [Psalm 22:5].

“For if the bread that descended from heaven is the Lord’s body, and the wine that he gave to the disciples is his blood of the New Testament, which was poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, let us reject Jewish fables, and let us ascend with the Lord to the large, furnished, and cleansed upper room. There let us receive from him the cup of the New Testament above, and, celebrating the Passover with him, let us become drunk with the wine of sobriety.

“For the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness, joy, and peace in the Holy Spirit [Romans 14:17]. Nor did Moses give us the true bread, but the Lord Jesus—himself both guest and banquet, himself both the one who eats and the one who is eaten. We drink his blood, and without him we cannot drink. Every day in his sacrifices we tread out red must from the fruit of the true vine and of the vine of Sorek, which is interpreted as ‘chosen’; and from these we drink new wine in the kingdom of the Father. We sing not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit the new song, which no one can sing except in the kingdom of the Church, which is the kingdom of the Father.”

In his Exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, at the passage where he explains the Apostle’s statement, “In whom we have redemption through his blood” [Ephesians 1:7], he says:

“Christ’s blood and flesh are understood in two ways: either as that spiritual and divine reality of which he himself says, ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink’ [John 6:56], and, ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life’ [ibid., 34]; or as the flesh that was crucified and the blood that was poured out by the soldier’s lance.

“According to this distinction, a diversity of blood and flesh is also understood in his saints, so that one is the flesh that will see the salvation of God, while another is flesh and blood that cannot possess the kingdom of God.”

Likewise, in his treatise on the prophet Isaiah, at the passage where it says, “What do I want with the multitude of your sacrifices?” and shortly afterward, “For who has asked these things from your hands?” [Isaiah 1:11–12], he says:

“Let the Ebionites hear this—those who think that, after Christ’s passion has been abolished, the law must still be observed. Let the companions of the Ebionites hear it, those who decree that these observances belong only to the Jews and to those of Israelite descent.

“The slaughtering of hosts and victims, therefore, was not principally demanded by God, but so that they would not be offered to idols, and so that from bodily victims, as through a type and image, we might pass over to spiritual sacrifices.

“By saying that he did not seek sacrifices, he shows that the law is spiritual and that everything the Jews do bodily is fulfilled by us spiritually.”

But in his explanation of the prophet Malachi, at the chapter where it says, “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts,” and shortly afterward, “In every place sacrifice is made, and a pure offering is offered to my name” [Malachi 1:10–11], after much else he says:

“Some think that what is said specifically to the Jews, because their victims are unclean and polluted, and that the sacrifice is transferred to the nations, must be understood of the priests of the Church who offer victims to the Lord negligently.

“But if we accept this, then the victims must again be transferred from the Church to another religion. And how, just as the Gospel succeeded the law, will things that are not destined to come again succeed the Gospel?”

Saint Augustine, in his exposition of the Gospel of John [tractate 26], at the same passage where it says, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” [John 6:51], expresses himself as follows. After asking why they were proud, he continues:

“‘Your fathers ate manna and died’ [ibid., 49]. What is the source of your pride? They ate and died. Why did they eat and die? Because they believed what they saw, and they did not understand what they did not see.”

And a little later:

“‘They ate manna,’ he says, ‘both Moses and the other holy men ate it, and they did not die a spiritual death. Why? Because they understood the visible food spiritually, and so were spiritually satisfied.’
