“For we too receive visible food today, but the sacrament is one thing and the power of the sacrament another. How many receive from the altar and die—and die by receiving! Hence the Apostle says: ‘He eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ [1 Corinthians 11:27].

“Was not the Lord’s morsel poison to Judas? Yet he received it, and when he had received it, the enemy entered into him—not because he received something evil, but because an evil man received something good.

“See, therefore, brothers: eat the heavenly bread spiritually.”

And after much else:

“This, therefore, is the bread that came down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die [John 6:50]—but this refers to the power of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament; to the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; to the one who eats in the heart, not to the one who presses with the tooth.

“‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven’ [ibid., 51]. It is living for this reason: because it came down from heaven. Manna also came down from heaven, but manna was a shadow; this is the truth.

“If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. ‘And the bread that I shall give for the life of the world is my flesh’ [ibid., 52]. When could flesh comprehend this—that he called bread flesh? What flesh cannot comprehend is called flesh; and for this reason flesh comprehends it even less, because it is called flesh.

“For this is what they recoiled from; this is what they said was too much for them; this is what they thought could not happen. ‘It is my flesh,’ he says, ‘for the life of the world.’”

Likewise, concerning the morsel that Judas received, after much else he says [tractate 62]:

“Remember where it is written: ‘Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord’ [1 Corinthians 11:27].

“The Apostle was speaking of those people when he said this: they were taking the Lord’s body indiscriminately and carelessly, as though it were any other food.

“If the one who does not judge—that is, does not distinguish the Lord’s body from other foods—is rebuked; if an enemy approaches the table of God while pretending to be a friend . . . if negligence at the banquet is touched by rebuke, with what punishment is the seller of the one who invites struck?

“What, then, was the bread given to the betrayer except a demonstration of the grace toward which he had been ungrateful?

“After this bread, Satan entered the Lord’s betrayer, so that he might possess him fully as one already handed over to him—he into whom he had previously entered in order to deceive him.

“For he was not with him when he went to the Jews and agreed on the price for betraying the Lord; the evangelist Luke plainly testifies to this when he says: ‘Satan entered into Judas, who was called Iscariot, one of the twelve; and he went away and spoke with the chief priests’ [Luke 22:3–4].

“See where it is shown that Satan had already entered Judas. He had entered him earlier by putting into his heart the thought of betraying Christ; for such a man had already come to dine.

“Now, after the bread, he entered him—not still to tempt someone belonging to another, but to possess someone who was his own.

“Yet, as some careless readers think, it is not to be understood that Judas then received Christ’s body. For it must be understood that the Lord had already distributed to all of them the sacrament of his body and blood, and Judas himself was among them, as Saint Luke narrates [ibid., 19, 21].

“Afterward they came to the point where, according to John’s account, he most clearly identified his betrayer by the dipped and extended morsel.”

On the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood he also delivered a brief homily during the days of the Resurrection, in these words:

> “What you see on the altar of God you also saw last night; but what it was, and what great mystery it contained, you have not yet heard. As far as what you see is concerned, it is bread and a cup, as your own eyes tell you; but what your faith demands to be instructed in is this: the bread is Christ’s body, and the cup is Christ’s blood.”

In his *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, which he composed, when discussing the ancient Passover, he speaks thus concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood:

> “For the purified alone, cleansed by the bath of heavenly forgiveness, the sacred capacity [for you] to receive Christ’s body is offered. Thus, what had been prefigured for the Israelites has been confirmed in us; what were images among them are realities themselves in us. They imitated the celebration of Passover while they were being exercised through likenesses; Christ’s disciples alone would celebrate the true Passover.”

Moreover, in the thirty-ninth Psalm, in the verse that says, “You desired neither sacrifice nor offering,” he explains most aptly and clearly how the Lord’s body is to be received, saying as follows (*Exposition of the Psalms*):

> “When what was promised has been given, the words of promise have been taken away, and the words of fulfillment have been given. Those sacrifices, therefore, were taken away as words of promise. What is the thing given in fulfillment? The body which you know, which not all of you know; and would that all who know it may not know it to their condemnation.”

And shortly afterward:

> “What then? Have we at this time been dismissed without a sacrifice? Far be it! ‘But you perfected a body for me.’ Therefore you did not desire those sacrifices in order to perfect this one; you desired them before you perfected this one. The perfection of the promises removed the words that promised them; for if they are still promising, what was promised has not yet been fulfilled. This was promised through certain signs; the signs that promised it have been removed, because the promised reality has been presented. We are in this body; we are participants in this body. We know what we receive; and you who do not know, come to know it—and when you have learned, may you not receive it to your condemnation. For ‘whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ (1 Cor. 11:29). The body has been perfected for us; may we be perfected in the body.”

And much later:

> “The Jews remained in the shadow; they cannot bear the sun of glory. We are already in the light; we hold Christ’s body, we hold Christ’s blood.”

Moreover, Saint Gregory, explaining in his homilies the passages of Exodus concerning the blood of the Lamb upon the doorposts and lintel, says as follows (*Homily 22 on the Gospels*, Book II):

> “You have learned what the blood of the Lamb is, not now by hearing, but by drinking. That blood is placed upon both doorposts when it is received not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart. For the blood of the Lamb is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of his Passion is received with the mouth for redemption and also pondered with an attentive mind for imitation. Whoever receives the blood of his Redeemer in such a way that he is not yet willing to imitate his Passion places the blood upon only one doorpost.”

Likewise, in the *Dialogues*, concerning the power and mystery of the saving victim, he says (*Book IV, chapter 58*):

> “Meanwhile, we must consider that the safer course is for each person to perform himself, while he is alive, the good which he hopes will be done on his behalf by others after his death. For it is happier to depart free than to seek freedom after imprisonment. We must therefore despise the present age with our whole mind, since we already see that it has passed away; we must offer God daily sacrifices of tears and daily sacrifices of his flesh. For this sacrifice uniquely saves the soul from eternal destruction; the following wording is lacunose and materially uncertain: “which … restores to us through the mystery the death *congenitam*.” Although, rising from the dead, he no longer dies, and death shall no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9), nevertheless, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering. For there his body is received; his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured out no longer into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful. From this, then, let us consider what this sacrifice is for us: it always imitates, for our absolution, the Passion of the only-begotten Son. For what believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the sacrifice, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest and lowest are joined; that earthly and heavenly things are united; and that one thing is made from visible and invisible realities?”

Cyprian, whose memory is deservedly illustrious, when expounding the Lord’s Prayer and coming to the words “Our daily bread” (Matt. 6:11), says:

> “It can be understood in two ways, both spiritually and simply, since each interpretation, through divine usefulness, contributes to salvation. For Christ is the bread of life, and he is not the bread of everyone but our bread. Just as we say ‘Our Father’ (ibid., 9), because he is the Father of those who understand and believe, so also we call him our bread, because Christ is ours, and we who touch his body have him as bread. We ask that this bread be given to us daily, so that we who are in Christ and receive the Eucharist daily as food for salvation may not, because of some more serious offense, be kept from the heavenly bread while being excluded and not communicating, and thus be separated from Christ’s body. He himself proclaims and warns: ‘I am the bread of life who came down from heaven; if anyone eats of my bread, he will live forever. The bread which I shall give for the life of the world is my flesh’ (John 6:51–52). When, therefore, he says that whoever eats of his bread will live forever, it is clear that those live who touch his body and receive the Eucharist by right of communion. Conversely, we must fear and pray lest, while someone is excluded and separated from Christ’s body, he remain apart from salvation … , since he threatens and says: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves’ (John 6:54). Therefore we ask that our bread—that is, Christ—be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not depart from his sanctification and body.”

[Col. 0953]

# Life of Saint Aigulf, Abbot of Lérins and Martyr

By Adrevald, a monk

(From Mabillon, in the place cited above.)

[Note: Preliminary Observation. Laurentius Surius had read the Life of Saint Aigulf—or Aygulf [Aigulfe; elsewhere Saint Ayoul]—written by Adrevald, though without the author’s name, and had published it in 1580 in an abridged form and in a different style. Vincent Barrali was not pleased with Surius’s Life. Wishing to obscure the memory of Saint Benedict’s translation to Gaul, Barrali published another Life in his *Lérins Chronicle* in 1613, compiled from various very ancient manuscripts and codices of the monastery of Lérins, with the account of that translation removed. This may in some measure be tolerated in a monk attached to the Cassinese congregation, but it certainly cannot be approved in the Surius recension made at Cologne in 1618, in which Barrali’s compilation was inserted after the earlier history approved by Surius had been rejected. In the Floriacensis manuscript, the Life of Saint Aigulf, which we reproduce here in its genuine and native style, bears the following heading:]

## Prologue of Father Adrevald concerning the Life and Passion of the Venerable Monk Aigulf, at Floriacum

[Col. 0953C] Useful lives of the saints.

### 1

Almost no one fails to understand that it is not the task of just anyone to commit to writing and transmit to later generations the pious and arduous struggles of the saints and most courageous athletes of Christ, by which they triumphed over the devil and the savage world. For such accounts provide the foundations of believers and the beginnings of faith; they strengthen the mature through confidence in hope; they delight the perfected through the sweetness of holy charity; they pour caution over the combatant, lest he fall, as though with a kind of oil; and, if they grow weary, they restore them to their former strength by this remedy.

To this is added the fact that, attracted by these accounts, we frequently associate ourselves with the company of the saints, whom the bosom of blessedness—which is still closed to us—already holds. For we love them not on account of their outward features, but because we know them to be beautiful through the distinction of their merits. When these merits are inserted into our hearts by the narration of their history, they are brought before the eyes of our minds, as though by a kind of mirror.

From their fellowship we have undertaken to commit to writing the life and passion of one man, Aigulf by name, moved by love for the one for whom he lived and suffered in this way. We do not rely upon the sharpness of our intellect, but upon the help of him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, and whose promise we hold as a most firm anchor when he says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80).

### 2

Yet I am not unaware of the practice of certain people who are always looking for a tooth into which they may drive their bite. Their opinion will perhaps be: “Why do you bring before us—or rather, invent—a crude martyr? Did some persecutor slaughter him for the faith of Christ? Such is the trophy of the martyrs of old, not that of some novice who was insufficiently cautious in avoiding the snares of his enemies, and to whom the briefest possible praise, if he escaped, ought to suffice.”

What difference does it make whether someone completed the course of his martyr’s contest four hundred or two hundred years ago? Is the spectator of the contest not always the same? Yet these matters are not to be weighed like wines, which generally become more agreeable the older they are.

But let us suppose that no persecutor killed him for confessing Christ. Did Herod behead that John who was greatest among those born of women because of Christ? Or did he not rather remove him from human affairs because John had opposed him in the way of iniquity, on account of the truth, which is God? Therefore, if anything should emerge from another source that he undertook for blessed John, let him remember that he ought to undertake the same for this venerable man.

Having briefly set these matters before us, let us proceed to the narrative, with Christ going before us and aiding our efforts.

# Here Begins the Life

[Col. 0955]

## Aigulf of Blois

[Col. 0955A]

### 3

It is evident even to the simplest people that ancient and modern writers have had the custom, when they were about to relate someone’s deeds, of first setting forth his family and native land. We too, not rejecting this custom, wish to make known the homeland and lineage of blessed Aigulf to those who do not know them.

The fortress of Blois is situated on the slope of a certain mountain, beside which lies the bank of the river Liger; and that same Liger (“le Loir”), flowing past it, supplies that place, more abundantly than others, not only with fish but also with a great bounty of other produce—namely wine, grain, and the other necessities of human life.

We have learned from the most certain report that the parents of blessed Aigulf were inhabitants of this district and fortress. They were not greatly exalted by the pride of ancient blood, nor puffed up by an abundance of worldly wealth, but they were made happy by a large number of children. For he was one of those of whom the Apostle says: “God chose the weak things of this world and the despised, and those things which are not” (1 Cor. 1).

It is difficult to relate how he passed the years of his childhood: namely, how he took delight in constantly wearing away the thresholds of the church, serving the priests, devoting himself to the watches of the vigils, coming to the aid of the needs of the poor according to his strength, and daily offering his whole self as a living and holy sacrifice, pleasing to God, spiritually sacrificing his spirit to the Lord upon the altar of his heart.

## He Entrusts Himself to the Discipline of Blessed Mummolus

### 4

But when he reached the years of youth, not only life itself but also secular dress and conduct began to weigh upon him. He considered how, by breaking its restraints and changing his condition, he might healthfully fasten his foot in the fetters of Christ.

While he was occupied with these thoughts and delaying according to the custom of delay, he soon sought a useful plan—for such a great matter ought not to be entrusted to rash desire, but such things require much reconsideration. Then the report of the blessed man Mummolus, abbot of Floriacum, reached his ears, for the fame of his life was carried far and wide.

Having heard this reputation, Aigulf eagerly sought to approach and hear the holy man. When he had come to him, he disclosed the desire with which he had long burned and asked, with the greatest humility, to be numbered among those whom Mummolus was educating in the school of Christ.

When the blessed man heard this, following the discipline that was always his custom, friendly to regular life, he united Aigulf to the body of his holy congregation as a suitable member, after the days of probation had passed and the appropriate period of testing had been completed.

## He Lives Religiously

[Col. 0956A]

### 5

Once he had obtained the enclosure of monastic life, he immediately began, through the working power of the Holy Spirit, to show himself a clean animal and suitable for the heavenly flock.

In him shone, as in a sheep, the purity of innocence; in the command of his own limbs, the true power of a ram; in the war he waged against demons, a certain inflexible authority like that of a bull; in purity of spirit, the sweetness of a dove; and in the chastity of mind and body, the surpassing purity of a turtledove.

Nor did he forget that the Law declares that animal clean which divides the hoof and chews the cud (Lev. 11). Accordingly, he understood the division of the hoof as discernment—not only between good and evil, but also concerning the inner person. In chewing the word of God, moreover, he maintained constant meditation, according to what the Lord says: “One ought always to pray and not grow weary” (Luke 18). And the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33).

With so many virtues gathered together in one place, grace of every virtue blossomed in him like a spiritual panel. And lest such great goods suffer any loss, he did what is written of the just man: “He will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1).

Through this exercise he rose to such a height that his teaching became a wonder not only to those of his own province but also to those living far away. It pleased the Divinity to show, by signs already evident, how highly he valued the one to whom he had granted such duties.

## He Brings the Relics of Saint Benedict to Gaul

### 6

Benedict, beloved of God, celebrated and worthy to be sung throughout the whole world, and the singular founder of regular life, had closed the final day of this life many years earlier in the province of Benevento and had received burial in the fortress of Cassino. But after not much time had passed, in accordance with the prophecy of that same most holy man, the place was captured by the Lombards and reduced to a wilderness.

Now, wishing both that the divine deposit and the relics of the aforesaid most holy man should be venerated with fitting honor, and that the regions of Gaul should be consoled by their arrival, he appeared to the aforesaid kindly abbot Mummolus and commanded him to send the aforementioned Aigulf to Mount Cassino, or to the fortress there, so that he might transport the bones of the most pious Benedict.

This is known to have been done. With God going before him and wonderfully prospering his journey, Aigulf traveled such a great distance, found what he was seeking by an easy indication, and, having found it, brought it back with the greatest rejoicing to the Father who had sent him.

Whoever wishes to know the details of this event more carefully may learn them by reading the little book composed about it (under the year 653).

## Aigulf Becomes Abbot of Lérins

### 7

Although Aigulf himself cared nothing for such matters, this deed produced in the holy man an immense reputation for holiness both with the king and with his courtiers.

Accordingly, when the fame of his virtue and the fragrance of his holiness had been scattered everywhere, and when the lamp kindled by divine fire ought by divine judgment to be placed upon a lampstand, behold, the monks of the monastery of Lérins appeared.

[Note: In the Acts compiled by Vincent Barrali, Aigulf is first said to have presided over the monastery of Saint Aignan near Orléans. Few people besides Barrali seem to have transmitted this report.]

They asked that a spiritual father be assigned to them. That monastery had flourished with an ancient distinction, so that under its direction many places suitable for divine service had been founded far and wide. Yet at that time, with discord arising through the agency of the devil, affairs were wavering in a manner contrary to what was proper.

When the monks’ request had been brought before the king and his nobles, and the king—as is customary—had consulted his advisers, by whose authority the state was known to be administered, about what should be done in such a matter, one voice was heard and there was no dissent: such a great man ought to be placed over such a place, through whom it would be certain that what had collapsed would be raised again and what had been neglected restored to its former condition.

Why say more? Blessed Aigulf, though resisting and reluctant, was brought before them, and the care of the aforesaid monastery was imposed upon him. The king rejoiced, and his princes exulted, because he had shown them such a shepherd to be placed over his flock.

Although the holy man would have preferred his own silence, he was not unmindful of the apostolic command that every soul must be subject to the higher authorities (Rom. 13). For he was an observant animal, looking all around, and, so that he might remain without blemish, he watched in every direction.

Now, placing his neck beneath the burden laid upon him, he approached the brothers he had received. Since his reputation had already attracted their ears, they embraced him with joyful arms of devotion; and he, in turn, cherished them with reciprocal and affectionate love.

## He Gives Excellent Admonitions to His People

### 8

Meanwhile, he began to sow the seeds of the divine word in the inner fields of their hearts, teaching them, after renouncing vices [elsewhere: vanities], to seize the summit of virtue.

He taught that the vision of the inner eyes must be purified, since God, being pure, can be seen only by clear sight; that the speck of anger and the beam of hatred must be entirely driven away; that the enemy of lust must be kept at the greatest distance not only from the body but also from the mind; and that a house is not worthy to be the dwelling of the Holy Spirit—indeed, that a heart accustomed to filthy pollution repels him.

He firmly asserted that the world and the things belonging to it must be entirely excluded from the love of the heart, and that nothing except what God commands should be placed in the seat of love, that is, in the ruling part of the heart: the love of God above all things, and of one’s neighbor after God.

Whoever extends the foot of love beyond these things and those pertaining to them does not escape the crime of fornication. Therefore the sentence of David must strike such a person: “You have destroyed all those who fornicate away from you” (Ps. 72).

With these and similar remedies, like a spiritual physician using mystical antidotes, he strove not only to heal present illnesses but also to forestall future troubles.

## The Monastery of Lérins Flourishes Again under His Care

### 9

The Lord was present with his efforts, without whose help those who build a house labor in vain.

Finally, the Lord deemed it right to bestow such grace upon his teaching that not only did those present listen to him with the greatest eagerness, but those who had formerly departed from the monastery also returned with the greatest fervor and rejoiced to unite themselves to the congregation.

The monastery could be seen receiving all who arrived like a kind of beehive—those who declared that they either were or wished to become the Lord’s bees. Many secular people also contributed their possessions and received spiritual things from the holy man; according to the Apostle, they exposed their carnal goods to be reaped by the one who sowed spiritual things (1 Cor. 9).

## He Suffers the Factions of Wicked Monks

### 10

The envious devil, whose envy brought death into the world, saw these things and was distressed. He grieved that he was being expelled from those whom he had formerly rejoiced to see subjected to him.

Therefore, the crafty investigator turned to his customary arts of wickedness, seeking whether he might find one of his own hidden among the Lord’s sheep beneath a sheep’s skin, knowing that those who belong to him imitate him.

At last he found two, whom he used like a serpent’s pipe in paradise to trouble the hearts of others and drive them toward discord. One was named Archadius; the other was called Columbus, using a name contrary to his own nature. His heart was not free from the wickedness of gall, but, as the apostle Peter said to Simon, it had been turned toward “the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8).

Into the hearts of these men, as into the heart of Judas, the devil entered, so that they might betray their master and, once he had been driven away, scatter the sheep, left without a shepherd, in conflict with one another.

For a long time they concealed their plans, secretly recruiting as many as they could to their treachery. But one day, when they had already gained confidence from their numbers and could no longer conceal their fury, they burst into public view like a flame long suppressed that suddenly breaks out.

The faction of the wicked, stirred up by these two standard-bearers, grew so strong that they scarcely restrained themselves from killing the master and laying hands upon the good men who adhered to him.

Those who saw the danger threatening them, and against whom the enemies [elsewhere: the wicked] had directed their designs, escaped their hands by flight and took refuge in the church of Saint John, commending their hearts and souls to the power and mercy of the Lord.

## He Tries to Soften Their Hearts

### 11

Blessed Aigulf, gentle in every respect and mindful of his customary patience and mildness, approached them and tried with the gentlest words to soften their swollen hearts.

He addressed them in these words:

> “O my sweetest and most beloved sons, by what impulse are you violating the bond of fatherhood and brotherhood? What is it that has made you fail to recognize your own brothers? Do you not know that the devil, because of pride and discord, was cast down from the summit of heaven? Has it escaped your minds that, as the highest punishment, the union of language was taken away from the proud alone, and that the bond of charity, signified by the appearance of fire, was never restored except through the coming of the Holy Spirit?
>
> “Learn, therefore, to renounce quarrels and obey the words of the Lord, who says: ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart’ (Matt. 11). But if this is being done on my account, I say to you in the words of Jonah: ‘Take me and throw me into the sea’ (Jon. 1). It is better for me to be separated from you in body than to be tormented by your present dissension.”

## Again, Shortly Afterward, He Tries to Pacify the Rebels

### 12

By this speech he seemed for a time to have restrained their agitation and calmed their fury, so much so that they themselves confessed their fault and offered satisfaction. Yet they were disguising their guilt by a stratagem.

For a whole year the devil hid in the caves of their hearts beneath such an appearance of simplicity. Nor could the man of God, by his frequent—or rather continual—admonitions, remove him from the hiding place of their minds, as though from a serpent with stopped ears; instead, they were always plotting how they might bring their undertaking to the desired conclusion.

But when such matters were already flying from mouth to mouth and had reached the king, the authors of the conspiracy, fearing that the king’s severity might act against them, decided that one of them, Archadius, should leave the monastery and stir up the clergy of the city and as many secular people as he could.

Columbus, however, remaining within the monastery, was to strengthen in their begun treachery those who had defected from the holy man and associate with himself anyone he could.

But Saint Aigulf continually persisted in his teaching, saying:

> “Brothers, these are the words of the Holy Spirit: ‘The Lord makes those of one mind dwell in a house’ (Ps. 67). Therefore those who do not preserve unity have lost their dwelling in the house of God and have passed into the devil’s lot. For this reason we must be bound by the ties of charity and not divided by schisms.”

## He Expels Archadius, the Instigator of the Sedition. He Is Seized and Bound with His Followers

[Col. 0959D]

### 13

While Aigulf was acting and speaking in this way, one day Archadius returned with feigned humility and false words, promising to correct his past conduct, and asked to be restored to his former dwelling.

But the man of God foresaw the hidden plague. With the brothers supporting him, he not only refused his request but also expelled him from the monastery.

Unable to bear this insult, Archadius went to a certain ruler of the city of Uzès—named Mummolus—and persuaded him to go to the monastery, as though he would find a great deal of money there.

[Note: Read “the ruler of the city of Uzès,” that is, the bishop; bishops are often called this. In the Life of Saint Amandus, chapter 23, under the year 679, Mummolus of Uzès—that is, the bishop of Uzès—is said to have plotted Saint Amandus’s death. The man’s cruelty, as well as his age, corresponds sufficiently to the present deed, although the island of Lérins is not a short distance from the city of Uzès in Narbonese Gaul. In the copy designated V. C. D. Herovallius, however, *Nicetiae*, or Nice, is read instead of *Vicetiae*; that city is closer to Lérins.]

When greed had kindled in Mummolus’s breast a torch familiar to him, he immediately set out and approached the monastery and the holy man. Since he had often been accustomed to confer with Mummolus about the welfare of his soul, Aigulf received him without fear and had him treated to a magnificent banquet.

By then he had learned the arrangements of the plot through Audoenus, the bishop [of Rouen]. While Mummolus was dining with the other conspirators in the crime, Archadius suddenly appeared, surrounded by a wicked crowd, like Judas. He ordered that the master be seized, bound, and beaten with clubs; and this was done.

Meanwhile, the man of complete patience, remembering God and that our Lord Jesus Christ had endured bitter things not for himself but for us, confidently sang:

> “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115).

Thus torn and bound, and held up to the mockery of his persecutors, he remained until night was brought over the light.

When night began at its appointed time to cover the earth, the ministers of Satan brought out from the monastery cloisters those whom they knew to have adhered most closely to the holy man and brought them to the Father, as though they were all to be heard together, but in reality so that they might suffer together. For the Divinity did not wish the shepherd to suffer alone, but to have the flock share in his suffering.

But the saints, strengthened by the Holy Spirit and possessing true virtue, as though they were already about to offer their throats to swords, said their final farewells to one another. Rushing into one another’s embraces, they commended themselves to the Lord, saying to him with the greatest confidence:

> “For your sake, Lord, we are put to death; all day long we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43). “Therefore do not reject us forever.”

They also said:

> “You have placed us in darkness like the dead of the age” (Ps. 142).

With these and similar words they consoled both the darkness of the night and their own afflictions.

## Aigulf Refuses to Escape from Prison

### 14

Meanwhile they armed one another with mutual words of encouragement, lest any of the weaker should fail under such circumstances, since the truthful Apostle says:

> “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

As is natural to the human body, sleep, made heavier by sorrow, overcame them all together—the prisoners, of course, and the guards. But one of the guards, touched by mercy, entered beneath the roof of the place of confinement, uncovered the roof, and invited the saints to escape.

Saint Aigulf thanked him for his devotion but did not at all accept his advice. He said:

> “Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s (Rom. 14). Since we have once placed ourselves in his hands and arrangement, we shall in no way resist his purpose. For we are his work, and he is our potter. It is not right for a clay vessel to complain against its maker. Therefore, let the Lord’s will be done.”

## The False Blandishments of Archadius

### 15

After these words had been spoken, the remainder of the night claimed divine praise for itself. When it had departed and daylight had succeeded it, Archadius, the bearer of calamity, imitating the practice of the devil and of all traitors, arrived with words sweetened in a certain manner, wishing to soothe the saints’ grief, although—as has been shown above—he himself had been the head of the entire crime.

One of them, named Trucarius, moved by righteous anger, confronted him face-to-face with whatever his mind and grief dictated. He said that anyone who, while driving another toward destruction, also desires to appear as his adviser was truly a son of the devil by imitation; and that Archadius was also a brother of Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, who, in imitation of Judas, brought words like a false kiss—words filled with the honey of flattery but with poisonous juices.

But the shameless face joined to cruelty did not heed the admonitions of the rebuke. Instead, he importunately persisted in the course he had begun.

For the wretched Archadius, in order to appear to prove that he had not deceitfully done what he had done, offered food and cups to the saints at the third hour and invited them to refresh themselves, as though sympathizing with their grief.

The saints, however, although distressed outwardly, did not therefore forget their purpose and regular custom. They replied that they could not violate the regular observances which at that time commanded that the fast be extended until the ninth hour. Thus, after the food had been removed, the solemn fast was postponed in the customary manner until the appointed hour.

When the time for ending their abstinence had arrived, they unanimously poured out prayers for Archadius, and then ate the food he had offered.

## Mummolus Plunders the Monastery’s Property

### 16

Mummolus, who had withdrawn from the monastery wishing to appear offended by these events, returned on the third day and began, with the greatest determination, to inquire into the money of each individual.

When the monks replied that those who had been placed under the authority of the holy man had never been permitted to possess anything as their own, not even according to their own will, but that everything was common to everyone, he saw that he had fallen from hope and turned elsewhere.

For, since he found no private property, he attacked the common property; and whatever belonging to the monastery his greed urged him to take, he left absolutely nothing behind.

## The Saints Are Put on a Ship

### 17

After Mummolus had departed, Saint Aigulf and the others were guarded according to the will of Archadius and Columbus. For ten days they were physically worn down in the prison, but they consoled one another with the Lord’s exhortations:

> “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12).

And again:

> “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14).

After this, the ministers of the devil—namely Columbus and Archadius—setting them in motion, placed Saint Aigulf and the other victims of the Holy Spirit upon a ship, and committed themselves to the sea.

The saints, now entirely aware that the sons of death had determined to destroy them, mutually encouraged one another with admonitions according to the Apostle, all the more because they saw the day approaching. They urged one another not to yield to their enemies through love of the present life or fear of uncertain death.

For present death, even if delayed, cannot be escaped; the future death of the wicked, however, never ends, since the Lord says to the impious:

> “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

But the blessedness of the saints will also have no end, since the Lord likewise says to his faithful, who persevere in his fidelity to the end:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.).

With these and similar words the athletes of Christ armed themselves in the spiritual arena against the wiles of the devil and his ministers, who were driven by demonic madness.

## They Are Tossed by a Storm

### 18

After the ship carrying both groups together—the persecutors and those suffering persecution—had reached the open sea, contrary winds arose. The persecutors were said to be driven in one direction by their will and in another by the force of the winds.

Thus, for forty days—a thing wondrous even to relate—they were whirled about, wandering throughout that strait, so that they could neither reach the shore nor could the waves of the sea sink the ship.

I believe that God was showing what the impious deserved. Yet, so that the guilty might not suffer what they deserved, the elements themselves seemed in a certain manner to cry out, not with their voices but by their actions, that the innocent were their obstacles:

> “It would have been right for these gallows-birds to be dashed upon shoals or swallowed by Charybdis, if those who did not deserve to experience such things had not been mixed with them.”

In the Flood, indeed, it was immediately possible for those who were harmful to be engulfed by the waters, since they had been separated from the company of the good. We freely swallowed the Egyptians because we saw no righteous person mixed among them.

We received Jonah to avenge disobedience, but we know him to be our fosterling, prepared by God, who would receive him in prison-like custody in order to save him; he would not pass him into his own members as food to be corrupted, but would present him as a deposit when he was reclaimed.

What the Creator wishes in such circumstances, our judgment fluctuates uncertainly. Yet here we recall one similar event, namely Paul’s shipwreck. He too, bound by the wicked, experienced maritime danger with them; but, so that he and the others might not perish, this was granted through his prayer.

Perhaps, therefore, even now an equal gift is being granted to this holy man amid an unequal danger. Thus, while his sentence is awaited, they are tossed here and there, but the way of escape is denied him, in accordance with Scripture: “The wicked walk about on every side” (Ps. 11).

## They Speak with Their Tongues Cut Out. Their Eyes Are Torn Out. They Are Dressed in Wretched Garments
19. Meanwhile, when Columbus saw that the sea was closed to him and considered that, if they reached land, both the innocence of the saints and his own cruelty would be exposed, he had the saints’ tongues cut out. After this was done, they sang as though their tongues were intact: “Lord, open our lips, and our mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Psalm 50). But he was in no way moved by so great a miracle; hardened in heart like Pharaoh, he ordered the tongues to be shaved out by the roots. One could see an open abyss, with nothing of a plectrum in it, and yet the words were perfectly articulated. When Columbus heard them speaking in this unheard-of manner, he increased his impiety and ordered their eyes to be pierced; nevertheless, they did not cease praising God. Although deprived of their external sight, they knew that they still possessed those eyes by which God is seen, and confidently sang before him—or rather, to him—saying: “To you we have lifted up our eyes, who dwell in the heavens” (Psalm 122). Yet the savagery of Columbus and his companion toward the saints did not even then cease. They ordered them to be stripped of the garments in which they were clothed and replaced with filthy and utterly worthless clothing, the wretches failing to consider that nothing old or filthy can dishonor the one who is clothed with Christ, according to the Apostle’s words: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13), and again: “Put on compassion” (Colossians 3), and so forth.

They celebrate Easter on the island of Capraria.

20. After they had been tossed about in this way for many days, they reached the island called Capraria. Its bay sheltered a very large community of monks. Turning aside to them on the Thursday before Easter, which is called Maundy Thursday, they were received with the greatest kindness and humanity—so, at least, I may say, as is fitting for monks. For once they had learned of the prolonged suffering through which the men had been tormented for so long and so miserably, they hastened to refresh them in whatever ways they could.

While they remained there, the most sacred day of the Easter solemnity arrived. As the office of the Mass was being celebrated, the most wretched and infamous of all men, Columbus, covered with the vestments appropriate to the diaconate, ministered as a deacon—conspicuous to human eyes, but hateful to the divine gaze. Moreover, when they had reached the point at which those about to receive the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood exchange kisses, that wretched man did not hesitate to offer kisses to those whom he had so cruelly mutilated—not dove-like kisses, but wholly raven-like, or certainly dog-like ones. The blessed man Aigulf, however, together with his companions, gave thanks to God with the greatest joy, insofar as they were able, not merely for their own refreshment, but still more for the immeasurable love of the brothers to whom Christ had led them.

After Columbus had gone to Ephesus, they remain there.

21. When the Easter celebration was completed, Columbus set out for Ephesus, being a man of the world intent on serving worldly business. In the meantime, he left Saint Aigulf with the other holy men in the same monastery, ordering them to await his return. Accordingly, until that wicked man came back, the Lord granted his holy servant Aigulf such great grace in speaking that the eagerness of his hearers was always accompanied by satisfaction. For the one who had given him the grace to speak though he was without a tongue now added grace to grace, so that he might be heard with greater pleasure.

From there they are taken away and slaughtered.

22. After returning from Ephesus, Columbus removed the saints from the monastery and put them on board a ship once more. When they had left the harbor and gone some distance, a certain ship coming from Africa met them. The holy martyrs were transferred to it, and Columbus ordered his agents that, when they reached an island called Amatim [Sur., Amatunam], situated between Corsica and Sardinia, they should kill the saints there by the sword. This was done.

When the executioners of the sacred victims reached the place assigned to them, they prepared to carry out their most impious orders and establish their workshop of wickedness. But when the saints asked for time to pray, the executioners granted their request. The saints, meanwhile, commended their souls to the Lord with ever greater devotion and for a longer time. At last they rose from prayer and, with complete confidence and cheerfulness, amid words of prayer and praise of the Lord, released their spirits from the vessels of their flesh, on the third day before the Nones of September.

[Note: Although Saint Aigulf’s memory is not recorded by the primary hand in the two oldest martyrologies of the monastery of Fleury, but by a later hand, it is nevertheless certain that his feast day was solemnly celebrated by the monks of Fleury six hundred years ago. This is attested by the author of the book about his miracles, who was living during the reign of Louis VI, as we shall see below in the Book of Miracles, no. 8.]

The devil’s deceit obscures their martyrdom.

23. Indeed, insofar as one may conjecture, the devil, the perpetual enemy of human salvation, was acting—so he thought—with excessive cunning, so that he might kill the saints in such a way that their passion would remain hidden from mortals. Thus the living would not have before them an example by which they might be strengthened to undertake the prize of endurance. For it is a very great incentive to virtue to behold in a companion and neighbor an inexhaustible vigor; and it is shameful to appear degenerate when one sees an equal attain glorious rewards by passing through the struggle of labors.

That most wicked one also begrudged mortals the benefits that would profit them, which he anxiously foresaw would be divinely bestowed upon them through the relics of the saints. But from this one may infer the truth of the hymn sung to God: “This dragon whom you formed to mock him” (Psalm 103).

Through Ricoinus it is revealed to Rigomirus, Aigulf’s successor, and to Angarisma.

24. For while the savage interrogators were occupied with the slaughter of the saints, one of them, named Ricoinus, driven by the divine Spirit, found a small boat and escaped, withdrawing himself from the fratricidal massacre. We believe that he was divinely preserved for this purpose, so that the saints’ passion would not be concealed. Through his account, both the manner of the saints’ passion was made known to mortals and their bodies, by God’s grace, were revealed for our consolation and brought back to our region.

It is right to believe that he was not deprived of a share in his brothers’ glory: fear did not hold him back from martyrdom; rather, God appointed him for so great a benefit. When he returned to the monastery, a man of venerable life, named Rigomirus, had already been appointed in the place of the holy man Aigulf. When the news was announced, great mourning was proclaimed both for him and for the brothers. Yet while they mourned in sympathy with the flesh, they rejoiced with regard to the spirit, knowing that, after their dwelling of clay, they had entered the inner chamber of the eternal city, whose king and founder is God.

Moreover, they shared the news with a woman named Angarisma, who presided over the consecrated sisters in a nearby monastery. From earliest childhood, this holy man had instructed her both in the divine Scriptures and in monastic learning.

The sacred bodies are brought back. Angarisma asks for Saint Aigulf’s body. She obtains his head and an arm.

25. Accordingly, by common counsel and effort, they prepared ships, appointed companions, and joined to them the man who knew the place. With God granting success, they traveled with favorable winds and a gentle temper of the air to the place where the glorious remains of the martyrs lay—abandoned by human guardianship, but defended by the protection of the divine hand.

When they found them as they had hoped, they placed them aboard ship with the greatest eagerness and the utmost reverence, as was fitting for martyrs, and returned by a swift journey. While, with God as their guide and their bringer-back, they enjoyed favorable conditions and prepared to carry the bodies of the saints into the monastery of Lérins, the aforesaid abbess Angarisma came to meet them. With many prayers she begged that permission be granted her to bury the body of her teacher in her own monastery, whose name was Oratorium.

[Note: A conspicuous error! There was never any monastery called Oratorium in Provence, but there was one in Belgic Gaul near the city of Beauvais, commonly called Oroer, over which Saint Angadrisma, a noble virgin, presided. According to her own Acts, she is not said ever to have lived in Provence or on the island of Lérins; those Acts are to be referred to the end of this Benedictine century. If any credence is to be given to the Acts of Saint Aigulf, interpolated by Vincent Barralis, Aigulf built or restored a monastery at a place called Arlucus and placed over it a consecrated virgin named Angarisma of Blois, whom he had ordered to come from Gaul with other virgins. Angarisma should therefore be distinguished from Angadrisma, who was originally from Thérouanne.]

Her devout request and the incomparable affection of the sons for their father were, so to speak, the sole source of this friendly dispute. The venerable woman, burning with desire, asked for the body; the disciples, however, did not wish to be separated from his presence even slightly. But amid these circumstances charity intervened as a mediator and obstacle-remover, as it is accustomed to settle such matters. It restrained the woman’s excessive eagerness and increased the disciples’ more devoted tenacity, to such an extent that the head of the holy body together with the right arm, which were granted to her, sufficed for her. The rest of the body, together with the relics of the other saints, was transferred by Blessed Rigomirus and the brothers to the monastery of Lérins for burial.

[Note: On the sixteenth day of May, as Vincent Barralis inserted.]

A blind woman receives her sight.

26. The devotion of the holy abbess was by no means left unrewarded. In her monastery there was a certain sister whose sight had been seized by glaucoma, rendering the windows of her eyes useless for seeing; the coverings of her eyelids concealed the globes of her eyes.

Accordingly, filled with faith, she joined the others in keeping the solemn vigil that they offered at the sacred burial. She filled the whole night with prayers and divine praises. At dawn, the light that had long been banished returned, and, although late, she was given the divine light and joyfully looked upon the world illuminated by the sun.

By this miracle the hearts of all who witnessed it were so deeply moved that they did not regret having lost their father in the body, since they rejoiced that he remained with them through so effective a manifestation of miracles.

Columbus, having seen Aigulf, pays the penalty.

27. The blessed Father was present not only to the devout, who sought benefits from God through him, but also offered the gift of assistance to his persecutor. Columbus, the contriver of his death, had retired to bed on the night following the day of the martyrdom, intending to relax his limbs in sleep, when suddenly the man of God stood before him. He rebuked him for having subjected an innocent man to such great evils and vehemently denounced the savagery of his cruelty, which had blazed forth even to the murder of the innocent.

After saying these things, he took with his finger a drop of the spilled blood and impressed upon Columbus’s chest and back a sign in the form of a circle. At the sight, the wretched man, trembling, fell at his feet and began to implore his accustomed and unconquerable mercy, begging that he not leave one so liable to such a judgment to the divine tribunal.

Then the saint, moved by his prayers, wiped away one mark. He indicated, however, that the other could not be erased until a remedy had been applied before King Chlodoveus [Note: The reading should be “Theodoricus.” In the Chronicle of Malleais, Saint Aigulf’s martyrdom is said to have occurred during the reign of King Theodoric and the mayor of the palace Ebroin. Certainly, after succeeding Erchinoald as prefect of the palace, Ebroin administered that office under Chlodoveus either not at all or for only a very brief period. We therefore place Saint Aigulf’s death around the year 675.] and Ebroin, mayor of the palace, and before the public judgment of the Franks. This is known to have happened. Sought out by royal command, Columbus was found, thrown into chains, and tormented by the severity of the punishments imposed by Frankish judgment until death.

The author’s pious meditation.

28. In these events we should not merely conjecture something, but clearly understand what they signified. The martyr’s spilled blood signifies innocence subjected to violence and demanding just vengeance. Thus God said of the first such man, Abel, to the first persecutor, Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me” (Genesis 1). The impression of blood upon the back or body of the persecutor signifies the execution of the vengeance owed him for the commission of his crime.

Thus also the Lord says to Ezekiel that he demands the sinner’s blood from the hand of the shepherd who does not proclaim it (Ezekiel 3). And the Lord says to the Jews: “That there may come upon you all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth” (Matthew 23)—that is, the vengeance for all the blood of the righteous innocently shed.

The figure of the circle foretold the unavoidable sentence of retribution: a circle returns upon itself and has no angular exit. Concerning this circle, the Lord says against Syria, under the figure of the devil: “I will put a circle in your nostrils and a bridle in your jaws” (2 Kings 19).

But because there were two circles, this signified that the wicked man would receive a twofold vengeance, as it is written: “With a double destruction destroy them” (Jeremiah 17). The circle’s figure, placed both before and after, signified by the divine judgment both the punishment imposed in the present and that which the malign man would suffer afterward.

The one circle that was wiped away, however, indicated that the same holy man, through his prayers, had obtained that his persecutor not be preserved for eternal torments, in accordance with the Savior’s command and example, by which we are instructed to pray for our persecutors.

The other circle, which remained and was to be erased by human judgment, indicates that although the saints obtain from God that future vengeance—whether their own or that of their enemies—be relaxed, so that they may not be consigned to eternal fires, they nevertheless do not wish crimes committed either against God or against their neighbors to go unpunished. Rather, the words of the Apostle must also be fulfilled by them: “If we judged ourselves, we should not be judged; but when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11).

Hence David, after sinning and confessing before the prophet who reproved him, said: “I have sinned against the Lord”; and he deserved to hear: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Samuel 12:13). Yet the reader of his history will be able to recognize by how many afflictions he was burdened because of the sin that had been forgiven.

Paul, the vessel of election (Acts 9), “labored more than all” (1 Corinthians 15); and because he had been a blasphemer, as he himself admits, and a persecutor (1 Timothy 1), he says that he bears in his body the marks of Christ (Galatians 6)—marks inflicted as satisfaction for his former life.

Let us therefore remember these examples. And if, as we know, our sins of action are forgiven us through the judgment of priests, let us nevertheless not think that we are spared until we have made satisfaction to God as is fitting, and to the human beings whom we have injured. Let us know how highly God values his servants, of whom he says: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zechariah 2).

Indeed, honoring those in whom we know that God dwells through faith and the practice of other good works, let us hear him say: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25). Then, with him, his Father, and the Holy Spirit, may we deserve to reign, with the help of him whose kingdom and dominion remain without end, for ages of ages. Amen.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 878. HINCMAR, BISHOP OF LAON.

[Col. 0967]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON HINCMAR.

(Collected in abbreviated form from the Life written by Cellotius.)

§ I. The education, studies, and character of the younger Hincmar.

[Col. 0967C]

The younger Hincmar was born in the district of Boulogne. His mother was the sister of Hincmar the archbishop; his father’s name is unknown to us. His parents were noble but not wealthy. Having lost his mother at the very threshold of childhood, he went to his uncle’s embrace to be raised and instructed in the liberal arts.

This must have happened when he was very young.[Note: [Col. 0967] These matters, and those which the author adduces hereafter, he has drawn in advance from the letters and treatises of Hincmar of Rheims. EDITOR.] For he was so ignorant of the language in which he had been born that, even after becoming a bishop, he could neither speak nor understand it except through an interpreter. His uncle admits that this education was provided at the expense of the church of Rheims, and that the boy was in a special sense his cleric: the church of Rheims had nourished him from what one might call his very cradle with tender kindness, had washed and stripped him of the garments of infancy, brought him to manhood, and advanced him to the episcopate.

As a boy he displayed an inclination toward grammar and poetry, though plainly of the sort cultivated in those times, as can be seen in his letters and verses. His nature revealed itself at once in his youthful studies: it was eager for novelty, display, and vanity. This appeared when he affected an obscure antiquity of expression; when he patched together a speech from the languages of several peoples like a cento; and when, for purposes of ostentation, he diligently sought out inappropriate words devoid of truthful meaning, which even he himself did not understand.

His uncle opposed and restrained him, but, so as not to extinguish his zeal for learning by harsher criticism or irritate him, already stubborn by nature, deferred correcting this perversity until he was more mature. Yet Hincmar shows that his hopes had been disappointed when, in a grammatical explanation of a single word offered by the younger man himself, he reproaches the bishop for allowing the new wine of his grammatical art and the bubbling of verbal distinctions to boil over.

Elsewhere, when he committed solecisms, he claimed that he was permitted to violate the rules of the grammarians because he was an ecclesiastical writer dealing seriously with weighty matters:

“But you,” he says, “new grammarian, who, like a leafy and dense tree adorned with foliage, must walk clothed in the trappings of words, puff up your inventions in lofty rhythms, and spit grammatical foam through puffed-out cheeks into every wind—you will not be permitted to say this.”

A substantial trace of this filthiness of expression survives in the articles sent by the provost Heddon to his uncle, in which one might think he had gathered barbarisms from alleys and crossroads.

Moreover, he sampled canon law and papal decrees with the same intellectual disposition toward vanity, even to the contempt of his uncle, who was highly esteemed in that field of learning. Yet he ventured to engage him with those weapons:

“Unhappy boy, and no match for Achilles in the encounter.”

From these things the character of the young man already begins to emerge: arrogant, restless, impatient of correction, obstinate, and rebellious. He brought these qualities with him to the episcopate, so that his uncle of Rheims repeatedly had nothing more to reproach in him:

“I have been told that among many people you boast because you are able to resist me and dare to despise me. Your madness—for so it is called by many—flies from mouth to mouth. Many also point you out as being carried away by pride, puffed up by empty glory, and overcome by arrogance.”

He produces a truly foolish and unbecoming example of this in a bishop:

“For from this fault comes the fact that many say you boast publicly of the strength and agility of your body, and that you frequently and willingly speak of battles and—as our people say—of vassal service; that you irreverently recount how you would conduct yourself if you had been a layman; and that you say and do many other things that do not suit you, nor do you report them to me.”

These are surely ridiculous accusations against a man who is said to have had a corpulent belly and fat limbs.

You rightly fit, wise man, what was once said:

> A swollen belly does not possess a subtle mind.

Swollen in character and deeds, as in body,  
you are said to be light in heart, in movements,  
and excessively frivolous in speech.

And in disordered movements there is a sign of pride and a most evil omen in a boy, as Nazianzen detected in Julian the Apostate.

But it is the mark of intolerable arrogance to wish to owe nothing to anyone and to attribute the benefits of others to one’s own merits. I omit the charge that was made against him almost constantly: that he wished to be subject to no one—not to the king, nor to his uncle and metropolitan.

On this point the entire heart of the controversy turns. It is therefore not surprising that he shook every censor off himself:

“Tell me, brother and son, what else have I required of you since you became a bishop and acquired earthly riches, except that you should have God made favorable to you, and, living as a bishop and bearing a bishop’s character, make yourself venerable to human beings? And I saw that this was burdensome to you. It may indeed have been burdensome to you until now, both because of your age and because you had not yet come to know the instability of this world and how changeable and fragile it is. But now it is time for us to rise from sleep; and we must not always remain young, just as a bad ox is always a calf.”

Thus, playing with meter, he calls him a young priest:

> From this title, young priest Hincmar,  
> it is fitting that I answer you in equal art.  
> In inverted verses, young priest Hincmar,  
> receive what has been returned to you, drawn from sacred springs.

He should be judged to have been considering not so much his age as the extreme immaturity of his character.

It should also be carefully considered that his uncle’s concern to admonish him—perhaps excessive at times and occasionally ill-timed—arose from the strict zeal for virtue and discipline with which he always burned. This, directed against his nephew’s insolence and rebellion, in a certain sense gave occasion for them; yet Hincmar himself assumed them only through his own very serious fault:

“For this reason also I admonished you very frequently and rebuked you so severely that you took offense against me and against those faithful to me, and strove to devise whatever and however many plots you could.”

Nevertheless, just as we favor friends and relatives through partiality rather than judgment, once Hincmar had matured in years his uncle sought, by seizing the opportunity, to make him fit for public affairs and bring him into the public light. Accordingly, the uncle sent to Charles, through his nephew, certain capitula written at Quierzy for King Louis of Germany concerning the provinces of Rheims and Rouen. He writes of them as follows:

“And do not neglect those capitula which the synod at Quierzy sent through Wenilo and Erchanraus to your brother Louis at Attigny in the preceding year; and, when I transmitted them, Hincmar my son gave them to you when he was with you in Burgundy.”

The nephew also records that he undertook an embassy to Gothia in the king’s name in the year 858, but he does not specify its date or cause.

We are certain of this: long before he acquired the sacred insignia, he ardently aspired to ecclesiastical honors—“only so that he might be a bishop in even one town; and even if,” as his uncle, his guardian, says, “circumstances and reason allowed, being desirous of honor and power, he would consent to become a rural bishop, who in Greek is called a chorepiscopus.”

§ II. The younger Hincmar is ordained bishop in the see of Laon.

At that time, when Pardulus had died and the see of Laon had become vacant, his uncle immediately obtained it for his nephew through the election of the clergy and people and the favor of the king. It was certainly suitable to his own designs, whether one considers the place—near Durocortorum of the Rhemians and peculiarly subject to the metropolitan—or the bond of affection, by which the nephew, through the favor of his patron and educator, would succeed him as a close associate.

For this reason, when the king tried to call him back from the journey he had undertaken, he addressed him as follows:

“First I consider it worthy to advise you that you should show due episcopal and pastoral kindness to the clergy and people entrusted to you. They chose you devotedly and earnestly asked that you be ordained their pastor, not because anyone compelled them, but because they were led by hope: they loved your uncle, who had benefited us, the kingdom, and the Church of our kingdom in many ways; they saw that you would follow in his footsteps and obey his counsels; and they knew that the municipality of Laon had anciently been united to the church of Rheims, in which you were raised. You should therefore repay them suitably.”

When the time for his ordination arrived, with the same favour of his uncle propelling him, and with no one objecting, he was consecrated bishop of Laon without examination by the primate, solely on his uncle’s testimony, in the presence of the bishops of the ecclesiastical province.

At that time, according to the custom of others, he promised faith and obedience to his metropolitan at the altar of Blessed Mary—promises that he afterward frequently broke and that his uncle frequently reproached him for breaking.

The elder Hincmar certainly did not know that this laying on of hands was preparing for him a harvest of cares, a seedbed of sorrows, a whetstone for ecclesiastical zeal, and a rock of patience. Favorable acclamations and public approval prevented him from looking ahead; all good men were, as commonly happens, vying to congratulate his uncle on the person of his nephew.

Thus the uncle commands him to remember the past:

“Finally, brother and son, I advise you to recall how you are now a byword, an object of head-shaking, and the subject of tale and song all day long; recall with what tranquility, free from the tumult of thoughts by which you are now pulled in different directions, you lived in your first days, when you came to the episcopate; with what kindness you were received by our lord the king; with what sweetness you enjoyed my company; with what unanimity you associated with our brothers and fellow bishops; with what affection you were honored by the courtiers and by the other men of this land; and with what loving reverence you were esteemed by those entrusted to you, as well as by our own people, among whom, by whom, and with whom you were raised—before an immoderate love of the world crept into you.”

King Charles wished to adorn him with offices and benefits. Just as earlier, for the sake of the elder Hincmar, he had restored to the church itself the property of the church of Rheims that had been divided among the courtiers, so, to win the younger man’s favor, he restored to the bishopric of Laon estates that had long been taken from it, specifically the villa of Pauliacum, detached from it in ancient times and later called the Field of Marathon by Hincmar.

In a letter to Pope Adrian, Charles himself declares that he enlarged the church of Laon with many estates and inheritances:

“We increased the church’s holdings by approximately two thousand manses beyond what it had possessed in the time of our predecessors; and even during his time we added more than six hundred.”

He also entrusted him with a palatine administration, without the knowledge of his uncle, and, through the intervention of external or secular powers, conferred upon him an abbey in a third province beyond the province of Rheims.

Although both actions were contrary to the canons, they nevertheless reveal the favorable disposition of the king and the courtiers toward him. The needs of the church and the poverty of the bishop also contributed—although the king later proved at a synod that the bishop had been one of those who possessed nothing and joined themselves to the clerical service.

The bishop of Laon himself declares that, if the villa of Pauliacum were taken from him, he would “have nothing from which to provide his people with sufficiency, indeed not even subsistence; nothing with which to prepare what was necessary for carrying out his services; and nothing from which he could make such frequent journeys or render temporal service to the king.”

The king’s generosity should therefore appear all the greater, since he supplied sufficient resources for all these needs.

[Col. 0971B]

During this period he was not altogether useless to his uncle, whom he always accompanied at councils. The controversies over theological doctrine with the faction of Gottschalk had indeed subsided, but the disputes of Rothad and the clergy of Rheims were then at their height. In these matters the uncle could expect no less assistance and obedience from his nephew than he had previously received from Pardulus.

Thus, imitating his educator in handling these affairs, Hincmar subscribed to all the acts. Later, when he proceeded with such lightness of mind as to pursue these judgments with laughter after they had been annulled by the Apostolic See, the archbishop of Rheims boldly replied:

“If you say this, you falsely accuse not only me but also very many bishops of many provinces—and even yourself, as you do not deny, indeed cannot deny, because you are a participant in our judgment in all these matters. You do not see the noose with which you are strangling yourself.”

Elsewhere, more explicitly, concerning the judgment against Rothad—or rather, as I interpret it, concerning the substitution of another in the place of Rothad after his deposition, before the appellant’s case had been heard at Rome—he writes:

“With regard to what you say about Rothad, that you did not consent to his deposition, the subscriptions written by your own hand refute you. I did nothing concerning it that you did not do with me; I subscribed nothing that you did not subscribe. For I have those very subscriptions written by your hand.”

We shall also see them disputing over the Second Synod of Toul at Tusiacum. The elder Hincmar affirms that those present subscribed his lengthy letter; the nephew denies that he subscribed anything other than a brief collection, not composed by him. In this matter, as we shall say, when he readily allowed himself to be drawn over to the side of the men of Lyon, opposed to his uncle in everything, he began to show how light-minded he was and how little steadfast in friendship and respect toward his uncle.

§ III. Raised to that rank before his virtue had matured. Having suffered an injury from King Charles, he receives help from his uncle.

[Col. 0971D]

Thus far we have spoken of him as a bishop brought up under the instruction of Hincmar of Rheims. We must now speak at greater length of the storm and tempest. If it was wisely and truly said in former times that human life is like a play, Hincmar certainly lived a tragedy, carried from happy beginnings through a turbulent rising action into a disastrous catastrophe.

Nothing was lighter than this cepphus [a bird; the precise allusion is uncertain], nothing more changeable than this Proteus, nothing more combative than this Ishmael. He desired the episcopate, a good work, like a little horse impatient of its rider and seeing before it an open field of freedom; like a theater and glory, as a slave to ambition; like a golden harvest, as an avaricious and impoverished mind.

At last his uncle was compelled to admit that Hincmar’s ordination had been premature, and that the young man, unwilling to advance under the severe discipline imposed in his household, had thrust his raw virtue into the world and its allurements. In the end, his uncle had to remind him that many people customarily reproached him for this:

“For this reason,” he says, “many accuse me of having ordained you, my nephew, through the favor of kinship: because you have become such a man—contrary to the arrangement of divine ordination, contrary to the king, contrary to me, contrary to the Church entrusted to you, and contrary to many others—that I ordained you a bishop.”

Although he is forced to excuse himself for this both in that place and before the pope himself, he nevertheless seems to have suffered something human: in that ordination he regarded flesh and blood rather than God’s purposes, and consecrated not an irreproachable man but his nephew.

We have just learned from his uncle who were the persons against whom this most troublesome man waged perpetual war; it is now our task to examine them in the order established by our subject. The first named is King Charles—not the cause but the pretext and occasion of the quarrels.

The king was compelled, not so much by his own fault as by that of the times, to tolerate palace mice gnawing away at ecclesiastical property. The bishops resisted them, vigorously and courageously defending the immunity of the Church, the patrimonies of the poor, and the offerings made for sins.

The courtiers claimed that the property of the churches was in the king’s power, so that he might distribute it at will. The bishops shouted that these laymen who seized sacred property were sacrilegious murderers of the poor, and they asserted that Charles Martel, the author of so great a sacrilege, had been condemned to eternal torments for this reason alone.

From these circumstances arose the war waged by Hincmar of Laon against King Charles and the king’s purple-clad officials, conducted with such tumult and outwardly in the just cause of defending the liberty of the Church. But it matters with what intention one acts and how far one proceeds; wise men command that good be done well.

The first confrontation recorded by history occurred in the year 868, at a certain legal hearing in the very parish of Laon. There, for a reason unknown to us, the proceedings began “with a reasonable beginning, namely, one not contrary to the sacred laws, and with some progress, since the matter began to be examined in an episcopal hearing, not in a public place but in a private and familiar inquiry.”

Suddenly the son of Luidon—whether a natural son conceived before entering the clergy, or a spiritual son, as Hincmar of Rheims habitually called Hincmar of Laon himself—approached the king as a suppliant and complained in Hincmar’s presence that, after obtaining his father’s benefice from Hincmar by means of a gift, he had afterward been unjustly deprived of it and excluded.

This was, at most, an unbecoming act of levity in a bishop—for at that time there was no dispute concerning the gift that had been given and accepted, although his uncle would recall the matter below.

But the king, inflamed by sudden anger, attacked the man with insults and reproaches before a large circle of nobles, going beyond what the matter required. Such words were unfit for a bishop to hear and for a king to speak. He must have been provoked by something else, although he also loved Luidon, the archdeacon of his old friend Pardulus.

Someone who examined the matter more deeply might judge that the crime of simony, overlooked by human beings, was punished by God in Luidon’s son through the bishop, and in the bishop through the king.

Nor did the king’s offense stop there. He summoned Hincmar to appear before him, that is, before a secular tribunal, to give an account of his action. When Hincmar offered excuses on the basis of the rights of the Church and did not send an advocate to represent him, the king proscribed all his property. Through the palace chancellor he forbade any of his subjects to render their lord bishop any service of due obedience.

And what is beyond all disgrace, he conducted that judgment through persons infamous under both sacred and secular law—persons whom laymen of free and sound legal standing would rightly have refused.

Nevertheless, we conclude from a letter of the archbishop of Rheims to Hincmar of Laon that the latter was not wholly free of blame in this affair:

“After this, following the custom of your instability and inconstancy, you rose up against our lord the king with such unreasonable obstinacy . . . and therefore, by letters and words, working on your behalf, I reconciled him to you.”

This is how the matter was conducted.

[Col. 0973A] Hincmar of Laon informs his uncle, Hincmar of Rheims, by letter of the injury he had received from the king—not, however, sincerely or with complete regard for the truth—pointing out only that ecclesiastical property had been proscribed because, when summoned to secular judgment, he had refused to appear. He repeats the same charge in person to the man who is present before him. The elder Hincmar, believing the bishop, immediately rises as the defender of the rights of the Church and, vehemently rebuking the king in the gravest of letters, recalls him to his duty and repentance.

Then, taking his nephew with him, he followed King Charles as he departed for Pîtres with the other bishops. Presenting the written dossiers again, and speaking at length, he “showed how great a prejudice the episcopal authority and the universal Church suffered in such an affair.” Thus he deployed the authority he had acquired at court—he is called a courtly bishop—with no ineffective result. For he obtained that the bishop should be restored to the possessions of which he had been stripped, and that the villa of Pailliac should be returned to him privately, until all the disputes had been settled by lawful judgment and everything remained at peace.

§ IV. He Offends King Charles in Many Ways

[Col. 0973B] The young man, overwhelmed by so great a favor, imprudently offended both the king, his uncle, and all the bishops when, in a headlong impulse, without consulting anyone, he reported the king’s action by letter to the Roman pontiff.
