Nor did he fail to do the same on other occasions, whenever he suffered any vexation from the king’s officials. The most Christian prince bore this especially bitterly, and the bishops condemned the act as having been done without his consent.

Again, on the same occasion, he accused both the king and his own archbishop before that same pontiff: the king as an invader of ecclesiastical affairs, and the archbishop as excessively patient under those injuries and, as Scripture says, a mute dog unable to bark. Consequently, after departing from him, he received neither the archbishop nor his envoys kindly thereafter.

But, disregarding all the bishops of his own province, he thereafter sought refuge with bishops of other provinces, asking counsel and assistance from them:

“Because, although I have twice sent envoys and letters to you, and some of your men have had the opportunity to speak with you and have spoken with you, you have neither sought the assistance of me or of our fellow bishops nor wished to use our counsel, just as you have acted on other occasions.”

And shortly afterward:

“Having also set me aside, and abandoning the common fellow bishops of your province—that is, mine and yours—you deliberately chose, contrary to the canons, to use in another province the counsel of bishops from other provinces rather than ours, although I was then in the vicinity of the place where the lord king was staying, and some of our fellow bishops were residing with the king.”

Do you think, reader, that it would be rash to suppose that those bishops of other provinces were the men who had been given the name of Lugdunensians? With them he had been joined from that time onward by a bond of friendship formed at the council at Tusiacum. Through their old hatred of King Charles and Archbishop Hincmar—an advantage which they had been unable to obtain through Gottschalk in theological questions—they had achieved through the troublesome nephew, in ecclesiastical property, [Col. 0973D] the result that these men were harassed by perpetual vexation and dragged out a life deserving of reproach for its cares and troubles.

Whatever ought to be believed, the bishop of Laon was at fault; and in the affairs that followed he always adhered to his long-standing and sluggish practice: neglecting the remedy that was readily available and placed in his hands, which he could have hoped for from his metropolitan uncle and from the neighboring bishops who perpetually surrounded the king, he sought protection far away and beyond the Alps. From there he began his defense, although, after trying everything in vain, he ought to have brought the matter to an end there.

Nor did the incautious man understand that, abandoned by bishops offended through contempt, he lay wholly exposed to injury; and that, where the struggle is conducted not by laws but by power, one subject man is no more to the king than a fly to an elephant.

§ V. He Rashly Attacks His Uncle, the Archbishop

In these circumstances even ordinary prudence required him to prepare a safe refuge for himself with his uncle, whom he had always honored and respected, who enjoyed the greatest favor with the king and the bishops, and by whose direction and counsels everything in public affairs was conducted. There he could have been protected against the assaults of the offended king and the nobles.

Yet, falsely reproaching his uncle that his friendship was of no benefit to him, but rather harmful, he contended with the man to whom he owed everything, though he had been anticipated by every kindness, and, as the most ungrateful of men, fought him in words, deeds, and writings, so that it may be said that he merely continued his quarrel with the king.

I say nothing here about many matters, because Hincmar of Rheims himself pursues the contempt shown toward him and toward the metropolitan see—truly without limit—in the Book of Fifty-Five Chapters, in other letters, and in his complaint before the synod, with equally limitless verbosity. I cannot read without astonishment the following words, which I do not know whether he wrote with rhetorical exaggeration:

“From the very day of your ordination, both by your words and writings and by your disorderly actions and movements, I have been so frequently burdened by your attacks and blows that I am weary of my life.”

And again:

“Would that I, who by reason of the office and rank of my position am bound to you, could fly far away from you and your people into a vast solitude, so that I might not be afflicted either by the obstinate persistence of your defiant presence, or by the harsh speech of your envoys, or by the disparagements in your writings and your useless trifles—or rather, tragedies—or by such reports about you as are unbefitting a bishop.”

I interpret this as follows: having become master of his own will through his ordination, he immediately shook off reverence for his censor, rejected his admonitions, adopted secular ways, and yearned for wealth, honors, and bodily pleasures, while his uncle grieved and repeatedly called him back. That quarrel remained for some time within private conversations and secret exchanges of letters, until at last it burst into the open, to the great offense of everyone, when the nephew inflicted upon his uncle—his fosterer and benefactor, and the bishop who had ordained him—everything that might have been feared from a stranger and bitter enemy.

Such acts included invading the possessions of the Church of Rheims; accepting the administration of the palace and an abbey without consulting him; traveling to that monastery, situated in another province, without letters from the metropolitan, and imprudently arranging matters there that did not concern him—matters which his uncle was later compelled to excuse and remove from synodal examination.

Summoned once and twice to a council, he neither appeared in person nor sent a representative with letters of commission. He received into his own care many persons whom his uncle had excommunicated as guilty of numerous crimes, such as Nivinus and his brother Bertricus. He excommunicated his uncle’s subjects, such as Amalbert, and, although admonished a third time, refused to revoke that sentence. For this reason Hincmar of Rheims had to summon a judicial assembly, at which bishops and laymen of every rank gathered; and there the young Hincmar said and did many disgraceful things.

At the entreaties of his uncle, he refused to grant pardon and communion to the cleric Senato, the presbyter Hadulf, and a certain monk sent by the king, all of whom had been excommunicated by him. Nevertheless, at the request of other bishops, the monk easily obtained both from him.

Despising his metropolitan, he sought a council of bishops from another province and wished to stand by their judgment. He would not even greet or look at his uncle when he was present; nor would he give him the kiss of peace at the council, although no one else refused it. In short, he did everything by which he might harass his uncle and attempt to throw off the metropolitan’s yoke.

Moreover, everywhere he attacked his uncle’s reputation; he kept saying that the king had been stirred up against him at his uncle’s instigation and by his counsel; he taunted him as one defeated in the two cases of Rothad and Vulfad; he demanded that Hincmar burn his own writings; he shouted that his uncle deserved deposition and interdiction from celebrating Mass, and threatened that he would bring this about.

He charged him with slander, alleging either that he falsified the writings of the ancient directors, or that he was doing only one thing: preventing him from pursuing his appeal before the Roman see—or even abolishing his right of appeal to the pontiff. This slander could have occurred to no other human being than himself.

I omit the enormously long writings against Hincmar of Rheims, swollen with arrogance and empty of substance because of their fables and corruptions: “monstrous little books, monstrously compiled.”

§ VI. He Harasses the Clergy and Laity of His Church

After offending the king and his uncle, the archbishop, he ought at least to have won the goodwill of his subjects by a peaceful and orderly administration of the Church of Laon. Let us see how he accomplished this.

He is convicted most manifestly of simony in the laying on of hands:

“You can remember well that I already admonished you, because I heard it from many people, and it even reached the ears of the lord king, that, in the laying on of hands for ordination to ecclesiastical orders, you even accepted gifts directly from the hand; that you demanded rewards for granting churches; and that you accepted payment from disreputable priests so that they would not be investigated. For this reason the lord king also sought to hear the truth from the sons of your Church; and, when such a matter arose—the matter is well known—he ceased pursuing the inquiry, while I warned you as forcefully as I could that you should in no way participate in such crimes.”

He was also accused for a long time of imposing many burdens upon his subjects:

“It is said by many that you burden the clerics and laymen entrusted to you in many ways, through various pretexts.”

And shortly afterward:

“For many say that scarcely a few—or rather, no one—can obtain any benefit from you except by giving a reward.”

His poverty when he came to the episcopate, as we said earlier, makes this highly credible. He says that this accusation is condemned by the canons as lending at interest and shameful usury, in the canons issued against clerics who pursue interest-bearing loans and disgraceful profits. From this disgrace he recalls him not only by other arguments but especially by his own example, since, following the example of Samuel, he accepted no payment from anyone for any reason.

[Col. 0975C] But the most disastrous disturbance of the Church of Laon occurred when, provoked by some injury, he excommunicated all the clerics of his parish. They were very numerous, and among them there must have been many innocent men.

That insult to the Church might in some measure have been endured if a few accused, confessed, and convicted persons had been expelled, or if there had been something doubtful or obscure in their accusation.

“But when, as is most manifest and as is known to everyone, three hundred, or four hundred, or five hundred men, expelled without any reason or guilt, contrary to all authority, had been expelled solely through your fury and because of the injuries done to you, and so forth…”

The order of the law required you to lay your complaint before me, your metropolitan, and to await my judgment concerning it. But you, driven by sudden anger and consulting no one, abruptly completed so great and harmful an act.

How many sins there were here! To avenge private injuries with the spiritual sword, which the canons strongly condemn; to wield that sword without any judicial procedure; to strike down so many innocent men with it; to undertake that novel and unprecedented action without the authority of the metropolitan.

§ VII. His Uncle, the Metropolitan, Lifts the Excommunication He Had Imposed

He maintained the deadly interdict for five days. During that time, it is credible that many infants in that very large parish were deprived of baptism, and dying persons of communion in the form of viaticum.

While the clerics of Laon, fearing a more prolonged disaster and seeking the remedy that was close at hand, appealed to the metropolitan “without schism or rebellion, in view of the shortness of the time and the imminent danger.”

What need was there then for the judgment of the Roman pontiff, to whom the bishop referred the matter, when the case was certain and had often been judged? The apostolic see should be consulted only about doubtful and obscure matters, where the canons are lacking or admit differing interpretations.

Thus, when the archbishop of Rheims had been appealed to, he released the clerics from the censure by lawful judgment, although without a provincial council and without a scrupulous examination of witnesses, and restored them to communion and to their ministry.

From this point the civil war between nephew and uncle grew fierce again. The nephew was indignant at having been openly caught in wrongdoing; and he demanded through Wenilo of Rouen that the collection containing the final sentence against him be destroyed by fire, declaring that otherwise he would never return to favor.

Rejecting that condition—not raising it with the laughter it deserved, but seriously refusing it as though it were a deadly cup offered him by the nephew—he cast away the man, lifted up by vain hope and boundless pride.

Finally, he compelled him to face synods, whose proceedings consisted of matters of this sort: accusers were aroused, written indictments prepared, and—what is remarkable—all the judges were offended: the king, the metropolitan, and the bishops.

For this reason he tried to avoid their judgment by repeatedly renewing his appeal to Rome, but the appeals were fraudulent and illusory. These matters must now be discussed.

At last King Charles resolved to restrain the rebel and slanderer. It is certain that Hincmar of Rheims claimed the rights and authority of his metropolitan see. The Gallican bishops did not doubt that a provincial judgment ought to precede an appeal. The circumstances and the man demanded a synod.

Three were granted: at Verberie, at Attigny, and at Douzy. At the first he declaimed; from the second he fled; to the third he came stripped of his possessions. Convicted on every point, he appealed from them all, and scarcely escaped from that one alive and free.

Afterward he pursued his appeal, but as one condemned; he was heard, but as one blinded; he was tolerated so that he might live, not so that he might rule. A powerless Samson, wretched for himself alone, at last succumbed beneath the burden he had so long increased.

§ VIII. Hincmar Is Sent by the King into Custody at Silvacus

[Col. 0976C] It is also established that, shortly after the Council of Verberie, he was detained by the king, as though in prison, at Silvacus, in the parish of Laon. He does not obscurely cast responsibility for this act upon his uncle when he writes to him:

“I have read through hastily the writings of your Excellency that you sent to be delivered to me, on the anniversary of my being handed over, which took place in my parish and at the place called Silvacus. I wrote ‘of my being handed over,’ not ‘of my handing over,’ so that the ambiguity between the person handing over and the person handed over might be removed through the possessive pronoun. For it is clear from the primary genitive construction that I was handed over, not that I was the one who handed over.”

And more explicitly he protested publicly at the council:

“I hold this charge against him: that he caused me to be sent into custody by the king.”

But that this is a slander is clear both from the king’s very serious assertion at the synod and from Hincmar of Rheims, who continues his account as follows:

“But you, adding worse things to those that came before, again so aggravated the lord king—as it would take me a long time to recount, and as many know—that he ordered you to be detained for a while as a punishment imposed upon you, without my will and without my consent.”

The expression “as a punishment imposed upon you” deserves notice. For we have just heard of a royal punishment, distinct from regular—that is, synodal—judgment: judgment belongs to the bishops, punishment to the king; judgment concerns sacred matters, punishment touches the body. In the same way, in the following year, in the case of Carloman, regular judgment produced excommunication, while punishment produced imprisonment at Senlis and afterward blinding.

A new consequence of contumacy and rebellion must therefore have arisen, one that had to be restrained by custody. What it was, who can say, since Hincmar omits to explain it? What if he then tried to accomplish what he had previously considered: fleeing from his own church and from the kingdom of Charles to his nephew Lothar in Austrasia? For Charles reports this plan of his, and the agreement made with Lothar, around the time of the Council of Verberie, in his petition to the synod.

The detention was not long, as the word “for a while” indicates. It may be inferred that this was due to the favor and admonitions of the bishops, who preferred that his case be examined in a synod and, if the matter required it, condemned by a canonical sentence rather than restrained by royal punishment.

§ IX. The Synod against Hincmar of Laon at the Palace of Douzy

[lacuna]

The synod had already been in progress for a long time when Hincmar finally arrived at Douzy, so that, after being questioned and heard in person, he might be convicted and condemned, however much he appealed and rejected the judges.

The Bertinian Annals recount the matter as follows:

“But Hincmar finally came to the synod with great arrogance. There, after King Charles had presented a petition according to the ecclesiastical canons, he was regularly accused and convicted on very certain charges, and accepted the regular judgment of deposition. As is contained in the acts of that synod, which the same synod sent through Actard, the venerable bishop who took part in it, to the apostolic see.”

Nevertheless, in two respects the reverence owed to Roman authority and to the appeal was preserved.

First, the Fathers concluded their sentence in these words: “Saving in all respects the judgment of the apostolic see.” This formula could not fail to be especially pleasing to Adrian, since it removed both the council from the danger of rashness and the danger of schism. For the pontiff replied that he could not approve the sentence against a bishop who had appealed to the apostolic see:

“Nevertheless, since, as is read in the proceedings of that council, you assert that he was judged by the bishops, with the judgment of the apostolic see preserved in all respects, we, moved by no hatred against anyone and desiring to cast no one’s guilt back upon another, wish,” and so forth.

Second, they appointed no one in the place of the deposed Hincmar, so as to reserve everything intact for the pontiff’s definitive judgment.

For Hincmar of Rheims remembered that he had once acted wrongly in a similar case: after deposing Rothad, he immediately supplied another in his place. Nicholas took this most unjustly and forbade the intruded man, without delay, to exercise any part of episcopal office.

Accordingly, the synodal letter rightly declares that they wish, insofar as they know and are able, to preserve and enlarge the privilege of the holy and first see of Rome.

§ X. The Judgment of Pope Adrian concerning the Synod of Douzy

The acts of the synod were sent to Rome to the pontiff through the envoy Actard, together with the king’s petition, the two complaints of Hincmar the metropolitan—both this one from Douzy and the one presented the previous year at Attigny—and also the proclamation of the clergy and people of Laon, although it was not read at that council because other business demanded attention.

Finally, there were three letters: one from the synod, one from Hincmar, and one from the king.

The embassy sought two things: first, the archbishopric of Tours for the envoy Actard, which Adrian most willingly granted; and second, confirmation of the synod and approval of Hincmar’s deposition, which was the principal object of the embassy.

But the pontiff consistently refused this, as Nicholas had once refused it in the case of Rothad. He objected that, “although he cried out in the synod that he wished to come without delay to the apostolic see and, in its presence, answer the charges brought against him by his adversary, a sentence of condemnation had been pronounced against him.”

He ordered Hincmar to come, and with him “a suitable accuser who could not be rejected by any legitimate authority,” so that the judgment might be reconsidered in the customary manner with the synodal assembly.

Meanwhile he forbade that, “until his case has again been reopened and concluded, another bishop should in any way be ordained in that very Church of Laon.”

These instructions were inserted into the pontiff’s private letter to the bishops generally and to King Charles. I find no reply here to Hincmar of Rheims.

Here, then, the statements, writings, and councils against Hincmar the Younger, formerly bishop, come to an end. The see of Laon remained vacant: the bishops sought that the expelled man not be restored, while Pope Adrian forbade anyone else to be appointed in his place.

The metropolitan of Rheims assumed the administration of the widowed church. We learn this from what he later wrote to Queen Richildis, who was herself then widowed, “informing her that, while the parish of Laon was vacant of a bishop, it was especially under his care,” and so forth.

No one took responsibility for the deposed Hincmar himself. The bishops and Hincmar his uncle had completely abandoned him in the letters they wrote to the pontiff from the synod.

Among the other matters that the emperor Charles settled at Rome with John, the confirmation of the Council of Douzy and of Hincmar’s deposition was not the least important. For, when asked by the pontiff, he related in detail before him the circumstances of the case, the man’s history of misconduct, the common complaints of everyone, and the legitimate examination conducted by the synod; and he brought the pontiff, who was thoroughly informed, to confirm it.

The pope immediately sent a letter to Hincmar the metropolitan, in which he approved his judgment and ordered another to be appointed in the place of the deposed man:

“Charles, the invincible emperor, after being most carefully questioned by us, reported to our apostolate the circumstances of the judgment pronounced against Hincmar, formerly bishop of Laon, by Your Beatitude and your fellow bishops. We recognized that the judgment was entirely just. For so great a prince could affirm nothing unless it were supported by the truth. Therefore we have considered that it would be wrong not to give his report an immediate hearing.”

This was especially so because the acts of the synod and the synodal letter agreed with the emperor’s account.

Accordingly, under the care of Hincmar of Rheims, the clergy and people of Laon elected Hedenulf, “a son of his own church, advanced within it, with the support of the merits of his service, even to the burden of the priesthood, approved in life, morals, and holy conduct.”

To this period, after the emperor Charles had returned to Gaul, I believe we should assign the final calamity of Hincmar of Laon. Expelled into exile, he spent two years there, during part of which he was held in chains in custody; toward the end he was deprived of his sight, as he laments in his protest. Thus the prince avenged his former rebellion and removed every possibility of future rebellion—although Hincmar, now wretched but not yet subdued, labored with all his strength, personally and through others, to bring it about.

At last God favored the wretched man. He had often refused to go to Rome when he appealed there and was himself appealed against; now he could not go, but reached Rome as it came to him, with little effort and not without benefit.

For Pope John, brought into Gaul after Charles’s death, was holding a general council at Troyes. There, among other matters, after hearing his complaint, which we have often cited, and at the urgent requests—almost the compulsion—of certain bishops, he released him from excommunication and irregularity and admitted him, if he wished, to celebrate Mass. He assigned him a portion of the revenues of the Church of Laon for his support.

This was granted, however, on the condition that Hedenulf, although he repeatedly requested release because of bodily infirmity and desired religious retirement, should retain the see and the episcopal office.

Not long afterward Hincmar of Laon died.

[Col. 0979]

# THE LITTLE WORKS AND LETTERS OF HINCMAR, BISHOP OF LAON

## I. LETTER OF HINCMAR OF LAON TO HINCMAR OF RHEIMS

He clears Nivinus and himself in his case, and reproaches Hincmar of Rheims.

[Col. 0979A] To the most reverend Hincmar, archbishop of the Rhemians, Hincmar, the least of the bishops of the Church of Laon: due devotion in Christ.

I confess that I never wished, nor do I wish, to speak or write to you in a way that might seem to oppose your serenity with harmfulness or displease you through deceptive discoloration, remembering Ham, Shem, and Japheth—namely, the paternal curse and blessing. But now the very circumstances of the time require that I reply briefly to certain matters about which you have written urgently.

Concerning Nivinus’s excommunication from your parish, as it was reported to me, this is how one ought to proceed with a person accused according to due procedure who refuses or is unable to purge himself, and who does not consent to confess, or who has been convicted by those who know the facts. Yet I heard otherwise: namely, that, after receiving from your authority [Col. 0979B] a period of time and accepting the terms, though no one accused him except on the basis of your assertion, you imputed the matter to him because of the suggestion of his rivals, requiring him to clear himself by eight kinsmen on his father’s side and four likewise on his mother’s side. He came on the appointed day and to the appointed place, prepared to carry this out, but found neither you nor anyone sent by you there.

Afterward, when summoned again before you and your people—although unexpectedly—he wished and was able to purge himself legally. But you explicitly sought from him, with his third hand, men of such a kind that they had no concern for him. He replied that he was a Frank and wished and was able, as a free man, to defend himself with men so suitable that no crime could be charged against them. When you rejected this, you excommunicated him, ordering that he should not remain even one night anywhere in your parish, and [Col. 0979C] earnestly entreating and protesting that he should nevertheless receive nothing from what he had labored to acquire. I could not believe this, nor ought I to have believed it, because what is worthy of your authority cannot escape or remain hidden from your wisdom.

For one ought not readily believe detractors, especially not concerning those who sing truthfully with you, as they do with blessed Job: “I diligently investigated the cause that I did not know” (Job 29:16); those to whom the blessing of the perishing came, who comforted the widow’s heart, clothed as with justice and crowned in judgment with a diadem; who were an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; whom the poor regarded as fathers; and who crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched [Col. 0980A] the prey from his teeth.

As for what you add—that you have heard from many that I accept his property as payment for him, and grant him ecclesiastical goods and resources as a benefice in return for shameful profit—you have heard lies. I could be astonished that such things are now being said to you by such a person of such standing, had I not known and perceived that you have often heard similar things and accepted and retained what you heard falsely as though it were true. There is no need to discuss these matters one by one at present.

I know that blessed Pope Anacletus says sufficiently (Epistle 3): “No one willingly reports anything to an unwilling hearer.” You ought not therefore to become irritated if I speak of matters that you know, since I can say nothing from the path of the Scriptures—at least, if it be wholesome—that you do not know. For “whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4). We may speak of what we know, and we can testify to what we have seen [Col. 0980B] and heard; but we may not rashly assert as true what we do not know.

Hence Pope Victor says (Epistle 1): “For we have heard that among you and your people various judgments are being made and uncertain matters judged. Let us not judge uncertain matters at all, beloved, until the Lord comes, who will bring hidden things to light, illuminate what is concealed in darkness, and reveal the counsels of hearts. For although such matters may be true, they are nevertheless not to be believed unless they are established by manifest indications, unless they are convicted by manifest judgment, unless they are published according to judicial procedure.”

Indeed, from the beginning of my life until now, by God’s mercy, you have never reproved me, nor known me to have accepted or exercised any payment for shameful profit; nor do you know this now, nor, with God’s protection, will you ever know it. The nature of a case either excuses each person [Col. 0980C] or, as the apostolic canons say, accuses him.

I add that your men Eutramnus and Humarus know the following: in years past, Nivinus himself transferred to me, freely and through their hands, certain possessions belonging to him. Since these lay adjacent to my own lands but were far removed from his, he sought my assistance because he was in great need. I nevertheless voluntarily helped him charitably in whatever ways I could, and I refused to receive those same possessions—something Eutramnus in particular knows, since afterward he often urged me to claim them. Nivinus himself has now given them to another, even though I did not resist him. Behold by what evidence it is shown that the charge brought against me is false.

I do not [Col. 0981A] fear being branded by any arguments as seeking payment for shameful profit. Nor do I deny that, where I ought and can, I wish and desire to assist the needy in fraternal charity. For a bishop ought to do good in all things and receive all the faithful.

Nor do I recall having granted a benefice to any of my relatives as though to a “sarga,” from which neither the integrity of the commonwealth nor the benefit of the Church over which, although unworthy, I preside would result. I do have, and do not deny having, relatives connected with me by blood. If I assist them both in acquiring property and in their other needs, I do not inflict harm upon the Church; rather, I contribute to the strengthening of its position, and I also add a useful support to the commonwealth.

Yet I hold no one so dear according to the flesh that, for the sake of shameful [Col. 0981B] profit, I would consent to his conducting a transaction with another in the acquisition of property when it does not accord with my purpose or would result in dangerous loss to the giver or receiver. The Lord says: “Whoever loves father or mother, or brother, or wife, or fields, more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

I give thanks for your testimony that, at my episcopal ordination, I received ecclesiastical property and resources without payment, for governing and dispensing them according to rule. And since, by God’s mercy, I attained this through your efforts, I never wished to become ungrateful to you, but strove to remain your most humble servant.

You pursue this matter sufficiently and more than sufficiently in a manner contrary to the authority of Holy Scripture and opposed to the decrees of the sacred canons. Therefore, as reason makes clear, I am not proved [Col. 0981C] in this matter to have inflicted an injury upon the sacred Scriptures or to have opposed the decrees of the sacred canons. Since those decrees have been strengthened by apostolic authority alone, I never wish to depart from them, nor do I believe that I departed from them in the past.

You also add, “If this is so,” that, as is being spread everywhere by many people and even publicly in public assemblies, I shall incur great danger and harm from it and bring great reproach upon the priestly ministry if I understand the matter correctly and possess sound judgment.

It is astonishing to me that this is being spread everywhere by many and even publicly in public assemblies—something that is not even secretly contemplated by me. Whether you had made a petition concerning this matter at any of those assemblies, I wonder, since blessed Pope Callistus insists (Epistle 1): “Therefore no one should accuse a teacher in writing, nor should he answer without a faithful [Col. 0981D] and legitimate accuser who also leads an irreproachable life and conduct.”

Pope Eleutherus likewise testifies (sole epistle, near the end): “Those who accuse or harass their brothers do not love them but rather neglect them, and they sin, as the Apostle says: ‘Love of neighbor works no evil’ (Rom. 13:10). Likewise: ‘A brother who helps his brother will be exalted, but he who strikes him down will be destroyed’ (Prov. 18:10).”

Pope Felix, warning us through a divine oracle, developed these matters in his instructions according to the occasion. For our predecessors and the holy Fathers who have gone before us repeatedly prohibited anyone from bringing detraction against the priests of the Lord—how much more accusations not arising from the root of charity?

[Col. 0982A] “Be silent,” they say (Felix II, Epistle 1), “and do not persecute those who serve God perfectly. Through their prayers earthly wars are quieted, the attacks of angels who have departed from God are driven away, and all demons, corrupters, are confounded by the persistence of their prayers. For truces must be granted not for a brief time but over a long period, so that the accused may prepare themselves, meet with all those who share communion and are located in the provinces, prepare witnesses, and fully arm themselves against their plotters.

“For judges and accusers ought to be such as are free from every suspicion and desire to pronounce their judgment from the root of charity. Having set these matters forth both legally and canonically, we also ask that all Christians rejoice in reverence, with [Col. 0982B] spiritual love intervening and with the fear of the Lord, through which human offense is removed and the building up of the Churches is placed above everything, so that all may labor more for the building up of their brothers than for their condemnation.

“For the Lord says: ‘By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another’ (John 13:35). We have already given a rule, and know that it was given by our predecessors: if anyone knows himself to be a Christian, let him observe what is known to have been handed down to the apostles, as the Apostle Paul says: ‘If anyone announces to you anything beyond what you received, let him be accursed’ (Gal. 1:9).

“For Christ, the Son of God and our Lord, granted the human race complete salvation through his own passion, in order to set us free. And if [Col. 0982C] God loved us so greatly that he did not spare even his own Son but handed him over for us all, in order to set us free, why do we not love our brothers, or why do we rashly judge them, when the aforementioned Apostle says: ‘Do not judge one another, but judge this rather: that you should not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother’ (Rom. 14:1)?

“For if those who love their brothers are born of God and see God, what then will become of those who persecute them and, by slandering, plotting against, accusing, and harassing them, strive to condemn them? If the former are sons of God, without doubt the latter are sons of the devil, who always goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour; so these men pursue their brothers in order to destroy them.

“Those who refuse to assist their brothers acquire a greater burden of sins and become guilty of denying fraternal support. ‘Woe,’ [Col. 0982D] says the prophet, ‘to him who gives drink to his friend, sending his own gall’ (Hab. 2:15). Again, the wisest Solomon says: ‘For he who speaks iniquity cannot remain hidden, nor will judgment, correcting him, pass him by. Therefore, the questioning of the ungodly will be about their thoughts, and the hearing of his words will reach the Lord for the correction of his iniquities, because the ear of jealousy hears everything, and the tumult of murmuring will not be concealed’ (Wis. 1:8).

“If they had wished to embrace these things with their own sound understanding, they would not have fallen into a reprobate mind. But by taking care, through the fear of God, to guard their words, they would certainly preserve the pious definition of the holy Fathers without presumptuous harm, since sacred Scripture says: [Col. 0983A] ‘Good counsel will preserve you, and sound understanding will guard you’ (Prov. 2:11).

“For such accusations and detractions do not proceed spiritually from life-giving springs toward the attainment of eternal life. Therefore blessed Paul the Apostle appropriately warns us: ‘We ought not to think more highly than we ought to think, but to think with sober judgment’ (Rom. 12:3). Let us persevere in the definition of piety. For those who pass beyond it are not merely falling away from their own firmness; they have also left to everyone a memorial of their folly, so that in those matters in which they sinned they could by no means remain hidden.”

Pope Damasus also wrote to all the bishops established throughout Italy (Epistle 4): “For it has been reported to the apostolic see that you receive written accusations against brothers without a legitimate accuser. We prohibit this from now on [Col. 0983B] throughout the whole world by apostolic authority, and we ask that what has recently been done be corrected without any delay. Nor may you ever examine the case of those who are accused in writing before they have been summoned canonically to a synod by the formal complaints of those bringing the charge, and before the person present has truthfully recognized and understood from the person present what is alleged against him.

“As Solomon’s wisdom rightly says: ‘Before you investigate, do not censure; first understand, and then rebuke; before you hear, do not answer’ (Ecclus. 11). And although the rebuke of the opposing parties may be entirely clear, an order must nevertheless be observed by those appointed to examine them, according to those who have been assigned to investigate in accordance with God’s will, so that, with the work cooperating, we may find God affirming this, who says: [Col. 0983C] ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matt. 18:20).

“Our Lord Jesus Christ knew that Judas was a thief; but because he was not accused in person, he was not expelled. Nor ought you in any way to do what he did not wish to do. For the laws of the world require accusers to be present, not absent through written documents. Hence the canonical constitutions of the Fathers repeatedly and emphatically declare that neither accusations nor testimony can be presented in writing, and that no one may give testimony concerning other matters except those known to have been conducted in their presence.

“Likewise, whoever chooses to accuse another must accuse him in person and not through someone else, with a written charge [Col. 0983D] presented beforehand. Nor may anyone ever be judged before he has legitimate accusers present and has been given an opportunity to defend himself and cleanse himself of the charges. Care must also be taken lest anger seize anyone and make him do immediately what is unlawful.”

Pope Adrian, long after Pope Innocent, successor of Peter, and together with many of his predecessors and successors, says in his decrees—using one example for the sake of brevity (Canon 4): “No metropolitan bishop may hear the cases of anyone without the insistence of all the other bishops of the province; otherwise the proceedings will be invalid, and he will even have to answer for the matter in a synod. Nor may any other bishop hear the cases of his priests [Col. 0984A] without the presence of his clergy, for the bishop’s sentence will be invalid unless it is confirmed by the presence of his clergy.”

Nor must we forget what Pope Damasus teaches and testifies (Epistle 2): “It is permitted for metropolitans, together with all their fellow provincial bishops, with none absent and with all agreeing concerning each individual case, to examine bishops and the most important ecclesiastical matters. But to define their highest disputes and those of the Churches, or to condemn bishops, is in no way permitted without the authority of this holy see, since all must appeal to it if necessary and be strengthened by its assistance.

“For, as you know, a synod held without its authority is not valid; nor can a bishop be definitively condemned except in a legitimate synod, convened at the proper time by apostolic summons. [Col. 0984B] Nor are any councils ever read as valid that were not supported by apostolic authority.”

Behold, it is clear which canons are to be received, venerated, and observed.

Let us now return to what came before. Since, unless a name is known, knowledge of the facts consequently disappears, what you falsely heard about me, and without any preceding proof, could just as easily now be rejected or disbelieved, even though it had seemed to be proved—as the Wise Man commanded: “Before you question, do not censure anyone” (Ecclus. 2:7); and again: “Before you hear, do not answer a word” (ibid. 8).

Likewise: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue. Make doors for your mouth and bolts for your ears. Melt down your gold and silver, [Col. 0984C] make a balance for your words, and set straight reins for your mouth” (Ecclus. 28:18).

And again: “He who willingly listens to lying words will have all the wicked as his servants; for he makes his ears the doors of death” (Prov. 29:12).

And again: “The whisperer and the double-tongued person are accursed, for he will disturb many who live in peace” (Ecclus. 28:15).

I do not boast of possessing sound judgment, since it is written: “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes” (Prov. 12:15). But concerning the fact that, because of this, I have been so hastily inflamed by you and might incur some danger or harm, I do not fear, being conscious of myself in this matter. Nor do I fear that reproach will thereby be brought upon the priestly ministry, since there is no evidence of it.

But so that I may be guarded from other things, by God’s mercy and protection, I, an unhappy man, implore the grace of that same God according to my knowledge and ability. And if I dared to entreat you to ask the same thing for me—since I know that you can obtain it more easily [Col. 0984D] from that same Lord—I would ask it earnestly and humbly.

Finally, concerning what you add about Bertricus, the principal matter is that you conclude decisively by saying: “I have taken care to make known to you what the sacred canons command.” Here it must be asked why you make this known to me: whether so that I must regard him as excommunicated, although, as you say, because he is not from your province, you ordered him and his people canonically to leave your parish; yet you do not say that you excommunicated him, nor whether he is forbidden to remain in the parish of any of your fellow provincial bishops.

For we learned from the Council of Nicaea (Canon 5) that those expelled by others ought not to be received. It is appropriate, however, to know the manner [Col. 0985A] of this expulsion. If, as you assert, he was regularly corrected for adulteries and other incestuous pollutions but was not reformed, and was tolerated for a long time, it must be known whether the correction was private or public; whether he was separated from the fellowship of Christians or from the body and blood of the Lord. I have not [Col. 0986A] heard that he was subjected to public penance.

I also ask to be instructed: if he belonged to your province but not to your parish, how would you have proceeded against him?

May the God of peace and love always be with us, so that, as the Apostle exhorts, everything we do may be done in charity, not through contention or vainglory (1 Cor. 16:14; Phil. 2:3).

## II. THE SAME TO THE SAME

He permits Hadulf, out of regard for Hincmar, the place of his former residence, but does not yet grant him his communion.

[Col. 0985]

[Col. 0985B] To the most reverend Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, Hincmar, by the mercy of God bishop of the Church of Laon, the devotion owed in the same Lord.

It now seems reasonable to reply urgently to certain matters concerning what you recently wrote about Hadulf. For the substance and conclusion of the matter, as well as the time and place, await an occasion that is not inappropriate.

You write that Hadulf has asked you to intervene with me so that he may be permitted to receive communion in my parish, to have fully his place and residence and the things he had administered under me, and to serve me canonically in peace; and, if this should be burdensome for me, that he may at least have communion in my parish, and be allowed, under religious discipline, to remain wherever he can find a suitable place for himself, and to be faithful to me.

[Col. 0985C] As for his administration, he has also complained about it in my presence, making a slanderous accusation against me among his other complaints. Concerning this, together with the other matters, at a suitable time and place, when he has deigned to hear me, I shall answer him fully.

For now I reply to you reasonably as follows: if it pleases you, you can properly ask him—who is making the request, hearing you, and speaking to you—why he has now reclaimed those things which, when no one compelled or persuaded him, he not only abandoned after having cast them from himself to the ground by the hem of his garment, [Col. 0986B] but despised with abhorrence, adding that it had been and was much better for him to be without the things I had given him.

Therefore, when he had cursed them in this way, ought not another person who desired to receive and possess them graciously then to have obtained them?

Accordingly, because of your intervention, I permit him his place in the canonry and the dwelling previously granted to him by me. I also consent that, from the time he returns, he may communicate with all who wish to do so with him.

But my own communion—which he rejected with hardened heart and hardened ears, fleeing stubbornly and maliciously with loud expressions of hatred against me, although no one pursued him or inflicted any force upon him, and from which, had I wished it, he would not have been deprived—he will receive at a suitable time and place [Col. 0986C] either judicially or obtain satisfactorily by making amends.

It is therefore fitting that, when he has now returned from you, your integrity should send him back seasoned with the salt of your wit, so that he does not appear to those with whom he has been staying as burdensome as he formerly appeared to me when he came from you—insulting me in a way he had never been before. For the one who said, “Have salt in yourselves,” himself added, “and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49).

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.

## III. THE SAME TO THE SAME

Concerning the ordination of the cleric Senatus, his detention in prison, and his appeal to the apostolic see.

[Col. 0985]

[Col. 0985D] To the most reverend Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, Hincmar, the least of the bishops of the Church of Laon, the devotion owed in the Lord.

I have hastily reread the writings of your Highness, which you arranged to have delivered to me as the anniversary approaches of my having been handed over in my parish, at the place called Silvacus. I wrote *mei traditionis*, not *meae traditionis*, so that the ambiguity between the one handing over and the one handed over may be removed by the possessive pronoun. For it is clear from the primitive genitive that I was the one handed over, not that I was the betrayer.

Having examined the documents of your Magnitude, I perceived that I was being bitten, as usual, but, thanks be to God, I did not feel myself wounded. Thus, resolved henceforth not to reply to you, though assailed by so many darts and marked with so great a blemish, I have been prepared until now to endure and have tried to dissemble; but, even after being driven into flight for a whole year, wishing to pass by like Abner, I am not permitted to do so, ground down by saws.

Accordingly, concerning the case of our fellow presbyter Haimeradus, having heard it regularly and canonically, I shall write my reply. As for the definition which you say I made concerning the same matter, I shall have to inquire of those who were present and are still alive, whom you identify in your writings, since I do not remember everything; and I shall then answer accordingly. Among them Hadulfus must be present at the synod to be held at Laon on the Ides of May, and it is also worthwhile for us that he be there. I wonder, however, why you do not send him back after delaying him for so long, especially since, as was right, I assented to your intervention concerning him.

Therefore, after carefully investigating a case which we do not know, and after learning through others what I think are the actions of your men—actions which we do not remember having taken ourselves—we shall pronounce our judgment once we have become certain; and, as truthful men, with God’s favor, we shall speak the truth with mouth and heart.

Regarding your cleric Senatus, you write to me as follows:

> “Therefore, if that cleric himself is not criminal and is teachable—which the sacred canons also require in a bishop—since he is offered to you to be ordained by us, you ought not to reject him from ordination in that very Church, to whom you consented for so long that he should have that same Church.””

That you say I consented, I do not know how you know, since the matter is well known and cannot even be twisted through circumstances or at least plausible forms. Therefore, you neither know that I consented nor can you prove it, while the sacred canons prescribe, concerning every bishop in the singular number, that a bishop must beware of saying about anyone what he cannot prove with clear evidence. Likewise, there is the canon: “Whoever cannot prove one crime must not be admitted to another.”

For you yourselves write later:

> “Because, when your presbyter was sent to me, I replied: Just as you acted toward me in your parish concerning my Church, so I shall act toward you in your parish concerning your Church.”

There you have proof that I did not consent.

What I replied to him, I replied in the presence of presbyters, deacons, and laymen, so that my judgment might not later be found void or calumnious. Namely, I sent word back to Sigebertus, who had sent him to me, recalling the place and time when and where I had spoken with him myself concerning that same Church: namely, beside the bridge at Cadamo. Even then I did not admonish him out of any emotional agitation, but peacefully, that he had not acted correctly in establishing him as a cleric in that Church without my knowledge and without a reasonable judgment concerning Haimeradus.

He replied that he had not done this without the consent of my ministers. When I persisted—“Whose?”—he identified Hadulfus. I gave him this answer: that I would speak with the presbyter Haimeradus, and that if Haimeradus were willing to withdraw without complaint, I would agree to Sigebertus’s requests; but if not, I would carry out what reason and authority dictated. This I did. Yet I was in no way able to obtain this from Haimeradus, and I sent the same message back to Sigebertus through Lairadus, his own man.

I did not think it necessary to recount these matters to his presbyter when he was sent to me. But I omitted them so that he might recall what grounds I had against him in this matter—namely, these. I also showed that afterward Haimeradus had brought the matter forward at the synod, as he often used to do, and that the same cleric, when sought, was not found there, just as he was not found on other occasions.

Therefore I instructed him that, before the matter was brought to judicial judgment, what had been taken from Haimeradus without ecclesiastical judgment should be peacefully restored to him. I was treating the matter graciously: he was to be restored to what had been unlawfully taken from him. Thus, if Sigebertus later thought that he had a just complaint, he could bring it forward at a suitable and canonical place and time.

I knew that chapter which you insert in your writings as though it were against me, although it acts in my favor. You write:

> “It is established in the first book of our synodal Capitularies, preserved by our ancestors from the time of our emperors” (Book I, chapter 90), “that presbyters must not be established or expelled in any Churches without the authority or consent of the bishops.”

The same collection also contains the following (Book V, chapter 43):

> “Concerning those who establish presbyters in their Churches, or expel them from their Churches, without the consent of the bishop, and who, when admonished by the bishop or by any royal envoy, refuse to obey: they shall be compelled to pay our ban and shall be ordered to come to our palace through sureties. Then we shall decide whether it pleases us that they pay that ban or undergo another penalty.”

Therefore I warned Sigebertus that what had been done without my consent should be corrected without detriment to him.

Let us return, then, to your writings, in which, after other matters, you add:

> “And if you wish to ordain that same cleric in the same Church, write to me according to custom, and I shall give him ecclesiastical liberty. But if that cleric, whom you consented for so long to have and to labor in that Church at Follanebraio, is not pleasing to you, and if you have rejected him on reasonable grounds, either because of a crime or because he is unteachable—although you ordained him contrary to the rules, without my permission and without my canonical grant of liberty—show this, and we shall find another.”

First, I ask why you did not investigate his irregular ordination during all that time. As for my lack of consent, I have already answered. But I confess that, in this matter, my ignorance is astonished at your wisdom, since you assert that I ordained him contrary to the rules, although you have not yet proved this, and yet you promise that, if I wish to ordain him in the same Church, I should write to you according to custom and you will give him ecclesiastical liberty.

For it is difficult, as the apostolic trumpet proclaims, that what had a bad beginning should have a good outcome. But if you had wished to observe in my case the saying of the Wise Man, “Before you inquire, do not censure anyone,” then, since no one is excluded, you ought first to have investigated the manner of the ordination. Only then should either the ordainer or the ordained have been judged according to law, or both struck with the canonical cautery.

Therefore, take up again in full the chapter which you have presented truncated from the book of our emperors, as though it were against me, although it acts in my favor (Book I, chapter 88):

### On the Ordination of Slaves

> “Concerning the ordination of slaves, who were being indiscriminately promoted everywhere to ecclesiastical orders, it pleased everyone that the matter should be brought into agreement with the sacred canons. It was therefore decreed that henceforth no bishop should presume to promote them to sacred orders unless they had first obtained liberty from their own masters.
>
> “If any slave, fleeing from or hiding from his master, or employing witnesses hired or bribed for payment, or using any other cunning or fraud, should reach ecclesiastical orders, it was decreed that he be deposed and that his master receive him.
>
> “But if a grandfather or father, migrating from one country to another, should beget a son in that province, and the son should be raised there and promoted to ecclesiastical orders, while it remained unknown whether he was a slave, and afterward his master should legally claim him, it was decreed that, if his master wished to grant him liberty, he should remain in his order. But if the master wished to draw him away from the Lord’s camp by the chain of slavery, he should lose his order, because, while remaining a person of low condition in relation to the sacred orders, he cannot exercise the dignity of the priesthood.
>
> “As for their possessions or peculium—their personal property—for they are granted liberty by their own masters so that they may lawfully be promoted to ecclesiastical orders, it was decreed that it should remain in the power of the masters whether they wished to grant it to them or claim it for themselves. But if they acquire anything after ordination, the rule established in the canons concerning consecrated persons possessing nothing shall be observed.
>
> “Concerning the slaves of Churches, it was decreed by common agreement that the archbishops established in the several provinces should possess our authority, while their suffragans should keep a copy of it. Whenever someone useful from the Church’s household is found who is to be ordained, this authority itself must be read aloud before the people in the ambon; and, before the priests or faithful laymen, in front of the altar’s horn, they must obtain liberty without any form of trickery, as our authority provides, and only then may they be promoted to ecclesiastical orders.
>
> “The same procedure must also be followed concerning those whom the superiors of canons or monks request to be ordained.”

Having considered the tenor of this chapter, await my answer concerning the ordination of your cleric—if it was made by me—at the appropriate time and place and according to the canonical requirements then in force. Meanwhile, cease judging my alleged irregular ordination, since you cannot be both accuser and judge.

Observe also what you yourselves write from later canons: no one bound by servile or peasant conditions may be admitted to ecclesiastical honors according to the statutes of the apostolic see unless it has first been legally established that he was freed either by testament or by written documents. If any bishop, knowing the status of the person being ordained, should perhaps wish to transgress by carrying out a forbidden ordination, he must not presume to celebrate Mass for a year.

As for knowledge of this cleric’s condition and the transgression involved in a forbidden ordination, it is clear what should be decided. These matters should first be brought forward, if you wish, and judgment should be imposed upon either one who confesses or one who is convicted. Yet, although I have neither been convicted nor confessed, without any synod, without any such interrogation, inquiry, or present summons, you have assumed and exercised the office of accuser and judge alike concerning both an absent man and one absent from the written proceedings, pronouncing as follows:

> “Since you ordained that cleric contrary to the rules, the sacred rule demonstrates this by saying” (Letter 1):
>
> “Leo says in his letter to all the bishops established throughout all the provinces:
>
> “ ‘People are admitted indiscriminately to sacred orders who possess no dignity of birth and no dignity of character, and who have been entirely unable to obtain liberty from their masters. They are advanced to the height of the priesthood as though servile baseness could receive this honor, and someone is believed capable of pleasing God who has not yet been able to prove himself to his master. There is therefore a double guilt in this matter: both the sacred ministry is polluted by the baseness of such companionship, and the rights of the masters are violated insofar as this constitutes the rashness of an unlawful usurpation.
>
> “ ‘Therefore, dearest brothers, let all the priests of your province abstain from such persons. And not only from them, but also from others who are bound to some hereditary condition, we wish them to refrain, unless perhaps the petition or consent of those who claim some power over them has been granted. For the person who is to be enrolled in divine service must be free from others, so that he may not be withdrawn by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s camp, in which his name has been registered.’ ”

And, as though interpreting these words against me, you add:

> “After decreeing the dignity of birth, he describes the character of those to be ordained and adds this conclusion” (Leo, in the same place, at the end):
>
> “Our admonition therefore declares that if any of the brothers should attempt to act against these decrees and dare to admit what has been forbidden, he should know that he will be removed from his office and will not be a sharer in our communion, since he was unwilling to be a companion in discipline.”

You further add:

> “It must be understood that these pronouns of the plural number—‘If any of the brothers should attempt to act against these decrees’—and the rest, until we continue with the words, ‘let us repeat the earlier passages of this letter,’ are not without discrimination and particular rational application.”

Know that neither this singular “this,” which concerns all, nor those plural pronouns—“these,” “those,” and the like—which refer to each individual, and which you either placed above from the statutes of the same pope or add below and interpret as you wish, in any way oppose me in the complaint you are pursuing.

For I neither understand nor have understood that those subject to slavery should be admitted to sacred orders unless they have been granted liberty by their masters. Nor do I decree that those who have been found or exposed should be retained. Nor have I ever agreed, or do I now agree, that the husbands of widows or men who have had numerous marriages should be received into these orders on any terms. Nor do I permit any cleric to practice usury for sordid profit, whether under his own name or another’s. Therefore I abhor both this singular “that” and these plural “these,” together with all the other things that have been prohibited.

But if you wish, first assume the office of accuser in judicial order, prosecute the matter canonically, and I shall be prepared to show canonically how these things do not apply to me. I shall also be prepared to explain how I understand and embrace them, word for word, down to a single iota, drawing from the fabric of faith what was woven by that same pope.

You also write:

> “As for these Gallican canons, which you often use in your writings and by which you make your complaint, I know that you will not reject them.”

Since it now seems lengthy and superfluous to respond to every other matter individually, I shall then answer fully concerning their reception as well.

As for what you wrote concerning your cleric:

> “But if you want him to come to your synod for this reason, because the canons of Chalcedon say” (canon 6) “that no presbyter or deacon should be ordained absolutely, nor anyone in an ecclesiastical order,”

since you did not touch upon the remainder, we supply it:

> “Unless the person to be ordained is specifically assigned to a church of a city, an estate, a martyr shrine, or a monastery. But those who are ordained absolutely—the synod decreed that the laying-on of hands in such a case should be considered invalid, and that the person ordained should nowhere be permitted to minister, to the injury of the one who ordained him.”

I know that I have never ordained anyone otherwise than with such a specific assignment. If I had done otherwise, the laying-on of hands would be considered invalid, and the ordained person could not minister without injury to me.

After this chapter, the council brings forward the following in harmony with it (canon 8):

> “Clerics placed in charge of poorhouses, or ordained in monasteries and basilicas of martyrs, shall remain under the authority of the bishops who are in each city, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers, and shall not withdraw rebelliously from their bishop. If anyone dares to overturn this arrangement in any way and does not submit to his own bishop, then, if he is a cleric, he shall be subject to the correction of the canons; but if he is a layman or monk, he shall be deprived of communion.”

Therefore, the manner of the ordination must also be investigated in the case of those subject to authority.

So that you may also learn from him, having forgotten, at whose persuasion you ordained him contrary to the rules, and so that, if you are challenged about this at the synod of bishops, you may have an answer to give, send instructions to me. Since he is the property of our Church and has been granted no liberty, I shall send him to your synod through my messengers, so that you may learn what blessed Leo writes to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople (Letter 87):

> “Just as one sins through bad persuasion, so one also sins through bad consent.”

I am astonished both at these statements and at what you yourselves wrote above, when you proposed in your present writings passages from blessed Gregory, worthy of proclamation:

> “Above all, no one who performs the office of shepherd ought to be unaware that, in carrying out the divine ministry, just as he must not be enticed by anyone’s favor into doing what is improper, so also he must not, through hatred of anyone or the zeal of private concern, delay or overturn what is proper.”

There you openly state that there is sin in bad persuasion and guilt in bad consent. And just as you perceive that I was badly persuaded and gave bad consent, you yourselves also seem to consent, saying what I have already quoted: that if I wish to ordain him, I should write to you according to custom and you will give him ecclesiastical liberty—the man whom you publicly declare to have reached ecclesiastical orders in this way.

Is hatred of someone boiling here, or is someone’s favor overflowing? Will you grant liberty for promotion so that the one who established him with evil intention may not be opposed, while the ordainer is seized because your cleric may perhaps have been ordained badly and irregularly? Does the former give birth to hatred? Does the latter produce favor?

As I have already indicated, although I had been somewhat softened by the former gracious address of that same Sigebertus, I did not presume, as though enticed by favor, to receive this cleric irregularly. Now, although he lies in wait for me, I am moved by no hatred. If justice favors his will from this point onward—which it has not done until now—the path of justice in our prosecution will not be held back from carrying out what reason and authority dictate.

I summoned the aforementioned cleric to the synod with this warning because he is accused by the presbyter Haimeradus. But now also, because you are accusing him concerning his ordination, I call him to appear, and I shall offer him what belongs to me.

If you intend to send your messengers to the synod, either with him or after him, to prove that he is subject to slavery—or, if he is unable to deny it, to hear his own confession—I have no objection. If he enters through the door, the sheepfold will retain him among the sheep; but if he climbs up from another direction, like a thief, he will be expelled as a robber.

As for what you write to me concerning him:

> “He himself, having been dispossessed contrary to reason and authority, ought not therefore to give you any regular account at the synod.”

Would that you would preserve this same principle for me, however unworthy a bishop I may be, since, as you know, I have been handed over to imprisonment, have been accused of no crime, and have never fled from synodal judgment, whether at any time or any place! Would that you would preserve it on this condition: that, contrary to reason and the authority of the apostolic see, adding grief to injury and inflicting it upon me and my parish, you would not demand from me—summoned by the apostolic see and appealing to it—a prejudicial answer, contrary to the decrees of all the apostles, at least until the synodal assembly!

For I had not merely been stripped of all my possessions and resources, but also of the power over my own body, by decree of blessed Pope Felix, together with his predecessors, Popes Julius, Lucius, Callistus, Zephyrinus, Victor, Anicetus, Hyginus, Xystus, and Alexander, and his successors Damasus, Gelasius, and Hadrian:

> “If any bishop has been stripped of his possessions or expelled from his Church by force or fear—which is hostile to every Christian name—it is necessary and fitting that the purpose of the bishops should always first contend openly so that everything taken from him may be legally restored to his authority, and that the bishop be restored first. Only afterward, not immediately but after a long period and extended intervals, once he has arranged his affairs with authority and prepared what is necessary for himself, should he come to the case and, if it seems just, answer his accusers.”

And later:

> “Whenever bishops think that they are oppressed by their fellow-provincial bishops or by their metropolitan, or regard them with suspicion, they should immediately appeal to the Roman see, to which they must be permitted to go freely, without any detention or seizure of their possessions. And when they have appealed to the aforesaid Roman Church, their mother, or have requested to be heard by it, no one may presume to excommunicate them, seize their sees, take away their possessions, or inflict any force upon them before the case of both parties has been settled by the authority of the Roman pontiff.
>
> “If anyone should presume otherwise, his action will be nothing and will lack force. For we do not rashly presume this either: you know well, Athanasius, that the same thing was established in the Council of Nicaea and was carried out by our predecessors. For when you and Paul of Constantinople, Asclepius of Gaza, and Lucian of Adrianople were condemned by the Eastern bishops without the advice of our predecessor Julius, of holy memory, and fled to him as to the head of the whole world, as has always been permitted to this holy see, he received you into communion after learning their wickedness and your justice. Caring for all of you, and out of regard for the dignity of his own see, he restored each of you to your Churches and wrote to the Eastern bishops, blaming them for having treated blameless men improperly by expelling them from their Churches and for failing to preserve the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.
>
> “He ordered some of them to appear before him on a fixed day, so that they might give a definite account of such presumptuous actions, and so that he might demonstrate in their presence that he had issued a just decree concerning them. He also warned them that the brothers would not thereafter endure such things, and that, unless they ceased from such presumptuous actions, they would withdraw from their proper orders.
>
> “By the privilege of this holy see, therefore, you and your brothers recovered your own Churches together with everything belonging to them.”

By these and many other documents it is clear that no bishop who has appealed to this holy see or taken it as his defender ought to be condemned or stripped of his possessions until he acknowledges the judgment of our apostolic authority—that is, of the prince of the apostles, Peter—for Christ Jesus alone entrusted this power to this holy, apostolic see. For the aforesaid prince of the apostles alone, above all others, is believed to have received and merited from Christ God, the King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

The twelve lights of the world proclaim these blessed things in concert with this Felix. By them I make my appeal, together with their predecessors and successors, and nothing will be held valid that differs from their constitutions.

Therefore, in this matter, he and they speak vainly together with all their predecessors, because the authority of each successor will be held valid only if, as Pope Symmachus says, he gives firmness to the acts of his predecessor. Thus, I do not know from where your cleric was stripped, nor do I yet know from where he ought to be clothed.

But if he has in my parish either a voice of complaint, a voice of expiation, or an accusation against anyone, you will be able to learn fully from my humility whether he ought to come to the synod which I am to hold.

Given on the Kalends of May, in the present third indiction.

## IV. HINCMARUS’S COLLECTION FROM THE LETTERS OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS, TO HINCMARUS OF RHEIMS

### From the letter of Pope Victor, addressed to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, who was the fifteenth after Peter

**Letter 1.**

> “For we have heard that among you and your people various judgments are being made and uncertain matters are being judged. Dearest brothers, let us in no way judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who will bring hidden things to light, illuminate what is concealed in darkness, and reveal the purposes of hearts (1 Cor. 4:3).
>
> “For although things may be true, they must not be believed unless they are proved by clear indications, unless they are established by manifest judgment, unless they are made public according to judicial order.
>
> “It has likewise been referred to the apostolic see that you judge matters which you are not permitted to decide without our authority—namely, the case of bishops. It is therefore clear that the following was established from the time of the apostles and thereafter:
>
> “If a bishop accused or judged by his fellow-provincial bishops in any matter appeals, he may freely approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who shall arrange for his case to be reconsidered either personally or through his representatives. While the pontiff is hearing the case anew, no other bishop may be placed or ordained in his position.
>
> “For although the provincial bishops may investigate the case of an accused pontiff, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since the Lord said to the blessed apostle Peter, and to no one other than him: ‘Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. 16:19).
>
> “Elsewhere it is read in the apostolic statutes: ‘If anyone thinks that he is oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the patriarch or primate of the diocese, or before the see of the universal apostolic Church.’
>
> “Brothers, such presumption is nothing other than transgressing the boundaries of the apostles and their successors and violating their decrees. For, as it is written, those brothers are blamed who presume to judge bishops in a manner other than the pope of the apostolic see has determined.”

### From the letter of Pope Callistus to all the bishops of the cities of Gaul, who was the seventeenth after Peter

**Letter 11.**

> “Let no primate or metropolitan presume to excommunicate or judge the Church of a diocesan bishop, or his parishioner, or anything belonging to his parish, or to do anything without his counsel or judgment. Instead, let them observe what was established by the apostles, the Fathers, and our predecessors and confirmed by us, namely:
>
> “If any metropolitan bishop, apart from what pertains solely to his own parish, attempts to do anything outside it without the counsel and consent of the bishops of the province, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank, and what he has done shall be considered invalid and void.
>
> “Whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of the provincial co-bishops, their Churches and clergy, and their secular needs, must be done with the consent of all the provincial bishops, not with any arrogance of domination but with the humblest and most harmonious administration, as the Lord says: ‘I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister’ (Matt. 20:26); and elsewhere: ‘The one who is greatest among you shall be your servant’ (ibid., verse 28), and so forth.”

Likewise, from the same material, concerning primates and metropolitans:

> “Let no primate, no metropolitan, and none of the other bishops enter another’s city or approach a possession that does not belong to him and that is the parish of another bishop, in order to arrange, ordain, or judge anything concerning its administration, unless he has been summoned by the one whose jurisdiction it is known to be, if he wishes to retain the honor of his rank.
>
> “If he presumes otherwise, he shall be condemned—and not only he, but also those who cooperate with him and consent to him. For just as ordination is forbidden to them, so also judgment and the administration of other matters are forbidden. For one who cannot ordain, how will he judge? He will certainly not judge, nor will he be able to judge, since just as another man’s wife may not be adulterated, judged, or disposed of by anyone except her own husband while he lives, so the bishop’s wife—that is, his Church or parish, which is unquestionably understood as such—may not, while he lives, be judged or administered by another without his judgment and consent, nor may another enjoy her intercourse, that is, her ordination.
>
> “Thus the Apostle says: ‘A wife is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but when her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband’ (1 Cor. 7:39). Likewise, since the Church is called the bishop’s bride and wife, she is bound to him while he lives. When he dies, she is released and may marry whomever she wishes, only in the Lord—that is, regularly.
>
> “If, while he lives, she marries another, she will be judged an adulteress. Likewise, if he willingly takes another, he will be considered an adulterer and will be deprived of communion.
>
> “But if he is persecuted in his own Church, he must flee to another and be joined to it, as the Lord says: ‘If they persecute you in one city, flee to another’ (Matt. 10:23).
>
> “If he must be transferred for the sake of usefulness, he must not do this on his own, but should do so at the invitation of the brothers and by the authority of this holy see—not for the sake of ambition, but for the sake of usefulness.”

### In the Decretals of Pope Lucius, concerning metropolitan bishops, who was the twenty-third after Peter

**Single letter.**

> “If any metropolitan bishop, apart from what pertains solely to his own parish, attempts to do anything outside it without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of the province, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank, and what he has done shall be considered invalid and void.
>
> “Likewise, supported by apostolic authority, we command that no metropolitan, without the insistence of all the other bishops of the province, hear the cases of anyone, since such judgments will be invalid and he himself will answer for what he has done.”

### In the Decretals of Pope Julius, concerning metropolitan bishops, who was the thirty-sixth after Peter

**Letter 1.**
