> “Because they wished the holy Roman Church to be the primate of all Churches, so that, just as the blessed apostle Peter was first among all the apostles, so this Church, consecrated in his name, might, by the Lord’s institution, be first and the head of the others, all greater ecclesiastical cases and episcopal judgments should return to it as to a mother and summit, and should receive their proper conclusion from its sentence.
>
> “Nothing concerning these matters should be decided outside the Roman pontiff, so that it may not be permitted to any metropolitan, as they were accustomed to act, rashly and according to anyone’s whim and private judgment, either to overturn the greater cases of the Church or to condemn bishops without consulting the Roman pontiff. Rather, with the common counsel of the bishops of the holy Roman see and through harmonious action, let them arrange whatever must be done with zeal for Christ; let them think rightly with one accord, and let them complete what they have thought, not by disagreeing among themselves, but in a manner pleasing to God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “If from this day forward anyone presumes to condemn a bishop or expel him from his own see contrary to the judgment of this holy see, let him know that he is irrecoverably condemned and will be perpetually deprived of his own honor.”

Likewise, from the decrees of the same pope, which he took from the Council of Nicaea (Letter 11 to the Easterners):

> “All bishops who are accused or charged with serious cases, whenever necessary, shall freely appeal to the apostolic see and flee to it as to a mother, so that they may be supported, defended, and liberated by it, as has always been the practice.
>
> “Ancient authority, that of the apostles, their successors, and the canons, has reserved to its disposition all greater ecclesiastical cases and the judgments of bishops, since those bishops are blamed who act toward their brothers in a way other than the pope of that same see has determined.
>
> “It was decided that a bishop accused or judged by his fellow-provincial bishops in any matter may freely appeal to and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who shall arrange for the case to be reconsidered either personally or through his representatives. While the pontiff is hearing his case anew, no other bishop may be placed or ordained in his position.
>
> “For although the provincial bishops may investigate the case of an accused pontiff, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since the Lord said to the blessed apostle Peter, and to no one other than him: ‘Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. 16:19).
>
> “If anyone thinks that he is oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pope of the universal apostolic Church.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let no bishop presume to retain or ordain the parishioner of another without the consent of that person’s bishop, or to judge him—although the authority of the apostolic see remains valid in all things—for just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment be invalid.
>
> “For we decree that no one is held by the sentence of any judge other than his own. Since one who could not ordain him will in no way be able to judge him.”

### From the Chapters of the most holy Archbishop Felix, taken from the Council of Nicaea

**Letter 11.**

> “Although the provincial bishops, together with their metropolitan, may charitably and harmoniously handle the cases of the bishops of their province, nevertheless, as was established in the aforesaid synod in your presence, they are not permitted to decide them without the authority of the Roman pontiff.
>
> “If certain persons presume to act otherwise, let those who have done this suffer the penalty of their presumption; and let those who have been wrongly excommunicated or condemned by them be released and restored by the authority of this holy see and by the power of our blessed teacher, the key-bearer Peter.
>
> “For the Lord himself says: ‘Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.’”

## Chapter 20

“Whenever bishops think that they are being excessively burdened by their fellow-provincial bishops or by their metropolitan, or regard them with suspicion, let them immediately appeal to the Roman see. They must be permitted to go freely to it, without any detention or confiscation of their possessions. Once they have appealed to the aforementioned Roman mother Church, or have requested to be heard by it, no one may presume to excommunicate them, usurp their sees, seize their property, or inflict any violence upon them before the case of both parties has been settled by the authority of the Roman pontiff. If anyone should presume otherwise, his action shall be null and void and without force. For we do not make this presumption without precedent: you know well, Athanasius, that it was established in the Council of Nicaea itself and practiced by our predecessors. When you and Paul of Constantinople, Asclepius of Gaza, and Lucian of Adrianople were condemned by the Eastern bishops without the knowledge of our predecessor of holy memory, Julius, and you fled to him—as to the head of the whole world, just as it has always been permitted to flee to this holy see—he investigated their wickedness and your justice, received you into communion, and, caring for all of you, restored each of you to his own Church in consideration of the dignity of his see. He wrote to the Easterners, blaming them because they had not dealt rightly, expelling blameless men from their Churches and failing to preserve the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. He ordered some of them to be present before him on a fixed day, so that they might give a definite account of such presumptions and so that he might demonstrate before them that he had issued a just decree against them. He also threatened that thereafter the brothers would not endure such treatment and that, unless they ceased from such presumptions, they would be removed from their own ranks. Through the privilege of this holy see, therefore, you and your brothers recovered your own Churches, together with everything belonging to them.

“By these and many other precedents it is manifest that no bishop who has appealed to this holy see or called it to his defense ought to be condemned or stripped of his possessions until he has acknowledged the judgment of our apostolic authority—that is, of Peter, the prince of the apostles—because Christ Jesus alone entrusted this power to this holy see, that is, to the apostolic see, since the aforesaid prince of the apostles alone is believed to have received and deserved to receive from Christ God, the King of kings, the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

Pope Damasus, who was the third successor of Felix II and the thirty-ninth after Peter, wrote to Archbishop Stephen concerning archbishops who readily wished to condemn bishops, saying:

[Col. 0998B]

### (Epistle 11)

“It is permitted to metropolitan bishops, together with their provincial bishops, provided that none of them is absent and that they all agree in the individual cases, to investigate bishops and the most important ecclesiastical matters. But they are not permitted to settle their most serious disputes or those of their Churches, or to condemn bishops, without the authority of this holy see. All must appeal to it, if necessary, and ought to be strengthened by its assistance. For, as you know, a synod held without its authority is not valid, nor can a bishop be definitively condemned except in a legitimate synod, convened at the proper time by apostolic summons. Nor is any council ever recorded as valid that was not supported by apostolic authority.”

[Col. 0998C] I remember that I have already written to you, in other volumes, these authorities of the apostolic see. But I now write to you again for this reason: so that you may know that, although you retain the booklet in which I collected these and similar authorities—the booklet through which, at the synod held at Attigny, I appealed to the universal pontiff of the holy Roman see, Lord Adrian, together with the letters he had sent me summoning me—although neither of these things helped me then, nevertheless, as long as breath remains in me, I shall not dissent from observing these principles.

And because you often reproach me concerning the subscription which you first extorted from me at that same synod by royal power and afterward fraudulently, I shall now give a brief answer, reserving fuller replies for their proper time, should they be necessary. For, as I have already written to you, you summoned me to that synod to answer the letters of the apostolic lord. When I came, you did not permit me to enter it, but ordered me to subscribe outside the doors, in accordance with the privilege of your see. I replied that I had never acted against your privilege; therefore there was neither necessity nor reason for you to demand that subscription from me.

When, on account of this, I was harassed more and more on the following day, I protested by citing the letter of Pope Leo sent to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (Epistle 88), where he says: “For it was not necessary that the man who had already demonstrated his obedience by the service of his voluntary arrival should be bound by a written statement.”

Finally, when even this did not help, I protested through the booklet mentioned above, reading this chapter (Felix II, Epistle 11, chapter 20): “Whenever bishops think that they are being excessively burdened by their fellow-provincial bishops or by their metropolitan, or regard them with suspicion, let them immediately appeal to the Roman see.” I read the chapter through to the end; I have also transcribed it in full above. I likewise read the letter summoning me from the apostolic lord, but neither action helped me.

While I was doing these things, the lord king, instigated by your faction—although on the preceding day he had said that he distrusted nothing on my account—threatened that he would burden me and my men as much as his power allowed unless I made that subscription. As for myself, I cared little. But when I saw that my men would be compelled to provide surety because they had followed me to the estate of Pauliacum, just as I was about to return home with Archbishop Harduic, Archbishop Frotarius approached me and asked why I did not agree to subscribe, since there was no danger for me.

I replied that I would not do so unless you also wrote to me that you would preserve the privilege due to my Church, as the Council of Antioch had established, so that afterward you would not attempt to inflict some prejudice upon me on the pretext of this subscription. He replied: “Certainly, he will in no way contradict this for you.” I promised that I would act on those terms, and I asked that the subscription itself be shown to me.

When you showed it to me, certain clauses to which I had not agreed had been deleted, and certain others had been added—namely, the phrase “according to the decrees of the apostolic see,” wherever it appeared. The subscription itself was as follows:

“I, Hincmar, bishop of the Church of Laon, hereby and henceforth shall be faithful and obedient to my lord Charles the king, according to my office, as a man ought to be to his lord and a bishop rightly ought to be to his king; and, according to the privilege of Hincmar, metropolitan of the province of Rheims, in accordance with the sacred canons and the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from the sacred canons, I profess that I shall obey to the best of my knowledge and ability.”

When I carried this home with me, I dictated the following for you to subscribe:

“And I, Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, shall preserve for you, Hincmar, co-bishop of the Church of Laon, your privilege, as required by the sacred canons, and in every ecclesiastical matter in which you have need, I shall, according to the sacred rules, provide you with the assistance due to you by right, through archiepiscopal authority.”

I sent this to you through Fredigisus, the priest of Archbishop Harduic. You sent word back to me through the same man that you were doing this voluntarily; and so, at the synod, I reread and subscribed to it. But you entirely abandoned the subscription you had promised. Instead, you professed verbally that in every matter in which you could justly and reasonably assist me according to your office, you would do so.

I, for my part, have never acted against the privilege of your see toward anyone, nor, with God’s favor, shall I ever act against the privilege of any bishop. Whether you subsequently acted toward me in accordance with your profession, anyone who reads the letter that you sent me from the same place, Attigny, through the deacon Hitto, will easily recognize. I have already answered you concerning that letter, so it would be superfluous to insert it here. You yourselves also know what assistance you offered me after this profession of yours, while I was writing these letters to you.

“To the most reverend Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, Hincmar, by God’s mercy bishop of the holy Church of Laon, sends due devotion in Christ.

“You know that I have twice been summoned by the pope of the universal holy Roman Church, our father Adrian. You yourselves, in the written sheets which you delivered at the palace of Attigny before the archbishops and bishops who were present, reproached me for refusing to come to that same see. If, because of a copyist’s error, *detrectem*—which means ‘I conceal or postpone’—should instead be read as *detractem*, meaning ‘I greatly delay,’ this may reasonably be understood, since the word was not marked with an interlinear stroke.

“Therefore, for the love of almighty God and out of reverence for Saint Peter, I now ask you—as I asked and pleaded with you at that same synod convened by you at Attigny, though I could not obtain it, and as I have already earnestly implored you for a full year, especially at the synod once held at the palace of Verberie [the text reads *ab horno*, uncertain]—that you obtain for me, through your archiepiscopal authority and with the favor of our lord, the most glorious King Charles, permission to obey the commands and ecclesiastical instructions of Lord Adrian, the universal pope, as is proper for everyone, since he has the right to judge concerning the whole Church. Specifically, I ask to be permitted to enter, as I vowed, the thresholds of Saints Peter and Paul, since I have moreover been summoned there by him.

“Otherwise, know that from now on I cannot obey you, as a co-bishop ought to obey an archbishop. For, as blessed Pope Gelasius decrees, those who oppose the decrees of the prelates of the holy Roman see as though they were canons do not know what they are saying; to resist them is to rise up against the canons themselves. This venerable and holy Pope Gelasius authoritatively decreed that the decretal letters should be received with reverence. Anyone who does not obey them does not receive them reverently, even if he bows his head deeply before the volume; rather, by stretching out his hands against them, he rejects them—an act that cannot be done without danger—since he does not foresee that he himself is being judged by them. Whether we wish it or not, we shall either obey them or be struck by the judgment of those whom no one among us is able to reject.

“As for the archbishops Remigius and Harduic, concerning whom you sent me instructions through the deacon Teutland, they do not prejudice the privilege of the holy Roman Church. Rather, that which the same holy see wished and arranged to entrust to them concerning me, it entrusted to them. You, however, do what belongs to you. Fare well in the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Even if that subscription contained something that might perhaps be intolerable, blessed Pope Alexander, fifth after Peter, prince of the apostles, would extend his hand to me. In his decrees he says as follows:

[Col. 1001A]

### (Epistle 1)

“Likewise, if any writing of this kind has in any way been extorted from such persons through fear, fraud, or force, or if they have composed or ratified anything by whatever ingenuity in order to free themselves, we decree that it shall bring them no prejudice or harm. With the authority of the Lord, the holy apostles, and their successors, we do not permit them ever to suffer infamy, accusation, or separation from their possessions on this account.

“A confession in such matters must not be compelled but voluntary, as he himself bears witness who says: ‘For from the heart come murders, adulteries, fornications, blasphemies’ (Matthew 15:19), and the other things pertaining to these. Nor should attention be paid only to what is done, but rather to the disposition with which it is done.”

If attention is not to be paid only to what is done, but rather to the disposition with which it is done, then no one who knows even a little can be unaware of the disposition with which I acted. At that time I would have done much more, if necessary, so that I might free my men, who were innocent and were being oppressed on my account.

And lest anyone think that only this holy Pope Alexander decreed such things, what blessed Gregory, whom you reverently receive, thought about the matter is clear from what he wrote to Constantius, bishop of Milan, concerning Bishop Pompeius:

### (Book VIII, Epistle 30)

“Now, since the matters alleged against him were not investigated with the strictness that was appropriate, and the proceedings subsequently drawn up before your fraternity are shown to be insufficient either for his condemnation or for his acquittal, this is no trivial matter and must not be decided carelessly or in passing. For it is exceedingly grave and improper that a definite sentence should be pronounced in a doubtful case.

“These proceedings could indeed have been sufficient for a decision if the accused person’s confession had followed them—provided, however, that the same confession had been elicited by the carefulness of the examination from hidden facts, and not extorted by severe affliction, which frequently causes even the innocent to be compelled to confess themselves guilty. Since the aforesaid bishop is said to have asserted that he was tortured by confinement and burned by hunger, you must know, if this is so, whether an extorted confession is harmful. Certainly, if an extorted confession is not harmful, neither is an extorted subscription.”

Would that you had then reasonably applied to me, however unworthy a bishop I may be, what you wrote to me about your villagers (the text reads *frustra villanis*), who were my parishioners, as I mentioned above—when you said that those who appealed ought not to suffer any violence. Was it fitting that violence should be inflicted upon me, who was appealing to the authority of the apostolic see, had been summoned by that same see, and was protesting by publicly reading the letters of its authority?

It is indeed established that the privilege of your see should serve charitable concord, not obstruct the negligence of judicial deliberation.

Moreover, you wrote to me as follows:

“You cannot be unaware how many evils the accomplices of Karloman have committed in the diocese of Rheims. Therefore, together with our brothers and fellow priests who were present, we have decreed, in the tenor appended below, that they should be excommunicated. Accordingly, after the matters appended below have been reread publicly, send me through your fellow minister a letter expressing your consent to this canonical excommunication, so that I may send it through the individual archbishops of the various provinces before the evil they have begun may grow more violently and spread farther and more widely.”

(See, concerning the letter discussed here, *The Works of Hincmar of Rheims*, in the immediately following volume.)

# V. Second Collection of Hincmar

From ancient letters of the Roman pontiffs, sent to Hincmar of Rheims at the estate of Gundulf through Archbishop Wenilo.

[Col. 1001]

## Preface

This little poem plainly brings forth and aptly teaches

That the apostolic see may be freely appealed to,

And that the appellant should not be constrained by any chains,

Nor a proper answer be demanded from one who is bound.

It distinguishes for the chief pontiff both the right and the limit,

As he soberly holds them with his fellow bishops.

May there be peace, life, and power for the devout King Charles,

Who, seeing these things, may approve them through his probity.

If anything is stolen from him by human efforts,

He rejects it by annulling it, when the truth returns.

[Col. 1002D]

Thus his mind, so ardent in the love of truth,

Does not allow what ought rightly to be frustrated to remain valid.

For gentle wisdom preserves his courage strong,

Whom piety specially redeems above all others.

O happy king, strong lover of the virtues,

Whom the piety of goodness alone so greatly surpasses.

But as he recognizes you, O Christ, as God and freely loves you,

He rejects what you reject and establishes what you establish.

Entrusting himself to you, he reveres your words;

Now and forever, protect what is yours.

## From the decrees of Pope Alexander, who was fifth after Peter

[Col. 1001D]

### (Epistle 3)

“Alexander, bishop, sends abundant peace and mercy to all who exercise the divine priesthood, and prays that wisdom and good will may increase and bear fruit in the Lord in all things.

“By the grace of God, dearest brothers, we are what we are. Therefore we must take care and strive earnestly lest we be found empty in this matter. Rather, with the same grace cooperating with us, we must bring forth abundant fruit for the Lord. This cannot happen otherwise than by searching out wisdom, meditating upon his commandments through readings and hymns, and, with his assistance, striving to fulfill his will as far as he grants us strength—by praying, keeping watch, and carrying it out.

“For the Lord has not given us grace to neglect, but has entrusted it to us to exercise faithfully. Love must be present and evident in us without pretense, because everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, while whoever loves God remains in God, and God in him (1 John 3). Therefore the Apostle also says: ‘Do not judge one another, brothers, but judge this rather, that you do not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brothers’ (Romans 14:13).

“And the Lord says: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.’ And elsewhere: ‘By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another’ (John 13:35). Solomon says: ‘A saving sacrifice is to heed the commandments and depart from all iniquity’ (Sirach 35:2).

“For the greatest iniquity is to slander and accuse one’s brothers. Hence it is written: ‘Everyone who slanders his brother is a murderer, and every murderer has no part or inheritance in the kingdom of God’ (1 John 3:15). And elsewhere: ‘Take care, dearest brothers, lest—God forbid—you become participants in their evils. Do not merely guard yourselves from them all, but teach others also to guard themselves from them and turn away from them.’”

## From the second epistle of Pope Sixtus, addressed to all the Churches; he was sixth after Peter

[Col. 1003C]

### (Epistle 11)

“If any one of you has been struck by adversity, let him freely appeal to this holy and apostolic see and take refuge in it as at his head, lest an innocent man be condemned or his Church suffer harm.

“If necessity should arise for him to appeal to it, but he should not dare to do so, and yet he should be summoned by this holy see, let him not refuse to come. Rather, as soon as he is notified, let him hasten to come, prudently arrange the matters for which he has been summoned, and, if anything needs correction, correct it with those whom he first finds here.

“Nevertheless, he must not return to his own Church until he has been fully instructed and, if there is any charge against him, cleared by apostolic letters or *formatae*. Then, after he has returned home, his neighbors may know how he settled his own case and that of others here, so that he may report and proclaim it to everyone without ambiguity.

“For bishops have been commanded by the holy apostles to be protected, defended, and liberated by this holy see, so that, just as they were first established by the disposition of the apostles under the ordering of the Lord, so in future times they may always be free from every perversity under the protection of this holy see, whose disposition they have observed in their cases and judgments.

“Therefore those are blamed who act toward their brothers otherwise than they know to be pleasing to the rulers of this see. Having considered these matters in this way, and having decreed them together with the other bishops as those who care for all, and because of the eminence of our own see, we decree that no pontiff may presume to excommunicate or judge a bishop who has been stripped of his possessions or expelled from his see, since one who has already been stripped has no privilege left from which he can be stripped.

“If anyone should presume to act otherwise, let him know that the censure of this holy see, together with all its members, will come upon him. As he has acted, so shall he receive: if well, well; if gravely, gravely; if most wickedly, most wickedly, because the laborer is worthy of his wages.

“We, brothers, wish to destroy no one; rather, he destroys himself who turns away from pious consideration and willingly violates the decrees of the apostles and of this holy see.

“And now, brothers, we commend you all to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to perfect you and give you an inheritance with all the saints. May the God of peace and consolation grant you to think the same thing according to Jesus Christ, so that you may help one another and not be divided; so that with one mind and one heart we may honor him in the concord and consolation of the brothers. He is able to strengthen you according to his Gospel, in accordance with the revelation of the eternal mystery, throughout all ages, in which the gifts of future joys are to be bestowed upon you.”

## In the decretal letters of Pope Hyginus, who was tenth after Peter, concerning metropolitan bishops

### (Epistle 1)

“Moreover, brothers, with the privilege of the Roman Church preserved in all things, no metropolitan may hear the cases of any bishops without the attendance of all the other bishops of the province, because otherwise the proceedings will be invalid; indeed, if he does so, he himself shall answer for it in synod and be corrected by his brothers.

“Accusations against men of higher rank must not be made by others, but by those who bring the charges themselves, provided that they appear worthy and irreproachable and demonstrate through public records that they are free from every suspicion and hostility and lead an irreproachable life and conduct.

“We also prohibit foreign cases and judgments, because it is unworthy that those who ought to have provincial judges chosen from among themselves should be judged by outsiders.

“We have cut off every opportunity by seizing it from all sides. Mindful of heavenly discipline, we extend our right hand to all who fall, raise from the precipice of ruin those whom we can, and desire with all our strength to provide the support of defense.

“Certainly, even if one’s conscience is aware of what is right, a person who becomes the cause of danger to another is worthy of punishment. Whoever persecutes an innocent person or a brother by any means strikes the throat of death against himself, as the divine and blessed herald says: ‘Do not slander, lest you be uprooted; do not accuse, lest you be accused; do not judge, lest you be judged; for with the judgment by which you judge, you shall be judged.’

“No one is thought to hate us whose report does not harm us. For the Lord says: ‘Every kingdom divided against itself shall not stand’ (Matthew 12:25); and every knowledge and rule divided against itself shall not stand.

“Therefore it is necessary that you receive these salutary exhortations concordantly, doing nothing through contention, but united in every zeal for devotion, obeying the divine and apostolic constitutions.”

## In the decretals of Pope Anicetus concerning contumacious metropolitans; he was thirteenth after Peter

### Unique epistle

“The archbishop himself shall do nothing concerning the cases of his fellow bishops or other common matters, according to the statutes of the apostles, without the counsel of all those bishops. Nor shall they act without him except insofar as their own parishes are concerned, because the Most High rejoices in such concord and glories in his members.

“The others who have obtained metropolitan sees shall be called not primates but metropolitans.

“If any metropolitan should become puffed up and wish to conduct the cases of the bishops of his province, or other cases, without the presence or counsel of all his fellow-provincial bishops—or to conduct any cases other than those belonging to his own parish—or if he should wish to burden them, let him be strictly corrected by all, so that he may not thereafter dare to presume such things.

“But if he should appear incorrigible and disobedient to them, let his contumacy be reported to this apostolic see, to which the termination of all episcopal judgments has been entrusted, so that punishment may be inflicted upon him and the others may be afraid.

“If, however, because of excessive distance, an inconvenient time, or the harshness of the journey, it should be difficult to bring his case to this see, then let the case be brought to his primate and judged before him by the authority of this holy see.

“Likewise, if any bishop should regard his own metropolitan with suspicion, let him be heard before the primate of the diocese or before this apostolic see.

“Let the one who is greater among you, according to the Lord’s command, be your servant; and the greater you are in all things, humble yourself.

“Dearest ones, do not contend among yourselves, and let no one seek to be greater. Rather, in accordance with the Apostle, love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.”

## From Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and decrees of Roman prelates and princes, delivered by Pope Adrian to Ingilramn, bishop of the city of Metz

[Col. 1006A]

### (Chapter 14)

“No metropolitan bishop may hear the cases of any bishops without the attendance of all the other bishops of the province, because otherwise the proceedings will be invalid; indeed, he will have to answer for the matter in synod. Nor may any other bishop hear the cases of his priests without the presence of his own clergy, because the bishop’s sentence will be invalid unless it is confirmed by the presence of the clergy.”

## From the decrees of Pope Eusebius

### (Epistle 2, toward the end)

“Sheep, therefore, who have been entrusted to their shepherd ought not to rebuke him unless he has departed from the true faith, nor can they accuse him in any way, because the deeds of shepherds are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even though they may appear rightly subject to correction.

“We say this because we find in your writings that certain bishops in your regions have been accused by their own sheep—some, evidently, on suspicion and others for a definite reason—and that, for this reason, some have been stripped of their possessions and others expelled from their own sees.

“You should know that they can be summoned neither to a provincial synod nor to a general one, nor judged in any matter, before everything taken from them has been legally restored to their authority. First, therefore, everything must legally be restored to them, and the Churches taken from them must be returned with all their privileges.

“Afterward, they must be granted not a short period of time, but as much time as they appear to have been dispossessed or expelled, before they are summoned to a synod and heard by all the bishops of their province.

“For one who has been dispossessed or expelled can neither be summoned to trial nor judged, since one who has already been stripped has no privilege left from which he can be stripped.

“Hence it was decreed in ancient times that, before joinder of issue, the recipient or primate must restore to the possessor all possessions, everything taken from him, and all revenues. Elsewhere it is written: ‘The one who has suffered violence shall recover everything in the condition in which it was, and shall securely hold what he possessed.’

“And elsewhere, in the synodal decrees of the Fathers and the edicts of kings, it is established and read: ‘Everything must be restored to bishops who have been dispossessed or expelled, by the personal order of the pontiffs, and they must be completely recalled to the places from which they departed, regardless of the circumstances of time—whether through fraud, captivity, the power of the great, or any unjust causes—they are known to have lost the property of their Church or their own possessions and substance before their accusation or their lawful summons to synod,’ and so forth.

“It is also decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that whoever invades another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore everything with increase. Hence it is written in the Gospel that if I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold (Luke 19:8). And in secular laws it is established: ‘Whoever steals another’s property shall restore to the person whose property was seized ten times what was taken.’

“And in the divine law it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who moves the boundary of his neighbor’; and all the people shall say, ‘Amen’ (Deuteronomy 27:17).

“Such things, therefore, must not be presumed without punishment, nor carried out without condemnation. Pursue peace, not the harm or injustice of anyone, among yourselves and toward all.

“But speaking the truth in love, let us grow in every respect into him who is the head, Christ. From him the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working in proportion to each member, makes the body grow for its building up in love.

“For the rest, dearest ones, rejoice and be perfect; exhort one another, be of one mind, and have peace. And the God of peace and love will be with you.

“May the Lord guard you, now and on the day of eternity. Amen.

“Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Constantius, illustrious man. Cons.”

## From the epistle of Pope Zephyrinus, addressed to the Egyptians; he was sixteenth after Peter

### (Epistle 11)

“For it has been reported to the apostolic see through your representatives that some of our brothers—namely, bishops—are being expelled from their Churches and their own sees, their goods being taken from them, and that, thus stripped and naked, they are being summoned to trial. This is entirely unreasonable, since the constitutions of the apostles and their successors, the commands of the emperors, and the provisions of the laws all establish the contrary, and the authority of the apostolic see forbids it.

“It was therefore commanded in the ancient statutes that bishops who had been expelled and stripped of their possessions should recover their own Churches; that all their property should first be restored to them; and that only afterward, if anyone wished to accuse them justly, he should do so at equal risk. The bishops who think rightly were appointed as judges, and they were to meet in the Church, where there would be witnesses for each of those who appeared to have been oppressed. They were not to answer before all their possessions, and those of their Churches, had been fully restored to them according to law.”

## From the epistle of Pope Julius

This letter was a reply to Eusebius, Theognis, Theodore, Berinthus, and the other Eastern bishops. It blamed them because they had presumed, contrary to canonical authority, to condemn Athanasius, Paul, and their other followers and expel them from their own sees without consulting the apostolic see.

[Col. 1007D] *(Letter 11, to the Eastern bishops.)* “It would have been fitting for you to speak about the holy Roman and apostolic Church with refinement and not ironically, since our Lord Jesus Christ himself addressed it appropriately, saying: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 16:18). For by a singular privilege granted to it, it has the power to open and close the gates of the heavenly kingdom to whomever it wishes. If you do not refrain from disparaging the one that was consecrated and exalted by the Lord’s own mouth, it is no wonder that you also do not cease to inflict injuries upon your brothers.

“Therefore the things decreed turbulently and stormily in your council are no longer concealed in silence. For it is evident that the truth was suppressed by a certain tumultuous lack of discipline: because you are heedless of what pleases God, on account of the quarrels you have with your neighbors, and insist that your resolutions are invincible. But it will be the work of divine providence that, from the opposite side, they can plainly be annulled, and that whatever you did there when assembled—without any grace, out of hatred or enmity—may be utterly rejected.

“Therefore I want all of you to hasten with all speed to the reverence of this holy see, so that through your own presence you may be able to demonstrate the integrity of what was done among you. For I believe that you cannot doubt that Athanasius, teacher of the sacred law, has been proved a defender of the true faith not only by us but also by the Council of Nicaea. After Alexander, that remarkable old man who had overthrown the blasphemies of Arius, had died, Athanasius assumed the episcopate of the Alexandrian Church five months after the Council of Nicaea.

“Against him and his followers you wove many lies and constructed barefaced slanders as though they were true accusations, declaring him to be the cause and head of many evils. You indicated in your writings that he was a disturber not only in Egypt but also in Palestine, Phoenicia, and the neighboring peoples. Therefore, following ecclesiastical rule, we summoned you and them to a regular judicial hearing at Rome on the appointed day—not within such a narrow period that an excuse could find a place—by letters and representatives. They accepted the summons and came on the appointed day; but you delayed coming, lest you be caught in your lies and your slanders be exposed.

“Nor have you been satisfied with these schemes alone. Seeing the sheep left without shepherds, you placed wolves over them in place of shepherds. It would therefore have been fitting for you to come to the regular summons, so that you might give a true account of these and your other presumptions; for the truth would have come forward if falsehood was displeasing. No one doubts that the guilty evade judgment in the same way that the guilty seek it in order to be acquitted. Nor is the one who disparages another with slanders free from suspicion of having spoken falsely, when he himself, summoned to judgment to prove what he had alleged, delayed coming.

“For I would have preferred you to come to the aforesaid canonical summons, so that before the universal council you might give an account of why you convened a synod to overthrow the condition of the Churches and brothers in Antioch and to destroy the great Council of Nicaea; or why, without consulting us, you summoned bishops to it, although neither Maximus of Jerusalem came nor our delegation was present—since the canons of the Council of Nicaea command that councils may in no way be held, nor bishops condemned, without the judgment of the Roman pontiff; or why, in place of the aforesaid brothers, you installed other adulterers before their case had been canonically examined and properly concluded before us or our representatives.

“For those who came to the aforementioned regular summons, wishing to withdraw you from the aforesaid accusations, report many things full of tears and pain, accusing you and saying that they have suffered unbearable things at your hands. You, therefore, refusing to come, while they persisted in the true account and protested against your slanders, and while the bishops of Egypt also protested in letters sent to us that the things you were contriving against Athanasius and his followers were false, and that everything was the fabrication of the Arians and their blasphemies: by such inventions it is clear that they are guiltless and you are guilty. For if you were confident in your true innocence, you would in no way have withdrawn from the aforesaid canonical summons, which was announced not suddenly but with ample time; rather, with every excuse removed, you would have hastened to come without delay and give an account of your actions.

“When these things had taken place, I wrote to you and to all who had assembled in Antioch against the apostolic and canonical rule without consulting us. First I reproved you for the injuries contained in your letters; then I asked why you had summoned Athanasius and his followers to your council, since the canons command that nothing be decided outside the Roman pontiff, to whom these and even greater affairs of the Churches have been entrusted by a special privilege, as has already been said, both by the Lord himself and by all the fathers of all the councils.

“But when you refused and, though summoned so many times to the council, did not wish to attend; when they persisted in their protest and just cause; when we learned your crimes and examined their just account; and when we found them all approved by the Council of Nicaea and obedient to our apostolic commands, it seemed right to us and to the whole council that you, instructed by divine commands and apostolic admonitions—we who ought to watch diligently and tirelessly for the condition of all the Churches—should, whenever anything liable to reproach is found, promptly correct it, whether it has arisen from ignorance and lack of understanding or from presumptuous usurpation.

“Having considered and decreed these matters in this way, and caring for everyone on account of the dignity of this see, we received them into communion and, by the authority of this holy see, restored to each of them his own Church together with its possessions. For, because of the snares of wicked men, this has always been and always will be permitted to this holy see, by the Lord’s institution and through the repeated confirmation of the holy Apostles and their successors in every council, with the Lord’s help, forever.

“Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over others should not resent having someone placed over him; rather, he should willingly render the obedience that he requires from others. For this reason I write to you in rebuke, because you did not properly treat men who were guiltless and had not been examined by us: you expelled them from their Churches after depriving them of communion, inflicted injury upon ecclesiastical discipline, and did not observe the decree of the Council of Nicaea. You did not fear to act in such an undisciplined way.

“Therefore, since you formerly refused to come, we now summon you again by letters and messengers to a definite day, namely the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, so that in your presence we may show that we pronounced a just judgment upon them [Col. 1010A] and that henceforth we will not tolerate such actions.

“For it is decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that whoever invades another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore it with increase. Hence it is also written in the Gospel: ‘If I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold’ (Luke 19:8). The Law likewise declares: ‘Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary marker’; and all the people shall say, ‘Amen’ (Deuteronomy 27:17).

“Why, then, do I wonder that you were so bold and acted so shamelessly, invading the boundaries and rights of blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles? For, as was briefly stated above, if it was a matter of law that without the authority of his holy see no one ought either to hold councils, summon bishops to a synod, condemn them, expel them from their own sees, or ordain others in their place, you did not fear to violate all these provisions.

“What, then, is such presumption other than a transgression of the decrees of the Apostles and their successors, and a failure to fear accepting the curse mentioned above, which was prescribed in the Law and which all the people confirmed with one voice and one accordant response by saying ‘Amen,’ that is, ‘Let it be’?”

Again, from the same letter:

“For no one can know a debtor better than the one who has suffered his injury and wickedness.

“And shortly afterward:

“As for what you have written—that he cannot be restored by fewer bishops than those by whom he was deposed—that is not so. Nor is this the rule of the orthodox bishops of the holy Church; rather, this invention of the Arians, your associates, was contrived for the destruction of orthodox bishops [Col. 1010C]. For, as trustworthy witnesses have reported to us, when you assembled at Antioch to condemn the faith concerning consubstantiality, you brought forward this rule out of hatred for the aforesaid Athanasius. It has no force, nor can it have any, since this council was neither conducted by orthodox bishops nor attended by a delegation of the Roman Church. The canons command that councils must not be held without its authority, and no council is, or ever will be, valid unless it has been supported by its authority.

“Therefore, in the matter of the flight for which you reproach Athanasius, you do not act rightly, since the Lord himself gave us this command: ‘When they persecute you in one city, flee into another’ (Matthew 10:23). The Lord himself also demonstrated this by his own example. When the Pharisees held a council against him in order to kill him, Jesus, knowing this, departed from there. Elsewhere it says: ‘The Jews took up stones to throw at him; but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple, and passing through their midst, departed.’ The disciples also withdrew because of fear of the Jews, concealing themselves. Paul, too, in Damascus (2 Corinthians 11), when sought by the ruler of the people, was lowered from the wall in a basket and escaped the hands of the one who sought him. Many other innumerable saints, both in the Old and the New Testament, are likewise read to have fled.

“If, then, you reproach those who flee for fleeing, blush rather to persecute them and cease laying snares; then those who flee will immediately cease fleeing. For whether you kill them—their death continually cries out against you—or whether you impose exile upon exile, everywhere you are known to send against yourselves the memory of evil; while they, by suffering, advance for their own good.

“Therefore the Lord says: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell’ (Matthew 10:28). For we have known many who were unjustly deposed through the worst schemes. Therefore it is my utmost duty—since, in the place of the prince of the Apostles, the care of the universal Church has been entrusted to me, with the assistance of that supreme Apostle—to ensure that such things do not happen again. For this reason the aforesaid privileges were specially granted to this holy see, both concerning the convocation of councils and the restoration of bishops, and concerning the greatest affairs of the Churches: so that from it all the oppressed may receive help and the unjustly condemned restoration, and so that such acts may neither be attempted by the wicked without punishment nor carried out without condemnation.

“And after a little more:

“The Lord did not wish his ministers to be treated so lightly as you treat them, or to be condemned by you; rather, as has been stated, he wished them either to be reserved to this holy see, to which they have been entrusted, or to his own judgment. For he says: ‘Whoever grieves you grieves me. Whoever does you an injury shall receive what he has done unjustly.’ The Gospel sufficiently explains what punishment awaits those who scandalize the Lord’s disciples, where it speaks of those who scandalize the disciples.

“That they are not to be condemned by you, but either by this holy see, as stated above, or reserved to him, he himself clearly demonstrates when he drove from the temple the sinful priests—whose place bishops now occupy in the holy Church—not through another but by his own authority, and overturned the tables of the money-changers with his own whip and expelled them from the temple. Elsewhere he himself says: ‘God stood in the assembly of gods, and in the midst he distinguishes among the gods’ (Psalm 81:1), and other statements of this kind and similar ones.

“Again, he himself says elsewhere: ‘Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned. For with the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged’ (Matthew 7:1–2).

“Therefore no one should presume, as rashly as you do, to spew forth his own wickedness. The one who judges must examine everything closely and investigate the order of events through a complete inquiry; he must in no way presume to judge matters that have not been entrusted to him. He must be granted patience for questioning, presenting charges, and adding further evidence, so that there the action of both parties may be fully limited and defined. He should not anticipate the litigants with his judgment until they themselves, after everything has been completed, have nothing further to present in the dispute.

“No one ought to be judged or condemned before he has his accusers present and receives ample opportunity to defend himself and cleanse himself of the charges. Likewise, it was established at the Council of Nicaea that permission to accuse must not extend beyond the boundaries of the province, unless an appeal has been made to this apostolic see, to which all who wish must be able to come freely and without the impediment of having to act through certain persons.”

Again, from what follows [Col. 1012A]:

“Judges ought to be no others than those whom the accused himself has chosen, or those whom this holy see has delegated with his consent, or whom its primates have delegated by the authority of this holy see. Yet from these and the other provisions established both in this holy see and by the Apostles and their successors, you granted nothing to the aforesaid bishops. Rather, using force against them and unjustly condemning them, as was mentioned above, you expelled some while they were absent—something contrary to every Christian law.

“In this it is evident that you have preserved neither the Lord’s rights for the Lord nor the rights of this holy mother and apostolic Church, which, as stated above, wished them to be reserved for its own judgment or for the judgment of this see, lest they be condemned or expelled by men as wicked as you are.

“In all these matters it is clear to every wise person that you are fools and transgressors of the Gospels and the canons. Nor were you satisfied with this transgression of yours: you also first expelled them and stripped them of their possessions, and then summoned and condemned them as though they had been present, although no one can regularly be summoned or judged before he has first been regularly restored and all his property has been completely restored to him according to law.

“For it was unanimously decreed in the aforementioned holy synod and confirmed by apostolic authority that if any bishop has been stripped of his possessions and summoned to face an accusation, the holy purpose of the bishops must first contend at the outset to ensure that everything he had lost through the accusations of his enemies is legally restored to his authority by an honorable council; that the bishop is first regularly restored to his former status; and that he then, after putting his affairs in order and arranging them, come at the appointed time to the case and, if it seems just, answer the allegations of his accusers.

“Why, then, have you transgressed the boundaries of the fathers, judging and condemning those whom you ought not to have judged? Why have you judged those whom you had not regularly approved?

“Nor did you observe what is written in the Book of Kings: ‘Man does not see as God sees, because man sees the face, but God sees the heart’ (1 Kings 16:7); and in Chronicles: ‘God searches all hearts and knows every thought’ (1 Chronicles 28:9). Elsewhere it is written: ‘The one whom God has reserved for his own judgment cannot be condemned by human examination.’

“All these matters must be guarded against with the greatest care, and accusations against bishops must not easily be accepted, since the Lord says: ‘You shall not receive a false report’ (Exodus 23:1), and the Apostle says: ‘Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter except on the evidence of two or three suitable witnesses’ (1 Timothy 5:19). If these precautions must be taken concerning presbyters and other faithful persons, how much more concerning bishops?

“Once these matters are understood, it is clear that you wish to rule rather than to care for your brothers or support them, because honor puffs up to pride, and what was provided for concord turns toward harm. It would have been fitting for you, in accordance with the aforesaid rules, if they had done anything against their order, to notify us and await what we would write in response to your inquiries. Even if they had committed something grave and intolerable, you ought to have awaited our censure and decreed nothing beforehand or otherwise than what you knew would please us, so that you would depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor through presumption.

“Let such presumption, now restrained by our authority, cease. Let such injuries be avoided, for we can in no way patiently endure such schemes, since it is fitting that we be diligent guardians of the sanctions of our fathers.”

From the letter of the most holy Archbishop Felix and his holy council, written in reply to Athanasius and all the bishops of the Egyptians, Thebans, and Libyans, in which their inquiries concerning the persecution and accusation of bishops are answered canonically.

**(Felix II, Letter 1.)** “Ecclesiastical affairs must not be handled in the same way as secular affairs. In secular matters, once someone has appeared after being summoned according to the laws and has begun to plead his case in court, he may not withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical matters, however, it is permitted to withdraw after the case has been stated, if necessity requires it or if one sees that he is being overburdened.

“Again, from the same letter:

“We have already given a rule, and we know that it was given by our predecessors: if anyone recognizes himself as a Christian, let him observe what is known to have been handed down by the Apostles. The Apostle Paul says: ‘If anyone announces to you anything other than what you received, let him be accursed’ (Galatians 1:8).

“For Christ, the Son of God and our Lord, granted the human race complete salvation through his own passion, so that he might free us. And if God loved us so greatly that he did not spare even his own Son but handed him over for us all, so that he might free us, why do we not love our brothers, or why do we rashly judge them, when the aforesaid Apostle says: ‘Let us not judge one another, but judge this rather: that you should not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother’ (Romans 14:13)?

“For if those who love their brothers are born of God and see God, what will become of those who persecute them and strive to condemn them by reviling, plotting against, accusing, and harassing them? If the former are sons of God, then without doubt the latter are sons of the devil, who, always like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour; so they pursue their brothers in order to destroy them.

“Those who refuse to help their brothers acquire a greater burden of sins and become liable for the deprivation of fraternal support.

“And after a little more:

“For such accusations and slanders do not proceed spiritually from the life-giving fountains toward the attainment of eternal life. Therefore blessed Paul the Apostle appropriately admonishes us, saying that we ought not to think more highly than we ought to think, but to think with sober judgment (Romans 12:3).

“Let us persevere in the definition of piety. Those who pass beyond it are not only themselves falling away from their own strengthening; they have also left to everyone a memory of their folly, so that they could not remain hidden in the very matters in which they sinned. For glory and disgrace are in speech, and a person’s downfall is in his tongue.

“Therefore it is appropriate that this demonstration of their reproaches be incorporated into our actions, so that you may no longer suffer such things, while they sow weeds and scandals, but may deserve to rejoice in your duties and teachings.

“Let them therefore be ashamed of such actions and hasten to remove such blasphemies, if they do not wish to be separated from our priestly fellowship and torn away from the society of the Christian people.

“For although we could have spoken and written many further and very necessary things found in the decrees of the apostolic see and established by the Apostles and their successors, nevertheless it seemed better to us to close the letter with a prayer.

“May almighty God, and his only-begotten Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, grant you this resolve: that you come to the aid with all your strength of all brothers and fellow bishops who are struggling under whatever tribulations, and that, sympathizing with them, you bear the cross of that same Lord and Savior, so that you may appear before all to be his true disciples; and so that both you and those who are with you may possess here and in the future the better things ‘which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart,’ which God has prepared for those who love him, through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory is due to God the almighty Father, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

“I wish you well, dearest brothers. Given on the Ides of February, in the consulship of Agarius and Julianus, men of illustrious rank.”

Again, from the Greek and Latin canons.

**(Chapter 5.)** “For if a bishop has been stripped of his possessions—or, God forbid, expelled from his own see, an act that ought to be alien to all the faithful—or has been separated from his own sheep by some form of detention, then, according to the canons, before he is restored to his former dignity and all his possessions that were taken from him through the schemes of his enemies are restored, he can neither be summoned nor judged, unless he himself, out of necessity, freely chooses to come, though not for the purpose of being judged.

“He must not be compelled by anyone to answer at all before everything that he lost through the accusations of his enemies has been completely restored to his authority by an honorable council, and before the bishop has first been restored to his former status. Then, after freely and securely arranging and putting his affairs in order, he may be canonically summoned and come at the appointed time to the synod for a legitimate and canonical hearing, and, if it seems just, answer the allegations of his accusers.”

From the decrees of Pope Celestine.

[Col. 1014D] **(Letter 11, to the bishops of Calabria and Apulia.)** “No priest may be ignorant of the canons, nor may anyone do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy order will remain with us if, at the whim of certain persons, and by a license granted to the people, the standard of the decretal constitutions is broken?

**Chapter 3: That the people must be taught, not followed.**

“The people must be taught, not followed. If they are ignorant, we must inform them what is permitted and what is not permitted; we must not give them our consent. Whoever attempts to try what is prohibited will learn that the censure of the apostolic see will certainly not be absent. What we do not correct solely by the authority of admonition, we must necessarily punish with a severity appropriate to the rules.

“We therefore wish this to be made known throughout all the Churches that lack their own rulers, so that no one may perhaps deceive himself with some hope or flattery.”

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Florentius and Dionysius.

Decretal letter of Pope Sixtus.

**(Letter 3 of Xystus III.)** “Sixtus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the Eastern bishops.

“We give thanks to your holiness because, in our tribulation and persecution, you sent to visit us, and because you desire to know that our case has a good outcome. You have entreated God in prayer to come to my aid in my tribulation, to help me, and to free me from my rivals who trouble and persecute me.

“Oh, how good is charity, which presents the absent as present through an image, and makes the present present to one another through love; which unites what is divided, orders what is confused, joins what is unequal, and strengthens what is imperfect. How rightly the outstanding preacher, namely the Apostle Paul, calls it ‘the bond of perfection’ (Colossians 3:14), since the other virtues indeed produce perfection, but charity binds them together in such a way that they can no longer be dissolved from the mind of the one who loves.

“By this virtue, brothers, I find that you are full of the grace of the Holy Spirit, since I perceive that you console me in my anxieties. Nor is it surprising, dearest ones, that my rivals persecute me, since our head, who is Christ, was formerly persecuted by the enemies of the holy Church of God and of its servants.

“Therefore the Truth itself says: ‘If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more the members of his household?’ (Matthew 10:25). It says again: ‘If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of this world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you’ (John 15:19).

“Although we know these things, brothers, and often preach them to others, and although we do not doubt that you know them perfectly, we must not turn either to the right or to the left because of the reproaches or accusations of those who lay snares, or because of the flatteries of those who praise us. Rather, amid the words of those who praise or reproach, we must always return to the mind.

“If the good that is said about us is not found there, it ought to produce great sadness. Again, if the evil that people say about us is not found there, we ought to leap into great joy. For what if everyone praises us while conscience accuses us? Or what if everyone accuses us while conscience proves us free?

“We have Paul saying: ‘This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience’ (2 Corinthians 1:12). Job also says: ‘Behold, my witness is in heaven’ (Job 16:19). If, then, we have a witness in heaven and a witness in the heart, let us allow fools outside to say what they wish.

“For what else do slanderers do except blow upon dust and stir up earth into their own eyes, so that the more slander they blow, the less they see any truth?

“Nevertheless, even they must be summoned and calmly admonished, and every effort must be made to satisfy them, remembering what the Truth says concerning the Jews: ‘lest we should scandalize them’ (Matthew 17:26).

“But if they do not wish to be satisfied by the truth, you have the consolation to look to in the Gospel. When it was said to the Lord, ‘Do you know that the Jews were scandalized when they heard this saying?’, he replied: ‘Leave them; they are blind leaders of the blind’ (Matthew 15:14).

“The Apostle Paul likewise admonishes us, saying: ‘If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people’ (Romans 12:18). In saying ‘live at peace with all people,’ he recognized that this is difficult; therefore he prefaced it with ‘if it is possible’ and added what can be done, saying ‘so far as it depends on you.’ For if we wish to preserve charity in our minds toward those who hate us, and if they do not have peace with us, we nevertheless undoubtedly have peace with them.”

“Therefore, since you commanded us to write to you how the dispute presently raised against me came about, or by whom it was raised, so that through your assistance it might be driven away and my case strengthened, know that I am accused and unjustly persecuted by a certain Bassus. When the Emperor Valentinian heard this, he ordered a synod to be convened by our authority; and when the council had been held, after satisfying everyone through a thorough investigation, although I could easily have escaped by other means, nevertheless, fleeing suspicion, I cleared myself before them all—liberating myself, that is, from suspicion and rivalry—but without thereby giving a rule or example to others who might be unwilling or might not voluntarily choose to do this, since it is written: ‘If anyone wishes to bring an accusation, let him first write that he will prove it’; and elsewhere: ‘Let no one receive accusations against a teacher’; and again: ‘If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or any cleric whatsoever, has been accused before a bishop by any person, whoever that person may be—whether a man of exalted rank or a person of any other condition—let the one who has undertaken this kind of blameworthy proceeding know that he must bring the charge with proofs capable of establishing it and with documents capable of demonstrating it. If anyone brings against such persons matters that cannot be proved, let him understand that he will suffer the loss of his reputation and be deported into exile under a severe excommunication.’ I set all these provisions aside, not to give an example to others, as was briefly stated above, but to free myself from the aforementioned disgrace and suspicion.

“The aforesaid Bassus was condemned by the synod just mentioned, but in such a way that the viaticum was not denied him on the last day, out of the Church’s humble compassion. The aforementioned Emperor Valentinian also condemned him in writing, together with his august mother Placidia, and united all his estates and possessions to the Catholic Church, thereby giving future men involved in such matters a precedent for acting in this way. Thus, not long afterward, the aforesaid Bassus died by divine will. Although his body was unworthy of burial, nevertheless, out of mercy, I buried him in his parents’ burial chamber.

“And although he had acted foolishly and shamelessly toward me, I acted mercifully toward him, remembering what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins’ (Matthew 6). And in the Lord’s Prayer itself, which our Savior taught his disciples to pray, we daily beseech the Lord, saying: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’; and many other things of the same kind.

“After these things had been done concerning me—against the will of all the bishops who were with us, because of my humility of mind, compelled by no judgment and subjected to no force, but choosing this voluntarily—I did these things, as has already been said, not to provide a model for others, but to purify myself. In the case of other bishops, however, an appropriate remedy must be applied to such wounds, lest an untimely readiness to cure should be unable to accomplish anything against the fatal plague of the head, while a destruction treated too slowly involves both the wounded and those who tend them in the guilt of an unlawful cure.

“Therefore we establish and decree that those who are not of good conduct, whose life is beyond defense, or whose faith, life, and liberty are unknown, may not accuse the Lord’s priests, lest base persons be admitted to accuse them. Likewise, those who are entangled in any crimes, or who are under suspicion, have no right to bring an accusation against their elders, because a suspicious and hostile voice customarily suppresses the truth.

“Foreign tribunals, while the apostolic authority is preserved in all respects, we prohibit by a general sanction. Therefore, if any bishop is accused of definite crimes, he must be heard by all the bishops of the province, because an accused person ought not to be heard anywhere other than in his own forum. If anyone finds the judge hostile to him, let him exercise his right of appeal. The appellant, however, must not be harmed by any affliction or insulted by detention in custody; rather, the appellant must be permitted to remedy an impaired case by means of appeal. It is also permitted to appeal in criminal cases, and the right of appeal must not be denied to one whom a sentence has condemned to punishment.

“Let the accused person state his case before his own judge; but if he is accused before a judge who is not his own, he may remain silent if he wishes. Let delays be granted to those who have been summoned, whenever they request them. If, therefore, anyone, being angry, rashly brings any accusation against anyone, the insult must not be treated as an accusation; rather, after a period has been allowed for reflection, let him acknowledge in writing that he will prove what he said in anger, so that, if perhaps he comes to his senses and does not wish to repeat or write down what he said in anger, he may not be held as guilty of a crime. Therefore, everyone who brings an accusation must write that he will prove it.

“Indeed, let a case always be conducted where the crime was committed; and whoever has not proved what he alleged must suffer the penalty that he himself imposed. It was also agreed that if an accused bishop appeals to the apostolic see, whatever the pontiff of that see decides must be established. Nevertheless, this rule must be observed absolutely in the case of priests, so that no one is bound by a sentence issued by a judge who is not his own.

“Every believer must also come to the aid of the ruins of the oppressed and the miserable, so that, by relieving another’s vengeance, they may be able to avert God’s vengeance from themselves. For one who drives adversity away from the afflicted makes a favorable offering to the Lord. Hence it is written: ‘A brother helping a brother will be exalted’ (Proverbs 18:19).

“For the Church of God must exist without stain or wrinkle; therefore it ought not to be trampled upon or defiled by certain persons, since it is written: ‘My dove is one, my perfect one’ (Song of Songs 6). Again, the Lord says to Moses: ‘There is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock’ (Exodus 33:21). What place is not the Lord’s, since all things are contained in him through whom they were created? Yet the place with him is, properly speaking, the unity of the holy Church, in which one stands upon the rock when the firmness of confession is humbly maintained.

“We admonish you also, and all our brothers who govern the Church of Christ redeemed by his blood, to restrain by every means available all those who are slipping into the precipice in which the brothers and the Lord’s shepherds fall through detraction and persecution in word and deed, and not to permit them to fall into the depths, since it is written: ‘The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God’ (James 1:20). Again it is said: ‘Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger’ (James 1:19).

“I do not doubt that, with God as author, you observe all these things. But since an occasion for admonition has arisen, I secretly join myself to your good desires and works, so that what you do without being admonished you may no longer do alone when an admonisher is added to you. Therefore, brothers, you and all the faithful ought to love one another and not slander or accuse one another.

“For it is written (Ecclesiasticus 27:18):

“‘Love your neighbor, and join yourself to him in faith. But if you uncover his secrets, do not pursue him afterward. For just as a person who destroys his friend is also one who destroys his neighbor’s friendship, and just as one who releases a bird from his hand, so you have abandoned your neighbor, and you will not seize him, nor pursue him, because he is far away. For he has escaped like a doe from a snare, because his soul has been wounded; you will no longer be able to bind him to you. And reconciliation belongs to the accursed. But to uncover a friend’s secrets is the despair of an unhappy soul. The one who signals with his eye contrives wicked things, and no one will cast him off. In the sight of your eyes he will sweeten his mouth, and he will marvel at your words; but finally he will pervert his mouth and give offense through your words. I have hated many things, but none as much as him; and the Lord will hate him. The one who throws a stone upward will have it fall upon his own head, and the wound of the deceitful will divide the wounds. The one who digs a pit will fall into it, and the one who sets a stone before his neighbor will stumble over it, and the one who places a snare for another will perish in it. The most wicked plan will roll back upon the one who devises it, and he will not recognize from where it has come upon him. Mockery and reproach are for the proud, and vengeance will lie in wait for him like a lion. Those who delight in the downfall of the righteous will perish by a snare; grief will consume them before they die. Anger and fury are both abominable, and the sinful man will be master of them’ (ibid. 28:1).

“‘The one who wishes to take revenge will find vengeance from the Lord, and he will surely preserve that person’s sins. Forgive your neighbor who has injured you, and then, when you pray, your sins will be forgiven. Does one person preserve anger against another and seek healing from God? Does he have no mercy on a person like himself and pray for his own sins before the Most High? Although he is flesh, he preserves anger and asks God for propitiation? Who will intercede for his offenses? Remember the last things, and cease from enmity. For decay and death threaten in his commandments. Remember the fear of God, and do not be angry with your neighbor. Remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook your neighbor’s ignorance. Keep away from strife, and you will lessen sins. For an angry person kindles strife, and a sinful man will disturb friends and bring enmity among those who are at peace.

“‘As the wood is, so the fire blazes; and as a person’s strength is, so will his anger be; and according to his substance he will exalt his anger. Hastened conflict kindles fire, and hastened quarrelling pours out blood, and a tongue that bears witness brings death. If you blow upon a spark, it will blaze like a fire; but if you spit upon it, it will be extinguished—and both proceed from the mouth. The whisperer and the double-tongued are accursed, for they have disturbed many who were at peace. The third tongue has stirred up many and scattered them from nation to nation. It has destroyed the fortified cities of the rich and dug up the houses of the great. It has overthrown the strength of peoples and dissolved strong nations. The third tongue has driven away women from their husbands and deprived them of their labors. Whoever watches it will have no rest, nor will he dwell in peace. The blow of a whip produces a bruise, but the blow of the tongue crushes bones. Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not so many as those who have perished through their own tongue. Blessed is the one who is protected from an evil tongue, who has not passed through its anger, who has not drawn its yoke, and who has not been bound by its bonds. For its yoke is an iron yoke, and its bond is a bronze bond. Its death is a most evil death, and the underworld is preferable and more useful than it. Its persistence will not endure, but it will possess the ways of the unjust; and in its flame it will not burn the righteous. Those who abandon God will fall into it; it will blaze against them and not be extinguished, and it will be sent against them like a lion and injure them like a leopard.

“‘Fence your ears with thorns, and do not hear an evil tongue; make doors for your mouth and bolts for your ears. Melt your gold and your silver, and make a scale for your words, and straight bridles for your mouth. Take care lest you slip with your tongue and fall in the sight of enemies lying in wait for you, and lest your fall be incurable unto death.’”

Let everyone beware of these things, restraining their tongues from evil, so that their lips may not speak deceit.

“Finally, dearest ones, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the world-governors of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and stand perfect in all things. Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth, clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

“These things that we have written to you, brothers, we wish to be made known generally to everyone, so that what concerns the others may become known to all. May almighty God protect you and our other brothers dwelling everywhere until the end—Jesus Christ our Lord, who deigned to redeem the whole world and who is blessed forever. Amen.

“Given on the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Valentinian and Florentius.”

### Also from the chapters written above

**Chapter 1.** “The holy Roman synod said:

“These are the provisions that, from now on, because of the snares of wicked men who ceaselessly rage against the Church and against ecclesiastical men, we wish to be preserved most firmly forever. If a bishop has been accused by those accusers who are to be admitted, after he has first been charitably admonished by them that he ought to correct and amend the matter itself, and he has refused to do so, then—and not earlier—his case is to be canonically referred to the highest primates.
