They must canonically summon a council at a suitable place within that province, at the time fixed by the canons of Nicaea, so that he may be heard there by all the bishops of the same province.

“He himself, having been canonically summoned, must be present, unless illness or some other grave necessity prevents him, because no one may be accused beyond the boundaries of the province before a hearing has been sought. For if he has been stripped of his possessions, or—God forbid, since this ought to be alien to all the faithful—has been expelled from his own see, or has been separated from his flock by some form of detention, then he may neither be summoned nor judged canonically until he has been restored to his former honor and all that had been taken from him through the snares of his enemies has been restored to him—unless, because of his necessity, he freely chooses to come, though he is not thereby to be judged.

“Let no one compel him to answer at all before everything that he had lost through the accusations of his enemies has been completely and honorably restored to his authority, the bishop has first been returned to his former status, and he has freely and securely arranged his affairs. Only then, canonically summoned at the appointed time, let him come to the synod in a legitimate and canonical manner and, if it seems just, answer the propositions of his accusers.

“For it must be provided above all that he not be compelled to answer before all these things have taken place, because contention must always be avoided. For no Christian can rightly regard it as permissible to deprive a bishop of his episcopate before the outcome of his case has become clear.”

Also from the same chapters (**chapter 14**):

“No metropolitan bishop may hear the cases of any persons without the insistence of all the other bishops of his province, because the proceedings will be invalid; indeed, they will even have to account in synod for what they have done. Nor may any other bishop hear the cases of his priests without the presence of his clergy, because the bishop’s sentence will be invalid unless it is confirmed by the presence of the clergy.”

### From a letter of Pope Gelasius to the Emperor Anastasius concerning Acacius, who was properly condemned in the Council of Chalcedon by the apostolic see

[Col. 1021A]

**Letter 11, to the bishops of Dardania.** “Let us certainly not remain silent about what the whole Church throughout the world knows: that the see of the blessed Apostle Peter has the right to loose those bound by the judgments of any bishops whatsoever, since it has the authority to judge concerning the whole Church; nor is anyone permitted to judge its judgment, if the canons have wished appeals from any part of the world to be made to it, while no one is permitted to appeal from it. Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see, as has often been said, according to the custom of our ancestors, has had the power, even without a preceding synod, both to release those whom a synod had unjustly condemned and to condemn, without any synod existing, those whom it was proper to condemn.”

And shortly afterward, in the same letter:

“Indeed, the synod of the East had condemned Athanasius, of blessed memory; yet the apostolic see, having received him and not consented to the condemnation of the Greeks, absolved him. Likewise, a synod of Catholic bishops had certainly condemned John of Constantinople, also of blessed memory; but the apostolic see, in the same way, because it did not consent, absolved him by itself alone. It likewise absolved the holy pontiff Flavian, condemned by the assembly of the Greeks, in the same manner, because the apostolic see alone did not consent; and by its own authority it condemned Dioscorus, the bishop of the second see, who had been accepted there, removed the impious synod by refusing to consent to it, and alone decreed that the synod of Chalcedon should be held for the sake of the truth. Therefore, since in that case alone it had the right to absolve those whom synodal decrees had struck down, it is likewise known to have condemned many in this same matter even without a synod.”

Also on the same matter:

“After five hundred years, they wish to overturn the constitutions of Christ, although the law of men cannot be broken after thirty years: that the holy Athanasius was not condemned by the synod of the East because this see did not consent; likewise the holy John of Constantinople and the holy Flavian. Therefore, if those condemned by a synod are [not] condemned when that see alone does not consent, then whoever is condemned when that same see alone condemns is condemned.”

### Saint Gregory says in his letter to the patrician Theoctista

[Col. 1021D]

**Book 9, letter 39, toward the end.** “If there are some who say that, when someone has been compelled by necessity, if he has been anathematized, or has presumed to do what is forbidden under an anathema, he is not held by the bond of the anathema, they themselves testify that they are not Christians, because they think that by empty efforts they can loosen the bonds of the holy Church; and consequently they consider the absolution that the holy Church grants to the faithful to be real while they do not consider its bindings effective.

“It is not necessary to argue with them at length, because they must be utterly despised and anathematized; and from the very point at which they think they deceive the truth, they are truly bound in their sins. Therefore, if there are some who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach these things or silently hold them within themselves, without any doubt we anathematize them—I and all the Catholic bishops and the whole Church—because they think and speak contrary to the truth.”

### If any priest acts against these prohibitions, he must be removed from his office  
**Leo, to the bishops established throughout the provinces**

**Letter 1.** “Accordingly, our admonition declares that if any of the brothers attempts to act against these statutes and dares to do what has been forbidden, let him know that he must be removed from his office, and that he will not share in our communion, since he was unwilling to be a companion in discipline.

“Moreover, lest anything be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions—both those of Innocent of blessed memory and those of all our predecessors—which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be so carefully observed by your devotion that anyone who violates them may know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him.”

### From the epitome of the venerable Pope Nicholas, predecessor of the present Pope Adrian, addressed to Michael, Emperor of the Greeks

**Letter 8.** “As for the decretals established by the holy pontiffs of the first see, the Roman Church, by whose authority and sanction all synods and holy councils are strengthened and receive their stability: why do you say that you neither possess nor observe them, except because they contradict your arrangement and resist your leaping suddenly from the lay state to the summit of the patriarchate, contrary to the apostolic injunction: ‘Do not lay hands quickly upon anyone’ (1 Timothy 5:21)? If you do not possess them, you must be accused of neglect and negligence; if you possess them and do not observe them, you must be corrected and rebuked for presumption.

“The sanctions of the holy Council of Chalcedon should also be recalled; they decree as follows (Canon 9): ‘If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or against another, let him be judged by the synod of the province. But if a bishop or cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan of that province, let him petition the primate of the diocese or the see of the royal city of Constantinople.’

“In this provision the following rule must be observed: if a cleric or bishop has a complaint against a metropolitan and is pressed by such necessity, or if he cannot endure the matter as a grave burden, wherever he may be, let him petition the primate of the diocese. But if one of them is established near Constantinople and wishes to be content with the judgment of that bishop alone, let him petition that royal city.

“For when the holy synod said, ‘Let him petition the primate of the diocese,’ it laid down a precept and established a rule. But when it added, with a disjunctive conjunction, ‘or the see of the royal city of Constantinople,’ it is plainly evident that it granted this second option by way of permission. Therefore, at least now, do you not see that one must proceed toward greater authorities? And the more the complaint is directed toward a judgment of greater authority, the more one must seek a higher summit, until one gradually reaches that see by whose decision the matter is either changed for the better when the merits of the case require it, or reserved without question to the judgment of God alone.

“By the primate of the diocese, however, the holy synod means no one whatsoever except the vicar of the chief Apostle. For he is the primate who is both first and supreme; these matters, if the occasion requires, we shall demonstrate individually in what follows.

“Let no one be disturbed because ‘of the diocese’ is expressed in the singular number. It must be understood that to say ‘the primate of the diocese’ has the same force as if he had said ‘of the dioceses.’ The holy Scriptures are full of this form of expression. Thus it is written: ‘A fountain went up from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth’ (Genesis 2:6). The text does not say, ‘one fountain went up from the earth,’ but says, ‘a fountain went up from the earth,’ using the singular in place of the plural, so that we understand many fountains watering their own places or regions throughout the whole earth. In the same way ‘soldier’ is said while many are understood; and ‘locust’ and ‘frog’ are said concerning the plagues with which the Egyptians were struck, although the number of locusts and frogs was innumerable. So here also he used ‘diocese’ in the singular, but wished it to be understood in the plural because of the unity of peace and faith.”

The same author also says:

“Having taken counsel with blessed Gelasius, bishop of our see, we shall say (Gelasius, Letter 6, to the bishops throughout Lucania and Bruttium): ‘We are constrained by the necessary ordering of affairs and bound by the governance of the apostolic see to weigh the decrees of the ancient canons and measure the instructions of earlier bishops and our predecessors in such a way that, after careful consideration, we moderate as far as possible whatever the necessity of the present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the churches.

“‘And since, concerning the persons of Ignatius and Photius, we judge nothing more prudent, mild, or beneficial than that both should come to Rome for a renewed examination, we greatly desire this and beneficially admonish you to announce it. But we grant this by way of indulgence; we do not give anyone permission to carry it out according to his own will.

“‘For since, according to the canons, where there is greater authority the judgment of inferiors must be deferred—whether for dissolving or for confirming—it is plainly evident that no one may review the judgment of the apostolic see, whose authority has no greater authority above it; nor is anyone permitted to judge its judgment. Since the canons have wished appeals from every part of the world to be made to it, no one is permitted to appeal from it.

“‘In accordance with this, the most holy bishops Boniface and Gelasius, not by their own inventions but because they knew the custom of the Roman Church, speak as follows. Boniface, writing to Rufus and the bishops established throughout Thessaly and the other provinces, says: “No one has ever boldly raised hostile hands against the apostolic dignity, whose judgment it is not permitted to review. No one has rebelled in this matter except one who wished to be judged concerning himself.”’”

“Gelasius, however, in a memorandum given to the master Faustus, who was serving as envoy at Constantinople, says (after Letter 8): ‘They bring the canons against us, although they do not know what they are saying. Yet by this very act they reveal themselves to be acting against them, because they refuse to obey the first see when it gives sound and upright counsel. The canons themselves are the ones that wished appeals from the whole Church to be brought to the examination of this see, while they decreed that no appeal whatsoever should be made from it. Thus they ordained that it should judge the whole Church, that it should submit to the judgment of no one, and that no one should ever judge its judgment; they established that its sentence ought not to be dissolved, since they commanded that its decrees should instead be followed.’

“Therefore, what we have said concerning the non-review of the Roman bishop’s judgment is confirmed, since not even custom requires such a review. We do not deny that the sentence of that see can be changed for the better, when something has been obtained from it by fraud, or when it has decided, for reasons of age, time, or grave necessities, to arrange some matter by way of dispensation. For we read that the distinguished Apostle Paul also acted dispensationally in certain matters which he is known afterward to have rejected.

“This applies when that Church—namely, the Roman Church—has chosen to act with the most discerning consideration, not when it has refused to reconsider things that have been rightly defined. Moreover, lest you say that we ordered Ignatius and Photius to come to Rome contrary to the law of the Church, know that in this we followed the example of the ancient father and our predecessor Julius. According to what is found in his letter, he is known to have given this instruction to those who had assembled at Antioch; and the historian Theodoret demonstrates the same thing in these words (Book 2, chapter 4):

“‘Eusebius and his associates sent the accusations made against Athanasius to Julius, the Roman pontiff. Following the law of the Church, he also ordered them to come to Rome and regularly summoned the venerable man to judgment; and he, immediately accepting the summons, came.’

“If you say in response that Julius summoned him, but that they themselves refused to come, continue reading what follows, and you will see whether that refusal was counted to them as praise or blame. The same historian adds:

“‘The bearers of the accusations did not travel to Rome, knowing that their lie could easily be exposed.’

“Therefore, do not say that we ordered the aforesaid men to come to Rome contrary to the law of the Church, since, as you have just heard from the historian, blessed Julius ordered both the accused and the accusers to come to Rome and summoned the venerable Athanasius to judgment. He, having a good conscience, came without resistance; but those who had a bad one refused, knowing, as it is written there, that their lie could easily be exposed.”

The same author also says:

“‘We wish and decree that such a pontiff receive what is worthy of his deeds, so that priestly dignity may not be utterly degraded, nor the episcopal crown so easily bent down to the ground. Thus, I say, we wish and decree that this man—or indeed any pontiff—be subjected to a just sentence, but not judged by any secular persons, not expelled tyrannically, not deprived of his own church before a hearing, and that he receive the decision of a correct judgment not from inferiors but from a person of greater authority.

“‘Thus, finally, we wish and decree that the cases of this man—or rather of all priests—be examined and their faults punished in such a way that we do not overstep the limits established by our fathers, trample upon the sacred canons, or violate in any way the decretal constitutions of the apostolic see, by which the whole Church is supported and protected.

“‘At the end, we wish and decree that a pontiff, whatever his character, be judged in such a way that the rights of the church over which he presides are violated by no rashness and no presumption. For no right of the Church can be preserved with due dignity if its bishop is hindered by anyone, at any time, or in any manner, and expelled so easily at anyone’s pleasure.

“‘Since this is so, we cannot meanwhile fail to count our brother Ignatius, whatever his condition, among the holiest and most blessed patriarchs. Although among you he has been wearied by so many reproaches and so many persecutions, nevertheless by us he is believed and venerated only as he was regarded by my predecessors. For in none of our examinations has he been found guilty of any crime, nor has he been found liable by any special judgment of ours. Consequently, he cannot be condemned by any sentence of ours, separated from the communion and fellowship of our Church, or addressed by any terms except honorable ones.’”

The same author also says:

“‘The judgment of superiors must always be feared by inferiors, lest, if they do not obey him, even though they may perhaps be unjustly bound by him, they deserve, because of another fault—that is, disobedience—the sentence of their own binding. Therefore one must dread condemning superiors indiscriminately. Those who possess lesser authority must carefully beware of being condemned and must not transgress the sentence of their superiors.

“‘Otherwise, even if they have sometimes been unjustly condemned, from that very rash transgression there will undoubtedly follow both the guilt that perhaps had not yet been committed and the punishment that the guilt had not yet deserved. For the forbidden tree itself contained nothing deadly; but the one who ate from it disobediently brought death upon himself and his descendants—not because the tree was evil, since God made everything he made good, but because transgression is evil, and condemnation rightly arose through it for the one unwilling to submit.’”

The same author also says:

“‘As we are taught by the apostolic canons, he may rightly be released by the one who separated him, or certainly absolved by the first see.’”

“Here it is shown most clearly that if anyone presumes to speak against the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, he is rightly accused of rashness.”

I have extracted these matters briefly, interweaving them here and there according to the nature of the subject, mixing them together indiscriminately, sometimes in reversed order and sometimes in arranged order, and also incorporating them gradually in a connected fashion. More fully, preserving a direct sequence, I collected them in another little book from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, culling a few small extracts from many sources.

## VI. HINCMAR OF LAON’S MEMORANDUM, PRESENTED TO THE BISHOPS AND THROUGH THEM TO THE KING

[Col. 1025]

Hincmar, bishop of Laon, presented this memorandum at Pîtres on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the first indiction, to the bishops of the province of Rheims: Hincmar [Note: [Col. 1025D] of Rheims], Odo [Note: [Col. 1025D] of Beauvais]; of the province of Rouen: Wenilo [Note: [Col. 1025D] of Rouen], Archambert [Note: [Col. 1025D] of Bayeux], Sigenand [Note: [Col. 1025D] of Coutances]; of the province of Sens: Aeneas [Note: [Col. 1026D] of Paris], Fulcric [Note: [Col. 1026D] of Troyes], Abbo [Note: [Col. 1026D] of Nevers]; of the province of Bordeaux: Engenold [Note: [Col. 1026D] of Poitiers], Helias [Note: [Col. 1026D] of Angoulême].

[Col. 1025C]

“I know that it is not hidden from you, lord fathers, brothers, and bishops worthy of God, that the property of the bishopric of the Church of Laon entrusted to me—or rather, everything I possessed in this kingdom, except the principal church, the bishop’s house, and the cloister—was first placed under a ban; so that no support or service whatsoever is supplied to me by anyone from the aforesaid property and resources.

“For when I had been ordered to appear within a short number of days, without any bishop of my province knowing of it, I did not attend the secular court, and I did not send an *exonia*—that is, a person who would establish that I could not come there; nor did I appoint an advocate in the secular court on my own behalf—that is, in my own case. Nevertheless, I sent an envoy of my excuse to our lord the king.

“And you know that the sacred laws have decreed that, for any civil or criminal case, no judge may summon, bring, or present an unwilling bishop before a public court (African Code, canon 15). And whoever among the bishops or the other clerical persons of the Church, for a criminal or civil case, abandons ecclesiastical judgment and proceeds to the public courts, wishing to be cleared there of a criminal charge, shall lose his position, even if a sentence has been issued in his favor; but in a civil case, if he prefers to retain his position, he shall lose what he has won.

“But if a cleric or any other person has a dispute against a bishop for any reason, the case must be judged before the metropolitan or the primate of the province, according to the sacred rules. And if the bishop contradicts anything that has been judged, the case must be referred to the most blessed pontiff of the Roman see, and he must bring the case to an end according to the canons and laws.”

After I had come with my metropolitan to this place, where I attended your assembly, pleasing to God, intending to seek your counsel and agreement, and through your reverence the clemency of our lord the king, as to what I ought to do and how I might live, having been stripped of ecclesiastical property and services without episcopal judgment, it was announced to me—not by unknown or uncertain persons—that, on the part of our lord the king, I should make acknowledgment to him and humbly make satisfaction to him. I also heard that the men on whose account his lordship’s anger had been aroused against me had come here in order to bring complaint against me.

Therefore, since I bind myself to regular judgment, and since a sentence pronounced without being written down, according to inviolable definitions, does not even deserve to bear the name of a sentence [or: “not even the name of a sentence”] (Gregory, Book II, Letter 54, indiction 6), I reply in writing with humble supplication:

If I am canonically restored to possession of the things of which I have been stripped, contrary to the sacred canons, the decrees of the pontiffs of the holy Roman see, and the laws by which the holy Church is governed together with the sacred regulations, and if he can show me that I have irrationally offended him in these matters, I will voluntarily acknowledge it and humbly make satisfaction to him, as I ought to do to my lord, superior, and king. Thereafter, having lawfully made use of what belongs to me, as the regulations command, and having been regularly summoned by the canons to a synod in my province, I will canonically give an account before my judges of whatever charges are brought against me there, and I will submit to canonical judgment.

Otherwise, according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the holy Roman see, in order that the memory of blessed Peter the apostle may be honored, I appeal to the apostolic see, by my own voice and in writing, so that no violence may be inflicted upon me by anyone. I therefore request that this profession and appeal of mine be delivered to our most Christian lord King Charles by the primate of my province, to whom I present it; and I ask you, together with him, to petition the clemency of that same lord of ours, so that, for the love of God, and of holy Mary, and of the holy apostles, and of all the saints together, he may preserve the ecclesiastical laws for me—he who, by royal piety, is admonished to preserve the law for all and to show mercy.

## VII. HINCMAR OF LAON’S SATISFACTION

Words of satisfaction by Hincmar, bishop of Laon, sent to Lord King Charles through Bishop Odo.

[Col. 1027]

My lord, I disturbed your mind, although there was no need for me to do so, and not through disloyalty, nor, so far as I was able to understand the intention of my mind, to your dishonor; but perhaps I offended you through my carelessness. And in proportion as I had regarded you as kind, so afterward I felt that you were offended. Therefore I beg your favor: may your mind be reconciled to me, and may I again experience your kindness toward me.

## VIII. LETTER OF HINCMAR OF LAON TO HINCMAR OF RHEIMS

He responds to Hincmar’s letter of fifty-five chapters and to other matters written or done against him.

[Col. 1027]

To the most reverend lord Father Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, Hincmar, the least of the bishops of the Church of Laon, fullness of every happiness in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Concerning what I instructed you by word through Hitto, provost of the church entrusted to me, and to which you replied to me in writing—that Hermund, a man of the Northman, had told me about property that I was to transfer—he did not tell me, but rather certain men of mine, and not unknown persons.

You also wrote that the same Hitto had said that I should be permitted to dispose of and govern the property of the church as I had represented. I do not wish to dispose of or govern it otherwise, nor to have any authority over it beyond the sanction of canonical institution; namely, as the Council of Antioch, which you accept fully and abundantly, decrees, saying (canon 25):

“The bishop shall have authority over ecclesiastical property, for its distribution among all who are in need, with the greatest reverence and fear of God.”

Likewise, in the same council it is established (canon 24):

“Let what belongs to the Church be preserved with every care and a good conscience, and with the faith that is in God, when all things are considered and judged; and let those things which are to be distributed be distributed according to the judgment and authority of the pontiff, to whom the people and the souls gathered within the Church have been entrusted.”

And the canons of the apostles conclude these provisions as follows (canon 41):

“We command that the bishop have the church’s property in his power.”

For if human souls, which are precious, have been entrusted to him, much more ought he to take care of money, so that everything may be distributed to the needy through priests and deacons under his authority and may be administered with fear and every care.

I also instructed you through the aforesaid man—who perhaps forgot this as well—that at the time when our lord the king withdrew from this kingdom for his own necessity, he entrusted to me the acceptance of more men than the size of my place could support, promising then that he would give me the means by which I could maintain them thereafter. At present I have no means to provide them with what is sufficient, indeed not even with the necessities of subsistence, or to prepare for myself what is necessary to perform his services. Unless I am permitted to arrange how I may live and from what means I may undertake such frequent journeys, I cannot render him temporal service, nor do I have the means to preserve the place over which, unworthy as I am, I preside.

Moreover, property that used to provide stipends both for me and for my clergy, and also for my predecessor, is being taken away from me and granted by royal authority to a man who was unable to obtain even a single mansus from my predecessor out of that bishopric. In addition, property that supplied lights for the church is being given to one whom for three years I was unable to persuade to come to me; he abandoned what he ought also to have worked on in the construction of the church and destroyed the same property that he holds, together with the church contained within it.

Other property is likewise being given to a man who, behold, has wandered here and there for eleven years at his own pleasure and has not deigned to come to me even once. He also provided no support for his son, who ought to have served me on his behalf; consequently, since I had nothing with which to give him another benefice, the son withdrew from me.

Thus men who confer no benefit upon me or upon my church, but rather bring harm, are, as the prophet says, “to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to demolish” (Jer. 1:10), being built up and planted by an external power over ecclesiastical administration.

As for what you wrote to me concerning the property taken from me—that the king had replied to you that he thought what he had already said to me at the palace of Attigny, before the bishops, with a kindly disposition and calm words, ought to be sufficient for me: namely, that it had come to his attention that I had presumed to claim more property than was due to the church entrusted to me, concerning which I had now written, because Flothar, his envoy, had delivered it to the Northman; and more than was contained in the royal charter by which he restored to me property long before taken from the Church of Laon, or granted it in response to my petition—just as was made entirely clear concerning those things which I had illegally and irregularly usurped against reason and justice, which were not contained in the charter and which his man had lawfully and reasonably recovered according to the law.

For that reason, he said, I was to receive immediately those properties—namely, the estate of Pauliac—which had long before been taken from the Church of Laon, while I was not to receive the other properties concerning which a complaint had reached him, but was merely to await the matter until I brought the charter, and his envoy and yours went into that district and investigated the truth of the matter; and whatever was found among those properties to belong justly and reasonably to the Church of Laon, he would not merely refrain from contesting, but would willingly grant to that Church. You wrote that I had contradicted none of this.

I shall begin my reply at the end. I contradicted none of these things because I heard nothing of them in this form. Indeed, when the receipt of that estate was being discussed, the king said that I had taken other things, as the Northman claimed, which were not contained in my charter. I replied that I had done nothing of the kind, except that what I had claimed belonged to that same estate or was named in my charter. If it pleased him, he could see the charter itself. He replied that it would be good for him to see it.

After this, one matter after another was introduced, until he came to the point of saying that he would grant me the same estate and everything contained in my charter, except for the five mansi held by Ansgar, his man. Concerning those, he wanted me—these were his very words—to leave them as they stood until, through his envoys together with your envoy and mine, he investigated the truth of the matter; and if he could find that they justly belonged to the estate of Pauliac, he would restore them to me.

But as long as I afterward remained at Attigny, he did not ask me for the charter, until Flothar reassigned those same properties to the Northman’s man. Later, at Attigny, with you present, the king saw the charter when my envoy Berthar brought it through the hands of Archbishop Harduic. You either saw the same places distinctly set out in that charter or heard them read again by Ansigis. Flothar, as I have said, had delivered them to the Northman’s man. The king told the same Berthar, as Berthar reported to me, that he had been misinformed and did not wish to alienate those properties from the Church of Laon; and Berthar kissed his foot. While you were briefly conferring with the king, the restoration was delayed.

As for what you wrote to me—“as was made entirely clear, concerning those things which you usurped illegally and irregularly against reason and justice”—the same charter states that the royal authority would restore the estate of Pauliac to me in its entirety, and it explains how the mansi justly and reasonably belong to that same estate of Pauliac. I have had certainty concerning the matter for sixty years and more. Therefore I possessed them legally and regularly, together with the other mansi belonging to Pauliac, for six months, until Ansgar obtained them by royal power, without my advocate being summoned to the mall, as the public laws require, to be formally notified concerning those properties.

Indeed, when a ban was sought at the palace concerning them from one of my men—who had no official responsibility there except that, at my command, he had recalled them to the authority of Saint Mary, as my other men had recalled the others, and because he had entered that mansus and was summoned to redeem the ban—my advocate appeared on behalf of these properties and demanded that the law be observed for him. He declared that the properties belonged to the authority of Saint Mary, the Church of Laon, that he was the advocate for them, and that he was willing to give an account concerning them according to the law.

He was immediately expelled, and with every kind of violence they compelled another man of mine, who had no connection with the matter, to redeem the ban on these properties. After the ban had been redeemed, they threatened that they would condemn him to death for disloyalty to the king unless he immediately gave such pledges, and such guarantors for the pledges, that on the appointed day he would reassign the same properties to the king’s envoy as though restoring possession. They compelled him to do this.

If this coercion can rightly be called a legal recovery, then these properties were recovered according to that law.

[Col. 1031B]

As for what you wrote to me in these words—“Concerning the benefices of your men about which you wrote, he replied that your men had appealed to him, claiming that you had unjustly and unreasonably taken away from them their benefices, which they had held under your predecessors and under you. Therefore, according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the holy Roman see promulgated from those sacred canons, you sought chosen judges from me, and by the judgment of these and of other God-fearing men it was decreed concerning certain of them that they should recover their benefices, which they had irrationally lost. The case of some others, however, because of certain intervening matters, remained undecided and was postponed for another hearing; and before the decision, without any necessity or reason, you fled contrary to the sacred canons and refused to await regular judgment”—I reply that the truth of the matter is as follows.

One day, when we should already have returned home, the king began asking you which of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims would be present on the following day to hear the case concerning these men. I said, however, that I did not have with me the clergy or laymen who had taken part in the case and through whom I could give an account of it. During the preceding days, all my men had been detained at the palace by royal summons; I alone had gone to Harduic’s residences with one of his clerks and three laymen.

The king also asked whom I could have there. I replied: Berthar the cleric and one layman who had taken part in the cases of some of these men. He ordered me to have them. Thus, Actard, Rainelm, and John having been designated, I accepted them as examiners in the manner stated above, lest I appear to wish to delay the case and deceitfully conceal the truth by delay.

We arrived on the following day. The first to bring a complaint was the man called Ragenard. Beginning from the outset, I gave the following account concerning him: when our lord the king had sent me to Gothia on his mission, Ragenard returned without my permission. Furthermore, three years had already passed since I had seen him; he had abandoned most of the work he ought to have performed from his benefice in the Church of Laon; and he had never come to any court proceedings convened because of my needs, to which my other men had come. He had never been willing to render justice concerning his own men, the villagers, who were bringing complaints against him.

More recently, when all men summoned for military service had been called out in the king’s service and I had come with my other men to Mouzon, not far from where his residence lay, he had neither come to me nor sent any envoy to explain his inability or any other excuse. Moreover, his son, whom he had entrusted to me, had been ordered by me to hold my residences with my other men from that district, but had sent him to hold the residences of Bishop Rothadus. When I passed through that estate, the son did not even deign to come into my presence.

I spoke with some of my men, from whom I also heard that this man belonged to Bishop Rothadus, as these indications plainly show. When I returned from that expedition and waited a long time, he did not come to me. Then a complaint reached me concerning Ragenard, that his benefice had been destroyed. I sent to find out whether this was true, and my envoy discovered that the demesne mansus and the church itself had been completely destroyed, the forest sold, and many other things besides.

The laymen present judged that it should be proved by oath on my part that he had left the king’s service without my permission and that he should lose that benefice—while they tithe mint, dill, and cumin, leave aside the weightier matters of the law, strain out the gnat, and swallow the camel—although the canons decree that the case should be concluded by episcopal judges.

Within the complete collection of the Capitularies of the most glorious emperors, our lords Charles and Louis, it is likewise established:

“Whatever has been established by individual kings concerning the most holy churches, or whatever each individual bishop has obtained concerning ecclesiastical matters, shall be preserved under penalty of perpetual and enduring sacrilege. Clerics, moreover, shall be reserved not for secular judges but for episcopal hearing. For it is not lawful that those who belong to God should be subjected to secular judgment.”

Likewise, the following has been taken from the sacred regulations in the same collection:

“Concerning men dedicated to God, or ecclesiastical property, no authority to dispose of anything is ever recorded as having been granted to laymen, even religious ones.”

Thus it was a matter for the superior judgment to destroy things consecrated to God and not to censure the failure to render the services owed to the church to which the things consecrated to God belonged, rather than to abandon that temporal service. But animal men do not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2), whereas spiritual men judge all things, as the spiritual man Pope Stephen, martyr, testifies (Letter 11). Whatever is unjustly done concerning things consecrated to God and concerning bishops will be reckoned as sacrilege.”

After him Grivo brought a complaint, and I replied that I did not have there the men who knew with me the matters I was about to relate. Nevertheless, at the king’s command I began to recount them.

I explained that I had informed him and Berald, who was present—as our lord the king knew—that they were to be sent to Rome and were to carry letters to the apostolic lord concerning my detention. One day Grivo came to me, and I verbally entrusted him with this mission. I wished to give him letters, but he withdrew his hand and said that he would not accept the letters until his companion arrived. I then told him that on the following Friday, which was approaching in that same week, he should come with his companion, namely Berald.

After hearing this, he wished to prostrate himself at my feet. I prevented him from doing so, and he then said that he had heard that I was angry with him, and that before beginning such a journey he needed to clear himself by oath; thereafter he would willingly do whatever I commanded. I replied that I did not conceal the fact that I had been moved against him, because I had heard from certain people that he had said he was not being asked to go to Rome for any other reason than to obtain “Scats” for me [the reading is uncertain]. I was surprised that he would say this, since I had freely given him whatever benefice he possessed, without any payment.

For, as you know, he left my predecessor Pardulus and commended himself to you. At the time of my ordination, you commended him to me. After he had served me for some time, his father died, and I gave him the benefice his father had possessed, together with twelve additional mansi.

When I disclosed these matters to him, he denied that he had ever said or thought such a thing and begged permission to clear himself by oath. I replied that from then on I would believe nothing contrary to him on this matter and would hold no further anger against him. If, by God’s favor, he went away and returned in good health, I would regard his service as deserving of reward and would permit him, as far as I could, to rest from those journeys.

After this I continued by saying that I had heard that he was destroying the forest his father had cultivated. I strictly warned him to take care that, if this had happened, it should not happen again. He replied that what I had heard was false; but while he was with me at the royal palace at Aachen—for our lord the king had told me that Ansigis was going to Rome as his envoy—some of his neighbors had devastated part of that forest. He said that he would make them redeem what they had done, and he departed after I had ordered him, as I have said, to return on the Friday of that same week.

But as soon as he had reached home, he had all his neighbors notified that whoever wished to take anything from that forest should take it before the appointed day, because he himself would no longer hold that benefice. They all came, both from that county and from the other surrounding regions, and ravaged the same forest. Grivo himself was present; he sold portions to some villagers and gave portions away to others. I heard of these things—as one would expect, since the matter had become so widely known—but endured them until the court session that I had appointed for him.

When he failed to come and did not send me an envoy to explain his absence, I finally sent to discover whether the reports were true. My envoys found the same forest being destroyed by countless villagers, with half-cut oaks left behind to be destroyed later, lying thickly across the surrounding fields because they could not be carried to the houses of those destroying them. I therefore ordered that everyone be forbidden, in my name, to destroy it any further.

I sent my envoys to recover what had remained in the fields. Grivo himself came armed with his relatives and resisted this being done. But when more of my men arrived, whom he could not withstand, he made compensation by pledges for the wrong he had committed. He sent word that he wished to come to me to obtain my favor and undergo whatever punishment I might impose upon him.

When my men who were petitioning on his behalf—Gerard, Hadoard, and Colsan—asked me about this, I replied that he should come on the following day and that, if this was truly his desire, I would willingly agree. He sent one of his relatives, named Magenfrid, to me for this very purpose. I gave him the same reply. Magenfrid came as though he intended to carry out the matter to the place where I was, called Montigny; but when I offered him precisely this, he departed, saying that he did not wish to have my land or to remain my man, and that he would never again travel on account of that benefice—not to Rome, nor even as far as the distance remaining to his own residence.

I added that he had utterly destroyed that benefice, as he had in fact done and as was evident, and that the dependents had been harassed in many ways contrary to law.

Before the king he denied that he had destroyed the forest, denied that his benefice had been destroyed, and denied that he had departed from me in this way. He said instead that he had been unable to come before me to give any account.

I did not have with me the men I have mentioned, nor the others who were with me at that time and who likewise knew these things, because during those days I had remained alone at the residences of Archbishop Harduic on account of the case described above.

Then our lord the king said that, if Grivo had cultivated that forest, as he claimed, which his father had begun to cultivate, and had given it to his friends not for destruction but with a measuring implement, or if he had taken from it in measured fashion for his own needs, he ought not to have lost that benefice on this account.

No one could deny this if he had acted in that way. But he acted as I have said, although, as I stated above, he denied it before the king. The king said that he was not offering this as a judgment, although what he said could, justly and reasonably, be said and judged if the man had not acted otherwise.

I persisted that I had enough of my own men there who could verify the truth of what I was saying. But when our lord the king saw that the case could not be concluded there, he postponed it until the Wednesday of the following week, when he would return from Senlis. The day on which these matters occurred was a Sunday. He ordered me to bring with me the men of mine who knew the facts, so that the case could then be concluded. I did so and appeared on the appointed day, but I found neither Actard nor Rainelm nor John, the bishops whom you had assigned to me as examiners; unless I thought their judgment had to be challenged and appealed to a synod, they could have served as judges. Without them the case could not be concluded.

Therefore, when you say that before the decision I fled contrary to the sacred canons, without any necessity or reason, and refused to await regular judgment, it is evident that I did not refuse, since I was present at the cases in the manner I have shown. Nor do I understand how it befits your greatness to describe me so often as a despiser of the canons, when you have not yet been able to prove this by even one clear document.

As for your statement that I fled without any necessity or reason, I confess that neither reason nor necessity ought to have led me to do this when I came into these final circumstances of the world. Nowhere and never have I done anything against anyone for which necessity could reasonably require me to flee or any occasion compel me to evade a hearing.

Therefore, it ought not to have been necessary for me to flee contrary to reason and contrary to all divine and human laws, if reason and authority had preserved their proper order and place in me, however unworthy a bishop I may be. But, as I instructed you at the beginning of your mission, I remembered Silvacy, where you were present. This did me no good but rather harm, since I was detained for the sole purpose of preventing me from going to Rome in obedience to the commands of the apostolic lord. Nothing of this kind has ever been heard from bishops concerning a bishop since the beginning of the world.

As for the flight with which you reproach me, let not I, who am nothing, answer, but the pope, venerable and worthy of veneration throughout the world, Julius, who wrote as follows to Eusebius, Theognius, Theodore, and Berinthus, and the other bishops of the East (Letter 11 to the Easterners):

“Therefore, concerning the flight for which you reproach Athanasius, you are acting wrongly, since the Lord himself gave us this command: ‘When they persecute you in one city, flee to another’ (Matt. 10). The Lord himself also demonstrated this example: when the Pharisees took counsel against him in order to kill him, ‘Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there’ (Matt. 12). And elsewhere: ‘The Jews took up stones to throw at him; but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple, and passing through their midst, he went away’ (Luke 4; John 8), and thus departed.

“For the disciples also withdrew because of fear of the Jews, hiding themselves (John 20); and Paul, sought by the governor of the nation in Damascus, was lowered from the wall in a basket and escaped the hands of the one who sought him (2 Cor. 11). Many other innumerable saints, both in the Old and in the New Testament, are likewise read to have fled.

“If, then, you reproach those who flee for their flight, be ashamed rather to persecute them and cease laying snares; and then those who flee will immediately cease fleeing. For whether you kill them—their death will always cry out against you—or impose exile upon them in turn, you will be known everywhere to send the memory of evil against yourselves, while they gain benefit through enduring.”

I shall therefore explain the signs of my necessity, showing that, although improperly and unworthily, I even now had to flee, because you compel me to do so, adding injury to suffering.

You summoned me by a letter issued under your authority to Attigny for a synod, stating that letters from the apostolic lord had been sent to Lord King Charles and to the bishops of his kingdom, and that no reply could be given to them without synodal deliberation. Although you had received those letters at Gundulf’s estate, where I was also present, you did not show them to me there.

When I came to Attigny, you gave me what you called a copy of those letters and asked me to read it, ordering me immediately afterward to reply to it and instructing me to return that same copy to you as soon as I had read it. But later, from another copy, I learned that several things were missing from the memorandum you had shown me.

At Attigny, our lord the king dealt for several days with matters that seemed appropriate. When a definite day was assigned to us on which only synodal matters were to be discussed—it was to be a Friday—I came, but you happened not to come.

All my men were also summoned for legal proceedings, so that not even one of them was permitted to accompany me when I returned from that palace. This was done by the Northman on account of the estate of Pauliac. Since I had received that estate by royal grant and, as you know, also by apostolic authority, these same men had followed me into it. Yet even if it had not been restored to me by royal grant, they ought to have been excused, because the estate lies within the parish granted to me by God, and because, under canonical sanction, they followed me as the man whose ministry required him to enter it.

But, in a remarkable manner, a new law was applied: the Northman himself—a robber and violator of sacred property, and therefore a sacrilegious man, indeed excommunicated by apostolic authority unless he divested himself of these properties, and, according to the authentic letters sent to you, to be repelled through your office, while also separated from the church by me, whatever kind of bishop I may be, because of the special offenses committed in the Church of Laon—was not compelled to make restitution in such a manner, even though we had not robbed them and did not consider it robbery, whether justly or belatedly, to recover and possess what was ours. He himself had not hesitated to plunder them with such unspeakable injustice for so many years.

Nor did the provisions included in the complete Capitularies of the emperors, Lords Charles and Louis, help us. They state:

“Whatever has been established by individual kings concerning the most holy churches, or whatever each individual bishop has obtained concerning ecclesiastical matters, shall be preserved under penalty of perpetual and enduring sacrilege. Clerics, moreover, shall be reserved not for secular judges but for episcopal hearing. For it is not lawful that those who belong to God should be subjected to secular judgment.”

Also in the same collection:

> “It has been decreed by synodal authority that laymen or secular persons must not suppose or presume that anything belonging to men consecrated to God or to the resources of the Church pertains to them, apart from the reverence due to them; for it is taught that God has entrusted the priests with undisputed responsibility for administering these things. If anyone should presume to act against this, let him be struck with anathema.”

Also in the same collection:

> “Concerning men consecrated to God, or ecclesiastical resources, no authority is ever recorded as having been granted to laymen, however religious they may be. Therefore, since those who have no authority to administer ecclesiastical property must not do so, it is pernicious for them to plunder it.”

Also in the same collection:

> “If anyone should break out into this kind of sacrilege, so that, rushing into churches and their property, he inflicts upon priests and ministers, or upon the worship itself and the place, some injury that ought not to be inflicted, let him know that, convicted or confessing his guilt in the injury to divine worship, he is to be punished by a capital sentence. Nor should it be awaited that the bishop demand vengeance for the injury, to whom holiness leaves alone the glory of forgiving; and thus let it be not merely permitted but even praiseworthy for everyone to prosecute, as a public crime, the atrocious injuries inflicted upon priests or ministers, and to secure the punishments due to the guilty.”

Now, on the contrary, it is permitted and praiseworthy for sacrilegious persons to invade sacred property, while the sons of the Church suffer punishment as though they were guilty when, at the bishop’s direction, they presume even to enter it.

You too, in the booklets you gave to the king, set out this chapter more fully from the book of those emperors from which it was taken; but in the book of our emperors it is inserted more briefly, as I have quoted above (*Codex Theodosianus*, concerning bishops):

> “If anyone should break out into this kind of sacrilege, so that, rushing into Catholic churches, he inflicts upon priests and ministers, or upon the worship itself and the place, some injury—let what has occurred be reported through written statements by the ranks of officials, magistrates, curators, and the notaries of the apparitors whom they call stationarii to the knowledge of the authorities, so that the names of those who can be identified may be declared. And if it is said that the deed was committed by a multitude, although not all can be identified, nevertheless some may be, and through their confession the names of their associates may be disclosed.

> “Accordingly, let the governor of the province know that the injury done to priests and ministers of the Catholic Church, as well as to the place itself and to divine worship, is to be punished by a capital sentence against those convicted or confessing their guilt. Nor should he await the bishop’s demand for vengeance for his personal injury, to whom holiness leaves alone the glory of forgiving. Rather, let it be not merely permitted but even praiseworthy for everyone to prosecute, as a public crime, the atrocious injuries inflicted upon priests or ministers, and to secure the punishment due to the guilty.

> “But if the violent multitude cannot be brought before the court through the execution of the civil authorities, with the assistance of the officials and landholders, because it protects itself with weapons and by the difficulty of the terrain, let the judges request the protection of an armed force from the illustrious count, by letters setting out the tenor of this law, so that the perpetrators of such crimes may not escape.”

You also included this:

> “If the venerable privileges of the Church have been violated through anyone’s rashness or neglected through dissimulation, let the offense be punished, as was also previously established, by condemnation to a fine of five pounds of gold.”

Was it fitting, my lord and father, that, having been summoned by you to the synod to give a response to be delivered to the apostolic lord, I should be excluded outside, while, as you sat together with my archbishops and fellow bishops, this Nortmannus—acting in such a manner and excommunicated by apostolic authority in such a manner, and one who, through the office of your mouth, ought to have been rejected—should come into your presence to accuse me concerning the very property he had received, and should be heard by you? From him, especially and in every respect concerning this matter, both I and all my people ought not merely to have been excused but wholly defended.

For this Nortmannus is one of those concerning whom, when it pleased you, you wrote in your booklets to the appropriate place on behalf of me and my Church:

> “Moreover, as is reported, this offense was committed and permitted through the prejudice of certain persons of the sort who are branded as infamous both in the laws and in the sacred canons. And if ecclesiastical discipline were as vigorous as it was in the time of your predecessors and our forefathers, they would be excluded from the thresholds of the Church among criminals, since, as the ministers say, they are criminals.

> “But now, through our dissolution, as some say, those who ought to have been separated from the Church themselves leap into the Church. We rightly attribute this to our sins, at the end of the ages, since, to our disgrace rather than to the glory of the Church, we are called priests—men who are trampled underfoot by such persons, while those very men sit in judgment upon the heads of priests. Yet laymen with sound and free judgment would not legally receive in a public court the judgment or accusation of such persons, if they wished to reject it.

> “In this deed, as Saint Celestine writes, the matter does not concern only the parties involved: the universal Church is struck by whatever novelty occurs. For what has now been done is new; it has never yet been heard of under this heaven, that a bishop with his Church should have been confiscated by any religious ruler under the title of proscription through the judgment of laymen.”

Behold with what distinguished weapons you then fought the battles of the Lord. But I shall tell you something that I neither ought nor dare keep silent about. I did not think it dishonorable to you that I sent to Rome, that I wished and still wish to go to Rome, or that I sought help from Rome—from which the whole episcopate received its beginning and continues to derive the increase of its progress and succession. Until now, the head has never harmed the feet, without which the feet are not accustomed to walk.

I hoped that the sword of your holiness would become sharper, not blunter, if it were sharpened by the steel of the vicar of the chief of the apostles, Peter. For the moment I say nothing about the treacherous attack you inflicted upon me at the same Attigny when I appealed to the holy Roman See for love of almighty God and in veneration of that same chief of the apostles, Peter—although, as you know, I had also been summoned by that See. Neither of these things benefited me, nor does either benefit me still; but I ought to have found from you some excuse for this, not have endured opposition. For this I have suffered, and continue to suffer, as much as my sins deserve, but not as much as is due to the reverence owed to so great a See.

As for what you wrote to me—that, when the lord king has returned from his brother, I should bring the royal order by which he restored or granted the aforesaid property to the Church of Laon, and that he would arrange to act as justice concerning that property once the facts had been established—I do not understand why it is again necessary for me to bring that order, since, in the presence of you all, Archbishop Harduic both heard and saw it when it was presented by his hands, and, as Bertharius reported to me, acknowledged that he himself had confirmed it.

But this is astonishing to many, and to me as well: what I had retained peacefully for more than six months by royal generosity, I immediately lost as soon as the synod had ended.

Concerning my men, about whom you write that their case remained not decided but unresolved, I have already given you a sufficient answer above; and therefore I did not depart, as you say, irregularly or illegally. But how their case can now justly and reasonably be examined and decided according to the sacred laws before I am revested with authority over that same property is not clear, since I justly and reasonably received them from that property and prohibited them from it. As I stated above, I was ready to prove this to him by clear documents.

As for what you wrote:

> “Furthermore, dearest brother, concerning the document said to contain the bishops’ decision at the synod held at Tusiacum, I am very much astonished where and how you found it. Before I heard of it through your cleric Hetto, I had never seen it or heard of it anywhere; nor have the bishops who are now present said that they had seen or heard of it.”

I too am not without reason astonished if Archbishop Harduic, who was present, said that he had neither seen nor heard it. For I received it from him, and, after rereading it, ordered it to be transcribed. It was transcribed by the hands of two deacons of the Church entrusted to me, one named Teutlandus and the other Hartgarius. I know that they do not know how to corrupt or abridge apostolic or synodal letters; they never learned this from me, for, God is my witness, I have never presumed to do such a thing.

But since you say that you neither heard nor saw it, and that you possess the authentic decision which, according to the sacred laws, was decreed at that same synod—the synod in which I took part with you—I earnestly ask you to show it to me, so that I too may be able to recognize in it the hand of my subscription. I know, nevertheless, that I was present at that synod, and I remember at whose particular urging this more concisely collected decision was subscribed.

You add that you cannot guess where this fabrication arose. You no longer need to guess, since in the meantime you have learned it from me, a human being. And if you show me an authentic version that differs from this one, you will prove it to be divine, because we human beings know truthfully that this was established and confirmed at that synod.

As for what you add:

> “As you can clearly recognize from those things which I have taken pains to write to you against your presumptions, it conflicts with certain sacred rules; and you could very easily have recognized it as false, if you had had in your head those eyes of which Scripture says: ‘The eyes of the wise are in his head’ (Ecclesiastes 2).”

What those things are that you wrote against my presumptions, by which I could clearly recognize that this decision conflicted with certain sacred rules, I do not know. Nor do I recognize from your writings that I acted presumptuously by doing nothing; for I examine myself, as far as I know, by the actions of my conscience, and do not cast myself down by your denunciation of the writings.

You say that I could very easily have recognized it as false if I had had in my head those eyes of which Scripture says, “The eyes of the wise are in his head.” I do not boast that I possess those eyes; rather, I desire, if only I may attain them. Nor do I wish to possess the eyes of those wise men of whom it is said: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jeremiah 4). I do not wish to be wiser than one ought to be, but to be wise unto sobriety (Romans 12), remembering the admonition: “Do not seek what is too high for you” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

Nevertheless, I ask you to show me where it is false and conflicts with the sacred rules. I confess that I do not see it; and if I had seen it then, I would not have subscribed.

As for what you say:

> “Your prudence is astonishing: how could it please you to possess and send me this false compilation, which, as I said, conflicts with certain sacred rules, rather than to possess the true definition of the synod, one that accords with the sacred rules, and to receive it from me, your primate, so that according to the sacred rules you might hold and follow it?”

I have with me the letter which you had dictated in your archiepiscopal office and caused to be read at that same synod. I remember that, because of its length, while certain persons were pressing the matter, we subscribed to this more concisely collected decision.

For, after prefacing your *Tetrastich* of devotion to the lord king, you begin as follows:

> “The holy synod assembled at Tusiacum, in the parish of Toul.”

But this document, which begins, “When in the name of almighty God,” begins its first chapter in this way:

> “First, therefore, because of the obstinacy of many who, although sacrilegious, corrupting the temple of God in themselves, do not fear to invade sacred things delivered to sacred places through the offerings and vows of the faithful, we decree according to the ancient rule of our fathers that if anyone wishes to receive or give outside the Church the offerings of fruits and of all things which are bestowed upon or collected for the ministers of the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person appointed by him to distribute what has been assigned to ecclesiastical office, both the giver and the receiver shall be anathema by the judgment of almighty God, condemned forever unless he repents—and so forth.”

In your letter you too seem to agree with this decree, saying among other things:

> “For those who reign in heaven and shine with miracles on earth—and who live with us even to this day and will live forever with our successors—say that their reward is with God. If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such responsibility has been entrusted, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.

> “Anathema is interpreted in the Roman language as ‘alienation.’ For everyone who does such things, so long as he remains in them, even if we bishops—who receive from God, in the apostles and with the apostles, not through our own merit but by divine grace, the power of binding and loosing—sometimes ignorant of divine understanding, sometimes unaware of what is entrusted to us, and sometimes unable to correct what has been entrusted as expediency requires, should dissemble or even neglect to carry out what has been established, and should not separate such a person from the Church and the fellowship of the faithful by excommunicating him, he has nevertheless already been excommunicated and condemned beforehand by the sacred canons, until he abandons that sin and, through ecclesiastical satisfaction and priestly reconciliation, receives the grace of the Lord and the fellowship of the faithful.

> “And whoever, entangled in his sins and such crimes, ends this life before making the necessary satisfaction will in no way be able to have communion and fellowship with the elect in the kingdom of God, nor will he ever be able to escape the punishments of hell and the company of demons.

> “But there are perhaps such persons who, disregarding the privileges concerning places and things dedicated to God and confirmed by the hands of the saints, mitigate, because they wish to do so rather than because they have the power, the excommunications pronounced by the saints of the Lord against usurpers of ecclesiastical property and resources. They say that they are not bound by the condemnation inflicted for this offense—that is, by the bond of anathema.

> “Concerning such people Saint Gregory says in his letter to the patrician Theoctista (*Book IX, Letter 39*):

> “‘They themselves bear witness against themselves that they are not Christians, those who suppose that they can loosen the bonds of the holy Church by various efforts, and therefore do not consider the absolution which the Church grants to the faithful to be genuine if they do not think that its bonds have force. There is no need to argue at length against them, for they must be despised and anathematized in every respect; and from the very point at which they think they are deceiving the truth, they are truly bound in their sins.’

> “Therefore, if there are any who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach these things or to keep them silently within themselves, I, together with all Catholic bishops and the universal Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak contrary to the truth.”

If this decree of apostolic authority, approved by your probity through being adopted in this manner, is to be followed and held, as you wrote to me, then certainly it must also be followed and held by all the sons of the holy Church who have chosen to possess the name of Christianity.

Therefore, it did not seem worthy of your excellence to say to Bertharius what he reported you had said: that if I excommunicated these men of mine who had committed and still commit such acts, they would not be held by excommunication, that is, would not be bound by the bond of anathema.

But it is not surprising if you despise the excommunication of my insignificance and perhaps judge it unreasonable, when you treat the excommunication of the apostolic See as nothing and proclaim that it ought to be treated as nothing, as though it were absurd.

Yet I am greatly astonished that, while saying such things, you think that your own excommunication or authority—which proceeds from the establishment of that See—will be considered by any of those who hear this, if indeed they believe you, to have any force. And those who fear God and retain knowledge of the truth do not believe you in these matters or agree with you in the conscience of their hearts; nevertheless, they cannot help feeling wounded by your wisdom and holiness. Rather, offended by the scruple of so abominable and detestable a transgression, they either grieve that the sincerity of your distinguished excellence has been degraded or detract from it.

I disclose this to you because “the wounds of a lover are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27), as Saint Jerome wrote to the holy Augustine:

> “I do not know whether those people should be considered Christian friends among whom the common proverb is more powerful—‘Flattery makes friends, truth produces hatred’—than the ecclesiastical saying, ‘The wounds of a friend are more faithful than the voluntary kisses of an enemy.’”

And the apostle Paul admonishes us:

> “Children, obey your parents in the Lord” (Ephesians 6).

To obey in the Lord, however, is—as the Lord himself teaches—“He who loves father more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10). Accordingly, he also says:

> “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out from you” (Matthew 5).

Saint Augustine explains this fully (*Sermon on the Mount*, Book I):

> “Here great strength is needed to cut off the limbs. For whatever the eye signifies is undoubtedly something that is loved intensely. Those who wish to express their affection strongly are accustomed to say, ‘I love him as my eye,’ or even, ‘as my eyes.’ Although these bodily eyes are commonly directed toward seeing, and if both are directed equally they are equally capable, people nevertheless fear losing the right one more.

> “Let this, then, be the meaning: whatever it is that you love so much that you regard it as your right eye, if it causes you to stumble—that is, if it is an obstacle to you in attaining true blessedness—tear it out and cast it away from you. For it is better for one of those things you love, which cling to you as limbs, to perish than for your whole body to go into Gehenna.

> “This compels us to inquire more carefully what he called the eye. In this inquiry nothing occurs to me more fitting than a most beloved friend. For this is surely something we can rightly call a limb, since we love it intensely; and this friend is a counselor, because an eye is like something that points out the way. In divine matters he is the right eye; the left eye is a beloved counselor in earthly matters relating to the needs of the body. If that counselor causes one to stumble, it would have been superfluous to say that he should be spared, since not even the right eye should be spared.

> “In divine matters, a counselor causes one to stumble if, under the name of religion and doctrine, he attempts to introduce some destructive heresy.”

Thus, I am not unaware that nothing ought to be dearer to you after God. But it is harmful to you to raise hostile hands against religion and the teaching of the apostolic See, and it is dangerous—indeed useless—for me to be so obscured by love of you that, by keeping silent, I might seem to agree with you. For even if I were silent and you cried out, you would never be able to accomplish that matter either because of my silence or because of your outcry.

Clearly, all the decretal letters of the apostolic See must be received—not merely received, but, as Gelasius decreed, they must be received with reverence.

But I do not understand what benefit there is in your saying in your booklets that I should merely read them reverently, if I am not also to obey them reverently and strive to follow their sanctions reverently.

You will not suppress bishops’ appeals to the supreme pontiff of the apostolic See. Nor will that African council prevail with you against countless apostolic decrees, where it says:

> “For we have found no provision established by any synod of the fathers that persons should be sent as though from the side of your holiness. For that which you previously transmitted through our fellow bishop Faustinus as though on behalf of the Council of Nicaea, we could not find in the more authentic councils received as Nicene, which were sent by our fellow bishop Saint Cyril of the Church of Alexandria and by the venerable Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, from authentic copies. These had also previously been sent to us through the priest Innocent and the subdeacon Marcellus, by whom they were forwarded to us from them, and we transmitted them to Boniface, bishop of venerable memory, your predecessor. In them we were unable to find anything of this kind.”

If these men could not find it—perhaps because they did not wish to—Marcus, the bishop of the apostolic See, could. He replied to Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt as follows:

> “Concerning the truth and number of the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, at which you indicated in your letter of brotherly affection that you had been present, we made careful inquiries among our own people who had been present there together with you. They explained the whole order to us exactly as your letter attests and testified that your letter was true in every respect—not because we suspected anything sinister on your part, but so that we might wish you, us, and them all to hold one opinion without any later hesitation, and so that the holy Roman Church, which has always remained immaculate and will remain so in the future through the providence of the Lord and the assistance of the blessed apostle Peter, might persist firmly and immovably at all times without any attack from heretics.

> “When this had been done, we carefully searched the archive of our holy apostolic See and found intact the same seventy chapters which, as you stated, had been sent to my predecessor of holy memory, Sylvester. We did not send them to you themselves because of the authority and subscription of so many Fathers and of that great council. But, in the presence of your representatives, we took care to write and send you other chapters containing similar material, the same number, the same words, and the same subscription, under a definite pledge and confirmation.

> “Who would dare deny such things to his brothers? For the Lord has taught us through the grace of the Holy Spirit not to neglect them, but to practice them faithfully; and he has assigned and entrusted them to be handed down and taught to the brethren. This is the living tradition of the apostles; this is true charity, which must be proclaimed and above all loved, fostered, and confidently held by everyone.

> “This holy and apostolic mother of all the Churches of Christ, the Church which, through the grace of almighty God, will be shown never to have erred from the path of apostolic tradition and never to have yielded to be corrupted by heretical innovations, received the rule of the Christian faith at its beginning from its founders, the chief apostles of Christ, and remains undefiled to the end, according to the divine promise of the Lord and Savior himself, who said in his Gospel to the chief of his disciples:

> “‘Peter, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail, and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers’ (Luke 22).”

Therefore the decrees of the apostles are not to be received merely as a shadow, nor did they arise after the confession of that same chief of the apostles, Peter, who said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” to whom the Lord replied:

> “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16).

From that time the old things passed away and new things came into being.

Nor are the decretal letters, established at different times for different circumstances as necessity required, found to be mutually opposed in any respect. It is one thing to administer different medicines at different times according to the variety of illnesses—that is, many and varied medicines—for just as new kinds of illness require new experiments in medicine, so many kinds of illness require many remedies and applications. It is another thing, at one and the same time, to introduce many teachings contrary to the truth. Such a thing can neither be found in these letters nor ought it to be said by anyone.

[Col. 1044B] As for what you say to me in your booklets specifically concerning the letters of Julius and Felix, as though they had been composed from the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, your response does not seem to be directed to me so much as an attempt to accuse those men themselves of falsehood.

The time at which the Council of Nicaea was assembled can be recognized from certain excerpts of the synodal acts of Pope Saint Sylvester. In their first chapter it is stated:

> “In the time of Pope Sylvester and the most devout Emperor Constantine Augustus, a great council was held at Nicaea in Bithynia, and three hundred and eighteen Catholic bishops were regularly assembled there at the summons of that same Pope Sylvester—and so forth.”

After this it adds:

> “At that same time, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, when the aforementioned great council was assembled at Nicaea, the aforesaid pope, having already issued a canonical summons, gathered two hundred and sixty-seven bishops in the city of Rome, and, with the counsel of the aforesaid Emperor Constantine Augustus, he himself—and so forth.”

The aforementioned Pope Marcus was his successor. He bears witness to Julius, his successor, concerning the chapters made at the Council of Nicaea—eighty in number and subsequently reduced to seventy—as I have written above.
