But you write in the same booklets as follows:

> “Furthermore, as for the fact that the letter in the name of Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops to Marcus, Sylvester’s successor, states that there were eighty chapters—namely, forty issued by the Greeks in the Greek language and likewise forty issued by the Latins in the Latin language—and that these were reduced to seventy chapters by the three hundred and eighteen bishops: if the chapters designated in Julius’s letter, those designated but omitted, and also those which we read in Felix’s letter are counted, more than eighty chapters are found, differing among themselves. Moreover, the chapters preserved from the Council of Nicaea by antiquity, and which the Church has maintained and venerated to the present, are not mentioned in those letters, much less counted among them.

> “The number of those chapters designated in Pope Julius’s letter is found as follows: 18, 19, 21, 23, 26, 27, 28, 29, 33, 41 and 5, 8 and 9, and 50, 52, 53, 54, 55 and 57, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63 and 66.

> “In the complete set of seventy chapters, the following are designated as having been set out by blessed Julius, inserted according to the significance of this numbering; therefore no more than twenty-four are counted by him here. If the twenty chapters that we possess are added to these, the total is forty-four, and they do not complete seventy—much less eighty—and thus this man is not shown here to be false by exceeding the number.”

But what you added—“The chapters read in Felix’s letter are also such that, if they are added to these, more than eighty differing chapters will be found”—has no bearing on the matter. For before arranging his chapters, Felix prefaced them as follows (*Letter I*):

> “Let us begin, therefore, with the help of God and the holy apostle Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ received their beginning. For many cases have often arisen which in some instances were not cases but crimes, since, as we have discovered, they were imposed upon the brethren more through iniquity than through charity.

> “And so that care may henceforth be taken that such things do not occur, let us set out certain chapters from the holy Fathers, established both in the Council of Nicaea and in this holy See, by which our brothers and fellow bishops, fortified, may be able with the Lord’s help to escape the ambushes of their enemies. And insofar as the Lord grants us ability, let us imitate, in fewer words, a concise account of so many evils; let us briefly review what we have found in the volume of your letters, and, as you request, let us add certain other matters necessary for the present time.”

And so he continues:

> “For it has been decreed by synodal institutions”—and so forth.

He therefore did not say that everything he set out had been taken from the Council of Nicaea, so that you could refute both him and Julius on that basis. Rather, he said that he was setting out certain matters both from the Council of Nicaea and from those established in the holy Roman See, which he judged to be of almost no lesser authority. Moreover, he added that he would set out certain other matters necessary for the present time, as they had been requested.

This is what his predecessors and successors did from the beginning, and what they will continue to do to the end: according to the necessity of the present times, they renew what has been established and establish what must be established. For this reason all decretal letters have been established at different times for different necessities. Therefore, according to blessed Gelasius, they must be received with reverence; and if they must be received, they must certainly be embraced and obeyed by all with reverence.

As for what you also said—that the matters set out by Pope Julius and those set out by Felix are found to differ from one another—if you wish “different” to be understood as different matters for different circumstances, according to what occurred in each man’s time, that is acceptable. But if you mean that they appear to oppose one another by establishing contradictory rules, then, unless you explain the point, I confess that I can perceive it in no way.

And when you said that the chapters taken from the Council of Nicaea which antiquity preserved and which the Church still maintains and venerates are not mentioned in their letters, much less counted there, both letters themselves reveal the reason why these matters were set out and those others left unmentioned.

Pope Felix says that he is setting out those things by which the brethren and fellow bishops, fortified, may with the Lord’s help escape the ambushes of their enemies; and he further says that he is establishing matters which they had requested from him because of the necessity of the present time.

If the subject had been the matters decreed by those twenty chapters of the Council of Nicaea which are commonly available, he would nevertheless have taken them up, and they would shine more brightly than daylight. Julius likewise clearly reveals a similar reason for setting out those twenty-four chapters. This is evident where he does not preserve the sequence of the numbering, but adds only those matters that suited the issue under discussion, just as everyone is accustomed to do.

For he prefaced them as follows (*Letter II*):

> “The holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea foresaw in spirit such plotters and established laws, which we call canons, so that the good might not easily be condemned by the wicked. We have judged it appropriate to insert some of their decisions here, so that our letter might be strengthened by the authority of so many Fathers, and so that all the bishops of the East and of the other regions, hearing these things, might not fall into so great a pit or suffer the condemnation decreed by the Fathers.”

Then follow those chapters extracted from the prescribed Council of Nicaea, drawn from its seventy chapters. And it is clear that, since the subject was the ambushes of enemies, he set out what pertained to opposing such ambushes.

Both men acted as prudent physicians. Every illness requires its own medicine.

As for what you said—that the chapters of the Council of Nicaea which we possess are not counted in those letters—I do not know what you mean by this statement. For, as I have already said, Pope Julius set out only twenty-four chapters by designation. But it is not apparent what Felix set out from the Council of Nicaea, because he does not distinguish the sources. He did not conceal that he had set out matters both from the Council of Nicaea and from those established in the holy Roman See, as well as certain others which he himself established, according to the requests of those who needed them because of the necessity of the present time.

Nor can one infer the number, since we do not possess the complete set of seventy chapters. We do not know whether he set out two, three, four, or ten chapters from the Council of Nicaea, or more than that. He could have set out twenty-six according to the numerical reckoning, and the twenty chapters which we possess here with us would still remain.

Therefore, what you have also set down in the same fascicles from the letter of the same Pope Julius must be examined to see how it coheres with itself. For you say:

[Col. 1046D]

> “But concerning this matter, namely that the most reverend Julius says in his letter that we have not inserted more of these chapters of the Nicene synod here, lest we should seem to empty out or cheapen the aforesaid synod, or lest the letter should cause weariness to readers and hearers: if anyone should wish to know more and fuller details about these matters, he will be able to find both what we have mentioned and more in the sacred archive of the church of our see. The very Divinity is witness that I speak the truth. No one can contradict this, because unless the see itself possessed what it sent, it could in no way have sent it; and since he possessed more, it is plainly true that the regulations established by the sacred Council of Nicaea are also preserved in the Roman archive.”

[Col. 1047A]

Thus he says that fuller and more extensive material is kept in the Roman archive, and nevertheless testifies that what he mentioned can be found there; and you admit that no one can contradict this, because unless he possessed the very documents which he sent, he could in no way have sent them. How, then, do you later write in the same fascicles that it is manifest that only the twenty chapters which we possess were established at the Council of Nicaea?

Indeed, the prolonged ages and extended periods inherited from ancient custom, during which only these twenty chapters of that council were received, are supported by the words of the historiographer Rufinus, which, you say, establish indubitable credibility. But both claims cannot stand together. For if it is believed with unquestionable confidence from the words of the historiographer that only twenty chapters were received, then Julius must be contradicted, since he asserts that fuller and more extensive material was available, and that what he had mentioned could also be found in the Roman archive—[Col. 1047B] material which he himself testifies in his letter that he had not included, lest he seem to empty out or cheapen the aforesaid synod, namely the Council of Nicaea.

It is right, therefore, that belief should rather be given to him for whom the very Divinity bears witness—the Divinity that promised: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18). And again: “If two of you agree about anything whatever that you ask, it will be done for you by my Father” (ibid.). And again, the Divinity and Truth itself says: “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19; Matthew 18).

Behold three competent witnesses—and not merely witnesses, but confirmers of those who testify—Mark, Julius, and Felix. [Col. 1047C] They demonstrate that more than twenty chapters drawn from the Council of Nicaea were preserved in the Roman archive through the lengthy periods of many generations. Nor do they add the number of these chapters to the Council of Antioch; rather, they produce regulations established at the Council of Nicaea, and they enumerate seventy or more, not forty-five or merely twenty chapters. Since it is not fitting for us to argue against the head, we must preserve what they have handed down and seek what we do not yet possess, rather than reject what we have obtained.

As for what you write in the same fascicles:

> “About twenty-three years after the Nicene synod, the Antiochene synod was held, and Julius’s letter is recognized as having been composed at the same time. In it many chapters are collected in a different form; and if they had been taken from one synod, they would not differ in this way. It is therefore more apparent that, since Julius composed his letter at the time when the Council of Antioch was being conducted, [Col. 1047D] he was not unaware of what had been established in that council—something which necessarily had to be strengthened by his authority—and consequently he did not confuse the regulations of the Nicene and Antiochene councils.”

But what do you mean by saying, “If they had been taken from one synod, they would not differ in this way”? If the material taken from synods differs, and the synods are represented as contradicting one another, what will now be mutually harmonious? What solid and stable structure will be found in the Church of God, since you do not conceal that the decretal letters of the apostolic see likewise differ?

[Col. 1048A]

Certainly, things adopted in different ways for different necessities do not differ, provided that they do not depart from the equity of reason and the path of truth. Julius took from the Nicene synod those matters which seemed at that time appropriate to him, as he himself says, so that his letter might be strengthened by the authority of so many Fathers. He also added, by establishing them with apostolic authority, those matters which had to be added because of the necessity of the present time, just as his successor Felix and his other predecessors and successors did.

But you add:

> “And if the matter of appeals, as it was established at the Council of Sardica, had previously been established at the Council of Nicaea, there would have been no need for it to be established again at this council. Rather, as is read in the other councils, it would have been written that what was established at the Council of Nicaea should be preserved by everyone.”

[Col. 1048B]

It is apparent that you do not at all believe the three aforementioned witnesses, who testify that the matter of bishops’ appeals to the bishop of the Roman see was established at the Nicene Synod (canon 7). Yet it does not conflict with reason or faith to say that this was not decreed at the Nicene synod because the same matter was also established at the Council of Sardica, where we read:

> “Bishop Hosius said: It has also been decided that if a bishop is accused, and the assembled bishops of that region judge him and depose him from his rank, and if the one who has been deposed appeals and takes refuge with the bishop of the Roman Church, wishing to be heard, and if he considers it just that the judgment or examination of the case be renewed, let him write to those bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they may investigate the matter very carefully and determine it according to the faith of truth. [Col. 1048C] But if the one who asks for his case to be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty to send a presbyter from his side, it shall be in the bishop’s power to decide what he wishes and what he judges appropriate. If he decides that those who are present with the bishops should be sent to judge, possessing the authority of the one by whom they are appointed, that shall remain within his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he judges by the wisest counsel.”

In the preceding chapter of the same council it is written: “If this pleases everyone.” The synod replied: “It pleases us.” In this chapter it is said: “It has also been decided.” Hosius therefore rightly said, “It has been decided,” if he already knew that it had been established in the Nicene synod, either in the same wording, or in wording equivalent to this, as it is found in the decretal letters.

[Col. 1048D]

Nor is it strange or absurd that the holy Fathers of the Council of Sardica were visited by the same grace of the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, even if they had not previously learned these things from Nicaea, they could have held the same opinion and established these provisions in honor of the memory of the holy Apostle Peter.

I think, however, that if the Sardican council had said only that “what was established at the Council of Nicaea should be preserved by everyone,” without saying anything about appeals—for the matter is not contained in these twenty chapters—you would have understood it to mean that only those twenty chapters were to be preserved. But now, since the matter of appeals is so explicitly shown to be something that must be observed, while the apostolic institution is preserved, and since this is also promulgated as deriving from the Nicene synod, I say “while apostolic authority is preserved” because the Nicene synod, as Pope Boniface wrote to the bishops established throughout Thessaly, [Col. 1049A] dared to establish nothing concerning the Roman see, to which it saw that nothing above its merit could be conferred. It knew, in fact, that everything had been granted to this see by the Lord’s word.

Therefore, whatever this council that you accept established as something to be preserved, allow it to be preserved, even if you believe that nothing concerning this matter was established at the Nicene synod. Just as those twenty chapters are held by everyone and judged worthy of observance—although even all twenty together are not sufficient for all the needs of the ecclesiastical order and of changing times—so let this chapter also be held and observed by you. It harms no one and benefits everyone.

For after the African council wrote to Pope Celestine in its letter at the relevant point (letter after the end of the synod):

[Col. 1049B]

> “For as to sending certain persons as if from the side of your Holiness, we find no such provision established by any synod of the Fathers. For what you previously sent through our fellow bishop Faustinus, as though from the Council of Nicaea, we were unable to find in the more authentic councils that are received as Nicene, which were sent by our fellow bishop Cyril of the Church of Alexandria and by the venerable Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, from authentic copies. These had also previously been sent to us through the presbyter Innocent and the subdeacon Marcellus, by whom they were transmitted to us from those bishops, and by us sent to Boniface, bishop and your predecessor of venerable memory. In these documents we were unable to find anything of the kind.”

And this was written by Pope Innocent, whom you conspicuously accept (letter 2), [Col. 1049C] to the bishops established throughout Macedonia:

> “It could not have seemed burdensome to your most devout minds that the judgment of anyone should be reconsidered, because truth, repeatedly tested, shines forth more brightly into the light, and an evil recalled for judgment is condemned more gravely and without repentance. For it is a divine fruit, dearest brothers, to review justice repeatedly.”

Furthermore, I say that what the African council asserts in the following words—“For as to sending certain persons as if from the side of your Holiness, we find no such provision established by any synod of the Fathers”—is a lie. [Col. 1049D] For it was established at the Council of Sardica in these words (canon 7):

> “But if the one who asks for his case to be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty to send a presbyter from his side, it shall be in the bishop’s power to decide what he wishes and what he judges appropriate.”

The Council of Sardica also wrote this to Pope Julius, among other matters, at the beginning of its letter:

> “It will seem most excellent and entirely fitting if, from the individual provinces, the Lord’s priests report to the head—that is, to the see of the Apostle Peter.”

Here it is clear that this council was not unaware of what Julius wrote concerning appeals from the Nicene synod. For this reason Hosius properly said, “It has been decided in that synod”—namely, the Nicene synod—which he himself had attended.

Or who, possessing sound judgment, would regard as trustworthy the claim that the chapters which Pope Celestine sent through Bishop Faustinus to the African bishops from the Council of Nicaea were not to be found in the authentic copies, [Col. 1050A] rather than supposing that they could have been omitted by the bishops of Alexandria or Constantinople? They may have been sent incompletely; or, if they were sent in full, they may have been reduced or corrupted by some—as we read happened with many documents—or altered by the Africans themselves, who did not want their judgments to be reconsidered. Just as they lied in saying that this had not been established by any synod of the Fathers, even though it cannot be concealed, so perhaps they also lied in saying that what they believed could be hidden had not been sent to them by the bishops of Alexandria or Constantinople. Yet, since the matter concerned Pope Celestine, they could not deny that it had been sent to them by him.

And so that the bishops of the apostolic see may not be the only ones to testify concerning this matter of appeals, let the testimony of the bishops of that very African province also be brought forward. [Col. 1050B] For Archbishop Stephen wrote, together with three councils, as follows (among the letters of Damasus):

> “To the most blessed Lord, exalted to the apostolic dignity, the holy father of fathers, Pope Damasus, supreme pontiff of all bishops: Stephen, archbishop of the council of Mauretania, and all the bishops of the three councils of the African province.
>
> “We make known to your Blessedness that certain brothers living in our vicinity are attempting, without consulting you, to depose certain of our brothers, namely venerable bishops, from their own rank. Yet the decrees of all the Fathers, in honor of the most blessed Peter, reserve to your see the judgments of bishops and the final determination of the highest ecclesiastical matters, together with the entire authority of inquiry concerning the things of God, which we must observe with every care and diligence.
>
> “[Col. 1050C] Above all, these matters ought rightly to be examined by the apostolic summit itself, whose ancient concern it is both to condemn what is evil and to restore what deserves praise. For it has been established by ancient regulations that whatever of this kind is done, even in distant or remote provinces, must not first be discussed or accepted unless it has first been brought to the knowledge of your nurturing see, so that, by its authority, it may be confirmed according to what has been pronounced.
>
> “And there are many other provisions of this kind, and similar ones, established concerning these matters. If anything has been done unlawfully, hasten to intervene, as has always been the custom of your see; and stand firmly on their behalf, fighting like a father for his sons, just as it is well said to Jesus son of Sirach: ‘Fight for the truth unto death, and the Lord God will fight for you’ (Sirach 4).”

[Col. 1050D]

Behold, lord father: these bishops of the African province testify that it was established by ancient regulations—something which those others said they had not found established in any synod. For it is a greater provision that nothing concerning the highest ecclesiastical matters, even when they are conducted in distant or remote provinces, should first be discussed or accepted unless it has first been brought to the knowledge of the nurturing Roman see and confirmed by its authority, than that an apostolic pronouncement should reconsider the episcopal judgments challenged by an appealing bishop—a pronouncement to which the care of all the Churches has been entrusted.

[Col. 1051A]

Neither this archbishop nor these councils considered it a diminution of their own honor; rather, they looked to the increase of salvation in obtaining this privilege for the bishop of the Roman see. I confess that I earnestly desire your paternity to become a participant in their unanimity.

Pope Damasus himself likewise replied to them at the relevant point in his letter (letter 4, at the beginning):

> “You know, dearest brothers, that the apostolic see has been established by God as a firmament fixed and immovable, and as the most brilliant title of his priests—that is, of all bishops—and as the summit of the Churches. For you are Peter, as the divine word truly declares, and upon your firmament the columns of the Churches, which are understood as the bishops, have been strengthened. And: ‘To you I have entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the power to bind and loose, which things are in heaven and which things are on earth, I have proclaimed’ (Matthew 16).
>
> “[Col. 1051B] You exist as prince and teacher of orthodox and immaculate faith over profane men and, above all, over my members and my disciples. In your place, by God’s grace, we today discharge an embassy for Christ, and all the bishops of this holy see have discharged, do discharge, and will discharge that office.
>
> “For this reason I would not have commanded that all the matters you have brought to our attention are unlawful unless I knew that you were so fully instructed that you would have no doubt that everything about which you consult us is unlawful.
>
> “It is permitted for a metropolitan, together with all his comprovincial bishops, with no one absent and with all agreeing in each individual case, to examine bishops and the highest ecclesiastical matters. But it is not permitted to define their cases, to settle the highest ecclesiastical disputes, or to condemn bishops without the authority of this see. If necessary, everyone must appeal to it and be supported by its assistance.
>
> “[Col. 1051C] For, as you know, it is not catholic to hold a synod without its authority. Nor can a bishop be definitively condemned except in a legitimate synod, convened at the proper time by apostolic summons. Nor are any councils ever read as ratified which have not been supported by apostolic authority.”

Here I note what you wrote in your fascicles:

[Col. 1051D]

> “The letter of Felix depends upon Julius’s letter. For it is the custom of the pontiffs of the apostolic see to place the words of their predecessors in their own letters as though they were their own, as anyone who reads understands.”

This is altogether true, because it is the custom of the pontiffs of the apostolic see to place the words of their predecessors in their own letters as though they were their own. For this reason the letters of the apostolic see are found to be all the more and thoroughly harmonious with one another, and in no respect or hardly at all discordant; nor are their constitutions opposed to one another in anything. Pope Symmachus wrote the following on this subject to Bishop Aeonius (letter 1):

> “How great a reverence will be judged due to the vicars of the most blessed Apostle Peter if what they prescribe in their priesthood is dissolved when they pass away? For we believe that this belongs to the very sacred religion, whose entire authority is undermined unless all things once established by the Lord’s priests remain perpetual. [Col. 1052A] This will happen if the successor does not give firmness to what has been done and, by strengthening what was enacted, make valid what his predecessor enacted.”

Therefore, lord father, since the foundation of these men is immovable, unshaken, and to be left unshaken, their structure also remains permanent and not to be disturbed, because in them there is one Spirit and one faith, one heart and one soul.

Do not attempt to oppose by your barriers what these men sanctioned in their decrees, for you will not be able to stand firm. Love has been ordered: possess authority in it and through it as an archbishop, just as the decrees of the apostolic see and the canons strengthened by their support prescribe, so that you may simply be a model suited to your fellow bishops.

Let episcopal dignity not be diminished in your days through your wisdom. Let the singular and universal power of the apostolic see be compared with no one, and let no one be troubled that it has been set above him, since it requires obedience from its subjects. [Col. 1052B] Let everyone look for from the Lord alone, and not from another prelate, the particular patience which it expects from its own subjects. Let no one detract from the one by whose gift each person has received what he possesses; let no one judge the judgments of the one who has the right to judge concerning the whole Church, whose judgment no mortal is permitted to reconsider. There is one Almighty who has reserved it for his special judgment.

Therefore, lord father, deign sincerely to consider why I say these things to you.

[Col. 1052C]

First, because the Lord threatens: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10). Therefore, we are one body in Christ, members of one another. But Christ is our head, Christ is our father, and Christ alone and the same is our teacher. He orders love, and he ordered it in blessed Peter, saying to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16), so that he himself, the author of our building, might be our foundation and head in him. We must not dissent from him. Whatever member perceives anyone leaping against this head cannot, and ought not, fail to grieve, both for itself and for the paternal confession.

Second, I am compelled, as one bound by the inward affection of a son devoted to you, with the fidelity that is owed to your paternal devotion, to babble—even though I am silent—about what I fear may happen to you.

I tell you the truth: I have not yet begun to go through your fascicles, which you gave me at Attigny, one by one, because I have been preoccupied with other matters of great necessity to me. But, looking ahead, I found that in the matters I have already mentioned [Col. 1052D] you argued against the autonomy of apostolic authority. You also brought forward many sharp arguments against what the venerable Pope Nicholas wrote to you and to us, and you stubbornly rejected what he impressed upon us—all the bishops of Gaul—as things to be retained. I summarized these matters in the memorandum that I gave you at Attigny.

Yet the same Pope Nicholas, worthy of remembrance, established nothing of his own as though it were new. Rather, he followed and explained the authority of Pope Leo and the institution of Gelasius, whose decrees you yourselves often place among your own writings.

I shall therefore set down here the very letter that he directed to us and that concerns this matter. I do not hesitate to say that it must be held and observed by everyone, just as he himself established it, although you say that he found something to say. He did find something—and something properly worthy of being said. He found what he should say, and what he said must be guarded by everyone.

And since it was sent generally to all of us, the bishops of Gaul, rebuking us and instructing us concerning the matters for which we were rebuked, and since I did not deserve to hear or receive it from you, as though you had not received any authentic letter sent to these regions, I have copied it here in full as I obtained it from others, taking an opportunity that is not inappropriate to the matter. Thus you may recognize that I embrace its soundness wholly with the devotion that is due. If you have it differently, I earnestly ask that this now be made known to me by you [the wording is uncertain]. For its text is as follows, and it must be held without weariness.

[Col. 1053A]

## General letter addressed to all the archbishops and bishops of Gaul

[Col. 1053B]

Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, etc. See this letter under no. 76 among the writings of Nicholas I, in volume CXIX of Migne’s *Patrologia*.

Moreover, just as you have written, it is the custom of the pontiffs of the apostolic see to place the words of their predecessors in their own letters, so that, as Pope Symmachus says, “by strengthening what has been done, they make valid what they have enacted.”

Accordingly, I firmly maintain that if your fascicles come to the attention of the apostolic see, they will have no force, since they speak against the decrees of the apostles. [Col. 1053C] For what the lord and venerable Pope Nicholas established by following the examples of his predecessors, the equally venerable lord Pope Adrian, his successor, will strengthen, so that he will make what he has enacted stand firm. And, as you have written, according to the custom of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, he will also place the words of this predecessor of his in his own letters as though they were his own, against all whom he perceives to be striving against what Nicholas promulgated.

Indeed, it is dangerous to raise hostile hands against the apostolic see—something no one has ever done, as you know better than anyone, who wanted to be judged by it.

Since, however, your fascicles contain many useful things, culled from the judgments of many authors as though from broad meadows irrigated by living springs, it seems to me that a cluster should be gathered from them and the thorn avoided.

[Col. 1053D]

As for what I have so far reread concerning myself in those writings, the answer is indeed very easy to make clear, but it requires a very extensive reply, full of verbosity and loquacity without the charm of wit. I therefore greatly fear that a reply will result from the cup so offered to me such as is written concerning a certain man—one which both you and I would be ashamed to read and which serious men would be weary even to hear.

For this reason, if I could, and if it pleased you, I would very much wish to avoid it. For the general matters set out there are answered sufficiently and abundantly by the decretal letters of the Roman see. No one possessing sound judgment will accept against them any labyrinth of propositions, any new invention, or any evasive interpretation.

This is the direct path, in which not even a fool will go astray—and along which, at Attigny, I was so insistently questioned concerning the excommunication I imposed in my parish.

[Col. 1054A]

For the moment I disclose only this: although you assert that the excommunication was unprecedented and contrary to apostolic teaching and ecclesiastical truth, I learned that it was to be imposed from no other source than your own teaching by living voice. You ought not to rebuild, without cause, what you rightly destroyed. Rather, I learned that this practice had been established at the Roman apostolic see by apostolic authority, and I claim that same see as its author. It is for that see to judge both the excommunication imposed by me and your ruling, since concerning it you write to me as follows:

> “As for what you attempt to assert concerning your parish—as though I could not enter it to determine some matter there—on the basis of the words of Callistus and of your other compilations, which do not agree with you, you understand the matter perversely. But from these and other constitutions of the regulations you will find that each metropolitan must observe this in the province of another metropolitan, which you perversely claim for yourself concerning your parish, subject to the metropolitan see of Reims. Perhaps there have been some metropolitans who have already attempted such things.”

[Col. 1054B]

Accordingly, the same Pope Callistus, in a reply to all the bishops of the cities of Gaul, completely prevented any ambiguity of interpretation in this matter. For he says (letter 11 to the bishops of Gaul):

[Col. 1054C]

> “Let no primate or metropolitan presume to excommunicate or judge the church, parishioner, or anything belonging to the parish of a diocesan bishop, or to do anything else without his counsel or judgment. Rather, they must observe what was established by the apostles, the Fathers, and our predecessors and confirmed by us: namely, if any metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything beyond what belongs solely to his own parish, without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he shall be subject to the peril of his rank, and what he has done shall be regarded as invalid and void.
>
> “But whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of the provincial fellow bishops, their churches, their clergy, and the needs of the laity, let it be done with the consent of all the provincial bishops—not with any arrogance of domination, but with the most humble and harmonious administration, as the Lord says: ‘I did not come to be served, but to serve’ (Matthew 20). And elsewhere: ‘The one who is greatest among you shall be your servant’ (Mark 10).”

And so forth.

[Col. 1054D]

Now, by saying, “Let no primate, no metropolitan, presume to excommunicate the church, parishioner, or anything belonging to the parish of a diocesan bishop, or to do anything without his counsel or judgment,” he does not appear here to have impressed upon primates in relation to their fellow primates, or metropolitans in relation to their fellow metropolitans, the rule that he has stated, since he specified “the church, parishioner, or anything belonging to his parish.” Rather, it must be understood there without ambiguity that it is not permitted to a primate, and even less to a metropolitan, to presume to excommunicate or judge the church, parishioner, or anything belonging to the parish of a diocesan bishop.

[Col. 1055A]

It is equally clear that a metropolitan is not permitted to usurp in the parish of another metropolitan what he is not permitted to attempt even in the parish of a diocesan bishop. The same chapter shows what is permitted and appropriate to him, where it continues:

> “But whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of the provincial bishops, their churches, their clergy, and the needs of the laity, let it be done with the consent of all the provincial bishops.”

Nor did he conceal the manner in which the action should be undertaken, saying:

> “Not with any arrogance of domination, but with the most humble and harmonious administration, as the Lord says: ‘I did not come to be served, but to serve’ (Matthew 20); and elsewhere: ‘The one who is greatest among you shall be your servant’ (Mark 10).”

No arrogance of domination could be understood here if they judged one another individually or reciprocally despised one another; the order would then be confused.

[Col. 1055B]

Let us also consider what is contained in the same chapter:

> “But they must observe what was established by the apostles, the Fathers, and our predecessors and confirmed by us: namely, if any metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything beyond what belongs solely to his own parish, without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he shall be subject to the peril of his rank, and what he has done shall be regarded as invalid and void.”

If this had been established for metropolitans to observe with their fellow metropolitans, and not with diocesan bishops, the wording would not have been “if any metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything beyond what belongs solely to his own parish.” Instead, it would have continued: “beyond what belongs solely to his own parish and diocese.”

[Col. 1055C]

And what follows—“without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, if he attempts to do anything beyond”—would mean that, if archbishops had to observe this rule in relation to archbishops, the canon you accept would fall: “A perfect council is one in which the metropolitan is present with his suffragans.” For no archbishop could, without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province—or, to use your own terminology, of all his fellow archbishops—consider or determine the cases of his fellow bishops. If he attempted to do anything beyond this, he would be subject to the peril of his rank, and what he did would be considered invalid and void.

[Col. 1055D]

Behold, in this way your archiepiscopal dignity is diminished rather than increased. For it is a lesser power if you can do nothing, except what belongs solely to your own parish, without the counsel and consent of all the archbishops of your province. It is a much greater power, as the holy Fathers established, that, with the counsel of your fellow provincial bishops, you may handle and definitively determine whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning their cases, their churches, their clergy, and the needs of the laity, provided that no contradiction arises from which an appeal may be made; and that you seek the consent of your fellow archbishops only in matters which reason and necessity demand.

[Col. 1056A]

The aforementioned Pope Callistus also wrote elsewhere, concerning this same matter, as follows (ibid.):

> “Let no primate, no metropolitan, and none of the other bishops enter the city or approach the possession of another—which does not belong to him and is the parish of another bishop—to make any disposition concerning it, unless he has been summoned by the one whose jurisdiction it is recognized to be, in order that he may arrange, ordain, or judge something there, if he wishes to retain the honor of his rank. If he presumes otherwise, he shall be condemned—and not he alone, but also those who cooperate and consent—for just as ordination is forbidden to them, so too are judgment and the disposition of other matters. For the one who cannot ordain, how will he judge? Without any doubt, he will not judge and will not be able to judge.
>
> “For just as another man’s wife may not be violated, judged, or disposed of by anyone except with the permission of her own husband while he is alive, so neither may the bishop’s wife—which undoubtedly means his Church or parish—[Col. 1056B] be judged or disposed of by another, or have another enjoy her intercourse, that is, her ordination, while he is alive, without his judgment and consent. Hence the Apostle says: ‘The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but when her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband’ (Romans 7).
>
> “Likewise, the bishop’s betrothed—for his Church is called his betrothed and wife—is bound to him while he lives, but when he dies she is released and may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord, that is, according to the rule. For if she marries another while he is alive, she will be judged an adulteress. Likewise, if he willingly takes another wife, he will be considered an adulterer and deprived of communion.”

[Col. 1056C]

If you said that this rule was to be observed only between primates and metropolitans, without the addition “and none of the other bishops,” then, by your archiepiscopal authority, you would claim the right to ordain priests and deacons in the parishes of your fellow bishops, and, without their consent, to settle alone and apart from a synod the judgments concerning them and their cases, and to appropriate to yourselves the disposition of other matters. Yet we find no such provision established by any synod of the Fathers.

Nor can what is contained in this chapter pertain to a bishop who is not an archbishop, since it says:

> “Just as another man’s wife may not be violated, judged, or disposed of by anyone except with the permission of her own husband while he is alive, so neither may the bishop’s wife—which undoubtedly means his Church or parish—be judged or disposed of by another, or have another enjoy her intercourse, that is, her ordination, while he is alive, without his judgment and consent.”

[Col. 1056D]

Pope Lucius, whom I know you have accepted, likewise promulgates the same rule as follows (single letter, at the beginning):

> “If any metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything beyond what belongs solely to his own parish, without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he shall be subject to the peril of his rank, and what he has done shall be regarded as invalid and void.
>
> “Likewise, supported by apostolic authority, we command that no metropolitan hear the cases of anyone without the instigation of all the other bishops of his province, because the proceedings will be invalid, and he himself will have to answer for what he has done.”

Behold: this pope also prohibited the archbishop from hearing the cases of litigants without the request of his fellow provincial bishops.

And since in your chapter which I cited above it is written thus: “But in these words of Callistus, and in the other constitutions of the canons [Col. 1057A], you will find that each metropolitan must observe this in the province of another metropolitan,” let Anicius, likewise a bishop of the Roman See and the predecessor of these men, come forward; and, if these statements are insufficient, let him remove every ambiguity from this interpretation. For he says as follows (Anicius, single letter):

“The archbishop himself shall undertake nothing concerning the cases of his fellow bishops, or other common matters, according to the statutes of the apostles, without the counsel of all of them; nor shall they, except insofar as pertains to their own parishes, undertake anything without his counsel, since the Most High rejoices in such concord and glories in his members. But the others who have obtained other metropolitan sees shall be called not primates but metropolitans.

“If, however, any metropolitan should become puffed up [Col. 1057B] and wish, without the present counsel of all the bishops of his province, to deal with their cases or other cases—except only those matters which pertain to his own parish—or to burden them, let him be strictly corrected by all, so that he may not dare to presume such things thereafter.

“If he should appear incorrigible and disobedient to them, let his contumacy be reported to this apostolic see, to which it has been commanded that all episcopal judgments be brought to an end, so that punishment may be inflicted upon him and the others may be afraid. But if, because of excessive distance, an inconvenient season, or the hardship of the journey, it should be difficult to bring his case to this see, then let the case be brought to his primate and judged by him with the authority of this holy see.

“Likewise, if any bishop should regard his own metropolitan with suspicion, let him be heard before the primate of the diocese or before this apostolic see. ‘Let the greater among you, according to the commandment, be your servant’ (Matt. XX); and: ‘The greater you are, humble yourself in all things’ (Eccli. III). Dearest ones, do not contend among yourselves, and let no one seek to be greater; rather, according to the Apostle, love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love” (1 John IV).

Indeed, when he says, “The archbishop himself shall undertake nothing concerning the cases of his fellow bishops, or other common matters, according to the statutes of the apostles, without the counsel of all of them,” by distinguishing “nothing concerning the cases of his fellow bishops,” he does not permit this to be interpreted as “nothing concerning fellow archbishops.” Moreover, when he adds, “without the counsel of all of them,” the relative and demonstrative pronoun “them” refers to the persons of the fellow bishops, and does not allow “fellow archbishops” to be understood.

It should suffice to have set forth the testimonies of these three men, to which the other pontiffs of the apostolic see bear supporting witness. I believe it is clear that what I gathered from the constitutions of Pope Callistus and of his other predecessors and successors I understood not perversely but plainly.

For the Council of Antioch decrees as follows (canon 9):

“In each region it is fitting that the bishops know that the metropolitan bishop has responsibility for the whole province. For this reason, all those who appear to have business should come together from every direction to the metropolitan city. Therefore it has seemed good that he excel in honor, and that the other bishops undertake nothing beyond him, according to the ancient rule established by our fathers, except only those matters which pertain to their own diocese and to the possessions subject to them. For each bishop has authority over his own parish, so that he may govern according to the reverence due to each person and exercise oversight over every possession that is under his authority. Thus he shall ordain priests and deacons and deal with individual matters according to his own judgment; but he shall attempt nothing more beyond the metropolitan bishop, nor shall the metropolitan act without the counsel of the other priests.”

Here it is shown that the metropolitan ought to have responsibility for the whole province, and that those who appear to have business ought to come together to the metropolitan city. Yet what specifically should be entrusted to the metropolitan’s care is not clearly expressed in this canon, because everything could not be included here, apart from what is said: “Nor shall the metropolitan act without the counsel of the other priests” [Col. 1058B].

But the African Council decrees the matter more openly:

“It was likewise decided that if priests, deacons, or other lower clergy, in cases which they have, should complain of the judgments of their own bishops, neighboring bishops, with the consent of their own bishop, shall hear them and decide between them, with bishops appointed by them. But if they should think that they ought also to appeal from these, let them appeal to the primates of their provinces, just as has been established concerning bishops” [Col. 1058C].

And it is set forth still more broadly in the Council of Sardica. Bishop Hosius said (canon 16):

“This also pleases all: if a deacon, priest, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his bishop and has gone to another bishop, and the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was rejected by his own bishop, the latter ought not to grant him communion. If he does so, he must know that, once the bishops have been summoned, he will have to give an account of the matter.”

All said: “This statute will preserve peace and safeguard harmony.”

And lest it be said that this canon does not prejudice archbishops, because it says, “if a deacon, priest, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his bishop and has gone to another bishop” [Col. 1058D], since it does not say “or to an archbishop,” the following canon of the same council examines this matter more carefully.

Bishop Hosius said (canon 17):

“What still troubles me I ought not to keep silent about. If some bishop, perhaps being angry—for he ought not to be—and quickly and harshly provoked against his own priest or deacon, should wish to expel him from the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. Therefore let the one who has been rejected have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, and let his case be heard and examined more carefully, because a hearing ought not to be denied to one who asks for it.

“And let that bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that his sentence may either be approved by many or corrected. Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no one ought to presume, before the inquiry, to restore to communion the one who has been separated from communion.

“But if those who have come together to hear the case should see arrogance and pride in the clerics—for it is no longer fitting that a bishop should suffer injury or insult—let them rebuke them in sterner words, so that they may obey the bishop who commands what is honorable. For just as he ought to show the clerics sincere charitable love, so also the ministers in return ought to show their bishop unstained obedience.”

What is said here—“Let the one who has been rejected have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, and let his case be heard and examined more carefully, because a hearing ought not to be denied to one who asks for it” [Col. 1059B]—makes it clear that, when the Antiochene Council says that they should come together to the metropolitan city and seek a hearing from the bishop who has responsibility for the province, the rejected man, having the authority to do so, ought to have the neighboring bishops gathered for this purpose. They, examining the matter, will either approve the bishop’s sentence or correct it. That sentence is to be changed by many, not overthrown by the deliberation of the archbishop alone. For when it adds, “Before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no one ought to presume, before the inquiry, to restore to communion the one who had been separated from communion,” it did not except the archbishop. For where “no one” is said, no one is passed over.

Let us also observe what the Council of Nicaea decrees concerning this matter. It says (canon 5):

“Concerning those who are deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the lay order, let the canonical sentence of the bishops in each province prevail, so that those who are rejected may not be received by others. Let inquiry also be made lest anyone appear to have been excluded from the congregation through faintheartedness, contentiousness, or any other fault of the bishop. Therefore, in order that this may be investigated more suitably, it has rightly seemed good that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that, when all the bishops of the province have been gathered together in common, such questions may be examined; and thus those who have clearly sinned against their own bishop may reasonably be regarded by all as excommunicated, until either the community or the bishop should see fit to pronounce a more humane sentence in such cases.”

Therefore these questions are commanded to be examined when all the bishops of the province have been gathered together in common [Col. 1059D], and those who have been excommunicated are to be reasonably regarded as such by all, until either the community or the bishop should see fit to pronounce a more humane sentence in such cases. No archbishop is granted the power to annul the sentence of a fellow bishop by his own authority alone. This privilege is owed only to the pontiff of the Roman see, since he has the right to judge concerning the whole Church.

Pope Alexander teaches at the end of his letter that “one must attend not so much to what is done as to the spirit in which it is done” (Letter 1). Indeed, when this has been examined with exactness, both in you and in me, the benefit of equity will immediately become evident [Col. 1060A]. Nevertheless, I shall say a few things concerning many matters that will have to be treated in their proper place.

When the Lord said to our first parent that on whatever day he ate from the forbidden tree, he would surely die (Gen. II), he did not say this so that he might eat and die—namely, in body and soul—but so that he might not eat and, by not dying, might live in life. When the devil persuaded our parents that, if they ate from the forbidden tree, they would become like gods, he did not persuade them in order that they should become what he promised, but in order that they should cease to be what they would have become if they had not eaten. Behold: the Lord’s prohibition preceded so that death might be escaped; the devil’s loosening of the prohibition was introduced so that life might be destroyed.

And since, according to that statute of Pope Alexander, “one must attend not so much to what is done as to the spirit in which it is done,” when, in its proper order, place, and time, he has heard my prohibition, he will judge with what spirit and intention I made it: whether so that some evil might follow from it, or danger to someone might result, or an opportunity might be opened for violating the decrees of the apostolic see, or, so to speak, whether the opportunity to offend against all divine and human laws might be granted; for the law was established on account of transgressors—or whether, rather, I preferred to take care that these things should not happen. He will weigh this no less.

The decrees of the apostolic see will be reviewed from the beginning, and it will be considered in them why excommunication should be imposed, upon whom and by whom, and also from whom one must withdraw and separate, with whom one ought not to eat, much less celebrate Mass [Col. 1060C].

Certainly, if one who does not correct what must be cut away commits it, and one who is silent in such matters is consequently restrained, and the prophetic woe threatens the one who remains silent, how much more is one who teaches the means by which such things may in any way be presumed by anyone shown to transgress—not merely against a human brother but against God the Lord, and therefore against the sacred religion itself.

Do not imagine that I say this on my own behalf, as though provoked by a personal injury. With God as my witness, I write to you rather to guard against harm to the ecclesiastical order, as it is written: “Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. IV). Know that I would not and do not wish even a single letter dictated by my mouth to appear displeasing to your fatherhood or unfitting for your dignity.

But I cannot, concerning those matters by which I am gratuitously attacked, refrain from saying what I know, or at least what I have been compelled to recognize as necessary. Perhaps I have exceeded the bounds in the manner of a hyperbaton; I shall look back to what was said above.

Concerning what you wrote:

“For although the memorandum sent to me by you appeared to contain something of reason or authority, you must nevertheless distinguish this: when a definite complaint is received, the case is debated and a reason is demanded, there is no presumption or rashness of usurpation, but justice is sought and equity preserved; therefore the strictness of canonical discipline is not left without force.”

If the memorandum contains something of reason or authority—the memorandum which above you described as false—it is good that this be observed. But concerning your statement about the reception of a definite complaint, I have described above how the complaint of those persons whom you mention was received, and I have shown how it was debated. It is sufficiently clear what legal standing their claim possesses, provided that justice was followed without presumption or rashness and equity was preserved for me.

As I explained above, I remained present until the appointed investigators, without whom no decision could be made, were absent, so that I might render an account of the case. To say nothing of the statutes of the canons, this may be understood from the writings of your authority concerning such a matter, and from the letters sent to the king, which I mentioned earlier. In them, at the relevant place, you decree as follows:

“Therefore it is clear that, if he must be deprived of what he obtained by lying, it is safer that the truth of the matter be investigated before he obtains anything through falsehood except an inquiry, as the holy and prudent king says: ‘I investigated most diligently the case which I did not know’ (Job XXIX). And therefore it can easily be discerned that in these matters the strictness of canonical discipline is not without force; rather, it ought to be intensified for the punishment of those who have departed from reason, authority, and equity and have become hardened in obstinate contempt” [Col. 1061B].

As for what you wrote to me: “I exhort and admonish you, dearest brother, by paternal and metropolitan authority according to the sacred canons, not to be rash, through these arguments which you sent me, in bringing forth a sentence, as you instructed me”—to speak according to your own words, concerning these arguments which you sometimes call false and sometimes say to possess something of reason or authority: since I answered above, and now omit much, it seems permissible to me to consider this rashness in light of what was generally set forth in your synodal letter at that same synod [Col. 1061C].

For in that letter you included an institution of Pope Lucius, who says (single letter, near the end):

“By apostolic authority we expel and condemn from the threshold of the holy Church the plunderers of ecclesiastical goods and resources, and we judge them to be sacrilegious; and not only them, but also all who consent to them, because not only those who do such things are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them. Equal punishment embraces both the perpetrators and those who consent.”

And, bearing witness in support of the words of so great a pope, you add:

“Those whose ministry it is to prohibit, restrain, and correct such things, and who are able to do so, cannot be free from the punishment of consent if they do not diligently correct them” [Col. 1061D].

Therefore it is not rash to prohibit and restrain such wicked despoilers and plunderers of ecclesiastical goods from sacrilege, and to deal more severely with the hardened according to the apostolic decrees.

Moreover, in your quires concerning this matter, given to the lord king, you wrote at the relevant place:

“Those, therefore, who receive the stipends of the Church, whatever their order, place, or dignity, if they do not labor earnestly and to the extent of their strength for its safety, peaceful honor, and defense, seize them unworthily, indeed even to their own judgment.”

Therefore, if the idle and unproductive seize these things to their own judgment, should those not also be judged who, as sacrilegious men, devastate ecclesiastical goods and rush upon them as plunderers? [Col. 1062A]

As for what you say—“especially since I have already admonished, rebuked, and even instructed you most sufficiently in this matter from divine authorities”—behold how you instructed me at that time. Yet you have not shown by any rebuke that I ever acted contrary to reason in any matter of mine; at that time it simply pleased you to say what you were permitted to say.

You also add:

“But meanwhile patiently endure what appears contrary to your authority, for you ought to say with the psalmist: ‘Sinners have built upon my back; they have prolonged their iniquity’ (Ps. CXXVIII). ‘In your patience,’ says the Lord, ‘you will possess your souls’ (Luke XXI),” together with many other teachings concerning patience.

Certainly, groaning, I answer that after I received, by God’s favor, the envoy of my lowliness who had been sent to Rome and had returned, and after I did not conceal from you that I wished to go there, as I had vowed and instructed him, I could find in you no other consolation for the needs of myself and my Church. For this reason, it would have been fitting for me to have experienced in you the sweetness of paternal compassion and affection, as well as the support of your archiepiscopal authority.

Concerning the building upon my back, I confess that it cannot be filled in proportion to my sins, nor am I worthy of such grace that I should even deserve to bear a small part of it with dignity. Yet the Comic poet, perhaps joking, spoke truly: “When we are well, we easily give advice to the sick.” I also remember blessed Job saying to his friends: “You are all troublesome comforters” (Job XVI).

But let holy, compassionate, and humble Augustine approach; let him deign to bend down and raise me, who lie prostrate, with the hand of his kindness.

## From Book One of *Various Questions*, Question 71, on the Apostle’s saying: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI), etc.

Because the observance of the Old Testament contained fear, it could not be indicated more clearly that love is the gift of the New Testament than in this passage where the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” He is understood to call this the law of Christ because the Lord himself commanded that we love one another, assigning such weight to this commandment that he said: “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John XIII) [Col. 1062D].

The service of this love is to bear one another’s burdens. Yet this service is not eternal. It will indeed lead to eternal blessedness, in which there will be none of our burdens that we are commanded to bear for one another. But now, while we are in this life—that is, on this road—let us bear our burdens so that we may reach that life which is free from every burden.

For, as some who have studied such matters have written about stags, when they cross a strait to the islands in search of pasture, they arrange themselves in such a way that they bear upon one another the burdens of their heads, which they carry on their antlers. The one behind rests his head upon the neck of the one in front; and since there must be one who leads the others and has no one before him upon whom he can incline his head, they are said to do this by turns: when the one who leads has grown tired under the burden of his head, he returns behind all the others and takes the place of the one whose head he had been carrying while he himself was in front. Thus, bearing one another’s burdens, they cross the strait until they reach solid land (Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 32) [Col. 1063A].

Perhaps Solomon had this nature of stags in mind when he says: “The stag of friendship and the fawn of your graces shall speak with you” (Prov. V, according to the Septuagint). For nothing proves a friend so much as bearing a friend’s burden.

Yet we would not bear one another’s burdens if the time of weakness were the same for both who bear their burdens, or if the kind of weakness were the same. Rather, different times and different kinds of weakness enable us to bear one another’s burdens.

For example, you will bear your brother’s anger when you are not angry against him, so that, in turn, at the time when anger has seized you, he may support you with gentleness and calmness. This example applies to the case in which the actions of those bearing the burdens are different, although the weakness itself is not different; for in both persons the burden is borne reciprocally in this way.

For a different kind of weakness, another example should be considered. Suppose that one person has overcome loquacity in himself but has not yet overcome stubbornness, while another is still talkative but is no longer stubborn. The first ought to bear the loquacity of the second, and the second the stubbornness of the first, until the one condition is healed in one person and the other in the other, bearing them through love.

For if the same weakness occurs in two people at the same time, they cannot tolerate one another when it is directed against each other. Two angry people, however, can unite against a third person and tolerate one another. Indeed, they do not merely tolerate one another but console each other, just as people who are sad over the same matter support one another more and lean upon one another, compared with a situation in which one person is sad while the other is rejoicing. But if they are sad against one another, they cannot tolerate each other at all.

Therefore, in such emotions, one must take upon oneself for a while the very suffering from which one wishes to free another through oneself, and take it up in such a way that it may serve as assistance, not as an equal share in misery—just as one bends down who extends a hand to someone lying on the ground. He does not throw himself down so that both may lie there, but he bends himself nevertheless in order to raise the one who is lying down.

Nothing makes this dutiful labor of willingly bearing the burdens of others readily undertaken except when we consider how much the Lord endured for us. Therefore the Apostle, admonishing us, says:

“Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus. Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

Earlier he had said: “Let no one look to his own interests, but each to those of others” (ibid.). He connected this with the sentence just quoted. For he continues: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus.”

This means only that, just as he, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I), and, although he was without sin, took upon himself our sins, did not attend to his own interests but to ours [Col. 1064A], so we too, in imitation of him, should willingly bear one another’s burdens.

To this thought another is added: he took upon himself a human being, whereas we are human beings; and we ought to consider that the illness, whether of mind or of body, which we see in another person, we also could have had or may have. Therefore let us show to the person whose weakness we wish to bear what we would wish him to show us if we happened to be in that condition and he were not.

This pertains to what the Apostle himself says: “I became all things to all people, so that I might gain all” (1 Cor. IX). He was thinking, of course, that he too might have been subject to the vice from which he desired to free another. He did this rather by compassion, not by lying, as some suppose—especially those who, when they cannot deny their lies, seek the protection of some great example to defend them [Col. 1064B].

Furthermore, we must consider that there is no human being who cannot possess some good which you do not yet possess, even if it remains hidden, and in which he may unquestionably be superior to you. This thought is useful for crushing and taming pride, lest, because certain goods of yours are prominent and visible, you think that another possesses no hidden goods, perhaps of greater weight, by which he surpasses you without your knowing it.

The Apostle does not command us to deceive ourselves or rather to flatter others when he says: “Do nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility of mind let each regard the other as superior to himself” (Phil. II). We must not understand this as meaning that we should pretend to think so without truly thinking it. Rather, we must truly believe that there may be something hidden in another by which he is superior to us, even if the good in which we appear superior to him is not hidden.

These thoughts, which diminish pride and increase love, make us bear our brothers’ burdens not merely with equanimity but most willingly. Yet no judgment should in any way be passed concerning an unknown person, and no one is known except through friendship. Therefore we bear the faults of friends more firmly because their virtues delight and hold us.

No one, then, who puts himself forward to establish a friendship should have his friendship rejected—not so that he may immediately be received, but so that it may be desired that he be received, and so that he may be treated in such a way that he can be received. We may call someone received into friendship when we dare to pour out all our counsels to him.

If there is someone who does not dare to offer himself for friendship unless he is summoned by some temporal honor or dignity of ours, we must descend to him and offer him, with a certain courtesy and humility of spirit, what he himself does not dare to seek.

Certainly, although it happens more rarely, it sometimes occurs that the faults of the person whom we wish to receive into friendship become known to us before his virtues. Offended and in a sense driven back by them, we abandon him and never reach an investigation of the virtues which may be more deeply hidden.

Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ, who wishes us to become his imitators, admonishes us to tolerate his weaknesses, so that through charitable endurance we may be led to certain healthy qualities in which we can rest with delight. For he says: “The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX).

Therefore, if for the sake of Christ’s love we ought not to reject from our hearts even someone who is perhaps sick in every respect, since he can be healed through the word of God, how much less should we reject someone who may appear to us to be entirely sick because, at the beginning of the friendship, we were unable to endure certain of his wounded qualities—and, what is more serious, because in our offense of mind we dared to pass a rash prejudicial judgment upon the whole person?

We do not fear what has been said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged”; and: “With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. VII).

Often the things that are good appear first. Even then, a rash judgment of benevolence must be avoided, lest, when you have thought someone entirely good, the evils that later appear find you secure and unprepared and offend you more severely, so that you hate more bitterly the person whom you had rashly loved—which is wicked.

For even if none of his virtues had preceded, and the evils that later appeared had emerged first, they nevertheless ought to have been endured until you had dealt with him concerning all the things by which such conditions are usually healed. How much more, then, when good qualities preceded—qualities which, like pledges, ought to bind us to endure what comes later?

This, then, is the law of Christ: that we bear one another’s burdens. By loving Christ, we easily endure another’s weakness, even when we do not yet love him for his own virtues. For we think that the Lord whom we love died for him.

The Apostle Paul impressed this love upon us when he said: “And the weak brother will perish through your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died” (1 Cor. XI). Thus, if we love that weak person less because of the vice by which he is weak, we should consider him in relation to the one who died for him.

Not to love Christ is not weakness but death. Therefore we must think with great care, imploring God’s mercy, lest we neglect Christ on account of the weak person, when we ought to love the weak person on account of Christ.

Therefore, father and lord, here your great fatherhood, perfected by an abundance of virtues, has found what it may perfectly consume; and here my smallness, supported by no defenses of good character, has found what it may imperfectly suck. For this is the form that has been placed before us, into which great and small may rightly be impressed. Nor is the person of this man, whom I have introduced as a mediator on my behalf, an objectionable one, whoever the brother may be.

I am unworthy to be called a son, lest I perish through your knowledge. For I confess that I do not understand these things which you write in this manner as proceeding from the root of love or flowing from the fountain of genuine compassion.

Your wisdom ought not to be disguised because of my foolishness, since my foolishness is of the kind to which no answer is necessary: “lest one who answers him become like him,” for I speak as I understand.

Certainly I have never written or spoken in order to exalt the privilege of the apostolic see in such a way that your standing might be diminished by it, but rather so that your authority toward us might increase. Pope Leo clearly demonstrates this when he says (Letter 93, to the bishops of the province of Vienne):

“Let each metropolitan defend the ordination of his own province, together with those who surpass the others in the antiquity of their priesthood, by the right restored to him through us. Let no one dare to claim another’s right for himself; let each be content with his own limits and boundaries.

“For we desire the order and harmony of all the Churches and of the priests to be preserved. We exhort you, bound together by the bond of love, to preserve for your peace and dignity those things which, with God’s inspiration and the blessed Apostle Peter, after all cases had been examined and approved, have now been decreed by us.

“Certainly, we know that your establishment of such things benefits not so much our honor as yours. We do not defend the ordinations of your provinces for ourselves; rather, through your own care, we vindicate them for you, so that no further opportunity may be given to innovation and no opening may remain for a presumptuous person to cancel your privileges.

“For we confess that our own joy increases only if the reverence due to the apostolic see remains inviolate among you and if, through the preservation of priestly discipline, we do not permit your honor to lose what belongs to it through wicked usurpations” [Col. 1066B].

Behold, the measures established in this way by the apostolic see benefit the honor of metropolitans more than they confer anything upon itself.

Therefore everyone who has a human heart ought to be moved by what is discussed in the same pope’s volume concerning anyone who attempts to violate his authority. He says (in the same letter, at the beginning):

“The worship of divine religion, which God’s grace willed to shine throughout all peoples and all nations, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, willed to belong to the office of all the apostles, but he established it principally in the most blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles. From him, as from a kind of head, he willed his gifts to flow into the whole body, so that anyone who dared to withdraw from the solidity of the rock might understand that he was excluded from the mystery of God.

“For he wished him, taken into the fellowship of indivisible unity, to be called what he himself was, saying: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ (Matt. XVI), so that the building of the eternal temple might stand, through the wondrous gift of God’s grace, upon Peter’s solidity.

“Yet whoever attempts to violate this most sacred firmness of the rock, built by God—as we have said—through excessive impious presumption, attempts to break his authority by favoring his own desires and by failing to follow what he received from the ancients. He regards himself as subject to no law and contained by none of the Lord’s institutions; he departs from your custom and ours through the circuit of a novel usurpation, presuming what is unlawful and neglecting what he ought to preserve.

“Nevertheless, trusting that God inspires us, and while the grace of our charity toward you is preserved—the grace which, as you remember, the apostolic see has always extended to your holiness—we strive to correct these matters through more mature counsel and to establish the order of your Churches through labor shared with you: instituting nothing new but renewing what is ancient, so that we may persevere in the established custom handed down to us by our fathers and please our God through the ministry of good works, once the scandals of disturbance have been removed” [Col. 1066C–1067A].

And by persevering in the established custom handed down by the fathers, this man and all his predecessors and successors chose to please God. They endowed archiepiscopal preeminence with due honor, built up episcopal dignity fittingly, and set it at such a height in the structure of the Lord’s house that it could not be struck down by the arrows of wicked men through any force.

“Every kingdom divided against itself,” says the Lord, “will be laid waste” (Matt. XII). This kingdom ought not to be divided, in which there is one heart and one soul in one Spirit.

But surely I shall disclose to my lord what is still turning over in my mind. The greater the apostolic power is proclaimed among secular people, the more strongly, after it, archiepiscopal authority prevailed among them. For the honor of a subject is the power of the prelate: if the prelate is humbled, all who are subject to him are consequently weakened by his diminishment. Thus episcopal dignity also becomes worthless if archiepiscopal primacy is not strengthened.

And I shall say more, Lord—I shall say it: will any archbishop ever have to be told that the excommunication imposed by his fellow bishop is invalid? I have explained many things above, but I shall add one point. Do not fellow bishops themselves ordain the same man as archbishop? Is the archiepiscopal blessing composed of words different from the episcopal blessing? Is not the fullness of the blessing bestowed upon the bishop as a divine gift? Or is a bishop able to be ordained by the archbishop alone, so that he ought consequently to be judged in his own judgments by that archbishop alone?
