For Pope Symmachus testifies (Epistle 1 to Aeonius): “In the likeness of the Trinity, whose power is one and indivisible, there is one priesthood through the various bishops,” neither holier in the just nor less so in the sinner. Nevertheless, provision was made lest everyone claim everything for himself; and therefore in each province there are those among the brethren whose sentence is first, and although they do not possess a dignity different from the common dignity, their order is of the same kind; hence it is also general.

But you, my lord and father, have been appointed guardian in the vineyards. Do not fail to guard your vineyard, seeking not your own interests but those of your fellow bishops, remembering him who desired to become accursed for the salvation of his brethren (Rom. IX).

Why, then, since I am dust and ashes, do I presume to whisper these things to you, the temple of the living God? Certainly, out of the devotion owed to you, not with language worthy of your greatness, unskilled in knowledge—but, having first confessed my ignorance, Augustine strengthens me with his honeyed voice, where he says:

“If, then, you do not have time to search through all the holy pages, to turn over all the volumes of sermons, and to penetrate all the secrets of the Scriptures, hold fast to charity, on which everything depends; thus you will hold fast what you have learned there.”

And again, the same writer says:

“Charity, therefore, is the bond of perfection; charity has the more excellent way; it surpasses knowledge and is above all commandments.”

And again:

“Love makes the saints distinct from the world and causes them to dwell with one accord in the house.”

And again:

“The Apostle placed charity above the tongues of human beings and of angels; he placed it above miracles of faith, above knowledge and prophecy; he placed it even above that great work of mercy by which each person distributes what he possesses to the poor; and finally he placed it above all the sufferings of the body (I Cor. XIII). He placed charity above such great things: possess it, and you will possess everything, because without it it will be of no benefit if you are able to possess anything.”

And again:

“What sort of good is this charity, brothers? What is more precious? What more radiant? What more steadfast? What more useful? What more secure? There are many gifts of God; yet many also possess them who will say: ‘Lord, in your name we prophesied; in your name we cast out demons; in your name we performed many mighty works’ [Col. 1068B] (Matt. VII). He does not answer them, ‘You did not do these things’; for they would not dare to lie before so great a judge, or boast of things they had not done. But because they did not possess charity, he answers them all: ‘I do not know you’ (ibid.). How can someone possess even a little charity who, even when convicted, does not love charity?”

And again:

“Therefore, if we desire to preserve charity whole, we must take care not to do any injury within ourselves to charity itself, which is God, fearing what is written: ‘The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit’ (Wis. I).”

And again:

“When a person begins to possess it, he will possess the Holy Spirit; if he does not possess it, he will be without the Holy Spirit. Just as your body, if it is without the spirit, is dead, so your soul, if it is without the Holy Spirit—that is, without charity—will be regarded as dead” [Col. 1068C].

And again:

“Consider, then, the greatness of this charity, which is poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit from God. Whoever desires to possess it with the Father and with God’s help, as has already been said, can have no vice ruling in him. And truly, since charity itself is God (I John IV), what evil can prevail against the person in whom charity, which is God, dwells?”

And again:

“It is our virtue, for if we are not in it, whatever else we may possess is of no benefit.”

And again:

“The excellence of charity is from God in such a way that charity itself is God. Nothing is more excellent than this gift of God. It alone distinguishes between the children of the eternal kingdom and the children of eternal perdition. Other gifts are also given through the Spirit, but without charity they are worthless. Unless, therefore, the Holy Spirit is bestowed upon each person in such measure as to make him a lover of God and of his neighbor, he does not pass from the left to the right; and the Spirit is not properly called a gift except because of the love which, if someone does not possess it, then—even if he speaks in the tongues of human beings and of angels—he is a clanging bronze and a ringing cymbal. Even if he has prophecy, knows all mysteries and all knowledge, and possesses all faith, so as to move mountains, he is nothing. And if he distributes all his property, and if he hands over his body to be burned, it profits him nothing (I Cor. XII). How great, then, is that good without which such great goods bring no one to eternal life?” And so forth.

[Col. 1069A] Many authors speak at length on this subject; but it was enough for me to catch the fragrance of a few blossoms from this one writer. I have set before your fervor the benefits of a man of such great integrity not to display them ostentatiously, but I have assumed the office of mediator out of fatherly affection and equal filial devotion.

Therefore I place before you, as words of the same writer addressed to Saint Jerome—which I trust you will not disdain—words urging you on my behalf. He says (Epistle 73):

“Why, then, do I try to move against the current of the river, rather than ask forgiveness? I beg you, therefore, by the gentleness of Christ: if I have injured you, forgive me, and do not in turn repay evil with evil by injuring me. You will injure me, however, if you conceal from me my error, should you find one in my actions or words. For if you reproach me for things that ought not to be reproached, you injure yourself more than me [Col. 1069B]. Far be it from your character and holy purpose to do this out of a desire to injure, blaming in me with a malicious tooth something which you know in a truthful mind ought not to be blamed. Therefore either reproach me with a benevolent heart, even if the fault you think should be reproved is absent; or soothe with paternal affection one whom you cannot cast away.

“For it may happen that something appears to you otherwise than the truth holds, while nevertheless you do nothing toward me except what charity requires. I shall gratefully accept even the most friendly reproach, although what can rightly be defended may not deserve reproach; or I shall recognize at once both your benevolence and my fault, and, insofar as the Lord grants it, I shall be found grateful in one respect and corrected in another.

“Why, then, should I fear your perhaps harsh but certainly salutary words, like the boxing gloves of Entellus? He was beaten, not treated; and therefore he was conquered, not healed. But if I receive your medicinal correction calmly, I shall not grieve. If, however, human weakness—or my own weakness—even when I am truthfully reproved, cannot help being somewhat saddened, it is better for the swelling of the head to hurt while it is being treated than while it is being spared and not healed.

“For this is what the man who said it saw sharply: that quarrelsome enemies are often more useful than friends who fear to rebuke. For while the former quarrel, they sometimes speak truths that we should correct; but the latter show less freedom in justice than they ought, fearing to embitter the sweetness of friendship.

“Therefore, even if you seem to yourself an ox—perhaps tired in body from old age, but not in the vigor of your spirit—still laboring with fruitful toil on the Lord’s threshing floor, here I am: if I have said anything wrongly, press your foot down more firmly. The weight of your age ought not to trouble me, provided the chaff of my fault is crushed.”

And so he adds (ibid.):

“Accordingly, what you wrote at the end of your letter, I read or recall with a sigh of great longing: ‘Would that we might deserve your embraces and, by mutual conversation, either teach or learn something!’ And I say in reply: Would that I might immediately deserve the longed-for embraces of your fatherhood more fully in life, and enjoy mutual conversation sweetened by a taste of paternal affection! And would that I might deserve to learn from you what would be useful to me, since I know that you are able to draw out for me everything necessary!

“For I know that I could never be educated in the knowledge of the Scriptures in comparison with you, even if I had devoted all the days of my life to pursuing this study. Therefore [lacuna] I would wish that those things might be written which would be useful for my smallness to read, desirable to recall, and praiseworthy to display to others, as befits your dignity; for a good name is better than great riches, lest at some later time someone write about your greatness and my smallness.”

This holy mediator Augustine writes the following in the same letter:

“Finally, what friend would not be feared as a future enemy, if what we lament could arise between Jerome and Rufinus? O wretched and pitiable condition! O uncertain knowledge of present circumstances in the intentions of friends, where there is no foreknowledge of the future! But why should I think that this ought to be lamented by one about another, when a human being is himself unknown to himself with respect to the future? For he may perhaps know, however imperfectly, what he is now; but what he will later be he does not know” [Col. 1070C].

And at the end of the same letter he says:

“Nevertheless, I should have found him somehow gentler than you, who are armed in this manner.”

May your armed fatherhood deign to hear this, because my gentle smallness is ready to obey this command, lest what he adds come to pass:

“This is a great and sad miracle: that from such friendships we have reached such enmities.”

But rather may he immediately pursue what he promises:

“It will be joyful, and much greater still, to return from such enmities to our former concord.”

This will immediately follow if knowledge that steals away ceases, and charity that restrains does not cease. To this may the Lord direct our hearts in the charity of God and the patience of Christ; and may the God of peace and love, who is Trinity and unity, always be with you.

## IX. THE SAME AUTHOR’S LETTER TO THE SAME MAN

Concerning agreement with the excommunication he had imposed, which he was seeking.

[Col. 1069]

[Col. 1069D] To the venerable archbishop of Rheims, Hincmar, Hincmar, the least of the bishops of the Church of Laon, offers the munificence of salvation in Christ.

Because you so earnestly request a letter expressing my agreement with the excommunication carried out by you, write back to me in your own letter as well, if you have added to that document the matters which I reported to you—through Heddon, the envoy of my smallness and my fellow minister, and also the head of the Church over which I unworthily preside—as seeming, at any rate, to accord with reason and authority.

For my own part, once the proper time has been received, as the matter requires, I shall finally seek to respond concerning my agreement, examining the matter thoroughly and respectfully—not evasively—in a manner regularly suitable to every matter and place under the sun. With God granting it, I shall promptly and carefully arrange to reply by a canonical letter, with my wish fulfilled and my life accompanying it [Col. 1071A]. Otherwise, in this matter also I recall that wise man whom you frequently mention, who says: “He who commands the impossible makes himself contemptible.”

## X. HINCMAR’S APPEAL AND PROTEST

He had once presided over the Church of Laon.

[Col. 1071]

[Col. 1071B] My lord and supreme father of fathers, ruler of bishops, called John in name and merit, hear the voice of my protest and heed the voice of my supplication, having compassion on the cause of my calamity.

I was summoned by the archbishop of Rheims to a synod at the village of Douzy, which he appointed for the first week of August, and he warned me to be prepared to answer there concerning certain matters. When I hurried to it, I was separated from my sheep in the middle of the journey by hostile violence; I was deprived and stripped of all my possessions; and by those same enemies I was brought as far as the aforesaid village.

When I arrived there, King Charles was already standing before my archbishop, holding a document in his hand and judging me to be a perjurer because I had sent to Rome without his permission [Col. 1071C], and charging me with having accused him. The same archbishop ordered me to answer these accusations.

I replied that, concerning the matters about which he had warned me to be prepared to answer at that synod, I was ready to respond in writing. I held those writings in my hands, but he did not allow the synod to receive them, because he ordered them to be handed over to him, while I was unwilling to give them to a man whom I suspected.

Concerning my cleric, named Bertarius, whom he suddenly demanded but who was not present when summoned, I replied that the men who had come with me would have verified the matter for him, if they had been allowed to come. But afterward the same archbishop did not question me about these things; instead, he repeatedly ordered me to answer the king’s accusation.

I protested that canonical authority did not teach that a man who had been stripped and deprived of his possessions, and who was additionally being detained by enemies, ought to answer at all [Col. 1071D]. I also added that I regarded him not merely as suspect but as manifestly hostile to me. Therefore I appealed to the apostolic see, for the love of God and the honor of Saint Peter, both concerning the king’s accusation itself and concerning the prejudice I was suffering from that archbishop [Col. 1072B].

Holding them in my hands, I read the authorities of Pope Julius and Pope Felix, namely, the provisions which they set forth concerning episcopal appeals. By appealing to the apostolic see, with my body prostrate, I begged that these provisions be observed for me; but my petition obtained none of these things.

Nor did the apostolic letters which he had personally given me have any force, although they summoned me and warned me not to delay coming by procrastination if I did not wish to suffer damage to my status.

The aforesaid archbishop imposed a judgment upon me, declaring that I was to be removed from episcopal office. But the others groaned and wept, among whom I deserved to have no enemy. They held in their hands writings imposed upon them by the same archbishop, but, unwilling to utter them aloud, they reluctantly stammered out scarcely a few words [Col. 1072C]. Nevertheless, they did not at all hope that access to the apostolic see could be denied to me. Therefore, preserving in every respect the judgment of the apostolic see, they brought the reading to an end.

After this I was sent into exile, where for two years I was kept in good health, though for some time I was guarded in fetters. When nearly two years had passed, I was additionally blinded, and I was held until now. As soon as I was released and able to come, I immediately approached you and the presence of your most merciful serenity.

Now I humbly beseech your clemency and your supreme fatherhood to prepare a judgment of equity concerning me. I have been, and remain, reserved for you according to canonical institution and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs [Col. 1072D]. I earnestly request that I obtain this through the love of God and the veneration of blessed Peter, from the piety of your fatherhood—both because of the multitude of my misery and because of the greatness of your piety—which may be kindled by love of the most merciful Redeemer, who acquired me with his own blood and consecrated me, whatever I may be, by his holy gift.

## In the year of the Lord 880

Isaac, bishop of Langres.

[Col. 1073]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

From *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV.

[Col. 1073A] Isaac, a cleric of the Church of Laon, attended the first synod of Quierzy in 849 as Pardulus’s deacon, and the second synod of Soissons in 855 as a deacon of the Church of Rheims—unless, perhaps, this was another man of the same name.

By the authority of Charles the Bald he was designated bishop of Langres. After long disputes and controversies with Wlfadus and Anscharius, who were striving for the see, he finally prevailed and peacefully held the episcopal staff. Hence it came about that, while the others were treated as of no account, he was regarded as Theutbald’s immediate successor.

Thus the Besançon Chronicle says: “After the death of Theutbald, Lord Isaac assumed the episcopate.” The Chronicle of Saint Benignus likewise says: “He acquired the surname ‘the Good’ because of the kindness of his character and his overflowing benevolence toward all.”

“This man,” says the old Martyrology of the Church of Saint Benignus, “shining with the grace of remarkable holiness, became a pattern of life to his followers and, strengthened by royal authority, enlarged the bishopric entrusted to him by God through wise diligence. Among other sanctuaries was this monastery at Dijon. [lacuna] It had been destroyed by the hostile devastation of the pagans. As the hour of his death brought his days to an end, he restored its condition as far as he was able, though not as he wished. In rebuilding it, he devoted himself with such complete dedication that he not only endowed it with lands and ornaments granted by royal gift, but also appointed an abbot according to the rule of the holy Father Benedict over the monastic flock, and designated there the place of his burial” [Col. 1073B].

The Chronicle of the same church reports the same things and adds: “He accomplished all this with the illustrious King Charles encouraging and assisting him.” In a similar manner the Besançon Chronicle says: “Following the good example of his predecessors, he bestowed many benefits upon this monastery.”

In 859 he took part in the Council of Langres, where sixteen canons or capitula were enacted, and in the Council of Toul at Saponaria, where Anscharius was ordered to make no further claim within the bishopric of Langres. The capitula of the Synod of Langres were confirmed, and he subscribed the letter of the Fathers to Wenilo, archbishop of Sens.

That same year, together with several bishops and Lothar, the nephew of Charles the Bald, he obtained the restoration of his Church at the village of Umbiliacum. He also subscribed the canons of the synod.

He attended the second Council of Toul at the village of Douzy in 860, and, at the request of Abbot Hilduin, subscribed the confirmation of the privileges of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours.

He also attended the Council of Pîtres, later transferred to the city of Soissons, where in 862 he confirmed by his subscription the privilege granted by Abbot Hilduin and King Charles to the monks of Saint-Denis.

Charles the Bald drew up a diploma in which he says: “Because our dearest Isaac, venerable bishop of the Church of Langres, has requested it, he grants to the churches of Saint Mammes and Saint Stephen of Dijon the right to mint money and to hold a market.”

But difficulty arises in dating the document. Perardus reports it and concludes as follows: “Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, in the second indiction, in the thirty-fourth year of the reign of the most glorious King Charles,” and in the margin he writes [Col. 1074A] the year of Christ 863. This cannot stand: Charles’s thirty-fourth regnal year corresponds to the Christian year 873, but the indiction conflicts with this, since in 873 it was not the second but the sixth. If we follow the indiction, it must be said that the document was issued in 863; but then the twenty-fourth year of Charles’s reign ought to be recorded.

At the request of Jonah, bishop of Autun, he granted two altars to Abbot Eigilo—later archbishop of Sens—and to the monastery of Flavigny in 865.

He attended the third Synod of Soissons in 866, and with the other bishops subscribed the synodal letter to Nicholas I, pontiff of the Roman Church, concerning the case of Wlfadus; likewise another letter to the same pope concerning the incursions of the Bretons, and so forth. Finally, he subscribed the solemn privilege granted by the synod to the monastery of Solignac.

He also attended the Council of Verberie in the same year, where, with the other Fathers, he strengthened by his subscription the privilege granted to the monastery of Saint Vedastus of Arras.

In 868 he transferred the body of Saint Variolus, also called Verolus or Vorlus, from the village of Marcigny, where it had lain since the time of King Guntram, to Châtillon on the Seine [Col. 1074B].

At the Council of Pîtres, held in the presence of Charles the Bald in 869, he subscribed the privilege of Egilo, archbishop of Sens, for the monastery of Saint Peter.

At Douzy, in 870, he added his name to the profession of obedience made by Hincmar of Laon to the king and to the metropolitan of Rheims.

That same year he was a royal envoy, as is clear from a charter reported by Perardus, in which the following is recorded: “Alcaudus came to the public court in the village called Curtanonus, before Isaac the bishop and Odo the count, or Bertramnus, the royal envoys,” and so forth.

In the thirtieth year of the reign of our lord King Charles—that is, 870—he vindicated the rights of Saint Benignus against a certain Hildebertus. In the same year, at the general synod in the village of Baziacum, he brought a certain dispute to an end.

In 871, when King Charles had come to Langres, Isaac obtained from him letters asserting all the properties previously granted to the Church of Saint Mammes and declaring them free from every burden of human servitude.

In 875 he attended the Council of Chalon, where, after the ordination of Adalgisus or Adalgarius, he confirmed with his colleagues the matters pertaining to the monastery of Tournus [Col. 1074C].

“Lord Isaac the bishop and Bertilo the chorepiscopus summoned the priest Andesualdus at the village of Siliacum, because he was unjustly retaining the property of Saint Benignus; eventually he restored it. Given on Wednesday, in the month of March, in the thirty-sixth year of the reign of our lord Charles, and in the second year of his empire”—the year of Christ 876 [that is, 877].

That same year he attended the Council of Ponthion and strengthened its canons with his subscription, as well as the foundation of the abbey of Carilocum.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirty-sixth year of King Charles’s reign but the first year of his empire, a certain Gislebertus, before Isaac [Col. 1074D] the bishop, gave his church at the village of Savigny to Saint Benignus and to Abbot Bertilo. In that same year he also ordered other property to be restored to the same monastery.

When Pope John VIII had come to Gaul, he wrote to Isaac, asking him to send envoys to Chalon who would guide the pope’s journey by the direct route to Troyes and prepare suitable lodgings for him throughout his own diocese [Col. 1075A]. Isaac did so, and in 878 he attended the Council at Troyes over which the aforesaid pope presided. Among the many matters settled there, the dispute that had arisen between the Churches of Troyes and Langres over the administration of Vandœuvre—which each claimed for itself—was brought to an end; the matter was assigned to the bishopric of Langres.

Finally, after carrying out many distinguished works, the devout bishop set out for Rheims, fell suddenly ill at Châlons, and there rested in Christ on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, after twenty-five years spent in episcopal government.

His body was transferred to Rheims and buried there. Later, with the permission of King Charles, called the Simple, and through the efforts of his successor, Bishop Argrimus, it was brought back to Dijon and buried in the Church of Saint Benignus on the fourth day before the Nones of February, as Isaac had ordered while alive. This is reported by the martyrology of the same church, already cited at the beginning of this article.

“He died around the year 880,” says the Chronicle of Langres. If this is so, the beginning of his episcopate should be dated not from 859, when he peacefully obtained possession of the bishopric, but approximately from 856.

His anniversary is celebrated every year on the seventh day before the Kalends of August. For this purpose revenues from the places called in French *Voisines* were assigned, says the Colbertine manuscript 765 [Col. 1076A].

He composed a book called the *Canons of Isaac*, because he selected whatever was most useful from the books of the canons and compressed it into a single volume. These are the words of the Chronicle of Saint Benignus.

Jacques Sirmond made the work public at the end of volume III of the Councils. It is also found in volume VIII of Labbe’s Councils, p. 698, and in volume II of Baluze’s *Capitularies*.

A letter concerning the canon of the Mass is also attributed to him, published by our Dom Lucas d’Achery in volume I of the *Spicilegium*. But Baluze proves that it does not belong to Isaac, bishop of Langres, but to another abbot of the same name, of the Cistercian order at Poitiers. Acherius himself acknowledges this in volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*, in the index of authors and treatises, etc., p. 33.

Hincmar wrote to Isaac on behalf of a certain soldier whom he had struck with an anathema, urging him to act more gently toward the man because of the pressing necessity arising from the pagan incursions. For that anathema does not last any longer than the person perseveres in sin. He also wrote concerning Isaac’s nephews, who had been brought up in the household of the same lord Hincmar, and on several other matters, as Flodoard reports [Col. 1076B].

[Col. 1075]

# THE CANONS OF ISAAC, BISHOP OF LANGRES

[Note: [Col. 1075D] There is no title in the ancient manuscript. We supplied the one suggested by the Chronicle of Saint Benignus, where this work is mentioned in these words: “The blessed bishop Isaac composed the book called the *Canons of Isaac*, and, selecting whatever was most useful from the books of the canons, compressed it into a single volume. He excerpted it from the books of the *Capitularies*, as he calls them, but especially from the three later books which Benedict the Levite added to the collection of Abbot Ansegisus [Col. 1076D]. Although everything contained in these books, as the same Benedict states near the end of Book VII, had been confirmed by legates of the apostolic see, it is nevertheless clear that not everything pertained to Boniface and Zacharias, as the following preface seems to suggest, but only those things described at the beginning of Book V. —SIRMOND.]

(From Sirmond, *General Councils*, vol. VIII, col. 598.)

## ISAAC’S PREFACE

[Col. 1075C] When ecclesiastical necessity has required a pastoral judgment to be pronounced against delinquents and those who err, it has frequently happened that the remedies which anxious fathers prepare with the greatest ardor of charity and piety are rejected by their sick children to their own ruin.

Because they do not properly consider either the affection of those who treat them or the danger of their own condemnation, they disdain whatever is offered and despise medicines as ineffective simply because they are familiar. Therefore I, Isaac, unworthy bishop of Langres, considering the negligence of certain people who are insufficiently compliant, their complaint against pastoral solicitude, and the insolence of the wicked, who chatter that everything said by us for their correction or protection is fabricated, contrived, and invented [Col. 1075D], have judged it useful to review certain most salutary capitula of decrees which Boniface, venerable archbishop of Mainz and legate of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, wrote together with Carloman, the orthodox prince of the Franks, in two councils of bishops for the honor and advancement of the Church of God.

Pope Zacharias also confirmed these capitula by apostolic authority in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 742 and established them as irrefragably binding upon all the faithful of the Church of God. I have therefore gathered from them certain matters that most frequently arise for discussion and collected them into a small unified body for my benefit and that of my people [Col. 1076C], so that if they slander our provisions or attempt to undermine them by a hostile interpretation, they may henceforth be silenced, restrained equally by apostolic and royal authority, and, when the need arises, submit—even unwillingly—to remedies that bring salvation.

## Concerning secular courts or assemblies, and the times when they ought not to be held

We wish to make a firm declaration to all counts and to all ministers of the commonwealth: from the Wednesday before the beginning of Lent, and even on that Wednesday, until after the octave of Easter, they must not presume to hold a public court or assembly, except concerning the reconciliation and pacification of those who are at discord [Col. 1076D].

Likewise, they must observe the same rule from the Wednesday before the Nativity of the Lord until after the consecrated days. They must also make every effort to honor with the same observance the days set apart during the fasts of the Four Seasons, during the Rogations, and during the days of Pentecost [Col. 1077A].

## No one may presume to hold a public court or assembly within the immunities of churches

It was decreed that no count, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, should presume to hold a court or assembly within the immunities or precincts of churches, or to injure any member of the household of those churches on any pretext or through any rash act.

If he does so, he shall pay the lord’s fine and, in addition, make full satisfaction according to canonical institution to God and to the church that he has injured. If he delays doing this, he shall be excluded from the assembly of the faithful until, having accepted penance, he makes amends for the guilt he has committed.

[Col. 1077B]## Concerning the holdings of each church

It has been decreed that one complete holding (*mansus*) be assigned to each church without any service being required from it, and that the priests established there perform no service except ecclesiastical service from the tithes, the offerings of the faithful, the houses, the courtyards or gardens situated beside the church, or the aforesaid holding.

If they possess anything more, they shall render from it what is owed to their superiors.

# FIRST TITLE: CONCERNING PENITENTS

## Chapter I. Penitents are not to be compelled to drink wine

From Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 54.

[Col. 1077C] No priest or layman shall compel a penitent to drink wine or eat meat unless he immediately gives one or two denarii on his behalf, according to the character of the penance.

## Chapter II. Concerning the killing of a man performing public penance

From the same book, chapter 107.

Whoever kills a man performing public penance shall pay our fine threefold and pay his *wergild* to his nearest relatives.

## Chapter III. Concerning a penitent whose crime has become widely known

From the same book, chapter 117 (Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 53).

At the Council of Carthage it is prescribed concerning this matter [Col. 1077D] that if someone’s public and notorious crime has disturbed the entire Church, hands are to be laid upon him before the apse.

Elsewhere, in the canons or decretals of Pope Leo, the same matter is prescribed: that the absolution of penitents should take place through the laying on of the bishops’ hands and their supplications. And there are many other provisions of this kind, and similar ones.

## Chapter IV. Concerning penitents who have received the Eucharist in illness

From the same book, chapter 108 (V, 54).

Penitents who have received the Eucharist as viaticum during illness must not consider themselves absolved without the laying on of hands if they recover.

## Chapter V. Absolution of penitents is to take place through the laying on of the hands of bishops or through the prayers of priests

From the same chapter, 120 (V, 56).

[Col. 1078A] If someone has undertaken penance in danger, in peace, or in illness, and it is immediately believed that he is about to die, he is to be reconciled through the laying on of hands, and the Eucharist is to be poured into his mouth.

## Chapter VI. A penitent is to receive Communion after showing the fruits of penance

From the same chapter, 121 (V, 57).

A penitent, after showing the necessary fruits of penance, is to receive legitimate Communion together with the reconciliatory laying on of hands.

## Chapter VII. When penitents seek penance, they are to receive sackcloth upon their heads from a priest

From the same chapter, 122 (V, 58).

[Col. 1078B] At the time when penitents seek penance, they are to receive from a priest the laying on of hands and sackcloth upon their heads, as has been established everywhere.

## Chapter VIII. During the entire time of fasting, hands are to be laid upon penitents by a priest

From the same book, chapter 123 (V, 59).

During the entire time of fasting, hands are to be laid upon penitents by a priest.

## Chapter IX. Those who have fallen are to be absolved through the laying on of a bishop’s hand

From the same chapter, 124 (V, 60).

We must not believe that those who have lapsed from the faith have been absolved unless [Col. 1078C] through the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

## Chapter X. Penitents who die before reconciliation are to receive Communion

From the same chapter, 125 (V, 61).

It has been decreed that those who, having undertaken penance, depart to God before reconciliation are to receive Communion because they honored penance. If they recover, they are to remain in the order of penitents, so that at the appointed time they may receive legitimate Communion through reconciliation and the laying on of the bishop’s hands, or of priests at his command.

## Chapter XI. Criminal sins are to be cleansed through many fasts and frequent layings on of hands by a priest

From the same chapter, 126 (V, 62).

It has been decreed that criminal sins be cleansed through many fasts, frequent layings on of the hands of priests [Col. 1078D], and their supplications, according to the statutes of the canons. No one is to believe himself absolved from his crimes without the laying on of the bishop’s hands, or of a priest at the bishop’s command.

It is not surprising that the absolution of sins takes place through the laying on of hands and the prayers of priests, since in the old law the Lord commanded that the priest’s hand be laid upon the head of the victim. For just as sins were then remitted through that victim, so now, through the invocation of the Holy Spirit—which is the remission of sins—and through the laying on of the hands of bishops, or of other priests acting by their authority, or through their supplications, sins are remitted.

For when the Lord raised Lazarus, he said to his disciples: “Take away the stone” (John XI)—that is understood to mean, so that the dead man might rise [Col. 1079A]. He thereby gave an example: just as they themselves take away the stone with their hands so that the dead man may rise, so they and their successors should lay hands upon penitents, so that through the laying on of hands and their prayers they may cause the dead man to rise from the tomb—that is, the sinner from his vices—and raise him up.

And just as they loosen Lazarus, bound with bands—that is, with cords—when the Lord commanded them, saying, “Unbind him and let him go,” so these priests, through their supplications, with the Lord’s help and the Holy Spirit accompanying them—the Spirit who always works in these matters—are to loosen the bonds of sins through the laying on of hands, give the absolved the holy Eucharist at the time established by the holy Fathers, and permit them to depart.

## Chapter XII. That penance should be given to penitents according to canonical authority, and that those suspended from communion should first be made to keep vigil at the church’s service

From the same, chapter 128 (V, 63).

[Col. 1079B]

Penance is to be imposed upon penitents according to the rule of the canons. First, they are to be suspended from communion and made to keep vigil at the church services; and among the other penitents they are to come frequently for the laying on of hands. When the period of satisfaction has been completed, the penitents are to be reconciled through the priest’s prayer and the laying on of hands, according to the order of the sacraments and the canons, and confirmed by holy communion.

## Chapter XIII. Concerning those penitents who have been separated from communion

From the same book, chapter 129 (V, 64).

[Col. 1079C]

Those who are separated from communion are to receive communion, through the laying on of hands, in the places where they had been secluded. Let no one believe himself absolved from sins without the reconciliatory laying on of hands; rather, through the laying on of hands and the prayers of the priests, let him be reconciled, as ecclesiastical authority prescribes.

## Chapter XIV. That a penitent at the approach of death should not be long suspended from reconciliation

From the same, chapter 130 (V, 65).

[Col. 1079D]

He who performs penance in danger of death is not to be kept long from the grace of reconciliation. But if the danger of death is certainly pressing, then, once penance has been received through the laying on of hands, reconciliation must immediately be supplied, lest the sick man depart from this human life before receiving the gift of reconciliation. Otherwise, it might somehow seem to those who survive that there is an unending grief, if the nature of death should suddenly remove from the present life a man cut off from the members of the Church, who certainly had not merited the grace of reconciliation.

Accordingly, in accordance with the decree of Pope Leo (Letter to Theodore of Fréjus):

> “For those who, in a time of necessity and at the moment of pressing danger, implore the protection of penance and immediately afterward reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied, because we can neither impose measures upon God’s mercy nor define its times.”

As for those who, having received penance, depart from this life before being reconciled, although there is a diversity of prescriptions [Col. 1080A] concerning this matter, we have nevertheless approved the judgment of those who, in greater number, have decreed more humanely in such cases: that the memory of such persons be commended in the churches and that an offering dedicated for their spirits be accepted on their behalf.

## Chapter XV. Concerning penitents who perform penance for more serious or less serious offenses

From the same, chapter 131 (V, 67).

Concerning penitents who perform penance either for more serious offenses or for less serious ones, the custom of the Roman Church indicates that, if no illness intervenes, they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter. Nevertheless, it belongs to the priest to judge the gravity of the offenses, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession [Col. 1080B] and to the tears and weeping by which he is corrected, and order him to be released when he sees that the satisfaction is appropriate. If someone falls ill and reaches the point of mortal danger, however, he is to be released before the time of Easter, lest he depart from this world without communion.

## Chapter XVI. That penitents who perform penance for more serious sins should remain three years among the hearers if they have performed true penance

From the same chapter 132 (V, 69).

Penitents who perform penance for more serious offenses, if they repent from the heart, are to remain three years among the hearers, as the Council of Nicaea decreed concerning the lapsed (canon 11). For five or seven years they are to remain among the penitents under the hands of the priests; [Col. 1080C] for two years they are not to be permitted to present offerings, but are merely to join the people in prayer.

Let them not be ashamed to bow their necks before God, since they did not fear to deny him. If, however, as mortal beings, they begin to be pressed by the end of life within the limits of the prescribed time, help is to be given to those who implore it—whether by the bishop who imposed the penance, or by another who has verified that it was imposed, or likewise by a priest, but only at the order or with the permission of their own bishop. Through the laying on of hands and the absolution of priestly prayers, viaticum is not to be denied to those departing from this world.

To children—so called because of their purity—or to clerics, or to laypeople, or even to comparable young women, whose age is supported by ignorance, communion is to be restored after they have been detained for some time under the laying on of hands. But if [Col. 1080D] before the appointed period of penance, they recover after being despaired of by physicians or oppressed by evident signs of death, let us observe in their case what the Nicene canons ordained: that they be counted among those who communicate only in prayer, until the period of time granted to them has been completed.

## Chapter XVII. That those who perform public penance should remain one year among the hearers in sackcloth

From the same, chapter 136 (V, 71).

[Col. 1081A]

Those who perform public penance ought to spend one year, or until the great day, among the hearers in sackcloth. When the people enter the church, they should, drenched in tears, ask pardon and humbly beg the people to pray for them.

For three years they are to remain among the penitents under the hands of the priests, in the place behind the church door appointed for penitents; and, separated from the people within the church itself, though no longer lying prostrate on the ground, they are to ask pardon humbly and from the heart, with bowed face and head, as stated above, and request that prayers be offered for them.

For two years they are in every way not to be permitted to present offerings, but are merely to join the people in prayer, so that in the seventh year, at the Lord’s Supper—that is, through the laying on of hands by the bishop, or, if he is absent, by other priests at his command—they may attain completion and receive the grace of Catholic communion through the absolution of priestly prayers.

During these seven years they are to persist in fasting, prayers, tears, almsgiving, and acts of generosity, [Col. 1081B] as best they can, and in weeping. They must take the greatest care that such things do not happen to them again, so that they may deserve to hear that saying of the Lord: “Go, and sin no more” (John 8).

## Chapter XVIII. Concerning transgressing penitents

From the same book, chapter 137 (V, 72).

Those who sin through frequent transgression, or repeat their penance, are to be restrained or condemned by repeated judgment unless they endeavor to correct through satisfaction the things in which they have transgressed, so that, unwillingly, they may amend what they did not willingly purge away.

If someone refuses and proves disobedient to the commands of his priest, [Col. 1081C] let him be excommunicated according to the measure of his fault. If anyone presumes to communicate with such persons before their reconciliation and satisfaction, without the permission of their own bishop, let him be subject to the same excommunication.

The priests to whom these matters are known to pertain, if they refuse to admonish such persons because of any gift, favor, or negligence; if they do not receive those returning through satisfaction; or if, when such persons show contempt, they do not expel them from the church, are to be punished by the same sentence, until either a sentence of correction or one of condemnation concerning them has been issued.

## Chapter XIX. Concerning more negligent penitents

From the same, chapter 139 (V, 74).

More negligent penitents are to be received more slowly.

## Chapter XX. Concerning one who asks for penance during illness

From the same, chapter 40 (V, 75).

[Col. 1081D]

If someone asks for penance during illness and, by chance, while the invited priest is coming to him, is rendered speechless by the illness or falls into delirium, those who heard him are to give testimony, and he is to receive penance. If he is believed to be immediately dying, he is to be reconciled through the laying on of hands, and the Eucharist is to be poured into his mouth.

If he survives, he is to be informed by the witnesses mentioned above that his request has been fulfilled, and he is to be subjected to the prescribed period of penance for as long as the priest who imposed the penance judges appropriate.

## Chapter XXI. That penitents should not believe themselves absolved without the laying on of hands

From the same, chapter 41 (V, 76).

[Col. 1082A]

Penitents who, during illness, have received the Eucharist as viaticum are not to believe themselves absolved without the laying on of hands, if they survive.

## Chapter XXII. Concerning penitents who die by chance on a journey or at sea before fulfilling the laws of penance

From the same, chapter 42 (V, 77).

Penitents who die by chance on a journey or at sea before fulfilling the laws of penance, where no priest could come to their aid, are to be commended in memory through prayers and offerings.

## Chapter XXIII. That no one should end his life without communion or be deprived of anointing with blessed oil

From book VI, chapter 75 (VI, 75).

[Col. 1082B]

If someone is found to be ill, he should not end his life without communion, nor be deprived of anointing with consecrated oil. If he perceives that his end is near, his soul is to be commended to God by the priest’s prayers with the most holy Body.

## Chapter XXIV. That no priest should claim more than one church for himself

From the same, chapter 76 (VI, 73).

[Col. 1082C]

Therefore it has pleased everyone that no priest should claim more than one church for himself. For just as each layman ought to have no more than one wife, so each priest ought to have no more than one church.

## Chapter XXV. Concerning the non-reception of other parishes’ penitents

From the same book, chapter 131 (VI, 129).

Those who are separated from communion on account of their offense are to receive communion in whatever places they had been excluded.

## Chapter XXVI. That the duration of penitents’ penance should depend upon the bishop’s judgment

From book VII, chapter 5 (VII, 3).

The bishops shall have the power, after examining the manner of life of penitents, either to deal with them more humanely or to add further time. Above all, their former and subsequent life is to be investigated; and humanity is then to be extended to them accordingly.

## Chapter XXVII. Concerning the conduct and faith of penitents

From the same book, chapter 6 (VII, 4).

The conduct and faith of penitents shorten the period.

## Chapter XXVIII. Concerning satisfaction in penance

From the same book, chapter 20 (VII, 12).

Satisfaction in penance is to be weighed not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart.

## Chapter XXIX. Concerning the measure of penance

From the same book, chapter 21 (V, 68).

The periods of penitence are to be established with moderation [Col. 1083A] and according to judgment, insofar as priests see the dispositions of those who have turned back to be devoted. They are likewise to consider advanced age and the necessities arising from any dangers or illnesses.

## Chapter XXX. Concerning the bishop’s judgment regarding penitents

From the same book, chapter 30 (VII, 18).

According to the difference among sins, the bishops are to determine the periods of penance by their judgment.

## Chapter XXXI. Concerning the remission of penance

From the same book, chapter 36 (V, 67).

Penitents, whoever they may be, who perform penance for more serious or less serious faults are to be released on the Thursday before Easter, if [Col. 1083B] no illness intervenes. Nevertheless, it belongs to the priest to judge the gravity of the offenses.

## Chapter XXXII. That penitents should not engage in profit-seeking commerce

From the same book, chapter 68 (VII, 44).

It is not fitting for penitents to engage in profit-seeking commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the transaction between seller and buyer.

## Chapter XXXIII. That no one should absolve a penitent from another parish

From the same book, chapter 77 (VII, 49).

No priest in another city or diocese, nor a priest in a parish or a bishop in a city, is to receive a penitent, one placed under the hand of a priest, [Col. 1083C] or one who says that he has been reconciled, without the consent and letters of the bishop or priest.

## Chapter XXXIV. Concerning those who die after receiving penance

From the same book, chapter 138 (VII, 101).

Concerning those who depart from the body after receiving penance, it has been decided that they should be admitted to communion without the reconciliatory laying on of hands, since this is sufficient consolation for the dying, according to the definitions of the Fathers, who appropriately called such communion viaticum.

If they survive, they are to remain in the order of penitents, so that, once they have displayed the necessary fruits of penance, [Col. 1083D] they may receive legitimate communion with the reconciliatory laying on of hands.

## Chapter XXXV. That no priest should dare to reconcile penitents without consulting the bishop

From the same book, chapter 202 (VII, 143).

It has been established and prohibited in the holy canons that no priest should presume to reconcile a public penitent without consulting the bishop, except, perhaps, one in danger of death.

Rather, all public penitents are to gather on the Thursday before Easter, which is the Lord’s Supper, in the city, in ashes and sackcloth, with bowed faces, into the presence of the bishop. There they are to be reconciled [Col. 1084A] and judged by the bishop canonically and in due order, as contained in the Sacramentary and the Roman Order. They are to be consoled and instructed, and it is to be preached to them what they must henceforth do and what they must avoid. Moreover, through divine prayers and the laying on of hands, they are to be healed by the bishop.

At no time has a priest been permitted to reconcile a penitent in the public Mass without the bishop’s permission. If anyone presumes to do this, he is to be punished by canonical correction.

## Chapter XXXVI. That one who mourns should abstain from banquets

From the same, chapter 243 (VII, 143).

One who mourns should abstain from banquets, ornaments, and white clothing.

## Chapter XXXVII. Concerning penitents, and how they should receive penance

From the same, chapter 310 (VII, 231).

[Col. 1084B]

At the time when penitents ask for penance, they are to receive the laying on of hands and sackcloth from the priest. If they have not cut their hair or changed their clothing, they are to be rejected; and unless they have performed penance worthily, they are not to be received.

Penance is not to be entrusted readily to young people, because of the frailty of their age. Nevertheless, viaticum is not to be denied to anyone who lies at the point of death.

## Chapter XXXVIII. Concerning female penitents who presume to marry other men after their husbands’ death

From the same, chapter 317 (VII, 237).

A female penitent who, after her husband’s death, presumes to marry another man, and one who joins herself to a stranger through either a suspect or forbidden [Col. 1084C] intimacy, is to be kept away from the thresholds of the church together with that man. It has likewise been decided that this rule is to be observed concerning a man placed under penance.

## Chapter XXXIX. Concerning the hearing of the faithful’s confessions, and how the period of penance is to be established according to its measure and character

From the same, chapter 78 (VII, 294).

When he hears the confession of sins from any member of the faithful, the priest must inquire first how the sin was committed: whether it was committed afterward again, or frequently; whether voluntarily or under compulsion; whether through drunkenness or by some other device. When he has discovered from what source the root of that sin proceeded, he is then to apply an appropriate remedy.

[Col. 1084D]

What kind of remedy is to be applied to the sin must be established according to the authoritative canons and the holy Fathers, not according to human preference but according to God’s will. In this matter, neither human will nor favor is to be pursued; rather, God’s will is to be sought in all things, so that through worthy prayers and worthy repentance one may be able to appease the vengeance of almighty God, which one has provoked by one’s own fault.

# Title II. Concerning Homicides

## Chapter I. Concerning priests who have been killed

From book V, chapter 186 (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 15).

A slain priest [Col. 1085A] is to be paid for to the bishop to whose parish he belongs, according to the capitulary of our glorious father Charles, specifically as follows: the bishop is to assign half of his wergeld to the needs of the church over which he presided, and is to distribute the other half justly in alms for him, because no heir of his seems closer to us than the one who joined him to the Lord.

## Chapter II. Concerning homicides committed in churches or in their atria

From the same, chapter 220 (IV, 13).

If anyone kills a man in a church, either for a trivial reason or without cause, he is to make composition for his life. But if they have quarreled outside, and one has fled into the church, and there, defending himself, has killed the other, then, if he has no witnesses to this deed, he is to affirm by oath, together with twelve [Col. 1085B] legitimate oath-helpers, that he killed him while defending himself. Afterward he is to be compelled to pay 600 solidi to the church whose portion he polluted by that homicide, and in addition our ban.

The man who was killed is to lie without composition; then the killer is to receive, according to canonical judgment, an appropriate penance for the crime he committed.

If a slave has committed this, he is to be examined by the judgment of boiling water, to determine whether he did it voluntarily or in self-defense. If his hand is burned, he is to be killed. If it is not, his master is to pay to the church according to the slave’s wergeld, or, if he wishes, hand him over to that church.

Concerning an ecclesiastical, fiscal, or beneficiary slave, we decree that on the first occasion his wergeld is to be paid for him; on the second [Col. 1085C] occasion the slave himself is to be handed over to punishment. Nevertheless, the inheritance of a free man who has been sentenced to death on account of such a crime is to pass to his legitimate heirs.

If such a homicide has been committed in the atrium of a church whose door has been consecrated with the relics of the saints, it is likewise to be amended or compounded. If the church door has not been consecrated, what is committed in the atrium is to be compounded in the manner required for an offense committed after the immunity has been violated.

## Chapter III. Concerning the killing of a man performing public penance

From the same, chapter 234 (V, 18).

Whoever kills a man performing public penance is to pay our ban threefold [Col. 1085D] and pay his wergeld to his relatives.

## Chapter IV. Concerning the prohibition of homicide

From the same, chapter 236 (IV, 20).

Whoever kills a man either for a trivial reason or without cause is to pay his wergeld in composition to those to whom he belongs. Because of such presumption, however, he himself is to be sent into exile for as long as we please; nevertheless, he is not to lose his property.

## Chapter V. Concerning the killing of clerics, priests, and monks

From the same, chapter 261 (III, 25).

Whoever kills a subdeacon is to pay 300 solidi; whoever kills a deacon, 400 solidi; whoever kills a priest, [Col. 1086A] 600 solidi; whoever kills a bishop, 900 solidi; whoever kills a monk is to be judged liable for 400 solidi.

## Chapter VI. Concerning one who abandons his own wife, or kills her without fault, and takes another

From the same, chapter 300 (V, 149).

Whoever, after abandoning his own wife or killing her without fault, takes another is to perform public penance after laying aside his weapons. If he is obstinate, he is to be arrested by the count, bound in irons, and placed in custody until the matter is brought to our attention.

## Chapter VII. That there should be no reckless shedding of Christian blood

From the same, chapter 332 (V, 180).

We wish and command, by our authority, [Col. 1086B] that it be announced to everyone and, indeed, preached by the priests, that such reckless shedding of Christian blood not be permitted to occur in our kingdom. We must always heed what the Lord said after the Flood to his servant Noah:

> “From the hand of man, and from the hand of man and his brother, I will require his life. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed, for man was made in the image of God” (Genesis 9).

And in the Law:

> “Whoever kills a man shall be put to death” (Leviticus 24).

And the Apostle:

> “For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it. For it is God’s servant to you for good. But if you do what is evil, be afraid, for it does not bear the sword without cause. For it is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does [Col. 1086C] evil” (Romans 15).

For divine authority says specifically of him:

> “He bears God’s sword for the vengeance of evildoers,”

and not of just anyone else.

On the contrary, we do not know by what device some have usurped the practice whereby those supported by no public office, on account of their hatreds and their most varied evil desires, have arrogated to themselves an unwarranted ministry of vengeance in avenging their neighbors and killing men.

What the king ought to exercise in one case, at least, for the terror of many, they do not fear shamelessly to perpetrate in many cases because of hatred. They think it is permitted them, in vengeance for enmities, to do what they do not want the king to do for the sake of God’s vengeance.

## Chapter VIII. Concerning one who kills a cleric or monk, and that he should lay aside his arms

From book VI, chapter 90 (VI, 90).

[Col. 1086D]

Whoever kills a monk or cleric is to lay aside his arms and serve God in a monastery all the days of his life, never to return to the world; and he is to perform public penance for seven years.

## Chapter IX. Concerning priests, Levites, and monks who have been killed or maimed

From the same, chapter 98 (VI, 97).

If anyone kills or maims a priest, Levite, or monk, he is to pay composition according to the statutes of the earlier capitularies that have been added to the Salic Law, and in addition pay us our ban, namely 70 [Col. 1087A] solidi. He is to lay aside his arms and serve God in a monastery all the days of his life under rigorous penance, never afterward to serve the world or worldly affairs, nor to be joined to a wife.

## Chapter X. That those who devastate church property are reckoned as homicides before God

From the same, chapter 421 (VI, 324).

We wish everyone to know that those who take away Christ’s and the Church’s funds, defraud, seize, devastate, or plunder its property are reckoned as homicides before God, because they plunder the possessions of the poor whom the Church ought to feed.

## Chapter XI. Concerning the killing of infants

From book VI, chapter 166 (VII, 121).

[Col. 1087B]

If anyone kills an infant, he is to be held as a homicide.

## Chapter XII. What is to be done with homicides

From the same book, chapter 255 (VII, 183).

Concerning homicides, we have ordered that the following be observed: whoever kills another without cause in reckless daring is to suffer the penalty of death and is never to be able to redeem himself by payment. If it should be agreed that someone may proceed to composition, none of his relatives or friends is to assist him in anything. If anyone does so, he must make full composition for his own wergeld.

## Chapter XIII. Concerning those who, having previously borne no hatred, kill someone while defending themselves, and how they are to be corrected

From the same, chapter 370 (VII, 295).

[Col. 1087C]

If someone is walking peacefully along the road, or is in his own house, or in a city street, or in a village, and another suddenly attacks him, or if, when a quarrel has arisen, he kills a man while wishing to defend himself, without previously bearing hatred against him, he is to perform penance for seven years according to canonical institution.

For three years he is to be deprived of communion. For the remaining four years, once he has been admitted to communion in prayers and offerings, it is to depend upon the priest’s judgment whether he is worthy to receive Christ’s Body or whether he should be separated from it until the completion of his penance.

Abstinence from food is to be determined by the priest according to the penitent’s ability, devotion, and disposition.

## Chapter XIV. Concerning women and men who suffocate infants

According to the preceding chapter (VII, 297).

[Col. 1087D]

A woman who, while sleeping, suffocates her son, so that he dies, is to perform penance for six years. Her husband, if he was in the house, is to perform penance for four years; if he was in the same bed, he is likewise to perform penance. For two years he is to live on bread and water, and for the remaining four the priest is to impose abstinence from food according to his judgment.

# Title III. Concerning Adulteries

## Chapter I. Concerning a man who has a lawful wife, if his brother commits adultery with her

From book V, chapter 21 (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 19).

If a man who has [Col. 1088A] a lawful wife has a brother who commits adultery with her, that brother and that woman who committed the adultery are never, as long as they live, to have another marriage. But the man whose wife she was has the power, if he wishes, to take another wife.

## Chapter II. Concerning those who join themselves to virgins consecrated to God

From book VI, chapter 402.

Concerning those who join themselves to consecrated virgins, the following is contained in chapter 20 of the decrees of Pope Gelasius:

> “We have learned that certain men rashly join themselves to consecrated virgins and, after a profession dedicated to God, mingle incestuous and sacrilegious unions with them. It is right that such men be immediately thrust away from holy communion; and unless they have performed public and approved [Col. 1088B] penance, they are not to be received at all. Nor, in any event, is viaticum to be denied to those who pass from this world in such a condition. If those who unite with consecrated virgins are struck so severely, how much more severely must those who abduct them be struck? Therefore, as stated above, this evil must necessarily be cut out by all who remain within the Christian religion, through the severity of divine or human authority.”

## Chapter III. That one who defiles a woman consecrated to God commits blasphemy against God

From the same book, chapter 403 (VI, 309).

You should know that he commits blasphemy against God who defiles himself with a woman consecrated to God or with a veiled woman.

## Chapter IV. If a cleric defiles a woman consecrated to God

From the same book, chapter 404 (VI, 310).

[Col. 1088C]

If a cleric defiles himself with a veiled woman or with a woman consecrated to God, he is to be deprived of his proper rank.

## Chapter V. That those who violate the bodies of consecrated women are sacrilegious and, according to the Apostle, sons of perdition

From the same, chapter 405 (VI, 313).

Everyone should know that the bodies of women consecrated to God are shown by the testimony of Scripture to be temples consecrated to God through the vow of their own commitment and through the words of the priest. Therefore those who violate them are sacrilegious and, according to the Apostle, are recognized as sons [Col. 1088D] of perdition.

## Chapter VI. That fornication is said to be more dangerous than almost every sin

From the same, chapter 406 (VI, 312).

Fornication is said to be more grievous and worse than almost all sins, and it can truly be called a snare of death, a pit of hell, and an abyss of destruction, because adulterers and the lustful, through poverty of heart, lose their souls.

For, as Scripture says:

> “The price of a prostitute is scarcely one loaf of bread” (Proverbs 6);

and:

> “He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body” (1 Corinthians 6);

and:

> “He who lives in sensual indulgence is dead while living in the body” (1 Timothy).

## Chapter VII. Concerning laymen who abandon their wives

From book VII, chapter 305 (VI, 226).

[Col. 1089A]

Those laymen who dismiss their wives without a grave fault, or who have dismissed them, offering no credible grounds for the separation, and who therefore abandon their marriages in order to presume upon either illicit or another person’s property, are to be cut off from communion with the Church and from the assembly of the holy people, because they stain both marriage and fidelity, unless they first state the causes of the separation before the bishops of the province and first reject their wives after a judicial condemnation.

## Chapter VIII. Concerning a woman who marries two brothers, and concerning her husband

From the same book, chapter 371 (VII, 296).

[Col. 1089B]

A woman who has married two brothers is to be subjected to penance until the day of her death. Nevertheless, out of humanity, she ought to be reconciled in her final sacraments, provided that the marriage is first dissolved and she remains unmarried; her husband is likewise to be subjected to similar penance without a wife.

If two brothers have committed fornication with one woman, without knowing of one another’s intercourse, as soon as they learn of the adultery, the one who has her as his wife is to dismiss her. After performing penance, he may be joined to another if his wife has died; while she is alive, he may not.

She, however, can never afterward be taken into marriage. Subjected to perpetual penance, she is to receive the grace of communion [Col. 1089C] until the end of her life.

## Chapter IX. Concerning a woman who commits adultery against her husband, and likewise concerning a man who commits adultery against his wife

From the same, chapter 383 (VII, 298).

[Col. 1089C]

If a married woman commits adultery and comes secretly to confession, she is to perform penance for seven years: three on bread and water, and for the remaining four the priest is to determine, according to what he sees she can bear, what abstinence from food is to be imposed upon her.

Likewise, if a married man commits adultery, he is to do the same—that is, he is not to communicate for three years.

If someone’s wife commits adultery, and this is discovered and made public by her husband, he may dismiss his wife on account of fornication if he wishes. She, however, [Col. 1089D] is to perform public penance according to what was inserted above. Her husband, while she lives, has no right whatsoever to take another wife.

If he wishes to reconcile the adulteress to himself, he has permission to do so, provided that he performs penance together with her and that, once the penance has been completed, both approach communion as the preceding provision states.

The same rule is to be observed concerning a woman. For if her husband commits adultery, she has the power to dismiss her husband on account of fornication; nevertheless, she is to remain unmarried for as long as her husband lives. Neither he has the power to take another wife while his first wife lives, nor she another husband while her first husband lives. They do, however, have the power to reconcile with each other.

# Title IV. Concerning Incest

[Col. 1090A]

## Chapter I. Concerning incest

From book V, chapter 9 (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 7).

If a man commits incest with a woman consecrated to God; with his mother; with his godmother from baptism or confirmation; with a mother and daughter; with two sisters; with his mother’s daughter; with his sister’s daughter; with a granddaughter or niece; with a female cousin; with an aunt on his father’s or mother’s side; or with those whom the canons forbid him to marry, he is to lose his property on account of these crimes, if he has any.

If he refuses to correct this, no one is to receive him or give him food. Anyone who does so is to pay 60 solidi to the lord king [Col. 1090B] until that man corrects himself.

If he has no property, then, if he is free, he is to be sent to prison until satisfaction; but if he is a slave or freedman, he is to be beaten with many blows. If his master permits him to fall again into such a transgression, the master himself is to pay 60 solidi to the lord king.

As for the other relatives, judgment is to be rendered according to the enactments of the holy Fathers and the decrees of the canons.

## Chapter II. Concerning incestuous persons

From the same book, chapter 91.

Concerning incestuous persons: they are to be examined canonically, and some are not to be released because of anyone’s friendship while others are subjected to constraint.

## Chapter III. Again, concerning incestuous persons

From the same book, chapter 165 (V, 98).

[Col. 1090C]

We strictly command that bishops diligently investigate incestuous persons. If they are unwilling to repent, they are to be expelled from the church until they return to penance.

## Chapter IV. That bishops should amend and correct incestuous persons

From the same, chapter 303 (V, 152).

Bishops are to correct incestuous persons and exercise great diligence concerning them. They are likewise to have authority to correct widows within their parish.

## Chapter V. That incestuous persons and parricides are to be restrained canonically

From book VI, chapter 71 (VI, 71).

[Col. 1090D]

Incestuous persons and parricides are to be restrained canonically, as judgment was rendered concerning the man who violated his maternal aunt’s daughter: he is not to seek marriage again, is to lay aside the military belt, and is either to seek a monastery or, if he wishes to remain outside, fully complete the periods of penance according to the canons.

## Chapter VI. Concerning incestuous and criminal persons, and concerning the sick and penitents, as well as the fast of the four seasons

From the same chapter 106 (VI, 105).

[Col. 1091A]

Priests are to exercise the greatest care concerning incestuous and criminal persons, lest they perish in their crimes and their souls be demanded from them by Christ, the strict judge.

Likewise, they are to care for the sick and penitents, so that the dying do not depart without reconciliation and viaticum, and so that the fasts of the four seasons are diligently observed by the faithful.

## Chapter VII. Concerning one who joins himself in an incestuous union to persons whom the rules forbid

From the same, chapter 400 (VI, 306).

If anyone joins himself, not in the permitted degree but in an incestuous union, to persons whom the divine rules forbid, both parties are to be deprived of communion until they demonstrate their penance through separation. They are also to have neither the right to hold military service at the palace nor permission to conduct cases in the forum.

For if they have in any way joined themselves in the aforesaid incest, [Col. 1091B] the bishops or priests in whose diocese or district it occurred are to announce the crime to the king or the judges, so that, once it has been reported to them, the parties may be separated from their communion or cohabitation.

Their property is to pass to their nearest parents until the separation, under this condition: before they are separated, their goods are not to come into their own possession by any device—neither through their parents, nor through purchase, nor through royal authority—unless they confess the aforesaid crime by separation and penance.

## Chapter VIII. From the third book of the laws of Theodosius, chapter 12. Concerning incest

From the same book, chapter 401 (VI, 307).

[Col. 1091C]

Incestuous persons are not legitimate heirs, but both parties are marked with infamy.

## Chapter IX. That no one should take a virgin or widow devoted to God as a spouse

From the same, chapter 402 (VI, 308).

Henceforth, as the ecclesiastical canons prohibit, no one shall take as a wife by unlawful marriage—whether by force or by consent—a virgin devoted to God, anyone living under a religious habit, a woman who has professed the continence of widowhood, a close relative, or indeed any woman through whose union he could incur the stigma of incestuous infamy. For a marriage cannot truly exist when someone is drawn from a better purpose into a worse one, and incestuous pollution and the uncleanness of fornication are perpetrated under the bond of a false name. If from now on persons of either sex from any people attempt to commit this abomination, then, under the insistence of a priest or judge, even if there is no accuser, they shall be separated from one another in every way and sent into perpetual exile.

## CHAPTER X. What must be done concerning incestuous unions

From Book VI, chapter 257 (VII, 185).

No one shall ever join himself in marriage to an incestuous partner. If this should happen, they shall be separated by the bishop of that place and shall perform public penance for seven years according to the canonical grades. Those who refuse to do this shall be regarded by all as anathema.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning those who have intercourse with animals, or who commit incest with their blood relatives according to the manner of beasts as far as the line of affinity, or who have intercourse with males

From the same, chapter 456 (VII, 273).

[Col. 1092A]

In this title occur the Greek words περὶ τῶν ἀλογευσαμένων, ἤ καὶ ἀλογευομένων, meaning “concerning those who have behaved irrationally, or behave irrationally,” which we may render in Latin as *De his qui irrationabiliter versati sunt, sive versantur*. In this sentence there is a double meaning: namely, concerning those who have had intercourse with animals, or who, in the manner of beasts, have committed incest with blood relatives as far as the line of affinity, or who have had intercourse with males. Whoever has committed any one of these acts shall either be punished capitally, or, if his life is spared, shall truly perform penance according to the decision of the Council of Ancyra, which is contained in chapter 16.

## CHAPTER XII. That incestuous persons must be diligently sought out by priests and God-fearing people and punished canonically

From the same, chapter 377 (VI, 292).

Incestuous persons must be sought out with every effort by priests through truthful men who keep the fear of God before their eyes. If they are discovered, the priests shall immediately strive either to correct them personally or, with the assistance of their bishop’s archdeacon, labor to eradicate this evil, lest the priests themselves be polluted and perish through so great a crime and offense, and lest others in their vicinity incur the wrath of almighty God.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the person who joins himself to his blood relative as far as the line of affinity commits incest

From the same, chapter 432 (VII, 335).

[Col. 1092C]

No member of the faithful shall marry his blood relative as far as the line of affinity—that is, as far as the seventh generation—or pollute her in any way with the stain of incest. If anyone knowingly presumes to violate this rule, then, if he is free, he shall pay to our treasury our fine, namely 60 solidi, and in addition shall suffer the canonical penalty for incest and perform public penance according to the canonical grades. If he is a slave or an ecclesiastical person, he shall be publicly flogged and shaved, and shall perform public and canonical penance according to the order of his own bishop.

If anyone, whether free, enslaved, ecclesiastical, or fiscally dependent, is disobedient or obstinate toward his own bishop, his priest, or his archdeacon, whether in this matter or in any other crime, all his property shall be seized from him by the count and the bishop’s *missus* until he obeys his bishop or performs canonical penance. If he does not correct himself in this way and delays coming to the bishop and to canonical penance, he shall be arrested by the count, shut up in prison under severe hardship, and deprived of control over his property until the bishop gives orders.

If the count or his officials delay carrying this out, he shall be excommunicated canonically by the bishop or by the bishop’s representative, and, until the count fully fulfills these obligations, he shall always be deprived of communion with Catholics, until the bishop sees fit to deal more mercifully with him.

But if—which we do not wish—the count himself proves disobedient or negligent toward his bishop, whether concerning the matters mentioned above or concerning the excommunication itself, he shall lose both the honor of the countship and communion until both of them come into our presence, so that we may correct him by episcopal authority and imperial fear in such a way that the others may be afraid and never again dare to commit such acts.

## CHAPTER XIV. That incestuous persons, as long as they remain in their crime, shall occupy the place not of faithful Christians but only of pagans, catechumens, or possessed persons

From the same book, chapter 404 (VII, 336).

While incestuous persons remain in that detestable and [Col. 1093B] abominable crime, they shall be regarded not among faithful Christians but among pagans, catechumens, or possessed persons. That is, they shall neither eat nor drink with Christians, nor eat or drink from the same vessel, but shall do so alone; they shall not kiss them, nor be greeted by them.

If they prove disobedient to their priests and refuse to be separated from so abominable a crime and to return to public penance, they shall be counted among those endangered by an unclean spirit, or even among those of whom Truth itself says: “If he does not listen to you, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matthew 18).

They shall not pray with the faithful or enter the church, but shall keep watch at the church door and, when people enter or leave it, ask pardon with their faces prostrate on the ground.
