They shall earnestly beg them not to disdain praying for them and shall appear before all with faces wet with tears, contrite hearts, and humbled spirits. They shall remain in this state until they have satisfied the Church and received canonical reconciliation from their own bishop, and they shall never return to their former incest.

Nor shall they conduct secular business or participate in assemblies, accusations, or testimony. Instead, they must be cleansed and healed through the frequent prayers of priests, the laying on of the hands of their own bishop, the distribution of alms, and the performance of every other good work.

## CHAPTER XV. Likewise, concerning incestuous persons

From the same book, chapter 434 (VII, 337).

[Col. 1093D]

We decree that incestuous persons are not to be covered by any name of marriage.

# TITLE V. CONCERNING ABDUCTORS

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the abduction of widows

From Book V, chapter 6 (Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 17).

Whoever joins a widow to himself within the first thirty days of her widowhood, whether against her will or with her consent, shall pay our fine—namely, 60 solidi—in triple amount. If he took her against her will, he shall pay her legal compensation and shall not approach her thereafter.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning abducted women and their abductors

From the same book, chapter 223 (I, 103).

[Col. 1094A]

Although we have specifically decreed what those who henceforth attempt to commit this abomination must suffer, we have nevertheless judged it necessary to insert here what the sacred canons prescribe concerning abducted women and their abductors, so that it may be clear to everyone how great an evil this is, and so that, constrained not only by human but also by divine authority, this evil may henceforth be avoided.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning abducted girls who have not yet been betrothed

From the same, chapter 224 (I, 104).

Concerning girls who have been abducted before betrothal, the Council of Chalcedon, at which 630 Fathers were present, states in chapter 28:

“The holy synod decreed that those who abduct girls under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or connive at the abductors, shall, if they are clerics, be deprived of their clerical rank; if they are laymen, they shall be anathematized.”

These words clearly show how the authors of this evil must be condemned, since those who participate in it or connive at it are struck with so great an anathema. Nor may the abductors, under any circumstances, lawfully claim the abducted women as wives according to canonical authority.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning betrothed girls abducted by others

From the same, chapter 225 (I, 105).

Concerning betrothed girls who have been abducted by others, the Council of Ancyra states in chapter 10:

“It was decided that betrothed girls who are afterward abducted by others should be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence was inflicted upon them by the abductors.”

Therefore the holy assembly decreed [Col. 1094C] that the abductor should be punished with public penance. If the betrothed man refuses to receive the abducted woman, and was not himself a participant in the same crime, she shall not be denied permission to marry another. But if she also consented, she shall be subject to the same judgment. If afterward they presume to join themselves together, both shall be anathematized.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the abduction of another man’s betrothed

From the same book, chapter 238 (IV, 22).

If anyone abducts another man’s betrothed, he shall return her, together with his legal compensation, either to her father or to the person who ought to be her lawful protector. Whatever he took away with her, he shall return separately, each item according to the law. If her protector consented to this act and therefore does not wish to demand anything from the abductor, the count shall exact from him, item by item, our *freda* for each thing; he shall remain in exile for as long as we wish, and he shall not be permitted to retain that woman.

## CHAPTER VI. That no one shall arrange a secret marriage or commit an abduction, nor marry a woman whom his kinsman has had, but shall take as his wife the woman he wishes to have, provided with a dowry and given by her parents, through the blessing of priests

From Book VII, chapter 70 (VII, 127).

It has been decreed that those who wish to marry shall celebrate a public marriage, because serious sins often increase and accumulate in secret marriages: with the betrothed spouses of others, with close relatives, in adulterous unions, and—what is worse to say—with blood relatives. From such unions, blind, lame, hunchbacked, and bleary-eyed children, or children marked by other shameful defects, are often born. Everyone must therefore take care that this does not happen again.

First, the priest in whose parish the marriage is to take place must be consulted, and the marriage must take place in the church before the people. There the priest, together with the people, must inquire whether the woman is his close relative, or the wife, betrothed, or adulterous partner of another. If he finds that everything is lawful and honorable, then, with the priest’s counsel and blessing and with the advice of other good men, he must betroth and lawfully endow her.

For blessed Augustine writes concerning lawful marriage:

“Let her be chaste in virginity, lawfully endowed, given by her parents to her bridegroom, received from the bridal attendants, and thus, according to the Law and the Gospel, honored by a public marriage and lawfully taken in wedlock. Throughout all the days of her life she must never be separated on account of a man, unless by mutual consent and for the sake of devoting herself to the Lord. If she has committed fornication, she may be dismissed if her husband wishes; but while she lives, he may not marry another, because adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God, and she must undertake penance. You men must not take wives whose former husbands are alive, for such marriages are adulterous.”

As we have said, it must be carefully ensured that she is not his close relative, because it is written: “No man shall approach his close relative to uncover her nakedness” (Leviticus 18). Likewise it is written: “You shall not lie with your neighbor’s wife, nor defile yourself by the mingling of his seed” (Leviticus 20).

And in the decretal letters of Pope Gregory it is read:

“If anyone takes as a wife a deaconess, or a nun, or a spiritual godmother, or his brother’s wife, or his niece, or his stepmother, or his daughter-in-law, or his cousin, or a woman from his own kinship, or one whom his kinsman has had, let him be anathema.” And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone abducts or steals away a widow as a wife, or those who consent to him, let him be anathema.” And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

“And if anyone abducts or steals away a virgin as a wife without having betrothed her, or those who consent to him, let him be anathema.” And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

Elsewhere the canons command that no one shall marry within the line of affinity arising from his blood relationship, and that no one shall presume to marry a virgin without the blessing of a priest. All these matters must be guarded against with the utmost care, lest they occur.

But after all these things have been investigated and no impediment has been found, then, if she is a virgin, she is to be taken publicly and not secretly as a wife, with the priest’s blessing as contained in the sacramentary and with the counsel of many good men, so that, by the Lord’s mercy, good children may be born from them, and not children of the kind mentioned above.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the abductors of widows or virgins, and that women shall not serve at sacred altars

From the same, chapter 248.

It has been decreed that the abductors of widows or virgins shall be expelled from communion with the Church, and that women shall not serve at sacred altars or presume to undertake any of the duties assigned to men.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning those who abduct women, so that they may not have them as wives, and how abducted women are to be treated

From the same, chapter 395 (VII, 311).

It has been decided that those who abduct, steal away, or seduce women shall under no circumstances have them as wives, even if they subsequently reach an agreement with them, endow them, or receive them in marriage with the consent of their parents.

If anyone wishes to have a wife, he shall take her canonically and lawfully, and shall not abduct her. Whoever abducts, steals away, or seduces a woman shall never have her as his wife. Instead, he shall return her according to the law to her relatives, pay the full royal fine in triple amount, and in addition perform public canonical penance.

To this they all cried out with one voice, saying: “We all firmly wish to uphold these things, and we desire that they be preserved by everyone forever.”

# TITLE VI. CONCERNING PLUNDERERS

## CHAPTER I. Concerning those who violently plunder anything within the kingdom

From Book V, chapter 341 (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 189).

If anyone in the army, within the kingdom and without royal command, wishes to seize anything by hostile force, carry off hay or grain, take large or small livestock, break into houses, or burn them, we absolutely forbid these things from being done. If anyone presumptuously does so, then, if he is free, he shall be liable for 60 solidi and shall restore everything of the same kind, or clear himself by twelve witnesses.

If a slave does this, he shall be subject to capital punishment, and his master shall restore everything of the same kind, because he did not correct or guard his slave so that he would not commit such acts. If we ourselves consume these resources, we shall soon fail. Nevertheless, each person must guard his army so that no plundering takes place within the kingdom.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning those who commit plunder within the kingdom

From Book VI, chapter 97 (VI, 96).

If anyone commits plunder within the kingdom or forcibly takes anything from any of our faithful or from one of their men, he shall pay legal compensation in triple amount to the person from whom he took it, and in addition shall pay us our fine, namely 60 solidi. Afterward he shall be brought before us by the count, so that he may be shut up in the *bastonicon* and suffer punishment until it pleases us.

If the act was public, he shall perform public penance for it according to the sanction of the holy canons. If it was secret, he shall perform penance for it on the advice of priests, because, as the Apostle says, plunderers will not possess the kingdom of God unless they perform true penance (1 Corinthians 6).

Whoever takes anything belonging to churches shall be judged more severely, because the removal of sacred property is sacrilege, and the person who takes or plunders anything from it is called a sacrilegious person. Such persons are also to be regarded as infamous until they have satisfied the Church whom they injured.

## CHAPTER III. That he shall name his accomplices when part of the plunder is found with him

From the same, chapter 355 (VI, 135).

Anyone with whom the crime is acknowledged and part of the plunder is found shall immediately be compelled to name his accomplices. If he refuses to name them, he shall be held for punishment. If he is a person of higher status, he shall give an account for himself and restore fourfold whatever was taken or destroyed.

If, however, part of the plunder is found with a slave, he shall receive 150 lashes publicly while stretched out, and shall not delay naming his accomplices.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning those who are found to have given information for plunder

From the same, chapter 356 (VI, 136).

[Col. 1097B]

Whoever, free or slave, gives information so that someone’s property may be destroyed or his livestock or draft animals plundered, and is found publicly convicted of this on firm evidence, shall, for having given the information, restore double whatever was taken or destroyed, if he is free, and pay us our fine, namely 60 solidi.

If he is a slave or tenant, he shall receive 150 lashes publicly while stretched out and thoroughly beaten, as above, and in addition shall restore whatever was taken according to his legal status.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning one who grants permission for plunder

From the same book, chapter 375 (VI, 288).

[Col. 1097C]

If anyone, through a criminal conspiracy, grants permission for plunder, or if anyone divides up plunder that has been committed, he shall be burned alive.

## CHAPTER VI. That those who invade, devastate, or plunder Church property shall be deprived of communion if they do not correct themselves after the bishop’s warning

From Book VII, chapter 267 (VI, 132).

If anyone, by wicked cunning, takes away, defrauds, invades, retains, or suppresses any gift bestowed upon any church by the authority of the holy Scriptures, and, after being warned by a priest, does not immediately return what was given to God, let him be expelled from communion with the Catholic Church.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning those who invade or devastate property entrusted to the Church, or receive it without the consent of their own bishop

From the same, chapter 275 (VII, 199).

[Col. 1097D]

If anyone, driven by horrible greed, occupies or retains property owed to the Church or belonging to a priest, or receives it from a power acquired through litigation, and does not restore it, let him be deprived of communion.

If, after recognizing the ecclesiastical right, he does not immediately restore it to the Church or priest, or delays appearing before the chosen judges so that he may recognize that right, let him be suspended from ecclesiastical communion for as long as he fails, by restoring the property, to make both the Church and the priest whole.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning those who retain the offerings of the dead

From the same, chapter 20 (VII, 199).

[Col. 1098A]

The form of ecclesiastical discipline established by the earlier canons shall likewise be applied to those who in any way delay assigning to churches or priests the offerings of the dead lawfully left to them, or presume to retain them. Whoever presumes, in any manner, to reclaim for himself what he gave to churches out of devotion shall also be subject to this judgment.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning abbots, priests, and other ministers, and the prohibition against alienating Church property

From the same, chapter 36.

Abbots, priests, and other ministers shall not be permitted to alienate or pledge anything from Church property or from property entrusted to the sacred ministry without the permission and signature of their bishop. If they presume to do so, they shall be degraded from the communion granted to them, and whatever was rashly presumed or alienated shall be restored by order of the bishop.

# TITLE VII. CONCERNING SACRILEGIOUS PERSONS

## CHAPTER I. That the plunderers of the Church are sacrilegious, as is proved by the testimony of Scripture

From Book VI, chapter 385 (Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 295).

The plunderers of the Church are sacrilegious. Thus, in the Council of Agde, the following decree is found under chapter 4:

“To steal something from a friend is theft; but to defraud, remove, or secretly take away anything from the Church is sacrilege.”

For all who act against the law, plunder Church property, or harass churches and priests contrary to the divine ordinances are called sacrilegious and must unquestionably be regarded as infamous and sacrilegious.

## CHAPTER II. That the things consecrated to the Lord belong to ecclesiastical right

From the same, chapter 386 (VI, 296).

The things offered or consecrated to the Lord belong to the right of priests, and all who remove them or transfer them elsewhere are sacrilegious.

## CHAPTER III. That if anyone presumes to assume a dignity he has not deserved, he shall be regarded as sacrilegious by the prince or a just elder

From the same book, chapter 387 (VI, 297).

[Col. 1098D]

If anyone presumes to assume a dignity he has not deserved from a prince or just elder, he shall be regarded as sacrilegious. Homicides, malefactors, thieves, sacrilegious persons, abductors, poisoners, adulterers, those who commit abduction, those who give false testimony, and those who resort to diviners and magicians shall in no way be admitted to bring accusations or give testimony.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning sacrilegious persons, who are thieves according to the testimony of Scripture

From the same, chapter 395 (VI, 312).

Everyone must know that all who plunder, devastate, invade, or harass Church property, or unjustly alienate it from the churches to which it had been entrusted, are sacrilegious thieves.

Thus blessed Augustine says in his forty-eighth homily on the Gospel of John:

“Behold, Judas is among the saints; behold, Judas is a thief. And do not disregard the fact: a thief and a sacrilegious person—not just any thief, but a thief of the money box, of the Lord’s money box; a thief of the money box, but of sacred things. If crimes are distinguished in theft, he is not just any thief, but guilty of peculation. Peculation is theft from public property, and theft from private property is not judged in the same way as theft from public property. How much more severely, then, must the sacrilegious thief be judged—one who does not take from just anywhere, but takes from the Church? Whoever takes or steals anything from the Church is compared with the lost Judas.”

Note that blessed Augustine asserts that taking anything from the Church is theft, calls the perpetrator of so great a theft a sacrilegious thief, and compares him with the lost Judas. And shortly afterward:

“Why,” he says, “did he have the money box, when angels ministered to him? Was it not because his Church was to have a money box?”

Behold by what teachings of so great a doctor we are instructed: what went before in the Head appears to have been fulfilled in his Body, which is the Church. We know that Christ and the Church are one person; therefore what belongs to the Church belongs to Christ, what is offered to the Church is offered to Christ, and what is taken from the Church is unquestionably taken from Christ.

It was therefore destined that the Church of Christ should have money; and if money, then certainly estates, slaves, and countless ornaments of various kinds. Since it is unlawful to take away what is given to the Church, the words of blessed Jerome, written in his exposition of the evangelist Matthew, bear witness to this:

“All those who misuse the temple contribution and the things given for the uses of the Church for other purposes by which they may satisfy their own will are like the scribes and priests who purchase the lie and the blood of the Savior.”

## CHAPTER V. That whatever is offered to the Lord is the Holy of Holies and belongs to the right of priests

From the same, chapter 396 (VI, 303).

No one may be ignorant that everything consecrated to the Lord—whether it is a human being, an animal, a field, or anything whatsoever once consecrated to God—shall be the Holy of Holies of the Lord and belongs to the right of priests. Therefore everyone who removes, devastates, invades, or plunders what belongs to the Lord and the Church shall be without excuse until he makes amends and satisfies the Church; he is sacrilegious, and not merely sacrilegious, but a sacrilegious thief.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning those sacrilegious persons who inflict injuries upon the Church and its priests

From the same book, chapter 397 (VI, 304).

If anyone breaks out into this kind of sacrilege, so that he attacks churches and their property and inflicts any injury upon priests, ministers, the worship itself, or the place, or brings injury against divine worship, he must know that, once convicted or confessed, he shall be punished by capital sentence.

The bishop should not be expected to demand vengeance for his own injury, since the holiness of his office has been left with the sole glory of forgiving. It shall be not only permitted but even praiseworthy for everyone to prosecute as a public crime the atrocious injuries committed against priests or ministers and to obtain vengeance against such offenders.

## CHAPTER VII. That everything offered to the Lord is unquestionably consecrated

From the same book, chapter 398 (VI, 305).

Everything offered to the Lord is unquestionably also consecrated. Not only are the sacrifices consecrated by priests to the Lord upon the altar called the offerings of the faithful, but whatever the faithful offer to him—whether slaves, fields, vineyards, woods, meadows, waters and watercourses, workshops, books, utensils, stones, buildings, clothing, skins, woolen goods, livestock, pastures, parchment, movable and immovable property, or anything from these things that is made for the praise of God or can contribute to the support and adornment of the holy Church of God and its priests—when voluntarily offered by anyone to the Lord and his Church is undoubtedly consecrated to the Lord and belongs to the right of priests.

Since we truly acknowledge that Christ and the Church are one person, whatever belongs to the Church belongs to Christ. Whatever is offered to the Church—whether in the forms mentioned above or in any other form, whether by promises, pledges, written documents, or [Col. 1100C] physical property—is offered to Christ.

Whatever is alienated or taken from his Church by any device—whether by alienating, devastating, invading, diminishing, or plundering—is taken from Christ. If stealing something from a friend is theft, then especially to take away, alienate, secretly remove, or devastate anything from Christ our Lord, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, is sacrilege.

All plunderers of the Church are therefore manifestly sacrilegious, and no sacrilegious person shall possess the kingdom of God except through pure, proven, and public penance, satisfaction rendered to the Church, and reconciliation by the laying on of the bishops’ hands according to the canonical sanctions. Such a person is not only excluded from the kingdom of God but also, until the aforesaid satisfaction, becomes an outcast from the thresholds of the holy Church, especially from the Church he injured.

Until that satisfaction has been made, we must not communicate with the perpetrators of such crimes, whether living or dead. For whoever steals his neighbor’s money commits iniquity. Such persons are not only sacrilegious but also sacrilegious thieves, wolves, and murderers and killers of the poor; moreover, they are condemned before God and his saints by the bond of anathema.

## CHAPTER VIII. That everyone must recognize how great an evil it is to defile women consecrated to God or other women

From the same book, chapter 425 (VI, 319).

We command everyone to know, and priests to preach to all peoples, how great an evil and how grave an offense it is to have intercourse with women devoted to God—widows or virgins—or with veiled women, or with women devoted to God, and especially with nuns and virgins or widows consecrated to God, whether in monasteries or outside monasteries.

There is no doubt that this sin is twofold. For example, let us consider what vengeance awaits a servant before his master if he violates his master’s wife through adultery. How much greater, then, is the guilt of the man who defiles with the corruption of his lust the bride of Christ, the Creator of heaven and earth?

As blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who have intercourse with males, nor revilers, nor plunderers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

## CHAPTER IX. That those who commit sacrilege, adultery, plunder, or devastation shall be punished by capital sentence

From the same chapter, 422 (VI, 325).

Under penalty of death, we prohibit anyone from committing sacrilege, adultery, plunder, or devastation in our kingdom. If anyone voluntarily commits one of these acts, he shall pay the composition for his life, and all his property, movable as well as immovable, shall be joined to our treasury, or handed over to the Church whose property he devastated, alienated, or took away.

For it is the greatest sacrilege to take away, devastate, alienate, invade, or secretly remove the offerings of the faithful, which are the property of the churches. For, as Scripture says, neither sacrilegious persons, nor adulterers, nor plunderers, nor devastators will possess the kingdom of God.

If those who plunder the property of their brothers are excluded from the kingdom of God, what do you suppose will happen to those who plunder or take away property dedicated to God? For the more gravely someone sins in this world, the more severely he will be tortured in hell.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the protection of the people from sacrilegious persons

From Book VII, chapter 55 (VII, 37).

Before the Lord’s tribunal, no one will be able to excuse himself for the guilt of negligence if he refuses to protect his people from the authors of sacrilegious persuasion.

# TITLE VIII. CONCERNING OATHS

## CHAPTER I. Concerning not swearing oaths lightly

From Book V, chapter 349 (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 197).

[Col. 1101D]

We wish oaths not to be taken hastily. Each judge must first investigate the case truthfully, so that the truth cannot remain hidden from him and so that people do not come too readily to an oath.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the avoidance of perjury

From Book VI, chapter 278 (III, 10).

We command that perjury be avoided and that witnesses not be admitted to swear an oath until they have been examined. If they cannot otherwise be examined, they shall be separated from one another and questioned individually.

An accuser alone may not choose witnesses in the absence of his adversary. No one at all shall be admitted to an oath or to testimony unless fasting. If anyone is rejected, the person rejecting him shall state and prove why he does not wish him to be accepted.

Witnesses shall be chosen from that *pagus*, not from another, unless perhaps the case must be investigated at a greater distance outside the county. If anyone is convicted of perjury, he shall lose his hand or redeem it.

# TITLE IX. CONCERNING EXCOMMUNICATED PERSONS

## CHAPTER I. That it is not permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons

From Book V, chapter 25 (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 23).

It is not permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons, nor to pray together with those who meet in houses while avoiding the prayers of the Church. A person who does not assemble in one church shall not be received by another church.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning one who has been excommunicated because of his own negligence

From the same book, chapter 238 (V, 28).

If anyone has been excommunicated because of his own negligence and, during his excommunication, presumes to communicate before a hearing, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning those who communicate with an excommunicated person

From the same book, chapter 75 (I, 36).

Whoever presumptuously communicates with an excommunicated person shall himself be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning those who despise the summons or correction of bishops

From Book VI, chapter 88 (VI, 88).

[Col. 1102C]

If any secular person, whether of higher or lower rank, commits a sin and, summoned by the authority of his bishop, delays coming to correction and penance, he shall remain an outcast from the Church and separated from the fellowship of Catholics until he corrects what he has committed, canonically washes away his guilt through satisfaction, obtains forgiveness through the divine prayers and reconciliation of his own bishop, and, after making satisfaction, is canonically restored to the bosom of the Church, from whose womb he had strayed, improved by that same bishop.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning those who inflict an injury or dishonor upon a bishop

From the same book, chapter 99 (VI, 98).

[Col. 1102D]

If anyone inflicts any injury or unjust dishonor upon a bishop, he shall pay with his life, and everything he appears to possess shall be joined in its entirety to the Church over which that bishop is known to preside. He shall also pay us our fine in triple amount, namely 60 solidi, or he himself shall be permanently assigned to service in our treasury until he can redeem himself at three times his lawful *wergild*.

The holy Church consists in its priests. Therefore those who inflict injury or insult upon bishops or other priests must be punished with a great penalty. For detraction against priests concerns Christ, in whose place they exercise an embassy in the Church.

## CHAPTER VI. That the excommunication of priests must not be treated lightly

From the same, chapter 248 (VI, 224).

[Col. 1103A]

It has been decided that the faithful must not treat the excommunication of their priests lightly, because if they do so, they will rightly be separated from the assembly of Christians.

## CHAPTER VII. That whoever violates synodal excommunication shall have no hope of restoration at another synod

From Book VII, chapter 9 (VII, 6).

If a bishop condemned by a synod, or a priest or deacon condemned by his own bishop, dares to perform anything belonging to the sacred ministry—whether a bishop according to the earlier custom, or a priest or deacon—he shall in no way be permitted either to have hope of restoration or a place for making satisfaction at another synod. All who communicate with him shall also be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that this has occurred, they attempt to communicate with him.

## CHAPTER VIII. That those excommunicated by a priest may not accuse persons of higher rank before they are canonically reconciled

From the same, chapter 180 (VI, 128).

An excommunicated person shall not presume to accuse persons of higher rank as long as he remains under excommunication. If he presumes to do so, he shall not be received; instead, he shall either be subjected to a greater excommunication or expelled from the Church.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the forms of excommunication, both for clerics and for laypeople

From Book V, chapter 63 (V, 42).

[Col. 1103C]

If any presbyter has been degraded or excommunicated by his bishop and afterward, in contempt, has presumed to perform anything belonging to his office without authorization, and has subsequently been corrected and excommunicated by the bishop, whoever knowingly communicates with him shall know that he too is similarly excommunicated. If any cleric, layman, or woman commits incest, and, after being corrected by his or her bishop, refuses to amend and is excommunicated by him, whoever afterward communicates with that person shall likewise be excommunicated. And so that you may know what the character of this excommunication is: the person must not enter a church, eat or drink with any Christian, have anyone accept his or her gifts or offer a kiss, join in prayer, or give or receive greetings, until reconciled by the person’s own bishop. But if anyone appeals, claiming to have been unjustly excommunicated, he or she shall have permission to come to the metropolitan bishop, so that the matter may there be judged according to canonical institution; meanwhile, the person shall observe the excommunication. If anyone disregards all these provisions, and the bishop is entirely unable to correct the matter, the offender shall be condemned by royal judgment.

## CHAPTER X. Likewise, on the same matter.

From the same book, chapter 64.

You can read all these provisions individually in the statutes of the Council of Nicaea, or in the synodal decrees of other holy Fathers, and in the Council of Antioch: those who have been condemned by a synod or by their own bishop, and afterward presume to minister, it is commanded that no one dare communicate with them. Whoever communicates with them shall likewise be subject to judgment, just as the condemned person is.

# TITLE X. ON THE STABILITY OF PRIESTS IN THEIR OWN TITULAR CHURCHES

## CHAPTER I. That a cleric should remain in the church to which he has been assigned.

From Book V, chapter 28 (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 26).

A cleric ought to remain in the church to which he was initially assigned and appointed by the bishop, and to which he has fled as though to a superior one. Anyone who rejects this arrangement must be recalled to his own church, in which he was first ordained, and minister there alone. If anyone transgresses this definition, the holy synod has decreed that he be removed from his own rank.

## CHAPTER II. That, in the titular churches where presbyters are consecrated, they should promise stability before their promotion.

From the same chapter, 75 (V, 108).

Presbyters who are consecrated in titular churches must, according to the canons, make a promise of stability in that place before they are ordained.

# TITLE XI. HERE BEGIN OTHER CHAPTERS COLLECTED FROM THE FIFTH, SIXTH, AND SEVENTH BOOKS OF THE CAPITULARIES, VERY APPROPRIATE TO ECCLESIASTICAL NEEDS

## CHAPTER I. On one who has held a stepson or stepdaughter before a bishop.

From Book V, chapter 7 (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 5).

If anyone has held a stepson or stepdaughter before a bishop for confirmation, he shall separate from his wife and shall not take another. Likewise, the woman shall not take another husband.

## CHAPTER II. On one who gives his stepdaughter against her will to a free man or a slave.

From the same book, chapter 19 (V, 17).

If any man gives his stepdaughter, against her will and against the will of her mother and relatives, to a free man, or to a cleric, or to a slave, and she refuses to live with him and leaves him, her parents shall have the power to give her another husband.

## CHAPTER III. On a suspect presbyter.

From the same book, chapter 36.

If a priest is regarded with suspicion or disbelief by his bishop, by his fellow priests, or by good and upright men of his people or congregation, so that he may not remain under accusation or the suspicion mentioned above, he shall, together with three, five, or seven good and neighboring fellow priests—following the example of Pope Leo, who had twelve bishops for his purgation—or with even more, if this seems appropriate to his bishop or if he recognizes that it is necessary because of the disturbance of the people, and together with other good and upright men, clear himself by oath before the people upon the four Gospels and restore himself to the Church. If anyone wishes to know what sort of witnesses ought to be admitted for the accusation of priests, and what should be done with the accuser, it can be found fully in the canons.

## CHAPTER IV. That presbyters should carefully guard the chrism.

From the same book, chapter 165 (V, 80).

Presbyters shall guard the chrism under seal and shall presume to give it to no one on the pretext of medicine or sorcery. If they do so, they shall be deprived of their office.

## CHAPTER V. Likewise, concerning the foregoing, in the same book.

Chapter 104.

A presbyter who has given the holy chrism in order to overturn a judgment shall, after being deposed from his rank, lose his hand.

## CHAPTER VI. That the evil of drunkenness should be completely avoided.

From the same book, chapter 161 (V, 96).

We command that the great evil of drunkenness, from which all vices spring, be avoided by every means. We have decreed that anyone unwilling to avoid it is to be excommunicated until he makes suitable amends.

## CHAPTER VII. On the building of a church.

From the same book, chapter 382 (V, 229).

No one shall build a church before the bishop of the city has arrived and publicly planted a cross there, and before the person who wishes to build has first specified what will suffice for the lights, the custodianship, and the stipends of the custodians; after making the donation, let him then build the house.

## CHAPTER VIII. That no one is to be judged without a legitimate accuser.

From the same book, chapter 298 (V, 244).

It is not the judge’s place to judge or condemn anyone without a legitimate accuser, for the Lord also knew that Judas was a thief; but because he was not accused, he was not expelled.

## CHAPTER IX. That laymen should not presume to exercise authority concerning religion.

From the same book, chapter 403 (V, 249).

Although they may be religious, laymen are nevertheless to be granted no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical resources or of persons dedicated to God.

## CHAPTER X. If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon goes to war, he shall be deposed.

From Book VI, chapter 61 (VI, 61).

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon goes to war and puts on military arms for fighting, he shall be deposed from every office, to such an extent that he shall not even have lay communion.

## CHAPTER XI. On those who wish to receive consecrated water on Holy Saturday.

From the same book, chapter 82 (VI, 77).

On Holy Saturday of Easter, or on Pentecost Saturday, if anyone wishes to receive consecrated water for sprinkling in his house, he must first receive the infusion of chrism.

## CHAPTER XII. That confirmation by the bishop should be earnestly sought by the people.

From the same book, chapter 73 (VI, 82).

Everyone must take the greatest care that no one ends his life without the bishop’s confirmation and thereby places his soul in danger.

## CHAPTER XIII. On a man and woman joined in marriage, when she later says that he cannot have intercourse with her.

From the same book, chapter 91 (VI, 55).

If a man and woman have joined themselves in marriage, and afterward the woman says that her husband cannot have intercourse with her, then, if she can prove that this is true, she may take another, because, according to the Apostle, her husband was unable to render her the marital due (1 Corinthians 7).

## CHAPTER XIV. On abductors and abducted virgins and widows.

From the same book, chapter 96 (VI, 95).

If anyone abducts or steals another man’s betrothed—a virgin or a widow not yet betrothed—it is decreed that, whether he subsequently betroths her, endows her, or does neither, and whether he has been able to take or retain her by any device, even with the consent of her parents, he shall never have her as his wife. Rather, she shall be taken away from the abductor or thief and restored to her relatives, to be married to another man at a suitable time and endowed according to law, provided she did not consent to this evil. The abductor or thief, and all who consented to him, shall be punished by public penance according to canonical authority; and they shall pay to her relatives threefold whatever they unjustly committed in this abominable crime, restoring each individual thing separately threefold according to law.

But the woman who was abducted, if she willingly consented to so abominable a crime, whether at first or afterward, shall never marry again. She shall be punished by public penance and placed under such custody that she may in no way engage in sexual relations with anyone. Thus are the aforesaid crimes to be punished, so that all may know that neither the laws of the world consent to such abominable unions, nor do the sacred canons offer them any approval.

## CHAPTER XV. On those who have established an oratory in their house.

From the same book, chapter 102 (V, 101).

Anyone who has an oratory in his house may pray there, but he must not presume to celebrate Mass there, nor permit anyone else to do so, without the permission and dedication of the bishop of that place. If he does so, his house shall be confiscated to the treasury. The count who knew of this and did not prohibit it shall be punished by public penance or deprived of his office.

## CHAPTER XVI. On exposed infants and their reception.

From the same book, chapter 154 (VI, 142).

If an exposed child has been taken in out of compassion before someone’s church, the person who took the child in shall draw up a letter of attestation. If the child who has been taken in has not been sought and recognized within ten days, the person who took the child in shall have the child securely. Anyone who afterward brings a claim against him shall be condemned by ecclesiastical discipline as a murderer, as the authority of the Fathers has decreed.

## CHAPTER XVII. On those whose baptism is doubted without reservation: it is prescribed that they be baptized again.

From the same book, chapter 184 (VI, 181).

Those concerning whom there is doubt whether they have been baptized or not are to be baptized in every respect without any scruple, with these words said beforehand: “I do not rebaptize you, but if you have not yet been baptized, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. How many days constitute a woman’s purification.

From the same book, chapter 207 (VI, 204).

After a woman has given birth, how many days must pass before she enters the church? We have learned from the precept of the Old Testament that she must abstain for thirty-three days in the case of a male child and sixty-six in the case of a female child. Yet, Saint Gregory says, it must be understood that this is taken mystically. For if she enters the church to give thanks in the very hour in which she has given birth, she is burdened by no weight of sin. It is the pleasure of the flesh, not the pain, that is at fault. In the union of the flesh there is pleasure, but in the bringing forth of offspring there are groans. Hence it is said even to the first mother: “In pains you shall give birth” (Genesis 3). Therefore, if we forbid that woman to enter the church, we attribute her punishment to her guilt.

## CHAPTER XIX. On preserving fidelity between husband and wife.

From the same book, chapter 424 (VI, 327).

We want everyone to know, just as we have often been admonished by the lord bishops and the other servants of God, that husbands must truly preserve fidelity and affection toward their wives, and wives likewise toward their husbands, and must not deviate from them in any respect. Married people are not permitted to have either a mistress or a concubine.

## CHAPTER XX. On priests who are unable to fulfill their ministry.

From Book VII, chapter 137 (VII, 100).

Priests who do not properly understand how to fulfill their ministry, and who do not strive with all their strength to learn in accordance with the commands of their bishops, or who are contemptuous of the canons, are to be removed from their office until they have completely corrected this fault.

## CHAPTER XXI. That no judge may punish a presbyter, deacon, or cleric without the knowledge of his bishop.

From the same book, chapter 139 (VI, 154).

No judge shall on his own authority punish or presume to condemn a presbyter, deacon, cleric, or junior member of the church without the knowledge of the bishop. If he does so, he shall be separated from the church to which he has inflicted the injury, which he is known to have committed, until he recognizes and corrects his offense.

## CHAPTER XXII. That presbyters are not to be appointed in churches without consulting the bishop, nor expelled from churches.

From the same book, chapter 145 (VII, 120).

It has been decreed that presbyters shall neither be appointed nor expelled from any churches without the authority or consent of the bishops. If anyone afterward attempts to do this, he shall be severely struck by synodal judgment.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That women’s unlawful access to the altar must not occur, and that no women should presume to handle the sacred vessels or the body and blood of the Lord.

From the same book, chapter 190 (VII, 134).

It has been decreed that women’s unlawful access to the altar must not occur, because it is contrary to all divine authority and canonical institution for women to thrust themselves forward at the holy altars, immodestly touch the sacred vessels, minister priestly vestments to presbyters, or touch the body and blood of the Lord and distribute them to the people. This is entirely without justification, and it is absolutely forbidden that it happen again. Any women who afterward presume to do these things shall be subjected to canonical judgment until they make satisfaction. That women must not enter the altar area is found at great length in the Council of Chalcedon and in the decrees of Pope Gelasius.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On violators of tombs.

From the same chapter, 192 (VII, 136).

Those who violate tombs shall be punished, whether free persons or slaves. If a person of higher standing is found guilty of this crime, he shall lose half his property and be marked with perpetual infamy. If he is a cleric, he shall be stripped of all clerical honor and assigned to perpetual exile. If a judge delays prosecuting or carrying this out, he shall be deprived of his property and office.

## CHAPTER XXV. On clerics who do not avoid drunkenness: they are either to be excommunicated or flogged.

From the same chapter, 270.

Above all, clerics must avoid drunkenness, which is the tinder and nurse of every vice; no one under its influence can retain free judgment of body and mind. Whoever is seized by wine is shown to be alienated from his senses, and a weakened mind is led more readily toward judgment; moreover, a person often incurs sin or crime without knowing it. Such ignorance cannot escape the punishment that clearly arose from voluntary madness. Therefore, whoever is proved to have been drunk shall, as the order permits, either be removed from communion for forty days or subjected to corporal punishment.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That witnesses must be bound by oath before they are questioned concerning a case.

From the same chapter, 283 (VII, 207).

Before witnesses are questioned concerning a case, they must be bound by an oath, so that they swear that they will say nothing but the truth. We also command that greater credence be given to more honorable witnesses than to inferior ones. The testimony of a single person, however distinguished and suitable that person may appear, must in no way be heard.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That slaves whom Jews have purchased or circumcised are to be removed from their power.

From the same chapter, 286 (VII, 209).

If any Jew purchases or circumcises a Christian slave or one belonging to any other sect, that person shall be removed from the Jew’s power and remain free.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On wandering and fickle priests and clerics.

From the same chapter, 296 (VII, 217).

It has also been decreed that a wandering and unstable cleric, even if established in the diaconal ministry or presbyteral office, shall, if he does not obey the commands of the bishop by whom he was ordained—to perform his office continually in the church assigned to him—be deprived of communion and honor for as long as he persists in his fault.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the chastity of those joined in marriage.

From the same book, chapter 389 (VII, 305).

Everyone must know and firmly retain that those who wish to take wives, just as they desire to find them chaste and undefiled, must approach them chaste and undefiled, and receive them with the blessing of a priest, as is contained in the Sacramentary. But first they must bind them by a marriage settlement.

## CHAPTER XXX. On those confirmed by a chorepiscopus.

From the same book, chapter 402 (VII, 317).

If anyone has been confirmed not by a bishop but by a chorepiscopus, who is not a bishop but a bishop’s vicar, before they were forbidden to do so, the confirmation must be repeated with other blessings. For before the apostolic and synodal prohibition, chorepiscopi belonged not to the number of the apostles but, as the sacred canons testify, to the order of the 160 disciples; and we know that they never transmitted the Paraclete Spirit. But since, as has been said, the aforementioned chorepiscopi were long ago prohibited, they are now nothing, and they were never able to transmit the Paraclete Spirit at any time, nor are they able to do so now.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Likewise, on chorepiscopi.

From the same book, chapter 423 (VII, 328).

It has been decreed that, just as we have determined by the general and synodal counsel of Pope Leo, all our bishops, and the other faithful, no chorepiscopus shall presume by the laying on of hands to transmit the Holy Spirit, consecrate priests, Levites, or subdeacons, veil virgins, prepare the holy chrism, consecrate churches or altars, or give the blessing to the people at a public Mass. All these things belong to the highest pontiffs, that is, cathedral bishops, and not to chorepiscopi or presbyters, whose form chorepiscopi represent according to the decrees of the saints. If they attempt to do any of these things, what they perform shall be invalid, and they themselves shall be utterly deprived of all ecclesiastical honor.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On those who kill themselves.

From the same chapter, 443 (VII, 144).

Whoever, by his own will, throws himself into water, hangs himself, casts himself from a tree, strikes himself with a weapon, or gives himself over to any voluntary death shall not have his offering accepted.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How these statutes are to be observed, and what is to be done with those who despise them, whether clerics or laymen.

From the same chapter, 476 (VII, 375).

We decree that all these ecclesiastical constitutions, which we have briefly and summarily touched upon, shall remain with perpetual stability, as they are more fully contained in the canons. Therefore, if any cleric or layman wishes to disobey these sanctions, then, if he is a cleric, he shall be subject to excommunication. If he is a layman and a person of higher standing, he shall lose half his property, which shall benefit the treasury; but if he is a person of lower standing, he shall be fined by the loss of his possessions and assigned to exile.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 880. ODO, BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS

[Col. 1109]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From *Gallia christiana*, volume IX.)

From the abbacy of Corbie, Odo was appointed bishop of Beauvais at the end of the year 860 or the beginning of 861, after Hincmar and the bishops of the province had rejected, as insufficiently worthy or capable, a certain Frimold. His name is found in the year 858 among the defective subscriptions to a charter of Charles the Bald, in which the possessions of the monastery of the blessed Mary of Soissons are listed and confirmed.

In 862 he attended the Council of Pîtres, to whose synodal letters concerning the monastery of Saint-Denis and the privilege of Saint Martin of Tours he subscribed. In the same year he brought to Rome, to Pope Nicholas, the Acts of the Synod of Soissons, at which Rothad, bishop of Soissons, had been unjustly deprived of office; from him, in the following year, he obtained confirmation both of the privilege of the monastery of Corbie and of the abbeys of Oratory and Saint-Geremar, which Charles the Bald had granted to the church of Beauvais at Odo’s request. The diploma of this latter confirmation, following Lhuet and the Sainte-Marthe brothers, is given here in the appendix (see volume CXIX of *Patrologia*, among the letters of Pope Nicholas).

The supreme pontiff certainly held him in high esteem. This is shown by his letters to Hubert, abbot and brother of Queen Teutberga; to Rothad, bishop of Soissons; and to the sons of Charles the Bald, in which Nicholas calls Odo “his most holy brother and fellow bishop.”

In 864 he was again sent to Rome by King Charles the Bald, to obtain from the Apostolic See confirmation of the liberty of the monastery of Anisolus, asserted at the assembly of Verberie. In the same year he attended another synod at Pîtres, at which the possessions of the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre were confirmed; then, two years later, the Council of Soissons, at which Queen Ermentrude was crowned with solemn rite.

In the same year, according to volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, page 504, he gave the monastery of Centula certain relics both of Saint Lucian and of Saint Justus the martyr. At about the same time he attended the Council of Verberie.

In the following year, when Hincmar of Reims had received from Pope Nicholas certain chapters of the Greeks against the Latins, to be refuted by the bishops of Gaul, this task was entrusted in the province of Reims to Odo of Beauvais. Hincmar wrote to him about this matter more than once, and especially in these words:

> “Therefore, dearest brother, following the recommendation of the apostolic lord, strive to investigate and gather together in one place, by the path of the Scriptures and the tradition of our forebears, what we may suitably write back to him about these matters; so that, when we come together, with the Lord’s help, we may reread with common effort, one by one, what each of us has found, and arrange what we are to write from this concerning the same lord pope. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the first indiction.”

Odo carried this out, both personally and through Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, and sent Hincmar his responses to those objections in a single booklet. Hincmar nevertheless thought that certain points in it needed to be reconsidered and corrected.

Odo had also ordered the same Ratramnus to refute the insane opinion of a certain monk who maintained that there was one soul in all human beings. Ratramnus fulfilled this assignment in a disputation dedicated to Odo.

In the same year, 867, Odo attended the Council of Troyes; in 868, the examination of Wildebert, bishop of Châlons; and in 869, the consecration of Bertulf, archbishop of Trier. In that same year, at the Council of Verberie, he confirmed certain royal precepts for the monastery of Carrof.

Again in the same year he stood beside King Charles at Metz at his coronation for the acquisition of the kingdom of Lothair. He was also responsible for Charles’s granting the estate of Luziacum to the monastery of Saint Lucian; the charter concerning this is found in Loisell, pages 242 and 244.

In 870 he took part in the assembly at Aachen concerning the division of the kingdom of Lothair between Kings Louis and Charles. In the following year he attended the Council of Douzy, at which Hincmar of Laon was deprived of office.

In 874 he built the church of Hussia, subject to Corbie, in the diocese of Tournai. In 876 he attended the Council of Pontigny, at whose eighth session he is said to have read:

> “Certain chapters dictated by the apostolic legates, Ansegisus, and Odo himself, without the knowledge of the synod; discordant among themselves and of no benefit, indeed lacking both reason and authority; and therefore they are not appended here.”

In 877, on the Kalends of July, Charles the Bald appointed him counselor to his son Louis the Stammerer, together with certain others, whether bishops or abbots.

In the following year Pope John VIII wrote him Letter 146 concerning the ordination of certain monks of Saint-Denis.

In 879, when Louis the Stammerer was near death at Compiègne, he entrusted to Odo and Count Albuin the crown, sword, and the rest of the royal regalia, to be carried to his son Louis, ordering them to strive to have him anointed and crowned king. But both men, after handing the royal insignia over to Theodoric the chamberlain, hastened back immediately to their own affairs.

At the beginning of 881, Odo received with due veneration the relics of Saint Vedast, which had been carried to Beauvais, and shortly afterward, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, exchanged life for death. That prelate accomplished many things useful to his church. Among other matters, he is said to have increased the number of his canons to fifty and assigned them suitable revenues, in letters found in Lhuet, Loisell, Sirmond, and Labbe; these we have arranged to reprint here after the Sainte-Marthe brothers.

But apart from the fact that those letters are defective—either nearly all the subscriptions of the bishops or other chronological indications being faulty—who could easily persuade himself that the common life of the canons, than which nothing was more important to the Fathers of the various councils of this age, disappeared so quickly from the church of Beauvais? See his eulogy in volume VIII of Labbe’s *Councils*, page 1723. Some believe, indeed, that he wrote a very corrupt Life of Saint Lucian.

# ODO’S SERMON ON SAINT LUCIAN

(In Bollandus, volume I, January, page 461.)

## CHAPTER ONE. Saint Lucian is sent to Gaul

### 1.

To recount the victories and deeds of the precious martyrs, dearest brothers, is nothing other than to proclaim the praises of Christ and to preach, for the glory of his name, the triumph of his power in his martyrs, because in all things he himself proved victorious—the one who said to his own: “Take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). Thus in all things the most merciful Jesus himself conquered, he who alone first fought on behalf of all.

Therefore the holy martyrs are honored in glory as being closer to Christ than all others, in proportion as they were his imitators in suffering. [Note: So, in fact, Saint Paul says in his Epistle to the Colossians 1:24: “I complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for his body, which is the Church.”]

They indeed supplied what was lacking in Christ’s sufferings; and therefore it is rightly said again that in all these people Christ suffered, because they were his members. Hence he is also rightly proclaimed victorious in them, because through them he conquered as often as a martyr, victorious in suffering for Christ, fell in death. [Note: The manuscript of Saint-Maximin inserts here something about imitating the martyrs who are praised.]

We ought, therefore, to praise the glorious men through whose teachings the glorious Church of Christ shines far and wide throughout the world. They themselves rest happily beneath God’s altar, clothed in shining robes, purpled with their own blood and whitened in the blood of Christ.

### 2.

Among their company was the most blessed Lucian, a distinguished and glorious martyr. [Note: The manuscript of Saint-Maximin adds: “who, once, from childhood, was consecrated by the Lord through holy baptism and fully instructed in heavenly disciplines.” Lhuet, Book II, chapter II, says that he was converted by Saint Peter at Rome. Renatus Benedictus says that he came from the East to Rome with Saint Peter.]

At the washing of the very font, divine grace poured over him, [Note: The manuscript of Saint-Maximin adds: “as he himself declares in his responses”] so that the outcome of the matter would give an indication that he would become great among the people because of the merit of his holiness.

For he was called Lucius by his parents according to the flesh, deriving from the great consul Lucius not only his bodily origin but also his name. But afterward, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, his name was changed for the better, in the manner of the holy Fathers. Thus the one who had been called Lucius by his parents was afterward called Lucianus by God, through grace and with an enlarged name, so that this might make clear that, begotten in a new light and himself made light in the Lord, he would eventually first preach among the nations, together with the other holy men, that same light in which he had been reborn in Christ.

It is therefore clear that he was Roman by descent, from a noble lineage; but he became nobler in spirit, because through the adoption of grace he was found to be a son of the eternal King. If it is asked whose teaching formed and whose instruction educated him, he was truly a disciple of the Apostle Peter, founded upon his faith and imbued with heavenly disciplines. The sequence, time, and order of his deeds speak sufficiently to this. [Note: Lhuet writes that he was most learned in Greek and Latin; the manuscript of Saint-Maximin adds several details about his steadfastness, zeal, and other virtues. Saussay says that after Peter’s death he traveled through various parts of Italy and scattered the seed of the divine word far and wide.]

After being reborn in Christ, he lived as a perfected soldier of Christ at Rome, as though in a military camp, so that when he eventually went forth to the nations he might be found a vigorous warrior and a most courageous champion of the faith.

### 3.

As he was nourished by the teaching of God into a mature man, it happened that the illustrious martyr Dionysius came to Rome under Christ’s leadership. [Note: Lhuet writes that Dionysius came to Rome to visit Peter and Paul in captivity; but when he arrived, he found that they had been killed and that Clement had already been made pope. Several years passed between Peter’s death and Clement’s election, during which Linus and Cletus held the pontificate; we shall discuss the former on 23 September, the latter on 23 April, and Clement on 23 November.]

There he found the blessed Clement already governing the summit of the Apostolic See after the departure of the apostles. Saint Dionysius, who was also called Macarius, was received by him with the greatest courtesy and treated with fitting and ample honor, both because of the merit of his holiness and because of their long-standing familiarity in Christ. He therefore remained with that supreme pontiff for a considerable time, so that they might refresh one another by their presence, warm one another through divine conversations, [Col. 1113D] and strengthen one another in turn by the examples of their virtues.

Among very many conversations concerning the Holy Scriptures, the blessed Clement, inspired by the divine Spirit, said to him:

“Do you see, my dearest brother Dionysius, how great is the harvest of the Lord’s sowing among the nations, and how few are the laborers in the word of divine preaching? Since, therefore, you have been sufficiently instructed in all the teachings of the Catholic faith, imbued with every Christian observance, and strengthened by virtues, go, I beg you, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the western regions like a good soldier, and fight the battles of the Lord your God against the most savage enemies.”

### 4.

When the blessed Dionysius had assented to depart in response to these commands, Saint Clement began to seek companions and energetic helpers for him in the word, as well as men suitable in life and holiness, and also numerous distinguished ministers of divine service. Among them the same pontiff chose this highly approved man, Lucian, as his companion, and ordained him bishop, [Note: Others say that he was consecrated by Saint Dionysius; according to Lhuet, the Martyrologies of Senlis report that he was consecrated bishop by Saint Regulus] because he had been thoroughly instructed in the faith under the teaching of the Apostle Peter, so that none of the individual offices of ecclesiastical discipline would be lacking among such highly approved men.

Because he was an older disciple of Christ and Peter, Saint Clement joined him to Dionysius so that he might be his interpreter and, for the others, like a venerable father and eminent teacher in the doctrine and religion of holiness.

After arranging these matters, and after giving them many teachings of Christ and exhortations to piety, he addressed them at last in these words:

“Go, dearest and strongest, most energetic warriors of Christ. And just as the Lord was with our holy Fathers, the apostles, and with their fellow workers, so may he be with you in all the works of the divine word. For you are going to acquire for the Lord a great and innumerable people from the nations and lead them into the promised land.”

After entrusting many things to each of them and revealing the sacraments of the faith to them all together, he gave peace to everyone, dismissed them, and ordered that this holy brotherhood depart in peace.

## CHAPTER TWO. He preaches in Italy and comes to Arles

### 5.

As they traveled and preached the word of God together, first throughout all Italy, before they approached Ticinum, [Note: Fidentia Julia, as will soon become clear, between Parma and Piacenza] it appeared to the most blessed Lucian, at a certain place not far from the city called Parma, on the road, that he should evangelize the people in that same place with the word of God and recall them from vain superstition and the worship of idols, in accordance with what is sung in the psalm: “Going forth, they went and wept, casting their seeds”; and that he should distribute among the people what he had received, as a faithful steward.

But because the people of that place were still pagans and deeply entangled in the worship of idols, they could not tolerate insults to their gods, nor the divine word being preached to them. They immediately seized the most holy Lucian, subjected him to abuse, and placed him in the public prison, which is still shown today to all who pass through that place.

When he entered it, he sang with great joy, saying:

“Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall enter into your truth”; and also:

“Make my steps firm in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be moved.”

[Col. 1115B] **6.** Thus the holy man conducted himself in this custody as though beneath the shadow of God’s wings, and, placing himself wholly in the hope of Christ’s protection, prayed to the Lord, saying:

“Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name; for the righteous await me, so that through me, Christ, Savior of the world, those among the Gentiles who are predestined to life may be justified before you.”

As the blessed man, holy in heart, sang such and similar words to the Lord, his petition immediately penetrated the heavens: he was not to remain without his companions on the journey, since he desired to go with them to suffering and to reach those to whom he had been sent. Thus the illustrious athlete of Christ did not shrink from accepting the loss of life for Christ’s sake; rather, he devoutly asked that he might first produce the fruit promised him by the Lord, and that only afterward, when the harvest had arrived with abundant interest, he might reach the palm of martyrdom and the reward of life together with his companions.

Divine power therefore soon came to his aid.

[Note: [Col. 1115C] The manuscripts of Saint Maximinus and Lovetus, drawing on another manuscript, add: “For there was already there a disciple of Christ named Domninus, who, still a perfect confessor of Christ, rests gloriously in the body in that same place on account of such works. Indeed, the place itself took its name from him,” and so forth. The account relates that he led Lucian out of prison by night; for this reason, on the following day, the inhabitants cast Domninus himself into [Col. 1115D] prison. Sussajus reports the same story, except that he wishes these events to have taken place at Parma. But if these things were written by Odo, I am not surprised that they have been omitted from other copies. For whether Lucian came into Gaul in the time of Saint Clement or under Decius, Saint Domninus could not have rescued him at the risk of his own head: as we shall say on 9 October, forty years after Decius he was chamberlain to Maximian, and, having been killed there for the faith of Christ, subsequently gave his name to the place now called the Borough of Saint Domninus.]

There were already certain Christians there, whom divine power moved. Knowing what had happened to the holy man, they came to him by night in the prison and, by whatever means they could, freed him from the dungeon for the love of Christ; [Col. 1116A] together with his holy fellow soldiers, they enabled him to depart free.

**7.** Meanwhile that holy company, advancing with favorable success from place to place, came from there to Ticinum, [Note: [Col. 1115D] Ticinum, or Pavia, was a royal city only in the time of the Goths.] the royal city of Italy. There, resting for a short while, they did not cease from divine praises, nor did they fail to preach the word of God everywhere, so that one could recognize in them the prophecy: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things” (Romans 10:15).

Running here and there, they acted confidently, trusting in God’s help. They went forth rejoicing, mindful of what is read in the Acts of the Apostles: that they too had already become participants in Christ’s sufferings and had been deemed worthy to suffer insults for his name (Acts 5:41). As they traveled together, no one can say [Col. 1116B] how many thousands of people were converted to Christ in that period. They preached, proclaiming the word of salvation to everyone.

Divine power accompanied them, so that those who saw them—like citizens of heaven and lambs among wolves—shining with signs and miracles, could perceive them bearing and illuminating the souls of God’s elect.

**8.** At last, leaving Italy, they entered the sea under favorable conditions, with the winds blowing, and by ship arrived where the Holy Spirit led them directly; they happily reached the harbor of the city of Arles. On leaving the ship, they were received as guests by the inhabitants of that city, who showed them no small kindness.

When they had assembled together there, following the custom of the holy Apostles they began to confer among themselves, each deciding what region [Col. 1116C] to choose for preaching and which companions should travel together. Thus it came about that they sent the most holy Marcellinus, with a few companions, as is said, to Spain.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Lovetus omits this name, and I cannot determine who he was, unless perhaps Saint Eugenius Marcellus, the first bishop of Toledo, who is said to have been a disciple of Saint Dionysius and is commemorated on 15 November.]

They directed Saturninus to Toulouse,

[Note: [Col. 1115D] The Roman Martyrology, Ado, and others state that he was killed at Toulouse in the time of Decius; the Acts that we shall give on 29 November agree with them, contrary to the tradition of the Church of Toulouse, as is clear from Guilielmus Catellius.]

as though to the capital of Aquitaine, so that they might spread the Gospel of the eternal kingdom far and wide among the nations and plant the churches of Christ everywhere as far as the British Ocean.

[Note: [Col. 1116C] Toulouse is not a city of Aquitaine, but of Gallia Narbonensis. The author calls it the capital of Aquitaine because the kings of Aquitaine, Aripert, brother of Dagobert, and Louis the Pious, established their royal seat at Toulouse. Catellius discusses these matters more fully.]

[Note: [Col. 1116C] Lovetus lists several more of their companions, assigned to various peoples as preachers of the Gospel: Saint Regulus to the people of Arles, entered in the sacred calendar on 30 March; Ursinus to the Bituriges, whom some claim to have been Nathanael, on 9 November and 29 December; Clement to the people of Metz, on 23 November; Crescent to the people of Vienne, on 27 June, although they report that he was crowned with martyrdom before Clement’s pontificate; Andochius to the Aedui, on 24 September, although the Roman Martyrology and others report that he was sent into Gaul by Saint Polycarp; Benignus to the Lingones, on 1 November, though he too is said to have been a disciple of Polycarp; Austremonius to the Arverni, on 1 November. Savaro, himself an Arvernian, disagrees and insists that Austremonius came there only under the consuls Decius and Gratus; Fronto to the people of Périgueux, on 25 October, though his life says that Saint Peter sent him into Gaul; Eutropius to the Santones, on 30 April; Mellonius to the people of Rouen, on 22 October. Yet Mellonius is said to have been made bishop by Pope Stephen in the time of Aurelian (Lovetus should more correctly have written “Nica­sius,” in agreement with other authors, concerning whom see 11 October); Taurinus to the Eburovices, on 11 August; Valerius to Trier, on 29 January. The people of Trier, however, say that Saint Peter sent him to them; Mansuetus to the Leuci, on 3 September. Adso the Abbot likewise writes in his Life that Peter sent him; Caraunus to the Carnutes, on 28 May.]

### CHAPTER III. He preaches at Beauvais; Saints Maximianus and Julianus are crowned with martyrdom.

[Col. 1117A]

**9.** After these arrangements, the blessed Dionysius—also called Macarius because of his exceptional religious holiness—who had received the honor of the apostolate and the privilege of preaching among the nations from the blessed Clement, is known to have retained the most sacred Lucian with him until he reached the town of Lutetia of the Parisians.

[Note: [Col. 1117C] The manuscript of Saint Maximinus adds that Dionysius remained there, because he recognized that the savagery of error was raging more fiercely in that place.]

Keeping only a few companions with him, he sent Saint Lucian to Beauvais for the purpose of evangelizing. Faith in Christ had united Lucian to him as a companion of noble faith and had made him his brother; uprightness and zeal had soon joined them together.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] The manuscript of Saint Maximinus and Lovetus state that they had been converted by Saint Lucian and had attached themselves to him; here the author makes them natives of Beauvais.]

He sent him together with the priest Saint Maximianus and the deacon Julianus to Beauvais, where, as we read, a Roman garrison and military force were stationed, since the people of Beauvais are said always to have been warlike.

Accordingly, as is recorded in the public histories, from that district alone [Note: [Col. 1117D] Caesar, in Book II of *The Gallic War*, writes that they could field one hundred thousand men and that, at the council of the Belgae, they promised sixty thousand against the Romans.] more than sixty thousand armed men are said to have gone out to battle against Julius Caesar and the Roman army, together with the other inhabitants of Gaul. Therefore, because of the protection of the other cities, the Roman army was stationed there at that time.

**10.** Against the savagery of both peoples the strongest athlete of Christ, relying on the consolation of his disciples, was not afraid to come, girded with the arms of Christ and strengthened by divine grace.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] The manuscript of Saint Maximinus contains a lengthy interpolation here concerning his virtues and miracles, and the many people converted by him, Maximianus, and Julianus in the city, its districts, and villages. Lovetus also quotes the following, among other material, from another manuscript:

“In these labors, although he sometimes appeared exhausted by old age, he was strengthened in vigor of mind and by the power of the Holy Spirit, so that he could say with the Apostle: ‘I am strong and can do everything in him who strengthens me.’ Indeed, these holy men had chosen such contiguous and neighboring regions for preaching the Gospel that they could often console one another at close hand with divine words and see one another face to face. Thus they were of one heart, one soul, and one charity of divine love. Because they could not be together on account of the preaching duties entrusted to them and the gains of souls, they could not long endure being far apart without refreshing one another through holy conversation. Hence, even today, public monuments of the blessed Dionysius are shown on the road called by his name. It is said that the supreme pontiff used to travel along it to illuminate these regions by his presence and refresh the holy old man and the blessed Lucian by his sight; together they would strive by their preaching to direct the savagery of the pagans toward the service of the true God.”]

For he was exceedingly steadfast in faith, most eloquent in speech, and admirable in every virtue. He therefore began to preach the Lord’s name, to wage war against the powers of the air, and to plant the Church of Christ. Drunk with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he instructed the people no less by his example than by his words.

The power of miracles accompanied him, and by the Lord’s power he drove away every disease. He had received such grace in expelling demons that, as soon as they heard his command, they immediately departed from the bodies they possessed.

Continuing without ceasing to preach by day and by night, he persisted in affirming the true and only Lord. He was always occupied in prayer and [Note: [Col. 1118D] The constant tradition of Beauvais holds that the building in which he once used to celebrate the divine offices was later consecrated as a church, first in his name and afterward in the name of Saint Nicholas. In memory of this, Mass is celebrated on his feast day above the first vault of the high altar.] divine service, in many vigils and daily fasts, in abstinence from food, and in every affliction of the flesh by which he daily mortified himself, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, he might present himself to Christ the Lord as a living and acceptable sacrifice (Romans 12:1).

Thus his regular food consisted of nothing else but a little bread and the eating of herbs, with cold water to drink. Divine power sustained him, and Christ’s grace strengthened his weakened limbs. The blessed man yearned so intensely to reach the palm of martyrdom that, already dead to the world, he carried his cross daily after Christ the Lord. For he knew with certainty that there are two kinds of martyrdom: one hidden and the other manifest. He was already undergoing the first in secret—although the power of his abstinence was evident to everyone—in order that he might afterward attain the second and be crowned by the Lord.

He was worn down by the mortification of the flesh, adorned with patience, grounded in remarkable humility, and filled with gentleness. Thus the power of good works had grown so greatly around him that, while he was still on earth in the body, he seemed already in spirit to dwell with the angels in heaven. Hence he always appeared calm in countenance and tranquil in mind, adorned with remarkable white hair, so that in conduct and body alike he was judged conspicuous and distinguished.

**11.** When his fame had spread far and wide, many came to him to be baptized by him [Col. 1118C] in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The idols that had been manufactured were destroyed.

Therefore, when the ancient enemy saw that those whom Christ was gaining through his servants were being lost to him, he turned all the machinery of his craft against the holy Church of God.

[Note: [Col. 1118D] The persecution of Domitian had begun before Lucian came into Gaul, if he came under Clement’s pontificate; perhaps, however, the edicts had not yet reached all the provinces.]
