He so inflamed Domitian—who, after Nero, the son of perdition, conducted the second persecution against Christians—and stirred him to such furious indignation [Col. 1119A] that, wherever Christians were found throughout the Roman world, he compelled them either to sacrifice to the gods or to be cruelly killed after being subjected to various tortures.

Accordingly, throughout the entire world subject to him, a public edict was posted in every city, town, municipality, and village, ordering all officials of the state to compel Christians to worship idols and sacrifice to the gods, or else to kill them by various punishments.

**12.** Persecutors of the Christian name were therefore dispatched here and there. Among them Fescenninus Sisinnius, together with the other officials, was ordered to come swiftly to Gaul to search out Christ’s soldiers, especially those who had recently left Rome and whose fame had already grown, so that they might drive the Christian name out of Gaul.

At that time three exceptionally savage men were sent [Col. 1119B]—namely Latinus, [Note: [Col. 1119D] Others have Jachinus; Vincentius has Jacinus; Petrus de Natalibus has Latrinus.] Jarius, [Note: [Col. 1119D] The manuscript of Saint Maximinus has Januarius; Petrus has Larius.] and Antor [Note: [Col. 1119D] Vincentius and Petrus have Antrus; Belfort has Andrus; Mombrizius, Antius; Lovetus, Anterus; the manuscript of Saint Maximinus, Auctor.]—specifically to search for God’s servant Lucian, with their agents. Wherever they found him, they were either to present him before the governor’s tribunal or immediately strike him with the sword if he refused to sacrifice to the idols.

When these men had traveled through the cities and places concerned, they did not find him at once. Meanwhile news reached them about the man of God: by preaching the Gospel of the eternal kingdom, he had won over the people of Beauvais. On hearing this, consumed more and more by anger and indignation, they hurried there at the fastest possible pace.

**13.** Shortly before they arrived, the blessed martyr, informed by the Holy Spirit that they were near, remained in the place where he was teaching [Col. 1119C] the people the words of life. A very large crowd was with him, already converted to the faith of Christ through the preaching of the blessed man of God.

He exhorted them all the more attentively because he was more certain of the glory of eternal reward, saying:

“Behold, dearest brothers and sons: my Lord Jesus Christ will now deign to grant me the fruit of my labors and the rewards promised long ago. Therefore, beloved, persevere bravely in the faith of Christ. I, already wearied by extreme old age, hasten joyfully to Christ with the palm of martyrdom. But you must remain steadfast in the grace you have received.

“Let not the terror of rulers turn you away from the faith of Christ; let not threats frighten you; let not flattering persuasion deceive you; let no promise of advantage call you back. Thus eternal joys may receive you there, where ineffable rewards have been prepared for you. I hasten there fearlessly, and therefore I do not fear the persecutors’ savagery.”

After saying this, he raised his eyes to heaven and gave thanks to God before them all, because God had deemed him worthy to be counted among the holy martyrs and not separated from his holy companions.

“I give you thanks,” he said, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who at the end have joined me to the blessed Dionysius and his companions and made me equal with them in labors. Therefore I ask that you deign to count me among their number and make me a participant in your kingdom.”

**14.** When he had finished speaking, he left the city of Beauvais and, in accordance with the Lord’s command, withdrew a short distance from the city—not out of fear of punishment, but to provide an example to the flock in accordance with the Lord’s command (Matthew 10:23).

Traveling with the blessed martyrs Maximianus [Col. 1120B] and Julianus, he did not cease from divine conversations and prayers throughout the journey, until he reached the summit of the mountain toward which he was traveling.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] Papirius Massonus, in his work on the rivers of Gaul, writes:

“Among the peoples of Picardy in Beauvais, whose territory extends widely, I must not omit the Thérain, the greater river, and the Thérain, the lesser. Both flow from the west, and both run toward the east, which is extremely rare. Milliacum is a place of the Beauvaisis, a castellany now dependent on Clermont and belonging to the kings, though a certain part belongs to Hadrian Boflerius, a very noble man whose residence we state to be in the Beauvaisis, in the village of Cagny. These two little rivers meet and merge, mixing their waters, and abound in trout and crayfish.”

A little later he adds:

“Near Milliacum there is a mountain called Millius, and at its summit a meadow is visible, where the martyr Lucian was beheaded and lost his life.”

Lovetus, as witness, says that the mountain is called Montmille in French. Renatus Benedictus writes that Lucian came there not to escape the fury of the persecutors but to meet their arrival.]

The mountain lies beside the river Thérain, nearly three miles from the city. When he arrived there, he could not remain hidden, like a city set upon a mountain, since the mountain itself offers the people a beautiful prospect above the river. There, placed as though on a watchtower, the most blessed man resolved to await his crown of martyrdom.

**15.** Meanwhile the soldiers mentioned above reached the city of Beauvais with swift flight. When they sought God’s holy Lucian there and did not find him, they began to investigate more carefully where he had gone. They were told that he was teaching the people not far from the city.

They immediately remounted their horses and, riding with winged speed, suddenly approached the mountain where the man of God was staying with the people and his disciples.

[Note: [Col. 1120D] The manuscript of Saint Maximinus inserts here an exhortation by Saint Lucian to his followers.]

When they arrived, before making any inquiry before a judicial authority, they seized God’s saints—namely Maximianus and Julianus. Perhaps they intended to frighten the holy old man by their punishments and bring him back to the worship of the gods.

After arresting them, they ordered Lucian, with all the fury of royal authority, to sacrifice to the idols. “Otherwise,” they said, “unless you sacrifice to the immortal gods, we order you to be punished immediately by the sword.”

But, strong in faith, they answered that they would never sacrifice to idols, because idols are vain and are the works of human hands. “For we know,” they said, “the one true Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, for whose faith we are prepared to die.”

On hearing this, they immediately ordered them to be punished by the sword before the eyes of the blessed Lucian. When this had been done, they received the imperishable crowns promised them by the Lord and were received in peace into the number of the holy martyrs.

In praise of their glory, the blessed Lucian extolled the Lord and said joyfully before them all:

“I rejoice and am glad in you, my God, because I see my sons going before me to the crown.”

### CHAPTER IV. Saint Lucian is tortured in various ways and killed.

**16.** Then Latinus, Jarius, and Antor, in anger and indignation, addressed him savagely, as though with one voice:

“Are you that man,” they said, “who by your sorceries lead the people astray so that they do not obey the commands of the unconquered Augustus and the Roman Senate by offering pleasing sacrifices to the immortal gods?”

Saint Lucian answered them:

“I am not a sorcerer; I am a servant of Jesus Christ, instructed in divine teachings. Therefore I show God’s people the way of truth and explain how they ought to follow without stumbling my Lord Jesus Christ, who came into the world to redeem his creation and turn it away from the worship of demons, so that, recalled to the light above and rescued from their darkness, they may be saved. For it is just that they bow the neck of their hearts only to him who chose to die, crucified for the salvation of all.”

**17.** They replied:

“How do you assert as God one whom you declare not only to have died but also to have been crucified?”

Saint Lucian answered:

“Although your infidelity does not deserve to hear the mysteries of the most merciful King, nevertheless, for the sake of the crowd standing here, I shall explain them briefly.

“God the Son of God, who was always with the Father before the ages, because of the transgression of the first man, at the end of time chose, for the restoration of the human race, to become truly human from a virgin, so that he might be true God and true man, the same one God and man, one Christ, true Son of God and of man.

“Thus he who, remaining always impassible in his divinity with the Father, was invisible, became not only visible but also capable of suffering for us according to his humanity. Therefore he became obedient to God the Father for our redemption unto death, even death on a cross.

“Otherwise, unless the Son of God had deigned also to become the Son of man, neither would the human race return to forgiveness [Col. 1121D], nor would mortals return to life.”

As the most blessed Lucian continued with these and many other words, the soldiers became increasingly filled with fury. They said:

“The time had already summoned you, in your old age, to recover from childish notions. But because excessive vanity deceives you and unnecessary loquacity entices you, you do not fear to go to your death, relying on reckless boldness.

“Nevertheless, unless you quickly come to your senses, withdraw from this audacity, and offer pleasing sacrifices to the immortal gods, we shall subject your old age to many torments.”

**18.** Then, sitting down, they ordered him to stand before them. They addressed him in a threatening voice:

“Declare your name and status to us immediately.”

The athlete of Christ answered:

“Among my forebears I was truly called Lucius; but in the regeneration by which I was reborn to eternal life in Christ, I am called Lucianus.

“As for my status, I acknowledge that I am Roman by birth, a name known throughout the world. But I show what is nobler for me: that I am a servant of Christ Jesus. This is clearly evident, because for me to live is nothing other than my Lord Jesus Christ, and to die is gain. Therefore I rejoice and confess that I am his servant.”

Then the soldiers said:

“This is precisely what we said: you are a magician and a seducer of those who listen to you. Moreover, you are proved obstinate, since you continue to speak insolently and finally do not know how to come to the aid of your weary old age.

“If you are a Roman, why have you madly withdrawn from the worship of the gods whom Augustus Caesar, together with the entire Roman Senate, venerates, and whom the whole world worships?”

Saint Lucian answered:

“Since I was reborn in Christ and came to know my true Lord Jesus Christ, I have renounced in faith not only the devil and idols but also all his works. But what I say and confess about Christ the Lord you neither perceive with your ears nor can retain in your minds.

“For the infidelity of your hearts has blinded you—and Caesar Augustus together with the Senate—from whom you have brought such decrees: that we rational human beings should sacrifice to demons and bow our necks to idols made by human hands.”

**19.** When Latinus, Januarius, and Antor heard this, they could not bear the insult to Caesar. Seizing him, they handed him over with his hands bound to the torturers. They stretched him out and savagely beat him with dreadful whips.

Although they flogged him excessively and held him tightly bound, and although the athlete of God was tortured for a long time by torments, he was neither overcome by pain nor frightened by threats. Strong in the faith of Christ, he strengthened the limbs of his nearly decrepit old age with the pure vigor of his spirit, so that throughout the blows, maintaining the same countenance and the same mind, he did not cease to confess Christ’s name aloud, saying:

“I believe Christ, the Son of God, in my heart, and I shall never cease to praise him with my mouth.”

**20.** Then, moved by fury, they pronounced sentence and ordered him to be struck with the sword. One of the soldiers drew his sword; and, when the holy neck was already prepared, he cut off the holy and precious head.

As the body of the holy man lay there [Col. 1122D] and still quivered though lifeless, a great light from heaven shone over the holy body in the sight of everyone, even the servants of death themselves. A loud voice came together with the light, saying:

“Bravo, good servant Lucian, who did not hesitate to pour out your blood for me. Come and receive the crown promised to you long ago, for you shall rejoice with the saints in heaven. Come and receive the dwelling of glory prepared for you long ago with the angels.”

This voice was not made for him, since he had always carried this promise in his heart through faith, but for those standing by, so that they might hold with complete certainty the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ that Saint Lucian had long preached and might be more firmly convinced of the holy man’s merits.

This occurred on Saturday [Col. 1123A] at the hour [Note: [Col. 1123D] Lovetus adds: “after midday.”] on the mountain mentioned above, three miles from the city, on the sixth day before the Ides of January [8 January].

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Lovetus gives 7 January.]

When the men who had believed—and those who had not believed—saw and heard these things, they were all struck with overwhelming terror. By divine prompting some fled; others, stunned and amazed with joy because they saw themselves freed from the devil’s snares, nevertheless withdrew for a short time from the place because they could not endure the brightness of the light.

### CHAPTER V. He carries his own head and is buried.

**21.** Then the lifeless body of the holy man rose, took the severed holy head in its own hands, and, by the grace of the Holy Spirit—whose members and instruments the body’s limbs had been—together with angelic assistance, began to travel on the firmest feet as though still alive in the body.

Carrying the precious head under angelic guidance, he traveled about three miles from the mountain and, after fording the riverbed, reached a place [Note: [Col. 1123D] The manuscript of Saint Maximinus says, “after crossing the ford of the Thérain.” Massonus, drawing from a manuscript Life, has “after crossing the Thérain,” hence Lovetus says that he crossed the Thérain at the village of Miauroy. The path by which he walked carrying his head can still be seen on Mount Millius; it is called Rosea, or Rosetum, *la Rosière*, and roses of extraordinary redness grow there, although roses transplanted elsewhere into the same kind of garden do not produce them. Although Mount Millius is steep and precipitous on one side, no one has ever suffered the loss of horses, wine, or any other property through the overturning of carts or wagons. Even heretics, who reject the veneration of saints and deny that they aid mortals, have often confessed that they themselves witnessed their carts overturning there and rolling down the slope, yet, when they reached the bottom, found both all the wine safe and the horses unharmed.] nearly one mile from the aforesaid city, the place that the holy man had chosen to be entrusted with his burial. There, in a public field, the saint rested in peace with the palm of victory.

**22.** [Note: [Col. 1124D] “The struggles of the martyrs.” The men of that place.]

The most devout men who had been converted through his preaching came out to meet him with spices. Wrapping the body in clean linen cloths, they buried it with great honor and reverence in a tomb that appeared to be newly made.

Nevertheless, so that the funeral rites might not seem to have been celebrated without the service of angels, while the most holy body was being placed in the tomb, their nostrils suddenly opened, and everyone present sensed wonderfully fragrant odors until the funeral rites of the blessed man had been completed and the body covered with earth.

The men, astonished and amazed with joy, said to one another:

“What is this? Glory to you, Lord Jesus Christ, because our nostrils have never before sensed such a great and wonderful fragrance. Glory to you, Christ the Savior, because we have been so filled that we believe nothing further good is lacking for us.”

The more they said such things, the more abundantly the divine fragrance flowed, so that no one could doubt that the ministries of angels had been present at these funeral rites from the beginning of his passion.

**23.** When these rites had been duly completed, all prostrated themselves on the ground in great fear and deep devotion of heart, crying out and saying:

“We believe in you, Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, reigning in heaven with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as we heard with our ears and learned in our minds from your holy martyr Lucian.”

When the multitude of people who had gathered from various regions, villages, and hamlets as though for a spectacle saw or heard these things from the believers, nearly five hundred men and women, as was estimated, were pierced in heart and believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, on that same day.

Already no fewer than thirty thousand people, or many more, of different kinds and ages had been converted throughout Gaul through the preaching of the blessed Lucian. Abandoning their idols, they confessed God the Father, unbegotten, and his only-begotten Son, together with the Holy Spirit, as the one true God in the Trinity.

Reborn and renewed through this faith by the bath of regeneration, some of them immediately built for the Lord, with great devotion, a basilica in the same place over the holy body, in honor of that martyr.

**24.** The bodies of Saints Maximianus and Julianus were buried on the mountain where they had been beheaded. But as the number and devotion of Christians increased, the faithful lifted them from there and joined them to the body of the blessed Lucian.

Later, when the church had been improved and adorned, the Lord the Father cooperating, many benefits were rightly granted by the Lord Jesus Christ to those who asked, through the merits and intercession of the holy martyrs.

Because they had one faith, one charity, and one confession in martyrdom, we rightly believe that their fellowship in eternal blessedness is one and that their sharing in merits is one. Therefore let us give thanks to our Creator, because three witnesses of Christ, taken together in number, completed a faithful martyrdom on earth for the sake of faith in the Trinity. Since we know that this happened, we venerate it, faithfully remember it, [Col. 1124C] and acknowledge it.

**25.** Behold, brothers: although the whole earth has been made purple with the blood of martyrs, our city too has been made purple by the blood of these men, sprinkled with the blood of Christ. Although heaven blooms with the crowns of martyrs, our land also blooms, adorned with their virtues.

The other churches are adorned with the memorials of martyrs; this one is adorned with the triumphs of these three and consecrated by their relics. The seasons are marked by the anniversaries of martyrs; the present festival also is marked by the anniversary of these men, celebrated because of their ascent to heaven.

Here too, at their tomb, the signs of their virtues multiply and the benefits of healing abound: the sick come and are healed; the blind are enlightened; the lame are cured; those afflicted by demons are freed. And what is greater, the prayers of the faithful are heard, vows are received, the bonds of sinners are loosened, heaven is opened to those who knock, and the Church receives its rewards.

How exceedingly blessed and pleasing to God is the fellowship of these holy martyrs! Through their association, choirs of angels rejoice in heaven, while through their merits and prayers the worthy petitions of all the faithful are granted on earth, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the co-eternal Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 1126A] lives and reigns through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1125]

## ODO’S CANONS

Issued at the Synod of Pontigonis.

*(In Baluzius, *Capitularia*, vol. II, p. 245.)*

[Col. 1125A] The holy synod, which was assembled in the name of the Lord at the summons of the lord John, thrice-blessed and universal pope, and by the command of the lord Charles, perpetual Augustus, at the place called Pontigonis, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 876, in the ninth indiction, in the thirty-seventh year of the reign of the aforementioned unconquered emperor, and in the first year of his empire, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, established the following chapters.

### CHAPTER I

When Louis, who governed the rights of the Roman Empire, died, the lord John, thrice-blessed pope, invited the lord Charles, then king, to the threshold of the blessed Apostles through Gadericus of Velletri, Formosus of Porto, and John of Arezzo, venerable bishops. He chose him as defender and protector of that Church and crowned him with the imperial diadem, choosing him alone and specially above all others to hold the scepter of the Roman Empire.

Obeying his sacred institutions as duty requires, we establish what he established, and, with unanimous consent, we all confirm what he confirmed.

### CHAPTER II

After a holy synod had been assembled in the city of Rome, before the arrival of the aforementioned lord emperor, it sent, with everyone’s consent, letters to King Louis, to his sons, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other leading men of his kingdom. In these letters it admonished them, with apostolic authority and in paternal fashion, to preserve the things that belong to peace, and not, in particular, to attempt any incursion easily into the kingdom of the aforementioned Augustus until they could come together for mutual discussion. He himself, according to the ministry entrusted to him by God, would then decide and discern among them both how peace should be preserved and what belonged to the rights of the kingdoms.

They wholly refused to receive these letters, which had been sent to them and delivered twice through Odo, the venerable bishop of Beauvais.

### CHAPTER III
He himself, however, disregarding the apostolic and paternal admonitions and breaking the fraternal treaties, invaded his brother’s kingdom with a hostile force in tyrannical fashion, laying it waste; and, through the authority of those who carried them out, perpetrated murders, rapes, adulteries, sacrileges, and countless other evils that cannot be enumerated.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 1126A] When the thrice-blessed pope heard that these evils had been perpetrated in the kingdom of the spiritual son of the lord Charles, ever Augustus, he was touched with grief of heart and hastened to send his representatives—namely John and John, venerable bishops—with other letters of his own. He wished to admonish him to repent of the past evil and at last to cease invading [Col. 1126B] his brother’s kingdom. Though admonished a second time, he still did not wish to receive their embassy.

## CHAPTER V

After these men, finally, he sent other envoys: namely Leo, most holy bishop of Gabii and envoy and *apocrisiarius* of the holy Roman Church, and likewise Peter, venerable bishop of Fossombrone. He protested, entreating and admonishing him concerning these same matters. It remains uncertain whether he will receive their admonitions.

## CHAPTER VI

But since the aforesaid Leo, most reverend bishop of Gabii and envoy and *apocrisiarius* of the holy Roman Church, and likewise Peter, bishop of Fossombrone [Col. 1126C], cannot remain here longer because of certain ecclesiastical necessities, nor is it fitting to weary bishops who have come from afar any further, they decided that John, bishop of Tuscany, and John, bishop of Arezzo, venerable bishops, should undertake the embassy of the aforesaid men together with the earlier embassy. Along with the other bishops whom they shall choose by common agreement, they are to define freely, in the place of all the bishops and by apostolic authority, whatever they determine must be done, whether in summoning people or in striking down the contemptuous. Whatever they themselves deliberate, the lord apostolicus, together with the whole holy Roman Church, shall determine, establish as enduring forever, and confirm.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 1126D] Just as the lord Pope John decreed, with the concurrence, consent, and joint decision of the lord and most glorious emperor Charles, ever Augustus, we unanimously praise with all devotion the decision that Ansigisus, venerable bishop and archbishop of Sens, should hold the pope’s place, and that he should be granted primacy over Gaul and Germany for summoning a synod and canonically deciding whatever necessary matters may arise; and that he should refer more serious matters to the pope’s attention. We decree and sanction that he should indeed hold primacy over Gaul and Germany.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 1127A] The synod which the lord John, apostolic and universal pope, recently instituted concerning the deposition of certain men—namely Formosus, bishop of Porto, and Gregory the *nomenclator*, together with Stephen the *secundicerius*, George the *vesterarius*, and the rest of their accomplices—as is contained in the letter he sent to us: in accordance with his command, and dissenting from its head in nothing, we consent to it and decree it. Obeying all his apostolic sanctions in every respect, as is proper, we submit to them.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1128A] The censure which the lord apostolicus established and confirmed concerning the utterly wicked deeds of King Louis and his accomplices—unless they come to their senses and render due obedience to the apostolic see—we all who have assembled for the present synod unanimously decree and confirm.

[Col. 1127]

# ODO’S INSTITUTION CONCERNING THE PROPERTY ASSIGNED TO THE COMMUNITY OF SAINT PETER

And concerning the number of fifty canons in it.

*(In Labbé, Councils, vol. IX.)*

[Col. 1127B] Odo, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ bishop of the Church of Beauvais.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, and especially to our successors, that the unanimous community and equal vote of the canons of Saint Peter’s Church, to which by God’s authorization I minister, earnestly requested our generosity: namely, that I should assign to them canonically, according to the custom of other churches, by a gift of generosity and by royal command, without anyone’s contradiction or disturbance, the properties that had been granted to them by our predecessors according to the boundaries of the individual estates, and that had likewise been secured for them by our own confirmation.

But seeing that such a matter exceeded the powers of my sole decision, and at the same time, with the grace of heavenly counsel going before me, taking thought for the aforesaid community to seek what would benefit it, and fearing—while granting them my assent in this matter—that the sheepfolds of the Lord’s flock might, God forbid, at some time be broken into by tyrannical attack, I sought the counsel both of Hincmar of the metropolitan province of Rheims and of the other venerable archbishops and my fellow bishops. Thus, through the sanction of those by whose authority ecclesiastical affairs are conducted, their assessment, inspired by the grace of the heavenly deity, might bring a useful and salutary outcome to me and to our Church.

On their advice I approached the serenity of the most pious King Charles, asking that, in his customary mercy, just as he looks peacefully upon all who everywhere serve the heavenly Majesty, so he might also look peacefully upon this Church, entrusted to me to govern without any preceding merits, and provide a command of solid permanence.

He, with his gratuitous clemency, graciously assenting to our prayers, decreed by his most orderly authority that what our benevolence had also foreseen should be stable.

Therefore, by canonical institution, we assign to the needs of the aforesaid community the villages written below in the county of Beauvais, with all their appurtenances and with all inhabitants legally belonging to them. These are: Burcinas, Pretiosas, Velena, Haverciaco, Frotmaro-Curte, Hilgia, and Cambariaco.

In the valley of Ballicinum: one vineyard at Bunnar, four [units] and one arpent.

In the suburb of our city: two mills, two *cambae*, two cultivated gardens, ten small farms, and one meadow.

A *precaria* in which there are twenty-four *mansi*, S., which Sigebert holds with its rent.

We entreat that none of our successors should thereafter diminish or withdraw anything from what, with God’s authorization, has been established by us, nor allot anything from it to his own use or that of his people. Rather, let them preserve undisturbed what we have accomplished out of divine love and for the salvation of souls, hoping with us for an equal and single reward from the Lord.

We also wish, and strive expressly to secure, that the number of canons living there, unless properties are added that provide the means of support, should not exceed the number fifty. And whenever any one of them departs by divine summons, let another be substituted, so that the aforesaid number may not be diminished.

Moreover, so that the authority of our devotion may possess firmer force, we have earnestly decided to strengthen this by canonical authority—not only through the command of the great and most pious King Charles, but also through that of the venerable lords and my fellow bishops, with whose consent we carried this out.

Hincmar, archbishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims: I have subscribed.

Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens: subscribed.

Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen: I have subscribed.

Rothadus, bishop of the Church of Soissons: subscribed.

Immo, bishop of the Church of Noyon: subscribed.

Lupus, bishop of the city of Châlons: subscribed.

Folcoinus, bishop of the city of Thérouanne: subscribed.

Theoderic, bishop of the Church of Cambrai: I have subscribed.

Ragenarius, bishop of the Church of Amiens: I have subscribed.

Erpoinus, bishop of the Church of Senlis: I have subscribed.

Given on the Kalends of March themselves, in the city of Soissons, before the altar of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, in the thirty-fifth year of the reign of the glorious lord King Charles, who in his piety consented to this privilege and confirmed it by royal authority, in the eighth indiction (in the year of Christ 875).

# In the Year of the Lord 881. Hericus, Monk of Auxerre

[Col. 1129]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Fabricius, Medieval and Later Latin Library.)*

[Col. 1129A] Hericus, or Herricus—corruptly Liricus or Firicus—a Benedictine monk of Auxerre, around the year 880, according to Sigebert of Gembloux, chapter 104, wrote in verse for Charles the Fat, already emperor: the *Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre* in six books, in the *Acts of the Saints*, volume seven, July 31, from the Paris edition of 1543, in duodecimo.

Caspar Barthius, who illuminates many passages of Germanus’s *Life* in his *Adversaria*, also published a hymn, book XXXIV, section 20. Labbe had already published two prose books on the miracles of the same Germanus in volume I of the *New Library of Manuscripts*, pp. 531, 569. Mabillon praises an as-yet unpublished sermon on this Germanus.

The *Life of Saint Alban the Martyr*, which Possevinus mentions as written in verse—Hericus here being for him Henricus of Luxeuil; compare Vossius, p. 332—exists at the beginning of the fourth book of the *Life of Saint Germanus*, as correctly observed in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. IV, June, p. 831.

Trithemius praises several of his letters and sermons in chapter 289 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and in II.56 of *Illustrious Benedictines*. Some of those sermons are read in the *Homiliary* of Paul the Deacon, though they must have been added by a later hand. See, if you please, volume XIII of the *Greek Library*, p. 795.

Combefisius inserted some passages from his homilies on John into his *Preaching Library*, calling them brilliant, learned, and sufficiently polished in style. Thomas Aquinas cites him sometimes under Bede’s name and sometimes under Alcuin’s.

Finally, it is useful to add what Mabillon brought to light in the *Analecta*, p. 422ff. (old edition, vol. I, p. 413): elegiac verses addressed to Hildebold, bishop of Auxerre, which this monk Hericus had prefixed to his *Collectanea*. The learned editor notes the following:

> “Heiricus, or Hericus or Ericus, was born in the territory of Auxerre, in a village called Hery after him, two leagues below the city, on the river Armançon. That place is still subject to the monastery of Saint Germanus. As a boy, I believe, he was given to that same monastery. As a young man he had Haymo, later bishop of Halberstadt, and Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, as teachers, as he himself testifies in these verses:
>
> “Here are the beautiful playful works of two teachers,
>
> “By whom I cultivated my intellect under bishops;
>
> “Lupus and Haymo played upon these in pleasing order,” etc.
>
> “This is the preface to the *Collectanea*, excerpted from the words of his teachers. I found these *Collectanea* in a Corbie manuscript copied by hand seven hundred years ago, bound together with the *Life of Saint Adalhard the Abbot*. In them fragments are reported first from Valerius Maximus, then from the Fathers, Jerome, Augustine, Bede, and others.

Hericus wrote many other works, including the *Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre*, in collaboration with the canons Rainogala and Alago, as is clear from chapter 39, where Hericus is called both Theosophus and a monk. Finally, he also composed homilies on the Gospels, as Honorius of Autun attests in IV.49, and John Trithemius agrees in chapter 289,” and so forth.

[Col. 1129]

# PREFACE OF THE MONK HERICUS TO HIS SIXTY-FOUR HOMILIES ON THE SEASONS AND THE SAINTS

*(Pez, Most Recent Treasury of Anecdotes.)*

[Col. 1129C] I, the humble brother Heinricus, a monk, prompted by the requests of my especially beloved Fathers to publish homilies—that is, sermons in the vernacular—to the extent of my intellectual ability, inclined my ears to their entreaties, although not willingly, but almost against my will. Nevertheless, I placed my hope in him who says, “Open your mouth,” and so forth.

Also, for the cultivation of divine praise, I undertook this labor as a burden of devotion and obedience. Therefore I beg your entire company, like an ignorant man going to war who does not know how to enter a duel, or rather, armed by your earnest prayers, that I may be able to begin this little work so discreetly and clearly that the beginning does not disagree with the middle, nor the middle with the end.

I ask this more earnestly of those who may wish to labor over this little work for the sake of improvement: if they find anything in it that needs correction, let them diligently polish it with the file of charitable correction.

May the grace of the Holy Spirit deign to be present with us. We fix our hope upon the mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God, beginning in this way: “Behold, the Desired One will come,” and so forth.

## The First Homily Begins: On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

“As the most sacred solemnity was now approaching, on which our Savior mercifully willed to be born among human beings,” and so forth.

[Col. 1131]

# VERSES OF HERICUS TO HILDEBOLD, BISHOP OF AUXERRE, IN HIS *COLLECTANEA*

[Col. 1131A]

Hildebold, rest and glory of your people,  
great in the honor of the earth, greater in the honor of God:

Receive graciously what Hericus here wisely offers,  
filled with love for your head.

I am ashamed to offer small things, since you deserve the greatest;  
yet it is fitting that great things should depend upon small ones.

And whoever gives this little thing is already proved to have given more:  
whatever he is and whatever he can be, he has surely given here.

Here are the beautiful playful works of two teachers,  
by whom I cultivated my intellect under bishops.

Lupus and Haymo played upon these in pleasing order,  
whenever time and occasion provided something to play at.

The one excelled in human learning, the other in divine;  
each is renowned and surpasses in his own titles.

Then, learned in handling these little notes,  
I grasped them swiftly with my fingers, aided by art.

Nor had I previously taken care to arrange them clearly in verse,  
until now, when they were to be given to you.

Remember, Father, to delight your mind with these violets,  
when your breast gapes beneath the weight of cares.

Increase the natural brightness of your brow and face  
whenever you wish to be more joyful.

If you deign to receive this with a tranquil expression,  
soon *comm... an* [the reading is materially incomplete in the source]—will the ardor be more pleasing.

These things Lupus was continually turning over on his shining lips,  
balancing each one according to its appropriate time.

[Col. 1131]

# THE *COLLECTANEA* BEGIN

## From the Books of Valerius Maximus on Memorable Deeds and Sayings

[Col. 1131B] While Sulpicius the priest was performing a sacrifice, a slip of the head covering removed him from the priesthood. The squeak of a mouse was heard by Fabius M. during his dictatorship. King Tarquin, once, because he had given a book of civic secrets to someone to copy, had him thrown into the sea sewn into a sack, and so forth.

[Col. 1131]

# LIFE OF SAINT GERMANUS, BISHOP OF AUXERRE

By Hericus the Monk, rendered from the prose style of Constantius [Note: Constantius was the author of the prose *Life* of the same Germanus of Auxerre, which is prefixed to the metrical *Life* in the Bollandists; editor’s note] into connected verse; from the very old manuscript of Lobbes, collated with a very ancient manuscript of Lyon and the Belfort manuscript.

*(In Bollandus, July, volume VII.)*

[Note: In the Lyon manuscript this title was read: “Commendation of the following work to the glorious King Charles, made by letter.” Concerning this letter, our preliminary commentary [that is, the Bollandist commentary], §4, from no. 39 onward, must necessarily be consulted. The same letter, though truncated, appears in Chesne, vol. II, p. 470.]

# DEDICATORY LETTER OF THE AUTHOR TO CHARLES (THE BALD), MOST DISTINGUISHED KING AND EMPEROR AT ONCE

[Col. 1131C] To Charles, predestined to immortal scepters and most distinguished of all kings, perpetual victor and ever Augustus: Hericus, least of the cenobites, wishes immediate and perpetual happiness in the Lord.

### 1

Whenever I recall that Your Highness [Belfort manuscript: “you,” throughout] governs your paternal scepters not only by courage, counsel, and prudence, but also, with no less zeal, draws the colors of true beauty from the innermost mirrors of wisdom and shapes with them an age defiled by depraved morals, I am repeatedly raised to the best hopes. I am often pierced by the truth of that saying uttered before our time: that a republic would be happy if either kings philosophized or philosophers ruled.

Although I am not unaware that what is now called a republic has become so worn out through the flood of every vice [another reading: “so befouled”] that many reasonably despair of its salvation, since it allows itself to be mastered neither by virtue nor governed by wisdom, there are many monuments of your clemency and many tokens of your piety.

Above all, this prepares eternal memory for you [Belfort manuscript: “for you alone,” throughout]: you not only represent equally the devotion of your celebrated grandfather Charles [that is, Charlemagne, the father of Louis the Pious and grandfather of Charles the Bald; the Lyon manuscript always writes *Karolus*] toward the immortal disciplines, but surpass it with incomparable fervor. What he drew from extinguished ashes, you advance everywhere through the manifold encouragement both of benefactions and of authority; indeed, to match lofty things with loftier, you drive it upward to the stars.

Thus, in your age, human talents strive with twofold support: you attract everyone by your example to pursue the hidden things of wisdom, while you invite certain people also by rewards.

### 2

To this is added that unassailable proof of truth by which your singular prudence protects itself with sufficiently vigilant reason against complaints that might arise. Lest our inertia, which willingly embraces its own blindness, place over itself a veil of excuse concerning ignorance, or reasonably complain of a lack of teachers, you have made it your distinctive concern that, wherever teachers of the arts flourished—arts whose principal task philosophy promises—Your Highness should bring them from every place for public instruction, attract them by courtesy, and summon them by generosity.

Greece mourns this, assailed by new goads of envy. Her former inhabitants, who long ago despised her together with the wealth of Asia, now prefer to delight in your magnanimity, are drawn by your studies, and place their confidence in your liberality. She grieves, I say, that she, once uniquely marvelous and marvelously unique, is abandoned by her own people. She certainly grieves that her privileges—something she had never previously feared—are transferred to our regions.

Why should I mention Ireland, which, disregarding the danger of the sea, is migrating almost entirely with its flock of philosophers to our shores? Each of them who is more learned voluntarily imposes exile upon himself in order to serve the wisest Solomon according to his desire.

### 3

Therefore, most invincible Caesar, it is almost as though the whole world were preparing new controversies against you and launching new declamations against you: while you strive to illuminate yourself and your people with the ornaments of wisdom, you have removed the schools and studies of nearly all nations. For once their teachers were removed, it necessarily followed that the talents of all easily froze in idleness.

Thus, with the others disregarded, all study of the best arts flowed into that part of the world embraced by your power. I am inclined to believe that they would long ago have withdrawn entirely from the earth, weary of human inertia, had they not been held there by the greatness of your integrity. In it, as is plainly evident, they have wonderfully established the unique summit and pinnacle of their profession.

Hence, although the very ancient saying is that “the laws are silent amid arms,” nevertheless, both in wartime and in peacetime, they have always possessed the greatest dignity among you. So much so that the palace is rightly called a school: its summit daily becomes accustomed to disciplines no less scholarly than military.

Whatever letters can do, whatever talents achieve, they owe to you—to you, I say, who, born always to accomplish something worthy of a man, both excel in courage and shine with wisdom.

### 4

The reason I have brought forward these matters is this. I openly confess that Lotharius, of divine memory, the son of Your Majesty, though a boy in years, was a philosopher in mind and, in natural disposition and resources of intelligence—if I may concede this uniquely to you—was more precious than the other mortals of his age.

Because, by your arrangement, he had been devoted to God and entrusted to blessed Germanus for education, he had conceived such devotion toward the saint and such ardor for the place that it may reasonably be thought that pale death envied us his life.

[Note: Lotharius, son of Charles the Bald and commendatory abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre, died around the feast of Christ’s Nativity—that is, either at the end of the year 865, as the *Annals of Bertin* at Chesne suggest, or at the beginning of 866, as Saint Ado indicates in his *Chronicle* near the end. See also the Benedictine *Annals* under the year 865, no. 35.]

Since he was a boy of divine intelligence and extremely eager for knowledge of things, it happened that one day, while searching out the hidden contents [Lyon manuscript: *penita*] of a certain book, he came upon two letters. In one of them, the most holy Aunarius, sixth bishop of Auxerre after blessed Germanus, earnestly entreated Stephen, an African priest, to arrange the life of that same most holy father Germanus in metrical form. In the other, Stephen indicated by his reply that he would obey the aforesaid bishop.

I judged it best to insert the text of these letters here also, so that the account intended to be conveyed to royal ears might overcome every scruple of ambiguity.

[Note: Both of the following letters also exist in the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapter 19. Saint Aunarius is said to have presided over the Church of Auxerre from approximately the year 571 to 603. This may be examined more fully on September 25, the day on which he is commemorated.]

### 5. Letter of Bishop Aunarius to Stephen, African Priest

[Alternative: priest of the province of Africa.]

> To Stephen, the most beloved and dearly loved brother, joined to me by the inward bond of charity, priest; Aunarius, bishop by the grace of God: eternal salvation in the Lord.
>
> The prudence of your teaching, already approved by many experiences, compelled us to place upon your shoulders a certain authoritative little burden—but one that would be not a burden to you but an honor, and would not press downward with an unjust weight, but rather raise you all the way to heaven.
>
> You know, dearest brother, how diverse human minds are, and how not only the empty crowd but the whole nobility is divided by pursuits into opposing directions. Some take delight in a prose style; others confess that they delight in meters, rhythms, or the songs of verses.
>
> Therefore, to meet everyone’s wishes and deprive no one of what he desired, it pleased me to describe some lives of the most blessed teachers in prose, but to arrange others constrained by metrical law.
>
> For this reason I beg you not to cease converting the life of the most blessed Bishop Germanus into verse, joined as you are to me by the friendship of affection; but describe that of Saint Amator in prose rhythm. Thus, becoming followers of apostolic preaching, we may become all things to all people and owe nothing to anyone except that we love one another.
>
> May divine mercy preserve your undivided charity toward me, venerable brother.

### 6. Reply of the Aforesaid Priest

> To the most blessed lord, adorned with apostolic insignia, spiritual father, Bishop Aunarius: Stephen, servant of all Christ’s servants.
>
> Having read through the letters of Your Apostolate, I have recognized, clearer than daylight, how the ardor of your holy desire presses forward with supreme eagerness.
>
> Your devout intention, therefore, is to describe the noble deeds of the flourishing lives of the celebrated men Germanus and Amator. But direct your purpose toward those most elegant men of your circle who can adorn the lights of their virtues with eloquence equal to them.
>
> [Note: The excellent Lyon manuscript reads *aequiperis affatibus inspicare*. The Belfort manuscript instead reads *convenienti oratione celebrare*, “to celebrate with suitable speech”; but that manuscript is interpolated throughout. The *History of the Bishops of Auxerre* reads *aequiparis afflatibus inspicere*, incorrectly. For the author’s sense is: “Seek for yourself another writer, Bishop Aunarius, who can illuminate the surpassingly excellent virtues of Saints Amator and Germanus with language no less elevated.” To *inspicare* the lights or torches of virtues with equal utterances means to ornament those virtues in speech so that, through rhetoric, they appear *inspicatae*—cut in the manner of an ear of grain—and, by that means, cast light more brilliantly in every direction than they could by themselves. Virgil used the same word, *Georgics* I.291: “And one keeps vigil late beside winter’s fires, and spikes the torches with sharp iron.”]
>
> But I, whose sluggish intellect grows numb under a double constraint, and whose stammering tongue, impeded by filthy roughness amid hoarse passages of the throat, does not speak but rather hisses: how shall I be able to set forth in polished speech the divinely inspired gifts of these most holy men, when I cannot even explain private affairs brought to completion by human misfortune?
>
> Whoever assumes a burden beyond the possibility of his strength entangles himself—if I am not mistaken—in ridiculous, inexplicable folly and disgrace. If the followers of wild beasts are not shaped by cunning skill, will not audacious recklessness destroy them? A novice will never carry the painted shield of victory as a monument if the trained examples of a veteran have not instructed him.
>
> Nor will a bird safely cut across the open path of the air if a feathered mother has not gone before it as guide. He will surely lie broken by the battering of the waves, whoever, relying on the guarantee of his own rashness, applies an untrained hand to the rudder.
>
> Thus everyone is cut upon the hook of inexperience in a different direction if he is not assisted by the favor of the learned.
>
> Therefore, most blessed man, I beg you to impose upon me the summit of your authority, which does not doubt that I can easily complete what it demands. Yet if, in this work also, you will bear with equanimity whatever rustic chatter may arrange inelegantly or ungracefully, I shall undertake it, and I shall do what paternal authority commands and orders.
>
> Farewell for a long time, my ever-lord and apostolic pope.

### 7

When I had carefully read through these letters and finally discovered, from the report of those present, that such a work had never existed anywhere among us, I was seized by great agitation that so considerable a work had perished uselessly from human knowledge. For several days I was consumed by inward anguish.

At last he summoned me, who had only recently emerged from the schools, disclosed his hidden grief, and insistently charged me to remedy it by whatever means I could: namely, to repeat what he had once read as having been composed in the aforesaid letters, and, to satisfy his wishes, to transfer the most excellent deeds of Germanus from prose into meter.

I was terrified by the task, I confess, and, judging what was imposed upon me to be beyond my strength, I withdrew my neck from it as far as I could. Finally, however, I was bound by the rule of the chapter, which prescribes that even impossible commands of an abbot must by no means be rejected. I accepted, as was proper, the command of the one giving orders, although conscious of no ability to do it; yet, as the rule teaches beforehand, I trusted in charity and obeyed in reliance upon God’s help.

I had scarcely reached the opening parts of the work when—alas, the miserable condition of human fate!—that abbot of mine, soon destined to be a marvel throughout the world, departed this life by untimely death, leaving his tender body.

This event, so mournful and bitter, shook all my studies and all my cares, unless that plausible saying came to my aid: that grief is diminished by time, and that what length of time would bring about—since age removes the greatest sorrows—we ought to anticipate by judgment and prudence.

With this thought I urged my mind to obey him dead just as I had been obedient to him alive, and, for the sake of the deceased, to apply stubborn perseverance to the work I had begun. I pressed on as I could; and, with Minerva not unwilling, allowing the reins to hang loose for good intention, I sometimes lightened my conceived griefs through the companionship of the Muses, as though by the art of a familiar remedy.

### 8

I was displeased to publish the completed work, because I had not sufficiently considered in my mind to whom specifically I should dedicate it. While I hesitated for a long time, you, most distinguished Caesar—you, I say, the nearest heir of a child who died without issue—came before me. His possessions returned to you by law.

Having reflected upon these matters, I dared [Lyon manuscript: “I began”] to send this literary offering first to Your Majesty, so that, after arranging the order of the argument, it might commend the contents of the work that follows.

Therefore, after the funeral of your most beloved son, accept this hereditary pledge, by which you may both sweetly refresh the memory of the deceased and recognize the complete devotion of a faithful servant, who in no way allowed you to be deprived of at least the benefit of a final service.

### 9

Moreover, I have composed another little work from the miracles of the most distinguished Germanus, divided into two books. Since mention of both your name and your age occurs in it frequently, I nevertheless preferred that it be dedicated to Your Highness [alternative: that it be dedicated].

Accept this also, and conceive toward Germanus that spirit of reverence which truly befits royal majesty.

Although it is characteristic of the cunning to refer everything to his own advantage, yet in this labor, however great it may be, and for its sake, I seek the praise of blessed Germanus rather than favor for my own person. How highly I esteem him, you can easily learn if you read through the sequence of our poem.

Thus I eagerly desire to obtain this return for my long labor: that God may be glorified in miracles, he who willed to be admired in his saints; that reverence and glory may increase on earth for the most holy Germanus, who obtained them in heaven through the increase of good works; that edification may be acquired by readers, peace by believers, salvation by imitators, and immortality by those who persevere in faith.

May you flourish in these things forever. This we both wish and tirelessly pray for you, greatest of kings, perpetual victor, and ever Augustus.

# INVOCATION OF THE AUTHOR

Composed in Phalaecian hendecasyllables.

[Col. 1137]

### 10

Eternal pattern and splendor of things,  
order of causes, origin of light,

summit of nature and father of truth,  
fountain and beginning, fullness of goodness,

with this hymn we humbly sing of you;  
we pray that you receive the gift from our mouth.

O fruitful Trinity (*Τριὰς*, “Trinity”), also a simple Unity (*Μονάς*, “unity”),

or, according to the Greeks (*Ἕλληνας κατὰ*),  
“one essence in three hypostases” (*Οὐσίαν μίαν εἰς τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις*);

[Note: That is, “one substance/essence in three persons.”]

or, as the Latin world confesses,  
“one hypostasis, three persons” (*Μίαν ὑπόστασιν, τρία πρόσωπα*):

[Note: A marginal note, probably by Hericus, distinguishes Greek *ousia* (*οὐσία*, “essence”) from *hypostasis* (*ὑπόστασις*, “individual substance”): the Greeks speak of one essence in three substances, whereas Augustine and Latin Fathers express the same faith as one substance in three persons. The difficulty was removed once *hypostasis* came to be rendered in Latin not as *substantia* but as *subsistentia*.]

you are always the same, established as the same yourself [Belfort manuscript: “and the same”],

begetting, unbegotten, you are called Father.

You, the Son born and begotten, Wisdom applauds;

the living Spirit flows forth from both.

In three persons we consecrate one,  
in these we gather one divinity (*θεῶτεν*).

[Note: *Theiōten* is used instead of *theiotēta* or *theotēta*, “divinity.”]

It is pleasing that it is so called because it sees everything,

or rather because it runs through everything.

[Note: As though *theotēs* were derived from *theaomai*, “I look at, I see.”]

[Note: From the verb *theō*, “I run.”]

Yet in such a way that nowhere outside itself

[Note: “Outside” has the second syllable long. The meter is therefore defective here. But our author was not so scrupulous in these matters, as six hundred examples below will make clear. Accordingly, we do not even think such points need to be noted, much less foolishly emended on the basis of the interpolated Belfort manuscript, since the Lobbes and Lyon manuscripts agree. The Belfort manuscript corrects the verse as follows:

> “So that it may never be carried elsewhere outside itself.”]

does it move beyond itself,

since it is motion and is itself also rest,

and stable motion; as the ancients once said,

“mobile rest,” and so I find the more learned have said.

### 11

Being (*ὤν*), which gives substance [Note: masculine *ōn* for neuter *on*, which Latin now calls *ens*]; place (*τόπος*) of things [Note: “place”; for all things are within it, according to the Lyon-manuscript notes];

goodness through itself; the idea of the world;

wise through itself; likewise without beginning (*ἄναρχος*) [Note: *anarchos*, “lacking a beginning”].

It is not; for it is above being and grants existence:

“This” is not, nor is “that”; but everything exists.

Not here, not there; but wholly throughout everything.

Small and great and middle God (*Μικρὸς καὶ μέγαλος μέσος θεός*).

[Note: That is, “small, great, and middle God”; *megalos* is used for *megas*.]

Small, when he provides help to the least;

middle, when he governs the inmost equally;

in the great he is shown to be the same.

Thus he is present to the small, the middle, and the great,

himself undivided, remaining wholly present.

O Being, beginning, middle, and end of all things [Note: [Col. 1138D] That is, Being, the beginning, middle, and end of all things.]

For from him, and through him,

[Col. 1139A] Are all things that live; toward him likewise

All things tend, as toward their rest.

Himself the πρωτότυπον [Note: [Col. 1139C] That is, the principal exemplar.], him likewise

They affirm to be nothingness, so that you may marvel still more;

Because he exists incomprehensibly beyond all

Nature, surpassing the damaged printed *νοερός λόγοστε* [Note: [Col. 1139C] B. has *νώας λόγουστε*; the note explains the phrase as “intellect and reasons.”];

Who, while he cannot be grasped, is called nothing;

Whenever he appears as a *θεωφανιις* [Note: [Col. 1139C] The source proposes the damaged forms *θεφανί οις θεωφανίαις*. “Theophany (*Θεωφάνια*), however,” as Maximus says, “is the divine manifestation that occurs through the condescension of the divine Word to human nature and the exaltation of that same nature to the aforementioned Word [Col. 1139D] through divine love.” Notes of the manuscripts of the Lugdunensis codex.],

He is said to come forth from nothing into something.

They write that all things were created from this nothingness.

Hence it is that he is likewise called darkness:

For the sacred *Ψαλμὶστης* thus says [Note: [Col. 1139D] The proposed reading is *Ψάλτης*, “Psalmist/singer.”]:

“As are the darknesses, so is his light”;

Since, to one who desires but is unable

To gaze upon him, black darknesses seem to exist;

[Col. 1139B] And he dwells in inaccessible light.

12. Since the streams of truth are thus ordered,

You will readily understand that it is necessary

For us, by no intellect or elegance,

To set limits to the true and supreme Good,

God; nor is it easy to say

What sort of being, how great, or who he may be.

You will better and more nearly entrust

To your mind whatever you prepare for prayer [Note: [Col. 1139D] For *allegabis*, according to the manuscript notes.],

If you compose it secretly [Note: [Col. 1139D] That is, if you prepare it inwardly; ibid.]:

He wishes to be prayed to in gentle words,

He is ready to grant and prompt to give.

Approach the Father, then, in these measures,

The Father with the Begotten, and the kindly Πνεῦμα [Note: [Col. 1140C] The Spirit.]:

Light, and our salvation and redemption,

Giver of *φύσεως, χάριντε*—of nature and grace—grant it [Note: [Col. 1140C] The manuscript note here says “that is, darkened,” apparently displaced in the damaged passage.],

[Col. 1139C] Bringing light into the blue-grey shadows [Note: [Col. 1140C] That is, “you who gave nature, grant grace.” Notes of the Lugdunensis manuscript.],

To the blind open the fiery heavens [Note: [Col. 1140C] For ἐμπτρίους.].

Once you brought Moses, the lawgiver,

Into the darkness [Note: [Col. 1140C] Into darkness.] of Sinai.

Help those who seek you with your mighty right hand,

Since no one is able to approach you,

Unless you grant that you yourself come to him:

Yet it is fitting for you to show your face

To those who ask for nothing other than you:

[Col. 1140A] For they will not be able to do even this [B., “For not even this will they be able”], unless it comes from you.

Tear apart the clouds and evil imaginings (φαντασίαι),

By which the mind’s vision, struck back,

Is not permitted to behold God purely,

As though he makes himself invisible to those

Who have learned to thirst for the light-bearing fountain,

Their rest and their end.

13. If anything remains, if anything presses upon us, I say,

We ask that you set in order our present works,

Which are in need of you; and favor our request,

Fill our senses, and loosen our mouths;

So that clear words may flow from the mute,

As you are accustomed to grant, and not without power.

[Col. 1140B] The subject matter urges us to prepare a title of praise

For Germanus; love constrains us,

Love for you, wondrous boy Lotharius,

To whom it would not be right to deny anything—

Neither mouth nor spirit, nor certainly those things

That are friendly to noble duties.

For whatever is fitting, whatever may be done decently,

And every hope, together with the sum of hope,

We place in you, discoverer of the art

By which the human breast, made pre-eminent [Note: [Col. 1140C] That is, strengthened, as it were, by an omen. Notes of the [Col. 1140D] manuscripts of the Lugdunensis codex.]

By a certain auspice,

Climbs the starry fields of honor,

Distinguished from beasts by the brilliance of reason [Note: [Col. 1140D] That is, by keenness of understanding. Ibid.].

I do not ask these things for Germanus on account

Of the blessedness of his merit, but through his goodness,

If he has accomplished anything light-bearing

That might have been praise to the heavenly Father;

If, following your standards as a hero,

He sternly crushed the hardened enemy;

If he endured fasts, unjust crosses,

And restless nights;

If he did not fear to enter

The threatening jaws of the sea,

Secure amid the waves;

If he patiently despised whatever sword

Or flame can inflict, for love of Christ.

## ADDRESS OF THE SAME TO THE BOOK, COMPOSED IN A TWO-LINE, DOUBLE-TURNED FORM

[Note: [Col. 1139D] This Address is found here in the excellent Lugdunensis codex, although it is absent from the Lobiensis and Belfortian manuscripts.]

[Col. 1139]

[Col. 1139D] 14. If we behold you with a perfectly clear eye,

And sleeplessness does not deceive the mind,

I would not have you suffer, little book, in vain

Because you attach such importance to popular opinion;

Hating your native hiding-place, you willingly

Take delight in the mad tumult.

Weariness of seclusion marks you, unhappy book, in no small degree [Note: [Col. 1140D] The sense is: these are signs of the bad fortune threatening you, little book—your hatred of secrecy and your unwillingness to avoid or postpone, at least for a while, breaking the seals that are so necessary to chaste studies. For if Danaë, daughter of Acrisius, was not sufficiently protected even in a bronze tower from shameless Jupiter, what will become of you, who neither wish to be shut away nor remain concealed?],

And you shrink for a while from breaking [Note: [Col. 1141C] Supply: “to break.”] the seals

That are always friendly to chaste studies;

Although that famous Danaë was scarcely protected

By a bronze tower from the golden rain.

What profit are streets that spew forth crowds?

What profit cities abounding in talkative critics?

You, whom correction has not yet touched, nor has color yet enhanced

After blemishes have been removed.

If an unintelligent augur is not wandering astray:

O you who are destined to suffer excessive shame!

They say that Maro polished and elaborated

His *Bucolics* through a labor of three years,

And likewise polished the fourfold *Georgics*

Through seven years of toil.

Afterward he brought the printed, textually damaged *Aenedas in arma pulchros / Endecas*

To the file and refined them; the precise construction and the force of *endecas* remain uncertain.

Nor do you weigh in your mind what he achieved, what we;

What another Rome hoped for;

What the least of the lesser, unequal to them,

Might achieve, though he must not be counted

Among the very least.

And yet, impatient one, you rush into the mouths

Of the common people and refuse the key?

15. Severe omens and terrifying sounds

Shake the unwilling poet;

Nor does the gnostic virtue permit one who wishes

To spare himself words that are unwelcome:

You will receive these things unwillingly and willingly alike;

With these words we oppose you, speaking in contradiction (ἀντιλέγοντα) [Note: [Col. 1141C] That is, contradicting.].

You will enter the public sphere, your hope favoring you.

But, ah, upon how great a wave will you be tossed!

One man will spit foully here; another, with wrinkled nose,

Will purse his lips against you and utter something unspeakable

And hostile;

Another will clap his profane hands;

Another will strike the earth three times with his foot;

Another will search with his finger for swelling faults [Note: [Col. 1141C] That is, defects in the poem. Notes of the manuscripts.],

Although none is visible anywhere,

And will mark them with his mouth,

Being skilled, forsooth, at overturning what is whole.

And the more lost and profane a man is,

The more fiercely he will be carried into anger.

At last, overcome by every kind of mockery,

Will you be thrust into a Μυροκότου [Note: [Col. 1141C] That is, a perfumer’s.] shop,

Or will you carry a little nard or pepper,

And whatever is wrapped in papers

For the idle [Note: [Col. 1141C] “Idle,” that is, empty, because, containing nothing worth reading [Col. 1142C], they are put to sordid uses.], once the adviser who was formerly rejected

Has ceased to take care of you [Note: [Col. 1142C] That is: if you are ever reduced to that state, little book, then I, who now advise you, will leave you to your fate and completely disown you.].

16. And lest you complain that you were cheated

Of our counsel [Note: [Col. 1142C] Namely, the counsel.], consider this within yourself:

Wherever the title assigns a place at the front,

Let no author prefix the name ὄνομα [Note: [Col. 1142C] That is, our name.];

Let Germanus enter first into the stronghold

Of the earlier auspice; let him mark the beginnings.

Perhaps you will then be able, unarmed, to despise

The common crowd or a thousand dangers.

The battalions of insolence would scarcely dare

To disregard the obstacle of so great a name.

Their madness will soften; they will spare their spittle,

And cease to rage with a cynical [Note: [Col. 1142C] That is, dog-like or envious.] tooth.

Go now, driven forward on Maeonian [Note: [Col. 1142C] That is, Homeric.] wings;

Go, book, happy beneath a favorable bird.

And do not be troubled that you departed

Neither unwarned nor without advice.

[Col. 1142C] For the rest, entrust yourself to uncertain fate.

And may better things follow you!

# BOOK ONE

## The Life of the Great Father GERMANUS, transferred from prose into verse

[Col. 1141]

### CHAPTER ONE. The saint’s homeland, nobility, studies, marriage, honors, love of hunting, and superstition

[Col. 1141D]

17. Where Celtic Gaul spreads out the middle regions,

And where the land—or at least its inhabitants—is gentler,

The earlier Gauls established a not unknown city,

Rich in fertile soil and in the gift of generous Bacchus [Note: [Col. 1141D] Concerning the vineyards of Antissiodorum, formerly bearers of exceptionally fine wine, see Le Beuf in the Preface to *Capti receptique Antissiodori*, p. 29 and following.],

And by the pleasant usefulness of the river flowing past [Note: [Col. 1141D] The Icauna, that is, the river commonly called the Yonne.],

[Col. 1142D] Which can rank itself among many great cities;

It is reported to have once been called Autricus

By the ancients [Note: [Col. 1141D] “He who thinks that Antissiodurum was previously called Autricum,” says Valesius in the *Notitia Galliarum*, in the section on Antissiodurum, “reveals his ignorance of geography.”].

A later age placed towers and heights

Upon the ancestral walls, defenses against harsh war;

From the enlarged walls, with the name altered,

Whether you call it Antissiodorum by customary usage,

Or wish to mutilate the name and call it Altiodorum [Note: [Col. 1142D] Concerning the very different alteration of this name among authors, see Valesius in the same place. There you will also find this etymology of Hericus rejected, because *Dor*, *Dur*, *Deur*, or *Dour* means not walls or ramparts in Celtic but water. We have also discussed this matter more than once elsewhere.],

Under a different name the same thing is more fully described.

[Col. 1143A] This is our native soil, this the fatherland of our Father;

Born within these borders, he blessed the fields of his birth.

18. There is no need to recount at length, in the saint,

The glory of his related nobility, which shone

With twin splendor and abundance, rich in wealth

And in offspring:

Numerous estates retain the evidence and proof of this,

Formerly well known through records renewed from time to time [Note: [Col. 1143D] The patrimonial estates of Saint Germanus will be discussed in the *Miracles of Hericus*, no. 19.].

19. The brief springtime of his life and the charm of his first flower

Were steeped, with ready effort, in the seven arts [Note: [Col. 1143D] Although the liberal arts are more numerous, they are commonly counted as seven: grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, music, arithmetic, geometry, and astrology.].

The generous grace that enlarged the child’s breast

With twin gifts [Note: [Col. 1143D] That is, talent and diligence. Notes of the Lugdunensis manuscript.] had heaped upon one person

What is usually pleasant and sufficient for two:

For, so that wisdom resting upon seven columns

Might be able to fashion a dwelling in his beloved breast,

[Col. 1143B] A lively intellect aided every effort;

And, as his mind expanded by nature in every direction [Note: [Col. 1143D] That is, naturally most receptive. Notes of the manuscripts, ibid.],

Studious diligence offered

The help of a teacher.

Both qualities, under God’s direction, advanced

The fortunate periods of the young man’s growing age.

Many seeds are scattered through barren furrows

With scanty or, at most, moderate yield;

But the grains that enter fertile new fields

Flow with a twofold hope, both from the soil and from the sowing;

And full abundance answers the conspicuous horn.

20. And since he was vigorous and eager in spirit toward everything,

He left nothing unattempted, nothing finally unexhausted,

Whatever could flow from native teachers:

For, almost still a boy and before youth,

He had absorbed everything. An inward ardor raged

In his bones to pursue what lay beyond, and, if opportunity

Were not lacking, to spend his leisure in study,

To devote himself to study, and to die in study.

Whatever is very small and insignificant to know,

If it is anywhere exposed, he considers worthless;

Whatever is hidden, he regards as precious and immense.

At that time there was constant honor for liberal arts,

And glory added a spur to study.

Driven by these impulses and bound by such desire,

He made his way to the place that is the head of the world,

Rome, greatest of things, to learn the intricacies

Of Latin law; and he learned them, and soon won

The palm of his labor.

21. To know was not much, unless he also undertook to be able [Note: [Col. 1143D] “To be able”: supply, “to use the knowledge already acquired.”].

A wise man is thought little better than a fool

If he is not also able to act. The two joined together

Are carried more effectively:

If you separate them, one is lost; thus one

Demands the allied aid of the other,

And they conspire together in friendship.

Therefore, so that what he had contemplated

Within the shelter of his room

Might afterward proclaim wisdom through marble streets [Note: [Col. 1143D] It is written: “Wisdom is learned in silence.” Likewise: “In the streets she gives forth her voice.” Therefore it is first learned in silence, so that afterward it may cry aloud in the streets. Notes of the manuscripts, ibid.]

And finally give laws to the proud,

The young man was soon elevated to patrician honors;

Chosen as an advocate of cases through public votes,

He restrained urban disputes with the bridle of law.

22. Latium rejoices in possessing so great a censor [Note: [Col. 1143D] Censors were those who judged morals. Notes of the manuscripts. Yet Constantius does not say that Germanus was a censor.]; and merely

To enjoy him while present seems too little. It thinks

Of posterity: so that the man might not lack

The glory of offspring, and so that Rome might not be deprived

Of the man’s descendants, there is hope in a wife;

Wealth, age subject to the flesh, love of offspring,

Integrity of mind in a beautiful spouse,

Riches, character, and the distinction of chaste modesty

Do not permit such a hope to be absent.

When such a woman appeared, she could be pointed out [Note: [Col. 1143D] In accordance with the saying: “How beautiful it is to be pointed out with the finger and to be told, ‘This is he’?”];

For she was a rare bird in our lands,

More unknown than a white raven [Note: [Col. 1143D] Solomon: “Among a thousand men I found one; among all women I found none.” Notes of the manuscripts, ibid.].

23. The Roman world was once skilled in countless practices.

Devouring antiquity has consumed one part completely [Note: [Col. 1144D] That is, from the whole.];

Another part wears away the traces of things in ancient books.

That people was shrewd, skilled in warfare,

Yet also knowledgeable in forming morals

And careful in arranging them.

And lest tender childhood wither under a blemish

(For the mind is wax-like and easily bent toward vice,

And when an uncertain path led it to branching crossroads

[Belfortian and Lugdunensis manuscripts: *ambivium*, “a divided way”;]

And the Samian had shown a two-forked road [Note: [Col. 1144D] Pythagoras of Samos compared the quality of human life to the letter Y. Notes of the manuscripts, ibid. From this you may infer what is meant by “branching crossroads” and “two-forked road.”];

The sluggish hesitates to follow the right-hand branch

And, with malicious desire, clings to the left),

That path then seemed straighter to the Romans [Note: [Col. 1144D] The sense is that, at the time when childhood was easily turned from vice toward virtue, the Roman people thought that children should be led toward virtue by this route—namely, by assigning guardians to them, and so forth.]:

An ever-watchful guard preserved their tender years,

Along with chaste companions, and the teacher’s red line [Note: [Col. 1144D] The line used by craftsmen, so called from its red color. It is used here for the diligence of a teacher. Notes of the manuscripts, ibid.]

Was applied, and a rule correcting crooked morals,

And a mind pressed by reason and striving to be mastered,

And a face guided beneath the teacher’s thumb:

The toga praetexta marked minds that trembled,

Still lacking reason and without counsel,

As most suitable to them [supply: the toga],

So called because a border of Tyrian purple was woven upon it,

And embossed ornaments fastened upon it [Note: [Col. 1144D] That is, golden amulets. Notes of the manuscripts, ibid. They were not fastened to the toga praetexta, however, but hung from the necks of the boys.], in the Greek fashion—

The Italians drew this custom from the Greeks [Note: [Col. 1144D] Rather, Wolfgang Lazius teaches and proves that this custom was derived from the Etruscans in *Commentaries on the Roman Republic*, book VIII, chapter 2, where he discusses the *praetexta* at greater length. He also treats the *bulla* separately in book IX, chapter 13.]—

As a mark of nobility.

24. Such was the custom then. After childhood had been passed,

When soft down clothed the tender cheeks

(That is, after he had completed twice eight Decembers),

The *praetexta* yielded to the toga, and they attached

To the household gods of his fathers the ancestral

Childhood gifts, the *bullae*.

Here hesitant infancy obtained its desired end;

Here it fixed its boundaries. Thereafter each person

Was thought useful in war and at home,

And capable of handling affairs in every respect

At a mature age.

He had drunk in this period of life, and as a young man

Wearing the toga he passed through a substantial part

Of his age with strength accumulated,

When, as governor and commander, he was elevated

Over the assigned regions where the Gallic axis lies,

Both avenger of crimes and dispenser of honors.

At that time victorious Rome possessed the whole world [Note: [Col. 1145D] By hyperbole.],

Wherever sea, land, and either pole extend;

[Col. 1145B] Whatever strait existed in the world, whatever hidden gulf,

Whatever climate lay beyond the reach of Phoebus’ lamp,

Whatever region produced yellow gold,

Lived only under the shadow of the Roman name;

Everything stood by the will of the sacred senate.

Scepters, magistracies, titles, praetorian offices, curule chairs,

The *praetexta* [Belfortian manuscript: “the praetexta and”], the *trabea*, the fasces, the mark of the tribunal,

The aedile, quaestor, dictator, and legal magistrate,

And the monarch, to whom the whole administration of affairs

Is open and obedient,

And the careful regulation of laws to be forged among nations,

Peace and war, dispute and concord among things—

All once served the enrolled fathers,

[Col. 1145C] In whose hands stood the guardianship of the boundless world;

And while they sat enclosed in one part of the shrine,

They fashioned the four-cornered world according to divine laws.

The sequence of events has been interrupted for a while;

It will be pleasing to resume it after this digression.

25. The hero, enriched by his merits and advancing through success,

Pressed forward with tireless strides toward the first citadel [Note: [Col. 1145D] Namely, of wisdom and virtue. Notes of the manuscripts.]

Of perfection, so that he might soon be sacred

And a bishop, perfect in every respect.

And so that he might be able to confront the deadly pests

And drive out heresies wherever they had emerged

[Belfortian manuscript: “heretical plagues”],

A lively eloquence armed his learned tongue.

[Col. 1145D] A teacher of justice and destined also to be

A standard of law, he rightly devoted himself

To learning law in due course.

And since he was destined to give the peoples examples

Of chastity and to establish decrees

For a chaste marriage-bed,

He entered into the lawful bonds of marriage

In a distinguished order, and while leading his life

With a chaste wife, he allowed no rights
