To forbidden pleasure,

Content to live solely for the begetting of offspring.

26. Although public and private concern for the many affairs

Of the earth’s broad and wide-ranging realm

Wearied the man greatly,

His natural affection had fixed his mind more readily

Upon his ancestral lands,

Which he continually tempered with gentle duties

And bent with a soft rein,

Strengthening the present with the present through a present divine power.

This was his home, his rest,

The delight of his life:

Either because he possessed there a considerable abundance

Of estates, memorials of his paternal inheritance;

Or because—as earthborn men have some pleasure

In such things—the young man possessed

A very great abundance of wild beasts,

Which supplied the riches of the forest.

Devoted to hunting, and contemplating spectacles

Of fleeting things,

He fed his idle mind on sportive pursuits [Note: [Col. 1145D] “Sportive,” that is, chaste indeed, but nevertheless youthful and empty pursuits of hunting; by them he fed his idle mind, that is, one free from the cares of his duty and resting between them. [Col. 1146D]]:

And although he had been washed in the fountain

Of sacred liquid,

He rejoiced to be called a Christian

Only in name; everything else about him

Savored of the muddy age.

27. In the middle of the city there once stood

A most pleasing pear tree, tall and broad,

Visible to all the people;

Not because it gleamed with the glory of hanging pears,

Nor because it renewed itself with the gift of perpetual leaves,

But because the heads of captured wild beasts,

Fastened here and there to the spreading branches

Of the obscene tree,

Provided empty applause and spectacles for the crowd.

There the branching antlers of frightened deer bristled [Note: [Col. 1146D] The manuscript note glosses *ramalia* as “horns.”],

As did the savage tusks and teeth of the bristling boar,

Planning destruction for fierce Molossian hounds.

Then too, clothed in such varied trophies,

The tree poured forth seeds of wanton laughter

For the uneducated.

The young man had fixed these trophies there,

A seeker of praise and of the breath

By which pliable minds are accustomed

To be nourished and captured.

### CHAPTER II. Saint Amator’s zeal against Germanus’s superstition and the latter’s anger

28. Amator, the lover of our city and the restorer

Of the sacred flock, was its bishop,

Enriched by a name he deserved.

A magnificent teacher, radiant with the light of his merits,

Celebrated far and wide by the titles of his miracles.

He knew how to set a limit to rushing flames;

He knew how to drive away hostile plagues by his word;

How to open the way for speech to stopped ears;

How to restore their function to tongues bound by command;

How to grant the use of light to those dead after burial.

He who was able to do all things

Gave the saint power to do all things.

[Col. 1146D] Holy guardian of the flock, rightly called Amator,

Not a lover of gold or the world, but of Christ above all,

Do not be angry with me for saying very little about you.

It would be sweet for me to commemorate your deeds

And to traverse the whole fabric of your life with my lyre;

But the long sequence of the work I have undertaken calls me back

And does not allow me to turn aside anywhere

From the path on which I began.

And I would have wished you to have nourished

Lofty-speaking poets,

Who could sing of you with a many-voiced Muse.

That you lack poets is the fault of your successors [Note: [Col. 1146D] He seems to be reproaching the bishops of Antissiodorum for not having encouraged poetic art more in the clergy.].

[Col. 1147A] We shall assign another time and place to these complaints.

Meanwhile, pastor, make use of the services now before you;

And if anything worthy of my account

Can be brought forward as praise of our Father [Note: [Col. 1147D] Namely, Saint Germanus.],

Think that it can be added to your praises.

You are the father; he, finally, born through Christ,

Is your son.

Believe me: it is counted a great part of praise

When the image of a son is praised in the face of his father.

Let the Muse now resume the account she began.

29. His spirit could scarcely endure the saint’s insane rites

And harmful amusements; nor did he delay to restrain

That proud beginning, already then, with gentle speech,

Addressing him in these words after choosing the occasion:

When Roman industry preferred you

For governing the lands,

And entrusted you with being father and leader

For the protection of your country,

It believed you to be a man; nor did the thing then believed

Fall short of the truth.

Many things constrain you to be a man at last:

The title of your lineage, the height of great honor,

And, governing both, a breast enriched

With divine gifts, and a mind wholly conscious of right.

Light-mindedness alone defiles and drives away

Manly distinction—light-mindedness alone, I say.

Behold, this tree, the witness nearest to madness,

Must be uprooted with its own roots

As soon as possible.

Let those who are deprived of knowledge of the divine power

Pursue such things; our religious profession

Loves something else [B., “not these things”],

Since, when practice asks what it should seek more,

The meditation of death alone answers.

Gravity has earned much praise in its own ages;

No one of distinction has been made by fickle inconstancy.

Cease to hurl the pliant and slippery minds

Of the common people headlong toward deviations.

It is known to no one as an unfamiliar fact:

Crimes performed under the authority of great men

Corrupt more quickly;

And domestic examples

Spread much more widely than those from outside,

Since people, naturally inclined to follow,

Seize upon the examples first displayed by their leaders.

Therefore, come now, and, leaving aside

Whatever is thought to be mere amusement,

O you of outstanding spirit, embrace serious things alone.

These are the signs that the republic asks to see

In the man it seeks; such signs befit a ruler.

The bishop often let these words drip into the man’s ear;

[Col. 1147D] But he bore them lightly [Note: [Col. 1147D] “To bear lightly,” in place of “to make little of.” The Belfortian manuscript changes the verse as follows [Col. 1148D]: “With such admonitions he did not cease to hunt.”],

And persisted in his proud undertakings:

For swift winds carried everything away in vain.

30. One day the young man had a definite reason

For visiting his estates; his journey from the city

At last offered the bishop the hour he had desired.

Since he was wholly fixed upon the love of the Lord

And, by this right, a despiser of human fear,

He summoned as quickly as possible the sacred clergy

And approached the ridiculous tree, immensely rich

In heads.

With as much authority as he could command,

He ordered it to be cut down with an axe and brought low.

The hands of the cutters trembled, and, terrified

By the revered majesty of the leader,

They feared that, if they struck the beloved timber,

The axes would be turned against their own necks.

When the saint saw the cutters trembling

In frightened paralysis,

He was the first to dare to seize the double axe

And, with the iron plunged into the wood that was to be violated,

Said: “Now let none of you hesitate to cut it down.

Let the origin of the offense be attributed to this one head alone:

Say that I committed the crime.”

He spoke, and the whole crowd obeyed the commands

Of the one giving the order,

Although it was unsafe [B., “although it was ill-advised”].

The tree resounded as it was cut by repeated blows;

Struck, it gave groans; and when it had been defeated

By the iron and by its own great weight,

It fell and collapsed.

Then for the first time the earth beneath it,

Touched by the gift of sunlight,

Admitted the day;

The tree, which had been offered to empty things,

Perished, and was gathered into deserved flames.

The little effigies of wild beasts that had long been fastened to it

Were entirely removed from the city

By order of the bishop.

All this was done while the leader was away in the countryside.

31. Rumor sees what is done in heaven,

On the sea, and on earth,

And is conscious of the whole world;

Whatever exists anywhere, though it be distant

From the entire globe,

She observes and penetrates the hollow hiding places

Where evil things lie concealed.

As soon as she has learned everything,

She immediately reveals everything to everyone.

And because some charm of words follows the speaker,

And eloquence grows through new subjects,

The common people grant her much credence.

She does not carry out her business by shouting,

But with the murmur of her voice,

In her foolishness croaking something hoarse and grave,

I know not what, like a raven:

She drags a thousand rumors and a thousand whispers

Along with her;

And falsehoods are mixed with truths in equal measure.

When she fills the empty air with fresh talk,

Empty joys sometimes follow as her companions;

Now fear, sometimes the hated madness of rage.

This rumor flies to the young man,

Announcing the harm that had been inflicted:

The tree’s fall, and the despised leader

And insulted tribunal [B., “the despised and insulted tribunal”];

She complains that the rights of her own fear

Have been wickedly taken away,

And that afterward she will possess no power

Anywhere in the world,

Unless the bishop then paid the penalty

Throughout the city for violating censorial honor [read: *censorii*].

Anger seized the man; fiercer than anger itself,

[Col. 1148D] He growled menacingly and drew a flush across his face,

As a spirited horse neighs when the martial trumpeter

Moves the standards with ringing bronze

And awakens [B., “inflames”] the love of battle.

Neither reverence for the great episcopate

Nor respect for sacred religion restrained him.

Right, piety, and shame withdrew from his eyes:

The savage man raged and plotted an unjust death

Against the saint; and he said:

“O companions, noblest of hearts,

Seize this man headlong,

Give his limbs over to punishments

Most deserving of his crimes,

And send the guilty man down to Stygian death.

Let him learn that there are men.”

Having spoken thus, and with anger growing fiercer,

He ordered his companions to prepare arms

And gather together with their whole spirit for battle.

And lest the populace be able to oppose his fury

Or defend the entrance by barricading the gates,

He seized the unsuspecting city with concentrated forces.

32. When the saint learned of the ruler’s inflamed anger,

He desired to receive the palm he had earned

Through battle as a martyr,

And to be drenched in the fountain of his own blood;

He poured forth these words with an unafraid face:

“We have lived up to this point long enough,

And more than enough.

Now my burning spirit longs to penetrate

Your face, O Christ;

It is weary of the road, weary of labor.

Where the shorter paths of righteousness lie open,

It is a pleasure to go;

Although the way may be exceedingly difficult

For those who tremble,

We shall soon be granted access to the starry fields,

If the tracks of our shed blood lead us there.

With outstretched arms we embrace the title of martyrdom,

And willingly seek the beautiful death through wounds.

Only deem us worthy to be witnesses

For your name.”

Saying this, he prepared both his spirit for death

And his neck for the executioner;

The sentence of death stood fixed in the fearless man.

But, O Christ, in your purest camp

Lilies gleaming white bloom together with roses;

Nor does martyrdom alone earn your favor,

Nor is one a martyr only through the shedding of blood.

Often a devout life has also won a crown for many;

And the pure confession of your priests,

Whom perfection of justice clothes,

Is pleasing to you.

And you, most savage ruler, whose mind,

Filled to the brim with black gall,

Urges you to sin against the saint [another reading: “moves you”],

Count nothing—nothing—as having been granted to you,

Since your evil desire has not succeeded;

And you too will one day certainly be a bishop,

Most widely known throughout the world.

The eternal Judge foresaw this long ago,

And does not permit the hands foreseen for sacred things

To be stained by the blood of an innocent man—

Those hands through which, it is believed,

A healing remedy will flow to countless sick people.

### CHAPTER III. The revelation made to Saint Amator concerning his death and Germanus’s succession; and the latter’s conversion and miraculous ordination

33. It was time for the bishop to receive

The palm he had earned through much struggle,

Having been taken into a place in the divine senate;

And the man was permitted to learn beforehand

The appointed time:

Who would be the successor to his sacred honor

After him, under God’s inspiration

And with concern for the people’s salvation.

There was an ancient city, famous throughout the whole world,

Previously called Aedua.

When its foundations were first laid in the soil,

The story tells that twin kids were seen

Engaging in playful combats.

The ancients, accustomed to their first auspices,

Once assigned names to cities as they were founded [Note: [Col. 1149D] This is mere fable; for it is not credible that the Celtic city received a Latin name from a kid before it knew the Romans.].

When Caesar first came to it from the Alpine heights,

At the time when Gaul still practiced barbarian customs [B., “was beginning to grow barbarous”],

He took it as an ally,

Drew the people into treaty with the Romulan race,

And called them new allies and brothers [Note: [Col. 1149D] Rather, Valesius shows in the *Notitia Galliarum*, in the section on Augustodunum of the Aedui, that this occurred long before Julius Caesar’s arrival in Gaul. Yet the same author denies that Augustodunum ever possessed metropolitan authority over other provinces, or even over Lugdunensis. See below, note e.];

And ordered it to assume the primacy as the head of the kingdom.

Celtic Rome then wished and began to be called [Note: [Col. 1149D] But when, or by which writers, was the head of the Aeduan people called “Celtic Rome”? Valesius asks this question there by way of denial.].

34. The strength of the friendship gradually grew through the years;

The city also advanced in merit and name,

And finally began to be called Augustodunum [Note: [Col. 1150D] It received the Latin-Gallic name Augustodunum from Augustus, by whom it was perhaps enlarged through benefactions or adorned with buildings, and from the neighboring mountain; commonly Autun. Valesius, ibid.],

A name that in the Celtic language translates

“Augustus’s mountain.”

That land was not fertile in grain through the ages,

Nor sufficiently wealthy: for forests surround everything,

With steeply rugged mountains,

And the soil is sterile for seeds,

Unsuited to the plowshare and exempt from the curved plow;

The harshness of the climate harasses the hard earth.

Yet no land produced men more distinguished in arms,

Or men more select in spirit for battles.

Therefore, when the saint and ever-memorable Amator

Sensed that the time of his approaching death was near,

He hastened without delay toward the walls

Of the city just mentioned.

Julius held there the highest office [Note: [Col. 1150D] Hericus seems to have thought that Augustodunum was the ordinary seat of the prefect of Gaul during this period. Hence, I suppose, just above he called it the head of the kingdom; but this is known to be false.],

A distinguished man, famous both for the rank

Of prefect and for the purity of his faith,

His vows, and his name as a worshiper.

The holy bishop Simplicius was also there,

A man of great merit and a minister

Of great honor.

Royal power, joined by law to the pontiff,

Restrained the people entrusted to them

With equal reins:

The former pressed the swelling nation

With stern authority;

The latter shaped it through the ministry

Of the saving word.

35. When the bishop and the blessed governor

Perceived that the man was approaching,

They prepared, having gathered troops

Of clergy and people from every side,

To meet the approaching saint.

They welcomed the man; after words of greeting

Had been spoken and received,

They solemnly led him into the bosom of their city.

They devoted the night to joy and praise.

When watchful Dawn, glowing brightly,

Opened her purple doors in the shining east,

And, having driven away the stars,

The Morning Star marked the end of night,

The bishop said that he wished to proceed

To the governor’s lofty tribunal,

And hastened along the road.

The governor came forward to meet him,

Honored the saint with every service he could offer,

And humbly asked to be blessed.

Then, having obtained his wish,

He led him into the lofty praetorium.

[Col. 1151A] When an opportunity to speak freely had been granted

In the presence of the governor,

He addressed him in these words:

“I would not have you think, most distinguished man,

That our coming occurred by chance [Note: [Col. 1151D] The source uses an indicative form in place of the subjunctive.].

A serious matter alone persuaded us

To undertake so much travel and so much labor.

The Founder of our death hastens the time

Of our departure,

Relieves the burden of heavy labors by their end,

And grants us to learn beforehand

The day of their completion.

Nor does the prospect and nearness of death itself

Strike us so much as concern

For the pious flock after us.

And since there is not a great abundance

Of magnanimous men

To whom the governance of a holy people

Can rightly be entrusted,

And since a rich harvest requires

A strong and good farmer,

This matter especially requires your aid;

For it cannot be undertaken without the ruler’s command.

Your majesty possesses so much dignity

That it itself makes the matter more weighty.

The whole matter is this:

We ask—do not reject the petitioner—

That Germanus be permitted to cut

The hair from his blond head.

He will be a vessel chosen by God

And sacred to the uses of the Church

[B., “and likewise useful”]

And to honorable studies.”

36. He was struck motionless by the novelty of the matter

And considered it at length.

“Although,” he said, “he was most welcome

To the whole kingdom,

We think it wrong to prefer human things

To divine things.

Therefore, what you foresee must be done,

With God’s breath upon you,

Hasten to accomplish;

You will not be deprived of our service.”

Having obtained his request and returned to the familiar city,

[he …] the people solemnly through the spacious courts of the church—

[The supplied source ends here, leaving this final construction incomplete.]

## Recovered Greek and damaged-form register

The following register preserves all twenty recovered strings in their source spelling and identifies their local sense without silently normalizing damaged print:

1. *Ὤν ἀρχὴ, μέσον, ὢν τέλοστε πάντων*: “Being the beginning, middle, and end of all things” (the ending of *τέλοστε* is damaged). 2. *πρωτότυπον*: “primary exemplar.” 3. *νοερός λόγοστε*: damaged printed wording explained by the note as “intellect and reasons.” 4. *νώας λόγουστε*: B’s likewise damaged reading, with the same editorial explanation. 5. *θεωφανιις*: a damaged form associated with “theophany.” 6. *θεφανί οις θεωφανίαις*: the source’s proposed damaged forms. 7. *Θεωφάνια*: “Theophany,” divine manifestation. 8. *Ψαλμὶστης*: the damaged printed “Psalmist.” 9. *Ψάλτης*: the proposed “Psalmist/singer.” 10. *Πνεῦμα*: “Spirit.”

11. *φύσεως, χάριντε*: “of nature, and grace,” in damaged syntax. 12. *ἐμπυρίος*: “fiery.” 13. *ἐμπτρίους*: the source’s proposed damaged inflection. 14. *θεσμοφόρον*: “law-bearing,” applied to Moses. 15. *Εἰς γνόφον*: “into darkness.” 16. *φαντασίας*: “imaginations/appearances.” 17. *Δικώλῳ διστρόφῳ*: “in a two-line, double-turned form.” 18. *αν` τιλέγοντα*: damaged print glossed “contradicting.” 19. *Μυροκότου*: “of a perfumer.” 20. *ὄνομα*: “name.”

## Source column map

- **[Col. 1139A]** all things proceed from and return to God; **[Col. 1139B]** darkness and inaccessible light; **[Col. 1139C]** the prayer for illumination; **[Col. 1140A]** clouds and harmful imaginations; **[Col. 1140B]** the proposed praise of Germanus; **[Col. 1140C]** Germanus’s trials and merits.
- In the address to the book, **[Col. 1139D]** opens the warning; **[Col. 1140D]** treats the book’s weariness of seclusion; **[Col. 1141A]** the seals and Danaë; **[Col. 1141B]** Virgil’s long polishing; **[Col. 1141C]** hostile public reception; **[Col. 1142A]** fault-finding; **[Col. 1142B]** the counsel to use Germanus’s name; and **[Col. 1142C]** the farewell.
- In Book I, **[Col. 1141D]** introduces Auxerre; **[Col. 1142D]** its names and walls; **[Col. 1143A]** Germanus’s homeland and birth; **[Col. 1143B]** his education; **[Col. 1143C]** his pursuit of further study at Rome; **[Col. 1144A]** knowledge put into legal practice; **[Col. 1144B]** marriage; and **[Col. 1144C]** Roman education and discipline.
- **[Col. 1145A]** adulthood and office; **[Col. 1145B]** Roman dominion and magistracies; **[Col. 1145C]** the senate and return to the narrative; **[Col. 1145D]** Germanus’s legal study and chaste marriage; **[Col. 1146A]** his attachment to home and hunting; **[Col. 1146B]** nominal Christianity; **[Col. 1146C]** the pear-tree trophies; and **[Col. 1146D]** Amator’s miracles and the poet’s apostrophe.
- **[Col. 1147A]** Amator and Germanus as spiritual father and son; **[Col. 1147B]** Amator’s rebuke; **[Col. 1147C]** rulers’ corrupting example; **[Col. 1147D]** Germanus’s refusal; **[Col. 1148A]** the felling of the tree; **[Col. 1148B]** its burning and removal of the effigies; **[Col. 1148C]** Rumor’s report; and **[Col. 1148D]** Germanus’s anger.
- **[Col. 1149A]** the armed seizure of the city; **[Col. 1149B]** Amator’s desire for martyrdom; **[Col. 1149C]** Germanus’s future episcopate; **[Col. 1149D]** the revelation and the Aeduan foundation story; **[Col. 1150A]** Caesar and the city; **[Col. 1150B]** Augustodunum’s land and warriors; **[Col. 1150C]** Julius and Simplicius; **[Col. 1150D]** Amator’s reception; **[Col. 1151A]** his speech to the governor; and **[Col. 1151B]** his request for Germanus’s tonsure.

[Col. 1151C] He orders everyone to stand, and when the assembly has gathered according to custom, he begins:

“Brothers and sons, receive the reward of our toil; allow me to set forth the matter in a few words. After endless labors of monstrous weight, amid the straitened circumstances that we have endured up to this point; after traversing the successive volumes of an unstable life; after the harsh burdens of grievous exile, now that I am weary and permitted at last to behold my longed-for true homeland—

although we rejoice to be released from the fetters of the flesh, so that the spirit may rightly deserve to be with Christ, anxious concern for our flock still troubles us.

Therefore, come: while you gaze upon this great assembly of thousands, designate for the Church a worthy leader after me.

[Col. 1151D] Set one man over all the others, one who at the appointed time can adequately supply your tables with the daily portion of saving doctrine.”

Everyone fell silent; each pondered the matter in his heart.

The man to whom the conclusion and ordering of the affair were more clearly apparent turns and hastens his steps toward the threshold of the church.

37. The whole people follows the man, and they were preparing to enter the temple with the holy man. But he resisted them, soothing everyone with calm speech:

“It is the duty of our office and of our vow throughout the ages to care for the house of God, and to admit ministers of peace into the divine dwellings in peaceful order;

[Col. 1152A] but those whom the love of slaughter and the insane desire for war incite, we must immediately keep away from the entire sanctuary. For this house was established as a place of prayer, not to provide spectacles of frenzied Mars.

Therefore, so that everyone may be granted access to the magnificent sacraments, unload your hands of the malign weapons of spear and sword.”

He spoke, and time did not allow him to say more. For all laid down the burden of iron; they freed and lifted their sides from the sword and their hands from the spear. The earth beneath resounded with the clashing of arms.

Thus the people attempted to follow the holy man, who was proceeding into the inner sanctuary of the temple. Once their threatening expression had been laid aside, the leader—unaware of his disposition and of the stratagem prepared—was present and entered first; such was the order required.

[Col. 1152B] When the bishop saw Germanus with his weapons put away, he ordered the doors of the temple to be fastened with strong bolts.

What he had ordered to be done was accomplished sooner than the word itself. What expression was yours, great Leo, when you saw such things? What thought first came to you, while turning over so many possibilities?

“You will strive in vain. If you wish to rage, the points of your weapons are lacking; if you wish to slip away in flight, there is no exit anywhere here.

Rather, grow gentle; this course is better. Learn to endure the hand, and do not flee human contact. In the end, let it not shame you to be enclosed in a mild fold.

This affair will once be celebrated by the mouths of many, if it should happen that a lion lies down among sheep.”

38. The bishop, surrounded by a gathered company of the sacred clergy, first forced his way by strength and hand upon the unarmed man,

[Col. 1152C] with great God granting him the courage to attempt it. Calling upon God’s name, he plucked the hair from the crown of his head; changing the garment, he changed the man’s state of mind as well, and ordered him to be advanced to the second rank of honor [Note: [Col. 1152D] That is, of the presbyterate. Manuscript note.].

He warned him to be sufficiently watchful and to preserve unharmed, in faithful keeping, the pledge that had been received. He knew that this very man would immediately become first in the governance of the church after him, heir to the place and successor to the master.

Learn, teachers, authors of decrees, shepherds of the flock—but many in name only—you who deny that the mystical sacraments of God can be entrusted to the unlearned (and we do not deny that this is true):

learn instead to submit yourselves to the Holy Spirit, whose work is law and whose administration is order. Wherever he wills, he breathes, since he shares equal majesty with the Son and the Father. In teaching he needs no delay: for to have touched is to teach, to have willed is to act; and at last he changes what he purifies.

39. The road is long and the journey difficult. To hasten it, we are delayed by feeble horses—those who undertake what they have begun vigorously at the first onslaught, yet scarcely complete the course at last: for they retain the will to do good, but possess little ability.

Therefore, dear companion, take counsel both for them and for yourself; having departed from home, set your first milestones here. To have begun something is already some part of its accomplishment.

PREFACE TO THE SECOND BOOK, COMPOSED IN A Τεικώλῳ τετραστρόφῳ [a four-stanza poem; first metrical designation uncertain].

[Col. 1153]

[Col. 1153A] 40. When the care of poetry seized the ancient noble poets—for once it was considered a mark of refinement to write in a pure, soft, melodious style—

they offered powerful vows to Phoebus’ household gods, in their customary religious observances, believing that the Muses would spread their sails for the future poem.

One poet more eagerly summoned forth a mouth resounding with a hundred voices, another as many tongues, a brazen breast, and iron plectra for the mouth.

But robust faith and a mind trusting in goodness stir me to seek something different, and indeed more fitting—not to say more dutiful.

[Col. 1153B] O light added to the minds of earthborn beings! O Spirit, wondrous beyond measure, creator! O giver of honors! O fertile eloquence!

Once you were carried above, sustaining and giving form to the shape-flowing waters; for without you, Creator, all things existed without form.

[Col. 1154A] 41. Breathe upon my undertakings with a gentle breeze, and supply easy dactyls and reluctant spondees; for this union is the more pleasing.

Yet flowing words are not enough unless the subject matter of the poem is splendid. Practice approves both, and we demand both,

although this matter is so great and so overflowing that the mind and intellect rightly shudder before such a mass of rough terrain and untouched peaks.

Nevertheless, it demands some labor: to force a swollen river into its banks when it spreads itself more broadly across open fields,

[Col. 1154B] O crosses of our mighty bishop! Words are not enough for them; hands are needed as well. I would not say that they can be borne under any covenant.

With you as my guide, I shall set my pen to these things, for whom he endured every hardship—not twice, nor once, but with more reluctance than life itself [Note: [Col. 1153] As if he were saying: The holy man did not cease tormenting himself before he ceased living.].

THE SECOND BOOK.

[Col. 1153]

CHAPTER ONE. The death of Saint Amator; the succession of Saint Germanus; and the beginning of his exceedingly austere life.

[Col. 1153C]

42. Amator, distinguished by excellent character and merits, for whom to live was Christ and the final lot was gain, full of the titles of virtue and full of days, had begun to receive the palm earned by his labors as their reward, transformed into the heavens in the likeness of a shining dove.

Then you could see the peoples rushing together into harmonious prayers, as God breathed upon them. The ranks of the clergy, joined with the noblemen, hastened forward; the rural populace sang together with the urban people. The judgment of all was equal, their voice the same; all burned with a common zeal to confer upon Germanus the title of bishopric:

to choose him for his noble merits, to choose him for his nobility, foremost in doctrine, first in his generous heart, known to princes and, in some measure, revered, cautious in counsels sought from the divine fountain.

Many praises of the man accumulated to crown his chaste renown. His high merits supplied the material; from the mouths of willing speakers the declarations of truth flowed freely.

Each person had no other subject and no greater abundance of speech than to repeat Germanus, to raise Germanus to the stars. Wherever you directed your eyes, wherever you tried to turn your ears, everything was Germanus. So great was the harmony of their voices.

43. Although he resisted much and prepared to reject the office, they resolved to wage a civil contest against the Primate. Their minds stood firm on pursuing what they had begun; they would not withdraw their appointed purpose in any direction.

What can a conquered authority do? What can it do against the resistance of thousands of peoples? Let him yield to custom, and recognize that the cause of the pressing affair had proceeded from the seat above.

44. If he had perhaps prepared certain patrons or obstacles on his own behalf, soon, when the axis of affairs had turned, he perceived that their minds were laying down their arms and joining the opposing side. He had learned that, when God wills, everything else is bent in this direction.

45. The honor was assumed, though not voluntarily, and he was made a priest. If there was anything of clay in him, with prudent judgment he turned it into gold; and with the advancement of his rank, an abundance of virtues flowed forth.

He left behind the wealth and offices of a declining kingdom, its profits together with its pomp, and everything that is fleeting, has fallen, or might be thought destined to fall. His mind considered all of it worthless.

Indeed, he preferred poverty to perishable riches. Whatever he had lawfully accumulated for human use,

[Col. 1155A] in hope of better things he lavishly distributed to the needy [Note: [Col. 1155D] Or “greedy”?] [B., with generous hand], content with the present day and caring nothing for tomorrow.

His wife, entirely faithful to chaste embraces, had been joined to him only to this extent; she exchanged her lot for that of a sister and was thereafter to lead a celibate heavenly life with her holy spouse.

This was the change wrought by the lofty God. By whose gift it was accomplished: whenever someone, having hated the left with sound mind, is borne more readily toward the right by a vigorous effort.

46. A difficult mass rises before the runner in the poem, grim with its own weight. It is something not seen in former times, not heard of by an unlearned age; for this reason unknown to all, believed by not all, and finally attempted by only a few.

Come, gracious Spirit; by whatever power you gave the means by which this could be done, now grant also the power to speak of it.

Having received the dignity and likeness of an apostle [B., “the dignity, and also the likeness”], he led an apostolic life in deeds and in name. Soon he declared difficult battles against his own flesh and devised everlasting crosses for his courageous spirit [Note: [Col. 1155D] That is, for his noble spirit. Manuscript note.].

47. From the day on which he began to be called and to be a holy man, he subdued his flesh with such merciless severity that thereafter he excluded his mouth from every kind of food by which human inventions seek to stimulate greedy taste.

He did not then permit even the tips of his lips to touch the use of grain, or finally of wine; he used neither oil nor vinegar in his food, without which even the most lavish dishes are pleasing, although they may be present in abundance.

[Col. 1155C] He denied even dry fare the assistance of salt.

48. Whenever he had proclaimed a festival day or holiday to the world—whether the day on which the Word, clothed in flesh from the Virgin, was born, or when, returning victorious from the infernal abyss, he brought forth with himself the standards of human salvation—

they say that on each solemn day, out of religious observance, he allowed himself cups at a modest expense. But wines buried beneath abundant streams of water had lost their natural taste and were no longer really wines.

49. To sustain his foodless body with inert nourishment, remembering the goodness of David, who cared for songs, he first tasted ashes; thus he took barley.

This alone was bread. He considered it sinful to consume what had been prepared by another’s hands, unless he himself, energetic in the task, shook it out and ground it with his own. He knew how to distinguish whether he obtained his food through another’s or his own sweat, and what might be made fortunate by the integrity of his hands.

Perhaps it was a pleasure to take food somewhat earlier, whatever it might be. When Phoebus, hastening from the fields and leaning toward the western waters at his setting,

[Col. 1155D] he had prescribed a fixed hour for his very dry fare.

How often did his fast last through half a week? More often he extended his fasting across seven nights.

50. For as much of the year as he endured the summer heat, he also endured the rigid frosts in that same garment.

[Col. 1156A] His clothing consisted of a cowl laid over a thin tunic, with a haircloth garment concealed within [B., hidden inside]. This made his limbs rough and his skin hard, and never allowed his body the softness of sleep.

Once taken up, it never ceased from constant use, unless it was handed over to the poor when another garment replaced it, or unless, worn out, it was no longer fit for any use.

And just as each attacker, rushing forward, casts hostile towers to the ground and presses the rebels with a powerful siege, never ceasing with engines [B., stratagems] or cleverly contrived hiding places, and fighting outside with the sword and within with terrors, never desisting until, victorious, he holds the walls—

so the fiercest enemy harassed his body with the same determination, hostile to himself, attacking now by one method, now by another, to mortify it. He afflicted it inwardly with fasts, outwardly with harshness; and, having subdued it like a monstrous lion, he set harsh things before it and then threatened worse.

O unprecedented constancy of flesh subdued beyond measure, to which it was given to overcome the laws of powerful nature and to trample beneath its feet the πάθος [passion] implanted in humanity!

51. His bed was a thin arrangement of four pieces of wood, filled to the rim with the remnants of flames and a hard sprinkling of ash. The ash, already compacted by the weight of the one lying there, had grown hard and presented a rigid back to the ground.

Hard bristles served as bedding, laid beneath a very thin cloak. Though many a stag’s antlers rise toward the lofty summit of its head, no object ever supported the man’s head beneath it.

Thus he had condemned his limbs to the ground. What garment did he not remove from his weary body at night? He wore coverings for his feet only rarely, and likewise belts only rarely. He did not remove the pledges of the saints from his holy neck.

His breast was never free from groaning, nor his mouth from prayer. Amid such torments, who could fail to be deprived of sleep?

“Proceed in the poem,” said the anxious mind; “further matters call you.” Then, touched by another inspiration, it said, “Let us stop; the chief matters recall our course. It is not enough to have lingered over these only once; when rubbed anew, they will be more pleasing.

The holy man’s transformation must be examined, and the new man weighed against the old on an equal scale: what he had been, what he became, and who emerged from what.”

52. Once, when he was about to dine in royal luxury, estates brought forth various dishes on ancient platters.

There was no limit to expense, nor was the abundance of food simple. Cheap things grown at home, and all that was domestic, were not enough; things sought by art and purchased through the hard labor of those who pursued them were preferred.

Whatever exists in the deepest earth among beasts, whatever is in the sky among birds, and whatever swims in the hidden depths of the sea, was brought together for the unrestrained uses of the prince—not because hunger commanded it, but to provide varied flavor [Note: [Col. 1155D] That is, not to remove hunger, but to increase pleasure [Col. 1156D]. Manuscript note of the codex of Lyon.].

These banquets, these deceptive world’s delights, once consumed by the young man—what a marvelous exchange of circumstances!—were later repaid by barley for twice three decades [Note: [Col. 1156D] That is, by the thirty years during which he was bishop.], ashes that had first been tasted, and long fasts of days.

The wines that come first and most abundantly from native lands were served in capacious, precious gems, to say nothing of the inventions of various liquids.

[Col. 1157A] At times he raised water drawn from a spring in hollowed hands; you might consider even this a fault, unless he drank sparingly.

53. Why should I mention garments inscribed by a Phrygian comb, or garments more than once steeped in Tyrian dyes; gold sewn onto them more thickly than on these, and emeralds embroidered upon them; then white byssus, downy silk, and necklaces—many things that generous Fortune gave to the proud leader, each destined to be made into a separate garment for a different day?

Upon these limbs he put on the hairy fibers of the pungent goat, having once been accustomed to sweat in his inner garments in tricaptas [τρικάπτοις] [Note: [Col. 1157D] We call *interulae* the inner tunics; *trichapta* means garments of hair-like fineness, for τρίχαι—or rather τρίχες—means “hairs” in Greek. Thus the manuscript notes here. Otherwise, *trichapton* properly denotes a certain silk fabric from which the hair of the head is bound, called in Latin a *crinale*. But it is clear that here a thin tunic is meant, contrasted with the harshness of the haircloth.].

What of the fact that, when he had properly completed his daily duties—sometimes handling games, sometimes serious affairs—when he withdrew from the crowd to the safety of a quiet bedroom, a softer cushion, most splendid in gleaming scarlet, invited him to draw healthful [reading uncertain: *salubres*] sleep?

This same earth, exceedingly harsh to his rigid back, received his limbs, which had already unlearned the white down of cushions.

He did not devote himself to sleep, but to lamentation. Upon his own bed, remembering the omnipotent Lord and recalling the traces of his former life even then, he washed away his inward hiding places with healing tears [Note: [Col. 1157D] For *eluit* or *diluit*.].

A living and pleasing victim, supported by the sharp insights of reason, thus sacrificed himself upon the pure altar of virtues; knowing that, after Christ, he must carry the cross, deny himself, and strive toward the starry heights of heaven—he for whom the world had been crucified, and he, finally, to the world:

CHAPTER TWO. The saint compared with apostles, martyrs, and others; his hospitality, solitude, and monastery.

[Col. 1157C]

54. Let prudent men, adopting the man’s judgment and composing their minds, weigh the causes and meaning of this affair, and let each person report what he considers most worthy after deliberation.

For my part, the same judgment remains with me, and day by day it sinks more firmly into my mind: Germanus, for as many days as he lived under this lot, endured a noble martyrdom for that same number of days.

Let no dullard take offense; let no one deem these things superfluous. Germanus will be a martyr to me, and I shall not be thought foolish when I say, “Great martyr, pray for us.”

55. And what is more important than these things—although I may be called presumptuous, I would dare to enroll Germanus among the apostolic grains, where the great harvest has spread across the whole world.

If not in number, the number whose limit its author fixed, then at least in merit. It is not forbidden for him to rival Peter in merits; Peter does not envy equal merits.

Read the life and virtues enacted by our bishop,

[Col. 1158A] and his teachings [B., “read”]. If he cannot both be and be called an apostle, either call him one, or call the speaker deceptive [Note: [Col. 1157D] For *dicito*, “say.”].

56. How many splendors he adds to the chairs of bishops, there is no need to say much here, since what is sufficient already stands out.

Inferior to no one and surpassing many, he bears this private gift as a gift of Christ: radiant in doctrine, mighty through frequent signs, he accomplished everything both by word and by illustrious deeds.

57. Why should anyone not attempt to place him beneath the virginal garland, since he entered into the lawful covenants of the marriage bed?

His incorrupt faith and mind conscious of a righteous vow never suffered the stain of snow-white chastity.

It is little merely to have preserved the brilliance of untouched flesh if a man is not inwardly pure from obscene action and strives to maintain the integrity of his own honor.

58. Come, then, and with the reasons set forth before you, carry your mind in order through all the saints. There are many things in every respect fitting for our Father.

When the world is compelled to come before the face of the future Judge with its great assembly, and when that apostolic senate has also taken its seat, Germanus himself, supported upon a radiant throne, will render as judge censorial decrees concerning the great world.

Then, when brave rewards are hung for the sacred martyrs, he will bear a rose-colored crown, which long crosses produced in a body devoted to them.

And when cautious priests enter the inner chambers of the kingdom in due order, receiving their reward for the talent, for their subdued flesh, and for the profit earned by their deeds,

[Col. 1158C] with the victorious palm assigned to Germanus, it will be said: “Excellent servant, receive the greatest things in return for small ones, because you have been faithful with your whole heart.”

59. Fertile earth rejoices in the threefold [B., threefold] abundance of its farmer; so the Sower taught when he cast the seeds of the word.

When others bring shining sheaves above the stars, each reclaiming the reward corresponding to his labor, you will see Germanus shining with three crowns.

He who advanced from thirtyfold to sixtyfold [Note: [Col. 1158D] He alludes to the parable of the seed falling on good soil and producing a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold, Matthew 13. It is cited in the manuscript notes. The hundredfold number, transferred from the left to the right, is a symbol of virginity.],

and always led his footsteps from the left toward the right, will flourish in happiness with a plainly virginal crown.

Given as companion to virgins, he will follow the Lamb wherever the Lamb goes; and, which is the destiny of the chaste, he will sing a resonant song with heavenly sweetness.

[Col. 1158D] That he became so great is your work, Christ, without whom nothing is right, and with whom all things are right.

60. The virtue by which the fathers of old pleased the heavenly guests whom they received [Note: [Col. 1158D] Abraham and Lot. Manuscript note.]—hospitality—was native to the saint.

Mindful of the command so often repeated by the human Teacher, that no one to whom you can soon do good should be rejected, and that the righteous man’s doors stood open to the traveler, he offered everyone the full use of hospitality.

No one was excluded; no one suffered rejection. He gathered everyone in and prepared banquets for everyone. He himself brought in the food, and when everyone had been refreshed from every source, he alone remained hungry.

How great was the care—or the affection [Note: [Col. 1159C] That is, diligence. Manuscript note.]—with which he did these things! It was as though Christ embraced all these duties and was then most fully present in his members.

He knew that God had done this and commanded it to be done: to remove the dirt from feet with chaste hands and to press kisses insistently upon feet that had been wiped clean.

With extraordinary compassion he always restored the weak. While he tended ulcers that had long been regarded as hopeless and no longer subject to medical treatment, how often did he recall many from death?

Here he was an eye for the blind, a foot for the lame, and a father to the poor. Thus he became all things to all people: he harmed no one and strove to benefit everyone.

61. Although at this time you see many, secluded from the people in a private place and without shame, likewise seeking popular favor with relaxed minds, here the order was reversed.

A rare thing among men, he obtained among the people a radiant life of seclusion. And what is astonishing: while dealing with worldly matters, he acquired none of the contagion of the deceitful world.

Wonderful! Someone touches pitchy filth and is not defiled by pitch. Wonderful! Fire enclosed in the deepest recesses advances, and the garments are carried away unburned.

62. It was his greatest concern always to benefit the Church over which he was rector. Arranging it with wondrous order through the growth of holy religion,

[Col. 1159C] he established two ways by which people might go to the heavenly realms.

Both were successfully perfected;

[Col. 1160A] both strive toward heaven by equal steps.

One, traveling more broadly—this one is said to be canonical—has long practiced the Πρακτικήν [practical life] [Note: [Col. 1159C] Πρακτικήν, that is, the active life. Manuscript note.] according to accustomed practice [B., “the accustomed practice”].

The other is narrow, confined on every side by restricted boundaries; it does not travel across level ground but always labors toward steep heights.

This one is also apostolic, and at the same time θεορικά [the contemplative life] [Note: [Col. 1159C] That is, contemplative. Manuscript note.], rejoicing only in withdrawal and happy in perpetual seclusion.

For those entering this life he established beautiful walls, rising beyond the sight of the city, where it projects beside the swollen river and rises toward the sun, though a river lies between it and the city. Ancient times gave it the name Icauna.

In this way the Church’s estate grew distinct, and it grew without limit. With eager devotion, everyone migrated in orderly fashion to the holy life, happy under a good shepherd whose preceding virtue had made him outstanding and set him forward as one to follow.

Who would not have acquired civil manners under such a bishop, even if he had recently arrived as a barbarian [B., “had been”]?

Who could fail to burn as a pure worshiper of the faith, even if he had sworn allegiance to a hundred sacred gods?

Who could be so savage that the grace of the holy man would not compel him to grow gentle?

He never accomplished his work by words alone. He could ultimately have been despised if he had not also acted; and a teacher is thought contemptible in eloquence unless deeds lend support to his words.

Nor is there any ability to proclaim oneself the mouth of God unless, by a humble art dear to Christ, one can draw out of the clay each person’s foul vapors [Note: [Col. 1159C] God says through Isaiah: “If you separate the precious from the worthless, you will be as my mouth” [Col. 1160C]. To God, the worthless thing is this world; the precious thing is the soul created in his image. Manuscript note at this passage. The meaning, therefore, is: it cannot be said how that man could win souls for God through teaching if he did not add the example of teaching to his doctrine.].

63. Since the third book takes its beginning from signs, the second must finish the account of his moral works,

although it complains that it is being compelled into brevity unworthy of the subject.

PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK, EXPOUNDED IN A Μονόκωλον [“single-membered” form].

[Col. 1159]

[Col. 1159D] 64. As I turn over the ranks of Christ’s worshipers whom the earth has produced, a consideration presents itself that is at once forceful and moderate.

With your permission, reader, let me reveal it more plainly; it diminishes no one’s magnificent service.

You observe one surpassing others in the gifts of renowned doctrine, another rising to the stars because of his merits, and another, celebrated for signs, made illustrious by more blessed fame. You will scarcely find one person in whom all these things converge at once.

They proclaim Hilary [Note: Hilary of Poitiers, renowned for the seven liberal arts.] famous for the seven-branched arts; Martin [Note: Martin, bishop of Tours, exceedingly well known, as was Saint Antony the abbot, who follows.] strikes the stars with the titles of his power in signs; Antony carried off [B., “brought forward”] the palm of a holy way of life.

Each shines by his own praise throughout perpetual time.

[Col. 1160D] Thus the Spirit, generous in gifts, endows human beings. Although he subsists simple, uncompounded, and one, the heavenly page nevertheless proclaims his sevenfold charisms, rich in their manifold endowment.

65. O thrice, four times, and finally a thousand times magnificent is the man fortunate enough to have deserved a share in one good!

To say nothing of that man who accomplished so many things, here is Germanus, here is the man whom we applaud in melodious [B., lyrical] song.

He is adorned with the highest mastery of καθολικὴ σοφία [universal wisdom] [Note: καθολικὴ σοφία, that is, universal wisdom. Manuscript note.].

In clear merits he has shone inferior to no one.

Yet compare him with the magnificent apostles in signs, if he too does not shine as powerful under a similar right.

Britain, freed from Pelagius’ flood, bears witness; the cell in which he endured harsh crosses bears witness; the churches standing wherever he once set his easy foot bear witness, as do the tokens of his life-giving name.

Thus, having passed through the beginning with excellent moral conduct, the signs shining across the fourfold world call us forward.

Grant, illustrious source and father of lights, who are rightly called both, that we may proceed here under good auspices.

THE THIRD BOOK.

[Col. 1161]

CHAPTER ONE. His wondrous power over demons; the conversion of Saint Mamertinus.

[Col. 1161A]

66. His deeds grew wondrous as his merits grew; crosses produced for the man a famous name through signs and power. The more severe their use, the greater his excellence in performing miracles.

Their beginning did not come from a vain experience of his own authority, nor from the light instability of a mind deprived of office, by which the sluggish are once captured;

rather, it came from compassion for a distressed brother, a quality familiar to good men, for whom failing to lend a hand is an unworthy share in guilt [Note: [Col. 1161D] The prose Life briefly says this: “And when, as his merits increased, it was time to proceed to the trials of virtue, the beginning was not one of presumption but of mercy.”].

67. His age raised the man through frugal pursuits, making him suitable for his first duties. January was his gentile name. Under a governor he was chosen as the chief official appointed to burden the people with taxes.

At that time he happened to be carrying the exact sum of money collected from the assessment, so that, with his purse full, he could add foreign riches to the public treasuries.

[Col. 1161C] Since he was a devoted servant of the holy man’s fear, he turned his steps toward the city to visit the bishop. He considered it unworthy of piety to have passed by the man when he was so near; therefore he directed his steps toward the walls.

Soon, after the tax-payer suffered the loss of his purse, he was already liable, yet did not know that his life was still in danger. Someone possessed by a demon seized the lost money together with the purse; when every judge was present, he hid it away.

Assigned to bitter losses [Note: [Col. 1162D] Namely, January.], from whom could he recover what he had entrusted to no one?

In anxiety he filled the city with uncertain complaints. He went and returned along the road, retracing in vain the footprints where he had now trodden, since the matter remained unknown.

When his hopes collapsed, only this decision remained: to transfer the means of repairing the loss to the holy man; to assail him with prayers and true tears, just as if he were liable for the deposit.

The bishop, pitying the mourner’s unjust lot, promised that the loss to the treasury could be restored. He wished to relieve the man’s mind of its womanish complaints.

The bishop’s edict soon hung throughout the city, and a delay of three days was announced for searching out the matter.

68. When the wretched man had spent this time and had been deceived by an empty promise, he rushed impatiently to the holy man’s footprints and said:

“If the public money is not discovered, you will soon weep to see my life strangled by a noose as I depart.”

What could piety do? He ordered one of the patients to be summoned. By chance the author of the crime was brought forward. He commanded him to disclose and announce the contagion of the agreed theft.

The man concealed the hiding place. The bishop soon ordered him, though unwilling, to be brought before the people. Then he solemnly prepared himself for the sacred rites.

Raising his hands and greeting the people according to custom, he prostrated himself, pressing the earth with his outstretched body, and groaned. The stars drank in the voice of the one praying.

Without delay, the captive was driven into the air and carried upward, so that at least through punishments he might provide evidence of the truth.

A shout filled the church, and trembling filled the people. That day displayed wondrous spectacles: the accused and the judge weighed their case in a fierce contest.

The one lies on the ground; the other is raised up. The former presses down the earth with prayers; the latter with complaints. The one touched the ground; the other fled from touching it, unhappy and not daring to stand in the same place for even a short time.

As though surrounded by a great fire, he called upon Germanus and set forth the crime in due order. The bishop lifted his limbs from the dust, roused the wretched man, and ordered him to stand before him and recount to the people the sequence of the theft; then to bring out into the open the solid money from its hidden place.

The people’s raised shout struck the stars, bearing witness to Germanus’ merit and to the insignia of Christ.

69. This experience is said to have applauded the man at the beginning of his career, since the matter had been carried out publicly.

Yet he had often driven out proud spirits [Note: [Col. 1162D] That is, spirits.]; because he desired secrecy, he wished to reveal it to no one.

70. The hostile forces contended against the holy man in a bitter dispute. At a certain time the war pressed more fiercely upon him.

When they saw that, though attacked by much art, he did not yield openly to their weapons, they turned the wickedness conceived in their hearts into harm for the people and at last shot their dark arrows against them.

Immediately disaster grew hot across the broad fields, and dire contagions crept through the widespread populace.

A spirit tightening the chests of the possessed within their confines and driving sick sighs through their swollen throats compelled the people to succumb to a hostile death.

Thus the enemy plague, scarcely lasting three days, submerged the wretched citizens in an undeserved funeral.

Their salvation was publicly lamented; confidence in life departed. Day by day the seeds [B., “the beginnings”] of the disease grew more savage; no one could lend a hand, no one could meet the fates.

The pious bishop recognized the signs of the ancient serpent [*chelydrus*] and grieved. Then he consecrated the ointment brought to him with the form of the sacred sign and with powerful words.

By this the plague was driven away; by this the people were restored to life. Their breath and food, restored by contact with the liquid, drove away destruction, and health quickly returned.

The physician cleansed whatever the serpent had infected.

Afterward it became clear that demonic spirits had sown such ruin. For when the spirit was driven from one wretched man, it reported that, while the holy man was giving his hands to heaven [Note: [Col. 1163D] The manuscript of Belfort, whose many corrections I often omit because of the antiquity of the other codices and the recent authority of this one, restores these two verses as follows:

“Afterward it became clear: when the spirit leaves the wretched man, it reported this, while the holy man was calling the heavenly powers to his prayers,

by a whirlwind …”],

it had suffered an ugly repulse in the whirlwind of his words.

[Col. 1163B] 71. Setting before everyone the rewards of emulous virtue, he summoned now the monks, now the clergy to difficult heights.

While he made himself equally present to them in turn, one day he happened to be asked to visit the brothers. He refused, held back by the burden of another matter.

But, once freed from his concern and released from the knot of business, after a short time he went out to visit the brothers, who knew nothing of it.

One of the possessed, suffering at the brothers’ threshold and raving more violently than usual, raised his voice through the empty air:

“They say that Germanus is present on the banks of the neighboring river, and that he cannot cross the open water [B., “river”] without first using a boat [Note: [Col. 1163D] Supply “being able to.”]. The deceitful prophet is deceiving the deceitful with a deceitful heart.”

For a long time they asserted this, but the increasingly insistent cry urged them to learn that it was more certain and that they should not delay the matter.

[Col. 1163C] A brother was sent to investigate and returned with certainty concerning the bishop:

“The boat flies and carries its welcome burden most faithfully.”

The priest was received with the brothers’ customary fervor. He applied himself to prayers, and the whole assembly followed him.

Immediately the enemy, bound in powerful bonds, lifted his captive high into the air. While the holy man lingered in prayer, the demon raged and filled the air with complaints.

Gnashing fiercely, he begged that he himself might at least be thrust from the wretched man’s breast and permitted to injure his bodily limbs. But, certain that even this would not be granted, he departed, compelled to break wind in an obscene manner.

A stench worthy of the thief followed in his footsteps.

Thus the place became illustrious through the merits and honor of its master, and for a long time through the governance of his successors’ disciples. Brevity of the pen keeps us from such matters [Note: [Col. 1163D] This seems to refer to the history of Saint Mamertinus, which Constantius develops at greater length on the occasion of this monastery, while Hericus adds it very briefly below.].

[Col. 1163D] 72. Mamertinus was a priest of Phoebus and Jupiter, and at that time still worshiped all the gods as best he could.

After he had spent several years in these forms of worship, the wretched man was deprived of the use of one eye and likewise suffered loss of his right hand.

After he had long struck the altars he had once ruled, he learned that deaf gods were summoned to prayers in vain. Having happened upon Sabinus, a Christian judge [Note: [Col. 1164D] For “whom he happened to meet”], who was shaping monastic rules by noble examples, he sought out Germanus.

Germanus, already informed of the matter, had indicated to him the man’s cause, his vow, and the manner of its fulfillment. The sacred dwelling was almost within reach, and by chance the bishop himself was approaching.

The man, suppliant, prostrated himself upon the ground and worshiped the holy man. The bishop raised him and soothed him with wondrous kindness; he entered and addressed the man with gracious words.

They went to the church; trusting, he was bathed in the waters. At last stripped of the squalor of his former self, he put on a snow-white form with a changed mind.

He also felt his bodily illnesses depart. Rejoicing that he had received light through the hand, he spent the remainder of his life under the holy man’s protection.

CHAPTER TWO. His piety toward the dead; the recompense of hospitality; his election for the British expedition; the consecration of Saint Genevieve the virgin.

[Col. 1161]

73. God declared in a truthful saying that he would not be of help to one who lets the innermost things, covered beneath a bushel, lie inert …
the lamp.

Our shepherd knew this through his lofty teaching,

and did not allow it to remain concealed in blind hiding places.

[Textual apparatus not otherwise represented in the translation: In the description of the haunted dwelling, B reads *prope* (“near”) for *fere* (“almost”). In §74, *acta* is perhaps to be corrected to *aucta* (“enlarged”). In §75 B reads *impensa est integra rebus* (“the whole night was entirely spent in sacred matters”). In §76 B has *ferme* (“almost”) for *pene* (“almost”); the printed Greek *μονάζος* is glossed “monk,” while the note proposes *μοναζόντων*, “of those leading a solitary life,” since *μονάζος* is not Greek. In §82 B reads *pernicior* (“swifter”) for *penetralior* (“more penetrating”). In §83 an alternative reads *diri* (“dreadful”) for *duri* (“hard”), and *liburna* is the feminine form of *liburnus*, “small boat.” In §87 B reads *potius* (“rather”) for *vulgo* (“commonly”), and *timoris* (“of fear”) for *timori* (“to fear”). In §88 the text reads *incesta fronte* (“with unchaste/shameful face”), while B reads *demissa fronte* (“with lowered face”). In §89 B has plural *refovent* (“they restore”) for singular *refovet* (“he restores”). In §90 B reads *et adhuc* (“and still”) for *adhuc* (“still”). In §91 C Lugd. and B read feminine *quaeque* (“which”) for masculine *quemque* (“whom”). In §92 B reads *prope* (“nearly”) for *fere* (“almost”). In §98 B reads *inferior* (“inferior”) for *impar* (“unequal”). In §103 B reads *caballum* (“horse”) for *jumentum* (“beast of burden”).

Horrible winter had grown severe over the frosty lands;

he, pressing on his journey, as night drew near, was warned

to protect from the darkness the limbs of the weary by hospitality.

That alone—for the fasts he had begun continued for the man.

By chance, from afar, traces of an ancient dwelling appeared,

with age-old roofs already decayed through prolonged desolation;

lofty shrubs enclosed the ruins grown old with decay:

savage was the appearance of the place, and savage its surroundings.

It was better to withdraw for the night beneath the rigid sky

than to entrust a doubtful head to such great horror,

since such a place, almost beset by the hostile perils of nocturnal phantoms, would properly allow no rest.

The bishop learned these things from the speech of two old men;

and, having measured out the place, he said: “Enter beneath the roofs,

my companions; here, amid uncertainties, a broad hope of triumph lies open.”

Here scarcely one dwelling among many was visible,

resembling an old hut (it had once been one).

He sought it, and transferred his companions and the scanty baggage of the journey there.

[Note: The Belfort manuscript emends both these lines as follows:

“Resembling an ancient hut (it had once been one):

He sought it; here the baggage was transferred, here the companions.”]

A brief supper nourished some, and holy psalmody nourished the others;

it was night, and all were enjoying deep sleep;

the reader applied his eyes to the divine books:

this was the man’s custom. Yet his weary limbs yielded to sleep,

and bodily substance overcame his steadfast spirit.

[Note: The frailty of the flesh. Manuscript note.]

Meanwhile, before the eyes of the unhappy reader,

a shadow stood, not very large at first; soon, growing from above,

it increased without limit. A rocky rain battered the building;

the house shook beneath the missiles, and the roused earth trembled.

A cold terror invaded the frightened man’s breast;

his words vanished, and his voice stuck in his constricted throat.

His one hope, as he swayed, was to awaken

the bishop from sleep. He saw him; and in the great name of Christ

the bishop ordered him to declare openly who he was and what he sought.

### 74

In a subdued voice the terrifying figure pressed

that he and his companion had committed many contagions of crime,

had paid savage penalties,

and had not deserved the gifts of burial;

and because no rest had ever been granted to the wretched,

they continued to trouble human beings. He begged that, if the bishop possessed any compassion,

if he possessed any pity, he should urgently entreat the Almighty

on behalf of himself and his companion—for such was the man’s concern—

that, after so many ages, they might be received into secure dwelling places

and allowed to find tranquil rest in their misery.

The bishop grieved, and, uttering sighs from the depths of his heart,

ordered him to show where they lay. The shadow, guide of the light,

went before him, and entered grimly among the ancient, shattered ruins:

that place was subject to the two men.

When the color of things shone beneath the bright sky,

the teacher invited the rugged peasants to work;

he urged the men, after assembling them in companies on either side,

to cleanse the place. Although the filth had been piled up for a long time,

swift labor overcame everything.

At last two corpses were seen scattered about,

long compressed beneath a shapeless mass: scarcely did decay allow

them to be recognized as human corpses;

iron, eaten away by rough rust, was visible,

and chains still clung to limbs that were then already dry.

The holy man’s compassion groaned over the human lot,

and brought the wretched whatever care he could;

a grave was opened, suitable for two burials;

soft linen took the place of the chains once removed;

their faces were covered with an accumulation of grave dust;

the place was marked, so that a future age might know it;

then the Father’s pious intercession for the wretched was offered,

to bring rest to the dead and peace to the living.

After this the fearless settlers occupied the ground,

and a generation free from evil filled the village.

### 75

A few days later, driven by the same circumstance,

he entered, weary from the journey, the lodging of poorer people,

as was his custom—for, wishing by such a device

to avoid the vanity of the winds, he often cherished such a refuge.

That entire night was devoted to divine affairs.

[Variant: “The whole night was spent in sacred matters.”]

And now Phoebus, advancing on the course of his flame-footed horses,

had scattered a noble redness throughout everything,

announcing the light that had arisen without any crowing of roosters.

[Note: Supply “to be announced.”]

The bishop was astonished, although some abundance of birds

was then visible around those houses.

When questioned, they replied that these losses had begun

to afflict them in ancient years.

The piety sought by the men’s prayers came to their aid

through the gift of the blessed grain.

Having been fed with this, the birds laid aside their defective silence of night

and hastened the sluggish day with their songs.

They regretted having been silent so long; for, once their throats were released,

they deprived the people of sleep. Thus, when the hinge was turned,

the singing birds displeased them no less than the mute ones had.

Having bestowed immense joy amid small circumstances,

he left the lodging, inclined toward such a gift.

[Variant: “Repaid with such interest.”]

### 76

The instruments of our earlier fathers relate that Ocean

had encircled the outermost boundaries of the earth with an endless rim.

Certainly he had made the end of the square-shaped world

where the swift waves wash the shores of Gaul;

unless an island, extending through a vast tract of land,

almost deserved the name of another world,

called Britain by the decree of the ancients, because

through its barbarous customs the entire savage people strike and torment others.

Of all the islands it stands almost in the middle

of those that are greatest or first in size:

for, stretched across very broad distances,

it extends in length for about three times thirty miles,

and, extending across its breadth, lies three hundred miles wide.

[Note: The length of Greater Britain, from the northern coast of Scotland to the town of Antona on the southern coast of England, is calculated at 530 miles; its breadth, between the promontory of Kent in the east and Bolerium in the west, at 320.]

Stretched between the west and the seven northern stars,

it exercises its chief seed upon its own soil;

[Note: *Medioxima* means “middle”; *invidiosa* means “chief” or “pre-eminent.”]

and as fertile as it is in crops, so fertile is it in men.

A dreadful error polluted this island in the aforesaid period—

an error that could persuade people that freedom alone

might contribute sufficiently to their own salvation,

even if grace were absent.

A certain Pelagius, a monk from a vain people,

breathing the livid blackness of Tartarean gall,

infected mortal hearts with such poisons,

perverse in his breast and still more perverse in his foul speech.

[Note: “Monk.” Manuscript note in the Lyon codex. Perhaps the text should read *monazontōn*, that is, “of those leading a solitary life”; for *monazos* is not a Greek word.]

### 77

A trustworthy delegation disclosed to the Gallic bishops

the danger to the faith threatening those regions in their downfall,

and how one might first of all come to the aid of the fallen peoples.

Compassion for the religious men moved their minds

to rescue their brothers exposed to terrible danger.

Therefore a numerous synod assembled: there the common cause

lay amid shared tears, and each beat his breast;

what speech denied, their sighs accomplished in prayer:

all wept over the plague, yet all were unable to help.

Among all, one was sought who might relieve everyone’s wound—

a man holy through his merits and cautious through his keen doctrine,

and readily available through his miracles. Such a patron

so great a dispute demanded.

“Father, these matters concern you; you were born for deeds,

and by a repeated lot you will now enter these dangers also.

Do not tremble; such trials produce an eternal laurel:

great things seek the great, while trivial things are granted to the small.

They judged that these gifts resided in Germanus:

that he could meet the enemy in close and fierce combat;

that he was powerful with tongue and hands, and through nobility,

and would easily bring splendid triumphs from the enemy.”

This was in everyone’s heart; this opinion held them all.

He was sought with prayers, and love at last yielded,

having sworn to die for the glory of his brothers.

### 78

Mindful of the command, they select a companion for the one who is to depart.

[Note: That is, “they choose.” Manuscript note.]

For two are better assigned to one lot,

and one companion hastens to aid the fallen man:

thus two take peaceful sleep at night;

when one is attacked, the strength of two presses back the assault.

The one chosen to provide this assistance was Lupus by name,

who had once, by chance, been bishop of the city of Troyes,

noble and supreme in signs and in his illustrious name.

The guiding grace joined together the apostolic prophets,

who cultivated the earth with their bodies and heaven with their virtue.

And the more difficult the labor, and the harsher the undertaking seemed

(for everything that is very great costs greatly),

the more swiftly they applied themselves to every arduous task,

trained to cross the course by tireless running.

### 79

Their journey turned toward the regions around Paris.

Metodorus provided the weary men with a night’s lodging.

The local crowd, having learned that these proven men were approaching,

hurried forward in a hastened throng,

and bestowed upon the saints who met them the honors that were due.

A present blessing was poured upon the entire people;

then Germanus undertook to adapt their uncultivated minds to heavenly admonitions

and to scatter nectar-like waters over their dry fields;

with immovable faces they attentively approached the wisdom

that flowed from the full fountain.

From afar the bishop saw a divine maiden standing in the midst.

He stretched his face over the crowds;

and as though he were considering some heavenly matter in her,

he soothed her when she came near with gentle speech.

So, when an auctioneer displays gems for sale,

while everyone gapes at the wares, he notices one precious stone;

he seizes it, wishes it to be worth many talents to him,

and, setting it apart from the others, carries it close in his grasp.

The men were immensely astonished. Stroking the frightened girl’s head

with his sacred hand, he asked in kindly speech

from what parents she had sprung and what her name was.

The girl’s parents were brought forward,

and it was properly stated that she bore the family name Genovefa.

[Note: *Ritu* is used for *ritu*, “according to custom.” Manuscript note.]

### 80

At once the sacred Spirit of the divine Prophet filled his breast,

and thus the priest thundered from his radiant mouth:

“O truly charming head! O heart worthy of praise!

O parents always deserving of such offspring!

“At whose birth, if it is right to believe the truth,

the citizens poured forth immense joys toward the powers above;

once brought into closest contact with the hidden heavenly things,

she will prove exceedingly dear to God, brilliantly glorious to the world,

and worthy even of the men themselves to imitate.”

Having spoken thus, and embracing the girl herself, he said:

“Tell me, O most holy one—and do not refuse the Father

who asks you—whether you take delight in the title

of the great Bridegroom, into whose embrace, unless she remains pure,

she passes.”

[Note: The word order is: “into whose embrace she does not pass unless she is pure.” Manuscript note.]

She eagerly seized the word and, with bolder speech, said:

“For a long time I have been borne by love for him, in all its fervor;

I embrace the title of kindred virginity,

by which I may, while unmarried, be wedded to my heavenly Bridegroom.

If you deem me worthy, I desire that this be strengthened through you;

and I submit my head to your hands: offer your prayers for the one who prays.”

The bishop rejoiced over the spoil, and, pressing her in chaste embraces,

ordered her to remain strong-hearted. Then, joyful, he entered

the threshold of the church, and, placing his right hand upon her head,

performed the solemn prayers and vows according to custom,

preparing an immaculate vessel for the Holy Spirit.

### 81

When the matters were completed, they refreshed their mortal bodies with food.

Then, entrusting the pledge to her faithful parent,

[Note: To her father and mother. Manuscript note.]

he ordered her to return to the light. Thus it was finally done.

“Do you remain mindful, daughter, of yesterday’s vow?” the bishop asked.

Certainly, the virgin declared that she remembered it;

and that, under his protection—him of whom she would otherwise be greatly in need—she would preserve the marriage covenant she had pledged.

A marvelous event followed in that place: you might have seen Christ

favoring the prayers of both by a shared gift.

The bishop immediately fixed his hanging eyes upon the ground;

a bronze coin flashed in the upper dust,

engraved with a cross. The priest lifted it from the earth

and dedicated the gift to the neck of his foster daughter, saying:

“Have this as the token of our dowry;

often, when you depart from before my eyes, call this to mind;

but remember to keep away from your neck and fingers

the other things that display worldly pomp in their adornment.

Let external insignia subdue the carnal bride;

as one wedded to God, adorn your spirit with chaste jewels.

“Now, precious one, farewell for a long time.”

After this he entrusted her to her parents to keep.

But he himself continued the journey he had begun,

following his familiar course.

## CHAPTER III  
The storm calmed by the saint’s prayers; the Pelagians defeated by his arguments and miracle

### 82

From there they embarked upon the sea, using Christ as their guide,

trusting that all dangers would yield to them—

he who protects his servants amid dangers

and, after darkness, grants tested men greater joys.

At first their progress was gentle beneath light breezes,

toward the middle of the sea, while the lands were withdrawn in the distance

and only the face of the sea, embraced by the sky, was visible.

Although the malign spirits had been deprived of glory

and thereby made guilty, their original substance remains:

their innate lightness is more penetrating than every wind,

their livid mind is always set against the pursuits of the righteous;

and whatever they see approaching the holy profits of God,

they grieve as having been lost to themselves. They groaned

at the blessed men’s haste to come to the aid of the captive people,
