and they confronted them, stirring dangers throughout the whole sea.

The winds pressed upon them, rushing swiftly from their several seats,

and drove waves that rose to the stars;

night fell, and dense darkness covered the sky.

The dry axis thundered through its trembling joints;

lightning bolts flew mingled together. It seemed that

the elements had confused their harmonious alternations,

and that the world’s ruin would return to its first chaos.

The sails could scarcely bear the fury of the winds.

The sea yawned headlong from its deepest jaws

and already displayed the sands of the underworld.

The merciless wave lashed the trembling keel

with alternating blows: the sailor’s skill gave way;

their strength failed; they surrendered everything to the winds.

### 83

The weary men had one salvation: the presence of the great Father.

Labor had overwhelmed him beneath the hard [variant: dreadful] hindrance of sleep;

the hated storm’s fury sensed that the man had grown slack,

and, as though no barrier opposed it, doubled the danger

and carried the ship’s mass up toward the stars.

All hope of life and escape had been torn from the men;

now they wished only to die, so that they might be free from fear of death.

After this, the tenth wave, leaning upon them—woeful sight!—

wrapped the frightened stern in a deadly whirlpool;

already it had tilted the side beneath the waves pouring over it.

Lupus and the terrified sailors roused the man,

horrified by what had happened, from his stupor.

One hope remained for all:

to set the old man alone before the waves and placate them.

He rose, his face unmoved amid the powerful storms,

and, invoking beforehand the name of Jesus, ruler of the world,

rebuked the audacious sea with exalted courage.

Then, sprinkling the swollen waves with sacred chrism,

he poured forth prayers according to custom.

Present grace accompanied his prayer:

the enemies sat down, their arts exposed;

night was changed into day. Joy balanced grief;

the sails, driven by the wind, moved forward according to his prayers,

and the ship flew as the waves served it.

### 84

Within a short time they traversed the immense stretches of sea

with the desired breeze, and on the shore they discharged their vows.

A nameless crowd, hurrying from various regions,

received the men—men whom, long before,

a sinister prophet had foretold in a troubled voice would come.

As they entered, a fortunate glory accompanied their works;

first, judgment was proclaimed against the savage demons.

For, while they were being driven out of the house they had occupied,

they disclosed to the saints that they had created dangers upon the sea:

they had contrived, amid a great tumult of heaven and sea,

to keep from the people the salvation sent from heaven,

and, defeated by the merits and divine power of the priests,

had yielded to the sea. Everyone marveled at these things.

### 85

Swift rumor, penetrating to the borders of the vast region,

spread that the men had come, whose footsteps

were followed by manifest salvation.

All rejoiced with a common spirit: a supreme fervor filled their breasts,

as they everywhere surrendered themselves to the heavenly leaders.

The grace of their speech was poured into every place.

Cities, churches, assemblies, crossroads, and countryside—

everything breathed meditation upon the heavenly law.

The whole island was filled with divine trophies.

Those in whom the plague had driven its fierce claw,

when they displayed their wounds, received the remedies of life.

The ardor of faith was strengthened in everyone’s minds;

everything breathed faith, and everything stood bound by the covenant of faith.

An apostolic dignity prevailed in the Fathers:

the gravity of their office, the grace of their natural appearance,

an ancient splendor, and a certain pre-eminence;

an uncorrupted mind, always conscious of what was right,

and a skill furnished with excellent arts,

whose sharpness of speech could rout hostile armies.

“Rejoice, Gaul; rejoice, Britain: such advocates

she sends you, by a heavenly gift, to pronounce the law for you.”

### 86

Truthful assertion compelled the wavering peoples

to return to a sound mind. As the darkness gave way,

faith, enlivened by miracles, burned brightly;

the hidden plague lay concealed, and its frightened authors were hidden.

The destruction buried in gloomy caverns wept over its losses

and, in the manner of the devil, groaned that the peoples

were escaping death.

### 87

Yet terrible alarm departed through minds divided between alternatives.

The opponents feared that, if they entered the contest,

they would be overthrown by the weight of reason;

or that, if they withdrew from the place,

their silence would condemn them.

Fear on one side and shame on the other equally prejudiced their cause.

Shame forced their hearts to enter the dispute publicly

rather than condemn themselves to fear without having engaged.

Now the day had arrived that would disclose their faith

through a splendid contest.

The opponents came forward from a distance,

with many acts of service and the flatteries of their followers,

shining with riches and fierce with pomp leading the way.

Their purple garments were marked out by costly material,

and the reverence lacking in their merits yielded to their wealth.

Here Germanus, the standard-bearer of the faith and glory of the age,

blazing with a lightning-like shield and heavenly weapons,

advanced, while his kindly colleague came beside him.

Rumor stirred the peoples; the whole region gathered as one

to watch the day. At last, after equal advances,

they stood face to face—but not with equal strength:

on this side was sincere faith; on that, treacherous error;

on this side Christ the author; on that, Pelagius the author;

on this side piety; on that, the deadly meditation of fraud.

[Variant: “of death.”]

### 88

At first the opportunity to speak was granted to the opponents.

Their position rested solely upon empty words,

and, content with nothing but this, wearied both time and ears:

chattering, savage, shameless, barren, wicked, and lying.

It was like a flame whose fuel, deficient in material,

roars horribly while it is being kindled, like a shapeless mass

being cooked in a furnace, when a lack of air takes in

the blasts from a smith’s bellows.

After the very just men had brought to an end

the weariness produced by the opponents’ prolonged words,

the priests, with breath inspired from above,

brandishing fiery weapons of heavenly speech,

poured forth immense thunder and immense lightning.

The mingled vernacular words with apostolic expressions,

and the harmonious reading of Scripture,

confirmed their chaste discourse.

[Note: “Reading,” namely, the readings of the texts of Holy Scripture by which they supported their statements.]

The savage parties blushed, their eyes downcast;

treacherous error grew warm with foul torpor.

They bared their backs for flight and confessed themselves defeated

in every particular, acknowledging with shameful, lowered faces

what they could not oppose.

But the people, acting as judge, scarcely at last

restrained their hands from avenging steel.

The only thing finally permitted was this:

they condemned the guilty with their shouting.

Thus the assembly burned with zeal,

revering the pious as much as it detested the profane.

### 89

A certain prince burst into the midst with his wife.

For a long time their only daughter, already in her second five-year period,

had been passing her life in the darkness of an unknown blindness.

He brought her before the saints. The defeated opponents judged

that she should be offered to them.

But once their presumption had been driven away,

he fled from attempting their power; and he and his wife,

joined in prayer, begged that the wretched girl be freed from her calamity.

Piety was moved by this, pitying the wretched parents.

They poured out prayer according to custom.

Then Father Germanus, properly invoking the friendly divine power,

removed the holy relics from his neck with his hands,

brought them to the girl’s forehead,

and revived the condemned lamps of her eyes by his renowned power.

A mighty remedy sprang forth, and, the darkness driven away,

filled the empty windows with an unknown sun.

The joyful parents could no longer contain their vows;

indeed, a salutary fear grew among the people:

faith was kindled on this side and grew brilliantly bright,

until no trace of error remained anywhere.

Thus another person’s salvation becomes the cause of salvation for others.

### 90

Although, trembling, we have scarcely completed half our sea,

and the Britons who have begun the journey are not yet permitted

to leave it, the final stage warns us to stop.

Now, poet, exhausted by the weight of your material,

rest for a little; when your strength is restored,

you will perhaps run through what remains.

[Note: In the sole manuscript of Lobbes there followed here a hymn for the saint’s feast, substantially as it is printed in the ancient Breviaries of Auxerre for both Vespers; then two profane stanzas unrelated to Germanus, which will therefore be omitted.]

## PREFACE TO THE FOURTH BOOK  
Composed in four lines and four stanzas.

### 91

Christ had once commanded

the company of disciples

to board the ship

and cross the sea.

He ordered the crowd

to withdraw, each to his own place;

then he climbed the heights

of the mountain and invoked the Father’s divinity.

In the drowsy night

everything had grown numb,

and the blue ship was cutting

through the threatening waters.

The sea had boiled

beneath an adverse wind;

hope of salvation had been extinguished

by so great an image of death.

Now Lucifer had driven

the heavens forward,

when, during the fourth watch,

the sleepless soldier arranged the order.

Christ, his friend,

carried his footsteps across

the liquid waves,

and entered among the horrors.

At once trembling

seized their chilled limbs;

a cry struck the stars;

terror beat their breasts.

“Behold, I am Christ,”

the holy one thundered.

Simon, taking courage,

leaped forward with these words:

“If your compassion

has truly come to us,

command me also, by your familiar order,

to go with you.

For no matter is burdensome

to the highest God;

you will see me carry

dry footsteps across the sea.”

The Lord immediately took pity

and granted his request.

Peter, trusting in the divine power,

quickly leaped from the ship.

The old man moved

his hanging limbs over the sea,

and, leaning upon the waters,

set his footsteps upon the waves.

A new event

had struck his trembling mind.

Then, boiling with fierce tension,

the sea brought dangers;

the waters that had lifted

the faithful man,

you could see gradually

dissolve and sink.

Now Peter, his body submerged

in the midst of the sea,

cries: “Good Jesus,

rescue me from these waves.”

The hand of Christ

caught him as he came toward it;

and, once he had climbed aboard the small ship,

the harmful winds gave way.

### 92

We too, not long ago,

entered the swelling sea,

trusting in the name

of the Most High Christ.

Now we have almost reached

the middle of our course:

only the blue sea

and the sky are visible on every side.

An increasing fear

now drains our breasts.

The waves raise up their mass;

the beginnings of our undertaking

also repent.

Yet, Christ, reveal

your serene face,

and look upon our falling hopes:

may everything yield to our prayers.

Now extend

your powerful hand to the trembling man.

I would dare to climb with you,

although the dangers are grim.

# BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER ONE  
The remaining events in Britain, and especially the Alleluia victory

### 93

Happy steadfastness, relying upon God,

had overthrown the unspeakable plague,

and faith, kindled in pure serenity,

was burning with chaste flames in everyone’s breasts.

A just decision compelled the Fathers, who were about to return,

to seek the tomb of the martyr Alban through their prayers.

He protects his Britons by his merits and prayers,

having suffered thousands of punishments for Christ’s name.

The final sentence of execution carried him away by the head;

but the matter did not remain secure for the proud executioner:

when his sacred head fell, the executioner’s eyes fell also.

Thus, Christ, sometimes avenge your servants.

### 94

Do not refuse, martyr, to be touched by words

that are shorter than justice would permit;

for, if better things had not called me elsewhere,

perhaps you too would have been subject to my pen.

And this now appears to me by no means unwelcome:

I hear that you once favored blessed Germanus,

who, preparing duly to render handsome thanks to his benefactor,

opened the precious barriers of your tomb,

and, reverently covering your holy ashes

with sacred gifts, stored the relics of the saints,

gathered from various places.

Thus, finally, it was right and fitting

that those whom the same glory bound together

through beautiful merits should be enclosed in one small tomb.

And, in return for the gift, he lifted a portion

from the sacred dust.

A turf stained with poured blood

then too rivaled the memorials of the ancient triumph.

The bishop, filled with virtue, carried this back with him—

[Reading: *revixit* is to be read as *revexit*, “carried back.”]

and from it an imposing sanctuary arose for you

within our walls, constructed by blessed hands.

[Note: See our author below, *Miracles*, no. 17.]

Here, Alban, you hear prayers; here you hear the vows of the pious;

here the just citizens have often felt the heavenly powers.

### 95

Whoever lived piously soon found himself

engaged face to face in a deadly contest with the savage enemy.

After completing his divine tasks according to the ancient custom,

and now returning, the hostile force attacks the saint;

then, as he bore peace and heralded salvation,

it happened by chance that the unwary man’s foot slipped,

broken by the burden.

By this art, impious one, you always prepare slippery traps;

but sometimes you forget that gold is tested in the furnace.

It would have been useful to remember the ancient battle.

Once Job, renowned for his abundant merits,

returned even more renowned as victor after the contest had been completed.

And although thunderbolts strike the highest mountains,

the mountains do not cease to remain what they are.

### 96

When the Father, weary, was confined in the same place,

one could see a lamp, covered by a bushel, lying numb.

By chance flames burst forth beneath powerful blasts,

devastating the neighboring houses; now the victorious fire held everything.

All hope vanished; the thatched roofs, consumed, crackled;

the fire raged, and now the great flame was borne

toward the bishop’s lodging, driven by the west winds.

The crowd flew about, and, lifting the Father in friendly hands,

prayed with united vows that he might escape the danger.

The bishop refused, and, having rebuked the uproar,

reproached the faithless, himself allowing no argument

to move him;

so great was the steadfastness of faith in the holy man.

It soon became clear that the people trembled with fear,

and that human efforts to resist the flame had suffered

a shameful defeat.

For, after consuming whatever the crowd tried to protect,

anything the sick bishop had defended

escaped the raging vapors, merit fighting on his side.

And although, after conquering spaces on either side,

the destructive flame spread its savage fury,

it was afraid to touch the roof of the little hut

in which the Father remained enclosed and which he preserved from the grim fire.

Immense joy seized the hearts of the people,

and they rejoiced still more that they had been defeated

by the heavenly power.

### 97

Neither numbers can contain, nor words convey,

what the bishop, weakened by illness, accomplished in that lodging.

Night and day a crowd of wretched people kept watch

before the doors of the man who lay there;

some, with weakened spirits, sought support,

others, with failing bodies, sought strength.

When no remedy was able to enter his illness,

one night a figure resembling a beautiful divine presence

was seen before the man, breathing something heavenly

both from its face and from its garment.

It extended its right hand and ordered him to stand upright,

and raised the wavering man to his feet.

Having received strength, he hurried along,

while the shadows yielded, unaware of sparing his swift steps.

### 98

Fame tells that the Saxons, with the Picts as accomplices

in their known crimes, had once raged more grievously against the innocent Britons.

For savagery feeds entirely upon quarrels

and, through an innate fury, drives everything into fierce rage;

then the seeds of an ancient dispute had kindled fires

of rigid warfare on both sides.

Now the two peoples, their forces joined,

prepared to clash with one another, setting up camps on either side,

and from a distance were testing preliminary maneuvers

for the certain battle, with varying success.

Germanus had not yet lifted his foot

from the friendly region, although, impatient of the prepared sea,

he was already urging his return.

A violent fear had struck the trembling Britons,

because their modest forces and military resources

were far inferior to those of the enemy.

A happy decision, instilled into their uncertain minds

by a heavenly sign, prevailed:

in their desperate circumstances they should seek the support

of the great Father. This seemed to the fearful their one salvation.

He promised protection and did not delay the prayers of his people;

he approached the camp, and his faithful colleague followed.

Those whose blood had grown rigid in their breasts

took up immense courage and immense hearts.

The unbroken line brought joy to its leaders under heaven,

as though it were a great army, trusting in the merits of the two men.

### 99

It was the time always venerable to the whole world,

when the people, having labored for forty days,

grow rich through emaciation [B.: “waste away”] and, intent only upon heavenly things,

sigh for holy Easter with purified hearts.

The presence of the Fathers added the service of splendor

to the holy days [B.: “festivals”];

and the better part of the people, instructed in the sacred word,

entered the white baptismal waters.

With the troops drawn up in battle order, in the name of the Paschal feast,

the church was woven like a city, filled with interlaced branches;

the open fields breathed immense praises.

The soldier emerged wet from the beautiful baptism,

with faith as his cuirass, hope as his most faithful sword,

and mutual love of the brothers as his strong shield.

All other use of weapons was despised,

for the merits of the bishops caused the weapons of the world to yield.

The unfamiliar camp was revealed to the suspicious enemy.

A great hope of victory arose: the unarmed men were mocked,

and, once they had joined hands, nothing seemed likely

except that they would soon become booty.

All that remained was for the fiercest enemy

to rush upon the unwary, invade them, tear them apart,

and crush them all while they hesitated.

The day had been appointed for the slaughter

that had been too confidently anticipated;

but the tricks did not remain hidden, and the detected fraud became evident.

Now the day had arrived, marked out by Paschal celebrations,

not by funerals, as the enemy had already presumed.

When the sacred rites were completed,

the soldier, radiant with the splendor of the washing,

rushed to arms, prepared by his vows for heroic deeds,

and prepared to stand against the enemy,

resolved at last to yield only to death.

The bishop, judge of this battle, properly arranging

the troops whose position was uncertain,

placed himself in the midst; and, raising his right hand to the stars,

he said:

“With me as your leader, the whole battle will be conducted.

As standard-bearer, I shall undertake the beginning of the appointed fight.”

### 100

When he had spoken these words, he advanced a long way into the army

and selected companions from the entire number.

After examining the places where the enemy might burst in,

he saw a valley lying beneath mountains and stretching downward.

Here the army, radiant in its splendid armor, was stationed.

On that day the Britons joyfully saw something

that had never happened before: a battle arranged

under the command of a great leader, the bishop.

It was a new event; but, insofar as it was unknown

through the long ages, it was all the more worthy

of eternal records.

Now the fierce enemy approached, trusting in its forces,

trusting in its hiding places—although everything lay exposed

and had been sufficiently investigated by careful labor.

Then the Father issued an order to all the companies:

whatever song he first uttered in measured voice,

let the entire army answer with raised voices,

secure from booty and finally secure from slaughter.

The enemy was present; the bishop, mindful of the agreed hour,

drew forth a mighty voice from his full breast,

pressing the holy “Alleluia” through three repetitions.

The cry of everyone followed, raised to heaven;

the mountains, receiving it more closely, tripled the sound.

### 101

The wretched enemy was thrown down, its courage failing,

and feared not only that the vast cliffs would collapse upon it,

but even the vaulted heavens above.

What remained, and what alone they thought left for salvation,

they entrusted to their feet—their lives’ trembling means of exchange.

But swift feet were not enough for this task;

and although wings seemed to clap for the fugitives,

they considered everything sluggish, and the fugitives had no wings.

They threw away their weapons far off,

rejoicing merely to have withdrawn their bodies from death.

We learn that the river swept away many who were spent;

for each thought it a light thing to meet death,

provided that he might escape unharmed

from the hard hands of those pursuing him.

Vengeance, driven by heavenly winds, raged,

and offered no respite to the terrified.

The victorious army stood and increased the deed

with a new song, composing hymns to Christ, their avenger.

Then, under fortunate divine power, it rested among the spoils,

attributing and carrying everything to powerful God,

claiming nothing for itself.

The bishops applauded the splendor of so great a triumph:

the happy victory, achieved under new auspices

and with no bloodshed, rejoiced over the defeated enemies.

## CHAPTER II  
The return from Britain; the journey to Arles made illustrious by miracles

### 102

When matters had been settled, constant concern for his own flock,

always eager, urged him to return as quickly as possible.

The sea invited them, ready under Christ’s direction;

his mind approved, conscious that his merits were not fruitless;

the martyr Alban accompanied the travelers with prayers,

until they should reach their desired friendly homes.

Gaul rejoiced as the Fathers returned;

the grace of the desired light arose for the churches,

while a harsh torture of pain arose against the demons.

When Germanus was at last brought to the familiar city,

his people surrounded the shepherd with a twofold affection.

The crowd rushed to meet him, showing grief through mourning

and joy through applause; such great throngs poured forward

in mingled expressions of both feelings, but joy gave way to tears.

Fortune had pressed a beam-nail upon the wretched,

[Note: A *clavus trabalis* (“beam-nail”) was believed in antiquity to have been used for punishment and torture. Hence Horace, *Odes* I.35: “Cruel Necessity always goes before you, carrying beam-nails and wedges in her bronze hand,” etc.]

while the kindly Father was absent;

yet he learned the causes in due order:

the citizens, long oppressed beneath the censor’s weight,

had been ground down more harshly by extraordinary taxes.

He groaned over their suffering and opened the entrails of compassion.

He searched for some means by which he could lift the wretched

from their calamity; and with great sweat

he had vowed his head to every kind of labor without restraint.

Concern pressed upon the man, and he no longer delayed his assistance.

Still weary from the sea, he attempted the roads again;

he entered the route along which stretching Gaul

opens a long journey; carrying Christ in his holy breast,

he advanced, content with modest expenditure in all things.

### 103

The bishop was crossing open countryside at a measured pace,

and evening was hiding the day in the waters,

for the whole sky had been overwhelmed by rainy cold.

Exhausted by leanness, exhausted by filth, behold,

a certain man of perverse heart joined himself as a companion,

bare right down to his feet. Compassion moved everyone.

A robber, disguised as a poor man, joined them at their lodging,

and laid his limbs down among the innocent servants.

Sleep pressed upon the latter; the savage meditation of fraud pressed upon him.

Knowing that the time was favorable for crime,

he rose and, through wicked deception,

led away from the stables the animal assigned

to the use of the holy old man.

[Variant: “horse.”]

When daylight returned, the loss of the familiar vehicle was discovered;

but the author of the theft had already withdrawn.

And so that the priest would not lack transportation,

a cleric accustomed to perform service for the holy man

was changed from horseman into pedestrian; thus necessity required.

And while they hastened on their journey, drenched in clear … [The supplied source breaks off here.]
serene
The man’s clear face shone with sober composure;

but upon his brow he restrained the stirrings of an unusually joyful spirit. His companions saw it, and all were astonished; one of them, bolder and somewhat more outspoken, asked what great cause there was for such a joyful countenance.

104. At this he said, “Wait a little, companions; before your eyes that wretched man will soon be exposed—both laughable and pitiable in his unhappy plight—whom presently the conscience of his shameful deed will torment.”

He spoke; and, turning their gaze to one side, they saw from afar a foot-soldier dragging behind him, with downcast face, an animal seized by its halter and by his hand. While he hastened on, and they lingered only briefly, he soon overtook them and prostrated himself at their feet. In due order he confessed each part of the crime he had committed, and that he was so entangled in the entire affair of that night (B., “bound”) that he could not possibly turn aside by any means, unless he at once vowed to return the captured four-footed animal.

Then the holy man grieved, and, soothing him with gentle speech, said:

“See, if I had perhaps given you what you lacked, you would have had no impulse to commit the crime. Now take what you need; return what is ours.”

Thus the guilty man carried back, together with the gift, the peace that had been granted him.

105. Eager for solitude, a man filled with holy power, no more skilled at avoiding outsiders’ favors than [B., “and”] the frequent consolations of his own attendants, had vowed to seek solitude and to maintain a lasting hiding-place, living a life exempt from publicity for as long as it lasted.

But the promise of great Jesus remains unshaken: a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden from sight. The glory that conceals you when you withdraw amid your noble merits reveals you, while grace illuminates you with outstanding signs. Wherever he easily carried his step along roads, in cities and villages alike, the mixed crowd would hasten to meet him, stirred by his illustrious deeds, and, although his labor was long, would endure it confidently and with ease.

106. Nor would I rightly refuse to entrust you also, Alesia, fatal to Caesar’s camps, to my reeds; you who, because you nourish your own inhabitants with exceptionally rich bread, are thought once to have been designated by that addition to your name [Note: [Col. 1178D] On Alesia see Valesius, *Notitia Galliarum*, where, following Diodorus Siculus, he derives its etymology from ἀπὸ τῆς ἄλης, “from wandering,” or from Hercules’ error. See also Julius Caesar, *The Gallic War*, Book VII, near the end.].

Caesar once attacked you, guarding the borders of the Haedui and their outermost approaches, in savage conflict, and nearly brought the Latin phalanxes to defeat in an unequal battle, having learned what Gaul could accomplish with native weapons. Now only traces of the ancient camp remain.

There a presbyter of distinguished birth had arisen, still more distinguished in intelligence; at that time he bore the native name Senator. His wife, equal to him in life and merit, matched the resolve of her chaste husband in devotion. Both advanced in years, both blessed with success.

107. The bishop praised here was joined to them by the bond of holy affection. When he happened to visit them, they welcomed him with as much honor as their means allowed.

There the matron devised a pious deception beneath the bishop: she placed straw beneath him, on which, unaware, he lay down, accustomed otherwise to rest upon the earth’s surface. When the sun, with a new breath, drove away the chill from the earth, he resumed his journey. The household rejoiced, and the attendants rejoiced that they had been illumined by the solace of the renowned Father.

The matron gathered the remains from the bed and, carefully arranged, hid them away for medical purposes [Note: [Col. 1178D] That is, for medicinal purposes. Manuscript note.].

Several days later, a certain man, splendid beneath the lamp of his birth and proud of his great dominion over worldly affairs, was inflated by a demon. No aid was available, and because Germanus was absent, all hope had failed.

The matron presumed upon her faith; she called upon Christ and wrapped the wretched man’s body in the straw that had been preserved. By reason of the absent man’s merit, the difficult matter yielded to her prayer.

At night the wretched man, as though surrounded by a great fire, burned and groaned, repeating the name of Germanus; at last he was snatched from the jaws of the savage lion, and thereafter remained safe, having rendered his gift.

108. The Arar, hiding itself beneath the walls of the Rhône, carried him toward the citadels of Lugdunum. The Gauls maintain that Lugdunum received its name long ago because it is “the luminous hill” [Note: [Col. 1179D] See the refutation of this in the same Valesius, in the passage concerning Lugdunum of the Segusiavi.].

The populace embraces him with eager devotion. Every age rushes forth; both sexes come together. They are pleased not merely to touch him, but frequently even to look upon him. A blessing full of salvation proceeds for all; then, with a gracious word, he revives every heart. Although he is hurrying onward, he certainly refreshes their thirsty hearts with as much living doctrine as suffices.

109. Although for a long time delay had stood in the way of their earnest prayers, at last the city of Arelas is borne with wondrous eagerness to meet Germanus, its crowds pouring forth from every quarter. They say that it derived its name in an uncertain age from the name of its first founder [Note: [Col. 1179D] Valesius also rejects this explanation in the same passage, where he discusses Arelate.].

At that time Hilary was there, renowned from that place to the stars; he discharged the office of bishop in word and deed. Fiery in faith, pouring forth heavenly speech, he devoted himself tirelessly to blessed commands (B., “untiringly to honorable [commands]”).

He received Germanus as though he were the likeness of an apostle from a glorious age, and honored the saint with humble devotion: as a father in affection, as a teacher in the splendor of his merit.

Auxiliaris also restrained the fierce people in the name of the prefect. For him, the bishop’s arrival shone with great joy in answer to his twofold prayer: he had long burned with love for the man and desired to see him, while a fever had for a long time been tormenting his wife.

110. As he entered, the prince hurried to meet him with a long procession. He welcomed him, delighted him, refreshed him, revered him, and adored him. Then he surveyed his whole body with an easy glance: a face worthy of the man, a breast filled with divine power, gravity in speech, illustrious splendor in his countenance, a reputation surpassed by his merits, and the excellence of a great heart.

Thereupon he poured out gifts from his richest treasures and asked that the bishop deign to extend his hand over them. After this he humbly added his wife’s illness to his prayers.

The bishop consented in faith and did not delay the reward. He entered, and manifest healing accompanied him as he went. As he entered, he drove the disease from the sick body; trembling and fever were dispelled in the same instant.

Thus the happy matron received the relief she had desired.

Afterward, setting out in order the reasons for his arrival, and having won over the governor, he enjoyed the fulfillment of his just and moderate wishes [Note: [Col. 1180D] That is, just and moderate. Manuscript note.]. He brought back the standards of peace to oppressed citizens; although the highest salvation for the whole city was restored, it was restored solely through the presence of the great shepherd.

## CHAPTER III. A revelation made to the holy man concerning the birthday of Saint Julian the martyr; a new expedition into Britain; a visit to Saint Genovefa; and a fortunate return.

[Col. 1180A]

Unaware that he was about to enter a rest free from toil, the bishop, once departing toward the regions of the Arverni, turned his steps toward the village of Brioude.

Here, martyr Julian, although you suffered thousands of punishments in a savage age for the sake of the supreme Name, antiquity, which has always opposed the good without impunity, everywhere diminished the monuments of your lofty triumph. And although, a martyr renowned by your famous name, you were already being carried from the setting sun toward the rising sun, you had in this respect been somewhat more obscure than you yourself deserved: the people, having forgotten the day that must always be honored, did not grant you fixed solemn rites according to the celebrated custom.

Germanus, on his arrival, did not allow the error to grow old through long ages. First, with friendly speech, he asked at what time they celebrated the sacred feast of the saint. The unlearned populace admitted that they did not know.

111. Then the Father said:

“Let that be sought from the highest dwelling, which the human mind cannot determine.

Night fell, and the assembly dispersed; each person withdrew to his own home. The bishop spent the night in the sacred building. When the golden dawn, shining with rosy hair, had scarcely reddened the sky with its morning chariot, the bishop appeared and of his own accord asked whether God had revealed the cause to anyone. They declared that they had no knowledge of the matter.

Then the priest spoke these words:

‘Know first that, in the seventh month of the year, this feast shines upon the world four days earlier [Note: [Col. 1180D] That is, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September]. These are the saint’s birthday rites; he was made a martyr on these fortunate Kalends and, having shed his blood, was admitted to the heavenly camps. This matter has been made known to me by heavenly instructions.’”

He spoke, and immense joy flooded the people. From that time onward the martyr’s festival has been celebrated wherever Gaul extends broadly in every direction.

112. Again you stir up wars; again you breathe fires. Will you, a more wicked beast rising with its neck severed [B., “a more wicked one, with its neck cut off”], not be ashamed to kindle weapons once more against the wretched Britons, weapons lately struck down in a strong duel?

Spare yourself—now spare yourself, I beg you. The more often you raise your black, poisonous head, the more certainly you will be cast down [B., “you will have your throat cut”], and your repeated schemes will bring swift ruin. What is once madness, when repeated, becomes more dreadful in its madness; and wounds reopened twice bring greater pain.

The bishop had scarcely laid down his arms, weary from immense exertion, and returned to his own city, when messages were brought, forced from the prayers of all the pious, reporting that the plague of insane doctrine had again fallen upon the wretched Britons and that no hope of salvation remained unless he defended, in his customary manner, the cause once obtained through noble struggle.

There remained a sure hope of victory if he would move his hands on behalf of the wretched; nor would glory go forth first to its own sails if the final hand were not laid upon the undertaking infected by evil [Note: [Col. 1181D] That is, if the final touch were not placed upon the matter begun. Manuscript note, C. Lugd.].

At these words he rouses his anger; impatient of delay, he immediately calls for his arms—his arms swiftly—and clothes his limbs in his familiar armor.

He had vowed, for the sake of faith, to expose his breast to whatever death chance might bring. He went through the world with peace-bearing steps, carrying holy seeds and revealing, through noble doctrine, what and how great rewards are prepared in heaven for those who follow Christ, and what punishments await the rejected after death [B., “remain for the rejected”].

113. And you also, illustrious Lutetia, again famous by your ancient name, enshrine your renown in my song. For me, mention of you is always welcome, because now the Bride of my Lord, once most renowned for her signs [Note: [Col. 1182D] Namely, Saint Genovefa.], adorns you with her bones.

When the bishop Germanus entered you at that time, he was received with wondrous affection. His blessing, offered with humility, warmed the people; everything resounded with immense applause.

Mindful of the matter he had entrusted to her, he soon asked in friendly concern what circumstances were affecting Genovefa. I believe that many dangers had touched her heart, which she had endured during that period, as piety commonly succumbs to harsh accusations.

It was equally possible to detect the poison of a black mind, when the envious populace did not suppress the seeds of furious flame once they had been conceived, even in the presence of the holy man; yet she is better known to him than to her own parent.

114. Thereupon he withdrew into the hidden recesses of the maiden’s cell, surrounded by the people. Soon the maiden came forth to meet him. The great Father greeted her with immense reverence, so that one might rightly have thought her to be a temple of the divine power.

Then, looking upon the people and commanding silence with his right hand, he renewed, under the maiden’s auspices, the praises he had begun:

“In her blessed childhood she dedicated her sacred body to Christ, never to be violated throughout the ages in any way; and she bears witness that she too has always remained in virginal chastity, although separated in bodily seclusion.”

“And so, to establish your minds in certainty, learn the proofs of this matter through true signs.”

He spoke, and the virgin pointed with her finger to the earth stained by a stream of tears where she had bent her limbs in prayer. From that moment the fury was driven away and soothed the raging people; you would have seen them all repent of what they had begun.

By common agreement all declared her innocent; united in praise, they all confessed her innocence. The true assertion composed the raging disturbances and drove the contagions of black gall from their minds.

Afterward the renowned Genovefa obtained throughout the Parisian region the praises due to her merit and victory.

115. Every detail of your deeds, most illustrious virgin, had been the object of my devotion to entrust to my reeds; but great undertakings involving many volumes recall the poet to his task. Yet, so that I may not pour forth these verses without just repayment, remember your suppliant and protect your faithful servant with your prayers.

Whatever gifts you know have accrued to your Bridegroom, consider that, by a shared lot, they have accrued to you. And now farewell, united with God, and remember the world.

116. From there they board the sea. Everything cooperates with their prayers; the vessel arranges its course in obedience to them; you would see the storms hostile to the waves give way. Living strength overcame the blows of the winds.

And you, savage one, were far away; the demon did not dare to be present, for you had not yet forgotten what you had suffered in the sea itself. Yet although your mind was envious, and you grieved eternally that peoples should emerge from the throat of the ancient dragon, the most holy virtue compelled you, unwilling, to proclaim to the peoples the bishop’s arrival.

He had not yet reached land, but the whole island was already resounding with Germanus. By chance Helaphius, the ruler of the place, hurried to meet him, so certain is it to trust the prophet.

Helaphius had brought with him his son, condemned from his earliest years by a bent knee and suffering the wasting of a withered leg. The whole province followed him, together with a throng of priests and an unknowing crowd.

Blessing went forth to everyone in due order as they bowed down; from it doctrine flowed in speech and watered them all. He recognized that the people were still steadfast in the faith and discovered that only a few were the authors of the crime. They were sought out, and a judgment of punishment struck the guilty.

117. Helaphius himself broke through the dense crowds, displaying his son, deformed by his crippled body.

No words were needed; many things pleaded their cause: the boy’s age, his weakness, and above all his father’s tears.

A just compassion drew immense grief from the hearts of all. The bishop, deeply moved, as usual turned to the heavenly protections. Then he ordered the young man to sit. Soon, instructed by the art of healing, he extended his learned hand to help him, touching the dry sinews with a gentle caress.

Immediately, as though health-giving medicine were flowing from his fingers, swift healing followed. The dry joints absorbed the returning sap; the sinews returned to their former state, and the forbidden limbs recovered their bent movement. The gifts of healing shone before the eyes of many (C. Lugd. and B., “of the Creator”).

The father received his son safe and sound after so long a time, and the son received his applauding father amid joy.

Thus, Christ, your praises grow fragrant in wondrous ways, and they instill invincible strength in hearts that embrace the faith.

Thereupon the holy man addressed the whole people concerning their fall and the efforts by which a fall might be repaired.

A secure faith, founded upon immovable pillars, held its ground; all fought for the covenant of faith. A very few pupils of the exposed fraud remained. They were brought before the assembly [B. omits “before the assembly”]; the same judgment remained fixed for all: to punish them with perpetual exile.

Thus the fortunate island, freed then from the Tartarean plague, still now shines with the pure splendor of the distinguished faith.

When peace had been established in those places, Germanus, richly adorned with splendid spoils, returned to the city under a favorable omen, deservedly most pleasing to the heavenly stars.

118. And you, to whom it was granted to penetrate the Britons, separated from the whole world, twice, and twice to see the innermost monsters of the great sea, at last turn your sails here after laying them down. As a sailor saved, pay your vows upon the shore, and, in whatever way you can, remember to cultivate your talent. Prepare yourself for the future, since the outcome of events is uncertain, so that, if some labor should arise, you may be equal to it.

## PREFACE TO THE FIFTH BOOK, completed in a distichic, two-strophe metre (Δικώλῳ διστρόφῳ).

[Col. 1183]

Rich Hecatopolis once brought forth Daedalus, skilled in many arts and highly renowned [Note: [Col. 1183C] Ἑκατόπολις means “the island of a hundred cities,” namely Crete. Manuscript note.]. Once, fleeing the palace of Minos, he joined wings with wax, believing that the empty air could safely be traversed on swift feathers.

Reckless lightness took his son as companion in an ill-omened bond: winged Icarus came to his father’s side, compelled to imitate his father.

Then people first saw two four-footed monsters of the sky flying.

The tireless father flew toward the frozen Bears, safe from the hostile cold; at last he stood above the Chalcidian heights and first touched those lands. There he dedicated a noble temple to you, Phoebus, and shed his weary wings.

His son, less perfect in Daedalian arts and heedless of danger, entered the lofty region of fire more than was right (B., Greek: “of the fiery region … of the climate”). Soon, when his wings dissolved, Icarus gave his name to the sea that lay before him, overwhelmed by savage waves.

119. These monsters seek you; this tale applies to you, unwary poet.

You are now too swift an Icarus for Daedalus, leaving the lowest regions of the earth behind, while your subject matter draws you too forcefully to stretch your wings toward heaven.

And if you were carried away into a sweet-singing bird, and feathers streamed melodiously from your fingers and shoulders as you flew, then, as through the liquid ether you joined well-varied limmata—“half-tones” [Note: [Col. 1184C] That is, semitones. Manuscript note.]; B., *lemmata*, “headings”—with musical measures, living plumage would adorn you.

Ah, let not reckless games overpower you while you attempt lofty things.

Ah, let not the fierce lightning bolts, rushing headlong into the inner regions, drive you down into Tartarus, since it is forbidden to pursue things excessively lofty or to rise beyond one’s strength.

You alone, Christ, can heal me in these matters and elude these weapons; and to you, who had the power to make such things come to be [B., “to be completed”], I would not deny the power to grant a fitting advantage to a chaste poem. Nor does hope ever go astray.

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER I. The miraculous defense of the Armoricans, and a new expedition undertaken for them into Italy; miracles performed along the journey as far as the Alps.

[Col. 1183C]

120. Scarcely had he been permitted to return, weary from the sea, to the shores of his native land when a deputation, advancing in an extended line with outstretched hands, came directly to meet him, having long awaited the holy man’s return to his homeland.

The people formerly called Armorican by their ancient name are enclosed between two rivers [Note: [Col. 1183D] The Seine and the Loire. Manuscript note.]. They are grim, fierce, windy, forward, heedless, rebellious, changeable, and unlike themselves in their love of novelty; lavish of words, though not lavish of deeds. It is considered respectable among them to say more and do less.

It had often been proved that they never preserved the tenor of loyalty toward their kings. Therefore, when the commonwealth was then flourishing under a ruler with its ancient titles, its great salvation, whose name was Aetius, utterly weary of the proud customs and crimes of the people, at last allowed them to be ravaged by the stern Alans.

Their king was Eochar, a beast more savage than any other. Why should I recount the slaughter and the tyrant’s frenzied deeds? He had experienced them widely throughout every region of the world.

Therefore, the license to slaughter that they desired was granted, and it goaded the savage people’s throats toward death. The barbarian mind hungered for throats, intending to test what its ferocity could accomplish. The wicked man led on the savage army, burning to fall upon the desired prey as soon as possible.

121. A dreadful expectation struck the wretched people, together with impatient fear and an immense horror of their situation. Nor did a simple terror press upon their hearts: the thought arose that they could neither meet the enemy in battle, nor defend their borders, nor even attempt flight.

Each person imagined for himself the dangers of various kinds of death, and the mere delay of the suspected death tortured them.

One means of salvation remained for the wretched: if the bishop would deign to oppose himself to the swords.

This was the sum of the envoys’ appeal:

“What will you do now also, holy man? What will you do? If you try to withdraw yourself, you know what it is to close the bowels of a captured brother. But if you wish to help, how many things terrify one who wishes to do so?

“The savage king, the unknown madness of a dreadful people, their language and customs, and the insolence of their grim faces; and, besides, the fact that your frail strength, exhausted by the burden of continual labor, may abandon you as you undertake great things.”

Trust in God. Brotherly affection will carry off the victory. He who gave the will will grant the power; although the matter is difficult, he will soon yield to just prayers through a favorable divine influence.

122. Therefore he undertakes the journey. The faithless people were already present, having crossed their own borders; armored cavalry filled the open face of the land. The barbarian king stood in the midst of the dark army, dreadful in his savage armor, gaping with hope of the slaughter he desired.

Then, trusting in the Lord as his guide, Germanus broke into the midst of the enemy and fearlessly thrust himself before the armed leader—wondrous to say!—and, through an interpreter, first pleaded with him and poured forth prayers on every side.

The king, like some wild beast untrained to endure hands (B., “as a certain beast”), recoiled from the man who was praying. The bishop rebuked the struggles of his savage heart. Nevertheless, the king refused.

At last, determined to persevere in his undertaking, the bishop laid hold of him and seized the reins of his bridle.

All were struck with immense astonishment. The armies were fixed in the same place, and no force could move from its position or turn its steps in any direction. Such a radiance of heavenly light poured upon the bishop that he was like Moses, whose horned face reflected the Lord from his countenance. The splendor of his brow terrified the savage ranks; they did not dare to resist or to advance against him.

123. The savage king was ordered to lay aside his untamed spirit and instead marveled; the miracles, being beyond understanding, terrified him.

What steadfastness could make the holy man so great-hearted? How great was the old man’s virtue, how great the reverence of his countenance, that one man should stand as superior or stronger than thousands?

At once the warlike ardor was laid aside for peace. Human affairs yielded to God; the violent condition of fury, once the wars had been abandoned, dealt with civil matters—how the matter should be settled, as the priest rightly decreed, not as the raging ardor had prescribed.

After the love of slaughter and the force of fury had been restrained, they composed their minds. Then, joining right hands in a strong covenant, they undertook the duties of secure peace.

Afterward they returned to their camps. Thus, deservedly, the Armorican people laid aside their fearful anxiety through the good bishop. In this manner they finally emerged from the throat of savage beasts, provided that the Roman emperor should furnish a pledge for the peace obtained by treaty.

124. It is easy enough to declare where these things are tending.

These things concern you again, Father; certainly such things concern you. The starry Olympus has long been calling for you, and long ago it begrudged you to the wretched fields more sharply.

Yet it is not permitted for those born of earth to leave the camps until you yourself, turning your step toward the Latin lands, make the heavenly harvest grow golden here also.

Perhaps this too is the judgment recorded in the heavenly books: that, when the end of great labors has been completed, you should seize in Italy a splendid prize—a crown sought through merits and won through virtue, a diadem distinguished and gleaming with beautiful beryls.

O Father! O man who has passed through the great dangers of the sea! Yet very many things still remain for you to undergo on earth. Wherever fortune carries you, go more boldly.

Although you have often endured more grievous dangers, fortunate steadfastness will at some time bring these to an end.

125. Nor was there delay—for what delays could one burning with heavenly fires have? Having departed from his native land, he turned his swift steps toward the Alpine citadels.

As he journeyed on again, Germanus, in the devotion of their former friendship, sought out Senator, dear for his merits and piety, intending to repay with grateful interest the gift of hospitality.

Suddenly a girl appeared before his eyes, incapable of every kind of speech. For twice ten years the misfortune of her age had worn away in silence.

The bishop received her when she was brought close to him, with wondrous dignity. Then, with a friendly hand, he passed over her face, caressing her mouth, forehead, and entire countenance with oil. Afterward he mixed three morsels of bread with wine, placed one in the astonished virgin’s mouth, and commanded her to pronounce a blessing over the bread she had received.

She, obedient to the priest in every detail, declared with full voice what the bishop had ordered.

Thus speech, arising through a new ritual and flowing forth, endured thereafter through the remaining years of her life.

126. As he was about to depart, he embraced his like-minded friend more closely than was his custom. Amid the embraces, soothing him with the gentlest speech, he said:

“Farewell forever, dearest brother, inseparable portion of my mind throughout the ages.

“May the Almighty grant that, when the final end of all things has come and He is required to set the final boundary, we may look upon one another with joyful, shadowed faces” [Note: [Col. 1185D] Perhaps: “that we may not look upon one another with joyful, shadowed faces.”].

“For until this burden of flesh is dissolved [B., “For indeed until this burden of flesh is dissolved”], it is henceforth forbidden for us to meet one another’s gaze.”

The Father uttered these words at their final parting and, as he departed, left his friend with this farewell.

Let anyone who wishes say that the saint was unaware of the time of his own death when he left his city [Note: [Col. 1187D] The meaning is: Let whoever wishes now say that, when the saint departed from Auxerre for Italy, the time of his blessed death had not been revealed to him; for this farewell itself plainly proves the contrary.].

He continued his journey with a few attendants, as was customary. But a crowd gathered in organized groups to surround him wherever he went. To these the Father poured out the seeds of the eternal Word.

It is especially pleasing to remember this because, if he had once passed through any place either praying or teaching, those places remain today renowned for their sacred chapels, or a venerable sign of the cross raised there shines forth.

127. Afterward, as he traversed the borders of the Haeduan district, he was received, as usual, with gentle services and the utmost devotion and favor. Swarms of people burned with eagerness; every age was present; both sexes came together.

It is neither possible nor appropriate to entrust to a fragile pen how great was the ardor in the minds of all for the holy man, with what affection and devotion they honored him, whom they knew to be the supreme friend of the supreme Divinity.

128. Once, after wandering through the whole circuit of the city, while, fervent with devotion, he was going around the sacred buildings, he came to the place where the venerable body of Cassian, once a bishop, lay in an honored tomb. In him the signs of heavenly virtue shone forth, bearing witness to the famous triumph of an outstanding soldier.

The marble was Parian, beautiful in wondrous whiteness; the enclosure of the sacred tomb was closed with it.

But from heaven a different appearance of red color impressed upon the varied marble a life-giving sign, so that a new form of the cross, marked out by heavenly hands, showed that Cassian, even after death, lived through the merits of his renown.

Father Germanus, seeing this with fixed eyes, pondered long and deeply how generous Christ is toward his servants throughout the ages.

129. Soon, after pouring forth prayers, he said:

“What are you doing now, most illustrious one? What are you doing now, brother?”

A man’s voice was heard answering from the very bottom of the tomb:

“Placed in a blessed dwelling, I have been granted a better portion of the desired light, in the tranquil gift of which I await Christ’s coming with the Father’s divine power.”

“Therefore,” said the bishop, “rest for a long time, most welcome brother, in the august dwelling assigned to you by lot. And, when the saving trumpet that restores the dead fills your ears one day with heavenly harmonies, pray more earnestly for us and for this people.”

O sublime merit of the man whom the grace of supreme Christ has raised so far to the summit of virtue, to whom all things are subject and to whose prayers all things respond.

Even though they lie asleep in the deepest tombs, do they not yield?

Nor is it surprising if one citizen was able to recognize another: one reigning with Christ and handling earthly matters in the world could recognize one dwelling in harbour while cutting through sea and storm.

“Give me a little time; a brief hour will remove whatever, up to now, separates innocent friends.”

130. Meanwhile, the parents approached before him, trembling with tears, and laid their limbs upon the ground.

A marriageable girl followed them with lowered face, suffering from an affliction congenital and well known to her. Her mother’s womb had brought her forth with her fingers bent back into her palm, their sinews withered.

The passing of time had increased the cruel pain. Her nails had grown excessively long in their hard progression and pierced the tender flesh within. As many fingers as the hand possessed, so many dreadful wounds it contained. The sores had already pierced the palm, unless their sharp points had been checked upon reaching the bones.

The bishop touched her right hand with healing medicine. Raising each finger with gentle control and pouring the gift of vital sap into the sinews, he restored the flexible hand to its use in wondrous order.

The girl, overjoyed, was restored to the use of her hands; the festal fulfillment of her wishes could no longer contain her.

The saint’s compassion added something memorable: he corrected the hand and removed whatever was excessive, cutting back the nails that had grown beyond all measure. He did not consider it beneath his holy hands to accomplish this.

## CHAPTER II. Continuation of the same journey and of the miracles performed through Italy.

131. Having traversed the fields of Gaul accompanied by signs, he then rose, made more exalted by his merits, toward the lofty Alps.

This boundary separates the Ausonian lands from Gaul; it lies numb beneath eternal snows and eternal cold. It had never before been passable for humankind, until Hannibal, returning victorious from the Spanish coast, split the rocks and broke through the mountain with vinegar [Note: [Col. 1188D] For Hannibal’s expedition into Italy during the Second Punic War, see Livy, Book XXI; or Silius Italicus, Book III; or also Cluverius, *Ancient Italy* I.1, chapter 33.].

Yet the Carthaginian, struck by unfamiliar cold, grew numb and left the king bereft of a soldier. Hannibal himself, worn down by the loss of one eye, felt the Alpine snow drive away the Carthaginians’ warmth, while the Moorish beast bore its one-eyed leader [Note: [Col. 1188D] That is, an elephant.].

Here the bishop Germanus obtained the honor he deserved and won the monument and glory of a famous triumph.

132. The sun was already staining its robes red in the ocean. The laborers, having received the wage owed for their day’s work, were returning together to their homes as night approached.

The Father, pressing his way along the trackless slopes with a determined step, was making his way along the route they had taken. The wretched burden-bearers, oppressed by heavy loads, were climbing the mountain with groans.

A torrent stood in their way, rushing down the steep heights and twisting its enormous fury in a violent current through roaring masses of water. It delayed the travelers, since the swollen stream could not safely receive their footsteps.

One man was exhausted by old age and, finally, by illness; a double burden weighed upon the wretched man. Scarcely able to carry his trembling limbs on unsteady feet, he groaned anxiously beneath the heavy load placed upon him.

The bishop, as usual showing compassion toward the lame and the old, lifted the wretched man’s burden into his own arms and carried it across the torrent. Then, after crossing the river again, he took upon his neck the man who was filthy and finally exhausted in his trembling body, raised him through the middle of the waters, and set him safely down on the farther bank.

133. Between the things I have said and the things I must say, I, the poet, am carried along. These recall me; those summon me; both are owed their due.

Remain here with me, wherever I depart. Many things will strike the stunned mind. Everything is marvelous; everything emerges in new forms. Yet reason has not fixed itself upon any single appearance. The heart is weighed down more heavily beneath the burden of events; each detail drives it on with carefully weighed words.

“Germanus carried the wretched man across the waters on his neck.”

Germanus carried the wretched man. Thus the very person tires you: illustrious and second to no one in the splendor of his lineage, he deigns to lift the wretched man upon his noble shoulders—something that even the least of our age would not do.

Seek his rank: the bishop is known throughout the whole world. Show me one who would prefer to humble himself so greatly as a bishop.

Do you ask his age? He was an elder, full of days; you would not truthfully say that he had forgotten his own years.

Do you continue to ask how great his health and strength were? He was squalid, dried up by a perpetual covenant of fasting; emaciation had wasted his entrails and pallor his face. After seven days, harsh barley cakes restored him.

The earth’s surface bore the exhausted man’s pause. Scarcely able to bear his limbs, scarcely able to bear himself, scarcely clinging to his bones, he conceived an immense flame of compassion in his breast. Not broken by the weight, not wholly averse to danger, himself exhausted and worn out by age, he first set down the burden and then carried the old man in his trembling arms.

You are reckoned great in the heavenly Olympus by merit, bishop joined to God, to whom it was granted to sacrifice so many offerings of the pious to the King of heaven.

134. As he proceeded farther, he was carried into a renowned city which antiquity is said to have called Mediolanum.

Tradition spreads the story—although not every tradition is to be believed—that Gaul, once blazing with internal wars, expelled its own settlers from their native homes by violent warfare. Compelled by circumstances to move into Latium, they built this city by pooling their contributions.

They called it Mediolanum, from what had occurred, saying that, when they first laid the foundations of the new walls, a half-woolly sow was reportedly discovered there [Note: [Col. 1189D] Concerning this origin of the name Mediolanum, consult Leander Albertus, in his discussion of this city in Transpadane Lombardy, near the middle.].

When the bishop came there, he avoided the empty air, striving, as usual, to veil himself in hidden places. Yet he did not remain concealed: immediately the whole city clearly learned who and how great he was.

135. On that occasion a solemn day had perhaps brought together several bishops, and sacred honors were being performed at the altar of the divine mysteries by which the followers of Christ are strengthened.

The bishop Germanus entered the peaceful church unknown and humble, clothed in the covering of an insignificant garment.

Immediately a certain man, whom the enemy had bound in demonic bondage, filled the empty air with cries:

“Why do you drive us beneath the Italian skies, Germanus? What do you think we wretched beings have deserved from you?

“Alas for the cruelty! Alas for the merciless violence of circumstances! There is no place for us in the sea; we are excluded even from the lands themselves. Recently driven from the shores of Gaul, the Ocean offered us a hiding-place amid the vastness of the sea. From there too, Germanus, you have driven us away by your prayers.

“Why do you penetrate everything? Why do you traverse the remote places of the world? Stop, and allow the rest we desire to those who are weary.”

Their minds were stunned. Trembling seized their bloodless limbs at these words. Everywhere people began asking who Germanus was, the man whom the voice they had heard addressed.

136. At last he was recognized by the likeness of his splendid face; all his other features indicated the dress of an ordinary man.

When questioned, he did not deny his rank, nor did he deny who he was. The assembly of bishops bowed before the holy man.

They all urged him, joining prayers and common vows, to visit the bearer of his name [Note: [Col. 1189D] That is, the demoniac who revealed his identity.]. The bishop, considering it necessary to obey the holy men for the moment, entered the secluded retreat, accompanied by the wretched man.

There was little delay before their prayers were fulfilled. He came forth, restoring to the people the man cleansed of the foul plague, sound again through his splendid power.

This was the first sign by which the Father became known in the Italian lands. Soon people came together from various regions and thronged the widely publicized
A gift of aid. Then, with signs joined to doctrine [Note: “With signs joined to doctrine,” that is, with miracles added to teaching],

Thus he relieved souls from reproaches, and bodies from affliction.

**137.** Thereafter the bishop, departing from the many-streamed city,

Was advancing on his journey with auspicious words:

[Col. 1190C] A needy band came to meet him and asked for alms,

Trained and able to live on another’s morsel.

The bishop asked his minister about the funds [Note: *Pro de ratione*, “instead of *de ratione*,” that is, “about the account.”].

The man, conscious that he had three coins remaining,

Replied that he had no more funds for everyone.

At once he ordered him to distribute everything to the needy poor.

“From where,” said the deacon, “do you think we shall live today,

Holy Father?” “It is not lawful to distrust Christ,” he said;

“But he will feed his own poor—let us fear nothing now.

Only remember to care for the helpless as far as you can.”

The cautious minister, though not rightly cautious about the future,

Gives two, and keeps one for the next day.

Not merely profit but loss, prudent man, how great a loss

You have built up on this occasion, despising the Master’s commands;

[Col. 1190D] Gaining little, you have deserved to lose much.

Thus swift vengeance followed; thus it mocked the greedy wish.

**138.** While they were preparing the journey, with rapid ardor hastening on,

Behold, men are seen coming on horseback behind them.

They dismount after a short while; thrown down in the dust before the holy man’s feet,

They then break into these words:

“Not far from here we have a lord of distinguished rank,

Of renowned fortune and exalted jurisdiction,

Whom domestic loss oppresses with savage bonds.

With his servants and his entire household—miserable to say—

[Col. 1191A] He lies ill, finally given over to countless diseases;

So surely he is ill, so is he himself, and so are his people.

Groaning beneath his calamity, he seeks as quickly as possible

To break off his wretched life and bring his hated sufferings to an end.

But after he learned that you were traveling through our regions,

Hope of recovery has returned to his uncertain heart.

Now we bring you his tears and prayers:

If your compassion can deem him worthy of this,

Visit the sick man; he asks it with bowed breast.

Or, if serious matters violently consume our prayers [B., “cut short”],

And it is not possible for you to abandon the journey once begun,

May a healing blessing joined to just prayers

Make up for the pleasure of a countenance denied;

[Col. 1191B] Let him be granted one, if he does not deserve both.”

**139.** Then the Father, marveling at the venerable pledge of faith,

Was moved to pity, and the image of compassion tightened his heart.

Although concern for the labor he had undertaken urged him

Not to delay a day, the straighter road seemed to be

The one by which the reward owed to just labor is preserved.

Without delay he turns aside. His companions oppose him;

The envoys, straining with all their strength, insist against him.

While these contend, and those contend [Note: Supply “contend”],

A long dispute arises.

He favors the needy more, saying that through the ages

Nothing was more important to him than to fulfill Christ’s commands,

And that he was ready to die twice over for the Lord’s precepts.

O Father worthy of the highest summit of splendor!

O man who refuses to expend his own life for himself,

Living wholly for God—indeed, for whom to live is Christ—

[Col. 1191C] Who prefers to place his soul at risk for his brothers’ gain!

Therefore, Father, remember to persist in the pious undertaking you have begun.

Believe me, the holy labor will not lack its prize.

**140.** A fitting joy takes possession of the happy envoys.

Because the bishop deigned to yield to their prayers,

They bring out two hundred solidi as an arranged gift [Note: *Soldos* for *solidos*, which were gold coins],

And give them to the man.

The bishop is glad not so much at the gift

As at the pledge of faith; he entrusts everything to the minister:

“Take these now,” he says, “and learn to suffer loss;”

For, when you were devising fraud against the poor wretches,

You preferred to be grasping. For if you had yielded

What I ordered you to give, Christ, in his customary generosity,

Would have returned to you three hundred solidi today as interest.”

Terror seizes the man: he realizes that the hidden secrets of his guilt

[Col. 1192A] Have been disclosed to Germanus.

“Do not regard this as astonishing, good man,” he says,

“That the Prophet’s closed chambers of the heart should gape open.

Filled with the power of the holy Spirit,

He is already God and already receives divine honors.”

**141.** So that delay might not burden those in need of aid,

He hastens, and with rapid step, as their prayers require,

Arrives ready to provide what was promised, accompanied by the same envoys.

Soon, as though manifest salvation had entered among them,

The long-awaited presence of the Father lifts everyone’s spirits.

Here you would have seen the familiar arts of the Physician displayed:

On one side compassion shines, on the other perfect skill.

He throws himself down and, as usual, prostrate, adores Christ;

Then seeking higher things all the more, as he became more bowed toward the earth.

From here a healing prayer poured forth to the heavenly ears;

Tears made a path for it as it flew above the stars,

[Col. 1192B] Tears whose streams purchased the joy of many.

He visits the masters, and finally visits the servants;

With equally ardent care he searches through every bedchamber;

To all alike he imparts heavenly remedies by right.

The matter was completed within the space of one day;

One day poured out the remedies of salvation for everyone.

After this he departs; the master of the house himself accompanies him as he leaves.

All rejoice, their strength restored;

Applause resounds everywhere, and the melody of beautiful praise.

Everything cries out “Christ”; everything echoes “Germanus.”

Thus glory to the Lord increases, and thus opinion of his servant,

As he scattered a delightful fragrance wherever he went.

An inborn ardor compels everyone’s hearts

To know the man, radiant with the marvelous light of his merits.

Many things contributed to producing his renowned name:

[Col. 1192C] Doctrine, labor, courtesy, character, steadfastness, ardor;

And, above all, the greatest love for his brothers,

By which he bore whatever was burdensome, on land and sea.

**142.** Why, I ask, are you hastening your steps through byways?

Why do you bend the shortcuts into a winding course?

You could have gone by a short route; instead you weary yourself along the long road.

The royal road certainly leads more directly to Ravenna.

I would not without reason say that you are seeking detours:

Indeed, so my mind seems to bear it, so at last it appears to me—

I believe that Ravenna portends something rather gloomy,

Something that may result either in destruction or in loss,

Since you dread approaching so close to its walls.

Whatever it is, pause for a little while, and, having recovered your breath,

Whatever remains for you to undergo, you will meet it with resolute courage.

**PREFACE OF BOOK SIX, varied in a two-membered, two-stanza form.**

[Col. 1191]

[Col. 1191D] **143.** The most beautiful *hexad* closes the expenses of the work [Note: *Hexad* (ἑξάς), that is, the number six, into which the author divides his books. He calls it “most beautiful” because it is considered the most perfect, as will soon be shown. [Col. 1192D] But why is *hexad* here treated as masculine? I answer: because it signifies a number, in accordance with the following:

“Sometimes the poet regards a general noun.”],

As you see, friendly reader.

If you ask for its causes and mystical symbols,

[Col. 1192D] I shall diligently set them forth.

The Creator, intending to make the solid sphere of the world,

Set this before himself:

For he distinguished all his work by the same number,

As the sacred page reports.

Although true theology sings that everything was created

Together and at once,

Yet the perfection of a number marks a perfect work,

A perfection suited to its several parts.

If you examine this number through the theorems of the first cardinal [Note: The first range of numbers extends from one to ten. The manuscript notes say that the meaning is: if you consider this number six attentively, you will find that it stands out among the first ten],

It shines forth as excellent.

For alone it confines itself within its own sphere,

Knowing how to keep within measure.

It neither diminishes the whole nor wishes to transcend the whole,

But is complete in its parts [Note: Both verses amount to the same thing, and mean that this perfection is proper to the number six: all its aliquot parts taken together neither diminish nor increase its total. For it has only three aliquot parts: the sixth, which is one; the third, which is two; and the half, which is three. If you join them—1, 2, and 3—they make six. This is not so with other numbers. For example, eight has as aliquot parts the eighth (that is, 1), the quarter (2), and the half (4). If you join these, they do not make eight, but only seven.].

One is its sixth; two its third; three its half;

Together they restore six.

**144.** Do you want me to relate something else, reader,

Something you will marvel at even more?

[Col. 1193B] Come here and hear it.

When its parts are drawn into a sequence and then mixed together again,

This number constructs a *decad* (δεκάς) [Note: *Decad* is used for *δεκάδα*, that is, the number ten].

The sixth part is the *monad* (μονάς), the first step of the number;

It enters first.

For the third is the *dyad* (δυάς) [Note: *Dyad*, that is, the binary number, which is the third part of six],

And occupies the second place;

It is the source of evenness.

The half, the *triad* (τριάς) [Note: *Triad*, the ternary number, the half of six],

Follows it in the third order;

From this flows oddness.

When the sixth joins the half, the monad joins the triad;

From these flows the nourishing *tetrad* (τετράς) [Note: That is, the sixth part of six, which is one, joined to the half, which is the number three, produces four, or the quaternary number, called in Greek *tetrad* (τετράς). It seems to be called “nourishing” because it contains the four elements, from which all bodies are constituted and nourished.].

When the third joins the half, it unites the dyad with the triad;

From these arises the *pentad* (πεντάς) [Note: *Pentad*, that is, the quinary number, arises from the third part of six (the dyad) and the half of six (the triad); for 2 and 3 make 5].

The parts, arranged in every possible order and poured back together,

Restore the *hexad* (ἕξα) [Note: For 1, 2, and 3 make 6].

[Col. 1194A] When the sixth with the whole produces the useful *heptad* (ἑπτάς) [Note: That is, 1 and 6 make the number seven, or *heptad* (ἑπτάς), “useful” because it is effective in many ways],

They call it sterile [Note: Because, among the numbers within ten, seven alone neither generates nor is generated. The manuscript notes say this],

But the third with the whole creates the *octad* (ὀκτάς) [Note: For 2 and 6 make 8, or an *octad* (ὀκτάς)]. From this flows hope,

To live after the ashes [Note: *Elpis* (ἐλπίς), “to live after the ashes,” that is, the hope of resurrection. For, according to Bongus, in the divine Scriptures the number eight signifies the New Testament, the resurrection of bodies, and the majesty of God’s kingdom. He explains and demonstrates this in his work entitled *The Book of the Mystical Meaning of Numbers*. There the reader curious about such matters will find much learned material collected, with a special significance assigned to each number.].

The whole with the half numerically produces *nine* (ἐννέα);

It triples the triad.

When the monad is added to these, the end of all numbers

Advances into the *decad*.

Thus the reward of the work will be followed by a lasting recompense,

Which the *decad* (δεκάς) represents [Note: As the same Bongus shows in his discussion of the number ten, beyond the midpoint.].

This remains as true as the sun that stands above all things;

Nor does the reasoning falter.

Do I seem to you, reader, to have drawn out too little

From the symbols of six?

If you can, produce another number renowned by a similar principle;

[Col. 1194B] Let that one also take its place.

But if you cannot, learn that the perfect triumphs

Belong to my bishop,

Whom the number holds enclosed—a number you may rightly now

Call the συνεργός (“co-worker”) of God [Note: A clever conclusion indeed: I recount the triumphs of Saint Germanus in six books; yet the number six is perfect, and therefore his triumphs too are perfect. But this must be forgiven the poet, who is playing.].

**145.** What remains of the labor you will complete more successfully through prayer,

And with little effort.

O merciful Trinity, source also of our trinity,
