For everything is subject to three:

They speak of essence, power, and operation—

Οὐσίαν, δύναμιν, ἐνέργειαν;

Without these there is no nature (φύσις) [Note: That is, essence, power, and operation, without which there is no *physis*, or nature. In every rational and intellectual nature, these three are considered to remain inseparably, perpetually, and incorruptibly. An example is given. There is no rational or intellectual nature that does not know that it exists, even though it may not know what it is. When, therefore, I say, “I understand that I exist,” do I not signify three inseparable things in this single word “I understand”? For I demonstrate both that I exist, that I have the power to understand, and that I understand that I exist: I would not understand if I did not exist, nor would I understand if I lacked the power of understanding; nor is that power silent within me, but it bursts forth into the activity of understanding. Thus read the manuscript notes, Codex of Lyon.].

There is also a trinity bordering upon our soul,

By which it becomes the image of God:

This is called mind, reason, and thought—

Νοῦς, λόγος, and also διάνοια [Note: That is, mind, reason, and thought or deliberation. The manuscript notes of the Lyon codex add: “By these three the essential trinity of the soul, constituted in the image of God, subsists.” Moreover, how greatly the Fathers labored, and how diverse were the paths they took, to discover and explain that image and likeness of God which certainly exists in the human being, the interpreters of sacred Scripture teach in their treatment of Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” If you wish, consult our Benedictus Pererius, *Commentary on Genesis*, vol. I, book IV, almost at the beginning.].

You too attribute this to it.

[Col. 1195A] Come, then, and grant us to reach the desired goals,

Highest God, O Trinity.

[Col. 1196A] Yet, lest weariness enter the exhausted mind,

With you as our guide we advance.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1195]

## CHAPTER ONE  
**The arrival of Saint Germanus at the royal city of Ravenna is welcomed by the emperor and all the others; the abundance of his miracles there**

[Col. 1195A]

**146.** The advance report, rushing ahead, had stirred the Latin world,

Announcing that Germanus, recently departed from his native shores,

Was hastening by a definite route to Ravenna.

The people spread the report, confirmed by many voices.

In cities and villages, at crossroads and through the streets,

[Col. 1195B] Men and women, infants and old people alike,

Young men, and whatever divides the young from the old—

All shook the air with powerful voices.

Everything was in turmoil; everything pressed forward with prayers.

Rich and poor alike resounded everywhere with the cry

That Germanus was coming.

Such was the love for the holy man, such the urgency among the people,

To see the bishop and report a sure recovery.

Although, in view of the labor already undertaken [B. “and already”],

He was plainly impatient and pressed on with his journey,

Yet the greatest ardor could scarcely endure the obstacles,

The bonds and delays, rebuking his sluggish steps

With a biting heart.

Thus delay is always said to increase thirst through desire;

But if desires, once deferred, subside,

Then surely they were not desires [B. “this supplies”], they were not what they claimed to be.

[Col. 1195C] At last you are received, bishop most welcome to the world,

Long awaited, although perhaps not in the manner desired [Note: Because he preferred to enter unknown. The manuscript notes say this],

As he sought, in his customary way, the silence of night.

Yet it was not possible for him there to avoid the watchful guards,

Nor did the stratagem devised for eager watchers deceive them,

So that they did not see him and enjoy seeing him.

Peter, distinguished by the rank and title of chief of the Church

[Note: Namely, Peter Chrysologus],

Was then preserving the apostolic flock in the city.

He was a man conspicuous for the splendid distinction of his ancestral lineage,

And radiant with much moral excellence.

**147.** At that time Valentinian, still a young man with his mother,

Held the Romulan scepter and guided the reins of affairs,

Great in imperial power and great in deeds and name [Note: This might have been omitted, at least if it is to be understood as referring to the whole period of his reign.].

[Col. 1195D] Placidia, the boy’s mother, distinguished by devotion to the Catholic faith,

Had formed him from tender infancy,

Worthy one day of his lineage and his father’s scepters.

Although he surpassed everyone in the order of authority

(For he was father of his country and ruler of the great world),

Such love of religion filled his heart

That, together with his pious mother, he offered full honor

And the proper service to Christ’s servants established in different places.

[Col. 1196A] Thus he adorned his father’s scepter of glory,

Already a sober lover of virtue [B. “holy virtue”].

They received Germanus as he entered the walls of the great city,

With the piety with which it was fitting to treat so great a Father.

You would have seen the order of affairs reversed:

While he fled from pomp, the pursuing pomp of the crowd

Pressed upon him in eager rivalry.

At the emperor’s command all the nobles came to meet him;

The common people hurried together;

[Col. 1196B] Then the sacred clergy of the church rushed forward in a dense procession.

Some applauded him with praises, others leapt about amid applause,

And all greeted the common glory with equal devotion.

**148.** A very great ardor had filled the imperial hearts

To heap services upon the man.

The queen, most careful in household affairs, prepared a large vessel

With royal foods, but without any admixture of meat,

And sent it to the bishop.

After receiving such a gift,

He divided all the delicacies among his own servants.

He kept the silver, intending to break it up for the miserable poor.

Then he visibly repaid gift with gift:

A wooden vessel, filled with cheap and modest bread,

Which the bishop had brought forth for his frugal uses,

Was sent to the empress.

She reverently received the gift and, as though she were receiving heavenly things, stored it away;

Happy at the gift given, but happier still at the gift received.

How precious the gift flowing from the bishop had been

Soon became clear: she ordered the wooden vessel to be enclosed in gold,

And the bread to be preserved with various remedies.

O deed certainly worthy of the eternal annals!

O grace that bends exalted minds

And subdues the necks of worldly pride to Christ!

O queen, honoring the divine power in the bishop!

O bishop, to whom Roman power now offers itself!

It will not be long before the heavenly chariot,

Following him more swiftly to the stars,

Carries him to heaven with its countless hosts.

**149.** One day, by chance, while the people crowded around him,

He entered a street, calmly surveying everything as he walked,

And came to a place where the public prisons

Had condemned a crowd of guilty men to wretched darkness.

These men, with their feet fastened in deeply sunken wood,

Were uncertain whether they should hope or fear more

To end the day amid punishments;

All other hope lay numb.

“Do not tremble, men, and do not surrender yourselves to death.

All hope has not been taken away.

The salvation thought impossible will bring the desired relief,

Removing your calamity.”

When the prisoners learned that the priest was passing by,

[Col. 1197A] They all raised their voices together toward the stars.

As the people explained the causes of their grief, he understood them.

He was moved to compassion and readily tightened his tender heart.

With gentle kindness he summoned the harsh keepers of the prison.

They withdrew from the holy man’s sight,

Those whom they could not release by any means—

Men whom the officials of the palace had condemned

To be plunged into dreadful death.

Where can you turn now, compassion?

I fear that you will not be able to persist in what you have begun;

Or, if your mind is determined to persist,

That, after making the attempt, you may suffer an undignified refusal.

Look: savagery recoils from prayers and scorns the one who prays.

It is better to test divine favor;

To ask majesty for what human beings deny.

Thus once you used to overcome all other things;

Thus you should overcome them now.

[Col. 1197B] **150.** The bishop turns his steps toward the punishment-house.

He throws his body upon the ground and, bowed down, prays to the Godhead.

Nor was the man’s compassion frustrated:

Suddenly the grace became manifest with which Christ had filled his beloved fosterling.

At once the prison was shaken from its deepest foundations,

It came undone, and the rigid doorposts yielded their bonds.

The iron gate, its massive locks loosened, stood open.

It was marvelous to see the hard fetters grow weak

And the threefold chains renounce their use.

Necks were relieved and lifted from their heavy burden—

Necks, hands, feet, and every part of the wretched bodies

That savage force had bound with rigid iron.

Compassion released what black rage had fettered.

O faith, always powerful,

To which everything that nature denies is subject,

Which the Omnipotent forbids by fixed laws to occur,

Whenever it compels what, by nature’s testimony, is proved unusual to happen!

The crowd of wretched men rushed out, freed from their chains,

Squalid, sluggish, filthy, miserable, bristling, and withered,

Carrying before them the now-light burden of the empty fetters,

Fetters with which savagery had previously bound their entangled limbs.

At last, after so long a time, the prison is left harmless,

And opens to those who enter a hall free from death.

With the triumph of peace going before him,

Germanus brings the returning company into the bosom of the Church

Through his wondrous compassion.

The Church applauds, leaping with a new song.

**151.** The fame of the great Father, furnished with blessed merits,

Was advancing without limit.

The glory of his signs likewise, its bright companion,

Was stirring peoples to the holy doctrines

[Col. 1197D] From every place where his lofty virtue had long been known.

Although eloquence were now available to me,

Such as poets usually utter from their hundred-tongued throats,

And with just as many languages demand,

I could not touch, in modest words,

Upon each miracle the Father performed in the lands of Ausonia,

While God magnified the gifts of his beloved endowment.

Who did not draw from him the sought-for remedy

For body or for soul?

Who did not find his prayers favorably received when he asked?

Who did not feel himself heaped with a generous gift?

The foolish recognized a teacher in him;

The poor recognized a father;

The least recognized one who humbled himself to them;

The greatest recognized one worthy of reverence.

And, as Paul teaches, becoming all things to all people,

He strove to pour divine benefits into everyone.

[Col. 1198A] **152.** Yet, lest this life, not inferior to angelic radiance,

Should be without witnesses, it is said that six bishops

Of distinguished merit and name remained with the holy man

For an uninterrupted period,

Whether he was displaying miracles to the world

Or subduing his body and limbs with crosses.

These men remained witnesses of his works for many days.

**153.** Although we have come this far with difficult steps,

Now, as I try to extend my progress farther,

The novelty of the subject presses upon me;

Then, exhausted by its weight,

I cannot go on, yet I am ashamed to lay down my burden.

If only, as events continually grow beneath heaven,

You would grant the words to grow as well,

You who gave birth to words!

I would choose to die beneath the burden

Rather than withdraw from what I have begun.

But what am I doing?

Am I to let my former labor perish?

After nearly reaching the shore of the sea,

Am I, because of one rock obstructing my way

And the trembling fear it inspires,

To turn back my sails and allow myself to succumb to guilt?

[Col. 1198B] Father, I beg you, rise to meet these mighty prayers,

And pour back into the chambers of my heart the hopes

That have been scattered far away.

You who once were able to restore the vital soul

To limbs dead beneath a muddy mass,

Give me at least these signs of your favor,

If only you grant me to pass correctly through what I remember.

## CHAPTER TWO  
**There he raises a dead man; frees a possessed man; foretells his own death**

**154.** There was a certain Volusianus, a man of very distinguished name,

A patrician of the city, beloved by the entire city,

And, according to ancient custom, a minister from the imperial offices.

He had a son greatly loved in his earliest years,

Already nurturing the hope of a posterity to be proclaimed.

Yet the boy, struck by the lash of an excessive fever,

Wasted away in misery.

A raging disease burned within his bones,

And had already ravaged his fluid marrow.

Feverish cold and heat, pestilential, insane,

Miserable, and immoderate, scorched the wretched boy in turn.

He had grown utterly weary of food, utterly weary even of drink,

And an iron sleep continued to drive him toward death.

The physicians now gave up; hope of recovery was removed.

Only the parents’ lamentations struck the terrified attendants,

As they prepared to close his jaundiced eyes in everlasting death.

But, friends, you brought your prayers to the holy man almost too late.

Swift death, which knows how to spare no one, forestalled you.

Nevertheless he hurries on, accompanied by a company of the devout.

Meanwhile a messenger frightens those who are traveling,

Saying that the bishop would wear himself out for nothing,

Since the boy, ordered to yield to his final fate,

Had already scattered the last breath of life into the thin air.

**155.** Then everyone, by common prayers, compels him

To persist in his pious duty; and he did not delay.

They find rigid limbs, their fibers withered,

And a chest already congealed by the chill of death.

As is both the custom and the saving care of Christians,

They commend to the King, for whom all things live,

The soul that had fallen by violent fate after completing its appointed duties.

Then they prepare to return.

A tremendous mourning rises,

And the mixed wailing of the people strikes the stars,

[Col. 1199A] Filling the house with dreadful cries.

The bishops press kisses upon the holy man’s hands.

They pray that he may have pity on the grieving parents

And call the dead man back from the deepest abyss by his prayers.

For a long time he resisted, out of holy modesty,

Confessing that virtue ought not rashly to be sought,

Nor ought one to risk whatever one may be able to do.

At last, taught to yield to the commands of faith,

He consents.

Then he girds his mind with beautiful weapons,

Which he knew belonged to the warfare above.

With these the hero brandishes his arms and orders the crowd to withdraw.

He then lies prostrate upon the ground [Note: That is, on the earth],

All the nearer to the stars.

He fills the earth with tears, shakes Olympus with groaning,

And prays to Christ with tears, prays to Christ with lamentation.

**156.** The Omnipotent heard him and did not delay the faithful man’s prayers.

He ordered the soul, drawn out from the lowest caverns,

To return and, by whatever power it could, to reweave what had been unwoven.

At once the limbs grow warm, their joints beginning to move,

And little by little recover their former [B. “vigorous”] proper senses [B. “proper places”].

With blood restored, living warmth revisits the bones.

The eyes that sleep had oppressed now breathe forth light.

The fingers already sparkle; the tongue seeks to move.

All the limbs perform the motions of life.

Nor does the bishop lift the body from the dust

Until, exerting himself close beside him, each rises together with the other—

The boy and the bishop:

The latter from tears, the former from death.

Germanus raises the young man snatched from cruel death

And, once raised, carries him before the rejoicing crowd.

Newly come from death, with his breath restored,

He breathes, sits, is revived, looks around, and shudders;

He is astonished to find that he himself still survives.

Soon, after strength has returned,

His body emerges into solid vigor, braced by its own power.

The joyful appearance of the event deceived bitter mourning,

And the joys received made the day a festival,

With loud voices.

The power of God, magnified, touches the stars.

Thus, Christ, thus you will soon heap upon your servant,

Who will be with you in the future,

A rich harvest of praises.

Highest glory to you, victor over bitter death,

Who command the depths of hell to yield to your chosen servants.

**157.** At that time the royal prince’s chamberlain,

And, as it happened, reputed keeper of the treasury,

Was Accolius, a eunuch famous for his distinguished name.

This nobleman was tormented by the loss of his fosterling,

Already a young man and already skilled in every art you might desire.

[Col. 1199D] A dreadful frenzy had crept into the wretched man,

Breathed into him by a demon.

The demon, harmful through its own plague,

Dashed captive minds against a foul peril,

When the moon gathers back its falling fires each month.

At the queen’s request, as she pitied such a condition,

He was offered to the holy man, to be healed at last from his long affliction.

He receives him, but postponed his cleansing until that day,

Although it was customary to drive such pestilences from a body

Only after a great fast had been imposed.

For the blind enemy had penetrated so deeply into the wretched man,

And had settled so far into his innermost and fluid marrow,

That he seemed to have been a fixed house,

Or a special vessel assigned to malign uses,

Held captive by fate.

The Father ordered him to shut this man in with him until nightfall.

Soon, as though the demon were driven by bitter tortures,

It bursts forth from the blind hiding places through the power of words.

It declares that it had seized him in his tender years

And says that he belonged to its jurisdiction, if the Father would consent to yield him,

For it was certain that he had served it for so many days.

The Father could not endure this.

He ordered it to depart far away,

And not to attempt anything further after this display of divine majesty.

It fled and breathed its feeble pulses into the thin air.

The young man, cleansed, was restored to the applauding palace.

**158.** He had indeed come at the request of the Armoricans,

To arrange a pardon for the crime of the wicked [Note: *Scaevae* for *malae* and *perversae*, “bad” and “perverse”] nation.

The matter yielded to the prayers; soon the emperor consented.

Everything depended upon the will of the blessed Father [Note: *Constarunt* for *constiterunt*, “stood” or “was established”].

[Col. 1200B] And that would certainly have been the strongest guarantee of peace.

But the nation, reviving the contagions of its former deceit,

Plotting its customary pestilential war,

Dared to arm the Roman axes against itself.

Thus the bishop’s intercession also proved fruitless,

And if imperial savagery had imposed any condition,

The conflagration fell upon the wretched people with a cruel fate.

**159.** While we move through the wondrous deeds of Germanus,

While it delights us to mark his distinguished labors with the pen,

And to comprehend what is countless within a number—

To say what would be a crime, as though he had performed

Such rare deeds that they could rightly submit to our words—

The better part of the events lies inert in dense darkness,

Certain to bring destruction upon the trembling poet.

[Col. 1200C] And you, reader, will one day complain,

Defrauded of a very great benefit and fruit,

With lamentation and tears,

If the Muse refuses to lay her hand upon the labor she began,

When this is the whole labor:

To run with a clear reed through the way in which Germanus,

Victorious, entered life through the threshold of death.

So be it.

Yet my prophetic mind shudders to enter into funeral measures.

O deed worthy to be kept silent!

It was pleasant to entrust the combat to the peaceful lyre.

Do you refuse to celebrate the victor with a radiant triumph?

Was he welcome as an exile, but not more welcome as a king?

If you fear to say that he died in a mortal body,

Then celebrate the immortal man with abundant praise.

Truly immortal, he truly lives through the ages.

[Col. 1200D] He lives and increases the splendor of the heavenly cohorts,

Joined to the Lord, finally conformed to Christ,

And—something still more astonishing—

United and made one with him,

Transfused into God as a human being,

Made *theosis* (θέωσις), deification.

**160.** The Light-bearer (Φωσφόρος) [Note: Lucifer],

Who had released lands submerged in shadow-wandering darkness

And knew how to restore the natural color to things,

And draw the fire-bearing stars from heaven,

Had risen.

Father Germanus, after completing the customary praise

That rouses the morning sleep with song,

Was exchanging words about religion with the blessed bishops,

A most renowned teacher with shining eloquence.

With ears open and senses gathered,

They all inscribed his joyful words upon receptive minds.

“Why, eloquent Father, do you linger over different matters?

Say what must be said, though it is sad—

Sad, threatening, plaintive, tearful, and portentous.”

At last he said:

“Brothers joined to Germanus by a beloved bond,

Receive these words and fix them deeply in your hearts.

We have lived, and have traversed the appointed boundaries of life.

Now, because a fixed sentence remains for our race,

And it is certain that everything created which flourishes

Will weaken and grow old,

The final things are now calling.

Christ is calling, I say; we must go.

The soul, thrust into its penal prison, wishes to be released.

Now, mindful of its origin, it rejects sluggish corruption

And willingly returns to the ether,

From which it drew its beginning.

Therefore I must be dissolved and go toward the light [B. “threshold”] of heaven.

[Col. 1201B] I entrust myself and my end to you.”

**161.** One night, when by chance I was taking peaceful sleep,

A face appeared to me, like that of a noble divine power,

Confessing itself to be God.

Neither voice nor words sounded human.

It was Christ; he is accustomed to visit his own in this form.

He extended his right hand toward me with a gentle gesture,

Smiled, and added these words with a radiant mouth:

“Dear one, as you are about to undertake a journey to foreign regions,

Receive the heavenly provisions already prepared,

The supplies for the road.”

Moved by such words,

I asked the reason for the journey and the reason for the labor.

“Do not fear,” he said.

“You are being recalled to your lofty homeland,

And heaven already, already claims an excellent citizen,

Where soon you will receive perpetual rest without end;

Where day runs without night, times without time,

And there are peace, rest, light, and everlasting glory.”

He spoke, and balanced himself upon the heavenly air.

Thus the Father was singing the final things of his approaching destiny.

The bishops interpreted the portents of another dream,

Unable to believe what they feared might happen.

Fear itself had taken away their faith.

But the breathless bishop, more eagerly intent on returning

To the bosom of his homeland,

Continued to entrust to everyone the cause of his final day,

Saying that he knew it well enough, that he knew himself thoroughly enough,

And knew what homeland the Ruler of the world promised to his servants.

## CHAPTER THREE  
**The saint’s illness; his death; his glory; his inheritance; his funeral and translation to Gaul**

[Col. 1201D]

**162.** Scarcely had a few suns passed, as the interval moved on,

When the swift fulfillment followed the prophet’s foretellings.

His most holy limbs are seized by an easy pain.

An inward flame attacks his delicate marrow.

Now his feet grow numb; now his soft legs tremble.

His eyes grow weak, dry in the dying body.

Everything fails; only his mind sees and grasps God.

**163.** But when the disease began to grow harsher with its advance,

The city trembled with fear and set heaven ablaze with mourning.

Alas, the fate once fashioned for earthly colonists!

We scarcely had time to see you.

Now, best of Fathers, are you leaving us?

Christ does not permit his beloved servant

To be tormented through the ages,

Or to remain apart from the kingdom he has partly entered.

His life was martyrdom.

He now invites him, exhausted by the mass of his labors,

After approximately thirty years,

Into the heavenly citadels of the ruler of all things.

**164.** Placidia, fortunate among the august women

Whom the world has ever produced,

Setting aside the pride of royal power,

Visits the sick man, restores him, embraces him, and surrounds him.

Taught to submit her rigid head to divine commands,

She offers and declares whatever his anxious mind seeks.

There is no delay in granting it, provided he does not fail to ask.

Soon the image of his homeland pierced the Father’s mind:

The homeland which he, its Pastor, had once left sorrowful when departing,

Because he had preferred to devote himself to the affairs of his brothers.

Unaware of events and ignorant of its future lot,

[Col. 1202B] It waited in helpless hope for the bishop’s return.

**165.** Why, people, why homeland, do you burden heavenly things with heavy prayers?

Why do you continue to nourish useless hopes?

The Fates are preparing something else,

And on this occasion the supreme Author of things

Does not favor willing people with his customary kindness.

He weighs what he provides, and what is better, more heavily.

The time has come for Germanus to receive his merited triumph without end,

As he climbs the Capitols of the clear heaven.

Nor does the shining procession allow itself to be confined or to dwell within narrow walls; rather, spread more widely through the Latian lands, it seeks to display spectacles to the fourfold world.

Others will look upon it; but you will possess the one who is looked upon. You will receive him in your bosom and shelter him beneath your tender foliage.

Your bishop has not forgotten his former love; and, though dead, he teaches how greatly he loved you while alive. He returns to you; when he has been restored to you, you will offer pious incense to the buried man.

This special service she undertook to request from the queen; never did she grant anything more readily to one who asked against her own inclination. She realized that what otherwise might never happen as he wished could not be refused to the man.

Thrice-blessed Father, thrice glorious, thrice venerable: after Christ, your flock and your people offer you every kind of song—your people to whom, at your return, you bring so many mercies of heart, so many joys of mind, such great hopes and such great benefits; with you all things are favorable, and without you none would be so, unless they were frivolous, blind, and adverse.

### 166

What shall I say of the peoples rushing from every region of Latium to the place where the physician lies? The same eagerness remains in all: to see him and to gather for worthy services to the Saint. And they do what each can, as his rank requires. Every hour is measured out in choirs singing psalms; praise resounds instead of tears, a hymn instead of mourning, inviting the heavenly hosts to the Father’s final rites.

### 167

Phoebus, in his swift chariot, had already breathed upon earthly things for the seventh time, returning brighter from the western waters. But the spirit, burning to emerge from its earthly bonds—*coicis* [Note: *Coicis*, that is, “earthly.” The manuscript notes say so; but it should be written *choicis*, from the Greek χοϊκός, “earthly.”]—leaps forth, and, set free, is borne into the liquid air, while heaven sings a joyful *alalagma* [Note: *Alalagma*, that is, “a hymn of victory.” The manuscript notes derive it from ἀλαλάζω, “I rejoice, I exult.”].

The heavenly companions surrounded him with wondrous splendor, carry the joyful victor beyond the fiery stars, and set him upon the throne of the supreme King for all ages.

### 168

He marvels at the lofty summits of the tranquil kingdom; he marvels at the certainly unknown light of Olympus. And now he sees clouds and stars beneath his feet; he looks down upon the shining radiance of the rosy sun; he looks down upon the dew-covered stars of the cold moon, and upon every star that pursues its wandering courses; upon the mass of the earth and the darkness spread around it; upon the spirits of the winds and the swelling of the storms.

He observes why spring is calm, why blazing summer appears; why autumn is laden with grapes, winter with hoarfrost; and whatever the structure of the threefold world revolves, and whatever physical causes are said to govern. Whatever things are active through numbers, measures, or weights; whatever things lie hidden, and whatever things lie open in the framework of reality—he contemplates the cause of all with pure light.

He sees everything beneath him, and Christ above everything.

He even laughs at the pageantry and summits of the age: dreadful kings, diadems, scepters, tyrants, and treasures acquired with the fervor of many crimes; garments mocked by a thin distinction of gold, and whatever worldly furnishings can alter.

Moreover, he laughs at the vain *κακοπάθεια* of the mind [Note: “Evil affections”], its joys and new hopes, its angers and dark fears, and the smoking torches that envy is accustomed to scatter.

He tramples these beneath his feet; as victor, at last he crushes them. Indeed, he subdues the poisons of the pestiferous dragon, crushes his head, and presses down his crests and hissing neck. He lies there, not daring to raise himself against him.

### 169

Meanwhile Christ himself crowns his head with a triple crown. The first blooms with thirtyfold jasper; the next, which rises beside it, is made sixtyfold [B: “made twice three times tenfold”]; the third, most beautiful, gleams with a hundredfold yield [Note: This alludes, as above, to the parable of the seed bearing fruit in good soil, Matthew 13].

O glory! O most noble inhabitant of the great heaven! Delight of the world, bishop, hail through the ages! Thrice and four times it is a joy—or a thousand times—to add: hail! Hail, and may you prosper; welcome, and supreme good health to you!

### 170

What remains is this: when a vigorous dispute arose among the parties, each eagerly demanded a portion of the bishop’s remains. Each longed for them, each struggled to seize them for himself. No sharper contention usually arises over the greatest riches: all desire to grow rich from a modest spoil, although it cannot be yielded to everyone.

The body is brought out into the midst, but the palace claims one part; the bishops, drawing lots, take another. The impatient queen takes the case containing the saint’s relics as a divine gift. Then Peter, the most holy bishop of the city, exults over the precious spoil and seizes the hair shirt; he himself seizes the sacred cowl. The other bishops contend to tear away the old man’s remaining garments: one anticipates the belt, another the cloak; two tear away the tunic, two the mantle.

These monuments, Father, you leave along the Italian shores. By the emperor’s decree you are to be carried back to the city that has honored you; Ravenna renders you these deserved honors.

### 171

With united devotion they hasten the expenses of the funeral, for such a great man deserved no small glory.

Accolius anointed the body with solid perfume. Queen Placidia raised it upon garments and a soft support, and carefully covered the sacred limbs. The emperor arranged the journey, companions, expenses, vehicles, and every provision and convenience for travel; he attended the chosen ministers with generous royal gifts [C, Lugd., and B: “with gifts from the summit”].

The bishops, whose chief concern was this, burned with care both to prepare the present service and to remain watchful for what would be needed later. Then, whatever the dignity of religion required, funeral provisions of every kind were furnished from every source.

Thus, in a splendid procession, they were brought to your shores, Gaul—rejoice, made glad by the return of your bishop.

### 172

Nor will I consider you deprived of divine gifts, Placentia, not unfruitful in Italian soil, to which the holy funeral soon deigned to proceed. When it had been placed at night within the church’s hidden recesses, while devout vigilance guarded it with hymn and light, a local matron happened to enter. A disease long called paralysis had weakened her wretched limbs.

It was already possible to see the miserable woman living with limbs as though dead, her nerves loosened and dissolved from their joints [*fluidum*; variant *fluidam*].

She asks to be placed beneath the holy bier as a suppliant. She is placed there; and, lying down for the whole length of the night, she draws in heavenly cures while Christ gives her strength.

Her body is drawn together into solidity; her nerves are restored to their former condition, and she rises to receive calm vigor, the disease put to sleep.

Day returns, and they resume the journey they had begun. The coffin is lifted, and the woman rises completely healed, having received healthy life through the gift of the dead man.

The people marvel to see her walking on her natural feet, though until then she had been entirely incapable of using them.

The other deeds accomplished throughout the regions then visited cannot be numbered or compressed into verse. Indeed, we are compelled to restrain the six books with a double triple knot [Note: By “a double triple cord” he means these six books], and to bring the course to its turning-posts. The things read will provide other tokens of a devoted mind.

### 173

Gaul, instructed by heavenly admonition and exercised by divine commands, hastens in procession toward the Pennine Alps, ready to receive her Father with a twofold devotion—he who is brought back from a nearby place and he who is brought back from a distant region.

Love presses the citizens forward; reverence certainly presses them forward. What they fear, they love; and what they love, that indeed they fear. Happy are they, if by an enduring wish they both fear and love what must be feared and must always be loved.

### 174

Every class of people runs to its several duties. Some level the roads by removing the obstacles; others make the banks passable by constructing bridges. These resound with psalms; those applaud with harmonies. Some carry the burden; many contribute expenses. Those who can are glad to relieve one another in turn. Those who cannot do this perform the only thing they can: they escort him with their eyes and follow him with eyes and voice.

Lights constructed with varied equipment obscure the shining flames of Phoebus’s lamp. If such a procession of worldly things is granted to perishable ashes, how great is the glory that marks the soul among the heavenly armies? How great in heaven, if it is so great on earth?

Through you, Redeemer, the death of your saints is always precious. With this splendor, Father, carried from the shores of Latium, you are returned in magnificent order to the beloved city, where a most holy tomb preserves your noble limbs.

But your enduring spirit, blooming through the ages by the lamp of its merits, lives on and raises the centuries with eternal signs.

## EPILOGUE

### The benefits conferred by God and Saint Germanus upon the author, the principal causes of this work

### 175

Now, Jesus, we consecrate to you the honors you deserve—you who, seated upon your Father’s throne, bend all things beneath you; Word, creating all things, uttered from the Father’s breast; King and beginning, peace and light from light; art and counsel, law and harmony of things; cause of causes, and fiery source of souls; the same beginning, the same middle, the same end.

You who never were not, and never endured not to be; you who always possess being, granting being to all; the pure and simple essence of existing things; infused through all their members, moving through the whole world, wholly present throughout the whole, with no single part enclosing you.

We worship you as the radiance of the Father, Christ, coeternal with the Father; after this, born from a Virgin by the coming of the Spirit, proceeding from the heavenly citadel by the decree of the Trinity, upon which all things depend.

Thus the Word becomes flesh—the Word that once made flesh—so that flesh in turn might become the wondrous Word.

Thus, with pure understanding, we confess you as *Σαρκάλογος* [Note: “Flesh-Word,” that is, “the Word [as] flesh,” according to the manuscript notes], the true offspring of God and the truest offspring of humanity; true man and God—here created, there Creator. Thus a twofold *φύσις*—“nature”—orders one person.

You, the loving champion of the human race through the ages, washed the world, drenched in blood, of its crime. Sent down to the Stygian shades as the restorer of life, so that at last, having recovered the spoils from the prostrate enemy, you might return in splendor as victor to the heavenly citadels—*οὐρανίαις* [Note: “Heavenly”]—where the many-eyed Seraphim receive you and, with melodious song, sing a manifold *δοξολογία* [printed *δωξολογία*; Note: for *δοξολογία*, “a hymn of praise”].

They spread six wings apiece with gentle applause, burning with the highest love of the supreme Deity.

Here, wielding your star-bearing scepter and dispensing all things, you distribute manifold gifts to your own servants.

One, allotted five talents, diligently employs his time in active works. Another, better instructed, compensates doctrine with deeds, proving that he has returned the two talents he received. There is one whose learning is followed only by an abundance of teaching; he will be reckoned a debtor of one talent.

Would that he not be cast back into dark shadows, and wash away with eternal grief the loss of his reward!

### 176

Nor, great King, would I rightly make myself deprived of your treasures. The charge of my own talent too rests upon me; for each person has the gain of his own recompense. Yet money buried in muddy caves condemns the idle servant both for theft and for fraud.

When the final day brings you back to the fields, and you establish equal distinctions among your servants, one will report his abundant thanks and the profits of his treasury, admitted to the heavenly dwellings and joys of the kingdom. The other will pay the deserved penalties for the business neglected [Note: That is, “transactions”], expelled from the beautiful walls of the peaceful court.

Reflecting on this in my mind and fearing such immense danger, I diligently considered how I might withdraw myself from so great a crime. After pondering many things, something drove me to this—though I do not know whether it was chance or God—to make Germanus, illustrious, resound through melodious songs; to test for the first time the vein of my talent in this venture; to make the first trial [B: “specimen”] of unattempted poetry.

Many things gave me courage: love and reverence for the Saint, abundant material, and above all the fact that my conscience warned me that I owed the man much—far too much.

When I was scarcely seven years old, my parents transferred me into the service of the Saint, helpless in understanding and defenseless in prudent judgment. He gently took up the tender pupil in pity; he fed me with bread, gave me coverings, and provided warmth. He strengthened me in body; then enlarged my understanding, granting my difficult and vigorous mind a rich capacity for learning. He drove away my illnesses; he overcame every danger. When I was absent, he helped me by his prayers; when present, by his power. He bestowed every good and restrained every evil.

Would he depart without praise in my songs?

### 177

As I turned these things over in my mind, many fears opposed me: the gravity of the subject, the dryness and poverty of my tongue, the appearance of the work, the lowly person of the poet, and the fact that the praise of God would be uttered by sinful lips without adornment.

Present confidence came to the trembling poet’s aid: you can strengthen the plectrum of an unsteady mouth, you who readily restore speech to the mute.

Relying upon powerful prayers, I compelled myself to undertake the work, thinking thus and worshiping you, Ruler of all things:

“If what I ask is yours, O God; if, by your gift, Germanus has enabled me to do this, then rightly grant gifts to the one who asks—gifts of a tongue whose gifts are yours. Grace has given me the will; may grace grant the ability.”

You heard me, and whatever I was able to do, you granted me the ability to do.

From this point onward, may your praise always grow upon my lips, King of kings, gracious Father of humanity, bright hope of your people. Your creation rejoices in you with its gathered clamors: the stars, the heavens, the clouds, and the whole mechanism of the skies; the sun and its sister [Note: That is, the moon]; snow and waters; every spirit; heat and frost; day and the thick clouds of night; dry lands; mountains and hills; the blue expanse of the sea; rivers and springs; then all living things; whatever the earth carries; whatever the lofty air bears onward; and whatever the sea’s swirling current carries for its varied uses.

### 178

Come, then, and descend upon the vows I offer. May what you have chosen to give please you to receive willingly; as once you blessed the widow with her smallest coin.

Forgive me, and break apart the bonds of my guilt; for I am oppressed by great fear of punishments.

Behold, my wretched life has now revolved through three decades; to these is added a second year, as my age continues to grow. I remember that I have never done anything good. Therefore anxieties goad me and bite into the innermost places of my mind.

Now raise me up, fallen as I am; now cleanse me of filth, Creator. Strip away my past, protect me in the present, and make me sufficiently guarded against future sins.

Grant that I may remember you, as it is necessary to remember you—before the golden band falls apart when its fastening is broken, before the silver cord pours out liquid streams, and before the cistern wears down the wheel and the flowing fountain the jar.

Then, whenever the frail substance of my life has departed from these limbs, and the material of ashes lies there after the death-cry, merciful Redeemer, spare me. Let no force of the Tartarean minister seize me, and let the savage flame of Gehenna not devour this soul.

And when the fourfold world has been consumed by its end, and you have come as judge in the divine power of your Father, and judgment sits with you among open books—alas, who will defend me then from the impending wrath?

I believe that then, Germanus, bishop, supported by an everlasting robe, I shall see you among the heavenly nobles.

Therefore, holy Father, then have mercy on your poet. When from afar you look upon me bound among stinking goats [B: “joined to” goats]—this is what the record of my crimes promises me—remember then to entreat the King with kindly prayers.

He will certainly be moved; and, once moved, he will say to his servant:

“Germanus asks; it is not right to reject one who pleads. Transfer this goat as soon as possible among the snow-white sheep. Let the lamb go to the right; let him be adorned with beautiful fleece.”

# Miracles of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre, by the same author, Hericus the Monk

Compared with a very old parchment manuscript from Lyon, together with other manuscripts and the edition of Labbe.

(In the Bollandists, July, volume VII.)

## Author’s Prologue

### 1

The Life and Miracles of the bishop Lord Germanus—whose apostolic memory must be named with the highest reverence—remained hidden for too long in silence, without any literary support, through lack of labor, or rather through irreverence. A careful consultation of antiquity, the teacher of events, bears witness to this.

For it is clear that, until the time of Saint Censurius, the fourth man to govern the Church of Auxerre after the most blessed Germanus, this undertaking had remained unattempted by everyone. As time passed, each younger generation was content with the simple reports of its elders, never imagining that these things could fade from memory. For ordinary uncultivated practice then considers itself to provide best for posterity when it allows all that is illustrious and greatest to flow down to later generations through mere oral narration.

This matter, no less irrational than improvident, at times caused harmful damage to the praises of the saints. For one rarely finds anyone who can establish confidence in unlearned rusticity, since the things it reports are judged partly fabulous, partly foolish and ridiculous, and therefore unworthy of the sanctuaries of letters. Thus some matters were completely forgotten, while others, flowing insincerely into the knowledge of later generations, obscured, with great disservice, the lofty memories of many great saints.

### 2

If, then, some curious investigator should perhaps regard what is reported in the *Acts* concerning so great a bishop as less reliable, less complete, and finally less supported by truth, because several intervals of time are said to have elapsed before these things were published, we correct him, after more careful examination, by the protection afforded by antiquity, since he does not hold a sound opinion.

For, as it is recorded in the archives of our church, after the most blessed Germanus had been removed from human affairs, Alodius was appointed to the episcopate and fulfilled the office of his pontificate for nearly thirty years.

After his death, because of the fury of the barbarians arising within Gaul, the privileges of ecclesiastical liberty were submerged, dignity was overthrown, splendor dimmed, and the whole force of Christian strength was lost. Thus the city remained widowed of its bishop for ten years. When these years had passed, Fraternus—third in succession to the episcopate after Saint Germanus—was appointed.

On the very day on which he was ordained, he was also killed by those same barbarians and crowned with martyrdom. In the fourth place, the previously named Censurius was substituted for him.

Thus, from the death of the most blessed Germanus down to this Censurius, approximately forty years can be counted, passing in the order just described.

### 3

When Censurius was distinguished by the dignity of ecclesiastical primacy, Constantius of Lyon, a man of outstanding learning, at the urging or prayers of Saint Patient, then bishop of that city, produced a book on the life and virtues of the most blessed Germanus, with remarkable elegance of expression and an abundant selection of words.

At that time the Saint’s memory still breathed freshly from the mouths of everyone, and many survived who had seen him living in the world. Their unquestionable testimony conveyed the greatness of his holiness while it was still pure and had not yet suffered the stain of variation.

Nor would I deny that some of those six bishops who had constantly attended the holy man while he was staying in Italy were still alive at that time. According to the testimony of the same historian, they had been witnesses of his deeds for many years.

### 4

At that time the city of Lyon, first and foremost among the cities of Gaul, had also raised its head above all others in the practice of learning and the disciplines of the arts.

For wisdom—which ought to be desired for its own sake—had been offended by the shameful profits of certain people, by the undisciplined life of many, and finally by the dishonorable indolence of all who pursued it half-heartedly. With teachers lacking and the studies of earlier generations nearly collapsed, wisdom, deadly in its hatred of our region, established its familiar seat at Lyon for some time.

There, expertise in what are called the liberal disciplines—and in those studies which, according to the proper order, are now said to proceed, though at this time that claim is merely a fable—grew so strong that, with regard to the schools, it was called the public university of the world on this side of the sea.

To offer some rational evidence for this, we infer it from the fact that anyone who was moved by a desire to profess the arts was not permitted to enroll among those who had already professed them until he had first been examined here with tested diligence and then departed.

The Satirist also supports this point. To make the matter clear by the circumstances of his example, after attacking the shameless for a long time and with severity in the first book of his work, he reports that they grow pale from consciousness of habitual crime,

> As a rhetorician from Lyon, about to speak at the altar [Note: Juvenal, Book 1 of the *Satires*, verse 44. Papirius Masson gives an exposition of the passage in his *Description of the Rivers of Gaul*, in the section on the river Saône].

Thus it is clear that Lyon once bestowed both palms and titles upon the learned.

### 5

We have touched on these matters briefly so that you may understand that, from so great a city, not an unskilled man but a most eloquent one was summoned by the industry of its bishop to revise the miracles of blessed Germanus.

Although, as the work placed below demonstrates, he was distinguished by eloquence, expressed in moderate and polished sentences, extremely fond of brevity, and excessively eager to avoid tediousness, he nevertheless acknowledges that he undertook the labor of so great a difficulty only after overcoming hesitation and shame. He must be judged justified by the lowliness of his own humility; and, apart from the fact that he knowingly passed over many things, he deserves praise of many kinds.

Having completed the work and for a long time carefully revised it privately, he subsequently sent it, at the request of the aforementioned Saint Censurius, to the Church of Auxerre, so that the bishop himself might publish it more widely.

There, since he truthfully testifies—though we are least grateful for this truth—that God knows hidden things, he admits that he remained silent about several deeds of Lord Germanus which he had learned and verified. By suppressing what divine power had wondrously accomplished for the benefit of all, he also declares himself guilty.

For a long time I have therefore resolved in my mind that it would be fitting for religion, useful for salvation, and certainly beneficial for edification if some of these matters that were omitted, or that could be recovered from knowledge, should happen to be entrusted to writing by someone more skilled.

### 6

Since this has not yet been done, it is certain that these matters should neither be passed over with impunity nor touched upon without fruit. Although, except through divine assistance, I have no awareness of being capable of this, I nevertheless undertake this work—one that ought not to be attempted by me or those like me, namely the unlearned—out of devotion to God and affection for the Saint.

I am all the more encouraged by the hope that the One whom all creation universally praises through its service declares that, if human beings suppress his praises, the stones will cry out.

We consider the plan of the undertaking most firmly established if, after first setting down certain matters sufficiently attested by report as having been accomplished through him before his glorious passing, we proceed in order to those things which we have seen happen, or learned to have happened, after his sacred memory.

But lest the previously mentioned brief work take offense at a more extended introduction—that is, lest the preface become too long—let us, with the Lord giving us courage, proceed to the matter at hand.

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE

### Saint Germanus’s conversation with a deceased disciple, the resurrection of the dead man, and other miracles during his lifetime

### 7

Both the authority of the records and the very well-known monuments of the places through which he traveled testify that the journeys of the holy man always shone with heavenly miracles.

For it was not permitted that a star-like lamp should be obscured by worldly darkness—a lamp that God, arranging all things gently to dispel the gloom of error, had placed high upon a lampstand.

Since he had devoted himself wholly to the interests of the Church, it happened, on a matter of definite importance, that he undertook a necessary journey with chosen companions.

When he had already advanced some distance, one of his disciples, who had accompanied the holy man from Ireland [Note: See the preliminary commentary, no. 74. “Ireland” is found in all our manuscripts and therefore seems to be the reading that should be retained, although our Papebrochius once expressed doubt about it on 30 April, p. 776], set out in pursuit of his master’s footsteps. His name was Michomeres. He had been selected for this very expedition but had been unable to depart with him.

When he reached the fortress called Tharnodorus [Note: Tharnodorus, otherwise Ternodorus, now Tonnerre, in the French region of Champagne], situated about eighteen miles from the city—that is, Auxerre—he was overcome by illness and lay down there. A few days later he died and was entrusted by the faithful to burial on the slope of the same rock.

### 8

After some days, it happened that the most blessed Germanus, retracing his journey, reached the same place. I believe that the Spirit forewarned him of his disciple’s death.

Approaching the place where he had been buried, and first offering a prayer, he ordered the grave to be opened. Michomeres was called by name and is said to have sat up after recovering the use of life.

The most holy bishop questioned him carefully about what he was doing and whether he enjoyed peace. He is confirmed to have received this answer:

“Thank you, most holy Father. I both give and retain thanks for your exceptional merits, because through the favor of your blessedness I have suffered nothing troublesome, nothing sad. Everything is peaceful for me; all things are sound.”

The bishop said to him: “Do you wish to continue laboring with me in the ministry of preaching, or, as you had begun, to rest?”

He replied: “Provided that it is not burdensome to your holiness, I have no need to wander any longer away from Christ. It is best for me to cling to him as I had begun; and I ask to be recalled as quickly as possible by your prayers from the place from which I have just been called away.”

When the bishop agreed to this request [Note: This is all the more marvelous, and therefore seems all the less likely to have been either unknown to or omitted by Constantius, if it is true. Hericus himself does not seem to have regarded it as certain, as the beginning of the following section suggests], he laid down his head again and, to everyone’s amazement, rested in peace.

I would confidently say that He then dwelt in Germanus who once called Lazarus, dead for four days, from a tomb already sealed.

This miracle was then widely known, and it still circulates most famously on everyone’s lips. An oratory was later built at the very place of blessed Michomeres, where divine benefits are still bestowed today upon those who worthily venerate the holy man of God.

### 9

The deed said to have been performed near the city of Aquilisima—or, as common usage more frequently calls it, Egolissima [Note: Now Angoulême, an episcopal city under the archbishopric of Bordeaux]—is believed all the more firmly because its evidence is displayed before the eyes.

When he had been brought there by the continuation of his journey, he was honored with an appropriate reception, one worthy of an apostolic man. He was earnestly asked to consecrate and dedicate a new altar in the older church to the honor of the chief of the apostles, and he complied with the charitable request.

While he was carrying this out according to the solemn rite, the innocence and purity of his holy hands were immediately revealed by a heavenly miracle.

Whenever and wherever he marked the horns of the altar and its middle with the sign of the cross, using the liquid of consecrated oil, the marble melted beneath the impression of his thumb and withdrew, so that at the touch of his finger one would have thought that a snowy softness had yielded.

That same marble still lies above the altar, both a spectacle and an object of veneration. Consecrated by the blessing of the holy man, it testifies to the singular grace of his merits.

### 10

In the suburb of Orléans there is a church dedicated in his name and frequently made illustrious by his merits. They say that the principal reason for building it was this.

When he had settled the ecclesiastical affairs that had pressed him most urgently and was returning briskly to his own people, as he approached the city of Orléans, the bells of the older basilica suddenly began to shake of their own accord and, with spontaneous ringing—wondrous to relate—to announce his arrival.

At that time Saint Anianus [Note: The life of Saint Anianus, bishop of Orléans, is to be treated on 17 November. The Sammarthani say that he sat for a very long time, approximately from the year 390 to 453] was bishop of the city, himself glorious in holiness and miracles. Taught inwardly by a revelation of the spirit, he went out beyond the city with all the gathered forces of clergy and people to meet the most blessed Germanus. He welcomed and venerated him, and refreshed him, exhausted by the journey, with all the diligence of service that was appropriate.

O what joys filled that day! How much honor, how great a treasure, did that city bear, supported by two apostolic columns, enriched by twin olive trees, and illumined by the most splendid candlesticks!

At the place where the priests solemnly welcomed one another in a mutual embrace, a church was later built in the name of blessed Germanus. Through the abundance of divine benefits, it continues to offer memorable testimony to his merits.

### 11

After they had feasted together in Christ with spiritual sweetness and, in turn, filled one another with the most joyful banquets of virtue, Anianus, a man equally distinguished in merits, accompanied the most holy Germanus for almost two miles from the city, out of genuine affection.

As they traveled, behold, a widowed woman carrying the corpse of her only son to be buried fell at the feet of the saints and earnestly begged them to have pity on her. Their presence had been offered to her not by chance but by heavenly providence. She firmly believed that, through the merits of both men, her son could be restored to his grieving mother.

For a long time there was uncertainty between the two, and they argued stubbornly over which of them should undertake the miracle. Germanus maintained that blessed Anianus ought to undertake the miracle because the matter belonged to his diocese; Anianus affirmed that, if anything was to be done, it could be obtained more quickly from the most holy Germanus.

Germanus therefore yielded partly to the mother’s tears and partly to the bishop’s insistence, trusting in the charity that bears all things. He devoted himself, as usual, to prayer and, purchasing the dead man’s life with abundant tears, restored the son alive from the funeral to his grieving mother, to the immense joy of everyone.

A church built in his honor at that same place later became famous for countless miracles. Even today it displays the tomb of the man who was raised; after completing the proper span of his life, he deserved an honorable burial there in perpetual memory of the miracle.

The patch of turf on which the saint lay prostrate in prayer is also still held in great veneration by everyone. A wooden railing has been placed before it to protect the small plot of sacred earth from the feet of passersby.

### 12

The same territory contains, on the public road, a village called Basilicas from ancient times, which still displays conspicuous evidence of a miracle once performed there.

A certain inhabitant of the place, distinguished by birth and wealthy in resources, was constructing a large church on his estate with craftsmen whom he had hired. When the building had already risen to some height and the anxious diligence of the builders was pressing to complete what remained, the architects were one day standing on the summit of the same structure and hastening the work.

Then the wall on which they stood split and broke from its summit down to the foundations, so that the tottering sections threatened ruin to themselves, while those standing above them faced immediate death.

Whether the work collapsed through the builders’ incompetence, or whether the material for a miracle was provided by the dispensation that orders human affairs in due arrangement [variant: “directs”], I cannot easily determine.

### 13

By chance Germanus was walking along the public road directly opposite. He saw the danger, raised his hand on high, and, having made the sign of the cross, forbade the wall—already tipping and hanging—to fall.

At the opposition of his most holy hand, the wall resisted; as though caught by a most powerful support, it returned to the upright firmness of its original position.

Thus, by the effect of a single act of power, he rescued both the wall from collapse and the people from death.

When this had been accomplished, and his merits had been proclaimed by still greater praises, he continued the journey he had begun.

After some time, when the work had finally been unfolded and the construction of the temple completed, discussion arose about its consecration. The owner of the work, moved by a prudent judgment, said:

“No one will more appropriately illumine this church with his name than the most holy Germanus, whose lofty merits are known to have already consecrated it.”

This church still stands today, most illustrious under the title of the most blessed Germanus and frequented because of the display of miracles. It still exhibits the same wall, marked by a conspicuous scar of fissure, and bearing upon itself the testimony of apostolic holiness [Note: Viola testifies, in the Gallic *Life of Saint Germanus*, chapter 28, p. 207, that only the walls and altar of this church remained when he wrote].

### 14

Rarely did he stay or teach anywhere without leaving behind magnificent monuments of his singular excellence. For pious minds that think devoutly about God, the small number noted here among the many will be sufficient.

These accounts are all the safer because they are known with greater certainty and seen more directly in the present.

As he traveled through the district of Toul, he was met by a multitude of peoples. At a certain place he sat down, intending to shape the assembled crowd through an exhortation in the saving word. He had happened to be carrying a hazel staff, which he planted in the ground.

When the preaching was finished—wondrous to see and wondrous even to relate—it had already produced little branches and leaves.

As a testimony to his holiness, it grew into a hazel tree of immense size. Even today everyone venerates it with great care, so that no one dares to pluck a branch from it or perpetrate anything improper beneath it or around it.

The place is also commonly called “At the Staff of Saint Germanus” [Note: *Cambuta* or *cambutta* means a staff or walking-stick on which travelers lean, as Cange explains in his *Glossary*].

15. In the pagus of Vastine [Note: The pagus of Vastine, commonly called the Gâtinais, is a district of Gaul in the province of the Île-de-France. In that district is the monastery of Gaiacum, subject to the convent of Saint Fara, about three leagues from the town of Montargis; Mabillon mentions this monastery in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 841, no. 41.], near the monastery of Gaiacum, with the river Odon lying between them, there stands a beech tree of astonishing size: lofty in trunk, immense in the spread of its branches, and dark with dense foliage. It is confidently asserted that this tree likewise grew together through the power of the holy bishop, when, after delivering a sermon to the people in that place, he thrust into the earth the staff with which he supported his aged limbs. Because of its extraordinary size, it has drawn many people from the neighboring regions to see it. Beside the tree there is a church distinguished by his name, and the place is now popularly called “At the Beech of Saint Germanus.”

16. Who, rightly, would judge it necessary to exclude from the category of miracles the fact that the tombs of venerable martyrs became known and celebrated during his episcopate? The most sacred bodies of that holy multitude, whom the savagery of Aurelian’s persecution slaughtered together with blessed Priscus [Note: Saint Priscus and his fellow martyrs are commemorated on 26 May, beginning at p. 365, where this matter is also explained.], were secretly carried away by Christians—then exceedingly few—because of the raging violence, and were heaped indiscriminately into a very large cistern. Their memory, obscured and gradually swept away by the long passage of time, remained hidden from everyone until the time of the most holy Germanus. Then God, in whose sight the death of his saints is always precious, determining to aid the peoples through their intercession, made their venerable bodies known; and, by marvelous means, he also revealed the head of the blessed martyr Priscus to the same man. Germanus built and consecrated a church for its burial four miles from the city; the continual abundance of miracles and the crowds of people flocking there make it famous. This has not been invented from elsewhere; rather, it has been inserted here from a truthful account of their Passion.

## CHAPTER II. Other matters concerning his life, up to his death and funeral rites

17. Since almost no one doubts that, in the churches he himself dedicated, the greater evidence of divine power was displayed through the miracles performed, it is judged most inhuman and inappropriate to exclude this from the salutary praises of his merits. To make this clear, we shall rely upon a single example, and one by no means obscure.

Returning from Britain, he brought with him relics of the very ancient and precious martyr Alban. Within the walls of Auxerre he built a basilica to house them and dedicated it in the name of the aforementioned martyr. They say that a certain devout priest served there with anxious zeal. Among his other efforts toward holiness, he had made it habitual that, when the signal from the elder basilica called him, he would snatch himself from bed and hasten as quickly as possible to the church. While he maintained such vigilant devotion to divine service, one night, as he was leaving his own house, which adjoined the aforesaid basilica, he heard an angelic choir singing with harmonious concord, “Alleluia,” together with Psalm 148, entitled “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” through to the end of the Psalter. Listening more attentively at the door of the oratory with astonished ears, he learned the melody by heart.

18. The Alleluia was one which our church customarily sings only on the Sunday of Septuagesima, together with the psalm mentioned above. In the first verse it is repeated once, in the second twice, in the third three times, and in the fourth it is finally repeated from the beginning. As I think, it is appropriately sung in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity.

When he had committed it to memory, he summoned the brothers after solemn Matins and, having reported the revelation he had received, taught them the melody as well, so that the matter might be better attested. Immediately, however, all its sweetness slipped from his mind, so that afterward he could remember nothing except the word itself. He is rightly thought to have suffered this because, having rashly disclosed to others the heavenly secrets revealed to him, while they retained them for the praise of God, he was punished by his own ignorance alone [alternative reading: he alone, through ignorance]. The apostle Paul, indicating that he feared this, admits that he heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak. John, too, is commanded not to seal [Note: “Not to seal,” and so forth. In fact, Apocalypse 10:4 reads: “Seal the things which the seven thunders spoke, and do not write them.” There “to seal” means the same as to seal with a seal and keep hidden. Hericus therefore follows the sense here, not the wording, understanding “do not seal” as “do not disclose, write down, or make public.”] what the seven thunders spoke. The soul, likewise, while contemplating divine things, is commanded: “Hear, Israel, and be silent” [Note: “Hear, Israel, and be silent” is not read in this form in the Vulgate, but among the Septuagint, Deuteronomy 27:9 reads: “Be silent and hear, Israel.” Saint Jerome also attributes these words to Moses in his letter to the monk Rusticus: “Hear, Israel, and be silent.”].

Many benefits are recorded as having been conferred at that same oratory, both in the expulsion of demons and in the restoration of sight to the blind; especially upon those who, afflicted by different attacks of fever, came to the place after invoking the patronage of the saints.

19. He enriched the church over which he presided not only with spiritual but also with the greatest abundance of temporal increases. How meager its resources had been before him can easily be inferred if one considers with fair judgment the wealth with which he left it endowed. For, noble among the noblest in birth, and, in fortune, the richest of the rich in possessions and estates, he made the Church his heir during his lifetime to everything that had come to him by paternal right; and we know that it still consists for the most part of his patrimonial property.

These estates are very numerous, extremely large in extent, broad in their boundaries, adjoining one another, most pleasant in the character of their locations, and distinguished by the abundance of their revenues [Note: The *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapter 7, enumerates some of them in these words: “This most blessed bishop gave to the basilica of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr a most noble estate called Varsiacus, with all its equipment and dependencies.” D. Le Beuf asserts in *Auxerre Captured and Liberated*, p. 284, that a church dedicated to Saint Eugenia the Roman martyr had been erected there by the saint. “Likewise Vercisum, containing within itself a marvelous palace, with its dependencies; also Poliacum, or Marciniacum; and likewise Jociacum with its dependencies; also the estate of Patriniacum, and Cutiacum likewise with its dependencies; and finally many others unknown to us moderns but all known to God. Read there what else he gave to other churches, and also in Viola, chapter 7.”].

In one of these estates, anciently called Epponiacus, his venerable father, named Rusticus, together with his mother, named Germanilla, rests honorably buried in a church dedicated under the name of the Prince of the Apostles, with their altars placed above their heads [Note: “Dedicated under the name of the Prince of the Apostles”: the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, at the passage cited, instead reads, “dedicated under the name of Blessed John.” Perhaps he honored both patrons.].

Thus Rusticus and Germanilla seem in some manner to have been canonized, says our Chiffletius in his manuscript annotations; and Viola says the same in his French *Life*, chapter 1. Indeed, unless they had been regarded as saints, such veneration would not have been appropriate for their tombs. Yet, as far as I have been able to determine, no one dares to number them among the saints. Moreover, of those two altars, the one on the right was later consecrated to Saint Germanus and is said to have become famous for miracles, especially for the resurrection of infants whom mothers who had given birth to them dead were accustomed to offer there, as Viola testifies in the chapter just cited [Note: Thus Rusticus and Germanilla seem in some manner to have been canonized, says our Chiffletius in his manuscript annotations; and Viola says the same in his French *Life*, chapter 1. Indeed, unless they had been regarded as saints, such veneration would not have been appropriate for their tombs. Yet, as far as I have been able to determine, no one dares to number them among the saints. Moreover, of those two altars, the one on the right was later consecrated to Saint Germanus and is said to have become famous for miracles, especially for the resurrection of infants whom mothers who had given birth to them dead were accustomed to offer there, as Viola testifies in the chapter just cited.].

They rest there decently buried.

20. O man to whom the highest honors are always owed, who, embracing voluntary poverty through love of eternal life, gave everything to Christ and kept nothing for himself! Who could easily express the openness of his spirit in this matter, an openness truly worthy of a noble soul? Who could encompass in an account the blessings which the Church of Christ now enjoys through him? Whatever now enriches bishops, provides sustenance for clerics, supports monks, and refreshes the needy was his; it was poured forth from his most fruitful generosity upon these people. How many examples of his virtues and holiness have flowed down to us! How much broader a record could have been composed, how many volumes assembled, if some inquisitive person had accompanied him while he lived in the world, recording his words as they flowed singly from his mouth, observing all his actions with careful attention, and finally entrusting to a tenacious memory the miracles that were always readily present with him?

For that brilliant abridger of his deeds—not to call him an expositor, since I have never read or heard him read without misgiving—declares that, if he were to traverse all his journeys and recount everything, he would prepare for his readers the weariness of an accumulation made tedious by its length.

21. Since the glory of a father shines forth in the conduct of his sons, of the many whom he is believed to have had as sons in Christ and disciples in religion, it will suffice to insert, in restrained brevity, a mention of one, and he the most famous.

Patrick, as the series of his Deeds reveals, the special apostle of the Irish region, was devoted to his most holy discipleship for eighteen years [Note: Observe that all our copies give eighteen years; accordingly, the note of our Papebrochius in the *Life of Saint Patrick* on 17 March, p. 546, must be corrected]. From so great a fountain he drew no ordinary learning in the heavenly Scriptures. The most divine bishop recognized him as magnanimous in religion, excellent in virtues, and vigorous in teaching. Considering it unworthy that so robust a farmer should languish in cultivating the Lord’s field, he sent him, through his own priest Segetius, to the holy Pope Celestine of the city of Rome, so that Segetius might present to the apostolic see testimony of the man’s ecclesiastical integrity.

Approved by the pope’s judgment, supported by his authority, and finally strengthened by his blessing, Patrick went to Ireland. Given specifically to that people as its apostle, he then and still now, and forever, illumines it by the marvelous privileges of his apostleship—then through doctrine and miracles, and now through their enduring effects.

22. The singular power of his merits is defended by this evidence: throughout all the roads of his journeys, wherever he either prayed or taught, chapels and elevated signs of the Cross still shine conspicuously to this day. Even today, in the monastery he himself built, an oratory is pointed out that was later consecrated in his name. There, we know without hesitation, is a cell witness to his afflictions and sufferings. I scarcely know whether to call its opening a little door or a window; it was so exceedingly small in its humility that no one, however tiny his body, could creep through it except lying prone.

What sighs were uttered there, what tears poured out; how many divine revelations were brought to this most godly man as he contemplated God; how many angelic consolations were provided; and, finally, how often the peoples who flocked there received remedies for soul and body—it would take much to recount. Who at least could adequately weigh what they were, how great they were, and how frequent? Their measure is known only to God.

Having advanced the undertaking begun in a few words, I shall now, with the Lord invoked, proceed to explain a small part of what followed his glorious passage from this life.

23. The most illustrious bishop Germanus, given as an unfailing light to a world living in darkness, after an incomparable life in this world, after sprinkling Gaul, Britain, and finally Italy itself with doctrine and miracles, was called by Christ the Lord and strengthened by the saving Viaticum. Full of the Holy Spirit, he died at Ravenna, a city of Italy, while the younger Valentinian, son of Constantius, together with his mother Placidia, held the monarchy of the world.

They received him there honorably, out of admiration for his holiness and because of the constant occurrence of his miracles, as the book of his Deeds more fully explains. When the Lord Christ appeared to him, he learned beforehand the day of his death and, although only with great difficulty, obtained that the clay of his body should be returned to his own city.

24. The reason for his journey to Ravenna, and the fact that it was neither uncertain nor accidental, is made clear by the text of his Life. A brief recapitulation here may not be inappropriate.

At that time the eminent Aetius had been appointed patrician and governor of the state. Provoked by the insolence of the Armorican people—whose fickle and undisciplined spirits have rarely preserved steadfast loyalty toward their rulers—he permitted the most ferocious king of the Alans, Eochar, to invade, subjugate, and lay waste that region as punishment for its rebellion.

When the barbarian had invaded it with the utmost cruelty, attracted not so much by the accumulation of booty as by slaughter and blood, the most blessed Germanus, who had already advanced to meet him while he was armed and pressing forward amid the attacks of the enemy, compelled his savage spirit, by a marvelous firmness of authority—and, as I judge, by an act preferable to all the miracles he performed—to lay down its fury, recall the army, and desist from ravaging the province. This was on the condition, however, that the pardon which the barbarian had granted should be sought from the emperor or from Aetius.

Accordingly, to complete the work of mercy he had begun, Germanus traveled through the Gallic and Italian cities and, after displaying many miracles along the way, reached Ravenna, where the emperor was then residing with his august mother.
