Although he had been long awaited, he obtained there, according to his request, peace and security for those on whose behalf he petitioned.

25. But because the treachery of a fickle spirit recalled the undisciplined people to their former rebellion, not long after his death a tyrannical savagery, which he had suppressed during his lifetime, rose more violently against the unhappy inhabitants. The Alans, Goths, and Vandals advanced from Spain into Africa and from there into Gaul, trampling everything beneath the sword, fire, and devastation.

The most holy Anianus mentioned above had not yet died; and his most reverend colleague Lupus, bishop of Troyes, was still living a heavenly life on earth. Protecting his people from barbarian ferocity by his prayers, as is sung in the hymn of his feast, according to Bede’s testimony, “While all the wars were laying waste, by praying he fortified Troyes” [Note: That hymn is said still to survive intact in Cousinet’s *Analecta concerning Saint Lupus, Bishop of Troyes*, manuscripts of which are preserved in Paris at Saint Geneviève.].

Since matters stood thus, no one will doubt that divine grace also provided this for the most blessed Germanus: he who, as an invincible advocate of divine law, had carried out Christ’s embassy in the world should end his temporal life in the confirmation of holy peace—the peace for whose restoration between God and humanity the Author of life had endured a voluntary death. For in what more fitting order could he complete the course of his contest than by laying down his soul for the one and for the attainment of that same end for which he had run through so long a stage of this life?

26. It is truly an impious thought to suppose that the blessed man undertook so great an expedition in ignorance of his approaching death. If he had recognized that the end of his life was immediately at hand, he would not have allowed himself to carry his foot even a little distance from his own city. We refer the reader to the book composed on his life; there, by the truth brought before him, he may cast off this error and learn that, even when he departed, he was not unprepared for the nearness of his passage.

When, because of the business mentioned above, he was preparing to visit Italy, he stopped, as was his custom, to visit his friend Senator, a priest. As he was about to depart from him, Germanus rushed upon his friend with more affection than usual; and, after many embraces and very tender kisses, he left him with these words of farewell:

“Farewell forever, dearest brother; farewell, portion of my soul. May God grant that we may see one another without confusion on the day of judgment. But in this light we shall never again enjoy one another’s sight.”

Since it is clear that this happened as he said, who can doubt his foreknowledge of his passage, when he was able to predict such things about himself, so clearly and so precisely?

Thus the saint, anxious in charity and not unaware that his death was now immediately approaching, considered nothing more important than to fulfill the Lord’s commands and to expend himself, near the end, for the relief of Christ’s sheep. With these matters established, let us return to the subject begun above.

27. Everyone competed in contributing his efforts to prepare the dead man. Acolius, the royal chamberlain, whose son he had formerly cured of the plague of a most savage demon, prepared the venerable body with a varied mixture of aromatics.

The empress, who had waited upon him while he was alive and desired from her heart to honor him also in death, covered the sacred body with elaborate and very fine garments, placing it in a most carefully cleansed cypress coffin prepared for transporting and preserving it.

When these things had been arranged, the emperor, anxious that nothing should be lacking among the rites due to the saint, made preparations with care, organized the journey, supplied the necessary means of transport, and assigned ministers and companions to escort the funeral. He generously furnished them with the expenses and all the provisions required for their service.

The bishops took the greatest care that the offices of religion should not be absent even for an hour from the sacred funeral rites. They themselves arranged those offices for the present occasion and, anticipating the continuation of the journey, made provision in advance so that they would not fail along the way.

Thus the funeral, splendidly equipped, advanced toward Gaul with a great procession of escorts.

## CHAPTER III. The Translation of His Body into Gaul; Its Reception and Burial

28. Since the funeral of one whose merit was so strong, whose glory so excellent, and whose position with Christ so exalted illuminated the public roads, it was fitting that the abundance of signs should declare his standing before God. Very many stories are circulated by popular report, but they lose credibility because they are related variously and without order.

There is one noble and precious account which, besides being especially worthy of remembrance, has also been committed to writing from ancient times. It both establishes belief and contributes to edification.

During the journey mentioned above, Germanus was honorably received by the venerable Eusebius [Note: The Roman Martyrology treats Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, on 1 August; but since, by a recent Roman decree, his feast and Office have been assigned to 16 December, we shall refer his Acts to that day. It is clear from this passage how little versed our Hericus was in ancient chronology: he did not hesitate to write these things about Eusebius, who died approximately seventy years before Germanus. Ughellus therefore argues, in his account of the bishops of Vercelli in the revised *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, col. 761, that Saint Albinus should be written in place of Eusebius, whom all our manuscripts present.

I am nevertheless sufficiently afraid that this will not satisfy everyone. For another history, very similar to this one, is related by Saint Ado, archbishop of Vienne and a contemporary of Hericus, in his *Chronicle*, sixth age, under the year 452. Its substance is as follows: When Saint Germanus, on his way to Ravenna, was passing through Vienne in Gaul, Saint Severus the priest asked him to consecrate the recently built church of Saint Stephen. Germanus promised that he would do so on his return. But after he had been awaited in vain for a long time and did not return, and the dedication was being arranged through another, behold: at that very moment the body of Saint Germanus, who had died, was being sent from Ravenna to his people. It was brought through Vienne and deposited for a time in that same church of Saint Stephen, so that it might rest there; thus the promise of the man of God was fulfilled.

Ado adds: “At that time Isicius governed the church of Vienne.” Here too he is seriously mistaken, since Isichius I did not occupy the see before at least the year 472, as has been shown on 16 March, under Isichius, p. 448, and on 5 February, where Saint Avitus, son and successor of Isichius, is treated, p. 661.

The resemblance between the two histories, and the palpable errors of both authors in them, certainly do not commend the truth of either. Yet let us not therefore call either one entirely false. Viola, in chapter 23, detected an error in Hericus, but not in Ado. Accordingly, what Hericus relates about Saint Eusebius and the church of Vercelli, Viola applies to Saint Isichius and the church of Vienne, confusing the two narratives.], bishop of Vercelli, and, as was fitting, was treated with every courtesy.

That same Eusebius, after long struggles against the ancient enemy, after he had shattered the plots of the heretics—by whom he had suffered much—and finally after that most celebrated exile in Phrygia, from which he returned after four years, was now worn out by old age. With peace restored, he was then founding a new church in his own city, like a veteran soldier.

He earnestly begged that the most blessed Germanus, on his return from Ravenna, would dedicate it. Germanus solemnly promised that he would fulfill this request with the greatest devotion.

29. When the death of the most blessed confessor became known, the aforesaid bishop prepared, according to ecclesiastical custom, for the consecration of his basilica. As he was solemnly about to enter it [readings: *quod*; alternatively *quam*], he ordered the customary lamps to be arranged and lit. But—strange to say—the flame could not be made to catch in any of the lamps, although the ministers repeatedly attempted it by various methods, and their persistent efforts were in vain.

When, for several days, repeated labor without result continued to be obstructed by these disturbances, the bishop, troubled by the unusual interruption of the undertaking, judged that he must abandon the project before him. It was evident to him and to everyone that the completion of the dedication was either being prevented, postponed to another time, or reserved for the service of another bishop.

Meanwhile, word arrived through the report that had preceded it that the procession bearing the venerable body was approaching. Who would not rise to meet it? Whom would concern for his own salvation not urge forward?

The bishop gathered the crowd from every side and, after receiving the body with the acts of devotion it deserved, brought it within the precincts of the aforementioned basilica. As soon as it reached the first part of the building, the entire mass of lamps was kindled from heaven and shone brilliantly, making it clear that the presence of the divine majesty had not been absent from the funeral rites of the sacred body. What human skill had been unable to accomplish readily obeyed the divine command.

30. Then the most holy Eusebius, mindful of his vow and not forgetting the promise received from the saint, considered the matter more deeply. Since what had been accomplished by heavenly auspices was unfit to be delayed by human efforts, he said:

“The most holy Germanus, mindful of the pledge agreed, did not delay, though dead, to fulfill what he had promised while alive, lest we be tormented by the incompletion of our vow. Therefore, having received such clear, such exalted, and finally such singular testimonies to his holiness, let us invoke the Lord and prepare ourselves to carry out what remains to be done in these divine mysteries.”

Having spoken thus, he went to the altar and, singing “Glory to God in the highest” as loudly as he could, proclaimed a festival day for the people.

After the sacred rites had been celebrated according to episcopal custom, and discussion had arisen concerning the splendor of the miracle, he devoted the remaining hours of the day to religious vigils around the sacred funeral.

O sweet and ever-unfailing memory of the just! O death of the saints, always precious in the sight of the Lord! No one could thereafter doubt what standing Germanus had merited before the Lord. Before his honored [alternative: adored] remains, such splendor of signs had also shone forth in foreign regions—something perhaps known only to God, had not the frequency of the wonders revealed it to the human race.

31. When these rites had been completed, the procession returned to the road, and a new fervor of service, born in everyone’s heart, was added to the duties owed to the saint’s funeral. The immense number of peoples arriving from every direction continued to grow, as new groups of companions joined at each place and none of those who accompanied the body grew weary of continuing the journey.

No opportunity to carry the body could be granted to everyone, although they pressed forward forcefully. Those who were able to approach took their turns; but those whom the surging crowd prevented from handling it at close range had this form of service: to accompany it with their eyes and to make the air resound with voices flowing from the innermost spring of devotion.

Throughout the entire journey, numerous memorials of his blessedness are displayed, both in churches dedicated in his name and in inscriptions affixed here and there. Wherever he spent the night or paused, the memory of his holiness still flourishes conspicuously.

32. It will be considered worthwhile not to pass over this matter untouched: namely, how divine providence, always caring for all, wished the death of the holy bishop to become known even to his own people, who still did not know that they had been deprived of him.

Saturnus [Note: On this Saturnus, see the *Praetermissi* for this day.] was the priest and disciple of the most blessed Germanus, equally distinguished in life and dearly loved by the holy man as a close companion. When Germanus departed for Italy, Saturnus had remained in the city at his command.

On the night when the glorious confessor and bishop of the Lord passed from this life happily at Ravenna, Saturnus, though stationed at Auxerre, learned of his splendid passage when an angel revealed it to him. Instructed by a divine revelation, he announced it to the people. Gathering a great multitude with him, he hastened to the Alpine passes, where the Gauls received their own patron, prepared to serve his great funeral with all the greater devotion because a love mingled with reverence compelled them to offer a more excellent service.

This is not a fabrication, nor something forced out from the itch of a fertile imagination. Rather, it is preserved among us to this day, engraved upon very ancient marble, whose writing itself displays the character of antiquity.

33. I would readily believe that some people, from Ravenna, having had the experience of his holiness, voluntarily imposed upon themselves the pilgrimage with the sacred body, and thus, with tireless spirits, followed the venerable funeral even though the route was longer.

Among them five exceptionally famous virgins, sisters by birth, are reported to have undertaken this purpose [Note: In the manuscript *Life of Saint Magnentia*, these virgins are not said to have been sisters of one another, but companions and associates of Saint Magnentia. Furthermore, only four are numbered there, Maxima being omitted. Bargedaeus argues in his manuscript *Collection of the Saints of Auxerre*, under 26 November, that Maxima either did not belong to this group or must be confused with Magnentia. He bases this on the fact that, in the very ancient stone chest in which the body of Saint Magnentia is preserved, she is represented lying on her deathbed with only three virgins attending her; and also because no more are shown in the paintings of the church of Saint Palladia.

Nevertheless, that Maxima was distinct from Magnentia is proved by her tomb and body, which were preserved at Auxerre in the monastery of Saint Germanus until the Calvinist profanation of 1567, as is clear from the records of the Siguier visitation. Her Gallic epitaph is said still to survive there: “Here lies the body of the lady Saint Maxima, a virgin, who accompanied the body of Saint Germanus from Ravenna to this monastery, together with Saint Palladia, Saint Magnentia, Saint Camilla, and Saint Porcaria.” As for the day on which Saint Maxima is celebrated, although she has a chapel in the monastery mentioned, we have so far been unable to determine it. Castellanus numbers her among the saints without a fixed day.].

Their names or merits have long preserved a celebrated memory in our province. Three of them—Magnentia, Palladia, and Camilla [Note: Magnentia will be treated on 26 November; Saints Palladia and Porcaria on 8 October; Saint Camilla has already been treated on 3 March, p. 242, where the year of her death must be corrected]—were each divinely summoned during the journey itself and brought their final day to a close [Note: If they died during the journey, then either they are not celebrated on the day of their death—the journey lasted from the beginning of August until 22 September—or, after falling ill along the way, they must be said to have remained bedridden for a long time before dying.].

They received noble burial beside the public road, with churches built over them and dedicated to their holiness. These churches remain famous today for the evidence of their miracles and are frequented by crowds with immense devotion.

Of the two to whom it was granted to see the burial of the sacred body, one, whose name was Maxima, deserved to be buried near the same basilica, although later she was enclosed within the structure of a larger building. The other, called Porcaria, rests about nine miles from the city in a church distinguished by her renowned merits.

34. From the day before the Kalends of August, when the distinguished Confessor, freed from the burden of the flesh, was admitted into the heavenly sanctuaries, the fifty-third day was passing [Note: He therefore arrived on 22 September, the arrival celebrated in the preliminary Commentary, no. 4], when the treasure of the sacred body, returned to its own city, was received with the solemn homage of the people and placed within the precincts of the principal church over which he had presided [Note: That is, the church of Saint Stephen, which is the cathedral; nevertheless, he was not buried there, as will soon become clear.].

There it was honored for ten continuous days with the most lavish expenditure on the rites [Note: Namely, until the Kalends of October, which, as shown above, were solemnly consecrated to the memory of this event, as will follow in no. 37. Saint Gregory of Tours, cited below in no. 41, included the whole period within the round number of sixty days, but less accurately.], until everything pertaining to the rights of the tomb had been prepared with the greatest care. Then, with a considerable multitude of the human race gathered together, he was committed to burial, as an apostolic man deserved.

Yet, since in individual matters everyone is permitted to form opinions according to his capacity without penalty, I would not rashly say that, during so many intervening days, provision was made only for the preparation of the funeral. Rather, by delaying the burial of the bishop, provision was also made for the priests and peoples who would arrive from every distant part of the earth; if they had been absent from the saint’s funeral rites, they would have borne that absence with the greatest distress.

35. Because we enjoy the presence of your sacred body; because we are illumined by the glorious memory of a man most illustrious after the apostles; and because, finally, we possess the surest refuge to which our weakness may flee amid all dangers, we both owe and render you, most holy Father, every kind of thanksgiving, after first proclaiming the ineffable praise of the holy and undivided Trinity.

We proclaim you a lover of your homeland, a protector of your flock, and the most merciful father of your children. Although you could have been laid to rest in the imperial seats by the hands of the emperors themselves, and could have been placed upon a summit all the higher because Roman excellence is more elevated than Gallic modesty—so that Rome might remain illustrious for the apostles and Ravenna for Germanus—nevertheless, paternal and maternal affection prevailed. The love and devotion of your desolate children prevailed: those whom you had loved so greatly and so earnestly while alive, you showed by your death how dear they were to you.

Thus, most just Father, it was fitting for your holiness: since you had so often spent yourself for the benefit of outsiders, traversed lands and seas, and finally endured every hardship, you should not neglect your own people, over whom the supreme Ruler of all things had appointed you a special shepherd.

O how well you deserved of them, and with what sincere services you must be honored—you who provided for their bitterest bereavement such an immediate, such an outstanding, and finally such a familiar aid, by which you would assist not only those living at the present time but also their descendants!

Nature, the arranger of all things, placed our city upon barren rocks, supported by no resources and defended neither by the advantages of its location nor by human skill. It would not even exist under a worthy name if it lacked the treasure of your body. Because it deserved to be marvelously illumined by that treasure, it shines more gloriously than all else in this respect: after the apostles, no other city preserves a more precious pearl.

36. I am not capable of fully expressing what I think about the character of the reception mentioned above, since, after long and repeated reflection, I cannot discern the matter sufficiently even with the insight of my own mind.

Whether that day should be called a day of joy or of grief is uncertain. And if I praise one without the other, I fear that I may truly detract both from the devotion and from the prudence of so many religious citizens.

For whose face would not be occupied with tears? Whom would not the bereavement of a flock deprived of its shepherd remind of grief? What seemed most grievous was that the most devoted sons had not even been permitted to take part in the death of their bishop, who was dying abroad.

Yet how ineffable was the joy! How pure the affections from which that gladness was formed! The sons were receiving back their father, the wards their protector, the despairing their counsel, and the trembling their support.

O festive day, rich in such abundant tears and heavy with such great joys! Whoever [the printed text has *quisque* for *quisquis*] was not present missed the greatest possible part of the spectacle. No day brought a sadder breath upon the city, nor a more joyful one upon the world.

37. When everything had been duly prepared, and there was no respite from the crowds converging [Col. 1225A], while those who had gathered could scarcely now be contained by the extent of the place, on the day of the Kalends of October the heavenly treasure was placed in the hidden chamber of the tomb—with such devotion from the whole world and such piety from the human race that it became clearer than daylight to everyone that he whose earthly honor was being provided for with such care must possess the highest merit in heaven.

At that time the site of this tomb was a very small oratory on his own estate, dedicated to the merits of the martyr Mauritius [Note: [Col. 1225C] In the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapter 7, the following is said of our saint: “He also built a basilica in honor of the holy martyrs of Agaunum, namely Mauritius and his companions; there he offered these gifts: Warchiacus in the Senonais, with all its appurtenances; in the Auxerre district also Corvalle with its appurtenances; and likewise Molinis, with its appurtenances. In that same oratory he ordained as priest Saint Saturninus, a man of thoroughly proven life and his own disciple, [Col. 1225D] so that, under the profession of the priestly dignity, he might serve the memorials of the martyrs there.”], which the aforementioned very illustrious man had once assigned to Saturninus, so that, under the profession of the priestly dignity, he might serve the martyrs’ memorials there.

The enormity of pagan superstition had not yet grown obsolete; Christianity was still confined and oppressed within narrow boundaries; and, while shrines flourished everywhere throughout the world, only limited space, modest expense, and scant adornment were devoted to building churches of Christ [Col. 1225B]. The zeal of the faithful had not yet spread itself around such works; indeed, in those regions before Saint Germanus there had been a great scarcity of them. Since he himself was the seventh in succession to govern the church in his city, it is plainly evident that the bishops who had existed before him, hindered by the savage fury of the pagans opposing them, established the beginnings of religion less freely and less fully. Yet this man, against whose nobility, virtue, and wisdom no one could generally prevail, gave them manifold growth in his own time.

## CHAPTER IV. The royal magnificence of the Basilica of Saint Germanus and of his tomb, adorned by continual miracles

[Col. 1225C]

38. As the insignia of the sacred faith were extended everywhere with the passage of time, and the Frankish nobles themselves submitted their necks to the heavenly decrees, the venerable Queen Crotechildis [Note: [Col. 1225D] Saint Crotechildis. We published her Acts on 3 June, beginning at page 292; they contain no specific mention of this matter.], worthy of perpetual memorial, wife of the great prince Clovis, moved by the divine Spirit, built above the tomb of the holy bishop a basilica of immense construction and elaborate size [Col. 1226A], trusting that she and her family could be advanced greatly by the prayers of one whose signs of holiness were so numerous and so wondrous.

At that same time, when the aforementioned Augusta was present, Saint Lupus the bishop came from the regions of Upper Burgundy [Note: [Col. 1225D] That is, where the kingdom of Burgundy once existed, whose royal seat was Arles. It is not known, however, of which church this Lupus was bishop. See Mabillon’s conjecture in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 593, no. 40.]. He died not long afterward, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 1225D] Nevertheless, our predecessors omitted him on that day, although he is called a saint here, as also in his epitaph in the crypts of the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre. His body was found there by the most illustrious Siguier during the frequently mentioned visitation of 1636. I say that he was omitted because, as I believe, there was insufficient certainty concerning his cult.], and, at the queen’s direction, was decently and reverently laid to rest in the same church. An ancient inscription engraved on Parian marble in our possession makes this known to anyone who wishes to read it.

39. Thereafter the elder Clotharius, son of the aforementioned Crotechildis, raised to the throne of the kingdom and the most faithful executor and heir of his mother’s devotion, after his mother’s death, erected above the venerable memory of blessed Germanus, through the hands of Saint Desiderius, then bishop of that same city [Col. 1226B], a *freda* at royal expense [Note: [Col. 1226D] *Freda*, as Cangius demonstrates, is an ornament or canopy, customarily placed in the form of a small shrine over the coffins and reliquaries of the saints.]. It was most elegantly decorated with gold and silver and endured even into our own age, identifying through an inscription in letters carved upon it the patron and the servant of the work.

Moreover, the memorable wife of that same Clotharius, named Ingundis, famous not only for her religion but also for her exceptional generosity and care toward churches, presented at the same time many ornaments of vessels and vestments to the tomb of blessed Germanus. Among them we saw an outstanding chalice, fashioned of splendid gold and gems, bearing in letters set with precious stones the memory of the queen, who had devoutly bestowed this gift upon blessed Germanus through the hands of the aforementioned bishop Desiderius.

[Note: [Col. 1225D] Clotharius I, who eventually became monarch of Gaul, had several wives after Ingundis, who was the first. [Col. 1226C] That Clotharius died in the year of Christ 561. How, then, could either his first wife, or he himself, who long outlived her, have expressed their generosity toward this place through the hands of Saint Desiderius, bishop of Auxerre, who, according to the *History of the Bishops* of that city, chapter 20, first began to occupy the see toward the end of the sixth century? Or perhaps Clotharius I is incorrectly understood instead of Clotharius II? Yet Ingundis is not known to have been the wife of the latter. Or was Desiderius mistakenly placed here for some other predecessor of his? Or should we rather say that there is a serious chronological error concerning Desiderius, as other such errors frequently occur in this *History*? Certainly the letter of Saint Gregory the Great cited there does not stand in the way, as though it were addressed to Desiderius, bishop of Auxerre. For, according to Gregory’s *Register*, book VII, among the letters written in the second indiction, that is, in the year of Christ 599, this same letter, number 116, is found addressed simply to Desiderius the bishop, without the location of his see. Mabillon, however, thinks that the Desiderius mentioned there is not our man but the bishop of Vienne. See him in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 622, no. 34.]

40. No one could reasonably doubt that this place, because of the privilege of possessing the sacred body, has always been most frequented for the glory of its miracles. Since these could neither be gathered by number [Note: [Col. 1226D] See the corresponding testimony of Saint Nicetius, bishop of Trier, cited above in the commentary on the Acts of Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, §1, no. 3, p. 51.] nor could the names of the persons on whom they were performed be retained—for whatever is quickly and readily obtained tends to become cheap—they have fallen into torpor, covered alike by the squalor of neglect and oblivion. Yet that they were exceedingly numerous can at least be inferred from the fact that some elderly men are still alive who affirm that they saw countless tokens of miracles performed hanging before the doors of this sacred temple. These tokens, deposited there by possessed persons, the weak, the deaf, and the mute after their recovery, long preserved a useful memorial of the divine benefits bestowed upon the sick [Col. 1227A].

41. Finally, Gregory, bishop of Tours, a most inquisitive investigator and diligent editor of miracles, records several performed in memory of this blessed Father and through his agency. We have preferred to report them in his words rather than ours, lest by exchanging the work without gain we diminish the credibility of the matter.

[Col. 1227B] “The glorious confessor Germanus,” he says, “died in the city of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1227C] Thus all our manuscripts read. In Gregory himself, however, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 41, from which this is copied, *Rome* is read instead of *Ravenna*. But that reading is wrong, at least in most manuscript and printed copies.]. From there his body was taken up and, after sixty days, brought to the city of Auxerre and committed to burial.

“During the time of Queen Teudechilda [Note: [Col. 1227D] Queen Teudechilda—not the one whom Charibert, king of Paris and son of Clotharius I, took from a humble station and introduced, like several others, alongside his lawful wife Ingoberga; he died in the year 567, and Gregory of Tours reports more about her in his *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 26. Rather, this was another woman, the daughter of Theodoric, king of Austrasia until the year 534, and sister of Theodebert, who died in 547. See more about her in Valesius, *Frankish History*, book VII. Consult also the notes on Gregory’s *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 26, in the Paris edition of his works of 1699.], a certain Nonninus, a tribune from Auvergne, returning from Francia after paying tribute to the queen, visited the city of Auxerre solely for religious reasons. Having prostrated himself at the tomb of blessed Germanus and prayed for a very long time, he drew a *tigre* [Note: [Col. 1227D] *Tigre*, that is, a large knife, as is noted in the margin of the Lyon manuscript by the same hand that wrote the text. Cangius understands it as a sword in his *Glossary*.] from its sheath and, without anyone seeing, struck the stone that lay over the venerable tomb. A small fragment having been knocked from it, he became rigid as bronze, so that he could not move any limb whatsoever or utter a voice [Note: [Col. 1227D] *Vindicare*: thus the Lyon manuscript reads, while Valcellensis and Chifflet’s manuscript have *vendicare*, which amounts to the same thing. It means either *vindicare* or *vendicare*, to make something one’s own and turn it to one’s own use, so that one may use it according to one’s will. This is certainly preferable to the reading found in the printed Gregory, *judicare*, or in the Labbean edition of Hericus, *indicare*. [Col. 1228C]].

“When the boys saw him lying on the ground in this condition, they did not know what had happened to him. One of them approached, and when he addressed him, he received no answer. Then, while he remained rigid, understanding in his heart that he had been condemned, he made a vow, saying: ‘I know that I have acted presumptuously, blessed confessor; but devotion required me to presume. Therefore, if you deign to absolve me and permit me to return safely to my own people with your favor, I shall place these relics in the basilica and take care to celebrate your feast most devoutly every year.’

“The holy man understood this silent prayer locked within him, absolved him, and permitted him to depart unharmed. He returned and placed those relics in the church [Col. 1228A], and faithfully celebrated the saint’s feast every year.”

42. At a certain time we went to the aforementioned basilica, where the relics had been placed, together with Avitus, my maternal uncle, bishop of Auvergne [Note: [Col. 1228D] Thus our manuscripts again read, although in Labbe’s edition and in Gregory’s own edition only *with Avitus the bishop* is found. Gregory had Saint Gallus as his paternal uncle and calls him so; Gallus preceded Avitus in governing the church of Clermont. But he never calls this Saint Avitus, whom he nevertheless frequently mentions as his teacher in sacred letters, either his maternal uncle or by any other title of kinship.]. When the holy bishop entered fasting at about the tenth hour, all of us who entered with him breathed in the fragrance of lilies and roses. We do not doubt that this was granted to us through the merits of blessed Germanus, for it was the ninth month. It occurred in the village of Musciacas [Note: [Col. 1228D] Musciacas, commonly Mauzac or Mozac, in the Riom district among the Auvergnats.]. Gregory relates it as follows.

Having prefaced this, let us now transfer the course of our writing to events that either came near to or reached our own age. Since spiritual things are sown among spiritual things, however, and the dignity of the Lord is measured in the integrity of his servants, I judge it fitting briefly to show that, toward the end especially, the divine favor toward the inhabitants of this place shone forth clearly through the merits of so great a Father [Col. 1228B].

43. A certain little boy was named Esopus. When he had scarcely reached five years of age, his parents dedicated him to the holy order, and, as his tender age permitted, he was trained in the first letters more through play than through serious instruction [Note: [Col. 1228D] Chifflet reads *ludo quamserio*. But why could the meaning not be that a boy scarcely five years old was not instructed seriously but through play, since at that age he was incapable of serious instruction? This shows clearly how tender an age pious parents once considered suitable for dedicating their children to the holy Order, that is, to the discipline of monks. Hericus made the same statement about himself above in the Epilogue to the metrical Life, no. 176.].

He was seized by dysentery and endured the distress of severe illness in his tiny body. One morning at dawn, when one of the elders asked him how he was, he replied that everything was in good health; that shortly before he had recited from memory the whole sequence of his lesson, which had brought him great cheerfulness and confidence. When asked what his lesson had concerned, he recited the first verse of Psalm 117, beyond what one could expect from his age, saying: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

Since he could neither have read this from writing nor, given his age and lack of practice, have conveyed it from memory, he was asked from whom he had learned it. “Do you not see,” he said, “the little ones leaning upon the steps of this most exalted ladder and striving toward heavenly things?” He said no more; and, just as he brought his words to an end, he also brought his life to an end.

It is certain that angelic spirits, appearing in the form of boys, were shown to him as pleasing to God in their innocence, and that they received his soul, freed from the fetters of frailty [Col. 1229A]. We know that the hour of approaching death was also revealed to others, so clearly that, while they were still alive, they themselves voluntarily anticipated the baths and changes of clothing customarily provided for the dead.

To some, the person of that same most blessed Father appeared with an exceedingly beautiful countenance, venerable white hair, and pontifical dignity, bringing them great consolation and no little security. We have perhaps touched on this among many examples without treating it as extraordinary, so that it may be evident that he anxiously cares for the servants who devoutly obey him. Let us proceed from here to the remaining matters.

44. Immoderate appetite for food, by which we all succumb to sin and death, is considered a light and trivial matter; but the less it is guarded against, the more cruelly it destroys. The holy man extinguished it in himself and also took care to teach that it displeased him in others [Col. 1229B].

As is customary among the faithful, who express their devotion by whatever means they can, apples flourishing with autumnal freshness had been laid before the tomb of the sacred body. Different in kind and most pleasing also in fragrance, they offered those who approached a double delight to sight and smell. Meanwhile, as crowds customarily streamed in for the feast of the blessed bishop and those who were permitted approached to kiss the pavement of the sacred tomb with religious veneration, a certain peasant from the countryside called Nantilla—which is not far from the city—happened to be present.

Attracted by the temptation to see and eat, he stealthily thrust his hand among the sacred objects and snatched an apple. As though he intended to indulge his appetite with it, he departed. Punishment immediately followed his presumption: when he had satisfied his desire by the unlawful eating of the apple, he was deprived of the use of speech and became mute, miserably recognizing himself guilty of the offense [Col. 1229C].

A year brought an end to his calamity. When the annual spectacle of the same solemnity returned, he went back to the saint’s tomb, washed away his guilt with tears, and, bound by many vows, carried away both his speech and forgiveness. This was not known beforehand, until the man on whom it had been performed disclosed the sequence of events. It took place on the feast that occurs on the Kalends of October, a feast that the ancient authority of our predecessors commended as more splendid than the others because of the deposition of his sacred body.

45. There is said to be a noble estate in the district of the Vexin called Cordibilias [Col. 1229D]. One of its inhabitants, as he was reaching the years of puberty, was afflicted with an unfortunate weakness of the knees. He hastened to the joys of the aforementioned feast and was restored to his natural uprightness, of which he was especially deprived; he returned home carrying with him the benefits of the health he had desired.

46. We are instructed by the teaching of the prince of the apostles to exercise steadfastly spiritual and unfailing vigilance against the aged stratagems of the malicious enemy. Like a lion always hostile to the Lord’s sheepfolds, he seizes, tears apart, and shuts out anyone who is unwary and negligent [Col. 1230A]. We are warned by this example to avoid his traps, as deceptive as they are subtle.

A certain inhabitant of the Senonais, diligently attending to his livestock and industriously managing his household affairs, happened to place his own son in charge of providing pasture and food for the pigs. One day before dawn, as is customary in such circumstances, he woke the boy from sleep and ordered him to drive the pigs to pasture. The boy, seized by an extremely violent thirst, hurried to a bucket, drew a drink of water, and swallowed it without first making the sign of salvation. The heat of the burning thirst—for, as is clear, the demon was inciting it—had invaded the boy’s marrow.

It is grievous to relate: in the same miserable draught he swallowed both the plague and the drink. Immediately struck down by the demon and tormented for a very long time, he was placed in chains [Col. 1230B] and confined in very strong restraints.

47. After he had been oppressed for some time by restless misery, his parents, inspired with wiser counsel, decided that he should be taken to the famous memorial of Saint Germanus. They believed, with complete truth, that unclean spirits yield before the presence of the sacred body, whose power and merits they were known to fear frequently.

When they had done this, they laid the boy, stretched out on the ground, before the venerable tomb, earnestly accompanying the sum of their vows with abundant prayer and tears. The brothers whose duty it was to watch over the holy place through religious vigils, moved both by the boy’s torment and by his parents’ devotion, approached closely. Applying the ecclesiastical exorcisms, they prayed that relief might be granted to the wretched boy through the power of the sacred bishop.

After a very brief passage of time [Col. 1230C], he rose unharmed, and returned home with his joyful parents carrying the happiness of the health he had received. Many still survive who confess, on the strength of sufficiently well-supported testimony, that they were present at the event.

48. I would consider it wrong to pass over a matter that must be wholly avoided and that many have unquestionably experienced, since it is evident that even in the smallest matters the greatest manifestation of divine power sometimes appears.

Since it is plainly known that the memory of the holy confessor radiates miracles continually, both within and outside the church, he is also proved to be no sluggish avenger of perjurers. It is thus clearly evident that the pledges, or relics, of the saints are sometimes assailed by human presumption only at the assailant’s peril.

For if anyone, enticed by greed or driven by obstinacy of mind, resolved to support a lie and dared to complete an oath even while touching the door-ring [Note: [Col. 1229D] I have not yet discovered what *armilla januae* means. I suspect that it signifies a ring—for *armilla* is also used for a ring—by which a door is customarily pulled by those leaving, so that it can be closed from outside. The sense would therefore be: if anyone, standing outside at the door while the church or chapel of Saint Germanus was closed, and even touching the door-ring, dared to swear falsely and invoke the holy bishop as witness to a lie, then, because he was guilty of perjury, etc.], vengeance immediately overtakes him. It seizes him either through loss of his property or through damage to his bodily health, without delay, and, entangling him in harsh bonds, either makes him free through prompt satisfaction or condemns him to near-term destruction [Col. 1230D].

This power was not earned only by the presence of his intact body. Wherever his memory is honored for its holiness, it has likewise obtained such reverence that, in a basilica consecrated under the name of Germanus, scarcely anyone, however savage, dares to swear falsely [Col. 1231A].

49. How powerfully he displays his presence around the enclosure of his own tomb has been experienced most particularly and clearly by those who, to speak truly, have been assigned the special guardianship of the holy of holies.

For the oil of the lamp hanging before the sacred tomb has often been found to have increased. It remained unextinguished for nearly fifteen days and nights and suffered no diminution whatsoever.

50. Nor should I pass over without due attention how much diligence the sacred place requires in its service. If the lamp that specifically serves the most holy body should happen to go out during the night, the custodians are granted no rest and no opportunity to indulge in sleep until the deficiency in the light has been repaired with greater care [Col. 1231B].

At times they are pressed more severely, as though by the thrust of someone’s hand, so that no one may safely doubt that the services owed to the place must be performed properly and without negligence.

Why should I mention that some who knelt more privately in prayer before the venerable altar of this tomb have felt, through a shaking of the place, the efficacy of their prayers and the attention of heavenly favor?

I omit the fact that invocation of this sacred name has also brought the most immediate assistance to many who were absent and near to danger.

51. It is very widely known that the bread of the same monastery provides many wonderful remedies for the sick [Col. 1231C]. Indeed, if someone, however severely bedridden, should feel a desire for it, this is considered a most effective sign that recovery is approaching.

We do not attribute this to the holiness of the inhabitants. Rather, the faith of those who devoutly ask obtains such things, and the merit of blessed Germanus, in whose name the bread is inscribed, is able to accomplish far greater things.

These are your gifts, Christ, who are wonderful in the power of your saints. While you glorify them through miracles, you inflame us to imitate them.

These excerpts concerning what has happened or is happening around his sacred body have, by the assistance of brevity, perhaps escaped the weariness of distaste. Let us therefore touch briefly upon those places where his relics are venerated [Note: [Col. 1231D] It therefore seems that there was once some portion of Saint Germanus’s relics in each of the churches about which Hericus now writes,] and hasten more quickly toward the end of the little book.

## CHAPTER V. Miracles performed in other churches of Saint Germanus throughout Gaul

[Col. 1231D]

52. In the monastery of Meleredum [Note: [Col. 1231D] Meleredum, also called Meleretum, Melerense, and so forth; now commonly Moutier, in the district of Auxerre. Concerning its foundation, see the monk Robert in his *Chronology* after the year 729, and more fully Mabillon in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 721, no. 47, and elsewhere.], the principal church is known to be dedicated under the name of this most excellent Father.

That monastery is both accessible and familiar to the Britons who tirelessly make their way to Rome [Col. 1232A]. Among their company there came a certain deaf man. Since he had no other lodging, he spent the night before the church doors, with a stone beneath his head. When daylight returned, he awoke; and soon, greatly rejoicing, he realized that through the intercession of blessed Germanus he had been freed from the affliction of deafness.

The stone that had lain beneath his head bore witness to his recovered health, for when he rose it appeared stained with blood. He gave votive thanks for his restored health and immediately continued on his way with his companions, who were making haste. The continued presence of many who still survive and saw the event confirms its truth.

53. In the district of Latice, which belongs to the diocese of Langres (commonly called Langres), there is a well-known estate called Ladriacus. There stands a church consecrated to the relics of this most precious bishop [Col. 1232B]. It is situated on a mountain summit and lies some distance from the village.

For this reason certain bishops of Langres attempted to demolish it and build another basilica in its place within the village. They wasted their efforts, however, since the attempt was made not once or twice but repeatedly. Whenever they tried to remove the sacred altar stone in order to take out the relics, it remained fixed and immovable with such weight that one could easily perceive that divine providence had not permitted the ancient worship of the place to be transferred elsewhere.

At this site, where miracles both numerous and great are continually performed, divine benefits are poured out even more abundantly upon the devout crowds who gather for the splendid feast of the Kalends of October.

54. On one occasion, when the people were gathering as usual for the annual day of that celebration, a woman from the village called Marcenniacus—which is not far from the place just mentioned—happened to attend, having been deprived of her sight.

She entered the basilica and, with abundant prayers and vows, begged a remedy for her blindness. While the faithful were carrying out the appointed vigils and the whole assembly watched, blood began to flow drop by drop from her eyes.

Within a very few hours all the darkness had been dispelled. She deserved to see the radiance of returning daylight and to view everything clearly. She spent that day in thanksgiving and praise; and, after completing the salutary rites of her restoration, she returned home [Col. 1232D] full of vows.

55. The following year brought back the joys of the same feast. Among the crowds hurrying there, a certain member of the household of Saint Mammes [Note: [Col. 1232D] Saint Mammes, or Mammas; understand “of the basilica.” This martyr became famous in Gaul after Queen Saint Radegund obtained his relics from the East in the sixth century. In the twelfth century, after also obtaining notable relics of him, the people of Langres dedicated their cathedral church under his name.], a tenant of that same village, weak and crawling with his whole body, happened to arrive.

As he turned his heart toward God, he recovered, through the intercession of the blessed bishop, the support of natural uprightness in the presence of many witnesses.

Remedies repeatedly received by those suffering from daily, third-day, or fourth-day fevers made the place extremely well attended by an unending stream of the fever-stricken [Col. 1233A]. No one who approached the holy threshold full of faith returned without relief.

56. The rash have also learned by experience that no violence may be done to that place or to anything belonging to it.

Once, as a certain man was traveling with his companions, one of them, whose duty it was, attempted to lead the horses with which they were traveling into the church’s meadow. When one of the peasants told him that the meadow belonged to blessed Germanus and that, out of respect for so great a name, he should refrain from invading it, the man thought that mere words were being addressed to him and nevertheless led the horses in.

The first horse to enter, as soon as it seized the grass with its teeth, was afflicted with a condemnable deformity: its throat was twisted crosswise into the shape of the letter X [Col. 1233B].

The keeper of the horses, seeing what had happened, drove the others away as quickly as possible and reported the outcome to their owner. Repenting of the offense, the owner brought a candle as long as a horse as a penalty, made satisfaction to Saint Germanus, and obtained the restoration of his mount—that is, his horse.

We have touched briefly on a few of the many examples, lest we seem to have passed over a place distinguished by such privileges.

57. We are compelled to mention Pauliacum, an estate in the Senonais, if only briefly, not so much because of its proximity as because of its importance.

That estate, subject to the authority of blessed Germanus, also has a church famous under his name and outstanding for its miracles [Col. 1233C]. Since these are difficult or impossible to explain either by number or in sequence, we omit what antiquity has worn away and briefly touch on a few of those about which, should doubt arise, we can overwhelm it with the multitude of witnesses.

An inhabitant of the Auxerre district, named Peter, had lost the natural ability to walk because of contracted knees. He made vows and crawled to the holy threshold. Soon, freed from his infirmity, he rejoiced that, through the patronage of blessed Germanus, he had obtained the sound use of his legs. The *sabbella*—an unidentified form of aid—which had long hung before the doors remained for a long time as evidence of what had occurred.

From a neighboring estate called Blariacus [Col. 1233D], a woman named Nonnula, rendered completely helpless by contraction of her entire body, had herself carried in a litter to the same basilica. Soon restored by the merit of blessed Germanus to the proper functions of her limbs, she departed full of health and joy.

58. Another woman from the same estate, called Alda after her parents, likewise lamenting the debility of her contracted body, asked to be carried there in a litter. With the support of the present healing power, her limbs yielded and returned to their former condition, and she departed healthy and joyful.

From the Auxerre district, from a place called Pratilis, another woman named Berlindis, whose limbs were likewise contracted, was brought by conveyance to the aforementioned basilica. She devoted herself to prayer and laid her vows before the Saint [Col. 1234A]. Soon, having experienced God’s presence, she recovered and grew strong after being restored to the natural use of her limbs.

From the estate of Lusciniacum, a woman named Tedvisa, whose entire body was contracted, had been brought here by the fame of the miracles. With the merit of the blessed Father assisting her, she obtained the beauty and uprightness of her limbs and demonstrated her awareness of the benefits by serving there for several days.

Many also repeatedly proved that the majesty of this place is not insignificant, having been afflicted by various attacks of fever. A certain Alcharius, wasting away hopelessly under a quartan fever, happened to come there. He entered the church, kept vigil, and proclaimed with great praise that through the most powerful aid of the blessed Father he had been restored to health as quickly as possible.

Agius, a priest of that place, had long suffered from the weakness of a tertian fever. When he devoted himself to God, he was promptly granted healing through the intercession of the blessed bishop and soon escaped the persistent disease [Col. 1234B].

Beatus, a cleric of that basilica, was severely tormented by the daily recurrence of his illness. He sought divine remedies through blessed Germanus and suddenly felt himself freed from his restless affliction.

59. If I wished to mention everyone in our own time who has been rescued from troubles of this kind at that place, I believe the number of persons who would present themselves would produce weariness. We should therefore spare such details and turn to matters more useful for edification.

A woman of that place named Doda, treating the sacred holy days carelessly, dared to violate by her customary woolworking even the majesty of the Lord’s Day [Col. 1234C], which all Christians are especially bound to observe.

The severity of punishment immediately followed her presumption. Her hands, accustomed to unlawful work, were soon deprived of their necessary functions. The result was that they could not satisfy the needs of nature, although they had not feared to provoke the Author of nature by profaning his day.

At last the wretched woman acknowledged her guilt and sought the aid of blessed Germanus. She bound herself by a vow not to repeat such actions. Through the mercy granted by the most compassionate Father, she recovered, in the sight of many, both the health of her hands and forgiveness for her crime.

Because she had likewise profaned the same day, a woman named Nonnula [al.: *nonnulla*, “a certain woman”] deserved to have her hands contracted. Conscious of her offense, she went to the church and multiplied her vows. Through the intervention of the blessed Father, she returned home safe and sound, corrected in her conduct [Col. 1234D].

Another woman, named Fredegardis, was punished with the same penalty for a similar crime. Repenting of what she had done and not despairing of mercy, she went to the place mentioned above. She burdened her face with tears and heaven with her groaning. The priest of the place offered public prayer for the recovery of the unfortunate woman. Through the intervention of blessed Germanus, she obtained both forgiveness for her offense and the restoration of health to her hands.

60. That the things belonging to this place are sacred and must not be improperly transferred to other uses has been demonstrated by the frequent chastisement of presumptuous persons.

The priest of the place, as the mind of the foolish is accustomed to be careless about such matters, placed a halter around a horse’s head. This was the rope that had formerly been used to ring the church bell [Col. 1235A].

It immediately became clear that something once made sacred was not suitable for domestic use. For as soon as it was placed on the horse’s head, everything enclosed by the rope was suddenly consumed, so that the entire flesh, together with the hide and hair, seemed to have been cut away down to the bones by a sword.

Thus that harmless horse thereafter preserved the signs of another person’s presumption, since it was never again able to acquire either flesh in full measure, sound hide, or a covering of hair.

From the countryside called Villaris, a woman named Maria came to this place under the pretext of prayer. Finding an opportunity for sacrilege, she stole a linen cloth from the ambo. Returning home with the stolen object [Col. 1235B], she girded her profane loins with the sacred covering.

Immediately, when all her limbs were rendered powerless, she felt the punishment’s presence through the destruction of her body. Soon repenting of what she had done, she acknowledged her guilt and asked to be carried back to the place she had previously approached wickedly. She publicly confessed her offense and expiated the sacrilege with tears.

Thus, through the intervention of the priest and the people, she obtained mercy. Thereafter, through the compassion of blessed Germanus, she departed not only unharmed but also chastened. By such and similar privileges, that place, constantly frequented, easily claimed for itself a renowned title of reverence.

61. Moreover, in the district of Rouen there is a royal estate which the inhabitants, on account of the antiquity of its palace, call the Old House. A chapel adjoining the palace, famous under the name of the most blessed Germanus, has deservedly acquired for itself the highest veneration through its distinguished abundance of miracles [Col. 1235C]. One example will suffice for the brevity we have proposed—an event we are compelled to mention because we know it to be publicly known.

King Charles [Note: [Col. 1235] Charles, surnamed the Bald, to whom the author dedicated this work. Mabillon places this meeting in the Benedictine Annals under the year 851, no. 27.] had perhaps come there to negotiate with Herispo, leader of the Britons, and to conduct serious business concerning the affairs of the kingdom. As is customary at such a great assembly, an excessive crowd of poor people flocked there from every direction. Among them was a mute girl, who had learned by a contrivance for seeking alms to moderate the familiar misfortune of poverty.

Since she found no opportunity for lodging, she withdrew within the chapel precinct. Around midnight, the most holy Germanus appeared to her as she kept vigil and, soothing her with gentle speech, said: “The hospitality denied you by human beings [al., by all people], I shall make up for with the kindness I am able to offer.” Having said this, he gently lifted the mute girl’s chin with his hand and spat into her mouth; then he immediately withdrew the visible presence of his manifestation [Col. 1235D]. Through the power of the remedy, the innermost parts of her throat were ruptured and discharged a very great quantity of blood, so much so that the entire surface of the pavement seemed to have been flooded with it.

62. When the shadows had receded and daylight returned, the still-unrecognized outcome of the miracle was more clearly revealed by its indications. The girl had recovered the use of speech and related in order what had happened to her; and the blood that had flowed in a stream from the mouth of the speaker was still extremely fresh upon the pavement, providing the clearest evidence of the deed [Col. 1236A].

Meanwhile, when some people questioned her more inquisitively about the appearance in which blessed Germanus had shown himself to her, she testified that she had seen a person most splendid in the dignity of his face, of medium height, beautiful in the quality of his hair, yet venerable because of its mixture of gray. She said that she had noticed these and other features in him; and certain people who had once been privileged to handle his sacred body when it was being transferred asserted that they had seen them to be exceedingly similar.

There were as many witnesses to this miracle as could come from every part of the kingdom to witness this general assembly.

## CHAPTER VI  
### Continuation of the miracles performed in various places dedicated there to his name

[Col. 1236B]

63. The most holy and illustrious Remigius, the precious bishop of Rheims, built with his own hand a basilica in honor of the most blessed Germanus at the place where he had decided to be buried, situated about a mile from the city of Rheims, as the most ancient authority of his Testament reveals. This basilica remains as renowned for the splendor of its miracles as for its great antiquity.

It is also commonly known that the feasts of these two pontiffs shine upon the world together on the Kalends of October. To celebrate them with the customary spectacle, the people had gathered as usual at the place mentioned above, where, specifically, the venerable body of the most holy Remigius rests. After the evening services had been completed, it happened that the entire multitude of the people was expelled from the church enclosure by the vigilance of the custodians, as is customary in monasteries [Col. 1236C].

Some friends had brought in a certain cripple on a vehicle. After he had been driven out of the church of blessed Remigius, they carried him into the aforesaid basilica of Saint Germanus, which stood before the doors. Keeping watch there for a while during the night, he was restored to health through the merits of the most blessed Germanus and thereafter was permitted to enjoy the natural function of walking.

Thus the man of apostolic eminence also commended the greatness of his dignity by his own deed, showing that on the feast day of Remigius he held a place of special distinction, a day which he wished to make glorious also through the privileges of his own merits.

The places whose mention we have inserted in this little work abound in almost continual miracles. Yet we have decided to touch upon only those which, being widely known to all, have deserved to escape every uncertainty [Col. 1236D].

64. In the suburb of Soissons stands a church of Blessed Germanus. A tradition conscious of its antiquity claims that it was once built by twelve famous merchants of the world. Since they were constantly traveling from kingdom to kingdom and frequently pitched their tents near the bank of the Axona, they decided to establish a memorial of their repeated presence at that place: pooling their expenses, they would build a basilica to blessed Germanus, trusting that by his merits and prayers they would be especially protected amid the dangers of land and sea.

We have learned a great many things concerning the holiness of this place, but the brevity of this work does not permit us to explain them [Col. 1237A]. We shall mention a few matters which, through the priest of that basilica, we know to have been faithfully established.

This priest himself had gone out one day to inspect the church’s fields. He discovered that, through the deceit of a certain neighbor, the field boundaries had been altered and confused, not without injury to his own portion. After once again making a lawful declaration in the presence of witnesses, he set up a stone on the boundary. Concerned for the case, he said: “Holy Germanus, if any care for your priest holds you, protect these boundaries of your field from the slanderous encroachment of those who cross them.” Having said this, he returned home.

65. Meanwhile, the neighbor, driven on by the sharpness of his greed, came to the field by night, removed the stone from the boundary, and moved it far away, improperly enlarging his own property and narrowing what belonged to another [Col. 1237B].

When day returned, the priest came back. He saw that the boundary had been violated and, unable to tolerate this repeated act of audacity, said in anger: “Holy Germanus, had I not entrusted this matter to your faith?” The moment he had finished speaking in the field, punishment already struck the sacrilegious man within his own household walls. He was seized by sudden pains and, with all his limbs contracted, was deprived of the support of his strength.

Soon remembering his rash act, he summoned his friends and begged for salutary counsel. Through his friends the matter was brought before the priest, and they humbly implored him to provide compassionate help for the wretched man. The priest declared that he knew no more immediate remedy than that the man, having made his vows, should go to the church of the one whose offense had clearly caused him to suffer such things.

Carried there on a litter, he arrived and, after performing penance there for several days [Col. 1237C], earned mercy. Restored afterward to health, he departed—not merely corrected himself, but destined to serve as an example to the others, so that they would not thereafter dare to commit anything of the kind.

66. This same priest, while celebrating the solemn office one Sunday night in the church, was overcome by a light sleep. He sensed that he had been prompted by the arrival of someone and warned to enter his house quickly.

He immediately rose, seized a candle, and entered his house. There he found thieves in the bedroom, packing up the bedclothes and whatever garments they had found. He handed them over to custody, returned to the church, and carefully completed the remainder of the office.

It is clear that blessed Germanus took thought for the minister of his basilica, lest, while he attended to divine praise, he should suffer losses in his household property [Col. 1237D].

67. It is less useful to recount things merely heard unless some matters perceived by the eyes are also included. On the day before the Kalends of August, the passing of blessed Germanus was being celebrated at the city of Soissons with fervent devotion. Since the celebration of divine praise had continued toward evening both in the city churches and in those of the suburbs and monasteries, I became anxious and thought of crossing the Axona and hastening to the aforesaid basilica, lest—as I was considering—because of the priest’s absence the evening offices might perhaps be lacking there [Col. 1238A].

Taking several brothers with me, I hurried anxiously. As we were entering the church atrium, the bells gave their customary peal. We quickened our pace and approached the door, which we found closed but not bolted. We had scarcely set foot on the threshold when the bells ceased to be rung.

Looking around in every direction, we saw no one in the church. There was no other door through which anyone could have escaped. We entered the priest’s house with the utmost speed and carefully searched everything; we saw no person, but found the entire place empty. As the priest later acknowledged, he and all his household had left the empty house long before and gone into the city to dine.

While I silently pondered the matter, everyone concluded that blessed Germanus had not lacked the divine evening service, which appeared to have been openly neglected by human beings [Col. 1238B].

After the service was completed, we departed cheerfully, leaving the lamps arranged for the night and securing the doors of the church with greater care. Although my mind, conscious of the miracle, rejoiced in the inner chambers of the heart, I preferred that the heavenly portent be proclaimed by others. I did not want anyone to suspect me of having wished, as a particular servant of blessed Germanus, to magnify favor by seeking greater things from lesser ones.

68. The district of Cinomannus [Note: [Col. 1237D] The districts Cinomannicus and Cenomannicus are what is commonly called Le Maine. It borders Normandy and lesser Brittany.] is especially devoted to the merits of the most blessed Germanus and proclaims innumerable miracles of his at various places. If all of them were committed to writing, they could by themselves fill a very large volume [Col. 1238C].

In that district is the village of Cadriacus, possessing a church glorious for his miracles. Since the place has long shone through the abundance of its signs, it is frequented by the most fervent and unwearied devotion of peoples who continually flock there.

Those who have very often seen it testify that the walls of the entire basilica, inside and out, are covered with cloths and linens [Note: [Col. 1237D] *Pallis*, that is, hangings. See Du Cange.]. The devotion of the faithful, in gratitude for the heavenly gifts of healing they have received, hangs these in the sacred place.

Because the building was constructed within a narrow enclosure and could not accommodate the gathering crowds, the inhabitants of the place surrounded it on both sides with wooden porticoes.

On one occasion Vivianus the prince [Note: [Col. 1237D] This Vivianus was a duke of Charles the Bald. He was killed in battle against Herispo, duke of Brittany, in the year 851, according to the Chronicle of Ademar in Labbe’s *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum librorum*, vol. II, pp. 161 ff.] came there. He then ruled that estate and, intending to sit down to dinner, ordered the hawks (*capos*) [Note: [Col. 1238D] Etymologists, together with Du Cange, frequently teach that *capos* are called falcons, from *capere*, “to seize.” Labbe reads “birds”; I prefer to follow our manuscripts.]—commonly called falcons, and brought there with him—to be placed in the basilica’s porticoes [Col. 1238D].

Having done this, he devoted himself to the banquet. When he rose from it, he found all the falcons dead, hanging from the same snares in which they had been caught.

The prince’s rashness was punished by the loss of a pleasure he valued greatly; this brought him sorrow but astonishment to the others. The most holy Germanus, vindicating reverence for his own place, clearly showed how displeasing savage rapacity was to him, pursuing even in birds that live by seizing prey the same vice with such severity.

69. He is also so great an avenger of perjurers that no one dares to swear—even to the truth—at the altar of his basilica [Col. 1239A]. Yet if some have attempted to swear at least at the church door, some have soon expired, struck by unavoidable vengeance; others have been rendered weak and paid the penalty for their profane audacity by suffering permanent incapacity.

Very many blind people recovered light at that very place; the lame, the use of their legs; lepers, the cleansing of their polluted skin; and those suffering from chills—that is, feverish people—health.

We have touched on these matters briefly so that this place, made illustrious by daily benefits, would not be excluded from our remembrance. But in the districts of Cinomannus, Anjou, and Bayeux [Note: [Col. 1239D] These territories are well known: Bayeux, commonly called *Bajocasinum*, lies in Normandy; Cenomannus, as I have said, adjoins Normandy; and Anjou, commonly called Anjou, likewise adjoins Cenomannus.], they most certainly assert that the glory of the most blessed Germanus is venerated by the whole people almost more abundantly there than—if one may say so—in the place where his holy limbs lie buried. So numerous are the miracles performed through him in these regions that they cannot even be touched upon in words, much less inserted into books [Col. 1239B].

70. Nor should we pass over without thought the fact that small portions given as relics from the shrine of the sacred body have at times shone forth through heavenly miracles. We remember that, when a certain distinguished man requested relics of blessed Germanus, a splinter [Note: [Col. 1239D] Thus the manuscripts read. *Astula* is a word commonly used by medieval writers for a fragment; see Du Cange.] of cypress wood was given to him by the chief keeper of the church [commonly, the treasurer]. The sacred body had once been covered with this wood.

He received it with the greatest devotion and built, on his own estate in the upper parts of the district of Auxerre, a chapel in honor of the holy bishop. The place is called Heldinnus.

One day a certain crawling girl came there. She had been afflicted by such a horrible force of weakness that, with her legs contracted and her feet twisted backward, she had entirely lost the ability to walk [Col. 1239C].

After she had remained for some time within the chapel and devoted herself more earnestly to prayer, the structure of her joints and nerves suddenly burst apart so violently that one would have thought something fractured had fallen into pieces. The bones of her joints themselves burst through the thickness of her skin with blood so forcefully that it seemed as though the wretched skin had been pierced by as many little spikes.

At that moment she was almost lifeless. Shortly afterward, however, having recovered the functions of her limbs, she walked about here and there and dedicated a great proclamation of the miracle to the whole surrounding region.

From then on, the place, rich in miracles and renowned for gatherings, also claimed for itself a special reverence in divine worship.

71. No one unfamiliar with the region can fail to know that the forests of Morvennus are filled with oratories of this kind [Note: [Col. 1239D] Valesius, in his *Notitia Galliarum*, makes Morvennus, or Morvinnus, into a very mountainous and wooded small district. He says that it belongs partly to the district of Nevers, partly to the lordship of Château-Chinon, and partly to Burgundy.] [Col. 1240D]. They are so famous that every uncertainty of the roads that can arise in wooded country is clarified by knowledge of these places, as though by a stone milestone.

Thus the most blessed Germanus, with fortunate patronage and as a guide going before, directs travelers’ journeys, orders their roads, and assists those who walk. He not only frees them from error but also protects them from the attack of dangers [Col. 1240A].

We know of several basilicas dedicated to him in these places. It is repeatedly confirmed, both by the frequency of miracles and by the testimony of many people, that oil often flows abundantly there. We consider it superfluous to mention the expulsion of fevers, since this benefit is now regarded as an everyday occurrence rather than a miracle.

We also know of other basilicas spread throughout the vastness of that solitude. The less human cultivation is bestowed upon them, the more powerfully the presence of divinity is revealed in them.

72. For even when the lamps there happen to be lit late, or when, after being lit, they are extinguished, they have very often been discovered to be kindled again by heavenly agency. The church bells also sometimes ring without anyone striking them, reproving by spontaneous service the dangerous negligence of the custodians toward the divine hours [Col. 1240B].

Thus it plainly appears that, when human diligence ceases, the guardianship of angels is not absent from the place.

Nor should it be considered unworthy if even small matters are included among the great benefits of God. Blessed Germanus protects things belonging to him with such authority, even from beasts, that if a fox—as is natural in wooded country—should attack a priest’s hen, it is in no way allowed to carry off its prey. Rather, it is held fast to the spot, unable either to flee or to injure its victim, until people arrive and capture both the predator and its prey.

He acts graciously in small matters, who powerfully accomplishes the greatest things in great ones; he who is both creator and governor of universal nature does not permit even one sparrow to perish without purpose.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Miracles performed at the monastery of Saint Germanus at Montfaucon

[Col. 1240C]

73. I should not pass over Falcon’s Mountain, as it has been called from ancient times, lest I seem to have suppressed a noble place, rich in miracles, through negligence as well as forgetfulness. That monastery, exalted by the merits of the most blessed Germanus, is adorned with miracles just as it is made illustrious by his name.

There, much glory of miracles and many benefits are bestowed upon mortals from heaven. The blind have frequently received sight; the weak, restoration; the deaf, hearing; and those suffering from chills have received many unexpected remedies, especially those lying ill with quartan fever who have experienced more severe attacks of fever.

It must not be left unmentioned how fiercely vengeance rages against those who invade the place [Col. 1240D]. For anyone who has rashly attempted to perpetrate anything there has brought death upon himself. If anyone has attempted to rule there tyrannically, to act harshly toward the monastery’s household, or to seize ecclesiastical property, vengeance is not long delayed. He is carried off by the swiftest death and immediately pays the penalty for his sacrilegious audacity [Col. 1241A].

This is absolutely certain and proven among all the inhabitants of the place. It is repeated in their mouths like a natural proverb: whoever is violent toward holy Germanus without fearing him is either crushed by the savage teeth of wolves or immediately swallowed in the swift whirlpool of the river Meuse.

By this marvelous dispensation of the just Judge, affection of love for the holy servant of the Lord is instilled in the devout, while great fear is instilled in the wicked, restraining their criminal attempts. Let the powers of this world hear such things and learn not to inflict injury upon churches, knowing with complete certainty that God is the avenger of injuries done to his servants.

74. Moreover, a certain thief accustomed to breaking into churches, having seized an opportunity for fraud, entered the aforesaid basilica of the blessed Father and lowered by a rope a silver crown hanging before the altar [Col. 1241B]. As soon as he grasped it with profane hands, he was divinely fixed to the spot, unable either to withdraw his foot or in any way to bring his rash hands back toward himself, until the custodian of the sacred place returned and the sacrilegious man was caught together with his theft.

There is a castle called Adrian’s Castle, belonging to the authority of the monastery mentioned above.
