Although it is situated in a difficult position on the summit of a precipitous mountain, it nevertheless contains a church of blessed Germanus. Its abundant miracles have won it great reverence and honor.

A certain blind man, widely known in that region, had set out from a village called “At the Lions,” which antiquity placed at the foot of the same mountain. Hoping to regain his sight, he was hurrying over the mountain’s rocky slopes toward the basilica. But when the difficulty of the ascent prevented him from overcoming the mountain’s height, he collapsed, overcome alike by weakness and exertion, and gave his weary limbs over to sleep [Col. 1241C].

While he slept, the most merciful Germanus appeared to him and, caressing the wretched man with gentle compassion, ordered him to spare himself the labor. Then, pointing out the trunk of an old thorn tree on the side of the mountain, he commanded him to dig the earth with a staff and wash his eyes with water from the flowing spring [al., emerging stream].

Roused from sleep, he sought the place under the guidance of a boy. He dug into the earth with his staff and awaited the outcome of the miracle. A most abundant spring burst forth. He bathed his eyes in it for some time; then, when the darkness was shaken off, he enjoyed a new day.

Urged on by his vows, he climbed to the summit of the mountain, proclaimed the miracle, and heaped manifold thanks upon his restorer. That spring, exceedingly fertile in remedies, is frequented by many even from distant places; it refreshes them by bathing and delights them by drinking its water [Col. 1241D].

75. One day the lord’s deputy of that place, while devoting special effort to settling affairs, was oppressing the ecclesiastical household with unjust commands. As everyone protested and testified to the open violence by tumultuous shouting, he ordered one of those who appeared more distinguished than the rest to be tied to a stake and beaten with rods.

Moved by this cruelty, everyone fell at his feet and earnestly begged him to avert the disgrace of the beating by offering compensation from their resources [Col. 1242A]. This did not soften the man’s savagery; rather, it provoked him more bitterly.

When they were already dragging the wretched man away to violent punishment, he began to call upon the protection of blessed Germanus with anxious cries. The judge, angered, said: “Even if holy Germanus should soon come to your aid on this occasion, you will experience what blows can do in your own punishment.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when, turning aside, he fell violently and paid for the rashness of his words by the breaking of his legs. Thus blessed Germanus showed himself to be immediately present: he granted the wretched man release and subdued the insolent man by a punishment proportionate to his deserts.

When swift rumor spread the deed everywhere, a certain noble matron learned of it through a report and became puffed up with indignation. Inflaming her foolish mind with frivolous words, she burst into this complaint: “It was not fitting for Saint Germanus to have been so lenient in this matter that he destroyed a man who was pursuing his own rights with such cruelty.”

Sudden vengeance seized her blasphemous speech. For as soon as she had uttered these words in her fury and twisted her foot while speaking, avenging punishment crushed her right foot so severely that she was carried almost lifeless into her chamber in the arms of her maids [Col. 1242B].

Thus she who shortly before had complained about another’s misfortune now anxiously sought a remedy for her own calamity. The one whom she had called unjust in punishing the proud man she now proclaimed in every respect just in bringing about her own crushing.

She summoned friends and relatives, confessed the matter, rebuked her own levity of mind, and condemned the facility of her speech. At last, burdened with vows and gifts, she went to the church, expiated her crime with tears, and asked blessed Germanus for forgiveness together with health [Col. 1242C]. Before much time had passed, she experienced as merciful the one whom she had recently found severe.

Restored to health, she returned chastened to her home and taught, by the example of this recent punishment, that immoderate speech must be avoided.

76. We remember that something similar happened in a village of the district of Auxerre called Abundiacus. There a distinguished man, known to almost the entire region, had ordered one of the inhabitants of the place to be beaten cruelly. When the man called upon the assistance of the precious Father, the distinguished man was not moved; indeed, he ordered the cruel business to be hastened and mounted his horse in haste.

Before he could leave through the gate, the horse reared into the air, threw its rider from its back, and, with his hip broken sideways, cast him down in a wretched fall [Col. 1242D]. He did not deserve to recover his health until he had made satisfaction through due repentance to blessed Germanus, whose name he had despised.

Having inserted this account because of the similarity of the deed, let us return the sequence to the place that we omitted [Note: [Col. 1241D] Namely, Montfaucon.]. [Note: [Col. 1241D] Here Labbe follows with the story of a resurrected little donkey, which we shall give below in the second Appendix, no. 4 [Col. 1242D]. It was inserted here quite ineptly, contrary to the evident context of Hericus and the testimony of all our manuscripts.]

77. The lord of the aforementioned castle, indulging a wicked greed, rashly seized property belonging to the church. When the bishop of Rheims, to whose diocese that place is known to belong, learned of this, he summoned the priest and forbade him to provide the sacrilegious man with the office of Mass [Col. 1243A].

Not long afterward, the lord arrived and demanded from the priest the celebration of the customary office. When he learned that the bishop had forbidden it, he summoned the steward of the place and ordered that, after guarantees had been given, whatever had been taken from the church should be returned.

Having thus obtained the celebration of Mass, he was driven on by the spur of his evil will. He ordered that what he had shortly before commanded to be returned should again be taken away, breaking the pledge of his sworn undertaking.

He did not enjoy his satisfaction for long before punishment seized upon the sacrilege. He had scarcely returned home when, possessed by an evil spirit, he was being tormented miserably.

His wife, aware of his rashness, sent candles and vows to the church for her husband’s recovery. Yet not one of them could be lit, for the sign of divine indignation toward the wretched man persisted—an indignation he had not feared to provoke against himself by an act of sacrilegious greed [Col. 1243B].

He was finally freed from this monstrous calamity when, persuaded by the counsel of his wife and parents, he both returned to the church what he had previously taken and donated an equal amount from his lawful patrimony.

A nocturnal thief entered the same basilica and carried away with sacrilegious hands everything belonging to the adornment of the altar. When he tried to set himself on his feet as usual, divine power so entangled him that he could not leave the church atrium by any means. He therefore walked throughout the entire night and, at dawn the following morning, was found in the basilica’s portico, trembling with guilt and burdened with his theft.

Thus the robber is confounded, the booty is recovered, and blessed Germanus clearly demonstrates through evident proofs that he acts generously in his own place [Col. 1243C].

We have nothing to say concerning level and habitable places unless we demonstrate that every mountainous and difficult place—and therefore almost inaccessible to human footsteps—is accessible to the miracles of Germanus [Note: [Col. 1243D] This transition to the following narrative is found only in the Lyon manuscript.]

## CHAPTER VIII  
### His miracles that occurred in the Alps and in Britain

78. The ridges of the Pennine Alps are illuminated by his merits no less than by the whiteness of snow; this is all the more certain because it has been tested by experience. For on the mountain called Lesser Jupiter [Note: [Col. 1243D] Cluverius, in *Ancient Italy*, book I, chapter 32, identifies Summus Penninus, or Mount Jupiter—called Mont-Jou in French and Monte-Giove in Italian—with the mountain marked on geographical maps as the greater Mount Saint Bernard (*le grand Saint-Bernard*). Why, then, should that mountain not be considered Lesser Jupiter which, being not very far from the other, is called Lesser Mount Saint Bernard (*le petit Saint-Bernard*)? Through these passes lies the route from Gaul into the territory of Milan. Both, however, are marked in Savoy on the borders of the duchy of Augusta.] there is a church modest in size but great in miracles. It is known to have been built at that place because the sacred body was rested there while being carried back from Ravenna [Col. 1243D].

This church is unavoidably accessible to those traveling to Rome and returning from there, since the public road on which it stands, because of the narrowness of the route, denies travelers every opportunity to turn aside from it. Innumerable benefits of divine generosity continually shine forth there. They compensate for the harshness and solitude of the place with a rich abundance of remedies, so that one may rightly confess that the majesty of heavenly munificence is not absent even from barren rocks [Col. 1244A].

That travelers who are compelled to pass under the church’s roof by the onset of night, by the difficulty of fatigue, or by the burden of illness receive gifts of healing there is made as clear as daylight by the following fact. The priest responsible for the place usually lives on a distant plain. Whenever he climbs into the mountains to perform the sacred office as customary, he sees there many proofs of sick people recovering.

There are frequently found tablets of the mute, by shaking which they ask for alms; also litters for the crippled; sometimes the pavement is wet with blood; and votive offerings of various little gifts left at night after miracles performed at the place have established its credibility.

79. It had once been customary for the holy man to seek solitude and withdrawal from human eyes, committing the deeds he performed miraculously to secret shadows and, as far as he could, concealing all his miracles beneath the darkness of perpetual ignorance.

This surely explains why, although many of his miracles have become known to the world and could not be hidden by the obscurity of the places where they occurred, he was exposed through his miracles; nevertheless, there are innumerable others which, fleeing publicity, he did not permit to come to human knowledge. He had surpassed the measure of human possibility and enjoyed the awareness of angels and the testimony of heaven.

Even today the eminent Father preserves this custom. Although he possesses incomparable merit with God, he sometimes displays more visible signs of miracles in obscure little places bearing only the title of his name than in the place where we continually venerate the sacred presence of his ever-adorable body [Col. 1244C].

But because it is characteristic of unbelievers and of those who measure invisible things only by visible ones to seek signs like the Jews and delight only in present benefits, these benefits will always be more precious to me. My faith has now grown strong; I am resolved to enter into life; and I do not doubt that souls surpass bodies, immortal things mortal things, and things enduring things perishable, incomparably.

Accordingly, those benefits that spiritually and perpetually bless the inner person will always be dearer to me than those that bodily and temporarily relieve the outer person. No sane person can doubt that these former benefits flow abundantly, day and night, from Germanus’s tomb.

80. As we traveled through the inland regions and carefully investigated each matter, we almost excluded the Ocean, which marvelously surrounds the outermost parts of the world, from the privileges of our most excellent Father. Yet although the whole world overflows with these privileges, Britain, an island either first or greatest among all islands, rejoices in them more abundantly.

Concerning Britain, as the authority says—for it is a repeated phrase—“The shore of the Gallic coast would have been the end of the world, unless the island of Britain, by its singular size, had almost deserved the name of another world” [Note: [Col. 1244D] These are the words of Solinus in the *Polyhistor*, chapter 22.]

Britain, subject to blessed Germanus with particular devotion [Col. 1245A], testifies through many expenditures of benefits that it is indebted to his holiness: it was illuminated by his teachings; through him it was more than once cleansed of the filth of heresies; and finally it was illumined by the many-lamped light of miracles. Since these matters have been committed to writing to some extent through the efforts of distinguished teachers, they require no repetition.

One famous event is reported among the rest, knowledge of which reached us through the holy old man Mark, a bishop of that same people. He was a Briton by birth but was educated in Ireland. After long exercises in episcopal holiness, he voluntarily imposed exile upon himself.

Thus he was brought to Gaul and, attracted by the generosity of the most pious King Charles, lived an anchorite’s life at the monastery of the blessed Medard and Sebastian [Note: [Col. 1245D] He means the monastery near Soissons, famous for the relics of Saints Medard and Sebastian. Mabillon discusses it in several places in the *Benedictine Annals*.], a philosopher of singular and unparalleled holiness in our time [Col. 1245B].

This man was accustomed to relate repeatedly, often in my presence, that the most holy Germanus—“the apostle of his nation,” to use Mark’s own words—once entered the royal palace with his disciples while traveling through Britain. It was then a harsh winter, violently hostile not only to human beings but also to the very beasts.

Germanus therefore sent an intermediary to the king and requested lodging for the coming night. The king refused and, being barbarous both by race and in disposition, treated the matter as worthless. Meanwhile Germanus remained with his disciples under the open sky and endured the severity of the weather with steadfast spirits.

81. When the day had already turned toward evening, the king’s swineherd returned from the pastures, carrying from the palace to his own cottage the portion of his daily wage that he had received [Col. 1245C].

When he saw the most blessed Germanus and his disciples wasting away in the winter cold, he approached closely and humbly begged him to say who he was and for what reason he was remaining there amid such severe frost.

When he received no definite answer, he was moved by the dignity of the man and said: “I beg you, my lord, whoever you are, spare your body and be willing to enter the lodging of your servant. If my poverty has any services to offer, accept them. For I see that it matters greatly to temper the hardships of the approaching night, however humble the dwelling may be.”

Germanus did not disdain the man’s station and entered his lodging. He willingly accepted the services offered him by the poor man.

The swineherd possessed only a cow and a calf. Turning to his wife, he said: “Do you not understand what sort of guest you have received? Gird yourself, then, slaughter the only calf we have, and set it before those who are about to dine” [Col. 1245D].

She obeyed immediately, cooked the calf, and placed it on the table. The bishop, abstaining as usual, instructed the others to eat.

When the meal was over, blessed Germanus summoned the woman and ordered her to collect the calf’s bones carefully and place them on its hide before its mother in the stall.

When this had been done—wondrous to relate—the calf immediately rose and, standing beside its mother, began to eat fodder.

Then the bishop turned to both of them and said: “Without diminishing the reward of your charity, receive back the rights of hospitality, compensated for the moment by such a benefit.”

They all proclaimed the wondrous outcome of the event with a common chorus of praise.

82. On the following day the bishop returns to the palace and awaits the king’s public appearance. As he came forth from [Col. 1246B] his private apartments, Germanus met him and sternly demanded, with a forceful rebuke, why he had refused him lodging the day before. The king stood speechless in astonishment and, stunned by the man’s firmness, was unable to answer. Then Germanus, with wondrous authority, said: “Come out, and yield the royal scepters to one better.” When he hesitated, Germanus pushed him with his staff and said: “You shall come out; and, as has been determined by the Lord, you shall never again abuse royal power for all eternity.” The barbarian, fearing the heavenly authority in the bishop, immediately—that is, without delay—went out with his wife and children, and thereafter made no attempt by any means to retain possession of the palace gates. Then Germanus sent one of his disciples, summoned the swineherd with his wife, and, while the entire palace stood amazed, installed him at the summit of the kingdom. From that time to the present, kings descended from the swineherd’s stock have ruled the nation of the Britons, while God, through blessed Germanus, wondrously orders human affairs. The aforesaid bishop firmly attested under oath that these things are contained in Catholic writings preserved in Britain; and anyone who has tested his integrity will have no doubt that his words deserve credence [Note: [Col. 1246D] See also what is said about all these matters above in the Commentary, § 7.]. O man singular among the ranks of mortals! O man already displaying the very signs of divinity! He has not yet laid aside his earthly mass, and already he contends with the world together with Christ, orders powers, and disposes kingdoms. I openly declare you mad, whoever despair that peoples can be advanced by Germanus’s merit to the heavenly kingdoms, when you consider that, while still carrying an earthly body, he was able to accomplish such things.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1245]

## PROLOGUE

83. Having traversed the sequence of the preceding little book, as best I could according to the capacity of my intellect, the second book, which remains, demands personal labor—labor that must now be undertaken urgently, though it cannot yet be completed in every respect and in due sequence. For, once I have examined the matters presently before me, if anything concerning the merits of our apostolic Father should thereafter present itself, I shall diligently carry it out; and whatever it may please the Divinity to provide, I shall not hesitate to insert immediately—that is, at once—into my notes [Note: [Col. 1247D] If Hericus recorded anything about the miracles of St. Germanus after this work had been published, it must necessarily have perished together with his notes—unless you wish to suppose that Hericus inserted certain miracles into this very work after its dedication and, indeed, after the death of Charles the Bald, just as we shall note that some others were inserted in no. 90.].

Gladly, however, let me bind myself to this obligation, and may I never wish to be released from it; and, as one who is always in debt and never able to discharge it, may I escape the bonds of the body while the privilege of the highest and most ancient sanctity toward the memory of Germanus endures. He has others more suited to so great an undertaking, and, if his own were lacking, the services of outsiders would certainly volunteer themselves to his desire. Yet, when he once dealt with secular affairs, he knew how to drink from gold, and he also knew at times how to dine from earthenware; and although jeweled cups were available to a prince, he nevertheless did not shrink, when circumstances required, from using wooden vessels in the service of many different functions. I believe he will not disdain to have his praises arranged by the lowliest and most speechless of men, for the glory of his merits is so great that it is sufficient to grant even the mute the ability to speak about him. It will be a kind of distinction to draw modest things from modest sources for one who is able to receive every great thing from the greatest.

For a long time now, as I have been preparing to speak, many matters have pressed forward together; yet I think that nothing should be placed first or more suitably at the entrance of this little book than an account of how our most munificent Father, within our own memory, resolved that provision should be made for this place. The sequence of that affair is explained in the account that follows.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### The new church of St. Germanus in the monastery at Auxerre, begun and completed through miracles

84. The most celebrated prince Chuonradus, colleague of kings and especially renowned among the leading courtiers, at that time shone with the greatest honors, worthy of his nobility, through royal munificence [Note: [Col. 1247D] He was the brother of Judith of Bavaria, the second wife of the emperor Louis the Pious and the mother of Charles the Bald; as his maternal uncle, that Conrad was held in very high esteem by him. Many call him Count of Paris, and also the Elder or Senior, in relation to his namesake son, mentioned below. See the Sammarthani, *History of the House of France*, book VII, where they discuss the sons of Louis the Pious.].

His wife was named Adheleidh, herself likewise distinguished by the titles of an eminent birth; for, descended from the ancestral line of ancient nobles, she matched the splendor of her family with the dignity of a most august lineage [Note: [Col. 1247D] Adheleidh, or Adelais, was the daughter of Louis the Pious by his first wife, Ermengarde, as the Sammarthani state in the same place.]. Conjugal affection and the grace of shared virtue joined them, and they equaled the greatness of their fortunes by their devotion to God and their moderation in worldly affairs. Their dutifulness was remarkable for secular persons, their devotion immense, and their faith immeasurable; so that it would be difficult to judge which of them was more inclined toward religion, more fervent toward the saints, or more abundant in care for the poor [Lab.: in relieving their need]. Thus they vied with one another in acts of piety, excelling all others both in the height of their dignity and in their eagerness to rival one another in virtue.

85. Although in our time you see very many secular men eagerly seeking ecclesiastical dignities in order to foster their ambition, I may say, with the permission of all, that these two were perhaps the first or the only ones in our age who, having undertaken authority over sacred places, wished not so much to preside as to be of service [Note: [Col. 1248D] Thus, in accordance with the custom of those times, when kings assigned abbeys—often several to a single person—to the chief nobles of the kingdom, this Conrad of ours presided over one or more monasteries. Mabillon proves this concerning the monastery of Lebrah in *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. III, under the year 853, no. 54; and concerning Auxerre, Viola does so from this passage in the manuscript of Auxerre, where he counts him as the thirteenth abbot of St. Germanus of Auxerre.], and did not satisfy cunning avarice by oppressing the servants of God, but either wholly excluded the needs creeping upon them by their own resources or mitigated them to a tolerable degree. Without my saying anything, the various Churches throughout the world proclaim this everywhere: through their incomparable devotion, they either increased those places in material resources or made them notably distinguished by the splendor of suitable adornments. Our own place bears especially strong witness to this; enriched by their manifold gifts, it began, through the orderly providence of the Divinity, to be marked by the following undertaking.

86. As the aforementioned prince daily rose to the summit of power through magnificent advances in honor, it happened that his prosperity was suddenly disturbed by the distress of an unforeseen misfortune. For a disease had so terribly destroyed one of his eyes that, as time passed, a thick glaucoma spread over it and the failing pupil daily accumulated greater increases of pain together with the intolerable loss of sight. A crowd of physicians had gathered from the palace and from every part of the kingdom, prepared to expend upon the prince the varied industry of their art by joining their powers of expertise. They labored long and hard without result; whatever human experience could offer was spent in vain. Thus the mature disease and its morbid force gradually grew worse, and had eluded both the hopes and the hands of the most distinguished physicians. Therefore they decided that what remained—what was greatest or most extreme in the art—must be attempted with the knife and the cautery. The prince urged that it be done, since, with the disease established, all hope of recovery was being abandoned. As they undertook the procedure, the appointed day earnestly challenged the physicians’ pious yet impious workshops—that is, their services.

87. The day had now arrived. He, sufficiently anxious between hope and fear, having spent almost the entire night sleepless, thought it was time before dawn [Note: [Col. 1248D] *Antelucandum*. Thus our manuscripts read, as though from *anteculari*, that is, “to anticipate the light” or sunrise.]. Wishing first to seek heavenly remedies through prayers, he approached the tomb of the most blessed Germanus, full of vows; and while the brothers were carrying out the nocturnal vigil according to custom, he lay prostrate in prayer for a long time, stretched out with his entire body. Meanwhile the pain raged more fiercely, but he nevertheless persisted in what he had begun. The place was strewn with herbs [Note: [Col. 1248D] *Consitus*, that is, “sprinkled over”; for it is not credible that herbs grew inside the church, whatever Viola may have thought in chapter 26. It is established from Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8, concerning St. Nicetius of Lyons, no. 6, that the tombs of saints were once accustomed to be sprinkled with herbs by the faithful.]. He placed his hand upon them and, seeking some refreshment, applied them to his eye for a while. After a short interval, he withdrew his hand from his forehead and, removing the herbs, was astonished to find that the darkness had entirely vanished together with the pain. Thus the prince, most devoutly, was restored through the merits of blessed Germanus, so that by the use of a single dawn he escaped both the threatening terrors of the physicians and the unavoidable necessity of his unrelieved illness, and thereafter enjoyed the complete restoration of his dormant sight.

Unceasing praises to God and thanks to the saint were poured forth; and the benefit bestowed was received with double rejoicing, because it had come suddenly and had confined the inevitable necessity of an unrelieved illness beyond what anyone could have hoped for. What was then found at hand—a pair of golden bracelets—he offered to the sacred tomb; but he conceived such devotion and goodwill toward the place of the saint that the immense effect of his possessions later proved it. When these matters had been completed, he withdrew to his estates under his own jurisdiction.

88. From then on, with each passing day, an inward fervor grew in him to undertake something new and fitting, something that would both match his own devotion and contribute to the dignity of the blessed confessor. That pious thoughts concerning God do not lack a happy outcome was also made clear by the result of this undertaking. He summoned his wife, of excellent memory, and, having discussed the matter with her, explained more fully what he had in mind and what he had decided should be done. She, being of singular intelligence, born not only into the highest rank but also endowed with an exceptional gift of innate prudence, immediately saw the matter with great acuity. She seized upon the prince’s word and strongly urged that what had been divinely inspired should be hastened as much as possible; she gladly undertook the entire burden of the enterprise. If anything appeared difficult, she said, it would easily yield to a just desire; and the undertaking, though arduous, would soon reach the summit of its desired completion.

Animated by such considerations, she judged that the matter must be hastened. Impatient of every delay, she departed by the prince’s command and reached the monastery of blessed Germanus. First, after carefully examining the position of the site, and then seeing that everything corresponded to her plan, it is impossible to say with what fervor she devoted herself to pursuing the undertaking—provided that the Divinity, moved by the arrangements of religion, would grant her the ability to accomplish what it had given her the will to do.

89. The place was especially convenient by its natural situation; and on the eastern side, where the slope of the mountain gradually grew gentler, it hung suitably inclined and readily offered itself to the conception of some immense structure. The matter was entrusted to craftsmen highly experienced in such works. Their skill adapting itself to the advantages of the site, a model of the proposed work was produced; and, as a kind of prelude to the future mass of the building, its dimensions were shaped in a small wax model with a beauty and delicacy worthy of the king of angels and men, worthy of the assembly of saints, and worthy even of the majesty of the place itself.

With suitable funds prepared, overseers and master builders were selected. Through their tireless labor and supreme diligence, the immense work was completed with incredible speed, with such ease in the circumstances and such eagerness among the workers that it was evident to everyone that divine favor had joined in the undertaking. There would be much to say about the character of this structure, which could rightly be committed to writing in praise of the work. But since it is visible to the eyes and almost universally known throughout the surrounding region, the page should be spared such matters, so that it may later be expanded on more necessary subjects.

90. The work was completed with sturdy diligence; and, with God’s assistance, it would endure for many centuries and henceforth bear immortal witness to the merits of Prince Chuonradus and his most gracious wife. Their willing and incomparable goodwill toward us and our place was also confirmed by the hereditary devotion of their descendants. Their sons [Note: [Col. 1249D] Three sons of Conrad and Adelais are counted: Welf, or Guelf, to whom two monasteries were subject, Centula of St. Richarius and Senonais St. Columba; Conrad the younger, who, after Welf’s death, succeeded him in the administration of St. Columba and followed him to eternity in that same year of Christ 881, as Mabillon testifies in the *Annals* under that year, no. 53; and finally Hugh, commonly called “Abbot” because he held several abbeys. Since, as will shortly be stated, he alone survived when Hericus wrote this, it follows that what is related here about them was inserted by our author after the year 881 and before the year 886, in which Hugh died according to the *Benedictine Annals*; and therefore that these additions to the work were made long after its dedication to Charles the Bald.], as most faithful reflections of parents equally distinguished for uprightness and piety, clearly showed that this place had likewise settled deeply in their hearts and had become dear to them with indescribable love. Since you had long been tortured by the successes of our budding prosperity, O fate, ever envious of the progress of the ages, you removed them after they had been overtaken by a bitter end. Yet, so that you would not utterly overthrow us, deprived of every hope of support as you had begun to do, the wisest governor frustrated your unrestrained efforts and grim designs by reserving this man—still alive beneath a propitious heaven and drawing vital breath—for our first salvation, then for the use of many, and finally for the advancement of all.

91. This is Hugh, who, if I speak the truth without the taint of flattery, is both in name and office an abbot. Whatever I say about him falls far below his merit; and it is better to be entirely silent about him than to say too little. For I have not now undertaken to discuss him, except to say that this outstanding offspring, descended from illustrious parents, represents them most faithfully both in dignity and in character. Thus, with God’s approval, he succeeded to his father’s honors and, mindful of his ancestral glory, stands as the strongest heir to his father’s power and integrity. With blessed Germanus protecting him, he will flourish for a very long time and happily, in accordance with the wishes of ourselves and all the faithful, for the glory of holy Church. But all the years to come will preserve the memory of that man.

It would indeed have been pleasant to linger over affairs flowing along in such a gentle course—were it possible (the reading *pro esses* is uncertain)—unless the matters that follow in due order were drawing minds naturally inclined toward pleasure away from it.

92. Whatever might contribute to the adornment of the magnificently executed work was prepared with the greatest urgency. Since our province had almost no supply of marble, they decided that it must be sought in distant regions. For this reason certain brothers twice undertook the difficulty of a dangerous expedition and, traversing the mighty currents of the Rhône on a perilous journey, proceeded to Arles and then to Marseille, which is the farthest city of Gaul. Their state of mind was such that they would have endured all hardships, every unfamiliar circumstance, and every extreme situation not only bravely but willingly.

There they encountered immense dangers and overcame many things through cunning and many through boldness—cleverly audacious and audaciously clever—remembering that great things come at great cost and that fortune aids the daring. After excavating the ruins of ancient buildings all around, they gathered an immense quantity of precious marble, partly by solicitation and partly by purchase. Having loaded the ships with their highly desirable prize, they twice achieved, through victorious success, a memorable triumph over their bold undertakings.

I may say without hesitation that divine favor did not fail them on their dreadful journey: undaunted in spirit and undiminished in strength, they passed beyond both the threatening swell of the sea and the ferocity of an untrustworthy people. Many times they experienced the most immediate protection of blessed Germanus; and when they invoked his name, they were rescued from deadly dangers and were amazed to find that adversity had suddenly been changed into prosperity.

93. Consider also how remarkable and manifest was the following event, which we think sufficient to represent the many for the sake of brevity. Having completed the tasks for which they had traveled and hastening their return with all urgency, they entrusted themselves to the rapacious Rhône. One day, deceived—as is customary—by the false calm of a tranquil morning, they boarded the ship intending to set out. But suddenly a storm arose, and the approaching squalls intensified the sea’s natural fury. Great terror seized them all; they were weary of the waves and afraid of the dangers. At first, when the helmsman carefully examined the appearance of the elements, it seemed to him that they should make for the shore as quickly as possible, withdraw from the danger, and abandon the voyage they had then begun; for the air, stirred more violently than usual, would scarcely open a calm passage through the waves within the next three days.

They therefore stretched their gaze far ahead and saw a church. Steering toward it, they reached the safety of the desired land. Once they had disembarked, a pressing need to care for their bodies afflicted them. As they sought various remedies for this purpose, the inhabitants of the place informed them that the church was sacred to blessed Germanus by both name and merits, and that it had secured such reverence among everyone that no one dared presume to take anything belonging to the place, nor even to appropriate a twig from the hedges surrounding it. Moreover, the entire neighboring countryside was so protected by the majesty of the place that people could leave their clothing hanging here and there on hedges and trees for whole days or nights and remain in their own homes without fear or danger from thieves.

Thus, through faith in the most blessed Germanus, everything remains safe; and it is a kind of miracle that things exposed to danger do not perish beside danger.

94. Once they learned this, they relieved their minds of anxiety and eagerly sought the place. They embraced the name of their special Father with familiar affection; devoting themselves more fervently to prayer, they gave thanks for what had passed and formed vows for what was to come. Thus commending themselves and all their possessions to God more familiarly through the merit of their glorious protector, they returned to their station on the shore. Suddenly, with their eyes directed all around, they saw at a long distance that the entire harshness of the atmosphere had subsided beyond what could have been hoped; the winds and all the elements, having laid aside their destructive violence, had returned to their former gentleness.

Without delay they eagerly resumed the journey they had despaired of completing. Summoning their strength for bold action, they pursued a favorable course across the sea, secure from danger because they had once tasted confidence, and despising whatever storms might arise to obstruct them in view of the favor of the Divinity reconciled through Germanus.

He had once prostrated a hostile legion in the British Ocean, when the spiteful obstinacy of the ancient enemy begrudged him as he sought the restoration of peoples who were perishing. Who now could doubt that it was through his power and merit that, after the sudden dangers of the waves, the loudly proclaimed joys of calm weather shone forth again?

95. I judge the following event nearly miraculous. When the marbles had been brought to their intended location, all the columns that had been transported fitted the various parts of the structure so perfectly that they seemed to correspond exactly to the model, fashioned—as they say—to the very “nail,” with the same lines and without any discrepancy. I think that one remarkable and evident feature of their placement should not be left unmentioned.

One of them, of no negligible size, had been set upon a base. A group of strong men joined their efforts and, having drawn an arch above it, attempted to insert it with combined strength. As everyone strained with all his might and the column was almost standing upright, the enormous mass overcame those pushing it. It slipped from their hands and, driven by its own weight, began to fall toward destruction. Everyone withdrew in fear of the danger, awaiting, not without inward grief, the fall of the marble, which they expected shortly to be crushed into fragments.

But, in God’s presence, the event turned out contrary to expectation. What human hands had been unable to accomplish was completed by the intervention of divine power, with far greater wonder and far greater ease; and, with the same force with which it had first rushed downward, it soon seemed, without any visible support, to reclaim its place above by its own mass. Fixed in its position, it now offers a beautiful reminder of an enduring and unshaken miracle.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### The translations of St. Germanus illuminated by miracles; the relics of Saints Amator the bishop, and Urbanus and Tiburtius the martyrs, also brought to his church

96. Once the work had been completed and everything contributing to its beauty had been finished, the most holy and venerated body of blessed Germanus throughout the whole world was transferred, with great preparation and an immense display of service, into a crypt worthy of so great a treasure [Note: [Col. 1253D] Namely, in the year of Christ 859, as will soon be stated.]. Some years earlier [Note: [Col. 1253D] Namely, in the year of Christ 841, as will follow.], by command of the emperors Charles and Louis [Note: [Col. 1253D] Louis, king of Germany, who was the brother of Charles the Bald but older, since he was born of Ermengarde. Both are called emperors because they were sons of the emperor Louis, namely Louis the Pious.], it had already been moved by the venerable bishop Heribald [Note: [Col. 1253D] The life of St. Heribald, also called Heribold, bishop of Auxerre, was treated on 25 April, p. 378, before our predecessors had seen the history of the bishops of that church, where he has an extensive eulogy.]. From the time of its translation from Ravenna, it had rested for approximately four hundred years in the same church, in the place where it had been committed to its original burial.

On that occasion too, the principal proofs of his merits were solemnly commended by special miracles. When the interior of the precious tomb was finally opened, the venerable body appeared intact, untouched, and beautiful in every aspect of incorruption, with all its clothing in place; so that anyone ignorant of the circumstances could easily have been persuaded that the man had only recently died, had only recently been placed in the tomb, and was surrounded by freshly prepared garments. To this was added the public splendor of a miracle that, given its magnitude, must not be passed over.

97. A certain unfortunate man named Helenus had been so ravaged by a terrible affliction that, besides the grievous loss of his tongue and ears, he had also long been miserably tormented by the violence of a black demon. As the Creator in his mercy looked favorably upon his calamity, it happened that he was present at the spectacle of the translation just mentioned. He later reported that, when he tried three times to leave the church, he had been recalled into it three times by the appearance of a certain grave and venerable person.

It is plausible that during those successive departures and returns a struggle had continued for some time between the malignant and the benevolent spirit over whether the man should be saved or not saved: for one thought it intolerable to abandon a vessel once possessed, while the other could not bear that the workmanship of the heavenly Craftsman should remain any longer in the enemy’s keeping. On his third return, as though driven by some violent force, he fell upon the pavement; immediately a powerful stream of blood poured forth from his mouth, ears, and nostrils [variant: *proluxit*]. Thus, through the intervention of the one whose sacred relics were being transferred, he was restored to health: he was freed from the demon’s plague and received again, for their former uses, the revived services of his necessary senses.

98. As confirmation of the miracle, he lived on for many days thereafter and, mindful of the benefit he had received, demonstrated his gratitude at the memory of blessed Germanus through services appropriate to his humble condition.

This took place in the year 841 of the God-man’s incarnation, while the most pious Charles, son of the emperor Louis, was already reigning—after he had returned victorious from the civil war [Note: [Col. 1253D] Specifically, the famous and bloody battle of Fontenay; it was fought in the same year, in June [Col. 1254D], whereas this translation took place on the Kalends of September, according to the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapter 36, and Robert the monk of Auxerre in his *Chronology* under the year of Christ 841.] and had raised the summit of royal power above all his brothers.

But in the year 859 of the incarnation of the same Word, the nineteenth year of King Charles, when the same basilica had been enlarged and the crypts adorned with the beauty described above, the most holy mausoleum of our often-mentioned and often-to-be-mentioned Father was again removed from the place of its original translation and transferred, amid public devotion, to the burial place described above, newly prepared with elaborate care [Col. 1254A]. The matter proceeded in the following manner, as is almost universally known.

99. Louis, king of Germany, violently emerging from the regions beyond the Rhine, rashly desired the kingdom belonging to his brother’s portion, although it had formerly been confirmed by the judgment of the Franks through the most sacred intervention of an oath [Note: [Col. 1254D] In the year 843, in August, when an agreement had been reached at Verdun concerning the division of the kingdoms among Lothair, Louis, and Charles, the sons of Louis the Pious.]. He did so without any regard for the treaty he had struck [Note: [Col. 1254D] This occurred in the year 858, through the faction of rebels who hated Charles and had invited Louis into Gaul against his brother.].

This had been carried out by treacherous factions of rebels, whose minds could not endure peace and whose bestial rage and animal restlessness supplied strength and courage for daring anything whatsoever, however monstrous. These men, rushing of their own accord toward slaughter and madness, turned their impious right hands against the killing of citizens. By then almost all the nobles of the kingdom had defected from one side to the other; nothing rested on equity, and everything depended on force. All things were carried away by slaughter, plunder, and fires. Neither the title of Christianity recalled them from their monstrous undertakings, nor consideration of the human bond, nor God, everywhere and in every place fully and truly present, and therefore observing all things from above, nor finally consideration of the future judgment, when, after the completion of the world, the deeds of the deserving and the guilty would be weighed in equal scales.

100. Meanwhile the most gentle king Charles, who in the arts of war and peace was always comparable to David’s modesty, perceived that he could not resist by human forces on equal terms the savagery of his brother, which grew stubbornly harsher with each passing day. Since he knew that everything turns in cycles and had from childhood been accustomed to bear disasters bravely and, with God’s favor, to overcome them, he judged that he ought to yield to circumstances rather than, at the expense of himself and the commonwealth, throw himself blindly into extraordinary dangers.

Thus, encouraged by a healthier counsel, and one befitting so great a prince, he abandoned hope of temporal assistance and turned to divine protection, knowing that it is sufficiently ruinous both to distrust divine aid and to rely too rashly on human strength. Standing between hope and fear, he visited the monastery of blessed Germanus on the expedition just mentioned, moved by God.

101. Therefore, taking advantage of the suitability of place and time, he decided that the translation of the sacred body should be completed without delay. He was uncertain whether he would return, and he did not doubt that he could acquire great strength for himself through acts of devotion toward the saint.

Accordingly, on the solemn feast of Epiphany [Note: [Col. 1254D] Namely, in the year mentioned shortly before: 859 of the incarnation of the Word.], when everything had been prepared, he reverently approached the memorial of the glorious body. Only a few stood around: venerable bishops and highly approved priests, accompanying the king within the holy of holies; he excluded the rest from the interior. He ordered them to continue tirelessly in their service, deliberately persevering in hymns and psalmody.

Then, hastening the reverent undertaking, he opened the tomb. Seeing the most precious limbs intact, just as before, with supplicating eyes, he venerated them with fitting honor. What vows he formed there, what affection he offered, and how purely he sacrificed himself upon that very altar through spiritual contrition, was and remains known to God alone; and that this was most pleasing to him, he immediately made clear.

Afterward, allowing the venerable body to be handled only by the hands of bishops, he once again wrapped it appropriately in elaborate coverings. In addition, offering to the Creator, who looks upon all things, a pleasing fragrance of faith through blessed Germanus by the abundant expenditure of balsam and incense, he transferred and placed the incomparable treasure of that worshipful body in the place where it is now venerated and honored, with lavish preparation, immense glory, and finally princely reverence.

He magnificently enriched the place with royal generosity and gifts, and he proclaimed that day, completed with festive ceremonies, should be celebrated perpetually throughout succeeding ages.

102. Thus, immediately after completing the salutary acts of his devotion, he commended himself through a humble vow to the mighty God who grants salvation to kings, through the intercession of the most blessed Germanus. Confident in spirit and as secure as though victory had already been won, he selected his forces and hastened without delay to meet the enemy, intending to conduct the war more by faith than by arms.

With Christ as his leader, he drove away the hostile forces without bloodshed. He was granted a double benefit: he won a trophy over the enemy and avoided the guilt of homicide, or rather of fratricide, while God protected him in all things. Thereafter, by God’s generosity and with blessed Germanus protecting him, he was destined to prosper and reign successfully [Note: [Col. 1255] These matters are narrated more fully in the *Fulda Annals of the Franks* under the years 858 and the following year, in Chesnius, vol. II, pp. 555 ff.].

103. It will be fitting for piety, and salutary for us, to add to the honor of the blessed bishop whatever miracles afterward illuminated the course of time.

Not many days later, a certain young man, weak and deformed alike through an affliction of the knees, visited the temple of the blessed Father. For several days he earnestly kept vigil there, praying through the merits of the sacred body to recover the use of walking that he needed. It was the night preceding the Sunday that is known to fall in the middle of the observance of the sacred forty-day fast. While the brothers were carrying out the nocturnal service around cockcrow, he was powerfully restored by the bishop’s merits to the natural straightness of his knees. He provided a great spectacle for the people standing by and a noble occasion and memorable increase for divine praise through the mouths of all.

Another miracle followed this one in the same period, also publicly celebrated before the eyes of many. A certain man deprived of the use of speech came to the saint, placing himself under the protection of strong faith, and escaped the harmful prison of silence through the assistance he received of restored speech. Tessellated tablets, hung in the vestibule of the church, served as a memorial of the event.

104. The year 869 of the Lord’s incarnation was passing when the following miracle was revealed. A certain Adalricus, a native of Sens, whose very kind of disability had made him universally known, was dragged along crawling on his entire body, so that his weakness, added to his deformity, seemed to have deprived him of the more necessary functions of the body. Nature had not produced him in such a condition; rather, an unforeseen calamity had suddenly overtaken him, for a reason known only to God, and had continued for twelve years.

On frequent visits to the memorials of the saints, he anxiously sought relief from his misfortune, but without success [variant: *frequenter*, “frequently”]. It is entirely clear that he had been reserved for the merits of our most blessed Father. Accordingly, when a large multitude of peoples had gathered, as was customary, for the solemnity of the Kalends of October, celebrated with public rejoicing throughout the world, he too made an effort to attend the assembly as best he could. As he later admitted, he did not do so chiefly in the hope of recovering his health, but in order to be helped by the alms gathered from those who had come together.

Yet God, the craftsman of human kindness, whose custom it is to bestow many gifts freely even upon those who do not ask, granted both glory to the day and, to the wretched man, the healing he had despaired of, through the expenditure of a single miracle. When nearly half of the sacred vigils had passed and, as the alternating choirs took their turns, the psalm entitled “Praise befits you, O God, in Zion” began to be sung, such a cry from the man recovering filled the church that trembling terror penetrated not only the crowd of ordinary people but even the divine choirs of the service to their very depths.

The arrival of health had stirred his weakened joints and his limbs returning to their former strength, and had driven the unfortunate man into uncontrolled cries. People hurried from every side toward the voice; and he was found collapsed, with his body and limbs almost lifeless. Shortly afterward, having recovered his strength and with the use of his legs returning, he brought the ferment of divine praise to those present and passed it on to those yet to come. As confirmation of this deed, he remains alive to this day and, expending upon the sacred body the service he rightly owes according to his strength, carries with him the signs of his restored health.

105. The night of his holy passing was spent, as usual, in devoted vigils. One of the brothers was so religiously minded that inward grief grievously exhausted his vital powers. He was overcome by an inconsolable sorrow and immoderate mourning—not so much because he was oppressed by the violence of his illness as because, weakened in strength, he could not take part in the solemn observances owed to the occasion. Meanwhile, sleep overcame his weary limbs.

Saint Germanus appeared to him as he slept and ordered him to state without hesitation what he was doing and what he was suffering. When the man declared his painful illness, Germanus seemed to lay a gentle hand upon the place of pain. At once the man rose full of strength [Col. 1257A] and, to the immense wonder of all, joyfully joined the choirs of those singing psalms. It cannot be said how greatly the ardor of all their hearts increased in praise of God.

106. The feast day of his most holy predecessor, Amator, had arrived [that is, 1 May], and, with the bishops assembled, his venerable body was being transferred with the reverence due to a principal saint. It would have been not merely improper but sacrilegious for the company of blessed Germanus also to remain absent from that spectacle. When they were to receive relics of the sacred body, they decided that nothing could be more fitting to request than the fingers of the right hand with which Amator had once violently torn Germanus’s hair. Having obtained them, they carried them back amid elaborate ceremony and festive rejoicing.

When they entered the basilica and, intending to celebrate the divine service, placed the sacred relic [Col. 1257B] before the tomb of blessed Germanus, it became immediately apparent that two lights of outstanding merit had met in pious joy and renewed glory. For a certain woman, carried on a litter because she crawled with her whole body and lacked the proper use of her limbs, was soon restored to a becoming upright posture and, filled with the merits of both saints, brought back the joy of soundness. The clergy exalted the deed with praises and the people with acclamations; thus the day seemed to have been illumined, and the ancient familiarity between the holy bishops appeared to have been confirmed by unmistakable evidence.

The days of the sacred Lent were passing, and a deaf woman from the Senonian district happened to arrive. She had been warned in a dream to make a rope for the bell and carry it to the basilica of blessed Germanus [Col. 1257C]. She obeyed the command, brought the rope, and attached it to the bell. When she struck it with her own hand, at that very moment the bronze gave forth a sound, and the woman recovered her hearing.

107. In the year 873, the public devotion of the faithful toward the Word made human among men was celebrating the Kalends of October with votive rejoicing. Among the others there was a native of the county of Angers, from a village called Basilicas, named Adalsadus, who had endured for nearly thirty-three years the disability of contracted knees. When the solemn celebration of Mass began, he entered the church and, as he himself reports, began to burn with immense fervor. Seeking a place where that fervor might be calmed, he went outside again. But as the heat subsided, he was immediately seized by such a terrible chill [Col. 1257D] that he thought he was nearly dying unless he reentered the church. Once he had gone inside again, he was inflamed with his former warmth.

Meanwhile, his knees burst apart and his sinews relaxed; the church was filled with shouting. A responsory was then being sung on the ambo. He was brought close to the holy tomb; before everyone’s eyes, the joints that had long been deadened were stretched out, the dryness of his sinews was revived, and his knees were restored to their former position. The gathering of the faithful was enkindled to praise God; and with joy doubled, their mouths were filled with voices and their cheeks with tears. The sermon turned to the splendor of the feast, and it was plainly demonstrated by this evident benefit that blessed Germanus was present on his own feast day.

The man of whom we speak still survives and, mindful of the benefit he received, confesses his gratitude by serving as best he can. Christ, you possess great and manifold remedies: since you are the creator of the universe, you both set in order, by pleasing methods, things that stand awry, and restore them by ordering them.

108. I fear that I should omit from the praises of our supreme and incomparable Father the fact that, through the intervention of the grace of his merits, this same place also deserved to be enriched with the relics of holy martyrs from the city of Rome [Col. 1258B]. I believe that divine providence was already foreshadowing this when, among the other furnishings of the work mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1257D] That is, of the basilica, which Conrad extended eastward in an immense building.], it prepared a chamber of burial [Note: [Col. 1257D] Among ecclesiastical writers, *secretarium* generally means a treasury or sacristy, as the common people call it; but here it is clear that the crypts are intended—those which Conrad had constructed beneath the new building like an underground choir, so that the body of Saint Germanus might henceforth be preserved there with greater reverence.] that was intended neither for one relic nor for one alone: namely, because other patrons from elsewhere would soon come, who would supplement the place by their presence, protect it by their merits, and illumine it by their virtues. Since it would be monstrous to consign this to silence, I see no place where it could more suitably be inserted—or where it could have been inserted at all.

109. Accordingly, in the year 862 of the incarnate God, certain brothers, equipped alike with mandates and royal letters, set out for the city of Rome, both for the sake of prayer and to pursue certain ecclesiastical matters. With God directing the affair, they argued these matters vigorously [Col. 1258C] and brought them to an effective conclusion.

Pope Nicholas, a most prudent man and one to be regarded with the greatest reverence [Note: [Col. 1258D] The first of that name.], then presiding over the Roman see, displayed the dignity and zeal appropriate to the apostolic summit. After making himself fully available to the aforementioned envoys for several days in every matter they desired, he graciously gave them, as they were departing, the relics of the holy martyrs Urban and Tiburtius [Note: [Col. 1258D] But which Urban and which Tiburtius? Was it Urban, the pope and martyr? The people of Auxerre agree with Hericus on this point; but see what is said about it on 25 May, especially pages 9 and following. And was it also that Tiburtius of whom the Acts of Saint Cecilia, virgin and martyr, speak? They too thought so; but consult our Acts for 14 April, especially page 210.], both precious in power and distinguished in quantity. Thus, by God’s favor and through the agency of King Charles, they accomplished with ease what otherwise would have been exceedingly difficult or impossible.

CHAPTER III. Miracles performed during the translation of the holy martyrs Urban and Tiburtius; likewise of the holy martyrs Mauritius and Innocentius; catalogue of the saints buried in the crypts of Saint Germanus at Auxerre.

[Col. 1258D]

110. What kind of relic and treasure was being brought from the city of Romulus began immediately to be revealed by the abundance of the miracles that followed. Omitting what is superfluous, I shall make whatever must be reported more pleasing by brevity.

After leaving the city, they reached the church of Saint Alexander at their first stopping-place [Col. 1259A]. When they spent the night there, a candle of extraordinary length, lit at one end, soon appeared to be burning at the other as well and to shine brightly from both ends. They embraced the event with great devotion and understood that, in honor of the memories of the two principal saints, they ought thereafter to serve them with twin lights.

The distinguished man Lotharius, count and a member of the expedition, then became afflicted with a very severe fever. He brought a candle proportionate to his condition and, spending the night before the sacred relics, felt himself relieved of all the distress of his illness by the following day. This took place at Volterra [Note: [Col. 1259C] Volterra, also called Volaterra, is a very ancient city in Etruria and in the territory of Pisa.].

Meginarius, the priest of the same Lotharius, was not long afterward inflamed by a most violent fever. When a candle was applied to the saints, he was cured as remarkably as he was easily. From then on it became familiar to everyone that the bodily weaknesses attacking them throughout the journey were to be averted by constant appeals to the saints’ patronage [Col. 1259B].

111. Having crossed the Alps, they turned aside to the martyrs of Agaunum [Note: [Col. 1259C] That is, to the monastery famous under the name of these martyrs, at the place where they suffered and were buried, Agaunum or Acaunum, in the diocese of Sion on the Rhône River, between Sion and Lake Geneva, though nearer the latter; today Saint-Maurice. For this monastery, see the Sammarthani, *Abbeys of Gaul*, under Agaunum. These martyrs are Saint Mauritius and his fellow soldiers of the Theban Legion, whom we shall discuss on 22 September.].

There they were received by Hucbert [Note: [Col. 1259D] Hucbert was the brother of Queen Theodeberga, wife of Lotharius, king of Lotharingia—the Lotharius who was known for nothing so much as his infamous intercourse with the concubine Waldrada, a relationship that he dared to defend at Rome by perjury and sacrilege, and for which he and his associates suffered terrible punishment from God the avenger in 869. Though Hucbert had at one time been a cleric, he subsequently adopted a secular life. Meanwhile he became a very famous abbot of many monasteries, some of which he had received and some of which he had seized—not famous for virtues but for vices, and especially for having squandered and plundered the resources of the monasteries over which he presided. He too met an unhappy end in the year 864, according to the Bertinian Frankish Annals. More about him may be found in the Benedictine Annals, volume 3, at various places.], a most notorious abbot. They were received with complete familiarity, and the great fatigue of the journey was relieved by the man’s full benevolence, the immense affection of the religious, and, finally, the lavish generosity of his every kindness.

Afterward, judging that they ought not to neglect the opportunity for their undertaking that had been presented to them, they decided to request from the aforementioned prince the relics of the saints of Agaunum. By God’s will, he received their request most willingly, being both exceptionally friendly toward these men and, since he devoted his thoughts only to worldly matters, not sufficiently sparing in distributing the patronage of the saints.

Accordingly, after summoning the custodian of the sacred bodies, he unhesitatingly ordered that they be given a portion of the relics of the precious martyr Mauritius, together with the venerable head of Saint Innocentius, once his fellow soldier of the legion. Although everyone bore this with the greatest reluctance, the prince’s command prevailed, and what he wished was carried out without delay—that is, immediately. Having obtained what they desired, they resumed their journey, praising God fervently, who always favors just arrangements.

The splendor of the services rendered to the saints and the frequency of the signs gathered the surrounding peoples from every side to behold them [Col. 1260A]. As some departed, others took their place: the former were happily impelled to return home by the fresh grace of the benefits they had received, while the latter were eagerly driven to hasten forward by hope of receiving benefits.

112. There is a place publicly famous and famously public, commonly called Orbe [Note: [Col. 1260C] Orbe is a town of Switzerland, toward the County of Burgundy, situated on the river of the same name, between Lake Geneva and another lake lying immediately to its north, Lake Neuchâtel.].

When they arrived there, a little girl of that place, named Osanna, whom birth had made both mute and contracted, heard the voices of the people singing psalms and was seized by an extraordinary longing to reach the saints. Since she could not express this in words, she displayed it by bodily gestures and the shrillness of her throat. At last, dragging herself forward on her stiffened sinews, she reached them with whatever effort she could make. Immediately rewarded with the fruit of such faith, she recovered, to everyone’s astonishment, the use of an upright posture previously unknown to her.

Then, having shared in the sacred rites, she responded at the priest’s command, “Amen.” From that point, fully endowed with the power of speech, she followed the saints as far as the place called Arlia.

Afterward, when they had come to a village called Botgalia [Note: [Col. 1260D] Commonly Bougeaille, between Orbe and Salins, which will be mentioned shortly.], a certain man of that place, subject from childhood to falling fits, so that every day he suffered a fall and violent impact more than once, ran swiftly to the saints. He carried the bier and followed them for three days; afterward he suffered no further misfortune.

113. From there they came to Salins [Note: [Col. 1260D] Salins, in the vernacular, is a town in the County of Burgundy, about thirteen leagues west of Orbe.]. A father carrying on his shoulders his little son, weakened by contracted limbs, placed him beneath the bier. Shortly afterward the boy began to stand up and call anxiously to his father. Awakened by his cries, everyone ran from every side and found him sound. The father, receiving his son back healthy before everyone’s eyes, carried him home with immense joy. This took place in the church of Saint John the Baptist, in the public village [Col. 1260C].

When they entered the forest of Mortkalia [Note: [Col. 1260D] Mortkalia. Thus our Lyon manuscript reads, as does Chifflet, who adds that the forest is commonly called the Bois de Mouchar. The Valcellian manuscript has Mortalia; Labbe has Montiskattae. It is clear that the place lay in the County of Burgundy, between Salins and the Saône.], a new joy breathed upon them. For amid violent winds and heavy rains, two candles carried before the sacred relics remained alight throughout the entire day, their flames unextinguished. Thus, evidently protected by the grace of the saints to whom they were being carried, they endured both rain and storm winds with tireless service.

When they came to a village in the county of Amaous called the Field of Vellius [Note: [Col. 1260D] In the vernacular, Chamblay, as Chifflet noted in the margin of his text. I have found nothing about the county of Amaous; it nevertheless appears from this journey to have lain approximately in this region.], a woman who had been mute from her mother’s womb ran forward, filled with faith. She poured out her prayer [Col. 1261A] and obtained the result of her petition. Immediately the innermost parts of her throat, which had long been denied a voice, began to sound melodiously, and a ready abundance of speech compensated for the losses of her long silence. Thus, magnifying the gift she had received by exercising her speech, she followed them as far as the Saône [Note: [Col. 1261D] The Saône, or Arar, is a very well-known river of Gaul. It was mentioned above.], praising God with both affection and words for having taken pity on his creature.

114. As they passed through the county of Ouche [Note: [Col. 1261D] The county of Ouche takes its name from the river Ouche, which flows into the Saône at Lauda-Saint-Jean, otherwise Saint-Jean-de-Losne, in the Duchy of Burgundy. It therefore seems to have extended from there as far as the county of Dijon.], a little girl of honorable birth, who likewise suffered the loss of speech, sprang from her nurse’s lap and came at a rapid run to the saints. Embracing the bier, she repeatedly cried out, with insatiable delight, that her lords were present. Thus, once the bond of her tongue had been released, she heaped praises upon praises and remained an inseparable companion as far as the castle of Dijon [Note: [Col. 1261D] Dijon, also called Divio or Divionum, is a very celebrated city on the Ouche and the capital of the Duchy of Burgundy.]. Her father and mother later sent suitable gifts for the journey to those who were traveling.

After this, as they passed through the county of Alise [Note: [Col. 1262D] The county of Alise, or Alesia, was discussed above. It lies between Dijon and Auxerre, though nearer Dijon.], they decided to spend the night in a village called Fanum. The church of that place is solemnly dedicated to Saint Germanus. In it they placed the precious relics of the saints.

A girl of nearly twelve years had arrived there, whose neck and nape, contracted and twisted around her shoulder, disfigured her with a deformity of shocking ugliness. Spending the night in vigilant prayer in the church, she was restored both to the health she desired and to complete beauty, and she burdened heaven itself with her vows and praises. Following the authors of her benefit to Auxerre, she spent an entire year in salutary service.

When they came to a village called Pompeiacum, they kept watch during the night in the church of Saint Christopher [Col. 1261C]. A well-born boy named Herimbert was being tormented by a terrible attack of fever. Carried there by his parents, he cast off his illness and filled those who desired it with joy at his vigorous health.

115. From there, as they set out, a solemn reception was being prepared for them at Auxerre. At last they arrived on the day before the Kalends of November, amid great glory, immense ceremony, and an indescribable excellence of events. From that time miracles increased visibly in bodily matters and invisibly in spiritual ones; the more subtle they were, the more useful; unceasingly abundant, unquestionably beneficial; and the longer they were destined to endure, the more certainly they would bring profit.

Folcoldus [also Fucaldus, elsewhere Fulcoldus], a cleric from the monastery of Saint Julian [Note: [Col. 1262D] There were several monasteries bearing this title, including one at Auxerre, where Le Beuf teaches in his preface to *Auxerre Captured and Liberated* that monks and nuns once lived, though separately.], had been afflicted with quartan fever [Col. 1261D] for almost a year. He humbly went to the saints. Soon, granted the reward of faith, he was restored to health and escaped his illness.

Not many days later, a certain tenant of Saint Germanus’s estate, from the rural district called Sorgiacus [Col. 1262A], learned of the fame of the miracles and resolved to make his way there. He was completely crippled by violent paralysis in all his limbs.

On the night before the day on which he planned to depart, as he slept, a man appeared to him wearing the appearance of a bishop and displaying beautiful white hair. He identified himself as Urbanus and said: “Behold, you have been made well; you have escaped your infirmity. Nevertheless, go straight on to the place you had resolved to reach, and remember to fulfill suitable vows in return for the health you have received.”

Obedience accompanied the command of the one who ordered him. He proceeded as instructed and openly explained what had happened to him.

116. From then on, the saints granted innumerable benefits to the many who sought the place. Finally, to all who made their petitions properly, they showed themselves unmistakably present through evident events. That they take pleasure in having honorable services brought to them in their place will be established by many examples, though one brief account will suffice.

The anniversary of the passion of the blessed martyr Tiburtius had arrived, and the pious devotion of the brothers was devoting itself with particular diligence to the nocturnal vigils. Meanwhile, one of the brothers had withdrawn to pray in greater secrecy and, having been somewhat carried away to the heights of divine contemplation, was granted a vision of the saint. Tiburtius appeared in the form and youthful beauty in which he is more expressly described in the text of his Passion.

He seemed to be standing before the chest containing his relics, his steps poised in the air, and to be praying earnestly for the salvation of the entire people, his hands extended toward the east; in one of them he held a golden staff. He later reported this to us with tears. It greatly benefited both the devotion of the present and that of the future [Col. 1262C].

Moreover, in the year 864 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the venerable Herchenraus, bishop of Châlons, came to the monastery of Saint Germanus and, through the generosity of the brothers, obtained relics of the precious pope and martyr Urbanus. Having received them, he built a monastery in the county of Perth in his honor. So many and such frequent miracles later shone forth in that place that, if all of them were committed to writing, they could themselves supply a volume [Note: [Col. 1262D] On these matters, see the Acts of Saint Urban, pope and martyr, 25 May. “This monastery still exists under the Benedictine congregation of Saint Vanne,” says Mabillon, *Annals*, volume 3, book 36, no. 43.].

I believe that we have now briefly honored the commemoration of the saints brought from Rome. The matter now requires us, leaving those events either delayed or omitted, to proceed with what follows.

117. Once the work described much earlier [Col. 1262D] had appeared both suitable to ecclesiastical dignity and worthy of housing the relics of the saints, the judgment of the wise, after deliberation, decided that the best course was to transfer the aforementioned relics of the martyrs, as well as the bodies of the blessed bishops of Auxerre [Col. 1263A], formerly buried in the church itself, into the crypts and to place them around the body of the most blessed Germanus with the greatest care of religious service. This was done with divine purpose and sound judgment: that those whom the same royal court of heaven contains might also be joined by the capacity of the same dwelling place on earth.

And so it was done. On the right side, that is, toward the south, the bones of blessed Pope Urbanus were placed in the same chest as the head of Saint Innocentius the martyr. Next came the body of the venerable Alodius, once his successor [Note: [Col. 1263D] “His,” that is, Saint Germanus’s. Saint Alodius is discussed on 28 September; Saint Ursus on 30 July; Saint Theodosius on 17 July; Saint Romanus may be treated on 6 October; Saint Aunarius on 25 September; Saint Fraternus on 29 September; and Censurius was discussed above. Saint Gregory is commemorated on 19 December; Desiderius on 27 October. For Bishop Lupus, see the note above at no. 38. We treated Saint Moderatus on 1 July. See also, if desired, the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*.], followed by the three holy bishops Ursus, Romanus, and Theodosius.

At the foot, that is, toward the east, beside the altar, rest the most sacred remains of the precious confessor and bishop Aunarius. The left side, that is, toward the north, was occupied by the relics of the glorious martyr Tiburtius, together with the venerable bodies of five bishops: Saint Fraternus, bishop and martyr, Censurius, Gregory, Desiderius, and Lupus; and outside these, Saint Moderatus, a boy once crowned with martyrdom.

Since we have introduced their names, let us briefly recount whatever about them has come to our knowledge.

118. From this it can be inferred what sort of merit or dignity Alodius possessed: while blessed Germanus was still alive, Alodius presided as abbot over his monastery, and after Germanus was raised to heaven, Alodius deserved to succeed him in the episcopate. As imitator and heir of his master, after ruling the church of Auxerre for thirty years, one month, and twelve days, he died in peace, rich in the rewards of outstanding merits, and was decently buried in the same basilica of blessed Germanus [Col. 1263C].

After his death, the city remained without a bishop for ten years, as we also noted at the beginning of this little work, because of the savagery of the barbarians who were ravaging Gaul. When these troubles had ended, Saint Fraternus was appointed to the episcopal throne. On the very day on which he was ordained bishop by the faithful, he was crowned with martyrdom by the barbarians, on the third day before the Kalends of October.

Censurius was then appointed to the episcopate. He was the man during whose time Constantius the orator, at the request of Saint Patient, bishop of Lyons, composed the Life of blessed Germanus in a remarkable style and, having worked on it with every care, later sent it to him for possession.
