After administering the priesthood properly for thirty-eight years, three months, and six days, Censurius died on the fourth day before the Ides of June, full of holiness and rich in every good thing. He was buried in the church of the most blessed Germanus [Col. 1263D].

Blessed Aunarius’s outstanding privilege is more than sufficiently declared by the account of his Deeds [Col. 1264A]. Among the other distinctions of his holiness, he also enriched the basilica of blessed Germanus with magnificent estates; for he was both of splendid birth and abundantly wealthy in possessions. In life and in death he shone with the glory of miracles. After serving as bishop for forty-three years, ten months, and twenty days, he died full of the Holy Spirit on the seventh day before the Kalends of October and was placed beside his fathers in the basilica of blessed Germanus with the reverence due to him.

119. Why should I recall blessed Desiderius? His secular dignity was so great that no one, however powerful, could compare with him on equal terms. He was related to Queen Brunhild and to her sons, the kings of the Franks [Col. 1264B]; through their royal generosity he also acquired an immense abundance of estates.

His mother, named Nectaria, lies buried in the monastery of Saint Amantius, situated in the county of Périgord [Note: [Col. 1263D] Rather, in the county of Quercy, as it is more correctly read in the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapter 20. See the Benedictine *Annals*, volume 1, book 2, no. 34.]. In memory of his mother he afterward adorned that monastery with honorable gifts and a very large endowment of lands, as the text of his will declares.

As far as could be investigated by comparing the dates, he was a contemporary of blessed Pope Gregory. Letters of his to Gregory are extant, commending the man’s renown also in apostolic writings [Note: [Col. 1263D] See the notes above at book I, chapter 4, no. 39, letter d.].

He was so rich in estates that no principal church of either central Burgundy [Note: [Col. 1264D] “Central Burgundy” here means the Duchy of Burgundy. For authors of declining Latin use *medianus* for *medius*, “middle.” Burgundy was formerly divided into three parts, as Brietius teaches in *Parallels of Ancient and Modern Geography*, volume 1, book 7, chapter 5: first, Transjuran Burgundy; second, Ducal Burgundy; and third, what they call the Free County, or County of Burgundy.] or the province of Aquitaine can be found that he did not increase with excellent possessions.

He greatly enlarged the church of Saint Stephen, in which he held office, with extraordinary splendor, adding a great vaulted structure on the eastern side and decorating it most magnificently with gold and mosaic, after the model of the one that Syagrius, bishop of Autun [Note: [Col. 1264D] Saint Siagrius, or Syagrius, bishop of Autun, flourished until approximately the year 600; he is commemorated on 27 August, when he will be treated.], is known to have built. He also transferred the ancient altar there and dedicated it on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May. He solemnly endowed the same church with many large estates, in various places and especially in the county of Saintonge [Note: [Col. 1264D] Saintonge is a province of Gaul on the Aquitanian Ocean.].

120. He also enriched the basilica of blessed Germanus, in which he had arranged to rest after death, with many gifts—gifts that still testify equally to the man’s generosity and excellence. He presented numerous golden and silver vessels, and, being exceptionally meticulous in such matters, included in the will he made both the workmanship of each and its individual weight [Col. 1264D].

He ordered the basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius to be built through his deacon Marinus [Note: [Col. 1265D] That Marinus later became a priest, under which title he is commemorated at Auxerre on 20 July.] and endowed it with his own property. Marinus himself also rests in that church.

How he appointed Christ and the church heirs to his possessions is made clear by the authority of his most ancient will, mentioned twice above. That will, still preserved in our archives, bears abundant witness to the man’s great dignity, his extraordinary generosity, and his arrangements, always considered with cautious diligence.

Since these matters offer more than the brevity of our undertaking can explain, let us omit them and continue with the rest. Having completed the course of his life, he met his final day on the sixth day before the Kalends of November and was transferred with due reverence into the church of blessed Germanus.

[Col. 1265B] 121. Romanus was appointed to the episcopal see. It is reported that, although he was a most holy man, he completed his martyrdom by decapitation on the day before the Nones of October, after serving for three years and fifteen days.

A faithful account commonly reports of blessed Ursus that, shut away near the basilica of Saint Amator, he led the life of a hermit. There is still an oratory there, consecrated to the memory of his name.

At that time the city happened to be consumed by a sudden and violent fire. When the people’s great cry, raised on high, reached the man of God, he judged that the danger must be confronted and sent there his familiar staff; meanwhile he applied himself earnestly to fervent prayers. Once it had been placed among the threatening flames and what still remained intact, the entire fire was extinguished more quickly than words can say.

On this occasion the holy man’s merit having been made manifest, when the city’s bishop died, the people forcibly brought Ursus out and appointed him to the episcopate. His cell was converted into a church. He served as bishop for six years and four months, and, precious in character and merits, departed from the burden of mortality on the third day before the Kalends of August.

Bishop Theodosius, after governing the see for eight years and twenty-four days, met his final day on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August and, in accordance with his holiness, received an honorable burial in the church of blessed Germanus.

122. Gregory, himself also a holy bishop, presided over the church for twelve years and six months. Having completed the service of his office, he laid down his human life on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January and earned his final resting place in the church of blessed Germanus [Col. 1265D].

As is noted on his ancient marble epitaph, and as we recalled in the preceding book, Bishop Lupus came there with the venerable Queen Crotechilde at the time when Saint Germanus was building his basilica. Overtaken by his own end, he was buried there.

In the same basilica rests Saint Optatus, bishop, with two priests, Sanctinus and Memorius. They were first buried together in the church of Saint Christopher the martyr, which Optatus himself had built. Later, after the years had passed, their bodies were transferred to the church of Saint Germanus with such devotion and solemnity [Col. 1266A] that the day of their translation is recorded in all the Martyrologies, especially the oldest ones, on the sixth day before the Nones of the third month—that is, May. Their passing or burial is recorded on the day before the Kalends of September. All of them rest together in the same sarcophagus.

Concerning the boy Moderatus, this alone has been learned: as a boy crowned with martyrdom, he long rested in his own basilica. Later, when miracles began to shine forth around his tomb, he was transferred to the church of blessed Germanus, where he is honored with a fuller observance of the Offices and a greater expenditure of lights.

CHAPTER IV. Eulogy of the church of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, and the pious exhortation of Saint Hericus to the brothers.

[Col. 1266B] 123. When a place is illustrious for such and so magnificent honors, enriched with titles and privileges, who would not consider it worthy of reverence because of its majesty?

The Hebrews once revered the Holy of Holies because there were kept the Ark of the Covenant, and within it Aaron’s staff and the heavenly manna; there was the altar called the Altar of Incense; there were the golden cherubim with the Mercy Seat; and there were the other symbols, intellectually typical and typically intellectual, which thereby bore the foreshadowing of the truth that was one day to come.

Do you not think it much more deserving of reverence that dwelling of supreme holiness, splendid with the memorials of so many saints and exalted by their trophies? The former was opened once a year to one priest alone, who was to make petition for his own transgressions and those of the entire people [Col. 1266C]. These holy places of ours, holy both in reality and in name, are open to each person and to everyone: accessible every day and easily made daily. And the more insistently a sinner presents himself, the richer the reward of his religious importunity will be.

If any outsider approached the former, he paid for his boldness with death. To these, however, we outsiders all approach, so that we may compensate the sentence of death with the payment of immortality.

There the blood of brute animals was brought by the priest into the sanctuary. Here the living body and most holy blood of the supremely good priest are made, through the use of the heavenly mystery, for the salvation of all Christians.

Such dignity belongs to the place; such is the holiness of its principal reverence. Whenever you enter it devoutly, you may behold Christ following the apostles, fighting alongside the martyrs, conversing with the confessors [Col. 1266D], rejoicing with the virgins, and finally reigning together with all the saints.

Moreover, there are so many places of prayer there and so many altars of the saints that, when you have visited them all and wept before each one, you may rejoice that the better part of your day has been turned to profit.

124. Nor do I consider those who rave that the souls of the saints have settled either in Abraham’s bosom, or in a place of refreshment, or above God’s altar—and cannot be present at their own tombs and wherever they wish—to be tolerated. It is altogether absurd, as the interpreter of sacred history testifies [Note: [Col. 1266D] He means St Jerome in his treatise Against Vigilantius, from which Hericus has copied several passages. [Col. 1267C] On this opinion of Vigilantius and others concerning [Col. 1267D] the state of the saints after life until the day of judgment, see further Cardinal Bellarmine, On the Beatitude and Canonization of the Saints, book I, chapter 1.], to cast the saints into chains, so that they should be held in penal custody until the day of judgment and should not be with their Lord, of whom it is written: “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes.” If the Lamb is everywhere, then those who are with the Lamb must also be believed to be everywhere [Note: [Col. 1267D] These words too are St Jerome’s. He does not mean that the Lamb—that is, Christ God and man—is properly in every place according to his human nature as well as according to his divine nature, which is the heresy of the Ubiquitarians; rather, he says that Christ is endowed with such supreme freedom and agility that he can immediately be wherever he wishes, and that this same freedom has also been communicated to those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Accordingly, it is false—as Vigilantius maintained—that they sit detained either in Abraham’s bosom, or in a place of refreshment, or beneath God’s altar, and cannot be present at their own tombs and wherever they wish. You see that he does not say that they are everywhere present, but that they can be present at their own tombs and wherever they wish.]. And since they enjoy the God who sees all things, penetrates all things, and knows all things, there is nothing in the manifold variety of nature that they too do not see, penetrate, and know without the obstruction of tedious difficulty [Note: [Col. 1268C] St Thomas may be consulted on this opinion in Part I, question 12, article 8, and elsewhere, where he rejects it. Nevertheless, the same author teaches that the saints know whatever on earth concerns them, especially the petitions of those who invoke them: see II–II, question 83, article 4, and Part III, question 10, article 2. As to the manner in which they know these things, Bellarmine says that there are four opinions of the theologians; see the cited work, chapter 20, where they are briefly set out.].

Therefore, although I have believed—and shall rightly believe—that the souls of the saints are nowhere and never absent from God, and consequently are always and everywhere present to those who rightly invoke them, nor shall I readily be driven from this opinion [Note: [Col. 1268D] Hericus was evidently of the opinion which Jerome also seems to suggest: that the souls of the saints, like the angels, are in a certain marvelous way, by the agility of their nature, everywhere, and hear the prayers of those who beseech them directly. See Bellarmine in the same place refuting this view.], nevertheless I shall unhesitatingly hold in my mind, and shall firmly proclaim with my voice, declare with my mouth, and profess privately and publicly, without fear of prejudice, that they love and hover around their own ashes and are always present with them.

125. And when, unworthy as I am, I approach the memorial of Germanus, I shall look upon him with the eyes of faith; I shall contemplate from time to time his angelic face, more frequently illumined through fellowship with the word of God and dreadful even to kings; I shall admire, as I prostrate myself, the gravity of his soul tempered with gentleness, the steadfastness of his purpose, and the reverence of his old age; and, kissing the holy stone, I shall venerate it most humbly as though it towered above my own head. At times, if the opportunity is granted, I shall even clasp his footprints; but if he does not deem that worthy, I shall certainly not cease faithfully to adore the place where his feet stood. I gratefully remember that he did many things even for me while absent, and I shall never allow my mind to be driven to doubt that, when duly venerated, he will also be present with me much more fully and diligently.

On the occasion provided by the undertaking proposed, something has been composed by which I think a scruple has been injected into the rash and something beneficial secured for sincere worshipers of the saints. I judge that they must be congratulated above all because, although winds may rage, storms may rage fiercely, and rivers may swell, the house of God—whose worshipers and ministers they are—will eternally possess the firm stability of its strength, unshaken, immovable, and inviolate; for it does not rest upon shifting sands but, supported by heavenly columns and joined eternally to the rock, has been built solidly by God the architect.

126. Come, then, you professors of spiritual discipline, companions in an excellent purpose, philosophers of supreme holiness, whom foresighted grace chose in advance to become accustomed to the sacred order, to grow old in religion, and to die into virtues; whom the will trained and the chaste devotion of your parents consecrated: take care, show diligence, weigh your vigilance, lest the evil spirit infect the dwelling of your breast, lest, mingling with your innermost senses, he defile the soul’s holiness, and lest he cloud that most splendid eye of divine contemplation with the enticement of a contrived persuasion.

Permit me to set forth before you, both in thought and in words, a subject once conceived by an author who is not wholly to be despised [Note: [Col. 1268D] In the margin of our Lyons manuscript, in a very old hand, Fonteius—some Carthaginian, I do not know who—is cited. In Labbe, however, the text itself, somewhat farther below, reads: “What the pagan Fonteius wrote to the Carthaginians concerning cleansing the mind in order to see God.”]. The ancient enemy’s evil creeps through every sensory entrance; it presents itself in figures; adapts itself to colors; clings to sounds; submits itself to odors; pours itself into flavors; and fills all the passages of understanding with dark affections, as with certain clouds—passages through which the ray of the mind ordinarily opens the light of reason.

In this God is reflected; in this innocent will; in this the merit of right action. God is present everywhere; but he is present together with each one of us when the undefiled purity of our mind has opened itself in his presence. For just as, if the sight of the eyes has been impaired, whatever it cannot see it does not consider to be present—for the present image of things surrounds the eyes in vain if the eyes lack integrity—so God, who is absent nowhere, is present in vain to polluted souls, whom the blindness of the mind cannot see.

What I have said is not my own; I do not claim it for myself or ascribe it to myself—for I do not presume that the club can easily be snatched from the hand of any very strong man—though a pagan wrote it concerning cleansing the mind in order to see God. Yet it was unfitting that what that same man, a Christian, baptized, and dead, had once said well should become obsolete.

Why have I sought these matters from so lofty a beginning? Clearly so that you may recall what is written: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour.” And: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” The one saying serves vigilance; the other contributes to divine contemplation.

127. In turn, see to it that you remember that Christ died for you, so that you who live may no longer live for yourselves but for him who died for you; and do not become arrogant against God because of his gift. Receive also what is written: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world”—not because we were holy and blameless, or because we were going to be holy and blameless—for otherwise this would be considered not so much a prerogative of grace as an exchange or relation of merit—but “he chose us so that we might be holy and blameless,” that is, by choosing he brought it about that we should be holy and blameless; for unless he willed it, we could not even exist at all.

Submit your head to him; place your confidence not in your own goodness but in his; humble yourselves beneath his most powerful hand. You will find a safe refuge in his mercy, for he is always ready to spare the submissive and overthrow the proud.

You are God’s athletes; you contend in the spiritual arena. One must compete lawfully in order to reach the prize. You have been made a spectacle to this world; everyone’s eyes are directed toward you. Your way of life, set as though in a mirror, is a teacher of public discipline: whatever you do, everyone thinks he ought to do.

Beware of doing anything that may be exposed to your critics or drive your imitators to ruin. Set before yourselves, with emulative devotion, the leaders of this way of life; imitate their truthful teaching and holy works, and hasten toward the pastures of the heavenly kingdom.

Meditate constantly upon the death that hangs over every hour, knowing that nothing is lasting in which there can be an end; and that all must die, though it is uncertain whether death will come on that very day. When that moment arrives, whatever has passed has flowed away; only what you have attained through virtue and right actions remains.

Resist your desires; oppose pleasures, lest you too become subject to the destruction of those concerning whom the Prophet complained that they had passed into the inclination of their heart, and prayed that their image in the city of God might be reduced to nothing.

128. If you have vowed anything to God, fulfill it without hesitation, remembering that after vows it is ruinous for a man to reconsider them [Note: [Col. 1269C] “Reconsider”—namely, those things that oppose the vows. Or perhaps “reconsider” may be understood as delaying or drawing out the fulfillment of the vows. Labbe reads “retract.”]. It is better not to vow than not to fulfill one’s vows.

The offerings of our vows are neither far away nor outside us; rather, as the Psalmist confesses: “My vows are upon me, O God; I shall render praises to you.” Persevere in these without weariness; compose them by day, compose them by night; add to them whatever you can with sobriety. For although he does not need our praise, the devotion of his creature is nevertheless pleasing to him. Your praise does not benefit him in the least; yet in pious zeal you act so that you yourselves may profit greatly from it.

While some wage war and others cultivate the fields, you are a third order, whom he has called to share in a private lot: the more free from external affairs, the more occupied with the duties of his service. And just as others undergo harsh conditions on your behalf, whether of military service or labor, so you remain obligated to them, attending to them through the urgency of your prayers and Office.

And to show that one thing is owed to those who share our nature and another to God himself, always turn this first and foremost over in your minds: that he himself made you, restored you when you were lost, and advanced you through benefits so frequent, so abundant, and finally so profitable that from this you may gain the material for praising him. While you give him fitting thanks for the gifts you have received and continue to return thanks for them, you become more worthy of receiving still more and greater gifts.

Now, so that the glorious members of the supreme Head may also be shown to share somewhat in his praise, receive that Davidic summons in these words: “Praise the Lord in his saints.” As though explaining the same judgment in another way, he says: “You do not act prudently enough if you think that the triumphs and merits of the most faithful soldiers of an unconquered commander should be excluded from their commander’s glory. Therefore glorify God with all your strength and with your utmost powers, since he freely grants you all good things; venerate blessed Germanus, who obtains these things for you through the support of his most powerful intercession; and pursue the others, who share with him both the temple and merit, with devout devotion and implore them with anxious affection. May they rescue from calamities, lead away from ruin, support by their merits, protect by their prayers, and defend from every kind of horror of present and future dangers the place which they chose and willed to be most flourishing through their presence and holiness, after all the forces of the enemies on land and sea have been defeated and the savage tyranny of demons excluded.”

SERMON OF THE SAME HERICUS, TO BE RECITED ON THE SOLEMNITY OF SAINT GERMANUS [Note: [Col. 1269D] This title, together with the sermon that follows, is found in our Lyons manuscript—not, however, in this position, but before the two books on the Life and Miracles. Chiffletius likewise found the same sermon in his manuscripts and copied it for us.]. (C)*

[Col. 1269]

[Col. 1269D] 129. You recall, beloved, the day dedicated to the public rejoicing of the Church. Although preaching is silent concerning its splendor, the gathering and devotion of religious people proclaim it. For you have conspired in such honorable efforts and with such united vows for the worship and joy of this day that the magnificence of the feast itself stands out sufficiently by its own titles, even though the diligence of its herald should abstain from praising it.

You have therefore learned through frequent, indeed continuous, readings the causes and fuel of such rejoicing; and you have shown by no obscure sign that you received them with attentive minds, while you honored the majesty of the heavenly miracles resounding through the sacred pages with inward sighs and evident affection at every point.

For today precious Germanus, once the distinguished chief bishop of this Church and now also an outstanding protector of the whole world before God, leaving the earth through a glorious passing, entering heaven, has been restored to the presence of the Lord.

Why do I say that he left the earth, when, according to the Apostle, his manner of life was always in heaven? Why say that he was restored to the presence of the Lord, when together with the most holy Elijah he stood perpetually and tirelessly before the sight of the living God?

I shall say something about him—though not with complete precision, certainly not ineptly; though with less boldness, still with sufficient truth. I say, then, that this is the day of blessed Germanus: not a mournful day but a celebrated one; not a sorrowful one but a saving one. On it, bringing a long struggle to an end, trampling down the world and overthrowing the devil, he shone forth as a glorious victor and, like another Elijah carried forward in an angelic chariot, ascended as a triumphant athlete to the heavenly Capitol.

130. The triumph of Elijah is rightly attributed to him, since he is shown to have answered him equally in all the marks of holiness and virtue. To pass over the other matters in which the holy men of God surpass one another in pious emulation and emulous devotion, in that singular privilege either of abstinence or continence I do not dare, with sufficient generosity, to place one before the other. For reliable authority testifies that both were most holy and both most abstinent.

Yet I have not forgotten that the prophet’s hunger was moderated by loaves in the morning and meat in the evening, supplied by ravens [Note: [Col. 1271D] Our author follows the version of the Septuagint, for in the Vulgate, 3 Kings 17, it reads: “Ravens also brought him [Elijah] bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening.”]; whereas the bishop’s fasting, after usually more than seven days, was revived only by barley bread. In Elijah the fortieth day brought his fast to an end; in Germanus the thirtieth year closed his profession of abstinence.

Elijah, strengthened by eating bread baked under ashes, prolonged his fast as far as Mount Horeb, the mountain of God. Germanus, strengthened by the grace of the almighty Spirit, ascended the citadel of the heavenly city through fasting and prayer.

In Elijah, the widow’s generosity relieved the hardships of his completed labor; in Germanus, the daily cross consumed the familiar abundance of birth and riches. Elijah, avoiding the fury of his persecutors, lived for a time alone among wild beasts; Germanus, whose memory nourishes us today, fleeing the favor of those who wished to serve him—a thing not so much rare as marvelous—remained a hermit among the people.

And, to pass from labors to the rewards of labors: an earthly paradise carried Elijah away in a fiery chariot, though he was destined to die in his own time; a starry throne received Germanus, supported by an angelic host, so that he might also rise in glory with the apostles to judge the world.

131. Not undeservedly, then, does Mother Church rejoice in these triumphs, for she is adorned by his singular examples. Indeed, reason persuades us to rejoice universally in the commemoration of all the saints; but in the excellence of this Father we rightly glory more abundantly. As our pastor in this city and teacher throughout the whole world, he obtained such dignity in that body whose head is Christ that he is numbered among its principal members both by name and by merit.

Although his exceptional holiness deserved celebrated renown throughout the whole world, he must nevertheless be venerated more fervently among us and by us, whom the presence of his sacred body ennobles, makes grateful through his benefits, and preserves through his intercession.

This, this is the man through whom the light of the Gospel flashed upon you, Gaul; in him and through him the radiance of holiness and miracles shone upon you. He is your Father; he is your own pastor. By his word he nourished the infancy of your untutored religion and formed it by his example; he protected you in adversity and advanced you in prosperity, reconciling divine things and arranging human affairs.

He endured much on your behalf. Because of his great love for you, he undertook difficult journeys by land and sea. He did not yield to labors or spare himself sweat, forgetting bodily weakness and disregarding the burdens of advanced age. For your salvation he opposed himself to rulers; for your peace he exposed his head to barbarians. After God he preferred nothing to his love for you, for whose sake and in whose service he consented to endure every extremity.

132. Although the several regions of the world competed to carry him away in turn—for at that time the salvation and hopes of all depended especially upon him and arose from him—he nevertheless preferred you to all. He always cared for your public and private interests with paternal affection.

You welcomed him when he returned; you comforted him when he was weary. You were the relief of his journey and the gentle rest of his labor. Therefore, even if he is not an apostle to others, he is certainly one to you: “For we are all the signs of his apostleship in the Lord.”

Finally, what could be a more striking or more forceful sign of charity, a more memorable proof of a father’s—or rather a mother’s—heart? He was already worn out by long service, and the heavenly calling pressed upon him. He sensed that death was near; his spirit was hastening toward the end and the reward of eternal recompense. Yet, to bring relief to the afflicted, he imposed upon himself an arduous journey. As an old man he did not fear the passes of the Alps or the obstacles of torrents; finally—and this is the greatest point—he did not fear dying abroad, but treated as little whatever in death could be most grievous.

[Col. 1272B] 133. Thus, as I think, thus the order of events required it, that your warrior, Christ, whom Gaul had seen fighting, Italy should receive in triumph. He fought in one place and was crowned in another.

The Italian world, which had long awaited him and received him late, embraced him; through imperial entertainments and the services of priests it wove pleasant delays around the man. Meanwhile Christ was present: he supplied provisions for the journey and invited his friend to the banquet of angels.

Joy mingled with mourning was indiscriminately spread through the spacious palaces, while they both offered tears to the dying man and—though in vain—rejoiced at the prospect of inheriting the pledge of his sacred remains. They were planning such things; but the unchanging Judge had ordained better things.

For Germanus was returning his spirit to heaven and providing saving benefits for his beloved citizens. Thus both sides were satisfied according to the proper time: by dying he illumined Italy; dead, he visited Gaul. But he would not visit it after death unless he were also alive in death.

I say that the dead man lives—the man who, while alive, had raised the dead. The dead man consecrated this day for us, and, if we duly venerate it, he will secure eternity for us.

See, then, how greatly he has deserved well of us, since he wished so earnestly to be our patron. When you render him the worship of due veneration, you prepare for yourselves manifold interest through fruitful lending, since through the presence of his sacred body you receive more than you offer.

Because we can say nothing worthy of his glory, let us now turn both our voices and our vows toward him. With submissive minds and fruitful prayers, let us seek his holiness.

134. Remember, most splendid Father, remember your sons throughout the ages, and may the ever-watchful care of the shepherd not forget his flock. We believe that you stand undefiled before the tribunal of the Most High; do not, then, refuse to relieve our frailty from the filth of monstrous sins.

You can indeed obtain for us a period of repentance from the most gentle Judge, since you were deemed worthy to sing the new song in the presence of the Lamb. You who deserved to be his attendant, deign also to be our patron.

Be the most faithful interpreter before God of the prayers that we pour out at your tomb. You who were our most vigorous preacher, be no less a most merciful intercessor for our calamities.

Ask for correction of morals, tranquility for our times, pardon for all sins, and the shortening of the way to eternal joys. You will easily obtain what you ask, since we believe that you are so closely joined to your most powerful Emperor that you can neither wish what he does not wish nor wish to request anything in which you have not recognized his delight—he who lives, reigns, and rules in every nation, place, and time, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## Back matter of the volume

[Col. 1273]

## INDEX OF ALL THE SAINTS CONTAINED IN THE TEXT OF USUARD

[Note: [Col. 1273] This index refers to the Martyrology of Usuard in PL 123 and 124.]

### A

[Column 1331] Usuardus, monk of Saint-Germain.

The Martyrology of Usuard follows. May, 9. June, 9. July, 109. August, 213. September, 319. October, 423. November, 525. December, 641.  

Charles the Bald, king of the Franks.

## The Letters of Charles the Bald

Letter I. To Pope Nicholas.—He intercedes for Bishop Adventius and asks that he be received back into favor. 861.

Letter II. Synodal letter to the bishops and counts of Gaul, in the name of King Charles. 862.

Letter III. Charles to Pope Nicholas I.—Written shortly before the Synod of Soissons, asking that it be permitted to entrust the Church of Bourges temporarily to Vulfadus. 867.

Letter IV. To the same.—Concerning what had been done at the synod. 869.

Letter V. To the same.—He writes at great length concerning the case of Ebbo, as the pontiff had instructed through Ansegisus. He then excuses Vulfadus’s hurried promotion and asks for the pallium for him. He also commends Bishop Actardus, his envoy. 870.

Letter VI. To Adon, archbishop of Vienne.—Concerning the ordination of Bernarius as bishop of Grenoble. 875.

Letter VII. To Adrian II. 876.

Letter VIII. To the same.—Irritated by two letters from Adrian, he replies to both with a somewhat more agitated spirit. 881.

Letter IX. To the same, sent at the same time as the preceding letter. 896.

A booklet of accusation against Wenilo, archbishop of Sens. 897.

Chapter XXXI.—Another similar case. 935.

Chapter XXXV.—A perjurer is chastised through Saint Benedict. A penitent recovers. 940.

Chapter XXXVI.—A lame woman is cured. 941.

Chapter XXXVII.—A fire is extinguished. 942.

Chapter XXXVIII.—A man invading the monastery’s vineyard is struck by death. 943.

Chapter XXXIX.—The unfortunate reign of Charles the Bald. A boy is rescued from a wolf’s jaws. 943.

Appendix of Adelerius the monk. 944.

Chapter XLI.—Charles the Bald is praised. Returning from Rome, he dies at Pavia from poison (in the year 877). When Louis succeeds him, the Northmen renew their incursions. They are defeated by Hugh. 946.
